case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 34-year-old man; Karnofsky Performance Status 100.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache and right ear tinnitus for 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4, IDH-mutant.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected brain lesion was reported as astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4, IDH-mutant. OLIG2 was positive. 1p/19q co-deletion was not detected.

[ imaging findings ]: Pre-operative MRI brain with contrast demonstrated a solitary intra-axial lesion in the right parietal lobe, T1 hypointense and T2/FLAIR hyperintense, with minimal patchy post-contrast enhancement and some central T2 hypointense solid components corresponding to enhancing areas. The lesion extended into the temporal lobe and caused minimal effacement of the ipsilateral temporal horn. No additional intracranial lesion was identified. No significant subfalcine or descending transtentorial herniation was seen.

Post-operative MRI brain with contrast demonstrated right-sided craniotomy changes with post-surgical/post-operative hemorrhagic change in the surgical bed. There was interval reduction in lesion size, with probable residual lesion in the surgical bed, particularly along the posterior aspect, with patchy enhancement. No new lesion was identified. No post-operative collection was seen.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-mutant; 1p/19q co-deletion negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent neuronavigation-guided right frontoparietal awake craniotomy with maximal safe resection in November 2025. Post-operative imaging showed interval reduction in tumor size with residual disease in the surgical bed.

[ current disease status ]: Residual tumor remained in the surgical bed on post-operative MRI. No new intracranial lesion was identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Lesion was described radiologically as a primary neoplastic brain lesion.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old woman from Sydney, Australia.

[ chief complaint ]: Multinodular goiter identified incidentally during CT pulmonary angiography performed after a lower-limb deep venous thrombosis following knee injury.

[ diagnosis ]: Minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC), 35 mm, arising in the right thyroid lobe; subsequent iodine-avid pulmonary metastases detected on post-ablation imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial fine-needle biopsy of the dominant right thyroid nodule was Bethesda category III (atypia/follicular lesion of uncertain significance). Right hemithyroidectomy pathology showed a 35 mm minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma with capsular invasion. Surgical margins were clear. There was no extrathyroidal extension. No vascular invasion was identified. Mitotic rate was low.

[ imaging findings ]: CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolus and incidentally identified a multinodular goiter. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a mildly enlarged thyroid gland with multiple TI-RADS 1-3 nodules in both lobes; the largest lesion was a 35 mm TI-RADS 3 nodule in the right lobe. Post-ablation whole-body scan showed uptake in the thyroid bed consistent with remnant thyroid tissue and multiple bilateral pulmonary foci. SPECT/CT demonstrated iodine-avid foci corresponding to very small nodules in both lungs.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF negative. NRAS positive.

[ laboratory results ]: Stimulated thyroglobulin was 11 one day after Thyrogen at the time of post-ablation assessment. Thyroglobulin antibodies were present. No postoperative thyroglobulin result prior to radioactive iodine was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right hemithyroidectomy followed by completion thyroidectomy (left hemithyroidectomy). She was treated with thyroxine after completion thyroidectomy. Radioactive iodine was administered at 1 GBq. Post-ablation imaging demonstrated iodine-avid bilateral pulmonary micrometastatic disease and thyroid bed remnant uptake.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history of thyroid cancer was reported. The patient had previously developed a deep venous thrombosis in the leg after knee injury.

Actually, the newly revised Japanese guidelines also do not recommend operational thyrodectomy for minimally invasive folliculocyte cancer. But personally, I consider the thick tumor capsule to be a risk factor for distant metastasis in follicular carcinoma from the clinical view. Although this view might be outdated, but I believe that the capsule formation is a response of normal tissue to the tumor. And the more aggressive the cancer, the thicker the capsule becomes. So the one remarkable point in this case is a thick capsule, I believe.
Yeah, I agree. I mean, that's a perception that I think most thyroid pathologists have, although I don't know if it's been proven. But at least the thicker the capsule, the higher the suspicion.
Fantastic. All righty. Great case. Thanks, Jeremy. Let's do another one. Poorly differentiated.

reference_conclusion: Following completion thyroidectomy for a 3.5 cm minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma with capsular invasion and no vascular invasion, postoperative assessment should include serum thyroglobulin measurement approximately 4 weeks after surgery to exclude persistent or recurrent disease before considering additional therapy. Radioactive iodine is not clearly beneficial in all such cases; however, in the setting of low but nonzero recurrence risk, low-dose radioactive iodine ablation at 1 GBq (approximately 30 mCi) was recommended rather than 4 GBq. After identification of iodine-avid small pulmonary metastases on the post-ablation scan, no immediate additional radioactive iodine was advised; instead, surveillance with structural follow-up and serial measurable tumor marker assessment was recommended, with consideration of a subsequent dose only if indicated by later evidence of disease.
reference_conclusion_quote: there's not clearly a benefit to radioactive iodine in all cases. [...] I'll reassure patients and generally not order radioactive iodine, but we'll definitely look at a postoperative thyroglobulin usually around four weeks post-surgery so that I can just make sure there's no concern for recurring or persisting cancer. Even though we say the risk of recurrence is low, it's not zero. And so it is really important to make sure that that postoperative thyroglobulin is nice and low before you consider any additional treatment. [...] But because we felt that the risk of recurrence is low, we recommended 1 gig. [...] Well, I mean, I think you have to look at the response. [...] she appears to have had a very good response and I don't think you lose anything by waiting. You can follow her structurally and she has a measurable tumor marker that we can follow. So I think, I mean, it may be that she needs another dose down the track, but at the moment there's not good evidence that we should be treating her earlier rather than later.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old postmenopausal woman. No reported comorbidities. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Newly diagnosed breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IB breast carcinoma, pT1b pN0 M0. Triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast.

[ histopathology results ]: Lumpectomy specimen showed invasive ductal carcinoma measuring 10 mm. Nottingham score was 8, grade 3. Surgical margins were reported as negative. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Staging evaluation was negative for metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Estrogen receptor negative. Progesterone receptor negative. HER2 negative. No other molecular or genomic test results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent lumpectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy. No residual nodal disease was identified on sentinel node assessment.

[ current disease status ]: Localized node-negative breast cancer following breast-conserving surgery. No distant metastatic disease was identified.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

reference_discussion.text: And Dr. Marino is going to be joining us soon. And also a very special welcome and thanks to our panelists from Boston and around the United States. So we can start collecting pictures of everybody who attends the tumor board. We'd be very grateful if you send those to Jessica. So I believe the first question would be does she qualify for consideration for chemotherapy? The answer, yes. She's ERPR negative and the Oncotype data have really been validated only for hormone receptor positive patients. So I don't think that the Oncotype would be informative in a case like this. I have something to add. Sorry about my voice this morning. I'm getting over a cold. I do want to stress that we tend to only send Oncotype in patients that have hormone receptor positive and HER2 negative disease.

So let me just get this clear for everybody. When you have a grade 3 tumor or a triple negative tumor, you're going to recommend chemo anyway and you're not going to send the Oncotype or a HER2 positive tumor. If you've got a tumor that's HER2 positive or a tumor that's triple negative or a tumor that's just grade 3 or triple negative, whatever, biology grade 3, do you have a lower size cut-off?

Yes, so I can comment on the HER2 positive patients. Our size cut-off is 5 millimeters. If they're HER2 positive, ER positive and PR positive, and it's three millimeters if there's a hormone receptor negative and HER2 positive. The patients where we tend to send Oncotype are those patients that have T1c, no negative, and maybe high or intermediate grade, T2 and zero intermediate grade. and any patient with one to three positive nodes, which is low and intermediate grade.

Right. Did everybody get that? Are you satisfied, Diego, with that? Yeah. I think we covered the ONCA type and the recommendation for chemotherapy. The general consensus is to give chemotherapy. Yeah. And so your next question, Diego. You were asking about the regimen. What type of regimen of chemotherapy would this patient be recommended in terms of TC versus anthracycline followed by taxanes? I think I would probably prefer giving her ACT.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so you highlighted the difference in this case, which is that the patient already has symptoms of their cirrhosis. They have the fluid in their belly. And, you know, We talked about during my talk that when we try to cut out part of the liver, yes, it can regenerate, but not immediately. It can take time. So of course, we always try to consider resection in everybody. One of the things that the surgeon will actually do is they'll calculate something called FLR, which is how much liver will be left after a surgery and try to calculate, is that enough for the patient to survive or do well? When somebody's at this point where they've already developed symptoms of cirrhosis, they're not going to have enough liver remaining to be able to survive the surgery. And so in this case, you would need to replace the whole liver with a transplant. And so for in this patient, I would recommend that they, you know, go to a transplant center, get referred there, have a transplant evaluation and kind of be checked out head to toe. And then in the interim see, you know, Dr. Chaudhry, Dr. Benjamin, to see if we can try to burn the tumor or embolize the tumor while we wait on the transplant list, knowing that from the time they meet me till when they actually get a transplant can be up to a year. So that would be my recommendation is urgent evaluation for transplant and then to see what are these two folks.

Yeah, so the analogy that I use here is it's almost like a car towing on an edge where it hasn't fallen off that cliff. But if you just remove more of that liver, there wouldn't be enough liver there to function. And so thereby, this patient who's actually doing okay right now, the complications are controlled, the labs look okay. But if you cut out any of the liver that's there, they wouldn't have enough left to thereby function. And this patient could thereby get sicker from their underlying liver disease. And this really highlights the complexity of this cancer, because we talked about this happening in the setting of liver disease and cirrhosis. And so whenever we think through the treatments, the tolerability, the outcomes, it's not just treating the cancer. It's also not upsetting or worsening the underlying liver disease. And so it really comes into all of our decision making of what's the stage of cancer, how well is the liver working or not working, and how strong is the patient. I always tell my patients the easiest way, the worst way to kill off a cancer is to kill the entire liver or to kill the patient, right? And this is one thing that we need to make sure that we don't do, that we treat the cancer effectively while preserving the patient and their liver function. And so this is one of the key things that always comes into our tumor board and highlights the importance of us getting together to discuss these things. So this patient, to Dr. Richard's point, was referred and enlisted for liver transplantation, underwent bridging therapy to Dr. Chaudhry's discussion, underwent bridging therapy with a local ablation, actually underwent a living donor liver transplantation. And I would argue this is the other thing that we need to think through as a group here. is that unfortunately for as many people who need a liver transplant, we don't have enough organs available. And so we need to make sure that we continue doing our part to get the word out that for those that are able to do so, that they consider donating if and when possible. And so living donation saves a lot of lives. Okay. Final case, and then I'm going to leave time for questions. I know we cut this short, but I think it's important to do so, so we have some time for questions before lunch. So 57-year-old female here with cirrhosis related to metabolic dysfunction. And conversely to like our last couple of patients, this patient unfortunately was not undergoing screening. and was found to have an eight-centimeter mass that was consistent with liver cancer and disease outside the liver. So also has a lymph node that's two centimeters in size. So liver's functioning well, but unfortunately, large tumor and metastatic spread, disease spread outside the liver. So I'm going to start just, Nicole, Moaz, would you guys consider this patient for a surgical therapy or local therapy? And you can be brief here.

reference_conclusion: The patient is not an appropriate candidate for hepatic resection because symptomatic cirrhosis indicates insufficient future liver remnant to tolerate surgery. Urgent referral to a transplant center for comprehensive liver transplant evaluation is recommended. While awaiting transplantation, bridging locoregional therapy with tumor ablation or embolization should be pursued.

And then in the interim see, you know, Dr. Chaudhry, Dr. Benjamin, to see if we can try to burn the tumor or embolize the tumor while we wait on the transplant list [...] So that would be my recommendation is urgent evaluation for transplant

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent ovarian carcinoma with progressive disease.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, stage IV at diagnosis on 25 December 2019; recurrent/progressive disease with last documented progression/relapse on 24 September 2025.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from a left internal lymph node showed carcinoma of ovarian origin with papillary pattern. Microscopy showed low lymphoid tissue and papillary architecture. Findings were interpreted as consistent with high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Latest PET-CT showed progressive disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- NGS identified TP53 frameshift mutation and TP53 missense mutation.  
- ERBB2 alteration was detected on NGS; activating ERBB2 S310Y mutation in the extracellular domain was reported.  
- ERBB2 variant allele frequency was reported at approximately 1.58%–1.8% in tissue and was described as subclonal.  
- No other actionable mutations were identified.  
- The ERBB2 alteration was not detected in plasma/liquid biopsy.  
- Germline BRCA1 testing was negative.  
- HRD testing at baseline was negative.  
- ESR1 was negative.  
- MSI-high status was not reported; MSI negativity was referenced.  

[ laboratory results ]:  
- IHC: Ki-67 approximately 60%.  
- WT1 positive.  
- PAX8 positive.  
- Estrogen receptor positive in 80% of tumor cells.  
- PD-L1 CPS: 8.  
- HER2 FISH had been sent and was pending at the time of documentation.  
- Tumor content in tissue sample was approximately 60%.  
- Plasma tumor fraction was reported as 37%.  
- TP53 mutation in tissue had variant allele frequency 50.6%; the same alteration was present at minimal level in plasma DNA.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Six cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin in 2015.  
- Recurrence in 2019 with omental metastasis; treated again with paclitaxel plus carboplatin.  
- Subsequently treated with liposomal doxorubicin plus carboplatin.  
- Cytoreductive surgery was performed thereafter; no macroscopic disease was reported postoperatively.  
- Tamoxifen was given subsequently.  
- Later treated with gemcitabine plus carboplatin plus bevacizumab.  
- Maintenance bevacizumab plus olaparib was administered for approximately two years.  
- Additional prior systemic agents mentioned included irinotecan and liposomal doxorubicin.  
- Total number of prior treatment lines was reported as five.  
- Last platinum exposure was approximately two years before the current progression.  
- Disease control on bevacizumab plus olaparib maintenance was reported until current progression.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease as of 24 September 2025 after multiple prior lines of therapy. ECOG performance status was 1.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbidities were reported. No significant family history was reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Worsening flushing, worsening diarrhea, and shortness of breath in the setting of metastatic neuroendocrine tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid) with hepatic metastases, mesenteric involvement, and later extensive osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Repeat biopsy demonstrated interval increase in Ki-67 proliferation index and mitotic count compared with an earlier biopsy, consistent with higher-grade transformation/progression. Exact numeric values were not provided.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Prior to referral in 2003, metastatic midgut disease had been treated with radioembolization.  
- February 2015 imaging showed relatively stable disease with small liver metastases and one small lymph node.  
- May 2015 imaging showed marked interval increase in the number of liver lesions, described as innumerable small hepatic lesions, with new extensive bone metastases.  
- Disease progression between February 2015 and May 2015 was described as clear-cut on repeated scan review.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2003: Radioembolization for metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor prior to transfer of care.  
- 2005: Pancreaticoduodenectomy and right hemicolectomy for mesenteric/root of mesentery involvement.  
- Long-term somatostatin analogue therapy with Sandostatin LAR 30 mg monthly for approximately 9 years.  
- Over subsequent years, hepatic recurrences/progression were managed with repeated local therapies, including percutaneous ablation and laparoscopic ablation.  
- Disease course had been relatively indolent over 7–8 years, with intermittent new hepatic lesions appearing every 1–2 years and treated locally. Symptoms had been relatively well controlled during much of this interval.

[ current disease status ]: Rapid systemic progression was present by May 2015, with innumerable hepatic metastases, extensive bone metastases, worsening carcinoid-type symptoms, and biopsy evidence of increased proliferative activity compared with prior pathology.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had chronic diarrhea, attributed in part to prior pancreaticoduodenectomy.  
- Prior pancreaticoduodenectomy resulted in biliary-enteric anastomosis/hepaticojejunostomy anatomy, which was relevant to subsequent liver-directed procedural risk.

Thank you for picking me first. Actually, I'm not sure if this is a midgut or is it a pancreas?
It was midgut. It was just involving the root of the mesentery, and that's why the whipple. It was relatively complicated.

So, you know, asymptomatic, somewhat progressive neuroendocrine tumor on somatostatin analog. Nowadays, there's, going back, if I were to have this person with progressive disease, especially things that are not resectable. First question in any patient is, is this operable? Can most or all of the disease can be removed, whether it's metastatic recurrence or not? If the answer is no, I try to find standard of care. If there's none, then I go to clinical trials. So at the time this is going on, I think there is the radian 2 that is possibly an option for the patient if she or he is not a surgical candidate. In this era, the question to ask is that should we give not yet FDA-approved Afinitor or Evalimus for a progressing neuroendocrine tumor of the midgut? That is a question that I think everybody has to decide with the patient on one-on-one discussion with the result. The RADIAN4 result is back, or it's been announced. So perhaps there's more data. And I think the RADIAN2 is enough data for me to start using that affinitory and adding to the somatostatin analog.

So before we go to the next slide, Mark and Gabe, can I ask you, she's had a Whipple, so she's got a, again, that means the bile duct's been connected to the intestine. As the years have gone by, we've avoided arterial therapy. She did have a radioembolization in the past. How scared should we be, Mark, for arterial therapy and Gabriel for poking needles in and burning things in the liver? Or is this overkill, we can use a Mad Lib?

I think each patient needs to be looked at on an individual basis, but I still have significant reservation about going forward with regional therapy in patients who've had any kind of compromise of the bile duct connection to the small intestines. The risk of hepatic abscess after chemoembolization or radioembolization is very small. It's probably less than 1%. But if you look at retrospective series of patients who have developed hepatic abscess, the very large majority of them have had an incompetent sphincter. And that hepatic abscess complication can be a very severe, life-threatening complication. So you really have to look at each patient individually, but I still have relatively strong reservation about being aggressive in those circumstances.
Gabe, what about alcohol, nano knife, are these things okay? Or is all ablation bad in a liver with a hepatical jejunostomy?

I think, you know, you run the same risks. And so, you know, for patients who we decided the risk is worth taking, we also we do a bowel prep. We treat with antibiotics before and after the procedure for a certain amount of time. And since we've been doing that in the literature, infection rates have been less, but the risk is still, you know, fairly significant.

Well, the question at hand was this, and that is that in February 2005, things looked pretty stable. There were some small liver metastases. Again, we did intervene periodically with ablation nervously when these grew, but we're talking a seven or eight year time period. One small lymph node. But then in March, more flushing, some shortness of breath actually, some worsening diarrhea. And the May 2015 report comes back with marked increase in the number of liver lesions and now extensive bone metastases. We went over the scan repeatedly, and there really was a very clear-cut progression between February and May. Innumerable small liver lesions with bone lesions. I guess the first question is, what happened? And I'll show you, in fact, I will show you the films now. what happened here with this biology? Did the biology change? Did we miss something? What does the whole group think? Have they seen this? And this concept of rapid progression from stable to seems to be growing fast. Yeah, jump in.

All right, I'll be happy to give a jump in. A couple of things. First of all, I agree entirely with what's been said about surgery up front. I think it's really important. Debulking really makes a big impact in terms of the long-term outcome. I'm not so sure that I would repetitively do it, though. I think you need to realize that eventually you're losing more and you're gaining less with repetitive interventions. But if you can render somebody R0 or R1 early, I think it's very, very important. I think the issue here is that this is the natural history of the disease. This is what actually will occur. As time goes on, you're going to start selecting out clones that are going to be more resistant, and you're going to have, you know, the old VINIC slide where you get the sort of ramping up effect many, many years later. And I think in this particular situation, you've probably going to have selected out a higher grade lesion that is going to be less amenable to therapy, and in fact may not even necessarily be octreotide avid at this point. So a couple of issues here. This person needs systemic therapy, there's no doubt about it. And I think going and working on specific lesions in the liver is not going to make an impact. The reason to focus therapy on the liver early on is really important, because many patients ultimately are going to succumb to liver disease. So you'll have a bigger bulk in the liver, and you're going to have to hammer the liver. But if you reach a point where you've broken out of the liver and you now have systemic disease, I think you really need some kind of systemic therapy. So you're going to have to have a discussion here. This is going to be some kind of clinical trial, which I would certainly support. I'd be personally wary in this particular patient of PRRT having previously seen radiospheres. There's certainly a dose effect, but we've had some unhappy outcomes in that situation, although I think it is something that should be considered here seriously. And I'm sure the man on my left is going to be supporting that. We actually have an MIBG trial at the University of Pennsylvania that is something to consider. That's another radio pharmaceutical. But something needs to be done at this situation. So I think you've reached a point now where you've got to go global.

In order to answer your questions, there are things that can be done in understanding the pathophysiology that we're dealing with. What we do is a combination of F18, FDG, PET, CT, as well as either gallium or actuarial scan, mostly gallium. And we are, in some of these patients, we see, for instance, that a previously negative FDG PET CT scan becomes positive in certain areas. That tells us that the tumor is becoming more aggressive and confirms our sort of guess that these tumors, they are changing their behavior, actually. At this point, obviously, the patient is progressing, is not responding to the prior therapies. Systemic therapy is definitely an indication because of the bone lesions, because of other new lesions that you're seeing. And regarding previously treated patients with SIRT, of course, depending on the number of procedures, Still, we can guesstimate in terms of the dose that liver has received and based on that, essentially justify the PRRT. I don't think this patient, there is, I mean, necessarily there is an absolute contraindication for PRRT. PRRT needs to be considered at this point as well.
So we've got PRRT, we've got Dr. Fan, midgut, but we're in trouble. What would you do? Outside of a trial, you know, with the available drugs right now.
Well, I think at this point you ask yourself if the patient has symptoms or not.
Yeah, a lot of flushing and actually worsening pulmonary issues as well from the heart, cardiac.

So remember I said that the two goals of treatment of patient would advanced disease is symptoms control and disease control. Both of these are not control at the moment. So if you can add an agent that actually potentially can treat both the symptoms and the disease, I think that is the ideal thing. So this person is on stomatostatin analog. In a sub-study of the RADIAN3, there is actually some benefit of adding Afinitor to stomatostatin analog to improve symptoms control as well. It is something that, again, I would probably do at this time. The only question is that looking at the KI-67 and the mitotic figure, what if that was 20? That's actually more of an interesting question, is that it's 20 or more, it becomes high-grade neuroendocrine tumor, regardless of the primary site. So then you have to question whether somatostatin analog, TKI, are they adequately treating the patient or not?

And we did a biopsy, and in fact, as you pointed out, it had changed quite a bit from the one a few years ago, a much higher Ki67 and mitotic count. Here are the two biopsies side by side, but I don't want to get stuck on this case, so we'll move on to another case. Any other comments from the panel? Is this, by the way, the expectation that a person who's five, six, seven years with stable disease, do they unfortunately have to always be worried that their next scan might show this? Is there a way to predict this? Is there a way to not Select out these clones immunotherapy. What's the role of that? I mean, maybe it's not here yet Is there anything we can do or do we just get scans month to month and hope? That's not our turn

Well, so in terms of immunotherapy, I suppose, and maybe Alex can comment, is the PD-L1 inhibitors may be well something that would be reasonable to consider here, but you need a biopsy and you need to show that the receptor is present. I must tell you, we're zero for about 20 tries at Penn. We haven't yet found one person, but that's something I think to consider. In terms of our kind, you know, standard immunotherapy, we're a long way away from that. I mean, one day we certainly will be hoping that that would be the way to go here.

It's very important to remember a patient is symptomatic. You need to address it now. And being on a clinical trial, that there's still some option that you have to try. I think that's first. PD-L1 expression or overexpression in immunohistochemistry does not predict respond to an immuno checkpoint inhibitor. So I'm not sure. I mean, I think that's why there's study that's going on. I'm not sure that would rule my out for a patient being referred to immuno-checkpoint therapy on clinical trials. But, yeah. So if you keep remembering those tenets, symptoms control and disease control, and if you can find one that treat both, that's the ideal thing. And if you can't, you address the symptoms because oftentimes disease is very hard to control and the patient's quality of life is very important.

So, when you respond to our question about markers of prognosis, for small bowel carcinoma, there's really not a lot of great markers other than the clinical markers such as grade and stage. But for pancreatic, there are a few experimental markers, even including somatic mutations that are sort of in development. But for small bowel carcinoma, there really has not been a clear molecular marker to predict the natural history of the tumor.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board concluded that the patient has biologically progressive metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor with extensive hepatic and osseous disease and requires systemic rather than further focal liver-directed therapy. Clinical trial enrollment was supported, with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy to be considered despite prior radioembolization if dosimetry is acceptable. Outside a trial, addition of everolimus to ongoing somatostatin analogue therapy was identified as a reasonable option to address both symptom burden and disease progression, with management prioritizing symptom control given active flushing, diarrhea, and cardiopulmonary manifestations.
reference_conclusion_quote: This person needs systemic therapy, there's no doubt about it. And I think going and working on specific lesions in the liver is not going to make an impact. [...] This is going to be some kind of clinical trial, which I would certainly support. [...] PRRT needs to be considered at this point as well. [...] It is something that, again, I would probably do at this time. [...] It's very important to remember a patient is symptomatic. You need to address it now.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male. Age 38 years in 2011; age 43 years in 2016.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent subcutaneous neck nodules following prior right thyroid lobectomy for a large thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Widely invasive/angioinvasive oncocytic (Hürthle cell) follicular thyroid carcinoma, initially misclassified as follicular adenoma on original pathology, with recurrent subcutaneous soft-tissue metastatic deposits in the neck/chest inlet region. Subsequent 2021 recurrent deposit showed progression to poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma, oncocytic type, by Memorial criteria.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2011 right thyroid lobectomy specimen: original diagnosis was follicular adenoma.  
- Pathology review of the original thyroid tumor identified an encapsulated angioinvasive follicular oncocytic carcinoma/Hürthle cell carcinoma measuring approximately 6.2-6.5 cm, with follicular architecture, oncocytic cytomorphology, fibrous capsule, and vascular invasion with tumor embolus attached to vessel wall and covered by endothelium. No extrathyroidal extension was reported. Thyroglobulin immunostaining was positive.  
- 2016 subcutaneous nodule beneath prior thyroidectomy incision: core biopsy showed Hürthle cell carcinoma. Excision with completion thyroidectomy and excision of old incision/subcutaneous nodule was reported as widely invasive Hürthle cell carcinoma.  
- 2018 recurrent subcutaneous lesion: differentiated Hürthle cell carcinoma in subcutaneous tissue; morphology similar to primary tumor with oncocytic features, macrofollicular architecture, and abundant colloid. No surrounding scar tissue or foreign-body reaction was identified.  
- 2021 recurrent subcutaneous lesion: oncocytic carcinoma deposit in subcutaneous tissue measuring 4.1 cm, with trabecular and microfollicular areas, reduced colloid, increased mitotic activity (13 mitoses per 10 high-power fields), Ki-67 approximately 10.5%, attenuated thyroglobulin staining compared with prior tumor, and vascular invasion. No necrosis was seen. Resection margin was uninvolved. This was classified as poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma, oncocytic type, by Memorial criteria.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2016 neck ultrasound demonstrated a 1.5 cm subcutaneous nodule just beneath the prior thyroidectomy incision.  
- Approximately 17 months after completion thyroidectomy, imaging identified a 1.2 cm nodule in the sternal notch.  
- FDG-PET performed during evaluation of recurrence showed FDG-avid disease in the recurrent lesion, with no disease elsewhere.  
- I-123 scan showed no uptake in the recurrent lesion.  
- Preoperative imaging before reoperation at approximately 29 months after completion thyroidectomy demonstrated two enlarging nodules in the level VII/manubrial/subcutaneous region.  
- Follow-up anatomic imaging after resection showed no evident disease in the neck; persistent chest nodules were present and attributed to sarcoidosis.  
- Approximately 31 months after the second nodule resection, a third subcutaneous nodule developed in the supraclavicular region; FDG-PET showed PET-avid disease.  
- CT shortly before the 2021 excision showed interval growth of the lesion from approximately 3 cm to nearly 4 cm over 3 months.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Stimulated thyroglobulin was elevated at initial postoperative assessment.  
- At approximately 17 months after completion thyroidectomy, unstimulated thyroglobulin was similar to stimulated thyroglobulin.  
- During evaluation of recurrent PET-avid disease, stimulated thyroglobulin was 16.  
- Thyroglobulin increased before the second lesion excision, then became undetectable after resection and remained undetectable for a period; thyroglobulin was 0.8 in July 2020.  
- Before the later recurrence, stimulated thyroglobulin rose again and increased further with interval tumor growth.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2011: Right thyroid lobectomy for a 6.5 cm solid thyroid nodule; original pathology reported follicular adenoma.  
- 2016: Completion thyroidectomy with excision of prior incision and subcutaneous nodule after pathology review established Hürthle cell carcinoma; pathology showed widely invasive oncocytic carcinoma.  
- February 2017: Radioactive iodine administered at 30 mCi.  
- 2018: Fine-needle aspiration of recurrent 1.2 cm sternal notch nodule confirmed Hürthle cell carcinoma.  
- Approximately 29 months after completion thyroidectomy: re-excision of two enlarging subcutaneous nodules in the lower central neck/chest inlet region; postoperative thyroglobulin became undetectable.  
- 2021: Planned wide local excision was delayed; lesion enlarged during delay. In November 2021, wide excision of recurrent supraclavicular/subcutaneous disease with large skin resection was performed, followed by temporary collagen graft and split-thickness skin graft 2 weeks later. Pathology showed a 4.1 cm poorly differentiated oncocytic thyroid carcinoma deposit with negative margins.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic oncocytic thyroid carcinoma involving subcutaneous soft tissues of the neck/chest inlet region, resected in 2021 with negative margins. Disease had shown serial locoregional/subcutaneous recurrences with interval growth and histologic progression to poorly differentiated carcinoma. No distant metastatic disease was identified on the reported FDG-PET studies. Persistent thoracic nodules remained present in the setting of known pulmonary sarcoidosis.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included pulmonary sarcoidosis.  
- Bronchoscopy with biopsy had confirmed sarcoidosis in thoracic lesions/nodules.

reference_discussion.text: Super. So everybody, you can see my slides? Perfect. So, thank you. And I'm from the University of Calgary and Chris and Santa and I are really pleased to be here to present. In the spirit of truth and reconciliation, I would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge that I have the privilege of working and playing on traditional territories of the Treaty 7 First Nations and the Métis Nations of Alberta Region 3. For those that don't know where Calgary is, we sit at the foothills of the Canadian Rockies and this is our cancer center and our hospital over here. This is obviously a summer shot as it is snowing outside as we speak. I think if anything that COVID did for us, the positive has brought a Zoom platform. which I'm sure other centers have found the same thing, that this has really enhanced multidisciplinary tumor boards and tumor care. Instead of having to drive across the city to the cancer center once a month, our team is able to link in electronically. And these are the players that consistently show up and are at our tumor board, but anybody is welcome. And you can see we have all of the various disciplines covered. No financial disclosures. I am an executive board member of Tyro and I would encourage all of you to download this app. And I would also say that I have the patient's permission to present this case. We have three cases for you. The first one is on her full cell carcinoma that's metastatic to the subcutaneous tissue. We have a follicular carcinoma with a rising thyroglobulin. And then we have a young man with metastatic papillary thyroid cancer with a very aggressive regional disease, but now we're questioning what to do with his metastatic disease. So this is the first case. This gentleman at the age of 38, his story started in 2011. He had a 6.5 centimeter solid thyroid nodule. And he was living in Edmonton at that time. And he underwent a right thyroid lobectomy. The final pathology came back as a follicular adenoma. And that was all that was done. Fast forward, he moves to Calgary. And in 2016, he is seeing a pulmonologist here in town. because he has the diagnosis of pulmonary sarcoidosis. He's 43 years old, and this clinician astutely picks up a 1.5 centimeter subcutaneous nodule sitting just under the incision of his thyroidectomy. So this is just an ultrasound of it. You can see it was just in the subcutaneous tissue. A core biopsy is done, and it came back as a hurtful cell carcinoma. That's when I got to see him and proceeded getting the path reviewed, which Musa will go into in just a minute. And then I proceeded to do a completion thyroidectomy and then excise the old incision, as well as this subcutaneous nodule, which was then reported as widely invasive herthal cell carcinoma. So, Moussa, if you want to, I will advance your slides for you. Just tell me when.

Sure. Thank you. So, the tumor was, in the gross description of the original report, over six centimeters. I didn't have the opportunity to see the gross of the tumor because it was done at an outside institution, but this is a whole-mount slide of one of the representative sections, and as you can see, it has an undulating, pushing margin. Please move to the next slide. and it has a fibrous capsule that separates the tumor, which is towards the right, from the residual thyroid parenchyma, which is the upper left. Next, please. The tumor has a follicular architecture, and you can see a large follicle at the center almost of the screen with colloid in it, and then the cytomorphology, which you see in the inset on the right side, is onchocytic. By that, I mean large voluminous cells with granular onchocytic cytoplasm or eosinophilic cytoplasm, and round nuclei with prominent nuclei. We used to call these Hertzel cells, but now we call them onchocytic follicular cells. So, with that, that's an onchocytic follicular neoplasm. Next slide, please. In one of the sections that were submitted, and I have to say not the entire capsule was submitted or at least not clearly indicated in the gross description of the original report, you can see that the capsule separating the tumor to the right from the rest of the thyroid to the left is having a vein and an artery running parallel to that capsule. And within the vein, you can see a part of the tumor or a tumor embolus within that vein. Next, please. That tumor embolus was partially attached to the vessel wall in the upper right, and it is also covered by endothelium where you see the long arrows. Next, please. So that would be a vascular invasion. And with that, this tumor would be an encapsulated angioinvasive follicular oncocytic carcinoma or Hertel-Serk carcinoma. Thyroglobulin was done as part of the workup of that case originally. And you can see that the tumor is staining positively in an equivalent manner to the normal thyroid tissue outside. I think that's the end of that part of the pathology.

Yeah. So this was then re-diagnosed as an encapsulated herthal cell or oncocytic tumor, 6.2 centimeters, no extra thyroidal extension. And so in February of 2017, the patient was given 30 millicuries. And I guess my first question, Mike, is, is that enough? I know these are considered intermediate, but is 30 enough for a oncocytic tumor with vascular invasion?

Yeah. Dr. Ghassani, let's go, let's go with you. So a couple of comments about hurtful cell cancer in general and radioactive iodine responsiveness and PET scanning. How are you thinking about hurtful cell cancer when it's coming to you as a nuclear medicine person?

So, in general, you want to have as much molecular signature of the tumor as possible so that it can help you in the subsequent treatment planning. If there is any known site of disease, like in this patient's subcutaneous nodule, and if we were able to look at both iodine and FDG PET, It gives us the idea of what is the relevant presence of sodium iodide supporters, which will be effective in terms of the treatment as opposed to the differentiation with FTG uptake. So that would be very beneficial. But in this particular case, 30 millicurie, I would think was probably insufficient dose.
But what if I argued that 30 was just as insufficient as 150 because these cell cancers don't concentrate radioactive iodine, right?

Right, right. Which is why I started off by mentioning that, you know, ideally would be nice to have that molecular signature up front. So you can decide whether you to give higher than 30 or not to give anything at all.
Yeah. Janice and then Lori. Janice, the subcutaneous nodule, where was this nodule?

So this nodule, this one was just underneath the actual incision in his neck. And so, you know, question was this, was the tumor broached and is this seeding? But the difference was that in the operative report, there was no evidence or any mention that they got into the tumor, but it was right underneath the incision. So when I excised this, I excised the incision as well.

Let me do Mark and then Lori. Mark, we often see either a poorly differentiated cancer or herthal cell cancer with these subcutaneous nodules right around the scar somewhere, you know, underneath where you guys are operating. There's never a note that says we ruptured this stuff, we spilled it, we had it everywhere. They're often these kind of encapsulated. So the question is, is this seeding from the time of the operation or is this a metastasis? Any idea?

Yeah, I think it's really intriguing and I can't say that I'm gonna be able to give you that much insight on what the pathophysiology is. I think certainly with that degree of vascular invasion that was highlighted, I gotta believe that that's probably the greater likelihood rather than that this was spilling of a tumor.

Yeah, I just wanted to weigh in. There was a nice paper done by the group at Hopkins a few years back that showed, especially with these hurtle cell carcinomas, often these kind of rounded deposits that we see in soft tissue, that if you go back and look at them closely and use vascular markers, that the majority of them, you know, do represent, you know, venous deposits, not always easily recognizable just on routine histology.

and would make sense because these are usually angioinvasive and that's the piece to it. Lori, you see a ton of purple cell cancers and they go weird places. Do you see them in the skin and other places?

Generally, no. I think unless they are very poorly differentiated and then they kind of can turn up anywhere. But no, generally not. It's funny, because herthal cell carcinomas generally don't spread to lymph nodes in the regional lymph nodes, but you can see other nodal disease elsewhere. You can see bone mets in these patients, lung mets. I certainly have a bad feeling about this guy.

I agree. Dr. Liu, anytime we see thyroid cancer in soft tissue or in other deposits, we're always thinking, is there a role for external beam? It sounds like in this one, Dr. Paseka got a nice complete resection, but are you thinking you're going to have any part of this upfront treatment where we are here?

Given the patient's age, despite the hurtle cell histology, I think most of us are hesitant to give external beam radiation when there's a complete resection, even though there are subcutaneous nodules here. But to the point about this histology perhaps not being iodine avid, even at a higher dose does bring to mind maybe the utility of radiation, either now or subsequently.

Jeff, he mentioned the age. I mean, I'm used to seeing heart-cell cancer in 50 and 60-year-olds. You occasionally see it in 20 and 30-year-olds. Does it look the same to you, Jeff? Is it any different? Does it ring any bells?
Yeah, I have to say, morphologically, I don't feel like I see anything particularly distinctive based on age range.

All right, so Janice so at our place we would have probably given this guy 100 and apologized for it, although there would have been some argument to use 30 sort of as high dose diagnostic scanning so you'd have been in the ballgame so let's keep going. Yeah, Mike, Mike.

Yeah, let me just ask you a quick, quick question and direct this to manure and anyone else's or any anyone who would advocate giving. a low-dose whole body, doing a whole body scan prior to the resection. Just to settle the question, is this at all trapping iodine?

Yeah, so if there is a possibility of putting the patient on a low iodine diet, and not only at that point we can document the presence of activity in the lesion, but that will also help in the treatment planning, because as Mike mentioned, you know, 30 millicurie may be too much or too little, depending on, you know, these heart cell tumors that are notoriously not radioiodine avid, if there is a way to document their uptake. So in a case like this, not only we would consider doing the radioiodine scan, but I would even propose that an FDG PET up front might be helpful if there are any, knowing the histology that we just saw, It's high likelihood that patient probably may have distant disease as well.

And, and then FDG pet will be able to delineate that right so in his, in his particular, sorry Mike but can you do that he had his, he had a whole lobe of his thyroid in right so he only had a low back to me so. We didn't go with a scan first because we needed to do the completion thyroidectomy, I thought.
I agree totally, Jan.
But in terms of the FPG PET, it can actually help you to see if there was any distant disease in that case.

But Mark's point is good, because in somebody that's had total thyroidectomy before, I think it is wise to do a diagnostic scan, even if you're going to surgically resect those lymph nodes, so that we have an idea about whether they're RAI avid or not. If they're negative, it doesn't necessarily mean they can't concentrate radioactive, but it gives you a little feel for the lesion of asymmetry. One of the questions before we move on, Laurie, apparently you're a fan of molecular testing on some of these tumors. You were worried about this guy. Would you go ahead and send molecular testing on him? And if it's a hurtful cell, are you going to find anything that's helpful?

So, yes, yes, and no. So, as you know, Mike, with herthal cell cancers, what we now understand is that there are frequently mutations in the mitochondrial DNA that are not druggable. We also often see widespread loss of heterozygosity. in these cancers that, you know, we think also is another driver alteration, also not targetable. We rarely find things that are potentially druggable, like a BRAF600E mutation or gene fusions. If I saw a herthal cell with, say, an Ntrek fusion, I would ask the pathologist to go back and tell me, is it really? So we, so we do, I think, you know, the, the right answer is only if you expect that the patient's going to need systemic therapy, should you do molecular diagnostics? case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in November 2021 with several months of diminished sense of smell and epistaxis. She had no visual symptoms and no other neurologic symptoms at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Olfactory neuroblastoma (esthesioneuroblastoma), locally advanced at presentation, with no regional nodal or distant metastatic disease on initial staging workup.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside biopsy demonstrated olfactory neuroblastoma, Hyams grade 2. Institutional pathology review of the initial biopsy also classified the tumor as Hyams grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI demonstrated a tumor centered in the olfactory cleft/nasal cavity with intracranial extension. The lesion abutted both orbits, more closely on the left than the right. There was extension toward the frontal sinus. The lamina papyracea was eroded. No gross orbital invasion was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ current disease status ]: No objective evidence of regional or distant metastatic disease had been documented at presentation; no later metastatic disease status was provided.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial regional and distant disease workup was negative.

reference_discussion.text: All right. Let's shift gears a little bit. This is our second case. This was a 61-year-old woman who presented in November of 2021. She had a few months of sense of smell, diminishment, and some nosebleeds. Otherwise, had no other visual symptoms or no other neurologic symptoms. She ended up getting some image on the outside, which is shown there with a snapshot of a coronal MRI scan. This was biopsied as an olfactory neuroblastoma or anesthesio-neuroblastoma. The outside biopsy was a Himes grade 2. In the grand scheme, at that juncture, a relatively low grade tumor, two out of four. Otherwise, her regional and distant disease workup was negative. This would be a locally advanced tumor, but no regional or distant disease at the time of presentation. I'll flip through, this is a coronal T1 post-GAD MRI scan.
Tumor, whoops, excuse me.

Horsovac, resin olfactory cleft with some intracranial extension, as you can see here. Kind of go through, slowly through a couple of these slides so you can see them well. Abutting the bilateral orbits probably a little bit more closely on the left side than the right side. Again, no visual symptoms to date. I have a sagittal MRI next. Anyone see additional slices there a little more closely on that coronal MRI scan?
We'll go to the sagittal scan. Again, a T1 post-GAD sag.
So a fairly typical appearance for a locally advanced olfactory neuroblastoma. Little extension towards the frontal sinus there, but nothing too much to write home about.
Can you stop in the midline to see the sinus?
Absolutely.
Yeah, interesting.
One, since you're on right now, any general comments about the imaging studies before we get into management of this patient?

Well, in addition to MRI, to me, it's of great importance to get CT scan, you know, CT angiogram to look at the bony anatomy and the vascular anatomy, for sure. For example, is the lamina preparation intact or not? That's an important consideration. Yeah.

In this case, certainly the lamina was at minimum eroded. We'll get some questions later about the orbit in particular in imaging studies, but no gross invasion, but certainly abutting it in the bone was eroded. So when we look at a case like this, so, you know, we think of aesthesios largely as favorable players compared to some other tumors. Now, caveat of course being, you know, high grade tumors and those kind of things. In many cases, these are prime tumors for endoscopic resections. That being said, there's a number of factors that may lead you towards an open or a combined resection for these particular tumors. Perhaps, Dr. Sargi, anything off the bat here when you think about open and endoscopic resection for asthesios and this particular case, what are your initial thoughts?

So my initial thoughts about this case is I did not like the dual enhancement tracking laterally along the roof of the orbit. way beyond what you could easily reach endoscopically. And if this is, I would discuss with my neuroradiologist, if you can point with your arrow, Dr. Chobi, about this enhancement on both sides, that would be an area of concern for me. And I would discuss with the neuroradiologist, and if they think this is indeed neural enhancement, you know, that up front would be a reason. not to plan on doing an exclusively endoscopic approach. Another area on the sagittal cuts as was alluded to as well is a superior extension you know you reach the limit of what you can resect endoscopically even if you can see the area of concern endoscopically, you reach the limit because of the instruments and the adequacy of the resection is compromised. Obviously, if you have an anterior table of the frontal sinus involvement or skin involvement, obviously, if you have, you know, bulky superior orbit lateral involvement, then an endoscopic approach is an exclusively endoscopic approach would not be a good option for the patient. That being said, even doing an open craniofacial resection, some intranasal cuts are best done using an endoscope. So you could always do an open approach and use your endoscope for the cuts in the nose. You could use them either going through the nostrils or going through the transcranial cuts just to enhance visualization and make sure the cuts that you are making are in what you think is normal tissue, so you can adequately sample the margins.

Really, really good points. Thank you. Thank you for that. Dr. Parasota, you know, we talked a lot about in some of these studies and malignancies, it's tough to know whether it's truly dural enhancement and tumor involvement or occasionally reactive dura. In asthesios, we see a lot over the orbits and over the plenum. Those are two primaries that we sort of debate quite a bit as far as, you know, planning for a combined approach. Any thoughts you have on imaging studies preoperatively and predicting whether it's truly involved dura versus merely reactive dura.

I think it's very hard to know. I think as when we look at these these years and you know, of course, like we look at the enhancement and we don't quite know without pathology, whether that's in, you know, reactive or true tumor. But I think we have to look at number one, what is invading, what the tumor is invading and number two, the options for reconstruction. So in this case, we really don't have, you know, the tumor goes and basically like occupies the whole nasal cavity almost. There's really nothing that, and I would like to get your opinion about that, but I don't think there's any free septum from disease basically there. And so In this case, I would opt for a combined approach. So a craniotomy, and also there's like some, looks like some invasion of the dura of the sagittal sinus, which will make that, you know, really, really hard from an endoscopic standpoint, and you cannot get margins. I think in this case, I would offer a combined approach, doing the resection and getting the neural edges and margins transcranially. And just we get like a big piece of fascia lata and we can suture that watertight and then use the pericranial flap for reconstruction. And then we go through, before doing that, we go through the nose and we resect, you know, the areas that are not as readily accessible from the transcranial part of it. I think it's really critical to think about the reconstruction in these cases before you know, while you're thinking of the resection.

Yeah. Those are really good points. Thank you, Dr. Parasota. I think, you know, as we talk through this, I think a couple of key points sort of keep arising for this particular disease process. The first is which the primary goal of surgery is to get a negative margin resection, and whatever it takes to get that negative margin is the most critical portion. And the second one is, of course, prior preparation. So preparing for recon even before you've been in the case is really important. Dr. Thorpe, before we get to the next question, maybe not about this individual case, but for stesios or sinus malignancies in general, if you have someone who you don't have many intranasal options for reconstruction, but perhaps you can achieve a negative margin resection purely endoscopically, do you favor bringing in a pericranial flap endonasally, or would you simply convert to an open approach to get a better reconstruction?

It's a great question. So, you know, obviously that's, it's extremely center dependent. If you're asking me specifically, you know, I like using an extra nasal flap brought in through a nasion incision with a nasionectomy. And that's, you know, was part of my training paradigm. With that said, you know, I've started to use a lot more additional adjuncts like tensor fasciae latae has been, has been discussed with others. you know, and is it really a tried and true reconstructive option. Again, all done through the endonasal corridor. So just, you know, the reconstruction alone, again, you have to think about, but that wouldn't necessarily require an open approach, especially in a setting where you're able to accomplish all your oncologic goals endonasally. But again, you don't want to sacrifice your oncologic goals for your reconstruction right and so in this case, specifically everyone is highlighted all the pitfalls, particularly with the lateral extension and you know there's there's, you know, people that are able to do, you know, techniques with the orbit where they're able to work on the orbit and decompress things but still, I think the benefit of having the open option here is one the watertight closure and to really being able to survey that that dura and get a get a very good margin, not a close margin, right? Because, you know, there's nothing worse than getting a, you know, a, you know, a microscopically, you know, single cell margin free area, you know, in the most challenging place, and then a 10 centimeter margin somewhere else, right? So I think you really have to think about those pitfalls early, not only with the reconstruction, but the oncologic piece.

Awesome, thank you. That's a really good point. Getting back to that question I sort of brought up earlier, almost every asthesio is at least going to abut the orbit. The question always becomes, you know, how much is it truly, is it involving the periorbita? Is there truly intraconal extension? And it's quite hard to tell sometimes, but Apparius sort of mentioned the challenges in sort of turning that on imaging studies. Dr. Fernandez-Mirando, when we're working around the orbit for a lot of these tumors, let's say where the lamina has been eroded, there's no gross orbital involvement and patient has no symptoms from a vision standpoint. What do you tend to rely on for a margin in that area? Is clearing the periorbita as a margin enough? If that's involved, do you convert to an exoneration or you sample the fat underneath the periorbita? What's your general technique in that region?

So, if I can jump backwards one step, I think this case is not really about, you know, endoscopic or opiate, because we all agree we need to combine if we're going to do surgery. It's whether we do surgery or not up front, right? Whether we use induction chemotherapy in this case. When I see an anesthesiologist, anesthesiologists in general, we all agree, they are a surgical disease. They're a surgical disease in most cases, but some of them, they're so invasive. This one worries me, the superior oblique on that right side, the tumor extends along the folks of the superior sinus, I would really talk to the oncologists here, Tim, and decide whether induction chemotherapy is a fair option that could make sure the safer and preservation of, you know, orbital structures, etc.

That's a really good point. And there's a series out of Anderson about induction therapy for aesthesia. We have a series as well that we've published on induction for aesthesia. It's a really good point. And we actually brought that up in the workup for this patient. Interestingly, with the original biopsy and the review at our institution being a Heinz grade two, sort of thought that it wasn't the most active from a tumor grade standpoint to respond to induction. We'll circle back to that in a minute, but that's certainly a great option, especially for higher grade tumors. I agree. And that was considered for this particular patient.

Yeah, but yes, it's a general principle. I try not to do it. I wouldn't recommend exanteration in this disease, especially with that low grade pathology. You can take periorbita. You even, you know, a couple times take the supraoblique muscle, which happens to be the most often involved. Patients get diplopia, but you know, it's tolerable. But I wouldn't do an exanteration for this.

Yeah, very good. Moving on, assuming the patient had a margin of negative resection, there's a lot of factors going to choosing or selecting adjuvant therapy and whether that's purely radiation therapy or a combination of chemo radiotherapy. Dr. Hallis, would you mind talking to us about, in your experience treating a seizure neuroblastoma, what are your main deciding factors for selecting radiotherapy and when would you maybe lean towards pushing for some chemotherapy as well?

Well, this is another case where I feel that the chemotherapy, including induction chemotherapy or adjuvant chemotherapy and adjuvant radiation is a bit different from center to center. And I know I was much more used to kind of induction chemotherapy, where I trained as well as chemo RT after. At the University of Washington, for the most part, Our medical oncologists have not been as much in favor of chemotherapy and so we tend to do adjuvant radiation in these areas. And so really we're looking at the margin status and kind of overall the patient's age and sort of fit and kind of looking long term as you look at the literature, there are sort of It's hard to necessarily tease up how much adjuvant radiation does improve things, but I think overall these tumors are generally pretty highly aggressive and coming back, so we tend to look at those higher grades and treat them. The type of radiation really has to do with where this is located and our targets, as you're talking about with the dural spread and kind of the areas right next to the orbits. We have, since being online with protons for the last 10 years, have used protons simply because the plans will look better. I mean, the treatment will be the same as photon or IMRT, and that certainly can give a good treatment. But when you're really trying to get a large field like this in between places where you want to get less radiation, then the proton plans tend to come out better.

Those are really good insights, thank you. To take this a step further, Dr. Sargent, you can comment on this question. There's some discrepancy in aesthesios and clinically end-zero neck. I would say that most centers probably would not offer an elective neck dissection, but some centers may consider electively treating the neck with radiotherapies. In your experience with this disease process, we know that a good portion will recur much later on in the neck, five years, six years, eight years out. However, there is some morbidity to elective neck irradiation as well. So what's your experience or your opinion with treating a clinically N0 neck anesthesia?

So the discussion between treating an N0 neck with prophylactic radiation or surgically treating or addressing a negative neck is completely different. The reason for that is, you know, Yes, esthesia neuroblastomas recur in lymph nodes, but the location of the recurrence is very unpredictable. Some of them recur in retropharyngeal nodes. Some of them recur in parotid nodes. Some of them recur in level 1B, in level 2A nodes, in level 5 nodes. It's very hard to predict which nodal basin to electively address, at least surgically. I can assure you that even in the best hands, there is consequences of doing an elective neck dissection, especially if you follow the patients long enough. We do not prophylactically address with surgery negative necks at University of Miami. We always discuss prophylactically radiating the neck, especially in high-grade tumors and in tumors that involve the dura. Once the dura is involved, you know that the chances of nodal involvement becomes much more significant.

Very good, thank you. A quick adjunctor side, Dr. Fernandez-Miranda, any thoughts on the role of dural lymphatics with the regional spread of this perhaps to dural metastases and those kind of things?

A great question. I actually don't know. I wish I would know. But we all we've all seen the dural mets, right of dural mets of these tumors. They're so typical. And that might be a way of for these tumors to spread now.
It's definitely been, you know, maybe at least discuss, you know, something, Dr. Parra-Sutter, perhaps in the lab, we can, we can look at that a little bit.
I don't know about that. But

Very good. I think in the second time we'll move on a little bit to the next portion of this. So, as the group mentioned, this patient underwent a combined endoscopic assisted open craniofacial resection. We achieved negative margins. Now she did have a delayed positive margin, a week after surgery. Thankfully it was on the nasal septum, so I did take her back and re-resect that margin secondarily. Interestingly, her final pathology was a Himes grade four tumor. So certainly, you know, some sampling error with that very large tumor of that initial biopsy, despite being reviewed our institution as well as a very high grade tumor. We offer her adjuvant chemo radiotherapy, she declined the chemotherapy, she'd undergo adjuvant proton beam radiotherapy to both the bilateral necks as well as the primary site has been discussed a little bit. The last slide I'll show, that's a follow-up scan from June of 2022. It was doing fairly well at that point in time. I will just mention that in these cases, I do like to, if I can find anything in the nose to put on the pericranium to get a little remucosalization, I like to do it. Even if it's just a floor flap with a margin checked around it, I'll throw something up there to get a little mucosalization on there. Um, we have noticed quite a bit recently that in our open craniofacial resections with adjuvant proton deradiotherapy, we do notice some long term side effects from that as many of you I'm sure have experienced as well. She had a lot of long term crusting and some issues in the nose end up having some distance of her hardware on her scalp and it's a breakdown there. and developed a lot of vasogenic edema. So I'm just curious, Dr. Hallis, we've been seeing this more and more with our open craniofacials with adjuvant proton beam radiotherapy, this really significant vasogenic edema that seems to be persistent. Have you noticed that in your practice at all? And if so, any tips on treating it?

No, we hate seeing that. I saw that on your slides. No, I think that this is something that's really an active area study for proton, and certainly Mayo, as well as us are really looking into this to really figure out with the proton beam at the end of range, are you having a higher effect on those frontal lobes? And so I think part of it is kind of where we place our beams and where we end, because proton therapy, because it's a heavy particle, gives most of its energy at the very end called the Bragg peak. And so that's where sometimes we are seeing some increased enhancement in long-term late effects from radiation. I think a lot of that can be worked on as there's more and more sort of proton outcomes in looking at these cases. Overall, our goal really is to kind of decrease the amount of radiation that goes to other parts. But I do think that we need to get really smart about exactly how we use our technique to bring in those beams. So the answer really is we don't know, but we're highly interested in this. And we have noticed some increase, sort of edema where we wouldn't expect it.

Yeah, very good. Thank you. The last point here is her bone flap ended up sort of dying. So she ended up going back for a free flap. We resected some of that necrotic tissue at that time as well. And she's actually doing really well now, but certainly has had some ongoing side effects from the therapies that we put her through.

Yeah, that's the other thing you will get with protons is that the skin, sort of the shallow sparing, so the sparing of the flaps does not occur as much as photons. And so I think overall with these complex surgeries and then high dose radiation, you'll start to see more of that, but there are techniques that we can do to kind of decrease those doses of the anterior aspens.
Thanks for those insights, appreciate it.

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent a combined endoscopic-assisted open craniofacial resection with achievement of negative margins; a delayed positive nasal septal margin identified postoperatively was managed with return to the operating room for secondary re-resection. Final pathology demonstrated Hyams grade 4 olfactory neuroblastoma. Adjuvant chemoradiotherapy was offered; chemotherapy was declined, and adjuvant proton beam radiotherapy was delivered to the primary site and bilateral necks.
reference_conclusion_quote: this patient underwent a combined endoscopic assisted open craniofacial resection. We achieved negative margins. Now she did have a delayed positive margin, a week after surgery. Thankfully it was on the nasal septum, so I did take her back and re-resect that margin secondarily. Interestingly, her final pathology was a Himes grade four tumor. [...] We offer her adjuvant chemo radiotherapy, she declined the chemotherapy, she'd undergo adjuvant proton beam radiotherapy to both the bilateral necks as well as the primary site

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of an enlarging left supraclavicular neck mass. No other presenting complaints were reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Malignant melanoma involving a left supraclavicular cervical lymph node, presenting as nodal melanoma with no identifiable primary lesion on clinical examination. History included basal cell carcinoma of the cheek and melanoma in situ of the posterior neck in 1999.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the left supraclavicular mass showed malignant melanoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Ultrasound of the neck was performed and led to tissue sampling. PET/CT showed FDG avidity confined to the palpable left supraclavicular nodal lesion, with no other sites of abnormal uptake identified. MRI brain was negative for intracranial disease. Office examination did not identify lesions in the oropharynx or nasopharynx, and no other obvious skin lesions were found.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Basal cell carcinoma of the cheek had been treated previously; details were not reported.  
- Melanoma in situ of the posterior neck in 1999 had been treated surgically, with no evidence of recurrence at the primary site thereafter.

[ other clinical data ]: Comprehensive head and neck examination did not identify an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal primary lesion. No other obvious cutaneous lesion was identified on examination.
