reference_discussion.text: All right. So this is a patient who, 71-year-old, he came in with a six-month history of an enlarging left supraclavicular neck mass, really had no complaints otherwise. And upon further digging, it sounds like he did have a very distant history of having a basal cell carcinoma of the cheek and then back in 1999 had a melanoma in site two of the posterior neck. It looked like it was mainly midline possibly to the right. It was treated with surgery and he hadn't had any evidence of occurrence in that primary site since then. And I will say given that he does have a lymph node with a technically unknown primary, there was a full exam done as well in the office. It did not identify anything in the oropharynx or nasopharynx as well, and there was no other obvious skin lesions. So this is some of the MRI, the imaging that he got. He did get an ultrasound. ultimately got an FNA that did show malignant melanoma, and a PET CT as well that only showed a FDG ability in that area that was palpable on exam. He also had a MRI brain that was negative.
Okay, let me pause you right there. So I'm sorry, you said you'd say that there is FDG. Good. So this is your next slide with a Steve, I think.
I do. But I also have what we ended up doing with it.
So TJ, is this, you agree with this workup?

I think so. Maybe throw in an ophthalmology exam. I guess you could have a UVL. I don't know. But yeah, I think, you know, I also I'd have a dermatologist, I might have missed it, but I have a dermatologist do a thorough body scan, you know, make sure there's no lesion that we're missing.
Okay. Audrey, anything to add from the workup standpoint? some PET, MRI.

I mean, you know, recently, and we never used to do this, but recently at our tumor ward, we had somebody present like this who actually had an undiagnosed vaginal melanoma. So now we always say, Oh, if it's a female patient, you know, does this patient have regular OBGYN exams? But I can't say that that used to be our standard of care.
Yeah. Super clav is a kind of a funny spot. So yeah, definitely a lot of acral type of lesion for sure, which you might not think of.
And the PET-CT didn't pick up the vaginal lesion, Audrey?
No, a PET-CT did not pick up the vaginal lesion. It was like a mucosal lesion.
Interesting. So I'm going to go to TJ. So what would your team offer this patient at this point for a known primary single focus in the neck?

Yeah, within isolated, but it seems like a pretty large MET. You know, I think the two options for this patient would be surgery with adjuvant treatment versus neoadjuvant treatment followed by surgery. And I think more and more people are kind of leaning towards the neoadjuvant. I guess one other thing, you know, the FNA probably isn't adequate to get a BRAF. So maybe a core, if you're not going to do, I guess, if you're not going to do surgery, probably a core for sure to get adequate tissue to try to think of what type of neoadjuvant approach you'd use.
Awesome. Audrey, what do you think your team would do? And then I'll go to Tony next.
That's what our team would do. Exactly. We would make sure we have adequate tissue to delineate neoadjuvant treatment for this patient.

So both of you are favoring, Audrey, definitely neoadjuvant and TJ, at least entertainment of neoadjuvant. Tony, What do you think about this case? And do you definitely want to know the BRAF status before initiating a next step versus kind of it's okay with what we have?

Yeah. So based on the emerging data that we have now from ECOG 1801 and the Abdulag study and the Prado study or the Opposite Neo study, neoadjuvant therapy really does seem to be the way to go. It is flooding the oncology community in triple negative breast cancer and lung cancer in many, many other areas because we're recognizing that we can get really great pathologic responses, which does seem to be a valid biomarker for relapse-free survival and potentially even now overall survival. So we're really much in favor now of neoadjuvant. This patient would have been a great candidate for neoadjuvant therapy because they have an unknown primary, but a clinically detected node that we can see on this PET scan. And so it would fit all the criteria for the trial inclusion I don't care about the BRAF status right now. I would get it. I would look for it, clearly. But in the neoadjuvant setting, as opposed to the adjuvant setting where we don't actually know if IO or BRAF is better, we do know that in the neoadjuvant setting. IO therapy clearly trumps BRAF MEK inhibition. If we give BRAF MEK inhibition, There's about a 70% chance that this would go down or go away, almost a 50% chance of a complete pathologic response, which sounds wonderful. But the recurrence after surgery seems to be exceedingly high. Whereas if we give neoadjuvant immunotherapy, we see that the complete response rate again can be up to 50 percent if we're using dual immunotherapy. But on the other hand, we also see durability and we see many, many patients never having disease again. We would want to offer this patient neoadjuvant again in a multidisciplinary setting, but I'm almost always leaning now towards IO therapy. Very rarely would I pull the trigger on Dirafenib, Intrametanib, or any other of the BRAF MEK inhibitors, at least up front.

What is your IO cocktail of choice for a case like this? Are you doing Ipinevo? Are you doing Pembro? Are you doing with a lag-3 inhibitor on top of it? I'm very curious because it seems like, and I'm sure there are also trial opportunities, but I'm curious what you're sort of using off trial.

Yeah, so right now we're using a lot of combination immunotherapy, so that would be ipinivo. Ipinivo is actually flip dosing, so ipi1 and nivo3. It's a lot easier to tolerate. I teach my fellows that I can always get one dose of ipinivo into every patient. And in fact, in the Prado trial, there were two doses, one dose every three weeks before surgery. And in that trial, 90% of patients, 90% of 100 patients, so literally 90 patients, got two doses. Only 10% didn't. And those 10% that had immune-related adverse events did not have delayed surgery. They took these patients to surgery with steroids. it didn't impact healing surprisingly to me. Because I always hear the case that steroids are really bad, but these patients apparently did really well. I use ipinevo a lot. I do that based off of extrapolating from the metastatic setting, where ipinevo is the immunotherapy du jour because of the really outstanding survival that we have at six years, 50 percent of patients are still alive. Actually, melanoma-specific survival is better than 50% at six years, which is really amazing. So we're using a lot of ipinevo flip dose. Obdualag is using rilatilamab plus nivolumab, a lag three inhibitor. And it also has a pathologic complete response rate in patients like this of around 50%, actually 57% in a small 30 patient trial. So I think that's also a good medication to use. It has a much lower toxicity rate than ipinevo, and so we've been using that a lot. But the big trowel, the biggest trowel that we have is the ECOG 1801. and that was about a 300 patient trial. And that used three doses of pembrolizumab, 200 milligrams every three weeks, and then surgery versus just doing adjuvant pembrolizumab. And in that trial, pembrolizumab neoadjuvant really did win, had a much better relapse-free survival. And importantly though, if we look at complete responses, complete pathologic responses, that was only seen in 21% of patients. So Pembrolizumab, 21%, OpdioLag, 57% based off of a small trial, and Ipinevo, a complete response rate of 50%. So I usually pull the gun to try to give dual immunotherapy if I can.

That's great, Tony. Thank you. And I think the study you just referred to about neoadjuvant versus adjuvant randomized with Pembro for N-positive disease or resectable disease with or without M1 disease is a link I just put in. Someone should check me, but I think that's the one I just put in. So great, Jessica, why don't you tell me what you did next?

So he did exactly what Dr. Olzanski had recommended with that specific dose. He was actually on trial, on the Opus in Neo trial, and he actually got randomized into that favorable arm with the low dose IPI of one mg per kg and high dose NEVO of three mg per kg for two cycles. He had that every three weeks, and then this was his response. PET scan really didn't show much FDG ambidity at all. So the next step was to take him to surgery. And really he had a complete posterolateral neck dissection and had no tumor present. There was one lymph node, which was the one that was probably visible on PET scan that did not have any viable tumor cells. So essentially he had a pathologic complete response.

Thanks, Zach. If you could just pause there for a second. Audrey, when you do these cases, do you do the, two through five. This is more of a posterior level five lymph node. You do two through five with a posterior lateral because you might think it might be a posterior primary that disappeared. Would you just do a very focused 5A, 5B? I'm sure there are more lymph nodes here, but I'm just curious what you think about in terms of what levels you would do for neck dissection.

Yeah, I, I think it depends. For this, this was really a level five lymph node, I would do a thorough clean out of level five. But, you know, it's pretty easy to get at least some of two, three and four while you're in five. So usually it ends up turning into a classic Boconac where I'm doing two through five.
Okay, TJ? Two to five?

Yeah, I think similar. You don't know where the original primary was, but I think this looked like almost like accessory chain level five kind of thing. So I would treat it like a posterolateral type of lesion and do a posterolateral neck like they did. Plus I treated MD Anderson, so I can't not do what they did at MD Anderson.

Can I ask a question here? In the Opus in Neo trial, complete lymph node dissection was required for that trial. But when that trial was amended and became the Prado trial, that was not necessary. And they did not do a TLND in all patients. So would you actually do a TLND if you thought that this patient had a complete pathologic response? Could you do an index node marker, take out that index node and get pathology?

Tony, great question. Audrey or TJ, who wants to take the first crack at that? If you know that it's likely to be a CR based on some by the FDG avidity and maybe even a biopsy that was negative, would you still do like a limited or?

So in this patient, that PET scan makes me too nervous to call that a CR. So in this patient, I would definitely at least take out that lymph node. I would like to do an act dissection. I'm glad that it turned out to be nothing. but that would make me pretty nervous. If the PET scan was like totally stone cold negative, yeah, I would talk with the patient about maybe just following with serial PET scans.
TJ?

Yeah, if a patient, even in a patient who had a like Complete CR, nothing on the scan. I don't know about you guys, but I can't find that one node. I mean, that's really impossible. So I think you have to at least take out a compartment. And if you're there, I think at least one level, essentially quote, like one level above, one level below, that compartment is probably the safest approach at this point. And probably what I would do at the minimum.

I think I'll just say one more thing, because I think it's so intriguing. In all of the trials so far, imaging underpredicted pathologic response by a lot. And so it was not actually a good representation of what disease would or would not be there.

That was my exact question is, how good is the interval imaging after neoadjuvant prior to your definitive surgery? And my understanding it's very poor at predicting that you can, and there can be look like there's a residual disease that is a CR, or there can be look like there's been a profound response that is still residual disease. Is that right? I don't wanna speak for you, Tony.

No, that is right. It's rare to have a CR on imaging and then find positive disease. That can happen, but it's rare. It's much more likely that you would have a PR or stable disease on imaging and then find that you have a major pathologic response. or complete pathologic response. Complete pathologic response is defined as no tumor cells present. A major is less than 10 percent of tumor cells present. In pathology, it's really nice to see necrosis, dead tumor cells, but fibrosis or scarring is actually even better because that's actually telling you that the tumor area, if you will, is undergoing real healing, and that is prognostically related.
Thanks, Tony. Dr. Neil Gross, thank you for joining. I see you have your hand up. Or is that an accident?

Yeah, no, I'm here. Thank you. And thank you, Jess, for presenting this case. Great, really great discussion. And obviously, this is an area that there's a tremendous amount of interest in. And I just kind of echo the comments that were made already around how imaging underestimates the pathologic response. And so that's sort of the holy grail now, both in melanomas leading the way, but also in cutaneous cremosal carcinomas, how to predict response better. And we currently don't really have a good substitute for tissue, but again, melanoma has led the way. And I think as was kind of mentioned, You know, it is possible, and this is being done now at our Center for Melanoma, you know, where you can mark the node of interest and then target that specifically for surgery. Now, I haven't done, personally haven't done a lot of that, and I'm a little nervous about missing, you know, missing the index node, but it certainly, partly, I think, depends on on the location and the risk of side effects with a more complete dissection. I think of a limited selective neck dissection a lot differently than perhaps the side effects from a groin dissection or axillary dissection.

That's great. Thanks, Neil, for your comments. Tony, can you break it down for me? What would you recommend for this patient next based on the pathology? Maybe you can outline when you have a PATH-PR, PATH-PR, or PATH-NR, maybe those three buckets, like I'm sure each of those will be a little bit different.

Yeah, so if you actually look at the trials, the way they were treated was different, but the way that I treat them in clinic is essentially the same. I offer now everybody adjuvant therapy after they get surgery. I do it for every patient. And I do it for a couple of reasons, a couple of really intriguing reasons. If you actually look at the Prado trial, which was using ipinevo flip dosing, the primary endpoint there was relapse-free survival. And they were expecting to see one relapse out of the patients that they had. They actually had four. So that patient did, that trial actually did not meet their primary endpoint. of avoiding adjuvant therapy. Those patients got two doses of ipinevo and then they did not get adjuvant therapy if they had a complete pathologic response. So that trial essentially was negative even though it gave us a lot of great data really supporting the use of neoadjuvant therapy. On the other hand, if you look at that same trial, they talk in the paper about patients who had non-response. So they did not have a pathologic response. And the patients who went on to get adjuvant immunotherapy did better than the patients who did not. And the interesting thing is, because I would put my hands up too, like what in the world is going on? We see the same thing in lung cancer. We see the same thing in triple negative breast cancer. Patients who get neoadjuvant and don't have a response, inevitably do better if they continue with adjuvant therapy, with immunotherapy, even if they haven't had that response. And that would suggest to us that there may be latent responses and that somehow the immune system figures out what antigen is going to actually attack and go after it. Based on the fact that we have that data now to support that, and of course, both the ECOG trial as well as the Opdulag trial used adjuvant therapy after the surgery in both arms. In the neoadjuvant, they got neoadjuvant, then surgery, then they got documented adjuvant therapy. We're now following that as well for these patients.
If I could just summarize, you're not using the pathological response to risk-adapt the adjuvant. You're just going to continue on with ibuprofen at this point, at least in your practice?
So just to clarify, we don't continue with ibuprofen. We just give the two doses of ibuprofen up front, and then we'll give ibuprofen out back.
Thank you. Got it. One more minute. Jess, you want to finish your slide deck?
Yeah, that was it, really. So I guess the question was if he needed adjuvant therapy, which we had a discussion about. Based on the trial, he actually did not, and he's been doing well since.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old woman; gravida 1, with one pregnancy 15 years previously. Light smoker. No prior substance use reported.

[ chief complaint ]: In the first quarter of 2015, she presented with vaginal discharge and post-coital bleeding.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma diagnosed in 2015. Clinical examination showed a bleeding exophytic cervical lesion with superinfection and cervical induration, without clinical vaginal or parametrial involvement. Initial body CT showed no metastatic disease. Surgical pathology demonstrated nodal involvement in 1 of 19 lymph nodes examined, involving a left iliac node. The case was documented as surgical stage IIIB.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy showed infiltrating, moderately differentiated squamous carcinoma of the cervix. Surgical pathology after hysterectomy showed invasive keratinizing large-cell, poorly differentiated carcinoma of the cervix with lymphovascular invasion. There was no parametrial, vaginal, or ovarian involvement. Surgical margins were negative. One of 19 lymph nodes was positive for tumor; the involved node was a left iliac node.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT prior to surgery showed no metastases and no lymphadenopathy identified. Post-treatment MRI in the third quarter of 2015 showed a latero-aortic lymph node extending from the left renal vein to the left common iliac artery, with no evidence of pelvic recurrence.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She underwent hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy and lymph node dissection in the first quarter of 2015. In the second quarter of 2015, she received adjuvant chemoradiation consisting of pelvic radiotherapy, cesium implant brachytherapy, and concurrent cisplatin. Post-treatment MRI showed no pelvic recurrence but demonstrated a latero-aortic nodal abnormality.

[ current disease status ]: After surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation, there was no radiologic evidence of pelvic recurrence on post-treatment MRI. A persistent/enlarged latero-aortic nodal lesion was present on MRI performed approximately 2 months after completion of chemoradiation.

[ other clinical data ]: Lesion size was not documented. The positive pelvic lymph node had not been identified intraoperatively and was detected only on final pathology.

reference_discussion.text: Okay. The case we are presenting today is a 38-year-old woman with one pregnancy 15 years ago. She's a light smoker with no previous substance. And in the first quarter of 2015, she presented with vaginal discharge, post-coital bleeding, and her physical exam showed at the spinoscopy there was a bleeding exopedic lesion that was over-infected. And there was also shown cervical induration with no clinical vaginal or parametric involvement. So the biopsy shows an infiltrating, moderately differentiated squousal carcinoma of the cervix, and the body CV showed no metastases. So we performed a surgery, and it was a hysterectomy plus bilateral anexectomy plus line blood dissection. And the pathology showed an invasive keratinizing large stem, poorly differentiated carcinoma of the cervix. lymphovascular invasion, no paramedial, vaginal, or ovarian involvement, with negative margin. And there was one light node with tumor in 19 examined. And that corresponded to a left agliac node. So the surgical stage of this tumor was stage 3b. And in the second quarter of 2015, We performed actual chemoradiation therapy with radiotherapy in pelvis and cesium implant. And cisplatin concluded during radiotherapy. In the third-quartile of 2015, we did a post-treatment MRI that showed a lateral articulating node from left vena brain to left common iliac artery with no signs of pelvic recurrence. So the questions for discussion are, what is the optimal systemic treatment option?
Can we just do the questions one at a time and discuss them one at a time, please?
OK. So the first one would be, what is the optimal systemic treatment option for this patient?
Should we read out all the questions? What do you prefer, Gans?
Why don't we stop the case and just sort of see. So in terms of the extent of disease, was the nodal involvement detected by CT scan?
No. Previously, first of all, we did a CT. And then we operated on the patient. That CT didn't show any life notes.
OK. And in terms of the size of the lesion, I know it says it was super infected, but any idea of what the lesion's size was?
We don't have that. OK. We have a big exam. It didn't say. But it was clinically, it didn't detect by a lesion.
So in terms of the stage, again, I'm not sure I understand why you're calling her surgical stage 3B.
Because in the pathologic review, it said there was one lymph node in the ear.

So that's just an interesting point that the Commission on Cancer, the staging group for AJCC, has recognized that it's not consistent with FIGO staging right now. That nodal involvement is not in the FIGO staging, but it is in the AJCC staging. We're trying to reconcile that with FIGO. But generally speaking, you know, with FIGO staging, we wouldn't consider the nodes on FIGO. So, I'm not sure, I'm not sure, it sounds to me like she was a stage one with positive nodes. Whether that would have impacted treatment in post-surgery, probably not, but it is a problem between the staging systems.
And just for everyone's education, the staging is done

That's actually clinical, and cervix is very funny because they don't allow extensive imaging. It's really a clinical stage, you know, you want to talk, it's like systole. You can do a systole, you can do a proctor, you can do an x-ray. Yeah, you can't do extensive radiographic staging, and it's actually a point that AJCC has made to FIGO that it's actually only cancer where we don't allow radiographic imaging. We allow CT scans for, you know, ovary, uterus. We allow it for brain, lung, breast, but for some reason in cervix it's considered in poor resource, poor countries is not appropriate. And I actually would like to challenge that. But having said that, FIGO staging is clinical. And ET imaging of nodes is not used. And nodal involvement is not actually considered in FIGO. So are you happy with this being called Stage 3 by FIGO or by AJCCP? I would actually clarify that as AJCCP 3B.

Right, which I think the thing is, though, Don, that it's going to be something that has to be resolved, because both the clinical and the surgical staging have important implications for management. And so there needs to be some kind of classification that reports both.

Yeah, I totally agree. And hopefully, the AJCC is going to put out their next staging guidelines in 2015. I actually was fortunate to be one of the members for the gynecologic group who's doing the AJC staging. And we're taking that back to FIGO that they need to incorporate nodes.
But are you suggesting to me that today this patient may be treated quite differently with one or the other staging, even though she's not?

You know, with a stage one, you know, if it's not a bulky tumor, we probably would have offered her surgery. But if this was a bulky tumor, we would have you know, done a CT, maybe biopsy of some nodes, and we would not have performed surgery. We would have done definitive chemoradiation. It was a locally advanced tumor. In this case, you know, again, I'm considering if it was super infected, it's likely it would look like a larger tumor than it probably was, and you know, the question of did you treat it, treat it for its super infection for a couple of weeks and then reassess for size, or did you go directly to surgery for local indications, which is perfectly appropriate, but that would have been the difference. Okay.
Okay. So anybody want to have a stab at whether What systemic options are appropriate, and what systemic option would be chosen?

I just want to make one more comment that I think is interesting in this case. She had a post-relief, and she had radiation to the pelvis only. In some situations, at least here, I'm curious to see what they do at MD Anderson. But here, we will treat also the parotid lymph nodes with radiation. And in this case, apparently, she was not treated to the parotid nodes.
Anuja, do you want to comment on the treatment of the para-aortic nodes with radiation?
Yes.
Sorry, somebody's got their microphone on. Can everybody turn their microphone off, please? In Argentina, the microphone is on. Sorry.
Wait, Kathleen's going to ask a question, and then I'm going to comment on the radiation therapy part.

Go ahead, Kathleen. One question is whether intra-op, the lymph node was noted to be positive or abnormal. Because when we operate and come across a grossly positive pelvic lymph node, we actually abort the hysterectomy. And at a minimum, we usually sample the parotid lymph nodes, if we're already in surgery, to see what to better tailor the fields. So that was just a question of intraoperatively, did you notice that it was enlarged?
Cecilia, do you want to try and answer that question?
No, it was shown only in the pathology.
Only in the pathology, okay. Marcella, do you want to add to that?

Yeah, I mean, I think I agree with Kathleen. Certainly that's the way that I would manage this patient if there's recognition of intraoperability. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 22-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive left subclavicular/left lateral neck mass first noticed in 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with extensive cervical nodal metastases and bilateral pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle biopsy of a left cervical lymph node was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Following surgery, pathology showed a unifocal 5.2 cm classic-type papillary thyroid carcinoma. Extensive lymphovascular invasion was present. Extensive gross extrathyroidal extension was present. A total of 83 lymph nodes were removed, of which 30 were positive for metastatic disease. The largest metastatic lymph node measured 5.9 cm. Extranodal extension was present.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT chest showed multiple thyroid nodules, with the largest reported at approximately 3 cm in the isthmus, enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with substernal extension, tracheal deviation, and extensive left lateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Thyroid ultrasound showed multiple suspicious thyroid nodules, including an isthmus nodule measuring approximately 1.7 cm in transverse view, a left-sided mixed cystic-solid nodule measuring approximately 5.4-6 cm, two dominant nodules in the isthmus, and a subcentimeter hypoechoic right-sided nodule. Multiple abnormal left lateral cervical lymph nodes were identified. Ultrasound of the right lateral neck showed no abnormal lymph nodes. CT chest demonstrated innumerable bilateral pulmonary nodules, largest approximately 5 mm. Post-treatment whole-body radioiodine scan showed diffuse bilateral pulmonary uptake and uptake in the right lateral neck. CT chest performed 6 months after radioiodine treatment showed decreased number and size of pulmonary nodules. Neck ultrasound performed 6 months after radioiodine treatment showed no suspicious findings. Diagnostic radioiodine scan performed 12 months after initial radioiodine treatment was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperative thyroglobulin measured 43 with TSH 0.07 approximately 4-6 weeks after surgery. At the time of radioiodine treatment, thyroglobulin was 272 with TSH 41. Six months after radioiodine treatment, thyroglobulin was 12 with TSH 1.6. Most recent thyroglobulin was 7.1 with TSH 0.04. Stimulated thyroglobulin at the time of the 12-month diagnostic scan was reported to be substantially lower than the pretreatment value and approximately 15-20. Pulmonary function testing was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, and left lateral neck dissection. She subsequently underwent diagnostic radioiodine imaging confirming pulmonary metastatic disease, followed by treatment with 150 mCi radioactive iodine after thyroid hormone withdrawal. After radioiodine treatment, thyroglobulin declined without additional therapy, CT chest showed interval improvement in pulmonary nodules, and follow-up neck ultrasound showed no suspicious cervical disease.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent but improving metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with biochemical response and radiographic improvement in pulmonary metastases after initial radioactive iodine therapy. No suspicious findings were identified on follow-up neck ultrasound. Twelve-month diagnostic radioiodine scan was negative.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included obesity and depression. There was no family history of thyroid cancer. There was no personal history of head and neck radiation exposure. Initial physical examination identified a 5 cm palpable mass in the left lateral neck and a palpable thyroid nodule in the isthmus.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 37-year-old Asian male.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache and blurring of vision for approximately 5 months prior to presentation in May 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Solid-cystic sellar/suprasellar craniopharyngioma, WHO grade 1, with postoperative residual suprasellar disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection specimen from May 2025 showed WHO grade 1 craniopharyngioma. No granulomas or malignancy were identified.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Preoperative imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous solid-cystic lesion in the sellar/suprasellar region. Limited axial and FLAIR images were available; the lesion was described as FLAIR hyperintense in the sphenoid sinus/suprasellar region.  
- Postoperative MRI in June 2025 showed residual heterogeneously enhancing solid-cystic lesion in the suprasellar region above the pituitary gland, consistent with residual craniopharyngioma. The pituitary gland was visualized in the sella, with bilateral cavernous internal carotid arteries and cavernous sinuses appearing normal. The residual lesion caused compression on the third ventricle. Hydrocephalus was present with bilateral prominence of the temporal horns.  
- MRI in November 2025 showed persistent residual enhancing solid component with adjacent cystic component in the left suprasellar/left paracellar region, left of midline, adjacent to the left MCA and optic chiasm. The sella was not expanded, and the pituitary gland remained in the sella. The lesion was slightly hyperintense on FLAIR. Hydrocephalus persisted.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Pituitary hormonal laboratory values were not available. The patient was under endocrinology follow-up.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- May 2025: Endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection of sellar/suprasellar lesion.  
- Postoperatively, residual suprasellar craniopharyngioma remained on imaging.  
- Following surgery, headache resolved and vision improved significantly. The patient became asymptomatic and returned to work.

[ current disease status ]: Residual left suprasellar/paracellar craniopharyngioma persisted on MRI as of November 2025, with associated hydrocephalus. Clinically, the patient was asymptomatic, with significantly improved vision and no headache.

[ other clinical data ]: Profession: welder. The patient had undergone one surgery only. No prior radiation therapy had been given.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 24-year-old female at initial presentation; 34 weeks pregnant with her second child at time of diagnosis. She was 27 years old at 30 months post-treatment.

[ chief complaint ]: Three-year history of intermittent left-sided neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma involving the left base of tongue with metastatic left cervical nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside biopsy and fine-needle aspiration, rereviewed internally, lacked clear high-grade features and favored mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Internal pathology/cytology review subsequently classified the lesion as intermediate-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Initial tissue diagnosis was based on FNA only; no direct laryngoscopy biopsy was performed at that stage. At approximately 5 months after completion of chemoradiation, direct laryngoscopy biopsy and FNA of left neck tissue were both negative for malignancy. At 24 months after treatment, 13 biopsies obtained in the operating room were all negative for carcinoma. At 30 months post-treatment, FNA of a left level III neck mass was diagnostic for mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial examination identified a mobile 3 cm left level II neck mass and fullness of the left base of tongue on nasopharyngolaryngoscopic examination. Imaging demonstrated an enhancing base-of-tongue mass extending deep and anteriorly, over the hyoid, approaching the midline. Three-month post-treatment imaging demonstrated persistent disease in the left neck corresponding to a persistently palpable left level II node. Serial CT and PET imaging after treatment showed stable or decreasing size of both the base-of-tongue lesion and nodal disease until approximately 2 years post-treatment, when enlargement was identified on imaging. At 30 months post-treatment, PET imaging showed persistent uptake at the base of tongue, similar to prior studies, without interval increase. During the same interval, a left neck mass enlarged rapidly from subcentimeter size to 2.2 cm over a period of weeks on interval imaging. Repeat CT demonstrated rapid enlargement of the left neck mass.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor profiling (Tempus) showed HER2 0, androgen receptor negative, and PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) 50 in the neck specimen.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She was induced at 36 weeks’ gestation and delivered her second child. She declined primary surgical resection because of the potential need for subtotal or total glossectomy. She then received cisplatin with 66 Gy radiation therapy. Post-treatment, a left neck node remained palpable, but direct laryngoscopy biopsy and FNA at approximately 5 months were negative for malignancy. Subsequent PET and CT surveillance demonstrated stable or decreasing disease burden until approximately 24 months after treatment, when radiographic enlargement developed.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent/progressive mucoepidermoid carcinoma was present 30 months after chemoradiation, with rapidly enlarging left cervical nodal disease and persistent base-of-tongue lesion.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was otherwise non-contributory.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 35-year-old married female. Right-eyed. Non-hypertensive and non-diabetic.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache for 2 years; generalized tonic-clonic seizures for 1 year; progressive right-sided visual loss for 5 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Skull base extra-axial cystic lesion centered in the pre-/suprasellar region, radiologically favored to represent an epidermoid cyst.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available.

[ imaging findings ]: CT brain demonstrated an ill-defined cystic lesion arising from the skull base in the precellar/suprasellar region. The lesion was described as extra-axial and cystic-appearing, following CSF density on CT. MRI characteristics described included T1- and T2-weighted signal following CSF intensity, without contrast enhancement. The lesion was described as insinuating along the margins of the brain without well-defined borders. Multicompartment involvement was described, including the middle cranial fossa, part of the anterior cranial fossa, and posterior cranial fossa with prepontine extension. Differential diagnostic considerations on imaging included epidermoid cyst and arachnoid cyst; craniopharyngioma was considered less likely due to absence of contrast enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging was not available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Hormonal workup was within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior treatment was documented. Past medical history was non-significant. Past surgical history was present but details were not provided.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic intracranial skull base lesion with persistent headaches, seizures, and complete right-sided visual loss. Neurological examination showed intact higher mental functions with MMSE 30/30, frontal lobe function intact apart from behavioral changes/aggression, no significant parietal or temporal lobe deficits, intact cranial nerves except visual deficit, right primary optic atrophy on fundoscopy, no motor deficit, no sensory loss, and bilateral upgoing plantar responses.

[ other clinical data ]: Cerebellar signs were negative. Right eye had complete vision loss. Fundoscopy showed right-sided primary optic atrophy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for consideration of curative-intent treatment for newly diagnosed prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 3+4=7, ISUP grade group 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Prostate biopsy confirmed Gleason 3+4=7 prostate cancer, grade group 2.

[ imaging findings ]: Multiparametric prostate MRI demonstrated a PI-RADS 4 lesion. No pelvic lymphadenopathy was identified on MRI. PSMA PET/CT demonstrated a highly PSMA-avid lesion in the left mid prostate with SUVmax 14. No suspicious pelvic nodal disease was identified on PSMA PET/CT. A retroperitoneal focus of uptake with SUVmax 6 corresponded to a small elongated soft tissue structure measuring approximately 0.5 mm by 1.2 cm; this was bilateral and linear in morphology.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 6.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed Gleason 3+4=7, grade group 2 prostate cancer referred for consideration of curative-intent treatment, with no pelvic lymphadenopathy on MRI or PSMA PET/CT and a retroperitoneal focus of PSMA uptake.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had been referred for possible surgery as curative-intent treatment. An external PET report had described the retroperitoneal finding as a nodal metastasis.

James, do you want to add anything else about standardised reporting and teaching and templates?

No, I think it's just good to think clinicians are watching. They do use this information, even what could seem seemingly unimportant, like what kind of tracer was used, what dose. It can have implications, for example, for the referrals to any research projects. They do pay attention. They do expect a certain quality. So I think it's good to keep that in mind. It's the only idea they have of the case.

And looking on earlier, George showed a couple of reports that were quite drastically different, and making it in a way that's easy for the clinician to actually understand without spending 15 minutes on it, that would be, I'm sure you'd appreciate that in the safety of time.

I guess, I don't know, Shankar, do you have any thoughts about? I think from a clinician point of view, as Declan had mentioned, you don't want to steer away this patient from having potentially curative local therapy for their prostate cancer. But even for myself, I've been saved a few times by nuclear medicine colleagues who've reported what has been uptaken, sacral ganglia or celiac ganglia, which are really an ask. And the question is, can I give sabre to these oligometastatic nodal disease? And clearly I shouldn't be because they're not actually nodes, but they can be reported externally and you can be led down the wrong pathway.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET/CT findings were interpreted as physiologic ganglion uptake rather than nodal metastasis, with no evidence of metastatic disease. The patient should proceed with definitive curative-intent local therapy for favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer, with either radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy.
reference_conclusion_quote: I'd consider it benign, and this patient does not have any metastatic disease. [...] Yeah, so it's actually physiologic ganglion uptake. It's not actually a lymph node. [...] This man should have surgery or radiotherapy [...] you don't want to steer away this patient from having potentially curative local therapy for their prostate cancer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 31-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Left temporomandibular joint region swelling for approximately 11 months, with associated jaw pain, xerostomia, and oral fullness. No upper aerodigestive tract symptoms were reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Left TMJ lesion with preliminary pathologic diagnosis of calcified chondromesenchymal neoplasm.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsies were non-diagnostic. Subsequent biopsy demonstrated features less concerning for malignancy, with no atypia, no mitotic activity, and no necrosis. Preliminary diagnosis was calcified chondromesenchymal neoplasm.

[ imaging findings ]: CT and MRI demonstrated a soft tissue lesion surrounding the left TMJ capsule with skull base involvement extending into the floor of the middle cranial fossa. MRI showed enhancement within the joint space with encroachment on the middle cranial fossa and sparing of the dura. Axial imaging showed the lesion in close proximity to the horizontal petrous internal carotid artery. Imaging also demonstrated extension into the parotid region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Fusion profiling was referenced for this tumor type, but no specific molecular alteration was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially underwent multiple non-diagnostic biopsies.

[ current disease status ]: Left TMJ calcified chondromesenchymal neoplasm with extradural extension to the floor of the middle cranial fossa and into the parotid region, in close proximity to the horizontal petrous internal carotid artery.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion was described radiographically as extradural at the middle cranial fossa floor. The disease had progressed between imaging and the planned operation.

reference_discussion.text: So the case I'm presenting is more so a school-based case. and hopefully a lot of interesting discussion points to highlight here. So it's a 31-year-old male who presents with a left TMJ lesion. Diagnosis preliminary is a calcified chondromysclimal neoplasm. Essentially noticed swelling over the TMJ area for about 11 months. Initially had a few non-diagnostic biopsies, only had some associated jaw pain, xerostomia, and oral fullness, and otherwise no upper air digest tract symptoms. Imaging, which I'll show in a second, showed a lesion in the TMJ involving the middle cranial fossa floor. And there was initially concern for possible sarcoma prompting further biopsy, which clarified the diagnosis. So I'll show you the imaging here. So you can see this soft tissue lesion surrounding the TMJ capsule. And on the coronal, You can more clearly see its skull base involvement extending into the middle cranial fossa floor on this image. And on the patient's MRI, you can see the similar lesion enhancing the joint space there, encroaching on the middle cranial fossa, but sparing the dura. And then in the axial imaging, you can see that it gets very close to the petrous horizontal internal carotid arteries here. And so before moving on to the discussion part, I just want to highlight that the initial biopsy came back with some features less concerning for malignancy with no atypia, no mitotic activity or necrosis, and the preliminary diagnosis as discussed was a calcified chondromedial mesenchymal neoplasm. In terms of discussion, I had a few points to highlight here and then I can move on to the rest of the case if there's no further points, but essentially, are there any additional concerns about the preliminary pathologic diagnosis given the extent of the lesion? Would anyone consider any radiation in the role of management of this lesion? And then since we're talking about surgical approaches for treatment, would anyone have any recommendations for any approaches that would achieve an on block resection? And then additionally, given the location of lesion and function, Any considerations for reconstruction?

OK, Michael, let's let's break there and maybe get some input from our. from our faculty members. Maybe let's start with Dr. Vancouvering, if that's okay. Obviously not your run-of-the-mill skull-based tumor, just a very weird and wonderful.
We see like 20 of these a year. I don't know, what are you guys doing in Canada?

You guys are the highest volume center in the world for this, for sure. Yeah, definitely. So this is a benign sort of locally aggressive pathology, obviously with resectability issues on imaging. Let's say you are going to offer this patient surgery. How are you going to? How are you thinking of approaching this co?

Yeah, great point. And maybe can you pull up the axials down into the window there? And so for me, this would obviously be an open approach where I would do a preauricular and extend that into at least a hemicoronal, if not a full coronal. uh, incision, depending on some of your cosmetic preferences on how you'd like to make that incision and bring that down. Uh, it looks like it's going well into the parotid as well. And so you probably are going to need to dissect the facial nerve in order to help deliver this tumor and get the TMJ, uh, exposed through a pre-auricular route. Uh, so sort of defining that frontal branch and the upper division of the, of the facial nerve may be needed here. Um, so I would probably extend that into some degree of a modified Blair incision, to get the exposure. And then, uh, you know, in a combined fashion with neurosurgery, this is going to involve a sub-temporal craniotomy to try and get around this tumor on block from above and below. And you'll have to take a cut across the, the, uh, the condyle, uh, or, or through the ramus, perhaps even, I can't remember how far down the TMJ it goes there on the coronal. Once you have that mobilized, the deep dissection is really the hard part where the, where the, where the carotid comes into play. And so it's really a slow dissection, probably working over top of the tumor to get to the petrous segment at the floor of the middle fossa, trying to peel dura the whole way. That's a tough dissection, no doubt about it. But that would be the approach I would probably take.
Dr. Montero, can we get this out on block, you think, in one piece?

You're going to try, but I think you probably can, John. It's going to be a little bit challenging, but I think you can. I agree with Kyle that that's how I would approach it as well. This wasn't my case, but I think a hemi-coronal probably would be enough here. Sometimes you have to extend a little bit over just to get enough mobility of the skin flap. Neurosurgery could go from above to sort of clear the middle cranial fossa floor. It looks all extradural on the imaging. Yeah, I agree with Kyle. It looks like it's quite a lot into the parotid gland, so I would dissect out the facial nerve and particularly just mobilize the upper branch because it'll all be deep to those upper branches. I think some of the zygoma has to go anteriorly as well and then the carotid could probably be approached through the neurosurgical approach of the middle cranial fossa four because that will give you some exposure to the petrous carotid and then similar to what Kyle said you can also approach the cervical and parapharyngeal carotid through the neck just to kind of protect that. So I agree with what he said and I think you know, an on block resection is going to be doable. Positive margins might be risky for microscopic positive margins, depending on how close it is to the facial nerve on the deep side of the facial nerve. So I'm not sure what you encountered, John, when you did the case, but I suspect it'll be a little close there.

And maybe from our senior discussants or Karina, any other approaches other than what Dr. Vancouver suggested, preauricular to a hemichronal or full coronal? Are there any other approaches to get to this?
It would not go endoscopically.

I agree. I think the concerns are definitely the carotid and the facial nerve. And I think that approach is probably the best and the safest so you can identify those structures and try to preserve them. I would be concerned a little bit about pathology. It's not a common tumor that we see a lot and it wouldn't hurt to maybe send it out for another opinion just to make sure it's not another rare type of mesenchymal tumor because you'll, or it could be sent out, you know, after the tumor is out, that might actually be more helpful when they have a lot of tissue to look at.

Yeah, that's generally what happens, Marlene. I think John can speak to it because I think it was his case, but we, all the sort of starcoma type lesions basically get regionalized to one center that both John and I work at just because the pathologists have basically been regionalized for our entire province to the one center. So I can't remember whether the initial biopsy, John, was read at Sinai or whether it was the post-op, but that's exactly right. The pathologist will often just reflexively send it to the sarcoma center for the reasons that you spoke about. It's just that these can be really challenging. And sometimes, you know, even after the post-op and they have a lot of tissue, they always can't properly characterize these things 100% either, right? They'll sometimes hedge on what they think it is.
Yeah, these rare pathologies are tough, but your radiation oncologist is going to want to know. They're very reluctant to radiate anything that's benign.

Dr. Delmeda, I think this tumor has some fusion profile that I can't quite remember, growth factor something or other. Oh, yeah. OK, there we go at the bottom there. I have no idea, to be honest with you. Is that amenable to any targeted therapies?

Yeah, that was a good question. We actually had one of our sarcoma med-oncs enter into the discussion before we proceeded with surgery, which we did. This is amenable on clinical trial to what are called CSF inhibitors or colony stimulating factor inhibitors. There's some data on that in the clinical trial space. These tumors are actually probably seen a lot more by oral maxillofacial surgeons. And so it's probably not in the average sort of skull-based surgeons' wheelhouse. It's kind of rare, but they're not as rare, I think, for maxillofacial surgeons. And the data generally supports, you know, why local resection where possible, and where concerning margins, there is a role for radiation treatment to minimize the risk of local recurrence, particularly in areas where it's close to unresectable structures. So that's kind of where the general thinking is with this approach. Maybe we'll switch over to Eric Wong. Your thoughts, I know you have an interest in reconstructive surgery. Do we need to reconstruct this? What do you think? How would you approach this and what would be your considerations here?

I think I would in a 31 year old. He's obviously have significant shortening of his ramus, I mean, it's almost. Yeah, that's a beautiful cut. Thank you, Michael. I mean that you're going to have, you're going to shorten his ramus by three or four centimeters. So it seems like he will have long-term dysfunction of his jaw, of his mandible, excuse me, if there's not a reconstructive option. You know, it looks like it's going to be extradural, but, you know, that's going to be close as you go through it. It's going to need sort of almost a patrosal approach as they come down from above. And then obviously there's the, so then there's going to be that portion of the temporalis that you're going to sacrifice as it attaches all of the muscles of mastication to that space. You're going to have a pretty large dead space. So John, you are definitely a better reconstructive surgeon than I, but I would guess that you're going to try to do something to restore some of that height, even maybe with one of those TMJ prosthesis that oral surgery sometimes uses for very recalcitrant situations. I guess the question is whether you do it at the same time as your resection or if you go back and do it later. I'm guessing it'd probably be best because you're going to come from above and below and it's really quite an impressive approach you'd have to take for it. I was trying to contemplate if there was any way um, to not have to do a, uh, you know, a full, um, hemichrono to a Blair like incision, but it just feels like the product has to be dissected to get this clear. So, um, I don't know that there's another option at first. I was trying to contemplate if you could get, you know, if you just pop up, Eric mentioned, you're going to have to take probably the, um, zygomatic arch, if that would allow you to rotate enough out that you could make an inferior incision, like, through a cervical approach, and then deliver it without the prodded, but it sure seems like the prodded is directly involved with this. Is that accurate, John?

Yeah, yeah, yeah, it definitely was, and that's kind of how we approached it. Michael will kind of wrap up the case in a second, but I want to just address one other issue, and maybe with Dr. Wang, Marilyn, your thoughts. This is very close, as you can see, on the CT to the carotid. What are your approaches here? How do you prepare for, you know, for potential carotid injury? Are there any things you do in terms of investigations, either preoperatively or or considerations intraoperatively for carotid management.

Yeah, there's things to consider. He's a young person, so you do worry that he doesn't have a lot of collateral if you do injure the left carotid. But you certainly could do an angiogram, you could do a carotid balloon occlusion in advance just to see if it were necessary. I don't think it would be, but it certainly wouldn't hurt to do an angiogram and see what the circulation looks like.

And intraoperatively, let's say you get into it at the petrous carotid, which is where it's very close. What are the options here if we injure the carotid intraoperatively? We're very close to the horizontal petrous carotid, taking the tumor out.

Yeah, I think you have to be prepared for that to harvest some muscle, some kind of a graft to put there. Fortunately, with an open approach, you have a little bit more access. I think you can plug it, so to speak, a little easier than endoscopically. And then, of course, he would need an angiopost-op just to make sure there wasn't any embolus or a clot there.

I agree with Marilyn. I mean, you definitely need to get immediate control, probably through directed packing. And then subsequently, Angiography is going to be the answer because actually I think in most 31-year-olds, they tend to have pretty reasonable collateral. Certainly pediatric patients have really great collaterals. So they can sometimes tolerate quite well the sacrifice. John, did you consider like reflecting the temporalis down and then actually drilling the floor anteriorly to give you even more access with, like in this cut that we see here?
Yeah. Yeah. So, um, maybe Michael, why don't you pick, pick the, show the pictures of what we actually did.
We did follow the temporal fossa, right. And actually remove some of that to give you more access to the anterior portion of the Petrus.

That's right. Yeah, we did. I mean, we did essentially neurosurgery came in to do a, uh, teratonal crania. And as Kyle mentioned, uh, we, he needed a sub-temporal sort of craniotomy, uh, to get rid of the disease that was extradural. So Michael, why don't, why don't you show kind of how we managed it?

Sure, yeah, I'll highlight some of the points I've mentioned. So the hemichronal blare and then the neck dissection incision. This is the final resection. We have basically a total parotidectomy. We mobilize the facial nerve and we did a transparotid approach into the TMJ. The toronial approach, subcranial craniectomy as shown here. And then we did take essentially the posterior part of the mandible, just a vertical osteotomy through the sigmoid notch down. And some of the other points that I wanted to highlight was obviously occlusion is important in this case and MMF we performed with rapid arch bars, which you can see here. And one of the learning points we had was you can't mobilize the TMJ when the patient's in MMF. you have to take the patient out of MMF to do your cuts, remove the tumor, and then go back to MMF for your reconstruction. And I think Dr. Montero mentioned taking out part of the ligoma, so we did also take out a segment of the lateral ligoma for access from a neurosurgery perspective. And then we, in terms of managing the infernal carotid artery, followed it from the neck through the peripheral space up to the skull base for not only control during a resection, but as we mentioned, in case there's any concern about injuring it at the petrous intracranial portion. And in terms of reconstruction, we performed a chimeric scapula tip myogenous latissimus dorsi free flap. So you can see the scapula tip here sitting, reconstructing TMJ with the tip into the TMJ fossa, and then the latissimus dorsi was used to cover. We had a free bone graft to reconstruct the zygoma. We mentioned and discussed previously about these custom TMJ prostheses, which you can actually modify them so that they don't need to sit specifically in the glenoid fossa, but you can actually butt them against, for example, the zygoma, as well as the cranium itself. But the concern was, given that medial margin and potential need for radiation afterwards, we want to reduce the risk of any hardware complications associated in that region. So that's why we chose to go for a free flat reconstruction. And just to end the case, I can show you the post-op imaging here, which shows some of the structures that we've reconstructed. So you can see here that that's the zygoma free bone graft. As we go down, we can see the scapula tip on the posterior mandible there.
So John, it looks like you just brought the scapula a little bit forward so that it's sitting below floating below the middle cranial fossa floor that wasn't resected. Is that right?

Yeah, that's right. We buttressed it against some residual sphenoid bone. There is a thought around doing a custom TMJ prosthesis, but the concern there, obviously, in patients who, if they do get radiated, you know, that we'll see a hardware complication, almost like that first case that we saw. And there really is still a possibility of coming in secondarily down the road and putting in a secondary TMJ implant. The other thing in our center, custom TMJ prostheses take three months to develop or to get them manufactured. And this was progressing. In fact, it progressed from imaging to surgery. And so that's a consideration as well. But when you put the patient in MMF for a period of four to six weeks, you almost let them create a pseudoarthrosis there and they kind of scar into place and their occlusion actually prevents migration of the scapula into the middle fossa because their bite prevents that scapula from actually pushing intracranial. So that was kind of the thought around that. So maybe in the interest of time, we'll move to the last case. Nadine and Dr. Levine, please take it away. Yes.

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus favored primary surgical management with attempted en bloc resection via an open preauricular to hemicoronal/Blair-type transparotid approach combined with neurosurgical subtemporal craniotomy/craniectomy to clear the extradural middle cranial fossa component, with facial nerve mobilization and carotid control from the neck to the skull base. Reconstruction was planned with vascularized free flap restoration of mandibular/TMJ height and soft-tissue obliteration of the defect; a custom TMJ prosthesis was deferred because of disease progression and concern for hardware complications if postoperative radiation were required. Additional pathology review at a sarcoma center was considered appropriate given the rarity of the mesenchymal neoplasm, and adjuvant radiation was recognized as a consideration in the setting of concerning or close margins near unresectable structures to reduce local recurrence risk.

[...] it wouldn't hurt to maybe send it out for another opinion just to make sure it's not another rare type of mesenchymal tumor [...] The data generally supports, you know, why local resection where possible, and where concerning margins, there is a role for radiation treatment to minimize the risk of local recurrence, particularly in areas where it's close to unresectable structures. [...] We have basically a total parotidectomy. We mobilize the facial nerve and we did a transparotid approach into the TMJ. The toronial approach, subcranial craniectomy as shown here. [...] in terms of managing the infernal carotid artery, followed it from the neck through the peripheral space up to the skull base for not only control during a resection [...] in terms of reconstruction, we performed a chimeric scapula tip myogenous latissimus dorsi free flap. [...] the concern was, given that medial margin and potential need for radiation afterwards, we want to reduce the risk of any hardware complications associated in that region. So that's why we chose to go for a free flat reconstruction.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Young male patient. Thyroid cancer journey began at age 7 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/persistent papillary thyroid carcinoma of the neck with tracheostomy dependence following postoperative bilateral vocal cord paralysis; evaluation of locoregional disease and pulmonary nodules.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffusely infiltrative multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) of the thyroid with dominant 2.5 cm left-sided mass, bilateral cervical nodal metastases, extrathyroidal extension, vascular invasion, positive margins, and soft tissue/tracheal region involvement. Disease course included persistent/recurrent locoregional nodal and soft tissue metastases and pulmonary nodules highly suspicious for metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial thyroidectomy pathology from July 2018 showed multifocal thyroid carcinoma with extrathyroidal extension involving muscle and adipose tissue; tumor was in contact with anterior and posterior margins; extensive vascular invasion was present. Two parathyroid glands were identified in the specimen. A pretracheal wall biopsy showed infiltration by papillary thyroid carcinoma without lymphoid tissue. There was extensive nodal involvement with extranodal extension. Pathology review described diffusely infiltrative PTC with a dominant 2.5 cm mass in the left lobe, with classic, follicular variant, and solid/paraganglioma-like features; no tall-cell component was identified. Tumor necrosis was present in the primary tumor and in metastatic tumor. Multifocal microscopic extrathyroidal extension, muscle invasion, extensive vascular invasion, and positive margins were present. At least 29 of 65 lymph nodes were positive at initial surgery.  
Third resection in July 2020 (left paratracheal resection) showed soft tissue infiltration by papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
Fourth surgery in September 2020 removed 5 of 13 positive lymph nodes and showed carcinoma in soft tissue.  
Fifth surgery in July 2021 removed bilateral lateral compartment nodal disease; no metastatic nodes were identified on the right, and 2 positive nodes were removed on the left.  
Sixth surgery in March 2022 removed bilateral lateral neck lymph nodes; pathology showed 26 right lateral compartment lymph nodes negative for malignancy and 2 positive left lateral compartment lymph nodes without extranodal extension.  
Fine-needle aspiration of a left central compartment lesion showed cytology consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular variant; nuclei were low grade, with no high-grade component identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Post-therapy radioiodine scan after 150 mCi in November 2018 showed intense uptake in thyroid remnant tissue without mediastinal, lateral neck, or distant systemic uptake.  
Diagnostic whole-body scan in June 2019 showed uptake on both sides of the trachea consistent with central compartment nodal disease, with an additional focus interpreted as retrotracheal and right lateral compartment disease.  
Post-therapy scan after second 150 mCi treatment in September 2019 showed uptake in the left central compartment interpreted as thyroid remnant, without other definite sites of disease identified.  
PET-CT in March 2021 demonstrated subcentimeter lateral neck and paratracheal nodal disease. Pulmonary findings were present but were too small for metabolic characterization. No other systemic disease was identified.  
Stimulated PET-CT and I-123 scan in 2021 demonstrated iodine uptake in soft tissue in the left thyroid bed and activity corresponding to left anterior pretracheal/paratracheal adenopathy at the level of the sternal notch. Left lateral compartment nodes were identified. Subcentimeter pulmonary nodules again were not metabolically characterizable on PET/I-123 imaging.  
Chest CT from June 2022 showed multiple pulmonary nodules highly suspicious for pulmonary metastatic disease.  
Subsequent neck/chest CT demonstrated multifocal tumor deposits in the neck, including a lesion anterior to the airway, likely lateral cervical nodal metastasis, and an enhancing lesion in the paraglottic space concerning for aggressive local invasion. Imaging also showed uptake in the low central neck/upper mediastinum (high level VII region) and activity in the left thyroidectomy bed on PET. The tracheostomy tube had an oblique course and abutted the tracheal wall.  
Ultrasound examination identified multiple abnormal lymph nodes, including bilateral central compartment nodes and right lateral compartment level IV and V nodes. A pretracheal lesion was not visualized on that examination. Biopsies were performed; only the superior left central compartment lesion was positive, while a deeper left central lesion was reactive.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified a RET/PTC rearrangement. Pathology review noted solid/paraganglioma-like morphology associated with RET/PTC3 rearrangement.

[ laboratory results ]: Stimulated thyroglobulin in June 2019 was 42, with no thyroglobulin antibodies detected. Thyroglobulin subsequently remained largely unchanged despite multiple surgeries and two courses of radioiodine; by December 2021 it was reported to be trending in the range of 20-30.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- July 2018: Total thyroidectomy with central compartment lymph node dissection and bilateral lateral neck dissection.  
- November 2018: First therapeutic radioiodine treatment, 150 mCi. Post-therapy scan showed thyroid remnant uptake only.  
- Postoperative complications after initial surgery included bilateral vocal cord paralysis and hypoparathyroidism.  
- February 2019: Respiratory failure requiring intubation and tracheostomy.  
- September 2019: Second therapeutic radioiodine treatment, 150 mCi, following diagnostic evidence of persistent central/retrotracheal/right lateral compartment disease. Post-therapy scan showed only left central compartment/remnant uptake.  
- July 2020: Third cancer resection, left paratracheal resection; pathology showed soft tissue infiltration by PTC.  
- September 2020: Fourth surgical procedure; 5/13 lymph nodes positive and carcinoma present in soft tissue.  
- July 2021: Fifth surgical procedure; bilateral lateral compartment dissection with 2 positive nodes on the left and none on the right.  
- March 2022: Sixth surgical procedure; bilateral lateral lymph node removal. Central compartment was not explored because of extensive scar tissue. Pathology showed no right-sided nodal metastases and 2 positive left lateral nodes.  
- Between 2019 and 2020 there were several tracheostomy-related problems.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent/recurrent locoregional disease remained present in the central neck/thyroid bed with biopsy-proven left central compartment metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. Cross-sectional imaging showed multifocal cervical tumor deposits, including a lesion in the paraglottic space concerning for locally invasive disease. Multiple pulmonary nodules were present and were highly suspicious for metastatic disease. Since 2021, the patient had been clinically stable and remained active in sports including soccer and tennis.

[ other clinical data ]: Laryngeal examination showed very little vocal fold movement, consistent with bilateral vocal cord paralysis. Tracheostomy remained in place. Extensive postoperative scar tissue was encountered at the March 2022 surgery.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus was that no further neck surgery for nodal disease or additional radioactive iodine should be pursued at present, given refractory disease and cumulative prior treatment. Short-term selective RET-targeted systemic therapy was favored with the goal of achieving meaningful tumor shrinkage and disease stabilization, primarily to facilitate eventual airway intervention and possible decannulation. Airway-directed surgery should be considered only after response or stabilization over approximately 6–12 months, with posterior cricoid expansion graft regarded as the most practical option and reinnervation remaining a consideration if durable control is achieved and further neck reoperation is not anticipated. Overall management should be palliative and goal-directed, with emphasis on airway function rather than cure.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 21-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache for 2 years and left-sided weakness for 6 months at presentation in October 2023.

[ diagnosis ]: Right temporal/basal ganglia/insular pilocytic astrocytoma, low-grade, with residual tumor after subtotal resection and subsequent radiologic regrowth.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from October 2023 showed a low-grade tumor consistent with pilocytic astrocytoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Historical imaging from 2014 reportedly showed an enhancing lesion in the right temporal region; digital subtraction angiography was unremarkable for vascular anomaly.  
- CT brain in October 2023 showed a heterogeneous lesion in the right temporal region involving the insula, with compression of the third ventricle.  
- Radiologic review described a mass lesion in the right basal ganglia region extending into the temporal region with extensive vasogenic edema, central hyperdensity, and peripheral hypodensity.  
- MRI demonstrated a solitary lobulated lesion with marked mass effect, associated vasogenic edema, and right-sided descending transtentorial herniation with distortion of the midbrain and effacement of the basal cisterns.  
- The lesion had mixed components: a central T1-hyperintense component interpreted as probable hemorrhagic component, surrounding soft-tissue component, and peripheral cystic component with CSF signal intensity.  
- Post-contrast MRI showed significant enhancement of the soft-tissue component with multiple enhancing nodules along the inferior aspect of the lesion in the temporal region.  
- No additional intracranial lesions were identified.  
- First postoperative CT showed subtotal resection/biopsy changes with persistent mass effect.  
- Follow-up imaging in the second week of May showed residual tumor with regrowth; mass effect and descending transtentorial herniation were reduced relative to preoperative imaging but not completely resolved.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- In 2014, the patient had sudden-onset left-sided weakness that gradually improved with symptomatic treatment/steroids; she regained ability to walk.  
- Surgical treatment/biopsy was offered in 2014 but declined by family.  
- In October 2023, she underwent subtotal resection and biopsy of the lesion. Approximately two-thirds of the tumor was reported to have been removed.  
- No new postoperative neurological deficit was reported after surgery.  
- Radiation therapy was deferred after histopathologic diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma.  
- On follow-up after surgery, the patient was symptom-free and family declined further surgery at that time.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Residual right-sided tumor remained present on follow-up imaging with interval regrowth by May after subtotal resection.  
- At latest clinical status described, left-sided weakness had improved; the patient was mobile and otherwise symptom-free.  
- No headache or other new neurological change was reported.  
- No signs of raised intracranial pressure were reported.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On examination in October 2023, Glasgow Coma Scale was 15/15. Higher mental functions were intact.  
- Left-sided weakness was present with increased tone. Plantar responses were bilaterally extensor.  
- The patient was able to walk with support and had preserved mentation and sphincter control.  
- The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 78-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Breathlessness; pleural effusion detected on initial evaluation.

[ diagnosis ]: Pulmonary adenocarcinoma diagnosed on axillary lymph node biopsy, with TTF-1 positivity. Clinical disease involved bilateral axillary lymph nodes, pleura, mediastinal nodes, and pulmonary consolidative lesions.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Pleural biopsy/excision: inflammatory pathology.  
- Axillary lymph node biopsy: adenocarcinoma, TTF-1 positive, consistent with pulmonary adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan showed:  
- Bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy, right greater than left  
- Moderate right pleural effusion  
- Pleural nodule(s)  
- Mediastinal lymph nodes  
- Consolidatory pulmonary patches  
- Inflammatory retroperitoneal nodules

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- 50-gene panel performed.  
- EGFR exon 21 p.L858R mutation detected.  
- EML4-ALK fusion detected.  
- EGFR variant allele fraction reported at 5.2%.  
- EML4-ALK fusion reported with 28 reads.  
- RNA sequencing was included in the assay.  
- EML4-ALK transcript reported as V1, involving exon 13.  
- Separate EGFR PCR testing was also positive.  
- ALK IHC was attempted but could not be completed.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Cytotoxic chemotherapy had not been administered because of advanced age and poor performance status.  
- Alectinib 300 mg twice daily was started 2 days before referral.  
- No treatment response data were yet available.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Wheelchair bound since diagnosis.  
- Able to walk only with support to the washroom.  
- Breathlessness occurred with minimal movement.  
- Performance status documented as PS 3.  
- Glasgow Coma Scale: 15.  
- Karnofsky Performance Status: 50.  
- No response assessment after initiation of alectinib was available.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No major comorbidities apart from hypertension, which was controlled.  
- Ejection fraction: 50%.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging left neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid with a small papillary thyroid carcinoma component; metastatic disease to lungs and central neck lymph nodes. Mediastinal nodal metastatic disease was suspected on PET imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the left thyroid nodule showed malignant cells, favoring anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Subsequent total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection demonstrated a 3.5 cm anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with a small component of papillary thyroid carcinoma. There was gross extrathyroidal extension into the muscles, focally positive margins, extensive lymphovascular invasion, and metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma in 3 of 10 central neck lymph nodes; largest nodal metastasis measured 9 mm, without extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial outside ultrasound showed a large left thyroid nodule measuring 3.3 cm, described as solid, with no suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy. CT imaging demonstrated matted soft tissue in the thyroid bed and left neck, inseparable from the left common carotid artery and jugular vein, with mild flattening of the tracheal wall concerning for possible tracheal invasion. Chest imaging showed pulmonary nodules measuring approximately 10-12 mm. PET imaging showed intense FDG uptake in the left neck mass and lung nodules, and a right paratracheal nodal station suspicious for mediastinal metastatic lymphadenopathy. After 2 months of selpercatinib, pulmonary nodules had nearly resolved on imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: RET fusion identified on molecular testing. Rapid BRAF testing and next-generation sequencing were performed; no specific BRAF result was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection. She subsequently received selpercatinib. Imaging after 2 months showed near-complete resolution of pulmonary nodules.

[ current disease status ]: Ongoing radiographic response on selpercatinib.

[ other clinical data ]: At presentation, she denied dysphagia and voice change. No suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy was identified on initial ultrasound.
