So, Frank, if she didn't have distant metastasis, I assume we would probably go in for external beam radiation because there was gross extra thyroid extension. In the setting of distant metastasis, how do I do radiation and then sulprocatinib together? Where are you on that now, Frank?

Yeah, so what I would do in this case, assuming she has what she has with distant metastasis, well, first of all, if there wasn't anything there, yes, I do external radiation therapy and they probably would have observed that the patient, but in this case, there's distant mets there. Again, back to the whole immunotherapy story that, you know, Mark and I both kind of brought up, I actually would Start immunotherapy in addition to radiation therapy. The reason being is that you can get more bang for your buck. Immunotherapy or checkpoint inhibitors aren't radiation sensitizers, so you're not going to get an advantage of making the radiation stronger or even causing more toxicity in that case, but it will treat the systemic disease. I would not give selprocatinib in combination with radiation because of the concern for radiation sensitization there. So what would happen in this particular case, we would do PEMBRO with radiation. Once the radiation is finished, we would go ahead and reassess imaging, but probably start up selprocatinib and continue the immunotherapy.
Perfect. Amanda, you put her on SELPR-Cut. Show the response that she had.

Here's the starting of the treatment. We started this and the two-month treatment is the picture on the right. These two pulmonary nodules almost resolved, even this area here. This is two months into SELPR-Cutting.
Perfect. And then you've got one more longer term.

Yeah. And then this is 20 months of treatment with selprocatinib. This is the largest pulmonary nodule that we could see, which is, I think, four or five millimeters. And there's no disease on her neck. I didn't put a picture because it was long. No evidence of disease on her neck.
So Frank, in 30 seconds, selprocatinib clearly working here. This has changed the natural history of anaplastic.

Yes, yes. And like I said, this is a lady who has had a remarkable response. And I have seen this too. I have another gentleman very similar to this case. Very, very similar. So yeah, no, this is great. Again, we don't necessarily know how these are going to behave. Again, I'd probably consider, because immunotherapy is available to add that. In addition, way back when. But nonetheless, zeproketin up here is doing the trick. So we would continue the treatment just as you are doing until any side effects are the patients really can't tolerate treatments. Perhaps if they need a break, we could consider a break at some point in time as well. Fantastic.

reference_conclusion: For RET fusion-positive anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with extrathyroidal extension and distant metastatic disease, the agreed approach was to initiate upfront systemic therapy with a RET inhibitor and immunotherapy in a neoadjuvant fashion rather than proceed directly to surgery. If postoperative locoregional radiation is administered in the setting of metastatic disease, pembrolizumab should be given concurrently with radiation, while selpercatinib should be withheld during radiation because of concern for radiosensitization. After completion of radiation, imaging should be reassessed and selpercatinib initiated or resumed with continuation of immunotherapy; selpercatinib should be continued thereafter until intolerance or other need for treatment interruption.

And then consider surgery, followed by radiation and other adjuvant therapy. [...] if the patient, as is shown here, does have a RET fusion, we haven't done surgery, we would start the patient on a neoadjuvant approach with, just as Frank mentioned, a RET inhibitor plus immunotherapy, given the patient has extra thoroidal extension and the patient has distant metastasis. And so I think getting that patient on up of front systemic therapy as soon as possible is probably is what we're the way we would go with it. So what would happen in this particular case, we would do PEMBRO with radiation. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old female. Active smoker. Comorbid chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and congestive heart failure.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented with a large malignant pleural effusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Pulmonary adenocarcinoma / non-small cell lung cancer with malignant pleural effusion, subcentimeter pulmonary nodules, and mediastinal mass.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural fluid cytology was compatible with pulmonary adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Large pleural effusion. Subcentimeter pulmonary nodules. Mediastinal mass that had been considered a pericardial cyst.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling by liquid biopsy identified an ERBB2 alteration, specifically an exon 20 insertion, with variant allele frequency 0.7%. Additional alterations included TP53 alteration. Tumor mutational burden was reported on the assay. Microsatellite instability was not detected. Tumor fraction could not be determined.

[ laboratory results ]: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 76.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Pleural fluid was drained. The patient was considered not to be a candidate for chemotherapy. No first-line eligibility for trastuzumab deruxtecan was documented.

[ current disease status ]: At the time of referral, the patient had newly identified ERBB2-mutated pulmonary adenocarcinoma with malignant pleural effusion and thoracic disease burden including pulmonary nodules and mediastinal mass.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

Sure. So in this case, what we're seeing is a liquid test and liquid profiling, you know, rather than getting a sample of the tumor directly, what we're getting is the shed from the tumor of circulating tumor DNA, but that's not the only source of DNA in blood. We also have DNA from normal cells as well as white blood cells. So in order to be able to detect variants in DNA, or sorry, excuse me, blood, you have to be sequencing in a very sensitive manner. This may be because there was not very much tumor DNA in the blood. However, we were still able to find this ERBB2 mutation, and this mutation in particular is an exon 20 insertion. You may also be familiar with exon 20 insertions from the EGFR gene. Those are also seen in lung cancer, and so thinking about ERBB2 in lung cancer, instead of seeing amplifications as we did in the the previous urethelial case, we actually most commonly see these exon 20 insertions. And you can see, looking at the right, a fat nib is listed as being approved in the patient's tumor type because it's approved for EGFR. alterations in non-small cell lung cancer, and then therapies with clinical relevance in other tumor type. And so IRB2 mutations in non-small cell lung cancer are definitely of interest. One question that comes up, we have from the audience, Mary is, It's still unclear to me the significance of lower levels of allele frequency. If you have a 5% allele frequency, what is the other 95%?

So in a tissue sample, you know, you would have cancerous cells, but you'd also have the normal tissue cells. And so, you know, any cell that's that doesn't have that variant, you're not going to see it there. So if, you know, 5% of cells have the variant, you'll see an approximately, you know, 5% variant allele frequency. So, you know, some cells Some cells may have a variant, some cells may not. And so we get into the thought of clonality, you know, how similar are all the cells in the tumor? And again, in this case with liquid, it's even more complicated because tumor DNA is not the only DNA we have in the blood. So we're also getting, you know, normal DNA and then DNA from white blood cells. So it's a question that doesn't necessarily have a simple answer, but as Holly said, you know, when we see a result on a test like this, we are confident that it is a real result.
Thank you. Jason, you're a specialist in lung cancer. How would you approach this patient?

You know, I was looking there on the first slide and I saw that the plan was to consider starting Afetinib. And I've used Afetinib in these patients. And, you know, I'm sure that you all have used Afetinib. It can be pretty rough to tolerate. And the diarrhea was actually prohibited for my patient. And she ended up hospitalized not once, but twice with dehydration from the diarrhea. We dose reduced. And in a clinical trial, there was a phase two trial several years ago with the Afetinib. So I continued my patient on just 20 milligrams and she tolerated that okay. I brought her in. probably about once every other week for IV fluids and just to make sure that she was doing okay with diarrhea. But the side effects from neophatinib could be an issue. And so we see trastuzumab duruxtacan listed here as an option in other tumor types. And we know that it's been recently approved in some other tumor types, but it's actually probably a little bit more well tolerated. I know it's got some side effects. We think about things like interstitial lung disease with the trastuzumab duruxtacan. But I think that probably as far as the diarrhea and the aphademia goes, it can actually be an issue. So if I could get the durex to can, I may actually look to start with that and then come back to the TKI if the patient progressed or did not tolerate the trastuzumab durex to can. That would be the way I approached it.
Harry, do you know if that was tried and wasn't successful or no clinical trials available?
Well, I don't think for first line that would be eligible for my tactic. But I think the plan was to obtain the fat in them on this patient initially, she was considered a candidate for chemo either.

reference_conclusion: Comprehensive genomic profiling identified an ERBB2 exon 20 insertion in non-small cell lung cancer. The agreed next step was to initiate afatinib, with recognition that dose reduction may be required because of tolerability concerns, particularly diarrhea. Trastuzumab deruxtecan was discussed as a potential alternative if accessible, with consideration for use if afatinib is not tolerated or if the disease progresses.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 79-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Right renal pelvis upper tract urothelial carcinoma, high-grade, initially identified as a 2.5 cm papillary tumor on ureteroscopic evaluation.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy from the right renal pelvis lesion showed high-grade urothelial carcinoma. Urinary washings showed rare atypical cells.

[ imaging findings ]: CT urogram demonstrated findings prompting ureteroscopic evaluation of the right upper tract. Ureteroscopy identified a 2.5 cm papillary tumor in the right renal pelvis. At initial endoscopic management, most of the tumor was laser ablated, with residual tumor remaining.

[ laboratory results ]: Baseline renal function was reported as good, with GFR 80 mL/min/1.73 m². Mild anemia was present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past history included prostate cancer treated with proton therapy. For the current upper tract lesion, ureteroscopic evaluation and opportunistic laser ablation of most of the visible tumor were performed, with residual tumor left in situ. The patient subsequently underwent robotic nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision, lymph node dissection, and intraoperative intravesical gemcitabine.

[ current disease status ]: Status post robotic nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision and lymph node dissection for right renal pelvis high-grade urothelial carcinoma.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities were present, including diabetes mellitus. Performance status was described as good. Kidney function before surgery was described as preserved despite comorbidities.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable right neck lump present for approximately 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma with tall cell morphology, metastatic cervical nodal disease, gross unresected right level IV nodal disease, and pulmonary metastases. Disease was considered radioactive iodine refractory based on post-thyroidectomy iodine imaging showing uptake limited to the thyroid bed and no meaningful uptake in the residual neck mass or lung nodules.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the right level IV lymph node was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Resected cervical lymph node showed metastatic papillary carcinoma with extranodal extension and tall cell features; tumor cells were described as 2–3 times taller than wide with papillary architecture and characteristic nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. Thyroidectomy pathology showed multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma; largest right-sided focus measured 1.6 cm. Morphology was focal classic and tall cell. No angiolymphatic invasion was identified. There was extrathyroidal extension into soft tissue. Central neck dissection showed one microscopic metastatic central neck lymph node.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound showed an irregular lobulated right thyroid nodule with coarse and punctate calcifications, suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Abnormal right lateral neck lymph nodes were present with loss of normal nodal architecture and coarse calcifications, including right level IV and higher-level nodal disease. Office laryngoscopy demonstrated right vocal cord paresis; left vocal cord was mobile. Contrast-enhanced CT neck showed right level IV nodal disease with cystic change and calcifications, and additional right level III nodal disease. CT chest showed multiple well-defined pulmonary nodules, including nodules in the medial left fissure region and medial right lower lobe, suspicious for pulmonary metastases. FDG PET showed FDG-avid necrotic calcified right level IV mass measuring approximately 2.5 cm, FDG avidity in the right thyroid nodule, and multiple subcentimeter FDG-avid lung nodules. Postoperative iodine scan showed minimal uptake in the thyroid bed only; the residual right level IV mass and subcentimeter lung nodules were not iodine avid.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor testing identified an atypical BRAF V600E-type alteration involving deletion/insertion around codons 600–605, interpreted as behaving like BRAF V600E. A NOTCH2 variant of uncertain significance was also reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroglobulin was 17. Thyroglobulin antibodies were elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial surgical exploration was planned for total thyroidectomy with central and right lateral neck dissection. Right neck dissection levels II and III were completed. The level III lymph node was adherent to but not invading the internal jugular vein. A 2.5 cm right level IV mass extended toward the clavicle/subclavian vein region and was inseparable from the internal jugular vein; the phrenic nerve coursed into the mass. The mass was not resected, and the procedure was aborted at that stage because safe mobilization was not possible without major morbidity. Biopsies were obtained. Subsequently, total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection were performed; the residual right level IV mass was not resected. Radioactive iodine was not administered after postoperative iodine imaging demonstrated no clinically meaningful uptake outside the thyroid bed. External beam radiotherapy was delivered to the residual gross right level IV disease.

[ current disease status ]: No systemic therapy had been initiated.

[ other clinical data ]: The neck mass was nonpainful. There was no dysphagia, dyspnea, or voice change reported at presentation. Physical examination showed a normal thyroid gland and a palpable fixed right level IV lymph node measuring approximately 3 cm. Past medical history included well-controlled hypertension and prediabetes. The patient was described as thin built and not obese.

Yeah, great question. I think we would get CT neck and chest imaging with contrast. Oftentimes you see some little tiny lung nodules and you don't know what to do with it, but it at least gives you a baseline to follow. Yeah, we do the same thing on these aggressive ones.
All right, Jared, go ahead. All right, so we decided to get an FNA of this right level four lymph node, and it was consistent very clearly with papillary.
What am I looking at there, Rachel?

So on the left-hand side, we've got a conventional smear sample, which is fixed and stained with Papaniklaostain, which is my favourite. And you can see tissue fragments with fibrovascular cores in keeping with papillary carcinoma and complex folded sheets. We don't have a very high power view, but I imagine that the nuclear features are pretty good based on our low power view. and then the right-hand side is the cell block, so you have a tissue fragment, and it's forming some follicles. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Hypercalcemia and hyperparathyroidism, initially diagnosed in 2021. Associated symptoms at presentation in mid-2024 included fatigue, cognitive difficulty (“brain fog”), muscle weakness, constipation, reflux, new lower-extremity bone pain, and a 3-month history of dysphonia and dysphagia following prior stroke.

[ diagnosis ]: Primary hyperparathyroidism with multigland disease. Osteopenia diagnosed in 2013, later osteoporosis. History of calcium nephrolithiasis, with last stone passed in 2023.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Left superior parathyroid excision: parathyroid adenoma, 750 mg, with oncocytic features.  
- Right superior parathyroid excision: enlarged hypercellular parathyroid gland; frozen section described no definite normal gland to diagnose adenoma.  

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Parathyroid/thyroid ultrasound in 2022: subcentimeter left-sided nodules and one isthmus nodule reported as TR5 on one report and later TR4; no parathyroid lesion visualized.  
- Repeat ultrasound in 2023: multiple subcentimeter nodules; no visualized parathyroid lesion.  
- Repeat parathyroid ultrasound in 2024: scattered subcentimeter thyroid nodules, including TR3 and TR4 nodules; no corroborating parathyroid adenoma identified. A 6 mm lesion posterior-inferior to the right thyroid lobe was described as more suggestive of a lymph node than parathyroid adenoma.  
- Nuclear medicine sestamibi with fused SPECT in 2024: findings suggestive of an adenoma in the mid left thyroid region.  
- Flexible laryngoscopy at clinic presentation: findings suggestive of laryngopharyngeal reflux.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Confirmatory preoperative laboratory testing demonstrated elevated calcium and elevated parathyroid hormone.  
- Renal function was normal.  
- Magnesium was normal.  
- Phosphorus was normal.  
- Vitamin D was normal.  
- Creatinine clearance was normal.  
- C-telopeptide was normal.  
- Intraoperative baseline PTH: 133.1.  
- Post-excision intraoperative PTH after left superior parathyroidectomy: 58 at first measurement, 54.8 at second measurement.  
- After right superior parathyroidectomy: PTH 15 at 10 minutes, 12.9 at 15 minutes, 12 at 20 minutes.  
- One hour postoperatively: PTH 7.5; calcium 2.4.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient had undergone serial imaging evaluation from 2022 to 2024 without definitive localization on ultrasound.  
- She underwent parathyroid surgery in 2024. Initial exploration of the left side identified and excised a grossly enlarged left superior parathyroid gland. Due to inadequate continued decline in intraoperative PTH, the neck was re-explored on the right side, where a grossly enlarged right superior parathyroid gland was excised; the right inferior parathyroid gland appeared normal.

[ current disease status ]: Status post excision of left superior parathyroid adenoma and enlarged right superior hypercellular parathyroid gland in 2024.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included essential hypertension, spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage, ischemic stroke in 2023, osteoporosis, and nephrolithiasis. The patient had been taking calcium carbonate (Tums) 3-4 times daily for reflux symptoms at presentation. No history of excess vitamin D intake, loop diuretic use, lithium use, or thiazide use was reported. Most recent DEXA scan was performed in 2024; T-scores were not provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old man; otherwise healthy; never smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent left retromolar trigone/oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma in a previously irradiated field.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Initial diagnosis: T2N0 p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the left palate.  
- First recurrence (approximately 4 years prior): recurrent squamous cell carcinoma involving the left retromolar trigone, considered contiguous with the prior primary site; pathology staged as pT4a with bone invasion and one positive lymph node; margins were negative.  
- Subsequent recurrence (fall of the prior year): recurrent tumor at the left retromolar trigone/adjacent posterior mandibular region in the previously operated and irradiated field.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- After prior left marginal mandibulectomy and neck dissection: tumor invaded bone; margins were negative; one lymph node was positive; stage reported as T4a.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Review of earlier imaging before the prior salvage operation showed scalloping of the mandible without widening of the inferior alveolar canal; lesion was centered at the retromolar trigone/posterior mandible.  
- Preoperative imaging before the later salvage surgery demonstrated recurrent tumor beginning just posterior to the prior resection site in the left retromolar trigone/posterior mandibular region.  
- PET scan showed isolated disease at the lateral cortex.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT showed no frank bony destruction.  
- Clinical assessment documented no mental nerve numbness.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Primary radiation therapy for T2N0 p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the left palate; completed 5 years prior.  
- Approximately 4 years prior, underwent left marginal mandibulectomy, neck dissection, and radial forearm free flap reconstruction of the retromolar trigone defect with a small buccal component for recurrent disease; pathology showed bone invasion, one positive lymph node, and negative margins.  
- At the end of the prior year, underwent left segmental mandibulectomy for further recurrence in the previously treated field; the resection included all previously marginally resected mandibular bone.

[ current disease status ]: Status post left segmental mandibulectomy for recurrent left retromolar trigone/posterior mandibular squamous cell carcinoma.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Prior mandibular resection involved the retromolar trigone and posterior mandible/angle region, with preservation of mandibular height sufficient for the initial marginal resection.  
- The recurrent lesion was located adjacent to the molar/attached gingival region in a previously irradiated and previously operated mandible.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female child. Exact age was not documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Sacrococcygeal/pelvic mass with metastatic disease at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Sacrococcygeal germ cell tumor/teratoma with recurrence and metastatic disease (pulmonary nodules, inguinal lymph node involvement, and vertebral metastatic involvement/collapse). Disease was described as stage IV.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Resected primary specimen had previously been reported as mature teratoma with benign ectodermal, mesodermal, and endodermal components; no immature or malignant component was identified on review. Approximately 9-10 sections had been examined from a mass measuring about 5 cm.  
- Post-chemotherapy resection specimen after excision of the mass with coccygectomy showed no residual viable tumor. Histology showed histiocytes only, with no tumor cells identified.  
- The post-chemotherapy specimen was AFP-negative on pathology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Repeat metastatic workup after chemotherapy showed reduction in size of the primary mass compared with prior PET-CT, with decreased metabolic activity.  
- Pulmonary nodules decreased in both size and number after chemotherapy.  
- Follow-up PET-CT showed absence of FDG uptake in the lung nodules and inguinal lymph nodes.  
- D11 vertebral collapse persisted on imaging; no FDG uptake was seen in the collapsed vertebra.  
- No FDG uptake was reported in lung nodules and also no uptake in D5 vertebra.  
- Before chemotherapy, there had been multiple pulmonary nodules, reportedly about 50, with the largest measuring 1.8 × 1.2 cm. Chest imaging showed numerous bilateral rounded pulmonary metastases/cannonball lesions, particularly in the upper lobes.  
- After chemotherapy, residual pulmonary nodules persisted, approximately 4-5 nodules on CT, including at least two nodules near the hila.  
- A metabolically active soft-tissue lesion in the mid-pelvic region measured 3.6 × 3.4 × 3.3 cm on PET-CT, consistent with local recurrence.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum AFP at presentation was reported as approximately 96,000 ng/mL.  
- A preoperative AFP value of 94 ng/mL was documented at the time of initial pathology review.  
- Postoperative AFP after the initial surgery was reported as 36 ng/mL at day 7.  
- AFP normalized at 3 months after surgery, then rose again at 6 months to >10,000 ng/mL, with one value described as approximately 36,000 ng/mL during relapse evaluation.  
- After post-chemotherapy surgery, serum AFP on postoperative day 3 was 6.5 ng/mL.  
- At 1 month after completion of chemotherapy, AFP was 1.5 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surgery had been performed for sacrococcygeal teratoma via sacral approach.  
- Local recurrence developed after the initial surgery, with rising AFP and a metabolically active mid-pelvic lesion on PET-CT.  
- Chemotherapy was administered for recurrent/metastatic disease. The patient completed 4 cycles initially, with good response documented radiologically and metabolically.  
- Following response to chemotherapy, the patient underwent excision of the residual mass with coccygectomy; inguinal lymph node excision was also performed.  
- Postoperative recovery was uneventful.  
- Chemotherapy was completed to a total of 6 cycles.  
- Treatment response included marked decline in AFP, reduction in size and number of lung nodules, decreased size/metabolic activity of the primary mass, and no residual viable tumor in the resected specimen.

[ current disease status ]:  
- At the time documented, the patient was on follow-up 1 month after completion of 6 cycles of chemotherapy.  
- AFP had fallen to 1.5 ng/mL.  
- Resected post-chemotherapy specimen showed no residual tumor.  
- Residual pulmonary nodules persisted radiologically but were metabolically inactive on PET-CT.  
- D11 vertebral collapse persisted without FDG uptake.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The immediate postoperative period after excision with coccygectomy was uneventful.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 81-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: De novo metastatic prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic prostate cancer; Grade Group 3 disease.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET was performed before and after enzalutamide treatment. Post-treatment imaging showed increased PSMA uptake in most lesions, with approximately 50% increase in SUVmax in multiple sites. A lesion in the proximal right femur increased in SUVmax from 30 to 45. A lesion in the lower dorsal spine increased in SUVmax from 40 to 60. The number of PSMA-avid lesions also appeared to have increased on the post-treatment scan.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA declined from 390 to 210 during enzalutamide treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient was enrolled in a clinical trial and received enzalutamide. PSA decreased from 390 to 210. PSMA PET after enzalutamide demonstrated increased uptake intensity in existing lesions and an apparent increase in lesion number.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease remained present on post-enzalutamide PSMA PET, with increased tracer uptake and apparent increase in lesion burden.

[ other clinical data ]: None documented.

Yeah, the PPP criteria. So this essentially defines sort of one or two new lesions. So you're not, you know, a change of intensity of uptake alone does not define progression. Even if your SUV's gone from 30 to 60, that's not progression. You've got to have new sites of disease. That's the key here. And I think that is an important differentiator. If you do the same PET scan on a patient every day for seven days, the SUV does have some natural variability. And that has been looked at. Here's a study of Gallium PSMA-11, where they took the same patients, intra-patient variability, 14 days apart, repeated the PET, and there was a variability in SUV, which was quite consistent with FDG. And there's also a study of DCFPYL showing exactly the same. The same with FDG. So you do need to have a big difference for it to be significant. Throw in a drug like enzalutamide that's not actually causing progression, but just up-regulation of a receptor expression, then you may get a doubling of SUV and it's not progression at all, it could be response. So we really do need to be seeing new sites of disease. I think throwing in CT is very useful if it's a lymph node. Is it getting bigger? If it's not getting bigger, it's not progression. Bone is more difficult because you can't really measure it. Whole body MR, which is not really done in Australia, is useful for measuring these bone lesions. It may be useful.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Shortness of breath.

[ diagnosis ]: Left lung adenocarcinoma, stage IV (T4 N2 M1a).

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the lingular lung mass showed adenocarcinoma with lepidic growth pattern.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT showed a 4.2 × 3.5 × 4.5 cm lesion involving the apicoposterior and superior lingular segment of the left lung. Multiple discrete parenchymal nodules of varying size and FDG uptake were present in both lungs. Mediastinal nodal disease was present in the right lower paratracheal, subaortic, subcarinal, and right hilar regions. No metastatic lesions were identified outside the thorax. Bilateral lung nodules were reported to measure approximately 9–10 mm. The largest mediastinal lymph node measured 1.2 cm. No brain metastases were present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing showed EGFR exon 19 deletion positivity and TP53 mutation. PD-L1 expression was 0% (negative).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior systemic anticancer treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated metastatic thoracic disease involving the primary left lung lesion, bilateral pulmonary nodules, and mediastinal/hilar nodal metastases, without documented extrathoracic or intracranial metastases.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination, decreased breath sounds were present over the left thoracic region.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal wall mass with peritoneal deposits identified approximately 3 years after cholecystectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Cholangiocarcinoma with abdominal wall involvement and peritoneal metastatic disease; initially deemed inoperable.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the abdominal wall mass was consistent with cholangiocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- At presentation after prior cholecystectomy, imaging/documentation described an abdominal wall mass with peritoneal deposits; disease was considered not operable.  
- After 6 cycles of gemcitabine plus oxaliplatin, there was reduction in size of the mass.  
- Subsequent imaging performed in the setting of rising CA 19-9 showed disease progression.  
- After 2 cycles of gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, PET scan showed progressive disease.  
- On later repeat imaging, no peritoneal disease was seen; predominant disease remained a large abdominal wall mass measuring approximately 9 cm. A previously described peritoneal deposit was small.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Initial liquid biopsy showed TP53 mutation and PIK3CA mutation.  
- Subsequent tissue-based NGS after progression on gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel showed:  
  - Tumor mutational burden (TMB): 15.8 mutations/Mb  
  - TP53 mutation, variant allele frequency 52%  
  - PIK3CA mutation, variant allele frequency 42%  
  - SMAD4 point mutation, variant allele frequency 38%  
  - CCNE1 copy number gain  
  - RICTOR copy number gain  
- No IDH mutation was identified.  
- No FGFR alteration was identified.

[ laboratory results ]: CA 19-9 showed an increasing trend prior to imaging-confirmed progression.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Cholecystectomy was performed in 2021.  
- Gemcitabine plus oxaliplatin was administered for 6 cycles from October 2024 to January 2025, with reduction in size of the mass.  
- Capecitabine was given subsequently for approximately 1 month.  
- Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel was then administered for 2 cycles; PET scan thereafter showed progressive disease.  
- Radiotherapy to the abdominal wall mass was completed.  
- Tissue was initially unavailable for NGS at an earlier time point, prompting liquid biopsy; repeat tissue biopsy for NGS was later obtained after progression on gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive cholangiocarcinoma after two prior systemic treatment lines, with predominant residual disease in the abdominal wall. Most recent described disease burden was a large abdominal wall mass of approximately 9 cm; no peritoneal disease was seen on the latest reported imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Performance status was documented as 2.  
- Persistent neuropathy was present following prior oxaliplatin exposure.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 4-year-old male child. Neurodevelopmental history included autism spectrum disorder.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected abdominal mass noted by the mother approximately 1 month prior to presentation, with rapid increase in size and progressive abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) arising in a horseshoe kidney, centered in the isthmic/interpolar region. The case had been managed as stage V/bilateral Wilms tumor for treatment planning purposes. No distant metastases were identified on available imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided core-cut biopsy was performed. Histopathology was suggestive of triphasic nephroblastoma. WT1 was positive. IRC status was reported positive.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound abdomen/pelvis showed a horseshoe kidney with fusion at the lower poles and a large solid-cystic lesion measuring 11.6 × 6.6 cm arising from the isthmus, with mild internal vascularity; nephroblastoma was queried.  
- Initial outside CECT had described a crossed fused right ectopic kidney in the midline at L3-L5 level with upper pole fusion to the lower pole of the left kidney, and a multiseptated solid-cystic lesion measuring 7.7 × 7.8 × 9.1 cm arising from the interpolar region of the ectopic kidney and extending to the left renal pelvis.  
- Review of CT imaging favored a horseshoe kidney with lower pole fusion rather than crossed fused ectopia. The mass appeared to arise from the isthmus and right renal hilar/interpolar region, extending into the left renal hilum.  
- Initial CT showed complete encasement of the renal arterial structures, described as involving both left and right renal arteries.  
- Bilateral lungs were clear on CT, with no evidence of pulmonary metastasis.  
- Associated skeletal anomalies on CT included multiple rib and spinal deformities, hemivertebrae, partial fusion of D4-D5 vertebrae, and levoscoliosis.  
- Post 6 weeks of vincristine/dactinomycin, repeat CECT abdomen/pelvis with CT angiography showed reduction in tumor size. The lesion remained centered in the interpolar region of the horseshoe kidney and extended into the left renal hilum. A left accessory renal artery arising from the distal aorta was identified; the right renal artery, left renal artery, and accessory left renal artery were all described as encased. The IVC was compressed without infiltration. No significant lymphadenopathy was seen. No renal vein thrombus or IVC thrombus was identified. Ureters and suprarenals were normal.  
- After 2 cycles of etoposide/carboplatin, repeat CECT abdomen/pelvis showed significant further reduction in tumor size. The tumor remained centered in the interpolar region of the right renal moiety, extending into the left pararenal space and left renal hilum. A single accessory renal artery supplying the upper pole of the left kidney was free from encasement. The right renal artery coursed along the periphery of the mass but was encased near the hilum. The right renal vein was encased. The left main renal artery was encased. A tributary from the left renal vein to the upper pole was free.  
- Delayed phase assessment reportedly showed no ureteric encasement; tumor infiltration into the left renal pelvicalyceal system was described without extension into the ureter.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Clinical exome sequencing showed heterozygous carrier status for Fanconi anemia.

[ laboratory results ]: Hematological and biochemical parameters were reported within normal limits at presentation. Urinary VMA was normal/negative. Estimated GFR after chemotherapy had not yet been obtained at the time of documentation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided core-cut biopsy was attempted via retroperitoneal approach but required a partially transperitoneal route to obtain tissue.  
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered per SIOP Umbrella-based institutional protocol.  
- First-line preoperative chemotherapy consisted of 6 weeks of vincristine and dactinomycin.  
- Clinical response after 6 weeks: abdominal mass was no longer well palpable on examination.  
- Radiologic response after 6 weeks: reduction in tumor size on CECT/CT angiography.  
- Because nephron-sparing surgery was not considered feasible at that stage, treatment was escalated to 2 cycles of etoposide and carboplatin, given 3 weeks apart.  
- Radiologic response after etoposide/carboplatin: significant further reduction in tumor size.

[ current disease status ]: Residual Wilms tumor persisted in the horseshoe kidney after 8 total chemotherapy cycles, centered in the interpolar/isthmic region with extension into the left renal hilum/pararenal space. Persistent vascular involvement remained, including encasement of the right renal artery near the hilum, right renal vein, and left main renal artery; one accessory artery to the left upper pole remained free. No pulmonary metastases, renal vein thrombus, IVC thrombus, or significant lymphadenopathy were identified on the latest reported imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past surgical history included surgery in infancy for right knee flexion deformity; records were unavailable.  
- Family history was non-significant.  
- Antenatal history was reportedly unremarkable.  
- Examination at presentation showed abdominal distension with inferior displacement of the umbilicus and a firm-to-hard, lobulated, non-tender abdominal mass approximately 6 × 5 cm, extending from the right lumbar region across the umbilical/epigastric/suprapubic region to the left lumbar region; margins were well defined. The mass was bimanually palpable on the left.  
- External genitalia and testes were normal.  
- Spine examination showed dorsolumbar scoliosis/abnormal curvature with suspected vertebral defect at the lumbosacral junction; no cutaneous stigmata of spinal dysraphism were described.

reference_conclusion: Further local control should proceed after obtaining high-quality 3D image reconstruction and CT angiographic delineation of the renal vasculature and collecting systems to guide operative planning. The family should be counseled that surgery may result in an anephric state, with likely need for postoperative hemodialysis and later consideration of renal transplantation if feasible. Tumor bed radiotherapy is indicated because of the transperitoneal biopsy, with renal dose to the remaining moiety limited as far as possible.

[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Surveillance-detected new filling defect in the right renal pelvis 11 years after prior surgery for right-sided upper tract urothelial carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent right upper tract urothelial carcinoma involving the ipsilateral renal pelvis; low-grade, non-invasive disease on ureteroscopic biopsy. Prior history of right distal ureteral urothelial carcinoma, stage Ta low grade, treated in 2012.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2012 right distal ureterectomy specimen: Ta low-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma; all surgical margins negative.  
- Subsequent ureteroscopic biopsy of right renal pelvis lesion: low-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Surveillance cross-sectional imaging with delayed phase demonstrated a new filling defect in the right/ipsilateral renal pelvis.  
- Ureteroscopic evaluation demonstrated a sizable tumor within the right renal pelvis, including a lower pole component that was initially difficult to access.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Estimated glomerular filtration rate: 85 mL/min/1.73 m².  
- Most recent serum creatinine: 0.97 mg/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2012: Right distal ureterectomy with ureteral reimplantation for moderate-sized Ta low-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma; margins negative.  
- For recurrent right renal pelvis tumor: endoscopic treatment with thulium laser.  
- Post-treatment surveillance was performed at 3-month intervals.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No remarkable past medical history was reported.  
- Performance status was described as fairly good.
slides: <image> Case 1: A 66-year-old man with prior right distal ureterectomy/reimplant for low-grade UTUC presents on surveillance imaging in 11/2023 with a new right renal pelvis filling defect.

reference_discussion.text: Absolutely. And so am I. I think what I've done for today is I've assembled four, what I would consider to be real world cases, real cases that have come across our practice here. I think summarize many of the nuances and challenges that we may face in upper track urothelial cancer. And I think this would be a great opportunity to gain some insights from experts in the field, both Dr. Hoffman-Sentzitz and Dr. Schmidt, to hear how you would manage these complicated scenarios and to hear some more of the contemporary evidence. So without further ado, let's get started with our first case. This is the case of a 66-year-old male, no remarkable history, who in 2012 had undergone a right distal ureterectomy and re-implant for ultimately a moderate-sized tumor that was TA low-grade upper tracheoethelial cancer. All margins were negative. 11 years later, during surveillance, he was found to have a new filling defect in the right or ipsilateral renal pelvis, as you can see here on the cross-section in a delayed view. He underwent a ureteroscopic evaluation that revealed a sizable tumor within the renal pelvis and a biopsy that was acquired that revealed low-grade UTUC. He has fairly decent performance status and his GFR is 85, most recent creatinine 0.97. So Dr. Schmidt, I'm going to pitch this one to you. With this information, how would you counsel this gentleman on his options?

Yeah, so I think in general, this patient is in a relatively favorable position. So he still has good kidneys on both sides. He's overall healthy. It took him 11 years to recur. So you think this probably is not a tumor with a lot of aggressive features, no high-grade found. So I think this person has options. Certainly, more aggressive treatment would involve nephro-U. I probably would lean away from starting with that. But you have a local treatment option, so laser ablation, whether that would be retrograde laser or PERC ablation. You can consider some focal treatments like gelmito or reverse thermogel mitomycin. It could be an option here. I would probably not use BCG in this setting. I think this is a conversation with the patient saying, like, there's a couple different ways you can approach this. I probably would not start by removing the kidney. And then very, very careful surveillance with any endoscopic approach, making sure that we continue to monitor. So if it were me, I'd probably start with a laser ablation. Just looking at the location of it, I'd probably start retrograde. but certainly you could perk into it. Looks like it's about a centimeter maybe, a centimeter and a half, so I think retrograde's reasonable. Anything over two centimeters in the pelvis, I think maybe a perk would be better. And with respect to laser, I mostly have access to the homeum. I've tried the thulium before. I like it a little bit more. I think the coag on it's a little bit nicer. I think the tumor ablation features are a little bit better. But in my practice, I have to borrow that from my benign colleagues, and sometimes I can, and sometimes they're using it. So, homeo works just fine. I use low settings, 0.2 and 50, and kind of go to town.

Yeah, that's really excellent. Excellent overview, very comprehensive discussion of the different options. It sounds like with the low-grade diagnosis, you'd be very comfortable with a nephron-sparing approach rather than jumping straight to a radical nephro-uredectomy. You know, I actually share the same sentiment when it comes to the choice of laser. We also have the luxury of having access to thulium. And I personally have found as well that the coagulative properties of the holmium laser, particularly for fulguration of upper tract tumors, seems to be a bit more hemostatic in nature compared to the holmium. So I feel like I tend to buy more more time with the full duration approach, especially for larger tumors. And, you know, if this patient were to have an incomplete treatment session, or if this patient had recurred, again, with, let's say, low grade disease in the same spot, Dr. Schmidt, would you consider like repeating the same type of an approach? Would that push you more to consider something like gel mito?

I would consider it in the adjuvant setting. Yeah, I think I would go back in, I'd try to get rid of as much tumor as possible, and I would consider the gelmito. I would do it antigrade, so you'd have to, patient would need a nephrostomy tube. I think I worry about the stricture rate using it in a retrograde fashion. As long as the patient lived nearby where he could get a nephrostomy tube, come in for six weeks at a time where we could take care of him that way, then I would definitely consider antigrade gelmido. If you look at their data, the patients that respond, the durability of response is quite good. I think you're looking at 80% at a year of the responders. That's quite favorable. But again, with any endoscopic approach, I'm very vigilant about going back in every three months. which is a real challenge with the anesthesia risk to these patients. You have to consider it. But I worry a lot about these tumors growing back and just sitting on them.

Absolutely. And I share the same sentiments. We, when it comes to gel mito, also tend to utilize an anti-grade approach. But the ureal stenosis, it is a real phenomenon, both anecdotally and as we can see from the literature. In terms of durability, actually, just hot off the press in this month's Journal of Urology, You may have come across the long-term follow-up from the Olympus trial that was just published, which seemed to show, just like you said, fairly durable outcomes with the use of gel mitos. So it's certainly a fine balance. In terms of how this patient did, ultimately, we went ahead and just treated him endoscopically. We used the thulium laser fiber. He did require two sessions to fully treat and debulk the tumor. You can't really appreciate it so much in this single cut, but there was some lower pole component of the tumor that was a little bit harder to access initially. But after two sessions, we continued to monitor him at three-month intervals. And now, since his most recent fulguration session, he has been NED for 12 months. And so hopefully this is a testament to the relative indolence with respect to the natural history of low-grade disease.

I will point out that right now, one of the challenges with low-grade is we are so reliant on our weather imaging with CT eargram or just direct visualization with repeat trips to the OR. What I'm really looking forward to is some of these urine-based assays. that can be helpful in this space right now. That's a space that's growing. Certainly nothing out there right now, but I'm looking forward to that in the next couple of years, whether it's for high-grade or low-grade disease, to see if we can potentially stagger our direct vision looks with maybe a urine-based assay. I think that would help these patients quite a bit, because I think we obviously, for our own fears, overlook, meaning check too many times.

Absolutely. And I think especially when it comes to undergrading limitations, multiple large series may report even as high as a 50% undergrade discordance between biopsies and final pathologies. And so I share very much the same sentiment that urine-based tests may be the way of the future. The last, I'll just put a plug out for a clinical trial that is also in this space. I think kudos to the Olympus Trial Consortium for being able to achieve FDA approval for an agent in the low-grade UTU space, the UTUC space, let alone complete a clinical trial. But there is also a phase three trial called the Enlighted Trial. It's also actually part of the SUO CTC. And it's investigating a novel approach that leverages something called vascular-targeted photodynamic therapy, or using something called pataliporphin, or 2CAD, to, in a more direct manner, with a certain wavelength of activation, essentially have a targeted approach to treating certain tumors. Certainly very encouraging results that were published recently from the Phase I trial of this, and we're eager to see the results from the Phase III trial once they emerge.
And, Nirmish, this is the one where you have to give something IV, right, a tracer IV, and then you bring kind of the laser fiber intra-op and you shine the fiber on the tumor?

That's exactly right. And the laser itself activates at a very specific wavelength that would then activate this compound called pataliporphin to induce necrosis within that region. And so that exactly is the concept behind it. And it'll be very interesting to see the data once it comes out.
Absolutely. And given how rare this disease is and how much data we need in this space, open the trial, enroll your patients, change the future.

reference_conclusion: Kidney-sparing management was favored for this low-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma, with initial endoscopic tumor ablation rather than upfront nephroureterectomy. Retrograde laser ablation was considered a reasonable first approach, with close endoscopic surveillance at approximately 3-month intervals. If treatment were incomplete or if low-grade recurrence developed, repeat endoscopic debulking with consideration of adjuvant antegrade mitomycin gel via nephrostomy tube was discussed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old male; occupation: engineer.

[ chief complaint ]: Second-opinion evaluation in August 2024 for an incidentally detected thyroid nodule identified on routine health screening.

[ diagnosis ]: Thyroid nodule in the posterior middle third of the thyroid, measuring 1.8 cm on ultrasound, with suspicious sonographic features. A second 1.0 cm low-risk thyroid nodule was also present.

[ histopathology results ]: No thyroid histopathology was available. Past medical history included partial nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma measuring 1.7 cm in 2024.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a 1.8 cm hypoechoic nodule in the posterior middle third of the thyroid with irregular margins and type 3 vascular flow. The lesion was described as close to the outer border of the thyroid gland and strap muscle. Additional sonographic features described included marked echogenicity, multiple echogenic foci, halo, ill-defined posterior border, and irregular lateral borders. A second 1.0 cm low-risk thyroid nodule was identified. Initial nodule volume was 1.7 cm³. Immediate post-ablation ultrasound demonstrated expected enlargement with necrotic change.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroid function was normal. TgAb was positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In 2024, the patient underwent partial nephrectomy for 1.7 cm clear cell renal cell carcinoma. For the thyroid nodule, active surveillance was discussed. The patient declined surgery. Radiofrequency ablation was performed in September 2024. The procedure was brief and uncomplicated.

[ current disease status ]: The patient was clinically well.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was significant for clear cell renal cell carcinoma treated with partial nephrectomy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old woman from Palakkad.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast lump of 1 month duration.

[ diagnosis ]:  
1. Left breast invasive carcinoma, post modified radical mastectomy, pathologic stage pT2N2a; triple-negative phenotype on immunohistochemistry.  
2. Left renal cell carcinoma, post radical nephrectomy, pathologic stage pT3aN0.  
3. Papillary thyroid carcinoma, classic subtype, pathologic stage pT1aNx.  
4. Ovarian mature teratoma, post oophorectomy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Breast core biopsy: infiltrating ductal carcinoma.  
- Modified radical mastectomy specimen: invasive carcinoma, grade 2; no lymphovascular invasion; surgical margins free; 6 of 19 lymph nodes positive; metastatic focus measured 1 cm.  
- Left nephrectomy specimen: renal cell carcinoma with extension to the renal sinus and pelvis; 15 dissected nodes negative.  
- Parotid node dissected: negative for malignancy.  
- Thyroidectomy specimen: papillary carcinoma, classic subtype; no lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion, no capsular invasion; nodal dissection not performed.  
- Oophorectomy specimen: mature teratoma.  
- Renal tumor immunohistochemistry: no specific subtype identified.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Mammogram: BI-RADS 4C lesion in the breast measuring 2.0 × 1.7 cm; axillary lymph nodes present, largest 1.7 × 1.5 cm.  
- PET-CT: primary breast carcinoma with axillary and deep pectoral nodal involvement; soft tissue mass in the upper pole of the left kidney, favored synchronous renal malignancy; mild left pleural effusion; FDG-avid hypoenhancing lesion in the lower pole of the left thyroid lobe; ovarian cystic lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Breast tumor immunohistochemistry: triple negative.  
- Comprehensive hereditary cancer panel: no deletions or mutations detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent modified radical mastectomy, radical left nephrectomy, oophorectomy, and thyroidectomy.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Postoperative status following resection of breast carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and ovarian mature teratoma.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No other associated symptoms were documented at presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Four-month history of progressive dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left hypopharynx/piriform sinus, with left vocal fold paralysis. No metastatic disease was identified at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Endoscopic biopsy from the left piriform sinus/hypopharyngeal lesion showed adenoid cystic carcinoma. Histology demonstrated a cribriform pattern with infiltration into muscle and fat.

[ imaging findings ]: CT neck demonstrated an infiltrative tumor in the left hypopharynx. No definite laryngeal mass was seen on CT. Endoscopic evaluation with microlaryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy identified a lesion coating the left piriform sinus; the lesion was partly exophytic but infiltrative, with a clear visible tumor interface, and was fixed to the larynx. Paraglottic space extension was present on operative assessment/specimen review. No metastatic disease was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial office evaluation including speech-language assessment showed poor swallowing function and left vocal fold paralysis. The patient underwent microlaryngoscopy with biopsy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy for diagnostic evaluation.

[ current disease status ]: No metastatic disease had been identified at diagnosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Office swallowing function was poor. Left vocal fold paralysis was present at initial evaluation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female child, aged 4.5 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in June 2024 with abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral multifocal Wilms tumor involving both kidneys.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial ultrasound-guided core biopsy from a right renal lesion showed triphasic Wilms tumor with anaplasia reported on biopsy.  
- Ultrasound-guided core biopsy from a left renal lesion after 6 weeks of chemotherapy was inconclusive.  
- Right robotic radical nephrectomy specimen showed multifocal Wilms tumor with two distinct lesions. Sections showed triphasic tumor morphology. No anaplastic features were identified in the nephrectomy specimen.  
- No evidence of tumor disruption, renal sinus involvement, renal vein involvement, extension beyond the renal capsule by viable tumor, or direct extension to adjacent organs.  
- Surgical margins were negative for viable and non-viable tumor.  
- Viable tumor was >33%, with blastemal component >66% of viable tumor.  
- One sampled lymph node was uninvolved.  
- Pathology was reported as local stage I high-risk histology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline abdominal imaging demonstrated:  
  - Right kidney: heterogeneous lesion measuring 12 × 10 cm in the interpolar region/lower pole with heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement; additional upper pole lesion measuring 4.3 × 3.9 cm.  
  - Left kidney: three lesions, including one measuring 3.7 × 3.3 cm in the posterior interpolar cortex, another interpolar cortical lesion laterally, and one lesion in the lower pole.  
- HRCT chest at presentation was normal.  
- Reassessment CT abdomen after 6 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed reduction in size of all renal lesions.  
- Whole-body PET-CT showed uptake only in the right lower pole lesion.  
- CT was repeated approximately 1 month later during a period off chemotherapy.  
- After completion of 27 weeks of chemotherapy, residual disease persisted in the left kidney as three subcentimetric lesions: posterior interpolar, lateral interpolar, and lower pole lesions. The largest residual lesion measured 14 × 6 mm in the lateral interpolar region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Received 3-drug neoadjuvant chemotherapy for 6 weeks prior to surgery; regimen included vincristine, dactinomycin, and doxorubicin.  
- Post-neoadjuvant imaging showed reduction in size of all bilateral renal lesions.  
- Underwent right robotic radical nephrectomy. There was no capsular breach or intraoperative tumor spillage.  
- Following nephrectomy pathology reported as local stage I high-risk histology, the patient started adjuvant chemotherapy for 26–27 weeks as per SIOP-based protocol with vincristine, dactinomycin, and doxorubicin.  
- After 7 weeks of adjuvant therapy, referral for nephron-sparing surgery of the left kidney was made, but surgery was deferred until completion of chemotherapy.  
- Interventional radiology assessed for radiofrequency ablation of residual left renal lesions; this was considered unsuitable because of multiple small lesions and anticipated loss of surrounding normal renal parenchyma.  
- Chemotherapy was continued to completion.  
- Despite completion of 27 weeks of chemotherapy, three residual left renal lesions remained.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post right radical nephrectomy for multifocal Wilms tumor.  
- Persistent residual disease in the left kidney after completion of systemic therapy, with three subcentimetric lesions remaining; largest 14 × 6 mm.  
- No pulmonary metastases were identified on chest HRCT at presentation.  
- PET-CT demonstrated metabolic uptake confined to the right lower pole lesion at the time of that study.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The child was referred after initial management at another institution.  
- During right nephrectomy, only one lymph node was sampled.  
- The left kidney was not surgically addressed at the time of right nephrectomy.

Radiofrequency ablation is not considered appropriate for Wilms tumor in this setting.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 48-year-old man. No significant past medical history was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented with B symptoms and lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), frontline setting. Modified Rai stage: intermediate risk, based on lymphocytosis, splenomegaly, and adenopathy.

[ histopathology results ]: Bone marrow biopsy showed substantial involvement by CLL.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IGHV mutation testing showed unmutated IGHV. FISH demonstrated deletion 6q, deletion 13q, and deletion 17p. TP53 sequencing was positive for TP53 mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: CBC showed leukocytosis to 38.5. Flow cytometry showed an immunophenotype consistent with CLL. No significant cytopenias were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed, previously untreated CLL with symptomatic disease and high-risk molecular features, including del(17p), TP53 mutation, and unmutated IGHV.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination showed splenomegaly. Adenopathy was present. Mantle cell lymphoma exclusion was referenced as an important diagnostic consideration in CLL workup, but no specific mantle cell lymphoma testing result was provided for this patient.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so with that, let's look into our case number two, and then we will go into the literature review after that.

So this is also in the frontline setting. This is a younger patient, though, with a, I'd say, less common, different initial presentation where the disease a bit more aggressive to start. So, this 48-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents with B symptoms and lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly on exam, and a leukocytosis up to 38.5 on the CBC with a similar immunophenotype on flow cytometry that we saw in the first case. Despite a no significant set of penias here, the bone marrow biopsy did show substantial CLL involvement. And so, in the bottom here, we just see this is modified Rye staging where this patient would fall in the intermediate risk group by virtue of that lymphocytosis and enlarged spleen with adenopathy. So, I make a point to bring up the Rye stages. This is, of course, the molecular tumor board, but to recall that the Rye and Binet staging, which were developed in the 70s and 80s, These two staging systems still remain today. They rely solely on physical exam and your standard CBC without imaging studies for those findings of adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. They're inexpensive and can be readily and consistently applied across patients, so not to lose sight of the importance of these. Then, considering molecular biomarkers, this is coming from NCCN guidelines. This table is really providing information or variables that can have prognostic information for survival and time to progression in patients who receive treatment. So, this patient clearly we're thinking about treatment already. When we think about IGHV mutations, that's a particularly important one. Recall these are generated through somatic hypermutation. This is a physiologic process to generate immunoglobulin diversity during the normal B cell maturation. B cells with mutated IgHV have undergone this process, whereas those with unmutated IgHV have not. The flow cytometry correlates to this, which are somewhat less established, would be the CD38 and ZAP70. And then as far as other sequencing, it includes TP53, which we'll talk more about in just a moment, and then FISH, which we've discussed a bit. already at this point, and then karyotyping or conventional karyotyping of stimulated CLL cells. The definition of complex karyotype varies a bit from paper to paper, but typically at least, you know, three unrelated chromosome abnormalities in more than one cell on karyotype.
Paul, could you also highlight what are the abnormalities then that would be associated with favorable and those with unfavorable?

Yeah. Yeah, absolutely. This is kind of a busy slide. So mutated IGHV, so a CLL clone that has gone through that process is favorable, whereas unmutated is unfavorable. And then you see the CD38 and ZAP70 that fall beneath each of those categories, which would be correlated or associated with mutated or unmutated, rather, IGHV. TP53 mutation, along with which often goes with deletion 17P, are unfavorable. The other fish carrier finding which is in the unfavorable group, which was present in our first case, was deletion 11Q. In the intermediate or neutral group would be having no findings on your fish probes or quote-unquote normal or trisomy 12 and then deletion 13Q as the sole abnormality being considered favorable. So, in this patient, the IgHV mutation testing did show unmutated IgHV, and FISH showed a number of abnormalities, including deletion 6q, which is a fairly rare finding, deletion 13q, and then, most notably, the del 17p, and clipped from the pivotal paper from Professor Donor with the establishment of a hierarchical model of chromosomal abnormalities. Deletion 17P is kind of the one that carries the day here. The worst of these findings is what you go with. And, you know, just one other point to make, as you see the FISH panel here, and there's a translocation 1114 Either by fish probe or by cyclin D1 expression, it's important to exclude mantle cell lymphoma when you're looking at cases of CLL, which can have a similar immunophenotype, but, of course, varied treatment and courses. And then, lastly, this patient did have TP53 sequencing as well, which was positive. The point to make here is that TP53 aberrations can include deletion 17p and or TP53 mutation. And so it's estimated that up to a third of patients who have a TP53 aberration, meaning either one of those, may carry only the mutation in the gene and thus would not be detected by FISH, which is the argument for doing both FISH and either Sanger sequencing or some high-throughput sequencing of TP53 prior to initiation of a treatment where that's going to potentially, you know, would dictate your treatment decision?

So, I think at this point, you know, we saw that this patient obviously has TP5317B deletion, but we also saw or talked about some of the molecular abnormalities. And now I would like to bring in our panel, and we will obviously review some of the literature behind this, but Just talking about this from an approach perspective, I mean, how do you sort of make sense of all of these molecular abnormalities to decide on treatment? That's question one. And then the question two, I think Paul brought up a good point, is in a lot of places, especially in developing countries, do not have the ability to do sequencing. What do you think about, like, the importance of doing a FISH and a Sanger sequencing or a MGS for TP53? So, let's start with Dr. Choudhury. Let me bring in Dr. Choudhury and see what his thoughts are.

Well, yes. So, my thoughts for this case would be that the – obviously, the TP53 mutation kind of is the driver of prognosis in this situation, so that's where I think the most important molecular abnormality I would consider. Now, the others, obviously, for the 13q, as the previous slide also suggested, that if it's the only abnormality, then it's favorable, but when it's associated with others, then it's not. So, I'd say, you know, he's got sort of unfavorable characteristics of the T53 mutation. So, I'd use that as the prognostic treatment marker for this case. As far as the thoughts about the gene sequencing, of course, the more deeper down we can actually sort of tease out the mutation, the better information we'll have, so one can always make a justification for more information. But it's also important to understand that then we are talking sort of lower numbers, and if there's countries where this is not available, we'll have to use the information that we have. So, those are my thoughts. Dr. Adelaide?

Oh, I think that was really well said, and I agree with all the points. We don't typically do gene sequencing studies here at Virginia Mason, but we'll do the molecular studies through FISH, and we'll do the P53, recognizing that we may check or may find an additional 25% of patients who have the P53 deletion. And in terms of treatment, you know, this would definitely catch my eye in terms of what his situation is and where he's moving.

Yeah, I mean, I think there are two parts of your question that are important. I mean, number one, obviously, in a resource-constrained environment, what do you do? And that's a very tough question to answer, to be honest, because you just have to utilize the resources available to make these decisions. Many years ago, I used to think that 17, everybody who has 17P will have a TP53 mutation, so really you can get that through the fish by default, but as Paul actually mentioned, and I'm sure he's gonna show later on, not all patients, you could see TP53 mutation, or even in patients who don't have the 17P deletion. Not in a lot, but there's enough out there. So, in a resource-constrained environment, utilize the information that you have and you proceed. I think the good news, or the silver lining in that, is that the frontline therapy in these patients has, you can make an argument that it's probably going to be the same nowadays regardless of whether the P53 is mutated or not based on the randomized studies. So I think that's maybe the silver lining. And the other thing that I was gonna say is I haven't And I'm curious what the other panelists and listeners have been doing, but I haven't been utilizing the IGHV mutation status in decision making except if I'm considering chemotherapy, obviously. So you want to do it, but it's also not available to everyone. So it's a tough question to answer because if you can't If you can't get the mutational status of the IGHV, then you're going to miss on the proportion of patients that might still benefit from systemic chemoimmunotherapy. So I'm curious, really, from listeners and others, what they do about this, because we sometimes are spoiled in the U.S., to be honest.
That's a very good point. Dr. Aboulafia or Dr. Chaudhry, any comments on the IGHV mutation status and use of chemoimmunotherapy?

You know, I usually order it more or less reflexively now that it's part of NCCM guidelines, and I know that the insurance carriers will cover it. Previous to that, it wasn't always covered. It's very expensive. You know, in truth, as Ken Achadri mentions, I'm not sure I would use FCR, you know, not in this context, but in maybe a different context, but with mutated form in a young patient, I'd still probably move toward novel agents. And so it's becoming less important to me.

I don't have anything to add to that. And I think the utility of the HIV mutation for determining therapies sort of now become very, very narrow. And just like David said, the decision-making for a young, fit, first-line CLL with, you know, are we going to use FCR or not? I think that would be the only place where I'd consider it. But again, that's not even a deciding factor anymore. And I think we're all using kind of novel agents. Two years ago it would have been a different discussion. But now I'd say it's having diminished utility.
Perfect.
So with that, let's review the literature on frontline treatment of CLL and how the field has evolved over the last several years. So Paul, I'll hand it back to you.

Thank you, yeah, excellent discussion. This patient, being 48 years old, unfortunately ended up having a number of adverse and high-risk molecular features where the conversation or consideration for a time-limiter immunotherapy approach appeared less of an option here, and we'll see why. So this is looking at CLL8 study, which compared a flutarabine and cyclophosphamide to flutarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. and shown to improve survival. And then on the right, we see the prognostic impact of deletion 17P in both groups, in PFS and OS. The circle is kind of highlighting the darker line being FCR and the dashed line being FC, but PFS on the top and OS on the bottom. And then on the left, really, you see that top curve, which has really a nice plateau, which we'll see again in the next couple of slides, but in the FCR group, the IGHV mutated patients doing quite well. So CLL10 compared FCR to BR, and you see that this benefit, the best outcomes amongst those patients with IGHV mutated disease in both the patients treated with FCR and BR. This is a PFS slide. And then this interesting report with extensive follow-up, nearly 13 years of follow-up, this was a phase two study evaluating FCR at MD Anderson, showed not only the IgHV mutated patients did the best, but that also this MRD negativity post-treatment was highly predictive of long-term PFS. And you see that top plateau and the year stretching out along the x-axis, which is really remarkable and I think leads to that allure of chemoimmunotherapy that has persisted despite a lot of these advances with novel agents. And MRD is something we'll revisit as well. So here, moving then to those novel agents, this was the PIVL-Resonate 2 trial. You see the much superior PFS improvements with the ibrutinib treatment compared to chlorambucil, and that's irrespective of IGHV mutation status. Then moving to the large cooperative group trials from the past reported within the last couple years. This is the ECOG1912 showing progression-free and overall survival benefit with ibrutinib plus rituximab versus that gold standard chemoimmunotherapy of FCR in the younger, fit, untreated CLL patients. Of note, given what we've already talked about today and seen in the prior slides, patients with deletion 17P were excluded here. There was patients with TP53 mutation, which snuck in, but it made up a small amount, only around 5 or 6 percent. So the small boxes here are simply showing the PFS for all patients, the middle slide showing that most dramatic difference among the patients with IGHV unmutated status, and then the intention to treat overall survival showing a superiority with ibrudinib. And then the Alliance trial was similar setup, but looking at ibrutinib with or without rituximab versus bandimustine rituximab, or BR, in untreated CLL in older patients. And this did have a small amount of del 17P in it and mutated TP53, but you see that regardless of ibrutinib with or without rituximab, it was superior in PFS to BR. And then most recently, the CLL14 trial, this is from the original publication. They actually just published a three-year efficacy update in Lancet Oncology last week, but continued to show this progression-free survival benefit with venetoclex plus obinutuzumab versus chlorambucil and obinutuzumab in untreated patients with comorbidities. And so that was the key here. And some other important points on this is that it's a time-limited option. And in the bottom slides here, I give the TP53 and IGHV status. These are kind of hard to see. I think these are from the supplement. But the top two lines there on the left side are the venetoclex obinutuzumab-treated arms. And you see in that solid line, the second one down, yep, that the, a lot of, that's the TP53 aberration, either deletion or mutation, patients treated with venetoclaxonobinutuzumab, and most of those events are coming after 12 months, or after that treatment duration. Excellent presentation, Paul. So I think looking at the data now, I think there are a few questions that comes up with what Paul presented. So, starting with the first question, let's start with the chemoimmunotherapy question. So, going back to the panel, do you think chemoimmunotherapy is still sort of your first line for any subset of patients? And I will start with Dr. Abulafi.

Dr. Chaudhary?

Yes, I would completely agree. Dr. Ahmed? Well, I may be less antagonistic to FCR than my co-panelists in the subset of patients that have the mutated IGHV. Yeah.
Sorry, go ahead, David.
No, no, no, I'm sorry. Go ahead.

The only thing I would add is we just have to wait for the trials. And so I'd say we've got to keep doing what we are doing now until the trials show that limited duration is as effective as prolonged.

Yeah, I agree. And just that young patient who has mutated isoform and who has P53 deletions, this is a perfect person to consider for a clinical trial looking at triple therapy. So if I was ever going to think about triple therapy, this would be the context, adding a BTKI with phenetoclax and open it to Zimab. But this wouldn't be in my clinic. This would be as part of a clinical trial.
So moving forward, then, in the interest of time, so Paul.
