case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Demographic details were not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Poor tolerance of lorlatinib with development of a Guillain-Barré syndrome-like demyelinating polyneuropathy causing facial weakness and lower-limb weakness with impaired ambulation.

[ diagnosis ]: ALK-rearranged lung malignancy with EML4-ALK fusion and TP53 co-mutation. Neurological complication described as GBS-like demyelinating polyneuropathy/autoimmune polyneuropathy.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology details were not provided.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT thorax showed good reduction in size of the primary lung lesion and mediastinal lymph nodes.  
- MRI brain and spine were repeated and showed maintained CNS control; no further radiologic details were provided.  
- PET scan was performed on the day of review; detailed report was not provided.  
- Chest radiograph showed near-complete response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- EML4-ALK fusion positive.  
- TP53 co-mutation present.  
- NGS/electrophysiologic assessment was described as showing demyelinating-type changes; axonal involvement was also stated.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Paraneoplastic antibody panel was negative, including ANNA-1/2/3, PCA-1/2/3, AGNA, CRMP5, and amphiphysin.  
- Anti-ganglioside antibodies were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Received first cycle of chemotherapy.  
- Received radiation therapy.  
- Subsequently received lorlatinib 100 mg daily.  
- Received intravenous immunoglobulin for 5 days.  
- Following IV immunoglobulin, neurological recovery was observed: facial nerve function recovered completely; proximal and distal muscle weakness improved; lower-limb power increased to approximately 3–4/5; patient was able to walk with support.  
- Systemic and CNS disease control were reported as good on treatment, with near-complete thoracic response.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Good CNS control was present.  
- Good thoracic disease control was present, with near-complete response on chest imaging.  
- Neurological deficits were improving after IV immunoglobulin. Facial weakness had completely resolved; lower-limb weakness had improved, and the patient was ambulant with support.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- CSF cytology had not been performed.  
- MRI brain and spine had been performed in the neurological workup.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-month history of a right preauricular facial mass with progressive enlargement.

[ diagnosis ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma involving the right parotid/preauricular region. Regional nodal metastatic disease was present in the ipsilateral neck.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial ultrasound-guided needle biopsy from an outside institution showed malignancy without further classification.

[ imaging findings ]: Ultrasound identified a mass in the right preauricular region. CT imaging demonstrated an infiltrative right preauricular/parotid-region mass without a clear plane along the masseter. The mass did not encroach on the stylomastoid foramen, with preserved distance from that structure. Anteriorly, there was thickening extending along the salivary duct over the masseter to the buccal space. PET imaging showed ipsilateral FDG-avid lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had undergone liver transplantation 7 years earlier. He had remained on chronic immunosuppression with mycophenolate and tacrolimus; for the preceding 3 years these had been at the lowest dose possible.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was significant for liver transplantation. Dermatologic evaluation did not identify concerning ipsilateral facial cutaneous lesions. There was no history of cutaneous lesions on the involved side of the face; a remote, very superficial squamous lesion had been treated on the contralateral earlobe. Preoperatively, facial nerve function was intact. MRI had been performed and showed no enhancement along the facial nerve near the stylomastoid foramen.

[ chief complaint ]: Advanced symptomatic metastatic prostate cancer with severe disease burden, pain requiring opioids, weight loss, and poor performance status (ECOG 3).

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic prostate cancer with widespread nodal and hepatic metastatic disease. Obstructive uropathy requiring nephrostomy; nephrostomy-dependent single functioning kidney situation was described, with an atrophic left kidney.

[ histopathology results ]: Not available.

[ imaging findings ]: FDG PET dated 28 February and PSMA PET dated 1 March were performed. The left kidney was atrophic. A nephrostomy was present, with right-sided line/nephrostomy in situ. Hepatic metastases demonstrated high PSMA uptake without evident FDG/PSMA mismatch.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: FDG PET metrics: SUVmax 55, SUVmean 11, metabolic tumour volume (MTV) 2 L. PSMA PET SUVmean was reported as approximately 10.8-11. PSA had been rising rapidly before treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had received multiple prior life-prolonging therapies before lutetium treatment; specific agents were not detailed.

[ other clinical data ]: The disease burden was described as extensive and symptomatic. The patient had hepatic metastases with high tracer uptake. Urine output reduction over several days was noted as a typical indicator of nephrostomy blockage in this nephrostomy-dependent setting.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: One-year history of neck swelling.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical nodal metastases, central neck nodal disease, and left retropharyngeal nodal metastasis. Background history of Graves’ disease diagnosed at age 18.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion had shown papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Physical examination had demonstrated an easily palpable left thyroid nodule measuring approximately 3 cm, massive left-sided cervical adenopathy with multiple mobile lymph nodes greater than 5 cm in levels II-IV, and a mobile right level IV lymph node measuring approximately 4-5 cm. Vocal cords were mobile on examination. Office ultrasound had shown a 3 cm left thyroid nodule that was hypoechoic, solid, with ill-defined borders and microcalcifications. Ultrasound had also shown bulky cystic adenopathy in the left lateral neck, involving levels III and IV, suspicious nodes in left level II, concerning right-sided cervical nodes, and central neck disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck had demonstrated bilateral lateral neck adenopathy, central neck adenopathy, and left retropharyngeal adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had previously been evaluated by another surgeon and then sought a second opinion.

[ current disease status ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical nodal metastases, central neck nodal disease, and left retropharyngeal nodal metastasis, referred for a second surgical opinion.

[ other clinical data ]: There was no family history of thyroid cancer. Other physical examination findings were otherwise unremarkable. Evaluation had been delayed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

reference_discussion.text: I need to see how I can get all your pictures off of my screen so I can read it. There we go. So this was a 26-year-old female that I had seen with a history of Graves' disease, diagnosed at age 18. So she'd been dealing with that for several years. She had a one year history of neck swelling. And, you know, like a lot of folks delayed evaluation due to the coven pandemic. She had seen another surgeon and came to me for a second opinion. And she had no family history of really any relevant diseases, but namely, no history of thyroid cancer. On physical examination, she had a easily palpable left thyroid nodule, which was about three centimeters. And she had massive left-sided adenopathy, multiple nodes greater than five centimeters throughout levels two through four. And she also had a right level four lymph node, which was about four to five centimeters. All these nodes were mobile. And other than this, she had a very unremarkable physical examination. Both of her vocal cords are mobile, in fact, her optic exam.

Okay, let me stop you right here, Dan. Dr. Orloff, you're an ultrasound guru, so forget that part. Patient comes to you with just obvious upfront lymphadenopathy. Do you just go to the axial imaging CT scan, or do you still say, no, I'll do the ultrasound? You're muted, by the way.

So sorry. Nope, I consider ultrasound a part of my evaluation, my initial evaluation, so I can glean a lot of information and it can guide ordering of cross-sectional imaging, whether it would be a CT scan or an MRI, CT of the neck alone, CT of the neck and mediastinum. PET-CT if it were something that appeared to be something beyond your typical thyroid cancer. So yeah, I think ultrasound still provides initial information on the disease at hand and on what further studies to order.
Dr. Smith, what are your thoughts on getting axial imaging in these cases?

So I agree with Lisa that ultrasound gives us a tremendous amount of information and in the vast majority of patients, all the information we need. If the ultrasound suggests that there may be very extensive extrathoracial extension of the primary tumor and I'm worried about tracheal or laryngeal invasion, then that would prompt me to think about other imaging. If the disease extends low in the central neck and I don't feel like I see the inferior extent of it going into the superior amoeba stynum, then that would prompt me to get more imaging with a cross-sectional imaging study. If everything here looks like I can see it well with the ultrasound, I would be comfortable with ultrasound alone on this patient.
All right. Okay, Dan, tell us what you decided to do.

All right. Yeah, I do a lot of ultrasound in my clinic as well, like Lisa and Russell. She had, I don't unfortunately have the images for her, but she had a left three centimeter thyroid nodule that was very suspicious hypoechoic solid ill-defined borders of microcalcification. And not surprisingly, she had pretty massive cystic adenopathy on the left side in levels three and four, and then suspicious nodes in level two also. And then some more concerning nodes on the right side. She had central neck disease on the ultrasound as well, although it was a little bit difficult to see.
Okay. Did you have an F, did she come with an FNA to you or you didn't have any biopsies?
She came with an FNA. Yeah. Which was, papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Okay. So Dr. Smith, patients come to you with the FNA already. What's your routine? Do you repeat the FNA? Do you do the nodes? Do you just do the thyroid? When do you say it's good? So when you say, no, I need more information.

So I think with one biopsy, either of a node or of the primary tumor, you've established the diagnosis. It sounds like her imaging is very pathognomonic of having a larger primary tumor. with fairly extensive nodal disease in the central neck and the bilateral lateral necks. And so I don't see a need for any additional biopsies because it sounds like one biopsy confirms our suspicion and the remainder of the imaging kind of tells the rest of our story.
Let me ask Dr. Allen and Cedars, do you guys do repeat the biopsy? Do you? Sorry. What would you do?

In regards to your question about repeating the biopsy, generally speaking, the diagnosis of papillothiazard cancer is fairly routine. I don't think you need a subspecialized pathologist to repeat the biopsy. So if they come with an outside FNA that says papillothiazard carcinoma, unless there's something that doesn't add up, we tend to trust it. We'll request the slides if they come, but we wouldn't necessarily wait for them. I generally find that when we do request them that our pathologists will agree with something as commonplace, vanilla diagnoses as papillary.
Okay. Do you stand for genetic testing at this point for finding out any mutations or it doesn't matter?

I'm more of a minimalist, Babak. I don't find that it will necessarily make or break our surgical planning. For me, it's more downstream if the patient has something along the lines of a targeted therapy.
Dr. Orloff, do you insist on having biopsy at Stanford? Do you do both thyroid and the neck? Do you stand for genetic testing?

So it's my institutional policy that slides are reviewed because of the not infrequent change in diagnosis. Especially for planned cancer treatment, we would review outside slides and not necessarily repeat them. It's my understanding that that is more cost-effective than repeating them as well as less invasive. But if the metastatic disease was biopsied and positive, I wouldn't go back and biopsy the primary. But if the primary were biopsied and the nodes had not been biopsied, it may be appropriate to biopsy the nodes if there's not the obvious distinction between just prominent reactives and phadenopathy and metastatic disease. Sometimes you just can't get to the metastatic nodes and you'll still operate on them, so it's not a hard and fast rule. And we don't usually do genetic testing up front if the diagnosis is papillary carcinoma. Perfect.
Thank you. All right, Dan.

Yeah, so we did get a CT with contrast. I tend to do this on people who have very bulky disease. It showed a lot of what we expected to see. It showed adenopathy in both bilateral lateral neck compartments and the central neck. And it also showed left-sided retropharyngeal adenopathy, which you can see in the axial and coronal planes here.

All right, so a question from the audience. I'll ask Dr. Orloff first and then Dr. Smith. The MRI versus CT, when do you do MRI, when do you do CT? And every time you want to do a CT, there is an endocrinologist in the audience that, oh my God, you're going to get a contract. How do you answer that?

Yeah. Yeah. Thanks, Babak. I just actually typed into the chat response because I think Tanya had asked the same thing, but I do try to minimize radiation exposure. So I think about MRI whenever possible in lieu of CT, but having said that, MRI is more prone to claustrophobia. It takes a lot longer to acquire the MRI images, and therefore the images are more susceptible to motion artifact. And sometimes it's just more expeditious to get the CT. It's slightly less expensive. And for the interface between the airway especially and the tumor, I think CT is better. Generally speaking, soft tissue is ideal with MRI, but I don't know about others, but when I get MRI images, there are all these sequences that the radiologist gets that I have no idea what to do with. They have all these weird names and they show images that I can't interpret anyway. So I think CT is very straightforward and being conscious of minimizing radiation exposure, I think it's the most expeditious.
Dr. Smith.

Yeah, I think one of the misconceptions about MRI scan is that it gives you more soft, soft tissue detail, but it only does that if you image a very finite area. So looking at the skull base, looking at the larynx, looking at a very specific organ, it gives you great imaging. If you try to do the entire neck from the skull base down into the mediastinum with MRI, it's really substandard imaging. It just doesn't give you the detail. And so I really tried to avoid using MRI of the neck as a global exam because I just think it doesn't give you the same information as a more focused MRI that's looking at specific pathology in specific areas. So I go ahead and get the CT scans. And if the endocrinologist are balking about, you know, iodine load, you can check. iodine levels in urine before you give them iodine therapy to help ease their anxiety. But for the most part, people clear their iodine from a CT scan pretty quickly because you're getting it probably a few weeks pre-op. You're not going to treat them for six weeks post-op with iodine therapy. And so within two months, most people can clear their contrast iodine load before any concerns about treating with radioactive iodine.
All right. We've got six more minutes to finish this case. Let's go. Dan?

All right, yeah, so, oh God, there we go. So she had a total thyroidectomy, bilateral central and lateral nectis section and a left retropharyngeal nectis section as well. The pathology was pretty much what you would expect in a 23-year-old classic PTC with multiple satellite nodules of tumor in both sides of the thyroid, negative margins and 23 of 65 nodes positive for PTC. No ENE, largest node was 3.5 centimeters, and there was that left retropharyngeal node.
Okay, some nitty-gritty questions. So, let me ask Dr. Mays, Ashley, if this patient comes to you, do you do this all in one session, or are you staging?

No, good question. I've actually never staged it personally. I've always done the neck and the thyroid at the same time. I guess the question becomes the retropharyngeal. Maybe that's what you're getting at. But no, I've never staged these.
Okay. Do you do the thyroid first or do you do the neck first?
I personally do the thyroid first.
Okay. Dr. Smith, do you stage these or do you do it one day, just clean up the calendar?

Yeah, I wouldn't post this as the third case of the day. I'd probably make it the only case of the day. I would do this all in one setting. I would do the thyroid and central neck first. I actually paralyzed my patients for their lateral neck dissections. And so from a a practicality perspective that eliminates the need for reversal of paralytics if you do the necks before the central neck from a nerve monitoring perspective.
And then do you do the retropharyngeal at the end after you do the lateral neck?
Yeah, I would just include that as part of my access for that left lateral neck dissection just to kind of go ahead and open up the parapharyngeal space from the upper part of the neck.

Yeah, I actually, I actually, I prefer to do the lateral next first. I don't think there's a right or wrong way but my thinking is that I leave the parathyroids and the nerve, the laryngeal nerves, less exposed for less period of time or I have less period of time for a patient to develop hypocalcemia. I know that there's the argument that you're more tired at the end of the case, maybe your attention to the detail in the central neck is more fresh and optimized early in the case, but I find also the access to the thyroid is perhaps enhanced by having dissected the lateral neck first. And that includes the retropharyngeal space if I can get to it. And if I can't get to it, if it's just too high, too close to the skull base, I think there is the option of doing it as a separate procedure through a transoral robotic approach or even a mandibular osteotomy approach. But I do as much as I can with the lateral neck. So, and I think maybe that was your point about the cross sectional imaging, which should be a point that we highlight here because when there is so much bulky adenopathy, I think that we really need to remember that the retro pharynx, as well as the retro sternal and mediastinal areas are going to be the hardest, or the areas that you miss with ultrasound. So I do routinely get cross-sectional imaging when I have a patient with, as Russ said, adenopathetic, that extends to the limits of my view, especially, you know, concern about the presence of retropharyngeal disease that I wouldn't see otherwise.
So this patient comes to your office, when you see that much of a disease in the low neck, do you also get a chest CT?

Yeah, I mean, in my office, our practice, we call it a thyroid CT, which includes the skull base to the aortic arch. You know, it's a mediastinal CT. It's not necessarily a pulmonary CT. But often, you know, in collaboration with whomever is my referring physician, there will be a neck and chest CT done. So one way or the other, it gets covered.
Okay. Dan, how did you do this case? Did you do the thyroid first? Did you do the neck first? What's your routine?

Yeah. I always do the lateral neck first. Like Lisa said, I think the exposure that you get in the total thyroid is so much better when you do the lateral neck compartments first than if you're worried about, you know, can I find the nerve? You can always go and stimulate the vagus very easily. So that's just how I've done it. I mean, get all the other reasons to do it the other way, but I did both lateral sections and the retrofringal node dissection first and then the total power.
yeah. Okay.

I am. I didn't know if you were going to go there with this, going back to the original presentation of the patient with Graves' disease. And I have the privilege of working right now with the ATA on revising the ATA guidelines for thyroid nodules. And one of the questions that we're asking is whether patients who are diagnosed with Graves' disease should routinely have thyroid imaging. Also, patients with Graves' disease do tend to have enlarged thyroids and I think that our ability to detect abnormalities, just by manual palpation, is limited. So I think it's very low risk and low cost to get an ultrasound in somebody with newly diagnosed Graves. This patient It sounds like she'd had Graves' disease for quite a few years before she presented with the nodular disease. So perhaps this might have been caught at an earlier stage. I don't know if it would have made a difference, but.
And Dan, how scarred was the thyroid when you, I mean, with Graves, they can be pretty sticky and pretty bloody. How bad was the thyroid when you took it out?
Well, I don't remember, so it must not have been too bad. Um, no, I think, I don't think it was too bad actually. Okay.
All right. Do you have another slide?

Great. Great. So this is nice work. Yes. Let's start with the next case, Dr. Ashley May. Is it Ashley or is it Alan?

Postoperatively, Thyrogen-stimulated radioiodine scanning at four months demonstrated only a small amount of thyroid bed uptake with no uptake elsewhere, and radioactive iodine was not administered. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old male. Moderately obese. Otherwise reasonably healthy, active, and working.

[ chief complaint ]: Longstanding difficulty voiding associated with a meatal lesion, splayed urinary stream, and desire to preserve normal function. At presentation in 2023, he had a tender erosive distal penile mass with urethral drainage.

[ diagnosis ]: Penile squamous cell carcinoma, HPV-independent, clinically T2N0 at initial oncologic diagnosis.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- June 2023 shave biopsy: epidermal hyperplasia with possible carcinoma in situ.  
- Subsequent wedge biopsy of the penile lesion: well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pelvic MRI at initial workup demonstrated a mass occupying the glans penis.  
- Clinical examination and imaging were consistent with an invasive distal penile/glanular mass.  
- Post-induction chemotherapy imaging showed marked interval local improvement.  
- Follow-up MRI approximately 2 months later demonstrated rapid local recurrence.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HPV-independent tumor.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- History from 1998 onward of meatal stenosis and lichen sclerosus with multiple prior local procedures, including meatal dilations, removal of painless lesions, circumcision with urethral meatal dilation, and circumcision revisions.  
- Initial definitive surgery was refused.  
- Initial radiation therapy was also refused.  
- Received induction TIP chemotherapy for 4 cycles. This produced substantial initial local response on post-treatment imaging and examination.  
- After a lapse in follow-up of several months, he developed worsening firmness and difficulty voiding, with rapid local recurrence within approximately 2 months.

[ current disease status ]: Rapid local recurrence of HPV-independent penile squamous cell carcinoma after 4 cycles of induction TIP chemotherapy, with worsening local firmness and difficulty voiding. He remained clinically node-negative.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past history included meatal stenosis and lichen sclerosus.  
- Examination findings at oncologic presentation included significant scarring of the remaining glans, slight hypospadias related to prior dilations/surgeries, a lobulated tender erosive firm mass at the tip of the glans, urethral drainage, difficult examination due to discomfort, and partially buried penis related to obesity.  
- He remained clinically node-negative at initial diagnosis and at the time of first documented local recurrence.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly progressive very hard left neck mass involving levels III and IV over 3–4 weeks. No signs of infection.

[ diagnosis ]: Thyroid malignancy consisting of tall-cell variant papillary thyroid carcinoma in the thyroid with metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma in a left cervical lymph node. BRAF-positive disease. Suspected bilateral pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the thyroid nodule was consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma; pathology comment indicated possible tall-cell or columnar features. Biopsy/FNA of a left level III/IV cervical lymph node showed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Final surgical pathology demonstrated tall-cell carcinoma in the thyroid with metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Tumor was PAX8 positive and strongly PD-L1 positive. Four of 23 lymph nodes were positive. The anaplastic component was described as massively invading muscle. Resection was considered grossly substantial, with suspected residual microscopic disease and possible small-volume gross residual disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Office ultrasound demonstrated a thyroid mass and a separate irregular fixed lateral neck mass/lymph node lateral to the carotid artery. Thyroid nodule was categorized as TI-RADS 5. Pathologic left level III lymph node measured 4.4 cm on ultrasound. CT neck showed a 1.5 cm left superior thyroid mass and a large necrotic left neck mass/lymph node. The left internal jugular vein was not visualized. The left common carotid artery was not encased. CT chest demonstrated tiny pulmonary nodules suspicious for metastases. PET imaging showed bilateral pulmonary lesions/nodules, concerning for bilateral lung metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF positive in the involved level IV lymph node/final tumor. Ki-67 was 25–30% in the lymph node specimen. p53 was negative. PAX8 was positive. PD-L1 was strongly expressed.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative thyroglobulin was not markedly elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past surgical history included right hemithyroidectomy and left parathyroidectomy years earlier; prior thyroid pathology had been benign. Flexible laryngeal assessment showed mobile vocal cords preoperatively. Surgical resection of the thyroid and neck disease was performed; disease was considered resectable based on imaging and operative assessment. Postoperatively, substantial tumor removal was achieved, but residual microscopic disease and possible minimal gross residual disease were suspected.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after resection of tall-cell papillary thyroid carcinoma with metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Bilateral pulmonary metastases were suspected on PET/CT. Thyroglobulin was considered unreliable for surveillance because of dedifferentiated/aggressive disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Neck mass was clinically hard and fixed. No evidence of infection was present at presentation.

And the level four lymph node is positive for BRAF. And look at the KI67. It's at 25 to 30%. So for us, that's setting off alarm bells.

Mike, do you want to take over here? You want me to stop at this point or should I continue?

Let's do surgery first and then we'll talk to Bruce about anaplastic and BRAF. In fact, let me go to Bruce first. Bruce, we got a papillary thyroid cancer inside the thyroid. We've got an anaplastic that's BRAF positive in a lymph node. All of this data now about BRAF and MEK inhibitors and who goes first in surgery, how would you be thinking about this case, Bruce?

Well, I mean, I think anytime you have an anaplastic cancer. You have to, you have to, with the positive you have to, you know, at least consider whether or not surgery should be first, or if you should start treatment with rapid and intermittent because I think We know over the last couple of years the great responses we see with the drugs with or without immunotherapy. So I think it's always a consideration. I think part of it, just like with any anaplastic cancer, it also depends on receptability at the time of diagnosis, whether or not it's really, do you really need to start treatment, you know, medical treatment or go ahead with surgery first. So I think if it's resectable and, you know, doesn't involve any major structures or vessels, then it's reasonable to do upfront surgery. But if you think you're going to, we know we can get, you know, with so many patients, we get so much benefit from initiating treatment first. So it's always, I think should always be discussed. And it's between, you know, the whole team has to make a decision where to go first. I think it's, you know, this patient, I think, definitely has treatment from me coming. Yeah, I should be pre-op or not. I don't, you know, I think, I think surgery is reasonable, based on everything we've said.

Ashok, help me. Ashok, help me understand, because many of these anaplastics are not are not resectable, and then they go straight to Bruce. Ones like this, I think Rick has made the case, it's not encasing the carotid. This is probably technically resectable. It may not be a lot of fun, but probably resectable. Operate now or try to make it shrink? What do you think in here?

I think, you know, in the past, I would have said three years back, I would have said operate because I can operate on the patient. But I know at the end of the operation, I'm going to be very frustrated and happy knowing the response that we have been seeing on anaplastic, our own cases. I think I'm very excited with the BRAP positive anaplastic to treat them with the new targeted therapy. And you can make a decision in four weeks. Because if the tumor shrinks in four weeks, I will probably go for three months and then operate on the patient. Will this have major impact on the long-term outcome? I don't have the answer. But would I feel more comfortable with the surgery? Absolutely, yes. And I'm saying this based on other cases that we have done.

Bruce, the one thing that worries me, I mean, we know that the BRAF MEK inhibitors shrink the vast majority of these anaplastics, but what if this is a patient that it doesn't shrink, and we missed the boat? I mean, if it doesn't work, this could go to un-resectable, right?

Exactly, and that's actually a point that we bring up for this in many cases when you talk about, you know, a neoadjuvant approach, that you may lose receptability. So I think that always has to be considered. And in this case, I think, you know, again, we have many cases where it's not even a question, you know, for many anaplastic, it's BRAP positive. I think the vast majority, we're going to go with, you know, upfront, you know, treatment with me.

So, but I do think it's it's a very good point and that's one reason I think it's reasonable to do surgery, if it's feasible, with absolutely so they always call me the most aggressive surgeon at Memorial because I'm not the surgeon, and I'm not the patient right so I, I can be very valiant. I pull you over to the side and say, look, can you get this out of there? I mean, I know what's technically resectable, but do you think you can get 99% of this out of here now? So how are you guys thinking about surgery versus the upfront BRFMEC?

So the discussion here is almost, it's echoing what we discussed at McGill with our team, the same specialties discussing, always looking at what's best for the patient. The surgeon saying, you know what, you do so well with your anti-BRAF and MEK inhibitors, let's start there. And then the endocrinologist or a medical oncologist say, well, if you can cut it out, cut it out, we'll see what happens. And so it's amazing how things have changed through my practice past 15 to 20 years. And so we did feel it was resectable. We did take it out. And we really did have good imaging, which showed us, and I felt with our ultrasound, with our CT, we could get it out safely with the patient. And it went well. And here are the slides. It ended up being a tall cell in the thyroid with a metastatic ATC. That's just invasion. Here's where all the stains, PD-L1 positive. And the final pathology showed a BRAF positive tumor, PAX8 positive as well, PD-L1 strongly expressed. Only four to 23 lymph nodes positive. The ATC, as was mentioned before, it was fixed. It was massively invading the muscle everywhere. We got a pretty good resection. We think we got most of it out, but there's for sure some microscopic, probably a little bit of gross disease. And so then we go to the next point and the final point, and the TG. Interestingly, but not so surprisingly pre op wasn't very high the thyroid globulin, because it was so aggressive it forgot how to express the thyroid globulin obviously. And so post up we can't rely on it too much. We suspect that there's something in the lungs. right now, which we see on PET scan on the right and left side. So bilateral lung metastases. And so our current plan right now, and this is all fresh, right to the original, our discussion was, do we give radiation, radioactive iodine, or go straight to targeted therapy? And that was a big discussion after the surgery, knowing what we dealt with. And after a long discussion, we figured we'd treat the primary site with IMRT because we can really ensure that any gross or microscopic disease is taken care of. Our plan right now is to follow with I-131 as per protocol, starting with 150 and then going once everything is gone. But if it doesn't respond to the I-131, if we don't see any take up, then to go straight to targeted therapy so we don't miss that window in the lungs.

Yeah, so Bruce helped me out here a little bit. So I'm trying to figure out when to get you involved and when do we go with systemic therapy, right? Because you're going to have six weeks of IMRT, then they're not going to feel like swallowing for a month or two after that. Now, they'll get the radioactive iodine. We're going to be three, four, or five months down the road before we figure out whether these lung things concentrate. So how do you integrate into all that?

Well, I mean, I'm concerned, you know, with this case, it's an anaplastic. So we know that this patient could be in trouble sooner than later. So I do think, I agree totally, radiation with doxorubicin is very reasonable. And that's what we would do for most of our patients after surgery for anaplastic. So that shouldn't change. I'm not sure how, again, I leave that to the team, but as far as the, you know, radioactive iodine, yes or no, I don't think it's unreasonable to consider targeted therapy now, you know, as soon as that is done, as soon as possible, even included, because this patient has a very high chance of recurrence and death from anaplastic thyroid cancer, I think. So I think targeted therapy, even considering with immunotherapy, Pembro, you know, which seems to give you a longer progression-free survival is a reasonable approach. I would say as soon as possible, I would consider it. I would discuss it for sure.
Yeah, I would too. George, what do you think in terms of timing? Because he's got a well-differentiated component as well.

Yeah, I think timing as planned is quite OK. I think the main concern is local recurrence from the anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. So radioactive iodine can be in a second plan. there was small landmass and sometimes we see CT that does not even show the nodules and have radioactive iodine concentration. So in this case, before planning radioactive iodine therapy, maybe I would consider pre-therapy scan and maybe if it does not show any uptake, I would consider treating focused only in the anaplastic thyroid cancer.

Yeah, so we're winding down the end. I think our approach would be when we start the IMRT, they almost always get a repeat FTG PET scan as part of that staging. So that's going to give you a two-month gap, right? December to February. If the lung things are rapidly progressing, then Bruce is on and we're not doing radioactive iodine. If they're stable, we do CT scans again when IMRT ends. And again, if they're progressive, Bruce is on. If not, it's radioactive iodine. So this is not somebody that you just sit back and watch for a long time. because if those lung mets are anaplastic, they're likely to change in just a few weeks. And I think there could be some good logic, as Bruce said, for just upfront Pembro or targeted therapy. So that would definitely be on the arranged form there. So let's answer a few questions from the audience before we finally down. Mark, was there a couple more on there from the audience about any topic that's still out there?

Yeah. I actually am not seeing anything that is terribly significant that we haven't covered in some form or not here. I think we are good. I have one quick question for George. George, the SUVs on those lung nodules was not very high. Can we take any comfort in that or is that irrelevant?

Well, I think one problem is the size of the nodules. We can have an effect of partial volume, and we are measuring lower than it really is due to the small size. So I would not take comfort relying only in SUVs.

reference_conclusion: Following resection of the thyroid primary and metastatic anaplastic disease, adjuvant IMRT to the primary site was selected to address residual gross or microscopic locoregional disease. The plan is to proceed with I-131 therapy thereafter, beginning with 150 mCi per protocol, provided interval imaging does not demonstrate progressive pulmonary metastases and pre-therapy evaluation suggests iodine avidity. If there is no iodine uptake or if the pulmonary lesions progress, management will transition promptly to systemic targeted therapy, with consideration of pembrolizumab-based therapy for the anaplastic component.
reference_conclusion_quote: And after a long discussion, we figured we'd treat the primary site with IMRT because we can really ensure that any gross or microscopic disease is taken care of. Our plan right now is to follow with I-131 as per protocol, starting with 150 and then going once everything is gone. But if it doesn't respond to the I-131, if we don't see any take up, then to go straight to targeted therapy so we don't miss that window in the lungs. [...] If the lung things are rapidly progressing, then Bruce is on and we're not doing radioactive iodine. If they're stable, we do CT scans again when IMRT ends. And again, if they're progressive, Bruce is on. If not, it's radioactive iodine.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 79-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic disease with bulky retroperitoneal nodal involvement causing right ureteric obstruction and impaired renal function.

[ diagnosis ]: PSMA-avid metastatic prostate cancer with bulky retroperitoneal nodal disease. Right-sided obstructive uropathy was present secondary to nodal disease.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET demonstrated bulky, intensely avid retroperitoneal nodal disease with very high SUV uptake. There was absent physiologic activity in the right kidney, with nodal disease adjacent to the right ureter consistent with right ureteric obstruction. The right kidney was described as non-atrophic in appearance.

[ laboratory results ]: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 19 prior to treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Right nephrostomy/stenting was performed for right renal obstruction prior to lutetium-PSMA therapy.

[ current disease status ]: The patient remained active.

[ other clinical data ]: Severe renal impairment was present in the setting of obstructive uropathy from nodal disease.

That's not a kidney that's, you know, shriveled up and atrophic and there's no point trying to rescue it. Correct.

Yeah, so very low doses to the kidneys. That gives us confidence that one, we could proceed to cycle two if we need. We don't need to be concerned. We don't need to dose reduce or delay treatment. And you can see we did dose reduce for the first cycle because of that low GFR by to 6.8 and he had four cycles of treatment despite such a low EGFR. he's had quite an exceptional response with, you can see that graph of PSA. Happy to see this because a lot of them were actually complicated and a little difficult. I think the bulk of our patients do quite well. This is a nice, happy one. He wasn't climbing ladders, but he was happy to just continue watching his PSA and wait to treat when the time was ripe.
I might just throw to Liz, we've made this point about ladders a couple of times. Liz, do you want to just sort of go over that a little bit?

Yeah, I think when we make people feel better, they think that they are invincible and that they can climb ladders when they haven't climbed ladders for 10 years. So it's a gentle reminder to remind patients that we don't fix everything. And if they fall off ladders, they still break things. So we haven't worked that one out just yet.

Excellent. Is there another slide? Ah, if you want to read more about this case, we published it recently. One of our fellows wrote this up about giving lutetium piercimine in the setting of severe renal impairment. I think a message here is that actually the obstruction was caused by nodal disease and if we can treat the cause of the obstruction, we're not going to make things worse, we're more likely to make things better.
Get a coffee for your urologist and get him down.

Now the problem here is he's had four cycles and along, you know, you can see on that graph, it looks like quite a durable response. I think that graph is actually out to about 15 months. The question is, when should we retreat him with cycle five? What's the trigger for that?

It's difficult, isn't it, because you could consider treating at first PSA rise. Obviously, you'd want to know what the volume of disease is. Do you wait for high-volume disease before you retreat? If you wait for high-volume disease, you can run into problems. It can be harder to get a good response. At the same time, you've got that GFR that's just hovering, so I think it's really tricky.

I think you don't want to wait too long, like especially not, you don't want to wait, like what we've looked at is we don't want the peak to go, higher than the peak at cycle one. So you want to treat a bit earlier than that, but yeah, timing is difficult. It depends a lot on what the patient priorities are. How were the previous responses? Did they get, you know, exceptional responders one, two cycles? Do they live very far away? It's many considerations.

Yeah, I think the message is to have clear communication amongst the team. This patient's not going to be followed up on nuclear medicine in this sort of one and a half year period when they're doing well. They're probably going to be seeing their primary medical oncologist. So it's good to communicate a plan and to check PSA regularly, I think every four to six weeks, you know, not to let the patient go for too long without seeing a doctor. then for the medical oncologist to re-refer this patient when PSA is definitively rising for consideration of another cycle and then we can have a chat in the MDT about when to re-challenge.

reference_conclusion: Following relief of the right-sided ureteric obstruction with stenting, lutetium PSMA therapy was administered with renal dosimetry; the first cycle was dose-reduced to 6.8 because of low eGFR, and treatment was continued for four cycles without further dose reduction or delay given low renal radiation doses and stable renal function. The patient achieved an excellent biochemical response, and treatment was stopped after four cycles. Ongoing management is surveillance with PSA monitoring every 4–6 weeks and re-referral for multidisciplinary review when PSA is definitively rising to consider retreatment with a subsequent cycle.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 3-year-old girl.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected right lumbar mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Right renal Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), post-neoadjuvant therapy radical nephrectomy specimen showing triphasic Wilms tumor with anaplasia; stage II disease due to extrarenal vascular invasion. Eleven sampled lymph nodes were negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial ultrasound-guided biopsy in January 2026 showed tubules lined by columnar cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and nests of immature blastemal cells. Radical nephrectomy specimen showed residual viable tumor involving the lower pole, extending into the mid region and upper pole, pushing the ureter downward and displacing the hilum. Tumor was extensively sampled, including ureteral, hilar, renal sinus, and margin sections. Microscopy showed classic triphasic Wilms tumor with predominant stromal component (>60%), epithelial component approximately 10–20%, and blastemal component approximately 10–15%. Viable tumor constituted >70%. Two focal areas measuring approximately 2–3 mm each showed anaplasia with markedly pleomorphic enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, multinucleated/bizarre forms, and atypical enlarged mitoses. One focus involved stromal component; another involved both epithelial and stromal components. Additional multiple areas showed marked nuclear pleomorphism/nuclear unrest without atypical mitoses. Extrarenal vascular invasion was present. Eleven lymph nodes were negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Outside ultrasound abdomen showed a large lobulated lesion measuring 13 x 6.5 cm in the right lumbar region, displacing the right kidney, likely retroperitoneal in origin. CT abdomen showed a large well-defined lobulated lesion measuring 10.2 x 9.2 x 13.2 cm with epicenter in the right kidney and associated mass effect. Post-neoadjuvant reassessment CT showed a large enhancing solid mass measuring 9.4 x 5.8 x 6.5 cm, reduced compared with prior CT. Imaging demonstrated a claw sign, with the mass arising from the upper and interpolar region of the right kidney, extending into the pelvis and compressing the renal parenchyma. No calcification was seen. No renal vein thrombosis was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: WT1 immunohistochemistry showed variable diffuse staining in the tumor, strong in the stromal component and variable in the epithelial component. PAX8 highlighted the epithelial component. p53 immunohistochemistry showed wild-type pattern in the anaplastic areas. Molecular workup was pending.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: After referral, neoadjuvant chemotherapy was started per umbrella protocol with vincristine and dactinomycin for 4 weeks. Interval imaging showed reduction in tumor size from 10.2 x 9.2 x 13.2 cm to 9.4 x 5.8 x 6.5 cm. The patient subsequently underwent radical excision/radical nephrectomy with Gerota’s fascia and perinephric fat.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status following radical nephrectomy for right Wilms tumor. Residual viable tumor had been present in the nephrectomy specimen. Pathologic stage was II with negative regional lymph nodes (11/11).

[ other clinical data ]: Renal sinus was reported as obliterated by tumor on gross examination. Margins were sampled extensively. No calcification or renal vein thrombosis was identified on imaging.

reference_discussion.text: We invite Dr. Satish from the RELA team to proceed. So Dr. Madhulika is presenting on our behalf. She is our pediatric hematology registrar and Dr. Julius has joined us. Dr. Vidyalakshmi, our pathologist and Dr. Gauripriya, they are also online. Welcome everybody. Very nice to have a board.
Ma'am, am I audible?
Yes, you are very clearly audible.

Good evening everyone. Our case is a three-year-old girl who presented as an incidentally detected right lumbar mass. She was evaluated outside at her native place. So, she imaging done outside was with an ultrasound abdomen which reported a large lobulated lesion.

Your slides are not moving. Have you shared the right screen? Yes, ma'am. We just see one slide here. Now, ma'am? No, only one slide is visible. So just unshare and share the right window. Yeah, now it's OK. Carry on.
Quick. One second. Yeah. Mom, is it visible now?
Yes, Madhulika, it's visible.

Ultrasound was done which showed a large lobulated lesion of size 13 x 6.5 in the right lumbar region displacing the right kidney, likely a retroperitoneal tumor. CT abdomen was done, which showed a large, well-defined lobulated lesion measuring 10.2 x 9.2 x 13.2 cm, noted with its epicenter in the right kidney and having a mass effect, possibly a Blum's tumor. So, she underwent an ultrasound-guided biopsy in January 2026, which the A HPE report suggested tubules were lined by the columnar cells with high nuclear cytoplasmic ratio with crest of immature blastema cells. So then she was referred to our hospital and she was started with neoadjuvant chemotherapy according to the umbrella protocol with vincristine and tantinomycin as a four-week regimen. And she underwent a reassessment with the CEC of them. which showed a large enhancing solid mass of 9.4 x 5.8 x 6.5 cm, which showed a reduction compared to the previous CT. On the left side, we can see that there is a large heterogeneous lesion making a claw sign. And on the right side, there are coronal and sagittal images which show that the mass is arising from the upper and the interpole with the extension into the pelvis with the compression of the renal parenchyma. There were no calcification and no renal vein thrombosis. So, she underwent a radical excision of the tumor along with the geratospacia and the perinephric fat. Next, I will request our pathologist consultant Dr. Vidyalakshmi Ma'am to speak about the HPE.

Thank you. I'll carry on from here. So here we can see the gross image which is cut open of the radical nephrectomy specimen. So there was a residual viable tumor which was involving the lower pole and it was actually pushing the ureter downwards and displacing the hilum also and extending into the mid region and into the upper pole. Now the tumor was extensively sampled. It was mapped sequentially. and multiple sections were taken from the ureter to look for the renal sinus because it was obliterated by the tumor and from the hilar regions and for the margins as well. Next slide please. we'll see the histopathology. So this is a microscopic image. Here we had a residual tumor which showed a classic triphasic Wilms. It had a predominantly stromal component which was more than 60% and followed by epithelial component which was around 10 to 20% and blastomal component was about 10 to 15% in many of the areas. And in the inset we can see the immunohistochemistry. WT1 showed variable staining diffusely in the tumor it was strong in the stromal component and it had a variable staining in the epithelial component and below is the image of PAX8 where we can find the epithelial component highlighted on PAX8 and viable tumor constituted about more than 70%. So next image. So in this we found two focal areas which showed anaplasia. So we would like to discuss more about it. So this was one nodular area within the otherwise non-anaplastic Wimbs tumor which was about 2 to 3 mm and this showed markedly pleomorphic large cells which had enlarged nucleus almost three times size and it had hyperchromatia along with some bizarre forms and multinucleated forms. This was seen in the stromal component in one section. So the next slide please. In these areas we also found atypical large enlarged mitosis. So with this it was taken as a focal anaplasia. P53 immunohistochemistry done was wild type in this particular area. Next slide please. And this was another focus which showed anaplasia again. Here we found the anaplastic cells in both the epithelial and the stromal component. So in this again there were large enlarged bizarre cells and multinucleated hyperchromatic cells. and multiple mitosis which were atypical and enlarged were also noted in this. Again p53 was wild type in this. So in this tumor after extensive sampling and examination we had two areas which were focal showing anaplasia. Let's move on to other slides. Now, there were other areas in the tumor where we found marked nuclear preomorphism. So these, each slide is from, each picture is from multiple areas of the tumor. So we can find that within the epithelial and stromal component, there were markedly enlarged preomorphic cells like what we saw previously. However, we could not find any atypical mitosis in these areas. Now, this was not any atypia related to previous chemotherapy. The changes were exceeding any chemotherapy-related degenerated changes. and this could be taken as a marked nuclear unrest. So with this having two focus of focal anaplasia with any multiple other areas showing nuclear unrest we would thought of considering it as a diffuse anaplasia. So now this point is, this comes under a high risk category. So we would like to have a discussion on how we go about when we find multiple areas like these in a treated case of Wilms tuber. So this was the final report given. So there was an extradenal vascular environment present, so it was stage 2. And 11 lymph nodes sampled from this was negative. So in this, because there was focal anaplasia, which fits with the criteria in two areas, and nuclear unrest found in other areas, we favored diffuse anaplasia according to the SIOP guidelines. a little bit about this. So WHO clearly says anaplasia is defined when you have enlarged atypical tripolar mitosis, marked nuclear enlargement at least three times the size and hypochromatia and all three features have to be present to call some area as anaplasia. So in our case we had two such areas and Focal anaplasia is when you can have according to SIOP is when you have one or two areas with anaplasia but the rest of the non Wimbs tumor should have no other areas of marked nuclear ATP or unrest. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 36-year-old male; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Focal seizures and slow response for 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent/residual intracranial astrocytic neoplasm involving the third ventricular and right temporal regions. Prior diagnosis in 2023 had been pyelocytic astrocytoma. Following resection in 2025, the third ventricular lesion was reported as astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4, IDH-wild type on immunohistochemistry; the temporal lesion was reported as low-grade astrocytoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2023 biopsy/resection: pyelocytic astrocytoma.  
- 2025 resection, third ventricular lesion: astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4, IDH-wild type on immunohistochemistry; pilocytic astrocytoma features were present.  
- 2025 resection, temporal lesion: low-grade astrocytoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain, December 2025, in the setting of prior right frontal craniotomy: focal abnormality centered in the right subfrontal and medial temporal region, around the MCA territory, with a large cystic component.  
- Lesion was T1 hypointense with patchy, heterogeneous/ring-like post-contrast enhancement in the subfrontal and medial temporal solid components.  
- Associated findings included vasogenic edema, including bilateral frontal lobe edema, dilatation/ballooning of the third ventricle, and hydrocephalus. Lateral ventricles were not markedly dilated.  
- Imaging demonstrated right-sided craniotomy defect/postoperative change from prior surgery.  
- Overall radiologic impression was enhancing neoplastic soft tissue mass with increased bulk, concerning for recurrence/residual tumor.  
- Immediate postoperative MRI within 24 hours after second surgery showed postsurgical changes, including air-fluid levels/pneumocephalus, smooth reactive pachymeningeal enhancement, patchy peripheral enhancement at the operative site, and residual soft tissue/residual tumor at the primary tumor site. The cystic component was hyperintense on FLAIR.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-wild type on immunohistochemistry in the third ventricular lesion. No PCR-based molecular confirmation was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2023: Right frontal craniotomy for third ventricular pyelocytic astrocytoma.  
- 2023: VP shunt placement had been performed; subsequent shunt-related interventions/procedures were required intermittently.  
- No prior radiotherapy had been given.  
- 2025: Neuronavigation-guided right parasagittal craniotomy with resection of third ventricular cystic lesion, and neuronavigation-guided right temporal craniotomy with lesion resection.  
- Postoperative MRI after the second surgery demonstrated residual tumor.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative residual enhancing tumor remained at the primary site after the 2025 resections, with residual disease in the right-sided lesion involving third ventricular/subfrontal-medial temporal regions.

[ other clinical data ]: Symptoms had worsened over time prior to the 2025 surgery.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old male; resident of Tamil Nadu; known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Former smoker and social alcohol consumer. No family history of malignancy or known genetic disorders.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain, constipation, backache, urinary straining with increased frequency and poor urinary flow, and unintentional weight loss over approximately 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma with extensive nodal and osseous metastases, with calvarial and dural metastatic involvement.

[ histopathology results ]: Prostate biopsy showed acinar adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 4+4=8. Perineural invasion was present. Lymphovascular invasion was absent. Periprostatic fat invasion and seminal vesicle invasion were present.

[ imaging findings ]: Ultrasound showed grade 2 prostatomegaly with hypoechoic areas in the prostate and a simple right renal cyst. CT abdomen/pelvis showed homogeneously enhancing abdominopelvic lymphadenopathy, prostatomegaly with irregular lobulated contour, thickening of the posterior urinary bladder wall with indistinct intervening fat planes, perivesical lymphadenopathy, mesorectal deposits, and multiple bony lesions. PSMA PET scan showed a PSMA-avid heterogeneous prostatic lesion measuring 6.4 × 4.5 × 7.6 cm with SUV 29.9, involving the prostate and bilateral seminal vesicles, extending to the mesorectal fascia and abutting the anterior wall of the mid and lower rectum, with multiple pelvic and retroperitoneal lymph nodes and multiple bone metastases. MRI brain showed diffuse asymmetric meningeal thickening with enhancement and multiple variably sized calvarial enhancing lesions, consistent with calvarial and dural metastases. No lacunar infarcts or other gross structural abnormalities typical of a primary dementia syndrome were identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Routine hematological and biochemical parameters were within normal limits except for elevated ESR, elevated LDH, serum PSA 150 ng/mL, and borderline hyponatremia. Albumin was 3.9 g/dL. CSF analysis was essentially normal; malignant cells were not detected. CSF meningitis panel was negative. MTB-PCR was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Borderline hyponatremia was corrected. Analgesic treatment with paracetamol, gabapentin, and tramadol did not provide adequate pain relief. Fentanyl transdermal patch 25 micrograms/hour every 3 days provided good pain relief and improved sleep.

[ current disease status ]: At presentation, the patient was conscious but appeared dazed and disoriented, with severe cognitive impairment and complete dependence for activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living. Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 7/27, with deficits predominantly in executive function, visuospatial function, recent memory, and working memory. There was no focal neurological deficit and no clinical parkinsonism. He had bony tenderness over the dorsal and lumbar vertebrae. Abdomen was soft. Digital rectal examination identified a hard prostatic swelling. He remained with metastatic high-volume prostate cancer involving pelvic/retroperitoneal nodes, bone, calvarium, and dura.

[ other clinical data ]: Abdominal pain was diffuse, non-radiating, colicky, aggravated by constipation, and relieved by passage of stool. Constipation was characterized by bowel movements once every 3-4 days, straining, incomplete evacuation, and requirement for laxatives/enema, without obstipation or vomiting. Back pain involved the lower and mid back, was non-radiating, aggravated by movement, partially relieved by analgesics, and worse at night. There was no history of fever or night sweats. He was afebrile, moderately built, and hemodynamically stable on examination. Chest and cardiovascular examinations were normal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Three months of headaches and dry eye, followed by one week of severe nausea and vomiting prompting emergency department evaluation.

[ diagnosis ]: Low-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma of the sinonasal/skull base region, with local extension into Meckel’s cave and the left cavernous sinus. Clinical neck status was N0. PET-CT showed no regional or distant metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside endonasal biopsy demonstrated low-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma with cribriform pattern. HPV testing was negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT demonstrated a sinonasal mass with significant erosion of the lateral wall of the sphenoid and erosion at the foramen rotundum, with lateral extension.  
- MRI demonstrated lateral extension into Meckel’s cave with contact of the medial temporal lobe, and extension into the left cavernous sinus lateral to the carotid artery.  
- PET-CT demonstrated no regional or distant disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HPV negative. No other molecular or genomic results were reported.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No diplopia or cranial neuropathies were present at initial presentation.

reference_conclusion: The consensus recommendation was for maximal safe surgical resection of the primary tumor, recognizing that complete resection and negative margins were not achievable given cavernous sinus and perineural involvement. Resection should prioritize removal of as much tumor as possible without causing new neurologic deficits, particularly diplopia, with acceptance of V2 sacrifice if required. Postoperative radiation therapy was recommended as an essential component of local treatment. Management should focus on local disease control rather than elective surgical treatment of the clinically N0 neck.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old male. No known comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: New-onset seizures and right hemiparesis.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffuse glioma, WHO grade 2, involving the left frontal region.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical pathology reported diffuse glioma, WHO grade 2. The report did not further classify the tumor as astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain demonstrated a large, well-demarcated left frontal solid-cystic lesion with enhancing components and septations. The lesion extended slightly across to the right side, caused mass effect with left-to-right midline shift, and displaced the corpus callosum and ventricles. The solid component was predominantly medial and posterior, with much of the remainder appearing cystic. Imaging appearance on T1 sequences favored a low- to intermediate-grade glioma / low-grade tumor. Postoperative MRI demonstrated a large resection cavity with air-fluid level and intrinsic T1 hyperintensity consistent with blood products. No definite residual tumor was identified; postoperative imaging was interpreted as gross total resection.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular testing was performed. 1p/19q codeletion testing and IDH1/IDH2 testing were not obtained.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Dexamethasone was started for right hemiparesis, with subsequent clinical improvement. The patient underwent surgical resection of the tumor via modified unicoronal incision under general anesthesia. Postoperatively, he was reported to be doing well without neurological deficits. No adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Status post gross total resection of a WHO grade 2 diffuse glioma. No definite residual tumor was seen on postoperative imaging. Neurologically, no postoperative deficits were reported.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion was located in the dominant hemisphere, in a premotor/mesial left frontal region, and extended to the ventricle intraoperatively. The case was performed as a charity case. Financial constraints limited access to molecular testing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old male. Past medical history included hypertension and asthma. He was a never smoker and never drinker.

[ chief complaint ]: Five months of left facial swelling and pain, with progressive trismus and odynophagia. Oral intake had been mostly liquids. Associated symptoms included 20-pound weight loss and two weeks of numbness of the left lower face and chin. He had initially been treated for presumed dental infection with mandibular molar extractions and antibiotics without improvement.

[ diagnosis ]: Invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the left oral cavity/buccal region, clinically staged cT4b cN2b cM0. Primary tumor involved the left buccal cheek/retromolar trigone region with extension into the masticator space and infratemporal fossa, with perineural spread along the mandibular nerve to the skull base. Regional nodal disease involved left level IB and level II nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: Buccal biopsy showed invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT neck demonstrated an endophytic mass involving the retromolar trigone and masticator space, with erosion of the pterygoid plates and posterior maxilla, and involvement of the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles. Tumor approached the coronoid attachment of the temporalis and extended into the buccal space. No clear cortical invasion of the mandible was identified.  
- MRI with contrast demonstrated tumor between the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles with thickening, inflammation, and enhancement of the mandibular nerve tracking to the skull base/foramen, concerning for perineural spread to the skull base. Coronal imaging showed extensive buccal edema and enhancement.  
- PET-CT demonstrated FDG-avid primary tumor centered in the masticator space and FDG-avid level II and level IB lymph nodes. No pulmonary, hepatic, or other distant metastatic disease was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Prior to oncologic evaluation, mandibular molars were extracted and antibiotics were administered for presumed dental infection, without improvement.

[ current disease status ]: Very locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the left oral cavity, clinically staged cT4b cN2b cM0, with extension into the masticator space and infratemporal fossa and perineural spread along the mandibular nerve to the skull base, and clinically involved left level IB and level II nodes. No distant metastatic disease had been identified on PET-CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination showed left facial swelling, severe trismus to approximately 1 cm, and an ulcerated endophytic mass of the left buccal cheek extending to the retromolar trigone, tonsil, lateral soft palate, maxillary alveolar ridge, hard palate, and second and third mandibular molars.  
- Tumor extension onto the buccal cheek was near full thickness without skin involvement and approached the oral commissure.  
- Left V3 numbness was present.  
- Palpable mobile left level IB and level II lymph nodes were present.  
- Endoscopic examination showed no extension to the posterior pharynx, base of tongue, or nasopharynx.
