There's no clear cortical invasion of the mandible, but certainly obviously cortical invasion of the pterygoid plates and the posterior maxilla. And then on the right is just a snapshot of the tumor at the level of the pterygoid plates with erosion of the plates and then clear involvement of the pterygoid muscles. We also obtained an MRI on this patient, and this is a T1 with contrast given the lower lip, lower chin and facial numbness. There was concern for mandibular nerve invasion. So this is a T1 with contrast, and we can see that tumor sort of redemonstrated. And if you look in between sort of the lateral medial pterygoid muscles, and follow it up, you can see that the mandibular nerve, there's thickening and inflammation of the mandibular nerve and enhancement, and it tracks all the way to the foramen. And then this is a coronal, you can see extensive sort of buckle edema and enhancement, and re-demonstrated is the nerve as it goes into the skull base. So we were concerned obviously at this point that there was perigross intraneural or perineural invasion to the level of the skull base. And we did end up getting a PET-CT scan like we do for many of our patients, but especially in someone with pretty concern for novel disease, but it's such advanced oral cavity cancer. We did obtain a PET scan. It redemonstrates that tumor centered in the masticator space and then some level two and level one B nodes that are FDG avid. The scan doesn't show this, but there was no pulmonary or liver or any other distant metastatic disease on the pet. So the buccal biopsy was positive for invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell cancer. We tentatively staged this clinically as a T4B, N2B, M0. T4B, given there was invasion of the masticator space and the infratemporal fossa, the pterygoid plates, and also imaging and clinical evidence of perinatal invasion to the skull base. And so, management of this patient, you know, our first initial questions were, you know, which T4B tumors are considered resectable? You know, we're sort of classically taught that T4B tumors are unresectable. but we know from practice that not all T4V tumors are the same and that we do tend to offer definitive surgery to many patients. And if we do offer surgery, you know, what is the goal of surgery? Is it truly that we think we can get an R0 resection versus, you know, resecting macroscopic disease knowing that we may leave some microscopic disease behind? And what is the goal in terms of, are we trying to truly improve survival or disease control in these patients? or is this more of a palliative surgery as these surgery, I mean, these patients can be very difficult to palliate with non-surgical treatment. And then with regards to skull base management, you know, how much skull base disease is too much for surgery. And then, you know, later we'll sort of get into what the decision-making was at tumor board, but what is the role of, you know, induction or new adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with very locally advanced oral cavity cancer.

Catherine, this is a very challenging case. Maybe we'll start with Peter on this one. What's your thought on discussions with a patient like this? Obviously young, sounds like fairly robust and healthy individual who has obviously a very advanced tumor, the likelihood of getting, well, maybe you can comment on whether you think that it's surgically perceptible or not and how you would approach this in your conversations with the patient.

Sure, I would be very realistic with the patient, starting off with discussing how extensive disease is and what the reality is of every treatment option. You know, the survival rate is not going to be high no matter what we do. But if we do nothing or opt for non-surgical treatments, the outcome is going to be miserable. And, you know, as you mentioned, you know, palliation through surgery might be the best option in any way you look at it. And then is surgery, is the goal of surgery and RZO resection possible? And I think it is possible in this case. I don't think you're gonna get wide margins on this. That's, I think, probably quite impossible to do, but the best chance of this patient surviving with any decent outcome would be to start with surgery. So that's how I would look at it, but have a very frank discussion with the patient about exactly what that means and how big the surgery is going to be and what the recovery is going to be like and the importance of recovering in a way that he can get to the next step of treatment because surgery alone is not going to do it. He's obviously going to need adjuvant treatment as well.

What's your thoughts on the last line there, the consideration of neoadjuvant therapy in a patient like this? A lot of times it sounds great, but in practice, it's always a question of whether it has a role or not. I'm curious how it's managed at your institution. Obviously, I'd love to get Jen's thoughts as well.

Yeah, every now and then we get a patient who really wants to do something like that and the reality is in a situation like this, we don't have a lot of room for this tumor to get worse. So, if we did neoadjuvant chemo or neoadjuvant immunotherapy and the tumor grew, the next place it's going to grow through is the skull base or in case the carotid or you know, or grow in any number of directions. So I think discussing that with the patient would be like, it's very risky, but it could get much worse. And then we're not gonna be left with any other option. On the other hand, you know, there's a small chance it could get better, but I haven't seen that. I haven't seen this play out in a good way. I haven't seen it many times, but the times I've seen it, it's always gone south.
Dr. Gross, your thoughts?

If this was a T4A tumor, we have some trial options for neoadjuvant immunotherapy. I think for chemotherapy, I agree with Peter. It's really all about having a frank discussion with the patient and the family and seeing, you know, sometimes they I feel one way versus another. I think one thing to note is that with the extent of disease and especially intraneural and just the size of it, I would expect there's a very high probability of positive margins with this surgical resection. I mean, it's not impossible to get our zero, but so. Keeping that in mind, I think we are, we do offer chemotherapy, induction chemotherapy in these cases, kind of depending on the medical oncologist because of that reason. And knowing that, you know, regardless of what we offer them, they're not gonna do well. So it's a very unfortunate kind of place to be in.

With regards to the skull base involvement here, it looks like it's primarily perineural invasion. Uh, it looked like obviously the, the pterygoid plates and the, the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles were involved, but as far as bone erosion, and maybe I missed it, it looked like it was primarily going up B3 through a valley into the lower, you know, basically, um, the lower part of the trigeminal. nerve. And so on those, you know, if you're approaching them surgically, sometimes they have a little bit, you feel a little bit better about being able to at least more precisely address the area of concern. I think you recognize it's still going to be almost a certainty there's going to be some microscopic residual disease, at least in my practice. I've never seen one where there's a fat nerve on an MRI that's going through a skull base foramen. that you can then get a very widely clear proximal margin that's negative. You may be able to, you know, I guess the only one is sometimes the facial nerve because you have a larger, you know, area that you can resect of that. But, you know, things like V3, you know, you can sometimes go and find ovale and rotundum, remove the intervening bone, and that gives you a little bit more wiggle room to get up and resect more of the nerve. you know, if, and I'm curious to see in the next slides, what was done here, but if you're going to approach this surgically, what sort of soft tissue approach would you do? And then for the diffuse, you know, even with the absence of bone erosion on the mandible, how would you address kind of the diffuse pterygoid muscle involvement here? As far, as far as that goes, maybe I'll start with you, Peter.

And this is always a challenge, number one, to get to that area. And in a case like this, I would want big exposure, lots of comfort. I would split the lip and peel the face off laterally. We don't need a mandibulotomy because we're going to be taking bone anyway. So we're essentially making a mandibulotomy. And it's probably going to be a hemimandibulotomy in this case, all the way up to the TMJ. So it probably makes the cut somewhere around maybe down the midline or parasympathesis, and then essentially you're creating a mandibulotomy that way. The other part is it looked like it may have been invading the posterior aspect of the maxilla. So I would make that maxillary cut posteriorly as well to kind of detach the pterygoids from there, and then work my way up towards the skull base. And in this case, it may even remove a zygoma and potentially replace it later, plate it back together to get into the infratemporal fossa. But I'd want to get all along the sphenoid bone and the skull base as much as possible to get all the pterygoids and their attachments out as much as we can. That's our best chance for, I think, getting a R0 resection, though we know there's a good chance we're going to be leaving some microscopic disease behind somewhere. And then as I do that, I expect lots of bleeding from the pterygoid plexus. So keep my bipolar up really high, like at 80. Use, you know, other energy devices like ligature or harmonic scalpel. Crank the bovie up pretty high. And just work my way around that with the idea being I want to clear everything off that skull base out of the infratemporal fall zone.
Jen, do you have any additional thoughts on how you tackle it, you know, these tumors extending to the pterygoid muscles?

Yeah, so I think that I've been able to, obviously totally case dependent, do a segmental mandible where you just remove the coronoid, you know, like the anterior mandible, so you don't have to Late or recon the bone and then by. Removing the anterior segment of the mandible there, you can then get access to, like, the lateral terracotta. Origin at the condyle and kind of go all the way to the condor head. If you need to, you can get the entire the terracotta muscles. It also helps. to get the teragoid plates. This patient in particular did have cutaneous involvement, so it made that part, it would make that part a lot easier for access as well. But generally for these patients, it will require some radical parotidectomy just because of the proximity to the parotid. And just the multi directional approach, if you don't have the continuous involvement, you know, obviously, you have to go trans oral trans cervical. I, I mentioned, I don't like doing him and a lot of me if I don't have to. So, with this patient, you know, I would. if there wasn't the cutaneous involvement, extend the incision kind of like a parotid and lift the skin as high as possible to get access because of the trismus and just kind of go from all angles to get what I need to do.

You know, and I think one of the things that's a challenge when things get into the pterygoid is there's so little resistance for tumor spread. And, you know, I think when instances like that happen, it's sometimes at least I've found it's helpful. Think of the muscle going to attach its attachments and depending on the morbidity it would impart, you know, you sometimes need to actually take those areas out on block. So here, you know, if it's extending to the pterygoid plates, you know, you have to take those out. You know, the, you know, depending on how lateral the, um, tumor extension is, you know, it's to the mandible, uh, you know, at, right at the retromolar trigone, it would be a little tricky to save the posterior ramus. If possibly you could, I think I'd have to look at the image again, but sometimes then if you unblock or removing the ramus as part of the resection, then it, it helps to just think about what is it. It's always tight to deliver that down. So what are your attachments? So you can detach. you know, the condyle of the mandible. You can obviously detach the temporalis muscle attachments. You got the spheno-mandibular and the stylo-mandibular ligaments down below. And then a lot of times, mainly what you're set on, if you've made your pterygoid plate cuts, that's usually an attachment as well. You take your distal and your proximal, you know, ECA branches. And then, as Peter mentioned, obviously there's always bleeding either in the pterygoid plexus or in those distal kind of terminal branches off the external carotid going up to, you know, spinosum with the middle meningeal. You'll want to address also coming right back behind the mandible, the auriculotemporal nerve, But sometimes that and the lingual nerve can kind of help guide you towards where that's going up to a valley. Cause they're both going to join V3 near the skull base. And that's usually your last attachment. So you've detached all these other ones cause they're easier to address on the way in. And then it's that last kind of battle to be able to dissect down. And, and, uh, Peter mentioned a great approach, you know, sometimes going from up above, um, you know, either taking down the zygoma and peeling down the temporalis muscle. or if you come at it from below and are able to move the facial nerve branches out of the way and still get access and divide through some of the temporalis, you can get, you know, to the skull base and then, you know, dissect down and looking back kind of back behind where those kind of lateral turquoise plates extend, you can see a valley there and address it almost from up above where the tumor is. These are hard, though, because it's always a challenge. You never, unless you kind of take those wider approaches, you never really feel like you get a legitimate margin when they get into the kind of these muscular beds like this. Well, Catherine, you want to take us through the rest of the case here?

Okay, so So we discussed this patient at our tumor board and we essentially offered two treatment options. One was induction TPF followed by surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation versus surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation. And we did have a frank discussion that obtaining negative surgical margins would be difficult and that his prognosis was fairly poor, especially given the perineural invasion either way. And there was a discussion of proton therapy as an adjuvant treatment for the perineural skull base disease. Ultimately, the patient chose option two. And we did discuss that with induction, you know, chemotherapy, there was no guarantee at all that he would have any regression of disease. But certainly there was potential that he would have progression of disease and he didn't have a lot of space to go there. So the patient underwent surgery, which was a subtotal maxillectomy, sparing the orbital floor with an infratemporal fossa resection. Um, because the, um, tumor and the buckle space approach the skin, we did start with just sort of a wide local excision, um, of the cheek, um, full thickness, um, and we were able to access the mandible and connect that with our neck incision. Um, we did do a segmental or, um, uh, marginal mandibular ectomy of just the ramus and took the coronoid and release the temporalis muscle, which gave us a little more mouth opening. And we did take, release the masseter and we're able to make some of those cuts through the external facial incision. And then we were able to get enough mouth opening after doing those maneuvers to do some of this intraorally as well. We then did a bilateral neck dissection and reconstructed with a fibula free flap. We ended up taking the hard palate basically to the K9 and did a subtotal maxillectomy, resected the pterygoid plates, and then we followed…we resected most…basically the entirety of the masticator muscles with the exception of the temporalis that was sitting in the temporalis fossa…temporal fossa. Of note, so the maxillary mandibular nerve did have positive margins intraoperatively, and so those nerves were followed back to their respective foramen. and were drilled down actually to obtain additional margins, which were set for permanent. We did note, unfortunately, gross disease in the foramen ovale. And then initially in our resection specimen, we had two margins that had microscopic disease, the infratemporal fossa muscles kind of superiorly, and then also the posterior pharyngeal margin. We had to take our cuts kind of almost to the lateral soft palate. Those were actually positive and we had to resect twice and we ended up sending them both for just permanence on final. And this is just a picture of the resection. You can see sort of extended all the way to, we actually ended up having to take part of the commissure. You can see the buckle space and then sort of the maxillectomy. And then posteriorly, you can see the pterygoid muscles that we had to take. And then on the superior aspect is the hard palate and the nasal floor. And then the bottom right shows kind of a superior view of that specimen and the sort of extra oral resection that we had to do. So final pathology, this was a really large 7.7 centimeter tumor with a depth of invasion of 23 millimeters with LVI and gross PNI. The final specimen margins did end up being negative. We were able to clear the infratemporal fossa and pharyngeal margins, but again, they were resected twice due to microscopic disease on frozen. And then the final on the mandibular maxillary nerve were positive for carcinoma with intraneural involvement with the mandibular nerve. And then four of the 31 lymph nodes were positive with major E and E. Um, and so sort of my last set of questions, you know, obviously we discussed that this patient would certainly need chemo radiation. Um, we discussed with them. Discuss that option with an upfront, given just how aggressive, um, locally the cancer was. Um, and then sort of what our other thoughts about this case, um, were, you know, management of skull base disease in the setting of perineural invasion. And so initially on the scan, we didn't see sort of the gross tumor kind of going up to the level of the skull base. It was mostly tracking along the mandibular nerve. And so how far do you chase PNI into the skull base? And what is the role of adjuvant proton therapy in patients with gross paranormal invasion, especially if you are unable to clear that margin? And then the last question is like kind of a loaded question, but how far do you chase a positive margin in a patient like this? How much benefit are they really getting in this setting?

Well, this is a great case, Dr Chang, and thank you so much for putting it together and really amazing surgery. I'll comment briefly. Actually, I know Natalia has been able to join us. I do want to give her a little time to present here in a moment. So maybe we could just go briefly through this. I know my mentor at one point when I was in training always said, you know, your closest margin is your closest margin. So at least my take on chasing margins is if you feel like without a lot of additional morbidity, you're going to actually improve their margin status, I consider doing it. But if it's something where you already have a known positive margin. How much you're going to go chasing after other ones, especially if you're imparting a lot of additional morbidity, is something that I typically would shy away from just depending, because you know at that point you're really dependent on the biology of the disease, whether it's going to respond to this adjuvant therapy or not. Certainly, with proximal nerve involvement near the skull base, we'd consider protons if available here. But at the same time, I think IMRT can also offer it. One question came up from the audience I'd love to briefly get. Maybe I'll have Jen comment on this just because, you know, she was involved in the case. Commenting on the approach to reconstruction, this was, it sounds like accomplished with a fibula. I don't know if there was an additional soft tissue flap on top of that. It sounds like the fibula was used more for maxillary reconstruction since you did a marginal mandibulectomy and left the lower ramus of the mandible. Was there additional soft tissue component or just a massive fibula skin paddle?
So, I'm actually on maternity leave, so I did not do this case. I haven't even seen Catherine in person yet. Catherine, do you want to comment? My, my guess is the city was for the maxilla though.

Yeah. Yes. So, um, we did a one segment fibula to reconstruct the maxilla and we did use a very massive, um, fibula skin paddle. Um, initially we were going to try to do like a chimeric skin, um, skin paddle where, cause we did find, um, a proximal and a distal perforator, but we use like spy fluorescence and actually saw that this like huge, like 15, 16 meters centimeter skin paddle was supplied by that one perforator. And we just de-upped it and sort of folded it to reconstruct the intraoral component. And then at the commissure was sort of where the DF portion, we sutured it sort of to the mucosal, I guess, lip or mucosal lip and then the external paddle within just to reconstruct the face.
So just because this is such an interesting reconstructive challenge, Peter, your approach to that one, how would you have tackled it?
You know, it sounds like a fairly, you know, subtotal maxillectomy, a large soft tissue void that's there, but the mandible itself has continuity in it.

The way I would think about this is a couple of things that don't always come to mind. Number one would be the infratemporal fossa. You're going to leave a big dead space in there if you don't fill it with something. You have some facial skin and then you have some mid-face as well to reconstruct. So I would think I need some bulk. A little bit of bone would be good. You could do this whole thing with soft tissue. I mean, you could say, this prognosis is terrible. Let's do the quickest possible flap just to have a safe wound and get the patient off the table. I think that would be perfectly reasonable. You could do a big rectus, ALT, or latissimus. But if you wanted to achieve all the goals, I think scap tip with a pedicle lat with skin, not necessarily a Tdap, but latissimus with skin would be good. You can also take some serratus anterior if you need to fill in that infratemporal fossa so you don't get this big, hollowed, sunken in look after the patient gets out of your treatment. that'd probably be my first choice. But if this patient wasn't in the best of health and we needed to get them off the table sooner, I might say, let's do something that we can do a little quicker in a two-team manner and maybe just soft tissue, a big ALT or a rectus flap.
Yeah, I think that's a great point.

And, Catherine, maybe I'll have you stop sharing just so we can be getting Natalia's slides loaded up. While we're making that transition, the comment on the infratemporal vasa dead space is a critical one because you're going to basically clear off the entire skull base and then radiate it. So getting some sort of soft tissue bulk in there to fill that, because if it starts to fall down, there's no way to get it back up there. And so, you know, not only getting something in, but trying to tack it up in a way that it's favored to swell and almost push against that bone really gives the best chance of it kind of sealing in. Occasionally you can get these little kind of potential spaces in there that become a big hassle down the road because they're virtually impossible to repair. Well, Natalia Hodges, I appreciate very much you joining us. I know it sounds like you've had a busy day. So thank you for being nimble and being here at UT Southwestern. Welcome to fellowship. I'm glad to have you a part of the session. We're a little late on time, but I think we'll still be able to get through this case. We may just abbreviate it a little more than some, but we'll probably just spill over a little bit past the normal time. So yeah, if you will, why don't you take it away.

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus was to offer either induction TPF followed by surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation or upfront surgery followed by adjuvant chemoradiation, with counseling that negative margins would be difficult to achieve and prognosis remained poor given perineural skull base involvement. The patient elected upfront surgical management. Resection was performed with subtotal maxillectomy sparing the orbital floor, infratemporal fossa resection, bilateral neck dissection, and fibula free flap reconstruction. Postoperatively, adjuvant chemoradiation was indicated, and proton therapy was discussed as a potential adjuvant option for perineural skull base disease.

And there was a discussion of proton therapy as an adjuvant treatment for the perineural skull base disease. Ultimately, the patient chose option two. [...] So the patient underwent surgery, which was a subtotal maxillectomy, sparing the orbital floor with an infratemporal fossa resection. [...] We then did a bilateral neck dissection and reconstructed with a fibula free flap. [...] obviously we discussed that this patient would certainly need chemo radiation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 78-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Found down at home; subsequent CT demonstrated ruptured hepatic tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma involving liver segments 2 and 3, initially presumed and subsequently biopsy proven; presentation complicated by tumor rupture.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT scan showed rupture of the hepatic lesion. Imaging demonstrated a large hematoma with active extravasation. Follow-up imaging performed a couple of months later showed resolution of the hematoma with persistent viable tumor in the previously embolized lesion. No obvious cirrhosis was identified on the available imaging description. No overt peritoneal disease was described.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Bland embolization was performed for ruptured hepatocellular carcinoma. Follow-up imaging a couple of months later showed resolved hematoma but persistent viable tumor.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent viable hepatocellular carcinoma remained in segments 2 and 3 after prior bland embolization. Hematoma had resolved. No overt peritoneal disease was described.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described as unstable at presentation with ruptured tumor.

<image> Axial abdominal CT image showing a left hepatic mass with adjacent rupture/hemorrhagic change, presented in discussion of management of a ruptured liver tumor.
<image> Follow-up abdominal MRI after bland embolization showing residual viable tumor, with the slide posing management options including surgery, locoregional therapy, or systemic therapy.

reference_discussion.text: Great. Moving on. This is a 78-year-old male. He has a segment 2, 3 presumed HTC and eventually biopsy proven HTC who presents, found down at home, a CT scan shows rupture. How do you, Sid, manage HTC that's ruptured?

So he's obviously, I'm assuming he's critically ill, right? So it's your ground rules in the beginning. And so we were presented with this. This guy is, let's say he's unstable. he's going to get an embolization at this point. And in this case, we typically do a bland embolization, whether that's particles or gel foam, it really tends to be dealer's choice. If you have a CT appearance like this with a big hematoma, active extravasation.

So that's what we did. We did a bland embolization, which tends to be our approach. I usually use smaller particles because this might be your best shot at getting any sort of oncologic benefit, at least local regionally. He has viable tumor. This is a couple months later, so you can see the hematomas resolved, but clearly he has viable tumor. He had a big tumor that we just bland-embolized. What do you think about resecting this? He doesn't have at least obvious cirrhosis. Gabe, do you think about resection in patients who have ruptured previously?

Yeah, I think it's still a legitimate option. You know, we used to historically look at the, you know, the rupture as, oh, now they've got disseminated disease. And I don't think that's always the case. I mean, certainly that can occur. We can see peritoneal metastasis, but I don't think it's reliable. And I think that, you know, in someone who's got, without cirrhosis, he's got just in the left lateral section, I think it's pretty safe and straightforward surgery. So, I would offer surgery.
And what do you think about immunotherapy from rupture? Do you think it's a disseminated process or do you think local-regional if we don't have overt peritoneal disease?

I agree with Gabe. If we don't have overt peritoneal disease, give them the benefit of the doubt. And if they're a candidate for a local approach for either surgery or interarterial directed therapy, I think that that would be fine. I would avoid Bevacizumab in a person like this that's had rupture if I was to choose systemic therapy, but they would still technically be a candidate for checkpoint inhibitors if we felt that that was in their best interest either now or down the line.

reference_conclusion: Following initial bland embolization for ruptured hepatocellular carcinoma, the patient demonstrated residual viable tumor on interval imaging. In the absence of overt peritoneal disease or obvious cirrhosis, surgical resection remained an appropriate local treatment option and would be offered. If systemic therapy were required, bevacizumab should be avoided given the history of rupture, although checkpoint inhibitor therapy would remain a potential option.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Sex was female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive lung cancer after prior ALK-directed therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Initial testing identified an ALK alteration. Subsequent broader panel testing identified ATM deficiency, HRD positivity, and loss of heterozygosity of 20%. A rare alteration with allele frequency of 50% was also reported; the gene name was not clearly documented in the available record.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received ALK-directed therapy initially and did not respond. Subsequent treatment with lorlatinib was administered and disease control was maintained for approximately 1 year. The disease later progressed.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer after prior ALK-directed therapy and lorlatinib.

[ other clinical data ]: PD-L1 expression was reported as 98%.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old woman. Gravida 3, para 2, cesarean section 1. Menarche occurred at age 12 years. No relevant past medical history was documented. Prior surgery included cesarean section and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in 2005.

[ chief complaint ]: In the second quarter of 2011, she presented with transvaginal bleeding, lower back pain, and a self-detected right breast lump.

[ diagnosis ]: Synchronous primary malignancies:
1. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, FIGO stage IB2.
2. Right breast invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER2-negative; reported as T1 pathologic, clinical N2, M0, clinical stage IIIA.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy demonstrated invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Breast lumpectomy demonstrated invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 2, measuring 1.22 cm in greatest diameter, with negative surgical margins. The breast tumor was estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, and HER2-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Gynecologic examination initially identified a 6 cm exophytic cervical lesion without parametrial involvement. Subsequent physical examination documented an 8 cm cervical lesion with clear parametria. Breast examination identified a right breast mass at the 11 o’clock position measuring 4 cm initially, without clinically evident axillary involvement at that time; later examination documented an axillary mass measuring 3 cm. Hepatic ultrasound, bone scan, and chest radiograph showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Breast carcinoma was hormone receptor-positive (estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive) and HER2-negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She underwent cervical biopsy and right breast lumpectomy. She then received concurrent chemoradiation for cervical cancer with external beam radiotherapy to 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions, with weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m² and paclitaxel 60 mg/m², followed by brachytherapy to 35 Gy. She subsequently received weekly paclitaxel for 12 doses, followed by AC for 4 cycles. She then underwent axillary lymph node dissection. She received adjuvant external beam radiotherapy and endocrine therapy with tamoxifen for 5 years.

[ current disease status ]: She was under surveillance. No metastatic disease had been identified on documented staging studies. She was receiving tamoxifen.

[ other clinical data ]: Occupation was recorded as farm worker.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old postmenopausal woman. No comorbidities were reported. Family history included lung cancer in both parents and uterine malignancy in a sister.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in March 2025 with left-sided weakness.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma presenting with brain metastases and patchy meningeal metastases; primary site was not identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Excision biopsy of the space-occupying brain lesion showed high-grade malignant neoplasm. Immunohistochemistry was consistent with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. CK7 and EMA were positive. CK20, TTF1, HMB45, and ALK were negative. MIB-1/Ki-67 index was approximately 10–12%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain showed a 1.9 × 2.1 cm lesion in the right frontal lobe and a 2.0 × 1.5 cm lesion in the right basal frontal region.  
- CT showed corresponding avid brain lesions and multiple foci of ground-glass opacities in the right lung, interpreted as suggestive of infective etiology.  
- Repeat MRI brain after excision biopsy showed new enhancing dural nodules suggestive of patchy meningeal metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Targeted/broad-panel NGS identified ARID1A alteration, PTEN alteration, and MAP kinase 1 (MAPK1) in-frame deletion described as loss-of-function/deactivating. PMS2 variant was reported as a variant of uncertain significance.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent excision biopsy of the brain lesion. Received whole-brain radiotherapy with hippocampal avoidance, 30 Gy in 10 fractions. Following radiotherapy, neurological symptoms improved, with improvement in limb power.

[ current disease status ]: At last documentation, the patient was not receiving active systemic treatment and was on follow-up. Clinical status had improved relative to presentation.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination at presentation, ECOG/performance status was 2. Power in the left upper and lower limbs was 3/5. No prior history of hysterectomy was reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female. Performance status was documented as APS 90; KPS 100.

[ chief complaint ]: Right nasal blockage and progressive right eye proptosis for 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Olfactory neuroblastoma involving the right nasal cavity with extension into the right orbit and intracranial parasagittal/right gyrus rectus region.

[ histopathology results ]: Endoscopic biopsy of the lesion performed on 12 November 2024 showed olfactory neuroblastoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain with contrast dated 27 October 2024 demonstrated a contrast-enhancing lesion extending from the right nasal cavity into the right orbit and intracranially to the right parasagittal region. Imaging review described a mass filling the right nasal cavity, causing mild right proptosis, with remodeling of the medial orbital wall. The lesion had an intracranial component in the region of the right gyrus rectus near the midline/parasagittal location. The lesion was T2 hyperintense. Post-contrast imaging showed significant enhancement, with intense enhancement of the intracranial component and heterogeneous enhancement of the nasal cavity component. Coronal and sagittal images demonstrated continuity between the intranasal and intracranial components through the olfactory groove region. There was extension into the right orbit up to the right optic nerve. The right medial rectus was not appreciable, and portions of the right superior and inferior rectus muscles appeared infiltrated. No abnormal signal intensity was described within the brain parenchyma. Postoperative MRI brain with contrast dated 11 December 2024 showed near-complete resection; residual enhancing tissue along the surgical tract was questioned on imaging review. PET scan showed pulmonary lesions suspicious for metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available. CT-guided biopsy of pulmonary lesions had been performed, and pathology results were pending.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially presented to ENT clinic. Endoscopic biopsy was performed on 12 November 2024 and established the diagnosis. Open craniofacial resection was performed on 10 December 2024 using a combined surgical approach involving neurosurgery, ENT, and plastic surgery; the operative approach was described as craniotomy extended to lateral rhinotomy. Postoperative MRI on 11 December 2024 demonstrated near-complete resection.

[ current disease status ]: Status post open craniofacial resection with near-complete resection on postoperative MRI. Pulmonary lesions remained under evaluation for possible metastatic disease; CT-guided biopsy results were awaited. Vision was intact.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had initially presented to the ENT clinic. Orbit involvement was present radiologically on the right side.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic relapse in 2016 with liver and bone involvement after prior treatment for early breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, with liver and bone metastases. Primary diagnosis in 2013 was invasive ductal carcinoma, pT2N0, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-negative, HER2-negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Primary breast tumor was invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-negative, HER2-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: CT imaging at metastatic relapse demonstrated multiple liver metastases. Bone metastases were also present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Circulating tumor DNA testing by next-generation sequencing identified:
- ESR1 p.D538G mutation, reported variant allele frequency 5.9%
- PIK3CA mutation, reported variant allele frequency 13.1%

Both alterations were described as single nucleotide variants and activating.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- 2013: Surgery for primary breast cancer.
- Adjuvant chemotherapy: FEC followed by docetaxel.
- Adjuvant endocrine therapy: letrozole.
- 2016: Developed metastatic relapse involving liver and bone while on/after adjuvant letrozole.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with documented liver and bone disease at relapse.

[ other clinical data ]: Metastatic relapse occurred approximately 3 years after the initial diagnosis.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you, George. And then finally, we need to look at what data is out there, the levels of evidence. So there are multiple tools now to rank the genomic alterations that we find, because genomic alteration is important, the context is also important, and the evidence that we have collected. And in this study in metastatic breast cancer called SAFIRO2, the learning is when you target molecular alteration with a high level of evidence, and in this study they used the ESMO scale that is called SCAT, so level one and level two, these are the highest levels of evidence for molecular alteration, you see that the patient outcome is better. a prolonged progression-free survival when you use structured therapy versus standard of care, whilst if you use genomic alterations that are with less levels of evidence, there was no difference in the study. So with that, we can maybe go to our cases. So the first case is a case of hormone receptor positive to negative metastatic breast cancer with multiple genomic alterations. So we are going to discuss the impact on first-line therapy. How do we prioritize target, but also the input of liquid biopsies? So the patient is a 60-year-old lady who was diagnosed in 2013 with invasive ductal carcinoma. PT2N0, grade 2, estrogen receptor positive, PR negative, R2 negative. She had surgery. She had adjuvant chemotherapy, FEC, followed by docetaxel, and was on an aromatase inhibitor, letrozole, as adjuvant therapy. And in 2016, she presented with a metastatic relapse in the liver and the bones. And you can see here images from the CT scan. And you see the multiple liver meds. So I would like first to ask a question to George. So how important is a biopsy here?

From the perspective of understanding evolution here, it can be incredibly informative, given that the heterogeneity of tumor with this profile, starting from that baseline of being ER positive but relatively high proliferation, we can expect that there will be some degree of genetic instability that can result in heterogeneity. Having a sampling of tumor DNA here would be important through a biopsy here, or in this case, through more comprehensive sequencing by plasma DNA as well.

So this patient had the liquid biopsy. And you see in this slide how we can use liquid biopsies based on circulating tumor DNA. We're not going to discuss today early cancer detection, but this is something to watch out for the future. It's in a very important space for screening for cancer. You can also use that surveillance for micrometastatic disease after the end of adjuvant therapy. And what we're interested here is the treatment selection and response monitoring. And treatment selection meaning that we can identify these alterations in DNA from plasma. So maybe a question for you, Jenna. So can you base your treatment mainly on a liquid biopsy without performing a tissue biopsy? What's your take on that?

I think in general, yes, but it depends a little bit about specifically what alteration you're looking for. I think there are certain types of alterations that are easier to detect in tissue sequencing compared to liquid biopsy, so specifically thinking about P10 loss is very difficult to detect in liquid biopsy. But in this case, with these two targetable alterations that were detected, I think that that's probably sufficient. I would say the other place where we sometimes run into problems is if there's low circulating tumor levels in the liquid biopsy. And so then if you're not detecting something, that doesn't necessarily mean that it's not there. And then I would maybe want to pursue tumor tissue sequencing at that time.

And I think this is such an important point that a negative result, depending on the limit of detection of the assay being used, does not equate with the absence of that molecular alteration in cancer cells. And we have to separate those two concepts. A positive result has one. level of significance in terms of treating the patient here. The absence, depending on the levels of ctDNA in the plasma, may not mean the absence of the alteration. Maybe the absence of detectable ctDNA with that sampling, with that assay. So we need to have this very clear in our minds.
And a question to Bob. So the advent of liquid biopsies, is this a game changer for patients? How do patients feel about that?

I think patients are excited about it, but we're also wary, just in terms of not quite knowing when it's really ready for prime time. I think it has exciting information, but we're looking towards our oncologist to really guide us with how to use that information.

So, liquid biopsy was performed using next-generation sequencing panel and two alterations were identified, a mutation in ESR1, which is a gene coding the estrogen receptor, and a mutation in PIX3CA. So, Dara, can you guide us through the results? So what does the numbers mean after?

Sure. So I'll start by saying that what you're seeing here for ESR1P.D538G, that P dot refers to the protein coding sequence. So in the parlance of molecular diagnostics, a P dot is a protein change, and a C dot is a coding mRNA change. And so you might see those on all of the reports that come out. And it's important to understand that the C dot is there in large part for people like me to be able to read in my lab, to be able to look down to the level of the individual nucleic acid. So if I'm testing a comparator, sample, it's possible to get an ESR1 mutation with the same P. mutation, but different C. mutations. So both of those pieces of information are important. These are both single nucleotide variations, and both of them are known to be activating And the VAF that's listed here at 5.9 and 13.1 is the proportion of all of the reads in the assay that are showing the mutation. And I think it's really important to understand that VAF can be very useful to infer pieces of information, but it's also very easy to over-interpret VAF and draw more meaning out of it than might be there. So I think interpreting VAF is actually very nuanced and is something that oftentimes the data that comes out in the report doesn't give you enough information to fully interpret what a VAF might mean.

So Phil, now I'm going to you. So this is a patient with a hormone receptor positive or negative metastatic breast cancer that relapsed three years after starting adjuvant letrozole. Would these results impact your first-line therapy?

Yeah, so definitely. I mean, I think it's important to know this information. Perhaps it's not entirely surprising, particularly the ESR1 variant, given that this patient is relapsing on litrosol. I think there are a few important clinical considerations. First of all, we want to know how well the patient is clinically, what their liver function is, because the scan that you showed showed pretty extensive metastatic disease. The clinical course is important as well. This is a patient who had a relatively low-risk breast cancer. T2N0 was treated with an anthracycline taxing chemotherapy, then had adjuvant endocrine therapy, and is now relapsing about three years after diagnosis. So that tells you something about the biology, potential endocrine resistance. So in this case with ESR mutation, having relapsed on letrozole, you would avoid, if you were choosing endocrine therapy, another aromatase inhibitor, and would prefer a selective estrogen receptor degrader like Fulvestrin. I think the standard of care would be to consider a CDK4-6 inhibitor as well. And now there's recently a drug approval, and this patient would have been eligible for the ANAVA 120 trial to also consider Inivolisib, which is an alpha-selective PI3 kinase inhibitor that also is a mutant degrader. So those provided that the patient was well and had adequate liver function. Those would be my thoughts in this situation.

Okay, thank you. Yeah, so those were the questions. So, well, based on the guidelines, the patients who had received endocrine therapy and a CDK for a six millimeter, as Phil said, so the in vivo data is not yet in the treatment guidelines, at least for ESMO. I think it was recently FDA approved. And upon progression, what would you do?
I would sequence again. I would get another liquid biopsy and see if there are any potentially new emerging mechanisms of resistance and then think about enrollment on a clinical trial.

So just put a slide about some of the data we have on the mutations. So SR1 mutations in the second line setting can also make patients eligible for treatment with the novel oral SIRDS. So LSS strand was approved by the FDA a few years ago, and yesterday we saw the data from EMBR3. And then I also put the data coming from the SWOLAR1 study, which got Alpelizib approved. And I chose this slide because this shows you that you can be confident in the result of a PQC mutation coming from a liquid biopsy, and you get the same benefit. So when you have different alterations, how do you, and this is a question for Jenna and Phil, how do you prioritize which one to target first?

Well, I think you consider the patient context and then you look at the concept of clinical action ability. So you want to know which mutations are really biologically important and which are associated with predictive benefit from a drug. So in this situation, you have two potential level one alterations that have been identified with the circulating tumor DNA test that can inform your decision making.
As much as we can, I like to try to combine things. So that's why I like clinical trials where you're doing combinations.

Indeed. So I chose this slide from the number one study. So this was a phase one study testing the novel third immunostrant, where there was a combination of immunostrant and alpelizib, which was quite active. So I don't know if there are any questions regarding this case from the audience. We have a couple of questions online. I'll go to the online questions. One question is, are we worried that this patient may have lost the RPR expression? So should we push for a biopsy? And I think you discussed that, George.

In the evolution, we do observe a small but significant proportion of patients that actually evolve to become not estrogen receptor positive anymore or dependent anymore. And I think it's very important, as it was mentioned before, that we understand what is What's the trajectory of the progression? Because there are multiple ways that a breast cancer, an IR-positive breast cancer, can become resistant after all these lines of treatment that we're opting to have here.

And the second question, so I would say this would be for Dara and George also. So when you see multiple clones on liquid biopsy, Do you know which one is actually the driver mutation? Can we assume the one with the highest percentage as the driver?
The short and the long just having the VAF there, no.

Yeah, I agree. I think it's very hard to extrapolate VAF into assumptions about clonality. You know, on first pass for the case we're talking about, you could say, oh, well, the PIK3CA is the driver and the ESR1 is subclonal. That's entirely possible, but there are alternate explanations for those VAF distributions that you really can't exclude. So, I think it's important to understand that when you're thinking about a heterogeneous disease, that all of the ways that heterogeneity can contribute to variable numbers can can be true at an individual site of disease and in the periphery.

And I think it's very important for us to acknowledge here that to understand the clonality, we'd need to derive local copy number information and employ it. And based on a ctDNA assay, this is by no means a trivial task. So I think extrapolating that in a context exactly like this case to say this is clonal, this is subclonal would be very, very challenging.
Thank you. And there are many questions, but I think I'm going to ask the last one. So can you use the variant frequency to monitor response?

Again, I really struggle to suggest that monitoring VAF in isolation can be the best approach. I think when you're putting it in the context of other pieces of information, it is another piece of data that you can use. But again, this concept of global heterogeneity I think can really contribute to VAF being a confounder as opposed to something that is very straightforward. You know, the example of needing local copy number plots I think is really important because, you know, using this PIK3CA example, if one site of disease has PIK3CA mutation and amplification, then you're completely shifting the VAF profile in a way that isn't really reflective of the global disease as much as it is that one site.

Thinking the other way around, if you go on chromosome 6, there is a duplication of the wild type chromosome 6. You look, you see the SR1 mutation, it looks lower VEF, but it does not mean that less cells. I think one interesting concept, however, that is becoming more and more adopted is the idea of molecular responses versus ctDNA fraction when you can calculate that ctDNA fraction, which is still not a trivial task depending on the footprint of your ctDNA assay.

reference_conclusion: Liquid biopsy identified ESR1 and PIK3CA mutations sufficient to inform first-line management in metastatic hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. In the setting of relapse on letrozole with an ESR1 mutation, aromatase inhibitor therapy should be avoided and endocrine therapy with fulvestrant is preferred, with addition of a CDK4/6 inhibitor as standard of care if the patient is clinically well and has adequate liver function. Upon progression, repeat liquid biopsy should be performed to assess for emerging resistance mechanisms and clinical trial enrollment should be considered.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation and management of a left thyroid nodule in the context of planned pregnancy.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, subsequently characterized as RET-rearranged papillary thyroid carcinoma with features consistent with diffuse sclerosing subtype/infiltration pattern. Background Hashimoto’s thyroiditis was present in the initial surgical specimen. Subsequent Graves hyperthyroidism developed in the remaining right thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left thyroid nodule was atypia of undetermined significance (AUS; Bethesda category III). Following left lobectomy with left central neck dissection, pathology showed papillary thyroid carcinoma in the left lobe with metastatic involvement of 3 of 10 central lymph nodes. Background Hashimoto’s thyroiditis was present. On later pathology review/second opinion, the tumor was classified as a different subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma associated with RET rearrangement, with morphology described as compatible with diffuse sclerosing-type features.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound in 2022 showed a solid hypoechoic nodule in the upper left thyroid lobe measuring 1.2 cm, with ill-defined margins, non-taller-than-wide shape, and microcalcifications. Multiple macrocalcifications involved an area measuring 2.3 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E was negative on initial evaluation. Subsequent gene panel testing demonstrated a RET rearrangement in the papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ laboratory results ]: In 2022, thyroid function was normal and thyroid peroxidase antibody was elevated. After the initial surgery, levothyroxine was administered with TSH maintained around 0.1. Nine months after the initial surgery, TSH remained within target range. In October 2023, after COVID infection, TSH was below the normal range with slight elevation of FT3 and FT4; TRAb was elevated. Levothyroxine was stopped for 2 months. In March 2024, TSH was normal and TRAb remained elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent left thyroid lobectomy with left central neck dissection in 2022. Pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma with 3/10 positive central lymph nodes and background Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. She was subsequently managed with levothyroxine suppression therapy. Six months after the initial surgery, there were no signs of recurrence. She conceived 9 months after surgery but the pregnancy was terminated at 11 weeks. In October 2023, she developed Graves hyperthyroidism in the remaining right lobe and was treated with methimazole. She later underwent completion thyroidectomy with right central neck dissection.

[ other clinical data ]: COVID infection preceded the episode of thyrotoxicosis/Graves hyperthyroidism in October 2023.

[ patient demographics ]: 44-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Right lung carcinoma with progressive disease and right pleural effusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease involving bone and paraesophageal lymph node. ECOG performance status was 1. Comorbidity: hypertension.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy was obtained from a paraesophageal lymph node and showed adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CK, TTF1, MUC5AC, and Napsin A; negative for P40, CDX2, synaptophysin, PAX8, and NKX3.1. Pleural fluid cytology was positive for malignant cells.

[ imaging findings ]: Entire right lung was collapsed at the time of current reassessment. Disease progression was present in both the primary site and metastatic sites. Right pleural effusion was present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing was not performed at initial diagnosis because of financial constraints. Repeat tissue acquisition for NGS was being planned via CT-guided biopsy after pleural drainage. The patient had received osimertinib as part of prior systemic therapy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Diagnosed on 3 August. Received 6 cycles of pemetrexed plus carboplatin with osimertinib, with partial response. Subsequently continued on maintenance pemetrexed plus osimertinib. One cycle of maintenance pemetrexed plus osimertinib was administered on 29 September. For bone metastases, received palliative radiotherapy and zoledronic acid monthly for 1 year, followed by administration every 3 months.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease on maintenance pemetrexed plus osimertinib, with progression in both primary and metastatic sites. Malignant right pleural effusion was present. Pleural drainage was being performed via pigtail catheter; the drained fluid was hemorrhagic, and cell block yield was limited due to low malignant cell number.

[ other clinical data ]: Repeat biopsy had not yet been completed and was being planned after pleural fluid drainage and repeat CT imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressively enlarging lower neck mass with local pain and pressure for approximately 1 year. Associated intermittent cough and choking. No dysphagia or voice change at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated insular thyroid carcinoma arising from the right thyroid lobe, locally advanced and unresectable after initial partial resection. Permanent tracheostomy was required following postoperative bilateral vocal cord palsy. Additional diagnoses included extensive uterine leiomyomatosis/fibroids, bilateral non-functioning adrenal adenomas, remote history of right nephrectomy at age 9 years for undocumented indication, and hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma (HLRCC) syndrome due to fumarate hydratase mutation.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside thyroid pathology was reported as poorly differentiated insular thyroid carcinoma, approximately 3 cm, with very extensive angioinvasion, extension into skeletal muscle, high mitotic index of approximately 5 per 2 mm², and extensive extrathyroidal extension. Histologic review described features consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma lineage with aggressive/high-grade differentiated features, including mitotic activity and soft tissue invasion. Tumor testing demonstrated loss of heterozygosity involving fumarate hydratase, and fumarate hydratase immunostaining was negative in the thyroid tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial outside CT neck showed a 9 cm thyroid mass arising from the right thyroid lobe with invasion of thyroid and surrounding tissues, encasement of the right carotid artery, and involvement of the esophagotracheal space.  
- Post-thyroidectomy CT at referral showed persistent right-sided neck mass in the thyroidectomy bed extending to the level of the isthmus, with tracheostomy tube in place. The lesion was inseparable from the esophagus on imaging. Residual invasive mass was present after partial thyroidectomy. Reported carotid involvement/engulfment was described on the formal report.  
- Abdominopelvic imaging showed a multilobulated uterine mass consistent with extensive fibroids/leiomyomatosis and bilateral adrenal masses, greater on the right.  
- PET scan demonstrated FDG-avid neck mass and FDG uptake in the uterine fibroids.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Tumor molecular profiling identified KRAS, PIK3CA, and BIRC3 alterations; no targetable fusion or mutation was identified.  
- Germline testing demonstrated a heterozygous fumarate hydratase (FH) mutation, consistent with hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma syndrome.  
- Thyroid tumor analysis showed FH loss of heterozygosity and negative FH immunostaining.

[ laboratory results ]: Evaluation for hormonally functional adrenal lesions was negative. Hypertension was identified during the initial workup and was medically treated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- At an outside hospital, attempted surgical resection of the thyroid mass achieved only limited debulking, estimated at approximately 30% removal, because of extensive invasion into surrounding tissues.  
- The postoperative course was complicated by bilateral vocal cord palsy requiring permanent tracheostomy and prolonged intensive care unit stay of 9 months.  
- After referral and multidisciplinary surgical evaluation, the residual disease was considered inoperable.

[ current disease status ]: Alive with tracheostomy in place. Residual infiltrative thyroid bed mass persisted with vascular encasement and probable persistent local unresectability.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On evaluation after recovery from the outside surgery, she was comfortable with tracheostomy and had no dyspnea, pain, hemoptysis, or dysphagia; occasional choking and cough persisted.  
- Past medical history included right nephrectomy at age 9 years for undocumented reason and hypertension treated with losartan and amlodipine.  
- Physical examination showed obesity, tracheostomy in situ, a fixed hard right neck mass of approximately 4 cm, and a non-tender mobile lower abdominal/pelvic mass extending into the mid-abdomen. Skin examination was normal.  
- There was no history of head and neck irradiation and no family history of thyroid cancer.  
- Family history included parental consanguinity; mother had hypertension and diabetes; father had died of unspecified abdominal cancer and had a history of nephrolithiasis.  
- She was nulligravid, had never married, and reported regular menses.

reference_conclusion: Multidisciplinary surgical review determined that the residual poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma was inoperable. Molecular profiling was recommended and performed; in the absence of an actionable alteration, treatment with a broad-spectrum multikinase inhibitor was initiated, with lenvatinib producing symptomatic and radiographic response consistent with stable disease. Given persistent unresectability after approximately one year of systemic therapy, external beam radiation therapy should be considered for local control.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Three-month history of worsening deep-seated headaches unresponsive to medication, diplopia worse on left gaze, impaired coordination, dropping objects, difficulty walking, and altered speech/articulation. There was no history of seizures.

[ diagnosis ]: Clival/petroclival meningioma causing brainstem compression, left cranial nerve VI palsy, left pupillary abnormality, and cerebellar signs predominantly affecting the right side.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a midline clival mass with imaging features described as classical for meningioma. The lesion extended superiorly into the suprasellar cistern, abutted both internal carotid arteries, and displaced the optic chiasm with greater left-sided effect. It displaced the midbrain and pons posteriorly and caused slight abutment/displacement of the fourth ventricle. There was approximately 270-degree envelopment of the basilar artery and encasement of both posterior communicating arteries. The lesion also encased and thickened the left cranial nerve VI. There was no restricted diffusion and no susceptibility blooming on SWI. T2 signal was described as very high.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No tumor-directed treatment had been administered. The patient had been discharged home and was awaiting return for surgery.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic untreated skull base meningioma with persistent cranial neuropathy and cerebellar dysfunction. At the time of reporting, the patient was at home pending operative management.

[ other clinical data ]: Neurological examination showed a dilated left pupil measuring 6 mm with poor direct light response and preserved consensual reflex. Visual acuity was unaffected, and confrontation visual fields were intact; formal visual acuity and visual field testing were pending as an outpatient. There was a left lateral rectus palsy without other gross cranial nerve deficits on examination. Dysarthria, right-sided dysdiadochokinesia, and dysmetria were present. The remainder of the neurological examination was normal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old female. Karnofsky performance status was 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial presentation in January 2020 with left-sided weakness. Re-presented in July 2025 with worsening left-sided weakness.

[ diagnosis ]: Intracranial solitary fibrous tumor, WHO grade 2, involving a right parasagittal/falcine midline dural-based lesion. Recurrent disease was documented in 2025 after prior resection.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- January 2020 resection specimen: solitary fibrous tumor, WHO grade 2.  
- 2025 repeat resection specimen: solitary fibrous tumor, WHO grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Preoperative MRI brain with contrast, January 2020: solid-cystic midline lesion above the corpus callosum, centered on the falx, with bilateral falcine extension and displacement of both cerebral hemispheres. The cystic component was T2 hyperintense. The anterior solid component was T2 hypointense and enhancing on post-contrast imaging. Associated anterior vasogenic edema was present. Imaging appearance favored an extra-axial dural-based lesion.  
- Early postoperative MRI brain with contrast after first surgery, January 2020: decompression of the cystic component, right occipital craniotomy changes, postoperative heterogeneity within the surgical bed with probable blood products, small residual solid component in the surgical bed, reactive enhancement, bilateral dural-centered postoperative change, and pathological edema in the surgical bed.  
- MRI brain with contrast, May 2020: interval regression compared with January 2020, with minimal residual solid component, subtle enhancement, associated dural thickening, minimal hemosiderin/blood-related postoperative products, possible tiny residual cystic component on the left, and significantly decreased residual edema.  
- Pre-second-operation MRI brain with contrast, July 2025: marked interval increase in lesion size compared with May 2020, centered in the prior surgical bed and predominantly right of midline, adjacent to dura, extending to the occipital horn of the right lateral ventricle, with additional component left of midline. The lesion was heterogeneous with cystic T2-hyperintense areas, dense solid T2-hypointense areas, multiple enhancing regions, and peripheral enhancement around cystic areas. There was significant mass effect and extension across the corpus callosum, with imaging concern for parenchymal infiltration.  
- Early postoperative MRI brain with contrast after second surgery, performed within 24 hours: most of the lesion had been resected. Residual deep-seated solid component remained adjacent to the ventricle with persistent mass effect on the right lateral ventricle. Residual peripheral/nodular enhancement was present, greatest along the anterior and lateral aspects near the ventricle. Additional postoperative blood products, postoperative scalp changes, residual lesion component along the left side of the falx, and persistent surrounding vasogenic edema, greater in the right cerebral hemisphere, were present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- January 2020: neuronavigation-guided resection of the right parasagittal lesion was performed.  
- Postoperative imaging in January 2020 and May 2020 demonstrated residual disease with interval postoperative regression but persistent minimal residual solid component.  
- Adjuvant radiation therapy was advised in 2020 because of residual disease but was not received.  
- July 2025: repeat surgery was performed for recurrent enlarging lesion. Early postoperative MRI demonstrated subtotal resection with residual enhancing deep-seated disease.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent solitary fibrous tumor, WHO grade 2, status post second resection in 2025, with residual enhancing tumor in the surgical bed adjacent to the ventricle, residual component along the left falx, and persistent surrounding vasogenic edema.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- CT neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis for staging showed no evidence of extracranial disease.

Conventional fractionated external beam radiotherapy should be delivered within 6 weeks of surgery using IMRT or VMAT rather than SRS, with a dose in the range of 54–60 Gy, favoring the higher dose range if organ-at-risk constraints permit. Chemotherapy has no established role in this case. Dexamethasone with PPI cover should be initiated before radiotherapy and tapered during and after treatment as clinically tolerated.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Sex was male. Performance/fitness was described as fit.

[ chief complaint ]: Symptomatic local pelvic disease with hematuria and requirement for Foley catheter at the time of recent progression.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic high-risk, high-volume prostate carcinoma diagnosed in March 2023, with subsequent neuroendocrine transformation. Disease progression occurred in the prostate and iliac lymph nodes after platinum-based chemotherapy plus immunotherapy.

[ histopathology results ]: Neuroendocrine transformation was documented. Ki-67 proliferation index was 80%.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET was normal at the time of neuroendocrine progression. FDG PET demonstrated disease in the prostate and iliac nodal region. After 3 cycles of etoposide/carboplatin plus toripalimab, iliac nodal disease increased in size and new nodal disease appeared. No disease was identified outside the prostate and iliac nodal sites on the available imaging before radiotherapy. No post-radiotherapy imaging had yet been performed; reassessment imaging was planned after 12 weeks from radiotherapy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No patient-specific molecular/genomic alteration was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was normal at the time FDG PET identified recurrent/progressive disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Orchiectomy was performed after diagnosis. The patient received docetaxel with abiraterone for high-risk, high-volume disease, followed by abiraterone maintenance for approximately 2.5 years. On subsequent progression with neuroendocrine-transformed disease, the patient received 3 cycles of etoposide/carboplatin plus toripalimab. Disease progressed on this regimen, with increase in iliac nodal size and appearance of new nodes. Curative-dose radiotherapy was then delivered to the involved sites for symptomatic progression. Following radiotherapy, symptoms improved; the patient was off Foley catheter and hematuria had resolved.

[ current disease status ]: Following radiotherapy, the patient was clinically improved and somewhat better symptomatically, with no hematuria and no Foley catheter requirement. Biological/radiological post-radiotherapy response had not yet been assessed. The last documented disease distribution before radiotherapy remained confined to the prostate and iliac lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: Platinum plus immunotherapy had already been administered before the latest local radiotherapy. No other metastatic sites were reported on the available pre-radiotherapy imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 48-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of a right-sided cervical lymph node identified on surveillance ultrasound after prior treatment for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, right-sided, previously staged pT2Nx status post total thyroidectomy. Subsequent ultrasound demonstrated a suspicious right level IV cervical lymph node measuring 8 mm, concerning for persistent or recurrent nodal disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound demonstrated an 8 mm right-sided level IV lymph node.

[ laboratory results ]: Suppressed thyroglobulin was 1. Thyroglobulin antibodies were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Total thyroidectomy had been performed approximately 2 years earlier for right-sided papillary thyroid carcinoma, staged pT2Nx. Radioactive iodine treatment had been administered after thyroidectomy approximately 2 years earlier.

[ current disease status ]: Small-volume structural cervical disease was suspected on ultrasound, consisting of a subcentimeter right level IV lymph node. No additional objective current disease data were available.

[ other clinical data ]: No biopsy result for the lymph node was available. No operative pathology details beyond pT2Nx were available. No cross-sectional imaging, functional imaging, or molecular/genomic data were available.

reference_conclusion: For a subcentimeter right level IV lymph node after prior total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine, the panel favored confirmation with biopsy only after discussion of localization and resectability with the surgeon, while recognizing the potential for ultrasound false positivity. Given the low-volume lateral neck disease, the preferred management is active monitoring with serial surveillance rather than empiric radioactive iodine or immediate surgery. If the lesion is not resectable and requires further evaluation, thyroid hormone withdrawal with I-124 PET/CT may be used to assess iodine avidity and guide radioactive iodine therapy; absence of uptake would indicate iodine-refractory disease and treatment-dose radioactive iodine would not be pursued.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Bilateral nasal obstruction and right-sided epiphora for approximately 2.5 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Grade 2 sinonasal chondrosarcoma, staged as T4aN0. PET-CT showed no regional or distant metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy demonstrated grade 2 chondrosarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging showed a very large mass filling the sinonasal cavity with significant extension into both orbits, greater on the left than the right. There was erosion of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa, erosion into the orbits, and mild maxillary erosion. MRI sequences including T1 post-contrast, fat-suppressed, and T2 images demonstrated the extent of intraorbital extension. PET-CT showed no regional or distant metastatic disease.

[ current disease status ]: No regional or distant metastatic disease had been identified on PET-CT at diagnosis.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination, there was hypertelorism, bilateral proptosis, expanded nasal bones, and a nasal mass visible on anterior rhinoscopy. There were no cranial neuropathies, vision was normal without reduced visual acuity or diplopia, and there were no neck masses.

Assuming that, you know, we were able to kind of peel things off the periorbita and peel things off the dura, but we didn't actually have to, but we didn't resect the periorbita on either side. We didn't resect the dura. So it was kind of gross total resection with, you know, in a case like this, it's kind of hard to ever know that you truly cleared all of the, the margin surgically do you primarily radiate a grade two converse arc up front, or not. And what modality.

Typically only would radiate if there was gross residual disease, otherwise I'd recommend monitoring. This is a young patient and I think likely to do well without radiation. If radiation is required, the dose is high. We typically give 70 gray and again, target the gross residual disease that we see on a scan. So I would not recommend radiation for this patient. I would recommend if there was residual proton radiation to be able to achieve a high dose with a, sparing of healthy tissues and avoidance of tissues and risks for, again, a young patient who has many years to live after radiation, we hope.

Yeah, for sure. Thank you so much. So I think we can go ahead and just finish up this case and move on to the next one. So I think we did exactly what the panel suggested. We did a bilateral purely endoscopic resection. We did not need to reconstruct the orbits. We deferred any adjuvant therapy. She's four or five years out. She's doing great. So yeah, that's the first case. We should move on to the second one, Dr. Jolie. Thank you.

reference_conclusion: The consensus management was bilateral purely endoscopic endonasal resection with the goal of gross total excision while preserving both orbits if feasible. The bony skull base would be resected as indicated, with dural resection only in the presence of gross dural invasion and multilayer skull base reconstruction if the dura were entered. Orbital reconstruction would be avoided if the periorbita remained intact and the defect was not expected to cause significant enophthalmos. No adjuvant radiation was recommended after gross total resection; surveillance was favored, with proton radiation reserved for gross residual disease.

If there was clear sort of gross invasion of the dura, I would resect the dura. And, you know, I would certainly tackle this endoscopically. You know, reconstruction-wise, if we had to take down the dura, I would do a multi-layer closure with a pericranial flap as the last sort of layer covering everything. [...] if the periorbita is intact, generally, unless it's a huge, huge bony defect, yeah, and in most cases, you can get away with not reconstructing the lamina and the floor. [...] So I think we did exactly what the panel suggested. We did a bilateral purely endoscopic resection. We did not need to reconstruct the orbits. We deferred any adjuvant therapy.
