reference_discussion.text: Okay, well, indications for brachytherapy would be, you know, a tumor that's generally under four centimeters in maximum dimension. The patient has to be circumcised first, if they have not been circumcised, and the tumor should not straddle the coronal sulcus. So, assuming we've got a patient that fits that, there are two basic ways of doing the brachytherapy. The traditional way was a low dose rate implant. Much of the historical literature was manually afterloaded implants using iridium wires. But now this can be done with a pulse dose rate machine, which treats the patient at the same dose rate. So it's still a low dose rate implant given in pulses once per hour. And the effectiveness and the radiobiology is the same. So it's usually two or three planes of needles, four to nine needles in total. The spacing is prescribed. The dose would be 60 to 65 gray. And that takes four to five days in hospital. And what you see in the top picture there is just a styrofoam slab that holds the penis separated from the other normal tissues. You can see in the lower slide that he's got the styrofoam plate under the implant just to distance it a little bit because this radiation doesn't go very far and a little bit of distance makes a big difference. And the bottom slide shows the pulse dose rate machine connected with cables to each of the needles. It's not as uncomfortable as it looks. They usually need minimal analgesia, but they are in hospital for the four to five days. Next slide. That's a result of one patient eight years after his implant. You can see the depressed white scar just proximal to the meatus. And, you know, he has excellent cosmesis, excellent function, and he's, you know, very happy with his results. Next slide. Now most of these would be done with a high-dose rate implant, and this is, you know, radiobiologically quite different. The approach is a little different. This guy was only 36 when he had his diagnosis. He had an excisional biopsy with positive margins. His urologist says it has to come off, and he said, no way. He found his way to me, and I did a HDR brachytherapy procedure. You can see the implant slide up in the top corner there. It looks like a lot of needles. There are actually only three in tissue, and the other three are just adjacent to the penis with some tissue-equivalent material in between. And that ensures that you're getting a full, even dose to the skin's surface. So it's just a way of improving the cosmesis, and the coverage without any trauma to the patient or the penis. And he's without evidence of disease 10 years later. And this is done with two treatments per day, usually over a six-day period. And again, they're usually in hospital because this is, you know, it's not that they're radioactive, but it's just, you know, they can't really be very mobile.

Next slide. Can I ask you one question there? So low dose versus high dose, the biggest thing I heard you mention is that the high dose, they're only receiving two to three treatments, whereas low dose, they're going to get more frequent treatments. Is that correct?

Yeah. It's actually low dose rate versus high dose rate. So the low dose rate implant gives a higher dose continuously over that five or six day period, whereas the high dose rate gives a lower dose, but gives it very quickly. So radiobiologically, it's more effective with a lower total number of gray delivered.

Let me break it down from my understanding as the urologist here. You know, when we looked at low dose brachytherapy for prostate cancer, you implant all the slaves and they stay there. In this case, you're putting the seeds in there, but you're not leaving the wires or whatever you're using for your radioactive source. You're not leaving them in there per se. You're providing a venue for them to stay in there and deliver radiation over a longer period, whereas the high dose is similar. You're putting in a seed or a wire that's coming out sooner. Is that correct?
That's correct. And for prostate, it's all delivered while they're under anesthetic. So it's, you know, it's delivered over 20 minutes instead of six months for prostate. Right. OK. But we diverge.
Great. Great.

This is another HDR example. This guy was 72 at an HPV positive squamous cell cancer. He'd had multiple local excisions, which left some deformity in his glands because he always refused penectomy. And the surgeon finally threw up his hands and said, we cannot take any more bits. It has to come off. And he refused. So I treated him with high-dose rate brachytherapy using, again, two templates. This gives you more flexibility than with a low-dose rate implant in that you can put the needles where they're needed. It looks like a lot of needles, but if you look at that picture in the top right corner, there's only six needles that are in tissue. And the ones in the arc around the outside are outside the penis for the same reason, as I already explained, to modulate the dose and make sure that you get full dose to the skin surface without hot spots. So it was six interstitial needles and eight that were just around the outside. And this treatment was given over seven days. Afterwards, he's disease-free. Five years later, he has the deformities from the previous excisions, but tumor-free. Next slide. This can be done in other centers without templates. Now, this means that all needles are interstitial, embedded in the penis, because you don't have any template to hold things adjacent. But this is from Jay Seesky at the Cleveland Clinic. And similar fractionation, six-day treatment, but plastic needles and no templates. Next slide. And this is from Peter Johnson's group at the Lee Moffitt Cancer Center, and they've actually turned the HDR brachytherapy into an outpatient treatment. They also see the advantage of using the template and having the needles adjacent to the penis, but the templates are very, very light. You can put the whole thing into a jockstrap and the guy can go home or stay at an adjacent lodge or hotel and just come back twice a day for his treatments. Next slide. And they do get acute moist desquamation that can take a couple of months to heal up. And it's just basically cleanliness and hygiene, which will help it heal. There are other things that can be added if necessary, such as antibiotics or steroids, whatever. But they generally heal up pretty well. Next slide. You can also get a complication called radiation necrosis or ulceration. This is more common with deeply invasive bigger tumors, which makes sense, and can be quite painful. But these will heal after hyperbaric oxygen treatments, as in this example here. Next. Oh, anyway, that's all I was going to say about this one. The radiation necrosis in those smaller tumors is extremely uncommon. You do get some ulceration, but that heals with just local hygiene. But as I said, the deeper, more invasive cancers, you can get deeper necrosis.

So Dr. Kirk, that's impressive. This is really, really good for all of us to see what you're capable of doing. I have a couple questions for you. So you mentioned that, you know, you must be circumcised and the tumor must be located to basically the glands. Is that right? So if you have a tumor that's more proximal or invasive, more into the corpora, mid-shaft or something like that, are they not necessarily a candidate?

They can be. The ABS guidelines suggest that this should be limited to tumors on the glands. But I know of colleagues who have treated mid-shaft tumors. And I mean, it works just as well. It's just a bit more complicated. It's not something you do for your first case.

Right. Well, this is really, really good information. And I think there's a lot of urologists and folks out there that don't even know that we can do this or this is possible. So really good to see. I really appreciate you enlightening us here because often, you know, we're not thinking I would ask that, do you think that a radiation oncologist community who has a specialty in brachytherapy, no matter what, would be able to do this? Or is this someone that's highly selected that's done it before? Or how would you approach that?

There are videos out there. The ABS and other Canadian societies do workshops. So we try to teach as many people as possible how to do it. I also get emails for advice. How do I do this? What do I go about? And so there's counseling that can happen as well. Technically, it's not hard to do. It's you're putting needles into an area that is very accessible. So it's not difficult and you just follow the guidelines.

reference_conclusion: For appropriately selected penile tumors, brachytherapy is an organ-preserving treatment option when the lesion is generally less than 4 cm, the patient is circumcised, and the tumor does not straddle the coronal sulcus. Treatment may be delivered as low-dose-rate or pulse-dose-rate interstitial brachytherapy to 60–65 Gy over 4–5 days in hospital, or more commonly as high-dose-rate brachytherapy administered twice daily over approximately 6–7 days. Acute moist desquamation and limited ulceration are managed primarily with local hygiene, with antibiotics or steroids if needed; deeper radiation necrosis or ulceration in more invasive tumors may heal with hyperbaric oxygen treatment.

The patient has to be circumcised first, if they have not been circumcised, and the tumor should not straddle the coronal sulcus. [...] The dose would be 60 to 65 gray. And that takes four to five days in hospital. [...] Now most of these would be done with a high-dose rate implant [...] And this is done with two treatments per day, usually over a six-day period. [...] And this treatment was given over seven days. [...] They do get acute moist desquamation that can take a couple of months to heal up. And it's just basically cleanliness and hygiene, which will help it heal. There are other things that can be added if necessary, such as antibiotics or steroids, whatever. But they generally heal up pretty well. [...] You can also get a complication called radiation necrosis or ulceration. [...] But these will heal after hyperbaric oxygen treatments

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old woman. No comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable right breast tumour.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast invasive lobular carcinoma, stage IIIC at initial diagnosis in 2014; pathologic nodal status showed 14 metastatic lymph nodes of 16 examined after mastectomy and axillary dissection. Subsequent metastatic progression to bone in 2015 and later to liver.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the breast mass showed invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 2. Surgical histology after right mastectomy confirmed infiltrating lobular carcinoma. Fourteen of 16 axillary lymph nodes contained metastases. Hormone receptor/HER2 reporting in the record was inconsistent; ER was reported as strongly positive (3+), PR as 1+, and HER2 status was described as positive in later clinical discussion, although the original immunohistochemical notation was unclear.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- At presentation in 2014, chest CT demonstrated a right breast mass measuring approximately 3.6 cm with ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy.  
- Initial staging information available from chest imaging indicated no lung metastases; no abdominal staging at presentation was documented.  
- In 2015, CT identified multiple bone metastases involving the sternum, coccyx, mandible, and humeral head.  
- Bone scintigraphy confirmed osseous metastatic disease with hyperfixation in the vertebrae, sternum, greater trochanter, and coccyx.  
- Liver metastases were identified approximately one month before the case review.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Hormone receptor/HER2 data were incompletely and inconsistently documented. Reported biomarkers included ER 3+, PR 1+, and an unclear HER2 immunohistochemical result; HER2 positivity was referenced subsequently, but no confirmatory in situ hybridization or other genomic testing was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Right mastectomy with radical axillary dissection was performed in 2014.  
- Adjuvant chemotherapy: 6 cycles of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and fluorouracil.  
- Toxicities during chemotherapy included grade 3 vomiting and alopecia.  
- Adjuvant radiotherapy was delivered at 2 Gy per fraction, Monday to Friday, to a total dose of 40 Gy to the right chest wall/scar and axilla; regional nodal fields including supraclavicular/infraclavicular/parasternal areas were included in the treatment field documentation.  
- After diagnosis of bone metastases, treatment included letrozole and zoledronic acid.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with documented bone metastases and subsequent liver metastases despite prior surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy, endocrine therapy, and zoledronic acid.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Primary tumour was described clinically as a 3.5 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast with two mobile ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes at presentation.  
- Initial clinical stage notation was corrected in the record from T3 to T2; M0 was documented at initial diagnosis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old female. Gravida 5, para 2, abortion 3. Never smoker. No family history of cancer. Obesity with body mass index 34 kg/m².

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for management after incidental identification of invasive cervical squamous cell carcinoma following prior excisional procedure and subsequent hysterectomy. The patient had been asymptomatic.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, FIGO 2018 stage IA2.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial Papanicolaou smear was suspicious for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (CIN 2/3). Subsequent colposcopy-directed cervical biopsy confirmed high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion without suspicious invasion. Excisional procedure (LEEP/conization) demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma in situ measuring 1 cm, with glandular involvement; the endocervical margin was positive for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion/CIN 2/3. Pathology review at the receiving institution confirmed the same findings in the excisional specimen. Review of the hysterectomy specimen by two pathologists demonstrated invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix with 2.5 mm horizontal spread and 5 mm stromal invasion, no lymphovascular space invasion, and negative surgical margins.

[ imaging findings ]: Pelvic MRI showed no evidence of disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial evaluation and treatment were performed at another institution. After abnormal cervical cytology and confirmatory biopsy, the patient underwent LEEP/conization. Two months later, she underwent total laparoscopic extrafascial hysterectomy. Following referral, physical examination showed no evidence of residual disease, and pelvic MRI showed no evidence of disease.

[ current disease status ]: No clinical or radiologic evidence of residual disease after hysterectomy. Physical examination was normal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old man. Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) 100.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented to the emergency department with generalized tonic-clonic seizure and behavioral changes of 6 months’ duration.

[ diagnosis ]: Bifrontal atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2, status post neurosurgical resection.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from the resected lesion was consistent with atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain with contrast performed in August 2025 demonstrated homogeneously enhancing lobulated bifrontal extra-axial lesions attached to the falx and anterior meninges.  
- Lesions showed surrounding vasogenic edema and mass effect on the ventricles and corpus callosum.  
- Signal characteristics included heterogeneous T2 signal, relatively isointense to gray matter.  
- No hydrocephalus was identified.  
- Postoperative MRI demonstrated hemorrhage in the surgical bed, marginal enhancement around the resection cavity, and enhancement along the anterior bifrontal dura.  
- Post-surgical hemorrhagic change and edema were present, with some relief of mass effect after surgery.  
- Small residual disease could not be excluded on postoperative imaging; overall, good/maximum resection was described.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent neuronavigation-guided bifrontal craniotomy with maximum safe resection of the lesion in August 2025.  
- Postoperative imaging showed postoperative hemorrhagic change and edema with reduced mass effect; possible small residual enhancing tissue remained indeterminate.

[ current disease status ]: Status post maximum safe resection of bifrontal WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma. Postoperative MRI showed postoperative cavity enhancement and anterior dural enhancement; residual disease was not definitively confirmed but could not be excluded.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Large bifrontal extra-axial lesion with dural/falcine attachment.  
- Behavioral symptoms had been present for 6 months before presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Demographic data were not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Right frontal lobe brain tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Grade 3 oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, located in the right frontal lobe in or very near the motor cortex/corticospinal tract region.

[ histopathology results ]: Histology showed an infiltrating glioma with oligodendroglial morphology, including relatively round nuclei with perinuclear halos. Tumor heterogeneity was present, with areas of low cellularity and areas of increased cellularity with more back-to-back cells. Mitotic activity was identified. Ki-67 proliferation index was reported at 10-12%. Under the 2007 WHO classification, the tumor was reported as anaplastic oligoendroglioma (grade III). Under current WHO terminology, it was classified as oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant, and 1p/19q-codeleted, grade 3.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI demonstrated an area of abnormally bright signal intensity in the right frontal lobe on T2-weighted imaging, with little to no corresponding contrast enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted imaging. Functional MRI and DTI tractography demonstrated the lesion to be either within or very close to the motor cortex, with the tumor closely associated with motor hand activation areas and adjacent corticospinal motor fibers. Postoperative imaging demonstrated resection of the vast majority of the tumor, with possible small residual tumor along the posterior aspect of the resection cavity.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation was detected by PCR. 1p/19q codeletion was present. MGMT promoter was unmethylated. Chromosome 10 findings were reported without EGFR amplification.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgical resection using intraoperative cortical and subcortical motor mapping/neurophysiologic monitoring because of proximity to eloquent motor pathways. Gross resection was limited by involvement of functional motor structures. The vast majority of tumor was resected, with a small posterior rim of residual disease possibly left to preserve motor function. The patient remained neurologically intact with preserved motor strength and function postoperatively.

[ current disease status ]: Status post subtotal resection of a right frontal grade 3 oligodendroglioma with possible small residual tumor along the posterior resection margin; neurologically intact in motor function after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion was described radiographically as non-enhancing and consistent with a lower-grade appearing tumor despite grade 3 histopathologic features.

reference_discussion.text: Sure. So again, we have our classic T2-weighted image, and this looks to be a post-contrast T1-weighted image. And we do see, again, an area of abnormally bright signal intensity. in the right frontal lobe, but in contrast to the cases we saw previously, we don't really see much in the way of enhancement of that same area. So in this case, we would be concerned for tumor as we were previously, but the fact that there's no contrast enhancement would suggest that this may be a lower grade tumor.
So I'll have Dr. Everson discuss the surgery decision.

Yeah. So as Dr. Pope described, what we think we're dealing with here is a lower grade tumor. Anatomically, it looks like it's located either within or very close to a very functional and eloquent part of the brain called the motor cortex. And with our fMRI and DTI mapping, we can outline that. And we're overlaying here the motor fibers in green with the motor hand activations, which are seen there in yellow, and the tumor, which is seen in purple. And as you can see, it's really pretty wrapped up or at least adherent to one side of that really critical connection between the motor cortex of the brain in the cortical spinal tract, which travels through the brain into the spinal cord and out into the distal musculature, which allows for movement. So if we cut or interrupt that with our surgery, we can cause paralysis that may be irreversible. So any manipulation in this area has to be done extremely carefully. The second feature is because it's one of these non-enhancing, what appears to be potentially lower grade tumors, we know that they often have a pretty indistinct margin. It's hard to tell under the microscope even where the tumor begins and ends. They grow more in a gradient fashion. There's not a clear idea of exactly where to stop, especially when you're in a homogeneously appearing subcortical portion of the brain. In this case, we can't look just visually at what happens with the tumor, we have to use physiology. And our next slide outlines kind of the techniques that we do. You know, the brain, the nervous system is all electrically mediated. We can test and find the resulting sort of activation of this motor system by putting a strip of electrodes on the brain over the region of interest. And we can stimulate a little current through each one of those silver electrodes. And we can find which area results in movement, you know, the motor system being activated. that helps us outline where it begins and ends. We measure that in real time with neurophysiology team, looking there at the responses on a monitor and seeing the different waveforms. And we can see that in that middle graph there that we get the most robust activation of the motor fibers over a certain area of the brain. That gives us a map of where we can go in. Once we're on the inside though, we have to continue our physiologic mapping. As we start our resection, we're probably going to start as far away from the motor fibers as possible and continue to shave down or remove tumor bit by bit, getting closer and closer while we're monitoring to make sure that we do not enter into the motor fibers. I think Dr. Kibben's talk earlier may have explained how we do this, but basically we can stimulate Now the subcortical, deeper parts of the brain with a electrode, and that's what's depicted here on the right-hand side. And we can do that each time to see if we trigger a motor response at a given amount of amperage. And as we get closer and closer to the actual tracks, the amount of stimulus required to trigger that response will get smaller and smaller until we're right on it. And that tells us really, how far we have, how much of a margin do we have before we really enter into those motor fibers? And that gives us an idea of where to stop removing tumor as it could be entering into those motor fibers and further resection would result in potentially irreversible paralysis. So when we use those kinds of techniques in something like this, we're taking it out in a different technique altogether. This we're sort of shaving down bit by bit a portion of the tumor, whereas in the previous cases, we might be able to cut all the way around it and remove the tumor in a single solitary piece. So very different approach surgically, a different operation altogether, but using these kinds of techniques to keep everything safe, we can still accomplish a lot. Now, knowing that this is wrapped up in the motor, we're probably not going to be able to remove 100% of it, but we can remove the vast, vast majority and leave a little margin as it enters into that functional area because we know that doing that and relying on subsequent treatments, chemotherapy and radiation is a much better situation to be in than taking out the entire tumor but leaving someone hemiplegic, meaning they can't move half of their body because they will not be able to go on and get benefit from those additional treatments. And so our next slide shows what we're able to accomplish in this case by chasing the margin posteriorly as it entered into the motor cortex, perhaps leaving a small rim of disease there, but keeping our patient neurologically functionally intact in terms of their motor strength and function. Our other images here give a few more looks at that. Maybe Whitney, if you want to comment on that.

I would just reinforce what you said that certainly the vast majority of the tumor has been resected successfully. Again, the margins look very clean. As you mentioned, there could be a small amount of residual tumor along the posterior or back part of the resecting cavity.
I'll have Dr. Rodriguez go over the pathology.

All right, so here we are seeing another example of an infiltrating glioma. On the upper left-hand side, you have something that we sometimes describe as cellular monotony, that the cells look a bit round and have some clear halos around. This will show some of it a little bit in the previous case, in which it was a component of a more aggressive neoplasm. But here we see that the cellularity is low, which is reassuring. And the cells, they don't vary much from each other. And they have this round nucleus with halos. That's something that helps us recognize it as oligodendrolytic-like. because referring to their similarity to oligodendrocytes, which are a specific cell type that you see that is responsible for the, that you see in the white matter of the brain. On the right-hand side, in contrast, you see this increase in cellularity. The cells look more back-to-back. At low power, we sometimes refer to it as being too blue. That is something also that tells you you have more cells. And this can vary from part of the tumor. tumors now we know can be very heterogeneous, can have areas that look more low grade and higher grade and more cellular like that one on the right hand side. On the lower left, this is a special immunostain K67 which recognizes cells that are proliferating, they are growing. So they are dividing. So here is 10 to 12 percent, it's somewhat increased, not as much as that glioblastoma that we saw, but it's going a little bit up there compared to normal brain. And then you have mitosis, which we can see still with H&E, which also tells you, this combination tells you the tumor is having areas of proliferation. So using the 2007 WHO, this was reported as anaplastic oligoendoglioma, meaning it's oligoendoglial, but then in addition to that, it has areas of increased cellularity and increased proliferation, which puts it into a high grade and a grade three. And oligoendogliomas are only common two grades. They're called, they're a low grade, a grade twos, most of them are initially at least. And then you have the great threes, so there are only two grades there's no great for if you notice here and that's the because they. irrespective of how high grade they can be, they don't act as aggressive as glioblastomas do. These are some of the information that we use. We report the K67 usually in our reports. 1p19q covalent lesion is one of the basic alterations that is required now for the diagnosis. So in the past, we will put it as an addendum, but now it has become, in the newer WHOs, part of the integral part of the diagnosis. So you see it in the lower field. that we need to add that information to the diagnosis to make it meaningful. And IDH mutation was detected by PCR. So there you have the combination of IDH mutation and 1P19 cochlear lesion is really characteristic of oligoendoglioma. It's one of the main features that we recognize. And it's essential, actually, for the diagnosis. So at the current time, you cannot make a precise diagnosis of oligoendoglioma without at least those two markers being positive. The MGMT here was unmethylated. It's a bit surprising because most are methylated. And there was some chromosome 10 that looks like no EGFR amplification. So those alterations, again, that you tend to see more with glioblastomas and diffuse astros. So in the more current WHO, we call it oligodendroglioma, IDH mutant, and 1P19Q coloration. We don't use the terminology anaplastic. We use a numerical grade. And something else that has changed also is that we're using the more friendly Arabic numbers for the classification now for the grades compared to the past that we used to have Roman numerals. And so those are some minor changes that have come up in the classification. Then a list of all the other relevant alterations that were found.

So in this case, now this patient has a slightly different diagnosis than the other patients. So we're going to discuss the different treatment options. So Dr. Lai, I'm going to ask if you could weigh in.

I'd be happy to. So this, as Dr. Rodriguez mentioned, this is now what we call a grade three oligodendroglioma. And the most important factor there is the 1p19q. Interestingly, as he said, the patient was unmethylated for MGMT, and you've heard how important that is. We did a retrospective study here at UCLA and found that the MGMT methylation is really important for the glioblastomas that we were just talking about in case one and two, and also for grade four IDH gliomas, but not so much for the grade two and threes. If your tumor is unmethylated, but you have an oligodendroglioma, I wouldn't worry about it too much. It doesn't seem to affect outcome. So the options that we have for this patient, radiation therapy at a dose of 60 gray over six weeks. I think Dr. Kapralian will talk about the radiation dosing. Option one plus concurrent adjuvant temozolomide. And option three, as you can see, it's in red, is PCV, which is a combination of procarbazine, CCN1, and bincristine. before or after option one, which is radiation therapy. What we do here at UCLA is that we do the radiation alone, unlike for the glioblastoma where there is chemotherapy combined with the radiation. In this case, for oligodendrogliomas that are 1p19q co-deleted, Radiation is given alone, followed by a two to four week break, and then continue with PCV. The other options here, radiation therapy at a dose of 50 gray over five weeks. chemotherapy alone, best supportive care. Best supportive care is always possible. I did want to take one little step back and explain why at a patient conference we're showing all of this data. I think everything that we do here at UCLA is to some degree data-driven. That gives us the structure, that gives us the starting point by which we can start making recommendations. Obviously, as Dr. Klausi said, every single patient is different, and we end up tailoring the treatments, you know, based on other factors, but the starting point is all data-driven. So this is a trial, EORTC. This was done in Europe, 26951. And there's just so many things in these curves that I want to point out to you. And the main thing is that when they looked at the specific 1p19q co-deleted group, so they took out the ones that were molecularly oligodendrogliomas, and these were anaplastic oligodendrogliomas, so grade three. What you see here, and I hope I can show, so the circle is when you added PCV to radiation versus the blue curve where you just have radiation alone. And there's this clear separation. There's a couple of things that we've learned from these trials is that sometimes the publications are prepared and published early on. So at seven years, Because these curves are overlapping, there's no apparent difference. But then as you let the data mature, as you get even at eight years, 10 years, 12 years, 14 years, that's where you see the greatest separation. What we're seeing here is with 1p90q co-deleted patients that have received radiation and PCV, we're seeing this curve plateau or flatten out, it's going down. And each time it goes down, that reflects a patient dying. But when it stops going down, it means that, and then we look at the percentage of patients where this has stopped going down, and that's actually at over 50%. So what this is telling us is in this specific trial, At 14 years, greater than 50 percent of the patients were still alive. When I see patients with the 1p19q co-related tumors that I think can withstand the treatments, I'm extremely enthusiastic and optimistic for them. I'm also making a very strong recommendation that we need to do treatment, this regimen of radiation and PCV.
Let's talk about the radiation.

So the radiation that we've been doing is very similar to the one I described for the grade four glioblastoma, which is true grade A for 30 treatments. There isn't currently data based on all the new categories that are coming up as you know, how Dr. Rodriguez just described. Currently, the radiation doses are lumped more together, high grade versus low grade. That being said, just like Dr. Clausey mentioned earlier, sometimes we take things case by case, and there have been a couple of patients who had a lower aggressive profile, and it was an oligodendroglioma, and we've kind of tweaked the dose a little bit and brought it down. But for the most part, just kind of standard overall, its high grade gets 60 gray, and then the low grades get a little bit lower at typically 54 gray. So this patient got 60 gray, similar margins were used, I guess, Can I use an arrow or just a point? You can do that. And you see this arrow now or no?
Yeah, the arrow won't work. You have to do the circle thing.
Well, I just can you see that?
Yeah.

OK, so that's my gross tumor area or resection cavity. And then the blue is my margin. And again, focusing in on all the dose to that area. You can also tweak the margins a little bit. So if it's a higher graded glioma, but we think it has a lower risk profile than a grade four, such as this case, you can go smaller on your margins. than a grade four that's more aggressive, like a glioblastoma. So there are things that we can do case by case.

reference_conclusion: Following subtotal resection of the right frontal grade 3 oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, adjuvant therapy should consist of radiotherapy followed by PCV chemotherapy. Radiotherapy should be delivered alone to a total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks, with a subsequent 2- to 4-week break before initiation of PCV. This approach is favored over concurrent temozolomide-based chemoradiation for this 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma.
reference_conclusion_quote: Now, knowing that this is wrapped up in the motor, we're probably not going to be able to remove 100% of it, but we can remove the vast, vast majority and leave a little margin as it enters into that functional area [...] So in this case, for oligodendrogliomas that are 1p19q co-deleted, Radiation is given alone, followed by a two to four week break, and then continue with PCV. [...] I'm also making a very strong recommendation that we need to do treatment, this regimen of radiation and PCV. [...] So this patient got 60 gray

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Follow-up for recurrent cervical nodal disease after prior treatment for thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Multicentric medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) of the thyroid, with greatest tumor in the right lobe measuring 2.2 cm, and synchronous papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in the left lobe; later biopsy-proven right lateral cervical lymph node metastasis from MTC.

[ histopathology results ]: Total thyroidectomy specimen in 2010 showed multicentric MTC, greatest focus in the right lobe measuring 2.2 cm, with angiolymphatic invasion, and PTC in the left lobe. Fine-needle aspiration of a right lateral cervical lymph node was positive for MTC; calcitonin in needle washout was markedly elevated.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- December 2022: Neck ultrasound was negative. Neck and chest CT were negative. Laryngoscopy was normal.  
- After 19 months of follow-up: Ultrasound identified an approximately 1.0 cm indeterminate right lateral cervical lymph node with altered Doppler signal and microcalcifications.  
- Three months after radiofrequency ablation: Ultrasound showed reduction in lymph node volume, with a reported volume reduction rate of 77%.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: RET-positive somatic mutation.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- December 2022: Thyroid function was normal. Calcitonin was approximately 60. CEA was 5.  
- One day after radiofrequency ablation: Calcitonin decreased to 26.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2010: Total thyroidectomy with tracheostomy for multicentric MTC and contralateral PTC.  
- 2010: Received 100 mCi radioactive iodine.  
- Approximately 10 years later: Received chemotherapy for acute leukemia.  
- For biopsy-proven right lateral cervical nodal recurrence of MTC: Underwent radiofrequency ablation under local anesthesia. The procedure was short, without complications, and she was discharged 2 hours later. Post-ablation biochemical response was documented with reduction in calcitonin, and ultrasound at 3 months showed 77% volume reduction.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-confirmed right lateral cervical nodal recurrence of MTC had been treated with radiofrequency ablation, with early biochemical and sonographic response. The patient was clinically well after the procedure.

[ other clinical data ]: Prior treatment had been performed outside the current hospital, and detailed historical records were limited. The patient had declined repeat surgery.

reference_conclusion: Following radiofrequency ablation of the biopsy-proven right lateral cervical lymph node metastasis, management should consist of active surveillance with longitudinal follow-up rather than additional focal interventions for small nodal disease. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 44-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Eighteen months of fatigue, arthralgias, night sweats, and weight loss; fever of unknown origin prompted abdominal ultrasound.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney, stage II at initial surgery, with subsequent solitary pulmonary nodule in the right middle lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Right nephrectomy specimen showed very high-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma with 2% sarcomatoid features; reported as Furman grade 4.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a right renal mass measuring 10 x 8 x 10 cm. CT abdomen and pelvis confirmed a 10 x 9 cm right upper pole renal mass with partial duplication of the collecting system and no lymphadenopathy. CT chest at initial staging was negative for metastatic disease. One year later, staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a right middle lobe pulmonary nodule at the medial edge measuring 1.3 x 1.4 cm, increased from 0.8 x 0.9 cm three months earlier. No other definite evidence of metastases was identified on that study.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Infectious disease and rheumatologic evaluations were extensive and negative. Two courses of treatment for presumed tick-borne illnesses had been given prior to renal mass diagnosis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right laparoscopic nephrectomy with regional lymph node dissection for the primary renal tumor.

[ current disease status ]: One year after nephrectomy, a solitary enlarging right middle lobe pulmonary nodule was present, with no other identified sites of disease. Abdominal and pelvic CT remained negative.

reference_discussion.text: Very good, thank you. That wraps up our first case and we'll move on to our second case. Our second case today features a 44-year-old man who presented with 18 months of fatigue, arthrages, night sweats, and weight loss. He had extensive infectious disease and rheumatologic workups, which were all negative, including two courses of treatment for tick-borne illnesses. An abdominal ultrasound was performed for fever of unknown origin, which demonstrated a right renal mass measuring 10 by 8 by 10 centimeters. He underwent a CT of the abdomen and pelvis which confirmed a 10 by 9 centimeter right upper pole renal mass with partial duplication of the collecting system, no lymphadenopathy, and a CT chest was negative for metastatic disease. He had an initial surgery with a right laparoscopic nephrectomy and regional lymph node dissection. Dr. Fu, can you describe his pathology?

Sure, so he had a very high-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma with 2% sarcomatoid features. So when we say that there are sarcomatoid features in a carcinoma, that typically means we're seeing morphology that is very atypical hybrid in appearance, often spindled in appearance, and that is generally associated with a poorer prognosis. And so even if it's very focal, we would still report a Furman grade four.

Great, thank you. One year later, he was undergoing staging CT when he had a chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT performed. This showed in the medial edge of the right middle lobe of the lung, he had a nodule that was previously measuring 0.8 by 0.9 centimeters. three months prior, and that had increased in size to 1.3 by 1.4 centimeters. There were no other definite evidence of metastases. So for this patient, we were hoping to discuss additional staging as well as role for biopsies or metastasectomies at this point.

I'd like to make a comment first about the history. The first question that pops up, I think, for many, many patients is, at the time of his first surgery, when he had stage 2 high-grade sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma, was there a role at that point for adjuvant therapy? Should he have received systemic therapy after nephrectomy? And this is a common question that patients ask when I tell them they're at a little bit increased risk of recurrence because of the sarcomatoid features in their tumor. They ask if there's anything that we can give to prevent that. And I was wondering, Mike, if you could comment on that. What do you think?

Sure. No, this is a great question. And this, again, is a question that's commonly asked by patients. Given the activity of drugs like sutent, serafinib, et cetera, in the metastatic setting, it could be reasonably wondered, maybe we should try to treat high-risk patients to try to reduce the risk of recurrence, or at least delay recurrence. So as far as the evidence that is known right now, recently the ASURE study, which was looking at adjuvant sunitinib or serafinib, did not show a benefit to adjuvant treatment for high-risk patients with localized renal cell carcinoma. There are multiple other studies, S-TRAC, Everest, using other agents, including oxytinib, everolimus, et cetera, that have accrued and are waiting to read out. But at least the first results that we have do not support adjuvant therapy at this point, unfortunately, for patients.

Yeah, I think that's exactly what I would tell the patient, too. And the other thing is patients with sarcomatoid tumors in general are not generally very responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibition or mTOR inhibitors that we know of. So, you know, there's maybe those two reasons. As for this patient's lung lesion, it's small, it's unifocal. For me, at this size, 1.4 centimeters, it might be very difficult to biopsy. Generally, lesions at a centimeter in size can be tricky, but I would consider this potentially for a resection. This is a tumor on the imaging that is very peripheral in the lung. and would look to me to be amenable to thoracoscopic wedge resection. So my first thought would be, well, it's a unifocal site of disease. Maybe it can be resected, but before doing that, I'd want to make sure that there was no other disease elsewhere. And for me, that would include a bone scan to look for disease in the bone. And if he hadn't had a CT of the abdomen and pelvis, but I think he did, I would check that. But if the CT of the abdomen and pelvis was fine, the bone scan was clear, and with a solitary lung lesion, I personally wouldn't scan the brain. I would generally do that when the burden of disease above the diaphragm is high. So multiple or lung metastases is when I would, or multiple lung and bone metastases, that's when I would consider checking his head.

Yeah, no, I agree. And I think certainly in this patient, a metastasectomy would make sense. I think the thing to realize with systemic therapy is that it has real side effects. The progression-free survival, depending on what drug you use, sunitinib, pazopanib might be appropriate in this patient, would be about eight to nine months. But during that time, the patient is having side effects. fatigue, hypertension, et cetera, et cetera. Whereas if you could treat the patient with local therapy, potentially do a wedge resection or some other way, pluck out this nodule, even if all you did is delay the time to systemic therapy, that would be a benefit to the patient.

Yeah, and for thoracoscopic wedge resections, the recovery period is remarkably quick. Patients leave the hospital usually within a couple of days, and usually within six weeks are pretty much back to baseline, assuming that there's no complications.

So the patient did undergo a right thoracoscopic wedge resection when the pathology showed a 1.3 by 1.2 by 1 centimeter clear cell carcinoma with negative margins. Dr. Fu, do you want to comment on his immunohistochemistry staining?

Sure, so the immunohistochemical findings on the lung nodule showed positive staining for RCC and CD10, as well as some patchy staining for vimentin and anti-cytokeratins, and those are all very consistent with a diagnosis of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. A TTF1 immunostain was negative, and that was done to make sure that it wasn't a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, and those tend to be positive for TTF1, whereas a renal cell carcinoma would be negative, as this case was.

I think this case demonstrates really the role of metastasectomy in renal cell carcinoma. It also demonstrates the patients that tend to benefit. So metastasectomies tend to work best in people who have lung-only disease versus disease in other sites, although it can be beneficial in those other sites. It tends to benefit patients who have asynchronous recurrence of disease rather than synchronous disease. And it tends to benefit patients who have a low number of metastases, one or two versus three or more. So this patient basically had several risk factors that would suggest a good outcome with metastasectomy, solitary lung only disease.

Thanks very much for that commentary. And the patient has remained without evidence of disease now four years after metastasectomy. So he met all those criteria. That concludes this case. Thank you for joining us for this session of the Renal Cell Carcinoma Tumor Board.

reference_conclusion: Additional staging should be completed with bone scintigraphy to exclude osseous metastatic disease; if abdominal and pelvic CT remains negative and the bone scan is clear, brain imaging is not indicated in the setting of a solitary pulmonary lesion. Given the small, peripheral, unifocal right middle lobe nodule, thoracoscopic wedge resection/metastasectomy is the preferred next step rather than biopsy or immediate systemic therapy. Adjuvant systemic therapy after nephrectomy is not supported by the available evidence discussed.

But if the CT of the abdomen and pelvis was fine, the bone scan was clear, and with a solitary lung lesion, I personally wouldn't scan the brain. [...] Yeah, no, I agree. And I think certainly in this patient, a metastasectomy would make sense. [...] But at least the first results that we have do not support adjuvant therapy at this point, unfortunately, for patients.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old Hispanic woman. No family history of cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of vaginal discharge and vaginal bleeding in June 2014. No other symptoms were reported at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IIB cervical cancer diagnosed in 2014. Subsequent brain metastasis to the cerebellum was diagnosed in October 2014.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy demonstrated moderately differentiated ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma. Histopathology from resected cerebellar lesion confirmed metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Gynecologic examination demonstrated a 7 cm bleeding exophytic cervical mass with necrotic center and parametrial involvement. Post-treatment imaging after chemoradiation showed no evidence of disease. Brain MRI in October 2014 demonstrated a cerebellar expansive lesion consistent with metastasis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In July 2014, the patient received concurrent chemoradiation consisting of weekly cisplatin for 8 weeks and radiotherapy for 10 weeks. At completion of treatment, imaging showed no evidence of disease. After identification of the cerebellar metastasis, she underwent suboccipital craniotomy with wide tumor resection. She then started whole-brain radiotherapy as palliative treatment in November 2014.

[ current disease status ]: Resected solitary cerebellar metastasis from stage IIB cervical squamous cell carcinoma, with no evidence of disease at the primary site after chemoradiation, receiving palliative whole-brain radiotherapy.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, thank you. This case is about a 41-year-old Hispanic woman without family history of cancer. In June 2014, the patient comes to the institution with a six-month history of vaginal discharge. and bleeding and no other symptoms. The gynecological examination revealed a seven centimeter bleeding exophytic cervical mass with necrotic center and dry paramedial involvement. A cervical biopsy was performed showing moderately differentiated ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma. Next please. and the patient was diagnosed with stage 2b cervical cancer. In July, she received concurrent chemo-radiation with weekly c-studying for 8 weeks and 10 weeks of radiotherapy. At the end of the treatment, there was no evidence of disease in the imagined studies. And in October 2014, with a history of headache for one month, a brain MRI was performed showing a cerebellar expansive process assisted with metastasis. She underwent a suboccipital craniotomy, a wide resection of the tumor, and confirmed the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma brain metastasis. She started olocranial radiotherapy as a palliative treatment in November 2014. And she was taken to the emergency room with severe neurological impairment in December, five days after her family reported her death. The first question is, cervix cancer in young women have different behavior and response to treatment?

So maybe we take that question first, if you don't mind. So the real question about this very full presentation and tragic ending with the patient's death is, does this disease behave differently in young women? And is the response to treatment different in young women?

I don't know of any data. I mean, I think we tend to think that these cancers, in general, that age is a prognostic indicator with older women doing worse. But that may be confounded by ability to complete all intended treatment, cycles of treatment, And then I think there may be some data that we tend to be less aggressive with older patients, even if you factor in medical comorbidities. I don't know of any data that would, in a non-immunocompromised patient, that would support that younger women have a different disease course. I don't know if Mike wants to weigh in.

Yeah, I would agree on that. If anything, in the States, the age relationship is inverse, which is the older patients with cervical cancer tend to do poorer, and I think for the reasons that Dr. DelCorno mentioned.
Is there any biological subtype that's confined to young women that makes it worse, like triple negative in breast cancer, young women with breast cancer? Is there something like that?

I would wonder if the histology here is different. I mean, I don't know if it's read as squamous, but certainly we see a more aggressive biology, some of the more rare types of cervical cancer, but it's not a I don't think brain methasis are that common.

The histologic distribution is really roughly the same in terms of squamous and adeno. I think we all think adeno tends to be a little more aggressive. In this case, it was a moderately differentiated squamous.
Is it common for these, you just said, no. Do you concur that it's not common to get brain mints from this particular cancer?

Yeah, so the interesting point here is you can certainly rest assured you had brain mints at the time the whole diagnosis was made. It was only three months between the radiation. And then once you became down with neurologic symptoms, it's a rare enough event for us that we would never recommend, you know, head CTs or MRIs as a screening issue at the time that you treat these patients. In an asymptomatic patient, we would go only with neurologic symptoms. So the way this played out is actually, I think, was handled reasonably well. It's just in this particular patient appeared to be a very aggressive tumor.

And the management of the brain meds? Kathleen, if you want to chime in, please feel free. The management of the brain meds in this young patient, she's got cerebellar metastasis from a squamous cell crossing over the cervix. What's the best management for that?

Just to take a step back, I agree with Mike and Marcella that I think when we see these cases, we usually go back and review the pathology. I mean, I just wonder if it's a neuroendocrine tumor or some other very aggressive pathology. When we have brain mats, usually we work with a radiation oncologist and the neurosurgeons. Sometimes if it's an isolated brain mat, our neurosurgeons are very aggressive. We do a lot of surgery. If it's multiple brain mats, then usually it's whole brain radiation and sometimes stereotactic radiotherapy as well.

Can I just say, Kathleen, thank you, can I just say, very often We have cases presented on these tumor boards from South America where the patient coming into a tertiary care cancer center from a peripheral center, and the management to date from the peripheral center has been suboptimal. But just to give you a reality check here, at Massachusetts General Hospital, when we get a breast cancer patient arrive for a second opinion or for a referral from an outside community hospital, it's standard practice to review the pathology in every single patient like that. So rather than sort of insulting the pathology expertise of the referring center, we just routinely redo the pathology, we routinely do the biomarkers, and it is really remarkable how often we have a change in the pathology and a change in the biomarkers by reviewing it. I don't know what the practice is like in South America, but that's what we do here. We review all cases. We have all the x-rays reviewed by our radiologists, re-read, sometimes we repeat the x-rays, we even sometimes repeat the biopsy, but we make sure that the information we're getting on the patient is accurate. And unfortunately, it very often isn't accurate from a referring center. So that might be a good idea for a patient like this who presents with a very atypical presentation of brain metastasis before accepting the pathology diagnosis, perhaps reviewing the path or repeating the biopsy would be appropriate. Do you want to make any comment about the case from INEN? Oh, they're still asking what's the treatment. treatment and management of—I don't know that we've got a brain radiotherapist yet, but— Well, I would just say, Leon— Yes, Leon.

So I do—I agree with the comments that were made. Here at Mass General, we're remarkably aggressive with neurosurgery for these patients. And as was pointed out before, if it's a solitary med, that's a clear indication of surgery. But even in the setting of multiple meds, If there's one, if there's any question about the pathology or two, if there's one that predominates in terms of edema and it's thought to be inducing neurologic symptoms, then that will be removed. And then the substance therapy is usually a whole brain with obviously concomitant toxicity, which probably is ultimately what happened in this patient. It seems to me most of what was done was quite reasonable.

Yeah, I would agree. I think that, just as Kathleen said, our neurosurgical group tends to be pretty aggressive, especially in a young patient. If it's an isolated med that is amenable to surgery, they'll resect and then will radiate the brain. We're lucky that we have protons, and that spares some toxicity of the brain. So at MGH, these patients will go through proton radiation therapy, so they have less mobility radiation, but I think that we would have treated her very similarly to how she was managed.
Do you imply that this patient may have died as a result of her radiation?

Well, it was awfully acute, so there was no evaluation on that. Could she have had a bleed, some sort of event from a tumor, that's also possible. But we do see with whole brain standard kind of approaches, there is, there can be a significant impact on neurologic function in certain patients. She sort of has to compromise a cerebral function because of all the meds, then she gets whole brain. I mean, I- Is it usually from edema or could be anything? Could be, it could be sort of, for lack of better terminology, neuronal degeneration from the radiation. It could be edema, it could be bleed. Okay. Yeah.

All right. Well, thank you for presenting that case. And then our third patient is going to be presented by Dr. Graziella del Molin from San Paolo. This is Dr. Molin's first visit to our tumor board. So welcome, Dr. Molin. And please feel free to begin presenting your case when you see the slides projected.

reference_conclusion: The panel concluded that this presentation was managed appropriately, with brain imaging indicated only after the onset of neurologic symptoms rather than as routine screening in an asymptomatic patient. For brain metastasis, pathology review or repeat biopsy was advised given the atypical presentation, and management should involve multidisciplinary evaluation with neurosurgery and radiation oncology. In the setting of a solitary or surgically amenable dominant lesion, resection followed by brain radiotherapy was supported; for multiple brain metastases, whole-brain radiation, with consideration of stereotactic radiotherapy in selected cases, was described as standard management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain, back pain, flushing, night sweats, watery diarrhea, and occasional postprandial abdominal cramping.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic well-differentiated small bowel neuroendocrine tumor, grade 2, arising in the terminal ileum, with hepatic metastases. Functional neuroendocrine tumor syndrome was present, with flushing and diarrhea.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial liver biopsy: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 2, Ki-67 10%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial abdominal ultrasound: multiple hepatic masses.  
- Initial CT abdomen/pelvis: terminal ileum lesion, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly with multiple liver lesions, and porta hepatis lymphadenopathy. Terminal ileal lesion measured approximately 2 x 3 cm.  
- MRI abdomen with hepatobiliary contrast (Eovist): multiple liver lesions.  
- Initial Ga-68 DOTATATE PET: avid uptake in multiple liver lesions, terminal ileum lesion, and mesenteric lymph nodes.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Liver function tests were normal at diagnosis.  
- Serum serotonin at diagnosis: 1423.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Echocardiogram at diagnosis was essentially normal.  
- No weight loss was reported initially; oral intake of solid food was maintained.  
- The primary terminal ileal lesion was described radiographically as near-occlusive, correlating with postprandial cramping symptoms.
