reference_discussion.text: Okay, so our first case is a 45-year-old woman. She presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and also back pain. She also had flushing and night sweats and watery diarrhea. And she says she has occasional abdominal cramping after eating. So she went to her primary care doctor who did an ultrasound and they showed multiple masses in the liver. that was followed by a CT abdomen pelvis, which showed a terminal ileum lesion, mesenteric lymph nodes, enlarged liver with liver lesions, and then portal hepatic lymph nodes. And I'll show you the images in the next slide. But she had a liver biopsy, and that showed a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. It was grade 2 and KSC 7 of 10%. Her labs showed normal liver function. Her serotonin was 1423, and she had an echocardiogram that was essentially normal. So if you look at her CT abdomen pelvis, so on the left hand side, you see in the circle area, that's where the terminal ileal lesion is. It's like a two by three centimeter lesion. And then on the right hand picture, you see one of the examples of the mesenteric lymph nodes that she has. And this is her MRI abdomen, and this was done with EOVIS contrast, so hepatobiliary phase contrast, which really, really produces clear pictures of the liver lesions, as you can see here. Just show you two representative cuts of her MRI abdomen with EOVIS. And then this is a DOTATATE PET scan. This is gallium DOTATATE, and so it showed a lot of uptake in all of these liver lesions, as well as the terminal ileum lesion and the mesenteric lymph nodes. So basically, we have a 45-year-old woman who was newly diagnosed with a metastatic, well-differentiated grade 2, small bowel neuroendocrine tumor, and she has liver metastasis. So I'm going to open this for discussion. How do we best approach this case? So I'll start by asking Dr. Koitgen, do you see a role for surgery here, either resection of the primary tumor or liver debulking surgery?

Thank you, Andy. So I think from a surgical perspective, there are two things that we look at, especially with small bowel neuroendocrine tumor. We look at the primary tumor, the size of the primary tumor, and if the primary tumor is causing any symptoms. You mentioned she had diarrhea. Was she complaining of any cramping or any pain after eating?
Yeah, she did say that after eating, she feels abdominal cramping, but she hasn't lost any weight and she's able to eat solid foods and keep everything down.

And then the second point is obviously from a liver debulking surgery, not all centers do that, but that's another question to ask. So, one of the things that strikes me on the abdominal CT on the left-hand side is that that lesion seems to be quite large. It seems to occupy a majority of the small bowel lumen. It's not that common actually that the primary tumors are that big and certainly here you could see you have these white little streaks of contrast that fill the bowel lumen and there really isn't much contrast that goes along the lesion here. So, I would say that this is a near occlusive small bowel tumor in addition to the story that she tells us with the cramping. After she eats, I would suggest that this probably needs to be removed surgically just in order to avoid a situation where she gets treated systemically and we end up having a bowel blockage that would interrupt this treatment and then potentially end up having to have an urgent or an emergent surgery, which are always more complicated and have higher rates of complications. From a liver debulking perspective, I think this is a little bit too enthusiastic for me. I think there are a lot of tumors here and I don't think that this would be the first line of treatments, but I could certainly imagine that there might be a role for liver-directed therapy either now or at a later point. Thank you.

So, Dr. Khan, liver jerky therapy-wise, would she be a good candidate for this? And if so, what would you use? Would you use embolization, either blend embolization or chemo embolization or radio embolization or Y90? And what about histotripsy? Everyone asks about that in clinic nowadays.

Yeah, so certainly there's a significant amount of liver disease here. I think that, you know, addressing the small bowel tumor initially would be something kind of focused on primarily, and then maybe subsequently looking at performing liver directed therapy. This is sort of diffuse, a bulky tumor, both sides. And so I think in this case that sort of favor a bland nebulization. not too much of a significant difference between bland normalization and taste, especially based on the initial results of a recent trial, a retinit trial. And then Tara, I would sort of favor for larger single lesions. And so I think she's a good candidate for bland. You could do histotripsy as well. Once again, histotripsy is a new technology, not a lot of data, We have performed it at our institution. And certainly some of those, if we go back to the MRI, there are a few of those that are pretty close to the front surface of the liver, which look to be amenable to visualization with ultrasound. And so maybe treating one or two of those lesions and sort of hopefully stimulating a potential immune, getting some immunostimulation with PRT is a possibility. I think blind nebulization may do a little bit more here. And then certainly, Andy, if I kick it back to you for systemic treatment, that might be more of the road to go down.
You mentioned something interesting. Is there any data to support this scopo effect like the histotripsy engendering an immune response and specifically for neuroendocrine tumor patients?

not any in human data specifically. Certainly there's been some basic science and some mice models that have shown some upregulation based on cytokine release and antigen release, but nothing in human. And so that's.

So we still need to wait for clinical trial data. Okay. Thank you. And then for the oncologist in the room, what would we do for systemic therapy? What would you give this patient? So I'll pick on Dr. Chandrasekaran.

Thanks, Andy. So, yeah, and this patient, you know, she also had a functional tumor based on her symptomatology, flushing and diarrhea. So I think the consideration of somatostatin analog is definitely, you know, one of the first things in terms of timing, whether the surgeon takes the primary tumor, before or after. I think, ideally, I would get her strontium, so I'm just adding analogs for the syndrome presented to the surgeon for consideration of the primary tumor, given her symptomatology would be the way to go. I think the question of first-line PRRT is interesting. I can see the patient has a key 67 of 10 percent, which is kind of the cutoff for the NETR2 trial, which looked at upfront PRRT as an option. These are patients within six months of diagnosis, and she probably meets the criteria. Personally, though, I think without a clear benefit on overall survival with upfront PRRT, I have not adopted it for the patients all upfront. given the distribution of the disease and the symptom analogy, you could make an argument that PRRT has good data for symptom control, quality of life preservation, et cetera. But again, these are studied in the second line setting when I'm talking about the quality of life. So I think get the primary tumor out of symptomatic, start on SSA analog therapy first, and kind of reassess with imaging and symptoms later would be my choice.
Great. Would any of the oncologists here disagree and say this patient should, or you would start this patient on first time PRRT?

So I wouldn't. So for a couple of reasons, so number one, we do not have data on overall survival with upfront PRRT. We know from NetR2 that progression-free survival was markedly longer with PRRT upfront. But it will also say that this patient would barely have made it onto the trial with the lowest possible KS7. And we have data, the somatization analog therapy works up front. So my take has been just to play that card first, the somatization analog card, and just see what mileage you got.
Great. Dr. Saras, Eids, any other thoughts?

Yeah, I agree. I think that someone by the book will certainly meet the criteria, but I haven't incorporated it really in the first line setting. I think one thing that probably many of us will do is to scan this patient a little bit more closely. I typically scan patients with small bowel neuroendocrine tumors every six months, the majority of them. this patient is someone that will probably do a repeat MRI in the three months mark or four months mark, just to have a sense. Because I didn't have a sense from the beginning of the presentation of for how long she has been living with the symptoms to sort of indirectly guide me if it is someone that the disease suggests that's really truly indolent or this is one of these tumors that might behave a little bit more aggressive that you would expect. So for these reasons, I will skin hair in a little bit of a shorter timeline than I normally do.

If I could just add to that, I agree that starting with a somatostatin analog makes the most sense and is what I would do in this situation for both anti-tumor control and for hormone-mediated symptoms. But I agree with Eloisa as well that, you know, wanting to take a look early would be wise, especially in someone who has a relatively large degree of tumor burden in the liver, and it is a patient with liver dominant disease. So oftentimes at our institution, we may consider doing somatostatin analog, and then if symptoms are either not optimally controlled, Or if we're worried about the pace of disease in the liver, we'll layer on the embolization in addition to the somatostatin analog, just to try to make sure that we maintain good control over the liver, because in a patient with this distribution of disease, oftentimes the liver involvement is where we get into the most trouble.

Yeah, that's a great point. So this is the timeline. So she was diagnosed in September, 2020. We started her on first-line lanyreotide, and then because she was symptomatic from her primary tumor, she had surgical resection of the primary tumor, cholecystectomy, but also a liver watch resection that showed a grade two well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, KS676%. And then in April of 2021, so about six months later, there is mild increase in size of several of her liver meds, but her serotonin almost doubled and she was having worsening flushing and diarrhea. And so you can see here the tumors, they're only mildly increase in size. So for reference here, this lesion here went from 32 millimeters to 36. So four millimeter increase, but it seems like her symptoms are clearly worse. So what would we do next in this situation, Dr. Khan?

Yeah, I mean, at this point, I'd be a little bit more stronger advocate of liver therapy. Still, we have bilobar disease, so I suggest treating with bilinear nebulization, breaking treatment up to like each lobe, kind of four weeks apart.
And then Dr. Kokian already told us this was too much tumor for Liberty Belkin. For the medical oncologists, would you change the systemic therapy at this juncture?

I would not necessarily do it, but I would obviously start prepping for it, though. So there is progression, there is an increase in the serotonin and symptoms might be worsening. And we know that radioligand therapy with lutetium does help with symptoms. We have evidence from NETR1, we have retrospective data from the Netherlands. So I think this would be sort of the time where I would really start thinking of radioligand therapy. And personally, that's where I would go next.

So that's indeed what we did for this patient. So she had blind embolization, one lobe at a time. And then nine months later, her MRI and Delta-T PET scan showed disease progressions. So you can see here in the Delta-T PET scan, there's progression in the liver, but also she seems to have developed new Delta-T avid retrocrural lymph nodes and then bone metastasis in the T3 area. Dr. Hop Donnison said that you would do PRT. Does anyone else agree or any other thoughts?

I think ideally, of course, with every patient, every discussion involves all the treatment options. So even at the prior step, you know, I would want to have a good discussion about all the options at this time. Technically, you could think about, quote, any systemic therapy, Everline, Ms. Cabozian, with the approval, or PRRT, or a clinical trial, if you have. With that discussion, probably, yes, I agree with Dr. Heffernan-Erson that I would be leaning towards PRRT. She's got definitely good receptor uptake, as one can see, kind of has also extra hepatic disease burden. I'm not sure if at this progression, May of 2022, she had a symptom progression as well. But regardless, I think from a quality of life perspective slash disease perspective, that may be a good next step. But again, there are patients who would take another option as well. So a discussion and then proceeding towards my code recommendation.
Okay. And everyone asks about alpha PRT nowadays. So what do we know about alpha PRT? And is it better than conventional dutapera?

So alpha particle therapy, just a quick introduction to that. So it is the same concept as with the lutetium-177 or lutethera. We're delivering a radioactive particle to the tumor cells. It's given IV. It's glued to a octreotetralangreotide-like drug. It floats around in the body. It latches onto the tumor cells like two pieces of Velcro. and deliver its radiation charge to the tumor. So alpha particles have much higher energy, they travel much less in terms of distance, and they have never been compared to beta particle therapy like lutetium. Those trials are actually coming. What we do know is that the two trials that have looked at something called lead 212 or PV212, There are two different types of that. The initial results are actually very promising, but the question is really, will it hold up over time? And so, yes, there seems to be a higher response rate. We shrink more tumors and we shrink them more than we do with lutetia, at least seemingly, but the question is really, how long does it hold up? So I'd say if you have an alpha study, by all means, introduce it, talk to your patient about possibly participating in that, but we don't have any comparative studies yet.

Great summary. So let's move on to the next slide. So she indeed was treated with PRRT with standard lutethera, and then two and a half years later, her scan showed disease progression. So this is an example. She had mild progression of many of her liver lesions, but this one in particular in segment three got significantly larger. And then she also developed new bone mass. As you can see here, they're all very small, very subtle. So at this juncture, what will we do next?

So especially when I have a patient who has a one rogue lesion kind of growing faster than the others, I would think about re-biopsying the patient at that juncture, specifically the lesion that is growing disproportionately to the others to make sure that we're still dealing with the tumor biology that we think we are. Oftentimes over the course of having this disease for several years, we will see some grade creep, so the Ki-67 may increase over time and become maybe less likely to respond to things that well-differentiated tumors do. Provided that that still showed a grade 2 tumor that didn't seem too particularly aggressive, I would think of a couple of options. sometimes, especially for a liver lesion that's kind of growing disproportionately, we will do some targeted embolization just to that lesion and then treat the rest of the disease sort of a different way. It also looks like this patient responded quite well to PRRT and so could be considered perhaps for either retreatment with the standard PRRT with lutetium-177, dodatate, or could be a good candidate for alpha therapy, ideally on study, to give it another go that way.
Great, thank you. Dr. Cincho-Sacara-Nosores, any other systemic options you would consider here?

Yeah, if I may say, and I know that's not usually majority of standard of care, but this is when I see this disagreement between the growth in addition to chasing the lesion. I like to sometimes, if possible, do an FTG PET. because that helps me to decide if I'm going to go on a more systemic approach that could potentially even include more traditional chemotherapy. And if I see that there are several lesions that are positive on the FDG PET, my limit towards there, that rather than just chasing one or the two lesions in the liver, and it's not unfrequent that we see this thing. So that's one additional test or tool that could help, at least in my thought process, how to decide on next steps.
That's a great point. Dr. Chandrasekaran, any other systemic options you would consider?

Yeah, I think I would incorporate pretty much all the steps mentioned about if especially one or two lesions are growing, re-biopsy, FDG PET, which could also guide in choosing the lesion to biopsy. Ideally, you would go for an FDG PET lesion. I would probably also repeat a gallium PET just to see because you may still have receptors retained in these patients. I think it's, again, even though she had a two-year demonstrated stability post-PRRT, if there is, quote, this grade creep happening, you know, we expect maybe even lesser from that PRRT if we repeat it. So, again, I would still offer it as an option and discuss. We have very little data for everolimus in the grade creep setting or, you know, higher grade. Cabozin technically has data in grade three, but that's a very small subset of patients, so I think it's a little hard. So I guess technically, again, a discussion, but I would maybe, if still receptor positive, go for a PRRT type of option if receptors are present. Or consider an embolization to that one lesion, which is receptor agnostic, get the cancer to declare itself better as to what's going to do, and then decide the next option.
Great. Dr. Koykan, any role for surgery here?

Surgery is a big biopsy, right? If you think about it, surgeons are just big biopsy people in the setting of metastatic disease. So, it depends. So, I would argue, having known this case actually, because this is our common patient, if I remember well, her symptoms got significantly worse again. Having learned from liver directed therapy that the bland embol part, you know, didn't really control symptoms very long, I would argue if it's just a few lesions that are rogue, that rather than just doing a biopsy, if she had a good response to PRT, and because she's symptomatic, and her symptoms are getting worse, and her serotonin is going up, if there's a role for debulking, and I would say it again depends on the overall liver tumor burden, but she hasn't been debulked yet. So certainly you can debulk after PRT. And interestingly, we see it more and more, you know, the patients get PRT kind of not first line, but, you know, second line after progression on long-acting octreotide and now have had some response to it, delivered tumor burden decrease, but now they're slowly progressing again. So that doesn't really take them out of contention for debulking, especially in those cases, I would say that have a high serotonin level and with worsening symptoms. So it might be an option in her, depending on what the scan looks like.

So we consider all these points that everyone brought up. This was shared decision-making with the patient. So she decided to go through surgery. So she actually had liver debulking surgery in January. And so the pathology is very interesting. So still show a well-differentiated neoendocrine tumor. But if you look at the different liver lesions that were taken out, so the segment one lesion, KSC7, was 20%. Segment three was 45% with 40 mitoses. Segment 4b was only 1%, segment 5 was 12.4%, and then segment 8 was 1.4%. And then we did next-generation sequencing on this segment 3 lesion because the KSC-7 was highest. And so that showed RB1 LAT4 loss, low tumor mutation burden, and mycosis stable disease. So like several of you were already alluding, there seems to be this great creep phenomenon going on. So Dr. East, how often do we see this in small bowel neuroendocrine tumor and why do you think that causes this?

Well, we actually see it quite a bit. Our group at Penn had looked at this actually and shown that with the grade creep phenomenon that the KI-67 generally increases about 1% per year. This is a little bit more beyond that, but it's not uncommon for these tumors to actually be very heterogeneous, not just within cross tumors, but also within one tumor. So I think it's actually not too surprising that there are several different Ki67s represented across all of these different segments. And I don't know if we necessarily have a great understanding of why one necessarily takes off. Certainly, the next generation sequencing showing the RB1 loss is something that we do see in the higher grade tumors. Oftentimes, it's more in the poorly differentiated setting as opposed to the still well differentiated histologies, but it's definitely demonstrating features that are suggesting that it's kind of transitioning into a more aggressive tumor biology.

Yeah, great points. So at this juncture, so she just had her liver debulking surgery, and she's still in real time. Will anyone offer additional or change in systemic therapy given this surgical pathology?

I would probably wait and see what happens. Technically, this is the rogue lesion, which is bad biology, but, you know, it's done for now. Hopefully she has symptom relief from this. India didn't tell me if she still had receptors prior to this. I think she, for the gallium pet, probably did. So I would kind of wait it out and see what happens and treat based on that, and not necessarily give something right away. I think this grape feed is very interesting for all of us, as we know.

Yeah. So let's go to the next slide. So that's indeed what we did. So we waited and then let her recover from the surgery, continue the lanyotide, and then six months later, her scans for tracheal disease progression. So this is the MRI comparison between April and July. You can see there's a significant increase in her liver metastases. And this is a dotal hip pet. So in addition to the worsening liver metastasis, there's also now diffuse bone metastasis. So what will we do in terms of treatment at this juncture? So Dr. Suarez?

Yeah, I think I will do a two-step approach, something that you can get it right away. I probably I'll start her on full Fox and prep her, do up to four months or full Fox, hopefully get a little bit more control and then set it up for potentially, if possible, repeated PRRT, which probably have to be off-label. I don't know if she would necessarily qualify for that trial. But unfortunately, this is a situation that the biology of disease is not being kind to us and to the patient, and you already have to start, like, really setting up, boom, boom, boom, all the steps because you're not outside of the initial PRRT. Disease control is not being held for too long. And it takes a little bit of time to get PRT in place, right? So especially if it's off-label. So I will do full FOX personally, but we'll have to see what my colleagues will do.
Yeah. Dr. Hoft-Andersen, what would you do?

So you have, so one option you have is cabosanthinib. So keep in mind cabosanthinib will not control the syndrome, but refractory small bowel or non-pancreatic NETs may control the disease for about eight to nine months, probably a bit shorter in this high grade. So this is all based on data from the cabinet trial. There was not a whole lot of grade three patients there. So that probably would be what I would do next. So it would be Cabo's antidote, continue the somatostatin analog. If the syndrome is uncontrolled, you have two options. You can increase the dose of the somatostatin analog, even shorter the cycle. and you can add telotristat to control the serotonin production, keeping in mind that the Kavos antiderivative is not going to do that, or at least not the symptoms reliably. And then you have Averolimus, but we have no data on Averolimus, or not at least prospective data, but we have some retrospective studies and we've all seen Averolimus work in this situation. So we have a repeat PRT on option two.
Okay, Dr. Chandrasekaran, how would you do in this situation?

I'll first say this is probably the most interesting part of the tumor board because you're going to get this discussion and I guess maybe differing opinions, but still the same, but I'm going to probably start by something that's probably everybody does actually counsel the patient because, you know, I think a lot of times patients have this perception. I've been told I'm not going to die from this cancer. Just a 45 year old was diagnosed with a grade two, a indolent small bowel neuroendocrine tumor. Now, I think it's important to emphasize to the patient first, this is not maybe quote, the same disease they've been dealing with in the past few years. I think that is important because no matter what we do probably in this situation, the benefit and the time it's going to have is going to be lesser than any other conventional therapy. With such a liver burden and such a short time, the The threat of a liver, impending liver failure when this disease takes off is very real. You know, I think we should counsel all our patients. We all do. I think this is a little bit more urgent situation, so I'll start there. I think I may lean towards what Dr. Suarez was alluding to. Just based on the April to July scan that you showed, there was quite a bit of progression, ROV loss, even though it was a well-differentiated neurendocrine, but very high. It's kind of behaving like, to me, clinically poorly differentiated. I have probably a little bit more faith in oxaliplatin or platinum-based regimen. but I'm glad to see she still has receptors, so I would not exclude PRRT. Certainly, I would have a discussion about CABLES, Anthony, but maybe not my first choice in this situation.
Great, thank you. And then last question, Dr. Eats, what would you do, and would this patient be a candidate for CAR-T therapy?

So yeah, that's an interesting question. So I'm inclined to agree with Dr. Suarez and Dr. Chandrasekaran in the sense that I am uncomfortable with the pace of disease. The rate of progression has been quite fast and we're really going to want to be able to get good control or ideally good control in a short period of time. I probably would do an FDG PET to see again like how much of this disease looks FDG avid versus dodatate avid and would favor some full FOX perhaps then followed by consolidation with PRRT. The other thing to remember about PRRT is that it does not work quickly and it's a treatment that we administer over several months. So when you need a rapid response, it just isn't maybe the thing to be looking toward. As for the question about CAR T therapy, so certainly a very interesting area that we are investigating at Penn in this particular patient population. It's something only available through clinical trials at this time. It's not something that would be standard of care. I think that I would be a bit nervous about it in a patient with rapidly progressive disease like this. It takes time to go through the CAR T process. We have to harvest T cells from the patient, manufacture them to be targeted toward the cancer, and then give them back to the patient, and all of that takes some time. Additionally, I think we're still not quite certain about how safe it is in patients who have a large degree of liver burden. So in this particular instance, I might be cautious that way as well. But as we learn more about it and hopefully get faster at manufacturing the cells as well, it may be an option. But why we participate in trials.
Yeah, definitely. Thank you. Dr. Chhatrasekaran, you had a question?

I don't know if we are short on time, but I just wanted to throw a question out. I know we just had a big surgical biopsy that Dr. Quagen gave us, but I'm wondering if even within that information, again, at a quite a bit of progression, would anybody re-biopsy? What if the tumor mutation burden has increased or something? I know the phenomenon has been described more in temozolomide-exposed patients, but I just kind of wanted to throw that thing out there. I may consider biopsying again.
Great point. Great point.
Well, thank you for bringing that up. Thanks to all of you. It's not easy to, you know, get you all out here and doing this. So thank you very much.

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended initial management with a somatostatin analog for hormonal symptom control and antitumor therapy, with surgical resection of the symptomatic near-occlusive primary ileal tumor. Postoperatively, close interval reassessment with imaging was advised, with consideration of liver-directed embolization if hepatic symptoms or liver-dominant disease remained inadequately controlled. Upfront PRRT was not favored in the first-line setting.
reference_conclusion_quote: So I think get the primary tumor out of symptomatic, start on SSA analog therapy first, and kind of reassess with imaging and symptoms later would be my choice. [...] I agree that starting with a somatostatin analog makes the most sense and is what I would do in this situation for both anti-tumor control and for hormone-mediated symptoms. [...] oftentimes at our institution, we may consider doing somatostatin analog, and then if symptoms are either not optimally controlled, Or if we're worried about the pace of disease in the liver, we'll layer on the embolization in addition to the somatostatin analog [...] Personally, though, I think without a clear benefit on overall survival with upfront PRRT, I have not adopted it for the patients all upfront.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism in the setting of stage 4 chronic kidney disease, referred for management prior to anticipated renal transplantation.

[ diagnosis ]: Secondary hyperparathyroidism associated with stage 4 chronic kidney disease; hypercalcemia developed over time as renal function declined. Chronic kidney disease was attributed to long-term NSAID use. The patient was not on dialysis.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative neck ultrasound identified a 17 mm potential parathyroid candidate posterior/inferior to the right thyroid lower pole with vascularity on color Doppler, and a second 10 mm potential candidate posterolateral to the left thyroid upper pole. CT neck without contrast was obtained due to impaired renal function; assessment was limited, but findings were thought to correspond to the right-sided lesion inferior/posterior to the right thyroid lobe and the left-sided 10 mm lesion posterolateral to the left upper pole.

[ laboratory results ]: At presentation, serum calcium was 11.3 mg/dL and parathyroid hormone was in the thousands.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had been managed medically prior to surgical referral.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension and osteoporosis. Physical examination before surgery was otherwise normal, including normal vocal cord motion. The patient was undergoing evaluation for renal transplantation or was in the process of being placed on the transplant waiting list due to progressive decline in kidney function.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah. Thank you. Thank you, Brendan. All right. So, in the interest of time, we're going to move on to our last case, which is really kind of distinct, which is that we're going to be talking about secondary or renal hyperparathyroidism. So, Natalia, thank you for joining us. If you want to just get started with your case, that'd be great.

So, the case is a 63-year-old female with stage 4 CKD, currently not on dialysis. with refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism was referred by the endocrinology team. She was on the waiting list for a renal transplant or in the process of becoming on the transplant list due to her progressive decline in kidney function. And the recommendation was for treatment of her hyperparathyroidism prior to transplantation. Her past medical history includes hypertension, osteoporosis, and her CKD was induced by long-term NSAID use. Listed are her medications. When BSAR in clinic, she otherwise had a normal exam, normal cord motion. Her labs at presentation were notable for an elevated calcium of 11.3 and PTH in the thousands. For preoperative, thank you.

I'm telling you, you have a, I don't know if, you know, you have a whole fan club on on the, or did I, I saw that. So, Brendan, I'll just start with you on this question. These patients, and this is true certainly for pre-transplant, post-transplant, they're very, these are distinctly different than primary hyperparathyroidism patients. Just in terms of the way kind of you think about approaching these patients in terms of Imaging because these patients, by definition, have all glands. And when I say all glands, I say that because they can also have supernumerary glands, but all gland involvement. So what do you do in terms of imaging in these patients?

So that's a great question. I mean, I think there are at least two schools of thought that I can identify for this group. One is, they're going to get a bilateral exploration. So why bother with the imaging. Well, I guess I'm a bit of a imaging good Nick, in that I like to have images I like to have images in the OR that I can refer to. And I think every patient is different. So my personal thing is, if I'm not going to cause kidney damage, that is going to complicate this situation. So in other words, if their kidneys have given up the ghost and they're not going to be prone to any insult from contrast, My preference would be to get a 4DCT, so I have an intraoperative map of where I need to go, what I should expect to find as far as size, up, down, right, left. But if people are sort of on the fence as to whether they're going to get a transplant, they still have a functioning kidney, albeit compromised, then you wouldn't want to use any imaging in those cases that would put a contrast load on the kidneys and potentially knock out some nephrons.
Okay, great. Thank you. All right. So, Natalia, so why don't you carry on? Can I ask a question?

Please, please. So, hypercalcemia begs the question of which comes first. So, I just want to go back in the patient's record and see if the hypercalcemia preceded the chronic renal disease, I would think this is primary hyperpara, and it would change my paradigm quite a bit. Now, the PTH of 1,000 does kind of suggest it. And so this may be one of those secondary turned tertiary cases. And I would certainly believe that as a possibility, but particularly in somebody who is not on dialysis yet, I would want to make sure that I went back and looked at those levels. So do we have any of that, Natalia?
Yes, she was a normal calcemic initially. And over time, as her kidney function declined, she became hypercalcemic.

Dave, I think that's a really excellent point, which is, and this is one of the things that my mentor Dave Terrace has taught me, which is that just because you are a dialysis patient, for example, doesn't mean you can't have primary hyperparathyroidism that's caused, in fact, by a single gland. But I think for the sake of this conversation, we're going to go ahead with the the more kind of standard secondary hyperparasites.
Multi-gland premise, yeah.

That's okay. But I think your point is a very good one. It's not just because you have kidney disease you can't develop primary disease. By the way, that's pre- or post-transplant. So, Natalia, please.

And so pre-operating ultrasounds obtained and There was a 17 millimeter potential candidate, just posterior and baro to the right thyroid, lower bowl. They can see here and there's purple vascularity on color Doppler ultrasound. There was also a potential second candidate, a 10 millimeter on the left side, just posterior lateral to the left thyroid lobe at the upper bowl. And because of her kidney function, you know, weren't able to get the 4D CT scan. And so a CT neck without contrast was done and hard to fully assess, but what we thought we saw was the right-sided candidate, just inferior and poster to the right lobe, which coincided with the ultrasound. And then on the left side, potentially that area, the 10 millimeter, target that was seen on ultrasound, just posterolateral to the left upper pole. And so I'll keep going. So the operative plan, so we preoperatively, there was a discussion with the nephrologist to establish the extent of surgery and what the PTH post-op goal would be, given that she's an anticipated renal transplantation patient. We wanted to bring up parathyroid reserve. So the goal was to establish at less than 300. And so the plan going in was for a bilateral parathyroid gland exploration with a subtotal three gland excision, leaving the gland behind.

So, Natalia, I'm just going to hold off for a second, because I think there's a ton of really important points to be made from this slide. So, I'll have you start, Dave. Just in terms of target, these patients are obviously, PTH-wise, this is a completely different situation than primary patients. So does this goal kind of fit with what you're looking for? And what happens if you achieve a goal? I mean, are we looking for a number of 20, like we're looking in for in primary hyperparathyroidism, for example?

Well, this reminds me of some advice I got from some more senior surgical colleagues, renal transplant surgeons, that said, if the patient is not on dialysis, do not make them hypoparathyroid. That will be a real disaster. So I don't think you're as aggressive in this patient as you might be in somebody that is in stage, on dialysis, never going to be transplanted. I actually think the goal for this surgery should be to get the calcium normalized because you're going to transplant them and they're still hypercalcemia. that's not gonna work. So while I agree that we don't want their PTH to be too low, I would certainly feel like I failed if the calcium remained high.
So let me interrupt you for a second. So surgically, and Brendan, I'm gonna ask you this question in a second. Surgically, Dave, in this patient, what is your kind of surgical approach?

So I think it's a four gland exploration and it's either going to be a three or a three and a half gland excision depending upon how the glands look. If you've got a relatively normal appearing gland and three abnormal glands, I definitely would just take three. If they're all four grossly abnormal, I'd probably take part of that fourth gland. I wouldn't take the first three and then try to take that portion of the fourth gland. I'd take the portion of the fourth gland first and make sure that I thought I had some viable you know, bleeding parathyroid tissue there. And I agree, the PTH, I would probably have guessed that I'd wanted the PTH to be more like 100, but the point is don't make them hypopara.

Yep. Brendan, in terms of choosing, and Natalia, maybe you can just go ahead to the next slide because I think the pictures are on there and I think it's valuable to see those, is Brendan, in terms of choosing kind of what to leave behind or which gland to leave behind or what part of the parathyroid gland to leave behind, do you have any suggestions for people?

Well, my suggestion is if you have multi-gland disease, find all the glands and leave them in situ and vascularized until all are exposed and all can be evaluated. And then what I like to do is either, as David had explained, a three or a three and a half, probably more frequently a three and a half, and I do the half gland on the most normal, of the four, assuming we're not dealing with supernumerary cases, parathyroid gland and make sure that there's good vascular appearance, that the vasculature is intact, because sometimes with these large lesions, You can sort of get coiling of the polar vessels and stuff like this. So you want to make sure that the remnant that you leave behind isn't going to become Venus congested and infarcted. One other thing I want to say to Natalia, and this perhaps may be one of the most important things projected all tonight. is your two-by-two table. Two-by-two tables are excellent. I think they're excellent both in primary surgery and certainly in revision surgery. And we present the two-by-two table concept among other things in the revision guidelines.

Natalia, sorry, I think there's actually an important part. You have in this two-by-two table, as Brendan just talked about, you have this comment about nodular. Does that mean anything to Brendan, Dave? Does that mean anything in particular, like nodular parathyroid versus non-nodular parathyroid?

Well, I definitely like the term nodular hyperplasia as a good description grossly for what renal failure parathyroid glands look like. And, you know, the nodular, you know, it has a density that is often stiffer and closer to thyroid. than a typical parathyroid adenoma in a primary hyperparakase and different than I think hyperplasia in a primary hyperparakase. So they're clearly abnormal and those are the ones you'd want to take out. I think sometimes it is hard to tell if they're thyroid or parathyroid in those cases. And this one shows two very close together. And the other thing that I think can be hard on the imaging and even intraoperatively is, is it one gland or those two glands that are sort of just pushed together because they're so big.

Yeah. I think that, that, that's an excellent point. And I think your comment about how the, the, the abnormal glands in these cases is very different than the way they look abnormally in primary cases. And a lot of times I think people can eat, you can easily overlook, um, hyperplastic, uh, say renal related, uh, parathyroid glands because they can look like just part of the, the thyroid gland. I'll say that for myself, that when I'm trying to leave behind a remnant, I try and avoid leaving behind nodular remnants of these glands and try and leave behind something that at least looks a little bit more like, say, foregland hyperplasia-type glands, where it looks just more like an enlarged normal parathyroid gland. I think that once it becomes nodular like that, I think that represents such abnormal tissue that, say, for example, the chances of them going on and having persistent hyperparathyroidism even after a transplant, I think, is probably just higher. And there's some data to suggest that's true. So Natalia, do you want to just finish up your presentation?

Yeah. So in the OR, We first started on the right side because the larger of the identified candidates were on that side. They identified all four before, you know, making a decision there. And so on final path, you know, it did in fact, our decision, it dropped what was concordant with our decision intraoperatively. And so all three plans that were removed were in fact enlarged and hypercellular. with modular hyperplastic change. And the PTH pre-op before incision was 1,343, and it came down to 252 after surgery. The calcium also didn't normalize. I don't have it written here, but it was 9.7.
So, first of all, thank you. I just, I'm going to have Dave, it sounds like you have a comment, and then I'm going to have one last question, then we're going to wrap things up. Please, Dave.

So these patients, they need to stay overnight because they can really drop their calciums. And so it's different than the primary hyperparapatients, which we can almost always send home. So that's one comment. And then the other is I find that the kinetics are much slower in these renal failure patients. So I like to get another PTH on post-op day one, and it can drop substantially. Typically, for a primary hyperparapatient, it's going to be at the NADER by the PACU. but not for the renal failure patients.

Yeah, I agree. I have a similar experience. Brendan or Dave or both, historically people have talked routinely about doing thymectomies in these patients. What is your approach, thoughts about thymectomy? Is it always needed? Is it sometimes needed? Brendan.

If I'm having trouble finding it, I certainly have no compunction about taking out thymus, either on one side or both sides. But if the disease is obvious to me, and I'm able to take it out, if I get otherwise, the surgery goes the way that I would expect it to go. No, I do not routinely take out the thymus in these cases. Dave.

I would agree with Brendan. I think that sometimes you feel like you need to, but you don't routinely. I would say MEN1 though, I always do. I think those patients have a high, persistent recurrent rate.
Different population, but I agree with that too.

Yeah, I mean, just so people are aware that the thymectomy idea is that theoretically, these patients, these renal patients, because of the intense drive to make PTH, they have a higher rate, theoretically, of supernumerary glands. So that's kind of the idea of doing the thymectomy. But I think it's important just to hear two, again, very experienced parathyroid surgeons who say they do not routinely do that. And I would add that I don't routinely do that either. So with that, I'm going to wrap up. I really want to thank everyone who joined, who presented. I know that everyone's really busy, and so to take out time, it really just shows your kind of commitment to the education of the fellows. So thank you.

reference_conclusion: For refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism in the setting of stage 4 chronic kidney disease and anticipated renal transplantation, the agreed operative approach was bilateral parathyroid exploration with subtotal parathyroidectomy, targeting preservation of parathyroid reserve rather than complete suppression. The preoperative goal was a postoperative parathyroid hormone level below 300 while avoiding hypoparathyroidism, with normalization of serum calcium also considered important. Postoperatively, overnight inpatient monitoring was recommended because of the risk of significant hypocalcemia, and repeat parathyroid hormone measurement on postoperative day 1 was advised given the slower biochemical kinetics in renal failure patients. Routine thymectomy was not recommended unless required to localize missing disease intraoperatively.

We wanted to bring up parathyroid reserve. So the goal was to establish at less than 300. And so the plan going in was for a bilateral parathyroid gland exploration with a subtotal three gland excision, leaving the gland behind. [...] So I think it's a four gland exploration and it's either going to be a three or a three and a half gland excision depending upon how the glands look. [...] So these patients, they need to stay overnight because they can really drop their calciums. [...] So I like to get another PTH on post-op day one, and it can drop substantially. [...] No, I do not routinely take out the thymus in these cases.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/metastatic HER2-positive breast carcinoma with progression after multiple lines of systemic therapy; history of left breast lump in 2021.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma, HER2-positive, hormone receptor-negative/low-positive on serial biopsies, with skeletal metastases, nodal disease, skin recurrence, right axillary nodal involvement, and brain metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial details from bilateral lumpectomies performed in 2009 were not available. Following left breast recurrence in 2021, post-mastectomy tumor biomarkers were ER negative, PR negative, HER2 3+, Ki-67 25–30%, and androgen receptor strongly positive at >90%. Right axillary node biopsy at progression in November 2024 showed ER 0, PR 3, HER2 3+, and Ki-67 30%. Re-biopsy in October 2025 showed ER Allred score 2, PR 4, and HER2 3+.

[ imaging findings ]: Disease progression during maintenance trastuzumab was associated with skeletal metastases. After T-DM1, there was local progression with nodal disease, skin recurrence, and skeletal metastases. On lapatinib/capecitabine, there was partial response at some disease sites with new right axillary lesions. Interim PET after 6 cycles of docetaxel and 11 doses of PHESGO showed good response. PET in November 2024 showed disease progression with brain metastases. Subsequent PET after initiation of trastuzumab deruxtecan showed good response. PET in October 2025 showed disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NGS identified MSH6 positivity as a variant of uncertain significance. This testing was described as germline testing. Family history was positive for endometrial carcinoma in the patient’s mother and maternal grandmother.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Bilateral lumpectomies were performed in 2009; operative/pathology details were unavailable. In 2021, after presentation with a left breast lump, the patient underwent modified radical mastectomy. She then received adjuvant treatment with 8 cycles of AC and docetaxel with trastuzumab, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and maintenance trastuzumab for 16 doses. During maintenance trastuzumab, after an approximately 3-month delay, metastatic progression with skeletal metastases occurred. She received T-DM1 from July 2023 to August 2023, followed by progression with local, nodal, skin, and skeletal disease. Treatment was changed to lapatinib plus capecitabine, with partial response at some sites but new right axillary lesions. She then received docetaxel plus PHESGO; after 6 cycles of docetaxel and 11 doses of PHESGO, interim PET showed good response, and maintenance PHESGO was continued. In November 2024, PET demonstrated progression with brain metastases. She was then treated with gemcitabine, carboplatin, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab, with progression again by February after approximately 2–3 months. Treatment was changed to trastuzumab deruxtecan, with good PET response, and this was continued for 8 cycles. PET in October 2025 showed progression. She was then started on tucatinib, capecitabine, and trastuzumab.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic HER2-positive breast carcinoma after multiple prior lines of HER2-directed and cytotoxic therapy. At the time of reporting, the patient had completed 2 cycles of tucatinib, capecitabine, and trastuzumab, started on 27 October 2025. Brain metastases had been documented by November 2024. Performance status was described as clinically good apart from radiologic disease progression.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbidities were reported. Family history was significant for endometrial carcinoma in the mother and maternal grandmother.

Again, her treatment was changed to dositaxel and she also received Fesco. Then, after 6 cycles of dositaxel and 11 doses of Fesco, her interim PET showed good response. So, we put her on maintenance Fesco. Subsequently, in November 2024, when her pet was repeated, we saw that she had a disease progression. Now, she was presenting with brain mets as well. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 2-year-old male child; first by birth order; born to non-consanguineous parents. Conceived naturally. Full-term normal vaginal delivery. Birth weight 3.4 kg. Postnatal period was unremarkable. Development was age-appropriate. Immunizations were up to date.

[ chief complaint ]: Sudden-onset gross hematuria for 1 day, with 2-3 episodes of blood in the entire urinary stream, increased urinary frequency, and low-grade fever occurring every 6-8 hours. There was no dysuria, abdominal pain, trauma, drug or food trigger, significant weight loss, body swelling, edema, or palpable abdominal swelling/mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Unilateral right Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) with pulmonary metastases; stage IV disease on the basis of distant lung metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: USG-guided core needle renal biopsy was performed via a posterior approach by interventional radiology. Histopathology showed a poorly differentiated malignant biphasic tumor with blastemal and mesenchymal differentiation, without anaplasia, consistent with Wilms tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Abdominal ultrasonography showed a solid mass involving the upper pole of the right kidney; the lesion had mixed solid and cystic components. The left kidney was normal.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the upper and middle pole of the right kidney with moderate dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system. No thrombus was seen in the renal vein or inferior vena cava. Regional lymph node involvement was present.  
- CT chest showed 3-4 ground-glass nodular lesions in the left lower lobe of the lung, each measuring more than 5 mm, consistent with pulmonary metastases.  
- No abdominal mass was palpable on clinical examination.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hemoglobin was low, with microcytic anemia.  
- Ferritin was low, consistent with iron deficiency.  
- Coagulation studies showed elevated INR and prolonged prothrombin time.  
- Urinary catecholamines were normal.  
- Calcium was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Infectious causes of hematuria were clinically excluded.  
- Preoperative chemotherapy was initiated with actinomycin D, vincristine, and doxorubicin for metastatic Wilms tumor.  
- The first dose of AVD had been administered.  
- Planned schedule included weekly vincristine, actinomycin at alternate intervals as per protocol, and doxorubicin dosing with cumulative dose limitation.  
- Radiologic reassessment after 6 weeks of chemotherapy was planned, followed by surgery.

[ current disease status ]: At the time of reporting, the child had biopsy-confirmed right-sided Wilms tumor with CT-detected pulmonary metastases and regional nodal involvement. The left kidney was normal. There was no renal vein or IVC thrombus. Preoperative chemotherapy had commenced, and nephrectomy had not yet been performed.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination showed pallor.  
- Blood pressure was 128/80 mmHg, approximately at the 90th centile for age.  
- Abdomen was soft, with no tenderness, organomegaly, or palpable mass.  
- Anthropometry was within normal range.  
- No significant past medical history or family history of similar illness was reported.  
- Evaluation for dysmorphism/syndromic associations related to Wilms tumor was negative.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thigh pain on weight bearing, with left quadriceps weakness, presenting to the emergency department in early last year.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic differentiated thyroid carcinoma involving bone, initially identified on core biopsy of an iliac bone lesion as metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma; subsequent thyroidectomy pathology was reported as poorly differentiated thyroid cancer.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Core biopsy of a pelvic/iliac bone metastasis showed features of metastatic follicular thyroid cancer.  
- Histopathology from the left femoral lesion showed metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma with follicular architecture.  
- Total thyroidectomy specimen was reported as poorly differentiated thyroid cancer, with papillary thyroid carcinoma-type nuclear features and vascular invasion described.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial plain radiograph demonstrated a 30 mm lytic lesion in the left femur with cortical thinning and no obvious fracture.  
- MRI performed after preceding left hip/buttock pain radiating to the left thigh demonstrated multiple osseous lesions, including:  
  - a large right iliac lesion with adjacent soft-tissue extension,  
  - an extensive L4 vertebral lesion with extension to the left pedicle and into the adjacent psoas muscle,  
  - additional lesions in both acetabula, both ilia, and the sacrum.  
- Review of imaging from two years earlier showed that the right iliac and L4 osseous lesions had already been present but were smaller.  
- Thyroid ultrasound showed an approximately 50 mm TI-RADS 5 nodule in the left thyroid lobe.  
- CT showed no metastases outside bone.  
- FDG-PET demonstrated mild uptake in the right iliac lesion, mild uptake in the L4 lesion, and very mild uptake in the thyroid gland; most lesions were mildly FDG-avid, with SUVs reported as less than 4.  
- Post-ablation radioiodine scan showed iodine uptake in the left femur lesion and a small additional lesion in the left femoral head not previously appreciated. Most other bony lesions showed no significant iodine uptake, including the right iliac lesion.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Postoperative thyroglobulin after total thyroidectomy: 480 mcg/L.  
- Stimulated thyroglobulin at the time of radioiodine therapy: 529.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Prophylactic gamma nail fixation of the left femur was performed because of concern for impending pathological fracture.  
- Total thyroidectomy was performed.  
- Resection of the L4/L5 spinal metastasis was performed because of concern for L4 nerve root involvement and possible developing pathological fracture.  
- High-dose radioactive iodine therapy was administered: 5.9 GBq (150 mCi).

[ current disease status ]: Persistent metastatic bone disease with heterogeneous and predominantly poor radioiodine avidity. Disease remained confined to bone on available staging CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had been independent at baseline.  
- Past medical history included asymptomatic coronary artery disease, sleep apnea, and lower-limb lymphedema.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old White female.

[ chief complaint ]: Five-month history of headaches with recent development of a left-sided visual field deficit, prompting neuroimaging.

[ diagnosis ]: Large right occipital-parietal brain mass crossing the midline, radiographically most consistent with a high-grade primary CNS neoplasm, specifically glioblastoma multiforme.

[ imaging findings ]: Brain MRI with FLAIR and post-contrast T1-weighted sequences demonstrated a large area of abnormal signal in the right occipital-parietal lobe with extension across the midline. Post-contrast imaging showed a large irregular enhancing mass corresponding to the signal abnormality. Central irregular non-enhancing areas were present, consistent with tumor necrosis. Associated swelling/mass effect was described. Differential considerations of metastatic disease and lymphoma were considered less typical on imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No tumor molecular or genomic test results were available. Biomarkers identified for potential evaluation included MGMT, 1p/19q translocation, IDH1 immunostaining, and PTFR/P3 molecular studies.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior oncologic treatment, surgery, biopsy, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated large invasive intracranial mass involving critical structures and extending into the contralateral hemisphere, with symptomatic headaches and left visual field deficit. No histologic confirmation had yet been obtained.

reference_discussion.text: This is a 57-year-old white female who presents with a history of five months of headaches, and recently she has developed a left-sided visual field deficit, which prompted the current imaging.
Mary, could you please review the MRI scans?

We have a flare and post-contrast T1-weighted images. On the flare image, you can see a large area of abnormal signal in the right occipital parietal lobe with extension across midline. On the post-contrast one image, we can see a large irregular enhancing mass that corresponds with the signal abnormality. If you look at the central irregular areas of non-enhancement, that's indicative of necrosis of the tumor. Due to the overall appearance of the lesion, the signal characteristics, the location, the necrosis, this is most consistent. with a high-grade CNS primary neoplasm, such as a glioblastoma multiforme. Other etiologies would be less typical, including metastatic disease, lymphoma. So again, most likely a GBM.

There are two main options for—surgical options for treating this patient. One is a large operation to remove the tumor, and the other is stereotactic biopsy. On one hand, the tumor is very large and has swelling associated with it, so that would favor a larger operation. On the other hand, it's a very invasive tumor. It involves critical structures, and it crosses over to the opposite hemisphere.
So as I look at these set of MRIs, I would favor stereotactic biopsy to establish a diagnosis for this patient, and then moving on with the appropriate therapy.

Other opinion, surgical opinions? Dr. McPherson. Yeah, I would probably fall in the Other end of the spectrum, we have a lot of evidence that extensive resection certainly benefits. I think she could have a hard time with radiation, given the amount of mass effect and swelling. I do agree this is a big tumor and there's certainly a lot of risk from surgery, but she already has a visual field deficit, which would be the primary deficit I would expect. So I do think that we can achieve an extensive resection without too much risk to her, so I would recommend a craniotomy with the extensive resection, maximal resection of what could be safely achieved. Dr. Chu, what do you think about this patient?

Well, I don't think there's any wrong answer here. The patient always has a chance to hear what the experts say and weigh in their own opinion. You're obviously dealing with a very aggressive tumor in a 57-year-old individual, so there's some Longevity, you want to get the very best you can for the patient. So I think I might come down on the side of offering the patient a radical operation, take out as much of the tumor as possible, which I think, based on our experience and literature, gives the patient the best long run probability quality of life. Obviously, you have to add to that other adjunctive therapies, such as radiation. chemotherapy, but ultimately the patient will make the decision. Dr. Kader, what's your opinion regarding radiation for this patient?

So for a glioblastoma, the recommended radiation therapy would be 30 treatments of radiation to all 60 gray radiation. We would use IMRT or intensity modulated radiation therapy as well as image guidance to try to increase the amount of normal tissue that's exposed to radiation. We would also get a fusion MRI after either the biopsy or the resection to try to better determine the area that needs to be treated with radiation. Using those different techniques specific to the resection question, I don't think there's a significant difference in the normal tissue that would be exposed or certainly not in the planned schedule of radiation based on the biopsy versus resection. And when would you typically start radiation after either of those scenarios? So we typically wait a couple of weeks, but the main determinant there is the surgeon's opinion about how well the patient has healed from the surgery. And so if there are any complications or anything like that, we would certainly take the neurosurgeon's opinion into account for when to start. Additionally, there can be trials or protocols that would determine more specifically when we should start the radiation. Dr. Briggs, so what clinical trial would this patient qualify for?

So here, the standard option after surgery would be chemoradiation, so the combination of radiation and chemotherapy with Stimodar, given at the same time for seven weeks, followed by maintenance Stimodar for a year. I think that's a standard recommendation we can make the patient. But also, this young patient is a candidate for a clinical trial we have here, the RTOG trial. which compares, you know, chemoradiation versus chemoradiation plus citerinib. Citerinib is an anti-vascular agent. And these are two good options we can discuss with a patient in the multidisciplinary clinic on Wednesday. And I think, again, the patient is eligible for the clinical trial. So I would even favor the clinical trial if the patient agrees with that. Any other opinions?
Dr. Kimler, what biomarkers would you normally perform in order to gain information regarding clinical trials?

We have a number of molecular markers that we can utilize, both for a prognosis and then we have markers useful for research study. The molecular markers for prognosis include molecular studies for MGMT, 1p19q translocation, immunostains for IDH1, And then we also have PTFR, P3 molecular studies which are useful for clinical studies. Any other opinions?
So the official recommendation of Tumor Board is surgery.
There seems to be an opinion that the enlarged operation is favored based on the size of the tumor and then followed by either standard treatment with radiation antenna bar or
consideration for clinical trial. We'll have the clinical trials there to meet with the patient to discuss that.
The case has been reviewed in accordance with the NCCN guidelines.

Postoperatively, treatment should proceed with standard chemoradiation consisting of IMRT to 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide, followed by maintenance temozolomide, with fusion MRI obtained after biopsy or resection for radiation planning and treatment initiation after adequate surgical healing. Consideration should also be given to enrollment in the RTOG clinical trial comparing chemoradiation alone versus chemoradiation plus cediranib, with discussion in the multidisciplinary clinic.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal swelling two years after treatment for breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, initially diagnosed two years earlier as stage III disease with axillary nodal involvement; subsequent metastatic recurrence involving liver and lung.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive ductal carcinoma. Receptor status was triple negative: estrogen receptor negative, progesterone receptor negative, and HER2 negative. Initial primary tumor measured approximately 4 cm. Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, residual invasive tumor measured approximately 1 cm at surgery. Residual nodal disease was present in 2 of 18 axillary lymph nodes removed.

[ imaging findings ]: Metastatic workup performed for abdominal swelling demonstrated a pulmonary lesion and liver metastasis. The liver lesion(s) were described as large.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No genetic testing had been performed at the time of initial diagnosis. No tumor genomic sequencing results were available. No PD-L1 testing results were available. No germline BRCA or other inherited cancer predisposition testing results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered with doxorubicin (Adriamycin), cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan), and paclitaxel (Taxol). The breast tumor decreased in size from approximately 4 cm to approximately 1 cm. The patient subsequently underwent bilateral mastectomies and axillary lymph node dissection. Surgical pathology demonstrated residual breast tumor and persistent nodal disease in 2/18 lymph nodes. Capecitabine (Xeloda) was offered postoperatively in the setting of residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic triple-negative breast cancer identified two years after initial diagnosis, with documented liver and pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: At initial presentation, axillary nodes were described as fixed. Residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy was present; a pathologic complete response was not achieved.
