reference_discussion.text: Well, great. We're going to move on to the next case and we'll take a few questions at the end. Next case, she's 56 years old, most common type of breast cancer as well, invasive ductal carcinoma. She's what we call triple negative. No estrogen, no progesterone, and no HER2 new. She was diagnosed two years ago. At that time, the facility that she was treated at, they did not do genetic testing. At that stage, at that time, she was stage three. Tumor was significant, had fixed nodes in the axilla, Chemotherapy was given prior to surgery, which is a good thing. She had adriamycin, citoxin, and taxol. She opted to have, although she had disease in only one part of her breast, she chose to have bilateral mastectomies, and she had all the lymph nodes removed. And the initial tumor size was about four centimeters. It shrank down to one, and she had two out of 18 lymph nodes after chemotherapy. Her provider offered her Zolota, which is often done with triple negative breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and residual disease is found. So she comes back in two years, has some abdominal swelling, and she has a metastatic workup. And on the right to you guys, that's actually the heart in the center. At the bottom there, there's a little round lesion right at the spine, and that is a pulmonary lesion. On the next slide to the left, the figure to your right, that's your liver. And the dark gray areas, that's a liver metastasis. So we're going to talk about what we would offer her. Want to get started, Dr. Bobby?
Sure. I think Dr. French is supposed to go first. Oh, he's supposed to go first. No, no, no. I didn't want to.
It's easier if you go first, right?

All right. So first of all, unfortunately, this is a more common situation that we'd like to see with triple negative breast cancers. Triple negative breast cancers do, unfortunately, account for a smaller subset of women, but they tend to have more aggressive disease. And oftentimes, we do see recurrence after we've attempted curative intent therapy. The first thing that I would recommend for a patient like her is, again, to get a biopsy of a metastatic site. Not so much to prove what the receptors are, but also to send the tumor for genomic sequencing to identify potentially any targeted options available for the patient. Also to send the tumor for a certain protein expression in the immune cells called PD-L1, for which we now have an FDA-approved immunotherapy to offer women that are PD-L1 positive in the metastatic setting for triple negative breast cancer. So that's the first thing that I would do. There's a number of genomic sequencing modalities that can be used, Foundation One, Tempest, Keras, so a lot of different companies that are offering genomic sequencing. It makes it very easy for patients and potentially, again, offers them targeted therapies or clinical trial options in the future down the road. In terms of our current standard of care, if a woman does have PD-L1 positive triple negative breast cancer, then we can actually offer them immunotherapy, which is an exciting new therapy for breast cancer patients that was previously not approved. So it's a combination of atezolizumab, again, which is an immunotherapy in combination with chemotherapy that has improved both how long we can control a woman's cancer and also overall survival in women that are PD-L1 positive. So that is something that I would strongly consider in this woman if she does have a PD-L1 positive breast cancer. If it's PD-L1 negative, then we do start talking about standard of care chemotherapy options versus potentially clinical trial if we are able to identify a matched clinical trial or a clinical trial that the patient would be eligible for.

That's a tough one. The other thing that she is, if she hasn't had genetics already, she needs genetic testing. You know, you're looking for, again, as we're going to talk, she'll probably talk about kind of the BRCA1 and 2 mutations because that does, you might not start with these drugs looking at Olaparib or some of these BRCA inhibitors or these drugs that work on these pathways, but the name of the game at this point is to try to open up your armament to say how many options can I have in my back pocket when I need them. If you look at the data with the Impassion 130 trial, that was with the addition of the tezolizumab, you know, it does increase progression-free survival and at the last, I think it was AACR update, they actually had an overall survival update. So it does add more toxicities to the regimen now because now you're adding immunotherapy. But with the survival advantage, it is FDA approved and that's probably the new standard of care that is as of just in the last 12 months or so. It's actually probably less than that, less than six months ago. You want to talk about that? I do. Yeah.
Thank you.

Yeah, so as Dr. French said, this patient clearly meets the criteria for genetic testing because any woman diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer under 60, regardless of her family history, her stage, anything else, is recommended to have genetic counseling and testing. And given that we've brought up genomic tumor sequencing, I just want to make sure everybody understands that there's, we've talked a lot about genomics and genetics already today, and a lot of that discussion is around tumor genetics and genomics. What I do in my clinic is different. We're testing inherited, your DNA that a person is born with. You can do that type of genetic testing on a person with cancer, without cancer. It's not dependent on the tumor. It's talking about your genes that you were born with and whether a person is predisposed to certain types of cancer due to something that they inherited almost always from one of their parents. So sometimes in these talks and even in papers or articles online, it can get confusing to know whether they're talking about BRCA or a gene that's isolated in a tumor or whether it's inherited. So you always want to make sure if you've had a tumor genomic test, that doesn't rule out the need for inherited mutation testing because a small percentage of people could have an inherited BRCA mutation that does not show up in their tumor testing. So you always want to make sure if your doctors are talking to you about BRCA, you've had both types of testing to completely, like Dr. French said, make sure that all your eligibility is known because usually the indications are for either tumor or germline or both. And germline means inherited. That's, if you see that word, that's talking about inherited DNA versus somatic or tumor or talking about mutations in a tumor.

Okay, so one of the reasons that you do tumor board with multidisciplinary approaches is that sometimes you read the body language and the tone of voice of your colleagues. Did you guys hear how excited they are? This gene and that gene will do immunotherapy, a new standard of care. From the radiation point of view, they've got something to offer, right? Now you might say, wait a minute, didn't you just say on the last patient a few mets and only a couple of organs and you should go to the races with the radiation? Yeah, those were little mets. Those were little mets. This liver, even if you called that two, they're huge and they move every time the patient breathes, right? So that's why you can't do medicine just by algorithm. You have to have some common sense in there and you have to have some teamwork. This is just not a radiation case at the moment. They've got things they can offer that can extend life, and they may shrink targets up. And maybe you invite a radiation oncologist to review the case again down the line, but at the moment, this is a systemic therapy case.

I'm going to add one other comment in terms of the gene sequencing is that I think there is a lot of education going on both in the academic world where not all triple negative breast cancer is the same. And so I think with Foundation One testing is I think eventually what we're going to find is that triple negative breast cancer is going to be kind of what we see in lung cancer, is that we're looking for a driver mutation where we used to think, oh, you have small cell or non-small cell lung cancer. Well, now non-small cell lung cancer is broken into two different parts, and now we're actually saying, oh, well, you have a met-mutated non-small cell lung cancer. I know it's a little bit complicated, but triple negative breast cancer is not all one disease. And I think there are a lot of clinical trials looking for specific targets to say, okay, you have triple negative, but what's driving it? And whether that's something to say, oh, this is an androgen positive breast cancer, so we're using therapies like you would use in prostate, or you're using pills to target that specific mutation, is very important in our triple negative cases.

I think that's a really good point and I do think that a lot of the trials nowadays that are focused on triple negative are looking at the up to six subsets of triple negative breast cancer and how to best target each of those as perhaps different type, as Dr. French mentioned, different drivers for each subset of triple negative. We do also have clinical trials available for triple negative breast cancer at Emory, and I'm sure WellStar does as well. The one that is coming to Emory soon is actually the use of a PARP inhibitor, which has been currently FDA approved only for women that have the BRCA germline mutation. There is a trial looking at the combination of a PARP inhibitor with another type of targeted therapy, also an oral drug, that perhaps works together to better control triple negative breast cancer. And that is actually offered for all triple negative breast cancer patients who have progressed on chemotherapy, irregardless of whether they have a BRCA mutation. So again, offers an oral targeted therapy to more women with this clinical trial.

And then the last, do I have time? The last thing I want to say, because this is a community forum, is just education. In terms of, this is going to be one of the first immunotherapy drugs that is approved for breast cancer space, but we've been using immunotherapies in melanoma and lung cancer for years now. So there's this guy out of Harvard named Hal Bernstein, when this got FDA approved, he said, you know, when immunotherapy comes to breast cancer, all the doctors are now immunotherapists. And so we have to be aware of the toxicities are different than chemo, right? So, you know, when we're thinking chemo, you're thinking nausea, vomiting, I'm going to lose my hair, fatigue, diarrhea. And immunotherapy toxicities are very different. And people in the community, when you go see your primary care doctors, might not recognize those. So there needs to be an education for our community and even not just medical oncologists, but our endocrinologists, our pulmonologists, your primary care doctors to say, hey, I'm not just on chemo, I'm on immunotherapy. So if you go there and you have normal blood sugars and you go see your PCP and they say, your blood sugar is 400, you have diabetes now. Well, maybe the immunotherapy took out or injured your pancreas and now you need to be on insulin and the therapy he's prescribing is not right. So we've seen this several times, and we're going to see it more, especially as this immunotherapy comes to our breast cancer patients. And there is a revolution of this immunotherapy that there needs to be education in the community and our community doctors, because you're seeing us, but most people probably have two, three, sometimes four other doctors they're seeing. And the toxicities we're seeing are not like chemo. So if you're fatigued all the time and you're saying, oh, well, it's just chemo fatigue, well, maybe that's not true. Maybe you've developed low thyroid now. And so there are things that they need to be checking for, at least communicating with us, to say, hey, my patient's in the office, and they're having this issue. What do you think about this? And I think sometimes I'm a stickler on proper nomenclature, and I don't call it chemotherapy. I call it immunotherapy, because it helps delineate that, hey, it's a different type of therapy, and the mechanisms work differently, and that profile of toxicity is different.

All right, just to go back on that patient, the reason why I brought her up, triple negative is very important when we look at stage four disease, but I did want to bring up one point just on the surgery side. So this was a woman that had breast cancer, only one part of her breast, and she actually had chemo first. The tumor had gotten much smaller. She still had the choice to do a lumpectomy and for her lymph nodes to be removed. The reason why I bring that up, because a lot of women think that if you have bilateral mastectomies, you're cured. You have no risk of the disease coming back, and that's absolutely an untrue statement. So, if you have the opportunity to preserve your breasts, or if you need a unilateral mastectomy, in most cases, it will not change your outcome if you choose a lesser invasive procedure. As well, when she had chemo initially, and then she had surgery, and she had residual tumor noted, that's another risk factor for her to have recurrence to come back. So, as providers, we were not totally shocked because she had advanced stage disease on presentation. When she had chemo, the tumor was not totally resolved, and when it's totally resolved, that's what we call a pathological complete response. just for you to be familiar with the verbiage there.

Dr. Johnson, can I make one more comment about this case? So there are some misunderstandings out there about what choice you're really making when you choose a mastectomy or a double mastectomy, and I'm really glad Dr. Johnson brought that up. One of the misconceptions out there is in a case like this, If I have a double mastectomy or even a single mastectomy, I'll avoid radiation therapy. Absolutely not true in this case. This is advanced disease, triple negative with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemo. This is a radiation patient every single day. So we really want our breast patients to meet with their radiation oncologist early in the process because they can explain when they would and would not need radiation. One of the things we have a hard time with in the community is a radiation doctor in the community often doesn't want to see a patient unless they're sure that the patient's going to need radiation. And we need to push back on that. You need a consultation with all of your specialists whether or not it's clear you'll need their services simply because a multidisciplinary approach requires all the expertise at the table.

reference_conclusion: Biopsy of a metastatic site is recommended to confirm recurrent disease and to obtain tissue for tumor genomic sequencing and PD-L1 testing. If the metastatic triple-negative breast cancer is PD-L1 positive, treatment with atezolizumab in combination with chemotherapy is the current standard systemic therapy; if PD-L1 negative, standard chemotherapy or an appropriate clinical trial should be considered. Germline genetic counseling and testing, including BRCA1/2 evaluation, is also indicated. At present, this is not a radiation case and should be managed as a systemic therapy case, with reconsideration of radiation oncology if disease sites become more amenable later in the course.

Also to send the tumor for a certain protein expression in the immune cells called PD-L1, for which we now have an FDA-approved immunotherapy to offer women that are PD-L1 positive in the metastatic setting for triple negative breast cancer. [...] The other thing that she is, if she hasn't had genetics already, she needs genetic testing. [...] this patient clearly meets the criteria for genetic testing because any woman diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer under 60, regardless of her family history, her stage, anything else, is recommended to have genetic counseling and testing. [...] This is just not a radiation case at the moment. They've got things they can offer that can extend life, and they may shrink targets up. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for consideration of curative-intent treatment for newly diagnosed high-risk prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Biopsy-proven prostate adenocarcinoma with PSA 16 and Gleason score 9 (grade group 5).

[ histopathology results ]: Prostate biopsy demonstrated Gleason 9 carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: External staging PSMA PET had initially been reported as showing bilateral pelvic nodal metastases, left axillary metastases, bone metastases in the right iliac bone and L3, and multiple lung metastases.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior treatment data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed high-risk prostate cancer with PSA 16 and Gleason score 9, referred for consideration of curative-intent treatment, with an external staging PSMA PET report describing bilateral pelvic nodal, left axillary, osseous, and pulmonary metastatic disease.

reference_discussion.text: Fantastic. Thanks, Michael, for that. So we will just push on with the cases. And if, Michael, you can advance those slides, that would be great. Thanks. Good. OK. So case one is actually a case of a 58-year-old man with a PSA of 16 who had a Gleason 9 biopsy-proven cancer. and he was referred for consideration of curative intent treatment, and an external staging PSMA PET was done, and it came in with the report of bilateral pelvic nodal metastases, left axillary metastases, bone metastases in the right iliac bone and L3, and multiple lung metastases. This was accompanied by some safe screens that were sent in with the report. So the question for the MDT panel actually, firstly, is What would you guys do as the referring clinicians of this patient and you got this report, what would your first step be? I guess we'll start with Shankar or Declan actually, we'll start with Declan.

Yeah, so we showed in the Pro PSMA trial that the use of PSMA PET-CT provided greater accuracy compared to conventional imaging. And that's been well borne out in other data. However, it's still very important that we scrutinize these images. There is variability in the quality of PSMA PET-CT, although again within Pro PSMA. We did do central review from the 10 sites and did show the concordance was very high, especially compared to MRI, for example. But nonetheless, it's still very important to review these images. So that's the first point I think I'd made to Yiting is that we do like to review all these images ourselves because it's a big call. Does this patient have distant metastatic disease? Does he have high volume distant metastatic disease? It's very important that we have confidence in the findings before we make a management recommendation.
Excellent. OK, well, we might actually move on to the next slide and actually get James to present the case for us.

All right, thank you. So we did get the images imported and had a look. You can see that this is the MIP to the right, and it's quite saturated. So I think that if we have a look down here, you do see the prostate cancer very highly avid, just below the bladder. There is quite a bit of noise, as you'd expect for BSMA PET, but it's very, very saturated. So usually Peter Mac will window it with 15 upper windows, so it looks a little bit more like this when you're interpreting and you have a little bit less of that noise that isn't actually significant. And if we have a look at those screen caps, you actually just had a lot of noise down here in the lower lobes of the lungs. So it wasn't actually, there weren't actually metastases, nothing on CT there. And you just look at the PET image itself, it doesn't look like there's anything that actually stands out. Same for the nodes down here in the pelvis. So again, it does look a little bit more alarming. But then when you look at it in a more appropriate window, there isn't anything suspicious. And same for those bone metastases. So windowing is quite important. It does change how you interpret. It's OK to change it. So you can adjust the windowing. As you see, we say 15. So anything above 15 is very red or very dark. Here, anything that was above 4 had that same appearance, so it's good to have it more around 0 to 15. You can change it just to increase sensitivity while you're reporting, so it's good to change that windowing, especially if you're looking for little pelvic nodes and you just want to have a higher sensitivity.

Thanks for describing that and the importance of windowing. So my question for the panel would actually be, does every PSMA PET that you get from an external site or even internally need to be presented at a MDT? Any one of you?

Yeah, I think at the moment, definitely yes. Because outside of clinical trials, we're doing PSMA PET scans either to aid in diagnosis or to assess whether a patient's suitable for radionuclide therapy. And I think those are decisions that really need to be made in the multidisciplinary setting. But this case also really highlights the danger of not doing an expert review of the PSMA PET scan because obviously in centers that aren't used to reporting PSMA PET scans, there can be variability in the quality of the reports. And also emphasizes the importance of doing PSMA PET scans in the appropriate setting. In this case, it was appropriate because the patient had high-risk disease. I think it was grade group five. So according to the PRO-PSMA trial, it's appropriate. But for example, in a patient with lower risk disease, having this particular PSMA pair report could have caused them a lot of danger, particularly if it wasn't reviewed in an MDT. Fantastic.

reference_conclusion: External PSMA PET findings should undergo expert multidisciplinary review before treatment decisions are made, particularly when the report suggests distant high-volume metastatic disease. In this case, MDT review of the imported images determined that the apparent lung, pelvic nodal, and osseous lesions reflected image noise and windowing artifact rather than true metastases; management should therefore be based on the reviewed imaging rather than the external report.
reference_conclusion_quote: it's still very important to review these images. So that's the first point I think I'd made to Yiting is that we do like to review all these images ourselves because it's a big call. Does this patient have distant metastatic disease? Does he have high volume distant metastatic disease? It's very important that we have confidence in the findings before we make a management recommendation. [...] So it wasn't actually, there weren't actually metastases, nothing on CT there. [...] Same for the nodes down here in the pelvis. So again, it does look a little bit more alarming. But then when you look at it in a more appropriate window, there isn't anything suspicious. And same for those bone metastases. [...] this case also really highlights the danger of not doing an expert review of the PSMA PET scan

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Referral for consideration of radioactive iodine following surgery for oncocytic thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Left thyroid oncocytic carcinoma, 4 cm, widely invasive; categorized as high risk of recurrence based on initial pathology.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial left lobectomy at an outside institution showed a 4 cm left thyroid oncocytic carcinoma. Capsular invasion was present. Vascular invasion was present with more than 4 foci. No lymphatic invasion was identified. No microscopic extrathyroidal extension was identified. Surgical margins were negative. No lymph node metastasis was identified. Subsequent completion thyroidectomy showed benign pathology in the contralateral lobe.

[ imaging findings ]: FDG PET scan after completion thyroidectomy was negative except for a small level II lymph node.

[ laboratory results ]: Post-lobectomy thyroglobulin was 0.2. Later laboratory values showed TSH 0.12, free T4 1.4, thyroglobulin 1.7, and negative thyroglobulin antibodies.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent left thyroid lobectomy at an outside institution, followed by completion thyroidectomy.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was lost to follow-up for approximately 1 year after initial surgical evaluation, then established care with a local endocrinologist before referral.

reference_discussion.text: For the case number two, we have a 67-year-old male with four centimeters left on conciliatory thyroid carcinoma. He underwent left lobectomy in an outside institution. There was no lymphatic invasion, and the invasion was present with more than four foci. He had a capsular invasion present, there was no microscopic estradiol extension, negative margins, and there was no lymph node positive.

Okay, hold for me right there for just a second. Dr. Alexander, the ATA guidelines in 2015 and more in 2025 leads us down this pathway of lobectomy in these three or four centimeters. And we can't tell this beforehand. So now the question is, you've got somebody that's going to be relatively high risk with four foci. but it's an onchocytic thyroid cancer. So talk me through that decision about completion or completion plus radioactive iodine. Eric, how are you thinking about this?

Yeah, I think we used to have that discussion a lot more with the patient directly, preoperatively 10 to 15 years ago. And now, as the guidelines would suggest, kind of less is more in general. But it's important to kind of always lean in, I think, in advance to say, here's the possibility of where this could go. And I think we all do that so the patient doesn't get too worried. I mean, in this case, I definitely would like the other half removed for a number of reasons. One, we'll question here whether to give radioiodine. We'll push that off for another point here. But I also think when you remove the other half, you improve the sensitivity of detecting recurrence. If nothing else, you get thyroglobulin to be very low, and then even if it's not zero, choosing radioiodine or not, the trend will be much more sensitive. So I tend to favor leaning in that direction. I talk to the patient quite directly that you're in the hands of a good surgeon, obviously, but there's a reason why we're thinking about this, and the long-term interest here is going to be the key.
Janice, how are you thinking about this one? Because they always say I'm the most aggressive surgeon at Memorial. I don't have to do the surgery. So unmute and tell us what you're thinking.

Yeah, no, I think this needs a completion thyroidectomy for all of the reasons that Eric has outlined going forward. And once again, no lymph nodes. I'd like to know the number of lymph nodes that were recovered and how many were negative, positive. If they're all negative and there were eight lymph nodes, then that would change the discussion a little bit. But if there were two lymph nodes and they were negative, we don't know what's going on. And the angioinvasion would say, let's take the other side out to help with ongoing treatment down the road and surveillance.
Eric, what is post-op thyroglobin 0.2?

0.2 with half the thyroid out. First of all, I'd be, that's surprising with half the thyroid out. Nonetheless, I'm kind of leaning here and we'll get to that discussion that I would favor radioactive iodine. And I know it's going to be a good discussion on that here upcoming, but I need the other half out to do that, even with a very low thyroid globulin.

So if it's 0.2, we got unmeasured antibodies or something, right? So even in the setting of a lobectomy, even a low-ish thyroid globulin, I guess the only thing that would help you if it was like, thousands or really high than you would know. Mabel, how are you thinking about these now?

So I'm going to be the outlier in the group, unfortunately. And I'm thinking about this for the last case as well. So these come by way of oncocytic neoplasm. So we don't know if it's cancer. And so these, in my opinion, are very rarely multifocal. Our pathologist can correct me if I'm wrong on that. And I truly view these as intrinsically radioiodine refractory. And so to me, I don't. So one of the things I do, and it's, I think, different than the guidelines, and that's my practice, but I actually stage these patients at the time preoperatively. So if I know it's an oncocytic neoplasm, at Mayo, our risk for malignancy is 15%. And often, especially if it's a follicular thyroid cancer, I would stage it, which means I do a CT test to see if there's distant disease. We have very good neck ultrasounds like you do at Memorial and other sites. So I'm very trusting of our ultrasound. If there's no nodal disease and no distant disease, then when the patient undergoes lobectomy and we find that it's capsular invasion or angioinvasion and it's a carcinoma, I'm fine with that. And I don't send these patients back for completion because I've already staged them. And if there's no distant disease, I'm certainly not gonna do radioactive iodine. That's my practice. If there is distant disease, I understand you could still, many endocrinologists would then say, let's do a total or make sure we have a total so we do iodine. I think that's how you could get around this. And so you don't, then you can, have the scan, don't have to go back for a second surgery. So I do a lot of staging before they go to surgery, so I know the lay of the land. And I would have done that with the first case as well. And I probably, even if it's eight centimeters, if it's an oncocytic, I don't send them back for completion.
Yeah, gotcha. George, what's sort of your guys' approach there in Sao Paulo?

Well, in these cases, usually they would go for a completion thyroidectomy and many of these patients are referred to radioiodine. In my opinion, I like to assess with an FDG PET before going to radioiodine. But in the first case, due to elevated TG, I was already thinking about doing a radioiodine. So I chose to use a whole body scan before to decide if I was going to proceed or not with a radioiodine. But in this case, I would go for probably a completion of the thyroid resection and we would go for an FDG to see if there was distant mets and then proceed to redo iodine.

That's great. I don't want Mabel to feel alone here. You're probably not surprised that I don't do a completion thyroidectomy and I don't do radioactive iodine. We don't generally stage before but we would absolutely stage this with 18-FDG PET scan because I want to know the extent of disease and the PET is going to be far better than radioactive iodine. I don't worry about the contralateral lobe. That's easy to follow. It's distant mets that I worry about. So we also think oncocytic is RAI refractory, just out the gate, out the board. So if we don't have, if we're not going to use radioactive iodine, we wouldn't automatically do completion. Sometimes these guys, thyroglobin is 50 or 75, and they've got some little nodules on the other side. You don't know if they have distant mets. So occasionally, we'll do a completion for staging for that. But we see these as really not very RAI responsive at all, and so we'll generally follow them. So take us up through a little bit what the guidelines said, Alina.

So, we did not, in his case, he was an outside institution. He did complete the, had a total thyroidectomy, and he was benign in the pathology. And based on his initial pathology, because of the widely invasive, he will be put in the category of high risk of recurrence.

Yeah, I think it is worth saying that high risk is not 100%, right? Because Mabel talked about cases that had high vascular invasion, and they did great. In fact, the majority will do great. It's not 70, 80% that met out, at least over a decade or two. So it's important to remember that some of these patients will do fine, and it's not 100% risk of recurrence over time. So depending on the size and the case, I agree it's more than 30%, but it's not like 90%. Keep going, Lynn.

So that is reflected in this follow up. So he was he saw first the surgeon, lost follow up for a year and then established care with a local endocrinologist who referred to us for radioactive iodine. And he came with these labs, the TSH of 0.12, free T4 of 1.4, and a paraglobulin that was 1.7 with negative antibodies.
Keep going.

So we wanted to go ahead with additional imaging. So we get a PET scan, according to the recommendations from the guidelines in this case, and his PET scan, it was a negative. We had only a small level 2 lymph node. So now the question was, are we going to give him radioactive iodine? That was the reason for referral. So we brought again the guidelines to the discussion. Okay.

Thank you. So you can tell in the guidelines there. I mean, I wasn't on the guidelines committee this time, but you can tell as a community. Most of us are thinking radioactive and certainly is not as effective as we want it to be. but maybe there's still some hope, the few cases you can do it and to facilitate follow-up. And you can kind of see that in the wording of the guidelines here. It's often impossible to prove a negative, right? How do you prove that this doesn't work and we don't have randomized prospective trials? But I think this certainly opens the door for the ones of us like Mabel and I that don't wanna do a completion thyroidectomy radioactive iodine to say within the big context, we're still fine, but also tends to still lean toward using it if I'm reading between the words there.

You know, I think you nailed it. And I love this discussion. I mean, this is the constant one where we're all shaking our heads at the national meetings, these types of cases. And I'll give you just a share of the way I share it with my fellows, not to be right or wrong, but how I walk into it. And I really think that's the key is how do we each approach the clinical translation of data into the care of the individual patient? And we're all different as clinicians. And I'll just share my approach, which is, if you will, I walked into the field as a standard being surgery, radioiodine, TSH suppression. There's no doubt I've watched the field kind of pull back and we use much less radioiodine, just across the board, every type, right? for the right reasons. Having said that, I like the clinical endpoint, and I'm always struggling where there's a lack of a good trial that tells me there's no reduction in disease recurrence, no reduction in mortality, things like that. I just don't think we have it yet, so I'm using less doses of radioiodine. I'm using less in terms of the quantity of the dose. But in this case, if I've already committed to kind of taking the other half out, I'm kind of worried about the patient. You know, I'm asking myself, there are other considerations beyond whether the science truly is telling us that those cells are not iodine avid, which I would agree with. There is also the innocent bystander kind of phenomenon that a beta particle can travel one to two millimeters. Could you get a little bit of perhaps destruction of an innocent bystander cancer cell? So I just don't know. And I'm just a little more conservative, I guess, is the way to finish it. as to why I still give it, but I know where the field's going. I think we will ultimately say there's no utility here down the road.

Yeah. Jorge, what are you thinking about this? I mean, are we already at the point, we're drawing back some, but are we still giving it to everybody? I mean, this is widespread vascular invasion. If you're going to give it to anybody, this is who you're going to worry about. How are you thinking about it, Jorge?

Yeah. Here in Brazil, we have sometimes some difficulty in the follow-up of patients. Though most endocrinologists and head and neck surgeons still prefer to give radioiodine to these oncocytic thyroid carcinomas, but mostly due to follow-up problems here. We see that they are mostly not very respondent to radioiodine. So I think here the thing is we could use more FDG PET-CTs to manage these patients. And even though we can lose their follow-up, with a negative PET-CT and this low thyroglobulin, I would be comfortable to say the patient was going to be cured if he had a complete thyroidectomy.

Yeah. Janice helped me here at the Big Picture. You've taken a couple of thyroids out over the years. I'm in a situation where I've got a high-risk patient, no question about it. I'm in a situation where I've got an adjuvant therapy that may or may not work, and in fact probably won't work. Then I've got to come to you and say, oh, tell me the real risk of a completion of thyroidectomy, not necessarily on the people on this. panel, but the real risk of a thyroidectomy in people in the real world that are going to be in surgeries done all over the United States. So help me understand what that risk is relative to the potential benefit, Janice.

Yeah, and I think that's one of the reasons the ATA guidelines have really sort of de-escalated surgery because not everybody has access to experts that do this surgery well. So hypoparathyroidism, it's not a benign disease. It's serious. And so to go into a completion thyroidectomy, the risk is what happened at the first operation? How many parathyroids were seen? What was the skill set that took out the first side when you're going after the other side? And so I think as surgeons, generally we tell them, oh yes, there's a risk of hypoparathyroidism, but the surgeons aren't the ones that long-term are following these patients. It's the endocrinologist, and that's a devastating disease, particularly for a young patient. So one does have to be cautious about recommending a completion thyroidectomy and who you get to do that.

Yeah, I mean, it's a balance. Mabel, Eric sort of mentioned that the basic biology was helping us understand this was a different tumor. Can I have you and then sort of Zuber talk about sort of the molecular biology of these onchocytics and how that may inform, you know, RAI responsiveness or avidity? Mabel first.

Yeah. So I think, you know, 60, 80 years ago when we used iodine for the first patients, you know, with thyroid cancer and had good luck with probably a follicular thyroid cancer that was functional, that really changed the tone and it was rational sense that we should use radioactive iodine than for all differentiated thyroid cancers. And I think 80 years ago, without more data and enough experience, that was the right answer. And then we had studies saying that if you get iodine, your outcomes are better, which I think are again skewed by certain populations of very REI avid patients that makes it a blanket statement. And now we fast forward from the work from the lab showing that we understand the biology of these diseases much more distinctly now, and that genomics impact iodine uptake or refractoriness. And in oncocytics, which used to be thought of as follicular thyroid cancers, the new WHO 2022 has really reclassified these as a separate entity. And I view them as that. And we know work from Ian Ganley and Dave McFadden that really it's mitochondrial mutations in class one of the electron transport chain. It's really, it's a metabolic disease, which is why it probably lights up so strongly on PET scan is the mitochondria that are full. While they do have nuclear mutations, and Ian Ganley showed a lot of loss of heterozygosity, some RAS mutations, some mTOR pathways, they are very different. And so these are probably reasons why I think they're intrinsically resistant to radioiodine and have a different biology.
Yeah. Subbara, thoughts about that sort of general area?

No, so I completely agree with what Mabel was saying. You know, it's always interesting that if you look at these oncositic tumors, we all knew even before molecular that they are a different kind of group of tumors, the way they grow. If you look at the angioinvasive oncocytic tumors that have been described in the literature, this will be the cancer where it will be the smallest size. You know, so I have seen small oncocytic carcinomas actually infiltrated and very angioinvasive. Also, the lymph node data shows us that it was initially thought that they really are the tumors which go through blood vessels and invade the lymph nodes. And this is where the whole radioactive iodine treatment literature came from. But when you really look at these tumors and what a couple of the studies from Hopkins and stuff shown, that some of these deposits that we saw completely replaced lymph nodes are actually soft tissue foci of angioinvasion that were interpreted as lymph node maps. So I think And that's when you look at the molecular makeup of these tumors, as Mabel was pointing out, it doesn't follow the normal BRAF and RAS pathway like food groups. It's a completely different tumors. Yes, you do see RAS mutated oncocytic tumors. And as we know, RAS mutated tumors have a higher differentiation scores. and they do respond to radioactive iodine differently than BRAF mutated tumors do. But then you have a layering of chromosomal alterations. Aggressive oncocytic tumors have third promoter mutations. So I think all these molecular profiles with a high risk on additional molecular alterations really affect how these tumors are going to respond. So I have, when I have an oncocytic tumor, which has not been nicely sampled by the trainee or somebody else, or even a pathologist, I always ask for more sections, because I know that these tumors can be very tricky. They can look really nice in the center. On the edges, you will see like multiple, multiple foci of vascular invasion, or even beyond the capsule. So when I see these tumors, I already am on a trigger to say, okay, you know what, this needs much more thorough evaluation because this is an oncocytic tumor. And even you can have poorly differentiated transformation in a very small oncocytic tumor. They don't need to be eight or nine centimeters. So I think this is a really different biology. And that's why I'm so glad that WHO and even ATA guidelines separated them out from the variety, garden variety, papillary and follicular parurin carcinomas.
I agree completely. Okay, Lena, finish this case up for me so I can get to number three. Show us what happened.

So, he was an oximalist patient also, so we decided to give him 30 MCI of radioactive iodine. This is a post-therapy scan. There was only uptake in the neck, but there was no evidence of local or regional or taste and metastasis. So, the long-term follow-up with him, two years with a suppressed TSH at the beginning, and then with normal TSH two years post-radioactive iodine showing an excellent response. He had an ecultrasound every year. They didn't show any suspicious nodules. And then going back to the guylines with the dynamic risk stratification, he initially was started here, but with the excellent response, he currently is in this category with 350% risk of recurrence. So yes, this is the last.

He's great. So the other teaching point is when they start out high risk, even if they have an excellent response, they still have some significant risk, right? And the natural history of these are when they look great like this to begin with, when they recur, they often have that thyroid globulin start going up around two or three years and you find the structural disease around year five. So these guys that are high risk to start with, I'm always cautiously optimistic. Let's watch those thyroid globulins because one pattern that I think is most common for them to recur is around that five year point. And it probably just has to do with the tumor volume doubling time. It's just little small stuff that grew there. Okay, let's look at the third one. I think we take it up a notch for the third one. Considering the aquasitic theme, I think very good. And Dr. Tarasova, we've let her off this morning so far. We'll have her share the slides.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

[ diagnosis ]: Localized prostate adenocarcinoma involving a right posterior peripheral zone lesion, clinically palpable on the right side. Baseline clinical stage was consistent with cT1c/T2a eligibility criteria for focal therapy registry enrollment.

[ histopathology results ]: Transperineal targeted biopsy plus template biopsy demonstrated Grade Group 2 prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 3+4) in the right mid/posterior target region, with only a very small proportion of Gleason pattern 4 reported. Template biopsy also showed a small incidental contralateral focus in the left mid prostate measuring 2 mm, reported as Gleason 6 / Grade Group 1.

[ imaging findings ]: Pre-treatment multiparametric prostate MRI demonstrated a right posterior peripheral zone lesion at approximately the mid-gland, visible as a hypointense area, particularly on ADC imaging. The lesion was MRI-positive and categorized within the PI-RADS 3-5 eligibility range.

[ laboratory results ]: Baseline PSA was 6.7 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent focal low-dose-rate brachytherapy to the right posterior lesion. Treatment consisted of 45 iodine-125 seeds delivered via 11 needles. Prescribed dose was 145 Gy to the focal planned target volume. The treatment volume included an expansion of approximately 7 mm beyond the initially targeted lesion. Because of the posterior lesion location, approximately 15 mL of hydrogel rectal spacer was placed to separate the prostate from the rectum.

[ other clinical data ]: At presentation, the patient had no urinary symptoms and no erectile dysfunction. The lesion was located close to the right neurovascular bundle. Follow-up was conducted with serial PSA testing every 3 months and post-treatment MRI plus repeat transperineal targeted/template biopsy at 18 months.

reference_discussion.text: All right, thank you so much, Jack, for the invitation, and thank you to the Focal Therapy Society. It's a fantastic opportunity to present on our experience in one aspect of focal, and I'm delighted to be sharing the panel with our other experts today, and I'm really looking forward to hearing their experience as well. So our experience is in focal low dose rate brachytherapy, and as Jack mentioned, we're gonna be talking about patient selection today. So before I get on to the case, just a really quick summary of why we have chosen focal brachytherapy as our energy source, because obviously we're going to hear about other energy sources today. Well, the answer is that, as you all know, it's already a standard of care for whole gland treatment of intermediate risk prostate cancer. Now that's obviously a good thing, the downside is that it's not novel and it's not sexy so it may be harder to enthuse people in that respect but at least I guess the positive is it's not an experimental modality as such. It's an experimental way of using the modality. In Melbourne, here in Australia, my radiation oncology colleagues have been early adopters of whole gland brachytherapy a long time ago, so we've really got decades of experience and expertise. That's a pragmatic reason, I guess, for choosing it. And finally, also pragmatic is the fact that brachytherapy is reimbursed by both our Medicare or government system, as well as the private health fund. So there's a significant reduction in potential financial toxicity that's sometimes associated with other modalities, particularly in the Australian context. So, as you all know, as the guidelines tell us, it's really important if you're going to do focal therapy to do it as either part of a study or at least a prospective registry. And that's what we've chosen to do. We created a registry a few years ago now called Liberate, and you can Google that. to find out more details. But really important, and this comes down to patient selection, is this eligibility criteria for these cases. So PSA less than 15, clinical stage T1C or 2A. Obviously, all patients have had an MRI. This is an MRI-based type of treatment, and they need to be positive for pyroids three to five. Our biopsies are very thorough. They're all transperineal. We do targeted cause plus a minimum of 18 template cause, obviously needing to match where the lesion is on the MRI. And in terms of grade of cancer, we do include patients with larger volume grade group one, although in the eligibility criteria, as it happens, we haven't actually had any of those patients yet. We're really focusing on the Gleason sevens. In other words, the grade group twos of any length, core or smaller grade group threes. So the Gleason four plus threes. So, going on to the case then, this is pretty typical, really, of what we're doing. 64-year-old guy, elevated PSA of 6.7, no urinary symptoms, no erectile dysfunction, and a clinically palpable lesion on the right-hand side. So he went on as per standard practice to get a multi-parametric prostate MRI. And hopefully you can see here, right posterior peripheral zone, this is about midway along the prostate, this hypo-intense area, particularly visible on the ADC map in the middle there. And so this patient underwent a targeted and template biopsy. And this is what the biopsy report looks like. So you can see on the right-hand side, mid, posterior and target, you can see those grade group two prostate cancers with only a very small percentage of Gleason pattern four. So, you know, you might be thinking perhaps even about active surveillance, but with such a tiny amount of Gleason pattern four and knowing what the lesion looks like on MRI, it's one of these classic cases where treating the entire prostate when there's no significant disease anywhere else seems to be somewhat excessive. Just notably on the template biopsy, you can see left mid, halfway down the slide there, there was two millimeters of grade group two of, sorry, it should be grade group one, it was Gleason six. I mean, that is really clinically insignificant disease and doesn't make any difference to our treatment decision. So in terms of doing the actual case, he obviously went on to have focal brachytherapy, even though it was a posterior lesion, and it was obviously pretty close to that right neurovascular bundle. And so in this particular case, there were 45 iodine 125 seeds administered via 11 needles. And if you look at that photo on the right-hand side there, you can just see the needles going into the template grid, and there's obviously a lot less needles than you would otherwise use for a whole gland brachy. 145 gray are administered to the focal planned, should be targeted volume actually. And the tumor volume actually expands out to seven millimeters beyond the actual targeted volume initially. And that's obviously because we need to take into account the fact that MRI always under calls the volume of the actual cancer. So obviously, we don't want to leave any cancer cells untreated at the periphery of the lesion. Now, this was a posterior lesion. So we always for the posterior ones, we always use 15 mils or thereabouts of hydrogel called space or to separate the prostate away from the rectum, minimizing on some and often nullifying any sort of radiation dose to the to the rectum, the anterior rectal wall. Follow-up is crucial, obviously, but because it's a novel focal therapy itself being novel, we need to collect the data and do it really rigorously. So we do that as part of the Liberate registry, serial PSAs every three months. And remember, this guy started off with a PSA of 6.7, it dropped way down to 1.4, 1.3, and then eventually 0.8. In terms of functionally, he certainly did have some initial post-treatment lower unitrax symptoms, only grade 2, and these settled with time. But interestingly, this particular patient had no erectile dysfunction. We do obviously see some erectile dysfunction depending on the location of treatment in other patients. but this guy didn't have any despite the location of his tumor and had no bowel symptoms throughout. And that is very typical of what we're seeing in other patients. Now, importantly, again, and this goes along with the guidelines as well in this field, we do a post-treatment MRI and exactly the same type of biopsy, target and transperineal. and obviously targeting the same area. We do that at 18 months. We started doing it at 12 months, but because it's radiotherapy, we were finding that it was too difficult to interpret the biopsy results because of the ongoing radiation effects. So we pushed it out to 18 months. So the top row of images is what you saw before, that's that pretreatment MRI with the lesion right posterior peripheral zone. And probably if you look at the bottom middle ADC map, what you can see instead of the tumor is a whole bunch of hypointensity, which actually represent all of the brachytherapy seeds. So the actual tumor has really been replaced and scarred, and what you can see instead of the seeds, going from pyroids four to pyroids two. So MRI becoming negative, even though we get a negative MRI, we always do a biopsy as well. And this is the post-treatment biopsy at 18 months result. As you can see, it's basically the target and all of the right posterior side has become negative. And on the left-hand side, again, incidental finding of one millimeter of Gleason six or gray grit one. So that's really, I guess, a very rapid summary of a typical focal brachytherapy case that we're doing as part of the Liberate Registry here in Melbourne. Happy to take any questions now or later.
Thanks, Jeremy. That was a beautiful case. Any questions or comments from the rest of the faculty?

Yeah. The first comment I'd just like to make is that I view the three plus five percent pattern four as a special group, and there's a number of papers, the one I'm most familiar with is from NYU, that the pathology Sorry, I'm just trying to get my video back up there.
Hey, Laurie. Yeah. When you say, sorry to interrupt you, but when you say three plus five, you might've mistaken, this guy had three plus four.

No, no, sorry, I misspoke. Three plus four with 5% pattern four. Yeah, yeah. That's, I'm trying to juggle my link here at the same time. I see my video is off anyway. So there's a number of papers showing that if you do radical prostatectomy on patients with Gleason 3 plus 5% or less pattern 4, the distribution of the RP pathology is exactly the same as if it was 3 plus 3. In other words, it's an artifact of tangential cut of a Gleason 3 asinous. It's pure artifact in most cases. And so I think treatment of these patients is probably unnecessary in most cases. Now, the The fact that he's got a PIRADS 4 lesion on MRI might drive treatment to some degree, but I just want to emphasize this point, which I don't think is as well known as it should be, that about 70% of Gleason 3 plus 5% or less pattern 4 actually only have 3 plus 3 in their final pathology. and these patients really should be managed in most cases by active surveillance. It's not a criticism of what you've done because I think the alternative is clearly focal therapy where kind of less is more, but they are a very special group and should be managed as such.

Yeah, I think it's a really worthwhile point, Laurie. I suppose a couple of things you touched on, in particular the MRMF positivity, but also it was clinically palpable as well. And so when you start to add those things together on top, in a guy who's in his early 60s who sort of start to wonder and hence focal therapy, I guess, keeping his sight. I mean, the whole reason we want to avoid, as you know, radical treatment in the first place is to avoid all the effects that come with it. So, I mean, this guy, we've managed to treat him and really get away with absolutely minimal symptoms. What we're finding with focal brachy is because it's this exactly the same administration basically as the biopsy itself that that's how patients are experiencing and it's almost like they're just going in for another biopsy. So side effects really have been and we have got a retrospective paper out on it that was just published in November last year, just on our pilot study, which was the impetus for going forward and doing the prospective liberate registry. But the last thing we want to do is overtreat these patients. This is not, focal therapy should, in my view, should never be a replacement for active surveillance. It really should be the next step along that middle path between active surveillance and and radical treatment for patients with more significant disease.

May I comment? A comment and a question. So comment on this very interesting topic of 3 plus 4s. Maybe one of the solutions to treat them on progression that you can observe on the MRI, then actually whatever is, I would say, the underlying pathology, pending they don't have a grade, you know that something is happening, he says that that was a comment on that. And I have a question, a technical question about, do you think you can deliver focal brachy at the very apex where actually most of the energy struggles actually, whatever you take really?

Yeah, I think that's a fantastic question, Clement. So the answer is, I guess, that we have given focal brachytherapy for apical lesions, but at the same time, we do it very cautiously and warily for that exact reason. You know, when the Prostate is narrowing down rapidly, getting the right dose within the prostate and minimizing it outside the prostate with obviously, you know, nerves, sphincter, urethra, all just sitting right there at the apex. You've got to be super careful. So it's not ideal. And certainly I have turned patients away who have got an apical tumor. I just decided it's really not appropriate. But if you go further up the prostate, it's a non-issue. And of course, the absolute best, of course, are the anterior lesions, easy access transperineally. And those patients we're finding just literally near zero side effects because you're away from all the important structures.

Art, you have some experience with the issue of gold nanoparticles. So I just wonder, is there any difference? I mean, just to quickly poll the panel, you guys do HIFU, Cryo, we have Tulsa here and gold nanoparticles. I just did a guy with an anterior apical tumor today. I really think what works best is what you're most comfortable with. Let's start with that, because if you don't understand your energy and how you're depositing, you're going to fail. And I counsel people, I use cryo, nano is a little different, but understand that at the apex, the nerves travel up the front towards the penis. And I think people forget when you're doing a transperineal procedure, that there's nerves that are coming at the apex head and anterior, not staying posterior, like when we think of the radical prostatectomy dissection. And I think that's an important thing, especially at the apex to take that into consideration. I even do a hydrodynamic section at the anterior part of the apex to push the prostate back to work in that space to maybe get some more nerves away, just as an extra safety measure. The nanoparticle on trial is closed currently. We're just finalizing our a hundred patient data by November, but that the idea was it's more of a tumor specific ablation. Sometimes I'd really miss it because I think it was focal, but if you plan incorrectly, if you undertreat, there's where your challenges are. In today's case, I pulled a case that was a failure and talk about what do you do and how do you stage for my discussion. So that's where I'm leaving that and I'll get to my talk when we do that.
That's great. And Dr. Klotz, very quickly, what about Tulsa? Do you have any challenges in the anterior apex?

And so, we don't hesitate to treat apical lesions with Tulsa. In the non-apical patients, we leave two or three millimeters at the apex. If the patients are having so-called whole gland treatment, I call it kind of subtotal treatment. But our experience to date is that in the limited number of patients who've had apical treatment with Tulsa, continence has not been an issue and it's very feasible.

Right, thanks a lot. So I think in the interest of time, let's move on to our next presentation. We're going to have lots of material for discussion, so please continue to jump in. I think the next case is by Dr. Klotz. Dr. Klotz, please carry it away.

reference_conclusion: The panel considered focal therapy an appropriate management strategy for this MRI-visible, clinically palpable, localized prostate lesion in order to avoid overtreatment associated with whole-gland therapy, while emphasizing that focal therapy should not replace active surveillance. The patient proceeded with focal low-dose-rate brachytherapy to the right posterior lesion using iodine-125 seed implantation with hydrogel rectal spacing. Post-treatment surveillance consists of prospective registry follow-up with serial PSA testing every three months, multiparametric MRI, and repeat targeted plus transperineal template biopsy at 18 months.

[...] we do a post-treatment MRI and exactly the same type of biopsy, target and transperineal. and obviously targeting the same area. We do that at 18 months.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old man. Past medical history included primary hypothyroidism. He was married. He worked as a Catholic missionary.

[ chief complaint ]: Increased work of breathing in spring 2021. Subsequent clinical neck fullness prompted thyroid and neck evaluation after relocation to Alberta in summer 2021.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with extensive locoregional disease involving the thyroid and cervical lymph nodes, with gross invasion of adjacent aerodigestive and neurovascular structures. Disease involved both sides of the thyroid and was associated with bilateral vocal cord impaired mobility. There was residual unresected right retropharyngeal/peripharyngeal nodal disease after surgery. Imaging also raised concern for metastatic disease to bone and indeterminate pulmonary nodules.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle biopsy of the thyroid isthmus nodule was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Biopsy of a right lateral cervical lymph node was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Surgical pathology showed papillary thyroid carcinoma measuring 9 cm, involving both sides of the thyroid, with gross invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound demonstrated multinodular goiter and abnormal cervical lymph nodes. Cross-sectional neck imaging showed tumor with suspected gross invasion into surrounding structures, specifically the trachea and esophagus, and partial encasement of the right common carotid artery by nodal disease. Bilateral vocal cord impaired mobility was documented. CT chest showed small indeterminate pulmonary nodules and a sclerotic lesion in the T3 vertebral body. Bone scan showed no uptake in the T3 lesion but demonstrated uptake in multiple ribs and the right ilium in a distribution concerning for osseous metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: He was initially evaluated for increased work of breathing and was diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea; CPAP was started. He subsequently underwent extensive surgical treatment consisting of total thyroidectomy, bilateral neck dissection, and laryngopharyngectomy with radial forearm flap reconstruction. Intraoperative findings included gross invasion into multiple surrounding structures, including both recurrent laryngeal nerves. Extensive disease was present in the right and left lateral neck. The right internal jugular vein and right vagus nerve were resected. Left-sided disease was resected. Residual unresectable right retropharyngeal/peripharyngeal nodal disease remained because it was not surgically accessible. Postoperatively, he was admitted for management of a fistula, which healed with bedside wound care.

[ current disease status ]: Status post extensive locoregional resection for grossly invasive papillary thyroid carcinoma, with persistent residual unresected right retropharyngeal/peripharyngeal nodal disease. He was asymptomatic from the bone lesions identified on bone scan. Small indeterminate pulmonary nodules remained present on CT chest.

[ other clinical data ]: The extent of surgery resulted in permanent major functional morbidity, including loss of the larynx.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented with a left axillary mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma of lung origin, ALK fusion-positive, with diffuse thoracic and nodal disease at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsies of involved sites demonstrated adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin. PD-L1 expression was 95%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial PET-CT demonstrated a left lung mass extending into the mediastinum, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and a left axillary mass, consistent with extensive metastatic disease.  
- After initiation of brigatinib in August 2020, follow-up imaging showed complete response.  
- By January 2022, PET imaging showed progression with FDG-avid mediastinal lymph node disease; progression at that time was described as limited to a lymph node focus.  
- After subsequent lorlatinib, imaging within a few months showed further progression with persistent/progressive nodal activity.  
- After carboplatin/pemetrexed/pembrolizumab, imaging again showed complete remission.  
- Approximately 5 months later, imaging showed further progression with recurrent lymph node disease; later disease burden was described as minimal and localized to approximately three lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive genomic profiling identified an ALK fusion.  
- Canonical fusion: EML4-ALK, variant 2.  
- Non-canonical fusion: ALK-PPP1CB.  
- TP53 mutation was present.  
- MET amplification was present at baseline and remained present on repeat biopsy/sequencing at progression.  
- CCNA1 amplification was present.  
- Tumor mutation burden was low.  
- Microsatellite status was stable.  
- Repeat biopsy at progression demonstrated the same ALK fusions as at diagnosis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- August 2020: Started brigatinib as initial ALK-directed therapy; achieved complete response.  
- January 2022: Disease progression after approximately 1.5 years on brigatinib.  
- Subsequently treated with lorlatinib; disease progressed again within a few months.  
- Subsequently treated with carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab; achieved complete remission.  
- Further progression occurred after approximately 5 months.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent progressive disease after prior responses to brigatinib, lorlatinib, and carboplatin/pemetrexed/pembrolizumab. Most recent documented disease burden was minimal, localized recurrent nodal disease with approximately three lesions.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Re-biopsy and repeat molecular testing were performed at progression.  
- MET amplification was documented both at diagnosis and on repeat testing after progression.

reference_discussion.text: All right, let's do case one, Ram.

So first case is a patient with AlkFusion positive non-sponsored lung cancer. Now, AlkFusion, you know, this is like old news in some ways, because We've known AlkFusion as physicians that take care of patients with lung cancer. Alk is a well-known driver target. We know to look for it. And there is so many Alk inhibitors now available that you are sometimes pressed for choosing which one is the right drug in a clinical situation. So why this case? And as we go forward, you will see why, because there are some interesting issues with ALK patients, because we still don't cure these patients. We still have to deal with progression after several of these new ALK inhibitors, and then we struggle how to best take care of these patients. So this is a 66-year-old gentleman who presented with a left axillary mass, but on further imaging with a PET-CT, was found to have more diffuse disease, which is what you see on the PET scan. You can see the left lung mass, which is extending into the mediastinum, You have these supraclavicular nodes and then also the axillary mass. So quite extensive disease. So biopsies were done, which proved this was an adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin. And case in point here, PD-L1 expression high at 95%. A lot of these tumors have high PD-L1 expression, but wait for the molecular testing. You have a better target with ALK rather than giving them PD-L1. And we are seeing a lot of data that PD-L1 with chemotherapy or by itself may not be very effective in this population. So it pays to wait, get the testing done, and then proceeding on treatment. So this is the test report. And you can see that there is an ALK fusion. Actually, there are two of them. There is the well-known EML4-ALK, which is common. And then there is this ALK-PPP1CB, non-canonical fusion. And we also see some other changes, TP53 mutation, but we also see amplification in MET and CCNA1. Now the MET amplification we'll discuss down the line as to why that is important. But as we do better, as we get better and better in the next generation sequencing, it is not uncommon to find non-canonical fusions. They do happen. And the fusion partners you'll see can be of different varieties of genes. And particularly if you do RNA-seq, you tend to find more of this. But EML4-ALK is the most common. [ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old White male.

[ chief complaint ]: Increasing headaches, progressive difficulty with speech/word finding, and incoordination of the right hand over the preceding few months. Initial presentation had included two seizures.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma with radiographic recurrence in the left frontal lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior surgical pathology had established glioblastoma. No additional histopathology details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Brain MRI studies obtained approximately 4-5 months apart were reviewed. Earlier post-contrast T1-weighted axial MRI showed postoperative changes without abnormal parenchymal enhancement. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a large irregular enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe, concerning for recurrent tumor. Metabolic imaging, including MR spectroscopy and perfusion imaging, showed findings most consistent with recurrent high-grade tumor. The lesion was located in the left frontal lobe in the dominant hemisphere.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Biomarker studies had been planned/pending from tissue analysis. Anti-EGFRvIII-directed trial eligibility was described as dependent on biomarker results. Potential molecular targeting of PI3 kinase and mTOR pathways was also referenced in relation to tissue-based biomarker analysis. No confirmed biomarker result was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgery approximately 1 year earlier, followed by radiation therapy and chemotherapy with temozolomide (Temodar). Subsequent imaging initially showed postoperative changes without abnormal enhancement, followed months later by imaging findings consistent with recurrent high-grade tumor.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic recurrent left frontal glioblastoma, with imaging and metabolic studies consistent with recurrent high-grade disease after prior surgery, radiation, and temozolomide.

[ other clinical data ]: The recurrent lesion involved the dominant hemisphere. Functional MRI for speech and motor mapping had been considered for operative planning. Biomarker testing turnaround was expected to be approximately 1 week.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male; otherwise healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Groin mass developing approximately 1 year after prior excisional biopsy of a penile lesion.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent penile cancer with fixed bulky groin nodal mass measuring 7 cm.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior excisional biopsy of penile lesion had clear margins. Subsequent biopsies of the groin mass ultimately confirmed recurrent penile cancer.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a 7 cm fixed groin mass.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial penile lesion had been managed in the community with excisional biopsy.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-confirmed recurrent penile carcinoma presenting as a fixed bulky 7 cm inguinal nodal mass.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence following radical prostatectomy for prostate adenocarcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, pathologic stage pT3bN0, Gleason score 4+3=7, Grade Group 3, with seminal vesicle invasion and subsequent biochemical recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial prostate biopsy demonstrated bilateral high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia without carcinoma.  
- Subsequent transperineal saturation biopsy demonstrated 4 cores with Grade Group 4 disease and 1 core with Grade Group 3 disease.  
- Radical prostatectomy specimen demonstrated adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3), composed of approximately 90% pattern 4 and 10% pattern 3, with cribriform Gleason pattern 4 present.  
- Seminal vesicle involvement was present.  
- Pelvic lymph nodes were negative (pN0).  
- Surgical margins were negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Prostate MRI in 2015 demonstrated a 41 cc gland with no focal abnormality; PI-RADS 2.  
- Repeat prostate MRI in 2016 demonstrated no change from prior imaging.  
- Preoperative bone scan and CT scan demonstrated no evidence of metastatic disease.  
- Preoperative PSMA PET performed on a research protocol was negative.  
- Restaging CT scan and bone scan obtained at biochemical recurrence demonstrated no evidence of metastatic disease or local recurrence in the prostate bed.  
- Bone scan showed uptake consistent with degenerative change at the acromioclavicular joints and sternomanubrial joint; no findings suggestive of osseous metastatic disease.  
- CT pelvis demonstrated postoperative changes without evidence of recurrence and no pathologic pelvic adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA was in the 2 ng/mL range in 2014.  
- PSA increased to 7.8 ng/mL in July 2015; free PSA was 10%.  
- In May 2016, PSA increased to 20.2 ng/mL; free PSA was 7.6%.  
- Prostate Health Index was 96 in May 2016.  
- Postoperatively, PSA remained relatively stable initially.  
- PSA began rising approximately 31 months after surgery and reached 0.13 ng/mL at 46 months after surgery.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent prostate biopsy after initial PSA rise; biopsy showed bilateral high-grade PIN only.  
- Underwent repeat MRI and then transperineal saturation biopsy after further PSA rise; biopsy confirmed prostate adenocarcinoma.  
- Underwent robotic-assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection in September 2016.  
- Postoperative course was characterized by initially stable ultrasensitive PSA values, followed by biochemical recurrence.  
- Restaging CT and bone scan at PSA 0.13 ng/mL were negative.

[ current disease status ]: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy, with PSA 0.13 ng/mL and no radiographic evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease on CT and bone scan.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Digital rectal examination was small and symmetric without abnormalities at initial evaluation.  
- No urinary tract symptoms were reported prior to diagnosis.  
- Erectile function was intact preoperatively, with no erectile dysfunction reported.  
- Family history was significant for bladder cancer.  
- At recurrence evaluation, urinary tract symptoms were minimal.
