reference_discussion.text: All right, thank you everyone for your comments. So the next case is a 70-year-old gentleman with biochemical occurrence. So initially presented with a rising PSA, twos in 2014, all the way up to 7.8 in July, 2015, with a 10% free value. His DRE was small and symmetric with no abnormalities. He underwent a prostate MRI, which showed a 41cc gland. Again, no focal abnormalities, which was read as a pyrites two. Given his concern, he did undergo a prostate biopsy, which showed bilateral high-grade PIN. There's no really evidence of true prostate cancer, potentially a precursor. And then, however, in May of 2016, his PSA sharply rose to 20.2, and his free PSA was down to 7.6, and his prostate health index was 96, which was pretty convincing that he potentially had some sort of clinically significant disease in his prostate. He underwent a repeat MRI, which actually revealed no change from his prior. Given the lab values, he underwent a transperineal saturated biopsy, which revealed four cores showing gray group four disease and one core of gray group three disease. Of note, he had an excellent shim with no erectile dysfunction and no urinary tract symptoms. His family history was significant for bladder cancer. He underwent a bone scan and a CT scan, which showed no evidence of metastatic disease. He underwent a PSMA PET scan on research protocol, which was negative as well. And subsequently underwent a robotic assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection. And in September, 2016, which showed a path of T3B with seminal vesicle invasion, grade group three disease. also sensitive PSAs. And you can look at this chart. His PSAs remain relatively stable postoperatively. However, around month 31 after his surgery, it started to rise to 0.13 in 46 months after surgery. He underwent restaging CT scan and both scan given his rise of his PSA, which was negative. Again, his lorinary tract symptoms were very minimal and his erectile function was actually mediocre and actually quite well at 19. We'll review his pathology and radiology right now.

Great, so this is a slide from his radical prostatectomy specimen. We're looking at a slide section through the prostate now. All of the pink is the muscle that surrounds the prostatic glands. And in the upper left-hand corner, or sorry, in the upper right-hand corner, you can see normal prostate glands with some pink secretions within them. On the left-hand side, almost all of the epithelial cells that you see are tumor, and they're forming what we call cribriform pattern, Gleason pattern 4, which is when we see not a single lumen in the center or a single hole in the center of a kind of a circle of glandular cells, but instead we see multiple back-to-back small lumens kind of punched out, appearing like a sieve. Cribiform just means sieve-like in Latin. So this is Criboform Gleason Pattern 4. and his overall grade group was grade group three. So he was mostly cribriform pattern four, 90%, and then 10% of the tumor was pattern three. So it was four plus three equals seven. This is similar to a patient that we saw in the last cases. Gentleman also had seminal vesicle involvement. On the left side, you can see the seminal vesicle epithelium and the lumen of the seminal vesicle, which is the white space you can see there. That's where all the seminal vesicle secretions end up. And then on the right side, you can see tumor just adjacent to that seminal vesicle epithelium. And again, more of this sort of cribiform pattern. So his overall pathologic grade was four plus three equals seven, 90% pattern four with some cribiform pattern. And he was on pathologic stage P, T3B because of the seminal vesicle involvement, but he had no lymph node involvement, so it was N0. And the surgical margins were actually negative.

All right, so this patient underwent a bone scan and a CT scan, which is not surprising. These have been standards of care for patients with biochemical recurrence for decades. But in a patient with a low PSA biochemical recurrence, we'd expect both of these tests to be negative in more than 90% of patients. And the few percent of patients that they may show an unexpected metastasis, that's important, as it obviously is going to impact the patient's subsequent management. But again, the vast majority of these patients will have a negative bone scan and CT. Here, we'll start with this bone scan. And this utilizes a radio tracer called methylene diphosphonate, which just adsorbs onto the surfaces of bones. And anywhere there's bone turnover, there tends to be more accumulation of this agent. And we can see this in a couple of spots that are related to degenerative arthritis. shoulders, there's these bright spots at the acromioclavicular joints, which are degenerative. And there's also a spot kind of in the middle of the sternum, which is the sternum manubrial joint, which often has degenerative change. The right elbow is sort of where the radio tracer was ejected, and that's just a little bit of contamination. But there's nothing to suggest metastatic disease. And then where the CT really can be helpful is in identifying small lymph nodes or sites of local recurrence in the prostate bed. And here are a couple of representative slices, one through the pelvis showing sort of the obturator fossa and the internal and external iliac vessels, where we would often find nodes that would be recurrent prostate cancer. And then in the right-hand image is a part of the prostate bed. which shows kind of normal post-operative changes and no evidence of recurrence there either. So again, it comes as no surprise that these two tests would be negative, but they are important to do in case they do uncover something unexpected.

So in summary, we have a 70-year-old gentleman with grade group four prostate cancer, status post prostatectomy PT3BN0 with seminal vesicle invasion negative margins with biochemical recurrence with a slow prostatectomy, PSA is 0.13 with a negative CT scan and bone scan. And really the question is whether there's the role for PSMA scan and also the role for salvage radiation.

Maybe the PSMA scans, the easier of the two. So I'll just kind of weigh in on that briefly. So most of our data with PSMA scans is in patients with PSAs at least 0.2 in the post-operative setting. And the detection efficiency of PSMA scans between a PSA of 0.2 and 0.5 is about 50%. So about half of patients will have a positive scan and about half of patients won't have a positive scan. That's much better than CT and bone scan in the same setting where, again, we're talking about detection efficiencies in the single digits. So PSMA is really a remarkable advance in identifying sites of disease in these patients. And I guess from my perspective, probably the patients it's most important in are the about 25 or 30% of patients that are gonna wind up having evidence of a disease that's outside of what would be the traditional salvage radiation field, so that that salvage radiation field can be adjusted or the patient can have alternative treatment. I think PSMA is really important. Again, at this PSA level, it's not particularly well studied, but there's a decent chance that the patient would have a positive scan that may be helpful.

Before Kurt weighs in, I would just say that to the audience that PSMA scanning has been approved for biochemical recurrence now and will be used more and more as insurance figures out approvals and sites come online to do that. And I do wanna emphasize that Dr. Rowe was one of the major drivers of PSMA scans being approved in this country and we should all thank him for that. And he also just recently published a paper showing that when you combine the rise in PSA, the speed at which it's rising, with the absolute PSA value, he can predict pretty accurately who's going to have a positive PSMA scan and who's not. I'll stop there and turn it over to Kurt.

No, I think those are all important, great comments and how we think about salvage radiation and kind of plan salvage radiation. I think often folks are thinking that, you know, if you don't have a positive scan or something visible on the skin, that means you don't treat, which, you know, I think Dr. Rowe articulated well, that really we're just looking to see if there's something that alters the management that might help us or we're often going to see something which is within the field that we were going to treat. So it's sort of somewhat reassuring from that perspective. So in this setting, it's fairly straightforward in the sense that the patient is a candidate for salvage radiation. We know that men do well when we essentially treat the prostate bed, the space where the prostate was removed or the prostatic fossa. And there's somewhat of a debate in our field, ongoing studies, whether we also include the adjacent pelvic lymph nodes, as with some of the vessel invasion, a high initial PSA, that they're still at risk for that micrometastatic disease, which is within the lymph nodes. And then there's also a question of whether we include hormonal therapy with that salvage radiation, often what we call short course, so six months of testosterone suppression overlapping with their radiation treatment. And there's a few studies that have shown some benefit to doing that, although we're still trying to refine, you know, again, what features, risk factors, Gleason score, indications for that. And then also I think an additional thing to consider, we can use genomic studies that the CIPR score is an example of one genomic classifier, which gives sort of a risk score of the tumor. And there is data that men who have a high risk genomic score, you know, do better when salvage radiation is applied earlier as opposed to a late salvage. So those are just some of the considerations when we're evaluating for salvage radiation and the timing of when to proceed.

reference_conclusion: The patient is a candidate for salvage radiotherapy for biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy. Salvage treatment would target the prostate bed/prostatic fossa, with consideration of inclusion of the adjacent pelvic lymph nodes given seminal vesicle invasion and high initial PSA as risk factors for micrometastatic nodal disease. Short-course androgen suppression for approximately 6 months overlapping with radiation may also be considered. PSMA PET may be obtained to identify disease outside the traditional salvage radiation field that could alter management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 79-year-old right-handed man. No prior past medical history was documented. Functional status was reported as 90%.

[ chief complaint ]: Sudden fall, prompting emergency evaluation and cranial imaging.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected tumor demonstrated a hypercellular diffuse astrocytic neoplasm composed of neoplastic astrocytes with microvascular proliferation and necrosis. Areas with oligodendroglioma-like morphology were present, with round cells and perinuclear clearing, but molecular findings did not support oligodendroglioma. Histologic and molecular features supported classification as glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial head imaging after the fall identified a right frontal mass. MRI from 2014 demonstrated a large abnormal lesion involving the frontal lobes, centered in the right frontal lobe, with extensive T2 hyperintensity in the anterior half of the brain. Post-contrast T1 imaging showed avidly enhancing regions within the larger abnormal area and a central irregular non-enhancing component consistent with necrosis. Tumor extended across the corpus callosum into the contralateral hemisphere. DOPA PET demonstrated greater metabolic activity in the right frontal lobe component, with less metabolic activity in the portion extending across the corpus callosum. Postoperative imaging showed resection of the large right frontal lobe mass with residual tumor at the corpus callosum/cross-midline component.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH1 was negative by immunohistochemistry and by sequencing. There was no 1p/19q codeletion. MGMT promoter methylation was present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient was placed on levetiracetam. He underwent surgical resection of the large right frontal lobe component of tumor; resection was stopped at the corpus callosum/cross-midline component.

[ other clinical data ]: Tumor location involved both frontal lobes via extension across the corpus callosum.

reference_discussion.text: We'll start with the second case. This one is a young-looking 79-year-old right-handed man who had actually no previous past medical history. He had a sudden fall and was taken to the emergency room. And because of the fall, he needed imaging of his head and then a subsequent MRI that revealed a right frontal mass. His medications were then, he was then placed on levopressin. otherwise very good functional status at 90%. So Dr. Pullman, if you can go over the imaging.

Sure. Okay, so this is from 2014 and we again have a T2-weighted image and a pre-contrast and post-contrast T1-weighted image. And we can see right away that there's a large area of abnormality in the front half of the brain centered in the frontal lobes where you see all this bright T2, this more white T2 signal intensity. Then if we look on the post-contrast images, there's areas of avid enhancement within that larger area of abnormality that we saw in the T2-weighted images. Again, we see this non-enhancing irregular portion centrally to these masses, so that suggests a necrotic higher grade tumor.
So Dr. Everson, what do you think about doing surgery on this patient?

So there's a couple of important considerations, I think, to make on this situation compared to the previous one. You know, one is the age and sort of frailty or robustness of the patient and their ability to undergo an operation safely and recover from it. Now, in decades past, you know, doing a operation, a craniotomy and resection of a brain tumor on someone, you know, in their 80s and 90s would have been, you know, looked upon as futile or unnecessary. You know, in more modern times, as we have improved and refined surgical techniques and decreased our complication rates and just gain more experience with it is much more feasible and a safe concept to take such a patient like that through an operation and expect a good recovery. So that's one aspect of it. Now, the second is the anatomical features of this tumor are pretty different from what we saw before. In this one, we see two major components of this. One is the large mass in the frontal lobe, then there's this other portion which really reaches and extends across the midline, across the corpus callosum, and goes to the other side of the brain. Thinking about those two components separately, knowing the anticipated functional effects of removing each one is quite different. The portion that's in the right frontal lobe, one would expect very little in the way of major functional side effects, but the part that's reaching across the corpus callosum, reaching that, number one, increases the complexity, the technical aspects of the surgery. It's not always as feasible to really reach over there and remove that portion. Secondly, it can lead to types of symptoms postoperatively related to disconnection in terms of severing the connection between the hemispheres of the brain, which can affect things more often like personality, higher cognitive function, executive function, things like math and reasoning and some higher order cognition things that are sometimes subtle to measure, but very much there. So that's a little bit more of a challenging area to reach surgically and with less rationale to do so. Now, one of the things that we can get beyond this is some more refined imaging to understand biologically or metabolically which parts of the tumor might be more active and have more rapidly dividing or more malignant cells in it. That's where advanced imaging modalities like our DOPA PET scan, which is shown here, or some of our cerebral blood flow and some other types of MR techniques can be used. And so this DOPA PET scan here is going to show basically amino acid metabolism in the tumor. And it's shown on this gradient scale where the red area is really a very metabolically active part of the tumor. And so that adds further rationale to target that area specifically to kind of get the most bang for our buck, if you will, for removing more aggressive components of disease. whereas the portion that is going across the corvus callosum is not as metabolically active. Therefore, if there's a part of this to leave in place and not risk these levels of complication, it's that part there. So combining these two modalities, understanding the anatomy and functional implications as well as what's happening metabolically, create a strategy where going after the big bulk disease that's in the frontal lobe makes sense. where chasing the components that go across really don't. And so that's the kind of strategy that's undertaken in this patient here. And our next slide shows what we're able to achieve surgically with removal of really the large mass in the frontal lobe and stopping the resection as it starts to enter into the corpus callosum and cross into the left cerebral hemisphere.
discuss the neuropathology on this patient, Dr. Rodriguez.

All right. So we may say that some of the features here from the neuropathology are similar to the previous one. We do have a proliferation of neoplastic cells, what we call neoplastic astrocytes in between. It's two cellar for normal brain. And it's composed of tumors that have some, a lot of processes, which is typical of astrocytes, and have these, where it labels MVP, that's microvascular proliferation, that is always a worrisome feature in some of these diffuse gliomas. So that kind of starts suggesting, even at this power, that it may be more on the higher grade end of the spectrum. So next. There is necrosis as well. So many of the features that were present in the first case are also present here. And so you have necrosis, you have proliferation, microscopic proliferation. That's also, again, a very difficult problem. These are features that are worrisome, everything else being equal. On the right-hand side, there's something that is being highlighted. It's oligo and glioma-like components. We historically always get like to see if there's any areas that pertain a better prognosis and oligandroglioma, historically, that has been the case. So we try to find areas like these, you see, compared to the other fields, these areas, the cells are round and have these clearing around the nuclei, which is very typical of oligandroglioma. We want to make sure that we don't miss that, since those are tumors that have a much better prognosis compared to the astrocytic, diffuse astrocytoma. Now, there has been a lot of debate through the years of what to do when you have part of the tumor has these and there was a term in the past that was called oligoastrocytoma or mixed neoplasm or mixed tumor, which but it's actually being superseded more currently by molecular information. So, in the, if you see that the larger classification as it changes over the years, this was recognized in the past as a global stomach we we just because global stomachs and astrocytic tumor. In the past, in the 2007 classification, there was a recognition that you can, if you identify areas that look only on the glial, you can add it to that with the idea that some of these portend a better prognosis. With time, now we know that what is more important in that context is the alteration. So if you don't have 1-Pinetic Euclid lesion or IDH mutation, So it's negative also for IDH1 by immunohistochemistry and by sequencing, and then there's no 1P-Net nucleic lesion. You cannot call that oligoendoglioma. That defaults it into the astrocytic category. And since it doesn't have IDH1 mutation, that will make it IDH1 type, and then you have all the other histologic features, necrosis, proliferation, that allows us now to put it more confidently in the glioblastoma IDH wild type category, even if it has areas that are somewhat resemble a better tumor. So the genetics here drive us confidently in the direction of glioblastoma. And that is really the difference. I tried to highlight that in my lecture earlier, the difference with the new WHO classifications, that these molecular alterations that we understand are helping us to be more objective in actually adding more precise information to our histologic diagnosis. So the diagnosis is similar, and also you have the MGMT methylation that we add. This one in contrast to the other one, so there is something biologically that is better. Here is the presence of the MGMT methylation, which is a good thing for treatment purposes. So the histology here is similar to the previous one, has areas that are a little bit what we call bland, that makes you think about an oligoendoglioma, but molecularly ends up not being, but then has something biologically that is also a bit more favorable, which is the presence of MGMT methylation.

So at this point, We, the patient is then sent to see neuro oncology and radiation oncology. And we also have to make a decision about how to treat these patients. So if you remember Dr. Cosley talk about the very old data, as someone pointed out. a standard treatment for glioblastoma using radiation with temozolomide chemotherapy. However, that trial actually excluded any patients over the age of 70. So that trial actually technically does not apply to this patient who is 79 years old. So the question is then, how would we treat a patient who is older in age, even though we otherwise have very good functional status and is otherwise doing well? In this patient population, again, I always want to make sure that despite being oncologists, we always say it's a reasonable option to think about supportive and palliative care. But we can also think about treatment. Is it popular to do treatment with hemozoloma chemotherapy alone or with radiation alone or with combination therapy? Hoping Dr. Kapurlian, if you can help us maybe understand the difference between the hypofractionated and the standard protocol a little bit of radiation.

Yeah, of course. So the standard radiation, we went over in the prior case, which is 60 grade in 30 fractions. But one option for us, certain groups of patients, one being those over 70 years old, is a shorter course, so 40 gray and 15 fractions, which has shown in these studies to be equivalent in the short time span with the 60 gray and 30 fractions. So the next slide shows a study, one of these studies that was done using this course, comparing doing nothing, so just observation, with radiation alone after surgery. And the study was stopped early. There was a short benefit up a little under three months, 2.8 months with the use of radiation alone. The outcomes were relatively equivalent with the six-week course. When we are faced with making this decision in this group of patients, we talk as a team to see if the patient has a good performance status, if they're able to come in for six weeks, And if not, then we can consider the shorter course, which is that three-week course.
And Dr. Clousey, you want to talk about some studies that talk about just using chemotherapy alone in this population?

Sure. One of the reasons why on that original study, that they didn't include patients who were over 70 was because it was predominantly done in Europe and Europe had been doing evaluations and trying to understand what the impact was with radiation or chemotherapy and patients who were over 65 in particular. I'll also say just, I think in general, I wouldn't pay attention to these median overall survivals. Many patients who are in their 70s or 80s can end up doing fairly well. The ones that are selected for many of these studies are the ones that the investigator didn't think could tolerate the full dose of radiation and or the chemotherapy. This is usually a patient population that isn't functioning as well. These numbers look a lot worse than we're used to seeing. But one of the studies that was done, this NOAA-08, was an evaluation that looked at giving patients radiation therapy, and then upon progression, they would get chemotherapy, but not as adjuvant, or they would get chemotherapy, and then upon progression, they would get radiation therapy. Basically, when you look at those data, the median survivals are similar between the two. This next slide really gets at trying to differentiate between the impact of the patients who are MGMT methylated, like this patient is, versus those that are not MGMT methylated. Let me see, I know that Dr. Niafu is gonna help me point these things out, but I might as well see if... You can annotate, Dr. Kelsey, you know how. Yeah, I'm wondering, oh, the mouse, I could use the mouse. Okay, let me know if you guys see this. Do you see this or not really?
No, you have to do the drawing. All right, I'll do the drawing.
Arrow maybe? Okay, so this, where I put a little circle, This here, or also I put the other little circle, are the patients that are MGMT methylated, I believe. Let me see if I got that right.
Yeah. Correct.

Yeah. The group up here in this area is the group that received temozolomide, and this is the group that received just radiation alone. What you can see is, and this is overall survival, so this is how the patients eventually survived. There was an improvement in overall survival in the patient population that was MGMT methylated, that received temozolomide alone, and then later went on to receive radiation if there was tumor progression compared to the group that just received radiation alone. In the end, their final analysis, which was done later than this, showed that there was a statistically significant difference between those two. On the contrary, if you're MGMT unmethylated, and let me get rid of my little circles here for a second. This group here is a group that got temozolomide compared to the group that's intermixed here that you'll see that received, I'm sorry, yeah, this group received temozolomide and the other group received radiation. You can see that the MGMT unmethylated population that got temozolomide first and then eventually followed by radiation and those who got it did much worse than those who had received radiation therapy initially. So in the patient population that is older, we tend to think there's an opportunity, depending on what's going on with the patient and what their functional status is, of giving temozolomide alone instead of giving radiation at that time and maybe potentially holding off to give radiation. Of course, that would not be a consideration at all in an unmethylated population. I don't know if Dr. Karpelian has anything to add to that, because I just want to make sure we have a good balanced discussion on it.

Yeah, I completely agree. As our team here knows, when we're faced with some of these patients and cases, I'll often chime in, and I also agree, if we can do TIMIDAR alone first, and then we see how the patient's doing, potentially even shrink the area so that if and when we do have to do radiation, maybe it'll be a smaller target. So I'm very supportive of this approach.
Dr. Kelsey, you want to continue with this? Yeah.

And so, you know, none of those studies addressed the real issue, which is, you know, okay, well, and they're still not going to completely address it. The question would be, how do patients over 65 do when you do radiation versus radiation and chemotherapy at full dose radiation therapy? That is not going to be answered, but the study that was done in Canada was a study using this short course of radiation again, and they randomized patients to receive radiation therapy alone. Again, this population who's over 65, and again, probably poor functioning because investigators thought they wouldn't be able to tolerate a full dose of radiation. Compared to the population that gets the short course of radiation plus daily temozolomide followed by temozolomide five days on, 23 days off. You can see the blue is showing that there's an improvement in overall survival. That's essentially showing that the addition of temozolomide is beneficial. I think even if the next one maybe shows issues around MGMT methylation status, I don't know if you have that or not. Again, the majority of the effect that we see in that original population comes from the MGMT methylated group. Meaning that they get the best survival compared to who are getting chemotherapy compared to the group that got radiation alone. It should be noted that over on the other side here where we show the MGMT unmethylated, that those patients also have a statistically significant or near statistically significant benefit of overall survival when adding temozolomide to radiation therapy compared to radiation therapy alone. It does pretty much mimic what we're seeing in the population who is under 70.

So pretty much what this patient then ended up doing is actually ended up getting, well, kind of summary of what we were trying to say is that in patients who's methylated for the MGMT who is older, the decision could be short course radiation with hemozolomide, better than, but hemozolomide alone may be a consideration, again, depending on a long conversation with the patient. versus in the unmethylated MGMT patients, we'd recommend that they should have some form of radiation therapy. And it seems that at least it's also okay to do short course of radiation, unclear if one is better than the other, right? With current data, whether the long course is better than the short course or not, we actually don't know the answer to that, but at least we know the short course with hemozolomide is a safe option for the older patient population. These are some of the criteria for deciding therapy for older patients. Dr. Clousey, you want to discuss a little bit about it? Sure. Just a summary.

Again, these are discussions that we have together with Dr. Comprelle and trying to understand the size of the radiation field and then the relative sensitivity of the areas being radiated. We know the temporal lobes and the frontal lobes are a bit tough. Like in this patient, it would be a big field, it would be in both frontal lobes. Now, that may not just be the best way if we didn't have to consider radiation for the patient. If it's more posteriorly placed, smaller, I think there's a huge advantage to radiation. So you really have to be considering that. It's more about what's going to happen a couple months after they're done. with radiation. Of course, the MGMT methylation status we discussed, the performance status, whether or not we feel they can tolerate radiation therapy at the 60 gray giving a full six weeks or the 40 gray. Fragility is maybe even a little different than performance status because it takes into account a number of other things, but it's kind of hard to measure. But when we see the patient, we know what we mean. And I think maybe the family understands that too. But really the most important thing, nobody understands more about what they want to do than the patient themselves. And especially a patient who is a bit older, who just has a clear understanding of what they would like to do, what they wouldn't like to do. So they're the ones who finally decide our job is to educate and provide the best information we can so that they can make a final decision about how to move forward.

Great, thank you. Pretty much just so, in summary for the patient, the patient actually opted to start just temozolomide alone as his own decision. And the patient actually, even after nine cycles of chemotherapy, which is a little bit longer than we would probably do these days, but still did very well without any tumor growth. I'll move on to the next case. This is on the opposite end of younger patients, 41-year-old, who also presented with a left arm focal motor seizure, also a very healthy patient with no past medical history. So Dr. Pope, if you could help with the imaging.

For an older patient with good functional status, the board discussed short-course radiation with temozolomide as a safe option and temozolomide alone as a reasonable consideration in MGMT-methylated disease. The patient ultimately elected temozolomide monotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 31-year-old woman. No previous medical disease was reported. No family history of cancer was reported. Gynecologic history included three pregnancies. Menarche occurred at age 13 years. Last menstrual period was in April 2014.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly growing left breast mass for 2 months at initial presentation. In August 2015, she presented with headache and vomiting since July 2015.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive ductal carcinoma, clinical stage cT4 cN2 at initial staging, ER low-positive, PR low-positive, HER2-negative. After surgery, pathologic stage was ypT3 ypN3. Subsequent isolated central nervous system metastatic disease was identified in August 2015.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the left breast showed invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2. Estrogen receptor was 8% positive. Progesterone receptor was 10% positive. HER2 was negative. Ki-67 was 40%.  
Post-mastectomy pathology showed residual invasive carcinoma, grade 2, measuring 5.3 cm, with associated grade 3 ductal carcinoma in situ. Surgical margins were tumor-free. Twenty-one of 39 axillary lymph nodes were positive. Residual cancer burden was 3.

[ imaging findings ]: Breast MRI demonstrated a suspicious heterogeneous nodule with irregular margins in the medial quadrant of the left breast measuring 8.9 × 5.6 × 4.6 cm. Several confluent satellite nodules were present in the superior medial quadrant, the largest measuring 2.3 × 2.0 × 1.3 cm. Positive left-sided lymph nodes were identified. The right breast showed simple cysts.  
PET-CT in April 2014 was negative for distant metastatic disease.  
In 2015, CT imaging and bone scan were negative for extracranial metastases.  
CNS MRI in August 2015 showed multiple metastatic lesions with vasogenic edema involving the cerebellar vermis, left capsular region, left temporal lobe, and right frontal lobe, with ventricular compression and rightward midline shift.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No genetic testing results were available. She was referred for genetic counseling but did not attend.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant paclitaxel was administered for 7 weeks, with local progression during treatment. She subsequently received doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide through August 2014.  
In September 2014, she underwent left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection.  
She received adjuvant radiotherapy through December 2014.  
Tamoxifen was administered from October 2014 until August 2015.  
She underwent bilateral oophorectomy in May 2015.  
Whole-brain radiotherapy was completed by August 2015 for brain metastases.

[ current disease status ]: As of August 2015, she had multiple brain metastases with associated edema and mass effect, without documented extracranial metastatic disease on CT and bone scan. ECOG performance status was 2 at that time.

[ other clinical data ]: ECOG performance status was 0 at initial presentation.

reference_conclusion: In the absence of extracranial metastatic disease, systemic chemotherapy was not recommended; endocrine therapy alone was favored, with transition from tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor following oophorectomy-induced postmenopausal status. For intracranial disease management, neurosurgical evaluation for possible resection of a safely accessible peripheral lesion was advised, with stereotactic radiosurgery preferred for the brain metastases and whole-brain radiation reserved for recurrence because of concerns regarding late cognitive toxicity.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Painless palpable midline neck mass. No dysphagia or dysphonia.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma arising in a thyroglossal duct cyst/thyroglossal duct tract region.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the midline neck lesion was diagnostic for papillary thyroid carcinoma (Bethesda VI). Cytology showed cystic change with macrophages and psammoma bodies, compatible with papillary thyroid carcinoma of thyroid origin.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound report described a mixed cystic-solid isoechoic lesion, taller-than-wide, with irregular margins and punctate echogenic foci in the solid component; TI-RADS 5.  
- Lesion was located above the isthmus and connected to the expected thyroglossal duct tract region.  
- Reported size was 5.2 × 1.9 × 4.0 cm.  
- Thyroid lobes were reported as normal in morphology and size, with no lesions identified.  
- Suspicious cervical adenopathy was identified, including a rounded node with punctate echogenic foci.  
- CT neck demonstrated a midline cystic lesion with septations and a solid component, inseparable from the strap muscles, without tracheal invasion.  
- CT also demonstrated a suspicious hypodense right lateral compartment level IV lymph node.  
- CT interpretation described a solid-cystic tumor with multiple septae adjacent to the thyroid gland/pyramidal lobe, considered compatible with carcinoma related to a thyroglossal duct cyst.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the midline lesion confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history was unremarkable.  
- No history of thyroid cancer.  
- No history of benign thyroid disease.  
- No history of radiation exposure.  
- Tumor was staged as T3a, stage I based on age younger than 55 years.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old male. Known history of hypertension.

[ chief complaint ]: High-grade fever for 2-3 days in the last week of October 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Pancytopenia with marrow dysplasia and molecular abnormalities consistent with a myelodysplastic neoplasm/myelodysplastic syndrome phenotype. Risk stratification: IPSS-R score 2.5 (low risk); IPSS-M score 0.18 (moderate-low risk).

[ histopathology results ]: Peripheral smear showed occasional tear-drop cells and macrocytic normochromic red cells, with impression of macrocytic anemia with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular, with erythroid hyperplasia and megaloblastic reaction; binucleated erythroid forms were present. Plasma cells were 2%. Blasts were less than 1%. Bone marrow biopsy showed increased cellularity and 1% ring sideroblasts.

[ imaging findings ]: Splenomegaly was identified radiologically; spleen measured approximately 13 cm. The spleen was not clinically palpable.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Conventional cytogenetics showed normal karyotype. Next-generation sequencing identified a ZRSR2 mutation reported as likely pathogenic and an ETV6 alteration reported as likely pathogenic/variant of uncertain significance. ZRSR2 variant allele frequency was approximately 74%.

[ laboratory results ]: At admission: hemoglobin 9 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2,820/µL, absolute neutrophil count 1,015/µL, platelet count 60,000/µL, LDH within normal range. Fever profile was negative. Infectious causes of fever were ruled out. APLA panel was negative. Latest available counts: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, total leukocyte count approximately 3,200/µL, platelet count 90,000/µL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No disease-directed treatment for the hematologic disorder was documented. Blood counts showed partial recovery trend without specific intervention; platelet count increased from 60,000/µL to 90,000/µL.

[ current disease status ]: Clinically improved from the initial febrile presentation. Currently asymptomatic. Persistent cytopenias remained present, with partial count recovery.

[ other clinical data ]: There were no bleeding manifestations. Infectious evaluation during the febrile admission was negative.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Renal mass with metastatic disease; one episode of gross hematuria. Performance status was 0.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a left renal mass with metastatic disease involving the lungs and liver, including multiple small pulmonary nodules and small liver lesions. The majority of tumor burden was in the kidney. A small contralateral renal mass was also present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin was within normal limits. Calcium, LDH, platelet count, and white blood cell count were within normal limits. No hypercalcemia was present.

[ other clinical data ]: Risk assessment was described as intermediate risk on the basis of presentation with advanced disease. Gross hematuria had resolved, and urine was clear at the time described.

[ chief complaint ]: Esophageal malignancy diagnosed in March 2025; referred with residual disease after chemoradiotherapy and subsequent metastatic lung lesion.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage III esophageal cancer at initial diagnosis on 06 March 2025. Residual disease was documented after definitive chemoradiotherapy. Subsequent PET imaging showed response in the esophagus with a lung lesion treated as metastatic disease.

Stereotactic body radiotherapy was delivered to the lung lesion at a dose of 50 Gy in 10 fractions. Four cycles of palliative chemotherapy with irinotecan had been planned.

[ current disease status ]: No residual lesion was seen in the esophagus on post-treatment PET imaging. A lung lesion had been identified and treated with SBRT. Disease status following SBRT and before planned irinotecan-based palliative chemotherapy was consistent with treated metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: PD-L1 testing had not been documented. Tumor mutational burden and MSI status had not been reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Slowly progressive enlargement of the anterior neck. At recurrence in late 2023 to early 2024, symptoms included intermittent dysphagia since 2019 and shortness of breath, particularly when lying down.

[ diagnosis ]: Cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma, high-grade by reported necrosis, with locoregional recurrence and pulmonary metastases. Initial outside diagnosis after prior thyroidectomy had been reported as follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial outside thyroidectomy pathology had been reported as an 8 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with necrosis and metastasis in 1 perithyroid lymph node. Following resection on 08-May-2024, pathology from the tumor and right central dissection described a 9 cm mass. Microscopy was reported as cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma rather than follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry showed TTF1 positive, PAX8 positive, thyroglobulin negative, Ki-67 positive, cyclin D1 positive, beta-catenin positive, estrogen receptor positive, and progesterone receptor positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound demonstrated a large right-sided neck mass, residual left-sided thyroid tissue, calcifications within the mass, low vascularity, and a cystic right level II lymph node. CT imaging showed a very large neck tumor displacing the trachea to the left and compressing the esophagus; the mass was described as partly necrotic. Chest CT demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases, including one cavitary pulmonary nodule. Postoperative imaging showed residual right-sided tissue measuring 2.3 cm, poorly defined, and persistent pulmonary metastases. FDG PET/CT demonstrated FDG-avid pulmonary metastatic disease, with one pulmonary nodule showing particularly high uptake.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Selected mutation testing was reported as BRAF V600E negative, HRAS negative, NRAS negative, and KRAS positive. APC germline mutation assessment had not yet been performed.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had presented with a thyroid nodule at age 27. The lesion enlarged slowly over time and had been described as a cold thyroid nodule. She subsequently underwent total thyroidectomy at an outside institution. She did not receive radioactive iodine therapy. She received external beam neck radiotherapy, reported as 20 Gy in 5 fractions. Over the subsequent 6 years, she underwent intermittent surveillance with ultrasound and CT without additional treatment. She was referred in March 2024 after renewed anterior neck enlargement and identification of pulmonary nodules on chest CT. On 08-May-2024, she underwent R2 resection, indicating gross residual disease remained postoperatively.

[ current disease status ]: Residual disease remained in the neck after R2 resection, with persistent pulmonary metastatic disease on postoperative imaging. Disease was described as stable at the time of reporting.

[ other clinical data ]: Colonoscopy showed no polyps. The tumor was thyroglobulin negative on immunohistochemistry. No diagnostic radioactive iodine scan had been performed.

She presented the tumor started around 25 or 26 years old, 27, and that's typical of the one that I related to. to FAP, but you can have a sporadic also Kriby-Foy-Murdoch case.

Absolutely. Ron points out excellent points. There's a real spectrum here. I'll even share, I had a case three weeks ago of a 17-year-old who came in, ended up with this in the thyroid, quite isolated and seems to be doing well, no evidence of spread, but indeed went for colonoscopy and had 67 polyps throughout the colon. So, its signal as a link potentially, not always, but a link potentially to FAP is so important. So, let's have you keep moving forward, Nicole, to keep us on time.

Very good.

So after surgery, you can see this is what was left of the right. It's a 2.3, not very well defined here, tissue. And these are the pulmonary metastases. She did have also an FDG PET CT, where you can see that this nodule especially is more FDG avid.
And Dr. Li, I'm just going to quickly pull you in on that PET scan and just any quick comments on this. And also, can you just give a quick review of how we should think about SUV kind of numbers?

Thanks for that. Firstly, SUV, high SUV, I mean, it just means that there's a lot of intensity in the tumor. It does not necessarily differentiate between the malignant or even an inflammatory lesion can have extensive in quite very high SUVs. But in this particular scenario, of course, the fact that the SUV is so high in that particular lesion, and there are also a couple more FDG avid lesions, I think, in the chest, is that correct? that, you know, would point towards the tumor being more aggressive in these particular lesions and having that degree of de-differentiation compared to iodine avid component. I think what you showed in the neck with the CT, and as Ron mentioned, you know, we don't know what the radioiodine status of CMV is, so it'd be interesting to actually have an iodine scan to see what that shows as well, and maybe you've got that differential disease present.
And, Nicole, let's go to your last slide with some of those important questions.

Yeah, I just wanted to add here. We did it like a local tumor board. Most reports don't suggest that these tumor express needs the sodium isoimporter. So we haven't treated her with radiated. We do not have like a diagnostic scan. So the questions that I was wondering was what should we do treatment wise? Have you had any experience with this type of thyroid cancer? And since this thyroid cancer is usually it usually slowly grows, and with good prognosis, there's not much information of what to do once it has spread distantly. She is stable for now, so we decided just to watch for now and see if it progresses. We might do something, but I was wondering what everybody thinks.
Just a few targeted questions to the unknown questions. Eyal, I'm going to bring you in. We each have a handful of these. Radioiodine, what's your norm on this?

So the only case reports, we don't really have data, but if you look at the molecular level, the likelihood of response is really, really low. So I see patients from all over, some get it, some don't. We don't expect the patient to respond in this case.

And also, Dr. Ghossein pointed out that a few years ago, they kind of carved out, this isn't even called anymore, I believe, Cribriform Morular Thyroid Carcinoma. It's just Cribriform Morular Carcinoma. It's unique genomic. kind of world. But what always struck me is the staining and molecular kind of profiling is that it's thyroglobulin negative. So my other question, Eyal, is when you follow these patients, is there any role in our usual kind of serial thyroglobulin measurements in the serum?

No, there's no, and it's pretty frustrating. So we follow with imaging. In this case, PEPCT will be the best one. And it's challenging not to have a simple blood test like l-Citonin or Thioglobulin when you follow the patient. Even antibodies give you something. In this case, we don't. It's just imaging.

All right, Dr. Warden, we always do our best in endocrine and then it doesn't work and we end up with the medical oncologist. So I'm going to pull you in just a minute or two. I don't know if there's a lot to say, but how do you think about an advanced tumor like this? And if it were starting to anatomically progress, what would you do?

Yeah, yeah. No, it's really interesting, Nicole. I have a patient just like this, about the same age. So the screening for FEP, yes, is most important here to look for a colon cancer. But in terms of the thyroid cancer, I agree. You talked about how she relatively is asymptomatic. So watching her, I don't think is unreasonable. Some of these more intense lesions, if they're growing bigger, for example, compared to the other ones, you could consult radiation oncology, or if you're concerned about one of these lesions invading an important vital structure, maybe focal radiation would be warranted. reference_conclusion: Given the low expected likelihood of radioiodine responsiveness in cribriform-morular carcinoma and the absence of a reliable serum thyroglobulin marker, the current plan is active surveillance with imaging-based follow-up, with PET/CT favored for monitoring. If there is anatomical progression or growth of specific lesions, focal radiation may be considered for threatening or enlarging sites. Systemic therapy with a multitargeted kinase inhibitor may be considered if progression occurs, with attention to bleeding risk related to the cavitary pulmonary lesion and consideration of radiation to that lesion before TKI therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]:  
Case 1: 8-month-old female infant.  
Case 2: 14-month-old female infant.

[ chief complaint ]:  
Case 1: Slow-growing sacral region mass present since birth.  
Case 2: Slow-growing sacrococcygeal region mass for 3 months, with serosanguinous discharge from a non-healing ulcer for 15 days, high-grade intermittent fever for 10 days, and straining during defecation.

[ diagnosis ]:  
Case 1: Sacrococcygeal mature teratoma, subsequently with recurrent metabolically active pelvic soft-tissue lesion and markedly elevated AFP consistent with recurrence.  
Case 2: Sacrococcygeal yolk sac tumor with metastatic disease involving lungs/pleura, right inguinal lymph nodes, and vertebral involvement.

[ histopathology results ]:  
Case 1: Resected specimen showed mature sacrococcygeal teratoma with no immature elements. Mature ectodermal components included squamous epithelium, keratin-filled cystic spaces, mature glial tissue, and sebaceous glands. Endodermal components included glandular spaces lined by columnar epithelium. Mesodermal components included cartilage and blood vessels.  
Case 2: Review of outside tissue biopsy showed small round cell tumor with hyalinized tissue; immunopositivity for AFP and CD99, reported as suggestive of yolk sac tumor. Postoperative pathology after mass excision and coccygectomy showed no residual tumor; specimen contained histiocytes without tumor cells and was AFP-negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
Case 1:  
- Chest radiograph was normal.  
- Ultrasound showed a heterogeneously hypoechoic presacral lesion measuring 2.5 × 2.3 cm at the level of the coccygeal tip, with calcification and cystic areas.  
- MRI pelvis showed a solid-cystic lesion posterior to the rectum and anterior to the sacrum, extending into the subcutaneous plane up to the skin surface, with slight extrapelvic extension and no extension into the spinal canal.  
- At 6-month follow-up, FDG PET-CT showed a metabolically active soft-tissue lesion in the mid pelvis measuring 3.6 × 3.4 × 3.3 cm, with no other metabolically active lesions.

Case 2:  
- Chest radiograph showed multiple bilateral nodules involving lung parenchyma and pleura, suggestive of pulmonary metastases.  
- Ultrasound showed a heterogeneous solid sacral mass without internal calcification or necrotic areas.  
- Cross-sectional imaging showed a solid-cystic mass measuring 12.5 × 7 × 7.4 cm, displacing the rectum anteriorly and abutting both iliac arteries.  
- Imaging also demonstrated erosion of the S5 vertebra and collapse of D11.  
- Metastatic workup/PET-CT showed a heterodense mass measuring 7.4 × 5.8 × 4.8 cm arising from the sacrum and coccyx, with avid uptake in bilateral pleura and lung parenchyma and in right inguinal lymph nodes; partial collapse of D11 was present.  
- After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, repeat imaging showed decrease in size of the primary mass, improvement in size and number of lung nodules, persistent D11 collapse, decreased size/metabolic activity of the sacrococcygeal mass, and absence of uptake in lung nodules and inguinal lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
Case 2: Tumor biopsy was positive for AFP and CD99 on immunohistochemistry.

[ laboratory results ]:  
Case 1:  
- Routine blood investigations were within normal limits.  
- Serum AFP at presentation: 94.1 ng/mL.  
- hCG: within normal limits.  
- LDH: 800 U/L, mildly elevated.  
- Postoperative day 3 AFP: 36.5 ng/mL.  
- AFP at 3-month follow-up: 8.5 ng/mL.  
- AFP at 6-month follow-up: 13,000 ng/mL.

Case 2:  
- Hemoglobin: 5.6 g/dL.  
- Serum AFP at presentation: 96,000 ng/mL.  
- Other tumor markers including beta-hCG were within normal limits.  
- LDH was elevated.  
- Postoperative day 3 AFP: 6.5 ng/mL.  
- At 1-month follow-up after completion of chemotherapy: AFP 1.5 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
Case 1:  
- Underwent upfront sacrococcygeal mass excision with coccygectomy.  
- Postoperative course was uneventful.  
- Follow-up at 3 months was clinically normal with normalized AFP.  
- At 6 months, biochemical and PET-CT evidence of recurrence was identified.

Case 2:  
- Prior to tertiary presentation, underwent incision and drainage twice elsewhere for presumed abscess; recurrence followed, and a biopsy was taken during the second procedure.  
- At tertiary center, received optimization with blood/blood product transfusion, antibiotics, and supportive care.  
- Started on PEB chemotherapy for metastatic yolk sac tumor.  
- Completed 4 cycles preoperatively, tolerated without neutropenia or immunosuppression, with reduction in mass size, healing of ulcer, and falling AFP.  
- Subsequently underwent excision of the mass with coccygectomy.  
- Postoperative course was uneventful.  
- Completed a total of 6 cycles of chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]:  
Case 2: On follow-up 1 month after completion of 6 cycles of chemotherapy and surgery; AFP was 1.5 ng/mL, with postoperative pathology showing no residual tumor.

[ other clinical data ]:  
Case 1:  
- Perinatal history was uneventful.  
- Parents reported rupture of the lesion during the first week of life with serous discharge for 2-3 days.  
- On examination, the child was active. Abdomen was soft with no palpable mass and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.  
- Local examination showed a firm, immobile sacral/natal cleft mass measuring 4 × 3 cm with a sinus opening and no active discharge.  
- Digital rectal examination showed a firm mass palpable on the posterior rectal wall with mobile rectal mucosa and no anal canal narrowing.

Case 2:  
- Perinatal history was uneventful.  
- On examination, there was a hard sacral mass measuring 6 × 5 cm and an ulcer measuring 3 × 1 cm with inflamed margins, slough-covered base, and active serous ooze.  
- Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was present.  
- Digital rectal examination showed hard nodularity over the posterior rectal wall with rounded upper border, immobile mucosa, and narrowing of the anal canal.  
- The child was irritable and dehydrated at presentation.

reference_discussion.text: Go ahead. Greetings, everyone. I'm Dr. Pushna, five-year MCH resident in the Department of Pediatric Surgery, SGPG, Lucknow. Today, we are going to start the tumor board meeting, and our discussion today is sacrocoxygial mass. We are going to share two interesting cases of the sacrocoxygial mass that we had dealt in the last year. So our first case is an eight-month-old female child presented to our department with the complaints of slow-growing mass in the sacral region observed by the parents themselves since the birth. Economically, they are socially very poor, and also, Approach to the hospital services and also other medical services is also very poor. So, according to the description by the mother, it was initially the size of the marble observed by herself and it was progressed to the present size as can be seen on the picture, clinical picture here. and she also had said that it had ruptured in the first week of the life itself and there was a serious discharge for two to three days observed by the mother and she had shown this symptom to the local practitioner who was a quack and who had assured her that it was okay for this child and that child can be managed conservatively only and child doesn't have any other constitutional symptoms and also entire perinatal history of the child is uneventful. So, but still the parent had the concern, so she had presented here and when we had examined the patient, she was very active and also for abdomen and also we had examined the local area of the sacral region. per abdomen there is no mass or any inguinal lymphadenopathy but there is a mass of size 4 into 3 centimeters which was firm in nature and also immobile just present over the natal cleft and we can also appreciate a sinus opening seen over the mass with no active discharge. Correctly there was the firm mass palpable on the posterior wall of the rectum with mobile mucosa over the mass and there is no narrowing of the anal canal. So we had proceeded with the investigations of the patient starting with the routine blood investigations which were within the normal limits and her tumor markers especially serum alpha-beta protein is slightly raised. According to the AFP mammogram for her age it should be less than 10 but for her as we can see here it is almost 94.1 nanograms per milliliters and rest of the tumor markers like hCG and LDH HCC is normal limits but whereas LDH is slightly raised i.e. 800 units per litre. Chest X-ray is normal. So, we had proceeded with the other radiological investigations in the form of ultrasound and also CT angio and MRI. Ultrasound had shown that there is a heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion of the size 2.5 x 2.3 cm in the pre-sacral region at the level of the tip of the coccyx with the area of calcification and also cystic areas. CT angio unfortunately we are not able to retrieve them but MRI pelvis was done which had showed the solid cystic region as can be appreciated here behind the rectum but in front of the sacrum and also it is extending into the subcutaneous plane as can be seen here with the lesion reaching up to the skin surface and there is no obvious extension into the spinal canal as can be appreciated here in the fourth picture and also in the third picture and also here we can appreciate that that is entirely pre-sacral mass with slight extension into the extra pelvic region. So, after the counseling of the parents and also in the view of our presentation, we had taken the patient for the upfront surgery in the, that is, sacrococcygeal excision, mass excision along with the coccygectomy. Here in the interoperative picture, we can appreciate the plane of the dissection that we had done and also here we can appreciate the coccygectomy post-tissue dissection here. So after the surgery, entire post-surgery period was uneventful and we had repeated serum alpha beta proteins after day three, which was the 36.5 nanograms per milliliters. Histopathology examination was reported as the mature sacrocoxygial teratoma with no immature elements. It had shown three components that is ectodermal, here we can appreciate the squamous and the keratin-filled cystic space. Here we can appreciate the mature glial tissue. And here we can appreciate the sebaceous glands also. And endodermal components like glandular spaces flanked by columnar epithelium. And also mesodermal components like cartilage and also the blood vessels. So, as it was suggestive of the mature teratoma only, she was advised for the regular follow-ups, that is a three-month interval. So, at the three-month follow-up, her serum alpha-fetoprotein was 8.5 nanograms per milliliters, and the rest of the clinical examination was also within the normal limits. But at the six-month follow-up, all the clinical examination was within the normal limits, like per-abdomen, there is no mass or any recurrence, and per-rectally also no mass palpable, But there is raised AFP of 13,000 nanograms per milliliter. So suspecting the recurrence, we had proceeded with the metastatic workup in view of their restrained finances also. We had straightaway proceeded with the FDG PET-CT as it can give the entire information, whether it is metastatic or the local recurrence or recurrence anywhere. It had shown that there is a metabolically active soft tissue in the mid pelvis region of the size 3.6 into 3.4 into 3.3 centimeters. And there is no other metabolically active region. Unfortunately, we are not able to retrieve the PET CT. I'm sorry for that. So for the recurrence, a patient was started on the PEB regimen, that is bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. Presently, she's at the follow-up with the completion of two cycles of the chemo with a good response to chemo. That is in the terms of decreasing trends of the alpha-beta protein levels. So post-second cycle completion, her serum alpha-beta proteins are 624 nanograms per ml. Moving on to the second case, a 14-month-old female child with uneventful perinatal history presented with complaints of slow-growing mass observed by the parents in the sacrocoxygial region for the three months. Here we can appreciate the mass in the sacrocoxygial region. So, they had taken the patient to a local practitioner who had diagnosed the mass as abscess and he had done incision and drainage and then again there is a recurrence in the size of the mass. So, he had proceeded with the repetition of the incision and drainage and he had taken a tissue biopsy at that time. And also there was a non-healing ulcer that was developed after the second time incision and the drainage. So a patient had presented here with the complaint of serosanguinous discharge also from the ulcer for the 15 days and also there is a history of high grade intermittent fever for 10 days. And there are other symptoms like straining to pass the stool and but no difficulty in the maturation. So on examination, there is a single hard mass of the size of the six into five centimeters over the sacral region was present as I had shown in the previous picture. And also here we can appreciate the mass along with the ulcer regions which was of the size 3 into 1 centimeters with inflamed margins and with the base covered with the slough and active serous sinus ooze was there. There was a bilateral inguinal lymphendopathy of variable size also. But rectally, there is a hard nodularity palpable over the posterior wall with rounded upper border but with immobile mucosa and also there is a narrowing of the anal canal. So general examination also, Shail was very irritable and dehydrated with the Hb of 5.6 gram percent. And also her tumor markers like serum alpha-beta protein was highly elevated, that is 96,000 nanograms per milliliters. But other tumor markers like SCZ was within the normal limits. Again, LDH was elevated. So we had optimized the patient in the terms of blood and blood products transfusion and also other support to treatment. including the antibiotics. We had done the chest x-ray which had showed the features suggestive of the lung metastasis as can be appreciated on the x-ray here and ultrasound showed that a heterogeneous mass solid mass noted in the sacral region with no internal calcifications or necrotic regions. Further imaging had revealed that there is a solid cystic mass as can be seen here of the size 12.5 x 7 x 7.4 cm that was anteriorly displacing the rectum and also it was abutting the bilateral iliac arteries. And on the chest x-ray there was multiple nodules seen bilaterally involving the lung parenchyma and also the pleura. And also there is an erosion of the S5 vertebra and also collapse of the D11. We had proceeded with the metastatic workup also, which had showed the heterodense mass of the size 7.4 into 5.8 into 4.8 centimeters arising from the sacrum and the coccyx. And also there was a heavy uptake in the pleura and the parenchyma of the lung, bilateral lungs. And also there is uptake in the right inguinal lymph nodes also. And also partial collapse of the D11 vertebra was appreciated. So the outside tissue biopsy that was taken by the local practitioner, we had retrieved that and was sent for the histopathology in the institute. It was suggestive of the small Roma cell tumor as can be appreciated here with the hyaluronized tissue also. And it was positive for the AFP and also CD99. So these are the features suggestive of the Yorkshire tumor. So after the counseling of the parents about the malignant nature and also the metastasis, we had started the patient on the PEB regimen and we had given the child four cycles. Patient had tolerated chemotherapy well with no complications like neutropenia or immunosuppression. And there is a clinical improvement in the mass size also. And also there is a healing of ulcer. And we had observed decreasing trend in the serum AFP levels also, which I will show later. So after the completion of the four cycles, we had proceeded with the repeat imaging mainly for the preoperative evaluation, which had showed a decrease in the size of the mass, as can be appreciated here, but with the persistence of D11 collapse. And as can be seen here, lung nodules had improved in their size and also in their number. We had repeated the metastatic workup also, which had showed that the mass had decreased in the size compared to the previous PET-CT in the terms of the mainly in the size and also epideptic. And also, there is absence of uptake in the lung nodules and also in the inguinal lymph nodes. Again, a collapse of the D11 vertebra was noted. So, as the patient had completed four cycles and also had shown the good chemo response, we had taken the patient for this surgery, that is excision of the mass along the coccygectomy. Here we are unable to retrieve the entire intro pictures, but this is the post-operative picture after the small dissection or the incomplete dissection of the tumor. After this, we had proceeded with the further dissection of the tumor and the coccygectomy also. and post-operative period was uneventful and the immediate post-operative period that we had repeated after day three serum alpha-fetoprotein was 6.5 nanograms per milliliters. Mr. Pathology has shown that the tumor we had sent is free of the residual tumor and here we can appreciate that there is only histiocytes with no tumor cells and it was also AFP negative. Right now, patient is under follow-up after the completion of all the six cycles of the chemo. And right now, she's under one month follow-up. Here, we can appreciate the decreasing trend of the AFP since from the presentation, that is 96,000 nanograms per milliliters. And at one month follow-up after the chemo completion, the AFP levels of 1.5 nanograms per milliliters.

Okay, but that collapse was assumed as a bone metastasis. Yes. But metastatic compromise of the tumor. Okay.
Yes, sir. Agreed. It is metastasis, but probably chemotherapy take care of that.

I had one query about meaning about the both the patients in the first patient you had mentioned that CT angio was done so what was the indication for CT angio CT angio for receptability look for receptability man we can remove it So is that a routine which is done generally?
Yes, yes, yes ma'am. Definitely CT chest and local area is routine at our center.
No, no, NGO, NGO. I'm talking of CT NGO. Yes, ma'am.
This is routine. We always do CT NGO, triple face CT NGO.
Okay, okay. So there in first patient as well as in second patient, I was actually wondering in the first patient alpha-beta protein was raised right in the beginning itself, right?

Yeah, this is my query ma'am. Actually, first case if we look carefully, it presented as a sacrococcygeal teratoma, most probably it is a benign lesion. and only apart from two issues are there only child is presented late that is eight month of age and other is alpha-fetoprotein is raised but it denotes that there is immature component is there or some malignant component is there but histopathology showed and it was reviewed when child presented after six months. Dr. Neha herself reviewed the cut the multiple section and saw there was complete mature cells. There was no any immaturity or any malignant cell is there and in spite of that after six months she presented with raised alpha-fetoprotein. So is it possible if we excise a teratoma or a benign lesion in sacrococcygeal area and if we leave some kind of tissue, little bit tissue there, that is it is a suboptimal excision, so is it possible that tissue can change to malignant behavior?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 15-year-old adolescent.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-week history of non-painful neck swelling, associated with anxiousness, increased resting heart rate, and occasional palpitations.

[ diagnosis ]: Autonomous thyroid nodule of the left thyroid lobe; post-operative minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed crowded groups of follicular cells with absent background colloid, categorized as Bethesda IV: follicular neoplasm.  
- Cytology showed no nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Surgical pathology demonstrated a very cellular tumor with scant colloid and a thick fibrous capsule.  
- Higher-power examination showed papillary/pseudopapillary architecture without nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Minimal capsular invasion was identified.  
- No angioinvasion was detected.  
- Pathologic interpretation was minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Point-of-care thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a large mostly solid left thyroid lobe lesion with a few small cystic spaces comprising less than 25% of lesion volume.  
- The lesion measured 4.0 x 3.5 x 2.9 cm.  
- The lesion had color flow but was not hypervascular.  
- It was described as mostly hypoechoic, with smooth margins and no echogenic foci.  
- Ultrasound-based assessment was TI-RADS 3.  
- No sonographic evidence of capsular involvement or extrathyroidal extension was described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Post-operative testing identified an activating TSH receptor (TSHR) mutation.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- TSH was undetectable.  
- T4 was elevated initially.  
- T3 was described as only marginally elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Methimazole was started pre-operatively.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was performed.  
- Thyroid uptake scan was not performed.  
- Surgical treatment consisted of thyroid lobectomy with preservation of remaining thyroid tissue; no prophylactic central neck dissection was performed.  
- Post-operatively, levothyroxine was not started because the patient was asymptomatic.

[ current disease status ]:  
- No angioinvasion was present on pathology.  
- No nodal disease was identified (N0).  
- The patient remained under active follow-up, with repeat thyroid function testing planned in 6 months.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis were mild but clinically present.  
- The thyroid lesion was described intraoperatively/pathologically as well circumscribed and readily separable from surrounding tissues.

reference_discussion.text: All right. Good morning, everybody. So we have three cases. If we make it through all three, that's our goal, but it's not a requirement. So my turn?

There's a large, we would call this a mostly solid lesion. It's got a few small cystic spaces, but that's less than 25% of its volume. It's got color flow, which almost every thyroid nodule has. It's not a hypervascular nodule by any means. It's over, it's quite large in size. It's four by three and a half by 2.9. And so if we go ahead and use the TIRADS scoring system, we would give this two points for being solid. And one point, I would call it mostly hypoechoic, no echogenic foci, it's pretty smooth margins. So it would get a TIRADS three. For adults, we would recommend a biopsy because of its size. Typically, the radiologist looking at the thyroid nodules will not have any information about the thyroid function, so we do not take the function of this nodule into account. For children or adults, I would recommend an FNA.
And Lucienne or Jonathan, the labs consistent with an autonomous nodule, would you do a thyroid uptake and scan? What's the next step in addition to considering an FNA?

So, you know, I can pipe in. I think along the lines of what Mary said, not all autonomous nodules need to be biopsied in kids. If they're Any suspicious features? Maybe Mary, I can put her on the line to comment on the applicability of tirads in children, because she's had a lot of thought about that. But only if there are suspicious sonographic features. I probably would consider an uptake and scan for this patient if we're thinking about surgical intervention for the patient. And although the thyroid function tests are only marginally abnormal apart from the TSH, the T4 is normal, the T3 is only marginally elevated. So we expect this to be probably what we would call a warm nodule rather than a hot nodule. And I'd also, from the scan, want to know whether or not there's any extra thyroidal uptake, because that would inform our assessment of the underlying pathology.
I'll just add, I agree with an uptake scan. We normally do this in any patient with a nodule and a suppressed TSH. It's like an automatic part of our algorithm.

I'll just toss in my thoughts about Tyrades. So, you know, Tyrades were designed to be used in adults. and they were designed to decrease the number of unnecessary biopsies and still, excuse me, maintain a high level of diagnostic ability for aggressive cancers, right? So we're trying to get the aggressive cancers in adults and we're trying to avoid biopsying the benign cancers in adults because we know what the natural history of the disease is in adults. We also know that that's different for children and what our group has suggested from from the Brigham, which seems to be sort of where people are falling in line, is to use the same descriptive categories and categorize the same way, but shift the recommendation sizes over one category. So the numbers that we would use at TR4 in an adult, we would move those numbers over to TR3 in kids, and we would take the numbers from three and move them to TR2 for children. So you just are upping the number of nodules that you'll biopsy, but we know that's more important in children than it is in, say, a 72-year-old, right? But in this case, the nodule is so big that it meets criteria, because the other thing that we've shown when we looked at a large series of nodules in children at the Brigham is that the nodules that are over four centimeters can fool you. And when they get this big, they probably actually need to come out, and FNA may not even be sufficient to tell you what the nodule is.

Just one thing to add to what Mary said, and I know Kaké wanted to speak as well, but I think buried in a lot of important stuff that she mentioned was needing to know the criteria of tirads. And for us in children in particular, just getting a referral with that this is a Tyrans4 nodule isn't sufficient. I'd like to know why was it a Tyrans4 nodule and what were the features that made it Tyrans4 or 5. So that's an important part of the referral for me.

I was just going to mention that in Michigan, our paediatric endocrinologist would look at the TSH being suppressed and order a thyroid scan and uptake. It looks like a T3 thyrotoxicosis, which has been described with autonomous nodules. And then in our literature, once you confirm it's a hard nodule, then it's recommended not to biopsy them because they'll come back as follicular lesions. Now, there are rare case reports of hot nodules that end up being thyroid cancer, but they're supposed to be exceedingly rare. So I think there's individual characteristics of the patients that have to come into play here.

So that's a perfect lead-in, which I think we kind of already talked about the indication and what would be the next step. And this is a proposed near-final. Jonathan is co-chair with me with Steven Wagesbeck on our updated ATA pediatric guidelines. So this is the tentative draft, as you can see written here, not final version. Yeah, I find it in, in this age group is it's very similar to working on an adult. If we start getting younger, There's a lot more issues like thymus, brown fat, things that are gonna make it a little more difficult for you to identify the parathyroids in the central bed. But by the time they're like 15 or late teenagers, they've lost a lot of that brown fat and the thymus has regressed. So it really is a little more straightforward.
