I would leave it.
Yeah. Based on ultrasound and psychology, no prophylactic central neck dissection. Right. All right. So kind of successful in removing.

So everybody predicted the TSHR mutation, which is a low risk for malignancy. The tumor shown here, it's very cellular, not much colloid at all as we expected based on the cytology. And it does have a very thick fibrous capsule. which is not a very specific finding, but it makes me a little more concerned when I'm evaluating thyroid nodules. If it's got a thick capsule, that's more characteristic of something that could potentially be carcinoma. not highly indicative of that. And I think the next slide.
Bill, that one area kind of at four to five o'clock, are those FNA changes or is that just a large nodule that's lost a little bit of vascular supply? Or am I over reading that eosinophil area?

Yeah, that looks, it may very well be due to FNA changes causing some fibrosis and degenerative change. Yeah, I mean, unfortunately, surgical pathologists have to be on the lookout for things that are FNA changes and they can even cause features that can mimic minimal capsular invasion.
Alright, and then higher power.

Again, this is the kind of thing though where we would probably do multiple deeper levels just to make sure we're not seeing hemocytorin or other features that could suggest it's related to

uh... an f in a type of artifact based on this it's a minimally invasive uh... polyethyroid carcinoma rights so it's a carcinoma sure you're in the other side and you know i think we're looking at a very it's a carcinoma but just barely from a few cells going into the house but that's a that's what i think i think i think that's like being a little bit pregnant right out there so this is a little bit pregnant yet now it's it's so it From what Bill showed us, it just barely meet criteria for carcinoma, and there's no angioinvasion. We were told it's N0 based on the WHO. We don't have separate pathology outcomes data in children, so we rely on the WHO criteria. And we really look at the likelihood of residual or recurrent disease as a function largely of the extent of angioinvasion. And if there were no vessels involved here, the likelihood of recurrent disease or distal metastases is going to be pretty low. I would agree with that. With our minimally invasive follicular thyroid cancer patients, we do just offer surveillance. So I would reassure family that there's no evidence of angioinvasion. Of course, like Bill said, we are relying on good pathology review of this.

You can think about it. I think it's always reasonable to think about Cowden syndrome. In kids, we will see other, often, very often, see other features of Cowden or P10 Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome. Gotcha. More of a mouthful, but they often will have macrocephaly. which may not be apparent visually, I always do measure them and plot them. And not uncommon, we'll have features of autistic spectrum disorder, learning disability, and then family history. So it's reasonable to think about it. Dicer-1's also there, and the problem with Dicer-1 is clinically it can be lower expression, no penetrance in a family. So LT4 replacement, just quickly to wrap this one up, would you start or would you wait?

Depends if she's symptomatic. I think she's symptomatic. reference_conclusion: Given the suppressed TSH and thyroid nodule, thyroid uptake and scan was discussed as part of the evaluation; however, because the lesion was a solid 4 cm nodule and management was already proceeding toward intervention, uptake and scan was not performed. Fine-needle aspiration was obtained at family request, and methimazole was initiated as a temporizing measure. Following lobectomy, pathology demonstrated minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma without angioinvasion; completion thyroidectomy was not recommended, and surveillance was advised. Levothyroxine replacement was deferred because the patient was asymptomatic, with expectation of recovery of thyroid function and interval reassessment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Large right hepatic mass in the setting of hepatocellular carcinoma and portal hypertension.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma involving essentially the entirety of the right hepatic lobe, with portal hypertension. No macrovascular invasion was described.

[ histopathology results ]: Not available.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a 10 cm hepatic tumor occupying essentially the entire right lobe of the liver, with splenomegaly consistent with portal hypertension. No macrovascular invasion was described. After systemic therapy, the previously large tumor had markedly regressed to a small cavity, with a new/enlarging focal lesion measuring approximately 14 mm. Subsequent SPECT-CT after regional treatment demonstrated treatment of the involved region. Follow-up imaging showed complete response with no evidence of disease and expected T1 hyperintensity attributed to radiation effect.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Platelet count was approximately 50 ×10^9/L.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial surgical management was not pursued because of portal hypertension. Mapping angiography for radioembolization demonstrated a lung shunt fraction of 37%, precluding delivery of an effective radioembolization dose. The patient subsequently underwent one round of transarterial chemoembolization. Repeat mapping after chemoembolization reduced the lung shunt fraction to approximately 20–25%, but this was still considered insufficient for effective dosing given tumor size and treatment territory. Systemic therapy with STRIDE was then administered, with a marked radiographic response. During treatment, a new/enlarging 14 mm focus developed within the treated area while the dominant tumor had regressed to a small cavity. Regional therapy was then delivered to the whole involved region, after which imaging demonstrated complete response with no evidence of disease.

[ current disease status ]: Complete radiographic response with no evidence of disease following multimodality treatment.

[ other clinical data ]: Portal hypertension was clinically significant, with recurrent variceal banding required. Splenomegaly was present. The patient had severe thrombocytopenia in the setting of portal hypertension.

reference_discussion.text: So, variations on the theme. Let's talk about this guy. 67-year-old male. He also has HTC, but this time he has portal hypertension, as you can see by a big spleen there. 10-centimeter tumor. Sit at your tumor board. What are you guys looking at?

With portal hypertension, it looks like he's going to need at least a right, I'm assuming not an extended right hepatectomy, and I don't think our surgeons are going to do an operation. Correct me if I'm wrong, would you do a surgery here? I would not. You did not, don't worry. And so without macrovascular invasion, this patient's going to get local regional therapy. The question becomes, are they going to be ever considered for a liver transplant, you know, with downstaging? And that's always a huge gray zone as to, you know, what is the official downstaging criteria? I would argue there's nothing official anymore. It's, you know, it's kind of individualized at this point. But we would start with local regional therapy in this case. And given the size of the tumor, it would be a radio embolization.

And I don't know if I mentioned for the listeners, this is a 10-centimeter tumor that's occupying essentially the entirety of the right lobe of the liver. Dr. Burgoyne, would you offer systemic therapy over local regional therapy for this patient?

Not outside of a clinical trial. I mean, if it's a targetable lesion by Y90, that is going to have a higher response rate than immunotherapy and a higher likelihood of downstaging this patient if that's our goal.

Are there any current clinical trials in the US for BCLC, this would be actually A, so this is actually technically BCLC-A, are there any ongoing trials in BCLC-A right now? It may not be offered at UCSD or UCLA, I'm just curious.

There are, and Zach can comment on this too, but the studies that are asking this question of tear plus immunotherapy typically don't stratify by BCLCC, more as what is the amount of tumor in the liver and is it targetable Y90? So a patient like this would potentially be eligible for one of those studies for combination, exactly.
So we took Sid's advice and took them for a mapping procedure and their lung shunt was 37%. could not get an effective, or at least what I would consider an effective dose of radioembolization. Okay.

What would you do now? So if they can't get an effective dose, there's a couple of things that you can do. You'd have to look at your angiogram to see if there was some shunting that you could shut down, and that obviously takes a lot of study to look at your angiogram and so on. The other option is to switch, right? So in our practice, if let's say we can't figure out a way around it, we switch therapies. You go to plan B, and in this case, that's chemoembolization. We kind of forget about chemoembolization because our practice tends to be so Y90 heavy, similar to yours. But keep in mind, chemoembolization has been the mainstay of BCLC A and B for the last 25 years. or close to 25 years, and so this patient would most likely get a chemoembolization without me looking at the mapping angiogram. And then we can always do the TACE, restage, and then put all options on the table again. It doesn't have to be, once you're doing TACE, you still have to do it. You can always switch back. You're not really set into one specific treatment algorithm. You can switch to systemic, et cetera.

Yeah, so we did a round of tastes and then redid the mapping procedure and we got their lung shunt down to about 20-25%. Still, you know, not quite happy with the amount of dose given how large the tumor was and the size of the territory. How do you feel about systemic therapy in this setting?

Well, if all of my colleagues have said no to their technologies, this is how patients sometimes land in my clinic. But yes, if they're not a candidate for surgery due to portal hypertension, if they're not a candidate for Y90 due to lung shunting, if they've already had a taste, we need to try something else. So, I think starting a person like this on systemic therapy, either with, depending on their degree of portal hypertension and, you know, presence of varices or not, if those are controlled, considering a tezobev, and if not, considering the stride regimen.

The other option just to think about, and again, you do the taste, restage them. You can also consider external beam radiation. That's something that we really haven't discussed. It's localized to that one side. It's not diffuse. If our radiation oncology colleagues can feel like they can conform it reasonably well without getting a lot of non-target dose, that's another option you can consider.

We ended up going with Stride, and this guy had a phenomenal response to Stride. However, he did start having an area grow, now 14 millimeters, and that huge tumor is now this small little cavity. And so, this is definitely new compared to prior scans. And so, do we consider switching to a different immunotherapy, or what are your thoughts?

You could switch to a different treatment, a systemic therapy to second line for someone that is progressing that would be within sort of the tenets of oncology. I think putting our common sense caps on though, looking at this, it's very small. Is this targetable now by local regional therapy and thinking outside the box and doing a laser focus therapy on that may make more sense than treating their whole body with a new regimen that might be more toxic.

And we've seen this a lot now, especially since a lot of patients with advanced tumors, large tumors, infiltrated tumors, got immunotherapy, had an awesome response. And then, I don't know, one year, two years later, they have this little nodular recurrence that looks just like this. And we've been anecdotally very successful in getting them back to a complete response. And they've been able to stay on their systemic therapy whether it's Stride or Atisobeb and so on. The one thing is, in terms of adding a local regional therapy approach here, it's not just that 13.5 millimeter nodule. Every time, every single time we do a mapping angiogram, it's going to be more than that. So to target that with, let's say, an ablation is going to be inadequate. You're going to miss. You see that small nodule, but there's probably three or four others tucked in there as well. So every time we do a mapping angiogram, we'll see three to four times as much tumor. But as long as it's all localized, it's very targetable, and it tends to be very straightforward as well. And so we've done that and kept them on the same regimen, just as you said, because it doesn't make sense to completely switch and you're burning a bridge, and you may not need to burn that bridge because you want to get them five years, seven years, whatever. And we've gotten durability from doing that. Completely non-science-based, of course.

That's the approach we took. And you can see on the left is the SPECT-CT taking your advice and treating the whole region, knowing that there's more disease that we can see there. And now we see we're back to a complete response, no evidence of disease. And you can see the expected kind of T1 hyperintensity from the radiation effect. So now we're in a situation where did we successfully downstage? Can we think about transplant? Does the immunotherapy give either of you guys pause with transplant?

Well, so what I'm gathering is that the total sort of presumed tumor diameter with the issues in getting that precisely measured that you raised looks to be that it would be within a downstage criteria that we could consider transplantation for this patient. As to the immunotherapy, yes, this does become an issue. Most programs are looking to discontinue that for three months or so ahead of going into transplant to avoid problems with rejection.

Yeah, I think Adam and I have a lot of experience with this. Fortunately or unfortunately, we were early dipping our toe in the water, the post-immunotherapy transplant, and found that if you have an insufficient washout period, then your risk of having very dramatic hepatotoxicity that looks like severe refractory rejection is super high. And I think that we were the center that came up with three months. out of experience, you know, that six weeks was inadequate for us and three months seemed to work from having gone through it. So yeah, we would definitely consider transplant, but again, they have to have that washout period to ensure that or to lower your risk. I think we still don't completely understand the process that's involved in Adam being much smarter than me could probably explain the immunology behind the, you know, the immunotherapy and how it really kind of changes your immune system dramatically, perhaps permanently, and again, in ways that we don't fully understand. So I think we have to be thoughtful and careful, but I do think immunotherapy can be used for downstaging.

And I would just say like from a pharmacology perspective, just remember these aren't oral medicines metabolized by the liver and the kidneys that wash out in a few days after stopping treatment, as you mentioned, Gabe. These are monoclonal antibodies that last in the system for weeks and probably do have some amount of you know, long-lasting remodulation of the immune system that we don't fully understand, but we need to be very mindful of. And the other point that I just would throw out there as we're thinking about transplant for not versus not is for patients that are complete responders with immunotherapy or multimodality therapy, we know that the tails of these curves are quite long now, you know, stride data now out to five years showing overall survivors of 20%. Do patients need transplant? And I think for someone like this, the case is a bit clearer. This person, their portal hypertension actually is quite bad. They're requiring recurrent banding for their varices. Their platelets are hanging out about 50. I think, you know, I'd be curious on Heather's input on what's their risk of death from cirrhosis alone and portal hypertension alone.

Actually, if you look at all the things that we look at to help inform prognosis, cortal hypertension is the biggest predictor of mortality still. And so I would definitely encourage, assuming that they are transplantable from all the other angles, that that be pursued for this person, if that's what they want.

It's interesting. I think Adam and I have had some cases as well, not transplant, but resection after long durations of stable immunotherapy with mixed results. I mean, sometimes you stop the immunotherapy and all of a sudden it's everywhere again, right? So I think we're still figuring this out. It's such novel therapy and new drugs keep coming up, new monoclonal antibodies keep coming up. So I think it's, It's an exciting time, but also one to be approached with some caution.

reference_conclusion: The patient was not considered a surgical candidate because of portal hypertension, and initial management was local-regional therapy with radioembolization as the preferred modality for downstaging. After mapping demonstrated prohibitive lung shunting precluding an effective Y90 dose, chemoembolization was performed, followed by initiation of systemic therapy with the STRIDE regimen when further locoregional options were not feasible. Following a marked response with a small localized recurrence, regional treatment to the entire involved area was undertaken while maintaining the same systemic regimen, resulting in a complete response. Given successful downstaging and significant portal hypertension, transplant evaluation was supported, with discontinuation of immunotherapy for approximately 3 months before transplantation to reduce rejection risk.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old male. He had been described as exceedingly healthy, thin, and an ultramarathon runner. He had no personal history of radiation exposure and no family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Eight- to ten-month history of enlarging thyroid gland. He had one episode of anterior neck pain that resolved spontaneously over approximately one month. He also had a single disabling vertiginous episode lasting approximately 3 hours. He denied headache, vision changes, palpitations, dysphagia, odynophagia, dyspnea, voice change, recurrent neck pain, and restriction of neck motion.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma involving bilateral thyroid nodules, with suspected pulmonary metastatic disease. Clinical stage was documented as cT3a N0 M1, stage IVC.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of both thyroid nodules was consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Outside thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a dominant 6.7 cm right thyroid nodule categorized as TI-RADS 3 and a left thyroid nodule categorized as TI-RADS 4.  
CT imaging demonstrated a 7.6 x 6.1 x 6.4 cm heterogeneous enhancing mass centered in the right thyroid lobe with minimal substernal extension. There was marked displacement of adjacent structures including the trachea, without definitive tracheal invasion or definite extrathyroidal extension. No enlarged lateral neck lymph nodes were identified on CT. A rounded lesion was present in the right palatine tonsil; this was considered a possible metastatic focus on CT, although later review indicated the lesion was within the tonsil and was not DOTATATE-avid. Pulmonary nodules were identified, prompting further evaluation.  
PET DOTATATE demonstrated avidity in the primary thyroid tumor, a PET-avid right pleural-based nodule, and a PET-avid right upper lobe pulmonary nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Proprietary molecular testing on FNA material and germline genomic testing were ordered but were canceled before completion. RET status was not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Calcitonin was >1200. CEA was 125. Serum calcium was normal. Urine metanephrines were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No cancer-directed treatment had been administered at the time of review. Diagnostic workup had included thyroid ultrasound, FNA of bilateral thyroid nodules, CT imaging, PET DOTATATE imaging, and laboratory evaluation.

[ current disease status ]: Bulky bilateral medullary thyroid carcinoma was present, with dominant right-sided disease and suspected distant metastatic disease involving the lung/pleural region. There was no definitive radiographic evidence of tracheal invasion, extrathyroidal extension, or enlarged lateral neck lymphadenopathy. Flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated normal vocal fold motion.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination demonstrated moderate visible neck asymmetry, right greater than left, with a palpable thyroid gland that was mobile and non-tender. No obvious lateral neck lymphadenopathy was detected on examination. Overall concern for multiple endocrine neoplasia was low based on normal calcium and negative urine metanephrines.

Really excited to get to hang out today and chat about this case. And I hope it stimulates as much discussion as we had when we first went over it. As a 41 year old, exceedingly healthy male, he had an eight to 10 month history of an enlarging thyroid gland. He also has no personal history of radiation exposure and no family history of cancer. On physical exam, he's thin, healthy, he's an ultramarathon runner. He did have a moderate right or greater than left visible neck asymmetry with a palpable thyroid gland, but it was overall mobile and non-tender at the time of exam. He also did not have any obvious lateral neck lymphadenopathy, and on scope, he had normal vocal fold motion. An outside provider had obtained an ultrasound and an FNA, and this is the information we had when he arrived in our clinic. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old man from Junagadh, Gujarat.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with new multiple pulmonary nodules and nodal recurrence on recent PET-CT after prior multimodality treatment.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus, initially diagnosed in 2024 as stage III disease; subsequently developed recurrent metastatic disease involving the paraesophageal region and lungs.

[ histopathology results ]: Residual disease was present after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery. Paraesophageal nodal recurrence and a lung nodule were surgically resected subsequently. Histologic subtype was squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Routine PET-CT performed during adjuvant nivolumab identified recurrence with a small paraesophageal nodule and a small lung nodule.  
- Most recent PET-CT demonstrated multiple lung nodules, one new paraesophageal lymph node, and a parietal lymph node.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive genomic profiling performed on surgical tissue demonstrated PTEN mutation, TP53 mutation, CCND1 alteration/amplification, and CDK6 alteration/amplification.  
- Additional reported amplifications included FGF19, FGF3, and FGF4.  
- PD-L1 CPS: 10.  
- MSI/TMB were reported as low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- In 2024, the patient underwent neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery for stage III esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Due to residual disease after surgery, adjuvant nivolumab was administered for 1 year.  
- Approximately 6 months into adjuvant nivolumab, PET-CT showed recurrence with a paraesophageal lesion and a lung nodule.  
- Robotic-assisted surgery was performed with resection of the paraesophageal lymph node and the lung nodule.  
- The patient was subsequently rechallenged with paclitaxel plus carboplatin administered every 3 weeks. Two cycles were completed.  
- Paclitaxel/carboplatin was poorly tolerated, with recurrent malaise and difficulty tolerating chemotherapy.  
- Despite prior surgery and systemic therapy, subsequent PET-CT showed further progression with multiple lung nodules and new nodal disease.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with progressive pulmonary and nodal disease after prior neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, surgery, adjuvant nivolumab, metastasectomy, and 2 cycles of paclitaxel/carboplatin.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- ECOG performance status had been 0 after surgery.  
- The patient subsequently experienced intermittent poor tolerance to systemic chemotherapy, including recurrent malaise.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old postmenopausal woman. Past medical history included mild hypertension. Family history was notable for a brother with prostate cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly progressive nodularity of the right breast at presentation in late 2013.

[ diagnosis ]: 
1. Right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, ER-positive, HER2-positive, clinical stage IIA at initial diagnosis in late 2013.  
2. Synchronous high-grade serous adenocarcinoma involving both ovaries, left fallopian tube, and omentum, FIGO stage IIIC ovarian cancer, diagnosed in 2014.

[ histopathology results ]: 
- Initial breast biopsy: invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3, ER-positive, HER2-positive.  
- Post-neoadjuvant breast surgery pathology: residual invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, with 1.1 cm residual disease; axillary lymph nodes negative; no lymphovascular invasion; no residual nodal disease.  
- Gynecologic surgical pathology: high-grade serous adenocarcinoma involving both ovaries, left fallopian tube, and omentum; stage IIIC ovarian carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: 
- Initial pelvic ultrasound during breast cancer workup showed increased bilateral ovarian volume; findings were described at that time as multiple follicles.  
- Repeat pelvic ultrasound in mid-2014 demonstrated a right adnexal mass measuring 8.4 cm, without ascites.  
- Imaging performed in early 2016 showed no evidence of disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: 
- Breast cancer was HER2-positive and estrogen receptor-positive.  
- BRCA1/2 testing was being pursued; no result was available.

[ laboratory results ]: 
- CA-125 was elevated prior to ovarian cancer surgery.  
- Postoperative CA-125 was 18.9, within normal range.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- Early 2014: neoadjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer with doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by weekly paclitaxel; trastuzumab was not available at that time. Clinical response in the breast was partial, approximately 50%.  
- Mid-2014: breast-conserving surgery with axillary dissection.  
- Subsequently underwent total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, peritoneal washings, and biopsies for suspected synchronous ovarian malignancy. Cytoreduction was considered complete. Lymph node dissection was not performed during gynecologic surgery because of operative difficulty.  
- Received adjuvant radiotherapy to the right breast.  
- Received adjuvant chemotherapy for ovarian cancer with carboplatin plus paclitaxel for 6 cycles.  
- Subsequently received approximately 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab for breast cancer, without adverse events.  
- Started adjuvant tamoxifen after completion of carboplatin/paclitaxel and completed the first year of tamoxifen.

[ current disease status ]: No evidence of disease on surveillance as of early 2016.

[ other clinical data ]: 
- No ascites was identified on pelvic ultrasound at the time the adnexal mass was detected.  
- Peritoneal washings and biopsies were performed at gynecologic surgery.

And I agree with what others were saying that our primary goal really needs to be to get her family tested so that we don't see 10 other family members of hers, you know, coming in with either breast or ovarian cancer that could be totally prevented. And then just quickly about the prophylactic mastectomies, we never used to do those in our ovarian cancer patients because we thought the prognosis was not great. And now in the last five years, we've started here at MD Anderson to do them, and we just counsel the patients. I mean, I think if the patients are watched closely and breast cancer is found early, it's a little bit different scenario than the prophylactic ooperectomy where, you know, obviously we strongly, strongly recommend that in the breast patients. But we are starting to do some prophylactic mastectomy.

In a funny sort of way, the longer you wait and the patient remains well, the greater the rationale for performing a bilateral mastectomy. So if you hesitate at the beginning and she's well later, I sort of implied that, but I think Don's answer was correct. I think somebody said if she's 54 when she gets her first breast cancer, she may not get a second breast cancer. So I think the role of prophylactic mastectomy in this patient with these uncertain prognoses from the two cancers really up in the air. I think it's a very difficult decision. I think it's one of those empirical decisions, actually.

We've been using a two-year mark in ovarian cancer. That's just sort of what the plastic surgeons in our group have done. But for patients with ovarian cancer, not with breast cancer, who are BRCA positive, if they're well after two years, then we consider, you know, then they're offered proprotic mastectomy.
That sounds reasonable, yeah. And do you think that in this particular patient, because she only got cancer at 54, that she is a BRCA1-2 mutation carrier? Do you think it's likely?
I do. Yeah.
Yeah, okay. You already said there's a 20% risk of it with this particular kind of ovarian cancer.
Yeah, the breast cancer, yeah.
Yeah. Okay.

And I think with the cost of the testing coming down, I mean, I think this is an area we really need to – I know Brazil – our colleagues in Brazil have been doing a lot of work, but I think, you know, sort of like the HPV vaccine, I mean, I think that BRCA testing and prophylactic surgery needs to be on the top of our agenda. I mean, we really can prevent ovarian cancer in a lot of patients if we can figure out who's BRCA positive.

reference_conclusion: No additional breast cancer-directed chemotherapy is indicated at this time; ongoing management should consist of endocrine therapy and routine breast surveillance with annual mammography and clinical follow-up, without routine staging scans or blood work. Ovarian cancer surveillance should consist of physical examination, pelvic examination, and CA-125 measurement every three months, with CT imaging reserved for symptoms or abnormal findings. Germline BRCA1/2 testing is indicated given the high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, primarily to inform familial risk assessment and potential future therapeutic implications. In the setting of synchronous cancers, management should continue to prioritize treatment with curative intent, with the ovarian cancer taking precedence because of its worse prognosis; prophylactic mastectomy is not recommended at present.
reference_conclusion_quote: I think at this point, I'm not sure I would give any further chemotherapy for her breast cancer. [...] we do yearly mammograms, clinical follow-up as well. We don't routinely do staging scans or blood work as a routine standard of care. [...] I would not follow her with CT scans. I would follow her solely with CA125s, a physical exam, and pelvic every three months. [...] So we will follow three months and get a CA-125, reserving CT scans for findings or symptoms. [...] what we're doing for everyone with a high-volume serous carcinoma of the ovary, we are testing everyone for genetic for BRCA. [...] So, you're right. I mean, I think that she should be tested. [...] In the past, at least, our approach has always been to treat each cancer with curative intent [...] The cancer with the worst prognosis takes priority. [...] in our BRCA patients who have synchronous breast and ovary, the ovary always trumps. [...] I would not be so inclined to strongly consider or even recommend a bilateral mastectomy in the context of ovarian cancer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive goiter; persistent elevation of thyroglobulin following thyroid surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the thyroid, classical variant, well differentiated.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- October 2017: Subtotal left hemithyroidectomy/lobectomy specimen showed a 6.0 cm encapsulated well-differentiated classical variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Capsular invasion was present.  
- Vascular invasion was present in more than four vessels.  
- No lymphatic invasion was identified.  
- No minor extrathyroidal extension was identified.  
- Completion thyroidectomy specimen showed no carcinoma in the remaining lobe.  
- Biopsy of indeterminate cervical lymph nodes showed no lymph node involvement.  
- Biopsy of a left level II lymph node in 2020 was benign.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid/neck ultrasound after initial surgery showed multiple nodules in the right thyroid lobe and indeterminate level V lymph nodes.  
- CT neck showed small indeterminate lymph nodes.  
- Preoperative CT chest showed no pathologically enlarged mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes; two subcentimeter pulmonary nodules measuring 4 mm and 3 mm were present.  
- CT chest also showed soft tissue attenuation in the anterior mediastinum, favored to represent thymus.  
- CT identified an indeterminate enhancing 1.8 cm hepatic lesion and a lesion in the abdominal wall.  
- MRI abdomen characterized the 1.8 cm hepatic lesion as most consistent with focal nodular hyperplasia; this lesion remained stable on follow-up MRI.  
- Post-therapy radioactive iodine scan after first treatment showed residual uptake in the neck and no radioactive iodine-avid metastatic disease in the lungs or bones.  
- Follow-up neck ultrasound after radioactive iodine showed no worrisome findings in the thyroid bed and no suspicious lymph nodes.  
- Follow-up CT neck and chest with contrast showed no metastatic lymphadenopathy.  
- CT chest demonstrated patchy ground-glass opacities in the right upper lobe; the previously noted small pulmonary nodules were not significantly characterized on that study.  
- Follow-up MRI abdomen showed a stable T2-hyperintense lesion at T11, considered possibly a hemangioma.  
- Subsequent neck ultrasound showed bilateral upper neck level II lymph nodes that were not highly suspicious initially; later, left level II lymph nodes became more prominent.  
- Bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease and demonstrated degenerative changes only.  
- A subsequent radioactive iodine treatment was followed by a scan that again showed no evident metastatic uptake.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Preoperative TSH: 1.5.  
- Thyroglobulin before completion thyroidectomy: 158.  
- Thyroglobulin after completion thyroidectomy: 37.  
- August 2019 TSH: 130.  
- Six months after first radioactive iodine therapy, thyroglobulin remained elevated at 26.9.  
- Thyroglobulin values subsequently fluctuated, including values around 70 and 46, without clear correlation to TSH stimulation or suppression.  
- Thyroglobulin was described as not clearly TSH responsive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- October 2017: Subtotal left hemithyroidectomy/lobectomy performed for progressive goiter; surgery had not included total thyroidectomy at that time.  
- Completion thyroidectomy was subsequently performed; no residual carcinoma was found in the remaining lobe.  
- First radioactive iodine therapy: 200 mCi, prepared by thyroid hormone withdrawal. Preparation was described as suboptimal with incomplete adherence to a low-iodine diet, although TSH elevation was adequate for treatment. Post-therapy scan showed residual neck uptake without iodine-avid distant metastatic disease.  
- Second radioactive iodine therapy: 150 mCi. Subsequent scan again did not identify metastatic radioactive iodine uptake.  
- Serial imaging and biopsies did not identify structural metastatic disease.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent biochemical abnormality with elevated thyroglobulin after surgery and two courses of radioactive iodine.  
- No confirmed structural disease in the neck, lungs, bones, liver, or lymph nodes on available imaging and biopsies.  
- Current status was consistent with persistent biochemical evidence of disease without localized structural correlate on available studies.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Initial surgery was complicated by recurrent laryngeal nerve injury/tear during traction on the goiter.

So lymphatic invasion usually means that there's real emboli within lymphatic channels. There is another definition to that term, which I'm just going to mention as an aside. And in fact, You know, this might be from a PTC, which often has nuclei that look like follicular carcinoma. But look at the large vascular channel. It's obviously vascular, not lymphatic because of the RBCs. And the emboli are basically stuck onto the wall of the vascular space. And the shape of the emboli is very different from the shape of the vessel. That's important because more often what we really see is a retraction artifact. And so the reason for discrepancies between pathologists, if one person says yes, another person says no, is that there may be an over-reading of retraction artifact. OK, let's go to the next slide. And so that's what I'm taking the time out to show you now. And so again, here you see it's stuck onto the wall, meaning it can't be some kind of floater that's masquerading as an endovascular embolus. It's stuck onto the wall, and it's a different shape than the vascular space, meaning it can't be a retraction artifact. Good.

Of course, these anesthetic findings are not possible to discard completely. Okay. And by higher dose, probably 150 millicuries or something like that?
Okay. So, Valentina, we're all worried about little stuff. Let's take us through the rest of the story with the radioactive iodine and see where we are.

All right, so she received 200 millicuries of radioactive iodine prepared by withdrawal, and she had some optimal preparation. She did not really follow strictly low iodine diet, and basically, but her TSH was at the proper levels for radioactive iodine therapy. So, and here is her post-therapy scan, which was right as they did not show evidence of radioactive iodine, avid metastatic disease in the lungs and bones. But at that time, she had T2 hyperintense lesion at T11 that could represent also hemangioma. Next slide.

Okay, let me skip ahead a little bit for time. Show me slide number 28, Gabby. So on slide number 28, she gets another 150 millicuries of radioactive iodine. Slide 29, Gabby. And Valentina, again, nothing here.
Nothing here.
Okay, and then slide 30. And this is where we are. Okay, and that's where she is now, Valentina.

Yes, so she was at taroglobulin. Taroglobulin is actually not, does not correlate well with the TSH levels. As we can see that it's really not stimulated with a high TSH. And even with suppression, it fluctuates. So sometimes, so this is, we can see two radioactive iodine therapies highlighted in red. And then the taroglobulin went all the way up to 70. And interestingly, with stimulation, it went to 46, it went down. and then after it's almost, after radioactive iodine, her thyroid globulin was at baseline at 70, and then with appropriate suppression, it went down to 46.

So, Dr. Patoi, we've got a 38-year-old female that easily could have distant mets, right? This was a six-centimeter tumor of vascular invasion, so she's high risk for that. But we've got this thyroid globulin that is not TSH responsive, doesn't really seem to be trending, kind of bounces around, and still non-specific findings. So she comes to you now. Well, I would put in doubt this thyroglobulin value because we have seen a couple of patients like this with the expected this patient may not have enough TSH receptors in their cells and then they cannot be stimulated to produce more thyroglobulin. But this is very, very strange and has not been shown. What this was, probably what it was shown is the presence of human anti-mouse antibodies or heterophilic antibodies that may give this pattern of non-stimulating seroglobulin always the same with TSH of 130, 40, and then with seroglobulin 0.1, 30. Monica, the role of 18-FTG PET scan and chasing these?

Yeah, well, I would have Before the second dose, when she was TSH stimulated, you could do a PET scan in the morning before you gave her the second dose. So she's got a biochemical incomplete response. I don't think there's any point at this stage giving more radioactive iodine. And an FDG PET will show de-differentiated disease. So it's like a flip-flop. If there's nothing on iodine, you may find something on FDG. The other thing is that thyroid cancer often doesn't show up on bone scanning. So bone scanning isn't very sensitive for metastatic disease in thyroid cancer. Yeah, I agree. I worry that we're getting fooled with the thyroid globulin assay, Valentina. So when I see these thyroglobin numbers that don't really track at all with TSH and they tend to bounce around and they're not really growing, that does make me wonder if we have some false positive antibody messing up our thyroglobin assay. You know, it's usually lower, but an endocrinologist love blood tests and we love to rely on our blood tests, but every once in a while you have to take a step back and say, we're missing something. The other scenario I've seen like this is she's just got really small volume pulmonary metastasis that we just haven't seen yet. They're not poorly differentiated, so unlikely to pop up on the PET, but we've seen cases like these that we've chased for like five or 10 years. And then eventually they say new pulmonary nodules that are four or five millimeters. So I was wondering these guys, if sometimes we're missing just low level background pulmonary nodules.

Yeah. I was just going to say, um, it was kind of weird. Uh, decades ago, I saw autopsy lungs from a young woman. I don't, she, she, I don't remember why she died, but, um, she did have a history of PTC and there were all these tiny little nodules in the lungs that she died with, not of.

Yeah. Yeah. And we see, particularly in this kind of case, this is the typical case. 15 years later, I find it in the lungs. vascular invasion, six centimeter, young people. These are the ones that should have concentrated radioactive iodine, but for whatever reason, she didn't. They don't explode. They don't get out of control. The PET scans are usually negative. And then sometimes when we find their disease down the road, then we put them down sort of the re-differentiation trials to try to make radioactive iodine work better. Last thoughts on her, Valentina. You spent a lot of time with her. What are you guys sort of thinking?

So I think that once we encounter patients with biochemical incomplete response, I think initially we have very limited information. So that makes us quite uncomfortable and we'll try to understand where disease is. But once we did all the various studies and observed for a couple of years, that definitely tells us that there is nothing really rapidly growing, nothing evolving. So clinically, whatever it is, it's probably not as meaningful to the patient. So definitely we'll slow down the follow-up and definitely she will have like long life ahead of her. So I definitely will not be chasing that pulmonary nodules every six months with a CAT scan, even though probably it will be, I'm curious to know how they are, but like I have to balance the exposure from radiation and really what imaging modalities would be actually meaningful and helpful in terms of determining plan of care. So I think that, and I definitely seen all that trend and analyzing it further, I think that definitely there is something wrong with her paraglobulin level and I will be much more conservative in terms of the follow-up of the patient.

Yeah, I think you're exactly right. These are challenging because the patients worry about it, their husbands and wives worry about it. Honestly, I worry about it every time I see them thinking what am I missing and going back through everything. So, all right, very good case. That's a good one. All right, let's go to our next junior fellow that's going to present. Let's go to slide 33. I believe this is Dr. Erkin presenting. What you got, Mark?

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended reassessment of the persistently elevated thyroglobulin with repeat testing using a different assay to evaluate for assay interference, including heterophilic or human anti-mouse antibodies. FDG PET-CT was advised to further characterize the extent of possible metastatic disease in the setting of biochemical incomplete response and negative radioiodine imaging. Additional radioactive iodine was not favored at this stage. Given the absence of structurally progressive disease after serial evaluation, follow-up should be de-escalated and managed conservatively.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient; described as young. Performance status was 4.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/progressive glioma after multiple prior lines of therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade glioma/GBM arising from a previously lower-grade glioma, with features consistent with transformed IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglial tumor. Disease had progressed multiple times after prior treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumor tissue immunohistochemistry had identified an IDH1 mutation.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- 1p/19q codeletion was present; this was identified after primary progression.  
- MGMT promoter methylation was present.  
- PD-L1 was negative.  
- Tissue NGS identified IDH1 R132C mutation.  
- PTEN mutation was present.  
- ATRX alteration was present.  
- MLH1 c.618 deletion was present.  
- MSH6 mutation was present.  
- Two TP53 mutations were present.  
- Microsatellite status was stable.  
- Tumor mutational burden was 66.76 mutations/Mb.  
- Variant allele fractions reported included ATRX 48%, MSH6 5%, and MLH1 1.1%.

[ laboratory results ]: No routine hematology or biochemistry results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surgical resection was performed.  
- Temozolomide was administered after surgery.  
- Subsequent disease progression occurred after temozolomide.  
- There were 2-3 episodes of progression overall.  
- Additional systemic treatments administered included bevacizumab, vincristine, and PCV regimen.  
- Disease progressed after multiple lines of therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Multiply relapsed/progressive high-grade glioma following surgery and several systemic regimens. Functional status was poor, with ECOG performance status 4.

[ other clinical data ]: The genomic profiling discussed was performed on tumor tissue rather than blood.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 83-year-old female; resident of Bihar.

[ chief complaint ]: Intermittent abdominal pain for 1 year with bowel irregularity in the form of constipation for 1 year. No tenesmus. No obstipation.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the colon involving the ascending colon/hepatic flexure with bilobar liver metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopic multiple biopsies showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Ultrasound-guided liver lesion biopsy also showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Review of outside pathology demonstrated immunohistochemistry positive for CK19, CK20, and CDX2, and negative for CK7. Mismatch repair status was proficient (pMMR).

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen performed in August showed long-segment irregular wall thickening in the ascending colon and hepatic flexure with a small segment of colocolonic intussusception, pericolic fat stranding, and pericolonic lymph nodes. Bilobar liver metastases were present, described as small and scattered in both lobes. Colonoscopy performed outside was incomplete.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mismatch repair proficient. No additional molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL. Anemia workup was consistent with iron deficiency anemia. CEA 69. CA 19-9 <2. Creatinine 0.69 mg/dL. Albumin 3.08 g/dL. AST 42 U/L. ALT 19 U/L.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior to oncologic evaluation, the patient had received local symptomatic treatment for abdominal pain and constipation without relief.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma with primary disease in the ascending colon/hepatic flexure and bilobar hepatic metastases. At presentation to the tertiary center, ECOG performance status was 3. She was not clinically obstructed.

[ other clinical data ]: Known coronary artery disease with prior acute coronary syndrome. Medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, rosuvastatin, and nicorandil; Rosocor Gold 20 mg was taken at night. No addiction history. No family history of cancer. On examination, abdomen was soft and non-tender with present bowel sounds and abdominal distension; digital rectal examination was normal. Geriatric assessment: G8 score 7.5; ADL 6/6; IADL 5/8; Timed Up and Go 13.55 seconds; HMSE 26/31; Geriatric Depression Scale 12; Generalized Anxiety Disorder score 4; BMI 20.5 kg/m²; MNA 14.5; Charlson Comorbidity Index included coronary artery disease/acute coronary syndrome. Social history: lived with son; good caregiver support; limited financial resources. Chemotherapy toxicity risk score was 8, corresponding to intermediate risk.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Postoperative management of carcinoma endometrium.

[ diagnosis ]: Endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma, FIGO stage IIIC, grade 1. Diagnosis date was recorded as 1 October.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical pathology was reported as endometrioid carcinoma, grade 1.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry demonstrated loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression, consistent with deficient mismatch repair. MSI status was reported as MSI-high. Next-generation sequencing on an endometrial hotspot panel did not detect clinically significant variants in the MMR genes assessed. TP53 was reported as wild type in one report; a pathogenic loss-of-function TP53 mutation was also reported on NGS.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgery consisting of total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy. She subsequently received paclitaxel plus carboplatin every 3 weeks for 6 cycles. After completion of 6 cycles of chemotherapy, she was referred for radiotherapy. No treatment response or toxicity data were provided.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative stage IIIC endometrial carcinoma after completion of adjuvant paclitaxel/carboplatin x6; referred for radiotherapy. No documented evidence of recurrence or metastatic progression was provided.

[ other clinical data ]: Biomarker testing had been sent on the biopsy specimen for MMR immunohistochemistry and NGS panel analysis. No clinically significant variants were detected on the reported biomarker studies apart from the TP53 finding noted above.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genetic panel was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Diagnostic biopsy had been performed prior to referral. No other treatment data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Localized resectable sinonasal mucosal melanoma confined to the primary site, with no regional nodal disease and no distant metastatic disease on PET imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Endoscopic examination image of the lesion was available.

Postoperative management should include discussion of adjuvant radiation to improve local control, with consideration of adjuvant immunotherapy in multidisciplinary follow-up. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Right facial numbness in the V2 distribution.

[ diagnosis ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma involving the right midface/maxillary sinus region with cutaneous lesion overlying the involved area and clinical perineural involvement of V2/infraorbital nerve.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the lesion in the involved midface/maxillary sinus region showed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Biopsy of an overlying skin lesion in the same region also showed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Biopsy of V2/infraorbital nerve tissue was benign at initial diagnostic workup. Additional sinus contents sampled were reported as normal tissue. The initial diagnostic procedure was described as an aggressive biopsy rather than an en bloc resection.

[ imaging findings ]: Coronal CT demonstrated a soft tissue lesion in the midface with extension along the infraorbital nerve and a component within the maxillary sinus. MRI demonstrated enhancement along V2; foramen rotundum was mildly enlarged. No pterygopalatine fossa involvement was identified. No other involved areas were described posteriorly.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a history of right facial cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma treated with unspecified office-based radiation completed approximately 4 months before presentation. During that treatment period, facial numbness developed. Further treatment of the skin cancer was discontinued at that time. The patient had prior sinus surgery, with prior sphenoethmoidectomy noted on nasal endoscopy. On examination before oncologic treatment, palpable nodularity was present in the midface; V2 sensation was impaired, while V1 and V3 were intact. Ocular examination was normal, with normal extraocular movements and vision. Nasal endoscopy did not show a visible maxillary sinus mass with a 0-degree scope; polyploid tissue was seen anteriorly in the sinus with a 70-degree scope. Definitive surgery was declined because of the extent of proposed resection.

[ current disease status ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the right midface and maxillary sinus region with clinical perineural involvement of V2, manifest as impaired V2 sensation and palpable midface nodularity. MRI demonstrated enhancement along V2 with mild enlargement of foramen rotundum, and no pterygopalatine fossa involvement was identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial neurologic evaluation had identified bilateral petrous cephaloceles, which were subsequently considered unrelated to the facial numbness by neurotology/neurosurgery assessment. The lesion extended through the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus into the subdermal midface soft tissues. The posterior aspect of V2 before the skull base was described as clear at initial assessment.

reference_conclusion: For this cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma with clinical perineural invasion along V2, the tumor board favored surgical resection with curative intent, using an open or combined open-endoscopic approach to obtain negative margins along the infraorbital nerve/foramen rotundum, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. Neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy with cemiplimab or pembrolizumab was considered appropriate to improve resectability, but not as a substitute for definitive local therapy. Because surgery was declined, cemiplimab was administered with interval MRI surveillance; the medical oncology recommendation was to continue treatment for 24 months. If surgery continues to be refused after immunotherapy, definitive radiotherapy may be offered as a reasonable nonstandard local therapy option rather than observation alone.

From a surgery standpoint, I also would do an open approach, probably a combined approach." [...] "I would still push the patient towards a resection with adjuvant radiotherapy being part of the plan, period, at the current standard." [...] "I'm trying to do surgical resection adjuvant radiotherapy. If they get immuno up front, great." [...] "So she's now 21 months into semiplumab, and that was the ultimate recommendation by medical oncology was to continue this for 24 months." case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient in her 40s.

[ chief complaint ]: New-onset debilitating headaches.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with heavy cervical nodal burden (N1b disease), BRAF V600E-mutated, previously treated with surgery and radioactive iodine; persistent/metastatic right retropharyngeal lymph node disease. High-risk features included extranodal extension.

[ histopathology results ]: Resection specimen from the right retropharyngeal node showed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma involving a lymph node. Histology was described as typical for papillary thyroid carcinoma. No mitoses, no necrosis, no high-grade features, and no extranodal extension were identified in the resected retropharyngeal node specimen.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Brain MRI performed for headaches showed no intracranial abnormality but identified a suspicious right retropharyngeal lymph node concerning for metastatic disease.  
- Neck ultrasound did not identify corresponding disease.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT neck demonstrated a necrotic right retropharyngeal lymph node in the retropharyngeal space adjacent to the carotid space; this lesion had been present on preoperative CT before the initial thyroid surgery and showed interval growth on subsequent CT.  
- Whole-body FDG PET-CT showed no abnormal uptake anywhere in the body.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E mutation was present.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- TSH: 0.13  
- Thyroglobulin: approximately 1.3 and described as essentially stable after radioactive iodine treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment had included thyroid surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.  
- Post-radioactive iodine thyroglobulin remained low but detectable and was essentially stable.  
- Laryngeal examination after prior treatment was normal.  
- Because of interval growth of the right retropharyngeal node, the patient underwent transoral robotic excision of the node. Intraoperative ultrasound demonstrated the node in close proximity to the carotid artery and jugular vein. The lesion was removed transorally through the lateral pharyngeal wall, and the pharyngeal incision was closed primarily.

[ current disease status ]: Four weeks after transoral resection of the right retropharyngeal nodal metastasis, postoperative thyroglobulin had not yet been reported. No FDG-avid distant metastatic disease had been identified on PET-CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The retropharyngeal node was considered anatomically high at the skull base.  
- The patient had undergone initial surgery at an outside institution.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of suspected local recurrence in the ipsilateral nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal region identified on MRI in 2020 during workup for transient ischemic attack symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma, initially staged T4N0M0. Suspected local recurrence in the ipsilateral deep nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal space approximately 15 years after initial treatment. Separate thoracic metastatic disease was present and remained stable.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial malignancy was adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Last routine imaging before recurrence surveillance gap was in 2015.  
- MRI in 2020 demonstrated an area in the pharynx/deep nasopharyngeal space concerning for recurrence, ipsilateral to the original tumor.  
- CTA demonstrated some separation from the cervical carotid, with very close proximity along the petrous carotid.  
- Thoracic metastatic lesions were identified separately and had not changed over time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment for T4N0M0 adenoid cystic carcinoma consisted of partial palatectomy, pharyngectomy with free flap reconstruction, and postoperative IMRT to 62 Gy.  
- The patient underwent long-term follow-up with medical oncology and otolaryngology.  
- Thoracic metastases remained stable and had not required systemic therapy to date.

[ current disease status ]: Suspected localized recurrence on MRI in the previously operated and irradiated ipsilateral deep nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal space, approximately 15 years after initial treatment. Thoracic metastatic disease remained stable without systemic treatment requirement to date.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The suspected recurrent lesion was located in a previously operated and irradiated ipsilateral field.  
- Balloon test occlusion had not been performed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of management for a solitary thyroid nodule diagnosed as papillary thyroid carcinoma; patient had planned total thyroidectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma involving a solitary thyroid nodule measuring 2.5 cm.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was diagnostic for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative neck ultrasound demonstrated a 2.5 cm solitary thyroid nodule. There was no evidence of extrathyroidal extension. There was no sonographic evidence of cervical lymph node disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Total thyroidectomy had been planned. No prior oncologic treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Localized papillary thyroid carcinoma confined to the thyroid on available preoperative assessment, without identified extrathyroidal extension or nodal metastases on ultrasound. No distant disease evaluation was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had elected to undergo total thyroidectomy and sought evaluation regarding prophylactic central neck dissection.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Right neck desmoid tumor with interval increase in volume on surveillance MRI and mild symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Desmoid tumor of the right neck, first diagnosed in August 2017.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy confirmed desmoid tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI surveillance initially showed stable disease after diagnosis.  
- MRI in September 2019 showed mild increase in tumor volume compared with prior imaging over the preceding year; RECIST progression was confirmed over that year.  
- Lesion was described as clinically quite close to the temporomandibular joint.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing was performed to assess for T41A substitution.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial management after diagnosis consisted of observation with regular surveillance.  
- Local treatment options were assessed; surgery was considered not feasible. Interventional radiology had no procedural option to offer.  
- Following confirmed progression in 2019, the patient was considered potentially eligible for the DEFI trial.  
- The trial was discussed, but the patient chose chemotherapy instead.  
- Methotrexate and vinorelbine were commenced.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included testicular cancer in early life and epilepsy.  
- Family history included grandfather with bowel cancer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive weakness of the left upper limb, later involving the left lower limb; subsequent inability to speak and bedridden state.

[ diagnosis ]: Right parietal atypical meningioma, status post surgical resection and adjuvant radiotherapy, with subsequent abnormal right hemispheric post-treatment imaging changes and recurrent midline shift.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical biopsy specimen reviewed at Shaukat Khanum Hospital reported atypical meningioma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain in November 2023 showed a right parietal/right convexity space-occupying lesion described as a small peripheral enhancing lesion with associated intraparenchymal edema.  
- Repeat MRI in February 2024, after an interval of approximately 3-4 months, showed marked increase in tumor size with increased edema, midline shift, subfalcine herniation, and ventricular compression/replacement.  
- Postoperative/post-radiotherapy MRI showed extensive edema involving nearly the entire right cerebral hemisphere, including an MCA-territory distribution, with central non-enhancement and peripheral nodular enhancement.  
- Most recent MRI showed persistent midline shift and residual/recurrent tumor visible on imaging.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initially managed with antiepileptic medication after first MRI in November 2023.  
- Surgery had been advised after initial imaging but was delayed for approximately 3 months.  
- Surgical resection was performed in February 2024; resection was described as complete, including dural excision.  
- The patient subsequently received 27 fractions of radiotherapy at A&M Hospital, Peshawar.  
- Steroid therapy was started after later clinical deterioration; slight improvement was observed, with some movement on the right side and eye opening reported.

[ current disease status ]:  
- At latest assessment, the patient had complete left-sided weakness.  
- Right-sided motor power was documented as 3/5.  
- The patient was unable to speak and was bedridden.  
- GCS was reported as 7/15.  
- Persistent midline shift and residual/recurrent lesion were present on latest MRI.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On delayed presentation before surgery, the patient was unable to move the left upper and lower limbs.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Hepatic mass identified on surveillance imaging after cure of hepatitis C.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosed radiographically in the setting of cirrhosis and prior hepatitis C infection; solitary lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: No biopsy was performed.

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a single hepatic lesion measuring approximately 3.5 cm. The lesion showed arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout on delayed phase imaging, with imaging features categorized as LI-RADS 5.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver-related laboratory studies were reported as normal. Platelet count was relatively preserved. Liver function was described as good.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had previously been treated for hepatitis C and was cured.

[ current disease status ]: Early-stage disease at presentation, with a single small hepatic tumor and preserved liver function in the setting of cirrhosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Underlying cirrhosis persisted despite hepatitis C cure. No evidence of impaired hepatic synthetic function was described.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so thanks all for sort of sitting steady for the last two and a half hours here. So what we're going to try to do is we're trying to go through a couple cases just to highlight a couple points here. And then, of course, try to leave some minutes for question and answer for this last session. So I've tried to keep this relatively simple to just highlight a couple points. But the first patient that we have here is a 54-year-old male who was undergoing screening after being cured for his hepatitis C. This is important. He was found to have a mass on imaging. You can see there a single lesion that was about three and a half centimeters. So, Moraz, do you want to just briefly describe how you would think about this from a radiology perspective in terms of describing sort of the imaging there, understanding obviously you're not an IR guy, but from going back to your diagnostic days, like how would you describe this lesion from your perspective?

Good. Well, thank you very much for having me. So what we see here are two slices for CT scan and basically, you know, for lack of a better word, I always tell my patients, it's like we're looking into your body from the feet towards your head. Okay, and you see where the green arrow is, that's the right side of your body. And then where the circle or white dot is, that's the aorta. So at the bottom of the thing is the spine, right? So that's your right, this is the back, and then the front and left on that side. And all this gray thing that you see under the green arrow, that huge lobular thing is the liver that we've been talking about all this entire afternoon. So normal liver on these scans and these CTs are done we give contrast or x-ray dye in the IV and then we wait for a few seconds and then image them in a subsequent sequence and you know the way we find this tumor is one if you see the entire liver has a different shade, and then right under the first image, under the arrow, there is a lot of white deposition. That basically shows that it is an abnormal focus of tissue that is taking up contrast, that has a lot of blood supply. And then over like decades of research, we've learned that liver tumors have a very particular way of taking up contrast. So what we see in most of the tumors is in the first sequence, we see they take up a lot of contrast. So we call them hypervascular. Vascular means blood. They take a lot of blood. And in the second phase, we see that you see how now it is actually darker than the surrounding liver. So when the tumors form, they form leaky blood vessels. So they make a lot of blood vessels and they're leaky. So these two image characteristics kind of make us very confident in calling this as a liver tumor. Now, over time, we've developed a grading system where we would say that this is something and we've kind of read them based on probability. It's called LIRADS, right? So, LIRADS 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which basically gives us a probability of how sure we are that this is true or not. So in somebody who has underlying risk factors, that's an important thing. Somebody with underlying risk factors, with a new mass, massless tumor, with arterial phase enhancement, which is the white uptake of contrast I spoke about, and washout, these characteristics make us, make this allowance five. And in layman terms, what that means is this is more likely 100% tumor, unless proven otherwise.

Yeah, so I think that, you know, the key thing that like, so thanks, Mara. So really what we're talking about here is that this lesion that was seen on imaging has a definite appearance for liver cancer. And I had referenced before, when you're going through screening, we often don't need to do a biopsy. So Mara's talked about this system of radiology grading. And this has classic appearance on imaging where we can say with 95% certainty, that this is a liver cancer. And so we treat this actually without needing to do a biopsy because of this characteristic appearance. Not all liver cancers have this appearance, but when it's present in the right clinical setting, once again, we treat accordingly. So it's a very unique aspect of liver cancer compared to other cancers. So this patient, because they were treated for their hepatitis C, fortunately continues to have good liver function. They still have cirrhosis, but their liver is functioning well. So we have grading scores for cirrhosis, and this patient has good labs. You can see the labs actually look normal from a liver perspective. The platelet count looks relatively preserved. This patient's liver, once again, is working well. So let me ask, Nicole, if you saw this patient, it was being discussed at our tumor board, this patient who has a single lesion, three and a half centimeters, good liver function, how would you think the treatment here?

Well, as you mentioned, you know, fortunately this patient was found early. So they have just a single small tumor and they have good liver function. So I think the first thing we would want to do is see is the patient a candidate for surgery to have it removed or resected while they keep their own liver.

Yeah. So that's exactly right. So the nice thing here is that this person's liver is working well. This is a patient who was found early. We have curative therapies available. And so this patient should be eligible for surgical resection, where you go in, you cut out that part of the liver with the tumor, and this patient once again can continue to do fine with their underlying liver intact. Let me ask, Morris, if this patient, for some reason, wasn't a surgical candidate, let's say, you know, they had, I don't know, significant other cardiovascular disease, et cetera, how would you think through local therapies, non-surgical therapies for this patient? Good.

Yeah, so like Dr. Singhal mentioned, every time we see a patient, we meet in the tumor board, and if they're not a surgical candidate, that's where our role comes in as doing minimally invasive local regional therapies. So there are a few that are more commonly used. Dr. Benjamin went over them. One of them is ablation, where we put an antenna and kind of burn the tumor under anesthesia, of course. But that has been shown to be effective to up to three centimeter tumors. So now this, I think, measures four point something. Three and a half. Three and a half. Right. So this is at the borderline of where we think we have other therapies which offer a better result. So then we talk about the role of trans arterial therapies. What that means is therapies that we deliver to the blood vessels. And as I discussed previously, these tumors have a lot of blood vessels. So we go into those teeny tiny blood vessels that supply the tumor very close to them under x-ray, and then we can inject two options. We can inject chemotherapy, or we can inject beads, which are reabsorbable beads that are coated with radiation, which is known as trans-arterial radioembolization, and the first one I mentioned was trans-arterial chemoembolization. Historically, before the radiation therapy came, we used to treat them with chemoembolization, and that has good results. But more and more, as our research progresses, we're getting more data that show that when we actually inject radioembolization or we inject radiation-coated beads, they have a longer response rate and more curative. By curative, I mean they can treat the tumor. So we have three options. I think given the size of this, we can either talk about trans-arterial radioembolization, or Y90, or trans-arterial chemoembolization, based on where the patient is, what facilities are available.

Yeah, so I think that this is like a common situation that we'll see in our tumor boards. So once again, with the idea that we try to do surgical therapies if possible. And if somebody isn't eligible for surgical therapies, then the next thing that we often think about is what local therapies are possible. Like Dr. Chowdhury was saying, that you basically have multiple different local regional therapies available. You have these therapies where you can inject beads with either chemotherapy or radiation directly into the tumor. And we heard from Dr. Benjamin that this is nice because it spares the patient from lots of other side effects. It gives local therapy. You're able to really shrink the tumor in the vast majority of cases. We have an ablation where you can try to burn it. The other therapy that we didn't talk about very much, unfortunately, our radiation oncologist wasn't able to be here today, is external beam radiation therapy. So, you know, we talked about the internal delivery, but you can also do external radiation therapy to this where you deliver high doses of radiation, also, once again, are able to typically shrink these cancers well. We talked about this. So this patient underwent a robotic resection. This is also an interesting phenomenon where we can now do this in a minimally invasive manner, laparoscopically essentially, where you can have it so the patient is able to recover quicker and go home in a very quick period of time after the surgery. So given time, I'm going to skip that. I want to talk about one other aspect here. So Nicole, I'm going to obviously send this one your way in terms of what do you think here. So this is somewhat of a similar case in the sense that we have a 62-year-old male with alcohol-associated cirrhosis has stopped drinking. But this patient has liver dysfunction, meaning that their liver is not working well. They've had complications of their cirrhosis, including ascites. And we haven't gone through these in detail, but this is the fact that the liver is not functioning well. You have an accumulation of fluid in the abdomen because of the liver not being able to operate perfectly. So this patient was found to have a small tumor, a small cancer of 2.1 centimeters. So similar to the last patient, this patient was found early. But in contrast, the liver is not functioning well in this case. So Nicole, can you talk through like what your thoughts here are? You know, before we went to surgical resection, would you recommend surgical resection in this case?

reference_conclusion: The hepatic lesion demonstrates classic imaging features of hepatocellular carcinoma in the appropriate clinical setting and may be managed without biopsy. Given preserved liver function, compensated cirrhosis, and a solitary 3.5 cm tumor, the patient is considered eligible for curative surgical resection. If the patient is not a surgical candidate, liver-directed therapy with transarterial radioembolization (Y90) or transarterial chemoembolization would be appropriate alternatives.
