case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive left epiphora. Stable left cheek numbness since prior surgery. Recurrent lesion identified on routine surveillance imaging beneath the left orbital floor implant.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the left maxillary sinus. Prior history of T3N1 squamous cell carcinoma of the left maxillary sinus.

[ histopathology results ]: Office biopsy of friable tissue arising from the residual left maxillary sinus cavity showed invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT neck/facial imaging with contrast demonstrated enhancing soft tissue along the lateral wall of the left maxillary sinus.  
- Enhancing tissue was present inferior and superior to the left orbital floor reconstruction plate and extended posteriorly along the plate toward the orbit.  
- MRI T1 fat-suppressed post-contrast imaging demonstrated enhancing tissue in the left maxillary sinus.  
- MRI also demonstrated enhancement along the left V2 distribution and at the left foramen rotundum.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- April 2024: Maxillectomy, neck dissection, and reconstruction with osteocutaneous forearm free flap for T3N1 squamous cell carcinoma of the left maxillary sinus.  
- Adjuvant radiation therapy was administered after initial surgery.  
- Surveillance imaging subsequently demonstrated recurrent disease.  
- For recurrence, the patient underwent left total maxillectomy with orbital exenteration after intraoperative identification of tumor extending through a gap near the prior orbital floor plate into the orbit and periorbital fat.  
- Vidian canal and foramen rotundum were drilled during resection.  
- Completion neck dissection was performed because the prior neck dissection had included only levels I and IIa.  
- Reconstruction was performed with a large anterolateral thigh free flap for soft tissue obliteration of the defect.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included hypertension and gout.  
- Former smoker; smoking cessation had occurred decades earlier.  
- Preoperative examination showed intact extraocular movements and no globe malposition.  
- Incisions were well healed.  
- Edentulous.  
- Intraoral examination was otherwise unremarkable.  
- No cervical adenopathy was identified on examination.  
- Endoscopic examination demonstrated friable tissue arising from the residual left maxillary sinus region.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 24-year-old African-American woman; married; student; postpartum following a term pregnancy with natural vaginal delivery in November 2015; one newborn. No known comorbidities. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Vaginal bleeding and dry cough beginning in January 2016, approximately 3 months postpartum.

[ diagnosis ]: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, FIGO stage IV, high-risk score 12.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were available. Biopsy of the cervical/vaginal lesion was not documented.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Chest radiograph showed multiple pulmonary nodules suspicious for lung metastases.  
- Pelvic examination identified a vaginal lesion, cervical tumor, and uterine enlargement.  
- Pelvic ultrasound showed enlargement of the cervix and uterus with a 12 cm lesion infiltrating the myometrium.  
- CT imaging of the brain, thorax, and abdomen demonstrated brain metastases, multiple lung metastases, and liver metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Anemia.  
- Serum hCG greater than 600,000.  
- During treatment, hCG decreased by approximately 1 log every 18 days.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial induction chemotherapy consisted of 3 cycles of low-dose cisplatin and etoposide.  
- Treatment was then escalated to EMA-CO regimen.  
- Intrathecal methotrexate was administered for brain metastases.  
- After the third cycle of low-dose EP, there was rapid treatment response accompanied by intense vaginal bleeding, managed clinically without a procedural intervention.  
- During the second cycle of EMA-CO, toxicity consisted of mucositis.

[ current disease status ]: Receiving second cycle of EMA-CO at the time of reporting, with biochemical response evidenced by falling hCG and prior rapid clinical response.

[ other clinical data ]: Pregnancy in 2015 was reported as normal, with uncomplicated natural labor at term.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 42-year-old Asian man.

[ chief complaint ]: Left hearing loss and diplopia of 2 weeks’ duration.

[ diagnosis ]: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma with de novo metastatic disease to the liver.

[ histopathology results ]: Nasopharyngeal mass pathology was reported as MPC and EBER-positive. Liver metastasis was biopsy-confirmed.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a locally aggressive, extensive nasopharyngeal tumor. Subsequent post-treatment imaging identified recurrent/progressive disease associated with new left cranial nerve VI weakness and right V2 weakness approximately 2 months after completion of initial chemoradiation. Later imaging after re-irradiation showed clival destruction/necrosis with an isolated appearing bony fragment and extensive skull base necrotic change near the parapharyngeal/paraclival carotid region. Contrast imaging later was interpreted as highly suggestive of a pseudoaneurysm arising from the left petrous internal carotid artery. Pretreatment angiography demonstrated a large pseudoaneurysm at that junction. Follow-up imaging showed a visibly patent carotid stent. Subsequent imaging demonstrated brainstem necrosis. The brainstem lesion later improved on interval imaging. Further imaging showed very extensive progressive necrotic/intracranial change extending posteriorly, and later an additional intracranial focus was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: EBER-positive tumor. The patient was described as PD-1 naïve prior to pembrolizumab.

[ laboratory results ]: Sinus cultures were obtained and guided antibiotic therapy. During presentation with epistaxis, hemoglobin did not show a significant drop.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment consisted of induction chemotherapy followed by definitive chemoradiation, administered outside the treating institution; exact treatment records were unavailable. He had a very good initial response, and liver metastatic disease cleared radiographically after treatment. Approximately 2 months after completion of initial therapy, he developed left cranial nerve VI weakness and right V2 weakness with imaging evidence of recurrent/progressive disease. He subsequently underwent repeat radiation approximately 7 months after the end of prior treatment. After re-irradiation, diplopia resolved, facial sensation remained stable, and imaging showed a good response. He later developed sinusitis and skull base necrotic changes; pentoxifylline/clodronate-based therapy was started, and antibiotics were given based on sinus cultures, with clinical improvement. He later presented with left greater than right epistaxis of relatively high volume that stopped spontaneously. Angiography confirmed a left petrous ICA pseudoaneurysm, which was treated with endovascular stenting. No further bleeding was reported after stent placement. He was subsequently maintained on pembrolizumab every 3 weeks. While on pembrolizumab and pentoxifylline/clodronate-based therapy, the brainstem necrotic lesion improved on imaging.

[ current disease status ]: He remained alive and under follow-up. The carotid stent remained patent on surveillance imaging. The previously affected nasopharyngeal/skull base area had remucosalized and appeared stabilized at one point, but he later developed progressive necrotic/intracranial changes and another brain lesion. Clinically, he became increasingly frail over time, with later episodes of weakness, intermittent mental status changes, and repeated hospitalizations. No recurrent bleeding was reported after carotid stenting.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension. He had a history of smoking but was not a current smoker. He was described as otherwise clinically well early in the course despite skull base necrotic changes, but later had deterioration in functional and nutritional status. Neurologic deficits after initial recurrence included left cranial nerve VI palsy and right V2 weakness; diplopia later resolved after re-irradiation. At the time brainstem necrosis was identified radiographically, no corresponding neurologic symptoms were reported.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, Dr. Kwon.

All right, thank you very much. I'm going to kind of hit the salient points of my very straightforward case of nasal pharyngeal carcinoma. So this is a 42-year-old gentleman, Asian, and he had history of his hypertension and history of smoking, though not current smoker. Presented with left hearing loss, diplopia for two weeks, large mass in the nasal pharynx found to be MPC, EBER positive. Here's our scan, so pretty standard appearance of a locally aggressive extensive tumor. And of course, the curve ball that starts is liver metastasis biopsy confirmed. And so the initial treatment for this gentleman was induction chemotherapy followed by primary CRT. We don't have those done outside of our institution, so we don't have the exact records. And he had a very good response to it. Two months after completion, he developed left cranial nerve 6 weakness and right V2 weakness. And he was found to have this on the scan. So my first question is to Dr. McBride, what do you think happened here? Because I don't have the records. And what would be your management strategies that you would recommend to this gentleman at this point?

Well, you know, coming back to it always starts with what was the prior radiation fields. I mean, this is probably a marginal. I mean, by the looks of it, probably a marginal miss here versus giving the outside team credit. Maybe it's an attempt to to spare some of the critical organs at risk, thinking that this is a relatively radiation sensitive tumor. But either way, the tumor is probably underdosed in this area. Now, we're two months after completion. I mean, No role for additional radiation at this point. So, you know, I would obviously probably restage this individual with a PET CT and you've already gotten the MRI and then talk to Neil about what the systemic options would best look like here.

Dr. McBride, I know we're running out of time, but I just want to ask a quick question. So if you have a patient who's had a substantial response to chemotherapy, do you go back and radiate all of the previous field, the entire area where the tumor was? Yeah, that is a great question.

That is a great question, Dr. Seay. Yes, so this is typically, at our institution, we've shifted more towards just treating the gross residual disease to 70 gray after a neoadjuvant strategy. And that's proven to be just as effective in terms of local regional control. There is some data on that. So that's what we do in practice. So obviously, almost all of our NPCs with stage two, stage three, for MPCs are getting induction, and so that's a real benefit in terms of reducing the volume given the full dose.
And so, Dr. McBride had read my slides, of course, and he decides to kick it over to Dr. Akave. So, what are your thoughts in terms of any systemic options for this gentleman at this point?
Yeah, I mean, this guy's in a very difficult circumstance. I'm assuming systemic staging still shows that he has no disease, his liver metastases are gone.
So that actually cleared, yes.

Yeah, okay. I mean, I think the initial approach was very reasonable. I don't think it would have been wrong to give GEMSYS toripalumab for initial disease and then consolidate with chemoradiation. But recognizing that he's PD-1 naive, the standard of care option here would be to consider single agent PD-1 inhibitors. There is sort of provocative data, which I think is reasonable that was published in Lancet earlier this year of Pembro plus Bevacizumab, which led to a significant extension, a significant improvement in response rates and an extension of overall survival, which I think is also reasonable to use in a population. The biggest challenge of that, it did lead, there was an increased rates of nasopharyngeal necrosis, which you'd have to consider here. Nevertheless, if my radiation oncologist said, you know, this is great options. This is a reasonable option to try. Either single-agent PD-1 or immunotherapy plus a VEGF inhibitor would be a reasonable option here.

Thank you very much. Yeah, very challenging situation at this point. So he does undergo repeat radiation. Oh my gosh. Which has completed seven months at the end of a prior treatment, ish. And his diplomia resolved and his facial sensation ended up being stable. And he does have a good response. He's got some sinusitis there now. You know, of course, this is, you know, the setup for something to come later. So, of course, we start with the calm before the storm in this situation as you hear the story. So, this is his repeat scan at six months and then three months later. Dr. Wang, do you want to tell me anything interesting about the scans at this point from your observations?
Yeah, the the clibus looks like it's, yeah, the clibus looks like it's kind of not disappearing but falling apart. Yeah. And this looks like a isolated piece of bone that's floating around.
Yeah, I was trying to figure out what that is. It was just like a different view of his skin. I think that's the left parapharyngeal carotid or the paraclebocarotid swimming in necrosis.
Yeah.

So we were pretty concerned about this, as we talked about now. He does start pentochloro based on these findings and what it looks like on endoscopy, which I didn't show here, is just crusting. There's nothing that looks exposed. It's very hard to tell. You don't really want to tamper with it. He's actually clinically otherwise well. a young gentleman who's otherwise pretty healthy. And so he actually does get started on pentaclone antibiotics based on sinus cultures. And he has clinical improvement, although we said we need to watch closely or telling him danger signs about any possibility. So six months later, he presents the outside ED with less to greater than right-sided epistaxis. It was relatively high volume by report, but it does stop spontaneously, and he's quite stable with only not a significant drop of hemoglobin. So the ER says, hey, he's not bleeding now, so we're going to have him follow up as an outpatient. So I said, please transfer him immediately so we can take a good look. And so what we see here is something quite different. Dr. Cohen, what do you think about these scans at this point in time? This is a contrast scan.

I think this dude's in big, deep trouble. I actually was going to take a step back. Dr. McBride, what would you tell this patient before the re-irradiation, seven months after the first radiation, their chances of having a complication like this would be? And again, I don't know if there was protons or not. Just seems like this is like, this is a crazy story.

You know, I think the risk of ORN or soft tissue necrosis, the combined risk with a re-irradiation that soon after the primary radiation, I probably would have quoted him something north of 50%. I mean, I think you can argue here that what I do with, you know, there's not a data for this, but what I do with all of my patients is start them prophylactically on vitamin E and actually Boswellia, which is frankincense. There's some data that that can help with reduced risk of radiation necrosis, but I mean, I think substantial risk here going in.
Yeah, so I always answer questions by asking the radiation oncologist a question. It looks like there is an issue with that. That left carotid for sure. Yeah.

Yeah, like that. So from the read, it's very suggestive of a pseudoaneurysm from the left petrous ICA. So, oof, for me. So the storm continues. Here's the pretreatment angio. Fortunately was able to get him here. He did not bleed. And we see this pretty large pseudo aneurysm at that junction that is pretty characteristic. But very fortunate to have some outstanding neuro IR colleagues who were able to stent this. He did very well, actually. He has actually not had any bleeding since then. And question to Dr. Su, Dr. Wong, Dr. Cohen, any differences in how you would have managed this in the acute setting, aside from, or any differences from what we did here?

We probably would, you know, obviously this is a conversation with the neuro IR folks in a situation where we don't have vascularized coverage and I'd anticipate that this process will continue despite your best medical efforts. We probably would embolize off the bat. we probably would not put a stent. And I just, that's just sort of our institutional sort of preference for a situation where, again, the process is gonna continue. Did the patient like fail balloon occlusion or something? Was there, or is there consideration for that?
Yeah, so he passed it.
I'm curious what the other folks think.

Dr. Kwong, can you please go back to the previous MRI? Just go back one slide. Yeah. So, you know, that carotid, there's a communication between the nasal pharynx, through the where the staging tube, cartilages, the staging tube had been. So that's all dead. And now you have all the mucus from the upper area digestive tract, bathing that carotid artery. And it's probably going to do the same on the other side as well, the bone is going to, you know, start to be exposed and because it's going to die off and So I think this is a situation where he does need some sort of flap coverage. I would have done exactly what you have done in terms of stenting the patient. I would have also, you know, right off the bat after that would have, you know, perhaps debrided him. For smaller defects, I've sworn nasal septum flaps across, even if they've been radiated, I've just want somebody to cover it. For bigger defects, we put a free flap in there.

Yeah, those were definitely considerations down the line. And we can talk a little bit about that as it kind of evolves. Let me go back to this. So continued surveillance. He's been doing OK, improving clinically again. Obviously, he's gotten more and more frail. So there was always kind of the bouncing back and forth of goals of care discussions. And it actually remucosalizes over in this area, as well as it's kind of stabilized. And then he has this stent that you can see that's visibly patent. So he's now currently on Pembroke every three weeks for maintenance. What is your surveillance protocol to our panelists, again, in terms of using a combination of imaging, endoscopy, and EVV DNA levels? How do you usually check for these patients, and how often, I guess?

Well, and I think he's pretty recent from his treatment, so he does need follow-up every few months. I think that he, like other people have said, he actually, I think, should have flap coverage sooner rather than later. But I think combination of endoscopy, maybe imaging every three to six months, EBDNA periodically.
Sounds good.

In general, though, I would say when he's on system, he's on systemic therapy with Pembro. In general, our approach there would be to do scans. I mean, just for, for disease status evaluation, six to nine weeks or so. So probably more, more frequent than that.

So we were all in talks of doing something prophylactic for him. Uh, and then we have some signs of the next storm coming up so far clinically. Great. And then we have this. So, what do you guys think now? Back to Dr. McBride and Dr. Akave in this case.

He had some brainstem necrosis, presumably from his twice irradiated brainstem. So I think in this kind of situation, you've got a variety of options. You could do hyperbaric oxygen. There's obviously data for bevacizumab, and there's emerging data in the CNS radonc world of, again, Boswellia, which is frankincense, which has shown some actually substantial regressions of radiation necrosis in CNS tissue. I mean, unfortunate finding, but I'd say you've got a triple option there for the radiation that grows.
Are you really arguing that frankincense would have prevented this, Sean?
Mark, don't poo poo it. There's data out there. It's available on Amazon. I give every patient a flyer. Plus, it helps my slack option with the company.
I don't have much to state on the systemic side, but I guess my question would be, functionally, how is he doing, Ed? I mean, now with this radiation necrosis.
Well, that's the thing. He comes in and out of us, you know, doing well clinically. He's extraordinarily resilient, as you guys can see. And you'll see some other additional storms coming up as well.
And that's why I think, you know, we've always kind of... Neurologically, he's not experiencing any issues from this brainstem involvement now?
No.
Amazing.

Yeah. It's a finding on imaging, you know, so. All right, so the next storm comes, continues on Pembro and Pentaclo. Brainstem lesion improves, and then he has this. Okay, and that was about the time when we were trying to talk about doing something, and this gave us pause. So this is actually a pretty, you know, I've never seen it this extensive before. And what is the role, you know, we talk about doing free flaps, we talk about trying local flap coverage with some vascularized tissue. When you guys see something like this, what is your, you know, in retrospect, you know, hindsight is 2020, what is your time frame for intervention and for something like this extensive, how would you approach it? So again, to Mark, Marilyn and Shirley.
I just point fingers and ask the radiation oncologist to manage it.
No, I don't. Is he symptomatic?

At this point, when this change started happening, he started having more clinical deterioration, a little bit of mental status changes, definitely much weaker in and out of the hospital. So his health condition was also not as great either, or nutrition.

I mean, unfortunately, this patient needed a goals of care conversation because you can do a radical resection. And there is data on temporal lobe resection for temporal lobe necrosis and how it helps to reverse the process. You could put a bunch of free flaps on top, but something else is going to start getting picked up. This is not sustainable. And unfortunately, someone has to have a real conversation with this patient to let them know that the end is probably coming sooner rather than later.

Yeah, and I think that's something we've always kind of broached pretty early, given that he presented with M1 disease. And it's just an ongoing thing, especially with basically one step up, three steps down consistently. But this is one of those very challenging situations where you're seeing a pretty extensive focus. I mean, it's all the way to the back of the head. Anyways, I think resilience is really the key to this case. He actually improved spontaneously, but now he has another focus in the brain. So it's always like, Really, are we going to really do anything to help him with any type of progressive surgery if this is going to be the case? So I agree, a goals-cared discussion. He's holding on tight. I still see him. And the one question to end for everybody is, how would you have changed this, the management, if there were no distant meds up front? Or would you have changed it, any of the panelists?
in terms of the management of the ORN or the soft tissue necrosis or just the decision to do the radiation so soon after?
Any of the above. I think just some type of guidance going forward for if we see another straightforward case of MPC.

I mean, I would have tried some, you know, he hadn't seen IO as part of his initial treatment. There is obviously good data for IO and NPC. It's a virally driven malignancy. I would have tried that up front and seen his response to that before committing to basically re-RT.

Yeah, I think I would agree with that. I think his initial approach of induction chemotherapy or conversion chemotherapy, we know the response rates are close to 90% in EPV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, so to do chemoradiation even in the setting of de novo metastatic disease, not unreasonable at all, and then consolidating with chemoradiation, I really think that the misstep potentially was on the re-irradiation side so close. In that instance, I think I would have also given immunotherapy.

You know, I think, Ed, it's like skull base is such a hard area to radiate. You know, we think about, you know, coming out of head and neck rhinology fellowship and doing, you know, subspecialty training to do skull base surgery. I think it will be the same for our radiation oncologists. The more common tumors are a little bit easier to treat. In the skull base, there are all these structures. And I think the experience of radiation oncologists who you send your patients to is also very important. And it's really important because you as a surgeon manage a lot of these sequelae. You can't send them back to the radiation oncologist, unfortunately, at that point.

So I guess here's a question for you guys then. Would you have put on, if the patient didn't have METs to start with, would you have been earlier to jump to some type of tissue coverage for the carotids, or would you have waited first to see that this was an issue?

Look, I think I've been in this situation of patients with meds and they're on systemic therapy and it's very slow progressing. And I know that if I don't put a flap in there, I'm going to be the one being called back, right? Like having another carotid blowout on the other side, thrombosis carotid, getting into a massive stroke. I think it's pretty reasonably straightforward. You put a flap in there, it's just soft tissue, you know. connects to the facial or the temporal tunneling through a quadrilateral arc, and you're there. So I've just had such a low threshold for putting free flaps in there now.
Well, I appreciate all the input on this. That's the end of my case. And thank you again, Dr. Su.

reference_conclusion: Restaging with PET/CT and MRI was recommended, with no role for additional radiation at that time, followed by consideration of systemic therapy. Given PD-1–naive recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma, treatment options discussed were single-agent PD-1 inhibition or immunotherapy combined with a VEGF inhibitor. Ongoing surveillance was advised with close follow-up using endoscopy, periodic imaging, and EBV DNA monitoring, with more frequent cross-sectional imaging while receiving pembrolizumab. Flap coverage of the exposed carotid/skull base defect was favored sooner rather than later, alongside continued goals-of-care discussions given progressive treatment-related necrosis and overall frailty.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidental liver mass identified during renal ultrasound performed in the evaluation of urinary frequency/prostate-related symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic non-functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pancreatic head primary) with bilobar liver metastases; well-differentiated NET, grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of a liver metastasis showed well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 2. Ki-67 proliferation index was 8%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Renal ultrasound detected a 3.1 cm liver mass incidentally.  
- MRI abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a 5.2 cm pancreatic head mass and multiple liver lesions.  
- Gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/CT showed avid uptake in the pancreatic head mass and in bilobar hepatic metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No evidence of an inherited syndrome.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Capecitabine/temozolomide was administered with the goal of tumor shrinkage.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Functional evaluation for hormone-producing NET was negative; tumor was non-functional.  
- Past medical history included Crohn’s disease.

reference_discussion.text: Great. Hi, everybody. I'm Pam Koons. I am co-directing today with Dr. Jen Chan. I'm an associate professor of medicine and medical oncology at Yale. I focus on caring for patients with NETs, and I love doing these events. So thank you for sticking with us to the bitter end. I thought, so I don't know if we have the next case one. OK. I'm going to just define, like pull back the curtains on what a tumor board is. You may have heard this term. Your case may have been presented at a tumor board. All of our institutions offer tumor boards. They may be slightly different, but basically it is a gathering of multiple disciplines where you, I call it one-stop shopping. So one of your doctors can bring a case to the tumor board, and then you get the benefit of input from multiple experts. At Yale, it actually happens virtually. We sort of transitioned to Zoom, and there are about 30 doctors that are on the tumor board. It includes medical oncologists like myself, surgical oncologists, radiation oncologists, nuclear medicine specialists who review DOTA pets, radiologists who look at CTs and MRIs. And I just think it's one of my favorite meetings of the week. It is critical to excellent patient care, especially for neuroendocrine tumors. So we're going to pretend that we're a tumor board. And in reality, we kind of have rapid fire discussions. But we're going to kind of go through this. And we have two cases to present for you. And so I'm going to present the first case. Dr. Chan is going to present the second case. I'm going to pose questions to our esteemed tumor board. We're missing radiology, so we're going to pretend that we have, I don't know, Dr. Clancy, do you want to be a radiologist? Yeah. So we'll all weigh in. So this is a 58-year-old man who underwent a renal ultrasound for a prostate evaluation. He had had some urinary frequency. And then incidentally, so kind of surprise, was found to have a 3.1 centimeter liver mass detected. This prompted an MRI of the abdomen and pelvis. And that actually showed a 5.2 centimeter pancreatic head mass and multiple liver lesions. We take into consideration what other medical issues a patient may have. So he actually had a history of Crohn's disease, which is an inflammatory bowel disease. The workup that was done included, so I'm bringing all this, I'm presenting this to the tumor board. This is almost exactly verbatim what I would say. The patient had a gallium dotatate PET CT. It showed that that pancreatic head mass was bright. So were the bilobar, like liver mets. And then the patient had a biopsy of one of the liver metastases. It showed a well-differentiated net, grade 2. KI67 was 8%. And then we did an evaluation for functional net that was negative. no evidence of an inherited syndrome. So what I'm trying to do is pull together all the things you learned today from all the different talks. And so Dr. Clancy, our radiologist, and surgeons are used to looking at, I mean, you look, I'm assuming, Dr. Clancy, you look at scans for your patients, right?
Correct.
Do you want to take, I only have really one slice through each of these, and normally we would run through kind of all of the imaging, but maybe talk to us a little bit.

That sounds perfect. So what we're looking at is an axial view of the MRI on the left side. And what that shows us is imagine the patient is lying down and we're slicing through the images like a loaf of bread and we're looking from the feet up. So on the right side of that image is really, sorry, the left side is the patient's right side as if we're looking from the feet up and vice versa. The right side of that image is the patient's left side. So in the area indicated by that dotted line is the head of the pancreas on the right side. Just immediately adjacent to that, that white area is the superior mesenteric vein and the artery.
I'm doing a good job.

You're doing a good job. Yeah, that's right. These are important vascular structures that might indicate whether a primary tumor is easily removed without damaging other structures. It just sits right above the kidney and vessels to the kidney, but it's a sizable mass in that area.
And there are also some liver lesions.
Right, and so on the right side with the Dodecay scan, we can see that on the right- Just imagine the patient's
for those of you who've had dodepet cysts, is looking at the patient like this.

Exactly. And in those darker areas above, sort of that squiggly area in the middle that represents the pancreas, right above that is the liver. So we see two darker areas in the liver, the right and the left side.

And just to make a comment, we see some normal uptake on a DOTA PET scan. So the pituitary gland is normally bright. That doesn't represent cancer. The spleen is normally bright. And then the contrast that you get injected gets excreted through the urinary system. And this is the bladder. So Dr. Hefty-Anderson. So as you're seeing this, you have a patient with a metastatic pancreatic net grade two. What are you starting to think about? What else are you wanting? Or what other questions might you have for the tumor board?

Yeah, so right now, we've done the diagnosis. We know what we're dealing with. We've completed the staging. We know where the tumor started, where it is. So my next question would be to know, is this what we call a functional tumor? Is the tumor producing hormones or chemicals causing symptoms?
Non-functional.

Non-functional, OK. So then the next thing is really to talk about the treatment. And sometimes the question comes up, do we need to treat at all? But with a tumor of this size, with these types of metastases, I think most of us would be inclined to start some therapy.
What would you start?

So all of these tumors light up like really, really bright. That means that the target for one of our therapies, what's called the somatostatin receptor, is abundantly present on the tumor cell. So I would probably start with monthly injections of a drug called octreotide or lanreotide.
Yeah. Dr. Clancy, would you ever go straight to surgery?

For a case like this, for a 5-centimeter tumor, we did not have any evidence of spread. That was certainly a case where we would recommend surgery. And the evidence with spread, particularly liver, I think it's challenging because we know we do have other options available. And I think also treatment of liver disease after a big pancreatic operation can be particularly challenging.

We also have a pathologist, not on this tumor board, but we normally do have a pathologist. We've talked a lot about pathology today. Dr. Hefty-Anderson reviewed this. So again, this is just showing, and our pathologists actually walk us through microscopic pictures and teach us a lot about what they're seeing. So this is almost exactly what we would be looking at. So really just confirming this KI67 of 8%. So systemic therapy, so either Chemotherapy, biologic therapy, somatostine analog was considered the most optimal approach given diffuse pancreatic involvement. And really there was a thought that the patient would even need perhaps a total pancreatectomy. So given the bulky disease, we actually decided to use capecitabine temozolomide with the hopes of yielding tumor shrinkage. The patient tolerated the treatment very well. However, there was no shrinkage. So this was the, on the left was the MRI before Keptem, and on the right was the MRI abdomen after just three months of Keptem, but there was really no response. So we took the case back to Tumor Board, and this can be an iterative process where the Tumor Board is really intended to be a resource for physicians, and I think that one thing I always like to say, it's really our way of getting other opinions, and what's the saying if your doctor won't do a second opinion, get another doctor. And I think it represents humility of all of us to say, I don't know, I want input, and you want your doctors to be doing that. So you can always ask, has my case been presented to the tumor board? When do you use a tumor board? And so we really decided, this was a little controversial, Dr. Clancy. So we decided to move forward with cytoreductive surgery. We just felt that this hadn't budged, it was technically feasible, but this was a big surgery for the patient. So I don't know if you have, sometimes these are tricky conversations, but I think another thing that this showed is that we didn't have progression and didn't have new spots. So this three months was a bit of a test of time and a test of biology. Dr. Asi, do you have anything to add to this or how your tumor boards work?

Yeah, I mean, as you can see here, multiple treatment options that we can consider for patients and different approaches. And really, the key here is really the discussion that happens between the different disciplines, medical oncology, surgery, interventional radiology, pathology, and nuclear medicine. So for example, Dr. Hab-Dinarson thought about giving this patient some instant analog. We thought about doing CAPTEM as a treatment. Given the recent NETR2 trial, we could have thought about doing Lutathera upfront as well. I mean, all these are different options, and determining it really is based on this discussion that we have amongst ourselves.

Yeah, yeah. I'm going to not spend a whole lot of time on this case, but I'm juxtaposing two cases. This was a patient who also had a pancreatic net and ultimately had a really robust shrinkage or response to CAPTEM. So I wanted to make a point with this, so I'm not going to. I'll show you some of the pictures here. And compared to the last one, you can see very large liver lesions. So there were multiple as compared to the last case. And then after six months of CAPTEM, we had really significant tumor shrinkage. And just to kind of juxtapose these two cases, and Dr. Chan, I might ask you to weigh in on this a little bit. So these two cases, I'm sorry, they're misnumbered here, case one and two, we had one patient with no response and another patient with a response. And there were a number of treatment options, as Dr. Ossie said. But how do we know, Dr. Chan, or do we? How can we select patients who are going to respond?

Yeah. For the most part, we really don't have a lot of predictive biomarkers. I think with the exception, perhaps, of somatostatin receptor expression, which does help us choose PRRT candidates. But I think choosing between these different options, we really do have to rely a lot on the clinical factors. For example, that second case you showed, where there was very extensive bulky disease, our goal really is to try to cytoreduce. So we're trying to get major shrinkage. So we're really probably trying to decide between something like chemotherapy or even PRRT. But how people are going to respond and to what degree is always really a bit unpredictable. I think in both of the cases you showed, one could make the argument chemo to shrink and then to think about surgery afterwards. I think you did some really great work in your ECOG study looking at possible predictive biomarkers for chemotherapy. So maybe we will in the future have some tools that we can use, but they're not routinely implemented right now. And I think that's why this discussion is so important, where we can think about the option, discuss the pros and cons, really try to be on the same page as a team about what we're hoping to achieve. work together with everybody on the care team to make sure we're making the right decisions.
That's right, yeah. And I'm going to ask one last question of Dr. Hefty-Anderson, and then I'll pass to Dr. Chan. So is there an optimal order in which we should be using these therapies?

So for a lot of them, there really isn't. And so we don't really have good studies that compare one treatment option to another. So in every case, it just has to be thought of very, very individually. And we take into account other health conditions. There are some people who, let's say, have diabetes, who might not tolerate a certain drug. Others who have high blood pressure, who might not tolerate a different drug. So you have to take a look at the whole picture. Also, what do the patients want to do? And so no ideal sequence we can debate. And that's actually why we use tumor boards. And the one point I wanted to get across, too, is that you can go to two or three different sensors of expertise and get completely different recommendations, all good, and very valid.

reference_conclusion: For metastatic, nonfunctional, well-differentiated grade 2 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with diffuse pancreatic and bilobar hepatic involvement, systemic therapy was considered the optimal initial approach rather than upfront surgery. Capecitabine/temozolomide was administered with the goal of tumor shrinkage; after three months, imaging demonstrated no objective response and no new sites of disease. On repeat multidisciplinary review, cytoreductive surgery was selected because the disease remained technically resectable and had not progressed.
reference_conclusion_quote: So systemic therapy, so either Chemotherapy, biologic therapy, somatostine analog was considered the most optimal approach given diffuse pancreatic involvement. And really there was a thought that the patient would even need perhaps a total pancreatectomy. So given the bulky disease, we actually decided to use capecitabine temozolomide with the hopes of yielding tumor shrinkage. [...] However, there was no shrinkage. [...] So we took the case back to Tumor Board [...] So we really decided, this was a little controversial, Dr. Clancy. So we decided to move forward with cytoreductive surgery. We just felt that this hadn't budged, it was technically feasible [...] we didn't have progression and didn't have new spots.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Right neck mass, presenting in approximately March 2023.

[ diagnosis ]: Cutaneous malignant melanoma of the right back/scapular region, initially diagnosed in November 2022, stage pT2a based on primary tumor depth 1.3 mm without ulceration; subsequent regional nodal metastatic melanoma involving the right neck, confirmed by fine-needle aspiration. PET imaging demonstrated regional disease only.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy of the pigmented lesion on the right back/scapular area showed malignant melanoma, Breslow depth 1.3 mm, classified as T2a. Wide local excision specimen also showed T2a malignant melanoma with one mitotic figure and no other adverse risk factors reported. Fine-needle aspiration of the right neck mass was positive for malignant melanoma.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan performed after identification of the right neck mass demonstrated regional disease only. The involved node was described as an isolated right level IV lymph node.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Gene expression profiling performed through Castle Biosciences classified the primary melanoma as class 1A, reported as low risk for a positive sentinel lymph node. No other molecular alterations were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In November 2022, the primary right back/scapular melanoma was biopsied and then treated with wide local excision by plastic surgery. No sentinel lymph node biopsy or other staging workup was performed at that time. Approximately four months later, the patient developed a right neck mass; fine-needle aspiration confirmed metastatic melanoma. The patient was subsequently started on neoadjuvant pembrolizumab. Surgery had not yet been performed.

[ current disease status ]: Regional nodal metastatic melanoma in the right neck without documented distant metastatic disease on PET imaging. The patient was receiving neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and was awaiting repeat imaging and planned neck dissection.

[ other clinical data ]: Planned restaging imaging included CT neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Planned surgical management was right neck dissection including levels III, IV, and V.

reference_discussion.text: Well, I thank you for this opportunity to be part of these virtual tumor boards. I think they're very important structure for our fellows so once again thank you for the opportunity to be a presenter today. First, the patient that I would like to discuss is a 67-year-old gentleman who presented to my office with a right neck mass. And that was the beginning of this year, around March of this year, so not too long ago. Back in November of 2022, he had a pigmented lesion on his right back scapular area, which I never got to see. It was evaluated by the dermatologist. A biopsy was performed on that, and it was a T2A malignant melanoma. It was 1.3 millimeters in depth. He was sent to a plastic surgeon. They did a gene expression profiling out through Castle Biosciences, which put him at a low risk of a class 1A of having a positive sentinel node. So the plastic surgeon did a wide local excision alone without any further sentinel node workup or any other staging workup. The final pathology from that specimen did return as a T2A malignant melanoma. It had one mitotic figure, no other adverse risk factors. Patient then presented to the clinic four months later with a right neck mass, which was FNAID for malignant melanoma. That's a picture of the neck mass. He had a PET scan performed, which demonstrated regional disease only. So the first question that I had put out there with this case is what is the role for gene expression profiling in cutaneous melanomas?
And how are people utilizing that? All right, that's a great question.
So hi, guys. My name is Devakar. I think I'm probably the only medical oncologist on this. So what have people heard about gene expression testing?
You may not get much response from the audience, Devakar.

All right, so the interesting thing about gene expression testing is You know, so we've got, we've got, uh, it's very important, I think, for you guys to know this because, uh, for the vast majority of, uh, head and neck oncologists, you're seeing two cutaneous malignancies, right? So it's melanoma, uh, we're in a rarely basal, but also melanoma and squam and their gene expression tests for both melanoma and squam. And so it's important, I think, for you guys to be, uh, familiar with the literature, but let, you know, let's very briefly think about a different paradigm and that is breast cancer. And so in breast cancer, if you have somebody with a two centimeter breast tumor, so that's a T1 lesion, you come in, the first thing you do is you either get mammoprint, oncotype, there's a third particular gene expression test as well. But the point is the idea that gene expression profiling is ingrained in the management of breast cancer is not news. In fact, it's information that's about 10 years old. And the reason for that is because the purpose of the gene expression test is not just to prognosticate, but it's also to predict value. So it predicts the value of adjuvant. So that's a very, very important distinction. It's not merely a prognostication tool, but it's also a predictive biomarker of the benefit of adjuvant therapy. In this case, in the context of breast cancer, at least for the benefit of adjuvant hormonal therapy. And the reason that's important is because, you know, when you think of the surgery that you guys are discussing, The primary reason for sentinel node staging, in this case, this is nodal dissection that is going to be discussed, but the primary role for sentinel node staging is actually prognostication. So the real question that you would have if you're a surgical oncologist is, does or how much does gene expression testing add to sentinel node staging? And as it turns out, we don't know that. In fact, we don't know the answer to that at all because that test, that experiment has just not been done. And as a result, we just don't know whether gene expression testing adds to sense and load staging. What we do know is that in the absence of knowing anything about the nodal status, gene expression profiling reasonably does a reasonable, decent job of predicting high risk, low risk, and intermediate risk patients. It adds a little bit to AJCC, not much, but a little bit. And so therefore, rightly so, opinion is divided. On the NCCN, this is a class two recommendation, so it's not strongly recommended. It's no level one evidence, but it's a class two recommendation. And as you've seen in this case, this particular instance, the gene expression testing, if it's completely relied upon, can actually lead you astray because it gives you a false sense of the reassurance of it being relatively low risk. So the takeaways are gene expression profile testing in other areas of oncology are ingrained. Gene expression profiling testing in melanoma and cutaneous squamous is something that a head and neck oncologist absolutely has to know about because it's very commonly done. Whether or not it's rightly interpreted is a separate question. But very importantly, it's because of the nature in which the tests were done and the way in which these tests were developed, there's no prospective level one data to guide the use and the interpretation of these tests. And they're interchangeably used for both prediction and prognostication, though they've got probably more value for prediction and very, more value for prognostication and very little value for prediction. They're unfortunately interchangeably used for both. So that's a really a medical oncologist's long-winded way of saying it's controversial. But you know, us medical oncologists, we like to talk.
Trevor, are you routinely using this testing? No.

We're not routinely using it either. I would agree with the sentiment that it doesn't supplant, in my opinion, the use or the need for Sentinel Node. It may be another adjunct if you have a negative Sentinel Node, but you think somebody is high risk. But I don't necessarily know that I would use it to supplant Sentinel Node.

And I would like to add, I did not send this because I agree with you guys. So this is just reiterating what current statements are on the NCCN guidelines regarding the gene expression profiling, that it is not recommended at this point in time. I utilize it for trying to figure out those patients that I need to follow closely, but I never do it as a treatment. maybe help guide the image that I would use afterwards for like a lower stage melanoma, but never in place of a standardized treatment. So now he's got a positive of FNA. He only has regional disease. And so these are the treatment options that were discussed with him. Do you do a neck dissection and what levels would you do if you were going to do this neck dissection in a primary tumor that was on his back slash scapular area? And he has this isolated level four lymph node. Would you do a neck dissection with possibility of adjuvant radiation therapy? Would you do a neck dissection with post-op immunotherapy? Or should this patient get neoadjuvant immunotherapy?

So this is a very, very interesting area. The level, the evidence for this has just dramatically changed in just the last couple of weeks, right? So again, I like to talk about paradigm. So in the paradigm of breast cancer, we've been doing perioperative immune therapy for eons, right? So we've been doing perioperative immune therapy, perioperative therapy, not necessarily immune therapy in breast cancer since the early 2000s. Perioperative immune therapy in melanoma was being done as a, you know, as an investigational area of interest for about a decade or so since the newer drugs emerged. But it really took a good friend, a close colleague of mine at MD Anderson, Sapna Patel, to design a, you know, what is probably the best evidence we have of doing this. And so this is SWOG 1801. It's a New England Journal paper, just came out a couple of weeks ago. It has been circulated, I think, in the meeting minutes, in the meeting notes. And SWAG-1801 is really a pivotal trial, right? So what SWAG-1801 did was it asked the really essential question, which was, if you give the same damn drug preoperative versus postoperative, are outcomes better? And as it turns out, it doesn't take a genius to realize that it actually does improve survival outcomes. So the study design is a randomized phase two. The key thing to understand is, unlike medical oncologists and surgical oncologists debating about CR rates and toxicity and all that sort of nonsense, the key thing in SWOG1801 was event-free survival. So the proportion of people who relapse or die from cancer, which is, as it turns out, exactly what you're communicating to your patients. So what SWOG1801 showed was that event-free survival with the same drug given perioperatively was significantly better than the drug given post-operatively. And the drug was Pembrolizumab, standard adjuvant therapy in the context of stage three melanoma, given perioperatively for nine weeks or three cycles, improves event-free survival significantly. So the hazard ratio is huge margin. The key thing that I explain to patients is that patients don't really understand hazard ratios. The way I explain to patients is you've heard of the Moderna vaccine and the benefit of neoadjuvant compared to adjuvant is the benefit of the Moderna vaccine. So it's pretty damn good. And the important thing I guess to understand is that the perioperative immunotherapy results in a 21% PCR rate. This is fairly consistent with what we've seen with single agent immunotherapy. The reference study to quote is Alex Wong from Penn. And the toxicity is negligible. The key problem with perioperative immunotherapy from a surgical perspective is really the fact that even though a certain proportion of patients are gonna respond and respond very nicely. A certain proportion of patients are actually going to fail perioperative immunotherapy and therefore close communication between the medical oncologist and the surgical oncologist in this setting is essential. In fact, in the SWAG 1801 trial, in Sapna's trial, about 10 patients actually did not make it a surgery. And those patients did not make it a surgery because their disease grew and they became unresectable. So Right now, if you had to ask this question, the answer would be, you'd have to discuss the surgical plan with the surgeons, but there's good level two evidence. It's not a phase three trial. Those trials will probably never happen, but a randomized phase two trial with a survival endpoint that has resulted in the drug getting an NCCN. has demonstrated that neoadjuvant immunotherapy improves survival. Now, there are many nuances to this. We talked about some of these nuances, but you have to think about close communication. I know when Dr. Sridharan and myself put patients on this trial, we are always talking to each other. And I think that kind of communication is very important. You need to be at a system where you can operationalize this too. So pathology, the role of the pathologist in helping you define who is a good responder and who is a poor responder, and then the areas that are completely unknown, which is extraordinarily good outcomes that we've seen with PCRs. Basically, if you have a PCR, your risk of relapse is less than 4%. in a paper that we published in Nature Medicine about two years ago now, is well known. But what if you have anything less than a PCR? What if you have a 10% residual tumor? What if you have 20%? What if you have 25%? We just don't know what those things mean, and we need larger studies for that. But the short answer at this point in time is, if you can and the patient is not contraindicated, no massive contraindications to immune therapy, perioperative immunotherapy, three cycles or nine weeks, level two evidence for improved EFS.

I would agree. I think if you were to ask my fellow from three years ago, they would probably tell you nectar section with adjuvant radiation therapy. The fellow a year ago, it's nectar section with post-op immunotherapy, and now I think the current fellow would tell you neoadjuvant. And I would agree. And furthermore, the patients that don't respond to the neoadjuvant regimen, you have to ask the question of, those are the patients that may not have done very well if you had done the surgery, done the radiation therapy, done everything else, and then they're still the ones that have a rapid relapse. And so, The question really with it with the neoadjuvant approach and are you identifying the patients that you know are just not going to do well and then you're not putting through the morbidity of surgeries and radiation therapy that were probably ultimately going to be ineffective, and you are capturing those that have the biologic capabilities of having long term. durable disease control with their melanoma. It doesn't really make the surgery harder. That was also a myth that people were worried about. In the realm of neoadjuvant immunotherapy, it also makes the surgery harder, dissection more difficult. It causes some inflammatory reactions, some fibrosis, but it's really not a major contradiction. It doesn't make surgery more difficult. I would favor at this point in time, the neoadjuvant approach as well.
Trevor, to follow up on that. What levels of the neck dissection which performed, this is a back melanoma now in the neck. So is it a level above and below or is it a one through five for you?

But I mean, this one, I think it's a back melanoma. So you've got to think about posterior triangle. And I think that you have to, if you're going to do that neck dissection, then yeah, you're doing a more comprehensive neck dissection because the intervening lymphatics, if you're going to do the neck, I would probably do probably a two through five. I don't know if I'd go up to level one. I don't know if there's much utility in that, but I probably would do a two through five if I was in the role of neck dissection with adjuvant therapy. In this role, if you get neoadjuvant immunotherapy, and then there's a, a radiographic CR, that also becomes then the difficult question, is it worth it to do the morbidity of a comprehensive neck dissection on what looks like a radiographic CR, or are you going to choose another modality of observation based on that response? That's another, I think, difficult question to answer. Right now, I'm leaning towards probably doing the surgery, but there'll be another role where if you have a phenomenal response, then the question is, do you accept that phenomenal response? Currently, I would do the surgery, but I'm leaning towards, can we trust radiographic CR in these settings?
Yeah, I think there's some more evidence to be had for that, for sure. Bob, you want to finish up your case?

Yeah, so this is the data that was presented with this paper that was published in March of this year. talking about the event-free survival at two years of 72% versus 49% in that neoadjuvant. So I think it's very compelling evidence to put patients on this neoadjuvant. So this patient was put on neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and we are awaiting to do his surgery. We have it with a coordination with our medical oncologist, we'll get re-imaging. And I plan on doing, and I'll throw that out there as a question too, we plan on doing a CT neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis. Would you do a PET scan for your imaging? And the neck dissection that I would plan on doing would be definitely a 3, 4, 5 in that area for afterwards.

Yeah, that's a great question. PET versus CT. I don't think it's wrong to get a pet, but I think I would be comfortable with a CT, neck, abdomen, chest, and pelvis. I think that would be appropriate. I don't have misgivings about doing a pet, but I don't necessarily know if it adds that much more value in my mind.

So I think the only point that I would want to educate my, want to clarify with my colleagues is that if you are talking about the initial staging scan, you should image the brain. In the perioperative trial that we've done, again, keep in mind that the interesting thing is this is a neoadjuvant cohort. What you have not seen is the patients before time zero. In this study, if you look at the consort diagram, about 20% of patients screen failed because of metastatic disease to the brain. So when you enroll a very high-risk cohort, about 20% to 25% of your patients will fail because melanoma is a CNS-tropic disease and because that is going to happen in this patient population. So in the initial staging, you have to scan the brain. Certainly at restaging, you don't have to. And whether or not you're going to get a PET or a CT, I think that really is up to the surgeon. The one interesting thing is, again, as somebody who does a lot of translational work in this space, I'll just throw this out there, is to think of the areas of novel imaging modalities. So myself, certainly some of my colleagues in Memorial, we're looking at novel PET traces. There's certainly a CD8 PET tracer, zirconium-8, and this zirconium-8 CD8 PET tracer essentially is able to essentially track T-cells that are moving into the tumor microenvironment. So what you might be seeing over the next couple of years is If PatCR predicts one-year RFS, what predicts PatCR? So to answer Trevor's question of who can you surgically you know, downstage. And as it turns out, we have increasingly developing tools that allow you to predict FAT-CR. There'll probably be two tools. One is ctDNA clearance. That's certainly predictive of FAT-CR. The second is non-invasive in vivo imaging. And look, at least in the context of immunotherapy, the most viable agent nearest to market is probably zirconium CD9 PET imaging from a company known as Imaginab.
Is there a change in your paradigm for wild type versus non-wild type?

You're talking about with BRAF. So I would say that the answer is not quite. So to summarize, essentially, BRAF is essentially a canonical mutation that is present in about 50% of melanoma. People have looked at perioperative trials. The really fascinating thing is that there have been two trials that were done that looked at perioperative targeted therapy as opposed to immune therapy. One was a non-randomized, one was a randomized trial that closed early. And this was done by my colleagues at MD Anderson, Rhoda Amaria, but also Jen Wago. And essentially what they showed was they actually had to close the neoadrenaline early because, you know, the response was extraordinary. The interesting thing about targeted therapy though, is that neoadrenaline targeted therapy has got two major advantages and two major disadvantages. So the major advantage of neoadrenaline targeted therapy is that it, you know, neoadrenaline immunotherapy, you have no idea if it's going to work or not. You don't know it's going to work until the tumor comes out. With neoadjuvant targeted therapy, 80% of the time you're seeing a response. You see a response within a week. So you can guarantee that you're going to debulk. The problem is, what does that response mean? So the whole purpose of neoadjuvant immunotherapy is to guarantee survival. You're like, if you have a path response 21% of the time, you're going to have a path response. But if you fall into that 21% of people, you're not dying of cancer. You don't need the adjuvant cycle. We don't know that yet, but we don't think you do. But the point is you're not getting cancer within a reasonable degree of possibility. With targeted therapy, you don't know that. In fact, these people with PCRs from targeted therapy relapse just as often, slightly more often than patients with neoadjuvant immunotherapy. And also the patients who don't respond to targeted therapy, well, those people are really in trouble. The second major, so the two major advantages of neoadjuvant targeted therapy are one, you can guarantee debulking. Two, if your whole purpose of therapy was conversion type surgery, right? And sometimes again, we're not in the paradigm of thinking about that in melanoma, but if you have somebody who's not, whose performance status is, you know, borderline and it's thought to be improved by the debulk, by, a reduction in bulk of tumor, or somebody is a few people who are complete neoadjuvant immunotherapy contraindicated, for example, organ transplant. or patients with autoimmune diseases, then you don't really have much of a choice. So those are the two major advantages. The two major disadvantages are what we just talked about, which is one, it's more toxic. So there's a significantly higher tox profile with the targeted therapy. People are going to be calling and complaining. They won't be calling and complaining to you guys. They'll be calling me and complaining to me about how much fevers they have, how many chills they have, how they can't go to sleep at night because of a hundred and four degree fever. So that's one issue. But then the biological problem, of neoadjuvant targeted therapy is that there's no satisfaction in telling the patient that you've had a great response. Because you could have had a decent response, but it's still coming back.

reference_conclusion: For regionally metastatic melanoma involving a right cervical lymph node, neoadjuvant pembrolizumab was selected as the preferred perioperative approach, with close coordination between medical oncology and surgery. Restaging imaging with CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis is planned prior to surgery; brain imaging is required for initial staging but not necessarily at restaging. Following neoadjuvant therapy, neck dissection remains planned, with anticipated dissection of levels III, IV, and V.
reference_conclusion_quote: But the short answer at this point in time is, if you can and the patient is not contraindicated, no massive contraindications to immune therapy, perioperative immunotherapy, three cycles or nine weeks, level two evidence for improved EFS. [...] I would favor at this point in time, the neoadjuvant approach as well. [...] So I think it's very compelling evidence to put patients on this neoadjuvant. So this patient was put on neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and we are awaiting to do his surgery. We have it with a coordination with our medical oncologist, we'll get re-imaging. And I plan on doing, and I'll throw that out there as a question too, we plan on doing a CT neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis. [...] In the initial staging, you have to scan the brain. Certainly at restaging, you don't have to. [...] And the neck dissection that I would plan on doing would be definitely a 3, 4, 5 in that area for afterwards.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent Hürthle cell carcinoma in the neck following prior right thyroid lobectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent/metastatic Hürthle cell carcinoma involving the right thyroid bed/central neck, central neck lymph nodes, and multiple intramuscular/subplatysmal soft-tissue nodules in the neck.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial outside pathology after right thyroid lobectomy had been described as Hürthle cell adenoma with microcarcinoma.  
- Needle biopsy of a new right ipsilateral paratracheal mass demonstrated Hürthle cells.  
- Pathology from revision right central neck dissection demonstrated metastatic Hürthle cell carcinoma with several foci in the central neck.  
- Additional excised subcutaneous/intramuscular nodules were identified at revision surgery.  
- Subsequent pathology review described a multinodular remaining thyroid lobe without particularly Hürthle-appearing nodules.  
- Central neck specimen showed a true nodal metastasis with lymphoid rim.  
- Soft-tissue/subcutaneous nodules showed Hürthle cell lesion morphology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Follow-up imaging identified a new right ipsilateral paratracheal mass.  
- CT at Johns Hopkins demonstrated a 5.3 cm mass with associated nodes.  
- Preoperative ultrasound later showed scattered cervical nodes, including right central neck and left central neck nodes, multiple subcutaneous nodules, and an intact left thyroid lobe.  
- Imaging demonstrated several soft-tissue nodules along the strap muscle/platysma region of the neck.  
- One right neck nodule was described as fairly small.  
- A central neck node on coronal imaging was enlarged and clinically suspicious.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- No patient-specific molecular testing results were reported.  
- Hürthle cell carcinoma biology was described as distinct from other thyroid cancers, with possible HRAS mutations reported in some tumors generally, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation abnormalities, characteristic mitochondrial DNA mutations involving complex I of the electron transport chain, and widespread chromosomal loss; these were not reported as confirmed findings in this individual patient.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent right thyroid lobectomy at an outside institution; pathology was reported as Hürthle cell adenoma with microcarcinoma.  
- After ipsilateral bed recurrence, underwent revision right central neck dissection at Johns Hopkins.  
- Planned surgery was limited to the right side because of loss of signal from the right recurrent laryngeal nerve intraoperatively.  
- Revision surgery was complicated by right vocal cord paralysis and pneumothorax.  
- Returned to the operating room the following day for bronchoscopy and neck exploration related to pneumothorax; additional excision of soft-tissue/subcutaneous nodules was performed at that time.  
- Disease recurrence had continued over time in the neck, with nodules recurring every 2-3 years by history provided in the case.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent/recurrent locoregional disease was present in the neck.  
- Disease sites included central neck nodal disease and multiple palpable soft-tissue/intramuscular nodules involving the platysma/strap muscle region and sternocleidomastoid region.  
- Left thyroid lobe remained in situ and was nodular.  
- At the time summarized, no confirmed distant metastatic disease had been documented.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history was otherwise reported as unremarkable.  
- Right vocal cord paralysis was present following revision neck surgery.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so this is a case of peripheral cell carcinoma recurrence. And so a 66-year-old who presented here with recurrent Hercules cell carcinoma. Her initial history started back at Hopkins, and this was no other past medical history. Right lobectomy at an outside institution. This was described as a right lobectomy. It was described as a Hercules cell adenoma and a microcarcinoma. In follow up then, a number of years later, a new right ipsilateral paratracheal mass was identified needle biopsy was done of that recurrent ipsilateral mass and it showed purple cells and so the patient went. from that outside right lobectomy with ipsilateral bed recurrence to Hopkins had CT scanning there. The mass was then 5.3 centimeters with nodes. Again, a little disconnect, the past history was benign herthal cell adenoma, at least by history. Now at Hopkins with recurrence.
Peter, help me out here. This is metastatic herthal cell adenoma or what's going on here? That's hilarious. I'm giving the pathologist the benefit of the doubt. Come on, you know.
Peter, it's a leading question. Don't you get it?

Yes. So, so, so no. In some ways it is. And we actually talk about this in other diseases in the head and neck. We talk about benign metastasizing, for instance, in women, benign metastasizing leiomyoma. We talk about benign metastasizing pleomorphic adenoma. These are tumors that have a very bland appearance that look exactly like the original lesion in the, in the, in the organ. but they metastasize and they look like for all intents and purposes, you're taking it out of the thigh of the skin and it looks like a thyroid nodule. So, you know, this is what we get. This is what we get with a really well-differentiated tumor. So I think the answer to your question is yes, and yet no. Okay, go ahead, Greg.
Well, that's helpful.

Yeah, I agree completely. I was, I was embarrassed many times when we first got these TKs and you guys would image and we'd find asymptomatic that I knew were there for a long time. Yeah, thanks, Dr. Tuttle. Awesome. We have about two minutes left, so get to me.
Okay, yeah.

I have a high power view here where you see these dark navy blue nuclei and small micro follicles. All right, next slide. This is the central neck. This is a normal hurtle cell lesion, which brings back the tautoloid question of the subcutaneous things. Is it a benign adenoma there? And this is the issue that will then bring in Laurie as the go-to, is like, what the hell do you do with this? The reason why Laurie is the hurtle cell professor of oncology is because of the fact that here and at Memorial, we're trying very, very hard to understand the molecular genetics of these hurtful cell tumors, because they're not the classic genetics of other thyroid cancers that we can think about targeting for drugs. They're very, very rich in mitochondria, which is the reason why they're particularly hypoxia sensitive. So the idea that these benign nodules appear in other parts of the body is absolutely curious to me, because if you put a needle in it, it can completely die because of the hypoxia that you're inducing. So they're really, really strange nodules. Sometimes they have HRAS mutations, but the truth is we start seeing they have the oxidative phosphorylation issues. They've got all sorts of things, and they're completely different than any other tumor, which is reminiscent of the fact that My colleague, who Bill Fagwin is sitting next door to me, had a case that he saw in 2011. And then six years later, the patient had a contralateral hurtle cell lesion that metastasized to lymph nodes and got a call from our good friends in Philadelphia who said, oh, I looked at your case from 2011, and that's hurtle cell cancer, too. But it's not. They all these benign appearing things that don't look like anything. No necrosis, no nothing. So, you know, how do we even say, so that's the reason why you want to know your pathologists are completely paranoid about misdiagnosing a hurtful cell carcinoma because they look like these benign things that you're finding underneath the skin. So how do you actually make the diagnosis of cancer? We need molecular markers that we don't have, and we need molecular therapies that we don't have. Well, I'd consider external radiation because we don't have good drugs for these herthal cell carcinomas yet, but I think we will be getting there. The Memorial Group and our group took a look at what drives herthocell carcinomas, and we found characteristic mitochondrial DNA mutations in a large proportion of these cancers that are all concentrated in the complex one of the electron transport chain of the mitochondria. There are other mutations that have been found as well. Another really interesting thing is that we found widespread chromosomal loss in herthal cell thyroid cancers. We've been able to develop now some cell lines and animal models. Also, David McFadden at UT Southwestern is working on on these models, and we're working on developing drugs that can leverage these unique molecular drivers of herthal cell carcinoma. Not quite there yet, though.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic breast adenocarcinoma with sternal metastasis.

[ diagnosis ]: Hormone receptor-positive breast adenocarcinoma; HER2 immunohistochemistry 2+ with negative FISH testing. Metastatic disease was present in the sternum.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of a sternal metastasis showed adenocarcinoma. Tumor cellularity in the specimen was 50%.

[ imaging findings ]: Sternal metastatic lesion was present. No additional imaging data were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: PIK3CA mutation was identified. Copy-number variation analysis did not show diagnostically significant findings. RNA sequencing had not been performed. Tumor mutational burden was 7.8 mutations/Mb.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior endocrine therapy included tamoxifen and letrozole. No treatment response data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic hormone receptor-positive breast cancer with documented sternal involvement.

[ other clinical data ]: HER2 status was equivocal by immunohistochemistry (2+) and negative by FISH.
