reference_discussion.text: Perfect, thank you very much. Let's start. We have a few patients, I think we have five clinical cases. These are virtual patients, so there is no way to recognize real patients, but we think these are good patients to learn about the function of molecular tumor boards and about how we think about targeted treatment in practice. The first patient is a patient with an adenocarcinoma, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-2+, and the FISH analysis is negative. She was biopsied on a sternal metastasis, 50% cancer cells in the sample. These are the previous treatments that she received, and these are the results of the molecular analysis. The mutational burden is 7.8, our usual cutoff is 10, or it depends on the tumor types. And I think one of the most interesting results is the mutation in PIK3CA, which is a gene frequently mutated in breast cancer and many other cancers. And the CNV did not provide any very interesting diagnostic uncertainty and the RNA-seq has not yet been done. So, Amaya, what would be your treatment proposal for these patients?

Looking at PIK3CA, that could be a target for which we could give treatment. But, I need to check whether we can give that in DROP, because we might have ALPELISIB available for PIK3CA mutations in DROP,
I think there were challenges for the patients, specifically with this type of tumor, with breast cancer, hormone receptor-positive for this cohort, right?

Yes, that is true. Because alpelisib in the Netherlands is registered for hormone-positive and negative patients with breast cancer, these patients are not applicable. But since these patients are hormone-positive as well, it is something that we should discuss with our PIs if it were an option. But looking at the other mutations found, there is nothing that we can give.
The challenge is the HER2 status, since it is ambiguous, with 2+, but FISH-negative, perhaps he could also receive alpelisib treatment.
Yes, so that would be outside the scope of treatment.
Paola, what would be your proposition in terms of treatments or trials?

So, in Italy, at the moment, we are lucky because we have a sponsored phase 1 trial that uses anti-PI3K drugs, including all types of PI3CA mutations for all metastatic bone-positive cancers, after CDK4N6 and endocrine therapy. and patients could potentially be enrolled.
Very well, that is an interesting option. So we do not have this clinical result, is it an RLY2760 something?
Yes, yes, yes. The good option is that for these patients, there is this drug combined with fulvestrant, so the patients can also have endocrine therapy.

So you are lucky. We do not have it at CLB, but other centers in France have this test, if it is the same one. At Centre Léon Bérard, we actually have a phase 3 trial called EPIC B5, which can recruit patients with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, but indeed it combines hormonal therapy with PI3KCA-targeted treatment, the matched treatment, and this patient had already had tamoxifen and letrozole, so that could be a challenge because it could be, I do not have the criteria in mind, but it could be an exclusion criterion to have had prior hormone therapy, at least with letrozole. But that is to be checked and indeed we do not have other clinical trials for this patient. Okay. Do you have any other ideas or thoughts from the team? INCa could also provide advice, but we will see next time if we have results. Okay. So, these are some previous proposals that we had mentioned. For patient 2, we remain with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative cancer. and this patient has a GATA3 mutation and we think that this is interesting because it is a relatively rare mutation, a gene that we do not know much about, at least for the previous years of therapy development, but it seems that there are new drugs on the horizon. There is also amplification of the FGF4-1 gene, which is quite common, can be found in gastric cancer, but we will discuss the relevance of this finding.

reference_conclusion: The discussion retained an orientation toward a treatment targeting PIK3CA, in particular alpelisib, subject to verification of regulatory and protocol eligibility given the HER2 2+ status with negative FISH. Inclusion in a phase I clinical trial evaluating an anti-PI3K in combination with fulvestrant after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy was identified as a potential option. A phase III trial combining hormone therapy and PIK3CA-targeted treatment was also mentioned, with a need to check the exclusion criteria related to prior hormone therapies. No other targeted treatment was retained on the basis of the other reported molecular alterations.

[ patient demographics ]: 86-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Re-referred for consideration of further ^177Lu-PSMA therapy in the setting of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with rising PSA; PSA doubling time was 2.5 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Subsequently developed acute myeloid leukemia (AML), described as therapy-associated on bone marrow biopsy and associated with very poor prognosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Bone marrow biopsy showed acute myeloid leukemia with a translocation considered associated with prior therapy.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline PSMA PET with paired FDG PET in May 2018, performed before first ^177Lu-PSMA cycle, showed predominantly nodal metastatic disease with bulky retroperitoneal nodal involvement and only a couple of subtle bony lesions. Restaging in August 2022 showed a changed disease pattern with multifocal osseous metastases. Subsequent restaging before consideration of a fourth treatment block again showed the same phenotype with multifocal bony disease. FDG PET was not performed at the last restaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Circulating tumor DNA analysis from baseline plasma reportedly identified clonal hematopoiesis prior to commencement of ^177Lu-PSMA therapy.

[ laboratory results ]: Pancytopenia was present at reassessment for further treatment. Hemoglobin was 71. White cell count was 0.6. Platelet count was 39. Platelet counts had declined over approximately 4-5 years and had more recently fallen from about 90 to 30 over 2023.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received a total of 9 doses of ^177Lu-PSMA. He initially received 4 cycles on a therapy trial; the fourth cycle was dose-reduced. Treatment during the initial block was ceased after cycle 4 in the context of platelet decline/thrombocytopenia and excellent response. Approximately 3 years later he received a further 2 treatments, followed subsequently by another 3 treatments. Overall response to prior ^177Lu-PSMA was described as excellent, with progression occurring approximately 4 years after treatment initiation. The interval from first ^177Lu-PSMA dose to re-referral was 4 years and 11 months.

[ current disease status ]: At latest reassessment, mCRPC remained PSMA-avid on imaging with multifocal bone metastases and rapid PSA rise, but the patient had severe pancytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed AML.

[ other clinical data ]: Early disease phenotype had been node-predominant despite subsequent significant thrombocytopenia during treatment. The patient was in his late 80s at the time of latest reassessment.

reference_discussion.text: So, case number six, an 86-year-old man, MCRPC, already had nine doses of lutetium piercemase, six of them on the therapy trial, and then a subsequent two treatment blocks, which were ceased after C4, something was ceased after C4 due to thrombocytemia, it must have been during the therapy trial, is that right? But also excellent response, is that what happened?
Yeah, yeah.
Okay, and then re-referred for consideration of further lutetium PSMA, four years and 11 months since the first lutetium PSMA dose. PSA doubling time, 2.5 months.

This is a bit of a summary. Looks like a complicated case. So he had four cycles on the therapy trial and then fourth cycle was dose reduced and then three years later he had two more treatments. So he did very well. and then had another three treatments. Maybe we'll have a look at the imaging to try to work out what's happening here.
Did he stop on the therapy trial for exceptional response?
Is that why he stopped? I think it was convenient that his platelets had dipped, but also he was doing really well. So they stopped in there.
So two of those extra ones were recommencing on therapy after exceptional response, fine.
Yeah, if we switch to the imaging, And we can see, Kerry, take us through.

Yeah, so we've got a number of scans here. So we can say starting in May of 2018, this is the baseline PSMA PET and paired FDG that were completed before his first cycle of lutetia and PSMA. Coming over to August 2022,
So just at baseline, is that just in the lymph nodes, or is it in bone as well?
It's node predominant. I think there were a couple of subtle bony lesions, but the majority is nodal disease, and we can see that particularly bulky in the retroperitoneal station.

So I think, you know, the common knowledge is that the thrombocytopenia is due to crossfire to normal marrow, and this guy has node-only disease. Louise, why did he get such a marked thrombocytopenia after lutetium?

Looking at the patient's history and then the baseline scan, it looks like predominantly nodal disease, is that right? Yeah. So I guess I wouldn't be expecting significant thrombocytopenia, especially in that first treatment block. It's definitely something we look out for and expect after multiple cycles, but after only three or four cycles, it is a little bit unusual to see that, especially enough to interrupt treatment.

We've had a handful of patients who actually get quite severe thrombocytemia in relation to Letitia and PSMA who don't have bone disease. And the interesting thing about those cases is they almost all do very well with treatment. And I wonder whether it's some kind of inherent radiation sensitivity that they've got I don't know what I'm talking about, but germline level, where they're... Germline radiosensitivity. Yeah, there you go.
We can call that Emmett syndrome.

The Emmett syndrome. So I do think some patients showed up. We had one patient on therapy. They got one dose. Their platelets went right down. It was inexplicable. They came up. We started them again on trial. They're still alive. They're doing extremely well. That was on therapy in 2018.
But it looks like when he progressed in 2022, which is four years later, which is quite remarkable, that his pattern of disease is a little bit different.

Yeah, so we go through the transaxles, can see this a little bit clearly, that we now have multifocal bony lesions, which is not the phenotype at baseline. And then when we've restaged him again prior to potential fourth treatment block, again, we can see that same phenotype. It's worth noting that for the last restaging, we didn't do an FDG, and part of the rationale for that was that he's had a suitable phenotype at each interval, he's in his late 80s, so we just have to be a little bit careful about what we're putting our older patients through if it's not going to change management.

Michael or Louise, listen to you say you've seen patients with thrombocytopenia without bone disease reminds us of when we bring these treatments way forward, like lutectomy, for example, you know, a lot of concerns were raised. Well, look, these are fit men who are not going to die of prostate cancer anytime soon. You know, if they do get marrow failure, myelodysplastic disease, we could directly affect their survival. So we were careful about it, but we did see some drops in platelets, James. Or we had one guy, I remember, he was real borderline platelets at entry and dropped a bit, so we didn't give a second cycle. Is this a question for the community as you bring the treatments forward about this direct thrombocytopenia without overwhelming bone metastases? It's not common, is it, or is it a concern for us?

Personally, I think it's not common. I think it's rare. I think it's super interesting. It'd be really nice to know what the phenotype is, or what it is that's causing that kind of response, whether those patients do have an exceptional response, and what it actually means. I think the myelodysplasia thing. Michael, you've got some pretty good indications from your patients about the level of myelodysplasia. You've had some myelodysplasia.
Well, in this case, he was being considered for further lutetium PSMA. Do we need any other clinical information, Louise?
Yeah, get back to the thing at hand. Well, I'd love to see his counts.
His counts? Oh, well, here's a graph of his hemoglobin over time, and it's his, let's see, it's hemoglobin 71.
Now, that graph goes back right to before the first lutetium cycle, and the endpoint is at our consult, considering him for this fourth treatment block.
So do we also have playlets?
Oh, platelet, oh you want, well here is white cells. These white cells are 0.6 and platelets, oh, this is platelets over a four, four, five year period. They're now 39.
So you've got an 86 year old with pancytopenia, multiple doses of previous lutetium. Perhaps it's what you're worried about, Declan.
Would you retreat him given the exceptional responses to date?

I think you really want to know why it's pancytopenic in terms of where that's heading, the speed at which that's going down. It looks pretty fast. I don't have a timeline on that. Is that all 2023 where it's gone from 90 down to 30? Is it very recent?

So he had a bone marrow biopsy. that actually showed acute myeloid leukemia with a translocation that was thought to be associated with prior therapy and associated with a very poor prognosis. And I think he died within one month of that. Do you think the lutetium PSMA was what caused this AML or do you think it was unrelated?
What do the oncologists think?

I guess we don't know for sure. I think the risk of MDS, it is generally low and although the patient did have nine cycles of lutetium, we've certainly given more than that at Peter Mac. So, you know, it would be interesting to know what the counts were before the first dose of lutetium and whether there was already MDS at baseline that has maybe transformed to AML.

Question I've got also for the oncologists is, so we talk about myelodysplasia and the concern when we're bringing it forward, but people get adjuvant chemotherapy as well, and what is the incidence of myelodysplasia and chronic marrow issues with chemo?

I mean, it depends on the, it's hard to generalize because it does depend on the agent. I mean, I think generally speaking that taxane drugs we use in prostate cancer, it's not something we typically see, as opposed to some of the chemotherapies we, for example, use in breast cancer where it's more common. I think in this case, with nine cycles, I think you'd have to, say it's suspicious for being related to lupus. Now, I mean, we, I mean, you know, the new med physicians can talk to this better than I can. But, you know, if you, the long-term data with lutetium dotatate in your endocrine tumors, there are, there is a, you know, not insubstantial MDS AML rate. I think as, Declan makes a good point, as lutetium presumably moves forward, it's a consideration. I do wonder about things like the PSMA addition trial that we saw yesterday. six cycles have been given to patients who may have very low disease burden after a couple of cycles because of their ADT and their AR pathway inhibitor. What's happening with giving those men big doses of circulating liquid radiation? So I think it's a real consideration.

Yeah, this is an interesting case. Look, in general, we just blame the medical oncologists. When we see AML or MDS, we say it was due to the prior chemotherapy. We say that with some confidence. No, no, but in all seriousness, you know, there probably is incidents of MDS or AML with lutetium piersomate that has not yet been defined in the literature because it has mainly been used in the late stage. In this case, there was unexpected thrombocytopenia which was prolonged in a patient that had node-only disease. Timing with the lutetium actually we're writing up this case at the moment because he participated in the therapy trial and we collected plasma from all these patients for circulating tumor DNA analysis and Ed Kwan, if he's in the audience up in Vancouver, has received a specimen of this patient and ran his fancy chip analysis. actually found some clonal hematopogenesis at baseline prior to administration of lutetium therapy. So it seemed that this was a patient who was susceptible to MDS, you know, five years prior to dying and then the lutetium treatment maybe has unmasked that. And we've now seen we've been doing this since 2015, we've seen several cases of MDS. And like a neuroendocrine experience, it's probably mounting. It's going to be a very low incidence. I suspect it's going to be somewhere between one to two percent, but not insignificant. And as we bring the treatment back earlier, as Declan was saying, it's something we need to be mindful of. So when you have your patient young and fit who says, look, I don't want ADT, I'm not having any of that, just give me this lutetium, I've seen Peter Max image of the year and that's the treatment I'm having. I refuse everything else. You should not do that because we don't know the long-term toxicities yet. That'll be defined over time and in trials.

I think just on a practical point with this case too, so this was a little bit of a tricky consult. It was a really busy day. We hadn't had a chance to have a look at the whole picture before immediately prior to the consult and that's when we detected the counts and then found that a bone biopsy had been taken in the prior week but that the patient hadn't actually received that result yet. So we made the decision that we would give the result in our consult because we had to have an explanation for why with a good imaging phenotype, we wouldn't be able to offer any further lutetium. But I think it's just, it's a good reminder to work closely with the multidisciplinary team so that we, when we're doing tests concurrently, that we're sharing our results and coming up with a combined strategy. So that, I think in this situation, that possibly should have been investigated first and might have saved the patient the extra consults with us when we weren't able to treat. Again, in the context of a busy clinic, we don't always get that right, but we just learn from these type of situations and continue to do the best we can for patients.

reference_conclusion: Further lutetium PSMA retreatment was not offered despite a favorable imaging phenotype because the patient had severe pancytopenia, and bone marrow biopsy demonstrated acute myeloid leukemia with a therapy-associated translocation and poor prognosis. The agreed next step was to explain the biopsy result during consultation and withhold additional lutetium PSMA, with multidisciplinary coordination emphasized for integrated review of concurrent investigations and management planning.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old female; Haitian resident.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive pelvic/right sacral mass with pain, present for approximately 1 year.

[ diagnosis ]: Low-grade conventional chondrosarcoma involving the pelvis/right sacral region, reported to originate from the sacral root.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy and immunohistochemical evaluation were reported as low-grade, well-differentiated conventional chondrosarcoma. No areas of dedifferentiation were identified. Pathology description included malignant cartilaginous neoplasia composed of chondrocyte-like cells with focal hyaline change.

[ imaging findings ]: Pelvic MRI demonstrated an expansile heterogeneous mass arising from the lumbosacral/presacral-pelvic region, measuring approximately 16.1 × 8.3 cm. The lesion showed heterogeneous contrast enhancement. The tumor was reported to originate from the sacral root. Pelvic organs were displaced anteriorly. Chest CT showed no lung lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Hospitalized since 19 September 2017. Diagnostic workup included biopsy, immunohistochemistry, pelvic MRI, and chest CT. No systemic therapy was administered.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent large low-grade conventional chondrosarcoma of the pelvis/right sacral region with progressive growth and vulvar deformity; no pulmonary metastatic disease identified on chest CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Symptoms began approximately 1 year before presentation. Approximately 7 months later, the patient developed a progressively enlarging mass in the upper tailbone/sacrococcygeal area with extension causing vulvar deformity.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male; right-handed; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Forgetfulness and generalized weakness.

[ diagnosis ]: WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, involving the left temporal lobe with multifocal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from left temporal lesion after resection showed astrocytoma grade IV, IDH-mutant. Ki-67 proliferation index was reported as 20–30%.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI brain showed a multifocal left temporal lobe lesion with cystic and necrotic components and heterogeneous infiltrative enhancement. There was surrounding vasogenic edema extending into the left insular cortex and ipsilateral basal ganglia. Abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signal was also present in the contralateral medial temporal lobe without significant enhancement. Imaging described bilateral temporal lobe abnormal signal, with edema appearing to cross the midline. The lesion demonstrated multifocal/nodular enhancement along the cyst wall. Descending transtentorial herniation and effacement of the basal cisterns were described on preoperative imaging. Postoperative MRI performed within 24 hours of surgery showed postsurgical changes and near-total resection of the enhancing lesion, with decreased size of the cystic component and a few residual enhancing foci along the superior aspect of the operative region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-mutant. MGMT methylation status had not been performed/reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neuronavigation-guided left temporal craniotomy with maximal safe resection. Postoperative imaging demonstrated near-total resection.

[ current disease status ]: Status post left temporal craniotomy and maximal safe resection, with residual enhancing disease on early postoperative MRI. Multifocal/bilateral temporal lobe signal abnormality remained evident on imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old man. He was documented as homeless. He had a history of very heavy tobacco use. Family history was unknown.

[ chief complaint ]: Profound weight loss and urinary retention.

[ diagnosis ]: De novo neuroendocrine small cell carcinoma arising from the prostate, with metastatic disease involving pelvic/inguinal and abdominopelvic lymph nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy was consistent with neuroendocrine small cell carcinoma arising from the prostate.

[ imaging findings ]: CT demonstrated a very large heterogeneous pelvic mass appearing to arise from the prostate, with extension to the pelvic sidewall and inguinal nodes. Bulky lymphadenopathy was present in the abdomen and pelvis. CT chest and bone scan showed no other evidence of metastasis. PET scan demonstrated extensive metastatic disease. No brain metastases were identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy identified an NTRK-FMO1 non-canonical fusion, NF1 frameshift alteration, and STK11 alteration. Additional findings were reported as consistent with clonal hematopoiesis. Tumor fraction on liquid assay was reported at 45%.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was 11.8.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Systemic treatment was initiated with carboplatin, etoposide, and atezolizumab. No treatment response or outcome data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic small cell/neuroendocrine prostate carcinoma with bulky pelvic primary tumor and extensive nodal metastatic disease on PET imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history was available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman at initial presentation; 67-year-old woman at time of symptomatic progression.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial incidental leukocytosis. Later developed symptomatic disease progression with B symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

[ histopathology results ]: Bone marrow evaluation confirmed that CLL was responsible for the cytopenias and that the cytopenias were not due to an autoimmune process.

[ imaging findings ]: Small adenopathy at initial presentation. At progression, enlarging adenopathy involving additional nodal regions and splenomegaly were present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Initial FISH showed no abnormalities. IGHV was mutated. At later progression, FISH showed trisomy 12. At relapse after chemoimmunotherapy, repeat FISH demonstrated del(17p), consistent with clonal evolution.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial white blood cell count was 110 with lymphocyte predominance on immunophenotyping. No significant cytopenias were present initially. At symptomatic progression, hemoglobin was 8.5 g/dL with borderline thrombocytopenia. At subsequent relapse four years after completion of frontline therapy, significant cytopenias recurred involving both hemoglobin and platelets.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial management was observation. Following symptomatic progression, she received 6 cycles of frontline BR (bendamustine plus rituximab) and achieved a complete response. She relapsed 4 years after completion of BR.

[ current disease status ]: Relapsed CLL after prior complete response to BR, with recurrent anemia and thrombocytopenia and acquisition of del(17p).

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was notable for hypertension and was otherwise minimal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old male; originally from Laos.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial presentation six years earlier with nasal obstruction and epistaxis. In 2024, presented four years after completion of treatment with 3–4 months of confusion and suspected seizures. Eight months later, developed progressive speech difficulty, dysarthria, bilateral hypoglossal nerve weakness (right greater than left), and mild aspiration.

[ diagnosis ]: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-related nasopharyngeal carcinoma, staged cT2N2 at initial diagnosis. Subsequent intracranial/temporal lobe process was clinically assessed as radiation necrosis rather than recurrent disease.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: At initial diagnosis, imaging demonstrated a large right nasopharyngeal mass encasing the carotid artery, PET-avid, with bilateral cervical adenopathy. No contrast-enhanced MRI had been obtained at that time. In 2024, MRI demonstrated a lesion with a classical appearance considered consistent with radiation necrosis. PET imaging showed asymmetry of intensity corresponding to the MRI abnormality. At later progression, imaging showed slight asymmetric enhancement near the right hypoglossal canal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: EBV-related disease. No additional molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial EBV titer was elevated at 540. At later progression, EBV remained negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received definitive concurrent chemoradiation for nasopharyngeal carcinoma with 70 Gy plus cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil. Four years after treatment, developed neurologic symptoms with imaging findings felt to represent radiation necrosis. Eight months after that presentation, symptoms progressed with dysarthria, bilateral hypoglossal weakness, and mild aspiration.

[ current disease status ]: No visible nasopharyngeal mass was identified on serial nasal endoscopy. Nasal endoscopy showed no masses, no purulence, and no exposed bone. EBV remained negative. The patient had progressive neurologic deficits and swallowing dysfunction in the setting of imaging findings considered most consistent with radiation necrosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial physical examination reportedly showed no other abnormalities. At later evaluation, there was no vocal fold immobility. Coworkers had reported episodes concerning for seizures. Speech and swallowing impairment were present, with aspiration beginning at the later time point.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic recurrence of adenoid cystic carcinoma with disease involving the left neck, lungs, and a liver lesion.

[ diagnosis ]: Intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma, initially diagnosed 4 years earlier, with subsequent metastatic recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]: Intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- After 3 years without evident disease following initial treatment, recurrent disease was identified in the left neck and lungs, with a possible liver lesion; lesions were described as subcentimeter at that time.  
- Repeat imaging 3 months later showed new pulmonary lesions and interval enlargement of a liver lesion to 6.1 cm.  
- During treatment on a clinical trial, pulmonary lesions decreased in size and liver lesions ceased growing initially.  
- Approximately 1 year after trial initiation, pulmonary lesions remained stable, while a dominant liver lesion enlarged from 6.1-6.5 cm to 8 cm.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment consisted of surgery followed by radiation therapy.  
- She remained without evident cancer for 3 years after initial treatment.  
- Radiation to all recurrent sites was discussed at the time of metastatic recurrence, but this was not pursued.  
- She subsequently enrolled on a clinical trial of a targeted agent.  
- On trial therapy, she had a marked response in the lungs, with shrinkage of pulmonary metastases, and initial stabilization of liver disease.  
- After approximately 1 year on trial, isolated progression occurred in the liver while other disease sites remained stable.

[ current disease status ]: Oligoprogressive metastatic disease, with stable pulmonary metastases and isolated progression of a dominant liver lesion to 8 cm.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- She was described as very active and working full time at the time of metastatic recurrence.

reference_discussion.text: This one's a pretty quick case. And so this 53 year old lady with metastatic adenocystic carcinoma was diagnosed 4 years ago with intermediate grade. She was treated surgery, followed by radiation and had no cancer for 3 years. And then, unfortunately, the cancer came back in her left neck, her lungs, and actually kind of concerning for her liver. Couldn't say for sure. It was all quite small, below a centimeter, even hard to tell. She decided she was very active, works full time, didn't want radiation. We talked to her actually about treating with radiation to all the spots they saw. And unfortunately, 3 months later, there was new spots in the lungs. There was a liver spot that was now 6.1 centimeters, so very large. So, at that point, she enrolled onto a clinical trial of a targeted drug we had at our institution as well as other places. And she had a great response. Her lung spots all shrink. She was doing very, very well, and her liver spots stopped growing. And the issue is that about a year into this, Her lung spots, although stable, finally her liver started to grow, went from 6.1, 6.5 centimeters to up to 8 centimeters. And here's what a picture of that would look like. Here's before the clinical trial. and here is now a year later. And per the clinical trial, there's very tight rules. What you do under certain circumstances should have to come off the clinical trial. But now we're having the question, everything's stable except for this one liver lesion. So what do we do? And so throw this to you. If this was in your clinic, what would you do?

Yeah. You know, Again, with with 1 dominant lesion, so sometimes there's oligo metastases as we talked about. There's another concept that we're kind of or another scenario, which is oligo progression, which is patients that are benefiting. So, you know, whatever drug usually that they're on and then have 1 area that's causing problems. And so we do try to try to target that area. The liver is a hard area for what I do, radiation often, because you want to preserve the liver. For smaller lesions, we often think about SBRT. That's most common for gastrointestinal tumors, but we do sometimes do ablations and SBRT for adenoid cystic carcinoma as well. When lesions typically grow this size, we often consider other options because we can't do SBRT usually for lesions this size.
John, what's the size in a small like, what do you mean by small.

Yeah, it's usually, I mean, there's, it depends on the, to be honest, it depends on the normal liver. I mean, this, this, this, this is complicated because it's, it's away from, you know, it's kind of at the side of the liver, but it's also close to the stomach. And so it depends on the other organs that it's close to. Um, but usually once we start to, you know, 5 centimeters or larger in most locations is not really appropriate for SBRT. Even once, you know, in many locations when it's larger than about 3 centimeters, 3 to 5 centimeters, we really start kind of thinking about other options.
Thank you.

And in this case, as you were saying, was progressing in a single lesion. All the others were doing quite well. She wanted some time off therapy. And so we decided to treat this aggressively with radiation. There's actually a clinical trial that's available here regarding treatment of liver lesions, and so they treated it quite aggressively with different types of radiation in combination, which I won't go into because I don't presume to step on your toes there with all the types of radiation. But the result here was that she was able to handle that spot well, developed a result, no symptoms there, and had endotherapy for some time.

This approach was selected in the context of an available clinical trial for liver lesions, using combined radiation modalities, with the goal of controlling the progressing site and permitting time off systemic therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Hoarseness for approximately 3 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Left thyroid nodule with preoperative left vocal fold paralysis.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the left thyroid nodule was Bethesda III.

[ imaging findings ]: Laryngeal examination demonstrated left vocal fold paralysis with bowed vocal fold and glottic gap. CT imaging from skull base through upper chest showed an enhancing nodule in the posterior aspect of the left thyroid lobe, ipsilateral to the vocal fold paralysis, measuring approximately 1 cm. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined hypoechoic nodule in the lower pole/posterior capsule region of the left thyroid lobe, described as sizable and suspicious for neoplasm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing on the Bethesda III thyroid nodule showed no detected mutations.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial empiric anti-reflux therapy for hoarseness did not resolve symptoms.

[ current disease status ]: No long-term follow-up was available.

[ other clinical data ]: No palpable neck mass was present on examination. The patient later reported a severe COVID infection around the time the vocal fold paralysis developed. No prior iatrogenic cause of vocal fold paralysis was documented.

reference_discussion.text: Oh boy, that's completely false actually. But I'm David Schanke. I'm a head and neck surgeon at the University of Virginia. And now I can actually focus on bringing the talk up. Okay. So good morning to everyone. Thank you. It's an honor to be here and we'll go through these three cases. So the first one is a 45 year old male who presented with three years of a horse voice. And this was initially diagnosed as reflux and managed with anti-reflux therapy. without resolution. So he came in initially to see one of our laryngologists. He had no palpable neck mass and a normal TSH level, but his laryngeal examination demonstrated left vocal fold paralysis and the vocal fold was bowed. And he also had a glottic gap, which explained his hoarseness.

Kerry, can you start with me? I mean, obviously, this is a tumor board, and this is going to be some horrible tumor invading something. But in the bigger picture, when we see somebody with sort of vocal cord paralysis, how do you begin thinking about that structurally, Kerry?

Well, I'm blessed at my institution to have a voice center with a world famous laryngologist. So not everyone has this, but, but I would, you know, there are other reasons for vocal vocal fold paralysis, especially in a 45 year old. So obviously if you see a nail and a hammer, I'm a thyroid surgeon, but I think the initial thing would be evaluated biologist or your nose and throat doctor.

And Dave, let me pick on you. Three years worth of horse voice? Should that be making me think of something else or still could be thinking about tumor or that long history sway you one way or the other, David?

So when I saw him, I was a little less worried about an invasive process just because it had been going on for so long. That being said, you know, I think a thyroid cancer in the right location could do this and potentially be fairly slow growing. And then, of course, you always wonder, you know, when someone gives you this history, you know, exactly what the process was. So I don't think he initially underwent a laryngeal examination when he had hoarseness. He saw his primary doctor about it, was treated with, you know, anti-reflux therapy. And so the initial laryngeal examination didn't happen until sometime later. And so It was a little unclear to us whether this actually had been going on for three years or whether it was a more recent issue.

Kerry, let me come back to you, probably because I work at a cancer center and the only vocal cords I ever see is taken up by cancer somewhere. Our immediate thing is to chase the entire course of the nerve with CT from neck all the way down into the chest. In real world, outside of a cancer center, what sort of imaging do you do to kind of chase this or evaluate this?

Well, I mean, I think doing a, actually even Dr. Wirth does a scope in the office to look at these and evaluate it in real time. I know that some folks, sometimes I can get it on ultrasound too to see if they're functioning on ultrasound and see what it looks like on there. I do ultrasound on everyone because I'm looking at the thyroid obviously, but I think that's really important. And you can have iatrogenic vocal cord paralysis from what I understand. And so imaging for me, I prefer ultrasound for all of my patients because of if it is an aggressive, at least well-differentiated thyrocarcinoma, I don't want to be giving someone a huge dose of iodine in preparation for potential radioactive iodine.
Gotcha. All right, David, what kind of imaging did we go through here? And we'll, Jeff, look at these.

Right. So, right. We did, did as described. So we also like to do a CT scan of the sort of from the base of the skull through the upper chest, just to follow the entire course of the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves as described. In my own practice, I've also started to just get ultrasounds of the thyroid on these patients as well, because occasionally, you know, CT will miss something, but this was the patient's CT scan and they did note this enhancing nodule in the posterior aspect of the left thyroid lobe, which was the same side as the vocal fold paralysis. And then here is the ultrasound.
All right Ian, Jeff, we'll just let you talk through this as it's rolling through if you want to.

Sure. So this is a transverse image of the ultrasound. We started superiorly, we're heading inferiorly. And what we see along the lower pole of the left lobe is a well-defined hypochord nodule. It's sizable, it's got imaging features of a neoplasm until proven otherwise, given a type of echogenicity, and the location along the posterior capsule is a great fit for the initial presentation in the history of unilateral vocal cord injury and or hoarseness related to it. And it's well-defined, and oftentimes we cannot see extracapsular extent on ultrasound even when it exists. But this is extremely well-defined, but it's in the location that's worrisome.
Yeah. Go backwards one for me, David. Let me have Jeff look at the, it's never fair to look at a single cut on the CT scan, Jeff, but what are you thinking here?

Well, you know, we, we, we have a non-specific enhancing nodule. A lot of nodules that are, you know, cancers, we don't really rely on the enhancement pattern so much for thyroid nodules. A lot of cancers don't enhance at all there. hypotenuating, meaning low density. But there are plenty that do enhance. And this is extremely nonspecific. And this would lead to an ultrasound, given its size. It's up to a centimeter. And with the history, you would definitely go right to ultrasound and followed by an FNA biopsy under ultrasound guidance.

So Kerry, this nodule looks a little lateral. It certainly looks posterior. Where's the RLN running at this point? I mean, we're on the left-hand side. Is it closer to the TE groove or is it still behind the thyroid over there?

Well, it depends. You know, if it's, you know, large goiter for any reason, it can, it can move the nerve medially. But in general, it's right where we're looking at it. So this would definitely make me very concerned. And the other thing I did want to mention, getting back to what you said, is once in a while, people forget to ask about someone having cardiothoracic surgery or anything in the, in the chest, um, thymectomy that no offense to the thoracic surgeons, but they're not quite as alarmed with taking the recurrent laryngeal nerve. So that's an important thing to ask as well.
Okay. All right, David, let's move ahead with your evaluation.

All right, so we decided based on the imaging appearance on ultrasound and the vocal fold paralysis to perform an FNA. And that came back as Bethesda 3. And so we had a discussion as to whether it was worth sending mutational testing on this at this point.

Mara, what do you think here? I mean, the surgeons are telling you they're worried about this. We've got a nerve out on this side. Are we about to spend $3,000 and not use this data? Or are we going to use this? What are you thinking, Mara?

Well, I think in this case it's a little bit tricky because you're potentially considering surgery regardless because of the impact on the recurrent laryngeal nerve. But I do think molecular testing can be quite helpful in this setting, particularly to help gauge the level of suspicion and concern around this nodule itself, as well as potentially to help guide the extent of surgery, whether or not you want to consider doing a total thyroidectomy, particularly in the setting where you're really concerned already about that recurrent laryngeal nerve on the left side. So I do think actually the molecular testing would be valuable here and could help, though it may not necessarily prevent a surgery in this case.

Mike, can I jump in here regarding, I just want to say regarding the deciding based on the molecular test, the extent of surgery, I have really some reservation regarding that. We published a paper where we found out that 30% of patients with TIRT have benign, TIRT mutation have benign nodules. you know, follicular adenoma, oncocytic adenoma. We even had a case who had RAS, TERT, and I think another mutation, three mutations, and it was an oncocytic adenoma histologically. So, I'm not a big fan of basing extent of surgery on the basis of the molecular results.
Dr. King, guide that way. All right. So, Dr. Roth wanted it, and we do whatever the West Coast wants, David. So, what did we get?

So we, in fairness, we kind of did both. I think Dr. Roth's points are perfect. I mean, we sort of said to him, even if the molecular testing is negative, I don't think we're going to be comfortable with just watching this, but we went ahead and sent it, but also at the same time scheduled a surgery date. So we got the results back before we were in the operating room and we saw no mutations on the testing.
Ronnie, how does that help us? It's a lowish risk. What are you thinking here now? Are you asking me? Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. I mean, this is, I guess, an example. I mean, yeah, if you go by the BETESTA-3 and the mutation, the molecular result, logically, this is a low-risk tumor, but you know that it looks like the imaging is different. This is really, again, proof that what we do at Memorial, and we can ask Dr. Shah, that we go more by the imaging and the clinical appearance to assess the extent of surgeries by far. better than just deciding on the basis of the mutational profile.
All right, Carrie, what's our next step here?

So, I kind of agree in this situation. Obviously, I have a long conversation with the patient regarding, you know, the risks of surgery, the morbidity, potential bilateral nerve injuries, right? Because that's a serious concern here. We don't have, I would also in this patient, send a calcitonin, a serum calcitonin. We're going to get into that conversation, I'm sure, is a whole other Pandora's box. But we have, because there are some misclassifications from final aspiration. But I would likely start with just the left because that's the the it's a young assuming young healthy patient who can tolerate a second surgery if needed and to get a definitive diagnosis and hopefully allow that nerve to recover. So I would start with the left if I see any lymph nodes in the operating room. I use a nerve monitor so I would have a better assessment of whether or not you know, where along the nerve course, you know, if it's distal to that, if the nerve still functioning and things like that. So I'd learn a lot more information in the operating room, but I personally would not start with a total.
And if there was just gross invasion, just of the nerve, you'd be, you'd stop with a lobectomy.

Keeping these questions very simple here. So that decision in the operating room, you're asking, do you take the nerve or not? Right? I think that's the question you're asking. I think if the nerve is for me, if the nerve is totally, the tumor is totally encasing there, which is unlikely in this case, given the imaging, then you take the nerve. If you can sharply dissect the tumor off of the nerve, then we don't even know the diagnosis at this point. So I would err towards leaving the nerve in place and sharply dissecting the tumor off of the nerve if needed. I got you.

David, what really happened? So yeah, all great points. And we were, we were prepared for kind of the worst case scenario, which would be nerve involvement. And one of my laryngologists was, the one who sent the patient to me was on standby just in case we needed to do a laryngeal re-enervation. But what we did, intra-ops, we started by finding the vagus nerve in the carotid sheath before we did anything with the thyroid and using nerve monitoring, stimulated the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath, which actually had a response, which to me, indicated that the nerve was intact. And because we had an intact signal through the nerve, I didn't see any reason to do a reinnervation procedure because those procedures don't give the nerve or the vocal cord movement. They just give a tone, which I expected that an electrical signal through the nerve should already be doing. I didn't really see that a reinnervation would improve the voice outcome. As Dr. Cunningham pointed out, at the beginning, occasionally patients can get what we call like an idiopathic vocal fold paralysis, which is essentially unexplained by any, you know, genic injury or, you know, prior intubation, which would potentially cause a crico-retinoid joint fixation. So, we just sort of chalk this up to maybe an idiopathic cause. And further questioning, he did report that around the time of his vocal fold paralysis, he had a pretty severe episode of COVID. So I don't know if that had anything to do with it, but this was our final pathology from the nodule.
One question before Ronnie reads this. So, interoperatively, David, was the nodule on the nerve or near the nerve, or was it completely unrelated?
It was right next to it, you know, as would be suggested by the ultrasound imaging, but there was nothing. I mean, it was a very easy nerve dissection. Nodule was totally contained within the gland.
So, interoperatively, we had a nodule that was just laying beside the nerve, not invading it, as far as you could tell. Correct. Gross exam. I got you. Ronnie, what are we looking at?

So yeah, so the first thing we look at, at least myself, when we look at the thyroid section, is microstaging. Basically, how invasive the tumor here, and here the news are good. It's an encapsulated tumor. It looks, based on this slide, that there is no invasion. So that already puts the patient in a much better category as far as tumor is concerned. Now here on high power, you see a actually follicular and solid growth pattern. And here you see some of the nuclear features of papillocasinoid. They're very, they're mild, like you have some large nuclei, some are irregular. You can see even grooves. So now, so if I assume the tumor, these are representative, so the tumor is an encapsulated non-invasive tumor. Now the solid growth pattern, I cannot judge the amount, but if it is less than 30% solid growth pattern, then this will fit the criteria for a non-invasive follicular tyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear feature, what we used to call in the past encapsulated follicular variants, non-invasive. And based on our studies, if this is the case, this is a tumor that do not recur if treated by lobectomy. In all the cases that we had, we never had a recurrence. And then now coming back, the cytology and the molecular are consistent within the this particular scenario. But again, I repeat that I don't think it's a good idea to base the extent of surgery on the molecular profile.
So, Maria, what do you tell people when they come back and they have this NIFT P tumor and they've already been on Dr. Google and GP Chat and everything we've ever heard of?

Well, you know, I mean, I think I talk about the fact that it was appropriate to have surgery, right? One of the first questions I get is why did I have surgery for this and could I have avoided it? And that I, you know, I talk about this can only really be defined on histopathology, that we can't confirm that it's NFP without being able to look at the entire capsule. So it was very important to go to surgery to have this definitively treated. But thankfully, given the extremely low risk for recurrence, this is a pre-malignant lesion. It does not actually show evidence of being invasive or having metastases or recurrence. And therefore, our surveillance for this is generally with a post-op ultrasound and periodic ultrasound, keeping their thyroid hormone in a normal range, but there's no rule for TSH suppression. So it's really the best outcome the patient could hope for in terms of a low risk, very low risk premalignant lesion.
Beautiful. Carrie, we still got a vocal cord paralysis. Where do we go from here now?

Well, you watch and wait a little bit. I would, I would have already had my fantastic laryngologist on board and even immediately following either before a following surgery to reevaluate them postoperatively once they're fully awake. So the anesthesia has worn off, but there's such great, you know, I love Ristalin injections. If someone's really having difficulty with phonating. depending on where the cord is, just where it's residing. Patients with grave disease often have nerve, you know, temporary nerve injuries. So I'm, I'm hopeful. I don't, I actually don't know in this case, I forgot with the slides, but, give it some time to recover, you know, months and months. And then if needed, if it's still difficult for the patient to phonate or if they're aspirating, things like that, there are other things they can do to medialize that cord. But I would give it some time, a solid, you know, four to six months.
Awesome. Dave, finish this one up for me. So how's she doing?
Yeah, great points.

I mean, we don't, unfortunately, all of these cases are from within the last month or two, so I don't have any long-term follow-up information for you, but our laryngologist felt exactly the same way. You know, we've got a nerve that's stimulating, so let's maybe give it some time and see if it recovers. He is not interested in sort of temporizing measures like an injection. He wants the one shot, fix it. So our laryngologist is planning a formal vocal fold medialization from an external approach, but wants to give it at least six months to see if it has some recovery now that the tumor's been removed. So we'll see. More to follow on that one. Very good. Fantastic. All right, let's go to case two. All right, so this next one is a 45 year old woman with a history of thyroid cancer. She had a PT1B, N1B, M0 papillary carcinoma. She had a total thyroidectomy, right central neck dissection, a right level 2, 3, and 4 dissection, and a left 3 and 4 dissection at an outside institution, and then got postoperative radioactive iodine. And this was about a year and a half prior to her initial visit with me. So from that initial surgery, they noted a multifocal PTC. The largest tumor was in the right side, and it was one and a half centimeters. But there was also a cancer within the isthmus and left lobe. There were 13 out of 41 nodes involved, the largest being 3.9 centimeters, and there was extra null extension for that. And there was also molecular testing done on that specimen, which demonstrated BRAF E600E mutation. So she got 152 millicuries of post-operative radioactive iodine, and this was the result of her radioiodine scan at the time. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 35-year-old premenopausal woman from Fortaleza, Brazil. Previously healthy. No family history of breast cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable right breast lump in January 2013.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, triple-negative, clinical stage II, cT2N0M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the right breast lesion showed invasive breast carcinoma, grade 3, triple-negative, Ki-67 70%, with no lymphovascular invasion and no perineural invasion. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of a right axillary lymph node was negative for malignant cells.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial breast ultrasound showed a BI-RADS 3 cystic lesion in the right breast measuring 2.6 x 1.5 cm at the 10 o’clock position, 1.1 cm from the nipple. Mammography was BI-RADS 1. PET-CT showed a right breast lesion measuring 2.8 x 2.6 cm and a right axillary lymph node measuring 1.3 x 1.2 cm with SUV 5.5. Breast MRI showed a right breast lesion measuring 2.7 x 2.6 x 2.4 cm in the upper quadrants and did not detect axillary adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline genetic testing performed in November 2013 showed a BRCA2 pathogenic variant. Genetic testing had initially been declined before treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered from March to September 2013 with an ACT regimen. This was followed by oncoplastic breast-conserving surgery using a round-block technique and sentinel lymph node biopsy in October 2013. Adjuvant radiotherapy was delivered to the right breast with 3D technique: 50 Gy to the breast with a 10 Gy boost, from November 2013 to January 2014.

[ other clinical data ]: The right axillary node assessment was discordant across imaging modalities: PET-CT was positive, MRI did not identify axillary disease, and ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy was negative for malignant cells.

So as many probably are familiar with, there's some data emerging that platinum agents in the neoadjuvant setting for triple negative disease may afford better outcomes or at least higher pathologic complete response rates. We have not routinely recommended, or at least I haven't, platinum for all young women who are triple negative in the absence of a positive BRCA or other types of germline mutations that are in the BRCA pathway. And that said, I think that there is a role, an emerging role again, for doing or adding some sort of platinum reagent to the neoadjuvant chemotherapy regimen for these women. So in this particular case, had she received the diagnosis of having a BRCA2 mutation, I think I would have considered adding carboplatin to her taxane, as some studies have suggested. Or if she had had a really striking family history, because I know in some parts of the world, BRCA testing isn't readily available. She did not, so it's a little bit hard to say. But again, this is a This is an ever-changing paradigm, so we don't really know. She achieved pathologic complete response, so that makes one feel better that she did quite fine with the retinib that she had. At the same time, we also know that pathologic complete response is not a perfect surrogate, and in some series, maybe up to 20% of patients will still relapse despite achieving PCR. So I think I would have been okay with this, but had I known the BRCA2 information ahead of time, I would have considered adding carboplatin.

I think I'm going to say, and I hope I'm still right, that at MGH we also don't routinely give platinum automatically to ultra-full negative young patients, but we do exactly the way Ben says, for patients who are BRCA positive or for patients in the absence of BRCA testing with a very strong family history but otherwise we don't give it. Actually, I'd like to ask Charlotte Gale. Charlotte, would you like to comment on the surgical approach because of discordant pet findings in the axilla? The second question here. Would you like to say something? It's just that this is Charlotte Gale.
Is it working? Yes.
Yeah, we can hear you. Thanks.

I think you would start based on your physical exam. If you have any suspicious nose that you can feel, you should try to biopsy them. And we always put a clip in anything that we biopsy so that we know which lymph nodes were positive at the time for clinical staging. And then after we give the chemo, we restage them as a Y, C, N, whatever. And if it is lymph node negative, then we'll do an extended sentinel lymph node biopsy, which is the radioactive tracer, the blue dye, as well as the clip itself. And we'll get a specimen radiograph to verify the clip. So I think that in the absence of the BRCA mutation, breast conservation with sentinel node is very reasonable in how I would proceed.
Great. Sima, do you want to say something?

Right, so I just want to add that ultrasound is actually a very useful imaging technique in this setting. It will show suspicious lymph nodes and facilitates a corneal biopsy and the placement of the clip as Shola mentioned. So the PET scan, of course, has limited resolution, but in this case it showed the node and the MRI didn't. The MRI is not nearly as sensitive for a diseased lymph node, so it's not a very reliable test for diseased lymph nodes. I think with a positive PET scan, I would certainly have looked for a lymph node with ultrasound and tried to biopsy it that way. And as Alphonse will probably elaborate on, that makes a difference to the radiation treatment planning in particular. The question I have is that the sequence of events seems to be that the patient consented to her BRCA test following surgery but prior to radiation. And so I wonder, was prophylactic mastectomy discussed at that point? Because the reconstruction, if she decides for it in the future, will certainly not be optimal given the use of radiotherapy on the treated side.
Thank you. There's a good bridge to Alphonse making some comments about this.

Right. So I want to go back to the issue of this lymph node based on the story presented here. So we have a PET scan positive, an MRI negative, and we have a triple negative tumor in a young woman. So it's likely that this lymph node was positive. And I would lean toward assuming it was. and chemotherapy, and this is happening 20 to 40 percent of the time. This will make a big difference from a radiation perspective, and although I would say the standard of treatment at this point in this scenario, assuming it was positive, which turned negative, is to give regular radiation. And this is a question raised in a large NSADP B51 R2G trial. which include women who had documented positive lymph nodes with FNA or with a biopsy. And it's nice also to put a clip there, like was mentioned. And after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, it is documented that these lymph nodes became negative. So the patient responded very well to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. These women will be randomized between breast radiation only, as this patient received, versus breast radiation and the original lymph node radiation including the supraclav and the IMC. So the question is actually raised in the radiation oncology field. But until we have an answer to that, I usually lean toward giving the original lymph node, especially based on how aggressive this tumor is.
And we will circulate details of the study of B51, NSABP B51, after the tumor board. Any other insights into this case before we move on? Anybody want to speak?
I guess the BRCA issue here is that we discussed whether the patient will have now bilateral methadone. It's a good point, yeah.

So what do you think about it? Does anybody have a… Let's go back to Charlotte again. What do you think about prophylactic mastectomy in light of the fact that she's now BRCA2 positive after her neoadjuvant mastectomy?

Well, I think that we know that her risk is going to be high if she's a BRCA carrier. The penetrance is different in every family, but we know that her risk is high with that mutation. So she should be counseled about risk-reducing surgery, not only for the breast, but as well as for her ovaries and whatever her fertility status is. you know, they need to talk to her about that, but, you know, the timing, I mean, she can get, the bilateral mastectomy is not going to change the cure for this breast cancer. It's just going to change the chance of her future genetic BRCA-related cancers in the future, so.

So actually, that's a point, Charlotte, thank you. That's a point I'd like to raise. You know, the role of preventative breast cancer surgery or medical therapy is diluted by the prognosis of the patient with first primary cancer. So if a patient after neoadjuvant therapy of a unilateral breast cancer has say like 10 positive nodes or 5 positive nodes post neoadjuvant therapy, It calls into question the mathematical modeling, the cost-effectiveness of performing a contralateral mastectomy. Even though she's at tremendous risk, what is the balance, you know, what on balance is the likelihood that she'll die from a second cancer as opposed to her first cancer? So I don't know whether you ever consider, Steve, do you ever think about that or do you just give her the benefit of the doubt and do prophylaxis anyway?

No, I think you make a very good point and that's something that should be considered every time. The burden of risk posed by the index cancer is a very important part of this sort of balancing. In this particular woman, though, she's had a complete pathologic response with neoadjuvant chemotherapies. and she had a smallish tumor to begin with, and so on. So I think with her, the risk-benefit balance favors prophylactic mastectomy somewhat, but there are certainly women who decline it, and in that case, she needs to be followed with a bilateral MRI. That would be another important component of her surveillance going forward. Her oophorectomy, of course, will decrease her risk of developing new primary cancers, particularly since she's BRCA2, since the benefit of prophylactic oophorectomy in reducing breast cancer risk seems to be somewhat larger for that group. So, prophylactic oophorectomy is something that should be pursued strongly with her, particularly as she gets close to 40. Prophylactic mastectomy is certainly something that should be discussed. And in someone who has, who's identified to be BRCA2 positive, or 1 for that matter, prior to radiation, you know, that's a useful window because the radiation does alter the reconstruction results.

I think the point I'm raising, thank you Seema, I think the point I'm raising is the issue of mathematical modeling around competing risks is a complicated business. I've had the benefit of sitting in with statisticians discussing this. I don't think we clinical oncologists have an accurate way of counseling our patients on competing risks. If a patient had non-small cell lung cancer two years ago, does she need you know, why much preventative for another cancer does she need? What's her real cumulative prognosis between a new cancer plus the old cancer? So it's like bilateral breast cancer. There's a competing risk and it depends on timing and stage and all kinds of factors. I do think there's an absence in clinical practice of an easy to apply, if such a thing exists, mathematical model of competing risks. You know, we all see papers on this about competing risks of if you've had a heart attack in the last five years, is it worth getting chemo for your breast cancer, and so on and so forth. I think competing risks is a complicated business about patient's age, different diseases, competing for the patient's health. And I think that this is just, I just raised it here because it's a very glaring example of competing risks. But thank you very much, Seema. I think we should go on to Yuli's case if we can, in the interest of time. So Yuli, we're getting ready for you to present your case, please if you could turn your microphone on from Mexico City.

Given the PET-positive axillary node despite negative biopsy and the aggressive tumor biology, regional nodal irradiation would be favored in addition to breast irradiation until further evidence clarifies management. After identification of a BRCA2 mutation, counseling regarding risk-reducing bilateral mastectomy and prophylactic oophorectomy was recommended, with bilateral breast MRI surveillance if prophylactic mastectomy is deferred.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Bulky ileal mass presenting with initially inoperable disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Ileal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy findings were consistent with GIST. Tumor showed c-KIT positivity. Necrosis was present. No further histologic differentiation data were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Disease was described as bulky at presentation and initially considered inoperable. No further imaging details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mutation profiling for GIST-associated alterations was negative. KIT mutations tested in exons 9, 11, 13, and 17 were negative. PDGFRA mutation was negative. BRAF mutation was negative. Other tested mutations were negative. SDH deficiency had not been assessed by immunohistochemistry.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant imatinib was started because of initially inoperable bulky disease. Imatinib was administered for approximately 1 month. Surgery was subsequently performed after mutation profiling showed no detectable mutation. Imatinib was discontinued prior to surgery. Response to imatinib was not established; sample size was reported as unchanged over that interval.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after resection of ileal GIST.

[ other clinical data ]: Tumor content for molecular testing was reported as adequate. An adequate mutation panel was reported to have been performed, although SDH deficiency testing by IHC had not been done.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented to the emergency department with worsening chest pain over 3 days.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma follicular variant, with extensive distant metastatic disease involving chest wall/ribs, right atrium/superior vena cava, pleural/posterior cul-de-sac region, multiple vertebral bodies, left humeral head, spine, and iliac crest.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Core biopsy of the chest wall mass was consistent with metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.  
- Thyroid ultrasound-guided biopsy of a 3.5 cm solid thyroid nodule (TI-RADS 4) showed papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular variant.  
- Histology of metastatic and thyroid lesions showed follicular architecture consistent with well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT demonstrated a 6.5 cm mass at the right manubriocostal junction protruding through the chest wall.  
- CT showed tracheal narrowing to 7 mm associated with thyroid goiter.  
- CT demonstrated a mass in the right atrium/superior vena cava region.  
- CT demonstrated a large left posterior cul-de-sac mass.  
- Multiple lytic lesions were present in the vertebral bodies.  
- A lytic lesion was present in the left humeral head.  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a 3.5 cm solid thyroid nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BRAF immunostain on chest wall biopsy was negative.  
- Molecular testing of the thyroid lesion showed no BRAF mutation.  
- NRAS mutation was detected.  
- TERT mutation was detected.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Ki-67 proliferation index was reported on pathology assessment; exact percentage was not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Anticoagulation was started after development of pulmonary emboli during workup.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Newly diagnosed widely metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma at initial presentation, with disease involving the chest wall/ribs, right atrium/superior vena cava, pleural/posterior cul-de-sac region, multiple vertebral bodies, left humeral head, spine, and iliac crest, and tracheal narrowing associated with thyroid goiter.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No notable past medical history was reported at presentation.  
- Physical examination showed an obvious protruding mass over the right chest.  
- Pulmonary emboli developed during diagnostic workup.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, thank you. I'm Rick Payne. I'm from McGill University in Montreal, Canada. I work in the Department of Otolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery. And before getting started, I'd like to say I have no conflicts of interest to report. I'd like to thank the Thank Foundation for inviting me to present these cases today. It's also a privilege to work with all of you, specialists, world experts on this topic. And so thank you. I hope that we have a great session together. And last but not least, I want to thank these individuals for helping put this together. As you all know, everything we do is collaborative. And especially at our center, McGill, this is how we do it. And so let's jump into the first case, if everyone's ready. Please cut me off at any time if you have any questions or comments. It's a 53-year-old male who presented to the emergency department with chest pain that had been getting worse over three days. There was no notable past medical history, and he had no other complaints. On exam, there was a very obvious protruding mass over the right chest. The emergency physicians worked him up, and they did a CT scan, and then they called my team, and this is what we found. Does anyone want to comment on this, or should I go through this?
Go ahead and go through it first Rick and then then we'll talk about it once we get the initial presentation.

Perfect. So this is, as you see here there's a mass coming through the chest wall and that's what was protruding through the end and lower down, there's a cut here you see the part of the thyroid, you see the trachea being narrowed somewhat. And then we have this and me as a thyroid surgeon, I don't know this part of the body so well. I just had our radiologist tell us that this was in the right atrium or superior vena cava. And so on the reports. They tell us that there's a six and a half centimeter right manubial costal junction mass, as I showed before, something in the right atrium, and a big left posterior cul-de-sac mass. And of note, the trachea was narrowed at seven millimeters at thyroid goiter. In the vertebral bodies, there were many lytic lesions and lytic lesions in the left humeral head. It looks like something that I actually know what it looks like.
Let me pause for just a second. Go back for me. Margie, it's totally not fair to ask you to read slides off a video, but initial impression looking at this?
Well, so I know that's well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma. And I know from experience this could be a widely invasive follicular carcinoma, or it could be follicular variant of PTC.

Well, you know, this is, it's okay. It's a very extreme, but yet classic example if it is follicular carcinoma, widely invasive follicular carcinoma. People, you know, even though this is part of a well-differentiated thyroid cancer family, it's, you know, a thing that follicular carcinoma comes to diagnosis with a bone metastasis, maybe not a metastasis protruding from the chest, but this is a known thing. And it's also a known thing that PTC follicular variant can behave like a widely invasive follicular carcinoma.

Yeah, so this is this is you're guessing from this presentation lots of bone mass that sort of stuff we're going to have some sort of follicular lesion probably with widespread vascular invasion and that's what this is going to turn out to be. Okay, so that's what we're thinking. All right, where are we going.

All right, let's see. So we have our bodies of the chest wall. This is the actual pathology report from Dr. Pustateri. He's one of our thyroid and head and neck pathologists at McGill. And you see here in red highlighted consistent with metastatic well-differentiated thyroid cancer, as Marge was saying. And we do IHC, or we've been doing it for a couple of years now, just looking with a BRAF stain. and it was negative for BRAF. We also do a KI-67. I don't know if all institutions are doing that right now. We do that fairly regularly now, just to have an idea of how aggressive it is. And for us, a KI-67 less than 5%, we're happy with that. 10 to 15% is a little bit aggressive, nothing crazy, but a little bit.
It's beyond what's normally expected.

So, um, if following on what Margie was talking about, are you surprised this is not BRAF or what, what mutation would, would you be guessing here? I mean, I thought all of these bad cancers were BRAF and tall cells. Does this surprise you here? Are you okay with this?

What's interesting is how we change our mind as things go along. So at first, if we've known it's thyroid cancer beforehand, we would have thought about anaplastic thyroid cancer, about poorly differentiated thyroid cancer, because it's so aggressive. We would need some more information about the history, how fast everything happened, if we could get some information. But then, we saw the biopsy. And on the biopsy, we saw follicles. We didn't see solid pattern. We didn't see anaplastic cells. We saw follicles. It looks like a thyroid. And this is when you, like Margaret said, it looks like a well-differentiated thyroid cancer. And then you think about other mutations, especially RAS mutation, which is typical to to follicular or follicular variant. And it causes us to be slightly optimistic about the chances of radioactive iodine, because if we see follicles, there's some production of thyroid hormones. So maybe, maybe we can be optimistic about some efficacy of radioactive iodine.

George, part of the decision making in what we do or don't do always is what's the likelihood that radioactive iodine is going to be helpful, right? He's got big disease that needs to be taken care of. But from what you know right now, do you think there's going to be a role for radioactive iodine and part of the process somewhere?

Well, I think maybe if you consider removing the thyroid, I think radioactive iodine would be considered. But I think at the present time, maybe an FDG PET-CT upfront would be interesting also to evaluate how active the glucose metabolism is and to predict poor prognosis.

Right, and it would help you understand likelihood of RAI-avidity and likelihood of Bruce having to be involved. Because if we had 1,000 places with SUVs of 30 that were really high, that may rethink, right? Ashok, obviously, everybody's thinking about surgery on this one. But before you talk about the surgery, he's got meds everywhere. I mean, when you look at that big picture, how do you think about getting him started and then headed towards surgery?

I think that's a great question. And one of the things we need to see and decide is, number one, He's young man, he's 54. So we cannot just say, you know, it is a big, big difference between 84 and 54, number one. Number two, probably this disease has been there for a long time. That's why you've got sternal met. For some reasons, follicular cancer with a vascular invasion or a capsular invasion, I don't know what is the link, but we, that sternal mets are not uncommon in thyroid cancer.
