case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent right knee pain in October 2022.

[ diagnosis ]: Osteoblastic osteosarcoma of the right distal femur, initially diagnosed in 2009. Recurrent high-grade pleomorphic spindle cell sarcoma in the right thigh/femur region in 2022, characterized as recurrent osteosarcoma. Metastatic pulmonary disease was identified on staging imaging. Segmental pulmonary embolism was diagnosed in January 2023.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical resection of the distal right femur mass in 2009 showed 35% necrosis. Biopsy of the new right thigh mass in October 2022 showed high-grade pleomorphic spindle cell sarcoma, best characterized as recurrent osteosarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- October 2022 radiograph followed by CT approximately 3 weeks later demonstrated a new 8.3 cm soft tissue mass in the vastus intermedius muscle.  
- Staging imaging after biopsy demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules, considered metastatic disease.  
- PET scan demonstrated uptake in the right femur mass and pulmonary metastases.  
- Subsequent surveillance/staging imaging showed enlargement of the femur mass, consistent with progression.  
- March 2023 imaging after total right femur replacement showed no recurrence in the femur and a mixed response in the lungs.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
Liquid biopsy performed after enrollment in the TRAC study showed:  
- TP53 splice-site mutation at approximately 0.5% variant allele frequency  
- No microsatellite instability detected  
- Tumor mutational burden not elevated  
- Tumor fraction not elevated

Tumor tissue profiling showed:  
- Microsatellite stable  
- Low tumor mutational burden  
- TP53 alteration present in tissue  
- KIT amplification  
- PDGFRA amplification  
- KDR amplification  
- TSC1 alteration  
- CDKN2A/B loss

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2009: Treated on protocol with methotrexate, doxorubicin, and cisplatin.  
- Underwent surgical resection of the distal right femur mass.  
- After resection, came off study and received cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, cisplatin, etoposide, and high-dose methotrexate.  
- Developed doxorubicin-associated cardiotoxicity.  
- Followed with surveillance imaging for 4 years after resection.  
- 2014: Right femur implant placement.  
- After recurrence/metastatic disease in 2022, treated with ifosfamide and etoposide.  
- Sustained a right femur fracture.  
- January 2023: Inferior vena cava filter placed because of bleeding complications limiting anticoagulation for pulmonary embolism.  
- January 2023: Underwent total right femur replacement.  
- From March 2023 to present: Treated with gemcitabine and docetaxel.  
- May 2023: Enrolled in the TRAC study.

[ current disease status ]: As of the latest update, she remained on gemcitabine and docetaxel. Postoperative imaging in March 2023 showed no local recurrence in the femur and mixed response of pulmonary metastases. She was reported to be clinically doing well on current therapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Right femur fracture occurred in the setting of recurrent disease.  
- Shortness of breath in January 2023 prompted CT, which demonstrated a new segmental pulmonary embolism.  
- Age at initial sarcoma diagnosis was in adolescence.

reference_discussion.text: So I'll tell you about our patient. She's a 28-year-old lady who was first diagnosed back in 2009 with osteoblastic osteosarcoma. She was started on a trial of methotrexate, adromycin, and cisplatin. She then underwent a surgical resection of a distal right femur mass, and that showed 35% necrosis. After that resection, She came off study and was treated with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, cisplatin, etoposide, and high-dose methotrexate, but then developed cardiotoxicity from the doxorubicin. And she had been followed. for four years with just surveillance imaging after the resection. She then in 2014 had a right femur implant placed and she continued beyond surveillance. And then about eight years later, she developed new pain. in her right knee, which was October of 22. That prompted an x-ray and then CAT scan about three weeks later that showed a new 8.3 centimeter soft tissue mass in the vastus intermedius muscle. That prompted a biopsy two days later that showed high-grade pleomorphic splendocell sarcoma, which was best characterized as a recurrent osteosarcoma from her eight years history. From that, she had a staging scan that showed multiple pulmonary nodules, believed to be metastatic disease, and a PET scan that also showed the right femur mass, and then the pulmonary mets lit up as well. She was started on a vasfomide and a topazide. She also had a fracture in her right femur as well again. And she developed shortness of breath in January, had a new CAT scan that was read as having a new segmental pulmonary embolism. And then a subsequent staging scan or surveillance scan that showed a femur mass was growing. So she was having some progression. She had an IVC filter placed because she had complications with bleeding, so she couldn't get beyond anticoagulation. She had underwent surgery in January of this year and had a total right femur replacement. And then a new scan in March showed that she continued to have this mixed response in her lungs, but no recurrence in her femur. March of this year until present, she's been on gemcitabine and docetaxel, and then May was enrolled in the TRAC study.

So thank you, Jacob. I don't know if anybody has any questions about the history. Basically, young person with a long history of osteosarcoma, which is a rare cancer, and with a lot of prior therapy, a lot of therapy of every type, surgery, and a lot of different types of chemotherapy. We will move on. And this is actually what usually happens. We get the liquid biopsy results first because all you have to do is draw a blood specimen. And for tissue biopsy, it takes longer because you have to find the tissue and ship the tissue and so forth. So Dr. Julia Albin, if you want to discuss the findings here. Thank you.

So just to orient everybody, a liquid biopsy is a peripheral blood sample that takes advantage of the fact that small amounts of DNA from both your normal cells and tumor cells are shed and are present in the plasma component. So we utilize this feature in the TRACK study to look for any information about the mutations that are present in the patient's tumor that we can make treatment decisions on. So this assay assesses over 324 different cancer-causing genes, looking for all types of alterations in those, including point mutations, insertion deletions, We can pick up fusions and copy number alterations in some of the genes. We also assess complex biomarkers such as microsatellite instability status, MSI, and can make an assessment of potentially the antigenicity of the tumor by the tumor mutation burden. So, as Dr. Kurzweil said, the patient was enrolled in May, this blood was drawn in June, and we had her results about a week later, ready to... ready to discuss at the tumor board. And so what we found was, first of all, there's another biomarker that we've come to report on and we think is very useful, which is called tumor fraction. So remember I said in the plasma, it's a mixture of DNA from normal cells and tumor cells. So if more than 10% of the DNA fragments are coming from the tumor, then we would know that the tumor fraction was elevated in this particular case. And that would give us confidence that there had been an abundance of tumor DNA to assess. Here, we didn't see it elevated. We also did not detect microsatellite instability or an elevated tumor mutation burden. What we did detect was a TP53 splice site mutation. Now, in a liquid biopsy, as we heard from Dr. Schwartz-Levine earlier about interpretation of P53 mutations, in the blood biopsy, we're thinking, is this coming from the tumor? Is this coming from CHIP, which is also one of the components that sheds DNA into the liquid biopsy, or is it potentially coming from the germline? With osteosarcoma being one of the kinds of tumors that are associated with P53 germline mutations. So in this case, the variant allele frequency of this was approximately 0.5%. So this is a very low allele fraction, and so not suggestive of it coming from the germline, and more consistent with either clonal hematopoiesis or the tumor. Luckily, in this trial, we get the tumor tissue for cases like this to help us sort out that final question about tumor-derived versus clonal hematopoiesis-derived, particularly in an osteosarcoma where P53 mutations are the most common alteration that we see in this tumor type.

So thank you. So that is one of the issues with liquid biopsies is that there is contamination by clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential that comes from the blood, not from the tumor. And as Dr. Elvin noted, The thing against this being CHIP would be the patient is young. That's usually something that occurs in older people. But you can see CHIP in younger people, too. But the tissue really helps tell the story there. So usually, as soon as we get results, we do a molecular tumor board. because we want to get something back to the patient. And we give some initial suggestions. And then those may be revised when we get the tissue results. They're often revised. So the only thing that we had here was a P53. And P53 is a tumor suppressor gene that is not considered targetable. But one thing we know about P53 is that it upregulates the VEGF, VEGFR, vascular endothelial growth factor axis. And we've published several papers showing that patients that have P53 mutations respond to inhibitors of VEGF or VEGFR. And other groups have published on this as well, including Kohler, who published specifically in P53 altered sarcomas. And including a group that was cooperative groups, Sloan Kettering, about P53 and gynecologic cancers, all showing that P53 makes tumors more susceptible to VEGF, VEGFR inhibitors. So when we had the initial discussion about this patient, the recommendation was to give pazopanib. Pazopanib is a small molecule inhibitor that is approved for sarcomas. And it does a lot of different things. But one of the things it does, it's a very potent VEGFR inhibitor. So, that was our first recommendation that went out with our first MTB. And again, if anybody has any questions, happy to entertain them. So, then, we found, And we got the tissue back. And now the tissue turned out, as it often does, not always, but often, to be very informative. And it showed, again, that the patient was microsatellite stable, tumor mutational burden low. This is important for immunotherapy. microsatellite status, unstable or high tumor mutational burden, predisposes to immunotherapy responses. But now the patient had a whole group of alterations. So the first thing that I think is very important to notice, which I tried to allude to in my previous talk. This patient has seven alterations. So, how lucky are we sometimes when we give a single drug that we actually get responses? But if people want to ask, why doesn't everybody respond? Well, the answer is sitting in front of you. It's because there's more than one driver. And probably we need to counteract as many drivers as possible. So the other thing that this tissue told us is that the p53 was not CHIP. It was there in the tissue. The same p53 mutation was there in the tissue. And so we have a scientist, Pradeep Deed, that works with us. And he's not here today, but he always prepares these beautiful diagrams of what is going on. in the patient's tumor. And he tries to put it together with what drugs can be used. So it turns out that KIT, PGFR-alpha, and KDR were amplified. And there's a good reason that they're co-amplified. They're all on the same amplicon. They're all on the same region of chromosome 4q12. That's the long arm of chromosome 4. And so there are drugs that can hit all three targets. Pazopanib is one of them, but it doesn't hit these three targets very strongly. There's another drug called oxitinib. which is approved for different cancers, like lung cancer, which actually hits all three targets very strongly with a very low IC50. And excitinib is also a VEGFR inhibitor. So even though pazopanib is still a good suggestion, excitinib is probably a better suggestion because it's a more potent drug against these particular targets. Patient has a TSC1 alteration. And TSC1 activates the PI3 kinase AKT mTOR pathway. And drugs that are approved, there are several of these. But the two that are mentioned are Everolimus and Tempserolimus that downregulate the mTOR pathway. Now, remember, none of these drugs are actually approved for osteosarcoma. It's a rare disease. And what is approved is... chemotherapy, and then pazopanib is approved for sarcomas. CDKN2AB loss, this patient does have CDKN2AB loss. And there are several FDA-approved drugs. There's actually three. target this abnormality. One is palbocyclob, one is abemocyclob, and rubocyclob. So, there's three. He mentions abemocyclob here, but it could be any one of the three drugs. So, now we're beginning to think about how do we co-target all of these alterations at the same time. So, based on the tissue results, the preferred match therapy recommendation was for exitinib, which was preferred, or pisopinib. Pasopinib, the advantage is it's approved for the indication. The disadvantage is it's not as strong an inhibitor, as I mentioned. And in combination with a CDK4-6 inhibitor, such as Bebaciclib, And we'll show you in a little while a case report that's very similar of a patient that we treated in this way at UCSD. And we also, in order to maintain safety, we recommend starting both drugs at 50% of the dose, and then titrating up to patient tolerance. And this is what we did in the iPREDICT study at UCSD, which was the precursor to the TRACK study, and again, found to be a very safe way of dosing drugs. And then, if a third drug is to be added, we would add an mTOR inhibitor such as temsorolimus or everolimus, again, reducing the dose significantly, at least at the beginning. So, that would be the recommendations that came out of the MTB as far a customized combination. So, Dr. Nakanjam, did you want to talk a little bit about dosing?

Sure. For iPredict and for our TRACK study, as Dr. Kershrock mentioned, it's really important to start at lower doses. But there's a fine line between a super low dose and one that's efficacious. So we needed information to guide us on what safe starting doses would be. So Dr. Kershrock and I did several studies over the past few years, which are listed in the references here, which looked at clinical trials and dosing combinations from phase 1, 2, and 3 data. And these studies encompassed information from close to 100,000 patients. And the observations we saw from these clinical trials was that some sorts of drugs, mTOR, PARP, and HDAC inhibitors, tend to be more toxic when given in combination. Antibody drugs tend to be less toxic than small molecule inhibitors or the classical cytotoxic chemotherapy. And if you have overlapping targets, for example, 2-VEGF inhibitors, these small molecules can be a little more toxic when given together. So based on what we saw and these rules, in general for patients that are enrolled on track when we're giving novel combinations, we start most of the small molecules at a 50% dose. Many of the antibodies will consider starting at full dose. And certain other drugs, especially those in the mTOR, PARP, and HDAC class, will often start those even lower at a 25% dose. And as Dr. Kershrock said, it's really important to start low and then escalate the dose within the patient so we can get to a dose that's still safe but also efficacious. So these rules are important for the TRACK and the TRACK trial and also for iPREDICT. Going to the next slide. If we think about patients that are on clinical trials, standard of care drugs, most patients that are getting standard of care treatment don't represent the clinical trials population. They're older, they're sicker, they're on more medications. So some would argue it's important to consider dose reductions initially for patients even on standard of care combinations or single agent chemotherapy. chemotherapy, or other drugs. So Dr. Kershrock and I had put together a commentary addressing this. And you can see on the left, there are many factors which can affect dosing and need to be considered in the starting dose. And if patients have these, we want to start them at a lower dose. And it's important to take the tools that we have on the right to come up with personalized, optimized dosing for both clinical trials patients, patients on the track trial, and patients getting standard of care treatments.

So, thank you. So, and I want to really emphasize that last point by Dr. Nakanjam. Although we started doing lower doses and escalating, we escalate by seeing the patient weekly, doing blood work and seeing how they're doing, or we may de-escalate. We discovered that this was not only good for de novo combinations, it's actually good for everybody. because a lot of patients don't tolerate the approved doses. And this is, you know, it just makes sense. And if you want to talk a little bit to us to what is available for this patient.

Thank you so much for the opportunity. As you can see here, this is one of the highest quality tumor boards that gives drug doses, combinations, combination regimens, and then clinical trial-based options now. So again, what are the clinical trial-based options based on the molecular profiling? As you saw that, there was a TAC alteration there. I see folks from the precision one study and from the Avopretinib group here. It was not intentional. I just happened to see both of you guys here from the companies. And interestingly, CDKN2A loss. Patient has CDKN2A loss and B loss. So again, this can open up doors for MTAP testing, MTAP IHC testing. Well, so there's a couple of different ways to detect it. So we can detect the gene loss, but that's not the only way that you can lose them. So the coincident or downstream effect of losing the protein is also a possibility. So I think that's what you're referring to. But we don't do it in this trial, but I think that's one of the great things about the Molecular Tumor Board is that we also talk about additional diagnostic testing that might be sought by the patient at their local institution if it's warranted.

Oh, absolutely. I think we just want to don't talk about the next line of therapy, but we want to be ready for the next to next to next lines of therapy for these patients. Again, pazopanib, right? Again, why do we need some, you know, some are wondering why pazopanib Why do you need a molecular tumor board for pazopinib for osteosarcoma? So I think, thank you Vivek, so I think that the important thing here is that we try to, we have expertise in clinical trials and customized combinations, and we try to offer to the patient many possibilities, including clinical trials and including customized combinations. So this is a young patient. So if Catherine Skifos could speak to germline testing.

Absolutely. So as Dr. Elvin mentioned before, the TP53 mutation that was identified on the somatic testing was at a low variant allele fraction, which makes us less suspicious that it would be of germline origin. Nevertheless, this patient was a teenager when she was diagnosed with a sarcoma. And so because of that, she should consider genetic counseling and testing. In patients under the age of 30 with osteosarcoma, about 5% or so will be found to have a germline mutation in TP53. But as a patient gets younger, that number increases. And even though the TP53 mutation was not particularly suspicious on this test, I did include here that NCCN guidelines Give a bit of guidance for when to consider testing. So to echo what Allie was saying in her previous presentation as well, TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene somatically. But in patients where there is a TP53 variant identified on tumor only sequencing, germline testing should be considered. if there's relevant family history or if the patient is diagnosed under the age of 30 with any cancer. So that does provide helpful guidance in taking that next step as to whether or not to recommend germline testing. And then other genes may also be considered for this patient's germline testing based on family history. There's some preliminary evidence of genes like CDKN2A and POT1 being related to osteosarcoma risk as well.

Thank you, Catherine. So, again, I want to point out the multifaceted expertise, multidisciplinary expertise that we've tried to arrange for this molecular tumor board. And really, in the post-COVID era, it was made possible because we can bring together the best experts at the best places. We can bring them together weekly for a Zoom meeting, something that we really could have done before COVID, but we didn't. And now we do this regularly. So this is the update. This patient was, I think, presented around July, August of 2023. And she was on gemcitabine and Taxotere. and doing well, and she actually continues to do well with this therapy. And so one of the questions you might ask is, so why did she go on the protocol? Because she's doing well with her current therapy. And what I want to say is from a lot of experience with these types of protocols, she went on the protocol at the exact right time. So, once the patient has progressive disease, especially if it's aggressive, that's late. It's not too late, but sometimes it's too late because patients don't have a lot of time, especially if they've relapsed multiple times. Tumors tend to be aggressive. there may be a very short window in which the physician really needs to treat the patient before they're going to deteriorate or even die. So this is exactly when we want patients to go on. We want them to go on while they're still doing well on their prior therapy. Now, if she's cured, great. But the likelihood of her being cured is very small at this point, because she's had multiple relapses. So at some point, we think that she will have progressive disease. And now we have a treatment plan for her. And if it turns out that she's responding for another year or two, we can always do another liquid biopsy. We can always update the molecular tumor board. There may be new clinical trials that are available and so forth. And then I want to talk about an example of a patient that we published from the University of California while I was there with the iPREDICT study. Very similar story. This is a 31, this publication is on a 31-year-old woman with heavily pretreated metastatic osteosarcoma, just like this patient. Just like this patient, she had alterations in the cyclin pathway. They were a little bit different than the current patient's alterations, but they essentially did the same thing. She had a CDK4 and CCND2 amplification, which upregulates the CDK4-6 pathway. And so we got a CDK4-6 inhibitor for her called palbocyclob. And that was one of our suggestions for this patient, palbocyclob or abemacyclob. The patient in question also had abnormalities in the FGFR pathway, so a little bit different than the current patient. But again, very much in keeping with that every patient is unique, but they often have some commonalities. So, she was given together with palbocyclob linvatinib. Another FDA-approved drug. Both drugs were, even though she's only 31 years old, both drugs were given at a considerably reduced dose, probably about 40% of the normal dose level. And although we tried to increase the dose, despite the fact that the patient was only 31, She could not tolerate an increased dose. But in spite of that, more drug for these targeted drugs is not necessarily better. For chemotherapy, we always thought more drug is better. But for targeted drugs, once you hit the target, everything else may be toxicity. So, her PET scan showed 68% reduction in metabolic activity. So, she had a very strong partial response. And she continued to do well 51 months. from the start of therapy. So, very durable, ongoing response with a customized combination that she tolerated very well. So, I think a good example for our current patient with osteosarcoma as well who has similar but not identical So, I think we will stop there and then we're happy to address any questions that anybody has.

reference_conclusion: Molecular tumor board review supported a matched therapy strategy for relapsed metastatic osteosarcoma consisting of axitinib as the preferred agent, with pazopanib as an alternative, in combination with a CDK4/6 inhibitor such as abemaciclib. Both agents should be initiated at 50% of standard dosing with subsequent titration according to tolerance. If additional therapy is required, an mTOR inhibitor such as temsirolimus or everolimus may be added with significant initial dose reduction. Germline genetic counseling and testing should also be considered given osteosarcoma diagnosed before age 30 and the identified TP53 variant on tumor sequencing.
reference_conclusion_quote: So, based on the tissue results, the preferred match therapy recommendation was for exitinib, which was preferred, or pisopinib. Pasopinib, the advantage is it's approved for the indication. The disadvantage is it's not as strong an inhibitor, as I mentioned. And in combination with a CDK4-6 inhibitor, such as Bebaciclib [...] And we also, in order to maintain safety, we recommend starting both drugs at 50% of the dose, and then titrating up to patient tolerance. [...] And then, if a third drug is to be added, we would add an mTOR inhibitor such as temsorolimus or everolimus, again, reducing the dose significantly, at least at the beginning. [...] Nevertheless, this patient was a teenager when she was diagnosed with a sarcoma. And so because of that, she should consider genetic counseling and testing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable and visible right supraclavicular/right lower neck mass. She had denied compressive neck symptoms and voice change and had remained asymptomatic.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma presenting with metastatic cervical, mediastinal, and pulmonary disease. Subsequent disease course included hepatic and osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle/core biopsy of the right supraclavicular mass showed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT demonstrated a 3.4 x 3.2 cm right supraclavicular mass. Neck/chest imaging and ultrasound showed:
- Right lateral neck nodal disease
- Bilateral central compartment lymphadenopathy
- Matted mediastinal lymphadenopathy extending through the mediastinum
- Additional pretracheal central compartment node
- Left inferior thyroid nodule measuring 2.3 cm on ultrasound
- Subcentimeter pulmonary nodules on chest CT, initially approximately 5 mm, suspicious for metastatic disease
- Thyroid gland appeared without a clear dominant invasive lesion on CT

Post-radioiodine SPECT/CT/post-therapy imaging demonstrated radioiodine-avid disease including:
- Small pulmonary nodules
- Solitary liver lesion

Follow-up CT imaging showed progression of pulmonary metastases, with the largest pulmonary nodule increasing from 5 mm initially to 11 mm. Later imaging also demonstrated bone metastases, including a spinal lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor molecular testing identified a BRAF V600E mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Approximately 6 weeks postoperatively:
- Thyroglobulin: 846
- Thyroglobulin antibodies: negative
- TSH: 0.45

Follow-up thyroglobulin increased from 846 in November 2019 to 7,000 by December at later follow-up.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She subsequently received radioactive iodine therapy with I-131, dose 150 mCi. Post-therapy imaging showed substantial radioiodine uptake in known metastatic sites, including pulmonary nodules and a liver lesion.

A spinal bone metastasis was treated with radiation.

She declined additional radioactive iodine therapy and declined tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with progressive disease after surgery and initial radioactive iodine treatment. Disease sites included cervical/mediastinal nodal disease, enlarging pulmonary metastases, hepatic metastasis, and bone metastases. She remained clinically asymptomatic.

[ other clinical data ]: She had pursued a holistic/metabolic-diet approach outside standard oncologic therapy.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, good morning everyone. I'm Amanda La Greca, faculty at the University of Colorado. I'm an endocrinologist and specialist on thyroid cancer. So this is a 51-year-old woman who noticed a lump on her right neck. It's more in a separate clavicular area than on the right lateral neck. She denies any neck compressive symptoms. She doesn't have any changes on her voice. She feels completely asymptomatic. And on exam, she has this right as superclavicular. 3 centimeter mass. Well, since it's palpable and visible. So, here's a picture of her 1st, um, CT scan showing the 3.4 by 3.2, um, right? Super particular mass.
Any thoughts on this?

Looks like she has central compartment and lateral compartment lymph nodes. It's heterogeneous. It's in the right location. So we'll be very suspicious for a thyroid person. Anything else we should be looking at?
I mean, this is a thyroid conference and everything is going to be thyroid. What else goes through your mind with that?

You know, the central compartment sort of makes it more thyroid, but you know, you always have to be suspicious when you have a really enlarged lymph node of lymphoma. They're generally more homogeneous, which this one image shows is more homogeneous. You always have to be aware of metastatic neck node from aerodigestive tract. The other thing in the supraclavicular region, one of the things that we think about it less because we all do ENT, is vercal nodes from GI malignancies.
Perfect, very good. And Amanda, I assume you went for a biopsy here?
Yeah, so she had a biopsy of that mouse and it was papillary theracarcinoma.
Okay, so show us your imaging now.
Okay, so here is the ultrasound of this patient. And the top two pictures are the right lateral neck and the top two, top bottom is a left inferior thyroid nodule.
Eric, any thoughts on this? Do you do your own ultrasounds or radiology does them? How do you do that?

We do it together with radiology, often in the same room, but I think the importance here is acknowledging surgical resection will be an important part of this patient's therapy likely ahead. And so mapping this out, giving them the best evidence of kind of where we see disease is going to be important.
OK. All right. And then I assume we did more than just the ultrasound, right, Amanda?
So she had some showing here. The center picture is her CT scan. She has subcentimeter pulmonary. I don't know if you want the radiologist to come.
I mean, this is always never fair to show your picture. Sure. No, no, no, no.

So the patient looks like not only they have a small nodule, at least in that one image in their lungs, so it makes it suspicious for a metastatic disease to the lung, but there's matted mediastinal lymph nodes. This is more than level seven. This is going throughout the mediastinum from what I could say on the coronal image. In addition, there is on the far right image, anterior to the trachea, there is an additional central compartment. So It's bilateral central compartment, you know, lateral compartment on the right. You know, once you have one, it's all lateral compartment. And what's worrisome is mediastinal and probable metastatic lung.

Zuber, anything else I need to be thinking about now? We've got sort of a biopsy of a superclavicular lymph node that says papillary cancer. With all of this, are you thinking anything different or just papillary?

Now papillary, I will be worried about it. It's one of these aggressive subtypes, but it can also happen with the classic subtypes. So the way it's presenting in the lymph node, most likely it's going to be the tumor which is forming papillae with a beautiful nuclei because cytology was able to outright call it papillary thyroid carcinoma. So at this point, I mean the size of the nodule in the thyroid and that lymph node. So I, you know, I will be at the papillary and I will, you know, what cytologists say.

So Eric, before we send this off to Dr. Zeferio, the endocrinologist often have done this workup, right? The ultrasound, the CT scans, you know, thyroid cancer is the one to have, you just do a surgery, everything is fine. How do you set up, yeah, you gotta go see Dr. Zeferio, but what's he likely to say? How do you frame that?

Yeah, I mean, a new diagnosis of cancer is not an easy thing for anyone, whether it's low, intermediate or high risk. And I think, you know, I think that should be approached with that kind of candor. You know, this is pretty extensive disease. And I think the key from the endocrine standpoint is you don't really know what you don't know. And while some people do have extensive neck disease, and that's all it is, and they do fine, certainly some people have distant disease. And in those rare cases, it can kind of go south pretty quickly.

So concerns with all of the snuff nodes in the neck that there may be distant as well, wouldn't surprise us, right? Mark, this is coming to you. Just from a real practical standpoint, what are you going to tell this patient and their family about surgery? You get a few minutes because this is a couple minutes sort of discussion here in terms of not only the surgery that you're thinking about, complications, expectations. How do you frame this on that initial visit with them, Mark?

Sure. Well, I think the appropriate workup has been done, which is a CT neck and chest. And then I would talk about sort of the surgery in a stepwise fashion. I mean, we'd obviously need to do a total thyroidectomy. We would need to do a central compartment dissection here. And that includes sort of resection of the superior mediastinal lymph nodes. And then the patient also needs a right lateral neck dissection. I'm assuming the lymph nodes in the left lateral neck are clear on the ultrasound. So, you know, that surgery may be about a five-hour surgery, sometimes a little more, sometimes a little less. And, you know, we talk about sequentially sort of the risks of thyroid surgery, of course. You know, we talk about the nerves and the parathyroid glands, and then we talk about the, you know, how the central compartment disease, this bulky central compartment disease, adds to that a little bit. This disease looks more bulky than invasive. So I think that the important structures there, you know, the nerve, there may be some adherence to these lymph nodes, but I doubt that they would be actually involved, involving the nerve. So it requires often some meticulous nerve dissection, but hopefully no invasion. But certainly those issues would be discussed. may have to implant the lower parathyroid glands. We really want to try to identify those parathyroid glands. Oftentimes they're in the thyrothymic ligament. We can, sometimes we can mobilize them out of the way. Sometimes we have to auto transplant them. So the patient should be aware that at least temporary hypocalcemia, temporary hyperthyroidism risk is high here. And then the lateral neck surgery, you know, there's risks with that. You know, we often have those patients see physical therapy afterwards for shoulder and neck exercises. So I would typically tell a patient like this to, they may need, you know, three weeks off. The only other issue, the last issue to be discussed here, and it is, it's not clearly apparent from these images is really how low that mediastinal disease goes. Because if, A lot of times this disease can be removed transcervically, and certainly we should always make an attempt to do that. But there are cases where if that disease goes below the innominate vein, we just can't reach that through the neck, and then we have to have our thoracic colleagues involved. Sometimes it's not clear up front, and you have thoracic surgeon on standby. This is discussed with the patient. Of course, if you're not able to get the disease out through the neck, you have to do what's called a median sternotomy, open up the sternum to get that disease out. In this case, again, I don't think it's the invasiveness of the disease, but if the disease, if there are some lymph nodes below the innominate vein, that could be a bit of a challenge and you may need sternotomy here as well. So those are some of the reef considerations here.

So Amanda, welcome to my panel. You get to present and answer questions too. What do you set up the expectation for this patient? Okay, so that's where we start. All right. And then so show us what happened with the surgeon.

Okay, so in data she had a. total thyroidectomy, bilateral central neck dissection, a right modified neck dissection, and a median sternotomy and a mediastinal mass resection. So I just put some of the pictures that the surgeon sent me, but I think it's very interesting that the primary tumor was half a millimeter PTC with no exothermic extension and no lymphovascular invasion. Remember that on the 1st ultrasound, she did have a left inferior thyroid nodule of 2.3 centimeters, but that lesion was benign and she has 35 out of 57 lymph nodes with metastatic PTC and the largest was 2.6 centimeters and she had external extension. As expected, you know, level 6, 7 out of 10, right level 2, no lymph nodes, right level 18 out of 21, and level 7, 4 out of 4 of 2.6 centimeters. Zuber, what the heck is going on here? I've been telling the world papillary microcarcinomas are no big deal. Watch them, no problem. Dr. LaGreca knows that. That's why she presents these cases. What up with a papillary microcarcinoma and a million lymph nodes?

So that's why in the new WHO, there's a strong recommendation not to use the term microcarcinoma because it always kind of reflects that there's nothing that's going to happen to the patient because 25% or more of us walking around with one, right? But I always say in pathology, never say never. So, you know, you are going to come across a case like this. This case is, to me, is a little bit surprising because I have seen some of these cases, and in those, you do see like some of the calcifications within the lymphatics, and you see a lot of this permeation, and all the cases that I've seen also have chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. We also know that sometimes the presentation is a distant metastasis, like a bone mat, and then you go into the thyroid, you basically put the whole thyroid under the glass and you find just one microcarcinoma. And if you are a little bit unlucky, you may just find a little scar with one kind of papilla in it. So we have all seen these cases. They are not common cases. And I'm really, for this to me, that many lymph nodes, you know, it does, has been reported and it does happen, and I'm sure all of you have seen it, but no LVI, no extrathyral extension. So that is, it's kind of a surprising for this tumor. I don't know what subtype it was, whether it was a tall cell, but, you know, already it has shown that this tumor has got, got out of the thyroid and, you know, has even caused METs to alarm. So, you know, we all seen it, but very rare.
I agree. And Amanda, you had at least some molecular testing on it towards the end.

I also wanted to mention this, Mike, since you said about the microcarcinoma. I don't want to scare the audience to stop doing surveillance of microcarcinomas. Typically, the ones that are aggressive present this way, and these are not obviously tumors that you're going to watch. So just to keep your business alive. which would be consistent with Zuber's field if there was something more going on. This may behave more like a tall cell or something like that. So post-op, where did we go?

Yeah, I mean, I think that's very reasonable in this setting of lots of lymph nodes, potentially distant mets, high TG to always remember the brain and to look at it. Munir, we're headed towards you for radioactive iodine. Is it going to work? Is it not going to work? What's going to go on here?

Yeah, so that's interesting. There are studies that show that these BRAF V600E mutations may have a variable degree of iodine uptake, but it is not all or none. We have seen the examples where despite the mutation there is significant uptake. And there are other examples where there's no uptake even in the known site. So at least it's worth pursuing the scan first and see what kind of symporter expression is there on the cell surface by looking at the degree of uptake.
Yeah, because there's definitely a subset of these tall cells that grab on to radioactive iodine.

And we also have a couple of sites that are not removed, including the lung nodules. So we have certain target sites that will allow us to see the expression. OK, so Amanda, I'm sure, got radioactive iodine.
Of course. She got 150 milligrams of iodine and 131 in the Sarkar post-therapy images.
What do you think? This looks like there's a storm coming in from the East Coast to me. That's what this looks like.
Yeah. To you, what does it look like? Yeah, so quite a high degree of expression as if this is a classic papillary thyroid carcinoma. You know, this is what we see in those classic patterns.

Yeah. Hey, Frank, something in the liver? I mean, you get these roads like this often end up in your clinic. I see lots of false positives and stuff in the liver. Do we really see thyroid cancer metastatic to the liver?
You can. I mean, I would say when I started this lady scared me from the beginning. So I kind of figured she's going to end up in my clinic someday. It's not common, but yes, it can happen.
So talk about that for half a second. Why did you think this was coming to you just from day one?

Well, first of all, you know, she shows up with this relatively aggressive, you know, picture, you know, radiology describes this. She has a lot of nodes. She already has pulmonary metastases. So we know that yes, people can be cured with surgery and RAI, but the degree of bulk, I think, you know, looking at this, I mean, it's interesting, Mark and I, their center has a study we're participating in, you know, for patients neoadjuvantally with like, with retin inhibitors, salprocatinib. Not that there is a study with like Linvatinib up front, and that is not standard of care. I'm not necessarily advocating that either, but it just made me wonder about these kinds of presentations. We know that in papillary up to 50% can de-differentiate, you know, and there were comments already thrown around here. Is this more aggressive picture? Is this, you know, could this be a, you know, somewhat of a de-differentiated, you know, component that's starting to arise? Obviously there's uptake with iodine. So at least that, you know, favors a more differentiated component. But I, based on what I see here and the liver metastases, it's getting so rare that this is a pretty aggressive tumor that eventually has become refractory to iodine.
So lots of red flags to everybody from radiology to pathology to surgery in this case. Amanda, take me a little bit more of the follow up here.
Yeah. So here is some of the, she has a, this is the SPECT CT images. And here is again the liver lesion and some of the small pulmonary nodules.
Azita, that liver lesion, thyroid, something else, can we tell from that single cut?

The liver lesion, I see a solitary liver lesion. That's what's concerning to me. But it's really picking up FDGs, which makes me more suspicious that this is aggressive. The other thing that I failed to talk about with the initial imaging that I think we all failed is the thyroid on CT looked normal. I only said that in retrospect. We were so concentrated on the nodes that we never talked about how There was nothing in the thyroid. There was no extra thyroidal extension. Nothing on CT would have told you this is from the thyroid except the location of the lymph nodes.

Yeah, that's awesome. And that's why when people always say papillary microcarcinoma never goes to lymph node metastasis, we don't think about this case like a papillary microcarcinoma, right? We ignored the entire thyroid. We're thinking about this as N1B disease, bulky disease. That's where they get lumped in there. What happened to her course, Amanda? Keep going for me.
So, these are this is her as you see, you know, she went from 846 in November of 2019. To 7,000 at her last follow up with me in December. So, doubling time there is there to comment if you want.
Eric, so we gave a dose of radioactive iodine in 2019. We got some uptake, maybe killed something, but clearly she's got residual disease here. What are you thinking about these thyroid globulins?

How do you follow this? I mean it's a very robust number it's continually going up, I mean the doubling time thing tends to stem more from medullary and calcitonin, you know, look at but you can't help but notice here you're approaching 10,000. There's active disease it's growing. You know, I think if you go back a decade ago, we would always consider a second dose of radioiodine. These are her her last to CT in August. She still has. Uh, metastasis on the enlarging, you know, the initial CT scan was 5 millimeters. Now, the largest pulmonary nodule is 11 millimeters and it's the 1 that I pointed with my arrow there. And then. She was found to have bone meds. I mean, she's getting in her middle age in life that she's going to have compression fractures, perhaps, or pathologic fractures. So those things we would do. The whole thing about therapy is always tricky. Yes, if someone shows up with bulky disease and they're very symptomatic, it's almost kind of like a slam dunk. And someone who has maybe isolated lesions, so let's say she just had the bony lesion that's presented here, that we treat with radiation or surgery, perhaps, and conservative measures. And it's always in the middle where we have to, like I said, watch these people. And if they're diseases, the tempo is growing fast. We know the doubling time here is fast. Usually, I've mentioned to these people, we're probably going to have to consider starting treatment with a TKI sooner than later. So I try to prepare them for that. And again, it's a total discussion that you have to have each time that the patients come back. They are knowledgeable, they read, and they do know that potential side effects. You get treatment. So I don't know. The question is, when is the right time? And I don't know that we've fully defined that yet, and we're still learning, so.

So maximizing the impact of the very first goal would be very important. The other important point I would like to bring up here is that when we see the patients for consults and when there's a big discordance between their symptoms and the extent of disease, oftentimes showing the images to really emphasize not only the total burden, but also some sensitive sites such as risk for compression fractures, it actually does make a difference in trying to convince them towards agreeing to get the therapy rather than saying, oh, I don't have any symptoms, why do I need the treatment?

Yeah, David Pfister taught me that years ago. Also taught me to ask the patient if they wanted to see it before I showed them, because every once in a while somebody says no, they don't want to see it. And then the last question on this one, there was a question about the solitary mass in the liver, could you do radio frequency or some? So yes, we will deal with focal lesions that are enlarging, just like they did with the spine to radiate that. So I've never done RFA, but that's sort of evolving now. We've done radiation, we've done surgery. So if there was one place outstripping everything else, and we weren't going to do a systemic therapy, that's something we'd consider.
Okay.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary review recommended initial operative management with total thyroidectomy, central compartment dissection including superior mediastinal lymph nodes, and right lateral neck dissection, with thoracic surgical involvement and possible median sternotomy if mediastinal disease extended below the innominate vein. Postoperatively, radioactive iodine therapy was pursued after brain MRI excluded intracranial metastases. Given persistent progressive metastatic disease, repeat radioactive iodine would require dosimetry to optimize dosing while limiting marrow and pulmonary toxicity; if additional radioactive iodine or tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy continued to be declined, close surveillance with serial chest and abdominal imaging and spinal imaging approximately every 3 months was advised, with focal radiation or other local therapy for symptomatic or dominant progressing lesions and bisphosphonate support for osseous disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old woman at initial hematology/oncology evaluation; 78 years old at time of treatment initiation.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred to medical oncology/hematology for clonal B-cell lymphocytosis meeting minimal criteria for chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

[ diagnosis ]: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / clonal B-cell lymphocytosis with bilateral axillary adenopathy. Prior history of stage I breast cancer, with no evidence of disease for approximately 15 years after treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Peripheral blood morphology showed absolute lymphocytosis with small mature-appearing lymphocytes.

[ imaging findings ]: Annual mammogram showed post-treatment changes from prior breast cancer therapy and new bilateral axillary adenopathy. Impression stated that bilateral adenopathy could represent lymphoma, leukemia, or another systemic reactive process. On physical examination, bilateral small axillary adenopathy was present; no hepatosplenomegaly was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Peripheral blood flow cytometry demonstrated an abnormal B-cell population measuring just over 5 × 10^9/L. Immunophenotype was positive for CD19, dim CD5, CD20, dim CD22, dim CD25, and CD23, with monotypic light-chain expression. FISH/cytogenetic testing showed 11q deletion and 13q deletion. At a later reassessment prior to treatment, 13q deletion was present in 81% of nuclei and 11q deletion in 90%.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with lymphocyte predominance of 62%, with normal hematocrit and platelet count. Chemistry panel and LDH were within normal limits. Over the subsequent two years, hematocrit declined. Iron studies were consistent with inflammatory block. Reticulocyte assessment indicated a hypoproliferative anemia. MCV was 94 fL, RDW was 13%, and direct Coombs testing was negative. The decline in hematocrit was accompanied by increasing white blood cell count and absolute lymphocyte count.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior stage I breast cancer had been treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and hormonal blockade. She remained without evidence of disease for approximately 15 years. For CLL, she was initially managed with observation.

[ current disease status ]: During observation, disease showed progression with rising white blood cell count/absolute lymphocyte count and development of anemia. At the time treatment was started, she had progressive lymphocytosis and anemia without documented hepatosplenomegaly.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included COPD, benign pulmonary nodules, bladder incontinence, chronic fatigue, episodic diaphoresis, mild coronary artery disease on cardiac catheterization, GERD, and Schatzky ring. Physical examination also identified a soft systolic ejection murmur.

Q in approximately 50% of nuclei, and I had read something about if it's less than 65, that offers a good prognosis, but if it's over 65, it may offer a lesser good prognosis. I'll have to tell you I'm not really certain that these trials are going to honestly answer the question just by virtue of the fact that the disease has such a long long natural history and patients do so well. So by the time, frankly, you have a control arm or the actual treatment arm, you know, the treatment has changed. So it will be interesting to see. But what I would tell your listeners and your audience is that this information is important to have a smarter conversation with the patient about prognosis, about what I'm going to do. But it really should not persuade you to start treatment earlier than what's indicated.
Thank you, Dr. Neumann. Dr. Chaudhary, do you have any additional comments on this?

No, I think I agree with what's been said so far. I think this is more of a prognostic sort of tool than anything else right now. I'd observe, just like the recommendations are now. You know, one could, I suspect that's your next question, but I'll I'll wait for you to ask the next question.
Okay.
So, Paul, moving forward, I'll hand it back to you.

Thank you. So, over the next two years, her hematocrit did decline. Iron studies showed an inflammatory block. This was hypoperliferative based on reticulocytes. Well, for somebody who's been untreated and been observed, I usually don't recheck a FISH panel. One can make an argument if the duration has been pretty long before any treatment, first line or subsequent line, that one should check a current FISH panel. In a situation like this, I'd probably you know, earned the side of taking what we have, but one could make the other argument as well. So, I'd actually go with what we have.

I'll just chime in. So, you know, I don't know if I would have done it. I agree with, you know, the idea that she probably did not need the FISH panel with the first cycle of evaluation because I think we could have provided her with reasonable information just on what we knew already, but given that instance and knowing that additional mutations can take place, I typically will, if I'm about to initiate therapy, I certainly would get a fish panel at that point. Because I think, and Paul, I mean, it may not change the treatment because we saw similar chromosomal abnormalities, but we may have seen something additional in clonal evolution, or maybe the karyotype has changed. So, I mean, I tend to believe that it's, you know, at the time when you really think that the patient needs therapy, rechecking a FISH panel is very reasonable. I mean, because it was five years, I believe, right? It was... Five and a half years. Yeah, you really don't know always what happened during that. I mean, I think as long as the patient is observation, I don't routinely recommend rechecking FISH panels because you're not doing anything with that. If you check it at diagnosis and then now something has changed, something has changed that made you decide to start therapy, something clinically has changed, you don't know on the molecular level or the genomic level if something has changed. So I tend to recommend checking the FISH panel at two points. Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, it's interesting. Anytime you ask these questions, five years ago would be different than maybe three years ago, different than today. So treatment is indicated. comments or disagreements on the treatment choice?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male. Exact age was not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Right testicular pain consistent with a symptomatic right-sided varicocele.

[ diagnosis ]: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with extensive local involvement of the inferior vena cava (IVC), initially considered locally advanced and unresectable.

[ histopathology results ]: Percutaneous biopsy confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT demonstrated a large right renal mass with extensive involvement/encasement of the IVC. The IVC was difficult to delineate over an approximately 6 cm segment, extending from just below the renal hilum to near the inferior edge of the liver.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No baseline laboratory values were provided.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with extensive local involvement of the inferior vena cava, initially considered locally advanced and unresectable.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had comorbid health factors affecting surgical candidacy, including smoking, alcohol use, and excess weight. Surgical planning initially considered the possibility of major vascular reconstruction or leaving the IVC in discontinuity.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so this is a good... I just remember when I found this out, and I don't know if it happened to you, Mark, when you go through training. You know, it's like when your first year anatomy class comes back and you're like, oh my gosh, I remember. So it is not uncommon. You actually see it. I think it's on our boards. You see it in question sets from time to time. But because of the gonadal vein for most guys usually comes off the IVC. if there's an occlusion or blockage of that IVC, those patients tend to develop varicoceles on that testicle, which most guys usually complain of the varicoceles as a dull ache, pain kind of stuff. So, while it's rare, I think any person who does this long enough gets these cases where they come in with no other complaint than my ball, you know, my testicle hurts. And it's the right one as opposed to the left one, which can happen too, but you just see it less often because of the anatomy that's usually coming off the left renal vein versus the IVC itself. So it has more collateralization to work with. So it's always an interesting thing when this happens.
Excellent. So this patient comes in, gets this workup, gets a CT, and kind of walk us through. This looks like a nasty process going on in the right kidney. What do we have here?

Yeah, so this was a, you know, incidental finding, sort of surprisingly, other than the testicular pain, I guess. But, you know, it's hard to capture, I think, on a still image, but you can see pretty clearly that it's really difficult, if not impossible, to make out his IVC. And this sort of continues if you scroll up and down for a good... six centimeters along the IVC. So I realized that whatever disease process going on, you know, sometimes it can be hard. Although this patient didn't have a history that fit it, but sometimes patients will have some spontaneous bleeds or a trauma event. And that blood, that capsule, which you can sort of make out a little bit on this patient too, can sort of fool you as, is this tumor, is this blood? You know, if I wait it out, we'll go away. It's hard because if you wait it out and it's not blood, guess what? Now it's grown bigger and you sort of missed your window. But if it's blood, you can sort of maybe get a little pullback. But I was concerned in this patient because he didn't have that history. I had to assume this was all tumor that was basically encased in his IBC. So in addition, as you can see, he wasn't, well, he's not terribly old. He wasn't the healthiest patient. So, this is sort of one of those cases where I knew we had to think a little more outside the box. And so, I knew surgical resection, if I got in there, was going to be a major thing. I don't think I'd probably have to either graft his IVC or leave it in discontinuity, which, you know, if you have to do, you have to do. This patient, and I don't think we've said it yet, you know, if he had other options to try and shrink this tumor or facilitate the surgery so I don't have to do as much. In addition, we sort of use that as a time for him to get himself healthier, stop smoking, stop drinking, lose some weight. And so there was an opportunity to not only maybe shrink the tumor, but optimize him as a surgical candidate as well.

Excellent. And just some more images here. And you can really see the extent of this process involving the IVC. And like you said, you kind of really lose the IVC sort of just below the renal hilum up to the edge of the liver, hard to make out. So you talked about taking some time to try to shrink the tumor and get him optimized for surgery. So I'm assuming that you are going to ask for a lifeline from your medical oncology colleagues here. Is that correct? Correct. So Reina, The urologist has this patient with a IVC tumor thrombus and a large tumor and has the intent of hoping to downstage for surgery. I'm sure this is a type of patient you see in your practice. How do you manage these patients?

So I would basically put this individual in the category of locally advanced unresectable. These patients were actually included in all of the phase three trials that tested various IO combination strategies. I think in the context of potential receptability down the road, where you're really looking at a regimen that's gonna be associated with the highest response rate, the lowest primary PD rate, the fastest time to response, so you could potentially get them to a potentially curative surgery, I generally go with an IOTKI combination and generally Lymvetinib Pembrolizumab in this context.

Excellent. So it looks like in this case the patient had a biopsy of course, confirmed that this is clear cell RCC and then started on Axi Pembro. Marina, can you just go back a little bit and tell us a little bit about sort of the kind of anticipated speed of response with TKI I.O. versus I.O. I.O. and how you think about if you want to get quick shrinkage, it sounds like you're going TKI I.O. Is that correct?

Yeah, I mean, I think if we think about Nebo IPI, for example, like the primary PD rates about 20%, which is a high primary PD rate for somebody you're trying to get to receptability. I mean, the caveat that I would use there is unless the patient had sarcomatoid differentiation of some kind. And also, the response rate's around 40%. Now, that response rate means 30% shrinkage or more. When we look at the data, for example, in vatneprimalizumab, the primary PD rate is less than 10%. The response rate is actually close to 70%. I could see the rationale for using Exitinib. Exitinib has a short half-life and, you know, is a favorable TKI when we think about stopping the agent for a planned surgical resection. But those are kind of the considerations to be had. I think you would expect, timing-wise, to see best response within a couple of months with an IO-TKI combination.

Hey, can I ask a question real quick for Rana, too? So, you know, traditionally, and I don't know if you're still in this game, because you mentioned it, if, like, say the biopsy showed sarcomatoid elements, and we always think epinevo when we see sarcomatoid, but do we really have data that shows that it's better than any other IO-containing regimen when it comes to sarcomatoid response?

We do. I mean, it's never been compared head to head, but I think if you're actually looking at the response data, the response rate is doubled in that population. And actually, what's really striking is the durability of response. is much more pronounced in those individuals. So when I think of like IOIO, we have one in five patients that have really no response, have primary resistant disease. We have one in five patients that can have a durable response. That's just your kind of all comer population. I think if we were to apply this to sarcomatoid, we really are bumping up the tail on the curve. And we see that when we look at the PFS curves actually in the subset analyses, though they're post hoc, demonstrating, you know, sustained durable response or durable benefit in that group of patients.
Thank you.

And Rakib, is there any role for radiotherapy to treat disease that's in the IVC? Is there, I guess, is there any data for efficacy? And on the other side, is there any concern for treating disease with major vascular invasion?

Yeah, not too much data that has matured yet. And we have started getting some experience with this, mainly started with treating a few cases of refractory and patients that are not eligible for surgery. And we started seeing actually very good 70 to 80 percent radiographic measurable response with radiation. So we went around because these cases are so rare combining a case report from multiple institutions that we published a case series of 15 patients and now we are updating that and we also have completed now enrolling on a small phase 2 feasibility trial of neoadjuvant radiation followed by surgery and nephrectomy. That trial, we hope to publish in the next couple of months, and it is feasible and safe. Now, I'll go over a few indications that we explored. One of them is the neoadjuvant, one of them is adjuvant, and another would be palliative. In the neoadjuvant case that I can remember, a patient similar to this, but a little bit more, a larger level, 4 thrombus with butt carry syndrome, so venous congestion. So that patient was not a candidate for surgery up front, but after SBRD of full dose, Within three months, the patient's SITs resolved, LFTs normalized, and then we had MRI showing that the venous congestion also relieved, and then patient was a surgical candidate and underwent surgery. So that was one case. Another case was an adjuvant case. So that is something that could apply to this patient where the patient wasn't really in good shape like this patient for an extensive surgery, but the patient was a candidate for a nephrectomy, a robotic nephrectomy, which is a much less complicated surgery as you know. So in a planned way, the patient underwent robotic surgery and the thrombus we gave local control with stereotactic radiation. So both together combined, the patient overall had local control. So this is something that I would like to eventually explore on prospective trials, because in many tertiary care centers, I mean, community setting, patients don't have access to surgeons that can do extensive surgery, but they will have surgeons who are able to do nephrectomy. And combined with radiation, you could probably give local control to this patient. So an area that we are exploring and the data is maturing, but we don't have long-term data yet.

Very cool to hear and look forward to seeing that for sure, to have more options for these complicated patients. So it looks like this patient went on to receive Axipimpro, had a decrease in the size of this mass and sort of stable lymphadenopathy over the next six months, developed, had some complications, DKA, ICU admission, and then six months later sort of was reevaluated for surgery. So, Dr. Manley, now we're a few months down the road. What do you see now compared to when you started?

You can start to make out the kidney actually, which is something you couldn't do before. You can actually see part of the IVC, which you couldn't see before. So, those are all good signs. So, you know, this was early in the experience for me of giving, you know, this wasn't standard of care, still not, but this is a case I think definitely deserving of neoadjuvant treatment, although some people could argue you could have resected him up front, but I think that would have been a tall task. So, I think we had a really great response. The sad thing was he did develop lifelong diabetes, so it's not without cause, but I still think and know the patient would do it all again if they needed to. So, they had a really good response and this sort of, is an emerging problem, I would say, or situation. I'd be interested to see what your take is, Mark. You know, after these patients have a good response, right, however you want to characterize that, decrease in size, change in enhancement, whatever, when do you offer these patients surgery and when do you not? Because, you know, now that we're seeing more of these patients come through and they still have their kidney intact and it's the only area that has any disease, do we really always go in, you know, and take these out? a little bit, right, some of these patients will start getting hits to their kidney, too, with treatment, too. So now they're not the same kidney function when you first met them, too. So I'm interested, you know, I've sort of adapted, but I'm interested how you sort of triage these patients, Mark.

Yeah, it's a great question, and there's not an easy answer to it. The PT0 rate, in my experience, is on the lower side, but it's definitely not zero. There are some patients that can have a complete response in the kidney, and then others who their disease is now somewhat more quiescent. Most of these patients, I would say, probably do end up having a resection if they are otherwise, if we deem it resectable, we can do it safely, and that we think the competing risks are favorable. And we do find viable disease more often than not, but are happily surprised when we get a YPT0, right? You know, sometimes These surgeries can be very challenging, especially after IO therapy and when there are big lymph nodes around the vasculature, sometimes you get a desmoplastic reaction and then sometimes It's, you don't really have any desmoplastic reaction at all. It's not like post-chemo testis cancer, right? So it's definitely a little bit of a box of chocolates.

And Rana, I'm sort of interested in, do you just send them to surgery? Like the surgeon will tell you if you need surgery or not. Or like, because you probably see these more and maybe they don't always come to us. And when do you decide, hey, I think that kidney needs to go or not, I guess?

Yeah, it's a very interesting conversation. I think we have a multidisciplinary tumor board actually that meets every Friday afternoon where we actually bring these cases and there's an assessment by a radiation oncologist, medical oncologist and surgeon and have a weekly tumor board as well. So I think that these are dynamic discussions. I can't emphasize enough the importance of just continued communication and collaboration because there's things that that I may see or have sort of insight into that maybe one of the other multidisciplines may not. And vice versa, there may be aspects from a surgical standpoint that I'm just not aware of that I will be enlightened by sort of reaching out to colleagues. But I think in general, my rule of thumb is, you know, if they've had two serial scans where they've maintained a sustained response with no other evidence of disease progression and they're clinically doing well, that's generally when I'm pulling the trigger to say, okay, let's have you go back and see the surgeon. I don't generally jump on the first scan because I want to ensure that response is maintained. There's been so many times where you kind of jump the gun too early, and then you stop their systemic therapy, and you're getting them teed up for surgery, and they met out in the middle of that process, and that's the worst thing you could do for somebody. So I like to ensure that there's sustainability in the response before we pull the trigger on actually taking somebody to the OR.

Excellent. So, Brandon, what did you end up doing here? Did surgery. And it was stuck. It was so, which again, sorry for, I feel like it's just me and Mark complaining about being surgeons, but he was so stuck. And when he looked at that scan, it didn't, it looks so much better that I think I got tricked a little bit, but it was really, really stuck. But we did discuss some of these other options. And again, we'll talk about it probably in a little bit, but you know, he, uh, we got him through surgery and he's doing fine. And yeah. I don't know if I would do anything different in his specific case again, but it has made me question other patients I saw subsequent to this about, you know, how to handle them. And every situation is different, but we ended up doing surgery, just an open radical nephrectomy, because I knew it would probably be stuck and wanted to make sure the vessel we had good control, but it was definitely more plastered than I thought it was going to be. Because like you had mentioned, I've done several cases of patient systemic treatment before. You always hear these horror stories about don't do it if it's CABO or no, IPI's the worst or, you know, this one's the worst. But in my experience, I really haven't found one that's worse than the other. It's just that sometimes some patients it's like horrible and other patients, it's like they never had anything.
Interesting. And did you have to do anything to the to the CAVA?

Yeah, so basically we, I sort of took a side swipe of it. So oddly enough, you know, this is, and again, there was no way to know. He never had a thrombus, and that's what I was worried about. The thrombus was never in there. What had happened is basically the tumor just closed off, just, you know, and you see this sometimes in testes too, it just basically, you know, compressed the IVC and had probably been there so long it just, you know, wasn't functional. So, you know, we didn't have to do a whole graft because it was slightly less than 50% of his circumferential IVC width. And considering that he had practically had no IVC before we started systemics, it was new blood flow. And so we didn't have to do, luckily, as much vascular work as I was fearing. Fantastic.

reference_conclusion: Biopsy confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and neoadjuvant systemic therapy with axitinib plus pembrolizumab was administered to downstage the locally advanced right renal mass with extensive IVC involvement. After approximately six months, imaging demonstrated reduction in tumor burden with improved visualization of the kidney and IVC, and the case was reassessed for operative management. The patient subsequently underwent open radical nephrectomy with partial caval resection/control; no true IVC thrombus was present, and full caval grafting was not required.

[...] we ended up doing surgery, just an open radical nephrectomy [...] we didn't have to do a whole graft because it was slightly less than 50% of his circumferential IVC width

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient. Age was not stated.

[ chief complaint ]: Right lateral neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with occult primary in the thyroid and metastatic right lateral cervical lymph node involvement. Pathologic stage was reported as T1a N1b. Distant metastatic status was not established.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroid pathology demonstrated a microscopic 3 mm focus of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Nodal pathology demonstrated a single involved lateral neck lymph node. No extranodal extension was identified. No soft tissue invasion was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound performed at a cancer center showed an ultrasonographically normal thyroid gland and was otherwise negative apart from a large right lateral neck mass. CT neck with contrast was reviewed and considered adequate quality; it demonstrated a solitary mass in the right high neck. The mass was described as approximately 4.5 cm and consistent with a level II/right high neck node. No chest imaging had been performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was 0.9.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Surgical treatment had been performed, with postoperative pathology showing T1a papillary thyroid carcinoma and N1b nodal disease as above.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status following resection of papillary thyroid carcinoma with a microscopic intrathyroidal primary and a single metastatic right lateral cervical lymph node. No extranodal extension or soft tissue invasion was present on pathology. Distant metastatic disease had not been evaluated with chest imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history was reported. No history of radiation exposure was reported.
