reference_discussion.text: That's a misnomer, and I think that terminology should be removed from the vocabulary for thyroid surgeons. Literally every patient who was described to have lateral aberrant thyroid was indeed a metastatic papillary carcinoma completely replacing the lymph node where the tumor was so well differentiated and there was no lymphoid follicle seen that it looked like normal thyroid tissue. Incidentally, the picture you showed is not the location for lateral labyrinth thyroid. Lateral labyrinth thyroids occur at level four or in the supraclavicular fossa. That's where they were called lateral labyrinth thyroids. Higher up in the neck, they are clearly metastatic thyroid carcinomas. Nevertheless, the terminology lateral aberrant thyroid is equal to well-differentiated carcinoma metastatic lymph node. So in 2014, there is no lateral aberrant thyroid.

So I would agree with that. And I gather, at least my interpretation of that concept of the lateral aberrant thyroid was much more of an incidental observation than a clinically apparent, what's obviously a metastatic node anyway. It was removing lymph nodes and finding benign appearing thyroid tissue in an incidental sort of fashion, as opposed to somebody presenting clinically like this that isn't even the phenotype of a lateral aberrant thyroid.

All right. I think those are fair criticisms of a term that we shouldn't be using anymore anyway, but sometimes it's fun to go back to the old history books. So how should we manage the thyroid gland? How should we manage the lateral neck on that side? And what should we do about the central neck in this case, where the thyroid gland itself is ultrasonographically normal?
Is there any family history or radiation exposure?
No family history, no radiation exposure on her TSH was 0.9.

So this patient would get a ultrasound, both of the central and lateral neck. This is a patient that I will often get both CT, contrasted CT, as well as a good ultrasound, clearly repeating it at my center.

So just to reassure you, the ultrasound was done at a cancer center and was negative apart from this big lateral neck mass. And the CT scan also was reviewed from the outside, was felt to be of adequate quality, so it was not repeated. But the review also suggested a solitary mass in the right high neck.

So, as has been pointed out, she still has quite a good prognosis. She's probably very worried, but she has a big operation in front of her. She needs a total thyroidectomy. In my practice, I would do an ipsilateral central compartment dissection as well as a lateral comprehensive neck dissection, levels two through five.
I would include. So, you would do the transverse incision and turn the corner and go all the way up to the back of the ear?
I would carry a COCR incision laterally in a skin crease that's less obtrusive, if you will.

So tell me about the pros and cons, if you will, of the extended cochlear incision versus a true lateral neck incision running along the lateral border of the sternocleidomastoid or medial border of sternocleidomastoid.

Well, I tend to make for squamous cell carcinomas a hockey stick type incision vertically behind the sternocleidomastoid. It's relatively unobtrusive, but in a patient like this, you can usually get around all of those lymph nodes with a single low incision in a horizontal plane, extending that cochlear incision, even if you extend it posterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle a bit for more superior exposure. Because that looked like a level two node, at least four and a half centimeter, some portion is going to be up in level two, 2A. I think you're obligated to dissect level 2B on this young woman as well. Of course, you have to be careful with the accessory nerve. That's the major concern. But level five is going to be, I think, of necessity as well. And so extending the COCR more posteriorly gives you access to level 5A and B.

And any other takers for an extended coca incision? Does everybody agree that that's an appropriate incision to reach this level 2 lymph node high in the neck and clear the remainder of compartments 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, at least ipsilateral?
It is not.
Good. Why not?

In 2004, The only incision for any type of neck dissection is a single transverse incision along an appropriate skin crease, regardless of the indication for the neck dissection. All you have to do is extend the length of the incision along the same skin crease, whether it's higher or lower. such that you should not be able to identify the neck incision in that patient standing six feet away, regardless of what neck dissection you have done. Cochlear incision is out of the vocabulary for modern day teaching in head and neck surgery. Double trifurcate incision is out of the vocabulary. And any incision that draws a vertical component in the neck is out of the vocabulary for head and neck surgery.
Out of the vocabulary for head and neck surgery, not only for thyroid surgery.
That is correct.
Those are fighting words, I feel sure. We'll have a squamous panel after this.
Squamous, carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, skin cancer, or thyroid cancer.

I think what you were describing is actually what Dr. Farris does, but maybe calls it a Cochra incision out of maybe tradition. I think another name that's sometimes used is the Addy decision or Addy incision after Joseph Addy. agree that you can access all of those levels of the neck through extension of your thyroidectomy incision. Maybe not calling it a cochlear incision, but designing the level of the incision to be able to adequately access the superior aspects of the central compartment and the thyroid as well as the inferior aspects of the central neck and just being able to extend that laterally.
So where for the hockey stick incision, where does that come in? Is there a role for a hockey stick incision in California?

You know, I think in this case dissecting level one, at least in my practice, is not a component that I spend a lot of time with. I think it's likely to be the area of most difficulty without a vertical portion. So I would say in that situation that it's when you're focused in the aerodigestive tract as opposed to level six and four where most of the lymph nodes metastatic from thyroid cancer are. That, to me, is where I distinguish the need for different incisions. And many more of these patients are young females where a less obtrusive scar is important. You know, it's a disease of morbidity as opposed to mortality, as opposed to squamous cell carcinoma where getting all of the disease out is obviously much more of a mortality issue.

So let me then turn to the audience because, again, I think there's some controversy potentially here. Who amongst the audience agree that the vertical component of an incision, call it what you will, but the thing that runs up behind the ear has gone out of the practice of head and neck surgery? Is there anybody here? So let me rephrase the question. I apologize. Let me make it clear. Is there anybody here who still feels that the vertical component of the incision is a requirement or a desirable attribute of a surgical approach? So we do still have some outstanding people.
What are we talking about? I think you need to rephrase that question for thyroid cancer.

I should make it clear. OK, let's try again. Vertical incision for metastatic thyroid cancer involving lymph nodes. Is there anybody who would still do that vertical incision? Wave your hands if you're raising them. There's a few smattered people, yes. And presumably, this is for ease of access to the upper part of the neck. How about morbidity of the vertical versus the skin crease incision? Is there a difference in morbidity in terms of neurologic function in the neck?
It's not the morbidity, Brian, but it's the aesthetic morbidity.
I count that as morbidity.

The functional morbidity of numbness of the skin is going to be the same. But the aesthetic morbidity of putting a hypertrophic scar in a woman's neck, or a man's neck for that matter, is not called for, because you can essentially do everything, including level 2B and 1A, through a single transverse incision. Bob, try it. Next time you will give me a call after the operation, Jay, you were right, I could do it.

All right, so pathology on this case revealed a T1A. There was a tiny microscopic focus, a three millimeter focus of papillary cancer. N1B, a single lymph node involved. No extra nodal extension, despite the size of that thing. There was not felt to be soft tissue invasion. How about adjuvant therapy? Is this somebody who should receive radioactive iodine? How about anemorrhy?

Yes, so this is a patient now with relatively small primary, but already you have evidence of node involvement. So this would be at least intermediate risk, so would benefit from adjuvant iodine therapy.
You said that very confidently, will benefit the data that supports you?

Well, that is the slippery slope there now to say I will benefit, so let me retrace my step. I will recommend the patient to receive adjuvant therapy for two reasons. One, given the nodal involvement, we know that the risk of recurrence in this patient is going to be higher than if you did not have lymph node involvement. Therefore, you want to closely monitor this patient in a reliable manner. So using iodine therapy at least as, not just as adjuvant, but to allow you to better monitor the patient in terms of thyroglobulin measurement will be of benefit.
So what if the post-operative thyroglobulin is not measurable? Would you still give RAI?
If you post-op thyroglobulin?
Yeah, six weeks after the operation, the thyroglobulin is not measurable, and there are no antibodies.
TG is less than 0.2 negative antibodies.

Well, at least the data out there will suggest that we know that pre-op thyroglobulin doesn't actually tell you what the survival outcome is going to be. The drop in thyroglobulin post-surgery also has not been shown to be a strong predictor of what the outcome is going to be. It may be that you have a tumor that is actually not thyroglobulin secreting. And then the question becomes, what would be the benefit of your iodine therapy in that instance? I guess that would be something that you have to discuss with the patient, that using iodine therapy in this instance is probably not going to help in terms of your monitoring. But I know where you're coming from, saying, show me the data, that adjuvant therapy will actually help with the outcome for this patient. I think there is some data to suggest that, not strong, a lot of it retrospective, showing that when you give I-131 as adjuvant therapy in this instance, it doesn't improve your overall survival, but it may at least reduce the risk of recurrence, which is what most of these patients will suffer from.

So I'll show my stripes at this point and emphasize that I'm a therapeutic minimalist when it comes to the use of radioactive iodine, having spent almost 20 years at Mayo Clinic under the tutelage of Ian Hay. So I come at this from a biased perspective. The data from Mayo, and we look very, very carefully at these patients, the data from Mayo is that node positive or node negative, size of tumor irrespective, so long as the patient was truly stage one and low risk by the prognostic scoring system of MASIS ages or aims, that we were unable to demonstrate any benefit to I131 ablative therapies in these patients. And the two groups had superimposable mortality rates and recurrence rates. And those data we've presented on a number of occasions. Having said that, there are others around the country who strongly disagree with us. It is the source of continuing exciting interactions at various national and international meetings. And of course, moving to Cancer Center as I have in Tampa, I've had to somewhat compromise my principles and acknowledge that most of my colleagues would be very uncomfortable not treating a patient like this with I131. So my bias then is to do it in a way that, if we're going to do it, minimizes the morbidity of the treatment and use low-dose remnant ablation using thyrogen stimulation to avoid hypothyroidism and use low doses of I-131, which are demonstrated to provide equally effective ablation of the thyroid remnant, which is all you're really achieving by doing this I-131. But could I get a comment from the Japanese perspective? Radioactive iodine, I understand, is less commonly used in Japan. Would you take an approach that involved RAI or not?
There is no merit to radioactive iodine, but recurrent and distant metastasis in the future is high, I think. So I recommend radioactive iodine.
You would administer radioactive iodine?
But I will check the thyroid globulin, the level of thyroid globulin. So if it's high, I strongly recommend.

So I think that one very strong argument in favor of some exposure to radioactive iodine in this patient is this search for distant metastatic spread. We've currently classified her as an MX. But we have no chest imaging. We haven't done a CT scan of the chest. It's quite helpful, I think, sometimes to do low-dose RAI and do a post-therapy scan to give yourself that extra level of reassurance that the chest is clear. I haven't found that to be a big issue with the N1B, just one or two lymph nodes. But if you have bulky lymphadenopathy extensively through the neck, I think that's a different beast.
Brian, you have been in the thyroid cancer business long enough. In this setting of this patient, how often have you found distant metastasis by RAI scan?
Never.
So I think we need to clarify that.
I'm trying to be nice.

Is Mike Tuttle in the audience? Michael? No. So our data of RAI mimics or reflects exactly what the Mayo Clinic showed. The administration of RAI post-operatively did not make any difference in local regional recurrence, recurrence pre-survival, or overall survival, whether they were treated or not. So our current philosophy is we do not give radioactive iodine unless the operative findings or the pathology report indicates an aggressive cancer. or the patient who is a low risk has persistently elevated thyroglobulin postoperatively done at about six weeks out, indicating that there may be a small node that we did not clear and that may need RAI treatment.

reference_conclusion: Management consisted of total thyroidectomy with ipsilateral central compartment dissection and a comprehensive lateral neck dissection encompassing levels II through V. Adjuvant radioactive iodine was discussed extensively; the panel noted that it is commonly recommended for nodal disease/intermediate-risk features, but also cited institutional practice to reserve postoperative radioactive iodine for aggressive pathologic findings or persistently elevated postoperative thyroglobulin approximately six weeks after surgery.

So this would be at least intermediate risk, so would benefit from adjuvant iodine therapy. [...] So our current philosophy is we do not give radioactive iodine unless the operative findings or the pathology report indicates an aggressive cancer. or the patient who is a low risk has persistently elevated thyroglobulin postoperatively done at about six weeks out, indicating that there may be a small node that we did not clear and that may need RAI treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old postmenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Painful right breast lump of 2 months’ duration in the first quarter of 2013.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Initial diagnosis in 2013: right breast invasive ductal carcinoma with extensive high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), triple-negative phenotype; pathologic stage I, pT1bN0M0.  
- Subsequent ipsilateral right breast recurrence/new lesion in 2015: DCIS with multiple foci of microinvasive/invasive ductal carcinoma, triple-negative phenotype.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial core biopsy: high-grade DCIS.  
- Initial lumpectomy pathology: infiltrating ductal carcinoma with extensive DCIS; invasive component represented 5% of the tumor; invasive carcinoma size 2 mm; high nuclear grade; surgical margins were in contact with DCIS.  
- Re-excision performed 2 weeks later: no residual carcinoma.  
- 2015 biopsy of right breast lesion: DCIS with foci of microinvasive carcinoma.  
- Mastectomy pathology in 2015: DCIS with multiple foci of invasive ductal carcinoma; largest invasive focus 2 mm; DCIS comprised >90% of the tumor; stromal fibrosis present; sentinel lymph nodes negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial mammogram and breast ultrasound in 2013: upper outer quadrant right breast lesion measuring 2.5 × 3 cm, described as high density with pleomorphic microcalcifications.  
- Surveillance mammogram and ultrasound in the third quarter of 2015: pleomorphic microcalcifications below the scar in the right breast measuring 19 × 4 mm; these findings had not been present on the prior year’s study.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Initial tumor immunohistochemistry: triple-negative breast cancer.  
- 2015 recurrent/right breast tumor immunohistochemistry: triple-negative; Ki-67 20%.  
- Family history: aunt and cousin with breast cancer.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2013: lumpectomy performed for right breast lesion.  
- 2 weeks later: re-excision performed; no residual carcinoma identified.  
- Adjuvant chemotherapy: weekly paclitaxel for 12 doses followed by FAC for 4 cycles.  
- Adjuvant radiotherapy administered after chemotherapy.  
- Follow-up surveillance thereafter.  
- 2015: right mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy and breast reconstruction with tissue expander performed for ipsilateral recurrence/new lesion.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Post-mastectomy pathology in 2015 demonstrated DCIS with multiple small invasive ductal carcinoma foci, largest 2 mm, with negative sentinel lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Right-sided breast primary.

The mammogram and the ultrasound shows in the upper outer quarter a high density of 2.5 by 3 centimeters with pneumorphic and microcalcifications. The biopsy shows DCIS, high grade, and she performed a lumpectomy and centrifuge with no biopsy. The pathology report Infiltral ductal carcinoma with extensive DCIS and the infiltrative compound represents the 5% of the tumor. The nuclear grade were high and the size of the invasive carcinoma was 2 millimeters. The surgical margins were in contact with the DCIS. The immunochemistry report a triple negative breast cancer, and two weeks later, she had a Y-local excision with no residual carcinoma. So we have a stage 1 triple negative right breast cancer, T1B, N0, M0. She put in adjuvant chemotherapy with Taxol weekly times 12 and FAC times 4. Then she received cryotherapy and then follow-up. Next, please. In the mammogram and ultrasound control, In the third quarter 2015, this year, the mammogram report a pleomorphic microcalcifications below the scar in the same breast, the right breast, 19 by 4 millimeters. These were not found in the study of the last year. positive and central peripheral vascular Doppler the biopsy report DCIS with foci of microinvasive carcinoma. She had a mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy and breast reconstruction with tissue spander. The pathology reports a DCIS with multiple foci of invasive ductal carcinoma. The largest foci was 2 millimeters, and the DCIS represents more than 90% of the tumor. A stromal fibrosis was found, and the lymph nodes were negative. The monochemistry reports a triple negative tumor with a K67 of 20%. Next, please. There are questions. The first question is the role of knowing the BCRR mutation status in an LUVANT plant.

Optimal treatment for no... Let's take the questions one at a time if you don't mind. So we'll start with the first question. What would, knowing the BRCA, in light of the family history which wasn't that strong actually, an aunt and a cousin, at age postmenopausal at 55, what is the value of knowing versus not knowing the BRCA mutational status in the neoadjuvant plan? So I'm not 100% sure I understand the question.

So probably you didn't mean in the neoadjuvant plan, because this patient was treated adjuvantly. But the NCCN guidelines now state that anyone diagnosed with a triple negative cancer under the age of 65, I think, either 60 or 65, we do routine testing for BRCA1 or 2, for whatever it's worth. So theoretically, she would have fallen in that category with her family history and the triple negative nature of her tumor. In our center, patients It's a choice, but they may at the initial operation have chosen mastectomy bilaterally in lieu of doing the lumpectomy.

Even for what is, what's being presented, I think, is an extensive DCIS with very minimal invasive ductal component, but it's still, that would still apply. If bilateral mastectomy would still be an option as the initial choice. If she was BRCA1 mutational positive, or just with her family history?
No, if she was BRCA1 positive.

Okay, if she'd been tested. So, for those doctors on camera here from around the world, Michelle, it's not common to have access to the BRCA1 and 2 mutational analysis. What do you advise those doctors to do in this tricky case of triple negative and strong family history? Do you have advice for them?

Well, I think that, I guess, to me it's not such a strong family history. You know, maybe diving down and really being very thorough about, you know, is this a paternal aunt? your father have other sisters, you know, really trying to get an understanding of the number of individuals that were unaffected versus individuals that are affected and if those individuals exist to determine the family history.

So Michelle and everybody on camera, it's routine in our setting. when a family history suspects hereditary breast cancer to have both counseling and analysis, mutational analysis performed. Does anybody, or would you advise, seeing as they don't have financial access to the mutational analysis, would you advise a counseling clinic even so to do the deeper dive that you were mentioning about family history and verification, all the issues that go on in our counseling setting?
Sure. I mean, I think that could be... Because that's an inexpensive thing, right? Yeah, it could be inexpensive, and who knows what you can get paid for.

Can I add something? So in the JEPAR-6TO trial, where they compared carboplatin versus non- and triple-negative breast cancer patients for the new adjuvant setting, those patients that had a family history positive for breast cancer had a 57% response compared to 30% without the family history. So I think for us that we don't have genetic testing available in most of our cases, that component might be very helpful to decide whether or not to add carboplatin.

But Cynthia, I think you're raising a different issue, if I may say. The question was, In the absence of most centers in South America and elsewhere around the world not having access to the laboratory estimation of VLC1-2 mutation, would you recommend, as you are doing in Monterey, would you recommend a genetic counseling clinic to do a deeper dive into the data around the family history before making a decision? Or is triple negative in any family history good enough for you to assume a mutational analysis?

I would say we did a study on 50-year-old or less triple negative breast cancer patients. There were 200, and in those, 23% had a BRCA mutation. And if they were less than 40 years old, 30% had a BRCA mutation. So, well, yes, if we have available genetic assessment, I think that would be worth
Would you mind, Cynthia, for the benefit of South American doctors to mention your study with the City of Hope Hospital on BRCA1-2 analysis?

Yes, so City of Hope has a registry, a prospective registry in the U.S. and in several sites among Latin America, specifically Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, as far as I know. And they are doing the genetic testing for free with a special panel called East Hispanil, where they test 114 prevalent mutations among Hispanics. It's without cost. It's a research project. And it has an 80% of sensitivity and a 100% of specificity. So we have been doing this for three years now.
And other people can get onto this collaboration, right?
Yes, so I've been referring the interested people to Dr. Jeffrey Weitzel, who is the PI of this important club.
So perhaps the second question is a provocative one. Hugo, do you want to just mention your second question?
well, the optimal treatment for a small node, negative, triple negative breast cancer. Is observation an option?

So, in other words, you don't mean after surgery, obviously, but you're asking is avoiding adjuvant chemotherapy ever an option in a triple negative tumor? So, perhaps I'll pick on, like, Jack Urban first to just give us your view of small triple negative cancer as relates to adjuvant chemotherapy.

Oh, Paul, thank you. These are very, very tricky. I would have to say yes, but I think that the criteria that I would use are several. First, a T1A is not a T1A. It could be multifocal invasive disease in an area of DCIS, and I view that somewhat differently biologically than a single focus of two millimeters or three millimeters of invasion. So I would want to look at the pathology very carefully to see whether or not we're really talking about unifocal disease as opposed to multifocal disease. In this case, I would think somewhat carefully about that and the possibility of retreatment with adjuvant therapy with, for example, a non-anthracycline combination of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide would not be out of the question for me. I believe activity has been established. I would not be enthusiastic about a platinum-based regimen without more information about family or genetics?

I think the current, if I'm speaking out of turn, Tony, but the current policy at MGH is not to use platinums routinely, but to give them in proven mutational analysis patients. If a patient has a BRCA1,2 mutation proved, we tend to in which we use platinum either in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting at the moment.
And I think that's ours as well. I perhaps might make an exception if I had a 30 year old where the family history was either incomplete or strongly positive and testing couldn't be completed.
I know the other people, thank you very much Jack. I think you've expressed the opinion of most people online. I'm going to take the prerogative of saying so. Michelle, can we go back to you?

I just want to be clear. You know, I think that originally this tumor was excised. It was 7 millimeters. It could have been multifocal in that nature, but I think even in that setting, a priority, we would have not offered neoadjuvant chemotherapy, because remember, the original core biopsy was high-grade DCIS. And we certainly, for a seven millimeter tumor, wouldn't have included a platinum-based agent. Our neoadjuvant protocol that's open right now is for tumors that are greater than two centimeters. If they're carriers, they get randomized to receive AC or a platinum-based chemotherapy on the informed trial. So this is pretty small.
So I think we might have mixed up two thoughts. I wasn't implying she should get it. I was saying when we get a neoadjuvant.
No, but Sophie was talking about this.

Oh, okay, right. So, okay, I think we've got consensus on that. Do you want to go back to after the recurrence in this that's being performed. Is now bilateral mastectomy an option or the option of choice?

It's not the option. It's always an option. We know the contralateral prophylactic mastectomy doesn't afford any increase in overall survival. Many women choose it because they don't want to go through the screening, but we carefully caution them that, you know, if there was an infection in the contralateral breast, if there was something that could delay her systemic therapy, if that's what she needed, That's a problem. So it's always an option, but we certainly don't force it upon anyone, because there's no survival benefit.
Shaila, I can see you nodding your head. Do you want to add something surgically to this?

What we do know is that the oncologic principles take first hand. So getting a tumor out, negative margins, orients in the margin, we all know that. But if you can do that, you have to keep in mind their cosmetic outcome. And so we know that women that have a unilateral mastectomy with implant reconstruction, their satisfaction long-term is very, very low. So sometimes if you're in a community where all you can get is implant-based reconstruction, you have to consider a contralateral mastectomy for symmetry procedures and their bras fitting properly and their clothes fitting. It's not for survival, but their quality of life is significantly impacted by how they look and their sexual life.
Alfonso, are there any radiation issues?

Yeah, a couple of comments. Just in general, and there is quite a bit of data on that, the risk of local failure for triple negative patients is significantly higher than luminal A or luminal B. So when you look at the data, you will see, let's say, at 5, 10, or 7 years of follow-up, luminal A will have 2% local failure is almost three and a half times the luminal age. Compared to her two positive patients before her septum, it used to be 11 after her septum, it's much less than that. So we still struggle with the local failure rate for triple negative. We'd like to bring it down to be close to 2 or 3 percent And there are some trials here and there, like actually giving concomitant cisplatin with radiation. And this is a trial from the Brigham that we also accrue for it here. But they include only 2 centimeter triple negative. So triple negative is an issue with local failure. I don't know how to overcome this, whether by adding something concomitant to this or including And what worries me here is that she had the local failure right away, within a year or two. And I don't know if this might reflect that maybe some DCIS was left behind. The radiation was absolutely fine. It was a British hypofractionation, which gave very good results. But it's just surprising that it came rather quickly. And then just the only treatment for this patient is mastectomy.

reference_conclusion: Following ipsilateral breast recurrence characterized by predominantly DCIS with multiple microinvasive foci and negative sentinel lymph nodes, mastectomy is the indicated local treatment. Contralateral prophylactic mastectomy may be discussed as an option for symmetry or patient preference, but it is not the preferred approach and does not confer an overall survival benefit. Platinum-based systemic therapy is not recommended routinely for this small node-negative triple-negative tumor and would generally be reserved for patients with a proven BRCA1/2 mutation; genetic counseling and BRCA assessment are appropriate if available.
reference_conclusion_quote: But the NCCN guidelines now state that anyone diagnosed with a triple negative cancer under the age of 65, I think, either 60 or 65, we do routine testing for BRCA1 or 2 [...] So theoretically, she would have fallen in that category with her family history and the triple negative nature of her tumor. [...] In this case, I would think somewhat carefully about that and the possibility of retreatment with adjuvant therapy with, for example, a non-anthracycline combination of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide would not be out of the question for me. I believe activity has been established. I would not be enthusiastic about a platinum-based regimen without more information about family or genetics [...] we certainly, for a seven millimeter tumor, wouldn't have included a platinum-based agent. [...] It's not the option. It's always an option. We know the contralateral prophylactic mastectomy doesn't afford any increase in overall survival. [...] And then just the only treatment for this patient is mastectomy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old woman. Never smoker. No alcohol use. Prior treated breast malignancy. Reported comorbidities were present. Functional status was described as good; she had still been working at presentation.

[ chief complaint ]: New dyspnea.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the left lower lobe lung. Clinical stage before brain MRI was described as T4N1 non-small cell lung cancer. A small brain lesion concerning for solitary metastasis was subsequently identified on MRI; stage designation under consideration included stage IIIA versus stage IVA.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy confirmed squamous carcinoma. Diagnostic tissue was obtained from a level 11 lymph node. Other sampled lymph nodes were negative aside from the involved level 11 node.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thoracic imaging showed a large left lower lobe mass. The mass obliterated the inferior pulmonary vein and abutted the airway and undersurface of the pulmonary artery. PET imaging showed the primary lesion to be metabolically active with probable central necrosis. An FDG-avid lymph node was present at the bifurcation/hilar region. No other mediastinal nodes were described as significantly FDG-avid. Brain MRI showed a small lesion concerning for metastasis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy was performed. Next-generation sequencing was also sent. Comprehensive molecular testing could not be completed on the biopsy specimen because of insufficient tissue. PD-L1 status was not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a prior breast malignancy that had been treated. For the current lung cancer, invasive mediastinal staging with biopsy was completed.

[ current disease status ]: Left lower lobe squamous non-small cell lung cancer with level 11 nodal involvement and an equivocal small brain lesion of uncertain significance. The patient was considered appropriate for resection, with possible need for complex left lower lobectomy with airway reconstruction/sleeve procedure based on local extent.

[ other clinical data ]: Mediastinal staging was completed by interventional pulmonology. Surgical local therapy, if pursued, was described as lobectomy rather than pneumonectomy if feasible.

<image> PET/CT imaging slide showing axial chest views of a left lower lobe/perihilar lung mass with FDG uptake, presented for tumor board review of local extent and nodal staging.
<image> Slide showing liquid biopsy/NGS results and PD-L1 biomarker associations as part of the tumor board discussion on molecular testing in this lung cancer case.
<image> Slide summarizing multidisciplinary discussion points for a potentially resectable lung cancer case, including stage uncertainty, fitness for surgery, and comparison of local and systemic management options.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, that's that hard. That's that box where it's tough and where I think part of the value of the tumor board is one is actually having persons of your own specialty there to kind of be a regulator. Because for any surgeon you have, you know, we have six surgeons in our group. It's not a bad idea to have five other surgeons go like, what are you what are you thinking? You should maybe dial it back. On the other hand, it's nice to have, you know, the other specialties where a medical oncologist can say, I know that if we can treat this, the outcome's going to be good. They're going to do well with chemo, you know, can you find a way to definitively treat this locally? And then you can feel the surgeon a little more comfortable saying, I am going to, in that gray box, I'm going to push a little bit more. It's technically on the edge, but clinically this is going to go well. Let's find a way to do this. Let's take that bigger step. Let's take a little bit more risk operatively. And I think that's worth it. So this is a case from our Artyom Bort. The quick background on her, 75-year-old woman, had prior breast malignancy, treated, who landed at her primary with some new dyspnea, carries a few comorbidities, but is actually great functional status, was still working, never smoke or no alcohol, no big family issues that came up. So she got some imaging. And I think the next slide, you can sort of see pretty clearly that there's a large mass in the left lower lobe. this thing kind of obliterates the inferior pulmonary vein, and then you can see abutting the airway and the undersurface of the pulmonary artery there. So she got a PET as well, and you can see metabolically active, probably central necrosis there, and then there's a lymph node there, the bifurcation, which is also FDG-avid, but nothing really in the mediastinum that looked too bright. So She was sent to our interventional pulmonologist to undergo biopsy and complete mediastinal staging.

And I think that that brings up a big question at this point, because I can say in our practice, I think that this case would be sent to us for a percutaneous biopsy. And that I find highly questionable. I believe that that is the pathway that would be chosen, maybe not if a thoracic surgeon saw the patient, because of ease of access and ease of procedure. Order the biopsy. It's reviewed. We schedule this biopsy. It can be done safely. We'll probably get a positive outcome as far as a diagnosis. I look at this case, and I see exactly what you described, that there's a lymph node in addition to this mass, and this is a big mass, right? When I look at this mass, initially, I think this may not be a resectable mass, ultimately, that this patient has a high likelihood of spread of whatever this is to mediastinal lymph nodes. I want to send to an interventional pulmonologist to get simultaneous tissue diagnosis of the lung mass and the lymph nodes. Scott, how do you see this?

Yeah, 100%. I think even if it's radiographically negative, I think that the chance, there's a reasonable chance of radiographically occult N1, N2, potentially even N3 disease. And so doing invasive mediastinal staging is absolutely imperative here.

Yeah, this was actually a great case from our side in the sense that this came back to what we started talking about, came from a pulmonologist who then immediately said, look, I've got this individual, I have this imaging, why don't we just see them in the multidisciplinary clinic right up front? And so that way, even before a diagnosis, they saw our interventional pulmonologist, they spoke with our medical oncologist, and they saw me. So we immediately were able to say, well, yeah, the staging plan we're going to need is to go this direction. And so they started out in that multidisciplinary format, and then I think it helped us make the best choices to get a diagnosis, a stage, and then move forward with them. They did end up, of course, getting an MRI. The nice thing in this case is because of some insurance coverage-related delays, this actually took a while to get aligned. So they had already had their diagnosis, but they did have what was concerning for a small metastasis. But this was identified kind of after everything else had already been completed. So the path is on the next slide, but essentially confirmed that this was a squamous carcinoma, but none of the lymph nodes outside of that one level 11, and that is actually what was biopsied for the diagnosis, was that lymph node, to your point. No other spread elsewhere. So what looked to be what we were calling a T4N1 squamous carcinoma, again, prior to having this brain MR.

I think even with the brain, I think it's a subtle finding, and I don't know that you would forego potentially curative, intense treatment in order to watch this brain. And so I think it's still an appropriate decision.
Can you talk a little bit about that with an isolated brain metastasis in the setting of non-small cell lung cancer and no other evidence of disease, how you generally approach these cases?

Right. And so we're always thinking about TNM staging regardless of the M part of it, you know, because we often get the patients when the metastasis has happened. And then we look at, you know, is this solitary? And the brain is a good example. And when we have a solitary or something not even all that clear on brain imaging, We think of the brain separate and think about what systemically they need and think we can treat the brain if we need to. And we would want them to get the treatment they would get for the rest of the lung disease first, you know, unless it was widely metastatic. So we do think about these oligometastatic patients and look at the T and M and N staging to think about how they might proceed forward.
Are there any other sites in the body?

So yeah, I mean, so I mean, if there's an adrenal, you know, anything that's kind of oligo, even a local bone lesion, if it's if it's one, the bone is a little tricky, often on subsequent imaging. Once they start getting treated, they become many. But again, we're looking toward. curing a patient if we can. And so that's kind of where our starting point is. I see this as metastatic. Is there a way to get a better outcome for local control? Because I know how to treat somebody systemically, but usually those outcomes are not as good as if we can get the local control to. And so we're always looking for that. And it's usually solitary mets. We will at least consider it. I think liver is a place where we probably start to treat systemically and not try to do local therapy and, you know, treat the liver, because the liver tends to be something that has more implications for higher level metastatic disease.

How do you feel about nodal involvement when you're thinking oligomet? Because we always, as surgeons, are kind of on the fence where if I see nodal disease, and yeah, we've got an isolated brain met, you know, you start to question, should we undergo surgical resection, which comes with a lot more morbidity, or is this someone we shift over to chemoradiation, immuno? and then can treat the brain with CyberKnife, still treat them that way, but take the surgical morbidity away when we start seeing nodal disease. That's always been my kind of hesitancy is that, is it really just that sort of, quote, oligomet pattern, or are we seeing local, we're seeing regional, and we're seeing distant, maybe we should treat them differently.

So, I mean, I think an N1 nodal disease is different than N2 or multistation N2 disease. So, I think with N1, I would still proceed. Also squamous cell. In our squamous cell patients, they tend to be, I know this was a large tumor, they tend to be larger or more localized. So, I would like to get that local control. If this was a diffuse adenocarcinoma, you know, and then you see these other small pulmonary nodules that we were ignoring, but now there's lymph node positivity and potentially another metastasis, that's looking more like this is really systemic disease. So I try to get that local control when we can, but I agree. If you start seeing mediastinal lymph node involvement and metastatic disease, sometimes getting that systemic treatment in, and again, now we have other options with chemo and immunotherapy and with targeted therapies. And sometimes then we're doing the consolidation local therapy later. And so I think we keep everything on the table for patients in ways that we never did before, even in the metastatic setting.
So what are the local treatment options for this patient?

So, based on her imaging, local therapy surgically would be some kind of probably complex lobectomy, meaning lobe plus airway reconstruction, maybe a sleeve based on its abutment of the airway itself. We really try and avoid pneumonectomy for lung cancers in most cases at this point. The morbidity is high and we have other really good therapies. So, but for now, it would be lobectomy would be the surgical local control that we would offer.
And obviously there's no interventional approach to this, but from a radiation standpoint, what would your approach be?

Yeah, I think the, well, the, I can give you the short answer, but the longer interesting answer is if we say they are M1, have metastatic disease, and then the surgeon says, well, you know, I don't know what the risk benefit would be compared to the risk given a huge surgery. Let's say they're in two or something, right? And then they get chemo immunotherapy. And the question is, is do we do chemo RT? Or do we do just radiation alone? Because a lot of these patients, what will happen is they'll get complete response radiographically in the mediastinum. Their tumor will shrink down to something very, very small. And I can just do SBRT to the primary target. and not have to worry about, you know, giving six weeks of radiation with chemo and causing them all sorts of toxicities. And then also, potentially, they could stay on their immunotherapy for the five treatments of radiation or three treatments of radiation I'm doing. So it gets a little bit more nuanced for these cases. Like I said, you know, these are the most complicated cases, right? Because there's no guidelines and there's no, you know, studies for this particular patient that has a metastatic lesion that we then get chemo I.O. and then they have a good response. And then what do we do? But long story short, I would do consolidation, radiation, or radiation up front. I think another interesting question is, like, if this were my family member or myself in this exact situation and they have an M1 lesion, I would want them to get chemoimmunotherapy, I think. Whether that's because they're going to get surgery or because they have metastatic disease, I feel like, in my heart of hearts, that's probably the best thing for them. Going straight to Pacific and then doing SRS to their brain lesion, I don't want to say that that's the wrong thing to do because we don't have data really, but I feel like the chemoimmunotherapy up front is going to move the needle the most for patients. I don't know how you guys feel about it.

I mean, this is a patient, when I see a large tumor, even before the lymph node was positive, my thought is, please send this patient to me because I think I can help this patient. Now we see it's squamous cell. They tend to have even better responses with immunotherapy. We don't know the PD-L1 status of this, but regardless, we would advocate for a neoadjuvant approach in this patient and give them neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy and then hopefully take them to surgery for a PATH-CR, right?

Yeah, so she had liquid biopsy and she had NGS because this is another, to your point earlier about biopsy samples and tissue, this was done on her lymphoid biopsy, but they could not do everything because there just wasn't enough tissue. But yeah, looks like someone who would do okay with the immunotherapies.

And for squamous cell, the next generation sequencing is less important. You don't expect, unless this person was a nonsmoker, you don't really expect them to have EGFR or ALK, which are things that could change their therapy and their outcomes. So that's a very reasonable thing.
Are these patients always getting a liquid biopsy up front? Is that something you're doing these days?

So patients with early stage disease, liquid biopsies are not always informative. You know, then we can talk, MRD is going to be a whole other conversation and not probably part of this group. But liquid biopsies are kind of uninformative in most people with lower stages. We're not at the place where we have ultrasensitive assays at this point. So they're better for metastatic disease.

Yeah, so this was just kind of the discussion we had again. She's appropriate for a section. You know, here's our stage. Are we calling her a 4A, a 3A? And then the options that we kind of had. And we landed on, again, what we were talking about, a neoadjuvant approach, chemo, you know. The brain actually, I didn't include it in this, but she had a repeat brain MRI about six weeks in and the lesion's not visible. So whether it was treated or not there, I don't know. We're going to just push forward either way with a sort of curative intent therapy.
What was the response on imaging? Do you have that?
Oh, you know, I don't. I didn't put everything together quick enough.
So you're always at what time point are you going to get a follow up imaging study?
So three months post resection, typically, though, they'll get some three to six just kind of depending on.

And do you tend to do imaging so now they're getting four cycles neoadjuvant? I think there's some question whether there's a benefit to looking at a scan in between again, especially with the pseudo progression and things like that. I'm not a big fan of getting a scan in between. I rather just do the therapy and move on because I'm not sure that it should stop you from giving more therapy.

I don't unless we have a really high expectation that there is something either they're progressing that can truly progressing. Maybe they're they're not tolerating a therapy or we're just concerned. Otherwise, I don't have any reason to look, you know, just wait till you're done. Don't look inside the box and we'll deal with it.
So you're not concerned about a patient about uncovering more widespread metastatic disease that would certainly sway a decision for a definitive local therapy.
Well, we would image them before after completion of their systemic. So, yeah, but we wouldn't do the kind of the two cycle reimage and then see where we're at.

And then to see more and more of them do it because in a standard metastatic setting, you might image after two cycles. And so that's kind of where people are going. And I've seen a lot of these now where then they end up coming back to tumor board because they don't look definitively like they're responding. And to me, that's insufficient. And once you decide on that neoadjuvant approach, you're going forward with it. You're not going to stop at halfway and then have to, you know, convert it to chemoradiation or something like that.
What about your your borderline cases? Because like the threshold for saying that they're operable, right?

So, you know, I think that's it's a good question. And it kind of I'll give a really long winded surgical answer. So I think resectability is something that comes up a lot. People, I think, use the term unresectable, surgeons include it inappropriately, because they assume it's just sort of a linear, it's a line of unresectable, resectable. But really, resectability is a plane. There's two axes of it. There's clinical resectability, there's technical resectability. Clinical resectability is, will my operation benefit this patient from the perspective of their disease burden? And so the answer is, even if you have a very small lesion with N3 disease, surgery is clinically not apt. You don't do that. That's a clinically unresectable tumor, right? Technically, sure, you can take all that out. That's not very hard. Technical resectability is the other piece of it. Technical is, can I do this operation and have a patient walk out the door, a whole patient walk out the door? And that is a different, that's a different thing to approach. So how extensive is the disease? So when I think about resectability, I'm thinking about those two axes. So you've got technically resectable, clinically resectable. That's an obvious yes. You've got technically unresectable, clinically unresectable. That's your obvious no. The gray zone is on either side. If you have a patient who is clinically resectable, where you feel like you can benefit, like this patient, we can benefit them if we can provide a definitive therapy. But technically, you're pushing a limit. Can you get them through this operation? And so the question is, well, am I going to get them through a lobe? I think so. A 75 drilled woman can get through a lobe. A sleeve? Yeah. Airway reconstructions are fairly straightforward. We can do that. A pneumonectomy? Are we going to believe that this 75-year-old is going to push through it? Well, it's a left side, probably okay. A right side, maybe not. Higher morbidity. So, yes, it is a resectable tumor, but we're pushing the limits of it. The other side of it is obviously the ones that are clinically technically and respectable but clinically you do well and so those are the harder decisions for us is you want to as a surgeon push really hard to do it you say look this patient it would be great if you could get this out this is they're going to do well but technically you're saying it's involving too many structures maybe You've got, you know, aortic involvement, for example, that's that's resectable, but it it starts pushing the difficulty level a bit. Will the patient tolerate it? So those two boxes of where it's discordant between the clinical and the technical resectability is what makes it hard. And then, like any good surgeon, I'll fall back to radiation oncologist.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, because I find myself pushing patients towards surgery because I feel like they're going to get chemo immunotherapy. And that seems to help the patients the most based on all the cases reviewed in the past. So, if they're technically resectable, and clinically, that dial can be turned up, you know, where it's like, in one, in two, multistation in two, you know, maybe like limited in three or something.

Yeah, that's that hard, that's that box where it's tough and where I think part of the value of the tumor board is, one is actually having persons of your own specialty there to kind of be a regulator because For any surgeon, you have, you know, we have six surgeons in our group. It's not a bad idea to have five other surgeons go like, what are you thinking? You should maybe dial it back. On the other hand, it's nice to have, you know, the other specialties where a medical oncologist can say, I know that if we can treat this, the outcome is going to be good. They're going to do well with chemoimmuno. Can you find a way to definitively treat this locally? And then you can feel the surgeon a little more comfortable saying, I am going to in that gray box, I'm going to push a little bit more. It's technically on the edge, but clinically, this is going to go well. Let's find a way to do this. Let's let's take that bigger step. Let's take a little bit more risk operatively. And I think that's worth.

reference_conclusion: Multidisciplinary review supported a curative-intent strategy for this T4N1 squamous non-small cell lung carcinoma, despite the equivocal small brain lesion, with treatment directed first at the thoracic disease. The agreed plan was neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy followed by reassessment after completion of systemic therapy and, if still appropriate, definitive surgical resection with lobectomy-based local control rather than upfront chemoradiation. Interval imaging during neoadjuvant treatment was not planned unless there were specific clinical concerns; restaging imaging would be obtained after completion of systemic therapy before definitive local therapy.

The brain actually, I didn't include it in this, but she had a repeat brain MRI about six weeks in and the lesion's not visible. So whether it was treated or not there, I don't know. We're going to just push forward either way with a sort of curative intent therapy. [...] but for now, it would be lobectomy would be the surgical local control that we would offer. [...] Well, we would image them before after completion of their systemic. So, yeah, but we wouldn't do the kind of the two cycle reimage and then see where we're at.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive breast cancer with increasing breast lump and axillary disease despite systemic therapy; breast lump was painful.

[ diagnosis ]: Initially diagnosed with locally advanced triple-negative breast cancer, clinical stage T3N2. Subsequent disease progression with extensive bone and nodal metastases. Performance status was 1. No known comorbidities.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial diagnosis: ductal carcinoma of the breast, triple-negative subtype.  
- Repeat biopsy in July after neoadjuvant chemotherapy: ductal carcinoma, triple-negative subtype.  
- Subsequent repeat biopsy after metastatic progression: infiltrative ductal carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial imaging had included contrast-enhanced CT chest.  
- Post-chemotherapy PET scan demonstrated extensive bone metastases and nodal metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing showed low tumor mutational burden.  
- Microsatellite status: stable.  
- HRD score/genomic aberration score: 44, reported as positive/borderline positive.  
- TP53 mutation detected.  
- MCL1 copy number gain detected; copy number reported as 16.  
- RICTOR copy number gain detected; copy number reported as 8.  
- TERT copy number gain detected; copy number reported as 8.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PD-L1 by immunohistochemistry: 0.  
- HER2 status from prior outside testing: 0.  
- ER/PR/HER2 were not repeated locally on the latest biopsy.  
- No other laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced disease:  
  - 4 cycles of doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (AC).  
  - 2 cycles of nab-paclitaxel.  
  - Followed by 2 cycles of nab-paclitaxel plus carboplatin.  
- Clinical response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy was poor.  
- After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, PET scan showed metastatic progression with extensive bone and nodal disease.  
- Subsequently treated with eribulin.  
- After 2 cycles of eribulin, there was no clinical response; breast and axillary lesions increased in size.  
- Additional prior systemic exposure was described as including anthracyclines, taxanes, carboplatin, capecitabine, and eribulin.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Progressive metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.  
- Clinical progression continued on eribulin, with enlarging breast lump, enlarging axillary disease, and a small additional nodule.  
- Pain was present in the breast lesion.  
- Performance status remained 1.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No known comorbidities.  
- Family history: doubtful/unclear history of malignancy in grandmother.

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended repeat biomarker assessment on the current specimen, specifically reassessment of HER2 status to determine whether HER2-low or ultra-low expression is present, and evaluation of androgen receptor status. If HER2-low or ultra-low expression is identified, trastuzumab deruxtecan may be considered; if not, sacituzumab govitecan was preferred, with datopotamab deruxtecan as another option where available. Clinical trial enrollment was considered the ideal next step, particularly for sacituzumab govitecan, and androgen receptor-directed therapy such as enzalutamide may be considered after exhaustion of standard options or if access to other therapies is limited. Immunotherapy was not favored in view of MSI-low/TMB-stable disease with PD-L1 0%.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 11-year-old girl.

[ chief complaint ]: Asymptomatic left supraclavicular neck mass present for more than 3 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with cervical nodal metastases and pulmonary metastases (M1 disease). Postoperative pathology described pulmonary thyroid cancer, diffusely infiltrating.

[ histopathology results ]: Excisional biopsy of the supraclavicular lymph node showed the node replaced by papillary thyroid carcinoma, classic type, with papillary architecture, focal follicular pattern, and classic papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclear features including pallor and grooves. Post-thyroidectomy pathology showed diffusely infiltrating papillary thyroid carcinoma with microscopic extrathyroidal extension. Thirty of 122 lymph nodes were involved; the largest metastatic lymph node measured 2 cm in the right lateral neck. Histology after neoadjuvant therapy showed irregular abnormal thyroid parenchyma with fibrosis and altered follicular-pattern tumor, interpreted as treatment effect.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound showed an enlarged heterogeneous thyroid gland with thickened isthmus, bulging anterior contour bilaterally, and diffuse punctate echogenic foci/speckling throughout both lobes, particularly on the left. CT neck showed a large enhancing supraclavicular lymph node and additional enhancing cervical lymph nodes on the left side. Preoperative chest CT demonstrated innumerable tiny bilateral pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic deposits. Restaging CT after approximately 3 months of larotrectinib showed decreased cervical adenopathy, with persistent bilateral cervical lymph nodes. At approximately 6 months, CT showed further mild decrease in size of cervical lymph nodes without complete resolution. Diagnostic I-123 scan after TSH stimulation showed very faint uptake in the neck and limited/underwhelming pulmonary uptake. Post-therapy radioiodine scan showed intense uptake in the bilateral neck and multifocal uptake in both lungs.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing identified an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion.

[ laboratory results ]: Baseline thyroglobulin was 146 with negative thyroglobulin antibodies. After 6 months of treatment, thyroglobulin was 36. Bilateral vocal cords were functioning on assessment prior to treatment. During larotrectinib therapy, grade 1 transaminitis occurred.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially underwent excisional biopsy of the supraclavicular lymph node, which established metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. Neoadjuvant larotrectinib was started because of concern for neurovascular/recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and potential surgical morbidity. Treatment was continued for approximately 6 months and was tolerated apart from grade 1 transaminitis; imaging showed partial response with reduction in cervical adenopathy, and pulmonary nodules became no longer visible on chest CT while on therapy. Larotrectinib was held prior to surgery. She then underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central and bilateral lateral neck dissection, including microdissection of both recurrent laryngeal nerves, right spinal accessory nerve dissection, and right retropharyngeal dissection. Postoperatively she required drains and had transient hypocalcemia; both recurrent laryngeal nerves stimulated well. Larotrectinib was restarted postoperatively. She subsequently received radioactive iodine therapy with 100 mCi following low-iodine diet and TSH stimulation/withdrawal.

[ other clinical data ]: She was a professional singer and had recently moved to the area.

reference_conclusion: Cross-sectional imaging and comprehensive cervical ultrasound assessment were recommended prior to any lymph node excision to define the thyroid primary and map nodal disease. Given concern for neurovascular and recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement in an NTRK fusion-positive papillary thyroid carcinoma, neoadjuvant larotrectinib was administered for six months, followed by total thyroidectomy with bilateral central and bilateral lateral neck dissection, including right retropharyngeal dissection. Postoperatively, larotrectinib was restarted and radioactive iodine therapy was administered; ongoing management consists of levothyroxine optimization and surveillance imaging, with reassurance that prognosis remains favorable despite pulmonary metastatic disease.
reference_conclusion_quote: we typically would not recommend it to do surgery for imaging [...] If you've got a lymph node, you've got to image the thyroid. You've got to get an ultrasound. [...] I do like to get a cross-sectional imaging. to look at the entire thyroid itself [...] So yes, we do get the molecular testing, which reveals an ETV6 and ChEK3 fusion [...] Yes, so she does get offered layer with tractinib. And this is started [...] We felt at this time, because it had reached somewhat stability and probably maximal response on the drug after six months, we decided to offer surgery at this time point. [...] She got a total thyroidectomy plus bilateral central and bilateral lateral neck dissection. She did end up requiring micro dissection of the bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerves, as well as the right spinal accessory nerve and right retroprangial dissection. [...] So we did elect to restart leotrectinib. [...] Yeah, so you gave a hundred millicures [...] We did intensify her levothyroxine. Her ultrasound CT of the neck was without recurrence. but her CT chest did show these multiple tiny little lung nodules. [...] we did reassure them about prognosis. And coming back to what Jonathan said, we know that regardless, prognosis is excellent in this population.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult patient with prostate cancer. No further demographic data were available.

[ chief complaint ]: Rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) following focal treatment of an extreme apical prostate tumour.

[ diagnosis ]: Localised prostate adenocarcinoma, initially staged as clinical T2a, with Gleason score 4+3. Subsequent adjacent/in-field recurrence at the prostatic apex was identified on follow-up imaging after focal irreversible electroporation (IRE).

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumour histology showed Gleason 4+3 adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Post-treatment T2-weighted MRI performed shortly after initial IRE showed haemorrhagic change in the treated area.  
- MRI at 1 year after initial treatment showed good resolution without concerning findings.  
- PSMA PET performed in 2019 for PSA rise demonstrated uptake in the treated region.  
- MRI in early 2020 demonstrated an abnormal area on ADC imaging adjacent to the prior treatment zone, consistent with adjacent/in-field recurrence and incomplete prior treatment coverage.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA was approximately 10 ng/mL in 2017 at initial diagnosis.  
- PSA rose again to approximately 10 ng/mL in 2019 after initial focal treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient underwent focal irreversible electroporation for an extreme apical prostate tumour in 2017.  
- Biochemical recurrence was observed by 2019 with PSA rise, and imaging subsequently demonstrated adjacent/in-field recurrence.

[ current disease status ]: Adjacent/in-field recurrence at the prostatic apex after focal IRE, with biochemical recurrence and imaging evidence of incomplete prior treatment coverage.

[ other clinical data ]: The recurrent lesion was located at the extreme prostatic apex, adjacent to the original treatment field. No additional comorbidity, age, family history, or performance status data were available.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks. I presented the results of our patients on the NanoKnife Masterclass two days ago, and so this is a denominator of about 600 cases up to date, with about 11-year follow-up. But what I thought I'd do is just share with you a couple of cases and some particular points with using irreversible electroporation. So the first one is a person who had an apical tumour, an extreme apical tumour, who then got a recurrence. The second one is a more typical extreme apical tumour that we treated. And the third one was just a tricky case in the anterior zone. So this patient had a PSA of about 10 in 2017, had a clinical T2A lesion and was a Gleason 4 plus 3 actually. After our treatment, we always do a T2 MRI image, which shows hemorrhage. I know Mark Emberton does a gadolinium at this point to look for perfusion, and having spoken to him, I think that might be a good idea. PSA dropped. One year MRI showed good resolution and nothing much to worry about. 2019, PSA went up to about 10. And then as a result of that, we did a PET scan and the PET scan did show some activity in that area. We have had a couple of people after IRE where you'll form a cavity and you'll get a false positive with the PSMA PET scan. So just a caution that when you see something bright there, you just have to look at the MRI as well. As a result of that, an MRI in early 2020 showed, as you can see, let me see here. It showed on the ADC an area just here which was adjacent to the area, so clearly I didn't treat that area completely. So that was an adjacent or infield recurrence. And so we retreated that, and the principles of treating the apex, I always put four needles into the apex. I know some people use three at the apex, but I always use four, just for a reliable ablation. And I always make sure that the distance of the active electrode is at least three millimetres from the edge. So that way I'm going to treat two millimetres outside of the capsule. One of the advantages of IRE that you can treat extracapsular disease. And this was the MRI at the two day mark afterwards showing the hemorrhage again. and PSA started to drop down to 3.7. The one year MRI showed retraction of that area and no perfusion, and biopsies of that area in 2022 was all clear, and the PSA up to today has stayed very stable. We then looked at our redo treatments, and the redo treatments, We've had 26 of the patients have had redos, and of those 26, 15 of them have had a durable response with biopsy-proven clearance. Overall, over time, that dropped down to 12. So there was some late recurrences as well. So overall, we actually ended up with half of the patients on a redo got a durable response. And again, there's treatment afterwards with either radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy. I thought I'd just share, I got one of our fellows just to look at exactly what's happened to the redos, because I think the redos are interesting. Over 344 primary RREs with a minimum of 18 months follow-up, the recurrence rate was 62 of them, as defined as any Gleason 4 pattern. Those recurrences had a redo and some had some active surveillance and just monitored a tiny little microscopic spot. Some were just Gleason 6 low-grade stuff. This was all recurrences. This is including Gleason 6. and we did redo IREs in 19 patients. And in those 19 patients, 10 of them ended up having a radical prostatectomy, two had more than two IREs, one's just been monitored and seven of them are clear from significant tumour. But what was interesting was This, when you look at the infield and outfield, the infield ones seem to do better with redo focal therapy, tiny numbers, four and two clear, although a lot of them decided that forget about it, I'm gonna actually have my prostate out. But the outfield, we had an extremely high 73% recurrence rate after redo in the outfield. which is different to what other people have presented. As a result of my general philosophy about infield tumours, if you get any biopsy recurrence on the infield, we are aggressive by doing a repeat treatment immediately, as opposed to outfield, which I think is more a disease phenomena. This is a more standard case. This is an anterior apical tumour. PSA was about 9.7. And then we treated that with, this is the PSMA PET scan. We treated that with a nanoknife. This was the MRI six months down the track. PSA fell down and biopsies were clear. This particular, was an anterior case, and the reason I'm showing you- It creates echo, literally covering my area. It is because- So that's unacceptable. We could probably turn the sound down. The reason I was showing it is, this is a biggish prostate, and so we put one needle in, and then I was trying to get the second needle in to treat this anterior zone. So what we do, we just re-angle the ultrasound probe. I suppose it's like precision point. and just go back in and it's much, much easier to place the electrodes in that extreme anterior zone. And you can see I'm placing them very, very close to the edge of the prostate, probably only three millimetres away is my preferred area. That's the fourth one that we put in, and this is the longitudinal plan, just to make sure that we're in the correct plane. We decide on the length of the electrode, and then the ablation is performed. One thing we've observed with IRE, in terms of feedback, the cancer itself tends to stay black, and you get the hydrolysis all around it, which is white. And it's one feedback that you get, not only the hydrolysis, which tells you about the tumour, but the black area which is often surrounded. So this was the black area here and as we placed it, as we electrocuted it, I showed this overall picture mainly because you'll see there's some movement of the patient when we're doing it. And when you're doing extreme anterior tumour, that amount of movement is still acceptable because we're getting direct obturator contraction. So you just need to be aware of the movement of the electrodes at the time when you're actually doing that type of movement there. And you can see the hydrolysis which is occurring there. So I thought I'd stop with that.

reference_conclusion: For biopsy-confirmed in-field recurrence after irreversible electroporation, repeat focal treatment is undertaken promptly, as in-field lesions appear to have better outcomes with redo focal therapy. Outfield recurrence is regarded as more reflective of underlying disease biology, with a high recurrence rate after redo treatment; subsequent management may include surveillance for minimal low-grade disease or definitive salvage therapy with radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy. Redo treatment outcomes should be interpreted with the understanding that approximately half of patients may achieve a durable biopsy-proven response.

[...] Those recurrences had a redo and some had some active surveillance and just monitored a tiny little microscopic spot. Some were just Gleason 6 low-grade stuff. [...] But the outfield, we had an extremely high 73% recurrence rate after redo in the outfield. [...] So overall, we actually ended up with half of the patients on a redo got a durable response.
