case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 11-year-old male child, born 16 November 2011, resident of rural/interior Maharashtra.

[ chief complaint ]: Longstanding constipation since age 6-8 months, characterized by difficulty passing stool for 24-36 hours, passage of small ribbon-like stools after excessive straining, and progressive dependence on laxatives; later presented with acute intestinal obstruction.

[ diagnosis ]: Pelvic/rectal inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor involving the rectum and anal canal, with extension to adjacent pelvic structures. Distal colonic acute intestinal obstruction had occurred at initial major hospitalization in November 2021.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Biopsy at outside hospital during emergency laparotomy in November 2021 was reported as inconclusive, suggesting an inflammatory tumor with possibility of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome; no evidence of malignancy was reported. Original slides were unavailable.  
- CT-guided biopsy performed in February 2022 showed dense hyalinized collagenous tissue with fibroblastic and myofibroblastic spindle cells, with scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells; findings were suggestive of a spindle cell tumor, and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor could not be ruled out.  
- Histopathology from piecemeal posterior excision showed fibrocollagenous tissue with fibroblastic cells between smooth muscle cells of the bowel wall, inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and lymphoid aggregates; differential diagnosis included inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor versus IgG4-related sclerosing disease.  
- Immunohistochemistry later showed CD138-positive plasma cells, very occasional plasma cells on IgG4 staining, and negative staining for MIC2 and desmin; findings were interpreted as supportive of inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Outside CT abdomen after initial laparotomy showed a neoplastic mass involving the lower rectum and anal canal with circumferential thickening of the rectosigmoid junction.  
- MRI pelvis (outside hospital, after November 2021 admission) showed an altered-signal-intensity mass measuring 3.7 x 4.3 x 5.3 cm, lying to the right of the rectum and extending inferiorly to the left of the anal canal, with loss of fat planes with the urinary bladder, extension into the presacral space, invasion of the right lateral pelvic wall, and loss of fat planes with the obturator internus muscle.  
- Ultrasound abdomen/pelvis in February 2022 showed a 3.7 x 2.1 x 2.0 cm hypoechoic mass along the right side of the rectum in close relation to the bladder, without sonographic evidence of bladder abutment/invasion at that time.  
- CT in February 2022 showed an unchanged right pararectal mass abutting the right vesicoureteric junction and right seminal vesicle, extending along the left lateral wall of the anal canal and abutting the puborectalis sling and left external anal sphincter. Multiple enlarged external iliac nodes were present; the largest nodal component measured 3.5 x 2.3 cm.  
- Ultrasound abdomen/pelvis with transperineal scan in November 2022 showed a similar mass in close relation to the bladder with high vascularity on Doppler; transperineal imaging showed the tumor extremely close to and invading the anal canal.  
- CT in November 2022 showed postoperative perineal changes with a bulky residual lesion encircling the rectum and anal canal, reduced in size to 3.0 x 2.7 cm, still abutting the trigone/right vesicoureteric junction, right seminal vesicle, and prostate.  
- CT after chemotherapy showed no significant improvement in tumor size or extent, with persistent invasion of surrounding structures.  
- CT in February 2023 after 14 fractions of radiotherapy showed mild reduction in tumor size with hemorrhagic and necrotic components and bladder wall invasion, considered post-radiation tissue destruction.  
- CT after completion of 30 fractions of radiotherapy showed minimal regression in tumor size, minimal reduction in external iliac nodal size, and minimal reduction in bladder wall thickening compared with the mid-radiotherapy scan.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Immunohistochemistry showed CD138 positivity, very occasional IgG4-positive plasma cells, and negative MIC2 and desmin.  
- No validated ALK or NTRK molecular result was documented in the available clinical record.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Routine blood investigations were normal at presentation in February 2022.  
- Urine routine examination was normal at presentation in February 2022.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- From infancy until approximately age 10 years, constipation had been managed intermittently and later almost daily with laxatives and over-the-counter medications, with progressive worsening of symptoms.  
- November 2021: admitted with acute distal colonic obstruction. Conservative management for approximately 24 hours failed. Emergency laparotomy via transverse abdominal incision showed dilated ascending and transverse colon and a hard pelvic mass thought to arise from bowel wall; because the mass was inseparable from the lateral pelvic wall and surrounding structures, loop sigmoid colostomy and biopsy were performed.  
- February 2022: after referral, CT-guided biopsy was performed.  
- 2022: posterior sagittal surgical approach was undertaken for attempted excision. Tumor was found to be extremely hard and densely adherent to anal canal, rectum, urethra, prostate, presacral space, sacrum, and lateral pelvic wall; complete excision was not possible. Posterior portion/piecemeal excision was performed for tissue diagnosis. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged after 1 week.  
- November 2022: readmitted with nodular lesion at mid-incision site, large distal colonic feculoma, and intermittent mild pus/fecal staining from the incision. Distal loop washes failed to evacuate the feculoma; evacuation under general anesthesia was performed. Conservative local care with sitz baths and antibiotic ointment led to cessation of discharge over 2-3 weeks.  
- December 2022: systemic therapy was started with vinblastine 5.1 mg weekly, methotrexate 25 mg weekly, plus celecoxib and tamoxifen. Four cycles were administered and were tolerated well. Follow-up CT showed no significant radiologic response.  
- Early 2023: three-dimensional conformal pelvic radiotherapy with daily imaging was delivered. Treatment was interrupted after 14 fractions because posterior wound discharge recurred and the patient developed significant pain with radiation dermatitis. CT at that stage showed mild tumor reduction with necrotic/hemorrhagic change. Radiotherapy was subsequently completed in March 2023 to a total dose of 54 Gy in 30 fractions over 41 days.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Residual pelvic inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor persisted after incomplete surgical excision, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.  
- Latest post-radiotherapy CT showed minimal regression in tumor size, minimal reduction in external iliac lymph node size, and minimal reduction in bladder wall thickening.  
- On post-radiotherapy per rectal examination, radiation dermatitis was present, but anal canal stenosis had improved from admitting only the fingertip previously to admitting the distal two phalanges of a finger.  
- Colostomy remained in situ and had previously been functioning well.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- At presentation in February 2022, examination showed a functioning loop sigmoid colostomy in the left iliac fossa.  
- A palpable hypogastric mass was initially suspected to represent tumor extension but was subsequently identified as feculoma in the distal colon.  
- Per rectal examination in February 2022 showed severe anal canal narrowing admitting only the tip of the finger, with a hard mass palpable circumferentially; a hard mass was also palpable near the left ischiorectal fossa close to the anal canal.  
- In November 2022, the anal canal remained stenosed on examination, similar to prior findings.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. Good evening, ma'am. Good evening to all the senior consultants. I am Dr. Neel Sheth, a third-year general surgical resident under ma'am at Bombay Hospital Institute of Medical Sciences, and I'll be presenting our case on infantile myofibroblastic tumor. So this was a very interesting case that we encountered last year in February of 2022. However, the history of the child starts as the child is 11-year-old boy who is a resident of the interiors of Maharashtra born on 16th of November 2011. The boy had symptoms from the age of around 6 to 8 months, wherein he would have difficulty to pass tools for 24 to 36 hours, following which he would pass small ribbon-like tools after excessive straining, but he was never truly relieved of his symptoms. This started from the age of 6 to 8 months, wherein his mother started taking him to a local doctor here and there, in their respective village, and the doctors would prescribe laxatives and over-the-counter medications. Initially, the child would require laxatives at an interval of around three to four months. This went on till the age of four to five years, following which the frequency of laxatives gradually kept on increasing until the child required laxatives almost daily, till he had an episode of which we are going to come to. Coming to 2021, when the child was 10 years of age in November 2021, he had his first episode of major hospitalization. Child complained of sudden onset severe pain in abdomen with inability to pass stools or flatus with severe abdominal distention. Going to the same local doctor who had been prescribing laxatives, looking at the condition of the patient, the doctor said he had to be taken to a larger hospital. He was taken by his mother to the nearest municipal hospital, wherein after some preliminary examination and x-rays, he was diagnosed as a distal colonic acute intestinal obstruction. Conservative management was opted and tried for around 24 hours, but looking at the child not settle down. The child was posted for an emergency laparotomy and a transverse abdominal incision was taken. The findings that were seen were a dilated ascending and transverse colon with a very hard and suspicious mass that was felt in the pelvic region that was thought to be arising from the wall of the bowel. Looking at the mass that was very inseparable and stuck to the lateral wall of the pelvis and everywhere, a decision was taken just to perform a loop sigmoid colostomy and a biopsy of the mass was done. Once the child settled down from the acute episode, the decision was taken to evaluate that mass a little more. So consequently, the child underwent a CCT abdomen, wherein a neoplastic mass involving the lower rectum and the anal canal with the circumferential thickening of the rectosigmoid junction was seen. Unfortunately, we don't have the films of this. But however, as the CT did not give too much information, they went for an MRI pelvis. So the MRI pelvis showed an altered signal intensity mass of 3.7 by 4.3 by 5.3 centimeters, lying on the right of the rectum, extending lower down to the left of the anal canal. Also, with loss of fat planes for the urinary bladder, extending into the presacral space and invading the right lateral pelvic wall with loss of fat planes of the obturator internus muscle. Once the histopathology was available, it showed inconclusive report suggesting an inflammatory tumor with the possibility of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome that was given in the report. However, the slides were not available as this was done at a far off hospital. However, the report did mention no evidence of malignancy. Fast forwarding four months, the child was referred to Mumbai and presented to us in February 2022. When the child presented on examination, as we can see in the image, there was a loop sigmoid colostomy in the left iliac fossa, which was functioning well. However, a very interesting finding we had was the palpable mass in the hypogastric region, which we initially thought could have been an extension of the tumor from the pelvis, but was later found to be just a feculoma in the distal colon. Coming to the PR examination, there was severe narrowing of the anal canal, admitting only the tip of the finger with the hard mass palpable in all the directions. Also, an interesting finding was on PR examination, there was a hard mass palpable somewhere around the left estiorectal fossa, a little closer to the anal canal. When we started investigating the child, the routine blood investigations and urine routine were normal. A USG abdomen with pelvis was done, which is shown in the image. Here we can see the mass lying in close relation to the bladder. However, USG did not show the mass abutting into the bladder. It was a 3.7 by 2.1 by 2 centimeters hypoechoic mass along the right side of the rectum. Later, a CT was done in the same month. The CT showed a mass in the right pararectal region with its size that was unchanged from the scan that was done outside. And it was seen abutting the right, it was seen abutting the right vesicouretic junction and the right seminal vesicle. As we can see here, it's in close relation to the right caudal part of the bladder, that is the trigone and the right seminal vesicle and the vesicouretic junction. then it was seen to extend along the lateral wall of the anal canal on the left side as we can see here it's involving the left side of the anal canal as well and butting the piborectalis sling and the left external anal sphincter. There were multiple enlarged external iliac nodes as well with the largest nodular component measuring 3.5 by 2.3 centimeters. Histopathology report, so a CT-guided biopsy was planned, and a CT-guided biopsy was done from a posterior approach, and multiple two-cut biopsies were taken. The report showed a dense hyalinized collagenous tissue with fibroblastic and myofibroblastic spindle cells, and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells. So the report was suggestive of either a spindle cell tumor. However, the possibility of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor could not be ruled out. Here we can see a 10x image, and then a 40x image. So once we had this report, we thought surgical excision of the tumor would be the best approach to deal with this. a complete excision of the tumor was planned from a posterior sagittal incision. Once the posterior sagittal incision was taken and the tumor was approached, however, the tumor was extremely hard and it was very adherent to the surrounding pelvic structures like the anal canal, the rectum, the urethra, the prostate. Also, it was completely stuck to the presacral space and the sacrum and even to the lateral pelvic wall, so adherent that It was not even, we were not even able to get our hands around the tumor or even lift up the tumor from any structure. So looking at the overall condition, the decision taken to excise the posterior most part of the tumor and send the specimen for histopathology. So consequently that was done. Here we can see the approach to the tumor. And this is once we reached the tumor. And now a few images of excision. This was a piecemeal excision of the tumor that we could achieve. And it was a considerable amount of tumor as we saw in the CT scans later. The histopathology report, when arrived, showed fibrocollagenous tissue with fibroblastic cells between the smooth muscle cells of the bowel wall, part of the rectal wall was also removed with the tumor, and inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and lymphoid aggregates. So differential diagnosis of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor or an IgG-4 sclerosing disease was given, and immunohistochemistry was advised. Postoperatively, patient recovered well and was discharged after one week. Fast forwarding to November 2022, when the patient returned to us and was readmitted. This time, the patient had a nodular lesion in the mid-incision site and a large feculoma in the distal colon. From the incision site, there was mild staining of pus and occasional fecal matter on and off. So multiple washes were given from the distal loop of the stoma to try and evacuate the feculoma, but the feculoma was very hard and was not evacuable with just washes. So evacuation of the feculoma under general anesthesia was done, following which, conservative management with Sitzbath antibiotic ointment was given, and the discharge subsequently stopped in around two to three weeks. Other clinical parameters were maintained, whereas the PR exam, the anal canal was just as stenosis as it was before. Then another USG of the abdomen and pelvis with a transperineal scan was planned. There was a similar mass in close relation to the bladder. This time the mass showed high vascularity on USG as well. Here we can see the space-occupying lesion lying very close to the bladder. And here we can see the Doppler image showing good vascularity in the tumor. In the transperineal scan, the tumor was extremely close to the anal canal and invading into the anal canal, as we can see here. Also, the Doppler image shows similar findings with the anal canal, the tumor almost invading into the anal canal.
I'll drink.

CT scan was repeated, which showed post-op changes in the perineum with a bulky residual lesion encircling the rectum and the anal canal. However, this time, the size of the lesion was reduced to 3 by 2.7 centimeters, and it was seen abutting the triangle on the right of a psychiatric junction and the right seminal vascular prostate as before. However, there was a subsequent reduction, there was a substantial reduction in the size of the tumor. Yeah, so what I'm trying to say is, these things should be taken,

Seriously, at the primary care level, a simple digital rectal exam may have helped, may or may not have helped, but sending up the chain to somebody who is better equipped to deal with these things early makes a big difference. I mean, this is for everything. I'm not talking just about this child. So I think that should be something that as apps so that we should be looking to convey to the general population. and general the primary care setup. That's all I have. Thank you for being with us.

reference_conclusion: Given unresectable residual pelvic inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor with limited response to vinblastine/methotrexate-based chemotherapy and low-dose radiotherapy, further management should prioritize molecular characterization. ALK testing should be performed, with additional evaluation for NTRK fusions and other actionable alterations by FISH and/or NGS as feasible. If an actionable alteration is identified, targeted therapy with an ALK inhibitor or TRK inhibitor should be considered to improve symptoms and potentially facilitate a less morbid surgical resection; complete surgical resection remains the definitive treatment when anatomically feasible, and margin-positive resection may be acceptable.
reference_conclusion_quote: Nowadays, what we do is we do the many of the biological markers like they are supposed to be all positive. And this all positivity can do. We do have an access to drugs which are targeting this deceptor. And you can use all inhibitors. And that targeted therapy perhaps is the way to go. [...] So I think the most important thing in this is to do the molecular workup. And the most important for myofibroblastic tumor is ALK positivity. And if it is ALK positive, then we can, it makes it very comfortable for a surgeon to do surgery also. [...] But ALK should be done, and also the TRK-A, B, and C. Because we have this MAP kinase and other pathways which can be explored for the treatment of such difficult diseases, rather than using modalities like radiation, which is which is not taking you anywhere. [...] Yeah, so I think in the chat that's happening on the side in our discussion here, you know, our approach here at St. Jude for these unresectable IMTs has usually now moved towards testing by fish for ALK and then also for NTRAC fusions. because there are two targeted agents that we've talked about, both crizotinib as well as larotrectinib, which could be used in TRAC fusion positive cases. And these have very, very high response rates and can often facilitate then a margin positive surgical resection, which would be acceptable. [...] Ultimately, like everyone has said, the ideal approach is a complete surgical resection. I think a margin-positive surgical resection would also be acceptable [...] Yes, if you have not done the ALK and NTRK so far, it should be done. [...] So you should do the fish and then it will be... It's required even in NGS, ma'am. Ntrek and Roths and all are new markers which come up in NGS. So you should do that because that is the only salvage for this cell.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Right neck fullness/tenderness with worsening neck swelling in the setting of a chronically fibrotic (“woody”) neck.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent regional squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx involving the right neck. Original disease had been T4N1 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior laryngeal malignancy was squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Prior PET scans after earlier treatment had been negative.  
- CT neck with contrast demonstrated recurrent right neck mass in a previously dissected neck, located posterior to the carotid bifurcation with loss of normal tissue planes.  
- More inferior images demonstrated greater disease burden with poor planes between the mass and the carotid artery.  
- Imaging appearance suggested less than 180 degrees carotid encasement.  
- Concern was raised on imaging for extension toward the prevertebral/paraspinal tissues and cervical rootlets.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Received chemoradiation for T4N1 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma approximately 4 years before current presentation.  
- Underwent salvage laryngectomy with bilateral neck dissections in January 2016.  
- Had prior flap reconstruction at the time of laryngectomy, described as a large ALT flap.

reference_discussion.text: So we'll start with 76-year-old male, T4N1 SCC of the larynx, status post-chemo radiation, underwent a salvage laryngectomy and neck dissections in January 2016. He now has some right fullness in his neck and some tenderness. In all honesty, I added the fullness and tenderness. He had kind of a woody neck. He had been salvaged several years before, and we were imaging him before revision pharyngoplasty because he was having worsening symptoms, swelling, but really asymptomatic in the same woody neck he had had for years. But in this setting, you know, with this gentleman's symptoms, if he's having pain, there's concern for recurrence. What sort of the folks' initial imaging, and I'll open it to the crew, what do you think is appropriate? Ever an ultrasound in this group? CAT scan? PET scan? What's your go-to initial imaging test?
That's a great question. How long ago was his chemo RT?
About four years ago.

Yeah. This is one of those challenging situation and we have all been in this scenario that you have a patient that you're, you do have this kind of weight pain that you really don't know and your exam with this woody neck and prior surgery is really not very conducive. I, to be honest with you, I was, I, and I, you know, as you know, NCCN guideline does not recommend routine imaging in asymptomatic patients. When it comes to symptomatic patients, they don't say anything. And I think it all depends on your local expertise and the comfort level. I think at this point, starting with just a normal CT, the regular CT scan is not unreasonable. If you have the possibility to do PET CT, it's also not. But I'm not sure if anybody knows exactly. I mean, we do have a PET MRI here, but I don't advocate for PET MRI on everybody. I think that's one of those things that it's a little bit, it's an art. And I am not sure if I have the answer. I'm curious to hear others.

I mean, I think a lot of it would depend on if you had any imaging after surgery before this time, because everything's going to obviously be distorted, and so a comparison image would be very helpful. Certainly don't lose by trying an office-based ultrasound. In my hands, I don't think it would be reliable in picking up somebody. in an operated womb bed, unless there was something focally there. So I often would start with a CT with contrast. Pet may have it run into the roadblock of insurance coverage if it's not biopsy-proven recurrence. So that's the only concern there.
Yeah, I would favor CT with contrast. You would do what?
I would favor CT net with contrast as the initial work, as part of the initial evaluation.
Perfect. Are there the Charlie, Don, Dr. Ridge,

Yeah, I certainly echo what Mike said in terms of the real challenge of ultrasound in these necks. On the other hand, if I've got the patient right there in my clinic and I've got the ultrasound right there in my clinic, you know, very low threshold to put the transducer up and if in fact I do see something that looks, you know, clearly targetable, I can go ahead and assess that with a needle right there. But if I'm left scratching my head after the ultrasound, I'm definitely going to get probably contrasted CT neck.
Perhaps I missed whether this was the previously dissected neck or is this the undissected side?

He had actually had bilateral necks. So this is his right neck at this time, which was a previously dissected neck that had disease. And he had negative PET scans too, to Dr. Moore's point, just to add that.
I think that somewhat informs what I'd expect of ultrasound. So I'd probably start with a CAT scan.
We have one more guest tonight is Dr. Jennifer Wong from MD Anderson. Hi, Jennifer. She joined us last minute. We're very gracious to accept. Jennifer, what would you do at MD Anderson?

Yeah. So thanks for having me on. We at MD Anderson don't do our own office space ultrasounds. So in this situation, I agree with what's been already said is that We start with the CT with contrast, but we often will set them up with the ultrasound with possible biopsy by our radiology team at the same time.
So let me ask our neuroradiologist, Dr. Zhang, would you recommend a fancy PET MRI or you start with the CT or PET CT?

I mean, I would like to see PET MR in probably any head on neck case. But in those cases, when they are surgically treated, when they receive chemoradiation, doing a contrast enhanced CT takes maybe five minutes, laying on the... scanner table, but doing an MRI will take at least half an hour. So during that half an hour, the patient needs to not swallow, not move, and keep very still for the image quality. It's really very hard in those radiated neck patients and when they come with woody necks. So the patient comfort really defines the quality of the neck. In that particular case, I would like to start with PET MR, but contrast-enhanced neck CT I think is the most reasonable option.

Excellent. Thank you. So this is a challenge that we all have to remember that doing an MRI for patients are not easy, especially when they have neck pain, neck fibrosis, the same lying flat for half an hour might not be easy. All right, Chad, let's continue.

Yeah, absolutely. And that's what we did. And I think I've got a few images here. With this first image on his right side, you can see just posterior to the carotid after it's bifurcated there. You lose your planes. Now, obviously, these are operated necks. So you're going to lose some of that. On this next set of images, you can see more disease burden as you go down inferiorly. and not great planes between it and the carotid artery. I'll let you guys look at this and if anybody has anything to add. I'm pleased he got a big ALT stuffed in there from his laryngectomy.

Yeah. Oh boy. Yeah, I agree with you. I think it's a plane, but it might be my imagination. Obviously these are limited imaging. So in these cases, I don't know. I don't know if PET will show you more than, obviously for distant mets, but that's not very high. MRI, do you think MRI would be more helpful? I'm not 100% sure, to be honest with you. Anybody else would do anything else?

I mean, I would get a PET CT. I think I would be interested to understand whether the patient has only recurrent regional disease versus any disease elsewhere. I think it'll inform, Not so much a decision-making, we'll be talking about management of the neck shortly, because that's a topic, but I think more just with the global aspect, if it's disease only in one place versus disease in multiple sites, I think it's very important to know.
Definitely. Mike, Arno?

Yeah, I mean, it looks like a pretty ominous recurrence just based on the borders of the mass and location. Maybe you could get it away from the carotid, but certainly based on that image, it looks pretty concerning. Either that or he's got a very hot plaque in his artery already. And it looked like it was going to have sucked into the prevertebral fascia on a pretty wide plane. That combined with kind of the extracapsular appearance of the borders is all pretty concerning for ability to easily remove it. Yeah, it's going to be a challenge.
Well, we can get off. Go ahead.

No, no, I was gonna say, you know, I think before we proceed. I'm curious what others would do in terms of number one, any role for a CTA and number or some sort of angiogram, or number two, based on this imaging, does anybody have enough, and Dr. Ridge in particular maybe, or just in terms of their threshold to consider resection of the carotid artery, and whether you get a balloon occlusion versus bypass, and how that comes into the fold with a patient like this.

Sure. I'll be the sacrificial lamb here and go first. You know, I'm memorial trained at the end of the day, and we were not very keen on sacrificing carotid. And in general, we thought, and this is all anecdotally evidence, it's not a clinical trial, but if the disease is extensive enough that you have to resect the carotid, you're not going to help the patient that much. But probably not. But, you know, there are cases, but I would be interested to see how others approach this. Let's go around the table.

I hadn't expected to be braced on this, so I didn't really carefully look. It doesn't seem to me as though the carotid is circumferentially involved. In that situation, I wouldn't seriously entertain replacing it. I think it's also worthwhile to remember that there's no point in increasing radicality in a single domain of your operation. So replacing the carotid is going to make you feel better about perhaps 20% of the circumference of this thing. And your concerns about the prevertebral fascia are, I think, very reasonable ones. so that we can go through a lot of effort to replace the carotid and feel a little better about that margin. But other margins are going to be thoroughly worrisome as well. I wouldn't think that carotid replacement is likely to be necessary in this case. I'd like a more sophisticated imaging response from a radiologist surrounding the amount of circumference involved.

One other question I would have too, is, you know, the MR actually may be helpful in looking along nerve roots. Sometimes these are perineural recurrences along cervical rootlets. This may just be extracapsular disease that's, you know, starting to blossom because I doubt it's a missed node. I mean, it could be. But, you know, if there was a a thorough clean-out before, then it's likely either extra capsule disease just coming back or disease along the rootlet. So, you know, check them for horners. You know, the progressive pain, a lot of times this can be, you know, perineural disease tracing and tracking along rootlets, which sometimes may be more evident on MRI. And certainly those things would be kind of deal breakers. If you see that, you know, that your ability to get any sort of semblance of a true margin is negligible. But if it seems more confined to what we've seen here, then I guess you could consider it. It would still be a real hail Mary.

Well, I think in the years to come, I'm going to call Dr. Riz that it doesn't make sense to increase radicality in one aspect of the operation. That's a great quote. Let me ask Elson. Elson, do you think MRI would be helpful here in particular with the two aspects, perivertebral fascia and the carotid artery?

MRI is like a sharp knife in those cases. It probably will overhaul the findings because of all the inflammation. There will be edema, there will be lots of enhancement. So I still like contrast CT for defining the degree of encasement. And here it definitely looks less than 180 degrees even maybe close to 120. But not CTA per se, because CTA, the contrast timing is very early. What you want to see in those cases is the enhancement between the mass and the carotid sheath and the prevertebral fascia. So I would run a delayed CTA, normal 72nd post contrast, and a delayed CT contrast, not CTA. I will do delayed CT imaging in that case. But on MR, we do have a high-resolution sequence and I think I showed two cases during prior presentations. When we do post-contrast KISS imaging with 0.6 millimeter resolution, we can give you an exact answer but not with the routine store contrast T1, T2 sequences.
How long does that take to do 0.6 millimeter MRI?

Yes, well, I have to sit at the scanner with the text and have to scan myself most of the time, or remote into the machine. And this case, I'm assuming this is probably cronial cradle three centimeter, it will take at least six to seven minutes. Okay.

So this is also where I'm sorry. I would have, you know, a goals of care discussion with this patient, right, I have to recognize that I cannot do a compartmental dissection, because the compartments are gone, he's already had a nodal dissection. And so, realistically, as everyone has alluded, the chance of achieving a true margin negative, meaningfully margin of negative resection, even with aggressive resection extending to and including the carotid is going to be low such that if surgery alone is all I've got, I don't know that I'm going to put him through that. This is a patient who would be offered any and every clinical trial option that he may have available, and that may include surgery as a portion of it, but as soon as he sees Ezra Cohen, he's going to have eight immunotherapy options laid out in front of him.

I think one of the important parts there too are the time of recurrence, right? We all know that if somebody like this recurs within three, six months, eight, nine months or not recurs then, but you know, within the first nine to 12 months, their prognosis is a lot worse than in a gentleman like this who's four and a half years out or four years out. And to me, that's a big factor in my aggressiveness. And so, and this guy is from good old middle of nowhere, Ohio, so he's all about whatever we need to do to get him taken care of. And so, in the interest of time, Bhavik, are you okay if I keep going? Yes, absolutely. So, just with that, I agree with most of what's said. Based on that imaging, I thought I was as likely to fail along the paraspinal musculature, the cervical rootlets, as I was the carotid. It seemed like that was not, enough that I went down the path of carotid resection. And so this is an illustration of a gentleman I took care of similar that had a resection in this way and going down a different path. We actually were able, this isn't his neck, this is another gentleman's, but we were able to clear it here. But really, we had actually resected a fair amount of the cervical rootlets into the paraspinal floor, and that's where he had some positive disease. I think the other point to what was mentioned is, in these patients, certainly if they're several years out, getting down to microscopic disease and getting healthy vascularized tissue in there so that you can you know, retreat with hopefully less morbidity has had, you know, some anecdotal success. But I think the biggest thing is time to recurrence. And we know the later they recur, the better the outcome. And salvage surgery still certainly plays a role in that. So with that, my next, you know, just to the group, what are some of the reconstructive options? You know, are there any thoughts or considerations when facing a defect like that?

Yeah, that's a great point. And really, to summarize, basically, at the end of the day, even as Charlie said, with 20 different clinical trials that we have, let's keep it very simple. It's basically that the decision is to cut or not to cut, because that's the main viewpoint here. And I agree with everything you said. Four years is long enough that we all would consider, especially single-site disease. In terms of reconstruction, I'm a big believer in having vascularized tissue there. You could do a quick and simple, dirty peck, or you can do a nice, beautiful ALT. You can also, in that location, you can bring back a, I mean, you can be as fancy as you want. You can do, you know, muscle only with a skin graft. You can do, well, musculocutaneous. You can do anything you like, but they are all possibilities, and it all depends on what's the best for the patient and what you are more comfortable with. Seems like you did a big, good old peck there, which is a great option, and to give you the option for re-radiation possibly.
Just curious about the other folks, ever in this case, or what would drive you all to a free flap?

I think you don't have a lot of vessels from the picture that you looked at. I mean, the jug is already gone. The real issue is, I mean, I don't think there's anyone who would disagree with putting in non-previously radiated tissue there. But I think the PEC flap, like a rotational flap, really gives you the most robust option for what I think is going to be a very harsh environment. And your vessels are going to be not great at best, and maybe even completely absent. You have to pull in a loop somewhere. I mean, I don't do any recon, so it's easy for me to ask someone else to do it, but I would still favor probably the pec flap like you did, just because I think it's straightforward. I think it's robust, and I think it's what you need. Whereas if you put in a vascular anastomosis with vessels that aren't great, I don't think that you're going to be, you know, there's real risk there. If this falls apart, you're in a very big, you have a very big problem.

Yeah, definitely, definitely need tissue, yeah. I would take him with the intention of trying to do an ALT from his other leg. A, he'd know what the morbidity of that is, so presumably he would say, that didn't bother me too much. B, you define your vessels after your neck, and if you don't have them, obviously the pec flap is the fallback. But the one caveat with the pec, and I like a pec flap, I do a lot of free flaps, but a pec flap is a great flap. is when you combine that with an extended radical neck dissection, the morbidity for the upper extremity is really amplified. So that would be why I would really look hard for vessels to do an ALT.

I agree. And that's a great point that I'm glad that Don brought it. We, you know, if we are thinking about these operations, it's not just the length of life, it's also quality of life and don't underestimate a dissected radical neck plus a pec slot, that shoulder is really, especially if it's a dominant hand, you really want to think about it. And a lot of time, even in the previously dissected neck, you might be able to find the transverse cervical vessels and those are very good vessels that you can use.

Sometimes it looks like this and I will say I agree 100% with Don and the point of going down this path was that and you can do this without necessarily burning the bridge of a pec flap and this is another patient just to illustrate is you can actually take branches of the thracochromial trunk and in particular the deltoid branch, and then you've got your cephalic right there, you can clean that out, flip it up over the clavicle, and that, believe it or not, you can get reasonable length. Now you have to have the right flap and the right defect for it. This lady here, this is, I thought I put that other slide, I may not have, but you can see here, this was an osteocutaneous radial forearm where we dropped it down in the neck, and that's right over the clavicle. But just to illustrate the point that, especially with the defects we showed, it is not hard and you can do it without burning the bridge of the pectoralis flap later to get vessels that are well out of your radiated field and give your flap a much better chance without having to go to like the mammary vessels or something like that.
So Chad, in the interest of time, for that patient that you discussed, what did you decide and what happened to that patient?

Well, we resected him, and he got an ALT. He's up getting proton therapy right now at our northern campus, and he's done quite well. He's a wonderful gentleman, so fortunate. I mean, but it's early out, so we'll see how he does.
Okay, great. Thank you. Were there any margins that were positive on that resection?
Like, you know, So not the carotid, carotid sheath was clear, but it was the paraspinal, the cervical root, which is, they were exiting, uh, in that area.
Yeah.

All right. To summarize again, as I said, it's really the decision is to cut or not to cut. And that's very important decision. Obviously there are a lot of clinical trials right now. I'm not sure any of them have been proven to be more effective as surgery upfront plus minus three radiation. But these things coming down the road, and remember, if you're doing this, you need to have a plan for reconstruction. You need to have a plan for adjuvant treatment. And you know, every once in a while, four years out, you might be doing well. Okay, great, thank you.
I am going to do- I was actually about to ask a similar question. Is this something anyone would consider brachycatheters underneath your flap?
Yes, we do consider that at NYU, absolutely.

We use this cesium and we actually have a clinical trial we've just gotten where we're combining interstitial cesium and hopefully the Jefferson crew and the case crew can do it as well. But using interstitial brachy with cesium plus immune therapy in this cohort. So I definitely think it's got some value.

reference_conclusion: Initial evaluation should proceed with contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, with ultrasound and possible biopsy if a targetable lesion is identified, followed by PET/CT to define the extent of disease and exclude additional sites of recurrence. Given the long interval from prior treatment and apparent single-site regional recurrence, salvage surgical resection was selected. Reconstruction with vascularized tissue was planned and performed using an anterolateral thigh free flap, with adjuvant proton re-irradiation subsequently administered.
reference_conclusion_quote: I would favor CT net with contrast as the initial work, as part of the initial evaluation. [...] We at MD Anderson don't do our own office space ultrasounds. So in this situation, I agree with what's been already said is that We start with the CT with contrast, but we often will set them up with the ultrasound with possible biopsy by our radiology team at the same time. [...] I mean, I would get a PET CT. I think I would be interested to understand whether the patient has only recurrent regional disease versus any disease elsewhere. [...] Four years is long enough that we all would consider, especially single-site disease. [...] Well, we resected him, and he got an ALT. He's up getting proton therapy right now at our northern campus, and he's done quite well.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old Hispanic woman. Menarche occurred at age 13. No family history of cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-year history of intermittent vaginal bleeding associated with chronic moderate-intensity pelvic pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical carcinoma, FIGO stage IIIB. Clinical examination identified an 8 cm ulcerated cervical mass with parametrial involvement. CT demonstrated extension to the lower third of the vagina and nodal disease in the common iliac and retroperitoneal regions.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma associated with high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for pancytokeratin and synaptophysin. Ki-67 was 84% in both components. Post-radical hysterectomy pathology showed chronic cervicitis, no malignant neoplasm identified in the uterus, and metastatic involvement in 1 of 24 pelvic lymph nodes; the positive node was pancytokeratin-positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominopelvic CT showed cervical malignancy extending to the lower third of the vagina, with positive lymph nodes in the common iliac and retroperitoneal areas. A subsequent abdominopelvic CT performed later showed no radiologically positive lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No numerical laboratory values were provided. Hematologic toxicity developed during chemoradiation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In December 2015, concurrent chemoradiation was initiated with carboplatin plus etoposide and pelvic-field radiotherapy. Radiotherapy was discontinued after 15 fractions because of hematologic toxicity. Chemotherapy was then continued, completing a total of five cycles of cisplatin plus etoposide, with partial response achieved. The patient subsequently underwent radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy.

[ current disease status ]: After surgery, no malignant neoplasm was identified in the uterus/cervix specimen, but residual metastatic disease was present in 1 of 24 pelvic lymph nodes. The most recent abdominopelvic CT showed no radiologically positive lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: Gynecologic examination at presentation demonstrated an 8 cm ulcerated cervical mass. Parametrial involvement was present.

reference_discussion.text: Hello, good morning. This case is about a 38-year-old Hispanic woman, Menarche, at age 13, no family history of cancer, with history of two years of intermittent vaginal bleeding associated with chronic pelvic pain of moderate intensity. In the gynecological examination, we found an 8 centimeters ulcerated cervical mass. Parametrium was involved. She underwent a cervical biopsy that showed a poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma associated with high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma. pancreatin-positive, synaptophisin-positive, and CHI-67, 84% for both components. In the abdominal pelvic CT, we can found cervical malignancy with extension to the lower third of the vagina, positive lymph nodes in the common iliac and the retroperitoneal area. The final diagnosis was stage 3b cervical cancer. On December 2015, she received concurrent chemo radiation with carboplatin plus etoposite and radiotherapy in pelvic fields. But radiotherapy was suspended after 15 sessions because she developed hematological toxicities. And then she continued chemotherapy until complete five cycles of cisplatin plus etoposite. and achieved a partial response. She underwent radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy, and the pathological anatomy reports chronic cervicitis, uterus nomalignal neoplasm, and pelvic lymph nodes 1 of 24, pancreatin-positive. Our first question, in light of surgical findings, should these patients begin follow-up? And the other question, considering an epidermoid component of the tumor, should this patient complete radiotherapy?
OK. The other questions.
Can you help me understand why the original decision was to give carboplatin with etoposide if you were planning to give radiation therapy?
The doctors considered, yes, the toxicity and the neuroendocrine component of the tumor. And because of that, they begin with carboplatin etoposide.

I think Don raised a good point. I think all of this is extrapolated from lung cancer. I think most people treat initially with cisplatin and cisplatin on the post side. I think if you have a lot of toxicities, I mean, if the patient has poor renal function, then you can switch to CARBO. But I think a lot of people maybe would have started with cisplatin right away, I think.

Minor point. And I just think particularly, you know, if you're giving—and Anuja, I'd be interested in your thoughts on this, too. If you're going to give radiation therapy, we just—we know that you can do it with cysts. I think with carboplatin, especially if you're combining with a second agent, I think it's not surprising she had hematologic toxicities. And, you know, I would be concerned about, you know, basically not completing the radiation therapy as part of her original plan.

I totally agree. We do cis and etoposide for neuroendocrine tumors with our pelvic radiation therapy, but we do use a lower dose of etoposide. I need to get that to you guys. We don't use 100 milligrams. I can't remember what dose we use, but we do use a lower dose. My other concern is that she had periodic nodes, and the periodic nodes were not treated. Do you know what happened with the- I mean, did she truly have Parodic Nodes originally? Because it's actually common iliac nodes and retroperitoneal nodes as well. That's what it says.
On the abdopelvic CT, it says positive lymph nodes in the common iliac and retroperitoneal areas. So you're quite right.

And they were never addressed either, because they did a radical hysterectomy and pelvic node dissection. They didn't do a periodic node dissection. So I guess that's the other question is, what happened with the periodics?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 18-year-old female. She had presented initially at age 17 years. She had no relevant past medical history and no relevant family history.

[ chief complaint ]: Dyspnea and cough.

[ diagnosis ]: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype; stage II disease.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration cytology from a lower deep cervical lymph node had previously shown lymphoma, without definitive subclassification.  
- Subsequent core biopsy established the diagnosis of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Chest radiograph had demonstrated a mediastinal mass.  
- CT had shown multiple mediastinal lymph nodes, with the largest measuring 6 × 9 cm.  
- Interval CT imaging over 4 days had shown marked thoracic disease burden with associated pulmonary infectious/inflammatory changes.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Tuberculosis testing was negative.  
- HIV testing was negative.  
- Blood cultures were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- She had been admitted for supportive management after acute respiratory deterioration with oxygen desaturation.  
- High-dose dexamethasone had been given as an initial pre-phase treatment at 40 mg once daily for 4 days, with prophylactic antibiotics and tumor lysis prophylaxis.  
- Despite this, respiratory status had worsened, with tachypnea up to 44/min and persistent tachycardia around 150/min, requiring ICU admission.  
- She had subsequently been readmitted to ICU 4 days later, mechanically ventilated, and treated with imipenem/cilastatin, linezolid, and caspofungin.  
- While ventilated, she had undergone core biopsy for diagnosis.  
- CVP chemotherapy had then been administered as a further pre-phase regimen. By the second day after CVP, she had been extubated with marked improvement in respiratory status and discharged from ICU.  
- Definitive treatment had consisted of 6 cycles of ABVD followed by involved-field radiotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- ECOG/performance status had been 2 at presentation.  
- Initial examination had shown hypotension, respiratory rate 28/min, pulse 150/min, normal temperature, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.  
- Chest examination had shown diminished air entry in the right upper and middle lung zones.  
- During examination, oxygen saturation had acutely fallen to 71% with worsening tachypnea.  
- She had no clinical features of superior vena cava syndrome.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Pediatric patient, age 14 years; sex not explicitly documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal mass with intermittent mild pain relieved by medication.

[ diagnosis ]: Left renal cell carcinoma, reported as translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma (TFE3-rearranged RCC impression on immunohistochemistry), with regional nodal involvement. Pathologic stage was reported as pT3. Clinical stage IV disease was considered on the basis of mediastinal lymphadenopathy and a pulmonary nodule on imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided renal biopsy showed renal cell carcinoma. Following radical nephrectomy with left template lymph node dissection, histopathology confirmed renal cell carcinoma. Tumor was reported as pT3 and limited within Gerota’s fascia. Microscopy showed nests/cystic spaces of polygonal cells with prominent nuclei and pale eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm. No lymphovascular invasion was identified. Urinary/ureteric margin was reported positive. Renal vessel margin was negative. Fourteen lymph nodes were examined, of which 3 were positive for tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: CT abdomen showed a solid mass replacing almost the entire left kidney. No contrast extravasation from the left kidney was seen. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were present in the left para-aortic/renal and mesenteric regions; the largest measured approximately 3.1 × 2.9 cm. CT thorax showed multiple enlarged mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes, largest approximately 3.1 × 2.9 cm. A 7 × 5 × 5 mm irregular enhancing nodule was present in the left upper lobe, superior lingular segment. No renal vein thrombosis or inferior vena cava thrombosis was identified intraoperatively. No gross peritoneal disease was seen intraoperatively.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for PAX8, CD10, EMA, and vimentin. INI1 was retained. CK7, CD117, HMB45, and Melan-A were negative. Overall impression was TFE3-rearranged/translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma. No confirmatory molecular genetic study was documented.

[ laboratory results ]: Blood pressure was within the 50th–90th centile. Estimated glomerular filtration rate was reported as 126.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent ultrasound-guided biopsy followed by upfront radical nephrectomy with left template lymph node dissection. Intraoperatively, the mass measured approximately 18 × 16 × 12 cm. Multiple enlarged nodes encased the renal artery and renal vein. A large nodal conglomerate extended from the superior mesenteric vessel region to the aortic bifurcation. Approximately 2 cm of distal ureter appeared grossly normal at surgery. No chemotherapy had been administered before or after surgery at the time documented. Radiotherapy had not been given.

[ current disease status ]: Approximately 3–4 weeks after surgery, residual concern remained for metastatic disease based on mediastinal lymphadenopathy and a small left upper lobe pulmonary nodule seen on preoperative imaging. The abdomen was described as grossly clear postoperatively apart from the reported positive urinary/ureteric margin on histopathology. The child was clinically well and active on follow-up.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination before surgery, the abdominal mass was palpable in the left hypochondrial region extending to the lumbar region; it had regular margins, a bosselated surface, firm consistency, moved with respiration, and was bimanually palpable. Initial radiologic differential diagnosis included renal lymphoma, renal cell carcinoma, and Wilms tumor.

reference_conclusion: Postoperative FDG PET-CT is recommended after an appropriate interval from surgery to assess residual active disease and guide further management. If PET-CT identifies resectable residual disease, including lower urinary tract disease amenable to completion ureterectomy with bladder cuff or other surgically accessible metastatic deposits, second-look surgery/metastasectomy should be considered with the aim of complete resection where feasible. Radiotherapy has no established role, and systemic immunotherapy may be pursued if feasible, with close follow-up and reassessment after imaging; pathology review of the reported ureteric margin and molecular workup for translocation-associated RCC should also be undertaken.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old woman. No significant past medical history was documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent differentiated thyroid carcinoma with enlarging right superior mediastinal/peritracheal nodal disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Classical variant papillary thyroid carcinoma diagnosed in 2007 with central and right lateral cervical nodal metastases. Subsequent recurrent radioiodine-refractory nodal disease was identified in the right superior mediastinum/right peritracheal region.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial surgical pathology in 2007 showed a 4.0 cm classical variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with capsular extension. Nodal disease involved 2/2 central compartment lymph nodes and 12/15 lateral neck lymph nodes.

[ imaging findings ]: Post-thyroidectomy radioiodine whole-body scan after initial 200 mCi treatment showed uptake in the thyroid bed and right retrosternal region. After a second radioiodine dose of 150 mCi, follow-up whole-body scan showed persistent substernal uptake. A subsequent diagnostic scan was negative.  
Neck/chest CT in 2013 showed a 1.3 cm peritracheal lymph node in the superior mediastinum, corresponding to the previously observed retrosternal region and present since 2008.  
Later CT demonstrated interval enlargement of the right peritracheal/superior mediastinal adenopathy to 3.0 cm, with several additional approximately 1 cm nodes superior to it. The dominant lesion was closely associated with the great vessels, including the superior vena cava and aortic arch, and abutted the trachea and lung apex.  
Small pulmonary nodules were present but were described as too small to characterize and not necessarily suspicious for malignancy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were documented.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was maintained in a suppressed range during surveillance. Serum thyroglobulin remained consistently in the 2-3 range over several years. Thyroglobulin antibodies were present and increased over time: 1.5 in 2008, 2.9 in 2011, 6.6 in 2013, 4.4 in 2017, and 17 approximately one year later.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In 2007, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, and right neck dissection. The sternocleidomastoid muscle and internal jugular vein were resected. Surgery was complicated by injury to the right spinal accessory nerve.  
She subsequently received radioactive iodine 200 mCi, followed by a second radioactive iodine treatment of 150 mCi for persistent retrosternal/substernal uptake. Final diagnostic radioiodine scan was negative.  
The superior mediastinal/peritracheal node was observed for a period because of stability and difficult location.

[ other clinical data ]: The internal jugular vein had been previously resected.

So we don't know, I think, Ayaka, correct me if I'm wrong, that there were any anatomic studies that were done at that time.

Well, I'll get into it. We did see it when we ended up seeing her, but I don't think they decided at the time to really do anything about it surgically. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Anal bleeding.

[ diagnosis ]: Low rectal adenocarcinoma without distant metastases at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy demonstrated moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT thorax and abdomen showed no distant metastases.  
- Pelvic MRI demonstrated a low rectal tumor located 5.5 cm from the anal verge, semicircular in configuration, with deep central ulceration.  
- Digital rectal examination identified a tumoral mass 2 cm above the sphincter.  
- MRI showed more than nine small locoregional lymph nodes.  
- Distance from tumor to mesorectal fascia was greater than 5 mm.  
- Restaging MRI at the time of planned surgery showed residual abnormality on T2-weighted imaging but no residual signal on diffusion-weighted imaging (B1000).  
- At restaging, no remaining lymph nodes were seen on imaging.

[ laboratory results ]: Carcinoembryonic antigen was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient underwent long-course chemoradiotherapy with continuous-infusion 5-fluorouracil.  
- Clinical examination after chemoradiotherapy showed no remaining tumor.

[ other clinical data ]: No relevant past medical history. No family history of cancer.

reference_discussion.text: So we will now present two challenging cases in rectal cancer, and I will start with the first one. We don't have a voting system, so I suggest that you raise hands with the different questions. So the first patient I am going to present is a woman of 65 years old. She has no relevant medical history, no family history of cancer. She presents with anal bleeding and has no other symptoms. On digital rectal examination, she has a tumoral mass two centimeters above the sphincter. Her CA is normal. The biopsy shows a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. There are no distant metastases on CT scan of the thorax and the abdomen. On MR, there is a tumor at 5.5 centimeters of the anal verge. It's semicircular, it shows a deep central ulceration, and there are more than nine small local regional lymph nodes. The distance to the mesorectal fascia is more than five millimeters. So my question to you is, what is next? And here are some options. Either we go straight to surgery, or we use the short course immediately followed by surgery. We can use a long course of chemoradiation followed by APR after six to eight weeks. A long course of chemoradiation followed by TME after six to eight weeks, or maybe some of you have other ideas. So who would go for surgery only? Okay, one, two. Maybe you as a surgeon can comment on that?

In going for surgery alone, you know, we treat these patients in the multidisciplinary setting, and although I might be inclined, I don't think that my colleagues will let me do that. I heard that they have five lymph nodes, is that correct? Visible nodes?
There are more than eight small lymph nodes, but hard to say whether they are malignant or not.

You have more than five? millimeters to the mesorectal fascia. So I suspect your tumor is T3A, maybe early T3B. So this patient is actually unlikely to have, you can see nine lymph nodes. Gina will say, yes, you can see nine lymph nodes, but they're unlikely to be involved.
But it is a low seated tumor.
but it's above the dentate line. You wouldn't have a problem in the surgeons I work with in doing a resection there without a stoma?

I think surgically this patient will need a coloanal. The tumor is only two centimeters above the sphincter. I doubt that you will be able to do a double stapling, but a sphincter saving procedure is technically feasible. I think, I don't know if you want to say something, Andres, but in the United States we have now opened a prospect trial, intermediate risk tumors that will be randomized to induction chemotherapy. I think in our institution we also favor induction chemotherapy. A lot of leave notes give anything risk of distant metastasis. So one can argue about starting with induction chemotherapy and then see the response.
And so you don't use radiation then, or depending on the response?

That will be an option, just like the prospect trial, it will be the radiation will depend on the response. If this tumor responds very well to systemic chemotherapy, just some systemic chemotherapy, and then surgery. We typically do four months of phone calls.

Okay. Are there any other questions or remarks? We did something a bit different. So first of all, we discussed the patient at the multidisciplinary clinic, and we decided to go for the long course of chemo radiation with a continuous infusion of 5FU, and then the idea was that six to eight weeks after the end of the chemo radiation, we would go for TME and sphincter saving surgery. But then we did an MR before the start of the chemo radiation, you've seen the images, You also see the B1000 image on the bottom, and then at the time of surgery, you can still see some tumor on the T2 weighted image, but on the B1000 image, there is no signal left. On clinical examination, there is also no remaining tumor. So now the question is, what do we do? Do we go for a wait and see approach, Do we go for a TEM procedure, a TME procedure, a boost with brachytherapy, or something else? Who would go for wait and see? Yes, but the microphone is not on. Can you switch the microphone on?
I would talk to the patient.
But do we believe that the lymph nodes were involved or not? Because if we believe that it's involved, the decision will be different.
Well, these are endless discussions with our radiologists. The only thing I can say is that there are no remaining lymph nodes on the imaging at the time of surgery.

We usually have some kind of secretary during MDT, and secretary writes the decision. If the secretary writes N plus, the decision will be now different. If secretary at the start written N minus, but suspected.
We don't have a secretary, so we write ourselves.
So wait and see, because it was N minus.
OK. We wrote N plus.

Don't you need to sit down with the patient and say, look, we can do a wait and see here, it's not standard of care, but we can do a wait and see treatment here. What it will involve is you having a lot of tests over the next few years. How long was probably of debate. You probably have a 6 or 7% risk of recurrence that will be unresectable in the future, but you will avoid major surgery and the vast majority of people in this situation, 70% or so, will maintain a reasonable function and not require an operation. And which do you think you can cope with? Don't you need to sit down with the patient and go through that, rather than saying, wait and see, or 10, or whatever?
Of course. And as a surgeon, would you do a 10 procedure in this patient, or not?

Well, I guess, you know, still in the United States and most of the world, the standard treatment, it would be a total mesorectal excision. of the options that you present there, I don't think I would give more brachytherapy to this patient with radiation. I don't believe in tens in somebody who might have had positive leaf loss at baseline before the chemoradiation. My choice would be between having a total mesorectal excision or just watch and wait. And the decision is shared with the patients. We have some experience, we have some data from having done watch and wait for an embryogia retrospectively. We have now an ongoing prospective trial. This patient probably is a good candidate. If the patient has a clinical and radiological complete response six to eight weeks after finishing chemoradiation, probably is a patient that is a good candidate as long as, as it was emphasized before, she's willing to come for repeated exams. Because, as we know, 20% of the patients will regrow, the tumor will regrow, so we have to inform the patient very well. But I think she will be a good candidate for that. But you registered the patient in a prospective study? We have a prospective trial, but we do have many patients that are treated out of trial because You know, we have some requirements about the induction versus consolidation. We randomize patients. So, we treat a number of patients outside of the trial with full disclosure of what to expect. And some patients are willing to undergo watch and wait, and some patients don't. They are not willing to take the risk of tumor regrowth and the uncertainty about maybe just having the tumor progress to a point where we cannot do the same operation that we can do at that point.

So our patient underwent TME surgery. And at the time of the pathological evaluation, there was no residual viable tumor tissue, and zero out of the 15 lymph nodes were negative. So the clinical complete remission was confirmed. And then my last question is, What would you do next? Is there anyone who would give adjuvant chemotherapy after a pathological complete remission? No one? Okay. What do the clinical oncologists say? In the panel?

Well, normally, when I think about this patient, my preferred option would have been to go straight for surgery. And then perhaps if those lymph nodes are negative and it's an early stage, I wouldn't have offered any type of adjuvant chemotherapy. But even now, having a PCR, I think those patients are going to enjoy a very prolonged, high probability of prolonged survival. So in general, in cases that are favorable in MRI, in initial MRI, like this one, I do not recommend, and having a complete response, I do not recommend adjuvant chemotherapy.
Okay, thank you. And then Andres, it's your case now. Can we have the second case?

After pathologic complete response was confirmed, no adjuvant chemotherapy was recommended.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old patient with prostate cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for curative-intent treatment of prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 4.

[ imaging findings ]: Conventional staging imaging was normal. PSMA PET using DCFPyL demonstrated mildly to moderately PSMA-avid primary tumor in the left peripheral zone of the mid prostate, with SUVmax approximately 7. No suspicious nodal metastases were identified in the pelvic chains. A solitary focus of mild PSMA uptake was present in a rib, with SUVmax 2.2, corresponding on CT to very subtle, well-circumscribed mild sclerotic change. Physiologic/benign tracer uptake was also seen in the tracheal/submucosal region, ganglia, and bronchociliary activity.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 23.

[ current disease status ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 4, with normal conventional staging imaging and PSMA PET demonstrating a mildly to moderately avid primary tumor in the left peripheral zone of the mid prostate, no suspicious pelvic nodal metastases, and a solitary mildly avid rib focus.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic progression of submandibular gland carcinoma with brain and lung metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Submandibular gland mucoepidermoid carcinoma, initially diagnosed in 2023, with subsequent metastatic disease involving brain and lungs.

[ other clinical data ]: HER2 testing had not been performed. Androgen receptor testing had not been performed.

[ diagnosis ]: Ulcerated cutaneous melanoma of the right neck, pathologic stage pT4b. Clinical satellite lesions were present at the primary site, consistent with N1c disease. No proven distant metastases were identified. Overall stage was recorded as stage IIIC.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial shave biopsy of the right neck lesion showed nodular melanoma with Breslow depth at least 8.5 mm, ulceration present, and high mitotic activity with mitotic rate 21. Pathologic T stage was pT4b.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis was obtained for metastatic evaluation. Chest CT was normal. Abdominal/pelvic imaging showed several lytic foci in multiple bones considered concerning/suspicious but not diagnostic for metastases; these lesions were reportedly difficult to appreciate on CT. A large left renal calculus was present. Imaging also raised concern for inflammatory change involving the kidney. Brain MRI was normal. PET scan demonstrated a right thyroid nodule. The bony lesions were seen but were not FDG-avid and were considered too small for confident PET characterization; bone metastases were not confirmed. Preoperative repeat PET scan showed ventricular uptake concerning for possible myocarditis; subsequent cardio-oncology evaluation was reassuring and myocarditis was not diagnosed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF mutation was present in the melanoma.

[ laboratory results ]: Creatinine was slightly elevated initially. During treatment-related diarrhea/colitis, creatinine increased to 2.44 mg/dL from 1.23 mg/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Biopsy of the right neck lesion was performed by a local dermatologist.  
- Neoadjuvant systemic immunotherapy was administered with ipilimumab plus nivolumab; first dose was given on 26 November 2024. Two cycles were given 3 weeks apart. The primary cancer site flattened markedly after treatment.  
- Treatment was complicated by immune-mediated colitis with profuse diarrhea and acute kidney injury. CT during hospitalization showed colitis. The patient was admitted and treated with IV corticosteroids, then transitioned to oral steroids. Persistent loose stools 9 days after discharge led to treatment with infliximab, with marked improvement.  
- Definitive surgery was delayed while on high-dose steroids/infliximab.

[ other clinical data ]: Right thyroid nodule underwent fine-needle aspiration and was benign. Clinical examination before systemic therapy demonstrated satellite nodules at the primary site.

So, being new at UNC. Okay. All righty. Dr. Arohil, can you show us the slides? And Trish, I don't know if you're gonna, because we're gonna have to exit this and bring up yours. Yeah, we did send them in. I'm a dermatopathologist here at UNC. What we mainly do, our role is, if anyone takes a biopsy from you, or an excision, or a sample, or a needle core biopsy, that tissue, we look at it under the microscope in order for us to define what kind of tumors is happening in the skin. My specialty is dermatopathology, so it's specifically skin. So we assess the tumor, what type of cell it is. We assess the prognosis of the disease. So when we say, The depth of the melanoma, we measure it microscopically. It's not eyeballing, it's not a ruler. It's more of a microscopic measurement to tell what is the depth of the melanoma, and that's how we can decide if it's T1, T2, T3, T4. Ulcers, sometimes the ulcer is very obvious clinically, but they're microscopic ulcers that we only see under the microscope. So that's another thing that we assess microscopically to tell you, the patient, what is the pathologic stage of your disease. Other things we assess is lymph node status, when we get lymph nodes, so we detect the metastasis, if it's clinically occult, where you can't, where it's not felt, but it's micro millimeters, and we measure it, and we're able to see it under the microscope. So that's mainly our role in what we do in rheumatopathology, to assess, to allow for your surgical oncologist and your oncologist to later on decide what type of treatment and therapy for you to undergo. Great. So this is the shaved biopsy. That's how it looks on low power. So when the tissue is taken, we look at it at the bench. And after that, the tissue is processed so we can put it on a slide. And when it's placed on a slide, it's usually looking pink like that. That's how it looks like. And believe it or not, that's what we read. These are mainly how they look like to us. So we can see a big nodular lesion, like we see this almost mushroom-like growth on top over here. And here, the background shows you the normal skin being present. So this is the measurement of how we measure the thickness of this tumor. So this one is, it's a very thick lesion. So the highest thickness is four millimeter. Most melanomas that I diagnose in my practice that come mainly from dermatology clinics are usually less than one millimeter. Higher than four is rare, but it does happen. And usually, the thicker it is, the worse it is. For you to visualize what one millimeter is, one millimeter is basically a dime thickness. So the thickness of a dime is one millimeter, basically. So this is like eight dimes stacked on top of each other. So it has a lot of thickness to it. On closer inspection, when we look at it, we see on this side, this is the skin surface, which is called the epidermis. So this is what you're seeing on your skin surface. This is the epidermis. This is what it looks like microscopically. And on this side, we see it's absent. So this is a definition of ulceration. So we have ulceration that upstages the melanoma. And lastly, this is the tumor on closer inspection. So we can see this nested-like growth. There's like subtle nests and sheets of cells of really atypical cells with mitotic figures. And on close-up images, we see in the center, what we mean by mitosis is a cell that's undergoing division. Our normal cells, for the most part, like a regular nevus, is silent. It doesn't undergo mitosis. It doesn't regenerate. But melanoma, it's replicating. So that's why we see that even in our eyes, microscopically, of a cell undergoing division, cell division. So these are parameters that we record. So that's how we were able to reach thickness of 8.5 with ulceration, with multiple mitotic figures. And that's how it translates into PT4B, the pathologic stage T4B melanoma in this case.
