Thank you so much, sir.

OK. So then the ear, nose, and throat provider ordered a CT of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and neck looking for metastases. Can you hear me? Yeah. Looking for metastases. The chest CT was normal. The abdominal CT was concerning. It had several, when they say lytic foci, many of the bones had some lesions in them that looked concerning. And if you've ever read a radiology report, they don't say anything definitive. They can say things like concerning for, worrisome for, suspicious for, because they can't diagnose unless there's a biopsy. And then this gentleman happened to have a large kidney stone in his left kidney. And they also said suspicious for this fancy word that is inflammation of the kidney. And this is a picture of the CT scan and the pelvis, and the provider, the oncologist that took care of this patient said it was very hard even to appreciate those lesions on a CT scan. So the ENT provider said, we need some help here, and referred this gentleman to see one of our melanoma medical oncologists. And we saw him in November of 24. And we ordered a PET scan and a brain MRI just to get a better picture of the whole body, including the brain. The PET scan is not great for looking inside the brain, so that brain MRI is kind of the gold standard for looking for metastases in the brain. And then on clinical exam, you can see that there were some satellite nodules at the primary site. Thankfully, the brain MRI was normal. His creatinine, which reflects kidney function, was slightly elevated. And there was a finding on the scan of a thyroid nodule, which we did get a fine needle aspirate of it later, and it was benign. It was fine. The PET scan, as I said, showed this right thyroid nodule, and then they said, you know what, we looked at these bony lesions, and we can see them, but they're not really lighting up, and they're probably too small to appreciate on the PET anyway, so we weren't convinced that that was a bone metastasis that we were looking at there. So melanoma staging can be pretty complicated. They look at tumor depth, lymph node involvement, and metastases. And under that N for lymph node involvement is kind of a subtype of what we call satellites. So you may recall that the clinician saw satellites at the primary site. So the final staging was a T4B. reflecting that worrisome depth with ulceration. These satellites, which made it an N1C, and then no defined, proven metastases. So it came out to be a 3C. So the question is, what do we do next? do we lead with surgery? And Dr. Dougherty, do you want to comment now on what we should do as far as surgery?

So typically in this scenario with the satellite lesions, we would not lead with surgery because we would try to get rid of those and sort of quote unquote downstage the cancer with therapy up front, systemic therapy.

Okay. Dr. Chen from radiation could not stay for this tumor board, but I did ask him to chime in and he said radiation would not be his up front modality here. So then we've got a gentleman with a BRAF mutation for which we have pills, but we also know that immunotherapy can give you a more durable response. So Dear Dr. Medical Oncologist, what would you recommend next?

You know, probably over the last few years, probably the biggest advance that we've made from a systemic therapy perspective is our understanding that up front or otherwise known as neoadjuvant immunotherapy prior to surgery can really improve outcomes in the long term. So we really, whenever possible, we try to start these patients out with some form of immunotherapy before surgery.

OK, and that word, and Dr. Cliccio mentioned it, of treatment before surgery is called neoadjuvant treatment. But then we had another quandary. Do we lead with SWOG1801, which was pembrolizumab or Keytruda for three cycles prior to surgery, versus the Nadina protocol, which is immunotherapy of ipilimumab and nivolumab? What do we do next? Toss-up. Dr. Hanks?

Well, I think, truthfully, we don't really have any head-to-head comparison between those two strategies. So there's not necessarily a right or wrong way here. I think when you're looking at combination immunotherapy, which would be the Nadina protocol, you're looking at two cycles of ipinivo, ipilimumab, and olumab immunotherapy, While the objective response rate or the ability to shrink the tumor is quite high, you're looking at almost 60%, really 56, 57% response rates. However, the toxicity and the side effects are gonna also be much more significant. So we see anywhere between 35 to 40% of patients will develop a higher grade toxicity on that protocol. So that is something to consider. And then we compare that with the SWOG 18-01 protocol, which is an anti-PD-1 antibody, in this case Pimrilizumab or Keytruda, which is another form of immunotherapy. And that's given three doses before surgery. The response rates are somewhat modestly lower, but the toxicities are also quite a bit lower. you're looking at 7% grade three, four higher toxicity rates relative to over 30%. So I think there's, again, there's really no clear answer for a lot of these cases.
Now you may recall that he had some kidney concerns, some inflammation in the kidney. Would that weigh into your decision?

Yeah, absolutely. I think that would be a very reasonable thing to be concerned about. I think fortunately, The incidence of interstitial nephritis or kidney toxicity on these regimens is actually quite low. You're looking at higher grade toxicities at less than 5% of patients that are treated with these therapies. When you combine it with Yervoy or ipilimumab, it is gonna go up a little bit. So I think that that's reasonable to consider. And given the unusual read from the radiologist in terms of his kidneys, that would be something to be concerned about.
Okay. And I know for ipinivo in stage four disease, sometimes we do ipilimumab three milligrams per kilo versus one milligram per kilo. In this Nadina study, which dosing did they use?

They use the one milligram per kilogram dosing. And I think that fortunately we do have a clinical trial that was designed, a European trial that was designed that compares the ipilimumab one mig per kg versus ipilimumab three mig per kg with the Volumab. And what they found was actually quite similar outcomes from an efficacy standpoint. So the response rates are just a few percentage points lower when you're using the one microcig dosing. The toxicity rates, and of course that was really the main reason for doing the study, was to understand whether or not we could reduce the toxicity or side effects by lowering the dose of Urovoy. The dosing was, the side effects incidence was actually significantly less when we went to one mg per kg. So, I think it would be very reasonable to go one mg per kg whenever feasible.

So if the patient was treated with a combination regimen, which of course he was. I'm sorry, can we have a little more microphone? Sorry about that. So if the patient was 68 loose stools per day, relative to baseline, we generally would start out with an oral prednisone dose. And I prefer to try to keep that dose as low as possible, whenever possible.
Okay.

For a few minutes, we tried to manage this with Imodium and diet. Prednisone or any oral steroid can suppress the immune response, and we're trying to increase it with the immunotherapy. But we saw him in clinic two days later, and he still had profuse diarrhea. And his creatinine was up to 2.44. It had been 1.23. So we admitted him to the hospital. They did a CT scan, which did show colitis, or inflammation of the colon, and they gave him IV steroids, because oral steroids were probably going to go whooshing out with his poop. Whenever we have patients that are not responding the way that we would like them to, to oral steroids or even IV steroids, I think that we now try to transition fairly quickly to a drug like infliximab, which is a drug that inhibits an inflammatory pathway that has traditionally been used for treating inflammatory bowel disease, for example. It turns out that this drug can also be highly effective for managing colitis secondary to immunotherapy. Oftentimes patients after just one dose will improve significantly over a number of hours. So this is often the preferred direction to go.

Yep. So I guess he was doing okay enough on oral steroids when he got discharged. But nine days later, he's still having frequent loose stools. And then we did do infliximab and with a marked improvement. So you may recall that the initial plan was to do two cycles of immunotherapy and go to surgery. Well, that got postponed because surgeons are not too excited to do surgery when somebody is on high-dose steroids. Dr. Dower, why is that, please?

It's the, in this case, both the steroids and the infliximab. If you're decreasing the immune response, you have a higher infection risk having surgery. So in this case, if you're, if it's not an emergent surgery and you're able to delay, it's better for a healing perspective to wait.

Okay. So surgery was scheduled for February 18th. We did rescan prior to surgery because we don't want to put somebody through a surgery when knock on wood, there may have been disease progression elsewhere. So what do we have on the next PET scan? Myocarditis. Dr. Hanks, how often is myocarditis, which is a fancy word for inflammation of the heart, how often, if ever, is that seen with immunotherapy?
Fortunately, very infrequent.

Right. Very, very infrequently. But the PET scan said there is some uptake of the dye along the ventricle, yack, yack. So increases the risk for cardiac abnormality. So the physician sent him off to the emergency room. Because we get nervous when the heart is not looking so good on a PET scan. He had a consultation with our cardiologist, who has a subspecialty in oncology, and the workup was very reassuring, so they do not think this was myocarditis. OK, finally, they got to surgery. And Dr. Daugherty, this was done by an ear, nose, and throat surgeon. But can you tell us a little bit about what happened here during the surgery? I know it wasn't on your watch.

So they did a wide local excision and a sentinel lymph node biopsy. I imagine they took two centimeter margins given the stage of this melanoma and the depth. The depth is usually what will determine how wide of a margin of normal tissue we take around it. So two centimeters is a fairly wide margin. That's the widest we would ever need to go for a melanoma. And then we inject a dye at the beginning before we take out the melanoma to find what we call the sentinel lymph node, or that's the first one to usually three draining lymph nodes. And then we sample those and see if any cancer has spread to those lymph nodes.
So one lymph node was removed and it did not show any melanoma. Dr. Al-Rohail, it's a little difficult. If there had been melanoma there, how would the report have read?

Yeah, so one of the things that have evolved in what we practice is actually we're seeing treatment effect. So after a patient undergoes checkpoint inhibitor treatment or treatment targeting therapy, we can actually see the tumor dead or dying or the aftermath of death of melanocytes. So melanoma leaves a trial after it's killed. So either we see fibrosis, which is significant kind of like scar-like tissue kind of look, or we see the melanocytes dead, which is like the ghost of nuclei is basically like the death of the melanocytes, and they leave behind the melanin pigment. So we call it melanophages. If you read it in the report, that's mainly what we mean. We see the melanin pigment being deposited in the lymph node itself. So we can see if there was metastasis that got treated. In this case, this only says negative for melanoma and there was like no signs of previous metastasis to the lymph node that responded to therapy. However, the one thing I'll mention is his excision where we clinically saw that there was a satellite nodule from the main tumor. There was no residual satellite, so he did respond to therapy. That focus of melanoma completely regressed and there was no residual viable disease in the excision or signs of metastasis in the central lymph node.

So, as far as our naked eye and technology, as far as we know, he is what we call NED, no evidence of disease, both by pathology and by scans. So, Dr. Hanks, he got permanent adena, two cycles of ipinevo. What would you do next?

At this point, based on the pathology report, we would just monitor him. Okay. Put him on a surveillance program and monitor him closely, physical exams, as well as his imaging studies every couple of months.
Okay.

Yep, so we're doing close surveillance, which, as Dr. Hanks says, we're going to do scans at least every three months. He's got to see dermatology for the rest of his life, and he'll have very thorough clinical appointments as well every three months. And if he remains free of disease, we will space that out over time. He is just really hoping to stay away from more medical specialists and avoid any more side effects and just enjoy the spring. Are there any questions? Yes, Ms. Mazurka. Infliximab. It's also called Remicade. You may have heard of that.

reference_conclusion: Neoadjuvant systemic immunotherapy was selected rather than upfront surgery for this stage IIIC melanoma with satellite lesions; the patient received two cycles of ipilimumab plus nivolumab per the NADINA approach. Following marked clinical response and subsequent wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy demonstrating no residual viable melanoma and a negative sentinel node, no further immediate systemic therapy was recommended. The patient is to undergo close surveillance with serial physical examinations and imaging at approximately 3-month intervals, with interval spacing if he remains without evidence of disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Presentation with widespread metastatic malignancy.

[ diagnosis ]: Extensive-stage small cell lung carcinoma with brain metastases and soft tissue metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the left flank soft tissue showed metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma consistent with small cell lung carcinoma of lung origin. Immunophenotype was positive for cytokeratin, TTF-1, and INSM1.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a sizable lung mass with adenopathy, pleural effusion, and brain metastases. Imaging pattern was consistent with primary lung malignancy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: PD-L1 expression was low. Tumor cell score was 0%. Tumor-infiltrating immune cells were 1%. Genomic testing identified TP53 mutation including TP53 Y220C missense mutation, and a PIK3CA mutation at H1047R.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received carboplatin, etoposide, and atezolizumab for 4 cycles, followed by atezolizumab maintenance. Whole-brain radiation therapy was also administered for brain metastases.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic small cell lung cancer with intracranial involvement after completion of first-line chemoimmunotherapy and transition to maintenance atezolizumab.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was not an operative candidate.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you, Basim. This is a case that is something I see quite frequently. And many of you who are practicing oncologists, I'm sure have kind of faced the same situation. reference_conclusion: For extensive-stage small cell lung cancer with brain metastases, standard first-line therapy consists of platinum-etoposide plus a PD-L1 inhibitor, followed by maintenance atezolizumab, with whole-brain radiotherapy already administered. Given the TP53 Y220C alteration and the limited benefit of later-line chemotherapy, enrollment in a clinical trial targeting TP53 Y220C is favored early, particularly in the second-line setting while performance status remains adequate. If trial participation is not feasible, approved second-line options include lurbinectedin or topotecan. Thoracic radiation consolidation may be considered in extensive-stage disease if a good response is achieved after four cycles of chemoimmunotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe abdominal pain in February 2013.

[ diagnosis ]: Small intestine neuroendocrine tumor arising in the ileum, initially stage III based on regional nodal involvement; subsequent metastatic recurrence involving the liver and later liver and bone.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial small bowel resection pathology: well-differentiated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor of the ileum. Tumor invaded through the muscularis propria. Mitotic count was 1 per 2 mm². Ki-67 index was <2%. Lymphovascular invasion was present. Perineural invasion was absent. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor was identified in 1 of 12 regional lymph nodes.  
- Liver resection pathology: metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 2. Mitotic count was 1 per 2 mm². Ki-67 index was approximately 15%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- February 2013 CT abdomen/pelvis: mesenteric mass in the small bowel mesentery.  
- At exploratory surgery: mesenteric mass near the cecum; no visible spread elsewhere in the abdomen.  
- Postoperative Gallium-68 DOTATATE scan: no evidence of disease.  
- Surveillance imaging over several years: no recurrence on routine follow-up imaging, typically annual CT abdomen/pelvis.  
- Approximately 6 years after surgery, CT scan: 3.5 cm lesion in the left hepatic lobe, not seen on the prior year’s scan; additional smaller hepatic lesions too small to characterize.  
- MRI abdomen: left hepatic lobe mass measuring 4 cm; several additional millimetric hepatic lesions concerning for metastases.  
- Gallium-68 DOTATATE PET: intense uptake in the left hepatic lobe lesion and lesser uptake in additional smaller hepatic lesions.  
- Subsequent MRI abdomen about 1 year after liver resection: growth of smaller residual hepatic lesions.  
- Later imaging about 1 year after initiation of somatostatin analog therapy: continued increase in size and number of liver metastases; DOTATATE PET demonstrated persistent somatostatin receptor expression and metastatic disease in liver and bone.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Exploratory surgery with small bowel resection performed shortly after initial presentation in 2013.  
- Postoperative surveillance was undertaken after negative DOTATATE imaging.  
- Robotic left lateral liver resection performed for hepatic metastatic disease; larger hepatic lesion was resected.  
- Observation was undertaken after liver resection.  
- Somatostatin analog therapy was initiated after interval growth of residual hepatic metastases.  
- Disease progression occurred on somatostatin analog therapy, with increasing hepatic metastatic burden and subsequent osseous metastases.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic well-differentiated small intestine neuroendocrine tumor with prior progression in liver and bone after somatostatin analog therapy; persistent somatostatin receptor expression had been demonstrated on DOTATATE PET.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: non-melanoma skin cancer, nephrolithiasis, hypertension.  
- No carcinoid syndrome symptoms were reported.

reference_discussion.text: All right, we'll start with a second case, or second set of cases, and this is not pancreas neuroendocrine tumor, but we will talk about small intestine neuroendocrine tumors. What would the emergency room doctors be thinking? And what would you think comes next

So with a mesenteric mass, there are a few different things we'll think of, a few different types of diagnoses. So usually limited to about four things. And we don't see a lot of bowel obstruction. There's really no dilation of the other loops of bowel. And I might be concerned that we have some ischemia to the bowel, or maybe a low-grade obstruction. Typically, so I would say the emergency room doctors are going to be thinking of the same thing and ask some consultants to have a look at the case. If I were to see the case, I would first consider that, you know, whether or not this disease could be removed and safely preserve enough small bowel so the patient could avoid intestinal insufficiency. I would point out that many times a patient could be seen in a hospital where neuroendocrine tumors are not treated as frequently. And you might go to the operating room and have a small bowel tumor operated on and a mesenteric mass like that left behind because it was deemed to be unresectable. And patients can be quite upset about that and say, why did I need a surgery? Why did this person not remove the original tumor? But I view that as very sound judgment to not try to explore or intervene in a situation where you don't think it's safe. Because removing a mesenteric mass and getting bleeding can have really disastrous consequences. And it's relatively straightforward to go another time and remove that. So if the patient were not seen in a center where we see a lot of mesenteric disease, I think it's perfectly fine not to rush into the operating room.

So he did have, not immediately, but did have exploratory surgery shortly after that mass was seen. So they found a mesenteric mass that was near the cecum. So that's the first part of the large bowel. They did not see in the operating room any evidence of spread elsewhere in the abdomen. So there was a small bowel resection that was performed. So the pathology, and I don't have slides to show today, but the pathology revealed a well-differentiated, low-grade neuroendocrine tumor that was in the ileum. So that's the last part of the small intestine where we most commonly will find small intestinal neuroendocrine tumors. There was, under the microscope, evidence of invasion into small lymphatic vessels, no invasion around the nerves, but they did find a neuroendocrine tumor in one of 12 regional lymph nodes. So he's referred to an oncologist for discussion about what to do next. So I will ask Dr. Asi how you would counsel this patient and how you would manage this.

Sure. So yeah, the first thing is really to discuss what we found on pathology with the patient. So it's very important to notice that it's a well-differentiated tumor. And it's a low grade with a KIC7 that's less than 2%. So it just gives me a sense that This tumor was probably there for a while. It's kind of a slow-growing indolent tumor that's been there. But that being said, there's also some concerning factors that I see on pathology. So one, lymph nodes was involved. So this kind of ups the stage of the tumor. So because there's lymph node involvement, that's stage three, at least. I'll talk more about that. And there's also lymphobascular invasion. These are bad prognostic signs. Now, the next step, in my view, would be to make sure the cancer has not, to fully stage the patient and make sure the cancer has not gone elsewhere. So, getting a Gallium 68 DOTATATE scan would be my next step. I don't know if it's already been gotten.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old male; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Coccygeal pain and increasing urinary hesitancy for 6 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Sacrococcygeal mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Sacrococcygeal lesion biopsy was performed on 27 October 2024.  
- Intraoperative frozen section showed malignant pathology and was inconsistent with chordoma.  
- Final pathology favored mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.  
- Immunomarkers reported included CD99 and NKX2.2.  
- Tumor grade was not reported.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI lumbosacral spine with contrast dated 22 October 2024 showed a contrast-enhancing sacrococcygeal midline mass.  
- MRI review described a large sacral mass with intrapelvic and extrapelvic components, with the intrapelvic component larger. The lesion was hypointense on T1, heterogeneous on T2, showed internal necrotic areas, and demonstrated significant post-contrast enhancement. The distal sacrum and probably coccyx were involved. There was infiltration/surrounding of cauda equina/sacral nerve roots. The urinary bladder was markedly distended, consistent with neurogenic bladder. No lymphadenopathy was appreciated on the limited images reviewed.  
- CT chest/abdomen dated 31 October 2024 showed a sacroiliac/sacral midline mass with suspicion of a deposit in the left parapholic/left hypochondrial region and suspected peritoneal metastases.  
- PET scan dated 14 November 2024 showed a large hypermetabolic destructive mass arising from the distal sacrum with dense calcification and central necrosis. A morphologically stable subcentimeter nodule in the left hypochondrium was reported as most likely a splenule rather than metastatic disease. PET review showed FDG uptake confined to the primary lesion, with no abnormal FDG-avid lesion elsewhere.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Surgery was initially undertaken with intent for maximal safe resection; biopsy of the sacrococcygeal lesion was performed on 27 October 2024.  
- The initial resection procedure was abandoned because of significant intraoperative bleeding.  
- Preoperative angioembolization was subsequently performed.  
- Maximal safe resection was performed on 26 November 2024.  
- Operative assessment documented gross complete resection; no rectal resection was required, although the tumor was very close to the rectum.  
- No postoperative imaging had been performed at the time of documentation.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Post-resection status following gross complete excision of sacrococcygeal mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.  
- Significant microscopic residual disease could not be excluded on operative assessment because of close proximity to the rectum.  
- No confirmed distant metastatic disease was identified on PET imaging prior to surgery.  
- Postoperative radiologic disease status had not yet been assessed.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Initial radiologic differential diagnosis included chordoma and chondrosarcoma.  
- CT-guided biopsy of the intra-abdominal/left hypochondrial lesion had been considered but was deferred because it was assessed as high risk.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old patient with known Lynch syndrome.

[ chief complaint ]: Surveillance imaging demonstrated a new bulky right-sided proximal ureteral tumor with hydronephrosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Lynch syndrome with germline MSH2 and MSH6 mutations; history of colorectal cancer; recurrent upper tract urothelial carcinoma. Prior left upper tract urothelial carcinoma was initially high-grade and later recurred as low-grade disease. Subsequent right proximal ureteral urothelial tumor was concerning for cT3 disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Left upper tract tumor treated in 2013 was described as small-volume, high-grade disease. Left-sided recurrence 6 years later was described as low-grade disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance imaging 3 years after treatment of the left-sided recurrence showed a bulky obstructing right proximal ureteral tumor with hydronephrosis. Imaging raised concern for T3 disease, including periureteral irregularity/spiculation. No metastatic disease or enlarged lymph nodes were identified. CT performed 4 months after pembrolizumab showed a complete response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline MSH2 mutation and germline MSH6 mutation, consistent with Lynch syndrome.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: History of colorectal cancer treated with right hemicolectomy. In 2013, left small-volume high-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma was treated with laser ablation followed by adjuvant retrograde mitomycin. Six years later, left-sided recurrence was managed with repeat laser ablation and topical gemcitabine. For the subsequent bulky right proximal ureteral tumor, pembrolizumab was administered. CT after 4 months of pembrolizumab demonstrated complete response. Pembrolizumab was then discontinued because of severe immune-related toxicity.

[ current disease status ]: Radiographic complete response after pembrolizumab.

[ other clinical data ]: Pembrolizumab treatment was complicated by immunotherapy-related diabetes mellitus with diabetic ketoacidosis. The patient declined further invasive intervention.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma, pT2N0, arising in the thyroid isthmus.

[ histopathology results ]: Preoperative biopsy was suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma. [ imaging findings ]: Initial thyroid nodule measured 2.5 cm in the isthmus.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NRAS mutation and TERT promoter mutation were identified on molecular profiling.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy. Surgical pathology demonstrated pT2N0 disease with 3 negative lymph nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Post-thyroidectomy status following resection of pT2N0 high-grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma. No nodal metastasis was identified in the resected lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old woman; Tamil ethnicity. Performance status was PS 2. Comorbidity: hypertension. No family history was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic bilateral breast cancer diagnosed in 2020 with subsequent multiple lines of systemic therapy and progressive disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral breast carcinoma, stage IV, diagnosed in 2020. Hormone receptor-positive and HER2-positive disease (ER/PR positive, HER2 positive). Repeat biopsies continued to demonstrate HER2-positive disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Immunohistochemistry on repeat biopsy remained HER2 positive; HER2 was reported as IHC 3+. HER2 positivity had been confirmed on three separate biopsies. ER/PR positivity was present; strength of expression/Allred score was not available.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid-biopsy next-generation sequencing using a 118-gene panel identified a PIK3CA mutation and an ESR mutation. NF1 loss was also reported in the molecular profile. Variant allele frequency/tumor fraction was reported as 0.73%.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: First-line treatment consisted of trastuzumab, a CDK inhibitor (palbociclib), and fulvestrant. The patient subsequently received endocrine therapies including letrozole and exemestane. Disease progressed on prior endocrine therapy. T-DM1 was administered, with subsequent progressive disease. Capecitabine plus lapatinib plus trastuzumab was administered, with subsequent progressive disease. Palbociclib-based therapy had been continued for approximately 3 years initially. Trastuzumab deruxtecan was not administered because of financial constraints. At the current stage, gemcitabine/carboplatin had been started, and a repeat biopsy had been sent for molecular testing.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic HER2-positive, ER/PR-positive bilateral breast cancer after multiple prior lines of HER2-directed therapy, endocrine therapy, CDK inhibitor therapy, T-DM1, and capecitabine/lapatinib/trastuzumab. reference_conclusion: In the setting of persistent HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer with progression after prior trastuzumab-, lapatinib-, T-DM1-, endocrine-, and CDK4/6 inhibitor-based therapies, and with trastuzumab deruxtecan not feasible because of cost, the preferred next systemic option discussed was tucatinib-based HER2-directed therapy. Recommended regimens were tucatinib plus trastuzumab plus capecitabine, with tucatinib plus T-DM1 noted as an alternative where applicable. A repeat assessment of PIK3CA on an earlier tissue biopsy by PCR was also proposed to clarify whether alpelisib could be incorporated subsequently if the mutation is confirmed as a driver event.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic breast cancer with multiple bone metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast carcinoma with bone-only metastatic disease, diagnosed in November 2016.

[ histopathology results ]: Primary tumor was strongly estrogen receptor positive and progesterone receptor positive; HER2 negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Progressive disease was documented after approximately 3 years of initial systemic therapy, with increased activity of bone lesions. Bone-only metastatic pattern was described. Palliative radiotherapy was administered.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Circulating tumor DNA assay (Guardant360) identified ESR1 mutation, PIK3CA mutation, and EGFR amplification.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Initial systemic therapy consisted of palbociclib plus letrozole. Denosumab was also administered. The patient had clinical benefit for almost 3 years before disease progression in bone. Palliative radiotherapy was given.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic disease in bone after prior palbociclib plus letrozole, with increased activity of existing bone lesions.

[ other clinical data ]: Bone metastases were considered the only known sites of metastatic disease. ctDNA testing was used in the setting of bone-only disease. Germline hereditary breast/ovarian cancer testing had not been reported.

So what is one of the things I think, again, is being brought up is the cost of these things. So how much does Garden 360 or Hydro Tree Panels cost in Nepal or India, Dr. Siroyi?

So it's so so foundation costs about three point six lakhs. So three hundred and sixty thousand rupees and garden costs exactly the same. And there are a lot of Indians. So, you know, a lot of times when I do these meetings, I'm asked which company to go with, because there are so many companies which are doing these tests. And in India, you have a lot of homegrown companies as well, like Strand, Datar, MedGenome, quite a few others as well, which are doing it at a fraction of the cost, but quite a few of the data is not validated. And so like it is with foundation and garden. So so that is that that is the downside. But it is very expensive. So I do do the tests with some of the Indian Indian vendors. It fosters an issue.

Sure, certainly. That is always something that I think we all have to keep in mind, because it's…you know, when we are saying that, yeah, at every progression there could be new resistance developing, but if the cost is that high, I think we have to be judicious about when to order these tests. So, the other discussion moving forward, I think we are…if you look at ESR1 mutations and looking at the clinical significance of that, You know these are, so I think one of the things that I would want to highlight in this slide is that these are studies. These are from different studies, so you can't really compare the columns, but I think what would be important is to look at this within a particular drug. How is our one in mutations? In fact, the PFS and OS. If you look at full restaurant. This is looking at two clinical trials, Sophia and in fact what they found was those with ESR one mutations had a PFS of 3.9 months. ESR negative at 4.1 months. Very comparable survival as well was very comparable. 80% and 81% one year survival. Eczema stain, on the other hand, was this was very remarkable. If you look at it, ESR one mutation positives had 2.4 months PFS, whereas ESR negative at 4.8 months. Overall survival as well was very different. 62% for ESR1 mutation carriers and negative were 79%. If you look at eczema stain and everolimus as well, there was difference in overall survival between those with ESR1 mutation and those who did not carry ESR1 mutation. Bottom line is it appears that for fulvestrant with ESR1 mutation, it does not really seem to be different to the PFS or OS between those who carry ESR1 mutation or those who do not. Whereas for eczema stain or eczema stain and everolimus, it does seem like that the PFS and OS seem to be lower in those who have ESR1 mutation. Now, based on this data, I guess the question that…because if you look at…if you just look at the ESR1 mutations alone and we don't think of the PIK3 mutation, Would that sway you in any ways about choosing fulvestrant over eczema stain and everolimus if somebody has ESR1 mutations? Dr. Sirui, what are your thoughts on that?

So, I think you've answered the question. In the SOFIA and the AFFECT trial, which tried to look at fulvestrant versus a neuromatase inhibitor, patients who had ESR1 mutation did better with fulvestrant. So, and that was the dose used in these studies was 250 milligram, which we no longer use. We use 500 milligrams of fulvestrant. And we know that the ESR1 mutation actually can cause relative resistance to fulvastrin and tamoxifen as well. And in the CDK4-6 trials, we know that it is prognostic but not predictive, the ESR1 mutation. So, patients who carry an ESR1 mutation have a poorer prognosis. But looking at the SOFIA and the effect, as you have shown, I think I would go for full restraint 500 milligrams if the patient had an ESR1 mutation.
Gotcha. Dr. Rian, any thoughts on that?

Oh, yeah, I, uh, I check, uh, yes, I want mutation a lot, almost routinely, um, after patient actually. And actually, for me, uh, I'm running a research project that, uh, for my static passive her to negative, we tend to drag our feet to have the genomic test. But now, actually, I'm running a research projects that, you know, I'm advocating for genomic test upfront. reason of all those ESR mutations. They can be acquired later, but they could be de novo to start too. So, you know, I totally agree that, you know, ESR1 should be checked when the patient progress on the first line treatments. Yeah, I almost always check that too.

Okay, so moving forward. So that was the ESR1 part of this. Now looking at the PIK3 kinase, the PIK3CA mutation. So, this is where I think the field has moved forward, and it's very exciting. We had the SOLR1 trial published last year, and what this study did was they had two different cohorts. They had a PIK3CA mutant cohort and they had a PIK3CA non-mutant cohort. So, both…and in each of these cohorts, what they did was used a combination of L-penicillin with fulvestrant and compared it to placebo with fulvestrant. And what they found was…and so, if you look at the enrollment criteria, these were all postmenopausal women with hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, advanced breast cancer, with recurrence of progression on prior AI. And so what they found was very interesting, and this is just in the PIK3CA mutated cohort. They found that there was significant difference in the progress and free survival. So median PFS for L-pallisive with fulvestrant was 11 months, whereas placebo with fulvestrant was 5.7 months. Now, in the non-PIK3CA mutated…so, in the PIK3CA wild-type cohort, they did not find a difference in progress in free survival. The overall survival data has not been reported, and so we don't know if this makes any impact on overall survival or not. So, this sort of opens up a new treatment option, in this case, at least, with Fulvestrant and Alpil. So I guess that brings us to sort of towards the end of this case. With knowing the ESR1, knowing the PIK3CA, Dr. Sirui, what would be your choice of treatment in this case? Where would you, what would you favor proceeding with treatment after progression on pelliciclib and AI?
So I think that the data is quite impressive. I would go for fulvestrin and Alpilisib if it was available. And again, if costs were not an issue.
How much, again, I think we keep on going back to the question of cost and how much is the cost on the Alpilisib?

So, I think in my clinical setting, most of my patients, even full restraint is quite expensive. So, I would tend to go towards maybe not eczema stain and everolimus, but possibly tamoxifen and everolimus, because we know that ESR1 mutation is predictive of resistance to AI. So, and there's relative resistance to fulvestrin and tamoxifen. So, most of the times I would end up, because we have a generic everolimus, so I would go for tamoxifen and everolimus. And because full restraint is also quite expensive, it's about 30 to 35 to 40,000 per injection and patients need to get two doses intramuscular every month. which is for slim ladies it's quite painful and it seriously affects their quality of life. Alpalysib is again quite expensive, the cost is in lakhs and if you add it to fulvestrant, I think all of these trials are done in high-income group countries and they're combining two drugs, three drugs, four drugs, immunotherapy, which I think where 70% of the cancer patients live that's low and middle income group countries, we don't have access to because patients can't afford it. So all the other option and real world setting would be capecitabine. So you know, which is again, very easily affordable and easily available.
Yeah, definitely. Dr. Rian, how about since you practice in the US, and these some of these limitations may not be applicable, What would your choice be?

Because, you know, this is this is a young woman and with bone only disease. And, you know, to be honest, to be honest, you know, even because it's not an issue with bone only disease, you would anticipate this woman may potentially do well, actually, even on hormone therapy only because she had the ESR1 mutation. You know, if the patient is totally against any more treatments and just giving fulvastatin alone wouldn't be a very reasonable option just to kind of watch her. And also it's not unreasonable at all because you know it's bone only and you know it's kind of benign process. So I would be OK with fulvastatin only. But you know if the patient is really she wants to be aggressive, she does have the PRK3CA mutation and we all know that with the mutation the patient tend to progress quickly. So I have a handful of patients that actually is on felvastatin and alpalisib. It's actually a very appealing approach. And so it's actually very well tolerated. And I have the luxury, I have two nurses and they have 30 years of experience in oncology and they are expert in doing the felvastatin injection. So I don't even want to send my patient to any other nurses. So my nurse is here. on doing the injection for my patients. And most of the time, I barely have any side effects from the injection. So, you know, I know I have the luxury that I don't have to worry too much about the cost and I have access to the medications. But if you look at this young woman, she's young and, you know, she has the ESLR mutation and she has APRK3CA mutation. So I would advocate that nowadays we should be smart and we should target the mutation for patients.
Sounds reasonable. We have a question in the chat saying that would you continue denosumab or change the bone-modifying agent as well?

Oh no, I would continue the denosumab and there is no evidence to tell me that a denosumab is better or inferior to Zomeda. However, we have to be aware that the commercial name Xgeva is FDA approved every four weeks. And Zometa, however, we have data that you can space out to every 12 weeks. So often the time I have patients that we space out xGiva to every 12 weeks because of the data and it's just too frequent. And when it's bone only disease, and I often just go back to xGiva every four weeks and sometimes they just do the trick. But I'm not sure if that applies to this patient because she has a mutation, but often the time just kind of go back every four weeks can do the trick.

Sounds good, sounds good. So, kind of just a summary of this case, and as you see, you saw that these mutations can happen during the course of treatment, and we talked a little bit about the prohibitiveness of the cost and the challenge of getting these treatments in countries like Nepal or India. And in that context, I think Dr. Siroya brought up a good point about how expensive molecular labs are, and I think one of the things that BTFCC is trying to do is establish a molecular lab in Nepal, which will be, in my understanding, is one of the first NGS lab in Nepal to be able to run some of these BIK3, ESR1, these kind of mutation testing in Nepal. So we're very excited about that. I mean, it's a process. There are a lot of challenges to getting it done, but hopefully we should be there in the next few years.

Could I take this question? One more question, Sid, just so it says that will the garden cover all the genes and hereditary panel costs around 15,000, but garden panel. So I just want to make a point that garden panel testing for the somatic mutations. So if you do find something, you must do germline testing separately as well.
Yes.
So for genetic counseling and for family.

Yeah. Yes, definitely. I think we I think the garden 360 is mostly just we are trying to evaluate for somatic mutations. I would not order it for germline aspect of things, and the German panels should be very different. So, moving on to case two, since we're talking about some germline aspect of things. Can I interrupt for a second? Yes, definitely.

reference_conclusion: Following progression on palbociclib plus letrozole in metastatic ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer with ESR1 and PIK3CA alterations identified on ctDNA, the preferred next systemic therapy is fulvestrant plus alpelisib, if available and financially feasible. Fulvestrant monotherapy is a reasonable alternative in the setting of bone-only disease, particularly if a less intensive approach is desired. Denosumab should be continued as the bone-modifying agent. Germline hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel testing should also be performed separately from the liquid biopsy assay.

So I have a handful of patients that actually is on felvastatin and alpalisib. It's actually a very appealing approach. [...] Oh no, I would continue the denosumab [...] I would do the whole germline panel, which includes PALV2, ATM, CHECK, and the other mutations as well. The whole hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel in her.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman; never-smoker; married.

[ chief complaint ]: Intensive lower back pain in June 2024.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV EGFR-mutated primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma with metastatic involvement of mediastinal/peribronchovascular lymph nodes, liver, bone, and brain.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy of the right iliac crest demonstrated primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry showed PD-L1 negative, ALK negative, and ROS negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Lumbar MRI in June 2024 demonstrated bone metastasis.  
- Total body CT scan showed a cluster of large paramediastinal adenopathies, largest measuring 3.5 × 3.7 cm, with associated peribronchovascular lymphadenopathy.  
- CT scan also showed approximately 15 secondary liver nodules considered metastatic lesions and multiple lytic bone lesions.  
- PET scan confirmed extensive metastatic disease with multiple metastatic lung nodules, liver nodules, and bone metastases.  
- Brain MRI showed cerebellar lesions.  
- PET scan in August 2024, performed for treatment evaluation, showed major response to treatment; a lesion measuring 4.8 cm had decreased to 3.6 cm.  
- PET scan in October 2024 showed relatively stable skeletal metastatic disease with mild reappearance of activity associated with the right basilar lung mass.  
- In December 2024, imaging showed progression of the lung lesion and major progression of metastatic bone disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- RT-PCR identified EGFR exon 19 deletion.  
- FoundationOne CDx in December 2024 confirmed EGFR exon 19 deletion and detected TP53 alteration.  
- No additional new alteration was identified on FoundationOne CDx beyond EGFR exon 19 deletion and TP53 alteration.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Osimertinib was started in July 2024 as first-line systemic therapy.  
- By August 2024, PET evaluation showed major radiologic response, with marked clinical improvement; lower back pain resolved and the patient became asymptomatic.  
- Osimertinib was continued through December 2024.  
- Disease progression occurred after approximately 7 months of osimertinib, with progression in the lung lesion and major progression of bone metastases; bone progression was described as asymptomatic at that time.  
- In January 2025, second-line treatment was started with carboplatin, pemetrexed, first-dose amivantamab administered in a split schedule over 2 days, and zoledronic acid.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic EGFR exon 19-deleted pulmonary adenocarcinoma after first-line osimertinib; second-line treatment with carboplatin, pemetrexed, amivantamab, and zoledronic acid was initiated in January 2025.

[ other clinical data ]: Clinical course included rapid symptomatic improvement on first-line therapy followed by radiologic progression within 7 months of treatment initiation.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Dr. Mirva. Thank you for organizing this series of tumor board, thoracic tumor board, that you are rendering the level to next level in our region in thoracic oncology. Thank you very much for inviting us and for this very rich discussion that we had tonight and every time we are doing this Thoracic Tumor Board. Thank you for being such a great leader for us all. So in the next 20 minutes, I'll start by presenting the case and discussing the overcoming resistance to ozymertinib, the constant battle. Let's start with the case. Those are my disclosures. It's a 43 years old woman, non-smoker, married, presented with intensive back pain in June, 2024. A lumbar MRI, she was evaluated first by an orthopedic surgeon, presents of bone metastasis. A total body CT scan was done, showing a cluster of large paramediastinal adenopathies, the largest measuring 3.5 times 3.7, associated with peribronchovascular lymphadenopathy. Also, we had about 15 secondary liver nodules considered as metastatic lesions, also multipellitic bone lesions. The pathology findings of the CT-guided biopsy of the right iliac crest showed a primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma. The immunohistochemistry confirmed that the PD-L1 was negative, the ALK was negative, the ROS was negative, and the RT-PCR showed EGFR exon 19 deletion. The PET scan confirmed the extension of the disease, multiple metastatic lung and liver nodules, and bone metastasis. Also, a brain MRI showed cerebellar lesions. The patient in July 2024 started on ozymertinib. In August 2024, a PET scan of evaluation after three months showed major response to treatment. and we had an exceptional clinical amelioration. The patient who presented with an important lower back pain was completely asymptomatic and you can see here how the lesion that was 4.8 centimeters become in three months 3.6 and many of the symptoms were revealed. Also in October 2024, three months later, another PET scan done show skeletal metastatic disease was relatively stable, but we have mild reappearance of activity associated with the right basilar lung mass. The same treatment was also continued till December 2024, when we have a progression of the lung lesion with major progression of metastatic bone disease that was considered asymptomatic. At that point, since we had seven months of treatment on ozymertinib, we decided it was considered short period of response. Foundation one, CDX was done, showing and confirming that we had the EGFR exon 19 deletion. but also we had the appearance of TP53 alteration. So this one was of one of the explanation why we had this rapid progression of the disease. So in January 2025, the patient started with the combination of carboplatin pemetrexate with the first dose of amivamptamab, divided the first one in two days and injection of zoledronic acid. So as you can see, we started in June 2024 with symptomatic patient, rapid response after three months. We have appearance of some stigma of recurrence a few months later, till we had after seven months, a progression of the disease. The foundation one didn't show new alteration, despite the TP53 that was positive, and the patient started a second line treatment with abivantanab, carboplatin, pemetrexed, and zoledronic acid. Two interesting questions. Will you be treating this patient with ozibertinib as first line in 2025? And the second question, what will be your other possible treatment option in 2025 after ozymertinib or after another possible first-line treatment? Let's discuss the possible mechanism of overcoming the resistance to ozymertinib, which is a constant battle. Many of my colleagues presented how the landscape of the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer, and mainly the adenocarcinoma, is shifting. Today, we are treating base bone genetic alteration. And the two major EGFR alterations are the exon 19 deletion and the L 858R point mutation, they represent together the most frequent EGFR mutation, around 85%, but also we have some rare mutation and also the group of exon 20 insertion that has dedicated therapeutic agent today. The majority of the EGFR mutated patients are considered never smoker or previously smoker, 22%. Only 8% are current smoker. The percentage of EGFR mutation in our region in our last publication was around 15.7% in the Arab world compared to 47% in the Asian population. Also, our friend and colleague from Morocco, Zainab bin Ibrahim, published in 2018 another review paper evaluating the percentage of EGFR in our region, and it was considered around 20%. And we can say that in our Arab world, it's between 15% and 20%, and it can vary between the different countries. We published in 2023 this review in Cancer Treatment Reviews, the Acquired Resistant Mechanism to Osimertinib, the constant battle in collaboration with Gustave Roussier in France. And the concept behind it was the new challenge of resistance for anti-EGFR. The first challenge was resolved. The first and second generation EGFR TKI developed resistance, T790M, and it was overcome by osimertinib. However, the new challenge is how to overcome the resistance to ozimertinib, the third generation EGFR TKI. It's a busy slide, but the message is clear. We should target the EGFR dependent pathway and the EGFR independent pathway. And you can see the huge number of mechanism of resistance to ozimertinib. Mainly, we can talk about MET amplification, MET mutation, HER2 mutation, HER2 amplification, FGFR, AXL over expression. So it's important to build strategy to overcome this resistance. So we have two big strategies. The first one, using new drugs to combat EGFR-TKI resistance in the second line. Single-agent strategy using novel ADCs or fourth-generation EGFR-TKIs. Combination strategies with chemo-IO anti-angiogenic drugs, double TKI, bispecific antibodies and chemotherapy. and completely different strategy on changing and manipulating the first-line treatment to combat EGF-RTKI resistance by adding to the third generation maybe chemotherapy, anti-angiogenic agent, and by specific antibodies. So the concept of Combating resistance on TKI, on ozimertinib, it's on target by using fourth generation EGFR, off target by using combination of anti-angiogenic and anti-PD-1 therapies, combining on and off target therapy using anti-EGFR, anti-MEG, anti-EGFR, anti-MET chemotherapy, or using antibody drug conjugate targeting HERD3, MET, TROP2, targeting those tumor-associated antigens. Let's start with the last part, the novel antibody drug conjugate. We have the HER2 and HER3 ADCs, the Patri-Tumab de-Ruxtecan, we have the MAT ADCs, the Telisotuzumab Vedotin, and the DROP2, which is now showing a lot of interest in bladder and in breast cancer also. Datopotamab, Deruxtecan, targeting the TROP2. And those three trials, Hertenalangone, Luminosity, Tropsonlangone, who included some of them, EGFR, the Patritumab, Deryx tecan was only EGFR mutation, the other included EGFR-mutated patient, among others, showed overall response rate around 30%, which is really promising agents in the management of EGFR-mutated adenocarcinoma. The second way or modality is working on target by inhibiting the EGFR using forced generation EGFR TKI. Why the forced generation? Because the majority of on target resistance is based on the cysteine to serine mutation in EGFR, the C797S, which are confirming the resistance. And Overcoming this mutation will lead to offer to our patients better outcomes. Also, when we are talking about off-target inhibition, we are talking about combination of anti-angiogenic and anti-PD-L1 agent, or using on and off target by using the combination of anti-EGFR and MET-TKIs or anti-EGFR plus chemotherapy next to anti-MET by specific monoclonal antibodies. The question was asked before about the place of immune checkpoint inhibitor and clearly the Empower is the only one showing interesting result in this subcategory of EGFR mutated patients where the combination of atezolizumab and bevacizumab and chemotherapy showed interesting results, but also we have in the pipeline this specific antibody combining anti-angiogenic and anti-PD-1, the EVO Nesimab combined to doublet chemotherapy, who is showing in Harmonia trial, very interesting result. So this combination is not bad, but it's difficult to have a resurrection of this combination. Also, it's interesting to see this biomarker-driven study for each resistant mechanism after ozimertinib, we give different treatment to counteract this mechanism of resistance. The first arm is the MET alteration, where they combine ozimertinib and an anti-MET, the sovolitinib, and when it's EGFR mutated and we have MET-driven locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, adding this anti-MET, the sovolitinib, to the anti-EGFR and ozimertinib was considered one of the options, with the primary endpoint being the overall response rate. And also, when we see When we have more expression of meth in immunohistochemistry and in fish, we can reach around 49%. So in well-selected patients, this drug in combination with ozymertinib can be very interesting. So when we have this overexpression of meth. Finally, all those were experimental, which is really approved, is only the Mariposa trial, combining the bispecific antibody, targeting the EGFR, and targeting the meds next to chemotherapy after. after progression on ozimertinib, and this Mariposa 2 trial with its second interim analysis showed very interesting results on overall survival. So, the key eligibility criteria in this study is documented EGFR, the most frequent mutation, progressing after ozimertinib As monotherapy, as most recent line with good performance stated, three arms in this study, amivantamab, lazartamib, chemotherapy, chemotherapy, and amivantamab chemotherapy. The two last lines, chemo versus amivantamab and chemotherapy, showed very interesting results on overall survival. We have 17.7 versus 15.3 with the advantage of 2.5 months in overall survival with hazard ratio of 0.73 and with significant p-value. And at 18 months landmark for overall survival was 50% for amoebontamab chemotherapy versus 40% for chemotherapy all alone. Also, we can see that we have 27% reduction in the risk of symptomatic progression with amivantamab chemotherapy versus chemotherapy. Time to symptomatic progression was 16 months with amikimo versus 11.8 for chemotherapy. Also the time to treatment discontinuation for amivantamab chemotherapy was five-fold more patients remained on treatment at 18 months versus chemotherapy. So that was how to overcome the resistance in second line after starting the ozymertinib in first line. The second type of strategies is to overcome this resistance before it appears by working on the first line and by manipulating the first line treatment with combination strategy. TKI plus anti-angiogenic agents, TKI plus bispecific antibody and TKI plus chemotherapy. The RELACE trial was one of the first who showed very interesting results with ramicirumab and erlotinib compared to erlotinib, the first generation TKI. And we had an advantage of PFS of around eight months when adding this anti-angiogenic drug to the erlotinib. And also we have very interesting overall response rate. So this was very promising study. In ESMO 2023, the main, the same exercise this time was done with Ozimertinib, Lusamicirumab. We have contradictory outcomes between two trials. One was negative, the other one was considered positive. So we are not sure of the level of evidence of using this combination of ozimertinib and ramicirumab in the first-line setting. However, we should keep in mind that adding anti-angiogenic to our TKI may be an interesting option. Also, the FLORA2 that was also discussed before showed an advantage in progression-free survival. For the first time, the median was around 25, median overall progression-free survival was around 25 months versus 16.7 months with osimertinib monotherapy, but that was of high cost of toxicity, mainly in the hematologic toxicity, which was 71 versus 24. And finally, the Mariposa trial where the combination of amivantanab and lasertinib showed an interesting progression-free survival of 23.7 months versus 16.6 months on ozimertinib. So, we had these three possibilities of adding chemo, adding anti-angiogenic drugs, or adding the amivantamab next to those medication, the bispecific antibody, next to the third generation TKIs in the management of EGFR mutated adenocarcinomas. According to the NCCN guidelines, still the Osimertinib is considered the preferred Category 1 regimen, despite all we discussed about that this Osimertinib alone is losing territory against the other combination. Other recommended also, the Category 1, we have the Amivantamab Lasertinib, and also we have based on FLORA2 in non-squamous, the ozimertinib, premetrexate, and the platinum agent. When we have the progression and we have multiple lesion progression, the only one approved after ozimertinib, according to the NCCN guidelines, remain the combination of amivantamab plus carboplatin and premetrexate. So thank you very much. This was the new era also in Lebanon, where we are rebuilding strong relations between Lebanon and Saudi Arabia at multiple levels. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Professor Khoury. That was an excellent talk and sharing case and also a great update. Because of the time, we just only took two questions. First, if any of the panelists today want us to ask Professor Khoury about his presentation. Okay, so there's two questions from the attendees. Dr. Iman from Morocco, she's asking how to identify the primary resistance in such cases. I think she meant by time or by how we can say that the patient has a primary resistance. So what do you think?

I think we should start doing NGS systematically, large panels at upfront, not only weighting the progression. And then we can compare. Maybe the ideal world will be to do NGS on the tissue, NGS on liquid up front, and also at progression, we can do the liquid to see the different abnormalities and the different mechanism of resistance that we are developing. And this is really an important point because, for example, in my case, unfortunately, I did only the evaluation after progression by foundation one. So the main question was this TP53 found in this foundation was present at the beginning? it was a primary resistance or it appeared after the treatment. So that's why the ideal world, it's costlier. We know that the third party will be, and the government will not be very motivated to cover all these testing, but for science and to offer the best for our patient, it will be really interesting to evaluate the abnormalities that we can have, the mutation that we can have, as we do an antibiogram to see all the genetic abnormalities that we can have, mainly in this type of mutations.
Next question by Dr. Ahmed Al-Jassim from Qatar. He is asking about the subsequent therapy with amaventamib and lazartinib. And is there any rule now for ADCs or just only future direction?

Today, we don't have a clear approval of ADC, but they are in the pipeline, and for sure, we will see very interesting results, and also in EGFR-mutated patients, maybe in the third line to start, and this will be really interesting. Maybe the ADC targeting the MAT will play an important role. What we can offer after lasertinib and amivantamab, I think the chemotherapy will be the next option in this sequence of treatment. Now, our colleague also was mentioning we should use with it the IO and the anti-angiogenic use the EMPOWER trial or only use in second line because the EMPOWER was mainly in the first line, or we use only chemotherapy? This is also an important question. We should see how is the coverage, the patient will pay it, who will pay it. It can be sometimes beneficial, but also I'm not very encouraged to use the quadruplet. I will go maybe for double agent chemotherapy.

reference_conclusion: Following progression on first-line osimertinib after approximately seven months, circulating tumor DNA testing confirmed persistent EGFR exon 19 deletion with TP53 alteration and no new actionable resistance alteration. Second-line systemic therapy was initiated with amivantamab in combination with carboplatin and pemetrexed, together with zoledronic acid. This approach is consistent with the discussed post-osimertinib management strategy for multifocal progression in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer.
reference_conclusion_quote: At that point, since we had seven months of treatment on ozymertinib, we decided it was considered short period of response. Foundation one, CDX was done, showing and confirming that we had the EGFR exon 19 deletion. but also we had the appearance of TP53 alteration. [...] So in January 2025, the patient started with the combination of carboplatin pemetrexate with the first dose of amivamptamab, divided the first one in two days and injection of zoledronic acid. [...] The foundation one didn't show new alteration, despite the TP53 that was positive, and the patient started a second line treatment with abivantanab, carboplatin, pemetrexed, and zoledronic acid. [...] When we have the progression and we have multiple lesion progression, the only one approved after ozimertinib, according to the NCCN guidelines, remain the combination of amivantamab plus carboplatin and premetrexate.

[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old man; smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Shortness of breath.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Bone-guided biopsy showed adenocarcinoma. Additional bone biopsy showed poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm with necrosis.

[ imaging findings ]: Staging PET scan showed a left lung mass with surrounding low metabolic activity and consolidation, and multiple metastatic osseous lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing showed EGFR-positive disease with exon 21 L858R mutation. TP53 alteration was reported as positive. PD-L1 expression was 30%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior systemic anticancer treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma involving the left lung and multiple bones; performance status was reported as good.

[ other clinical data ]: Bone metastasis was present at diagnosis.

So basically, just to lay out down the main roles that we have to play down by such cases. In endodrivers mutations, basically we only gave the targetable agent. We refer away from immunotherapy because definitely they do not work, period. And none of the studies basically that had looked at the immunotherapy when the eGFR or ALK or ROS1 even, I would say, they do not exert the same action that they would do in otherwise ribosomal mutation-negative patients. So this carries a higher risk of possible transformation. If even if the RB1 was possible, that it's like positive there, then that's basically a double whammy. So the possibility of small cell lung transformation is quite higher, even in that case. So in this particular situation, I would go with the FLORA2 as a retinib chemotherapy. Keeping in mind, the PD-L1, again, to reiterate, is not the best marker, even as a protection to the response to immunotherapy. So the idea of immunotherapy and driver's mutation patients is non-existent. We should not proceed with that at all, basically, in all lines to me, basically. I'm not convinced with any of the studies. especially with the quadruplet, they looked at patients who had received azimutinib or alektinib or basically crizotinib before, and it was done as a subgroup analysis. Great comment. Thank you, Dr. Ahmed. So, Prof. Umpeke, can you comment on the best approach on this patient?

Yes, I think the best approach, as mentioned by Dr. Ahmad, is the combination of lasertinib, amivantanab, and we have the exploratory analysis of mutational profile after using and the percentage of TP53. So, I think when we have the TP53, this combination will be the best option compared to a single-agent ozimertinib. For sure, the IO, there is no place independent of PD-L1 because when you have the EGFR, EGFR is driving PD-L1, no place for it.

reference_conclusion: For metastatic EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma with L858R and TP53 positivity, first-line targeted therapy with amivantamab plus lazertinib is favored over single-agent osimertinib. If amivantamab and lazertinib are unavailable, osimertinib combined with chemotherapy is the preferred alternative. Immunotherapy is not recommended despite PD-L1 expression, given the presence of an EGFR driver alteration.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old man; retired teacher; married with good family support.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough, exertional dyspnea, anorexia, and weight loss for several months in late 2022 to early 2023; one moderate-to-large episode of hemoptysis in February/March 2023 prompting emergency department presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma of the left lower lobe with malignant pleural effusion; thoracic nodal metastatic disease and later brain metastasis. Initial clinical status included ECOG performance status 2, approaching 3.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the left lower lobe mass showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, TTF-1 positive. Pleural fluid cytology was positive for malignant cells.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT chest demonstrated a large left lower lobe mass with pleural effusion.  
- CT chest dated 10 May 2023 showed an aggressive left lower lobe mass infiltrating to the mediastinum, with pleural effusion and pericardial effusion.  
- CT abdomen/pelvis showed no metastatic disease.  
- PET scan showed thoracic metastatic disease involving supraclavicular, mediastinal, and left hilar regions; no osseous metastases were identified.  
- MRI brain was initially negative for intracranial metastases.  
- Restaging CT dated 10 July 2023, after approximately 3 months of osimertinib, showed partial regression of the left lung mass and no recurrence of pleural effusion.  
- CT in February 2024 showed progressive disease in the left lower lobe.  
- CT brain in February 2024 showed a small left parietal lesion with associated vasogenic edema.  
- Subsequent CT chest remained stable for a period on later-line therapy, with possible minor progression, followed by significant progression with near-complete obliteration of the left lung, marked collapse, significant pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: EGFR pathogenic mutation positive: L858R. PD-L1 negative. Broader NGS had been sent. Repeat biopsy at progression to assess resistance mechanisms was discussed but not performed because the patient declined biopsy.

[ laboratory results ]: Severe acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease occurred during carboplatin/pemetrexed/amivantamab-based treatment, with significant reduction in eGFR, leading to discontinuation of pemetrexed and carboplatin.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line palliative systemic therapy: osimertinib initiated in 2023 for EGFR L858R-positive metastatic disease.  
- Clinical response to osimertinib included marked improvement in cough, exertional dyspnea, appetite, hemoptysis resolution, and improvement in performance status.  
- Radiologic response to osimertinib: partial regression on CT dated 10 July 2023.  
- Disease progression was documented in February 2024, with recurrent symptoms and new left parietal brain lesion.  
- Second-line systemic therapy: carboplatin plus pemetrexed initiated while awaiting amivantamab approval; 3 cycles were given.  
- After amivantamab became available, treatment continued with carboplatin/pemetrexed plus amivantamab for 2 additional cycles.  
- Chemotherapy was then stopped because of severe AKI on CKD with significant eGFR decline; amivantamab was continued.  
- Amivantamab total exposure was 7 cycles; the last cycle was administered on 12 January 2025.  
- Disease remained stable for a period on amivantamab before subsequent significant progression.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic lung adenocarcinoma after osimertinib and subsequent carboplatin/pemetrexed/amivantamab-based therapy, with extensive left thoracic progression causing near-complete left lung obliteration/collapse, significant pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and prior documented left parietal brain metastasis.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and chronic kidney disease. No known drug allergies. Home medications included metformin, an angiotensin receptor blocker, and aspirin. Family history was non-contributory. Smoking history was 50 pack-years. No alcohol use was reported.
