reference_discussion.text: Well, thank you very much, Dr. Humberbet. I really appreciate the kind introduction. I really apologize deeply for being late. I enjoyed the discussion part. That was very informative. So I'd like to extend my thanks and gratitude to Dr. Humberbet and the rest of the team, the organizing committee, for inviting me to give this case presentation. So it's going to be a short presentation, but it's going to be overlapping with the bulk of the discussion that took place with the rest of the colleagues. So the case is basically about this gentleman who is a 67-year-old gentleman who has been complaining of coughing, shortness of breath, and exertion for the past few months. And when I say past few months, I mean that was in the late 2022, early 2023. associated with anorexia and weight loss. He had one episode of hemoptysis that time, that was in February 2023, about that time, or March, that was moderate to large. He went to emergency department. He underwent CT tests, which showed large left lower lobe mass with effusion. Past medical history showed diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease. And there was some element of CKD as well. So background history, he's not allergic to any medications, medications at home, metformin, ARB, and aspirin. The family history is not contributory. Positive smoker, actually had 50 pack years smoking history. Alcohol, he's not alcoholic. Married with good family support. He's a retired teacher. So for the workup, we've done a pathology on the left lower lobe mass, and it was shown to be adenocarcinoma, moderately differentiated, and he had the TTF1 positive. The NGS and the PD-L1 were sent. He had a positive pleural fusion of malignant cells as well. Strikingly, the EGFR came back positive. It was the L858R pathogenic. So despite being a heavy smoker, he had that positive and the PD-L1 was negative for him. So the CT chest was done in May 10th, 2023. As you can see here, it shows the left lobe mass. It was quite aggressive looking, infiltrating all the way to the mid-stinum with pleural fusion and some pericardial fusion as well. There is no mets in the abdomen pelvis. PET scan was consistent with the testic disease as you can see there elsewhere, but mainly the supraclav, midostinum, lefthaler, and elsewhere, the bones were negative and the moral brain was negative. So the case was discussed in the tumor board, and the discussion was to proceed with palliative systemic treatment in the form of azimutinib at that time. We didn't have the data about the imivantumab and lazarotinib. Even if we had that, lazarotinib would not be accessible to us. So definitely we went with azimutinib, looking at the overall situation, the comorbidities, the ECOG of two approaching three for this gentleman, we decided upon azimutinib, as you can imagine. So upon follow-up, he had noticed significant improvement in his initial symptoms of coughing, shortness of breath and exertion, no more hemoptysis, and the appetite has improved quite significantly, and his ECOG as well. So restaging scans, this is the July 10th, 2023, after three months almost of initiating ozomertinib, he had partial regression of the left lung mass, his symptoms had improved quite significantly, no recurrence of pleural effusion as well. So, fast-forwarding until February 2024, reminding you that in November 2023, we witnessed the release of the emyventema studies, the mariposa 1 and 2, and in the interim, we had the flora 2 as well. So, the CT in February of 2024 showed progressive disease, unfortunately, in the left lower lobe. His symptoms recurred and he was feeling really sick. So CT brain as well was done, which showed a left parietal lesion. It was small, but there was some kind of esogenic edema going on at the same time. Minding you that we had frequent scans, and they were quite stable. Since we started, there was a meridian in May. So less than a year, he had recurrence with progressive disease, as you can see there. So the decision was, in light of the release of the mariposa 2 at that time, we decided to proceed with the amiventumab plus chemotherapy. So we applied for the amiventumab and we were waiting for it. So to buy us time, we decided to start him on chemo. Mind you, we had discussed with him the possibility of getting a biopsy done, and he refused that totally. It's just we needed to know if there's any resistant mechanisms that can be targeted. But in the mariposa 2, that was not required. So that gave us a leeway that we can go with amiventumab chemotherapy. So he had received three cycles of the treatment in the form of chemotherapy, carboplatin, pemotrexate, and then amivantamab arrived, and he was starting on chemo and amivantamab for two more cycles. Then we stopped chemotherapy, the maintenance pemotrexate, as well as the carboplatin, mainly because of the severe AKI on CKD with significant reduction in his EGFR. It was quite worrisome for us to continue the pemotrexate. He has already been on amiventumab, so we carried on with amiventumab in between. He had stable disease since he's been on it. He completed seven cycles altogether of amiventumab. Last cycle was given in January 12, 2025, only this month And unfortunately, the CT chest had been stable for the past little while, maybe some element of minor progression, but now we have significant progression of his disease. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to pull up his scan here. It was obliterating the left lung, significant collapse, significant pulmonary effusion, pericardial effusion as well. So we decided to declare him as DNAR and transfer him to palliative care for full supportive measures. So the main takeaway message of this particular case, and it's quite challenging because definitely we're going to run into such cases like that, So the addition of imiventumab to me amongst the artillery for treatment of VGFR-positive metastatic menstrual cell lung cancer, mainly the common mutations along with the exon 20, had improved the responses PFS and OS, especially in the second line setting. Mind you, the first line setting is quite intriguing to start patients with imiventumab and lazarotinib. The use of imiventumab was quite tolerable for my patient. There are absolutely no issues when it comes to premedications. The infusion rate reactions were nonexistent. He received almost eight cycles of imiventumab, as I said. We have to be very vigilant that we need to start these patients on an oxaparin once we commence them on chemotherapy with imiventumab as a prophylactic dose. And we always need to consider the possibility of a biopsy to lay that down as an option for the patient, just to be more informative in our decision-making process. And with that, I conclude my presentation. And thank you very much for your kind attention.

Thank you very much, Dr. Ahmed, for sharing your experience and also sharing your case. So, I think you hit a very important element. I think we all are a little bit vigilant about the infusion reaction and also the manifestations with imiventumab, and it can be one of the barriers, especially most of the patients with lung cancer, they receive as a first line, they may frail, they may not be candid. So in your experience, you give the patient seven cycles of Entamiv, and you also you pointed that with the good medications, pre-medications regarding the infusion, it went very well. So how you did this, perform this, and can you please illustrate more about what you did exactly, and also, your nursing team as well?

Yeah, I remember those days. So basically what we've done, and we didn't have that protocol initiated electronically or automated. So we have to put it down, like we had to write it down like in the old days when we wrote down the chemotherapy. So clearly write in the diphenhydramine, the doses basically to be initiated one to two hours before, the dexamethasone doses to be initiated properly as well. And most importantly is basically to give them that space before we initiate them, Ventimab, and we even had written down the rate of the amiventumab basically at initiating dose and how to reduce it should you face any reaction. Stop everything, give more pre-medications, the dafenhydramine, the dexamethasone, or the hydrocort if you have it available there. Give more fluids and initiate the rate at 50% reduction than the previous one and monitor for an hour. If everything's okay, then re-initiate back to the previous rate. So we definitely had no issues so far. So it is basically one of those things that we have to be very vigilant of the pre-medications and how to initiate them. It's the usual medications that we give, the dexamethasone, the diphenhydramine, and basically upon reaction, give more of those medication, not dose-reduced, but lower down the rate and go from there. No issues so far, alhamdulillah.
How about the skin manifestations? Do you face any?

So far, for my patients, I haven't seen any, to be honest. None of those reactions at all. None of the skin manifestations, none of the infusion reactions. The DBT definitely we had given them, so I haven't noticed that. So we've given them the prophylactic enoxaparin, Um, it was all in all very tolerable. Um, and again, he, he like received almost five cycles, a single agenda event about because of the severe AKI stable disease, good responses, similar to the chrysalis. So there were no issues with him until recently.
There is a question from Dr. Mohamed El-Arabi. He is asking, for the patient with MET amplification, what you will do for them? Also, amiventamib, or you will give a specific medication?

So it's an excellent question. So basically, we all know that imiventumab is the best specific monoclonal antibody that would target both the MIT14 as well as the GFR. I think this is the natural approach of how we go by these patients, basically, just continue with imiventumab because it should tackle it. That being said, we know that there's other studies that looked at the use of Tipartanib, whether it's Imertinib. These studies are Phase II studies, so none of them is a Phase III study like this one. So I would always go by the Phase III studies, so it's more reliable, more applicable in practice. So even if there is a mid-14, we go with emyventum chemotherapy. Mind you, the beauty about the monopositive is that they did not make the biopsy as a mandatory thing. So we always have a leeway to just go by in an automated way, just to go by basically the emyventum chemotherapy.

I think I agree with you totally but I think that possibility of biopsy is important and of course as you mentioned that but still we don't have a clear input like you mentioned that what to do for the patient with a mid-amplification, HER2-positive patient, or even for the small cell. So we may consider that this patient is a group of patients we identified. The patient with non-identifiable may go for the treatment. And if we are unable to go for a biopsy, this means consider the empirical treatment. As you pointed, it was not mandatory.
Yeah, absolutely.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board recommended palliative systemic therapy with osimertinib for EGFR L858R-positive metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, taking into account the overall clinical status, comorbidities, and poor performance status. At subsequent progression, the agreed next step was amivantamab plus chemotherapy; chemotherapy with carboplatin and pemetrexed was initiated while awaiting amivantamab approval, followed by combination treatment. After later marked disease progression with collapse of the left lung and pleural and pericardial effusions, the patient was designated DNAR and transferred to palliative care for full supportive measures.

So we applied for the amiventumab and we were waiting for it. So to buy us time, we decided to start him on chemo. [...] So we decided to declare him as DNAR and transfer him to palliative care for full supportive measures.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 42-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic recurrent follicular thyroid carcinoma with rising thyroglobulin and progressive distant metastatic disease over a prolonged course.

[ diagnosis ]: Follicular thyroid carcinoma, primary tumor 1.5 cm, staged pT1b cM0 at initial diagnosis. Disease later recurred with radioactive iodine-avid pulmonary metastases and subsequently progressed with osseous and hepatic metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial thyroid malignancy was reported as follicular thyroid carcinoma with capsular invasion and vascular invasion. Extent of vascular invasion was not available. Subsequent liver biopsy from metastatic disease confirmed well-differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma, concordant with the original primary lesion.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial post-treatment course achieved complete structural response after early radioactive iodine therapy.  
- At approximately 10 years from diagnosis, whole-body radioactive iodine imaging demonstrated an avid pulmonary lesion.  
- After radioactive iodine treatment at that time, follow-up imaging at approximately 3 months showed that the pulmonary lesion had apparently disappeared.  
- Between years 12 and 15 from diagnosis, imaging demonstrated recurrent pulmonary lesion(s); within approximately 3 months, the lesion doubled in size.  
- After additional radioactive iodine-based treatment during that interval, 3-month follow-up imaging showed significant structural reduction in the pulmonary lesion.  
- By year 17, imaging showed increased size of non-pulmonary metastatic disease involving right iliac bone, spine/L5, multiple hepatic lesions, and other osseous metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Metastatic tissue genomic testing identified NRAS mutation, PIK3CA mutation, and an activating TSH receptor mutation.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Initial incomplete biochemical response after surgery led to early radioactive iodine treatment.  
- Complete biochemical response was achieved after the first two radioactive iodine treatments.  
- At approximately 10 years from diagnosis, suppressed thyroglobulin rose to 43.7.  
- After radioactive iodine at that time, suppressed thyroglobulin decreased to 1.5.  
- Between years 12 and 15, thyroglobulin rose from 7.4 to 148.  
- After subsequent trial-associated treatment plus radioactive iodine, thyroglobulin decreased to 39, reported as an approximately 80% reduction.  
- By year 17, thyroglobulin rose to 8,000.  
- After lenvatinib, thyroglobulin decreased from 8,000 to 1,000.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surgical treatment consisted of hemithyroidectomy followed by completion thyroidectomy.  
- Within the first 2 years after diagnosis, the patient received two radioactive iodine treatments: 158 mCi and 182 mCi, for incomplete biochemical response. These resulted in complete structural and biochemical response.  
- At approximately 10 years from diagnosis, recurrent radioactive iodine-avid pulmonary metastatic disease was treated with 202 mCi radioactive iodine, bringing the cumulative dose to 542 mCi. This was associated with marked biochemical response and apparent radiographic resolution of the pulmonary lesion.  
- Between years 12 and 15, recurrent enlarging pulmonary metastatic disease was treated in the setting of enrollment on a selumetinib/placebo clinical trial, together with 148 mCi radioactive iodine, bringing the cumulative dose to 690 mCi. Follow-up showed biochemical improvement and significant structural reduction in the lung lesion.  
- At year 17, progressive metastatic disease involving bone and liver was treated with stereotactic radiotherapy to the right ilium and L5, and systemic lenvatinib was started. Lenvatinib reduced thyroglobulin but caused severe toxicity including hypertension, stomatitis, diarrhea, weight loss, myalgias, and fatigue; dose reduction was attempted, then treatment was discontinued because of grade 3-4 toxicities.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Concern for marrow toxicity arose after cumulative radioactive iodine exposure exceeded 600 mCi.

reference_conclusion: At progression with osseous and hepatic metastatic disease, stereotactic radiotherapy was delivered to the right ilium and L5, and systemic therapy with lenvatinib was initiated. After lenvatinib was discontinued because of grade 3–4 toxicities, repeat liver biopsy confirmed well-differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma and identified NRAS, PIK3CA, and activating TSH receptor mutations. Given prior radioiodine responsiveness, autologous stem cell cryopreservation was performed to permit additional high-dose radioactive iodine therapy despite cumulative marrow toxicity concerns; subsequent treatments produced mixed responses, with some lesions improving and others progressing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic pancreatic malignancy diagnosed in April 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Pancreatic lesion biopsy showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified clinically significant DNA alterations in KRAS, GNAS, and CDKN2A. KRAS alteration was reported as G12A. RNA fusion analysis showed no clinically significant gene fusions. Tumor mutational burden was very low. Microsatellite status was stable. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic alteration explaining the reported phenotype was detected on the germline/DNA test report.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line palliative chemotherapy: gemcitabine plus paclitaxel/nab-paclitaxel, 6 cycles completed.  
- Post-treatment follow-up CT showed progressive disease.  
- Second-line chemotherapy: weekly IFL initiated after progression on gemcitabine-based therapy.  
- No prior platinum exposure.  
- No prior nanoliposomal irinotecan exposure.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease after 6 cycles of first-line gemcitabine-based chemotherapy; subsequently receiving weekly IFL.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history was reported.

[ other clinical data ]: Clinical trial options referenced for relapse settings included fulvestrant with or without venetoclax; fulvestrant combined with immunotherapy with or without a CDK4/6 inhibitor; and fulvestrant combined with agents targeting the PI3 kinase and mTOR pathways.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy, with rising PSA.

[ diagnosis ]: High-risk prostate adenocarcinoma status post radical prostatectomy in 2012, followed by nodal metastatic recurrence involving pelvic and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, consistent with nodal metastatic disease (N1 and M1a).

[ histopathology results ]: Prostate cancer with Gleason score 9, ISUP grade group 5.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PSMA PET in March 2015 demonstrated moderately to highly PSMA-avid left pelvic nodal disease involving internal iliac, external iliac, and common iliac chains, with extension into the retroperitoneum including interaortocaval/periaortic nodal stations.  
- Disease extended to approximately the level of L3.  
- No bone metastases or visceral metastases were identified on that scan.  
- Largest involved node was subcentimeter, approximately 8 mm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA was undetectable for 3 years after radical prostatectomy.  
- PSA subsequently rose to 3.5.  
- PSA doubling time was 2 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Radical prostatectomy was performed in 2012.

[ current disease status ]: Nodal metastatic prostate cancer involving pelvic and retroperitoneal chains without bone or visceral metastases, with rapid PSA doubling time of 2 months.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

reference_discussion.text: This is a 64-year-old man who's had a radical prostatectomy in 2012.

For those who aren't familiar with PSA doubling times, we kind of divide that into less than 10 months, which is rapid, or greater than 10 months, which is slow. So two months suggests this is definitely disease, and that it's probably fairly aggressive disease. Now, I guess the PSMA PETs requested to localize where this recurrence is, which is an entirely appropriate indication, and James will show us the scan results.

So this was a very early use of PSMA PET. And when we saw these in our MDT seven, eight years ago, it created a lot of confusion because what do you do with this patient? Is it even real? Yeah, this is, you know, this is the classic Pokemon phenomenon that you're kind of alluding to here. And Declan wrote the paper on this in, was it 2017, Declan? In European Neurology. And then you're running a conference, and the theme is see it, treat it.
You're confusing me. You can treat it, you just shouldn't.
And look where we've come seven years on.
Maybe we can go back to the slides.
Slides, please.

I think we do have follow-up on this patient. I can tell you, for whatever reason, this patient was subjected to an extended retroperitoneal nodal dissection. That was deemed the appropriate treatment at the time. And four months later, you can see the result of that. Do you want to take us through the results, James?

Yes, you can see, we can flip back if you want back to the MIMS screen actually, but you do see there were, there was an extensive retroperitoneal and pelvic nodal dissection. And unfortunately you do see it was quite rapidly progressive disease. So you do see nodes. There was one node that was still in the pelvis, but you also see some coming up in the retrocrural Sorry, I'll just back this up. So there is one also, a retrocrural. It did creep all the way up into the mediastinum. There are two bone metastases as well. So it did spread quite quickly and it went all the way up into the left cervical chains. So just a few months later, it did spread quite quickly.
Back to the slides.

Back to the slides. Yes, so Declan wrote an editorial in European Urology titled, Pokermats, got to catch them all. And the message here was that salvage lymph node dissection or stereotactic radiotherapy, you may be feasible for that, but is it worthwhile? And you do need to select patients carefully. Do we really need to ablate all these lesions? And the long-term outcomes may not be any different. And in that short time frame, systemic therapies has evolved. Yeah, I think in a patient with a short doubling time and relatively high volume nodal disease, systemic therapy is definitely warranted and we can no longer say androgen deprivation therapy is enough. We do have to have a discussion about chemotherapy with docetaxel or one of the novel anti-androgens. There's now even an argument for triplet therapy in some patients. We are limited in Australia, though, as the antiandrogens, so enzalutamide and abiraterone, are not subsidised on the PBS yet, so it is a bit of a nuanced discussion with the patient, but it would definitely be ADT plus one of those agents. And I think I agree with Renu and Genevieve in that with the doubling time that quickly, local regional treatment I think would be inappropriate because the concern is micrometastatic disease that's being missed on the PET scan, which is clearly what happened and recurred.

[ chief complaint ]: Stage IV non-small cell lung cancer with persistent demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy/neuropathy following lorlatinib exposure.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV non-small cell lung cancer with ALK-EML fusion and TP53 co-mutation. Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy/Guillain-Barré syndrome-like neuropathy developed during treatment with lorlatinib.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified ALK and EML fusion and TP53 co-mutation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Thoracic radiation had been administered. Intravenous immunoglobulin was administered for the neuropathy. Neurological recovery occurred after treatment and lorlatinib cessation: facial weakness recovered completely, and ambulatory status improved from inability to walk to walking with support. Persistent proximal L4/L5-level neuropathy remained.

[ current disease status ]: As of February 2026, systemic disease was radiologically stable on PET-CT. Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy persisted, with residual proximal L4/L5 neuropathy and partial neurological recovery.

[ other clinical data ]: The neuropathy had been graded as severe, described in the record as grade 3-4 and specifically queried as grade 4 adverse event. CNS disease status was not otherwise documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70–71-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic left lower lobe lung malignancy with radiologic progression after systemic therapy; referred for second opinion.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV squamous cell carcinoma of the left lower lobe of the lung at initial diagnosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Lung biopsy dated 30 September 2024 showed squamous cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated p40 positivity and TTF-1 negativity.

[ imaging findings ]: CT imaging showed definite disease progression. No further imaging details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing performed on the original diagnostic biopsy specimen identified tier 2 pathogenic/likely pathogenic alterations in ALK, TP53, and HER2. TP53 had the highest variant allele frequency/weighting among the reported alterations. RNA sequencing did not identify an ALK fusion.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 6 cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin from approximately September/October 2024 until April 2025. This was followed by 14 doses of pembrolizumab. Disease progression was documented on CT imaging after pembrolizumab.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease on imaging after prior chemotherapy and subsequent pembrolizumab. Initial performance status was 2. At the time of current review, the patient was described as clinically doing well; current performance status was estimated to be approximately 1.

[ other clinical data ]: No repeat biopsy had been performed; molecular testing was conducted on the same biopsy specimen obtained at diagnosis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 17-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent, progressively enlarging bilateral cervical nodules/neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) involving both thyroid lobes, with biopsy-proven bilateral cervical nodal metastases; metastatic pulmonary disease with diffuse bilateral miliary-pattern lung nodules/micronodules. Focal leptomeningeal enhancement on brain MRI was identified without cytologic confirmation on subsequent lumbar punctures.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion was consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. Fine-needle aspiration of bilateral level III cervical lymph nodes showed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. Subsequent lymph node biopsy for molecular testing was performed.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound: Large right thyroid lobe hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications; left thyroid lobe mass with similar sonographic characteristics. Bilateral central compartment lymph nodes demonstrated microcalcifications, hypoechogenicity, and irregular margins. Bulky right and left lateral cervical lymphadenopathy and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy were present.  
- CT neck/chest: Right thyroid mass was closely related to the trachea with tracheal narrowing. Bulky lateral compartment lymphadenopathy was present; lateral compartment lymph nodes circumferentially involved the common carotid. An enlarged avidly enhancing level II lymph node was described. Diffuse bilateral pulmonary punctate miliary-pattern lesions/nodules were present, with lower-lobe predominance.  
- Brain MRI: Focal leptomeningeal enhancement over the left precentral sulcus.  
- PET-CT: Mild FDG uptake in the primary thyroid tumor and multiple cervical/supraclavicular lymph nodes; lesions were not markedly FDG-avid.  
- Interval imaging during lenvatinib: Neck tumor and adenopathy became smaller, with necrosis observed in the neck tumor; pulmonary nodules were largely stable.  
- CT after 6 weeks of selpercatinib: Further reduction in size of the right thyroid tumor and cervical adenopathy, including upper right level III nodal disease; some pulmonary nodules had resolved and overall lung disease had improved.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: RET fusion identified on lymph node biopsy molecular testing.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Thyroglobulin was >2,200 at initial evaluation.  
- After treatment, thyroglobulin decreased to 78.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial outside evaluation of palpable neck mass approximately 1 year earlier reportedly considered inflammatory lymphadenopathy.  
- Lenvatinib was started while access to selpercatinib was being arranged. After 1 month, there was clinical reduction in lymphadenopathy and right thyroid lobe mass size. During lenvatinib therapy, the patient developed right vocal cord palsy with dysphonia and dysphagia to solids, and underwent rehabilitation. Additional toxicities included diarrhea, weight loss, marked fatigue, prolonged bed rest, and inability to attend school. Despite toxicity, imaging showed tumor shrinkage/necrosis in the neck and stable pulmonary nodules. Lenvatinib was continued for 5 months.  
- Selpercatinib was subsequently started in early October. After 6 weeks, imaging showed marked reduction in the primary thyroid lesion and cervical nodal disease, with improvement in pulmonary metastases including resolution of some nodules. Treatment was well tolerated.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic RET fusion-positive papillary thyroid carcinoma remained present in the thyroid, cervical/supraclavicular lymph nodes, and lungs, with substantial radiographic and biochemical response on selpercatinib. Visible and palpable neck disease had markedly improved. Lung function assessment had been normal prior to systemic therapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Physical examination at presentation showed a firm palpable right lateral cervical mass adherent to deep planes, with bilateral cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.  
- Initial laryngeal examination showed normal vocal cord movement.  
- Subsequent flexible laryngoscopy during lenvatinib therapy demonstrated right vocal cord palsy with preserved glottic closure.  
- Subsequent lumbar punctures did not provide cytologic confirmation of leptomeningeal disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Postoperative metastatic progression of periampullary carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Periampullary carcinoma, pancreatic subtype. Postoperative stage IV disease with liver metastases and multiple abdominal nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Periampullary carcinoma, pancreatic subtype. Surgical tissue from the primary surgery was used for molecular testing.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- No imaging had been performed immediately before surgery.  
- Postoperative re-imaging demonstrated stage IV disease with liver metastases and newly appeared multiple abdominal lymph nodes.  
- After six cycles of chemotherapy, reassessment showed good response in abdominal nodes, with newly appeared liver metastases.  
- Recent PET-CT showed response in abdominal nodes and liver lesions, with a few newly appeared liver lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing performed on surgical tissue demonstrated KRAS G12A mutation.  
- Testing was performed on an Oncomine hotspot panel with hotspot SNVs and short indels; this was a targeted panel and did not cover BRCA.  
- Re-biopsy had not been performed.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent ERCP with biliary stenting.  
- Underwent surgery approximately four months later; procedure documented as Whipple surgery.  
- Following postoperative identification of metastatic disease, palliative chemotherapy was started.  
- At initiation of systemic therapy, general condition was poor with ECOG performance status 2; the patient was described as more wheelchair-bound.  
- Started on single-agent capecitabine, later escalated to CAPOX after improvement in performance status.  
- After six cycles of chemotherapy, abdominal nodal disease showed good response, but new liver metastases appeared.  
- Clinical performance status improved during treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic periampullary carcinoma with persistent liver metastatic disease and abdominal nodal disease after prior palliative chemotherapy, with mixed radiologic response and interval appearance of new liver lesions.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- ECOG performance status was 2 at the start of palliative chemotherapy.  
- Performance status improved during treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Unintentional weight loss of unquantified amount over approximately 2 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Hyperthyroidism associated with a right thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration was diagnostic of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Thyroid fine-needle aspiration cytology: findings consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma, with monotonous cell population forming pseudopapillae and nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Cytology also showed increased oncocytic/eosinophilic cytoplasm, raising concern for tall-cell component.  
- No documented lymph node metastases were identified in the material described.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Outside thyroid ultrasound: reported a 14 mm right thyroid lobe nodule; images were unavailable.  
- Repeat thyroid ultrasound at referral center: right thyroid nodule measured 0.8 cm in greatest dimension; taller-than-wide; well-defined/smooth borders on available image; lesion described as isoechoic to mildly hyperechoic relative to the remainder of the thyroid, with a hypoechoic outer border and echogenic foci. Classified as TI-RADS 5.  
- Doppler interrogation of the nodule was performed.  
- Radioiodine/iodine thyroid scan: relatively increased uptake in the right thyroid lobe compared with the left, consistent with a hyperfunctioning right-sided nodule.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT neck: right thyroid lesion appeared subcapsular/peripheral, measuring approximately 14 mm on the displayed images. Lateral border was described as irregular and concerning for possible extrathyroidal extension. No lateral or central compartment lymphadenopathy was identified on the images reviewed. CT also showed medialization of a vocal cord with enlargement of the ipsilateral piriform sinus on a single image, raising concern for possible vocal cord paralysis; laryngoscopy was not performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- TSH: suppressed.  
- T4: approximately 3- to 4-fold above the upper limit of normal.  
- Thyroid antibodies: not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Diagnostic workup included thyroid ultrasound, contrast-enhanced CT, and radioiodine thyroid scan.

[ current disease status ]: No documented nodal disease was identified on the imaging reviewed. No post-treatment disease assessment was available.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: prediabetes, hypertension.  
- At presentation to the referral center, hypertension and tachycardia were present.  
- No family history of thyroid cancer or benign thyroid disease.  
- No history of radiation exposure.  
- No reported hoarseness or dyspnea at clinical evaluation.  
- Interval between iodinated contrast CT and radioiodine uptake scan was 4 weeks.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old woman; Army veteran.

[ chief complaint ]: Second-opinion evaluation regarding management of a newly diagnosed right thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma involving a right thyroid nodule measuring 1.3 cm on biopsy/imaging. Incidentally identified bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules were also present.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right thyroid nodule was positive for malignancy, consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. Pathology review at Mayo Clinic concurred with the diagnosis.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- November 2020 CT imaging of the neck, obtained during evaluation of headaches, incidentally identified a right thyroid nodule and several bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules.  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a solitary right-sided hypoechoic nodule measuring 1.0 x 0.8 x 1.3 cm with posterior macrocalcification and associated posterior acoustic shadowing.  
- No cervical lymphadenopathy was identified on ultrasound.  
- Chest imaging demonstrated multiple scattered bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules; the largest remained subcentimeter.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH 3.2; patient was euthyroid at the time of evaluation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- No prior thyroid-directed treatment was reported.  
- Pulmonary evaluation of the lung nodules considered them most likely benign, although a neoplastic process was not excluded; surveillance imaging in 6 months was advised.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed right papillary thyroid carcinoma, solitary intrathyroidal-appearing lesion measuring 1.3 cm, without sonographic cervical lymphadenopathy. Multiple bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules remained under surveillance.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No prior history of thyroid disease.  
- No known family history of thyroid malignancy; family history was limited because the patient was adopted.  
- Possible prior radiation exposure was uncertain.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Follow-up for ALK-positive lung cancer; prior hemoptysis with two episodes.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-small cell lung cancer of the lung, diagnosed in July 2025. Disease was described as stage III at initial diagnosis; subsequent clinical characterization included unresectable stage III versus stage IV disease, with multiple lung nodules and oligometastatic/stage IV disease considered in the record. ALK-positive disease with EML4-ALK fusion.

[ histopathology results ]: Non-small cell lung cancer.

[ imaging findings ]: Multiple lung nodules were present. Post-radiation imaging showed partial response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified EML4-ALK fusion, transcript variant V1. TP53 co-mutation was present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Hemostatic arterial intervention was performed in the setting of hemoptysis. One cycle of chemotherapy with pemetrexed and carboplatin was administered, then discontinued. Definitive radiation therapy was delivered to the primary lung tumor to a total dose of 54 Gy. Partial response was achieved with radiation therapy. Lorlatinib procurement was delayed and treatment had not yet been initiated at the time documented.

[ current disease status ]: Post-radiation partial response. Lorlatinib had become available but had not yet started. Interval since completion of radiation therapy was 10 days at the time documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Radiation treatment had been continued because of delay in obtaining lorlatinib. V20 was documented as less than 35%.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough for 2 months, associated with occasional shortness of breath. Subsequently developed 2 episodes of hemoptysis after initiation of chemotherapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-small cell lung carcinoma, consistent with adenocarcinoma of the right lower lobe, grade 2; clinical stage cT3N3M1 (stage IV) ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy of the right lung lesion was suggestive of non-small cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse TTF-1 positivity and occasional tumor cell positivity for p40. Pathology interpretation was adenocarcinoma of lung, grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]: CT chest demonstrated a 4 × 4 cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the superior and anterior basal segments of the right lower lobe, with right hilar, lower paratracheal, and subcarinal lymphadenopathy, and moderate pleural effusion. MRI brain was normal. PET-CT showed an irregular lobulated metabolically active soft tissue mass in the lower lobe of the right lung abutting the pleura, measuring approximately 47 × 56 × 56 mm. PET-CT also demonstrated bilateral superior mediastinal, prevascular, pretracheal, right paratracheal, right hilar, and left supraclavicular nodal involvement. Multiple cervical lymph nodes were described as reactive. No other metastatic sites were identified on PET-CT.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NGS 12-gene panel detected ALK alteration and TP53 mutation. ALK fusion was described as EML4-ALK, exon 13 to exon 20 fusion, consistent with variant 1.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: One cycle of systemic chemotherapy with pemetrexed plus carboplatin was administered. After the first cycle, the patient developed hemoptysis. Hemostatic radiotherapy was delivered to the lung lesion at 3 Gy per fraction for 3 fractions (total 9 Gy), with resolution of hemoptysis. Radiotherapy was being continued; by day 12, a total dose of 50 Gy had been planned. Radiation field was limited to the lung lesion; mediastinal and supraclavicular nodes were not included.

[ current disease status ]: Patient was clinically stable. ECOG performance status was 1. Hemoptysis had resolved at the time of latest status assessment. No brain metastases were identified. No metastatic disease outside thoracic/supraclavicular nodal sites had been demonstrated on available imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Pleural effusion was moderate on initial CT chest. Total reported hemoptysis episodes: 2.

- The EGFR kinase domain duplication was described as a duplication involving exons 18 to 25.  
- No gene fusions were detected on the earlier panel.

- The EGFR kinase domain duplication was described as a rare alteration in lung cancer, with frequency reported as less than 1%.  
- Tissue adequacy and assay design were discussed as relevant to detection of structural variants such as kinase domain duplication.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient; older adult. Smoking history was present. Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable.

[ chief complaint ]: One month of nasal pain and nasal congestion, with tenderness and fullness at the base of the nose.

[ diagnosis ]: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma involving the caudal septum/collumellar region with extension onto the nasal floor bilaterally.

[ histopathology results ]: Preoperative biopsy was consistent with invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: CT sinus with contrast demonstrated an anterior nasal mass measuring approximately 2.0 x 1.0 cm. No bony erosion of the maxilla was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent radical resection of the nasal columella skin, a substantial portion of the septum, and the bilateral nasal floor. Reconstruction was performed with a small radial forearm free flap for three-layer reconstruction of nasal lining, septum, and skin. A small osteocutaneous component was harvested initially but was not used. The pedicle was tunneled through the face. Two nasal trumpets, cut in half, were placed postoperatively. Postoperative course was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged home shortly after surgery. Nasal trumpets were removed at the first postoperative visit.

[ current disease status ]: Status post surgical resection and reconstruction. No indication for adjuvant therapy had been identified. Follow-up at 3 months after surgery was planned to assess healing and discuss possible secondary reconstruction for maintenance of nasal projection.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial examination demonstrated fullness of the medial crura bilaterally and an approximately 1.5 cm mass at the base of the caudal septum extending onto the nasal floor bilaterally. There was no communication with the oral cavity; involvement was limited to the nasal floor without extension through the premaxilla.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 85-year-old woman. Past medical history included early-stage breast cancer diagnosed in 2016.

[ chief complaint ]: Recently diagnosed metastatic high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma initially attributed to pancreatic origin after discovery of pancreatic mass, large liver mass, and metastatic lymphadenopathy on imaging in December 2022.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma with neuroendocrine transformation. Disease manifestations included liver metastasis with poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma morphology and a separate right axillary metastasis consistent with invasive ductal carcinoma. Original breast primary was ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2016 right breast primary: low-grade invasive ductal carcinoma; ER 90%, PR 60%, HER2-negative. Sentinel lymph node biopsy had been performed.  
- Liver biopsy (metastatic lesion): metastatic poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma, non-small cell type, initially favored pancreatic origin; synaptophysin strongly positive, CD56 strongly positive; Ki-67 greater than 90%.  
- Right axillary biopsy: invasive ductal carcinoma; GATA3 strongly positive; ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative.  
- Comparative molecular/pathologic assessment of the 2016 primary tumor and liver metastasis showed shared alterations, supporting clonal relatedness and neuroendocrine transformation.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- December 2022 chest CT: large liver mass, pancreatic mass, multiple peripancreatic masses, and lymphadenopathy suspicious for metastatic disease.  
- Abdominal MRI in December 2022: pancreatic body mass approximately 4 cm; multiple peripancreatic, portocaval, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes; liver mass measuring approximately 10 cm.  
- CT imaging after initiation of systemic therapy demonstrated: large right axillary mass extending to the skin surface with deep extension involving a rib; pulmonary nodule along the left minor fissure; thoracic adenopathy including right perihilar and subcarinal nodes; periportal lymphadenopathy; liver mass; osseous metastases involving the sternum and anterior ribs.  
- May 2023 scan after carboplatin/etoposide: mixed response, with response in liver, pancreas, and abdomen but increased axillary adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Sequencing of the liver metastasis identified multiple alterations including PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss-of-function alteration, TP53 loss-of-function alteration, RB1 deep deletion, and ESR1 D538G mutation.  
- Tumor mutational burden was 21.4 mutations/Mb.  
- Microsatellite instability testing was not MSI-high.  
- Additional analysis demonstrated loss of heterozygosity involving TP53 and PTEN, consistent with biallelic loss; complete RB1 loss was also identified.  
- Mutational signature analysis showed a clear APOBEC signature.  
- Tumor type prediction algorithm based on genomic features favored breast cancer (77% likelihood).  
- Comparative analysis of the 2016 breast primary and liver metastasis showed shared rare alterations including PIK3CA mutation, ESR1 mutation, and PTEN loss; RB1 loss and TP53 alteration were newly present in the neuroendocrine-transformed tumor.  
- Likelihood of relatedness between the primary breast tumor and liver metastasis was reported as greater than 99.99%.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hyponatremia was present at initial GI oncology evaluation, with sodium 114 mmol/L, considered consistent with SIADH in the setting of neuroendocrine disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2016 early-stage breast cancer: treated with radiation therapy followed by anastrozole for 5 years.  
- First-line treatment for metastatic disease: carboplatin plus etoposide. This was associated with resolution of SIADH/hyponatremia. Imaging in May 2023 showed mixed response, with improvement in liver, pancreas, and abdominal disease but progression in axillary adenopathy.  
- Subsequent treatment: paclitaxel plus pembrolizumab.

[ current disease status ]:  
Metastatic breast carcinoma with neuroendocrine transformation remained present, involving liver, right axilla, thoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, lung, and bone.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient was described as otherwise healthy.  
- Initial presentation had suggested pancreatic-origin metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma, but subsequent pathology and genomic correlation supported metastatic breast carcinoma with neuroendocrine transformation.

reference_conclusion: Molecular and pathologic review supported that the liver lesion represented neuroendocrine transformation of metastatic ER-positive, HER2-negative breast carcinoma rather than a primary pancreatic neuroendocrine malignancy, broadening breast cancer-directed treatment options. Given the aggressive disease course and RB1 loss-associated concern for lack of benefit from CDK4/6 inhibition, endocrine therapy with CDK4/6 inhibitor was not favored. The patient was treated with paclitaxel plus pembrolizumab, with interval radiographic response; antibody-drug conjugate therapy remained a consideration if HER2-low expression were identified, and fulvestrant plus capivasertib was discussed as a potential future option in the setting of PTEN loss and ESR1 mutation.
reference_conclusion_quote: I would agree that I would, honestly, I would stay away from endocrine therapy. CDK4-6 is the next line of therapy. [...] Yeah, that's definitely an option for, because we know that capivacertib is active in cancers that have lost P10. And also, fulvestrin can have some activity against ESL1 mutations. So I think there's a lot of reasons to want to consider using fulvestrin and capivacertib recently approved by the FDA in her case. [...] So, actually this patient received paclitaxel plus pembrolizumab, and the reason was that they were not able to get the liver for, to perform ER, PR, and they were concerned that there might be ER negative. So, we started the patient with paclitaxel pembrolizumab [...] I think an antibody drug conjugate would be great for her. And I think the idea of using pembrolizumab would be great. I would be inclined to give her chemotherapy and would choose one of the regimens. She's just recently had platinum, so we would go with a taxane and pembrolizumab for her, but I would be intrigued by the antibody-derived conjugate if she's hurt too low.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 29-year-old woman. Occupation: attorney. No significant past medical history. No family history of thyroid disease or malignancy was reported. No history of radiation exposure. She lived with her husband and 7-month-old child.

[ chief complaint ]: Asymptomatic neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral thyroid involvement and bilateral cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Cytology was consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma, with bilateral proven metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a heavily calcified lesion in the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe, echogenic with marked posterior shadowing. In the right thyroid lobe mid-pole, there was an 8 x 8 mm mixed-echogenicity lesion with an anterior hypoechoic component, posterior echogenic component, and punctate echogenic foci. Ultrasound assessment assigned TI-RADS 4 to the left lobe lesion and TI-RADS 5 to the right lobe lesion. Cystic and septated lymph nodes were present in the central compartment and level IV neck.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a heavily calcified left thyroid lobe nodule and an 8 mm hypodense right thyroid lobe lesion. No vocal cord paralysis was present on imaging, and no definite extrathyroidal extension was initially identified radiographically. Metastatic cervical adenopathy was present in the left central compartment and left lateral neck, including levels II, III, and IV. A central compartment nodal mass extended inferiorly into the superior mediastinum to the level of the aortic arch. On the right, there was a calcified and cystic metastatic right level IV lymph node. Retrospective review described an irregular medial border of the left thyroid lesion, raising concern for extrathyroidal extension.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Fiberoptic laryngoscopic examination before surgery showed normal vocal cord mobility.

[ current disease status ]: Bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical nodal metastases and central compartment nodal extension into the superior mediastinum, with radiographic concern for extrathyroidal extension at the left medial border.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination showed diffuse thyroid enlargement, greater on the left than the right, with palpable cervical disease bilaterally. She denied voice change and dysphagia. Preoperative fiberoptic examination confirmed normal vocal cord mobility.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary panel supported definitive surgical management with total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, and bilateral lateral neck dissections performed in a single operation, with intraoperative neuromonitoring. For the mediastinal extension, resection through a cervical approach was favored, with possible manubrial swing if additional exposure were required; thoracic surgery involvement was not considered necessary. [ patient demographics ]: Sex was female. Exact age was not available.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic breast cancer with central nervous system involvement, including brain-related neurologic symptoms and spinal disease. Difficulty walking was described in association with spinal involvement.

[ diagnosis ]: HER2-positive breast carcinoma with metastatic disease. Metastatic sites/documented disease involvement included skull metastases, spinal metastases with L3 compression fracture, possible/concern for cauda equina syndrome, and leptomeningeal disease. CNS crisis/brain involvement was described. Triple-positive disease was referenced.

[ histopathology results ]: Breast primary histology details were not available. Re-biopsy had been discussed/performed in the context of progressive metastatic breast cancer, but no formal pathology report details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging had shown an L3 compression lesion/fracture. Skull metastases were present. Membrane/meningeal involvement was described, including leptomeningeal disease. Brain imaging abnormality adherent to the meningeal surface was described. Spinal imaging was being obtained/performed in view of symptoms and metastatic involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HER2-positive disease was documented. HER2 2+ status was also referenced in relation to available HER2 data. Hormone receptor-positive disease was implied by use of endocrine therapy and by reference to triple-positive disease. No additional genomic findings were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Platelet count was referenced in the context of considering procedures/radiation tolerance, but no numeric laboratory values were available. Bone marrow suppression risk was referenced. No other laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior systemic therapy included trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and leuprolide. CLEOPATRA-type treatment was referenced; paclitaxel had been used instead of docetaxel. Ongoing/previous HER2-directed therapy with trastuzumab and pertuzumab had been given. Hormonal therapy had been given. Steroids were being administered, with clinical improvement described. Overall well-being had improved, and symptoms were reported as absent at one point during follow-up. Disease progression had nevertheless occurred, including CNS/leptomeningeal progression.

[ current disease status ]: Active metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer with progression involving the CNS/leptomeninges and spine. Leptomeningeal disease was present. Spinal metastatic disease remained clinically significant, with L3 compression and impaired ambulation. Improvement on steroids was described, but metastatic disease remained active. CNS involvement had already occurred.

[ other clinical data ]: Intercurrent infections/medical complications referenced included UTI, typhoid, and anemia. Broca’s aphasia was mentioned. Neurosurgical procedure was referenced in discussion of management context, but no completed operative details were available. Craniospinal radiation was referenced, with concern regarding bone marrow effects.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Elderly female; housewife; mother of six children.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast cancer with persistent local disease despite multiple prior systemic therapies and palliative radiotherapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive ductal carcinoma, diagnosed in March 2017; grade II; ER-negative; PR-negative; HER2-positive by FISH. Chronic renal disease with compromised renal function was also documented.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, grade II. Estrogen receptor negative. Progesterone receptor negative. HER2/neu positive by FISH.

[ imaging findings ]: CT scan dated 8 March 2017 demonstrated a left breast mass with associated breast wall thickening and left axillary lymphadenopathy, consistent with locally advanced left breast tumor with left axillary nodal involvement. There was no CT evidence of metastases in the lungs, abdomen, or pelvis. An incidental 5 mm non-obstructive left lower pole calyceal calculus was reported.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HER2-positive by FISH.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Six cycles of paclitaxel plus trastuzumab were administered with minimal response. This was followed by three cycles of epirubicin and cyclophosphamide with minimal response of local disease. Two cycles of oral capecitabine were given from December 2017 without response. Palliative radiotherapy for local disease control was given from February 2018 and was completed on 4 February 2018, without response. Lapatinib was being taken subsequently; the most recent course had been completed in the week prior to assessment.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent local breast disease after multiple lines of therapy. On examination, performance status was ECOG 2. The patient appeared weak and sick-looking. She was not pale, not jaundiced, not dehydrated, had no edema, and was afebrile. Breast examination documented a right breast mass in the upper outer quadrant. The left breast was shrunken with skin changes described as a burnt area attributed to radiotherapy. No breast surgery had been performed.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history of cancer was reported. The patient had never smoked and did not drink alcohol. No known drug allergies were reported. Other systemic examination findings were otherwise unremarkable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, amenorrhea, and progressive increase in size of hands and feet for 4 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent functioning pituitary macroadenoma associated with acromegalic features and elevated IGF-1.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior biopsy demonstrated pituitary adenoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT axial imaging showed soft tissue in the prepontine cistern, left of midline, consistent with a pituitary-region lesion.  
- MRI demonstrated a sellar/suprasellar mass with no normal pituitary gland separately appreciable.  
- The lesion extended into the left cavernous sinus and had predominant left-sided extension.  
- The left internal carotid artery was completely encased; the right cavernous sinus was also involved with partial encasement of the right internal carotid artery.  
- The mass reached and pushed the optic chiasm; the left half of the optic chiasm was not separately visible on coronal imaging.  
- The lesion displaced the left medial temporal lobe.  
- The mass was described as iso-intense on T2-weighted imaging with modest post-contrast enhancement.  
- No necrosis was identified within the lesion.  
- No hydrocephalus or ventricular compression was present.  
- The lesion was described radiologically as a large pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Initial IGF-1 was approximately 1300.  
- Current IGF-1 was 1168.  
- Remaining hormonal profile was reported as normal, including early morning cortisol.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surgery was performed in Karachi prior to April 2022.  
- Repeat endoscopic transsphenoidal redo surgery was subsequently performed after recurrence.  
- Postoperative imaging after the redo surgery reportedly showed residual tumor with improvement compared with preoperative status; complete tumor removal was not achieved.  
- The patient later re-presented with recurrent/progressive tumor.

[ current disease status ]:  
- The patient was currently admitted with recurrent large residual/recurrent pituitary macroadenoma.  
- Clinical examination showed Glasgow Coma Scale 15/15.  
- Acromegalic features were present, including frontal bossing, macroglossia, prognathism, and gross enlargement of hands and feet.  
- Visual acuity was normal.  
- Fundoscopy was unremarkable.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Previous imaging from the earlier presentation was not available.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus favored surgical debulking as the initial management for this recurrent functional pituitary macroadenoma, given the large tumor burden, cavernous sinus involvement, and proximity to the optic apparatus. A transcranial approach was considered more suitable if feasible to achieve meaningful reduction of tumor within the cavernous sinus. Following adequate cytoreduction, radiotherapy was recommended, with conformal external-beam treatment preferred over stereotactic radiosurgery because of the lesion’s close relationship to the optic chiasm; if surgical reduction is not achievable, radiation therapy would remain the treatment option.
reference_conclusion_quote: But if you do go transcranial and you can achieve a significant set of reduction, then radiosurgery will be the reasonable option. [...] So, I would recommend that conformal radiosurgery would be a better option than radial surgery. Yes, then it can be done. [...] But surgical reduction will be done. Yes, it should be done. It should be done. The first choice should be surgery anyway. [...] And if there is no surgical reduction, then radiation is the only option.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old male; retired senior Air Force officer.

[ chief complaint ]: Painless hematuria and irritative lower urinary tract symptoms in May 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-metastatic muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma (transition cell carcinoma) of the urinary bladder, clinical stage cT3 with extravesical extension and transmural vesicoureteric junction involvement causing upstream left hydroureteronephrosis; cN0 cM0. Background comorbidities included Crohn’s disease, atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate, and sensorineural hearing loss.

[ histopathology results ]: Bladder biopsy from superficial and deep samples showed urothelial carcinoma with variant histology. Dominant papillary urothelial pattern comprised approximately 50% of the tumor. Additional components included clear cell change, rhabdoid differentiation, and nested architecture involving approximately half of the tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Cystoscopy demonstrated a 3 cm bladder tumor along the left lateral and posterolateral wall, grossly not typically papillary, involving the vesicoureteric junction and obscuring the ureteric orifice. The tumor required resection to visualize the orifice, and a stent was placed. No other multicentric bladder lesions were seen.  
- CT urography/enterography and PET imaging showed bladder tumor staged as T3 with some extravesical extension, transmural vesicoureteric junction involvement, and upstream hydronephrosis/hydroureteronephrosis. No nodal or distant metastatic disease was identified. Upper urinary tract imaging was otherwise clear.  
- CT enterography showed multiple segmental Crohn’s-related lesions extending from the duodenum to the ileum, with the ileum worst affected; descending colon and sigmoid colon were also involved. No imaging signs of active inflammatory bowel disease were present; severity was described as moderate.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: PD-L1 score was <1%. HER2 result was equivocal. Tumor was described as low immunogenic.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL.  
- Renal function was considered adequate for age.  
- Split renal function showed 37% function of the left kidney, attributed to hydronephrosis.  
- Hepatic function was largely preserved.  
- Pure tone audiometry confirmed sensorineural hearing loss.  
- Colonoscopy showed chronic quiescent Crohn’s disease involving the descending and sigmoid colon.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial cystoscopic tumor resection/biopsy was performed with ureteric stenting.  
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered with gemcitabine plus carboplatin for 2 cycles.  
- The patient subsequently underwent bladder-preservation treatment with concurrent chemoradiotherapy. Radiotherapy was delivered using IMRT with adaptive planning. Concurrent carboplatin was given.

[ current disease status ]: Completed concurrent chemoradiotherapy and was awaiting post-treatment review/evaluation. No nodal or distant metastatic disease had been identified on prior staging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Crohn’s disease was a known pre-existing diagnosis.  
- Crohn’s therapy included 5-aminosalicylic acid; no steroids or biologic therapy were being used.  
- Atrial fibrillation was present with controlled ventricular rate; the patient was receiving anticoagulation and beta-blocker therapy. No structural heart disease, hypertension, or uncontrolled tachyarrhythmia was documented.  
- Sensorineural hearing loss required hearing aid use.  
- Cognition was normal.  
- The patient was ambulant without aids, had no documented frailty on screening, and had good social support.  
- ASA physical status was recorded as ASA III.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable thyroid nodule identified incidentally on examination. No compressive or local thyroid nodule symptoms were reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe with multifocal disease and central compartment nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left thyroid nodule was reported as follicular neoplasm of undetermined significance, with mention of some peripheral cells. Surgical pathology after total thyroidectomy demonstrated two foci of medullary thyroid carcinoma in the left lobe, including a left upper lobe lesion measuring 1.8 cm and an additional small focus in the lower pole of the same lobe. No C-cell hyperplasia was identified. Twenty-two central compartment lymph nodes were examined; 3 were positive for metastatic carcinoma. One involved lymph node measured 1.4 cm, with metastatic deposit measuring 0.4 cm. No extranodal extension was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a TI-RADS 3 nodule in the right lobe and a TI-RADS 4 nodule in the left lobe. The left-sided lesion met biopsy criteria. Intraoperative ultrasound identified an abnormal left paratracheal lymph node. No lateral compartment lymphadenopathy was identified on intraoperative ultrasound.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Afirma testing on the biopsied thyroid nodule was suspicious and positive for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Germline RET sequencing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Calcitonin was elevated preoperatively. CEA was 32. Serum calcium was normal. Plasma metanephrines were obtained. Parathyroid hormone was slightly elevated preoperatively. Immediate postoperative PACU PTH was within acceptable range and was neither elevated nor low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central lymph node dissection. Nerve monitoring was used intraoperatively. Pathology confirmed multifocal medullary thyroid carcinoma with 3/22 positive central lymph nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Status post recent total thyroidectomy and bilateral central lymph node dissection for multifocal medullary thyroid carcinoma with central nodal metastases. No lateral compartment lymphadenopathy was identified intraoperatively.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypothyroidism, primary hypertension, and diabetes mellitus requiring intermittent insulin use. Medications included liothyronine (Cytomel), levothyroxine, semaglutide (Ozempic), amlodipine, metformin, and intermittent insulin. Blood pressure had been reported in the 140s to 160s. Family history was notable for paternal grandmother with breast cancer; no family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN syndrome was reported. Married, with one healthy son.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 29-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of a left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma, including a left papillary thyroid microcarcinoma and a contralateral microscopic focus, in the setting of Hashimoto thyroiditis/hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine since 2015.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration performed at another center was reported as Bethesda category VI, consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. Following total thyroidectomy, pathology demonstrated a 6 x 5 mm papillary thyroid microcarcinoma in the left lobe and an additional 2 mm focus in the contralateral lobe, consistent with multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: In 2015, a 7 mm thyroid nodule had been identified and had not been further evaluated at that time. At consultation in 2017, ultrasound showed a posterior left-lobe thyroid nodule with unchanged size and pattern compared with 2015. During follow-up, an incidental 3 mm thyroglossal duct cyst was identified. Post-radioiodine whole-body scanning demonstrated uptake in the thyroglossal duct cyst. PET-CT performed several years later showed no abnormal findings.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroglobulin levels remained undetectable during follow-up. TSH was maintained between 0.8 and 1.5 on levothyroxine. Thyroglobulin antibodies were present and remained stable during the first year after surgery, then decreased over the subsequent 4 years to approximately half of prior levels, with persistent positivity thereafter.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Total thyroidectomy was performed as initial surgical treatment. The patient remained on a stable levothyroxine dose of 88 micrograms daily. Follow-up consisted of laboratory surveillance and neck ultrasound every 6 months. Radioiodine remnant ablation was subsequently administered with 75 mCi after recombinant human TSH stimulation. Post-therapy whole-body scan showed uptake in the thyroglossal duct cyst. Subsequent PET-CT was negative.

[ current disease status ]: No structural disease had been identified on follow-up imaging. Thyroglobulin remained undetectable. Persistent thyroglobulin antibody positivity was present but had declined from baseline and then remained stable. No evidence of recurrent or metastatic disease was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Past thyroid history included Hashimoto thyroiditis/hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine since 2015.

reference_conclusion: Following total thyroidectomy for multifocal papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, surveillance with laboratory testing and neck ultrasound was recommended, with thyroglobulin antibodies interpreted as a follow-up marker rather than an indication for intervention if stable or declining. Because the patient strongly desired postoperative remnant ablation, radioactive iodine was administered after counseling regarding dose selection; 75 mCi was given with recombinant human TSH stimulation, and post-therapy whole-body scanning demonstrated uptake in the thyroglossal duct cyst. Subsequent persistent but stable thyroglobulin antibodies were managed conservatively, with reassurance and avoidance of repeated imaging or additional radioactive iodine in the absence of structural evidence of disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old woman; lifelong non-smoker; never drinker.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive oral tongue lesion present for approximately 2 years, with progressive pain, intermittent tongue bleeding, dysphagia/odynophagia, and approximately 20-pound weight loss over the preceding few months.

[ diagnosis ]: Well-differentiated papillary squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue, with possible anterior floor-of-mouth involvement and no clinical or radiographic nodal or distant metastatic disease at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial incisional biopsy of the tongue lesion demonstrated well-differentiated papillary squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT imaging demonstrated a 3.1 x 2.8 x 3.0 cm exophytic mass of the oral tongue.  
- Possible involvement of the anterior floor of mouth was reported.  
- No extension to the base of tongue was identified on CT.  
- No cervical adenopathy was identified on imaging.  
- No mandibular involvement was identified clinically or on CT.  
- Metastatic workup was negative.  
- Clinical head and neck examination showed no palpable adenopathy.  
- Endoscopic examination showed clear base of tongue, vallecula, and lateral pharyngeal walls.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- A biopsy had been offered by a local otolaryngologist approximately 2 years earlier, but was declined at that time.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue with possible anterior floor-of-mouth involvement; no clinical or radiographic nodal or distant metastatic disease had been identified on staging workup.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included leukemia at approximately 2 years of age, treated with total body radiation and bone marrow transplant.  
- Leukemia had remained in remission.  
- There was no prior history of head and neck cancer.  
- At presentation, the lesion was described clinically as a fungating exophytic mass involving most of the visible oral tongue and extending to the junction of the ventral tongue and floor of mouth.
