reference_discussion.text: All right. Good evening, everyone. It's an honor and a pleasure to be kicking off the virtual activities for this academic year. I'm Fab Al-Bahari. I'm a fellow at the University of Florida. The case that we'll be presenting today is around a patient that we saw not too long ago. She is a 30-year-old woman, a lifelong non-smoker, that presented to our clinic with progressive tongue lesion, with a progressive tongue lesion for about two years. She was offered a biopsy by her local ENT in Panama City two years ago, but refused. And then she presented for an assessment secondary to progressive pain and intermittent tongue bleeding, now two years later, referred by her local otolaryngologist. In terms of other head and neck symptoms, she had some dysphagia or dynaphagia and weight loss of about 20 pounds over the last few months of her symptoms. In terms of her risk factors, she had full body radiation at age of about two years for leukemia. She also had a bone marrow transplant around that time, but she has been in remission since. She's a never smoker, never drinker, and she has no previous head and neck cancers. And she presented to our clinic with no workup. So this is essentially what she presented with, a sort of a fungating exophytic lesion that was covering most of her visible oral tongue and reaching the junction of the eventual tongue with the floor mouth. In terms of her initial work, we did a full head and neck assessment. There were no palpable adenopathies. We scoped her. The base of tongue and molecular were clear. The lateral pharyngeal walls were clear. We also performed an initial incisional biopsy, and we got some head and neck imaging and metastatic workup going.

Just before we go on from there, how do you typically, maybe I'll start with Jen, when you see a patient like this in your office, obviously malignancy is high on the index of suspicion. So assessing somebody like that has got obviously a very large, I imagine quite tender tumor. How would you assess this relationship to the mandible if it's too tender for them to really touch it much on the tongue itself? And then how do you get your tissue diagnosis for these patients?
You're asking me?
Yes.

Okay. I mean, I try and do as good of an exam as I can. Sometimes I'll spray them with some topical anesthetic to get a better exam, um, and assess the mobility from the mandible. Um, obviously imaging is helpful with that. Um, obviously if they have any kind of, um, symptoms of V3 numbness, then I, you know, that will tell me that there is involvement in the mandible. Um, In terms of, sorry, in terms of how I would do a biopsy, I would also do a very basic incisional biopsy of trying to get a good piece of tissue using probably just a scalpel and pickups. Were those your two questions?

It is. Yeah, no, I think I have a very similar approach. I would say the only other subtle thing that you can add, sometimes just pushing under the chin, if it's really painful for them in the mouth, you can actually see how much it wiggles from the mandible. If it's one that's kind of endophytic onto the floor mouth and although not excellent, it gives you a little bit of appreciation for it. Incisional versus a version of that, sometimes doing a punch biopsy, the three millimeter is nice because it's about the exact size of a silver nitrate Q-tip as well. All right, Pod. Talk us through the rest of what you found.

Yeah, so her CT scan showed a 3.1 by 2.8 by 3 centimeter exophytic mass of the oral tongue with possible involvement of the anterior floor of mouth, but there was no extension to the base of tongue again, no adenopathy. Her pathology came back as well differentiated papillary squamous cell carcinoma. And again, this is sort of in the context of a slowly progressive over two years sort of lesion and her metastatic workup was negative. So, you know, in terms of the treatment options, we offered the patient our usual treatment options for oral cavity sclerosal carcinoma. Essentially, you know, on the top, we offered surgery followed by possible radiotherapy. We spoke to her about the extent, possible extent of a resection, her need for neck dissection, and her reconstructive options. We also offered her primary chemo and radiotherapy. We offered her as an option chemo and immuno-oncology or immunotherapy, and obviously no intervention or palliation.

She, after a thorough discussion, she... Before we, why don't we stop there just for a second, just to kind of get the thoughts of the group as well, and then we can maybe go through how you guys proceeded. So on the imaging, what, Peter, what imaging would you get for a patient like this with a pretty advanced oral tongue cancer? I guess more than anything to assess the extent of the primary, and why would you get that?

So for me, typical imaging would be a CT neck and chest or we call it here a CT max face neck you need both order them both of them to get the entire oral cavity so we get that. If there's too much dental artifact and I can't tell the relationship of the tumor to the mandible I'll get an MRI as well. In some cases, I'll also get a PET scan. I can't remember if we got one in this case, but in a case with something unusual like recurrence or someone with suspected aggressive pathology, I might get a PET scan right off the bat as well. But for most of them, a CT neck and chest is what I'll start with.
All right. And Jen, you have similar approach to that as far as when you get a pet. Do you look for adenopathy before considering a pet or?

We generally get pets on every start, unless there is limited time. and or the schedule is too full for a PET scan. And then we can just get a CT neck chest kind of faster. But we really try to get a PET on everyone to start.

As you guys were presenting this at your tumor board, did the history of leukemia and their prior therapy for that at all impact or what it impacted your institution? approach to treatment. And obviously there's still, there's no exact science to that. It sounds like I would imagine fairly low dose radiation for kind of whole body ablation, but also just your counseling with the patient on how the biology of the disease may behave in a patient whose status post prior kind of whole body ablative therapy, even if it was in the distant past. And Peter or Jenny, either one.

In our case up front, didn't really come into the treatment decision algorithm for this patient. Kind of kept it in the back of our mind. Discussing it with the patient, you know, her having been a lifetime non-smoker, she's already had a previous cancer. We discussed with her that she probably has some kind of a genetic defect that we don't know about, and this tumor may not behave like a usual one. That being said, she had it for two years, and it really hadn't spread anywhere, and it was just slowly growing. So we can't really predict exactly how things are going to go for her. She's young, so it's not a common age to get this type of cancer. So we had that discussion with the patient, but it didn't really factor much into the treatment decision, other than the fact she wanted the most aggressive treatment available, which for us was surgery followed by adequate treatment as needed. And then we haven't gotten that part yet, but post-op, you know, it did come in a little bit into the discussion and we can mention that once we get there.
Sure. All right. Well, Fahad, why don't you walk us through how you guys approached it?

Yeah, so one, you know, she opted obviously for surgery after discussing all the options. We essentially explained to her that she will require, you know, an ablative approach to the tongue with a wide resection, hopefully with negative margins. And then we discussed with her the need for neck dissection and reconstruction afterwards, both from a functional perspective and from a holistic treatment approach. The things that came up to mind when we were thinking about her consent were, are we gonna spare her base of tongue or not? Obviously there wasn't any obvious involvement on the CT scan. And we also had in the back of our minds, both pre-op and intra-op, you know, whether we will need a marginal mandibular ectomy or not. She did not have any obvious disease that was close to the mandible upon assessment in the clinic, nor on the CT scan, and interoperatively, we did not think that there was anything involving the mandible.

Which approach, yeah, oh, there you go. Yeah, so this is a great, great point. So what approach would you guys consider? Maybe I'll start with Jen, since Peter, I think this may have been your case. So why don't we get to Dr. Gross's thoughts.

actually have never found the need to do a mandibulotomy. I always try and do anything else. So, and especially in a patient like this, where you really don't, I don't think need one for the approach. I would just make, you know, a gingival incision intra-orally and just drop the whole tongue into the neck to make the posterior cuts. So pull through.

And we didn't really mention this earlier, but I think just since this is one of the first sessions of the year, this patient would obviously need a thorough dental evaluation, you know, high likelihood they may need some additional adjuvant therapy afterwards. These are going to be right in the high dose field for that. So if there are any teeth that need to be removed, especially if you're going to be doing, you know, some sort of a, you know, a lingual release or, or a pull through approach where you're going to be degloving the inner surface of the mandible, that's the time to get the teeth out of there. Cause you would then just overlay the sockets with your flap. And when you do your reconstruction. Yeah, I would say I would certainly use a similar approach. The only caveat of times where I sometimes consider a mandibulotomy is if there's a lot of the floor mouth musculature on one side that may give them some semblance of function. And, and you feel like that's your only chance to preserve that just given how, um, it's growth pattern would, uh, threaten things like the contralateral lingual artery. Uh, usually you can still do those just working above and below, but that's kind of one of the rare times if you're trying to really keep that mylohyoid and kind of the suprahyoid muscles on one side, it would give some semblance of, rather than just resuspending it, that can sometimes help. All right, why don't you talk us through that after the verse action there.

All right. We obviously consider her for bilateral neck dissection. We did not involve level four as she was an N0 neck. And then we also spoke to her about reconstruction. So this was the extent of our resection. We were all the way back to the circumvallic papillae, but we We did it through a pull-through approach, like a hemi-pull-through approach. So we saved, we preserved the super hard muscles on the left side and only sacrificed them on the right side, the side of the pull-through. And this essentially the defect that we ended up with intraoperatively. So that's the base of tongue at the very back and essentially the floor of mouth along with the oral tongue were all removed. So the next question for us was, you know, what are the goals of our reconstruction? Obviously we wanted to separate the oral cavity from the neck. We want to create and maintain bulk for deglutition, for speech intelligibility, to try and prevent aspiration. And the, you know, the famous question is, you know, how do you try to get back sensation by doing any neurophys or nerve transfers? And then also the choice of reconstruction, you know, as in terms of would you go for an ALT or rectus free flap, a thoracodorsal artery flap, rate of form with a beaver tail, or a regional flap in that case.

I see in our participant group here, Dr. Hoey, B. Hoey. I don't know if you can, if it's Dr. Hoey out of South Florida, if you can comment on your approach to reconstruction in this patient. I don't know if you're able to unmute. if he's available to comment. In the meantime, Dr. Gross, maybe you could comment on how you would approach it. Maybe first off, your choice of flap, and then whether or not you have any subtle tricks of the trade, and then whether you consider the nerve repair as well.

You know, I try to get something that has sub-q fat because I find that that doesn't atrophy as much as muscle. So, you know, especially in a female, I would say that an ALT would be my go-to option. You can also two-team, of course. I haven't done erectus, so I can't really comment on that, but my thought is that the donor site morbidity is probably higher with erectus than with an ALT. I also like getting the tensor fasciae latae with ALT for suspension reasons. I think regardless though of what you use, you know, you're trying to get the bulk to get that tongue, that neotongue to touch the hard palate to help with swallowing and speech if they can do that. But all these flaps do end up atrophying over time. I try to suture the TFL to the cutaneous paddle to the gingiva to try and suspend that tissue so it doesn't fall into the neck. But I wouldn't do a regional flap and a young person. I really try not to do tech flaps primarily unless I really have to. And then a radio forum generally just isn't enough bulk, I think.
Absolutely.

Dr. Zygielewski, your thought as well. I know you did this reconstruction, but if you can comment on it, as far as your approach, any subtle ways you do to minimize, kind of help it bunch up for you in a way that doesn't compromise the perforator circulation to the flap and your flap of choice for this.

I think the flap of choice, first of all, I agree. I want something with a lot of sub-Q fat, ideally, and it's going to depend on the patient's body habits. I've seen forearms that are as thick as ALTs, ALTs as thin as forearms. It depends on the patient. This young lady, she was somewhere around like 90 pounds, very, very tiny, very small BMI. Forearm definitely was completely out. Even her rectus was too thin. We looked at rectus versus ALT, and her ALT actually looked better than the rectus would have been in this case. So certainly want something with bulk. I usually measure it to overcorrect, kind of measure from one part of the defect. So like we'll say from one side of the teeth to the other with an arch that'll touch the palate to try to get a sense of some extra width on it. And then I don't have any really good tricks to get it to bunch up other than just travel along the flap more than I would around the teeth. It's pretty rare that you'd put too much in there and congest the flap or your perforators, but I have seen that happen before where I had to cut out a bunch of flap because it was too much. I think I've seen that once. Most of the other time, if it feels like it's too much and it's difficult to suture, you're probably doing it right, is what I tell our fellows. And then I like to use a TFL to suspend it. I do it on the undersurface of the mandible by drilling little holes into the mandible and suturing through there. And Fahad will show you what we did. Those are the main things. If it's a huge defect and I'm taking some muscle as well, like with an ALT, I'll do a neuroraphy between the nerve to the vastus to the hypoglossal nerve to try to maintain some of the muscle to keep some bulk over time, even though a lot of it's still going to atrophy, but if you reinnervate it, it'll keep some bulk. Um, you know, those are kind of the main things that I try to go for over correction and some suspension. And if you can keep some of the super high muscles, like we were able to in this case on one side, that's great. Um, I think those would be the main things I would think of.

Absolutely is a great case. I think it highlights so many important points. Um, You know, I think it is important to remember, you know, there were studies in years past to look at, and it was actually out of the Wash U group, that looked at using latissimus free flap and reinnervating the thoracodorsal nerve to the hypoglossal nerve, and they would kind of put it crossways. in a delayed fashion, you could see it kind of contract. And although you could see some movement, it didn't actually, there was a question of whether it actually had significant benefit to swallowing. And so I think it's not been used as much for that. Spending a little bit more time here because I think you're one a lot of great points and I'm not sure if Natalia is going to be able to join us we're still trying to reach her. So, while before we move on from this case maybe one additional points so for the subtotal or maybe if they say this had extended back to involve the base of tongue. When do you consider doing just a total glassectomy versus including a laryngectomy? Obviously, for a young person, that's a very difficult conversation. Dr. Gross, do you have a cut off? Do you offer a total glassectomy just by itself with necks and reconstruction? Or do you, you know, some some people I know have a philosophy of strongly considering an upfront laryngectomy in those patients?

I try and preserve the larynx at all costs, and even if, you know, a segment of the hyoid is, has to be resected, as long as the epiglottis is maintained, I will, you know, I'm going to try and save the larynx. And of course, I do warn them that there could be intractable aspiration if I'm getting kind of a little bit close, or I have to take even you know, some of the mucosa off of the epiglottis, for example. And we would, if that was the case, go back at a later date.
And Peter, do you have a similar approach?

Yeah, I agree. I like to preserve the larynx if possible, pretty much at all costs. I think patients can do very well that way. But once you're starting to remove part of the supraglottic structure like the epiglottis, then you're just creating a nice conduit for any food and liquid to just go straight down there. So once it's starting to involve resecting part of the supraglottic structures, then I would opt for a total laryngectomy. I agree, the hyoid doesn't play a huge role in it, you can still suspend the larynx through the thyroid cartilage if you want to do sutures to the mandible so that can help. If the patients had radiation therapy, I would be much more quick to do a total gloss total laryngectomy because those patients already have a huge swallowing deficit and they're probably going to be chronically aspirating. in a patient who's had a full dose of radiation before, I would push probably more towards a total laryngectomy with a total vasectomy. But otherwise, I think it's a good option in most patients to preserve the larynx.

Sometimes for these patients, we will offer them a neoadjuvant Um, chemo or, you know, just because obviously, I don't think she would be a trial candidate. So it might just be chemo. But because. If you're worried about a laryngectomy, that is with the hopes of trying to spare the larynx, because in the end, they're going to need a laryngectomy anyway, but I don't think that would be the case necessarily for this patient.

Yeah, I would agree that in surgery, if it persists, you know, it's a rare instance you consider something like that, because especially without a lot of nodal disease, it's unlikely you're going to go from that to an incurable cancer and the surgery would likely be similar. So there are certainly some patients who would would balk at, you know, that and would consider doing some sort of a non-surgical neoadjuvant. And it also gives you a sense on the biology of the disease, you know, as well. All right, well, why don't we transition to our next case. Dr. Chang, maybe if you could stop sharing. We'll have Dr. Chang call hers up and then.

reference_conclusion: The patient elected primary surgical management for oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. The agreed operative plan was wide ablative resection of the tongue and involved floor of mouth with the goal of negative margins, bilateral neck dissection excluding level IV in the clinically N0 neck, and immediate reconstruction. Mandibular resection was not planned because there was no clinical, radiographic, or intraoperative evidence of mandibular involvement.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old premenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast lesion detected in June of the same year on mammography and ultrasound.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with microinvasion after mastectomy pathology; positive medial surgical margin. Sentinel lymph node findings showed isolated groups of neoplastic cells. Right breast showed no malignancy. BRCA mutation was reported.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial breast biopsy showed DCIS, solid and papillary type, grade 3, with microcalcifications and comedonecrosis; no invasive component was detected. Subsequent left mastectomy pathology showed DCIS, comedo type, grade 2, with microinvasion and a positive medial margin. Estrogen receptor expression was 90%. Progesterone receptor expression was 40%. HER2 was negative. Left sentinel lymph nodes contained isolated groups of neoplastic cells. Right breast pathology was negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]: Mammogram and ultrasound demonstrated a BI-RADS 5 lesion with pleomorphic microcalcifications.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRCA mutation was present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In August of the same year, she underwent bilateral prophylactic mastectomy, left sentinel lymph node biopsy, and immediate reconstruction with tissue expanders. Surgical pathology demonstrated residual left-sided DCIS with microinvasion and a positive medial margin; right breast was free of malignancy.

[ current disease status ]: Status post bilateral mastectomy with immediate reconstruction. Residual pathologic risk features included positive medial margin, microinvasion in the left breast specimen, and isolated neoplastic cell groups in sentinel lymph nodes. No malignancy was identified in the right breast.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history was significant for breast cancer in her father and in a sister diagnosed at age 41 years. Previously healthy before this diagnosis.

Alphonse, do you want to add something? Thank you, Carol.

Yeah, it's not traditional to give post-mastectomy radiation for the CIS, but it is a very difficult question, and it depends on many things. What was the quality of surgery? Did the surgeon leave a significant breast tissue behind? Did the patient have these overwhelming something like a snowstorm of classification with DCIS all over the rest. What's exactly, what was in this positive median margin, was it focus, one focus of DCIS close to a margin or it's a longer broad front? There are a lot of questions here that need to be answered because this woman is a young woman and her survival is very long and then having local failure after mastectomy for DCIS is not unheard of. We have seen a few of those. So a lot of factors here really come into the decision whether you give post-mastectomy radiation or not. The other thing about the radiation-induced cancer, I think what was meant probably radiation-induced sarcoma. Yes, the patient could be at risk. The risk is 0.2% at 10 years and might increase a little bit at 20 years. The risk is low, but it's there. So this is not… So I don't know what is the risk of radiation with subcoma in brachycardia. It could be higher than that. So it is a difficult question. It's not 100% no, we should not give post-mastectomy radiation. It's not 100% we should give post-mastectomy radiation. And we struggle with this question all the time. A study from Kaiser Permanente showing that positive margins give a higher risk of local failure. In fact, for every common, the risk of local failure is actually 2%. I mean, it's 90% control rates after mastectomy for DCIS. But when you have those factors, it can go up to 7%. This will need a discussion, it's not an easy answer.
Maybe we could get some surgical perspective, Sima would you like to comment?

So I actually lean towards Alphonse's argument here because it Although the value of radiotherapy is not definitively proven, the risk certainly for this group of features is higher, particularly her young age. And if the patient is so inclined, I mean, agreeing that this is a relatively data-free zone, the risk may be high enough to actually justify radiotherapy.
Thank you Seema. Charlotte Gale, would you have the courage to disagree with Seema and Alphonse?

That's easy, no. What I would say is that if you look at this and it was a strictly an in situ cancer, and you're positive at the fibroglandular border, it's in situ. Additional local therapy would be treating non-breast tissue, but this isn't clearly in situ because it's in a lump node. Yes, she had reconstruction. How did she have it? With tissue expanders.
Okay, thank you.

And that's one of the things that some of the radiation oncologists are getting into about, you know, switching them out to permanent or keeping them over-inflated or, you know, there's a bunch of different regimens, so that would go into what, you know, what you would want to do from there, but that's not, that's a radiation oncology question.

Yeah, I mean about just a comment on the impact of radiation on reconstructed breasts, well it has a negative impact, no doubt about it, it increases the risk of complication, it increases the risk of encapsulation of tenderness, of cellulitis, And sometimes they have to remove the expander or the implant just because of radiation. But this is usually maybe around 20%. Sometimes we request the exchange before radiation and then the Memorial Sloan-Kettering technique, which we usually actually do it here also. Sometimes we do the exchange after radiation. Plastic surgeons don't like to operate in an irradiated field. It may seem more complicated, no doubt about it. But again, looking at the benefit, every time you give radiation, there is a reduced risk of local failure by two-thirds to 75%. So this is universal in almost every paper. The question is, what is the original risk? If you start with a risk of 7%, it will go down to 3% but this outweighs the potential side effects from radiation. If you start with a risk of 20% it goes down to 5% but here the benefit is big. And again this is a case where we really struggle and there is no right or wrong, there is no clear answer to it but all those things more things to discuss like this.
Thank you. Casino, can you send us the reference from the French study that you cited, please, to Jessica, she'll communicate. Carol, did you comment on this case?
Yes, I did. I was the dissenting voice saying that there are several studies saying there's no need for radiation.

I just thought you had a follow-up question. Thank you very much. Does anybody else have any questions? We had three very young patients presented today, all very worrisome, and so thank you very much. Has anybody got a comment? Here's a comment. What is it? Can you read it? We just have a comment from a viewer, if you don't mind. Alphonse, that is a good question. I don't know. I mean, if there is no evidence of invasion in her breast, it will be TIS, and then it will go to probably NI+. So it's still DCIS. reference_conclusion: Post-mastectomy radiotherapy was not endorsed as a routine recommendation after mastectomy for DCIS with a positive margin, given the generally low risk of locoregional recurrence in available series. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old woman; never smoker; former school teacher.

[ chief complaint ]: Shortness of breath. Associated symptoms at presentation included approximately 6-pound weight loss, exertional dyspnea, cough, and loose stools/diarrhea.

[ diagnosis ]: Left pleural malignant mesothelioma, epithelioid subtype, with extensive left hemithoracic disease and subsequent abdominal metastatic involvement.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical biopsy demonstrated epithelioid mesothelioma. PD-L1 expression was 50% by staining. BAP1 loss was present by immunohistochemistry.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial evaluation identified a left-sided pleural effusion.  
- PET imaging demonstrated extensive hypermetabolic disease at the left lung base/left pleura.  
- Axial imaging showed pleural mass extending between ribs with possible rib involvement, consistent with chest wall invasion.  
- Imaging also showed nodal uptake near/below the diaphragm, concerning for abdominal nodal involvement.  
- Repeat imaging approximately 3 months later showed substantial interval progression, with clear abdominal disease in addition to progression of thoracic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BAP1 loss on immunohistochemistry.  
- Tumor sequencing did not identify a BAP1 somatic mutation; germline BAP1 testing was therefore not pursued.  
- CDKN2A mutation was identified.  
- MTAP deletion was not identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Surgical biopsy was performed for tissue diagnosis.  
- Systemic chemotherapy with carboplatin plus pemetrexed was administered.  
- Four cycles were completed initially.  
- A total of six cycles of carboplatin/pemetrexed was planned/recommended; the patient was nearing completion of cycle 6 within 2 weeks of the documented update.  
- Bevacizumab was not given because of underlying giant cell arteritis/vasculitis.  
- Immunotherapy was not used in the documented treatment course.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Disease had shown rapid progression over a 3-month interval before treatment, with development of definite abdominal involvement.  
- No pemetrexed maintenance had been initiated at the time documented.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: giant cell arteritis diagnosed within the prior year and still requiring steroids; prior small stroke; eczema.  
- Occupational/environmental history: reported asbestos remediation in her classroom during her employment as a teacher.  
- Family history: no family history of mesothelioma, melanoma, kidney cancer, or breast cancer.  
- Examination findings at presentation: vital signs stable; no palpable lymphadenopathy; lungs clear with decreased breath sounds at the left base; tenderness to palpation over the left central back without palpable mass.  
- Performance status: ECOG 0.

reference_discussion.text: I think also in this day and age with data that is a little bit equivocal about how much surgery is beneficial, we're all looking for reasons not to do surgery. I'm sorry. We're trying to figure out why surgery is a bad idea. And if we get to the end of that questioning and we say, wow, I really couldn't think of a reason why it's not a bad idea, then we proceed. But we've become much more picky. OK, I'm going to move on. This, we're about to answer, so we can talk a little about that. Okay, so this is our next case. So this is a 76-year-old woman. She presented with shortness of breath, and she was found to have a left-sided pleural effusion, again, fluid on the outside of the lung on the left side. ROS means review of systems, so these are like the symptoms that she reported. So she reported some weight loss, about six pounds. She said that when she was walking, she felt more short of breath. She had a cough and she had her bowel movements were loose. She said she was having some diarrhea. In terms of her past medical history, she actually had giant cell arteritis, which is an autoimmune disease. She'd had a small stroke in the past, and she had a history of eczema. She was a never smoker. She worked as a school teacher. She knew that her classroom had undergone asbestos remediation during a period of time that she was the teacher there. She did not have a family history of mesothelioma, melanoma, kidney, or breast cancers. These are some of the cancers associated with BAP1. And on exam, she looked pretty good. Her vital signs were stable. I couldn't feel any lymph nodes. When I listened to her lungs, her lungs were clear. They were moving. She had decreased sounds at the left base of her lung, which was probably the fluid that was there. She had some tenderness to palpation of her left central back, but I couldn't feel a mass. And her performance status was a zero, which basically means she's up walking around. She doesn't really have any symptom that is limiting her activities during the day. Okay, so we have a left-sided pleural effusion. We still don't have a diagnosis at this point. So what would we do next? We've talked a little bit about this, but let me have somebody walk us through.

For the most part, this type of a diagnosis, you may be in a primary care office, a pulmonologist's office, you don't have a diagnosis yet, you just have fluid. So a lot of the times, kind of as we've discussed before, imaging and then sampling of the fluid, and then depending on your kind of what we would call pre-test probability, but that just meets your suspicion, even if that fluid is negative, you may still want to go towards a more invasive approach to sample. I would get some dedicated imaging first and that would probably guide what to do next.

OK, you asked for imaging. We have it. All right, so this is a PET scan again. I'm going to use my laser pointer. So in this one, the patient is actually, it's as though you're standing up, even though all of you guys know that when you go through a scanner, you're lying down. But I find people have, it's a little easier to look at this way. A little different from our other case, we see there's quite a bit of activity here at the left base of the lung. So this is all presumably disease that's taking up the dye. It does seem to be isolated to that area, but it's fairly extensive. When we look at the axial section, so now the patient is lying down, their feet are coming out towards us and their head's on the other side. These are slices like a hoagie. We're going to go back. You can tell we're in Philadelphia when I call it a hoagie, right? So we can tell here from this plural mass that these little white things along the side are ribs. So it's going in between the rib, maybe even into the rib. So this is chest wall invasion. And then as we go towards the bottom of the diaphragm, we can see there's some lymph nodes here that are probably on the other side of the diaphragm. So there's probably a lymph node that's taking up the dye that's in the abdomen. Anybody want to make any comments about the imaging?

A large tumor burden in this location is particularly hard to clear in the operating room, in the sulcus where the diaphragm goes down and meets the chest wall, and then more specifically medially where the diaphragm comes over towards the center of the chest. It's a little hard to see on there. You gotta trust me on this, the esophagus comes up there, the aorta's there, there's a lot of other structures that are there medially and posteriorly, so a large tumor burden in that spot in particular tends to be pretty hard to clear in the operating room, unfortunately.

Okay, so I think what we know from these images is that the disease is fairly extensive on the left side of the chest, and it might have spread into one or two spots in the abdomen. So what would we do next? Emmett, maybe I can have you walk us through.

What we know from these images, this is a pretty extensive involvement. So we saw in both sides of the diaphragm and there has been some local extension. We would like to understand what the biology is. This is highly suspicious for cancer and we need a tissue diagnosis. And once we identify the diagnosis, then we, of course, need to start thinking about the patient's current state of health and how their organ functions are so that we can start thinking about what medical management can be considered. So basically, blood work, clinical exam, and tissue diagnosis will be the next step.

Great, so we did get a biopsy. It was a surgical biopsy again. So the pathology came back as the epithelioid type, so the vanilla in our analogy there. And then there was staining for PD-L1, which was 50%. That is a marker for immunotherapy, not a great predictor in meso, but we can talk a little bit about that. And there was BAP1 loss within the path, not necessarily a germline BAP1, but there was loss there. Anyone want to comment on any of this? Dr. Offen.

Just that I would make sure it was sent for pathology, and then I'm assuming during this procedure they probably did something to help with the effusion. So in general, you know, we can talk all the science and the fun stuff on the stage, but the patient in front of you is what matters. So if the person's got fluid there and they're short of breath, we want a diagnosis. We want to figure that out. But the first thing is help the shortness of breath. So during a procedure like this, I would assume they would have sampled the fluid, placed a catheter if needed. To me, that's like the first step. The first step is try to help with the symptom.
That's a great point. OK, any additional information that you need? Maybe go back to you, Dr. Offen. Do you have everything you need to make a decision?

Organ function, blood work, and patient preferences are going to be paramount here. I think looking at the imaging, to me, this is leaning towards initiation of something through the vein first before we would consider anything else. And to figure out what makes sense, we know it's the vanilla, which In the modern setting is what I like to say dealer's choice. We have three FDA approved options, and theoretically they're all on an equal keel for epithelioids, so that's dual immunotherapy, chemo by itself, or chemo plus immunotherapy. I have strong inclinations one way or another, but that's personal preference. All three of them are reasonable in epithelioid, and it's gonna depend on the patient's goals, the patient's wants, and what's safe to give based on the labs. So I have a question for you guys, actually. So one of the things that's come up a lot for us is potential autoimmune problems in giving immunotherapies. Do you guys have any absolute no's, gray areas, and ones that you're like, that's not a big deal? So I have and do give immunotherapy to patients with underlying autoimmune disease in close collaboration with the rheumatologist. If it's well-controlled and depending, if hopefully it hasn't required anti-inflammatory biologic-type drugs. Regine cell arteritis, it to me would really depend on what vessels were involved and how active it was. It may give me an inclination that if I had the option of chemo, to start with chemo because of the concern for toxicity for this individual. There are lots of like, I always like to say, Malin and I are both chefs and we both cook the same dishes but we have slightly different recipes. So there's different ways you can dose the drugs, different ways you can lean the patient into the medicines. So it's not a direct contraindication in this patient, again, just based on the information given. Ones that I would usually say definitively no would be an underlying autoimmune lung disease where they're on oxygen. I cannot risk loss of pulmonary function with those medications. Aring that, destructive rheumatoid arthritis, which is debilitating quality of life. But in reality, it's talking to the patient about risk and benefit.

So just for everybody in the room, so giant cell arteritis, if flares, if it flares badly, you can lose your sight. Okay, so it's one that you can, in my opinion, it's one you don't want to mess with. This particular patient had been diagnosed within the last year and was still on steroids.

And a couple of additional things about that. So giant cell arthritis is involving generally the vessels that are going to the brain. And one of the common symptoms can be vision loss if it is an active you know, inflammation in this vessel, but also it can cause stroke, and sometimes it can, because of inflammation of certain vessels, it can increase the risk of aneurysms and dissections in major vessels. So this is definitely a very concerning diagnosis, and we do not know very well what are the incidence rates when we give immunotherapy, how many patients or what is the percentage we may flare. What we know from immunotherapy, even in patients who never had this problem, this has been in case reports a reported potential risk of an immunotherapy. It's very rare. But we know in a biology, probably this is something immunotherapy can flare. So that is why when we have different treatment options, definitely this pre-underlying autoimmune disease is one thing that can help you to decide what should be not probably a first treatment option.

All right, so this patient actually had a pretty long journey to get to us. And the imaging findings actually were three months prior to when I met them. And so I got new imaging. And the summary of the new imaging is that the disease in the three months actually had grown quite a bit. And there was now clear abdominal disease, whereas before we thought maybe there was a lymph node. So that's just the update on the imaging. So I think we've answered a little bit of this, but certainly we're thinking more about how quickly we can start systemic therapy. I do think about these people that have quick disease growth, a lot of weight loss. I do think more about chemotherapy for patients like that because I think we see some faster responses with chemotherapy. So again, I think we're all kind of leaning that way. So this is what ended up happening with this patient. They had four cycles of chemotherapy. The thickness along the left side really decreased very nicely. The lymph nodes decreased in size. The abdominal lymph nodes, the abdominal implants decreased and she felt it much, much better after starting treatment. So I wanted to provide an example of chemo because we talk a lot about immunotherapy, but for some patients, I do think that chemo is a really important tool or at least part of what we can do. I'll pause there for comments.

Did you happen to get any sequencing? I would just say in general, in mesothelioma, the guidelines and our feelings are if there's adequate sample and the patient's agreeable, doing sequencing off of the tumor that can help inform clinical trials can also be somewhat prognostic. If we find certain genes, we may know that it may be a bit more of an aggressive biology. It may open up, you know, matched therapies later on in terms of a trial setting. There's also the possibility of the inherited genetic panel that can be considered. That may also have prognostic implications. We'll talk more about that in the peritoneal session tomorrow. But BAP1 may mean a little bit of a different biology. But there are other inherited conditions that go along with mesothelioma. We say it's around 10 to 13% of the time, regardless of known or suspected asbestos exposure. It could be an inherited family predisposition. And that could be anything from BAP1 to the BRCA breast cancer gene to the Lynch syndrome colon cancer gene. It's not just the classic one we think about on our test questions. So I would routinely recommend a broad-based genetic panel for those interested.

Yeah, so this patient did get a genetic panel. They did not have a BAP1 somatic mutation, so we did not proceed to germline testing. I believe this patient had a CDKN2A mutation, but not MTAP deletion.
So they were BAP1 wild type? They're wild type. So they lost it on IHC, though?
On IHC, yeah.

So that's an important, interesting thing. You're going to see BAP1 potentially in reports in several different places. Seeing the word BAP1 doesn't mean it's an inherited BAP1. So this patient's tumor lost BAP1 expression in the cell, but the gene in the tumor was normal, and the gene they were born with was normal. So they actually lost it. beyond the DNA, when the DNA was becoming a protein. And so when you see BAP1 in your report, it doesn't necessarily mean you lost it at birth.

So the next question I have here is kind of what happens next. And I think this is an area we don't have a lot of data for. So this patient got carboplatin and pemetrexid. They got four cycles. They tried to do a trial where they flipped a coin for patients like this. And they said, OK, continue one chemotherapy or just do surveillance every three months with your scans. And that trial didn't accrue quite enough patients. They accrued about 50 patients. But from what they were able to see, there wasn't much difference between continuing one of the chemos and actually just watching. So I think we all have slightly different practices about this. And probably it differs patient to patient. But I'd like to ask the medical oncologist what they do.

I feel like this can become very frustrating to the patients that when they see two or three providers, everyone have a different opinion. And that is pretty much because we don't have the existing data and we are trying to extrapolate the information from other tumors or from our experiences. But at the end of the day, when we have these conversations, we need to talk about what are the justifications. So this is a patient who has a quite high risk for immunotherapy-induced toxicities. So we know the standard of care for the second line for this patient, if at that point, after a discussion with the patient, it's going to be chemotherapy or a dual checkpoint inhibition. immunotherapy, toxin rates are higher than one. That is not an easy decision to go for a relatively weaker chemo versus dual checkpoint inhibition. So one question that is going to come up is in a patient where the second line treatment options are less than ideal, how we can prolong the duration of response. And I think that is one of the reasons patients coming with these comorbidities, it is important to talk about how many cycles of chemotherapy should be given and if we need to give any maintenance chemotherapy. So, as we discussed, the clinical trials that has very limited data about the benefit of conjugation of ametrexate in the maintenance setting, it is because those studies did not enroll much and their endpoints changed. And at the end of the day, we also had to see a patient population in two different arms receiving a little bit of different treatments, like cisplatin versus carboplatin, and different histologies, like sarcomatoid epithelioids. So there were some imbalances, which makes that information very hard to understand and interpret. But what we know for certain maintenance therapies in certain settings, like non-small cell lung cancer, suggest there is a relative side effects related with chemotherapies in that setting. There can be a prolonging of the containment of the cancer. what we call progression-free survival. This is specific to lung adenocarcinomas. So I think in this situation, it would be reasonable to consider a maintenance strategy with the hope that you can prolong the duration of control of the disease. So, you know, this is one of those situations you can consider metrics of maintenance, and if the patient have a good tolerance, Again, it is the same thing with radiation surgery. In order to decrease the disease burden as much as possible, you can consider the induction regimen, which is dual chemotherapy, to be longer. There are a couple of variables we need to be very careful of. considering. Number one, there are the cumulative toxicities of this treatment, how the patient is feeling with this treatment, because some of these toxicities can be irreversible. The second thing, how much of a deepening response we are getting from these therapies. So after two cycles, if you are really reducing the cancer burden in the sequential scan. If you are seeing you reach the maximum cytoreduction, you reach to more of a plateau from that tumor shrinkage, you know, it suggests that maybe the treatment is not as effective as it has been because you are trying to kill these cancer cells with chemotherapy. But chemotherapy generally kills most of the chemotherapy senses and whatever left behind may not be as responsive to chemotherapy. Along these lines, I think this is a patient we need to consider if there's going to be four or six cycles of carboplatin pemetrexate, and if a pemetrexate maintenance can be considered with the hope to prolong the containment of the cancer. And that is what I would suggest.

I also think it's important to consider if their recurrence or their progression is symptomatic or not. So if she has, for instance, progression in the chest wall with significant pain, I think it'd be a good time to bring in other treatment modalities like radiation or protons or whatever. I think that's important. I think, I know I sometimes fall into this trap of treating imaging rather than the person. So I think you have to think about is it a symptomatic recurrence also, that's important to consider. Just to give us a slight counterpoint to the use of Pemetrexid maintenance. With all the nuances therein, there is a negative randomized trial for the use of Pemetrexid, which did not improve survival or outcomes and did lead to a detriment in quality. And so it has to be a very select person you would consider it for. My counterpoint being, we define the reutilization of the chemo double. If somebody's cancer responded and didn't grow for six months or a year, it depends on who you ask, but many months of benefit before the cancer regrows. If you're gonna continue a maintenance, you have to be mindful if that maintenance drug hurts the kidneys, hurts the blood count, hurts the person's functional status and quality, and the cancer recurs on the maintenance, you may not be able to repurpose the platinum again. And so it's a very delicate tightrope walk. But what I would say is, as it stands right now in the guidelines and in my head, it's a rare person that I tend to continue on Pemetrex at maintenance for that reason. But this is a very unique case where immunotherapy is much less attractive. And so thinking outside of the box here is by no means incorrect.

And these are the concern that we generally have in terms of chemotherapy, that cumulative toxities can be detrimental by their self as well. That's why before each treatment, the patients are seen by the providers and we'll get the blood work and do clinical exams. Because, for example, for pemetrexate, there are a couple of toxicities that are very relevant, which is fatigue, bone marrow suppression, and problems in the kidney. So if you see any of those toxicities, you know that things can get worse. The other thing that we know, again, that comes from non-small cell lung cancer data that also kind of maybe give a little bit more clarity about the maintenance, even in patients where we believe there is a benefit from pemetrexate, like non-small cell lung cancer, adenocarcinoma, in 85, 90% of the patients within one year, we have to stop it either because of disease progression or because of an organ dysfunction or because of progressive worsening of the side effects. So, in no means this is not indefinite, but again, in case to case, I think these are the nuances that makes us think about how many cycles, if there is a role for maintenance, because there is not a really high level of evidence that's available that can give us more clear answers.

Great, so I ended up recommending six cycles of carboplatin pemotrexate for this patient. And so she's just completing that MS here in two weeks. So I appreciate this was actually just me trying to get everybody's opinion about what to do. But most likely we're not going to do pemmetrexid maintenance. She's starting to feel the chemo a little bit. And I think she would appreciate a break. And I don't have great evidence that it's going to benefit her to continue the pemmetrexid. So I think that's what we're going to consider. And she knows we're talking about her today. She's not here. But she knows we're chatting about her. So I'm going to open it up to questions. Yes.
What makes you choose carboplatin over cisplatin?

Yeah, great question. I can start off. So the original studies were done with cisplatin. There are some people that are still very much cisplatin loyalists. And they feel that this is a, and actually, Dr. Offen comes from an institution that is generally a cisplatin loyalist. They have done retrospective studies, meaning they looked back and they said, okay, this person got cisplatin, this person got carboplatin, and they compared them, and there's no difference, okay? Now, that's not a perfect comparison because you're not, you know, flipping a coin and making sure all the different characteristics are equal, but I generally only use carboplatin. It's a very rare situation that I'll use cisplatin, and that's only post-surgery in a very young patient.

As a quick aside, I am not a cisplatin loyalist. And I see many of my patients in this room who can probably attest to the fact that I use carboplatin quite frequently. It's the person in front of you. If you have no reason not to use cisplatin, then I would say there is some anecdotal experience in older papers where cisplatin had slightly better outcomes. But those tend to be healthier people who can tolerate cisplatin. You treat the person in front of you, and I would say the vast majority of people I see will get carboplatin because it's likely the one they'll tolerate the best.
My question is, in your experience, and everything I read, people are in their 70s, 60s, are you starting to see younger people coming in?

So this is like a little plug to Prasad Adasimile. We have a paper under review on that exact topic. So we have polled what we call the young diagnosis, which we defined as patients less than 50. Very young is less than 35. We've identified 500 patients seen at our institution over the years, 200 or so of which we were able to annotate. The youngest patient I have ever personally seen and managed was eight. This is a disease with a bimodal distribution. We tend to think of it as a 60, 70-year-old Caucasian male veteran. That's not the case. We have to really start integrating our understanding of a younger patient population's needs into clinical trials in terms of fertility preservation, in terms of all the things we know from other malignancies, and we have to have a high level of suspicion in a younger individual with recurrent pleural effusion that meso's not off the table just based on demographics. So it can happen in a younger population. We anecdotally see they may be more or less responsive to certain drugs. They may have slightly different genetic backgrounds. Those are active fields of investigation right now. Everyone is treated by the same playbook, but whether that's the right thing, I don't know.

I'll make one other comment, which is it is a very hard disease to diagnose. And so we're getting better at it, actually. And that's probably contributing somewhat to seeing it in younger patients as well.
There were comments about continuing with mextrad as a maintenance drug. But none of you talked about Avastin. Did you touch on that?

Yeah, I was hoping someone would ask that question, so thank you for being the plant. So the patient we talked about did not get Avastin because of their history of giant cell arteritis, which is a vasculitis. And Avastin is an antibody that affects blood vessels. Okay, but generally if I were giving carboplatin and pemetrexid, I would give avastin with it. And you're right that there is data to continue avastin in the maintenance setting. So if this patient had gotten avastin, they would have continued avastin in the maintenance.

As an aside, if there's a person in the room or family member, people you know who couldn't get Avastin maintenance because there are lots of lists of reasons why Avastin may be less attractive to continue. The trial that showed Avastin was beneficial showed it was better than chemo by several weeks when you added Avastin. It was enough to get it into the guidelines and it's something I use routinely. But I like to say to my patients, if there's a reason you can't get it, the chemo is the part I don't want to miss out on. I'd love to add the Avastin when we can. I agree. If there's no reason not to, I would give it. First of all, thanks. This is fascinating and so important, this information, because I Each one of us, I think, has had a scan happen and then gotten in front of an oncologist. And this is going on behind the scenes. We don't know this. This is not explained to us how this happened. I heard a mention of a tumor board one time. So it's fascinating to see how it works. I hope it happens every time. My question is, how do I know, because there's too much to talk about, OK, with an oncologist, honestly, with this disease. I would need hours of time to satisfy every question I have, we have, about the disease. It's unrealistic. They did germline testing on him. And they did tumor marker testing on him. How do I know that the treatment he's currently receiving Receives the consideration that I just saw happen up here where you discussed among yourselves the tumor marker Results and the relation to the germline results We don't get that communication How do I know his treatment is guided by that those tests that were paid for and sit there in his portal? I was hoping you'd say, assume that it's done. I would never make the assumption. Assume they did it and just didn't talk to you. I mean, I would hope and assume that, you know, people at centers like this, yes, they are appreciating the results, they're reviewing the results, they're integrating them into their decisions. But the most important thing to integrate into a decision is the person getting the treatment. So I do think it's important. If you have a question about a fancy diagnostic test, that is not time wasted to bring up. So I advocate that you bring that up, like that's an important, like for instance, not to get in the weeds here, there's a new gene we're very interested in in terms of clinical trials. We've only found out about that gene of being interesting in the last few years. So if I have a person that was diagnosed three, four years ago and had a genetic test, we never tested for that gene on that panel. But that panel may give me a hint. because there's a gene that co-deletes with it. And a patient bringing that up to me and saying like, hey, what's going on with my genetic sequencing? You know what, maybe that scratches an itch I wasn't thinking about. And so I think it's very important, constantly advocate for yourself. These tests belong to you. Is that a good way to word it? How are the tests being used to infirm? I mean, my patients will come in and be like, are my genetics result back? I would like to discuss them, and that's it. I mean, that's as easy as it needs to be. It's like a CAT scan. The assumption is you should be discussing them.

And I think the reality is right now for standard of care treatments, other than some small nuances, we aren't making decisions based on the molecular testing yet. Most of the time we're making the decisions is about clinical trials. So just to be explicit about what Dr. Offen is saying, so we're talking about things like MTAP deletion. So these are maybe words you're starting to hear, M-T-A-P. So you can ask, have I been tested for MTAP deletion? or NF2 loss, that's another gene, NF2, and those are going to set up a patient's eligibility for certain clinical trials. So that's the type of conversation that we're starting to have, but this is all really new because we're finally seeing some drugs that, you know, potentially can target these things.
So the genetic testing done three years ago, is it still relevant?

I mean, genetic testing, like any test, is relevant in context, right? So if the gene you're interested in knowing about, like, let's say it's a trial. Let's say you walked in the clinic and said, am I eligible for this company's drug that says I must have this gene being wrong to get on? If it was in that panel? then that's still relevant. If it wasn't in that panel, then there are several ways you could actually go back and try to recapture genes and do, like using old specimens to get new answers is theoretically possible. But I would say it's still relevant, but if, you know, it was a new gene or you've had several intervening treatments in between, a repeat biopsy for repeat testing is also reasonable.
He's asking about somatic testing, and I think what Dr. Offen's saying is if you've had treatments that you would need, you may need.

The treatments we use in mesothelioma, unlike lung cancer and other things, don't have as much evidence that it could completely change the genetic makeup of the tumor, that could like, this gene wasn't there, I gave this drug, I would expect this drug to make this gene get messed up, and I expect to see it now, so let me biopsy it. We don't have that amount of, Equipoise, like we may have in lung cancer, like if somebody's on a pill, the pill stops working, you expect there's gonna be resistance and you repeat the biopsy. With that said, I do routinely, and if there's an easily accessible, like let's say somebody has a lymph node that we can feel, or something just under the skin, doing a repeat biopsy for repeat genetic testing, if you've had lots of treatments in between, is reasonable considering the current state of our clinical trials.
So I just had surgery, and there's a lot of biopsy material.

Should I request another nomics? I mean, again, without knowing your specific situation, depending on when the last genetic testing was done, how old that panel was, it's not unreasonable to discuss. I can't chime in too much about fancy genetics and stuff like that, but you should never feel shy to ask questions to your doctors. And if they get frustrated with you asking questions, you should get another doctor. Serious, totally serious.

You might have alluded to this, but I'm not quite clear. The genetic testing, I'm assuming for most people, was done when you had a fresh biopsy sample. And I know people can request slides and at least pick up a gene mutation or two, but can you really get a full genetic workup from saved I mean, I don't know. I don't know. I mean, I don't know.

As long as there's enough cells in there, the technology exists to extract the DNA. It doesn't have to be fresh material to do that. Often it's actually fixed in slides first and then DNA is extracted even on a fresh sample.

And mesothelioma, because we do such big biopsies a lot of the time, you know, we're doing surgical biopsies, we're actually lucky that there's usually a lot of tissue that's there. So in lung cancer, that's not always the case. In lung cancer, we sometimes have to, you know, decide what we're going to use the tissue for, but I haven't really had that problem with mesothelioma.
Quick question.

Just having all of you on the panel, first of all, thank you for making the time and flying out for all of us patients and so forth, feels a little bit misleading in that I feel like you guys are all Hall of Famer baseball players, so to speak.

And so to have you on a panel like this on a tumor board would be unusual. For us patients, if we're in an area where there's maybe, luckily, having one all-star, then they have a tumor board with a bunch of bench players and minimum salary folks. Do you know what I mean? It's like, how do we?
No insult, but how do we?
I mean, you're at UPenn, you're at Swedish, you're at MSK, MD Anderson, I'm sorry, you know what I'm saying. How do we do that as patients? Does that make sense?

I would turn around to Julie. So this foundation is imperative to that kind of streamlining for patients with this diagnosis. I get emails from Julie on the weekly for this exact reason. The most common patient I see, and I'm assuming most of us see, their second, third, fourth opinions for that exact reason. That's what we're here for. I'm very happy to review a colleague's kind of plan of care, testing that was done, agree or disagree and give comment. That's the easiest way to do it. The unfortunate truth is we've been trying to organize a virtual tumor board. That's very hard to do. It's like herding cats. But the easiest way is seeking second, third, fourth opinions and kind of figure out who those people you may want to speak to. The Marf Foundation, IMIG, these types of groups are a great resource.
And there's nothing wrong at all with seeking several opinions, right?

So actually, this is something the board, I'll speak for the board, is very interested in. We're talking about this idea of mesocenters of excellence. Certainly that's something I think this organization can work to provide. There are a lot of hurdles that really don't allow us to do telemedicine and other things. For example, I was raised in the area where touching and laying hands on the patient was critical and how dare you diagnose a patient you've never seen. But by and large, we can get a lot of things right on a telemedicine visit. And we kind of learned during the pandemic I diagnosed a pulmonary embolus very early in the pandemic, because the person was looking funny. And I was like, does anybody have a finger oxygen? They're like, oh, I just got one from Amazon. Put it on, and now run to the ER. You have a pulmonary embolus. So there's a lot we can do. We're currently, so as an organization, that's what we're here for. We're working on that. I would also say for advocacy, everyone is trying to put hurdles back up, or many people are trying to put hurdles back up. The federal government, different states are putting up hurdles so that we can't see across state lines and we can't provide opinions and I can't take care of my patients when they move to Virginia because I'm not licensed there and then I have to find someone who knows about a really rare cancer. It's very stressful. I think this is something in the modern world that is utterly unacceptable. There can be a person in the darkest corner of Appalachia with a perfectly good iPhone that I can give a great medical opinion to, and they can share their medical record with me, and I think it's unacceptable that we allow roadblocks to continue. You know, physicians can't complain about doctoring not being any good or payment not being any good. Scientists can't complain about no research funding because it's too self-interested. What really helps is where patients advocate, patient groups advocate for these changes. Because I think, again, if you can talk to your grandmother in Thailand without any trouble whatsoever, I've had conversations with people in the International Space Station, it's unacceptable to have area where you feel like you're being treated by guys who ride the pine? I think centralization in the care of certain diseases is very important. I think it's one of the things that Canada actually does very well in terms of mesothelioma. It's very centralized. I guess I'm lucky and unlucky to work in a place where we have a very large encatchment area. So I see people from Alaska, Montana, Dakotas, Oregon. And I do a lot of visits virtually, and it works out just fine. And when we need people to come in, you know, if they come in once, it's way better than having to schlep in four, five, six times, right? I mean, and you're right. We can call space from Texas, for crying out loud. Like, but you can't, like, do virtual visits? Like, it's nuts. So I think it's important to really push the virtual platform because there is a lot of stuff you can do remotely. And as long as they have a good physical exam locally, that's fine. And hopefully they can pick up on red flags and things like that. You can do a lot of directing and guidance of care remotely. And the best thing that might come out of it is you come up with an organized care plan that's put together by a bunch of people who are used to seeing something like this, and it gets carried out locally. And as long as the person locally doesn't have a major ego problem, then usually that's fine.

I do agree that it is probably for rare cancers particularly a second opinion especially if this diagnosis was made in the community to have the academic side is very critical but it needs to be a true second opinion. So I would not recommend just a chart review. Pathology needs to be reviewed. Imaging studies needs to be updated in an acceptable quality because what really makes centers, maybe a little bit more meticulous, is that it is a team effort. So, I am as good as my pathologist give me the right diagnosis. So, that is why it needs to be a true second opinion, not just a chart review. But this is a patient's right. It is not about physicians. It's about an individual's health. So, that is why I would be very supportive of that. I do agree that it is not very easy for every state or patients to be able to travel and foundations like this has been a great source, so it's very fortunate. I just have one more question now. I'm just I'm in the sports. Right. But I. The question is you know with the funding cuts on NIH. How has that affected the ability to learn from your colleagues across the country. What's going on with your field or do you have. your own kind of network that you deal with that is not that critical. And then the other question is, how are these clinical trials funded and supported? And how has that been affected by the decrease in federal funding?

It's a difficult question to answer on a recorded stage. The world continues to spin, medicine continues to lurch forward, and our patients remain our utmost concern. There are, in my colleagues' terms, a lot more roadblocks now than there were. Fortunate that we have several federal grants. I know many of us on the stage do. Mesothelioma, in particular, being the demographic that it tends to affect, at least on paper, the funding line there has not been as dramatically affected for some other areas of research, like DEI and things of that nature. But it's definitely become a much more difficult environment to get substantive funding. Our ability to communicate doesn't change, thankfully. So I texted Melina twice last week about patients. We constantly talk. What will become more difficult will be the ability to do cooperative group trials with federal funding and the way to combat that as the people sitting in this room in this foundation. Constant advocacy that this is important. This is not a partisan disease. Again, I'm not going to sit here and give my opinion on federal cuts in general because I have strong opinions, but for this specific disease state and the people affected by it this should not be a partisan discussion and Funding should remain in my opinion and that's what we keep advocating for I know doctors outer is not on stage right now But she's been instrumental in advocating for continued mesothelioma support last meeting We marched on Capitol Hill to continue the support for this I think it's acts like that That'll keep me so in the limelight as a nonpartisan need

And just to answer your question about clinical trials briefly. So most clinical trials are funded by pharmaceutical companies that are making the drug. And that's great. They're amazing partners in this disease. And it's awesome that they're developing drugs in mesothelioma. So we enjoy partnering with them. It does leave out some of the questions that they're not interested in. You know, maybe it doesn't involve their drug. And that's where these cooperative groups come in. So trials with ECOG, Alliance, SWOG, these are names of cooperative oncology group trials. And those are the groups that have a significant amount of federal funding and they are having some trouble with those trials. Thankfully, again, our industry partners are stepping up. and they are helping with those trials, but that's where we need the advocacy.

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended prompt initiation of systemic therapy rather than surgery, given extensive pleural disease with transdiaphragmatic and abdominal involvement and the patient’s underlying giant cell arteritis, which made immunotherapy less attractive as first-line treatment. Carboplatin plus pemetrexed was selected, with a total of six cycles recommended after initial response to chemotherapy. Pemetrexed maintenance was discussed but was not favored because of emerging cumulative toxicity, the patient’s preference for a treatment break, and lack of strong evidence for benefit. Ongoing management should include clinical and laboratory monitoring, with consideration of radiation if future progression is symptomatic, particularly for chest wall pain.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Lower urinary tract symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, initially low-risk disease diagnosed in 2015; subsequently upgraded on repeat biopsy in April 2019 to Grade Group 2, Gleason score 3+4=7, favorable intermediate-risk, left-sided disease.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial prostate biopsy in 2015: 1/12 cores positive for prostate cancer, Grade Group 1, involving 30% of a left-sided core.  
- Confirmatory biopsy after initial diagnosis: 1/12 cores positive in the same left-sided region, Grade Group 1, involving 30% of the core.  
- Repeat biopsy in April 2019: 2/12 cores positive, both left-sided. One core from the left apex showed Grade Group 2 disease; one core from the left mid gland showed Grade Group 2 disease involving 10% of the core.  
- Biopsy pathology demonstrated Gleason pattern 3 and pattern 4, overall Gleason score 3+4=7, with pattern 3 predominating.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial prostate MRI: prostate volume 73 cc; no obvious lesions identified.  
- Repeat prostate MRI: prostate volume approximately 100 cc; PI-RADS 3 lesion on the left side.  
- MRI also showed marked benign prostatic hyperplasia with heterogeneous enlargement of the gland.  
- Left seminal vesicle appeared diminutive, darker in signal, and atrophic.  
- Tumor localization on MRI was not clearly defined.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA in 2015: 4.9 ng/mL.  
- PSA in April 2019: 8.5 ng/mL.  
- Digital rectal examination at initial workup was normal.  
- IPSS: 25.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Active surveillance was elected after initial diagnosis in 2015.  
- Active surveillance continued through at least February following the April 2019 biopsy, during which PSA rose and repeat biopsy demonstrated upgrading from Grade Group 1 to Grade Group 2 disease.  
- The patient underwent consultations with radiation oncology and obtained second opinions during this interval.

[ current disease status ]: Localized unilateral prostate cancer, left-sided, Grade Group 2 in 2/12 biopsy cores, with PSA 8.5 ng/mL and enlarged prostate gland.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No erectile dysfunction was reported.  
- No contributory family history was reported.  
- Prostate gland size increased from 73 cc to approximately 100 cc over the documented interval.

And so an aggressive dose regimen may be potentially a little bit more risky in that setting. But those would be his radiation options to consider.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 15-year-old female student (Form 2), from Kisii.

[ chief complaint ]: Dry cough, chest pain, and difficulty in breathing for 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET) / small round blue cell tumor involving the right labia majora, with pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the right labia majora mass performed in November of the previous year showed an extensive infiltrate of monotonous round blue cells with scant cytoplasm. Scattered abnormal mitotic figures were present, reported as 4 per 10 high-power fields in areas. Tumor cells were arranged in nodules with thickened hyalinized fibrotic intervening stroma, with prominent vascularity. Hemorrhage was present. Necrosis was not identified microscopically. Tumor extended to the margins of excision. Gross description reported two large tissue biopsies together weighing 200 g, with rough surfaces; the largest measured 10 × 9 × 4 cm and another measured 8 × 9 × 6 cm; cut section was variegated and hemorrhagic with necrotic areas.

[ imaging findings ]: Chest CT showed widespread nodular masses of varying sizes in both lungs, with the largest measuring up to 7 cm in diameter. Central hypodense areas were present within the nodules. There was bilateral pleural infiltration and minimal right-sided pleural effusion. Heart and bones were reported as normal. Radiologic impression was widespread bilateral lung nodules with associated right-sided pleural effusion, consistent with chest metastases from an unknown primary at the time of imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: GeneXpert was negative. Pregnancy test was negative. Alpha-fetoprotein was within normal range. Beta-hCG was within normal range. LDH was elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Thoracocentesis was performed after identification of pleural effusion. The vulval mass had been biopsied in November of the previous year. Immunohistochemistry was subsequently performed early in the current month and supported the diagnosis of PNET. No prior medical or surgical ward admissions were reported.

[ current disease status ]: At presentation on 29th of the previous month, the patient had symptomatic metastatic disease involving both lungs with pleural involvement and right-sided pleural effusion, and a persistent right labia majora mass. On examination, she was in fair general condition with mild distress. She was not pale, jaundiced, or cyanosed. Respiratory examination demonstrated bilateral bronchial breath sounds. Local examination showed a right labia majora mass measuring 6 × 4 cm, firm, mobile, and non-tender, with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination showed no fullness, organomegaly, masses, or tenderness. Other systems were essentially normal.

[ other clinical data ]: Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse CD99 positivity and negativity for desmin, EMA, S100, synaptophysin, chromogranin, and MPO. These findings were reported as compatible with PNET in the appropriate clinicoradiologic context.
