case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging multinodular thyroid disease with development of symptoms from a left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, identified after left lobectomy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2015 fine-needle aspiration (outside institution) of a 3.6 cm left thyroid nodule showed nodular hyperplasia; follicular neoplasm could not be ruled out.  
- Subsequent fine-needle aspiration (outside institution) of the enlarging left thyroid nodule showed benign follicular cells with lymphocytes, with possible lymphocytic thyroiditis.  
- Cytopathology from outside institutions was not reviewed at the treating institution.  
- Left thyroid lobectomy pathology showed a 4.5 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma without extrathyroidal extension, lymphatic invasion, or vascular invasion. Tumor was completely resected with negative margins.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Left thyroid nodule measured 3.6 cm in 2015, 3.7 cm in 2016, 3.8 cm in 2018, and 4.2 cm in 2019.  
- Two contralateral thyroid nodules measured 0.6 cm and 0.4 cm in 2019 and did not meet biopsy criteria.  
- Post-lobectomy neck ultrasound for lymph node mapping showed no highly suspicious lymph nodes and no lesion suitable for biopsy.  
- CT neck with contrast showed no suspicious lymph nodes.  
- CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis with three-phase contrast showed scattered small subcentimeter pulmonary nodules, a 6.5 cm hepatic hemangioma, a calcified splenic granuloma, an adnexal cyst, and a kidney stone.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Germline genetic testing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Five weeks after lobectomy, calcitonin was undetectable.  
- Five weeks after lobectomy, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 77.5.  
- Calcium and parathyroid hormone were within normal limits.  
- Subsequently, calcitonin and CEA decreased to undetectable levels prior to completion surgery.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Left thyroid nodule was observed serially from 2015 to 2019 due to gradual enlargement.  
- Left thyroid lobectomy was performed for interval growth and symptom development. Pathology demonstrated a 4.5 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma, completely resected with negative margins.  
- Completion thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck dissection was performed approximately 90 days later.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Family history was negative for medullary thyroid cancer.  
- Brother had recurrent kidney stones.  
- The adnexal cyst prompted gynecology referral.  
- Colonoscopy was performed because she was due for screening.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-positive left breast invasive ductal carcinoma (estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER2-positive), presenting with fixed axillary lymphadenopathy and synchronous liver metastasis, consistent with stage IV oligometastatic breast cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. Liver lesion at presentation was biopsy-confirmed metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial breast evaluation demonstrated a 3 cm left breast mass. Regional lymph nodes were at least 2 cm and fixed. Metastatic workup identified a liver lesion in one lobe of the liver; both described metastatic sites were less than 2 cm in size.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Estrogen receptor positive. Progesterone receptor positive. HER2 positive.

[ current disease status ]: De novo oligometastatic, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-positive breast cancer with fixed axillary nodal disease and a single biopsy-proven liver metastasis.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history included a great-aunt with melanoma. First mammogram was performed at age 58.

reference_discussion.text: All right, we'll move on to our next case. She's 58 years old. She presented with a breast mass in the left breast. She actually had her first mammogram at 58, which we know is not good. Most common type of breast cancer as well, invasive ductal carcinoma. She's estrogen positive as well, progesterone positive, and HER2 new positive. So that's what we call triple positive breast cancer. She had a family history of a great aunt with melanoma. The breast itself, she had a three centimeter mass. Her lymph nodes were at least two centimeters in size and fixed. So the doctors did what we call a metastatic workup. She had a lesion in one lobe of the liver. Both areas were less than two centimeters in size. and we're gonna go with, start talking about the chemotherapy regimen that will be recommended and possible clinical trials and move on.

I guess I get to go first. So I haven't seen that, she had surgery, right? No. Yeah, so this is one of those kind of oligo metastatic cases again, where there's kind of these isolated liver lesions. And so I think for this case, you know, again, Yes, this is stage four disease. This is devastating. Can I cure the patient? When we say cure, is there a way to get rid of all the tumor and not leave anything behind? I think this case is yes, but this person needs treatment. The kind of way to do this is you can kind of take a neoadjuvant approach. So there's a lot of different ways to do this. I think giving her a combination of Taxotere, Carboplatin, Herceptin, and Progetta up front. So that's kind of two different chemo drugs and then two different anti-HER2 drugs, assess for a response, and then you can take that patient for surgical resection. Afterwards, then you need, and again, up front, you need a multidisciplinary approach because I need my surgeon on board and I need my radiation doctor on board because the chemo is not going to cure this person. The chemo will shrink the tumor. It will make it go away. I may even make it not detectable on scans, but unless you can either cut it out or burn it out, that person is going to have a relapse. So I need buy-in from these two, and we're going to hear from them in a second about getting it out afterwards. Once that is finished, if there's any residual tumor, and maybe we can kind of come back and circle back and we'll talk about this, is what do you do afterwards? Because typically for HER2-positive disease, you need anti-HER2 therapy to complete one year total of therapy, and she's going to need an anti-estrogen because of the ERPR positivity. So once she gets through chemo and surgery and radiation, we'll hear from our colleagues there, she still needs more stuff for a whole nother year.

There's a little bit of uncertainty here based on response, but let me just generally speak. So in some centers, because the chemotherapists are so outstanding at their job, Keeping track of the liver lesion is going to be a little bit of a trick, because if you didn't put anything there, you don't know where it is anymore. And image fusion with pre- and post-therapy is tricky. It's not as accurate as, say, putting a fiducia in or marking the tumor somehow. The reality is that if you're talking about post-upfront, what we call neoadjuvant chemotherapy, or post-surgical radiation in the adjuvant setting, we're fighting an invisible disease, right? So a woman has a lumpectomy or a mastectomy, and there's a statistical risk. Technically, that patient is no evidence of disease, but the radiation doctor doesn't believe it because we're professional pessimists, and so we treat the area despite there being no detectable disease. In this case, you have a patient who presented oligometastatic, And there is a little bit of a question right now in the radiation oncology literature, how do we help the most? Because if the lesions disappear, you can't really do, we talked about the difference a little while ago about ablative versus radiotherapy. Am I destroying the target or am I scrubbing and cleansing the target? This woman can have the area of the breast or chest wall cleansed by fractionated radiation. But if the targets have disappeared, you cannot ablate a target you can't define. You can't destroy the entire contents of a volume you can't draw. So in a very good way, the radiation doctor may have been booted out of this case in terms of the metastatic disease. And that's good. We're fine with that. and in a complete response. In an incomplete response, then we would be back in that oligometastatic setting and we'd probably go to tumor board and come up with a way to treat this. The last thing I'd like to say about this case is let's pretend the liver lesion was there and we wanted it out. Although, It is true that the first prospective randomized trial was using a technology from my department. That doesn't mean you can't extrapolate from the data. There is a real role for surgical oncology to address liver metastases. There's an absolute real role for interventional radiology. So we don't want to get caught up too much in this. For your radiation oncologist to address a liver lesion, they're often going to want a fiducial marker placed. But if the interventional radiologist is sitting with a needle in the middle of the lesion, it's pretty easy to use energy at that time to destroy that lesion. Why go through the extra effort of having radiation afterwards? So these are the things that you work out in a multidisciplinary tumor board. And I'm sorry I couldn't give more specific advice, but again, the response kind of boots me out for a minute. Yeah. All right.

All right. OK. So Dr. French brought up the role of surgery in stage 4 disease. So in most cases, there is a questionable benefit, but the data is changing. So at our facility, patients who present with stage four disease, the best patients who do well are patients that have bone metastasis fibrillates sites. It's changing now for her to new positive patients. The reason being is because once you get that treatment, a lot of times when we go to surgery, particularly if they're not stage four, we see very little disease there. So, there's some current literature out now, say for instance, this is that particular patient with liver metastasis. You know, the study is not all the way conclusive, but I will tell you there are some patients who would offer her surgical intervention. The latest literature, based on what I know, is about 27 percent increase in survival. And so she would be given that choice. And I will tell you, when I talk to patients and they have stage four disease, a lot of them want it out because their goal is to get this out. But what I tell them is that in some cases we can't get that out, what's already spread. The best treatment for stage four patients is usually what we call systemic treatment radiation therapy. So in some cases we would offer it to them, but like I said, we would present this case in tumor board and see how she did after chemotherapy.

I agree. I also just want to reiterate, these are challenging cases in women who have oligometastatic disease, and I do think that it requires an upfront multidisciplinary discussion. The only reason why we're able to even offer potentially a multidisciplinary approach is because we do have very good, now systemic agents that offer prolonged survival in these women, even with oligometastatic disease. So, but I do think that these are case-by-case discussions and unfortunately it doesn't apply to every woman. And so, in some women we do solely offer systemic therapy with actually very good survival and very good quality of life and control of their symptoms related to their breast cancer. And in other women we may offer a more aggressive approach with a combination of surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy.

So, she did have surgery on this patient, so we're still, this is going to be quick for the medical oncologist. So she had residual tumor, 1.5 centimeters, 4 out of 18 positive lymph nodes. What would you offer at this point?

So for this woman, we have gone with a more aggressive approach with upfront neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a very good response of her cancer, and then the woman has gone for surgical resection at this point. So now we're at a point where we have no evidence of disease in the woman, but we still are looking for treatment to prevent the recurrence of her breast cancer in the future. There is actually some newer data that just came out in December of 2018 that utilizes a new drug called Kedsilo, which was previously used only in the metastatic setting for HER2-positive disease. We're now looking to use that in women who have residual HER2-positive breast cancer at the time of their breast surgery. And that has actually offered an improvement in both in invasive breast cancer survival. And shortly, I think we will get some survival data on this as well that will show overall survival benefit. Kedsila is given similarly to Herceptin, which was used previously in these women, IV every three weeks. So the options that we would have would be Kedsila, IV every three weeks to complete a full year of HER2-directed therapy versus Herceptin with or without Progetta to complete a full year of therapy. For this woman, given the aggressive nature of her disease with liver metastases, I would offer her KEDSILA, although she does not perfectly fit the patients that were studied in the KEDSILA, in the Catherine trial for KEDSILA. I would still offer her KEDSILA, given the improvement that we've seen in invasive breast cancer recurrence with the use of that drug.

Yeah, I would agree with that. I think if you look at the Catherine data that was published in the New England Journal of Medicine, you know, the hazard ratio is like 50%. So that basically means there's a 50% reduction in someone's invasive disease-free survival or invasive disease-free survival from their breast cancer. So you can take someone who's, you know, 77% and bump them up to 88% chance that maybe those people are cured. You're extrapolating that data because this person had a liver lesion So you're kind of extrapolating that data to say, yes, this drug works better if there is residual tumor left behind. If the person had a pathologic complete response, meaning at the time of surgery, yes, we know we marked those tumors, we cut them out, and there's just scar tissue, it might be reasonable to continue the Herceptin or even just the Herceptin Progetta and not switch the drug. But because there was a little bit of tumor left behind with this new data that came out in December, we would probably switch her. She also has one other option, which is after, now we're oncologists, so we keep doing things to patients, right? Is after she finishes that anti-HER2 therapy, she does have the option to take a pill, which is called neratinib, which is an anti-HER2 directed pill. Again, this is being extrapolated from adjuvant therapy, meaning these are not stage four patients, but there was an invasive disease survival increase by about 2% if you add this pill for another year after you've already done the year of anti-HER2 therapies. Now we're talking, after surgical resection, two more years, one of IV and one of pills, to add to this woman for about maybe a 2% to 4% benefit. This is a little tough because on the pill, I don't think there's a lot of people that are prescribing this for a 2% benefit. Now, obviously, if it's stage four and you're trying to cure these people, maybe there's some data there. But, you know, the cost is an issue. You want to talk about that?

Yeah, I totally agree, Dr. French, with what you're saying, and I do think it is worth a discussion to talk about the use of Neurotinib after CAD-SILA. The one thing I will say about it is there are specificities seen with the Neurotinib, the primary one being pretty severe diarrhea. And so if it does end up being a quality of life issue, I think at that point you do have to weigh the risks and the benefits of how much survival improvement do we get with what are we doing with the quality of life for our patient. The other thing I would also like to mention is that women was triple positive, so we would add hormonal therapy in addition to any HER2-directed therapy that we would do after surgery. And so I do think that there is a chance potentially for what we call cure for this patient, although she would need very close follow-up given still a higher risk of recurrence with the fact that she had liver metastases at the time of her diagnosis.

So she comes back now, she comes back a year later, and just has some memory loss, just doesn't feel like herself. And so we do a metastatic workup, including brain MRI, and she does have a single foci. Dr. Cavanaugh, you want to address that?

I'm glad that we've moved on to a brain metastasis because the post-mastectomy radiation question in this case is impossibly tough, and I don't have a study. So let's move on to the brain, Matt. So in this case, I believe we have a biopsy-confirmed lesion in the liver at presentation. OK, so we have evidence of hematogenous spread, right? Cancer can spread three ways. It can invade what's next. Next to it, it can go through lymph nodes. It can go through the blood. This one already learned how to go through the blood. That's really important. Because if the brain lesion is the first presentation, you've got a real trick on your hands. Do you blast away as if you know what you're doing, or do you require some proof? In this case, we can probably just go ahead and take care of the problem. So you would have a neurosurgery consult, and you'd have a radiation oncology consult. And you deserve both. And most patients, unless the neurosurgery is going to be very easy, it's a place that's going to induce very little deficit, most patients in this situation are going to lean towards stereotactic radiosurgery. And the reason is, if you have the lesion resected, you're still going to need radiation. And so why not just take care of it with a single shot of radiation? A lesion under two cm, what did we say the size was? I'm sorry. In the brain?
Two centimeters.

Okay, so your radiation doctor is probably going to be on the fence between a single shot and a few shots, but that should be a lesion they should be able to control fairly readily. Under no circumstances in 2019 would a woman in that situation receive whole brain radiotherapy. because we would want to treat again. We're not going to use radiotherapy, which is scrubbing something clean with repeated daily treatments. We're going to use radio ablation or radiosurgery, which is let's destroy the target in a very, very thin rind around the target. In this case, your margin on the target would be about 1.5 millimeters. So if you can imagine that, it's a very, very tight situation. You're just destroying everything inside because there's no functional brain tissue in there. That's all disease. And so that's how that would be managed. From that point onward, your radiation oncologist is likely to be your brain manager going forward. So yes, you're going to see your medical oncologist just as much. We're not taking anything away from them. But the radon could be expected to continue to follow indefinitely. And we actually aren't able to tell you right now what the survival data are for repeated SRS, SRT, as we call it. in situations like this because they're changing so rapidly. I have many patients who have had a half a dozen or more stereotactic interventions in the brain over several years. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Liver nodules identified on surveillance ultrasound in the setting of cirrhosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal infiltrative hepatocellular carcinoma involving the right hepatic lobe and lower liver, in the setting of cirrhosis secondary to previously treated hepatitis C virus infection with sustained virologic response. Child-Pugh class A6 liver function.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance ultrasound demonstrated liver nodules. Contrast-enhanced CT showed diagnostic imaging appearance of hepatocellular carcinoma with two measurable nodules in the right lobe. Additional lower hepatic lesions included nodules and confluent irregular infiltrative disease; the dominant infiltrative mass measured slightly greater than 5 cm. No portal vein tumor involvement was identified; the main portal vein, right portal vein, and segmental branches were patent and free of disease. Extensive gastroesophageal varices were present. No extrahepatic spread was described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Platelet count 106. INR normal. Sodium normal. Creatinine normal. Alkaline phosphatase 99. ALT 35. AST 63. Bilirubin at the upper limit of normal. Albumin 3.5 g/dL. Iron deficiency anemia was present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Hepatitis C virus infection had been treated successfully, with sustained virologic response. The patient had been taking iron supplementation for iron deficiency anemia. No prior cancer-directed therapy was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated multifocal intrahepatic disease without documented vascular invasion or extrahepatic metastases. Preserved liver function with Child-Pugh A6 cirrhosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Cirrhosis was present. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable apart from obesity and mild hypertension. Past medical history was otherwise not significant.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old Asian man. No past medical history was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache and seizure.

[ diagnosis ]: Left insular/temporal astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Diffuse infiltrating glioma with astrocytic morphology. Cellularity was moderately increased compared with normal brain. Nuclear pleomorphism/variation in morphology was present, consistent with an astrocytic tumor. GFAP immunohistochemistry was positive. Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 1-2%.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a homogeneous T2-hyperintense, non-enhancing tumor centered in the left insula with extension into the overlying temporal lobe. Post-contrast imaging showed no tumor enhancement. Preoperative functional assessment demonstrated left hemispheric dominance for language and memory. Postoperative imaging demonstrated resection of a sizable portion of the lateral temporal lobe, with residual deep tumor involving the insula and beyond left in situ.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation was detected by PCR. MGMT promoter was methylated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent subtotal surgical resection consisting of a modified minimal temporal lobectomy. The hippocampus and deep insular portions of tumor were not resected because of involvement of eloquent/deep structures. After surgery, the patient initially deferred further treatment despite residual disease. Subsequently, seizures increased in frequency.

[ current disease status ]: Residual non-enhancing low-grade glioma remained in the left insular/deep temporal region following subtotal resection. The patient had ongoing/increasing seizures after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion involved anatomically high-risk regions including the temporal lobe, insula, and deep structures adjacent to the basal ganglia/internal capsule. Functional risk considerations included potential involvement of memory, language, motor, and sensory systems. A Wada test was referenced as an available confirmatory study for hemispheric dominance.

Sure. Here we see in the region of what's called the insula and the overlying temporal lobe, we see an area of rather homogeneous T2 signal increase. Again, this kind of whiter color on the scan. When we look at the post-contrast images, we just see some spots here and those are the blood vessels, so those are normal, but we don't really see any enhancement of the tumor itself. This looks like a non-enhancing tumor that's centered in the left insula.
Surgery on this patient.

Lesions like this can pose a real challenge to us as surgeons for several reasons which The location here anatomically involves potentially multiple functional systems in the brain. The portion that's in the temporal lobe might involve the hippocampus, which is involved in memory formation, and other portions in the insula and beyond are involved potentially in the speech language system. Then the deep portion of this as it gets towards structures in the brain called the basal ganglia and internal capsule can border on motor and sensory systems. So really all of the major systems are potentially at risk for a surgery to remove a tumor like this. And we'll typically need to balance that between the apparent low-grade type appearance of this and balance all of those factors together. Again, we rely on our presurgical mapping, our functional MRI studies to understand where the language systems might be located, as well as proving and confirming which hemisphere of this patient's brain is dominant for language and memory systems. The probability studies would tell us that about 90 plus percent of people, their left hemisphere is dominant, and that was the case in this patient here. There's an additional type of study, which is mentioned on the next slide, called a WADA test, which is a test that's done in interventional radiology, where a drug is injected into one hemisphere of the brain, which sort of temporarily inactivates that hemisphere. And that further can confirm whether or not, you know, sort of taking that hemisphere offline knocks out the language and memory systems and further confirms hemispheric dominance of the brain. So if a test like that or the functional MRI proved that the left hemisphere was dominant, we would know that a surgical attempt to remove this entire lesion really would put all of those major functional systems at play. Beyond that, beyond just the functional systems are the sort of deep, arterial anatomy of the brain gets complicated for tumors in this region. You've basically got, in the depths of this mass, a bunch of fine blood vessels, which each supply blood to really important parts of the deep structures in the brain, the basal ganglia and thalamus, as well as blood vessels, which sort of travel over this area, which go on to supply other critical regions of the brain, like the motor cortex. And so, you know, we were really entering into high risk territory with a surgery on a tumor like this. And for this instance, you know, weighing all these factors, we elected a strategy to mitigate against all that risk, but still establish some important things that we can do surgically, number one, reducing the number of cells, and number two, confirming the diagnosis. So using our pre-surgical mapping, we can determine that parts of the temporal lobe are going to be the safest surgical target. And so in this instance, that's what was done at surgery, a modified sort of minimal temporal lobectomy, excluding the deep structures of the hippocampus, excluding the part that enters into the insula and puts all those speech and motor functions at risk. And what we've got on the next slide here is sort of the results of that in that, you know, a sizable part of the lateral temporal lobe is removed surgically, but the deep structures, the deep portions of the tumor that crawl into the insula and beyond are left intact, you know, in place to mitigate against the risk of the functional deficits that could be acquired by to cavalierly entering into those areas. That other slide there does make a note. To do this well, you have to understand the full three-dimensional anatomy and some looks can be deceiving. But in this day with our really amazing imaging that we can get here, that's not such a surprise anymore.
We'll go through neural pathology.

Okay, and here we have and yes you can see as a theme of what we call diffuse gliomas, these are tumors in which the cells kind of infiltrate their brain in a single cell level that's why they are in many ways, very challenging. to treat. So you have in the in the left hand side, what we call a low power view, and the similarity I will say is kind of moderate is increased, we can recognize as increased compared to normal brain. but not to the extent that we saw with an anaplastic oligoendoglioma and the glioblastomas. Here on the right-hand side, upper corner, you see a higher magnification view. You can start seeing the individual nuclei. And here, you can see the variation in the morphology and the shape. That is something very typical of astrocytic tumors compared to oligoendogliomas, for example, that we saw earlier. And the lower left side, you have an immunostain. We stain for proteins with a variety, for a variety of proteins. That's the technique that we use as immunohistochemistry. And here we stain for GFAP, which is a marker of glial tumor. tumors, particularly astrocytic tumors, they tend to have all these processes that are GFIP positive. It's one way how we recognize it as astrocytomas by other methods. And you see here that on the right hand side, the Ki67, again, a marker of cells that are dividing or in the cell cycle that are actively dividing is something that you don't see in normal brain. Here, you do have some increase. compared to normal rate, 1 to 2%, but not to the extent that we saw again in the other higher grade tumors. So this is actually reassuring. It tells you that the tumor is proliferating, but at a very low rate. We can go to the next. So in 2007, and even 2016, we will have called these diffuse astrocytoma WHO grade 2. Now, in 2016, the IDH information was added. So we need to add it with the signet whether IDH mutant or not. And in the more current one, the terminology of diffuse astrocytoma has been supplanted by just calling it astrocytoma, specifying whether it's IDH mutant, and also the grades. And they can go from grade 2 to grade 3 to grade 4. Grade 2 is at the lower grade of the spectrum. They all start at grade 2s, these diffuse gliomas. And they have very little proliferation like this tumor. So this is, in some ways, the best you can get within that group of tumors. In a grade three, we'll have more proliferation. In a grade four, we'll have areas that are very similar to glioblastoma with a lot of necrosis and vascular changes. So this is at the lower end of the spectrum based on proliferation. It does have IDH mutation detected by PCR. And it's MGMT methylated, which, again, is a good pregnancy factor. And many of these IDH mutant tumors, both astrocytic and oligos, The majority of them are MDMT methylated. So there is some, they're somewhat related, not 100%, but there's a big overlap there.

So there's no need for immediate treatment. In terms of, incompletely resected tumors. This goes into this high-risk, low-grade category. What we found here was that the early radiotherapy improved progression-free survival, but there was no difference in overall survival. What it said was also in the incompletely resected group, we could also delay radiation. I wanted to make one comment, though. You know, there was a question about, you know, why are we showing data that's this old? And the main reason is that that's what we have right now. But there is a complication because low-grade tumors at that time were not categorize the way they are in 2021 with everything that Dr. Rodriguez is talking about. While the majority may have been IDH mutant tumors, not all of them were, and plus we weren't able to, didn't necessarily have the 1p19q as well.

In this case, a patient actually decided that he didn't want to undergo treatment yet, although technically he would be in the high-risk group. But he did start having more and more seizures and then decided that he wanted to undergo treatment after. I'm sorry, I'd like to answer some patients' questions. So I thought I'd go a little faster with some of these cases at this point. So for a patient who then opted to get treatment Dr. Lai, do you want to start talking about?

Yeah, so these are the options. Radiation therapy alone, and I think Dr. Cabralian will talk about the dosing PCV before or after option one. Enrollment in a phase three clinical trial with AD881, that's something that we have finished enrolling in. chemotherapy alone, radiation therapy, 60 grade, surgical resection. Option number two here is radiation plus concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide. So what we are doing here at UCLA, or we're trying to do, and this again is, we will tailor it for a patient, but we are trying to do PCV before or after radiation. And typically we're doing it after radiation. instead of temozolomide and I think the next slide will talk about some of the data so yeah this is our to G 9802 and this 98 signifies that it was this this this was actually initiated in 1998 so. That is 24 years ago, but what it clearly showed in the high risk, low grade astrocytomas and oligo astrocytomas that radiation plus PCV was superior to radiation alone and. Hopefully, you've gotten used to looking at these Kaplan-Meier curves. And we look at overall survival. And this just shows that with the circle in the yellow, that's radiation plus PCB. And that is radiation alone. And you can also see here with eight years of follow-up, greater than 50% are alive. doing well at eight years. But there are the caveats, as I said, there was insufficient 1p19q biomarker data. The samples were, I don't think they had enough to really, really even differentiate which ones were IDH mutant in there, although we do know that most of them would have been, but still, that can definitely create noise. And I think, so what you might be saying, well, why are we using PCV if you said PCV is really, really great for all of our endotheliomas? Again, we're following the data. So this, even though it's from 1998, it was read out more recently, we don't have a head-to-head comparison between PCV, which is a combination of three chemotherapies, procarbazine, CCNU, and vincristine versus temozolomide. Temozolomide would not be the wrong answer and a lot of institutions are using temozolomide. But we have this data which clearly shows the benefit of adding PCV to radiation. We don't really have the same data comparing PCV and temozolomide. I think that's coming up. But we do tailor our treatments based on the patient. I think most people would agree that temozolomide is easier to administer than PCV and it's easier on the patient. But with data like this, we are trying to do radiation plus PCV for these patients.
Dr. Kapoli, you want to talk a little bit about radiation?

Yeah, it's very similar to the prior images that we saw. The only difference is that the margin would be smaller than a high-grade glioma, and the standard dose for a low-grade glioma is 54 gray. Typically, we would do it at 1.8 gray daily fractions over 30 treatments. Really, that's the main difference between the two.

So just a summary of a lot of the things that Dr. Lai spoke about. We do consider watchful waiting for the grade 2 gliomas if they had gross total resection. So we really would consider what's the extent of their residual tumor. We want to make sure that they have an IDH mutation. Of course, that's changed a little bit now. They have to have an IDH mutation to stay at the low grade. Anyway, their patient's age, how much of the pathology may be indicating a higher, faster growing tumor. And it does look like if we do treat, we want to treat with radiation and chemotherapy since those data show that it's better than radiation alone. And again, because of the data, we do prefer using PCV for the low-grade tumors. That is what is available in our data, although we really don't know yet what to make of temozolomide. So if we have results that may change. Again, I think also to just explain why these data are so old is, you know, these patients with low grade tumors do well. And so it can take many years before we start seeing some definitive results to actually make sense and make treatment decisions. There's also the idea of IDH inhibitor, which I spoke about in my experimental therapy lecture. However, the trial that we have currently is close to enrollment, but that is will have results in the next few years. And that may change what we do in the future for the lower grade IDH mutant tumors. So onto case five. This is a 45-year-old Asian gentleman who presented with headache and also a seizure. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Sex was male.

[ chief complaint ]: Right renal mass with tumor thrombus extending through the inferior vena cava into the right atrium.

[ diagnosis ]: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney, with inferior vena cava tumor thrombus extending to the right atrium. No evidence of adenopathy was reported.

[ imaging findings ]: Tumor thrombus extended from the right renal vein/inferior vena cava to the right atrium. No adenopathy was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right radical nephrectomy with inferior vena cava thrombectomy and atrial thrombectomy in conjunction with vascular surgery.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status following right radical nephrectomy, inferior vena cava thrombectomy, and atrial thrombectomy. No nodal disease was identified in the available clinical data.

[ other clinical data ]: Lymph node dissection was discussed in the operative context, but no pathologic nodal involvement was reported. No laboratory or molecular/genomic data were available.
slides: <image> Axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT image shown during discussion of a right renal mass with associated venous tumor thrombus extension.

reference_discussion.text: Right nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy and atrial thrombectomy in conjunction with our vascular surgery colleagues.
Okay. What would your approach be? What decision would you make?

I would do a midline incision, and then the vascular surgeon might decide to do a sternotomy if they cannot get the heart thrombus from the abdomen. So that will be one long incision from the, basically from the neck down all the way to the pubic bone.
Okay.
But it could be done in different ways, but that's the approach I would do.
Okay. Dr. Chapin, I presume you're allowed to do this. What would be your approach?

Yeah, so in conjunction with you or Dr. Karam or Dr. Mateen, I would perform a right radical nephrectomy and thrombectomy with the help of the vascular team. Again, I'd do the same through a midline approach. In the absence of, you know, we talk about lymph node dissections and you're probably either going to bring that up or if you haven't already. I would do a lymph node dissection and this just as a function of trying to dissect out the vessels anyway.

Would anybody consider preoperative embolization? So just for the audience, preoperative embolization means that just prior to surgery, basically putting a cork in the renal artery to cut off blood flow to the kidney with the tumor in it. And in past series, that is actually, that used to be the sort of standard approach for this type of a tumor. Would anyone consider it?
No.

Okay. In the old days, we used to do that, and the thought process behind it was that these tumor thrombi are very vascular, and so by cutting off blood flow to the tumor thrombus, the hope was that you could get it to shrink down and avoid the complications associated with having a median sternotomy and having to be put on cardiopulmonary bypass and so forth. And there are anecdotes in the literature where you see this tumor thrombus much like this that shrinks way, way down almost to the renal vein. The problem is that that almost never happens. And so the morbidity or the side effects associated with embolization are probably not worth the potential benefits. And so we rarely, if ever, will embolize patients nowadays before surgery.
Can I ask you, if the patient had compromised liver function, would you do it in that scenario? Not in the setting of planning to do the operation, but in the setting of trying to treat what's there?
That's a good question. I'll throw that one over to Dr. Karam. What do you think?

So I had this in my presentation, but just for the sake of time, I didn't include it. So what you're referring to is when the tumor thrombus and the vena cava goes to the veins of the liver and basically blocks the liver outflow. And that's called Bud-Chiari syndrome. And for those patients, we routinely do not take them to surgery immediately, but we first do the embolization procedure. to try to shrink the tumor from those veins and allow the liver to recover, and then if they recover well, we will take them to do the operation.

Yeah, so in our experience with Bud-Kiari syndrome, and Bud-Kiari, Bud was a doctor and Kiari was a doctor who described this syndrome. It's hepatic outflow obstruction associated with abnormalities in LFTs, they develop abdominal ascites, they develop lower extremity edema, and they develop liver perfusion abnormalities, clotting, clotting factors that the liver produce become abnormal. And in our experience with taking these patients to surgery, the in-hospital mortality rate is in excess of 80 percent, meaning that 80 percent of the time these patients never leave the hospital, they die in the hospital. So now we approach them with this embolization process, again, hoping that the tumor thrombus is vascular, hoping that it shrinks a little bit so that they can, again, regain hepatic outflow and return their liver function to normal. The problem with embolization, however, is that if you do not operate within the first 48 hours after embolization, you have to wait three months. And the reason for that is that the changes that occur as a consequence of embolization in the abdomen, it's like a bomb went off in there. And the tissue planes are basically like wet Kleenex. So trying to take somebody to the operating room before the embolization has had time to mature can be a catastrophe.
How successful is this embolization?

It's hard to say because, you know, the only ones we know about are the success stories. The ones that are not successful usually go home and die and we don't hear about them. So this patient underwent right radical nephrectomy, IBC thrombectomy. You can see the pathology here. He had evidence of rhabdoid features. That sounds bad. Twenty to 30 percent, and it was a T3C tumor, obviously, because it was up to the renal, up to the right atrium. No evidence of any adenopathy. Dr. Karam, rhabdoid. Sounds weird.

Yes, that's an aggressive subtype of kidney cancer and you hear in this situation it's clear cell kidney cancer. You could see it alone or you could see it with another very aggressive tumor called sarcomatoid. These are all very high grade tumors, you know, grade three or four. And they, basically all it's saying here, we have a patient who has an advanced tumor going all the way to the heart and a high-grade tumor, so that this patient is at a very high risk of recurrence in the future. Which, you know, goes down to your question there, how often would you, you know, follow a patient, how would you treat them? Unless there's an adjuvant clinical trial, the standard would be to just watch the patient with imaging, which we would do every three months or so the first year.
If he wants to know his risk of recurrence, what number are you going to tell him?
I'd say at least 50%.
50% risk of recurrence? At least. Dr. Mateen, you agree with that?
Yes, perfectly.
Anybody else have any differing opinion?

Rhebdoid is really different from sarcomatoid. And all it says, this is a high-grade tumor. It shows the tumor cells are round. But it is different than circumvent. All it says is basically high grade.

reference_conclusion: The agreed management was surgical resection consisting of right radical nephrectomy with inferior vena cava thrombectomy and atrial thrombectomy in conjunction with the vascular surgery team, performed through a midline approach, with sternotomy if abdominal access proved insufficient to retrieve the cardiac thrombus. Lymph node dissection was to be performed as part of the vascular dissection. Preoperative embolization was not recommended in this setting. Given the high risk of recurrence, postoperative management was surveillance imaging approximately every 3 months during the first year unless an adjuvant clinical trial became available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable thyroid nodule identified on routine clinical examination; patient was asymptomatic.

[ diagnosis ]: Right thyroid nodule, 4.4 cm, with indeterminate cytology (atypia of undetermined significance). Additional left thyroid spongiform nodule, 1.5 cm.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology from the right thyroid nodule showed atypia of undetermined significance. Subsequent core needle biopsy of the right thyroid nodule did not show papillary thyroid carcinoma; follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma/NIFTP was considered excluded on the biopsy material. Lack of thyroglobulin expression was described on the core biopsy.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a 4.4 cm right-sided thyroid nodule and a 1.5 cm left-sided spongiform nodule. The right-sided nodule was described as echogenic, cystic, heterogeneous, and wider-than-tall. No sonographic evidence of extrathyroidal extension was identified, including no invasion of the tracheal interface or strap muscles. No suspicious cervical lymph nodes were seen on ultrasound.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Afirma testing on the right thyroid nodule was reported as suspicious. No driver gene alteration was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Diagnostic evaluation included thyroid ultrasound, fine-needle aspiration, molecular testing, and core needle biopsy. No surgery had been performed. The patient preferred to avoid surgery if possible.

[ current disease status ]: Asymptomatic thyroid nodules under active surveillance.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient declined operative intervention at the time of evaluation.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, perfect. Yeah, so this one is actually shorter, but I think it's something that we commonly find in our day-to-day. You know, the ultrasound, I always, my first thing, believe it or not, I look for extra-thyroidal extension. You know, everybody else can see the lesion is echogenic, it's cystic, it's heterogeneous, you know, It's wider than taller, but I think if you look at it at its interface with the trachea, at least from what I see, I don't see any invasion. I don't see any invasion through the strap muscle for, so there is no extra thyroidal extension. And after that we have to do tissue sampling. The only thing I'll be cautious about is where you do your tissue sampling, which portion of this nodule.
Dr. Sugitani, in Japan, when you see this sort of 4.4 centimeter right-sided thyroid nodule, what's your usual evaluation?

Of course, ultrasound and fine needle aspiration, because we don't have commercially available molecular testing. So we are reluctant to perform surgery on every tumor over four centimeters, but the symptoms and the patient's preference is the most valuable determinant for surgery.
Awesome. Okay, David?
So we did FNA, and then cytology was ATP of undetermined significance. Of course it was.
Yep. And then you work at the Mayo Clinic, so we sent off three different molecular tests. Is that how it works up there?
So actually, this was actually done outside of the Mayo Clinic initially. But yes, someone actually did a firma, and this was what the firma resulted.
All right, suspicious, but we don't have a driver gene. All right, Camillo, what do we do with this?

So in most of Mexico, the behavior would be very similar to what Dr. Sujitani said. There's people that would even push if we, and I'm going to go to David, the rest of the thyroid gland is clear. Do we have any lymph nodes that we could see from the ultrasound? There were no lymph nodes that were worrisome. So yeah, based on preference, I would go at this point, anywhere from a lobectomy to a 12th thyroidectomy.
Now, what if I tell you that the patient's asymptomatic? And they don't want to do anything? They don't want surgery, if at all possible.

So this is an uncomfortable situation. Because you said suspicious, yeah, you didn't give me a gene variation, fusion, mutation. So if this was BRAF positive, I would still lean towards the same. If it was not, there's a big trend towards ablative techniques. But I don't know if this is, going back to Dr. Tuttle's wording, this might not be the ideal case for that, but I could accept surveillance.

So, JP, help me through the logic here. I mean, we see this all the time. Somebody does molecular testing and the patient doesn't want surgery anyway. Was this a good use of molecular testing? Go ahead.

So this is exactly the goal of the case. This is a benign-looking tumor to begin with. And that drives pretty much everything else in decision-making. When you have an AUS, in reality, the AUS for different institutions has different thresholds of cancer and the AUS might still not change significantly the risk of malignancy. Here in Mayo Clinic, it's about 10 to 15%, for instance. And within the AUS, you have the nuclear atypia and you have the architectural atypia that sometimes doesn't get reported. But when you build the case here, you start with a benign-looking tumor that has an AUS and it comes as suspicious for, it comes in affirmations of follicular aneuplasia. So probably telling us to some extent that is likely an architectural level of atypia. And those ones, when you have a benign looking nodule and an architectural atypia, the majority of those tend to be benign, which goes against to the idea that 50% of these positive affirmations are cancer. So just to maybe, trying to decompose the idea that if a firm is positive, we are 50% of malignancy, which is not always the case.
Perfect. And what else did you do to this young man, David? Or did somebody else on the outside do?
So this patient came to us, and then we decided, OK, then let's do a core biopsy. And this was the result of our core biopsy.

Margie, help me here with this logic, because we've got what, you know, when we're down this AUS follicular neoplasia pathway, we're down a follicular neoplasm pathway, and you need to see the capsule to tell me whether it's cancer or not. Right.

So this satisfies do something. Yeah. So something was done. And so a core needle biopsy is, unless you know you're thinking about anaplasty, it's a low yield thing. So what can I tell you here just based on histology alone, it's not PTC in this core needle biopsy. So something was done.
Really? Your report says something was done, Margie? You're going to charge for that?
You know, I don't write a fraction of the things I think.
That's probably good for both of us. That's very good. All right. So at least it told us it's not a papillary thyroid cancer. Probably not a follicular variant of papillary as well, right, Margie?

Exactly. Right. So, you know, NIFTP is off the table. Now, certainly, I just want to point out that the lack of thyroglobulin here is kind of unusual, and it may correlate with the fact that this is thought to be spongiform.
Perfect. All right, so Camilo, bottom line, what are you gonna do for this gentleman?

So you see, we see a lot of patients that come, you get the workup done or you get treated, and then they never come back. Mexico is like that. So with that in mind, I would still push at least for a lobectomy. And you're putting me in a hotspot here, but if this was a patient that was very educated and was very... I don't know, thorough with this, with this workup and follow up, I would definitely lean towards a more conservative approach. And David is, I think, hinting towards that when he was asking his question. And I do love that. still there's there's a problem that needs to be solved and I don't see this disappearing in any in any way so if we wanted to go to an ablative technique this is a gray gray zone so still I'm gonna say watch and wait there's there's a lot of things in in these partially cystic solid nodules that will change in the ATA guidelines so I'm not sure if I wanna follow my heart and just watch this patient or do something really conservative here in Mexico at least.

Yeah, I agree. I get to see a lot of these folks. Obviously they come to see us because they don't want surgery, right? They don't want, they're seeking out a very minimalistic management. And so I've become very comfortable following exactly the logic that JP outlined. I probably wouldn't have biopsied this to begin with. Um, and I certainly wouldn't have done the molecular testing on it. So in patients that can understand that this could be a follicular thyroid cancer, it could be one with some vascular invasion that I can't tell about, but I think that's pretty low. And if they're comfortable following that with me, I'll follow along with them. And so what did you guys decide to do?
That is exactly what we're doing with this particular patient. So we're doing active surveillance with him.

Yeah, so I mean, it's a risk benefit, it's a value preference of the patient, right? So what I personally would do might be different than what the patient would do. So as long as they understand what those risks and benefits are, then I try to respect their things. And at least in our situation, if I tell them it's okay to do that, a lot of times they will come back in two or three years and not just be completely lost to follow up. So great case, JP. All right, let's do one more.

reference_conclusion: Given the benign sonographic appearance, absence of extrathyroidal extension or suspicious lymphadenopathy, and indeterminate cytology/molecular findings without a driver alteration, the agreed management is active surveillance. This approach is contingent on patient preference and informed understanding of the residual possibility of follicular thyroid carcinoma, including the inability to exclude vascular invasion without surgery. Continued follow-up is planned rather than immediate operative intervention.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old male; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Multiple cranial nerve palsies. Left hemiparesis and facial weakness developed in 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma in the sellar/suprasellar region with residual/recurrent disease after surgery and CyberKnife treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from resection performed on 05 December 2017 showed adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain dated 02 August 2017 showed a heterogeneous midline sellar/suprasellar lesion posterior to the optic chiasm, with a large T2 hypointense component in the midline likely at or inferior to the third ventricle.  
- The lesion extended into the right cavernous sinus/paracavernous region and inferiorly into the sphenoid sinus.  
- It caused significant mass effect with compression of the midbrain and upward displacement/lifting of the third ventricle.  
- Temporal horns appeared mildly prominent, suggesting possible hydrocephalus.  
- The lesion demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement with both enhancing and non-enhancing components.  
- The optic chiasm was not separately visualized on the provided images.  
- Postoperative MRI in November 2017 showed significant residual disease/large residual lesion with persistent heterogeneous enhancement, residual suprasellar component along the floor of the third ventricle, and right paracavernous involvement.  
- MRI in 2021 showed reduction in tumor size compared with prior studies.  
- Comparative imaging through December 2021 demonstrated decreased enhancing component after radiotherapy, with persistent residual mass effect.  
- MRI dated 18 December 2024 showed mild progression of the lesion, with multiple internal non-enhancing areas/necrotic change, persistent residual mass, involvement of the right cavernous sinus, and mass effect on the pons/brainstem.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Right craniotomy and resection of sellar/suprasellar tumor performed on 05 December 2017.  
- Postoperative MRI showed significant residual disease.  
- CyberKnife treatment was administered in March 2018.  
- Follow-up MRI in 2021 showed reduction in tumor size after treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Residual/recurrent sellar-suprasellar craniopharyngioma with mild radiologic progression on MRI dated 18 December 2024 and ongoing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion had longstanding mass effect on adjacent critical structures including the midbrain/brainstem and third ventricle, with right cavernous sinus involvement.

[ patient demographics ]: Demographic details were not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma with new PET/CT abnormality after prior definitive chemoradiation, salvage stereotactic radiation, and pembrolizumab.

[ diagnosis ]: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, initially stage IIIB. The patient achieved a complete response after definitive chemoradiation. Five years later, recurrent disease developed in the right masticator space. Subsequent biopsy-proven recurrent disease in the nasopharynx was identified. A right temporal lobe lesion was present.

[ histopathology results ]: Recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma in the nasopharynx was biopsy proven.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial recurrence occurred in the right masticator space 5 years after definitive treatment.  
- A subsequent PET/CT demonstrated a nasopharyngeal-region abnormality and a right temporal lobe lesion.  
- CT imaging demonstrated bony involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic findings were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory results were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Definitive chemoradiation was administered for stage IIIB nasopharyngeal carcinoma, with complete response.  
- Five years later, recurrence in the right masticator space was treated with stereotactic radiation in 5 fractions and pembrolizumab for 5 cycles.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven locally recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma of the nasopharynx after prior definitive chemoradiation, salvage stereotactic re-irradiation, and pembrolizumab, with bony involvement demonstrated on CT. A right temporal lobe lesion was also present.

[ other clinical data ]: Prior radiation exposure included definitive chemoradiation followed by salvage stereotactic re-irradiation.

reference_discussion.text: Great, thank you very much, Dr. Choby. So, the third case is going to shift gears a little bit to another very well developed area but also kind of a frontier in many other senses. So nasopharyngeal carcinoma which really has a lot of challenges of its own. This is a patient who initially presented stage 3b and was treated with definitive chemoradiation with a complete response. Five years later, the patient developed a recurrence within the right masticator space and was treated with stereotactic radiation, five rounds, and then also Pembroke for five cycles, and now moves over to a different area and now presents with a new PET CT demonstrating this finding right here. I'm going to start by pulling the panel and asking, how do you surveillance patients? Dr. Price, what is your paradigm for this?

So I think if you look at the head and neck guidelines for NCCN, they talk about doing pre-treatment imaging, doing your post-treatment kind of curative imaging. And then there's not a lot of really recommended imaging when there aren't any symptoms. So it's kind of left up as clinically indicated. I always struggle with this for nasopharynx because you can't really see, or at least those of us without fun scopes can't really see very well. And it's kind of like with some of the sinus tumors too, you sort of feel a little bit blind because you can't really feel as well or see as well. we do tend to kind of get some intermittent imaging on these patients, both MRI imaging generally to look at the nasopharynx as well as some form of distant metastatic assessment, whether that's PET or whether that's CT scans. For those that are EBV related, we'll incorporate the EBV quantitative DNA in the blood as kind of a biomarker. And of course, history and physical exam and all of the important things that we do for everyone.
Thank you. And then, Dr. Liao, just to add to that, what is your intervals for assessing surveillance for these patients?

Yeah, like Dr. Price said, there's not great guidance as far as national guidelines with this, with what exactly to do. It is a little bit individualized, I think, from risk from patient to patient, but our starting point is usually Q3 to four months with office visit, endoscopy, MRI, and then Q6 months after that, and a little bit more space with systemic imaging, either CT, chest, abdomen, pelvis, sort of Q6 months. We don't routinely get PET-CT scan, necessarily, unless we're concerned the patient hasn't had a CR. You know, sometimes we'll get that in three or six months to verify that, but I know there's many institutions that do.

Great, thank you. So just wanted to also point out, we do cover this partly within the document itself and especially for the ones that are EBV positive, there was a recommendation that was very strong from the Asian literature on the use of the EBV DNA serum test for surveillance and assessing recurrence. So this is some representative scans of the patient once we saw that PET CT. So we draw your attention to this very cloudy area, as well as the temporal lobe lesion that you're seeing very obviously on the bottom there. Dr. Gardner, would you biopsy the right temporal lobe lesion if you see something like this, knowing the patient has had prior treatment as well as a little bit more radiation treatment than the typical course?

I definitely would not. I fight this battle on a regular basis where patients with sinonasal tumors of any sort get temporal lesions in any time period from even six months to three and four or five years later. And it often is read as tumor recurrence, but these tumors, it's not the right substrate. These are not brain tumors. They don't grow in the brain. They don't like the brain. This is not a solid looking lesion. And I always have to fight back about biopsy, and I definitely would not biopsy the temporal lobe.

Thank you. Yeah, I love the way you said that. All right. And then one representative scan for the CT, you can see a little bit of that bony involvement. Dr. London, when would you consider nasal pharyngectomy for nasopharyngeal cancer patients?

In the question, that would be, you know, in the setting of a recurrent NPC, you know, this patient you said has already had CRT with a recurrence and even already had immunotherapy. This looks like a fairly easy recyclable lesion. So, you know, I would recommend proceeding with endoscopic nasopharyngectomy at this point.
Yeah, it was biopsy proven again so technical considerations for surgery if elected Dr. Levine with regards to nasal pharyngectomy.

Yeah, I think, you know, there's some of the kind of the classic ones here, you know, whenever you're, you're doing this type of surgery, obviously, you want to have enough imaging to really see, you know, that you don't have any aberrant carotid lesions, that you're not going to be super close to anything that, that is a abnormal, but a lot of times that when you're doing this type of a a resection, I think the biggest part of this in many ways is just preparing the patient for what it's going to be like afterwards and making sure that you have a really good frank discussion with them about that. A lot of times, the biggest challenge is not actually the surgery itself, although I can say it can be challenging, it's really getting the patient through that post-operative period and making sure that they can cooperate with you in that process. Going through that with them, I think is really helpful.

Just kind of to piggyback off of that, I know we always worry about critical neurovascular structures for nasal pharyngectomy, especially the carotid artery. Do you counsel them about eustachian tube symptoms? I know they probably have a pre-op, but it's likely to be a permanent problem going forward. So what is your strategy for talking to patients on that?

So usually I tell them that what they have at that time, which most people, you're right, have symptoms, is going to either stay the same or get worse. So I try to usually set low expectations, and then if it's anything better than that, they tend to be pretty happy. But I think it's really important to discuss that because often patients have this idea that you do surgery and then everything will get better. And I think it's just very important to dissuade them of that notion and to have a really realistic set of things like this is the bad part through the healing period, but these are the long-term things that you're going to be dealing with. And I think that's the piece that everybody needs to have the right expectations for. And usually they need to hear that more than once.

Great. So we do also cover nasal pharyngectomy in the document itself. So it's been getting a lot of growing evidence base, especially also pioneered in Asia, especially for select early stage and maybe a couple of more advanced stage lesions. Of course, there's some frontiers being pushed on this where you see very amazing videos of carotid bypasses and sacrifices and, you know, I think it's probably going to get a lot more adoption as we learn more about this disease. Dr. Gardner, you had a comment?

It's a question for really anyone in the panel is, what do people do for coverage after an endoscopic nasopharyngectomy, especially these patients who have been radiated and you may have exposed a clival bone in that setting? Just curious as to thoughts on that.

I mean, I think in this setting, it's really important to cover, you know, the great vessels after surgery. If you can use a contralateral and there's a septal flap, that's helpful, or a, you know, pedicled temporal parietal fascia flap, or even, you know, if there's a really big defect, you know, free flap, if you really had to. Those would be some things I would think about.
Would you do that if the carotid is, only if the carotid is exposed, or would you routinely do it, Dr. London?

I mean, I think it's hard to tell based on those two cuts from the CT, but for that particular patient, I'd probably try to use a contralateral nasoceptal flap to cover that area. It should be usable.
Dr. Roderick?

Yeah, thanks. I would do exactly the same as what Dr. London had said. But the ICAR document is absolutely wonderful, but there's been Chinese guidelines from several communities of care there that are really quite good that were recently published. And they go through different scenarios of also nasopharyngeal cancer, but osteomyelitis of the skull base, which is also a terrible problem as well. So I'd encourage anybody to take a look at that who's interested.

Definitely. I remember seeing that as well. Okay. So the patient ended up getting the nasopharyngectomy, negative margins, and then end up having bevacizumab and some steroids for the temporal lobe necrosis, and it ended up getting better. But of course, the saga always continues. So question kind of before we get to kind of the end of the saga, Dr. Price, when would you consider immunotherapy for MPC patients? What are your main indications for using it?

So we're using immunotherapy now routinely in recurrent metastatic disease for nasopharynx cancer. So there was a recent phase three study from Asia, the Jupiter study, that used it for first-line treatment in combination with cisplatin gemcitabine and showed survival benefit. But even before that study, there had been a number of phase two studies looking at single agent immunotherapy, typically after platinum chemotherapy, similar to mucosal head and neck that showed activity. So we routinely will use it in the recurrent metastatic setting, either by itself or with chemotherapy, depending on the amount of disease, whether the patient's symptomatic from their disease. a good tool, of course, you know, not everybody responds to immunotherapy, but it is part of standard care now.

Great, thank you for sharing that. So, this is also kind of summarized also in the document as well. Again, for recurrent and metastatic MPC as you had mentioned. And we briefly already, our STOOT panelists already talked about this a little bit. So several months post-treatment, of course, there's new clival enhancement and the nasal pharynx is demonstrating a little bit of mucosal necrosis. So I think this is a great segue into how do you manage a likely impending ORN of the skull base? So Dr. Widerich, I know we were just talking about this, so. I'll share your thoughts.

Yeah, you know, it's the bane of existence on this. So, I mean, we have a late effects clinic and there's various medications that can be used to try to increase blood flow and I'm not really sure they work. And then we also have hyperbaric and I'm not sure that works. And if we really think that there's something going on, you know, you can watch for a while, but if it's progressing, then I would move towards putting some sort of vascularized tissue on it to try and prevent a carotid blowout. So it all depends on how it's progressing. Some of it stays stable. You know, I think of hyperbaric oxygen as just sort of delaying. It's like a delaying tactic. It's something to do while you're waiting to see what happens. Maybe I'm offending some people by saying that, but I think definitively you have to decide whether they really need surgery and a flap.
And then when you offer them surgery, you would debride it to, what is your end point that you use for debride?

It's until my coronaries act up enough that I have to put nitrates on, because sometimes you just can't get the bone to bleed and it's terrible moth-eaten, And you just sort of, you know, your coronaries go into spasm. Yeah, so that's the limits.
Dr. Gardner, do you ever chase it to incorporate resection of dura? I think I know the answer, but what is your thought on that?

Usually, you know, we're monitoring Ian's coronary vessels throughout the procedure, and we use that as our marker as well. But it is, all kidding aside, you take it until your degree of comfort. I would never resect dura in this setting. There are very rare situations where you go and you do see even a small hole in the dura, and I think those patients we found They really need something robust like a free flap if Dura is involved. But I would do, I think that coronary spasm time point is when you really think you're risking Dura. If you think you're risking Dura, it's time to stop.

And then Dr. Liao, with regards to the risk of patients developing ORN, how do you counsel them? And then what are some other tips and tricks you can offer us from the surgical side to try to mitigate this risk? Or are there any at all?

Yeah, tough one. You're talking about in the re-irradiation setting. Yeah. Yeah, there is no perfect solution, unfortunately. I'm very glad to do less and less re-irradiation and endoscopic resection is an option for these patients. And it's feasible when you have a patient with more limited disease. That's something I think that's in discussion. We route patients towards just systemic therapy palliation sometimes. If we retreat, I tend to usually to do hyperfractionated accelerated course, BID, in the retreatment setting. And there's actually a randomized trial that was recently reported in the endemic Asian experience. It was randomized to conventional versus accelerated course hyperfractionated re-radiation. And there was decreased grade three toxicity in the patients that had BID radiation. So if you're gonna do aggressive re-radiation, I think that's our favorite approach, is hyper-fractionating it.

Great. Well, fortunately this patient stabilized in terms of this development. So active surveillance on immunotherapy, kind of seeing what the next steps are for this. Keep watching until my coronaries can't take it either. All right, so that was the end of my case. Thank you all for sharing your expertise. Dr. Chovy, I think maybe we could go to Q&A.

reference_conclusion: For biopsy-proven locally recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma after prior chemoradiation, stereotactic radiation, and immunotherapy, the agreed management was to proceed with endoscopic nasopharyngectomy. Reconstruction should include vascularized coverage of exposed critical structures, with a contralateral nasoseptal flap favored for this defect. The temporal lobe lesion was not recommended for biopsy and was managed as radiation necrosis with bevacizumab and corticosteroids, with subsequent radiographic improvement. Ongoing management consisted of active surveillance while receiving immunotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old woman; gravida 3/para 3; regularly menstruating.

[ chief complaint ]: Irregular per-vaginal bleeding for 8–9 months, moderate in amount and intermittent, associated with generalized weakness for 3–4 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. Initial clinical stage was recorded as FIGO stage IIA2. Subsequent pelvic MRI and CT abdomen/pelvis described locally advanced cervical malignancy with parametrial involvement and suspected posterior bladder wall/base involvement. Cystoscopy was normal. In the absence of bladder mucosal involvement, disease was discussed as stage IIB if no nodal disease was present; stage IIIC would apply if lymph nodes were involved.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology showed grade 2 squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pelvic examination showed an exophytic cervical lesion approximately 6 cm in diameter arising from the anterior lip of the cervix and extending to the upper one-fifth of the anterior vaginal wall.  
- MRI of the lower abdomen/pelvis showed a locally advanced cervical growth protruding into the upper vaginal canal with parametrial involvement and posterior bladder wall involvement; reported TNM stage was T4a M0.  
- CT scan of the whole abdomen showed locally advanced cervical cancer confined to the pelvis with bladder base and vaginal invasion, without vesicoureteric junction or ureteric junction involvement; reported TNM stage was unchanged from MRI.  
- No hydronephrosis or hydroureter was described.  
- Nodal status was not documented as positive on the available imaging summary.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic findings were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Severe anemia was documented on general examination. No numerical hematology or biochemistry values were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior oncologic treatment was documented. Diagnostic cystoscopy was performed and showed normal bladder blood vessels/mucosa, with no cystoscopic evidence of bladder involvement.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated locally advanced cervical carcinoma with vaginal extension and parametrial involvement. Bladder invasion was suspected on imaging but not confirmed on cystoscopy. No distant metastasis was documented (M0 on reported imaging).

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Abdominal examination was normal.  
- Vaginal examination: exophytic lesion about 6 cm in diameter in the anterior lip of the cervix extending to the upper one-fifth of the anterior vaginal wall.  
- Bimanual examination: anterior fornix shallow; other fornices filled.  
- Rectovaginal examination: both parametria were free on initial clinical examination.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Long-standing right thyroid nodule; reassessment was prompted by unexplained 25-pound weight loss over approximately 1 year.

[ diagnosis ]: Right thyroid nodule, 2.0-2.4 cm, classified on ultrasound as TI-RADS 5; fine-needle aspiration cytology was Bethesda V (suspicious for malignancy).

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Office/formal thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a right-sided thyroid nodule measuring approximately 2.0 cm, with multiple suspicious sonographic features, classified as TI-RADS 5.  
- Interval growth was described as minimal over several years, from approximately 2.0 cm to 2.4 cm.  
- CT neck redemonstrated the right thyroid nodule without appreciable extrathyroidal extension and without evidence of cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- Clinical examination demonstrated a smooth, mobile right thyroid nodule without palpable adenopathy.  
- Flexible laryngoscopic examination showed normal vocal cord mobility.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing identified an isolated TERT mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroid laboratory testing was ordered during evaluation for weight loss; specific results were not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- More than 10 years earlier, the right thyroid nodule had been identified incidentally during a routine work physical.  
- Initial FNA at that time had been indeterminate.  
- The patient had been followed by endocrinology with annual thyroid ultrasounds for approximately 5 years and was subsequently discharged from surveillance.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No thyroid cancer risk factors were reported.  
- No significant family history was reported.  
- No personal history of radiation exposure was reported.  
- No cervical adenopathy was palpable on examination.

Yeah, I think you're right. To me, we are using too much of mutations. and making clinical decision. Keep in mind, this lady is 70. She has a nodule for a long time. Yeah, I agree.

Yeah, I was going to make a point is that I think we have to be careful to not to extrapolate what a certain molecular test is designed to do. Chris, I really like how you shared decision-making. Amit, you have clearly, clearly trained your fellow very, very well in terms of how this was taken care of. So Amit, do you have any last words before we move on to the next case?

No, I just thought it'd be a great case to share with the group just because it kind of merges a lot of what we're kind of learning in the current day and age about molecular medicine and thyroid cancer and kind of how you can be led down a certain way. So.
Absolutely. Absolutely. All right. Thanks, Ahmed. And thanks, Chris. Let's move on.

reference_conclusion: For this 2.4 cm Bethesda V thyroid nodule without radiographic extrathyroidal extension or cervical nodal disease, the panel favored surgical management with thyroid lobectomy/hemithyroidectomy as the appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic procedure. Total thyroidectomy was not supported on the basis of an isolated TERT alteration alone, and extent of surgery should be guided primarily by the clinical and imaging findings rather than molecular testing in isolation.
