case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: In 2007, he presented with flushing and pain. Seven years after initial lung surgery, he was found to have elevated liver enzymes; subsequent ultrasound demonstrated liver lesions.

[ diagnosis ]: Typical lung carcinoid (low-grade well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor) of the right lower lobe, initially resected in 2007. Subsequent recurrent/metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor involving the liver, described as bilobar hepatic metastases.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Primary lung tumor pathology after right lower lobectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy: typical lung carcinoid, 2.5 cm.  
- Mitotic rate: fewer than 2 mitoses per 10 high-power fields.  
- Ki-67: less than 5%.  
- Synaptophysin positive.  
- Chromogranin positive.  
- Liver biopsy from recurrent disease: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial imaging in 2007 showed a lesion in the right lower lobe of the lung.  
- Seven years later, liver ultrasound showed liver lesions.  
- MRI of the liver at recurrence demonstrated a large hepatic lesion; disease was described as bilobar liver metastases with significant right lobe involvement.  
- Octreotide scan was performed at the time of hepatic recurrence.  
- Post-surgical imaging after hepatic debulking demonstrated two small residual subcentimeter hepatic lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Elevated liver enzymes were identified at the time hepatic recurrence was detected.  
- Elevated liver function tests/liver numbers were described in association with hepatic metastatic disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2007: Right lower lobectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy for typical lung carcinoid.  
- No adjuvant treatment was given after initial surgery.  
- After hepatic recurrence, he underwent surgery consisting of removal of several confluent liver masses, microwave ablation, alcohol ablation, and lymph node dissection.  
- Residual gross disease remained after hepatic debulking, with postoperative imaging showing two small residual subcentimeter lesions.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of pulmonary origin with bilobar hepatic metastases, status post hepatic cytoreductive surgery with microwave ablation, alcohol ablation, and lymph node dissection. Residual gross disease remained, with postoperative imaging showing two small residual subcentimeter hepatic lesions. The primary lung lesion had been completely resected and no thoracic recurrence was described; disease was described as confined to the liver at that stage.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Hepatic disease was described as bulky and not amenable to ablation at one stage because of lesion size.  
- Surgical candidacy for hepatic disease was limited by bilobar involvement, significant right lobe tumor burden, and abnormal liver tests.  
- After hepatic debulking, the patient was asymptomatic.

reference_discussion.text: So the tumor board is a very important part of the care of our patients. And that's because a lot of the patients required more than one discipline. And as you know, in a hospital environment, I'm sure many of you have tried to get in touch with me. It's not so easy, right? And even us getting in touch with each other. And sometimes we need to get in touch with three or four people. And sometimes we all need to be looking at the same thing at the same time. in order to come to a decision. And as you'll see from today, there's not always one right decision. Sometimes these decisions in the care of a patient are quite nuanced. So it takes everybody coming together, reviewing the pathology, reviewing the radiology, the case, special considerations to develop a good treatment plan. Now, tumor boards tend to be recurring, and they should be not a looking back, so to speak, but looking forward. So they should be done on a – usually we do it weekly. Some places do it monthly. But as the patient care is being provided, it's an ongoing thing. So we're going to present a few cases today. And we have representatives from all the specialties. And this year we did something special is that we included the patient perspective. because I've noticed that a lot of times we'll have recommendations from our tumor board, and of course you know who has veto power, right? Right, right, okay. So case number one. So poor Josh, he's 53. In 2007. I wish, we'll get back to it one day. In 2007, he had flushing and some pain. He went to his primary doctor. He had some imaging that showed a lesion in the right lower lobe of his lung. Afterwards, he had a right lower lobectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy. Here's a picture of the lesion. And this was the pathology results. It was a typical lung carcinoid, two and a half centimeters in size, Less than two mitoses per 10 high-powered fields. KI67 is less than 5%. Synaptophysin and comogranin was positive. Dr. Marchewski, any thoughts?

Well, this is basically a low-grade neuroendocrine tumor. We use a different terminology in different organs. In the lung, we like carcinoid. The tumor was 2.5 centimeters in size. which smaller than three centimeters is lower risk category. We use mitosis, how fast the tumor is growing. And there is a limit of two in 10 high power fields. That is good news. Higher than that makes it an atypical carcinoid. Tumors are known to have a little more aggressive behavior. So you have size is good, the number of mitosis is good, and then the Ki67 is less than five, which is another cutoff for good news versus not so less good news. The last two features are immunostains that we used to determine that a tumor is neuroendocrine. So both were positive, which classified the tumor as a low-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm.
Okay. Does anyone have any recommendations for this patient now that we're discussing in tumor board after surgery? Dr. Halperin, does this patient need any kind of treatment at this point?
No. Next question.
Okay.

Does anyone want to venture as to what the surveillance plan should be for a patient like this? Do they just need a chest x-ray once in a while and we're good? Anyone have any thoughts? What do we have to do to check to see if the tumor is going to come back or not? Dr. Lee, do you have a plan for this patient? Yeah, so surveillance imaging, I think there's not complete consensus in terms of guidelines. So this is a relatively low grade neuroendocrine tumor where the risk of recurrence is still low, but there is still that risk of recurrence. Imaging can either be CT of the chest imaging, usually about either three to six months intervals to see whether or not there's a recurrence moving forward. So this patient was told by the surgeon, you're good. This is done. Tumor's gone. You can maybe get a CT scan once in a while, you're in the clear. Giovanna, do you have any thoughts about this, this recommendation from the surgeon?

On the one hand, I think as a patient, I'm going to feel really good about that. Like, I want to believe that I'm cured. On the other hand, I may be a little suspicious. Like, is it really true? Am I doing the right thing? But if this is my first experience with being diagnosed with something really major, I'm probably going to believe the physician and just go with it, because I really want to believe that I'm done.

Yeah, it's a tough case. And then how long would you do surveillance for the medical oncologist? How long would you continue to check scans? Or surgeons? I know there's no thoracic surgeon here today, so I know it's a tough one. But you're tumor surgeons. How long would you do surveillance if you were going to do imaging? How long would it be done for?

Yeah, I think, you know, the movement more recently, particularly with GI, but I think even if we look at sort of the way we've adjusted the NCCN guidelines over the last year or two, has been to extend surveillance out, right? So I think we would typically say you may do the same number of scans, but over more years. So, you know, if you're doing them once a year, you may tend towards 10 years, I think The data aren't quite clear on, particularly with low-risk patients, exactly when and where those recurrences will be, but 10 or, for some folks, even longer may be appropriate.
Josh, how do you feel about all this? This is a tough problem.

I feel good so far, but I've read online that I'm never really cured and that I should be getting imaging or some other follow-up more often. So I'm a little nervous about waiting six months, but I'll try.

It's understandable. So this gentleman, seven years later, I think the idea that he had cancer even left his mind completely. He was found to have elevated liver enzymes, and an ultrasound showed liver lesions, and these are biopsy. So this is what an MRI at that time looks like. And here you see these, these are the tumors, and then this is the liver, normal liver here. So you see, it's a pretty large lesion. So not only is the patient, is Josh, shocked that it's come back, but he's also surprised again. That's concerning. And an actria scan, this is an olden days radiology. Gabe, what do you think about, you can't see it. It's not very impressive. Yeah, it doesn't look too good. But it's pretty similar to how we do with arterioscans. It's just kind of like blurbs of light, yeah. Anyways, so a biopsy was done. Dr. Marchevsky, what do you think about this biopsy result?

Well, again, the patient has a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. In this situation, you have to consider could it be a recurrence of the tumor from many years ago. Or could the patient have a new tumor, as the neuroendocrine tumors are known to be multiple in some people. So before you make sure that this is a metastasis from the previous tumor, it's a good idea to compare the two lesions, which in this situation is not going to help all that much, because they all tend to look similar. But then clinically, you have to make sure the patient doesn't have a carcinoid tumor elsewhere, particularly in the small bowel. that may benefit from surgery before labeling this metastatic tumor from the lung into the liver.
And Giovanna, as a patient, how do you feel right now?

I think right now I'm pretty frightened. I was told I was good, and here I am some years later, and I feel like I have really greatly metastatic cancer. So I think one of the things that might cross my mind is, am I getting the best opinion that would come up?
Yeah.
How about you, Josh?

Josh, how are you feeling? I'm trying to find out what the next treatment would be, what my options are. I'm probably not running around yet to find what else to do. I'm waiting to see what comes back from the tumor board or from my oncologist.

OK. So does anyone from the surgical or interventional radiology have any perspectives on what they would recommend, or medical oncology at this point? So a patient with recurrent lung neuroendocrine tumor, well differentiated. by low-bar metastases to the liver seven years later. I think we would want to really discuss this kind of in this similar fashion in real life in terms of multidisciplinary team. One of the questions I would have for the surgeons as well as interventional radiologists is the tumors appeared relatively bulky. Whether or not that's going to potentially compromise venous outflow The patient already has elevated liver function tests, so the concern is that if it potentially leads to anus outflow obstruction, then that patient is in big trouble in terms of their underlying disease with the liver, and they can go into impending liver failure as a result of that. So that's, I think, question number one because that will really determine how aggressive we might want to be with our systemic therapies going forward. We know that the patient will need some form of systemic therapy because we're not going to be able to completely clear the disease. But question number one would be for, you know, the multidisciplinary team in that sense. Dr. Ganji, any thoughts? Our surgeon, if you haven't had a chance to meet her, she's our tumor surgeon specializing in endocrine tumors.

So, I apologize for my voice, but from the one cut, we see he has pretty significant disease in the right lobe of the liver, and you're saying he has bilobar metastases with some evidence of liver compromise based on his elevated liver numbers. So, I don't think he would be an optimal surgical candidate at this point. I think there would be some option to potentially see if our IR colleagues can offer some embolization therapies to kind of control or decrease the tumor size, followed potentially by some systemic therapy. and then reassess for potential resection depending on response.
That's my liver function.

Yeah, so I think there are several options for us in the interventional radiology realm. These are too big for ablation, so we're looking at the trans-arterial techniques. And we'd also, there are elevated liver enzymes here, so we'd look at the liver enzymes and make sure that it was safe to treat, actually, assuming that it is safe. I think bland chemo or radiation, it's kind of dealer's choice here, are all, they're all viable options.
So, Dr. Kasari knows what's happened.

So, I think one of the points that should be brought up is that, especially surgeons, I, first of all, I agree with all the comments of my colleagues. Surgeons are spatial, spatially oriented species. We like to see it, we like to have the information. So if you get calls from our offices saying, hey, we really got to have the actual images, that's the reason why. Because something that's in the report, most good surgeons will tell you they look at the images first, they make up their own mind about what's going on, and then they check to make sure that the radiologist read the film correctly. when it comes to liver disease for sure. So you got to see the images and see for yourself, what is the distribution of disease? What are the chances of resection now? What are the chances of resection later? How can we bring in this multimodality treatment to hopefully get the patient to the point where something more can be done, if it can't be done like this is right now.
Great. And Dr. Halperin, if someone's recommended to have a large cytoreductive surgery like this, How would you consult the patient as far as the risk-benefit ratio of doing something like that?

Yeah. This is really one of the things, sorry, like many things Giovanna says, like this was sort of true genius this morning when you said that really the calculation about quality of life and how much you're sort of buying with whatever sort of cost to yourself and your body you're willing to endure is so critical. Because the way I counsel my patients is when they see our surgeons, we tell them if you follow large surgical series long enough, almost everybody recurs eventually. And in fact, many series will show you an average time to recurrence on the order of a couple of years for many folks. And so it becomes very much how much risk is there to the surgery? What anatomic considerations will there be? How much of a hit to your quality of life? Like you guys, my surgeons are phenomenal. So, you know, the surgeons, we have very low morbidity and mortality, but what do you really get for that, even if it is just a week in the hospital or heaven forbid longer? And how do we weigh that against the other treatment options we might have in light of knowing what the benefits of all those things might be?

Great, so this patient did have a surgery. As you can see here, it was removal of several confluent masses, microwave ablation, and alcohol ablation, and a lymph node dissection. So even within the techniques, there's sometimes multidisciplinary, right? So now the patient has been debulked, or CIDR reduced. Anyone have any recommendations on what to do from here?
What should we do, tumor board? So I'm sorry, this was R2? Is that what we're saying? It was gross R2 debulking? Or did they... Let's assume it's R2.
Okay. Can you explain what R2 means?

Sorry, yeah, so the main question is do we still have visible cancer that was left behind sort of deliberately? Not deliberately, but because it was not... Forgive me, because it wasn't amenable to the many techniques that our colleagues had available at the time.

Yeah. No, I mean, I think as a medical oncologist, you know, we're aware that our systemic therapies have significant benefit for folks, right? So a lot of times, if you're dealing with low-volume indolent disease, We'll take that opportunity to understand if and when the disease is going to grow before we start deploying the systemic therapies and really sort of try to maximize, because I think the lowest toxicity option you have is going to be observation, other than the anxiety, which is worth considering in that risk-benefit balance. And so we may try for that first.

That's been a big question in our group.

There's no parking.

Yeah, coffee is awful.
Coffee is awful, but we're used to that.

So you'll be kind of privileged to other patient identifiers and patient information. So what we do say is that, you know, we have a robust discussion and we do kind of keep notes in terms of what happened in the tumor board. We're very open in terms of how the case was discussed. So oftentimes for my patients, I do tell them that if there was discrepancies between different opinions, what are the different reasons why people had discrepancies so that we can really kind of weigh those risks and benefits and make a conscious decision together.

Can I comment on that too, please? So anyone shop on Amazon? Have you ever spent like three hours looking up, you know, a different type of wallet that you want to buy? The problem with information is that The more access to information you have, sometimes the harder it gets to try and interpret it correctly. It's not because we don't want you in the tumor board. It's that information has to be digested by someone that you trust and be given to you in the way that it makes sense. I bet you if you sat through tumor board for your own case, you're not going to understand maybe, you know, 30, 40% of sometimes the material that's being presented to you. And that's doing you a disservice. You shouldn't worry about the background stuff that goes out. You should find the right people that you trust, and then get that information. Check it with other folks if you'd like to. But that's part of the reason. I haven't seen anyone include patients in tumor boards across the country.
Keep this moving along. I'm going to assume I don't have any symptoms, and I'm OK. So I'll let it be active surveillance, and you tell me how often I should come back.

Yeah, that's so typically for well-differentiated, low-grade disease, our surveillance imaging plan is about every six months. But of course, depends on the situation, that might vary. So in April 2016, how long did you say, Dr. Halperin, the average amount of time was? Around a couple years. Yeah, well, two years later, there's some disease growth in the right lobe of the liver. So go back to the tumor board. Can you see it? Unfortunately, the screen is kind of dark. We can see it pretty good here.
My selfie doesn't look very good. Dr. Lipschitz, what do you think about that?
I would ask the surgeons if they want to resect again.
we'd have to see the rest of the images. Yeah, that's it.
Those are all the images. I mean, assuming that this- You would do a surgery again in two years?

Yeah, I don't rule things out. I mean, you have to have the full data set, as much data as you can, but repeat operations is doable. If this looks to be like in the right lower liver towards the back, and it's far enough away from the main vein that's draining the right side of the liver, So it is possible to go back in there and locally just excise that area.
Okay, any other ideas?

I think the question with excision I would have there is he's had a pretty extensive surgery so I'd like to know what remnant liver he has and what his liver function is and it looks, I assume it's about under two centimeters or so. So it's pretty central and I think an ablation would be another option for a short interval recurrence in this patient.
All right. So these are the options. How about Everolimus, Dr. Halperin-Ali, standard approved agent?
Agreed.
Agreed. That's true. That's true.

I think that I think the question in all of these situations is really, you know, what do we know about the biology of this? Sorry. It's sort of what's at the confluence of the anatomy of the situation as was described, the biology of the cancer and the condition of the patient. Right. And I think that the biology of the disease is telling us we just did the experiment that a local therapy is going to give us a relatively short interval recurrence. And my question would be, are we sure we want to bark up the same tree again, regardless of modality, IR surgery, or alternative technique, personally.
OK, great. So this patient did receive embolization, then received Everolimus and other therapies. But moving forward, we have a gallium 68 scan. Can you see that?
So another two years pass.
Yeah, we can say another two years, about the time the gallium is approved in the US. So we have a gallium 68 scan. Dr. Thompson, do you have any feelings about this scan?

Gallium 68 PET is a huge advantage over the octreotide because of the brightness of the lesions when they show up compared to background and the fusion of the lesions with the anatomy so you can see where the heart is up the top and the liver and then the blob down the bottom of the bladder. It's always surprising to our patients to find gallium 68 PET showing up things that they didn't know they had and that's the problem with sharpening the lens and taking a look at the fine detail is You're using a different tool. It's a more sensitive tool for detection of small things, and frequently it shows up things that you didn't know you had that were not evident on other imaging before. But sometimes that's really important to get a sense of the bigger picture of where the disease is rather than just focusing in on one organ.

And how does that change our treatment algorithm? Now that a patient has progressive disease, the gallium scan is positive, but they have a lung tumor. Does any of the medical oncologists have a feeling of what you would recommend for this patient? It's not an easy one. Yeah. So this is a, you know, I think you're going to get. You're probably four different opinions if you see four different medical oncologists. I'm being very honest. Yeah, yeah, maybe. Yeah, probably six different opinions on it. So at least off of your list here, I think a lot of major academic centers, we do encourage clinical trials. The reason why is we understand that for lung neuroendocrine tumors, there are limited FDA approved treatment options. Therefore, whenever we think about a clinical trial, We're really trying to give you another opportunity to see a medication that you might not have otherwise. So that we give you as many possibilities in terms of many chances to potentially respond to the various different types of treatments. Obviously that does require kind of a similar mindset from the patient perspective. and potential toxicities incurred in the clinical trial drug. But I think all of these are options. But usually, I would favor a clinical trial, in this case, over standard therapies.

And I'll do a quick follow-up. Would it matter the fact that my lung primary is completely removed and it doesn't seem to be re-showing up? That isn't the area recurrence, it's just my liver. Would that change some of the mathematics to what you were thinking?

Yeah, absolutely. So if it's just localized in one area, then potentially local regional approaches might be more appropriate, along with the same line of thought of being able to have as many therapies still on the table as possible going forward.

And can I just add, I think there's an important element here for the patient to understand how you are about information and decisions, and how do you make decisions, and how much information you feel you need. Like you said, I'm more the person who will be on Amazon for six hours looking for the wallet. So I feel my comfort level is there to make a decision once I feel like I have enough information. Some people are just the opposite. They're like, no, I don't wanna do the research, just tell me what to do. So it's important to know who you are in this process and what you need in terms of information or not having an overload of information. And that's individual.

reference_conclusion: Following resection of the typical low-grade pulmonary carcinoid, no adjuvant therapy was recommended. Surveillance imaging with chest CT was advised, initially at 3- to 6-month intervals and then extended over a prolonged period, potentially up to 10 years or longer. After hepatic recurrence with bilobar metastases and residual low-volume disease following cytoreductive surgery, the plan was for active surveillance with imaging approximately every 6 months rather than immediate systemic therapy. With subsequent progression, liver-directed embolization and everolimus were used, and for further progressive Ga-68-avid disease, clinical trial enrollment was favored over standard therapies, with consideration of additional locoregional treatment if disease remained confined to one area.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Young adult male.

[ chief complaint ]: Reflux symptoms in 2011; recurrent ascites.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffuse malignant peritoneal mesothelioma, epithelioid type, initially diagnosed in 2016; subsequent biopsy-proven pleural involvement with bicavitary mesothelioma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2016 paracentesis cytology showed mesothelial proliferation.  
- Omental biopsy obtained at laparoscopy in 2016 showed epithelioid mesothelioma.  
- External pathology review confirmed intermediate-grade epithelioid mesothelioma.  
- Thoracoscopic pleural biopsy performed after recurrent pneumothorax demonstrated epithelioid mesothelioma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2011 abdominal ultrasound showed ascites.  
- CT imaging in 2011, reviewed retrospectively, showed ascites and abnormal omental density.  
- Abdominal ultrasound in 2016 showed increased intra-abdominal fluid.  
- CT scan in June 2016 showed omental caking suspicious for malignancy, a very small right pleural effusion, and a very small right pneumothorax.  
- PET-CT demonstrated diffuse uptake associated with omental caking, peritoneal thickening, moderate ascites, and mildly increased small right pneumothorax.  
- Post-neoadjuvant systemic therapy imaging showed stable disease without tumor shrinkage.  
- CT in January 2022 showed disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Germline BAP1 mutation identified on germline testing.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Serial surveillance with annual abdominal ultrasound from 2011 to 2016.  
- Paracenteses performed for ascites, including removal of 2 liters in 2016; later required monthly paracentesis during progression.  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy in 2016 with pemetrexed, platinum, and bevacizumab. Bevacizumab was discontinued because of toxicity; treatment continued with pemetrexed and platinum. Best radiographic response was stable disease.  
- November 2016: cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC performed. Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) was 39/39. Cytoreduction was incomplete (CC1/CC2) with unresectable confluent mesenteric bowel disease. Postoperative recovery was prolonged.  
- Observation was undertaken after surgery.  
- The following summer, recurrent pneumothorax led to thoracoscopic pleural biopsy confirming pleural mesothelioma.  
- In August of the following year, laparoscopy for suspected progression showed ascites without visible disease; observation continued.  
- In January 2022, repeat laparoscopy again showed PCI 39 and unresectable disease.  
- Enrolled on a clinical trial of an EZH2-targeted agent for BAP1-mutated disease. Adverse effects included diarrhea, abdominal cramping, altered taste, and skin rash. Disease remained stable for a little over 1 year before CT-confirmed progression.  
- With later progression associated with monthly paracentesis requirement and recurrent GERD, laparoscopic HIPEC was performed for palliation; disease remained unresectable at laparoscopy.  
- One month later, enrolled on a clinical trial of an oral TID inhibitor.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Functional status was described as fully functional.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Occupational/environmental history was notable for para-occupational asbestos exposure via father’s work clothes; father worked in a boiler room at a pharmaceutical company with exposure to steam pipes, boilers, and asbestos.  
- Family history was notable for multiple family members with cancer.  
- Recurrent right pneumothoraces occurred during the disease course.

reference_discussion.text: OK, so in 2011, this young gentleman developed some reflux symptoms, nothing abnormal. He, for some reason, underwent an ultrasound and it showed ascites. He had a paracentesis, he had a CT scan, and these failed to identify a cause. He was following with a primary care doctor, and he had really no other symptoms, and so his doctor followed him with yearly abdominal ultrasound. It comes to be 2016, and the ultrasound was showing some increase in fluid, and they removed two liters from a paracentesis. At this point, cytology, the cells in the fluid, revealed a mesothelial proliferation. In other words, something subnormal but doesn't look quite like cancer. So we're now two months later in June 2016, they do a CT scan finally. And it showed a mental caking, the apron on the abdomen had disease and it was suspicious for cancer. There was also a very tiny right pleural effusion fluid around the lung and a very tiny right pneumothorax. So that's an air leak between the lung and the chest wall. And this was later compared to a CT from 2011. And now in retrospect, they saw not only the ascites, but also some abnormal omental density. So he had this even back in 2011. Gives you an idea about a slow natural history of this disease. So he finally undergoes a laparoscopy. They put a scope inside. They do an omental biopsy. And lo and behold, the pathology revealed an epithelioid mesothelioma. He had a PET-CT, which showed, and I don't do them either, but this was ordered elsewhere. And it showed a diffuse uptake associated with omental caking, peritoneal thickening, moderate ascites, and mildly increase in that small right pneumothorax. He then was referred to our mesothelioma clinic. So our pathology review, indeed we always review the pathology from the outside, and it confirmed an intermediate grade epithelioid mesothelioma. We now have a two-stage system, low and high grade. In those days it was a three-grade system, so this was in the middle. We do standardly do germline testing on all of our patients and this revealed that he had a germline BAP1 mutation. When we looked at his exposure history because we take an occupational history from all of our patients. His father worked in a boiler room at a pharmaceutical company and was around steam pipes, boilers, and asbestos. So he had both a germline mutation and para-occupational exposure. His dad wore his work clothes home and he was exposed that way. BAP1 is what we think of as a gene-environment interaction, so maybe you have a lower threshold for developing the cancer, just like I have a lower threshold for developing sunburn when I'm out in the sun. He also had multiple family members who had cancer. We know that patients with germline mutations tend to be young, tend to have more commonly peritoneal disease, and have multiple family members with cancer. So we had a discussion regarding preoperative, or what we'd call neoadjuvant chemo. or upfront surgery. And the decision was made at that time that he received neoadjuvant chemo because one, and I think most important, his wife was expecting a baby in two months and he didn't want to be recuperating from surgery at the time of the birth. This occurs in young patients and there are other family issues that are involved. And secondly, the presence of that tiny pneumothorax suggested that we were concerned that there might be disease outside of the peritoneum. A spontaneous pneumothorax is a not uncommon presentation for a pleural meso, but it just didn't quite merit doing a thoracoscopy at that point. So he received what was standard at the time, Pametrexed platinum and Bevacizumab. He had some toxicity from Bevacizumab and had to stop it, so continued on just Pametrexed and platinum. And one does also have to hold the Bevacizumab because it can affect clotting and bleeding before you're going to do a surgery. Now the scan just showed stable disease. He hadn't actually had any tumor shrinkage. So we're now in November, and he underwent a CRS Hypex, so the cytoreductive surgery with the heated chemotherapy. And at that time, the PCI was 39 on a scale of 0 to 39. So he underwent a CC1 to CIDR reduction. Some areas were CC2, others were CC1. This was clearly an incomplete resection. There was confluent disease over the mesentery of the bowel which could not be removed. And he had a prolonged operative recovery. And he opted for observation afterwards. We had a discussion. You've got disease left. Do you want to get treatment now or not? This was before immunotherapy was standard of care. He'd had a prolonged recovery, he had young children, and he had disease that he knew had been there since at least 2011. So it was reasonable to offer observation in the absence of very active therapies and having such indolent disease. So the next summer, he had a recurrent pneumothorax. And at that point, we did a thoracoscopic pleural biopsy. And I remember my surgeon describing it as very thin and filmy, like you could barely really identify it there. But the biopsy did show an epithelioid mesothelioma. So he now had proven bicavitary disease. In August of the next year, he underwent a laparoscopy to better assess a concern for disease progression, and it showed no evidence of disease, just ascites, and continued observation was recommended. This was a little bit strange, but hey. So then in January of 2022, we are four years out, he finally has some disease progression on CAT scan. Laparoscopy again showed that PCI of 39 and he clearly was not considered resectable. So he was now offered chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or a clinical trial. How do we decide? Well, chemotherapy, his disease was at best stable from it, although maybe he had a delayed response. We don't know. He had a tough time with it, and he was not eager to resume it. Immunotherapy was, at that point in time, challenging to obtain from an insurance perspective for peritoneal meso, as it was approved only for pleural. And there was limited data on it in peritoneal patients. And a trial that Kiran Turaga and I were running concurrently actually showed an increase in ascites fluid in these patients getting immunotherapy. and some other challenging issues, and so we were a little reluctant to offer that to him, but his insurance basically wouldn't let us anyway. Or a clinical trial. At the time, we had a clinical trial of a drug targeting something called EZH2. And this was specifically for patients with BAP1 mutations, so it looked kind of perfect. Basically, if BAP1 goes down if you have a mutation, EZH2 goes up. And so this drug brings EZH2 down. So sounded pretty good. He did have a lot of side effects, including diarrhea, abdominal cramping, altered taste, skin rash. And however, he had stable disease for another year, a little over a year, when his disease finally progressed on CAT scan. But at that point, he was requiring monthly paracentesis, and he had recurrent GERD. Basically, thank you. Thank you so much, Julie. Definitely a caregiver. All right. So for him, whenever he would develop GERD, he would know that he needed a paracentesis. And so he was requiring monthly paracentesis had recurrent GERD. So we first wanted to see is there a surgical approach that we could use, we knew he wasn't a surgical candidate, but is there a surgical approach that we could use short of a CRS-HYPEC that might palliate ascites. We know that the CRS-HYPEC itself can control ascites well. And for a durable period, laparoscopic HIPAC, where you put a scope in and you put the heated chemotherapy in, can sometimes control ascites fluid. And so that was what we offered him. These days we're also doing PPAC where you spray the chemotherapy in. And on laparoscopy again we checked just in case and yeah, it wasn't resectable but he got his HIPEC. He then a month later was offered again the same options, chemo, immuno or a clinical trial. We had the same discussion. This time he said, I don't want chemotherapy. I know about immunotherapy. But if you got a trial, I did well before, can I try one again? It's a good lifestyle thing. I want to be able to play sports with my kids. And I'd rather take a pill than get immunotherapy with potentially unknown side effects. So he started on a trial of an oral TID inhibitor. Side effects include increased urine protein. And he continues on this trial for over two years. He no longer needs the monthly paracenteses. He no longer has GERD symptoms. His disease is more than 30% smaller. Basically, at every CAT scan, it gets about 2% smaller. And he is fully functional and quite happy. And I hope he can continue on this study for quite some time. So, that is a germline on receptacles.

So Eddie that's a quite a remarkable case. I think there are some things we can take from this. I think one the thing that stands out is here's a gentleman who made the choice even though we recommended treatment. He said I want to be observed and I think the key for all of us is we have to respect patients decisions you do and go through this disease on your own terms in terms of whether you want surgery or treatment or when you decide to act or not act. It's not compulsory that you get on therapy you have to appraise what you want. look at your own history and make decisions. And he had a significant amount of time after the interventions that were done before he faced having to go back on therapy. And I sometimes say patients are smarter than us. Like sometimes they make these calls and you're just like, wow, you just made a great decision. And we're looking at it through the prism of science all the time. So I think that's paramount. in a forum like this. Then I think the other thing that was interesting, there's always this debate about what does HIPEC do, but if indeed the laparoscopy said that his CC1-2 was cleared when they went back and looked, it argues that there was a therapeutic effect in that synergism of the systemic therapy, the surgery, that went down. And I will say that I've brought people back for second looks that have HIPEC'd, and know that there's malaria disease and it's gone and it's just scar. So there is this because we don't have clinical trials major clinical trials that sort of appraise the response. But there are definitely responders in there. And then I guess the last thing I would say the two things I'd ask you Hedy or one if you could tell us a little bit about the T inhibitor how that works. That was one thing I would want you to do if you don't mind.

So this is a very exciting class of drugs and there are several different drug companies So I'm not here to advertise drugs or trials or anything. So I'll just talk about this as a class. And there are several different drug companies that have drugs of this class. And so we think about this as a drug that targets one of the abnormal molecular on off switches. And so in me so most of the growth switches are actually off switches whereas in lung cancer they're mostly on switches and it's kind of a complex pathway. And this hits something called teed permit elation it hits something called the hippo yap pathway and it was thought initially to be something that was useful for patients who have what we call an F2 deletions. But now we know that they work even in patients who don't have these NF2 deletions. And so exactly the molecular mechanism is not fully clear. I would say that these several of these are in what we call phase 1B expansion cohorts. So these are trials where they're testing in multiple different diseases and at multiple different dose levels to find the right dose. This particular drug is moving to a phase 3 trial which will be age hopefully drug approval trial in which patients will be randomized to this drug or other drug or standard of care drugs. So they are promising enough. These data were recently presented at an international meeting and definitely show great promise for this disease. One of many classes of targeted therapies that are really exciting these days.

Awesome. And then the second thing I would say so if this weren't a germline mutated patient with bicarb disease how might this impact the decision making and sort of the course that we're observing how does that BAP one germline mutation sort of impact this case versus someone with bicarbonate disease with wild type.

We actually don't know that I know of other BAP one patients on this trial and I think that needs to be analyzed and looked at. Certainly patients with BAP1 germline status as this gentleman is have more indolent you know slower growing low grade disease and what is the impact of a drug that might take a while to work being able to do that in somebody who had slow growing disease as opposed to somebody with explosive disease. Maybe it doesn't have time to ramp up enough but I think we'll have to do analyses of the patient cohorts to know that.

And just the general tenor of this progression, if this would have been a wild type case, would you have, do you think we would have seen this same level of survivorship in someone with biocompartment disease with an intermediate to high grader? Or Mike can speak to that as well. Like have you had any biocompartment disease that are not BAP1 disease?

BAP1 germline wild type in a male with a high disease burden in the abdomen involving the chest. It's probably a more kind of aggressive disease course. I think the BAP1 germline here is a very important portion of this specific patient's long-term outcome.

I think there's also a difference between the patient whose disease is predominantly in the peritoneum versus the patient whose disease is predominantly in the chest and then moves to the peritoneum. It's the one that starts in the chest and moves to the peritoneum. That's usually a more advanced disease. The patient who starts in the abdomen and might have trivial disease in the pleura, you might still, if they're very symptomatic in the peritoneum, have ascites, et cetera, you may choose to operate in the peritoneum. But you would generally not do it in the reverse of a non-germline patient.
I wanted the non surgeons to speak to these things that how where it starts and the different factors that impact how the course will go. George has any thoughts.

Two things first that I wanted to really highlight what Jason said before how this has to be a conversation constantly with our patients their families not only for the reason that it is the right thing to do but also because we have limited scientific evidence to help us guide what we do. So I always bring the example with my patients about comparing this to, say, breast cancer. And those of you in the room who know somebody who has gone through breast cancer, there's so much literature there, so much knowledge that I jokingly like to say that we know if it's better for the patient to walk in the room with the right foot first or the left foot first. In mesothelioma, we don't know nearly as much. And in peritoneal mesothelioma, even less still. So I like to keep a little bit of an open mind. And in this case, the patient made a very reasonable and, in retrospect, a very correct decision by going potentially that route. But it is very important to know, and for us, kind of sitting on this side of the panel, acknowledge our limitations in what we do know and what we don't know and what we think we know. The second thing I wanted to really highlight, which everybody else has already, even though this is a wonderful, inspiring case, it is not the average case of the patient who comes in with a bicavitary disease. I think two things that will probably drive this home is, one, you had diagnosed pleural disease in 2018 or 2019, for which essentially he didn't get any treatment until five years later. Something that will ring true to anybody in this room who, again, knows of pleural mesothelioma, how many patients can go five years from diagnosis to first treatment. So there's something there that we have to use as we think about how some treatment worked or another didn't. He was fortunate enough to get years out of observation alone, which is again, wonderful, inspiring, maybe helps us identify different patients that may be getting similar treatment approaches. But I would caution against not using this as a benchmark to feel bad if we don't achieve the same outcomes with other patients, because that's unfortunately not nearly the average.

What's also interesting for this case is that we were just learning about the natural history of germline back one disease during this course. I mean this has not been identified or very long and so we didn't really know how insolent this disease was and we learned so much from our patients. But indeed and I really agree with you about the whole joint decision making on patients. It is so very important. You need to hear that patient voice.

Yeah, we'll have Giorgio's come up. I guess my final thoughts, I think the panel's done an excellent job just talking about all the angles of this particular problem. So I think we'll go on and do another case. This one will have more of a recurrence flavor, I believe.

reference_conclusion: The patient initially received neoadjuvant pemetrexed, platinum, and bevacizumab, with discontinuation of bevacizumab for toxicity, followed by cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC; given residual disease and prolonged postoperative recovery, observation was pursued. After subsequent confirmation of bicavitary disease and later progression with unresectable peritoneal recurrence, continued observation was recommended when laparoscopy showed no visible disease, and at later progression the management options discussed were chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or clinical trial enrollment. For symptomatic ascites, laparoscopic HIPEC was performed for palliation, after which the patient enrolled on a clinical trial of an oral TEAD inhibitor rather than chemotherapy or immunotherapy.

[...] So we're now in November, and he underwent a CRS Hypex [...] And he opted for observation afterwards. [...] In August of the next year, he underwent a laparoscopy to better assess a concern for disease progression, and it showed no evidence of disease, just ascites, and continued observation was recommended. [...] So he was now offered chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or a clinical trial. [...] And so that was what we offered him. [...] and yeah, it wasn't resectable but he got his HIPEC. He then a month later was offered again the same options, chemo, immuno or a clinical trial. [...] So he started on a trial of an oral TID inhibitor.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for consideration of completion thyroidectomy following prior outside thyroid surgery complicated by left vocal cord paralysis and persistent hoarse, breathy voice.

[ diagnosis ]: Widely invasive Hürthle cell (oncocytic) thyroid carcinoma, 8 cm, with gross extrathyroidal extension, positive margins, and extensive vascular invasion. Metastatic intrathoracic/mediastinal disease was present. Subsequent recurrent disease developed in the central neck bilaterally, predominantly on the right.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside thyroid surgery pathology demonstrated widely invasive Hürthle cell carcinoma measuring 8 cm with gross extrathyroidal extension, positive surgical margins, and extensive vascular invasion (>4 foci). Parathyroid tissue was present in the specimen. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy of intrathoracic/chest lesions was positive for metastatic disease. Biopsy of suspicious neck lymph nodes was negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging and ultrasound after outside surgery demonstrated bulky intrathoracic metastases. Mediastinal adenopathy was present and was considered unresectable by thoracic surgery. Over the subsequent years, lung nodules showed slow progression. Previously irradiated mediastinal disease remained stable. Recurrent disease later appeared in the central neck bilaterally, mostly on the right.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor profiling (Moffitt STAR/FoundationOne-type panel) identified no actionable alteration. An MSH1 mutation was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperative laboratory studies after the initial surgery were reported without major abnormalities. Thyroglobulin was elevated after surgery and slowly increased over the following years. After completion thyroidectomy, postoperative parathyroid hormone was within normal range.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial outside thyroid surgery was performed for an 8 cm thyroid nodule.  
- Preoperative FNA had been Bethesda II, described as colloid, macrophages, and follicular cells with some Hürthle cell change, favoring a colloid nodule.  
- The outside surgery was complicated by left vocal cord paralysis.  
- Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy confirmed metastatic intrathoracic disease.  
- Suspicious neck lymph nodes were biopsied and were negative.  
- Mediastinal nodal disease was treated with radiation therapy.  
- Completion thyroidectomy was subsequently performed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Left parotid tail mass present for 6 months, with mild interval growth during the preceding month.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma involving intraparotid lymph nodes, favored to represent metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma from an unknown primary.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside core biopsy of the left parotid tail mass showed neoplastic squamous epithelium; differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma versus mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Intraoperative frozen section was positive for squamous cell carcinoma. Final pathology showed squamous cell carcinoma, with a 1.1 cm deposit involving 2 intraparotid lymph nodes. Adjacent normal parotid tissue was present, supporting a non-primary parotid origin. Selective neck dissection specimen contained 15 lymph nodes, all negative for metastatic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 1.3 x 0.9 cm soft tissue mass along the superficial aspect of the left parotid tail. No pathologically enlarged cervical lymph nodes were identified on imaging.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent superficial parotidectomy. Following intraoperative frozen section confirmation of squamous cell carcinoma, a selective neck dissection of levels II-IV was performed.

[ current disease status ]: Status post superficial parotidectomy, selective neck dissection levels II-IV. Pathology demonstrated metastatic squamous cell carcinoma limited to 2 intraparotid lymph nodes, with 0/15 cervical lymph nodes involved.

[ other clinical data ]: There was no overlying skin ulceration, no associated pain, and no facial weakness. There was no history of prior skin cancer, prior head and neck cancer, or prior head and neck radiation. Past medical history included dyslipidemia and obstructive sleep apnea. Physical examination showed a 1.5 cm mobile, non-tender left parotid tail mass without overlying skin ulceration. Facial nerve function was intact. No visible skin lesions or scars were present on the scalp or face. No cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. Oral cavity and oropharyngeal examination were normal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Right breast swelling, change in skin color and texture over the right breast, and nipple retraction/detraction for more than 1 year prior to presentation in August 2017. Cough had been present for approximately 2 months at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast carcinoma diagnosed in late 2017. Invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, no special type, hormone receptor-positive and HER2-positive. CT chest demonstrated metastatic disease with widespread osseous metastases and enlarged right intramammary and axillary nodes, consistent with metastatic breast cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided breast biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type. Overall histologic grade was grade 2, with total score reported as 6/7.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial breast ultrasound showed a right subareolar breast mass measuring 1.7 × 1.7 cm with associated breast edema and nipple retraction, suggestive of neoplasm; BI-RADS 4.  
- Subsequent mammogram showed a right subareolar mass, BI-RADS 5, highly suspicious for malignancy.  
- Repeat breast ultrasound showed the mass measured 2.1 × 1.9 cm, with skin thickening, subcutaneous edema, and nipple retraction, suggestive of malignancy; minimal increase in size compared with the prior scan.  
- Chest radiograph showed no evidence of pulmonary metastasis; pneumonia was reported.  
- CT chest showed a right breast tumor with lymphangitis carcinomatosa, bilateral small pleural effusions (right greater than left), widespread osseous metastases, and enlarged right intramammary and axillary lymph nodes.  
- Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal abdominopelvic study.  
- Repeat mammogram showed increased right breast retroareolar density with areas of coarse calcification, right nipple retraction, and skin thickening. Left breast upper outer quadrant showed a 0.6 cm well-circumscribed opacity with scattered intraparenchymal calcifications; no left breast skin thickening or nipple retraction. Impression remained consistent with right breast carcinoma.  
- On recent clinical examination, the right breast lesion remained palpable at approximately 3 × 2 cm with nipple retraction and purulent skin changes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, and HER2 positive disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient was worked up for ACT chemotherapy.  
- She received 1 cycle of AC.  
- Two weeks after cycle 1 AC, she developed congestive cardiac failure and required admission.  
- Anthracycline-containing therapy was discontinued thereafter.  
- She was subsequently treated with single-agent paclitaxel at 175 mg/m² every 3 weeks.  
- She completed 6 cycles of paclitaxel; the last cycle had been administered 2 months prior to current review.  
- She was receiving letrozole 2.5 mg daily.  
- Trastuzumab had been advised but was not administered because she could not afford it.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent right breast mass remained present after chemotherapy, with ongoing nipple retraction and purulent skin changes. Recent palpable lesion size was approximately 3 × 2 cm. ECOG performance status was 1. Metastatic disease had been documented on CT chest, including widespread bone metastases and bilateral pleural effusions.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included hypertension.  
- No prior hospital admissions were reported before cancer treatment.  
- No prior blood transfusions were reported.  
- No family history of cancer was reported.  
- No other chronic illnesses were reported.  
- No known food allergy history was reported; fennel allergy was reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Follow-up after treatment for right breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma right breast, triple-negative breast cancer, stage II at diagnosis in January 2024. ECOG performance status was 1 at diagnosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Right modified radical mastectomy performed in May 2025 showed pathological complete response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Hereditary cancer germline panel identified a pathogenic APC gene mutation. BRCA1 and BRCA2 were negative on the reported panel.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent wide local excision of the right breast mass. Received systemic therapy including pembrolizumab with paclitaxel and carboplatin; regimen was subsequently modified to paclitaxel-carboplatin due to toxicity. Pembrolizumab was reportedly administered for 1-2 cycles and then stopped because of toxicity. Underwent right modified radical mastectomy in May 2025, with pathological complete response. Received postoperative radiotherapy. Received maintenance capecitabine for 1 year, continued until August 2025. Last imaging showed complete response.

[ current disease status ]: Complete response on last imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Family history was significant for carcinoma endometrium in an elder sister.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected brain tumor showed an infiltrating astrocytic neoplasm with mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for GFAP. Ki-67 proliferation index was 40%. IDH1 immunostain was negative. Integrated pathologic diagnosis was glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4. MGMT testing was sent. EGFR FISH was sent.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial brain MRI demonstrated a mass lesion in the left posterior temporal region with mass effect, T2 hyperintensity, irregular contrast enhancement, a central non-enhancing necrotic component, and surrounding edema, consistent with an aggressive tumor. Preoperative functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging were performed for surgical planning because of proximity to language pathways; the lesion was also assessed relative to visual and sensory tracts. Postoperative MRI demonstrated complete resection of the contrast-enhancing tumor, with no nodular enhancement and no residual hazy T2 signal abnormality to suggest residual enhancing or non-enhancing tumor. Approximately 6 months after chemoradiation, follow-up MRI showed nodular enhancement at the margin of the resection cavity with associated concern for recurrence versus treatment effect. Perfusion imaging demonstrated increased blood flow within an enhancing area adjacent to the original tumor site, a finding concerning for viable recurrent tumor. Subsequent perfusion imaging of another enhancing area showed low perfusion, which was less concerning for tumor recurrence and more compatible with treatment effect.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH1 was negative by immunostaining, consistent with IDH-wildtype status. EGFR testing by FISH was ordered. MGMT status was ordered but no result was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: After diagnostic workup, the patient underwent craniotomy with gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing lesion. Postoperative imaging showed no radiographic residual enhancing tumor. In the newly diagnosed setting, he received radiation therapy with concurrent temozolomide, followed by adjuvant temozolomide. He enrolled in a clinical trial and received an EGFR inhibitor together with radiation and concurrent temozolomide, followed by adjuvant temozolomide plus the EGFR inhibitor. Tumor treating fields were not used during adjuvant therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Several months after completion of initial therapy, imaging changes developed at the resection cavity margin. The differential included recurrent glioblastoma versus treatment effect/pseudoprogression/radiation necrosis. Perfusion MRI findings were concerning for recurrent tumor in at least one enhancing focus.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypothyroidism. He was started on levetiracetam after presentation with seizure. Radiation therapy for glioblastoma was described as 60 Gy in 30 daily fractions.

And if there is definite progression, there's also clinical trial options that can be explored.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female. Past medical history included congenital optic atrophy, reported as probably bilateral.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred in early 2019 after resection of a 12 cm parieto-occipital scalp mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (FVPTC/FBPTC reported in record), with osseous and orbital metastatic disease. Documented metastatic sites included parieto-occipital scalp/calvarial lesion, temporal bone involvement, and right orbital metastasis with intracranial extension.

[ histopathology results ]:
- Outside pathology from a 4.8 cm right thyroid nodule resected approximately 2 years earlier had initially been reported as benign after right thyroidectomy/lobectomy.
- Following diagnosis of metastatic thyroid carcinoma, outside thyroid pathology was reviewed for second opinion and amended to metastatic follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Pathology from the resected 12 cm parieto-occipital scalp mass showed metastatic FVPTC.
- Pathology from urgent anterior orbitotomy specimen again showed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma, with a small amount of background necrosis.

[ imaging findings ]:
- In 2019, CT head and MRI demonstrated metastasis involving the temporal bones and right orbit.
- Post-radioactive iodine treatment scan after 175 mCi showed only small uptake in the right thyroid bed and occipital region.
- Whole-body scan and PET imaging performed in late 2022 with levothyroxine withdrawal showed no metastasis.
- Repeat PET-CT in mid-2024 showed no abnormalities despite rising thyroglobulin.
- After recombinant TSH stimulation, scan demonstrated intense right orbital uptake.
- CT showed right orbital disease with intracranial extension.
- Imaging of the orbital mass showed proptosis, significant mass effect on the right globe, and areas of flow void consistent with marked vascularity.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:
- At initial detection of metastatic disease, serum thyroglobulin was 778.
- After surgical resection of the scalp mass, thyroglobulin became undetectable.
- Thyroglobulin remained completely undetectable until late 2022.
- In late 2022, thyroglobulin rose to 10 over 6 months.
- Thyroglobulin then remained detectable but below 10 until mid-2024.
- In mid-2024, thyroglobulin increased to 64.
- Five months later, thyroglobulin increased to 181.
- After recombinant TSH stimulation (0.9 mg IM twice), stimulated thyroglobulin was 1300 and TSH was approximately 80.
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:
- Approximately 2 years before referral, the patient underwent right thyroidectomy/lobectomy for a 4.8 cm thyroid nodule; original outside pathology had been reported as benign.
- In early 2019, the patient underwent surgical resection of a 12 cm parieto-occipital scalp mass; pathology showed metastatic FVPTC. Postoperatively, thyroglobulin became undetectable.
- In 2019, the patient underwent completion thyroidectomy.
- Following identification of temporal bone/right orbital metastatic disease, the patient underwent additional surgical resection of this mass.
- The patient received radioactive iodine, 175 mCi. Post-treatment scan showed only small uptake in the right thyroid bed and occipital region.
- After development of right eye proptosis and edema following recombinant TSH stimulation, high-dose corticosteroids were administered.
- The patient subsequently underwent urgent anterior orbitotomy; pathology again showed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with small background necrosis.

[ current disease status ]: Rising thyroglobulin in 2024 was followed by clinically and radiographically evident progressive right orbital metastatic disease with intracranial extension.

[ other clinical data ]:
- The patient had poor tolerance to levothyroxine withdrawal, prompting use of recombinant TSH for subsequent stimulated evaluation.
- Right orbital disease developed with right eye proptosis and edema.
- Vision preservation was a significant clinical consideration because of pre-existing optic nerve atrophy.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so this is a long story, but I will try to summarize it. So this patient was referred to us in early 2019. She's a 70-year-old female, past medical history of congenital optic atrophy. She came in after a removal of a 12-centimeter parieto-occipital scalp mass, and the pathology was metastatic FBPTC. The patient had two years prior to that. She had a right thyroidectomy or lobectomy, for a 4.8 centimeter nodule. The final pathology was in an outside hospital that showed as benign, but then when we received the diagnosis of the FVPTC, we send it again for a second opinion and it was amended to be metastatic. So at the time of initial detection of the metastasis, the serum thyroglobulin was 778, which was consistent with active metastatic disease. The patient had a surgical resection of the scalp mass, her thyroglobulin was undetected, reflecting the reduction of the tumor burden. Then afterwards, she'd had a completion thyroidectomy in 2019 and a CAT scan of her head showed, an MRI as well, showed a metastasis in the temporal bones in the right orbit. Then the patient had another surgery and we resected this mass and she received 175 microcurie of the radioactive iodine. The post-treatment scan showed only small uptake in the right thyroid bit and the occipital region.

Laurie, help me with this sort of natural history here. Somebody presenting with this big tumor and then a bone mat. What are you sort of thinking about natural histories likely to happen here, Laurie?

Well, so, you know, that big 12 centimeter calvarial lesion probably had been there for a long time. And so, I think that this seems like a very rapidly aggressive, progressive cancer, but it may not be. However, with this lesion here on the CT scan invading the right orbit, it makes you wonder because with the calvarial lesion, the patient would have had good head imaging and a lesion there should have been appreciated even if it was a little bit smaller. So I am a little bit worried about this being a more aggressive variant than a typical follicular variant PTC. And you can see disease that's been around for a long time becoming more more de-differentiated and have one area in particular becoming more de-differentiated than disease elsewhere. So, I'm a little bit concerned about what the histology of that particular orbital lesion is.
Azita, any comments on that imaging other than there's a big blob there?

No, well, the mass, if you look at it, has areas of flow void, which means it's very vascular, which you typically see. It has proptosis. It has significant mass effect against the right globe. And there is one thing that's very important that was in the histories. The patient already has optic nerve atrophy, and it's probably bilateral. So in terms of, you know, vision preservation is very important in this patient.
Very good. Okay, and where do we go from here, Dr. Imer?

Yeah, so the patient had like the completion thyroidectomy in 2019 and she has been following up with us. She had like a completely undetectable thyroglobulin until late 2022, which like subsequently it rose to 10 over six months. We did an i9 whole body scan and also PET scanning with levothyroxine withdrawal that showed no metastasis. Thyroglobulin was like stabilized, was below 10. It was detectable but was below 10 until mid of 2024. Then suddenly the thyroglobulin increased to 64 and then we were thinking about like possible de-differentiation like given the prior negative scanning. So we repeated again like the PET-CT that showed like no abnormalities. But five months later, the thyroglobulin increased to 181. And then during that time, we decided to do the precombinant TSH with the scanning because the patient had poor tolerance to the levothyroxine withdrawal. So the protocol that we used was like 0.9 IM twice and the patient had like a stimulated thyroglobin of 1300, TSH was around 80 and the thyroglobin level was antibody was negative. Suddenly after the recombinant TSH patient started to have right eye proptosis, edema, and then the scan showed intense right orbital uptake with intracranial extension on the CAT scan. I have a video here, hopefully you can detect a little bit of the uptakes.

All right, so David, help me here. We always were, when we got thyrogen years ago, we were always worried that we were going to see big swelling either in the spine or in the brain. How often does that happen and if you do, how do you deal with it, David?

Yeah, so it's rare. It is very rare when it occurs. Clearly it is a concern. I mean, I haven't personally had this, you know, happen to me in this scenario, but really, you know, the key is in those patients that are at particular risk, you know, it's worthwhile doing, you know, appropriate staging beforehand when you are suspecting either clinically metastases or otherwise, if there is a significant likelihood, particularly of cerebral or spinal mets to do imaging, to confirm that before you know, treatment, but then really if it does occur, you know, that key step is giving things like steroids to try to reduce that, you know, edema and swelling and inflammation and, you know, manage accordingly on spec in this case.

Yeah, because our usual approach in the setting of these widespread distant meds is to treat any of them that we know about before we give the thyrogen. Like we radiate before, we give them steroids and stuff before, but every once in a while you get surprised because you didn't know one was there. Okay and so you guys had some swelling with the thyrogen and then where did you go from there?

Correct, so we gave her a high dose of corticosteroids but then the patient unfortunately she went for another surgery which was an urgent anterior orbitotomy and then the specimen again showed a follicular barium PTC. was a small amount of background necrosis and this was the CAT scan after the MRI. The tumor board in our institution recommended orbital inoculation with limited craniotomy. because of the progressive orbital metastasis invading the intracranial space. The patient underwent the surgery in late 2024. It was a big surgery. We have people from ophthalmology, neurosurgery, ENT, and this is the pathology. Also, the patient got external beam radiation and the surgical pathology confirmed the follicular variant BTC.
I mean, this just seems like way out of control for a follicular variant.

Sure. So, you know, like, this is not the typical story. You know, I have seen, unfortunately, you know, a benign thyroidectomy and then a bone mat. So this is not the first time I've seen this. And then go back to the original benign histology and find out something that is not benign. But even then, you know, it's not the typical story for for PPC follicular variant. So I would put money down that, you know, if they go back and they look at the original thyroid lesion, that they're going to find the high mitotic rate or some necrosis, you know. And so I think from the get go, this is acting like high grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma. And so from here, all I could see is, well, this is thyroid and, you know, I'm sure it's TTF1. And then, you know, you have to look at the overall picture for four prognostic. You know, it's not the picture of, as you say, a usual follicular variant PTC.

Yeah. Laurie, thoughts about this one for me? I mean, this is, it's a weird pattern. I suspect Margie's probably right. If we looked into it, it'd be. some molecular combination? How are you thinking about this, Laurie?

So I think, you know, we don't quite know the extent of disease elsewhere, but this is bad disease and in bad places. And so even if there's not a large tumor burden elsewhere, if there is some residual disease, my interest in starting an effective systemic therapy is a sooner rather than later thing. For the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the word on the street used to be that they don't work in bone. But we actually, when we took a look at the select patients from the lenbatin and phase three trial who had bony disease, they had the same progression-free survival benefit that patients with other METs like lung METs had. So I do actually think that there is a role for Linvatinib offering benefit when patients biggest problems are bone metastases. So that's one thing, you know, we definitely want to know the genotype. What I'd really like to know is, you know, in addition to a driver alteration here, Are there additional alterations that are suggesting this is a much more aggressive disease, like an ARID1A commutation or a P53 commutation? Again, those aren't drugable, but they can give us an idea of what to expect going down the road.
Dr. Wang, what are you thinking here to help them out?

You know, first of all, we didn't have a research until end of last year in China. So, so we only do withdraw of ILT4 in China. But right now, we do have a recombination TSH now in China, so we are hearing what kind of thing will happen. Especially this is a very special case, but it's very interesting case and I noticed this case was published already, so I will introduce this case to my to my colleagues. And the second for this patient. So why do we should put further therapy or treatment. So, I will discuss with my oncologist and not endocrinologist. So, in China, most endocrinologists actually do not treat cell cancer at this late stage.

Yeah, same way in the United States. Laurie, the role for bisphosphonates or zoledronic acid in people with bone meds, it seems to wax and wane. We use it some years and we don't. Where are we sort of, I mean, this patient's going to have other bone meds because it's coming up in the bone. Do you use the zoledronic acid or one of the other ones? How do you do that, Laurie?

Yeah we do. So you know unfortunately we don't have randomized phase 3 trials in people with thyroid cancer with bone modifying agents and bone metastases but there have been studies done across other solid tumors that have shown both with zoledronic acid as well as denosumab that the bone modifying agents do decrease the risk of complications related to bone metastases, including things that are really meaningful like pain, need for surgery, pathologic fracture. So we use them. I think one of the things that's different about the thyroid cancer patient population is that they tend to live for a long time. And so what's the right frequency of using those drugs and for how long do we use them? We don't have great data, but I usually give the bone-modifying agents every three months, and I might stop after two or three years. The other thing is, you know, with this patient population with radioactive iodine, they have xerostomia. Our patients may be at a slightly higher risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw on bone-modifying agents, so you definitely want to make sure that the patient's dental health is in good shape.

Dr. Demers, let me bring you back in. Just from the practical clinical aspects of taking somebody like that. I mean, we endocrinologists do thyroid cancer and people do well, and we send them back for surgery. We're not usually sending them back for big eye surgeries or, you know, even taking tracheas out and that sort of stuff. How do you sort of think through that discussion with the patient? I know the discussion happens at the disease management team, but how does that get translated back to this individual patient at your Geist Center?

So I think it's a hard discussion. It's going to be a hard discussion because it's going to be compromising the eye. It's going to be a tough discussion. That would be a tough one. I don't have a real answer, but I would probably put it out in a way that here is the disease, and this is what we are kind of Making a decision as a team, we think this is a better idea to do and I would probably bring up to the patient and we'll kind of, you know, get the patient's output and see what the patient thinks about the, because some patients don't want to do anything, you know, they will just say, I'm fine, I don't want to lose my eye. Yeah, it depends on the patient, yeah. So I would try to do with the patient like, we'll try to be on the same page with the patient, yeah.

David, can you speak to sort of how your disease management team communicates this information with the patient? Is there one person that's the lead of everything or is it the person that's known them the longest or is it different? How does that really work on these difficult discussions, David?

Yeah, I think it really depends on which clinician has had the most, you know, contact and has the best rapport with the patient. So, you know, some patients will have, you know, been predominantly followed in nuclear medicine or within radiation oncology or endocrinology. So it really depends on who has that best rapport with the patient and their family. or a medical oncologist. I mean, in this case, I think it would be a discussion with the surgeon, who's really that key decision maker. But yeah, I think it really depends on who has that best rapport, and also, in this case, who's actually gonna be delivering the intervention as the best.

Exactly, yeah, that everybody's on the same page, somebody's not being too optimistic, too pessimistic, we're giving the same message, and then we do the same thing. Whoever's really delivering that, aggressive treatment, whether it's the oncologist or the radiation oncologist. They're making the final decisions, but all of us are supporting that in the background. Difficult things that we're not traditionally trained to do as endocrinologists, part of that. Fantastic. Well, let me say thank you very much to our team from Missouri. These were great cases. They were some wonderful discussions. Oh, perfect. And that's the publication that we were talking about. Beautiful. That's there. Perfect. All right. Thank you again for doing that. So coming up will be Dr. Nair, an interesting discussion next week, and then you can see the other ones coming. And then just a reminder about the Voices of Wisdom. I got it right this time. Wonderful podcast, great things to listen to. Thanks again to our panelists. We stuck to the landing right on time. Wonderful cases. Thanks, team. Bye-bye.
