case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria and increased lower urinary tract symptoms at initial presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: High-risk localized prostate cancer. Initial biopsy demonstrated Gleason score 5+5=10, Grade Group 5 adenocarcinoma. Subsequent pathology demonstrated very high-grade adenocarcinoma with possible neuroendocrine/small cell features on re-biopsy after initiation of androgen deprivation therapy.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial prostate biopsy showed the index lesion in the left prostate with Gleason score 5+5=10, Grade Group 5 disease involving >90% of that core; right-sided biopsy cores were negative. Re-biopsy after initial androgen deprivation therapy showed a very high-grade poorly differentiated tumor with almost no glandular differentiation, sheets of poorly differentiated cells, and Ki-67 proliferation index approximately 80%. Neuroendocrine markers including synaptophysin were negative. This specimen was signed out as Gleason score 5+5=10, Grade Group 5 adenocarcinoma with a note of possible neuroendocrine differentiation/small cell features.

[ imaging findings ]: Prostate MRI demonstrated a PI-RADS 5 lesion in the left lobe of a 44 cc prostate, with suspicion for neurovascular bundle involvement and possible seminal vesicle and pelvic sidewall invasion. MRI appearance was described as involving nearly the entire left side of the gland with extraprostatic extension and aggressive diffusion characteristics. Initial metastatic workup with bone scan and CT showed no evidence of metastasis. Research PSMA PET demonstrated avid uptake in the primary prostatic lesion without definite extraprostatic disease on pelvic imaging and identified a 7 mm right upper lobe pulmonary nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genetic testing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial PSA was 3.9 ng/mL. Repeat PSA was 3.5 ng/mL. IPSS was approximately 25. SHIM score was 13.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient enrolled on protocol J1560. Planned androgen deprivation therapy consisted of leuprolide for 2 years plus bicalutamide. Androgen deprivation therapy was initiated.

[ current disease status ]: High-risk localized prostate cancer with very high-grade adenocarcinoma and possible neuroendocrine/small cell features on re-biopsy after initiation of androgen deprivation therapy. No evidence of distant metastatic disease was identified on conventional imaging with bone scan and CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history included uncles with prostate cancer at older age and a mother with an unspecified kidney tumor.

reference_discussion.text: We're going to get started with these three patients. Our next patients are a 52-year-old gentleman with a high-risk localized disease, a second gentleman with biochemical recurrence, and a third gentleman with focal therapy options. So in our first patient is a 52-year-old gentleman who initially presented with gross hematuria with increased lower urinary tract symptoms on his gross hematuria workup. He was noted to have a PSA at 3.9 with an abnormal digital rectal exam, which prompted a prosthetic MRI, which revealed a Pirates 5 lesion in his left lobe with suspicion for neurovascular bundle involvement, as well as potential seminal vesicle and sidewall invasion. He had a 44cc gland. He underwent a prostate biopsy, which showed a left, which that lesion showed a Gleason 5 plus 5 or gray group 5 disease greater than 90% of that core. The whole right side of his biopsy was negative. He underwent a metastatic workup given his advanced disease, including a bone scan and a CT scan, which showed no evidence of metastasis. Under a research protocol, he underwent a PSMA PET scan, which showed a primary prostatic lesion and a seven millimeter right upper lobe pulmonary nodule. Genetic testing was negative at that time. His repeat PSA was still 3.5. Of note, his family history was significant with uncles with prostate cancer at a late age and a mother with an unknown type of kidney tumor. Otherwise, his preoperative IPSS or his voiding symptoms were roughly 25, so moderate to severe lower urinary tract symptoms, and his SHIM, which is a marker for his erectile function, was 13, indicating moderate to severe erectile dysfunction. He underwent discussion at our prostate multidisciplinary clinic, and the decision was made to enroll the patient on a J1560 trial, which included androgen deprivation therapy, as well as radiation. The androgen deprivation therapy was going to include two years of Luprolide, as well as bicalutamide. He started his ADT. And on the research protocol was a re-biopsy at Hopkins, which revealed actually small cell features of his prostate cancer. He was re-discussed at our tumor board, which the tumor board consensus was recommending continuation of ADT and radiation therapy, however, chemotherapy given his small cell features. He completed four cycles of his chemotherapy from December last year to March of this year. However, he was having ongoing hematuria, his lower urinary tract symptoms persisted, as well as horrible nocturia. He underwent a restaging physical exam with his digital rectal exam, revealing a prostate that was relatively mobile, and underwent a cystoscopy, which showed no involvement of his ureral orifices or prostatic involvement of his bladder neck. And his repeat PSMA showed resolved pulmonary nodules. if we can review our pathology or the pathology and radiology review.

Great. So this is the biopsy we received following his initial course of ADT. And it's a very unusual and very high grade appearing tumor. There's almost no glandular differentiation in this tumor. You can see just sort of sheets of very blue cells here. And the blue is the nuclei of the cells, which is taking up most of the space within the cytoplasm or within the body of the cell. So the nuclei are very large. And again, no glandular differentiation whatsoever. So, given the lack of glandular differentiation, we suspected that this might have some features of neuroendocrine differentiation, which is when the prostate cells sort of lose their identity, often because we've applied some selective pressure, such as androgen deprivation therapy. And so the pathologist examining this case looked first at a proliferation marker to see what fraction of the tumor cells are proliferating. In a typical prostate tumor, it's not larger than about 5% of cells overall, so actually a very low proliferation fraction compared to other types of tumors. But you could see here in this prostate tumor, all the brown cells on the left, all the brown dots are the nuclei that are proliferating actively, meaning dividing actively within this tumor. And so the proliferation rate or the percentage of cells that are dividing is probably, you know, 80% at least, which is very, very high and unusual for a prosthetic adenocarcinoma. And that would be more typical of a neuroendocrine differentiated tumor. However, when we looked at neuroendocrine markers, these are sort of neural cell markers that prostate cancer cells can begin to express. particularly after they're put under some kind of pressure like androgen deprivation therapy or some kind of treatment, we don't see any synaptophysin or any neural marker expression. So it's a little bit of a hybrid case, the proliferation rate or the rate of cell division is suggestive of some neuroendocrine or very, very high-grade features, but we don't have a complete picture of neuroendocrine differentiation because the cells are not expressing neuroendocrine markers. So it was eventually signed out as a glucine 5 plus 5 equals 10 or grade group 5 adenocarcinoma with a note suggesting that it might have some neuroendocrine differentiation and perhaps chemotherapy could be useful in that context. So in this slide, you can see his prostatectomy sample. And at this point, we have sort of a tumor with divided features. So on the left side, you can see tumor cells that are making some glands, some sort of circular structures or glands that resemble the normal prostate. So these are cancer cells that are better differentiated. They're adenocarcinoma cells. And on the right, you can see just sheets of very poorly differentiated cells. These still have overall more features of adenocarcinoma than neuroendocrine carcinoma, but this may have been, you know, this area may be better related to that very poorly differentiated area we saw on the biopsy here. and may have differentiated after additional therapy. So this was, again, signed out as a 5 plus 4 is 9 adenocarcinoma. And then this is just an example of seminal vesicle invasion that we saw in this case. So the case was pathologic stage 3B, meaning there was invasion of the adjacent seminal vesicle glands adjacent to the prostate. On the left, you can see with some brown pigment in them, the normal seminal vesicle epithelium. And on the right, you can see the cancer cells invading in the muscle layer around the seminal vesicle there. Again, these are adenocarcinoma appearing cells. There was also a metastasis in a lymph node. And so this was stages P or pathologic stage 3B and 1 at radical prostatectomy.

All right, so we'll take a look at some imaging for this patient. He has both an MRI and a PSMA PET. And similar to the pathology, the appearance of this tumor is highly unusual on MRI. On the left-hand side of the screen is the TT-weighted or anatomic sequence, and on the right-hand side is a diffusion-weighted or more functional biological sequence of the MRI. And nearly the entire left side of the gland and extending outside of the gland is a heterogeneous tumor with a very odd growth pattern. So we don't normally see such obvious violation of the capsule around the prostate and growth of tumor in this fashion, all the way up to the sidewall of the pelvis. So a very unusual appearing tumor on MRI. And the right-hand image we're able to see is decreased signal on diffusion-weighted imaging. Admittedly, diffusion-weighted imaging is sort of the Rorschach test of radiology. You really have to sort of be honed in I'd be looking at something very specific to make anything out of all the sort of gray and white dots. But in the area where the tumor is, again, occupying the left side of the gland, there's relatively low signal, which indicates sort of tightly packed cells and is very suggestive of an aggressive tumor type. So can we move on to the PSMA PET? Perfect. So PSMA PET's a relatively new tool. The first PSMA radio tracer was FDA approved in the US in December of last year. And then an agent that's more nationally available was approved in May of this year. This was done on a research protocol. And most of what we see here is completely normal. So the lacrimal glands above the eyes, the salivary glands around the face, all have normal uptake. The liver, the spleen, the kidneys, the bowel, all normal. And then there's excreted radiotracer in the urinary bladder. And then right below that, there's this fuzzier, less well-defined area of uptake. And that's the tumor in this case. On this whole body image, there's really no evidence to suggest that there's anything outside of the prostate. There's just the primary tumor. And we'll look at a few sort of slices through the pelvis on these images. And these are the PSMA PET fused to CT for anatomic correlation. And in the upper left, the bright spot, there is actually just urine in the right ureter. And we see that again in the bottom right. There's really nothing else abnormal, or nothing actually abnormal in any of these images. That is at least suggestive of this being a tumor that's confined to the prostate. Although, as Dr. Lotan told us, there was a pathologic evidence of disease in the lymph nodes. And in spite of how great PSMA PET is and how sensitive it is for sites of prostate cancer, it doesn't replace true pathologic surgical staging in these cases. And the sensitivity is relatively marginal for pelvic lymph node involvement. However, we can see there's very bright uptake in the primary tumor in the prostate. And this is also in keeping with the pathologic findings of this still being an adenocarcinoma. Neuroendocrine differentiated prostate cancers tend to lose PSMA expression and will not appear hot on PSMA PET. So this is additional evidence that this is at least somewhat behaving as an adenocarcinoma.

So, in summary, we have a 52-year-old gentleman with initial diagnosis of gray group 5, high-risk prostate cancer, with initial decision to pursue ADT as well as radiation therapy on a research protocol. He was re-biopsied, which was significant for some evidence of small cell features. Now, sounds close, chemotherapy with persistent significant lower urinary tract symptoms with no evidence of metastatic disease and a negative cystoscopy for trigonal involvement.

So I would just comment that to give a patient this type of chemotherapy is not what we usually do for an average prostate cancer. Cisplatinamide and etoposide is reserved for patients we're very concerned about who have at least some indication of These neuro endocrine features and as you saw from the pathology that ki 67 staining with 80% of the lesion, even though there's some nap device and was negative made us concerned that this patient would have micro metastatic disease and so. We actually treat, when we worry about that, we think about using what's a regimen that's usually used for neuroendocrine lung cancer, and that's this cisplatinum etoposide regimen. And we gave four cycles of that to try and shrink everything we could, even things we couldn't see. And it's interesting for us that it was noted that the patient had a small lesion in the lung that did go away on a subsequent scan, which suggests that that might have been a metastatic foci that we treated with the chemo.

You know, we're learning so much about these PSMA scans and Dr. Rowe, you've been a leader in that, but, you know, this case is fascinating because, you know, typical prostate cancer is an adenocarcinoma, which you would expect to light up in a PSMA scan. Do we know yet, or are we still learning about variant histology within prostate cancer and how PSMAs do or do not detect that?

Yeah, great question, Max. And I would say that because these tend to be such rare tumors, there's not necessarily a big prospective clinical trial that's told us exactly how PSMA behaves in an imaging sense. Although at the pathologic level, it does seem as though most of these tumors will lose PSMA expression and I think we'd expect them to be cold on imaging. And the small sort of retrospective case series and case reports that we do have are consistent with that, where we don't necessarily reliably image these with PSMA PET. Although, again, his primary tumor was quite hot. So I do think that is suggestive of at least some some maintenance of kind of the adenocarcinoma phenotype or otherwise, again, we wouldn't have even seen it on the PET scan. As to whether potential metastases might be sort of more differentiated along a neuroendocrine phenotype and we might miss them with PSMA PET, that's certainly possible, although I don't think we know that definitively yet.

Just to add a comment from the radiation oncology perspective, I think this is also a positive plug for research and considering research trials as part of the continuum of care. In this case, we have a trial that was designed for patients with high-risk prostate cancer who were considering radiation and hormonal therapy. And prior to it becoming commercially available, we had it available just under research, wanting to detect, see if we could detect patients with, know, distant disease not being picked up on their conventional scans. But also it included this second scan and baseline biopsy and second biopsy trying to assess response to hormonal therapy and see if there are some sort of correlates with imaging and biology. And in this case, you know, I think it was helpful, you know, hopefully had a positive impact on the patient's course. And it was that research biopsy that really detected the small cell differentiation and altered the course and advising, you know, additional systemic therapy. And then later he was, you know, kind of steered towards surgery, you know, perhaps taking that into consideration and also some of his response to the treatment.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary review supported continuation of androgen deprivation therapy and radiation therapy, with the addition of platinum-etoposide chemotherapy because of the biopsy findings concerning for small cell/neuroendocrine features. Four cycles of cisplatin and etoposide were administered from December through March. Given persistent significant lower urinary tract symptoms, absence of metastatic disease, and negative cystoscopy for trigonal involvement, the subsequent course included direction toward surgical management.
reference_conclusion_quote: He was re-discussed at our tumor board, which the tumor board consensus was recommending continuation of ADT and radiation therapy, however, chemotherapy given his small cell features. He completed four cycles of his chemotherapy from December last year to March of this year. [...] And in this case, you know, I think it was helpful, you know, hopefully had a positive impact on the patient's course. And it was that research biopsy that really detected the small cell differentiation and altered the course and advising, you know, additional systemic therapy. And then later he was, you know, kind of steered towards surgery, you know, perhaps taking that into consideration and also some of his response to the treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial presentation to the emergency department with inability to void.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IVA squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, with extension into the posterior bladder base. Patient was COVID-19 positive at the time of initial definitive treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Multiple biopsies obtained from the cervical/vaginal tumor and from bladder lesions identified on cystoscopy showed poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Cervical, vaginal, and bladder biopsies were all positive for squamous cell carcinoma. Tumor stained positive for p16.

[ imaging findings ]: Pelvic evaluation demonstrated a large pelvic mass. Examination under anesthesia identified a 6 cm firm mass extending down the vagina to the level of the introitus, completely obliterating the vagina; the mass was fixed and extended to both pelvic sidewalls. Cystoscopy demonstrated friable nodules at the posterior base of the bladder. Imaging showed right hydroureteronephrosis. Staging PET-CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic cervical malignancy and multiple peripheral ground-glass opacities in both lungs with low-level hypermetabolic activity. No lymphadenopathy was identified in the pelvis, para-aortic region, or mediastinum. Differential interpretation of the pulmonary findings on PET-CT included metastatic disease versus infectious/inflammatory process. Dedicated chest CT and lung biopsy were planned but were not performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Right nephrostomy tube and Foley catheter were placed for obstructive uropathy/urinary retention. Definitive chemoradiation was initiated. Radiation therapy was held for a few days during evaluation.

[ current disease status ]: Patient remained asymptomatic from COVID-19 infection, without fever, cough, shortness of breath, or known sick contacts.

[ other clinical data ]: No significant past medical history, surgical history, or family history was reported. Patient had normal BMI. Patient was a frequent traveler and often flew to and from New Orleans for work. SARS-CoV-2 testing returned positive approximately 24 hours after testing.

<image> Histopathology showing poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with p16 positivity.
<image> PET/CT findings of bilateral hypermetabolic ground-glass lung opacities, an intensely avid cervical mass, and no hypermetabolic lymph nodes, with infection or inflammation in the differential.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. As Rami said, my name is Navya Nair, and I'm a GYN oncologist at Louisiana State University in New Orleans. Before I start with the case, please note that Project ECHO case consultations do not create or otherwise establish a provider-patient relationship between any IGCS volunteer clinician and any patient whose case is being presented in a Project ECHO setting. Responsibility for the patient remains with the medical team who cares for the patient at the presenting institution. So let's begin. So this is a case of a 74-year-old female who initially presented to the emergency department with an inability to void. Evaluation revealed a large pelvic mass that was the source of the patient's symptoms. The patient had no significant past medical, surgical, or family history. Of note, the patient was a frequent traveler and often flew to and from New Orleans for work. On physical exam, the patient was of a normal BMI. Exam under anesthesia was performed due to her significant symptoms with a bedside exam, and that revealed a six centimeter firm mass extending down the vagina to the level of the introitus, completely obliterating the vagina. The mass was fixed and extended to both pelvic sidewalls. A cystoscopy was also performed at that time, and that revealed friable nodules at the posterior base of the bladder. Multiple biopsies were taken of both cystoscopy and the tumor within the vagina. In addition, imaging revealed right hydroureteronephrosis and a right nephrostomy tube as well as a Foley catheter were placed. Pathology on all the biopsies returned as a poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Given the extent of disease extending into the posterior bladder base, this placed the patient at a stage 4A squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. And on the right, you'll see that the tumor stained positive for P16. A staging PET CT was done. And on that PET CT, there were multiple ground glass opacities noted with low-level hypermetabolic activity. at the peripheries of both lungs. In addition, the known cervical cancer was also seen, and that was noted to be hypermetabolic as well. Of note, there was no lymphadenopathy in the pelvis, periordic region, or mediastinum. The PET-CT, the lung findings were read with a differential diagnosis of metastatic disease versus an infectious or inflammatory process. The recommendation was to get a dedicated chest CT as well as consider a lung biopsy for further evaluation of these lung findings. Here are some images of the PET scan. On the left, you see the CT component, and on the right, you see the PET component. The arrows are pointing to these ground glass opacities, and on the right, you'll see the hypermetabolic activity that is noted. And here is another image of the PET. The imaging was reviewed by the treating clinicians, myself and the radiation oncologist, and we felt that the lung findings were unlikely due to metastatic disease, given their distribution and the fact that there was no upper abdominal disease. The patient was very symptomatic from her cancer, and we decided to go ahead and start treatment with definitive chemoradiation while the chest findings were being worked up concurrently. A chest CT and lung biopsy were planned to be performed. However, before that happened, COVID-19 entered into the differential diagnosis. Given this possibility, additional testing was canceled when we felt that it was important to get this patient tested as soon as possible for this virus. At that time, we did not have rapid testing available for asymptomatic patients, so this actually required hospital administration approval to get this patient tested. The patient was brought in, the test was completed, and 24 hours later, the test returned as positive for COVID-19. Throughout this period, the patient remained asymptomatic with no fevers, cough, no shortness of breath, and no known sick contacts. So we were left with one of three options. One, we could hold the treatment that had already been started for two weeks. Two, we could hold the chemotherapy alone for two weeks and continue the daily radiation with appropriate personal protective equipment. Or three, we could continue the treatment as scheduled with appropriate personal protective equipment.

Navia, thank you very much. We are now going to open up the panel for discussion of the case. And Dr. Rahm, I would like to start with you. As a radiation oncologist in the group, what is the standard of care, regardless of the COVID-19 diagnosis, what is the standard of care therapy for patients with stage four locally advanced cervical cancer?

Yes, we've seen this particular patient and we know that most of the current guidelines currently recommend concurrent chemo radiation. As Navya has also just mentioned, that's what they plan for this patient, especially for when there's a minimal bladder and rectal involvement. But we have situations sometimes where we have a high volume stage four disease. So some people can consider starting with like a neoadjuvant chemo for three to four cycles, see how the patient is and then a more radical treatment is offered. In a scenario where there is a very extensive rectal or bladder infiltration and the patient has significant, mainly obstructive symptoms, then after a suitable diversion, some of these patients are offered palliative hypofractionated regimen.
Okay. And now that you know that the patient is COVID-19 positive, how would you change your approach, if at all?

Yeah, so in the context of COVID-19 being positive in a patient, and I can share it from the more of a perspective of how will you handle this in a low resource situation. The principles which I normally like to follow is what we'll do for mitigation and the preparedness to deal with this kind of a situation. And the factors which primarily come into play in this situation is factors which are related to the patient and factors which are related to the resources available at that particular center. So the whole concept of risk versus benefit ratio needs recalibration in the situation. And also the result optimization and prioritization on strategies mainly for the treatment needs to be redefined. And as far as coming to this kind of a particular patient, if you have a low resource setting, we know this patient is an elderly patient. She has lung findings, and she's COVID positive. And if you look at the data, which has just come out from China, where some few patients were treated for cancer, and they were COVID positive, and those who are having increasing age, and they have received treatment for less than 14 days, and had lung findings, they had a higher risk of severe illness. And hence, this patient, though is asymptomatic for COVID-related illness, but the findings which have just come out places her at a high risk of risk for developing severe illness due to COVID. And the other risk of this kind of a patient, again, in low-resource setting, is the probability of exposing, say, the other patients. And we are working with a very limited staff in the departments. So those factors have to be considered. Because again, the accessibility of testing in this situation, accessibility for appropriate PPEs in the setting is still a challenge in many areas. And also, it is a huge resource constraint, again, in low-resource settings, especially when you have a patient who goes into the machine area for treatment. And the protocol which needs to be followed for cleaning up the treatment area, the machines, especially each vendors have their own protocol, which kind of chemical can be used. So in a situation like this, it is very resource draining activity. And the same thing stands for the treating professionals. And there is an urgent need for resource optimization. So if this particular patient happens to be in a low resource setting, I would suggest that this kind of patient, we defer the radiation therapy and the patient be given care in the hospital as per the national guidelines for a COVID positive, but an asymptomatic patient. And some people suggest that we do because we need to see when we should start treatment for this patient. Weekly testing can be suggested till the patient becomes negative, and this will be desirable. And once the patient becomes negative, thorough clinical evaluations to be done to reassess the level of the COVID related illness, and then make a call on restarting the treatment as well. So that is what I feel from the low-resource perspective is a solution from my side.

OK. Dr. Botha, I'd like to ask you first about the case. Dr. Naira showed us the results of the PET CT and the confusion it initially caused in treating the patient. What is your take on using images in these imaging in these circumstances?

Well, good afternoon. First of all, I think when we see imaging, we always need to use the information we get in combination with clinical evidence of our clinical examination of the symptoms of the patient in order to make a decision about further clinical management. In this case, I think the PET-CT potentially showed lung metastases. We, from our unit, Anna Simons, published a series of patients with locally advanced cervical cancer, about 280 patients of which about 30% were living with HIV. So in our population, Many patients will have HIV as a comorbidity and also things like TB, which can significantly change the picture on something like PET-CT. And I think the answer is really colleagues at nuclear medicine and to have a multidisciplinary team to make a decision about the patient's management. And I think in this case, Navya showed that the CT showed no paraortic or pelvic lymphadenopathy and with lung, potential lung metastasis and that in my opinion wouldn't really make sense. So I think whatever imaging we use in staging and in treatment needs to be put into context of the entire patient.
Do you screen all patients for COVID-19 these days in South Africa?

At the moment, I think we're still in a fairly early phase of the epidemic. We definitely screen everybody that enters the hospital with a series of questions. You know, all the simple things like fever, contact with somebody with symptoms, etc. If they screen positive, then they will be offered testing. So I think every single person that enters the hospital will be screened, but not necessarily tested. And I think testing, Navya, I think you said earlier that you are now testing all your patients in the system, which I think is difficult if we, I think we just wouldn't have the resources to test all our patients. But I think screening and testing those with positive screening results is really the way to go. And I think it also depends a little bit on where in the epidemic you are in your environment. If you have very few cases of community transmission, I don't think it makes sense to test everybody. However, if there's a lot of community transmission, it might be a different situation.
This patient, her only risk factor was travel, basically, right? She didn't have, and she was completely asymptomatic.
Right, this is an asymptomatic patient.
And Gerda, I just want to ask you a last question before we move on. How would a patient like this be treated in the New Region Radium Hospital?

Hi Ram, thank you for that. So at the Norwegian Radium Hospital, any patient that presents with a new cervical cancer will undergo a CT, chest, abdomen, pelvis, for metastatic disease. And importantly, and maybe differently from what's been presented here, we always do a MRI of the pelvis. And that's really to evaluate locally the main tumor and its extent. We also feel that we get a better sense of possible nodal metastases in the pelvis with an MRI versus a CT scan. Then we also do an exam under anesthesia with all our new cervical cancer patients, both with and attending from our radiation oncology team and our GYN oncology team. And if the patient is not thought to be a candidate for surgery, then we will also do a PET scan before we plan for And in this case, you know, we would really heavily rely on our radiologists and in regards to if this was felt to be metastases in the lungs versus infectious disease and COVID, because this is very important in regards to the therapy. She's, this is a symptomatic patient. She needs to initiate her therapy shortly. And we also know that the therapy that would be most helpful for her now is radiation. You know, if this was a large tumor and we felt we needed to shrink it to give curative radiotherapy, we might start with neoadjuvant chemo. However, that wouldn't really help her symptoms that quickly, very likely. So if we felt that we needed a biopsy, we would try to get this. And then, you know, we'd look at the potential risks of transmission of disease, both to the staff there in other patients, but also we would consider, you know, what are the risks to the patient? It's rare, but you could have complications like primothorax, which again would delay maybe initiation of her definitive therapy. So I think once we, we have as much knowledge as we can, we would go move forward as well with chemoRT. Intensive intent for this woman.
So Navya, can you wrap it up for us? What did you end up doing?

Yeah, and I do thank you for mentioning what you did, Gerd. I do want to also say that we do also rely heavily on our radiologists, but at that point, pet findings of COVID were really not widely published. And so it was not something that the radiologists really knew to look for at that time either. There was a question about whether the bladder biopsy was positive, and I just want to confirm that both the cervical, vaginal, and bladder biopsies were all positive for squamous cell carcinoma. So we were left in a difficult position because she had already started her definitive treatment, and then here we were with this COVID positive result. And we had an interdisciplinary discussion with our cancer center director, our lead infectious disease physician about the risks and benefits of continuing her treatment. We felt that chemotherapy would be too high risk to continue given that these infusions last six to seven hours, and she's in the infusion center with other immunocompromised patients and our staff, so that was held for two weeks. The radiation did get held for a few days while all of this workup was being done. We looked at the risk benefits as Thomas had very well put about continuing her radiation versus holding it, and at the end, decided that if the patient was masked, treated at the very end of the day, and remained asymptomatic in that she was not coughing or aerosolizing particles, we would continue with her radiation treatment. So that's what happened. She continued the radiation, but she came in masked, and she was the last patient treated so that they could sterilize it after her treatments were complete. And she's currently ongoing with her treatment.

reference_conclusion: For this patient with stage IVA squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, concurrent chemotherapy was held for two weeks because of active COVID-19 infection and the associated exposure risk in the infusion setting. Radiation therapy was resumed after a brief interruption and continued with definitive intent, with the patient masked, treated at the end of the day, and managed under appropriate post-treatment sterilization precautions while she remained asymptomatic.

We looked at the risk benefits as Thomas had very well put about continuing her radiation versus holding it, and at the end, decided that if the patient was masked, treated at the very end of the day, and remained asymptomatic in that she was not coughing or aerosolizing particles, we would continue with her radiation treatment. So that's what happened. She continued the radiation, but she came in masked, and she was the last patient treated so that they could sterilize it after her treatments were complete.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 39-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Ovarian cyst with infertility history; peritoneal nodules were identified at diagnostic laparoscopy.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary, stage III. Diagnosis was established in October 2025.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of a peritoneal nodule showed high-grade serous carcinoma.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Hereditary germline NGS panel detected a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation with autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and a likely pathogenic MLH1 mutation. Both alterations were detected in blood.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial diagnostic laparoscopy was performed for an ovarian cyst. An incomplete cytoreductive surgery was subsequently performed at an outside center. This was followed by 3 cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin chemotherapy. Completion cytoreductive surgery was then performed. Further chemotherapy cycles were ongoing. Treatment had otherwise been described as completed at the time of referral.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative systemic treatment was ongoing following completion cytoreductive surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism. Family history was significant for breast cancer in both twin sisters at approximately 40 and 45 years of age, gastrointestinal cancer in the mother (primary site/details unclear), and brain cancer in a maternal aunt.

So, you know, whenever we talk about Lynch-related ovarian cancer, it's usually the endometrioid or the clear cell. I mean, that's usually more common if you're talking about Lynch-driven ovarian cancer. Here, you know, it's a high-grade serous ovarian cancer. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old male. Non-smoker. Occupation: mechanic.

[ chief complaint ]: Penile mass present for approximately 4–6 months, described as slightly painful with minimal bleeding. No urinary difficulty.

[ diagnosis ]: Penile squamous cell carcinoma of the glans penis, clinically node-negative at presentation. Clinical stage was reported as cT2N0, stage IIA.

[ histopathology results ]: Confirmatory biopsy demonstrated HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma. Partial penectomy specimen showed squamous cell carcinoma measuring 2.7 cm with lymphovascular invasion. Intraoperative margins were negative. Dynamic sentinel lymph node sampling identified two left groin nodes positive for squamous cell carcinoma without extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Physical examination demonstrated a 2 cm firm red ulcerated mass of the glans penis with no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. CT imaging showed possible invasion of the penile glans and no inguinal adenopathy. SPECT/CT following radiotracer injection to the partial penectomy scar demonstrated drainage to selected inguinal sentinel nodes; two left groin sentinel nodes were subsequently identified intraoperatively.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor was HPV negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Confirmatory biopsy was performed. The patient then underwent partial penectomy. Pathology showed a 2.7 cm squamous cell carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion and negative margins. The patient declined upfront inguinal lymph node dissection and underwent dynamic sentinel lymph node sampling instead. Two left inguinal sentinel nodes were positive for squamous cell carcinoma; no extranodal extension was present. A plan was described to proceed with superficial and deep lymph node dissection on the involved side.

[ current disease status ]: Post-partial penectomy with negative primary surgical margins. Pathologically node-positive disease was present in two left inguinal sentinel lymph nodes without extranodal extension.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical and surgical history were described as otherwise standard. No inguinal lymphadenopathy was present on examination at initial presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 84-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent hyperparathyroidism with persistent hypercalcemia after two prior parathyroid operations; worsening systemic symptoms over the preceding 6 months, including severe weakness, loss of appetite, cognitive changes, and significant mood changes.

[ diagnosis ]: Primary hyperparathyroidism with persistent disease after prior parathyroidectomies.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Prior surgery in approximately 2005–2006 reportedly involved removal of a single parathyroid gland, pathologically confirmed; operative and pathology reports were unavailable, and the gland laterality/site was unknown.  
- Prior reoperative surgery in 2019 reportedly involved removal of the left inferior parathyroid gland, pathologically confirmed; operative and pathology reports were unavailable.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Nuclear medicine scan performed the day before endocrine surgical evaluation showed no identifiable abnormal parathyroid focus.  
- Office ultrasound on 20 December 2024 showed no obvious parathyroid gland. A small hypoechoic lesion was seen posterior to the superior aspect of the left thyroid lobe, but this was not considered definitive.  
- 4D CT subsequently demonstrated two hyperenhancing right central compartment nodules:  
  - Right periesophageal lesion superior to the right thyroid lobe measuring 2 × 6 × 6 mm.  
  - Lesion overlying the anterior wall of the proximal right subclavian artery at the thoracic inlet measuring 3 × 6 × 7 mm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- 20 December 2024: PTH 108 pg/mL; vitamin D normal; corrected calcium 10.5 mg/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Early 2000s: diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism.  
- Approximately 2005–2006: parathyroidectomy at an outside hospital with reported removal of one gland. Persistent hypercalcemia remained postoperatively.  
- 2019: attempted reoperative parathyroidectomy at an outside hospital with bilateral exploration and radioguidance; reported removal of the left inferior parathyroid gland with intraoperative PTH drop. Persistent hypercalcemia remained postoperatively.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: Hashimoto thyroiditis, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension.  
- Physical examination before reoperation: well-healed midline cervical incision.  
- No history of nephrolithiasis was reported.  
- Bone density had reportedly been described as good historically, but after prior back surgery she was told bone density was poor.

You're relying on the word of the surgeon. on the reporting of the patient, the patient's family, so you don't necessarily have a lot to go on. But you really want to think about what glands probably have been removed, were likely removed. And so, you know, based off of the reporting and based off of the fact that an inferior gland was removed at the second case, you know, the glands that are less likely to be found by someone who I think is probably just, you know, a less experienced parathyroid surgeon, the glands that are most likely to be found are going to be the inferior glands. It's going to be the superior glands that are more likely going to have not been identified during the case. And so that also influenced just my thinking about kind of which glands probably we're going to be thinking about finding in this case.

Tell us a little more about this backdoor approach, Michael. It's almost like you have magic fingers, but what is it about the backdoor or strap approach that so-called led you to the gland? Is there some particular technique to it?

No, it's essentially going—by the way, this is very helpful in reoperative surgery, additionally for kind of re-op thyroid cases, like re-op central necks and whatever else, which is the plane that is going to be the most scarred in these cases is the strap muscle onto the thyroid. So if you can find a plane between the strap muscles, that plane is usually has not been explored, hasn't been opened up, and oftentimes it's scar-free. And if you just trace that out laterally, you go between those strap muscles, that leads you then to the carotid sheath. And that carotid sheath oftentimes kind of, you can then work from lateral to medial, and again, less likely to encounter scar tissue. And honestly, it sets the depth for you in a very helpful way, particularly for superior parathyroid glands.

Thanks. We have a question, Russ. Go ahead. I just want to make one, I think Michael made a great point about the superior glands, because I think the other aspect of it is that we can unroof a superior gland that looks normal. But the abnoma actually sets on the backside of it and gets in tucked in behind the esophagus. And I think occasionally people are a little anxious to completely mobilize that gland because they don't want to devascularize it. And you end up seeing what looks like a normal cap. but you don't look all the way behind. And I think those are frequently that missed land is that you even may see it, but you just don't trust that it looks abnormal and you don't take the time to completely mobilize it because you don't want to run the risk of devascularization. Yeah, that's a good technical tip. I've noticed that myself. Last question, Jeremy, would you be able to answer the question in the chat about medical management with Sensipar? Have you ever recommended it, pros and cons? Yes. Well, the cons are that it's very expensive. It's about $1,500 or $1,600 Canadian for a month, which is about $1.50 American. But anyway, it's very expensive. The other thing is, I've had a long talk with John Belzikian about this years ago, and we still don't know what the long-term effects of Sensipar are going forward. And, but I've used it for intractable cases where it's virtually impossible to find the disease where also a patient with real bad renal hyperparathyroidism that's got multiple comorbidities and it's had multiple surgical procedures. I think there's a place for it there. May I make another comment about surgery? I've approached these cases and I find it's very helpful to, and I've presented this at World Congress, it's very helpful for better exposure to cut all the straps right across and reflect them superiorly and inferiorly. And that displays the whole central compartment very nicely and doesn't give you a keyhole to operate through. I find that very helpful and you can just suture them up at the end and patients have a normal neck without any tugging of the trachea. The second thing I'd like to ask is, I told you I'm bad at math. I think there were three parathyroid disease parathyroids that were removed in this case. Am I wrong on that?

So there was three that had, there had been two removed in prior surgeries. I personally don't think that those were diseased. I mean, the patient showed no improvement in their hypercalcemia afterwards. And so I think that essentially what were removed were two normal glands. And in fact, I think this represented single gland parathyroid disease.

Okay. In the event, just, just for discussion in the event that those other two were parathyroid diseases, diseased glands, and the one you removed, Michael, was diseased gland, you can be sure as shootin' that that last one you thought was normal at one point is going to turn bad. So would you have given consideration to removing that and maybe cutting off a little bit of it or putting the whole thing into a pocket into the pectoralis for function and future reference if it goes bad?

Yeah, I mean, generally my approach for foregland hyperplasia in general is a subtotal, you know, taking out three and a quarter, maybe three and, you know, 40%, something like that. I don't do totals with reimplantation. I'm talking now for primary disease, not for renal disease, but for primary disease, I do subtotals. In this patient, I think given her life expectancy and her overall situation, I think the likelihood that, you know, she's going to develop the disease again if, say, I leave behind a significant chunk is unlikely, but definitely there. So what I did was I, and this wasn't the case in her, but I would take a little bit of it, make sure it's vascularized market very clearly with vascular clips and maybe a proline stitch and then leave it behind. I, I, I personally in primary patients, I really don't like the idea of doing a total parathyroidectomy with re-implantation.

Yeah. So if the fourth gland at one is left, not saying in this case, but that might've turned into hyperplasia again. If you have to go back in there, I would submit, perhaps it'd be better just to take the thing out and re-implant it in a better accessible area. And my area of choice would be infraclavicular into the pectoralis muscle. I've tried in the forearm and then when those go bad, our friendly orthopod causes some hand dysfunction when he tries to take it out. So I like the pectoralis.
I would just say, Jeremy, that your comment is very well taken and particularly is relevant, at least in my experience, in MEN patients. Those are a real challenge in that regard.

reference_conclusion: Additional localization with 4D CT was obtained, demonstrating two subtle right-sided central compartment hyperenhancing nodules. Given the patient’s symptomatic persistent primary hyperparathyroidism and biochemical indication for intervention, reoperative parathyroidectomy was offered despite challenging localization. The patient subsequently underwent reoperative bilateral neck exploration, with identification and excision of a right superior enlarged hypercellular parathyroid adenoma and biopsy confirmation of a normal left superior gland. Postoperatively, intraoperative and early postoperative biochemical findings were consistent with cure, with marked PTH decline and normalization of corrected serum calcium.
reference_conclusion_quote: So, we ended up following this up with a 40 CT. They did note that there were two hyper-enhancing central compartment nodules that were both on the right side. [...] But it sounds like the patient has symptoms and is a reasonable candidate to offer a surgical intervention for. [...] Yes, I would because this patient needs surgery based on symptomatology. [...] So patient in February underwent reoperative parathyroidectomy with bilateral exploration. [...] And overall, this appeared to be disease consistent with a single right superior adenoma, and this was removed. [...] A few days after surgery, the PTH was eight and the corrected calcium came back into normal range.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging left neck mass in April 2019, with pain radiating from the left neck posteriorly to the occiput and dysphagia to solids without aspiration symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, clinically staged cT1b cN1b cM0, stage IVB, with no distant metastatic disease at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the neck mass confirmed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. No differentiated thyroid cancer component was identified on the biopsy specimen.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a large left-sided thyroid/neck mass extending posteriorly, marked deviation of the airway to the contralateral side, contralateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and retropharyngeal FDG uptake on PET imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E mutation detected on tumour molecular testing.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Previously diagnosed with a benign thyroid mass approximately 2 years before presentation. Enrolled in an international tissue bank. Initially treated on a phase I study of intralesional STING agonist with pembrolizumab; an initial clinical and radiological response was observed, followed by disease progression with ulceration. Received palliative radiotherapy to the neck for pain and ulcerating local disease, with good symptom control.

[ current disease status ]: BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, stage IVB, with local disease that progressed with ulceration after intralesional STING agonist plus pembrolizumab and was subsequently treated with palliative radiotherapy to the neck with good symptom control. No distant metastatic disease had been identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Examination at presentation showed a large left neck mass with posterior extension and minimal palpable abnormality on the right.

reference_discussion.text: So let's, so let's move on. Let's do case two. We're going to aim for 15 minutes here for case two. So let's do case two. And I see Dr. Kim signed on. Dave, if you want to turn your camera on, just sign on and join in here with us. And we'll let Kate introduce Dr. Kim.

There we go. So Prof Kim is here. Prof Kim is a thyroid and head and neck surgeon who works with us here at the Royal Marsden. And his particular interest really is thyroid cancer, but also the preclinical and the molecular side of thyroid cancer is looking into some circulating tumour DNA studies with us as well, which is All very exciting. So I'm moving on. Thank you for joining day and moving on now to our second case. This is a 64 year old lady who presented back in April 2019, which is important because at that period we did have limited treatment options, and I'll talk about that in a moment. But she presented with a rapidly enlarging left neck mass, associated pain radiating from the left neck posteriorly to occiput, and she also had some dysphagia to solids, but no symptoms specifically of aspiration. She'd previously been diagnosed with a benign thyroid mass two years prior to this and this was the appearance clinically. She had a large mass which was extending posteriorly on the left side particularly, not a lot to feel on the right side and this was the imaging at the time and I think the sagittal PET is quite helpful here and also highlights this retropharyngeal uptake as well. You can see she had a lot of deviation of the airway to the contralateral side but also had contralateral lymphadenopathy as well. She had a core biopsy which was confirmed as the clinical picture suggested of anaplastic thyroid cancer. Unfortunately, no areas on the biopsy have differentiated thyroid cancer. We sent her tissue for molecular pathology. At that time, it was slow, but we did get a result eventually which showed us that she had a BRAF V600E mutation present. She was staged clinically as a T1B, N1B with no distant disease, so stage 4B anaplastic thyroid. So at that stage she actually, we enrolled her in the International Tissue Bank that Dr Laura Moss was chairing at the time, so her tissue went off to that. She had no, we didn't have access to targeted therapies at that time but there was a phase one study of intralesional sting agonist with pembrolizumab which she enrolled in under my colleague Professor Kevin Harrington and she had an initial response to this both clinically and radiologically but not long afterwards her disease started to progress again and you can see the ulceration that was associated with this disease. We made an application for Dibrafenib and Tremetanib at that stage, as we had the early data then available, but there was no predefined pathway for this. I think we were the first to apply for this in the UK at the time. So in the meantime, we gave her some palliative radiotherapy as she was getting a lot of pain and this was ulcerating. So very old-fashioned, simple, Maltese cross arrangement of radiotherapy, anterior-posterior beam, just so that we could get her on treatment within a day and treat for some palliation. And actually that did give her quite good symptom control. So we did then get approval through expanded access program it's now set up for the graph and it's been tremendous nib based on the mutation to be roughly 600 D, and you can see that very rapidly. she got remarkable clinical response which we are now thankfully all getting accustomed to seeing which is such a brilliant move forward for anaplastic. But she did have some of the toxicities so not uncommonly we see nausea and she actually also had vomiting requiring admission to her local hospital unfortunately. However, just the first dose reduction of her drometinib improved that significantly and she was able to continue to tolerate this. So we can see radiologically, sorry, another mix of modalities, but we had a reduction quite significantly in the tumour. with the dibrafinib and trimetanib, and this MRI also at 10 weeks was done because we were considering heading towards surgery.

Okay, let's pause there for just a second, Kate. Go back one for me. Lori, this dibrafinib, trimetanib thing has really been on our radar screen the last two or three years, and we've seen some really remarkable responses. Now that more have been done, do you get a feel for, like, how many of them get this traumatic response and kind of what duration this response is now? I know there's not a ton of data, but anecdotally, what are you sort of feeling about that right now?

So I originally was skeptical of the data from that small group of 15 patients from the dibrafinib basket trial. But as these patients do trickle into clinic and we get more and more experience, I've actually had several patients have incredible responses to Dibrafinib and Trematinib, quite durable responses. So I think that there is, you know, real activity. And then there was an updated publication with a number of more patients that were treated in the study that, again, showed very high response rates for anaplastic thyroid cancer with good durability as well. It's important, though, to note that not everybody achieves responses, and sometimes you can see a response but have it be very short-lived, and I don't think that we really quite understand what the mechanism of resistance is yet in these patients.
And Kate, your experience, have you had many with on Dabtram? Nobody's had a ton, but that same sort of field that Laurie has there?

Yes, so within the expanded access in the UK, I think we've had approaching 30 patients now. And in fact, we're just publishing the outcomes for UK wide for the first 18 patients. And the results are not as good as the single center publication in term, but they're still, you know, they're still pretty good. And we've, my personal experience is, has been very impressive results, although I have had a primary resistance. And as Laurie says, you know, it's, it's not the complete answer. Unfortunately, not everyone, all of our anaplastics have, have this mutation. And so we've still got a lot of work to do with the BRAF wild type tumors as well. but yes our experience has been generally positive and generally well tolerated but most patients I have need a dose reduction quite often due to nausea and we'll talk about another toxicity with this lady.
Okay so let's go ahead and talk about the toxicities and then we'll pause next when it comes to the surgical decision making.

So quite early on in her treatment with this, she developed blurred vision and described floaters. So she had an urgent ophthalmic review and she was diagnosed with bilateral granulomatous uveitis, which is reported, but not as very common. She was advised to stop her diprafenib at that time. She continued the trimetanib and started some dexamethasone topically. and the uveitis improved and we restarted at a dibrafinib dose reduction and she seemed to be okay for that. She had a continued response as we've seen on the imaging and she was assessed for surgical resection including EUA and esophagoscopy at that time. She, however, declined surgery at that point, and she wanted to continue. She was feeling much better. She didn't want to go for a big op, and so she continued on the medical treatment for a bit longer, in fact, until 16 months post her diagnosis. At that stage, we did opt to go for surgery, and Day, I don't know if you were able to or wish to chip in at this point to discuss the surgical approach.
Should I do that now, Mike, or do you want to?

Yeah, go ahead. I was going to ask you, Dave. So tell us, A, sort of the way you think about, you know, when is it time for you to do your surgery? And then, interesting for us non-surgeons, what do you actually find when you get in there?

Yeah, so I think that's a key question, and it'd be great to learn from other surgeons and other units. It's the timing, How long can you take the drug off for? Because it often has antigenic properties. It's individual, it's for that patient. What are we trying to achieve for each drug? What is the window period? How are they responding? All those things I think factor in. So I think for myself, I'm there to offer Kate support, knowing that these patients will develop resistance and it may be too late then. um to try and agree when a reasonable time to intervene with surgery if we both feel that that has a role both either temporarily for salvage reasons locally or possibly to to provide more long-term progression free survival so so that's what we're always thinking and therefore there's no exact timings so for this lady we we had numerous discussions but So when I assess this patient, I'm thinking, you know, what problem will I cause? Will I be able to excise most of this tumor? Can I actually provide some material benefit for this patient and therefore give Kate a reasonable chance for other treatments or continue the treatments? and get more robust results. And when I examined this patient, everything was rock hard. She's had radiotherapy. She's had everything. She's had injectables. And so it was challenging, but at the same time, we saw a fantastic response. So it was really radiologically made the decision for this patient. So when I looked at it, I thought, look, this is really doable now. And so we did the oesophagoscopy. I was convinced that there was no gross invasion of the oesophagus. Although having said that, we did consent her for reconstruction. We consented her for PET major because we had to take some of the skin. Really, really didn't know what we were expecting, but we went in there. And as expected, it was very much easier than normal. Everything stuck down. So we started from first principles about preserving the carotid artery. We had to take the vagus because it was part of the tumor, but she had a left vocal cord palsy anyway. We managed to save the esophagus. We did a myomectomy, but we preserved the mucosa. We left an NG tube just in case, but she didn't have any perforation issues. And so it was a learning case, it was a challenging case, but she didn't need a PET major reconstruction, we closed primarily, and she did very well. So we don't have much experience, but we're building that with one or two other patients. So I don't know if that gives you some insight, but it is certainly challenging.

It does. And there was a question in the chat. Laurie, maybe you can take this one. Out of everybody that gets down the neoadjuvant therapy pathway of all of these target agents, how many of them really get surgery? I know we don't have an exact number, but what's your gut on that right now?

We definitely don't have any data yet from the studies that have been done. But anecdotally, I can say that we're using therapies that have very high response rates in the range of 65, And those response rates really do translate, I think, into a better opportunity to do resection. So we've we're so far with our clinical trials that are underway. We're fairly pleased with what we're seeing.
Dr. Lubitz.

Yeah, I just want to make one for the comment I agree with Dr. Kim's approach at minimizing harm when you know you're not going to completely entirely, you know, this is not going to be an R0 resection and just want to be careful about and involve the patient. The one thing actually, Dr. Wirth and I had a patient. that after this treatment where the tumor sort of melts away, you actually have to be concerned about the absence of tumor. If you remember, Laurie, we had a patient who had a tracheal, basically a hole in the trachea from the absence of the tumor or the treatment of the tumor. So that's something also to consider that the wall of the trachea and other surrounding structures may be weakened by the actual treatment itself. So consideration of a tracheostomy in certain cases is something we need to think about.
That's great. Kate, show me the next, yep, where was that?
Yep. Yeah, quick question for Kerry and Dr. Kim. Does frozen section play any role intraoperatively during these delayed resections here?

Sorry, go ahead, Dr. Kim. So as in this case, sometimes when you reset this tumor, actually you don't find any anaplastic and you find the differential component it may have developed. But I don't think that would change the decision to perform the surgery, nor the way we perform the surgery. So in my opinion, I don't think so. I don't know if Dr. Lubitz has a different opinion, but not really.

No, I agree with that. It's pretty obvious when you're in there where the tumor is. It's pretty sticky, either tumor or the effects of radiation and treatment. So it's hard to differentiate even on frozen section between those things, between the changes from radiation and involvement directly with the tumor. So no, I don't normally send frozen sections during them.

Okay, take me to the next slide, then I'm gonna come to Zuber. Zuber, the path reports I see on some of these are like this one, no anaplastic, but there's almost always some residual well differentiated. How do we make sense out of those path reports? I mean, Dabtram is pretty magic, but it made the anaplastic go away and leave some papillary behind. How do you think about that?

I mean, to be honest, I have seen only one case like this, depending upon how much the anaplastic component was there. You know, when the whole tumor is anaplastic carcinoma, greater than, I mean, I call them like a blind man's tumor. I mean, anybody can look at it and say, that looks bad, right? So that is not the problem. The problem is to really look at the cases where the anaplastic is only present at the invasive edge, or there are cases of this small anaplastic carcinomas arising de novo in the background of multinodular goiter, and that's when really the problem starts. And then there's a lot of bleeding of the stains when you're doing these differentiated stains, so-called anaplastic should be thyroglobulin stain positive, but if they're in the mix of all this other benign thyroid disease or papillary carcinomas, you're going to get some bleed over. For me, those are the hardest cases, depending upon how much the anaplastic component was there and where it was located in the surgery. Was it in the middle of the tumor or was it situated at the invasive edge? I mean, this case, to me, looking at the amino profile, it looks pretty clear. But I mean, I have only seen one case where the anaplastic disappeared, but there was a tall cell and hobnail, which was sitting. And that was not, there was nothing happened. So that nidus was still there of a well differentiated, but I mean, you know, these are not such common tumors. So, you know, I, I have only seen one where there was no anaplastic on there, but the core biopsy and FNA did show the anaplastic carcinoma completely.

So Eyal, we need to move on to the next case. But teaching points for this one are things that endocrinologists and regular thyroid folks need to think about as you're listening to this complicated case.

Yeah, there was a question in the chat about the original nodule that this patient had. Now, today we're treating less, we're doing active surveillance. People are afraid maybe it's going to turn into anaplastic. So it doesn't happen. It's extremely rare. We can't prevent that. many patients with people without cancer don't know that they have thyroid cancer. So I think it's not something we need to consider when we treated differentiated low, not intermediate, not poorly. So it happens, but it's not, we can't prevent it and it's unexpected.

This has been an exciting field to see how this Dab Tram has changed what we do, but as Dave mentioned, I think it's given us more questions than answers. When do you intervene? When do you stop the Dab Tram? When do you restart it? Is it different if they have distant METs? Is it different if they don't have distant METs? I think we're still doing these very much as a one-off. as individual cases within the disease management team but I think for the for the general audience knowing that anaplastic cancer we actually have options now for beyond the standard treatment things that were so disastrous and things to think about in terms of this test and get these folks in a rapid fashion to people that can deal with these because you know hardly anybody does a bunch of these except at specialized centers so these are great cases and so tell me the last couple of sentences on her Kate how's she doing now just to round out.

So we did start restart the debriefing of a tremetinoid because she had residual thyroid tissue because we didn't really know. whether to or not but she got a reappearance of the uveitis and in spite of further dose reductions this continued to be a problem so we stopped and actually she wanted to stop and she's been off treatment now for over a year and fingers crossed everything is stable as post-op appearances so you know she is doing well and we just keep our fingers crossed now we're in unknown territory.

reference_conclusion: Following an initial response to intralesional STING agonist plus pembrolizumab and subsequent progression, palliative radiotherapy was delivered for pain and ulceration, after which dabrafenib plus trametinib was initiated via expanded access for BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Treatment-related nausea, vomiting, and bilateral granulomatous uveitis were managed with dose reduction, temporary interruption of dabrafenib, continuation of trametinib, and topical dexamethasone, with maintained radiologic response. After initial deferral, surgical resection was performed at 16 months from diagnosis following favorable response assessment; postoperatively, dabrafenib and trametinib were restarted because of residual thyroid tissue but were ultimately discontinued because of recurrent uveitis, and the patient has remained clinically and radiographically stable off treatment.

She continued the trimetanib and started some dexamethasone topically. and the uveitis improved and we restarted at a dibrafinib dose reduction and she seemed to be okay for that. [...] She, however, declined surgery at that point, and she wanted to continue. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old right-handed man from a rural area. He was partnered, had two young children, and worked locally as a concreter. He had no past medical history and took no regular medications.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidental intracranial/skull base mass identified on trauma imaging after a motorbike accident. He was neurologically intact at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Multicompartment skull base meningioma, WHO grade 1, involving the middle cranial fossa with extension into the posterior fossa, cavernous sinus region, and extracranially through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected tumour showed a medium-cellularity neoplasm with some mesenchymal features, low pleomorphism, clear nuclei, limited whorl formation, intranuclear pseudoinclusions, and rare psammoma bodies. SSTR2A immunostaining was strongly positive. Final histopathological diagnosis was WHO grade 1 meningioma. Tissue adherent to the inferior temporal gyrus was not submitted separately. Sequencing had not been performed. TERT promoter and CDKN2A/B status were not tested.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial non-contrast CT brain demonstrated an ill-defined mass throughout the middle cranial fossa, extending into the posterior fossa and inferiorly through the skull base.  
- MRI demonstrated a large extensive tumour abutting and displacing the pons, extending anteriorly into the middle fossa, involving the cavernous sinus region with encasement of the internal carotid artery, and extending through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.  
- Coronal imaging showed a posterior fossa component adjacent to the basilar artery, a middle fossa component, cavernous sinus involvement, and extracranial extension into the infratemporal fossa.  
- Axial imaging showed displacement of the pons and a large supratentorial component.  
- CT demonstrated hyperostosis/osseous remodeling including expansion of the foramen ovale, hyperostosis of the sphenoid wing, and remodeling of the maxillary sinus region.  
- Postoperative MRI after first-stage surgery showed resection of the main middle fossa component with residual tumour bulging in the cavernous sinus region, preserved MCA flow voids, persistent posterior fossa component, and coagulated thickened middle fossa floor.  
- Postoperative CT after second-stage surgery showed resection of the posterior fossa component that had been compressing the brainstem. No postoperative MRI after the second-stage procedure was available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular sequencing had been performed. CDKN2A/B deletion status and TERT promoter status were unknown.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- L1 fracture from motorbike accident was managed conservatively by the spinal team.  
- First-stage tumour surgery: pterional craniotomy with piecemeal resection of the middle fossa component down to the opticocarotid triangle; the tumour was adherent to the inferior temporal gyrus and some of that tissue was resected. The middle fossa floor was coagulated without entering the cavernous sinus. Residual tumour remained in the cavernous sinus region and posterior fossa.  
- The patient initially deferred second-stage surgery after returning home.  
- Second-stage tumour surgery: retrosigmoid craniotomy with NIMS monitoring for resection of the posterior fossa component compressing the brainstem. Cranial nerves III, IV, VI, VII, and VIII were identified and preserved; cranial nerve VII stimulated well at the end of the case. Cranial nerves IX–XII were located inferior to the tumour. Cranial nerve V was displaced inferiorly and encapsulated over the tumour. A small residual tumour was left adjacent to the basilar artery.  
- No adjuvant radiotherapy or systemic therapy had been given at the time described.

[ current disease status ]: Following two-stage surgery, residual disease remained in the cavernous sinus region and extracranially in the infratemporal fossa. A small residual component remained adjacent to the basilar artery after posterior fossa resection. The patient was back at home, remained neurologically intact, and had no documented new deficits.

[ other clinical data ]: The tumour was discovered incidentally during trauma workup after a motorbike accident. The patient’s major traumatic injury was an L1 fracture. He was examined on more than one occasion and remained neurologically intact throughout the documented preoperative period and after staged surgery.
