reference_discussion.text: How does that look?
Yep.

All good? Yep, good. Cool. Thank you for the opportunity to speak tonight on this case. I'm a neurosurgeon at the Royal Melbourne. I work with Professor Drummond. I'm dual fellowship trained. I was lucky enough to do my neuro-oncology fellowship with Professor Drummond in the Brain Cancer Centre, where we did our IDH inhibitor trial. And then I went off to Cambridge to do a Skull Base Fellowship. And now I'm back at the Royal Melbourne working there with some work at the Peter MacCallum. So this case came in before I went to Cambridge when I was on call. It was a 30-year-old right-handed man from the country who had a motorbike accident and hence had a CT trauma series. He had no past medical history, didn't take any medications. He was partnered with two young children and he worked locally as a concreter. His major injury from the motorbike accident was this L1 fracture, which was managed conservatively by the spinal team. The reason he was referred to me was this is his non-contrast CT brain, which showed this ill-defined mass throughout the middle fossa, extended into the posterior fossa and down through the skull base. So upon referral, we ask for a MRI scan. I'll put some videos in because it's a little bit easier to see the tumour, which I'll scroll through for you. So the T1 post front, you can see this tumour here, pressing up against the pons and then forward. into the middle fossa down there, you can see it going through foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa. So quite an extensive tumour. So I'll just show you on coronal view here, you can see that posterior fossa component there coming up against the basilar, the middle fossa component, The sun there going through in the cavernous sinus encasing the RCA, and you can see that component there going down into the infratemporal fossa. And just finally on axial, you can see how that is displacing the pons there and how extensive that supratentorial component is there. So just to show you the CT brain, you can see that there is some hyperextosis there, some expansion of the foramen ovale and some hyperextosis there of the sphenoid wing. And coming down here, you can see that sort of remodelling there of the auxiliary sinus. I've got this young 30-year-old gentleman who's completely neurologically intact. He just stacked his motorbike while out on the farm. And he's got this multi-compartmental large tumour. So just wondering everyone's initial thoughts about what we should do here. Okay, surgeons, Linda.

I know this very tough case. I think he has two great things going for him, which is that he's young and, or three things, two, that he does not yet have symptoms, and three, that this tumor is all connected in some sense. So thinking about, you know, the basic reasons why we offer surgery for anybody, which is to improve their quality of life or their quantity of life, either immediate or in the future, I think to be very clear with this person, their ability to recover, the tempo of recovery, and the potential for future treatments, I would think about this in a, do you think he would benefit from surgery? Because these phenoid mean, or this region of tumors that go into the infratemporal fossa, I find have a higher incidence of atypical behavior. than the pure sphenoid wing or sphenoid orbital meningiomas. I think the goals of the surgery would be, number one, to decompress the brainstem and to preserve his future vision. So at least for me, I would offer him a surgery, probably starting with a cranial orbital zygomatic approach to broaden the access to the infratemporal fossa, drilling of that sphenoid wing to widen the door into the infratemporal fossa, anterior clinodectomy to peel the cavernous sinus, possibly looking at your window into the, posterior fossa component, possibly an anterior putresectomy. In terms of all of this, within the cavernous sinus will depend on the texture and whatnot. Of all this, the infratemporal fossa component, which is quite large, I think the extent of resection there depends on the texture of the tumor. Sometimes it's not, it's quite firm for whatever reason within that region and not so easy to distinguish between the pterygoid muscles and such. I think the main issue with that, I know after counseling for trigeminal sort of distribution numbness is that of jaw pain and trismus and such. And so that component on the T2s, it looks like there is a capsule or some sort of boundary once we get past that initial window, past the pterygoids. But I think that will be an interoperative decision making. Probably the biggest risk of this operation at least in my mind, is that of CSF leak. And so if there was an extensive infratemporal fossa resection, to be careful not to violate kind of the walls into the sinus because it would be a massive hole such that it can still be reconstructed with fat or localized rotational of the muscles if that were to be resected would be the kind of biggest concern in my mind.
That was comprehensive. Aristotle, do you have anything to add?

Yeah, first of all, I would discuss, you know, differential diagnosis with him. I would say that's most probably meningioma. We see some bone remodeling, thickening, but we also see some anatomical-driven growth that we also see in schwannomas. I would put that in my differential as well. as a second working diagnosis. And then I would discuss with him the nature of both diseases and say that most probable surgical intervention would be to his benefit. I would lay down the risks. I agree with Linda, one of the major risks would be the CSF leak. In terms of the goal of the resection, I would probably be straightforward with the patient and say that we cannot get a gross total resection of this. There is a cavernous sinus component of the tumor with encasement of the ICA. So I would plan for a general subtotal resection and leave that cavernous sinus component for a later adjuvant treatment according to the pathology, with SRS and fractionated radiotherapy being options. Now in terms of the surgical approach for this, it's quite complex. I guess many options are out there. I would probably do a stage approach and leave the extracranial component to deal with a kind of a second stage operation. I would do a you know kind of a orbital zygomatic as Linda suggested or a pre-temporal and then see what's the consistency of this. The tumor in a sense has done the Cavase approach itself so if you do an anterocleanidectomy extra-dural pilling of the middle cranial fossa. You probably have a pitreous apex which is invaded by the tumor itself, so probably not a lot of hard drilling there. And the first goal would be with this operation to decompress the brainstem and get a maximal safer section. And then according to the texture to the consistency of the tumor, I would decide on my second stage operation for the infratemporal fossa. One option is if it's a hard and vascular, I would continue kind of a preauricular incision, have my ENT colleagues or head and neck involved and try to do an open approach. I guess drilling of the middle fossa is necessary there to expand on the Foramenon valley and get access to the infratemporal fossa from lateral. It's quite large. Otherwise, if it was smaller, I would also, you know, discuss If it was smaller and it was not vascular in the first operation, I would also discuss an endoscopic approach, either a transmaxillary or a transperigoid, incorporating probably both nostrils with resection of the posterior septum to get access laterally to the infertemporal fossa. So yeah, this would be my discussion, my options laid out to the patient.

Sarah? What did we do? First I brought the patient down from the country and met him. Yes, remembering that this is a young Australian man who just wants to ride motorbikes around on a farm. And I examined him twice and he was definitely neurologically intact. And we went through his scans in a lot of detail. And unfortunately he was referred just before I was leaving for fellowship. So I handed him over to one of my colleagues. But nonetheless, when we were looking at this tumour, as you all said, it's quite an extensive tumour. And we were looking at the different components and how we would stage surgery and how we would approach it. And the patient was very risk adverse. He wanted to stay on the farm with his kids and not have any deficits. So we first looked at the middle fossa component and thought, you know, we could do an extended tereornal and move that component. The cavernous sinus component, initially we thought, we'll leave that alone, we won't go in there. The infratemporal, the extracranial component, again, in the first step, we were leaving that alone. And then we'd look at a second stage doing a retrosigmo craniotomy to remove the component that's compressing the brainstem. So his stage one was that tereonal craniotomy. Stage two, we've left these two sections. So that's how we sort of broke it down. And I guess we've spoken about what we'd do first and how people would combine it. But we went ahead and did the pterianal, standard pterianal dissection down to the octago-carotid triangle, showed optic and oculomotor, everything pretty routine. The tumours resected piecemeal. It was quite adherent to the inferior temporal gyrus. So there was some resection of that. and the coagulation of the middle fossil floor without entering into the cavernous sinus. So this is his post-op MRI scan. And you can see that tumour is still there bulging out the cavernous sinus with that main component all removed with preservation of the MCA running through there. And you can still see that posterior fossil component, obviously, just in all three planes. You can see how that floor of that little fossas just got that thickened area that was coagulated. And again, just on sagittal. So after this surgery, he went back to the country and he decided he didn't want to do the second stage surgery. So it took quite a while. And I just got back from Cambridge time for his second stage, which we did via a retrosigmoid craniotomy with NIMS monitoring. We opened up and 9 to 12 were down below the tumour. We saw 3, 4 and 6, which we preserved. In this picture here, you can see 7 and 8. 7 was stimming great at the end of the case. Five was our main problem. It was pushed inferiorly and quite encapsulated over the tumour. You can see what this is, the cavity of tumour here that we're still resecting, but we managed to get it off. However, we did leave a smaller amount, which is up against the basilar, but otherwise got a good resection. And this was only just done recently, and I don't have a post-op MRI scan, but this is his CT. where you can see the resection of that component that was compressing the brainstem. So for the neuropathologist on the panel, I've got some slides for you of his results, which I could describe, or you can expertly describe. I might make a comment. We did, I think we sent them earlier as well.

Yeah, so I think it's very nicely described. So we have a medium cellularity tumor that has some mesenchymal aspect to it. It is rather of lower pleomorphy. It has some clear nuclei in that and a very limited world formation. So for us, this would very nicely fit to a meningioma, of course.

Yeah, and just some other pictures here. There was some intranuclear pseudo-inclusions and we highlighted some very rare simone bodies throughout the HNA staining. And then we had the SSTR2A, which was strongly positive. So the histopathology report came back with SWHO grade one meningioma. As we all know, the classification was slightly altered in the 2021 change with the addition of the TERT promoter and the CDK2NA and some change with the grade three meningiomas. And I point this out because in this paper that they published, it was mentioned, you know, this case where there's a patient, two patients which had histologically grade one meningiomas. However, one had the CDK2NA KN2 deletion, which is the bottom one you can see on the post-op one year scan, very strong recurrence. So although our tumor is histologically grade one, we haven't done any sequencing on it. So I guess where to now for this young guy, we've done two staged surgery. We've still got this extracranial component and we've still got this cavernous sinus component. Should we be sequencing this to guide how aggressive we need to be? Should we attack the extracranial component? And what should we do for the cavernous sinus component? And I think we've discussed it a little bit, but basically- Before you go on, Michael, what do you think about this multi-staged approach to the tumour?
Yeah, I just wanted to have one question, Ed. Did you do any sampling from that adherence to the inferior temporal gyrus? Did you get an extra sampling, send that off separately to rule out right?
It wasn't sent separately.

Because there's a discussion currently going on in Germany, and there's a study running, an observational study called the INVADER study run by a friend of mine called Felix Behling from Augsburg, Germany. They're sort of looking into that. I think that is something that we as surgeons should definitely keep in mind that we should not only send off the chunks, but to really, if we see a brain invasion or feel that there's brain invasion, to send it off separately. Yeah, regarding the multistage, I mean, I like Linda's idea of doing a very generous approach, like FTOZ or FTZ or whatever, to really get it all in one stage. I mean, that's definitely something you can discuss with a patient and how risk-friendly he or she is.

Well, so I think there's a question about how aggressive you need to be for the extracranial part of the tumor, but I guess you're going to say something about that. Dr. Lazaridis, would you be jumping in with any adjuvant therapy at this point?

No, I would not be jumping in with any adjuvant therapy. I think surgical resection is gold standard. Then radiotherapy plays a vital role when surgery is incomplete or not possible. And chemotherapy, I think, demonstrates limited benefit and advanced molecular testing and profiling would be good for me to have more options.

I just have one question regarding this case, Kate. So a 30-year-old with a stuffed tumor, that's very rare. And so he has no radio, so no exposition in the past to any radiotherapy or something. I have one question. Could it be a case of NF2 without bilateral acoustic neuroenomas? Does that make sense? It's just that such an uncommon case. I don't know, maybe in Australia it's different, but we don't generally see these large tumors in 30-year-olds, what do you think?
No, very unusual. It was very rare.

Yeah. No, I agree with everything that's been said here. I would probably go for the orbital psychomatic and try to do the trans-patrosal approach and see if I can't get that mobilized in the initial approach, but I would do the SAGE also for the sub-temporal part. We wouldn't do that at the beginning, for sure.

Okay, Sarah, we have five minutes. Okay, I'll zoom through, but basically that, as we said, that extracranial component, it's rare, it only occurs in 2% of meningiomas, and Hoy postulated four theories for that, and obviously our case is due to that extension through the foramen ovale, which forms a part of the roof of the infratemporal fossa. I mean, when you look through the literature about approaches and how to attack these tumours, it is quite sparse, to be real. There's a lot of case reports out there, but not a lot of studies. There's an old study from Tokyo in 2009 that suggests some of the approaches that you've all suggested on how to attack this in one approach. But I think the discussions between the surgeon who actually did the surgery with the patient, who was very risk adverse, was to just try and reduce the bulk of the tumour with least risk to him. In regards to the cavernous sinus component of it, I mean, this is the consensus statement from the ENS skull base section published in 2022. And as they suggest, you need a multidisciplinary team approach and you can consider surgery for those aggressive lesions in young patients. and endoscopic combined with radiation is effective. And I quite like how they in this paper, explore the anatomy and the tumour growth and describe the tumour growth which are favourable to surgery. In this picture they show that pattern 2 where the tumour is growing laterally is more favourable to open surgery, where your pattern 3 where they're pushing the nerves laterally is more favourable to endoscopic approaches, but your pattern 1 and 1a obviously are less favourable to surgery. I think if you look at our patient scan, it's more in keeping with one eye than it is with two or three. So that leaves us with stereotactic radiosurgery, which has a reasonably good five-year progression for his survival of 96% and only dropping to 90% at 10 years. So that's where we're at with him at the moment. He's had that two-stage surgery. He's back on the farm. He's still neurologically intact. He's happy, but we're still seeking a head and neck opinion on the extracanial component and a radiation opinion on the cavernous sinus component. Thank you. Any comments from the panel?

I have a very academic question. Would you really say that this is a cavernous sinus man in general, or was it, I mean, I haven't looked at the images that thoroughly as you did, but would that be a spinal petroglybal, or what was your impression from intraoperatively?
It looked like it was within the cavernous sinus. Obviously, I wasn't there for that surgery, but that's what I was told.
Can I just clarify, did you say that this particular tumor has CDKN2AB loss? Or was that just referring to the report?

No, I was saying that we haven't tested for that. And I was postulating, is this something in a young patient with an unusually large tumor, something that we should consider routinely checking to guide how aggressive we should be? Because if he does have a deletion, maybe we would then be more aggressive in our initial surgery despite his risk aversion.

We do have the luxury of doing chromosomal copy number alteration in every meningioma. And as you probably know, pediatric meningiomas are far more enriched for higher grade tumors, also more likely to be non-dural based and to be in unique anatomic compartments. So at age 30, tough to know if this originally was emerged or was born as a pediatric meningioma. and then evolved over the subsequent decade or 12 plus years to be this multi-compartmental entity, and especially since he remained without symptoms. My sense is that the excellent control rate in some of the cavernous sinus radiosurgery studies are because it combines both lower grade and higher grade tumors. And many of the observed cavernous sinus components or true cavernous sinus tumors can be very indolent for a long time, whereas those that progress in our truly higher grade may not have such perfect control and will track up the tectorium and other compartments in a very insidious way. I think, too, I think Michael's question of is, do you consider this a, you know, pedroclival versus a cavernous sinus meningioma, even though there is infiltration of the cavernous sinus, the bulk of the cavernous sinus component does not seem to be expansile. And so the epicenter of the tumor may still be more in that sphenoid wing compartment, allowing it to both grow down into the infratemporal fossa and posteriorly into the petrous apex sort of region. The petrous apex, but although I may have misremembered this when you were scrolling, the CT itself did not seem to be particularly remodeled or eroded or hyperostatic. So it seemed to be a secondary extension through Meikle's cave to that posterior fossa causing the brainstem compression there. But I guess the bottom line is that we probably would do some sort of copy number or molecular sequencing if it was low grade to watch as long as possible, because I do worry that in higher grade tumors, in a young person that there is a durability to any form of treatment we give, whether it's surgery, radiation, or both, and to try to stretch out, kind of get the most bang for the buck for every intervention so that they get closer to their natural lifespan, you know, has been our formula.

reference_conclusion: Following staged surgical management, the patient has residual extracranial/infratemporal and cavernous sinus disease after resection of the middle fossa and posterior fossa components, including decompression of the brainstem. No immediate adjuvant therapy is planned. Further management consists of obtaining a head and neck opinion regarding the extracranial component and a radiation oncology opinion regarding the cavernous sinus component; advanced molecular testing/profiling may be considered to inform future treatment options.

And chemotherapy, I think, demonstrates limited benefit and advanced molecular testing and profiling would be good for me to have more options. [...] So that's where we're at with him at the moment. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 22-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: In May 2020, he presented with 20 days of abdominal enlargement, left hypochondrial discomfort, generalized bone pain, weight loss, night sweats, and fever.

[ diagnosis ]: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), chronic phase, Philadelphia chromosome-positive. Low-risk disease at initial diagnosis. Post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation course was complicated by chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) involving skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver, and later by pulmonary infectious complications including Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and suspected tissue-invasive CMV infection.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial bone marrow biopsy (2020): hypercellular marrow (~95%) with myeloid proliferation and maturation, consistent with a myeloproliferative neoplasm; findings supported CML chronic phase.  
- Bone marrow evaluation after dasatinib (approximately July 2021): BCR-ABL remained elevated at 34%; marrow details not otherwise specified.  
- Bone marrow evaluation in December 2021: hypercellular marrow with 2% blast cells; bone marrow biopsy showed approximately 5% blasts with CD117 positivity; consistent with CML chronic phase, without evidence of accelerated phase or blast phase.  
- Donor marrow aspirate/biopsy (sister): normocellular marrow, no blasts.  
- Skin biopsy during post-transplant GVHD evaluation: very thin epidermis with collagen deposition and hyalinization in the dermis, pigment incontinence, no lymphocytic infiltrate, no atypia or malignancy; consistent with sclerodermatous stage of GVHD.  
- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopic biopsies: mild chronic gastritis/duodenitis; esophagitis and biliary reflux were also reported.  
- Lung biopsy (September 2024 admission): alveoli with scattered enlarged cells showing viral inclusions, reported as likely CMV inclusions.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- At presentation, examination showed splenomegaly approximately 11 fingerbreadths below the costal margin.  
- CT chest at day +94 post-transplant (approximately September 2022): multiple patchy areas of ground-glass opacity with predominantly peripheral upper-lobe distribution; radiologic severity described as CORADS 5; COVID testing was negative twice. Follow-up CT showed resolution of ground-glass opacities.  
- CT chest at day +140 post-transplant (October 2022): prior ground-glass opacities had resolved.  
- CT chest in September 2024: multiple central and peripheral ground-glass opacities with associated reticular opacities, mainly basal, with left basal patchy consolidation and left pneumothorax; pulmonary GVHD was included in the differential diagnosis.  
- Follow-up imaging by March 2025: more resolution of previously noted abnormalities, with residual atypical segmental changes in the left lower lobe; otherwise stationary course.  
- Pulmonary function testing pre-transplant: FEV1 90%.  
- Pulmonary function testing in September 2024: obstructive pattern with some restriction.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Philadelphia chromosome detected by FISH at diagnosis.  
- BCR-ABL quantitative PCR at diagnosis: 32%.  
- BCR-ABL qPCR after 3 months of imatinib: 12%.  
- BCR-ABL qPCR after 6 months of imatinib: 32%.  
- BCR-ABL qPCR in January 2021: 35%.  
- BCR-ABL qPCR in June 2021: 34%.  
- BCR-ABL qPCR in December 2021: 55%.  
- Post-transplant BCR-ABL PCR at day +26: negative.  
- BCR-ABL PCR in August 2022: negative.  
- FISH/chimerism after transplant: XX karyotype/chimerism 99%, XY 1%, consistent with predominant donor engraftment.  
- BCR-ABL PCR in November 2022: negative.  
- BCR-ABL PCR in June 2024: negative.  
- BCR-ABL PCR in November 2024: negative.  
- No kinase domain mutation testing was reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Initial CBC (May 2020): total leukocyte count 174,000/µL; absolute neutrophil count 138,000/µL; hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL; platelets 518,000/µL; normocytic normochromic anemia.  
- Initial differential/peripheral smear: myelocytes 3%, metamyelocytes 12%, polymorphs 68%.  
- CBC in June 2021: total leukocyte count 20,000/µL; hemoglobin 14 g/dL; platelets 140,000/µL.  
- Pre-transplant recipient infectious workup: EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, HSV-1, and HSV-2 IgM negative; corresponding IgG positive. CMV PCR below detection limit. Bacterial cultures showed no growth.  
- Donor infectious workup: EBV IgG positive; EBV IgM reported as equivocal at 12.13 (reference positive >13); toxoplasma IgM and IgG negative; CMV and HSV-1/2 IgM negative, IgG positive; CMV PCR below detection limit. Hemoglobin electrophoresis normal.  
- Day +6 post-transplant blood culture: Staphylococcus epidermidis isolated.  
- October 2022 liver profile: ALT/AST elevated to approximately 3 times the upper limit of normal; glucose reported as elevated to 1.4 (units not specified).  
- During chronic GVHD course in 2024: ALT 470 U/L, AST 412 U/L, bilirubin 2 mg/dL.  
- During pulmonary infection episode in late 2024: ALT 232 U/L, AST 172 U/L, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL.  
- By March 2025: ALT 108 U/L, AST 72 U/L.  
- BAL/culture studies during September 2024 admission: bacterial cultures no growth; Candida albicans isolated; respiratory viral PCR negative; immunostain for Pneumocystis positive.  
- CMV PCR in blood during pulmonary infection episode: negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial cytoreduction with hydroxyurea.  
- Imatinib 400 mg daily started June 2020; given for approximately 3 months, then interrupted because of cytopenia. Molecular response was inadequate (BCR-ABL 12% at 3 months, 32% at 6 months).  
- Switched to nilotinib in February 2021; treatment was not tolerated.  
- Switched to dasatinib in April 2021; after approximately 3 months, BCR-ABL remained elevated (34% in June/July 2021).  
- Referred for allogeneic transplantation workup; fully HLA-matched sister donor identified.  
- Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed on 29 May 2022 using peripheral blood stem cells from matched sibling donor. Conditioning regimen included busulfan and cyclophosphamide. Stem cell dose infused was 7.9 million/kg.  
- GVHD prophylaxis: cyclosporine and methotrexate, with antimicrobial prophylaxis.  
- Early post-transplant complications: febrile neutropenia and mucositis on day +6; treated with meropenem and vancomycin according to culture results. Possible engraftment syndrome around day +10 with fever, desaturation, and skin rash; treated with dexamethasone 8 mg every 12 hours for 3 days followed by taper. Neutrophil engraftment occurred on day +16. Discharged on day +20 on cyclosporine 250 mg.  
- Approximately 1 month after discharge: hemorrhagic cystitis/emergency urinary bleeding, improved with intravenous fluids and bladder irrigation.  
- Cyclosporine was tapered and discontinued by approximately day +100, then restarted in October 2022 when chronic GVHD developed.  
- Day +94 admission for fever/chest infection with bilateral ground-glass opacities; treated with meropenem, vancomycin, and supportive care; radiologic improvement occurred within 1 week.  
- October 2022 chronic GVHD presentation with weight loss, skin changes, vomiting, cough, mucositis, and liver dysfunction; treated with intravenous cyclosporine 75 mg every 12 hours, methylprednisolone 19 mg every 12 hours, hydrocortisone 100 mg, and total parenteral nutrition.  
- Ruxolitinib started at day +162 at 5 mg twice daily with prednisolone 30 mg for 1 week followed by taper; cyclosporine continued. Weight increased from 46 kg to 50 kg, later to 58 kg; gastrointestinal symptoms improved. Ruxolitinib was later increased to 10 mg twice daily. Skin lesions improved with PUVA.  
- Steroids were subsequently withdrawn; cyclosporine and ruxolitinib were continued long term because of persistent chronic GVHD activity, particularly hepatic involvement.  
- September 2024 ICU admission for fever, hypoxemia, productive cough, sore throat, and left pneumothorax. Intercostal tube was inserted. Lung biopsy/BAL demonstrated Pneumocystis positivity, Candida albicans in BAL, and histologic viral inclusions suggestive of CMV; blood CMV PCR was negative. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, acyclovir, and levofloxacin; fluconazole was later stopped. Clinical and radiologic improvement occurred, with regression of pneumothorax and removal of chest tube.

[ current disease status ]:  
- CML remained in molecular remission after allogeneic transplantation, with serial BCR-ABL PCR negative through at least November 2024; June 2024 PCR was also negative.  
- At last documented follow-up on 2 March 2025 (approximately 2 years 7 months post-transplant), he was clinically stable. Chest imaging showed further resolution of prior pulmonary abnormalities with residual atypical left lower lobe changes. Liver enzymes had improved but remained abnormal (ALT 108 U/L, AST 72 U/L).  
- He remained on ruxolitinib 15 mg twice daily, cyclosporine 25 mg twice daily, acyclovir, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and liver supportive therapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Matched sibling donor: 18-year-old female, 100% matched sister.  
- Pre-transplant dental, dermatology, ENT, and cardiology assessments did not identify contraindicating infectious foci or cardiac disease.  
- Recipient pulmonary function before transplant was preserved.  
- Weight loss during chronic GVHD flare in October 2022 was approximately 11 kg over 2 months.  
- Skin manifestations included dark pigmentation, desquamative/disfiguring skin changes, photosensitivity, and mucositis/lip lesions.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old female. Non-smoker. No prior comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe breathlessness with hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated neoplasm/carcinoma, treated clinically as probable non-small cell lung carcinoma with suspected lung primary. Radiologic pattern was considered consistent with lymphangitic carcinomatosis.

[ histopathology results ]: EBUS-guided biopsy of a subcarinal lymph node was performed. Initial pathology impression was non-small cell lung carcinoma. After extensive immunohistochemistry, the specimen was reported as a poorly differentiated neoplasm. TTF-1 positivity was reported.

[ imaging findings ]: Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral haziness. HRCT thorax showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities and multiple lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm. Multiple lytic bone lesions were also described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Limited NGS panel reported MET amplification at a borderline threshold and stated it was not commentable. ALK point mutation was reported as a variant of uncertain significance. No ALK fusion was documented. The panel was described as covering major mutations including EGFR and ALK.

[ laboratory results ]: PD-L1 tumor proportion score was reported as approximately 8–10%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received carboplatin and paclitaxel. Clinical improvement was observed after treatment, including improvement in breathlessness and hypoxia; oxygen dependence resolved. A second cycle of paclitaxel/carboplatin was being planned.

[ current disease status ]: Marked symptomatic improvement after paclitaxel/carboplatin. Performance status improved from poor functional status at presentation to approximately ECOG PS 1 at the time of review.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had initially been admitted under pulmonology. Lymphoma had been considered initially because of thoracic and infradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old premenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Self-palpated right breast nodule during the third trimester of pregnancy in 2015.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, pathologic stage IIB (T2N1).

[ histopathology results ]: Mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection specimen showed invasive ductal carcinoma measuring 2.5 cm. Scarff-Bloom-Richardson score was 7 (grade 2). Lymphovascular invasion was present. Surgical margins were negative. One axillary lymph node was positive for metastatic carcinoma, with metastatic deposit measuring 7 mm.

[ imaging findings ]: Mammography was performed following detection of the right breast nodule. No further imaging details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor positive (reported as R7), progesterone receptor negative, and Ki-67 approximately 50%. Genetic risk assessment was pending.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. One month later she presented for adjuvant treatment planning. Adjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel was initiated. The first cycle was administered on 5 November. No treatment response or toxicity data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative early-stage breast cancer after mastectomy and axillary dissection, receiving adjuvant chemotherapy. No documented evidence of recurrent or metastatic disease was provided.

[ other clinical data ]: The breast cancer was hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative by available data. The patient was pregnant at the time of initial presentation, in the third trimester.

reference_discussion.text: Our case is a 38-year-old premenopausal woman and now with breast cancer at age 50. and all the risk factors. In the third trimester of 2015, she self-pulpated a right breast nodule. A mammogram was performed and after that, a mastectomy plus axodialytic nodule dissection was performed. In the pathologic report, an invasive ductal carcinoma, well documented, of 2.5 centimeters, with SBR of 7, lymph vascular invasion positive, negative surgical margins, and one lymph node positive for a metastasis of 7 millimeters. The immunochemistry report, estrogen receptors positive, with R7, progesterone receptor negative, to negative and the CAI 57 off 50%. One month later, the patient presented to our center to advise adjuvant treatment. Next, please. So we have a patient with breast cancer, stage 2B, and we indicated adjuvant chemotherapy with dog bends of AC followed by paclitaxel. And the first cycle was on November 5th. A genetic risk assessment was pending. It's pending. Next.

So we have several questions regarding this case. So the first one is, what would be the optimal active and hormonal therapy for her being a 38-year-old woman with an N1 grade 2? And we would consider extended therapy or ovarian suppression. And we would like to know your opinion about we should consider for all premenopausal patients the combination of OFS plus adjuvant aromatase inhibitors.

So that's a very clear question. Jack, could you tell us your view after soft and text, what do you do with premenopausal patients who are already receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for perceived risk? How do you manage the endocrine therapy?

So this patient clearly does have major risk issues. She's 38. I would consider her probably closer to 35 than 40. She's requiring chemotherapy. She's PR negative. There's a whole host of factors that make one want to be concerned about her prognosis. But it's important to remember that the patients who entered SOFT were really premenopausal, if you will, by virtue of their estradiol levels or continuing to have menstrual function. And so I think it shouldn't be yet, in my opinion, and Paula would certainly be the expert, certainly yet wouldn't be my practice to put all patients on therapy. Going back to ECOG years ago, the addition of Lupron without Tamoxifen did not add to chemotherapy in the premenopausal woman who had just completed chemotherapy unselected. So I would follow the standards of SOFT. I would want to know what her estradiol was before committing her to ovarian suppression.

think that not all hospitals attaining this tumor board will have an easy estradiol assessment available. And particularly as the levels decline toward menopause and into menopause, most hospitals don't have that technology. But the question really, Jack, I'm going to push you on this a bit. The question from Montserrat, from Mexico City is, if you've already decided the patient is justified to give chemotherapy, I think you've answered this, does the administration of chemotherapy mandate a soft text approach because they were considered requiring chemotherapy? I think that's the question.

So if I could make it a little bit cleaner and make her just a little bit younger and I would have to say that I think the evidence is compelling that a very young woman in her 30s with no positive requiring chemotherapy, hormone sensitive, probably should have additional combined therapy. And the question of the aromatase inhibitor versus tamoxifen I think deserves a second discussion and in some cases will be correct. So I think yes, ovarian suppression should be considered.
Okay. Any agreement or disagreement with that, Susan?

Yeah, so I think if you look at the published data, I mean, the patients who received chemotherapy and who were part of these studies were a group, regardless of age, that benefited from ovarian suppression. So looking at the data of tamoxifen versus ovarian suppression with eczemastine, the difference at five years was like 7%. Yeah, so if you don't have access to hormonal levels, you could start with tamoxifen, and then if she gets a period, add in ovarian suppression, or take a different approach and say that the majority of women treated with ACT at this age will resume menstrual function within a year and just be aggressive with the treatment of her breast cancer.

I must say I'm inclined to be in that camp of thought. I agree that she's going to be premenopausal at 38 regardless of what happens, I think. So I think that at least here, I know several of my respective medical oncologists would agree with that opinion that Jack and Susan have just given. If anybody disagrees, please say so. But I think you're hearing that a soft text approach should be given to patients with chemotherapy, adjuvant chemotherapy.

I would just add one that I think the B30 trial was very informative as to who would or wouldn't become menopausal based on chemotherapy and by age I think you can get some very nice data as to what that outcome is going to be.
Okay, I'd like to ask Cynthia to give a second question, the next question.
Can you put the presentation, please, again, Jessica?
Or I can see it over here.
The second question is, what is the role of adjuvant bisphosphonates in premenopausal patients that receive ovarian suppression, and if there are any other features that guide us on this decision?

Another very good controversial issue, and I'm going to turf the ball to, let me give it to Susan first. Susan, do you routinely give bisphosphonates? There are two questions buried here, I think. The first one is, is bisphosphonate desirable for a young person getting ovarian suppression? for bone metabolism reasons, and I think the answer to that is yes. For one year at least, definitely. But the deeper question is, with the presentations that have been given at the major meetings, is adjuvant bisphosphonate now a routine anti-breast cancer five-year adjuvant therapy in all patients? In whom should it be given? When should it be given? That's the question.

Yeah, so I think, again, this is a controversial issue. In my young patients who I'm offering ovarian suppression as their primary endocrine therapy, particularly with an aromatase inhibitor, those are the patients that I'm normally recommending bisphosphonate for. Based on the SWOG study, I think you have your option right now, whether you use an oral versus an IV bisphosphonate. But I would consider, in this population, that would be standard. For me, although I think the national guidelines and NCCN are still not quite certain who to give bisphosphonates to.
Susan, can I interrupt you? Are you influenced if the patient expresses interest in subsequent pregnancy by the use of bisphosphonates or not?
You know, I honestly don't know that data, Paul. My guess is that would make me nervous, but I have not researched that. Does anyone else who's listening know that answer?

Yeah, hi. I would be very nervous. I think the evidence, at least in clinical studies I'm aware of, is that you can measure terminal half-life of excretion of the drug even a year out from a dose. There is drug that is stored and slowly released over time and so I think it would be, in my practice, an absolute contraindication if somebody were considering future pregnancy.
And for either oral or IV bisphosphonate?
Yes, I would avoid that because of the long half-life in the patient.
And then the question that I should probably answer, but I'll let others answer. What about denosumab? Would you consider denosumab differently or the same?
That's a great question. I actually don't know the evidence for the terminal half-life, but I would say any drug that could exist in the body for a long period of time, I'd be nervous about.

I think donosumab's got a long half-life like most antibodies, but not as long as the meto or those other agents. But I think that in patients wanting children or pregnancy after treatment, I think bisphosphonates currently are still contraindicated, actually, and probably donosumab as well, because of possible teratogenicity.
So Paul, I just researched that quickly as we were talking and both of those agents are contraindicated with pregnancy.
Right. Thank you, Susan. That's great. So Cynthia, is that the answer you were looking for or did you want to probe deeper on this question?
No, it was that because then in the meta-analysis, even the patients that were deemed postmenopausal were the ones that benefited.

And I realize I've got two experts on the line that I haven't asked a question of. So the radiation question, that's next. Perhaps Dr. Carol Marquez can address. And as well, the last question. So Dr. Chu, maybe you'd like to say something as well about the post-mastectomy radiation for this young patient. So you ask the question, Cynthia, please. The last two questions.

The question is, the third one, what is the role of post-mastectomy radiotherapy for this young patient with a T1N1, with a one-node positive, HIV-positive hormone, we said, to deposit her to negative breast cancer, and if should all young women with one, two, three positive nodes should receive adjuvant radiotherapy?
So...
It's Julia.
Julia, yes, please.

Yes, hi. So the question is always debated at our own tumor board at Penn. So because of your young age and her having one positive lymph node, we would err on the side of being more aggressive and will most likely recommend post-mastectomy radiation at our institution.
Maybe Alphonse, you want to add something to that? Dr. Marquez, would you like to say something, please?

I agree with that, and I'd agree with it also because of her other negative features, which would include the LVSI and the size of the tumor. I think all of those features together would make me recommend radiation for her.

And Alphonse is nodding his head. Absolutely right. It's beyond the age. It's beyond one positive lymph node. will bring her risk a little bit higher. So I fully agree with you. We look now at multiple risk factors. We look at the big picture. And instead of being cornered into one positive lymph node, she should have post-mastectomy radiation. So she has LVI. She's young. She didn't have enough lymph nodes removed. And the tumor was large. So she had multiple risk factors. I agree with you.
Can I add something about it? Otherwise, we would have positive features. Illuminal A of breast cancer with a grade one. But with one to three notes, H would guide you towards giving radiotherapy.

I mean, in regards to your last question, so like what you're saying is, just because she's young and just because she has one to three positive nodes, would you always give radiation? I don't think that's the case, because I think, as we discussed in, you know, the previous case, I think it depends on the amount of the nodal burden, how involved the node is. I think it does depend on the pathologic subtype, and I think the presence or absence of LVSI is really an important feature. in determining local regional recurrence after a mastectomy. So I think it is, as Dr. Takian says, kind of looking at the whole picture, at the whole combination of factors, not just age and positive notes.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old right-handed man. Retired from law enforcement. Newly divorced. Lived alone. No children. Residence was approximately 45 minutes from the treating medical facility.

[ chief complaint ]: Confusion and headache.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected brain tumor tissue showed large pleomorphic tumor cells with mitotic activity and microvascular proliferation. Histopathologic and molecular classification was glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, IDH-wildtype.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial brain MRI demonstrated an aggressive-appearing enhancing mass in the right posterior temporal/inferior parietal region with central necrosis and surrounding edema, consistent with a high-grade glioma. Postoperative MRI obtained within 48 hours demonstrated gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing tumor.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation negative. MGMT promoter hypermethylated. TERT promoter mutation present. EGFR amplification present. CDKN2A deletion present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgical resection with gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing lesion. Postoperative course was uneventful; he was ambulatory the next day and headaches resolved. He received dexamethasone postoperatively. Despite no prior seizure history, he was discharged on antiseizure medication.

[ current disease status ]: Status post gross total resection of a right posterior temporal/inferior parietal glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, IDH-wildtype with MGMT promoter hypermethylation. Postoperative MRI within 48 hours demonstrated gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing tumor. He was ambulatory the day after surgery with resolution of headaches.

[ other clinical data ]: Symptoms began approximately 2 months before presentation with mild daily headaches that progressed to severe, intolerable headaches. Family noted confusion and forgetfulness for approximately 2 weeks before presentation. Past medical history included hypertension and pre-diabetes. Family history was notable for a father who died of colon cancer. Visual field assessment was considered preoperatively because of lesion location. No seizure history was documented at presentation.

reference_discussion.text: And now we'll kick off the first official session of today's conference, Behind the Scenes of a Brain Tumor Board. This will consist of a multidisciplinary panel of expert clinicians who will simulate the review of brain tumor cases to determine the best course of treatment for patients. The goal of this session is to show you how treatment decisions truly involve teamwork among physicians to ensure that we're giving the best care possible for our patients and how those conversations are had. I'm going to introduce everyone to come up to the stage. First, I'd like to introduce our moderator for this session, Dr. Mark Gilbert from the NIH, a neuro-oncologist. Our panelists. Our panelists include our neuro-oncologist for the panel, Dr. Akanksha Sharma, who's at Sutter Health. Our neurosurgeon for the panelists is Dr. Michael Lim, who's the Chair of Neurosurgery at Stanford University. Our radiation oncologist is Helen Shi, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Hospital in Boston. Our neuropathologist is Matthias Nutterl from NYU Langone Health. Our radiologist is Javier Villanueva-Meyer from the University of California, San Francisco. And our neuro-oncology nurse navigator is Jenny Lynn Owalu from the Brain Tumor Network. Thank you so much. It is certainly a great honor to be moderating this session. Reminiscing, I realized I gave my first talk at the ABTA in 1997. I was 12. So, all kidding aside, actually my daughter, who was 11, was in the audience and she had just written a report for school on brain tumors. I don't know where she got that idea. And her final paragraph talked about how much hope she had because people like her father were in the field. And I presented that, she was in the audience, and I got a clap, she got a standing ovation. Tough act to follow. So this is my favorite session. As you may have surmised, I have retired. But I came back because I was asked. And it really is such a tremendous opportunity for all of you to understand what we go through as physicians taking care of folks with brain tumors to make sure that the best decisions are made. And what these guys don't realize is that I'm going to go a little off script. And that's what happens, right? What we're looking for is discussion and consensus building. And so you can hear the controversy, the discussions, the importance of really getting everybody's opinion coming to a consensus. And we're so fortunate to have such a fantastic panel of colleagues. It's a small field, so I kind of know everybody. I was in the field for 38 years, so you would hope I'd know everybody. And we will actually go through two cases, and with each we will get input from all of our esteemed colleagues. So these are the disclosures. And just to quickly review, a neuro-oncologist, typically it's either a neurologist or a medical oncologist who's received specialized training in the treatment of patients with brain tumors, so medical therapy, the neurosurgeon. a surgical treatment, radiation oncologist, radiation therapy. The neuropathologist is a specialized pathologist who focused on diseases of the central nervous system, also peripheral nervous system. Radiologist, of course, interprets imaging, but I would say that to get the best care, it should be a neuroradiologist, and we're very fortunate to have actually one of the top neuroradiologists in the country. And then the neuro-oncology nurse navigator, right? So to integrate all of this care to make sure that the patients get the optimal treatment, the logistics, the family support, et cetera, this person is incredibly important. And of course, the supportive care services, which we we'll talk about a little bit today also. So first case. So a 61-year-old right-handed man presents with confusion and headache. Symptoms started about two months ago, mild daily headaches, now they're severe and intolerable. Two weeks prior to this, family noted some confusion, forgetfulness. His past history, not surprisingly, hypertension and pre-diabetes quite common. And the patient is retired from law enforcement, newly divorced, lives alone, no children, home, is about 45 minutes away from the medical facility. And his family history, remarkable, just for a father who died of colon cancer. So with this, of course, seen in an emergency facility with that history, an image would be done, and I'll ask Dr. Villanueva to not only describe what we see here, but also to give you all an overview of imaging, MR being the magnetic resonance imaging being the most common, just to give a quick overview so your interpretation will be more complete. Thank you, Mark. So, as Mark just noted, MR imaging is the mainstay for assessing the status of tumors in the brain, in the spine, and the bread and butter sequences, which are the types of images that we acquire, are T1 post-contrast, which is what you're seeing here on the screen, and T2, and a particular type of T2 image, it's called a T2 flare image, which you may have heard of. And we look at those two as the main sets of images to help us understand the characteristics of a tumor, where a tumor may be, But as you can all imagine, the story doesn't stop there. There's additional images that are also acquired. Here we're going to focus on some of the more basic things initially and then we'll maybe fold into the discussion some of those other sequences. In this patient's case, what we're seeing here, as I mentioned earlier, this is a T1 post-contrast image. It's an axial view, meaning it's a view you're looking from the top down or from the bottom up. We're sort of at the level of the ventricles, as you can see. And in imaging, when we're describing findings, we like to mix things up, and so the right side of the screen is actually the left side of the body, and the left side of the screen is the right side of the body. So in this patient's case, we're seeing a tumor that's posteriorly along the right-hand side involving kind of the temporal and maybe inferior parietal areas. You can see there's some contrast enhancement. That's that bright signal or the bright area on the back part on the your left-hand side of the screen, but the right-hand side of the patient. And inside of that, we see some lack of contrast enhancement, that's what we would describe as necrosis. I'm only showing you a T1 post-contrast image here, so you can't see the T2 flare, but the areas that are dark, that are at the periphery outside of that, that represents edema or swelling related to the tumor. What we're seeing here would be described as something that looks aggressive. This looks like a high-grade glioma very clearly. reference_conclusion: Following gross total resection of the right temporal high-grade glioma, molecular profiling established glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, IDH-wildtype with MGMT hypermethylation. The agreed postoperative management is standard chemoradiation with daily radiation therapy over six weeks administered with concurrent daily oral temozolomide, initiated within 6 to 8 weeks after surgery if no clinical trial is pursued. After a 3- to 4-week recovery interval following radiation, adjuvant temozolomide is to be started on a 5-days-per-month schedule for 6 months, with discussion of Optune/tumor treating fields at that time. Subsequent imaging changes in this case were interpreted as pseudoprogression, and the plan is continued close observation with serial MRI rather than immediate change in therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 86-year-old female from Louisville, Kentucky. She lived independently and was described as relatively functional. She was a never smoker and had no history of alcohol use.

[ chief complaint ]: New ventral tongue lesion present for approximately 3 months, associated with mild discomfort.

[ diagnosis ]: Oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma of the ventral tongue, predominantly right-sided with extension to the midline region. Final pathologic findings were consistent with node-positive oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy performed by an oral surgeon showed squamous cell carcinoma with an estimated depth of invasion of approximately 3.6 mm. The lesion was described at biopsy as an erythematous lesion measuring approximately 1.5 cm. Final surgical pathology after partial glossectomy showed a 3.0 cm squamous cell carcinoma with depth of invasion 7.5 mm. Margins were negative; closest margin was 4 mm. Perineural invasion was present. Three lymph nodes were positive for metastatic disease: one level IB node on each side and one ipsilateral level III node. The largest positive node measured 0.9 cm.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging of the neck/oral cavity was limited by dental artifact, with poor visualization of the oral cavity tumor. Imaging report indicated no appreciable cervical adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past medical history included breast cancer treated approximately 10 years earlier. She had a history of DVT at that time and remained on anticoagulation. Additional history included hypertension and idiopathic left vocal cord paralysis diagnosed approximately 7 years earlier; medialization had previously been discussed but not performed at that time.

For the current malignancy, she underwent partial glossectomy with bilateral neck dissection. Reconstruction was performed with a radial forearm free flap because of concern for tethering related to ventral tongue/floor-of-mouth involvement. During the postoperative hospitalization, left vocal cord medialization injection was performed approximately 6-7 days after flap surgery to support swallowing function. A feeding tube was placed. Postoperatively, she was hospitalized for approximately 1 week, then discharged to rehabilitation for approximately 1 additional week. By discharge from rehabilitation, she was eating by mouth while also receiving nutrition via gastrostomy tube.

[ current disease status ]: Status post surgical resection of ventral tongue squamous cell carcinoma with bilateral nodal metastases identified on final pathology. She tolerated surgery and postoperative recovery well.

[ other clinical data ]: On preoperative examination, the ventral tongue lesion was estimated clinically at approximately 2.5 cm, with mild induration and tenderness. It was predominantly right-sided but approached the midline. No palpable cervical adenopathy was appreciated clinically. Flexible laryngoscopy confirmed persistent left vocal cord paralysis. She had breathy dysphonia consistent with the vocal cord paralysis. She maintained oral intake preoperatively without significant weight loss. Dentition was described as moderate, with a lower partial denture in place.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old male. Former smoker. No reported comorbidities. No reported family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain of approximately 1 month’s duration. On physical examination, there was a large right flank abdominal wall mass measuring approximately 8 cm, hard in consistency and firmly adherent to deep tissues.

[ diagnosis ]: Undifferentiated high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma of the abdominal wall, also described as malignant fibrous histiocytoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Percutaneous biopsy showed an undifferentiated pleomorphic malignant neoplasm with necrosis and numerous mitoses. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin and alpha-smooth muscle actin (alpha-SMA). Final pathology diagnosis was undifferentiated high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma / malignant fibrous histiocytoma. Following surgical excision, pathology again showed malignant fibrous histiocytoma, giant cells type, with free margins.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT imaging demonstrated a large abdominal wall mass. No definite metastatic disease was identified at initial staging. A focal liver abnormality was present but was not confirmed as metastatic disease. Three months after resection, imaging showed progressive disease with four new hepatic lesions and bone metastasis. After first-line palliative chemotherapy, there was further progression with a new bone lesion and a breast implant lesion. Subsequent imaging after spinal cord compression surgery showed systemic progression with new liver lesions, bone disease, retroperitoneal implants, pleural implants, and pulmonary embolism.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Hematologic toxicity occurred during radiotherapy. No specific laboratory values were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial local treatment consisted of radiotherapy for pain control, with 25 fractions planned; treatment was stopped after 18 sessions because of disease progression and hematologic toxicity. The patient then underwent surgical excision of the abdominal wall tumor; pathology confirmed malignant fibrous histiocytoma, giant cells type, with negative margins. No adjuvant chemotherapy was given after surgery, and the patient was followed clinically. Three months after resection, metastatic progression was documented in the liver and bone. Palliative systemic chemotherapy with doxorubicin was started; disease progressed with a new bone lesion and a breast implant lesion. Second-line ifosfamide was then administered; after three cycles, best response was progressive disease. The patient subsequently developed spinal cord compression and underwent neurosurgical decompression plus radiotherapy. After further systemic progression, third-line docetaxel was started and was associated with clinical improvement, including reduced bone pain, decreased opioid requirement, and improved quality of life.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic progressive high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma involving liver, bone, retroperitoneum, pleura, and breast implant region, with prior spinal cord compression and pulmonary embolism. At the time of latest update, the patient was receiving third-line docetaxel with clinical symptomatic improvement; interval CT reassessment was pending.

[ other clinical data ]: Performance status was described as good at the time third-line docetaxel was initiated.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma with disease progression after multiple lines of systemic therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma diagnosed in May 2025. Stage IV disease at diagnosis with lung and liver metastases. Comorbid diabetes mellitus. ECOG/performance status 2.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue next-generation sequencing showed low tumor mutational burden and microsatellite stable status. Detected alterations included KRAS mutation, TP53 mutation, CDKN2A missense mutation, ARID1A frameshift deletion, TERT promoter mutation, and SMARCB1 frameshift deletion.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: First-line treatment consisted of gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel. Partial response was achieved, with duration of response approximately 6-7 months. Treatment was complicated by neuropathy. Therapy was then changed to gemcitabine plus capecitabine. After approximately 2 months, disease progression occurred with increase in lesion size and rise in CA 19-9. Third-line chemotherapy consisted of irinotecan plus oxaliplatin. After 3 cycles, progressive disease was documented. There was no decrease in CA 19-9 during this treatment, and imaging also showed progression. Neuropathy had subsequently recovered.

[ laboratory results ]: CA 19-9 increased at progression on gemcitabine plus capecitabine. No decline in CA 19-9 was observed during irinotecan plus oxaliplatin.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic disease after three cycles of third-line irinotecan plus oxaliplatin.

[ other clinical data ]: Diabetes mellitus. Performance status 2.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Large frontal extra-axial brain mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected tumor showed features of a meningothelial neoplasm with closely apposed cells, indistinct cell borders, and whorl formation. Mitotic activity was present at 6 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. Necrosis was present. Ki-67 proliferation index was greater than 5%. Pathologic classification was atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]: Pre-operative MRI brain with T1 post-contrast and T2-weighted sequences demonstrated a large, well-defined, avidly and relatively homogeneously enhancing frontal mass. A circumferential CSF cleft was present, indicating an extra-axial lesion arising from the meninges/dura rather than intra-axial brain parenchyma. Sagittal and coronal imaging showed extension to the meninges. Imaging appearance was classic for meningioma. The lesion originated from/was attached to the superior sagittal sinus region, with preserved blood flow through the sinus. Post-operative MRI demonstrated excellent resection with removal of all nodular enhancing tumor, preservation of the superior sagittal sinus, no visible adjacent vascular injury, and persistent T2 hyperintense edema/swelling in the adjacent brain.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 27-year-old premenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Vague lump in the left breast, first presenting in February 2023.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive lobular carcinoma, initially staged as pT3N3a after left mastectomy, with de novo metastatic bone disease on PET-CT. Hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer. Subsequent contralateral breast progression in May 2025 with ipsilateral axillary nodal involvement on imaging and biopsy-confirmed invasive lobular carcinoma in the opposite breast.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Left mastectomy specimen: invasive lobular carcinoma. Pathologic stage reported as T3N3a.  
- Biopsy of contralateral breast lesion in 2025: invasive lobular carcinoma.  
- Repeat immunohistochemistry on progressive lesion: ER strongly positive, PR negative, HER2 negative (HER2 0).

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Post-mastectomy PET-CT in 2023 demonstrated multiple sclerotic and lytic osseous metastases involving the sternum, left scapula, bilateral ribs, sacrum, and dorsal/lumbar vertebrae, consistent with extensive bone metastatic disease.  
- Serial PET-CT assessments were performed approximately every 4 months during treatment. Initial response imaging showed good response, with vertebral and other bony lesions healing and becoming sclerotic.  
- PET-CT in May 2025 demonstrated a 1.5 cm lesion in the opposite breast in the subcutaneous plane and multiple abnormal axillary lymph nodes.  
- On later PET-CT, bone lesions remained of low uptake; sclerosis had increased, and progression versus stable treated disease could not be clearly determined from the available data.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Tissue NGS from the progressive breast lesion identified an NTRK3 fusion involving VPS13C-NTRK3.  
- Tissue report referenced 177 transcripts identified.  
- Liquid biopsy NGS was negative for ESR1 mutation, PIK3CA mutation, and AKT mutation.  
- Liquid biopsy tumor fraction was reported as 0.4%.  
- TP53 variant was detected on liquid biopsy at 0.3%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Left mastectomy was performed before systemic therapy.  
- First-line systemic treatment for metastatic hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative disease consisted of leuprolide, letrozole, and ribociclib, started in 2023.  
- This regimen was continued for approximately 1.5 to 2 years.  
- Initial treatment response was favorable on serial PET-CT, with healing/sclerosis of bone lesions.  
- First documented progression occurred in May 2025 with a new contralateral breast lesion and axillary lymphadenopathy.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Progressive metastatic hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative invasive lobular carcinoma after approximately 1.5-2 years of first-line ovarian suppression plus letrozole plus ribociclib.  
- Current documented sites of disease included contralateral breast lesion, axillary lymph nodes, and previously known extensive osseous metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Premenopausal status was documented.  
- Bone metastases were described as extensive at initial metastatic presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma involving the left thyroid lobe with cervical nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration was diagnostic of anaplastic carcinoma. No differentiated thyroid cancer component was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: CT of the neck demonstrated a tumor in the left thyroid lobe and left cervical lymph node enlargement, both with central necrosis. The trachea was distorted. Esophageal muscular layer invasion was considered possible. The carotid artery appeared intact on imaging. Internal jugular vein invasion was suspected. FDG-PET showed no evidence of distant metastasis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified NRAS and TP53 mutations and a promoter mutation. No actionable mutation was identified. Microsatellite instability was stable. Tumor mutational burden was low.

[ laboratory results ]: White blood cell count was >10,000/µL. Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was 3.7.

[ current disease status ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe with cervical nodal disease and no distant metastasis on FDG-PET.

[ other clinical data ]: On presentation, there was an approximately 8 cm large, firm neck mass with slight mobility. There was no hoarseness, dyspnea, or dysphagia. Prognostic index for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma was 3.

And this was a trial that looked at patients with either primary advanced endometrial cancer or recurrent disease. And in this study, 71% of patients had primary disease, 29% had recurrent disease, and they had to have a treatment-free interval of more than six months from the last platinum treatment. But when this was broken down to patients who got first-line versus treatment in the recurrent setting, what they found was that there was a huge amount of benefit in the first-line setting of a difference in 17.9 months, almost 18 months versus 9 months. in terms of progression-free survival whereas you still saw the benefit in the recurrent setting but this was a much smaller PFS benefit of 9 versus 6 months. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Nine patients from India were presented as a grouped hepatocellular carcinoma cohort. Individual ages and sexes were not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Advanced liver malignancy. A representative case had stage IV liver cancer with pulmonary metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), stage IV/metastatic in the presented cohort. Lung metastases were documented in a representative case. The cohort included patients with differing underlying etiologies of HCC; many had hepatitis B, and some had hepatitis C. Cirrhosis was described as the principal underlying risk factor for HCC in this population.

[ imaging findings ]: Representative imaging demonstrated metastatic HCC involving the liver with lung metastases. Imaging was not available for all nine patients. Multiple micrometastatic lesions were described in association with TP53 R249S-mutant disease biology. Tumor size reduction after sorafenib was described in an HCC case with FGF19 overexpression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: All nine cases shared a recurrent molecular profile including:
- 11q13.3 amplicon involving CCND1, FGF19, FGF3, and FGF4
- TERT promoter mutation, reported as the same promoter mutation across all nine cases
- TP53 mutation in all nine cases

TP53 hotspot variants reported within the cohort included:
- TP53 R249S in 4/9 cases
- TP53 R249M in 4/9 cases

Additional genomic findings reported in a subset:
- Tumor mutational burden of 10 mutations/Mb in some cases
- NTRK1 amplification in 3 cases

[ laboratory results ]: No routine hematology, biochemistry, liver function, AFP, or viral serology values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Sorafenib treatment was described in an HCC case with FGF19 overexpression, with reduction in tumor size after treatment. No patient-specific systemic treatment histories for the full nine-patient cohort were provided. No surgical treatment was reported for these nine stage IV cases.

[ current disease status ]: The cohort had advanced/metastatic HCC. For the nine presented cases, no meaningful surgical option was described because of stage IV disease. A representative case had metastatic disease to the lungs.

[ other clinical data ]: Viral-associated hepatocarcinogenesis was emphasized, particularly hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Aflatoxin exposure was described as relevant to TP53 codon 249-mutant HCC biology, particularly in conjunction with hepatitis B infection. The TP53 R249S alteration was described in the DNA-binding domain. RB1 loss/mutation was described as occurring in approximately 30% of liver cancers in general, but no RB1 status was provided for these nine patients.

And the prevention of the phosphorylation on top using the PD compound, the two act as a double whammy. And that leads to destabilization of the CMIG and its degradation, which would then further bring down the proliferation of the hepatocellular cells in the carcinoma. This was very elegantly also shown that if you use single agents, either multiple concentrations of C1, that's your P53 activator, or P1, which is your cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, you don't get as much good response as you would see in the bottom graph, P2 plus C2, that's a higher concentration of both the P53 stabilizer and the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor. When you have both of them on the bottom left graph, you know, the last little bar, you see the maximum inhibition of cell proliferation or cell confluence. So they do act synergistically. That's extremely promising for these patients. And that's the further, another readout of that on the bottom right is the CMIC band on the very right side of the graph. at higher concentration of PD and CP, the CMIG is getting degraded, and that's another marker for ensuring that the cells are not proliferating. So this kind of a combination therapy that is very, very unique to the hepatocellular carcinoma that is predominant in African, Asian, Southeast Asian countries, that comes from a combination of alcohol consumption, aflatoxin, probably from the contaminated food grains, and also from hepatitis B infection. These tend to seem to almost select for this mutation, and the mutation is not a simple amino acid change, it's missense. It is leading to activation of a whole new pathway But the pathway now having been tracked and elucidated well also throws up a synergistic combination of targets that can be targeted, both as an activator of P53 and an inhibitor of cycle-independent kinase, together hold tremendous promise in these cases to take it forward to actual human clinical trials, and hopefully that will reduce some of the disease burden in this case. It's a very promising field, but needs to be tested and seen. Thanks, Basim.

reference_conclusion: For metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma in this cohort, no meaningful surgical option was identified, and management should proceed with systemic therapy. Standard first-line treatment favored atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, with durvalumab plus tremelimumab also considered a first-line option and sorafenib or lenvatinib recognized as alternatives; lenvatinib may be particularly relevant in tumors with FGF19 amplification, and immunotherapy may be considered in cases with tumor mutational burden of 10. Clinical trial enrollment was emphasized, particularly biomarker-directed studies incorporating a CDK4/6 inhibitor with an immunotherapy-based backbone in tumors harboring the cyclin D1 amplicon with intact RB1 expression.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Abnormal screening mammogram leading to recall diagnostic breast imaging for a left breast mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative, clinically early stage; final pathologic tumor size 1.8 cm; sentinel lymph nodes negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the left breast mass demonstrated ductal breast carcinoma, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive. Final surgical pathology showed a 1.8 cm tumor with clear margins. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was negative for nodal involvement.

[ imaging findings ]: Diagnostic mammography identified a mass in the left breast upper inner quadrant, near the chest wall. Ultrasound demonstrated a corresponding left breast mass close to the pectoralis/chest wall muscle. Physical examination identified a very small palpable mass in the upper inner left breast without clinically concerning lymphadenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Oncotype DX 21-gene recurrence score was 23. The reported estimated 9- to 10-year recurrence risk with endocrine therapy alone was 9%, with estimated chemotherapy benefit less than 1%. Family history met NCCN criteria for consideration of hereditary cancer genetic testing. Genes specifically identified as relevant to assessment included BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, and ATM. No germline test result was reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent breast-conserving surgery for the upper inner quadrant left breast cancer with excision of the lesion and bilateral breast reshaping/breast-lift type oncoplastic procedure. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed. Surgical outcome showed complete excision with clear margins and no nodal metastases.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after breast-conserving surgery for left breast cancer; primary tumor resected with negative margins and node-negative disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included osteoporosis. Medications were reported only for osteoporosis treatment. Family history included mother with breast cancer at age 68 and maternal uncle with pancreatic cancer at age 60. Physical examination was otherwise normal.
