reference_discussion.text: Thank you, Dr. Westberg. So this team gets to work together every week, which is the best part of my job. So I'm glad we get to share this tumor board with you tonight. Our first patient is a 62 year old woman who has an abnormal screening mammogram. She was called back and had diagnostic imaging that identified a mass in the left breast, the upper inner part of the breast near the chest wall. She's otherwise very healthy with only osteoporosis, and the only medications she takes is for the treatment of her osteoporosis. Next slide. Her family history is interesting. Her mother had breast cancer at the age of 68, and her mother's brother, her maternal uncle, had pancreatic cancer at the age of 60. She has a very normal physical exam, except for a very small mass that can be felt in the upper inner part of the left breast, and she has no concerning lymph nodes on physical exam. So here's a representative. These cases are also representative cases. specific patients. But here's an example of a mass that would be concerning on a mammogram. Mammograms are taken in two views. And so the first view looks at the breast from side to side. So you can see that the mass is in the inner part of the breast. And the second image shows the breast from top to bottom. So you can see that the mass is in the top of the breast as well, and very close to the muscle of the chest wall. The ultrasound showed this mass. And as you look at the ultrasound, you see the stripes on the bottom of the screen, that's the muscle of the chest wall. So you can see again that this tumor mass is close to the muscle. So she had a biopsy and the biopsy demonstrated that this area was a breast cancer. It's a ductal cancer, grade two, and it's estrogen receptor positive, which is a favorable tumor biology. So this is where patients will usually see a surgeon as first course of treatment. And so we'll review medical history, surgical history, her social and her family history. And then we'll make, surgeons will make the referral to the tumor board for discussion of the primary team. In general, someone with a good early stage and favorable biology cancer will be referred for surgery as the first course of treatment. So I'd like to turn it over to Pam Fitzgerald, who is our patient navigator, who will sit with patients at this initial consultation and will start the process of helping patients work their way through the system.

Hi, can you see me? Yeah, I'm Pam Fitzgerald and I am one of the navigators at Smilow, Trumbull and Fairfield. I am a social worker and what I would do is sit with the patient at initial consultation with Dr. Lynch and get to understand a little bit about their social history and their family history, who their supports are. We would also review the distress screening tool at this time and see what in particular this woman generally speaking, would indicate we're her stressors, and we would try to help problem solve those issues. So for example, in a 62-year-old woman, we would talk sometimes about loss of loved ones. She may have recently had a family member pass away. Her children may be moving away. She may still be working and worried about financial stressors. So in that period of time, would talk about what supports are available to her in the community. We do have financial grants that we can help with. We can also help her with paperwork for work, whether it be FMLA or short-term disability. We also can refer her to counseling. if it's felt that she would benefit from that. The integrative medicine services that we have available are numerous. We have support groups, dietary counseling. We, you know, we have acupuncture and also massage someone very helpful throughout their course of treatment. But what's kind of unique to navigation is that we can travel, so to speak, with the woman throughout her continuum of care. So we can meet with her to discuss her options for treatment, but also explain why things are happening in a certain way, sort of in layman's terms. We're available. We tell them as soon as they walk out of the office, if they have a question, please call us. Call us tomorrow, call us next week, whatever we can do to alleviate stress. We can also meet with them, with the medical oncologist and the radiation oncologist. And again, assess at that time, oftentimes in radiation oncology, people have problems with transportation, we have resources for that as well. So again, we're here to eliminate barriers to care and to also help you from diagnosis through till survivorship. And, you know, we're just like to say we're, you know, a new sort of friend that you would make and please call us if you need us. And with that, I'll turn over to Amanda.

All right, we can go to the next slide. I'm Amanda Ganczak. I'm one of the genetic counselors. We have several who are staffed in the Bridgeport Trumbull location. And basically what we do is help to review an individual's personal and family history of cancer to determine the likelihood that the cancers are hereditary, meaning a gene is running in the family, placing them and their family members at high risk for particular types of cancers. And with that information, we can then target and help the providers plan how to attack those increased risks, how to offer different surgical approaches, how to discuss various chemo prevention or other risk reducing options that might be available based on those increased risks. So if we take this case one as our example, some of the factors that I would be looking at in terms of assessing for the likelihood of a hereditary risk for cancer is the patient's own breast cancer diagnosis, although she was diagnosed after the age of 50. So that alone is not something that would highly be concerning for a hereditary risk. However, she has a family history of both breast cancer in her mother and pancreatic cancer in her maternal uncle. So we see two affected relatives on the same side of the family, combining both breast and pancreatic cancer, which for me are all red flags to see, you know, to further assess this family for a potential hereditary risk. Next slide. So we utilize the NCCN guidelines, which are published on an annual basis out of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network. These are ever-changing and involving as new data and information is collected from our hereditary cancer families. So it can certainly be difficult to keep a bridge to these year to year, but that's what we hope to be there for, and particularly in tumor boards. We help to review these guidelines and all the cases that are presented to determine how eligible someone may be for referral to cancer genetics for an evaluation and discussion of genetic testing. And so, if you just hit next for me, please. In looking at this, this particular patient was diagnosed with breast cancer over the age of 50, and she has a close relative with breast cancer and a close relative with pancreatic cancer. So using these guidelines, we see that she does meet criteria for consideration of genetic testing. Next. And so historically, BRCA1 and BRCA2 are the genes that we see most often associated with hereditary breast cancer. But these genes cause other cancers like ovarian and pancreatic cancer. So for me, kind of top on my radar of assessment for this patient would be BRCA1 and 2. Although they are not the only genes that link breast and pancreatic cancer. The other genes that we might think about in this particular case are PALB2 and ATM. And so in the kind of world of genetic testing nowadays, we do what's called a multi-gene panel where we can test multiple genes for hereditary cancer risk. And I think that would be the best test suited for this patient. And she does meet NCCN guidelines. And so more than likely, she would also meet her insurance guidelines for genetic testing. And that test would help us determine, does she have a hereditary risk? Does she have future risk for other cancers that are higher than we would expect in the general population and our other family members at risk. That testing comes back in a couple of weeks and we can help facilitate that, disclose those results and help facilitate next steps as needed. I'll pass it along to Dr. Mastroni.

It comes back to surgery. Okay. So our breast surgery is certainly continuing to evolve as we develop new techniques to make sure that we are both curing the cancer and also providing patients with a good result and minimizing the morbidity or complications of our operations or symptoms associated with them. And we've moved from mastectomy to being able to offer breast conservation or lumpectomy to more patients and the Pictures in the bottom show the difference between axillary dissection, which was the standard of care when I was a medical student, to now sentinel lymph node biopsy, removing only one or two lymph nodes at each operation, as you see in the picture in the lower corner. Next slide. And so now we've moved into the area of oncoplastic breast surgery, which is providing the best possible operation for patients to achieve a good cosmetic and functional outcome, as well as ensuring that we are providing the best oncologic outcome, that we are contributing to the cure of a cancer. Oncoplastic surgery as often requires teamwork from a breast surgeon and a plastic surgeon working together to come up with the best operation for a patient, and also making sure that we understand what the patient's goals are. Next slide. This is Dr. Mastriani's slide.

Now I'll jump in. So oncoplastic breast surgery is not a cookie cutter operation. And as you can imagine, based on your tumor size and the ratio of that tumor size to the rest of the breast size, breasts come in all shapes and sizes in many different patients and women. So typically we're looking at a ratio of the tumor and the tissue that we need to remove in relation to the rest of the breast. simple slam dunks or smaller tumors in larger breasts. Patients will hardly notice the difference if we remove that lump and we may not necessarily have to do anything very complicated to yield you with a normal looking breast at the end of your operation. However, as you approach the 20 and 40 percent range where you're going to be removing a significant portion of the breast. Oftentimes, and the literature shows this too, it's important to consult with a plastic surgeon because there are options that don't involve more surgery or implants or anything that's going to cause more scars on your body besides that lumpectomy scar. Occasionally we can do things to match the other breast too. So this is our sort of basic guidelines where if you have less than 20% of breast tissue being needed to be removed, you oftentimes can close very simply and you're not going to have a very cosmetically noticeable difference. As you approach the 20 to 40% range, there are a variety of different techniques that we can use to essentially squish tissue from one area into the area that is now a hole where the cancer used to be. Once we go beyond that, then you need to think about volume replacement or removing tissue from somewhere else outside the breast to help fill in that volume and to make sure that you're in your own skin look normal. Next slide, please. And as you can imagine, there are nearly limitless possibilities. So this is one of the fun parts of my job, where I get to talk closely and work with Dr. Lynch, where we figure out exactly where that tumor is, and how can we best design an incision that's going to be cosmetically sensitive. It's not going to be right in the middle of your face every time you look at yourself. And that can easily be hidden in clothing. And also, how can we make this look nicer for you? Sometimes this often requires an operation on the other breast too to help it match. So these are just some examples of what we can do. Next.

So this patient had a cancer in the upper inner quadrant of the breast. And so we planned an operation to excise that to remove underlying tissue and to reshape both breasts in a breast lift type operation. Next slide. And so many studies have been done to demonstrate that this kind of approach to breast surgery is both safe from a surgical standpoint and provides a good oncologic outcome that we can ensure that we are also curing the cancer in the same way that we would be doing it with a simple lumpectomy. So two large trials have shown that they're both safe and effective. And next slide. This is kind of a busy slide, but if those two last columns, oncoplastic breast surgery and therapeutic mammoplasty, the type of operation that we just showed you, also have the best patient-reported outcomes, including sexual well-being, appearance, emotional well-being, and physical well-being. Next slide. So this was the outcome of the case for this patient where the final tumor was 1.8 centimeters in size. We achieved clear margins. We did a sentinel lymph node biopsy, a limited axillary surgery, and the lymph nodes were not involved. Next slide. We sent a test called an oncotype, and we'll move from here to the next slide and to Dr. Phan.

So hi. So as a medical oncologist, I typically will see patients such as this one who have small lymph node negative tumors that are hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, to discuss treatments that we can offer to reduce the risk of recurrence. long-term. And as a medical oncologist, I'm particularly interested at reducing the risk of distant recurrence. That means cancer outside of the breast and the lymph nodes, lungs, you know, liver to reduce or increase the chance that patients will survive long-term cancer-free. And so for this type of breast cancer, one tool that we have to assess whether a patient needs chemotherapy is called the oncotype. And we'll move to the next slide, and I might go back to this one. So historically, many patients with this profile were offered chemotherapy, but we now know that many patients, in fact, most patients with node negative hormone receptor positive breast cancer actually don't benefit from post-operative or what we call adjuvant chemotherapy, though there is a subset of patients that do benefit in reducing their risk by receiving chemotherapy. So our goal is to identify the patients who will benefit and offer them chemotherapy and then, you know, reassure the patients who won't benefit that chemotherapy is not necessary and the side effects that potentially could come thereof are, you know, we can avoid them by avoiding chemotherapy. So this Oncotype DX test is what we call 21-gene recurrence score. This is a test that was developed by researchers by looking at a whole array of genes that are involved in breast cancer biology and identifying 16 genes that are very strongly associated with breast cancer recurrence, as well as five reference genes. So when we send this test, this test is a test sent on the tumor tissue. It's sent out to a lab. And the levels of those 21 genes are assessed. And then using a mathematical model, a recurrence score that ranges from zero to 100 is resulted as in that report that you just saw on the previous slide. So this test is what we call both prognostic and predictive. It can allow us to estimate the chance that cancer comes back in nine to 10 years with endocrine therapy, which I'll talk about in the next slide alone. And then it can also predict, you know, how much can we lower that risk by adding on chemotherapy to that pill that I'll discuss. So when this test was developed, you know, it was shown when they looked at patients treated on previous clinical trials that there's a subset of patients with a high recurrence score who really do benefit from chemotherapy, whereas patients who have lower scores, you know, the benefit's less clear. So with this oncotype score result from zero to 100, we consider up to 10 to be low risk, 11 to 25 to be intermediate risk, and 26 and above to be high risk. And so this, you know, is validated in a clinical trial called Taylor X, in which patients who had low recurrence scores did not receive chemotherapy and did quite well long term, whereas those patients who had high recurrence scores did because we knew that already that these patients are at high risk of recurrence. And then patients with an intermediate score between 11 and 25 were randomized. a flip of a coin to receive chemotherapy and followed by a pill, endocrine therapy, or endocrine therapy alone. And the results of this study show that for patients with a recurrence score of 25 and below, these patients did not, in general, benefit from additional chemotherapy after surgery. And so, you know, I say here postmenopausal women, but really women who are over 50, like our patient here, with a recurrence score at or under 25, really, we don't think benefit from chemotherapy. And you can see that on the report on the previous slide, they give an estimate of recurrence risk at nine to 10 years as patients was 9%. and they estimated that really we can't lower it any further by giving chemotherapy. That was less than 1% benefit. For those patients, unlike our patient who are younger, under 50 years old, there might be some benefit from chemotherapy in the high intermediate range. And often we take into account other features such as the size of the tumor and the grade. But again, for this patient with a recurrence score of 23, I would not recommend adjuvant chemotherapy. So that brings us to a quick discussion about endocrine therapy. So certainly, though chemotherapy is not needed, adjuvant endocrine therapy will be a really important part of this patient's care. So by this, I mean a pill that's taken once a day for we say at least five years or five to 10 years, which yields a really significant reduction in the risk of recurrence by about half and death from breast cancer, and then has a secondary benefit of reducing the risk of a second breast cancer. So for postmenopausal women, just a really brief overview. A class of pills called aromatase inhibitors, really the preferred therapy to reduce breast cancer recurrence risk. Pills that many of you may have heard of in this class include anastrozole, letrozole, eczema stain. These pills reduce estrogen levels. And in general, these pills can be quite tolerable in many patients with no to few side effects. And side effects are often very manageable with various strategies. But it's important to know that they can carry some side effects. For these particular aromatase inhibitors, joint stiffness and pain may occur. as well as some hormonal like symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. We also look out for bone loss on vermicase inhibitors. This patient had osteoporosis. which is not in and of itself a reason not to offer an aromatase inhibitor, but we would want to make sure that we are working with her primary doctor or endocrinologist to make sure that we're reversing any other causes of osteoporosis, make sure that her vitamin D levels are optimized, and then also potentially offer an IV medication to enhance, you know, bone strength and reduce bone loss. The alternative endocrine therapy is called tamoxifen. This can be offered to either pre or postmenopausal women. But in studies comparing aromatase inhibitors and tamoxifen is slightly less effective in postmenopausal women. These pills can have similar hormonal-like symptoms and also carry a small but increased risk of side effects such as blood clots and uterine cancer. So really, this is a kind of personalized discussion with the oncologist and the patient to decide on endocrine therapy. But for this patient, I would potentially discuss with her an aromatase inhibitor. Then really briefly, in terms of how long do we treat patients for, you know, our standard is at least five years, though there are studies, many studies that are looking at or have looked at extending this treatment to seven to 10 years. And in general, it's an area of controversy. You know, these studies generally show that there's a increased reduction in the risk of recurrence by extending therapy. But this benefit might be more significant in patients who have higher risk disease. This includes patients with larger size or lymph node positive disease who we really might strongly feel to extend to 10 years. For this patient with a small node negative tumor, it's an individualized decision depending on how well the patient's tolerating treatment at five years. I will mention briefly there is a test called the breast cancer index that is also a gene expression assay similar in concept to the Oncotype DX. a score, which can sometimes allow or help for patients who are on the fence, predict, you know, the risk of recurrence in the years five to 10 after treatment, you know, treatment, and also predict benefit of extending treatment. And so this is something that is not right for every patient, but it's something that, you know, potentially might be right for this patient if she's on the fence and continuing endocrine therapy at year five.

It's really enabled what Dr. Lynch referred to earlier, which is an approach called breast conservation therapy. It's been really a big advance in terms of combination therapy between modern surgeries, chemotherapy, systemic therapies, and radiation therapies. That's been a huge advance in breast cancer care in recent years. As I'm showing here on the slide, we use radiation to reduce the risk of recurrence and to help cure cancer. But in addition, and very importantly for radiation treatment as well as all our treatments, we also want to reduce the risk of side effects from treatment. This is very important. In my earlier comment about understanding patient priority, It's a very important thing to understand the priorities and what a patient is hoping for out of treatment. This is very important to tailor treatment around the relative benefits and the relative toxicities of treatment. For radiation treatment, what we do typically is after surgery, after systemic therapies, we treat the breast with x-rays, and we use x-rays to clean up any possible remaining cancer cells. It may be just a few cells that no one can really see, but we use radiation to clean up those cells. And what you're seeing here is actually a a patient similar to the patient that Dr. Lynch presented with a left-sided breast cancer. What we're looking at here is a CT scan of the patient laying down on my radiation table, my treatment table. We're looking at a CT scan where the patient is laying down on their back, and we're looking from the feet up through to the head in kind of bread loaf slices. And in the front, at the top of this image are the patient's breasts, and on the back, the patient's spine, and in the red contours, the patient's heart, and these black areas to both sides of the heart are the lungs. just to orient you to what we're looking at. You can see that close to the breast on the left side where the heart is, the breast is actually very close to the lungs and the heart. These are very important things that we pay attention to when we're thinking about how to aim the radiation. and things that we worry about when we worry about the side effects of radiation. There's some things that we can do that are very simple conceptually. Of course, we need to make sure that we execute them correctly in order to reduce the side effects of radiation. This is one technique where very simply we ask the patient to take a deep breath when we treat them with radiation. You can see, that by taking a deep breath, your chest expands, and during the breath hold here on the right-hand side of the screen, you can see that, and I had arrows here, I apologize, I don't know where the arrows went, but you can see in the space between the breast, which is in pink, and the heart, which is in red, that that black area, the lung, expands out and puts more space between the heart and the lungs and the breast where I'm aiming the radiation. And so this pink line is actually an actual dose of radiation that I've delivered to a patient. And you can see that it very nicely avoids the lung, maybe just a little bit of catching the lung here and in the along the, where you can see a little bit of black area encompassed by the pink, and entirely avoids the heart. And so this is one technique that we can use to reduce the toxicities of radiation while still maintaining cure rates. Next slide. And then another technique that we use commonly to reduce side effects of radiation is to simply have the patient lay down on their stomachs instead of laying on their back. And you can see in this pink foam board here, which this simulated patient is laying on, is called a prone breast board. And there's an opening here where the breast will fall into that opening and away from the patient's body. And you can see on the, again, on the right side of the screen where I have my radiation doses on, again, this CT scan, that treating a patient supine really, while we're treating the breast well, really captures a lot of this black area, the lung. And we don't want that. So, and you can see that by simply repositioning the patient the breast falls away from the body in the lower panel away from the body and, and you can actually avoid entirely long exposure by simple techniques like this so. Next slide. So, I. Traditionally, a radiation therapy would be delivered by over six to seven weeks of daily radiation. Each treatment of radiation is only about 10 minutes, but Even so, with this reduction from six, seven weeks to four weeks, you know, every day when I talk to my patients I can still tell that four weeks is a lot of visits for them. And in recent, just the last few years there have been more of a data, more of a push, more clinical trial results, which support, in fact, perhaps even shorter treatments than that, potentially even as short as five treatments for radiation treatments. And I think the, the discussion here that I have with my patients is that probably the most standard treatment is the rather lengthy four weeks of daily treatment. However, in selected patients and if it's right for them. You know that. potentially shorter courses of treatment would be appropriate and safe for them to choose. I think the point here, as the slide alludes to, it's not a one-size-fit-all approach for radiation. A lot of it is really just with the surgical approaches and the chemotherapy, the medical oncology approaches. that it does depend a lot on the biology, you know, the discussion between all the folks on this panel, the medical oncologists, the surgeons, in order to come up with a tailored approach and most importantly, the patients. And this again goes back to what I was first saying, which is it is very important to understand what the patient hopes for, what they're looking for out of treatment, and to be able to help them meet what they need. That's my take on the radiation. I think in terms of all these different approaches, probably the four-week regimen is what I would recommend for this patient.

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent breast-conserving surgery with excision of the upper inner quadrant lesion, bilateral reshaping in a breast-lift type oncoplastic procedure, and sentinel lymph node biopsy; final pathology demonstrated a 1.8 cm tumor with clear margins and no nodal involvement. Multigene germline testing is indicated based on the family history and NCCN criteria. The Oncotype recurrence score of 23 does not support adjuvant chemotherapy in this postmenopausal, node-negative, hormone receptor-positive case. Adjuvant endocrine therapy is recommended, with discussion of an aromatase inhibitor, and adjuvant whole-breast radiation is recommended, with a four-week regimen favored for this patient.

And so we planned an operation to excise that to remove underlying tissue and to reshape both breasts in a breast lift type operation. [...] So this was the outcome of the case for this patient where the final tumor was 1.8 centimeters in size. We achieved clear margins. We did a sentinel lymph node biopsy, a limited axillary surgery, and the lymph nodes were not involved. [...] In looking at this, this particular patient was diagnosed with breast cancer over the age of 50, and she has a close relative with breast cancer and a close relative with pancreatic cancer. So using these guidelines, we see that she does meet criteria for consideration of genetic testing. [...] And I think that would be the best test suited for this patient. [...] But again, for this patient with a recurrence score of 23, I would not recommend adjuvant chemotherapy. [...] But for this patient, I would potentially discuss with her an aromatase inhibitor. [...] I think in terms of all these different approaches, probably the four-week regimen is what I would recommend for this patient.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Healthy 8-year-old boy.

[ chief complaint ]: Four months of nasal obstruction and headaches, with weight loss and poor oral intake.

[ diagnosis ]: Clival chordoma presenting as a large nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal mass with skull base, upper cervical spine, and intracranial extension.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mass showed chordoma. No dedifferentiated or poorly differentiated features were identified. Ki-67 was low.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI showed a very large tumor filling the nasopharynx, with extension to the bilateral parapharyngeal carotid arteries. There was erosion of the clivus, C1, and part of C2. The mass extended inferiorly to C2 and had significant intracranial extension posteriorly up to the dura overlying the medulla/brainstem. Imaging demonstrated tumor around the craniovertebral junction, including involvement of the atlanto-occipital region. Axial imaging showed persistent extension to the bilateral parapharyngeal carotid spaces and intracranial disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient was initially taken to the operating room for planned adenoidectomy; a large nasopharyngeal tumor was identified and biopsied.

[ other clinical data ]: The tumor was discovered during attempted adenoidectomy by community otolaryngology.

reference_discussion.text: All right, Tyler. Yeah, great discussion. So we'll move on to our third case. This is a healthy eight-year-old boy who had four months of nasal obstruction and headaches. He was losing weight, not eating well. And otolaryngologists in our community took him to the operating room to do an adenoidectomy. And when they looked back there, they saw a giant tumor. They took a biopsy and that showed a chordoma. There was no de-differentiation or poorly de-differentiated features with a low KI67. Next slide. So here's some of the imaging. This is a first MRI. As you can see, there's a very large tumor filling the nasopharynx. It's extending out to the bilateral parapharyngeal carotid arteries and extending back with erosion of the clivus in the C1 and part of C2. Here's it on sagittal, a very large tumor. You can pause it there for a second, Garrett. You can not only see the extension down to C2, but also the hypo, The area that's non-enhancing is extending back intracranially up to the dura of the medulla, to the brainstem. So keep going. Thank you. So a significant intracranial extension. And we'll just show an axial just to complete the picture, and then we'll do some bony anatomy too. You can see it's extending out to the bilateral parapharyngeal carotid arteries in addition to the significant intracranial extension. And there's some of that intracranial extension, large tumor. So let's move on to the next slide. So, Dr. Paracelda, when you see a patient with a very large clival chordoma that's both intracranial as well as an extending down to the spine, but also a significant portion in the sinuses, in this case, the nasopharynx and oropharynx, how do you think about a patient like this?

So I think we know that, you know, we have to look at the surgical treatment first. And, you know, the resection, the, you know, radicology of resection is very important. And so, you know, looking at like this patient may or any patient with like a large clival chordoma, we think about two things mainly, and especially when it goes into the spine. So surgical resectability, and if so, the approach, and number two, stability of the perineal cervical junction. So I think that's key as two main points for resection of these chordomas, so the clivus and, you know, low clivus and pericervical junction. And then, you know, the third part is, you know, how we are going to reconstruct that as well, our options for reconstruction. So I think those are like the key points of surgical treatment of gordomas. So in this case, we are faced with a large tumor that is going to, you know, I haven't looked at the images of the bone, but that is going to create awesome stability and has lateral extension as well.

Yeah, so continuing on with that part of the discussion, Dr. Thorpe, how would you think about approaching this type of tumor surgically? Would you go transnasal, transoral? Would you split the palate? Would you think you would need some type of far lateral craniotomy? How would you think about this?

Exactly like you're stating. So this is, this is, this is an incredibly challenging case that really requires a thoughtful multi likely multi portal approach in addition to stabilization right. I think there's a couple sticking points obviously the paraphernalia carotids, you need to make sure that you have a plan for being able to surgically manipulate manipulate those obviously the intracranial extension and then the degree to which you're going to have to chase it intracranially and then reconstruct right so as I'm thinking about the different pieces those are kind of the main aspects, but I agree. As soon as I saw the images, I was like, okay, there's a fair amount of this that I could assess endonasally, potentially with a combined transoral approach. I would try not to split the pallet, frankly, if I was able to, because there's a lot of reasons for that, especially since we're going to stabilize this child, you know, that's going to result in a lot of, you know, potential issues postoperatively with swallowing and the like, probably going to need a nasogastric tube, child's going to be intubated for a period of time, C. septivers, and all these things, right? And then a far lateral would be also a very reasonable thing to have in your sort of arm inventory for this. And so those are, those are kind of the first two things that that that came to mind, but certainly I would not, I would not limit myself with a singular approach on this, this is something that's going to require a thoughtful multimodal approach.
Go on to the next question, Garrett. So, actually maybe one more after that too. Dr. Sargi, when you're thinking about extremely large chordomas, how do you think about margins?

Well, there will be places where you can easily take margins and you can resect more if you need to, and those are the places that probably won't matter as much. So, I mean, you can do it just to make yourself feel good, but I think the areas that matter the most, you will never be able to assess the margins accurately. That's my opinion. I echo what Dr. Thorpe said in terms of not splitting the palate, absolutely not splitting the palate on an eight-year-old for speech, for swallowing, for multiple other reasons. And another comment I would add is that, you know, it's okay to stage this procedure, not to look for one surgical approach that's going to give you access to all those different pieces of the tumor, because I don't think of any single approach that would give you adequate enough access to all of those, starting with the easy part maybe the endonasal approach gives you a feel of how this cordoma is, is it dissecting easily is it, you know, is it separating from the structures or is it going to be a nightmare, that would be, you know, one way, one way to go. as a first approach but this is a very, very challenging case. In addition to stabilizing the spine which is, I think something you mentioned, airway becomes an issue in those giant chordomas and sometimes prophylactic tracheostomy is needed post-operatively just to secure the airway. You know, there could be some central depression of the respiratory mechanisms or needing to ventilate or suction the patient's post-op for multiple reasons. So for giant chordomas, sometimes I recommend upfront tracheostomy. I'd rather have it with a fused neck than have a patient with an airway disaster post-op and potentially dying from inability to secure a transoral airway.

Great. Thank you for that. Dr. Fernandez-Miranda, just continuing on with that part of the discussion. If a tumor like this extends intracranial and you can resect it off of the dura and there's no CSF leak, would you resect the dura just to get a negative margin?

You know, as a general principle, chordomas may sometimes not invade the dura. They always invade the interdural space. So often you can actually peel off the periosteal dura and leave a thin inner meningial dura. That is an option in some tumors. Others do penetrate through both layers of dura and then I chase it, of course.
Yeah.
Can you show the T2 again? Sure.
It's the last one.
It is a real difficult case. You know, these lower clavicle domas are, are the, you know, the worst.

So it looks like it extends pretty far intracranially on the left, kind of back by this and back to the high cervical spine. But actually intraoperatively, we were able to take that all out without a leak.

The problem is the tumor that is around the cranocervical junction, right, C1, C2. And yeah, I would consider for this one, say, an anterolateral transcendental approach, as combined with the nasal, starting probably with the neck, actually, to preserve the verte and dissect the vertebrate that is really displaced by tumor, especially on that left side.

Yeah. Yeah, it was definitely a challenging case we go back to the questions for a second. So, um, So just for the sake of the discussion, so we did a two-stage. The first day was an endonasal and transoral combined approach to take out all the tumor extracranially and dissect it all off the carotids. And we took everything back to the clivus and the C-spine without dealing with any of the tumor past the bone. And on the second day, we did the additional bony work and took out all of the tumor that was intracranial and by the cervical spine. So moving on to the next question, Dr. Paracelda, how do you think about stabilization of the spine in patients like this? How do you think about it?

Yeah, so there's quite a lot of debate about the timing. So certainly like what do you do first? Do you fuse first and then you resect and then you have already like the patient already fused or do you do it the other way around. And then in the meantime, just stabilize the neck of the patient. So there's, um, so I would, uh, potential, I would do probably in this case, just, uh, the stabilization first, just to make sure that, uh, everything is, uh, but you know, of course, like I would think about even doing that trick because of the reason that was exposed earlier, uh, just to make sure that we secure the airway. So I think it's, uh, yeah. So about, occiput to C2 versus C1 to C2. I think this tumor involves also the allantooccipital joints, if I'm not mistaken. So in this case, I think that would make that articulation completely unstable. So I think it has to be fused to the occiput, in my opinion.
Have you noticed that patients have substantially more swallowing and swallowing and airway issues if you include the oxyput in the fusion?

So I haven't, I haven't experienced more or less with that, but I do think that, you know, that I wouldn't do the fusion myself. I would talk to my spine colleagues for that, but, but I do think that it's, probably important in this case for that reason.
Dr. Fernandez-Miranda, any additional thoughts about spinal fusion?
Yeah, I'm not a spinal surgeon myself, but what I do know from this case is that they do go to C4, C5. You go occipital to at least C4 or C5, not C2. C2 is too short.

Matt, can I just make one comment? More so in the adult population, you know, when you've got patients with, it's really important to look at the spine imaging. If you have someone with osteophytic disease, that's really had a lot of compensatory mechanisms with, you know, with, you know, dipping their chin or moving their head for swallowing, those patients are an absolute setup for a G-tube afterwards. And so some of those folks, I talked to them pretty early about that and talking about going back later on, you know, for, you know, removal of their osteophytes and just kind of that discussion. So, Again, maybe not, you know, critical for the, for the pediatric population but certainly something to think about as you're counseling the patients.
Great. Thank you for that. Brian, we go to the next question. Dr. Hollis can you talk to us a little bit about protons versus photons, especially in the setting of someone who's had a fusion.

Yes, no, it's a good question. So for a lot of the more superior skull-based chordomas, we often will use protons because just in that area, anterior to the brainstem, you're able to get a better looking plan. The ones that are lower down, often the photon plans where we use IMRT and kind of beam angles from around a 360 can look quite good. And the problem with fusion and protons is that protons are very sensitive to the density that they go through. So when you hit metal, it's hard to necessarily map that out in our computer algorithms. And then there is a bit of a shadowing effect that has shown that overall that patients with hardware when treated with protons for spinal cordomas and chondrosarcomas have worse local control. So that's what the issue is. We've done a few cases where we use carbon fiber, if we can kind of swing that and get the hospital to look at that expense and kind of think about it ahead of time. In the spine, we sometimes, MGH has really published on sort of preoperative radiation. then surgery and then adding more. But in the skull base, I think that's a bit of a harder sell in terms of the difficulty of all these surgeries. So I think overall, some of these patients have gotten a combined of photons and protons. But you really have to look at sort of how good you are at measuring the dose with that hardware there and being able to count for it.

Great, thanks. And how about thinking about the timing, especially if someone's going to be getting fused perioperatively? Normally, you know, for other types of head and neck cancers, we like to radiate people within four to six weeks. When do you do it for these chordomas if someone who's been fused?

Yeah, I will wait three to six months sometimes, I think, for neurologic recovery and just recovery in general. There's been very few chordomas that I've found have really taken off, although I would say I think the ones that I can think of are pediatric. I don't know if that was just bad luck in those cases. But in general, unlike other head and neck cancers, we tend to let these patients recover from their very large surgeries before starting.

Great. Let's move on to the next and we'll just answer any questions at the end. So we did a two-stage procedure. Like I mentioned before, we also used intraoperative MRI. We did everything endoscopic endonasal and endoscopic transoral. We did not split the palate. We just kind of held it out of the way with a red rubber catheter. We put the patient in a halo after the second day, which is when the predominant bony work was done by the spine. Then the patient underwent a fusion shortly thereafter and got adjuvant photon radiation, like Dr. Hollis was saying, and he's doing great and is currently NED. Maybe just a couple of questions at the end here to finish up. kind of out to anybody. Does anyone use IMRI in this context or any context? Do they find it to be a useful technology? Yeah.

You know, we have one that we are starting to use. I haven't used it yet for this pathology, but I think it's a good indication for it. These very large chordomas, the same as the very large Jayana venomas, you know, these are good indications.

And then lastly, does anybody commonly stage endoscopic procedures with lateral procedures or even just two endoscopic procedures on the same patient? How do you kind of do those with your teams? How do you kind of set all that up? And in what context?

Yeah, those sometimes tend to be very long and very painful procedures and I think, you know, you get tired of drilling and you, you know, It probably is in the best interest of the patient to, you know, stage and give the patient to properly done surgeries then one extremely long surgery where when you leave disease behind that's my, my perspective, you know on on on many of those cases. halfway through the case or at the end of the case, I swear to myself that this is the last time I get involved in a case like this, and I see myself doing this again. And I'm sure I'm not the only one in that situation. So those tend to be very long and very painful cases. And I think for especially an eight-year-old child, you know, giving the patient the best possible surgical outcome sometimes requires staging the procedure.

That's a good point. I'll just mention one thing, Matt. This is a bit akin to pediatric JNAs. An eight-year-old child, you really got to think about blood loss as well. And obviously, you can transfuse, but for very large JNAs with excessive blood loss, it's always prudent to stop, give them a day or two to recover, get some transfusion, get some more blood volume, go back again, because some chordomas can be extremely light.

Yeah. For sure. And yeah, just for completeness for the end, we used fascia and then fat, and then a nasal septal flap to reconstruct, put in a lumbar drain. The patient did great. And yeah, we were very pleased. So it looks like we're coming up on an hour. I just wanted to thank everyone for attending tonight, and also thank all of our panelists, and also Dr. Joby for helping moderate with me. We really, really appreciate the support of all three societies in putting this collaboration together, and we look forward to doing more in the future. So thank you all so very much.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent epistaxis. At the current recurrence, the only symptom was mild bloody nose. He had no orbital symptoms, vision was intact, and extraocular movements were intact.

[ diagnosis ]: SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma. Initial diagnosis was biopsy proven. A first local recurrence in the right ethmoid region was biopsy proven and treated. A later recurrence was also biopsy proven and showed the same tumor type. Disease recurred locally without evidence of systemic metastatic disease at the times described.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy confirmed SMARCB1-deficient sinus carcinoma. Tissue specimens obtained during bilateral sinus surgery performed for post-radiation sinusitis were negative for tumor. Biopsy of a right-sided ethmoid mass confirmed recurrent disease. After two cycles of additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection yielded no tumor in the specimen; frozen sections and all margins were negative. A subsequent later lesion was again biopsy proven recurrent disease of the same histologic type.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PET/CT performed one year after bilateral sinus surgery showed no evidence of disease.  
- Surveillance MRI obtained three months later demonstrated a right-sided ethmoid mass.  
- At the first recurrence, disease was described as localized, in the frontal ethmoid region/medial orbit, within the prior radiation field.  
- Repeat imaging after two cycles of additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed interval increase in tumor size in the vertical dimension inferiorly.  
- Postoperative PET imaging performed soon after that resection showed no additional disease.  
- Approximately one year later, imaging demonstrated a new recurrence in a slightly more anterior location, with greater orbital involvement than previously described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: SMARCB1 deficiency was identified. No additional molecular profiling results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment consisted of induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation, with a complete response.  
- Nine months after completion of treatment, bilateral sinus surgery was performed for post-radiation sinusitis; pathology was negative for tumor.  
- At the first local recurrence, the patient received additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy for two cycles.  
- Repeat imaging after these two cycles showed progression, with increased inferior vertical extent of the mass.  
- Surgical resection was then performed. Pathology from the resection specimen showed no residual tumor; frozen sections and margins were negative.  
- Approximately one year later, a further biopsy-proven local recurrence developed.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven second local recurrence of SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, more anterior than the prior recurrence and with greater orbital involvement, within a previously irradiated field and without documented systemic disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The recurrent disease occurred less than two years from primary treatment.  
- The patient had previously received a full course of radiation to the local site.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, well, the basic facts about doing a history and physical examination and seeing what the orbit is doing, and then often we get a pathology review, so assuming that it is what it is, and then review what imaging we have, and then decide on other imaging, so obviously an MRI would be appropriate here, and then whatever type of metastatic workup that you would normally do. In this case, I think a PET CT would be very worthwhile to look at for metastatic disease. And then putting that all together then would be discussed in a multidisciplinary tumor board.

Great. And then knowing that it is now a SMARCB1 deficient sinus carcinoma where you have the biopsy proven diagnosis, what is, how would you recommend treatment if there is no metastatic disease in this patient?

Well, we would normally start with discussions around neoadjuvant type treatment and then look at the response and then go on to consider chemoradiation and look at the response there and then versus surgery with that. So we have to look at a whole host of factors and patient preference.

Wonderful. Thank you so much for sharing that. It's very, very comprehensive and well said. So we did cover this in the Icarcine nasal tumors document where we talk a little bit about management options for different tumors based on histopathology. So in this case, as you mentioned earlier, Dr. Widerich, we do look at neoadjuvant chemotherapy response as a guide for treatment based off of the MD Anderson paper, And it was provided really strong evidence for us to be able to delineate out responses and subsequent treatment methods. So then this patient underwent initial treatment with induction chemotherapy followed by chemo radiation and he had a complete response. Nine months after his treatment, he continued to have really bothersome quality of life issues. So he underwent a bilateral sinus surgery for post-radiation sinusitis. Tissue specimens sent during the sinus surgery were all negative for tumor. He did not have any signs of that. One year after his sinus surgery, his PET CT demonstrated no evidence of any disease. So he was still disease-free. And then three months later, in surveillance MRI, he developed a right-sided ethmoid mass, and the biopsy confirms recurrent disease. Dr. Gelsiler, what are your thoughts about this phenomenon at this point?

Yeah, that's a rapid recurrence, unfortunately. So we're looking at basically less than two years from primary treatment. Yes. Which isn't surprising. I would want to completely restate this patient with another PET scan just to make sure it didn't pop up with any regional or distant metastatic disease. Um, and then, you know, assuming that he was able to get full dose radiation to the local site, he's within two years. Um, I would want to know more about how that orbit's doing. Um, Is he having any double vision? And then, you know, it's hard to tell from this single slice if, you know, how, what that dura too is exactly doing. I would kind of want to look more closely also at a CT scan, just to kind of get a better sense. And if I felt like there was dural involvement, but general principle would be, I would send this tumor off for genetic analysis to see if there was any systemic therapy. But I would likely offer this patient surgery, assuming that there's no T2 signal change in the brain. And then regarding the orbit, I'd have a pretty low threshold to exonerate a patient like this, although it almost looks like on this slice that you could maybe try to preserve it. But I would go into the surgery telling the patient that if we couldn't clear that orbital margin, we would have to take it.

Very well said, and definitely a little additional information is he did have no evidence of other systemic disease, just localized. A couple of questions in, since you brought up some of the treatment algorithms and possibilities for this patient. Dr. Liao, would you consider re-irradiation if the patient had a full course of radiation in this case?

Yeah, that's a good question. I think this soon from his prior treatment, I would be reluctant. We're pretty selective about re-radiation in general, you know, in this region. This looks to be kind of within field recurrence, you know, along this frontal ethmoid region and medial orbit. So it would have been, I think, within his prior field and received full dose. I don't see relationship to the, you know, orbital apex there, but the frontal lobe there would have received full dose and would have had 60 gray. I think if this is resectable disease, and that's an option, I think that would be preferred versus systemic therapy. But tough case, I definitely have seen cases of local infield relapse for this entity.

Appreciate it. And also to Dr. Gelsinger, back to your question. He actually had no orbital symptoms at all. Yeah. Intact vision, extraocular movements intact. The only symptom he had was a little bit of bloody nose. So of course these are very challenging. Repeating chemotherapy, Dr. Price, what is your thought on about this regarding, you know, he just had quite a few doses and he has this local recurrence.

So I would definitely consider that as an option. I would look to see, you know, what his response was to the induction chemotherapy by itself to see if he did have chemotherapy sensitive disease at that time. This is a relatively fast recurrence, but it still would have been quite a while since his last chemotherapy dose. So I wouldn't take that off the table. We don't have a, you know, you know, huge list of effective chemotherapies for this disease. So, you know, I wouldn't want to throw something out too early. So I would definitely, you know, look back at his original regimen if he'd had a good response to reduction chemotherapy, you know, offer that as an option to retreat. Agree completely with getting, you know, molecular testing to see is there something targetable because even if, you know, best case scenario, he'd responded to that initial therapy, which was probably a platinum-based regimen and you retreat, you know, that still is only going to buy you a certain amount of time. You know, you can't continue somebody on platinum doublet chemotherapy indefinitely, so you kind of have to start in parallel looking for other options, you know, that you might be able to use, you know, as kind of a maintenance therapy if you're successful at debulking it initially, or just to have in the future, certainly if this patient were to go to surgery and then be followed afterwards, you might put those in your back pocket immediately. You know, in my experience with these cancers, they're often not as chemotherapy sensitive as some of the other sinonasal cancers that we see. So I think it's a little bit tricky. And so looking at kind of what actually happened in vivo with somebody with chemotherapy response can be helpful.

Thank you for sharing that. Yeah, his initial response to the chemotherapy was pretty dramatic. So he actually did fortunately have a good response to the neoadjuvant treatment. So we're also brought up a little bit when touched upon it by Dr. Geldseiler, management considerations for the orbit. Dr. Levine, any additional commentary on just what you would do with the orbit in this case, knowing that there's no symptoms related to it?

Yeah, I mean, obviously it's much harder when there's no symptoms. I think that some of that is a discussion with the patient themselves and kind of talking to them about their prognosis now that they've had a recurrence. One thing that we have done previously is to take periorbita and take orbital fat and then try to kind of recover that area so that we're still taking a margin on it. It's not always the best margin, but we've had some success with that. And I do think that that would be something I would talk to them about as an option, especially since that could preserve a lot of the function and still give you a little bit more cushion. But I do think that that is a really tough discussion with a patient, especially when they have really good function.

Great points. and definitely not a lot of consensus in that, as you'll see in the ICAR document. Dr. Gardner, if we resected the skull base regarding reconstruction, especially with the history of recent radiation, what are some considerations and any changes in the strategy for you?

Sure. I think this appears to have pretty clear dural involvement. And even if you're unsure, I think if you're doing surgery for this, you're trying to get margin on it. And that would mean an anterior craniofacial resection. In this setting, a vascularized reconstruction, which usually would involve pericranial flap, but the absence of any nasal tissues and also the aggressiveness of the tumor, we would probably do a pericranial flap. I like to take out just the frontal sinus itself, the anterior table, the frontal sinus, so it's not perhaps a true craniotomy, but a transfrontal sinus approach. take out the anterior sable, remove the posterior table so you cranialize it and use a pericranial flap with temporalis fascia as your dural substitute and suture in as much as you can the temporalis fascia and lay the extra durally tunneled pericranial flap on top of that. And that creates a very nice barrier. And at least you have a two layer, one of which is vascularized reconstruction. And that's really quite a good option in this setting.

Yeah, these are challenging reconstructions because of the radiation as well. And then role of immunotherapy, and we briefly touched on this. Dr. Price, can you expand a little bit more on kind of your experience with immunotherapy in patients with these problems?

So definitely a tough question. I don't think we have a lot of really good data. I think in the face of a bad tumor, especially a recurrent one, you know, we'll often throw a lot of things at it. And so, you know, thinking about chemo immunotherapy, you know, is reasonable, but, you know, it would be better or nice to see if there are some markers of immunotherapy response, you know, if you were doing some additional sequencing or testing, if you saw, you know, higher mutation burden, or had other surrogate markers. PD-L1 can be done, although it's an imperfect predictor of response. Again, I haven't seen a lot of great responses with immunotherapy as single agents in these tumors. So I tend to incorporate it with chemotherapy if there's a reason to do that. That's not to say still wouldn't do it, especially if they had a marker that would suggest benefit. But I, you know, I haven't seen a lot of sort of really durable, good responses like we'll see, you know, a little bit more frequently in some of the squamous cell cancers. Great.

So he underwent, we talked about his case at Tumor Board again. He actually underwent additional courses of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. He went through two cycles and had a repeat scan. That was his new repeat scan. It looks like the tumor grew a little bit more in the vertical dimension inferiorly. So the thought was, okay, well, he's not responding. He's progressing through something that he responded to earlier. So to surgery we go. I took him to surgery, I sent frozens, there's no tumor in the specimen anywhere, all margins were negative, and then he had a PET done relatively soon afterwards, which also showed no additional disease anywhere. that's what it looked like post-op. Very limited resection really because there was no tumor in the specimen, nothing along the lamina, nothing along the skull base. So Dr. London, have you seen this type of phenomenon before and what are your thoughts about it?

That's actually quite surprising. So he previously biopsy positive when you said after three months of that PET-CT, that was biopsied in clinic, it was positive, and then got two more rounds of chemo? Yes. Interesting. I don't know that I've seen that with chemo, maybe with some patients with immunotherapy, but not necessarily for SMART-B1 deficient carcinoma. Very surprising.

Yeah, this was a huge surprise to me. I actually asked a couple of colleagues around and some people have seen it before just because I think it worked so well the first time and I guess it did work really well this time. It's just that the mass itself did not fully regress at this point. So I thought that was just really interesting. And I think we're gonna probably see it more and more as we adopt this treatment strategy for different tumors.
How long ago was that?

That was a year ago, and then I have the next part of the story. So he then developed this about a year afterwards, being completely free of disease, but this is different appearing and in a different location or close, but it's actually a little more anterior. Okay. So this was interesting as well. So actually, Dr. Geltzer, I listened to you, brought it up. What do you think, options at this point?

I mean, it's the same thing I said. I would restage him again. I mean, this disease has a propensity to have distant metastatic failure. So I would worry that's going to happen at some point. This looks like, at least in the left-sided image, that it's even more in his orbit. Again, I would ask him about symptoms related to that. And I mean, it's, it almost looks more unilateral than it did last time. You know, this, if I was going to, I would definitely offer upfront surgery. Now that he's kind of failed this treatment strategy twice, you certainly could do it again, give him another more induction and do it again. But I mean, this thing keeps on recurring and now the interval is actually earlier. And I would, I wouldn't try to preserve the orbit with that scan. I would do. an orbital exoneration with neurosurgery and we could take out that adjacent dura directly through the orbit and then reconstruct it with a free flap.
Yeah. So, you know, the, it's interesting to say that he again had no symptoms except for nose bleeding, that's really what it turned out to be.
You biopsy that, that was biopsy proven recurrence.

Yeah, same tumor type as well. So this patient is very much against highly aggressive surgery, of course, so we had the discussion. He ended up getting, he ended up wanting to go with the option of getting treated again with a similar regimen, although he's now also on immunotherapy. He's about six months out again, without any disease again, and also no metastasis. So the saga continues, but I felt this case was not your typical scenario for an undifferentiated carcinoma and felt like it was a worthwhile discussion. I learned so much from everybody. So appreciate all of your thoughts. I think the next case is going to be Dr. Chobi. So Dr. Chobi, go ahead and take it away.

reference_conclusion: For localized recurrent SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, repeat staging with PET/CT was recommended to exclude regional or distant metastatic disease, with additional assessment of orbital and possible dural involvement and molecular/genetic analysis to identify potential systemic therapy options. If the recurrence remained resectable and confined locally, surgical salvage was favored over re-irradiation or systemic therapy; given repeated recurrence after prior induction chemotherapy, upfront surgery was advised, with low threshold for orbital exenteration if orbital margins could not be cleared and consideration of craniofacial resection with dural resection/reconstruction when indicated. Re-treatment with the prior chemotherapy regimen was considered a possible option because of the prior dramatic response, with immunotherapy viewed primarily in combination with chemotherapy rather than as a single agent.
reference_conclusion_quote: I would want to completely restate this patient with another PET scan just to make sure it didn't pop up with any regional or distant metastatic disease. [...] general principle would be, I would send this tumor off for genetic analysis to see if there was any systemic therapy. But I would likely offer this patient surgery, assuming that there's no T2 signal change in the brain. And then regarding the orbit, I'd have a pretty low threshold to exonerate a patient like this [...] if we couldn't clear that orbital margin, we would have to take it. [...] I think if this is resectable disease, and that's an option, I think that would be preferred versus systemic therapy. [...] I would definitely, you know, look back at his original regimen if he'd had a good response to reduction chemotherapy, you know, offer that as an option to retreat. Agree completely with getting, you know, molecular testing to see is there something targetable [...] I haven't seen a lot of great responses with immunotherapy as single agents in these tumors. So I tend to incorporate it with chemotherapy if there's a reason to do that. [...] I would definitely offer upfront surgery. Now that he's kind of failed this treatment strategy twice [...] I wouldn't try to preserve the orbit with that scan. I would do an orbital exoneration with neurosurgery and we could take out that adjacent dura directly through the orbit and then reconstruct it with a free flap.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male.

[ chief complaint ]: Rising PSA after prior definitive local therapy for prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with oligometastatic/low-volume metastatic disease involving a single hilar thoracic lymph node after prior prostatectomy and salvage radiation.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration obtained by endobronchial biopsy of the hilar lesion showed metastatic prostate cancer.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET demonstrated a single PSMA-avid focus near the hilum of the lung, consistent with a central thoracic/hilar lymph node. No other sites of disease were described on that scan.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient previously underwent prostatectomy at an outside facility. Postoperatively, PSA did not become undetectable. He subsequently received salvage radiation. PSA continued to rise after salvage radiation.

[ current disease status ]: Oligometastatic recurrent/metastatic prostate cancer after prior prostatectomy and salvage radiation, with biopsy-confirmed solitary hilar nodal metastatic involvement.

[ other clinical data ]: Biochemical recurrence was documented by persistently detectable PSA after prostatectomy followed by continued PSA rise after salvage radiation.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you very much for having me and it's great to be here with Drs. VanderWil and Sajdev. We work together frequently and seamlessly and I think that's been a wonderful part of being at Northwestern. I'll talk about a couple cases that often will require a multidisciplinary approach. We had one gentleman recently, he had had a prostatectomy at an outside facility. He had then had radiation in the salvage setting when his PSA did not go to undetectable. And then his PSA continued to rise and he had come to see me after treatment asking what to do. We got a PET PSMA scan, which is a type of imaging that is more specific and sensitive for prostate cancer. And it showed only one hotspot near the hilum of the lung. So a lymph node kind of near the central portion of the chest and lung. A couple of quick approaches before he even got to multidisciplinary oncology clinic, I reached out to some of my colleagues, one of Dr. Vanderbilt's colleagues, Dr. Fenton, and asked her like, which way did she go about doing these biopsies of these things to figure out what they are? And she recommended an interventional pulmonologist who could do an endobronchial biopsy and get a little bit of a cellular sample of this through an FNA. That came back showing that it indeed was prostate cancer. So this is a guy with oligometastatic or low-volume metastatic prostate cancer. who has had complete treatment to his prostate and pelvis, and the question is what to do. And so, that's the kind of case that I often will bring to the multicellular oncology tumor board to ask opinions about machine of radiation alone, radiation and hormonal therapy, radiation and a combination of hormonal therapy with antigen deprivation and an antigen receptor signaling inhibitor, what should the duration be, and What are the different clinical trials that are open for this patient? And this is a patient that's going on to be managed by Dr. VanderWaal and Dr. Sajdev with both hormonal therapy and radiation. This patient, although somewhat straightforward, it really galvanizes and sort of puts us all on the same page about their care. And they're allowed to then go through like an accelerated approach to those findings. And there's lots of times where, again, the literature is unclear. And having the opinions of not just David and Sean, but often dozens of us on the conference is very helpful. The other minor point I'll make, and it was already sort of suggested, is how do we deal with these multidisciplinary tumor boards? You know, how do we actually make this into a practical solution for folks? And there's lots of different models of tumor boards that have been made. Some of them have all the providers seeing the same patient the same day, including ancillary providers, etc. The problem is that we have an increasing population, all of which needs expert care. There's uncertainty about decisions, and we want to make sure that everyone has access to different clinical trials. I think that our approach, and I think Dr. VanderWaal mentioned this, that maybe it was helped by COVID, our approach by saying, let's have the patients come in wherever they come in, whether it's through urology, medical oncology, or radiation oncology. And if their case is complicated or maybe requires multiple sets of eyes, then elevate them to our tumor board discussion where we can have all of us together on a conference, go through these cases quickly, maybe present as many as 10 difficult cases, have review by radiology and pathology if needed at that conference, and then move forward from there. And I think that this approach, which maybe was not born out of COVID, but became much more kind of operationalized during this time, I really think it is the winner to serve a growing population of aging Americans that are unfortunately going to have not only prostate cancer, but other cancers as they're controlling their heart disease and other things more effectively. So maybe a long-winded answer, but I wanted to give my two cents on how happy I've been with this system for other hospital systems that are thinking about how they want to operationalize their tumor board.

Yeah, and I'll chime in that we seem to be having a growing number of these cases where we're operating a little bit in a gray area of what to do. I think often it's patients with kind of recurrent prostate cancer. There have been some major disruptions in the fields. We've been blessed by having these PSMA PET scans become more widely available. which is great because they're much more sensitive than the older scans, but all of our ways of establishing what to do in response to the imaging comes from the older scans. And then even though the new scans are very sensitive, we're not exactly sure what the best way to response them with different therapies. And at the same time, we've had a lot of data suggesting that if you're more aggressive earlier on treating cancers that have better outcomes, but we're not really sure. had that data and the new PET scans around long enough to know for a lot of these patients who are kind of newly diagnosed a little bit of metastatic disease but a relatively low burden or patients who are newly recurrent after surgery It's kind of a gray area right now and really sort of the intersection of all of our specialties, what's the best approach to take. So often we have clinical trials available and we have a couple clinical trials in these spaces kind of depending on what the exact clinical scenario is. So often it's a discussion about those trials or the patient might not be interested in the trial or maybe they don't really quite fit the criteria for the trial. And then it's a discussion of, okay, we're moving ahead with standard of care, what do we do? And it really is helpful to have everybody's input often before we see the patient, again after the patient, and then again at our tumor board meeting, reaching a consensus about how we move forward.

Also add a few comments here to what was well said by both Dr. Ross and Dr. VanderWaal. When we look from a high-level view of prostate cancer, we see that we are dealing with a malignancy where we're finding better and better ways to treat different stages of prostate cancer. And not only are we doing that, we're actually realizing that patients are doing better and better. We're seeing improved clinical outcomes. And I believe a lot of that arises from teamwork. If we go back historically, as I often explain to patients, modern cancer care is a three-headed beast of different cancer doctors that bring individual expertise, their own individual expertise, to the table. A surgical oncologist like Dr. Ross has a lot of expertise, a lot of extensive training in being able to remove some cancer from a certain location in the body. Myself, as a radiation oncologist, I can harness the power of radiation and ionizing energy to, again, go after one or a few spots in the body. And if it's anything more extensive than that, then historically we would always think of a skilled medical oncologist like Dr. VanderWaal, who is in charge and oversees any treatment that goes in through the mouth or through an IV. If we go back historically, we perhaps operated in a very siloed manner. If a patient needs surgery, they're going to Dr. Ross after he does a biopsy. If they have a biochemical recurrence, by which I simply mean that the PSA is rising after surgery, or maybe they got some localized radiation to a certain region of the body, and if it becomes more extensive than that, then we have the patient see Dr. VanderWaal for expertise on how to manage a systemic burden of disease. But a lot of the newer data And in fact, we just had a national meeting this past week, and all three of us were in attendance. A lot of the newer data continue to show that with more improvement in research, more improvement in our understanding of how we can harness our individual expertise and specialties, the best outcomes emerge from when we all work together. So going back to the case that Dr. Ross presented just a few minutes ago, a patient who initially had surgery that had recurrence after surgery, got radiation, but not radiation by itself, radiation with modern systemic agents, and now has a different area of disease which was picked up with very modern molecular imaging. And here again, while I can be of use in this kind of a scenario where I can focally go after one area of new disease, but not just by myself, also utilizing the expertise and opinion of Dr. VanderWaal to add something on like hormonal therapy or androgen deprivation therapy at a newer modern agent, which would be an androgen receptor signaling inhibitor. So we find, to the benefit of our patients, that as we continue to work together, as we continue to bring all of our modalities onto the table, oftentimes increasingly in close coordination and at once, we find that patients are doing better and better.

reference_conclusion: For oligometastatic, low-volume metastatic prostate cancer identified after prior prostatectomy and salvage radiation, management will proceed with combined hormonal therapy and radiation. The case was reviewed in multidisciplinary tumor board to align treatment selection and expedite coordinated care.
reference_conclusion_quote: And this is a patient that's going on to be managed by Dr. VanderWaal and Dr. Sajdev with both hormonal therapy and radiation. [...] So this is a guy with oligometastatic or low-volume metastatic prostate cancer. who has had complete treatment to his prostate and pelvis

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Demographic data were not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Discomfort/pain associated with hepatomegaly from liver metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Intermediate-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor arising in the head of the pancreas, with metastatic disease to the liver and cervical lymph nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: Tumor grade was described as intermediate grade. No additional histopathologic details were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: CT abdomen demonstrated a mass in the head of the pancreas abutting the superior mesenteric vein. CT also demonstrated extensive hepatic metastatic disease, including a large lesion occupying most of the right hepatic lobe and an additional large lesion posterior to it; coronal imaging showed a large mass in the right lobe of the liver and another lesion in the left lobe. The hepatic lesions were described as relatively hypoenhancing/darker in appearance compared with more typical enhancing lesions. Octreotide scan demonstrated uptake in the liver and an additional focus in the neck consistent with metastatic spread to cervical lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No patient-specific laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior cancer-directed treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with liver-predominant disease and extrahepatic spread to cervical lymph nodes. The patient was symptomatic from enlarged liver/hepatic capsular stretch.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were provided.
