<image> Abdominal CT images highlighting a pancreatic head mass and multiple liver lesions in a patient with right upper quadrant pain.
<image> CT abdomen images highlighting a pancreatic head mass and multiple liver lesions for discussion of disease extent.
<image> Slide comparing coronal abdominal CT findings with an octreotide scan, highlighting abdominal disease extent and a neck lymph node focus.

reference_discussion.text: So I hope you can see this little arrow moving here. So again, this is another CT cross-section of the abdomen at pretty much the same level as the last one. Again, kidneys back here, spine back here. And the red arrow is indicating this mass that's, again, in the head of the pancreas. And this is the superior mesenteric vein here. It's coming right up against the superior mesenteric vein. So that's its local extent. But in this case, that isn't as critical because we can see when we look at the liver, which is this organ right here, normally the entire liver should look the way it does back here, pretty uniform, bright appearance. But I think it's pretty obvious that there are these big, dark areas within the liver that represent metastatic disease. So this is a pretty large lesion that's occupying most of the right portion of the liver, and then there's another one right behind it. So these are quite large liver metastases, which makes the question of whether the tumor doesn't involve the vessels or does involve the vessels not nearly as much of an issue.

And you'll notice that, as opposed to the pictures I showed earlier, where these tend to be bright white, this is actually darker, which might go along then with a less well-differentiated. The better the tumor behaves like neuroendocrine, the more likely they are to be the enhancing type. So, it's another clue that maybe this might be a more aggressive tumor than what we otherwise want to deal with.

And in addition to the CT scan, this patient also had an octreotide scan. This CT scan is taken at a different plane. This shows in the coronal plane the extent of this big mass in the right lobe of the liver. Then there's another one here in the left. And in addition, on this octreotide scan, not only is the liver lighting up, but we can see there's a bright spot here in the neck, which shows that the tumor has spread all the way up to the neck. And it's a little bit complicated why tumors tend to go up there, which probably doesn't matter, but it's clearly this particular tumor has spread not just beyond the pancreas to the liver, but up into lymph nodes in the neck as well.

All right, so now we have a... intermediate grade tumor, which we tend to put in with the better behaving as opposed to the very high grade, but still not good enough. And we have liver spots, we have a spot in the neck, we have a person who's having some discomfort associated with the enlarged liver. John, do you want to mention anything that you might do for that enlarged liver? Would you consider any local treatment before we ask Dr. Koontz what she'd do?

So this person has liver-predominant disease and is symptomatic. There's a thing covering over the liver that is very sensitive. And so when the tumors grow and stretch that liver capsule, it can be very painful. And this would be someone who would benefit from liver-directed therapy, such as chemoembolization or radioembolization, although we're not able to treat all the tumor in the entire body. I think our goal here is improving symptoms and addressing the biggest tumor. And before I usually treat patients, besides just looking at the scans, we'll see the patient, make sure their labs are good too, because that would limit my ability to treat the patient if the liver was failing. For example, if the total bilirubin was above two, that would tell me that the liver is not doing so well. I would just hasten their death and not really improve their life. So other markers I look for would be five times normal, AST, ALT, or nuance ascites, meaning the liver's not doing so well as well. Those are all indications. And I would also make sure that the patient has a fairly good functional status. So if they're already not doing so well, maybe sleeping most of the day, that's not someone I would like to treat because, once again, I'm here to help people, not make their life worse. So that's what we do, chemoembolization or radioembolization to treat the symptoms and perhaps help them live a little longer.

So, in the tumor ward, this would be one of those situations where we'd ask John what he could do, and even if he felt that he could help in this particular situation, we might defer to Dr. Kuhn's first, simply because she has treatments that go everywhere. And if they work, then they would work not only in the liver, but also in the lymph node, and also in the pancreas. But it's helpful to know that this person would be a candidate for a liver-directed approach if, in fact, that became the symptom-limiting organ. So, Pam, you want to talk about what you might consider?

Sure. And I think that this is sort of a good case to discuss an internal tumor board because I think the sequence of how we would offer treatments is really important. I think knowing that we could do a chemo embolization or radio embolization is important. We don't really know. if it's important to do that early in the disease course or later in the disease course. I think that for this particular patient, I would probably offer a systemic treatment first and kind of keep the liver directed treatment in my back pocket. And what's exciting is that I think you may have addressed this earlier in the morning cases, but two new drugs, as many of you know, have been approved for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors just in May. So Sunitinib or Sutent. and Everolimus or Afinitor, and those are both oral agents. They are used separately. Both were studied in large phase three clinical trials, and both showed improvement in terms of slowing the growth of the disease, and in some cases, shrinking tumors. And I think one or one of those, and again, we don't know which one should be started first, but I would probably choose one of those. And I tell most of my patients with metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors that they will likely see both of those agents in their lifetime. But the sequence right now, we just don't know what is better.

reference_conclusion: The agreed management is to initiate systemic therapy first for metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, using one of the newly approved oral agents sunitinib or everolimus. Liver-directed therapy with chemoembolization or radioembolization is recognized as an option for this symptomatic, liver-predominant disease but is to be reserved for later use if the liver becomes the symptom-limiting site, contingent on adequate hepatic function and performance status. This sequencing is intended to prioritize treatment with whole-body activity given metastatic involvement of the liver, lymph nodes, and pancreas.
reference_conclusion_quote: I think that for this particular patient, I would probably offer a systemic treatment first and kind of keep the liver directed treatment in my back pocket. [...] So Sunitinib or Sutent. and Everolimus or Afinitor, and those are both oral agents. They are used separately. [...] And I think one or one of those, and again, we don't know which one should be started first, but I would probably choose one of those. [...] But it's helpful to know that this person would be a candidate for a liver-directed approach if, in fact, that became the symptom-limiting organ. [...] So that's what we do, chemoembolization or radioembolization to treat the symptoms and perhaps help them live a little longer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old man; otherwise healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Multiply recurrent sinonasal adenoid cystic carcinoma with severe facial/orbital pain, ectropion, and worsening diplopia; visual acuity in the affected eye had been preserved.

[ diagnosis ]: Multiply recurrent intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left sinonasal/maxillary region with involvement of the left orbit, pterygoid skull base region, sphenoid sinus, infratemporal fossa, and nasopharyngeal bulging; prior isolated pulmonary metastasis had been resected in 2022.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 1999: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the maxilla.  
- 2018 resection: R2 resection with positive margins along the orbital floor and pterygoid plates.  
- 2023 biopsy: Recurrent intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- Pathology over time had been described as possibly initially lower grade, subsequently read as intermediate grade.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2021 imaging showed soft tissue prominence in the posterior left nasal cavity at the pterygoid plate, masticator space, and orbit; this was observed.  
- MRI demonstrated recurrent tumor in the left orbit involving the rectus muscles and lacrimal gland, without intracranial extension.  
- MRI also demonstrated a second component at the pterygoid base extending into the sphenoid sinus and infratemporal fossa, with bulging into the nasopharynx.  
- Tumor involved the foramen rotundum below the skull base and encroached on the foramen ovale.  
- No overt intracranial extension or cavernous sinus extension was identified on imaging.  
- PET demonstrated a large hypermetabolic exophytic tumor at the nasal-maxillary junction.  
- PET showed no evidence of distant metastatic disease at the time of current evaluation.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Oncomine/targeted molecular profiling was negative for actionable alterations.  
- No NOTCH mutation was detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 1999: Infrastructure maxillectomy for maxillary adenoid cystic carcinoma followed by adjuvant neutron radiotherapy.  
- Approximately 2009: Revision surgery for recurrence at a second center.  
- 2018: Total maxillectomy without orbital exenteration with fibula free flap reconstruction for recurrence in the maxillectomy bed with orbital and masticator space extension; resection was R2 with positive margins at the orbital floor and pterygoid plates.  
- 2021: Imaging-detected soft tissue recurrence was observed.  
- 2022: Isolated lung metastasis underwent resection.  
- 2023: Hardware removal for hardware exposure and cutaneous deformity; radial forearm free flap reconstruction was performed. Residual skull base disease was not dissected.  
- 2023: Biopsy confirmed recurrent intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]:  
Locoregionally recurrent disease remained present in the left orbit and skull base/pterygoid region, with orbital muscle and lacrimal gland involvement, extension into the sphenoid sinus and infratemporal fossa, and involvement of the foramen rotundum with encroachment on the foramen ovale. No overt intracranial or cavernous sinus extension was identified. No distant metastatic disease was identified on current PET imaging. Symptoms included severe facial/orbital pain, ectropion, and worsening diplopia with preserved visual acuity.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Prior neutron radiotherapy records from 1999 were not available despite attempts to obtain the treatment profile.  
- Chronic opioid therapy had been used over more than a decade, with opioid dependence/addiction reported.  
- Possible infected mesh had been considered as a contributor to pain prior to hardware removal.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks for the opportunity. For discussion today, we have Mr. G, who is a 57-year-old gentleman, otherwise healthy, with a 26-year history of multiply recurrent adenoid cystic carcinoma of the sinonasal cavity. He's been treated at several centers across the United States. So to briefly recap, his journey started in 1999 when he developed an ACC of the maxilla. He underwent a infrastructure maxillectomy and adjuvant neutron therapy. He did well for about a decade until about 2009 when he presented to a second center and got revision surgery. The notes on that are a little bit sparse, but we do know well that he did well for about another decade until about 2018 when he developed a second recurrence in the maxilectomy bed with orbital and masticator space extension. He then went to his sort of third surgical team where he underwent a total maxillectomy without orbital exteneration and reconstructed with a fibula free flap reconstruction. This was an R2 resection with positive margins along both the orbital floor and pterygoid plates. The imaging done about 2 years later in 2021 showed that he had a soft tissue prominence in the posterior left nasal cavity at the pterygoid plate, masticator space, and orbit. This was observed. He later developed an isolated lung met and underwent a red trasection in 2022. In 2023, he developed some hardware exposure and a bit of a cutaneous deformity so that the hardware was removed. He had a second free flap, a radial forearm done at that time, but the residual disease in his skull vase was undissected. And then he finally had a biopsy done later that year by a rhinologist, which confirmed recurrent intermediate grade adenoid cystic carcinoma. So that brings us to kind of earlier this year, where he presented to us for really kind of a second opinion, and he's really just seeking further treatment options. He was really suffering from severe facial pain, ectropion, and worsening diplopia, though his visual acuity in that eye was preserved. I think the tumor is best captured with MR. So starting with the coronal, he's got a recurrent tumor in the left orbit that involves the rectus muscles and lacrimal gland without intracranial extension. There's a second component at the pterygoid base that extends into the sphenoid sinus and for temporal fossa, kind of bulges into nasal pharynx. The tumor involves the foramen rotundum below the skull base and kind of encroaches on ovale, but there's no, overt sort of intracranial or cavernous sinus extension. He's had a, we had a PET done as well, which sort of re-demonstrates this large hypermetabolic exophytic tumor at the nasal maxillary junction. Notably, though I don't show it here, there's no evidence of any distant or metastatic disease. So we thought this was a good time to bring it up to sort of turn it to the discussants. I guess we have a couple questions that we've prepared just to shape the conversation a little bit.

Chris, maybe to sort of facilitate discussion, can you bring up your imaging again? Sure. And then we'll turn it around to, we'll start with our... I just paused at a good spot. faculty members and then turn it to our senior discussants. Maybe we'll start with Dr. Levine, if that's okay, your thoughts on receptability and we'll go around the table.

Yeah, this is always, you know, an area that's gonna be a challenge because, you know, resectability at a rate cystic carcinoma is, you know, kind of variable, right? You know, there's great studies to show that, you know, gross total resection and getting decent margins is going to make a difference for you. And that even in some cases, close margins are still gonna have very similar prognosis. Yeah.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult female treated at Massachusetts General Hospital.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent right neck masses following initial treatment for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma, initially diagnosed in 2016. Initial surgical stage was pT3N1bM0. Recurrent locoregional nodal disease developed postoperatively. Somatic RET-mutant disease with later oligoprogression in a right supraclavicular lymph node while on selpercatinib.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial thyroidectomy pathology demonstrated a 2.5 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma with extrathyroidal extension, lymphovascular invasion, and positive margins. Immunohistochemistry was positive for calcitonin and CEA. Numerous lymph nodes were involved. Several additional microscopic medullary thyroid carcinoma foci were present in the remaining thyroid gland. Revision neck dissection in January 2017 showed metastatic disease in 4 of 9 lymph nodes; the largest metastatic node measured 3.2 cm and showed extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial staging evaluation after January 2017 revision neck surgery showed no evidence of distant metastases. PET/CT performed after development of four new palpable right neck masses over subsequent months demonstrated uptake in multiple nodal stations; the largest node measured 1.6 cm. Restaging CT after 2 months of cabozantinib showed a mixed response, with regression of some cervical lymph nodes but a new 1.0 cm right supraclavicular node. CT after 8 months of cabozantinib showed significant progression. On selpercatinib, serial imaging showed a partial response within the first few months, with a 51% decrease in sum of target lesion diameters, followed by a durable response and eventual radiographic complete response by 2022. In February 2024, evaluation identified a solitary recurrent right supraclavicular lymph node measuring 1.4 cm, radiographically concerning for extranodal extension.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET testing was negative. Tumor next-generation sequencing identified a somatic RET M918T mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperative calcitonin was 181 and CEA was 15.7. After subsequent nodal recurrence, calcitonin was 270 and CEA was 17.1. During cabozantinib treatment, calcitonin and CEA initially decreased, then rose again at progression after 8 months. During selpercatinib treatment, calcitonin and CEA decreased markedly and subsequently normalized for a prolonged interval. With the February 2024 recurrence, calcitonin increased slightly from previously normal levels.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial surgery for medullary thyroid carcinoma was performed in 2016. Revision neck surgery was performed in January 2017 for a new right upper neck mass. Cabozantinib was started in April 2017 for recurrent locoregional disease. Adverse effects on cabozantinib included hypertension, mild diarrhea, mild nausea, hoarseness, hair depigmentation, and later hand-foot syndrome. Best early radiographic assessment on cabozantinib showed mixed response at 2 months; disease progressed significantly by 8 months. Selpercatinib was started in March 2018 on LIBRETTO-001 at 240 mg twice daily. Early treatment response was a partial response with 51% reduction in target lesion measurements. No adverse events were reported on selpercatinib. Treatment produced a long durable response, with radiographic complete response achieved by 2022.

[ current disease status ]: As of February 2024, there was isolated oligoprogressive locoregional recurrence consisting of a solitary 1.4 cm right supraclavicular lymph node. No other active disease sites were described. Selpercatinib treatment was ongoing.

[ other clinical data ]: Four new palpable right neck masses, including one in the right supraclavicular fossa, developed within months after the January 2017 revision surgery.

So when you're looking for the rest of the body, you want to scale it differently compared to looking at the liver. So you can, even though these may be small, many of them have such a high expression of somatostatin that you can see them incrementally higher intensity than liver based on dynamically scaling the display window. And if you have completely negative, as you said, many of these are malaria, and that becomes an issue with all imaging modalities, whether it's DOPA, F-DOPA, whether it's gallium dotatate or whether it's FTG. Whenever there are miliary, we miss across the board in molecular imaging, but because they have such a high degree of signal expression, many of them, even when they're small, we see them. So, what we typically do is scale the intensity of the liver. If we see that, the specificity is extremely high. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male, 60 years old.

[ chief complaint ]: Left neck pain causing inability to sleep.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma involving the left carotid space/left level II neck.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial thyroid cancer surgery in 2007 showed stage T3N1bM1 disease with extrathyroidal extension.  
- Cervical nodal disease was extensive, with 23 of 47 lymph nodes positive.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the recurrent left neck lesion was positive for malignancy but was non-conclusive for definitive classification.  
- CT-guided core biopsy of the left neck mass demonstrated poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI neck with contrast demonstrated an enhancing, infiltrative, ill-defined left carotid space versus level II mass. The lesion extended superiorly toward the prevertebral muscle level.  
- PET imaging demonstrated a markedly FDG-avid left neck mass with SUV 22.  
- PET imaging showed no other disease elsewhere; chest and abdomen were clear.  
- A surgical clip was present at the level of the lesion from prior surgery.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- CT-guided core biopsy provided sufficient tissue for molecular testing.  
- NTRK fusion was identified: ETV6-NTRK3.  
- TERT alteration was positive.  
- BRAF was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent thyroid surgery with extensive neck dissection in 2007.  
- Received radioactive iodine, 200 mCi, in 2007.  
- Had no evidence of disease for approximately 14 years after initial treatment.  
- CT-guided core biopsy of the recurrent lesion was performed as an outpatient and was tolerated without procedural complication.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Isolated FDG-avid recurrent left neck disease was present in the carotid space/level II region.  
- No distant disease was identified on PET imaging of the chest and abdomen.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Voice was normal on presentation.  
- Cranial nerve XII function was normal on presentation.  
- Prior concern for kidney metastasis at initial staging was later considered not to represent metastatic disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Ascites and peritoneal disease at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, FIGO stage IIIC.

[ histopathology results ]: High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary.

[ imaging findings ]: Peritoneal disease was present at diagnosis. Ascites was present at diagnosis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue next-generation sequencing showed low tumor mutational burden, microsatellite stable status, and homologous recombination deficiency positivity with genomic aberration score 77. TP53 mutation was detected. Copy number gains were reported in HER2, EMSY, CD274, PDCD1LG2, NBN, MYBL1, NOTCH3, and TEAD. Germline hereditary cancer panel showed an MSH2 variant of uncertain significance; no other germline mutations were detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 3 cycles of neoadjuvant paclitaxel plus carboplatin, with good clinical response. She subsequently underwent cytoreductive surgery. Surgical outcome was described as complete cytoreduction with minimal residual tumor. She was continuing adjuvant chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed advanced-stage disease after interval cytoreductive surgery, with response to platinum-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy and currently on adjuvant chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history was significant for breast cancer in a maternal aunt at age 32 years.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male; otherwise healthy at initial presentation.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe abdominal pain after months of severe reflux and diarrhea.

[ diagnosis ]: Functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma/Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), arising from the uncinate process/head of pancreas; well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor with nodal and later hepatic, retroperitoneal nodal, and osseous metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy of pancreatic head mass showed well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with Ki-67 12%.  
- Whipple resection specimen demonstrated well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor in the pancreatic head/uncinate process with Ki-67 23%; 3 of 17 lymph nodes were involved.  
- Repeat biopsy performed later in the disease course showed Ki-67 in the mid-30% range; tumor remained well-differentiated.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT at emergency presentation showed free intraperitoneal air consistent with duodenal perforation.  
- Subsequent abdominal MRI demonstrated a pancreatic mass concerning for neuroendocrine tumor.  
- Endoscopic ultrasound identified a mass in the head of the pancreas.  
- Somatostatin receptor imaging in 2016 showed intensely avid disease localized to the pancreas/peripancreatic region without metastases.  
- Further imaging and repeat endoscopic evaluation localized the primary tumor to the uncinate process of the pancreas; no obvious gastric or duodenal mass was identified.  
- Approximately 1 year after surgery, MRI showed a small new liver lesion and enlargement of a postoperative lymph node.  
- Somatostatin receptor PET/CT demonstrated approximately 5-10 small hepatic lesions and several retroperitoneal lymph nodes, interpreted as metastatic disease.  
- Follow-up imaging after initiation of octreotide showed slight interval increase in some lesions at 3 months, and by December 2017 showed further growth with new liver lesions and enlarging lymph nodes, including additional retroperitoneal adenopathy.  
- Repeat somatostatin receptor PET showed all lesions were avid; no non-avid lesions were identified.  
- After capecitabine/temozolomide, imaging at approximately 6 months showed progression in the liver with enlarging and additional hepatic metastases.  
- PET/MRI after everolimus showed intensely somatostatin receptor-avid disease in liver and extrahepatic sites.  
- After PRRT, imaging showed partial response in liver and lymph nodes, followed by stable disease in February 2020 and continued favorable imaging in September 2020.  
- Later imaging demonstrated renewed hepatic progression with multiple new and larger liver lesions.  
- Subsequent somatostatin receptor PET continued to show avid disease despite progression.  
- Later imaging showed relatively similar liver disease but marked new osseous metastatic progression on DOTATATE PET.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genomic sequencing was performed later in the disease course and did not identify actionable findings.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum gastrin was elevated at diagnosis.  
- After Whipple resection, gastrin decreased but did not normalize, remaining approximately twice the upper limit of normal.  
- Gastrin later began to rise again during metastatic recurrence/progression.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Emergent surgery for duodenal perforation was performed at presentation; this was not oncologic resection.  
- Whipple resection was subsequently performed in 2016 for localized pancreatic primary.  
- Postoperative management consisted of surveillance imaging without adjuvant systemic therapy.  
- Long-acting octreotide was started for metastatic recurrence at 20 mg with concurrent proton pump inhibitor therapy; dose was increased to 30 mg after slight progression at 3 months. Disease subsequently progressed with new hepatic lesions and enlarging nodal disease.  
- Capecitabine plus temozolomide was administered in 2017; treatment was well tolerated, but imaging after approximately 6 months showed hepatic progression.  
- Everolimus was then started; imaging after 3-4 months showed persistent/progressive somatostatin receptor-avid disease.  
- Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with lutetium-177 dotatate was administered for 4 cycles, with continuation of somatostatin analogue therapy. This produced a partial response in liver and lymph nodes followed by durable disease control/stable disease for approximately 2 years.  
- On later progression, the patient enrolled on the CABINET trial; early progression occurred after approximately 3 months, and unblinding showed placebo assignment. He then crossed over to cabozantinib.  
- With subsequent progression, including marked osseous disease, retreatment with lutetium-based PRRT was attempted for 2 cycles without response.  
- FOLFOX was started in May 2022; mild improvement was observed after 5 cycles, but treatment was stopped because of neuropathy and other adverse effects.

[ current disease status ]: After discontinuation of FOLFOX at the end of 2022, disease remained stable. Most recent documented status was stable disease, with follow-up imaging pending.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Clinical syndrome was consistent with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, with reflux and diarrhea improving after resection and acid suppression.  
- Symptoms worsened later with rising gastrin levels, though without recurrence of the severe reflux seen initially.  
- Somatostatin receptor imaging remained avid throughout the disease course, including at later progression.

reference_discussion.text: Hello, my name is Thor Haff-Denarsson. I'm a medical oncologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, and I will be presenting the next case, a case of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. So this is a gentleman who presented to us with a history of severe abdominal pain and a little bit of a backstory. So he had months of really bad reflux and diarrhea and eventually got severe abdominal pain relatively suddenly presented to his local emergency room, had the CT that showed free abdominal air. And he had a perforation of the duodenum, so essentially a hole in the duodenum and underwent emergent surgery that was fixed. And then obviously, as we talked about before, this was emergent surgery. This was not cancer directed surgery. So there was no resection or removal of any tumors. So then after this, he had the ongoing evaluation locally, which was all really well done, and had an MRI of the abdomen. And now they see that there's a mass in the pancreas that's really concerning for a neuroendocrine tumor, at least as per the MRI. So an upper endoscopy with ultrasound was ordered, and there was a mass in the pancreas, and the head of the pancreas was biopsied and was a well-differentiated, degraded-to-neuroendocrine tumor with a KS67 nuclear grade of 12%. At that time, he also had a gastrin level that was fairly elevated. I can't remember the actual number, but it was up. So he came to us for another evaluation and had a CT scan, and he had what you see on the right hand there is a blast from the past. This is an arterioscan. So this is in 2016. This is just before we got our SSTR PET scans. So you can see the liver here. You can see this is a mass, either a lymph node or a mass in the pancreas, and it lights up really bright. And there were no metastases at that time. This seemed to be limited to the pancreas and was clearly producing this hormone called gastrin. So now the question is, what do we do now? So we have someone who is otherwise pretty healthy, that do a dental perforation, had diarrhea, had elevated gastrin. And maybe we'll start with the surgeon, Dr. Koitgen, So what is going on there? So how do you connect all of these dots?

I'm honored. Thank you for letting me start here. So a couple of things I think of, first of all, if you said the gastrin was above 1000, it's sort of almost diagnostic for gastrinoma, although you can have occasionally high gastrin levels, you know, when patients are on PPI, but that high is usually pretty diagnostic for gastrinoma. So gastrinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor that produces gastrin and it can either be found in the duodenum or in the head of the pancreas. Most commonly, these can present with actual ulceration or damaging of the mucosa of the duodenum or the stomach, which can cause perforations, which is probably what he had the first surgery when they went in and they saw free. I don't know exactly what they sewed up and where they saw it, but assuming that it was somewhere in the duodenum or the stomach, that's probably what we're dealing with here. The interesting part on your CT is and on your OcteoScan is that it was hard for me to say whether this was truly part of the pancreas or as you said whether this was a lymph node. So I would push my endoscopist to make sure that they essentially evaluated like the entirety of the duodenum because gastronomas are often found in the duodenum and it can be sometimes in the third or fourth portion of the duodenum And so if they're pretty sure that there's nothing in the stomach in terms of, you know, mass or nodularity and nothing in the entirety of the duodenum, then you could certainly assume that perhaps what you see on the CT is part of the uncinate process of the pancreas and is a neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas. primarily that came from there. I would say an MRI perhaps is helpful also sometimes in being able to differentiate that. And then one last thing is I would consider certainly checking out whether there's a family history. There are some gastronomas that are essentially associated with what's called MEN1 syndrome, so primary hyperparathyroidism, as well as pituitary tumors. So if there's no strong family history, then this could be certainly a sporadic gastronoma, but it is something that we ought to consider. And after all of these things, Assuming that, you know, things are still localized, I think he buys himself a surgery so we can go resect whatever needs to be resected, whether it's the peripancreatic lymph nodes and the duodenotomy and the duodenal mass, or whether it is the primary mass that's within the ulcerative process of the pancreas.

So we got some more imaging and I think he had another endoscopy and eventually it was concluded that this was femur of the uncertain process of the pancreas. It was sort of like exophytic and hanging off the pancreas and there wasn't really anything obvious in the stomach or duodenum. So he underwent a Whipple resection, so removal of the pancreatic head and part of the duodenum. And there was a well-differentiated NET in the pancreatic heads or the unscented process, actually. And now the KF7 was 23%. There was well-differentiated three of 17 lymph nodes were involved. And this is actually where I got involved. So this is back in 2016. So now the question, this may be a good one for the medical oncologist, Dr. Liao and Dr. Suarez. So what are we going to do now? So back then, we didn't really have much information. Are we going to observe, or give adjuvant chemotherapy, or what's the way forward?

So now I would enroll this patient in the ongoing trial. Right answer. Yeah, so this patient had many high risk features, you know, the lymph nodes, the high KSC symptoms. So there's actually an adjuvant therapy trials, adjuvant therapy are treatments to help, you know, reduce the chance of recurrence of people live longer. So there's an adjuvant therapy trial of kipsetamine and temozolomide chemotherapy. But seven years ago that the trial was not in place. I would be curious to see what the patient did.

That's an excellent point. And just to want to emphasize that this is really the only way we move the field forward is that we do trials for particular scenarios like that. We didn't have that information that we didn't, we don't have that information now because the trial is ongoing, but maybe this will be effective therapy. So back then, ultimately it was decided to watch him carefully and nothing was done other than repeat imaging. So did the gastrin level normalize? Yeah, gastrin levels actually came down, didn't normalize completely, but were sort of hanging above the upper limit of normal, about twice the upper limit of normal. Definitely a lot better. And the reflux got a whole lot better. So I think this was like real Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, so overproduction of gastrin. So we follow him, and then a little bit over a year later, he comes in, and here I'm doing the MRI. Even back in 2017, it was sold on MRI. So it's really following with MRI. And now we can see that there is a small lesion, a little dot on the liver here that wasn't really seen previously. And this lymph node that had been there after the surgery, but the smaller is now getting bigger. So now we have someone's adenoreceptor PET CT. This is prior to us using MRI routinely. And we can see that these are just representative shots. And as I think Dr. Lon Heath said before, we have to take a look at the whole picture. The liver probably had about the five to 10 of these little dots and a few of these lymph nodes back there. So these were presumed to be small liver metastases. We didn't go ahead and biopsy it. We thought we had enough evidence here. So maybe a question for Dr. Amateur. So how many is too many for liver directed therapy?

You know, there's no such thing as too many, in that as long as the patient's underlying or normal liver is functioning well, and the patient is doing well, you know, clinically or physically, you know, able to tolerate normal activities, we indiscriminately can do bland embolization, I think, as we've mentioned before. When the question really then I think becomes, what's too many to do what we call ablation, where we put the needle in and directly burn the tumors. And in that situation, we tend to not do more than three or four lesions at a time. Doesn't mean we can't do more, but it becomes very time consuming. So those are sort of the ways that we look at it. If we're looking at more than three or four lesions, then we lean more towards bland embolization.

Thank you. And another question for Dr. Koitkin here with If you have a liver with 5 or 10 lesions, and I think you just showed us before that you can easily remove more than that. What about if you have these lymph nodes in what we call the retroperitoneum? Is it still worth going after the liver and getting to those lymph nodes?

Yeah, so you can get to them, but it's not always that straightforward. If you have very extensive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, most of the time the appetite to do surgery becomes a lot less because it gets very complex. And there certainly are a lot of really important structures in that area, including, like you see here, the blood supply to you know, the left kidney, but we can certainly do that surgically. It's not that it's not possible. I would say the overall question for this patient is, a year later, do they really want to go through surgery again? I mean, surgically speaking, this is, both of these lesions are resectable, but I would tell the patients that I would rather probably wait a little longer, maybe do something a little bit more systemic, like maybe long-acting obturatitis or so, and sort of see how much more declares itself because that lymph node on the left side is sort of an atypical location for localized disease, right? So it's not just the liver, but it's also away from where the tumor was, which was on the right side of the abdomen. So I would assume that there are more lymph nodes around the chain on the left side and possibly on the right side that are going to show up over time. So I'm not sure I would recommend surgery right now.

Okay. And then there's a question for Dr. Long-Heath. So here we have an SSTR or somatostatin receptor PET, and keep in mind that these tumors are crept into the grade three range, barely, but still made it. What should we do with the other PET, the FDG PET?

Well, that's a great question. So first of all, it's very difficult in our insurance environment in the U.S. to get both a DOTATATE and an FDG PET approved. Those are looking at two different things, right? FDG PET is looking at metabolic activity of the tumors, whereas SSTR PET like DOTATATE PET is looking at how to what extent are these tumors expressing functional somatostatin receptors. So theoretically insurance should be willing to pay for both. They're asking two different questions, but it's very difficult. So generally, if I'm making a decision about whether to treat somebody with PRRT, I don't care if you tell me that it's grade three. I don't care what the KI 67 is. I mean, I do for, you know, to just figure out how well they're going to do and that kind of thing. But what's the most important by far is the DOTATATE PET CT and how avid the tumors are on that. If the only reason that I would recommend an FDG PET CT in a case like this would be if I saw a finding on the CT or the MRI that looked suspicious, but was not lighting up on the DOTATATE PET, then I think we would need further investigation to make sure that that's not a metastasis that has become more de-differentiated. Otherwise, I just let the DOTATATE PET or the somatostatin receptor PET stand.

Thank you. And that's pretty much what we did. So back then we didn't really have much information on adding FDG PET CT and figured we would not get it approved anyway. So then a question again for Dr. Suarez and Dr. Leo. So with the grade three tumor, does this mean that we're dealing with a different tumor or what's this all about?

Great question. And I think there is great trees with a Ki67 of 20 to 30 that behave very aggressive. And there is great trees with a Ki67 of 20 to 30 that tend to behave more as a great tool with more indolence. In this particular situation, I will probably give the test of time and start this patient on a somatoste analog with a very short intervals of scanning, right? In some patients, you can go six months without scanning. This is someone that I probably would scan with a cross, cross-sectional imaging every three months in the beginning to have a sense. In addition to what was already said about the FDG PET, I probably, in the idea, I wouldn't have done at that time, but if after that I was considering going for the PRRT, that's when I would be very interested, if I could, in the ideal world to get the FDG in addition to repeating the DOTATATE. So what I would have done here is starting the somatocin along with short intervals of scans every three months initially and see what happens.

And we did not compare notes before I presented her. So this is exactly what happened. So although back then it was started long acting on the triotide was started at 20 milligrams. One could argue we should have started at 30, but you can start, that would be the typical tumor controlling dose. And we continued the protein pump therapy for acid suppression as I didn't tell you that the gastrin levels were starting to creep up, but there were no symptoms. And then we repeated the imaging in three months, and there was a slight increase in some of the lesions. So we just bumped up the actreotide dose to 30 milligrams. So in December of 2017, then we do another scan. And I'm not comparing the old scans to the new scans, but now there is some growth of the tumor, and there are some new lesions in the liver that were clearly not there before. So what do we do now? So keep in mind, this is a well-differentiated grade three neuro-tumor of pancreatic origin. New lesions, lymph nodes also getting bigger, and we're starting to see more retroperitoneal lymph nodes a little bit further down.

I guess my prediction was right. More retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Yeah, I'm going to bail out here, surgically speaking. Grade three, you know, progression of disease on somatostatin. I think if I debulk him, he's going to come, things are going to come back pretty quickly. So I'll take a break. Dr. Suarez and Dr. Liao.

I think that's a perfect patient for us to discuss the current Alliant trial that compares PRRT versus CAPE10 in patients that had progression on somatocinalogues or Bokeh disease of the pancreas. So that will be what I will be discussing with the patient, these two options under the trial.
Okay. So Dr. Ahmed, in terms of progressive liver lesions, if you're starting to see new liver lesions pop up, Is it worth trying to ablate the new stuff or should we do something like drug therapy?

Yeah. I mean, to me personally, I probably would lean against doing something local regional because this doesn't seem like a local progression in general. I think we tend to apply our therapies as we talked about for symptomatic control, but also now in cases where there's only sort of various focal progression in the liver, for example. So I would lean against it probably.
Thank you. Do we know if those new lesions are totally avid, or are they one of the non-avid ones that Courtney was talking about?

Great question. At this time, we didn't have that information, but a few months later, we repeated an SSTR PET, and these were all avid. There were no lesions that we were not accounted for on the SSTR PET. So this being 2017, we proceeded with Cape Tem, Cape Cytopen and Temozolomide, which was very well tolerated. But then a few months later, six months later, there was now progression in the liver. So the liver lesions were getting larger and there were again, more liver lesions. So what do we do now? So any thoughts on where, and again, this reflect, also pay attention to the timing of this, this is 2017. So maybe Dr. Long, you can tell us a little bit about when did we get puberty in the US?

Well, yeah, so PRRT was done for a long time in Europe and Australia prior to it coming to the U.S. We started doing PRRT at UCSF on a clinical trial basis around 2016, but it was not FDA approved until 2018. So this would have been a referral to some kind of clinical trial at that time if PRRT were indicated. Although I would want to see a repeat DOTATATE PET to make sure those meths are avid.

And that was indeed done. I don't show, I'm not showing that, but that was still AVID. So we presented the case at the tumor board, and at that time we didn't have access to, or PRT was sort of coming on board, and the practice was not really up and running yet. And there were progressive and new liver metastases. So we started Everolimus. And after three or four months of Everolimus, we did another imaging study. And now I'm showing you a little bit more information. So on the left-hand side, we see the fused delta-tetra-SSTR PET images. It's actually a PET MRI. We see the MRI part just showing one of the lesions. And then we see the, what's called the MIP. We always forget what that stands for.
So sort of a- Maximum intensity projection.

That's what it is. I always find, I find these very helpful for patients because you can rotate these and these are very easy sort of anatomically for both me and the patients to talk about. So now everything is very, like everything lights up really bright and there's nothing that doesn't light up. So what are we going to do now? So I think we can all weigh in here.

So can I weigh in first? I was going to say, so this is where I would, in my local tumor board, become very annoying and start pushing very hard for PRRT. So there's significant extra hepatic progression, right? As well as a lot of disease in the liver. And most importantly, it's extremely avid. And to me, even if there was a lower burden of disease with this level of intensity of uptake, it's an indication that those tumors are going to take up a lot of radioactivity. and definitely bumps up my willingness and my desire to do PRRT. I would push for PRRT here at this time.

Excellent. Keep in mind, now we've gone through a Somosatin analog, Cape Tem and Averolimus, and things are progressing. And indeed, we proceeded with PRRT. So he received the four cycles of lutetium-1787-dilutate, also known as lutetarum. We continued this almost in analogs, and actually we'll get there in a moment. So had a partial response in the liver and lymph nodes with mildly decreased size and a little bit of decreased intensity, although we didn't do a lot of PET like early after we completed the PRRT. So February 2020, stable disease. Then we did another PET imaging in September of 2020. So this is now almost two years after completing PRRT, and things were actually looking pretty good. So here's a question for probably all of you, but maybe mostly the medical oncologists. So should we continue the octreotide or lanreotide after PRRT? These are not inexpensive drugs.

So I personally do, especially if it was given for symptom reason. So, you know, patients who have a lot of secretion symptoms in that situation, I definitely continue. Now, if they have a non-functioning tumor and they've technically progressed on octreotide before, you could argue, then what's the point of continuing with that toxicity, both physical, but also financial.

So, and so, any thoughts from any of you here? So there's

What about re-biopsying these lesions and perhaps looking at whether, number one, the grade has changed, probably repeating the PET scan, making sure that there's still obviously uptake and they haven't de-differentiated. And then I don't know if you guys routinely use genomic profiling, if that ever changes your treatment sequence, especially when you sort of start slowly running out of options.

Great question. So somewhere along the way, I can't remember exactly when we re-biopsied, and now the KF system was up in the mid-30s. And so with this one, I think we did genomic sequencing. We haven't done a lot of it for well-differentiated grade 3 NETs, and we haven't really found a whole lot when we do it. So we do it for all of the poorly differentiated American carcinomas. It's more sort of a gradual progression. And thankfully, not any worsening of his symptoms.

Well, the only thing, I mean, not the only thing, but one of the things that the patient hasn't seen is tunitinib, right, which could have been used. I mean, I was itching to also considering fufox, but if the overall burden of disease is not super great and we feel that the timeline of progression is acceptable, we can probably hold off on fufox, which is something that sometimes we use when disease is picking up more speed. So on the time, tunitinib and We also have the cabinet trial that is looking into cabozatinib for patients. And I don't recall on the top of my head, but I think the grade is not necessarily, as long as the tumors are well differentiated, cabozatinib can be considered as part of a trial as well.
And you were spot on.
Okay, and we didn't exchange notes. All right.

So we had the cabinet trial open at the time, and you're absolutely right that there is no All grades are allowed as long as they're well differentiated, so having KS7 of 35 was not a contraindication. It's a randomized trial, 2 to 1 randomization, so one third of patients get placebo, two thirds get the CABO, and there was progression shortly after starting, probably about three months, which it probably was in late May. So we unblinded, that is, we looked under the hood, see what he was on, and he was on placebo. So we switched over to cabozantidib. Then he started having worsening symptoms. I'm gonna fast forward to the next scan. That was that. Well, that takes us to the end of my case.

reference_conclusion: Following Whipple resection of the localized pancreatic gastrinoma, the patient was managed with close surveillance and serial imaging rather than adjuvant therapy. After subsequent metastatic progression involving liver and retroperitoneal nodal disease, treatment was initiated with a somatostatin analogue and proton pump inhibition, with cross-sectional imaging every three months and dose escalation of octreotide for early progression. With further progression on somatostatin analogue therapy, systemic therapy with capecitabine and temozolomide was administered, followed by everolimus, and then peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with lutetium-177 dotatate because of persistent somatostatin receptor avid disease; the somatostatin analogue was continued thereafter given the prior functional syndrome. At later progression, management included trial enrollment with crossover from placebo to cabozantinib, PRRT retreatment without response, and subsequent FOLFOX, which was discontinued after five cycles because of neuropathy and other adverse effects, after which disease remained stable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Sex was female. Age was not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidental suprasellar/interpeduncular lesion identified during evaluation after an episode of confusion. Headaches were present. Vision was reported as normal.

[ diagnosis ]: Undiagnosed nonenhancing mass centered in the interpeduncular fossa/retroinfundibular region, located posterior to the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk and anterior to the brainstem. No tissue diagnosis had been obtained.

[ histopathology results ]: No biopsy specimen was obtained. No histopathology was available.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI demonstrated a lesion in the interpeduncular fossa. The lesion was described as posterior to the chiasm and posterior to the pituitary stalk, with the stalk displaced anteriorly and slight anterior displacement of the optic apparatus. The lesion was anterior to the brainstem. It was very bright on T2-weighted imaging, approximately isointense to slightly hypointense on T1-weighted post-contrast imaging, and did not enhance. No surrounding brain edema was described. Mild calcification was reportedly present. The lesion was initially thought to be cystic on imaging, but intraoperatively it appeared firm and neural-tissue-like rather than cystic. Postoperative imaging was reported to be unchanged from preoperative imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Pituitary hormonal function was reported as otherwise intact after surgery. No numerical laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent an attempted endonasal transsphenoidal/endoscopic approach by an experienced surgeon, including pituitary gland transposition and attempted dorsum sella removal. The lesion could not be biopsied or resected because of limited operative corridor and venous bleeding. No tissue was obtained. The postoperative course was complicated by transient diabetes insipidus, which resolved after a couple of weeks. Surgery had occurred a few weeks before the current referral.

[ current disease status ]: The lesion remained radiographically unchanged after the attempted operation. The patient was clinically doing well, with normal vision and resolved transient postoperative diabetes insipidus. Headaches persisted. No seizure-like events were reported. No mass-related visual deficit was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion had been considered radiographically cystic preoperatively, including possible craniopharyngioma, but this was not confirmed. Differential diagnostic considerations documented in the record included hypothalamic hamartoma, optic pathway glioma/exophytic glioma, and other low-grade glioma. No definitive diagnosis had been established.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old man. General health was described as excellent. Past medical history included well-controlled hypertension. Performance status was excellent.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain, nausea, and bloating at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Transverse colon adenocarcinoma with a large locally advanced mass adherent to the anterior abdominal wall. Tumor was mismatch repair deficient / MSI-high.

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopy biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial evaluation demonstrated a large transverse colon mass adherent to the anterior abdominal wall. Postoperative imaging after 12 cycles of FOLFOX showed persistent residual tumor without response. Imaging obtained after approximately 6 months of pembrolizumab showed near-complete resolution with hardly any tumor remaining. Most recent scan showed no evidence of residual disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mismatch repair deficient tumor (dMMR/MSI-high).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent surgery for the primary tumor; postoperative residual tumor remained. Subsequently received FOLFOX for 12 cycles with no response. After referral, received single-agent pembrolizumab. After approximately 6 months of pembrolizumab, imaging showed marked response with near-complete resolution, and subsequent imaging showed no evidence of disease.

[ current disease status ]: No radiographic evidence of residual disease on the most recent scan.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had presented approximately 1.5 years after initial diagnosis for subsequent oncologic evaluation. At the time of referral for immunotherapy, residual tumor was present and the patient remained relatively symptomatic.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Large ureteral tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma of the ureter. The tumor was described as heterogeneous, predominantly low grade with focal high-grade areas.

[ histopathology results ]: Urothelial carcinoma with predominantly low-grade histology and foci of high-grade disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a large ureteral mass. Available imaging review was limited; the base of the tumor was not visualized, and it was not determined whether the lesion had a broad base or narrow pedicle. No additional objective radiographic staging details were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Glomerular filtration rate was 100 mL/min/1.73 m². Predicted postoperative renal function remained within cisplatin-eligibility range.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No chemotherapy or immunotherapy administration was documented.

[ current disease status ]: No metastatic disease status was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Risk estimates cited for this case included approximately 30% risk for T2 disease or higher and 20% risk for T3 disease preoperatively. The case was categorized as high risk by EAU criteria and high-risk favorable by AUA criteria.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 80-year-old female. Lifetime non-smoker and non-drinker. Edentulous mandible. Otherwise healthy and described as active.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of progressive pain involving a lesion of the left gingivobuccal sulcus. No numbness was reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Oral cavity malignancy arising in the left gingivobuccal sulcus, with rapid interval progression to direct cutaneous invasion involving the facial/submental skin and oral commissure. Disease was classified as T4a after progression with skin invasion.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology details were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial lesion measured approximately 3 cm at the left anterior oral cavity adjacent to the oral commissure. The lesion extended from the mucosal side toward the oral commissure and appeared to creep onto the gingiva, but was initially entirely mobile from the mandible on examination. Imaging showed no mandibular erosion. Sagittal imaging demonstrated markedly atrophic edentulous mandible with vertical mandibular height of approximately 1.5 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient proceeded to surgery approximately 3 weeks after initial presentation because of significant interval progression. At operation, the tumor had progressed by direct extension to involve skin and had extended over and down the alveolar ridge to involve both the buccal and lingual surfaces of the mandible.

[ current disease status ]: The patient was considered willing to proceed with radiation therapy.

[ other clinical data ]: Cutaneous involvement represented direct tumor extension rather than dermal metastases. An Allen test was satisfactory, and multiple donor sites were considered available if needed.

Reconstruction was performed with a fibula free flap using two separate skin paddles for internal and external lining, with closure of the commissure to preserve oral competence.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes mellitus. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: In the first quarter of 2015, she presented with anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal distention.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade serous ovarian adenocarcinoma, FIGO stage IV.

[ histopathology results ]: Preoperative biopsy showed serous adenocarcinoma, grade 3. Immunohistochemistry was estrogen receptor positive and WT1 positive, consistent with serous ovarian adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal ultrasound showed ascites and peritoneal carcinomatosis. PET-CT demonstrated a 2 cm hepatic lesion with increased FDG uptake, increased uptake at the lower diaphragm, ascites, and increased uptake in the parametrial region and left ovary.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: CA-125 was 345 at presentation. Hemoglobin was 9 g/dL, consistent with anemia.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She underwent suboptimal cytoreductive surgery with resection of the hepatic lesion; residual disease greater than 1 cm remained postoperatively.

[ current disease status ]: Stage IV high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma after suboptimal primary cytoreduction, with residual postoperative disease greater than 1 cm.

[ other clinical data ]: Hepatic involvement was surgically resected at cytoreduction. Residual postoperative disease burden was greater than 1 cm.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old man; ECOG performance status 1.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe headache and rapid blurring/deterioration of vision.

[ diagnosis ]: Astrocytoma, WHO grade 3.

[ histopathology results ]: Stereotactic/open biopsy via right frontal mini-craniotomy showed astrocytoma grade 3.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain showed a diffuse, ill-defined infiltrative lesion centered in the corpus callosum, crossing the midline and infiltrating the adjacent cerebral hemispheres. T2-weighted imaging demonstrated hyperintense infiltrative signal involving predominantly the corpus callosum with extension into subcortical white matter and cortex, posterior extension into the corona radiata, involvement of the frontal and parietal lobes, and inferior extension into the temporal lobes. The lesion involved more than three lobes bilaterally. Post-contrast T1-weighted imaging showed no discrete enhancement, no cystic component, and no necrosis. Postoperative MRI showed a right frontal surgical tract/post-surgical changes after biopsy; the lesion size was reported as more or less unchanged, with interval increase in the infiltrative component also described on postoperative imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: 1p/19q codeletion not detected. IDH1 and IDH2 alterations not detected. MGMT promoter methylation not detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent biopsy only; extensive resection was not performed because of diffuse lesion extent. Postoperative imaging demonstrated post-surgical changes in the right frontal lobe without meaningful reduction in tumor burden.

[ current disease status ]: Diffuse non-enhancing infiltrative supratentorial astrocytoma involving the corpus callosum and bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal regions, symptomatic with headache and visual blurring, status post biopsy.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional laboratory results were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 78-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Altered bowel habits, anemia, and intermittent rectal bleeding for 4 months; recent subacute intestinal obstruction managed conservatively with Ryle’s tube decompression and intravenous fluids.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon, stage IIIC (T4a N2 M0), non-metastatic.

[ histopathology results ]: Adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon.

[ imaging findings ]: Locally advanced sigmoid colon malignancy with nodal disease; non-metastatic disease. Subacute intestinal obstruction was present.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL. Estimated glomerular filtration rate 25 mL/min. Anemia was described as mixed anemia of chronic disease and iron deficiency anemia secondary to rectal bleeding.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Subacute intestinal obstruction was managed conservatively with Ryle’s tube decompression and fluids.

[ current disease status ]: Non-metastatic locally advanced sigmoid colon cancer with nodal involvement and ongoing intermittent rectal bleeding. The patient remained medically complex with subacute obstruction and significant frailty/comorbidity burden.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Hypertension for 25 years, treated with calcium channel blocker and ACE inhibitor.  
- Diabetes mellitus for 20 years with diabetic nephropathy.  
- Chronic kidney disease stage 4.  
- COPD with frequent exacerbations; on home nebulization.  
- Congestive cardiac failure, NYHA class II–III; ejection fraction 38%.  
- Mild cognitive impairment; MMSE 25/30.  
- Activities of daily living partially dependent; instrumental activities of daily living dependent.  
- Moderate depression on geriatric assessment.  
- Recent weight loss and malnutrition were documented.  
- Charlson Comorbidity Index 9.  
- Polypharmacy was present, with approximately 10 medications.  
- High fall risk; no recent falls reported.  
- Required a walker; walking limited to approximately one block.  
- CARG score indicated very high risk for chemotherapy-related toxicity.  
- No hearing impairment was reported.  
- MSI status was not available.  
- DPYD testing had not been reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Many months of otalgia and odynophagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the supraglottic larynx involving the epiglottis. Clinical stage at presentation was cT1N0. Final pathologic stage after resection was pT3N0 due to focal cartilage involvement and pre-epiglottic space invasion.

[ histopathology results ]: Direct laryngoscopy biopsy demonstrated invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Final surgical pathology after transoral laser microsurgery supraglottic laryngectomy showed focal cartilage involvement and invasion of the pre-epiglottic space. Margins were negative. Perineural invasion was absent. Bilateral neck dissections were pathologically node-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Nasal endoscopy demonstrated an exophytic mass on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis without involvement of other supraglottic structures; vocal fold movement was normal and the vocal folds did not appear involved. CT neck showed thickening of the epiglottis with normal appearance toward the glottis and no cervical lymphadenopathy. CT chest showed no evidence of metastatic disease. Retrospective review suggested possible subtle cartilage erosion on imaging.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent direct laryngoscopy with biopsy confirming invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. He subsequently underwent upfront bilateral neck dissections, which were pathologically N0, followed by transoral laser microsurgery supraglottic laryngectomy. No tracheostomy was required postoperatively. Postoperatively, he developed COVID-19 infection. He experienced dysphagia requiring hospital admission. Postoperative swallowing analysis performed approximately 1-2 weeks after surgery demonstrated penetration and frank aspiration. He required Dobhoff tube feeding for supplemental nutrition. He was started on a pureed diet despite aspiration findings and progressed to a normal diet over approximately 6 months. Voice outcome was mild dysphonia with otherwise good voice function.

[ current disease status ]: Status post surgical treatment for supraglottic squamous cell carcinoma with negative margins and pathologically node-negative neck dissections. Postoperative functional recovery included improvement from tube supplementation/pureed diet to normal diet over approximately 6 months.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included acute myeloid leukemia treated with bone marrow transplant, complicated by graft-versus-host disease. On physical examination at presentation, there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. No formal preoperative swallowing assessment had been performed.
