reference_discussion.text: All right. So thank you so much for having me to the H&S. So I'll be presenting a case of a T1N0 squeam of the super goddess. So this is a 68-year-old male. He's a former smoker. He had a 45-pack-year history, and he presented to clinic with many months of otalgia and odynophagia. His other pertinent past medical history is that he does have a history of AML and had had a bone marrow transplant complicated by graft-versus-host disease. On exam, he had no palpable lymphadenopathy. We did nasal endoscopy and there was a exophytic mass of the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis. There was no involvement of any other supraglottic structures and he had normal vocal fold movement. They did not appear to be involved. This is varying pictures of his CT. You can see thickening of the epiglottis and then down towards the glottis, everything appears normal. And again, he had no lymphadenopathy. So for his workup, he got a CT chest, no evidence of metastatic disease. And then we went to the OR for a DL biopsy. And as expected, he had invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. So this is a early stage supraglottic, very contained to the epiglottis. And so for the panel, some of the treatment considerations, Is this someone you consider for surgery or XRT? And then how you address the neck, particularly for a supraglottic lesion, and then open versus endoscopic surgery. And then if we're talking about surgery, sort of the approach, so we can take each of those sort of little by little.
Dr. Neal, before you jump in and talk about treatment, can I ask for clarification about the history?
Absolutely.
Patient had a dynaphagia, but did the patient have any actual dysphagia and or was there any formal assessment of swallowing function performed?
He was doing okay with swallowing before. It was mostly pain related. And I do not believe he had any formal swallowing preoperatively because symptomatically he was doing okay.
So Dr. DuPore, do you think this is someone that you would consider for upfront radio, single modality radiotherapy, or would he be a sort of candidate in your eyes? Yes.

So the reality is that this is really dealer's choice, right? So I think that to Dr. Neal's point, there is evidence, it seems to be that this guy's swallowing well, and we can easily attribute the dysphagia or whatever amount of dysphagia he might have to pain, but I think it is really important to get these people evaluated because there are silent aspirators, there are silent issues that we may miss. Assuming that that doesn't exist and clearly the goal of the treatment of this patient is to preserve the organ and that organ preservation, which in many centers automatically equates to non-surgical treatment is a misnomer. I think you can preserve the organ with surgery and you can preserve the organ and the function of the organ with radiation. If he really is T1 and zero that I think that that's a very valid valuable point but we know the data suggests that up to 25 to 30% of these patients can have occult nodal metastasis with a T1 and zero of the superglottis. And of course, I'd be remiss if I didn't cite the data from my alma mater Pittsburgh which demonstrated that. So the reality here is that it's the other's choice in terms of what the patient wants. In my hands, I think that this patient, if he really is T1 and 0, would be well treated with surgical resection alone without the need for adjuvant therapy. And I think that's really the bottom line. All of these questions are getting to what is the least you can do to cure the cancer, to preserve the patient's function, that really is a multidisciplinary care decision. In my hands, I would advocate for surgery, but clearly it has to be done with the team-based approach.

Dr. Young, from a staging the procedure standpoint, that's a good question. Would you stage between the endoscopic or what have you, the resection and the nodal dissection, and why would you advocate for that?
Did you direct that at me?
I did. I'm just kind of going through the panelists, you know.

And I appreciate greatly your efforts to engage me. I will tell you as a laryngologist, I haven't done a neck dissection in too long. I would say I would do whatever Dr. DeVore, Dr. Schroeder and told me to do or whatever they would like to do. I think that, I think it's a challenging conundrum, and I have to say, while I have an opportunity, I love Dr. DeVore's stance of minimizing morbidity, because we know that surgery carries risks, but so does radiation with regard to swallowing function, right? And it's all a matter of balancing it out. I would just have to put in a plug for careful observation, monitoring, and actual measurement of patient swallowing function throughout however you're going to approach this treatment.
So Dr Neil how to go.

So we can talk about we did consider the staging aspects so we talked to the patient he was interested in surgery, and so, given the high rates of nodal occult nodal disease particularly with superglottis tumors. common at Michigan that we do upfront neck dissections before, since nodal disease is what drives adjuvant therapy in many of the cases. And so we did a, this is one of my partner's cases, upfront bilateral neck disease, and indeed was pathologically N0. And so then did a TLM, supraglottic laryngectomy. And on final path actually the T stage was more advanced than initially thought because there was focal involvement of the cartilage and the pre-epiglottic space. He had negative margins and no PNI. And so he was pathologically technically T3. And so he was presented at tumor board. And the question was, so you don't know disease had no PNI but he's T three based on this focal cartilage involvement. And so I think there's another good question for the panelists. This is a multidisciplinary discussion but when, when do these people get observation and when do they get. radiation for adjuvant therapy.

So Molly, if I can, if I can sort of poke at that a little bit, if you were to go and look back with a retrospective scope, do you think that you would have seen that pre-epiglottic space invasion, or was that just not caught on the imaging?

I don't think it was caught on the imaging. We can go back to the, if I go back to his his scan, it looked pretty exophytic, and it was mostly on the laryngeal surface, but I think you may be able to see a little bit of cartilage erosion here. I think even with that information and discussing with the patient that there's still a chance for observation, knowing that there's a higher risk of vocal recurrence and trying again to minimize the number of modalities they're receiving may still have been a consideration, but yeah, it's a very good, very valid point.

So just for the trainees, I think one thing to consider when we talk about endoscopic versus open, you know, the standard sort of textbook method here is the open supraglottic langectomy. You make a horizontal cut, you take the epiglottis and supraglottis, and then you basically sew the remnant thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. And in that scenario, you basically do the neck dissection at the same time because the guy or lady ends up with a really fairly big incision. But then you also have to trick these patients, right? So the tracheotomy is a real valid concern because it's an open procedure with the concomitant lymphedema. So it's evolved over the time to move towards endoscopy really to avoid having to trick these patients, right? So most high volume endoscopic surgeons now don't trick these patients anymore. You can get a one-stop shop and the patients will recover pretty well, especially if they have good adjuvant therapy in the context of rehabilitation. I really like this concept of doing the next sort of first because the nodal staging drives the treatment for these patients most of the time. But it is sometimes hard to convince somebody that you can do bilateral neck dissections on them and then give a radiation afterwards anyway for the primary tumor, especially if you keep more radiation in some cases. It's a provocative concept, but I think it's one that probably warrants further study. Again, just from the trainee standpoint of things. And so I'm assuming that you didn't trick this patient, right?

Yes, so that leads nicely. So he, from a post-op perspective, he did not require a trach. He did immediately get COVID after his procedure, and then from a functional standpoint, was struggling with dysphagia, and he was admitted. And so we have a post-op swallowing analysis here, and he required a Dovhoff tube feeding tube for supplemental nutrition. So this is in the hospital with COVID. So keep that in mind. And this is about, I think, a week or two post-op. So this is actually, it looks relatively good, but it does have penetration and some frank aspiration. And so I think a lot of our speech language pathologists work in clinic closely with us and with all of our head and neck cancer patients and are very willing to sort of even with evidence of some aspiration, you know, we know these patients are going to aspirate, whether they get radiation or surgery. And so being willing to sort of tolerate some amount of aspiration, getting at sort of what was their lung health preoperatively. And so they did start him on a pureed diet, even in the setting of having some gross aspiration. And he was able to work up towards a normal diet after, you know, six months or so. From a voice perspective, he had mild dysphonia, but actually had pretty good voice outcomes. And so that was one of the other aspects I wanted to discuss with the panel was what kind of preoperative counseling and expectations for swallowing and speech functional outcomes do you tell patients when you're having, I mean, this drives a lot of the XRT versus surgery treatment discussions as well.

One of the things that I'm really proud that we have at UCSF is that actually we have a extensive cadre of voice and swallowing expertise driven SLPs. and they are embedded in the head and neck clinic. So these are conversations exactly as you talk about that are started early, right? So this patient didn't have any dysphagia up front, but I hope that somebody talked to them about the potential for that before they got to the, I'm admitted to the hospital because I've aspirated and now I've got a feeding tube in. Right, I think that having I think that having a pre op exam could have been helpful free up MBS can be helpful to have a baseline understanding of function, but at the least a pre op. conversation, whether it's with you or the speech pathologist or preferably both, just to lay the groundwork for what the patient needs to anticipate that they are going to be facing and how they're going to work through it, right? So regardless of whether the patient has surgery or radiation, the involvement, the continued involvement of the speech language pathologist, I think is critical for their ability to have an optimal outcome, for sure.

I would actually push on a step further. I know the data from Kate Hutchinson is pretty compelling that preoperative therapy or pretreatment therapy actually impacts greatly the functional outcomes post-treatment, whether it's surgical or non-surgical. So one of the, I think the big steps that we've taken here at NYU at the Permanent Cancer Center is to actually get patients preoperative and not just counseling, but preoperative therapy. So before they start, they actually see a speech pathologist. They have an assessment, but they also have some intervention. And you can think about it this way. If any of the trainees have tried a supraglottic swallow or a supra-supraglottic swallow, which is hold your breath, swallow, cough, swallow again, it's really hard. It's hard to do that now. So you can imagine once you've had surgery and you've got pain in your throat and you can't swallow well, to ask people to now do those techniques and to do those complex techniques for weeks is even more difficult. And people often give up. And that's why it takes them a long time sometimes to recover from this, especially post-radiation. So getting people into that frame of mind and strengthening these muscles and doing this sort of work is, I think, of paramount importance.
Do you guys believe in NG tube or G tube for these patients? Do you believe that the G tube could be a crutch that they don't do enough swallowing therapy? And what do you do before surgery?

Yeah, so I agree with Uma. All these patients, all our head and neck patients actually undergo a pre-op, pre-treatment, not even pre-op, pre-treatment swallow evaluation with the SLPs. That's great, thank you.

[ patient demographics ]: 80-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive disease/recurrence of pancreatic carcinoma identified in October 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, initially diagnosed in 2015 as stage III pancreatic cancer; current disease described as stage IV progressive metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the left psoas muscle showed metastatic adenocarcinoma deposit.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor was reported as homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) positive. BRCA mutation was detected, specifically BRCA2 with a truncating/termination loss-of-function alteration. NGS interpretation described two clonal populations of BRCA2 mutations. Germline versus somatic status had not been established.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In 2015, the patient underwent Whipple procedure. He subsequently received adjuvant chemotherapy abroad; regimen details were unavailable. Disease progression/recurrence was documented in October 2025.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma with biopsy-proven metastatic involvement of the left psoas muscle.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history of cancer was reported. Details regarding disease burden on imaging were not available. CA 19-9 result was not available. Germline BRCA1/2 testing had not yet been performed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 39-year-old woman at initial breast cancer diagnosis in 2011.

[ chief complaint ]: In November, she was admitted with chest pain and back pain.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- 2011: ER-positive/PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast with associated ductal carcinoma in situ, stage T2N1.  
- Metastatic recurrence identified in November with osseous involvement at T2 and hepatic metastasis.  
- Liver biopsy confirmed metastatic carcinoma of breast origin, ER-positive, HER2-negative (IHC 2+, HER2-low).

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Primary breast cancer: invasive ductal carcinoma with associated DCIS; ER/PR positive, HER2 negative.  
- Nodal disease at initial diagnosis: 2–3 sentinel lymph nodes positive.  
- Liver biopsy: metastatic carcinoma consistent with breast primary; ER positive; HER2 negative, 2+ by immunohistochemistry.  
- Bone biopsy from T2 lesion was inconclusive.  
- Prophylactic total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy specimen showed no malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial primary breast tumor measured 4 cm.  
- In November, workup demonstrated a pathologic fracture at T2 in the thoracic spine.  
- PET scan showed a hypermetabolic lesion at T2 and a single relatively large liver lesion.  
- Surveillance pancreatic MRI had been performed in October in the setting of BRCA2-associated pancreatic surveillance.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Germline testing identified a pathogenic BRCA2 variant.  
- Tumor comprehensive genomic profiling demonstrated BRCA2 alteration corresponding to the known hereditary mutation; reported as a 4-base pair deletion.  
- Genomic loss of heterozygosity was high at 34%.  
- Tumor mutational burden was 12 mutations/Mb.  
- Microsatellite status was stable.  
- PIK3CA mutation was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: White male. Age 62 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Hematuria. Weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma with a locally advanced left renal primary and pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of a lung lesion showed metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging showed a locally advanced tumor involving the left kidney and multiple pulmonary metastatic lesions/nodules. Post-sunitinib imaging showed central necrosis within the primary renal tumor with persistent local extension into the retroperitoneal musculature. Pulmonary metastases were overall stable, with possible slight progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Anemia was present. Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated. Other laboratory values were within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient enrolled in a presurgical trial and received two courses of sunitinib. This produced a good response in the primary renal tumor, with central necrosis, and overall stable metastatic disease with possible slight progression in the lungs.

[ current disease status ]: Following presurgical systemic therapy, the primary tumor had responded and pulmonary metastatic disease had remained largely stable with possible minor progression.

[ other clinical data ]: Performance status remained excellent prior to cytoreductive surgery. Bone scan and MRI were negative for metastatic disease. No significant past medical history was documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 90-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with biochemical progression on androgen deprivation therapy and darolutamide; asymptomatic at assessment.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), chemotherapy-naive, with multiple bone metastases.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET/FDG imaging demonstrated very intense PSMA uptake in multiple bone metastases. Maximum SUV was approximately 150-151. Whole-body bone lesion SUV mean was 19.8. No FDG-avid metastases were identified. Disease was confined to bone on the described contouring workflow.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA rose from 0 to approximately 80 between 2019 and 2023. PSA at current assessment was 84, with a PSA doubling time of 2.6 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Androgen deprivation therapy alone had been administered for the preceding 9 years. Darolutamide was subsequently commenced.

[ current disease status ]: Asymptomatic, ECOG performance status 1. Biochemical progression was present with rapidly rising PSA despite prior ADT and darolutamide.

[ other clinical data ]: Lived at home with his wife and was fully independent. He was chemotherapy-naive.

[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old female. No comorbidities were reported. She was a non-smoker. No family history was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough with expectoration, breathing difficulty, and occasional fever.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma with malignant right pleural effusion/pleural involvement. Disease later progressed with lumbar bone metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural fluid cytology was positive for malignancy. FNAC from a pleural nodule showed atypical cells of a poorly differentiated neoplasm. Biopsy from pleural nodules showed immunohistochemical features of adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial evaluation showed a massive right pleural effusion; therapeutic pleural tapping was performed. CT chest showed a lesion in the collapsed right middle lobe and a heterogeneous enhancing lesion. PET-CT after six cycles of pemetrexed and carboplatin showed stable disease. Repeat PET-CT performed after presentation with back pain showed progressive disease with bone metastasis in the lumbar region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Immunohistochemistry showed TTF-1 positive, CK7 positive, calretinin negative, and p63 negative. Tumor proportion score for PD-L1 was 30%. NGS showed RET positivity. KIF5B-RET fusion was referenced.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Therapeutic pleural tapping was performed for the right pleural effusion. Systemic treatment was started with pemetrexed and carboplatin. After completion of two cycles, pembrolizumab was added based on PD-L1 tumor proportion score of 30%, beginning from the third cycle. After six cycles of pemetrexed and carboplatin, PET-CT showed stable disease. The patient was then continued on maintenance pemetrexed and pembrolizumab.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease was documented on repeat PET-CT, with bone metastasis in the lumbar region, after prior stable disease on chemoimmunotherapy and maintenance treatment. The patient had presented with back pain at the time of progression.

[ other clinical data ]: Selpercatinib was not arranged.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old postmenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: One month of pelvic pain, with subsequent worsening abdominal pain over the following two weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Right adnexal mass highly suspicious for ovarian malignancy with omental involvement and small-volume ascites; advanced-stage intra-abdominal malignancy was suspected clinically. Pathologic confirmation had not been obtained.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathologic diagnosis was available. Omental biopsy had been planned but was not performed.

[ imaging findings ]: CT demonstrated a complex 9 cm right adnexal mass with omental nodularity and small-volume ascites. The lesion was reported as not amenable to ultrasound-guided drainage. Imaging appearance was considered highly suspicious for malignancy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: CA-125 was elevated at 579 initially and subsequently increased to 1,253 over approximately two weeks. CEA was slightly elevated at 8.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for three cycles followed by interval surgery had been planned because of concern regarding surgical tolerance. Chemotherapy was not initiated. Omental biopsy was scheduled for diagnostic confirmation but was not performed. Endoscopic evaluation for elevated CEA was not performed.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic untreated pelvic/adnexal malignancy was suspected, with worsening pain and rising CA-125. No tissue diagnosis had been established, and no systemic therapy or surgery had been delivered.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. BMI was 42. ECOG performance status was 2. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination demonstrated obesity and a slightly tender 9 cm right adnexal mass; no other abnormal examination findings were described.

reference_discussion.text: So, please note that this case consultations do not create or otherwise establish a provider-patient relationship between any IGCS volunteer, clinician, and any patient whose case is being presented. Responsibility for the patient remains with the medical team who cares for the patient at the presenting institution. So we have for our case presentation a 71-year-old woman who is postmenopausal and has had about one month of pelvic pain. Her past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. Her family history is relatively unremarkable. The CT scan shows a complex 9-centimeter right adnexal mass with omental nodularity and small volume ascites, which is not amenable to ultrasound drainage. Abnormal labs include an elevated CA125 at 579 and a slightly elevated CEA at 8. Physical exam, patient is obese with a BMI of 42. She is somewhat limited in her mobility with an ECOG score of 2. And on physical exam, the only finding is a nine centimeter, slightly tender, right adnexal mass. CT scan has shown the mass looks highly suspicious for malignancy. So the plan of treatment was because the patient was somewhat frail and, um, We were a little bit worried about the ability for her to tolerate surgery. We were going to get a biopsy of the omentum to confirm the diagnosis. And we had planned to treat her with three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed by surgery, possibly minimally invasive, after three cycles. This was scheduled, but CT scan called and informed us that we could not do a biopsy as the case was considered nonessential due to the COVID-19 epidemic. I called the radiology department and they still refused to do the biopsy because they were so busy. We were informed that all surgeries that are not immediately life-threatening are on hold due to increased surge in our hospital. And I could not get an endoscopy scheduled for the same reason to evaluate her elevated CEA. So our options at this point were to give chemotherapy without pathologic confirmation or to wait until she was symptomatic. So over the next two weeks, the symptoms got worse with increasing abdominal pain. Her CO125 increased to 1,253. After discussion, the patient opted for chemotherapy without a biopsy, but now the infusion unit is closed. due to the need for additional hospital bed space. So I think this highlights the rapidly changing situation that we have in many places. I think the situation is different for everybody, but we have to remember that this doubles every three to five days, depending on where you are. And so short-term plans will change rapidly. And I just wanted to discuss this in terms of deviations from standard of care and see what our panelists had to say about this.

We can open it up to the panel to make a couple of comments on situations that they've experienced regarding delay of care, particularly diagnostics. Daniella, being in Italy, I'd like to start with you.

In fact, in this particular moment, when we're planning a treatment for our patients, it's mandatory to consider multiple factors, such as comorbidities, age, immunostatus, because first of all, we should prevent the patients becoming infected, but also we should preserve the hospital resources for COVID-19 patients. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes, it's the same.
And Jun, from China, you probably have experience also. Do you have any comments?

Yeah. I do agree to give this patient maybe the new agent of chemotherapy first. but it's hard to get the biopsy, get the pathology results. So at this time, maybe we can more often to use some non-invasive methods to make a more clear diagnosis. Sometimes, such as for this lady, maybe we can test HE4, another tumor mark. If HE4 increased, obviously, maybe just indicate there's a malignancy and also high-grade malignancies, I think there's another way. Also, I think, could we just give the patients a new adjuvant chemotherapy for the cycle if she had a good response to the chemo, maybe to help us to make the right diagnosis?

Thank you. So what we're going to do next is a couple of poll questions. If we can move to the next slide. So we clearly know that there's lots of delays. I just want to see how it's assessing you. So the first question is, are you anticipating significant delays in surgery, radiation, imaging, or chemotherapy as a result of the pandemic compared to a normal schedule? And then the second question, which you may need to scroll down for, how have these changes impacted cancer care? from no changes to care to currently cannot deliver cancer care, as you heard in this case. And while you're voting, I'd like to ask Dr. Pereja if he has any comments on these questions that we just posed to the group before we get to the didactic. Renee, any comments?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 84-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Inferior vena cava mass identified in summer 2024; high-grade sarcoma on catheter-based intraluminal biopsy pathology.

[ histopathology results ]: Intraluminal catheter-based biopsy of the inferior vena cava mass showed a pleomorphic epithelioid and spindle cell tumor with indistinct cell borders. Mitotic activity was reported as 17 mitoses per high-power fields. Tumor cells were vimentin-positive. Pathologic conclusion was high-grade sarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]: CT in summer 2024 demonstrated a mass involving the inferior vena cava, described as arising from the vena cava.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue molecular testing showed tumor mutational burden of 47. Genomic prevalence score yielded a 58% call for melanoma. Mutational signature analysis demonstrated a UV mutational signature.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described clinically as very fair-skinned.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarged thyroid of unknown duration; subsequently presented with right humerus fracture.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic high-grade thyroid carcinoma. Outside neck mass biopsy had reportedly shown poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. Subsequent pathology from tracheostomy/isthmus specimen was reported as high-grade oncocytic thyroid carcinoma; morphologic description was consistent with poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. Disease involved the neck with extensive distant metastatic spread, including osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Core/specimen obtained at time of tracheostomy with partial isthmusectomy showed solid/nested growth pattern, tumor necrosis, and absence of nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Extensive lymphatic invasion and angioinvasion were present. p53 immunostaining showed complete loss (null phenotype). BRAF V600E was negative by immunohistochemistry. Final pathology was reported as high-grade oncocytic thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT neck demonstrated a very large neck mass, greater on the right than left, with marked tracheal deviation to the left. Imaging showed osseous metastatic disease involving the sternum. There was extensive metastatic disease throughout the neck, including multiple nodal compartments, with lymphadenopathy involving supraclavicular, subpectoral, and intrathoracic regions. Possible metastatic involvement of musculature around the right shoulder was described. Clinical history also included a pathologic right humerus fracture consistent with metastatic bone involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry was negative. p53 showed null phenotype by immunostaining. Next-generation sequencing had been planned/pending; no additional genomic results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Mild hypothyroidism was present. Thyroglobulin was markedly elevated at approximately 3,300. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet count were all reduced.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had undergone neck mass biopsy at an outside facility. During admission, he was initially observed for airway status. He later developed acute respiratory distress/anxiety with air hunger overnight; ICU intubation attempts were unsuccessful until fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation was performed by the head and neck service. He subsequently underwent tracheostomy with partial isthmusectomy/isthmusectomy specimen collection. Radiation oncology and medical oncology evaluations were completed. Initial nonoperative treatment with cytotoxic therapy pending next-generation sequencing had been proposed.

[ current disease status ]: Extensive metastatic thyroid carcinoma remained present in the neck and at distant osseous sites. The disease was not resected.

[ other clinical data ]: No significant past medical history was reported. Flexible laryngoscopy showed evidence of aspiration; bilateral vocal cord movement was confirmed, although assessment was difficult. He had lost weight but had been eating adequately. Before airway decompensation, he had been saturating adequately and had no noisy breathing. He relied heavily on his parents for care discussions.

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus was that this represented unresectable metastatic high-grade/poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma with extensive locoregional and distant disease, and that upfront surgery was not appropriate beyond airway stabilization already performed. Recommended next steps were urgent comprehensive molecular profiling, including BRAF and RAS immunohistochemistry with next-generation sequencing, and initiation of noncurative systemic therapy, with preference for cytotoxic chemotherapy combined with radiation while awaiting molecular results. If palliation rather than disease-directed therapy were pursued, a very short course of radiation for local symptom control was discussed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 2.5-year-old male child.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive, asymptomatic upper abdominal mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatoblastoma involving both lobes of the liver; staged as PRETEXT III, standard risk.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous liver mass measuring 8.6 × 7.6 cm involving both hepatic lobes.  
- Initial CT angiography showed a heterogeneous hepatic mass involving segments 4A, 4B, 5, and part of segment 8. The left and right hepatic veins were splayed over the mass; the middle hepatic vein was not visible. The left portal vein was not visible. The main portal vein and arterial phase vessels were visualized.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Jaundice was present at presentation.  
- Gamma-glutamyl transferase was raised.  
- Alpha-fetoprotein was >180,000.  
- LDH was 1545.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed hepatoblastoma involving both lobes of the liver, staged as PRETEXT III, standard risk, with a heterogeneous hepatic mass involving segments 4A, 4B, 5, and part of segment 8, and alpha-fetoprotein >180,000. The child was otherwise asymptomatic apart from the progressively enlarging upper abdominal mass.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination at presentation showed generalized abdominal distension, with liver palpable approximately 10 cm below the costal margin; the mass was firm and dull on percussion and was continuous with the liver.  
- Left inguinal hernia was present.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Localized prostate cancer with suspected residual/recurrent right-sided lesion following primary focal HIFU.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, initially localized to the right peripheral zone, Gleason score 3+4 on initial biopsy. Subsequent residual/recurrent clinically significant disease was confirmed on repeat targeted biopsy as Gleason score 4+3 in the right side. Additional low-volume Gleason score 3+3 disease was identified in the left posterior prostate.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial external biopsy showed Gleason score 3+4 disease on the right side only. After primary HIFU, a targeted biopsy of the right-sided lesion near the prior ablation zone was negative, with only partial tissue available for laboratory analysis. Repeat targeted biopsy subsequently confirmed Gleason score 4+3 disease, measuring 5 mm, on the right side, and Gleason score 3+3 disease, measuring 1 mm, in the left posterior side.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial external MRI showed a lesion in the right peripheral zone. Repeat high-quality MRI confirmed a clearly visible right-sided lesion with radiologic-pathologic concordance. The anterior-most part of the disease was 36 mm from the rectum. Imaging before primary HIFU demonstrated a right-sided lesion with anterior extent suitable for focal ablation. Post-HIFU MRI performed after PSA concern at approximately 1 year demonstrated a persistent suspicious right-sided lesion near the prior ablation margin. MRI localized the lesion anteriorly at the anterior margin of the previous ablation zone.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Baseline PSA was reported as 6. After primary HIFU, PSA fell by approximately 70%. At approximately 1 year after HIFU, PSA was higher than expected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent primary focal HIFU to the right-sided prostate lesion after confirmation of MRI-pathology concordance and technical suitability for complete focal ablation with margin. Intra-procedural imaging demonstrated treatment reaching the anterior part of the target with expected ultrasound treatment changes. Early functional outcome after HIFU was favorable, with complete continence and preserved erectile function with PDE5 inhibitors.

[ other clinical data ]: Follow-up had been PSA- and MRI-driven. The residual/recurrent right-sided disease after HIFU was located at the anterior-most margin of the previous ablation zone. The left-sided Gleason 3+3 focus was low volume and located in the left posterior prostate.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you everyone for the invitation to speak today and thank you to Mr. Orteig for presenting a case on his behalf. So today I'm going to present a case, a second chance of treatment, redo cryotherapy after primary HIFU. I know I'm conscious about time so I'll try to keep to the facts. We have his external referral of a 68-year-old man who initially had some external diagnostic workup with a PSCO6, an external MRI showing a lycophyte lesion in the right PZ, an external trust biopsy showing lesion 3 plus 4 on the right side only. This was a repeat MRI scan that we did when we saw him to have high quality imaging as that is essential for our investigation and you can clearly see the lesion on the right side here. So in order to evaluate him for eligibility for focal therapy, we put it through our focal multidisciplinary team meeting in the presence of our radiologists and pathologists, where we reviewed the MRI and we reached a consensus between the concordance of the pathology and the MRI. We also looked at the localization of the disease and confirmed that the anterior most part of the disease was at 36 mm from the rectum and therefore confirmed the suitability for a focal hyphae. We confirmed that we would be able to reach a complete ablationary target with a margin and respecting the anatomy as well. So here you can see the images from the Haifu treatment with the anterior most treatment zone reaching very well the anterior part and also good Haifu Uchida changes on ultrasound. The initial follow-up was good with complete continence and maintained record function using some PDE5 inhibitors and we reached a very good drop in PSA from 70%. But after one year, we saw that the PSA was higher than we would expect and we repeat an MRI scan. As you can see, And we did a targeted biopsy of his lesion on the right side, near part of the previous ablation. Unfortunately, the biopsy came back as negative, which was surprising given the likelihood, but there was only a partial amount of tissue analyzed in the lab. So what we decided to do, because we believed in the positivity of the lesion on radiology, going back to what we discussed before, we repeated an early MRI scan. and repeated a target biopsy, which did confirm plisone 4 plus 3, not 5 millimeters in the right side, and there was only one millimeter of plisone 3 plus 3 in the left posterior side. Therefore, we discuss this in our focal MDT. and we were discussing potential options for the patient going between prostatectomy and radiotherapy, or we discussed whether it would be possible to offer him or redo right focal therapy and maintaining the left side on active surveillance given the low grade and low volume. So the rationale in this case for repeating focal treatment was that we had the initial treatment was really good at the posterior part and the residual disease was anterior most margin where there's little overlap in the treatment. The focal therapy would have been ipsilateral, therefore having low damage to the contralateral side and therefore maintaining good functional outcomes. And based on the MRI and the anterior location of the lesion, we decided for an interstitial treatment for easy access to anterior portion of the gland with cryotherapy. So this was all discussed with the patient who preferred radiofocal therapy in view of minimizing the side effects. Here you can see again the pre-HIFU images and the MRI that was done pre-HIFU. So the location of the lesion was very well located anteriorly at the anterior margin of the previous ablation zone. In May 2019, we performed a reduced cryoablation and you can see on the right side the treatment plan with the position of the two cryo needles and the thermoprops as well. We had two cycles of freezing and thawing with excellent coverage with the ice bowl and no intraoperative complications. Again, this you can see the early post-cryo scan that we do regularly, routinely at two weeks after the cryotherapy treatment. And you can also see the isotones where we reach minus 40 degrees at the location of the tumor and zero degrees at the more extensive treatment. There was good coverage of the lesion and no complications. The follow-up is PSA and MRI driven. We are five years down the line from the initial HIFU and the PSA has been very well stable. The one-year post-op MRI showed good treatment and visual coverage with no new lesion and no recurrence. We're currently awaiting for the three-year post-cryo MRI, which is planned in July. And the functional outcome so far has been very good with complete continence, still good erection function using PDE5 inhibitors and no complication afterwards. This is, as you can see, we can see really well the one year post-op MRI scan after the cryo where there is no evidence of residual tumor.
That's so much, David. Yeah. Great presentation. Yeah. I'd like to invite any comments from the faculty. Uh, what do you guys think?

It's a fantastic case. Uh, it raises the question about sequencing basically. And if you have a failure with one modality, is there an advantage to switching to a different focal, a different form of energy? And, uh, I have absolutely no idea, and I don't think we have any data on this. It's a very interesting and unexplored question.

So I'm going to jump in. So yes, the case was to show that the choice of energy has to be based on the location where you are. Then you can change one or the other. But I may leave all the comment before I say more, actually.

Yeah. Well, I noticed your beautiful MRI pictures and I noticed that you seem to have a schedule where you will do the MRI one year post-treatment. And if I'm not wrong, your protocol seems to be that if you don't see a target, maybe you'll do an MRI again three years later. So I just, I just, am I, am I right to say that? Is that, is that your, how you do it?

Yeah, exactly. So we've got to schedule for, depending on the risk of the disease. So we do an early MRI post-op, because I think it doesn't say if you've eradicated everything, but it will indicate for the follow-up what has been ablated. and the quality of the ablations and what went one year, three years, five years. And then we are very much guided by the MRI, but the PSA as well. So if there is any discrepancy between a PSA which is rising and we don't really understand why, we still trigger a biopsy. If the MRI is positive, but the PSA is still stable, we still trigger, we trigger even more a biopsy. So it's a very much image-driven protocol we have. And in terms of data about that, I think we've got long-term data now showing we don't have patient metastasizing. So I think this is really reassuring. And in terms of data, I think we've got 20, 25 cases like cryo plus HIFU, and I think changing modalities. And we learned from these cases as well that probably the entire component was too much on this case for HIFU. And another comment I wanted to do about HIFU, the HIFU technology, is really about what we do now is a dose escalation. It's like we do overlay multiple times a treatment on one zone to make sure that we have enough energy going there. So in this case, probably only one layer on the core of the lesion was not enough.

Perfect. And, uh, just a question to the other faculty, Art, and maybe Jeremy, perhaps you could weigh in on what's your follow-up protocol after focal therapy. I mean, we agreed that we should do biopsies maybe a year later, but how about down the road? What do you tell your patients?

So I'll go first, at least Clement and the team from UCL, these guys are leading the area in the thought or their mental progression of follow-up. If at one year I do a biopsy because I'll have a lot of trials and another plug for the focal therapy society registry. We want to get more people included. We have I think up to over 500 cases already put into the registry and we're looking forward to expand that every day. So please participate. Um, it's agnostic to the modality, but I do a biopsy at one year and then I more or less use an active surveillance protocol looking at, you know, what does our initial pathology was, what the PSA trend is. And then I image, as you saw my case, it was a four year post ablation biopsy. So it was three years from his one year biopsy. And I used imaging, not as PSA to drive the conversation and, It's a difficult task because someone's like, what's a PSA be a metric of success? I don't think there's any clear cut what each patient produces because PSA is a function of leakage into the bloodstream. Depending on the tumor architecture can, I think, change a little bit. I just look at it as a leaky silo. How are the glands maintaining the PSA? Post focal, if you've ablated everything, and you can see my patient went from 13 to 1.2, 1.9, somewhere around there. That's kind of how we've approached it. So imaging drives more of our intervention and our imaging occurs at, at the most, I wait three years and re-image like an active surveillance Prius protocol, which is that three to four years post confirmatory biopsy.
Thanks Alex. How about you, Jeremy?

Yeah, similar. So as I mentioned, with regard to focal brachy, we get an MRI and targeted and template transplanting a biopsy at 18 months for everybody, regardless of PSA, even if their MRI has become negative, we'll do the biopsy anyway. After that, the protocol is much less prescriptive. We still do six months, well, three monthly PSAs after two years and then six monthly. But after that, it does depend actually on the PSA to an extent, if presuming that that post-treatment biopsy shows no significant cancer at all. And like Art said, you'll often have a tiny amount of low-grade disease elsewhere. So I think we are actively surveying the rest of the prostate, you know, the untreated portion of the prostate. So I think an active surveillance type of follow-up is appropriate.

Thanks. I guess the, hopefully the evidence for more mature series, as well as the focal therapy registry will help us, help to inform us about that. Well, you know, we had a wonderful hour, but I'm always mindful of the time. We are now at the end of our allotted hour. So I just want to thank all of you. We had an excellent discussion covering the points of treating limited volume intermediate grade cancer with focal brachytherapy. We had a case of salvage focal therapy after radiation therapy, and we had some excellent points on when to do repeat focal therapy or fall back on whole gland salvage. So I'd really like to thank the faculty panel for the wonderful discussion, and the audience for being here to learn and share these lessons with us. Now, this is the third webinar in our series, and this, together with our first two webinars, are available on the Focal Therapy Society website, which is at FocalTherapy.org. So please, for those of your friends and colleagues who have missed it, please send them there too. We are planning for our next iteration in August 2022, so please look out for our next email and join us again. We're always looking to improve, so also take a moment to fill out the evaluation form before you log out of the Zoom meeting. Again, thank you for your participation, and I wish you a great day or evening ahead. So thank you, everybody.

reference_conclusion: Following multidisciplinary review, management proceeded with repeat right-sided focal therapy using interstitial cryotherapy for the anterior residual lesion, while the low-volume Gleason 3+3 focus in the left posterior prostate was managed with active surveillance. Follow-up was planned with a PSA- and MRI-driven surveillance protocol, including early post-treatment MRI, MRI at 1, 3, and 5 years according to risk, and biopsy triggered by concerning MRI findings or unexplained PSA rise. At the time of review, the 3-year post-cryo MRI was scheduled for July.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Right distal ureter high-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma with regional lymph node involvement; clinical stage cTx N2 M0. Chronic kidney disease stage 3 was present at diagnosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Ureteral biopsy demonstrated high-grade urothelial carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a sessile tumor in the right distal ureter, an atrophic right kidney, and multiple enlarged right-sided regional lymph nodes including hilar, retrocaval, and interaortocaval nodal stations. No distant metastatic disease was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Screening for Lynch syndrome showed no indication of Lynch syndrome.

[ laboratory results ]: Estimated glomerular filtration rate at presentation was 42 mL/min/1.73 m². Differential renal function study confirmed poor function of the right kidney.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: A ureteral stent was placed locally at initial presentation.

[ other clinical data ]: The primary tumor was described as sessile. The case was characterized as lymph node-positive upper tract disease without evidence of distant metastasis.

Yeah, and I was obviously playing the devil's advocate, not the devil, I was playing the devil, not the devil's advocate, necessarily, in suggesting we do surgery first, but the point being that this is not a surgical situation. Yes, we can maybe feel immediately gratified because we're removing all the disease, but that patient is going to recur, as that graph shows you. They're going to recur very quickly, and they're going to have explosive disease, and survival is going to be awful while they're recovering from the surgery that they should not have had at the first place. The point here is that systemic therapy would be indicated with lymph node positive disease. And then, you know, as Dr. Cole already mentioned, her go-to at this point would be EV Pembro, which is a recent development within the past year. As it turns out, this case is a bit more historical, before this was available. And so, you know, this may not be relevant now, although there may be situations where it could be if a patient isn't a candidate for EV Pembro. At our institution, with someone who's got, is not cisplatin eligible, they give this gem taxoladriamycin as a nephron-sparing initial chemotherapy because what we notice and have observed and have published on this is that many times as this chemotherapy is working and the cancer responds, their kidney function improves for reasons we don't fully understand, but we definitely have observed. And once that kidney function improves to a certain threshold, then they switch to cisplatin. And then so the patient got MVAC for five cycles. And so just to kind of cut to the chase, because of the very satisfying radiographic response to chemotherapy, the patient then underwent open nephro-ureterectomy with an extensive lymph node dissection of all the previously diseased sites and then maybe a little bit more intravesticular chemotherapy. That's a great point. That's a great point. Not by the post. Thank you. This is like out of the playbook with my fellows, because when I go to those cases, I usually look to see which films they put up. And usually, it's the post-chemo films. Thank you very much. Because there's no clear template, right? Yeah, we didn't plan that. I'm really happy to see that we think alike. So again, chemotherapy is the primary treatment. So honestly, if you do choose to go EV Pembro, you're basically saying this is out of the box and you may never go to surgery. So we're very clear with the patients that we're really hoping to control your disease. If we get a really great response, we might be able to pause for surgery. But if you're in that 30% who has the complete response, you may not need anything else. You know, kind of like the Lynch syndrome patients. It's a way to kind of overcome the fact that not all of us are gonna have Lynch syndrome and respond beautifully to immunotherapy, that Infortimab is a really strong partner.

Very good. And so this goes back to one of the pre-test questions you got, which is that surgery here provides consolidation after we see that there's been a good response to chemotherapy. So if it's an extremely rare situation where the patient is progressing on chemotherapy, surgery would not be the answer either. Correct? Would you agree? Yeah.

And just one more thing I'll throw in there is, you know, this is early days for us with just seeing what happens to patients on EV Pembro who may have never been, you know, operable to begin with. But we're also doing quite a bit of radiation therapy to the areas of disease that were present to consolidate without operating on them and taking something out of their body, particularly when it comes to intact bladder patients. which I know isn't this session, but we're definitely going down.

Not long-lasting radiation, but we're walking into those realms.

Susanna, I have a question. If there was active viable tumor in the nodes, would you consider giving adjuvant NEVO? And what happens if you give someone who has had Pembro or Nevo? I don't know the answer to that.
If we had started with Kibo and then give Nevo?
You've given EV Pembro. Can you, there's data on adjuvant Nevo, you know what I'm saying?

There's no data on post-EV Pembro immunotherapy. We're actually running a trial that's almost live from ECOG looking at that question. But I would only do adjuvant Nevo. I have actually done sometimes for patients who did not receive any neoadjuvant, anything, ended up having very bad disease. I have sometimes given them a full course of chemotherapy, whether it's Gemsys or CarboGem, and then I've moved right into Nevo because they're so high risk. And I can't always get that paid for, but sometimes I can, so I just try.

reference_conclusion: Primary management should consist of systemic therapy rather than upfront surgery for lymph node-positive, locally advanced upper tract urothelial carcinoma. Current preferred systemic treatment is enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab; if this is not feasible, initial nephron-sparing chemotherapy may be used with transition to cisplatin-based therapy if renal function improves. Surgical intervention, if pursued, should be reserved as consolidative treatment after a favorable radiographic response to systemic therapy, with lymph node dissection planned according to pre-treatment imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration/biopsy of the thyroid nodule was classified as Bethesda VI, diagnostic of thyroid cancer with papillary features. Cytologic features included nuclear clearing, prominent nucleoli, irregular nuclear contours, and nuclear grooves.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a right-sided solid nodule measuring 3.2 cm in longitudinal dimension and 2.0 x 1.5 cm in the other recorded dimensions. The nodule was heterogeneous, contained hypoechoic areas, and demonstrated internal blood flow. It was described as somewhat suspicious. Preoperative ultrasound of the neck showed no involved lateral cervical lymph nodes. The lesion abutted the thyroid capsule laterally and approached the trachea.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF positive.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH 1.2.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, at least 3.2 cm in size, abutting the thyroid capsule and approaching the trachea. No lateral neck nodal involvement had been identified on preoperative ultrasound. Distant metastatic status was not documented.
