TSH was 1.2. Thank you. So there is the nodule, Dr. Ferris.

This one looks a little more irregular, looks more worrisome, certainly less well-circumscribed. It's a little hard to tell from the projection whether those are cystic low-density areas or just poor projection, but certainly looks like a solid nodule.

And on ultrasound real time, it was definitely a solid nodule, but with those hypoechoic areas within it, somewhat heterogeneous. Blood flow pattern? So it contains blood flow. And so it was felt to be at least a somewhat suspicious nodule. That's the biopsy material. I don't think you can see it all that well, but there's nuclear clearing and prominent nucleoli and some irregularity in the shape of the nuclei. Nuclear grooves are present as well. And so this was classified as Bethesda 6 diagnostic for thyroid cancer with papillary features, so papillary thyroid cancer. So, ultrasound scan was done preoperatively, no lateral nodes were noted to be involved at the time. On then to management of the central neck in this case, clearly we're going to do a thyroidectomy. I suppose I should ask first, is anybody on the panel going to do a lobectomy?
Sure, why not?
Good, I'm glad.

No, no, what is it in this patient that makes her a candidate for total thyroidectomy. Unless you tell me she has gross extra thyroid extension, which matters. Unless you tell me this is poorly differentiated histology, that matters. Or unless you tell me that the tumor has invasion of central compartment viscera. Her age of 46 does not put her into the high-risk category. And I think, if you give me a moment, I want to address the myth of 45-year-age cutoff.
That's why I made her 46.

Because there is nothing that happens on your 45th birthday that makes you high risk. So we have carefully looked at this and validated that from data from our institution, from Toronto, from MD Anderson, from Brazil, and from Australia. So there is a validation by five different institutions. using recursive partitioning curves, ROC curves, to see where does the line for worsening of prognosis for recurrence and death due to cancer fall. That's not 45. That line actually drops at 56, and the recommendation to the AJCC-UICC staging committee in the coming year is going to shift the age cutoff line from 45 to 55. By doing that, we would be moving 17% of thyroid patients who get unnecessarily aggressive treatment because they just happen to be 46.

So let me challenge you just a little because here's a patient she's got. Although these two dimensions are 2 and 1.5 centimeters in longitudinal dimension, It's 3.2 centimeters. So this is going to be at least a T2 tumor. A large papillary of classic subtype is going to have lymph nodes involved in the central compartment in more than 60 to 70 percent of cases. So she's going to be a node positive T2, N1A at least, M unknown, papillary cancer when you have resected this. And that is going to give her a stage probably three designation at a minimum. So now we're talking about a stage three cancer in this woman, and you're only going to do a lobectomy. Let's take a poll of the audience and tell me.

Wait, wait, wait, before you take the poll. You exactly enumerated the problem of the staging system. Because thyroid cancer is not like a pregnancy test. There are many gradations of thyroid cancer. So this patient will go to the operating room at my institution with the following consent, right thyroid lobectomy, possible total thyroidectomy, possible central compartment dissection. Because those decisions are made intraoperatively. If she has no enlarged lymph nodes identified at the time of surgery, if she has no gross extra thyroid extension demonstrated at the time of surgery, there is no data that doing more than a lobectomy makes any difference.

So let us then say you're going to do a lobectomy at this end of the table, a total thyroidectomy at the other end of the table, but both of you would agree, I think, the central neck is very important. Dr. Shah, you would presumably do something in this ipsilateral central neck. Dr. Ferris, I'm assuming you would do something in the bilateral central neck. What something would you do? We'll explore the central nodule. Hold on. Dr. Farris answer.

I don't think there's an indication for a bilateral central compartment dissection in this case, unless you told me that the nodule was straight in the middle in the isthmus, for instance. But other than that, I think a ipsilateral central compartment staging procedure is reasonable.

So how are you going to stage it? Are you going to ignore it, inspect it, dissect it, reset it? What exactly are you going to do surgically? Again, remind me, remember I'm an endocrinologist here, I think in simplistic terms.
So if you're asking what is removed, are you saying whether to make the decision to do so or not?
Well, what I'm saying is you're going in to operate on this woman's thyroid. I presume you're going to do a removal of the thyroid and you will at least look into the central neck.
Sure.
And I think identify the nerve and those kind of things.

Dr. Shah makes the point that we always inspect the central neck nodes. And that would be one situation where a frozen section could be valuable if there was something concerning or if there are features with regard to the gland itself, that lobe that looked worrisome and it looked more aggressive than the ultrasound suggested. But I think in this case, I would say I would be leaning toward it. Leaning towards? Doing a central peritracheal dissection on that side.
So can you describe what you mean by a peritracheal dissection? What do you actually take out?
Skeletonizing the nerve, removing the peritracheal, pretracheal, and paralaryngeal lymph nodes.
And Dr. Orloff, is that what would happen in California?

I wouldn't be satisfied. I have to put in a plug for a dynamic ultrasound, because that ultrasound picture you showed us has other worrisome features. The tumor at least abuts the capsule laterally in the thyroid. It approaches the trachea immediately. I think you would see lymph nodes in the central compartment, in spite of what you read and hear about ultrasound being poor in the presence of the thyroid gland for the central neck. most often see macroscopic nodes in the central neck if you look for them. And so I think you would have a better sense preoperatively of whether there were bilateral or ipsilateral central nodes if you did a more, or you had a dynamic ultrasound to review. So depending on what that showed, I think I would most likely do at least an ipsilateral central neck along the lines of what Dr. Farris described, but possibly bilateral if there were nodes on ultrasound bilaterally.
So you would want to remove the node-bearing tissue, or you would pluck out the nodes?
No. Plucking is not in my vocabulary.
All right. And Dr. Shah, I presume you would say the same thing. If there were visible nodes, you would do something about them.
Visible or palpable, yes.
OK. What about this idea of a distinction between central compartment dissection and central compartment resection, which in ICD-10 are going to be two different codes? What's the difference?
Semantics.
Semantics, nothing other? So you do the same procedure? for those two codes? What do you code it as?

I think, you know, Brian, we need to clarify what does a central compartment lymph node dissection mean. And I would like to have the surgeons on the panel define when they do a central compartment dissection, what do they actually do?
So there's the challenge to the surgeons, please.

Well, in this setting where you're doing it at the time of the total thyroidectomy, the nerve is skeletonized. If we're not going to do it, there's a large portion of the nerve that's not usually exposed and dissected. In a case where you're doing a comprehensive ipsilateral dissection, then the nerve is going to be skeletonized so that the lymph node packet, lateral, medial, to the nerve as well as A pre-tracheal, the central portion of the pre-laryngeal and pre-tracheal nodes are also dissected. They're not always kept in continuity, just given their orientation. But it's a comprehensive dissection where the nerve is dissected in its entirety down to the level of the innominate artery from the cricoid insertion point.
And that sounds like a definition that I'm comfortable with.

So this lesion was on the right side, and I think it bears mentioning that the recurrent laryngeal nerve on the right divides the central compartment in a way different from the left, and that there's a substantial nodal packet posterior deep to the recurrent nerve on the right side. So it doesn't disagree with what Bob just described, but there is a larger volume of nodal disease posterior and lateral to the nerve. I think otherwise, you know, it's the management of the parathyroids is the real challenge in these central compartments. And so, to some extent, depends on where those parathyroids were and how their blood supply was oriented at the time of the thyroidectomy. I typically would do the thyroidectomy first and do the central compartment dissection after removing the thyroid. So, it's, there's some variation to it.

So one of the reasons that I bring this case up again is to emphasize the difference in mindset between surgeons and endocrinologists, because we tend to think as endocrinologists very simplistically, that you either operate and dissect those compartments in the central area, or you ignore them altogether. And I think the subtleties are often lost on us. And I think it's those subtleties that lead to some of these very heated debates about how we should actually manage the central neck. When you really sit down with at least the surgeons at Moffitt and you talk through exactly what they do, just as you described, it's actually exactly the same at Moffitt as at Mayo and I suspect as it is at Memorial. These terms that we use are used loosely and don't really describe what the surgeons truly do. So I would make a plea for clearer language and you know, clarity of communication back to the endocrinologists who get upset with you if you don't do something in the central neck. Would it change your management of central neck if it was BRAF positive? We've kind of answered that question before, but does everybody agree that it shouldn't change your management? Anybody in the audience disagree with that? Do you think BRAF is really important in managing the central neck? One hand, one hand.

Please, use. First question is for everybody's central neck in a second. Where is the fascial plane that divides the right and left central neck? I've never understood that. How do you know how far to go over on the other neck to know that you're staying on one side? That's one question. The other question is, do you guys have any pearls on how to preserve the parathyroids when you're taking all the soft tissue out with all the nodes that look like parathyroids?
Sounds like a question for the surgical team.

Well, I don't do elective dissections because I have not been convinced it has any benefit to the patient. And I was going to ask Lisa and Bob both, what do your patients benefit? And how many of them benefit out of the 100 you do? So maybe think about the response to that. Superior parathyroid is easier to preserve because it is tucked away from the lymph node bearing area. And a proper central compartment lymph node dissection means clearance of all lymph nodes from hyoid to innominate and from carotid to carotid. I bet my boots 80 out of 100 surgeons doing elective central compartment dissections don't do that and challenge me on that one.
But what about that definition of left versus right central compartment? Where is the dividing line?

Well, I think it's an arbitrary midline. You clear pre-tracheal lymph nodes up to the lateral aspect of the lower pole of the contralateral lobe. Is that about correct? So you clear pre-tracheal lymph nodes up to the lower pore of the contralateral lobe. But it's an arbitrary line. There is no finite division. Keep also in mind that there is crisscross lymphatic drainage also. Inject dye in one lobe of thyroid and you will harvest it from the contralateral paratracheal area. So it is not strictly unilateral. So Gary has his hand up. Gary, use the microphone. Thank you.

So there is going to be a VA cooperative trial that's going to be looking at elective dissection. This VA cooperative trial is not powered to look at recurrence. It's powered to look at morbidity of the surgery. They define the neck dissection as stopping at the contralateral thymus. I think that was as arbitrary as anything else. There is no fascial plane there. Actually, when you showed that one ultrasound, there's a posterior carotid lymph node there that's more than one centimeter in size. Would not be removed in a standard central compartment dissection, just as you know.

So not only were lymph nodes in the central compartment involved, this tumor was also BRAF positive, but also when the surgeon went in, it was clinically adherent or invasive into the trachea. So this is where head and neck surgeons excel, is doing stuff to the viscera of the neck. So what is the appropriate management of tracheal adherence versus invasion? Anyone who wants to volunteer, please.

Well, I can tell you what it sounds like would happen in my practice is if this were discovered intraoperatively, then attempts would be made to obtain a negative margin on the cartilage to the extent that even a ring could potentially be shaved. But this is where frozen section would be useful. I think in the absence of having a thorough discussion and a plan, I would not be more extensive than that at this stage.

So you would not propose to reset part of the trachea or do anything more aggressive with this disease? You would just shave it down to a negative surgical margin? How far will you shave it? Right into the lumen?
Well, that is occasionally what happens and requires buttressing that and supporting that with strap muscle or some other maneuvers, but hopefully avoidance.
And the rest of the panelists agree with that approach?

We haven't really talked about imaging, preoperative imaging, but I think the best management of tracheal invasion is to anticipate it and really be thinking about it before you get to the operating room. So if you have any suspicion of its presence, getting cross-sectional imaging is appropriate preoperatively. And performing bronchoscopy at the time of intubation to assess for intraluminal disease is also very valuable. difficult once you've already resected the thyroid and haven't really assessed the depth of invasion from the inside out or cross-sectional.

Which raises a crucially important question. When should we be doing cross-sectional imaging in the preoperative neck? And should we be doing it with CAT scan or MRI or some other imaging? And should we, if we're using CAT scan, do it with contrast material? So let's have a little discussion about that.

So if you're going to do a CAT scan, don't waste your time and money doing a non-contrast CAT scan. It's totally useless. And giving contrast dye and getting better imaging to give you better assessment of the central compartment viscera and the tumor is the crucial part. No inadequate operation is going to be patched off by RAI. So only administration of contrast to do a CAT scan implies that your radioiodine administration would be delayed by a few weeks, maybe two months even. I'm not aware of any patient ever even reported as a case report who has died because of delay in RAI administration by two months.

And as an endocrinologist, I would support your view on that 100%. You know, it doesn't take that long for the iodine load to be washed out. typically would check urinary iodine excretion rates to confirm that the iodine load is gone and then move ahead with RAI if that's indicated. But how about...

So Brian, you indicated adherence versus invasion. Yes. Adherence to me implies that you can peel the tumor off the trachea. Invasion to me implies you need to investigate more by imaging, by endoscopy, and be prepared for visceral resection.
So I agree with that, but then the question is, who should be submitted to cross-sectional imaging preoperatively? Is this something we do to every patient or not?
Go back to your ultrasound. Can you show the imaging back?
OK.

So if you see here, you do not see any intraluminal tumor. But you do have concern about the irregularity of the tracheal wall on the right-hand side. I would be inclined to do cross-sectional imaging on this. Keep in mind, you don't have to have intraluminal tumor to have full thickness tracheal wall invasion. The tracheal wall may look smooth. on ultrasound or on cross-sectional imaging, but simple hypervascularity of the mucosa of the trachea and fixation of the tumor to the tracheal wall is tracheal invasion. That tumor you will not be able to peel off. You will actually transact the tumor trying to peel it off. So endoscopic assessment of the trachea to see the area of hypervascularity or telangiectasia is a crucial point which will tell you that the tumor is just next to the trachea or it infiltrates the tracheal wall.
So you would recommend CT with contrast to evaluate this neck preoperatively? Absolutely. Is that the case in Kobe as well? Would you do cross-sectional imaging with contrast material?
Yes, relatively. I checked the CT scan, so contrast.
And in Emory, you would also cross-sectionally image?

Yeah, at times we try to do MRI pre-op, but eventually we end up doing the CT with contrast because you still end up with the same problem of we can't identify the planes, we don't know which one is lymph node and what is blood vessel and things like that.

So again, the question would be to the panel, is this something we should recommend in everybody going through thyroid surgery now, or should we be selective? And if we're going to be selective, what criteria should we use to select a patient for cross-sectional imaging pre-op? Dr. Arsha has suggested, because we're not really seeing the lateral wall of the trachea, medial to this tumor, maybe that's an indication. Should we base it on that? Should we base it on size? How are we going to make this determination? Because once again, I'll point out, ATA guidelines, ACE guidelines, and I think AAES guidelines, none of them call for routine cross-sectional imaging.

So I've been privileged to be part of a writing group from the ATA that is about to publish, and Bob is as well, guidelines on preoperative imaging in thyroid cancer. And most of the focus of this writing project was on nodal disease. and disease that appears to extend beyond the thyroid, not really focusing on characteristics of thyroid nodules within the thyroid. But I think a sort of simple summary is that if you are not confident that you can see everything that might be there to see with ultrasound alone, then cross-sectional imaging is complementary. So it may be the disease that appears to extend beyond your ultrasound limit, and it may be that the patient's body habitus or prior treatment of thyroid-related or unrelated in the neck distorts anatomy such that you just, you can't see completely around the disease, then it's appropriate to do cross-sectional imaging.

So again, I think the message to the endocrinologists would be, you know, be more liberal with your cross-sectional imaging rather than just relying on ultrasound. Sorry, question at the microphone if you will.

I'm Hisham Mahana from Birmingham. I guess what our discussion is saying is that, what Bob alluded to earlier, is that really it's the quality of your ultrasound that's pretty important and that, you know, we often get radiographers and community ultrasound operators doing these regular ultrasounds, and it really has to be somebody who's very experienced at doing ultrasound radiography, or else you get bitten by these, basically.

Absolutely, 100% agree with that. All right, so let's, since we're running remarkably short of time, let's move on to this case, case number three. She's a 28-year-old woman, You can see the problem there in her neck. It's been present for a few months and treated with antibiotics to no benefit. It's felt to be about four and a half centimeters in the right lateral neck, and that was confirmed on ultrasound. Ultrasound otherwise was reported to be negative. There was nothing in the thyroid gland visible. CT scan was otherwise negative, apart from a mass in the right region, too. and a core biopsy was performed elsewhere and was positive for papillary thyroid cancer. So this sounds like it's the old-fashioned lateral aberrant thyroid. Since we're 100 years into the Memorial Sloan Kettering Head and Neck Surgical Service, Dr. Shah, how often do you see lateral aberrant thyroid at Memorial?

reference_conclusion: The agreed operative plan is right thyroid lobectomy with possible conversion to total thyroidectomy and possible central compartment dissection, with final extent determined intraoperatively based on nodal status and gross extrathyroidal extension. In the absence of enlarged lymph nodes or gross extrathyroidal extension at surgery, lobectomy alone is considered appropriate; if central nodal disease is identified, at least an ipsilateral comprehensive central neck dissection/peritracheal dissection should be performed, removing the peritracheal, pretracheal, and paralaryngeal nodal tissue. Given concern for possible tracheal involvement, preoperative cross-sectional neck imaging with contrast-enhanced CT is recommended, with endoscopic assessment as indicated to evaluate for invasion and guide the need for visceral resection planning.
reference_conclusion_quote: So this patient will go to the operating room at my institution with the following consent, right thyroid lobectomy, possible total thyroidectomy, possible central compartment dissection. Because those decisions are made intraoperatively. If she has no enlarged lymph nodes identified at the time of surgery, if she has no gross extra thyroid extension demonstrated at the time of surgery, there is no data that doing more than a lobectomy makes any difference. [...] I don't think there's an indication for a bilateral central compartment dissection in this case, unless you told me that the nodule was straight in the middle in the isthmus, for instance. But other than that, I think a ipsilateral central compartment staging procedure is reasonable. [...] Dr. Shah makes the point that we always inspect the central neck nodes. And that would be one situation where a frozen section could be valuable if there was something concerning or if there are features with regard to the gland itself, that lobe that looked worrisome and it looked more aggressive than the ultrasound suggested. But I think in this case, I would say I would be leaning toward it. Leaning towards? Doing a central peritracheal dissection on that side. [...] Skeletonizing the nerve, removing the peritracheal, pretracheal, and paralaryngeal lymph nodes. [...] So you would recommend CT with contrast to evaluate this neck preoperatively? Absolutely.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you, Tom and everybody and all of you who die hards for staying in the meeting with us. So this will be just a small case to kind of take away the point that things that we routinely do. So 65-year-old gentleman with a PSA of 7.6 and a negative DRE. did not get the MRI images, but we got an MRI that showed a couple of pyrus 3 lesions, and we did the biopsy as shown there on the screen. Came back for a lesion 7, 3 plus 4, and 3 plus 3 prostate cancer. Interestingly, the tumor was located in the, you can see in the right anterior area and the mid area, mostly anterior as well. And with that, we were able to formulate a treatment plan. So, in order to treat this gentleman, we go in ahead and we do it under fusion in the office setting, so we need the fusion platform, the energy platform, and again, you need a registration module, the stepper, and again, we usually do this in the office setting, and this illustrates how we treated this gentleman. We infiltrate the perineum with local anesthesia, usually lidocaine, either 1% or a diluted 2%, and we put in then the Foley catheter. And as we go, then we make sure that the prostate is in the actual place, just above that one number, and we go ahead and do then the deeper block. We try to block on each side of the urethra, and then do kind of like the onych maneuver with the lidocaine, so it spreads laterally, and then we kind of numb up each novabascular bundle, or especially the area, like in this gentleman, that we're gonna treat on the right side. make sure that the ultrasound is calibrated with the fusion device and once this is in place, we go ahead and do the swap of the prostate. We will acquire the prostate ultrasound images coming. This can be done either in transverse or actual view and once we have that ultrasound set up, then we will start the scanning and that's what you see as we go through the prostate. The screen is in green, meaning that all these pictures are coming in, and then you want to capture at a rate that is smooth, so you get great quality. And then the fusion really is done, we just tell the system where is the prostate, the front, the end, I mean the apex and the base and the boundaries, and the system is the one that does the actual fusion, the core registration. So you hit that. orange button, and then the prostate will show up. And this gives you the perspective on how to treat these patients where you have your intended ablation zone, and it will also tell you where you should go in the grid and where you should place the cryoprobes so you can achieve the ablation that you desire. Of course, if you want to modify it while you're doing it, you can do that, and you can see also the prostate in both the sagittal view and transverse view. And this gives us a good perspective on the lateral boundaries, especially when the ablation starts and the whole hypoachronicity is evident. So you can see how we nail it there. We like to see that right on the point, and then we go through the freezing and thawing process, and we have our goals set up in order to treat. And this is how we basically treated this gentleman. So, you know, I know that there's much controversy, like this is the type of patient that you could say, well, you put him on surveillance as well, you could do that. But in our philosophy, it's like if you know exactly where those tumors are, why not treat it? Because the harm associated with this is extremely low, thankfully. And that's what we've done. We've made a recent analysis over 1,300 men that we have treated in this same way. It's what we define as targeted therapy, which usually means ablating less than 40% of the gland, so it's not hemiablation or hemiablation plus. And we were looking at the differences in conversion, really to surgery, radiation, or initiation of handwriting deprivation, what we call the disease progression or development of METs, where we have about 65 events recorded. And we didn't see real differences between the Gleason's. 3 plus 3 and the 3 plus 4, and then when you combine that and you see to the Gleason's, 4 plus 3, is that where you start making a slight difference, but if you were to see those curves, they look like prostatectomy curves when I was a resident doing research or a fellow. This is the sweet spot also about focal therapy, that there is an improvement in IPSS scores that is sustained over time, and that's one of the benefits to the patient. Furthermore, you're not talking about incontinence and other issues, but basically there is a great quality of life associated with this procedure, so it's not a traumatic or dramatic change in lifestyle. And the same happens even with erections without PDE5 inhibitors, you can see that there's a, a change, and then with PD-5 inhibitors, they go almost to the 20 score, so it's a pretty good outcome. Here we show in this slide, and this QR code shows our publisher technique, so you can see it step by step. And one of the most intriguing aspects of this is that there will be, as we are not seeing a whole lot of predictors, we see the PSA density, however, and the absolute PSA level, looking at this respiration tree, are one of the most important indicators. So maybe have predictors of what's, going to be the success of what we do. So, as I said, thank you very much, and I'm open to any questions. Yes.

Thank you, Fernando. Great presentation. I have two questions, and I always wonder, you do a lot of this and talk to people around the country. There's this concept about the time that you hold the temperature. After you reach your diameter, is there a value of holding the temperature for a while, and if that is the case, how long?

Yeah, that's a great question, Dr. Pausan. So, you know, we did a lot of studies in the beginning, measuring the time it takes to expand that ice ball, depending on which probes are you using, I mean, were you using EndoCare or were you using the Galil system? And for most of them, the first I wanna say four to five minutes is where you have that expansion and it holds. Now one of the advantages of this type of treatment is that you, since you're not treating the entire gland, you can go full speed and full power. So we start at 100%. We don't start low and then it go crescendo. We start at 100% and if anything, then you taper it off. But we like to hold it at least for three minutes. keep that ice ball really packed, and you could see the edge of the ball, which is usually at zero degrees, and you hold it tight for at least three minutes. Our typical cycles last eight minutes. We thaw, now it's a little bit more. anywhere between 10 and 13 minutes, we're actually thawing passively because of the expense and sometimes the supply of helium, and then we go ahead and do another thaw, another freezing cycle at eight minutes, and then we thaw up to the point that we can move the needles, and then we take them out, and the whole thing is passive.

Great talk, and I was wondering, in your massive experience and long follow-up, whether your selection of patients excluded certain patients, whether it excluded extreme apical tumors, whether it excluded periurethral tumors, and were there any nature of tissue that you excluded as well?

Yeah, so when the tumors are close to urethra, we use the termocoupler. and we'll be very sensitive to the temperature around that area. And sometimes if it's very close, we'll use a warmer. I will say that we use warmers about one every 15 cases or so, so not routinely. But we've been able to treat every tumor so far. So we don't restrict it based on that location. Aaron?

Yeah, okay, great. Great case, you know, having done a few cryos myself in my career, I've always done it with urethral warmer. So that was my question, you know, as to how you feel. I mean, you haven't had any sloughing? No, we do. We have had. And so how often do you have that and how do you manage that?

Yeah, that's a great question. So that occurs every now and then. So we, as a routine, we try to take the foley out about a week later. And then the overall adverse event rate that we have associated with this patient is about 8%. And if you go there, 75% of those adverse events are related to urinary retention. So 1% of the patients, okay, we have had, out of the 1,300, we have 14 that we had to do a TURP.
Yeah.
Okay. But most of the time when they have some of that sloughing, it doesn't bother them. They tell you, and then it goes away within. Yeah.
I guess the question is, why not put the warmer in?
Why not use it?

Yeah. I mean, if you've ever dealt with it, and I'm sure you have, and I've dealt with it in the years past before we had a great warming system, it's difficult. You know, you have intermittent catheterization, prolonged catheterization, TUR, et cetera, et cetera. Why not? Why not?

Well, often what you see when you're doing this is that the urethra gets pushed to the opposite side. So it's not even close. I mean... And even if the tumor is closed, then you want to take it completely, because sometimes you have the catheter in the middle. But I guess that we have started that way. It hasn't become a big enough problem to make us change so far. But many people use it like you do all the time. I mean, Dr. Shanti uses a wormer all the time. And it's good practice, I'm not saying it's not, but I tell you, it's another, just getting it in, I guess it adds a little bit of time sometimes.
Well, it also seems like you're treating more primary cancers than you are salvage cases, so maybe in the salvage cases it clearly has a role, maybe not in the primary, untreated cases. Great.

Hi, thanks, great presentation. Could you elaborate on how, if at all, your treatment planning has changed? I mean, I noticed you're sort of, the way that you marginated with your planning around your tumor. Yeah. I guess, do you feel that is limited at all by the software? Are you able to adjust that, and has that sort of planning in your margin changed over time as these 1,300 cases have been performed?

Yeah, it certainly has changed, and as we migrated to transpreneal biopsies, because we started back in 13, really, that's where we start having more change. So since 2017, we haven't done a transrectal biopsy, right? So now we use the information of the positive course, and we also use information that's driven by the negative course, and that helps us set up the boundaries of where we wanna go, and of course, then the natural boundaries, the lateral boundaries of the prostate, we try to stop right there. So then we measure, based on the estimates of the ice balls, how that's gonna go, and then depending on the cryo machine that we're using, in Miami we use mostly V-Probes, so you can measure the length, and all that is done before we take the patient to the procedure, so all that is done when we plan the procedure, so the day of the procedure, you know, really what we're doing is executing the case. We don't worry about the planning. If we have to change something on the fly, we'll do it, but it happens less often than, I mean, it really doesn't happen that much.
And a quick follow-up, so in your post-biopsy, the post-treatment biopsy, there's typically four cause, and when they are done, are they targeted only, or are they targeted plus a template?

So, great point. Okay, so we were doing it, encouraging all of our patients to have this biopsies routinely and we did this up to 2019 where we did an analysis where we have about 70% of our patients up to that point that had a biopsy and we noticed that if you apply the PI-RADS to the untreated prostate and that was a one or a two and you did not have contrast enhancement really, the positivity of that biopsy was about 4%. Now we have a big series that we're gonna be submitting soon with a lot of these patients. And that's where we said, for those, we don't now, we give them the alternative. We said, you know, if you want to be very, very intense, you would get another biopsy. Otherwise, if the PSA is non-trending and the MRI is essentially negative, we're just watching. And after that point, the other amendment we had done is that we want to do an MRI at least at year five for everybody, so we're encouraging that since we have many. And in between time is for costs. It depends on the PSA fluctuation.

Great presentation, Wei Pintan, NYU. I wanted to get your thoughts on whether you think the type of biopsy actually matters after cryoablation. Because usually when we freeze for cryo, we freeze based on the length of the prostate, right? So you're going from base to apex. So, technically, you shouldn't recur on the base or the apex if you didn't leave residual tissue there. But what happens is that the freeze going down, if you don't freeze enough, you may get recurrence on the APXS of it. So, if you're only doing transperineal biopsy, you may miss that and you may not pick that up. Whereas, if you come from the rectum, you have a higher tendency to pick that up. And full disclosure, I only do transperineal biopsy.

I mean, I think that how you do the biopsy matters. And the information that you get from your pathology matters as well. We've been working with a pathologist out of PathNet that gives you the actual amount of tumor that's in that core and where it is. So now we can map that to the fusion system and have an idea of the cancer distribution. One of the advantages of a transprenal biopsy is that you move away from this concept based mid apex. You're often biopsying two zones at the time and you understand then the tract. And yes, you can measure it based on the length of the prostate. If it's not going to really harm the urethra or the bundles, then you can take more tissue if you wanted to. All right. Okay, thank you.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board-supported management consisted of office-based MRI/ultrasound fusion-guided focal cryoablation targeting the right-sided anterior and mid-gland lesions, using a targeted ablation approach involving less than 40% of the prostate. The procedure was performed transperineally under local anesthesia with Foley catheter placement, image registration and treatment planning on the fusion platform, followed by cryoprobe placement and freeze-thaw cycles to achieve the planned ablation zone. Post-procedure management included Foley catheter removal at approximately 1 week. Subsequent surveillance was to be guided by PSA trend and MRI findings, with repeat biopsy offered selectively if intensive follow-up was desired and MRI remained negative with non-rising PSA, and MRI encouraged at year 5.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Four weeks of right neck swelling.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bulky locoregional nodal metastases. Structural distant metastatic disease to the lungs was present.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial needle biopsy was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Core biopsy identified a RET fusion–positive papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Outside ultrasound demonstrated a 3.3 cm right thyroid nodule and an approximately 11.5 cm right neck mass described as a group of matted nodes.  
- Physical examination showed right thyroid bed fullness and a large oblong right neck mass extending from just below the ear inferiorly into the neck.  
- Flexible fiberoptic endoscopy showed normal voice and normal vocal cord motion.  
- CT neck showed diffuse calcifications in the enlarged thyroid; an approximately 12 cm group of matted right cervical lymph nodes; additional left neck nodes; and bilateral central compartment nodes.  
- CT demonstrated nodal disease extending from the lateral neck into the central neck, with tumor abutting the vertebral artery; additional potential interfaces involved the sternocleidomastoid muscle and jugular vein.  
- Chest CT demonstrated pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Core biopsy molecular testing identified CCDC6-RET fusion (RET-PTC1).

[ current disease status ]:  
- Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bulky right cervical nodal disease extending from the lateral neck into the central neck.  
- Tumor abutted the vertebral artery, with additional potential interfaces involving the sternocleidomastoid muscle and jugular vein.  
- Structural distant pulmonary metastatic disease was present on chest CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had otherwise been healthy.  
- Examination outside the neck was negative.

reference_discussion.text: Yes, hi, I'm Greg Randolph. I'm an otolaryngologist at Mass Eye and Ear and Mass General, and I'm very honored. I want to thank Mark and thank Mike for putting this wonderful program together. And so this will be a thyroid tumor board. I appreciate also Peter Sadow, our expert pathologist. He really helped a lot with many of the slides here relating to pathology. And it's really my honor to be here with such a elite group of panelists. So we're going to do three cases, and I'm going to just kind of present the case and then Mike will take it and moderate through the panel. So the first one is a case number one, which is a case of local regionally advanced DTC. I wanna first think that when I say these are my cases, they're really our cases. We have a very, very large group of people. And I think all of us would admit that all of our activity research and otherwise is really multi-pronged and based on all of our colleagues that we work together. This is a sampling of all of the people that help to treat these patients and research the problems that these patients present. So this is a lovely 26 year old woman who came up from North I think from New Hampshire or so and she had a four weeks of right neck swelling, otherwise completely healthy. She had a outside ultrasound when she came down that showed a 3.3 centimeter right thyroid nodule and an 11.5 centimeter something or other in her neck, a group of matted nodes, they thought perhaps, and she had a needle biopsy that was positive for PTC, and then it was referred to our practice. So, Mike?

Yeah, so when we have these, we'll start with Eric, and then we'll go to Mark. Eric, sort of, what initial thoughts when you're seeing this and sort of, you know, what are you thinking about as we're sort of thinking out loud here a little bit?

I didn't have the ultrasound. I mean, I'd say, you know, acute onset of enlargement of the anterior neck. And I'd be wondering, is there a cyst that bled? Is there some maybe even de Quervin's thyroiditis that's showing kind of a mass? Those are more common issues that would kind of acutely grow. I will say the ultrasound here, you know, that shows a very large lymph node. So that is not a subtle, a small thing. And that kind of changes everything. And I would try and get a handle on whether the patient really feels there's been that rapid of growth, and that would lead to really concern for a very aggressive process.

Yeah. Now, Mark, this, you know, it's a tumor board. So, we all know this is going to be thyroid, but you don't always know that when people walk in your door, right? So, are there, what else is going through your mind when you're looking at this beyond just the sort of typical thyroid cancer stuff, Mark?

Thanks, Mike. So, yeah, I think, as Eric mentioned, I mean, I think if you didn't have the, you know, the ultrasound and the biopsy, you would be looking at the possibility of some type of benign you know, thyroiditis, of course, once you see sort of the enlargement of the significant enlargement of these lymph nodes, you're not thinking that anymore. But the other thing in this age group, I mean, lymphoma, of course, would be in your differential. So, you'd be asking the patient if they have had fevers, night sweats, weight loss, those types of things.
Okay. And Greg, tell us about your physical exam now when they got to you.

Yeah, so we have a right thyroid bed fullness, she's a fairly thin person and you can feel it feel felt like I remember it felt like a banana in her neck, there was this oblong ovoid. mass that started just below her ear and extended downward into the neck. There was some lobulation to it, but it felt like one large mass. We examined her otherwise negative, and her voice and vocal cord motion were normal on flexible fibro-optic endoscopy. And so then the next question is, what sort of imaging would you get? She had had an outside ultrasound, but In these sorts of patients, I really never ever rely on outside imaging, especially when the findings are quite extreme on exam. I worry about the accuracy and cuts of the CAT scan and so forth. So these are usually people who get, you know, clean slate new imaging here. But what would everyone, Mike, what would you think about imaging ultrasound alone? What else? Anything?

Yeah. So, I mean, I think when you, there's very little question when we have these big, lots of lymph nodes in the neck and big masses, we're going to go to imaging beyond ultrasound, right? So, we've all seen ultrasound underrepresented that. To Dr. Ghassandi, in some patients, some centers go to MRI with contrast, other folks do CT with contrast. It seems to be very kind of center and physician specific. Is there any reason to pick one versus the other when we're looking at neck and lymph nodes in the neck?

I prefer CT. It's quicker. most patients cannot stay in the scanner for that long. MRI scanners are longer. The second thing is that most of the lymph nodes for thyroid disease are lower in the neck. So that's when patients are breathing and you get a lot of artifact, particularly from shoulders and breathing by the thoracic inlet. So evaluation of central compartment is much harder, evaluation of level five and four, lateral compartment, neck nodes are much harder. I prefer CT. In addition, the biggest challenge with ultrasound is that you will never be able to evaluate a lateral retrofringal lymph node. So that's why, especially with someone with such bulky disease, which if you don't know the first diagnosis without a biopsy in this age group with lymphoma, you have to consider lateral retrofringal nodal disease. I would go to a CT. Easy, low radiation these days with the new equipment.

Yeah. Dr. Erkin, Dr. Shaha, the young surgeon that I work with over here, he loves CT scans with contrast. That's generally what we do. It seems like you order a lot of MRIs in this setting. Am I sort of dreaming that up or do you have a preference there, Mark?

No, I would agree with Dr. Versandi. Obviously, this question of an iodine load from the contrast, but that really is not something that we pay much attention. The value added is significantly outweighs the delay in RAI.

Dr. Alexander, should we be thinking about anything beyond the neck? We're all focused on the neck with cross-sectional imaging in the neck to guide the surgery. Chest, anything else that you'd be doing? I think so.

I mean just putting this in perspective, if we are dealing with thyroid cancer, I think we had a biopsy or we certainly would get one if we didn't. When you have this amount of disease, you'd be worried about distant disease as well. So you're kind of thinking to yourself, you have to address, diagnose what's going on in the neck. You'd be worried at the rapidity of growth potentially, but you do want to look at the lungs.

Dr. Zeferio, you know, a lot of times I'll see people just operate off the neck and they'll miss these upper mediastinal lymph nodes when somebody has a ton of disease in the neck like this. So, in your cross-sexual imaging, do you do neck and chest or does your neck CT see far enough down to the upper mediastinum? How do you think about that, Mark?

Thanks, Mike. So, yeah, typically the neck CTs do go down and get the superior mediastinum anyway, but we would definitely get a CT neck and chest on this patient as described, just because this demographic of patient would suggest she's in her mid-20s, that this is probably like a pediatric thyroid cancer almost that may have been there for years and even decades and grown over that time. Those patients, in addition to bulky lymph node disease, often have tiny little lung nodules, you know, representing metastasis, and these aren't particularly threatening. They grow, you know, slowly over the years, but they're typically there, and it's a good baseline to have for the patient.

I just want to mention something, emphasize something that Dr. Khorsandi said, which I think is really important, that there's always this debate, MR versus CAT scan. It's all about, you know, cross-sectional imaging is what we want, but that blurring, that MR artifact from breathing in the neck base, that's a very big ticket item, as is the readability and speed of CT scan to quickly have that information, have it read by the surgeons who are going to be bringing the patient to the OR. Those are really good points that are subtle, but I think trump the MRI scan in the setting of getting a quick and easily read CAT scan were very good points. Yeah.

Dr. Rossley, before we move on to look at the imaging, 26-year-old papillary thyroid cancer at some point, is there any role for other nuclear medicine imaging here, or we're just starting down the pathway with the CT scans as you're thinking about this one, Monica?

I don't think a preoperative assessment with nuclear medicine is necessary. You might change your mind after the operation when you've got the surgeon's findings in the operation and the histology, but we don't do any preoperative scanning.
Awesome. Thanks. All right, Greg, let's go ahead and look at it.

We got, I'll show you the image in a second, the CT scan showed diffuse calcifications in the enlarged thyroid, the 12 centimeter a group of matted nodes on the right, some left neck nodes and bilateral central compartment nodes. And the way we're thinking about this now, and I'd be interested in both Mark's commentary on this, is with neoadjuvant trials now, we think of like, where is this tumor going to beat me? That is, what is a potential R2 interface based on this imaging. And so that is where might I leave gross disease if I don't take something outside of the thyroid. That's very helpful for me as I summarize the CAT scan findings and so here, it looked to me like the right RLN, the right trachea, right straps, and that was in terms of potential R2 interfaces relative to the primary in the right thyroid? And then where might this large nodal mass give me problems with an R2 interface? And that was SCM, jugular, and vertebral artery. And so SCM, no problem at all. Jugular vein, no problem at all. Vertebral artery, that's an issue. So I think this is a helpful way of looking at it. I'll show you the images in a second. In terms of ultrasound, I was trying to force the discussion that we've already had, and we obtained it, and it added nothing. Chest CT scan Y, we did get that. And as Mark outlined, I mean, the mediastinum, I think, is well evaluated by our NET-CAT scan. Mary Beth Kinane does a great job with that. But it's really, you want to get more of a robust local regional evaluation. Lori always appreciates this information with the patient coming in. Maybe she can comment on what is this information important for her to have right out of the gate.

But before you move on, I really like this concept of R2 interface. Now, most of the endocrinologists and most of us deal with, we know TNM, but we don't know the R. Can you say just in a second what you mean by that R2?

Yeah, R0, these are the three types of surgical resections. R0 means all tumor macroscopic and microscopic has been resected. R1 means all gross disease has been resected, but there's a microscopic positive margin. And R2 means you cut across gross disease. There's gross disease left in the neck.
So, you're trying to make that decision up front.

These are areas that you would potentially have to leave gross disease, which would be... Or configure a surgery that would encompass that R2 interface. Like, where are the extrathyroidal extension frontiers? Possibly, based on imaging. And, you know, with a good forensic evaluation of your imaging, you can do this.

Okay, so let's, let's look at his imaging, and then look at the molecular testing, because somebody's already mentioned sort of neoadjuvant stuff. And then let's go from there. So what are we looking at?

So this is this is the lateral neck node. So you know, in general, and I'd be interested in Mark, Erkin and Zeferio commenting on, you know, generally, these are pushing nodes, they're keeping everything away, you can often dissect them away from even a jugular vein that's strapped, splayed over them. But you see, in the coronal images, you see, this is not the simple straightforward set of nodes, there's a finger of this group of matted nodes that is extending lateral to the subclavian common carotid bifurcation, and then a finger of disease that is extending into the central neck, and that's where I thought the vertebral artery was being abutted by this tumor. This is not a typical pattern of extension, but when tumor starts to extend dorsally in the neck base, you have to think about things like phrenic and vertebral artery that you typically don't have to worry about for routine thyroid nodal distribution. This also kind of helps to confuse the nomenclature of the neck locations, central versus lateral, because the nodal disease is not in any way respecting that. It's jumping the fence and extending. This is all one group of nodes that will bring you from the lateral neck into the central neck. I'll show these are the other sets of images here with the pulmonary images. And so then we did not automatically bring her to surgery because of that long list of potential R2 interfaces. And so a test was ordered and that would be the next step, but I'll stop for discussion of imaging.

Dr. Wirth, come in here for me for a second. So normally, we're thinking about molecular testing and somatic testing. Normally, it's a long ways down the road to get you involved in it. But now, what's the setting in this pre-op thing we should be thinking about the molecular testing, Lori?

Well, exactly a case like this, although this case is so dramatic. It's kind of a no brainer, but I think that idea of, you know, when the when the surgeon is going to be leaving our to disease behind. I think we're getting to the point where we might want to begin doing something about that in the neoadjuvant setting. Then also, this woman is only 26 years old. I'd be jumping all over Greg to do a core needle biopsy so that we could do molecular testing. I'd be particularly excited about the potential for finding an actionable fusion in this young adult. The pediatric and young adult patients with PTC are much more likely to harbor RET fusions, ENTREC fusions. We even see ALK fusions and rarely ROS1 fusions. You can't do that molecular testing well off of an FNA. A core needle biopsy in this patient would be quite easy to do. It's definitely the right next step to see if we can identify something actionable.

I just want to comment on something subtly that Lori said, which relates in part to something that Mark Zufferio implied, that as you get a multidisciplinary evaluation of this, like I've learned from Peter, learned from Lori, so we're dealing with a young patient, you know, you think about solid variant, you think about pediatric kind of areas like Mark was implying, and so then With Peter and Lori's input, you start to think about this could be a fusion patient, you know, like this is something that you kind of seeing the headlights come down you on the road, but this is really an idea that is generated by a group of people really focused on this a multidisciplinary group.
All right, let's show Lori the somatic testing, and then we'll come to Mark to see where he's going to use that.

And that is exactly what we did. We brought together the group in our Mass General Mass Eye Near Advanced Thyroid Cancer Clinic that Lori and Peter participate in, and a core biopsy was done. And this is the fusion. What I know about this fusion, you could fit on the head of a pin comfortably. And so I'll let Peter or Lori comment on this.
If in doubt, always go to Lori. Lori, you ordered the test. Is this what you were looking for?

I told you so. Actually, I mean, obviously, I know the patient, but this is exactly what we'd be thinking about. This is a RET-PTC1 in the older nomenclature fusion or a CCDC6 RET gene fusion. This is the most common RET gene fusion that we see. The CCDC6 is the five prime fusion partner to the RET part of the gene that contains the intracellular business end or kinase domain of RET. And this fusion leads to constitutive activation of the RET kinase. So that's a driver alteration. And because it's an oncogenic kinase, it should be druggable. Several years ago, there were a couple of drugs that were designed to potently and specifically inhibit the activated Rett kinases that can be activated by these gene fusions in papillary thyroid cancer, also in a small subset of non-small cell lung carcinomas, and then also the drugs were designed to inhibit the Rett mutations that we see in medullary thyroid cancer.
Perfect. Okay, Greg, in the interest of time, take me through the clinical course and then stop once you get the surgery done. And then we'll have Mark comment on his experience with this as well.

Very good. So patient was started on selprocatenib, one of the two new RET inhibitor agents. She basically tolerated this one pill a day incredibly well. In fact, when I said, so how was the medicine? She goes, well, the minute I took it, it started shrinking down my neck disease. And I said, so What about the complications? Were there problems with this? She goes, well, to be honest with you, I didn't know I was on the medicine. They told me right before surgery that my liver function tests went up a little bit, but I didn't really know that I was on the medicine. So this was incredibly well tolerated. This is the before and after coronal images that she had after four months on neoadjuvant cell percatenib, no more R2 interface in the SCM, just in terms of the nodal mass, no more R2 interface with the jugular vein, no more R2 interface with the vertebral artery. This improves my mood considerably as I bring this young woman to the OR. Again, you still have nodal disease, but this is the result. We divide sometimes for more complicated patients, we'll stage the surgery. She had initially a right lateral neck dissection. These are the images that you see there, and then followed by a total thyroidectomy. The right neck dissection showed 10 of 37 nodes. Peter will talk about the path in just a second. We have some images. Then the total thyroidectomy showed this to be right lobe about five centimeters, diffuse sclerosing. Eight of 46 nodes in the central and left lateral neck. And these nodes, just at surgery the and Mark and probably Mark so Pharaoh can comment on this, but these nodes, when we dissected them look like someone had taken a baseball back to them. They were shrunken and hemorrhagic, and they looked beat up. There was some mild desmoplastic reaction around them, but not ponderous. But they had clearly shrunken. There was this rind of desmoplastic reaction around them, but not too, too difficult to dissect. But the nodes themselves looked hemorrhagic and beat up. And so again, the pathology confirmed what we knew based on the core. And Peter, I'll go through these slides as you tell me to here.

Yep. Hold on a second for me. Before we do the path. Dr. Cefario, give me sort of some 30,000 feet observations here. So this is cell per cat nib, it's a red fusion. How long do you generally leave these folks on before you take them to surgery? How much shrinkage do you want to see before you take them to surgery just from a, you know, practical standpoint, Mark?

Thanks, Mike. So yeah, this is a classic, great example of a very, I think, wise use of neoadjuvant RET-specific inhibitors, sulfurcatinib in this case. And yeah, we do have a trial looking at this where ret-altered thyroid cancers, and we've enrolled about 14 patients on that trial, most of which are medullaries, but there's been about four ret-fusion patients we've enrolled in that trial, and they've all been patients like this who were essentially patients in their 20s, have a pediatric-type thyroid cancer presentation with bulky lymphadenopathy. often little lung nodules and they end up having a ret fusion. I completely agree with Greg. From that imaging, it appears that certainly neoadjuvant therapy could help with the R2 interfaces especially. Often, as I think Dr. Randolph mentioned, often these are pushing margins in these types of patients, but you really don't know until you get in there. The last thing you want is to be in a situation where you have to leave gross disease on the recurrent nerve or the vertebral artery or somewhere like that. And so I think this is a great. example of how the R2 interfaces can dictate neoadjuvant therapy. In terms of the timing, in the trial, we typically leave patients on for a maximum of six months. I don't think we have any good data. As Dr. Randolph mentioned, in this case, you typically do see responses in the first month or two. What I've noticed is that the responses are the most dramatic in the first couple of months and then they tend to level off, you know, after that in months three, four, five, and six in terms of the trial. So I think you're at least going to want to leave patients on for two or three months. And, you know, we leave them on up to six months. The other minor point to make is we've had quite a few patients, although these drugs are pretty well tolerated, The issues that we've typically seen and had to dose reduce is due to a lot of patients do have fatigue. That's a very common complaint on the RET inhibitor. Certainly, the increased LFTs were mentioned. Then the other thing that we've seen in a couple of patients is some pancytopenia that we've had to dose reduce for. Those are a few highlights.

Can I just make a comment because I've spoken a lot to Mark and also to your colleague, Rich Wong, both of whom I respect quite a bit about neoadjuvant and how we think about it. And I think for the endocrinologists and oncologists, we're thinking like, so we can shrink the tumor down. So what, what would be the outcomes of this? Like, what are we really trying to do? You know, one would be to say, We will do the same surgery we would have otherwise done but with neoadjuvant therapy, we may get a better margin. That's goal number one. this is an aspirational goal, we may or may not see this, that we may not need to resect that thing that is representing the R2 interface, trachea, esophagus, and I think that will be borne out. Nerve, I'm not so sure about nerve, is linear and gets gummed up in the tumor and that often will still need to come. But trachea and esophagus, I got a feeling we may end up resecting less of those in some circumstances, depending on the degree of invasion that the patient presents with. surface adherence, transmural invasion, there are different degrees.

One quick word of caution. I've had two cases now with neoadjuvant therapy where I had a great response and on treatment, I missed a window and the patient started to progress on treatment. We're still in the nascent stage of this, but just a word of caution.
Very good. Okay, so we're running a little bit long here. I want to look at the slides from Peter, because we're going to talk about adjuvant therapy at several journal clubs going ahead.

I'll pop right through them, Mike. So this is a lymph node. I just wanted to give people a relative lay of the land that where you see those arrows, those blue circles with the purple in the middle, those are germinal centers, which allows us to know it's a lymph node. The asterisk represents where you have viable carcinoma. You'll see some fluffy stuff in the bottom right in white, which those are papillae of metastatic capillary thyroid carcinoma, or you can see architecturally. And then the giant end in the middle is necrosis, and this is actually a response to the drug. Next slide, Greg. This is higher power, and you can just see those areas more closely. Next one, Greg. This is what I wanted to show you. This is actually in the thyroid proper. This is diffuse sclerosing variant of capillary thyroid carcinoma. And I wanted to point out to everyone, just so you can get a great, perfect view of it, those pink bands are what is called sclerosis. Oftentimes there's actually no nodule seen at all in the thyroid because the thyroid's diffusely involved, you don't see a mass. So you could look and see a normal thyroid and then actually see lymphadenopathy, especially in young patients. So the one thing that actually, we could diagnose the fusion based on looking at the slide without actually even needing molecular diagnostics, And the reason we can do that is all those tiny little microcalcifications that you see, which are represented here by me before I became exhausted, the yellow arrowheads, are all pointing toward the calcifications, but there's many, many more. And so that's these microsomoma bodies, tiny little calcifications, are diagnostic of diffuse sclerosing variant and further CCDC6 RET fusion. So this is actually a diagnostic look at this. So next slide, Greg. And this is one sort of small papillary area that's left over. And then next slide. This is what I wanted to point out is that you have these areas that are kind of interspersed within normal thyroid. So that's why I say it's sometimes very difficult to even see a proper mass because it is spread evenly throughout the thyroid. And then next slide. And the other thing I want to point out, this is not typical changes that you see in papillary thyroid carcinoma in terms of the nuclei. They're more round, there are fewer grooves, there are barely any intranuclear pseudo-inclusions. This has a different morphology to the tumor. And so although we call them papillary thyroid carcinomas, it really isn't. And in some ways, it's a very specific tumor that's very distinct from what your classic papillary thyroid carcinoma would look like. And like I said, as we learn more about the genetics, as well as the morphology of these tumors, we're able to actually say, by the way, the genetics are going to be this, because this is what the morphology of the tumor looks like, this is the architecture of the tumor, and although it's still currently classified as we speak as a papillary thyroid carcinoma, I honestly feel by the next edition of WHO, we're going to be classifying these tumors in a different way. Okay, I think that should be it for me, Greg.

Awesome. Thanks, Peter. Laurie, finish this one out for me and Monica. I'll go to Monica first. So, we've used the suppercat neb as neoadjuvant, they've done the surgery. Should we leave them on the suppercat neb to try to do the radioactive iodine scan as a re-differentiation thing? way out there. But Monica, what are you sort of thinking about that if you see one of these that has been treated this way?

Well, I haven't actually seen any treated this way, but because I would have thought diffuse sclerosing variant, you don't need to continue re-differentiation, but I see that you guys did. And that's interesting. I have I mean, I've had cases where we didn't have uptake in known mets and then we have done the re-differentiation in a lot older patients. And then we retreated when the scan showed uptake following re-differentiation. So I thought it was interesting that you kept her on the cell percatinib.

Okay. Laurie, talk about that just a little bit, because I'm going to see this exact patient, honest to God, at 10 o'clock this morning. Same case, same mutation, same diffuse sclerosing, cell percatinib, Dr. Shaha whining about the surgery, and I'm going to have to decide whether or not to leave him on for the radioactive iodine. So what do I do, Laurie?

Well, so I think Monica makes a good point that a young patient like this should be responsive to radioiodine. So why do you need it? One of the reasons that we did it was because we knew that she had the structural distant metastases, and because she tolerated sulprocatenib so well, it was a known entity, and we knew that she wouldn't have any difficulty if we gave her sulprocatenib leading into the radioactive iodine treatment. That fusion does activate the MAP kinase cascade, and so it may indeed downregulate the thyroid differentiation genes, TIPO, the sodium iodine symporter expression. There have been a couple of case reports published now in patients with retfusion positive iodine refractory disease, showing that pretreatment with selprocatinib does bring about uptake of radioactive iodine. So that was the rationale for her treatment and so far she's doing quite well.

That's good for her. So I mean, I think that the teaching points in this case is the imaging when we have all that bulky disease up front, making sure we're doing the adduct surgery, recognizing that you do, that this may not be an easy surgery and shrinkage would help with that, which will lead us down the molecular testing, the ideas of using a neoadjuvant and then still that opening if they're on the drug already, can you just go ahead and do the radioactive iodine while they're on drugs? I think those are good. Greg, how about if I do a player trade for you? Let's do case number three. Because I want to be able to talk about case number three. Can I just have you pop ahead?

reference_conclusion: Cross-sectional staging with contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest was obtained, and preoperative nuclear medicine imaging was not pursued. Given the extensive locoregional disease with concern for potential gross residual disease at critical interfaces, a core needle biopsy was performed for molecular profiling and identified a CCDC6-RET fusion. Neoadjuvant selpercatinib was initiated and continued for four months with marked reduction in disease burden, followed by staged surgical management consisting of right lateral neck dissection and subsequent total thyroidectomy.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after two prior lines of systemic treatment.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Adenocarcinoma of pancreatic origin was reported. No further histopathology details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular profiling identified a KRAS mutation; the specific KRAS variant was not provided. Additional reported alterations included ATM, CHEK2, NF2, CDH1, and TP53. The ATM and CHEK2 findings were described as potentially compatible with clonal hematopoiesis rather than confirmed tumor-derived alterations. No confirmed biallelic loss or homologous recombination deficiency result was reported.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging findings were not provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had received two prior lines of treatment for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Specific regimens and response assessments were not provided.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease persisted following two prior treatment lines.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

So for Gaël's question, indeed, I like to ask the advice from a hematologist to be sure there is no and it is good to have a standard blood test. So, if everything is normal, there is a low risk that there is an underlying hematologic disease, but indeed, the JAK2 mutation could be associated with abnormalities in the blood test that could lead to indications of a hematologic disease. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly progressive metastatic breast cancer on first-line CDK4/6 inhibitor plus aromatase inhibitor.

[ diagnosis ]: ER-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer of invasive lobular histology, initially diagnosed in 2022 as locally advanced breast cancer and subsequently found to have osseous metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Primary left breast mastectomy specimen showed moderately differentiated invasive lobular carcinoma with discohesive neoplastic cells in classic single-file pattern and loss of E-cadherin expression. Residual invasive tumor measured 75 mm. One of two evaluated lymph nodes was positive. Pathologic stage was ypT3N1a. Tumor was strongly ER-positive, PR-positive, and HER2-negative.  
T10 bone biopsy showed metastatic breast carcinoma morphologically similar to the primary lesion. Metastatic lesion was ER-positive at 20%, PR-negative, and HER2-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial PET imaging at diagnosis demonstrated primary breast and axillary disease without definite extra-thoracic metastatic disease; subcentimeter bilateral lung nodules were present and considered nonspecific.  
A routine CT scan in May 2022 identified metastatic bone disease.  
MRI spine demonstrated extensive osseous metastases. Axial imaging through the T6 vertebral body showed osseous metastatic involvement with posterior mass effect causing spinal cord compression.  
Disease progression in bone was documented in December 2022.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor sequencing was performed on both the primary tumor and the bone metastasis. The tumors were clonally related and shared multiple alterations. A clonal BRAF V600E mutation was identified. BRCA2 deep deletion was present. Further analysis demonstrated a large intragenic deletion of one BRCA2 allele with loss of heterozygosity of the other allele, resulting in complete homozygous BRCA2 loss involving most exonic regions. MYC amplification was also identified. Germline testing showed no germline pathogenic variants.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received neoadjuvant dose-dense AC-T chemotherapy for locally advanced breast cancer, followed by mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy. She then completed post-mastectomy radiation therapy. Endocrine therapy with ovarian suppression plus aromatase inhibitor was given; after bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy/oophorectomy, ovarian suppression was discontinued. Adjuvant abemaciclib was delayed for bariatric surgery and started in May 2022. Metastatic bone disease was identified at that time. She subsequently received first-line CDK4/6 inhibitor plus aromatase inhibitor for metastatic disease, with progression in bone by December 2022.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer with extensive osseous involvement, including spinal metastatic disease with cord compression at T6 on MRI. Disease had shown rapid progression on first-line CDK4/6 inhibitor plus aromatase inhibitor.

[ other clinical data ]: Primary tumor size at diagnosis was reported as 9 cm with multiple axillary nodes involved clinically. Surgical pathology showed clear margins. Subcentimeter bilateral lung nodules were present on initial staging imaging and were considered nonspecific.

So the history goes back to 2022 when she was diagnosed with locally advanced breast cancer. She had a PET scan that showed the primary breast and axillary disease, but no disease outside. There were some sub-centimeter bilateral lung nodules that were considered to be nonspecific. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in 2018 with mild hypercalcemia and osteoporosis identified on routine medical assessment, followed by a rapid rise in serum calcium over approximately 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic parathyroid carcinoma with liver metastases and subsequent pulmonary metastases; associated refractory hypercalcemia due to hyperparathyroidism.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial left parathyroidectomy had been performed for presumed benign parathyroid adenoma. Subsequent clinical course and identification of metastatic liver disease established the diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Further investigations in 2018 demonstrated liver metastases. Restaging CT later showed progression in multiple liver metastases. Subsequent CT confirmed progression in both liver and lungs. Disease had initially been confined to the liver before later development of lung metastases. Gallium DOTATATE PET imaging in parathyroid carcinoma had shown only low-level uptake and had not supported peptide receptor radionuclide therapy; no patient-specific positive somatostatin receptor imaging result was documented.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular profiling identified a TERT promoter mutation and a SMARCE1 variant. PD-L1 testing showed CPS >20.

[ laboratory results ]: At the time of marked biochemical progression, serum calcium was 3.9 mmol/L and PTH was 85 pmol/L. Hypercalcemia persisted after initial parathyroidectomy. During later progression, calcium rose to approximately 3.3-3.5 mmol/L. Renal function remained preserved during the documented course.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Left parathyroidectomy was performed in 2018; calcium and PTH did not normalize postoperatively. Medical therapy included cinacalcet and pamidronate without adequate biochemical control. Liver metastases were resected later in 2018, after which calcium and PTH normalized, but both rose again approximately 6 months later. Bisphosphonate therapy was continued during this period. Owing to symptomatic and difficult-to-control hypercalcemia, bisphosphonate was changed to denosumab. Bland embolization/trans-arterial embolization of liver metastases was performed when disease was confined to the liver, with good initial effect; calcium remained only mildly elevated for most of the following year. With later hepatic progression and new lung metastases, repeat trans-arterial embolization was performed just over a year later, with virtually no improvement in calcium. Systemic chemotherapy with ECX (epirubicin, cisplatin, capecitabine) was administered for 6 cycles; this stabilized disease temporarily and reduced calcium to below 3.0 mmol/L, but progression recurred soon after completion, predominantly in the liver. Further liver embolization produced no significant improvement. The patient alternated supportive calcium-lowering therapy with cinacalcet, bisphosphonate, and denosumab. Weekly paclitaxel was given as interim systemic therapy and produced limited temporary disease control but caused toxicity.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic parathyroid carcinoma involving the liver and lungs, with refractory hypercalcemia despite calcium-lowering therapy, repeat liver-directed embolization, and prior systemic chemotherapy. The patient remained clinically well despite marked hypercalcemia.

[ other clinical data ]: Hypercalcemia had become symptomatic during the disease course, although the patient was later described as remarkably well clinically despite elevated calcium levels. He was not eligible for phase I studies because of hypercalcemia.
