reference_discussion.text: I was hoping that Dr Morgenstein would also be on online for this one but this is a 50 year old gentleman. Brilliant, brilliant. Daniel, would you like me to, you can chip in at any point. So this is a 50 year old chap who presented with mild hypercalcemia and osteoporosis to another centre back in 2018 just on a routine medical. But his calcium levels then suddenly dramatically rose over just a short period of just over a month. So his calcium was 3.9 millimoles and his PTH at that point was 85 picomoles per litre. I don't know whether that's your units.
No, we don't speak the Queen's English despite the anniversary. So that's a calcium level around 15 and a PTH probably in the 800-ish range, right Dan?
Yeah, so our upper limit of normal on most assays is 2.6 millimoles per liter. So that's, yeah, anything above three we would consider life-threatening.

Yeah, so these are sky high, I mean high calcium numbers that would be around 15 and a half in our range and a PTH in our assay that goes to 65, this would be around 800 or something in our assay. So clearly way above the range, okay.

So he had a left parathyroidectomy for what was thought at the time to be a benign parathyroid adenoma, but his calcium and his PTH levels didn't fall. all despite sinicalcid and pomidronate and further investigations led to what looked like liver metastases and he was in fact diagnosed with metastatic parathyroid carcinoma. So he actually had resection of those liver metastases later that year and his calcium and PTH normalized but rose again about six months later. and all this time he was receiving bisphosphonate. Restaging CT scan revealed progression within multiple liver metastases. Daniel, would you like to take over the story from here, because I think you know it very well.

Yeah, so this was when he came to see me, and he essentially was not struggling to control his hypercalcemia. He was becoming symptomatic. We switched him from bisphosphonate to denosumab, and there was a case series suggesting that there's a greater response rate in parathyroid carcinoma. and we restaged him to look to see if we could pursue any local ablative treatment. At that stage he only had disease within the liver and we proceeded to a bland embolization of the liver metastasis which worked very well. Calcium was controlled only mildly elevated for the best part of a year. after that, but then started to rise with progression within the liver and development of some lung metastases. We did repeat the trans-arterial embolization almost just over a year later and unfortunately saw virtually no improvement in his calcium after the second embolization. And that's, so after those were so gradual rise despite monthly denosumab and high dose Sinocalcet, that's a point at which we got Kate involved to see him.

Yes, so then, when I saw him, his calcium was rising again, his CT scan confirmed progression, both within the liver and the lungs. I mean, when I saw him, I thought, crumbs, you're going to be ill, you're going to feel terrible, but actually he was symptomatically remarkably well. Clearly, he was used to tolerating these high levels of calcium. and remarkably his renal function remained pretty good. So what were we going to do? We had progressing cancer and our experience for these within our unit is that we end up treating them as a generic carcinoma because there's very little evidence evidence for specific therapies for this situation.

Let me ask, let me ask David, is there anything from like the neuroendocrine land, you know, there's this peptide receptor therapies, lutetium, I don't know what dotatate is, or gallium or that, so I mean, this is kind of a neuroendocrine thing, is there, is there anything you guys could leverage from that?

Yeah, look, it is. I mean, we've had two patients like this in probably the last couple of years. And we tried imaging them with gallium dilatate PET scans. So with a view to potentially treating them with a radionuclide therapy, which is what we do for our new endocrine tumors. So if they express somatostatin receptors, then we get uptake and we can then treat them with lutetium bound to that. But unfortunately, in the cases we've tried this, it just hasn't been very successful. So unfortunately, but yeah, it's something we try.
Laurie, I mean, who was that? Daniel. We've done gallium dosatate PETs on three or four patients now and have seen only low-level uptake and never sufficient PRRT.
Laurie, any sort of high-level thoughts in your vast experience of parathyroid persona? Sorry, you're the oncologist. Tag, you're it. What are you sort of thinking here, Laurie?

Well, I was really deeply appreciative of the comment on the bullet down on the bottom, generic chemotherapy for carcinoma, which is what my high level approach to as well. And I've been raked over the coals for trying generic chemotherapy in these cases because it quote unquote doesn't work. And, you know, the alternative is doing nothing. And that doesn't work very well either. So it's perfectly fine in the world of oncology when you're treating a rare, rare disease that you extrapolate from other cancers and use your best judgment to try to do something to help a patient.

I was going to say, Dan, any information on molecular biology of these parathyroid cancers that can inform us or help us or still just a black box? Do I get you, Dan? Just, you know, the next-gen sequencing or anything?
Yeah. So, Raj Vakha has published a paper looking at mutation mapping, suggesting mutations in the mTOR pathway, but there's no therapeutic data to date.

And we always have a sort of window of opportunity with these patients with renal function, because at some point their renal function is going to go off and that will limit from an oncology point of view what we can give. So we actually gave ECX chemotherapy, which is a combination that we've given in this situation before. So epirubicin, cisplatin and capecitabine, so like a sort of sledgehammer for a carcinoma. And he showed, it sort of stabilised his disease for a period of time and his calcium came down below three on our measurements. and he proceeded to six cycles, which is the limit which we normally stop at, but actually pretty quickly after that, his disease started to progress once again in the liver and he was referred for further liver embolization. Unfortunately, he had no significant improvement with this. He's not eligible for any phase one studies because of the hypercalcemia. And we did do some molecular profiling and we identified TERT promoter mutation and a SMARCE1 variant, but nothing that we had drugs to target. So he switched to sinicalcid backwards and forwards with bisphosphonate and denosumab. And at the same time, we requested a PDL-1 status because I read a case report about this and his CPS came back as greater than 20. Now, there's no significant data on immunotherapy in parathyroid, but based on his fitness, he's very well. we'd exhausted our options as calcium continued to climb. We were sort of at 3.3, 3.5 levels on our assay, so creeping up to the highest it had been. We requested permission. In the meantime, we gave some weekly paclitaxel just while we waited, and that held things a little bit, but he obviously started to get toxicity from that. And actually, we then did get permission for pembrolizumab, and he started at the end of April, he's tolerating this well, his calcium has come down from around 3.5 on our assay to 2.7 and Daniel nicely summarised his levels for us at the moment. So we are in again unknown territory but it's you know it's interesting and we will see how he does with immunotherapy but you know this is not something that we have lots of data on from a teaching point of view or any data sorry.

Dan, from just the teaching point for this regular endocrinologists that don't see this stuff, what are the flags that the once in your lifetime you're going to see a parathyroid carcinoma out of all of the hyperparathyroid you guys see? Can you help us understand what were the flags maybe in this case or other case that would make you say, hey, I need to go look for something else?

So, the pre-op calcium is the big clue. I mean, all the aggressive paraphyroid carcinomas we've seen all had presented with pre-op calcium as well, well above 3 millimoles per litre in SI units. They all had high calciums, they all had short histories. I think that is crucial because clearly the best chance of cure is the right surgery up front and an on block resection with a hemiphyroidectomy. And so I think recognition of the unusual cases which present with much higher calciums than standard primary hyperthyroidism. And then I think the other group is patients like this whose calcium does not return to normal despite appropriate upfront surgery.

Yeah, let me do day and then super day. Anything special about a parathyroid cancer when you're doing the operation or does it look like a parathyroid adenoma is there anything that's like signals you if you're in there doing the surgery.

So, unfortunately, Most of the parathyroid cancers that I've been involved with, we diagnose afterwards. There's nothing obvious sometimes. But if you have an indication like this, I'd like to say that we didn't operate on this, something like this where you have a high suspicion, then you're going in for wide local excision and doing the lobectomy and trying to clear as much as you can. And clearly the classical teaching is that there is invasion, there is adhesion, and it just feels hard and different. But last week, I had a case where I thought this must be parathyroid carcinoma and turned out to be just adenoma, just very inflamed and very active. So it's challenging. But, you know, I think it's challenging. It's just trying to be upfront, just to be aware, certainly high, very high calciums like these cases. Maybe we should be thinking more wider resection.

Yeah. Zubair, finish me up, Zubair, with pathologically differentiating an adenoma from a cancer. If we're not going to give you the labs and we're not going to tell you anything else, we just put you in a room and give you the slides, how are you going to do?

First of all, very difficult diagnosis to make because you don't see them every day. Mostly you see adenomas. You really have to rely on few features and they have to be very clear cut to really differentiate them from parathyroid adenomas. or some of those parathyroid adenomas which have been needled mistakenly for thyroid nodules and caused a lot of reactive changes. You have to have a clear-cut invasion either in the blood vessels, which includes in the angio-invasion or in the lymphatics, or there has to be perineural or intra-neural invasion. Infiltrative growth is in the eyes of beholder, but it has to be clear-cut infiltrative growth into the surrounding. There are other features, but that's why they really overlap with a lot of adenomas. So that's why the diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma now is on a spectrum. So according to the new WHO, there's going to be three types of parathyroid tumors. One is going to be your run-of-the-mill parathyroid adenoma. The one which sits in the middle is going to be called as atypical parathyroid tumor, which used to be called as atypical parathyroid adenomas. Clinically behave like adenomas, but have some really kind of iffy invasive features, and then you have parathyroid carcinoma. This is a case that is still, if I'm going to make a parathyroid carcinoma case, a diagnosis on histology, I personally will show it to somebody else just to make sure that I'm making this, because I think there's so much overlap that you can really mistakenly call something which is just fibrosis in a parathyroid adenoma as a carcinoma.

reference_conclusion: For progressive metastatic parathyroid carcinoma involving the liver and lungs with refractory hypercalcemia, systemic therapy was administered with ECX chemotherapy, resulting in temporary disease stabilization and reduction in serum calcium, followed by further liver embolization without significant benefit. Given PD-L1 CPS greater than 20, preserved performance status, and exhaustion of other options, pembrolizumab was approved and initiated; treatment has been well tolerated with improvement in hypercalcemia.

reference_conclusion: The panel supported operative management for normocalcemic hyperparathyroidism in the setting of persistent nephrolithiasis, with recognition that surgery in such cases is reserved for carefully selected patients and is driven primarily by stone disease or significant skeletal involvement. Four-gland exploration was performed with resection of the enlarged right inferior and right superior parathyroid glands, identification and biopsy confirmation of the left inferior gland within the thymus, and preservation of the left inferior gland while removing the left superior gland; intraoperative parathyroid hormone levels normalized following resection. The discussion emphasized the high likelihood of multigland disease in this clinical setting and the preference to leave an inferior gland in situ if a gland is to be preserved.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old male; occupation: IT professional.

[ chief complaint ]: Breathlessness during a hiking trip.

[ diagnosis ]: Lung adenocarcinoma involving the left lower lobe, with pleural effusion and pleural fluid cytology positive for malignant cells.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology showed scattered tumor cells, with a few atypical cells demonstrating significant pleomorphism and hyperchromatism. Immunohistochemistry was positive for TTF-1 and Napsin A, confirming pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Additional immunohistochemistry reported pancytokeratin positive and CK7 positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Chest radiograph showed massive left pleural effusion. CT thorax showed an enhancing soft-tissue lesion in the left lower lobe with associated subcentimetric lung nodules and enhancing left pleural nodules.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Initial targeted testing with an 11-gene panel was negative for actionable alterations. Subsequent 52-gene next-generation sequencing identified a kinase domain duplication. Microsatellite status was stable. Tumor mutational burden was 4. PD-L1 testing by SP263 assay showed expression of approximately 3–4%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab for 4 cycles. Disease progression occurred on treatment. The patient was subsequently reported as not responding to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease after 4 cycles of chemo-immunotherapy; persistent non-response to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: Pleural fluid cytology was positive for malignant cells.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Left cheek mass present for approximately 2 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced basal cell carcinoma of the left cheek/left lateral zygomatic-temporal region; clinical stage T3N0M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy was positive for basal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a large plaque-like lesion of the left zygomatic region involving the cutaneous and subcutaneous soft tissues and extending onto the temporal scalp. The lesion was adjacent to the lateral orbital rim and periauricular soft tissues. Loss of fat planes with the masseter muscle was reported. Focal erosions through the lateral cortex of the zygoma were reported. Tumor depth was estimated at approximately 1 cm. No regional metastases were identified.  
Preoperative reassessment imaging after neoadjuvant therapy demonstrated focal dermal thickening with retraction over the left malar eminence and a small residual band of tethering over the underlying masseter muscle, significantly decreased from baseline.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were reported. No PD-L1 testing was reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Basal cell carcinoma of the left lower eyelid in 2019 was treated with Mohs surgery. No prior radiation therapy or chemotherapy was reported.  
For the current lesion, neoadjuvant cemiplimab was administered on a clinical trial. After 2 cycles, there was a significant decrease in lesion size with increased mobility of the mass; ulceration and bleeding were present. Pruritus was reported as a treatment-related adverse effect. After cycles 3 and 4, the lesion continued to decrease in size; fatigue was reported. After 4 cycles, lesion size was 2.5 x 0.98 cm. After cycles 5 and 6, the lesion continued to decrease in size; a persistent wound over the malar eminence remained.

[ current disease status ]: Status post neoadjuvant cemiplimab.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was notable for no history of autoimmune disorders or immunodeficiency. No other malignancies were reported aside from prior left lower eyelid basal cell carcinoma. No social risk factors were reported.  
Physical examination before treatment demonstrated a 6.7 x 5.8 cm exophytic mass of the left lateral zygomatic and temporal region, partially affixed to the periosteum. Bone fixation or invasion could not be determined on examination. The lesion encroached on the lateral orbit but did not involve the eyelid or canthus. No clinical lymphadenopathy was present. Facial movement was intact.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. As we can see, we have an excellent panel today. And with that, we're going to discuss our first case. This is a 46-year-old male who presented to the emergency department complaint of epigastric pain. A CT scan of the abdomen reported a 15.8 centimeter pancreatic tilt mass with multiple liver lesions and with the greatest dimension being three centimeters in size. CT scan guided biopsy of the liver mass reported a grade two well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with a KI67 of 15%. So this is the scan. of the patient. And Dr. Mitra, as we're showing the scans, could you please describe what we're seeing in the scans and what would you recommend as the next step?

Sure. So for evaluation of these types of tumors, especially for staging, but also restaging, both CT and MRI have a very important role. So this is the MRI that was done. It's particularly good for the liver and for the pancreas, which is exactly where this patient has their disease. And so you can actually see the very large pancreatic tail mass, as well as multiple enhancing lesions within the liver, which are likely the metastases that are there.

I'm fond of MRIs, but I think sometimes when you're looking for vascular definition, I prefer a good CT for anatomical purposes and for planning surgery. I think a good CT for vascular definition and a delayed, you know, 20-minute delay on the ovious phase for the burden of liver disease.
And Dr. Singh, for our patients, could you please describe what is SMA and what is relevant in this case?

So the SMA is the superior mesenteric artery which supplies the entire intestines. And so it is critical to actually make an effort to save that, because if you compromise that, you're compromising the vascularity of the entire small intestines and two-thirds of the large intestines. The celiac axis, on the other hand, has three dominant branches. One goes up towards the liver, one goes up to the stomach, and the third goes up to the spleen and the body and tail of the pancreas. So once again, It's a good idea to save the celiac axis and not take it, although you can reconstruct these vessels. But I think it's always a better idea to have before you go into the operating room as to do you have the degree of freedom to be able to resect these without needing complex vascular reconstruction.
Okay. Dr. Mitra, anything that you would like to add?

No, I just wanted to reiterate Dr. Singh's point that both CT and MRI, as I mentioned, have an important role for the evaluation, but they do have different pros and cons. I think for patients, it's important to understand that in either case, it's important to get a multi-phase CT or a multi-phase MRI. Oftentimes patients only get one phase, and that's not quite sufficient to evaluate all the different things.
And Dr. Oz, anything else that you would like to add in this case?

Not much. I think it's a great discussion. I would probably echo a lot of what Dr. Singh said as a vascular interventional radiologist. You know, we are particularly keen on getting CTs for vascular planning, and I would agree that this mass looks like it's well away from the SMA and celiac axis. It does look like it's draping over the splenic vein, but I imagine the spleen is easier to sacrifice than other parts of the body.

So I think it's important to get good vascular definition on these scans, and particularly if the mass is encroaching on the superior mesenteric artery, which supplies almost two-thirds of the large intestine and the entire small intestine, it's important to make sure that the mass is away from that so it can be safely removed. And with regards to the celiac axis, that actually has three dominant branches, one that's going up towards the spleen, one to the stomach, and the other towards the liver. And once again, it's a good idea to actually save those blood vessels in surgery when you're doing that, except for the splenic artery and vein, which is going to come out in continuity with the mass itself. You can do complex vascular reconstructions, but you like to be well-prepared ahead of time before you go into these operations. You want to make sure you have good vascular definition on your scans before you go into the operating room.

And what I'm hearing in the discussions, especially in this case that we have a patient with a pancreas, large pancreas, mass, and liver lesions consistent with neuroendocrine tumors, and it seems that based on the discussions, surgery is an option. Would you recommend anything more, any other scans prior to surgery?

I'm actually fond of making sure that these are somatostatin receptor positive scans, tumors, because that determines a lot of the adjuvant treatment. So, a good gallium 68 PET scan is in order, I think.
And as we can see, this is the 68 gallium dot that they scanned. And Dr. Mitra, could you please describe what we see on the scans?

Yeah, so this scan is targeting the somatostatin receptors that are expressed on these tumors and based on the key 67. 15%, you would expect that most of these tumors should have high expression of somatostatin receptors. So it's a great thing that's an adjuvant to the CT scan or MRI scan to see what the expression there is. And as we're scrolling through, you're seeing all those same lesions in the liver as well as the large pancreatic mass that are showing that high uptake. The pancreatic mass also shows some areas of not high expression, which are probably necrotic or areas that have actually died within the tumor. And you can see that as sort of the holes within there as well. And you can probably make out some lymph nodes locally as well.

And can I ask you a follow-up question? Some of our patients ask whether there is any difference between 68 gallium dotted scans or 64 copper Could you please describe more in detail whether there's a difference or if any preference one versus the other?

Sure. So there's a lot of technical differences, but I think the bottom line that patients should understand is that there's these two different isotopes. Gallium 68 and copper 64, both of them are targeting the somatostatin receptor as we just talked about. And if the scanners are set up properly for the isotope, then essentially they're equivalent as far as imaging quality and effectiveness. So I don't think patients should really be worried too much about that. There are technical differences between them in terms of the half-life and the energies and things like that. But more or less, either one is good as long as the institution is set up for that.

Great. Thank you so much. Based on this information, Dr. Steens, now we have this patient that have a pancreas neuroendocrine tumors with liver metastasis. You already saw the dot of the scan, which is Abbott. So the tumor expressed the receptors. So what would you do next? Well, what would you recommend next on this patient?

the most important thing is to take the primary out. That is one single action that promotes longevity, okay? Whether you touch the liver, you don't touch the liver. And, you know, a lot of groups have published that, including our group. So that's one thing. So she would end up with a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy for sure. Now, since there's no vascular reconstruction, and if the first portion of the operation is fairly straightforward. I'm a proponent of doing the liver at the same time. And as long as you think you can achieve in today's day and age what we say, 70% reduction of the total liver tumor volume, somewhere about eight or nine lesions is what I calculated, but there might be more, you know, which would definitely be more obvious on a 20 minute delay on the MRI. If there's no vascular reconstruction necessary, then I tend to do the liver at the same time. If there's going to be some major vascular reconstruction, I like to do it as a staged fashion. There is no data to suggest that the staged liver resection is anything wrong. So if you don't feel comfortable doing it at the first sitting, or you think the surgery's already taken, been fairly major, it's absolutely fine to stage it and do the liver in, you know, six weeks to three months.
Okay. And Dr. Oz, as an interventional oncologist, do you think that's something that you could address via liver directed therapies? And when would you recommend?

Yeah, that's a great question. I would echo what Dr. Singh said that, you know, in our practice, we would probably prefer if there is a surgical option with respect to obviously the primary, but also to the liver, to try to debulk as much as possible, especially if the tumor burden is feasible enough to do that. I think the role of interventional radiology or oncology here would be twofold. One would be If Dr. Singh, for example, felt that he could get 80% of the tumors, but maybe a few would be difficult to reach, then we could potentially offer local regional therapy like a percutaneous ablation. And or if he felt that the tumor burden was too high to address surgically, we could also offer what we call intra-arterial therapies, which are under that umbrella include things like bland embolization, as well as radio embolization.

I would like to add one more thing. You know, usually at the time of surgery, I tend to debulk them surgically. You don't need a margin on these tumors. All you need to do is enucleate these tumors. So it's like taking a hard-boiled egg out of a, you know, a shell basically, but you're not leaving any residual tumor behind. So you can do that safely. A couple of the deeper lesions, you can ablate in the operating room at the same time. But I think what Dr. Oz just said is there are certain, sometimes you're left with disease that you cannot get to, or you're going to be pushing the envelope a bit too much and, you know, not leave enough liver behind. At that juncture, you then, you know, put a pause on it and then do that either in a staged fashion or you get your interventional colleagues involved to address that disease while they're on systemic therapy.

Great. Thank you so much. Just as Dr. Singh recommended, this patient did underwent a distal pancreatectomy, a splenectomy, and cholecystectomy, meaning that the distal pan of the pancreas was resected, the spleen was resected, and the gallbladder was resected. Pathology was consistent with a grade three well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. So the K67 is 30%. As we discussed earlier, the K67 was 15%. But now we can see that the final pathology said that it's 30% and there was lymph nodes that were also positive for neuroendocrine tumor. Patient then have a follow CT scans. The liver lynchings were unchanged and the patient was started on Lanreotide every four weeks with a follow scans every three months. After nine months of being on Lanreotide, follow scans revealed that the tumors in the liver grew. And at that moment, Landry type was stopped. And Dr. Mitra, what would you think? Would you do any other workup for this patient based on the Ki-67, based on what we've seen here?
Before I answer your question, I'm curious what your answer is. How often do you see that, that the Ki-67 changes? And what does that mean to you from an oncology perspective?

Right. So the initial KS67 of 15% was from a biopsy. And sometimes when the biopsy is done, it's possible that maybe they could biopsy a necrotic area. And sometimes when there is a necrotic area, sometimes the percentage of KS67 cannot be accurately calculated. So in the fact that this patient underwent surgery and there is a lot more tissue to kind of review this number. So I do believe that this KS67 is more accurate and it was 30% from the very beginning. And I feel like the initial KS67 that was done for a biopsy is possible that there is more necrotic tissue and unable to accurately calculate as I said, but now that this 30% seems to be more accurate in 30% is what I think has been from the very beginning of the diagnosis of neuroendocrine tumor. But yes, that's a good question. Sometimes I get the question that I get a K67 and a biopsy of this percentage and then a repeated one is higher. But usually we, our decision is to always take the highest K67 because as I said, you know, sometimes, you know, the lower K67, there may be an area that there was, like I said, necrotic tissue. And as I said, the pathology is the call of the pathologist to calculate this number. But I do believe that the higher guess 67 is a more accurate for the neuroendocrine tumor.

So let's say if the KI67 came back at 30% on the initial biopsy, based on the new data that's coming out with CAPETEM, would you start the patient on CAPETEM to see a response and then go to surgery? Or would you still want us to debulk it and then go to surgery?

Our recommendations for our patients with neuroendocrine tumors, as we all discussed, is multidisciplinary. And I think it's important always to have our surgeon, nuclear medicine, interventional radiologists, medical oncologists, because it's not one size fits all. And I think we all know that. So the treatment of neuroendocrine tumors is quite personalized from patient to patient. And in this situation, yes, I do agree that systemic therapy is an option. And the reason why is because of the volume of disease. It's important to know as well. What is the vol to know whether the tumors or outside the liver, wheth receptors because that a as well as what therapies in this situation because a large pancreatic mass, l metastasis. I do think th to my first follow up th line of therapy will be cap 10 just to see if that also shrink the tumors because we know that the tumors can shrink up to 40 percent. So and if we can do that, maybe it's possible that surgery it will be easier later on. But in this situation, yes, I think I will have opted to start Gibbs Iodine intramusolomide.

Yeah, so this brings up a couple of interesting points. So one is that, you know, we did see that area of necrosis on the initial scan. So what you said about the biopsy, you know, makes a lot of sense. And in addition to that, always the surgical biopsies is generally more accurate than the ones that are done with the core. Now we know that the patient has progressed based on the CT scan already. So just for that reason alone, it would be important to potentially restage again with somatostatin receptor PET, the DOTATATE PET, to see what is going on now. And then also because the Ki67 is increased, as the number goes higher, you begin to lose somatostatin receptor expression. At 30%, I would still expect to see good uptake, but it would be good to reevaluate that. And on the scan, as we're going through, You're seeing many, many more liver lesions than you saw previously. The majority of them appear to be still showing somatostatin receptor expression, but it would be very important to correlate that very closely with the CT or MRI to make sure that some of these small lesions are not beginning to lose the expression that was just mentioned. And then you also have their FDG scan. And that also starts becoming important as the Ki-67 starts going up, especially above 20%. Because you start losing somatostatin receptor expression, then those lesions will start having increased glucose uptake, which is what the FDG scan shows. So many people advocate that it would be ideal to do both types of scans to fully evaluate all the different tumors and what is expressing what.

Right. Thank you so much, Dr. Mitra. And as you suggested, this patient did had glucose scans, and the glucose scans is on the top end of the picture. And then the dot of the scan is on the bottom. And as we can see in this patient, it still highly expresses somatostatin receptor, which we know that is the tumor response to somatostatin receptors. It can open also the possibilities of other therapies as well. But as you suggested, I think you know, you say like, well, we need to sometimes do both the scans to really understand more about the biology of these tumors. Maybe there may be some tumors that may be more DOTATATE avid and maybe some tumors may be more FDG avid. But maybe if you could, for our patients, maybe to discuss more in detail, when would you do the two scans and how that help us to make clinical recommendations?

Yeah, in a very general sense, sort of rule of thumb, if the Ki-67 is less than 20%, you can probably get away with just the DOTATATE PET scan, again, as long as you correlate with the CT or MRI and you don't see any discrepancies there. Above Ki-67 of 55% on the opposite end of the spectrum, you almost always want to go with FDG. scan and it'll be less likely to show the DOTATATE expression. But that still leaves a very wide range between 20 to 55 percent where, again, you might need to do both types of scans. And the best advice I can give, again, is to correlate it with the CT and MRI. As far as therapeutic decisions, if you have somatostatin receptor expression, as you're alluding to, that opens up those types of therapies such as somatostatin analogs and PRRT, whereas the more you lose that and the higher the FDG uptake goes, then you're not going to be well served with those therapies and you'll want to do other types of systemic therapies such as CAPETEL. In this case, like you said, the FDG uptake is very, very low compared to the DOTATATE, so that's very good.

And one last question. Sometimes our patients have difficulties getting both scans approved. Is there any recommendation, anything that you will suggest, you know, for our patients or how to approach their physicians in order to get the scans done whenever it's needed?

Yeah, that's a really important point and frustrating for ourselves as well as for patients. And I think a lot of the difficulties, the fact that they're both two different types of PET scans and insurance companies often see them as sort of in the same bucket, even though they're completely ultimately types of scans. So oftentimes it's just an education with the insurance company and having them understand what is the benefit of these two different types of scans as we just discussed. So doing a peer-to-peer evaluation discussion with the insurance company can sometimes help alleviate that, but it is a problem and also there's a lot of regional variability. with that as well. But the first thing is to kind of understand the importance of it. And then secondly, is to kind of push for it with the insurance company.

Thank you. So just to follow with our case, this patient did get a combination oral chemotherapy with kefcidabine and temosolomide. And kefcidabine was discontinued due to coronary phase of spasms. And what is that mean is when your heart already suddenly constrict, causing spasms that trigger symptoms like a heart attack. It very rarely occur, it's less than 4%, but it has been documented. So this patient only got temosolomide alone for two more cycles. And as we can see on these scans, you know, there was evidence of the tumors grew and there were more tumors seen on the skins. And maybe that will be a question for Dr. Oz, you know, what would you recommend here?

This would be an ideal scenario for an interventional radiology intervention, particularly because the bulk, if not all of the disease seems to be confined to the liver, which is where most of our therapies are sort of confined to. Given the amount of tumors and the distribution of the tumors involving both lobes of the liver, we would typically favor doing something intra-arterial, meaning we go through the artery, deliver it, stage it into two procedures, right and left lobe. And we, in our practice, typically do what's known as bland embolization. So we would inject basically inert particles that would occlude the arteries and basically starve the tumors of their blood supply.

And could you please explain the difference between gland embolization, radio embolization, chemo embolization, because we know that there's different type of embolizations, and why would you recommend gland versus radio embolization? I know that some of our other colleagues may recommend radio embolization, and the question will be, if that's an option, when would you recommend that?

Yeah, that's a great question. You know, I think the procedures are all very similar in that the idea is that the tumors with neuroendocrine cancer are hypervascular. And hypervascular is a fancy word for they get a lot of blood flow or a lot of blood supply. So we take advantage of that by going into the artery of the liver and directly and injecting some material. And that material could be basically, like I said, just like grains of sand, just bland beads. That's called bland embolization. You can mix those beads with chemotherapy and or you could inject radioactive microspheres and that's called radio embolization. It's a form of radiation therapy. The sort of why one is picked over the other, a lot of that will just be variations in practice of the IR that you're seeing. And a lot of it is also just preference of the surgeon that you may be working with. The reason that we particularly like bland embolization is because A, it gets good results, but B, you can repeat the therapy with little to no sort of collateral damage to the liver. With neuroendocrine cancer, you know, radioembolization has become a little bit less favored because it causes sort of underlying liver damage. And we talked about other therapies like PRRT and things like that, where, you know, that will also directly target tumors and may cause some liver damage as well. So we want to try to minimize that as much as possible. Fortunately, because neuroendocrine cancer patients have generally a favorable prognosis, we want to minimize the chance of a patient developing cirrhosis down the road. So we favor bland embolization because it tends to sort of cause less cloud damage. It doesn't mean that you can't have Brady embolization, but more often than not, that will be sort of, at least in our practice, would be more of a bailout if the bland embolization didn't seem to work well.

Thank you so much for that answer. And Dr. Mitra, the fact that, you know, we have these tumors very avid on and this patient have not received 177 Lutetian DOTATAY, would you recommend in this situation?

Yeah, it's a great question, one that is very, very relevant right now in terms of the data that's coming out from several clinical trials, such as NEDR2, which is a big one that included patients with this type of high-grade tumors, but still expressed somatostatin receptors exactly as this patient does. At our institution, this patient would exactly go, as Dr. Oz is saying, between sort of these options, so the tumors are what, as he said, looks like either entirely or mostly limited to the liver. So liver-directed therapies would be a great option, but also because they're so somatostatin receptor avid, they would also potentially be a good candidate for PRRT. So that would, I think, be the big discussion point at our institution. And in often cases, it would go between one versus the other. It's just a matter of which one is done first.

Thank you so much. I think it's important to know and make our patients aware of the data with the NETR2 that it was given in the first line settings and for higher grade neuroendocrine tumors. And they saw that the tumors did shrink with that. And I think it's something that needs to be discussed as well with our patients.

Can I ask a quick question to the interventional radiologist? Do you tend to target the bigger lesions first and then leave the smaller lesions for the nuclear medicine people to take care with PRRT? Or do you randomly go after one side and then the other side? How do you plan treatment with bilobar disease like this?

Yeah, great question. So, the answer is somewhere in between. So, we do treat the whole liver when we do bland embolization, if you have tumors in both sides. If you only had it on the right or on the left, we would only treat that half. Typically, when we're doing interventions for neuroendocrine cancer, and if we're doing one of these arterial therapies like bland embolization, we're doing it because there's widespread tumors. If you only have a few tumors, then we're talking about surgery versus ablation or even something like histotripsy. So because we're doing it for patients who have tumors everywhere in their liver, more often than not, we will do what are called lobar infusions. So we go into the right hepatic artery. or the right side of the liver, and we inject the beads very proximally or very, you know, far away from the tumor and distribute the beads throughout the entire liver. Because the tumors are very hypervascular, meaning they're like vacuum cleaners, they kind of suck up those beads as you inject them. We indiscriminately inject those beads. So the intention is to treat all the tumors on that side that's being treated. And then we would repeat that procedure for the other side of the liver, you know, four to six weeks. The side of the liver we typically start with is the side that typically has the most tumor and the largest tumors. So more often than not, that tends to be the right side of the liver, but not uncommonly, we start with the left.
So with the bland embolization, do you feel that the smaller tumors completely go away and the bigger ones get a little bit smaller? What is your experience on that?

Yeah, I would say that's generally what I like to tell patients to expect is don't focus on the tumors disappearing. Focus hopefully more that these tumors are like light bulbs, as we've seen on these scans. We want to basically burn the light bulbs out. We want to basically get rid of the blood supply to them. So what we see more often than not is that those larger tumors, yeah, they may shrink a little bit, but we don't want to see them enhance or get contrast on the follow-up scans. Similarly, the tiny tumors, hopefully because they're so small, they may disappear, but we're looking for sort of a lack of enhancement more than anything.
Dr. Mitra, you wanted to make a comment?
Oh, I was just going to ask what your opinion is in this case between liver-directed therapy versus PRRT.

Right. And yes, we discussed our case, this case in our tumor board, and we discussed about liver-directed therapies. As Dr. Oz mentioned, that was an option. We also discussed about Lutathera. At that moment, the data of the NETHER2 was not out when this patient, you know, and what we know now is that 177 lutetium dodecane is approved for low grade neuroendocrine tumors. So the fact that we have this information that can also be used for higher grades is very important. But at that time, you know, we didn't have that information. So this patient actually was enrolled in our clinical trial with in combination with Olaparib. Dr. Kunz will discuss more about clinical trials, but this is a study that is available here at the NIH. And the idea is that we want to make 177-nutrition Dr. Tay more effective by adding Olaparib, but that will be. And just to mention, LACNATS has also a clinical trials information and a video about this study. Please refer to that video if you have an interest in this study. Now let's discuss our second case. This is a 45-year-old female. At age 40, she was complaining of intermittent flushing, postural hypotension, that means when the blood pressure drops when you go from lying down to sitting up, presyncope, so that's the feeling that you have when you faint or when you want to faint, and diarrhea. Five years later, she was admitted to the emergency room with no clear etiology of the symptoms, and she was having worse enough of diarrhea up to 20 times a day. Initially, her primary care physician thought that maybe there was an immune condition. She was sent to see a immunologist and it was him who recommended for evaluation. And as we can see here, the plasma serotonin was very elevated as well as the 5-HIAA was also elevated. She then underwent a CT scan of the abdomen and we can see here that there is multiple liver metastasis, which are the more darker area that we see in the liver. But maybe for further view, we can see the dot that they scanned. And the dot that they scanned also was positive as well with the tumors having the receptors. And as we can see, the scan is also positive. And a question for Dr. Mitra, what would you recommend here, Dr. Mitra?

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus favored resection of the pancreatic primary with distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy, with consideration of synchronous hepatic debulking if no major vascular reconstruction was required and at least 70% of total liver tumor volume could be reduced; otherwise, staged liver-directed treatment was considered appropriate. Following progression on lanreotide and intolerance/progression on capecitabine-temozolomide, repeat functional imaging with somatostatin receptor PET and FDG PET was used to reassess disease biology. Given liver-dominant, bilobar metastatic disease with persistent somatostatin receptor avidity, liver-directed intra-arterial therapy, particularly staged bland embolization, and PRRT were both considered appropriate options, with subsequent enrollment on a clinical trial combining 177-lutetium DOTATATE with olaparib.

Now, since there's no vascular reconstruction, and if the first portion of the operation is fairly straightforward. I'm a proponent of doing the liver at the same time. And as long as you think you can achieve in today's day and age what we say, 70% reduction of the total liver tumor volume [...] If there's no vascular reconstruction necessary, then I tend to do the liver at the same time. If there's going to be some major vascular reconstruction, I like to do it as a staged fashion. There is no data to suggest that the staged liver resection is anything wrong. So if you don't feel comfortable doing it at the first sitting, or you think the surgery's already taken, been fairly major, it's absolutely fine to stage it and do the liver in, you know, six weeks to three months. [...] So just for that reason alone, it would be important to potentially restage again with somatostatin receptor PET, the DOTATATE PET, to see what is going on now. [...] And then you also have their FDG scan. And that also starts becoming important as the Ki-67 starts going up, especially above 20%. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for evaluation of primary hyperparathyroidism. Reported musculoskeletal pain. No history of nephrolithiasis or pathologic fractures.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Primary hyperparathyroidism.  
- Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, tall cell subtype, multifocal, with nodal metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was diagnostic of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Thyroidectomy pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell subtype.  
- Multifocal disease was present.  
- Metastatic carcinoma was identified in a lymph node deposit measuring approximately 0.2 cm.  
- Two parathyroid glands were excised: right upper parathyroid gland and intrathymic left lower parathyroid gland.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound demonstrated a highly suspicious right thyroid nodule, 1.8 cm in greatest dimension, described as solid, hypoechoic, with infiltrative ill-defined margins; categorized as ATA highly suspicious / ACR TI-RADS 5.  
- Ultrasound also demonstrated an enlarged right upper parathyroid gland.  
- Post-radioiodine imaging showed uptake including a focus above the left clavicle consistent with a supraclavicular lymph node; a right-sided focus could represent residual thyroid bed uptake.  
- Follow-up neck ultrasound demonstrated a central compartment (level VI) lymph node measuring 4 x 8 x 6 mm, indeterminate in appearance, without definite cystic change.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- No tumor molecular testing results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hypercalcemia was present.  
- Parathyroid hormone: 122.  
- Vitamin D: normal.  
- 24-hour urinary calcium: increased.  
- Postoperative thyroglobulin became undetectable.  
- TSH was suppressed postoperatively.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent total thyroidectomy.  
- Underwent excision of the right upper parathyroid gland and an intrathymic left lower parathyroid gland.  
- Received radioactive iodine therapy, 80 mCi, approximately 5 years before the current review.  
- A small central neck lesion was biopsied after treatment.

[ current disease status ]:  
- No biochemical evidence of persistent thyroid carcinoma was documented, with undetectable thyroglobulin after treatment.  
- Persistent small-volume structural disease was present in the central neck as a level VI lymph node measuring 4 x 8 x 6 mm.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation.  
- Family, social, and surgical history were otherwise unremarkable.  
- The patient had been anticoagulated for atrial fibrillation.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. Thank you for allowing us to present today. I wanted to bring this case up because it was actually after Dr. Tuttle visited us that my management of this patient really changed. So this is a 69 year old female who was actually referred for primary hyperparathyroidism. Her biochemical profile is pretty consistent with primary parathyroidism, elevated calcium, PTH of 122, and a setting of normal vitamin D and an increased 24-hour urinary calcium. Her medical history, just hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, otherwise unremarkable family, social, or surgical history. Her presenting symptom, she felt overwhelmed except for some musculoskeletal pain, otherwise no kidney stones or pathologic fractures. And with all of our patients, we started examining her and obviously doing a neck ultrasound.
All right, Jill, let's take a look at the ultrasound. What do you see in there?

Yeah, so we do see a very highly suspicious nodule using ATA lingo, a TYRAT5 nodule using American ACR. So this almost certainly would be a neoplasm. It's solid, it's hypoechoic, it has infiltrating ill-defined margins, highly suspect for a papillary cancer.
So this was a, you know, greatest dementia 1.8 centimeters, exactly what you said, and also very obvious right upper parathyroid gland.

So Jill, help me out here a little bit. This is obvious to surgeons and you guys that look at that, but help me understand why is that not a lymph node? Why is that a parathyroid gland? How do you sort of think through that, Jill?

Yeah, that's a very good question. And certainly there's overlap. So for a classic enlarged parathyroid gland, the color Doppler is actually really helpful. It'll have rim or arc-like flow as opposed to a lymph node, which would have sort of central arborizing flow or no flow. Of course, not all parathyroids read the book. And if I were to see cystic change or echogenic foci calcifications, that would favor that it's a metastatic lymph node. In some patients, particularly the renal failure patients, however, that have secondary tertiary hyperpara, they can have those more atypical findings. But when all is said and done, this does look like it favors a enlarged parathyroid gland.
Okay. Joyce? I'm trying to find my cursor. Okay. So we did an FNA, pretty classic, PTC, and cytology.

Pause there for me for a second. So normally when we're having this discussion, we're having the argument of 1.8 centimeter, do we do a lobectomy, do a total thyroidectomy? Now that you've got this parathyroid thing going on the same side, I mean, it's the nodules on the right side, the parathyroid gland looks on the right side. How does that dealing with the parathyroid change how you think about total versus low from a practical standpoint, Mark? Thanks, Mike.

I think it's a good question. I mean, I think every once in a while, a couple times a year, we'll get a case that's got a concurrent type of parathyroidism plus a capillary thyroid cancer. In this case, it's incidental. So yeah, if it's on the same side, it makes it more straightforward. Most of us who do parathyroid surgery We'll still use intraoperative PTHs to confirm that we have successfully helped the patient by reducing their PTH according to the Miami criteria, at least 50% drop at 10 minutes. But I think when I'm thinking about lobe versus total, I'm typically even more likely to do a lobe in somebody who as primary hair parathyroidism if the parathyroid adenoma, suspected adenoma, is on the same cell side. It's a little bit trickier. You have to think about what are the risks that you have to go back to in the future. I still, in most cases, do a low, but it's a little bit more discussion.
Perfect. All right. So it'd be one or the other. And Joyce, what did you guys choose to do?

So with the discussion with the patient, this is my patient, so I remember she was a little bit nervous going off of her anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation. Here at the Cleveland Clinic, we always do a four-gallon expiration, so they will be scarring on both sides if we ever needed to go back for a completion. So all those discussions were had and she opted for a total thyroidectomy. although the cancer is small enough to potentially undergo a lobectomy. We also did excise two glands, the right upper as we've seen, and there was an intrathemic left lower parathyroid gland as well.
Perfect.
Alrighty, and let's look at the pathology. Dr. Golosh, this is my favorite thing to do, show you two pictures and have you give us a formal opinion. What do you see, Zuber?

OK, so on the left hand side, as you can see, that's like a medium to high power picture of papillary thyroid carcinoma. And if you look at the right, my right, actually, at the edge of that picture here, the cells, if you take an individual cells, they are actually tall. So they are about almost two to three times the width of the cell. And the nuclei you can see in the middle where there's a lot of blood is actually the papillary core is. You can see beautiful intranuclear holes, and there's many of those. Now, if you go to the, almost again to the right side, you see the cells are kind of lining up what is called the tram track appearance. So they are very parallel to each other, the way cells are lining up. So those are the typical features of a papillary thyroid carcinoma tall cell subtype. And on the right hand side, you see a lymph node metastatic deposit in a lymph node, and which, you know, from even the screen looks like about 0.2 centimeter or a little less, almost to 0.2 centimeters. I mean, that has to be measured. So this is a classic case of a tall cell subtype of PTC with a lymph node met.

Perfect. Nicole, what are you thinking now? We'll assume the parathyroid gland is all taken care of. We've got It looks like a little multifocal. It's a tall cell subtype. What's the prognosis here? Help me risk, and then I'll come to JP and Monica, and we'll talk about maybe the role of radioactive iodine. risk and sort of prognosis? What are we thinking here?

Well, we're thinking it's incidental, so the presentation would be low itself. The tall cell variant does make it a probable BRF-driven thyroid cancer, but it's small, it's two centimeters, and so I would think this would be a low-risk thyroid.
And at your center in Mexico, Nicole, would you normally give radioactive iodine here or talk about it with the patient or normally don't give?
We talk about it with the patient. In the past it was given like almost to everybody but now we're trying to selectively give the radioactive iodine.

I got you. JP, a lot of discussion over the last sort of five or ten years about radioactive iodine responsiveness and tall cell and whether to use it or not use it. Where are you and the team at the Mayo on this right now?

I think the way of thinking about this, rather than subtypes, is to think about the buckets of risk. Because the studies are very difficult to understand just based on the told cell versus not told cell. So it's easier just to say where the told cell actually fits. And I agree with Nicole that this looks like more low risk. If we go by the guidelines, probably they increase it to low to intermediate risk just because of the tall cell. But, you know, 20% of cancers are tall cell, papillary thyroid cancers, and they do behave very well. So I don't think it changes that much. I will go with baseline risk. What is the chances of this cancer to recur as a whole? Understanding the lymph node, understanding the size, and it's still considered less than 10% chances for this cancer to come back. So it will be very unlikely radioactive iodine will change that.

Monica, I mean, you get, obviously, folks refer to you all the time for radioactive iodine. Your feel about the tall cells and responsiveness to radioactive iodine and the BRAF tumor, any sort of thoughts on that, Monica?

Well, I think we would have considered tall cell variant and aggressive histology. And so we would, and in this case, it was multifocal. There wasn't formal lymph node sampling, but there was involvement in that, in a lymph node. So I think, although I am aware there's some literature to suggest, such as that article in clinical thyroidology last year that tall cell variant prognosis doesn't change with radioiodine, we would have offered the patient radioiodine.
Yeah, I think so. Dr. Lanshan, where are you guys sort of in this tall cell radioactive iodine discussion story?

Yeah, we kind of thought along the same lines too. We thought this was more intermediate. And although we thought the risk wouldn't change, risk overcomes wouldn't change with the treatment, but we thought about offering the patient that as well.
Okay. All right. And Joyce, how did you guys move forward?

So I'll just skip this because it was explained so beautifully. The patient actually did have radic dividine treatment. This was a case from approximately five years ago. So our thought process back then was to treat the patient with radic dividine.

Yep. And that's one of the challenging things, Monica, is what I'm trying to figure out, like in some of these, high-grade thyroid cancers and some of the tall cell variants, is the post-therapy scan showing me RAI-AVID disease? Like if you see it in the distant mets, I know that it's real. Some of these dots in the neck, how can I tell that that's thyroid cancer versus the superior or inferior pole of the thyroid or residual? Well, we would have to rely on the CT component of the SPECT CT to differentiate between thyroid bed and a lymph node. But this focus just above the left clavicle is more in keeping with a supraclavicular lymph node rather than residual thyroid tissue. So I would think that there was some lymph node uptake on that scan. The right focus could well be residual thyroid bed.

Yeah, I agree. I think that's one of the things that makes this discussion in tall cells challenging, because we've all seen some tall cell variants that are RAI avid. To me, it seems like a smaller percentage than the folliculars or that. So I'll often tell people that I generally don't use radioactive iodine in the tall cells, but there's a small likelihood that it would be helpful. And some people choose to do that, other ones don't. Which is good. So where do we go on our follow-up, Joyce? So we gave her radioactive iodine, 80 millicuries. and a little uptake like Monica showed there. Yep.

So these are biochemical profiles for her surgery was in September of 2023. We had to buy an instrument in November. I do not have the labs while she was being, I believe it was thyrogen, but obviously she's well suppressed afterwards with undetectable thyroglobin levels.

So go back for me one step. Nicole, just from a real practical standpoint, so we've got either a low-ish or intermediate risk patient, they had radioactive iodine, we're not finding lots of distant mets. What's your follow-up for that next year or so in an average patient like this, Nicole? When do you see them back, ultrasounds, blood tests, just from a practical standpoint?

Well, I will usually see it back like around six months if everything's doing well. If I'm worried about there being like a persistent disease, I would check it at three months post-surgery and go from there.
Perfect. And JP? What if I said this patient should never ever have another ultrasound the rest of their life? Would you argue with me that we should be doing ultrasounds in these patients?

Yeah, it's difficult to see where the benefits of ultrasound in these patients, but I think we do it because of how we've been doing this for a long time. It's difficult to deescalate, but evidence actually suggests in these patients the likelihood of finding something is high, but the likelihood of finding something relevant is extremely low. So I think we have to distinguish what is, I think you call it clinically relevant, which is, you know, actionable findings, is extremely low. And the end result happening is that we find lymph nodes are pretty much reactive. Patients get anxious about it. A lot of reutilization happens. But it's very difficult to move from, you know, something to nothing. And I think there is a process, as Nicole said, to have some degree of follow-up for these patients. I also wanted to comment that I never ordered tyroglobulin before surgery, but I always like it when I see it. It's kind of, I'm curious to see how it drops. I always find it interesting. And in this case, it took a little bit of time to drop, but it seems that it has dropped after surgery.

Yeah, I'm the same way. If I had my way, I would probably do a thyroglobulin before every surgery, even though that's like totally against the guidelines. And what I'm really looking for is an inappropriately low thyroglobulin, right? They have all these lymph nodes, but the thyroglobulin is really low. So I know I can't use it as a marker, but that's way out there. Nicole, TSH goals for somebody like this, where would you normally keep their TSH? Let's just say the first year when you're kind of going started here.

I mean, if we decided that we're treating this patient as an intermediate risk, so we will keep the patient between 0.1 and 0.5 of TSH around that, not completely suppressed, because it was not high risk from start, or even to the lower range of that 0.1 to 0.5.
Gotcha, perfect. All right, Joyce, and then you showed us an ultrasound, and we're headed down the pathway. So, Jill, what do we see in here?

Yes. So, what we see is a central compartment level six lymph node, which is a little bit big for that compartment. It looks like it's about four by eight by six millimeters. It's not particularly rounded. It does not definitely show cystic changes. We don't have the color Doppler. And, you know, I think all of you are alluding to the difference between clinically relevant disease versus low burden of disease versus no disease. And there's no real way for ultrasound to distinguish between those. We basically just report this in the absence of other findings. So it would just be size. We would say it's indeterminate, but could represent a low burden of disease. We do not recommend a biopsy. I see that in a lot of reports because as you're alluding to, it does not trigger a management decision in the vast majority of cases. But we do see a lot of reports that do say, you know, to biopsy.

So Mark, how do you have this discussion with the patient? I think we're zero surprised we find a little lymph node in the central neck with a tall cell variant of papillary despite radioactive iodine. If you don't wanna treat this right now, when do you change your mind to treat this? How do you have this discussion with the patient, Mark?

Yeah, I mean, I think we would just tell the patient that this is a relatively low-risk cancer, so we think, that it's likely to have indolent growth, and that we'll have to watch these little lymph nodes over the years, and I would stress years, because this is really a long-term, active surveillance situation at this point. I wouldn't even think that you would need to do it that closely. I mean, six months would be the soonest I would recommend. I mean, and even if these are stable at six months, I think you can go yearly pretty quickly with the follow-up. And, you know, there is some possibility over time that these will progress. But, I mean, these can likely be watched for for years, even if there is some slow progression, and understand it is possible the patient could need more surgery down the road.

Yeah. JP, where are we with like killing little lymph nodes with alcohol or ablation or that sort of stuff versus surgery? You guys have been killing these little things for a long, long time. Where are you sort of, how do you think about that in this situation here, JP?

So yeah, we like it a lot. So the reason why we tend to like ethanol ablation is that it all depends on how patients have been prepared to have the follow-up. For instance, if they were to be patients that come to us for the first time, we kind of prepare the patient to say, we're going to find something, do something sweet. Sometimes we don't do anything for years. those patients usually are fine watching. But if they come for the first time, second opinion, third opinion, we tend to say, you know, it's difficult to convince them to wait. And in those circumstances, surgery seems too extreme. And finding ethanol ablation is actually, has been a very good opportunity to treat mostly the patient's feeling and anxiety about this. And actually, we see patients actually like it quite a bit. I mean, we know that we are treating just the tip of the iceberg sometimes, we know about treating just a nodule, no change in the prognosis, but patients do find it beneficial in that way.

Very good. A common scenario for us to have. Jill, from your perspective, I mean, you live in this radiology land. How should we be thinking about doing ultrasounds? You know, we're thinking about doing less of them as we're getting long-range, but, you know, trying to get this balance between relevant versus non-relevant. How are you sort of thinking about that now, Jill?

Yeah, I think, you know, it's people talk about sort of, you know, you know, over diagnosis, if we see something, of course, we have to put it in the report, then the pendulum swings, just as JP said about potentially treatment versus versus over treatment. So I think particularly if you have somebody who's low risk or intermediate risk of recurrence, not scanning a bunch, This does correlate with that PET finding, so it's probably the real thing, but we don't get such a good look at the central compartment of the neck preoperatively. Postoperatively, with ultrasound, we see everything. We're going to see normal nodes, normal parathyroid. So, also, we have to be a little judicious in not making the report alarming about reporting every single thing and give a lot of the pertinent negatives, and then, you know, just saying it's uncertain if this is a normal postoperative finding or not. But yeah, I think if less is more here, if it's a low risk histologic recurrence.
Fantastic. All right, Dr. Shin, what'd you really do with this person?

So being the mean surgeon that I am, we did biopsy that small thing. However, like I said, after you had a visit at the Cleveland Clinic, we opted not to. do anything in terms of surgery. Um, all the possible treatment options were discussed and I've been following her for now three years. It has not increased in size. She's very comfortable with just watching it. It's not near any, you know, um, you know, important structure. So now I guess the question is how long do I follow this patient? I'll do the next question.

Yeah. I know when we started watching these, Dr. Shah and I were talking about this the other day, When we started watching these 20 years ago, we thought we'd just been watching for three or four or five years. And now some of these patients we've watched for 20 years at this point, and they really haven't changed at all. And do we keep following them for the rest of their life? So Dr. Shah has a really expensive house, so he thinks we should keep following them so he can make his mortgage payments and new cars. All right, so let's go on to case two. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old female. ECOG performance status was 0 at initial presentation. Weight was reported as approximately 50–52 kg.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in September 2020 with a large right breast mass measuring approximately 5 × 7 cm. During later follow-up after autologous stem cell transplantation, developed blurring of vision, dull aching right eye pain, and subsequently two convulsive episodes at home.

[ diagnosis ]: Primary breast diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), stage IIE at initial diagnosis, with subsequent right axillary nodal relapse and later secondary central nervous system lymphoma involving the brain parenchyma.

[ histopathology results ]: Excisional biopsy of the right breast mass showed an undifferentiated round cell tumor consistent with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Morphology demonstrated diffuse pleomorphic infiltrate composed of mature and transformed lymphocytes with inflammatory cells, mainly plasma cells and histiocytes, separated by fibrous tissue bands. Final diagnosis was non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell type. Immunohistochemistry showed CD20 diffuse membranous positivity in neoplastic cells, Ki-67 positivity in more than 80%, and negative staining for cytokeratin and CD3.

Excisional biopsy of a recurrent right axillary lymph node later showed involvement by non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell type, with CD20 diffuse positivity.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial post-contrast CT in 2020 showed a right breast mass, enlarged right axillary lymph node measuring 20 × 24 mm, and a few bilateral small upper deep cervical lymph nodes measuring up to 13 × 7 mm. No other abnormalities were detected.

Bone marrow evaluation showed a small hypercellular marrow, approximately 30%, with no lymphomatous deposits.

Post-first-line PET-CT showed enlarged right axillary lymph nodes measuring 16 × 7 mm with SUV 1.8, considered likely residual, and a peripherally enhancing avid right iliac cystic lesion with SUV 5.1. Subsequent PET-CT demonstrated no nodal metabolic activity and anatomical resolution of the previously reported right axillary lymph node. The right iliac cystic lesion was characterized as a non-metabolically active ovarian functional cyst, largest 17 × 15 mm.

Ultrasound of the axillary region after approximately 6 months of follow-up showed an enlarged right axillary lymph node with loss of hilum, globular shape, and cystic degeneration, measuring 3.2 cm, with suspicious features, plus another subcentimetric ipsilateral lymph node; no left axillary lymphadenopathy was seen.

Restaging PET-CT after axillary relapse showed no other pathological lymph nodes.

PET-CT in May 2023 remained consistent with complete remission.

PET-CT in July 2025 showed a well-defined hypodense non-enhancing area in the right frontoparietal lobe with associated mass effect and mild compression of the ipsilateral ventricle.

MRI/MRS demonstrated a superficial cortical space-occupying lesion measuring 34 × 20 × 30 mm with moderate perifocal edema, effacement of adjacent cortical sulci, and mild leftward midline shift; imaging was suggestive of lymphoma.

CT brain after one cycle of CNS-directed therapy showed regression of the previously reported right parietal lesion to 13 × 9 mm with mild edema and minimal mass effect.

MRI in November 2025 showed regression of the frontal lobe subcortical space-occupying lesion but new faintly enhancing patches in different brain sites, including subthalamic and frontal subcortical regions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BCL2 and BCL6 testing were not performed. CD10, CD19, and CD30 were not performed. No double-hit lymphoma testing was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: LDH at initial presentation was approximately 600. Serum methotrexate level measured one week after high-dose methotrexate was 0.04 and was considered toxic. Serum creatinine was reported as normal, around 1. Liver function tests were reported as normal. Kidney function was reported as normal by serum creatinine assessment. During toxicity admission, neutropenia was present. No B symptoms were reported at initial presentation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received 6 cycles of CHOP chemotherapy without rituximab as first-line treatment, completed in March 2021. Response assessment PET-CT showed likely residual right axillary nodal disease.

Subsequently received 6 cycles of rituximab. Re-evaluation PET-CT in January 2022 showed complete remission with no metabolically active nodal disease.

After isolated right axillary relapse approximately 6 months later, received second-line chemotherapy with R-GemOx-based treatment for 6 cycles; prophylactic intrathecal therapy was given during this treatment. PET-CT after 3 cycles in January 2023 showed complete remission, and PET-CT in May 2023 remained in complete remission.

Underwent autologous stem cell transplantation as consolidation, with day 0 stem cell infusion on 7 November 2023. Conditioning regimen was BEAM.

Following CNS relapse, received high-dose methotrexate plus cytarabine; methotrexate dose was 3 g/m². First cycle was administered on 8 July 2025.

One week after chemotherapy, developed febrile neutropenia, bullous skin eruption involving both arms and back, oral mucositis, diarrhea, scleral redness progressing to subconjunctival hemorrhage, and extensive ulcerative skin lesions. Dermatology assessment considered drug-induced skin toxicity and possible toxic epidermal necrolysis. Management included calcium leucovorin 50 mg every 6 hours for 2 days, then escalation to 100 mg every 6 hours, oral steroids, cyclosporine 100 mg every 12 hours, dexamethasone every 24 hours, and topical steroids. Marked improvement occurred on cyclosporine, which was continued for approximately 14 days and then tapered. Hospitalization lasted approximately 3 weeks.

After subsequent treatment, the patient received 3 cycles of the HAB protocol. Latest MRI in November 2025 showed regression of the original lesion but new enhancing brain lesions.

[ current disease status ]: After autologous stem cell transplantation, remained in complete remission until April 2025, approximately 18 months post-transplant. Subsequently developed secondary CNS relapse. After initial CNS-directed therapy, the dominant right frontoparietal/frontal lesion regressed radiologically, but MRI in November 2025 demonstrated new enhancing lesions in multiple brain regions, consistent with progressive intracranial disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Ophthalmology review during CNS relapse recommended retinal injection. CSF analysis had not been performed at the time the brain space-occupying lesion was identified. No lymphomatous bone marrow involvement was documented at initial staging.
