If you're comparing a toxicity of a certain thing compared to death, then it's less toxic.
And what do you give after progression on CAR T?

You can try bispecific. But I mean, generally, if you have secondary CNS disease and you get progression on CAR T, you're pretty much at an end-of-life situation. You can certainly try by specifics after CAR-T. There is some interesting data that, and this have been true in my own personal experience. If you have progression after CAR-T, in general, not specific to CNS, but in general, if you have progression after CAR-T, one of the reason, there are two main reason for progression after CAR-T. One of them is that you lose a target, which is usually CD19 for the commercial CAR-T. or you have T cell exhaustion because you make the CAR T out of the patient on T cell. So if you can use medication like lenalidomide in a small dose, there is proven data that this can reverse T cell exhaustion. So you could restore or rekindle the CAR T response. So when you give lenalidomide for relapse post-CAR TFC, that personally happening in a handful of patient, and there is few published smaller report that you could have a more, you can have durable remissions after CAR T progression if you use a drug like lenalidomide. The other thought is some of the relapses after CAR T tend to be localized. So there's some data that if you irradiate those lesion, again, we're not talking about CNS disease, we're talking in general, you can irradiate those and keep the patient remission for longer. So not all relapses after CAR T are equally terrible. Some of them are worse than other, and that's still something that's being, that's being investigated. One of the things that you should never do after CAR T is to give cytotoxic chemotherapy. Because what you will establish is you're dealing with a chemorefractory disease, mean if you give chemotherapy, it's not going to kill the lymphoma. What it will do, it will kill the CAR T. And then you can transform, and I've seen that happening before. You can transform an indolent type of relapse into an explosive type of relapse. So CAR T might be still having some therapeutic effect, but the lymphoma is breaking through. It's sort of like a tug of war. You have two sides pulling on the rope. But the CAR T still have some effect. The disease is not fully explosive. But then you give cytotoxic chemotherapy and you don't kill the lymphoma, you kill the CAR T. And you can transform a slow, indolent relapse into an explosive relapse. So one thing you should never do after CAR T is to give chemotherapy, particularly if you use an agent that kills lymphocytes, something like Bendamastin or something like that.
That would be one thing that you should never do after CAR T. So we can't use the CAR T at the bridge for a transplant?

You can, depending on the disease. So typically with ALL, the relapse rate is high and ALL is a disease of younger people. So there is a little bit of a controversy, mostly in the pediatric world. that if Kymriah, for instance, that's enough for curing LL, pediatric LL, or you need to follow it with an allogeneic transplant. And our adult diseases, usually not, because usually our patient are older, they're pretty beaten up. once you get them through CAR T, you're pretty much done. You're hoping for remission and then you're done. Now, if the relapses after CAR T, especially if you, usually, I don't know, I haven't seen that happening a whole lot. Right now, especially with B-cell lymphoma, We have a lot of different choices that you try to cycle all of those different things and kind of try to keep the patient alive one way or the other. But you don't use it just as a bridge. Usually a CAR T in aggressive B-cell lymphoma is your final step, usually. And then if they relapse, you try a bispecific if you haven't tried a bispecific before.

One other thing to say about the CD30 question, this would be a rare circumstance, but there is Brentuximab, which has some good activity peripherally and even to some degree CNS. So if this patient was CD30 positive, that might be another avenue, though that would be very rare. More likely, again, something like a BTK and one of the other drugs that has been mentioned will be the way to go.

And I wanted to just as a kind of a shout out for the FDA approved AxiCell like a couple months ago for primary CNS lymphoma based off an investigator initiated study. So, I know investigator-initiated is always surrounded by difficulty and sometimes are not taken, but the FDA took an investigator-initiated study on only less than 20 patients and expanded the label for CHITES products in primary CNS lymphoma as well as it included patients with secondary CNS involvement to receive CD19 cortisotherapy. I think there is definitely a good role here. And the alternative, I know 50% might not be great, but the alternative is death. So I think 50% against death is really a good outcome.
Thank you. You have answered all the questions of discussion.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary panel concluded that no further conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy should be administered, given chemotherapy-refractory relapsed secondary CNS lymphoma and severe prior toxicity. Management should be palliative and include localized radiotherapy to the CNS lesion(s), with consideration of intrathecal therapy if leptomeningeal/CSF involvement is demonstrated. If available, treatment with a BTK inhibitor with CNS penetration in combination with rituximab, with or without lenalidomide or nivolumab, was recommended as the preferred systemic approach. Reduced-intensity allogeneic transplantation with a thiotepa-containing conditioning regimen could be considered only if good disease control/remission is achieved and a donor is available.
reference_conclusion_quote: I don't think there is any point in continuing chemotherapy if you don't have an exit plan. [...] Yeah, then your best case scenario here is to radiate that area, not whole brain radiation, just radiate the mass. Again, palliative, and maybe consider intrathecal therapy and then put her on xenobrutinib plus rituximab, and that's gonna be the best you could do. And it's going to be completely palliative here. [...] Then you have, I think, you know, you could, the consensus is there is no point in doing any more chemotherapy, traditional chemotherapy. You're probably gonna need the retoxin. There is good data that you can give that at a higher dose, like 1,000 milligram per meter square, you get better CNS penetration. Along with Ibrutinib, or another BTK inhibitor, then you could either try what Dr. Emmons proposed with an ibrutinib and niflumab. I have had good luck with that regimen before. You could also try ibrutinib, lenalidomide, and ritoxin. [...] And do give that regimen for a good two months. And then repeat an MRI, repeat the LP. And if she enters remission and you have a a sibling donor that's available, you could do a reduced intensity allo with a Sayotepa-based regimen. [...] I concur that radiation, localized radiation, is maybe your best first step in getting BTK inhibitors. I hope that Ibrazenib runab is available. I know Ibrunib is, along with Rituxan and Lunalidomide, is a reasonable move to try to get the patient in remission. [...] I mean, you are in the palliation realm at this point. [...] I don't recommend you give any more chemo, any more cytotoxic chemo. You can use targeted agent, you can do radiation, but I wouldn't give any different combination of chemo at this point.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old African-American man.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent metastatic papillary renal cell carcinoma involving the adrenal glands/adrenal fossae and later para-aortic renal fossa recurrence.

[ diagnosis ]: Type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma of the left kidney, initially stage pT1a, with subsequent ipsilateral renal recurrence (pT1b), metastatic involvement of the right adrenal gland, bilateral adrenal/adrenal fossa recurrence, and later para-aortic renal fossa recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2003 left partial nephrectomy: type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma, pT1a, margins negative.  
- 2007 salvage left radical nephrectomy for left renal recurrence: type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma, pT1b, margins negative.  
- 2009 right adrenalectomy: metastatic type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma.  
- April 2011 exploratory laparotomy with left radical adrenalectomy and excision of right retroperitoneal mass, including en bloc cholecystectomy and partial hepatectomy: pathology confirmed resected disease; surgeon reported complete resection.  

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2010 non-contrast imaging demonstrated:  
  - recurrent mass in the right adrenal fossa at the prior adrenalectomy site;  
  - large locally advanced left adrenal mass;  
  - extension of tumor inferiorly along the aorta/lateral aspect of the vena cava;  
  - pancreas draped over and intimately involved with the left-sided mass.  
- Complete metastatic workup at that time was negative for distant metastatic disease.  
- Bone scan was negative despite minimally elevated alkaline phosphatase.  
- October 2013 staging evaluation demonstrated a para-aortic renal fossa recurrence adjacent to the aorta.  
- CT chest and bone scan at that time were negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No tumor molecular or genomic test results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Significant renal insufficiency after nephrectomy and in the setting of hypertension.  
- Estimated glomerular filtration rate was 27 mL/min/1.73 m² at the time of recurrent bilateral adrenal/adrenal fossa disease.  
- Anemia was present.  
- Alkaline phosphatase was minimally elevated.  
- At recurrence in October 2013, renal function had worsened: GFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m², creatinine 3.19 mg/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2003: Left partial nephrectomy for incidental left renal mass; margins negative.  
- 2007: Salvage left radical nephrectomy for left renal recurrence; left adrenal gland was preserved because it was radiographically and grossly normal; margins negative.  
- 2009: Right adrenalectomy for enlarging right adrenal mass; pathology showed metastatic type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma.  
- 2010: Developed right adrenal fossa recurrence and left adrenal mass.  
- Initial systemic therapy for recurrent disease: sunitinib; best response stable disease, followed by progression at 5 months; significant toxicity occurred.  
- Subsequent systemic therapy: everolimus; stable disease; significant toxicity occurred.  
- April 2011: Exploratory laparotomy, left radical adrenalectomy, excision of right retroperitoneal mass, en bloc cholecystectomy, and partial hepatectomy. Postoperative recovery was good.  
- No postoperative systemic therapy was given after the April 2011 resection.  
- October 2013: Para-aortic renal fossa recurrence identified.  

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: hypertension, ulcerative colitis, chronic renal insufficiency, anemia.  
- Prior surgeries included total abdominal colectomy, left partial nephrectomy, left radical nephrectomy, right adrenalectomy, lung surgery for a benign tumor, and transurethral resection of the prostate.  
- Former smoker; quit in 2003.  
- Performance status was 1.  
- Because both adrenal glands were ultimately removed, lifelong adrenal replacement therapy was required.

reference_discussion.text: All right, let's do one more case, and then we'll break. We'll let you go out and get the lunches and bring them back in here, and we'll continue on with the case presentations while we eat lunch. So, this is an interesting case. This is a 72-year-old African-American gentleman initially presented to an outside physician back in 2003 with an incidental finding of a left renal mass, and he underwent left partial nephrectomy. Margins were negative. It was a type 2 papillary T1A tumor, so stage 1 type 2 papillary tumor. A node dissection was not done at the time of surgery. He did well until 2007, and then he developed a left renal recurrence, and he underwent a salvaged left radical nephrectomy. At the time, the left adrenal gland was left in situ because it was radiographically and phenotypically normal at the time of surgery. And the final pathology demonstrated a type two papillary renal cell carcinoma, stage T1B, with negative margins. He did well until 2009, and then he developed an enlarging mass in the right adrenal gland and he underwent a right adrenalectomy. Thank God we spared that left adrenal. And this revealed metastatic type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma. He did well until 2010, and then he developed a right adrenal mass, sorry, a right adrenal fossa recurrence, as well as a left adrenal mass. And he comes to MD Anderson. His past medical history is fairly extensive. He has a history of hypertension and ulcerative colitis. He's had innumerable surgeries. He's had a total abdominal colectomy for his ulcerative colitis. He's had a left partial nephrectomy, a left radical nephrectomy, a right adrenalectomy. He's had lung surgery in the past for a benign tumor. And he's had a TURP, or resection of the prostate. You can see the medicines he's on. He does have a smoking history, but quit back in 2003. And he has fairly significant renal insufficiency following his nephrectomy because of the hypertension. And so his scans could not be done with contrast. They had to be done without contrast. But just to show you, so here's the vena cava. Here's the aorta. He's got this mass present where the right adrenal gland used to be, which is a recurrence in the right adrenal fossa. And he also has this locally advanced mass here. where the left adrenal gland should be. You can see this is the pancreas draped over it. Here's the beginning of the spleen, but the pancreas is sort of intimately involved with it. Very large mass. And here you can see the extent of the mass extending down along the aorta. So again, he has an adrenal fossil recurrence after adrenalectomy, and he has what looks to be a locally advanced left adrenal metastasis. with extension down along the lateral aspect of the vena cava and has probably a significant chance of having a hostile abdomen from all of the surgery that he's had done in the past. And he comes to MD Anderson and sits down with Dr. Chapin. And Dr. Chapin, what are your recommendations for this patient?

It's obviously a difficult problem. I mean, in patients who've had retroperitoneal recurrences who undergo re-resection, there is a real mortality risk of dying of the operation itself or dying while in the hospital. This patient's had multiple abdominal surgeries. Would it be difficult, at best, even to get access? You're also dealing with other organs that seem to be involved with the tumor at this time. Although, in the absence of other metastatic disease, a lot of this appears to be local tumor. So, I honestly, it would be a difficult problem, and I probably would seek consultation from you.
You're killing me. And I would, I'm not in the hospital. I'm traveling. So, you're on your own. What are you going to do?

You know, there's not really good systemic therapy for this, and in the absence of distant disease, I mean, I think if the patient wants to go for it, you tend to be heroic here and try to go for it, but I'd be very hesitant.
So, the disease is progressing while you're talking. Why don't you tell us what you're going to do?

I probably would seek the help of some of my surgeon colleagues for hepatobiliary, just to make sure I don't need assistance with the pancreas. And I would do a midline approach to resect his left fossil recurrence and his right adrenal recurrence, or adrenal fossil recurrence.
Okay, and he would not have any adrenal glands left, so what are the implications of that?
He'd have to be on replacement therapy. Which is? Mineral corticoid and a glucocorticoid.
So prednisone and Florine for the rest of his life.
Yeah, what's left of his life.
Dr. Karam, Dr. Chapin's office is next to yours. He comes by for consultation. What would you tell him?
Just a quick question. Is this something significant here or just a little artifact?
I don't know.
I have two pictures to look at, since you've seen the films, just to see if it's a local recurrence. Suppose it is. The first thing to do is to make sure to do a complete metastatic workup.
Which we've done and it's negative.

To summarize it, if the patient is healthy enough and willing to take the risk of doing an operation, In the absence of metastatic disease and in the absence of effective drugs, his only chance of prolonging his life is to go back to surgery and removing the left adrenal gland and the recurrence on the right side completely.

To find healthy enough because he's got renal insufficiency to the point that he can't get contrast for CT and he's got a history of hypertension and had multiple abdominal surgeries. Is that healthy to you?

Yes. And in our clinics, I mean, this is standard. So if the patient, what we normally do is send our patients to the internal medicine clinic for evaluation before major surgery. And if the patient can tolerate an operation and it's his only chance of survival, then that's what we have to do.
Okay. There's another look for you to see. Sorry, I didn't know that was going to pop up.

The one thing to point out about his disease kinetics is, you know, his disease was fairly indolent over the course of about the first seven years. And then suddenly in the past, this recurred within a year, right?
Last surgery was 2009.

Yeah, and this was 2010. So I think that's something to make note of because it's, for whatever reason, the tumor had a genetic shift or something, and now it's not quite as you know, sort of sputtering along over the course of six, seven years. And now, over the course of one year, it did more than it did the previous, you know, six. Okay. So what would you do? I actually would call Nizar because he's got a lot of experience with unconventional histologies or non-clear cell and see if there's either a clinical trial or there's something off trial that may be worth trying. But that does not negate anything that Dr. Karam said. His real chance is surgery. But the fact is, the likelihood is, is that he would recur pretty quickly afterward. But I would still, you know, explore all possibilities with Nezar.

So as it turns out, he has fairly significant renal insufficiency with a GFR of 27. He is anemic. His L-COS is minimally elevated, but his bone scan is negative. And the patient says, all right, you know what? I'm really tired of having surgery. So Dr. Tenhir, he comes over to your clinic. What are you going to tell him?

Unfortunately, he is not a candidate for a clinical trial because of his real insufficiency. So as we discussed this morning, all these good therapies that we have, unfortunately, they're not established or they have not been demonstrated. to be effective in the non-clear cell histology, especially papillary type 2. Papillary type 2, in my opinion, in my experience, is one of the toughest ones to treat. There have been retrospective studies. single arm phase two trial in non-clear cell and we had 27 patients with papillary RCC. We treated with sunitinib on that phase two trial and the results were not impressive at all. In fact, of the 27 patients with papillary treated with sunitinib, zero responded and the median progression-free survival was 1.6 months. We published this in 2012 in European Urology. Now some of these patients maybe were like him with comorbid illnesses. Some may have had a performance status of two. But these drugs that we discussed this morning don't really produce the results that we see with clear cells. So I would try to convince the patient and convince the surgeon to go and do surgery. If he's adamant against half surgery, then we will try. Try what? Try sunitinib.
Sunitinib would be your first choice?
Well, I will try to see if his insurance would cover off-label drugs.
He's independently wealthy. He can cover it by whatever. So why don't you tell us what you would choose?
Well, I think the drug that Tom mentioned this morning, Cometric or Cabozantinib, would be a drug that I would consider. You know, Tarceva, Erlotinib has been shown to have some activity in it.
He wants to know what Dr. Tenir would recommend.
I would recommend if his insurance would cover Cabozantinib, then we'll give him Cabozantinib.
Okay, and if he's indigent, what would you recommend then?
Then, you know, again, if he's not going to be able to get Erlotinib or Cabozantinib, then, what did you tell us about his performance status as well?
Performance status is one.
Yeah, I mean, then you can try sunitinib and tell him that the results are not that good. We can try that.
Okay.
There's one other option.
What's that?

That is to either use his archival tissue or do a biopsy and have it go through the, in our group, it would be the phase one group or the molecular markers group. And, you know, basically what happens now is that it's so much easier to test for the gene mutations in these tumors. And now what, in fact, we just got an email this week where they've been able to go from, instead of testing 50, they can test 400 known mutations. And some of those mutations are targetable, meaning that there's drugs that will act against that. So that would be another option. And actually, I think he would fit that trial. JJ, you and I have done a couple of cases like this.

What's that? I totally agree with you. However, phase one will decline him up front because his kidney function is low. So, but even in that case, you can still do the exome sequencing. He's papillary type 2, so it's possible that he has C-met mutation. And if that's the case, just like what Dr. Tannier said, we can try carboxanthinib. which is a cement inhibitor. So if you can match the mutation with the drug, then the likelihood for success can be up to, you know, 70 percent. So...
Okay, so your choice would be carboxanthin if you can get it, otherwise...
Otherwise, I mean, you can try one of the TKIs, you know. Yeah, what one do you want to try? I would agree with Dr. Tenier, try Sununtunib up front.
Sununtunib, okay. Tom, any different thoughts?

No, all of the above. I tend to use Nexavir a lot for my non-traditional histologies that don't fit any other pigeonhole for anything and with anecdotal evidence of some people do well for long periods of time. And one strategy in this guy who's not going to do well, he has a lot of negative features up front with his disease, his past medical history, his borderline renal insufficiency. I mean, he's in GFR of 27. For you all in the room, the normal should be in the 60 to 70 range for someone. So he has impaired kidney function. He probably, my concerns going to surgery right away is that he wouldn't make it through the surgery. He'd come up with a complication. So one of the things that could stratify is if you put him on an agent and he had a period of stable disease that you could contemplate some type of resection later, because at least you know that he wasn't exploding, because it seems like my experience has been whenever we've taken patients for multiple metastectomies, that one of the biggest concerns is it just pops right up again, and it's spreading while you're recovering. And so if he was able to demonstrate control on a targeted therapy, although that may be rare and not common, maybe one in five, But if he declared himself that way, then he may have a chance with being more aggressive surgically.

Okay. Thankfully, his disease hasn't progressed while you guys have been babbling on up here. He was initially treated with sunitinib, stable disease, progression at five months, changed to everolimus, stable disease, significant toxicity noted with both the sunitinib as well as the everolimus. What do you think?
Cut, cut. Cut, cut.
Cut, cut. Cut him.
He may not think surgery is so bad now after getting all that poison.

Anybody disagree with taking him to surgery? Okay. He was taken to the operating room, had an exploratory lab, left a radical adrenalectomy, excision of the right retroperitoneal mass. It was actually invading into the gallbladder, so he had an unblocked cholecystectomy and also partial hepatectomy. This was done in April of 2011. You can see the pathology. Thankfully, he had a good surgeon, so he recovered nicely from surgery and did well until October of 2013. He then showed up on staging evaluation to have a para-aortic renal fossa recurrence with a CT chest and bone scan that were negative. His kidney function's even worse with a GFR of 23, creatinine of 3.19, although he's no- Did he get any therapy after surgery or no? Would you have given him therapy after surgery?
Well, I wouldn't have done it. That would be somewhat malpractice. But I would be curious, because most of the time, the medical oncologist would like to give more.
So, well, OK, let's ask him. Dr. Tenhir, would you have given this guy therapy after surgery? Tom says no.

No. As I said, I was arguing for surgery all the way. But no, I think after the surgery, you rendered him without evidence of disease. You resected everything visible in the abdomen. So I would have followed him like you did.

So would anybody have given him systemic therapy after the surgery? No. Okay, good. All right, so here's his films, and you can see, and I'll show the audience here, he's got this one little area of recurrence right here, right next to the aorta. His kidney function's even worse, and he has an even more hostile abdomen because of his previous multiple, multiple surgeries. So, again, brief, please. Dr., let's see, Dr. Mateen, what would you do?

Well, he had a reasonable response to the first couple of agents. And so I would, again, call Tom or Nizar and talk to them about putting him back on therapy. An alternative would be to observe him for a short period of time just to see if he's developing explosive disease, just to spare him, you know, the suffering. The suffering of what?
Treatment. Of you doing surgery?
No, no, I wouldn't offer surgery.
You would not offer surgery? No. Okay. Dr. Karam?

So now it's been two and a half years since his last operation? It's been three years, actually. Three years. So, I mean, I agree with what Dr. Mateen said. The other thing is I would consult with my interventional radiology colleagues to see if there is any way they can do an ablation on this mass. I know it's very close to the aorta, but at least it's a question worth asking during the course of the disease, while it's still small, or if it can even be shrunken.
You do realize this is a small bowel right here, sitting on top of it?
Well, I can't see it. It's pretty dark and I have one picture to look at, but if you say so, I'll take your word for it.
It is.
Trust me. But that's the only other thing. I would not go back to do surgery at this point.
Okay. Dr. Chapin?

Yeah. I mean, the same as what the other two said. I mean, essentially systemic, send them back to Dr. Tenier for consideration of systemic treatments and then see where things go over the next course of the next year.
So for this solitary, small recurrence in the retroperitoneum, all the surgeons say no. Medical oncology, anybody in medical oncology want to do surgery?
I think the theme is surgery for today. I'm sorry, say that again? I think the theme is surgery today.
You would offer surgery?

Well, at least some local intervention, if it's possible. You know, I don't know if you repeat, like, those target agents, whether they, you know, the tumor apparently didn't respond. It became refractory. If you treat, I don't know the, you know, how much chance you have for this to respond.

Yeah, so to be honest with you, from my perspective, he did not tolerate the targeted therapy as well. He had a lot of toxicity. His renal function is terrible. This is a small isolated recurrence. We took him to surgery, and he had a salvage resection. There's the pathology. Margins are all negative. We also took out some of the lymph nodes. And, you know, it's been three months so far so good. He was able to get through the surgery fairly well. But I thought my feeling at the time was that, you know, additional systemic therapy, we know what this thing is. It's not going to shrink it. It's not going to make it go away. It's going to make him feel terrible and probably make him a worse surgical candidate. So, you know, I thought that aggressive local resection was probably the best way to go. So one of the things we're remiss about, and it's my fault that I apologize, but did anyone have any questions that they wanted to ask? I was asked one question during the break that I just wanted to allude to, and that is, you know, one of the concerns when you integrate systemic therapy with surgery is the issues of wound healing, which I brought up during my talk. And, you know, it's very important to understand that when you commit to performing a surgical procedure on a patient, they are going to need somewhere between four and six weeks of time to recover from that surgery before they can get any targeted therapy, regardless of what's going on. And that's always, at times, not always, but at times it can be a real crapshoot where, you know, you'll have a patient that you operate on whose disease, for whatever reasons, decides to explode after surgery. And you sit there and you watch this disease consume this person, and there's really almost nothing you can do because of the dangers associated with receiving targeted therapy and the issues associated with wound healing. Did anyone else have any other questions? If you do, we'd ask you to come to the microphone just so that we can record the question. Did you have a question? Anyone? If not, we'll proceed with some more cases. If questions do come up, please don't hesitate to get up and come to the microphone, and we'd be happy to take those questions at any time. If you have a question about the case, or if you have a question about one of these guys' judgment, just step up to the mic and let us know. All right, with that said, why don't we go ahead and move on. So the next case is a 50-year-old gentleman who presents with shortness of breath and chest pain. Those are sort of classic symptoms for somebody who has a pulmonary embolus, and that's always a concern. He reports a 60-pound weight loss and fatigue over the last six months. He had a CT, which was negative for metastatic disease, but also negative for pulmonary embolus, importantly. He has some evidence of renal insufficiency with a creatinine of 1.49, GFR of 50. He's got some anemia, although his LDH and LFTs are all within normal limits. LFT stands for liver function test. LDH is lactate dehydrogenase, which is just a blood test that we get an enzyme that circulates in the blood. And here are his films. So what we can see is he appears to have a tumor originating in the right kidney, and this is a tumor thrombus that extends up the vena cava all the way into the heart. Here's the heart right here. And you can see that he's got a very large tumor thrombus present within the right atrium, which is one of the chambers of the heart. Here's another view, which again shows a locally advanced tumor involving the right kidney here. with the thrombus going up to the heart, and here's a cross-sectional image. Here's the renal artery going to the kidney. Here's the tumor invading into the vena cava right here, and a locally advanced tumor involving the right kidney. The left kidney appears to be normal, and his metastatic evaluation appears to be negative. So with that said, Dr. Karam. You're always whining that you don't have enough patients at clinics. So this guy shows up in clinic for you. What are you going to do?

reference_conclusion: In the setting of isolated recurrent papillary type 2 renal cell carcinoma and poor tolerance of prior targeted therapy, aggressive local surgical management was selected. The patient underwent salvage resection of the small isolated retroperitoneal recurrence with negative margins and nodal excision. No postoperative systemic therapy was recommended after complete resection, and surveillance was planned.
reference_conclusion_quote: This is a small isolated recurrence. We took him to surgery, and he had a salvage resection. There's the pathology. Margins are all negative. We also took out some of the lymph nodes. [...] But I thought my feeling at the time was that, you know, additional systemic therapy, we know what this thing is. It's not going to shrink it. It's not going to make it go away. It's going to make him feel terrible and probably make him a worse surgical candidate. So, you know, I thought that aggressive local resection was probably the best way to go. [...] No. As I said, I was arguing for surgery all the way. But no, I think after the surgery, you rendered him without evidence of disease. You resected everything visible in the abdomen. So I would have followed him like you did.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive left nasal obstruction with rhinorrhea and hyposmia for 5-6 months, with associated dizziness, headache, and diplopia.

[ diagnosis ]: Olfactory neuroblastoma (esthesioneuroblastoma) of the left sinonasal cavity with skull base invasion, intracranial extension, meningeal/dural enhancement, and cervical nodal metastasis. Staged as Kadish D. Neck disease was identified on CT neck as a positive left cervical lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Intraoperative biopsy with frozen section demonstrated a malignant neoplasm suggestive of carcinoma. Final pathology was olfactory neuroblastoma, Hyams grade 3. Pathology demonstrated pseudorosettes.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a large mass in the left nasal cavity obstructing nearly all left-sided sinuses, with intracranial extension and abutment of the left orbit. CT demonstrated no invasion of the medial orbital wall, with chronic bony changes involving the sphenoid, clivus, and ethmoid roof. CT neck demonstrated a positive lymph node on the left. DOTATATE PET demonstrated tumor involvement in the primary site and neck.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past surgical history included prior nasal polypectomy performed outside the United States and prior tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy. Office biopsy was not performed because of marked lesion vascularity and patient anxiety. The patient underwent intraoperative biopsy.

[ current disease status ]: Hyams grade 3 olfactory neuroblastoma of the left sinonasal cavity with skull base invasion and intracranial extension, and a positive left cervical lymph node, staged as Kadish D.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination, there was no neurologic deficit and cranial nerves were intact. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated a highly vascular, pulsatile mass filling the left nasal cavity, extending beyond the middle turbinate without reaching the nasal floor or nasopharynx, with surrounding watery polyps. Fibrous dysplasia of the skull base was present.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so hello everyone. We'll be presenting our case for today. This is a 68-year-old patient who presented to our clinic with an MRI finding of a large sinonasal mass. I'll be showing his MRI shortly. His symptoms were a five to six month duration of a progressive left nasal obstruction with rhinorrhea and hyposmia, along with dizziness, headache and diplopia. Previous past medical history that is a bit related to us is he had a nasal polypectomy outside the US and a tonsil and adenoidectomy. On exam, he had no neurologic deficit and his cranial nerves were intact. On scope exam, he had a highly vascular pulsatile nasal mass that was filling the left nasal cavity. However, this mass was extending beyond the middle turbinate but not reaching the nasal floor nor the nasopharynx. And he had surrounding that watery polyps. This is his MRI. So as you can see, he has this large mass in the left nasal cavity obstructing almost all of his left sinuses with intracranial extension as well, and abutting the left orbit as well. This is his CT scan. to assess for any further bone involvement. His medial orbital wall did not look invaded, but he had some chronic bone changes, mostly in the sphenoid and in the clivus, and the roof of the ethmoid as well. We needed to get tissue biopsy to get further assessment of what this patient was presenting to our clinic with, but given the vascularity of the lesion that was on our exam and the anxiety of the patient, we were unable to have the biopsy in a clinic setting. And we could not also ask for a PET scan early on because the insurance company refused to get clearances before a biopsy proven malignancy, which was highly suspected on those imaging findings. So we ended up taking the patient for an intra-op biopsy and on frozen section, the patient had a malignant neoplasm that was suggestive of carcinoma. Thinking of what could be part of our differential diagnosis for malignant nasal mass, these can be a long list, but if we want to name some of them, we have the neuroendocrine tumors, the pituitary adenomas, melanomas, lymphomas, SCC, snot, rhabdomyosarcomas, or even Ewing sarcomas. And if we want to compare neuroendocrine tumors to olfactory neuroblastomas, usually, astesial neuroblastomas, they have a less aggressive clinical course compared to the neuroendocrine tumors. So the pathology of our frozen section ended up being indeed an olfactory neuroblastoma, and it was read as a grade three on HIAMS. Basically, the high M grading system is what will be categorizing the pathology or the histopathology of these tumors based on their architecture of the cells that they have, and this will further give us information on the prognosis with higher grades. meaning that the patient will likely have or present with metastasis, mostly in the neck, and will have a worse survivor rate. These are our own patients' pathological slides. These were provided by our pathology department, in which you can see some of the clinical findings that points out to the olfactory neuroblastoma with the grade three, and some of the key points or key cellular structures related to the diagnosis of the olfactory neuroblastoma. We have specific pseudorosette in him as well. So my question for the panel are the following. What would you order for additional imaging for a patient that presents with such a scenario to your clinic? What are some of the referrals you might consider? And if his neck is negative, what would you actually do with the treatment of the neck?

OK, maybe that's a good opportunity to stop and focus on some of these questions that you've posed here. Dr. Montero, maybe your thoughts on, let's just focus, let's focus on maybe the neck for now. He or she is N0, I believe, Nadine, is that right on imaging?
So this is my initial question. Would you ask for imaging for the neck to start with?

OK, let's say the imaging is done and it's negative. Eric, what are you doing for the neck? Himes 3 or high grade Himes? Are you doing an elective neck dissection? Are you? observing the neck or elective neck irradiation? What are you thinking for this patient?

Sorry, right now I'm just trying to deal with my post-viral cough, which I think is becoming more functional in nature than actually pathologic. But yeah, so that's a good question, Nadine, and it's a topic of controversy, as many will talk about how to manage the neck. Generally, so generally we would not operate on an N0 neck in the setting of anesthesia neuroblastoma. I don't know how my esteemed panelists, whether they would agree with that, but generally we would not approach that with primary surgery. However, where it's controversial is the radiation side of things and whether you give elective neck radiation to patients with Ends your neck disease. There's been lots of studies on this. And, you know, in our study actually Himes grade was not predictive of neck metastases. John can speak to this as well, but we did a study where there's actually comparable rates of neck failure in low grade and versus high grade hymes. So we're not sure whether that's necessarily true. However, other things can predict regional failure. I think out of the Pittsburgh group, Eric can correct me if I'm wrong, but when you look at something like dural invasion, for example, is actually quite predictable of neck neck failure as opposed to Heim's grade. So, our radiation doctors sometimes do treat the neck electively as part of management, about 20 to 25% of patients will fail on the neck over time generally I think was most of the studies have shown. And actually, the neck has also been shown to be relatively salvageable surgically. And when you add postoperative radiation to a previously non radiated neck in the salvage setting that can show some decent control options. Long answer is that we don't tend to treat the neck electively in these scenarios. However, the neck is often treated to some degree, whether that's microscopic radiotherapy, dosages of 50 gray or more, kind of is dependent on our radiation doctors. But I do tell patients that they do have about a 20 to 25% chance over time of failing regionally.
Kyle, are you guys, how are you guys addressing the neck at Ohio State?

Yeah, great question. I think Eric brought up a lot of key points. And like he said, there's been some several retrospective analyses that have looked at nodal failure rates. And like he said, for K-B and especially K-C disease, which this is, the risk of nodal disease or nodal failure is significantly higher. And so for us at Ohio State, we would routinely treat the neck with elective nodal radiation. And that allows us to include level one as well as the retropharyngeal basin. which is tough for the patients. Um, but that, that can be pretty comprehensive there.

Yeah. In Toronto, we, we electively treat high grade tumors, bilateral level two, three, actually, and RP nodes. Um, the, uh, um, we don't treat electively level one, Eric, to your point about regional failure, there's actually a lot of data with elective nodal irradiation that the regional failure rate is very low. In fact, in the Michigan series, and I think MD Anderson series with elective nodal radiation close to zero, that 20 to 30 percent is when you don't treat the neck. In fact, yeah, we did a neck dissection recently on a a low Himes grade patient who recurred isolated level two in the neck. Marilyn, your thoughts on neck management? Is anyone doing neck dissections here?

Not for clinically negative neck. You know, I agree with what's been said that because of the risk, especially in this patient with the intracranial extension, I would, well, my radiation oncologist would radiate the neck because you can't really access this retropharyngeal nose real well. With elective neck dissection, you can't really argue to do an elective neck dissection when there's no clinical or radiographic evidence of disease. So, you know, I think after the surgery, they would see our radiation oncologist who would very likely recommend post-op radiation, including the neck.

Yeah, sorry, John, I should have clarified that before, but yeah, I meant that 20 to 25% is exactly why most of our adults give it, right? Because I think our data shows it's less than, we've had less than 5% failures with elective neck radiation, right? Which I think is similar to the Michigan data. I don't know if it's 0%, but I remember something between less than six or 7% sort of the data, but I could be wrong.

And Dr. Levine, let's say this is a 20 year old patient with a, a Hymes I with the same volume of disease on imaging, so a low Hymes grade, asthesio-neuroblastoma. What are you thinking at your institution in terms of managing the neck or not managing the neck?

Yeah, that's a great question. You know, we, I think one of the great advantages is to kind of go through that at tumor board and we'll often, you know, have that discussion. You know, this is a young person then who has a high volume of disease and a long life in front of them. And I think they really also need to be part of that discussion. We know that neck recurrence is one of the most likely areas and that can be very delayed in this pathology. So we do really want to make sure that they understand that if we decide not to do the neck, there's a possibility that this is going to be the recurrence. I did have a significantly younger person, I want to say 16 or 18, that had an anesthesio-neuroblastoma with a clinically negative neck. And after talking with the patient as well as the family and our radiation oncologist and looking at the intracranial extension, we did actually decide to do treatment to the neck as well. that was very much a discussion that they were involved with. But I do think that that ends up being a much more kind of personalized decision and also a little bit focused on what kind of the risk tolerance level is of the patient and the family.

I think for the fellows, it's important that, you know, in young patients, these bilateral neck irradiation doesn't come without side effects. And salvage rates on recurrent neck disease anesthesia are not small. What I mean by that is you probably have a 70 to 80% likelihood of salvaging a nodal recurrence. So that should definitely be a point of discussion. If they recur, it's not like those are going to be catastrophic recurrences necessarily. They're very salvageable typically. So maybe Nadine, take us through what you guys did here.

So we did order imaging of the neck. We ordered a CT scan of the neck that showed a positive lymph node on the left. And we asked for also referrers to have the neck and neurosurgery for the extent of the disease in the neck and through the skull base. As for additional imaging, we also asked for a DOTATATE PET. And I want to talk a bit about this studying specifically because Esthesia neuroblastomas are known to express somatostatin, and the DOTADATE PET scan is a somatostatin receptor-targeted PET. It has multiple advantages over the regular FTG PET CT. Mostly it has better resolution and accuracy. We have less radiation dose on the patient. It costs less and it's much more comfortable for the patient. Most of the time it's used when the tumor is difficult to visualize, when we have extension through the brain or through the skull. skull base, and with the regular FTG PET scan, usually with Estesio, these have low metabolic activity, so the PET scan might be falsely negative. So many authors now are recommending the Delta Tate PET scan to detect lymph node metastases rather than the regular FTG PET scan. So as all the panelists have been discussing with the N0 or the N1 neck, we all agree that with the N1 neck, the patient will undergo a neck dissection. Most of the literature also recommends radiotherapy after that, plus or minus chemotherapy, which I'll be asking you about that in a few minutes. And with the N0 neck, the literature also is being geared into going with the prophylactic radiotherapy to the neck, given the high rate of regional failures in patients who do not receive this elective neck radiation, even in those Kaddish stage B or C tumors. So this is the DOTATATE PET scan of the patient. You can see the tumor involvement in here, and this is his neck scan. Next would be how would we stage our tumor and we have multiple staging system. The most common one is the Kaddish versus the Dolgorov stage. We are mostly familiar with those stages. the Kaddish is less detailed about where the tumor actually invades versus the other staging system, which is the Dilgarov, it goes more into details of what which entity is the tumor is invading. This will also help us if we follow one of those stages, let it be the Dulgerov, to know what approach the surgery should be or the surgeon should follow and it will correlate with further assessment of this tumor based on the involvement of either the crib reform, the orbit, or the dura, which will eventually play a role in the risk of recurrence and the death over time. Versus with the Kaddish, mostly like the Kaddish stage C, will have all of the tumors grouped in a single entity, regardless of which structures they are invading.
This is an interesting study. For the sake of time, I think we can skip forward since we're a little slow for where we are to talking a little bit about the risk action.

Okay, so this is in summary our tumor. It's a tumor that is invading the skull base. It has intracranial extension with meningeal enhancement at the positive neck. It is staged as a Kaddish D and a high M3 on pathology. So what would be your approach for surgery for this patient?
Maybe Nadine, why don't you show us what you guys did and then we can get some feedback from the panelists.

Okay, so what we ended up doing is a combined approach with neurosurgery going from above and below at the same time. This is our endoscopic view working on the ethmoid and this is the above the view. We ended up just like we would treat with any craniofacial approach following the tumor opening up the maxillary sinuses, the sphenoid, clearing it from different areas to get better access and to control the bleeding. So this is our endoscopic approach. This is the repair that was eventually done with the alloderm being sutured to the dura. And this is the immediate post-op CT showing the resection and the repair. These secretions are from the packing that were placed in the nose.
Can you just clarify, did you guys go from above with the craniotomy or everything entirely from below?
So this is the above procedure. So a craniotomy was done at the same time as the tumor from the endoscopic approach.

Okay, maybe pull up your images and we'll get some feedback from the group. Dr. Wong from UPMC. Eric, your thoughts on combined craniofacial resection with endoscopic assist versus strictly endo approach here?

So, I mean, I think actually in our team, we probably would have done this purely endoscopic, but in truth, I don't know that it matters as long as you get an R0 resection from a margin standpoint. If your team is more comfortable using a craniotomy to achieve that, I think it's... It doesn't, it doesn't matter. I mean our team we probably would have done this because it's behind enough. It's behind the frontal enough it certainly has a reasonable lateral extension, but I think it's well within the reach of the midplane in the orbit. So we probably would have done this and the nasal. I will say though, I probably, these surgeries are pretty long. So in my hands, I probably would have done the neck dissection actually on stage one. And I like to do the neck first because I don't really love re-intubating my fresh, you know, open craniofacial resection or endoscopic craniofacial resection with the re-intubation of the neck. So I tend to do the neck first, because I think it's a pretty straightforward operation. At least the node that you show, Nadine, was pretty significant in size. So I would have at least done the left neck first, and then probably done an endoscopic craniofacial resection for clearance.
Marilyn, your thoughts on when to do a craniotomy versus, indications for a craniotomy versus endoscopic approach.
Yeah, Corrina, how did you reconstruct the defect? Did you use a paracranoflap or a nasoceptal flap? Because that is one of the things we think about in deciding on the approach.

There was no nasoceptal flap that was going to be available because of the involvement with the sphenoid and the extension. We knew we wouldn't have one. And the, you know, I think one of the things that is an advantage here that you don't get to see is that for us, when we talk to the patient and I took him for an intraoperative biopsy, I said, well, if we know that it's something that we expect to be resectable, I can debulk some of it at the time. So when you can breathe into our second stage surgery will be much faster. So I think Eric's point is excellent. And for us, this was about half the size of what you see by the time that we went to do the second stage where we did it from above and below. And then we actually did the neck all in the same day. And because we do above and below at the same time, we actually work simultaneously. that saves us a lot of time to do it that way. But I think that's part of the reason is that we knew we wouldn't have a nasal septal flap. This is an older gentleman. And so this was a pericranial flap that we used.

Yeah, I think that would definitely weigh into the decision. I think that the tumor itself looks accessible and resectable from below. But if there's a concern about reconstruction, it's good to have that option of coming from above so you can do the pericranial flap.

Karina, correct me if I'm wrong, I imagine you guys chose to go from above because of that dural enhancement that goes almost to about the pupil on the left-hand side. Was that, because to me, you kind of scrolled over, it looks like the dural enhancement goes about to the level of the pupil, but maybe I'm just right there, a little bit back. So is that kind of what tipped your neurosurgeons? Because that's hard to get endoscopically if it really does go towards the pupil and beyond.

Yes, and I think that, you know, our concern was that we wanted to make sure that we got good margins on him we definitely wanted to get a good reception. And we were worried that, you know, if we were there and struggling and then we had to stage it versus doing it all at once. We really felt that then we got a better reconstruction, we got a better opportunity to get the really good resection for him, and then to make sure that we can really get him to radiation. You know, sometimes we will do this at Miami with just an allergy reconstruction and no, you know, vascularized covering there. But if we're going to try to get him as an older person to radiation quickly, and we knew that we would want to do that, this was, I thought, just a better option for him in general.

And then I guess a quick second question is the fibrosius appearing bone throughout the entire skull base. Did you biopsy that just to confirm that that was a separate fibrosius lesion or how did you manage that?

Yeah. So we, um, he definitely has a whole bunch of, um, fibrous dysplasia. And so a lot of it does come back as fibrous dysplasia, but we also then had to drill quite a bit of that bone, um, to get kind of all the stuff that was in the nooks and crannies, which, um, was less than pleasant.
OK, Kyle, final word. Combined crani endo versus endo alone and reconstructive options at Ohio State.

Yeah, great question. I think if you go through that MRI, the one thing that kind of leans me slightly towards the combined approach in addition to the reconstructive ability, because you're going to need a pair of cranium either way. is that the tumor has a fairly narrow waste right there that you're kind of working through, and then it kind of mushrooms out. So you're going to be fighting with that right frontal lobe quite a bit endoscopically, and you're going to be able to manage that perhaps a little bit better in an open approach, and then the extension up over the orbit on that left side. So, you know, we might start endoscopically, and then After we've struggled long enough, decided to go open or maybe just plan for it straight ahead of time. Frankly, I think, you know, it depends a little bit on the patient's age and all those things. This has been noted, but I would perhaps lean a little bit towards a combined approach here.

Postoperative radiation therapy, including treatment of the neck, was planned.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old White female.

[ chief complaint ]: Pituitary lesion identified after failing a vision test; referred for evaluation of interval growth on serial MRI.

[ diagnosis ]: Pituitary adenoma, initially diagnosed as pituitary microadenoma approximately 6 years earlier.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a lesion in the left sella, best visualized on post-contrast T1-weighted coronal images. Lesion size measured 0.7 cm on MRI in 2005, 1.1 cm on MRI in 2010, and 1.3 cm on the most recent MRI. Imaging showed gradual interval enlargement across serial studies. There was very mild suprasellar extension. The lesion was closest to the left pre-chiasmatic optic nerve at approximately 2-3 mm. No cavernous sinus involvement was identified.

[ laboratory results ]: Endocrine laboratory evaluation was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial management after diagnosis was observation following neurologic evaluation. Observation was continued after MRI the prior year despite interval growth. No surgery, radiation therapy, or systemic therapy had been administered.

[ current disease status ]: Slowly progressive pituitary adenoma with serial radiographic enlargement. Recent visual field testing was intact. Endocrine function remained normal.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion remained confined to the pituitary region aside from mild suprasellar extension.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so the next case is a benign tumor and certainly we spend a lot of time in tumor ward talking about gliomas and glioblastoma. but we spend probably as much time talking about the benign tumors, the pituitary tumors, the acoustic tumors, meningiomas, and we even spend a lot of time talking about things that we don't necessarily know whether they're tumors or not. Sometimes lesions, spots on MRIs that we're not sure of, we'll review at our tumor board too. So this is a case of a pituitary tumor, and certainly for this one, you'll see the importance of the radiology review, especially for these lesions when we're not exactly sure what they are. and then a focus on the treatment options of surgery and radiation.
Dr. McPherson, would you like to present the patient?

I would. This is a 41-year-old white female who was initially diagnosed six years ago with pituitary microadenoma. She failed a vision test with her ophthalmologist and got an MRI that showed a tumor. She saw a neurologist who recommended observation. She then had an MRI last year, which showed some growth, but again, further observation was recommended. She then presented to my office this year with another MRI with some more change. Her visual fields, when recently checked, are intact. She's had all of the endocrine lab work and all of that is normal.

We have three MR scans on this woman. This is her most recent one, which shows a lesion in the left stella. We can see it best on the post-contrast T1-weighted chronal images. On this study, it currently measures 1.3 centimeters in transverse dimensions. If we compare that to the scan done in 2005, it measured 0.7 sonometers and then on the scan from 2010 it measured, increased to 1.1 and again on the current study it measures 1.3 sonometers. So gradual increase over the three scans and it is considered a pituitary adenoma.
And how close to the optic nerves?
There's actually a very mild supercellular extension. The point where it's closest to the left pre-chiasmatic optic nerve is about two to three millimeters. There's no cavernous sinus involvement.
Well, in terms of treatment option, Dr. Tu, what do you think about this patient?

Well, I think this patient actually is best suited for surgical treatment. You could consider radiation, but she's young. You've followed her for a period of five years. It's doubled in size. The tumor is still confined to the pituitary area. It's not causing supercellular compression of the optic apparatus. So it's an elective procedure, but given the increased enlargement and the ability of surgery to cure this tumor, I think that would be the best approach. The technique would also offer a very low morbidity, and that's the technique where you actually go through the nose, so there's no incision on the skin, has very low morbidity, and a low probability of causing pituitary decline or pituitary insufficiency, because the patient still has, as I understand, a normal functioning pituitary gland, although it's compressed increasingly by the tumor. So I would recommend that approach to the patient, but I'm sure that there are those who may want to consider radiation. Dr. Brenner, what are the radiation options for this patient?

Yes, well, I do agree that treatment is indicated in this instance with the progression seen on the serial scans. There are a couple of radiation options. There would be the choice of using a fractionated radiotherapy regimen that would be daily treatment five days a week over five and a half weeks. pathway. I think that radiosurgery, a single fraction treatment, is also an option as well.
That has the advantages, of course, of being done in a much more compressed fashion with much less difficulty for the patient in terms of back and forth treatment.
Both of those options do give pretty good tumor control.

I think though in a young patient where there's a lifespan ahead of them of many decades, there's just not as much data about radiotherapy being effective 30, 40 years would favor surgery as well, and I agree with Dr. Tu. If a patient wished to pursue radiation, which of those would you choose for them, and what would be the risk in terms of hormonal dysfunction?

The radio surgery would be a good option because it is that single treatment. Now, the hormonal dysfunction after radio surgery is probably going to be a higher risk than it is with surgical excision. It would, over the period of the following 5 or 10 years, run about 30%, about a third

Dr. Pater, what's your opinion regarding radiation for this patient? Again, I think given the relative lack of long-term data going out 30 to 40 years for radiation, I think surgery would be preferable. I think if the patient did want radiation and wanted to avoid surgery for whatever reason, the stereotactic treatment would be the preferred method, again, because of the distance between the critical structures being sufficient for that treatment.

And can one of the two radiation oncologists here address the potentially for radiation after surgery? If this is a complete resection, then there would be no indication for radiation. If there was some concern that there was residual tumor afterwards, then I think depending upon what the degree of concern was, you could either observe for a period of time or consider radiosurgery to the remnants at that point.

Dr. McPherson, after hearing all of these recommendations, what is your final recommendation to the patient? I agree with Dr. Tu that given her young age and progression over time that surgery with the endoscopic approach would be my recommendation, but obviously radiation would be an option to discuss with her. So our official tumor board consensus is surgery is the primary option. And as you'll see in this case, certainly, again, radiology is very important. Determining recurrence versus treatment effect, especially in recurrent tumors, is a difficult thing and certainly something that radiologists help out a lot with. Obviously, treatment options, but especially for the recurrent tumors, a big part here is clinical trials. So we'll present this case.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/progressive ovarian carcinoma after multiple prior lines of systemic therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade papillary serous carcinoma of the ovary, initially diagnosed in September 2021; stage III at initial diagnosis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy next-generation sequencing demonstrated tumor fraction 12.1%. Reported alterations included MRE11 mutation, CHEK2 mutation, multiple TP53 alterations including TP53 R249S, and amplifications involving FGFR, KIT, and PDGFRA. Genomic instability status was reported as not detected. Tumor mutational burden was reported as 16.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent cytoreductive surgery, followed by paclitaxel plus carboplatin. Subsequently developed recurrent disease and received gemcitabine plus carboplatin, with good response; treatment was discontinued because of cytopenias, tolerance issues, and transfusion requirement. Thereafter received oral cyclophosphamide, oral etoposide, megestrol, and letrozole. Most recent regimen was pazopanib; disease progression occurred on pazopanib. Carboplatin-containing regimens had been associated with prior responses, and the disease had behaved as platinum-sensitive.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease after pazopanib. ECOG performance status was 1.

[ other clinical data ]: Prior gemcitabine/carboplatin course was complicated by cytopenias and transfusion needs.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Vague abdominal pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Malignant peritoneal mesothelioma. Initial biopsy diagnosis was epithelioid mesothelioma. In a separate but otherwise similar case described for comparison, final pathology after resection demonstrated sarcomatoid/biphasic histology.

[ histopathology results ]: Percutaneous CT-guided biopsy was obtained. Pathology review at the treating institution was performed. In the primary case, tumor histology was low-grade epithelioid malignant peritoneal mesothelioma. Ki-67 proliferation index was 1–2%. Tumor grade was reported as intermediate (grade 2). Final surgical pathology showed multiple sites of tumor of varying size. Cytoreduction achieved CC-0 status with no visible residual disease. In the comparison case, initial biopsy showed epithelioid histology, but final resection pathology showed sarcomatoid-type disease; this case was described as biphasic with both epithelioid and sarcomatoid components.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT performed during emergency evaluation for possible gallbladder disease or nephrolithiasis showed omental nodules, prompting surgical referral. Subsequent high-quality cross-sectional imaging was obtained, including thin-cut CT and MRI. Imaging and laparoscopy demonstrated residual/visible pelvic peritoneal disease with small white peritoneal implants. PET/CT was not used routinely for operative planning. Baseline chest CT was obtained to assess for thoracic disease. Peritoneal carcinoma index was reported as 14.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Somatic BAP1 alteration was identified. Germline BAP1 mutation was not detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent upfront cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy. Operative procedures included extensive peritonectomies, omentectomy off the spleen, bowel side-bite excisions and/or formal bowel resections as required, and appendectomy as a standard component. Complete cytoreduction was achieved (CC-0). In the comparison case with sarcomatoid/biphasic histology after similar CC-0 cytoreduction, postoperative systemic therapy consisted of 4 cycles of chemotherapy plus immunotherapy, followed by 6 cycles of immunotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: After cytoreductive surgery and HIPEC, no visible residual intra-abdominal disease remained (CC-0).

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described as medically fit/healthy for major surgery. Diagnostic laparoscopy was used to assess disease extent because imaging could underestimate thin peritoneal tumor deposits. Fertility preservation was identified as a relevant consideration in patients of reproductive potential.

Diagnostic laparoscopy is preferred to define the true extent of peritoneal disease, as imaging may underestimate tumor burden. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 90-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Pain, loss of appetite, and weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV / extensive-stage large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, managed clinically as small cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Morphology was consistent with large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma. Tumor was described as highly proliferative with high Ki-67.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL.  
- Creatinine clearance: 47 mL/min.  
- Cardiac function was described as fairly preserved.

[ current disease status ]: Extensive-stage large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma in a 90-year-old man.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Functional assessment showed ADL and IADL largely preserved; he was able to perform most activities independently.  
- No falls were reported.  
- Cognition was intact on assessment.  
- Mild depression was present and was already on treatment.  
- Nutritional risk index indicated severe risk of malnutrition.  
- G8 screening indicated need for full comprehensive geriatric assessment.  
- Age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index predicted 10-year survival of 0%.  
- Chemotherapy toxicity score (CARG) was 12, indicating high risk for serious toxicity.  
- BMI was described as acceptable.  
- Social support was limited to one full-time helper.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old woman at initial diagnosis in August 2019; later described as 65 years old. She was in good general health with excellent performance status and minimal comorbidity. She relocated to Wisconsin from another state.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic colorectal cancer diagnosed in August 2019 after presentation with urinary symptoms attributable to a bladder dome mass. She later presented to the emergency department with bowel obstruction after an approximately 6- to 8-week interval without treatment during relocation.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic right-sided colon adenocarcinoma with peritoneal metastases and bladder dome involvement; BRAF V600E-mutated, microsatellite-stable disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopy confirmed well-differentiated adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a right-sided colonic/fecal mass, several peritoneal nodules, a moderate-sized cecal mass, and an ill-defined mass at the dome of the bladder. No lung or bone metastases were identified. At later presentation with bowel obstruction, imaging showed a large right-sided tumor and dilated small-bowel loops.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E mutation identified. Microsatellite stable.

[ laboratory results ]: Baseline CEA was 2.3 and was non-informative. CA 19-9 was persistently elevated at approximately 130-140 initially, later rose with symptomatic deterioration.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She received first-line treatment outside the current institution with modified FOLFOXIRI. Best response was partial response. Clinical benefit lasted approximately 7-8 months. In May of the subsequent year, she developed symptomatic deterioration with rising CA 19-9 and was recommended to start encorafenib plus cetuximab, but treatment was delayed for approximately 6-8 weeks during relocation. She then presented with bowel obstruction and underwent extensive debulking surgery. Postoperatively she recovered with some difficulties.

[ other clinical data ]: Extensive debulking surgery resulted in a positive margin related to incompletely resected bladder tumor involvement.

reference_conclusion: For metastatic right-sided colon adenocarcinoma with BRAF V600E mutation and peritoneal disease, initial management should consist of first-line systemic therapy rather than upfront surgery, with reassessment of surgical candidacy only if an excellent response is achieved. In a patient with good performance status, an intensive chemotherapy regimen such as FOLFOXIRI/FOLFIRINOX with bevacizumab, if no contraindication is present, is favored. BRAF-directed therapy with encorafenib plus cetuximab is supported in the previously treated setting and is not indicated as first-line therapy.
