reference_discussion.text: All right. OK. So thank you for giving me the opportunity to present this case. I'm Kate Larrabee. I'm from Henry Ford Hospital. I'm a PGY-4 resident. So this patient's a 63-year-old woman with hypercalcemia, incidentally noted on routine annual lab testing. It was identified several years ago, but she was told not to worry and to continue routine follow-up. Her most recent outside labs revealed elevated serum calcium with the highest value of being 10.9. So additional testing revealed a PTH that was also elevated at 110. And at this point, she was referred for primary hyperparathyroidism. At her first deployment, she reported a remote history of nephrolithiasis seven years ago. The stones passed on their own without complication. She complained of acid reflux and general aches in her legs, and she had no fracture history. From the outside workup, I mentioned her highest calcium was 10.9. Her DEXA-T score was negative 1.8, which was consistent with osteopenia, but the form was never tested, and 24-hour urine collection was not performed. Laboratory testing that was done in our clinic showed a calcium of 10.7 with corrected calcium 10.3, ionized calcium of 1.38, an elevated PTH of 133 and then a vitamin D level of 43. So the question for the group is whether she has an indication for surgery.
Yeah, thank you. Does she have insurance? No, I'm just kidding. I'm kidding. It's a joke. It's a joke.

So thank you, Kate. So this case, this is not a diagnostic quandary. That's not the point of this case. The point of this case, as Kate kind of showed there, is indications for surgery. So I'll open up with just a broad question. Dr. Tarras, how do you think about indications for surgery? For some people, the indication is having the disease. Is that your belief? Do you have more kind of restrictive approaches? How do you think about this?

Well, first of all, thank you for the privilege of participating in this webinar. It's certainly an honor, and I always enjoy talking about parathyroid disease. That's the only thing I know anything about anymore, so it all worked out well. Let me just make a couple of comments about the excellent presentation, Kate. Just a couple of things to think about. The patient was referred by a primary care physician as opposed to an endocrinologist. That makes a little difference to me just in terms of making sure all the ducks are in a row. The endocrinologist, especially if it's somebody you know well, you can almost anticipate that the patient has the disease and it's been appropriately worked up. When it comes from a primary care physician, sometimes it's vitamin D deficiency or something else. So that's one thing to make note of. The kidney stones, so you said seven years ago, maybe she's had this condition for seven years. A lot of patients have. Maybe it's just a red herring. But that's worth noting. And then for me, in terms of deciding on surgery, the big thing for me is family history in terms of ruling out. You said there was no 24-hour urine calcium. That doesn't bother me. Most of my patients don't have that. But as long as there's not a family history of a cousin that had surgery for parathyroid disease and never seemed to get better, that kind of thing. So if there's no family history, then the patient is, I would say, eligible for surgery. Again, assuming this is a straightforward case, I would say the age then starts to matter. For me, 63 is increasingly young. I think you've got the latest workshop guidelines. The thing that aggravates me over the past 20 years of doing just parathyroid and thyroid diseases, They have not changed the age you see it at the bottom age 50 5050, even though the surgery has gotten easier, safer, more effective and more dependable. We really need to raise that age so that more patients. seem to be eligible based on their criteria. This lady's 63 and I'll occasionally have that conversation with a patient like, are your parents alive and how old are they? And when you find out that their dad is still alive at 96 and the mom is 92, you can figure she's gonna be around for 30 years. And so the question is, when do you pull the trigger? And really the time to pull the trigger is early right when when she's relatively young and healthy and going to the stand of surgery, pretty easily and so, so I would say, you know, in my book, absent, you know, true hard indications like kidney stones or. bad osteoporosis, I think it's reasonable not to deprive the patient of the opportunity to feel better. And in those guidelines, they specifically talked about we can't make any promises about neurocognitive improvements and quality of life improvements, which I guess I agree with. But I'll tell you the way I say it to my patients, because I don't really talk about that when in my standard conversation, I talk about protecting your kidneys, protecting your bones, because it's really about kidney health and bone health. If they bring up other symptoms and, boy, I've had fatigue, I've got foggy brain, I don't sleep well, I've got bone pain, joint pain, what I tell them, and I don't know if I was saying it back when Michael was doing the fellowship with me, but what I tell them is, you know, the list of symptoms that you can have, got to get both my hands in there, the list of symptoms you can have related to this disease is very lengthy. The problem is everything on that list is nonspecific. So it means it could be from this condition, it could be from age or depression or other things. And then I say, the only thing that we have to agree on is if anything gets better after the surgery, I get full credit for it. And they laugh and everybody understands that maybe you're gonna get better, maybe you're not. And so that's sort of the bottom line for me as a 63 year old with hyperparathyroidism, Why wouldn't you operate there'd have to be a reason not to in my book is because by and large, they feel better and that's what I tell the patients I said I can't guarantee anything but it's the rare patient that doesn't feel better even the ones that that didn't think they were symptomatic. And some of them are, you know, sort of type A, they're from Connecticut or New York, and they're going 100 miles a minute, and they're sort of working through their fatigue or issues until you fix that problem. Then they say, oh, my God, I had no idea. I thought everybody felt this way and so forth. So those are my thoughts.

So, just because I, I think that the, the, the slide that Kate has up. I think probably a lot I assume a lot of the fellows kind of hear about this these is this is from this, this NIH or at least initially was an NIH kind of initiated group and they put out these. these guidelines every few years. And the way these guidelines are described, right, is as this is for asymptomatic patients, right. And so they say that at the very bottom, just like you said, if you come in, you have clearly related kidney stones, or you have compression fractures from from osteoporosis, okay, fine. But if you don't, these are kind of what they put out. And they, you know, changed a little bit over time, this way, that way, whatever else. because I assume many of the fellows see this, tell them what your thoughts are about this. Like, if someone doesn't meet one of these again, like, does that mean like, okay, you're out? Or do you look for these things if the someone doesn't come in with them?

Yeah, so I would say it's a bit confusing because they say it's the asymptomatic patient, but that's narrowly defined. As you said, kidney stones, fragility fractures, and neuromuscular syndrome, which I've never seen. So that's symptomatic. So they're calling these patients asymptomatic, but most of them have symptoms. They're just not specific to this disease according to the guidelines. So that's just one important thing to point out that it is a little bit confusing. And then the most important thing I can I can tell the fellows and then what I tell my fellows and residents is the way to think of these guys and endocrinologists that I interact with, because this this becomes the Bible for the endocrinologist, and I can't tell you how many referring documents. I get this, well, they don't meet the criteria, or they meet the criteria because they have this or the 48, so I guess I'm going to send them for surgery, and I do my best to gently educate them that the guidelines are really, it's not indications for surgery. These are guidelines which are the contraindications to observation. So if you were thinking about observation, but then they have one of these findings, then you cannot observe, you must send for surgeries, is really the way to think about them. The default should be surgery, because especially again, in 2023, it's usually a straightforward operation done in experienced hands, and outpatient, the patients recover easily. Now, a surgery is still a surgery and can have complications, sometimes dramatic. I would say less so with parathyroid disease than with thyroid disease but but it certainly can have complications. But by and large, many, many patients are benefited from the surgery and I think many, you know, are hurt by not having by not being offered the operation and, and the problem is, you know, Our internist friends are creatures of habit and they're sort of guideline driven. That's the way, especially the younger ones are sort of trained, which by and large is a good thing. But I just think they sort of do them a disservice with these guidelines. And I think you mentioned, Michael, the AAES guidelines.

Yeah. So one last question, then we're going to go on to the next case. Maybe, Natalia, you can get your slides ready while we're talking about this. How does imaging play into indications for surgery? Someone has, say, non-localizing studies. Does that influence the way you think about should they have surgery or not? Or is that a silly idea? Or what are your thoughts about that?
I'm sorry. Who did you ask, Michael? Oh, sorry.

That was for you. Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you said, oh, you said to tell you get your slides for me. Yeah. Imaging. Um, listen, it's always nice when they have localizing imaging, but, um, but I have, most of my endocrinologists are very well trained, uh, not to get any imaging, send the patient, I'm going to do the imaging. And so, um, so when I do the imaging, it's again, it's nice when you have, when you see something, but it doesn't change anything about what I'm going to do on primary surgery. On reoperative surgery, that's different. But we're talking now on primary surgery and no, of course we're gonna operate. I mean, of course I'm gonna operate. Now, if it's a morbidly obese patient, it's truly non-localizing, because there's a lot of non-localizing studies that are not actually non-localizing. And we had a great nuclear medicine physician I think just recently retired, sadly, but, but he looked at things like a surgeon like we do you know it's okay if you're not right 100% of the time but tell me what you're thinking and, you know, I see something here whatever, as opposed to, I see so many that say, you know, non localizer. nothing asymmetric and I turn I turn to my nurse and say, does that look asymmetric to you and she says yeah this there's something over on this side like, how was the radiologist that they, they're looking for the so called light bulb system maybe, which happens but mostly it doesn't happen and so, but anyway so if there's non localizing But if it's truly non-localizing and you don't see anything on ultrasound and the patient's big and maybe they're crotchety or whatever else, that's a good patient to refer unless you're doing a ton of this stuff. Because if you're a decently trained surgeon, you should do parathyroid surgery. But the ones that you can see coming down the hallway, not literally, but you can tell this is going to be a tough surgery, maybe refer those. Completely non-localizing, that might be the one.

All right, thank you. So Kate, thank you. And we're gonna move on to the next case just in the interest of time. And Mike, I just wanna make sure. So we'll save time at the end to allow people to ask questions. Is that okay for you?

Usually they'll just actually shoot them to the chat box and we can introduce them at any time. But yeah, as we're transitioning, I do think that's a really important point for the fellows. And I think it was great to get Dr. Terrace's insight on this as well. I think many people would argue that you almost want to determine whether you're going to operate or not before you get imaging. Obviously, imaging is nice because it can guide a more focused approach, but having something show up and seeing something that looks red as abnormal doesn't necessarily then obligate you to operate. You have to make that decision based on your clinical assessment of everything else.

Yeah, let me add on to that because that I see that as well that the endocrinologist orders their own imaging studies. It's negative. And so they say, well, I'm not going to that. That's not a case I would refer. And so that's that's the worst of all situations.

Yeah, I mean I think that Mike and, you know, as you said, emphasize that idea I mean it's amazing to me that endocrinologist still will use nuclear medicine. It's like, oh well we didn't see anything so therefore we're not sure if you have the disease. the scans are…they're not for diagnosis. They're not to…at least in my mind, they're not really influencing the idea of whether you should have surgery or not. It influences maybe the form of surgery you should have, but I couldn't agree with you more. Okay, so in the interest of time, we're going to move on to a slightly…you know, people refer to it as mild. It's not necessarily mild, but it it's maybe more of a nuanced idea in terms of potentially that certainly the diagnosis and and then maybe what you're going to find intraoperatively. So with that, Natalia, do you want to get started?

reference_conclusion: The panel concluded that this patient with primary hyperparathyroidism is an appropriate candidate for parathyroidectomy, provided there is no concerning family history suggestive of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia or related hereditary disease. Surgical decision-making should be based on the clinical diagnosis rather than imaging findings; nonlocalizing imaging does not preclude operative management in a primary case. If the studies are truly nonlocalizing and the operation is anticipated to be technically difficult, referral to a high-volume parathyroid surgeon is appropriate.
reference_conclusion_quote: So if there's no family history, then the patient is, I would say, eligible for surgery. [...] And so that's sort of the bottom line for me as a 63 year old with hyperparathyroidism, Why wouldn't you operate there'd have to be a reason not to in my book [...] The default should be surgery [...] but it doesn't change anything about what I'm going to do on primary surgery. [...] But if it's truly non-localizing and you don't see anything on ultrasound and the patient's big and maybe they're crotchety or whatever else, that's a good patient to refer unless you're doing a ton of this stuff. [...] Completely non-localizing, that might be the one.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent gross hematuria in the setting of prior urothelial malignancies.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent multifocal high-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) involving the contralateral solitary kidney, with disease in the renal pelvis and proximal ureter. Prior urothelial cancer history included high-grade Ta non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer diagnosed in 2019, subsequent bladder carcinoma in situ, and right-sided high-grade UTUC treated surgically in 2022.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2019: Ta high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.  
- Subsequent bladder recurrence: carcinoma in situ within the bladder.  
- 2022 right radical nephroureterectomy pathology: pTaN0 high-grade UTUC.  
- Biopsy of recurrent contralateral upper tract lesion: high-grade urothelial carcinoma with suggestion of possible lamina propria invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated mildly enhancing tissue thickening adjacent to the ureteral stent, corresponding to tumor seen endoscopically. Ureteroscopy identified high-volume, high-grade, multifocal UTUC in the solitary contralateral kidney, involving the renal pelvis and proximal ureter.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry demonstrated retained expression of MMR proteins.

[ laboratory results ]: Estimated glomerular filtration rate was 59. Good performance status was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2019: Intravesical BCG for Ta high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer; no recurrence for approximately 2.5 to 3 years after completion.  
- Subsequent bladder CIS: induction intravesical gemcitabine/docetaxel followed by maintenance therapy for 2 years.  
- 2022: Upfront right radical nephroureterectomy for high-volume, high-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma; final pathology pTaN0 high-grade UTUC.  

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidemia. The patient had a solitary kidney following prior right nephroureterectomy. Functional status was reported as good.

reference_discussion.text: Absolutely. And honestly, from a functional standpoint, he's living life as he was prior to a diagnosis of cancer. So even in the absence of one kidney, even with the degree of CKD that he has, he's staying away from dialysis and he's maintaining a very happy sort of quality of life at this juncture. So I agree, we've been pretty fortunate, I think, I would say, with his outcome. So let's move on to case three. This one, you know, I'm trying to stump the chumps here, so hopefully we can get something a little more tricky for you. So with this case, we have a 57-year-old male. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, relatively a clean slate of health, but he does have this history of recurrent urethelial cancer in various parts throughout his urinary tract. His urethelial cancer history dates back to 2019 when he was initially diagnosed with TA high-grade non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. This was treated with a course of BCG. Upon completion of the BCG, he had been initially without any recurrences for the first two and a half to three years and then was found to have a focus of CIS within the bladder. For that, he received induction course of gemcitabine dosotaxel and had been on maintenance treatments for two years. That being said, he did also in 2022, he was found to have a high-volume, high-grade upper tractor enthelial cancer within his right upper urinary tract and had undergone an upfront radical nephroureterectomy with a final pathology that had revealed PTAN0 high-grade UTUC. Two years later, he had redeveloped gross hematuria and underwent evaluation for this. Ultimately, he was found on ureteroscopy to unfortunately have a recurrence in his contralateral solitary kidney with high-volume, high-grade multifocal UTUC both within the renal pelvis and in the proximal ureter, a biopsy, as with an earlier case, had suggested the potential for lamina propria invasion. Of note, given the span of his urethelial cancers, MMR testing was performed. This is actually something that we try to perform routinely, but on the actual tumor itself, IHC stains for these MMR proteins were all demonstrated retention of the protein itself. I don't have the greatest images to highlight the degree of his disease. Unfortunately, there were no intraoperative photos or fluoroscopy acquired, but at least adjacent to the stent on these cross sections that you see here, the arrows try to do justice to the tumors if you can make out some of this mildly enhancing area of tissue thickening consistent with what was seen endoscopically as well. I should point out that he had good performance status and his EGFR was 59. So, with this situation, solitary kidney, high volume, recurrent high-grade UTUC, maybe I'll initially pitch this one to Dr. Schmidt. Can you provide us with some of your insights as to how you would approach this patient and counsel him on his options?

Oh, this is so rough. I mean, this is just one of those scenarios you really dread. First of all, this is a patient obviously I would look at genetic testing for making sure that we don't have a Lynch scenario. You mentioned MMR or IHC staining, but just doing full evaluation for that I think is important. He's got a solitary kidney. He has a history of bladder cancer. I really worry about this patient. Obviously, you take out that kidney. They're committed to dialysis. I've had a patient like that recently who chose that route and said she wants to avoid systemic therapy, would rather go with surgical therapy. I think that cuts off your options down the line for some systemic treatments, not having any renal units. You know, you can only get Pembro at that point, maybe. Not even, right?

No, I would actually say no. It's easier to actually give systemic therapy once a patient is on dialysis. This creatinine clearance is okay, but if somebody had end-stage renal disease with a creatinine of the clearance of 10 or 15, that's where it's much harder. So in this setting, it would be more reasonable.

So obviously, that's still an option. I think that's a real discussion with the patient. I think I would consider systemic therapy in this patient. While you can with that renal unit, especially given that you describe a fairly extensive tumor, I worry about this patient developing metastatic disease. I would consider this patient for intensified systemic therapy with chemo plus immunotherapy if you could do that. The alternative is you take out the renal units. You can do adjuvant. He recurs in the bladder. You take out the bladder, right? I mean, there's a lot of ways that this could progress in a 57-year-old. I don't know that there's a right answer. I think this is a lot of shared decision-making here.
Dr. Schmidt, do you see a role for topical installation of any agents such as BCG into the renal pelvis?

In a small tumor, in a solitary setting, maybe you could consider something like that, but I think that's kicking a can down the road and not very far down the road. When you have a large tumor like this, you have it in the proximal ureter, you have it in the pelvis. I don't think it's going to work. I think the way if we have a treatment that can sit in that space in the high-grade setting like the reverse thermogel, we know they looked at mitomycin in a high-grade setting a little bit. I think I saw a paper looking at it in some kind of small case scenarios. Maybe there's some promise. It's certainly not approved in that indication. I think BCG, in my experience in this case, has not been effective, whether you do it through percutaneous access and drip it down slowly, or you put it in the bladder with a stent. In a patient who was much, much older and really wanted to preserve their quality of life and just delay, delay, yes, maybe, but not in this patient.

So it sounds like, you know, the urologist toolkit is a bit limited in a setting such as this, you know, shy of committing this patient to being anephric and dialysis dependent versus maybe ineffective options like topical installations or futile endoscopic attempts at fulguration, particularly when the volume of disease is high and we know it's high grade. Dr. Hoffman-Sentzitz, do you have any tricks up your sleeves you could offer?

I have a few tricks. I think one of the important things for a patient like this is to really frame what the disease state is and what are the goals of care. This turns out because you and I have a multidisciplinary upper tract urethelial cancer clinic that we preferentially will book patients with really challenging disease that we feel like we both need to see at the same time. No, this is a not uncommon scenario that we see in our clinic. And I think that I try to imagine, OK, if this patient had two kidneys, how would we approach this? Then I have a conversation about, OK, perioperative cisplatin-based chemotherapy and nephrectomy going on dialysis. Because I think at the end of the day, surgery is still the gold standard. And I think patients need to be aware that that choice remains. It's a really tough choice. I wish we had the crystal ball to know who was going to be best suited for that. And the comorbidities that go along with dialysis, all the unknowns in that setting. And then patients ask other really good questions that Well, am I eligible to get a transplant later? There's so many things that kind of go into what does it look like if, you know, I go down that road. And then we go down, well, what would the other road look like, which is if we treat with palliative intent, if the feeling is this is a person who does not want to have their cancer resected, even in the setting where that's an option, then what are our other options? And so that's a situation where I feel like as an oncologist, I can open up my toolkit of medications and see if we can control disease when an operation is not feasible. And so that's kind of how I frame the discussion. And oftentimes, this is not just one consultation. It goes on. For patients with upper tract disease, in addition to having the comorbid issues and problems with renal function, the lack of tissue that we have as medical oncologists to oftentimes get additional information, like next generation sequencing, to see whether or not the patient's a candidate for an FGF inhibitor, we're limited to some extent by that. So I think for this patient, if they have good renal function, we can use a perioperative toolkit of cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Again, with good renal function, platinum-based chemotherapy with palliative intent with a goal of just downstaging and keeping that renal function as good as we can is also reasonable. And then we also have this new exciting tool of n4tumab plus pembrolizumab. that we can use for patients with, you know, locally advanced metastatic disease. And that's a great tool for many reasons. So one is, you know, these drugs are not necessarily neprotoxic, and they are suitable for a wider variety of patients, both, you know, traditionally platinum eligible and ineligible. And the response rates are generally quite high. You know, what is the response in the primary tumor versus a metastatic disease? I don't think we have a ton of prospective or even retrospective data to kind of understand what that looks like. But certainly, you know, preoperative trials are being done. And at least for bladder cancer, I think we'll hopefully be having that information soon. And then if a patient has intolerance or progression on our first treatment, there's certainly, you know, the ability to get subsequent treatments down the line. But I think still with the same conversation at each fork in the road of whether or not they want to kind of re-decide if they want to have surgery at that point in time or not. I think it's important to, if it's still feasible, there isn't any evidence of metastatic disease that we continue to have that ongoing conversation if surgery is still feasible.

So this gentleman was vehemently opposed to undergoing a radical surgery, and he wasn't really as excited about some of these other, let's say, topical options that were felt not to be really that effective. Dr. Hoffman says, is there sort of a go-to combination you may use? Are there any clinical trials you can think of for which he may qualify?

Yeah, well, thanks for asking that one. So as a labor of love, and because I do see patients in my clinic quite often with this scenario, and really felt like this was certainly a population with a huge unmet need, we do have a trial open now at Hopkins using n-fertumab and pembrolizumab for patients with non-metastatic upper tractor athelial cancer, where really it is their intention to keep that kidney. So we're looking at you know, tolerance, safety, outcomes, response, outcomes, which are not as, you know, easy sometimes to kind of determine. And then really also an outcome of can a patient keep their kidney and maintain their kidney function. So we do have that trial open. And I think others, you know, across the country are kind of thinking about using the EB-Pembro toolkit in this or various different settings for patients with hard to manage upper tract disease.

Yeah, and really, thank you for your efforts with this trial. I mean, as you had alluded to, it's a very challenging scenario, very much an unmet need for a lot of patients, either between having a solitary kidney or simply being very comorbid or decreased renal function at baseline. Sometimes there is a lot of morbidity that we would put a patient through by subjecting them to a radical nephrogenectomy. And so to be able to show, hopefully in due course, potential benefit from simply a strategy of utilizing systemic therapy alone, that it may be a feasible alternative to surgery, I think would certainly be very useful for a lot of patients that you encounter in practice with UTUC. And then I guess the last bit, since it is at this juncture very experimental, would there be a defined endpoint? Maybe if you can attest to how what's called the renal retention trial is designed, is there a certain duration for which you would treat this patient with EV Pembro or is it more of an indefinite sort of regimen you would use?

Yeah, I think the spirit in which EV Pembro was approved and kind of the thought about how we would give it in this trial is if the combination therapy is controlling disease and patient is tolerating treatment, it's reasonable to continue. What I tell patients when we start therapy outside of the trial in a metastatic setting is that if this combination is working, I think it makes sense to continue. With the knowledge that nobody can stay on Npr2Meb indefinitely, most patients who are doing exceptionally well on the treatment and are in later cycles, cycle 8, 10, 11, they start to develop cumulative peripheral neuropathy, which necessitates that we dose reduce or hold. And there are other reasons that we sometimes will hold earlier. Sometimes patients can maintain a durable response, whether it's a partial response or a complete response. If it's feasible, if the patient is tolerating immunotherapy, which tends to be easier to tolerate, then we can continue the immunotherapy. Sometimes we stop both drugs. If we see something like a high-grade rash, you're not quite sure which drug is causing the side effect. And sometimes we can see a durable outcome without. So just like in standard practice, patients can kind of pop on or off. those drugs, you know, ongoing in the setting of the trial, just depending on their tolerance.

The patient was treated with enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab and demonstrated no evidence of active disease on surveillance ureteroscopy, cytologic assessment, and radiographic evaluation after approximately five cycles. Ongoing treatment with this regimen was continued at the time of discussion based on the favorable response.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 42-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Chest pain in late 2019. She also had right pleural effusion and symptomatic thoracic disease. Later in the disease course she required supplemental oxygen with ambulation because of impaired lung function. Over the last 6-9 months of follow-up she developed recurrent chylous ascites and pleural effusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma diagnosed at age 3 years, with metastatic disease involving lungs, pleura, and bone. Disease was radioactive iodine-refractory at the time of referral based on a negative whole-body scan despite progressive metastatic disease, and later demonstrated some restored iodine uptake after RET inhibitor therapy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Total thyroidectomy had been performed in 1984 at an outside hospital for papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- CT-guided transthoracic lung biopsy confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Immunohistochemistry on metastatic tissue was positive for PAX8 and thyroglobulin.  
- Intraoperative tumor biopsy was obtained at the time of pleurodesis; surgery found intrathoracic disease to be more extensive than expected radiologically and unresectable.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT chest in 2009 showed scattered bilateral pulmonary nodular lesions, including right-sided masses.  
- CT chest in February 2020 showed interval enlargement of pulmonary lesions compared with 2009, with at least one new right lung lesion; large lung masses and right pleural effusion were present.  
- PET/CT in 2020 demonstrated hypermetabolic pulmonary metastases, pleural disease, and osseous metastatic disease including sacral involvement; possible thoracic vertebral metastatic involvement was also identified.  
- Interval imaging between February and April 2020 showed further growth of pulmonary lesions.  
- Operative assessment found right lower thoracic disease more extensive than suggested by CT and not amenable to resection.  
- Subsequent imaging during delay in access to RET-targeted therapy showed marked progression in chest and bone, including iliac crest metastasis.  
- Spine imaging demonstrated thoracic vertebral metastatic disease with compression deformity and epidural extension, lumbar vertebral metastasis, and a sacral lesion compressing sacral nerve roots. MRI confirmed epidural extension without clinical cord compression.  
- Six weeks after starting selpercatinib (March 2021), CT showed marked reduction in pulmonary metastases, decreased pleural/thoracic disease, decreased epidural extension at the thoracic spine lesion, and marked reduction in the sacral lesion with less enhancement/mass effect.  
- PET/CT approximately 1 year after starting selpercatinib showed significantly fewer and smaller pulmonary lesions, marked reduction in metabolic activity, improvement in thoracic vertebral disease, and no cord compression.  
- Pre-referral radioactive iodine whole-body scan from the local hospital was negative.  
- Diagnostic iodine scan after approximately 18 months of selpercatinib showed limited/low-volume uptake; this was interpreted locally as positive in the right lower lobe.  
- Post-therapy iodine imaging after 130 mCi radioactive iodine showed diffuse uptake in the right hemithorax and pleura, with avid uptake in symptomatic posterior right thoracic lesions.  
- CT and PET/CT in February 2023 showed sustained major partial response: marked reduction in right lower lobe disease, marked improvement in sacral metastasis, no visible thoracic lesion on the images reviewed, and only mild residual metabolic activity in some residual lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Broad next-generation sequencing (Oncomine panel, approximately 170 genes) identified TRIM24-RET fusion.  
- BRAF alteration was not detected.  
- NTRK alteration was not detected.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum thyroglobulin at discharge from outside follow-up in 2010 was 20 ng/dL.  
- By referral in 2020, serum thyroglobulin had risen to 300 while on thyroxine suppression.  
- At the time of diagnostic radioiodine reassessment after selpercatinib, stimulated thyroglobulin was 1600 and TSH had been stimulated with thyrotropin alfa.  
- Thyroglobulin subsequently declined on selpercatinib.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 1984: Total thyroidectomy.  
- Childhood/adolescence: Radioactive iodine therapy, cumulative dose 300 mCi (reported as 100 mCi on three occasions).  
- 1992: Lung metastases were identified. Details of management at that time were unavailable.  
- 2010: Discharged from outside follow-up despite persistent thyroglobulin elevation.  
- 2020: CT-guided lung biopsy confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- 2020: Surgical exploration for possible right lower lobectomy was undertaken because of symptomatic bulky right lower lobe disease; resection was not feasible because disease was too extensive. Pleurodesis and tumor biopsy were performed.  
- 2020: Sorafenib was started for progressive metastatic disease and stopped within weeks because of severe toxicity with marked cutaneous reaction/hand-foot syndrome.  
- 2020: Lenvatinib was started at 14 mg and increased to 18 mg; it was discontinued after approximately 3 weeks because of severe proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome with lower-limb edema.  
- 5 March 2021: Selpercatinib was started after access was obtained on a compassionate basis. This produced rapid radiologic and biochemical response within 6 weeks and durable disease control over at least 2 years.  
- After approximately 18 months on selpercatinib, radioactive iodine 130 mCi was administered following evidence of renewed iodine uptake on diagnostic assessment. No significant clinical improvement was observed after radioactive iodine treatment.  
- Recurrent chylous ascites during selpercatinib therapy was managed with temporary drug interruption and dose adjustment, with improvement during treatment holds and recurrence after rechallenge.

[ current disease status ]:  
- As of February 2023, metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma remained radiologically improved and clinically stable on selpercatinib, with sustained partial response in lung and bone metastases.  
- She was ambulatory.  
- Residual pulmonary impairment persisted, and she required oxygen with exertion.  
- Recurrent pleural effusion and chylous ascites had occurred during ongoing RET inhibitor therapy.  
- Cytologic/fluid evaluations of ascites reportedly did not show malignant disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had longstanding metastatic disease beginning in childhood.  
- Pleural effusion was present at symptomatic relapse in 2019/2020 and pleurodesis was performed during thoracic surgery.  
- Chylous ascites emerged during RET inhibitor therapy and improved with temporary interruption of selpercatinib.

Sorry, this is the whole body scan, the radioactive iodine whole body scan that was done in the local hospital before she was referred to us. And it was negative. This is a poor image of a speck. So there's no activity. So now after one year, I start to think that maybe now we re-differentiated this tumor enough to be treated with radioactive iodine. And this is actually a diagnostic for body scan done around 18 months on silver catenin. And again, maybe we can get somebody to comment on it. I know that the pictures may not be high resolution, but I think there are some obvious abnormalities. So our nuclear expert.

Yes, thank you. So these are I1, I2, I3, whole body planar. So these are the diagnostic scans, both at 24 hours, just with different intensity. So probably if we go to the set of images on the right and we start in the head and neck region, we do have some asymmetry in the head and neck region. Okay, so we, this was read, and actually we have some specs, a few, I included them or not in the next slide, but this was read as positive scan in the right lower lobe. This is the NT, and this is the lighter view. At that time, theroglobin was 1600, TSH was stimulated with tyrogine, and we wanted actually to give her the benefit of the doubt. So I actually went ahead and gave her 130 millicurie of radioactive iodine, and now this is the worst type of scam in plain films and specs. So again, could you comment on this, please?

Sure, thank you. Well, these are, we always say that I123 gives you a very low dose and you really don't get very good spatial resolution. It's a completely different picture. Even on the planar views, you can see in the hemithorax is quite diffuse uptake and quite a lot through the pleura as well. So there's some really good iodine uptake. And then again, on the spect, we've got some hybrid imaging here. You don't need it to take, you don't need all the lesions to take it up. But if the lesions that are causing her, if she's still symptomatic, we haven't really heard if she's still got back pain. But the lesions that were previously described, particularly posteriorly on the right, they're really avid. So I would think that it was a good call to give her some iodine. Sometimes it's hard to know. And as you've said, selprocatinib can in itself allow some re-differentiation. So yeah, interested to see what happened biochemically and clinically to this patient.

So, honestly, we did not observe any significant clinical improvement, but at least we thought that we did something that might be helpful. Now, this is now two years later. We are in February 2023, and these are the scans. And again, our radiologist here, if you can comment, remembering what she had initially.

And this is significant positive imaging response to treatment just just the most amazing one honestly is the sacrum, I have never seen such a large. blowout lesion. Of course, they're not bone windows, but even if we disregard that, a significant improvement and reduction in the size of the sacral lesion is what's the most outstanding. I no longer see the thoracic lesion. The lumbar spine lesion is just dot-like the one we had, and the lesion involving the right lower lobe is significantly smaller, and sometimes part of even what we're seeing may be atelectatic changes. So this is significant positive imaging response to treatment, I would say.
Thank you so much. So again, this is the PET scan before and two years later. This is before and this is two years later.

I don't want to grab anybody else's spot, but there is significant reduction in the not only metabolic activity, but size of the right lower lobe lesion we see on the pet and the lesion involving the sacrum in the interim, it was hyper metabolic, it was smaller. And then in the interim, the other images we saw, it significantly enlarged. And now we see very mild metabolic activity in that area. So again, significant positive response to treatment. However, if you look at the scout images, I think the right lower lobe, it's still some, yes, the lesion is still, there may be small three lesions that are persistent there. And even the lumbar spine lesion is still mildly hypermetabolic, again, in the scout image.

Okay, so the current status, patient is stable. She's ambulatory, but has two issues. One, her lung function is not great, probably because of the lung fibrosis, metastasis, infusion, so she needs oxygen when she walks around. Second thing that came recently over the last six to nine months is she started to develop recurrent cholecystitis and pleural effusion. And I would like to ask our colleagues here what they think about this or whether they have observed it in their own patients.
Anybody? Well,
Pearl effusions definitely right so no, no issue with that kind of societies Frank, that's probably more of your arena.

Yeah, I was going to say, I haven't seen this I mean it's interesting. we do know that selprocatinib can cause fluid retention. So it's not uncommon to see patients with edema. I had one lady who developed frank ascites and she came in thinking that she was actually pregnant. And it turned out that she had such ascites that we required a drain. Stopping the medication actually improved the ascites and then lowering the dose, she was able to go back on without complication. So I wouldn't say that that's uncommon, perhaps. The chylis component, it's interesting. I have not seen that. In terms of the effusion, yes. Again, because of the fluid retention and possibly related to hypertension, I definitely would want to tap the effusion to see if it was malignant and then involve our pulmonary people for placement of a Plerix catheter or something to that degree to relieve the effusion, especially if it is recurrent.

Thank you. So when she came with chylosocytes, we were not aware of a strong association, actually, between chylosocytes and RIT inhibitors. We thought initially that this is because of progression of the disease, fibrosis, and we tabbed repeatedly. We could not see any malignant disease. It turns out that this is now well-recognized complication of RIT inhibitors. This is a report that was just published in February, I think this year, a recent one, multi-center studies, including many patients from actually Memorial Hospital, where they looked at around 7,000 patients who received TKI in general, the lymphadenib, psorafinib, and other ones. And the incidence, sorry, the incidence in that one is not that high, but it seemed that the RET inhibitors are, you see, out of around more than 7,000 patients, of whom I think around 45 or 50 received selective RET inhibitors. So from the 7,000, only seven patients, and from the 45 around 15 patients, so the total was 22, and you can see the details of this. People from Italy also reported a dozen of patients who developed chirosocytes secondary to silvertanib and pransatinib, so it seems to be a rare complication of those drugs. And in fact, in this patient, one of the ways to manage this is to stop the drug for few days and she improves and then when she goes back on it she will be okay for another month or so and then she will come to me with again accumulation of the fluid. and we'll try to manage it by either decreasing the dose or even holding it for a few days. I know we are running short of time, so let me move unless you have a burning comment on this issue.

I was going to say just a couple of things here, too. I agree with what you're doing. I may also consider switching to prosetin if it's interesting. Sometimes if people have intolerance to one of these RET inhibitors, if you switch to a different one, some of those side effects may not occur. Now, you could get them recurrent in both patients. I've seen that. But I have had patients have issues with one who necessarily don't develop the same degree with another one. The other thing I just throw into this case is that I probably would consider, when we were talking about the spinal meds, treatment with bisphosphonate therapy and definitely perhaps an evaluation by, you know, a spinal clinic orthopedic surgeon to make sure there's, you know, stability of the spine, especially in a younger woman who may have several years, you know, to live with this disease.

reference_conclusion: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma was confirmed on transthoracic lung biopsy, and molecular profiling demonstrated a TRIM24-RET fusion. Surgical resection was attempted for symptomatic bulky right lower lobe disease but was not feasible intraoperatively; pleurodesis and tumor biopsy were performed instead. Because of progressive disease, systemic therapy was initiated with sorafenib and then lenvatinib, both of which were discontinued because of intolerance; treatment was subsequently transitioned to selpercatinib, with marked radiographic and biochemical response. After evidence of renewed iodine uptake on diagnostic imaging while receiving selpercatinib, radioactive iodine therapy was administered; ongoing management of recurrent pleural effusion and chylous ascites has consisted of selpercatinib dose interruption or reduction as needed.

So we had to stop. [...] this patient has TRIM24 red fusion. [...] 5th of March, 2021, we started her on silver catenin, a RET inhibitor. [...] I actually went ahead and gave her 130 millicurie of radioactive iodine [...] one of the ways to manage this is to stop the drug for few days and she improves and then when she goes back on it she will be okay for another month or so and then she will come to me with again accumulation of the fluid. and we'll try to manage it by either decreasing the dose or even holding it for a few days.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 18-year-old female at initial diagnosis in 2011; age 32 years at most recent documented follow-up.

[ chief complaint ]: Right ventral lateral tongue lesion present for approximately 3 months at initial presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent right oral tongue squamous neoplasia, including well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma and multiple episodes of carcinoma in situ/dysplasia. Initial stage was documented as T1N0 in 2011. A recurrent invasive lesion in 2018 was documented as T1.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial outside excision in 2011 showed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma arising in a papilloma; p16 negative; excision margin 0.2 mm. Subsequent partial glossectomy in 2011 showed squamous mucosa with focal mild dysplasia; margins negative for dysplasia and carcinoma. Right selective neck dissection levels I-IV in 2011 showed 0/19 lymph nodes positive. In 2014, direct laryngoscopy with biopsies of the base of tongue and oral tongue showed carcinoma in situ, suspicious for invasion; subsequent partial glossectomy from the same site showed carcinoma in situ. In 2016, partial glossectomy again showed carcinoma in situ. In 2017, there were benign biopsies, followed by partial glossectomy with final pathology showing well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma measuring 0.2 cm, depth of invasion 0.5 mm, no lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion, and closest margin 2.5 mm at the deep margin. In 2021, partial glossectomy showed moderate to severe dysplasia, with severe dysplasia 1 mm from the lateral margin. In April of the most recent documented year, partial glossectomy specimen was benign.

[ imaging findings ]: In 2011, CT neck and PET demonstrated FDG avidity corresponding to the oral tongue lesion; otherwise unremarkable. The lesion was initially misread as tongue base on imaging but clinically represented oral tongue disease. Over subsequent surveillance, there were two additional CT neck studies and two additional PET scans. Neck ultrasound was used as the primary surveillance imaging modality thereafter. Initial examination documented a 1.4 cm right ventral lateral tongue lesion sparing the floor of mouth, with no cervical lymphadenopathy; endoscopic examination was normal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 negative on the initial 2011 squamous cell carcinoma specimen. Formal genetic evaluation assessed low likelihood for Fanconi anemia; no formal genetic testing was performed because further testing was declined.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Outside hospital local resection of tongue lesion was performed in 2011 and identified squamous cell carcinoma. Re-resection with partial glossectomy was performed in 2011 and showed no residual carcinoma, with negative margins for dysplasia and carcinoma. Right selective neck dissection levels I-IV was performed in 2011 and was node-negative (0/19). In 2014, direct laryngoscopy with biopsies followed by partial glossectomy was performed for recurrent lesion; final pathology showed carcinoma in situ. In 2016, recurrent lesion was treated with partial glossectomy; pathology showed carcinoma in situ. In 2017, benign biopsies were followed by partial glossectomy; pathology showed a 0.2 cm well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with 0.5 mm depth of invasion, no LVI/PNI, and negative margins. In 2021, another recurrent lesion was resected by partial glossectomy; pathology showed moderate to severe dysplasia. In April of the most recent documented year, another partial glossectomy was performed for a new lesion; pathology was benign. No adjuvant therapy was administered.

[ current disease status ]: Most recent documented resection in April showed benign pathology. The patient remained under close surveillance approximately every 3 months.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was significant for beta-mannosidosis deficiency, described as a lysosomal storage disease. She was a non-smoker and non-drinker. Initial examination at referral after outside excision showed granulation tissue at the prior excision site. No cervical lymphadenopathy was documented at initial presentation.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah. And I think, you know, this case shouldn't take too long. I think it's just kind of a good little clinical topic. Not particularly complex from like a, you know, surgical or recon standpoint. So, all right, here we go. So this is an 18 year old female initially when she presented, she had a tongue lesion for three months and outside hospital, otolaryngologist kind of resected it. and had found that there was squamous cell carcinoma and had referred her over to Dr. Sumer. Her past medical history is significant for beta monocytes deficiency, which is essentially a lysosomal storage disease, kind of affects how you process sugars. It's not found to be related to squamous cell carcinoma. kind of presents with like hypotonia, some intellectual disability, amongst some kind of like ovarian issues. Non-smoker, non-drinker, and nothing particular about her social history otherwise either. on her physical exam, she had, this is like her physical exam when she had initially presented to the outside, ENT 1.4 centimeters, right ventral lateral tongue lesion, sparing the floor of mouth, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and her scope was normal. When she came to us, she had a like kind of just granulation tissue evidence of where this excision occurred. CT, neck, and pet at that time. This is from 2011, so unfortunately I didn't have access to the images for this, but it was misread as tongue-based. It really was the oral tongue and had corresponding FDG ability in that area, otherwise unremarkable. So her initial biopsy from the outside was well-differentiated squamous low carcinoma, arising in a papilloma, P16 negative, and the excision margins were 0.2 millimeters. She was counseled on re-resection with wide margins, knowing that, you know, the final pathology may not reveal carcinoma. That was done, and so she had a partial glassectomy. That pathology revealed squamous mucosal focal mouth dysplasia. Margins were negative for both dysplasia and carcinoma. The decision was also made to perform a right neck dissection, levels one through four, selective neck dissection. There were zero out of 19 lymph nodes that were positive. The reason for that was based on the description of how the lesion initially looked and the size in order to try to avoid any kind of radiation therapy. That's kind of the thought process behind the neck dissection at that time.

Can I just ask a quick question? So Peter, when do you consider doing, so say you have a fairly, you know, an oral lesion, doesn't feel overly deep. And, you know, your question whether it was just a surface lesion or a truly invasive, when do you make the cutoff or when you do an upfront neck dissection versus not, and do you ever base that on frozen section or wait for permanent pathology?

Good question. So I start off doing a punch biopsy in clinic, like you were mentioning earlier, and I try to get something that helps the punch so I can get a good sense of the thickness. So I'll start with that. If that can give me a definitive answer, then I can make the call up front. And I like to use two millimeters as a cutoff. Anything more than two, that's my cutoff for recommending a neck dissection in most oral cavity cancers. And if I don't have the depth of invasion on the biopsy, then I discuss the option with the patient and tell them, you know, we could do an FAS on front, it might be overkill, or we can do it in a staged fashion, cut it out, wait for the final. the final pathology and then come back and do the neck dissection after. I've talked to our pathologists and they haven't been able to tell me that they can do a reliable depth of invasion on frozen sections. They've always said what they prefer to do, final pathology. I would stage it if that's what the patient preferred to do.
Excellent. Thank you.

All right, so moving on a few years, in 2014 now, she had a recurrence of a suspicious lesion. She underwent a biopsy in the operating room, a drug laryngoscopy with biopsies of the base of tongue as well as the oral tongue. That revealed carcinoma in situ and suspicious for invasion, and so then was recommended to have a partial glaucectomy. Same site, that final pathology revealed carcinoma in situ.
Quick question, I guess, before we go from there.
On the invasive disease, Dr. Gross, how do you assess the margins at the time of surgery for those who have partial glassectomy for an invasive, like lateral tongue cancer, for example?
You mean with frozen section?
Right. Yeah. Do you do it as a specimen-based or a wound bed?

Oh, specimen base, I mean, I think there's enough literature out there showing that the. Outcomes are better and the risk of having to do a section is lower. And then, of course. If you had, if you're doing tumor bed based margins and it's positive, you know, the likelihood of getting to that same spot to re resect is pretty low. There's, I can't remember what percent it is, but it's, it's pretty low. So we at Emory, at least we do it all tumor based margins. We walk it over to the pathologist and review it. And we, you know, if I have any questions at all, we'll actually stay there and cut it with the pathologist so I can see exactly where the closest margin is, re-resect if needed. But hopefully you get it right on the first go around.
Peter, you have a similar approach?

Yeah, the way I do it is before cutting out the tumor, I kind of map out where my resection is going to be. And so I take a ruler, I like to do two centimeter surgical margins. So I measure out two centimeters all the way around. And then I take circumferential margins all the way around my plan resection, then do the resection and take the deepest margin off right before we remove the entire tumor. knowing that that's probably the least reliable of all the margins. I think the superficial mucosal ones are the most reliable and the easiest to re-excise if you have to, but I agree with Jen. It's that deep one that the chance of you getting right back to where it was is pretty pretty low. And then I do think that taking the specimen to the pathologist is key, not only for assessing, you know, potentially close margins that you can re-excise, but also for orienting the specimen for analysis afterwards. Many times they don't always understand the three-dimensional anatomy. So if you can show it to them, draw a picture, help them ink it, it can make a big difference in your pathology reporting.

Great question came up from Fahad on the role of sentinel node biopsy in this original one. Do you ever consider doing that for early oral cancers that are clinically in zero? Either Jen or Peter, either one of you have experience in that.

Yeah, I mean, we participate in the HN006 trial. So we actually are only offering sentinel node trials for oral cavity if they're, sorry, sentinel lymph node biopsies for oral cavity if they're on that trial. I think we tend to err on the side of neck dissection, especially if it's oral tongue, just because, you know, they can be very aggressive, they can come back even if it looks like it might be really superficial. It might be more, have more depth than you initially think. So we tend to just do a neck dissection on most patients unless they are not a good surgical candidate or they really, really, you know, insist, or if they are interested in the HN 066 trial and get randomized into the sentinel lymph node arm.

Sounds good. Yeah. And just remember, we do have level one evidence to show that you need to manage the neck somehow once it's above three millimeters deep. And some people certainly use a little lower cutoff from the D'Cruz study, you know, conspiring observation with close surveillance and therapeutic dissection if they develop nodes versus an up to front elective neck dissection. They shared a significant survival advantage when they did the upfront dissection, but that's what this HN006 is designed to look at. Well, would the sentinel node offer a similar benefit by kind of stratifying which one of those need the formal dissection by testing the most adverse nodes? Very good. Natalia, you want to continue on?

All right, so similarly, a couple of years later, in 2016, she had another recurrence of the lesion, had a partial glaucectomy, and that showed carcinoma in situ once again. A couple of benign biopsies in 2017, followed by another partial glaucectomy. This is probably the one that we have the most information from. Here she had final pathology showing a well-differentiated swing-missile carcinoma, 0.2 centimeters in size. Depth of invasion was 0.5 millimeters. No lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion. And then the closest margin was 2.5 millimeters away, and that was the deep margin. She then continued follow-up. Again, another lesion. She had no adjuvant treatment at that time. She had another recurrence of a lesion in 2021. Had that resected with partial gloss, moderate to severe dysplasia on that with severe dysplasia one millimeter away from the lateral margin. And then finally another lesion this year in April for which she went another partial glaucectomy and that was benign. So here's like a just summary kind of of her treatment history that we had just reviewed. So she was diagnosed at 18, she's now 32. Her staging as follows with T1 and zero, 2011 recurrence, T1 in 2018 with that summary of pathology right there that I just discussed. and kind of her entire history right there with the surgeries that she had.

So this is obviously one of the most challenging scenarios, and I'm glad I'm on this session because I'm hoping that you guys all tell me how to manage these people, because they are very, very difficult. I certainly have not found a great way. Peter, maybe I'll start with you. These patients with just kind of multifocal, this one seems like it's centered a bit more in one area, the right tongue, but certainly there are ones where it's proliferative rucous leukoplakia or like implantists where it's just popping up everywhere as dysplasia or pre-cancer, sometimes early invasive disease. How do you manage those? Your surveillance regimen, do you have any other non-surgical approaches that you use like topical agents or other chemopreventive agents that you believe in.

A great question. I think, just like you said, these are very challenging patients. I've got a number of these in my practice. For surveillance, they're usually very in tune. And so I tell them, we're going to see you every three months or so. Anytime you notice something new, call the office and I'll see you right away. And anytime they find something new, they're typically in there pretty quickly. And eventually, from my experience, they'll end up with something that needs a much bigger surgery. I had one recently that eventually ended up needing a mandibulectomy with these multiple recurrent areas. Some of the other ones, I tried to convince one of our medical oncologists to just give immunotherapy to them to see if this would help, because we had nothing else to offer. And we came up with a compromise. I don't know if you guys are using any of the circulating tumor DNA tests, but there's one signataria that we've been using. And so we decided, let's do that. And if it comes back positive, maybe we can convince the insurance company to pay for some rounds of Keytruda. Luckily, it was negative, but that was kind of our thinking about something we might be able to offer these patients that if they still have circulating tumor DNA after their latest resection, perhaps we can add in some immunotherapy as sort of a treatment slash preventative measure. But I don't have the answer to these, unfortunately.
Any topical agents or any other tricks of the trade, Dr. Gross?

Yeah, I mean, these are very challenging. I think there aren't great chemo preventative options for this problem. You know, we have a trial for active or previous smokers who can take metformin as a chemo prevention if they have any type of dysplasia. And there is some data from a phase 2 trial showing that in these patients. There is a greater likelihood that the dysplasia resolves so. I mean, if they aren't a smoker, I don't really have a good option for them. And kind of like what Peter said, unfortunately, I, in my, you know, few years of practice, have seen that these often progress to larger cancers, and you just have to keep a very close eye on them. So, preserving…sorry. So, preserving the radiation for the large cancer is kind of what we tend to do.

Yeah, I agree. I think one of the most tricky situations is people kind of overreact to a close margin or displeasure or something and try and then throw like radiation or some other adjuvant therapy at it. And like you said, you almost want to save that for a later time. I have heard of a clinical trial of using topical 5-FU, which is similar to what you use in early skin cancers, but not for invasive disease, for pre-cancers. There's a place out of Ohio, it's actually not an academic, it's a private practice group, but I've had a couple of patients who've interacted with, and actually so far I've been very impressed with the patients I've sent over there, And I think there actually may be one for ones where they have multifocal invasive disease. I believe there's an ongoing clinical trial that actually does use immunotherapy for that, I think for the similar reasons, but since it's done on trial, I think they were able to get it passed, but obviously it's a very challenging situation. One question from the audience came in, I think that leads to your next slide, Natalia, is, you know, was Fanconi's anemia ruled out or what other testing was done?

Yeah, so we she did formally see the genetic team over here. And they, they just clinically kind of determine her risk factors and whatnot and didn't do any formal genetic testing but they decided that she had a low likelihood for pancomenemia. Actually, she declined further genetic testing, I should say. Her surveillance with us has been kind of similar to what others have said about every three months or so she has been coming in. Over the course of these years, she had Aside from the initial CT and PET, she had like one other CT neck, or sorry, two other CT necks and two other PET scans. And then other than that, her main surveillance imaging modality has been a neck ultrasound. And yeah, that's no other kind of adjuvant treatments or adjuvant therapies or testing besides that.

reference_conclusion: The patient is to continue close surveillance with clinical follow-up approximately every three months and expedited evaluation for any new oral lesion. No adjuvant therapy is planned at this time; management remains surgical surveillance, with radiation reserved for development of a larger cancer. Surveillance imaging has primarily consisted of neck ultrasound.
reference_conclusion_quote: For surveillance, they're usually very in tune. And so I tell them, we're going to see you every three months or so. Anytime you notice something new, call the office and I'll see you right away. [...] I think there aren't great chemo preventative options for this problem. [...] you just have to keep a very close eye on them. So, preserving…sorry. So, preserving the radiation for the large cancer is kind of what we tend to do. [...] Her surveillance with us has been kind of similar to what others have said about every three months or so she has been coming in. [...] And yeah, that's no other kind of adjuvant treatments or adjuvant therapies or testing besides that.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 73-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Hematuria for 3 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder; prior outside TURBT had shown high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma. Subsequent evaluation demonstrated recurrent disease staged radiologically as at least cT3N0.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Prior outside TURBT: high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma.  
- Repeat cystoscopy and TURBT: recurrent muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI pelvis: urinary bladder mass, T3 lesion with extravesical spread; VI-RADS score 5. Lesion involved the left posterolateral bladder wall with involvement of the left vesicoureteric junction and mild left hydroureteronephrosis.  
- DTPA renal scan: GFR 45 mL/min; left kidney showed negligible cortical tracer uptake.  
- USG KUB: cortical thinning of the left kidney.  
- 2D echocardiography: left ventricular ejection fraction 56%.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hemoglobin: 9.1 g/dL after 3 units PRBC transfusion.  
- Serum folic acid: 5.5 ng/mL (reported lower limit of normal 8.2 ng/mL).  
- Transferrin saturation: 5%.  
- Serum ferritin: 12 ng/mL.  
- Serum creatinine: 1.4 mg/dL.  
- Other routine laboratory parameters: within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- TURBT performed outside institution: pathology showed high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma.  
- Repeat cystoscopy and TURBT at current center: recurrent muscle-invasive disease identified.  
- Received 3 units packed red blood cell transfusion for anemia.  

[ current disease status ]:

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old right-handed woman. Karnofsky Performance Status was 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache and memory disturbance for 1 month at presentation to neurosurgical clinic in 2023. Confusion and memory impairment were also documented.

[ diagnosis ]: Known right breast carcinoma, invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3. Subsequently developed a left frontal brain metastasis from breast primary. Metastatic disease was also identified in the L5 and D10 vertebral bodies and in axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: Brain lesion biopsy/resection specimen was consistent with metastatic breast carcinoma. Receptor testing on the brain metastasis was triple positive: ER positive, PR positive, HER2/neu positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain dated 18 June 2023 showed a left frontal, well-circumscribed solid-cystic contrast-enhancing lesion measuring approximately 8 × 6 cm, with marked surrounding vasogenic edema and mass effect. The lesion was described as dural-based/dural-attached. Possible ipsilateral pachymeningeal prominence/enhancement was described. No other intracranial metastases were identified on the imaging discussed.

PET scan demonstrated metastatic deposits in the L5 and D10 vertebral bodies and hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the axilla and mediastinum.

Immediate postoperative MRI brain showed postoperative change with concern for residual enhancing disease along the medial and posteromedial margins of the resection cavity.

Follow-up MRI brain in November 2023, obtained after wound debridement for radiation planning, showed nodular enhancing tissue posterior to the area of hemorrhage, extending into the meninges and involving the overlying bone/bone flap, concerning for residual/recurrent disease in the surgical bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: ER positive, PR positive, HER2/neu positive on the brain metastasis specimen.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy for breast carcinoma, 4 cycles. She underwent right-sided modified radical mastectomy in April 2022. She then received 30 fractions of chest radiotherapy in June 2022. She was on tamoxifen at the time of presentation with brain lesion.

Because of the size of the intracranial lesion and associated mass effect, she underwent neuronavigation-guided left frontal craniotomy with maximum safe resection in August 2023.

Postoperatively, she developed wound-site collection/infection and subsequently underwent wound debridement in October 2023. Poor wound healing was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with intracranial, osseous, and nodal disease. Post-craniotomy and post-debridement imaging in November 2023 demonstrated persistent/enlarging nodular enhancement in the surgical bed with meningeal and calvarial/bone flap involvement, consistent with residual/recurrent intracranial metastatic disease. Functional status remained good, with KPS 90. No paralysis was present.

[ other clinical data ]: No focal paralysis was reported. Activities were described as preserved despite poor wound healing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive bladder cancer with pelvic pain, back pain, obstructive acute kidney injury, and declining performance status.

[ diagnosis ]: Urothelial bladder cancer initially diagnosed in 2019, previously treated with intravesical BCG. Disease progressed in 2021 to muscle-invasive bladder cancer with a large bladder mass and metastatic retroperitoneal and pelvic adenopathy.

[ histopathology results ]: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor demonstrated muscle invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT showed a large bladder mass with widespread retroperitoneal and pelvic adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling showed ERBB2 (HER2) amplification and ERBB2 R103Q mutation; TP53 alteration; CCND3 amplification. Tumor mutational burden was not high. Microsatellite status was stable. No FGFR mutation was identified. ERBB2 R103Q variant allele frequency was 3.6%. PD-L1 immunohistochemistry was positive.

[ laboratory results ]: Creatinine was approximately 2.5 mg/dL in the setting of obstruction-associated acute kidney injury.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:
- Intravesical BCG for bladder cancer after initial diagnosis in 2019.
- Nephrostomy tubes were replaced for obstructive uropathy.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic muscle-invasive urothelial bladder cancer with a large bladder mass and widespread retroperitoneal and pelvic adenopathy, complicated by obstruction-associated acute kidney injury.

[ other clinical data ]: ECOG performance status was 2 and had worsened over the preceding 4 weeks. No contraindications to pembrolizumab were documented. The patient was otherwise described as healthy apart from the current malignancy-related issues.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old right-handed male.

[ chief complaint ]: Focal motor seizures of the left arm.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal IDH-wildtype diffuse glioma of the right insular/right frontal region, subsequently classified as molecular glioblastoma based on molecular features. Later multifocal progression involved the right frontal region and a left parietal lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial intraoperative frozen section from the right insular lesion was reported as diffuse astrocytoma. Final integrated assessment was compatible with molecular glioblastoma. Molecular glioblastoma classification was supported by chromosomal alterations including chromosome 7 gain, chromosome 10 loss, and homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT head showed a diffuse hypodense lesion in the right insular region with mild local mass effect and displacement of cortical structures. There was no intralesional hemorrhage, calcification, vasogenic edema, midline shift, hydrocephalus, or acute ischemia.  
Initial MRI demonstrated a diffuse right insular tumor and a separate right frontal lesion, consistent with a multifocal pattern.  
Preoperative FET PET showed moderately intense patchy uptake at the right-sided lesion; SUV, tumor-to-brain ratio, and kinetic profile were consistent with low-grade glioma, with slow increase to plateau and no early peak/decline. Diffuse uptake in the right hemisphere supported multifocal disease.  
Postoperative MRI after initial resection showed resection of the majority of the tumor with residual tumor involving the lentiform nucleus.  
MRI 2 months after radiotherapy showed stable disease without blood-brain barrier disruption. Follow-up FET PET at that time was unremarkable.  
After completion of adjuvant treatment, MRI showed new contrast-enhancing lesions/hotspots in the right frontal region and left parietal region. FET PET demonstrated increased tracer uptake consistent with high-grade tumor progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH wild type. MGMT promoter unmethylated. Chromosome 7 gain, chromosome 10 loss, and homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion were identified and supported the diagnosis of molecular glioblastoma.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Before neurosurgical evaluation, levetiracetam and dexamethasone had been prescribed.  
The patient underwent microsurgical resection of the right insular tumor via pterional craniotomy with microscope, neuronavigation including fiber tracking, 5-ALA fluorescence guidance, Sylvian fissure split, subpial technique, CST monitoring/mapping, and subcortical mapping. Intraoperatively there was absence of 5-ALA fluorescence. Tissue sampling was taken from the area of maximal amino-acid uptake on PET. Resection was limited to avoid basal ganglia and deep frontal white matter.  
He subsequently received radiochemotherapy with temozolomide according to the Stupp protocol. At 2-month post-radiotherapy follow-up he was clinically unremarkable and imaging showed stable disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial neurological examination was unremarkable. At the time multifocal recurrence was identified, performance status was reported as Karnofsky Performance Status 100.
