And one month later was still still, there were a new, was new contrast enhancement, right temporal, And the left remains sort of stable, because we don't know what we're actually seeing with PDT. You see these reactive changes all the time. And two months later, it progressed. So, obviously, for us, it wasn't a surgical patient anymore. The only thing I wanted to comment before we finalize this is those areas that we operated on, right, those areas, they remain clean. And it always tells me, well, we might be doing something sensible, even resecting these parts of the tumor, even multifocal disease, right, even though at the end, it's going to just continue. Okay, do you want to maybe show the last slide, Dole?
Yeah.
Oh, okay. So just very, very quickly.

Yeah. Yeah. Okay. So, um, the end, um, the, um, I thought it was changed. So, um, he, um, received an enter inhibitor, tenserolimus and also, um, paraphernalia, um, which inhibits, um, the N A N P a, uh, receptor and it's a neurobiome synopsis. And now that she got progressive disease, um, unfortunately we do not have the MRI scan of that. And then they switched to a muscular endothelial growth factor inhibitor, Vivakizumab, and the fibroblast growth factor receptor inhibitor, RFGNF. But then after weeks, there was progressive disease again. And finally, after a few weeks, the patient died, unfortunately. So I'll go to the take-home messages. First of all, molecular criteria may upstake histologically low grade lesions, as wolf in sheep's clothing. Then FET pad is useful in differentiating progression from radio necrosis. Targeted biopsies can be helpful to confirm multifocal progression and even a multifocal gliomas surgical intervention retains its value in tumor management. So I thank you for your intention and for the lovely discussion.

Okay, and I will suggest for the sake of time, if there's any questions or comments, please put them into the chat. And if we have more time at the end, we can address them. Otherwise, we'll move forward to the second case, if you agree, Kate, and the others.
Can I just ask one question? How long did the patient live? What was their overall survival in the end?
It was like two years, two years.

reference_conclusion: Following subtotal resection, adjuvant radiochemotherapy with temozolomide according to the Stupp protocol was recommended and administered for molecular glioblastoma. At multifocal progression, stereotactic biopsies of the left parietal and right frontal lesions were performed to confirm progression and obtain updated molecular profiling, followed by fluorescence-guided re-resection of the right-sided disease. The subsequent management plan included re-irradiation and CCNU administration, with repeat NGS undertaken to evaluate for newly targetable alterations.
reference_conclusion_quote: still the standard treatment protocol would be like combined radio chemotherapy, according to the protocol from 2005 with Timosulamide. [...] Yes. So what we do, we did radiochemotherapy with temozolomide, histoprotocol, as said before. [...] Yes, we did. We did a stereotactic biopsy of the left peritoneal lesion. We wanted to confirm tumour progression as we suspected. During the same procedure, we also took a stereotactic biopsy of the right frontal lesion because we wanted to differentiate if the contrast enhanced lesions or radiation necrosis or tumour progression. [...] And then we also aimed to do NGS panel again because during the first operation, we saw that there was no targetable mutation and perhaps now there's a choice that we can target that we have a suitable targeted therapy. And we plan to do re-irradiation and CCNU administration. [...] And then we also opted for a second surgery. We did a microsurgery called fluorescence guided tumor resection in the right inferior region again, and on the right frontal lobe under interoperative neural monitoring.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 82-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent pain involving the right mandibular teeth/mandible with nonhealing extraction sockets 6 months after extraction of two right mandibular molars.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right mandibular alveolus/gingiva.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial oral surgeon biopsy demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: PET/CT demonstrated FDG uptake at the primary right mandibular site without evidence of cervical nodal disease or distant metastatic disease. Contrast-enhanced CT soft tissue neck was interpreted as demonstrating cortical bone involvement of the mandible. Clinically, the lesion measured approximately 1-2 cm, involved the right mandibular alveolus with submucosal extension, appeared fixed to the mandible, and had no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The lesion was described as isolated to the right mandible/gingiva without midline involvement and with minimal to no floor-of-mouth or buccal involvement.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Two right mandibular molars were extracted by a dentist prior to cancer diagnosis; pain persisted and extraction sites remained unhealed at 6 months.

[ current disease status ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right mandibular alveolus/gingiva, clinically approximately 1-2 cm and fixed to the mandible, with cortical mandibular involvement on CT, no palpable or radiographic cervical nodal disease, and no distant metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Past history included remote tobacco use, discontinued approximately 20 years earlier. Baseline medications included metoprolol and simvastatin. The patient was otherwise described as healthy for age.

reference_discussion.text: All right, so we're now going to jump to Jeremiah Tracy, who has the next case for us.
I think you're muted, Jeremiah. Let's try that again. There you go.

Thanks to the organizers for having me present. And thanks, Dr. Yusefbegovich. That first case was very interesting. I like there are a lot of margin calls there. The case I have may be more straightforward. This is a 82-year-old who first presented with pain of what he thought were his mandibular teeth, possibly the mandible. His dentist pulled two of his right mandibular molars. Unfortunately, the pain persisted, and his two sockets had not yet healed six months later. He was seen by an oral surgeon who did a biopsy. And so when he got to me, he did have a pathologic diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. He was quite healthy for an 82-year-old. He had a history of tobacco use, but not for, I think, almost 20 years. And really, metoprolol and simvastatin were his only medications. He had this about 1 to 2 centimeter a lesion involving the right mandibular alveolus, kind of visible submucosal extension. It seemed to be fixed the mandible and there were no palpable lymph nodes. He had a PET CT scan at the time of my evaluation showing FDG uptake at the primary site, but no concern for nodal disease or metastatic disease. And I actually got a CT scan of the neck, soft tissue neck with contrast as part of preoperative planning. which we read as demonstrating cortical bone involvement. So I guess this would be my first pause. Any further workup to complete staging and initial management recommendation?
So he has a biopsy and a PET CT scan?
That's right.
OK. So with regard to the evaluation of the tumor, to me, that's pretty adequate.
And what was the time frame between the biopsy and the dental extraction?
So the dental extraction was six months prior. That's where the delay occurred. But between the biopsy and him seeing me was quite quick, a few weeks.
And the PET CT scan is pretty recent too, right? That's not that old.
That, yes, that was all ordered by the oral surgeon to identify the cancer. And then I did have also a CT soft tissue neck with contrast.

So we've all unfortunately seen these patients. First of all, you guys can't operate on anybody under the age of 80 apparently, but we've all seen these patients who come in, right, with loose dentition or stuff around the tooth. They pull the tooth and you've got cancer around the socket. So what's the, on Dr. Tracy's slide, are we doing a marginal mandibulectomy? Are you doing a segmental? What are you doing? And what are you doing with the neck?

In this case, I'm definitely doing a segmental mandibulectomy. The one thing is it's pretty straightforward with respect to the bony erosion. I also to your point, Trevor, just to again underscore for the fellows, you know, when there is a tooth extracted, presumably in the bed of where cancer was, you know, you almost have to assume that it's in the medullary space, meaning you can't afford to leave cancer behind there. And that's why I would err towards a segmental over a marginal But again, very straightforward with these nice images. And then I would do, certainly do a neck dissection as well on that side. It looks like from your photo that this is right-sided and that even with a good one centimeter margin, it's still right-sided. Is that fair to say there was no midline involvement?
That's right. It was very, very isolated to the mandible and the gingiva. There was really pretty minimal to no, you know, floor of mouth or buccal involvement.
Yeah, I agree with all the comments.

I'd just like to say that on the scans, like whenever you look at assessing mandibular tumors, you know, look for paramandibular spread, you know, look for the sublingual space and, you know, whether that is asymmetric as compared to the other side. Look at the symmetry of the, you know, midline tongue musculature. All of those things are important to decide whether this is truly sort of a lateralized tumor that has some medial component to it. I agree that in this case, it looks pretty obvious that the patient needs a segmental. There's too much of a body involvement to consider anything else.

Yeah, I agree. Segmental is a standard of care in this situation. But just to make the discussion a little bit more interesting, what if the patient said, hey, doc, for whatever reason, he loves his mandible, and he does not want to go through a segmental mandibulectomy? He says, there is no way I'm going to go through a segmental mandibulectomy. Explain to the patient that even if you do a marginal, the soft tissue defect will be large enough that he's going to need a flap to cover the soft tissue defect anyway. But for whatever reason, he does not want a fibular free flap in a segmental. How would you proceed? Would you do a marginal?

That's a really great sort of scenario, which I hope I never have to encounter. But if it did come down to that, then I have to be true to, you know, what I think is going to work. And in that situation, it could be an inadequate surgery, it wouldn't even be palliative, because you're going to kind of, you know, cut through tumor for the most part. and sort of leave the patient in a greater disadvantage. And I would just have them consider a non-surgical treatment option at that point, even though it's probably not the right option for them.

Yeah. Tracy, can you go back to the CT scan that you had shown previously? So on that axial, on that coronal cut, you can see the degree of bone invasion into the mandible there. Now, I had patients like this, a handful of patients in my career, who for whatever reason, they refused a segmental. And their tumor was eroding the mandible from the occlusal surface like we have here. So I've done I've relented on these patients, and I have done marginal on these people, but doing the marginal, but taking a very significant portion of the mandible, leaving a fairly thin rim along the inferior aspect and plating that to bolster it. By doing that, on three of these patients who had refusal segmental, I was able to get a negative margin on the bone, and with adjuvant therapy, they turned okay. On some of those cases, I have taken that approach. But I do agree with everyone that the standard care is. Sorry, I'll put one more step forward.

And that's why I asked Jeremiah the dental extraction was six months prior. So are you sure that this, this amount of bone loss is due to. the cancer or could it be from the dental extraction and from six months ago. And then, just to be devil's advocate, and, and there's a pretty big distance between that and where the nerve is that the patient doesn't have mental numbness they're not involved in the marrow space I still think is segmental is what most of us would do. But if you do a marginal. Steve, do you do a marginal and then wait for final path, and then go back and do a segmental neck if you need to, or are you doing a neck when you're doing the marginal, if you're doing a marginal and then you'd be like?

So if I'm doing a marginal on this patient, I'm doing the neck at the same time. The main reason is that to, in order to put the plate on, it's easier if you make a neck incision and raise the flap over the mandible. And so if patients have a neck incision, the neck's gonna be opened up, I'll do the neck dissection at that same time.
Yeah.

I mean, I, you know, it is, it is true that like sometimes you can get away with marginal mandiblectomies. Uh, I, this particular case, I think it would be really difficult to get away with one of those. Uh, but, but, you know, there are certainly something to consider. And I think if you have a proper discussion with the patient preoperatively and, um, look at all your options and say that I'm going to consider doing a marginal. But if things don't look, you can always have a backup of a segmental resection. And sometimes you can get away with it.

Yeah, I think there's a difference between mild cortical erosion and irregularity versus involvement in the medullary space. And this is actually, and Jeremiah, I don't know if you were hinting at this earlier, most neuroradiologists would actually prefer an MRI if we are really questioning bony involvement into that medullary space because they can look at the enhancement better. So that's just one thing to think about. But I will still stick to my segmental.

I would agree. That's a great point, Cecilia. And the last thing I'll put on there is if you're going to do a segmental for the trainees, you're going to take their mental nerve. So when you're doing the neck, you have to be very careful you don't take their marge. Because if you give them a numb lip and a weak lip, you affect their oral competence, which could be a big factor in the quality of life of anybody, especially this 82-year-old. So you have to be very careful. Once you've taken their sensation, don't also take their power. Go ahead, Jeremiah.

So this patient did indeed have a segmental mandibulectomy, an ipsilateral selective one through four neck dissection, and was reconstructed with a fibula. He did well perioperatively. The surgical pathology actually showed a 1.4 centimeter tumor, seven millimeter depth of invasion with no bone involvement. And this was confirmed with the pathologist pretty extensively. LVI, PNI negative, negative margins, no lymph nodes. So finally, final pathologic staging was T2, N0, M0. And I guess my question for concern is, I guess what I'm hinting at is, do we have any remorse for doing a segmental on this patient with the T2 disease? And any pearls that you have for identifying bone involvement preoperatively? And I guess final would be any role for adjuvant treatment in this case.

Yeah, first of all, no remorse at all. You've done the surgery that you thought was indicated based on the preoperative information. What I will tell the patient is, you know, emphasize the positive. Listen, you know, your cancer did not invade a bone. Your cancer has been taken care of. You don't need to adjuvate treatment. You're good. So I would reinforce the positive. But the surgery, if this was my patient and I'd done the segmental, then you've done the surgery that you thought were indicated based on the preoperative scan. So there's no remorse on that. In terms of identifying bone involvement, obviously, CT scan is what you start out with. And as Cecilia said, if you have any concern, MRI would be your second line study. But I have patients who on CT scan who had no evidence of bone invasion, and I do a marginal, and the path comes back with T4 cancer with positive bone margin. So that has happened to me as well. But I would say relying on the CT scan, using the MRI as necessary, and your clinical assessment is what you have to rely upon to assess for bone invasion.

I agree, Steve. And I think the onus is really on us as surgeons operatively to say, you know, please realize there's a chance we're going to go in. And despite, you know, thinking we need to do this segmental, we may not find bony erosion. And it's easy to look back and say, gee, I wish I didn't, but it's A, the only way to know and B, if that happens, we're going to celebrate because you don't need radiation. And that's just a great sign. It's early stage. So I think being transparent up front, explaining the why, and then finding the positive, as Steve was saying. And that's easier to do up front before you go to surgery, and then you can just reinforce it on the back end.

I think sometimes also, and again, I wouldn't say that this trumps getting a CT, but sometimes when patients come with OPGs or orthopentomograms, you get some really cool bone architecture and perspective that you don't get with a CT. And sometimes it's worth looking at that also. But again, there will be no doubt in my mind that I will change my management based on the scans that you showed us. So yeah, and no remorse, like Dr. Kim said, you did the right operation for the tumor.

Thank you, Jeremiah. That is a great case. And it is a challenging case. This one's maybe seemed like it was more straightforward because of bone erosion. And that was my question to you, Steve, is that sometimes I'll do a marginal, but I don't do the neck at the time of the marginal. And the main reason I don't is because if the bone is positive, then I haven't violated my neck and I can go back in and do my segmental and free flap. But what I would say in this case, too, is sometimes and you might speak to the Steve, sometimes the soft tissue margins are easier to get widely negative when you do a segmental when you're doing a marginal sometimes you don't get as good because because you're approaching it in a different way. or maybe your soft tissue margins on your path report, Dr. Tracy, wouldn't have been as widely negative if you had done a marginal. You may not have taken the same cuff of tissue because you're trying to kind of get the saw in there. And so doing the segmental may also not take the care of the bone, but expand a little bit how you manage the soft tissue around it too. Great. All right, Caitlin.
Before we move on, did you radiate this patient or observe?

No, and so I appreciate everyone's input and that's exactly what I think about it. I kind of think about it as, you know, the classic teaching for appendicitis, right? In general surgery, like they should remove a certain percentage of normal appendices to make sure they're not leaving appendicitis behind and having ruptures, right? And in this patient, it worked out great since he did have no nodes, otherwise no high-risk features. He had no radiation. He's two years out. He's getting implants placed shortly, so he's happy.

I think the other important point, I realize we're a little bit almost out of time, but he's fully dentate. So by doing that fibula, you now gave the opportunity to do dental restoration, whereas with a marginal mandibulectomy, I think for this particular case, that would have been nearly impossible.
Very good point.
Having dental

is not something which is commonly, like, you know, we don't commonly think about it as a part that at least we do as head and neck, you know, ablative surgeons. But a lot of the OMFS literature talks about, like, actually having the implants in the fibula at the time of reconstruction. And that has several advantages of, you know, not exposing that, you know, radiated fibula then to implants later on. So that's just something to consider.
All right. Thank you, Jeremiah. All right. Caitlin. Hey, sort of a less fun case, more depressing.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus supported primary surgical management with segmental mandibulectomy and ipsilateral neck dissection, given the extent of mandibular involvement on preoperative assessment. Following resection, reconstruction with a fibular free flap was performed. Final pathology demonstrated pT2N0M0 squamous cell carcinoma with negative margins, no lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion, no nodal metastases, and no bone involvement; therefore, observation without adjuvant therapy was recommended.
reference_conclusion_quote: In this case, I'm definitely doing a segmental mandibulectomy. [...] And then I would do, certainly do a neck dissection as well on that side. [...] Segmental is a standard of care in this situation. [...] So this patient did indeed have a segmental mandibulectomy, an ipsilateral selective one through four neck dissection, and was reconstructed with a fibula. [...] You don't need to adjuvate treatment. You're good. [...] He had no radiation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male. Age was not documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with hepatic metastatic disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor arising from the pancreatic tail with liver metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumor grade had been grade 2. Following systemic therapy and subsequent surgery, pathology from both the pancreatic primary and liver metastases showed grade 1 neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI performed after 12 months of CAPTEM plus octreotide showed significant decrease in size of multiple hepatic lesions and decrease in size of the primary pancreatic tumor. Fewer than 10 liver lesions remained visible on that study.  
- Repeat DOTATATE PET/CT before surgery showed no disease outside the liver and pancreatic tail mass and no significant extrahepatic tumor burden.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None documented.

[ laboratory results ]: None documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Treated with CAPTEM in combination with continued octreotide for a total of 12 months.  
- This was followed by marked radiographic response, with significant reduction in hepatic metastatic burden and reduction in the primary pancreatic tail lesion.  
- Subsequently underwent distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, liver debulking, and cholecystectomy.  
- Intraoperatively, 15 liver lesions were identified; 6 were ablated and 9 were resected.

[ other clinical data ]: No hormonal syndrome was documented.

reference_discussion.text: If it's mild progression and patient's overall clinically stable, you know, you could continue. treating, but then this may be a situation where you want to talk about the role of surgical treatment. So discuss that more to the tumor board and then send to Dr. Koykan.

Great. So in this case, he was discussed, and I thought that he would get more bang out of the box, so to speak, if we were able to shrink his liver disease. And so we came up with the idea to start on CAPTEM, which is a chemotherapeutic agent, and to continue Octreotide. So we continued for a total of 12 months, and lo and behold, the next MRI showed there was a significant decrease in size of multiple hepatic lesions, and also of the primary tumor. I mean, you're looking at now just really less than 10 lesions that were left. So he had a really amazing response. Dr. Chen, what would you do in this case?

I think where he's gotten a really excellent response to chemotherapy, it's worth, again, discussing back at the tumor board to think about resection to try to debulk some of this disease. It is actually really interesting. It's always hard to predict when you start chemotherapy, what type of response you're going to get. But I think especially in these excellent responders, it is, I think, worthwhile thinking about debulking where some of the lesions that you'd seen before, you don't clearly see right now. So I'd be curious to see what your thoughts were when you re-reviewed the case.

These were exactly our thoughts. So actually, we did repeat a dolatate PET CT just to make sure, you know, that there was nothing outside of the liver or no significant tumor burden that was outside of the liver and the pancreatic tail mass, just to be sure that it was worth our while going back in there. And we did take him to the OR. We did a distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and liver debulking. And you can see here, we could only find 15 lesions. So we ablated six, resected nine. We also did a cholecystectomy. And interestingly, the pathology showed that it was a grade one tumor now and not a grade two anymore. This is pathology from both the primary as well as the liver metastasis. So Dr. Liao, do you see that, that patients sometimes can have a lower grade after being treated with chemotherapy?

We do definitely see a lot of heterogeneity, depending on where you biopsy, depending on what is the primary tumor versus the metastatic lesion. And even depending on, you know, different metastatic lesions, and sometimes you can even see differences in terms of how these lesions light up on, for instance, on PET scan, you know, some of them will have more, so minus 10 receptor expression, they will light up more brightly. And then if you biopsy them, they may be of lower grade or lower KXCC7, then the faster growing the metastasis. So definitely a lot of heterogeneity.

Okay, we're back to the same question of octreotide. Dr. Chen, any ideas or advice? Do you treat your pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors differently than your small bowel neuroendocrine tumors after surgical resection for metastatic disease?

Yeah, I mean, I think as you look at this case and if all disease that you knew about preoperatively has been resected, there are no, you know, hormonal syndromes that you're trying to control with the SSA. I think it's very reasonable to stop treatment and just follow. So I would probably in this case favor stopping and watching very closely.

Okay, so that's what we did. Two years later, no evidence of disease progression. That's what his liver looks like. So that's a really good outcome. So now we got a 55-year-old female with a newly diagnosed pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Same start up, so to speak. It's a grade two, casting 77%. Stage four disease. The imaging again shows innumerable bilobular liver metastases in the pancreatic tail mass. Now this is what the liver looks like. There seem to be perhaps even more tumor than in the previous scan. And this is what the DOTATATE PET looks like. So you can see the dark spots are all liver disease. So he was started on long-acting erythrocytes, same story, returned three months for surveillance imaging. And now there's some mild progression of the liver tumors. What now? Oz, is this something that you would recommend liver director therapy for?

reference_conclusion: Tumor board review supported initiation of CAPTEM with continuation of octreotide to reduce hepatic tumor burden. Following a marked radiographic response, repeat DOTATATE PET/CT was performed to confirm absence of significant extrahepatic disease, after which distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and hepatic debulking were undertaken with ablation and resection of residual liver lesions. After resection of all known disease and in the absence of a hormonal syndrome requiring somatostatin analogue therapy, octreotide was discontinued and the patient was placed on close surveillance.
reference_conclusion_quote: we came up with the idea to start on CAPTEM, which is a chemotherapeutic agent, and to continue Octreotide. [...] we did repeat a dolatate PET CT just to make sure, you know, that there was nothing outside of the liver or no significant tumor burden that was outside of the liver and the pancreatic tail mass, just to be sure that it was worth our while going back in there. And we did take him to the OR. We did a distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and liver debulking. And you can see here, we could only find 15 lesions. So we ablated six, resected nine. We also did a cholecystectomy. [...] I think it's very reasonable to stop treatment and just follow. So I would probably in this case favor stopping and watching very closely. [...] Okay, so that's what we did.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, flushing, and occasional nausea.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, presumed midgut/small bowel primary, with mesenteric mass and hepatic metastases. Carcinoid syndrome symptoms were present.

[ histopathology results ]: Pathology demonstrated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI demonstrated multiple large liver masses, a mid-mesenteric mass, and a small bowel mass. Disease was described as bulky and predominantly hepatic. Octreoscan was positive. After two operations, follow-up imaging demonstrated residual bilobar hepatic disease with lesions measuring approximately 1-2 cm. No extra-abdominal metastases were identified; no metastases outside the liver were known at that time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent small bowel resection for symptomatic bowel disease. Hepatic disease was not addressed at the time of the initial bowel operation because of the extent of liver involvement. He subsequently underwent a second operation for hepatic tumor removal using a parenchymal-preserving approach. He recovered well after both operations. He was treated with Sandostatin LAR. Approximately 9 months after surgery, he developed increasing diarrhea and flushing while on Sandostatin LAR.

[ current disease status ]: Residual metastatic disease remained in both hepatic lobes, with small-volume lesions measuring approximately 1-2 cm. He was asymptomatic immediately after surgery, but by approximately 9 months postoperatively he had recurrent mild carcinoid-type symptoms, including increased diarrhea and flushing, while receiving Sandostatin LAR. Known disease at that time was confined to the liver.

[ other clinical data ]: He was otherwise described as healthy.

reference_discussion.text: All right, let's move to another case, get Dr. Amersi involved. 63-year-old male, abdominal pain, diarrhea, flushing, a lot of stuff going on, liver masses, a mass seen in bowel or next to bowel on the MRI, a mesenteric mass, noted otherwise healthy. These are the scans. The scans on the left are focusing on the liver, the two different projections on the liver. The scan on the right is meant to show, it shows some liver, but it's meant to show a mass sort of mid-mesentery. And again, you can't really see it here, but there's also a small bowel mass. It's got abdominal pain. You want to walk us through what we should do here? He's symptomatic with abdominal pain and occasional nausea and this amount of tumor.
I'll choose scan positive.
Pardon?
Octreoscan.
Octreoscan positive. What are you thinking? Early PRRT?
Well, I mean, to keep the disease, I mean, we can make it stable. I mean, the lesions are pretty big, very large lesions. But still, I mean, it works. We have treated many of these patients.
All right.

Sure. So I think, you know, with this patient, obviously, where would the primary be in terms of small bowel? Do you need to do double balloon on these patients? I can tell you that a lot of times when you go in for these patients, if they didn't have the mesenteric mass and just the liver metastases, then I think there's a role for a double balloon and aroscopy to try to identify the primary. Most of these patients, when you do go in for a surgical exploration, Wherever the mesenteric mass is, you can find the primary within the bowel in that area. And really, the question is looking at more cuts of the MRI in terms of the mesenteric mass. Is this involving what we call the superior mesenteric artery and vein, which is the blood supply to the entire small bowel? And trying to get all this disease out, are we going to compromise the potential blood supply to whatever else that's left behind? I think that's one important factor in consideration for surgery. And then more importantly, addressing it with a liver surgeon, is there something that's going to be done surgically at the same time to address the liver disease, or are we going to turn it over to our intervention colleagues after surgery and do something more in terms of chemoembolization or radioembolization or other targeted therapy?
I know you can't see the bowel mass, but laparoscopic, or is that mass too central and you just do this as an open case?
For this, I would do it open. I would not do it laparoscopic, purely because of the blood supply issue.

Let me say, this is a great example that you've chosen here of why you need a multidisciplinary center, because there are many ways to skin the cat here. So one option is to take out the primary and deal with the mesenteric nodes first, and go back and sort out the liver at a later stage with interventional radiology, making sure you do a COLI at the same time. We have that discussion. An alternative is to go in there laparoscopically, do as much as you can in terms of the liver, sort out what you're going to do with the mesenteric nodes, and then come back at a later stage and, sorry, start off with the liver directed therapy and then come back at a later stage and see what you're going to be doing with the surgical point of view. In terms of your scanning, you're going to certainly in this patient look for bony metastases and extensive disease out of the abdomen at this stage. And that may change you and make you want to go with some kind of systemic therapy. So this is a perfect example of why multidisciplinary care is everything that counts here. Because there's no one right or wrong way to do this patient's therapy. And you can change. And certainly, you can move as time goes, come back six months later and say, well, we've done X. Now the problem is Y. How are we going to deal with that? So I think it's a perfect example of why a multidisciplinary approach is so important.

In his case, the thought, and this is a great point, that's how we discussed it, and there was question about which direction. The thought was that he was symptomatic from the bowel lesion, so we as a group prioritized that. Mark and Gabe, anything interventional here? Let's take the bowel part out of the equation, because what ended up happening is a small bowel resection. There was a question, should the liver be dealt with surgically? Should the liver be dealt with interventional radiology? Should we use PRRT or just watch it for a while? What should we do? These big, bulky tumors, kind of one-sided.

Well, once these big bulky tumors really take a hold like this, get to be this size, my experience with radioembolization is that it's not quite as effective as we'd like it to be. So I think if we were going to go on the regional therapy tack, I think chemoembolization would probably be a better way to go in this situation. I think it's doable, but, you know, if surgery is an option in the clinical setting, I got to believe that that's going to be the best way of going about it, to debulk the liver at the time or at a separate time than the other surgery is done, and then come back. And if there has to be any kind of cleanup at that time, then we can address regional therapy then. That would be my opinion on that.
Gabe, what's the limit on ablation? What size would you no longer try or is there no limit?
There's no limit.
Perfect.

I think that you can use, you know, various strategies and you can combine therapies. So, you know, for tumors that are bigger than four centimeters, Ablation or chemoembolization alone tend not to be as efficacious, so you can combine the two, really, and chemoembolize before and then ablate the next day or a week later. And, you know, larger tumors, you can get a pretty good response with that.

So we didn't script this. I don't know that any of these people remember this case, but this is exactly the same dialogue we had in the multidisciplinary group. And ultimately, Dr. Amersi took this patient for a small bowel resection, and we felt that it was simply too much to tackle the liver at that time. It's a fairly big liver operation. After the fact, the case went to Dr. Friedman, who said, if you can do something surgically, that's going to put us miles ahead. So one of the videos we skipped over this morning was removal of that large lesion through kind of a parenchymal preserving approach. So that's just the pathology. It's a low grade. Let's move to his new scan. So this is now after two operations, which both he recovered quite well from. A little bit of disease left in the liver, both lobes, one centimeter, two centimeters, asymptomatic at this point in time. Again, this is mid-gut as far as we know, all the bowel, there's no other metastases, just some small disease left in the liver. What should we do, if anything? Now, I will tell you, just to add a bit, this was about nine months after the surgery, and he was actually starting to become symptomatic. He was having a little bit more diarrhea and flushing at this point in time. So, we have to do something, and he's already on his Sanistatin LAR. And this is all the disease we know of. What's the best way to tackle this small leftover disease by lobar in the liver? Andrew?

I mean, one thing that I would consider is that the clinical course doesn't seem typical. It seems to be rapidly progressing clinically. And I would probably want better imaging. Maybe this is the kind of patient you might get a gallium 68 to get more information.
All right. Still costs money. They're not covered yet. Any other thoughts? Mark, radioembo, chemoembo, it's not very big disease. You know, but he's symptomatic. Yeah.

At this point, based upon the carcinoid syndrome that you're describing, I think regional therapy would be an option at this point. And I would choose radioembolization because there's not that much disease, number one. Number two, it's much, easier to tolerate for most patients, radioembolization. It's outpatient. So I think in that setting, if the decision is made that something needs to be done, that's what I think would be the way to go.
Dr. Delbasan, where does PRRT fit? Any course in this illness, where does it fit?

Number one, I agree with Andrew regarding doing a more sensitive test. For a patient with this course, with those large lesions and essentially progressive disease, I won't be surprised that a diagnostic test like Allium shows more lesions at this point, or more lesions as our typical structural imaging modalities are showing. And you mentioned that the Arcturus scan has been positive. Of course, depending on how positive is that and how intense these tumors are expressing somatostatin receptors, I think PRRT is an option for this patient.

Would you choose, again, just because you mentioned earlier, you actually, the wheels were turning, you were wondering about doing it early on. Do you have experience with bulky liver disease before any other therapy? Do they do better to have it before we've done other things to their liver? Does it matter?

Actually, we have had very good responses with the, I mean, obviously seeing the bigger lesions initially, I mean, you feel, oh, wow, I mean, is this going to be really effective? But we have had several patients that I can tell with larger lesions, they have responded very well. And the way that the response is, I mean, we see the stabilization of the previously progressive disease for a relatively long time. And then, you know, kind of surveillance down the road just to make sure that they are staying stable. This has been our experience. I mean, still we can control this disease and function actually for the symptoms. I mean, our experience, about 77% of the patient, they experience symptomatic relief from the therapy. a structurally objective response by resist criteria might not really give the whole story to us. We see, I mean, our radiologists report this as a stable disease, but really, when you see a patient after two cycles, I mean, totally the clinic, the quality of life has changed. They say, okay, you know, I was having flushing, you know, five times a day. Now, occasionally I get it maybe, every, you know, two weeks. So that part, actually, we have seen very good response when they are functional.

I doubt his diarrhea and flushing actually due to the either new recurrent or residual tumor. I agree with Dr. Andrew Hanifar. Either he has actual hepatic diseases, significant advancement, or these are due to some dumping syndrome as a result of the bowel resection.

Let's just, all we found on it, because I'm just trying to create discussion points, forget this individual specifics. If all we found after an extensive workup was this liver disease, bilobar, relatively small volume disease, mildly symptomatic on Sandostatin LAR. Ablate it, inject it, change drugs, change to lanreotide, try a systemic agent. Where are we in this day and age? Because we've got six things to choose from now.

So there's another approach that actually hasn't been mentioned and I think is reasonable to consider. If you have a patient like this who's been maximally debulked, has very little residual disease. The residual disease doesn't look as if it's too aggressive, so it's reasonable to say, I want to wait a couple of months here, and I'll get another scan. And if this looks the same to me, and the progression of the tumor is mild and slow, it's reasonable to consider asymptomatic management, and that may be very well the place where a drug like Telotrastat could be useful here. I have a number of patients now that have done You know, I'm way in favor of being very aggressive up front. Take out as much tumor as you can, get us to an R0 if you possibly can. Be as aggressive as you can in terms of liver director therapy, systemic therapy up front. Make a new baseline, then follow your patient. If your patient actually looks like they're stable from a tumor perspective, but still a little symptomatic, deal with the symptoms. You may actually help them in the long term.

My problem with that is that that's a lot of disease there. I mean, it's bilobar, it's multiple sites, and it's the only place of disease. So symptoms control is a good reason to go after. But I think if you do regional liver-directed therapy, you don't have to have significant respond to get symptoms control, right? So I mean, being an oncologist and saying this, I actually think at this point, Regional therapy is not a bad option, both for disease control and symptoms control.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary review prioritized resection of the symptomatic small-bowel primary, and small-bowel resection was performed. Hepatic disease was deferred initially because the liver tumor burden was considered too extensive to address at the same operation; subsequent surgical debulking was favored when feasible to achieve maximal cytoreduction. For residual small-volume bilobar liver metastases with carcinoid symptoms despite Sandostatin LAR, regional liver-directed therapy was considered appropriate, with radioembolization favored in the setting of limited hepatic disease and PRRT considered an option after more sensitive imaging to better define disease extent.

And I would choose radioembolization because there's not that much disease [...] I think PRRT is an option for this patient.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old male. No significant comorbidity. No family history of prostate cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer after prior local therapies.

[ diagnosis ]: Localized recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma following prior HDR brachytherapy monotherapy and subsequent focal HIFU hemiablation.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2015 prostate biopsy: Gleason score 4+3 adenocarcinoma, identified only in the right lateral base lesion.  
- At first local recurrence: repeat biopsy confirmed Gleason 4+3 adenocarcinoma in the right side; biopsies of the remainder of the prostate were negative.  
- At subsequent recurrence after focal HIFU: biopsy of the left side showed Gleason 3+4 adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2015 conventional ultrasound: 12 x 14 mm nodule at the right lateral base.  
- At first recurrence: conventional staging was negative. PSMA imaging and MRI both demonstrated recurrence confined to the right side of the prostate, corresponding to the site of original disease. PSMA showed a high-intensity lesion in the right lobe; the left lobe was negative. MRI showed a corresponding lesion in the right peripheral zone.  
- At subsequent recurrence after right-sided focal HIFU: repeat imaging demonstrated recurrence on the left side; the previously treated right side was negative. PSMA uptake had shifted from the right to the left. MRI showed a left-sided lesion with T2 hypointensity and restricted diffusion, not present two years earlier.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2015: Treated with HDR brachytherapy monotherapy on a hypofractionation clinical trial, consisting of two fractions of 13.5 Gy with neoadjuvant therapy. Initial PSA response was good, followed by subsequent PSA rise.  
- At first intraprostatic recurrence: underwent focal HIFU with right-sided hemiablation. Initial PSA response was good, followed by subsequent PSA rise.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- PSA in 2015: 7.2 ng/mL.  
- PSA at first recurrence, approximately 3-4 years later: 5.2 ng/mL.  
- PSA after focal HIFU: 8.4 ng/mL.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. Thank you. If we can have the next slide. This is a healthy 75 year old male who's got no significant comorbidity and no family history of prostate cancer. And back in 2015, he had mild elevation of PSA to 7.2. He had an ultrasound at the time, conventional ultrasound showing a 12 by 14 millimeter nodule to right lateral base. Biopsy was Gleason four plus three, in that site only, and he went on to get radiation treatment, HDR monotherapy. This was a clinical trial of hypofractionation at the time, two fractions of 13.5 grade with neoadjuvant therapy, and he had a good PSA response, but subsequently a PSA rise. you'll see where I'm going with this case. It's not your typical case of primary treatment, but rather it's a salvage case. So he had a PSA rise and three or four years later, PSA now 5.2 conventional staging negative, PSMA had recently become available and both PSMA and MRI showed a recurrence confined to the right side, which was where he had original disease. And this was confirmed on biopsy again, showing four plus three biopsies of the remainder of the prostate were negative. If we can go to the next slide. And so here you see the imaging. the PSMA showing really a very striking area of high intensity in the right lobe, left lobe completely negative in the scan on the left, and the MRI showing essentially the same lesion in the right peripheral zone on the right side. Next slide. So, he went on to get focal HIFU. right-sided hemiablation, and with some confidence that, you know, based on PSMA and MRI imaging, this was all the disease he had. Initially, a good PSA response, subsequent rise, PSA up to 8.4, repeat imaging now shows a recurrence on the left side. The right side that had been treated previously was negative, and now the biopsy shows Gleason 3 plus 4 on the left. Next slide. So in here you see the imaging and it's really fairly striking how the PSMA has shifted from the right to the left and MRI shows a hypodense lesion on T2 and a restricted diffusion on the left side, not present two years ago. So next slide. I assume, Jack, you wouldn't want normal run-of-the-mill garden variety cases for this type of webinar. So I think in a case like this, there are limited options for local control. He's had two sets of therapy. And so we went on to do salvage Tulsa for this case. Focal Tulsa, in a sense, really treating just the left side. and go on to the next. So you can see there the treatment planning, mainly on the left, a little bit on the right, and go on to the next slide. So this should be a movie. If you can hit the next slide again, it should activate. And this just shows dramatically speeded up what this looks like. So you can see mainly the treatment on the left, the boundary. So I don't know, probably most people that have an interest in focal therapy have at least heard about TULSA MRI guided transurethral thermal ablation. It's kind of arguably the next generation of Haifu and the appeal of this technology, that's fine. We can go to the next slide. Sorry, before you do, the bottom shows the post-treatment gadolinium with essentially complete ablation of the treatment zone. Next slide. So the point of this is the appeal of Tulsa is that, we can go to the next slide. Yeah, so the appeal of Tulsa in a case like this is two things. I would say first of all that the thermometry which drives the amount of energy that's delivered gives you very accurate information as to the tissue effect that's been achieved. And this is really the unique thing about the technology Uh, there's no guesswork as to have you really delivered enough energy. And part of that, particularly in the salvage setting is that you don't have to. Over deliver energy. You just deliver enough energy to heat the tissue to 57 or 58 degrees Centigrade, 10 seconds at that temperature is a hundred percent lethal to epithelial cells. So it's quite appealing conceptually and in the salvage setting. The appeal is that the energy is not transrectal, unlike Haifu, which I also am an advocate of. But I think in the salvage setting, it's very appealing to have a technology that really doesn't drive any energy through the rectum at all. And therefore, at least theoretically, should be extremely safe. There are now been about 1,700 patients worldwide treated with Tulsa. There's not a single case yet of a prostatorectal fistula. So I think the sweet spot for this technology is really in the salvage setting, where I think it has at least some conceptual advantages over the transrectal energy-based technologies. And again, lends itself very much to focal therapy.

Thanks so much, Dr. Klotz. That's a really nice case that this is really cutting edge focal therapy. My hospital recently looked at acquiring a Tulsa Pro unit and it's very expensive. So there's a high capital expenditure in obtaining it and you need MRI time as well. But certainly it looks like, you know, the cutting edge, truly incisionless, transurethral, no needles, don't touch the rectum. Yeah.

Let me just respond to that. Definitely, the Achilles heel of this technology is the complexity. So it does require quite a lot of MRI expertise. And it requires a fair bit of time to get the positioning exactly right. So it is never going to be a cheap technology. You know, the question is, is there only going to be one winner in this competition for which is the best focal therapy? And I think this will remain a kind of a limousine quality form of focal therapy. And I think there'll be kind of Volkswagen level types of focal therapy as well. You kind of pick your poison.

I don't know if Dr. Klotz picked the best car right now to have a limousine, but everyone has their own choice. We've looked at this as well. They have different business models in the US, Jack, so it's a no cost placement and the finances sometimes are challenging, but my department of radiology has no interest in doing this. So they're like, if you'd like to have it, you do so many MRIs on the outside, we can work something out that if you wanted time. It's a give and take in the situation. If you have capacity, we have an MRI magnet for treatments here at Northwell. So that's kind of the direction of what's available to different platforms. So as we go through this, everyone should always remember, you do what you're comfortable with, and we have not determined any limousines versus Volkswagen's yet. Depends what the urologist drives after he does the case. It has to be electric.

Okay, great. I thought that was really good. I think, Dr. Klotz, I think you did prepare some discussion points, so I will visit them since we have a little bit of time. Just coming back to the MR, this is such a beautiful telling picture of where the cancer is and really tells us about the role of MR in localizing these cancers. So do we still need to do a biopsy in this case? Perhaps I'll ask Art. He's the most... No, no, no.
Ask Dr. Klotz.

I want to hear what Dr. Klotz has to say. Well, yeah. So I would say this is evolving. I mean, in the paradigmatic case where you have PSMA and MRI both point to a local recurrence in the same site, how much value is there to the biopsy? Now, I admit I'm kind of old school in this area. I still would like to confirm a positive biopsy, particularly if you're undertaking a therapy that really puts the patient at risk in terms of morbidity. I suppose if you have a very innocuous therapy, the downside risk of overtreatment if you have false positive lesion is less. But I still rely on biopsy before proceeding with particularly a salvage therapy because we know these patients are at risk for complications. But I think it's changing. So maybe a different story in a year or two. I think probably we need more data that, for example, if we knew that the combination of PSMA and MRI being positive for local recurrence was associated with virtually 100% chance of significant cancer in that site, then it's an easier argument. But we don't have that data yet that I'm aware of.

I just like to point out that the bar for prostate cancer we've created for ourselves is so much higher than kidney cancer that has, uh, how many partial effrectomies do you do with a biopsy proven disease? We don't, but the most part we just operate, um, maybe because there's two kidneys. I don't know. And Clement's here. So in Europe, you hear Everton talking, why are we even doing biopsies? It's a radiologic diagnosis. And that's what Dr. Klotz alluded to. And for me, I think I'm in the radiologic diagnosis camp. Hopefully in the future, that's where we land this. And we all, I think, agree as imaging improves. And I'm glad everyone shows their pictures because that's important. But my question is for Dr. Klotz and Jeremy, because the two of them are probably using more PET-CT than us in the US. I order a ton of it now. But the challenge is, how do you interpret those findings in patients if we don't have really what the outcomes are in selecting patients? So if there's concordance, great. If it's PET positive and the MRI lesion's positive, great. What if the PET is negative? is, you know, should we be treating? Does it impact your decision-making? Because PET does have a false negative rate with a Gleason 3 plus 4 part, and there's a recent paper on that. I just want to know how each of you use PET in your practices. PSMA PET, sorry.

I can respond to that. We only we're, we're way behind the Australians, I would say, but perhaps ahead of the Americans, which doesn't happen too often in this in the area of new technology, but we basically have PSMA pet in patients who have. recurrent disease, we still can't access it for primary treatment, primary staging prior to treatment. So in this kind of case that I just showed, it's pretty much readily available, and I think it was quite useful, but we have not, we just simply can't get it as a primary staging tool. So it's kind of a moot point, whether we'd be prepared to abandon the biopsy in patients with, you know, suspected prostate cancer who have a positive PSMA for primary local disease.

So not necessarily related to focal art, but we have been very fortunate in Australia with our access to PSMA PET. And we've been using it routinely for a few years now in both the upfront staging situation and also the PSA recurrence post-radical prostatectomy situation as well in particular. So obviously the latter is now sort of part of routine guidelines, and if your PSA is greater than 0.2, a PSMA PET is recommended. So we do that. But yeah, as I say, in the primary staging, basically grade group three and above, we've been routinely using it. As the guidelines will say, we still don't know whether it's positive or negative, whether we're making the right clinical decision about therapy after that. because we don't have the trials to support that, but we have found it still, we think it's still incredibly useful. And as of July 1, a bit like the MRI came in, in terms of reimbursement about two years ago, we're actually having all of the staging and restaging piece reimbursed by our Medicare system, which is really exciting because otherwise it's It's been—well, comparatively, it's not too bad. It's about $800 Australian. It's actually not that expensive, but from July 1, patients won't have to pay anything.

Yeah, that's great to hear. Now, it's, it seems a pretty niche to do focal therapy as a salvage after radiation failure. So I know some stuff has been published on it. What are your thoughts on, you know, focal salvage versus whole gland salvage? Clement, you have quite a lot of experience in ablation with both Haifu and Cryo. What are your thoughts on this?

So yeah, we're doing kind of, the alternative is hormones. So that's the baseline. I think it's doing a great benefit for patients who have been well selected. They all have a PSMA PET, MRI, biopsies. And actually, we've got a very good profile of success in terms of control of the disease. I think what the latest data we have is like at three years, 80% don't need any other form of treatment, which is quite good. As Dr. Claude said, you know, we don't want to harm the patient. So we're really cautious in terms of indications. You know, the rate of fistula with HIFU is higher than in a primary setting. So, but I think for the patients, it's really a great benefit for them. And very interestingly, even if we're treating some high-grade disease, which is probably the group where the disease is the most aggressive, we still have some good results with ablation. So I think it's really encouraging for fibrillation as a treatment modality. And then side effect-wise, They already have been treated with radiotherapy, so erections, I think it's a bit less relevant, but still some of them still have some good response. And the continence rate is a little bit worse, but like still 1 or 2% of urinary incontinence, not less than 1%. But selecting cases, and I think it's for the benefit of patients.
Thanks so much for that comment. Now let's go on to the third case. The next case is by Dr. Adesha Rastinahat.

reference_conclusion: Following prior HDR brachytherapy and right-sided focal HIFU for localized recurrent prostate cancer, subsequent PSA progression with imaging and biopsy demonstrated a new left-sided intraprostatic recurrence, with the previously treated right side negative. The multidisciplinary plan was focal salvage TULSA, consisting primarily of left-sided ablation with limited treatment on the right. This approach was selected as a local salvage strategy in the setting of limited remaining options for local control after two prior therapies.
reference_conclusion_quote: Initially, a good PSA response, subsequent rise, PSA up to 8.4, repeat imaging now shows a recurrence on the left side. The right side that had been treated previously was negative, and now the biopsy shows Gleason 3 plus 4 on the left. [...] So I think in a case like this, there are limited options for local control. He's had two sets of therapy. And so we went on to do salvage Tulsa for this case. Focal Tulsa, in a sense, really treating just the left side. [...] So you can see there the treatment planning, mainly on the left, a little bit on the right

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old male. Known diabetes mellitus and hypertension. No family history of malignancy. Baseline performance status was 1; current performance status was 2 following recent admission with acute kidney injury and urinary tract infection.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in November 2024 with intestinal obstruction.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the descending colon (stage IV) with liver metastases, peritoneal/omental deposits, and pericolic nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the colonic lesion showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with extracellular mucin. Mismatch repair status was proficient.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline CT demonstrated a primary lesion in the descending colon with wall thickness of 1.3 cm, multiple metastatic lesions in both lobes of the liver, subcentimeter pericolic lymph nodes, and omental and peritoneal deposits.  
Interim PET scan after 2 cycles of CAPOX showed persistence of the descending colon primary with increase in thickness from 1.3 cm to 2.2 cm; the largest liver lesion had decreased in size.  
MRI brain performed after seizure showed no metastases.  
PET scan after 7 cycles of nanoliposomal irinotecan showed increased size and metabolic activity of the primary descending colon lesion, mild increase in subcentimeter pericolonic nodes, decrease in liver metastatic lesions, and complete resolution of bilateral pleural effusions.  
Baseline echocardiogram was normal with ejection fraction 60%. Cardiac MRI later showed ejection fraction 25%, left ventricular global hypokinesia, and moderate bilateral pleural effusions. Recent 2D echocardiography showed ejection fraction 25%, mildly dilated LA/LV, and severe generalized left ventricular hypokinesia.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: MMR proficient.  
NGS colorectal panel showed KRAS G12 mutation with variant allele frequency approximately 40-41%, ATM mutation with variant allele frequency 36%, and FAT3 amplification (7 copies). PD-L1 TPS was 0%. APC and SMAD4 mutations were also reported. Tumor mutational burden was reported as 9 mutations/Mb. DPYD testing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial CEA, measured after 2 cycles of CAPOX, was 23. Follow-up CEA in April was approximately 144. After 2 cycles of irinotecan-based second-line therapy, CEA decreased to 31. Creatinine rose to 3 during admission after CAPOX. Kidney biopsy for persistent renal dysfunction showed acute tubular injury. Creatinine was 2 after 2 cycles of second-line irinotecan-based therapy. Most recent creatinine was 1.27.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent loop transverse colostomy for intestinal obstruction.  
Received first-line CAPOX. After 2 cycles, developed breathlessness, hypotension, septic shock, and underwent CPR; subsequently revived and was discharged in stable condition. During this period, creatinine increased to 3, with history of NSAID exposure.  
For persistent renal dysfunction, kidney biopsy confirmed acute tubular injury and steroids were started.  
Second-line treatment was initiated with irinotecan on day 1 and day 8 every 21 days. After the first cycle, the patient was admitted with petechiae, giddiness, and seizure; treated symptomatically and recovered.  
After 2 cycles of irinotecan-based therapy, CEA declined from 144 to 31 and creatinine was 2. Treatment was then changed to nanoliposomal irinotecan from cycles 3 through 8. After completion of 7 cycles of nanoliposomal irinotecan, PET imaging showed mixed response as detailed above.  
After 7 cycles of nanoliposomal irinotecan, the patient was admitted again with infective symptoms and pre-renal acute kidney injury; managed with supportive care and recovered.

[ current disease status ]: Following 7 cycles of nanoliposomal irinotecan, disease showed persistent primary descending colon lesion with increased size/metabolic activity, mild increase in pericolonic nodes, decreased liver metastatic burden, and resolution of bilateral pleural effusions. Current renal function had improved, with creatinine 1.27. Cardiac systolic dysfunction persisted with ejection fraction 25%. Current performance status was 2.

[ other clinical data ]: Septic episodes were associated with urinary tract infection. Coronary angiography was not performed because of renal dysfunction.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old male. Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He was a never-smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Dyspnea on exertion and back pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with massive pleural effusion and bone metastases at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural fluid cytology and cell block were positive for adenocarcinoma of lung origin. Immunohistochemistry showed Napsin positivity.

[ imaging findings ]: Massive pleural effusion was present. Bone metastases were present at baseline. No other imaging details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified BRAF V600E mutation, classified as Tier 1/pathogenic. RNA findings were consistent with MET exon 14 skipping, reported by the laboratory as a MET fusion with fusion gene A breakpoint at exon 13 and fusion gene B breakpoint at exon 15; this was interpreted as canonical MET exon 14 skipping and labeled Tier 1. BRAF V600E variant allele frequency was 20.6%. An additional MET variant of uncertain significance was reported with variant allele frequency 8%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: During admission, the patient required supplemental oxygen. Empiric gefitinib was started because of never-smoker status while awaiting molecular results. Clinical improvement was observed on gefitinib.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma remained present with pleural and osseous metastatic disease. Molecular profiling demonstrated concurrent BRAF V600E and MET exon 14 skipping alterations. PD-L1 testing had not been performed at the time of documentation.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described as financially able to access treatment. Chemotherapy was not favored by the patient.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive postoperative rise in serum thyroglobulin after thyroidectomy for follicular thyroid carcinoma, with initially occult structural disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Widely invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma of the thyroid, AJCC stage pT3aN0, stage II; high risk of recurrence. Disease subsequently demonstrated pulmonary metastatic involvement on FDG PET/CT.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroidectomy specimen showed widely invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma with extensive vascular invasion. Maximum tumor diameter was 6.2 cm. No nodal involvement was identified. No extrathyroidal extension was identified. Prior preoperative thyroid biopsies had been reported as benign Bethesda II.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial post-treatment radioactive iodine scan after 100 mCi showed significant central neck uptake only, consistent with thyroid remnant.  
- Second radioactive iodine treatment approximately 1 year later showed only very faint central neck uptake and no uptake elsewhere.  
- Early FDG PET/CT demonstrated a 0.3 cm focus in the right thyroid bed and a very small pulmonary nodule with mild FDG avidity; no other FDG-avid disease was identified.  
- Repeat FDG PET/CT studies in 2020 showed persistence of the same 0.3 cm nodule.  
- Additional investigations including neck ultrasound, CT neck/chest, nuclear medicine bone scan, and I-123 scan did not localize other disease.  
- FDG PET/CT from November showed five pulmonary nodules. The previously observed pulmonary nodule had enlarged and demonstrated markedly increased FDG uptake. Three nodules were new. One nodule measured 4 mm and had reportedly measured 2 mm previously. No lesions were identified elsewhere.  
- Representative right upper lobe pulmonary nodule showed SUV approximately 25 on the most recent FDG PET/CT, compared with SUV 2.66 on the prior study.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: TERT promoter mutation was identified in the primary tumor.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperatively, thyroglobulin rose progressively over approximately 3.5 years from 8.6 to the 300 ng/mL range under predominantly TSH-suppressed conditions. Thyroglobulin doubling time near the later course was approximately 8 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Total thyroid resection was performed in 2017; complete resection was achieved, including a large retroposterior component.  
- Radioactive iodine therapy was administered twice, with 100 mCi given initially and a second treatment approximately 1 year later. Post-therapy imaging demonstrated remnant uptake in the central neck only, with no convincing distant iodine-avid disease.  
- Serial surveillance imaging over several years did not initially localize definitive structural disease despite progressive thyroglobulin elevation.  
- The patient remained asymptomatic throughout this interval.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent and progressive biochemical disease with structurally evident pulmonary metastatic disease on the most recent FDG PET/CT. Disease burden was low volume and confined to the lungs on available imaging. No symptoms attributable to metastatic disease were reported.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Longstanding history of thyroid enlargement/goiter dating to 1996 with gradual progressive enlargement.  
- The patient had initially been reluctant to undergo surgery.  
- No relevant comorbidities were reported.  
- No identified risk factors for thyroid cancer were reported.  
- No bone pain or other cancer-related symptoms were reported; functional status was described as well preserved.
