reference_discussion.text: Great, thanks very much. Dr. Tatelsan tells me you might call this case a case of where's Waldo. So this is, I'm going to try to go through this fairly expeditiously given time, you know, anesthesiologists or surgeons always complain about waiting for anesthesiologists. This is kind of the opposite way around, although I'm not an anesthesiologist. I had to wait for a surgeon to finish here. So this is a 60 year old lady. sorry, who presented initially to Dr. Psyka back in 2017. She actually had a longstanding history of what she called a goiter dating back to 1996, so quite some time. She had gradual progressive enlargement. She was reluctant to have surgery. She had several biopsies, which were reported clearly as benign Bethesda II. She had no relevant comorbidities, no risk factors for thyroid cancer. Eventually, given the size she did consent for surgery. This, she was us taken to the operating room by Dr. Sika now four years ago, complete resection was achieved there was a large retro posterior component. The pathology, which I'm not going to review, but will because I'm interested in some of the follow up, was felt to be a widely invasive follicular thyroid cancer. There was extensive vascular invasion. The maximal diameter of the tumor was six point two centimeters. There was no nodes involved. There was no extra thyroid extension. There was some molecular diagnostics done on this test, and there was felt to be a Turk promoter mutation. This patient staged A T3A tumor stage two, the recurrence risk was graded to be high. Post-operatively, the major problem has been ongoing and progressive elevation in thyroglobulin. We gave her over time, The first radioactive iodine treatment with 100 millicuries just showed simply fairly significant central neck uptake only in keeping with the remnant. Following along, we then actually ended up giving her a second dose a year later, which showed just very faint central neck uptake, really nothing anywhere else. And then we have done several FBG PETs on her. The first one, again, findings that all of us might see sometimes, it's very hard to know the significance of it. There's a 0.3 centimeter focus in the right thyroid bed, very small pulmonary nodule, notice with very mild FDG avidity, difficult to know the relevance of this with no FDG uptake anywhere else. I just show everyone here a table These are all mostly completely TGs with suppressed TSHs. There are a couple of stimulated on the right, but I just like to show you the progression over a three and a half year period from a TG of 8.6 up into the 300 range with a thyroglobulin doubling time of almost eight months towards the end. This is just representing it graphically, showing a log scale on the left and the gross values on the right. And you can see both the predicted and the actual values follow this algorithm actually quite nicely. So as things go on again, once again, we are hunting for Waldo. Another PET scan was repeated twice in 2020, showed this same 0.3 centimeter nodule. Throughout this time, the patient remained 100% asymptomatic. Apart from me making her anxious for doing all these tests, she was functioning, feeling well, no bone pain, really nothing. We did a number of other tests, which I've listed there, ultrasound, CT neck, chest, nuclear medicine bone scan, I-123 scan, really nothing. I have taken her to tumor board at least three times. There was question about, are we missing an occult bone metastasis? Finally, we seem to have cropped up with an answer here. This is a recent FDG PET just from last November. There are now five pulmonary nodules. The one we've been watching is larger. The SUV, as I'll show you in a slide in a minute, is markedly increased. There are three new nodules. And one that they're saying in retrospect was only two millimeters before is now four millimeters. But once again, there's no lesions anywhere else. So again, is there a disconnect between the level of thyroglobulin and what we're finding on both our anatomic and functional imaging? This is just a couple of screenshots from showing the representative right upper lobe nodule. And you can just see on the top half of this is the recent FDG PET with the SUV of 25. And then that same lesion a year previously at 2.66. And then again, this is just the new nodule shown on the capture image from the CT PET showing some of the differences there. So I'm going to wrap this up just and leave up for you these four questions that I have. And I guess the first one is the one that I just alluded to was comments on the discrepancy between the progressive and marked thyroglobulin rise and the challenges we've had in both functional and anatomic localization.

I got to work in the this this I was getting up in the two and three hundreds where you know the patients are going nuts because they're still trying to find them, what are you going to tell this year, this person, she's 60 years old so she's young by our criteria, what are you going to tell us going on here.

Well, she clearly has disease and through all of these studies trying to find it. I do think the question becomes how often do you image, what are you going to do to try to stem the tide and give her some comfort here? This is not a surgical problem. I think you've imaged the neck and I think this really obviously lies in the range of medical oncology and nuclear medicine.

Dr. Ghassani, the limited resolution like on the PET scan, has she had small volume lung meds the last three or four years and we just couldn't find it? Where do you start picking up lung things on the PET scan that you believe is real?

Yes, it depends on the generation of the scanners and our most recent generation scanners have better resolution, because they are digital detectors, so we are able to sometimes pick up the activity in the nodules. less than seven millimeter which was initially the benchmark that was considered for when the lung cancer application of FDG PET-CT was approved. Now the resolution has improved, but equally important is the notion of of the blooming, which is that if there is significantly high number of mitochondria in a given setting, then even though the nodule may be small, there's usually a blooming effect, such that the other pixels around the nodule start to take up some of the residual signal, and they, to your eyes, look larger than actual size of the nodule. And I think looking back in this particular patient, knowing that ultimately the STCV went up to 22.9, also explains that there's probably a very high expression of mitochondria. And that would also imply the fact that the next question about the tarot globulin we'll discuss, but it probably is a significantly high amount of tarot globulin being produced by these aggressive nodules.

I mean, these are always challenging. My kids had the book called Where's Waldo? And you're always chasing where these are. So I often tell these patients you could have lots of small volume pulmonary metastases because remember, the chest CT can't see less than three or four millimeters. So I think the disconnect you have here, if you did a biopsy, she's going to have lots of multifocal disease on the lungs that you're not seeing. I think that's where volume is coming from. So multiple small volumes that are very good TG producers. That's probably what you have here. Bone mets happen over and over that the fiber globins go up in the hundreds before you can find these small bone mets, because that for whatever reason, bone mets get this really out of out of proportion fiber globin for very, very small disease. The other place I always look is the skull and the base of the skull. I've seen over and over pet scans. missed disease at the base of the skull because where the brain takes up so if you wouldn't have been seeing stuff in the lungs I go look at the base of the skull and the calvarium because that's usually a little bit outside. The other place I see this is in the kidney, you'll occasionally see a kidney met from a follicular thyroid cancer. and it gets ignored because everybody calls it cystic lesions and nodules in the kidneys. So I think about small volume lung metastasis that takes several years to do. I tell patients they're below the radar screen at four millimeters and next year they'll say there's new ones. They're not new, they're just getting big enough to see. Basis skull, skull, and the kidneys. So I think you're there. Lori? Good Lord, we've been watching this poor lady and she's coming back every six months. When do we do something here?

Yeah, so that's a really important question and a question that I think is difficult to answer. I think the best approach is to really individualize pulling the trigger for the individual patients and what's important to them as well as what their disease is doing. But she has low volume disease that's not rapidly progressive. She doesn't have a lesion that's even as big as one centimeter in size. She would not meet criteria to enter any of the clinical trials for iodine refractory disease. I would say sit tight and we'll continue to monitor the disease. and try to minimize the anxiety. It's also a good time to talk to patients about the idea of prehabilitation. Likely an MKI is in her future, and we do think that patients who have good healthy lifestyles get plenty of exercise. even weight-bearing exercise, probably tolerate the MKIs better. So we're beginning to try to work that into our period of disease monitoring for these patients. So we don't have a randomized trial that tells us that people will live longer if they start earlier versus later. But we have actually looked at the select trial with lenbatinib that randomized patients to lenbatinib or placebo, and then the patients that received placebo crossed over to receive lenbatinib when they had disease progression. So it's difficult to really look for overall survival benefit because of that crossover. But nonetheless, we've looked at several different aspects of the data and post hoc analyses. And it does seem that people do derive a longer, better, deeper clinical benefit when the drug is started earlier versus later. There was an analysis that was done taking a look at patients with lung mets. Patients who had lung mets, who were randomized to lumbatinib or placebo, had a longer survival when they were randomized initially to lumbatinib, despite the fact that 89 percent of the patients crossed over and received lumbatinib at progression. So with lung meds, when patients have lung meds as small as one centimeter in size, they actually have an overall survival benefit when they start lenbatinib earlier. So that's one of the aspects that I think is important to discuss with patients. Then, of course, you also have to discuss the impact on quality of life. from side effects from therapy, which everybody has to expect to experience some side effects. And so there's a balance and the formula for which is most important to a patient depends on the individual patient.

Dr. Ghassani, we're in that space with this patient of probable structural progression. not rapid or not big enough to go with TKIs yet. She's fairly unresponsive to radioactive iodine, two doses of 100 millicurie. Is there any space in here for these re-differentiation trials? This is probably going to be a RAS-like tumor, right? It's a follicular tumor. It's probably going to be RAS-like. It's got the TERT mutation. Would you be thinking about re-differentiation or trying to use radioactive iodine in here?

Yes, in fact, we have done so. As you know, we have collaborations between Memorial and Mount Sinai, and we have either used the I-124 for the dosimetry planning or I-123 scan with the gamma camera imaging, and these patients actually do benefit after re-differentiation, so this patient could be a candidate for that.

Yeah, so, so in our place we would do full molecular testing to get some better feel for what it is and then one of our medical oncologists would probably put them on a re differentiation agent for about a month and repeat the scan to see if we can get some uptake. There's a couple of other questions that are tangential that I'll have you do. Lori, role for zoledronic acid in people with bone metastasis. Do we talk about it? Do you really do it? Worry on that. Then I'll come back to Dr. Ghassani. Something about a FAPI PET scan? I never heard of that. You can tell me about that. Lori first.

Yeah. There is a role, I think, for bone modifying agents in patients with bone metastases to reduce sequelae of bone metastases. There are good studies that have been done in multiple tumor types and studies that have enrolled thyroid cancer patients. So in general, we do start Zometa. One thing that I do is I don't do monthly Zometa, but do every three months Zometa, expecting that the patients are going to be on Zometa for a while. And then also, you know, we're really meticulous in terms of the dental evaluation and dental hygiene because of patients with xerostomia related to their radioactive iodine. And I think I tend to use Zometa as the drug of choice rather than Denosumab. But I think that Denosumab is also an option.

Yeah, so FAPI is a very promising new agent on the horizon. It has been studied extensively in Europe and Australia. And we now have discussions of having access to FAPI for multiple cancer applications, including thyroid. And it's a fibroblast activation protein, and it actually has more diverse localization in multiple tumor types, and also the target to background is considerably higher. We just had a review of hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma and there we also found extensively higher amount of FAPI uptake relative to traditional agents such as FTG or in the case of liver gallium 68. So, this could potentially be an application, but here we already have a FDG uptake localized. And as you said, Mike, there are probably multiple more underlying nodules. So, if we did a FAPI and compared it to FDG, it's very likely that higher tumor volume could be detected with FAPI in the lungs, and that can explain the rise of thyroglobulin values.

So I mean I think it's a great case I think what we would pretty much all follow along the same way, at least for me in terms of deciding when to do something I use five things, size of the metastasis location rate of change. Are they symptomatic are likely to get symptomatic and then patient preference. So those are the five things that I think about, size, location, rate of change, symptoms, and patient preference, because that'll be your next decision point in summary here. If there was a role for a re-differentiation scan, we would probably at least be talking to the patient about that in this intermediate space between just completely watching and moving to kinase inhibitor therapy. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive fatigue and dyspnea on exertion over approximately 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Acute myeloid leukemia with monocytic differentiation. Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow morphology showed monoblasts/promonocytes. Bone marrow was hypercellular. Cytogenetics showed a normal female karyotype.

[ histopathology results ]:  
Peripheral blood smear showed large immature cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, irregular nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, vacuolation, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and features consistent with promonocytes/monoblasts.  
Bone marrow core biopsy was markedly hypercellular for age with near absence of fat spaces and diffuse blast infiltration. There was reduced normal maturation of neutrophilic and erythroid lineages. Small megakaryocytes with hypolobated nuclei were present in the background.  
Bone marrow aspirate showed monocytic blasts/promonocytes with irregular nuclei and cytoplasmic vacuoles. Background dysplastic erythroid cells and some hypergranulation of myeloid cells were described, but the threshold for AML with myelodysplasia-related changes was not met on the material reviewed.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging results were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
Bone marrow next-generation sequencing panel identified mutations in NPM1, DNMT3A, and TET2.  
FLT3 was negative.  
CEBPA was negative.  
KIT was negative.  
IDH mutations were negative.  
KRAS was negative.  
Conventional cytogenetics demonstrated a normal female karyotype.

[ laboratory results ]:  
Initial complete blood count:  
- White blood cell count: 11.9 x10^9/L  
- Absolute neutrophil count: 1.1 x10^9/L  
- Hemoglobin: 7 g/dL  
- Platelets: 36,000/µL  

Chemistry/liver profile:  
- Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL  
- AST: elevated  
- ALT: elevated  
- Bilirubin: normal  
- LDH: slightly elevated  
- Albumin: 2.8 g/dL  
- Uric acid: normal  
- Fibrinogen: normal  

Red cell indices were described as consistent with normocytic anemia with increased RDW.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior leukemia-directed treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed AML with monocytic differentiation at initial evaluation. The patient was symptomatic from cytopenias, with anemia, thrombocytopenia, mild leukocytosis, and neutropenia. Karnofsky performance status was 80.

[ other clinical data ]:  
Past medical history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, arthritis.  
Home medications: hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, rosuvastatin, metformin.  
Family history: prostate cancer, coronary artery disease, diabetes.  
Review of systems: denied chest discomfort, lower extremity swelling, fever, and bleeding symptoms.  
Physical examination: afebrile; heart rate in the 90s; blood pressure approximately 140/90 mmHg; oxygen saturation 95%. Conjunctival pallor, bruising on extremities, and a soft systolic murmur were present. Cardiac rhythm was regular. Lungs were clear. Abdomen was normal without palpable organomegaly. No lymphadenopathy was present. Neurologic examination was nonfocal.

reference_conclusion: Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy should be performed to confirm suspected acute myeloid leukemia, with comprehensive diagnostic evaluation including flow cytometry, conventional cytogenetics/G-banding, and molecular testing including at minimum NPM1, CEBPA, RUNX1, and FLT3; peripheral blood flow cytometry and HLA typing at diagnosis before induction therapy should also be obtained. Additional pretreatment assessment should include echocardiography, evaluation of abnormal liver function tests, and planning for central venous access as indicated. Enrollment in a clinical trial is the preferred treatment approach. If no trial is available, management should be individualized between intensive induction chemotherapy and lower-intensity hypomethylating agent–based therapy, with consideration of allogeneic transplantation in first remission as the only reliable curative strategy in an older adult fit for transplant.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging right-sided neck mass first noted in October after a viral upper respiratory illness, with progressive hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea when lying flat, and 20-pound weight loss by December.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with sarcomatoid features on fine-needle aspiration of a right thyroid mass; metastatic disease was present on PET imaging.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Outside fine-needle aspiration: anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with sarcomatoid features.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Outside thyroid ultrasound: TI-RADS 5 thyroid nodule.  
- Flexible fiberoptic examination at presentation: marked supraglottic edema and limited right vocal fold movement.  
- CT neck/chest: large right-sided thyroid mass displacing the great vessels posterolaterally and deviating the trachea to the left.  
- MRI brain: performed; no specific findings were provided.  
- PET scan at presentation: diffuse metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Rapid mutational testing by immunohistochemistry: BRAF positive.  
- TERT positive.  
- p53 positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy was initiated after molecular results with dabrafenib, trametinib, and pembrolizumab.  
- The patient subsequently underwent total thyroidectomy, bilateral central compartment dissection, and bilateral lateral neck dissections.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post systemic therapy and surgical resection.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- At presentation, the airway was maintained without extremis.

reference_conclusion: Rapid BRAF testing was prioritized while closely monitoring the airway, with tracheostomy reserved only if absolutely necessary. After identification of a BRAF-positive anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, systemic therapy with dabrafenib, trametinib, and pembrolizumab was initiated, resulting in a near-complete metabolic response. Following this response, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central compartment dissection and bilateral lateral neck dissections. Postoperatively, continuation of triplet therapy was favored, with radiation considered selectively but targeted therapy prioritized over radiation in most cases.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old woman. Retired government employee. Good performance status. Lived with her younger brother. Past medical history included diabetes mellitus and hypertension for 15–20 years on regular medication, dyslipidemia for 4–5 years on statin therapy, and sleep disturbance/insomnia. She was taking more than five medications for comorbidities.

[ chief complaint ]: Right breast lump detected incidentally in April 2025, with associated vague bony pains.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic right breast carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, with nodal and osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy from the right breast lesion showed invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3. Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor strongly positive at 90%; HER2 was 2+ by IHC and negative by FISH. Ki-67 was approximately 60%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Mammogram: BI-RADS 5 right breast lesion measuring approximately 4 × 5 cm.  
- Initial PET-CT: primary right breast lesion with regional axillary nodal involvement, multiple non-regional nodal metastases in the cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal regions, and scattered bony metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- HER2 FISH negative.  
- Germline BRCA testing was performed.  
- Additional NGS testing was performed for potentially druggable targets.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Baseline frailty assessment was performed; no recent falls were reported.  
- Bone densitometry and cardiac evaluation were completed prior to systemic therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic ER-positive/HER2-negative breast carcinoma with nodal and osseous metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidity burden included diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia with polypharmacy. Performance status was good.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 39-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in 2021 with frontal lobe symptoms and seizures/fits.

[ diagnosis ]: Right frontal diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from February 2022 neuro-navigation-guided craniotomy/debulking showed diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 2. GFAP was positive. p53 was positive. ATRX loss was present. Ki-67 proliferation index was up to 5%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pre-operative MRI dated December 2021 showed a large right frontal lobe lesion crossing the genu of the corpus callosum, with a central cystic component, heterogeneous signal characteristics, vasogenic edema crossing the midline, subfalcine herniation, marked mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle and frontal horn of the contralateral lateral ventricle, and small subarachnoid seepage along the occipital horn of the left lateral ventricle. There were internal T1 hyperintense/T2 low-signal foci consistent with hemorrhagic areas. The lesion showed irregular peripheral/nodular enhancement of the cystic component.  
- Early post-operative MRI, approximately 6 weeks after surgery and before radiotherapy, showed reduction in bulk of the right frontal lesion with decreased mass effect and reduced subfalcine herniation. A new/enlarged enhancing lesion was seen contralaterally in the left frontal region, in an area that had previously shown edema. Post-surgical changes were confined to the right frontal side.  
- MRI from July 2022, approximately 5 months after completion of radiotherapy while temozolomide was ongoing, showed encephalomalacic/gliotic change in the right frontal resection bed with significantly reduced mass effect. The contralateral lesion had partially regressed in size, with residual enhancing component near the genu of the corpus callosum.  
- MRI from July 2024 showed no enhancement at the site of the prior contralateral lesion.  
- MRI from May 2025 showed recurrent enhancement in the contralateral frontal region.  
- MRI from August 2025 showed interval increase in enhancement in the left frontal lesion and also enhancement on the right side along the inferior/medial aspect of the lesion, anterior to the frontal horn.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation was present. ATRX loss was present. p53 was positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent neuro-navigation-guided craniotomy/debulking of the right frontal lesion in February 2022. The left-sided lesion was not surgically approached.  
- Received chemoradiotherapy after surgery, including concurrent temozolomide and whole-brain radiation.  
- Received temozolomide for 7 cycles (5 days per month).  
- Serial imaging showed initial reduction in the right frontal lesion and subsequent regression of the contralateral lesion, with no enhancement seen on July 2024 imaging.  
- Imaging in 2025 demonstrated recurrent/progressive enhancing disease.

[ current disease status ]: As of August 2025, there was radiologic progression with increasing enhancement in the left frontal region and additional enhancing abnormality on the right frontal side. Functional status was reported as class I. She had returned to work as a school teacher. She was neurologically and behaviorally well apart from urinary incontinence.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination at presentation showed subtle cognitive impairment and papilledema; otherwise no major abnormality was described.  
- The patient had shown significant clinical improvement over time after initial treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Referral 2 months after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma with known gross residual disease involving the anterior tracheal wall; postoperative persistent hypocalcemia, pain, and persistent globus sensation.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, partially resected at initial surgery, with gross residual tumor in the left thyroid bed and tracheal invasion/submucosal tracheal involvement. Tumor had been incidentally identified after CT chest/abdomen performed for rib pain demonstrated a thyroid mass.

[ histopathology results ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma. No additional histopathology details were available.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pre-referral CT chest/abdomen performed for rib pain demonstrated a thyroid mass.  
- Neck ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous soft tissue with punctate echogenic foci in the left thyroid bed, consistent with gross residual tumor. No lymphadenopathy was identified on sweep images of the lateral or central neck.  
- CT neck demonstrated hyperdensity/loss of tracheal cartilage below the cricoid with protrusion into the tracheal lumen. No pathologically enlarged lymph nodes were identified, although several ipsilateral level II and III lymph nodes were noted. Tumor abutted the cervical esophagus without obvious invasion.  
- Office flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated mobile vocal cords. Limited office tracheoscopy was not tolerated; the visualized subglottis appeared normal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing demonstrated both BRAF and TERT mutations.

[ laboratory results ]: Persistent postoperative hypocalcemia was present. No numerical laboratory values were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment at an outside hospital consisted of total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- At the initial operation, the surgeon identified tumor adherence to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and involvement of an estimated 3-4 cm of the anterior tracheal wall. The surgeon transected through tumor, preserved the nerve, and left gross tumor on the anterior tracheal wall.  
- Postoperative course after the initial thyroidectomy was complicated by persistent hypocalcemia, pain, and persistent globus sensation.  
- Subsequent operative management included direct laryngoscopy, rigid bronchoscopy, revision left thyroidectomy/completion resection, sacrifice of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, bilateral central/peritracheal neck dissections, left lateral neck dissection, and tracheotracheal resection with primary anastomosis.

[ current disease status ]: Following revision surgery, gross residual locally invasive disease had been surgically addressed with tracheotracheal resection, revision thyroid bed resection, bilateral central/peritracheal dissections, and left lateral neck dissection. No postoperative imaging or biochemical disease assessment after the revision procedure was available.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included remote cerebrovascular accident without residual deficits, remote seizure disorder, coronary artery disease approximately 15 years earlier, and moderate, reasonably well-controlled asthma.  
- No drug allergies were reported.  
- Never smoker.  
- No history of radiation exposure.  
- No family history of thyroid cancer.  
- Occupation: house cleaner.  
- Physical examination before revision surgery showed a well-healed collar incision and no palpable lymphadenopathy.

reference_discussion.text: Perfect, all right, so I'll kick us off with a very ugly case. So I'll preface this by saying that I had been in practice for about seven months when I saw this person. There are some things that I would do differently today, but this is a case of a partially resected papillary thyroid cancer with tracheal invasion that I saw after her initial thyroidectomy. I have no disclosures, but I do have very adorable pets who actually do cuddle like this, All right, so this is a 55 year old lady, she was referred to me by an outside hospital endocrinologist. This was two months after she had undergone a total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer. The cancer was incidentally diagnosed after a CT chest and abdomen that was performed for rib pain showed a thyroid mass. Interoperatively, the surgeon who did her original surgery noted some adherence to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, and he estimated three to four centimeters of the anterior tracheal wall. He elected to cut through the tumor, preserve the nerve, and leave gross tumor on the anterior tracheal wall. Her postoperative course was complicated by persistent hypocalcemia, pain, and a persistent globus sensation. Her outside hospital endocrinologist was managing her hypocalcemia and sent next-generation sequencing, and her tumor was notable for both BRAF and TERT mutations. Her past medical history, she had a remote CDA, no residual deficits. She had a seizure disorder. Again, the last kind of clinical activity of this was very remote. She had coronary artery disease, again, like 15 years prior, so relatively young presentation. And then she also had asthma, which was classified as moderate, reasonably well-controlled. She had no drug allergies, was not on any particularly exciting medications, never smoke her. She worked as a house cleaner. She had never had any radiation exposure, no history of thyroid cancer in the family. And then on exam, she had a well-heeled collar incision, no palpable lymphadenopathy. I scoped her in clinic, her focal cords were mobile. She wasn't really able to tolerate tracheoscopy in the office despite attempts at adequate topicalization, What I saw of her subglottis was normal in appearance. Because she was coming from a significant distance, as happens a lot here in Oregon, you know, when people are referred for kind of tertiary care, OHSU was one of the only places and she was coming from. five hours away. So before I saw her, I had arranged for an ultrasound with our ultrasonographers as well as a CT. And so that showed some heterogeneous soft tissue with punctate echogenic foci in the left thyroid bed consistent with gross residual tumor. There was no lymphadenopathy on sweep images of the lateral neck or the central neck. And then CT performed that same day, did show some hyperdensity loss of the tracheal cartilage below the cricoid. This picture here shows some protrusion into the tracheal lumen. There were no pathologically enlarged lymph nodes, but several level two and three lymph nodes on the ipsilateral side of the cancer were noted on the CT. And then the tumor was noted to be abutting, although not obviously invading the cervical esophagus.

So just before we start, so John, Amanda, let me ask you a couple of questions just to start with. So, because I know probably some of the fellows are like, wow, like this wasn't done upfront. How frequently do you see patients, not necessarily with this exact presentation, but who've had surgery where your, you know, people will say cleaning up after someone else, but patients who've had surgery where you're kind of dealing with the fact that maybe initially things weren't kind of handled properly.

Well, in my, in my environment, I see it probably less than those that are in a pure academic center. But I do, I do see it, I see it more in the context of patients that were suspected to have benign pathology, and we're kind of followed along until suddenly something erupts. or they were told, I have, you know, a number of, I'm thinking of a number of patients in my practice that are in their 80, you know, mid to upper 80s, and they were told, oh yeah, I was told it was thyroid cancer 10, 15 years ago, but it's a good cancer, and it wasn't going to hurt me, and so nothing was done, and now it's really at quite an advanced stage that's, you know, in some cases, unresectable. So, you know, we do see it. And I think that my comments speak more to kind of the changing of paradigms in terms of how things are managed and worked up. You know, I think we do things differently now than we did 10, 15, 20 years ago.

Yeah, I mean, I think that what's one of the things that's important again this is really for the fellows is that, unfortunately, depending on like Amanda said the practice location. You will see non infrequently, by the way, and this is just probably true for endocrine but for other head and neck stuff as well. You're going to see patients not infrequently, we're going to come to you, where kind of their initial management was, I would say less than ideal. And the reality is that that's what it is. you know, your kind of responsibility as the kind of beyond expert, hopefully, is to say, okay, that's not what I would have done up front, but now here's the reality and I'm gonna deal with that. John, tell me something, because this is kind of one of those standard questions. What do you think about the idea that the nerve was cut off? Like how do you handle that intraoperatively? So you find, have a patient, I'm assuming this patient, hopefully, that they had looked preoperatively, they saw the nerve was functionally intact. How do you handle that when you encounter a kind of significant disease involving the nerve with a functional nerve or a non-functional nerve?

So I actually appreciate kind of what they did, right? They recognized that they were maybe overmatched for the tumor and they said, hey, we're gonna preserve a functioning nerve and we're gonna know that there's disease there, and they left the nerve intact. For me, as the cleanup guy, that makes it a lot easier because I've got a bilateral functioning nerve at that point. I've got a lot more options and things that I can do. I think most of us kind of agree that when you scope somebody beforehand, if you have a functional nerve, at the end of your surgery, you should still have a functional nerve when it's well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma. And most of us wouldn't sacrifice the nerve. Kind of my thinking is I only sacrifice the nerve if it's to save a larynx. And so if there's frank invasion when the nerve inserts to go into the larynx, I'll sacrifice that nerve. But otherwise I will shave to the best of my ability, clean everything off. And I'll just acknowledge the fact that, hey, you know, five years from now we might have to come back and we might have to, we'll let the cancer take out the nerve. And when the cancer knocks out the nerve, then we'll move forward at that point with the bigger resection. Yeah.

Can, can I ask whoever's microphone is on just to mute themselves if they're not one of the presenters. So, I guess the, the, the question I would just have for you is, how about if. Do you make a distinction whether you can leave or not leave behind microscopic versus macroscopic disease. So, for example, if you need to maintain nerve function, but you're going to leave behind a big chunk of cancer, is that different than if you're going to be leaving behind really kind of minimal residual disease?
Right. I wouldn't leave a chunk. I would never leave macroscopic disease behind, but certainly shaving for microscopic disease, I'm not going to sacrifice a nerve for that.

Okay. And let me ask, either of you can comment on this. What do you think about the next generation sequencing kind of results? I think it was a TERT mutation, correct? And BRAF. And BRAF, yeah. So are you guys surprised by that in this context?

I would say no. The BRAF, certainly not. And the degree of disease or kind of how it was described and what was found, putting aside how we feel like maybe it was worked up preoperatively, speaks to a more aggressive clinical biology, which seems to be what we're seeing here. So that does not surprise me.

Yeah. And for all of the trainees, we always talk about how BRAF by itself historically was associated with worse cancer. Now we kind of don't make that association anymore. BRAF in isolation doesn't mean much for prognosis. And in fact, it gives us some good targets that we can focus on. But BRAF plus TERT for motor mutation, that combination is associated with a worse prognosis. And so that's something that should send off alarm bells in your head.

But you'll still see the BRAF written on reports as being associated with more aggressive behavior. So exactly what John said, just in isolation, it may not change what we do clinically, but it does often need to be addressed with the patients and or the endocrinologist or the referring doctors, just so they understand it, because if they just see BRAF in isolation, then they often panic with that.
Yeah, I think those are great points. Okay, so Alessa, why don't you carry on and tell us kind of next steps that you did?

Perfect. All right, excellent so started surgical planning, anticipating a tracheal resection. And so, kind of thinking through like putting in the order for surgery and thinking through what kind of procedures are going to be. needed, we put in for a DL, a rigid bronchoscopy, to assess the trachea and kind of see how much was going to need to be resected. Completion thyroidectomy was likely left to recurrently around general nerve sacrifice just based on the location of the residual tumor and the kind of bulk of the residual tumor. bilateral, central, and paratracheal neck dissections. I elected to do a left lateral neck dissection based on those rounded nodes, although they were not pathologically enlarged by size criteria and the ultrasound didn't call them, but the CT did. As I was thinking through doing a cricotracheal resection on this person, I would like to never come back to this neck, and so I elected to do a left lateral neck dissection as well. and a cricotracheal resection. I booked this as a co-surgery with one of my laryngology partners, and Dr. Shindo was gonna be kind of around that day as well. So intraoperatively on bronchoscopy, we noted that the tumor looked like it was about a centimeter below the true vocal cords, but extended three centimeters inferiorly to about the fourth tracheal ring. Once we opened up her neck, we encountered a lot of dense scar and tumor that was adhered to the recurrent laryngeal nerve all the way up to the cricothyroid joint. We did note some adherence to the esophageal muscle and had to resect some of that, but there was no invasion of the esophageal mucosa and we did do a quick esophagoscopy at the beginning of the case as well. I just don't have pictures from that.
And so obviously what you're showing, or I think what you're showing is just the tracheoscopy, right?
Correct. Yep. This is just the tracheoscopy pre-resection.

that there was some abnormal appearing tissue that was extending submucosally that started about a centimeter below the true vocal folds and came down to about tracheal ring four. This is kind of a crummy picture, but this is all I got.
But no true mucosal invasion? Correct. Correct.
Yes, but definitely some submucosal, like very obvious abnormality.
Okay, great.

Postoperatively, so ultimately we did all of the procedures that we anticipated doing. So did a tracheotracheal resection with primary anastomosis. Revision total thyroidectomy or revision left thyroidectomy, left tummy thyroidectomy with sacrifice of the left recurrent. peritracheal dissections on both sides and a left lateral neck dissection. On a couple elements here. What do we know or what is your approach and what do we know about the difference in outcomes? Amanda, do you want to start with that?

Sure. First of all, I think the way Dr. Coliani laid out, you know, the plan to kind of plan for the maximum. And you can always pare it back down, but you're kind of preparing the patient appropriately so that they're not surprised, you know, by what you do at the end. I think in terms of involvement of the cartilage itself, you can use your preoperative imaging to guide you. And so you should kind of anticipate plan for the worst, but you may see the intraoperatively something different than kind of what you were expecting. And I approach it similar to the way Dr. Russell was talking about the nerve that you do kind of as much as you need to and as little as you have to. So I wouldn't do more prophylactically. I would kind of go as far as you really see that you need to go through those gradations that you described, shaving it versus a little window versus true resection.

John, again, if everyone could just turn off their, their microphone who who's not a presenter, that'd be appreciated. John, just tell us because we have to go on to the next case. We could talk about this case honestly, for the whole hour. easily. Yeah, it's a great case. But just tell me again, what is your approach of, oh my goodness, it's extending, do I do a shave? Do I do a tracheal resection? What is your approach? Like what dictates that for you?

So I have adapted my approach a lot since I started. I think most of us come out of training and most of our training is with squamous cell carcinoma, where clean margins are vital to the survival of the patient. Tracheal resections, my experience with them is it's tough to always get a clean margin because where it inserts is, where your nerve inserts is in your larynx. And unless you're willing to sacrifice that larynx, at least your proximal margin is going to be positive at a relatively high rate. Your distal margin, sure, you can keep taking rings until you get a clean margin, but even that, these tumors are kind of insidious and they just kind of track down along that And yet, as far as outcomes go, those microscopic margins of a well-differentiated carcinoma don't seem to be what really drives your prognosis as much as a lot of other things. And at this point in my career, I am going to make the cancer take the larynx and cause the dysfunction before I am going to do it with the knowledge that for the most part, the worst that this cancer will do is will be to affect the larynx and make it non-functional. And so, why should I speed up that process by being overactive with my surgery? And so, I'm going to just take what this cancer gives me. I'm going to shave everything down as well as I can. There's a great Japanese series that talks about, you know, how likely are Are you to recur if you do a shave versus a window versus a full tracheal resection? And certainly a tracheal resection has the best as far as recurrence rates, as far as mortality, but there's a lot of nuance that goes into that. And for most well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma, it's not actually through and through those tracheal rings and into the lumen. Kind of, Mike, you pointed this out earlier. You said you don't see a big chunk of tumor hanging out in your lumen. That's fairly rare. Yeah, so I think those are all great points by both of you I do, just in the interest of time and thank you less we're gonna we're gonna move on to the next case but I do want to just raise that point that you just kind of suggested quickly at the end there john which is, in general, a well differentiated thyroid cancer, we don't think about external beam radiation. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Flushing, diarrhea, and postprandial cramping at initial presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV well-differentiated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, presumed small bowel primary, metastatic to liver and mesenteric lymph nodes, with carcinoid syndrome. Subsequent carcinoid heart disease was documented with tricuspid valve involvement.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Liver biopsy demonstrated well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, low grade, with Ki-67 less than 3%.  
- Emergent bowel resection pathology demonstrated a 2 cm well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with 1 of 2 lymph nodes positive.  
- At later operative intervention, an additional segment of small bowel was resected containing additional neuroendocrine tumor primaries.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial non-contrast CT demonstrated enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes around the mesenteric vessels.  
- Initial contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a suspicious right hepatic lesion.  
- DOTATATE PET/CT demonstrated somatostatin receptor-avid mesenteric lesion in the right lower quadrant and multiple hepatic metastases, more numerous than initially appreciated on CT.  
- Approximately 18 months after starting octreotide, contrast-enhanced CT performed during emergency presentation demonstrated bowel abnormality concerning for obstruction/compromised bowel associated with mesenteric disease; emergent bowel resection was performed.  
- At later restaging for recurrent symptoms, DOTATATE PET/CT did not show significant progression of liver disease.  
- MRI liver with Eovist demonstrated more extensive hepatic metastatic disease than seen on CT.  
- CT chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a 5 cm mass at the root of the mesentery.  
- Postoperative imaging after liver debulking demonstrated multiple post-treatment hepatic lesions and persistent mesenteric disease at the root of the mesentery.  
- Approximately 3 years after liver debulking, repeat MRI demonstrated recurrent hepatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Urinary 5-HIAA was positive at initial workup.  
- Chromogranin A was elevated at initial workup.  
- Serum serotonin was 1200 at the time of recurrent carcinoid symptoms and dyspnea.  
- Postoperative serotonin level decreased after liver debulking.  
- Approximately 3 years later, serotonin increased to 800 with recurrent symptoms.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Long-acting octreotide (Sandostatin monthly) was initiated after diagnosis; flushing and diarrhea improved, but mild persistent postprandial cramping remained.  
- Surveillance CT imaging was performed every 6 to 12 months while on octreotide.  
- Emergent bowel resection was performed for compromised/obstructed bowel approximately 18 months after starting octreotide. Postoperative course was complicated by wound dehiscence and wound infection, with hospitalization for 3 weeks. Cramping resolved after surgery but later recurred.  
- Cardiology evaluated tricuspid valve disease and managed it medically without surgical intervention.  
- Operative liver debulking was subsequently performed, with extensive treatment of hepatic metastases; approximately 58 liver lesions were resected or ablated. Additional small bowel resection was performed for further neuroendocrine tumor primaries, and a mesenteric mass greater than 5 cm was resected from a location lower in the mesentery. Symptoms normalized postoperatively, and serotonin normalized.  
- Long-acting octreotide was withheld after liver debulking.  
- Approximately 3 years later, octreotide was restarted for recurrent symptoms.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with hepatic recurrence after prior liver debulking. Carcinoid syndrome recurred intermittently with elevations in serotonin despite prior symptom-directed and liver-directed therapies.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Later symptoms included worsening flushing, diarrhea, recurrent cramping, shortness of breath on exertion, fatigue, and vomiting.  
- Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated a dilated, malfunctioning tricuspid annulus with moderate tricuspid regurgitation.

reference_discussion.text: Welcome everyone to our Neuroendocrine Tumor Research Foundation Virtual Meeting Treatment Sequencing Tumor Board. My co-moderator here is Thor Halfdanason from the Mayo Clinic, who is a medical oncologist. And then our outstanding panelists are Heloisa Soraris, who is a medical oncologist at the University of Utah, Courtney Long Heath, who is a nuclear medicine physician at UCSF, Andy Lau, who is a medical oncologist at the University of Chicago, and then Oz Ahmed, who is an interventional radiologist at the University of Chicago as well. We're very excited to share these two cases with you. The way this is working is that I will present the first case, and then Thor will present the second case. So welcome everyone. All right, let's jump straight into this. This is case number one. It's a 65 year old female who presents to an outside physician with flushing diarrhea and cramping after eating. A CT scan was performed at this outside hospital and it's found first a non-contrast CT as seen here and then later on a CT with IV contrast, and there are two things that I found on this CT. But the first CT, non-contour CT, shows that there are some lymph nodes here around the mesenteric vessels, so the vessels that supply your small bowel and your large bowel with blood, some lymph nodes that appear to be enlarged here, and then there's this lesion in the liver on the right-hand side on the CT with contrast that is sort of suspicious and should not belong there, although the read was that it is unclear what this actually could be. So the outside hospital referred this patient to an oncologist who recommended a biopsy and it was found to be a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, low grade, the Ki67 was less than 3% and it was a stage 4 disease because the biopsy was of the liver and the tumor is expected to have started somewhere in the small intestine and has spread to the liver. Now, additional tests made by the outside medical oncologists were urinary 5-HIAA, which is a tumor marker that we check for in patients that have symptoms such as flushing and diarrhea, and it was positive, and the chromogranin A, which was quite high as well. So, this is the DOTATATE PET-CT that was ordered by the outside medical oncologists. Courtney, can you give us a quick read on this? Is there anything in particular that looks suspicious to you?

Absolutely. I'm happy to talk about this image. So this image is going from the, we see from the top of the liver down through the pelvis, basically the area that was being shown on that prior CT. And in kind of the right lower quadrant area where we saw that mesenteric lymph node that was being pointed to, exactly, thank you, we do see uptake in that lesion. And so that is very suggestive and very consistent with the biopsy proven well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor in the liver. In addition, if you look in the liver, which is that gray triangle in the right upper quadrant, there's not one just abnormal polka dot in there. Unfortunately, there are many more than the CT seemed to originally suggest. including the one, presumably the one that was biopsied. So it looks like there are multiple liver metastases in this patient, in addition to that mesenteric lymph node metastasis.
Thank you very much. So the patient was started by his outside oncologist on Octreotide. Eloisa, is that the first move you would do in those patients generally?

Yeah, well, I do think, first of all, the patient should be discussed on a multidisciplinary setting, just to make sure that we all agree what's the best strategy. But in this case, my personal take would be to consider a somatocene analog, the initial approach. We do have now many centers have actually a clinical trial that we could consider in comparing two different somatostein analogs that we could have offer to this patient as well outside of standard of care use of somatostein analogs either with octreotide or laryotide. And I am okay with that. I think there's a few other things that I would like to do, but you might be discussing that.

Yeah, let's jump on that a little bit later. So the patient was started on Sandostatin monthly, had some improvement in flushing and diarrhea. Although she did complain of some mild persistent cramping after eating, the outside medical oncologist kept an eye on the tumor burden with CT scans every 6 to 12 months. Now a year and a half passes and the patient now presents to again an outside emergency department with shortness of breath, fatigue, as well as vomiting. The CT scan is done again with IV contrast and this time this shows. Andy, if you get consulted down in a patient with, down from the ED to go down to the ED to look at a patient in a CT like this, is this something that worries you as a medical oncologist?
Yeah, I worry we've heard the mesenteric lymph node is causing some obstruction symptoms.

Yeah, I would agree. And actually the general surgery service was consulted as well at this outside hospital and the patient underwent an emergent operation for what was thought to be compromised bowel, which you can see here, the swollen sort of, you know, wheel shaped bowel here that's much thicker than the normal bowel here on the right hand side. And so bowel resection was performed at the outside hospital and the pathology showed a two centimeter well differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with one out of two positive lymph nodes. Thor, is this worrisome to you, that pathology report highlighting the one out of two positive lymph nodes? Is this something that you care about? Meaning, does it matter how many lymph nodes people remove?

Well, for metastatic disease at this point, probably not. If this was someone who did not have metastases, I'd be a little worried about only getting or retrieving two lymph nodes in the entire specimen. One wonders, did you sample enough lymph nodes? Was it adequate resection? This is coming from the medical oncologist, not the surgeon. But in this particular patient, it wouldn't worry me particularly. Okay, great.

Yeah, and then this is, I think that's the difference between when we have a planned resection versus something that was done in the emergency setting, right? This is a patient when we were talking about things that we should have considered is whether or not we should have discussed the resection of the tumor when the cramping was not going away. Was the cramping related to the local disease. And if so, that's when having a resection of the tumor in an elective setting will have the ideal situation. And perhaps at that time, there could potentially have been more lymph nodes resected, whether that's beneficial or not, it's hard to say in the set of metastatic disease. And also, they could have planned to potentially resect the gallbladder as well, which is something that you might touch later or not, I don't know. again, the planning of how we do things in anticipation of some of the problems that we might be seeing in the future.

I absolutely agree. And as the surgeon on the panel, I can't tell you that I feel like you're the surgeon on the panel. So this is great. So yes, I agree with you. And that surgery in an emergent setting is always more challenging. It's always more complicated. You obviously have higher chance of having an issue. Like in this patient, this patient actually had a complicated post-operative course, complicated by a wound, a dehiscence at a wound infection, ended up staying three weeks in a hospital, which we rarely see when we actually do this in an elective manner. So I do think that that's a really very important point that you bring out. And I do think that We should really pay attention to our patients if the cramping doesn't go away, is the source of the pain related to the mesenteric mass and is it resectable. So the cramping did actually disappear after surgery in this particular case, so the patient was quite happy. And then finally, she was presented in our multidisciplinary neuroendocrine tumor clinic after all of this was down at an outside hospital. So she came for a second opinion. And actually at the time when she presented, which was another six months after surgery, she was complaining again of worsening flushing and diarrhea, despite continuing on the long-acting obturatide. She also had persistent cramping that came back after surgery, a couple of months after surgery, and shortness of breath on exercising. So what now? Dr. Liao, Andy, what do you think?

Yeah, I think these symptoms are suggesting that carcinoid syndrome might be getting worse. So definitely we want to confirm biochemically, but the shortness of breath on exercise is a little bit worrisome. You know, one of the things that carcinoid syndrome can affect is the tricuspid valve. And so I definitely want to get an echocardiogram to see if that's affected and start from there. And then restaging the disease also to see if there's disease progression.

Perfect. So we started with a DOTATATE PET CT, which didn't really show any significant progression of the liver disease. The MRI with EOVIST, which is what we do at our institution quite a bit to determine the lesions in the liver, actually showed quite a bit of disease in the liver that, again, on the DOTATATE was not that significantly different, but on the MRI compared to the CT actually showed that there were more lesions there, which is, I think, commonly what we see. Thor, do you have any preference to follow these lesions or to follow tumors with MRI versus CT scan when it comes to liver metastasis and maybe Courtney can chime in as well.

Sure, I am actually really warming up to MRI with the EFS. So I think there are definitely patients where you can see everything you need to see with just carefully done CT with arterial and venous phase contrast. As long as you're consistent in your methods, I think that's probably what matters more than anything else. We're seeing patients quite frequently who have had the CT scan and an MRI with a different contrast and MRI with EOBist and comparing all those and then an uncontrast enhanced dilated PET or SSTR PET. So as long as you're consistent, you just have to find the imaging study that works for that patient.

Yeah, as an amateur, I would just add, I think I do agree that the apples to apples is more important than anything else. So whatever you do, do it the same every time. And ideally at the same institution as well, because every institution does things a little differently as well. Just because that makes it increases the likelihood that we're going to catch slow growth over time if we do it the same way every time. But I would come down a little bit more firmly on MRI with hepatobiliary contrast being far preferable to any other imaging modality. We are taught as people that treat neuroendocrine tumors, we're taught certain ways that these things look on imaging. Oh, they always arterially hyper enhance. And actually it's really some of them do. A lot of them don't. I would say in my experience, probably most of them don't necessarily demonstrate the characteristics that we read about on imaging. The most reproducible way to image these and to catch them regardless, you know, that's not dependent on catching the contrast at exactly the right moment is going to be this sort of 15 to 20 minute delayed phase on an MRI with hepatobiliary contrast. Now there are some patients just can't do MRI or some, you know, because they, they're claustrophobic or hate it or have a pacemaker or, you know, so it's, it's not ideal breaker to not be able to get an MRI. And again, consistency is more important, but in an ideal world, all my patients would get hepatobiliary phase MRI.

Thank you. Yeah. And I would point out here as well that, you know, here you could see also the difference on the T2 sequence between a cyst as well as a tumor. What's brighter here is a cyst and, and, you know, what's darker is a tumor, which sometimes it's not that clear cut on the CT scan as well. So Andy wanted a TTE or TEE, in this case we just did a TTE, which is essentially an ultrasound of the heart, and it did show that there was a malfunctioning dilated tricuspid annulus with moderate reflux, so not horribly bad, but that could certainly explain some of the shortness of breath. The serotonin, which is an equivalent of the urinary 5-HIA, just as a blood test, was quite high at 1200. and the CT chest and abdomen pelvis also showed a five centimeter mass at the root of the mesentery, which was not clearly seen before. So it's a little unclear whether this was progression or not. So we sent the patient to cardiology just to make sure that the tricuspid valve issue was not a major concern. And they actually decided to manage this patient medically without the need for surgical intervention from a cardiologic or cardiothoracic perspective. So, Eloisa, does this serotonin of 1200 worry you? Do you like to get it lower in somebody that has a heart valve problem that's most likely due to the serotonin?

Yeah, correct. The serotonin and the 5-HIA definitely concern me. I typically tend to monitor patients with the 5-HIA just because I feel it's a little bit more reliable in terms of the variations through the day or through what the patient's serotonin can alternate a little bit more. But regardless, this is high as several times above your normal. So bringing this down will be certainly important to prevent further damage of the triclosper valve. And then how you bring down, there are several strategies, right, that you can use and really depends on if you consider the overall disease's progression, there's progression, then I think one of the ways that one could argue to bring it down is with escalating to something like Lutetium-177. If you feel that this is potentially a stable disease, you can bring it down quickly with leave-in embolizations that are very nice in achieving good symptomatic responses on patients. That's another option. And there is some medications. that one can use, short-celled teletrastat, that we can use to control carcinoid induced diarrhea and also bring the serotonin 5-HAA down. So there's, thankfully, we have a few strategies that we can use. And I'm surprised that the initial approach was not to go for a surgical intervention for the heart. I would love to learn more about the thought process and how the patient got followed long-term with the cardiothoracic service and cardiology.

So we talked about the different treatment options. I think you just brought them up very nicely. Heloise asked, can you comment on IR-BLAN-EMBO for these types of patients? And do you feel like you can get a pretty good symptom control in those patients that are not maybe actively progressing, at least in the liver, but where the tumors seem to be more active at producing serotonin than they were before?

Yeah, absolutely. Thanks, Xavier. And I think Heloise touched upon one of the advantages of embolization that we sort of advocate for when we see patients is that the results tend to be sort of quick in terms of the response to the therapy. You know, as you mentioned, oftentimes with neuroendocrine, as in this case, the disease tends to be confined to the liver and the liver is one of the few organs that is very friendly to our bland embolization procedures because it does have two ways that it gets blood. the normal liver getting blood from the portal vein and usually the tumor getting primarily its blood flow from the artery. So that facilitates us to be able to go in with a catheter-based approach and place a catheter into the hepatic artery or the arteries that feed the liver and deliver very small microspheres, usually on the order of 100 microns, so very small. And we usually split the procedure up into two. So we'll treat the right side and then wait about a month and do the left side or vice versa. So we do like this approach because as I mentioned, we do tend to get good response, even if the tumor is not actively growing, but we're doing it for symptomatic relief. Thank you.

Okay, so I'm going to move a little bit quicker here. I am obviously the surgeon presenting the case, so the patient ended up going to the operating room for liver debulking. We did resect an additional piece of small bowel with additional neuroendocrine tumor primaries that were found within that segment. It's not uncommon for patients to have more than one primary tumor, and in a mesenteric mass that was greater than five centimeters, not at the root of the mesentery, but a little bit lower down, and we felt would be a problem down the line potentially and cause further obstructions. We also debulked the liver quite extensively, as you can see here, about 58 lesions were either ablated or resected. The post-op serotonin level dropped nicely, like we mostly see with liver debulking, and historically, before us came around with Bland-EMBO, liver debulking was one of the major things that could be done to improve the symptoms in these patients, also before we had long-acting octreotide. So, the patient then, because of normalization of the symptoms and the serotonin, was kept off. As I say, this is a post-operative scan here. You can see all of these dark lesions are all post-treatment areas, and then you can see this area here at the root of the mesentery. So, what now? Anything else you would do? I guess we don't have to debate too long on whether this patient should go back on Octreotide or not. I think most people would probably, I think at Mayo and in Heloisa, you would probably keep them on long-acting Octreotide. I think it's certainly a valid point. I think in this case we chose not to because the patient also had preferences not to go back on it for a while and so we gave that patient a break which again, we thought was reasonable with a serotonin that had normalized.

Yeah. Can I just clarify, because I said about Lutathera, but then when I was rethinking, so even though some of the lesions on the DOTATATE were positive, some were less, but were the lesions overall considered everything that was positive on imaging or there was a mismatch?

No, it's a good question. All of it was considered to be positive. So she would have been certainly, and you will see, she will get PRT. So about three years later, sorry, anything else you want to add?

I was going to say, I generally, if there's that much disease just in a single organ, I usually, there's kind of a sweet spot for PRT. And to me, it's when there's more disease outside of the liver. So I'm in agreement with the management.

Thank you. Three years later, the patient had return of symptoms, serotonin increased again to 800. You know, what now? This is a repeat MRI and you can see some disease recurrence, so probably maybe some persistence of some lesions that have grown again. Oz, would this be a good candidate for a liver directed after surgery? Can you actually use liver directed therapy after surgical debulking?

Yeah, absolutely. I think I've probably touched upon this in other talks. You know, the liver is a very resilient organ, as you've illustrated by that fantastic, you know, surgical resection that you did. And is really the two limitations that we have to doing gland embolization is how is the patient doing from a sort of what we call functional status? So if the patient is active, healthy, able to tolerate daily activities, that's somebody that we can treat as well as long as the underlying liver function itself. So we look at the lab values for the liver function, and if those are all within normal limits or acceptable, we can proceed. So even if you've, as you've sort of illustrated, done an extensive cervical operation, we can still offer this patient bland embolization with the same approach that I mentioned before, where we would probably split it up into half and half, so right and left or left and right.

So in this case, we restarted Octreotide, which I think we can all agree upon, see if the symptoms improved. And actually a year later, this patient did undergo bland embol. We also tried Zamelo. It didn't seem to particularly improve her symptoms. Thor, what's your take on Zermelo? Is there anything in particular you think it's worth starting on all your patients that are symptomatic despite being on Octreotide? How long do you usually try it for and what has been your success rate? Great question.

So the Cermelo or Telotristat is a drug that inhibits or reduces the production or synthesis of serotonin. So it's really mostly used for carcinoid syndrome diarrhea, but that's a diarrhea caused by serotonin production. But I will say probably the majority of patients with neuroendocrine tumors and with diarrhea have diarrhea because of something else we did to them, such as small bowel resection. Now they have what's called bile acid diarrhea. Kaltrestin is not going to work for that. But if you don't look for it, you're not going to find it. And you might treat patients with a drug that's never going to work. And so I work everyone up for bile acid diarrhea. It's very simple to do. And I also ask very carefully about symptoms of steatorrhea. So that's a diarrhea secondary to the octreotide and lanreotide injections. And you need a totally different approach for that. But once you've sort of zoomed in on those who truly have carcinoid syndrome diarrhea from serotonin productions, The telotrix that the reservoir actually works pretty well. And I think the studies that were done did not carefully exclude patients with other causes of diarrhea. So I do use it for that. But it's hard to say. It reduces the number of stools a little bit. But some people have a really dramatic, like, life-altering response to it.

Definitely worth trying for six to eight weeks before you give up. Yeah, that's a very good point. Don't give up after two weeks. You've got to try it at least for a month and a half or two months. I think it's a really important point you bring up. And your point is very well taken with the post-surgical diarrhea that's usually due to reabsorption problems or like pancreatic insufficiency due to lanreotide or sandostatin. So very nice. One year later, the patient, like I said, underwent blend embolization, improvement in the symptoms, pretty dramatic actually, nice serotonin drop. Now, two and a half years later, recurrence of symptoms, serotonin back up again to 850. Andy, we eventually treated this patient with four cycles of PRT. Do you think that that was, in hindsight, the right treatment at that point? I have to mention here some progression of extra hepatic disease seen on the DOTATATE at that time as well, which I didn't mention.

Yeah, I think so. I think in the setting of disease progression and also worsening carcinoid syndrome, it seems that we should be dialing up the systemic therapy. So PRT is one of the great options for this.
I think that concludes our first case.

reference_conclusion: Biochemical reassessment and restaging were recommended for worsening carcinoid syndrome symptoms, including echocardiography to evaluate possible carcinoid heart disease and imaging to assess disease progression. Given the elevated serotonin/5-HIAA and tricuspid valve involvement, reduction of serotonin burden was prioritized; management options discussed included telotristat for carcinoid-related diarrhea, liver-directed bland embolization for rapid symptomatic control in the setting of liver-dominant disease without clear progression, and escalation to lutetium-177 PRRT if overall disease progression were present. Following subsequent extrahepatic progression with worsening carcinoid syndrome, systemic therapy was escalated with four cycles of PRRT.

And then restaging the disease also to see if there's disease progression. [...] bringing this down will be certainly important to prevent further damage of the triclosper valve. And then how you bring down, there are several strategies, right, that you can use and really depends on if you consider the overall disease's progression, there's progression, then I think one of the ways that one could argue to bring it down is with escalating to something like Lutetium-177. If you feel that this is potentially a stable disease, you can bring it down quickly with leave-in embolizations that are very nice in achieving good symptomatic responses on patients. That's another option. And there is some medications. that one can use, short-celled teletrastat, that we can use to control carcinoid induced diarrhea and also bring the serotonin 5-HAA down. [...] Yeah, I think so. I think in the setting of disease progression and also worsening carcinoid syndrome, it seems that we should be dialing up the systemic therapy. So PRT is one of the great options for this.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Breast carcinoma, referred for oncologic management.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage III triple-negative breast carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Post-surgical pathological stage was ypT1bN2. Residual disease was present after neoadjuvant systemic therapy; pathological complete response was not achieved.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Hereditary germline mutation panel was positive for PALB2.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy with epirubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel-carboplatin, with pembrolizumab. She subsequently underwent surgery. After surgery, she completed 17 cycles of pembrolizumab. Adjuvant capecitabine was also administered.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative residual triple-negative breast cancer following neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, with pathological stage ypT1bN2 after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: Germline hereditary mutation testing was performed at the end of pembrolizumab treatment.

reference_discussion.text: Yes, the next case also straightforward case. Just next slide, please. So. So, she is a carcinoma breast stage 3. She triple negative subset. Not really, sir. I don't think we should be offering it in clinical practice, because we should tell them that, you know, even though There are a lot of trials looking at addressing this question, but none of them have come into mainstream clinical practice, and especially in the curative setting. And given that, you've already given capsidabine as well, sir, because of the residual disease. So you've already given IO plus capsidabine, and you've continued that in the adjuvant as well, sir. The continuation of adjuvant IO and then capsidabine as well as part of response-adapted therapy or risk-adapted therapy. So I think PARP inhibitors in the adjuvant setting, except for a germline BRCA1 and 2, still remains experimental, sir.
I think we should not justify even offer it. Okay. Thank you. Thanks, Kripa. Anybody else?
Sir, what about TACI2MAP going to centre? Actually, there are some ongoing trials with the TACI group in Residual, TNBC. Any thoughts on that, sir?

I think there are ongoing drives addressing even taxi plus Pembroke as well. SG plus Pembroke also even in the adjuvant setting but again I mean like none of them have gotten approved and you know the data we're still waiting on all of that data so the ascent data again.

sorry being a mutation similar to BRCA and we have a drug which can target that pathway and we cannot extrapolate but can we even discuss that with the patient sir like an off-label use see that's what probably this was in the metastatic setting and if you're running out of options yes you know then you talk about off-label therapy where you know it's all fine but in the curative setting Kripa I think in metastatic it is approved no now the
They have approved PAL-B2 in this particular setting, right? Metastatic?

Not approved, sir. As far as the expert consensus and recommendation, guidelines have suggested that, sir. For example, NCCN, if you look at it right now also, even though SACSI and Dataportum have not been approved yet, they already give it as a preferred option for TNBC in the metastatic setting, especially if your PDL1 negative. So I think that that's the difference. I mean, like you'll have guidelines endorsing it, expert consensus and all of that saying it, but as of right now, still not yet been approved per se. So I, which is why in the adjuvant setting, I think it's fine.
Fair enough. I think I do agree. Thank you.

reference_conclusion: Adjuvant olaparib is not recommended in this case. In the absence of supporting adjuvant data for germline PALB2-mutated disease, and given that OlympiA included only germline BRCA1/2 carriers, PARP inhibition in the curative adjuvant setting remains experimental and should not be offered in routine clinical practice. The patient has already received response-adapted adjuvant therapy with pembrolizumab continuation and capecitabine for residual disease.
