case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Left hydronephrosis and left ureteral soft tissue lesion identified on surveillance imaging 6 years after prior cystectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Post-cystectomy left ureteral urothelial carcinoma, clinically concerning for locally advanced upper tract disease (radiographically concerning for T3 disease), without evidence of metastatic disease at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Percutaneous biopsy of the left ureteral lesion showed poorly differentiated carcinoma compatible with a urothelial primary.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance imaging demonstrated left hydronephrosis and soft tissue within the left ureter. Imaging showed a long segment of the ureter involved by bulky tumor with appearance concerning for extraluminal extension/speciculation, raising concern for T3 disease. No evidence of metastatic disease was identified on staging imaging.

[ laboratory results ]: Glomerular filtration rate declined from 47 to 22 at presentation with obstruction, then improved after nephrostomy/relief of obstruction to approximately baseline at 45-49.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had previously undergone cystectomy without lymph node dissection and Studer pouch urinary diversion for BCG-refractory carcinoma in situ many years earlier. A nephrostomy tube was placed and percutaneous biopsy was performed. The patient then received 3 cycles of cisplatin, gemcitabine, and ifosfamide. Subsequently, the patient underwent open nephroureterectomy with cuff of the pouch and lymph node dissection.

[ other clinical data ]: Significant comorbidities included Parkinson's disease, dementia, and pacemaker in situ. The spouse served as the major caregiver. Post-treatment renal function remained impaired.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected thyroid nodule on annual physical examination in 2020. The patient had been asymptomatic, with no voice change and no dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration of an isthmic thyroid nodule (Bethesda VI).

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology was Bethesda category VI, consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. No surgical pathology was available, as no operation had been performed.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound in 2020 demonstrated a 1.4 × 0.9 × 1.2 cm solid isoechoic nodule in the thyroid isthmus with well-defined borders and no calcifications.  
- No additional nodules were identified in the right or left thyroid lobes.  
- No cervical lymphadenopathy was identified on ultrasound.  
- Serial ultrasound surveillance from 2020 through 2024 showed no significant interval growth of the isthmic tumor over 4 years.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroid function testing was unremarkable at presentation and remained stable from 2020 through 2024.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Isthmusectomy had been offered because the lesion was confined to the isthmus and there were no bilateral thyroid nodules.  
- The patient did not undergo surgery.  
- The lesion had been managed with surveillance, with stable thyroid function and no significant tumor growth over 4 years.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent biopsy-proven papillary thyroid carcinoma in the thyroid isthmus under nonoperative surveillance. As of 2024, the lesion had shown no significant growth on serial ultrasound. No cervical nodal disease had been identified on available ultrasound imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

reference_discussion.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you so much for being here. So we have a first case. This is a 54-year-old man who was found to have a thyroid nodule on an annual physical exam that was back in 2020. The neck ultrasound showed the presence of a 1.4 by 0.9 by 1.2 centimeter solid isoechoic nodule in the isthmus with well defined borders and didn't have any calcification. He did not have any other nodules on the right or the left lobe and did not have any cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient was completely asymptomatic. He didn't have any changes in his voice or any difficulty swallowing. His blood test, his thyroid function test was also completely unremarkable. So he had an FNA that revealed Betesda 6-PTC.

OK, hold right there for me. Go backwards one. Jeff, when you're doing this ultrasound, I check off a box that says ultrasound. But in the community, do I order ultrasound? Do I order lymph nodes? From a practical standpoint, what do you want to see from us when we ask that question?

Well, standard at Memorial, we do a full survey of the thyroid, central neck, and lateral neck for obvious reasons. Unfortunately, for many, many years in the community, that was just not being done. People would just simply get the dimensions of the lobes, report on some of the nodules, and that would be the end of it. That, of course, is not the standard of care, and I think the community is catching on more and more, although we still do plenty of foreign interpretations where we just get the, imaging and thyroid, and we have no idea what the nodal status is, and that's extremely important for every single reason. So, yes, we do that as standard, and it should be done.

Gotcha. Ashok, just initial thoughts. This is a 50-year-old. Even I can probably fill this nodule in the estimates at one and a half centimeters. Sort of, what are you thinking about this case at this point?

Well, you know, the evaluation is very appropriate. I think Jeff mentioned at Memorial, we always look for the central and lateral nodes. That's our practice. You know, you go to Florida, you'd order two separate ultrasounds. So it is a little different, but it's a practice of the institution because Jeff and his colleagues, they know we're interested in the lymph nodes more also in the primary tumor. Now, if you look at this primary tumor, it's well encapsulated. It's involving the isthmus only, not going on either side of the thyroid lobes, which is very important to appreciate. Now, the nodules in the isthmus, which are mobile, and you can practically pull it up from the trachea, I think those are very favorable nodules. We try to avoid them on active surveillance as best as possible. Could they be actively surveyed for a while? Yes. Eventually, he's 54, he's going to come to surgery. in next 45 years his tumor is going to grow probably go in the either side of the thyroid lobe. So I think this is what we think all the time. This surgery is pretty simple. We'll talk a little more when you come to surgical intervention. I just want to add one more thing. As a surgeon, this ultrasound is very nice. It gives you the whole idea, but the CAT scan is something that is quite helpful. The three-dimensional view of the whole thyroid nodule, extend into the surrounding areas, how close it is to the trachea, and is there a plane of cleavage between the thyroid and the trachea? I think that is very important. The one last thing I just want to add, The isthmus is a very small organ, three centimeter thickness. So anything more than that is going to come out of the thyroid. So don't be surprised to find there is extra thyroidal extension in these tumors. That's almost a given in all isthmic thyroid tumors.

Jeff, let me come back to you for a second because you do ultrasounds and you do radiology. Help me understand what the CT scan tells us that maybe we don't see as well in the ultrasound and vice versa.

But with respect to nodal status, as we've discussed many times in DMT, it is extremely helpful to get a CT scan, especially, you know, as a baseline preoperatively. We've had over the last 15 years or so adopted that more and more, and I'm happy to see it. The reason is ultrasound is operated dependent, and depending on, you know, how meticulous the sonographer is going to be, how meticulous the attending, and how often they go into the room, depending on how busy the day is, Things can be missed and even recently we had a case that was scanned where unfortunately an operation was done six months later, came back for the normal surveillance. And lo and behold, there's all this lateral disease. Obviously, the lateral disease was there preoperatively. We just failed to recognize it. And that's one of the failures of ultrasound. So, you know, we used to worry about the radiation dose. Oh, my God, you know, should we? Radiate all these people. It's not that big of a deal. Let's do it. And I find that it helps a lot with nodal status. And, of course, the things that are hidden, like, retrofringal adenopathy, we're never going to see on all the time. Regarding thyroid, you can capture extension with both modality and ultrasound. You know, again, it's operating dependent on ultrasound, how meticulous you want to be. And also, you can create extra tapestry extension just by moving your hand a little bit, and you can hide it that way, too. With CT, you see ill-defined borders. It's sort of a hazy look, and you can find that to be very helpful. So they're complementary, and they're not perfect, but I'm glad that we're getting more and more CT imaging for patients.

Superior on a related question, the biopsy is Bethesda rheumatoid number six. And I always thought that was like 100% thyroid cancer. And we saw a case a couple of weeks ago that it was Bethesda six read by our team. And when we took it out, it wasn't thyroid cancer. But does that happen? Or, you know, should I be worried about that? Trade my cytologist in? Help me with that.

So, Mike, you can hear me clearly, right? Gotcha. Yeah. So, I mean, when you look at the studies, the risk of malignancy for apoptosis sex is between 98 and 100 plus percent. So naturally, some of the cases are going to be very rarely 1% or so that the Bethesda-6 call is going to lead to either a neoplasm or commonly the oncocytic nodules, because the oncocytic cells, which we used to call heart cell cells, can have very atypical nuclei. And sometimes these patients also have chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, which we know can cause horrific reactive change in the nuclei because they are being bombarded by all these inflammatory cytokines. So yes, it does happen, but very rarely it does. And I have seen also cases in which, and I'm sure the search path was also read by the same pathology group, but sometimes there are very small capillary carcinomas that are sitting very close to the main focus that is being biopsied, and that may show a few cells. And depending upon one's threshold, one may call it Bethesda 5 or Bethesda 6.
Okay. So Lena, let's go to the next slide. Give us a little more information. We'll bring Dr. Alexandra and Dr. Newbold into the discussion here. Go ahead.

So, given the location of the nodule that was in the isthmus and he did not have any additional nodules bilaterally, we offer him the possibility of isthmusectomy, but the patient didn't go through any surgical procedure. And as you can see here on the table, his thyroid function has remained stable since 2020 when we started to see him. So the next ultrasound, you will see that since 2020 to 2024, basically the tumor has not grown in the last four years.

So Jeff, I know it's not fair to have you look at two isolated ultrasound pictures without your hand. What's your initial thought when you look at this, understanding different planes and all that stuff?

Yeah, I was surprised that it didn't grow just based on these static images. On the left, wasn't very impressive. I'd give it a TIRADS 3 at most, only based on the fact that it's solid and it's isochoic. I wouldn't give it anything else. The lobularity, and it looks bigger to me on that side, but the lobularity is worrisome. That's something I would push it more into category 4. And given the size, it's 1.4, 1.5, we would definitely, we would buy it. On ATA, same thing. you know, low and intermediate there. We don't have calcifications, but the lobularity is worrisome, and that always pushes my hand into a biopsy.

So Eric, this is a real case. You run into these. How do you deal with this? I mean, we told him years ago to do a surgery. He hasn't. The ultrasound report is saying really no change in size. How do you deal with this and follow with this?

I mean, I think you meet the patient where they're at, and every patient certainly deserves their own autonomy and whatnot. I think, you know, as we all have gone through clinical medicine, you try and find the ability to keep the conversation going, and you certainly don't want to lose the patient knowing that you're dealing here with a malignancy. And certainly you can acknowledge there's some data that we can follow some malignancies conservatively, non-operatively, and they do fine, but there certainly are others. That do not. And the only thing I would share, and maybe this comes up in conversation two or conversation three, is there is some intriguing new data that isthmic nodules are not only higher risk, but molecularly different. And I've never understood why that is, but it is some new data that has caught the attention of many of us. So I would follow him at least every four to six months or so and keep the conversation going.

This seems to be a discussion I'm having more and more because we can never get the pendulum in the middle, right? It was like everybody needs surgery. Now people come to me and say, well, we heard you two never do surgery. In England, are you having this same sort of situation?

Yes, absolutely. And actually, the lower the risk, the more complicated the discussions are becoming, I think, almost. Because obviously, if there is a higher risk, the decision is more black and white. And I absolutely agree. We're having more of these discussions. And it's quite difficult, because we haven't got that level one evidence to point in one way, one direction or the other. What we do have is the natural history, which allows us time. And so, you know, with a case like this, again, it does very much, as Eric says, come down to the discussion of the individual patient. You know, some patients can live with a little bit of uncertainty. Some patients find they can't, and often that opinion changes for them as well as they go through. And, you know, if they get very anxious before each ultrasound scan, then, you know, you kind of tend towards to move towards some definitive surgical treatment. And I think with this picture, as Jeff said, even though the size may not have changed greatly, the features of it, I mean, just on that one image starts to look a little bit more concerning, and we may have that discussion.

Yeah, and this is one in particular, the three-dimensional volume helps you. Sometimes you get fooled by you're saying they're only changing a millimeter or two, but when you do the volume, you go, holy cow. Dr. Shah, you and I follow a bunch of these. My question always is, if we keep watching, is it going to make your surgery harder or is it going to invade anything? So how do you convey that to the patient there?

Yeah, if you look at the, you know, I mean, the four years is a good time to say, hey, it's time to do something. He bought four years without surgery. But if you look at the current ultrasound, if I can use the word funky looking, I don't like it, you know. And that is a new classification, you know, Shahad's classification, funky or non-funky. I don't like it. The lobulation that bothers me, it is swinging on one side rather than staying dead in the midline. Maybe this is one picture. So I would definitely push him for surgery. I would tell him that, look, you are going to come to surgery sooner or later. You want to buy another six months? Fine with me. But the other thing is, I'm more concerned about the extrathoracial extension and going into one lobe of the thyroid. So the surgery, which would have been just the isthmusectomy, may end up with left thyroid lobectomy and isthmusectomy, because we may not be able to get a good margin beyond that. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old man; university student.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-year history of left-sided suboccipital headache radiating to the neck, slurred speech, difficulty chewing food, blurred vision, and dysphagia predominantly for solid foods; semi-solids and liquids were tolerated.

[ diagnosis ]: Left hypoglossal canal dumbbell-shaped lesion, radiologically favored to represent a hypoglossal schwannoma.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a left-sided expansile hypoglossal canal lesion with intracranial and extracranial components, producing a dumbbell appearance. The lesion was described as ill-defined and isointense on T1-weighted imaging, heterogeneously enhancing on post-contrast imaging, and extended across the hypoglossal canal into the upper cervical region. It abutted the cerebellar hemisphere posteriorly and the brainstem at a lower level, without T2 hyperintense signal change within the brainstem. The ipsilateral vertebral artery lay anterior to and abutted the lesion. The lesion also abutted the ipsilateral petrous segment of the internal carotid artery and extended toward the ipsilateral jugular foramen. Coronal imaging showed extension beyond the hypoglossal canal to the upper cervical spine, reaching the level of the C1 lateral mass. Reported MRI dimensions were 20.4 mm anteroposterior, 26.1 mm transverse, and 23.4 mm craniocaudal. CT skull base imaging showed erosion/expansion of the ipsilateral occipital condyle with preserved cortical component.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior surgical treatment, radiotherapy, or systemic therapy was documented. No prior imaging was available for interval comparison.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic skull base lesion with established left hypoglossal nerve palsy. On examination, the patient was in fair general condition, alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Visual acuity and fundoscopy were normal. Cranial nerve examination showed left hypoglossal nerve palsy; other cranial nerves were clinically intact. There was left tongue hemiatrophy with ipsilateral deviation and intermittent fasciculations. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Systemic examination was normal. There was no radiologic evidence of brainstem edema or signal change.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbid illness was reported. There was no history of trauma or prior irradiation. Hoarseness was reported symptomatically, although lower cranial nerves other than XII were clinically intact on examination. Clinical and radiologic progression could not be assessed because the patient had only recently presented and no prior reference imaging was available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria. Associated fatigue and weight loss over several months.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic renal malignancy with a large left renal primary tumor and metastatic disease involving bilateral adrenal glands and lung.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a centrally located left renal mass measuring approximately 10 cm in maximal diameter, radiographically malignant in appearance. Bilateral adrenal nodules were present, with the right adrenal lesion larger and highly suspicious for metastasis. A lung nodule was also identified and considered suspicious for metastatic disease. No additional sites of disease were identified on staging imaging. Brain imaging was normal. No bone metastases were identified. On subsequent imaging after systemic therapy, the pulmonary lesion(s) had resolved, the left adrenal lesion was no longer visible, and persistent lesions remained in the left kidney and right adrenal gland. The residual left renal mass was described radiographically as non-enhancing/rim-enhancing, necrotic-appearing, and suggestive of treated or nonviable tumor.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received systemic therapy with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab. Disease was reported as fairly stable over the subsequent next couple of years. During treatment, chronic kidney disease/decline in renal function developed gradually. At later reassessment, systemic therapy had been discontinued. Residual radiographic abnormalities persisted in the left kidney and right adrenal gland, while prior lung disease had resolved and the left adrenal lesion had resolved. The patient was subsequently managed with surveillance. At approximately 1 year after this decision, he remained under observation.

[ current disease status ]: Off systemic therapy. Residual radiographic lesions persisted in the left kidney and right adrenal gland. Prior pulmonary metastatic disease had resolved, and the left adrenal lesion had resolved. Disease had been stable on surveillance. Renal dysfunction/chronic kidney disease was present.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included diabetes. Physical examination at presentation was unremarkable. No acute cause for the renal dysfunction was identified; the decline was gradual during systemic therapy, and no other associated symptoms were reported at the time treatment was stopped.

reference_discussion.text: All right then, let's move on to our last case then. Another case of Brandon's actually. 62 year old man, this time presents with gross hematuria. Looks like has some diabetes, some fatigue, some weight loss over several months, and an unremarkable physical exam. And to work up for all this, gets some scans. So Brandon, if you wouldn't mind again, tell us what you saw on these scans and

Yeah, so I think these highlight pretty much, but his primary tumor is on the left side. I think it's something around 10 centimeters was the total tumor diameter and very central, you know, looks malignant. He also had a contralateral right-sided adrenal lesion that also looked highly suspicious along with a lung nodule. And then in the left side, I think actually had bilateral adrenal nodules with the right side being the bigger. So those were the sites of disease that we identified. Everything else was negative.

So, large renal mass and suspicious areas look like metastases, bilateral adrenals, and in the lungs, you've got the, you know, no brain is normal, no bone mets. So, it looks like we've characterized the sites of disease. So, you know, this seems like the type of patient that would be presented at a multidisciplinary discussion. So, Reina, we've, the sort of the role of surgery versus upfront systemic therapy has really kind of maybe shifted over the past few years with CARMINA and SIRTIME and other trials. For this type of patient, I mean, every patient's a little different, but for this patient, what do you think the best next step would be?

Generally for patients who present like this, I am leaning towards systemic therapy first. And then it's not to say everybody's going to get resected. That's not the case, but a consideration down the road. I think it's really important to guard against patient expectations around surgery. I think a lot of times, depending on, you know, how the patients are kind of, you know, being seen or being evaluated or who sees the patient at any given time, I think that, you know, you could really do somebody a disservice if they have it in their mind that they're going to at some point in time get resected and that's just going to be an expectation. So I think I level set and say this is a systemic disease. You have a system problem. You need a system treatment, which is immunotherapy based. And then depending on what happens, we can always reassess surgical options, though that is not the primary goal here. So I try to level set that discussion up front.

Yeah, I think that level setting, the importance cannot be overstated. I would definitely agree and I think in my center, this patient would likely get systemic therapy first. Before we delve into the details here though, are there any types of patients who present with metastatic disease that you do consider maybe surgery first and that could be because of either of cause of histology or maybe because of the location or amount of metastatic disease? Do any of those things factor into your calculus?

Yeah, no, very good question. I mean, I think that, yes, it does. I think there are some individuals who are young, healthy, maybe have very low volume, minimal lung metastases, and that's really the only thing that's designating them metastatic. They've got the bulk of their disease is in their kidney as opposed to outside their kidney. They don't have poor risk features. They don't have this inflammatory phenotype of anemia, thrombocytosis, their calcium is not dysregulated. So I think their only IMDC risk factor is that they basically presented with metastatic disease at their initial diagnosis, but their other as well. So I think in that context, it makes sense. I have had patients who have had very symptomatic hematuria at the time of their presentation and otherwise had low burden disease where it made sense to treat the renal primary with a surgical resection. I think sometimes in that context we're actually embolizing to deal with the hematuria and then get them on their systemic therapy.

Excellent. So, for palliative purposes and, you know, I think it was maybe one of the European guidelines at least a couple of years ago that was if the amount of metastatic disease wouldn't warrant immediate systemic therapy, so maybe that low-volume lung-only disease, and I've carried that as a helpful heuristic for me. Okay, great. So, So it looks like this patient did go on to receive systemic therapy. Linvon Pimbrough, back to Rainer for a second. We talked in the last scenario about sort of your preferred regimens for unresectable local. Would you agree with the treatment here or what are your thoughts for a patient who presents like this?

So I think actually in this scenario, I'm a little bit shifted. In the other scenario where you had somebody who had localized disease, who maybe was borderline resectable and you're really trying to get them to a point where they could undergo a curative intent therapy, I think the goals of care are a little bit different there, where I do want to get them maximally slight or reduced with a regimen that's associated with the highest response rate and lowest primary PD rate, which is the IO of edge FTKIs. But in the context of somebody who's overtly metastatic, like in this scenario, even though they're intermediate risk, We've demonstrated long-term disease durability with IOIO that we just have not seen with the other regimens. And so while 1 in 5 progress and the response rate is numerically lower compared to the IOVEGF regimens, 1 in 5 are going to have a long, durable response. and potentially even cure. So I think that that is an important thing to consider when you're treating somebody with metastatic disease. And also the other piece to it, from a quality of life standpoint, though there are immune-related AEs that are associated with the chronicity of long-term TKI treatment, can have a negative impact on quality of life as well. So I generally favor NEVO-IPPE to give that individual the greatest chance of a long, durable remission. And then if they do progress, favor VEGF-TK monotherapy strategy.

I do have a comment here. Please. I think Raina may be too shy to mention that she is leading a trial that this patient may be eligible for, the SAMURAI trial, which is exploring the application of debulking with stereotactic radiation in the setting of metastatic diseases where primary is intact and the patient is starting an IO-based regimen. And we are trying to take advantage of both the immunogenic properties of stereotactic radiation, which is not clinically established yet, but has a lot of preclinical data, but at the same time debulking with the radiation. So again, we will not know until the trial matures. Cytoshrink, a similar trial, actually completed enrollment, but I have not seen the data for that yet either.
So that's fascinating. So I'll ask you both. So is the intent here to treat both the primary and the metastatic sites with radiation or just the primary?

Just the primary, yep. It's a trial of combination IO therapy, any standard of care combination regimen for patients presenting with de novo metastatic disease with an intact primary. And they're randomized between radiation to the renal primary versus observation with their systemic therapy of choice as deemed as selected by their investigator.

And the thought is that the radiation, there might be some immunogenic releasing antigens and maybe the, you know, the abscopal effect. Is that, am I reading too much into that or is that the, one of the thoughts?

Well, I think it's actually multifactorial. I think it's one, cytoreduction with SBRT actually, as opposed to cytoreduction with surgery. And two, could there actually be a synergistic effect with the IO therapy? So I do think it's the combination of the two. Fantastic.

So in this case, the patient went on to systemic therapy and it looks like, Brandon, like things were fairly stable over the next little while, really over the next couple of years, other than the patient developed some CKD. And then I guess a little while later, a couple of years later, we have this. So walk us through what we have now.

So in essence, the patient was on treatment I hadn't seen him for a couple years, seen one of my colleagues, but it came back to me. I don't know if they met the qualifications that Dr. McKay said, you know, they've had more than a couple scans, nothing else has shown up, the lung stuff went away, and it's left with basically two tumors. So the left adrenal one is gone, but the right one is still there, and the left renal mass is still there. And so I think this sort of probably borrows a little bit from our past conversation, What do you do with these patients now? And I think one thing maybe Dr. McKay can speak on, because I think this is also new, is historically a lot of our kidney cancer trials really were cognizant that many patients were coming into the trial probably with poor renal function, right? They already had their kidney removed, because that's used to be, I think, the early trials, the Mozart trials, 90% of patients had one kidney, right? So everything was sort of designed. But I've noticed some of the newer trials are starting to have you know, renal function qualifications for getting on trials. And in fact, this patient, because their kidney function took a pretty big hit with just the systemic therapy, this is a patient where I would feel really bad if I went and took out that left kidney and it was all dead tumor, and now he's not eligible for some trials. So I don't know if you can comment, Rana, about how that field sort of changed a little bit in having some of the inclusion-exclusion criteria around the renal function of patients, because that seems sort of new to me. I don't know, maybe it's not.

I mean, I think in the metastatic setting, I think we are a little bit more generous with our inclusion-exclusion criteria, but I think that, especially around renal function, and that varies. You know, if it's a Phase I study, it's obviously more restricted. If it's a Phase III study, it's... broader, I would pause and ask, why did this patient have renal dysfunction while on treatment? And what is the cause of this person's renal dysfunction? Did they have ridiculous sarcopenia at baseline from the disease, and they've actually been able to stabilize and gain some weight and gain some muscle, and this renal function is more reflective of their normal state? Or did this patient develop an aphritis? Like, what's going on?

There's no smoking gun, I can tell you that. You know, everyone sort of chalked it up to just cumulative IO. It sort of happened slow enough that nobody really sounded it. It's not like he came in for one lab meeting. It was like, oh my God. But when I looked back, I was like, nobody really even noticed it. I don't know. That's just because it happens a little tick here, a little tick there, and you just look. So I don't know.

So it's just kind of one of these things. I think these things can happen. Does it correspond with a parallel increase in weight? I see that all the time. Patients, they do better, they gain weight because they've lost weight and then their cramping goes up and it's because they've actually gained a ton of weight. But, you know, sometimes these patients need to get in, see a nephrologist, and actually get a biopsy and make sure they don't have nephritis, which can be reversed with steroids, actually, if that's what's going on. So that's where I was getting at.
At this point, he was already off treatment, too. So there was nothing more, and he wasn't having any other symptoms. So that was sort of the rationale, I guess. Yeah.

I mean, I think we have to think about, like, what's the ultimate goal, right? Like, what is the goal? Do we think that this person is going to have, like, Is the goal of therapy cure? What is actually our goal? So in the context of somebody kind of having been cytoreduced to this point and you're really running up against it from a GFR standpoint, I don't know that I would subject an individual like this to resection. I mean, also looking at the location of that tumor, you know, I'm not a surgeon, but that central location makes me a little nervous about how much, even though the rest of the renal parenchyma actually looks pretty good, but it's just location looks concerning. But I tend to have a more conservative strategy, I guess is what I'm saying.

Systemic therapy stopped at this point, stable disease and two locations, this mass in the left kidney and this right adrenal. So multiple options on the table here, surgery to remove everything, more systemic treatment, monitor radiation. Let's just go back to Rakhee for a second. Based on what you've taught us, these look like decent locations to consider SBRT, would you say?

Yeah, I agree. They are feasible and treatable, safely and effectively. Again, if there's no viable disease, then perhaps I would wonder why. Maybe we watch and see whether there is any activity or growth, and if there is, then we take them out with radiation. But yes, radiation is an option.
Now, do you typically require or at least want a biopsy before treatment? Or I guess it depends.

Yeah, that depends. I mean, it goes back to the earlier discussion we had. I mean, nowadays with MRIs, you're getting so much information and you're almost confirming the diagnosis. For this patient, of course, before IOT care, perhaps had a biopsy to confirm the histology. So we would not need another biopsy.

Okay, so Brandon, what did you end up doing here? So this patient I watched, and he's a year out, and I think this is an area that both for the surgeons, you know, do you operate or not, but to recoup to point two, do you radiate or not in these scenarios, it's equally same problem. One is we probably need a little more data on the radiological side. Some groups are looking at this. How can you tell if there's viable tumor there or not, you know? And I also think it's probably going to be a space where we start biopsying more of these lesions, you know, just to try and prove it. For this one, radiographically, you can sort of tell, like, it looks like a dead tumor, right? There wasn't really enhancement. It's sort of rimmed, looks necrotic. And so I sort of learned The problem with this guy is he had both adrenals involved at the beginning, and I didn't want to take both his adrenals. If you're going to go, that means both his adrenals, kidney goes, cranium goes over too, which I talked with the patient. This is, again, where I'm having to get more, you know, historically, I never had to do this. But I sort of talked with his medical oncologist and said, hey, if he progresses, what trials are you looking at? And then we looked at the inclusion and exclusion of those trials. And one of them was specifically, it was to his GFR. And so when I told him that, he was like, no, that's, That trial was his baby. He's like, I don't want to lose that trial. He really loves that trial. And so we agreed there's risks and benefits. But I think, again, how to select which ones you watch, which ones you don't, I think is still a moving target.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Ascending colon mass identified on first screening colonoscopy.

[ diagnosis ]: Colon adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon; pathologic stage pT3N0 (stage II).

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopic biopsy demonstrated adenocarcinoma. Surgical resection pathology demonstrated poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Tumor was pT3 with invasion into the serosal area without extension beyond the serosa. Lymphovascular invasion was present. Perineural invasion was absent. Fourteen lymph nodes were examined and all were negative for metastatic involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Universal screening for Lynch syndrome/mismatch repair proteins demonstrated proficient mismatch repair (pMMR).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Surgical resection of the primary ascending colon tumor was performed. Resection pathology showed pT3N0 disease with negative lymph nodes (14/14).

[ current disease status ]: Resected stage II colon cancer following surgery; no nodal involvement identified on pathology.

[ other clinical data ]: This was the patient’s first screening colonoscopy; no prior colonoscopy had been performed.

reference_discussion.text: So welcome to the Multidisciplinary Molecular Tumor Board on colorectal cancer today. We will mostly be focusing on colon cancer only today, so the rectal part, I think, we just didn't have enough time to include that. So starting with introductions, everybody is aware of Dr. Shah, who is the president of the Vinay Thara Foundation. My name is Dr. Siddharth Yadav. I'm assistant professor at Mayo Clinic. I'll be moderating the session today. Joining us today as featured faculty or experts are Dr. Rona Yeager from Memorial Sloan Kettering, Dr. Hagen Koenigke from Virginia Mason, Dr. Axel Grothy from West Kansas Center, and Dr. Sakpit Chakraborty from Medical College of Wisconsin. So before we go into our cases, I just want to briefly talk about colon cancer in the U.S. We have approximately 150,000 new cases every year, thousand plus deaths every year, and it is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S. if you combine male and females. So definitely something that is very common and very relevant to our today's discussion. So let's start with our cases. So case number one, patient is a 61-year-old female who was found to have a mass in ascending colon after undergoing first screening colonoscopy, so she has never undergone colonoscopy in the past. Biopsy demonstrated colon adenocarcinoma, and she undergoes surgical resection, and final pathology demonstrates it's poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. The P stage is T3, so it's invading into the serosal area, but it's not outside of the serosal. There is lymphovascular invasion present, but no perineural invasion. And a total of 14 lymph nodes were removed, and they were all negative for involvement. The final path at this time is PT3N0, and universal screening for Lynch syndrome and mismatch repair proteins. So this was performed, and there was a self-expression of lymphoid proteins. So the question here is, he's referred to medical oncology for further discussion on adjuvant therapy. And the question is, does he require chemotherapy or not? And so, I'm not a colon cancer person, but my thought process to going through fellowship was, stage one, observe, no chemotherapy. Stage three, give chemotherapy to everybody. And stage two, you sort of risk stratify and decide whether somebody needs chemotherapy or not. So what are the factors that we typically think of when we are thinking of risk stratifying in stage II colon cancer? So of course there is clinical pathological features, which would include your T4 lesions, then lymphobascular invasion, which is what our patient has, perineural invasion, which our patient does not have, if there is any obstruction caused by the tumor or perforation caused by tumor, and then poorly differentiated tumors, which our patient has. inadequate lymph node sampling, then of course that's also considered as a high risk factor. So if there are two or more of these risk factors present, then we typically tend to think of them, the patient being a high risk and consider adjuvant chemotherapy. Whereas then there is the other side of this is the molecular alteration. So MSI, MMR status obviously is a big factor in deciding who needs chemotherapy or not. And then there is oncotype DX and then there are a bunch of other factors. We will go through all of these separately and look at some of the evidence in terms of the molecular alterations. But at this point, I just want to bring in the panel right now just to get your initial thought on would you offer chemotherapy to this patient or not? And we can start with Dr. Grothier. I'll let you lead first.

Can you put me on the spot? So, when you look at the clinical pathologic features that you've listed here, they're not equally ranked, you know. So, I mean, PT4 is clearly the most important one, lymph node sampling less than 12. These two are the most important ones. And I actually believe that perineural invasion is underrated. So, from these standard clinical factors, you know, they're not equal. And if you do multivariate analysis, something like obstruction perforation actually normally falls out. I mean, so these are not necessarily the same thing. Poor differentiation also is completely useless if you have an MSI high tumor, for instance. That's not a risk factor. So these are the, let's say, soft risk factors that are associated here. Lymphovascular invasion, poor differentiation here. It's not T4. It's not less than 12 lymph nodes. So, this is really a shared decision-making between patients and physicians. We're eight-factor in patient expectation, et cetera. And I'm not trying to kind of wiggle myself out of a recommendation here, but here I really have equipoise. I would really think, you know, both decision ways are right. And I would actually think this is exactly where we'd like to see data like ctDNA, other molecular factors, to help us make a decision.
Got you. Let's go to Dr. Yeager from Memorial. Dr. Yeager, do you have any thoughts on this?

I agree with Axel, and I agree with the schema that you showed. So in patients who are stage two colon cancer, the decision about chemotherapy is not so straightforward. And both you look at these risk factors and you also speak with patients to understand how much risk they're willing to tolerate and if they're willing to leave any potential benefit on the table. I think at this point, most of our decisions are based on the clinical pathologic features other than MSI. And I think some of the other features we're going to talk about are hope for the future to refine who we treat.
Dr. Koenigke, what are your thoughts?

Yeah, I didn't hear you. Yeah, look, I agree with the comments. I agree that the histologic criteria in colorectal cancer for risk are a little bit on the weaker side. I am concerned about this 61-year-old woman's colon cancer and her risk of relapse. I think it is more elevated because of the LVI. I think is relevant given that it is a PMMR tumor. So, she would have been a candidate for the stage two high-risk idea study. I would discuss with her the value of chemotherapy. I don't know, we're talking about type and duration, but something like three months of PBOX I think would be appropriate if you're kind of going in the more, you know, cutting-edge ctDNA, COBRA study. I think those are also important considerations, and I think you're going to talk about those in a little bit.
Dr. Chakrabarty, any different thoughts than what everybody else has already mentioned?

No. I think the recommendation is that I'd like to add that, you know, these type of patients at the fertile ground for investigating the value of ctDNA and need of stroke. Not that we can use it right away outside of the clinical trial, or maybe because CMS has decided to cover ctDNA for stage two and three patients. So I would like to ask the panel, what would be your stand on offering ctDNA for this patient outside of the clinical trial after full disclosure of pros and cons, the fact that CMS is going to cover this test.

So I think we are going to come to ctDNA in just a little bit, so I'll let you, we can come back and address that question in just a few slides. So let's go and, so it seems like at least our panel at this point seems to be, you know, kind of undecided in terms of whether this patient truly needs chemotherapy or not, and it's a shared decision making at this point. So let's look at some of the molecular alterations in stage 1 to 3 colon cancer and their prognostic versus predictive impact on clinical outcomes. I think the big one that we always think of is MSI or MMR status. And if you look at stage two disease, so on your left, so these are your stage two patients. If you look at disease-free survival, those with DNA mismatch repair defect, which is in your yellow, they tend to do quite well with surgery alone. And 5-FU, in fact, leads to worse prognosis. So that's one of the reasons why if somebody has a defective mismatch repair in stage two, a lot of us would not probably offer chemotherapy. And I think that's where, but this patient that we are talking about has a proficient mismatch repair. And if you look at, that's where your curve C comes in, is with 5FU and surgery, they are pretty much overlapping, meaning there is no difference in the disease for survival with chemotherapy. This is looking at, which I found interesting, was looking at stage three colon cancer and looking at your KRAS, BRAF, and MMR status, and then classifying patients into low risk, which are your T1 to T3, or N1s, and then your high risk, which are your T4 or N2s, and looking at the overall outcomes. What was interesting to me was the five-year recurrence-free survival by MMR status. If you look at everybody, low versus high risk, low risk obviously does better compared to high risk. But if you classify it by mismatch repair protein status, so deficient mismatch repair protein in low risk tends to do better compared to those with proficient mismatch repair proteins. However, if you look at high risk, the difference does not exist between deficient mismatch repair and proficient mismatch repair. And so I think the first question that comes up is obviously how do you use MSI-MMR status in stage 2 and in stage 3 bone cancer? And the question would also be in terms of looking at do you, even in stage 3, do you sort of classify patients based on low risk versus high risk and use the MSI-MMR status? So let me start with Dr. Chakraborty. I'll go to you this time first.

Well, I think there are several unresolved issues here, although the NCCN guideline says stage 2 MSI-high, no chemotherapy is a reasonable choice. But I just wonder, how about T4 MSI-high stage 2 patients? And secondly, I think the Jerome Gallon group has published some data showing that in MSI, high patient immuno score has a good discriminative use. But I think overall, I'm in favor of not offering chemotherapy unless maybe it is due for a tumor.

Dr. Kinneke, I'll go to you next. What are your thoughts? on is there a subset of patients, even within stage 3, who are, let's say, MSI-high, who do not need chemotherapy, and within stage 2, who are MSI-high, who need chemotherapy?

Okay, I wish I knew. Obviously, MSI status is incredibly relevant in the stage 2 setting. And I think it's hard to argue to give adjuvant chemo even if it's with KFOX or FullFOX to DMMR stage 2. So, I generally would not do that in the setting of stage 3. I think that's a very nice finding that it's not a great prognostic factor in the no positive setting. although there have been other studies showing that it does confer a reduction in risk of relapse regardless of stage. Overall, I think I would offer adjuvant Folfax or KFOX in the setting of stage three DMMR, colon cancer. There's, again, the duration of therapy discussion. And then, of course, we have the atomic study. I put a couple patients on that. And it's an important question to answer. We definitely have equipoise there.
Dr. Yeager, what are your thoughts on this?

I would agree. So, as it showed in stage 2 NMR-deficient disease, patients have really good outcomes overall. So, I generally don't give adjuvant chemotherapy. And as mentioned, for stage 3 disease, we give doublet treatment with a platinum, not 550 alone. And I, as well, have been able to get some patients on the atomic study, looking at full FOX versus full FOX, what the T-doll is in that.

So I'll go back to Dr. Grothier. Dr. Grothier, what are your thoughts? I mean, is there like T4, N0 with high MSI that you would offer chemotherapy? And then maybe there is a subset within stage 3 with high MSI that you would not offer chemotherapy.

Yeah, these are exactly the holes in our knowledge that you just pointed out, because, I mean, there are Twitter discussions about the MSI high T4 stage 2 patient. And, you know, the opinions go across the board. So, I believe, you know, that overall we know the relevance of MSSI is more kind of important and more clarified in Stage 2 than in Stage 3. But there are the overlapping, you know, prognostic groups between T4 and 0 and the T3 and 1A, you know, which is kind of actually overall a better prognosis than T4 and 0. So I, again, this goes down to an individual discussion. I think if I give T4 and 0M as a high-cancer adjuvant treatment, it would be three months of KPOPS and not more. We need not subplot in this approach here, because low permittance alone wouldn't work. So that's really talking about, you know, expectations, et cetera, side effects that we would inflict on patients. There's not one clear answer. And I don't think, you know, we'll never have a prospective study that will really answer these questions. We will get some data from a more, you know, say, detailed MSI analysis from the IDEA collaboration and the IDEA having Stage 2 and Stage 3 patients, at least in core studies. So, stay tuned. Hopefully, we'll be able to answer this question at some point.

So the other thing that comes up is, in this patient, would you offer oncotype DX colon to decide on adjuvant chemotherapy? So we do know that the oncotype DX colon score is available, and that based on your high versus low score, you can decide whether somebody needs chemotherapy or not. What was also interesting to me was looking at the breakdown by MMR status. And so I think what was interesting to me was if somebody is T4 and MMR proficient, even with the low score, their risk is high enough that I think maybe everybody would offer chemotherapy. And if somebody is T3 and MMR deficient, even with a high Oncotype Cohen score, their risk is low enough that maybe chemotherapy could be avoided. And this is where our patient falls in T3 and MMR proficiency. Let me go back to the panel, and this time I'll start with Dr. Yeager. Would you order Oncotype DX on this patient to decide on chemotherapy?

So I think you show here that the Oncotype DX score has diagnostic information, but it doesn't really guide us on who will respond to the treatment, so who will benefit from adjuvant treatment. So in our center, we don't use Oncotype DX when we make decisions on adjuvant therapy. It doesn't provide predictive data for us, to guide us to say this person should go through treatment beyond what we have that's prognostic from the clinical pathologic features.
Dr. Grothy, what are your thoughts?

So, I completely agree. I mean, when you look at the breakdown, even the prognostic information, when you look at the risk groups that are being separated out by Oncotype DX, compare this to the risk group and prognostic implication of ctDNA. They are world apart. So I personally have never used Oncotype DX in my clinical practice because I'm just not convinced that it really guides my treatment approach as much as people think it would. When you go back one slide on the screen here, you'll also see when you look at how many patients fall in which area, they are clustered in the middle. And this is really where most of the patients will end up. So, for the average patient, the really, yeah, exactly, and the curve overall for the T3 and zero, T3 patient, it's pretty flat, you know, and it's not as steep, and you'll show the ctDNA data later, as you see with more, let's say, advanced and more innovative and more modern prognostic indicators. So, again, I don't think, you know, and I know breast cancer is all gung-ho about Oncotype DX. That's gospel, but in colon cancer, oncotype DX is disappointed.
Dr. Kenneke or Dr. Chakraborty, any other thoughts on this one?

It's nice to see Oncotype DX being mentioned. I think we all used to use it a little bit more, but really, sometimes it helps guide the patient discussion. I used to treat a lot of breast cancer, and in that setting, the Oncotype score Of course, it's a completely different molecular assay. It's not only prognostic, but it's also predictive. It'll predict benefit from chemo. Of course, we know that that is not the case with the archetype for the DX4 colon, so a whole lot less useful for that. I don't rely on it as much anymore.

Perfect. Okay. We talked about the prognostic versus predictive role of Oncotype DX. So it seems that this is more prognostic rather than predictive. So CTDNA, and this is where I think a lot of excitement is happening. And this is just looking at some of the data on CTDNA. We know that it's prognostic. The 30-day CTDNA sort of impacts your overall rates of recurrence-free survival if you are ctDNA positive versus negative. We also know that if you're ctDNA positive and then turn negative, maybe you have a better outcome compared to those who continue to be positive. So let me bring in the panel again at this time, and let's talk about ctDNA a little bit. So I'll start with Dr. Chakraborty. So how often do you use ctDNA, and how often have you found it to be useful?

Well, I am impatiently waiting to use this tool, because I think recently CMS has decided to cover it, so we'll be able to connect to our patients. Looking at the data, especially the data published by Dean Tai from Australia, and then the Reiner Group, this tool looks incredibly powerful. So, at this time, you know, if there's a stage 2 patient, like the patient you just described, if this patient shows CTDNA positive in the postoperative period, I think, and again, I would like to know other panel members' opinions. I think it will be very difficult not to offer exigent chemotherapy to that person.
So, Dr. Koenig, what are your thoughts on this?

So, it's certainly the most controversial and the newest kid on the block here. I'm assuming we're still talking about the early-stage setting, and I'm assuming we're talking about a custom tumor-informed assay. And overall, I think those are the ones, certainly in the early-stage setting, if we're going to talk about that, that I think have the most in terms of sensitivity. And do I use them routinely in clinical practice to guide recommendations for adjuvant therapy? I confess I do not. I have ordered them. I think there are big questions out there regarding, you know, is it just one assay or does it have to be sustained? If you do it, how frequently do you have to repeat it? The general guidance, if you look at the label, recommendations would be every three months. So, you know, that's a long time in terms of accurate decision-making deferral. So, I am really looking forward to doing the trials. I don't routinely use it in clinical practice at this time.
Thank you. Dr. Yeager, you earlier mentioned that you would not use Oncotype DX. What about CTDNA? Would you consider ordering CTDNA in this patient?

So, as was mentioned before, at this point, we don't use this. part of our standard approach to patients who are early stage. I've used CTD and tracked patients who had a static, but in early stage disease, it's not yet part of really guiding our clinical decisions. I think the data is clear that if someone has positive CTDNA, they have high risk for recurrence, and we would think that there still is some tumor there, and the specificity is there, but the sensitivity is not. And how to act on it is not clear. And the best way would be to send clinical trials. And there are trials now in stage 3 disease trying to guide the use of their treatment in stage 2 to look at outcomes based on ctDNA. In my practice, we have a few patients used it as something to follow, but not something to make decisions based on. Patients who don't have markers that are easy to follow, don't have CEA before, sometimes in a patient who is very educated and asked for the test. I think I've done this test in that setting, but I don't use it as a tool to make decisions in early stages.
Thank you. So, Dr. Grothy, you had mentioned earlier about ctDNA. Would you consider ordering it, and how often do you do this in your practice using ctDNA?

Since January, every patient of stage 2 and 3 colon cancer has received ctDNA testing. And so we have about 56 patients right now that were, that actually, of course, they need to agree to that, et cetera. There are two patients who actually made treatment decisions on the assay because, I mean, let me backtrack. There are a couple of decisions you can think about, making decisions, criteria where you can make decisions on. Number one, if you have a low-risk stage 2 cancer where you normally do not give adjuvant chemotherapy, and you have a CT DNA positivity, the specificity for recurrence within the next three years is 99.8 percent. So, that's really almost a guarantee. That's the performance characteristics of the study, of the test. Even with one test, if you add two positive tests sequentially, it goes up to virtually 100 percent. The sensitivity actually also goes up if you do sequential testing. There are data that, you know, once you're positive, and you give adjuvant therapy, that's the Rhino data, you actually can salvage at least short-term patients. They do not necessarily go down to 100% recurrence rate. They plateau up at 40% to 50%. OK. So how often is that? How common do we see low-risk stage 2 patients with positive CT DNA tests? That's about 5% to 6%. So many patients exist. And these two patients that I had, actually I talked to them, and we made a decision to use adjuvant chemotherapy. You can even follow the CT DNA levels and see whether these markers disappear. The question that I have on stage three, of course, is can we use a negative test to withhold treatment or treat at a later time point when the test turns positive, because we know the lead time to radiographic detection is about 10 months. There's still a curable situation. That's actually something that's going to be investigated in an upcoming, which I think is very important, intergroup trial, the Cairns ID study. Now, the other question is, of course, what do you have a negative test and you don't see anything on scans? That's, of course, the situation we're facing. Now, first of all, a positive test would trigger a more, let's say, comprehensive workup, and that's another situation where I actually saw a patient who would normally not have done an MRI liver or PET-CT scan at this point in time and be found with sectable disease. So, I mean, again, individual information, this is not yet validated on a large scale. I encourage people to enroll patients into ongoing randomized trials and also observation cohort studies. It's neat to figure out what's going on. But this is the one marker, this one test that's going to change the way how we treat patients in the adjuvant setting, and not just in colon cancer. virtually across medicine.
Absolutely. So my question to Dr. Grote though, when you are ordering these tests, on what postoperative day did you order the first blood test? Is it the 21st, the 25th?

It has to be more than two weeks after surgery. I mean, that's really the critical issue, because between, you know, up to two weeks, normally, you know, realistically, patients don't come within two weeks after surgery. They come after three to four weeks. But that's when the kind of surgery-based or, you know, pre-surgery-based DNA should be washed out. You know, the point is, the high specificity of this test is really intriguing, with 99.8 percent. That's actually tweaked just recently after one false positive test that wasn't by my patient, because there was admittedly one false positive test, you know, because really it happened to be actually two false positive tests in the United States and one was my patient, so they tweaked the performance of the test, and the sensitivity went from 99.6 percent to 99.8 percent, because, you know, that's really where we want to be.
Axel, can you comment on the assay? I'm assuming you're talking about the Tera. I'm talking about Tera, yeah.

Can you comment on the reimbursement experience that you've had? So first of all, I mean, so it's reimbursed now by Medicare. And the company actually says, you know, for cold cancer patients right now, if there's no coverage, they will perform the test for free. That's all I can tell you. We've never had reimbursement issues with it.
OK, thanks.

All right, so moving forward, so. Interrupt, Sid. Sure. So from attendees, if you have any questions, please type it in the chat box and the panelists will take your questions. If you have a question to a specific panelist, name that faculty. Otherwise, we can have the faculty just look at the chat and respond to you.

Perfect, thank you. Thank you, Dr. Shah. So moving on to looking at KRAS, BRAF, NRAS, and PIK3CA in the adjuvant setting. So if you look at KRAS versus BRAF, I mean, they are almost mutually exclusive. NRAS, you know, so KRAS constitutes the majority of molecular abnormalities in colon cancer, followed by PIK3CA, BRAF, and then NRAS. The question here really is, if you look at stage 2 and 3 colorectal cancer and then you look at BRAF mutation, you do see that cases with BRAF mutations tend to do worse compared to cases without BRAF or wild-type BRAF mutation. Now, this is more of a prognostic marker rather than a predictive marker. Question always is, how do you use BRAF along with your mismatch repair protein status? So even in MMR, those with mismatch repair protein proficient or deficient BRAF seems to further stratify these patients into higher risk or lower risk. So if you look at this curve over here, you can see that those with mismatch repair protein deficient and have a BRAF mutation have almost similar outcomes compared to those who are BRAF wild type and mismatch repair protein proficient. So that sort of always makes me wonder, should we also be in addition to MSI, MMR, should we also be looking at BRAF to look at prognosis and how would we use that information? So again, I'd like to bring back the panel and just talk briefly about, is there any role of checking for, checking KRAS, BRAF, NRAS in the adjuvant setting at all? So, I will start with Dr. Kenneke.

Yeah. These have always been an interesting and tempting question, looking at these biomarks that are so important in the advanced setting, in the earlier stage setting. I have seen the ROS data about the prognostic impact in the early stage setting. I think it is notable that the endpoints there are in the overall survival, which may relate to more distant events after the relapse event. I mean, overall, I have – I'm not familiar with good evidence of using these markers in the Stage 2, 3 setting, particularly not for decision-making. We don't – BRAF, you know, is associated with DMMR status, but that is really – doesn't drive the DMMR behavior that we know of. So, overall, I don't use the KRAS or BRAF in this stage 2, 3 setting in decision-making or even testing?

Dr. Grothiel? So, Hadam, what if you had a single trial available that you could accrue to for BRAF inhibition in this early-stage disease? I mean, we do it reflexively, you know, if you have an MMR-deficient tumor. Then you definitely get BRAF, you know, to see whether your lymph or somatic But I can – I hope, you know, that at some point with the emergence of more treatment options for patients in the adjuvant setting, you know, we will be able to – we would actually be encouraged to test for BRAF. Right now, as you say, it's not, let's say, one of the things that are on top of my mind at this point in time, but if I saw a clinical trial available with a BRAF-targeted approach, I would definitely think, you know, we need to test for BRAF. What do you think, Dr. Lamont?

Yeah. Of course, I agree. Hopefully, we'll have clinical trials. I think in terms of the graph you showed of the BRAF and MSI, if you look at the stage 3 deficient MMR or proficient MMR, the clinical features vary by BRAF status. There's more T4 and 2 in the BRAF mutated. There are traditional factors that will also segregate by BRAF status. So we don't use it right now in our clinical decision making. We can imagine kind of building off what Ashley said on the CFDNA, that we will come to a point where we'll have the BRAF therapy may be KRAF allele-specific treatment. And we'll use CFDNA to see who needs it. And we can hopefully one day have treatment that's going to be much more selective. against whatever the tumor is. And I think BRAF is a little bit ahead right now since we have targeted therapy, so hopefully we'll have the trials looking at that starting the analysis of that approach.

Perfect, thank you. So I think to sort of summarize what we are seeing, back to this case, I think there isn't a straightforward answer, but I think More so, I think we are coming at this point where we are thinking of do clinical pathological features along with molecular alterations, how do we use all of this? And then I just wanted to show this subset analysis of the idea, the study published in Indian. Dr. Brute is here as well, so he could comment. I think what was interesting to me was that there was a lot of subset analysis performed by the clinical pathological features, but none by molecular alterations. One of the questions that I had was, you know, while we are already using the clinical pathological features in deciding who gets three months versus six months of KPOCS, what about putting molecular abnormalities into this and looking at that as well and deciding on duration of treatment and treatment escalation or treatment de-escalation? At this point, I just want to bring the panel again to just give your final thoughts on adjuvant treatment and what directions where you are seeing that this field is heading in terms of how we will use molecular alterations and clinical pathological features together in the future. So, I'll start with you, Dr. Grothy, since this was your study.

So, I mean, this paper focused really on the clinical pathologic features, also because, This study took more than a decade from first patient to really publication in the end. So, all these molecular markers we talked about were emerging at that point. So, we don't have full data set on all these molecular markers. We're going actually back right now and see what we can salvage here. So, there will be a presentation or a publication about the molecular markers within the idea to see whether longer duration dose intensity makes sense in certain subgroups. I think, you know, at some point we need to—and I think we all have that in our mind—we need to go beyond T and N. classification to really identify the risk for patients. We've talked about CTD, and I think everyone acknowledges this is really one of the most important, one of the most intriguing factors you'll see. So if you have a marker that is associated with a virtually 100 percent risk of recurrence that trumps that work, but it trumps the T and N classification, it actually should, I think, potentially be even integrated in the AJCC classification, you know, like molecular residual disease. And, you know, this is going to change the way we look at our pathologic staging, because we cannot ignore the presence of tumor DNA as a marker of residual disease. And, you know, in the adjuvant setting, we talk about, you know, we need predictive markers. Not necessarily. We make a lot of decisions based on prognostic markers. We treat T4 and T2 different than T1 and T3N1. So, we already look at prognostic markers to make treatment decisions, duration of therapy, intensity of therapy. So, if we have a very strong prognostic marker, but we still need to show that we can turn the medical history around and provide benefit and not have this inevitably be, let's say, moving into stage 4, classic stage 4, I think then we can just use prognostic markers to make treatment decisions, and PTB makes one of those.
Dr. Kenneke, any final thoughts on molecular abnormalities in adjuvant treatment?

Yeah, I think that I suspect we'll see more about the molecular subtypes emerging from the IDEA studies. I think that the established markers that we're using are here to stay, including DMMR nodal status and TNN status. But I agree that ctDNA does have the ability to kind of a lot of those. But then the question is, what do you do? And I think it is worth emphasizing that at this time, You know, ctDNA is just, quote-unquote, a prognostic marker. We don't know whether it identifies those patients that we'll predict from therapy as well.

One arm had FALCOX and the other arm had FALCOX plus adipocinab. So, when we did the retrospective analysis and tried to figure out what's the impact of a pre-radiation in stage 3, we found something intriguing. And we presented that in ASCO last year. So, if you take a low-risk stage 3 disease, the MSR was protective. And so having BRAF did not impact their outcome. But if it is state-free high-risk disease, then BMMR did not matter. BRAF-positive patients had a worse outcome, and BMMR treatment did not have any protective effect at all.

In BRAF, as you showed in the graph, the effect is driven by the very poor survival after recurrence. Even though there is an increased risk of recurrence, the outcomes are really driven by the poor survival when they recur. So as we have treatments that may have an effect, we may start thinking about these molecular markers earlier.

Thank you. All right, so moving on to the metastatic setting. And I know we are sort of running out of time, so we'll try to run through this fairly quickly. But I'll hand this over to Dr. Chakrabarti to sort of lead the discussion on the metastatic aspect of things.

If adjuvant therapy is elected, a 3-month course of CAPOX would be an appropriate regimen. Oncotype DX was not recommended to guide this decision, and ctDNA was regarded as investigational for treatment selection in early-stage disease and best used within a clinical trial or as a non-decision-guiding adjunct.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male farmer. Heavy smoker with approximately 50 pack-year smoking history.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive dyspnea over 2 months (reported as mMRC grade 1 progressing to grade 3), cough with scant sputum for 1 month, low-grade fever, anorexia, and weight loss for 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Lung adenocarcinoma with concurrent left pleural effusion/hemorrhagic pleural fluid and coexistent isoniazid-monoresistant pleural tuberculosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural biopsy obtained after stabilization and thoracoscopic evaluation was reported as malignancy consistent with adenocarcinoma of lung.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial chest radiograph showed homogeneous left hemithoracic opacity.  
- Ultrasound confirmed pleural effusion; subsequently described as large/massive left pleural effusion.  
- CT chest dated 07 October showed left hemothorax, collapsed left lung with pleural effusion, significant pneumomediastinum, marked paraseptal emphysema, chest tube in situ, and areas of ground-glass opacity on the left.  
- Repeat CT chest dated 17 October showed interval resolution of pneumomediastinum with persistent pleural effusion.  
- Abdomen was reported as normal apart from a renal cyst described as simple cyst.  
- Clinical respiratory examination had shown findings of left pleural effusion with collapse.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Pleural fluid CBNAAT/GeneXpert for tuberculosis was negative.  
- Line probe assay on pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with isoniazid resistance.  
- Resistance-associated genes reported included katG and inhA.  
- No second-line LPA result was available.  
- No mycobacterial culture result was available; MGIT culture was not performed/reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Oxygen saturation was 90% on room air at presentation.  
- Blood investigations were reported as normal.  
- Pleural fluid was hemorrhagic.  
- Pleural fluid total cell count was approximately 220 cells/mm3.  
- Pleural fluid differential was lymphocyte predominant.  
- Pleural fluid LDH was 874 U/L.  
- Pleural fluid ADA was 22 U/L.  
- Pleural fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells.  
- Sputum culture grew Acinetobacter.  
- Arterial/ventilatory assessment showed type 2 respiratory failure with pCO2 around 100 mmHg.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient was admitted because of hypoxemia and large pleural effusion.  
- Diagnostic pleural tap was performed.  
- Intercostal chest drain was inserted; large-volume hemorrhagic fluid was drained, with symptomatic relief.  
- The patient required BiPAP/NIV support during acute respiratory failure.  
- Following BiPAP, pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax were documented on CT, considered in the setting of ruptured emphysematous bullae.  
- The patient was managed for Acinetobacter respiratory infection.  
- After approximately 10 days, clinical status and ECOG performance status had improved sufficiently to permit further diagnostic procedures including pleural biopsy/thoracoscopy.

[ current disease status ]:  
- After stabilization, the patient was clinically improved compared with presentation.  
- Pneumomediastinum had resolved on repeat CT.  
- Pleural malignancy had been confirmed on biopsy, and concurrent pleural tuberculosis with isoniazid resistance had been identified microbiologically.  
- Persistent pleural effusion remained present on follow-up imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past history included cerebrovascular accident in 2017, managed medically.  
- On initial examination, vital signs were stable.  
- Mild pedal edema and clubbing were present.  
- Emphysema was present on CT imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 31-year-old male; non-smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Exertional breathlessness and cough. Initial presentation included cardiac tamponade due to massive pericardial effusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic TTF1-positive poorly differentiated carcinoma consistent with primary lung malignancy.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from a supraclavicular/neck lymph node showed poorly differentiated carcinoma, TTF1 positive. Prior bronchoscopic biopsy was inconclusive; it showed malignancy only, and immunohistochemistry could not be performed.

[ imaging findings ]: Upfront PET scan demonstrated a left perihilar lung mass encasing the bronchus, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, a supraclavicular neck node, two brain lesions in the frontal and temporoparietal regions, lytic bone lesions, multiple intramuscular deposits, and multiple skin nodules. PET scan after 3 cycles of chemotherapy showed partial response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor next-generation sequencing identified a BRCA2 mutation characterized as a well-characterized pathogenic loss-of-function variant. Germline hereditary panel performed on blood showed the same BRCA2 mutation. No other genetic variation was identified in the tested tumor tissue. HRD testing was negative. PD-L1 immunohistochemistry was 40%. MSI was not high. Tumor mutational burden was low. Tumor content in the tested specimen was approximately 10%. Variant allele frequency for BRCA2 was reported as 48%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 3 cycles of pemetrexed plus carboplatin. He became symptomatically better. Response assessment by PET after 3 cycles showed partial response.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic lung malignancy with documented partial radiologic response after 3 cycles of platinum-doublet chemotherapy; symptomatically improved.

[ other clinical data ]: Pericardial effusion was exudative. Family history included mother diagnosed with breast cancer approximately 6 months before the patient’s diagnosis; maternal uncle reportedly had cancer, details unavailable. The patient was recently married.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Blood per rectum/rectal bleeding.

[ diagnosis ]: Rectal well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid) with liver-only metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Pathology from the rectal mass demonstrated a well-differentiated rectal carcinoid tumor. Histology showed a classic neuroendocrine tumor pattern with uniform cells, small round nuclei, and coarse/fine (“salt and pepper”) chromatin. No mitotic figures were identified in the described specimen. The tumor was classified on histology as grade 1, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Colonoscopy revealed a rectal mass. CT imaging demonstrated a brightly enhancing round lesion in the rectal wall consistent with the primary rectal carcinoid. CT also showed multiple large liver lesions, with most of the liver replaced by metastatic masses. The hepatic masses splayed the portal vein, extended toward the left side of the abdomen, and compressed the stomach. No evidence of extrahepatic metastatic disease was described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent colostomy for control of rectal bleeding and removal of the rectal primary tumor.

[ current disease status ]: Primary rectal tumor had been resected. Persistent bulky metastatic disease remained confined to the liver.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had no other reported symptoms and was otherwise healthy.

So, it's amazing that something that's smaller than your pinky can be associated with so many different types of tumors that can arise from it. Now, all relatively rare, but whenever that happens, that's why we rely on someone like Terry to try to sort out the different possibilities.
