But fortunately, many times, as Terry alluded, these people don't need treatment. All they need is to have their appendix out. And in fact, it's entirely possible that the appendiceal tumor precipitated the appendicitis just by blocking the appendix and it gets inflamed and bursts. It could have been that somebody had appendicitis, because that's common. And at the time of removing the appendix, you find a very slow-growing tumor that was probably there for 10 years and might have been there for another 20 years before anyone ever found it. So, it can be an incidental diagnosis, as alluded to. Well, unfortunately, it's not always incidental. And sometimes, instead of finding this at the time of an appendicitis attack, you find that there's metastatic disease. So here's a 70-year-old woman who presents with some blood per rectum. So she has some rectal bleeding. She has no other symptoms and otherwise healthy, but that always gets your attention. She has a colonoscopy, which reveals a mass in the rectum. And the pathology demonstrates what's described as a well-differentiated rectal carcinoid tumor. The CT scan shows multiple liver lesions, no evidence of disease outside the liver. And because of the rectal bleeding, she undergoes surgery to get rid of the bleeding source. And she has what's known as an APR, which means you have a permanent colostomy, but you've removed the tumor in the rectum. And then the question is, what other treatment should be considered? So this is a, I'll let Terry go ahead. We have two Terrys. They know which one I mean.

So I think it's pretty apparent what we have here. The image on the left shows a cross-section through the pelvis, and I have the uterus as this brightly enhancing structure here, and then just behind it we have a cross-section through the rectum, and the arrow is pointing to a round, brightly enhancing structure in the rectal wall, which is a pretty typical appearance for a carcinoid tumor in the gastrointestinal tract. One of the hallmarks of carcinoid tumors in the gastrointestinal tract is that, although they're often very small, they're commonly brightly enhancing. And so if the clinician knows that we're looking for a carcinoid, it's important for the radiologist to know that, too, because it affects how we acquire the scans. But in this case, we're actually able to see the primary rectal carcinoid. But then, unfortunately, you can see here in the liver that almost the majority of the liver is replaced by these large masses that are splaying here the portal vein and also extend even over to the left side of the abdomen and compressing the stomach. And so this is quite a bit of the tumor is replaced by these large metastases so much so that you would not be able to take these metastases out surgically because there's just so little liver left.

Okay, so this setting is one in which the grade really makes a huge difference, because you can see there's tumors spread into, there's quite a bulky liver involvement. And if this is a grade three tumor, they would do something different. They would treat completely different than if it was a grade one or two. So this, in this scenario, grade matters a whole lot. And sometimes all we're getting in pathology are these very, very small biopsies, and it can, and they get crushed from the biopsy pinchers, and so Sometimes it can be difficult to try and determine whether it's a low-grade or a high-grade tumor. And what we do is we do those immunostains for the prolitis as a stand in that key 67 that I showed you earlier, because that sort of helps us identify which cells are actually dividing and not. But this particular example, we've got a very nice biopsy, and this is very classic pattern for this is the usual neuroendocrine tumor. The cells are all uniform in size and shape. The nuclei are small. They're round. They have sort of what's referred to as coarse and fine or some pathologists will talk about salt and pepper chromatin because you see bigger blobs in them and smaller blobs. And you can see — whoops, I guess that's all we have. So, and sometimes what you can see is at the periphery — let me see if I can do this. Yeah, right here. You get this sort of palisading around these nests. But this is a very typical pattern, and there are no mitotic figures in this particular example at all. So, even though this tumor seems to have spread into the liver, we would classify this particular example, at least on the histology, as a grade one or a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.

Okay. Thank you, Terry. So, let's pause there for a second, and now we have a person whose primary tumor has been removed because it was bleeding, and we wanted to take care of the bleeding problem, who has a well-differentiated tumor that is limited to the liver, but the liver spots are relatively large. This would be another situation where, Dr. Norton, I would ask you first, but I suspect that you're not thrilled about taking out that much liver.

Yeah, I think it's important to realize with neuroendocrine tumors of the GI tract that location is an important variable. Not only is histology important, but location. For example, appendiceal tumors like the one we presented, they're almost always cured by simple appendectomy, and they have a very good prognosis. Ileal carcinoid tumors have a poor prognosis, and they commonly have liver metastases. or at least lymph node metastases, but they have a better prognosis than rectal carcinoids. For some reason, rectal carcinoids, although they're rare, like the case presented here, they commonly present with distant metastatic disease, and they do poorly. So, I think that in this case, you're right. I mean, there's no surgery, and you have to wonder about the wisdom of doing an APR for a patient like this.

So before people panic in the audience about this being a typical case of rectal carcinoid, Pam, you've done a search through the SEER database looking at neuroendocrine tumors and their different sites and those sites that are increasing most rapidly and what we think the relevance to that might be when people find very small ones. Do you want to comment on that?

So in reference to this case, rectal carcinoids are one of the sites that at least in this large population database, which covers about 30% of the US, it's the largest cancer database, we looked at a number of different sites of the body and how common neuroendocrine tumors are at these sites and what the incidence is and what their rates are. And so rectal carcinoids do seem to have increasing incidence rates over about a 30 year period as do gastric carcinoids. We don't know why that is. Perhaps it's because we're doing more colonoscopies or we have better diagnostic imaging. So that's something it's a future research question that we hope to delve into.

For very many, now that we are doing a lot of colonoscopies or sigmoidoscopies, because we've learned to screen for colon cancer, which we didn't do so well 20, 30 years ago, we're finding these little nubbins of neuroendocrine, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors in the rectum. at such a frequency that is far higher than the frequency of any patient you'd see like this. So, we don't think that those have the same clinical course that this does, and that perhaps by removing them, we can even eventually decrease the risk that such patients would have this. John, you want to just comment on the liver-specific therapy?

I think, once again, chemoembolization and radioembolization are options. I always get mixed up when patients ask me if they can do a, because they read radiofrequency ablation, because it sounds really similar. Both have radio in it, but radiofrequency ablation is more for small tumors. In this case, these are large tumors, three centimeters and below. is what we do for the freezing and burning of tumors. And this, we would do a more wide approach with chemoembolization and radioembolization, and would complement what Dr. Koontz and Dr. Fisher do, because they're not mutually exclusive. What I have to offer and what oncology has to offer, they're complementary.

reference_conclusion: Following resection of the bleeding rectal primary, no further hepatic surgery is indicated because the liver is extensively replaced by metastatic disease and is not surgically resectable. The metastatic well-differentiated grade 1 neuroendocrine tumor confined to the liver should be managed with liver-directed therapy, with chemoembolization or radioembolization identified as appropriate options.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Left medial brow pain and headaches, with worsening visual acuity and worsening diplopia.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the frontal sinus/frontal bone with extension into the left orbit. Prior malignancy had been diagnosed in 1998; recurrence had been treated in 2006.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Clinic biopsy of the recurrent lesion demonstrated low- to intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Imaging demonstrated a very large tumor involving the frontal sinus and frontal bone with extension into the left orbit.  
- There was significant left orbital extension.  
- There was erosion of the floor of the left anterior cranial fossa.  
- CT demonstrated erosion of the floor of the frontal sinus, crista galli, left lateral lamella, posterior table, and anterior table.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent surgery in 1998 for the original malignancy.  
- Underwent repeat surgery in 2006 for recurrence, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy.  
- For the current recurrence, underwent left orbital exenteration and left transorbital craniofacial resection with facial incisions and limited lateral rhinotomy.  
- Reconstruction was performed with an anterolateral thigh (ALT) free flap.  
- Subsequently underwent adjuvant neutron radiation with a proton boost.

[ current disease status ]:  
- PET-CT demonstrated no regional or distant metastatic disease at the time of evaluation for the current recurrence.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Longstanding bilateral V2 numbness had been present from prior surgeries.  
- Examination demonstrated slight restriction in left eye movement.  
- Vision in the left eye had been reduced but remained present prior to exenteration.  
- Subjective diplopia was present.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: In September 2006, she presented with a 1-year history of spontaneous vaginal bleeding without other symptoms. In December 2008, she re-presented with vaginal nodules and bleeding. In November 2013, she presented with hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, FIGO stage IIB.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy showed moderately differentiated ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- November 2013 abdominal CT demonstrated a 6 cm para-aortic lesion, 4 cm iliac lymphadenopathy, and a 5 cm adrenal lesion.  
- October 2014 chest and abdominal CT showed no evidence of disease.  
- August 2015 chest and abdominal CT showed no evidence of disease.

[ laboratory results ]: Pap test after completion of cisplatin/paclitaxel in June 2009 was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- September 2006: Received pelvic-field radiation therapy for stage IIB cervical cancer, including brachytherapy. She was subsequently observed.  
- December 2008 to June 2009: Treated with cisplatin plus paclitaxel for 6 cycles for recurrence with vaginal nodules and bleeding. Post-treatment Pap control was negative. She was subsequently observed.  
- November 2013 to June 2014: Treated with carboplatin plus paclitaxel for 6 cycles after CT demonstrated para-aortic disease, iliac lymphadenopathy, and an adrenal lesion. Follow-up chest and abdominal CT in October 2014 were negative.

[ current disease status ]: No evidence of measurable disease at last documented follow-up. Last control in August 2015 showed negative chest and abdominal CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Menarche at age 12 years.  
- First pregnancy at age 17 years.  
- Reported three sexual partners.  
- No family history of cancer.  
- Initial gynecologic examination in September 2006 showed a 6 cm exophytic bleeding cervical mass with left parametrial involvement.  
- Initial radiation field was limited to the pelvis.

reference_conclusion: No active antineoplastic therapy is indicated in the absence of measurable disease. The patient should undergo observation with symptomatic follow-up and treatment initiated only if there is evidence of recurrence. If relapse occurs after a prolonged treatment-free interval, re-challenge with carboplatin and paclitaxel may be considered; bevacizumab may be added if available. For an isolated local or nodal recurrence, local therapy with surgical resection or radiation should be considered rather than immediate systemic therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old male; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, vertigo, and vomiting for 8 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Posterior fossa ependymoma centered in the fourth ventricle; histologically WHO grade 3.

[ histopathology results ]: Ependymoma, WHO grade 3.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain demonstrated a heterogeneous T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesion expanding the fourth ventricle, centered predominantly along the floor of the fourth ventricle, with mass effect on the brainstem and adjacent parenchyma. No definite abnormal signal was identified within the adjacent brain parenchyma. There was complete obstruction at the level of the fourth ventricle, with no significant ventriculomegaly on the available study, in the setting of prior endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Post-contrast T1 imaging showed heterogeneous moderate enhancement within the lesion. Enhancement extended inferiorly through the obex to the foramen magnum. No extension into the foramina of Luschka was seen bilaterally. No other intracranial enhancing lesion was identified.

Postoperative MRI brain demonstrated suboccipital craniotomy changes with a midline resection cavity and postoperative heterogeneous signal change. The previously seen expansile fourth ventricular lesion was no longer visualized. Persistent signal abnormality remained around the fourth ventricle, slightly greater on the right. Post-contrast imaging showed a tiny nodular enhancing focus along the right lateral wall/aspect of the fourth ventricle, suspicious for small residual tumor. No large residual lesion was identified.

MRI of the complete neuraxis/spine had not been performed at the time of documentation.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy had been performed prior to tumor resection; symptoms persisted thereafter. Suboccipital craniotomy with resection of the lesion was performed in December 2025. Postoperative imaging showed no large residual fourth ventricular mass, with suspicion for a very small residual nodular focus along the right lateral wall of the fourth ventricle.

[ current disease status ]: Status post suboccipital craniotomy and resection of fourth ventricular WHO grade 3 ependymoma. Postoperative MRI brain was suspicious for minimal residual enhancing nodular disease along the right lateral wall of the fourth ventricle. No complete neuraxis staging had been completed at that time.

[ other clinical data ]: Clinical examination was unremarkable. CSF cytology results were not available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 34-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Chronic cough.

[ diagnosis ]: Left upper lobe lung squamous cell carcinoma, initially staged cT4N0M0; postoperative pathologic stage pT4N0. Subsequent isolated endotracheal recurrence was identified approximately 1 year after initial treatment.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- CT-guided biopsy from the left lung lesion showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- EBUS-FNAC of mediastinal nodal stations sampled for N2/N3 disease was negative.  
- Resection specimen showed poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Pathologic stage was pT4 pN0.  
- All resection margins were clear (R0 resection).  
- All dissected lymph nodes were negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT chest showed a left lung lesion.  
- Initial PET-CT showed a multilobulated soft tissue density in the left upper lobe with transfissural extension.  
- PET-CT also showed involvement of the left fifth rib region.  
- Mild FDG-avid para-aortic and left hilar lymph nodes were described as suspicious for metastases.  
- No other FDG-avid disease was seen elsewhere in the surveyed body on initial PET-CT.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Initially presented with gastric outlet obstruction. Re-presented in December 2025 with abdominal pain and abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Gastric adenocarcinoma, status post radical subtotal gastrectomy, with subsequent progressive metastatic gastric cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Postoperative histopathology showed pT2N0, grade 1 adenocarcinoma of the stomach. Lymph node dissection was inadequate: 5 lymph nodes were resected, with 0 positive nodes.

[ imaging findings ]: Outside PET-CT performed in December 2025 showed progressive metastatic gastric malignancy. Clinical progression included an umbilical nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- MMR IHC showed isolated MLH1 loss.  
- HER2 IHC was negative.  
- PD-L1 was negative.  
- NGS showed no actionable mutations.  
- No BRAF mutation was detected on NGS.  
- Tissue NGS report noted poor sample quality.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent radical subtotal gastrectomy with modified Billroth II reconstruction on 31 December 2024 at an outside center.  
- Planned for adjuvant chemotherapy followed by adjuvant radiotherapy after referral.  
- Received 4 cycles of CAPOX, completed by March 2025, then defaulted further treatment.  
- After metastatic progression in December 2025, started palliative FOLFOX.  
- Tolerance after the first cycle of FOLFOX was poor.  
- Disease was clinically progressive on FOLFOX, with non-response of the umbilical nodule and severe pain; chemotherapy was stopped.  
- Received palliative radiotherapy to the umbilical nodule.  
- Subsequently declined further intravenous chemotherapy.  
- Was continued on single-agent oral capecitabine.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic gastric cancer after prior surgery, incomplete adjuvant systemic therapy, and poor tolerance/progression on first-line palliative FOLFOX. Symptomatic disease included abdominal pain, distension, severe pain, and an umbilical metastatic nodule. At last update, the patient was on oral capecitabine after palliative radiotherapy and was unwilling to receive further intravenous chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent symptomatic hypercalcemia following prior right-sided parathyroidectomy. Reported symptoms included mental fogginess, bone pain, and abdominal pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Persistent primary hyperparathyroidism after prior unsuccessful right-sided parathyroid exploration/parathyroidectomy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Outside surgery: two specimens labeled as right inferior parathyroid tissue were reported as lymph node tissue with non-necrotizing granulomas; no parathyroid tissue was identified in either specimen.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- DEXA scan demonstrated progressive osteoporosis; numerical values/Z-scores were not available.  
- Reoperative localization included 4D CT and ultrasound.  
- 4D CT demonstrated surgical clips in the right paratracheal/right inferior thyroid region and a hypodense lesion adjacent to the right thyroid pole beneath a surgical clip on non-contrast imaging, with arterial enhancement on arterial phase imaging.  
- No additional abnormal lesions were identified on the contralateral side, in the anterior mediastinum, retropharyngeal space, or high cervical ectopic locations.  
- Ultrasound demonstrated a corresponding lesion in the inferior right thyroid/intrathyroidal region, considered concordant with the 4D CT target.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- On presentation after prior surgery, calcium and parathyroid hormone levels remained consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism.  
- TSH was normal.  
- Vitamin D was normal.  
- Urine calcium was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent prior right-sided parathyroidectomy/exploration several years earlier.  
- Operative report from the outside surgery described dark necrotic-appearing lymph nodes in the central compartment, biopsied and sent for frozen section; pathology was interpreted as granulomatous disease consistent with possible sarcoidosis. Further parathyroid dissection was halted.  
- No intraoperative PTH data from the outside surgery were available.  
- Persistent hypercalcemia and symptoms continued after the outside operation.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Prior operative field appeared limited rather than extensively dissected.  
- No prior imaging studies from the outside workup were available for review.

reference_conclusion: Following confirmation of persistent primary hyperparathyroidism and concordant localization on 4D CT and ultrasound to a right-sided intrathyroidal/inferior thyroid region lesion, reoperative parathyroidectomy was performed with a targeted right-sided exploration. Intraoperative ultrasound was used for localization, and a small thyroidotomy allowed excision of the suspected lesion beneath prior surgical clips; frozen section confirmed hypercellular parathyroid tissue. Intraoperative parathyroid hormone levels decreased appropriately from 94 at excision to 21 and then 18, and bilateral exploration was not undertaken. Postoperatively, the calcium normalized, consistent with successful treatment.
reference_conclusion_quote: we chose to do 4DCT and ultrasound [...] there was a hypodense lesion basically right next to some surgical clips [...] there was arterial enhancement to that same area [...] this correlates very well to the ultrasound that was done [...] suggestive of a parathyroid abnormality [...] With this information, you know, with the localizing studies being suggestive of, um, you know, a parathyroid abnormality in the bloodwork being indicative of still having primary hyperparathyroidism. We went to the OR [...] we at our institution do all intraoperative ultrasounds before anything [...] with just a small thyroidatomy. there's a parathyroid adenoma kind of sitting right underneath surgical clips [...] sent it for frozen to confirm it actually was hypercellular at the time [...] So interoperative PTHs were confirmatory, you know, it started at 52 pre-op and then it was, the baseline was 94 at excision and then 21 down to 18. [...] bilateral exploration was not undertaken, but we felt this was pretty successful treatment [...] the calcium actually went to normal post-op.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female, born in 1976. HIV-positive and on antiretroviral therapy.

[ chief complaint ]: Left eye swelling of 4 months’ duration at initial presentation in 2016. Re-presented in November 2017 with recurrent left upper eyelid swelling of 1 month’s duration, increasing in size. At later review, the orbital mass was reported to still be increasing in size. An episode of difficulty in breathing was also documented and was managed with antibiotics and salbutamol.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Initial diagnosis in 2016: left orbital plasmacytoma.  
- Subsequent diagnosis after recurrence workup: plasmablastic lymphoma involving the left orbital/upper eyelid region.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2016 biopsy of orbital mass: plasmacytoma. Histology described anaplastic cells with perinuclear halo and mitotic activity.  
- Initial immunohistochemistry: CD20 negative, CD138 positive, kappa stronger than lambda; findings were concluded to be consistent with plasmacytoma.  
- Biopsy of recurrent left upper lid mass: poorly differentiated carcinoma on initial pathology review, with suggestion to consider a post-nasal space primary and recommendation for immunohistochemistry.  
- Subsequent immunohistochemistry on recurrent specimen: CD138 positive, CD3 negative, CD20 focally positive, kappa strongly positive, lambda negative, EMA negative, CD45 negative, S100 negative. Final conclusion: plasmablastic lymphoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT scan in 2016: retro-orbital tumor with intracranial extension.  
- CT head and neck reassessment in May 2017 after 10 cycles of therapy: significant interval change compared with prior CT; residual enhancing tissue remained in the left globe with associated palpebral thickening. Clinically, proptosis had resolved.  
- MRI head during recurrence workup: left orbital soft tissue mass measuring 6 x 48 mm, extending to the left ethmoidal, maxillary, and sphenoid regions, with an anterior orbital component; findings were in keeping with recurrent orbital plasmacytoma.  
- No other disease sites or lymphadenopathy were documented; disease was described as confined to the eye/orbital region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None documented.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum protein electrophoresis (2016): M-component 5 g/L.  
- Serum protein electrophoresis (May 2017): M-component 0 g/L.  
- Serum protein electrophoresis during recurrence workup: M-component remained 0 g/L.  
- Serum free light chains during recurrence workup: kappa 30 (above upper reference limit of 19), lambda 18 (within reference range; upper limit 26), kappa/lambda ratio 1.71 (slightly elevated).  
- Bone marrow aspirate: normal marrow with plasma cells 2%.  
- Trephine biopsy: normal.  
- CBC: within normal limits initially.  
- Renal function: within normal limits initially.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Thalidomide plus dexamethasone (Thalidex) was started in August 2016 for presumed orbital plasmacytoma and was given monthly.  
- After 10 cycles (May 2017), reassessment showed good response: marked radiologic interval improvement, residual enhancing tissue only, clinical resolution of proptosis, and SPEP M-component decreased from 5 g/L to 0 g/L.  
- Thalidex was continued because of residual tumor.  
- Despite ongoing treatment, recurrent left upper eyelid/orbital mass developed by November 2017.  
- Thalidex was continued during the recurrence workup, then stopped in February 2018 after the recurrent lesion was classified as plasmablastic lymphoma.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent/progressive left orbital/upper eyelid mass with biopsy-confirmed plasmablastic lymphoma. The patient was off antineoplastic treatment at the time of documentation and remained on antiretroviral therapy only.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Financial constraints delayed investigations and affected access to care.  
- Radiotherapy had been offered previously but was not undertaken because of cost.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old woman; otherwise relatively healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal discomfort at initial presentation. Subsequent symptomatic recurrences included abdominal discomfort/pain, chest discomfort, and later hip pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Epithelioid peritoneal mesothelioma with peritoneal and omental implants along the diaphragm. Disease later progressed with lung involvement.

[ histopathology results ]: Pathology review confirmed epithelioid peritoneal mesothelioma. Following neoadjuvant therapy and attempted cytoreductive surgery, microscopic examination demonstrated residual viable tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial ultrasound demonstrated a substantial mass spanning essentially the entirety of the upper abdomen. Post-platinum/pemetrexed imaging showed a radiologic response. After a period of observation following surgery, subsequent imaging showed early regrowth of disease within 1-2 scans. Imaging during/after immunotherapy eventually showed progression, including lung involvement. Rechallenge with chemotherapy produced a robust radiologic response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Somatic tumor profiling of >500 genes identified two tumor alterations, including BAP1 loss in the tumor. Germline testing of 100 genes identified no inherited pathogenic findings; no inherited BAP1 loss was detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Exploratory laparotomy was performed at initial presentation and demonstrated extensive peritoneal and omental implants along the diaphragm. Surgical oncology assessment considered the disease borderline resectable. Neoadjuvant platinum plus pemetrexed was administered for 4 cycles and was tolerated well, with radiologic response. Attempted cytoreductive surgery was subsequently performed; extensive fibrosis and adhesions were encountered, and residual viable tumor was present pathologically. A period of observation followed, but disease regrew shortly thereafter. Immunotherapy was then administered; treatment was poorly tolerated due to marked fatigue and poor quality of life, and imaging showed disease progression. Chemotherapy was reintroduced, producing a very robust radiologic response. Bevacizumab (Avastin) was continued thereafter, with maintained quality of life for approximately 1.5 years. Bevacizumab was discontinued after development of hip pain attributed to avascular compromise of the hip, and hip replacement was performed. This was followed by approximately 1 year of surveillance.

[ other clinical data ]: There was approximately a 1-year interval from symptom onset to initial ultrasound imaging. A cellular therapy/CAR-T trial had also been considered as a trial option.

We tested 100 genes in the inherited setting and she had none of those. So no BAP1 inherited loss. The BAP1 she had was only lost in the tumor. She saw my GI surgical colleagues and they felt that she was borderline resectable and we all kind of came to the decision, the patient as well, that giving her something preoperatively to see if we could control the disease and figure out the biology a bit better would make sense. So we ended up giving her four cycles of platinum and pemetrexid, which thankfully she tolerated pretty well. Repeat imaging, according to the scans, looked like she had a nice response. So we did do an attempted cytoreductive surgery. But unfortunately there was a large amount of fibrosis and adhesions. And as Gio had mentioned, in the operating room we were kind of convinced this was hopefully scar and treatment response. But we did find a lot of viable tumor. An important caveat of this is in mesothelioma, we don't have a good definition of pathologic response. So if you're thinking about like a solid tumor, a lung cancer, a breast cancer, it's a ball. You give medicine, you take out the whole ball, and you can see what percent of the ball is living and what percent of the ball is dead. So you have a numerator and a denominator, and you get a percent. But in mesos, when you go in, even if you take the entire lining off, people assume it comes off in a solid piece. It comes off in hundreds of little slivers. And so you don't actually have a denominator. And then the cells themselves actually can look fibrotic and things of that nature. Is it response? Or is that just the tumor that looks like that? So understanding what is or isn't viable tumor, what a path response is, is very understudied in this realm, despite lots and lots of ongoing efforts. So operatively, we thought it was scar. Under the microscope, there was residual disease. She still had relatively robust symptoms. We gave her a period of time of observation. She didn't have any specific side effect to put her finger on. She was just extremely fatigued and a poor quality of life. And then the imaging overall eventually showed progression of disease with lung involvement. Because she had some response to the chemo on pictures and no response to the immunotherapy, I put her back on chemo, and she had a very robust response radiologically. We kept her on the Avastin, and she had a beautiful quality of life for a year and a half, and then came in with hip pain, and we actually had caused the bone in her hip to not get enough blood flow based on the Avastin, so she had to get a hip replacement, and we stopped the Avastin. This led to a period of time of surveillance. And that's actually where I left it two years ago. So we got away with about a year of surveillance. And then unfortunately, she did develop symptomatic recurrence of her disease, abdominal discomfort and pain, chest discomfort. We discussed several options. And similarly, I'm not here to work for a pharmaceutical company, so I'm not going to say the names. But I put her on the same Tead inhibitor trial. And she actually had a complete response And she's still on it well over a year later. So we can't see the tumor anymore, and her pain is resolved. It's important to say the two cases we've discussed are the best case scenarios of that drug. It's still being investigated. It doesn't work for all. But for those it works for, it can be very important and transformative, and it's a very exciting field of research. But it's just that. It's still research. And the big takeaway I get from this is, for a long time, and still, peritoneal mesothelioma is the orphan diagnosis of an orphan disease. There are more trials for pleural than there are peritoneal. And so I think disease-specific trials or mesothelioma trials that allow patients with either type of mesothelioma that we can analyze separately are 100% paramount here. Because peritoneal disease, for the most part, we're relegated. Basically, whatever we did in plural, we'll try in peritoneal once it's approved. This drug and drugs like it, they're specifically looking at peritoneal versus pleural, different genetic factors, and that should be the next iteration of these trials. We should have respect that these are two different diseases, and they can have different outcomes. So the reason behind this case was we kind of exhausted the most attractive first-line options. We also had her ready for cellular therapeutic, a CAR-T trial. So, again, discussing trials at every point is always an important standard of care consideration. Like, when you look at the guidelines for the management of mesothelioma, they'll list a bunch of the drugs we have, and right next to it will say clinical trial is also an option. So, I think this is an illustrative case of that kind of possibility. I think I probably forgot to advance, but I kind of verbally said what I wanted to. So again, just to reiterate, this class of drug is exciting. It is not standard of care. And so I just wanted to be careful with that. There's a lot more investigations ongoing, but this is an exciting time for this type of oral option drug.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old woman. Karnofsky Performance Status was approximately 70–80.

[ chief complaint ]: Seizures at initial presentation in 2021; recurrent seizures in May 2024.

[ diagnosis ]: Right frontal astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial resection specimen (September 2022): astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial preoperative MRI (July 2022): non-enhancing right frontal lesion involving the superior/middle frontal gyrus; T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesion with reported T2-FLAIR mismatch pattern; no significant contrast enhancement.  
- Postoperative MRI (October 2023): postsurgical changes in the right frontal region with partial/complete resection cavity, residual surrounding T2/FLAIR hyperintensity/gliosis, mild ex vacuo dilatation of the right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle, and no other abnormal lesion identified.  
- MRI (May/June 2024): interval increase in T2/FLAIR signal and bulk adjacent to the resection cavity in the right frontal region, extending more medially than on prior imaging; no definite new enhancing disease was initially described, although patchy enhancement was also reported on post-contrast review of the June 2024 study. Findings were interpreted as disease progression.  
- Post-radiotherapy imaging (before October 2024 surgery): enhancing right frontal lesion with central necrotic/hemorrhagic component, surrounding vasogenic edema with extension toward the periventricular region, nodular enhancement, and adjacent leptomeningeal nodularity; differential included progression versus radiation necrosis.  
- Perfusion imaging performed before the second operation showed high perfusion, favoring tumor progression rather than radiation necrosis.  
- Postoperative MRI after repeat surgery (October 2024): gross total resection of the enhancing disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation was present. No additional molecular data were documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- September 2022: right frontal craniotomy with maximal safe resection at AKUH. Postoperative imaging showed no residual disease.  
- Surveillance followed; disease remained stable for approximately 1.5 years, including stable imaging in October 2023.  
- Following radiologic progression in May/June 2024, she received radiotherapy to 5400 cGy, completed in September 2024.  
- Chemotherapy was also administered with radiotherapy; six cycles of PCV were reported.  
- October 2024: repeat craniotomy with maximal safe resection for recurrent/progressive right frontal lesion. Postoperative MRI showed gross total resection of the enhancing component.  
- Intraoperatively during the second surgery, seizures occurred; postoperative weakness was present and subsequently improved.

[ current disease status ]: Status post repeat right frontal resection in October 2024 with postoperative MRI demonstrating gross total resection of the enhancing lesion.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Lesion was located near the motor cortex.  
- No residual disease was reported after the first surgery.  
- No laboratory results were provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient, age reported as 75–77 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Incidentally detected pancreatic tail lesion, diagnosed on biopsy as a well-differentiated low-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the pancreatic tail lesion showed a well-differentiated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging performed during evaluation for possible nephrolithiasis identified a small lesion in the tail of the pancreas measuring approximately 14 mm. Gallium scan was positive at the pancreatic lesion and showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

Medical oncology, what do you guys think? When we're talking about personalized medicine, personalized approach, and individualized approach, host factors play a big role. For a 75-year-old, it's really important to gauge not only their chronologic age, but necessarily their functional age. an individual who's really, from a functional standpoint, more of a 55-year-old, or from a functional standpoint, potentially a 85-year-old, because that has significant differences in terms of your risk of mortality on a yearly basis from other conditions besides just the underlying neuroendocrine tumor. Giovanna, as a patient, what do you think? Your doctor comes back and gives you these recommendations or these opinions. How would you digest this?
I was going to pass this one to Josh.

So honestly, I do get these calls actually asking what to do, not that I just try to give out. It really is up to who you are and where you are in your life. Well, great.

Yeah, so just as we all have different levels and thresholds for information, we also have a threshold for I don't care, get it out. And somebody who says, you know, I'm What do you call it? Not wait, but learn.
Watch and learn.
Watch and learn. And that's OK. Well, great.
Well, thank you for your help, the tumor board. This has been great. The tumor board needs to stay up.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable abdominal mass and abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffuse peritoneal epithelioid mesothelioma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial laparoscopic biopsies established epithelioid mesothelioma.  
- Tumor was described as high grade.  
- Following initial cytoreductive surgery, pathology showed excellent treatment response with many tumor areas appearing non-viable.  
- Following later repeat cytoreductive surgery after immunotherapy, resected specimens were reported by pathology as showing tumor without identifiable histologic features of treatment response.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT abdomen/pelvis showed diffuse nodular mass-like thickening of the peritoneum, most pronounced in the right upper quadrant, with small-volume ascites and omental thickening/caking.  
- After 3 cycles of cisplatin/pemetrexed, imaging showed good response.  
- At 18 months after the original operation, CT showed several areas concerning for recurrence, including a lesion posterior to the liver and additional nodularity/small-volume disease in the abdominal cavity; lower abdominal nodularity was limited to one pelvic region.  
- After 8 months of immunotherapy, imaging showed no change.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent diagnostic laparoscopy with disease mapping and biopsy in the local setting prior to referral.  
- Received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and pemetrexed for 3 cycles; imaging demonstrated good response.  
- Subsequently underwent cytoreductive surgery. Procedures included splenectomy, cholecystectomy, partial hepatectomy, partial colectomy, and peritonectomy of involved peritoneal surfaces. Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) was 29. Complete cytoreduction was achieved. Postoperative recovery was uneventful.  
- Received postoperative intraperitoneal chemotherapy via abdominal port with cisplatin and mitomycin C for 4 cycles; treatment was tolerated well.  
- At recurrence, underwent operative re-exploration for repeat cytoreduction; procedure was aborted because disease involved vital intra-abdominal structures and could not be safely completely resected.  
- Subsequently received immunotherapy for 8 months. Treatment course was complicated by thyroiditis resulting in loss of thyroid function requiring thyroid hormone replacement, and diabetes mellitus severe enough to cause ICU admission with diabetic ketoacidosis.  
- After immunotherapy, underwent another surgical exploration and repeat cytoreductive surgery. Intraoperatively, disease burden was markedly improved, all visible gross disease was removed, and surgery was considered complete from a gross cytoreductive standpoint.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Disease was described as diffuse at presentation.  
- Recurrence occurred 18 months after the initial cytoreductive surgery.

reference_discussion.text: The next patient that I'll be discussing is that of a 26-year-old man who presented with a palpable abdominal mass and abdominal distension. And the first CT, before we even saw the patient, the report talked about diffuse nodular mass-like thickening of the peritoneum. So most pronounced in the right upper quadrant with small volume ascites. So a lot of terms there. But what this means is that when we looked at that scan, we saw some areas of some pockets of fluid. And then the omentum, which is that layer of fat we all have draped over our intestines, was thickened. So that is that caking that Jason mentioned before. So at this point, and without having much more information, I'll ask, I guess we'll start from the other. Mike, what are you thinking right now? follow the same pattern here. So what would be your first thought at this point?
Do you have a confirmed diagnosis?

See, one person falls into the trap and now everybody knows. But again, when I was preparing these cases, I thought that the pattern was already established. So this patient does have epithelioid mesothelioma. And in fact, before even that referral, this happened in a local setting, had a laparoscopy for mapping out the disease and obtaining biopsies. And at that point, CARE was transitioned to a referral center. So what would be your first thought? And again, I don't have all the pictures here, but this probably does it justice from one slide. You have, again, diffuse disease. Jason, what are your thoughts on that? Where do we go to next?

So in these scenarios, there's always a desire to repeat the laparoscopy to see it with my own eyes, but if I have good photos from the outside and this is fairly diffuse disease, and I've talked to my pathologist, this is high grade, and I'm talking with my medical oncologist just as the other case we discussed that we're gonna go down the path of some upfront therapy reassessment. I think this patient at that age, Surgically fitness wise as a candidate and we just need to get them through the first phase that they're not going to have Explosive or progressive disease would be my steps

And then something you alluded to, like, even if I meet the patient first or the surgeon meets him first, the utmost importance of having kind of a multidisciplinary discussion, even if the a priori thought the surgery doesn't make sense. I always like to tell my patient I'm a car mechanic, he's a boat mechanic. We both look at engines, but we look at them differently. So like, I like the surgeon to meet them. We kind of come up with a plan together. But I agree, this would be some sort of systemic therapy. The other thing. If you have adequate tissue, it would be genetic testing inherited in tissue. And then something not yet mentioned, but just important specific to peritoneal, there's a rare population that may actually have an ALK positivity, which is a specific gene we talk about a lot in lung cancer. So it's something that should be looked at. And next generation sequencing, or at least targeted sequencing in this disease, is actually considered standard.

And all excellent points, which I think apply very well to this gentleman. So he did receive chemotherapy first with cisplatin and pemetrexid for three cycles. The imaging did show good response, so we did proceed to surgery later on, where in that case, hydroreductive surgery included a significant impact on the patient with having to remove the spleen, the gallbladder, part of the liver, and part of the colon, along with the lining of the peritoneal cavities in the affected areas. The PCI, which we just discussed, ranging from 0 to 39, or I guess technically 1 to 39 if you're diagnosed with the disease, in this case was 29, so fairly extensive. But the ultimate outcome was very satisfying in the operating room, right? So we were able to achieve a complete cytoreduction. And even more interesting is when all these areas were looked at by the pathologist, There was mention of excellent response to therapy with a lot of the parts of the tumor looking like they were no longer viable. So we completed the recovery from the surgery was uneventful. Our version or our, I guess, flavor of adding some chemotherapy to the peritoneal cavity directly after treatment is not necessarily in the operating room, but rather in the post-operative setting where patients have a small port in their abdominal cavity. And we use that port to administer additional chemotherapy, in this case, cisplatin and mitomycin C. for another four cycles, which went well. So at that point, what are everybody's thoughts? How often would they want to see a patient in this scenario? And what would be going through their minds in terms of risk of this coming back?

Um, you know, this is a high risk patient for really relapse for sure. And, you know, standard general oncology boilerplate is every three months for the first year, every three to four months for year two. And, you know, the first two years are the high hotspots. I tell people 75% of the recurrences, if you're going to recur, are going to happen likely in the first two years. And ideally, if I'm thinking about another intervention, you want to get them through the first year, it doesn't mean you can't offer patients with isolated recurrence as something, but you want to see some biological control, some period before that happens in these recurrent patients would be my thought. But I don't think the patient needs anything else after this other than surveillance.

I agree with that. I would also keep in mind with the surveillance, like if they're having a good response, the fact that they are young and of childbearing potential, the modality of the imaging, contrast, things like that as well. So you always want to take into account the patient in front of you in terms of picking the imaging modality.

So I think all of these are very important things to highlight and I thank everyone for making these points because it's not, the course doesn't end at the end of the treatment, right? We still have what comes after, which sometimes is both less well-defined but also can be more stressful and checking more often or less often can be a double-edged sword. Now this patient, unfortunately, despite everything going well enough at the time of the original operation, 18 months later, has another CT scan that shows several areas of concerning for recurrence. One was behind the liver in an area that you can see there with a green arrow, but also some nodularity or small spots of involvement in the abdominal cavity. So we've gone through these treatment options. We are here now. What are everybody's thoughts? And I should highlight just before I frame this a little bit better that the areas of nodularity in the lower abdomen were actually more limited to one part in the pelvis. So Mike.

I mean, I would obviously discuss it with you to see if there was a role to repeat intervention. The fact that this person had a quite nice response to the initial chemo and it lasted again, the caveat that there was surgery in between, but they had a meaningful benefit from that intervention. I would consider recycling the same type of chemotherapy or immunotherapy could also be considered, but again, an open discussion with the patient would have to be had.
Do you share the same thoughts or is there a limit to how much chemotherapy how much surgery how much immunotherapy.

So I would of course have a discussion with my surgeon and she might want to do a laparoscopy to take a look to see how much disease there was or she might not. We have that discussion together and the patient may or may not want that. But indeed I think that this patient is platinum sensitive. And you do kind of want to stretch out the surgeries if possible. And so it might be worthwhile to offer a platinum-based treatment. If, however, a clinical trial were available, that also could be an option.

It's an excellent point about keeping those clinical trials in mind all the time. As I said before, we don't really know what the right treatment is at any given point as well as we would like. And the only way to overcome that is by studying it in a proper way. Now, the patient, and I will say I'm not exactly sure what the conversation was on the treatments before surgery, but eventually was taken back to the operating room. for repeat site reduction. And at the time of the surgical exploration, the procedure had to be stopped because there was disease that could not be safely removed. There were vital structures in the abdominal cavity that were involved. that did not allow the surgeon to safely clear the disease. So stopping there now, and let's just say that both Jason and I have agreed that this is not something that we could take out at that time. What do you have to offer the two medical oncologists? Or Jason, it seems like you have a comment.

Yeah, I just wanted to say, as Hedy and I were just talking, you can try to do a laparoscopy, and we can. Sometimes we get lucky after a high-pick that's been formidable, and you can get in and get good views. But in these scenarios, when I know there's gonna be a lot of scar that they faced, I may reflexively just talk with my oncologist and say, you know what, let's test this biology first before I subject them to the, at least my thinking with these patients. I know that they required systemic therapy to get us there the first time, so why wouldn't that be true in a multi-site recurrence? Let's see what these things do. And then can we treat to maximal benefit before we go in? Because you know you're going to deal with scar and be back in some difficult planes. Back to the oncologist in terms of what they would do now post-op.

I think in general, like we had said, platinum if able, just because they had a very nice disease-free interval with the platinum. Immunotherapy is also not incorrect, but it would be a discussion with the patient which one makes sense.

Yeah, and this is, I think, an excellent illustration of how it's so difficult to define what the right treatment course is or how a lot of reasonable individuals can disagree. This is from our institution, but neither myself nor Mike were involved. And then the next thing that happened was a patient who got on immunotherapy. So not what we would have discussed on this panel before based on the excellent treatment. Had you asked me, I would have said the same thing that, hey, chemotherapy worked so well the first time. Why not give it another go. I'm not sure if the rationale was there were toxicities that came the first time around that made the patient really hesitant to go back on that.
Mike maybe I reviewed this case for the paper. It had just become recently available in that space so it was like a hot off the press drug combo and very much wanted it.

Yeah. So interesting thing happened next is first we always think about immunotherapy and this is I was hoping this presentation can help give a little bit of a counter to some of the common I wouldn't say myths but common misconceptions we have about one treatment versus another. We all think at least on our perspective and I suspect it happens across the board that immunotherapy stimulating the immune system probably less toxic than getting chemotherapy which is essentially poison, but well intended. However, this patient, as the course showed, they developed thyroiditis, which essentially knocked out their thyroid gland and needed to have thyroid hormone supplementation from there on, and also developed diabetes that was bad enough to lead them to an ICU admission and get ketoacidosis. So obviously, again, we're talking some outliers here. Same as we said before, that case was not representative of every case of disease involving both the chest and the abdomen. This is certainly not representative of every case of patients receiving immune therapy. But things can happen out of the ordinary. The scan after the treatment was or the intended eight months of treatment were completed showed no change. So at that point, and given the patient's young age, the overall thought process was to give it another try and see if at that point, even though the imaging response was not certainly very impressive, the fact that there was no progression in the meantime. And we also know that sometimes immune treatments can have responses at the microscopic level, but not always necessarily at the level of looking at a scan and changing what we look at, the decision was made to take this patient back to surgery. And something interesting happened there. The patient had another exploration, and things looked to be much, much better, dramatically better, in fact. All gross disease that could be seen, anything that could be visibly seen with the naked eye was removed. And from a clinical perspective, this was judged to be an excellent clinical response to immunotherapy. Now, I will say, and I just put an asterisk on this because that could be a whole talk for about an hour, when the pathologists looked at those slides from the specimens that we sent to them or that the surgeons sent to them at the time, they said that they couldn't see anything that reminded them of response to treatment. They looked like it was pure tumor the same way that they were expecting it. Now, what does that mean? The immune treatment effects are, we know that they're going to be different than a chemotherapy effect, but sometimes you can have a lot of discrepancies. So it's not uncommon for your physician to tell you that the tumor is responding, and then your pathologist to tell you the opposite, or the other way around. Sometimes we see on pathology that once something is taken out, it looks dramatically different from what it was before, even though the CT scan, as in this case, looks the same. So the surgery this time around again was felt to be complete and thankfully the patient two years later remains without any signs or symptoms of disease on continued surveillance. So the one thing that I wanted to kind of delve a little bit into in this context is when do we. Consider somebody for repeat surgery and this is something that I've been asked many times Is this I've heard this is a one-and-done surgery or I've heard that this is one cannot have it again The reality like most things in life is much more complicated than that. There are certain things we know are going to work and better and certain things we know are going to work worse. So for instance somebody having one small spot versus a lot of them or having smaller versus larger spots or those spots and perhaps to me that's probably the most important factor here is having enough time between one surgery and when you're considering the next surgery. And I will explain a little bit why that is. The biology, we talked about some cases today that have favorable biology, BAP1 germline or other different subtypes. Of course, it's important to know, do we think that we can achieve, again, a complete cytoreduction? If we think that we're going to surgery but we're not going to be able to do that, the trade-off is not always warranted. And then finally, the fitness of the patient and their ability to tolerate this. But putting all those things together, the way that I try to rationalize this is, if we know that surgery is going to give somebody a few weeks, sometimes a few months of a recovery period where their quality of life is not going to be as good as it was the day before their surgery. what is the expectation that what they will get out of it, whether it is through living longer or living better once the recovery has been completed, enough to justify this. And that's where, for instance, that disease-free interval is so important. Doing a surgery that you need three months to recover from or two months to recover from sometimes leads to you having a CT scan that looks no difference four and a half months later. Is this something that you feel is a good trade off and again to everybody in this room and everybody on this panel. The answer may be different but that's in my opinion the way to approach this rather than a yes no or strict criteria. And the outcomes after repeat site reduction are actually better than one would think just thinking about it. But it is very important to know they are as good as they are because not everybody who has their tumor come back after the first site reduction is offered a second one. So by definition. where we are, we as both patients and providers, selecting a treatment that we think is going to be reasonable and I think the outcomes show that we are fairly good at selecting a reasonable treatment because people who do have that second site reduction, who choose to have it, do fairly well. And the safety profile is not that different from that of the original surgery, which means, again, if we do the right thing at the right time for the right reasons and with the right patient, it should have a very similar outcome. Recurrence is still very common, unfortunately. Same as the first operation, sometime between one and two years is when we tend to see things come back. So again the one key message to highlight one more time is this repeat surgery is an option and it's appropriate in highly selected patients who have both a good or who have a good biology or a favorable biology good performance and disease that can be taken care of. But again highlighting the importance of having that done in a context of people who have the both individual and institutional experience for that. Do we have any comments from or should we move on.

Yeah, I guess I would just... Say, forgot what I was going to say actually. I'll let you go if you had anything to say. In these recurrent patients, this is a challenge. I think the idea that they can undergo multiple procedures more than once. Like I've had patients who come back a third time for an intervention. So I don't think limiting the number of times, it's more about the context, as you said, is where I wanted to go. And then the other thing that was rattling in my head as you were talking, about this, and it also goes back to some of the first cases I wanted to ask our oncologists. You know, with the increasing efficacy of immune therapy, so for instance, the standard patient that we're going to do neoadjuvant chemotherapy on, how do you choose or not choose to add immuno? Is it routine? Is it, is there a certain context? And similarly in the recurrent patient, the choice to just do immuno or to do combination, like what, what's your preferred way to manage these patients now with these tools that are domain?

So I mean, as we've all alluded to, this is somewhat of a limited data zone. But we have more experience comparatively in plural. All things being equal, outside of a clinical trial, chemotherapy is the one that's most studied in terms of outcomes. If a person had something that would make me think immunotherapy would be more beneficial, be it the swirl histology or things of that nature, or patient preference also obviously comes into play if a person has or some reason I would be nervous to give chemotherapy. For the most part, the conversation I would have is the most studied in standard of care is chemo perioperatively.

Yeah, we really have, you know, three or four different options. We have planal chemo, we have planal immuno, and we have chemo immuno. There's even less data on chemo immuno in the peritoneum, although there is a large randomized trial. But in general, when choosing between chemotherapy and immunotherapy, in addition to The patient-related factors, do they have kidney disease? Do they have autoimmune disease? It's also a predictability of toxicity and a length of treatment issue. Because chemotherapy, you know what day you're going to have nausea or constipation or fatigue, and that cycle is predictable. With immunotherapy, oftentimes you may have less toxicity, but the side effects are much more unpredictable, and you just don't know which organ system is your immune system is going to take a left turn on and suddenly you've developed inflammation of this organ or that. For some patients, they want something that's tried and true and predictable. For other patients, the issue with immunotherapy is that if your immune system is activated to target the tumor, sometimes it can work for years and years, whereas chemotherapy tends to work for a shorter period, though not always. So you really have to balance that. And there's better data for germline patients with platinum. And so those are patients who you might encourage chemotherapy with. So really, it's a balance of patient factors and patient preference.
Thank you very much.

So I just put this in there because of the IP therapy that was given in this case and I know Memorial has a trial where they're enrolling optimally cytoreduced patients to IV IP versus IV alone and several centers are participating in this in terms of the mechanisms in terms of whether or not it gives us better disease control or has an impact on survival. He covered all of these in terms of, sometimes this is called iterative surgery, and to the point that I made that patients who get second site reductions, they're often candidates if they have isolated recurrences or limited recurrences for a third or fourth round, and there's probably some people in the audience that have had that done on more than one occasion with their disease. So, we're going to move on to our other panelist, Dr. Offen, who's going to present an unresectable case and its management.

reference_conclusion: For diffuse high-grade epithelioid peritoneal mesothelioma in a surgically fit patient, the agreed initial approach was multidisciplinary management with upfront systemic therapy, including comprehensive molecular profiling with germline and tumor genetic testing and assessment for ALK positivity. Following favorable response to cisplatin plus pemetrexed, cytoreductive surgery was performed with complete cytoreduction, followed by postoperative intraperitoneal cisplatin and mitomycin C. Thereafter, no additional therapy was recommended beyond surveillance, with imaging-based follow-up approximately every 3 months during the first year and every 3 to 4 months during the second year, with imaging modality individualized to the patient. At recurrence, if repeat cytoreduction was not feasible, the preferred systemic option discussed was re-treatment with platinum-based chemotherapy given the prior meaningful platinum-sensitive interval; immunotherapy or clinical trial enrollment were also considered appropriate alternatives after discussion with the patient.

I think this patient at that age, Surgically fitness wise as a candidate and we just need to get them through the first phase that they're not going to have Explosive or progressive disease would be my steps [...] But I agree, this would be some sort of systemic therapy. The other thing. If you have adequate tissue, it would be genetic testing inherited in tissue. And then something not yet mentioned, but just important specific to peritoneal, there's a rare population that may actually have an ALK positivity [...] And next generation sequencing, or at least targeted sequencing in this disease, is actually considered standard. [...] So he did receive chemotherapy first with cisplatin and pemetrexid for three cycles. The imaging did show good response, so we did proceed to surgery later on [...] we were able to achieve a complete cytoreduction. [...] we use that port to administer additional chemotherapy, in this case, cisplatin and mitomycin C. for another four cycles, which went well. [...] But I don't think the patient needs anything else after this other than surveillance. [...] standard general oncology boilerplate is every three months for the first year, every three to four months for year two [...] So you always want to take into account the patient in front of you in terms of picking the imaging modality. [...] indeed I think that this patient is platinum sensitive. And you do kind of want to stretch out the surgeries if possible. And so it might be worthwhile to offer a platinum-based treatment. If, however, a clinical trial were available, that also could be an option. [...] I think in general, like we had said, platinum if able, just because they had a very nice disease-free interval with the platinum. Immunotherapy is also not incorrect, but it would be a discussion with the patient which one makes sense.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old woman at time of recurrence evaluation in 2015; 80 years old at most recent status update.

[ chief complaint ]: Follow-up for papillary thyroid carcinoma with concern for recurrent cervical nodal disease and metastatic pulmonary disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma status post prior total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection, with recurrent/persistent disease in the left central neck and biopsy-proven pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial surgical pathology after total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection showed multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma, including a 1.3 cm focus in the right thyroid lobe, with 3 of 4 lymph nodes positive for metastatic disease measuring up to 5 mm; no extranodal extension was identified at that time. Fine-needle aspiration of suspicious cervical lymph nodes in 2015 showed cellular smears of atypical follicular thyroid cells consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. Pathology from redo left central neck dissection showed tumor invading the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, positive surgical margin with tumor present at inked/cauterized specimen edges, multiple positive lymph nodes, and extranodal extension. CT-guided biopsy of a pulmonary nodule showed metastatic papillary carcinoma; immunohistochemistry was positive for TTF-1 and thyroglobulin.

[ imaging findings ]: Post-radioactive iodine therapy scan after initial treatment showed findings concerning for metastatic lymphadenopathy in the thyroid bed and in the left chest. Routine surveillance neck ultrasound in 2015 identified suspicious cervical lymph nodes, which were subsequently biopsied. Serial ultrasound surveillance of residual disease in the left neck showed a persistent small focus that enlarged over time to approximately “M&M”-sized by most recent follow-up. Chest CT later demonstrated numerous subcentimeter and pericentimeter noncalcified pulmonary nodules throughout both lungs, in a pattern considered compatible with small-volume pulmonary metastases from thyroid carcinoma.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroglobulin after initial radioactive iodine treatment was 1.1. Subsequent thyroglobulin values increased over time to 3.6, 18.3, 45.0, and 45.4. Thyroglobulin antibody was negative. TSH was monitored during thyroid hormone replacement; a specific value was not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment at an outside institution consisted of total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy. Despite post-therapy scan concern for residual/metastatic disease, thyroglobulin remained low initially. In 2015, recurrent cervical nodal disease was identified on surveillance ultrasound and confirmed by FNA. The patient underwent redo left central neck dissection. Intraoperatively, disease involved the left sternocleidomastoid muscle and left recurrent laryngeal nerve; a small amount of tumor was intentionally left on the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Following reoperation, the residual neck lesion was monitored with annual ultrasound, and there was no apparent progression for approximately 3 years. Rising thyroglobulin later prompted chest imaging, which identified bilateral pulmonary nodules. CT-guided lung biopsy confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]: At latest follow-up, the patient was 80 years old with small-volume residual disease in the left neck and biopsy-proven small-volume pulmonary metastatic disease. Thyroglobulin had risen over time. The patient remained clinically well and asymptomatic.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described as highly functional, robust, and active at age 75, with good adherence to follow-up. No pulmonary symptoms were reported.
