reference_discussion.text: There are some things that are obvious, you know, there are times when a tumor is clearly just coming outside of the surface and grabbing on to muscle or there's a, most often we would see that in ultrasound. There are other times, and Dr. Levitz and I had a few cases of this every year, where there's some little lymph nodes, little lymph nodes, but they're clearly not normal lymph. They're not big enough to show up on the ultrasound, but they've got a funny color about them or a pool of colloid fluid in them. And so sometimes a negative lymph node, a surprise finding of an abnormal lymph node during surgery will flip a case from a lobectomy into a total thyroidectomy plus a lymph node dissection. Sometimes that happens. I think we're just going to do two cases today because I think the discussion is really good. I'm just going to go slow. This person may or may not be in the audience today. A 75-year-old woman when I met her and presented for follow-up of papillary thyroid carcinoma believed to be metastatic to the lungs. She had her first operation somewhere else. This was a total thyroidectomy in the central neck dissection. and pathology showed multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma. That means multiple islands of thyroid cancer within the thyroid. But most of the action, the big one, as you can see, was on the left lung. And the biology of papillary thyroid cancer, most cancers are dominated by the largest focus, usually. it was a 1.3 centimeter focus from the right and three out of four positive lymph nodes measuring up to five millimeters and none of them at the time had extra nodal extension. Extra nodal extension means you got this lymph node and the fingers of the tumor, little roots of the tumor, are coming through the surface of the lymph node and that's an independent risk factor for a tumor coming back. She did have radioactive iodine and she had a post-therapy scan which showed high concern for metastatic lymphadenopathy in the thyroid bed. So some lymph nodes were still glowing and in the left chest. However, her fibroglobulin was pretty reassuring. So here we have some conflicting data. And Dr. Leung, how should we interpret that? There's a post-therapy scan showing some worrisome areas, but the fibroglobulin is pretty good. What do we make of this?

Yeah, this was maybe what Dr. Levitz had alluded to earlier that not all types of thyroid cancer are able to make, you know, thyroglobulin as our tumor marker robustly. And sometimes, especially when the thyroid cancer turns into a sort of what we call a less differentiated thyroid cancer, it tends to secrete very little thyroglobulin. So this is a little bit of a mismatch here. We recognize that. This is why we don't use one test in isolation. we do imaging along with blood tests for thyroglobulin together. And if there's a mismatch, then we kind of go and sort out the answer of what that might be.

Yeah, excellent point. Some tumors are more efficient at secreting thyroglobulin than others. All right, so this is when I met her, 2015, and then suspicious cervical lymph nodes were found doing a routine ultrasound surveillance exam. And a needle biopsy was performed of these abnormal looking lymph nodes, which showed cellular smears of atypical follicular thyroid cells. And it looks like papillary thyroid carcinoma and the nuclei are a little weird. And this FNA result is basically a home run for a thyroid cancer in a lymph node. And maybe I'll turn it to Dr. Livitz at this point, what would you do for this patient? And I just want you to know, she was 75 at this time, but really very active, totally healthy, robust, wonderful family life, and highly functional.

First, I think this highlights the importance of imaging, not just the tumor markers. As Dr. Leung mentioned, some tumors produce less or more thyroglobulin, so it's really the combination of the blood testing for the tumor markers and the imaging. The ultrasound in particular is really the best imaging modality to look for a recurrence or cancer coming back in the neck, typically in the lymph nodes or perhaps in the soft tissue. In this case, the thyroglobulin wasn't such a great marker to pick up the recurrence, but it's really the ultrasound. So we know there's a recurrence in the neck. But the next point I'll mention is again the benefit of the tumor board. This patient had their initial treatment somewhere else. So the tumor board presentation really gives us an opportunity to go and collect all that data that we may not have otherwise. going to go back and really look for the prior reports of pathology and find the radiology images and kind of go back in time so we get that full history and we present all of that during our tumor board so everybody is up to date on that. In terms of what to do next, I would first evaluate how much disease does the patient have is there still concern about disease outside of the neck? And we had, you know, this patient had spread to the lungs. So I'd probably want to know what is the extent of metastasis in the lungs? And then what is the extent of disease in the neck? But if the disease in the neck, I thought, was something that could hurt the patient, depending on the location, could there be invasion into a major blood vessel or perhaps the trachea, that is something that could really hurt the patient in the near future. And then I would consider a reoperation in the neck to remove the disease and the potential complications from a local invasion.

Yeah, excellent points. In this particular case, we were not really able to confirm a significant amount of disease in the chest at this time. And it seemed like the fibroglobulin was a little low. It didn't seem to quite fit. A fibroglobulin for a patient with a significant amount of lung disease, I would have expected a little bit more than a fibroglobulin of 1.1. Dr. Leung, what do you think about that? I mean, how do we interpret the thyroid globulin number? Can we convert that thyroid globulin number to an approximate volume of thyroid cancer present in someone's body?

Yeah, we can, but only under the caveat that if that tumor or the collection of tumor in aggregate in the body is efficient in making thyroid globulin, So we roughly translate, you know, the thyroglobulin units into how many grams of thyroid tissue are remaining in the body. And so, you know, as Dr. Ye had suggested, a thyroglobulin of 1.1 translates to like only one gram of thyroid tissue, which is like nothing. So this is where our radar pops up and says, you know, is something else going on and why isn't making it thyroglobulin.

Yeah. And a gram of tissue, I sometimes think of like an M&M, right? Because Halloween's coming up, we use candy analogies. All right. So we did perform a left neck dissection and something Dr. Libitz alluded to is if this patient had widespread disease outside of the neck, we probably wouldn't be operating in the neck because we have Some treatments that are focal, where we're doing surgery or we're blowing away one little area of tumor, and that's good if we think the disease is limited to one area. If we think the disease is systemic and spread throughout the body, it doesn't quite make sense to pursue a focal therapy in that case, unless the patient's having symptoms, like a metastasis in the hip that makes it painful to walk, we would perform a focal therapy for that, probably a radiation treatment in order to restore the patient's function. All right, so this patient did have focal treatment, redo left central neck dissection, and Dr. Levitz, I found this. I found tumor in, you know, invading the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, which is this diagonal muscle here, which was easy to remove, several left central neck lymph nodes, which were easy to remove, and then I found a little like a smaller than a kernel of corn area of tumor, which was involving a left recurrent laryngeal nerve. And I had to make a choice whether or not I wanted to sacrifice the voice nerve or leave it alone and leave a little tumor there. And I know you've been in that position. So what is your thought process when you see something like that?

So yeah, this is always a very difficult situation. Sacrificing the recurrent laryngeal nerve means that the patient could have some hoarseness after surgery. There are procedures that we can do that can improve the quality of voice, but it does have some real consequences. So I would think about the patient's entire situation. This is a patient who's 75, I think you said. in who this is their second operation. There was some concern about spread outside of the neck. So I don't know that we're talking about a curative situation. You know, if this was a young person and sacrificing the nerve to remove this tumor would achieve a complete cure, then I would be much, you know, really considerate in that case. I think that in this case, I would probably prefer to leave a tiny bit of tumor along the nerve to try to just protect the patient's quality of life because I don't think this is going to be a definitive cure. I think the patient's still at risk for some disease coming back or perhaps being in the lung still.

Yeah, great point. Great point. So yeah, that was my reasoning. I thought she's 75 at the time, and I thought she was unlikely to have this little area of tumor end up shortening her life or causing significant morbidity. And I did think there was some risk lurking in the back of my mind, the possibility of lung disease. So You'd hate to sacrifice a nerve, give somebody really a permanent disability, hoarseness. We can rehabilitate the voice, as you said, the things we can do, but it's never perfect. And I hate to do all that, cause a significant disability and still have tumor present in the chest. So yeah, I did leave a small amount of tumor on the nerve. I spoke to the family and the patient extensively about this. And we agreed that we would just monitor that area with ultrasound every year. And so this is what the full pathology report looked like. There was tumor invading the muscle. This was a positive margin, so tumors present at the inked and cauterized specimen edges. Cauterized means we use this little heater probe to cut through tissue sometimes. But when tumor invades into muscle, it's hard to get a negative margin. She had a lymph node that was positive. A couple other lymph nodes were positive. And here, you see the extranodal extension presence. So tumors starting to crawl out, getting these little fingers outside of the lymph nodes. All right, so I'll turn it over to the group. What else does this patient need? And maybe for Dr. Liang, how do we decide focal versus systemic treatments? And this patient went on to do well for quite a few years. So what would you say in the tumor board? Would this patient need anything immediately to follow this operation?

Well, we have the luxury of looking back at her case, and it's nice that she did so wonderfully. But at the time, had we been back in time at the time of this case, further treatment is going to be sort of an individualized decision that probably her team of the endocrinologist, as well as her surgeon, Her family is going to probably want to be all discussing in detail. You know, are we talking about quality of life that we want to preserve or do we really want to eradicate every last trace of tumor and, you know, perhaps alleviate any anxiety if that is an issue in her life. When we talk about focal versus systemic treatments, focal treatments can be, you know, either getting rid of the tumor that we can see, so like let's say surgery for local areas, or using something called external beam radiation. Radiation using a beam from the outside, not something that she had already, that radioactive iodine dose that she swallowed by mouth a couple of years ago. versus systemic treatments, those are what we refer to as generally infusions of anti-cancer treatments that target the thyroid cancer, no matter where it is in the body. So an infusion in the arm, through the vein, every couple of weeks or so, the decision to do this, the systemic treatments, would be a little bit more intensive. It comes with a lot of side effects, and it may not necessarily cure her. We know she has a pretty extensive amount of disease, but at the same time, it seems really small and stable and perhaps focal, so using one of these large Large guns may not be might not be in her best interest so there's no one right answer for for her and this is where we have a just a really good conversation about her expectations and her wishes going forward.

Yeah, that's a great point. This patient tended to prefer less less treatment. And she had a very supportive environment always came to her follow up appointments. And so it was a good person for us to be able to monitor with accurate surveillance and she you know. In retrospect, it was doing nothing and just observing her was the right thing to do because three years went by and nothing at all happened. So, you know, this is an 11 year journey I'm presenting to you and I know that the people in the audience are all on long journeys. Thankfully, the survivorship after initial treatment for thyroid cancer is so good. We have the luxury of talking about these things. Here are some of her numbers. Maybe I'll ask Dr. Leung to help us interpret some of these values.

The big numbers that we are looking at is the thyroid globulin that becomes our tumor marker in a person who's had completely, their complete removal of their thyroid glands, and we can see that it, yeah, it started off at 1.1, and the tumor burden seemed to increase over the years, 3.6, 18.3, and then 45. Everything is relative. We can't sort of translate to say that 45 is the same type of morbidity, meaning the same health effects in one person versus somebody else. Someone can be completely asymptomatic with that amount of thyroglobulin versus someone else who may not be. It really depends on where that the tumor has sort of recurred and spread to. Is it really close to vital structures and that sort of thing? the thyroglobulin antibody, as Dr. Yeh had mentioned previously, we always get that just to be able to trust the thyroglobulin itself. So it's nice that that thyroid antibody was negative. And then the third value is that TSH. Again, just to remind everybody, that's a reflection of how much thyroid hormone replacement we're giving her. through the synthetic pill. And so we weigh the risks and benefits of having too much thyroid hormone replacement on board versus just enough to fill up the tank. I talked about previously that having too much really tries to keep the thyroid cancer away, but in an older person like this patient is, it can also have some detrimental effects to the heart and the bones specifically. So we weigh the risks and benefits of keeping her TSH too low, but yet not giving her other health problems. So I like this TSH right where it is if she's feeling asymptomatic.
And Dr. Levitz, you know, when you look at these numbers, especially that rising thyroglobin level, what does it make you think? And if you were to start looking for a tumor, where would you look?

Yeah, so this is a very clear pattern that this thyroglobulin is going up. And when you look at the doubling time, I mean, it's going up, you know, a fair amount. And now this thyroglobulin in the 40s certainly makes me think of disease outside of the neck. So spread outside the neck, perhaps to the lungs.

I agree. When I see a thyroid globulin in the single digits, I'm thinking a neck lymph node, double digits, maybe the lungs, triple digits, maybe the bone or somewhere else. We started looking in the chest because way back when we had some indication there was a little bit of disease in the chest. And indeed, she had a chest CT demonstrating numerous sub and pericentimeter non calcified pulmonary nodules throughout both lungs and, and I tried to pull up the images to show the audience but I couldn't get the website to work. But this just looks like, remember, the lungs are mostly air, right? And on our scans, air looks black. Tissue, solid tissue looks white or gray. And this was like little dots, little teeny dots. spread in several areas throughout the lungs. And this did look like a pattern compatible with a small amount of lung metastases of thyroid cancer. So this is a case we brought to the tumor board, the April tumor board. And so what should the next step be? And I'm going to ask Dr. Liang to pretend to be maybe one of the radiation oncologists or the medical oncologists in our group. What would that discussion look like?

Yeah, and this is where we really appreciate the expertise of so many disciplines in the room. But how we think about something like this is we try to figure out how many discrete areas in the lungs might be cancerous versus sometimes people just have pulmonary nodules in the lung for, you know, just a little blood of something that is not cancer. And indeed from the imaging, if it looks like, you know, there's lots of diffuse tumor, then it would be really hard to remove that, let's say by surgery. or through this really focused beam of external beam radiation that a radiation oncologist would be responsible for delivering the care for. So if it doesn't look like, you know, it's really one area that we can really eradicate through one of those means. And if the person herself, she's getting perhaps a little bit more symptomatic, we ask about her breathing. Sometimes we do some specific breathing tests, a pulmonary function test to see how much air she's able to move through the lungs If all of those things seem to be, you know, suggestive that she's really symptomatic, that her health is being impacted from these little lung nodules, then this is where we would consider referring her to one of our medical oncologists for one of these systemic therapies that I talked about recently. So it really kind of depends on her situation, asking all those questions.
Yeah, so she was totally- Dr. Yeh, we've got about 10 minutes officially left. We can run over a little bit.

Okay. All right. Thank you for that tip. Yeah, so Dr. Leung mentioned that these little dots can be thyroid cancer, but they might not be. There are other reasons to have these little dots in the lung. There are certain fungi or other infections that can cause it. So maybe I'll ask Dr. Levitz, do we need to prove that this is thyroid cancer before we give the patient any other treatments, potentially toxic chemicals with side effects or do we need to prove that?

Yeah. Generally, the radiation oncologist and the medical oncologist, they do want a biopsy that proves that there is metastatic disease before they treat with a treatment that can have some side effects like a systemic therapy or radiation. Usually, the biopsy of the lungs can be done in a fairly minimally invasive way guided by CT imaging. It's not a surgery, but we should get a biopsy of the lungs next.

Okay, so that's what we did. And it's amazing. These, these little dots are so teeny, like a little corn kernel. And yet, the interventional radiology guys can guide a needle into that without puncturing the lung. I don't know how they do that. But they were able to spear this little thing, and it showed metastatic papillary carcinoma. And again, we love the pathologists always helping us. They stain it for molecules that are only present in thyroid tissue. And these TTF1 and thyroglobulin markers are both positive. And that proves beyond a shadow of a doubt that this is metastatic thyroid cancer to the lungs. And so here we are, brings us up to today. Now she's 80, small volume in the left neck. And I should tell you that, you know, we ultrasound that area every year and it's a tiny little speck, but it's now a little bit of an M&M, you know, in the neck. Thyroglobulin trending upwards, which stimulated us to look at the lung. And then we found some lung nodules and we biopsied these showing metastatic cancer, but the patient's doing great. She's doing great. Doesn't feel anything. So what are the options now? Maybe Dr. Leung could comment. We could give a systemic treatment. We could give chemotherapy. What about radioactive iodine in this patient?

Yeah, I think the key is that she is doing well, so well clinically that we really have to weigh the risks of introducing one of these other therapies that have oftentimes been associated with side effects. And, you know, decrease quality of life from that point onward. And also with the, with the sense that we likely no matter what therapy we choose, if any, will be unlikely to totally eradicate her tumor right we won't ever sort of get rid of it completely but it doesn't mean that she won't be fine with that little bit of tumor resting in her. So Michael had talked a little bit about radioactive iodine. She had one round of it many years ago, more than a decade ago. Could her disease be receptive to receiving another dose and potentially getting rid of a little bit of that tumor? We would try to do a diagnostic radioactive iodine and scan if that was a consideration before we give her the real dose. If so, But, you know, in terms of talking about these systemic therapies, what we call, you know, chemotherapies for thyroid cancer, it seems like that would, the risks would really outweigh the benefits in this situation if she's doing so well. So we have many patients, many patients exactly like her who have a little, you know, a little bit of thyroid cancer in the lungs or elsewhere. We just monitor them every six months or so for years and years on end, and they tend to do quite well. So I would maybe leave it at that for her.

Yeah, all these options. And I think this is your point, if I'm hearing you right, is this is an example of living with cancer, you know, a small amount. And this patient is clearly thriving. And it's one of the most pleasant aspects of treating people with this disease is you can, you've been friends with them for so long and you see them live their lives and have fulfilling activities and relationships on the journey. This patient did have a second dose of radioactive iodine. and the post-therapy scan. So we give the patient a dose of radioactive iodine, we wait about five days, and we do a post-therapy scan. And we see, did those tumor areas drink up the radioactive iodine? And yes, it did. So here we have focal intense radioactivity in the left upper lobe corresponding to a lung granuloma. That's a collection of inflammatory tissue favored to represent reactive change versus less likely melanoma. Sometimes there's some ambiguity as to whether or not it's truly an area of thyroid cancer, but they had some iodine uptake in the lungs. And I felt reassured by this. I felt like the thyroid cancer cells there were taking up the radioactive iodine. And so here are tumor markers after that peak of 45.4. It did come down a little bit. And is it safe to say, Dr. Liang, that maybe she had some response to the radioactive iodine too early to say?

I think that's true. You know, radioactive iodine can stay and be effective in the body for up to a year. So the timeframe of this calendar seems to fit that response. But again, as we said, it's unlikely that we'll completely eradicate her tumor as long as that this number sort of stabilizes, remains kind of in this range. We're fairly happy with that.
Very good. So that brings us up to date with this patient. So we're happy to take some more questions from the audience.

reference_conclusion: Following reoperative left central neck dissection, a small amount of tumor was intentionally left on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve to preserve voice and quality of life, with planned annual ultrasound surveillance of the residual neck disease. Given the subsequently identified small-volume, asymptomatic pulmonary metastases, lung biopsy was obtained to confirm metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma before additional therapy. Because the patient remained clinically well with indolent disease burden, management favored observation with serial monitoring; a diagnostic radioactive iodine evaluation was considered if further radioactive iodine therapy were pursued, and the patient ultimately received a second dose of radioactive iodine with biochemical response requiring continued surveillance.

And we agreed that we would just monitor that area with ultrasound every year. [...] Usually, the biopsy of the lungs can be done in a fairly minimally invasive way guided by CT imaging. It's not a surgery, but we should get a biopsy of the lungs next. [...] So we have many patients, many patients exactly like her who have a little, you know, a little bit of thyroid cancer in the lungs or elsewhere. We just monitor them every six months or so for years and years on end, and they tend to do quite well. [...] We would try to do a diagnostic radioactive iodine and scan if that was a consideration before we give her the real dose. [...] This patient did have a second dose of radioactive iodine.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old woman from São Paulo, Brazil.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive visual field loss over approximately 1 year; headaches for 2 weeks prior to presentation. Additional symptoms before initial admission included headache associated with nausea, vomiting, and confusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Giant pituitary macroadenoma with sellar and suprasellar extension, associated obstructive hydrocephalus and visual pathway compression. Intratumoral hemorrhagic change/apoplexy was present at surgery.

[ histopathology results ]: Tumor consistency at resection was described as soft/suckable. No formal histopathology report was provided.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT head demonstrated a large sellar/suprasellar mass with hydrocephalus.  
- Post-shunt MRI demonstrated persistent ventricular asymmetry, with one lateral ventricle less dilated than the other, and a dumbbell-shaped lesion centered in the pituitary region with sellar and suprasellar extension, consistent with pituitary adenoma.  
- The lesion extended superiorly into the third ventricle.  
- Postoperative imaging showed a residual radiographic abnormality.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Prolactin level was normal.  
- Cortisol was reported as 0.9 on initial evaluation; no steroid replacement had been started at that time, and the low value was attributed to timing of sampling.  
- No postoperative diabetes insipidus was reported.  
- No postoperative cortisol change was reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- At initial presentation in 2020, cerebrospinal fluid diversion was performed with ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement under endoscopic guidance with septostomy because of hydrocephalus.  
- After shunt placement, the patient was discharged and was subsequently lost to follow-up during the COVID-19 period.  
- She later re-presented to the emergency department with visual loss and no headache.  
- Definitive tumor surgery was then performed as a combined procedure in a single anesthetic session: endonasal resection followed by transcallosal, transchoroidal/transfissural approach to the third ventricle for removal of remaining tumor.  
- Nasoseptal flap closure was performed after the endonasal stage.  
- Gross resection was achieved, with residual concern on postoperative imaging.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Immediately postoperative after combined endonasal and transcallosal resection, with a residual radiographic abnormality on postoperative imaging.  
- No CSF leak was reported postoperatively.  
- No diabetes insipidus was reported postoperatively.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Neurological examination at presentation showed reduced consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale 13.  
- Visual assessment documented visual acuity of 20/50 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye.  
- Bitemporal hemianopsia and papilledema were present.

reference_conclusion: The agreed management was staged urgent cerebrospinal fluid diversion followed by definitive tumor resection, with preference for temporary external ventricular drainage when feasible and subsequent resection after MRI. For the giant pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar and third ventricular extension, a combined approach in the same anesthesia was performed, consisting of endonasal resection followed by transcallosal resection of residual third ventricular tumor. Postoperatively, the patient was observed with close follow-up; the residual radiographic abnormality was interpreted as hemorrhage rather than residual tumor, and no reoperation for clot evacuation was undertaken.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Painless left cervical mass present for approximately 2–3 months at initial presentation. At relapse, he developed symptomatic enlarging left-sided cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), initially presenting as diffuse nodal disease with bone marrow involvement. At relapse, repeat biopsy was consistent with more aggressive pleomorphic, if not blastoid, mantle cell lymphoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial pathology confirmed mantle cell lymphoma. Tumor cells were SOX11 positive. Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 10%, with focal areas showing higher proliferation up to 40%. Bone marrow biopsy showed involvement by lymphoma. At relapse, lymph node biopsy showed complete effacement with increased B-cell size (small to medium-sized cells), SOX11 positivity, TP53 positivity, and increased Ki-67 to 50%; morphology was described as more consistent with pleomorphic, if not blastoid, mantle cell lymphoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial PET scan showed diffuse hypermetabolic disease above and below the diaphragm, with hypermetabolic splenomegaly. At relapse, PET/CT again showed diffuse hypermetabolism.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: FISH demonstrated t(11;14), confirming mantle cell lymphoma. TP53 abnormality was reported, with three copies of TP53 identified initially; at relapse, TP53 was strongly positive on biopsy.

[ laboratory results ]: LDH was elevated at initial presentation. Other laboratory studies were otherwise unremarkable.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 6 cycles of bendamustine plus rituximab as outpatient induction therapy. Treatment was well tolerated and resulted in a very good partial remission. He was subsequently lost to follow-up while overseas. Relapse occurred in less than 1 year after completion of therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Early relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma after a short remission duration of less than 1 year following bendamustine-rituximab. At the time of post-relapse treatment, disease was symptomatic with diffuse hypermetabolic involvement on PET/CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial physical examination showed a palpable left cervical mass with scattered diffuse lymphadenopathy. He had no significant constitutional symptoms at initial presentation. Splenomegaly was present on PET imaging.

<image> Slide summarizing 16-week response and MRD outcomes from the AIM study of venetoclax plus ibrutinib in relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma, with comparisons by PET assessment.

reference_conclusion: For early relapsed mantle cell lymphoma with a short response duration after prior bendamustine-rituximab, further management should prioritize novel targeted therapy rather than re-challenge with chemoimmunotherapy, given the aggressive clinical behavior and relative chemotherapy resistance of early relapse disease. Clinical trial participation is recommended. The patient was enrolled on a clinical trial using a BTK inhibitor backbone with ibrutinib plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor and has been responding well on treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Irregular menstrual bleeding/irregular menstrual cycle at initial presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Synchronous gynecologic malignancies diagnosed in March 2025:
- Ovarian carcinoma, stage III, involving the left ovary.
- Endometrial carcinoma, stage IA.

ECOG performance status was 1. Comorbidities included type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Family history was positive for endometrial cancer in the mother and maternal aunt.

[ histopathology results ]: Postoperative histopathology after total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic lymph node dissection showed:
- Left ovary: endometrial carcinoma, grade 2, with capsule breach; 10 lymph nodes were positive; reported as stage III.
- Endometrium: endometrial carcinoma, grade 1, stage IA, with less than 50% myometrial invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative imaging demonstrated an ovarian mass following initial endometrial biopsy diagnosis. Post-treatment imaging showed complete response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: 
- Tissue molecular testing performed on the endometrial biopsy specimen detected an MSH6 mutation.
- No mutation was detected in MLH1, POLE, MSH2, PMS2, or TP53 on the reported panel.
- Hereditary cancer gene panel identified a pathogenic MSH6 variant.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- Underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic lymph node dissection.
- Received adjuvant chemotherapy:
  - 2 cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin.
  - Followed by 4 cycles of nab-paclitaxel and carboplatin.
- Imaging after treatment demonstrated complete response.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative and post-adjuvant chemotherapy status with radiologic complete response.

[ other clinical data ]: 
- Tissue molecular analysis was performed from the endometrial biopsy block.
- Right ovary was reported as uninvolved.
- Mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry/MSI testing was not reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidental neck lump.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, tall cell variant, with extrathyroidal extension and metastatic cervical lymph node involvement (right central and right lateral neck).

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion was Bethesda VI papillary thyroid carcinoma. Surgical pathology after total thyroidectomy with right central and right lateral lymph node dissection showed a 1.7 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell variant. Vascular invasion was absent. Extrathyroidal extension was present. Right central compartment nodes: 2/3 positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; largest metastatic focus 1.3 cm; no extranodal extension. Right lateral neck nodes: 4/35 positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; largest metastatic focus 0.6 cm; no extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial neck ultrasound showed a 1.9 x 1.5 x 1.9 cm solid hypoechoic right thyroid nodule with extension beyond the capsule/posterior capsule involvement, and suspicious right-sided cervical lymph nodes. Post-radioiodine SPECT/CT showed uptake in the thyroid bed and intense uptake in a right level III lymph node. Ultrasound in January 2024 showed a right level IV lymph node measuring 1.2 x 0.7 x 0.6 cm. Follow-up ultrasound approximately 1 year later showed the same right level IV lymph node measuring 1.4 x 0.8 x 0.9 cm with microcalcifications.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperative laboratory studies showed normal TSH, free T4 1.7, thyroglobulin 0.9, and negative thyroglobulin antibodies. After radioactive iodine, thyroglobulin was suppressed. Subsequent thyroid function tests were reported as normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with right central and right lateral lymph node dissection. She subsequently received radioactive iodine, 150 mCi, at another hospital. Post-treatment SPECT/CT demonstrated uptake in the thyroid bed and a right level III lymph node. On follow-up, a persistent right level IV cervical lymph node remained detectable on ultrasound and increased from 1.2 x 0.7 x 0.6 cm to 1.4 x 0.8 x 0.9 cm over approximately 1 year, with microcalcifications.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent structural cervical nodal disease was present on surveillance ultrasound in the right lateral neck (level IV), with suppressed thyroglobulin and normal thyroid function tests.

[ other clinical data ]: Thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. No extranodal extension was identified in either the central or lateral neck nodal specimens.

All those details you heard Dr. Shah talk about, yeah, I know where level four is, but where is it within level four relative to the nerves and the vessels and that sort of stuff. And every once in a while it'll look to me, it'd be lateral and he'll call me back and he'll go, no, this is really sitting right on in a bad location to take a look at. So having, our surgical colleagues that really understand the anatomy of those. I often tell patients, if I ask the surgeons, if it got bigger, is it going to grow into anything? And if it got bigger, is it going to make your surgery harder? Those two questions would help us kind of know to move in the right direction. All right, Dr. Pedraza, you're on a roll. Let's do some more practical. Let's try one more and see what we get on number three here.

reference_conclusion: Following total thyroidectomy with right central and right lateral neck dissection and subsequent radioactive iodine administration, no second dose of radioactive iodine is recommended. The persistent right level IV nodal abnormality should be managed with active surveillance using serial neck ultrasound, with repeat imaging in approximately 6 months and consideration of interval CT to define anatomic relationships and assess for additional nodal disease. Fine-needle aspiration should be deferred while observation is ongoing, and surgical intervention should be reserved for clinically meaningful progression or the appearance of additional concerning nodal disease.
reference_conclusion_quote: No, I rarely, in the last decade, I can't even think on one hand how many times I've double-dosed. I mean, other than the setting of re-differentiated disease for advanced, not this scenario, so no. [...] Probably we could monitor him and rather than repeating the ultrasound in one year, I would do it in six months. and maybe in a year and a half I would repeat a CAT scan and compare the two CAT scans. So I think those are the important issues when we think about it. The one thing I need to be absolutely sure that in the next six months he doesn't come up with one more node at another level three or level two, which will push me into surgery. The last thing I want to describe is If you are thinking about not doing surgery, don't put a needle in it. Because once you put the needle and that is positive, there is no way, Jose, you're going to stop operating on the patient. [...] Okay, so no second dose radioactive iodine. We talked about surgery. And I really do think active surveillance in these guys.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 79-year-old woman at presentation; 80 years old at subsequent follow-up.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent hyperthyroidism in the setting of prior toxic multinodular goiter and a palpable left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Toxic multinodular goiter diagnosed at age 63.  
- Recurrent hyperthyroidism approximately 16 years after prior radioactive iodine treatment.  
- Left thyroid nodule with initial fine-needle aspiration reported as Bethesda category III, atypical cells of undetermined significance.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the left thyroid nodule was cellular, without nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma; interpreted as Bethesda category III, atypical cells of undetermined significance.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid scintigraphy at recurrence of hyperthyroidism showed heterogeneous uptake in a hyperfunctioning left thyroid nodule with suppression of the contralateral lobe.  
- Physical examination identified a firm, fixed 2–3 cm left thyroid nodule without palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- Follow-up neck ultrasound demonstrated a new suspicious left lateral neck finding corresponding to echogenic soft tissue within the jugular vein, described as an echogenic mass extending along the vein, consistent with tumor invasion/tumor thrombus.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Molecular testing on the FNA specimen identified a GNAS mutation.  
- The molecular report characterized this as a low-risk mutation.  
- High expression of the sodium-iodide symporter was also described on molecular analysis.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- TSH: <0.01.  
- Free T4: 2.07.  
- Total T3: 245 ng/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- At age 63, toxic multinodular goiter was treated with iodine-131, dose 29 mCi.  
- She remained euthyroid for approximately 16 years without levothyroxine or methimazole.  
- After recurrence of hyperthyroidism and evaluation of the left thyroid nodule, methimazole was started.  
- Interval follow-up ultrasound at 1 year identified a new suspicious left lateral neck/jugular vein lesion.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy was present on examination at initial recurrence.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: New diagnosis of multiple myeloma.

[ diagnosis ]: Newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) stage II. High-risk disease due to t(4;14). Transplant-eligible.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: High-risk translocation t(4;14).

[ laboratory results ]: Renal function was normal at diagnosis.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed disease. Performance status was good. No comorbidities were reported. The patient was considered clearly eligible for autologous stem cell transplantation.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you, Nina. So I'm going to start off with this gentleman who is a 60-year-old patient with a new diagnosis of multiple myeloma, who has a revised ISS stage 2 myeloma with a high-risk translocation for 14, good performance status, no comorbidities, has a normal renal function and diagnosis, and as you can see, is clearly eligible for an autologous stem cell transplant. Now, as Dr. Shah already mentioned, There has been significant change in the approach to treatment of multiple myeloma for the entire spectrum, especially the newly diagnosed myeloma, where many of these new therapies have made a significant difference. And it is important to remember that right now the standard of care has been the combination of bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone based on survival data from this walk trial, both progression-free and overall survival data. as well as the randomized phase 3 trial from the French group showing it to be an effective induction therapy prior to autologous stem cell transplant. Even though peripheral neuropathy has been a concern with Bortezomib, the use of subcutaneous dosing as well as once-weekly dosing has ameliorated this problem significantly and made this a suitable backbone for developing the quadruplets, particularly the antibody-based quadruplets that we are going to be talking about. While we have some initial data suggesting that these quadruplets can improve outcomes, both progression-free and overall survival, with some of the regimens, we still need long-term follow-up with some of the quadruplets that are likely to be used in this setting. We still have limited data in terms of what the impact would be on high-risk patients and whether this is a paradigm that can be used both for transplant-eligible and ineligible patients. And obviously, we want to see what the long-term toxicity data would be as well. So, let's take a look at the current paradigm. So, we have the Bortezomib-Lentex or Bortezomib-Lentex at reduced doses for transplant-eligible and transplant-ineligible patient populations, respectively. And we also have the Lentex in the frail population and VMB that has been used. And the recent phase 3 trials have all examined the role of adding daratumumab or isatexamab, the two monoclonal CD38-targeted antibodies, to these existing backbone regimens. We will focus our discussions more on the quadruplets today, but it's important to note that addition of daratumumab to a doublet-like lenalidomide and dexamethasone in the older patient population has not only been shown to improve the progression-free survival, but more recent data from the EHA this year shows that there's also an improvement in overall survival. Now, the initial phase three trials had focused on the transplant-eligible patient population and looked at the backbone of bortezomib thalidomide dexamethasone. That was a commonly used induction therapy in Europe. So the Cassiopeia trial randomized patients to receiving bortezomib thalidomide dexamethasone with or without direttumumab to look at its role as an induction therapy pre-transplant and consolidation. And the trial also looked at a second question as to whether direttumumab maintenance is better than just observation after consolidation therapy. The initial results of this study, with the longer follow-up, shows that the addition of direct imumab to induction and consolidation pre- and post-single autologous stem cell transplant improved both the progression-free survival and overall survival, suggesting that it has a significant synergy with this regimen. Now, there's data from ASCO that looked at the impact of maintenance with DirectMoveMap post-consolidation compared to observation and showed that the median progression-free survival for the entire cohort was significantly better with DirectMoveMap maintenance compared to no maintenance. However, it is important to note that with the the benefits seem to be primarily limited to those patients who did not get dretimumab as part of the induction and consolidation therapy. While the patients who did not see bortezomib, who got the bortezomib thalidomide dexamethasone induction therapy and consolidation had a significant improvement in their progression-free survival when dretimumab was used as maintenance therapy compared to none. Now, one of the disadvantages of the VTD regimen is that we don't use it very commonly in the U.S., primarily because of the increased risk of neuropathy. The GRIFFIN trial asked the question whether we can replicate these results with the addition of directamomab to the commonly used regimen, botosomab lenaldomide dexamethasone. It was a randomized phase two trial. And what we saw at the most recent presentation at ASH 2020 was that addition of the retinomab over time led to deepening of the responses with almost two thirds of the patients getting to be a complete response and significant proportion of those patients being MRD negative compared to just under half of those patients when they did not get retinomab in combination with RBD. Now, when you specifically look at the deeper responses, it is clear that the MRD negativity, particularly the durable MRD negativity, was almost 10-fold higher in the indirect MMF RVD arm compared to the RVD. And this translated to only some early trend in the PFS, but we don't have the long-term data to say that the DARA RVD PFS is definitely better than RVD, even though the trends appears to be in that direction. Now, specifically looking at this quadruplet regimen, I think one of the areas of great interest is its role in high-risk patient population. We know that with the standard approach of BRD, single transplant, and lenalidomide maintenance, our high-risk patients don't do as well. as the standard risk patients. So there have been attempts to try and improve the outcome of the high-risk patient population. There was a previous trial in this work that looked at adding elotuzumab to bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone that did not improve the outcomes of high-risk patients. More recently at ASCO, we had the OPTIMUM trial that looked at a five drug combination. So it's BRD with cyclophosphonate and retinumab added as part of injection therapy. And they studied 103 patients And after six cycles of induction therapy, they underwent an autologous stem cell transplant, followed by six cycles of consolidation with the directamomab VRD regimen, the quadruplet, followed by 12 more cycles of directamomab VR with the dexamethasone being dropped, and patients continue on directamomab lenalidomide until disease progression. Now, when you look at these patients, obviously we don't have the long-term data from these trials, but it's clear that these multi-drug combinations induce deep responses with almost half of the patients in CR after the autologous stem cell transplant. And the MRD negativity amongst these patients, just bone marrow MRD negativity was almost two-thirds of these patients being MRD negative. So clearly, these multi-drug combinations are highly effective in inducing deep responses in this high-risk patient population. And MRD negativity has already been shown to be one of the most important prognostic factors for high-risk patients. Now, this also in the context of high risk patients is important to note the results from the Forte trial that was presented at the ASCO this year, which clearly showed that in the high risk patient population, again, defined as patients with 414 translocation, 17p deletion and 1q abnormalities, the use of carfilzomib lenaldomide maintenance versus lenaldomide maintenance as a single agent was associated with better outcome than just using lenaldomide maintenance. And in fact, the NCCN guidelines for the newly diagnosed myeloma therapy already includes many of these quadruplets. So the direct imumab VMP is already included for the non-transplant eligible patient population. We also have the direct imumab VRD, which is included for the transplant eligible patient population as one of the recommended regimens. Now, while a lot of the focus has been on this transplant-eligible patient population in terms of exploring the quadruplets, there has been interest in exploring these antibody quadruplets in the older patient population. The DARA-VMP regimen was studied in the ALSION trial, and the DARA-VCD regimen was examined in the LIRA study. Now the ALSION trial, the addition of diatomumab given continuously to a limited duration BMP regimen was associated with a significant improvement in the PFS and overall survival for this patient population. So it's important to note that the initial therapy for myeloma is rapidly evolving with the introduction of CD38-targeted antibodies in order to create a variety of different triplets. And the important thing is the anti-CD38 approach seems to be very useful both in terms of efficacy but without a significant increase in toxicity when added to the standard of care regimens. It is important to define how well these quadruplet regimens are going to behave for the high-risk patients, which is an area that clearly needs significant improvement, as is the case with this particular patient that we talked about who has the 414 translocation. So clearly the quadruplets are important in the sense that create or lead to high rates of MRD negativity, which are important for these high-risk patients. And we hope that these quadruplets will also allow us to give limited duration therapy in some of these patients. And the ongoing clinical trials are examining the role of MRD-directed treatment duration, again, in a prospective manner. I'll hand this back to you, Nina.

Great, such a fantastic discussion about a part of myeloma therapy that's still with controversy, even though we're doing so well and newly diagnosed myeloma. I want to open it up for discussion to all of our panelists and talk about not just this case but in general, I think we're seeing small. specific questions being answered, you know, DERA RVD versus RVD. We're seeing, you know, DERA VMP versus VMP, DERA RD versus RD, but I was very impressed by the Forte data in the high-risk analysis. I mean, you showed the data there where getting KR maintenance after is doing a really good job. Now, that study is actually a randomized phase two. Can we extrapolate from there and say, okay, our new standard for maintenance, actually, if you start with KRD, should be KR maintenance. What do you think about that?

I think it's a very important question. I think what the Forte trial tells us is it adds to the body of evidence that a proteasome inhibitor plus an IMID is the appropriate maintenance for this high-risk patient population. So we have the retrospective data from Emory showing that a proteasome blend maintenance in high-risk patients were associated with a significant BFS, or better than what we would have expected historically. We have data from the SWARC trial, looking at VRD with or without elotuzumab, followed by VR maintenance, where the progression-free survival for the VR for the high-risk patients was comparable to the standard risk patients in the endurance trial getting a VRD induction therapy followed by LEN maintenance. And now we have the Forte data, similarly, quite consistent with what we have seen. So I think it's reasonable to say today, if you have a high-risk patient population, if you do VRD induction, continue with VR. If you do a KRD induction, continue with KR. I don't think we have the data quite yet for the data LEN maintenance in this patient population.

Yeah, I think it's just really interesting to think about what we're going to do for our high-risk patients. Thinking about the MYA trial, which had very interesting findings for transplant-ineligible patients, so maybe, Tom, I'll throw it out to you. With the data for DERA-RD being so good compared to RD, is there any reason to use a PI for this transplant-ineligible patient population? What do you think?

So, it's a really good question but it is amazing data from the Maya trial, the PFS in the Maya Maya trial for the transplant ineligible population actually is better than many transplant trials for transplant eligible patients in terms of PFS which which is truly amazing. But I still think there's one specific class or group of patients, the high-risk patients, that we still, I think, have some debate on what the best triplet is for induction therapy. And I think in my practice, I do tend to favor VRD as an induction therapy versus DRD in the truly high-risk population. But yeah, I think DRD should be our standard of care for transplant-ineligible patients. for induction therapy, pretty amazing results.

Yeah, I think it's just, we always talk about myelin with these alphabet soup combinations and sometimes it's hard to know what to do. Nupur, I want to ask you, with all this great data, I actually am really impressed with the PFS curves on the Forte data in general, not just for the high risk. Is there ever a case for you to do DERA, KRD, Nupur, have you ever been using that at all?

So again, as you've seen here, Nina, really good data with the quadruplets. And you can argue when you start seeing not just complete responses and deepening of responses, but MRD negative disease. I agree with everybody on the panel. I think it's specifically important for the high risk patient population, but I always go back to saying if what's good for high risk is going to be even better for standard risk. And that was actually highlighted in the Forte trial. When you looked at the data in the Forte trial, it was not as if the double maintenance did not help the standard risk patients. And in fact, if you're thinking about curing myeloma, you know, we assure the unmet medical need is in the high risk patient population, but the patients who are actually going to cure are the standard risk population and therefore give them the best possible treatment upfront. I think one additional thing which I will mention, which I think Tom alluded to, is, you know, it's not quite clear whether it's the antibody or the proteasome inhibitor, which is a better drug for the high-risk patient population. But even in the elderly patients now, we are doing quadruplets so that if you use dose attenuation with all of the drugs, you can actually give even older patients an attenuated RVD with daratumumab, for example.

Yeah. And I actually just thinking about all the choices that we have, you know, Shaji, I'll throw it back to you. What do you think, you know, it's 2021 now, what do you think is going to be 2025, the standard of care for upfront induction? What do you think from all of these options that we have?

Yeah, I think because the, I think a four-drug combination is probably going to be the standard initial therapy. Now, I think the big question in debate is, what are the four drugs going to be? You know, is it still going to be the direct-to-mammalide, bortezomib, lent-dex, or are we going to replace one of them with some of those fascinating immunotherapies that you and Nupur is going to be talking about later on? I think that's going to be the big question. You know, you said 2021, so 2025 isn't too far from here, four years. It's unlikely we will have phase three data to support many of those new therapies yet. So I suspect we will have the mature data from the current quadruplet. So I think it's reasonable to assume that either DARA-VRD or DARA-KRD would be the appropriate initial therapy. in 2025 with some of the others just trying to replace them.

So I think we've had a great discussion about all of the different options for newly diagnosed and particularly a discussion about high-risk patients. So let's turn it back to this case. Maybe I'll point to each of you and say, you know, we have this patient who's 60 years old, revised ISS2. This person has translocation 414. So just a note of that, doing pretty well, has very few comorbidities and is transplant eligible. How would you treat this patient? Ashaji, I'll start with you.

So this is a patient where I would give a dretumumab VRD induction therapy, a stem cell transplant, and then go on to a bortezomib len maintenance. I certainly will have the discussion of a tandem transplant with this patient, particularly if they are not MRD negative by the end of the first autologous stem cell transplant.
Perfect. Tom, what about you?

Well, I'm going to differ a little bit in terms of the induction, because actually here in California, we don't actually have the ability to give a quad just yet, mostly based on insurance approval. We can't get insurance approval. So, I would choose KRD vis-a-vis the Forte trial, and I would do KRD, an autologous transplant, and I would give KR slash KRD as maintenance-based therapy, and that would be my treatment for this patient.
Great. What about you, Nugur?

So I would do a four-drug combination in this patient. He's 60 years old with high-risk features. Certainly would either do DERA-RVD or DERA-KRD. We do, especially in the transplant-eligible younger fit patients without any comorbidities, KRD works extremely well. And we have ongoing studies looking at the combination of four drugs with the CD38 monoclonal. So KRD-DERA would be my choice with continuous KR for maintenance.

Yeah, I'm going to have to go with my boss, Tom, and say I would probably choose KRD. And that is actually a little bit of endurance data there, where the 414 seemed to do better with the KRD. They were included in the patient population. So I would probably go with KRD for transplant KRD and go KR maintenance, similar to the Forte trial. So at least we have one agreement here. So that's great. Great. So that brings this discussion to a close. And now we're going to move on to antibody platforms in early relapse, making therapeutic choices for optimal sequencing. And for this, I'll turn it to my colleague, Dr. Tom Martin.

reference_conclusion: For this transplant-eligible patient with newly diagnosed high-risk multiple myeloma characterized by t(4;14), the panel favored induction with a four-drug regimen, specifically daratumumab-RVD or daratumumab-KRD, followed by autologous stem cell transplantation. Post-transplant maintenance should incorporate a proteasome inhibitor plus an IMiD, with KR maintenance favored after KRD-based induction and bortezomib-lenalidomide maintenance also discussed. Tandem transplantation should be discussed, particularly if minimal residual disease negativity is not achieved after the first autologous transplant.
reference_conclusion_quote: So this is a patient where I would give a dretumumab VRD induction therapy, a stem cell transplant, and then go on to a bortezomib len maintenance. I certainly will have the discussion of a tandem transplant with this patient, particularly if they are not MRD negative by the end of the first autologous stem cell transplant. [...] So I would do a four-drug combination in this patient. He's 60 years old with high-risk features. Certainly would either do DERA-RVD or DERA-KRD. [...] So KRD-DERA would be my choice with continuous KR for maintenance. [...] So I would probably go with KRD for transplant KRD and go KR maintenance, similar to the Forte trial.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man; previously healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Right flank and rib pain associated with movement.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Right nephrectomy specimen showed clear cell renal cell carcinoma with abundant clear cytoplasm, enlarged round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and delicate vasculature. Tumor was predominantly Furman grade 3 with focal Furman grade 4 atypia. Chest wall/rib resection specimen showed metastatic carcinoma morphologically consistent with the renal primary. Left medial clavicle wide excision specimen showed metastatic carcinoma morphologically consistent with renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI demonstrated a large mass in the lower pole of the right kidney with apparent invasion of the renal hilum; the renal vein was not involved. MRI also demonstrated metastases involving the right lower ribs, including a large soft tissue component associated with the right 11th rib lesion. Postoperative bone scan demonstrated abnormal uptake in the right calvarium, left clavicle, and left tibia, consistent with metastatic disease; dedicated calvarial views confirmed a right calvarial metastasis. Four months later, CT brain was performed. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis obtained five months after initial presentation demonstrated a right lower lobe pulmonary nodule and a soft tissue mass arising from the left acetabulum, consistent with metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL; hematocrit 39%; white blood cell count 8.7 ×10^9/L; neutrophils 6.2 ×10^9/L; platelet count 212,000/µL; calcium 12 mg/dL; creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; LDH 108 U/L. Vital signs were normal. Karnofsky performance status was 100.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right adrenal-sparing nephrectomy with right 10th, 11th, and 12th rib resection. He subsequently underwent left medial clavicle wide excision. He received radiation therapy to the skull to 30 Gy in 10 fractions. Following local therapies, subsequent imaging demonstrated additional metastatic disease, including right calvarium, left tibia, right lower lobe lung nodule, and left acetabular soft tissue mass.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease persisted after nephrectomy, rib metastasectomy, clavicle metastasectomy, and skull radiation, with osseous metastases involving the calvarium, clavicle, tibia, and left acetabulum, and a pulmonary nodule in the right lower lobe.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination showed a well-appearing man in no acute distress; examination was otherwise benign.
