reference_discussion.text: So we'll start with our first case today. This is a 50-year-old previously healthy man who initially presented with right flank and rib pain associated with movement. Physical exam revealed normal vital signs, a Karnofsky performance status of 100, and he was a well-appearing man in no acute distress. And otherwise, the physical exam was benign. His labs were significant for hemoglobin of 12.5, but a normal hematocrit of 39, white blood cell count of 8.7, with neutrophils of 6.2. His platelet count was 212,000. His calcium was high at 12 and his creatinine was normal at 1.2. LDH was normal at 108. This ultimately led to an imaging study. Dr. Ho will discuss our initial imaging for this patient.

The imaging that he first received was an enhanced MRI of the abdomen, and this image shows that there is a large mass in the lower pole of the right kidney, and it looks to invade the renal hilum, but the renal vein was not involved. In addition, he had metastases involving the right lower ribs, and the arrow is pointing to a large topotitia component to this right 11th rib metastasis.
So that brings us to the first discussion point of this case, and that is the necessity of biopsy. And for that, we will turn to Dr. Inman.

Well, when I look at these images, it's more likely to me to be a renal mass metastasized to the bone than a bone lesion metastasized to the kidney. So, in this case, the presumptive diagnosis is one of kidney cancer. The question of whether or not you need a biopsy depends on what you're going to do next. If the patient is going to be a candidate for a nephrectomy, then I wouldn't do a biopsy because the biopsy is not going to change what I do. On the other hand, if it's a patient who's not going to go to nephrectomy, then I would consider a biopsy because we'd need the tissue diagnosis to decide on how best to manage the patient next. So in this particular patient, because I think he would potentially be a candidate for nephrectomy, I probably would not be considering a biopsy.
Great. In terms of prognostic categories, Dr. Harrison will now discuss the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center criteria as well as the HENG criteria.

Sure. So this is summarized on this slide. There are several prognostic criteria that are used. The first one that's probably the most widely used is the Memorial Sloan-Kettering criteria. It consists of five criteria. This was published in 1999 by Dr. Mozart et al., and the reference is at the bottom of the slide there. But again, it takes into account five clinical factors. So having a low Karnofsky performance status is a risk factor, as is having a high LDH, a low hemoglobin, a high corrected calcium, and having had no prior nephrectomy. All of these are risk factors. Then based upon the number of risk factors, you can group the patients into prognostic categories. So if a patient has zero risk factors, that corresponds to a favorable risk category, one to two intermediate risk, and three or greater is a poor risk. And these correspond to different survivals. Now that's been updated. The initial Memorial Sloan-Kettering criteria were published in the cytokine era. Now that we're firmly in the TKI era where we're using drugs like sunitinib, these criteria have been updated. And the first four were retained. What was added was a short time to diagnosis to therapy of less than one year. Thrombophilia was added, neutrophilia was added, and I'm sorry, LDH was actually omitted, the second prognostic factor, because it is not routinely checked. So to summarize, what's called the HENG criteria has six risk factors. And again, you can group those patients into risk categories. A patient with favorable risk, as is shown on the slide, has a prognosis of about three to four years. Our patient has two risk factors, so that patient would be expected to have a median survival of about 27 months, whereas poor risk patients have a survival of about nine months. So in summary, I would say, you know, looking at this patient, he would appear to have a good enough prognosis to think about things like cytoreductive nephrectomy and other local therapies.
That leads us to our second discussion point, which is what is the role of cytoreductive nephrectomy in this case?

Okay, so cytoreductive nephrectomy is when we remove the kidney in the presence of metastatic disease and when we have not removed all of the cancer because presumably there's metastasis somewhere else that we haven't removed. And there's two main reasons we might consider cytoreductive nephrectomy. The first is symptoms. So, a symptomatic kidney tumor that's bleeding or painful, even if they're a poor risk patient from a cancer standpoint, might be a good candidate for nephrectomy to improve their quality of life for whatever time they have left. And the second reason we might consider would be to improve their survival. And there's two large randomized trials in the cytokine era that have been conducted. One was a SWOG trial, and the other one was done by the EORTC. And those trials were pooled in a large analysis, and it showed that there was a benefit to doing cytoreductive nephrectomy in combination at that time with interferon versus interferon alone, and it improved survival by about six months. We don't have any trials that have been published in the current TKI era, although there are two that have enrolled, the CARMINA trial and the SIRTIME trial, and those are expected to produce results in the next couple years. But we expect to see probably a similar benefit, although it's really not known. So for me and this patient, the best current data that we have suggests that patients who have their kidneys removed, even in the presence of metastatic disease, live longer and have less local symptoms. And the complication rate of cytoreductive nephrectomy is pretty low. About 25% of patients will have a complication, but of those, really only 5% are grade 3 or higher. Grade 3 or higher are complications you actually need to do something about. So the majority are minor complications. So because there's very few complications and because there's a potential survival benefit and because there's a symptomatic benefit, in general, if the patient's in good condition and can tolerate the surgery reasonably well, we would recommend cytoreductive nephrectomy.

Great, so this patient initially underwent a right adrenal sparing nephrectomy and right 10th, 11th, and 12th rib resection. We have the pathology of his initial resection and Dr. Fu will talk us through that.

So the image that's shown here is from his nephrectomy specimen, and basically everything that you're seeing is tumor. So the tumor morphology of his particular cancer is actually pretty classic. So the cells have abundant, very clear cytoplasm. The nuclei are fairly round, but they're pretty enlarged, and the nucleoli are very prominent. The vasculature is relatively delicate, and there is a fair amount of it. All of this is really good for a diagnosis of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and this looks fairly high grade in appearance. The majority of the tumor was graded as a Furman grade 3. The next slide shows a higher magnification of some of the more focal areas of the tumor that had very large, very prominent pleomorphic nuclei that have some nucleoli that are actually the same size of the red blood cells that are on the slide as well. And that would be more consistent with the bizarre atypia that you see with the Furman grade 4 case. So, he had a very high grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Along with the nephrectomy came his chest wall resection, and along with the ribs, there was a large soft tissue tumor mass, and this is a representative section from that. If you take a look at the morphology of the tumor cells here, you can see that they look very similar to the initial image that I was showing of his kidney tumor. So morphologically, this is consistent with the metastasis from his clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
Thank you. Subsequently, the patient underwent a bone scan, and Dr. Ho will talk to us about that bone scan.

These are frontal and posterior images on the left from his bone scan. And you can see when the arrow is pointing to various sites, one in his right calvarium, his left clavicle, and his left tibia, are all sites of abnormal metabolic activity there, indicating that they're most likely to be metastases. The next image is a cone down view of his scalp, his calvarial region, again showing high activity in his right calvarium, consistent with metastatic disease.

So at this point, we considered local therapies for the patient, including metastasectomy, as well as external beam radiation. And I'll have Dr. Harrison talk a little bit about which to choose for this patient.

Okay. And, you know, I think the thing to recognize is that, you know, it doesn't have to be one or the other. It could be both. Dr. Edmund can maybe talk a little bit about this as well. Metastasectomy is appropriate when there are one or maybe a few lesions that we think we can remove, again, to debulk either all of the tumor or the vast majority of the tumor. Certainly, external beam radiation therapy is appropriate when a lesion can't be removed, for example, in the skull, not practical. So certainly, this is a multidisciplinary discussion amongst usually surgery, urology, that is, medical oncology, and potentially radiation oncology. I'll just add that several, you know, retrospective series looking at metastasectomy have shown that patients can have good outcomes. I don't know if you have anything to add there, Brian.

Well, I would comment that at the outset, this patient had a metastasectomy in his ribs. And the reason that was done was predominantly for symptoms, but also because at the time of initial treatment, it was the only known site of disease. And at this point, three months later, we now know that he has more extensive bony disease than we had previously. I think at this point, one of his metastases is in the clavicle, and it is quite symptomatic. So, one reason for doing a metastasectomy, other than for potential cure, would be for symptom control, because it can be very effective for that. And particularly in the clavicle, where it's prone to break, this is an area where we would consider bony resection. The data on metastasectomy for kidney cancer are actually pretty interesting. For patients who have lung-only metastases and that are completely resected, their five-year survival is almost 50%. For those patients who have disease in the bones, liver, or lymph nodes that are completely resected, it's not quite as good. It's maybe around 30 to 40%. but it's still a lot better than virtually any other treatment at five years for metastatic cancer. So, for me, if a patient is in good shape, has a good performance status, and that's key, has a limited number of metastases that we feel we can completely resect, then they're generally, and with minimal morbidity, I must say, because if you have to remove, for example, an entire leg, the morbidity of that would probably outweigh the benefit. So it has to be a procedure that has reasonable morbidity. Then there's a potential benefit to the patient, not only in terms of quality of life, but quantity of life. For those patients in whom we can't have a potential cure, then we really only consider it as a palliative maneuver and prefer radiation if it's possible. For example, for axial spine metastases, where there's multiple metastases, would prefer radiation in that setting.
Great, thank you.
So continuing on with our case, the patient underwent a left medial clavicle wide excision with pathology shown here.

So this is a representative image from his clavicle resection, and the bright pink material that you're seeing sort of in the upper right hand corner of the screen represents bone. So normal bone marrow is actually hypocellular. You should see hematopoietic elements and fat. And what you're seeing here in the majority of the screen is actually a very hypercellular infiltrate of epithelial cells. And if you sort of think back to the original morphology of his tumor, you can see that they look very similar. So this is consistent morphologically with a metastasis from his known renal cell carcinoma.

Thank you. So four months later the patient underwent a CT of his brain and he also underwent radiation to his skull to 30 gray in 10 fractions. After he underwent local therapy, he had a CT chest abdomen and pelvis five months after his initial presentation.

The image on the left shows lung bases. There is a nodule in the right lower lobe. And the image on your right is a soft tissue window image of his pelvis showing a soft tissue mass originating from his left acetabulum, also consistent with ptosis.
So at this point, we come to a role for systemic therapies for the patient. And Dr. Harrison, if you would discuss choosing his first line of systemic therapy at this point.

Sure. So now the patient has had a fairly aggressive surgical debulking, the patient has had a radiation therapy, and what systemic therapy do we choose? And certainly, based on the patient's risk factors, based on the patient's age, we did think about high-dose IL-2. High-dose IL-2, though, has a response rate in the neighborhood of about 15%, so maybe 7% complete responses, only half of which are durable, maybe 8% partial responses. So when we were thinking about how to treat this patient, we were thinking mainly of that lesion in his pelvis and thinking of the size of it and that if that continued to grow unchecked, he may start to have symptoms. So we needed something with a little bit higher response. And so for that reason, we actually chose sunitinib. Certainly, either sunitinib or pazotinib are first-line therapy choices in this setting, so a patient with clear cell metastatic renal cell carcinoma, good intermediate risk. The difference, again, between drugs like pazopanib and sunitinib and hydroxyl 2 are that the response rate is probably in the neighborhood of 30 to 40 percent. Now, they don't have the same chance of a long-term response, basically, if you just compare complete responses. So, complete responses are probably maybe 1 percent or non-existent with drugs like sunitinib. So, we did talk about this and counsel the patient very extensively about that. and elected to go at the agent with a higher chance of response. We also talked to the patient about anti-resorptive agents. So there are two drugs, zolandronic acid, which is a bisphosphonate or denosumab, a rank ligand inhibitor, which are reasonable to use in patients with skeletal metastases with renal cell carcinoma. If you look at the trial, which was in all solid tumors, it was a phase 3 trial. Actually, either one, they both included a significant proportion of patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma, and either one of these drugs did appear to delay or prevent skeletal-related events. So, I would say using a drug, either zoledronic acid or denosumab with the systemic therapy is important in this setting.
Do you think there's a role for any of these anti-absorption agents? Do they have an anti-neoplastic effect?

That's a good question. That's been investigated fairly extensively in different randomized phase three studies. It's not clear in renal cell carcinoma, at least clinically, that they do have an antineoplastic effect. But I would say they do add to the systemic therapy in terms of preventing important morbidity from the cancer. So they're very important in that regard.

Very good, thank you. That wraps up our first case and we'll move on to our second case. Our second case today features a 44-year-old man who presented with 18 months of fatigue, arthrages, night sweats, and weight loss. He had extensive infectious disease and rheumatologic workups, which were all negative, including two courses of treatment for tick-borne illnesses. An abdominal ultrasound was performed for fever of unknown origin, which demonstrated a right renal mass measuring 10 by 8 by 10 centimeters. He underwent a CT of the abdomen and pelvis which confirmed a 10 by 9 centimeter right upper pole renal mass with partial duplication of the collecting system, no lymphadenopathy, and a CT chest was negative for metastatic disease. He had an initial surgery with a right laparoscopic nephrectomy and regional lymph node dissection. Dr. Fu, can you describe his pathology?

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent cytoreductive management with right adrenal-sparing nephrectomy and resection of involved right 10th, 11th, and 12th ribs, followed by local treatment of metastatic sites including left medial clavicle wide excision and radiation therapy to the skull to 30 Gy in 10 fractions. With subsequent progression including a pelvic lesion, first-line systemic therapy with sunitinib was selected on the basis of the need for a higher response rate in metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Concurrent bone-targeted therapy with either zoledronic acid or denosumab was considered important to reduce skeletal-related events in the setting of osseous metastases.
reference_conclusion_quote: this patient initially underwent a right adrenal sparing nephrectomy and right 10th, 11th, and 12th rib resection. [...] So continuing on with our case, the patient underwent a left medial clavicle wide excision [...] four months later the patient underwent a CT of his brain and he also underwent radiation to his skull to 30 gray in 10 fractions. [...] And so for that reason, we actually chose sunitinib. Certainly, either sunitinib or pazotinib are first-line therapy choices in this setting [...] So, I would say using a drug, either zoledronic acid or denosumab with the systemic therapy is important in this setting.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Hoarseness/worsening dysphonia during surveillance following prior treatment for right true vocal fold carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent/persistent squamous cell carcinoma of the glottic larynx involving the anterior commissure after prior endoscopic treatment and definitive radiotherapy. Initial disease had arisen in the right true vocal fold with extension to the anterior commissure and involvement near the right arytenoid/vocal process.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Prior biopsies after initial endoscopic treatment demonstrated persistent disease at the anterior commissure.  
- Operative biopsy performed for suspicious post-radiation anterior commissure lesion returned squamous cell carcinoma. A deep biopsy was taken at the anterior commissure.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Flexible laryngoscopy during surveillance showed an irregular area at the anterior commissure; bilateral vocal fold mobility was preserved.  
- CT neck demonstrated no cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- CT showed an irregular lesion measuring approximately 6 x 3 mm extending to the anterior commissure, involving the right vocal cord more than the left, without obvious cartilage erosion on imaging.  
- Operative endoscopic assessment identified a shallow ulcer at the anterior commissure on the infraglottic aspect, with no significant subglottic extension seen.

[ laboratory results ]: ...

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent microlaryngoscopy with excision of right true vocal fold squamous cell carcinoma, followed by blue light laser ablation.  
- Required two operative procedures for endoscopic treatment.  
- Subsequent biopsies from multiple sites showed persistent disease limited to the anterior commissure.  
- Received radiotherapy to 63 Gy in 20 fractions without treatment breaks.  
- Six months after radiotherapy, surveillance evaluation identified a suspicious anterior commissure lesion; biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: hypertension; coronary artery disease without prior surgical or endovascular intervention; no history of angina or myocardial infarction.  
- Social history: never smoker; non-drinker.  
- Swallowing assessment, including FEES, was normal preoperatively; no swallowing dysfunction was present.  
- Pulmonary function was normal.  
- Performance status/functional capacity was described as very good.  
- Preoperative medical clearance included stress testing.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks so much. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm going to do some moderating and also present a case here. I'd like to thank everybody that joined and all the panelists and all the presenters. The first case will be a case that was relatively recently done All right, can you guys see okay?
Yes.

Perfect. So this is a 67 year old patient with a past medical history of hypertension and coronary artery disease. He's a non-smoker, he's a non-drinker, otherwise healthy gentleman. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old African-American woman; physician.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, clinical stage T1N1, grade 3. Germline BRCA1 mutation carrier.

[ histopathology results ]: Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy and bilateral nipple-sparing mastectomies, pathology showed complete pathologic response in the breast and lymph nodes. Twelve lymph nodes were removed; one of 12 nodes showed treatment effect.

[ imaging findings ]: Primary tumor size was reported as less than 2 cm on imaging, consistent with T1 disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRCA1 mutation positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received neoadjuvant weekly paclitaxel plus carboplatin for 12 cycles, followed by doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide. Subsequently underwent bilateral nipple-sparing mastectomies with axillary nodal evaluation. Surgical pathology demonstrated complete pathologic response in breast and nodes.

[ current disease status ]: No residual invasive disease identified in the breast or sampled lymph nodes after neoadjuvant therapy and surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension requiring two medications. Family history was significant for heart disease. Ovaries remained intact.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable thyroid nodule and subsequent palpable neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, classic variant, arising in the right thyroid lobe, with bilateral cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Right hemithyroidectomy specimen: 1.9 cm classic variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Focal angioinvasion present.  
- No lymphatic invasion identified.  
- No perineural invasion identified.  
- No extrathyroidal extension identified.  
- Posterior surgical margin positive.  
- Completion thyroidectomy with bilateral central and bilateral lateral neck dissection: metastatic nodal disease identified. Right neck: 7/26 lymph nodes positive, largest metastatic focus 9 mm, with extranodal extension. Left neck: 1 lymph node positive, 9 mm, with extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial thyroid ultrasound in 2022 demonstrated a diffusely hyperemic gland suggestive of thyroiditis and a solitary 1.8 cm right upper thyroid nodule classified as TI-RADS 5, with sonographic features including hypoechogenicity, taller-than-wide shape, infiltrative margins, and echogenic foci.  
- Repeat neck ultrasound after approximately 6 months demonstrated macroscopic right lateral neck nodal disease; one suspicious node was described in the right lateral neck, level II/III region.  
- Post-hemithyroidectomy nodal evaluation identified abnormal right lateral and left lateral cervical nodes; FNA later confirmed metastatic disease in a right level V node and a left level IV node.  
- Ultrasound at approximately 18 weeks’ gestation showed no recurrence in the thyroid bed but marked interval increase in size and number of abnormal lymph nodes bilaterally.  
- Postpartum neck ultrasound showed two hyperechoic indeterminate nodes in the upper right level II neck.  
- Non-contrast chest CT postpartum demonstrated small bilateral non-calcified pulmonary nodules, indeterminate in nature. Prior CT imaging from 2017 reportedly did not show these nodules.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- ThyroSeq testing on indeterminate thyroid FNA identified a ROS1 fusion, reported as associated with a high probability of malignancy.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Thyroid function testing was normal at initial evaluation.  
- Postpartum TSH was suppressed.  
- Postpartum thyroglobulin was 19.2.  
- Thyroglobulin remained elevated at 6 months postpartum, with slight decline from the initial postpartum value.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- History of aplastic anemia treated with allogeneic bone marrow transplant in 2016, including total body irradiation.  
- Prior transplant course was complicated by graft-versus-host disease, aspergillus pneumonia, and amphotericin-associated drug-induced hepatitis; these complications had resolved by 2017.  
- Initial thyroid nodule surveillance was chosen in lieu of immediate FNA.  
- Thyroid nodule FNA later yielded indeterminate cytology.  
- Right hemithyroidectomy was performed; pathology confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Subsequent FNA of cervical lymph nodes confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma in a right level V node and a left level IV node.  
- Completion thyroidectomy with bilateral central and bilateral lateral neck dissection was performed at 20 weeks’ gestation.  
- No postoperative parathyroid dysfunction was reported.  
- She later delivered a healthy infant.  
- Radioactive iodine therapy had not yet been administered; treatment was deferred while breastfeeding.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent biochemical disease was present after completion thyroidectomy and neck dissection, with elevated thyroglobulin postpartum and at 6 months postpartum.  
- Structural concern for persistent disease remained in the right upper level II neck on ultrasound.  
- Small bilateral indeterminate pulmonary nodules were present on chest CT.  
- She remained under interval surveillance, with plans for repeat ultrasound and CT imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past complications from prior treatment had resolved by 2017.  
- She had undergone infertility treatment, including ovarian stimulation for egg retrieval, IVF-related treatment, and intrauterine insemination attempts prior to pregnancy.  
- Pregnancy was identified after postoperative nodal FNA confirmation of metastatic disease.  
- Maternal-fetal medicine follow-up occurred during pregnancy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Recent clinic presentation following a single episode of altered level of consciousness.

[ diagnosis ]: Pineal region/posterior tectal plate extra-axial lesion; radiologic impression favored epidermoid cyst. History of obstructive hydrocephalus requiring VP shunt insertion in 2005.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available. No biopsy had been performed.

[ imaging findings ]: Recent MRI brain demonstrated a well-defined non-enhancing lesion in the pineal region/posterior tectal plate region. The lesion was described as extra-axial, with CSF-like but slightly heterogeneous/“dirty” signal characteristics, insinuating between the basal cisterns. It was hyperintense on FLAIR, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and showed no significant pathological post-contrast enhancement on axial or sagittal post-contrast T1 imaging. It caused mild mass effect on the posterior aspect of the midbrain. No associated vasogenic edema or other abnormal signal intensity areas were described. A VP shunt was visible with the tip in the lateral ventricle. Comparison with prior imaging dating back to 2005 showed long-term stability over approximately 19–20 years.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: VP shunt insertion was performed in 2005 outside AQH for hydrocephalus associated with a brain lesion. No other prior oncologic or surgical treatment was documented. Disease remained radiologically stable for approximately 19–20 years after shunt placement.

[ current disease status ]: At recent presentation, the patient was neurologically intact with no focal deficits. The intracranial lesion remained radiologically stable and non-enhancing, with persistent mild mass effect on the posterior midbrain.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial presentation in 2005 included a brain lesion with hydrocephalus. Diffusion-weighted imaging was referenced but no definitive diffusion result was documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 36-year-old man. Morbid obesity. Past medical history included poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP, and hypertension. Employed in the railroad industry as a freight train conductor.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent palpable nodules in the thyroidectomy scar/central neck following prior treatment for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid, primary tumor size 4.2 cm, initially staged as intermediate-risk pT3a N1b. Subsequently developed radioactive iodine-refractory, biochemically persistent and structurally recurrent locoregional metastatic disease involving pretracheal/Delphian nodal tissue, subcutaneous peri-incisional soft tissue, sternocleidomastoid muscle, thyroid bed, strap muscle, paratracheal nodes, and cervical lymph nodes. No distant metastatic disease was identified.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial total thyroidectomy specimen: 4.2 cm multifocal left papillary thyroid carcinoma; no extrathyroidal extension; no lymphovascular invasion; negative margins; 2 of 4 central compartment lymph nodes positive.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of a superficial peri-incisional/scar nodule: positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- First reoperation pathology: 4 of 9 lymph nodes from pretracheal, subcutaneous, and muscular specimens were positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; metastatic thyroid carcinoma also involved skeletal muscle of the sternocleidomastoid.  
- Subsequent resection specimens: metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Pathology review specifically assessed for tall cell variant and did not identify tall cell variant.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial neck ultrasound and FNA led to diagnosis of thyroid malignancy.  
- Pre- and post-radioactive iodine scans demonstrated uptake confined to the thyroid bed/pyramidal lobe region, with no evidence of distant metastases.  
- Neck ultrasound at 6 months after initial treatment identified several nodules in the thyroidectomy bed, including a palpable superficial left nodule in the surgical scar; a suspicious node anterior to the trachea/prelaryngeal-central compartment region was described.  
- Additional ultrasound characterization localized some lesions to subcutaneous tissues rather than the central compartment; another lesion was identified within the sternocleidomastoid muscle.  
- Later ultrasound demonstrated two enlarged left level I lymph nodes with significant interval growth.  
- PET/CT demonstrated a large left cervical level II malignant node, additional smaller cervical nodes, small mediastinal nodes, and focal uptake in scar-line tissue.  
- Follow-up ultrasound showed anatomic progression of locoregional disease.  
- Non-contrast chest CT showed no metastatic disease in the chest.  
- Ongoing surveillance included alternating neck ultrasound and intermittent contrast-enhanced neck CT to assess the neck, including the retropharyngeal space.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular testing results were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Stimulated thyroglobulin after Thyrogen stimulation prior to radioactive iodine: 4.9.  
- Thyroglobulin subsequently documented at 1.9, later increased to 4.9 by the time of referral for recurrent disease.  
- After resection of recurrent disease, postoperative thyroglobulin was 2.2.  
- Six months later, thyroglobulin rose to 3.6.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of a right level I node later showed no malignant cells; thyroglobulin washout was not sent.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent total thyroidectomy for primary papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Received radioactive iodine ablation, 96 mCi, following Thyrogen stimulation. Post-therapy imaging showed uptake limited to the thyroid bed/pyramidal lobe region and no distant metastases.  
- Developed biochemical persistent disease and structural recurrence within 6 months.  
- Underwent resection of pretracheal/Delphian nodal tissue overlying the cricothyroid membrane, subcutaneous peri-incisional tissue superficial to the platysma, and an additional nodule within the sternocleidomastoid muscle.  
- Subsequently underwent further resection for palpable lymph node recurrence and lateral neck adenopathy.  
- Later underwent another revision central neck dissection for multiple sites of disease in the thyroid bed, strap muscle, and paratracheal nodes.  
- In total, had undergone four surgeries for locoregional disease.  
- No significant complications from surgeries or prior treatment were reported.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent locoregional recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma with a small palpable peri-incisional/central neck recurrence under surveillance. Disease had shown multiple rapid recurrences in the central neck after surgery and radioactive iodine, consistent with radioactive iodine-refractory locoregional disease. No evidence of distant metastases had been identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history was notable for a daughter recently diagnosed with thyroid cancer who had undergone surgery approximately 2 months earlier.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old multiparous woman; four living children; all prior deliveries were home deliveries. She remained menstruating at presentation. She had no history of contraceptive use. She was non-diabetic.

[ chief complaint ]: Irregular per-vaginal bleeding for 3 years, with occasional post-coital bleeding for 2 years. During the 2 months prior to referral, bleeding became excessive.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical adenocarcinoma, grade 2, identified on biopsy from a cervical growth. Clinical examination showed a broad, barrel-shaped cervix with cervical ectropion and an ulcerated growth measuring approximately 5–6 cm on the posterior lip of the cervix. Bimanual and rectovaginal examination found both parametria free and all fornices free. MRI demonstrated a cervical lesion with stromal ring disruption and extension into the parametrium/left broad ligament. Primary site distinction between cervix and endometrium remained unresolved on available data.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the cervical growth showed adenocarcinoma, grade 2. Endometrial curettage was performed; the histopathology result was not documented.

[ imaging findings ]: Ultrasonography showed:
- Uterus measuring 10.3 × 6.3 × 6.4 cm
- Endometrial thickness 28 mm
- Inhomogeneous cervix with a hypoechoic area measuring approximately 4.5 × 3.4 cm
- No hydroureter or hydronephrosis

MRI showed:
- Hyperintense cervical lesion measuring 3.2 × 6 cm
- Distortion of the hypointense cervical stromal ring
- Tumor protruding through a defect in the ring into the parametrium
- Ill-defined extension from the tumor to the left broad ligament
- No MRI comment was documented regarding any endometrial lesion

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Immunohistochemistry had not been performed. No molecular or genomic results were available. HPV testing had not been reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Severe anemia developed in association with heavy vaginal bleeding. She received 4 units of blood transfusion.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior to referral, she had been treated repeatedly with oral progesterone for irregular bleeding by different physicians. Symptoms improved while on medication, but treatment adherence was irregular. Following worsening bleeding and development of severe anemia, she was referred to the National Institute of Cancer Research Hospital. Blood transfusion with 4 units was administered.

[ current disease status ]: At referral assessment, she was anemic. All accessible lymph nodes were not palpable. Abdominal examination was normal. Pelvic examination demonstrated a bulky uterus, broad barrel-shaped cervix, cervical ectropion, and a 5–6 cm ulcerated growth on the posterior cervical lip. Both parametria were free on rectovaginal examination. Imaging demonstrated a locally advanced cervical-region mass with parametrial/left broad ligament extension. No hydronephrosis or hydroureter was identified. No distant metastatic evaluation results were documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Menstrual history was notable for continued menstruation at age 55. No palpable accessible lymphadenopathy was found on examination.

reference_conclusion: Further diagnostic clarification is required to determine the primary site of the adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry of the biopsy specimen should be obtained, with hysteroscopic endometrial evaluation and biopsy preferred if feasible, in order to distinguish cervical from endometrial origin and guide treatment selection. Sometimes people are found not transplantable or resectable. These immunotherapies are able to shrink it and bring it into sort of criteria. So not all hope is lost anymore. So we have very effective therapies, clinical trials. And one thing that we didn't explicitly say, but sort of referenced in this tumor board, the most important thing that I would say is if somebody is found to have liver cancer is to go to a multidisciplinary center. Not all doctors, not all practices are the same. Go to a center that has a setup where you have all of the doctors that are talking to each other to figure out your best therapy, not only at diagnosis, but as you go through your course. Once again, the time that I typically see people who aren't treated with surgical therapies if they're found early is if they just go to whoever down the street. And if you're a hammer, everything in life is a nail. But you want to have a toolbox where you have all the therapies that are being considered and weighed.

reference_conclusion: Surgical resection is not recommended at present because nodal involvement indicates extrahepatic disease and hepatic resection would not address the involved lymph node. The consensus recommendation is to initiate systemic therapy, with an immunotherapy combination as the preferred first-line approach given the absence of contraindications and preserved liver function. Management should proceed in a multidisciplinary setting, with future reconsideration of local or surgical options contingent on response and disease course.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging right-sided neck mass. He had no dysphonia or dysphagia. Laryngeal examination was normal at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally invasive metastatic poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (insular form), with mediastinal nodal metastases, pulmonary metastases, and tumor thrombus involving the right internal jugular vein.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the thyroid mass demonstrated differentiated thyroid carcinoma of aggressive insular type.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial contrast-enhanced CT neck/chest showed a large right thyroid/neck mass causing marked leftward tracheal deviation.  
- The mass was poorly circumscribed, extended near the esophagus, and there was loss of visible soft-tissue plane between the mass and the internal jugular vein.  
- Tumor extended through the cricothyroid membrane; no definite invasion of the tracheal lumen or laryngeal lumen was seen on the described imaging.  
- Tumor thrombus was present in the internal jugular vein, extending via the middle thyroid vein.  
- Carotid axis was described as encased/obscured by tumor on baseline imaging.  
- Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes were present.  
- Multiple small pulmonary metastases were present.  
- FDG PET demonstrated intense uptake in the primary thyroid/neck mass, mediastinal nodal metastases, pulmonary metastases, and the internal jugular vein tumor thrombus.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified an NRAS mutation. No BRAF mutation was detected. Ki-67 had been performed, but no numerical result was provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Anticoagulation with heparin was started because of internal jugular vein thrombosis/tumor thrombus.

[ current disease status ]: Locally invasive poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid/neck with tumor thrombus in the right internal jugular vein, enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, and multiple pulmonary metastases. He remained clinically well apart from the neck mass.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included hypercholesterolemia/vascular disease and prior transient ischemic attack.  
- Medications at presentation included low-dose aspirin.  
- He remained clinically well at presentation apart from the neck mass.  
- Vocal fold mobility was intact on laryngeal examination.

[ patient demographics ]: Sex was reported as male.

[ chief complaint ]: Pancreatic head/periampullary mass with multiple pulmonary nodules/metastatic lung lesions identified in 2025.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- History of colon cancer resected in 2015, stage pT3N0.  
- Subsequent metastatic adenocarcinoma involving the lung, with biopsy showing intestinal differentiation and immunophenotype suggestive of colorectal origin.  
- Concurrent pancreatic head/periampullary mass was present on imaging.  
- MSI status was stable.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Lung lesion biopsy showed adenocarcinoma with intestinal differentiation.  
- Immunohistochemistry on the biopsied lesion showed CK20 positive, CDX2 positive, CK7 negative.  
- CK19 was positive.  
- SMAD4 expression was retained/positive.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PET-CT showed a pancreatic mass lesion in the head/periampullary region.  
- Imaging described a locally advanced appearance of the pancreatic head mass.  
- The mass was reported to be abutting the duodenum.  
- PET-CT did not show uptake in the colon or elsewhere in the lower gastrointestinal tract.  
- No pelvic nodal disease was seen.  
- No liver lesions were seen.  
- Multiple lung nodules/metastatic lung lesions were present.  
- No obstructive jaundice was present clinically despite the pancreatic head/periampullary mass.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing showed KRAS mutation, APC mutation, and TP53 mutation.  
- Tumor mutational burden was 15.82 mutations/Mb.  
- MSI testing showed microsatellite stable disease.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- CEA was elevated, approximately 100.  
- CA 19-9 had not been performed.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Colon cancer had been treated surgically in 2015.  
- Pathologic stage at that time was pT3N0.  
- No adjuvant chemotherapy was given.  
- No adjuvant radiotherapy was given.  
- Disease-free interval between the 2015 colon surgery and the 2025 presentation was approximately 10 years.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Active disease was present in 2025 with a pancreatic head/periampullary mass and multiple pulmonary metastases.  
- No evidence of recurrent colonic lesion was seen on PET-CT at the time described.  
- No liver metastases were identified.  
- No pelvic nodal disease was identified.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Colonoscopy had not yet been completed at the time described and was being considered to evaluate for an occult colonic primary.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), diagnosed in April 2024. Recurrent disease was identified on 19 December 2025. Re-excision specimen showed recurrent high-grade glioma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial intracranial space-occupying lesion was diagnosed as GBM. Following recurrence, re-excision histopathology showed high-grade glioma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI performed at recurrence demonstrated a recurrent lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing on recurrent tumor identified TP53 mutation.  
- MGMT promoter methylation was positive.  
- IDH1/IDH2 alterations were not detected.  
- HRD was negative.  
- Tumor mutational burden was low.  
- Germline testing was positive for TP53.  
- TP53 variant allele fraction on tissue testing was reported as 42%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent right frontoparietal craniotomy with near-total excision after initial diagnosis in April 2024.  
- Received adjuvant radiotherapy to 60 Gy with concurrent temozolomide.  
- Subsequently received adjuvant temozolomide.  
- Achieved a disease-free interval of approximately 1.5 years.  
- At recurrence in December 2025, underwent re-excision.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent intracranial high-grade glioma/GBM following prior surgery, chemoradiation, and adjuvant temozolomide; status post re-excision for recurrence in December 2025.

[ other clinical data ]: Intracranial lesion was located in the right frontal/parietal region.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old premenopausal woman. No comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast lump.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast carcinoma, clinically operable. Initial clinical findings were a 4 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with a single mobile left axillary lymph node measuring 1.5 cm. Clinical stage details were not otherwise specified.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy from the left breast lesion showed grade 3 carcinoma. Hormone receptor testing showed estrogen receptor negative and progesterone receptor negative disease. HER2 was 3+ by immunohistochemistry.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing beyond receptor status was provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No details of adjuvant systemic therapy or radiotherapy administered were provided.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial axillary examination had identified a single mobile left axillary node measuring 1.5 cm. No distant disease evaluation was documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected renal mass on abdominal imaging performed during evaluation for diverticulosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Localized renal cell carcinoma of the kidney; postoperative diagnosis was clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pathologic stage pT1a.

[ histopathology results ]: Robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy specimen showed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, low grade, with negative surgical margins.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial abdominal imaging demonstrated an incidental 3 cm renal mass. The lesion was described as solid and enhancing, in a favorable posterior location. The colon was approximately 1 cm from the lesion.

[ laboratory results ]: Renal function was good at baseline. Postoperative kidney function changed minimally.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy. Surgical pathology confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, pT1a, with negative margins. Postoperative renal function was largely preserved.

[ current disease status ]: Status post robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, pT1a, with negative surgical margins and largely preserved renal function.

[ other clinical data ]: Past surgical history included appendectomy. The patient was otherwise described as healthy.

So I think this type of case is probably going to be referred to the urologist first. So maybe, Brandon, is this a typical case that you would see in your practice? And if it is, how do you sort of counsel a patient on what their options are?

Yeah, thanks, Mark. So, this is a pretty classic case that, you know, I think anybody who does kidney cancer sees a lot of these, you know, the incidental diagnosis, typically a smaller renal mass, under 4 centimeters. These are pretty common. So, you know, first thing that I do when I see a patient like this is try and get a sense of what the patient knows. Obviously, being at a cancer center, I may be the second, third, fourth, but sometimes I'm the first, you know, if they went to the ER. So starting by trying to get a sense of, you know, what the patient knows, what they've heard, right? A lot of information before I even say anything. So I sort of know how to frame my discussion with them. Sometimes, as we all probably know, patients come in with their own idea, mindset of what they want, right? And so it's important to get that from the get-go, because then you're sort of addressing the patient's needs on that sense. When it comes to this patient specifically for their mass, They have quite a few options. You know, this mask looks like it's solid, obviously. I'm sort of guessing, but it looks like it enhances. So, you know, statistically speaking, this is more likely than not a malignancy. One of the considerations here would be a biopsy to really prove that. I think the field has changed quite dramatically over the last several decades where we used to you know, think it was taboo to biopsy these things. But me personally, I tend to biopsy a lot of these small renal masses, especially in patients where they may not be the healthiest or if I'm worried I'm going to have to take a kidney. I really want to make sure I'm doing it for the right reasons. So that's something to consider. But I also don't think in a case like this, in a healthy patient with a pretty sizable mass and radiographic features that are pretty strongly pointing towards malignancy, proceeding with surgery or some kind of intervention is also reasonable. A little bit depends on the patient's comfort level with that. When it comes to treatment options, this patient, three centimeters is sort of the typical landmark we use when we talk about ablative versus surgical having equivalency. So at three centimeters, I think it's still within the realm. And lucky for this patient, the location of the mass is in a pretty good location for ablation. It's not really close to anything. The colon's a little close to it, but I think they could get that off with some saline or something. So They would have that as an option. I think the gold standard still in this case in an otherwise healthy patient, 3 centimeters and above, would be a partial nephrectomy. So that would be my initial recommendation. But obviously tell them I'm biased, I'm a surgeon, but I don't think they're unreasonable if they want to get some more information with a biopsy or meet with my IR colleagues. I think those would be the ones I would consider in this situation.

Excellent. I think that all that sounds similar to my practice as well. Brendan, let me ask you this. You mentioned biopsy. I think biopsy is being increasingly utilized. Is it something that you use often in your practice?

Yeah, I do. When I say often, I guess I'm comparing it to historically through my training where I saw my attendings. Rarely getting a biopsy except for sort of the more complex cases. I don't think if I were back in residency and I mentioned getting a biopsy, my attending right then and there would be like, what are you doing? And they weren't wrong. It wasn't in a lot of our guidelines. It wasn't really an established practice. So, that was the way it is. But I think the field is changing. Part of it is, As a surgeon, I really don't like it when I go in, cut something out, and find out it wasn't cancer, or the patient didn't need that operation, technically. Now, sometimes if patients are proceeding directly with intervention, I caution them on that, saying, listen, this isn't a guarantee, this is cancer, and that's an important thing. It seems a little ludicrous. I'd never go in and take somebody's prostate out without proving that they had prostate cancer or something like that. So, you know, those are the situations I try and avoid. Unfortunately, they happen to all of us. The MRI are great, but they are not perfect. And neither is a biopsy for that part too, so I caution them on that. But I do think biopsy is becoming more common. It's just an extra way to ensure that you're selecting the right patient for the right intervention. Absolutely.

So, you counsel the patient on these options and they say, you know, doc, that sounds great, but I really don't want to do surgery. You've mentioned ablation. That is not really ringing as a great option for this patient either. Is it ever appropriate to do surveillance for a tumor this size?

So, again, in this patient, how do you describe them? It's a pretty healthy person. Yeah, they had some diverticulitis hypertrophy. I think we would all agree, especially those who do surgery, this is a good surgical candidate from everything I've heard thus far. So, if that wasn't the case, then I think that definitely opens the door for watching these. In those cases for active surveillance, right, anything under two centimeters, it's well in our guidelines to monitor those. tumors, you know, obviously selection based on the patient characteristics matter a little bit too. Sometimes I'm a little more hesitant to watch a tumor that's really central in the kidney and close to the vessels where I already know it's going to be difficult making it bigger just potentially as long as I'm trying to spare the kidney. But in a case like this, in a favorable location, you know, a couple, half a centimeter here or there is probably not going to change my management. So from a surgical perspective, I'd be okay watching this, but there's a cancer perspective. And if the patient's really sick, has some comorbidities, then I think it's reasonable to entertain that option as long as the patient's on board too. And in those cases, almost for sure, I'd get a biopsy if at all possible to help sort of guide management. And again, if this is a clear cell, which this, you know, statistically speaking, most likely to be, you just have to caution, you know, there's good data from Mayo and other places, you know, historical rates for the development of metastasis based on the primary tumor size. So, something like this, about three centimeters, I think looking at that data, you'd estimate, you know, probably a one to two percent, maybe up to a three percent chance if they had some bad histology.

Excellent. Well said. I'm gonna throw things over to Rakib. Rakib, you know, this patient, after meeting with the urologist, thinks surgery sounds okay, but wants to really explore all their options. And, you know, their brother had radiation for their prostate cancer, wants to hear what's going on in 2025 with radiation for kidney cancers. You know, in my training, just a little while ago, we used to say that renal cell carcinoma, you know, there's no role for radiation. And that's really not at all where we are now. So, Can you kind of tell us what's changed? What does the up-to-date data say for treatment of primary renal masses with radiation?

Absolutely. So, renal cancer used to be considered radio-resistant, but mainly to the older form of fractionated radiation, those radiation that was delivered over five, six, seven weeks. Now at that time we did not have the technology to deliver the high dose focused radiation to a target such as kidney which as you may know moves with breathing. So it becomes much more difficult to target and focus the radiation. But now we do have the technology that is what is called the stereotactic radiation. You may often hear the abbreviation SBRT or SABR. With the application of SABR, we have seen local controls that are on the order of 95% to even 100%. So far, three trials have been reported, the Fast Track 1, Fast Track 2, and our own Phase 2 trial. And we have data that is about five to six years out. So reasonable duration data, reasonable number of patients, and we have been able to get local controls on the order of 95% to 100%. The benefits, of course, with Savor, it takes one planning session and then either a single treatment or three treatments. These are completely non-invasive. The patient is just laying on the table for about an hour on the maximum. This particular case, it's a posterior location, favorable location for us. Colon is about a centimeter away, which does not bother me as much, particularly because, again, with the advancement of technology, we are able to do adaptive radiation. We can even take into account daily motions that may be there in this colon. And we should be able to deliver and adequately offer local control for this patient.
Fantastic. Are there any locations or any type of comorbidities that takes SBRT off the table?

So comorbidities, no. I mean, comorbidities actually, those are patients that we are seeing because they are not surgical candidates typically. Location-wise, and that's a good point, you know, size, I keep saying size is not an issue, but location is more key. So if you have an exophytic anterior tumor that is up against small bowel, That's something that I would worry about and something that, you know, there will be increased risk of bowel damage or small bowel damage. So that would be the one case where I would worry about.
Got it. Excellent. And, Reina, is there any role for systemic therapy for patients with localized small renal masses? We often think about for advanced disease, but what about in this space?

You know, quite honestly, if we weren't going to do any local treatment, the patient wasn't a candidate for surgery because of comorbidities, also wasn't a candidate for focal therapy, whether that be SBRT or cryoablation or some other radiofrequency ablation, then I think we really have to think and talk about our goals of care and what do we anticipate is going to be the risk of this renal mass impacting that individual's survival if they're not a candidate for any of the above items. And generally in that situation, I'm watching expectantly as opposed to putting somebody on systemic therapy for a three centimeter mass. So I think, you know, it all depends upon the risk of the mass and competing risks in the patient that may impact the patient's life expectancy.

Well said, and I think when we're thinking about any treatment, really weighing the risk and benefits and the competing morbidity and mortality risk is we should all be doing that whether we're treating with surgery, ablative therapies, radiation, or systemic therapy. So, excellent points. So, for this case, I think we sort of hit these topics. So, what we did here is we did surgery. We did a robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy and sort of what we would expect. This was a clear cell RCC, it was low grade, it was I sub grade 2, pathologic T1A with negative margins, kidney function didn't change much. So maybe back to Brandon, how do you surveil these patients post-surgery and is this a patient that you would be calling Reina about to think about adjuvant therapy or no?

Yeah, so for follow-up for these patients, so first of all, this patient has what we sort of expected, so I don't think there was any, you know, curveballs or anything in their post-op path. So hopefully the patient's sort of prepared for this. Again, this is a good prognosis. You know, I would tell the patient, based off this kind of pathology, you know, well over 90% cure rate. So that usually puts them at ease. And because of that, I probably wouldn't pick up the phone and call Dr. McKay for this specific patient. I think we're going to get into a little more of the role of adjuvant, which is obviously a big part of how we manage patients. But in this case, it's still a little classic bread and butter. And so for this one, I would just recommend surveillance. And for me, I pretty much follow the NCCN guidelines, which, you know, I'd usually get a patient imaging about six months, if that looks good, go to once a year at this point. And that's how I would follow them. Unless, of course, I had some suspicion about hereditary family genetics, something like that. But that would be the standard.

Excellent. And going back to Reina, when you see a patient post-surgery and just much like the radiation space has changed, really the adjuvant therapy space has changed over the last few years to something that was where we didn't have great options and then now with Pembro with a survival benefit to adjuvant Pembrolizumab, we're really talking about adjuvant therapy after surgery more and more. So who are your ideal candidates for to consider adjuvant therapy?

You know, I think I revert back to the Kino 564 eligibility criteria and that largely included patients who had T2 grade 4 tumors, T3, T4, N1. It also included patients who are M1 resected to NED. And there's some caveats there regarding the sites of resection that were permissible. And that did not include, which we'll get to probably later, people who were deemed NED because of SBRT as opposed to a surgical outcome. So this patient who's got a T1A grade 2 expected management, I mean, I would not offer any adjuvant treatment.

Excellent. And this patient went on to have NCCN-based surveillance and has done well. So I think we can move on to our next case. This is also a localized case, but this is a 45-year-old man who is found to have bilateral renal masses, no family history of kidney cancer, a few comorbidities that are well managed, and good kidney function. And he comes in with these scans, and I just have one cut of each, but just a single mass in each kidney. In the right kidney, a large, somewhat central mass. And in the left kidney, a completely endophytic mass, also somewhat central going into the renal sinus. We can start off with Rakib here. You kind of told us before about size doesn't really matter for SBRT and location as long as it's not abutting, you know, critical structures, which to me doesn't appear. So would this patient be a candidate, you think, for SBRT based on these imaging?

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy for the 3 cm renal mass. Final pathology demonstrated low-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, pathologic stage pT1a, with negative margins and preserved renal function. No adjuvant systemic therapy was indicated, and surveillance was recommended in accordance with NCCN guidelines, with imaging at approximately 6 months followed by annual imaging thereafter.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male.

[ chief complaint ]: Breathing difficulty/airway compromise in the setting of a large thyroid mass with intratracheal tumor extension.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced papillary thyroid carcinoma involving the thyroid, trachea, and cricoid, with gross extrathyroidal extension.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial fine-needle aspiration biopsy: well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma; no anaplastic or poorly differentiated component identified.  
- Core biopsy: well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma; no anaplastic component identified.  
- Intra-tracheal debulking specimen/biopsy from intraluminal tumor: well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma; no necrosis or anaplastic component identified.  
- Pathology review was performed at multiple institutions and remained consistent with well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline contrast-enhanced CT neck demonstrated a large partially calcified thyroid mass replacing the left thyroid lobe and isthmus.  
- The mass encased the trachea and extended through the anterior tracheal wall with intratracheal involvement.  
- The mass was inseparable from the esophagus, with possible esophageal infiltration.  
- Loss of the fat plane posteriorly was concerning for prevertebral muscle infiltration.  
- Fat planes between the mass and the carotid vessels were largely preserved; no definite direct carotid invasion was identified on imaging.  
- No abnormal cervical lymphadenopathy was identified on CT.  
- Esophagoscopy showed no luminal esophageal tumor.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular/genomic result was documented.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed and showed well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.  
- Core biopsy was performed and showed well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.  
- The patient underwent operative airway evaluation with intra-tracheal tumor debulking/microdebridement for breathing compromise; pathology again showed well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma without necrosis or anaplastic features.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Left renal mass consistent with locally advanced renal malignancy. In a separate metastatic presentation, there was a locally advanced left renal tumor with bilateral pulmonary nodules and multiple hypervascular liver nodules concerning for metastatic disease.

[ current disease status ]: In the metastatic presentation, disease burden included a locally advanced left renal tumor, multiple hypervascular liver nodules, and small-volume bilateral pulmonary nodules; bone scan and brain MRI showed no metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was unremarkable. Past surgical history was unremarkable. ECOG performance status was 0. Uncontrolled hypertension was present.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old man; university student.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-year history of left-sided suboccipital headache radiating to the neck, slurred speech, difficulty chewing food, blurred vision, and dysphagia predominantly for solid foods; semi-solids and liquids were tolerated. Hoarseness was also reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Left hypoglossal canal dumbbell-shaped lesion, radiologically favored to represent a hypoglossal schwannoma.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a left-sided expansile lesion centered on the hypoglossal canal with intracranial and extracranial components, producing a dumbbell configuration. The lesion was described as iso-intense and ill-defined on T1-weighted imaging and heterogeneously enhancing on post-contrast imaging. T2-weighted imaging showed the lesion abutting the brainstem without T2 hyperintense signal change within the brainstem. The lesion abutted the left cerebellar hemisphere posteriorly, extended toward the ipsilateral jugular foramen, and extended inferiorly beyond the hypoglossal canal into the upper cervical region to the level of the C1 lateral mass. The ipsilateral vertebral artery lay anterior to and abutted the lesion. The ipsilateral petrous internal carotid artery also abutted the lesion. MRI measurements were 20.4 mm anteroposterior, 26.1 mm transverse, and 23.4 mm craniocaudal. CT skull base imaging demonstrated erosion/expansion of the ipsilateral occipital condyle with preserved cortical/articular component.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior surgical treatment, radiotherapy, or systemic therapy was documented. No prior comparative imaging was available. Clinical follow-up had been limited to two clinic visits, and radiologic progression could not be assessed due to absence of reference imaging.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic skull base lesion with persistent left hypoglossal nerve palsy. Examination showed fair general condition; the patient was alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Visual acuity and fundoscopy were normal. Cranial nerve examination demonstrated left hypoglossal nerve palsy with left tongue hemiatrophy, ipsilateral tongue deviation, and intermittent fasciculations. Other cranial nerves were clinically intact. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Systemic examination was normal. There was no radiologic evidence of brainstem edema or signal change.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbid illness was reported. There was no history of trauma or prior irradiation. Dysphagia affected solids more than semi-solids or liquids.

Preoperative CT skull base imaging, with dynamic assessment for instability as needed, was advised to define condylar involvement and guide the need for fusion. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 83-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: New skin lesion on the left ear; interval development of a second enlarging nodule superior/posterior to the biopsy site prior to planned surgery.

[ diagnosis ]: Merkel cell carcinoma of the left ear with additional left upper neck cutaneous Merkel cell carcinoma and metastatic involvement of the left parotid lymph nodes. Reported stage was stage IIIA.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy of the left ear lesion was positive for Merkel cell carcinoma. Following surgery, pathology from the left ear lesion showed multicentric Merkel cell carcinoma; largest focus measured 1.0 x 0.9 cm, thickness 9 mm, with 13 mitoses and positive lymphovascular invasion; margins were negative. The left upper neck cutaneous lesion also showed Merkel cell carcinoma measuring 4 mm with negative margins. Left parotid specimen contained 2 of 8 lymph nodes positive for metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma; largest metastatic deposit measured 9 mm and showed extranodal extension. No additional metastatic nodes were identified in the neck dissection specimen.

[ imaging findings ]: CT showed an enhancing nodular soft tissue lesion in the left earlobe measuring 1.1 cm. No evidence of metastatic disease was identified on initial imaging. Subsequent post-treatment PET imaging showed no evidence of disease. Follow-up PET imaging 5 months later showed a hypermetabolic liver focus and several bony lesions suspicious for metastatic disease.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver biopsy was planned within 1-2 weeks following detection of the hypermetabolic liver lesion. No biopsy result was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past medical history included chronic lymphocytic leukemia, colon cancer diagnosed in 2013, hypertension, and a long history of cutaneous malignancies of the head and neck. He had undergone more than 50 nasal resections and received radiotherapy to the face and scalp in 2021 for prevention of recurrence of prior skin cancers. For the current Merkel cell carcinoma, he underwent left partial auriculectomy, resection of a new left neck cutaneous tumor, left parotidectomy, and neck dissection (levels II and III). Sentinel lymph node biopsy was not performed. He subsequently completed adjuvant radiotherapy. Post-treatment PET showed no evidence of disease.

[ current disease status ]: After initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy, post-treatment imaging showed no evidence of disease. At 5-month follow-up, PET demonstrated a hypermetabolic liver focus and multiple osseous lesions suspicious for metastatic recurrence; tissue confirmation was pending.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included chronic lymphocytic leukemia, colon cancer in 2013, and hypertension. He had an extensive history of head and neck skin cancers.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Paraparesis for 4 months.

[ diagnosis ]: D7 spinal anastomosing hemangioma with cord compression; residual disease remained after decompressive surgery.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from the paravertebral component was reported as anastomosing hemangioma. No histopathology specimen was taken from the intradural component.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative contrast-enhanced MRI of the dorsal spine dated 11 March 2024 showed an enhancing lesion with an extraspinal component at the D7 level. T2-weighted imaging demonstrated involvement of at least 2–3 vertebral bodies with heterogeneous punctate signal and extension into the posterior elements. Vertebral body heights and endplates were preserved, with no compression fracture described. There was extension into the thecal sac/intrathecal space and a right paravertebral component. T2 fat-suppressed images showed multiple punctate flow voids. Post-contrast T1-weighted imaging showed intense homogeneous enhancement. Additional smaller similar signal abnormalities were described in the lower cervical and upper dorsal vertebrae. PET scan performed as part of metastatic workup was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was negative/within normal limits on metastatic workup.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Dorsolaminectomy and spinal cord decompression were performed. Complete excision was not attempted because the lesion was highly vascular intraoperatively with significant bleeding; decompression and limited safe resection/biopsy were performed. Metastatic workup prior to surgery, including PET scan and PSA, was negative.

[ current disease status ]: Residual lesion remained after surgery. Neurological function improved postoperatively: preoperative motor power had been proximal 3/5 bilaterally and distal 2/5; subsequently proximal power improved to 4/5 and distal power to 3/5. The patient was able to walk with support.

[ other clinical data ]: At presentation, examination showed proximal motor power of both extremities 3/5 and distal power 2/5. The patient had signs of spinal cord compression and was paraplegic at the time of surgical intervention.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of progressive left-sided headache and painful ophthalmoplegia with diplopia, left-sided ptosis, vomiting, and unintentional weight loss of 26 pounds.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma in the setting of hepatitis C-related chronic liver disease/cirrhosis. Symptomatic left skull base/sellar-region lesion involving the pituitary, sphenoid sinus, and cavernous sinus, with differential not histologically confirmed at the time of reporting.

[ histopathology results ]: No liver biopsy had been performed. No histopathologic confirmation of the skull base/sellar lesion was available at the time of reporting.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal imaging demonstrated a cirrhotic liver with hypertrophy of the left lateral and caudate lobes and more than 15 variable-sized hypodense/hypointense lesions involving both hepatic lobes. The largest lesions measured 37 mm in segment 3 and 27 mm in segment 5. These lesions showed arterial phase enhancement with venous and delayed phase washout, consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma. MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated an ill-defined lesion involving the left pituitary, sphenoid sinus, and cavernous sinus with encasement of the left internal carotid artery, measuring 33 mm anteroposteriorly, 20 mm transversely, and 27 mm craniocaudally. Review of the MRI described extension into the sphenoid sinus and clivus, predominantly T2 hypointense signal, smooth appearance, complete filling of the left sphenoid sinus, preserved aeration of the right sphenoid sinus, and possible clival invasion; the epicenter was described as appearing more within the sphenoid sinus than the cavernous sinus.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Alpha-fetoprotein levels were 36.2 in February, 55.1 in April, 106.4 in June, and 167.5 on 19 September.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Trans-arterial chemoembolization was performed in February. Systemic therapy with lenvatinib and sofosbuvir was ongoing at the time of reporting.

[ current disease status ]: Multifocal hepatic disease remained present on imaging. The patient remained symptomatic from the left skull base/sellar-region lesion, with cranial neuropathies on examination including left pupil-sparing third nerve palsy and left sixth nerve palsy, with visual symptoms reported as worsening.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included diabetes mellitus and hepatitis C-related chronic liver disease. He was a non-smoker and did not consume alcohol. Family history was significant for hepatocellular carcinoma in his father; his brother had undergone liver transplantation. Examination demonstrated left pupil-sparing third cranial nerve palsy and sixth cranial nerve palsy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 85-year-old Taiwanese male.

[ chief complaint ]: Intermittent hemoptysis beginning in June, with progression over weeks to intermittent stridor. Associated cough was present. He had known right thyroid fullness and induration.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, stage IVC, with pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid demonstrated high-grade carcinoma with squamous features, interpreted as most consistent with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed normal vocal cords with a lesion beyond the cords in the subglottic/tracheal region. CT neck/chest demonstrated a thyroid mass involving the right side, invading the right lateral aspect of the trachea, with tracheal deviation and suspected tracheal erosion/invasion. CT chest demonstrated bilateral pulmonary nodules, including a large spiculated lesion in the left lung and additional right-sided and left lower lung nodules, reported as consistent with pulmonary metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E testing was negative. PAX8 was positive. Thyroglobulin was negative. TTF-1 was negative. Tumor mutation burden was low. PD-L1 status was low or negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: He had no prior surgery and was not taking thyroid medication. He was hospitalized for approximately 1 week with worsening airway distress. He declined tracheostomy, tracheal resection, radiation therapy, and toxic chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Stage IVC anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with pulmonary metastases and progressive airway compromise manifested by intermittent stridor and hemoptysis.

[ other clinical data ]: Otherwise healthy prior to presentation. No family history of thyroid cancer.
