case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old premenopausal woman. Previously healthy. No comorbidities. No family history of breast cancer. Past surgical history included myomectomy in 2009.

[ chief complaint ]: Suspicious left breast mass detected on screening mammography at the end of 2014.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive lobular carcinoma, stage IB, pT1c pN1mi M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial surgery consisted of quadrantectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. Pathology showed invasive lobular carcinoma measuring 1.1 cm, grade 2, with multiple foci of lobular carcinoma in situ. Surgical margin showed atypical lobular hyperplasia with one focus of lobular carcinoma in situ. Fourteen axillary lymph nodes were removed; 2/14 contained metastatic disease, each with diameter 0.1 cm, consistent with micrometastatic nodal involvement. Hormone receptor testing showed estrogen receptor positive and progesterone receptor positive disease. HER2 was negative. Ki-67 was 10%.

[ imaging findings ]: Screening mammogram demonstrated a suspicious mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, BI-RADS 4. Diagnostic ultrasound and breast MRI confirmed a 1.2 cm spiculated nodule at the 2 o’clock position in the left breast, 4 cm from the nipple. No suspicious axillary lymph nodes were identified on imaging. Staging workup showed no metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No genomic assay results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the breast lesion was positive for malignancy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent quadrantectomy with axillary lymph node dissection.

[ current disease status ]: After breast-conserving surgery and axillary dissection with staging evaluation, there was no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Lobular carcinoma in situ was present at the surgical margin.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

So in retrospect, what I would have done, I don't know if fentanyl node is being done or not in this place. But if it is, you could stop. You don't need to do a neutron dissection after a small, tiny positive neutrons like that. And you just give the treatment of the axilla to radiation, because she will get radiation anyhow. And I would just do high tensions, which will cover the level 1 and 2 in the axilla.

Now, I need a medical, like Susan, I'm going to hand you the question of, what are you doing in the era of post-text, post-soft data? This is a perimenopausal, declared premenopausal, 47-year-old patient with neopositive breast cancer, and the question is, what is the choice of optimal adjuvant endocrine therapy, and what is the duration? What is the duration? So, if you could just address this whole point, that'd be good.

Well, I guess the most important thing is to develop a regimen that a patient's going to be compliant with long term. So I think based on the soft and text study, the ideal treatment in my mind for someone who's a higher risk that you've given chemotherapy to would be to offer them ovarian suppression with an aromatase inhibitor. Having said that, many women cannot tolerate that. So this patient, I would view, is not in the highest risk category to really say, dogmatically, this is what I would prefer. But that would be the best therapy available. But in this particular case, I think I would have an honest discussion with her about various side effects, comparing ovarian suppression, starting that with first month, and then maybe adding in the aromatase inhibitor at month two. and she didn't tolerate ovarian suppression, then you could back off and think about extended tamoxifen or starting with tamoxifen and switching to an aromatase inhibitor once she's clearly post-menopausal.

So I think, Susan, you're saying that I think a trial of endocrine therapy is always the appropriate way to address patients. Anything we give, tamoxifen, ovarian suppression, or anything, it's always a trial. And I think in the first three months, patients sort of know how they're going to be on a treatment. I think patients between 45 and 55 are most vulnerable to side effects from endocrine therapy, more so than younger women and older women. So I think those are the problematic patients. She's in a problematic age and may not tolerate. But the good thing is these days we can reverse any kind of endocrine therapy decision. So that's good. And then I think that in my own mind, actually, it doesn't matter what kind of endocrine therapy you give, It's so much better than none. And any kind of endocrine therapy is a lot better than none. When you're talking about what kind of chemotherapy, you're talking about a difference between last year's model of a motor car and this year's model. But the difference between having a motor car or not is the big difference. And having some form of endocrine therapy, I think, is important. And in 2016, we are hoping to present data on MA17R, which we'll talk about five, ten years of aromatase inhibitor rather than five, as is the NSABP B42 trial going to present. So a lot of patients are asking after five years, should I continue my aromatase inhibitor or not? For the time being, I'm continuing because we're on the brink of a result. So for those patients where there's indecision, why not just continue if they're tolerating it well and have no financial duress or anything. Continue it until the results are available. But at the end of the day, longer endocrine therapy seems to be better than shorter. That's what all the data is pointing to. So some form of endocrine option is probably preferable to, and longer, is probably preferable to not. So that's my overall opinion about that subject. And then there's a question here about the best imaging modality for follow-up? I don't know quite what the question is. Michelle, can you comment on an invasive lobular that's been excised or had a mastectomy?

So with a lumpectomy, if she had completed the lumpectomy, it would be yearly screening mammography. We don't necessarily add breast MRI to one screening and follow-up. if they've had a lobular without a family history of breast cancer. In fact, I would argue that their risk of creating a new cancer in the contralateral breast is improved because the hormonal therapy they're on for the treatment of their known breast cancer. After bilateral mastectomy, I know that in this situation, you had noted some residual breast parenchyma, so it's kind of an interesting different situation, but we would, you know, not do any imaging Even our plastic surgeons feel like imaging the implants is not a have to and really any issues that we have with regards to implants are things that we can detect clinically. So it would be a yearly clinical exam by a surgeon and a yearly clinical chest wall exam with the other physicians involved in their care, the medical oncologist and the radiation oncologist.

reference_conclusion: The panel concluded that prophylactic contralateral skin-sparing mastectomy is not indicated solely on the basis of invasive lobular carcinoma, and that LCIS at the margin does not warrant re-excision because it does not increase local failure risk. For adjuvant systemic therapy, endocrine treatment was considered essential; for this premenopausal patient who received chemotherapy, ovarian suppression plus an aromatase inhibitor was identified as the preferred option, with tamoxifen or extended tamoxifen as acceptable alternatives based on tolerability and menopausal status. For follow-up after bilateral mastectomy, routine imaging was not recommended; surveillance should consist of annual clinical examination of the chest wall and surgical follow-up.

[...] when we have LCIS at the margin, we do not try to achieve negative margin, because there is no evidence that LCIS at the margin increase the risk of local failure. [...] So for me, just because someone has lobular cancer does not mean that they're going to automatically get a bilateral mastectomy. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old woman; gravida 4, para 3. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Postcoital bleeding.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, stage IB2 at initial diagnosis. Subsequent progressive disease with parametrial infiltration after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed later by pulmonary metastatic progression.

[ histopathology results ]: Pap smear/cervical cytology was reported as squamous carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial extension studies were negative, including CT, colonoscopy, and urography. After radiotherapy and brachytherapy, CT pelvis demonstrated parametrial infiltration. Subsequent CT scan demonstrated pulmonary progression with a few lung nodules/metastases.

[ laboratory results ]: HIV test was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial management at another hospital consisted of neoadjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin for 3 cycles; there was no response. She was then referred for radiation therapy followed by brachytherapy. Approximately 1 month later, she was admitted with abdominal pain; pelvic CT showed parametrial infiltration and pelvic examination demonstrated exophytic/infiltrative cervical disease, consistent with progression. She then received chemotherapy with cisplatin, topotecan, and bevacizumab. Bevacizumab was administered for 1 dose only. After 2 cycles of chemotherapy, she was admitted again because of pain. Repeat CT showed lung progression.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive cervical cancer after paclitaxel/carboplatin, radiation therapy, brachytherapy, and cisplatin/topotecan/bevacizumab, with parametrial involvement and pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: She had abdominal pain at the time of pelvic progression and pain again at the time of subsequent pulmonary progression.

reference_discussion.text: Okay. This is a case of a 49-year-old woman with four pregnancies and three natural births. She has no family history of cancer, and she consulted in another hospital because of bleeding after sexual intercourse. They made a pap smear with the SCAMOS carcinome, and she had negative extension studies, the CT, colonoscopy, and neurography. The diagnosis was Eskamos carcinoma E1B2. So the treatment plan in that center was neoadjuvant chemotherapy with Eclitaxel and carboplatin for three cycles. After that, she had no response. And she was referred to our hospital for radiation therapy, followed by brachytherapy. And after that, maybe one month after that, she was admitted in the hospital because of abdominal pain. And we made a CT pelvis, and she had parametral infiltration. And the pelvic exam was exofiltration in 4K. So the diagnosis was disease progression again. The treatment plan in our hospital was chemotherapy with cisplatin, topothecan, and bevacizumab. And after two cycles of chemotherapy, she was admitted again in the hospital because of pain. I want to say that the Bevacizumab, she received just one doses because of the delay on the drop. So we made a CT scan, and I have the result today, and she has a lung progression. So the question in this case is about the neoadjuvant treatment in cervical cancer. For which stage is appropriate, and what is the response that you have, because we have a lot of case. we don't have to respond with the neoadjuvant treatment. And in this case that the patient is progressive, what is the new treatment options?
So when you say disease progression, what exactly do you mean?
When she has the diagnosis, she had no parametral infiltration. And after the first chemotherapy, she has. And now she has a lung progression. She has a few nodes in the lungs.

Now, that's the second type of progression. She's got progression twice. After cisplatin and Topatit can do cisimide, she's been found to have lung meds. They got the CET result just today or yesterday.

And I want to say something, because this is not the regular treatment that we have. We always start with cisplatin and radiotherapy. And the second line is carboplatin plus faclitaxel. But she came from another hospital already with that drugs. So we didn't have another option than this last treatment with topotecan and bevacizumab.

So we don't really have a large experience doing neoadjuvant therapy here in the United States for cervical cancer. You know, if we extrapolate from breast – and Paul can correct me if I'm wrong – when you do neoadjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer and there's a lack of progression, we will automatically or oftentimes we'll just take them to surgery. Rather than try medical therapy for a second or rather even a third time, just try to get the tumor out and then restart again. You know, I know that the use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy is far more common in Latin America as well as Asia, but again, it's not something that we do routinely. Indications here, and what I've seen, is locally advanced cervical cancer, and then folks who are otherwise not candidates for surgery. I don't know, MD Anderson, are you guys, Kathleen, are you guys using much of the way of neoadjuvant?

We're using almost none. The only time we start with chemo is if they have disease outside the pelvis. So if they have locally advanced disease, that can be radiation. But we have had a few cases where they present with a super club node as well, something else, and we give them chemo. And then if they have a very dramatic response, We have gone back and radiated. But that's completely out of the box and not usual. But we don't. But I think it's a very interesting question. Tom Randall and I have talked a lot about this for countries that don't have a lot of radiation therapy available or the wait is really long. I mean, I think that here we don't use it because we have access to such great radiation. But I think it's a really important question. for us to answer, hopefully with studies, with our partners in Latin America.

I think the limitation that I think we have here is largely what Don hit on earlier, which is that there are no randomized data. The data that we have are largely from retrospective meta-analyses. And I think the problem with those studies is that the comparison arm, which is radiation, for the age of chemoradiation therapy, so it's very outdated. I think if you look at the studies, the largest meta-analysis includes about 21 studies, and it's a very heterogeneous group of chemotherapy regimens that were used to give the neoadjuvant treatment, so the studies that we have, the data that we have are problematic, but there is a, I think, here's the URTC, 5599, and I think there's another study in India that hopefully will give us a better sense of what right regimen is compared to chemo radiation therapy.
There's also a study that's opened in Europe, England has opened it, that's looking at neoadjuvant compared to chemoRT, and they're actually accruing right now as well.
Is that the interlace study?
Yes, the interlace study, exactly.
So we're making a note of all these studies, and we're going to distribute them to all the viewers and participants after this term of award. to be able to look at these studies.

But Mayra, you know, in terms of your question about the activity of carboplatin taxol, it's supposed to be really good. You know, 70 to 80 percent is what's reported in the literature in terms of response rates. So, you know, the question of, you know, why she didn't respond is a really interesting one, but it's rather uncommon, I think, that patients don't respond to carbolintaxol. And in fact, to see frank progression on carboplatin taxol is quite worrisome for a squamous cell.

I agree, and I think it means that... It's a terrible case, and I don't think that you should have a lot of feeling that anything was mismanaged in this case. It's highly unusual for a cancer to be this aggressive. Presenting locally advanced like this, there was a very high risk that there was microscopic metastatic disease that would not have been addressed by radical surgery, and that that disease was chemoresistant. And furthermore, Generally, the molecular changes that make something chemotherapy-resistant also make it radiotherapy-resistant, as we see in this case. And so I think the cards were stacked against us with this case, and I'm not sure that a different approach from the start or during her course would have made a difference from the fundamental things we see biologically about this cancer.
There was a nice review that was just published just this year on neoadjuvant chemotherapy. I can pull it for Paul and he can send it out to you if you'd like.

So it sounds like, am I right in concluding that in the US, The reason neoadjuvant chemotherapy has not been so well-explored is because of the accessibility of radiation, so radiation chemo is more usual.

Yeah. Al Cubbins from Canada and I tried to propose a neoadjuvant chemotherapy trial. It was not supported by the hysteria committee. And I think it's because, for the exact reason, that chemoradiation is so widely available. And for a large proportion of folks, we can cure people. There just wasn't much appetite, although Inuja was clearly in favor of doing the trial.

So the South Americans can look forward to data from, I think I heard, three ongoing trials. At least three ongoing clinical trials, Myra, will answer the question about chemoradiation versus a neoadjuvant chemo alone. And so the data aren't there today, but Don Dijon is going to give us a meta-analysis publication of the data that is available in the literature, and we will circulate it off this tumor board. So thank you very much for that case. And because we are...
I'm sorry, I just have one question. Do you have any equipment for this patient?
Ask the question again, please.
if you have any idea of the new treatment for this patient now that she's progressed again.
OK, just hang on. Anuta?

I don't think there's a good answer for this. I think it sounds like she's getting cis-topal, right? Cis-topal progression. Cis-topal bath progression. So I think you gave her kind of the best, in my mind, the best chance with cis-topal and Avastin. I don't think there is. wouldn't have good chemotherapy at this point. I mean, here we would offer a single agent chemotherapy for palliation, but that's about it. There's nothing good to offer her. Yeah, so the only treatments that probably have data that you could use is Olimta, or Pemetrexet, has some data. Although, again, a lot of our trials that were done were really an older population that didn't see path attacks all before. But Olimta is one that we use, and then Vinarelbin. A Phase I trialist is going to open a trial using a nivolumab, which is an immune checkpoint inhibitor, and that's fairly promising, particularly for virally-mediated malignancies. So that's going to be an option. Hopefully, that will be open here in the next few months. And they have an entire cohort for cervix vulva vaginal cancers, because all of those are HPV mediated. So there's some preliminary data that shows these checkpoint inhibitors are important for viral cancers. And if you are able to try to enroll her in a trial using an immune checkpoint inhibitor, it might be her best shot.
Just a reality check, I mean those drugs are like... a gazillion dollars, right? I mean, I...
I said clinical trial, not off-label.

Okay, I agree, but just, you know, when someone progresses through primary treatment with Taxol and Carboflatin, I mean, I know we're all oncologists and we're forever hopeful, but I think just the reality of the situation is that supportive care has been shown to work probably as well as all these chemo agents, and clearly, you know, we could try existing drugs like gemcitabine or nabalbine, but the probability of these working are extremely, extremely low. So I think here in Houston, we would send this patient obviously for, or offer this patient a clinical trial. A lot of times with something that you mentioned, Don, which I think are great options for the future, but I think you know, realistically, I think we'd be happy to realize that the prognosis for this patient is extremely poor and, you know, in the absence of the possibility of a clinical trial, that really to consider supportive care as our first recommendation.

Great. Just a small comment. One is to make sure that the pathology has been interpreted correctly. It's just that I agree with Tom that it's a very unusual presentation and progression of disease for your typical squamous cell. And the other thing is, if the patient has been tested for HIV, just to make sure that she doesn't have other life, we already did it, and she's negative.

And I'd like to make one commitment and comment that I've been itching to involve our very advanced palliative care services here at MGH for a tumor board, and we may be able to combine the cervix and breast cancer groups together, and we have a master end-of-life palliative care, supportive care tumor board, and I think this is an area you know, sort of great importance to doctors in South America. So we will be doing that this coming year in 2016 for sure. But anyway, thank you very much, Myra. You've done everything possible for this patient, we think. So thank you for presenting. And Zaida Marenti is from Lima, Peru, and she's ready. I think, Zaida, are you ready to present your case?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Asymptomatic late recurrence detected on routine surveillance imaging in 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Olfactory neuroblastoma with left cervical nodal metastasis, initially diagnosed in 2013; Kadish stage D; Dulguerov stage T4N1. Recurrent metastatic disease identified in 2025 involving bilateral cervical lymph nodes and sacrum.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology results from the 2025 recurrence were provided. Initial diagnosis was olfactory neuroblastoma.

[ imaging findings ]: At initial diagnosis in 2013, imaging demonstrated a left neck node. Surveillance MRI brain in 2025 showed a clean, well-healed primary site without concerning findings. Concurrent neck MRI in 2025 showed enlargement of a previously stable postoperative left neck node and additional right-sided cervical nodes. DOTATATE PET/MRI in 2025 demonstrated bilateral cervical disease and no uptake at the primary site. Additional intense uptake was present in the sacrum, consistent with metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Somatostatin receptor expression was inferred by DOTATATE-avid disease. No next-generation sequencing results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In 2013, the patient underwent endoscopic resection of the primary tumor and left neck dissection, followed by chemoradiation, completed in 2013. He was subsequently followed with serial imaging and endoscopy and remained asymptomatic for approximately 12 years.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic olfactory neuroblastoma was present in 2025 with bilateral cervical nodal disease and sacral metastasis. The patient remained asymptomatic from the sacral lesion at the time of detection.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had undergone annual surveillance with serial imaging and endoscopy. He had remained functionally active and continued professional work as a cellist.

reference_discussion.text: I have an interesting case. My fellow can't be here, so I'm going to present this. A patient, a 67-year-old male with a history of olfactory neuroblastoma with left neck metastasis diagnosed in 2013, so 12, 13 years ago, K-stage D, Dulgarov T4N1. He had a palpable and imaging positive left neck node. So he underwent endoscopy resection and a left neck dissection followed by chemotherapy radiation and completed in 2013. He's been followed annually with serial imaging and endoscopy has been asymptomatic. He's a professional cellist with the LA Philharmonic, still continue to play. During his routine surveillance MRI of the brain in 2025, so last summer, this is what it looked like. Here we can see the primary site, looks clean, well healed, no concerns, but then the neck MRI is concerning. He had had some postoperative changes in the left neck that were stable, really, for 12 years, you know, a small node. But then in this last one, it enlarged, and there were also a couple nodes on the other side. So I'm going to stop here and ask any of the panelists, what would you do next? Any further imaging, biopsy? Yeah, Dr. Kwon.

I think if we're seeing some changes in the neck, then an FNA would be helpful to start. So that would be something to establish whether there's a recurrence or not. And I didn't hear any recent systemic imaging. Has the patient also been getting serial PET scans as well for the routine surveillance, Dr. Wong?

No, it's interesting. I actually had to fight for his surveillance MRIs for the last five years because his insurance company kept saying after five years he doesn't need them anymore. So no, he did not have a PET CT, just the MRI of the brain and the neck.

Gotcha. So one other consideration is if we're looking at this, which can happen with olfactory neuroblastoma or lay recurrences, which are often out of field or distant from the local site can happen, I would certainly consider a PET-CT, probably a DOTATATE at this point, given the specificity.

Yes, so it leads to the next slide. So, DOTATET, PET, CT or MRI. Just a few things about DOTATET PET MRI. SSTR expression is consistent across olfactory neuroblastomas, and it's associated with DOTATET uptake. So this is a relatively newer nuclear medicine study. It's not FTG, but using the DOTATET, it can be specifically helpful for olfactory neuroblastoma. So we went ahead and got one for him. and it did show bilateral neck disease. And I'm not gonna show you the next one, but if this showed just bilateral neck disease, 12, 13 years after the initial diagnosis, and it did not light up in the primary site, what would your next recommendation be?
So perhaps we can ask Dr. Cohen, what would you do at this point?
I'm sorry, you said it did not light up?

The primary site did not light up. It lit up in the neck. And I'm not gonna show you the next one because there's another pointed section, but say the DOTATATE PET just showed activity increased in bilateral necks, no place else, 13 years after the initial surgery.
Were the necks radiated as part of the primary treatment?
They were, yes, yes.
Yeah, I mean, if the necks are the only site of disease and there's nothing throughout the body, I would do a salvage bilateral neck dissection.

Yes, that was what I was thinking, but I scrolled further down the PET scan and there's huge light in the sacrum. So this obviously changed everything. He was totally symptomatic from this, but with the sacrum being involved, we no longer think that there should be surgery on the table. So what are the treatment options now? Dr. Akabe, it's no longer a surgeon's case.

I mean, you could be creative here, you're right. I mean, are there multiple ways of using local therapy? This is a late asymptomatic recurrence, not huge volume, but certainly not low volume. Could you be creative in using local radiation to his pelvis along with bilateral neck dissection? I mean, I think you could, and I would say that it would be something to really consider in a disease type that has very limited standard of care options, and our options are quite, are modest in their efficacy. I think it's, I would biopsy that just to confirm that that is truly olfactory neuroblastoma. I'm amazed he's not symptomatic from it. You can order NGS. Again, this is how likely is that to yield an option that's going to be therapeutic. 30% of olfactory neuroblastomas happen to have IDH2 mutations. R172X that, at least from a clinical trial perspective, may be actionable, although the biology of this one does not seem to fit an IDH2 mutant sinonasal carcinoma, which are usually high Hymes grade and have relatively shorter disease-free interval. Considering that it is DOTATATE positive, like many olfactory neuroblastomas are, you could use PRRT, which is an extrapolation, again, from the neuroendocrine tumors of the GI tract and lung. That would be now a radionucleotide targeting somatostatin receptor. I think that's a very reasonable option. There have been case reports, and I say anecdotal experience with the use of VEGF inhibitors, also an olfactor and noreblastoma, which would be another consideration. Would I jump to using chemo? I feel a little hard-pressed to doing so in a person who's otherwise asymptomatic, so I probably would not opt for chemotherapy, which has very low response rates.
Yeah, thank you. Dr. McBride, any comments?

I actually agree with Dr. Abhi here. I think here you could use a radionuclide therapy. I think you're probably not going to get great local control with that alone in that massive sacral lesion. So I'd probably SBRT that sacral lesion. I think there's a good case to be made for the bilateral neck dissections, SBRT the sacral lesion. And if you have a radionuclide therapy available, use that to control micrometastatic disease. I mean, I think that would be a very appropriate way to handle this case.

Yeah, so I think I just want to say a few words about PPRT because it's relatively new. There's more literature in the GI malignancies, but it has been used in the literature, their small case series. So we did send him to talk to the nuclear medicine people, and he heard the indications risks and benefits. He also talked to the radiation oncologist. He had had his previous radiation at UCLA. And so, the upshot was after tumor board discussion, the decision was to actually not do the Lutathera therapy at the time, but he was placed in a pulse pal clinical trial and got SBRT, the sacrum, and 55 gray and five fractions of the bilateral neck. So, he actually just completed this literally last week. He did very well during the treatment, tolerated very well, very few symptoms. So, you know, we're still ongoing. It's an interesting question, though. We'll do imaging, but if he has disease left in the neck, you know, would it be indicated or a good idea to do a neck dissection, bilateral neck dissection for him? Yeah. Dr. Cohen.
I would love to operate on a doubly irradiated neck. That is my Tuesday.
That's your favorite thing. That's your favorite thing, Mark.

Listen, I think it's low likelihood that there'll be persistent disease after those dosage. But if there are, I would give it a go and put a vascularized tissue on top if there's any concern about the local area. I probably would have done it before, realistically. But I think it's a conversation after the trial.

Yeah, no, it's interesting because we brought that up in the tumor report, you know, how about his neck and everyone said, oh, he's got, you know, the sacral disease and it was not recommended, but it was a thought, you know, definitely worth considering. Dr. Kwan, would you do anything differently?

Now I think, you know, with the systemic disease, these options are probably the most state of the art and building evidence around these areas and, you know, the availability of DOTATATE has really changed how we can detect these very small metastatic foci. The other thing I just wanted to comment on is I think it's awesome that you surveillance them beyond five years and all the way to 13 years and out, because, you know, with all these olfactory neuroblastomas, if you continue with the traditional paradigm of five years and out, you're probably not capturing most of these recurrences that are going to be pretty late. So I think, you know, that's a pretty great catch on this part.

Well, I'm glad he was so reliable in coming back to see me. And I feel so bad because at 10 years, I told him, you know, you're done, you're past the 10-year mark. But I guess we have to keep on following our olfactory neuroblastoma patients even longer.

So that's it for me. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Wang. I would just add, I think, for our fellows that DOTATATE scan, it's really been a game changer for olfactory neoblastoma in the sense that it picks up very small metastasis, it's very sensitive and it's superior to PET because in the PET scan, the brain is FDG avid, but in a DOTATATE scan, you don't have that issue and you can actually see very small drill metastasis, which is another common site of metastasis for olfactory neoblastoma.

If there is time, Shirley, could I ask the group how, what is your interval of surveillance here for an olfactory neuroblastoma? I don't know, Marlene, if you were doing, if you had access, let's say you had access to DOTATATE PET, the introduction is not assigned, would you have been doing that yearly?

Yeah, I would have. Yeah, I think after annually, I think after about five years, and he was so rock solid stable, I was seeing him every every few months. And after about five years, we stretch it out to six months. After about 10 years, it was every once a year. So yeah, I guess it would be nice now in retrospect to see when that sacral met started.

reference_conclusion: Tumor board review concluded that, given DOTATATE-avid bilateral cervical disease with a sacral metastasis, surgical management was not recommended initially. The patient was referred for multidisciplinary evaluation, and the agreed treatment was enrollment on a clinical trial with radiotherapy consisting of SBRT to the sacral lesion and 55 Gy in 5 fractions to the bilateral neck. Lutathera/PRRT was discussed with nuclear medicine but was deferred at that time. If residual cervical disease persists after completion of trial-directed therapy, bilateral neck dissection may be reconsidered.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old male physician (pulmonologist). He resided in New Jersey and also worked in Palm Springs/Indian Wells, California.

[ chief complaint ]: Rising PSA following prior definitive radiation therapy and subsequent salvage cryoablation for recurrent prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, initially diagnosed in September 2011 as Gleason score 3+4=7 disease involving 3 of 12 biopsy cores, with presenting PSA 6 ng/mL. Biopsy-confirmed local recurrence was identified in 2018 as bilateral Gleason score 4+3=7 prostate cancer with PSA 3.6 ng/mL. Subsequent biochemical recurrence occurred after salvage cryotherapy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- September 2011 prostate biopsy: Gleason score 3+4=7 adenocarcinoma in 3/12 cores.  
- 2018 repeat prostate biopsy: bilateral Gleason score 4+3=7 adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Conventional CT and bone scan performed at the time of recurrence in 2018 were negative.  
- Recent PSMA PET (rhPSMA/PYLARIFY-equivalent agent referred to as PASLUMA) performed in Indian Wells, California, showed no identified uptake in or about the prostate gland or seminal vesicles, no abdominal/pelvic/retroperitoneal nodal uptake, and no osseous metastatic uptake. The scan was interpreted as negative, including no activity around the bladder neck, prostate, or adjacent lymph nodes.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA at diagnosis in September 2011: 6 ng/mL.  
- Post-IMRT nadir PSA: 1.1 ng/mL in August 2013.  
- PSA rose gradually to 4.38 ng/mL during 2014–2017.  
- PSA at 2018 biopsy-confirmed recurrence: 3.6 ng/mL.  
- After salvage cryotherapy, nadir PSA was 0.18 ng/mL at approximately 6 months.  
- Approximately 5 years after cryotherapy, PSA was 1.46 ng/mL.  
- PSA was described as having doubled between December 2022 and July 2023, corresponding to an estimated PSA doubling time of approximately 7–8 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Definitive IMRT was administered after initial diagnosis in 2011.  
- Finasteride was started during biochemical rise after radiation; a small PSA decline was observed.  
- Salvage cryotherapy was performed in New York in 2018 for biopsy-proven local recurrence.  
- Following cryotherapy, PSA declined to a nadir of 0.18 ng/mL at approximately 6 months.  
- Cryotherapy was complicated by treatment-related adverse effects.

[ current disease status ]: Biochemical recurrence after prior IMRT and salvage cryotherapy, with PSA 1.46 ng/mL and negative recent PSMA PET for local, nodal, or distant metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past history included radiation cystitis and hematuria.  
- Urethral meatal stricture was documented after prior treatment.

reference_discussion.text: Hi everyone, my name is E. David Crawford from the University of California in San Diego and welcome to our PET Tumor Board. PET imaging, especially PSMA PET, in my opinion, is one of the most significant advances in prostate cancer management in the last decade. It has created a lot of opportunities and also challenges. I have observed that in many tumor or second opinion boards, Almost half of the cases now are focused around PET scanning, particularly PSMA PET. We recently published our latest Radar 6 and 7 guidelines, which goes through in detail a lot of the indications for PET, the pitfalls and the ups and downs. We have a lot to learn, and we hope that these monthly tumor boards will broaden your knowledge in this area. I would like to thank Blue Earth Diagnostics who recently developed and launched a PSMA pet product called RH-PSMA or PASLUMA for this educational grant. We have gathered for this tumor board panel, three international experts in this field. They have not seen these cases beforehand, and so they are as blinded as you are to what's gonna happen in these cases. First panel member is Dr. Phil Koo. Phil is at MD Anderson Banner in Phoenix, Arizona. He is a nuclear medicine physician. Also, Dr. Daniel Petrulak, a medical oncologist from Yale, well-known in the field of prostate cancer, is joining us. And a radiation oncologist, Dr. Paul Nguyen from Harvard Brigham in Boston, Massachusetts. So gentlemen, let's go ahead and get started. Our first case is that of a 71-year-old pulmonologist who has a rising PSA. He was diagnosed in September of 2011. He had a PSA of six, the Gleason score of 347, and three of 12 cores. He was treated with the IMRT. His NADER PSA was 1.1. in August of 13. He lives in the East Coast in New Jersey and also commutes back and forth and works in Palm Springs, California. So let me start out with Paul. Paul, what nadir PSA do we like to see after radiation?

Yeah, so the lower the better with Nader PSAs. With brachytherapy, sometimes you can get down all the way to less than 0.1, like you can with surgery. With external beam IMRT, like this patient got, usually I'd like to get it down below 0.5. So 1.1 feels a little bit high to me.

Okay, so it's a red flag. You know, there's a lot of interest in these rectal spacers right now, you know, quite honestly, I can remember over the years with radiation oncologists saying that we don't have much rectal toxicity. So why are we putting all these rectal spacers in?

Yeah, so there's a couple of kinds of rectal spacers out there. One by One is the SPACE-OAR, another one's by Barigel, and both of them have shown in randomized trials that they can reduce rectal toxicity. I think, you know, there is data out there that some patients do get rectal toxicity, and that when you put these spacers in, it can reduce it by a certain percentage.

Well, yeah, and I know they're randomized trials, and that's sort of the key here. Probably the rectal irritation and things like that may have been sort of underestimated. Dan, you've spent a lot of time with adjuvant therapy and ADT and prostate cancer. What's your sort of, what do you tell patients before they see the radiation oncologist about how much ADT to get?

when we look at the different risks, intermediate versus high risk. And generally we would recommend for a high risk patient about 18 months of ADT. One of the contradictions about, oh, actually one of the caveats about antideprivation therapy is that the older the patient, the less likely the chance of the recovery of testosterone. And also the baseline testosterone levels are important to the recovery. So the absolute amount of ADT, I think, is a little bit controversial because the question is, when do these patients do truly recover? But it's important to emphasize the synergy between ADT and radiation therapy goes back to Bola's studies a number of years ago, where three years of ADT plus radiation showed a superior survival to radiation therapy alone. And so, of course, the duration and the proper patients are important for selection.
So, Paul, I don't think anybody uses the BOLA data much anymore, three years. What do you tell patients? A guy like this, is this six months okay or does he need radiation? Does he need ADT?

Yeah. Certainly, like Dan said, BOLA put ADT on the map, but now with a patient like this who has what we would call favorable intermediate risk prostate cancer, either you could give no ADT currently according to the NCCN guidelines, or if you want to give some typically it'd be short course like four to six months.

All right, so what happened to this guy? His follow-up was he did okay, but Paul hit the nail right on the head when he said that wasn't a good Nader PSA, and it wasn't. So his PSA slowly rose up to 4.38, and that was 2014 through 17. He had a biopsy following this. He was placed on finasteride and saw a little dip in his PSA, but he had a biopsy right after that in 2018 that showed that he has bilateral Gleason 437 cancer with a PSA of 3.6. We have a situation here where the guy has recurrence. He was offered cryotherapy. Actually, he contacted me. That's how I got to know the guy because of our work with cryotherapy. And he got cryotherapy in New York. Do you think that's a good option, Paul, for somebody that's like him that failed to respond to radiation or recurred?

Yeah, I mean, as far as we know, if somebody's got a local recurrence after radiation, Any of the local focal treatment options appear to have a similar chance of local control. They just have different side effect profiles. So whether you do focal brachytherapy, or focal cryotherapy, or HIFU, or maybe some laser things, currently the meta-analyses, which are all retrospective, seem to suggest pretty similar outcomes. So I'm okay with that.
Seems like we don't see a lot of patients referred from Rad-Onc for salvage therapy. Are they waiting to some specific PSA level or what's the holdup?

Well, usually I would check once the PSA hits nadir plus two. So in this case, the patient had a PSA of 1.1 for their nadir. So once they hit 3.1, that would be time to get an MRI, look for a local recurrence, and then make that referral if the biopsy shows a local recurrence. So reaffirm for focal brachy, focal cryo, hyphoo, laser, or even salvage prostatectomy for certain patients.
So Phil, this is 2018. What imaging should have been done on this guy?

You know, in 2018, unfortunately, we didn't have PSMA PET widely available. Otherwise, I would have definitely considered getting a PSMA PET. In 2018, we might have had, I believe, some other advanced imaging tools, perhaps Actium or Choline, though Choline availability was limited. But I think in these scenarios where a patient has a rising PSA following definitive therapy, you know, there's good evidence now that we should be a little bit more aggressive with imaging to identify either local disease or metastatic disease.

We had conventional imaging and CT and bone scan, and guess what? It didn't show anything, not surprising. Dan, is there any role for ADT in this guy at this point? Would you have gone with the cryotherapy?

Well, I've not seen any randomized data, but we recently had a case that was very, very similar to this, where the patient, we started ADT three months before we did the cryotherapy, then gave another three months afterwards. So certainly there isn't the same synergy, at least documentation synergy between cryotherapy, but certainly you worry about any distal mycomastatic disease, which would be taken care of by the ADT.

So well what happened so he had a nadir PSA point one eight about six months after the cryo and he was very happy, he did have some complications. as you might expect, and we'll get to those in a second. Now he comes to see me out here in San Diego a number of years later, five years later or so, and has PSA at 1.46. So what do we do? He was seen at MD Anderson in one of the satellite places in the Northeast. These are the exact notes copied out of the chart that he had history of radiation cystitis and hematuria in the past, cryoablation, and he had a structure of the urethral meatus. And this is his PSA history. What do we do now? Paul?

Well, unfortunately, it looks like his PSA is coming up. Certainly, I'd be suspicious about some kind of recurrence. I'd want to do an MRI, or maybe Phil would weigh in, maybe some kind of PET imaging, and see if there's yet another local recurrence. Although this time, I'd be pretty hesitant to go in again with focal therapy, unless it was very far away from the original lesion.

So Phil, what What would you do in a way of imaging in this guy? So his PSA is 1.46. I mean, we have approval for PET imaging for a number of agents right now for biochemical failure, which he is, a newly diagnosed disease. So would you jump in with something?

You know, it's interesting. Imaging in this setting where he had definitive treatment, he got cryotherapy. I think we need to sort of turn the tables and think, all right, what would we do with the imaging results? And really talk through how we might potentially manage this patient, look at his goals of care and sort of take it in reverse. If it is decided that we would be aggressive with his treatment, treat perhaps algomeths or whatnot, I would consider getting a PSMA PET. Pelvic MRI in this setting is interesting and we often use it to detect the recurrence. But I think I'd like to remind the readers that PyRide is actually not meant in that recurrent setting. So, but it is a good tool. That being said, we are learning more about PSMA PET to detect local recurrence and metastatic disease. And depending again, how we would manage this patient, I would consider that as a possibility at this time.

I think you said something very important. I'm going to ask Dan a question too now. If you're going to order a scan like this or something, it ought to be actionable what you're going to do with it, not just say, oh, I got the scan and it's interesting. We'll talk a little bit about false positives and false negatives. Dan, what are your thoughts? You wouldn't hit the sky with any hormone therapy at this point, would you?

Well, looking at his PSA and his PSA characteristics, he's doubled from December of 2022 to July of 2023. So it's about a seven to eight month doubling time overall. And generally in the past, if we had negative imaging, I would often base starting ADT on doubling time. So I would be inclined to start him on ADT I think it would be important to do some imaging to determine whether he had, as we were saying, a distal method may be radiated in addition to doing the ADT. So certainly, this is somebody that I would start being aggressive about because his PSA doubling time is fairly short.

Okay. You know, years ago, we used to use low-dose antiandrogens on these people. Jed Mylan, I published a paper of flutamide alone, and have some people out 10 years. So anyway, so we got a scan on him. As you know, there's a new scan out called PASLUMA, which is R-H-P-S-M-A. And so this was done at his home base in Indian Wells, California. And as you can see, this was done just a short, a couple of weeks ago, a week ago. So here are the findings. Bill, what do you think of that? I'll show you a film in a minute, but what do you think of this?

It says no identified uptake in or about the prostate gland or seminal vesicles. So that's good. Nothing in the abdominal pelvic retroperitoneal nodes, nothing in the bones, really not much to report that they're reporting on the PET so far.

So this is one of the first ones in these scans that were done and sort of happy to see that and unhappy in a way, but like Dan, I shared the concern about this. So this posthumous scan, RhPSMA is negative and we do not see any activity around the bladder, neck and the prostate or any adjacent lymph nodes. Let's just look at two other scans from patients who did have positive areas and asked Dr. Khoo to comment on those. Phil?

And this is not the patient that we just talked about. So looking at the first image on the screen left, you see very focal and heterogeneous activity in that pelvis, which I presume is the prostate gland. So something that would be concerning for recurrence. And I'd be curious to see, you know, if we had an MRI there. The image on the right, I think to two areas that you see that have low level activity might just be the ureters, but we'd want to trace it and make sure they follow the track of the ureter. And there's another focus of activity more anteriorly, which I think we'd want to interrogate that further and see perhaps if that's a lymph node or not.

The scans are helpful determining direction. I think we're going to see more like this with the positive scans. And I've got a, and I don't know about, anyone else, but we have an intense interest in two areas, radiation failures and salvage cryo and surgery and things like that, but also targeted focal therapy. The thing about targeted focal therapy is it's all about your target. People call it focal therapy. If you don't know where your target is, then you're gonna have a failure. There's lots of energy ways to get rid of prostate cancer, cryotherapy, lasers, Haifu, electroporation. You can inject alcohol until it can get rid of it, but it's all about the target. And I think there's a value for these scans and looking what's in the prostate and helping you determine where your target is. So with that, again, thank you all, and we will see you for the next case. Our recommendations following the negative POSLUMA scan is to follow the PSA about every four months looking for changes in the doubling time, consider ADT, or consider a clinical trial.

reference_conclusion: Following the negative PSMA PET scan, the plan is continued surveillance with serial PSA monitoring approximately every four months to assess for changes in PSA doubling time. Androgen deprivation therapy may be considered based on subsequent PSA kinetics, and clinical trial participation may also be considered.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old female. Past medical history was reported as non-significant.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid nodule under surveillance with interval growth.

[ diagnosis ]: Follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, with central compartment lymph node metastasis showing extranodal extension. Additional papillary thyroid microcarcinomas were identified in the right thyroid lobe after completion thyroidectomy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2019 biopsy of a 1.5 cm left thyroid nodule was Bethesda II.  
- Repeat FNA in March after interval growth to 1.9 cm was Bethesda III.  
- Left hemithyroidectomy in July demonstrated follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- A central compartment lymph node removed at the time of surgery measured 4 mm and contained metastatic carcinoma with extranodal extension.  
- Completion right thyroidectomy demonstrated papillary microcarcinomas; at least one focus was BRAF-positive.  
- No extrathyroidal extension of the primary tumor was described.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in 2019 showed a 1.5 cm left thyroid nodule.  
- Follow-up ultrasound 1–2 years later showed modest increase in size to 1.9 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Molecular testing on the Bethesda III left thyroid nodule identified an NRAS mutation with low allele frequency; the report estimated an approximately 50% likelihood of malignancy.  
- Immunostaining/molecular assessment of the metastatic lymph node was BRAF-positive.  
- At least one right-sided papillary microcarcinoma was BRAF-positive.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Postoperative thyroglobulin decreased from 61 to <0.1.  
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were absent.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surveillance was undertaken after Bethesda II cytology of the left thyroid nodule.  
- Repeat ultrasound-guided FNA was performed after interval growth and yielded Bethesda III cytology.  
- Left hemithyroidectomy with central compartment lymph node biopsy was performed in July. Pathology showed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with a 4 mm metastatic central lymph node demonstrating extranodal extension.  
- Right completion thyroidectomy was subsequently performed. Pathology showed papillary microcarcinomas in the right lobe.  
- Biochemical response after surgery was favorable, with thyroglobulin falling to <0.1 and negative antibodies.

[ current disease status ]:  
Post-completion thyroidectomy status with no biochemical evidence of persistent disease based on thyroglobulin <0.1 and negative thyroglobulin antibodies.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The metastatic central compartment lymph node was identified intraoperatively using methylene blue dye.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 44-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Increase in size of breast lump during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced breast carcinoma, clinical stage cT4bN2 at presentation. Post-mastectomy pathologic stage ypT3N2. Disease remained locoregionally confined on imaging, with no distant metastasis identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy showed breast carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry on the pretreatment specimen showed estrogen receptor (ER) 5%, progesterone receptor (PR) negative, HER2 0, and Ki-67 60%. Postoperative histopathology after modified radical mastectomy showed ypT3N2. No metaplastic component was identified. There was no pathological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging performed after clinical enlargement of the breast lump showed persistent locally advanced breast disease without evidence of metastasis. PET imaging showed local progression only, with no distant metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified TP53 mutation, GATA3 frameshift deletion, and MSH2 termination mutation. Microsatellite instability status was stable by NGS. Tumor mutation burden was reported as low. PD-L1 immunohistochemistry had been sent; result was not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with 4 cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin followed by 2 cycles of adriamycin plus cyclophosphamide. An initial clinical response was observed with paclitaxel/carboplatin. After the sixth cycle of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the patient reported increase in breast lump size. She subsequently underwent modified radical mastectomy. Postoperative pathology demonstrated ypT3N2 disease with no response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative wound had healed. There was no documented distant metastatic disease. Adjuvant radiotherapy was planned, followed by capecitabine.

[ other clinical data ]: Repeat ER/PR/HER2 testing on the postoperative specimen had not been performed. Mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry had not been reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 79-year-old White female.

[ chief complaint ]: Right-sided abdominal pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Incidentally detected right renal mass.

[ imaging findings ]: CT abdomen demonstrated an approximately 3.0-3.5 cm right renal mass. The lesion was described as deep/lateral in location with extension toward the central kidney and contact with the renal sinus/collecting system. No renal vein invasion was identified. Contralateral kidney was normal. CT chest was negative for metastatic disease. CT interpretation was partially limited by artifact from prior spinal instrumentation.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including renal function. Estimated glomerular filtration rate was approximately 75.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially presented with cholecystitis and underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

[ current disease status ]: No thoracic metastatic disease was identified on CT chest.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hepatitis B, and arthritis. Prior surgical history included hysterectomy, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and prior back surgery with spinal instrumentation.

I would offer a partial as well, but I actually would do this one open. I wouldn't do this robotically.
And she did go on to receive an open partial nephrectomy, and it was a stage T1A, clear cell. And her post-operative course was unremarkable. So would anybody do a biopsy ahead of time?
Only if I'm planning to do a radical nephrectomy.
So explain the logic of that.
Or active surveillance.
Just I would hate for someone to lose their kidney for a three centimeter mass that could be benign.
So if you're going to do a radical nephrectomy, you would do a biopsy to prove that?
For a small mass, yes. If I'm going to do a partial nephrectomy, there's no reason to do a biopsy because I know the rest of the kidney is still going to be there.
And if the biopsy came back as benign, you would observe?
Or I would not go for the radical. I'd change it and do a partial if that was the second option.
Huh? What?

If it's, you know, sometimes the biopsy doesn't always say benign, benign. Sometimes it's inconclusive or oncocytic. So, you know, observation or surveillance would be more of an option at that time as well. But if the patient is having symptoms such as hematuria, like you said, this is very close to the urinary system there on the second picture on the right. It might be an option to still do a partial nephrectomy.

I think it's an issue, you know, it's unconventional. We don't think about doing partial to decide to do a radical, I mean, to do a biopsy when you're considering a radical. But I think the logic of it actually makes sense. And it may not have 10 years ago when we weren't able to distinguish benign from malignant quite as well. But I kind of buy that argument.
What about the argument that if it's active, if we're going to do active surveillance, we should do a biopsy? Do you agree with that?

I do. You know, I've become, I used to leave it very optional for patients. It's still optional, but I do encourage it. I think most patients want to know if they have cancer or if they don't. And it also puts them in a position of power when we're observing it, and it does something that is unexpected, and that's not infrequent. So it may shrink, it may get bigger, but then you're in a position of more power as a patient, I think, when you kind of know what it is. So that is an unusual perspective for a urologist. Most of them would not biopsy or be, I don't know, what would the other guys do?
Yeah, show of hands, who would biopsy for active surveillance and who would not? So who would biopsy?
Not everybody.
Okay, Dr. Karam, what's your selection criteria?

So if I, you know, we have some patients, let's say if a patient's 85 year old and has a one centimeter mass, realistically, whatever that biopsy is going to show, we probably won't be doing anything. So unless a biopsy is going to change something that I'm going to do, I would not obtain a biopsy. Now, if a patient says, I will not do surveillance unless I have a biopsy, it's a different story. But if the patient's leaving gut, to us to decide or to help them decide, I would not do the biopsy unless it's going to change what I do, meaning if it's going to sway me from surveillance to do some form of intervention like surgery or ablation therapy.

But when would you use a biopsy for active surveillance? That's not the same question that you're answering. We've already decided we're going to go on active surveillance. Who do you biopsy? Who do you not?
So if you've decided already you're doing surveillance, why would you biopsy?
That's the question I'm asking.

Right. So in my way, I'm thinking of it backwards. I've used the result of the biopsy to see if I'm going to do surveillance or not. So if I'm doing surveillance, what is the biopsy going to tell me if I know 100% I'm doing that?

I think that's fine. The thing is, things don't always go the way you expect. And again, I think having information puts you and the patient in a position of power. So there's always unexpected outcomes. whether the patient gets better or the tumor does things you don't expect it to. So, you know, even in those, for me, even for cases where we know it may not change the management at that time period, I still encourage a biopsy.

I guess, so then my esteemed urology colleagues helped me as a simple medical oncologist understand because we've, I've had your colleagues from Philadelphia, you know, say that they want to avoid biopsy and they have all this data that they've published about monitoring how much growth rate there is in a small renal mass to predict whether or not the small renal mass is malignant based on a growth rate criteria. So it just doesn't make, it seems counterintuitive to want to biopsy that because I think the question's different. Your data sets would be different. If you knew there was cancer there and you were still going to observe them, then I think you're using data based upon low metastatic potential and the size versus the data that exists from Ouzo et al when it's a small renal mass that you don't know and you're basing the data set on whether it's malignant or not. So I'm just confused as to, I don't know, the rationale.
I'm not aware of data from them that talks about growth rate predicting malignancy.

I thought that's what the small renal mass whole debate was. Because with the small renal mass, the reason that you're observing is because there's a certain percentage of those. that are going to be benign. And so the growth rate per year is predicting the likelihood of malignancy. And that's a different mindset than if you knew it was cancer, you would want to monitor it because if it was below a certain size, it wouldn't metastasize. So are they two different?

Well, no, not really, because as it turns out, oncocytomas grow. And in fact, they may have a higher growth rate than small renal cell carcinomas. So the growth rate actually does not predict histology.

Although, I mean, alterations in growth rate may trigger an intervention. So, for instance, you know, they're normally growing at a rate of two to three millimeters per year, and all of a sudden, if it jumps up and grows seven millimeters, you might say, holy cow, we've got to do something. You know, my practice, I typically don't biopsy patients on active surveillance. You know, sort of like I've already decided that I'm not going to intervene, so I'm not sure I really want to know. And, you know, if the patient asks for one, I'll do it, but otherwise, we typically don't. All right, I think we beat this one to death. Let's move on. So, this is a 72-year-old white male who presents with uncontrolled hypertension. He underwent abdominal imaging, which revealed an asymptomatic renal mass. Past medical history significant for hypertension, peripheral vascular disease with a stent in the left lower extremity. Physical exam's unremarkable. CT chest, bone scan negative. Hemoglobin is nine. Creatinine is 1.3 with a GFR of 51. So GFR just means kidney function glomerular filtration rate. Dr. Chapin. These are the films. Give us your thoughts about this and how would you manage this patient?

reference_conclusion: The consensus management was nephron-sparing surgery with partial nephrectomy for this approximately 3–3.5 cm renal mass, rather than active surveillance, ablation, or neoadjuvant therapy. A minimally invasive robotic approach was favored by most discussants, although an open partial nephrectomy was also considered appropriate; the patient ultimately underwent open partial nephrectomy. Preoperative biopsy was not recommended if proceeding with partial nephrectomy, but would be considered if radical nephrectomy or active surveillance were being pursued.
reference_conclusion_quote: The main options I think here are partial nephrectomy or complete nephrectomy. If the patient's healthy enough, I would recommend a partial nephrectomy [...] Partial nephrectomy. [...] Robotic. [...] If she left it up to me, I would do a partial. [...] Yeah. [...] No. [...] I would offer a partial as well, but I actually would do this one open. I wouldn't do this robotically. [...] And she did go on to receive an open partial nephrectomy [...] Only if I'm planning to do a radical nephrectomy. [...] Or active surveillance. [...] If I'm going to do a partial nephrectomy, there's no reason to do a biopsy because I know the rest of the kidney is still going to be there.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Large left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the left thyroid nodule was Bethesda VI (malignant). Initial surgical pathology after lobectomy showed classic papillary thyroid carcinoma measuring 4.3 cm. One surgical margin was close at less than 1 mm but negative for tumor. One perithyroidal lymph node was negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a fairly large left thyroid tumor, estimated at 3.8 cm to nearly 4 cm, with mild capsular distortion but remaining within the capsule. No abnormal cervical lymph nodes were identified. No obvious local invasion was seen.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor testing was positive for BRAF V600E mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: One month after completion thyroid surgery, TSH was 0.99 and thyroglobulin was 0.6 with negative thyroglobulin antibodies. On subsequent follow-up, TSH was further suppressed and thyroglobulin decreased to 0.2.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially underwent thyroid lobectomy for presumed 3.8 cm intrathyroidal papillary thyroid carcinoma without radiographic nodal disease. Final pathology demonstrated a 4.3 cm classic papillary thyroid carcinoma with a close but negative margin and one negative perithyroidal lymph node. She subsequently underwent completion thyroidectomy. Postoperative thyroglobulin levels were low and decreased further on follow-up. No radioactive iodine had been administered.

[ current disease status ]: Status post lobectomy followed by completion thyroidectomy. Postoperative biochemical assessment showed negative thyroglobulin antibodies and very low thyroglobulin, decreasing from 0.6 to 0.2, consistent with minimal residual thyroid tissue burden. No structural residual or metastatic disease had been identified on the available imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No abnormal contralateral thyroid findings were documented. No evidence of cervical nodal metastasis was documented. Age was noted to be a favorable prognostic factor.
