reference_discussion.text: Sounds good. Can everybody see my screen now? I hope everybody can hear me. And the title of our session is a patient-focused tumor board for this year's virtual FICA meeting. So here's the question. Joel put it so well. Tumor board can be this kind of black box. And we kind of wanted to demystify the black box. It seemed like it would be a more fair thing to do. So what really happens when your case gets presented at tumor board? And we want to make sure you know how friendly it is. There are a number of patients that I see of our patients on the attendee list today. And several of their cases have been presented. presented at tumor board. A few of them have agreed to have their cases shared. So you've already met our faculty. Here are our disclosures, nothing too exciting. And here's what tumor board looks like. At least pre-pandemic, it looked like this. So Tumor Board is a working multidisciplinary conference, as we get a bunch of people in a room, sometimes we eat some tuna sandwiches, and this crowd represents everybody from all the various disciplines, different training backgrounds and skill sets, who can contribute value to the care of our thyroid cancer patients. We have a big screen, and literally, before the Tumor Board begins, So who are the representatives? Let's get into that. So endocrinology, those endocrinology doctors are most often the quarterback. Endocrine surgeons and head and neck surgeons are present. These are also known as the neck invaders, as Joel said. Nuclear medicine is there. They administer, this is obviously an oversimplification, right? They administer radioactive iodine and they help us with functional scans, such as radioactive iodine scans and PET scans. pathology, an increasingly important role. They analyze every tissue we biopsy, everything we remove from the neck surgically, pathology is analyzing. You know, I know a growing role for pathologists is molecular testing results, which are more and more common. You've probably heard about that at other sessions. Radiology is there to perform scans and help us to interpret scans. Radiation oncology, they're the ones that give external beam radiation therapy, such as SBRT. Medical oncology, and those are the people that give chemotherapy, including targeted agents. So everybody you need is there. What's the workflow well we hold UCLA we hold this conference at first Wednesday of every month, and anyone could submit a case I mean literally anyone, it could be a UCLA doctor it could be a doctor from the outside we will teleconference those people in, and we just want that people to submit their cases in advance. So we can present, we can prepare the slides and pathology slides and everything. We present anywhere from four to eight cases presented in an hour. There are times, months when we have too many cases, we have to hold an additional tumor board. And these are often complex or unusual cases where multiple skill sets are required to offer optimal care for the patient. There's a certain humility for the tumor board, right? Because you're admitting that We can't do it just with one person. You need a lot of people to work together. And it's a really invigorating conference. It's one of my favorite conferences, because I'm reminded why I enjoy working at UCLA so much. So I can't hide how proud I am of this team, because everywhere you look at UCLA, you're surrounded by intelligent people who really want to help. And so often you get yourself stuck in this situation, not sure what to do. And then you present it to the tumor board. And the ideas that are devised there are much more awesome than any one of us could devise alone. And the goal is to arrive upon a consensus and formulate an action plan for immediate implementation. We're not just sitting there teaching and pontificating. There is a little bit of that. But honestly, we're there to get work done. And then we put this consensus into the chart. It's documented, and then there's a phone call or a video conference that takes place within 24 hours after the tumor board where we convey the findings to the referring doctor and the patient and their family. All right. So that's the basic structure. And I'm just going to go through a few example cases. And now, since you know that when we say to you, we're going to present your case of tumor board, you know what the people look like, you know what the conference looks like, you know what it's for. So now, so here's our first case. This is a 26 year old woman with a fairly large left thyroid nodule. FNA reveals it's a Bethesda six means very likely to be it's a malignant aspirate. And that means the likelihood of thyroid cancer here is about 99%. and it's common for us to show the ultrasound images so the radiologist will then say see here's the trachea and here's the carotid artery and here's the tumor here and it's a fairly large tumor it's distorting the capsule a little bit but still inside the capsule we didn't see any abnormal lymph nodes and it's not an obviously invasive tumor and so I'll turn it over maybe to Dr. Livitz to discuss these findings and what she might do.

So we know that this is an almost four centimeter thyroid cancer. I'm assuming probably a papillary thyroid cancer. And this patient could be managed either with a thyroid lobectomy, removal of half the thyroid, or a total thyroidectomy, removal of the entire thyroid, based on the 2015 American Thyroid Association guidelines. So the things that I'm thinking about are the ultrasound findings that Dr. Yeh already mentioned. It's a tumor that seems to have clear borders. We don't see local invasion or spread to the lymph nodes. So either option is reasonable. The other things I'm thinking about are, are there any nodules in the other half of the thyroid? Is the patient already on thyroid hormone supplementation, in which case there might be less benefit in leaving the other half of the thyroid in? And the patient's preference, you know, the patient, how they feel about it. Are they somebody that prefers more maximal removal of the entire thyroid to have a little bit more reassurance, potentially be able to use tumor markers after surgery, or somebody who really wants to try to avoid thyroid hormone supplementation and try to leave the other half of the thyroid in? I think both options would be very reasonable in this patient. I would discuss both options with the patient. I think there are pros and cons to either one. If you would make me decide, I think that removal of half the thyroid would be reasonable to start with, really in the absence of any high-risk features.
And for Dr. Leong, what role does the endocrinologist play in this initial decision for the type of surgery and extent of surgery?

Yeah, thank you so much. I'm pleased to join everybody here. If the patient is coming to see me before the surgery, sometimes I am involved at that point. Sometimes as an endocrinologist, we get involved after the surgery has been done. Either way is fine. But things that I might be able to help in the endocrine perspective before the surgery would be to counsel them that this person is a very young person and age is so protective in thyroid cancer. Young people tend to do very, very well because it downstages their their eventual, the outcome of the stage that's arrived after surgery. I also recognize that she's a young woman. There's obviously plans potentially for childbearing. So I ask about all of that because it might have some influence when we talk about subsequent treatment, if it's required, if it's found that this cancer is found to be a little bit more aggressive or invasive after the surgery. But then I do what has been already implied and inferred is I refer to one of our endocrine surgeons. I always say that choosing an endocrine surgeon is important just because obviously there are potential risks with any procedure surgically. So I want to always reassure folks to find someone who's doing a lot of surgeries and with a lot of experience.

So yeah, these are all excellent points that go into this. I'm cognizant of the fact that among the audience members, there are a fair number of people who probably had surgery prior to 2015, and we had sort of fewer options then, right? Most everyone then was getting a total thyroidectomy, often with radioactive iodine. And then there's going to be a generation of FICA and attendees who have now been managed with therapeutic lobectomy, right? They just had a lobectomy only. if they had a tumor less than four centimeters in diameter without invasion and without positive lymph nodes. And I'm sure that's one of the new topics of discussion. There'll be a generational difference. So in this case, Dr. Libitz highlighted many of the factors that go in the decision. When there's ambiguity, I tend to do just a lobectomy. when we're kind of on the fence. Because I like to say to people, if we do a total and it ended up being not the right thing to do, we can't really put anything back in. Whereas if we do a lobectomy, it's okay to do a little bit more the following week if it turns out you need to. All right. So this is what the pathology looks like. And, you know, I know that some of you guys have all seen your pathology reports, but this is what the tissue actually looked like and it looks like. And you see these beautiful pink and purple colors. And this is, of course, not the natural state of the tissue, but the tissue has been stained with special stains to highlight certain cellular features. And this is a fairly classic papillary thyroid carcinoma. The normal thyroid has these big lakes, these big lakes of colloid fluid. But you see here that there are no lakes. It's mostly cells. So that tells you it's a neoplasm or a type of growth. Then, you know, some more details here, and especially these big white circles, which are the nuclei that look a little bit different. And so this was a classic papillary carcinoma. It's so nice, you know, whenever you meet with a pathologist and they describe to you exactly what's going on, you always get more information than you would from just reading the report. Likewise, when a radiologist describes to you blow by blow what's in a set of images, that's always better than a report. You can ask questions, you can interact with them, so more information almost comes forward. So this lady, we thought she had a 3.8 centimeter left thyroid nodule, but it turned out to be a little bit more than we bargained for. It was actually 4.3 centimeters, and one of the margins, a margin is like the safety factor you have between the tumor the adjacent and sort of where you actually cut it out of the patient's body. And one margin is pretty close, less than a millimeter, though negative, right? We didn't have any tumor present at the margin. And one negative perithyroidal lymph node. So in this case, we had a little bit more than we bargained for. And you probably heard many times during this meeting, that a lobectomy is acceptable for a tumor less than four centimeters, but now it turns out it was greater than four centimeters. So Dr. Levitz, what should we do with this little surprise?

So I think first it's an important point, as you already mentioned, if we're going to do a lobectomy, there's always a chance if we find something a little bit more high risk of the pathology, that you will have to come back for a second surgery to remove the other half of the thyroid lobe. So going into it, that just needs to factor into your decision that you're okay with the possibility of potentially having that second surgery if we think it's necessary based on the pathology. And patients often ask, what is it that we're looking for in that pathology report when we're looking at the cells under the microscope? So we're looking at the type of papillary thyroid cancer. So classic is what most people have that doesn't make it particularly more aggressive. But there are certain subtypes of papillary thyroid cancer, like tall cell, for example, that can be a little bit more aggressive. And then, of course, we're looking at the margins. Margins are less important for thyroid cancer than they are for some other things, other types of cancers. We do need to have negative margins, but we don't need to have a very large margin. We just need to have completely removed the tumor. So I would say this patient needs to go back to have the other half of the thyroid removed because it was already kind of on the border, but now we know it's over four centimeters in size and we do have that close margin. I think we need to remove the other half of the thyroid.
Right. And for Dr. Leung, is there something magical about the four centimeter cutoff? Is a 4.1 centimeter tumor that much worse than a 3.9 centimeter tumor?

This is a good point, and not. We know biologically the tumor doesn't act suddenly more aggressively just because it's crossed over that four centimeter mark. Our recommendations to go back and remove the other side are based on available data, what people call retrospective data, looking at people who've had thyroid cancer and it be a little bit larger than 4.0 centimeters, that tends to be the situation which we want to guarantee complete removal. I agree with Dr. Levitz that it's a good idea to go back and remove the other side, but not necessarily because we think you're at suddenly high, high risk.

Yeah, it's just sort of a result of how we study these things in terms of research. And Dr. Levitz, when would we do the second operation? And is it worse? Is it higher risk to have two operations as opposed to one? Is it bad?

Right. So there are two factors. One is a surgical factor. So in terms of timing, ideally for the second surgery, we'd like to go back almost right away within a week or so. before there's too much scar tissue that sets in. Sometimes we can't do that right away for whatever reason. The patient needs a little bit more time to recover. There are some logistical factors. In that case, we would wanna go back after six weeks. That time in between, things are very sticky in the neck. There's a lot of scar tissue and that can make the surgery a little bit more complicated. So we either wanna go back within a week or so or wait until all that scar tissue settles down and then after six weeks. In terms of the actual complications, they're really fairly similar to the initial surgery. We go back through the same scars. So you don't need a new scar. We just open it back up. And the good part is that whenever we remove one half of the thyroid, we really don't go to the other half of the thyroid in that deep space. And that's purposeful. It's to avoid creating scar tissue in that area. So when we do go back to remove the other half, we really haven't been in that deep space before where the critical structures are. the vocal cord nerves are in that area. The risk of complications in that second operation is fairly similar to the first one.

I noticed that the patients always say the second time is easier. I think it's because they know what the deal is, they walked that path before. All right, so this one, it was on the margin, the patient needed a little more time, so we decided to test this patient's tumor for mutations, and we found that it was positive for the BRAF V600E mutation. So Dr. Leung, can you tell us a little bit about the significance and the prevalence of this mutation, and should patients be worried if they have it?

It's a little bit of a complicated question just because we don't necessarily advise getting this mutation tested in everybody before the surgery happens. The reason for that is just because if it is found and it's found quite variably, studies say maybe it's found in up to even 80 percent of the time, but it could be as low as 30 percent of the time. It really depends on which groups of patients you're studying and all different conditions, age groups, and all that stuff. So even if we were to find like this person had the information, it doesn't necessarily change that much in terms of how we counsel her risk of recurrence of the disease, recurrence of the thyroid cancer in years to come. It alone itself doesn't probably predict enough information for us to say confidently it will, you know, recur in this degree, this percentage. But what we use it in and where it's helpful is if we put everything together, her entire package, right? Her age, other features of the tumor, the size of the tumor, whether or not it was completely excised, all that sort of stuff, where it itself in addition to all of those clinical factors can perhaps inform a risk of recurrence. So again, it's important to stress that we don't necessarily want to test for the mutation everybody before the surgery.

freak. So we were kind of on the fence, and we allowed this to kind of push us over. And just like Dr. Levitt said, we did do a completion thyroidectomy. And then we had some labs. So one question that we would pose to the tumor board in this patient's case is, should we do the completion if it's ambiguous? And the other one is, should we give radioactive iodine? Because everything about this case is kind of on the margin. It's kind of gray, and we could go either way. So one month post-op, she had a TSH of 0.99, which is in the normal range, and a nice low thyroglobulin with negative antibodies. And you probably remember that the absence of antibodies really allows us to fully interpret this number, the thyroglobulin number. And we thought 0.6 was pretty good. And we waited a little while longer because the patient was unsure in discussions with her endocrinologist whether or not she wanted to have radioactive iodine. and her TSH, you see here, got a little bit more suppressed and her thyroglobulin went down to 0.2. And I pulled this data from an encounter from just a few days ago. And the endocrinologist says the thyroglobulin of 0.2 indicates a very thorough operation. And that made me feel so warm and fuzzy because, you know, surgeons, we need love too. And so I asked Dr. Leung, if you see these TSH and thyroglobulin numbers, How does that influence the decision for radioactive iodine in this case?

Oh, this is so reassuring. I like to see thyroglobulins, you know, definitely less than one or fractions of that. So we are already there so quickly after thyroid surgery has been completed. And that, you know, that number really equates well with how much thyroid tissue is remaining, whether or not that thyroid tissue is cancerous or regular thyroid tissue is remaining microscopically. So there's really almost nothing left. So sometimes we talk about using this separate treatment called reductive iodine in some people to get rid of even more microscopic stuff. But we already shown that that amount is almost negligent. So I would say that she is not going to be benefiting much more from dosing reductive iodine. I would counsel her that we don't necessarily need to do that. In terms of her TSH, that reflects how much thyroid hormone replacement the person is on. So sometimes we, at least initially after surgery, we give them a little bit extra libothyroxine, a little bit too much thyroid hormone replacement just to try to keep the thyroid cancer away in terms of any thyroid cells that might be remaining to not be woken up and stimulated to make thyroid hormones. So I like a TSH that's sort of in that range, a little bit lower than normal around 0.1 and for her probably even up to 0.5 would be fine.

Yeah, this is something relatively new, you know, for patients who could go either way in terms of radioactive iodine or not. I find that more of my patients, we're waiting, we're checking the thyroglobulin and we're seeing whether or not that thyroglobulin level is reassuring. And sorry, Dr. Livitz, are you seeing a similar pattern? What role does the early post-op thyroglobulin play in your patients?

I absolutely agree. I think we have more of these patients that are a little bit in a gray area. There might be some slightly higher risk features, like this patient had a tumor over four centimeters. It did have the BRAF mutation, which has been associated with slightly more aggressive papillary thyroid cancers. However, that's more in older patients and more in male patients. So in a young woman who already has an excellent prognosis, you know, she's a little bit in this gray area. So I think that thyroglobulin level, when it comes back, you know, four to six weeks after surgery and is already very low, we feel fairly confident that there's no more disease at the time. And I would just mention this is one of the benefits of the tumor board is that we can immediately get multiple opinions from different endocrinologists and surgeons in a very efficient way. So rather than the patient, you know, potentially, let's say, you know, you want to know maybe what somebody else might think, and you would go to a separate consultation, you immediately have that entire room full of experts that can look at your specific case, all of the details, and give a group consensus.

Yeah, it's really the tumor board is like getting 25 second opinions at the same time for free. And sometimes there are disagreements, you know, people have to arm wrestle a little bit. But it's good to have a diversity of opinions. So in this case, you know, what I'm thinking is, you know, not all surgery is perfect, right? So I'm wondering in every case after I finish, is it possible that I could have missed something? And there are two ways you can miss something. You can miss it because you didn't see it on the ultrasound, or you can miss it because it was there on the ultrasound, but you didn't remove it. The presence of a thyroglobulin of 0.2 means that neither one of those things happen, right? It means that we have a complete resection. And what's amazing to me is how sensitive. Thyroglobulin tests are so darn sensitive now. They can detect, you know, I often say it's like a smoke alarm who can find There's a guy smoking one cigarette down the block from you and your smoke alarm can pick it up. So in this lady, we've decided to hold at this position. And so that's the end of the first case. And for our moderators, Anjali and Joel, are there questions that have bubbled up about this first case that you think we should answer? Maybe we'll take two of them or so.

reference_conclusion: Following initial lobectomy, completion thyroidectomy was recommended because final pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma measuring 4.3 cm with a close but negative margin. The completion procedure was to be performed either within approximately 1 week or deferred until after 6 weeks if immediate reoperation was not feasible. Postoperatively, given the very low thyroglobulin level after completion thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine was not recommended. Thyroid hormone replacement was to be titrated to maintain mild TSH suppression, with a target approximately 0.1 to 0.5.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging right thyroid mass for approximately 8 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration with ThyroSeq demonstrated medullary carcinoma. Immunostaining was reported as confirmatory for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a right thyroid nodule measuring 2.8 x 1.9 x 2.4 cm. Outside CT neck demonstrated the right thyroid primary lesion, a small nodule inferior to the lower pole, and a right upper cervical lymph node in the level II/III region with loss of fatty hilum. CT chest and MRI abdomen showed no evidence of distant disease. Repeat neck ultrasound identified a suspicious lateral neck lesion; fine-needle aspiration of the upper neck lymph node was benign. A 6 mm hypoechoic nodule inferior to the left lobe was not biopsied.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: RET testing was negative. The case was described as sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative calcitonin was 2053. CEA was normal. Other routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Catecholamine evaluation, including urinary testing, was within normal limits.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old man; physician.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of elevated PSA in the setting of strong family history of prostate cancer and ongoing anxiety regarding possible occult higher-grade disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 1 (Gleason score 3+3), initially identified in 2020 on biopsy.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial prostate biopsy in 2020 showed two foci of Gleason 3+3=6 adenocarcinoma (Grade Group 1) in the left base, involving small amounts of tissue reported as 20% and 5%.

[ imaging findings ]: Prostate MRI performed when PSA was 4.9 showed a PI-RADS 3 lesion at the left base and an approximately 40 g prostate. PSMA PET showed increased uptake within the prostate gland, a small left periaortic node, right adrenal gland uptake, and an osseous lesion in the fifth rib. Review of the PET findings described focal/intense uptake in the prostate and additional low-volume/incidental-appearing uptake elsewhere, including rib activity and vertebral/disc-space activity. Micro-ultrasound demonstrated a PRI-MUS 4/5 lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline testing was negative. Select MDx result was low risk. Oncotype DX on prior biopsy tissue showed very low risk disease, GPS score 17, with an estimated 11% chance of high-risk prostate cancer.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was 4.9 prior to initial MRI. Prostate volume was approximately 40 g. After initiation of finasteride, PSA decreased to less than 1.5 and remained stable thereafter.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent active surveillance following diagnosis of low-volume Grade Group 1 prostate cancer. Finasteride was started after discussion of low-risk disease biology and prostate size contribution to PSA; PSA subsequently decreased to <1.5 and remained stable.

[ current disease status ]: Intraprostatic Grade Group 1 prostate adenocarcinoma, with stable low PSA on finasteride. PSMA PET demonstrated intraprostatic uptake and additional extraprostatic foci (small left periaortic node, right adrenal uptake, fifth rib lesion), without pathologic confirmation of metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Strong family history of prostate cancer involving first-degree relatives, including father and brothers. The patient remained concerned about the possibility of occult higher-grade disease despite low-risk biopsy and genomic findings.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male from Louisiana. Fair-skinned. Non-smoker. Past medical history included non-melanoma skin cancers and cardiac/vascular comorbidity.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable bump/lesion behind the left ear, first noticed while washing hair.

[ diagnosis ]: Cutaneous melanoma of the left postauricular scalp/skin. Initial primary tumor was staged as T3a (stage IIA) on biopsy. Subsequent surgical pathology demonstrated microsatellites and regional nodal metastases in sentinel lymph nodes, with additional non-sentinel nodal involvement after completion lymphadenectomy.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial shave biopsy demonstrated melanoma measuring 3.8 mm in Breslow thickness, non-ulcerated, with mitotic activity, regression, and vascular invasion. Tumor was present at peripheral and deep margins on biopsy. Wide local excision specimen showed residual melanoma and microsatellites. Sentinel lymph node biopsy showed 3/3 positive nodes: 2 positive nodes in level II and 1 positive node in the suboccipital basin. Largest nodal tumor deposit measured 0.9 mm. Completion lymphadenectomy identified 3 additional positive lymph nodes; approximately 70 additional nodes were negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinical examination initially showed no palpable adenopathy. CT imaging showed no pathologically enlarged lymph nodes. Lymphoscintigraphy/SPECT-CT identified sentinel nodes in the suboccipital and level II regions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF wild type. PD-L1 expression was less than 1%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Wide local excision of the primary lesion was performed with 2 cm margins, with delayed reconstruction. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed in the mapped suboccipital and level II basins; 3/3 sentinel nodes were positive. The patient declined systemic therapy initially and underwent completion lymphadenectomy, which showed 3 additional positive nodes. Postoperatively, additional satellite disease developed inferior to the skin graft.

[ other clinical data ]: No nodularity or palpable adenopathy was present on initial examination. Surrounding small satellite lesions were suspected clinically at presentation and microsatellites were confirmed pathologically.

reference_discussion.text: Hi, everybody. Nice to see some familiar faces and names. I appreciate it. I'll keep this quick for discussion purposes. This gentleman who presented noticed a bump behind his left ear when he was washing his hair, seen by a local dermatologist with a biopsy demonstrating melanoma. He has a history of some non-melanoma skin cancers. He is from Louisiana, has some cardiac vascular histories, a non-smoker. The only picture I had of him was an intra-op photo, but essentially on exam, this gentleman is fair-skinned. He's, you know, ambulating and in fairly good physical condition. And he has this lesion behind his ear. It was a shaved biopsy and looks like there's some, no nodularity or palpable adenopathy, but some surrounding looks like small satellites. This is his review of his outside biopsy. It is a 3.8 millimeter, sorry, that does not transmit very well, 3.8 millimeters thick. There's some mitoses that is not ulcerated. There's some regression and vascular invasion. And it's present at peripheral and deep, but as a stage, it's overall 2A, it's a T3A lesion. presume that most surgeons would be worried about this, but would recommend a wide local excision with a sentinel node biopsy. And I was curious what type of imaging people would like, how they'd go about that. I thought that'd be a useful question.

So I guess in the absence of, you said nothing clinically on exam, I'm a person who has an ultrasound in my office, so I probably will be doing a bedside ultrasound in my office anyway, it's free of charge. But if that looks pretty normal to me, I don't feel anything, I'm probably not getting For this level, I'm probably not doing PET and random R. I'm probably leaning more towards Y local with Sentinel node. I don't think I would fault somebody for getting the imaging, but for a 2A, I think I probably would, in the absence of anything on ultrasound, I'd probably just do the Sentinel node.

Great. I completely agree with my colleague. I will say that one thing about the nuance of this case, though, is when you see regression. Regression is something that in AJCC 8 is not considered a high-risk creature, but historically has been considered a high-risk creature. And the reason for that is what are you essentially looking at the regressed melanoma as a melanoma that the actual Breslo appears to be a certain size, but actually was thicker than that. So when you see a regressed melanoma and you come away thinking, because the pathologist is measuring, is measuring the slice of actual viable tumors. So think of a cheesecake, right? So cheesecake is all the way from topping down to crust. And when you have a regressed melanoma, what you're really measuring, you know, hypothetically speaking, is just a crust. So the key question is, did you get any cheesecake, right? And so when you see a regressed melanoma, the thing about a regressed melanoma is that historically has been an idea that you should think about how long the tumor has been there, because the presence of a regression is both a favorable risk factor, a favorable factor, meaning the immune system is attempting to respond to the tumor, but also an unfavorable risk factor, an unfavorable factor, because it really means the tumor is slightly thicker than what it originally, at least now, appears to be. So just something to think about. Some people might, at least in this setting, some older medical oncologists have a preference when they see regressed lesions to strongly push their surgeons towards trying to do more imaging. Some of the newer guys, myself included, we're probably more just looking at the actual breast load depth.

Precisely what I took, I pointed that out and I'd be happy to share a meal with you given your analogies. So this patient, he had a CT scan. I'll tell you that it's usually an ultrasound we get, and he did not have any pathologically enlarged lymph nodes. He had a lymphocytography specced CT, which you can see here, demonstrating some sentinel nodes in the suboccipital and level two regions. Just out of patient counseling and interest, I'll point this out. This is not the only risk prediction Institute of Australia. We work a lot with that group. And just to point out, based upon these factors that you enter in, this is this actual patient. this generates a risk of a positive sentinel node of 70%. So we were all somewhat worried about this, but I find it particularly helpful in patient counseling to use a data-driven approach. And you can show them, there's actually a nice figure that is helpful for communication purposes that you can bring this up in the clinic and show the patient. This patient is from several years ago, but I'm just thinking on the top of my head about trial options already for this gentleman who has an intermediate thickness melanoma. There's a couple there, but he's not really eligible for either of them, just for purposes of discussion. This gentleman had exactly what Trevor was discussing. He had a wide local excision. He had two centimeter margins here, and we did a sentinel node biopsy from the areas that were lit up in the lithocytigraphy, and he had a delayed reconstruction. Anything specific you all want to comment about this? We like to delay the reconstruction, though I don't always do it for and convenience, given my concern about this patient and my concern about some small, you know, microsatellite or satellite lesions around it. That's why I did it.

I agree. I think delaying the recon on these cases makes a lot of sense. There's no wound care risk to doing it. There's no risk for vessel exposure. I would delay it as well, because you can always come back later and do it. And you can cover that with the dressing pretty well.

This is a lot of, sorry. a lot of information, but basically he had some residual melanoma there, and he had three out of three sentinel nodes positive. There were two in the level two, and there was one in the suboccipital. The largest tumor burden was only 0.9 millimeters, so less than one millimeter of largest tumor burden. They went ahead and did some adjuvant or ancillary studies. He was BRAF wild type. Dr. Dahmer, you can comment whether the CPS score here is important. In melanoma, PD-L1, less than 1%. You know, we talk about that a lot as a criteria for systemic therapy and other diseases, but this was his pathology report.
He did have microsatellites, as I said.
So then we came back to our multidisciplinary planning conference, and these are some options for the next step.

So just to go back to that earlier, I mean, not that you have to go back, but just to talk a little bit about the path report, I think there are two points to raise. The interesting thing is, from a staging perspective, the presence of satellites. Satellites is what is giving this guy the high-risk staging. So what you would consider is that the presence of the satellites is really what is upstaging this guy. When you've got microscopic node-positive disease, you could have a high absolute number of lymph nodes. with AJCC, the staging classification is really very weighted, especially with eight towards the depth of the primary tumor. So what would be very interesting in this guy's case is if he had multiple nodes that were just microscopically node positive, that would be a very different stage than if he had the presence of a satellite. So that's one kind of interesting feature, if you really wanted to nerd out over surgical staging. To me, just to talk about a point that Dr. Gephardt raised, which is the presence of trials. So two things. There are actually, interestingly enough, some trials that are going on in the space. So the University of Pennsylvania, really one of your guys' colleagues, George Karakousis, has done this very provocative trial of looking at pembrolizumab And so George has essentially looked at pre-sensital node immunotherapy in high-risk node negative clinically node negative melanoma.

So we discussed these various options with the patient. At this time, the patient was a candidate for some of these protocols that were discussed earlier. including neoadjuvant, or sorry, adjuvant systemic therapies. We had some adjuvant radiation protocols. We were particularly worried about the primary site having microsatellites and considering adjuvant radiation to that area, certainly a combination of these things. That thing being said, the patient's wife had had a previous immune-related adverse event, and he did not want to have systemic therapy. He was concerned about it for some valid reasons, given his experience, and the patient elected to have a completion lymphadenectomy, which he underwent. This had three additional lymph nodes positive, so there were six positive, including what we removed, and another 70 or so that were negative. So then here we have this patient with additional non-satellite, sorry, non-sentinel lepidodes positive. So this gentleman came back to our post-op appointment, and of course he has some additional satellite disease inferior to his skin graft, which we were disheartened by, but I don't think anybody would be completely surprised. We had another discussion at planning conference and here is where we can see the benefit of this neoadjuvant approach and why some of these patients did better. So this patient was, we knew that he needed something other than surgery. This is what Dr. Hackman was also talking about before patients recurring, you know, before you've had a chance to get them healed from their surgery. Essentially, what this patient went on to was a combination of nivolumab. He did not want double agent therapy, again, given his concern about a mean-related adverse event. And he also had TVEC injections. concurrently. After the fifth injection, all of these lesions disappeared. They were no longer clinically evident. There was a biopsy done of the area, which showed some rare viable melanoma cells, as you can see. And he completed one year of systemic nivolumab and stopped that again. At this time, then, the pandemic was beginning and most of his care he developed some small nodules, about eight millimeters. One was peripheral and a candidate for biopsy, which unfortunately demonstrated metastatic melanoma. Any comments at this point? I think I just have one more slide.

So, I'll say one thing I mean we talked about this, you present that last part about having this disease and it's sort of sad that the patient recur but let's let's take a step back and think about where we were five to 10 years ago with melanoma. And this patient's not making it 18 months. And so I think that. One thing to take a look at for the trainees now is that really immunotherapy TBAC has changed. These patients survive more than three, six, nine months and now it's recurrence, it's got bilateral lung nodules, but But that amount of disease-free survival is just impressive. It's the advanced melanoma that we really didn't have 10 years ago. It is a case that reminds you that melanoma is unforgiving, but at the same time, the response of therapy still is quite impressive and it did give some meaningful, durable control would be my thought.

I'd actually completely endorse that and highlight one thing. In the medical oncology community, TVEC has a rep as a drug that does not work. And I actually think that that is completely untrue. TVEC is actually a very effective drug that just happened to be developed at the same time as a more effective drug. So you can't be blamed if you're playing on the same team as Kobe and you only score 25 points a game, right? Just because there's somebody who's better than you doesn't make you a less good player. And the problem with TVEC was that it was FDA approved roundabout the same time that Pembrolizumab or Keytruda was. And so what we have now is a setting in which this drug is actually extraordinarily effective for this very small subpopulation of patients in whom it's designed to be utilized. And it's no surprise that MD Anderson is a place where they know clearly how to utilize this drug. But when you're at a large center, when you have appropriate multidisciplinary care, when you're triaging patients appropriately, there are indications where you can effectively use this agent, and it's really, truly very effective in the right hands, even it's checkpoint-inhibited refractory patients. So I'd highlight, actually in this case, this is actually a very good example of a very effective use of TVEC, because this guy really responded to TVEC. He did not respond to the checkpoint, because if you're gonna respond to checkpoint, you're not relapsing at a year, eight months, a year and six months with metastatic disease. This guy responded to TVEC, TVEC worked, didn't necessarily work Elsewhere, you don't generally have a response in uninjected disease, but this is a very good example of the suitable use and appropriate use of an intralesional therapy that unfortunately has not gotten wider traction. Now, hopefully, there are some newer agents that you guys might be hearing about in the next three to six months that are newer oncolytic viruses that are eliciting very, very durable responses in, and you might, that hopefully will have a path to registration.

So I'll ask you a question back. With the PATH report from his initial resection that showed microsatellites, what is your thought about preemptive TVEC injection, knowing that there's a high risk of, and was even mentioned, I mean, I think that was part of the concern was that Ryan mentioned was the risk of the microsatellites. What do you think about preventative or preemptive TVEC in the area?

So I think, Let me break that down into two questions, and that is preoperative, meaning neoadjuvant TVEC, and neoadjuvant immunotherapy in the setting of satellites. In the pooled analysis that was published by some of Dr. Gephardt's colleagues and myself, very interestingly, satellites and in-transit disease were two subgroups that did not derive as much benefit from neoadjuvant immunotherapy. So these are two sort of subgroups that just, for some reason, probably biological and actually more anatomical, just do not respond quite as well to neoadjuvant systemic immunotherapy with the same degree of response as, say, a nodal MET. So one issue is that the moment you see satellites, that's just a bad actor, clinically observed satellites. Neoadjuvant TVEC has been studied. There's a phase two trial by Reinhard Duhme looking at preoperative versus preoperative TVEC versus TVEC versus just surgery. And necessarily preoperative TVEC did quite produce a certain path response. There was not much RFS benefit. But to your point, there will be at ASCO, unfortunately the data is embargoed for at least another couple of weeks, but there will be a ASCO abstract discussing the role of perioperative immune therapy, combination of TVEC and systemic immunotherapy. So NEVL plus TVEC. been discussed by an Italian group that I'll draw your attention to in the melanoma session. Suffice to say that I think that in this subpopulation, this is actually a good idea. It's not obviously FDA approved. You have to just clarify that based on the Masterkey 265 data, the combination of checkpoint plus intralesional TVEC did not result in an improved survival benefit compared to, again, either PD-1 alone. Thanks, Dean Walker. We have about 13 minutes. I wanted to let Dr. Cain have some time to present her case.

reference_conclusion: Initial management consisted of wide local excision with 2 cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy, with delayed reconstruction given concern for microsatellites/satellite lesions at the primary site. After pathology demonstrated residual melanoma with microsatellites and positive sentinel nodes, adjuvant options including systemic therapy and radiation were reviewed; however, the patient declined systemic therapy and proceeded with completion lymphadenectomy. Following postoperative development of additional satellite disease, treatment was escalated to nivolumab in combination with concurrent T-VEC injections, with completion of one year of nivolumab after clinical regression of the lesions.

He had two centimeter margins here, and we did a sentinel node biopsy from the areas that were lit up in the lithocytigraphy, and he had a delayed reconstruction. [...] We were particularly worried about the primary site having microsatellites and considering adjuvant radiation to that area, certainly a combination of these things. That thing being said, the patient's wife had had a previous immune-related adverse event, and he did not want to have systemic therapy. He was concerned about it for some valid reasons, given his experience, and the patient elected to have a completion lymphadenectomy, which he underwent. [...] Essentially, what this patient went on to was a combination of nivolumab. He did not want double agent therapy, again, given his concern about a mean-related adverse event. And he also had TVEC injections. concurrently. After the fifth injection, all of these lesions disappeared. They were no longer clinically evident. [...] And he completed one year of systemic nivolumab and stopped that again.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 85-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma of the right neck/thyroid region with locoregional invasion and distant metastatic disease. Coexisting bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma was identified in the surgical specimen. A sigmoid colon lesion was identified on evaluation and biopsy showed adenoma with high-grade dysplasia.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the neck mass showed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Following surgery, pathology showed marked treatment effect with tumor liquefaction/necrosis. Residual viable anaplastic thyroid carcinoma comprised approximately 5% of the primary tumor, measuring 1.4 cm. Residual viable disease in the central lymph node dissection was approximately 1%. Bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma was present, with the largest papillary carcinoma focus measuring 1.2 cm. Multiple metastatic lateral lymph nodes were present. Microscopy demonstrated necrosis, residual anaplastic carcinoma, and papillary thyroid carcinoma components.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck CT showed a right necrotic tumor with coarse calcification and local/regional invasion. Initial FDG PET demonstrated a markedly FDG-avid neck mass extending posteriorly, with bilateral FDG-avid cervical lymph nodes. Distant metastatic disease was present. The primary disease was predominantly locally aggressive and was considered unresectable at presentation. Airway imaging showed marked leftward tracheal deviation with a widely patent airway and no suspected airway compromise. After 1 month of systemic therapy, imaging showed reduction in tumor size and FDG avidity, with improvement in metastatic disease. At 3 months, structural response was documented and the disease became resectable. Follow-up imaging after surgery and adjuvant treatment showed small-volume residual disease. Pulmonary metastases remained stable and demonstrated low FDG avidity. Persistent FDG uptake in the sigmoid colon had improved with systemic treatment.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF mutation testing was positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She was referred in July. Because the disease was unresectable at presentation, she was started on dabrafenib plus trametinib at standard doses. Treatment was well tolerated. At 1 month, there was radiographic and metabolic response in the neck tumor and improvement in metastatic disease. At 3 months, sufficient structural response had occurred to permit surgery. She subsequently underwent thyroid surgery with central and bilateral lymph node dissection. Postoperatively, she received IMRT to the neck. Dabrafenib plus trametinib was resumed after completion of radiotherapy. Immunotherapy was added thereafter, and she had received 3 doses at the time of follow-up.

[ current disease status ]: Residual disease persisted but was limited in volume on follow-up imaging. Pulmonary metastatic disease was stable and low FDG-avid. The sigmoid colon lesion remained under evaluation/treatment planning after colonoscopic biopsy demonstrated adenoma with high-grade dysplasia.

[ other clinical data ]: Colonoscopy of the sigmoid lesion showed adenoma with high-grade dysplasia. The sigmoid lesion was considered a second primary lesion rather than thyroid cancer metastasis.

They don't quite do as well as with the BRAF patients, but we would want to know what that main driver mutation is. So we would want a core then.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive metastatic breast cancer after prior endocrine-based systemic therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma, bilateral breast involvement, hormone receptor-positive and initially HER2-low by prior biopsy. Disease had involved bilateral breasts, cervical/supraclavicular and bilateral axillary lymph nodes, lungs, and bones. Left breast disease had been described as inflammatory at initial presentation; right breast disease had involved the retroareolar region with skin involvement.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial breast biopsy performed in November 2023 from the left breast showed estrogen receptor positive (ER 8+), progesterone receptor positive (PR 8+), and HER2 IHC 1+. Repeat biopsy was performed in September 2025 from the contralateral breast and supraclavicular node. IHC from the repeat biopsy was pending at the time of reporting.

[ imaging findings ]: At initial diagnosis in November 2023, metastatic disease was present in bilateral breasts, cervical nodes, bilateral axillary nodes, and bones. PET scan in October 2024 showed partial response after first-line systemic therapy. After approximately 12 months of treatment, imaging showed progression in bone lesions, bilateral breast lesions, lung nodules, and nodal disease, with new bone metastases. PET scan in August 2025 showed further progression in bones, nodes, and breast lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling on the September 2025 biopsy showed:
- Genomic scar/HRD score: 45
- PIK3CA mutation, variant allele frequency 58%
- ESR1 mutation
- ERBB2 (HER2) amplification with copy number approximately 10
- Additional amplifications reported in MYC, MDM4, and FGFR1

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Following diagnosis in November 2023, the patient initially pursued alternative treatment and did not start systemic oncologic therapy at that time. She presented again in April 2024 with progressive disease. First-line treatment with ribociclib plus letrozole was started in May 2024. This was tolerated for approximately 1 year and produced a partial response on PET imaging in October 2024. After subsequent progression at approximately 12 months, repeat biopsy and molecular testing were advised but initially declined. Ribociclib was continued and fulvestrant was added as subsequent endocrine-based therapy. After 3 months, PET imaging in August 2025 showed further progression. Following repeat biopsy in September 2025 and progression on two prior standard lines of therapy, systemic chemotherapy with paclitaxel plus carboplatin was started. At the time of reporting, she had received cycle 2.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with radiologic progression after ribociclib/letrozole and ribociclib/fulvestrant. At the time of reporting, she was receiving paclitaxel plus carboplatin, remained asymptomatic, and early clinical response had been observed after 2 cycles. Current repeat-biopsy HER2 IHC remained pending.

[ other clinical data ]: Follow-up compliance had been suboptimal during prior therapy, although treatment had been continued. Blocks from the repeat biopsy had been used for NGS; repeat IHC had not yet been completed at the time of reporting.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult female with breast cancer. Initial presentation occurred in 2010.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic breast cancer with disease progression after multiple prior systemic therapies; new liver lesion identified in July of the current year.

[ diagnosis ]: Initially diagnosed in 2010 with triple-positive breast cancer (ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-positive). Metastatic recurrence/progression was documented in 2014 with bone metastases. Subsequent metastatic progression involved lung, adrenal gland, and liver. On later biopsy of a liver lesion, the tumor remained ER-positive, became PR-negative, and was HER2-negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Liver lesion biopsy performed in July of the current year showed metastatic breast carcinoma that was ER-positive, PR-negative, and HER2-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Bone metastases were identified in 2014. Later progression occurred in the lung and adrenal gland. Within 1 year of second-line ado-trastuzumab emtansine, enlarging lung lesions were documented. A new liver lesion was identified in July of the current year.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling identified:
- PIK3CA p.H1047R mutation
- High tumor mutational burden
- BRCA2 alteration
- BRCA2 reversion alteration

Tumor mutational burden was 19 mutations/megabase.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- 2010: Received TCH (docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab), followed by trastuzumab, then maintenance endocrine therapy with a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor.
- 2014 metastatic progression to bone: Received first-line paclitaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab; subsequently continued trastuzumab plus pertuzumab, with fulvestrant added.
- This regimen achieved disease control for approximately 5 years.
- After progression in lung and adrenal gland: Switched to second-line ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1).
- Within 1 year on T-DM1: Developed enlarging lung lesions.
- Subsequently received trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd); treatment was discontinued because of interstitial lung disease of sufficient severity to require cessation.
- Thereafter received ribociclib plus fulvestrant.
- After identification of a new liver lesion in July of the current year, started capecitabine; capecitabine was poorly tolerated.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with prior receptor conversion from HER2-positive disease to HER2-negative disease on liver biopsy, persistent ER positivity, PR negativity, and recent progression following multiple prior lines of therapy. Most recent documented disease sites included liver, lung, adrenal gland, and bone.

[ other clinical data ]: Interstitial lung disease occurred during trastuzumab deruxtecan therapy and led to treatment discontinuation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 85-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally identified right thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with nodal metastases, including a metastatic left level II cervical lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside biopsy of the right thyroid nodule confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinic ultrasound demonstrated a right thyroid nodule measuring 4.2 x 2.6 x 1.9 cm with microcalcifications and irregular lateral borders. The interface between the right thyroid and trachea was difficult to define, and the strap musculature was difficult to ascertain. Minimal to no thyroid tissue was present on the left. One right level III lateral lymph node contained microcalcifications; central neck nodes were difficult to assess. Formal neck ultrasound showed indeterminate right level IV lymph nodes and indeterminate left level IA and IIA lymph nodes. CT neck demonstrated a large right thyroid nodule measuring 4.4 x 4.0 x 4.3 cm with several internal calcifications and no obvious concerning cervical lymph nodes. CT chest was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E positive.

[ current disease status ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with a metastatic left level II cervical lymph node confirmed on fine-needle aspiration.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was asymptomatic at presentation. He had no history of radiation exposure. Examination showed a palpable right thyroid nodule that was firm and fixed along the trachea; voice was strong without breathiness. Flexible laryngoscopic examination was unremarkable. Fine-needle aspiration of a left level II lymph node was positive for metastatic disease, and thyroglobulin washout was positive. Past medical history included coronary artery disease with two coronary stents, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Medications included aspirin 81 mg, metformin, levothyroxine, amlodipine, and lisinopril. No prior relevant head and neck surgery or prior anesthesia complications were reported.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, great. Can you see my screen? My name's Annie. I'm one of the PGY-3 residents from Walter Reed. So this was an 85-year-old male who presented back in August with a 3.5-centimeter right thyroid nodule. It was incidentally found during a hearing aid consult with a community ENT and he had an outside biopsy of his nodule and it was proven to be PTC. It was BRAF V600E positive on a firm of testing. And on presentation to Dr. Dillon's clinic, he was completely asymptomatic. He had no history of radiation exposure. In terms of past medical history, he has coronary artery disease with two stents in place on 81 milligrams of aspirin, type 2 diabetes on metformin. He's been hypothyroid for the past year on a stable dose of Synthroid. He has hypertension hyperlipidemia on amlodipine and lisinopril, and he had no relevant head and neck surgery with no past issues with anesthesia. On initial exam, he had a very palpable right thyroid nodule that was firm and fixed along the trachea, but his voice was strong without breathiness. His clinic scope was essentially unremarkable. Dr. Dillon's clinic ultrasound showed a 4.2 by 2.6 by 1.9 centimeter nodule with microcalcs and irregular lateral borders. He had a formal neck ultrasound a few days later, which showed indeterminate right level 4 lymph nodes and an indeterminate left 1A and 2A node. He had a CT neck that same day, which I'll play. And it shows this large right thyroid nodule, which was measured 4.4 by 4 by 4.3 centimeters with several internal calcifications and no obvious concerning neck nodes.
Very fishy looking there on the cartilage.
Agreed.
All right.
Agreed. He went a biopsy of those neck nodes. There was one positive left level two neck node and the thyroglobulin wash was notably positive.

It can confirm your suspicion, essentially? Yeah.
Sorry, I don't mean to put you guys on the spot.

Yeah, there's a high rate of sometimes an indeterminate cytology, or you can get mixed up with the lymphocytes, right, in a lymph node, and you may not be able to pick out that is papillary, but the thyroid globulin would be more specific. So it's a good indicator of a you know, thyroid cancer within the node.
Yeah. So anytime you're doing an FNA in this case, when you're suspicious of papillary, I'd recommend adding that on. All right, next slide.

Just be mindful, just one comment. If the patient has taroglobulin for positive antibodies, taroglobulin washout may be false negative in that lymph node. So just be mindful if it's negative, it may be due to antibodies too.

Hey Lynn, just because we have a lot of fellows, can you go through how you do one, how you interpret it, anything else you do at the time of a thyroglobulin washout? Because I think that'd be helpful for the fellows.

You send it for biochemistry for a thyroglobulin. And it's entirely useless. unless you also order a serum thyroglobulin at the same time. What you're looking for is a massive difference in ratio. So it's not a very complicated test. It's your FNA. You do FNAs in the clinic all the time. Very helpful, thank you. Excellent. Okay, let's keep going.

Do you wanna just summarize real quick what we have? We have a exercise papillary with where the neck disease is.

Yeah, I mean, I don't have my note off hand, but just to clarify our plan, given the disease was actually a total thyroid bilateral central and a left lateral neck. He didn't have right lateral neck disease and then based upon the findings of the right. lobectomy, which was basically effacing the cricothyroid cartilage with no invasion. Let me just summarize the findings and the outcome here, because I think it's a little bit, just to be totally clear. So we did the right thyroid lobe and the left thyroid lobe. So the thyroid's completely removed, but the right nerve is not working as well as we like. And so we've deferred the left lateral neck dissection because of some concern about injuring the vagus and ending up with a bilateral vocal cord paralysis.
Correct.

Okay. So just want to make sure that's clear for the fellows of why exactly we're not doing the left lateral neck dissection. So there's a lot of interesting intraoperative decision-making happening. Dr. Wang, if you do one side of a total thyroidectomy, a planned total thyroidectomy for cancer, and you are dissecting tumor off the nerve and you lose stem, what goes into your mind when you're deciding whether or not to proceed with the other side?

That's such a good question, Caitlin. The first thing is you want to see if the loss system is real or not. You can have a loss system for many reasons. It could be that the tube gets torqued, the tube gets pulled back, you're working and by pulling on it, You could have temporary paresis. You could have long-term paresis because you're rough on the nerve. So what I do first is I take a pause. I check the tube, make sure that everything is plugged in properly, and then do a little stim. If I can't get any kind of signal in the nerve, I just do the cricothyroid twitch palpation. I just hook my finger behind to the PCA, and then you touch the nerve. And if you feel a little twitch, you know it's intact and it's a system problem. If you can't feel a twitch, then you know it's really down. And if it's really down, you look at the number, you see what the amplitude is. You should know what it was to start with, and you see what the number is. If it's like 99, then you wait like five minutes, and it's back to 110, and you get a beep again. But there's nothing magical about 100. 100 is what most people use as a threshold. That's just a cutoff. But then if I really do lose signal, then I usually stop. I honestly usually stop and I do something else. I don't work on the nerve. If I feel like I was really good on the nerve and I feel like I don't think I really did anything bad, sometimes I'll go do something else without pulling on the nerve. I'll work on a different part of the thyroid where there's no tension on it, and then I'll re-stim it a little bit later. It could be 10, 15, 20 minutes later. if you have a temporary process from traction, sometimes it comes back like right away and you're like, oh my God, it's okay again. But then you have to be like super careful with how you're holding the thyroid and not yanking on it. Cause it's most of these injuries are not like traumatic sectioning or cutting or anything or burning. It's usually traction from pulling the poor nerve is getting yanked up and you just have to relax and let it recover. And if I can't get it to recover and it's really down, then I stop. I stop usually.

Yeah, I think that's a key point to take a pause, troubleshoot, stop. If it's really out, it's never the wrong answer. We're dealing with papillary thyroid cancer here, not squamous cell or something else like that. And they're still going to live a long time, even if you had done nothing originally, right? So you don't want to have them end up with bilateral vocal cord paralysis over this. So there's different ways to handle it. Sometimes people think about their own personal rate of nerve injury, if the risk benefit of going to the other side. One other tactic that sometimes people do is if you start to see that one side might be potentially at risk, going to the normal side, doing that one and getting that nerve out, feeling confident that you can be a little more aggressive on the tumor side. So there's several ways to handle it, but really just doing what you can to avoid a bilateral cord paralysis. Let's go to the next slide. We wanna have time for Dr. Jethwa's case as well.

All right, pathology showed what we expected, PTC in that right thyroid lobe measuring 4.2 centimeters. In the right central neck, there was three of nine lymph nodes that were positive. Left central neck, the nodes were negative. That is our last slide. He is- Thank you. He is scheduled for a left lateral neck dissection in December.
So did his nerve, when he woke up, was his nerve okay?

Yeah, he ended up having good mobility, but I'll be honest, he has an SLN paresis and the nuances of that, I mean, he's already had some voice change, which he could function with, but you know, there is some, it's not a paresis picture, but it does cause dysfunction. So, you know, I think it's important when we're thinking about lateral neck, lateral neck disease doesn't kill us, right, with papillary, but, if we do hit the vagus, we can cause more dysfunction even to that recurrent. So, you know, he were going for the stage surgery. He's willing to go through that, but it's still weak. But we're waiting for it to see if there's going to be any more kind of synkinesis. But if not, he's OK with proceeding with the mobility that he has. So it's not a perfect picture. But I think from a quality of life standpoint, this is what, you know, this is the best thing for him at his age and what he wants.

Yeah, older people tend to be much more sensitive to those nerve injuries. So great case. I think the keys for this one are what do you do when you suspect nerve paresis intraoperatively for a cancer case? So I think there's some great pearls from that discussion. Thank you. Let's go to our last case. Dr. Jethwa from the University of Minnesota pivoting a little bit to medullary thyroid cancer.

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck dissection; the right thyroid lobe was resected with a cuff of involved muscle, yielding an R1 resection, and the planned left lateral neck dissection was deferred intraoperatively because of decreased right recurrent laryngeal nerve stimulation and concern for bilateral vocal cord paralysis. A staged left lateral neck dissection is planned in December, with interval observation of vocal cord function and proceeding based on recovery and residual mobility.
