case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Partial right lung atelectatic change identified incidentally on routine breast MRI in 2016, prompting further evaluation.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma, ER-negative, consistent with primary lung origin, with pulmonary and osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Bronchoscopy with lymph node biopsy demonstrated adenocarcinoma. Immunophenotypic description included ER negativity and findings consistent with a pulmonary primary.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Routine breast MRI in 2016 suggested partial atelectasis of the right lung.  
- Subsequent CT chest demonstrated a large hilar mass.  
- Restaging imaging demonstrated no evidence of brain metastases.  
- Restaging imaging demonstrated bone metastases and pulmonary metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Tumor genotyping identified alterations in TP53, STAG2, NF1, and FOXL2.  
- TP53 alteration: p.Arg181Pro missense mutation.  
- STAG2 alteration: splice-region intronic variant.  
- NF1 alteration: splice-region intronic variant.  
- Rapid EGFR testing: negative.  
- ALK FISH testing: negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Remote history of ER-positive breast cancer approximately 20 years earlier.  
- Prior breast cancer treatment included standard chemotherapy followed by tamoxifen and an aromatase inhibitor.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic lung cancer with pulmonary and osseous metastatic disease; no brain metastases identified on restaging imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you for the panel. We have an excellent panel here. Dr. Ellison is a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and the program director for breast medical oncology at MGH. He's the co-leader of the breast cancer program at Dana-Farber Harvard Cancer Center. His personal clinical practice is focused on cancer risk assessment, and he leads our genetic clinic at MGH in breast cancer. And his lab is focused on revolutionizing cancer treatment through personalized cancer treatment with a particular focus on triple negative breast cancer and TP53. Dr. Daryl Berger is the co-director of the Translational Research Lab at MGH. He was instrumental in developing the snapshot tumor genotyping technology at MGH and leads a biomarker efforts for trials where we partner with industry. Justin Gaynor is an attending physician in thoracic oncology at MGH. He's involved in leading clinical trials, particularly related to immunotherapy and immunotherapy combinations. He's also the MGH principal investigator of the Stand Up to Cancer grant, focusing on targeting KRAS in lung cancer through immunotherapy and targeted therapy combination. So we have a wonderful panel here, and we thought we'll discuss two cases. So I'll start with the first case. The first case is of a 74-year-old female who had a remote history of breast cancer. 20 years ago, she was diagnosed with ER-positive breast cancer, had received standard chemotherapy, followed by tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitor. In 2016, during a routine breast MRI, it was noted that she might have partial atelectasis of her right side of the lung. So this was worked up further with a CAT scan, which demonstrated a large hyaluron mass, underwent a bronchoscopy and biopsy of the lymph nodes, which demonstrated adenocarcinoma that was ER negative and consistent with a pulmonary primary. She also had routine restaging scans done, which demonstrated no evidence of brain mets, but demonstrated evidence of bone mets, as well as pulmonary mets. So she was diagnosed with metastatic lung cancer. Her tumor was sent for genotyping, and the genotyping report showed an alteration in TP53, STAG2, NF1, FOXL2. She also had rapid EGFR and ALK fish testing done. That was negative. So I'll probably start here and start with Daryl. Daryl, do you want to comment on the genotyping results for this patient?

Yeah, so we have four different variants that were identified. All four of these are tumor suppressors. So maybe just kind of go down the list of what was found. So P53, no introduction needed for P53. Obviously, a primary tumor suppressor gene mutated in half of all cancers, including lung cancer. Very important, obviously, for DNA repair. The mutation that we see here, arginine 181 to proline, this is a missense mutation, so these are the hardest for us. We have to determine if this is deleterious or not, or if this is a passenger mutation. Fortunately for p53, there's some good databases that are available. The World Health Organization has a good one, the IARC, and so we would look there and find that this is in fact a deleterious mutation. So clearly a driver mechanism in this patient's tumor. In terms of lung cancer, PV3 mutations are associated with worse prognosis, particularly in lower grades. I don't know how that pertains to this patient here, but. Then going down to STAG2. This is a gene that is part of the cohesion complex that's required for proper segregation of chromosomes during mitosis. And mutations are known to drive aneuploidy. We found a splice region intronic variant here. And this would be deleterious. So this is a region that's required for recognition of the intron-exon boundaries. And if you have a mutation there, what happens is you can have a lot of intronic sequence that gets put into that RNA, or you have a lot of skipping of exons. And so that gets incorporated into the protein, and you would have an abnormal protein in that respect. In terms of implications in lung cancer, there's really not a lot of information prevalent to mutations across cancers as a whole. It is about, I think, 5 to 15% lung cancer is pretty much right in the middle of that. Interestingly, though, based on this signature, if you look at Ewing's sarcoma, which is a childhood malignancy, bone malignancy, Coalterations of STAG2 together with P53 actually suggest very poor prognosis. So this might be a signature of a very aggressive form of lung cancer. Then I'd probably jump down to the SMARC A4. That is the catalytic subunit of the SWI-SNF chromatin remodeling complex. So it's important for driving gene expression as well as DNA damage. We have a point mutation here. It's very rare in lung cancer to find these alterations, and this is a particularly rare variant here, so there's really no information as to what the clinical relevance of this might be, but there was a report, I think it was earlier this year, that showed at least reduced expression, RNA expression of SPARK4 in lung cancer was associated with not just poor prognosis, so we have another prognostic indicator here, but then also potential response to chemotherapy, but we know based on the history. that might not be the case. Then lastly, NF1, we have another splice region intronic variant, so we think that this is going to be relevant in this patient. NF1 is involved as a modulator of MAP kinase signaling. It is actually a negative modulator when it's intact, so mutation would lead to inactivation and drive the activity of a very important cancer signaling pathway. There's actually some cross-talk with another very important cancer pathway, the PI3K-AKT mTOR pathway. So this would be actually, I think, a significant finding in this patient.
and maybe multiple driver mutations. How do you distinguish clonal versus subclonal, driver versus passenger, because this would have big implications for therapy.

Yeah, absolutely. It's tough. This is actually a tough case. You pick probably one of the tougher cases, being tumor suppressors. Great for discussion. Unlike oncogenes, you know, oncogenes are leading to constitutive activation. So it's really a small number of mutations that would drive that, and those are very well characterized. With tumor suppressors, you can inactivate the protein many, many different ways. So what we look for is mutations that clearly lead to dysfunction of proteins. So a mutation that would lead to a nonsense mutation, introduction of a stop codon, you'd have a truncated protein. A frame shift where all the coding gets shifted. Usually what happens is you have a premature stop codon that gets introduced there. splice site mutations we talked about. But it's really the missense mutations that are difficult to really determine. Those are 80% of the mutations that we find. And so it's a painstaking process. I mean, everyone is on a case-by-case basis. We have to go into the literature. We probably start off going through some of the resources like the Cancer Genome Atlas and COSMIC to look at the frequency of these alterations that have been reported in cancer. I'll try to get some insight there. There are some predictions in terms of whether or not it's deleterious or not. But ultimately, we go into a ClinVar that might have some information as to its clinical relevance. But usually, we're going into PubMed on a case-by-case basis and looking for information as to the biological implications of that mutation. And if we're lucky, we'll get some information on therapeutic implications. So it can be difficult, it can take a lot of time. In terms of heterogeneity, what we look at is we actually look at the allelic frequency of that mutation and look at the sample that we tested in terms of the tumor cellularity. So if we had a tumor that was 50%, we had a tissue that was 50% tumor, we did testing and we found an allelic frequency of 10%. for a mutation, we would suggest that, you know, that was probably indication of heterogeneity. Sometimes we'll actually find mutations, concurrent mutations in the same gene at low allelic frequency, which would, again, indicate heterogeneity. Those are some of the things we look at.
Yeah, you know, I think absolutely. So the idea is that

You know, of course, a driver mutation is going to be in the founder clone. And so all clones that are derived from that will still have that underlying mutation. And so as Bruce mentioned, when we do sequencing, we have a readout in terms of how many reads had a mutation versus all the reads for that run. And that will give us an allelic frequency. And when we're looking at tumor suppressors, it's a little bit complex because there could be loss of heterozygosity. in terms of what that allelic frequency will be. But the idea is that if you have a 50% tumor and your allelic frequency is 50%, you probably have a loss of heterozygous event in a tumor suppressor and then a mutation that's found across pretty much all the clones in that tumor.

So you've lost the normal allele. Correct. And then since it's 50% that have the mutant allele, In 50% of the cells are tumor, virtually every tumor cell, at least you can presume it's in the tumor cell. They have that mutation.

But there's also the scenario, though, in that same context where you might find the mutation at 25%. So half. So there's probably likely another mechanism that silenced the other. And so that would be consistent also within 100%.
So what is the sort of baseline for allelic frequency that you use as saying this is actually likely to be important? Does it vary with genes and with?

You know, it's kind of a toolbox approach. I think that we really try to assimilate as much information as possible to really try to understand the potential clinical impact of these variants. So allelic frequency is just really one aspect of that. If we find, like I said, if there's like an 80%, a sample with 80% tumor, and then we find something at a 5% allelic frequency, more than likely that occurred late in evolution of that tumor. It's not really an underlying founder mutation. We would probably weigh that a little bit less than something that was in the vast majority of those tumor cells.

It's a great point, and I'm sure this gets also complicated by aneuploidy and other alterations that a tumor cell might possess. Absolutely. Leif, can you comment on TP53? What does the TP53 alteration signify in terms of functional consequence and consequence on the cellular signaling, and also some potential strategies to target TP53?

Thank you, Aditya. I think I'd maybe like to first take a step back, and Daryl has given a great perspective from the molecular pathologist about synthesizing data and interpreting reports. But ultimately, of course, the goal of the report is to make it interpretable for the oncologist. And it's a shame the audience can't see the report, because one of the most critical factors for the molecular pathologist is to synthesize the data to the degree that oncologist knows whether the findings are truly actionable in the clinical setting or not. And for example, the variants that are found in this case, none of them would really rise to the top two or three tiers of what would be considered clinically actionable. And so this is a good case of where very interesting variants are found, but one of the most important messages in the report would be to convey to the oncologist that these were things that were somewhat far afield from actionable. We've published on this about what is the optimal way to report these complex molecular findings in tumors, and we and others agree that really there has to be a very clear tiered system in terms of clinical reports of molecular pathology that oncologists can readily translate into therapeutic actionability. For example, top tier would be a mutation BRAF V600E linked to an FDA approved medication. Second tier would be perhaps mutations that are clearly associated with spot responses, but either perhaps not to an FDA approved, but an emerging agent, or perhaps an agent that's FDA approved for a different indication or different disease type. A third tier, and these need to be carefully delineated in these reports, would be, for example, variants that are related to pathways linked to response or variants not clearly associated with response. The talk we heard from Neil Rosen yesterday about the whole panoply of BRAF variants might fall into that third tier category because they haven't been correlated with clinical responses in a systematic way. And then fourth tier would be variants that probably are affecting the function of a gene, but unclear what we would do clinically about that. And then the fifth tier would be some of the ones which actually includes two of the variants here that are intronic, suspected to be deleterious in terms of gene function. but not entirely clear that they're affecting the function of the gene. So I don't know, did the audience get the reports at all, just so they know? But just so you know that this is not the report that a clinician would get and that the clinicians and pathologists currently and where the landscape of the field is are working very closely together to try to make these reports as interpretable as possible in terms of the actual meaning because the data is very complex. So on to p53. So p53, of course, the most common gene mutated in cancer. Currently, not directly therapeutically actionable, just so that folks know there's, of course, a lot of interest in how do we target P53. There's three general strategies to target P53 in the current thinking. Number one is for tumors that have wild-type P53, the idea of reactivating that wild-type P53 through inhibitors such as MDM2. The second class is mutations of P53 where there's loss of function. that changes the metabolism or properties of the cell that might create so-called synthetic lethalities. So a p53 mutant tumor would be sensitive to a particular drug that a p53 wild-type normal cell would not. So those are two of the ways. And then the third way, p53 is a rather unique tumor suppressor because its mutations not only lose the normal function, but actually gain an oncogenic function. P53, if you put the mutant protein in a cell, it actually promotes metastasis and other properties. And so other strategies have come up to try to refold in some cases the protein structure of that mutant p53 to make it behave more like wild type where it would then execute the tumor cell. And so those are the three approaches, none at the level of phase three trials yet, but the work goes on.

Well, that's excellent. Thank you so much for your comments, Leif. This is very helpful and good feedback for us for future tumor boards as well. Justin, do you want to comment on the role of immunotherapy, particularly in a tumor that might have multiple alterations and the role of TP53?

Yeah, so that's a great question. And I think this is a good segue from the previous talk, where Dr. Wu showed several papers looking at mutational load and responsiveness to immunotherapy. And really beginning with melanoma and moving towards lung cancer, and then more recently in colorectal cancer, showing that As one increases mutational load, it seems like there's an association with responsiveness to checkpoint blockade. And in fact, it's now become sort of an obligatory slide showing the TCGA data based on each cancer type. And we see that at the far end, so the cancers with the highest mutational load are cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, bladder cancer, and these are really the malignancies where we now have FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitors. Those are really the cancers that have high mutational loads, and then when we delve into those specific cancers, we find that there's a tremendous spectrum. So for example, as a thoracic oncologist treating lung cancer patients, we know that a smoking-induced cancer has a much, much higher mutational load compared to a lung cancer that arises in a never smoker. And that actually has clinical implications because when we look at use of checkpoint blockade in smokers, response rates higher than it is for never smokers. In fact, response rates among never smokers are actually quite low, three to 4% in our experience. So I think the mutational load, this hypothesis, we're certainly seeing it clinically. But I do think it's important to emphasize that there are certainly patients who have high, it's not perfect. There are patients who have high mutational loads who don't derive benefit from these drugs. And it speaks to this concept of this neo-antigen lottery. Just because you have a high mutational load doesn't mean that you're gonna have one of those mutations that generates a neoantigen. It just increases your probability that you're gonna generate a neoantigen.
Now Justin, this patient has a p53 mutation. Does that increase the chances that she has a more mutated tumor?

Yeah, I think it's interesting because I look at these reports a lot. I think it's important to note that, to begin with, comprehensive genotyping is standard of care in lung cancer. I think that's really an important point to emphasize, that patients should be having comprehensive genotyping in lung cancer. And looking at these reports, I would say, We see a few more alterations than is typical for standard lung cancer. But at the same time, this is a fairly limited panel of about 100 genes. And all of the studies to date have mainly looked at mutational load using whole exome sequencing. So I think it's intriguing, and as was alluded to, having a p53 mutation, perhaps there's a higher mutational load here, but we don't know because most of those studies used whole exome sequencing, and they were pretty small. So the RISV data that was published in Science last year that showed mutational load as being important in lung cancer, looked at 34 cases total. So I think we have to remember that, that it's still small amounts of data and we really need to then start validating this, both in larger subsets and also using smaller panels. You can't really use whole exome sequencing clinically right now, so can we actually get a sense of mutational load with a smaller targeted NGS panel and how large should that panel be to both be feasible, but also give us a sense of mutational load.
And for the mutation load, does it matter as to what specific mutation it is? There might be something about certain mutations that cause more new antigen than others.

Right, right. No, no, I think that's a great point. The data that I'm aware of in lung cancer was really focused on KRAS mutations. There's been a lot of emphasis on KRAS mutations. And we know that specific KRAS mutations so far really haven't given us a sense of prognosis, but the co-mutations with KRAS can. So there was interesting work published by MD Anderson last year showing that you can really subdivide KRAS mutations into three distinct buckets based on co-mutations. And it was the KRAS plus P53 subgroup that tended to have a higher mutational load compared to the KRAS plus LKB1 subset in that work. And so the authors hypothesized that that may be the subgroup that's more responsive to immunotherapy.

So that's quite interesting because we have this other gene that's mutated here, the NF1, which feeds into the, it's basically a KRAS activator. Correct. And maybe that plus P53 would be an indication that we have a high mutational load in the

Exactly. So I think that's one of the reasons why I wanted to bring up that. And we do know that for NF1 mutations, 75% of the time they occur by themselves outside of the context of another oncogenic driver. But when they do occur with other driver mutations, it tends to occur with KRAS mutations. And with P53 mutations, sorry.

So what I would say that, you know, in terms of molecular diagnostics and our panels that we use, they were really geared toward targeted therapy. And so we're still trying to kind of catch up to, you know, really implementing immunotherapy. And, you know, so we have a lot of these discussions internally in terms of how well do our platforms predict tumor burden. And we've looked at it somewhat, and what we do find is that definitely in cases with MSI, we do find a higher prevalence of mutations even with our 100 gene panel. How accurately do we predict that? I don't think that we know right now, but it seems to be even these relatively focused panels still provide some information. So what we're looking to do now is really try to expand our panels to have markers throughout the genome that we can better predict this and try to implement this as part of the routine care.

Excellent. So Justin, if you had this patient in clinic and you had access to all targeted therapies ever made, so in the perfect world, what targeted therapy or therapy combination would you choose for this patient?

Yeah, so I think it's important to go back to Leif's comment about how do we tier these alterations. And in lung cancer, The field is moving very quickly and really I talk to my patients, at least newly diagnosed patients, about three major classes of systemic therapies. Historically it had been all chemotherapy, really platinum-based chemotherapy had been the standard of care for a long time. In the middle, the second major class is targeted therapy, which you're alluding to. And there are certainly several tier one genetic alterations, where we know that using a targeted therapy is superior to using platinum-based chemotherapy. So for example, EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements, ROS1 rearrangements, those I would characterize as really tier one genetic alterations. We also have some really emerging targets as well. Targets where we have them in other malignancies. For example, BRAF mutations occur in about 4% of lung cancer. Met splice site mutations, RET rearrangements, NTRAC rearrangements, where we actually are now starting to see responses, but not necessarily having FDA approved therapies. So those are some of the alterations where if I see them, I'm going to pursue a targeted therapy in a patient who's newly diagnosed. The third major class, and this is really, I think, hot off the presses if people looked at the New England Journal of Medicine last week, is immunotherapy, but using first-line immunotherapy. So last week was published the findings of Keynote 24. This was a randomized phase three study comparing pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, versus platinum doublet chemotherapy in newly diagnosed lung cancer patients. And here they used a biomarker selection strategy, so all patients had to be PD-L1 positive in 50% of tumor cells or more. I should note that 30% of lung cancer patients enrolled in that study met that cutoff. So this is a big piece of the pie. And what's notable is the Pembrolizumab showed improvements in both progression-free survival and overall survival in that study. And so that has become the new standard of care for the subgroup of patients who are PD-L1 positive at greater than 50%. So for this patient, though, none of these alterations are in that tier one or tier two. I would test for PD-L1, and if it was greater than 50%, I would pursue immunotherapy. If it was less than 50%, then I would pursue standard chemotherapy. And then as the patient progressed in therapy, if we gave chemotherapy first, I would certainly want to include immunotherapy at some point in her care. And then when we start getting into third line or so, we start thinking about, are there clinical trials that interrogate the pathways based on some of the genotyping data? And so I would be interested in MEK inhibitors, for example. So there's some data looking in the pediatric literature showing that NF, And if one mutant patients have some responsiveness to MEK inhibitors, that also mirrors some preclinical data as well. So that would be something I'd be thinking about. But again, not as standard of care in first line.

That's great, and I think you highlight a very important point that when we look at a report, there are two layers. Even if you find something that is actionable, the first is can I act on it? But the second, which is equally, if not more important, is should I act on it? And that looks at what's the current landscape? Should you abandon the standard therapy in favor of something that is potentially actionable, but you might not get the same benefit? So any closing comments? When you see these reports in clinic, are there certain features that you really like? At MGH, we are a bit spoiled that we get snapshot reports, but sometimes we also get genotyping reports from other institutions or other diagnostic companies. So are there key features that you really like when you're looking at a genotyping report? And Leif, you alluded to some of these points before.

Well, I think there's some consensus that you have to make a clear statement to the oncologist about what's actionable and what's not. But I'm interested to hear from Justin about what you think of that versus commercial testing panels. Do you think there's a large variability in your impression about the sorts of reports you get? Or do you think that the companies and the private enterprises have come together to make these as interpretable as possible to oncologists?

I would say many times the commercial companies try to make them interpretable, but I think many times are off the mark in that you'll get a list of 100 different clinical trials that one should consider. But then when you actually look at the genetic alterations that you're seeing there, it's not something I'm very excited about. And so I completely agree with you. I really like this thoughtful, tiered system and how we should really think, just because you see a genetic alteration in a gene, doesn't mean that that's actionable, it's relevant to the function. So I think those are some of the things that oncologists need to wrap their heads around, and I think that's one of the beauties of the Molecular Tumor Board, in that we have molecular pathologists, clinicians, all working together to try to interpret what can be very complicated genotype data, especially if you're treating multiple different cancers out in the community, this could be something really difficult to try to digest.
We might have some questions from the audience about this, if there are any.

We've had a precision tumor board now at CINJ for over three years. And if you eliminate these tier one and two mutations, our data and others, I guess your data too, show about 30% of the time there is a actionable mutation. But what I haven't seen is what are the clinical results of those actionable mutations? Do you have any data on that?

I think that is a little bit the holy grail. I think that some of us, including our center, is trying to put together this data. I think that, you know, there's some disagreement about whether it needs to be done in a highly controlled setting for one gene or one variant or one drug versus trying to look at just a huge composite of data for outcomes. I mean, certainly certain studies have been published. Patients who go on a trial based on genotyping have a higher response rate than patients who might appear to be matched but did not go on a trial guided by genotyping. But these are very rough data. There are no large data sets to my knowledge, and I think it's going to take a little bit of big data to really answer that question because of the heterogeneity and the landscape of the reports, the genes, and the drugs.

Bruce, this would be a question as much for you in your capacity as editor-in-chief of the Journal of the Oncologist, as well as for this expert panel. If you were ever interested in getting a broad swath of the community oncologists who get lots of data, as you were obviously talking about, and get their opinion as to what really is helpful and what may be unhelpful, One of the thoughts would be, and Annie, this would be something for you and Bruce to talk about, is actually opening up in the journal, the oncologist, a section where you could actually have this kind of a tumor board published. And with, you're already laughing, you're right. And then with the forms that you're describing in a leaf, I'm sorry we don't have them up on the screen, but that would be really helpful. And then to ask for feedback and through a communication just with a journal, you know, letters, not just the editor published, but actually blog online, we certainly could give you direct feedback on that kind of a proposal if you're ever interested.

I think the panel is smiling because I think we all agree that this would be a very important contribution and there's discussion about precision medicine clinic section in the oncologist where we discuss these things and I think that would be very important for the community oncologist, absolutely.

I think there are some interesting aspects to that. One is certainly you can give comments back on what the importance or what's known about a certain mutation. Actually giving advice about how to treat any patient I think would be difficult. I would like to ask Leif one other question. So, P53 mutations have been associated, at least experimentally, with poor response to chemotherapy. Should that be taken into consideration? I'm not sure that that's, that probably doesn't get into the report, but should we be conscious of that?

Well, it's a fascinating question and to some degree it speaks a little bit to the duality of p53 and this issue of that it's also a gain of function and a loss of function. And in breast cancer I think is an area that's my clinical specialty that's particularly either interesting or confusing in that There are certainly multiple published reports that in the setting of primary disease, responses to chemotherapy, clinical responses, are higher in the subset of P53 mutant patients, and that's been attributed to the fact that those patients have cell cycle deregulation that is more amenable to targeting with chemotherapy. On the other hand, not all of those studies have taken into account, and then that's been validated in various mouse models. But those studies really haven't necessarily all taken into account the long-term outcome of those patients. Because you can imagine that it's not the idea whether 95% of the tumor cells disappear with the chemotherapy. It's a question about whether the other 5% are eventually going to grow out and metastasize and kill the patient. And I think that's where there is still some uncertainty in the field about whether P53 is going to be a strong, particularly chemotherapy predictor for that reason. Because it also engenders, it may be higher responses, but also potentially engender more resistance.
Right. Very good. Thanks.

Could you also comment on, Darren and Leif, in terms of if you're seeing a molecular alteration, when do you get concerned that this actually might be a germline alteration? And how do you, what's the workflow in terms of informing the patient or the oncologist and intake in a genetics clinic?

Yeah, you know, I think that that's a great question. It's a very complex question in that respect. You know, our testing is for somatic alterations. So, you know, we're a little careful in reporting germline. You know, there's a number of considerations. One is patient consent. Has the patient consented for that type of information because it's impacting not only that patient, but the relatives of that patient and the offspring. You know, there's clearly a number of genes that are associated with hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes that are in our panel. that we can find mutations that have been previously reported to be germline. And so we have these databases that we can look into. And when we find what we think could be a germline, so we're testing off tumor tissue, so we don't know the answer to that. We can just postulate that it could be germline. And if we think that it is germline, what we do is we have a close contact with the clinician. and discuss that result and whether it makes sense to, you know, pursue consent and, you know, really determine if it is germline by maybe getting a blood sample that we can actually determine that. And, you know, Leif will tell you that, you know, then you start bringing on a larger team of genetic counselors. And so it's just another example of really kind of a community-based effort.

I was just going to say that it's a little bit of an evolving area in the field. Number one, the question about if you're trying to assess the actual accuracy of the mutation calls in the panel, do you really need to compare directly to germline? So that's an issue that speaks to whether you're really giving the best somatic information you can without the germline. And then the second question, as Daryl alluded to, is what kind of complexities does it create in terms of the implications for hereditary cancer if you're unearthing genetic hereditary findings that the patient and their family may or may not be prepared for and then there's also the technical question about if you're just looking at the tumor whether you can distinguish between those two and what's the clinical workflow to do that in the cases where it's a possibility.
So in this case, we have a patient with a p53 mutation. Does that raise any alarms?

Well, in fact, three of the four genes have actually been associated with germline syndromes. Markov 4, NF1, of course, and p53 have all been associated rarely with germline syndromes, with NF1 being the most common, actually, but this variant not a common NF1 variant. So these are things that are not infrequent, and that's why it's an important area of discussion.

Question? Yeah, a question for Daryl. So I'm curious how you decide what markers to add to your panel, whether you've added epigenetic markers and also with the FDA now looking at regulating LDTs, what changes in your approach?

That's a very loaded question. You know, I think that in terms of what is the composition of the panels, You know, we try to focus on those that we think really have the most therapeutic, prognostic, diagnostic implications that will ultimately be important to our clinicians in guiding therapy for the patient. So, you know, we work very closely with our clinicians in terms of what those alterations are that should be included in that respect. And so in that respect, it's always kind of evolving. And just recently, we went from 20 genes to 100 genes, probably just a few months ago. So it's expanding very, very quickly. You had mentioned LDTs and the FDA. You know, the FDA has announced that they are going to start enforcing oversight of all laboratory-developed tests, which falls under our operations, that all the testing that we do are LDTs that we've developed internally and have clinically validated. And I think that that landscape is still evolving and becoming clear. I don't want to get into too much conjecture, hypothesis of what might be to come, but I think that clearly there is some need to provide information to patients and advocacy groups in terms of what are the tests that we have, how do they perform, Compared to other institutions, I think that that's information that's lacking. I think that that's actually very important information for patients to understand when trying to select what institute to go to. You know, we can argue as to whether FDA is really in the best position to regulate that or are there some other mechanisms that can be put in place, kind of like what we call proficiency testing in the clinic where there is an organization that has a panel of samples that they can then send across institutions across the country and have a standard. And as long as you meet that standard, then you are okay, so to speak, to implement that clinically. So, you know, I think that I'm kind of a little bit on the fence in that regard. I think we don't want over-regulation. It's gonna stifle our development and our ability to be able to deliver this in ways that we think are really best for our patients and for our institution. But at the same time, I think that there is, there's a lot of LDTs out there and that we do need to understand what are the differences and maybe some benefits and disadvantages.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent abdominal pain for more than 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral fallopian tube malignancy reported as suspicious for low-grade serous carcinoma. Abdominal wall lesion was reported as abscess formation. Uterus remained in situ following surgery.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy date: 03 December 2025. Specimens included right and left fallopian tubes with ovaries following bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Histopathology reported low-grade serous carcinoma involving the fallopian tubes, described as suspicious for low-grade serous carcinoma. Tumor measured 1.7 cm in the right tube and 1.5 cm in the left tube. Ovarian malignancy was not documented in the available histopathology description. Biopsy from the abdominal wall lesion showed abscess formation.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a cystic lesion in the region of the right fallopian tube and ovary measuring 7.9 × 4.45 × 2.62 cm. A separate abdominal wall lesion measured 7.6 × 3 × 4.7 cm.

[ laboratory results ]: CA-125 was reported as normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The abdominal wall lesion was explored surgically and was described intraoperatively as a pus-producing abscess. At laparotomy, a mass was found abutting adjacent pelvic structures including the uterus and bladder. Resection was incomplete. Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Total abdominal hysterectomy was not performed.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status following bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with residual pelvic disease suspected intraoperatively due to inability to achieve complete resection. Uterus remained in situ.

[ other clinical data ]: The available record described diagnostic uncertainty regarding the final pathologic classification of the tubal malignancy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for management of left-sided upper tract urothelial carcinoma in a solitary left kidney, with concurrent recurrent bladder carcinoma in situ.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal left upper tract urothelial carcinoma involving the ureteropelvic junction, mid ureter, and distal ureter in a solitary kidney; clinical stage was described as high-grade Tx with possible lamina propria invasion, consistent with possible cT1 disease. Concurrent active/recurrent bladder carcinoma in situ persisted after prior intravesical BCG induction.

[ histopathology results ]: Ureteroscopic biopsy of the left upper tract lesion showed high-grade urothelial carcinoma, staged as Tx, with suspicion for lamina propria invasion and possible T1 disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated multifocal left upper tract disease, including lesions at the ureteropelvic junction, mid ureter, and distal ureter. Multifocal ureteral disease was not well visualized but corresponding sites were identified on imaging review.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Renal function before treatment was described as adequate despite a solitary kidney. The patient was cisplatin-eligible. She was not on dialysis before surgery.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Prior right nephroureterectomy had been performed; original stage and grade were unavailable.  
- Bladder carcinoma in situ had been treated with intravesical BCG induction; maintenance BCG was not given.  
- Subsequent recurrent low-grade bladder tumors had been managed in the office.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had a solitary left kidney at presentation due to prior right nephroureterectomy.  
- Performance status and functional capacity were described as good; she was otherwise healthy and active.  
- No major comorbidities, cardiotoxicity, hearing loss, or other contraindications to cisplatin were reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 34-year-old woman. Karnofsky Performance Status was 80. No comorbidities were documented. No significant smoking history was reported. Family history was significant for multiple cancers on both paternal and maternal sides, predominantly hematologic and gastrointestinal malignancies.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, vomiting, left-sided weakness, and disorientation.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IVB metastatic lung carcinoma, suspected right lung primary, with brain, pulmonary, mediastinal nodal, left adrenal, and T8 vertebral metastases. Intracranial disease was symptomatic with mass effect from dominant right frontal and right parietal lesions.

[ histopathology results ]: Resection specimens from the right frontal and right parietal brain lesions showed metastatic adenocarcinoma with cribriform pattern, reported as likely lung in origin / metastatic lung carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white matter junction in both supratentorial and infratentorial compartments. Approximately 8-9 intracranial lesions were appreciated. Dominant lesions were located in the right frontal and right parietal regions and caused mass effect and midline shift. Additional lesions were present in the left and right cerebellum.

CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast demonstrated a large necrotic right upper lobe mass closely abutting the mediastinum, encasing the right upper lobe bronchus and right pulmonary artery. There was a large necrotic right hilar lymph node and necrotic subcarinal mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Subsegmental atelectatic change was present in the right upper lobe. Adjacent pulmonary soft tissue nodules/satellite lesions were seen in the surrounding parenchyma. No discrete contralateral pulmonary nodule suggestive of contralateral metastasis was described. A metastatic deposit was present in the T8 vertebra. A large necrotic metastatic deposit was present in the left adrenal gland. Overall imaging was consistent with bronchogenic carcinoma with metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were documented.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor markers were reported elevated, including CA-125, CA 19-9, and LDH.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neuronavigation-guided right frontal craniotomy and right parietal craniotomy with maximal safe resection of the dominant intracranial lesions using two separate incisions. Postoperatively, no new neurological deficits were documented.

[ current disease status ]: Residual multifocal intracranial metastatic disease remained, including supratentorial and infratentorial lesions. Systemic metastatic disease involved the lungs, mediastinal lymph nodes, left adrenal gland, and T8 vertebra. Preoperatively, left upper limb power was 4+/5. No lower limb weakness was present. After surgery, no new neurological deficit was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient presented through the emergency department. The dominant intracranial lesions were resected because of severe mass effect.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 84-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Left auricular lesion along the superior aspect of the helix.

[ diagnosis ]: Merkel cell carcinoma of the left auricle. Initial pathologic stage was T1N1a with clinically occult regional nodal metastasis, consistent with stage III disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy of the left auricular lesion confirmed Merkel cell carcinoma. Wide local excision of the primary lesion achieved negative margins. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was positive for metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma. Following neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and completion neck dissection, pathology showed 0/23 lymph nodes with viable tumor; significant fibrosis and inflammation were present, consistent with regressed tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial ultrasound showed no evident disease. Initial PET scan was negative beyond the primary tumor. Repeat PET-CT performed after sentinel lymph node biopsy demonstrated multifocal hypermetabolic disease in the neck. MRI brain was negative for brain metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Merkel cell polyomavirus serologies were drawn pre- and post-treatment. No results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent wide local excision of the left auricular primary lesion with negative margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy, which identified nodal metastasis. Approximately 1 month after the initial biopsy/sentinel node procedure, repeat PET-CT demonstrated multifocal cervical nodal disease. He then received 1 dose of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab on protocol, followed by completion neck dissection 1 month later. Postoperative pathology demonstrated no viable tumor in 23 dissected lymph nodes, with fibrosis and inflammation consistent with treatment response/regressed tumor.

[ current disease status ]: After neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and completion neck dissection, no viable tumor was identified in the neck dissection specimen. MRI brain remained negative for intracranial metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: He was described as a very healthy 84-year-old man. Intraoperatively, a firm level IV node near the junction of the subclavian vein and internal jugular vein adjacent to the thoracic duct was partially shaved rather than aggressively dissected because of concern for vascular injury and chyle leak.

I'm happy to jump in. Adam from Jefferson Kyle gave me a call this week and asked me to jump in for somebody so happy to be here. Sorry, Adam.

Yeah, no, just concurring. I think a lot depends on the clinical. One of the interesting things just for our fellows, You know, one thing I had recently is a patient came in with a melanoma. Great.
So I don't know that question out there. Would you you do you check that in all your Merkel cell carcinomas?

I do. reference_conclusion: For regionally metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma without distant disease, the standard management discussed was completion neck dissection followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. In the presented case, the patient was treated on a clinical trial with one dose of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab followed by completion neck dissection; given the robust pathologic response, the trial schema was to continue immunotherapy, whereas radiotherapy would be considered if there were minimal response. [...] It would have been a completion neck dissection and radiotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male.

[ chief complaint ]: Unexplained weight loss following COVID infection; initially fairly asymptomatic despite extensive intra-abdominal disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Extensive unresectable small bowel/peritoneal malignancy with high intra-abdominal tumor burden. Disease was initially considered not amenable to surgical resection and treatment was undertaken with palliative intent.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated extensive small bowel disease with complete encasement of small bowel. Disease extended inferiorly to the pelvis. Initial imaging findings were considered consistent with unresectable intra-abdominal disease.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks, Mike. That's a great case. I'm just going to do one more case in this arena, a unique case that I had. Similar scenario of an unresectable patient, and I was able to figure out how to put these in, so I'm going to play this. And you'll see here, if I pause, how severe some of the things we've been talking about. So you can just see up here, this is small bowel disease completely in case on this individual right here who came in, who actually was fairly asymptomatic after COVID, just had this unexplained weight loss and just extensive disease. And if I click on this one below, You can see the small bowel is the limiting step all the way down to the pelvis. So this is a gentleman we would all say isn't a surgical candidate, most likely won't become a surgical candidate. And this is sort of on that era when immunotherapy was starting. to get a spot as a possible treatment option. So I'm going to bypass this just for the sakes of time. This is a gentleman who, as we would expect, went on systemic therapy. There was a lot of difficulty getting the intruder, the Pembrozilumab, approved for this patient, but we did. And the patient was actually having some response, but again, This is another episode where these patients with high burdens got a DVT, this time lower extremity DVT, went on appropriate therapy, then had a GI bleed, and we all encounter that. When people have GI bleeds, you have to hold the blood thinners. So our natural instincts are we want to protect them from a PE. When we protect patients from a pulmonary embolism, we put something in called an IBC filter. It's a little net that catches any clots so that they don't go to the lung. Those are not benign either and unfortunately for this individual they developed extreme clot burden in the cava with Massive lower extremity edema that required another one of these vacuum assisted thrombectomies and just as a side note like our ability to take care of patients with these issues that often would have been life-threatening has just gotten so much better whether it's an IR person or a vascular surgeon who can declot some of these clots that would require open surgeries. And it's a game changer, because we do see this in our oncology world. So this individual had that, was able to successfully get back on Eliquis, was doing well. But some of the things that came up was the toxicity of immunotherapy, the unpredictability of it. And one that I had not seen was itching. I had not seen someone itching to the point where they were scratching their skin off. And that can be, you take it for granted, that itching happens, and we just scratch. But people who've had these immunotherapies, it's unbelievable how much itching and skin reaction that they're having. And it can be a reason to come off of therapy. Often, it can lead to other things, such as diarrhea and colitis. And that's what this individual had. So this individual came back, and that's what this shows. As I run through that, I can do it again. Just to kind of show you that what happened in all of this is that he had an unbelievable response over 18 months and it allowed us to reevaluate his surgical candidacy. Most of his symptoms have been down in the lower extremity but he became a candidate. So we took him back after this extensive treatment and he was unresectable. Again, this was palliative in nature because he was already considered somebody who wasn't going to be treated for cure. I put these specimens in. I'm going to quickly go over it because it might bother folks, but we ended up having to do lots of bowel resections. We ended up having to take out multiple areas where the bowels were stuck to this, but it turned out The therapy actually sort of took these things back. The way I view it is you get back to the root of where these tumors started, where were the original implants, the way that these things can work. Now, whether or not it was the immune therapy or the chemotherapy or the combination of both, it got us to this point. And this gentleman went on and had some significant control ended up having to go back on single agent immuno. Again, the itching was a little bit better at about 18 months down the road. So I do think we're in a different era. Like some of the things that have come up that you've heard here are sort of changing the paradigm for cancer control and potentially surgical candidacy at different points for people. And I think this is the thing it's always a conversation. Georgios and everybody said that we're constantly having conversations about people's options and also listening to the patients about what their desires are what risks they want to take or not want to take with this but they're in the driver's seat. So, I'll kind of close here, and hopefully these cases were illustrative of where we're going with these things, what our options are, and sort of the importance of just this open communication and being earnest about how you're feeling and everything else. We didn't talk about symptoms in terms of those things that come up and how we can use surgery and other things for that, but I imagine we may get some questions in that arena. But we'll open the floor to the audience.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Multiple thyroid nodules identified on palpation during gynecologic examination.

[ diagnosis ]: Multinodular thyroid disease/goiter; germline pathogenic PTEN mutation consistent with Cowden syndrome/PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided FNA of right mid-thyroid nodule (3.0 cm, TR4): Bethesda III, follicular lesion of undetermined significance.  
- Ultrasound-guided FNA of left thyroid nodule (1.5 cm, TR4): Bethesda II, benign.  
- Total thyroidectomy pathology: follicular nodular disease; pathology described as consistent with Cowden syndrome.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in August 2021 showed enlarged thyroid gland.  
- Right lobe measured 6.9 x 2.7 x 2.1 cm.  
- Left lobe measured 6.0 x 2.2 x 1.5 cm.  
- Isthmus measured 0.12 cm.  
- Bilateral multiple thyroid nodules were present, predominantly TI-RADS TR3 and TR4.  
- Right-sided nodules measured up to 3.1 cm, 2.1 cm, 1.4 cm, and 1.1 cm.  
- Left-sided nodules measured up to 2.2 cm.  
- Nodules were described as well demarcated without evidence of extrathyroidal extension and without highly suspicious sonographic features.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Molecular testing (ThyroSeq) was performed on the Bethesda III right thyroid nodule.  
- PTEN mutations were detected, including two mutations in the same gene.  
- Variant allele frequency was reported at 51%.  
- Germline genetic testing identified a pathogenic PTEN mutation, consistent with Cowden syndrome/PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroid function tests were within normal limits at the time of initial ultrasound evaluation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided FNA was performed on two dominant thyroid nodules.  
- The patient subsequently underwent total thyroidectomy.  
- Surgical pathology demonstrated follicular nodular disease without reported thyroid carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post total thyroidectomy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient did not perceive the nodules.  
- No compressive symptoms were reported.  
- No dysphagia or dysphonia were reported.  
- No history of head or neck radiation exposure.  
- Family history included multinodular goiter without known thyroid cancer.  
- Mother had a history of skin, ovarian, and endometrial cancers.  
- Two sisters were reported healthy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 27-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for further management following total thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Total thyroidectomy specimen reviewed at MSK showed a 3.5 cm left-sided poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. The tumor was completely encapsulated with extensive capsular invasion and marked mitotic activity. Necrosis was absent. Extensive vascular invasion was present in 7 foci. There was no extrathyroidal extension. Tumor was present at the surgical margins. Three perithyroidal lymph nodes were benign.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Approximately 3 months after surgery, serum thyroglobulin was 5.9.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a history of hyperthyroidism/Graves disease prior to surgery and was prepared preoperatively with methimazole and beta-blockade. He underwent total thyroidectomy in October 2024.

[ current disease status ]: Status post total thyroidectomy for poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma with extensive vascular invasion and positive surgical margins, with a thyroglobulin of 5.9 approximately 3 months after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: History of hyperthyroidism/Graves disease. A possible consideration of vocal cord paralysis was mentioned, but no confirmed clinical finding was documented.

reference_discussion.text: Yes, so we have a 27-year-old man who underwent a total tyroidectomy in October 2024. He came to MSK for further treatment, and then the pathology review here showed a left 3.5-centimeter poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. completely encapsulated with extensive capsular invasion with marked and methodic activity. There was no necrosis, and there was extensive vascular invasion of seven foci. No extraterritorial extension, and the tumor was present at the surgical margins. Three periterital lymph nodes were benign. And at the time of the visit, we have this a viral panel that showed that three months after the surgery, his seroglobulin was 5.9.

So, I mean, not much has changed. I mean, if you really look into it from the earlier classification, but what we have done, we have created an umbrella term of high-grade follicular drive, that means follicular cell drive carcinomas, and that includes the classic poorly differentiated which was based upon the criteria from what we call as Turin criteria. And now we have brought in also these well-differentiated carcinomas. They look like papillary, they look like tall cell, or they look like columnar cells, but have necrosis and mitosis, which is greater than five by two millimeters square. But the criteria for the poorly differentiated, for diagnosing it stays the same, but it is under that term of high grade. because these have that intermediate to high, you know, the prognostic on the risk of stratification.
And they signal RAS-like, BRAF-like? Do you get a feel for it?

So if it's a papillary thyroid carcinoma, which is high grade, they are BRAF or BRAF-like. but they can have additional like a tart promoter and stuff. Whereas the poorly differentiated carcinoma, depending upon which tumor it's coming from. So most of them are RAS and then they have a layering of other additional mutations or fusions.

Perfect. So Eric, I'll come to you on this, this thyroglobin level here. I mean, we were, we're already thinking this is potentially a higher risk. We're worried about distant metastasis, all that vascular invasion. What do you expect the Firework Goblin to be afterwards? And this one came back at that 5.9. Happy? Not happy? What do you think about that?

You know, as Ashok kind of mentioned, you get to know your team and your surgeons and you kind of fit within kind of the remnant that's normal for each surgeon. Everyone operates a little different. This is a little higher than we would typically see post-operatively, but it's not 40, you know, or something like that. So it's kind of in that middle ground. I find poorly differentiated carcinoma to be worrisome that sometimes it can go bad. Other times it does just fine. It's, it's kind of a very wide range, large standard deviation around this, this pathology in my opinion.

So Eric, I don't know anything about Graves' disease other than how to spell it usually. He had Graves' disease before surgery, No data whatsoever. You know, if you're stimulating the TSH receptor, which is a natural growth factor for the cells, I think the clinical reality that that's ever shown to be a negative prognostic factor or a causative problem is nil, really. So I don't lead into that or kind of blame it. I find it a curiosity.

Yeah, me too. Kate, where do you go with this? I would probably also do a PET CT at the same time as my iodine with the poorly differentiated components so that I would have both the post iodine scan and an FTG image to look at in just because of my suspicion that you know we may have some iodine non iodine avid disease present and I would want to make sure we weren't missing anything.

Yes, yes, absolutely, yeah. So that if you wanted to go ahead and give the radioactive iodine... Yeah, we kind of make the most of the raised TSH and do it just after they've had their thorogen. Yeah. I mean, if you're looking for golf balls, I mean, we, we wait longer than that usually, but, um, you know, we don't expect to find anything postoperative. And if it was rising, then we'd have to do some cross-sectional imaging. We've, of course, would start with the ultrasound, but then we'd have to, you have to go beyond that.
Perfect.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent hypercalcemia and persistent primary hyperparathyroidism, with transfer of care in April 2024 for pharyngocutaneous fistula, neck abscess, and electrolyte abnormalities following attempted reoperative parathyroid surgery.

[ diagnosis ]: Persistent primary hyperparathyroidism with ectopic left parathyroid adenoma in a retrocarotid location at the thoracic inlet. Postoperative pharyngeal injury with pharyngocutaneous fistula following prior attempted left parathyroidectomy.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior outside neck explorations did not yield histologically proven parathyroid tissue.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Nuclear medicine parathyroid scan (August 2020, outside facility): no evidence of parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia.  
- CT neck with and without contrast (October 2020, outside facility): nodular lesion in the left thyroid bed and a lesion in the left parapharyngeal space; differential included lymph node versus adenoma.  
- Nuclear medicine scan (June 2023, outside facility): subtle uptake in the left thyroid bed.  
- CT neck with contrast (2023, outside facility): unchanged 1.1 cm nodule just inferior to the left thyroid bed.  
- CT at Emory (April 2024): fistula identified.  
- Flexible laryngoscopy at presentation to Emory: hypomobile left vocal cord.  
- 4D CT (April 2024): 1.7 x 0.7 cm hyperenhancing mass posterior to the left carotid with avid arterial enhancement and rapid washout, consistent with parathyroid adenoma; resolving fistula also visualized.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- At presentation to Emory: PTH 825 pg/mL; calcium 11.6 mg/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- August 2020: admitted at an outside hospital for diverticulitis; hypercalcemia was identified during admission.  
- September 2020: underwent neck exploration by an outside general surgeon; no adenoma was found; hemithyroidectomy was performed.  
- 2020-2023: lost to follow-up for several years.  
- March 2024: underwent attempted inpatient left parathyroidectomy at an outside hospital for hypercalcemia; operative field was markedly scarred; procedure was complicated by pharyngotomy of the left piriform sinus, repaired intraoperatively; no parathyroid adenoma was found.  
- April 2024: developed pharyngocutaneous fistula, neck abscess, and multiple electrolyte abnormalities; transferred for higher-level care.  
- Day after transfer: underwent direct laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy, neck washout, and incision and drainage. A 3 cm linear injury to the left piriform sinus was identified with extensive granulation, scarring, and inflammation precluding primary closure. Salivary stent, Penrose drain, pressure dressing, antibiotics, and glycopyrrolate were used; parathyroidectomy was deferred.

[ current disease status ]: No subsequent outpatient follow-up data were available because follow-up appointments were not attended.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included bipolar disorder, neurocognitive decline, longstanding hypercalcemia, and hyperparathyroidism. Social barriers affected continuity of follow-up and access to regular medical care. No lithium use was identified in available records.

And they said, was this a lymph node or an adenoma? Unfortunately, she was lost to follow-up for several years, and then she represented to an outside ENT in about 2023. She got some more workup and scans. She had a nuclear medicine scan in June of 2023, which showed some subtle uptake in the left thyroid bed, and then a CT neck with contrast. I don't believe there was any 4DCT protocol with this, and had an unchanged 1.1 centimeter nodule just inferior to the left thyroid bed. Again, she was lost to follow-up, and then she presented to an outside hospital in March of 2024, hypercalcemic. And because she had so many issues with, you know, kind of keeping appointments and with the hypercalcemia, they decided to do an inpatient parathyroidectomy. And this surgeon attempted a left parathyroidectomy, but per operative reports, it was a really scarred field and difficult, ended up complicated by a pharyngotomy in the left piriform sinus that was repaired at the time, and no parathyroid adenoma was found. Then in April of 2024, she went back to the hospital because she started developing a pharyngocutaneous fistula and had a neck abscess and multiple electrolyte imbalances. And at this time, they decided to transfer her care to Emory.

Hold on for just a second. So Russ, could I ask you a question as our discussant? How often these days are you performing hemithyroidectomies when looking for parathyroids? Is this a common practice that you endorse still? No. I do all my own ultrasounds as Jeremy had stated. It's a very important part of, I think, being best informed about what you may find interoperatively. And if a patient has a completely normal thyroid lobe and I have done a failed exploration, I won't take that lobe out because the ultrasound is very sensitive. So if there's any intra-thyroidal lesion, you're going to know about it based upon your pre-op ultrasound. Now, if someone has had an exploration and there's an intra-thyroidal pathology and I haven't found things that would change my perspective. And I think even now we're becoming sophisticated enough with ultrasound that Even preoperatively, we ultrasound patients and things look like thyroid nodules and sometimes things look like parathyroid glands within the thyroid gland. You can see the polar blood supply. But I wouldn't routinely do it unless there was some intratheroidal pathology that I couldn't exclude. Negative ultrasound, I would never do a lobe. And if you're so confident with your ultrasounds, are you getting any other scans as a routine measure? Like looking at this scan, this is very familiar with what we see in our institution, you know, no evidence of this, subtle that. Are you getting any of those other scans? So I think that's a great discussion point and I'm glad it came up again. So everyone gets an ultrasound, so they'll want to make sure, do they have concurrent thyroid disease with their parathyroid problem? I want to try to localize the parathyroid adenoma. I think an important teaching point about cestamib scans is that unless your adenoma is greater than 500 milligrams, which makes it reasonably sized, you have a pretty high incidence of negative cestamibs. So if I've done an ultrasound and I don't see something, I think it's unlikely the cestamib is going to help. There may be something hidden in the mediastinum, and if that's the case, I'm going to get a CT to figure out where it is anyway. So I've kind of eliminated cestamib as part of my protocol. So I typically start with an ultrasound. If I see something great, If I don't see something, then I'll go to a phased CT scan to look for something smaller or something that may be hidden that I just can't see with the ultrasound. If everything's negative, I may get assessed to maybe just kind of be complete before I go explore, just to give me a little more information. But that's kind of the approach I use for my imaging preoperatively. Excellent. Okay, Alexa, proceed. Thank you.

Okay, so when she presented to Emory, she had, and here's the CT scan showing this fistula. She had significant erythema, two fistula tracts. On her flexible laryngoscopy, she had a hypomobile left vocal cord, and then her PTH on presentation was 825, and her calcium was 11.6. So the next day after arrival, Dr. Seabrook and team took her just for a neck washout. So did a DLB neck, neck IND. And there's a three centimeter linear injury to the left piriforme sinus and just a lot of granulation and scar and inflammation to make primary closure really not possible. So a salivary stent was placed for diversion, a pin rose was placed, a pressure dressing, she was placed on robinol, and the parathyroidectomy was delayed. And during this time of delay and just letting her be on antibiotics and heal, further imaging was ordered for localization. And I kind of interspersed some discussion points in this talk, and we can either...I know we sort of just kind of talked about this, so we can move past it or discuss it again, but what imaging modalities are preferred in revision cases for people?

Good question. Let's ask Jeremy. Jeremy, in a tough case like this, very challenging, do you go to any particular scan? What's in your toolbox? Yeah, for the revision ones, just before we go there, there was something in your last slide. They said they thought there was a parathyroid that they took out.
In all the other institutions, they never found parathyroids.
Okay, so histologically, there was never a proven parathyroid.
Correct.

That's correct. Okay, sorry. Okay, these revision ones, I just hit them with the book. I go with a Sestamibi, a SPECT CT, conventional CT, 4D usually, and see what I've got with that. Okay, excellent. Yeah, you had another discussion point too, right, Alexa, or was that the main one?
At the end, we have some discussion.
In that case, let me ask Mary, who probably knows this case so intimately well, could I ask what your practice is in these cases?

Well, to echo Russ, I repeat my own surgeon-performed ultrasound. And I'm not gonna give away this case at all, but this was a case incredibly supportive of surgeons looking themselves. But I, just like Dr. Freeman said, I kind of throw the book at them. I get a 4DCT, which of course is non-functional. It's not a functional scan, it's an anatomic scan. I do get a functional scan. I do get a cestamib just in case it, and it shows something. And you had a good question for the last discussants. I don't always, I'm not always enamored of the accuracy and even the technique done for sestamibes. I think that the technique is tricky and that can lead to
Moderate.

Ambiguity. Yes, thank you. Thank you. I don't even look at the outside ultrasounds. I just do an ultrasound myself. And so I think a revision case like this really does need to have every possible imaging modality, because this is a little bit of a rescue case. And also, I do want to make the point where this case is not meant to be critical of our preceding surgeons. I think especially the one who was operated with the really high calcium, I think it was somewhat heroic, but that surgeon was hampered by not having the skills of doing their own ultrasound. And so I really feel for the two prior teams. So this case is not meant to criticize anybody.

Alan, can I just make a brief comment? And this is just to reemphasize what Mary just said and what Jeremy just said. I do think it's just critical for the fellows to be aware that in general, reoperative parathyroidectomy is really, it's a distinct entity from primary surgery. And one of the ways that it is most clearly a distinct surgery and a distinct entity is that in most instances, most endocrine surgeons will say that you really should only be doing reoperative cases when you have a clear target. Now, that's not absolute as we'll get to in the next case, but I do think it is important to understand this. that reoperative surgery is not just like, yeah, there'll be some extra scar tissue. It really is important, I think, to think about it as a totally different kind of paradigm than we think about in primary parathyroid surgery.
Well put. Can I just ask one simple question? This was a bipolar individual. Was she on lithium at any point?
Not that we saw in her records, but that's a really good point.
Just curious.
Yeah, not that we saw in her records that transfer.
Not that it would change anything. All right, Alexa, let's proceed and we'll get to the end of the, find the conclusion, the surgical triumph. Yes, go ahead.

So, our team ordered a 4D CT scan, and these are the images here, and it had a very classic hyper-enhancing mass posterior to the left carotid, and that's seen right here measured, measuring 1.7 by 0.7, and very classic avid arterial enhancement and then rapid washout consistent with the parathyroid adenoma, and this is that right here. You can sort of see the resolving fistula. So she was taken to the OR on the 29th, this is roughly 10 days after her presentation, for a directed left parathyroidectomy. And as Dr. Seabrook mentioned before, Dr. Seabrook did a pre-incision ultrasound, which really confirmed this retrocarotid mass and also used the ultrasound intraoperatively to find this mass through scar tissue. and identified a two by one centimeter parathyroid adenoma posterior to the left common carotid at the thoracic inlet. This was also confirmed on frozen. That's sort of the protocol at our institution as well. And her PTH went from 829 to 154. And then on this next slide, so Dr. Sieblik, as she mentioned, did a directed approach. So this is the original incision and then where the new incision was sort of directed by the ultrasound of where to place it. and to keep it out of the operative field of the fistula and the previous surgeries. So, for conclusion, her fish still resolved with iodoform packing and conservative measures. She was able to get the salivary stent removed and a gastrograph in that didn't show a leak. She was transitioned to a regular diet. Her post-op PTH decreased to 22, and she was discharged to her personal care home in June of 2024. Unfortunately, as Zafra mentioned, we haven't been able to follow up with her because she hasn't made any of her follow-up appointments thus far. But some other discussion points, and again, we don't have to use these, we can do something else, but what is the preferred surgical approach in primary cases, and then what is the preferred surgical approach in revision cases for people?

Yeah, good question. Russ, with this merging together, do you ever deviate from the standard midline incision in your surgeries? Not for primary cases. I think in revision cases, you do have to start being creative, especially if you have a localized target, to try to minimize the amount of effort you put going through old scar tissue. Sometimes you can't help it. So if you have something that's setting behind the esophagus and somebody has already explored that side, but that's where you have to go, you have to go. But I think in this case, as Mary pointed out, I suspect Mary went lateral to the jug, lateral to the carotid, didn't even really get back into the central neck and kind of stayed in a lateral plane. And I think that's a really nice way to do these cases to, to simplify, you know, the morbidity. Cause this patient, I think going back into that central neck to try to find an adenoma, the risk of a recurrent nerve injury starts to skyrocket. And so I applaud her for taking a little more creative approach to get to this. Right. Because Alexa, do you know what happened to her bipolar state?
It did not improve much. Yeah.
Dr. Freeman, I said exactly the same thing. What if all of her mental health issues go away? Unfortunately, they did not.

One can only hope. Great, great. So the take-home points for this case, number one, do your own ultrasound, and number two, send all of your bipolar fistulized patients to Emory. Okay, great. Let's go on to, I'm just kidding, I'm just kidding. Mary would kill me. Please don't send your revision cases to her. Okay, let's move on to our third case, Jake and Michael, Dr. Singer. Go ahead, Jake. Thank you.
