reference_discussion.text: So here's a 53-year-old white female who presents with low back pain and weight loss. She has a past medical history significant for cervical cancer, which was treated with a cone biopsy. And she had a CT chest and an MRI of the brain that was negative. All of her laboratory studies are within normal limits. And here's her films. So there's a couple of points here. You can see she's got a tumor involving her right kidney. You can see that here in cross-section. But she's also got evidence of sacral involvement. You can see she's got a lesion right there. And we'll see that on the next film. Again, you can see she's got tumor involving her sacrum. So it's a metastasis from the, well, presumably a metastasis from the kidney tumor to the sacrum. You can see it again here. Does everyone appreciate that? Okay. So, first I'll throw it out to Dr. Gao. If this patient shows up in your clinic, what are you going to tell him?

I think, you know, first of all, you want to make sure the diagnosis. So, she has a history of cervical cancer. I assume that's, you know, that's early stage, but still with two sides of disease, so you want to I would biopsy of that sacrum mass.
So you would biopsy the sacral mass, okay. Dr. Karam, do you agree with that approach? Yes. So you would biopsy the sacral mass? Yes. Dr. Tenier, this is actually your patient, what would you do?
Yes, I would biopsy either the mass in the kidney or the sacral mass.

Here's the bone scan, and again, that just demonstrates, just for you all, the hot spot right here corresponds to the area of uptake or the area of concern on the CT scan, indicating that it might represent a metastasis. So everyone has said that they would do a biopsy. Anybody different from that?
I would just say we definitely want to biopsy the sacral mass over the kidney primarily. That would be my choice.

Yeah, the problem, nobody actually did, you didn't do a biopsy. She was, it was presumed that this represented metastatic disease and I guess on, you know, cervical cancer metastasizing to bone as well as to The kidney, I think that's...

But I'm not even like, I'm less concerned about the cervix since it was treated with a cone biopsy, but I would be more concerned about something else. Like? Like another primary. Like? Primary bone sarcoma or osteo...
Bone sarcoma metastasizing to the kidney?
No, I think that could be two separate primaries. Okay. But I'd want to know what the sacral lesion was before I went ahead with treating the kidney.
Why?
Because if it turned out that it was metastatic kidney, then there is possibly options for clinical trial in like a pre-surgical type setting.
Or if it's a sarcoma and the patient needs good kidney function for chemotherapy for sarcoma, then I would treat the sarcoma with chemo first and then do the nephrectomy at a later time.

But the chance of this being another primary, it's always yes in the first diagnosis, but that's, uh, you know, practically, pragmatically speaking, this is very unlikely to be anything else, but renal cell with mets to the sacrum. I mean, this is a pattern of behavior of RCC. It's unlikely. We've seen, I mean, we've seen, we have patients together where the patient has multiple lymph node enlargement up and down, you know, from chest all the way to the pelvis and has a renal mass. Yes, there you would biopsy one of those lymph nodes because the patient could have very well a lymphoma and a renal concurrently. I see all the time two malignancies concurrent. Both sometimes can be metastatic, but this is not, it's unlikely to be something else other than kidney going to the sacrum.
We have a saying in medicine, or in med school you learned, the saying goes, when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras. Apparently Dr. Karam and Dr. Chapin Didn't go to that medical school.
But we work here at MD Anderson.

So the patient subsequently was referred to me and underwent a cytoreductive nephrectomy. She received radiation therapy to her pelvis for the pelvis metastasis and her tumor was sent for processing and she too is being enrolled in the ADAPT trial, which is again the dendritic cell vaccine plus synitinib versus synitinbilone. We have a question.
Jose and I have a question to ask you. Would you have considered doing a partial nephrectomy in that patient?
That was what I was going to ask you actually.
Yes, I would have. That's why I'm asking.

So, Dr. Karam, I believe you have published or are beginning or just now publishing the role of partial nephrectomy in metastatic disease. What is the role of partial nephrectomy in the setting of metastatic disease?

I mean, the publication that we just have is a small number of patients over a long, you know, duration. It's about 33 patients. The bottom line is, whenever it's technically feasible to do a partial nephrectomy that's not a heroic type of partial nephrectomy, and this is a feasible partial nephrectomy, we should consider it, especially if the patient has, you know, borderline kidney function.

Okay, so this patient doesn't have borderline kidney function. She has normal contralateral kidney. So, you know, I agree with you, you could do a partial nephrectomy here. So there's two, I have two challenges, two things that occur to me for that, because I did consider it. First of all, it would probably be, would you do it robotically or would you do it open?
This looks like it's doable robotically based on this picture. I mean, it looks like it's not invading into anything like a lecting system, but.
You would not do this robotically. Yeah. No, you would not. Yeah. I know you, you would not.

Having said that, when we talk to the patient with a metastatic disease about a partial nephrectomy, we have to be very careful and tell them that there is a higher risk of complications with partial nephrectomies. So that might delay their, you know, receiving targeted therapy. So if we are doing a partial, I think we have to be sure that we can do a good partial with the lowest possible complication rate so that we don't. mess their chances in getting a clinical trial. So if it's a large mass invading into other things, I would definitely not do a partial, but for things that are doable, I think we should at least entertain the idea.

My approach would largely rest on whether or not I was planning on doing a lymph node dissection at the time. And in the setting of metastatic disease, I think there's a lot of thoughts about whether or not you do a lymph node dissection. I think in this patient, my thought is in this patient with a solitary metastasis, doing a lymph node dissection would be appropriate to show that the lymph nodes are negative. If your plan is to treat that metastasis as possible with a resection later on by metastasectomy.
Do you think that metastasis is resectable?

No, I don't think it is at this point, but you could also treat it. You could treat it locally. The point is in the absence of other metastatic sites, I think a lymph node dissection may provide some information here.
Okay. And then the patient develops callous societies and has a drain? Sure, there's risks with everything.
I'm actually amazed she had a radical.

The challenge with that, though, is, again, going back to the statement that I made before we started the case presentations again, if she has a complication, urine leak, bleed, what have you, that could potentially prevent her from getting systemic therapy for some period of time because you're going to need to have the urine leak heal up beforehand. So if she had a complication related to the partial,

But I think we're overstating those complications. I mean, urine leaks are very unusual in our practice these days. Not with a tumor that size. Yeah. And the overwhelming majority of the kidney is uninvolved by tumor. You have 90 percent of the kidney, which is completely healthy. You know, the real risk would be hemorrhage, but hemorrhage is something we can manage fairly quickly, and I don't think it would delay hair therapy overtly. So that would be my approach. Okay.

I mean, I would agree that if it's – that's pretty clear cut that that's separate. I mean, I think that that would be on the lower end of complication rate compared to something that was maybe a very endophytic or tumor that's inside the capsule of the kidney and not really extending outside of the kidney. So I think that's a scenario where it might be an option.

I agree, I'm not a surgeon, but I agree a partial nephrectomy would have been the preferred approach for treating the primary. And I would not do lymph node dissection in this patient with metastatic disease to bone in the absence of obvious enlarged lymph nodes by CT or at the time of surgery. So that's added time and it's really not gonna help her to have RP-LND in her case.

And so the thought, again, the thought process from my perspective was we could do a minimally invasive procedure that she's much likely to recover from very rapidly and go on to receive systemic therapy. If she needed it, if she didn't need it, she could just be observed. So let's move on. 57-year-old presents with cough, lower extremity edema. No real urologic complaints. Lab work indicates hypercalcemia and anemia. Imaging is obtained. She has a performance status of one. She has a past history of myasthenia gravis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and also ADHD. She's had a C-section and had a thymectomy, C-section times three, a thymectomy in the past for her myasthenia gravis. And here's a locally advanced tumor involving the right kidney with an IVC thrombus. And again, not to belabor this, Dr. Karam, how would you approach this? Did she have any metastatic disease? CT chest was negative, bone scan was negative.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in August 2022 with 2 months of left-sided body numbness and weakness, seizures, and headaches.

[ diagnosis ]: Right parietal anaplastic meningioma, WHO grade 3, status post craniotomy and gross total resection in August 2022, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. Subsequent follow-up imaging demonstrated a deep right-sided/corpus callosal ring-enhancing lesion with diffuse borders and extensive bilateral periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensity within the post-radiotherapy interval.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical biopsy/resection specimen was reported as anaplastic meningioma, grade 3. CAI index was 30–40%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial pre-operative CT/MRI in 2022 showed a well-defined right parietal extra-axial lesion, iso- to hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, with significant perilesional edema and vivid post-contrast enhancement with dural tail, radiologically suggestive of meningioma.  
- Immediate post-operative imaging showed gross total resection.  
- MRI at approximately 20 days post-operatively showed no residual lesion on post-contrast imaging; enhancement beneath the flap was described after cranioplasty and was considered postoperative change.  
- MRI at approximately 5 months post-operatively showed no residual lesion on T1-, T2-, or post-contrast images, with only subtle postoperative edema.  
- MRI at approximately 10 months post-operatively showed hyperintense changes on T2/FLAIR and a deep-seated enhancing lesion in the region of the corpus callosum, more on the right side, with ring enhancement and diffuse borders.  
- Additional described imaging features at that time included extensive bilateral periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and another nodular area with peripheral enhancement in the surgical bed with pachymeningeal thickening/enhancement.  
- MR spectroscopy was described as showing a lipid-lactate doublet in one nodular area.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent craniotomy and gross total resection of the right parietal lesion on 31 August 2022 at another center.  
- Post-operative recovery was smooth, and she was discharged a few days after surgery.  
- Received adjuvant conventional radiotherapy, 30 fractions, from 3 November 2022 to 14 December 2022.  
- Underwent regular clinical and radiological follow-up.

[ current disease status ]: At the time of latest clinical information, the patient was ambulatory and had left-sided weakness. Follow-up imaging had shown no residual disease early after surgery and at 5 months, but by 10 months post-operatively had shown new enhancing corpus callosal/right-sided deep lesion and multifocal post-treatment white matter signal abnormalities.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension and depression.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic recurrence of carcinoma endometrium with pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma endometrium, stage IV, with metastatic recurrence involving the lungs. Comorbid diabetes mellitus and hypertension were present.

[ histopathology results ]: Lung biopsy performed at recurrence after etoposide-based treatment showed adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry showed PR positive, TTF-1 negative, and PAX8 positive findings, consistent with metastatic endometrial carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Lung nodules had remained stable after 2 years of megestrol acetate therapy prior to radical treatment in 2021. PET imaging subsequently showed progression in the lungs and pleural effusion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing showed CTNNB1 mutation and PTEN mutation. Two PTEN variants were identified, with variant allele frequencies of 56% and 24%. APC variant(s) of uncertain significance were also reported. Microsatellite status was stable (MSS/MSI-stable).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Diagnosed on 18 December 2019. Initial treatment consisted of megestrol acetate for 2 years at an outside hospital. After stability of lung nodules, she underwent staging laparotomy followed by EBRT and IVBT in 2021 with radical intent. She remained on follow-up thereafter. Metastatic recurrence occurred in November 2024. Subsequent systemic treatment consisted of four cycles of carboplatin-based chemotherapy with oral etoposide over 6 months, after which disease progression occurred. She was then treated with liposomal doxorubicin plus carboplatin, and 4 cycles had been completed.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic disease while on liposomal doxorubicin plus carboplatin, with pulmonary progression and pleural effusion on recent PET imaging. Four cycles of current treatment had been completed, and next imaging evaluation was pending at that time.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described as fit for further treatment. She was apprehensive regarding intravenous treatment.

But as we get ready to get teed up for surgery, This happens the week before surgery. A huge saddle PE occurs, which we know, unfortunately, patients can have other unrelated problems. This can be something that leads to hypercoagulable states. They were able to do a vacuum-assisted thrombectomy. The patient went on Eloquist and actually did great. So when you face this, you face an obstacle to getting to surgery. What would the panel do? Obviously, we don't want to take a patient with an active PE straight to surgery. We know that our surgery is going to be even more clot-provoking, so we need to pause. So if you have somebody who's having a good response, what would be the thoughts at this point? So we obviously cancel surgery, take care of the problem.
I would treat to maximal benefit up to six cycles in buy time.

And that's exactly what we did here. And it actually worked out. So this particular provider decided to drop, which I think was reasonable, the Permatrexid and switched to Carbo in light of all of this. But the patient went on and had an even better response in the pelvis, which is going to make this a much more I won't say better, but still the surgery in terms of getting to the goals is going to be much more successful. So this patient, when I return after this meeting, will undergo their cytoreduction. But I thought this was a perfect example of not just how neoadjuvant can benefit patients, but how we adjust to the medical issues that occur for patients. So we're going to skip that and I'm going to yield this podium here to Dr. Kindler and she's going to provide a case about two compartment disease. You guys heard about it yesterday a little bit. You heard it from the pleural side. So just to briefly sort of tell you about it from the peritoneal side when you have people we have both disease in the peritoneum and in one chest cavity or sometimes both or pericardial, what do you do? In my mind, when you're thinking about patients who might be surgical candidates, there's kind of three scenarios. They can present with both. They can present with isolated peritoneal recurrence after management of something in the chest. And then they can present with more diffuse disease. This is where Hedy will talk about the impact of BAP1 status and germlines that can come up and impact this. And I think we're highly selective in this group of patients, but at the core, if you don't have disease amenable to surgical clearance, and if that surgical risk is absorbent, you're not going to have a surgical option in biocompartment disease. And I think when it does come up, I think it's a challenge for us. If people have already had a major lung resection, or if you have bicabitary disease that you think is of surgical consideration, you tend to want to do the peritoneum first because once you do a pneumonectomy, the anesthesia around pneumonectomies, even for elective procedures, and I think this is all our peritoneal group, like the idea of one lung ventilation gets very challenging and it's an issue in and of itself to take patients who have had a major pneumonectomy to the OR because A blowout of that stump can just be devastating for a patient. So you have to be really thoughtful in terms of what you're going to do in these scenarios. So I will yield and let Hedy.

reference_conclusion: Given the extent of intra-abdominal disease and the anticipated morbidity of a multivisceral operation, initial systemic therapy was favored over immediate cytoreductive surgery. Surgical reconsideration was to be based on treatment response, with neoadjuvant therapy used to assess disease biology and potentially reduce operative burden. After a favorable response, surgery was deferred because of an acute saddle pulmonary embolism; systemic therapy was continued to maximal benefit, up to six cycles, before proceeding with cytoreduction once medically optimized.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic penile cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Unresectable metastatic penile squamous cell carcinoma.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HPV positivity had been reported in approximately 50% of cases in some series and up to 80% in others. PD-L1 positivity and high tumor mutational burden had been described as potential biomarkers associated with immunotherapy susceptibility in penile tumors. No patient-specific molecular results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No patient-specific prior treatment history was available.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease was present. Morbidity described in the metastatic setting included severe lower-extremity lymphedema, scrotal edema, deep vein thromboses, hypotension with diuresis, and anasarca; no patient-specific current complications were documented.

[ other clinical data ]: A first-line systemic regimen discussed for metastatic penile cancer consisted of pembrolizumab with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, followed by pembrolizumab maintenance for up to 2 years. In a 2024 Brazilian multicenter study (11 centers, n=33) in penile cancer with unresectable metastatic disease, this regimen produced a reported response rate of 40%. TIP chemotherapy was described as a more intensive comparator regimen, but no patient-specific administration data were available.
slides: <image> Case slide presenting a 65-year-old man with a longstanding penile mass, inguinal adenopathy, systemic symptoms, and CT images showing pelvic and pulmonary findings, posed as a discussion of first-line options for chemo-naïve metastatic disease.

reference_discussion.text: So this is a great case because we often just extrapolate from the neoadjuvant setting and then use TIP in this setting. But recently at ASCO last year, 2024, we saw the results of the Hercules study. This is a Brazilian study from 11 different centers enrolled 33 patients with penile cancer or unrespectable metastatic penile cancer. And they were treated with pembrolizumab plus platinum-based chemotherapy, cisplatinum and 5-FU. every three weeks for six cycles, and they received the pembrolizumab for up to two years. And they saw a response rate of 40%. So that's great for us, because that's a lot gentler than TIP chemotherapy. And one of the questions is, there wasn't a long follow-up yet for this study, but will we have durable responses if we incorporate immunotherapy up front for these patients? So we're currently working on designing a first-line trial for patients with penile cancer, and we wanted to have a randomized component to it. We don't, you know, with this new data coming out, the Hercules data, and, you know, some data that I have from my phase one CAVONEVO study that enrolled about nine penile cancer patients, and we currently have the ICONIC study open right now that's enrolling more. The question is, is there equipoise to have a non-penile immunotherapy arm in the metastatic setting now? Should we have a TIP arm and then an IO plus chemo arm, kind of like the Hercules study? But then what about the TKIIO promise there and just kind of building on some data that we have? So these are kind of questions that we're having right now as we develop the next phase of first-line trials. and really trying to find the best therapies for our patients with metastatic penile cancer. And in the second line setting, again, like I said, we're testing antibody drug conjugates. A comment by Dr. Crook in the beginning about the HPV status, and although we don't have HPV-directed therapy, Seattle, though a lot have been tested. There's vaccines out there. There's IO therapies. There's even CAR therapies that are being tested right now on penile cancer. We just don't have any specific therapies for penile cancers per se, but we do have some that are being developed for HPV-positive squamous cell tumors that can potentially be extrapolated and used in this setting. And the incidence is kind of, it depends on which series you look at. In some, it's about 50% in terms of HPV positivity, but it can be as high as 80% in some series. And there's also other markers like PD-L1 positivity and TNB high that make these tumors a little bit more susceptible, that we think make these tumors a little bit more susceptible to IL. So therein goes back to the frontline option that I would give this gentleman, I would give him the Hercules regimen at this point because, you know, it's, it's, it's easier, it's easier to give than tip. I've given a lot of tip and I never like giving it. Iphosimide is tough. The patients really struggle through it. It's, it's a, it's a, it's a tough regimen.
Tell us the regimen again, the Hercules regimen.

So the Hercules regimen is an IO chemo. So it has pembrolizumab and it has 5-FU and cisplatinum. And it's given every three weeks and for six cycles, like metastatic disease. And then the pembrolizumab is kind of given maintenance over two years.

Right. Well, that's really interesting. I will tell you that I've had a couple one-offs here and there with my medical oncologist here doing chemo-immuno or penile cancer or urethral cancer, primary squamous urethral, and actually I've been really pleasantly surprised by it.

Yeah, yeah. For urethral cancers, we've seen some really nice responses in the ICONIC study, again, the Cabo Nebo study that I have, Cabo Nebo IPI. So there's activity there. And those, the issue with urethral tumors is that they can have different histologies, but I'm really focusing right now on the squamous histology. I've seen really nice responses, which is very in line with what we see in the penile cancer patients. But not all patients respond, right? So I'm talking about a 30% response. What about the 70% that don't respond? What do we do with those? They're coming to me for other clinical trials, and we're looking for better treatments. One of the things that I wanted to comment on, I know we talked a lot about primary treatment of the lymph node, bulky lymph nodes, and initially the diagnosis of penile cancer and doing a lymph node dissection, there's a lot of morbidity. And of course, I see all of the morbidity in the metastatic setting, right? So I see these terrible lymphedemas.
You see them after we're done with them, like, terrible.

They can't walk. They get scrotoedema because their legs are so swollen. that then it becomes scrotal edema, and we try wrapping them, they get DVTs, and we try diuresing, but then they get low blood pressure because it basically becomes anasarca. It's very difficult to manage these patients at the end of life. And, you know, we're trying to find better treatments to improve upon that. But even the primary treatments, I think, need improvement in order not to deal with this morbidity that happens post-surgery and could be also post-rehabilitation.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board favored first-line systemic therapy with the Hercules regimen for metastatic penile squamous cell carcinoma. This consists of pembrolizumab combined with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil administered every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, followed by maintenance pembrolizumab for up to 2 years. This approach was selected over TIP chemotherapy based on the discussed activity and more favorable tolerability.

I've given a lot of tip and I never like giving it. Iphosimide is tough. The patients really struggle through it. It's, it's a, it's a, it's a tough regimen. [...] So the Hercules regimen is an IO chemo. So it has pembrolizumab and it has 5-FU and cisplatinum. And it's given every three weeks and for six cycles, like metastatic disease. And then the pembrolizumab is kind of given maintenance over two years.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Easy fatigability and generalized muscle weakness.

[ diagnosis ]: Primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia and inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone level; osteoporosis.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative neck ultrasound demonstrated an approximately 2 cm lesion posterior to the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe. Four-dimensional CT confirmed an approximately 2 cm lesion in the left tracheoesophageal groove, posterior to the upper pole of the thyroid. DEXA scan showed osteoporosis of the lumbar spine with T-score -2.5 and osteopenia of the femoral neck.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum calcium was elevated on outpatient evaluation and remained elevated on repeat testing. Parathyroid hormone was within the normal range but near the upper limit; a value of 47 was reported. Magnesium, albumin, and vitamin D were within normal limits. Twenty-four-hour urine calcium was 325.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated normal vocal cord mobility preoperatively.

[ other clinical data ]: Past history was otherwise unremarkable. There was no personal history of nephrolithiasis. Family history was negative for parathyroid and thyroid disease. Physical examination was normal.
slides:
<image> Case Two slide summarizing a 60-year-old woman with fatigue, generalized muscle weakness, normal exam and laryngoscopy, and elevated calcium as part of the workup discussion.
<image> Case Two slide summarizing the patient’s laboratory evaluation, including elevated calcium with PTH in the upper-normal range and otherwise normal phosphorus, magnesium, albumin, and vitamin D levels.
<image> Ultrasound slide showing transverse and sagittal neck images of a measured lesion posterior to the left superior thyroid region as part of preoperative localization workup.
<image> Preoperative neck CT images in axial, coronal, and sagittal views showing a left-sided approximately 2 cm lesion in the tracheoesophageal groove posterior to the upper thyroid lobe.
<image> Slide summarizing a left-sided parathyroid lesion identified on preoperative imaging.

reference_discussion.text: Yep, sure. Thank you for inviting me to Dr. Singer and Dr. Terras to present our patient over here. So our patient is a 60-year-old female who came in complaining of easy fatigability, generalized muscle weakness. On outpatient work of bio-primary care, she was found to have hypercalcemia, otherwise healthy, no personal history of kidney stones, and family history is negative for parathyroid and thyroid disease. Her physical exam was normal. When we saw her, we did do a flexible laryngoscopy exam, which showed normal cord mobility. And so we ordered further lab testing when we saw her. full panel, calcium was elevated again, PTH was within the normal range towards the upper limit there. BOS Mag and albumin and vitamin D were all within the normal limits. And so she also did come in with a 24-urine calcium, which was at 325. And her DEXA scan did show osteoporosis with a T-score of negative 2.5 in the lumbar spine, and then osteopenia of the femoral neck.

All right. So, Natalia, I'm just going to ask you to take a break there for a minute. Do you mind just going back one slide? Yeah, so, you know, the idea of normal hormonal hyperparathyroidism is a little bit, it's a little bit paradoxical sounding, but so this patient comes in with clear hypercalcemia, there's no question about that. but their parathyroid number is well within the normal range, right? So Dr. Terras, how do you think about these kinds of patients and what do you think is like the critical part of understanding why this is still pathologic?

So the first thing I would say is that even some endocrinologists and certainly primary care doctors don't recognize this as being clear-cut hyperparathyroidism, and they have their little nomogram that we all got in medical school, and they don't understand that this patient has treatable disease. And so the way I try to explain it to my folks is the PTH, it's really about the relationship of the calcium to the parathyroid hormone level. And when one goes up, the other goes down like this, I see Brendan Stacks on the call. He introduced me to the concept of the teeter-totter. So it should be like a teeter-totter. And so when they're both up, that's clear-cut hyperparathyroidism. The parathyroid hormone level is technically normal, but in relation to the calcium, it's abnormal. So we call it inappropriately normal. And even patients can understand when the calcium's high, the parathyroid should be low, very low. And I say, maybe not zero, but close to it. When it's not, it means it's inappropriately normal or incompletely suppressed or not suppressed. So it's that relationship between the calcium and the parathyroid hormone level that's so important. And, you know, just another side point is the PTH varies kind of minute to minute, the calcium, you know, day to day. And so it's good to get those at the same time. And so if you have a confusing patient, comes from the outside, you know, get a set of labs. I hate repeating stuff like that, but we do because it can eliminate confusion. So, get them at the same time. But this is, I mean, I think this variant of classic hyperparathyroidism, I think, was described further ago, longer ago than the normal calcemic But still relatively recent in the last 20 years or so, it's sort of been recognized. And so, but this this one is hate to use the term no brainer but this is a no brainer, and partly because of the other things with the patient so the lumbar spine. minus 2.5, that's, I mean, that's a contraindication to observation. And then the most recent, I didn't see a lot of changes in the most recent guidelines other than the threshold for urine calcium. So it was 400 for a number of iterations, then they removed it, then it came back in, and now they've actually lowered it, which makes sense. So I think it's 250 for women, 300 for men, so she's at 325, I think it's on the next slide. So, she certainly meets my criteria for surgery, and the PTH of 47, I wouldn't even blink at that one. You know, when it gets into the 20s, I think it makes you, you know, at least have to step back and say, okay, let's make sure we got the right disease. But 47 is, yeah, that's every week I see two or three patients like that.

So I mean, I think that maybe the single most important thing that you said, and you said a lot of important things, but maybe the single most important thing is that it's the relationship between the PTH and the calcium. And so again, this is, I think for the fellows, I think it's critical to understand, you can't look at calcium or PTH in isolation. If someone tells you that someone has a PTH of 110, That literally means nothing. And if someone tells you you have an elevated calcium, it doesn't mean anything. It's about that relationship between the two and understanding whether that relationship, like you said, whether that relationship is abnormal or not. So in your experience, and Brendan Stack is on as well, and Brendan's a very experienced parathyroid surgeon, so maybe I'd ask him to just comment as well, is what is the lowest PTH that you've had that you've operated on preoperatively.

So, for me, it was like, I think, 21, 1921, around that level, although Alan Sipperstein presented a paper, actually, I was, I saw the presentation at the AAS, and then it was published. This is probably 10 or 12 years ago, something, it was a catchy title, like how, you know, normal hormonal hyperparathyroidism, how low can it go or something like that. Five, five, a PTH of five they operated on. So I'd have a tough time doing that. Brendan, how about you? What's your lowest? I would say my lowest would be in the low 30s that I recall at the moment. Yep.

I mean, I saw a patient today. And Michael, what about you? I mean, I definitely have operated in the 30s. I saw a patient today who has robust hypercalcemia. That's what's interesting. This is not, you would think, well, maybe because the PTH number is lower, that the patients are going to have hypercalcemia, but lower mild hypercalcemia. This patient's calcium levels were into the 12s. and his numbers were in the 20s. So it's just about understanding, I think, again, like you said, that idea that if you have high calcium, your PTH maybe not is zero, maybe it's not five, but it is very low. So say this patient comes to you, do you have any additional concerns about, I don't know, FHH or any other entity that it could be confused with?

Not one. I mean, this to me is classic primary hyperparathyroidism, except the PTH is a little bit on the low side. The biggest challenge is, not a challenge, but it's just explaining it to the patients so they understand for the sophisticated ones that have, you know, gone on MyChart and pulled up their numbers. But no, this is straightforward. You mentioned at the beginning something about mild. Like, I don't consider this mild disease. you know, and that's one of the things I, you know, again, educating my colleagues, my endocrinologists, the severity of the disease doesn't even really relate to these numbers. It's things like the 24-hour urine calcium, or the DEXA scan findings, or what's their creatinine, that is kind of the better measure of uh, the severity of the disease. And so, um, so yeah, this is again, this, I wouldn't even think twice about this patient, especially they're 60. That's an age I can relate to. So they need surgery stat.
You mean, because they're so old, they need to have, they need, yeah, quick before they die.
Yeah.

Let me ask a question that some people might be wondering about. And I know that you had looked at this at some point, at least. And again, Brendan may have comments on this. How about if someone says to you, I want to operate on this patient, but I like to use intraoperative PTH. Can I use intraoperative PTH? Is this patient's number going to be so low to begin with? What is your sense of that?

Yes, you can use intraoperative PTH. Oftentimes these patients, for whatever reason, it's a little bit, the baseline at surgery seems to be a little bit higher than what we got in the office. But I had a patient, was it today or yesterday, the baseline was 48 or 54, something like that, and it dropped to 12. And so I would say, if nothing else, you can feel confident that you've removed hyper-functional parathyroid tissue, because it won't change at all. And that's, again, for the fellows. And I see it in other surgeons' operative notes, that they think, well, I couldn't find the adenoma, but I found this normal gland. I'm going to remove that normal gland to help the patient a little bit. It doesn't do anything to help the patient. It only hurts them, because if you remove a normal gland when somebody has an adenoma, it doesn't do anything. The number is going to stay the same. So if the corollary is if the number comes down in a meaningful way, then you know you've removed hyperfunctional parathyroid tissue and you can feel confident that you found at least one abnormal gland. I mean, the reality is, I mean, it depends on imaging and a number of other things. And I don't know we will even get to the surgical aspect of things but but my threshold for looking at other glands is much lower than it has been in the past you do this long enough and you see and then it just makes the case go easier when you've looked at other glands and and when you're comfortable with that you can do it quickly and. and it's usually a good thing. In a patient like this, you find an adenoma, maybe there was localization, you find the adenoma, you remove it, you see the other gland on the same side, and I have a hard time not looking for that other gland on the same side, and it's normal. They don't have forward gland hyperplasia, I've removed an adenoma. If they have multi-gland disease, it's going to be a double adenoma. You know exactly where to find it because usually it's a double upper, so it saves a lot of time. at surgery, but so I would say the PTH assay, yeah, I find it very helpful.
Okay. So Natalia, why don't you- You do a lot of these surgeries.
Do you use it for these cases?

Absolutely. I mean, and first of all, there's no question and it's not clear why is a lot of times the baseline is actually ends up being above the normal range, even though preoperatively it's not, and that's very common. Yeah, that's been my experience. The way it drops in terms of the slope that you see, it's actually very similar to the slope as if it was starting at 150. It may end up lower, but the slope is similar. Natalia, why don't, because I know Dr. Terrace is itching to talk about the surgical side of this.
Well, the surgery is fun too, but this is an interesting disease even before surgery.
Yeah. Okay. So why don't you talk about what, what you guys found?

Yep. So we did get a preoperative imaging first ultrasound, which did show about a two centimeter potential lesion posterior to the upper lobe of the thyroid. And this was confirmed on our 40 CT scan. We usually get these in combination. And again, you see this two centimeter lesion, tracheoesophageal groove on the left, and just posterior to the upper bowl of the thyroid. And so we took this patient to the operating room. And so, oops, sorry. And so we took this patient to the operating room, and we did find an enlarged left superior gland and excised this. We also did take a look to see if, since we were operating on the left side, to take a look at the inferior gland, which appeared normal, so we preserved this. And a pathology did confirm that we did in fact have an adenoma. We don't typically get intra-op PTH, but our post-operative PTH did drop down to 27, our calcium normalized. And again, one month on follow-up, she was doing well. PTH was still in the normal range. Calcium was in the normal range as well. So overall, a success story.
You're muted, Michael.

Sorry, my, my, my, my, my children are big very supportive of the conference. So, let's have them weigh in. Trust me, you don't want that. So, a couple, a couple of things. So first of all, just generally. When you have a normal hormonal case, in your experience, does it change anything significantly about either what you're thinking about or looking for surgically? Multiglandular disease, smaller adenomas, does it have any impact on those things?

Me, no. No, not really. Normal calcemic is a different situation. Non-localizing imaging, different situation. But in a case like this, no, it wouldn't be in my brain at all. Can I comment on the surgery?
Can you comment? Yeah. Of course. And the best part is that Greg Randolph joined.
Greg Randolph just jumped on. I saw, yeah. That's why I'm going to comment.
He wants to hear a review of his surgical approach.
That would be very helpful to me.

I would never presume to review Gregory Randolph. and his surgical technique. It's just a different way of doing things. I haven't met the parathyroid gland that I wouldn't want a biopsy. And certainly if I get an operative note from Greg Randolph and he says, I found a normal gland and I judge it to be normal and it was definitely a parathyroid gland, who am I to question? But for every other surgeon on the planet, biopsy proof way better than surgeon judges this to be that or this or that. And even me, like I do a lot of this, But have I ever been wrong? A little reddish lymph node? Yeah, I've been wrong. So I much prefer biopsy proof. Why? Because I do a ton of reoperative surgery, and it can be exceptionally helpful to know, not what somebody judged, but to know. So personally, I would biopsy. Again, there's lots of different ways to do this. That's just my bias. And then the PTH assay, Oh, it's a pain to wait for that thing. I get it. It's a pain, but it has spared me from causing a second operative encounter for patients on enough times that I think it's worthwhile doing. I'm surprised, Greg, you don't use it, but like I said, lots of different ways to do things.

So, Greg, certainly if you have any comments, you're more than welcome. I think he's muted. So, a couple, a couple questions I have so I do think it is important to say because I know you're, you're very much a believer in biopsying of of parathyroid glands that you find. certainly some people that would make them nervous because somehow you're going to damage them. And I think, though, that your point is really a critical one. And this is true, I think, as you said, this is true for more beginner parathyroid surgeons, but this is for super senior parathyroid surgeons. Like we all think things are parathyroid glands and they're not. It's lymph node, thymus, thyroid, fat. I mean, I think it can be a very humbling surgery. And at the end of the day, at this point, and maybe Greg or maybe Natalia wants to make a comment about this. At this point, or certainly up until a few years ago, the only thing that we had to prove 100% that this is a parathyroid, that I found the parathyroid, that I clipped the parathyroid was pathology. I do think that, you know, and I think that the fellows will hear more about this in the next, you know, few years, because I think this is technology that's emerging, is this idea of autofluorescence, and some of the fellows may be familiar with it, autofluorescence imaging of parathyroid glands, and there's different devices that are on the market for this. And I do think that that is, at least intraoperatively, largely going to replace the need for frozen sections in terms of confirming tissue as parathyroid or not. But again, that idea that you know for sure that just not that just not how it works.

Funny that you say pathology is the only thing that's 100% because I was telling you I had an interesting case today where the imaging was backwards. The pathology was wrong they said I've removed an adenoma I did not. And then the, and then the levels came back it's it's a long story but like I was I was really up against it today and one of the things was the pathologist steered me wrong because they said, Yes, hypercellular parathyroid. Anyway, so it's not actually 100% maybe 99%, maybe one of fluorescence will be better than the pathology. Well, who's the lady, who's the lady in in Calgary, Greg, the general surgeon, Janice Jessica, Janice Jessica, we had her in Augusta, and one thing I remember her say this as many years ago before I was so want to do biopsies but I remember talking about intraoperatively a challenging case. She said, when you have one of those challenging cases. make sure you know what you think you know first. In other words, you found this claim, you found that plan, send a little piece to the pathologist intraoperatively, sort of tangential to our conversation, but that way you can verify what you believe you know in a difficult case because you think you found two on the left and maybe you only found one on the left and et cetera. So I just thought that that has sort of rung true with me is make sure you know what you think you know. So anyway.

So, just before we move on to the last case, because I, you know, we talked about it a little bit, but I think is, you know, we tend to talk about intraoperative PTH, and we tend to, like, people tend to, I think, think of it as something that's so easy to interpret all the time. And I think just like everything else that we do surgically, there is a lot, a lot of nuance. So, if you don't mind just And you could do it in more words or less, but just comment on generally what criteria you use for cure. I think that's a really important point to make. And the other thing is maybe if you comment a little bit on what you see intraoperatively in terms of IOPTH, depending on the type of disease you're addressing. So I think you'll talk first, obviously, about just single adenomas. But how about what you would see intraoperatively on IOPTH, say with a double adenoma versus say four gland hyperplasia, if you can.

Yeah, I'll try to keep it to like two or three minutes. So I remember when I was a young head and neck surgeon and learning from Bob Sofferman, and he came in to Augusta, was talking about parathyroid disease. And he said something about just because the PTH level gets below 65 doesn't mean the patient's cured. And I thought, well, of course, this is the normal range. No, it's going to get to the teens or 12. The question is, where do you stop operating because you believe it's on its way down there, but that's where it's going to get in everybody because the other glands that are normal are actually suppressed or dormant. And so the patient's going to get to the teens or maybe 20. Do we need to wait intraoperatively for that to happen? Not necessarily. But for me, so to answer your question, so when is it a cure? I would be hard pressed to wake a patient up if the PTH is above 40. That's kind of, you know, there's no hard and fast, but that's as close as I would get to hard and fast. If it's 45 and it started at 90, I'm probably waiting for one more level. And we get them, you know, that's the other thing, how do you do it? We get every five minutes, we get five, 10, 15, Then I get a 25 now. We used to have the really rapid assay, which was seven or eight minutes. Now it's about 25 minutes, which seems like an eternity to me. So I get that 25 just to have another data point in case we need it. So I get a five minute and it's 43. I'm waiting for another one. And if it's not in the 30s, I know the patient has a double adenoma. And it's really, and I think you alluded to this, Mike, it's a little bit to the trajectory of how it's falling. And I would confess that because I'm going and finding another gland and biopsy, my five minute may be closer to 10 minute. level, so it's such that I expect a significant drop. And so if it goes from, and my nurse is texting me the numbers because the fellows closed and I'm, you know, doing something else. And if it went from 130 to 70, or even let's call it 64, which is a 50% drop and in the normal range, it goes from 130 to 64, I'd respond, like, oh, that should have gone lower than that. in a typical patient. So you want to see that relatively quick drop. But some people are slow degraders. There are patients like that. And so you just have to be patient. And I've had patients where we waited an hour and 20 minutes. And I probably wouldn't do that nowadays. But each level came lower. And they got all the way down. They were cured. But there are slow degraders. As far as the different patients, so double adenomas, if they're both biochemically active, yeah, you'll get not necessarily 50% drop, but it'll drop approximately half of where it was, but then it will plateau if it's a double adenoma. And so those are straightforward. For four gland disease, I've had cases where, you know, with each gland, you know, years ago when I find a gland, remove it and get levels, you could actually map it out. So it incrementally drops with the four glands. I wouldn't be able to say that today because I'm a little bit too impatient to wait for that. If I see a gland, I look at the other gland on the same side, if it's abnormal, then I'm looking on the other side. And so I'm going to do all that work before I even start getting levels. And I would say I still wait for levels. If I've done a subtotal on somebody that has clear cut four gland, although you could argue that you don't need to, but there's that occasional, we all have that. Greg's got three of them. I've got a couple of them where it was the supernumerary abnormal gland. So the fifth gland. And so I'm still a little paranoid. I practice a little too close to Tampa to have failures. Like I gotta make sure that they're all cured. So I still wait for the levels, but theoretically, if you do a four gland exploration, you can wake the patient up. Which they do in Tampa, by the way, they do that. But in the recovery room, they get a PTH level. And if it hasn't dropped, they wheel them back into the operating room. They don't put that on the papers, but it's worth knowing that, that that's their practice pattern.

Yeah, I think it's, as you do more, you realize that if you're sitting there hoping that the PTH number is cured, it means that the patient's not cured. The number has to be demonstrably clear that the patient's cured. All right, so with that we're going to move on to, to normal calcemic hyperparathyroidism and I just want to say for the fellows. The reason we're presenting them in this order is because these are, these are things that you're going to see in your practice and you know and and again they present different, different challenges. This is an entity, and Alex is going to start in a second, but this is an entity that I think, as Dr. Tarras already mentioned, this was kind of first described much more recently. And this has now become, in some people's practices, really pervasive. And again, it seems somewhat paradoxical, and it's hard to understand exactly what it is. So with that, Alex, I appreciate you doing this. Thanks.

reference_conclusion: The panel concluded that the patient has primary hyperparathyroidism with inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone in the setting of hypercalcemia, osteoporosis, and elevated 24-hour urine calcium, meeting criteria for operative management. Preoperative localization with ultrasound and 4D CT identified a left superior lesion. The patient underwent parathyroidectomy with excision of an enlarged left superior parathyroid adenoma and preservation of a normal-appearing left inferior gland. Postoperatively, parathyroid hormone decreased and serum calcium normalized, consistent with successful treatment.

[...] this, I wouldn't even think twice about this patient, especially they're 60. That's an age I can relate to. So they need surgery stat." [...] "So we did get a preoperative imaging first ultrasound, which did show about a two centimeter potential lesion posterior to the upper lobe of the thyroid. And this was confirmed on our 40 CT scan." [...] "And so we took this patient to the operating room, and we did find an enlarged left superior gland and excised this. We also did take a look to see if, since we were operating on the left side, to take a look at the inferior gland, which appeared normal, so we preserved this. And a pathology did confirm that we did in fact have an adenoma. We don't typically get intra-op PTH, but our post-operative PTH did drop down to 27, our calcium normalized. And again, one month on follow-up, she was doing well. PTH was still in the normal range. Calcium was in the normal range as well. So overall, a success story."

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Four months of left-sided epiphora, slight blurring of vision, and mild diplopia.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma involving the left ethmoid/anterior sinonasal region with extension toward the lacrimal sac/orbit; staged clinically as T4aN0 sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: In-office biopsy of the left sinonasal mass demonstrated poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a left-sided mass filling the nasal cavity, with erosion of the nasal bones and extension into the left orbit. The lesion did not extend far posteriorly and was immediately adjacent to the lateral lamella.  
- MRI with contrast demonstrated an anterior left sinonasal lesion encroaching into the orbit, either abutting or invading the periorbita. The extraconal fat and medial rectus muscle were not invaded. The lesion extended through the nasal bones, with indistinct soft-tissue planes anteriorly involving the skin near the nasal bones/frontal sinus region.  
- PET scan for staging was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic results were reported. p16 testing was discussed, but no patient-specific result was documented.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- She denied nasal obstruction, epistaxis, cranial neuropathies, and neck masses at presentation.  
- Examination showed no ocular motion restriction, no cranial neuropathies, and no neck masses.  
- Rigid nasal endoscopy demonstrated a mass filling the left nasal cavity and middle meatus.  
- Performance status was described as reasonable, with Karnofsky status considered acceptable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman at initial diagnosis in 2016.

[ chief complaint ]: De novo metastatic breast cancer at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast, grade 3, estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, with de novo stage IV disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 3; ER-positive; PR-positive; HER2-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Metastatic disease involved multiple bulky lymph node masses, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and extensive osseous metastases at presentation. Disease progression was documented in 2019. Slow disease progression was documented again in the current year after prior disease control.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling identified CCND1 amplification, FGF3 amplification, FGFR amplification, and CDH1 mutation. CDH1 variant allele frequency was 69%. No microsatellite instability biomarker was identified. No tumor mutational burden biomarker was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment included tamoxifen. She then received a couple of cycles of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, which were discontinued because of toxicities. She subsequently pursued alternative therapy for a period. Thereafter she was treated with nab-paclitaxel (Abraxane) and had clinical benefit for a period. Following progression in 2019, she was treated with fulvestrant and abemaciclib, which achieved disease control and maintained quiescent bone disease for a prolonged interval. After subsequent slow progression, she was treated with everolimus and exemestane. Everolimus was associated with oral mucositis; otherwise treatment was tolerated fairly well.

[ current disease status ]: She experienced slow progression of metastatic disease in the months preceding comprehensive genomic profiling.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old patient with a family history of prostate cancer in the father and brother.

[ chief complaint ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen.

[ diagnosis ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen with PI-RADS 2 multiparametric MRI and a focal PSMA-avid lesion in the left transition zone.

[ imaging findings ]: Multiparametric MRI demonstrated PI-RADS 2 findings. Pelvic PSMA PET/CT using gallium-68 PSMA-11 demonstrated an obvious focal area of increased uptake in the left transition zone with SUVmax 12. Mild diffuse uptake was present throughout the remainder of the transition zone. No other focal abnormal uptake within the prostate was described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None available.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 8. PSA density 0.2.

[ current disease status ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen under evaluation, with discordant multiparametric MRI (PI-RADS 2) and PSMA PET/CT findings.

[ other clinical data ]: PSMA PET pattern was described as focal transition zone uptake with SUVmax above 12.

So if there's nothing, as you can see for score one, nothing that stands out, very mild uptake. We consider that's no pattern, it's very low grade. Score two is divided into two different parts. And then if you go to the right in red, you have those malignant patterns. So focal uptake within the transition zone for three. Anything that's focal within the peripheral zone without defining any minimal uptake with SUVmax. So anything that stands out is suspicious and should go on to have biopsy. And finally, score 5 is anything regardless with SUVmax above 12 that had a 100% probability of having prostate cancer.

So we've learned from our radiology colleagues with multi-parametric MRI that differentiating the peripheral zone from the rest of the prostate is really important, because most prostate tumors arise in the peripheral zone. So if you have focal uptake in the peripheral zone, even if it's lowish grade, we should be reporting that as malignant. And if it's really intense in the peripheral zone, then it's a score five. It's almost certainly malignant. So that's the way we're interpreting the prostate now. the intensity of uptake, but where is it? case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 25-year-old woman; gravida with a documented single live intrauterine pregnancy at 22 weeks 4 days on obstetric ultrasound; para 4.

[ chief complaint ]: Three-month history of progressive neck swelling, left breast swelling, left upper limb swelling, and breathlessness. Swelling reportedly began in the left breast, extended to the axilla, and later involved the neck. Associated weight loss was present but not quantified.

[ diagnosis ]: Large left chest/neck mass with mediastinal involvement causing tracheal deviation and respiratory compromise; tissue diagnosis was pending at the time of reporting.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsies of the lesions were obtained. Histopathology results were pending.

[ imaging findings ]: Chest radiograph demonstrated a huge mediastinal/chest mass with tracheal shift to the right. Neck ultrasound showed enlarged, nodular, heterogeneous thyroid lobes and isthmus, with an anechoic left thyroid lobe cyst measuring 1.1 × 1.2 cm. Breast ultrasound showed an enlarged left breast with a mixed echogenic mass involving the whole breast and multiple nodular masses in the left breast; right breast tissue appeared normal. Obstetric ultrasound demonstrated a single live intrauterine pregnancy at 22 weeks 4 days. MRI chest was planned but was aborted because the patient could not tolerate lying flat.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Serology was non-reactive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: During the index admission, the patient received pain management and nursing in a propped-up position. Diagnostic workup included chest radiography, neck ultrasound, breast ultrasound, obstetric ultrasound, and lesion core biopsy. MRI chest was not completed because of intolerance to supine positioning.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic bulky left chest/neck/anterior chest wall mass with left breast enlargement and left upper limb swelling. The patient was in respiratory distress with ECOG performance status 4. Examination findings included pulse 138/min, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 36.8°C, and blood pressure 130/80 mmHg. Trachea was shifted to the right. The left hemithorax was dull to percussion with absent air entry on the left. There was a firm upper anterior chest wall mass involving the neck and axilla, without bruit. The left breast was enlarged with palpable masses. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with normal S1 and S2 and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no palpable masses. Central nervous system examination was stable.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient reported skin nodular swellings since childhood. She had no history of diabetes mellitus or hypertension. No family history of chronic illness or cancer was reported. No food or drug allergies were reported. Prior admissions had been for deliveries only.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old male; never smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe breathlessness at presentation to the emergency department.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma subtype, with disease localized to the left pleura and malignant left pleural effusion.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural fluid cytology was positive for malignancy. Cell block from pleural fluid and pleural-based lesion showed adenocarcinoma with TTF-1 positivity. Tumor cellularity in available tissue/cell block material was approximately 5%.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan showed pleural-based nodules and left pleural effusion, with no disease identified elsewhere. Disease was described as localized to the left pleura. Brain imaging was normal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue was sent for next-generation sequencing, but testing could not be performed. Liquid biopsy obtained after the first cycle of chemotherapy showed no targetable mutation. A PD-L1-positive result was reported from blood-based testing; no tumor proportion score was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient was initially admitted under pulmonology. An intercostal drain had been placed and was subsequently removed. Pleurodesis was performed. Systemic chemotherapy with pemetrexed and carboplatin was started because of symptomatic disease. Liquid biopsy was performed after the first chemotherapy cycle. At the time of reporting, the patient had received two cycles of pemetrexed and carboplatin.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic malignant left pleural effusion and pleural-based disease at diagnosis; no extrathoracic disease identified on PET imaging and brain imaging was normal. Ongoing treatment with pemetrexed/carboplatin after two cycles.

[ other clinical data ]: Multiple tissue fragments from pleural fluid cell block and pleural-based lesion were combined for molecular testing because of low tumor cellularity.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Dizziness; increased cough with sputum.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic colon cancer diagnosed in October 2024, described as upper-end metastatic colon cancer. Metastatic sites documented in lung, liver, sigmoid colon, and brain.

[ histopathology results ]: Endobronchial/lung biopsy had been obtained via bronchoscopy by pulmonology. No formal histopathology description was available.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a new single hemorrhagic brain metastasis. A lung mass previously measuring approximately 10 cm had increased to 14 cm and subsequently occupied essentially the entire left lung. Concomitant infectious/inflammatory pulmonary changes were present. A 2 cm right lung lesion had disappeared after initiation of trifluridine/tipiracil. Sigmoid colon lesion and liver lesion had also disappeared after initiation of trifluridine/tipiracil. Overall imaging pattern was of mixed response, with progression of the dominant left lung lesion and new brain metastasis despite regression/disappearance of other lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing reported KRAS mutation, GATA mutation, APC mutation, mTOR mutations, and PIK3CG mutation. MET exon 14 skipping was reported. HRD was reported as positive/high. Microsatellite instability was not detected. Tumor mutational burden was low.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin was approximately 9 g/dL and had been falling. No overt bleeding was reported by history.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line XELOX had been administered after diagnosis; subsequent repeat imaging showed progression. Exact number of cycles was not available.  
- Second-line XELIRI had then been administered; disease progressed.  
- Trifluridine/tipiracil (Lonsurf) had subsequently been started; the patient presented while on cycle 2. After starting trifluridine/tipiracil, the small right lung lesion, sigmoid lesion, and liver lesion disappeared, but the previously 10 cm lung lesion enlarged to 14 cm and a new brain metastasis developed.

[ current disease status ]: ECOG performance status was 2. Ongoing cough persisted, with recent brown-colored sputum. Weight loss was ongoing; body weight was 40 kg. The patient had a concomitant fungal pulmonary infection and remained on oral antifungal therapy. She was described as systemically stable.

[ other clinical data ]: No peripheral neuropathy was reported. No hemoptysis was reported. The left lung was described as entirely occupied by tumor mass.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 80-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapid rise in PSA with lower urinary tract symptoms, including urgency and sensation of incomplete bladder emptying.

[ diagnosis ]: De novo metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with extensive nodal and osseous metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Transrectal 12-core prostate biopsy showed Gleason score 9 adenocarcinoma in all biopsy cores. Gleason pattern 4+5 was described.

[ imaging findings ]: Digital rectal examination had shown an enlarged prostate. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 65 g prostate with a PI-RADS 5 lesion in the left posterior base and suspicious pelvic lymph nodes measuring approximately 1.5-2.5 cm. F-18 PSMA PET/CT dated 13 July 2023 demonstrated metastatic disease involving multiple organ systems, including nodal disease and osseous metastases. Reported osseous sites included T1 vertebral body, right acetabular roof, and left posterior sacrum; additional bone involvement was later described in the skull and clavicle. Plain radiographs of the hip/pelvis showed no osseous abnormality despite concern for right acetabular involvement; prior left hip arthroplasty was present. Subsequent bone scan demonstrated widespread osteoblastic metastatic disease involving the spine, ribs, manubrium, sacrum, pelvis, clavicle, and left femur; the impression stated that multiple osteoblastic metastases were better demonstrated on the recent PSMA PET scan.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline testing for BRCA was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Historical PSA had been 3-4 ng/mL. In April, PSA rose to 9.7 ng/mL. After 4 weeks of ciprofloxacin, PSA decreased to 7.2 ng/mL. After initiation of systemic therapy, PSA declined to 0.05 ng/mL within 6 weeks.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: He had a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with tamsulosin for 3 years. He received ciprofloxacin empirically after PSA rise; PSA decreased from 9.7 to 7.2 ng/mL after 4 weeks. He was started on relugolix and a third-generation antiandrogen, with good biochemical response. Lower urinary tract symptoms reportedly improved on hormone therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer with high-volume osseous and nodal disease on conventional and PSMA-based imaging. Biochemical response to androgen-directed therapy was marked, with PSA 0.05 ng/mL at 6 weeks.

[ other clinical data ]: Past history included benign prostatic hyperplasia and prior left hip arthroplasty. He was described as otherwise in good general health and active. Prostate size was also later described as approximately 60 g.

One of those two things, most cancers don't do that. That's been my feeling. So I saw the guy in consultation and echoed what you had to say. and that was to get an MRI and possibly some biopsies. All right, does that sound reason? So, Bill, I'll just have you comment on this. I don't have the film to show, but he had a 65 gram prostate. Biopsy.
Biopsy. All right. So he had 12 core biopsies done and not by that urologist, but by another one. And he had Gleason 9 in every biopsy core.
That's interesting that we have that discrepancy between what the biopsy is showing versus the MRI, which was just talking about one focal lesion.

Well, I just skimmed the results off the top here, but there were some fours in there, and then diffuse enlargement suspicion within the prostate. But this thing at the left base was pretty prominent. All right. So what's next, guys?

Yeah, I think in this patient, you know, you have Gleason grade four plus five, high grade. I would get it. I would recommend a PSMA PET.
Yeah, I would as well. And I'm already pretty convinced that the lymph nodes are real in this patient, but we want to look for a distant disease.
Right. So why not do a bone scan?

I mean, we know based on multiple studies and just our own practices that the bone scans and CTs are not as sensitive. And in this case, just as all the guidelines recommend, if you're gonna go straight to PSMA PET, don't bother getting conventional imaging.

So we remember those radar, one thing we did, Phil, and this guy, you have to have, to get a bone scan, we started that because there were so many bone scans being done on people with Gleason scores of six and PSAs of six and CT scans and everything else. I agree that a scan was obtained. And here, Bill, if you want to take a look at this, this is the F-18 results from July 13th and 23. So not too long ago. Basically, you see a lot of disease.

Yeah, the head and neck, they divide this by organ system. There's pretty much something in every organ system. So I guess there's some bony lesions, the T1 vertebral body, the right acetabular roof and left posterior sacrum. So yeah, it looks like it's just a metastatic disease.

I don't think it would have shown quite as many bone lesions. I mean, it might have shown a bunch of these. It probably would have told us he's got high volume metastatic disease, but my guess is at least there are a few things that the PSMA picked up that the bone scan wouldn't.

Yeah. So let's just have some discussion here about Are these scans going to replace bone scans? A lot of people, even with lower PSAs and so forth, there are high PSAs. What if this PSA was 200? Bill, what are your thoughts?
My guess is over time, yes, it will slowly replace bone scans and CTs. I think clearly it performs better. It's more accurate and it does better at lower PSA level. So it's just a better test.
Okay. Tyler, what are your thoughts?

I think it definitely, Will already is replacing bone scan in a lot of places, but I would order a bone scan in this patient because I'd like to know where he would have been staged when all the clinical trials were done. So Dave, if I might interject, I think Tyler and Dan bring up really good points. And if we get a bone scan in this setting, should we blind the reader from the PSMA results or not? And oftentimes, some people think you should read the bone scan sort of in a vacuum. And I disagree. I think you should look at it in the context of all the other information that you have, in which case, sometimes you'll have subtle findings on the bone scans in which you might ignore, had you not been getting certain information, but you might sort of upstage knowing that the PSMA PET was positive. I think also you're making a great point because sometimes I'm just not comfortable taking one imaging technique and using that to tell me what to do as far as my treatment goes, especially if it doesn't fit as well as it should. But the The plain films here, as you can see, showed no Osseous abnormalities. Those patients have a poor overall outcome, so it would even be more...
He was tested and was negative. I'm sorry? He was tested and was negative. Negative.
So I think I still would favor triplet in this patient. Okay.

So, plain films were negative. He was started on Relagolax and a third-generation anti-androgen here. He did very well. Within six weeks, his PSA had gone down to 0.05. So, I guess there's a couple, and he had a discussion about and the Erickson's trial and so forth. And he had, the plan was that he was going to, he was going from Ohio to Florida, and that when he got to Florida, he would talk to Medoc about the chemotherapy, and in fact did. He tolerate, so let's talk about a couple, two other things here as we finish this up. Nader PSA down to 0.05. I think everybody'd say that's good stuff, right? Yeah, I mean, I'm wary. for this patient. He's 80 years old and he has a lot of lower urinary tract symptoms. And work on the side effects of ADT so he doesn't have them. I'm sure we both have a number of patients with disease like this, alive many, many years, 10 years even, some patients. You just never know.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Hepatic lesion subsequently managed as hepatocellular carcinoma, with later intrahepatic recurrence after prior hepatic resection.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-cirrhotic, biopsy-proven hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Initial presentation was a solitary LR-5 lesion in segment 7. Subsequent recurrence presented as a 26 mm hepatic lesion on the contralateral side.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial liver lesion was biopsy-proven HCC.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated an LR-5 lesion in segment 7 along the liver capsule, measuring 46-47 mm. After right posterior sectorectomy, recurrence developed approximately 6 years later as a 26 mm hepatic lesion located on the contralateral side. The recurrent lesion was in proximity to the stomach.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right posterior sectorectomy for the initial segment 7 HCC and did well for 6 years before developing recurrence. Thermal ablation was considered, but hydrodissection of the stomach was not felt to be easy.

[ other clinical data ]: No underlying cirrhosis. The patient was not considered a transplant candidate due to concurrent alcohol use and stated unwillingness to stop drinking.
