reference_discussion.text: Exactly. Well, don't worry. Your time is coming. Because now we have a second patient, 68-year-old female, also doesn't have cirrhosis, has this LR5 lesion up here. It's measuring 46, 47 millimeters up here in the segment 7, right along the liver capsule area. Thermal ablation still an option? Did they get a biopsy?

This one is also biopsy-proven HCC, just because no underlying cirrhosis are practices to get a biopsy. You can't assume that it's going to be HCC in a non-cirrhotic. So this is well beyond most ablation guidelines, including ours. While a thermal ablation is technically feasible, the recurrence rates are sky high once you start getting above three centimeters. In our series that my colleagues published, the recurrence rate after a thermal ablation is about 15% to 20% at one year. To me, that's pretty high when you compare it to, let's say, if you can do a partial right epitectomy and you get an R0 margin, your recurrence rate is probably in the single digits or even less, right? So my preference would be to see if you can do a partial right epitectomy.
Wow, thanks, Sid.
See, that would be my conversation with the patient. Say, go see our surgeons first. Yeah, I agree with that.

I think that's a, at least from what we see, a very minimal surgical resection. I think that's the best option for a tumor that size. And know that, Adam, we had a study, you had a study open that looked at adjuvant in this setting, right, that would meet the criteria for size. I can't recall exactly, but.

The cutoff for most of the adjuvant studies was five centimeters. So, you know, on the resection tissue, it could be a bit bigger, you know, depending on what the, that would, that would be the size that we would use. Adjuvant data is still coming. That study that we were participating in actually has not read out yet, but others have. The kind of most press has come from the Imbrave 050 study, which on its initial data analysis did look like there was an improvement in recurrence rates for those patients treated with adjuvant atezobev for a year versus those who are surveyed. Unfortunately, subsequent data analysis has been less promising, and it looks like those curves are mostly overlapping at this point. So I don't know that adjuvant atezobev is going to be the answer for such patients, but as I mentioned, there's other ongoing studies that are large phase 3 studies looking at different combinations of adjuvant immunotherapy that may have some promise.

I mean, if this patient was, let's say, again, let's say they refuse surgery again, right? Like the first one. From a local regional therapy standpoint, while ablation to me is off the table, it's easily amenable to a radio embolization, right? So this would be most likely a straightforward Y90. And in our series of patients with five centimeter tumors or less, we're looking at objective response rates in excess of about 96, 97%. Yeah.

So Gabe and your colleagues won this war, battle I should say, and she ended up going for a right posterior sectorectomy and she did quite well for six years until she eventually developed a recurrence. And this is what the recurrence looks like. Unfortunately, not a transplant candidate due to concurrent alcohol use and has expressed a strong interest to not stop drinking. So now we have this 26 millimeter recurrence. Knowing that she did have a previous surgery, what's our thought process here? Would you repeat surgery?

You know, if she still, despite her best efforts, has no cirrhosis, I think that's amenable to resection as well. And it's a smaller tumor, a little bit more painful on the surgical end with her previous hepatectomy, but I think it's definitely feasible considering it's on the contralateral side. And yeah, I think you can get away with doing it without taking too much liver, so I think that would be an option still.
And if she wanted to explore alternatives, what about the location for thermal ablation?

So I think that the biggest concern from a location standpoint comes due to its proximity to the stomach. This is a single slice, so it's one of those where you have to really kind of study it both in axial, coronal planes, et cetera. From a thermal ablation standpoint, I still think it's safe. you know, we were too close, this would probably be a relatively straightforward hydro dissection where we could put a small needle in between that segment two and the stomach and instill, you know, half a liter of fluid and should be fine. That being said, I think either a thermal ablation or a segmental radio embolization would be potentially, you know, get us a complete response in this case in greater than 90% of the time. So I think it ends up being dealer's choice. Okay.
And how about now with recurrence? Are we starting to talk transplant yet? Are we still?

Well, assuming she would ever stop drinking. Right, exactly. We led with that. So again, the fact that she is not cirrhotic and there are other options with potential curative outcomes, we would not pursue a transplant.
Gabe, question for you. Do you worry about continuing to chip away at someone's liver like this that is still drinking? You know, she's thankfully not cirrhotic now, but obviously at risk.

Yeah, definitely. I think there's the more liver you take out, the more at risk she becomes. You know, it's, I think that's a bit of a challenge, right? Because you, if they're not taking care of themselves and doing what they need to do to prevent their, you know, disease progression, it gets very frustrating to be chipping away at a problem that's just going to keep popping up. Because once you have one recurrence, the odds of getting a second recurrence, you know, it goes up substantially. So it's a good point and definitely frustrating and really you got to have, you know, real heart to heart, I think, with patients like this.
And probably say to the hepatologist, like, why don't you get this under control? Right.
Darn you, hepatologist.

Awesome. This patient chose to go with radioembolization. We didn't feel that the stomach would be very easy to hydrodissect away. So ended up having a complete response and is doing well to this day. So now, let's go a little bit more advanced. This is a 69-year-old male who also doesn't have cirrhosis, but has multifocal HCC. So this is an aggressive BCLC-B, technically. Definitely no macrovascular invasion that we can see. Bilobar, really a dominant 12-centimeter tumor, kind of in segment 5, 6, but also has some small, three additional small lesions up in segments 2 and 3. What does the discussion at your tumor board sound like?

reference_conclusion: For the initial 4.6–4.7 cm biopsy-proven hepatocellular carcinoma in a non-cirrhotic liver, the multidisciplinary consensus favored surgical management with partial right hepatectomy/right posterior sectorectomy as the preferred curative approach, given tumor size and lower expected recurrence risk relative to thermal ablation. At recurrence, repeat resection remained feasible; however, thermal ablation or segmental radioembolization were considered appropriate local therapies with high likelihood of complete response, and liver transplantation was not pursued because the patient was non-cirrhotic and had other potentially curative options.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Left base of tongue mass with left neck lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the left base of tongue with ipsilateral cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Multiple biopsies of the left base of tongue lesion were performed. Frozen sections from three rounds did not demonstrate carcinoma. Final permanent pathology identified carcinoma in the last section; most of the sampled tumor was papilloma. Fine-needle aspiration of a cervical lymph node demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma, p16 positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Non-contrast imaging demonstrated an exophytic mass in the left base of tongue and two left-sided cervical lymph nodes. PET imaging demonstrated FDG-avid disease in the left base of tongue and two pathologic left cervical lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor was p16 positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Diagnostic workup included examination, multiple biopsies of the primary lesion, and fine-needle aspiration of a cervical node.

[ current disease status ]: Left base of tongue primary tumor with two ipsilateral pathologic cervical lymph nodes was present at the time of referral.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea. No prior surgeries were reported. Tobacco history was cigar smoking at approximately one cigar per day. Alcohol intake was approximately 1-2 drinks per day. On examination, the left base of tongue lesion was described as an exophytic mass measuring approximately 2 cm, close to the midline medially, free from the tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall, without apparent deep invasion on palpation, and without palpable extension through the floor of mouth. Neck lymphadenopathy had developed approximately 2 weeks before evaluation.

So my patient's a 71-year-old gentleman with hypertension in OSA, actually was noted to have a left base of tongue mass on a dice for an NSPIRE evaluation. Was sent to us after that, and was also noted to have neck lymphadenopathy, which had developed about two weeks prior to seeing us. Otherwise, ultimately healthy, no past surgeries. He was a cigar a day smoker and drinks about one to two drinks a day. So on exam, he has this pretty exophytic two centimeter mass in the left base of tongue, which is really clearly comparable it's very clearly free from the molecular as well as a lot of pharyngeal wall. But, you know, it's pretty well otherwise here but pretty close to the midline on the medial aspect. Um, so we, uh, actually bobsled multiple times. So you can see here, we actually did three rounds of frozen sections. We took it out, basically half the tumor. Um, by the time we actually got, uh, I mean, we actually never actually got, um, cancer on the frozen sections. It came back in the final permanent, um, with the last, uh, section. So actually most of his tumor is, was just papilloma. Um, given that we weren't able to get the frozen, we actually did a FNA and while he was in house, which came back is, uh, scleromycel carcinoma, which was P16 positive. Looking at scans, unfortunately, he didn't get contrasted scans the first time, but you can sort of see this mass here within the left base of tongue, which is again, pretty exophytic. And then he's got two nodes here. So you've got the one here, and then this is a second node just below it. And then similarly, a PET scan, again, you can see this kind of FDG mass in the left base of tongue. And then there's the two pathologic nodes there on the left side. So I think for this case, there are a couple of discussion points. So first is like management of the contralateral neck. And we've sort of gotten a little bit into that in the first case. But I think this is a big, you know, hot topic, especially for, you know, cancers of the base of tongue, and then kind of leading into how that affects the decision between TORs and chemoradiation.

Well, let's take a step back. Let's go back to your imaging. I think these are, to me, these are the most challenging tumors that I deal with are these glossotocelar sulcus tumors. Much more challenging than do you treat both necks or one. It's harder to have a definitive algorithm on these just because there's so much involved. First step is how do you examine this patient to determine if you should or even can take this tumor out?

Yeah, so there are, I guess, a couple of things to look for. First thing is obviously palpation. So this tumor was pretty free from the tonsil and that really, you know, you have to get all the way down to your finger, all the way down to the vallecula to make sure that it's not involving the epiglottis. And similarly, I try to feel laterally to make sure that it's off the lateral pharyngeal wall. Um, this tumor didn't seem very deep. The other thing also I'll feel through the floor of mouth, um, and try to feel there for some of these tumors, you can actually feel the tumor through the floor of mouth, which is a sign of deeper invasion, which he didn't really have.

Yeah. Yeah. I think the, the floor of mouth palpation is exceedingly important on these patients because if they have tumor palpable on the floor of mouth, you're going to start getting into some hairy territory. Um, not Harry Kwan territory, a hairy situation, territory. Um, you might be getting into hairy territory too, because that patient might need some radiation treatments, but may hear from a surgical standpoint, you've done hundreds and hundreds of tourist cases. reference_conclusion: For this p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the left base of tongue with ipsilateral nodal disease and a non-lateralized primary, the multidisciplinary consensus was to proceed with definitive chemoradiation rather than transoral surgery. This decision was based on the anticipated need for bilateral neck irradiation at 60–66 Gy within the local practice environment even if contralateral neck dissection were negative, such that surgery was not expected to improve the overall treatment burden or functional outcome. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old male; never smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Right-sided neck swelling/lymphadenopathy following partial improvement of bilateral neck swelling after antibiotics.

[ diagnosis ]: HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma of the right palatine tonsil with metastatic right cervical lymph node involvement.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the tonsillar lesion showed squamous cell carcinoma, p16-positive and HPV ISH-positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT neck showed a small hyperdense nodule in the right palatine tonsil and cystic right neck nodal disease. PET-CT showed FDG-avid disease in the right palatine tonsil and right cervical nodal disease with peripheral FDG avidity and central non-avid cystic/necrotic change. Additional small mildly FDG-avid lymph nodes, including one in level V, were identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Preoperative circulating tumor HPV DNA (NavDx) was elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received antibiotics for bilateral neck swelling, with resolution of most symptoms but persistent right neck swelling.

[ other clinical data ]: Clinical examination of the right neck node found it to be mobile relative to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with less mobility near the angle of the mandible.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male. World Trade Center first responder.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging right-sided thyroid nodules with palpable goiter, initially identified incidentally on routine chest CT surveillance. Subsequent development of a right lateral neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, initially classic type with gross extrathyroidal extension into strap muscles and positive margins after partial resection; subsequent completion total thyroidectomy demonstrated a 5 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma with focal oncocytic and tall cell morphology, strap muscle invasion, and microscopic central neck nodal metastasis with extranodal extension. Later right lateral neck recurrence/metastatic disease showed high-grade transformation, with pathology described as at least poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and probably anaplastic transformation.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial outside pathology after right hemithyroidectomy/partial resection showed a 4.5 cm classic papillary thyroid carcinoma with gross and histologically confirmed extrathyroidal extension into strap muscles and positive margins. Completion thyroidectomy pathology showed a 5 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma with focal oncocytic and tall cell morphology; no necrosis, no mitoses, and no angiolymphatic invasion were identified. Extrathyroidal extension into strap muscles was present. Microscopic central neck lymph node metastasis measured up to 0.9 cm and showed extranodal extension into soft tissue. Fine-needle aspiration of a later right lateral neck mass was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Resection of the right lateral neck mass subsequently demonstrated invasive carcinoma with hobnail features, marked atypia, frequent mitotic figures, and necrosis, interpreted as at least poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and probably anaplastic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Routine chest CT surveillance had shown incidental right-sided thyroid nodules and subcentimeter pulmonary nodules. Outside CT/ultrasound imaging demonstrated a bulky multinodular-appearing right thyroid lobe with calcifications. Preoperative MRI of the neck showed no gross tracheal invasion, tumor separate from the carotid artery, and no grossly abnormal adenopathy. FDG PET after thyroidectomy showed nonspecific postsurgical changes, mild uptake in a subcentimeter right level IV lymph node, and subcentimeter pulmonary nodules less than 5 mm that were too small to characterize. Low-dose radioiodine imaging showed predominantly neck uptake. Follow-up neck ultrasounds were initially negative. Follow-up chest CT showed small pulmonary nodules without alarming features, with possible slight interval increase over time. Approximately two years later, ultrasound demonstrated a suspicious right level II mass measuring 2.7 cm and additional suspicious right lateral neck lymphadenopathy. The recurrent lateral neck disease was FDG-avid.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor molecular testing identified BRAF V600E mutation, TERT promoter alteration, PIK3CA alteration, and CDKN2A/B splice mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroglobulin was undetectable for almost the first year of follow-up, with negative thyroglobulin antibodies. By approximately two years, thyroglobulin became detectable at a low level. At the time of right lateral neck recurrence, thyroglobulin was approximately 1.2.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Multiple prior fine-needle aspirations of the right thyroid nodules were benign. The patient underwent right hemithyroidectomy/right lobectomy for enlarging multinodular goiter; intraoperatively, gross extrathyroidal extension to strap muscles and adherence to trachea and carotid sheath were encountered, and only partial resection was performed. He was then referred for completion surgery and underwent total thyroidectomy. At surgery, the tumor was significantly adherent to the trachea without clear invasion; there was no nerve injury. A small membranous tracheal injury occurred intraoperatively, and tracheotomy was performed because of body habitus, obesity, and COPD. The tracheostomy healed uneventfully, and decannulation occurred four weeks later. He subsequently received radioactive iodine therapy after low-dose iodine imaging because of high-risk features and indeterminate pulmonary nodules; post-treatment evaluation showed only thyroid bed/neck uptake, with no clear iodine-avid distant disease. He was followed with thyroglobulin, neck ultrasound, and chest CT. After development of FDG-avid right lateral neck disease, surgical resection of the mass was performed.

[ current disease status ]: The patient developed structural recurrent/metastatic disease in the right lateral neck after initial surgery and radioactive iodine therapy. Resected recurrent disease showed high-grade transformation, interpreted as at least poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and probably anaplastic carcinoma. Small bilateral/subcentimeter pulmonary nodules remained indeterminate on imaging and were too small to characterize by PET or radioiodine scan.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included COPD, sleep apnea, and severe obesity; body weight had been reported as greater than 400 pounds initially. Vocal cords were mobile before completion thyroidectomy. He had been treated with tirzepatide (Zepbound) for approximately two years, with reported loss of more than one-third of body weight and improvement in ambulation and sleep apnea.

reference_discussion.text: Yes, I'll move this along a little bit faster. So this is a 68-year-old male. He's a World Trade Center first responder. So he's been getting chest CT scans routinely. And at some point during his chest CT scans, he was noted to have incidental right-sided thyroid nodules. that were initially monitored for a few years, enlarging in size, multiple benign FNAs of those right-sided thyroid nodules. And he has some centimeter lung nodules on chest scans. Given the growth of these nodules over the years, some of them now like four and a half centimeter in size, visible palpable goiter, he decided to undergo a right hemithyroidectomy despite the benign cytology. He does have some medical history, COPD, sleep apnea, severe obesity. He's about more than 400 pounds. This is outside imaging. I tried to get the best that I could. So his initial management was done outside of our center before he was referred. So he has this sort of bulky looking right side of the thyroid, some calcifications in that right side as well, but overall like a multinodular goiter kind of appearance, both on CT and on the ultrasounds that he has had so far. So, he was taken for a right lobectomy for that benign multinodular goiter, but the surgeon out in the community saw that, interoperatively, he had gross extrathyroidal extension to the strap muscles, fibrotic tumor that was adherent to the trachea and carotid sheath. So, that surgeon performed only a partial resection of this tumor because he felt it was outside of his hands. and then referred him to a tertiary center, so to our center, to a high-volume thyroid surgeon for a total thyroidectomy. So the initial pathology from the outside center was a four and a half centimeter classic PTC with gross and histologically confirmed extra-thyroidal extension, but only into the strap muscles with positive margins. And now this patient had four alterations. He had a BRAF V600E, he had a TERT promoter, a PIK3CA, and a CDK N2AB splice mutation. So it's a very high-risk molecular signature.

This is a nice example of why I never do second opinions for Dr. Junaid's cases anymore. I don't know what to do with them. Rachel, tell me a little bit about this mutational pattern. And in a classic papillary, that seems a little odd to me.

Yeah, so you could have the BRAF V600E with the TERT in a classic papillary, that'd be fine, but the PIK3CA and the CDKN2A2B deletion are more associated with high-grade tumors or anaplastic tumors. So again, I'm worried about this patient.

And as opposed to the second case where Taneja said there was a really small tumor, like one and one and a half centimeter, now we've got four and a half centimeters. Now we've got gross extra thyroid extension. This is already starting to behave poorly, right? I mean, it's a nice, I'm glad you put this one on. Keep going, Sharad.

All right, so he got some interval imaging with an MRI of the neck before he went for more surgery. And there wasn't any gross invasion of the trachea. Tumor seemed to be separate from the carotid on imaging and no grossly abnormal adenopathy. Vocal cords were mobile. Our surgeon did take him for a total thyroidectomy. The total thyroidectomy went okay, there wasn't any injury to the nerves. But the tumor was significantly adherent to the trachea, though not clearly invading. There was a small injury to the membranous trachea during this surgery. And then given his habitus, his obesity, COPD, the decision was made to do a tracheotomy instead of just closing it. And the trach healed pretty uneventfully. Four weeks later, he was decanalated and the trach site healed pretty well. And then just going over the pathology really quickly from his thyroidectomy, he has classic papillary cancer with some areas of focal tall cell morphology. He does have that extra thyroid extension into the muscle that you see on the left. And then I just put one of his central neck lymph nodes here on the right as well with tumor.
Rachel, any major findings or anything on the images that they showed you there that worried us?

Yeah, well, you've got, again, nice tram tracks there, so tall cell variant on the right-hand side, and that invasion into skeletal muscle is never a good sign, so that's pretty worrying. Gotcha, okay.

All right, so the pathology was again a five centimeter papillary cancer with focal oncocytic and tall cell. But again, no necrosis, no mitoses here, no angiolymphatic invasion that invasion into strap muscles. And then he had some microscopic central neck lymphadenopathy up to 0.9 centimeter with extra nodal extension into the soft tissues. So he saw me after this surgery, so sometimes at our institution we will also get an upfront FDG and iodine-based imaging together. So we decided to do that for him. His FDG imaging was really non-specific. Some post-surgical changes, a little bit of uptake in the right level four sub-centimeter lymph node that wasn't, maybe a reactive lymph node, maybe something there. And then some sub-centimeter lung nodules less than five millimeter that were too small to characterize with the PET. He also got a low dose iodine scan that had only shown mainly neck iodine uptake, but we did decide to treat this one because he had those uncharacterized small lung nodules. And we were hopeful, you know, even though his molecular testing indicated that he's probably not going to have good response from RAI, but we decided to take our chances and treat him with RAI. And then to our surprise, you know, he didn't, nothing lit up really. He had some neck uptake in the thyroid bed, but that, FDG I would focus on the neck was not iodine avid, probably a reactive lymph node at that point. And then the lung nodules were also too small to characterize on this iodine scan.

Let me bring Dr. Ghassani in here. The issue is administered activity. I mean, over the years, we've really gone more toward 100 for most of these, or maybe 150 tops. We used to give lots of 200 and 300 administered activities. But where are you guys, I mean, this was gross extra thyroid extension, kind of a bad tumor. What range would you be thinking about there, Dr. Kasai?
We would go between 100 and 125. I would consider 200 millicurie for lung or bone metastasis, but for lymph node and if there is a local disease, then we go between 100 and 125.
And Mara, at Hutch, where are you guys with sort of administering activities these days in a higher risk patient like this?

Yeah, and it's similar where we would consider, you know, 100 to 150 if we can see actually disease in the neck elsewhere out beyond the central neck. If we're really thinking about adjuvant treatment, very rarely will we go above 150 without dosimetry, except in the setting, again, of distant metastases where we would consider it.
Okay. And Cherit, what happened here?

Right. All right. So nothing got picked up on that iodine scan. We were hoping we give a higher dose because of those lung nodules, but they didn't really pick up anything. And then he seemingly did well at his follow-ups. His thyroglobulin for almost the first year that I followed him was undetectable on the assay with no antibodies. neck ultrasounds negative, his chest CT with the lung nodules, really nothing alarming, maybe a small increase over time. And then by the time he's two years, his thyroglobulin is a little bit detectable, but nothing that's standing out or alarming from the thyroglobulin standpoint. with structural disease also not really alarming at this time. Just to bring in here, I hope it's not and I don't believe it is related to anything, but he's on Zeppon for the last two years with immense, immense benefit. His ambulation, his sleep apnea, everything has improved. He's lost more than a third of his weight. And I just wanted to put it on there that he's on that and he's doing well.

Awesome. This TG makes Kate's point that these BRAF tumors often don't make a lot of thyroglobulin, so just like you, you don't get excited about it, but you would pretty much almost ignore that in a classic papillary, but now that's sort of a sign. Dr. Roth, my nurses probably eight times a day are now answering the question in a non-medullary thyroid cancer, can I be on Zep-Bound, and the primary care doctors won't do it unless I write a letter. Please tell me the West Coast is more sane, or are you dealing with the same thing?

Nope, we have the exact same thing. I'm giving medical clearance for GLP-1 receptor agonists all the time to confirm, mostly because a lot of primary care doctors haven't seen the primary pathology. One was in my papillary microcarcinomas we were watching, and we watched them on these GLP-1s and off the GLP-1s, nobody grew. Rachel, what are we looking at here?
Yeah, that looks terrible. Sorry.
That's the new WHO staging system, Rachel. I haven't seen the new one yet.

100%, that's how we roll in Australia. Yeah, no, so we have Well, invasive carcinoma, it's a bit tricky to see at low power, but on the right hand side, the higher power, it looks like you've got marked ATPR, possibly some necrosis centrally. I'm very worried that this is turned into an anaplastic carcinoma. And then on the top left, you've got a very beautiful example of Hobnail variant. There's, again, bottom left is some more necrosis, and on the right-hand side, you've got marked atibia and frequent mitotic figures. So you've got at least a polydifferentiated tumor and probably anaplastic.

Cool. Kate, I've got two minutes left. Compare this case where we've had an anaplastic transformation and all those molecular findings with the second case that we showed, that small thing. How are they different and what's going on at the sort of 30,000 foot view here, Kate?

We've got multiple genetic alterations within this tumor. We've got large invasive disease. This patient needs to be treated rapidly, getting on to a very rapid care pathway. And we have got some targetable alterations. So we have got systemic therapy options.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in April 2024 with fever, abdominal pain, and cough.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma, stage IV at diagnosis in 2024. Date of diagnosis: 22 April 2024. Prior history of soft palate malignancy treated in 2007, with subsequent pathology reported as adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2007: Excision of a soft palate lesion for painful swelling showed malignancy; subsequent wide local excision showed adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- 22 April 2024: BAL/biopsy showed adenoid cystic carcinoma, grade 1.  
- Reflex immunohistochemistry: CD117 diffuse positive; TTF-1 scattered positive; Napsin A positive; p40 positive; p63 positive.  
- Ki-67: 15%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound abdomen/pelvis in April 2024 showed multiple space-occupying lesions in the liver with abdominal lymph nodes.  
- CT chest in April 2024 showed soft tissue lesions in the right upper lobe, right lower lobe, and left lower lobe.  
- PET-CT dated 14 March 2025 showed progressive disease after four cycles of second-line therapy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- PD-L1 expression: 0%.  
- NGS identified pathogenic alterations involving PPP2R1A, MYB-NFIB fusion, and ATM.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum creatinine: 2.8 mg/dL.  
- Non-oliguric.  

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2007: Excision of soft palate lesion followed by wide local excision; adjuvant radiotherapy administered.  
- First-line systemic therapy for metastatic disease: lenvatinib plus low-dose nivolumab. Progressive disease after 6 months.  
- Second-line systemic therapy: pemetrexed, carboplatin, and lenvatinib. PET-CT after 4 cycles in March 2025 showed progressive disease.  
- Subsequently continued on maintenance lenvatinib.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Progressive metastatic disease after two lines of systemic therapy.  
- ECOG performance status: 3.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Comorbidities: chronic kidney disease, hypertension, hypothyroidism.  
- Bilateral pedal edema present.  
- Not on dialysis.  
- No significant family history documented.

HER2 and androgen receptor testing may be performed, and if positive, corresponding targeted therapy may be considered; alternative tyrosine kinase inhibitors were discussed, but expected benefit is limited after prior TKI exposure. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man. Past medical history included hypertension treated with low-dose ramipril. He was an ex-smoker, having stopped 20 years previously, with a smoking history of less than 10 pack-years. No significant family history was reported. He worked as a postman.

[ chief complaint ]: Three-month history of a rapidly enlarging neck lump with hoarseness of voice. He later developed neck discomfort, dizziness, and headaches.

[ diagnosis ]: Differentiated high-grade thyroid carcinoma arising from the right thyroid lobe, with cervical nodal metastases, brain metastases, and subsequent pulmonary metastases. Initial clinical staging was cT3bN1bM0 before detection of intracranial metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Flexible nasal endoscopy demonstrated an immobile fixed right vocal cord. Fine-needle aspiration from the thyroid mass showed papillary thyroid carcinoma with focal de-differentiation. Fine-needle aspiration also confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma in right lateral neck nodes and central compartment lymph nodes. Subsequent core biopsy demonstrated differentiated high-grade thyroid carcinoma and did not show anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound showed a large multinodular goiter with suspicious malignant features, including involvement of the strap muscles, particularly on the right, and posterior extension into the tracheoesophageal groove. Pathological lymph nodes were present throughout the right neck, involving levels II, III, IV, and central compartment level VI. The thyroid lesion was graded U5.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a mass arising from the right thyroid lobe with extracapsular extension involving the esophageal groove, extending inferiorly to the sternal notch and into the superior mediastinum. Right cervical nodal disease involved levels II to IV and VI. No thoracic distant metastases were identified at that time.

FDG PET-CT showed no additional sites of disease beyond those already identified on ultrasound and CT.

Brain MRI demonstrated three lesions suspicious for metastatic disease: one right parietal lesion measuring approximately 2 cm with perilesional edema, and two sub-centimeter occipital lesions.

Repeat imaging performed after treatment of the brain lesions showed significant progression in the neck, with tumor invasion through the trachea and development of multiple small-volume pulmonary lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular profiling identified a RET fusion, a TERT promoter variant, and a TP53 variant. No other actionable alterations were identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Dexamethasone was given for symptomatic management of headaches and neck discomfort, with reported symptomatic benefit. Brain metastases were treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. Planned total thyroidectomy and right neck dissection were not undertaken after discovery of brain metastases and subsequent disease progression. Airway assessment found the airway to be safe, and no airway intervention was required.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic differentiated high-grade thyroid carcinoma with prior brain metastases treated by stereotactic radiosurgery, cervical locally invasive disease with tracheal invasion, and multiple small pulmonary metastases.

[ other clinical data ]: No evidence of distant thoracic metastases was present on initial CT thorax. FDG PET-CT did not identify disease outside the known neck findings prior to brain MRI.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Bleeding per rectum.

[ diagnosis ]: Rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease (stage IV), with liver and lung metastases on PET-CT.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the rectal growth showed adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT was suggestive of liver metastases and lung metastases. Rectal growth was identified on clinical examination.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed metastatic rectal cancer with synchronous hepatic and pulmonary metastatic disease. No treatment details were available.

reference_conclusion: For newly diagnosed stage IV rectal adenocarcinoma with liver and lung metastases, imaging should be reviewed to determine resectability and potential for later conversion, and baseline carcinoembryonic antigen with molecular profiling should be obtained. Molecular testing should include at least RAS, BRAF, and MSI, with broader next-generation sequencing considered based on logistics and affordability. Resection of the primary tumor is reserved for symptomatic indications such as obstruction, bleeding, or perforation. If metastatic disease is unresectable, systemic therapy should be initiated; if conversion to resectability is feasible, reassessment should be performed approximately every two months and surgery undertaken at the earliest point of resectability rather than prolonging preoperative chemotherapy beyond about two to three months.
reference_conclusion_quote: Still, I will evaluate the paired CT scan to look whether it's a sort of receptible liver and lung metastasis, which is unlikely. Likely, it's an unreceptible metastasis, but I need to look into that. and whether there is any possibility later on for the conversion. [...] then obviously we will go for the carcinoembronic antigen and depending on the affordability and what sort of the treatment patient can take then either limited panel like the RAS mutation, BRAF or MSI or maybe the full panel like NGS [...] Depending on the logistics, I will go for the molecular analysis. [...] in cases like if the patient is in obstruction, if there's a bleeding, perforation, or if there's anything which is related to symptomatology, mainly it is the symptomatology which is harsh. [...] Yeah, at least two to three months of systemic therapy. [...] every two months you go on evaluating the patient and whenever you feel earliest, you feel that the patient is resectable or conversion has happened. Hand over the patient to your good friend surgeon and let him do his job.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 80-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging left breast mass in August 2022.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma diagnosed in 2022, arising as a genomically distinct second primary from a prior left breast cancer. Prior breast cancer in 2019 had been ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast.

[ histopathology results ]: In 2019, left lumpectomy showed multifocal well-differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma with gland formation; tumor was strongly ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative. In August 2022, core biopsy of the left breast mass showed poorly differentiated invasive carcinoma without glandular architecture; no DCIS or benign tissue was identified in the background. Immunophenotype of the 2022 tumor was ER-negative, PR-negative, HER2-negative, AR-negative, CK7-positive, SOX10-positive, and GATA3-negative. Morphology of the 2022 tumor was dissimilar to the 2019 tumor. Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry showed loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression with retained MSH2 and MSH6 expression. PD-L1 staining (SP263) showed CPS greater than 10.

[ imaging findings ]: Breast imaging demonstrated an irregular dense mass in the upper inner quadrant of the left breast posterior depth on mammography and an irregular heterogeneous mass on ultrasound. In August 2022, ultrasound measured the lesion at 2.6 x 2.0 cm. PET/CT in August 2022 showed an FDG-avid multilobulated left breast mass, an FDG-avid right perihilar node, a mildly FDG-avid axillary lymph node, and an FDG-avid pleural-based right upper lobe pulmonary nodule suspicious for metastatic disease. At subsequent clinical evaluation, the breast tumor had enlarged to greater than 4-5 cm with skin involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy performed approximately 7 days after oncology evaluation identified 52 mutations, tumor mutational burden of 250 mutations/megabase, and MSI-high status. Tumor sequencing confirmed markedly elevated tumor mutational burden and MSI-high status. MSI score on tumor testing was 25; an additional reported MSI-high score was greater than 30. Mutational signature analysis demonstrated a dominant MSI/MMR-deficiency signature. Comparative sequencing of the 2019 primary tumor and the 2022 triple-negative tumor showed no shared mutations and no common copy-number changes, supporting that the 2022 tumor was a genomically distinct new primary. Germline testing was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In 2019, the patient underwent left lumpectomy for multifocal ER-positive/HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma. Lymph node staging was not performed. Radiation therapy was omitted. She received adjuvant aromatase inhibitor therapy from 2019 until presentation with the 2022 breast mass. She declined biopsy of metastatic sites because of health concerns.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities included prior cerebrovascular accidents x2, hip fracture, coronary artery disease with stent placement, cardiac rhythm disorder with pacemaker, atrial fibrillation, and anticoagulation use.

reference_discussion.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to San Antonio Breast Cancer Conference Symposium Molecular Tumor Board. I'm Pedram Razavi from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. I'm a breast oncologist. And I will be moderating this session, and I'm joined by a fantastic group of panelists to discuss the cases with you, and I will introduce them later on. So with that, let's move on to the session. We have 60 minutes and multiple cases to discuss, so I don't want to waste any time. So these are our disclosures. So the modern landscape of precision oncology, as all of us are aware, have changed very recently. We are using targeted therapies and precision oncology very routinely in clinic. And one big part of this precision oncology is identifying the targets using molecular assays and genomics. And we use them very routinely in clinic. Of course, on top of that, we also try to move the field forward. I'll be doing liquid biopsies, pre- and post-treatment, samples, pre- and post-treatment, understand the biology of disease better, understand the subgroup of patients who respond or do not respond to certain therapies to improve the outcomes. And then all of that will be hopefully translated back to clinic in terms of trials. And we've been using these type of genomic efforts since 2013, 14 very routinely. And we started using them more in clinic. The knowledge gap between what was known and what is unknown started to increase. There are alterations in genes, well-known drivers in cancer that we didn't know or we don't know. how they behave, and are they drivers, are they pathogenic alterations, oncogenic alterations or not. And there are also alterations in rare variants that we were not aware of, or rare genes that were not routinely seen on that type of cancer. So as these type of gaps started to grow, there was an absolute need to close this gap, and there is multiple efforts to develop these knowledge-based toolkits to help with precision oncology and curate these mutations and genes in a programmatic manner. And one of them that I would like to highlight to develop at MSK is the OncoKB that assigns, it's the manually curated database of genes and alterations in a disease-based manner, and gives the genes and the mutations a level of evidence, and that level of evidence can help the oncologists and the physicians in clinic to navigate this genomic data much better. But there is a gap still. There is much more interaction between genes, between the pathways. The genomic alteration of the tumor doesn't have only one driver. The tumor often has multiple drivers. They are sometimes working together, sometimes bypassing. There's some interactions with them. And that complicates the interpretation of these results more and more. And as we started sequencing and using genomic panel with this next-gen sequencing panels that use a wide range of genes, these type of interactions become even more significant. And it's not fair to ask oncologists in clinic to be able to interpret all of these results when they're busy seeing patients. And on top of that, the cancer evolves and changes very routinely, so there is a significant amount of spatial heterogeneity in the tumor, especially in breast cancer, as all of us are aware, and also there is temporal heterogeneity and evolution because of the bottlenecks that we impose with our treatments or because of the cancer itself, and that also complicates the results even more, to the point that, you know, when we have liquid biopsies, we have tumor, And also, we have multiple tumor samples from a patient interpreting these results need expertise. And putting all of this together, unfortunately, there has been a disconnect between what we have in our guidelines that we are referring to, to guide us through clinic, and ever-growing list of genes and alterations that we see in these reports. And again, it's not fair. to put all of this on the shoulder of busy physicians to be able to interpret this. So we thought, we saw the need at MSK a few years ago, and multiple other centers have done this the same. And considering our volume, we started having this breast molecular tumor board that we started in February of 2020. And there's a group of breast oncologists, pathologists, radiologists, radiation oncologists, and also translational scientists, genomic experts, all of us are sitting together as well as, you know, breast fellows to train the next generation of molecularly focused physicians and experts. And then we review the cases very routinely in clinic. But what is important for such molecular tumor board is the multidisciplinary nature of these. It's impossible to interpret the molecular data in an isolated manner. We need to have input from different aspects and different disciplines to help understand this and put them in the context. So we have also input from the pathologists and molecular pathologists and also radiologists, in addition to all the other providers. And also in addition to that, we do higher levels of genomic analysis to better understand these results. So with that, we would like to do a molecular tumor board this year at San Antonio that somehow mimics that multidisciplinary nature. So I would like to introduce our panelists. So from medical oncology, we have Dr. Joyce O'Shaughnessy from Baylor. We have Dr. Nick Turner from Royal Medicine Hospital Institute of Cancer Research UK. We have Dr. Giuseppe Coriano. from European Institute of Oncology, Milano. And we have Dr. Nancy Lin from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Dr. Gaurav Gupta is a radiation oncology expert. For breast radiology, we have Dr. Sarah S. Chris Winkler from MSK. And for surgical and molecular pathology, we have Dr. Mariam Shirazi from Tempest Lab. So without further ado, we're going to go to the cases. So case number one, this is an 80-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities with initial diagnosis of ER-positive HER2-negative disease, diagnosed in 2019, who was now recently diagnosed with a metastatic triple negative breast cancer. So the diagnosis goes back to 2019. She had a left lumpectomy. She had a multifocal, well-differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma. The tumor was strongly ER positive, PR negative, HER2 negative, and she didn't have a lymph node staging as appropriate for the age, and RT was omitted. She received adjuvant AI since then, and in August of 2022, she was presented with a rapidly growing left breast mass. Ultrasound showed a lesion that was 2.6 by 2 centimeter. There was a core biopsy of it done that showed a poorly differentiated invasive carcinoma. The tumor was ER negative, PR negative, and HER2 negative, and also AR negative. No DCIS or benign tissue was seen in the background. She had a PET scan that showed multilobal mass in the breast, but it also showed a right upper lobe long lesion with possible pleural involvement and multiple hyaluronidinopathy, FTG-AVID. that were all consistent with metastatic disease. So she established care at MSK at the time, and when she was seen in the clinic, she was noted to have even more growth of the disease. At the time, the tumor was more than four or five centimeters, with evidence that is involving the skin as well. And she declined the biopsy for the health reasons. So I just want to highlight some of the comorbidities that she had. She had a CVA times two. She had two strokes. She had a hip fracture. She had coronary artery disease and stent place. She has cardiac issues, pacemakers, arrhythmia, AFib, and anticoagulation. So multiple comorbidities in the family. So with that, we start with radiology.

So on the left, we have CC and MLO mammographic fused. The red arrow is depicting an irregular dense mass in the upper inner quadrant posterior depth. And on the right, we have the sonographic carlet in a regular mass with heterogeneous echo texture. Next slide. Thanks. So in August, she had a PET CT to look at the extent of disease. And if we start at the top right, we see in the left breast an FDG-AVID mass. Going to the top left, the yellow arrow is showing an FDG-AVID perihilar node. Then right below that, the blue arrow is showing a mildly FDG-AVID axillary lymph node. And in the bottom right, the yellow arrow shows a pleural-based pulmonary nodule, which is FDG-AVID and highly suspicious as well.
Dr. Shirazi?

Sure. So on the top, we have the morphology of the left breast from 2019. So this is a well-differentiated lesion. You see there is gland formation, all the tubular structures with the lumen in the middle. These are neoplastic glands. They are highly infiltrative, angulated. So this was a well-differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma, strongly positive for ER and negative for PR and HER2. On the bottom, we have the more recent lesion from also left breast from 2022. Just the overview of the H&E pictures, they don't look like each other. So the lesion on the bottom, this doesn't have glandular architecture. This is a high-grade lesion. cells are larger, more polymorphic. So when we see a lesion like this, for the most part, we try to approach it with an open mind. So this could be another primary. This could be even a lesion not coming from breast. And I think based on the panel of immunostains they performed, this lesion was positive for CK7 and SOX10, negative for GATO3. So this is a combination that pretty much could be, and also ER, PR, HER2 negative. So this combination is actually good enough for a metastatic breast cancer, triple negative.

Thank you, and in your opinion, these two tumors are morphologically dissimilar, correct? I was asking if these, I have a hard time hearing you, and you have a hard time hearing us, so how should we do this? So in your opinion, these are two different tumors morphologically dissimilar?
They don't look like each other. Yes.

Very good. So standard of care options and additional tests, what we're going to do. So Dr. Roshanasi, what do you think? This is a newly diagnosed metastatic triple negative breast cancer. How should we move forward?

I suppose the question is, you know, no DCIS was found on a biopsy. Could this be a metastasis from elsewhere? It doesn't look like it on the PET CT scan, not another primary, per se. It looks phenotypically consistent with metastatic triple negative breast cancer, but they're so disparate, they're so unusual. Certainly, we need the PD-L1 status as has been ordered. We also need germline BRCA status panel testing. It would be nice to know the germline PAL-B2 as well. And so, yeah, those otherwise we just need all the information we can get. But it would be nice to know if this really truly is a breast cancer.

Fantastic. So, Dr. Lin, while waiting for the results, we have a patient with rapidly progressing triple negative breast cancer. What are you thinking of the standard of care options for this elderly lady, multiple comorbidities?

Yeah, so if we were not to consider, first, just if we were to imagine somebody who is not elderly and fragile, what would we think about for first-line therapy for metastatic triple negative breast cancer? Typically, we would start with PD-L1 status. If the patient has PD-L1 positive cancer, they would receive chemotherapy with pembrolizumab. And if PD-L1 positive, could receive single-agent chemotherapy With the exception that if somebody has a germline BRCA1 or 2 alteration, or perhaps PALPY2 germline alteration, one might consider a PARP inhibitor instead of chemotherapy. Of course, in this person, we have to consider that she has quite a number of comorbidities. We didn't hear her performance status, but she's had two strokes. She has cardiac disease. And I think one of the values of the additional testing, which I think we'll go through in the rest of this case, is to identify whether there are additional targets that we could consider that would allow us to de-escalate or give her an option for less toxic therapy, particularly if she has PD-L1 positive cancer, where we would normally be giving cytotoxic chemotherapy, or if she's BRCA1 or 2 negative, where we, again, normally would be giving some sort of cytotoxic chemotherapy.

Fantastic. So the patient had a liquid biopsy. It was resulted seven days after the patient was seen in clinic. And it showed 52 mutations with a tumor mutational burden of 250. And MSI high was detected. Multiple alterations that we know that are relevant in breast cancer were seen here. But the tumor had many, many mutations. Let's just first talk about TMB. Dr. Turner, what are your thoughts on assessing the TMB and MSI on ctDNA?

Yes, there's two aspects here that are both really quite uncommon in breast cancer, but important. So most importantly, she's got microsatellite instability, and this can be measured very robustly in ctDNA and is a strong indication for the pan-tumor type indication for pembrolizumab. And this is one of the causes of high TMB. This is a very unusually high TMB for breast cancer and, well, pan-tumor. What's much more common is finding a TMB that's just slightly higher than the cutoff for pembrolizumab, which is 10 or higher mutations per megabase. And that can't really be assessed very reliably in circulating tumor DNA. because we have multiple reasons that can elevate the TMB in ctDNA. So mutations can come from clonal hematopoiesis that you have in circulating tumor DNA assays and also lots of subclonal mutations you can pick up in liquid biopsies, all of which can elevate the TMB. So if you see a TMB that's, you know, just above 10, that's uncertain really whether that's an indication for pembrolizumab on that individual pan-tumor indication, and that really needs to trigger getting tissue testing. But for this individual patient, she's got MSI high, which is a relatively strong indication to consider that pan-tumor indication of pembrolizumab.

I would like to do a comment, because pragmatically, you know, in Europe, in order to prescribe Pembrolizumab for an eye tumor of mutational burden, you need also assessment of PD-L1 on the primary tumor, or in the metastatic disease. So, in this specific case, since there is no previous exposure to any chemotherapy, the disease-free interval was three years, I believe on liquid biopsy, tumor mutational burden can be reliable in order to prescribe Pembro. But I would like also to know if the tumor is PD-L1 positive in order to prescribe in my country the indication to immunotherapy. And immunotherapy per se in an 80 years old should not be considered the contraindication. Because I know in the audience how many of you have elderly patients receiving immunotherapy. This is an important question.

Absolutely. So this is an astronomical high TMB and we actually confirmed this in the tumor as well. And there was a question also that was brought up. about the relatedness of this tumor. So we sequenced both the triple negative breast cancer and also the historic primary tumor. And this is the primary tumor from 2019, and these are the mutations that were multiple pages of alterations here. But what was very clear, that there was no mutations shared between these two tumors. Again, highlighting that this is a new primary that the patient developed, has no relatedness genomically with the previous one. The germline testing also showed it was negative, and the tumor had a significant high TNB. Just for those who don't have a reference here, usually a TNB in breast cancer is around two to three mutations per megabases. This is extremely high for breast cancer, and the MSI high score was more than 30 as well here. So this is the copy number profile. These are the chromosomes, and for a heterozygous, you know, or normal cell, you're going to see it a line in the middle, and you see that there were multiple alterations and copy number changes in the strip of negative breast cancer. This is a relatively low purity tumor, but you see that there are no common copy number changes comparing these two, again confirming that these two tumors are not the same, and this is a completely distinct tumor. So after that, we performed MSI score, showed an MSI score of 25. Usually in breast cancer, the FDA approval is for MSI score of more than 10. Here at MSK, we did a validation study, and we looked at the MSI scores in breast cancer. Anywhere between 3 to 10, we call them indeterminate. And we do additional testing in those patients. But this is unequivocally high. MSI score, we also performed signature analysis, and the signature analysis showed a very dominant MSI-MMR signature in this tumor. Further staining was done, so Dr. Shirazi, what do we see here?

Yeah, so the IHC also confirms all of these findings. So we have the picture of MLH1, PMS2, IHC1 of them, they both look the same. And all the blue you see, these are neoplastic cells that are not expressing MLH1 or PMS2. And then on the bottom, that's a great contrast. You see that the neoplastic cells, they are all expressing MSH2 and MSH6. So this is consistent with a more deficient tumor with loss of MLH1 and PMS2.
So this is a case of somatic MSI high tumor. And these are the PD-L1 staining.
Sure. And there is a PD-L1SP263, which is also, it has a CPS of more than 10, I guess this was interpreted as such.

So this is the perfect molecular storm to prescribe an immunotherapy. Microsatellite instability, high tumor mutational burden, and PD-L1. So unless you invented the case, I never saw a case like this.

This would be the Luis Diaz's story again in New York Times. So let's talk about hypermutated breast cancer. What are the reasons for hypermutation in breast cancer? Dr. Gupta, what are your thoughts?

I mean, you know, there are different etiologies of hypermutation. I think in breast cancer overall, the prevalence is relatively lower, but you know, as we saw here, MSI instability does occur and should be checked for in metastatic patients. You can also see pole epsilon mutations that can sometimes contribute, and another emerging mechanism that I think is important in breast cancer is APL-BEC mutagenesis, which, you know, we're still understanding when and how to identify it best, but I think could be relevant in immunotherapy response.

Dr. Shirazi, so just to expand on that, we know about APOBEC. What is the significance of APOBEC? What is the difference between APOBEC and MSI signatures as part of hypermutated phenotype? What else do we see here?

Sure. So, generally speaking, these are the major drivers of hypermutation in breast cancer. Dominant APOC back mutational signature in about 60 percent of these hypermutated cancers. So, this is a very important signature in breast cancer in general and enriched in these lesions. Also, mismatch report efficiency and, to a lesser extent, poly-mutated signature is also associated with hypermutation. I don't know if I should comment on the – okay.

So the clinical indication, we know that there is a FDA approval for single-agent pembrolizumab in this setting in a TNB high and also for MSI high. So just to update you on the case, she received a single dose of pembrolizumab in end of November of 2022. She developed, actually, unfortunately, immune-related adverse events. She had hypothyroidism, required admission to the hospital because of worsening of her And then after that, she came out of the hospital and she refused to come to clinic and said, I don't have any disease anymore. So got to the point that, you know, she finally came to clinic and she had no palpable disease in the breast. She was not interested in further imaging and she comes occasionally to clinic for visits with no evidence of disease. We haven't had a chance to convince her to get a PET scan yet. So hopefully that will happen. But we were able to convince her to get an ultrasound when she came for a visit in January. And this is what we see from the January of 23.

So here's the imaging evidence here. We have in August 2022 that irregular mass. And by January 2023, there's near complete resolution of the mass. It's very hard to see on ultrasound if it's even there at all.

Fantastic. So again, highlighting that even in an 80-year-old, doing genomic testing can completely change the therapeutic landscape for that patient. And this is a good example of it. It's extremely rare to see such a high MSI in breast cancer, but that one case worth doing the analysis. So let's just go to case number two. So this is a 49-year-old woman. with ER positive, HER2 negative metastatic breast cancer, and a rapidly progressive disease on the first line, CDK46 inhibitor plus AI. So the history goes back to 2022 when she was diagnosed with locally advanced breast cancer. It was moderately differentiated lobular carcinoma, nine centimeter, multiple axillary nodes, strongly ER, PR positive, HER2 negative. She had a PET scan that showed the primary breast and axillary disease, but no disease outside. There were some sub-centimeter bilateral lung nodules that were considered to be nonspecific. She received neoadjuvant doses, ACT, followed by lymph mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy that showed extensive amount of residual disease, T3N1A, seven and a half centimeter, but relatively good response in the lymph nodes, one out of two lymph nodes, clear margins. The disease was ERPR positive and HER2 negative. She completed post-mastectomy radiation therapy, followed by OSAI, and she had a BSO and oophorectomy, and the ovarian suppression was dropped. She asked for delay in starting abdomocyclic perimonarchy, as she wanted to go undergo bariatric surgery, and she started it in May of 2022. She had a routine CT scan at the time, that actually accidentally she was found to have metastatic disease with bone mets. She had a T10 bone biopsy that showed ER 20%, ER negative, HER2 negative breast disease. This tumor underwent sequencing. And unfortunately, relatively quickly after, in December of 2022, she had progression of disease in the bone. So imaging.

reference_conclusion: Comprehensive molecular characterization was recommended, including PD-L1 testing, germline BRCA panel testing with PALB2 assessment, and confirmation of the tumor origin. Given the metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with MSI-high status, very high tumor mutational burden, and PD-L1 positivity, pembrolizumab monotherapy was identified as the appropriate treatment approach under the pan-tumor indication. Immunotherapy was considered acceptable despite advanced age, with attention to comorbidity and treatment tolerance.

[...] the clinical indication, we know that there is a FDA approval for single-agent pembrolizumab in this setting in a TNB high and also for MSI high. [...] immunotherapy per se in an 80 years old should not be considered the contraindication.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Chronic back pain for 4 years prior to diagnosis; left upper abdominal pain for approximately 1 year prior to diagnosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with osseous, pulmonary, and later intracranial metastatic disease. Initial presentation in October 2020 with a thoracic vertebral/rib mass.

[ histopathology results ]: Aggressive resection of a thoracic mass at presentation demonstrated follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma, TTF1-positive and thyroglobulin-positive, measuring 9 cm, with lymphovascular invasion. Subsequent total thyroidectomy in October 2020 demonstrated follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma, 2.5 cm, with no positive lymph nodes reported.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT chest in October 2020 demonstrated a T8 tumor measuring 8.9 cm.  
- MRI showed infiltration of adjacent edges/ribs, depression of the pleural space, and lung compression.  
- Postoperative radioiodine imaging after first treatment demonstrated uptake in the thyroid bed, lung metastases, and the thoracic operative/metastatic site (reported as T9 region).  
- FDG PET/CT after initial radioiodine showed no abnormal FDG avidity.  
- Follow-up radioiodine imaging after second treatment demonstrated a new radioiodine-avid lytic frontal bone lesion.  
- Subsequent FDG PET/CT demonstrated an FDG-avid lytic frontal lesion.  
- Follow-up showed the frontal bone lesion enlarged to 3.3 cm; lungs remained stable with micrometastatic disease.  
- Brain MRI at that time showed no brain metastases.  
- Frontal bone metastasis later progressed and was subsequently resected.  
- After a third dose of radioiodine, FDG imaging demonstrated a right-sided hypodense lesion with cerebral edema, consistent with a new large brain metastasis measuring 4.5 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BRAF and KRAS testing on initial tumor were negative.  
- Next-generation sequencing later demonstrated an HRAS Q61R mutation and a TERT promoter mutation.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Stimulated thyroglobulin at first radioiodine treatment: 110.  
- Stimulated thyroglobulin at second radioiodine treatment, approximately 1.5 years after surgery: 226.  
- At referral for possible radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, thyroglobulin was approximately 300; anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were negative.  
- On follow-up, thyroglobulin increased to the thousands, later to the 4000s.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Aggressive surgical resection of thoracic metastatic mass at initial presentation.  
- Total thyroidectomy performed in October 2020.  
- First radioactive iodine treatment: 200 mCi; post-therapy imaging showed iodine-avid thyroid bed, lung metastases, and thoracic metastatic site.  
- Second radioactive iodine treatment: 200 mCi administered approximately 1.5 years after surgery; subsequent imaging showed a new iodine-avid frontal bone lesion.  
- External beam radiotherapy delivered to the frontal bone metastasis, with some decrease in tumor size.  
- Zoledronic acid initiated every 3 months.  
- Additional metastatic bone disease developed; external radiotherapy was delivered to pelvis and spine.  
- Left tibial metastasis with increased fracture risk was treated surgically.  
- C2 fracture occurred with concern for instability/fracture risk.  
- Frontal bone metastasis was eventually surgically removed.  
- Third radioactive iodine treatment was administered.  

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic disease with multiple symptomatic skeletal metastases and multiple skeletal-related events despite repeated radioactive iodine therapy. Lung micrometastatic disease remained stable on follow-up imaging, while bone disease progressed. Most recent imaging demonstrated a new large brain metastasis measuring 4.5 cm with associated cerebral edema.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- FDG PET/CT was initially negative despite radioiodine-avid metastatic disease.  
- The patient experienced a psychotic episode after the third dose of radioactive iodine.
