reference_discussion.text: So this is a 41-year-old woman. Prior to presenting, she had back pain for four years. She had some simple x-ray, nothing showed up. A year prior to her diagnosis, she started with some left upper abdominal pain, not very strong. In October 2020, at age 37, she She had a COVID test that was positive, so she decided to get a CT scan, and she was actually symptomatic. And on the CT chest, there was a T8 tumor, 8.9 centimeters. She got an MRI, and it was infiltrating the edges and ribs, depressing the pleural space, and causing lung compression. So, it was thought to be a primary bone tumor. So, she had an aggressive surgical resection at a different institution. And the pathology showed a follicular variant papillary thyroid cancer, TTF1 thyroid globulin positive 9 centimeter with lymphobascular invasion. these two mutations were assessed, BRF, basic syndrome, and KRES, they were negative. And so that same month she got, once they knew it was a thyroid origin, she had a total thyroidextramine. She had also follicular baron papillary thyroid cancer, 2.5 centimeters, no lymph nodes positives.

All right, and hold right there. Dr. Hussain, I'm going to pull in what I think Eyal and myself will be asking, but we would walk into our tumor board with our pathology colleagues and say, wait a second, a papillary carcinoma we always learned is kind of local spread. We'd expect to see some lymph node involvement if there was a big lesion. And in fact, it's follicular thyroid carcinoma that tends to be more bony mets, you know, is there a crossover? Is there any complexity in calling these out in terms of their microscopic appearance or what do you think on that?

It's a very good question and we did many studies at Memorial and I did study with your colleague Dr. Bailetta from Brigham. So basically the follicular vent of papillary carcinoma is a two disease. There's the encapsulated follicular vent that this patient has that it has the name of papillary carcinoma, but forget about it. It's not a papillary carcinoma. It's a RAS mutated tumor. It's basically a follicular carcinoma with clear nuclei. And we tried to, I tried to change the name. That's why actually when there is no invasion, we call it NIFT-P. So these actually, and it's interesting to see here that they don't go to leaf node, they bypass leaf node and go to distant site. So you have to look as a clinician, you have to look at the encapsulated follicular vent as a misclassified entity that's just another form of follicular carcinoma. It happens that the nuclei are clear.

So that is... Is this a parallel, similar but different, when occasionally we can get a follicular adenoma, maybe miss the invasion, and sometimes they pop up down the road with a distant metastatic site as well?

Yeah, so this is the other interesting things about this case is that, according to the report, although I did not look at the slides because there's enormous inter observability when it comes to diagnosing capsule invasion, but we have done a study once at Memorial and we thought that we found out that the encapsulated tumor with minimal invasion when they have distant metastasis, like this case, it's almost always at presentation. And it's interesting that the case has fibrosis because we have seen a lot of fibrosis in this case, and maybe it was a regression phenomenon like you see in melanoma. So yes, it is possible to have distant metastasis with minimally invasive tumor, almost always, however, they are at presentation, like in this case, and often they are RAS and TERT.
Right.

Two short points. It's extremely important to know these two types of follicular variant PTC because most physicians are not aware for the infiltrative type and encapsulated type and they behave completely differently. And if you do like a lobectomy for an encapsulated tumor, it can be follicular variant or follicular carcinoma, we do encourage to check with our globulin just to see that it's not 800, that it's not 1000, even if we don't see vascular invasion, just once to see there's nothing extreme there. That's it. That's great.
Nicole.

Okay, so she got her first dose of radioiodine 200 millicuries. The thyroid gland was 110 in that particular time. And I'll show you how it has radioiodine inhibited in the thyroid bed and in the lung metastasis, and in the area where the primary tumor was, well, the tumor was resected, the metastasis, that wasn't the primary tumor, was resected in T9. And she did have an FDG PET CT with no abnormal FDG ability. She got her second dose of 200mg a year and a half after surgery. Here the stimulated thyroglobin was higher in 226. And here she had a new lesion in the frontal bone. So here you can see the first radiodin dose. You can see how the lung metastases are avid. Quite avid. Yeah. And then this is the second dose. Here you can see the new lytic lesion radiodin avid in the frontal bone and here the area where she had the surgery.

So hold there. And Dr. Lee, I'm going to lead you on this one, but any first of all thoughts on the imaging. But number two is, is it more common, less common to see continued iodine avidity on the second treatment with radioiodine?

Uh, it depends on the location. Um, it's, you know, you'd expect that if it was an effective treatment, the radio iodine should be less, um, and get progressively less even in bony metastases, which tends to be a little bit more resistant to radio iodine. Um, but that's where you do the FDG PET to look for the differentiation component, which I believe is negative here. Um,

And I just pull out that point a little bit. I mean, if when we choose to give radioiodine and we're doing less of it now, certainly over the last decade, but when we do, we often are thinking one dose. And even if we consider a second dose, I got to say the expectation on the endocrine side is that you're usually not going to see as much uptake and you're going to certainly bring with it the siloadenitis and other things. But you do get these unique cases where there's continued iodine avidity. And it's going to foreshadow a little bit, I think the question some will ask, which is if you keep seeing the iodine avidity as kind of this targeted then uptake, should you keep using radioiodine or should we move to a more targeted approach? Let's not answer that yet for time, but keep moving us forward, Nicole, if we can.

Okay, perfect. So she was referred to the diagnosis of maybe a radioiodine refractory differentiated thyroid cancer. Her thyroid globulin at the time was around 300. She had an agriculture sign which was negative. She had the chastity only at lung micrometastasis, and she had an FDG PET-CT with dyslithic frontal lesion. And on follow-up, the thyroglobulin increased to the thousands, and the lung was still stable, but she has this dyslithic frontal lesion, now 3.3 centimeters with FDG-FBG. The brain MRI showed no brain mets. So, she did get external radiotherapy to the frontal bone meds. The tumor decreased in size a bit, the frontal tumor. She was also started on soliduronic acid every three months. She has developed new metastatic bone disease. Her thyroid globulin went to the 4000s. She was treated externally for the pelvis and spine. It has been very symptomatic for her. She has had multiple skeletal-related events. She had pain in her left tibia, so she had this metastasis that I'm going to show you that was with increased risk of fracture, so she had surgery for that. She had a C2 fraction that was risky for the fracture.
I'm going to move you forward to the genomics, if we can, just for the sake of time here.

Okay. Yeah. Sorry. Okay. Let me continue. And so basically, this is the frontal lesion. It progressed. This is the, she had this surgery. She had surgery, eventually the frontal metastasis was removed. And this is the genomics. She got an NGS and basically she has an R81 and a third promoter mutation.

And kind of a rare mutation, right? But certainly the dual mutation of anything with TERT catches our attention and classically affiliates with aggressive disease. What I'm going to do, I think next one is questions maybe, Nicole, if you just go forward.

Yeah. Okay. She did get a third dose of radioiodine and recently she had this symptoms. She had this psychotic episode and after the dose of the dose of radioiodine and an FDG was done at the same time, she had this hypodensity on the right that is actually cerebral edema. So it seems she has a new brain metastasis that is very large at 4.5 centimeters.

So the questions would be- All right, so hold there because I'm going to put one last question. I know time's going to be tight here. There's a lot to talk about. And in fact, Frank, I'm going to pull you in, but pull out the last moment of the brain metastasis and the argument that there's imminent issues to deal with. But the question I think that's really intriguing in front of all of us is going to be this issue that there's continued iodine avidity, and yet there's anatomic growth. And how do we think about, again, repeated doses of radioiodine? I've heard some people say give inorganic iodine afterwards, see if you can trap the iodine into those lesions, because it's very targeted and good. Or has the ship sailed, and our newer TKI therapy here is so important and so valuable that we should really jump here to something different?

I'll comment about that. What worries me here is the brain involvement with the TKIs. So there's a risk for bleeding. So if, you know, we're going to consider treatment with TKI therapy, in particular, Linvatinib, then we really need to make sure that the brain lesions are controlled either through, you know, surgery or radiation therapy. So I think anybody really who's starting these therapies should be checked to look for brain meds prior to treatment. In this particular case, that does take pause. It doesn't mean it couldn't be offered. The other thing too about bone disease, treatment with TKI therapy, it can have some benefit, but it's not as beneficial as someone who has visceral disease, such as lung disease or liver disease. In a case like this, this is somebody maybe I would consider because of the aggressive component. using actually cytotoxic chemotherapy. So the group from the Mayo Clinic reported a case series using carboplatin and pemetrexid, which I have used in such patients and had some responses to therapy. So that may be at the forefront versus actually using an anti-angiogenic.

reference_conclusion: Given progressive metastatic differentiated thyroid carcinoma with continued anatomic progression despite repeated radioiodine, the disease course is consistent with radioiodine-refractory disease. Immediate management should prioritize control of the large brain metastasis with surgery or radiation before consideration of systemic tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy because of bleeding risk. In view of the aggressive disease biology and extensive bone involvement, cytotoxic chemotherapy with carboplatin and pemetrexed may be considered preferentially over anti-angiogenic therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 23-year-old nulliparous woman at initial presentation in March 2017; infertility workup was ongoing at that time.

[ chief complaint ]: Ovarian cyst detected on ultrasonography during infertility evaluation in March 2017.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- 2017: Left ovarian borderline serous tumor following cystectomy.  
- May 2020: Right ovarian high-grade papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma, surgical stage IA.  
- December 2021: Recurrent disease 14 months after completion of adjuvant chemotherapy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2013: Left-sided cystectomy for left adnexal cyst; histopathology showed papillary serous cystadenoma.  
- April 2017: Frozen section from left adnexal mass was reported as benign; left cystectomy was performed. Final histopathology showed borderline serous ovarian tumor. Omental biopsy was normal.  
- May 2020: Frozen section from right ovarian mass was positive for malignancy. Final histopathology after total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and staging showed high-grade papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma. Ovarian capsule was not involved. Surgical pathological stage was IA.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- March 2017 CT scan: Left adnexal complex mass with solid component.  
- Routine antenatal ultrasonography in 2019: No adnexal pathology.  
- Peroperative findings at cesarean section in November 2019: No adnexal pathology.  
- Approximately 6 months postpartum (2020) transvaginal sonography: Right adnexal complex mass measuring approximately 8 × 9 cm.  
- Further imaging in 2020: Lobulated complex mass in right adnexa; no ascites; no lymphadenopathy.  
- May 2020 laparotomy findings: Uterus and left ovary were healthy; right ovarian mass measured 12 × 8 cm with smooth intact capsule; no ascitic fluid; no metastatic deposits.  
- December 2021 recurrence assessment: Three masses were identified, including one large mass with preserved fascial planes, one deposit adherent to the rectum at one point, and one additional peritoneal/abdominal cavity deposit; no ascites; no diaphragmatic deposits; no other disease elsewhere.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
No molecular or genomic test results were documented. ER/PR testing was referenced as routine practice for borderline and low-grade serous tumors, but no patient-specific result was provided. No BRCA result was documented. No p53 immunohistochemistry result was documented.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- March 2017: CA-125, LDH, AFP, and beta-hCG were within normal limits.  
- 2020 recurrence from contralateral ovary: CA-125 was 178 U/mL; other tumor markers were essentially normal.  
- After completion of adjuvant chemotherapy in October 2020: CA-125 was 65 U/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2013: Left cystectomy for left adnexal cyst; histopathology showed papillary serous cystadenoma.  
- April 2017: Laparotomy with frozen section in a neighboring country; frozen section was benign; left cystectomy and omental biopsy were performed. Final histopathology showed borderline serous ovarian tumor; omental tissue was normal. Right ovary and uterus were normal intraoperatively.  
- Post-2017 surgery: Managed with observation and ultrasound follow-up.  
- 2019: Conceived and delivered a male infant by cesarean section in November 2019.  
- May 2020: Laparotomy for right adnexal mass with frozen section positive for malignancy, followed by total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, peritoneal washings, infracolic omentectomy, right pelvic lymphadenectomy, and para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Final pathology showed stage IA high-grade papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma.  
- Adjuvant chemotherapy: Six cycles of paclitaxel and carboplatin were completed in October 2020.  
- December 2021 recurrence: Chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin was initiated; first cycle had been administered.

[ current disease status ]:  
Recurrent ovarian carcinoma was present as of December 2021, 14 months after completion of adjuvant paclitaxel/carboplatin. Disease burden included three intra-abdominal/pelvic masses, with no ascites and no diaphragmatic or other distant disease described. The patient had started systemic chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin and had received the first cycle.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Nulliparous at initial presentation; infertility evaluation was ongoing in 2017.  
- Follow-up after 2017 surgery was irregular.  
- The recurrent right ovarian malignancy arose in the contralateral ovary.  
- The December 2021 recurrence occurred after prior surgeries including multiple laparotomies.

But I still do think I might counsel the patient and might go ahead because she's so young. I think we should try everything in our armamentarium to prolong her life, which is, I think, doubtful because, you know, slowly, slowly, the interval between recurrence and treatment is certainly getting shortened.
No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no.

Intuitively, one may say, yes, we want to do, but currently there is no evidence to suggest that IPEC is beneficial in this setting. Though I must say that there is actually no good trial either ways. There is only one small phase two study from MSK less than 198, which I showed during my presentation also. where they used carboplatin for high-tech. And this study, although showed that it is tolerance-wise, there is no problem. Carboplatin in high-tech was all right, but there was no survival benefit. So whatever data we have, it doesn't really support. Having said that, we have actually got very limited data. And this is something we need more evidence to accept. And we won't do it at our center.

So I think this is the general consensus. In fact, all the faculty whosoever I asked today has given the same answer, that some centers probably may be carrying out and thinking that HIPEC is a kind of a treatment along with a secondary cytoreductive surgery. Many centers were doing it. But there are more and more evidence coming, again, back that that is not beneficial. A good cytoreductive surgery where we achieve a CC0 would all what is required. So the tumor board decision which was taken for this patient in the NIRH was that this patient should undergo a secondary cytoreductive surgery. However, Because this was going to be the fourth laparotomy in this particular case, the patient had reservations about it. And also, what I found out from Dr. Rubana was that she was told that there would be chances of stoma, which then made her go against the decision, against getting a laparotomy done. And so therefore, Then the tumor board said that the second option is chemotherapy. So this patient right now is undergoing chemotherapy with Paclitaxel and Carboplatin, and she has received first cycle of therapy. So this is the only point I would like to make here is that it is how you tell about the stoma to the patient. I feel that this patient was a very good candidate for a secondary cytoreductive surgery, which all the faculty here have agreed upon. And it is a way we counsel to a patient about the stoma. It can make her very fearful and totally go against stoma. Most of the cases, the stoma is not required. A LAR can be done and a stoma is not required. So thank you.

reference_conclusion: Following initial fertility-sparing cystectomy for serous borderline ovarian tumor, re-staging surgery was not recommended in the absence of poor prognostic features or residual disease; management consisted of close surveillance with clinical examination, tumor markers, and ultrasound every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then 6-monthly, with encouragement to attempt conception as early as possible. At later platinum-sensitive recurrence, the multidisciplinary consensus favored secondary cytoreductive surgery if complete gross resection was feasible; HIPEC was not supported by available evidence, and systemic paclitaxel-carboplatin was accepted as the alternative when surgery was declined.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Sex was male.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive liver-predominant metastatic neuroendocrine tumor with high hepatic tumor burden.

[ diagnosis ]: Pancreatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with liver-predominant metastatic disease. Tumor grade increased from grade 2 to grade 3 on repeat liver biopsy.

[ histopathology results ]: Repeat liver biopsy demonstrated persistent well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. Ki-67 proliferation index was 30%, consistent with progression from grade 2 to grade 3 disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated multiple hepatic lesions with marked liver tumor burden and hepatomegaly. Repeat imaging after 6 months of capecitabine/temozolomide showed mild progression of disease. Following bland embolization of the right hepatic lobe and then the left hepatic lobe, imaging showed decreased overall liver tumor burden. Nine months later, imaging demonstrated recurrent progression in the liver. DOTATATE imaging showed predominantly hepatic disease with persistent somatostatin receptor avidity.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing performed on the repeat biopsy specimen identified an ATRX mutation and RB loss.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver function tests were normal at the time intra-arterial liver-directed therapy was considered.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Capecitabine/temozolomide chemotherapy was initiated because of extensive liver disease burden. After 6 months, imaging showed mild disease progression. Liver-directed bland embolization was then performed sequentially to the right hepatic lobe and left hepatic lobe, with successful reduction in hepatic tumor burden on follow-up imaging. Disease progressed again in the liver 9 months after embolization.

[ current disease status ]: The patient had liver-predominant, DOTATATE-avid metastatic disease with progression in the liver after prior capecitabine/temozolomide and prior bilobar bland embolization. Current pathology remained well differentiated but with Ki-67 30% (grade 3).

[ other clinical data ]: Overall general health status was described as adequate at the time liver-directed therapy was undertaken. Bone marrow toxicity risk from prior capecitabine/temozolomide was identified as a consideration for subsequent therapy monitoring.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, I think, good question. And I think the same principles still apply here. So we don't really discriminate based on tumor burden, as long as there's still functioning liver there. And the liver function is normal, meaning the liver function tests are okay and the patient's overall general health status is okay. We can still do an intra-arterial therapy again, because there's more than a few lesions here. There's obviously multiple lesions here. I would favor something like a bland embolization if we wanted to go the liver directed therapy route.

Andy, any role for CAPETEM? Yeah, definitely. You know, for pancreatic neoendocrine tumors, it's one of the therapy options that can actually produce a objective response. So we need tumors shrinkage in a relatively short amount of time. So it might be, you know, someone, let's say you worry about them going into liver failure and you need that response. That may be a situation where you would start the CAPETEM.
Dr. Chen, what do you think?

I completely agree with Dr. Liao. I often, as I evaluate patients, when I see that much liver disease at the outset, where the liver is already enlarged, you worry about progression and how much more progression the liver might tolerate. So I sometimes start out with chemotherapy when there's a large burden of disease like this.

So that's what we did. We started chemotherapy and actually repeat imaging after six months of K10 showed mild progression of disease still. So then we went the IR route and the bland embolization was actually very successful in this patient. He had first the right and then the left lobe that was embolized. And you could see here that there's definitely decrease in his overall liver tumor burden. But unfortunately, nine months later, he again experienced progression of disease in his liver. So, what are we doing now? Courtney?

Kind of like a few cases ago, I would still probably give my interventional radiology colleague the right of first refusal here. Also, at my institution, in addition to Blandenboe, They do a lot of Y90 in situations like this, and so it's possible that interventional radiology may feel that another treatment, another round of treatment is indicated. But this could potentially be a time to consider PRRT. There are a couple of things that I would think about, though, in this patient. If there's not too much healthy liver left, sometimes we worry that radiation may damage some of the healthy remaining liver. But that's not a concern in this patient. The other thing that was giving me pause as we were talking through the case is, you know, generally when patients get CAPETEM, there is some risk to the bone marrow. And when patients get PRRT after getting CAPETEM, they may be at increased risk of marrow toxicity. It doesn't necessarily mean at all that they can't get PRRT or shouldn't get PRRT, but it's, one of those things that I would want to pay extra careful attention to their blood counts over time.

Outstanding. So let me just turf it right back to Oz. Oz, two points that Courtney brings up. The first one is giving you sort of the right of refusal again, right? So I think it's a very good point. Is there any timeframe that you say you know, liver directed, it's been nine months ago. He had good, good response granted, but it's nine months too short to go again. Or is there any timeframe where you would think oncologically wouldn't make sense to retreat? That's my first question. And then my second question is what about Y90? Do you use it for NETs?

Yeah. So yeah, to address your first question, I mean, um, you know, a lot of what we do isn't terribly scientific, you know, uh, in terms of the, you know, standardized protocols and algorithms. You know, to be honest with you, it's a lot more, it's a lot more common sense. So if a patient's doing well after a bland embolization, you know, for example, I mentioned when we do whole liver treatment, we separate each half of the liver, so right and left by one month. And I've done patients where I've done right, left, and then gone back and then the right again after, you know, sequential months just to sort of, you know, finish off the job, if that makes sense. So, you know, to answer your question, I would pursue treatment after nine months, again, provided the patient was healthy and did well the first time, which in this case she did. You know, when does it not make sense? I think it's more going to be based off of that MRI. If I don't see a lot of arterial enhancement or it looks more heterogeneous or the liver function is not doing well, I would probably, you know, shy away from that and then sort of rediscuss with Andy and you at the tumor board. With respect to Y90, I think we tend as an institution, as a group, to shy away from it. I think as a society of interventional radiologists, most academic interventional radiologists are not performing Y90 because of the risk of chronic hepatotoxicity, which is a very fancy way of saying that we cause liver cirrhosis with Y90. With Y90, we use it for a lot of other tumors, and unfortunately, you know, those patients don't have a long lifespan. And with NET, because our patients do have a longer lifespan, they actually, unfortunately, see the side effects or the toxicity of long-term Y90, which is basically this hepatotoxicity or cirrhosis. So we tend to shy away from it. Now, with that said, I know we were chatting very recently about some encouraging data from Penn about combining Y90 with CAPTEM for grade two NETs. But again, a lot of that's early, and it remains to be seen. I think the nice thing about NET is that we have a lot of treatment options available to us, including PRT. So I tend to stay away from it, you know, in the short term.
Courtney, do you have any reservation about giving PRT to someone that had Y90, so the Vortius Cumulative Rhetotoxicity?

Short answer is yes. I do have reservations worrying about cumulative radiotoxicity to the liver. This is something that just because of the practice patterns at my institution, though, we do end up actually doing PRRT very often after Y90, sometimes after multiple rounds of Y90. generally have not, you know, seen too much radiation-related hepatic toxicity, but we haven't seen zero. Do you know what I mean? So we do occasionally have a case. It's usually when the patient is heavily pretreated. has gotten multiple rounds of therapy, multiple rounds of Y90, potentially a bilobar Y90, even, you know, over various time points, and still has a really high burden of avid disease in the liver. So I think it's like a lot of factors that have to come together at once, but it's not my first choice in that sort of setting.

And then, Andy, so this patient, right, so had CAPTEM, didn't really respond, actually progressed mildly on CAPTEM. Initially responded well to liver erected, but is there any reason why you would want to re-biopsy this tumor at some point? I mean, the time frame is relatively short on how quickly the patient is progressing. I mean, is this something that you would consider?

Yeah, every now and then you see someone's disease kind of take on an unusual course, like, you know, indolent for a few years. And then after like CAPE 10 and PRT and all these treatments start to take off more rapidly. And when that happens, sometimes I, you know, I usually kind of re-image it and consider re-biopsy because every now and then you find this fast-growing clone that may even be poorly differentiated. So.

So in this case, we did a repeat liver biopsy, actually our interventional radiology colleagues did this for us, and showed this time that it was still a well-differentiated tumor, but the KR67 was 30%, so it went from sort of a grade 2 to a grade 3 tumor. While we had the biopsy specimen, we also did a next-generation sequencing panel on it, and it showed an ATRX mutation, which is very common, but also a loss of RB, which is a gene that has been associated with other types of tumors and sometimes can be associated with pancreatic endocrine tumors. The DOTATATE shows, again, mostly disease within the liver. It's still avid disease. Jen, what do you do in a patient like this?

Many of the conversations that we've already had with respect to should we go back and re-embolize, should we consider PRT, I think they're still very relevant topics to discuss given that it's liver predominant. I think when we tend to see higher grade disease, I think we also can consider chemotherapy. This patient has already had capecitabine and temozolomide. So I don't think we would necessarily return to that. But other regimens that do appear to be active with WellDiff grade 3 neuroendocrine tumors of the pancreas include regimens like Folfox. But I do think that there also is a role for PRRT and liver directed therapy. So I think those need to be discussed again in a multi-D setting just to figure out which one would be most appropriate now for the patient.
So Courtney, what's your experience? I think that's the last question, but what's your experience with grade three tumors and PRT?

We definitely do PRT in well diff grade three tumors. And essentially like for us, it's, it's not the grade that's important or the KI it's, it's the imaging and how hot are the tumors on imaging. And are there any significant tumors that are not hot on Dotatate? Because then we worry that we're going to be treating some tumors, and then other tumors are going to be sort of growing, like are not being treated. And so they may grow out of control. But barring something like that, as long as the uptake is as good as it is in this patient, we're very comfortable treating grade 3 patients, do generally find that response rates are somewhat lower and the duration of the response tends to be somewhat less. But particularly in patients like this that have already been through a few lines of therapy, this can definitely buy some time. This might just be the right time to do that in this patient.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Mid-abdominal pain/abdominal discomfort for several months.

[ diagnosis ]: Localized pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor involving the head/uncinate process of the pancreas.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy demonstrated a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: CT abdomen demonstrated an approximately 5 cm bilobed mass arising from the pancreatic head/uncinate process. The mass projected medially, abutted the superior mesenteric artery, and flattened/closely involved the posterior wall of the superior mesenteric vein. Reconstructed CT images showed a small margin from the superior mesenteric artery and close apposition to the superior mesenteric vein. Octreotide scan was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Hyperglycemia was present; the patient was described as borderline diabetic and was not receiving anti-diabetic medication.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Antacids had been tried for abdominal pain without benefit. Diagnostic biopsy was performed and confirmed well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. No systemic therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery had yet been documented.

[ current disease status ]: Localized pancreatic mass without documented distant metastatic disease on the available imaging summary. Tumor remained present in the pancreatic head/uncinate process with vascular abutment/involvement of the superior mesenteric vein and abutment of the superior mesenteric artery.

[ other clinical data ]: Weight had remained stable. No other significant symptoms were reported. Physical examination showed mild mid-epigastric tenderness; otherwise he appeared generally healthy.

reference_discussion.text: We actually did this for Palo Alto Cable. Terry, were you on that one? Terry Lonick? We did a cable co-op 15 years ago, mock tumor board. And they would run it, as cable stations would for health stations, at 2 in the morning and 3 in the morning when most people should be sleeping. And every time they ran it, we'd get a series of phone calls saying, we want to come to the tumor board. So we're going to give you sort of a flavor, I think, I hope, for the discussions that we have. And sometimes disagreements, and I think that disagreements, we have a room full of students, residents, fellows, upper GI surgeons, lower GI surgeons, there's colorectal surgeons, and then surgeons like you met with Dr. Polsedis and Dr. Norton who do stomach, esophageal, gastric, pancreas, liver surgeries. We highly value our pathologists, as everyone in this room should, because this is a tumor which I think really needs good pathologists to look at the tissue to feel comfortable that we're all talking about the same thing. And Terry Longmaker is a pathology specialist. We can't aim Dr. Kuhn's wonderful beams that you heard about earlier with millimeter precision, as he said, unless we can see the damn tumor with millimeter precision, right? I mean, you can't aim a beam unless you can see it. And we have some of the best radiology equipment in the country, and we have the best radiologists to run it. And Terry Desser helps us with our body imaging for all of our GI tumors, including neuroendocrine. And I would say, and will be the discussion I hope is part of this, the cases, is that a CT scan is not a CT scan as a CT scan. They actually differ. And there are different ways of using CT scans, and different CT scans have different capabilities that allow us to look at some unusual tumors in more accurate ways with greater resolution. So I hope to bring that to bear. And John Louie, who you met earlier, is an interventional radiologist. It's wonderful having them at the tumor board, because when there's something that Dr. Falsidis or Dr. Norton cannot remove, and Dr. Desser says, yes, but it's right there. I can see it. John Louis will say, yeah, well, just give me a try at it. And he can either ablate it or he can put a needle, a catheter up next to it and squirt something at it. So this is a multidisciplinary group. The only people that we're missing at this table would be gastroenterologists, a nuclear medicine specialist, a geneticist, which we sometimes have as well, because he's a card-carrying oncologist. And who else would it be missing? That plus about 30 students and residents and fellows. So, I think that the students, residents, and fellows always learn more from a good argument among experts than they do from reading a textbook. So, I hope that if we argue, I hope that doesn't confuse you. It's part of what we do in trying to find the best possible therapy for the patient whose scans we're reviewing. So, with that, I'm going to just launch into the first case. First case is a localized pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. And I'm going to describe the case much like a medical student would to us if a medical student had worked up this case and then was presenting the tumor board. This is a 55-year-old gentleman who presents with some mid-abdominal pain over the course of a couple months. He tried some antacids, but it wasn't helping. His weight was pretty stable and no other symptoms to speak of, so just some abdominal discomfort. He's got a high blood sugar, so he's borderline diabetic, but not on any anti-diabetic medications. His examination had a little bit of tenderness in the mid-epigastric region, but otherwise looked like a pretty healthy guy, and a CT scan revealed a pancreatic mass. We worked pretty quick at Stanford, so as soon as we saw the scan, he got a biopsy, and it was a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, and so the question comes up with treatments. I'm gonna, Jeff, why don't you come up here, if you don't mind, because it's hard to sit there and look at these scans. This is a CT scan, and I apologize for the projection, but I just wanted to have Dr. Norton talk about the CT scan. Because whenever, and this was alluded to in one of the questions, whenever we find a tumor in a person that's newly diagnosed, and it's in one place, the first question we ask ourselves is, can it be removed? And so, we defer to the surgeon and the radiologist, and I'll let Terry comment too.
Terry, why don't you describe the tumor, Terry? She's probably better to do it first. The pointer's that button.

So what we have here is a CT scan that's very magnified, and it's a close-up of the pancreatic region. And so just for orientation, it's a cross-section through the abdomen, and these are the kidneys back here and the spine here. And this is the region of a part of the pancreas called the head and uncinate process of the pancreas. And I'm not sure how well you're able to see this because the lights are on in the room, but normally the pancreatic tissue is pretty brightly enhancing like this. And coming off of it, we can see that there's this bilobed mass that's sticking out and going toward the middle of the patient. And it's coming up against these two bright dots right here, which are two intestinal blood vessels seen in cross-section. This is the superior mesenteric artery, and this is the superior mesenteric vein. And what we look at when we look at the tumor is Does the tumor come near any of these vessels? So we can see it comes and abuts this artery, as well as flattens the back wall of this vein. And we can see this in cross-section, but often for the surgeon it's helpful to see it in other ways too. The current state of the art in CT scans is that we can see things in cross section, but then we can also recreate images in almost any plane that we want. So what we do is we make an image that shows the length of the vessel we're interested in and how close the tumor comes to it. So this image on the right is a specially reconstructed image that shows this vessel, the superior mesenteric artery, all along its length. like this. So this is the superior mesenteric artery. And some of the other anatomy is distorted because of the projection here. But this is the pancreatic head and we can see the tumor now. And there's a small margin with the artery, but for the most part, it's pretty clear. But you can see that it comes up and abuts and lies against this vessel, the superior mesenteric vein. So that's helpful to the surgeons when planning it.

So I think that the other thing that's important is the size of the tumor. So it's about five centimeters. So that's a bigger tumor. And the fact that it involves the vein so closely, especially the posterior wall of the vein, if it was standard adenocarcinoma of the pancreas or pancreas cancer, we'd make it unresectable. So that's kind of why the biopsy is important. So the biopsy shows that it's a neuroendocrine or islet cell tumor. So these are the kind of patients we talked about where we would consider resecting the vein. And since the tumor comes off the artery, that's really a good sign. So we feel like there's a good margin on the artery and we could resect a segment of the vein and still take out the tumor and then reconstruct the vein. So we can use like the jugular vein from the neck or the superficial femoral vein. from the lower extremity. So we would plan, that's a bigger operation, but we would plan working with vascular surgery and, you know, develop a plan where we can actually do all these things.

And I think that one of the lessons here is that the usual limitations in surgical technique that might apply to an adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, don't always apply to neuroendocrine tumors. And so, we can be a little bit more bold with some neuroendocrine tumors than we can with adenocarcinomas. And in fact, Dr. Norton has a poster later on, and Dr. Pulsidas have posters talking about doing surgeries in patients who have vascular involvement like this and showing that you can still get very good results when that might make other surgeons shy away. So, and I have to apologize, this is really terrible, and I bet a third of the audience are throwing darts at me right now, because I didn't introduce Pam Kuntz, who's my colleague, and just joined us this afternoon. And Pam is a medical oncologist who joined Stanford to my delight and the benefit of all of our patients, and she's a rising star in the neuroendocrine world internationally now. And she made the mistake of having a third boy recently, and she complains of fatigue now. I just said, you know, 20 years of that, and you should take care of it. So this is the actreotide scan, and in the region of the pancreas, and it looks like It says it's negative. Can we trust that, Teri?

Teri Manolio This was a negative scan. The octreotide is a tracer that hones in on a particular kind of receptor that these tumors tend to have. And most of the time it's positive and allows you to see kind of in one imaging test, all the places that the tumor has spread to. But it is negative about 10% of the time. So having a negative octreotide scan doesn't rule out the presence of neuroendocrine tumor or its metastases.

And you can see that kidneys ordinarily take up the octreotide. So not everything that's positive in an octreotide scan is necessarily a tumor either. Whenever we see a negative bacteriotide scan, because that's the minority of the patients who have a negative bacteriotide scan, again, 80% or positive, 80%, 90% or positive, it does make me a little bit nervous, though, because an adenocarcinoma would be negative. So that's where we have to rely on the pathologist to give us better detail as to are we dealing with the right type of tumor here. And so Terry Longacre will guide us through that.

So these are a couple of pictures of fairly routine appearing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. And I think the main point to remember with pancreatic tumors is that they often show a lot more varied morphologic patterns under the microscope than the neuroendocrine tumors that tend to occur in the rest of the GI tract. And so sometimes it can be a bit of a problem trying to determine, particularly on a small biopsy, whether you actually have a neuroendocrine tumor, or as Dr. Norton was addressing earlier, a possible pancreatic adenocarcinoma. And as he mentioned, treating physicians' entire treatment and surgical plan would change tremendously if it wasn't a pancreatic endocrine tumor. But what you can see on the left, it's sort of a, you see sort of a ribbony, trabecular pattern, and that's really fairly common, I think, in association with most neuroendocrine tumors. And when you see this pattern, it's pretty reproducibly going to be a neuroendocrine tumor. So, what we can do is we can use immunohistochemical stains to try to identify whether or not these tumors are, in fact, endocrine tumors. And the two main stains, and probably most everybody in this room is familiar with them, or chromagranin A and synaptophycin. Now, chromagranin A is by far the most specific. In other words, if a tumor stains with chromagranin A, it's in like 99% all likelihood going to be a neuroendocrine tumor. Whereas if you use this less specific marker, synaptophysin, there are other tumors that can occur that may express synaptophysin that may not be neuroendocrine tumors. And it's basically three grades. It's the grade one, two, and three, and it's based entirely on how much of the cells are dividing or proliferating. So, there's two ways to do it. Or you can use an immunohistochemistry stain. And in fact, we do both now. So, we'll do a formal count, and then we'll stain for a key 67, which is basically just highlight cells that are going through the cell cycle and proliferating. And these are the cutoffs. And so anything less than or equal to 2% is grade 1, 3 to 20% is grade 2, and then greater than 20% is grade 3. And that's a neuroendocrine carcinoma. And again, if it's a grade 3 tumor, their entire management will change. It's a different sort of tumor. They tend to be much more, they tend to spread through the body a lot more rapidly. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old female. Karnofsky Performance Status: 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in June 2021 with a right middle cranial fossa/skull base lesion.

[ diagnosis ]: Atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2, involving the right temporal skull base/middle fossa with residual and subsequently progressive/recurrent disease after surgery and stereotactic radiosurgery.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical histopathology demonstrated atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging in June 2021 demonstrated an extensive right middle fossa lesion centered in the right temporal skull base, extending posteriorly to the tentorium, laterally to the convexity, medially to the cavernous sinus, and into the prepontine and suprasellar cisterns, with extension into the infratemporal fossa. Postoperative MRI after June 2021 resection demonstrated residual enhancing lesion near the base of the temporal fossa/skull base, including enhancement near the infratemporal fossa and a small medial residual component. Imaging after Gamma Knife treatment in 2021 was followed by interval imaging in July 2023, which demonstrated increased contrast enhancement and significant interval increase in lesion size, predominantly in the infratemporal fossa, with progression along the posterior margin/tentorium. The intracranial residual component showed cystic change with edema. There was significant edema and mass effect. Imaging also described radiation-related changes in the previously treated residual lesion. CT demonstrated extensive right temporal bone erosion. The lesion was described as close to the cavernous sinus, propagating through neural foramina, possibly via foramen ovale, with involvement of adjacent skull base neurovascular structures.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In June 2021, the patient underwent surgical resection via right pterional craniotomy for the skull base lesion. Postoperative imaging demonstrated residual disease at the skull base/temporal fossa, including infratemporal and medial residual components. In September 2021, the patient underwent Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery to the residual lesion. The patient was subsequently lost to follow-up from September 2021 until July 2023. Imaging in July 2023 demonstrated interval progression/recurrence with enlargement of the lesion, particularly in the infratemporal fossa and along the tentorial margin, with associated cystic change, edema, and mass effect.

[ current disease status ]: As of July 2023, there was progressive/recurrent residual atypical meningioma involving the right skull base with significant enlargement in the infratemporal fossa, interval increase along the tentorium/posterior margin, intracranial cystic change, marked edema, mass effect, and extensive right temporal bone erosion.

[ other clinical data ]: No preoperative embolization had been performed before the initial surgery.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old female. Otherwise healthy. History included tanning bed use and multiple lifetime sunburns.

[ chief complaint ]: Pigmented scalp lesion identified by hairdresser.

[ diagnosis ]: Nevoid melanoma of the scalp. Initial pathologic stage after excisional biopsy was pT2a Nx Mx. Final stage after wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy was pT2a N2a Mx, stage IIIA melanoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial shave biopsy demonstrated a combined nevus. Subsequent narrow-margin excisional biopsy, reviewed at Cleveland Clinic, demonstrated nevoid melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.3 mm. Ulceration was absent. Satellitosis was absent. Lymphovascular invasion was absent. Neurotropism was absent. Regression was absent. Mitotic count was 1. Narrow-margin excision had a 0.3 cm margin. Following wide local excision, no residual tumor was identified at the primary site. Sentinel lymph node biopsy removed 3 nodes, all positive for metastatic melanoma. One parotid sentinel node contained a 0.2 mm metastatic focus. Two level V sentinel nodes each contained rare metastatic cells with foci measuring less than 0.1 mm. Nodal melanoma deposits were demonstrated on H&E, S100, HMB45, and Melan-A stains, with subcapsular deposits described.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinical examination showed no clinically evident nodal disease. Physical examination otherwise showed actinic changes in a photodistributed pattern with no other concerning lesions. Preoperative lymphoscintigraphy/SPECT-CT identified sentinel drainage to a preauricular/parotid node and a level V node. No additional imaging was performed before wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial shave biopsy was performed and showed combined nevus. Narrow-margin excisional biopsy of the scalp lesion was then performed by an outside dermatologist. The patient subsequently underwent wide local excision with 2 cm surgical margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Scalp defect was managed by secondary intention, left open to granulate with pericranium down. No residual primary melanoma was found on wide local excision.

[ other clinical data ]: Primary lesion was located on the scalp. Nodes were clinically negative at presentation. Sentinel nodes sampled included one parotid node and two level V nodes.

reference_discussion.text: Great, thanks very much. I'm Dave Vorner. I'm one of the fellows at University of Michigan. Thanks very much for the opportunity to present this case. So this is a case of a 58-year-old female who's otherwise healthy. She does have a history of tanning bed use and had multiple sunburns throughout her life. She was at the hairdresser and her hairdresser noted a pigmented lesion on her scalp. Her physical exam otherwise just shows some actinic changes in a photo distributed pattern with no other concerning lesions. We're fortunate enough actually to get a picture of this pigmented lesion here on her scalp. So this is her before what her hairdresser saw. She ended up getting a shave biopsy first, which just initially demonstrated a combined nevus. She then went on to have an excisional narrow margin biopsy performed by an outside dermatologist that ended up being reviewed at the Cleveland Clinic. And you'll see those results here on the next slide. And then she was referred to our way at the University of Michigan. So that excisional biopsy showed a nevoid melanoma of 1.3 millimeters thickness. They ended up with that narrow margin having a 0.3 centimeter margin. And she didn't really have any other concerning features per se, no ulceration, no satellites, no LBI or neurotropism, no regression, and just one mitosis. So she ended up with a PT2ANXMX at this point in time.

Awesome. Oh, that's perfect. Can you go back one slide so we can see all the excellent data? So, um, Audrey, so this patient presents your clinic, what are some of the ways that you sort of size of the patient for work of imaging prior to an intervention.
It sounds like this patient had clinically negative nodes. Is that right, David? I missed that piece.
Correct, yeah.

Right. So, you know, this is a patient I would have a discussion with about, you know, I don't know how large the margins were. I think you said narrow margin excision. But this is a patient who I would discuss having a wide local excision in the operating room and at the same time having sentinel lymph node biopsy. It's interesting because now, you know, a lot of these patients are coming in with preoperative genetic testing. I don't know if you're also seeing that in some of your practices, but many of my patients will come in with a castle test that was ordered by their dermatologist and say, hey, I'm class 1A. You know, the chance that this metastasizes is really low. Do I still need to send a lymph node biopsy? And to that, I answer, yes, yes, you do. Those tests are not great. And until we have really great data showing, you know, some of the molecular testing, I think we still have to offer these patients the standard of care. So that's what I would do. At our institution, we don't use blue dye anymore. We found that it doesn't work as well in the head and neck as it does with some of the trunk and extremity melanomas. So we would just preoperatively inject her and take her to the operating room and find the lymph node and call it a day.
Awesome, thank you. What work of imaging do you do for these patients if they're clinically N0?
We don't do any imaging for these patients.
Okay, so you based it based on clinical exam alone?
Absolutely. Okay.
TJ, your thoughts on CASEL Biosciences testing in this, if you get the results anyway, are you integrating it and what is your work of imaging?

We are not integrating Kessel biosciences for melanomas. That's easy answer for that. Just to back up a little bit, when I get these referrals, I also worry a little bit about a couple of things. They had it reviewed at Cleveland Clinic and I'm guessing maybe at Michigan, but I always have my own dermatopathologist review the slides. I worry about a shave first and then a second, you know, excisional biopsy. Like maybe that's not the true thickness. you know, I want to really be sure about that. Because if you go from T2A to T2B, you're actually in the realm of adjuvant therapy. You know, that's a big, big, big crossover, you know. You know, that picture to me looked a little more worrisome than the pathology report. So anyway, that's what I did. And as far as imaging, yeah, I think, For early stage melanoma like this, you may not, but I think, again, given the history, and because I didn't do the workup myself, I might nudge it to a higher stage melanoma in my thought process, and I might get a CT. neck, just to be sure. Our ultrasonographers have had a lot of turnover here recently, and I don't think I have as much, you know, confidence in our ultrasonography here. So I would get a CT so I can look myself for necrotic nodes and large nodes and see if there's anything worrisome, you know, in addition to my own exam.
Okay, sounds good. David, you want to proceed? What happens next?

Yeah, so she does end up getting a wide local excision, two centimeters surgical margins were taken. And at that same time, a sentinel node biopsy was done. There was no additional imaging beforehand. This is her lymphocentigraphy. So you can see a pre-auricular and a level five node lighting up. Some of her lymphocentigraphy and spec CTs here as well for interest. And then I would manage to track down some pathology, just as quick interest here. So just a standard HNE stain. These are of her nodes, the sentinel nodes, which there was three removed. Here's an S100 stain showing some melanoma deposits here, subcapsular, more standard HMB45, and then some melanae and frame stains suggesting there's some melanoma deposits in the sentinel nodes. So ultimately, after the wide local excision, there was no residual tumor found at the primary site. So just as a reminder, original thickness of 1.3 millimeters, though excellent point that with the shave, this could have been more thick. She did end up being BRAF positive. And then those three nodes were all positive. So there was one in the parotid and two in level five each. One in the parotid was 0.2 millimeter focus. And then the other two are kind of rare cells, less than 0.1 millimeter focuses. Oops, sorry. So she ended up with a PT2A-N2A-MX for stage 3A at this point in time.
Thank you so much. And thank you for some of the molecular testing that can add to our conversation. Just out of curiosity, how did you reconstruct the defect?
This was secondary attention at this point in time.
So you kind of left it open to granulate, or did you use alloderm or skin graft, or you just kind of leave it open?
She would have been just left open, pericranial down.

Very good. Well, let's go back to TJ for a second. I'll ask Audrey a second in the reverse order. So TJ, if you see this, I'm sure you'll get your medical oncologist involved, but Do you do additional imaging or do you favor additional imaging at this point beyond the CT or ultrasound you might've gotten earlier?

Yeah, I mean, with positive nodes, I think you need to do a metastatic workup. you know, so I'd get an LDH, I would get either a PET CT, although after an operation, it might be a false positive. So you might get a CT, chest, abdomen, and pelvis. And we usually do get a brain MRI just to be sure there's not a brain mint. So I think that's the pretty standard.
Audrey, what would you do? Similar?

same thing we would do at our institution. You know, I have been getting PET scans right after an operation, even after a couple weeks. You can kind of tell the difference between post-operative change and a frank mass somewhere else. We also routinely get brain MRIs, and I would send this patient to medical oncology You know, the treatment of this patient over the last 10 years has trained drastically. I mean, when I was trained, I'm an old lady, so when I was training, we were doing completion neck dissections for these patients. And, you know, that has really fallen out of favor with the MSLT2 trial that was published in 2012. It's interesting because there are, as you guys know, there are some head and neck surgeons who would continue to do a completion neck dissection. There is a lot to be gained from that. But I think more and more people are coming away from that. I understand why somebody wouldn't want to go for with a completion dissection in the axilla or the groin. I mean, the chance for lymphedema is horrible. There's a lot of morbidity associated with those operations. But as you know, a neck dissection, I mean, that's no big deal. It's fun. It doesn't take that long. The risk of nerve injury and lymphedema is very low. And it can give you additional staging information if you have additional non sentinel lymph nodes positive in the neck. that can be important for staging and prognosis going forward.

Thanks, Audrey. I'm going to pause you because I definitely want to revisit that point, but I want to have Tony kind of weigh in here because Tony, because I definitely want to visit the complete hemophageal necromena and muscle T2. I think that's a very important point here. Tony, now this patient's in your shop. What are your thoughts on this case and what do you think you would do?

Yeah, so to very briefly start, we never look at the CASEL bioscience reports because they're very confusing and they don't advance our treatment in any way. It's gene expression profiling. It's not codified by any of the major like NCCN panels and stuff like that. So this patient is very interesting because we actually do think that this patient could potentially benefit from adjuvant therapy. The FDA approved adjuvant therapy for patients with stage 3 disease. They don't classify stage 3a, b, c, or d. And so this patient would be potentially a candidate for that. Importantly, pembrolizumab and nivolumab, when they were studied, they actually didn't study patients like this. Specifically, if they had stage 3A with less than a point, with less than a one millimeter focus of disease, then they excluded those patients. They had to have stage 3A with greater than a millimeter focus. And then as we see on the slide here, we also have in this BRAF positive patient, COMBI-AD, which is adjuvant dibrafinib and trimetinib in a patient like this. So in this patient, because we really do have three nodes positive, I think we really have to think about a risk benefit profile. If I had one node and I had less than a millimeter focus, I would probably talk to the patient about the cons and pros of therapy. Both of these therapies, immunotherapy or targeted therapy, are reasonable and rational in this patient. Again, I would offer the patient adjuvant therapy based on the studies that show improvement in relapse-free survival. I think a big difference right now and up for contention is do you start with immunotherapy or in a BRAF patient, BRAF positive patient, do you do instead targeted therapy?
Tony, I know that there's both excellent data for both adjuvant I.O. and adjuvant debraphic atrobatinative. Which one do you reach for first and why?

I typically reach for Pembrolizumab because it's every six week dosing. A patient only needs nine doses in a year. And although some toxicities can be serious, life-threatening or non-reversible, most toxicities are actually very mild and it's easy to get patients through that for the most part. 80% of patients really have no significant toxicity. Nine doses goes really fast for patients. On the other hand, dibrafenib and trimetanib has a higher rate of grade three toxicity, and you're taking at least five tablets. Some of them are tablets, some of them are capsules, but you're taking five pills a day. And when you multiply that times 365, that's a whole lot of tablets you're taking over the course of a year. Because the dose-limiting toxicity rate was about 50% with Dab-Tram, and the most significant toxicity is fever, pyrexia, seen in over 60% of patients, we have a pretty robust discussion of patients if we're going to start Dab-Tram.

Thanks, Tony. So, you know, David, would you go back, I think, a slide to the actual pathology again? You know, Tony, sometimes, you know, Audrey very nicely outlined the MSLT2 data in summary that completion lymphagnectomy doesn't offer a melanoma specific survival benefit, excuse me, yeah, an overall survival benefit, but there may be some other benefits from local regional control, et cetera. You know, as a medical oncologist, when you have a patient like this one, you know, this is when like there's multiple parameters here, right? Is it single node versus multiple nodes? Is it like a teeny tiny less than one millimeter focus or is it like E and E? Can you outline, you know, especially when, know, you're working with your fellow head and neck surgeons, when do you say, hey, you know, maybe we should think about a completion even in the face of MSLT2?

Certainly for patients with big bulky lymphadenopathy we found or extranodal extension, those are the kind of things that start making me a little bit more nervous. The odd thing here is that if I'm going to start immunotherapy, and we'll talk about this as we get to some of the other cases, having antigen load at the tumor bed can actually possibly be helpful. And so eradicating all the disease with surgery might not be actually the best way to use immunotherapy, which is very intriguing thought. And we know that surgery in and of itself is a locally immunosuppressive. and just from the healing process of the inflammatory component itself. That could actually decrease the rate of pembrolizumab or any PD-1. We're not just talking about pembrolizumab here and nivolumab is approved as well. Those medications might not work as well if we actually decrease the antigen load. I think what really needs to happen and what we're doing here is we present these patients in a multidisciplinary tumor board, and we really discuss the pros and cons. And this is really helpful because the surgeon is going to know what that operation is going to look like. What are the real risks? What are the real benefits potentially? What is making the surgeon sway for or against TLND? And a medical oncologist is going to do the same thing. And we usually can come to some kind of consensus.

We have about three minutes left. So TJ, Would you offer this patient a completion lymphadenectomy with this setting with this and with, or I should remember phrase. If this was your patient and you would discuss this in your team, what would your team recommend for this patient completion or not.

Yeah. The short answer is in majority of cases now we're not doing completion neck dissection for this. The discussion details I still, I kind of presented to the patient that, you know, there could be the melanoma and lymph nodes in your neck. And even though it would make sense to remove those surgically, it has not shown to have a major impact on overall survival. I do talk to them a little bit about regional control, and then I kind of let them, we make like a collective decision, usually, the patient and myself, but they're kind of being steered away from the dissection at this point.
Okay. Audrey, what would your team offer this patient? Completion or straight to IO?
We would go straight to immunotherapy, most likely. Okay, David, if there's a patient who can't get immunotherapy for any reason, then we might have that discussion as well.
Yeah, that's a good point. David, do you want to finish out the rest of the slide deck?
Absolutely. Thanks.
So what did you guys end up doing?

Yeah, of course, multidisciplinary tumor board. Interestingly, she was close friends with a local dermatologist who was a huge advocate for her. And that dermatologist happened to be very prominent at the University of Michigan. That person came to all of her appointments with her. She was obviously very well informed due to this. She had multiple discussions with head and neck surgery, oncology, medical oncology and dermatology. She had a little apprehension with immunotherapy and targeted therapies, and so completion lymphadenectomy was offered, but she ultimately decided on surveillance actually, so she got no adjuvant treatment and no completion lymphadenectomy. We ended up doing CT necks and neck ultrasounds as well as some additional CTs. We did offer her and recommend a brain MRI, but she did not undergo this. She didn't end up having any additional regional disease or distant metastatic disease. She's being followed now. She's almost three years, two years, and almost three years, and she's still disease-free at this point in time. But time will tell, I suppose.

reference_conclusion: Following wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy demonstrating stage IIIA melanoma with three positive sentinel nodes, metastatic staging with cross-sectional imaging was recommended, including CT or PET/CT and brain MRI, and referral to medical oncology was advised. Completion lymphadenectomy was generally not favored, with the panel indicating a preference to proceed directly to adjuvant systemic therapy rather than completion neck dissection. In this BRAF-positive patient, adjuvant therapy was considered appropriate, with pembrolizumab identified as the usual first choice over dabrafenib/trametinib based on toxicity and dosing considerations.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Increased left infraorbital swelling concerning for local recurrence.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent squamous cell carcinoma involving the left nasal cavity/maxilla/orbit region. Original diagnosis in 2021 was nasal cavity squamous cell carcinoma, p16-positive.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial tumor in 2021 was reported as p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the nasal cavity.  
- Outside biopsy at recurrence was positive for recurrent squamous cell carcinoma and was also reported as p16-positive.  
- Postoperative pathology after salvage resection showed a 4.5 cm squamous cell carcinoma involving bone, with perineural invasion.  
- Carcinoma was present focally at the posterior soft tissue margin.  
- Additional pterygopalatine fossa excision showed invasive squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Treatment-related change was estimated at 40%.  
- Cervical lymph nodes were negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI of the maxillofacial region showed an enhancing infiltrative soft tissue mass extending from the nasolabial fold into the orbit and medial canthus, abutting the inferior medial rectus muscle.  
- PET-CT showed hypermetabolic uptake along the nasal bridge with underlying erosion and extension into the orbit.  
- No distant metastatic disease was identified on PET-CT.  
- Level II cervical lymph nodes were described as equivocal.  
- Intraoperative findings included tumor involving the medial and inferior orbit and ethmoid air cells, extending up to but not involving the skull base.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- p16-positive primary tumor.  
- Recurrent biopsy was also p16-positive.  
- Combined positive score (CPS) for PD-L1 was 7.  
- No additional genomic sequencing results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- In 2021, the patient underwent partial maxillectomy and neck dissection at an outside hospital for nasal cavity squamous cell carcinoma.  
- He subsequently received adjuvant chemoradiotherapy with 3 cycles of cisplatin.  
- He was followed for approximately 4 years before recurrence was identified.  
- For recurrent disease, he received induction systemic therapy with paclitaxel, carboplatin, and pembrolizumab; response after 3 cycles was limited.  
- Treatment was then changed to cetuximab plus pembrolizumab; after 6 cycles there was no significant change on imaging or clinical examination.  
- He then underwent salvage surgery consisting of radical maxillectomy, orbital exenteration, hard palate resection, partial rhinectomy, pterygopalatine fossa and infratemporal fossa dissection/resection, left total ethmoidectomy, neck dissection, and free flap reconstruction with an anterolateral thigh flap.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent/recurrent locoregional squamous cell carcinoma remained present at salvage resection after neoadjuvant systemic therapy.  
- Postoperative pathology demonstrated residual invasive disease with bone involvement, perineural invasion, focal positive posterior soft tissue margin, and additional invasive carcinoma in the pterygopalatine fossa.  
- Neck nodes were negative.  
- No distant metastatic disease had been identified.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included prior deep venous thrombosis and alcohol dependence.  
- He was a non-smoker.  
- On examination before salvage treatment, there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- Left cheek and medial canthal induration were present, with a small fungating tumor at the medial canthus.  
- Flexible nasoendoscopy was limited by extensive crusting.
