case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old woman; highly functional physical therapist.

[ chief complaint ]: In February 2018, she developed left jaw pain, oral bleeding, and new numbness of the chin.

[ diagnosis ]: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma involving the left retromolar trigone/mandibular region, with clinical evidence of mandibular invasion and inferior alveolar/mental nerve involvement.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy of an approximately 1 cm heaped-up mucosal mass near the retromolar trigone showed mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Subsequent surgical pathology reportedly showed a positive margin. Pathology reportedly did not identify perineural invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated frank deep mandibular invasion. The mental nerve was enlarged on imaging, consistent with neural involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She underwent segmental mandibulectomy of the left mandible, extending from approximately the angle/sigmoid notch region to the mental foramen, with neck dissection and osteocutaneous fibula free flap reconstruction using a single bony segment. The bony defect was reconstructed from the angle to the mental foramen. She subsequently received postoperative radiation therapy, completed in June 2018.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had full dentition at presentation. The primary mucosal lesion was approximately 1 cm in size. The surgical defect was described as involving the mandibular body from the angle to the mental foramen.

And Ilya and Avi, if you have comments about Chase's case during your presentation, please feel free to go. All right, who's next?

reference_conclusion: The consensus management was surgical resection with segmental mandibulectomy rather than marginal mandibulectomy, including resection of the inferior alveolar nerve with an attempt to obtain a proximal negative margin at the skull base/V3 as feasible. Reconstruction was performed with an osteocutaneous fibula free flap, and a neck dissection was undertaken in conjunction with flap reconstruction and for assessment of occult nodal disease. Given the clinical perineural invasion, bony invasion, and positive margin, postoperative radiotherapy was indicated, with treatment fields extending to the skull base and including ipsilateral neck levels I–III.

That would be my plan for resection, but I would, I would also try to get a margin on the inferior alveolar nerve at the skull base to Dr. Shah's point. [...] We did go with an osteocutaneous fibula, one segment. [...] Yeah, obviously, as you see here, we did do a neck dissection. [...] Of course, he needs post-op radiation, no question about that. [...] the radiation port is going to be much higher than what you would normally think. I'm not worried about lymph nodes at level 405, but I'm more worried about proximal spread up to the foraminal valley. So the primary port is going to be high enough to the base of the skull and I would include the neck at least up to the lower border of the hyoid bone implying levels 1, 2 and 3.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 80-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic stage IV prostate cancer with disease progression after multiple lines of systemic therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV prostate adenocarcinoma diagnosed in 2016, with osseous metastatic disease. Subsequent castration-resistant progressive metastatic disease was documented.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: At diagnosis in 2016, multiple bone lesions were present. In March 2019, metastatic disease involved the humerus and left femur. Subsequent progression included a lesion in the left pelvis and a lesion in the scapula, both treated with radiation therapy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing performed after progression on multiple prior therapies demonstrated microsatellite instability-high (MSI-high) status and very high tumor mutational burden. Reported genomic alterations included NF1, PTEN, MEN1, APC, ASXL1, and BCL2 mutations. Alterations affecting the androgen receptor pathway were also described.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was approximately 600 at initial presentation, declined substantially on initial androgen deprivation therapy, later rose with progressive disease, reached nearly 1,000 before pembrolizumab, then declined to near zero after pembrolizumab, and subsequently rose again with later progression.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment consisted of androgen deprivation therapy with leuprolide (Lupron) plus bicalutamide (Casodex), with marked PSA response. In 2017, rising PSA prompted reintroduction of bicalutamide, followed by abiraterone (Zytiga) plus prednisone; bicalutamide was then stopped. With continued PSA progression, therapy was changed to enzalutamide (Xtandi). Further progression with rising PSA and new lesions led to docetaxel (Taxotere) plus prednisone; PSA initially declined, then resistance developed after 6 cycles. Subsequent cabazitaxel plus carboplatin was administered without meaningful disease control, and PSA rose rapidly. Molecular profiling was then obtained, demonstrating MSI-high disease, and pembrolizumab (Keytruda) was started, producing a marked PSA response from nearly 1,000 to near zero. With later progression on pembrolizumab, apalutamide (Erleada) was added. Oligoprogressive lesions in the left pelvis and scapula were treated with radiation therapy while pembrolizumab and apalutamide were continued, with disease control for several years. After further progression, everolimus (Afinitor) was given to target the PTEN alteration, without benefit. Darolutamide was subsequently administered.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after androgen deprivation therapy, multiple androgen receptor-directed agents, taxane-based chemotherapy, platinum-containing chemotherapy, pembrolizumab, radiation therapy, everolimus, and darolutamide.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Advanced oral cavity/oropharyngeal mass with severe trismus, weight loss, frailty, and left lip numbness.

[ diagnosis ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity/oropharyngeal region, involving the retromolar trigone, posterior buccal mucosa, posterior maxilla, lateral pharynx, mandible, and tongue. Clinical stage based on imaging was cT4b cN2c cM0.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside biopsy showed squamous cell carcinoma. Pathology review confirmed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. p16 was negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated extensive mandibular destruction crossing the midline, with tumor extension under the gingiva nearly to the midline. There was invasion of approximately half of the tongue, nearly to the midline, with involvement of the hemitongue. Tumor extended posteriorly into the medial pterygoid with masticator space involvement. The pterygoid plate was not clearly eroded. There was extensive pharyngeal involvement and extension into the posterior maxilla. Anterior soft tissue involvement approached but did not invade the skin. PET imaging demonstrated a contralateral cervical lymph node, consistent with bilateral nodal disease (N2c). No distant metastatic disease was reported (M0).

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver function tests were normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial management focused on supportive optimization because of poor nutritional status and frailty. A gastrostomy tube was placed. Nutrition and social work were involved. Pain control was improved. Smoking cessation efforts were initiated. The patient was evaluated by radiation oncology and medical oncology. Medical oncology determined he was not fit for concurrent chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Locally advanced, unresected head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with masticator space invasion and bilateral cervical nodal involvement, without documented distant metastasis. The patient remained frail with severe trismus and malnutrition.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had mild to moderate dementia and was taking memantine. He was able to answer questions appropriately and understood his condition, but was not fully independent in daily activities. He had a history of cirrhosis. He was a former heavy drinker and former heavy smoker; he was still actively smoking at the time of evaluation. Nutritional status was poor, with significant weight loss, BMI 17, temporal wasting, and marked frailty. Examination was limited by severe trismus. There was decreased sensation/numbness of the left lip. Airway was reported to be adequate. He lived at home with his wife, who was his primary support.

Thank you, guys. Obviously it's not the best modality, Honestly, I was not optimistic about surgery for him, and so I didn't want to put him through an MRI. But if I were really going to consider going to surgery, I probably would have ordered that. So this was staging based on imaging, T4B, mastigator space involvement, and 2CM0. Yeah, no, I agree with that T4B designation. I think that this tumor is, at that presentation, unresectable. If you had a patient with this type of tumor and they really wanted you to do everything possible, including consideration of surgery, I think one option is neoadjuvant treatment, whether that be chemo or a combination of chemo and immunotherapy and see how the patient's tumor responds. And in some cases, we have seen patients who do respond significantly where we think that surgery does become feasible, not easy, but feasible. So that's an option. Yeah, I definitely would lean on our tumor board You know, it's interesting, Caitlin, from the dementia standpoint, like, was he able to participate in his decision making?
He was. He could answer questions appropriately. He understood what was going on. But in terms of his day to day, he's not driving the car. He's not, you know, doing his bills.

Sure. So, you know, I think that you have a couple of options. Any surgery in this case would be heroic. There would certainly be positive margins. Yeah, I just, I totally agree. I just want to say that, like, you know, from the fellows perspective, that there are T4Bs, and then there are T4Bs, you know. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Painful chest wall mass developing approximately 4 years after prior treatment for colon cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage II colon adenocarcinoma diagnosed in 2017, subsequently recurrent/metastatic disease with biopsy-proven chest wall metastasis and a PET-avid suspicious right upper quadrant abdominal mass.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the chest wall mass showed immunohistochemistry consistent with the original colon adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PET scan demonstrated a painful chest wall mass and a minor suspicious mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen.  
- Repeat PET/CT after systemic therapy demonstrated response in the chest wall mass and resolution of the right upper quadrant abdominal mass, with persistent residual chest wall mass and ongoing chest wall discomfort.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: FoundationOne genomic profiling identified:  
- KRAS G12C mutation  
- NRAS wild type  
- Two PIK3CA mutations  
- Two APC mutations  
- SMAD4 mutation

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2017: No adjuvant therapy was administered after resection/diagnosis of stage II colon adenocarcinoma because no high-risk features were present.  
- The patient remained without evident disease for approximately 4 years.  
- After recurrence, treatment was initiated with FOLFOX plus bevacizumab.  
- The first cycle was poorly tolerated, with significant nausea and peripheral neuropathy.  
- Oxaliplatin was discontinued; treatment continued with infusional 5-FU plus bevacizumab.  
- The patient subsequently developed severe diarrheal syndrome and was diagnosed with enteritis.  
- The patient refused further 5-FU therapy.  
- Bevacizumab was tolerated.  
- Sotorasib was obtained for the patient.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent residual chest wall mass with associated discomfort remained after initial systemic therapy; the previously seen right upper quadrant abdominal lesion had resolved on repeat PET/CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Severe treatment-related gastrointestinal toxicity was documented during fluoropyrimidine-based therapy, including severe diarrhea/enteritis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Re-presented in February 2024 with new right-sided abdominal wall symptoms after prior spontaneous regression of a left abdominal wall desmoid.

[ diagnosis ]: 
- Left abdominal wall desmoid-type fibromatosis diagnosed in November 2019.
- Right abdominal wall desmoid-type fibromatosis identified in 2023/2024, anatomically separate from the prior left-sided lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: 
- 2019 biopsy of the left abdominal wall lesion confirmed desmoid-type fibromatosis.
- Biopsy of the right-sided lesion confirmed desmoid-type fibromatosis.
- The right-sided lesion was described as having the same diagnosis as the prior lesion but with a different mutation.

[ imaging findings ]: 
- Outside baseline imaging of the left abdominal wall lesion showed no persisting lesion, consistent with spontaneous regression.
- Subsequent imaging demonstrated a lesion on the contralateral right abdominal wall, separate from the original left-sided site.
- Imaging showed interval growth of the right-sided lesion between February 2024 and June 2024.
- The right-sided lesion was described as still relatively small.
- Vascular supply/location of the right-sided lesion was described in relation to the external iliac and inferior epigastric vessels.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: 
- Mutational analysis of the 2019 left abdominal wall desmoid demonstrated CTNNB1 S45P substitution.
- The right-sided desmoid harbored a different mutation from the 2019 lesion; the specific variant was not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- Left abdominal wall desmoid was managed with active surveillance after biopsy in 2019.
- The left-sided lesion spontaneously regressed.
- The patient was subsequently lost to follow-up for a period.
- She had a pregnancy during the interval before re-presentation.

[ current disease status ]: 
- As of the latest assessment, the prior left-sided lesion had regressed.
- A new right abdominal wall desmoid was present and had enlarged between February 2024 and June 2024.
- The patient had chosen surgery and was awaiting surgical consultation/discussion.

[ other clinical data ]: 
- Past medical history: no relevant comorbidity reported.
- Colonoscopy: negative; performed for unrelated reasons.
- Family history: no relevant family history reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent metastatic rectal cancer with bilateral pulmonary metastases after a disease-free interval of approximately 5–6 years following treatment for localized rectal cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Rectal adenocarcinoma, initially localized at first presentation; subsequently recurrent stage IV disease with unresectable bilateral lung metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of a lung lesion at recurrence confirmed metastatic disease consistent with the primary rectal carcinoma. Mismatch repair protein testing by immunohistochemistry showed deficient MMR.

[ imaging findings ]: Metastatic disease involved both lungs with multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules/lesions. One pulmonary lesion was described as large. Disease was considered unresectable. One lesion had encroached on the bronchus and was associated with hemoptysis. Most recent HRCT thorax showed stable thoracic disease. No liver metastases were identified on the imaging referred to.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Initial molecular profile: BRAF wild type; KRAS wild type.  
- Liquid biopsy NGS (Guardant): KRAS mutation detected, specified as KRAS G12S; TP53 alteration detected; SMAD4 mutation detected.  
- ctDNA/tumor DNA fraction on liquid biopsy was approximately 0.8%.  
- Variant allele fractions of detected alterations were reported as less than 1%.  
- Tumor mutational burden on liquid biopsy was reported as low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial localized rectal cancer had received protocol-based treatment.  
- After metastatic recurrence, first-line FOLFOX plus panitumumab was administered; disease progressed.  
- CAPOX plus bevacizumab was then administered; disease progressed.  
- TAS-102 (Lonsurf) plus bevacizumab was subsequently started and was associated with partial response/stable thoracic disease on latest HRCT.  
- Radiotherapy had been considered for a pulmonary lesion encroaching on the bronchus because of hemoptysis, but no radiotherapy administration was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic rectal cancer with lung-only disease, involving multiple bilateral pulmonary metastases. Disease remained unresectable. On current TAS-102 plus bevacizumab, the patient had partial response with low ctDNA fraction and stable disease on latest HRCT thorax. Hemoptysis had been settling. No hepatic metastases were documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Hemoptysis had occurred in relation to a pulmonary lesion with bronchial encroachment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old woman; para 2, living 2. Non-hypertensive and non-diabetic. Menarche occurred at age 12 years. She had used oral contraceptive pills for 10 years. There was no personal or family history of ovarian, endometrial, or colon cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: She presented in January 2022 with a lower abdominal mass and excessive per-vaginal discharge of approximately 1 year duration.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, grade 2, clinically stage IIB at initial presentation, with a synchronous malignant right ovarian/adnexal tumor reported on core biopsy as serous cystadenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy performed at initial presentation showed squamous cell carcinoma, grade 2. Core biopsy from the right ovarian tumor showed serous cystadenocarcinoma. Following surgery on 29 August 2022, histopathology of the ovary showed squamous metaplasia. Gross section of the cervix showed a visible growth; no further final postoperative cervical histopathology details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: CT scan of the whole abdomen in January 2022 showed a right-sided loculated complex mass adjacent to the right adnexa measuring approximately 6.7 × 7 × 9 cm, with right-sided hydronephrosis and hydroureter due to involvement of the mid portion of the right ureter within the mass. The cervix was enlarged with a cervical growth. CT chest performed on 21 January 2022 showed right lower lobe/right lower zone pulmonary consolidation. CT-guided FNAC of the pulmonary lesion showed an inflammatory lesion. After completion of chemotherapy, chest radiograph showed no consolidation. CT scan of the whole abdomen on 21 July 2022 showed interval increase in size of the pelvic mass, adherence to the abdominal wall, persistent right hydroureter and hydronephrosis, and a homogeneous cervix.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial CA-125 was 223 U/mL. Other tumor markers were within normal limits. Post-chemotherapy CA-125 was 36 U/mL. Serum creatinine was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She received 6 cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin, completed by 11 June 2022. On reassessment after chemotherapy, the abdominal mass had increased in size to approximately 15 × 10 cm, was firm, occupied the hypogastric and right lumbar regions, and had restricted mobility. Pelvic examination after chemotherapy showed a broad, barrel-shaped cervix with no visible growth; the mass remained continuous with the uterus, and both parametria were free. Before chemotherapy, the right parametrium had been involved; after chemotherapy, both parametria were free. Because of radiologic and clinical persistence/progression of the adnexal mass, she underwent laparotomy on 29 August 2022 with modified radical hysterectomy, debulking surgery, appendectomy, omentectomy, and pelvic lymphadenectomy.

[ current disease status ]: After neoadjuvant chemotherapy and before surgery, the pelvic/adnexal mass had enlarged clinically and radiologically, with persistent right hydroureter and hydronephrosis. Postoperative residual disease status was not documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial examination showed a 12 × 10 cm firm abdominal mass in the right lower abdomen. Pelvic examination at presentation showed an endophytic cervical growth; the pelvic mass was continuous with the uterus; the right parametrium was involved and the left parametrium was free. Operative findings on 29 August 2022 included a firm mass fixed and adherent to the rectus sheath/anterior abdominal wall, appendix embedded within the mass, encasement of the ureter and internal iliac artery by the mass, gross right hydroureter, and an enlarged right iliac lymph node.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old woman at initial presentation in November 2011. Migrated from the Philippines to Australia approximately 2 years before presentation. Past medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

[ chief complaint ]: Neck lump at presentation in November 2011.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma arising from follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma, with bilateral thyroid involvement. Subsequent biochemical and radiologic recurrence/metastatic disease involving pulmonary nodules and suspected cervical nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Total thyroidectomy specimen showed a 37 mm poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma arising from follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma in the left lobe, with mitoses and necrosis present. There was an additional focus in the right lobe. Margins were clear. No lymph nodes were included in the specimen.

[ imaging findings ]: Postoperative radioiodine whole-body scan after initial I-131 therapy demonstrated a significant thyroid remnant, localized on SPECT-CT to the right thyroid bed, with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Neck ultrasounds performed over the subsequent approximately 3 years were unremarkable and showed no lymphadenopathy. CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis in 2016 showed no demonstrable actionable findings. FDG PET in June 2017 showed mild uptake in bilateral upper cervical nodes/tonsils and in the left neck, with a few small nodes at the upper limit of normal in left level 3 and left level 4. It also showed a right middle lobe pulmonary nodule measuring just under 1 cm, not significantly FDG avid. Repeat FDG PET in January 2018 was essentially unchanged, with persistent mild uptake in neck nodes, stable size, unchanged right middle lobe nodule, and no bone lesions identified. Repeat CT neck/chest/abdomen in 2018 showed interval growth of the right middle lobe nodule to approximately 10 mm from 6 mm previously, and a new lateral right lower lobe nodule measuring up to 6 mm. I-124 PET dosimetry study performed with thyroxine withdrawal and TSH stimulation showed very faint uptake in the right middle lobe nodule at 24 hours with washout by 96 hours and no meaningful iodine retention. After trametinib re-differentiation therapy, repeat I-124 imaging showed intense iodine uptake in the right middle lobe lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genetic testing on the original tumor specimen identified an NRAS mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: At initial radioiodine treatment, stimulated thyroglobulin was 4.7 with thyroglobulin antibodies in the normal range. Over the next approximately 3 years, thyroglobulin remained low-level and variably slightly detectable, with negative antibodies and suppressed TSH. In early to mid-2016, thyroglobulin began to rise. By May 2017, thyroglobulin was approximately 80. After left level 4 node FNA in 2017, follow-up thyroglobulin had fallen slightly to 64. Through late 2017 to early 2018, thyroglobulin remained in the mid-70s range. During 2018, thyroglobulin rose to closer to 200. At the time of the I-124 PET dosimetry study, stimulated thyroglobulin was nearly 500. Lesional dosimetry before re-differentiation estimated approximately 1 Gy delivered to the right middle lobe nodule per GBq of I-131 administered. After trametinib, lesional dosimetry estimated approximately 75 Gy per GBq to the right middle lobe lesion.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Total thyroidectomy was performed in 2011. Shortly afterward, the patient received 4 GBq (>100 mCi) I-131 with recombinant human TSH stimulation. Post-treatment imaging showed thyroid remnant only and no distant metastatic disease. The patient was subsequently monitored with serial thyroglobulin measurements, neck ultrasound, CT imaging, and FDG PET. Ultrasound-guided FNA of a left level 4 cervical node demonstrated lymphocytes only, with no evidence of malignancy. Because I-124 PET dosimetry showed minimal uptake and no meaningful retention in the pulmonary lesion, I-131 therapy was not given at that time. The patient later received trametinib 2 mg for 4 weeks as re-differentiation therapy. Repeat I-124 imaging after trametinib showed markedly increased iodine avidity. She then received 6 GBq I-131.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial I-124 dosimetry was performed with dual time-point imaging at 24 and 96 hours after administration, using thyroxine withdrawal and TSH stimulation. The pre-re-differentiation pulmonary lesion demonstrated uptake washout by 96 hours, indicating lack of meaningful iodine retention.

That's awesome, Liz. Well, we're going to stop here. A special thanks to David and Jeremy. Great cases, different ones that we've discussed and helping us understand the I-124. reference_conclusion: Serial FDG PET/CT and CT surveillance was undertaken initially, with observation favored over immediate surgery or empiric radioactive iodine while disease remained indolent. After identification of an NRAS mutation, re-differentiation therapy with trametinib 2 mg for 4 weeks was administered, followed by thyroxine withdrawal and TSH stimulation; repeat imaging showed marked restoration of iodine avidity, and therapeutic I-131 was delivered at 6 GBq.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old woman; occupation: ophthalmologist.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation for hereditary breast/ovarian cancer risk in the setting of a strong family history of breast cancer in first-degree and second-degree relatives.

[ diagnosis ]: No personal malignancy was documented. Familial cancer predisposition evaluation was undertaken because of a family history of breast cancer and ovarian cancer. A pathogenic heterozygous BRCA1 mutation had been identified in one affected second-degree relative. The patient’s own germline testing identified a BRCA2 variant of uncertain significance (VUS).

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were available for the patient.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- A second-degree relative had prior testing performed in Canada that identified a heterozygous pathogenic BRCA1 mutation.  
- The patient underwent germline hereditary cancer panel testing in India, which identified a BRCA2 variant of uncertain significance.  
- The patient’s son and daughter underwent testing in India and were reported to carry the same BRCA2 variant of uncertain significance as the patient.  
- The BRCA1 pathogenic variant identified in the second-degree relative and the BRCA2 VUS identified in the patient/family were reported from different laboratories.

[ laboratory results ]: No non-genetic laboratory results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Germline testing was performed for the patient.  
- Germline testing was also performed for both her son and daughter.  
- No cancer-directed treatment was documented for the patient.

[ current disease status ]: No personal diagnosis of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, or other malignancy was documented for the patient at the time of referral. She remained under hereditary cancer risk evaluation.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Family history included multiple relatives with breast cancer in both first-degree and second-degree relatives.  
- Two second-degree relatives were reported to have cancer.  
- One first-degree relative was reported to have breast and ovarian cancer.  
- The first-degree relative with breast and ovarian cancer had not undergone genetic testing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old man; retired government employee. Primary caregiver was his wife. Son was identified as the family decision-maker and was living abroad, visiting India intermittently. Multiple comorbidities were present and were described as well controlled.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent oral cavity malignancy with a large proliferative lesion protruding from the oral cavity, submental ulceration, pain, discharging malignant ulcer, fever, bleeding from the oral lesion, purulent discharge from the tracheostomy wound, and desaturation. He had developed stridor requiring emergency airway intervention.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent carcinoma of the tongue with advanced locoregional disease. Current biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy showed squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Large proliferative lesion protruded from the oral cavity. Ulceration was present in the submental region. No additional radiologic findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: PD-L1 expression was 40%.

[ laboratory results ]: No specific laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- 2010: Treated for carcinoma tongue.
- 2022: Developed recurrence; underwent radical re-irradiation and chemotherapy.
- Subsequently developed stridor and underwent emergency tracheostomy.
- Underwent palliative debulking of the tumor protruding from the oral cavity under local anesthesia to improve oral closure and comfort.
- Received oral metronomic therapy and immunotherapy.
- Completed 2 cycles of immunotherapy.
- Developed moderate tumor bleed; underwent bilateral lingual artery and left facial artery embolization, after which bleeding ceased.
- Following embolization, further oncologic treatment was stopped and care was transitioned to comfort-focused management.

[ current disease status ]: Advanced recurrent head and neck squamous cell carcinoma after prior surgery/radiation-systemic treatment exposure, with poor functional condition, poor nutritional status, tracheostomy in situ, malignant ulceration, and prior tumor bleeding controlled after embolization. He was transferred to an assisted living facility for end-of-life care according to patient and family preference.

[ other clinical data ]: 
- Communication was impaired because he was unable to speak, although he was able to write.
- Home assessment documented fever, bleeding from the oral lesion, discharge from the malignant ulcer, purulent tracheostomy wound discharge, and desaturation, prompting hospital admission.
- Neck was described as woody bilaterally after two courses of irradiation.

Last but not the least, allocate time for counseling and educating the caregiver and suggest strategies to sort of empower them and identify caregiver burnout. Regarding the next question, so usually patients discharged from our hospital while transitioning to home care, usually they are given a well-formulated care plan usually with specific instructions for the home care physician. Thank you, thank you, Dr. Anupama. I think the transitional care plan is what we call in our hospital for all patients who get discharged. But now when it comes to when it when it is a paid facility, we are expected to give the best possible care best possible nutrition nursing. So this stigma is definitely reducing. And again, when it comes to challenges associated with assisted living, see, it is enormous. Okay, first of all, the clinical challenges itself. because managing the polypharmacy delirium behavioral symptoms this is for a geriatric patient when when it comes to oncology again the everything double and triple fold and then need for trained geriatric staff so that is something which is quite challenging because when you scale something like an assisted living when you want to have more centers like this training them with good clinical exposure is very very vital And often we found that we cannot restrict them with an SOP, especially when you handle geriatric patients. And most often we go out and ask them, are you planning a travel? Are you asking these for this? And again, the most important challenge is the financial challenge because most of the patients pay out of pocket. And it is really long term. And when it comes, you know, they have to repeatedly pay and when the care level goes up, the cost goes up. So that is when the patients feel the need for the insurance, the long term insurance, which is non existent here. So challenges are there. But still, with evolving needs, various models coming up, this is definitely a boon for geriatric oncology patients, especially this patient made use of our facility till his end of life. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Vasant.

So moving on to our patient, our patient was transferred to assisted living facility to receive end of life care in accordance with the patient and his family's preference. So as Dr. Vasant has told, this family had a very elderly caregiver. They wanted to have an end of life in a facility where that could happen in a very dignified manner. So we had also formulated the care plan for him, for which we have to do a goals of care discussion. Goals of care discussion is basically to find out what the patient wants and to match the care along, aligned with the wishes of the patient. So the general things that have discussed are usually regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation, any medical intervention, yes or no, or if needed. life-sustaining measure and need for any NG or a PEG insertion. So and also to discuss regarding the preferred place of care, whether they want it at home or at a facility. And which is regarding the final rights also needs to be discussed. Usually we have found a lot of patients who actually tell us where to do the last cremation and what kind of prayers they wanted. And many people even select the wood for their coffin box. So much is there, and all these make a lot of impact for them, because they feel that that is the last resting place for them. So right to refuse treatment. So any patient who is capable of making a decision can refuse treatment, and we should not force them to have any treatment. So this is in accordance with the judgment from the Supreme Court. So our patient passed with dignity, and his family also was with him in the assisted living facility.
Thank you, Dr. Bharati. I think we just finished on time and hand over the session back to the organizers.

Given poor performance status and lack of suitability for aggressive intravenous chemotherapy, oral metronomic therapy and immunotherapy were administered; after subsequent moderate tumor bleeding, bilateral lingual and left facial artery embolization was performed with control of bleeding. Thereafter, further oncologic treatment was discontinued and care was transitioned to comfort-focused end-of-life management, with transfer to an assisted living facility in accordance with the patient’s and family’s preferences.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Slow-growing right parotid mass present for approximately 1 year, with occasional discomfort.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the right parotid gland with oncocytic features.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial fine-needle aspiration of the right parotid lesion showed clusters of oncocytic cells with bland cytologic features and was interpreted as a low-grade oncocytic neoplasm, favored Warthin tumor; oncocytoma remained in the differential. Intraoperative frozen specimens from parotid tissue and proximal parotid duct were suspicious for carcinoma but were not definitive. Permanent pathology from subtotal parotid resection showed a high-grade salivary gland neoplasm with oncocytic features, most consistent with high-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Additional immunostains were consistent with mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Parotid ultrasound performed in April demonstrated a right parotid lesion. CT neck with contrast showed an enhancing right parotid mass involving both the superficial and deep lobes, without obvious CT evidence of perineural spread and without cervical lymphadenopathy. MRI showed an enhancing 3 cm lesion in the posterior right parotid gland. No metastatic disease was identified. There was questioned facial nerve enhancement in the mastoid segment near the stylomastoid foramen. No neck adenopathy was seen on MRI.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Salivary gland fusion panel identified a MAML2-CRTC1 fusion.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent subtotal right parotid resection with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was described as large, multilobulated, involving both deep and superficial lobes, and adherent to the main trunk of the facial nerve and pes anserinus. The facial nerve was left intact at that operation; at the end of the case, the main trunk did not stimulate. She subsequently underwent mastoidectomy with facial nerve dissection, transection of the nerve at the second genu with proximal nerve margin sent for pathology, completion total parotidectomy, resection of the nerve at the stylomastoid foramen as part of the parotid specimen, right neck dissection levels II-IV, left adipofascial anterolateral thigh free flap reconstruction, and additional facial reanimation procedures. She subsequently completed radiation therapy.

[ current disease status ]: She had completed radiation therapy.

[ other clinical data ]: On initial examination, there was a firm inferior right parotid mass abutting the tragus without overlying skin changes. Facial nerve function was fully intact and symmetric bilaterally at presentation. No palpable neck masses were present. No sensory deficits were documented on examination.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 88-year-old woman. Never smoker. Functionally independent and living alone.

[ chief complaint ]: Right facial numbness, initially described as vague discomfort and pressure in the right preauricular/periauricular region, progressing to hypoesthesia in the right mandibular dentition.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade salivary ductal carcinoma of the deep lobe of the right parotid gland with clinical inferior alveolar nerve involvement; clinical stage IVA. Disease later progressed in the right mandible without documented distant metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Image-guided core needle biopsy of the right parotid lesion demonstrated high-grade salivary ductal carcinoma. Subsequent biopsy of abnormal mandibular/oral mucosa after radiotherapy demonstrated progression of disease.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial brain MRI demonstrated a poorly infiltrating mass in the deep lobe of the right parotid with concern for perineural spread.  
- PET-CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic right deep lobe parotid tumor, a questionable mildly avid right level II node, an avid focus in the right posterior mandible, and no evidence of distant disease.  
- Repeat MRI with cranial nerve protocol demonstrated possible extension to the glenoid fossa and possible involvement of cranial nerves V, VII, and IX, greater petrosal nerve, and extension to the dura through the jugular foramen.  
- Facial nerve function was clinically intact. Tongue sensation was present.  
- Post-radiotherapy MRI obtained approximately 3 months after treatment demonstrated complete response at the primary parotid site, with new lytic lesions/progression involving the right mandible extending along the mandibular body to the right parasymphyseal mandible.  
- No distant metastatic disease was documented on interval assessment.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HER2 immunostaining was equivocal. HER2 FISH testing did not demonstrate amplification.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Definitive full-dose radiation therapy was administered to the primary site, without concurrent systemic therapy. Lower-dose neck irradiation was also delivered.  
- Radiation therapy was tolerated well.  
- Approximately 3 months after completion of radiation therapy, the patient developed discomfort in a molar; biopsy confirmed disease progression in the mandible despite MRI evidence of complete response at the primary site.  
- The patient subsequently underwent salvage cervical resection for mandibular disease.

[ current disease status ]: Status post salvage cervical resection for progressive mandibular disease. Post-treatment imaging was pending. No distant disease had been documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Head and neck review of systems was otherwise unremarkable at presentation, including no dysphagia. A questioned decrease in facial mobility was not confirmed on examination. The right posterior mandibular PET-avid focus had initially been considered possibly odontogenic/inflammatory versus tumor.

reference_conclusion: Multidisciplinary review concluded that the primary high-grade salivary duct carcinoma was resectable and that surgical resection was the preferred initial management, with anticipated postoperative external beam radiation therapy given the high likelihood of residual microscopic disease and the need to treat the neck. The patient elected definitive full-dose radiation therapy as a palliative-intent nonsurgical approach. Following subsequent mandibular progression, repeat multidisciplinary discussion supported cervical resection of the mandibular disease, with the patient proceeding with surgery after counseling regarding the aggressive biology and high risk of recurrence or metastasis.
reference_conclusion_quote: But overall, that surgical resection, and this was considered a resectable tumor, was the recommendation. But ultimately, she decided to pursue radiation therapy. [...] It was definitive, but it was presented, as Dr. Lee alluded to, as a palliative. But yes, it was a full dose. [...] So in general, what we've been doing is do adjuvant external beam radiation therapy, whether IMRT or proton, to allow us to shape the field better. And plus, this is high grade, even though clinically there is no evidence of nodes and salivary duct is very lymphatic prone, so we probably have to treat the neck anyway. [...] So again, we discussed it at tumor board and all of this great points came up and she again met with two of us and radiation oncology and medical oncology and palliative care. And this time she decided to pursue cervical resection, understanding that this is a very aggressive diagnosis and very likely to recur or metastasize.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Increasing left hip pain over several months.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with osseous metastasis to the left iliac/acetabular region, mediastinal/subcarinal nodal metastasis, and subsequent right cerebellar brain metastasis. Pathologic stage after nephrectomy was pT2 Nx M1.

[ histopathology results ]: Open right radical nephrectomy specimen showed a 9 x 9 cm right mid-pole clear cell renal cell carcinoma, Fuhrman/ISUP grade 2, without sarcomatoid features. There was no extracapsular spread. Extensive adhesions to the inferior vena cava were present, and IVC repair was required intraoperatively because of invasion of several accessory veins. Following resection of the brain lesion, pathology confirmed metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Brain metastasis resection was margin-negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial MRI demonstrated a large lytic mass in the left iliac wing.  
- Initial CT chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a very large heterogeneous hyperenhancing right renal mass with central necrosis, most compatible with renal cell carcinoma; a lytic focus in the superior acetabular region/left iliac bone; and a subcarinal lymph node measuring approximately 2.2 cm in short axis.  
- Bone-window imaging initially showed thinning of the cortex of the left iliac wing lesion without cortical breakthrough.  
- Postoperative restaging CT demonstrated progression of the left iliac lytic lesion with cortical erosion and extension into adjacent soft tissues.  
- CNS imaging obtained before high-dose IL-2 was normal.  
- Approximately 1 year after observation off therapy, brain MRI demonstrated a new isolated right cerebellar metastasis measuring 2.3 cm, with hemorrhagic features including a hemosiderin rim, surrounding edema on T2/FLAIR, and avid contrast enhancement on post-contrast T1 imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Post-nephrectomy LDH was normal.  
- Hemoglobin was improving to near normal postoperatively.  
- Renal function after nephrectomy stabilized at creatinine approximately 1.3.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent open right radical nephrectomy with IVC repair. Surgery was associated with substantial blood loss.  
- Left hip pain postoperatively was mild and relieved by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; radiation therapy was initially deferred.  
- Received high-dose interleukin-2. First cycle: 10 doses, limited by severe diarrhea and hallucinations. Second cycle (1B): 7 doses, limited by hypotension, diarrhea, pruritus, and somnolence. Subsequently completed cycles 3A and 3B. Best response was prolonged stable disease; mediastinal disease resolved, and the lytic iliac lesion remained stable.  
- After inability to tolerate further high-dose IL-2, he was observed off therapy.  
- Following development of symptomatic right cerebellar metastasis, he was admitted, treated with corticosteroids, underwent surgical resection of the lesion with negative margins, and then received postoperative stereotactic radiosurgery to the resection cavity.  
- He was then started on sunitinib on a 4-weeks-on/2-weeks-off schedule.  
- He also received denosumab for bone-directed antiresorptive therapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- ECOG performance status after nephrectomy was 0-1.  
- Left hip pain was initially mild and NSAID-responsive.  
- He later developed increasing neck pain and headaches at the time the cerebellar metastasis was diagnosed.

reference_discussion.text: All right, let's start with this first case. And this is a case of metastatic clear cell kidney cancer. And this is a fairly young man, 58 years old, who presented with increasing hip pain. He was a truck driver and felt pain while he was hauling boxes. And over several months, he consulted with an outside physician and eventually an orthopedic surgeon over his increasing left hip pain. He was found on MRI, actually, to have a large lytic left iliac wing mass, and referred to orthopedic surgery for further evaluation. A CT of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis did show a large right renal mass consistent with kidney cancer, and a lytic focus in his superior acetabular region of the left iliac bone, which was concerning for metastatic RCC. He also had a small subcrinal node, and we're gonna show you some imaging from this case. Dr. Gupta?

Thank you very much. So this is the original CT scan that we see here of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. And in the upper image, you can see, as denoted by the arrow, a very large, heterogeneous-appearing renal mass that is hyper-enhancing. And it is most compatible with renal cell carcinoma. On the bottom image, what you can see is the subcoronal lymph node that was referred to. And that measures approximately 2.2 centimeters in its short axis diameter. As we go here, we have another image seeing the same tumor at a different level. And this is really blown up on the bottom there to illustrate some of the different features of this mass. So there are central portions of necrosis inside of this mass, which is the low density areas within it. As we take a look at the bone windows, we can see, as denoted by the arrow, the yellow arrow there, that is the lytic mass that is seen inside the left iliac wing. And at this time there, it is beginning to thin the cortex of the bone, but not erode through it.

Okay, so back to the case. This patient underwent a open right radical nephrectomy and repair of the IVC, which was due to several accessory veins being invaded. And his pathologic specimen revealed a fairly large nine by nine centimeter right midpole clear cell renal cell carcinoma. It was classified as grade two, had no sarcomatoid features, pathologically staged as a T2NXM1 tumor. There was no extra capsular spread, but extensive adhesions to the IVC, which required repair and was associated with a great deal of blood loss at the time of surgery. So when he was assessed in our clinic post-operatively, he underwent restaging scans and blood work. His LDH was normal. His hemoglobin was improving, basically up to normal. His left hip pain was mild and relieved by non-steroidals, and thus radiation was deferred at this point. His functional status was back to really a ECOG of zero or to one, and his renal function was now at his new normal of about 1.3. Restaging scans at this point did show, though, progression in his left ilium and the lytic lesion with a soft tissue component. Dr. Gupta will review this again for us.

So this is a follow-up CT scan that is done, and if we take a look at the top image, we can see that is on bone windows, and we can see that the lesion in the left iliac wing is certainly increased in size from the initial imaging. What the soft tissue component that is being referred to is much better delineated on the soft tissue windows on the bottom of the image. where you can see that the lesion actually goes from the bone, now erodes through the cortex, and actually the high density that is pointed to by the arrow is actually showing where there's soft tissue tumor extending from the bone into the soft tissues adjacent.

Great, thank you. So at this point, I'm going to pose four questions for my expert discussant, Dr. Dan George. Number one is, what do you consider in 2016 to be the optimal frontline management strategy for this kind of patient who is considered good risk, has really two sites of metastatic disease at this point, a solitary bone metastasis, really minimally symptomatic, and a lymph node metastasis?

Yeah, you know, Andy, this is a great question. This is a scenario that is not uncommon. Unfortunately for renal cell carcinoma, we don't screen typically for this cancer. And so probably about a quarter of patients will present with metastatic disease as this gentleman did. And yet he's still got a relatively low volume disease at this point in time. He's only got a couple of sites of disease. His primary tumor is out. He's got a good performance status. The first thing we typically do for cases like this is we'll do something called risk stratification. And there's a couple of different scales we can use. Historically, the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center scale is what we've used. It includes five factors including elevated LDH, which he didn't have. uh... anemia which he does have a little bit of anemia uh... a uh... decreased performance status of ecog two or less or worse and he's he's clearly not that uh... a uh... presence of his primary tumor in place and elevated calcium, or instead of the presence of primary tumor, the time to systemic therapy. So the fact that he's presenting with metastatic disease that's mildly symptomatic, that's progressive in this time point, we're gonna start systemic therapy within a year of his diagnosis. And the fact that he's got some anemia, although it's mild, gives him sort of two intermediate, two risk factors, two poor risk factors, and that makes him an intermediate risk patient. So, even though I think on the surface, you know, this is a gentleman who has kind of, you know, low volume disease, I am a little bit concerned about the fact he's got a couple of risk factors and he's got this bony lesion that is in his pelvis and has caused some appearance of destruction. So, one option for somebody like this would be to start with systemic therapy. Another option would be to palliate that, even though it's mildly symptomatic, that bone lesion with some form of radiation therapy to treat that. Dr. Kim, do you want to comment on that before I talk about the systemic therapy? What's the role for radiation therapy in terms of palliation for a case like this?

So, radiation therapy is very effective in palliating pain, especially if we catch it earlier on, if it's a smaller lesion. I would say that the pain control, if you look at all studies, is somewhere around 80%. complete response and partial response lumped into that group. Of course, a smaller number have complete pain response, but a lot of times we're able to knock down the pain medicine a notch or two, which is very helpful in terms of quality of life. Now something in the pelvis we also want to be maybe more aggressive because it's a weight-bearing bone and so that can also affect quality of life. Usually radiation is very well tolerated because it's a focused beam, especially when we target bone and muscle. There's not symptoms like nausea or diarrhea. Sometimes patients have fatigue, but for the most part it's very well tolerated. So I think it's a, you know, depending on how fast they need to get to systemic chemotherapy, we could do anywhere from one to five to ten treatments depending on their performance status, depending on the durability of response that we want to achieve. So if we're expecting this person to live a long time, then we would choose 10, because in studies we see that 10 treatments, although equivalent to pain relief to one treatment, the need for retreatment is higher in the one fraction.

And this patient being intermediate risk, but with good performance status young and with overall low volume of disease, we'd expect him to live probably close to two and a half years on average, with some patients living much longer than that. So certainly, I think a more definitive course would be reasonable. From a systemic therapy standpoint, you know, he's really got sort of two options. Traditionally for patients like this, we'd consider a high-dose IL-2 therapy as an option. Now, that's not necessarily for all renal cell carcinoma patients. For our patients that are over 70, We worry about the cardiovascular strain in that population, and the risk of complications goes way up. So we generally think of that for a little bit younger patient population, and certainly a healthy patient population. But he has no cardiac risk factors that we know of at this point. He's somebody that is young and in good performance. So I would consider him a candidate for high docile tooth therapy. And the other advantage there is that if he does have some progression, particularly if we're able to kind of control that pelvic disease, then that lymph node disease or other sites of disease, even if that progresses, it's unlikely in that sort of three-month window of time that we would give the hydrosal to and look for a response, that the progression would get out of hand. So that would be an option four. The alternative option would be treatment with a VEGF receptor, tyrosine kinase inhibitor, like Synitinib or Pazopanib. And these are standard therapies now. They're available, widely used, been around for a number of years, and have a higher response rate than Hydosil-2, which traditionally has a response rate probably somewhere around 15 to 25% partial response rate, but maybe only a 5% or less complete response rate. For the VEGF receptor TKIs, the response rates are probably closer to somewhere around 30 to 40 percent in some cases for partial responses. And for stable disease, another 30 to 40 percent. So a number, the majority of patients showing at least some degree of tumor regression, some minor responses or whatnot. So that's an attractive option for many patients as well because it has overall a higher likelihood of controlling disease up front 2, because it seems to be tolerated in a wider population of patients. It does have its degree of side effects, but it's also active following hydrosol 2. So for a patient like this that chooses hydrosol 2, it can be that he can go then on to a VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor after that. So the way I present this to patients is typically If you're going to do that hydroxyl 2 therapy, let's do it up front. If we think that it's a reasonably safe window to try that in, and if it doesn't work, we still have this VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase strategy to try. If this isn't something that they want to put themselves through, or we're concerned about risk, or we're concerned about rapid progression, or more symptomatic disease, then we'll start with that VEGF receptor TKI up front.

Great. Thanks, Dan. I think that addresses questions one and three, but how about number two? So what trials would you consider 2016, 2017 to be the most important in this frontline setting and that may change the standard of care in the future? What would you be looking for for a guy like this?

Yeah, you know, there's several trials that I think this year have been real paradigm shifts for the field. And of course, we don't know the results of these yet, but I say paradigm shifts because it's really paradigm challenging studies where we're really looking at immunotherapies, novel immunotherapies, not hydroxyl 2, but newer, more targeted immunotherapies either combined with VEGF-targeted strategies or against VEGF-targeted strategies. And, well, one of these includes the study of ipilimumab and nivolumab versus sinitinib. Now, that study is just closed to accrual, and we're awaiting the results, but that's been a recent study, and we look forward to seeing if there's a population of patients or if all patients in general benefit from that upfront use of ipilimumab, nivolumab instead of a VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor. A second study is looking at the use of avastin and atezolizumab, a PD-L1 inhibitor, in combination versus sunitinib. And so that strategy there combines a VEGF inhibition with a PD-L1 inhibition and seeing if that's better than the traditional VEGF receptor TKI. And then a third strategy is looking at a vaccine, a dendritic cell vaccine made by the patient's own nephrectomy tumor And then that's used to create RNA from the tumor, to create a dendritic cell vaccine to stimulate the immune system in the setting of standard of care, Sinitinib or Pazopanib. And again, compared to Sinitinib or Pazopanib alone as standard of care. So again, three strategies involving immunotherapy in comparison to standard VEGF receptor TKI.

Great, and the final point is we've all heard about asymptomatic brain metastases and the question is when would you scan a patient with kidney cancers brain, CT, MRI, would you consider that in this case?

You know, this can be a challenge. I generally do consider, you know, especially before embarking on something like Heidel's interleukin 2 or a clinical trial, that some kind of CNS monitoring is warranted because we can find asymptomatic lesions in these patients, and when we find them asymptomatically, they're easier to treat, and they can be unifocal, and that can have a better prognosis. Problem is, sometimes insurance will deny that if it's not a symptom-driven indication. So that's something we do our peer-to-peer consultations on. I think we all challenge with that, but it's something that, in general, I think is worth considering in most patients.

So he actually had CNS imaging that was normal at the time, and he elected to go with what you described as IL-2, and high-dose IL-2 is administered in the hospital. He actually got 10 doses in his first cycle. This was limited by pretty severe diarrhea, some hallucinations. The second cycle, 1B, he got seven, and now this was limited by low blood pressure, diarrhea, itching, somnolence, pretty standard. He had stable disease after his first course. He actually got all the way through cycles 3A and 3B, did pretty well with prolonged stable disease. And at that point, he wasn't able to get much more high-dose IL-2 because of intolerance. And we simply observed him off therapy. Now, he didn't have a partial remission, other than in his mediastinum, which disappeared. His lytic lesion remained stable. So he had kind of a mixed stable disease, but symptomatically he was improved and we elected to observe him. Now about a year later, now off of all therapy, he developed some increasing neck and headaches. And he had an MRI which showed a new right cerebellar brain metastasis, 2.3 centimeters, and Dr. Gupta will show us this.

So this is the MRI of the brain, and we have two images here. And the first image demonstrates this large, isolated right cerebellar hemisphere met that has some pretty characteristic features of a bleeding lesion in that it has this hemocyterin rim of black or dark ipo-intensity around it. And then also it has these waves of high signal surrounding it on the T2-weighted flare image there, and that basically is some edema. And then when we take a look at the other image on the other side, what we can see here is very bright contrast enhancement on the axial T1 post-contrast image. Very compatible with what you'd expect to see in the setting of a metastatic renal cell carcinoma to the cerebellar hemisphere.

So let me start with Dr. Kim here. He's in the hospital, symptomatic. This is a fairly sizable tumor in a difficult region. Would you, as a radiation oncologist, recommend stereotactic radiation to this lesion, or would you suggest that the neurosurgical colleagues get involved?

I would talk to neurosurgery about this case. Anytime there's a solitary lesion that is sizable, not like two millimeters, but something like this, anytime there's any kind of edema, mass effect, we always want to consult our neurosurgery colleagues to take care of this.

Great. And fortunately, they agreed with you, and he was admitted, placed on some steroids. He went to surgery right away, actually, and had a full margin negative resection. It was clear cell, renal cell, and he got SRS to the bed post-operatively and did quite well with this, actually. Systemically, he was free of disease other than a stable lytic lesion in his left iliac. So Dan, let's go back to you again. So after failure of IL-2 now, even though he's not officially on it, he got his three courses, progressed with an isolated CNS metastasis, but still has some disease outside of his brain. What would you do at this point? Do you feel like the radiation was necessary for a completely resected brain metastasis? Would you consider whole brain radiation? And how would you image his brain from now on?

Yeah, you know, this is a challenging case because he doesn't really have measurable disease for us to judge a systemic therapy and whether or not it's working. As I mentioned earlier, our VEGF receptor TKIs, they have some side effects. They can cause you know, fatigue and high blood pressure and GI symptoms, and they don't work 100% of the time. So it's nice to be able to have some measurable disease to see that we're really having a positive impact on the patient, even if it's just stable disease in that setting, and to put up with the additional side effects that they'd have. But this case is different because this case had a known metastatic progression in the brain resected and we would be concerned that there could be other sites of disease in the brain or other parts of the body that would occur in the near future. So one option is to do whole brain radiation to kind of protect that try to treat that microscopic, if you will, other sites of disease before they get bigger. The other option would be use a drug like senitinib or pazopanib to try to change the blood flow in the brain in a way that might alter that tumor vasculature and prevent that kind of progression in the future. And I generally, for a patient with a single lesion like this, prefer the systemic therapy first, because I think it still keeps open the salvage radiation option later. And it is something that we're worried about progression, not just in the brain, but elsewhere. And we do know that these drugs can penetrate the blood-brain barrier and get in there and prevent that kind of a site of disease and show response in the brain as well as other organs. So I feel pretty comfortable that, you know, that would suffice in a case like this. So for me, I would probably start this patient on a VEGF receptor TKI. Great.
And you'd image his CNS along with restaging scans along the way?
Absolutely. Especially where he's had this lesion now, he'll be at risk for either recurrence or for new lesions in that organ.

So that's exactly what we did and over six years ago he was started on the typical four and two schedule sunitinib. He achieved a near complete remission. He had a little bit of sclerosis in his left hip but his soft tissue components in his chest disappeared. He was put on denosumab as as an agent for anti-resorptive therapy to improve his bone density and reduce his risk of fracture. He did have some difficulties with SNITINIB at this full dose and schedule. Really around year three or four, it became even more challenging, diarrhea, fatigue, and we switched him to the two-in-one schedule, and he actually remained in a near-CR for an additional two years, so this is about six years of a VEGF TKI. So he did quite well, and he actually developed some other medical complications really unrelated to his kidney cancer and aspiration pneumonia. And because of this, we actually had to stop his sunitinib. He was in a near CR, and the discussion came up about, does he really need this drug anymore? So this is a little bit of an unusual circumstance, but let me just ask you your experience. In a patient who's doing so well, have you actually stopped sunitinib, and what's been your experience with that?

Yeah, you know, this is a really great response and duration of response. And very fortunate for this case, it's not typical for synitinib, but we do see it. And in fact, there's been some nice literature out of France, kind of a retrospective collective that has sort of categorized a number of complete responses, either with drug alone or drug plus focal therapy. And the results are interesting, because about half of the patients in those scenarios actually did take a treatment break, and about half of those patients relapsed, and about half hadn't as of about two years. So there is a proportion of these patients that we can stop systemic therapy on, and they don't at least immediately recur. I can't say that that's cure, but I can say that there is sort of durable disease control in a number of these patients. So it's a very reasonable thing to do, particularly in somebody that's having other medical complications.

So he actually, about eight months after stopping the Sunitinib, developed increasing pain and disease progression. This was about a year ago and Sunitinib was restarted and he actually subsequently responded to therapy. So jumping to the final question is, let's say this patient now in 2016 progresses on Sunitinib, what would be your 2016 standard of care following a frontline VEGF TKI?

Yeah, you know, this is very challenging because, again, this is an outlier case. This is a guy that's responded now for five years now to VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase therapy. And it wouldn't be unreasonable to say, gee, he did so well on this one, could we try another one? But just in the last three months now, we have a new FDA approval in this space with a drug called Nivolumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, that has demonstrated a real survival advantage, not against VEGF receptor TKI, but against an mTOR inhibitor, Everolimus. But the overall survival associated with that agent was very, very impressive. It was almost two years. or a little over two years median overall survival. And it's impressive as well because we didn't see a change really in the progression-free survival. Median progression-free survival is around four to five months for both Everolimus as well as for Nivolumab. and yet we see this dramatic difference in improved overall survival associated with this. So to me that says that treating with an immunotherapy next like Nivolumab, even if it doesn't show a partial response, which 20% of patients did and have a really sustained duration of response in that scenario, that very well could happen. But even if that doesn't happen, if they end up with some progression over the next four or five months, that's a patient that's still likely to live for another couple years and very well could respond again to our VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase. strategies. So to me, this is another sort of ideal circumstance where we might try an agent like that. And again, what we're looking for is any kind of, sure, we'd love to see a partial response, but even stable disease to kind of keep that therapy going, but know that they can respond and benefit to subsequent therapy after that.

reference_conclusion: Following resection of the symptomatic solitary right cerebellar metastasis, adjuvant stereotactic radiosurgery to the resection cavity was administered. Given metastatic progression after high-dose IL-2 and residual extracranial disease, systemic therapy with a VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor was initiated, specifically sunitinib on the standard 4-weeks-on/2-weeks-off schedule. Ongoing surveillance was to include CNS imaging together with routine restaging studies. Denosumab was added as anti-resorptive therapy to improve bone density and reduce fracture risk.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Bilateral renal masses at initial presentation. At 10-year follow-up after nephron-sparing surgery, enlarged left renal hilar/retroperitoneal lymph nodes were identified.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral papillary renal cell carcinoma, type 1. Pathologic stage after staged bilateral partial nephrectomies: right renal tumor pT1b; left renal tumor pT1a. Subsequent nodal recurrence/metastatic disease in the left renal hilar/retroperitoneal lymph nodes, biopsy-proven metastatic papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Renal biopsy demonstrated papillary type 1 kidney tumor. Following staged bilateral partial nephrectomies, both renal tumors were papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated bilateral renal masses. The left renal mass was described as essentially entirely endophytic. Small bowel was within approximately 1.5 cm of the left renal lesion. The right renal lesion was not in close proximity to the hepatic flexure of the colon. At year 10 follow-up imaging, there was no tumor identified in either kidney, but there was a chain of enlarged lymph nodes along the left renal hilum/left renal artery in the retroperitoneum. Staging imaging demonstrated disease confined to the retroperitoneum. Brain imaging was negative. Bone scan was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline genetic panel was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent staged bilateral partial nephrectomies for bilateral renal masses. Postoperatively, surveillance imaging was performed according to guideline-based follow-up for the first 5 years, with no evidence of local recurrence. Imaging intervals were then extended to every 2 years. Imaging at year 7 was unremarkable. At year 10, nodal recurrence in the left renal hilum/retroperitoneum was detected.

[ current disease status ]: Isolated nodal recurrence along the left renal hilum/retroperitoneum after staged bilateral partial nephrectomies, biopsy-proven metastatic papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma, with staging imaging demonstrating disease confined to the retroperitoneum.

[ other clinical data ]: Bilateral renal masses at presentation and young age prompted hereditary evaluation. Concordant histology was present bilaterally. No evidence of intracranial or osseous metastatic disease was identified on staging studies.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, based on this imaging, the left kidney mass is mostly endophytic. I mean, pretty much actually entirely endophytic. A little bit of small bowel is coming about within a centimeter and a half of it, and that is treatable. The one on the right, I believe the hepatic flexure of the colon is again not too close. So yes, both of the lesions are treatable with SBRT.

Hey, Rakib, can I ask a question, maybe an obvious or silly question? You know, obviously when it comes to radiation treatment, you know, very familiar with the sensitivity of bowel and stuff, but what about some of the other organs? Do you even worry about liver proximity or spleen? Like, in my head, I sort of figure, just radiate it, what's the worst that can happen? But that may not be true, I guess.

Yeah, very good question. And I actually hear that often. So liver, as you know, it's what we call a parallel functioning organ. You can cut out half the liver, throw it out and patient's going to do perfectly okay. There's so much reserve. So liver, we don't worry about at all. Something like that is a serial functioning organ, which is colon or small bowel we worry about because you damage one part of it, it renders the entire organ non-functional. So that's something we worry about. Spleen, as you also know, splenectomy patients do perfectly okay. So yes, spleen doesn't bother me, liver doesn't bother me, you know, lung doesn't bother me. Large bowel is a lot more radio-resistant than small bowel. So large bowel for the most part doesn't bother me too much. Small bowel is the only thing that if it comes to proximity or if it's up against the tumor, then that bothers me.
Thank you. Excellent. Going back to Brendan then, this patient comes to you, 45-year-old, multiple renal masses. What are you thinking here and how do you start to work this patient up?

Yeah, so bilateral renal masses is not an uncommon thing I see in probably you too, Mark. You know, these patients tend to, and I think appropriately so, go to tertiary centers because the level of complexity does jump up once both kidneys are involved. The first thing, you know, that I think any of us do is do a good history and physical. History means a lot. This patient's age is, you know, they have a couple red flags, sort of, that I would make sure, you know, the trainees that are with me sort of know. One is the age, right? We all know that Average age for RCC development still right now is around 64, 65 in the US, so this is considerably younger. So that should be a red flag. In addition, having bilateral renal masses, which radiographically look to be homogeneous, and we know 90% of the time, pathology should be congruent. I also tell all the trainees, when you see bilateral renal masses, the diagnosis for clear cell RCC goes down the list. right, whereas most renal masses we see that's at the top of our list. When you have bilateral, the development of hereditary syndromes, which can include all varieties of RCC, but more commonly we see the papillaries and the chromophobes and the onchocytomas show up. So that's another sort of red flag. In these cases, I almost always get a biopsy. When both kidneys are at risk, I want to know what I'm dealing with so I can counsel the patient because Sometimes, rarely, you do have to think outside the box. So, and this is the kind of case where if we get some really rare things, we may have to get, you know, Dr. McKay involved. We may need to, you know, you can't always just tackle these surgically because sometimes they're hereditary or other medical issues. So, history and physical, and then a biopsy, and then I usually try and get them to genetics if I think it's going to affect my management up front. So that's sort of the first couple of steps before I come up with a treatment plan.

Fantastic. We thought very similarly to you. So yeah, you mentioned genetics. Just my only question is, I guess you said if it affects the treatment plan, so sometimes before surgery, sometimes after surgery, depending.

Yeah, a lot of times, I'd say about one out of four cases, I need it before surgery because to be honest, most of it comes in handy after you've taken care of the tumors that are there. It's what are you going to do with the next one? How are you going to follow those patients?

In this case, we did germline genetics. Actually, the germline panel was negative. We did a renal biopsy and it was a papillary type 1 kidney tumor. You know, Dr. McKay, we talked about the use of systemic therapy for a small renal mass in a clear cell tumor. Now we have a papillary tumor, what we used to call PAP type 1, now just kind of papillary RCC. Any role for systemic therapy in the localized setting in this disease space?

No is the sinful answer. So there's no level one evidence on utilization of perioperative systemic therapy for a localized papillary RCC, whether that be pre or post treatment. Now, I think that this case is complicated, and I think sometimes patients who present with complicated bilateral renal masses, particularly renal masses where they're larger or, you know, T3 or budding other structures, and they're going to be undergoing a staged approach to target both tumors, sometimes in that context, you almost treat the individual like a locally advanced unresectable patient and give them, you know, the best upfront systemic therapy for cytoreduction to see if you can potentially convert them to a resectable status. So that could be considered in this context, but just because one side is a papillary doesn't mean that the other side is too.

Excellent points. Yeah, can't take it for granted. Yeah, concordance rates, 75-80%, but you can definitely see mixed histologies. In this case, they were the same, though. We ended up doing stage bilateral partial nephrectomies, and they were both papillary type 1, RCC, T1B, just based on the size for the right, T1A for the tumor on the left. And then, so going back to Brendan, similar surveillance to the last patient, you think, after surgery?

So, you know, I think all of us know here we have made a lot of strides when it comes to characterizing hereditary syndromes, but I fully don't think we've done all of it. And, you know, for the hereditary papillary patients, right, they don't, some of these people, you know, have multiple family members, their kidneys look like, right, every other sign is telling you something's going on, they just don't have a gene to tie it to.
