So I usually just tie in some imaging at that point, I would probably treat this patient more like a T3 patient for the first at least couple years. And then this is a patient where I'd probably, as long as I can get their insurance to agree, I'd follow them longer than five years too as well. I try and, you know, do every other year with an MRI or something like that if I can get it for these patients. Because, again, part of it is probably just my bias because of the practice I have where I do see Patients recur long after our guidelines told them they shouldn't. And that's true for any cancer. But in a younger patient, bilateral kidneys are already exposed. You don't want to catch the next tumor that comes in that kidney when it's any bigger than it has to be, because then you're going to really start losing options for this person.

I agree 100% with your biases here. Who knows what's causing these? This patient could be a risk for developing de novo tumors in the future. I also sort of consider them lifelong risk. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old female. Known diabetes mellitus. Family history significant for colon cancer in her mother.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma diagnosed in 2021.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic carcinoma breast; hormone receptor-positive (ER/PR-positive), HER2-negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Estrogen receptor positive; progesterone receptor positive; HER2 negative.

[ imaging findings ]: PET imaging performed in the last week of August 2025 showed no active metabolic lesions. Pelvis demonstrated a right-sided hypoenhancing nodule without significant uptake.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Hereditary gene panel identified a RAD51C exon 3 variant, reported as a variant of uncertain significance, in heterozygous state. A CHEK2 exon-level variant of uncertain significance was also reported in heterozygous state.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor markers were within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received 6 cycles of palliative chemotherapy including cyclophosphamide after initial diagnosis of metastatic breast cancer in 2021, with good response. Since 2022, she had been on ribociclib plus letrozole.

[ current disease status ]: On ribociclib plus letrozole. No radiologically active metabolically avid disease was identified on PET imaging in August 2025. Tumor markers remained within normal limits. No disease progression was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Hereditary testing had been performed in the context of maternal history of colon cancer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Flushing, diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal cramping occurring approximately 30–60 minutes after eating.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV well-differentiated small bowel neuroendocrine tumor with liver metastases and carcinoid syndrome.

[ histopathology results ]: Liver biopsy demonstrated well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 1, with Ki-67 less than 3%. Subsequent operative pathology from liver resection remained consistent with well-differentiated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT abdomen demonstrated an approximately 2 cm distal small bowel tumor partially occluding the small bowel lumen. MRI liver with Eovist demonstrated innumerable liver metastases. DOTATATE PET/CT demonstrated predominantly intra-abdominal somatostatin receptor-avid disease, with extensive hepatic involvement, the small bowel primary tumor, and regional lymph nodes. Following liver-directed therapy, imaging demonstrated reduction in tumor burden with stabilization and shrinkage of hepatic disease. At approximately 2.5 years later, follow-up imaging demonstrated hepatic progression and two small extrahepatic foci outside the liver.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Serotonin was 1,330 at diagnosis. Chromogranin A was 4,119 at diagnosis. After liver-directed therapy, serotonin decreased to 350. At symptomatic progression approximately 2.5 years later, serotonin increased to 900.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Somatostatin analog therapy with long-acting octreotide was initiated. Flushing improved slightly, diarrhea improved minimally, and abdominal cramping persisted. Preoperative echocardiogram was obtained in the setting of carcinoid syndrome. The patient subsequently underwent laparoscopic right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and liver resection for pathology. After surgery, abdominal cramping improved, but flushing and diarrhea remained significant. Liver-directed intra-arterial therapy with bland embolization was then performed. Hepatic tumor burden decreased, disease stabilized with shrinkage on imaging, symptoms improved markedly, and serotonin declined from greater than 1,300 to 350. Octreotide was continued, and the patient had good quality of life for a prolonged interval.

[ current disease status ]: Approximately 2.5 years after liver-directed therapy, the patient developed recurrent worsening diarrhea and flushing. Imaging demonstrated progression of liver metastases with two small extrahepatic lesions. Biochemical progression was present with serotonin rising to 900.

[ other clinical data ]: Symptoms and biochemical profile were consistent with carcinoid syndrome. Extensive hepatic tumor burden was present at diagnosis. Surgical debulking of liver metastases was not performed due to high liver tumor burden.

reference_discussion.text: Welcome back again, and thank you for joining us. I'm Dr. Xavier Koitken from the University of Chicago Medicine, and we have our fantastic morning panel that is joining us today for the treatment sequencing panel. So we'll start with Dr. Oz Ahmed from the University of Chicago, who's our IR specialist, Dr. Courtney Lon Heath, who is our nuclear medicine from the University of San Francisco, Dr. Andy Liao from the University of Chicago, medical oncology, and then Dr. Jennifer Shen, who is also joining us as a medical oncologist from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. So we'll drive straight into the treatment sequencing panel slides. As you probably know, there are some guidelines out there that we use as clinicians to be able to, or at least to try to figure out how we treat certain cases and it was sequenced or in what order. we treat those patients. But if you look at, this is sort of a simplified version of things. If you look at the red part here, which is for metastatic disease, for neuroendocrine tumors, there are a lot of different options that we can fall back on depending on different cases. And so I hope that these four cases we're gonna talk to you about today will illustrate how different things can be from one patient to another. So let's jump right into the first case. This is a 49-year-old female who presents with flushing, diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal cramping after eating, usually about 30 to 60 minutes after eating. She gets an abdominal CT and an MRI. And the CT shows, as you can see here, that there is a roughly two centimeter tumor in the distal small bowel that's partially occluding the lumen of the small bowel. And then the MRI with Eovist shows that there are multiple liver metastases. The radiologist calls them innumerable. The blue arrows just point to some of them, but essentially all the dark spots here in the light gray liver are tumors. So let's start, so the patient gets a biopsy, a liver biopsy, which shows a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. It's a grade one tumor, the Ki67 is less than 3%, and obviously this is stage four because the tumor has spread. So serotonin is quite high at 1,330. Chromoglandinase, 4,119. And as good clinicians, we got a DOTATATE PET CT next, which showed that there was mostly disease within the abdomen, with most of the disease here in the liver quite a bit, actually a lot of disease, and then the primary tumor here with some lymph nodes in the right lower corner. So Dr. Chen, what would you do next for this patient when she comes to your clinic?

I think what's interesting to note about her case is the extent of liver disease that she has, as well as her symptoms that are compatible with carcinoid syndrome, with the flushing and diarrhea. I think whenever there's pain, especially after eating, you have to worry that there may be partial obstruction related to the primary tumor or even if there is mesenteric disease, some element of mesenteric ischemia that's causing some pain after eating. So I think in a case like this, there is a clear role for somatostatin analog therapy to help with her symptoms of carcinoid syndrome. But I would also make sure that she is seen in a multidisciplinary setting like this to especially get surgical input regarding resection of the primary tumor with the pain and symptoms she's having.

Great, so that's exactly what we did. We started on somatostatin analogs and her symptoms improved minimally. She states that her flushing got a little better, her diarrhea minimally improved, but the cramping remains. So she was, like you suggested, discussed at a multidisciplinary tumor board, like we are having right now. And the general consensus was exactly as you suggested, that perhaps because the cramping didn't really get better on the long-acting arcteotide, and because the CT suggested that there was quite a bit of narrowing of the small bowel, lumen where the small bowel tumor was, she could potentially benefit from surgery. Now, Dr. Liao, why did we get a preoperative echocardiogram in this patient? Does this matter before we would take somebody to the operating room?

Yeah, I think for anyone who has carcinoid syndrome like this patient has, we would always worry about carcinoid heart disease. So, you know, tricuspid valve abnormalities. And so, It's really to help with the surgical planning to make sure that, you know, if they have any underlying carcinoid heart disease, that that gets addressed first to optimize the surgical risk.

Thank you. So we took her to the operating room, did a laparoscopic right amycolectomy. We took out her gallbladder to prevent gallstones since she was expected to be with that much limited disease on long actinobutyrate. We also did a liver retrospection just for the pathology. and the pathology essentially remained the same as the liver biopsy. So this was a well-differentiated tumor, low grade. So at this point after the surgery, she says her cramping improved, but the symptoms are still pretty bad. So as a matter of fact, she thought that the flushing and the diarrhea really didn't get much better since we talked to her last. So now I would ask Dr. Lon Heath What are the options here for somebody that has bad flushing and diarrhea despite being on long-acting octreotide? Would you consider PRT for a patient like this, just for symptom control?

That's a great question. So we know PRT does help with these exact symptoms. And the patients in the NETR1 trial that led to, that sort of was the big trial to demonstrate how well PRT works, We're kind of in similar situations to this patient in that. They had avid tumors like this, but their symptoms were progressing on or at least persistent on somatostatin analogs. And also, I will say, if we could go back to a view of the case, thank you. You can see there that there's really excellent uptake in the tumors here. And so, from that perspective, the patient would be an excellent candidate. for PRRT. One thing I would say though, one hesitation that I would have for doing it right now, you know, PRRT is not something that you can do too many times. You want to do it at the right time when it's going to have the most benefit. And for right now, it seems to be really, especially now that the patient's had surgery, It's pretty much exclusively in the liver. And that kind of suggests to me that there might be a role for something directed just to the liver, and that we might hold off on PRRT until the disease has spread outside the liver.
Perfect. So that puts a beautiful transition to our colleague, Dr. Ahmed. So Oz, what do you think? Is this a candidate for liver-directed therapy? And if yes, what type of liver-directed therapy?

Yeah, definitely. You stole my thunder a little bit in explaining that this is an ideal candidate for liver-directed therapy, specifically because, you know, at this point, most, if not all, of the tumor burden is confined to the liver. You know, with liver-directed therapy, we have two primary treatment options that we use, one being percutaneous ablation and the other being intra-arterial therapy. In this situation, because there's multifocal tumor throughout the liver, we would opt for intra-arterial therapy so we could treat or blanket the liver with our therapy. So in this situation, I would choose something like bland embolization, where we would catheterize the hepatic artery doing an angiogram, and then inject bland beads into the right hepatic lobe, and then followed by one month, treat the left hepatic lobe.

And as the surgeon on the panel, I will add that this is way too much tumor for me to take out. So even if I wanted and I would be really motivated to try to get it out, this is a lot of liver tumor burden, right? So this is definitely not something that I would operate on. So this is what we did. We got liver directed therapy. This is actually a real case. And you see here, that it actually got a lot better already. So the tumor actually not only stabilized but shrunk and her symptoms dramatically improved. Her serotonin dropped to 350 from over 1300 and she was a really happy camper for quite some time and she did continue deoctreotide and had a really good quality of life. So Dr. Chan, would you continue the Octeotide in this case or because you said, well, liver directed therapy worked, serotonin dropped, you know, we can stop it?

I would also continue with the somatostatin analog. I think many patients who have carcinoid syndrome still benefit from continuation of the SSA to reduce hormone secretion as much as possible. And it also may in the long run by getting better hormone control. Also, we would hope prevent development of longer term complications from having sustained high levels of hormone like development of carcinoid heart disease or mesenteric fibrosis down the line. So I tend to continue even if there is improvement after embolization.

Perfect. Okay. So two and a half years later, she has a return of a symptom. She comes back to clinic, obviously, um, complaining this time again about diarrhea and flushing that gets worse. So serotonin increased again to 900. So what now, Dr. Liao?

Um, so I would want to get another set of imaging to see what's going on. Um, this sounds like she has disease progression. So it looks like she does have disease progression. Um, yeah. So MRI should deliver from outside the liver.

Right. So there are two tiny foci that you could see here that now are outside the liver. And like you suggested, Dr. Liao, clearly there has been progression in the liver. Dr. Heath, what are we doing now?

Well, you know, I will say because the disease is still mainly in liver, I would still probably at least run the idea by my interventional radiology colleague to see if they felt that there was something else that was indicated. However, The fact that it is starting to spread outside the liver is a sign that it might be time to consider PRRT. And just as on the prior study, it's tough to see those little lesions and the uptake probably looks really low because the lesions outside the liver are so little. But the lesions that are good enough size, we can see there's a lot of uptake there. And if something's that bright on the PET scan, you also know that a lot of PRRT is going to go there and treat those tumors. So I think this could be a good time to consider PRRT.

This is what we did. I took us out of the equation there. Although you're absolutely right. I think it would have been absolutely reasonable to go back to our interventional radiology group. And I would even add, and maybe you can comment on that, Oz, is there a limited amount of time you can use bland nebulization in a patient or can you use it over and over again?

No, I think those are all fantastic points, and I think it's very reasonable to proceed with PRRT here, as mentioned, for the reason that there is evidence of disease outside of the liver. But again, I think if we wanted to make an argument for, you know, repeat intra-arterial therapy here, given that probably, you know, 90, 95% of the disease is still localized within the liver, I think that's totally reasonable. There's two things that I would want to make sure of. I'd want to make sure that on this MRI that the tumors, that there is arterial enhancement, because what we are targeting is the arteries of the tumor. And so we want to make sure that there's arteries feeding, which again, usually is the case, if not almost always is the case. And then the second is I just want to make sure that the liver is still healthy. And by healthy meaning, I want to make sure that the liver function tests are acceptable and that the patient's in a good health status, just like Our oncology colleagues assess the health of the patient prior to treatment. We do the same exact thing. We want to make sure our patients are healthy and that specifically the liver can withstand another round of basically targeted therapy to the liver.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 37-year-old right-handed male. No known comorbidities.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in January 2023 with new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

[ diagnosis ]: Right frontal intra-axial brain lesion, radiologically consistent with glioma. Intraoperative frozen section favored low-grade glioma. Final histopathology was pending.

[ histopathology results ]: Intraoperative frozen section was reported as low-grade glioma. Limited immunohistochemistry available locally showed GFAP positive, p53 performed, and Ki-67 less than 1%. Histology also described abundant gemistocytic cells. Final permanent histopathology review had been sent to Aga Khan University and remained pending.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI in January 2023 demonstrated a right frontal intra-axial lesion. Follow-up MRI approximately 6 months later showed slight interval increase in lesion size. Available MRI sequences demonstrated a right frontal FLAIR/T2 hyperintense lesion with extension toward/across the corpus callosum. The lesion was reported as non-contrast-enhancing. There was slight mass effect without significant midline shift described. Postoperative MRI demonstrated subtotal resection with residual T2/FLAIR hyperintense disease in the medial/posterior/inferior aspect near the cingulate/anterior corpus callosum region adjacent to the ipsilateral ACA territory.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Final molecular testing, including IDH status, was pending. No completed molecular/genomic result was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: After initial presentation, the patient was treated with steroids and antiepileptic therapy and observed. Steroids were subsequently stopped. He remained on levetiracetam, with seizures reported as well controlled and no recurrent seizure until later specialist review. He subsequently underwent neuronavigation-guided craniotomy under general anesthesia with maximal safe resection. Postoperative imaging showed residual disease near the corpus callosum/cingulate region.

[ current disease status ]: Status post subtotal resection of a non-enhancing right frontal glioma with residual radiographic disease near the corpus callosum/cingulate region. Final histopathology remained pending.

[ other clinical data ]: Intraoperatively, concern was documented for risk to ipsilateral ACA branches along the medial/posterior/inferior tumor margin, contributing to intentional residual tumor left in that region.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 78-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with minor lower back pain and leg pain attributable to sites not previously treated with radiotherapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) with diffuse osseous metastatic disease, nodal metastatic disease, and a subtle liver lesion on functional imaging.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET and FDG PET performed on closely dated studies demonstrated diffuse bony metastatic involvement and nodal disease. A subtle liver lesion was also identified, with low conspicuity. Quantitative PSMA PET parameters included SUV mean 7.7 and SUV max 35.2. During subsequent hospitalization after lutetium therapy, spinal cord compression occurred and was treated with radiotherapy. Follow-up PET imaging was not repeated.

[ laboratory results ]: Before lutetium therapy, PSA was 500 with an estimated doubling time of 2 months. Hemoglobin was 112 g/L, white cell count 4 x10^9/L, and platelets 175 x10^9/L. After cycle 1 of lutetium PSMA therapy, PSA decreased. Platelets fell to 33 x10^9/L at 4 weeks. During hospitalization, pancytopenia and febrile neutropenia were documented. Four months after cycle 1, hemoglobin was 96 g/L and platelets had recovered to 138 x10^9/L.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had undergone radical prostatectomy. He had received androgen deprivation therapy and radiotherapy to multifocal bone lesions, with more than 80 radiotherapy sessions in total. He had also received docetaxel, abiraterone, and cabazitaxel. He subsequently received 1 cycle of lutetium-PSMA therapy. After cycle 1, PSA declined, but treatment was complicated 2 to 3 weeks later by hospital admission with pneumonia, ICU admission with pancytopenia and febrile neutropenia, and a prolonged hospitalization of approximately 1 month requiring antibiotics and infusions. Radiotherapy was administered for spinal cord compression during that admission. Lutetium-PSMA cycle 2 was not given.

[ current disease status ]: At the time of consideration of further lutetium therapy, the patient had recovered partially from severe hematologic toxicity and infection after cycle 1, with persistent anemia and platelet recovery. Performance status before lutetium therapy had been ECOG 1, and he remained active, walking for approximately 1 hour on most days.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient lived in rural Australia, approximately 4 to 6 hours from the treating center.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent cough from September of the preceding year, followed by a rapidly enlarging left posterior cervical neck mass noted by December. She later developed exertional dyspnea and discomfort/pressure from bulky neck disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, hobnail subtype, with extensive cervical and mediastinal nodal metastases, diffuse left lung involvement with a lymphangitic pattern, and subsequent osseous metastasis in the right ninth rib. Disease was metastatic and clinically aggressive at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsies were obtained from left level III cervical lymphadenopathy and the left thyroid lobe. EBUS-guided biopsy was obtained from mediastinal nodal disease at station 4. Pathology was reported as hobnail subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- February PET-CT demonstrated extensive bilateral FDG-avid cervical lymphadenopathy, FDG uptake within the thyroid gland, mediastinal nodal involvement, and diffuse left lung involvement described as a lymphangitic pattern. Overall disease burden was large at presentation.  
- MRI was also performed at baseline.  
- Repeat PET-CT approximately 4 weeks later, obtained before systemic therapy because of clinical progression, showed interval progression, including slight increase in neck disease and a newly reported lesion in the right ninth rib. Lung disease had not changed substantially.  
- MRI brain performed before systemic therapy was negative for intracranial metastases.  
- Early response-assessment CT after 6 weeks of systemic therapy showed radiologic stable disease by RECIST.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: ROS1 fusion identified on urgent molecular profiling of tumor tissue.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Entrectinib was started as systemic therapy.  
- Within the first 6 weeks of treatment, she developed a change in baseline cardiac findings requiring cardiology assessment.  
- Symptomatic improvement occurred on treatment: cough resolved and neck pressure reduced significantly.  
- First imaging assessment after 6 weeks showed stable disease by RECIST rather than partial response.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with persistent but symptomatically improved bulky cervical, mediastinal, pulmonary, and osseous disease while receiving entrectinib. At first on-treatment assessment, disease was radiologically stable.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Performance status was effectively near 0, limited by cough and exertional shortness of breath.  
- On examination at initial oncology review, there was a visible bulky left neck mass with palpable smaller right-sided cervical nodes in levels II-IV.  
- Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable except for COVID-19 infection in January of the same year.  
- She was undergoing IVF treatment when symptoms began.  
- She was taking no regular medications.  
- Family history was not significant.  
- Smoking history was less than 10 pack-years.  
- There was no prior radiation exposure.

reference_discussion.text: Brilliant. Thank you so much. And again, thank you very much for the invitation to present some cases on this tumor board. It's such a helpful forum and brilliant that we can access it at convenient times around the world as well. So thank you for that. So my name's Kate Newbold and I'm an oncologist in London, UK, and I'm a clinical oncologist, which in our country means that we do both the radiation and systemic therapies and isotope therapies. So that's the background for how I get my patient referrals. So we have three cases to discuss today and I hope they're interesting and I hope they spark some good discussions for everybody. So the first case we'll launch into it. This is a 43 year old lady who previously very well undergoing IVF treatment when she noticed a cough in September of last year. She didn't really take much notice of it as you wouldn't she didn't have any past medical history. But by Christmas she then noticed a lump in the left side of the neck quite posterior on the left side, but this increased over size quite rapidly over the next few months, and so she was referred to a respiratory physician. in view of this palpable lump within the neck, but also the persistent cough. And she underwent a CT scan and a PET-CT scan with them. So these are the images that she had. So she actually was looking at an MRI as well, obviously, and PET CT here. And this was in February of this year. And shall I just talk through them? So the main thing, obvious is on the MIP I think that you just get this big overall picture of what's going on so a huge amount of bilateral lymphadenopathy uptake within the thyroid gland as well but also this mediastinal involvement and a diffuse process of sort of lymphangitis picture going into the left lung as well. So pretty large volume disease at the outset. So she went on to have core biopsies. This was all before she was referred to us. So this is from reports that we had received. So she had core biopsies from the left level three lymphadenopathy and also from the left thyroid lobe. She also had EBUS for the medicinal disease and had a biopsy a biopsy at Station 4 as well. So we had pathology from both the neck and from the midostinum chest.

Let's pause there for just a second, Kate. Zubair, this hobnail thing popped on our radar screen a few years ago. Can you tell us a little bit about what this hobnail variant is and from the pathology standpoint, how you think about these tumors?

So just to make something clear, in the new WHO, which will be coming out for the classification of endocrine organ neoplasms, the word variant is going to disappear because the word variant is used for a lot of molecular stuff. So we're going to call them subtypes of papillary thyroid carcinoma. So let's make that clear. So this actually, the first cases were reported from Mayo Clinic by Dr. Lloyd in 2010. And this was really a seminal article, which did get a lot of press, but also a lot of pushback because everybody thought it's just a little growth pattern that is, you know, just caught an eye of a pathologist who's probably just wants to make another entity. But what we also realized that when the tumor has the small structures and it almost looks like a tiny flowers with a lot of petals. If you can consider, you know, thinking of in a layman terms and if you do not do pathology every day. We have recognized these type of structures and other organ systems like in urinary bladder. which have these micro papillary type carcinomas, and ovary, and even in the breast, and lung. And what we recognize that when these tumors have these small papillary structures, they tend to be more aggressive, because you can just imagine mechanically they can easily snip off, can go into the lymph nodes and blood vessels. And this tumor, when it was described, some of these cases were already associated with other aggressive subtypes, like tall cell subtype is the most common where you see these tumors. And as you can see on the high power, which is the bottom right picture, my screen, the right, there is these very smaller structures, but if you see the nucleus, it is kind of pushed to the edge of the cell. And that what is known as the hobnail appearance. And as you know, if what is hobnail is, if you go back into the Western times, you can see the, how the nails were, or sometimes what the cowboys kind of wear on their boots. And that's what comes out, the term comes out from. So what we see these tumors that they can have multiple molecular alterations, which will be talked about later in there, they tend to have increased lymph node metastases recurrences. Now you make the diagnosis, you call something all hobnail subtype of papillary carcinoma, when 30% or greater of the tumor mass that is examined on the slide shows hobnail features. And these tumors can be a little bit cystic also sometimes, but they are, what I have seen mostly, that they are very much associated with other aggressive subtypes. So you kind of have a mixture. Let me just make one more comment about the radioactive iodine. Thyroid cancer actually has the highest rate of oncogenic kinase fusions of any solid tumor. And so if we think about Ntrek targeting, ROS1 targeting, RET targeting, ALK targeting in non-small cell lung cancer, we should be thinking about it in thyroid cancer as well. And using a good assay that can detect those fusions is so important in patients who need systemic treatment.

Awesome. Right before we go to the next case, I can't resist. David, give us a couple words about re-differentiation therapy. I know you guys are using it and thinking about it. Where do you see that in sort of three or four sentences here?

Yeah, sure, certainly. So the first thing is, I think there has been a case series with larotrectinib with providing re-differentiation therapy for thyroid cancer. Would you recommend a diagnostic iodine or a PATI-124 pets in this situation in the first instance, or? Well, I think that I'd go with the thyroid. We've got the thyroid.

Yes, I'd go with the thyroidectomy first, but then I think I'd be hopeful. I mean, without the entrectinib, you know, I think I'd be pretty cautious and be relatively unlikely to get a good response. But I think you just have to hope and see and continue the entrectinib.
Yeah. Thank you. That's really, really interesting. Thanks.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus was to proceed with thyroidectomy first, with surgery undertaken only if feasible as a palliative debulking procedure rather than with curative intent given the extent of pulmonary and nodal disease. If operable, the proposed procedure would be total thyroidectomy with bilateral central and bilateral modified radical neck dissection, with preoperative laryngeal examination and consideration of MRI to better assess tracheal and esophageal invasion. Entrectinib should be continued, and radioactive iodine may be administered in conjunction with ROS1 inhibition to maximize the possibility of iodine uptake, while recognizing that the likelihood of meaningful response to radioactive iodine alone is low in this aggressive PET-avid disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Liver lesions detected on surveillance ultrasound in November 2019 in the setting of known cirrhosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma arising in a cirrhotic liver. Initial disease involved a dominant left hepatic lobe lesion with several additional subcentimeter hepatic lesions. Disease later progressed to multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance ultrasound in November 2019 demonstrated liver lesions. CT on 11 December 2019 demonstrated a hepatocellular carcinoma in the left lobe of the liver and several subcentimeter lesions throughout the remainder of the liver. The CT images also demonstrated varices. Staging arteriography on 20 February 2020 demonstrated a large hypervascular left lobe tumor supplied independently by segments II and III. Post-radioembolization PET demonstrated good targeting of the dominant tumor and an adjacent smaller posterior lesion. Follow-up imaging after radioembolization showed that the largest tumor had decreased in diameter and was no longer vascular. Multiple hypervascular subcentimeter nodules in the right lobe remained unchanged at that time. Approximately 7 months later, imaging remained stable overall. On more recent follow-up imaging, the previously treated radioembolized tumor was no longer visible, but the subcentimeter nodules had increased in diameter, consistent with multifocal disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Platelet count 107. INR 1.1. Creatinine 1.03. Alkaline phosphatase 289. ALT 49. AST 69. Total bilirubin 1.7. Albumin 3.1. AFP 334 at diagnosis. ALBI score -1.67. Child-Pugh class B7. AFP decreased after treatment and did not exceed 150; approximately 7 months later AFP was 107. On subsequent follow-up, AFP increased to 701.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Cirrhosis had been present for several years. The patient had required one prior paracentesis for ascites a few years earlier; ascites was subsequently managed with diuretics. No known varices had been identified before cancer workup; varices were later seen on CT. The patient underwent radioembolization of the dominant left lobe tumor, with treatment delivered to segment II and segment III arterial supply. Post-treatment course was clinically well tolerated. The dominant treated lesion decreased in size and lost vascularity. The adjacent smaller treated lesion was also targeted. The patient underwent transplant evaluation and was placed on the transplant list. No systemic therapy had been administered up to the time multifocal progression was identified.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive intrahepatic disease with enlargement of previously subcentimeter nodules and AFP rise to 701, consistent with multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma. The previously radioembolized dominant lesion had resolved on follow-up imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Cirrhosis with ascites controlled on diuretics. No known varices had been documented before diagnosis, but varices were subsequently identified on CT.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks Rich, and it is a pleasure to be here with you and Laura, and a pleasure to talk about the treatment of patients with liver cancer. This slide is fairly basic, but shows the treatments for people as they move through the BCLC staging and treatment algorithm. We in IR have had a preeminent role for years, decades, and for a long time, we provided the only therapy beyond resection and transplant, because systemic agents weren't terribly effective. That changed with serafinib, and we then were trying to figure out ways that we could work with people providing serafinib to provide good care to patients. It changed a lot in the last couple of years when really good systemic agents came on and they're supported by really good studies. So we have now a very changing environment in the management of patients with hepatocellular cancer and it's important that we figure out how to treat our patients well within that environment because Even though we're doing a good job, the mortality of patients with liver cancer is increasing. The incidence is increasing and the mortality is increasing. So we can do a better job. And our goal would be to treat patients earlier and get them toward curative therapies. Or in optimally, people take people who are further along to the right in the algorithm and move them toward the left or stage transition and prevent stage migration. The way to do that is working together. And so that's what this symposium is all about, is optimizing our care of patients by working with every member of the team and trying to figure out the best synergies between what we can provide. And so with that, I will move on to the first patient to discuss. And both of the patients we'll discuss are mine, and they're real. And the first patient is 58 years old. She had cirrhosis for several years and required her first paracentesis only a few years ago, after which her ascites was treated with diuretics. So she had one paracentesis, now has ascites, treated with diuretics. And at the time of her diagnosis and up until this point, she had no known varices. Her labs are as stated with a platelet count of 107, INR of 1.1, creatinine of 1.03, ALKFOS-289, ALT-49, AST-69, bilirubin 1.7, albumin 3.1, and AFP-334. Her ALB score is negative 1.67. So together, she's a child Pugh B7. and being followed, and surveillance ultrasound in November of 2019 showed liver lesions, so she was sent to us for further evaluation. The December 11, 19 CT scan demonstrated clearly a hepatocellular cancer in the left lobe of the liver and several subcentimeter lesions throughout the rest of the liver. The smaller slides also show the presence of varices on the bottom right of your screen, unknown up to that point. We went to multidisciplinary conference and decided that she would hopefully make it to transplant. And we wanted to try to stabilize her largest tumor, keep her within Milan, and then work toward getting her transplanted. So this is from the staging arteriogram on February 20th. She delayed because of COVID to come into us. And we eventually did get her in. And you can see the large hypervascular tumor in the left lobe. It was actually fed independently by segments two and three. So I treated both of them. And this is the post-radioembolization PET scan, and you can see good targeting of that tumor, and it actually hit the smaller tumor that was coddled to it and posterior. And the smaller slide just shows the correlation between the post-itrium PET and the CT prior. She did very well with that and her largest tumor decreased in diameter and no longer was vascular after that. And you can see multiple hypervascular nodules in the right lobe of the liver, all sub-centimeter and not changed from prior to her radioembolization. So we thought that was great. We started her evaluation for transplant and December, seven months later, everything looked about the same and her AFP was still 107. It hadn't ever been above 150 after treatment. So at this point she's on the list and she just came back for a follow-up study about a few weeks ago and unfortunately even though the tumor that we treated with radioembolization is gone, those subcentimeter nodules have increased in diameter, and her AFP is up to 701. So she has developed multifocal hepatocellular cancer that is now diagnostic of that. So we, up to this point, did not have her on systemic therapy. It was discussed, and we didn't have her on systemic therapy. But before I get to that, I should probably have asked a more important question, or at least a question of a more general nature, and that is, if she were child Pu-A at diagnosis, would that have changed any of your treatment options? What would it have changed for this patient? And I'll ask that of Laura.

So given that she is young and her AFP was relatively low when she was diagnosed and she'd already had some complications of liver disease requiring a paracentesis, I think the goal would be to get this woman to transplant. So I think I would have probably done similar to what you guys had performed with the goal of bridging her to transplant, regardless if she was an A or a B.

Thanks. And the reason I asked that one first is that the next three are best answered, I think, by Rich. So the first question is, would you have decided earlier to move on to systemic therapy for this patient?

So I think to Laura's point and how you guys manage her, our goal is cure and if we could get the patient a transplant, that's great. But as patients are waiting, their tumor biology will declare themselves. And I think as this patient advances, and what I've often said is patients who have intermediate liver cancer, if they don't get cured or die of some other comorbidity, they will stage progress to advance disease. And I think when we start seeing multifocal disease in the liver, in both lobes, we start to get concerned that local regional treatment won't be enough. And now, as you alluded to, we do have very good medical treatments available, not only frontline, but second line, and potentially even third line. Given all of these have been studied only in patients who are Child Pue A, and so the safety and efficacy of some of these regimens has not firmly been established. For patients who are candidates, atezolizumab and bevacizumab has clearly established a new standard of care for frontline liver cancer. One of the things we do get concerned about is this risk of bleeding. And in the Mbrave 150 study, all patients were required to have an endoscopy within six months of starting. And many patients did have varices. Some of them had to have them treated. But as long as they were not high risk for bleeding, then they were allowed to come on study. And we can't forget that there's a whole lot of regimens on the horizon, new combinations and ongoing clinical studies, which we should always consider how to get patients into these clinical trials to do better. But again, most of them do require patients to have good performance status in child PUA liver disease.
Well, what are the considerations for treating the varices before starting on atezolizumab and bevacizumab?

So not all varices need to be treated. Obviously, we would defer to the endoscopist if they're at high risk for bleeding. Small varices probably do not need to be treated. But if there are varices that are at high risk for bleeding based on the endoscopist assessment, then those should be banded. And then probably it's prudent to wait a week or two before starting the BEV. But this is a minor procedure. In reality, unless they're, again, high-risk for bleeding, a tezobev should be considered a treatment of choice for advanced liver cancer. You know, there's been a lot of advances in liver cancer treatment, and this slide comes from the NCCN, which highlights the role of a tezolizumab as a new option for patients, as well as what we have is the established TKIs of saraftib and lenvantinib. Interestingly, they maintained a potential recommendation for nivolumab, even though there was a phase 3 study of nevo versus serafinib that did not meet its statistical endpoint. But we did see nivolumab had a response rate of 15%, was well tolerated, and a survival of over 16 months. It just was not statistically different than serafinib. And that would be for patients who can't tolerate any anti-angiogenics. But for the large majority of patients, they will probably be candidates for a tezobev if they're candidates for systemic treatment. And this study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine last year, where it met both its primary endpoints of improving overall survival and progression-free survival. And at the time of the initial analysis, we did not reach the true median in the treatment arm. We did have a hazard ratio of about 0.58. That was stable and significant. And at GI-ASCO now, with an additional 12 months of follow-up, we see that the new frontline survival for advanced liver cancer is over 19 months. 19.2 months with a Tez-O-Bev, and the soraphin arm did not change. That was 13.4 months. The PFS data was very stable, because we had reached those medians at the time of the primary analysis. And what was very striking is that with longer follow-up, we've actually seen the response rate go up. At the time of the primary analysis, the response rate with the tezobev by conventional resist was 27%. And now, with longer follow-up, we see that response rate is 30%, including 8% complete responses with systemic treatment. And this regimen is pretty well tolerated, I would say. We don't see any new safety concerns with longer follow-up. Obviously, the autoimmune phenomena, which we are familiar with PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors like atezolizumab, can be seen, but generally they're low grade. Really, a lot of the side effects we've seen were related to Bevacizumab. And we see that here on this slide, where looking at the safety of Bev versus Serafinib, you can see the most common side effects with Atezobev were hypertension and protonuria. And in this slide, all grades are lighter, high grades are darker. But things that the patient really notices, such as diarrhea, hand-foot skin syndrome, anorexia, are really more common with seraphinib. And this type of data was very much supported by improved quality of life assessments with a tezobev over seraphinib. There is similar bleeding risks with both drugs. Most of it is low-grade, such as epistaxis. There are worse, more higher-grade bleeding events with the Tez-O-Bev, but again, this can be mitigated by patient selection, good performance status, child PUA, and doing your pre-operative endoscopies, or pre-treatment endoscopies, I should say. Now, You know, single agent PD-1 inhibitors have had challenges in phase three studies. Both nivolumab and pembrolizumab have accelerated approval for progression after serafinib. Now that we've seen IO move to the frontline space, the number of patients getting this beyond progression I think will be fewer because the patients who will get this will be the ones who get TKIs in the frontline. And again, a Tez-O-Bev is not gonna be for every frontline patient, but I think it'll be the majority. Maybe some of us estimate around 15, 20% of patients might not get a Tez-O-Bev frontline for various reasons. And if they get a frontline TKI, a progression, both Pembro and Nevo would be appropriate, as both of them gave response rates of about 15 to 20% that were very durable. The thing is, as you see here in Checkmate 459, nivolumab did not reach its primary endpoint of improving PFS statistically in the Checkmate 459 study. And interesting enough, at GI-ASCO, we saw data from the single arm Keynote 224 data a subset of patients who had got pembrolizumab frontline. Again, an uncontrolled study. And again, similarly, the survival was 17 months. So very similar data that single agent checkpoint inhibitors are active, we just don't have level one evidence. And there's ongoing studies, a lot of exciting combinations. Those include dual inhibitors of two checkpoints together, such as Dervalumab and Tremulumab, which is PD-L1 and CTLA-4 combinations, or CheckMate 90W, which is NEVO and IPI, and that's PD-1 and Tremulumab. CTLA-4 combo, and some combinations of immunotherapy and TKIs, such as atezolizumab and cabizantinib, which is already approved in second line CABO, and LEAP-002, which is pembrolizumab and linvantinib. So we've seen some early phase data with these combinations. This study from ASCO of last year looked at tremilumab and dervalumab in various arms looking at different dosing strategies or single agents versus combinations. What's very interesting is this dosing here with a single dose of TREMIE at 300 plus DERVALUMAB gave an overall response rate of 24% in second line with a duration of response that still had not been reached and a median survival of just under 19 months in the second line population with a tolerable safety profile. And this regimen is being compared to Seraftib in the Himalayas study, and we're waiting for those results. There's also several early stage studies with this combination, in combination with TACE or after resection or curative RFA. Looking at the study designs here, you see Himalaya with Derva versus Derva-Treme and Serafnib, and Checkmate 90W with Nevo-IPPE versus Serafnib or Lenvantinib. And we should comment that Nevo-IPPE itself is approved now in the United States for second line. It has accelerated approval, and it is based on response rates of about 30%, and that is what's driving this confirmatory study front line. Also in front line, we have the combination of Linvantinib and Pembro. Now Linvantinib is a multikinase inhibitor. It's approved front line based on non-inferiority to serafinib. And in this study published in JCO last year, we saw response rates, if you look at conventional resist of 36%, median duration of response is over a year. And disease control rate of 88%. And this is very exciting data, I would argue. Median survival was 22 months. And again, this is a single-arm frontline study, but not too similar from the single-arm IAMBRAVE-150 data or a TezOBev data that led to IAMBRAVE-150. And this study has completed accrual and we're waiting for results. And here you see the design of LEAP-002, which is LEN and PEMRO versus LEN. This is a placebo-controlled study for the Pemrolizumab component. And COSMIC-312 is looking at cabizantinib, the VEGF receptor inhibitor, Met and Axel inhibitor, in combination with the tezolizumab versus CABO or serafinib, which is really the control arm here. We don't have a lot of data on this combination in the public domain, but needless to say, many of the TKIs in combination with PD-L1 inhibitors or PD-1 inhibitors are showing very exciting responses. Now, we can't ignore the fact that we have several drugs available at progression. If we look at the I.O. approvals, as mentioned, NEVO and Pembro have approval, accelerated approval, as single agents. And NEVO and IPPE now has an approval as of last year, 2020. for accelerated approval after prior serafinib. And you see the response rates go up with the combination. There is more toxicity with the combination, about 50% in the combination in the phase 1b study actually needed steroids for immune-related adverse events. But needless to say, these are options for patients, and I think specifically for patients who do not get IO in the frontline setting. And also looking at second line approved TKIs. Regorafnib was the first drug approved since serafinib, and it was approved for patients who had tolerated serafinib. It was approved in second line based on an overall survival benefit versus placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.63. Similarly, cabizantinib was looked at versus serafinib or after serafinib progression. And interestingly, the Celestial study also had about 25% of patients who were third line. And again, an improvement in overall survival with a hazard ratio that's consistent, I would say, with the other drugs in the space, which also includes ramucirumab. the anti-VEGF antibody. So this is a monoclonal antibody to the VEGF receptor. This differs from Bevacizumab, which is to the VEGF ligand. And in this study, patients had to have an elevated alpha-beta protein in order to be enrolled. So this is a biomarker-selected cohort where we saw has a ratio of 0.69 for this cohort. So a risk reduction for death in this population of patients who have a worse prognosis based on the high AFP. And certainly the AE profiles of the TKIs are fairly similar. hypertension, Hanford Skin Syndrome, diarrhea, and anorexia. Ramicerumab, as a monoclonal antibody, has a little cleaner side-of-the-heck profile and really is related to its VEGF receptor engagement. And we've seen things such as hypertension, proteinuria, and some fluid retention. So before we go on to the next case, I see there's some questions coming in from the audience. And Matt, maybe this is a good one for you. As we talk about these newer combinations that are more active, how do you see them affecting where we stop LRT? You commented that before we had serafinib, LRT kind of filled a void. Then we had Serafinib, which improved survival, but not a high response rate. And now we have a new generation of drugs that seem more active.

And it's a great question. But I think it's not really stopping LRT because local regional therapy has occurred. It's whether you do it again. It's a different metric now. It's a different equation because if there wasn't anything else, then you would do the same thing. You'd pound your head against the wall again because it's the only wall you could pound on. Now it's not. Now if you've done something and it either it wasn't completely successful or it recurred afterward, you have to evaluate the patient at that moment and determine what's the best thing to do at that time. We don't know always what that is, but these drugs work. And so they should be actively considered rather than doing the same thing you already did that didn't work, that may have worked at one point, but isn't working now.

Yeah, I think that's a good way to put it. And I would also remind the audience that, you know, to have advanced liver cancer or liver cancer that's a candidate for systemic treatment, you don't necessarily need to have extra hepatic disease, right? Bulky progressive disease in the liver post-local regional therapy would be something to consider for systemic treatment. Laura, you're a hepatologist. You're very involved in the management of liver cancer and this idea of transplant. What about this idea of IO agents and downstaging? What are your thoughts and concerns?

So it's something we have started thinking about. Certainly there are people who will have a very robust response and a sustained response and should those patients be considered for transplant in the context that there's never been concern for extra hepatic spread. I think we need some more safety data. There have been case reports of patients undergoing transplant after receiving an IO and subsequently losing their graft very quickly. There is a recent publication, which was a letter to the editor that comes from the Mount Sinai group where they had a total of nine patients of which eight had received transplant within four weeks of their last IO. And they've only had one patient with mild rejection and no one has lost their graft. So I think we need to start thinking about it, but we need to do it safely. These grafts are very precious and we need to make sure that we are not putting patients at at risk of a more quicker demise as a result of graft failure due to a severe rejection.

Yeah, and I think we need to characterize who those patients are, right? I mean, I'm at a large transplant center, all of us are, and my sense is most patients can be controlled with local regional treatment, right? And who are those patients, to the discussion before, but here we're looking at curative intent, who are those patients who we stop LRT pre-transplant and say, look, you're still a transplant candidate, but now you need systemic treatment, right? What's their... clinical course look like? That I think we need to clearly define in order to target them. And it relates to our next question about safety. How does post-transplant status affect choice of drug? And I think this is referring to patients who have recurrent liver cancer after transplant. And I think many of us think that the TKIs are probably the first choice. Certainly the most safety data is with Seraphinib. Whether or not these drugs work the same post-transplant, we don't have those data sets. you know, assuming they're not going to die of liver failure, we would offer these patients some treatment. And to Laura's point, I think now in the post-transplant setting, we need to be very careful with IO because, you know, You know, the question is, are we hitting the brakes and the accelerator at the same time? Meaning, you know, patients are on immunosuppression, and then we want to give them drugs that activate their immune system, right? So maybe one of the first things is just to decrease the immunosuppression, see how they do. But I think IO in this setting is right now contraindicated. So for the sake of time, and there are good questions coming in, I think we will transition back to you, Matt, with your second case.

reference_conclusion: Following initial radioembolization as bridge therapy with the goal of transplantation, interval progression to multifocal bilobar hepatocellular carcinoma with rising AFP was recognized as advanced disease for which repeat locoregional therapy was not favored if prior treatment was no longer effective. Systemic therapy should be actively considered, with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab regarded as the preferred first-line regimen for eligible patients. Endoscopic evaluation for varices is required before initiation of bevacizumab; high-risk varices should be banded, with bevacizumab started after an interval of approximately 1–2 weeks.
reference_conclusion_quote: We went to multidisciplinary conference and decided that she would hopefully make it to transplant. And we wanted to try to stabilize her largest tumor, keep her within Milan, and then work toward getting her transplanted. [...] And I think when we start seeing multifocal disease in the liver, in both lobes, we start to get concerned that local regional treatment won't be enough. [...] For patients who are candidates, atezolizumab and bevacizumab has clearly established a new standard of care for frontline liver cancer. [...] all patients were required to have an endoscopy within six months of starting. And many patients did have varices. Some of them had to have them treated. But as long as they were not high risk for bleeding, then they were allowed to come on study. [...] But if there are varices that are at high risk for bleeding based on the endoscopist assessment, then those should be banded. And then probably it's prudent to wait a week or two before starting the BEV. [...] a tezobev should be considered a treatment of choice for advanced liver cancer. [...] Now if you've done something and it either it wasn't completely successful or it recurred afterward, you have to evaluate the patient at that moment and determine what's the best thing to do at that time. [...] these drugs work. And so they should be actively considered rather than doing the same thing you already did that didn't work

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old woman; nulliparous. No comorbidities were reported. Family history was significant for three paternal aunts with breast cancer diagnosed between ages 45 and 50 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable right breast lump detected on self-examination in the fourth quarter of 2015.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, grade II, triple-negative by immunohistochemistry; clinical stage IIA breast cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Core needle biopsy of the right breast lesion demonstrated invasive ductal carcinoma, grade II. Immunohistochemistry showed triple-negative phenotype. Sentinel lymph node biopsy identified two lymph nodes; both were negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]: Physical examination identified a 2.5 cm mass in the right breast at the 11 to 12 o’clock position, with no clinical axillary involvement. Breast ultrasound demonstrated a right breast lesion measuring 2.5 cm. Bone scan showed no distant osseous metastases. Hepatic ultrasound showed no distant metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Extended hereditary cancer panel testing (Myriad myRisk, 25 genes) identified no clinically significant mutation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Oocyte preservation was performed for fertility preservation. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed approximately 2 months after initial evaluation; 2 nodes were removed and both were negative. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy had been initiated with a planned regimen of doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide for 4 cycles followed by paclitaxel for 12 cycles. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist was planned during chemotherapy for fertility preservation.

[ current disease status ]: The patient was undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy at the time of reporting. No distant metastatic disease had been identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Fertility preservation was pursued because of desire for future fertility. No other gynecologic history was reported.

reference_discussion.text: Well, this case is about a 30-year-old woman. She has no comorbidity, but a family history characterized by three paternal aunts with breast cancer diagnosed between 45 and 50 years old. She's maliparous with no other gynecostatic history. By the fourth quarter of 2015, during a breast self-exam, she felt a right breast lump. During her physical exam, a 2.5-centimeter lump between 11 and 12 o'clock radio of her right breast was detected with no axillary involvement. An ultrasound reported a lesion of the same VRAT5, and a corneal biopsy shows an invasive ductal carcinoma grade II triple negative by immunohistochemistry. Bone scan and hepatic ultrasound demonstrate no distant metastasis, no distant disease. It's a young woman with fertility desire, so she underwent an oocyte preservation, and the patient go through a genetic cancer test, an extended myriad my risk with 25 genes evaluated, and no clinical significant mutation was identified. Two months later of her first evaluation, the surgeons underwent a lymph node biopsy, with two nodes detected, and both of them was negative. Arrived breast cancers, a stage 2A triple negative breast cancer was diagnosed, and the proposed plan for this patient is neoadjuvant chemotherapy, AC for four cycles, followed by Taxol for 12 cycles, plus agonist of the gonadotropin-released hormone for fertility preservation, followed by a conservative surgery, depending on the result of the neoadjuvant chemotherapy, more or less adjuvant radiation therapy. The patient is actually in the neoadjuvant phase. And so we asked the panel, This patient with a strong family history, but with a negative gene test, do you consider neoadjuvant chemotherapy, or do you consider up front?

Oh, can I just interrupt you? I'm sorry. We'll leave the questions up. I'd like any panelist just to have general comments about the case again, the way we did for the one before. So any comments about this case, any questions from the panel, any clarifications, please.

I'll make a comment about the sentinel node check two months after the fertility preservation. I think you're obviously doing the sentinel node in advance of neoadjuvant therapy to increase the chances that you'll find the sentinel node and not have false negative. There is a push now to use ultrasound evaluation of axillary lymph nodes and fine needle aspiration. So that might have been an option and you could have considered that probably early before the OO site preservation because in the case of this patient, if she had positive axillary lymph nodes, waiting two months for treatment might have been something we would have counseled the patient about thinking carefully if she really wanted to wait and do the oocyte preservation. Because at her age, she's probably likely to continue to be fertile after chemotherapy. Obviously, the medical oncologist can speak about that. But I probably just would have evaluated the lymph node differently.
Some other comments about her fertility preservation versus her neoadjuvant therapy, etc.

You know, we have started with our endocrine group, our fertility group, and they've got a grant. And they really like to do the fertility preservation prior to any chemo. I don't know if it's just because of our grant or what it is. But as we're working with these premenopausal women, they really want to do that before the chemo. They really push us.
Brittany, do you want to give a comment on this?

Sorry. Yeah, I kind of agree that maybe, you know, a complete nodal assessment should have been done before, like, making decision about fertility preservation, because she is young, and she probably will regain her fertility after chemotherapy. I do think that, like, the two-month delay seems a little bit long for the fertility preservation. I know it takes time. but I don't know if there are mechanisms to have that done a little bit quicker. I feel like we can usually do it in a one-month time.
But because of her young age, both you and Michelle have raised the question about her being so young. Would you have not performed fertility preservation because she's so young?
No, I think if she was indeed node negative and that had been assessed, I think fertility preservation definitely could have been done.

I'd like to point out that a number of clinics, including the Dana-Farber and other places, I'm sure, around the country, have specialized clinics now, specialized groups that evaluate fertility preservation. And I'd like to point to the Latin American countries, a study that's going on through Cynthia Villarreal. She has set up a specific clinic. and specific fertility preservation program, and she's interested in other people collaborating with her. So please communicate with us through Jessica if you want to join a group effort in evaluating this important endpoint and this important outcome in young patients. So that's just something for your interest. Other questions about this case? I'm sorry, I bumped in front of you. Please. Please, Joel, feel free to ask your questions. I think, what about the negative gene test, yeah, that you're saying? That's your first question? Sorry, one more comment, just generally. Yeah, I mean, what is the result of her surgery? What was left was the amount of residual disease, and could you give a little bit more information about the radiation she received?
She's actually in a neoadjuvant chemotherapy phase.
Okay, thank you. Any other general comments before discussion about the genetic testing and the strong family history with the negative gene test? Anybody want to speak to this topic?

Paul, I had a couple of comments. So in these young patients who truly want to maintain fertility, if it's possible, This patient kind of has a borderline tumor size. If it's going to take a while for them to have their OSI preservation, there may be a role to do surgery first, and as they're recovering from their surgery and before adjuvant chemotherapy, at that point do their OSI preservation. So this gal, 2.5 centimeter tumor, unknown nodal status, it's harder to know what the right answer is. And then I think the second question that was asked is, what do we do with this strong family history? You know, I think we feel reassured that her gene testing is negative, but I'm not sure that we understand all of the genetic predisposition to breast cancer in Hispanic women. And I don't know that anyone on the panel has more information about that. Maybe we just didn't test for the right genes in this 25-gene panel.

So, again, for the Latin American countries, I'll just say it again, Cynthia Villareal in Monterrey, Mexico, is collaborating with Dr. Weinstein, I think it is, from the City of Hope Hospital in the United States, and there are genetic mutations with strong family history being discovered. There are some Hispanic-founded mutations that are unique. And because of this as a study, he's invited, and Cynthia invites, anybody who wants to perform genetic testing on very young patients. to collaborate with her and have a blood sample sent to the United States, and under research conditions for free, the patients can get this testing done. Because I know this is frequently not a test that can be performed in South America. So just that comment. So then another surgical question is the role of samples in the box. I thought we already answered that, Michelle.

Well, it says before or after pre-op systemic chemotherapy. So after chemotherapy, well, this patient's already had a sentinel node, it looks like, removed. So there's no way to really go back and analyze the sentinel node at this time. But let's just say she had an ultrasound, they looked negative, and she got chemotherapy. We would do a sentinel node test during the time of the lumpectomy after systemic chemotherapy. a positive FNA and then had chemotherapy, she could have a sentinel node out back. I think the studies are showing that we can increase the chances that we find a sentinel node, and that we reduce the false negative rates by using both the radioactive isotope and the dye after neoadjuvant therapy, and that we attempt to try to remove at least two sentinel lymph nodes at that point.
And what do you do with that result, just to clarify about that result?

Well, the way we handle it right now, since there still is a little bit of controversy about how to handle a positive sentinel node after neoadjuvant therapy, we send that particular lymph node for a frozen section. And if it is negative, do not go on to do a lymph node dissection. If it's positive, we do a lymph node dissection. And usually, we have tried to have a conversation with our radiotherapists, radiation oncologists, in advance to decide whether or not this is going to impact their decisions about radiation therapy.
So, Julia, could you comment, please, from your perspective?

So the Centena trial and also the C1051, something like that, has given us some reassurance that sentinel biopsy is feasible after neoadjuvant chemotherapy with an acceptable low false negative rate. So at my institution, we often do the sentinel biopsy after completion of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. And I would suspect that this patient would yield also a negative central node. It probably won't change her additional adjuvant treatment, such as radiation therapy, given the results of the central node biopsy.

Thank you, Julia. Does anybody want to add to ovarian function suppression during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for the purpose of preserving fertility in these young patients? Does anybody have an opinion on this topic? Cezanne? Sure, yeah. So we do have some data looking at GnRH agonists in this setting, and that it can help with fertility preservation. In very young women, I think it's something you can certainly discuss for fertility preservation during chemotherapy in general, whether it's neoadjuvant or adjuvant. Brittany, you want to comment on that?
I agree, we do add that in for patients who are young.

And again to preserve fertility. Correct. So does everybody agree there? Jack and Susan, are you happy with that? I would certainly add it in. I think it's worth comment to differentiate menstruation from fertility preservation because a lot of the studies that have been published I've really used that as a surrogate having resuming menstrual cycles which is not the same as fertility preservation and the literature is very conflicted on whether this works but that said I am a favor of doing anything possible in this patient age and of course there's the additional benefit of amenorrhea in breast cancer outcomes so I would include it. Thank you, Jack. So in the last few minutes, if there are panellists I have failed to call on and you'd like to make some comments about any one of the three cases or some general comments, remember that these boards are held with a view to having expert panellists like yourself be of assistance to doctors in developing low and middle income countries. So if you have any general points about the cases we've heard, can you speak up now, just in the last remaining few minutes, if anybody has a comment?

I'll comment a little bit about surgery and how we're handling our lymph nodes. I know that in some places resources are limited and you have to be prudent of your dollars, but we really don't do frozen sections on the lymph nodes anymore. So we will send them off for permanent, whether or not it's neoadjuvant or know-what front therapy, and then we take that case to our tumor board, and if it will change any adjuvant treatment, then we go on with surgery because we know it's not prognostic. It's just telling you what has already happened. So instead of making a decision, you know, in the operating room, but it saved us having to have frozen section available, and that's just something that we've changed based on the data, and that's how we do it here.
Michelle, do you concur with that?

More is what's done here? We definitely have used much, much less frozen section for our sentinel nodes, and I believe only for the neoadjuvant, where if we found residual disease after they completed all their therapy, we knew we definitely were going to do a lymph node dissection. That's when we do it, just to save the patient another operation, only in those situations.
Julia, what is your practice about frozen section on neoadjuvant nodes?

Our pathologists are very hesitant in doing frozen section because it wastes some of the lymph node tissue. Also with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, there's some fibrosis involved in the treated lymph node, so it makes the interpretation of the histology more difficult, so our pathologists don't like to do them. So we often don't do frozen section and wait for the final pathology. And then we'll talk to the patient and let them aware that additional surgery may be necessary if the note is possible.

Okay, thank you. So Joel, I think those were very good questions and a little bit of controversy or differences in practice around those. sample nodes after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Yeah, make a comment. Have you seen a comment from Rosanna?

Not a question, actually. Regarding the last case and considering this very young patient with such a strong family history and under the results of the GEPR system, would anybody consider giving her platinum as neoadjuvant therapy?
Any takers for platinum neoadjuvant therapy in this patient because of the strong family history despite the negative test?
I would just comment here we are doing platinum therapy in the neoadjuvant setting but in a clinical trial in patients that are BRCA negative.

And I think that's the same in MDH. We don't routinely give platinum, even neoadjuvant or adjuvant. But under clinical trial conditions, we definitely do. So the literature is on the fence still. There will be more evidence forthcoming this year and next year about the use of platinums in this setting. Can you repeat, Jack? Oh, just one other quick option. In the U.S., there's a trial that's looking at neoadjuvant non-platinum-containing chemotherapy and then stratifying by residual disease or not. So the patient who has a CR doesn't go on, a patient who doesn't gets offered further therapy that might include the platinum and that might be an option if a trial were available. Right. So any questions from our presenters or are you all satisfied? I just want to thank everybody, don't forget to take a picture of yourselves, even if you're alone, a quick selfie would be very valuable, thank you. And of your room particularly, take a picture of your room, thank you very much. And thank you all for joining the CUMA board today, thank you very much indeed, bye now.

reference_conclusion: For this stage IIA triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma, the agreed management is neoadjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide for four cycles followed by weekly paclitaxel for 12 cycles, with concurrent gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist for fertility preservation. Breast-conserving surgery is planned after completion of neoadjuvant therapy, with adjuvant radiation therapy to be determined according to the response and surgical/pathologic findings. Platinum therapy is not recommended routinely in the neoadjuvant setting in the absence of a BRCA mutation and would be considered only in the context of a clinical trial.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient; age 62 years at time of radical prostatectomy in 2017.

[ chief complaint ]: Rising PSA after prior radical prostatectomy, salvage radiation therapy, and short-course androgen deprivation therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma with biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy and subsequent salvage treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Radical prostatectomy specimen in 2017 showed Gleason score 7 prostate adenocarcinoma. Surgical margins were negative.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET performed in March 2024 was interpreted as negative for local recurrence and negative for regional metastatic disease. A rib focus was described without definite corresponding osseous abnormality; no definite metastatic lesion was identified on the scan.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline BRCA2 positive.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA after radical prostatectomy was 0.81 ng/mL.  
- After salvage radiation therapy and 4 months of hormonal therapy, PSA decreased, then subsequently rose again in early 2024.  
- PSA immediately prior to consultation was 0.14 ng/mL.  
- PSA during March 2024 visit was 0.19 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Radical prostatectomy performed in 2017 in Italy.  
- Subsequent radiation therapy was administered for postoperative PSA of 0.81 ng/mL.  
- Four months of hormonal therapy were given with radiation.  
- Radiation dose to the prostatic fossa was 71.8 Gy.  
- PSA declined after radiation and hormonal therapy, then rose again by early 2024.

[ current disease status ]: Biochemical recurrence with PSA 0.19 ng/mL in March 2024 after prior prostatectomy, salvage prostatic fossa radiation, and short-course hormonal therapy. No definite local, regional, or distant disease was identified on PSMA PET.

[ other clinical data ]: Patient resided in Naples, Florida. Occupation was entrepreneur.
