reference_discussion.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to our educational series titled Pet Tumor Board. In this series, we present real-world cases, mostly drawn directly from my clinical practice, with the goal of highlighting practical scenarios and extracting meaningful, applicable learning points. Joining me for today's tumor board are several renowned experts in the respective fields. Dr. Dan Pestelkamp, medical oncologist from Yale. Dr. Sharif Ghami, a nuclear medicine physician from the University of California, San Diego. And Dr. Wayne Brisbane, a urologic oncologist from UCLA. Also joining us is Dr. Sean Collins, a radiation oncologist from the University of South Florida. None of our panelists have reviewed these cases in advance, ensuring fresh, candid insights. Let's dive in. This is a patient that I saw recently from actually Naples, Florida, that came to see me out in San Diego, was referred by a friend of mine. And he is an entrepreneur who at age 62 in 2017 had a radical prostatectomy. That was a Gleason, and it was actually done in Italy, but he had a Gleason score of seven negative surgical margins. For some reason, right after his surgery several years later, he had a PSA of 0.81, was treated with radiation and four months of hormonal therapy. Interestingly, he also was germline tested and BRCA to the positive. He came to see me. after his PSA began to rise. So after the radiation and the hormone therapy limited is on the right here, you see his PSA was down, but then it began to rise in early 24. When, right before I saw him, it was 0.14. And during our visit in March, it was 0.19. What's the next step? Who wants to chime in here? Dr. Collins?
I would get a PSMA scan.

Okay, nobody would disagree. In fact, that is what occurred, because this is a PSMA PET tumor board. So the posthumous scan comes back, read by Dr. Sharif Ghani as basically negative. There's no local recurrence, no regional disease, but he does comment on a rib. So, Sharif, why don't you dig into this a little bit deeper about lesions and false positives and negatives.

We keep coming across this rib findings that just throw everybody off. And I think if there's clearly no definite corresponding osseous abnormality, and I say that with a grain of salt, because sometimes if the osseous changes are sub-centimeter in size, this is where I'm at a disadvantage and I won't see it, so I won't call an osseous finding. In the absence of a clear-cut osseous finding, I would either chalk it up to post-traumatic or fibrous dysplasia kind of scenario and not hang the hat of the rising PSA on that rib finding.

That is an important statement because that seems to be one of the things we see all the time on the PET scans And I'm going to ask you if there's any difference between some of the pets out there. And that it really throws people off in what they want, how they treat the patients. Particularly, I guess if you had multiple ones, you'd feel different, right? Absolutely.
Absolutely.
How do you investigate this? MRI, what do you do?

I think an MRI can help. I think the first step would be ask the patient, have you got bumped there recently? Because a lot of times that it gives you the answer and it kind of just puts it to rest. An MRI would be a good next step to completely rule it out. But I think the other alternative would be to just get a follow-up study in a few months as far as PSMA.

Are the insurance companies going to pay for that, I wonder? Is there any difference between the different scans and rib positivity? Seems like when we first started out in this, we were seeing more positive ribs.

So we started out with gallium 68 PSMAs, and gallium 68 is a tracer that just its physical characteristics in terms of how it decays produces a photon that is not as well imaged by our, quote unquote, crystals that are part of the PET scanner. And so, since a lot of the practices now have shifted from Gallium 68 to F18, whether it's PosLuma or Pylarify, F18 has a little bit better imaging characteristics, and so there's not that much amount of scatter, if you will. And so that's why it's gone down a little bit. And Dr. Collins, you mentioned looking for something that's 0.5 centimeters or larger. That's for the new scanners. Older scanners are probably closer to 0.8. And so the technology now is out there 0.5. But if it's something that's smaller than a half a centimeter, it's anybody's guess.
That's really helpful. Thank you.

So, Dan Petrowak, micro-oncologists often are sort of supposed to be middle-of-the-road people between radiation oncologists and surgeons that render opinions in cases like this. What would you tell this guy?

So, you know, again, I think this rib lesion is a complete red herring based upon his clinical presentation. And with a negative PSMA PET scan, you could radiate his bed. That's one possibility. You still are below that 0.2 threshold where it's considered to be a relapse. So again, I think you could potentially observe this patient as well. It's really radiation therapy now versus delayed radiation therapy.
Let me ask Dr. Collins, if Dr. Petrowak wasn't sure and he sent this patient to you for radiation, what would you do?
I read the records and he had 71.8 gray to his prostatic fossa already.
Oh, okay. I didn't see that before, actually. Yeah.
I mean, to me, re-irradiating someone who's had prostatic fossa radiation would be highly dangerous and put him at risk for many things.
What about the rib though? That's what I'm talking about.

Oh, the rib. Oh, for the rib, I would not radiate that. I see lots of rib lesions that does not have any, there's no obvious soft tissue component to it. And so to me, I would not radiate the rib. I think it's unlikely to be the cause of that, the source of that PSA.
Okay. Anybody else have any comments?

You know, one of the things we also could consider, again, the PSA is below two, but if the PSA goes up and there's no change in the scans, you could also consider giving cingulation and zalutamide to this patient.

Yeah. Okay. I take that. So we talked about, should we repeat the scan? We talked about that. If you repeated the scan, Sharif, if you were worried about that or something else, how long would you wait? Three months? Six months?

I don't know if there's a real good number. I would look at the doubling time of the PSA. I mean, if his PSA is steady and it's just minor bump up in PSAs, I'm not sure that you could get it anytime before six to eight months, probably closer to eight months, I would say. But if the PSA is doubling or if it's rising fairly rapidly, I think you can make a case to get it probably as soon as six months.
So Blaine, what is your definition of a rapid doubling time when you're looking at PSA as a urologist?

I mean, in his, in this kind of clinical scenario, you could, you could, and Dr. Petralek will have to clarify this for me, but I think you can use the EMBARQ criteria, which was, is that 13 months or 16 months? It's, it's, I don't remember.
I believe it was 12 months.
A month. Yeah. It was, it was, it's pretty short. So on the, I think any time where your PSA doubling time is less than a year, that's considered fast by almost anybody's definition.

Okay. Well, great, great cases. A lot of this great case here, a lot of learning points about rib lesions and doubling times and things like that. Let me just ask Sharif this question and the rest of you. What's the lowest PSA level with biochemical recurrence that you would consider ordering a PSMA PET scan?

Obviously, knowing what the approved indications and pre-auths are, 0.2 is probably, that's the published known. But, you know, we've discussed a couple of cases here today where the sentiment and the recommendation was to get a PSMA scan even under 0.2. So, I think any rise in PSA, really, that is either making you, the urologist, the oncologist, the radiation oncologist nervous, or the patient is kind of now concerned, probably makes sense to go ahead and order it, since it's rising. Again, if it needers, and if it gets to undetectable.
Last comment, Wayne?

No, I agree. That's a nice case. The one thing I do wonder about is probably from an individual patient standpoint, I feel very vindicated when I'm being aggressive. From a cost standpoint, then I'm not sure what the right answer is.

Great. Let's just summarize what we've learned from this case. First of all, we discussed PSA levels at which time to perform the test. green on 0.2, but there are a lot of men that have positive tests when their PSA is less than 0.2 nanograms per ml. Kind of reminds me of bone scans years ago, and before we published the Radar 1 paper, in which we showed that Ordering bone scans a lot of times in men with PSAs of less than 20 is not very helpful, but there's always those exceptions, particularly with higher grade cancers. So we continue to move forward. And we do know that it also serves another purpose, and that's a baseline to compare to in the future. We talked a little bit about when to repeat these. And I think we're in a learning curve. They're very helpful at monitoring lesions. But I would say that it's important to do this. If the results are going to be actionable, that we're going to do something with it. And finally, we discussed lesions away from the pelvis, particularly like ribs. That's sometimes sort of in our red herring here and doesn't mean anything. So again, I want to thank everybody for taking part in this pet tumor board.

Re-irradiation of the previously treated prostatic fossa was not recommended because of prior 71.8 Gy exposure, and radiation to the rib lesion was not advised. The agreed next step was surveillance with interval reassessment, including consideration of repeat PSMA imaging based on PSA kinetics, generally at approximately 6–8 months unless the PSA doubling time becomes rapid; if PSA rises further without imaging progression, systemic therapy with enzalutamide could be considered.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient. Age was not stated.

[ chief complaint ]: Lower extremity edema associated with inferior vena cava involvement by renal tumor. Renal mass had been present in situ prior to surgery.

[ diagnosis ]: Renal cell carcinoma of the kidney with inferior vena cava thrombus. Disease had poor-risk features based on at least two abnormal laboratory parameters. There was no metastatic disease on workup.

[ histopathology results ]: Radical nephrectomy specimen demonstrated greater than 95% sarcomatoid/rhabdoid dedifferentiation. Tumor invaded the renal vein and the arterial wall. Tumor was present at the resection margin, including an arterial margin.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative evaluation showed no metastatic disease. Inferior vena cava thrombus was present. Lower extremity edema was attributed to back pressure from the inferior vena cava thrombus.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum albumin was normal. At least two laboratory parameters were abnormal and were cited as poor-risk features. Specific values were not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent radical nephrectomy with thrombectomy. Lymph node dissection was performed as part of the operation for the inferior vena cava thrombus.

[ other clinical data ]: No hypoalbuminemia was present.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 4-year-old male child.

[ chief complaint ]: Right-sided abdominal mass for 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Large right renal tumor, initially diagnosed as non-metastatic right Wilms tumor. Postoperative pathology was reported as unclassified malignant spindle cell sarcoma/malignant mesenchymal tumor of the kidney, with external review favoring clear cell sarcoma of the kidney. Final documented diagnostic consideration remained between Wilms tumor and clear cell sarcoma of the kidney.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial FNAC from the renal mass showed round blue cells, suggestive of Wilms tumor with predominant blastemal component.  
- Core needle biopsy after neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed multiple spindle-to-ovoid cells with high mitotic activity; reported as stromal-predominant possibility of monophasic Wilms tumor.  
- External review of the core biopsy reported mesenchymal component of a Wilms tumor; immunohistochemistry was inconclusive.  
- Nephroureterectomy specimen showed multiple sheets and nests of spindle cells with spindle- and ovoid-shaped nuclei separated by fascicles, with areas of cystic degeneration lined by epithelium and high mitotic activity.  
- Institutional final pathology on resection specimen: unclassified spindle cell sarcoma.  
- External pathology review: malignant spindle cell tumor, most probably clear cell sarcoma of the kidney.  
- Additional tertiary review: malignant mesenchymal tumor, possibly clear cell sarcoma of the kidney.  
- Resection status was documented as R0.  
- Lymph node sampling was performed; sampled nodes were negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound abdomen/pelvis identified a right renal mass.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis showed a large heterogeneous mass arising from the lower pole of the right kidney, in close association with the inferior border of the liver, compressing the inferior vena cava, with marked mass effect on surrounding structures.  
- Inferior vena cava and renal vein were free of thrombus.  
- Imaging features were initially considered consistent with right Wilms tumor.  
- Reassessment CT abdomen/pelvis after 5 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed no significant reduction in tumor size and no significant change in tumor characteristics.  
- Intraoperatively, the tumor was free from the inferior surface of the liver and arose from the lower pole of the right kidney.  
- Tumor bed was marked with titanium clips for radiotherapy planning.  
- Follow-up was conducted with clinical and radiological surveillance; imaging surveillance included ultrasound and chest radiography alternating with CT chest and abdomen at 3-month intervals.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None documented.

[ laboratory results ]: Routine blood workup was performed initially; specific values were not documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered according to the DD4A regimen: vincristine, actinomycin D, and doxorubicin.  
- Planned treatment course was 5 cycles; 2 cycles were given initially, followed by chemoport insertion and administration of the remaining cycles.  
- Interval imaging after the initial 5 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed no significant radiologic response.  
- Right nephroureterectomy with lymph node sampling was performed.  
- Adjuvant chemotherapy was continued postoperatively according to the Wilms tumor protocol because treatment had already progressed and the child was clinically well.  
- Flank radiotherapy was administered to a total dose of 10.8 Gy.

[ current disease status ]: Clinically well and disease-free for 9 months after completion of treatment, on close clinical and radiological follow-up.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On examination, the child was well preserved.  
- Abdominal examination showed a firm, non-tender mass measuring approximately 15 × 20 cm involving the entire right side of the abdomen and crossing the midline.  
- External genitalia were normal.  
- Per rectal examination showed no abnormal findings.  
- There were no urinary complaints, altered bowel habits, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

reference_discussion.text: We now invite Dr. Navya Bholu from ESIC Medical College, Sanathnagar, Hyderabad to do her presentation.
Thank you, sir.
Are my slides visible?
Yes, they are visible.

Good evening, everyone. Today I will be presenting a case. So we had a four-year-old male child who presented to us with complaints of a right-sided abdominal mass since one month. There were no other associated symptoms or urinary tract complaints, no altered bowel habits, and no GI symptoms. The child was otherwise doing well. On clinical examination, the child appeared to be well-preserved. And on examination of the abdomen, there was a large 15 into 20 centimeters a firm non-tender mass involving the entire right side of the abdomen and crossing the midline. External genitalia of the child was normal and per rectal examination also showed no abnormal signs. So after the initial investigations, which included the routine blood workup as well as an ultrasound abdomen and pelvis, we proceeded to get a CCT abdomen and pelvis, which showed a large heterogeneous mass that was arising from the lower pole of the right kidney. It was seen in close association with the inferior border of the liver. and it was also shown compressing the IVC. However, the IVC and the renal vein were both free of thrombus and it showed a large mass effect over the surrounding structures. So these features were consistent with Willem's tumor of the right kidney. As a part of our institutional protocol, we went ahead and did a histopathological diagnosis to help confirm the diagnosis. And we did a FNAC, which again showed, as you can see, round blue cells, which was suggestive of possibility of a Willem's tumor with a predominant blastomel component. An FNAC in our institution is usually done as an adjunct to the diagnosis and it can be done as a safe method which does not upstage the tumor and it is a simple and easier method which doesn't involve any sedation and is less pain-free as well with a quicker response rate. So at this point, our diagnosis was a non-metastatic right Wilms tumor. And in view of the large size of the tumor, as well as possible risk of tumor spill during surgery, we decided to give the child neoadjuvant chemotherapy, according to the DD4A regimen, which involves vincristin, actinomycin D, and doxorubicin. We plan to give five cycles and reassess. So this was our roadmap for the child. We decided to first give two cycles of chemotherapy, and following which we inserted a chemo port, and we have administered the remaining cycles. Now, following the initial five weeks of Neerjeevan chemotherapy, we reassessed with a CCT abdomen and pelvis again. However, there was no significant reduction in size, nor were there any changes in the features or the nature of the tumor. So to confirm our diagnosis and to reassess, we decided to go ahead with a core biopsy along with IHC markers. So after doing the core needle biopsy, we saw that this was the histopathological picture showing multiple spindle-to-ovoid cells, and there was a large mitotic activity as well. And this was the report that was given by our institution, which was suggestive of stromal predominant possibility of monophasic Wilms tumor. So just to confirm our diagnosis and to confirm our findings, we decided to get a second opinion at a regional prominent cancer center where we routinely send our specimens. And they had also reported it to be a mesenchymal component of a Wilms tumor and their IHC markers were inconclusive. So at this point, because the child was doing well, and we decided that it was possible for us to go in and do a surgical resection, we proceeded to do a right nephroureterectomy along with lymph node sampling. Intraoperatively, as you can see, the tumor was free from the inferior surface of the liver, and it appeared to be a solid tumor with fairly upfront and easy resectability. This was the tumor. which is arising from the lower pole of right kidney. And this is the tumor bed, which we have later marked with titanium clips to help in guiding us for future radiotherapy. So on histopathological examination of the specimen that was sent, this is the cut section, and this showed multiple sheets and nests of spindle cells with spindle and ovoid-shaped nuclei that was separated by fascicles. And there is also areas of cystic degeneration, which show areas lined by epithelium. And it was a fairly high mitotic activity that was noted. This was the final report that was given to us by our institution, where they classified it to be an unclassified spindle cell sarcoma with positive IHC staining for vimentin, cyclin D1, CD99, TLE1, and CD34, along with PANCK. And it was negative for BCL2, WT1, S100, desmin, synaptophysin, CD1A, glypecan 3, paxate, and myogenin. So at this point, we were slightly puzzled and we decided to get, as we did with the core needle biopsy, a second opinion from our local cancer center as well. And this report was given to us almost two weeks post-operatively. They have also mentioned it to be a malignant spindle cell tumor that was most probably a clear cell sarcoma of the kidney. which were positive for Cyclin D1, CD99 and Vimentin on IHC staining. Following this, so at this point, because two weeks of the report and the surgery had already passed, we decided to continue with our chemotherapy protocol and we continue to give the adjuvant chemotherapy as per the roadmap. At this point, we also discussed with a radiologist and because the reports were differing in terms of the final diagnosis, Both whelms and clear cell sarcoma of the kidney did not have any significant changes with respect to the radiotherapy administration. So we decided to proceed with radiotherapy, where we gave flank radiation for six cycles of 10.8 grade. Following this, just to confirm, we also sent it to AIMS New Delhi for another opinion and they have also reported it to be features of malignant mesenchymal tumor that was again possibly a clear cell sarcoma of the kidney. So at this point, these were the histopathology reports and these were the IHC stainings that were given to us by all three institutions. So in this, what I would like to highlight is BCOR and CD99, which are usually positive for clear cell sarcoma of the kidney. In this case, BCOR was negative in both the reports that we took for second opinion. CD99 was positive in our institutional report. WT1 was negative throughout, Vimentin was positive and Cyclin D1 was positive in both our report as well as the AIIMS report. So after discussing with the parents and giving them the option of either further continuing the chemotherapy as per the guidelines for clear cell sarcoma of the kidney, taking into consideration that the child was doing well post-operatively, we were able to get away with an R0 resection. We continued, and at this point, the child had almost completed chemotherapy. So the parents and the doctors involved decided that we would finished the chemotherapy as per the Wilms tumor protocol. And since then, he has been healthy and disease-free for the last nine months. And we have kept him on close follow-up, both with a clinical and radiological follow-up. This is our protocol that we follow. Coming to the discussion, so there has been documented confusion between the diagnosis of a clear cell sarcoma of the kidney. And in those cases where initially it is diagnosed or thought to be a Wilms tumor, 5% of these have actually been reclassified to be clear cell sarcoma of the kidney in literature. And the differences that come up are the following. So Wilms is a more risk adapted therapy. Clear cell sarcoma, all of them are considered to be high risk. Wilms tumor is usually treated with either a two or three drug regimen of chemotherapy. Clear cell sarcoma requires a more intensive and multidrug chemotherapy protocol. The duration coming to Wilms is given for a period of six months. For clear cell sarcoma, it is said that according to the latest guidelines of NWTS-5, that the duration can be six months, but with a more intensive protocol that includes cyclophosphamide and adipocyte. The 15-month protocol that was studied and compared to the six-month protocol shows that the 15-month protocol has better relapse-free survival rates, but coming to overall survival rate, both are similar. Surgery-wise, both have the same surgical protocol. They both require a nephrectomy with lymph node sampling. And in Wilms, selective radiation therapy is done based on the final histopathology report. However, in clear cell sarcoma, routine radiotherapy is recommended to all cases. So as of now, we have come to a point where we have given surgery and radiation for this patient. And this matches with both the Wilms and the clear cell sarcoma. Whether we are doing enough for this patient coming to the chemotherapy protocol, our decision was to stop and keep the child on follow-up after six months. So this is something that we wanted to discuss and whether we should be doing anything more for this child as well. Thank you.

Thank you, Dr. Navya. I think in the interest of time, we'll quickly ask Dr. Tejaswini from KMC Manipal to do a case presentation. It's very similar. So then we'll have a quick discussion after. Over to you, Dr. Tejaswini from KMC Manipal.

Can I be made a co-host? I'm not able to share my slides. You were the host. Yeah, I have been. I don't know. I'm no more the host. I'm much sorrier. Thank you, Suhasini, for joining. Thank you. Thank you. You can give a comment while she's loading her slides. Unmute yourself. Yeah, make host. Yeah. Yeah. I think I made a host. Yeah, please go ahead. Yes.
are my slides seen? Good evening, everyone. So there is a similar case to the previous case that was discussed by Dr. Navya.
Ours was a one-year-old, 10-month-old girl who was born by non-consanguineous marriage, first order by birth. There was no significant family history of any malignancy.
She presented with a mass per abdomen since 15 days. She was also noted to have hypertension with more than 95th centile readings and grade one protein energy malnutrition.

She had presented with an ultrasound report from outside, which was showing a large, well-defined hypoechoic solid mass lesion, which was involving the upper and middle pole of the left kidney, which was suggestive of Wilms tumor. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Colon carcinoma with radiologic disease progression during adjuvant chemotherapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Colon carcinoma, stage III at initial diagnosis. Progressive disease was documented after adjuvant chemotherapy, with new supraclavicular and mediastinal nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Mucinous histology was reported. Biopsy was performed after documentation of progression; no further biopsy histomorphologic details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: FAPI PET scan performed after 3 cycles of adjuvant CAPOX demonstrated progressive disease with new supraclavicular lymph nodes and new mediastinal lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NGS/hotspot panel on biopsy specimen showed BRAF V600E positive, TP53 positive, microsatellite stable/MSI negative, and HER2 negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Surgery for colon carcinoma was performed.  
- Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy was administered for 3 cycles.  
- Disease progression was documented after 3 cycles of CAPOX on FAPI PET scan.  
- FOLFIRI was started after progression while awaiting NGS results. Cycle 1 day 1 had been completed; cycle 2 was due at the time of reporting.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive disease after adjuvant CAPOX, with nodal metastatic progression involving supraclavicular and mediastinal lymph nodes. The patient had commenced first cycle of FOLFIRI following progression.

[ other clinical data ]: None further available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Draining left scalp lesion present for approximately 2.5 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Nodular melanoma of the left temporal scalp with regional metastatic disease to left parotid/preauricular and cervical lymph nodes; clinical stage pT2b cN2b, stage III locally advanced melanoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial shave biopsy of the left scalp lesion was positive for nodular melanoma. Breslow depth was at least 1.1 mm. Clark level was at least IV. Ulceration was present. Mitotic rate was 10/mm². The lesion extended to all margins. Primary tumor staging was reported as T2b. Fine-needle aspiration of a palpable left parotid/preauricular node was positive for metastatic melanoma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated several soft tissue nodules in the left parotid gland and left neck, including a necrotic left neck node, measuring approximately 13 mm and 15 mm. PET/CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic left scalp lesion, multiple hypermetabolic intraparotid lymph nodes, and hypermetabolic left cervical lymph nodes including level IIA and a smaller level IV node. Post-neoadjuvant repeat cross-sectional imaging/PET showed reduction in size of the lymphadenopathy and decreased metabolic activity of the previously described nodes. New small bilateral FDG-avid nodes were present and were interpreted as inflammatory changes related to immunotherapy. Surveillance imaging plan consisted of PET/CT every 3 months and brain MRI yearly.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF testing, next-generation sequencing, and circulating tumor DNA testing could not be performed due to insufficient viable cells.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received neoadjuvant ipilimumab plus nivolumab. Clinical response included decrease in size of the primary lesion and partial radiographic response with reduction in nodal size and FDG avidity. Reported treatment-related adverse effects during neoadjuvant therapy were pruritus and fatigue. He subsequently underwent wide local excision of the primary lesion, left superficial parotidectomy, and left neck dissection. Reconstruction was performed with a cervicofacial advancement flap. No adjuvant therapy was given.

[ current disease status ]: The patient was on surveillance.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination at presentation, there was a 1 cm scaly lesion in the hair-bearing left temporal scalp with surrounding erythema and a palpable left pretragal lymph node measuring approximately 1 cm. Past medical history was notable for no autoimmune disorders, no immune deficiencies, no prior oncologic history, and no reported social risk factors.

Although the data is probably around the corner that had you highlighted your index node, you could do just a node biopsy before doing complete neck dissection. Again, not there yet. Small trials have shown that that's safe, but the larger trial is in the works.

Yeah, this is why when I only taught a cursory glance of that pad, I was asking if that node was a deep lobe parotid node or not, because that would definitely, you know, can perhaps not be in your resection plan. And you definitely would want that in your resection plan. I think the Nadina trial, they actually put a little seed in all the positive nodes to ensure, as a quality measure, that those are resected. So if you have a complete response, it can be challenging to really be sure that you got out the nodes that were originally involved with disease. But yeah, I agree for this. I would do a wide excision of the primary site, and I would do a parotidectomy, neck dissection, including all those levels.
If this patient originally only had parotid mets and no neck adenopathy on the surgery, would you consider the neck dissection or just do a parotid?
That's a great question.

I have a good answer for you, but what I would generally do is try to be like, one level further than anything clinical. So I think I would probably make sure that I address the EJ nodes, because I would think of that as like the next chain. Maybe if there was just one node, a complete parotid would probably be good. So maybe you don't need to go that far, much further. But I think with more than one parotid node, I think I'd want to know that the next chain was clean.

That thing that is being discussed as a deep lobe parotid is a high external jugular node, and those have to be removed in this. It's commonly stated as a parotid node, but it's actually just behind the tail of a parotid. And I agree with what everybody else has said about extent.

Yeah, that's a great point. With skin cancers, you've got to remove those EJ nodes. I can hear Randy Weber's voice in my head when I do these cases, because back then for anyone with positive nodes, he would do a modified radical for all of those, because melanoma can have a pretty strange pattern of spread, you know, not our typical aerodigestive. And so often we would be doing level fives even for those. But, you know, in the setting of neoadjuvant therapy, I agree with Joe, like we don't know, you know, what the true resection has to be. I think to answer your question, Jessica, with the parotidectomy, with the parotid node, I would do a parotid and probably do level two, maybe slide down into three and like get one around. And again, I think the thinking behind that too is, you know, your surgery is not ultimately probably their life-changing thing. It's really their risk of dysmethia that's gonna be their problem. So their response immunotherapy is really important. The only comment about the nadina trial is the outcome was event-free survival. It wasn't overall survival. So again, we still don't have really mature data, even though those neoadjuvant curves look so fantastic, we don't know the long-term differences. And this all is related to this discussion. We don't know if any of these things are really impacting you know, even the extent of our neck dissection, if that's going to impact their long-term outcomes. They do look good, though. Yeah, I know, they look promising, but it's really just their time to their melanoma coming back. OS is going to be a goal.

Harleen, I think this is a great case, and I think all the comments and questions are really great. I work at Kaiser, it's a big managed care program, so We know our patients aren't generally on clinical trials, so we follow NCCM guidelines very closely. And the guideline is after neoadjuvant to do a therapeutic neck dissection. But looking at the PET, you mentioned that they thought that some of the lymph nodes were from an effective immunotherapy. And although we all learned about pseudoprogression with immunotherapy, like every immunotherapy paper just talks about pseudoprogression. But I haven't actually seen it that much in clinical practice, whereas meaning like there is an activity or increased activity in lymph node. Often I've removed the lymph node, it has cancer in it. I don't see that much pseudoprogression, meaning the pet shows activity and ends up being just benign. So I think that's something I learned in my practice in the last few years.

A handful of people didn't get surgery in that trial. And it was something like less than 3%, I don't know, TJ, it was like less than 3% that progressed and had true hyper progression and were no longer surgical candidates. So, I mean, it's another thing we think about, right? Like, so we, uh, It's the importance of the trial is not just the outcome, but the safety, right? I mean, people can die from immunotherapy. Fortunately, it's very rare, but it can happen. It's real. Actually, one patient did die in the... Yeah.

I mean, I just had a patient who had a myocarditis and had a cardiac arrest one day after getting immunotherapy. It's crazy. It does happen. Just to comment on the pseudoprogression, that specifically is often referring to their first cycle and having the tumor expand after the first cycle. So I just want to clarify that when they talk about pseudoprogression, that's usually referring to that kind of false progression of the tumor after that first infusion. But I've had a patient hyper-progress too, and we kind of delayed watching them to the second cycle, but his tumor was just exploding. And so you do have to be worried about missing that when you're thinking it's just pseudoprogression.
Yeah, I think my point is like yours, that you can't just count it to be like pseudoprogression or immunotherapy reaction. I would remove every lymph node that had activity on the PET.

I would just add to this really interesting discussion is that while we're talking about being more rather than less complete with regard to regional nodal disease, I think we're going to have more data sooner rather…well, not sooner, it's going to take a while for trials to mature. index lymph node resection to assess response and then determine whether or not there's going to be any further dissection similar to positive sentinel node not necessarily completing that dissection. The Proto trial is too small but suggests that that's safe to do. MSLT3 will answer that if that gets going. So, yeah. But the head and neck specifically, if your sentinel node or index lymph node is in the parotid, it would be – you're not going to do less than a reasonable dissection because you're not going to want to go back to the parotid. So, there are head and neck considerations that are really kind of distinct from these practice-changing trials that we always have to keep in mind too.

Great, really salient points. I know we're running a little short on time, but I will just go forward with the rest of the case here. So we did undergo surgery, and as everybody correctly stated, we did a wide local excision, a left superficial parotid, and a left neck dissection on this gentleman. His reconstruction was done by our plastics colleagues with a cervical facial advancement flap. And for our final pathology, he actually had a complete pathologic response. So we only had evidence of an intradermal melanotic nevus with ciliary elastosis on the main lesion. All of the notes were negative per tumor board discussion and then in a trial, no adjuvant therapy was recommended and he is on surveillance. The surveillance is dictated by a medic who is going to be doing Q3 month PET CTs and yearly brain MRI. Of note postoperatively, the patient was admitted for nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and ended up being secondary to adrenal insufficiency, which he's still dealing with, secondary to the immunotherapy. So just an important point to discuss. An endocrine is recommended, as stressed as the steroids for this patient, anytime he's undergoing an acute illness, surgery or hospitalization.
Did they get adjuvant immunotherapy though? No. No, he did not.
Because of the complete response.

Like crazy. I want to make a comment that I'm, you have to add this to your consent that you're going to do surgery and there's a possibility you do not find any tumor. Cause that's a kind of a new thing. We're saying a lot to patients and that's kind of a crazy thing to consider when you look at this surgery.
And, um, I just tell them that's their best, best path report. That's what we get.

Yeah, that's true. Yeah. But I've done like a resected part of a lip and done an ABA, you know, but then for no disease. So that's, you know, you have to really counsel them that you really, these are important decisions and that there's a possibility there's no cancer there.

I would say like you brought up another really good point, which is the adrenal and that's one of the things I kind of like about this design is like, You don't have to get it, which is maybe a little not the best for the drug company, but it certainly would be great if you're a patient and it pans out. Right. I mean, if the long term data is good, it's a very good thing.

I got three brief comments. One, if you're gonna do an advancement flap for melanoma at the same time, be careful with that. Even if you think you had a complete response of the primary, you can get burned. Two is that with these pathology reports, there is a synoptic way to report these after immune therapy that's standardized. The pathologist, I can't remember the name of it, but they should quantify Four things, Gil, please correct me if I'm wrong. There's fibrosis, there's melanosis, there is necrosis. What's the fourth one? Anyways, these should be, so when there's no tumor in the specimen, they should say, hey, this is what we see there. For melanoma, they will see evidence that there was a melanoma there. It's just all dead. Okay. That may not be the case for squaying where it's just fibrotic. And as TJ said, that can be distressing. Are you talking about a viral tumor for the other one? Yes, sir. Yeah. The last thing is that these immune-related adverse events, endocrinopathies, that will be permanent, very likely, this adrenal insufficiency. And that sucks.

Hey, Ryan, thanks for the comments. Just to add some clarification, not only did the pathologist report those things, so there was melanophagias and necrosis in three of the lymph nodes. The lymph node, the preauricular lymph node, which started off palpable, was pigmented. So when we opened them up, it was still pigmented. So the melanocytes are just in the macrophages.

Yeah, so that's off. I remember the first, you know, Very often, this is what it is. And it's distressing because you think, oh no, the PET CT looked like a good response. And then there can be black lymph nodes everywhere, and it's all dead.

It is also found with our melanin incontinence. which is sometimes it's just melanin in the lymph node, which I thought I got fooled by that. I thought it was the best term ever from a pathologist, but it's just pigment in the node from the tumor being broken down.
Are you sure your pathologist wasn't just jerking your chain? She might've been, she's pretty clever.
That's all I got for everyone. So I will stop sharing so we can get to the last case.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient. Age was not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma identified as high-grade cT1 disease.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma, clinically at least T1 at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy demonstrated high-grade T1 disease. Exact final pathologic TNM stage was not provided.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging did not demonstrate definitive locally advanced disease. Imaging was acknowledged to have limited sensitivity for excluding occult higher-stage local disease. No objective radiographic measurements or specific CT/MRI findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative renal function was discussed in terms of estimated post-nephroureterectomy glomerular filtration rate. Estimated post-nephroureterectomy GFR by nomogram was 45 mL/min/1.73 m².

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 4 cycles of neoadjuvant gemcitabine/cisplatin without difficulty. She subsequently underwent robotic nephroureterectomy with lymphadenectomy. Intravesical gemcitabine was administered perioperatively, consisting of 2 g instilled into the bladder intraoperatively with subsequent drainage and bladder irrigation.

[ current disease status ]: Status post neoadjuvant gemcitabine/cisplatin followed by robotic nephroureterectomy with lymphadenectomy. No documented metastatic disease was reported. Final postoperative pathologic stage and current surveillance status were not provided.

[ other clinical data ]: Risk stratification tools categorized the case as high risk for advanced pathologic stage. One calculator estimated approximately 60% probability of pT3 disease. Estimated recurrence-free probability following radical nephroureterectomy for high-grade disease was approximately 82% at 2 years and 70% at 5 years.

reference_discussion.text: So at our institution, we tend to lean towards offering people with good kidney function, high-grade disease, upfront neoadjuvant chemotherapy because the biopsies can be understaging people. We also have a clinical trial open that we're always thinking about for our patients, which is looking at MVAC with or without dervelumab, so an immunotherapy with chemotherapy in the neoadjuvant setting. And so we tend to lean heavily towards chemotherapy.
OK. Adam, agree? Disagree?

Yeah, well, I think you're going to show that, I mean, you have to think about this patient and what's there. If you were to do a nephro, so first of all, I think the patient needs a nephro-uterectomy. I just want to be clear. High-grade T1 disease, even if you, you know, the patient needs a nephro-uterectomy. It's at least T1 and maybe under stage. Then the question is, what's the post-NU GFR going to be? If that's going to result in a GFR that the patient is then cisplatin ineligible, then I think that is the ideal patient that should be considering neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Perfect. And that's really what we want to start highlighting. And the AUA guidelines have maybe don't explicitly go in. Well, they do explicitly go into it in terms of the idea that we should start thinking about what the kidney function is going to be before we create a new kidney function baseline. So don't wait until after a nephro-ureterectomy to think about it. Think about it at presentation. And there are ways of estimating this, and they're available in your syllabus. But you could do a very basic calculation of splitting the GFR in half, although that doesn't tell you how much that other side may have compensatory changes. So based on that, maybe it's between 30 and 40. There are nomograms available. There's RCC nomograms. We recently published a specific upper tract urothelial cancer nomogram as well. Based on those, her GFR would be 45. This will have an impact on the patient's ability to receive cisplatin chemotherapy. There are some centers that maybe would give it to a level of 50-55, but for most places are not going to give cisplatin below 55-60. Would you agree?

The POUT trial actually required patients who had a GFR of 50 or better, they had to go on the cisplatin arm. Once that was published, I became much more open and aggressive. And sometimes I will also go a little below that, depending on the patient. I do a lot of splitting the dose.
You can split dose or reduce dose, correct? So there's other ways of managing it.

Our medical oncologists will go to about 50. And I'll just comment that depending on who's part of your multidisciplinary team, there are times you may need to push them to give neoadjuvant in a situation like this.

So there's two factors here. One is the kidney function, which we talked about, but the other is what is the risk of disease? Are we over-treating or are we under-treating? And so I don't have this here, but according to the new AUA guidelines, this patient would have high-risk favorable disease. That data doesn't come with any objective values for you to guide yourself. All you know is that it's not unfavorable. And we've talked about the T1 staging potentially being understaged. And imaging, as you know, can also understage this disease. And so imaging is really more of a rule-in. It can confirm sometimes locally advanced disease, but it doesn't really rule it out. And so this is why we've developed risk stratification tools. And there's a variety of these available. I'm going to show you two of them. This one predicts T3 disease or higher. The accuracy is actually pretty reasonable for a clinical calculator, 82%. It's very simple to use. In this case, the patient meets high risk criteria. And then this one is on the basis of recurrence-free probability if they have an FRU for high-grade disease. And in this case, it's not quite as clear because it's roughly, let's see, yeah, 60% chance of T3 disease, and the recurrence-free probability at two and five years is 82 to 70%, so you could argue that's more intermediate, not really high risk. But either way, what we know is that if we do initial surgery, patient is not likely to get high, really good levels of curative chemotherapy. And so you need to have an honest conversation with the patient in terms of these are the risks and benefits. And the patient, given this data, is elected to proceed with neoadjuvant chemo.

And so I'll just make one quick comment. I know it's not your center, it's not my center, but if you go to cancernomograms.com, you can just plug the numbers in and it'll provide it for you. So you don't need to use the little, you know, yeah, exactly. You don't need to do that. Yeah.
And I'm a big, I can't remember if we got these on the Fox chase. I go to the Fox chase. It is awesome. Yeah.
That's cancer nomograms.com. Yeah.

So you can, you don't have to do these manually. Um, yep. So the patient received four cycles of, of gem cysts without difficulty. Uh, they underwent a robotic nephro ureterectomy with lymphadenectomy. It just as a side note, Adam, would you have done a lymph node dissection in this case?
I would have. It's high-grade disease. It's very informative.

Very good. Obviously, we don't really know what the stage was. We know it was at least a T1. By all accounts here, given the post-treatment pathologic stage, she was downstaged. Generally, this is considered effective response. As we can see, the GFR is a little lower than we predicted, and more than likely, that's a result of some cisplatin nephrotoxicity that occurred.

This might be a good time to comment on the intravesicular gemcitabine. I think that that's important. There are different ways to do it. It's been shown to reduce the risk of bladder recurrence distally. Historically, what people started doing, they were giving it around 48 hours. Some were doing it at the time of catheter removal, but we're giving it actually in the operating room. I think it's the same way you do it. Instill two grams of gemcitabine into the bladder, clamp the catheter. Once the artery is divided and ligated, then put a clip on the ureter and then allow the gemcitabine to drain out and then run a continuous bladder irrigation to irrigate the bladder. And we've had no issues with that. Exactly.

Because also when the patient leaves the hospital, you know you're done. Correct. It's much easier. We actually don't even, we do a cystogram in the hospital and take the catheter out before they leave.
And to me, it actually makes more sense because that's when the cells are floating and that's when you want to kill them. I totally agree.

The only other thing I will add to that is I ask anesthesia to minimize fluids, because you are clamping the bladder for up to an hour and a half to two hours. So we definitely don't want them to dilute the chemo or to get over distended. Is there any questions about that case before we move on?
And I'll just comment, use the chat to ask questions. I think that's the best way if you're going to do it through your phone.
How are you staging this patient? Are you using PET scan? And would that change your decision to do a lymphadenectomy?
We don't use PET routinely in urothelial. I don't know if you do. We use conventional iPlus imaging.

I hate PET scans. The resolution of a PET is not as good as a standard CT, number one. Number two, I think there are indications for it. And generally, when I've used it is when they can't get a contrasted CT. And we have concerns about an MRI. For whatever reason, they have a pacemaker, and we can't get an MRI either. So for me, it's a very narrow indication for a PET. Sometimes post-surgery I'll do it because they meet those indications. I don't know. Do you have any thoughts about that?

I do a PET on almost all of my patients that are metastatic because we find much more disease or if you're thinking they're kind of at the border of being operable versus locally advanced. It's very informative if you find a high lymph node in their superclav that's not palpable or super visible on the CT. So it's been very informative in the metastatic setting for us. We use a lot of MRIs and other modalities in the early stage, and these patients usually don't belong to me until they've been worked up. So the early stage is kind of your ballgame.

You know, I think potentially another situation would be an enlarged lymph node that you can't biopsy for whatever reason, and you just need some information as to guide treatment. I'm trying to think if I've been in that situation. But otherwise, I don't. You know, it doesn't help you with local staging at all, right? We agree. But potentially for ruling in or ruling out metastatic disease, maybe.
But I agree that the CT on a PET is suboptimal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old Caucasian male.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-month history of worsening epigastric pain, later associated with nausea and vomiting.

[ diagnosis ]: Myeloid sarcoma presenting as extramedullary abdominal/pelvic masses without morphologic evidence of acute leukemia in the bone marrow.

[ histopathology results ]: Laparoscopic biopsy of the mesenteric/anterior abdominal mass showed blasts in conglomeration. Immunophenotyping was reported as CD45 positive and CD117 positive, with morphology interpreted as consistent with myeloid sarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT abdomen/pelvis at an outside hospital demonstrated a mesenteric mass.  
- PET-CT demonstrated the biopsied anterior abdominal mass, a right hemipelvic mass with mass effect on the bladder, and additional soft-tissue sites of involvement. Disease was described in multiple separate areas.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- FISH testing on tissue was sent to Mayo Clinic for AML and MDS panels; results were negative.  
- FLT3 testing was negative for both ITD and TKD mutations.  
- NPM1 mutation was positive.  
- Next-generation sequencing was positive for DNMT3A; an additional mutation was reported but not clearly specified.

[ laboratory results ]: Routine laboratory studies were reported as completely normal at presentation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Colonoscopy was performed before laparoscopic biopsy.  
- Laparoscopic biopsy of the abdominal/mesenteric mass was performed by colorectal surgery.  
- Bone marrow biopsy was performed and was completely negative, including normal morphology; marrow genetic testing was also reported as completely normal.  
- Lumbar puncture was performed and was negative.  
- Intrathecal methotrexate was administered.  
- Induction systemic chemotherapy with 7+3 was initiated.  
- HLA typing was performed for the patient and one sister.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Multifocal extramedullary disease was present in the abdomen/pelvis and soft tissues on PET-CT.  
- No acute leukemia was evident in the bone marrow.  
- CNS evaluation by lumbar puncture was negative.  
- The patient was hospitalized and receiving 7+3 induction chemotherapy at the time of reporting.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: hypertension.  
- Social history: never smoker; alcohol use was reported as 1-2 drinks, 4-5 times per week.  
- Family history: breast cancer; no hematologic malignancy history reported.  
- Physical examination was reported as unremarkable.  
- Functional status appeared preserved; the patient exercised regularly and ran daily prior to presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Left renal pelvis upper tract urothelial carcinoma (high-grade), with regional retroperitoneal nodal involvement at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Ureteroscopic biopsy of the left renal pelvis mass was consistent with high-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial evaluation identified an infiltrative left renal pelvis mass. Multiple enlarged periaortic and perihilar lymph nodes were present, measuring up to 1.8 cm, described as bulky lymphadenopathy. No distant metastatic disease was identified. Pre-treatment FDG PET demonstrated avid lymphadenopathy throughout the nodal disease burden.

[ laboratory results ]: Renal function was preserved at presentation. MAG3 renal scan showed approximately 4% differential renal function in the left kidney.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent ureteroscopic evaluation with biopsy of the renal pelvis mass. She subsequently received 6 cycles of enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab. She then underwent left radical nephroureterectomy with extensive templated retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy.

[ other clinical data ]: No remarkable prior medical history was reported. Performance status was good at presentation. No distant metastases were identified at diagnosis.

reference_conclusion: The consensus recommendation was to manage the bulky retroperitoneal nodal upper tract urothelial carcinoma as systemic disease with prompt referral to medical oncology and initiation of systemic therapy rather than upfront nephroureterectomy or nodal resection. Surgery was not recommended initially, with consideration of consolidation resection only after a durable and substantial response, given the risk of delaying necessary systemic treatment and the absence of clear supporting data.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old female; performance status 1.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough and mild chest pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Inoperable pulmonary artery sarcoma with peripheral lung nodules/lung metastases. The lesion was described as an intraluminal pulmonary artery mass; intimal sarcoma was considered in the differential classification.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from a peripheral lung nodule showed undifferentiated sarcoma after extensive immunohistochemistry.

[ imaging findings ]: Echocardiography identified a space-occupying lesion. PET imaging demonstrated a pulmonary artery mass with peripheral lung nodules. The pulmonary artery lesion was described as intraluminal, with associated tumour thrombus. Cardiothoracic assessment deemed the pulmonary artery mass inoperable.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Soft tissue sarcoma-specific NGS panel identified two TP53 pathogenic missense variants. One TP53 variant had a variant allele frequency of approximately 40%. No sarcoma-associated fusion was detected on the panel.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine plus docetaxel was initiated for inoperable cardiothoracic sarcoma. The patient completed 2 cycles. Cough reduced and clinical symptoms improved after treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Clinically improved after 2 cycles of gemcitabine/docetaxel. No repeat imaging had yet been performed to assess radiologic response.

[ other clinical data ]: Cardiac function was reported to be preserved. No comorbidities were reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia; later sought operative management after progression of symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Biochemical primary hyperparathyroidism.

[ histopathology results ]: Pathology from the initial neck exploration demonstrated two parathyroid glands among submitted specimens; additional specimens consisted of fibroadipose tissue and thyroid tissue. A left lower parathyroid gland had been identified intraoperatively and preserved rather than excised.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- DEXA scan demonstrated osteoporosis at the distal radius and osteopenia at other measured sites.  
- Sestamibi scan in 2018 was non-localizing.  
- Preoperative 4D CT had not been performed before the initial surgery.  
- F18 choline PET scan subsequently localized a right lower parathyroid adenoma.  
- Office ultrasound later corroborated a right lower level VI candidate lesion at the site identified on PET.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Initial biochemical evaluation showed calcium 11.0 mg/dL and PTH 127 pg/mL.  
- Pre-incision PTH at the initial operation was 99 pg/mL.  
- During the initial operation, intraoperative PTH did not decrease after excision of a right upper parathyroid candidate and remained essentially at preoperative levels after further exploration and excision of a presumed left upper parathyroid candidate and a left retrosophageal nodule.  
- At later evaluation, PTH was 147 pg/mL and calcium 10.6 mg/dL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Surgical intervention was initially deferred after diagnosis despite meeting operative criteria on the basis of hypercalcemia and skeletal involvement.  
- Initial parathyroid operation was performed in November 2022 without prior 4D CT localization.  
- At that operation, a right upper parathyroid candidate was excised first without intraoperative PTH decline. The procedure was then converted to bilateral exploration through bilateral lateral approaches. A presumed large left upper parathyroid was excised, a right lower gland was not identified, a cervical thymectomy was performed, a left lower gland was identified and preserved, and a left retrosophageal nodule was excised. The operation did not achieve biochemical cure.  
- The postoperative course after the initial surgery was complicated by cervical hematoma requiring evacuation and ICU admission.  
- Following subsequent localization with F18 choline PET and confirmatory office ultrasound, revision surgery was performed with rapid identification and excision of a right lower parathyroid adenoma.

[ other clinical data ]: No parathyroid specimen weights were available from the initial pathology report.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging thyroid nodule in 2016.

[ diagnosis ]: Oncocytic (Hürthle cell) thyroid carcinoma. Concurrent chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) had also been diagnosed in 2017. Recurrent disease had involved the thyroid bed/neck soft tissues, including scar/subcutaneous tissue, skeletal muscle, and left paratracheal region.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2017 left hemithyroidectomy: initially interpreted as a benign oncocytic neoplasm with macrofollicular growth pattern and degenerative changes. External review at that time identified no carcinoma.  
- Subsequent review of the 2017 specimen showed the specimen had been fragmented; one slide demonstrated lesional tissue beyond the capsule, consistent with at least capsular invasion. Revised diagnosis: oncocytic carcinoma with at least capsular invasion. Extent of invasion could not be fully assessed because of specimen fragmentation. Tumor cells were oncocytic/Hürthle cells without nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- 2021 isthmus resection with central compartment lymph node dissection: Hürthle cell carcinoma involving the isthmus and surgical scar. Histology showed oncocytic thyroid cells in subcutaneous tissue and skeletal muscle, with vascular invasion identified. No lymph nodes were involved by carcinoma in that specimen.  
- Completion thyroidectomy specimen (including right lobectomy, skin/scar, and central compartment soft tissue): Hürthle cell carcinoma present, including growth in skeletal muscle. Lymphoma was also identified as a secondary diagnosis.  
- 2024 left paratracheal revision surgery/biopsy: frozen section and subsequent pathology confirmed Hürthle cell carcinoma. A 3.4 mm focus of disease was referenced.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2021 PET-CT performed for lymphoma evaluation demonstrated a hypermetabolic nodule in the thyroid isthmus.  
- Post-radioiodine scan showed uptake in the thyroid bed only.  
- 2024 PET-CT demonstrated increased FDG uptake in the left thyroid bed with SUV approximately 12. Adjacent lymph nodes were present but were less avid than the thyroid bed lesion.  
- 2024 CT documented interval increase in size of the left thyroid bed lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Initial molecular testing on the left thyroid nodule cytology was negative.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- February after the third operation: thyroglobulin 4.5.  
- Subsequent thyroglobulin values: 3.1, then 7.0, and 9.5 in 2023.  
- After the 2024 left paratracheal procedure, thyroglobulin changed from 9.2 to 7.0.  
- Thyroglobulin washout testing was not performed on the thyroid bed/central neck aspirates.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2017: left hemithyroidectomy for enlarging left thyroid nodule. Initial pathology was benign; later pathology review revised this to oncocytic carcinoma with at least capsular invasion.  
- 2021: resection of the isthmus with central compartment lymph node dissection for PET-avid isthmus lesion/FNA showing Hürthle cell neoplasm; pathology demonstrated Hürthle cell carcinoma involving isthmus and surgical scar, with soft tissue and vascular invasion.  
- Subsequent referral led to completion thyroidectomy with right lobectomy, excision of skin/scar, and central compartment soft tissue removal, with intent for radioiodine treatment. Pathology again showed Hürthle cell carcinoma.  
- Radioiodine therapy was administered; post-treatment uptake was confined to the thyroid bed.  
- 2024: two independent fine-needle aspiration biopsies of the PET-avid left thyroid bed/paratracheal lesion were both interpreted as CLL.  
- 2024: revision surgery in the left paratracheal region was performed; intraoperative frozen section confirmed Hürthle cell carcinoma, and the operation was limited after diagnostic confirmation.

[ current disease status ]:  
- The patient had remained asymptomatic during the period of rising thyroglobulin.  
- Most recent documented disease was recurrent Hürthle cell carcinoma in the left paratracheal/thyroid bed region, confirmed pathologically in 2024 after PET-avid recurrence and rising thyroglobulin.  
- No gross residual disease was described after the most recent limited revision procedure.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Four surgical procedures had been performed in total, including two at outside hospitals.  
- 2021 FNA of the isthmus lesion showed a Hürthle cell neoplasm with high cellularity and nuclear enlargement, elongation, and grooves.  
- Two later FNAs from the recurrent left thyroid bed/paratracheal lesion were interpreted as CLL despite imaging and biochemical concern for recurrent thyroid carcinoma.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so just to preface this, there were four surgical procedures done in this particular patient, and two of these were done at an outside hospital. And so Ronnie was actually involved in some of the reviews. So just to set the stage, this is a 68-year-old patient who presented back in 2016 with an enlarging thyroid nodule. She did have some other nodules in the right lobe and the isthmus, and she had a cytology done on that larger nodule in the left lobe that came back as peripheral cell neoplasm, undetermined significance, and molecular testing was negative. So she was taken to the OR in 2017, underwent a left hemithyroidectomy, and was found at that time to have had what was believed to be a benign oculocytic neoplasm with a macrofollicular growth pattern and some degenerative changes. She was also diagnosed at the same time with CLL, which will become important as we move forward in these slides were sent out for external review, and there was no evidence of carcinoma identified. So if we dial the clock ahead in 2021, the patient had a follow-up PET-CT for evaluation of her lymphoma and was found to have a hypermetamolic nodule in the isthmus, and an FNA showed herthocel neoplasm with high cellularity. And so there was deemed to be nuclear changes with enlargement and elongation and grooves. And so, again, at the outside hospital, she had a second operation that involved removal of the isthmus and central compartment lymph nodes. And this time, the diagnosis of peripheral cell carcinoma was including both the isthmus and the surgical scar. So, Ronnie, do you wanna just comment on this?
Yeah, can you put though the other, the initial surgery? that was done, the slide from the initial surgery, Mark?
Yeah, so... Oh, you don't want to show it now? Yeah, maybe if we just, I'll get to that in just a minute.

Okay, okay, okay, I got it. So here is a surgery. Actually, this is a strip of a skin, believe it or not. And what you see here is oncocytic cell, her two cells really living in the subcutaneous tissue. Next one, Mark, please. So these cells have cholerae, they're clearly thyroid cells, and also they do not have, by the way, the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. The next one. What you see a tumor plug hanging, sorry, hanging in the lumen of the vessel. You can see the red blood cells and the line by endothelial cells. I put the arrow and next to one. Here, actually, you can see it in the muscle. And again, these are oncocytic cells with non-nuclear feature of papillocasinoma. So this is hurtle cell casinoma growing in the muscle and the vessel in the neck, and there were no leaf nodes.

Hey, Ronnie, how did these thyroid, the hearth cell cancers get from the thyroid to subcutaneous tissue? Do we see lymphatic invasion? Is this, you know, fracture of the tumor at the time of surgery? Because a lot of these come back in the scar in the field.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Actually, to be honest with you, nobody knows exactly the mechanism. I mean, one, it's probably, maybe it comes from surgery, but that actually becomes an interesting point, because could it be just mechanical implantation? But the fact here that we saw it in a vessel, Mike, makes it that it is really biologically invasive. It's not implanted by the surgeon.
Yeah. Okay, go ahead.

So this was the diagnosis that was obtained at that second operation. And if we dial the clock ahead, Ronnie did get an opportunity to review the original histology from that initial surgery. And one of the things that I think is important to note here, which may or may not be mechanistic in terms of what you were asking, Mike, was that the specimen was fragmented that was removed back in 2017. And so, Ronnie, this is your review of that specimen.

Yeah, so again, the most important, there are two messages here. The most important thing that the specimen is fragmented, and then it makes the diagnosis of carcinoma in the thyroid very challenging because a lot of our entities, for example, oncocytic or hertocell carcinoma, the diagnosis is based on invasion. So next slide, please. So luckily here, by incredible chance, there was one slide that contained a lesional bud that is outside the capsule. And so this is an expression of capsular invasion. So in the diagnosis, we said oncocytic carcinoma with at least capsular invasion. Obviously, the extent of invasion, which is crucial in oncocytic carcinoma cannot be really assessed here. Next one.
But if this was only capsular invasion, right, this would still be relatively low risk, right?

Sure, of course. But here, unfortunately, Mike, that's why I said at least, unfortunately, we didn't analyze the whole capsule. That's why it is crucial that the whole capsule is analyzed. But now in North America, everybody does it, even in small community hospitals. But this is just something happened during surgery.
Gotcha.
And the cells here are typically oncocytic. Herto cells without the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. So it's an oncocytic carcinoma with at least capsule invasion. That's how it started.

So this patient was then referred for follow-up care once this diagnosis was changed from benign to malignant. And the patient did undergo a completion thyroidectomy with the plan for radioiodine. And so we do have, in addition to the right lobectomy, removal of skin and scar, as well as central compartment soft tissue.
Pause for just a second. JP and Monica, hurtle cell cancer, tell me the truth. Are you guys using radioactive iodine in the hurtle cell cancers? Are we not? JP first, then Monica. JP?

Yeah, it has been a while since I used radioactive iodine for a hurtle cell, probably three or four years now. We have been paying more attention to really the other aspects. Okay. Yeah. But there's certainly a trend toward at least agreeing it's probably less effective or less useful. I personally am using it almost never. So yeah, this is from that third procedure. Ronnie, I think it's more of the same here.

Yeah, basically, you see the hurtle cell carcinoma here, it's really growing in the skeletal muscle. Now, if I didn't know anything about this patient, it would be very challenging to make a diagnosis of cancer here because of mechanical implementation, but putting everything together, the fact that the nests are small, this is hurtle cell carcinoma.
Great.

Already, I'm going to skip forward here. And this is Ronnie's diagnosis with the secondary diagnosis of lymphoma. So, I guess either Azita or Monica.
Monica, take first shot at this one.

Well, you can see the lesion in the left thyroid bed is very FDG avid, indicating a high-grade malignancy. And, you know, you get a flip-flop if it's FDG avid, the chance of it being radioactive iodine as well, uptake as well, is low. Usually if it's hot on FDG, it's not going to accumulate O131.

Hey, Mark, how are you thinking through this? I mean, clinically, this looks like herthal cell cancer to us on the PET, but you're about to go operate in a dangerous position without a biopsy-proven cancer. How are you thinking about this, Mark?

Yeah, so this is really a tough discussion. And so when you present all the information that Lisa mentioned here, you've got something that doesn't look like CLL, even though that's been the diagnosis cytopathologically. You've got a rising thyroid globulin, and you've got this concern that if you wait, the thing that you're worried about surgically may actually happen due to the disease process. And so the patient was indeed understandably very anxious about all the information that was presented. And so this is one of my cardinal rules of revision surgery that as long as a nodule or the suspected lesion is readily amenable to ultrasound guidance, I usually will not go in. but we have the confounding information here that this was a very hot area on PET, and so the patient wanted to proceed with surgery, and so this was done. So, Ronnie, this is what was found.
Yeah, I mean, in view of the context, yeah, this is callable as HER2 cell carcinoma, yeah.

And so you just mentioned that, Marc, but tell me a little bit more. So you went in, you did the surgery. Why didn't you just resect it since you were there? You made the diagnosis and got out, or what happened right there?

Yeah, so, you know, did skeletonize, the nerve was functioning well. This is a situation where interoperative neuromonitoring was extremely helpful. And so I wanted to document that my suspicion was there was residual disease here. And as long as I found it, I was comfortable that I had accomplished my mission. One of the, and then, so I didn't really focus in on that 3.4 millimeters. So one of the questions for Monica is, for me, was the blossoming on that upfront PET scan consistent with a 3.4 millimeter focus of disease?
Looks bigger, doesn't it?

Yeah. Yeah, you look bigger than that. So, yeah, so, you know, I think one of the questions becomes, is there more disease present there? And so our follow up labs here, Mike, shows a TGM 9.2 going to 7.0, and kind of gets us to this final question. Where are we and what are next steps here?

Even after RAI. I've occasionally broken the rule and called central neck level four. I figure it's close enough, but yeah. So I think that was the initial thought. If it's central neck, you wouldn't do that, but on one like this, JP, I think that would have probably been helpful if it was positive. tell you it's not as likely to be CLL, right? But then again, a three millimeter one, so I wonder how much of that, yes. Probably wouldn't have got it. All right, Lisa and then Frank, where do we go from here? Yeah, no, I think that you know that this is multifocal. It's shown up in the subcutaneous tissue and muscle, now in a paratracheal, just soft tissue. So I do think external beam radiation is indicated. And I know my colleagues in radiation oncology really don't want to radiate gross disease. They want to radiate microscopic disease. So your best chance to be effective with it is now before she shows new foci of macroscopic disease. And I think she's already proven herself to warrant it. And her age would not argue against radiation. I think she'd be a better candidate now. And then I would also ask my colleague Frank or my medical oncology colleagues about systemic therapy as well. Although I think their typical response would be in that case to wait until she is more progressive because she's going to have to go on indefinite therapy once she starts. Frank, finish this one up for me.

Yeah, I would totally agree with Lisa. So, you know, we published a study RIFTOS, you know, looking at people who are refractory to iodine to, you know, when we would start therapy and we really didn't figure that out. to figure out when they became symptomatic progression, and it was about five or six years median. So there are some people we can follow effectively without systemic therapy. We always want to try to treat things focally with either surgery or radiation. So what Lisa is saying, it is spot on. The other thing I would do on this person is to look at next generation sequencing, because it's fertile cell, oncositic, doubtful, there is a driver mutation, sometimes Gentrec is present, more likely the mTOR pathway will be involved. We don't really have, you know, at this stage, a really good, you know, targeted therapy for, you know, such tumors. So I think I would treat with radiation first. I would continue to observe closely, probably scans every, you know, three months, at least to begin with, antiviral globulin antibody levels. And then, you know, accordingly, you know, treat if the patient becomes more symptomatic or the disease burden becomes greater pretty quickly. Gotcha.
JP, last comment?

Yeah, just one thing before, I guess, any decision making for treatment. And this patient really crossed my threshold of MRI of the brain. So when I see self metastasis, things like that, That's probably when they say, you know, let's MRI the brain. It's not like we do it in every patient, but this one might be one. Raising type of global markers, that kind of something is not round. It's not behaving in the right way. I agree completely.

reference_conclusion: Given multifocal recurrent Hürthle cell carcinoma involving subcutaneous tissue, skeletal muscle, and paratracheal soft tissue, with no gross residual disease currently identified, adjuvant external beam radiation therapy to the neck is indicated at this time to treat presumed microscopic disease. Systemic therapy is not recommended immediately; close surveillance should continue with imaging approximately every 3 months initially and serial thyroglobulin and thyroglobulin antibody measurements, with treatment escalation if the patient becomes symptomatic or demonstrates rapidly increasing disease burden. Next-generation sequencing should be obtained to assess for actionable alterations, and brain MRI should be considered given the pattern of soft tissue metastasis and rising thyroglobulin.
