case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Frequent diarrhea, reported at 18–20 bowel movements per day.

[ diagnosis ]: Widely metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, suspected small bowel primary. Clinical features and imaging favored terminal ileum or right-sided colon origin. Hepatic metastatic disease was present.

[ imaging findings ]: Anatomic imaging demonstrated a mesenteric lesion/mass, suggesting a small bowel primary. No obvious primary mass was seen on the referenced scan. Disease was described as very widely metastatic with extensive liver involvement. DOTATATE PET was indicated for staging, and the tumor was described as having high somatostatin expression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic findings were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Serotonin was markedly elevated. 5-HIAA was markedly elevated.

[ current disease status ]: Widely metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with extensive hepatic burden and a hormonally active syndrome.

[ other clinical data ]: The biochemical syndrome was consistent with hormonally active disease. Concern for carcinoid heart disease was raised in the setting of excess serotonin/5-HIAA.

reference_discussion.text: Imaging-wise, it's exactly what we need. We, again, want anatomic imaging and the DOTATATE PET for staging. Since this is the initial diagnosis, it would be important to find the primary tumor, which, again, can be done usually with a combination of those two things. There appears to be something there in the mesentery, which would suggest there may be a small bowel origin for the tumor. So that's something that would be important to find and can be helpful for the surgeons. But beyond that, it's clearly a very widely metastatic case.

And Dr. Sindh, what are your thoughts about this case? We think it's coming from this small bowel primary. So we know that serotonin and 5-HIA is very elevated, but there was not an obvious mass on this scan. So what are your thoughts about that?

I think the primary needs to come out. There's no question in my mind. I think there's a mesenteric mass. So this is most probably a terminal ileum or a right-sided colon primary. So if you don't see it, I would still recommend surgical intervention based on the mesenteric mass and go and do a right hemicolectomy if there is truly a mass in the right colon or in the terminal ileum. So that's number one. Number two, I think you have too much liver disease and this is not a liver that I could safely debulk to 70%. So I would again, actively engage my interventional colleagues and my med-on colleagues I would approach this in a stage-wise fashion. That's definitely an option, and that's what we did about 10 years ago. Today, you have Telerestat in your back pocket, so I've seen medical oncologists use Telerestat to control the bowel movements as well, and then keep an eye on the liver metastases. I'm an interventional radiologist. I like to do interventions. So, this patient is pretty symptomatic. So I would advocate for it, but as mentioned, I think it's also reasonable if there, if for any reason we wanted to hold off and see if medications could control it.

As a surgeon, I think it's imperative to remove the primary tumor because I think that largely determines the progression of metastatic disease and gives you an idea as to how the symptoms are controlled after the resection of the primary tumor. And so in that sort of a setting, I would definitely recommend proceeding with a right hemicolectomy in this patient and then reassessing. And if the diarrhea continues to be a big impending issue, then I think the options are to consider systemic therapy. with our medical oncology colleagues, and alternatively, interventional radiology to control the liver disease, which might be also participating in the secretion of the high 5-HIA.

Yeah, I just wanted to add, from my perspective as well, this is again why the NETR2 study was so powerful, because it was exactly in these types of patients who initially diagnosed, you know, it was within the diagnosis, that they were given Lutathera as long as they had high somatostatin expression, such as in this case. So I would throw that also into the mix as well, because in addition to controlling the tumor growth, it can definitely also help symptoms, and it can be given in conjunction with somatostatin analogs for additional symptomatic control. Absolutely. And as we all discussed, this patient underwent two radioembolizations. In this case, Dr. Oztet mentioned when it's needed or what, in terms of the difference between bioembolization or She also underwent surgery, as Dr. Singh mentioned, and underwent an elusive colectomy. Two separate tumors were identified, and three out of 12 lymph nodes that were resected was positive for neuroendocrine tumor. And pathology was consistent with a great one, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with a KS67, more than 1%, but less than 3%. And she then underwent two blind embolizations. And the symptoms of diarrhea significantly improved. But then she was complaining of worsening shortness of breath. And here, the point I want to make is that every patient I have small bowel neuroendocrine tumors, where there is excess of serotonin and 5-HIAA, it's important to see a cardiologist and have a routine echocardiogram, surveillance echocardiogram, maybe once every year, once every two years, depending on how the clinical presentation of this patient is. But that can also, and the reason why I'm saying this is because when we see something like this, we need to consider about carcinoid heart disease, meaning that the hormone, can also go to the heart valve and it can cause scar of the heart valve. And that can also then put a risk for the patient to develop heart failure. So I think it's important also that we're patients with a small bowel near endocrine tumors that has this excess of hormones that be evaluated by a cardiologist and have routine echocardiograms as well. And my last question for Dr. Oz, a lot of our patients are asking about histotripsy. So I think we understood in this situation, resecting the primary was important, doing the liver directed therapy with embolizations is also important, or considering this patient for the symptoms. But we get a lot of questions about histotripsy. Maybe would you mind describing what is that and how this plays in terms of the management of neuroendocrine tumors?

Sure. Yeah, I'm glad a lot of people are asking me too. So I'm happy to chat about it a little bit. Histotripsy is a non-thermal. So non-thermal means doesn't rely on using heat or freezing to kill tumors. Mechanism of using ultrasound energy to ablate or kill tumors. It's also non-invasive. So it's very attractive because it's non-thermal and it's non-invasive. Most of the tumors that we've discussed today through our case presentations involve patients who had tumors throughout their liver. Histotripsy would be more applicable in situations where patients only had a few liver tumors, where we would consider doing what's known as ablation or percutaneous ablation, where we take a needle, put it into the tumor, and burn it away. Histotripsy would mitigate the risk of the needle puncture and also would allow us to potentially treat tumors that would be hard to treat with traditional ablation, meaning tumors that are next to blood vessels, bile ducts, which happen to, you know, occur a lot in the liver. So histotripsy is a technology, we just received it, and so it technically doesn't allow us to treat any new patient per se, but it's another tool that we have available to us to treat tumors the way that we think of when we do ablation. So it's a very exciting technology. One of the other final things I'll mention about it, it's very interesting, unfortunately doesn't apply yet to neuroendocrine. But it seems that when you do histotripsy, it promotes a very immunogenic response. Meaning when you kill the tumor, it basically disintegrates the tumor such that all the tumor antigens are released. And it really basically, you know, sort of to sum it up, it wakes up the immune system very much. So there's a lot of interest that you can get what's known as a non-target response. And that's particularly in cancers where we use immunotherapies. So there's also some excitement there with histotripsy as well. And because it's so new, we don't really know a lot of the answers yet, but now histotripsy is FDA approved. There are at least 10 centers that have the technology and are offering it and evaluating patients. But yes, it's a very exciting time because of, you know, having that technology available to us.
One quick question on that same thing. How big a tumor can you treat with histotripsy and what's your size cut off at this point?

Yeah, a great question. So, hisotripsy is very similar to percutaneous ablation in that the sort of maximum size that you can sort of do in one session is about four centimeters. So, we typically will target tumors. If we want to treat the whole tumor, we always want to have some margin. So, we'll typically treat a tumor that's up to three centimeters. It doesn't mean you can't treat tumors that are larger than three centimeters. You just have to do multiple treatments, you know, of that same area. So right now we're probably limiting it to, at least in my practice, limiting it to patients who would be eligible for ablation. And this would be an alternative to ablation.
Any major disadvantage or complications associated with histotrip?

Yeah, I would say the major disadvantage currently is we can't get to every tumor the way that we can get to with percutaneous ablation, largely because this is a technology using ultrasound waves, essentially, to create cavitation within the tumor. We have to have a good sonographic window, so we have to be able to see with an ultrasound very well, and there's some more physics to it, but we have to, in a geometric way, be able to align the robot so that the tumor is very well visualized. So that limits sort of the parts of the liver that we can treat. With that said, there's a lot of technological updates coming to the system over the next year or two that will hopefully be able to allow us to treat actually any tumor. We're a little bit away from that, but right now we're largely limited to tumors that you can mainly see with an ultrasound from a subcostal approach. So meaning, you know, if you take the ultrasound, you can only see the tumor from under the ribs.

reference_conclusion: Staging should include anatomic imaging and DOTATATE PET to identify the primary lesion, which is suspected to arise from the terminal ileum or right colon. The agreed management was resection of the primary tumor with right hemicolectomy, followed by reassessment of symptoms and metastatic disease burden. Given extensive symptomatic hepatic metastases, liver-directed therapy with bland embolization was supported for symptom control, with systemic therapy options including somatostatin analogs, telotristat, and consideration of Lutathera in the setting of high somatostatin receptor expression. Ongoing cardiology evaluation with surveillance echocardiography was recommended because of elevated serotonin/5-HIAA and risk for carcinoid heart disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female; aged 50 years at presentation in 2017. Body weight was 57 kg.

[ chief complaint ]: Longstanding neck mass for more than 20 years, with significant enlargement over the preceding 6 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Follicular thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with capsular and lymphovascular invasion; subsequent iodine-avid pulmonary metastatic disease. Later disease progression included bone metastasis. Refractory hypothyroidism after thyroidectomy was documented, with persistently elevated TSH despite levothyroxine therapy.

[ histopathology results ]: Total thyroidectomy was performed in December 2017. Intraoperatively, the right thyroid lobe was entirely occupied by a large nodule measuring approximately 8 cm in greatest dimension. Significant inflammatory adhesion was present involving strap muscles and cricothyroid muscle. Intraoperative frozen section was reported as atypical adenoma, suspicious for capsular invasion; malignancy could not be excluded. Final pathology from the local hospital reported follicular thyroid carcinoma in the right lobe with capsular invasion and lymphovascular invasion.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in April 2015 showed a right thyroid nodule measuring 3.2 × 1.8 cm.  
- Preoperative physical examination in 2017 showed a 6 cm firm right neck nodule and a 2 cm firm left neck nodule, both with smooth surfaces.  
- Subsequent preoperative ultrasound demonstrated marked enlargement of the lesion, central hypoechogenic areas, vascularity, and irregular medial border.  
- Preoperative CT neck showed a thyroid mass without clear evidence of carotid or esophageal invasion; tracheal wall involvement could not be determined.  
- Chest radiograph demonstrated significant tracheal deviation and was interpreted as showing multiple lung nodules.  
- CT performed 2 months after thyroidectomy suggested pulmonary metastases.  
- Post-radioiodine whole-body scan in 2018 demonstrated residual cervical tissue and bilateral lung metastases with radioiodine uptake.  
- Diagnostic whole-body scan performed 3 months after radioiodine treatment, without levothyroxine withdrawal, again showed pulmonary uptake and focal head uptake.  
- Brain MRI showed no significant intracranial abnormality; pituitary hyperplasia was considered suspicious on one MRI.  
- A subsequent whole-body scan before planned second radioiodine treatment again showed cranial uptake; repeat brain MRI again showed no abnormality.  
- Later disease progression included bone metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor molecular testing identified a RAS mutation and an EIF1AX mutation.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Preoperative thyroid function was normal.  
- Serum calcium was normal.  
- Vitamin D was normal.  
- Liver function was normal.  
- T-SPOT.TB test was normal.  
- Hepatitis viral panel was normal.  
- Before initial radioiodine treatment, despite levothyroxine therapy, TSH was >20 and thyroglobulin was >300; thyroglobulin antibodies were negative.  
- Three months after radioiodine treatment, TSH was 12.  
- During follow-up on levothyroxine, TSH remained elevated, ranging from approximately 10–11 to >36, with low-normal T3 and T4.  
- Thyroglobulin remained >300 with negative thyroglobulin antibodies.  
- For preparation for second radioiodine treatment, levothyroxine was stopped for 18 days; TSH increased to >100.  
- Reverse T3 was low-normal.  
- Thyroid function testing performed at two hospitals showed similar results.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Total thyroidectomy was performed in December 2017.  
- Radioiodine therapy was administered in 2018. Post-therapy scan showed residual cervical tissue and bilateral iodine-avid pulmonary metastases.  
- Planned second radioiodine treatment was initially declined because of patient concern regarding persistent cranial uptake on whole-body scan despite negative brain MRI.  
- After transfer of care, the patient received second, third, and fourth radioiodine treatments.  
- Cumulative radioiodine activity reached 700 mCi.  
- Despite repeated radioiodine therapy, thyroglobulin remained markedly elevated and disease progressed to bone metastases.  
- The patient was subsequently enrolled in a RAS inhibitor clinical trial.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma with prior pulmonary metastases and later bone metastases. Refractory hypothyroidism persisted.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No significant family history was reported.  
- No significant past medical history was reported.  
- Evaluation for causes of refractory hypothyroidism included confirmation of laboratory results with different assays and exclusion of assay interference.  
- Medication adherence was reported as good by the patient and family.  
- Review of medication storage and tablet use was appropriate.  
- No concomitant medications, gastrointestinal symptoms, lactose intolerance, Helicobacter pylori infection, or other apparent causes of impaired levothyroxine absorption or increased turnover/excretion were identified.  
- Levothyroxine absorption testing was declined.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old female from Manipur. No known comorbidities. Past history included forearm fracture surgery. History of tobacco consumption for 30 years; had stopped 3 weeks prior to presentation. No known drug or food allergies. ECOG performance status was 1 at presentation.

[ chief complaint ]: Growth over the right buccal mucosa for 2 months, with difficulty opening the mouth for 3–4 weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right buccal mucosa. Disease involved the masticator space, masseter muscle, and infratemporal fossa, extending to the high infratemporal fossa. Clinical nodal disease was absent on examination. Radiologically, bilateral level IB and II lymph nodes were present. Disease was described as T4b with N2c nodal status.

[ histopathology results ]: Punch biopsy from the right buccal mucosa showed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: CT head, neck, and thorax showed a right buccal mucosal mass measuring approximately 3.5 × 2.8 × 1.5 cm with depth of invasion approximately 1.5 cm. The lesion involved the masticator space, masseter muscle, and infratemporal fossa, extending to the high infratemporal fossa. Bilateral level IB and II lymph nodes were seen, largest measuring approximately 1.5 × 0.8 cm. CT thorax/lung window showed no pulmonary nodules.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL. Platelet count 1,43,000/µL. Creatinine 0.59 mg/dL. DTPA GFR 99 mL/min. Albumin was reported as normal. One recorded blood pressure reading was 160/100 mmHg. Two-dimensional echocardiography showed left ventricular ejection fraction 40–45%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior oncologic treatment was documented. Supportive and allied health interventions included referral to physiotherapy and occupational therapy for jaw stretching exercises, speech and swallow therapy for swallowing difficulty, psycho-oncology assessment for mild depression and anxiety, and dietitian referral for high-protein diet and BMI monitoring. Cardio-oncology review was sought following reduced ejection fraction. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination were advised.

[ current disease status ]: At presentation, oral examination showed mouth opening of less than one finger breadth. There was a 3 × 3 cm ulcerative proliferative growth involving the right buccal mucosa extending toward the retromolar trigone. Examination was limited by trismus. A 5 × 5 cm hard indurated cheek lesion extended up to the zygoma; overlying skin was mobile. No palpable cervical lymph nodes were detected clinically. No distant pulmonary metastases were identified on CT thorax.

[ other clinical data ]: G8 screening score was 11. Comprehensive geriatric assessment showed Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale 3, ADL 6/6, IADL 8/8, Timed Up and Go 10 seconds, MMSE 26, GDS 5, GAD 14, and MNA 23. BMI was normal. Charlson Comorbidity Index was 0. The patient was on no regular medications. Social history documented that she lived with her son, had good family support, and had limited financial resources. CARG toxicity score was 4, indicating low predicted risk for chemotherapy-related toxicity.

reference_conclusion: The case was considered unresectable/borderline unresectable because of disease extent into the high infratemporal fossa and masticator space, and upfront surgery or definitive chemoradiotherapy was not favored. The agreed next step was initiation of neoadjuvant systemic therapy, with preference for an oral metronomic chemotherapy-containing regimen rather than DCF, given the patient’s age, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, and uncontrolled blood pressure. Geriatric-directed supportive interventions were also to be implemented, including physiotherapy/occupational therapy for jaw-stretching exercises, speech and swallow therapy, psycho-oncology input, dietitian review, cardio-oncology assessment, and blood pressure monitoring.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 22-year-old woman; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, initially relieved with oral analgesics and symptomatic measures but subsequently persistent; longstanding left-sided weakness for approximately 12 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Right deep hemispheric intracranial mass lesion, radiologically described as a well-circumscribed solid-cystic lesion centered in the right subcortical region/basal ganglia-thalamic region, with mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle and brainstem compression. Tissue diagnosis had not yet been finalized.

[ histopathology results ]: Stereotactic/open biopsy had been performed via right temporal craniotomy. Final histopathology was pending. Frozen section was not available.

[ imaging findings ]: CT brain showed a solid-cystic lesion in the right subcortical region involving the right thalamus and right basal ganglia, with perilesional edema. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed mixed-intensity solid-cystic lesion extensively involving the right thalamus and compressing the right lateral ventricle. T1-weighted imaging showed intrinsic hyperintense areas consistent with hemorrhagic/proteinaceous content. T2-weighted imaging showed a hyperintense lesion with minimal to mild surrounding edema. Post-contrast MRI showed heterogeneous enhancement, extension to the anterior temporal tip, involvement of the right parahippocampal gyrus, and significant mass effect with basal cistern effacement and descending transtentorial herniation. Brainstem involvement was described radiologically as significant compression without definite macroscopic invasion. Multiple adjacent satellite nodular enhancing lesions were also described inferior to the main lesion. Postoperative imaging after biopsy was obtained.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had experienced an initial episode of left-sided weakness in 2012 with partial improvement over 2-3 months. A further episode occurred in 2013 with incomplete recovery, leaving residual weakness. She subsequently underwent biopsy through a right temporal craniotomy. Postoperatively, she remained mobile and neurologically stable compared with baseline, with persistent pre-existing weakness.

[ current disease status ]: At latest assessment, the patient was fully conscious and oriented with GCS 15/15, ambulatory without support, and able to perform daily activities. Residual left-sided weakness persisted at the preoperative baseline. Karnofsky Performance Status was 80. Final biopsy result was still awaited.

[ other clinical data ]: Neurological examination showed left homonymous hemianopia, left spastic hemiparesis with power 4+/5, bilateral grade II papilledema, and an upgoing left plantar response. Past functional status remained relatively preserved despite residual weakness.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Hoarseness beginning in November 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma involving bilateral thyroid lobes with cervical lymph node metastases, multiple liver metastases, and pheochromocytoma. Left vocal cord paralysis was present. No parathyroid disease was identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology of thyroid tumors and cervical lymph nodes was suspicious for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial evaluation showed masses in both thyroid lobes and multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck. Abdominal CT demonstrated multiple liver metastases and bilateral adrenal nodules. CT findings at first visit to the treating department showed left upper neck and left middle neck lymphadenopathy, bilateral thyroid tumors, apparent invasion of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the left thyroid lobe tumor, multiple liver metastases, and left adrenal enlargement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET exon 11 codon 634 mutation was confirmed. The patient’s mother and two children were also found to carry the same RET mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum CEA was 295.9. Serum calcitonin was 7,260. Urinary metanephrine and normetanephrine were elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In June 2020, right laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed for pheochromocytoma.

[ current disease status ]: Advanced medullary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral thyroid tumours, bilateral cervical nodal disease, and documented liver metastases, following resection of the pheochromocytoma.

[ other clinical data ]: No significant past medical history was reported. There was no family history of thyroid disease. Left vocal cord paralysis was present at initial presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old male physician-scientist (MD, PhD).

[ chief complaint ]: Rising PSA.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, initially high-risk by biopsy (Gleason 9), clinically localized on PSMA PET without nodal or osseous metastatic disease; status post radical prostatectomy. Final surgical pathology demonstrated Gleason score 4+3=7 with tertiary pattern 5 (Grade Group 3) and extraprostatic extension.

[ histopathology results ]: Transrectal prostate biopsy performed 11/06 showed Grade Group 1 disease on the right side. At the MRI-positive left base lesion, biopsy showed Gleason score 4+5=9 in 2 cores with 80% tissue involvement. Radical prostatectomy specimen showed Gleason score 4+3=7 with tertiary pattern 5, Grade Group 3, with extraprostatic extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Prostate MRI demonstrated PI-RADS 4 and 5 lesions. PSMA PET showed prostate-confined tracer-avid disease, described as localized to possibly locally advanced along the prostatic capsule. No enlarged or PSMA-avid pelvic lymph nodes were identified. No osseous lesions were identified.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative PSA was 8.73 ng/mL. Postoperative PSA was 0.02 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Biopsy was delayed approximately 1.5 years after the initial MRI. The patient subsequently underwent radical prostatectomy. At approximately 6 weeks postoperatively, PSA was 0.02 ng/mL. Early postoperative course included urinary incontinence with improving control and absent erectile function.

[ current disease status ]: Post-radical prostatectomy state with PSA nadir/postoperative value of 0.02 ng/mL. No radiographic nodal or distant metastatic disease had been identified on PSMA PET. Persistent but improving postoperative urinary incontinence was present; erectile function had not recovered.

[ other clinical data ]: The MRI-positive lesion was located at the left base. The initial biopsy grade was higher than the final prostatectomy grade.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET imaging was obtained for staging and demonstrated localized, possibly locally advanced, high-risk prostate cancer without osseous or nodal metastatic disease. Management options for localized therapy included radical prostatectomy with extended pelvic lymph node dissection or dose-escalated radiation therapy with long-term androgen deprivation therapy; the patient proceeded with radical prostatectomy. Following surgery, given a postoperative PSA nadir of 0.02 with extraprostatic extension, the plan was surveillance with serial PSA monitoring rather than immediate adjuvant radiation. If salvage radiation were to become necessary, it should be deferred until urinary continence improves, with a minimum interval of 3–6 months postoperatively.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 21-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Right breast mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, grade 3, diagnosed in November 2017. Disease was described clinically as locally advanced and inoperable at initial surgical assessment.

[ histopathology results ]: Histology showed invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, grade 3 by Nottingham score. Lymphovascular invasion was present. Margins were involved by tumor. No lymph node sampling had been performed. Immunohistochemistry had not been performed.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging studies had been performed at the time of review.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing had been performed. ER, PR, and HER2 status were not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient was referred for neoadjuvant chemotherapy after the tumor was considered inoperable. She received 1 cycle of doxorubicin plus cyclophosphamide in December 2017, then had a treatment interruption of approximately 3 months due to financial constraints. Thereafter, she had received a total of 5 cycles of doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide and 2 cycles of paclitaxel; the most recent cycle had been administered 1 week before review. Clinical reduction in the right breast tumor burden was described, with the breast tissue having shrunk to the chest wall and no discrete right breast mass palpable on examination at that time.

[ current disease status ]: ECOG performance status was 1. General condition was fair. The patient was not pale, jaundiced, or cyanosed. No lymphadenopathy was identified on examination. No right axillary lymph nodes were palpable. Left breast examination showed no palpable mass, although the nipple-areolar region appeared abnormal on inspection. Right breast examination showed marked shrinkage of breast tissue to the chest wall with only a portion of the nipple remaining visible and no palpable mass. Other systems were reported stable.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial clinical documentation described a hard right breast mass measuring 15 × 15 cm and fixed to underlying tissues. The patient had achondroplasia/dwarfism. There was no reported history of chronic illness in the patient or family. HIV status was not available. The patient was not a National Hospital Fund contributor. Financial constraints had affected continuity of care.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 79-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Neck swelling.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with tall cell variant features and tumor necrosis; metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma to a right level IV cervical lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the right thyroid nodule showed papillary thyroid carcinoma with focal high-grade features and extensive necrosis. Surgical pathology reported papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell variant, with necrosis. Necrosis was classified as tumor necrosis. Ten lymph nodes were positive for metastatic disease. No extrathyroidal extension was identified on pathology.

[ imaging findings ]: CT neck showed a heterogeneous nodule involving the mid and upper pole of the right thyroid lobe measuring 2.5 x 2.7 x 3.2 cm, with suspicious features for extrathyroidal extension. No obvious cervical lymphadenopathy was identified in the central or lateral neck compartments on CT. CT chest showed a solitary ipsilateral 7 mm upper lung nodule. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous right thyroid nodule measuring 3.12 cm and a 0.66 cm right level IV lymph node.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Thyroid nodule FNA was positive for TERT mutation and BRAF V600E mutation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, central compartment neck dissection, and right lateral selective neck dissection levels II-IV. Past medical history included gastric cancer treated with surgery and chemotherapy in 1997.

[ current disease status ]: Status post thyroidectomy and neck dissection for papillary thyroid carcinoma with nodal metastases. A solitary 7 mm ipsilateral upper lung nodule had been identified on chest CT.

[ other clinical data ]: No history of radiation exposure. No family history of benign or malignant thyroid disease. Past medical history also included inactive hepatitis B.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Right breast mass with palpable lymph nodes at initial presentation; later developed abdominal pain in 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, final pathologic stage III at initial diagnosis; subsequent metastatic recurrent triple-negative breast cancer involving liver and bone in 2019.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the right breast mass showed grade 3 triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma. Bilateral mastectomy specimen showed invasive ductal carcinoma measuring 7 cm. Axillary nodal involvement was present in 7 of 27 lymph nodes. Liver biopsy in 2019 confirmed recurrent triple-negative breast cancer. PD-L1 was negative on recurrent disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial disease included a 2.6 cm right breast mass with palpable lymphadenopathy. CT scan performed in 2019 for abdominal pain was suggestive of metastatic disease in bone and liver.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline testing identified a pathogenic PALB2 variant consisting of deletion of exons 12-13. Tumor comprehensive genomic profiling (FoundationOne) identified FGFR2 amplification at 10q26.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Underwent bilateral mastectomy. Received adjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide for 4 cycles followed by weekly paclitaxel for 12 doses. Remained disease-free for 2 years after completion of adjuvant treatment. After metastatic recurrence in 2019, received capecitabine, then carboplatin. Subsequently received olaparib off-label.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with prior liver and bone involvement.

[ other clinical data ]: Bilateral mastectomy was chosen in the setting of germline PALB2 pathogenic variant and patient preference.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, diagnosed on fine-needle aspiration cytology in May 2017.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy performed at another center was reported as Bethesda category VI, consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thyroid ultrasound in May 2017 demonstrated a hypoechoic left thyroid lobe nodule measuring 7.5 x 5 mm with microcalcifications. The patient had a documented history of the same left thyroid nodule with unchanged measurements 6 years earlier. During pregnancy, at 20 weeks’ gestation in May 2018, ultrasound showed interval growth of approximately 3 mm in each dimension, with extension toward the posterior border of the left thyroid lobe.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroid-stimulating hormone remained normal throughout follow-up.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No thyroid surgery had been performed. The patient declined operative management and underwent active surveillance. Fine-needle aspiration established the diagnosis in 2017.

[ current disease status ]: Subcentimeter papillary thyroid carcinoma in the left thyroid lobe under active surveillance, with interval enlargement documented at 20 weeks’ gestation.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had sought multiple prior consultations and had declined recommendations for total thyroidectomy. Pregnancy was identified after initiation of surveillance; she presented at 20 weeks’ gestation in May 2018.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary panel supported continued active surveillance for this low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, including during pregnancy despite transient interval enlargement. The lesion enlarged modestly at 20 weeks’ gestation, but surveillance was maintained because pregnancy-related growth does not necessarily indicate aggressive behavior and deferral of intervention was not expected to adversely affect prognosis. Subsequent imaging demonstrated return to baseline size and ongoing stability, supporting continued observation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 13-year-old female from Saudi Arabia.

[ chief complaint ]: Thigh pain at initial presentation. Subsequently developed headache associated with a new posterior skull mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Ewing sarcoma of the thigh with pulmonary metastases at initial diagnosis; later developed a skull lesion consistent with relapsed/progressive disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the thigh mass showed Ewing sarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial radiography of the primary thigh lesion showed a fracture. MRI demonstrated the thigh mass. Imaging at relapse demonstrated a mass in the posterior skull, which initially responded to chemotherapy and subsequently enlarged with recurrent headaches. Venous reconstruction imaging of the skull lesion was available. Postoperative imaging of the lower extremity after limb-salvage reconstruction was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment was given per a standard European regimen. The patient had a good response to initial therapy, then underwent surgery for the primary tumor, followed by additional chemotherapy and whole-lung radiation. For the skull relapse, chemotherapy was administered with an initial good response, followed by recurrent headaches and regrowth of the skull mass while on second-line therapy. Up to the time of referral, prior radiation exposure had been limited to whole-lung irradiation.

[ current disease status ]: Active growing posterior skull mass with symptomatic progression manifested by recurrent headaches during second-line therapy. History of metastatic Ewing sarcoma with lung metastases at diagnosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Ectopic/malpositioned kidney with 13% function on the affected side; the contralateral kidney accounted for most renal function.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent thyroid carcinoma with cervical nodal/soft tissue recurrence after thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine treatment, and multiple neck operations.

[ diagnosis ]: Differentiated high-grade oncocytic (Hürthle cell) thyroid carcinoma, 2.0 cm primary in the left thyroid lobe, widely invasive, with extensive angiolymphatic invasion and nodal metastases. Disease subsequently became radioactive iodine-refractory and metastatic, with recurrent cervical disease, liver metastasis, pulmonary metastases, and osseous metastasis at T3. The patient had Wilcox-Dubetz syndrome.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial thyroid/neck surgery pathology showed a 2.0 cm high-grade oncocytic carcinoma that was widely invasive, with extensive angiolymphatic invasion. Necrosis was present and mitotic rate was high. There was no extrathyroidal extension. Surgical margins were negative. At least 10 lymph nodes were positive for metastatic involvement, predominantly in the central compartment and left levels III and IV. Subsequent left neck revision pathology showed lymph nodes involved by poorly differentiated oncocytic carcinoma, predominantly in level IV, with extranodal extension. Pathology details for one interim reoperation were not available.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Serial CT imaging performed for prior tongue rhabdomyoma surveillance incidentally identified a 2 cm left thyroid lobe nodule and left cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- Preoperative ultrasound/biopsy correlated with nodal disease in the left neck.  
- Post-thyroidectomy diagnostic radioiodine scan showed uptake confined to the neck, described as two iodine-avid left cervical foci, mainly in the lower central compartment (levels VI/VII). A pulmonary finding was described without iodine uptake.  
- Follow-up radioiodine scan after rising thyroglobulin showed no abnormal uptake.  
- FDG PET demonstrated a small FDG-avid midline level VI lesion consistent with recurrent disease.  
- Subsequent FDG PET after reoperation showed persistent disease in the left neck, including a left cervical lesion and possible bilateral supraclavicular lesions.  
- Later FDG PET demonstrated persistent small-volume left neck disease.  
- Further surveillance imaging identified a liver lesion on MRI/PET and a metastatic lesion at T3.  
- Small-volume pulmonary metastases were also present at later disease assessment.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor genetic testing identified TP53 alteration and a folliculin mutation associated with the patient’s syndrome.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroglobulin values after initial treatment were as follows: stimulated thyroglobulin 5.1 at the time of radioactive iodine treatment; subsequently 4.5, then 6.2, 10.5, 14, and 26. After reoperation, postoperative thyroglobulin was 30.5. At 18 months after initial diagnosis, thyroglobulin was 226. These later values were obtained with suppressed TSH.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Remote history of tongue rhabdomyoma resection, followed by recurrence and repeat resection.  
- Fine-needle biopsy of the left thyroid nodule was suspicious for Hürthle cell neoplasia; biopsy of a left neck lymph node was also suspicious for Hürthle cell involvement.  
- Total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection was performed.  
- Radioactive iodine therapy was administered after thyroid hormone withdrawal; post-treatment scan showed uptake only in the neck. The patient received 150 mCi I-131. Thyroglobulin did not meaningfully decline and subsequently rose progressively.  
- Reoperation for recurrent midline level VI disease was performed approximately 7 months after initial surgery; recurrent oncocytic carcinoma was removed, although the operative/pathology report did not clearly distinguish lymph node from soft tissue recurrence.  
- A third neck operation (left neck revision) was performed shortly thereafter for persistent/recurrent disease; pathology confirmed nodal poorly differentiated oncocytic carcinoma with extranodal extension. Operative findings included fixed, firm lymph nodes, and the sympathetic trunk was sacrificed during resection.  
- Systemic therapy had not been started because the patient declined it.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent/recurrent metastatic radioactive iodine-refractory differentiated high-grade oncocytic thyroid carcinoma. Residual small-volume disease remained in the left neck, with metastatic disease involving the lungs, liver, and T3 vertebra. The patient remained under close surveillance without systemic therapy.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had Wilcox-Dubetz syndrome. The syndrome-associated folliculin mutation was also identified on tumor testing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 17-year-old female from southern Brazil.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive giant right lateral neck mass with severe deformity, constant pain, difficulty swallowing, and inability to raise the right arm above shoulder level.

[ diagnosis ]: Neurofibromatosis type 1 with giant plexiform neurofibroma involving the lateral neck, bilateral occipital regions, and right temporoparietal scalp/head region, associated with marked craniovertebral junction and upper cervical spine deformity.

[ histopathology results ]: Lesion was described clinically as a giant plexiform neurofibroma. No formal pathology report details were available.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT scout demonstrated a very large mass involving the lateral neck.  
- MRI T2 coronal imaging demonstrated a large mass on the lateral surface of the neck.  
- The lesion extended circumferentially around the neck, into both occipital regions, and involved the entire right parietotemporal region, wrapping around much of the head in a plaque-like distribution beneath the skin.  
- The tumor extended to the prevertebral space.  
- There was marked deformity of the craniovertebral junction and upper cervical spine.  
- The clivus was largely absent on imaging.  
- CT sagittal bone window and 3D CT reconstruction showed severe upper cervical osseous abnormality, including C1-C4 hypoplasia with varying degrees of fusion.  
- Posterior cervical elements of the upper spine were absent/destroyed.  
- C1 and C2 appeared rotated outward posteriorly.  
- The odontoid was displaced/tilted anteriorly.  
- The spinal alignment at the upper cervical region was markedly abnormal with an S-shaped/swan-neck type deformity.  
- The vertebral canal was not directly invaded by tumor; spinal cord compromise was attributed to chronic deformity and bone destruction rather than direct intracanalar tumor compression.  
- No intracranial or cerebral disease was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Two prior cytoreductive surgeries had been performed by plastic surgery.  
- These procedures achieved limited reduction in tumor bulk and were not curative.  
- The patient reported no meaningful clinical benefit from the prior surgeries.  
- The lesion continued to enlarge over time with progressive deformity and persistent symptoms.  
- Diagnostic angiography had been performed and demonstrated vascular supply from bilateral external carotid artery branches, bilateral vertebral artery branches, and occipital arteries; the left vertebral artery was dominant.  
- Preoperative embolization had been considered technically feasible for reduction of tumor vascularity.

[ current disease status ]:  
- The mass had continued to grow slowly over years and was causing major visible deformity with leftward head deviation.  
- The patient had constant pain affecting daily activities and quality of life.  
- She had dysphagia and was able to tolerate liquids such as iced coffee; there was no reported malnutrition or weight loss at that time.  
- Neurologic function was largely preserved.  
- Sensation was preserved.  
- General muscle strength was preserved.  
- The only focal motor deficit described was inability to elevate the right upper extremity above shoulder level.  
- She remained ambulatory and able to stand, walk, and speak.  
- There was no airway compromise reported at that time.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The deformity involved long-standing bone destruction at the craniovertebral junction and upper cervical spine.  
- Reconstruction was considered anatomically challenging because the occipital bone was preserved but the posterior upper cervical elements were absent.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus was for conservative management of the craniovertebral junction and upper cervical spine lesion, with no neurosurgical or spinal intervention at present given the absence of significant progressive neurologic deficit and the high risk of major morbidity. Management should remain symptom-directed and palliative, with consideration of intervention only if serious progression develops, such as worsening swallowing dysfunction, spasticity, gait deterioration, or other progressive neurologic compromise. Any future operative consideration would require careful reassessment because resection may be feasible, but reconstruction and postoperative functional outcome are major concerns.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male. Heavy smoker. Obesity with BMI 35. History of obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP.

[ chief complaint ]: Gradually progressive hoarseness for 10 years, presenting in February. No neck mass, pain, dysphagia, dyspnea, or other associated symptoms at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]:  
1. Right true vocal fold squamous cell carcinoma, extending from the vocal process posteriorly to the anterior commissure and involving the saccule.  
2. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, with extrathyroidal extension and regional nodal metastases.  
3. Right vocal fold paralysis/immobility documented after initial biopsy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Operative laryngeal biopsy: right vocal fold squamous cell carcinoma extending from the vocal process posteriorly to the anterior commissure and involving the saccule. Posterior vocal process lesion showed necrosis; biopsy from that site was negative. Left vocal fold edema was present and was not biopsied.  
- FNA, right thyroid: poorly differentiated carcinoma with necrosis, consistent with squamous cell carcinoma; TTF1 negative; thyroglobulin washout negative. Immunoprofile showed positivity for p40 and p63, and negativity for PAX8 and TTF1.  
- FNA, right level III lymph node: rare atypical cells; flow cytometry negative; suspicious for malignancy. Cytology showed malignant pleomorphic cells.  
- FNA, left lymph node: markedly atypical cells with background necrosis; interpreted as positive for tumor, morphologically similar to the thyroid lesion.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial videostroboscopy: bilateral true vocal fold motion; edema of the right vocal fold; posterior vocal process thickening thought to represent inflammatory granuloma.  
- CT neck: right thyroid lobe lucent focus/nodule abutting the tracheoesophageal groove and posterior tracheal wall, suspicious for extrathyroidal extension. Bilateral enlarged level IV lymph nodes were present: left posterior to the left jugular vein and right lateral to the right common carotid artery.  
- Thyroid ultrasound: hypoechoic right thyroid lesion with irregular borders and loss of interface with adjacent structures, concerning for extrathyroidal extension.  
- Repeat office laryngeal examination on April 4: new right vocal fold immobility/paralysis.  
- CT chest: negative; no lesion identified along the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.  
- PET scan dated April 18: hypermetabolic right thyroid lobe/right thyroid lesion; hypermetabolic cervical lymph node(s), including right level III; no distant metastatic disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial operative laryngeal biopsy established right vocal fold squamous cell carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]:  
- No distant metastatic disease was identified on PET or CT chest.  
- Persistent right vocal fold paralysis had been documented after biopsy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No new symptoms were reported at follow-up after biopsy despite interval development of right vocal fold paralysis. Swallowing and breathing remained unchanged at that time.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus was to proceed with upfront thyroid-directed surgery because the thyroid lesion was considered the dominant aggressive process. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection and bilateral neck dissection, achieving gross complete resection despite microscopically positive margins. Postoperatively, adjuvant wide-field radiation with concurrent Taxol-based therapy was planned, incorporating treatment of the laryngeal primary.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Dysphonia.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, microcarcinoma, pathologic stage pT4aN1a. Disease involved the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and superficially invaded the esophagus.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial fine-needle aspiration at an outside institution had been reported as benign. Repeat cytology of the left thyroid nodule was malignant. Surgical pathology demonstrated classic papillary thyroid carcinoma with a 25% tall-cell component and vascular invasion. Tumor encased/invaded the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Superficial esophageal invasion was present. Resection status was R1 due to esophageal shaving margin. Two additional thyroid microcarcinomas were identified. Two micrometastatic nodal deposits were present in the central compartment.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial neck ultrasound demonstrated a solitary incidental left thyroid lobe nodule measuring 8.2 mm, classified as TI-RADS 5 / EU-TIRADS 5. Sonographically, the lesion was markedly hypoechoic, poorly marginated, and located posteriorly abutting the posterior thyroid capsule. Serial follow-up over approximately 3 years showed minimal interval change in size from 8.2 mm to 9 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest performed during evaluation of vocal fold immobility showed no explanatory lesion other than the small posterior left thyroid nodule.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The lesion had been followed with surveillance for approximately 3 years after an initial benign FNA result, with no significant growth. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated left vocal fold immobility. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection. Intraoperatively, the involved recurrent laryngeal nerve was nonfunctional on neurostimulation and was resected. Superficial esophageal tumor involvement was managed by shaving resection. Postoperatively, voice was unchanged from the preoperative baseline. Adjuvant radioactive iodine was administered at a dose of 100 mCi. The patient achieved an excellent response after radioactive iodine.

[ current disease status ]: At 4 years of follow-up after surgery and radioactive iodine, the patient remained disease-free with an excellent response. Cross-sectional imaging had not yet been performed during follow-up.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was notable only for gestational diabetes. There was no reported history of thyroiditis. Preoperative left vocal fold immobility had been documented on fiberoptic laryngoscopy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old man from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Performance status was reported as 2–3. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, cardiac disease, and dialysis dependence.

[ chief complaint ]: Presentation with massive pericardial and pleural effusions. Hepatic focal lesion was also identified at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenocarcinoma, grade 3, with metastatic disease manifested by pleural/pericardial effusions and a hepatic focal lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy showed grade 3 adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Massive pericardial effusion, massive pleural effusion, and a focal hepatic lesion were documented.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: PD-L1 expression was 10%. Next-generation sequencing showed BRAF positivity; V600E was referenced but not definitively documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior anticancer treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Advanced metastatic adenocarcinoma with poor functional status (performance status 2–3) in the setting of significant comorbidity, including dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease and cardiac disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and cardiac disease. The patient was on dialysis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 81-year-old man at initial presentation in 2018. Former smoker with an approximately 10-year smoking history.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally identified right cervical lymph node during emergency department evaluation for stroke-like symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary at presentation, subsequently localized to the tongue base. Cervical nodal metastatic squamous cell carcinoma involving a right level II lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the right level II lymph node performed on 10 December 2018 demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma. Tissue from the FNA was insufficient for p16 testing. Operative pathology from tongue base resection demonstrated a p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma, measuring 2 mm. The carcinoma involved the medial margin. Left tongue base resection specimen showed no tumor on final pathology.

[ imaging findings ]: CTA of the neck/carotid system and CT head obtained during emergency department evaluation on 29 November 2018 identified a pathologic cervical lymph node. Subsequent CT neck confirmed the cervical nodal abnormality. PET/CT performed on 19 December 2018 demonstrated a hypermetabolic lymph node without FDG-avid primary lesion in the nasopharynx or oropharynx. Head and neck examination, flexible endoscopy, repeat office examination, and direct laryngoscopy did not identify a visible primary lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Primary tumor was p16 positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent operative evaluation including direct laryngoscopy, ipsilateral tonsillectomy, right tongue base resection, and limited left tongue base resection. No lesion was identified on direct laryngoscopy or tonsillectomy specimen examination. A 2 mm p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma was identified on permanent pathology from the tongue base resection. Bilateral neck dissections were performed.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial emergency department head and neck examination was otherwise unremarkable. ENT endoscopic examination in the emergency department did not reveal a primary lesion, and no palpable cervical nodes were appreciated at that time. Repeat office examination including palpation of the tongue base and tonsils was also unremarkable.

<image> Slide summarizing the patient’s diagnostic workup timeline for a cervical lymph node finding, alongside an axial PET/CT neck image reviewed in discussion of occult primary evaluation.

reference_discussion.text: Perfect. So, yes, I'm Dante, I'm here over at Penn with Dr. Rajasekaran, and today we'll be talking about management of an oropharyngeal unknown primary tumor. So this is actually kind of an interesting case. We picked one from a while ago just because we have some long-term follow-up on the patient. This gentleman initially presented back in 2018 and was 81 years old at that time, a former smoker, not an extensive smoking history, but over that 10-year history that Dr. Raj did mention. And he essentially had an incidentally discovered neck node that was discovered when he presented to the emergency department for stroke-like symptoms. So he got a CTA to essentially evaluate his carotid system and a CT head. and they saw a pathologic node. In the ED at that time, he had an otherwise unremarkable head and neck exam. The ENT service was consulted and scoped him in the emergency department. Didn't see anything, couldn't palpate any nodes, but he was ultimately referred to ENT for follow-up, given the pathologic node that was identified. was obtained in the days following that CTA. Uh, and then just to, you know, briefly kind of talk about the workup for this gentleman, that initial emergency department visit was on the 29th of November. Uh, we got him in to, uh, see Dr. Raj on the fifth. And again, at that repeat exam, uh, scope was repeated and, you know, tongue based tonsils were palpated. Uh, everything was essentially unremarkable. Uh, that CT neck was performed, which I showed previously. And then an in-office ultrasound guided FNA of the right level 2 lymph node was performed on the 10th of December. That demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma. I think because it was an FNA, there was not sufficient tissue to perform P16 testing on that. A PET CT was performed on the 19th, so about like a week later, and it showed this, you know, a hypermetabolic lymph node, but no real FDG avidity in any of the potential primary sites, nasopharynx or pharynx. and so that he was taken on the 27th.

Oh, hang on one second, Dante, sorry about that. So I guess this is a good time to talk about, if I were to pull Dr. Sumer's nut on, but, you know, looking at this, would anyone order any other diagnostic imaging for this patient? I mean, would people order an MRI?

I would not. I'll let Linda answer as well, but I would not. I don't find it that valuable. I know some people love MRIs. I'm in the opposite camp. I don't understand them or know how to interpret them, to be honest with you. I examine the hell out of these patients. I smash on their tonsils and smash on their lingual tonsil, and then I do an endoscopy. And I'll pick up a few in the office that way. I see very few unknown primaries now going into the operating room just by Being a little rough with my exam, honestly, trying to stir something up and target something. But you're right. You don't find all of them. But if it's that small, I don't know what the resolution of MRI is to find a subcentimeter occult primary in tonsil tissue. Linda, what are your thoughts?

Yeah. We also don't use a lot of MRI. MRI, specifically for this unknown primary scenario, I don't know the literature on it very well, and I've never used it for that indication. But in general, for the existing tumors that we can see, the MRIs tend to upstage. And particularly for the base of tongue ones, they can get a bit confusing. And I worry about it upstaging. So no, I wouldn't I agree with Ryan, again, doing a really good exam and being pretty rough. Sometimes you see just a little bit of viability that clues you in. And I do think, as we'll probably get to talk to, the TORS workup for this is not all that morbid. It shouldn't be all that morbid to do a TORS workup for this.

I would also make another comment. I think a lot of people, talk themselves out of tumors on PET scans. I think the PET scan probably identifies it more often than we give it credit for. I'm not sure why, but I feel like, you know, tumor boards at these conferences, people say it's an unknown primary, and then they actually scroll through the PET. And it's like, well, no, it's right there. You can see it. So it'd be interesting to see all the images of the PET scan, because I think oftentimes there is some asymmetry in the GTS or in the tongue base or somewhere. It doesn't even have to be a lot of asymmetry, but something to at least give you a target.

Yeah, it's a good point. So I think the literature says PET scans, it's 40% false negative. But that doesn't mean it's a bad test to order. I mean, you don't hurt yourself by ordering it. And it gives you some information is better than none. And you, you know, you use it just with the rest of the information that you have. And it can kind of clue you in to maybe focusing in your initial look in that spot. And if it's not there, you're still going to complete the endoscopy. So perfect. So I mean, this is this case was one of my first ones, I think I did the six or early ones about six, seven years ago. So we changed our algorithm algorithm a little bit. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient. Smoking history was present.

[ chief complaint ]: Lung cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-small cell lung cancer, classified as poorly differentiated pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Molecular interpretation described non-small cell lung cancer with SMARCA4 alteration/deficiency and very high tumor mutational burden.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside pathology diagnosed poorly differentiated pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Tumor immunohistochemistry was positive for TTF-1. No in-house slide review was available. SMARCA4 immunohistochemistry was not performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive molecular profiling identified alterations in TP53, KEAP1, and SMARCA4. The SMARCA4 alteration was described as a class 1 event, specifically a homozygous deletion. Tissue and blood-based testing were concordant for TP53 and KEAP1 mutations. No EGFR or KRAS alteration was identified on the reported profiling.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor mutational burden was very high, reported as close to 100. PD-L1 testing results were not reported for this patient.

[ other clinical data ]: Primary diagnostic pathology had been performed outside the treating institution. Blood-based molecular testing was performed in addition to tissue-based next-generation sequencing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient. Age was not documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy, with slowly rising PSA.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, status post robotic radical prostatectomy, with subsequent biochemical recurrence and suspected solitary osseous metastatic recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]: Prostatectomy specimen showed Gleason score 9 disease, corresponding to ISUP Grade Group 5.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Preoperative prostate MRI showed a PI-RADS 5 lesion.  
- Initial PSMA PET at staging demonstrated localized disease only, with no nodal involvement.  
- Follow-up gallium-68 PSMA PET performed approximately 18 months after prostatectomy showed no abnormal uptake in the prostate bed and no pelvic nodal uptake.  
- The same scan demonstrated a single mild focal PSMA-avid lesion in the left side of the T2 vertebral body, SUVmax approximately 3.  
- No corresponding abnormality was identified on CT at the T2 lesion site.  
- Comparison with prior gallium-68 PSMA PET from approximately 9 months earlier showed no uptake or CT abnormality at T2 at that time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA at recurrence was 0.7.  
- PSA doubling time was approximately 12 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Robotic radical prostatectomy had been performed for high-risk localized prostate cancer.  
- At approximately 18 months post-prostatectomy, PSA had risen slowly to 0.7, consistent with biochemical recurrence.

[ current disease status ]: Approximately 1.5 years after prostatectomy, the patient had low-volume recurrent disease with a slowly rising PSA and a new solitary PSMA-avid T2 vertebral body lesion suspicious for metastasis. No local recurrence in the prostate bed and no nodal disease were identified on the most recent PSMA PET.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Both the prior and current PSMA PET scans were gallium-68 PSMA studies performed on the same scanner with similar acquisition conditions, including uptake time of 60 minutes.

No lymph node metastasis was identified; no lymph nodes were present/recovered in the specimen.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Total thyroidectomy had been performed. Postoperative FDG PET/CT showed no metastatic disease.

[ current disease status ]: At the latest documented postoperative assessment, there was no evidence of metastatic disease on FDG PET/CT. The patient remained under postoperative biochemical surveillance because of an elevated early postoperative thyroglobulin level.

[ other clinical data ]: Postoperative assessment occurred 4 weeks after surgery. Risk of recurrence was documented as intermediate-high, estimated at greater than 16% to 30%, based on tumor size and extent of vascular invasion.

All this is going to be driven off capsular and vascular invasion. These big ones, do I need to worry about that, ZooBear?

Um, well, I think it's very important to really set at least, you know, look at the entire capsule of this nodule and it usually don't need 8000 slides because if you take the sections, you can at least put two or three sections from the capsule in one cassette. So you can get this actually done between like eight to 10 slides. So that's why I think it's very important to have a piece of the tumor capsule and a little bit of a surrounding thyroid tissue because you need to see how it invades the capsule and the vessels. And that's becoming more and more important in these tumors because we really need to see how many real foci of angioinvasion are present, which is very important for defining these tumors.

From a practical standpoint, I mean, I guess I feel really good if it's two, three centimeters. I worry a little bit more about sampling if it's eight centimeters, or should I not worry about that? I can still trust the two vessels, or should I be a little more concerned with the bigger ones, Zubair, or are we okay with that?

So I think if you really look back at the literature, it's pretty sketchy, but whatever it's available, it comes from the institutions, which really spell out that the entire capsule was examined. Naturally, you're not going to go through the block to see it. And I think this is where the less than or four or more foci comes from. Because if you really think about a three-dimensional section of a thyroid, which is being placed on a slide, which is two-dimensional, you may be hitting the same vessels the way the vessels run. You may be hitting the same vessels twice in consecutive sections. So I think this type of less than four or four or more takes care of this. And when you apply that criteria, you have to be careful what is true vascular invasion. And I think most pathologists at this point who are specialty focused, who know how to read thyroid tumors, who know what is at stake, what are the pitfalls, really know how to diagnose true vascular invasion. I just want to add, because thyroid tumors are so vascular to begin with, and depending upon, no pun intended, how the surgeon handles the thyroid tumor in the OR, it has been shown that they really really are a little rough with these thyroid tumors because oncocytic tumors particularly do not have a lot of stroma. These are just a bag of just nothing but cells. So they can actually squeeze some of the tumor cells into the vessels. That's why there are strict criteria how to diagnose and how to confirm that this is foci of true vascular invasion. So once you are there, now the studies have shown even including from Memorial and us that if you have more foresight of true NGO invasion, it really affects the prognosis. Perfect. Mabel, let me ask you sort of a bigger question. I mean, there are certain patterns that we see here. Sorry. Yeah, as you're talking about this case, I'm thinking about the, you know, the different centers I've been in growing up at MEMS KCC and then coming to Mayo. And when I talked to our pathologist initially, they would call anything that's angioinvasive one, two, three, or four angioinvasive. It's eight centimeters. And I do pets after pets after pets. And after five years, even with vascular invasion, they don't recur. So these do exist. And so I was wondering if the ultrasound, although it's going backwards from pathology, but I think it tells a bigger picture with the pathology to incorporate what the ultrasound looked like, what the And the fact that there's no lymph nodes is unusual for a really aggressive oncocytic.
Yeah. Jill, any thoughts about that since we're bumping into ultrasound here?

Yeah, I mean, it can be very challenging when you have such a large lesion to really get a good look in and around the thyroid. That is a challenge, and there is a role for cross-sectional imaging, I think, when you have a very large lesion like this. Often, this patient's younger, but as we'll see in other cases, typically the patients are older and kyphotic, another complication to getting a really good ultrasound exam.
Perfect, very good. Okay, so let's go ahead and stage this one and see what happens.

Oh, we were discussing this. So basically this patient will be on the intermediate high with a risk of recurrence with more than 16 to 30%. And it's basically because we're gonna take the size of the tumor and the number of vascular invasion and that will put him on the intermediate high risk.
So for this we use- Hold on a second, yeah. Janice?

Could we just comment on no lymph nodes, like no lymph nodes in the specimen versus negative lymph nodes and how many were actually recovered? Because I think that is a really important piece when we're looking at the staging. And even if there was only a lymph node, one has to take it into context. We not leave note positive on the specimen.

So how many lymph nodes were recovered? Yeah. So what you're hearing for the rest of the crowd is by the time we see these things, eight centimeters, the vast majority have lymph node metastasis, or there's something different going on. And I suspect this one didn't know they were oxidic thyroid cancer when they got their initial surgery. It was probably a Bethesda three. So they're not thinking about big lymph node sampling. Again, back to that same concept that eight centimeters usually don't present as completely confined to the thyroid. Okay, go ahead, Lena.

So in order to have the calculation of the risk of recurrence, we wanted to highlight this initiative from TIDO. This is the risk of recurrence calculator. Okay, so keep going.

Okay, so going back to our case, our patient, so he came to us four weeks post-op, and as you can see, he has a TSH of 0.4, free T4 of 1.9, and tarot globulin of 152, and negative antibodies, and we were very surprised with this level of tarot globulin.
Dr. Alexander, Houston, we have a problem. What's going on here?

You know, we do. I mean, that certainly is a high value post-operatively. And usually thyroglobulin drops fairly precipitously after a near total thyroidectomy. Absolutely. Jorge, imaging and FDG PET, where would you be on this one now?
Well, OTC can be tricky. And sometimes it can have a low radio iodine uptake and higher FDG uptake. But with this highly elevated thyroid globulin, I would go firstly for a radio iodine scan.

Okay, so we've got an elevated thyroid, Bob. I would instantly be leaping to distant met somewhere because this is eight centimeters. I've been worried about it since day one when I saw the person. So I'm going through that filter. Fortunately, Dr. Pedraza is smarter than me. So what did you guys do, Lena?

So we have the question that you just did, but we did repeat labs on her and on him, sorry, and we also ordered a PET scan. So four weeks before, we have the steroid globulin, we ordered an FDG PET CT. There was no evidence of this metastatic disease. Dr. Reiner, what's going on? We just spent $3,000 on a PET scan, and apparently a $100 TG would help us. What's going on here?

Yeah, so I've had this case. This reminds me of a case back at Memorial when I was more junior, and I had a patient with a large hertho-oncositic thyroid cancer. He underwent surgery. I saw him back four weeks later. And I think the thyroglobulin was 1,000, if I'm not mistaken. And we did a PET scan. There was nothing. You know, sometimes I would have considered also an MRI brain if the PET was negative. That's the only other place we might find disease. But simply waiting four to seven half-lives for the thyroglobulin to come down is probably the answer here. And so I think that's what's happening. Herthal cell, like oncocytics, like follicular thyroid cancers are very good TG producers. And I think in papillary thyroid cancer, you get away with doing post-op TGs at four weeks, and it's fine. But in oncocytics, if we had measured this thyroglobulin before surgery, it was probably many, many thousands. And so what we're seeing is that it does take six to eight weeks to probably be patient before you measure the thyroglobulin. So I've had this case myself, and I've learned over time to be patient.
Keep going, Lina.

Yes, we assume that that was the reason. And we wanted to come back to the guidelines and use the data framework for initial therapy, where they are telling us step by step what we should do. And they highlight the assessment of the taraglolin should be at six weeks, between six to 12 weeks post-op. So here are the rationale behind this and what Dr. Ryder was mentioning, the half-life of the theroglobulin is about three days. So, to just make sure that there's a clearance of the theroglobulin, we need to at least wait 25 days. So, basically, the minimum biological clearance will be four weeks, but six weeks provides a more reliable and clinically meaningful measurement.

Yeah, I mean, this is absolutely accurate. I think this is one of the good things the ATA guidelines did for us, because we're using that post-op TG to make decisions about radioactive iodine, right? And so letting that drop down, I would bet you that this pre-op thyroglobulin was 20,000 or 30,000. These eight centimeter hurtful cells can legitimately do 20, 30,000 in thyroglobulin. and a week was just not long enough because you were starting at such a high level, right? And as Mabel mentioned, we usually get away with it in papillary because they're not as high to begin with, and so they're down to the lower level. So I think particularly when we're doing post-op decision-making in response to therapy, understanding that if you have a TG in that three, four, or five range, hold tight, repeat it again in a month, and watch and see where they go down. And this was a great teaching point, not specifically related to Herthel cell, but related to all of thyroid cancer. Very good. Okay, let's go on to case number two. That was a great teaching point. Now let's take it up a notch and see what we got.

reference_conclusion: The patient was classified as intermediate-high risk of recurrence, estimated at greater than 16% to 30%, based on the 8 cm primary tumor size and the presence of fewer than four foci of vascular invasion. Given the unexpectedly elevated postoperative thyroglobulin, repeat laboratory assessment was obtained and FDG PET/CT was performed, which showed no evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent management emphasized reassessment of thyroglobulin no earlier than 6 weeks postoperatively, preferably within 6 to 12 weeks, to allow adequate biochemical clearance before making further treatment decisions.
