case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female; age 51 years at initial presentation in 2019. Known HIV infection on antiretroviral treatment since 2011.

[ chief complaint ]: Four-month history of low abdominal pain and genital sores at presentation in 2019. Initial associated symptoms included localized genital pain and bleeding.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced invasive vulvar cancer diagnosed in October 2019. FIGO stage III at the time of starting radiotherapy. Subsequent recurrent/metastatic disease involving the left inguinal lymph node was confirmed later in follow-up.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy was performed with histologic confirmation of invasive vulvar cancer. Fine-needle aspiration of the left inguinal lymph node later confirmed recurrence.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial visual inspection with acetic acid screening for cervical cancer was normal. Later Doppler ultrasound and CT scan were requested to evaluate groin swelling, possible recurrence, and deep vein thrombosis. CT scan demonstrated metastatic involvement of the left inguinal lymph node. Doppler ultrasound confirmed deep vein thrombosis. On clinical examination at recurrence, there was a left inguinal lymph node measuring approximately 2 x 2 cm and vaginal stenosis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Chemoradiotherapy was administered. Cisplatin was given for 1 cycle. External beam radiotherapy dose was 46 Gy in 23 fractions, commenced on 7 April 2020 and completed on 12 May 2020. Planned boost was not delivered; treatment was therefore incomplete. During radiotherapy, by fraction 17, constipation developed and genital pain increased; morphine and lactulose were added. Post-treatment, abdominal pain persisted and perivulvar sores were necrotic; wound care twice daily with sitz baths was prescribed, and morphine 5 mL every 4 hours plus bisacodyl 10 mg nocte were continued. At 6 months post-treatment, genital pain persisted and analgesics were continued. At 1 year, low abdominal pain persisted and analgesics were continued. After later presentation with groin swelling and lower limb pain, analgesia was continued; tramadol was used in addition to paracetamol, and morphine had been discontinued at that stage.

[ current disease status ]: At 3 years and 4 months after initial treatment, recurrent disease was present with metastatic left inguinal nodal involvement and associated deep vein thrombosis. The left inguinal node subsequently progressed to a fungating nodular mass with progressive lower-limb swelling/lymphedema. ECOG performance status was 1.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was managed as an outpatient. She had palliative care involvement from early in the course of treatment, including counseling and analgesic review. Analgesic and supportive medications used during the disease course included paracetamol, morphine, tramadol, lactulose, and bisacodyl. Wound care was required for necrotic/fungating vulvar and inguinal lesions.

reference_discussion.text: The case study is of a female who was age 51 at the time of presentation that was in 2019. She had had complaints of low abdominal pain and genital sores for four months. And so she went to a local clinic for screening for cervical cancer by visual inspection with ascetic acid and the findings were normal. So then she was referred for further investigations. and she had a biopsy taken and histology done. And some background information also is that she had been on HIV treatment from 2011. So she first presented to Cancer Diseases Hospital in 2019 in October, and the diagnosis was locally advanced viral cancer type, locally advanced and invasive. Figo staging was stage three at the time of starting radiotherapy. So summary of the treatment was that she had chemo radiotherapy. She had one cycle of cisplatin and then she had 46 gray radiotherapy in 23 fractions. This was started on the 7th of April and her last session was on the 12th of May in 2020. A point to note was that she'd not get a boost So her treatment was considered incomplete. The initial patient problems was that she had localized genital pain. obviously because of the sores and then she had bleeding. And then she was on paracetamol one gram twice, three times a day orally. And also she had an encounter with the palliative care team. So this is something that the hospital tries to do to ensure that every new patient has an encounter with the palliative care team and starts interacting with them. So she had counseling and then also they had a relook at her pain meds. Then during radiation therapy at 17 fractions, she developed constipation. The genital pain seemed to have increased. So they added morphine and lactulose to her analgesic regimen. And then immediately post-treatment, she was seen and she had continued problems of abdominal pain. And then the perivalvelous sores were necrotic. So she was, prescribed wound care twice a day, which involved six baths. And then she continued on morphine, five mils every four hours, plus bisacordial 10 milligrams Nocte. So this lady was treated as an outpatient case. So mostly she would just come in for treatment and then she would go home. So any interventions were obviously through health education and then encouraging her to carry out those interventions for herself at home. And then she was followed up at six months post-treatment. The genital pain continued. So the anti-pain meds were continued. And then at one year again, she was seen. So she was being followed up now every six months. She still had complaints of low abdominal pain. So the pain meds were continued. And then she sort of dropped off the radar and this was during the time of COVID. So a lot of patients were not showing up and there were travel restrictions. So she was now seen about over a year later when she came in with a complaint of swelling in the groin, which had been there for about a month. And then also lower limb pain. And on examination, she had a left chinguinal lymph node that was about two by two centimeters. There was vaginal stenosis and the doctors requested for a Doppler and a CT scan to rule out recurrence of the cancer and also deep vein thrombosis. So she was continued on analgesics. And at this point she was taking Tramadol in addition to the paracetamol and the morphine had been discontinued. Then again, she fell off the radar after doing the CT scan. She came back now at three years and four months and the left inguinal lymph node, it showed that this was metastatic. This was from the CT scan report and the Doppler confirmed the deep vein thrombosis. So she was commenced on Clexane 60 milligrams once a day. And she only took this for 14 days and she continued on the Tramadol. and there was a recommendation for her to be reviewed in the gynecology clinic for fine needle aspiration of the lymph node. So this was done and it was confirmed from results that there was recurrence. So the swelling in the lower limb was progressive and then they left lymph node now became a fungating nodular mass. So at this point, she was ECOG 1 in performance status. And the recommendation was for her to have palliative chemotherapy of carboplatin and taxane for six cycles, which she completed in September of 2024. Her last visit to the hospital was this year in January on the 23rd. and the lesion had expanded and grown and the lymphedema also now had increased extent of what she was now a COG2. And she continued now on morphine. She was put back on morphine because her pain was unbearable. And then also there was a recommendation that the ulcer is treated with a crushed metronidazole. because it was foul-getting and foul-smelling. And now her mobility also had become severely compromised, and she was quite dependent on care. The conclusion of the case study was one for the radiation therapy, and also she should have had three cycles of chemo, but she only had one for the chemo-radiation therapy. And then also there were all these gaps in her follow-up resulting in delayed intervention for the problems she began to develop. So the issue is now how can nurses provide optimal follow-up remotely between visits or link these patients to their local primary health care providers for care? Because like in her case, there was a great need for wound management and pain management And the point to note is Cancer Diseases Hospital is based in the capital city. It's the only cancer center for the whole country. But through their presentation, so now we can discuss and have questions and contributions. Thank you.

Biemba, I have some questions just regarding payment for services in your area. Is it you have to pay per treatment? Is that part of the reason that you believe follow up may not have been as close for this patient?

Well, treatment itself is free, but some investigations people pay out of pocket. And of course, getting, accessing a health care facilities at the patient's own cost. So the economic factor sometimes is a huge impediment to patients accessing care. That's why sometimes people have missed appointments. Because for example, if they come from halfway across the country, they don't have any family in the city, It becomes very difficult and sometimes they have to raise the money that they have to pay for transportation and also have some money to support their stay while they're in the city accessing care.

Thank you. Here in Australia, we have. something called IPTAS or travel allowance schemes that allow, if the government provides patients who live a certain amount of, more than 100 kilometres away from their nearest treatment centre, some financial support. Is there anything like that available to your patients?

Unfortunately, no. The only thing is usually when a patient is referred for specialist care, sometimes there may be an ambulance service at their first visit. Because sometimes even the ambulance service, there may be such challenges as maybe there is no fuel at that point in time. and also because of the cost involved, they may have to wait a little so that it's a combined trip with some other services. So currently there is no transportation support, although at some point the Zambian Cancer Society was running a service called Hope Transport where they would engage the commercial passenger services who would offer free tickets to patients and sometimes the social workers department is able to find well-wishers who can subsidise patient travel, but this is not very reliable or consistent.
Now the question was going to be, so she had incomplete treatment, the reason behind that, especially the boost, she didn't have that, was there a reason behind that?

Unfortunately, in the case notes, there was no detailed information as to why the treatment was incomplete. But a point to note is by this time, our radiotherapy service was limping and sometimes our machines would be down because our machines had been in service from when the hospital opened in 2006, especially the linear accelerator. and the initial Cobalt 60 unit. And then we had a second Cobalt unit that was a Barbatron that was procured in 2016. Our brachytherapy unit as well was one that had been around from the time the hospital opened. So by 2019, our machines had more downtime than uptime and that would disrupt treatment.

Yeah, absolutely. We had our national gynae oncology meeting here in Australia last week and there was a radiation oncologist from Rwanda who presented and similar type of situation where, you know, the linacs were out of action, you know, a large amount of the time that really had an impact on being able to provide treatment to patients.
Diemba, do you know if the boost was going to be external beam boost or a breaky HDR boost?

Yes. At present right now, question, but I was also going to add that We have had no T22 working and because of age, spare parts were no longer available. Currently, the government has procured new machines and the bunkers are being redone. So hopefully before the end of the year, radiotherapy services will be back on. So what the government did is we're having to send patients out of the country to India at government cost. But obviously, you can only send so many patients at a time. So our waiting list for radiotherapy is actually over a thousand patients currently.

Thank you, Biamba. In the beginning of you answering, it completely cut out. We heard, I think, the second half, but we did not hear if it was going to be an external beam or a brachytherapy boost. You cut out for that part.

Okay, so this lady was obviously going to need brachytherapy, but Like I said, at that point, our machines were mostly down than working. So you find that a good number of the patients, even on external beam, would not complete all their treatment in the allocated time slot. So they would have to discontinue treatment until the machines were fixed. And for some who come from far away, that would have an impact on whether they came back in time to complete their treatment or not. So we've had a lot of progressive disease and recurrence, I think, in the recent past because of suboptimal treatment.

Thank you. I was able to hear all of that this time. Do you find that with the HDR units in particular, with the brachytherapy unit, do you see more issues with support for when the machines break? from the vendor, or is it also sources getting stuck in customs for source exchange?

Well, for source exchange, like when we, because we were using, it was an Iridium afterloader, so sometimes it would be transportation. All the paperwork would be done and all, but you'd find that finding an appropriate flight that can carry radioactive material would be an issue. And then sometimes also it would be issues of processes and procedures really to get the payments cleared because we are a government funded institution and it operates based on public funds. And so we usually have to get clearance from headquarters for anything that we're doing. So sometimes you would have delays in the brachytherapy source being brought in when the old one is done.

Thanks so much, Bamba. Amber, it's Bronwyn. Thank you so much for your presentation. At the start, you mentioned that when the patient had been diagnosed, she had met the palliative care team as an inpatient as standard practice. Is that for all cancer patients or just specific subgroups?
For palliative care, our aim is for every patient to have a palliative care assessment at diagnosis and first assessment. However, sometimes because of not having... Biemba seems to have dropped out.
Yeah, she looks like she completely dropped off. She was able to join. Yeah. How amazing that palliative care referral happens so early.

Yeah, I was thinking exactly the same thing. I think there's an Irish population who expect an imminent death when we bring up palliative care. So it's really interesting that they do it at the point of diagnosis.
That feels the same here within the US. A lot of the doctors that don't routinely use palliative are very reluctant to even consider bringing them in early.

but I think there's such benefit from allowing them to be met by palliative care when they're well and able to, I guess, voice their concerns, their goals, their wishes and things like that. But I think it's also about how you sell palliative care or how you, it's more about symptom control and symptom management as opposed to end of life and I think palliative care probably get a bad rap from that respect. And that's, I guess, the reticence from both the community, but as well as the medical profession too, for not wanting to refer early.

I think sometimes the barrier to not referring early also comes from, they feel like they can be that palliative care provider. And I think in some ways I can appreciate where they're coming from, But I also see where patients have a lot of gaps in the quality of care that they could receive if that referral was done early. And once they receive the education of the difference between hospice and palliative care, they're very interested in doing it. But for me, it's often convincing my providers that, you know, the more people have support from multidisciplinary teams, the better their outcomes, the better they feel emotionally, you know, even spiritually about their journey with cancer.

And what is the kind of end of life care in the US or in Australia? So in Ireland. people are very attached to their homes. And there's a lot of generational trauma around that. But we have a real, there's a palpable need for people to be at home and to pass away at home. And we have a community structure to try and support that. It's not always possible, but we, to the best of our ability, with a publicly funded health service, we try and facilitate that with nurses and carers going into the home. But I'm just curious, is it more hospice-based where you guys are or is it community-based?

It's more hospice-based, at least as far as Portland, Oregon is concerned. And interestingly, you know, patients can be divided in how they feel about that. Some people, that's absolutely where they want to be, is at home in their own comforts with their family around them. And then a lot of people really struggle with just the concept of dying and not being on the planet anymore. And so they feel more comfortable actually being in a hospital setting. They just let their symptoms get to the point where they have to be admitted and they end up passing away in the hospital.

I've found that family members actually aren't always comfortable with bringing the patients home. They are- Agreed. Yeah, they push admission more so than the patient themselves, even if the patient's wishes were to pass in their home. We try to, or at least where I'm out of, we do get hospice involved, but it can be a home hospice. So a visiting nurse would come in and take care of some of the needs that the patient had and teach the family how to do it. So it's interesting to see how different some families and communities.

Here in Australia, which I think is a little bit in contrast to Sarah's experience in Ireland, it's a lot more hospital based. There's not that connection and expectation of dying at home and dying with your family. Of course, that does vary according to the community and cultural background. So we have a lot of patients in hospitals and we can have palliative care type wards, but then some of the hospitals also have more hospice areas as well. We do also offer home palliative support, but that's probably less of a percentage than patients passing away either at home or in hospital or palliative care units.
It looks like Biemba is back in also. So I don't remember exactly where we left off, but it was definitely with palliative care. Hello, can you hear me? Yes.

Biemba, I'm curious to know how palliative care operates where you are. Is it a community service or is it based around centralized like the cancer hospital is for you? Was this patient be able to get palliative care in her local community or not?

So our palliative care service is still highly centralised because prior to HIV treatment with home based care, and there was a lot of hospices, they actually huge issue and mortality was high. But once ART came in, and people lived longer, the home based care service fizzled out, and very few hospitals were left. So we came up with putting up palliative care because in the beginning, when our cancer hospital was opened, obviously, we had a lot of advanced disease. And so we saw the need to have palliative care. But linkage to a primary health care level and the community is still not well structured. And as a consequence, also because of myths and beliefs, you have more families or patients being brought back to the hospital, even when they've reached end of life. So in our society, I think people would rather die in the hospital than die from their homes. And then also sometimes it's because, you know, death is not something we talk about or the concept of death and dying. So when we introduced it, it was a bit difficult even for us as healthcare workers, but slowly I think people began to appreciate the value of having this service and also talking about the fact that they had crossed that threshold from curative intent to palliative. and then they become end of life. But our families would still require a lot of support and having the difficult conversations. So like you saw from my, one of the things I raised was how do we strengthen the linkage between this specialized hospital and the communities where these patients are coming from probably we need to piggyback on the primary healthcare system because we do not have, like I think in the UK, you have the home, what you call, is it visiting nurse? You know, the nurses that work in the community and go to people's homes. We do not have that here. So it's a bit of a challenge when a patient goes home to have continuity of care.

Do most patients have a primary health care provider? I know it's often difficult in Australia even for people to have a general practitioner or a primary health doctor that they see. Is that something that your patients do have someone that they do see on a regular basis locally?
No, we don't. You're seen by whoever you find at the health facility when you show up.
Yep.
So you're not guaranteed of having the same clinician at every visit.
It makes that very difficult for people then having to. It becomes difficult. Yeah. Tell their whole story again.

Yes. And especially if your medical records have gaps, like obviously the file I accessed. And these are conversations we would have with the clinicians where sometimes somebody will not take a detailed history and they'll not document everything. So the next clinician still is not able to get the full story. And sometimes our clients, depending on their emotional state at the time of a visit, will not recall everything they were told. I've had patients whom when you ask what drugs are you taking, they'll say, well, I don't know, I just have a batch of pills. And that's not very helpful.

Yes, we also have community nurses here in Australia that can go out to the home to assist with wound care and also palliative care home visiting as well. They have access to that. So I guess it's difficult for women when they're looking after themselves as far as wound care in this situation to be able to manage if they don't have someone like that that can come and assess how it's going or change the plan if need be. And my other question was gonna be around the follow-up. So obviously there was a long time between follow-up for her. What's the routine follow-up plan for a woman with vulva cancer, Bimba? Like how often would they usually be seen?

So the standard follow-up plan that is there usually is once you complete the treatment, you're seen after six weeks. And then depending on how you're responding to treatment, then you're followed up like every three months in your first year. And then if you're okay, you're going to be followed up every six months for another two years. And then after that, you're seen annually. But patients are still told, if anything comes up, anything happens, please do not hesitate to come back.

Yeah, and just to kind of add from a, since I'm in radiation area as well, with these vulvar cases, as Biemba said, you know, it will vary depending on how they're doing. As a lot of us know, some of them get really nasty skin reactions after radiation, especially if we have to dose the skin very high, which usually we do in the vulva and even the distal vagina. Um, but, uh, yeah, sometimes we see them frequently if they live close by, but, um, you know, that's here in Los Angeles, we get patients from. Out of state, out of the country. So, you know, of course, then we have to figure out local care, but some of them need a lot of wound care and some of them do really well. It's just, it's, it's yeah. As Bamba said, you know, it depends on the patient.
But do you have visiting nurse services available to you or available to other parts of the country.

Well, something akin to visiting nurse services is what we call outreach. And mostly this is for maternal and child health services, because obviously our statistics for maternal mortality and infant and child mortality are not very good. So you have a lot of funding that supports this, but the same service is not really available for other conditions, unfortunately. There's something similar that has been started for tuberculosis because it is a problem and obviously there is funding under those programs. So, and then the other issue, of course, is resources like this team has to go out and maybe the institution only has the one vehicle. One thing we try to do with the palliative care team sometimes is if we have a patient that is out there and they're like on morphine and they don't really have to come back in because they don't have problems, we would then coordinate with their local health service provider. When they come to the city, they come with the the information about this patient, and we're able to get a medication refill that is taken back by the team that came to do something else. But that only would work well because you know somebody there, but we don't have an actual system that is intentional. So follow-up care is sporadic, like for those that are not in the facility, unfortunately.

I see, thank you. Hopefully, because you have not, as you said, intentional programs for this, but maybe they'll be able to build one based on some of the templates of the other ones right now, like the tuberculosis and the maternal, those type, if they already have something in place for going and checking on them, it would be great to be able to build it up to include, even if it was one, you know, nurse in that area for, it could be general oncology that's able to go and evaluate the patients and reach out to the team.

Yes, so one of the things is thankfully they're building two other regional hospitals, one south of the country, one a bit north. but also we did develop oncology nursing curricula. So we're having more oncology nurses trained, and then we are lobbying the government for nurse positions, not only at big hospitals, but within the district health system, so that then these nurses are able to provide the service, like you have said, at primary healthcare level. So that is the challenge that we still have, because I think until about 10 years ago, oncology was not really anybody's priority. And so people didn't really put money on it in terms of programmatic allocation. But now, We actually have a national cancer control strategic plan and we have prioritization of cancers. So like for adults, we have breast cancer, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and colorectal cancer as priorities that actually have been funded. And then we have also pediatric oncology, the six index cancers under the WHO program. So we have made some strides. We're not yet where we wanna be, but I think we're certainly not where we were 15, 20 years ago.
Yeah, that's incredible, moving in the right direction for sure.
Anyone else have any comments or questions?

I think, you know, just something that this is just another, you know, another example of you know, healthcare across the world, I'm finding, and I'm talking very broken right now, I have thoughts going through my head and I'm trying to figure out how to get them out. Doing a lot of education around the world, primarily with brachytherapy, but also with just general radiation, I'm finding, you know, there's barriers that are patient-related. and, you know, resource-related. And then there's barriers that are government-related, such as, you know, access to health care, but also just important things like a project we have with Nigeria right now, just equipment getting stuck in customs that can't get to the machines, and then their source can't get exchanged, or whether it's for external beam or for brachytherapy. And seeing it just in many different countries and across many different continents and just I wish there was a way, and this is way above my intelligence level, but a way to get government to realize how critical this equipment is and get it through more, more quickly or get vendor support more quickly. I, I don't have a good solution. It's just verbalizing seeing this repeated pattern, lots and lots and lots of places. And I don't know how we can, how we can tackle it as a specialty. more just a statement of frustration than wanting to fix it without knowing how to do it.

I agree, Kayla. I think it's quite eye-opening when you hear the vast differences across the world in the options that are available to patients and government support or lack of government support across there. But I think as nurses, it's about advocating for our patients and to get them what they need, you know, when they need it, where they need it. But I think, as Chrissie said, Bianba, it's fantastic that you've now got an oncology nursing program, which is amazing, and that, you know, the government, you have, you know, an oncology strategic plan and the government is seeing the importance in I guess those more common cancers or those cancers that probably have higher rates across your country. So yeah, definitely a step in the right direction, but unfortunately these things are slow to change, but yeah, heading in the right direction.

Yeah, it definitely, it gives me hope that I know that we can keep moving things. It's a great example from you, Biemba, Just coming back from Colombia, another great example is LDR brachytherapy. While I practice HDR, LDR is a great option for countries that are hit hard by the machines going down. But even Colombia, they said, we don't practice LDR anywhere because the government allowing the seeds in is basically, there's rules against it, so they don't even try. It's very eye opening. I think we've got a lot of work we can do as nurses to advocate and help what we can, and especially through education. But yeah, I think as oncology globally, there's there's a lot of opportunity to try to keep things moving, just learning a lot as we go here.

I would say also that we have one of the most robust cervical cancer screening programs, I think, in Sub-Saharan Africa. This was started in 2005, obviously, after seeing the association between HIV and development of cervical cancer. So people were no longer dying of AIDS, but they were living long enough to develop cancer. So for cancers like breast, it's also beginning to piggyback on the programming that is already available for cervical cancer. So cervical cancer screening, at least, is available almost countrywide now. The only aspect of cancer care that's still lagging a bit behind and is highly centralized is obviously treatment and then also, you know, supportive care. So if treatment can catch up and the fact that we are going to have two additional centers, I think is a step in the right direction, bearing in mind the cost of radiotherapy equipment. So it is a huge investment for a country like ours that is LMIC. So hopefully in the next 10, 15 years, we will see a much better picture and we will have more and more oncology nursing services available at lower levels of care, not just centralized. So again, we keep on learning. We look at other countries. The only, I think, area where we still have a lot of work to do is obviously generating research that is local. So for there, we actually need a lot of capacity because most of what we have, especially for nursing, is obviously just observational and anecdotal. But it would help if we could actually have data driven by science to support some of the things we tend to talk about.

I couldn't agree more, Biemba. And I suppose it'd be interesting if it was without the cameras on a show of hands, Has anyone got any active trials in vulval cancer? Because I feel there's a real paucity of evidence, particularly for vulval cancer. And I don't know of any trials that are open in Ireland at the moment.

Here in Australia, one of our nurses in Western Australia, which is the other side of the country from where Bronwyn and I are, has just started a local project but hoping to go national around the use of an antibacterial solution called Prontothan to for vulval wound care after vulval cancer surgery. So I think both Bronwyn and my units are also planning to be a part of that because we as a group of gynae oncology nurses here in Australia have seen the the issues that women have with vulva wound care, rates of infection, readmission to hospital and things like that. So that is something that is planning to be started in a few centres at the moment so that we can get a standard of care. Because as you say, a lot of the things we do as far as vulva wound care is all anecdotal and there's actually no evidence behind you know, the sits baths or the peri washes, people call it different things that we currently do. So being able to have a trial when this is a nurse led trial around using a solution to help with viable wound care will be fantastic because, yeah, we definitely need the evidence behind some of the things that we do.
Getting close to being on the hour here. Dre, I know you started a topic conversation. I'm not sure if you want to table it or discuss it in these next final minutes that we have.

That's so nice of you to circle back to that. I was actually about ready to type in the chat that I have to go see a patient for teaching. So thank you so much again for this meeting, everybody. And this was a really incredible topic and presentation for the group. And then I'm sure it's something that is an ongoing thing here, so I can bring it up at our next meeting. Thank you so much.

Thank you, Drea. As Ashley just said, also, we are coming towards the end of this, and if there's anyone out in the group that's with us right now that wants us to discuss their case or they want to present their case at our next meeting, we really love getting input from this international community, and not just from the cases that we think are important, but from the cases that you think are important. anyone has anything that they really want to talk about, please feel free to email us. If something comes up next week and you realize, hey, it would be great, please email myself and Sarah or Ashley. And she just sent her email in the group, so even better. Biemba, that was an incredible presentation, and I can't thank you enough for coming on and doing that with us and for us.

I'm also very thankful that you reached out and the falling off and on notwithstanding I've had an absolutely fruitful discussion and I'm looking forward to the findings of that study that's going on about wound care because like you saw already that was one of our issues and we do sometimes as nurses here we do a lot of things like you know you're going to use honey and stuff like that but we do not have you know, the evidence to support what we're doing. So I think that is an area that will really be of interest. So I'm very, very thankful and looking forward to interactions going forward.
Well done, Biemba. That was really interesting case. Thank you for presenting.

Well, great. Thank you, everyone. Biemba, thank you for the case, as I said, Our next ECHO is scheduled for May. We're doing these every other month. So looking forward to you all joining us in May. And like Chrissy mentioned, if you have a case, feel free to send that over our way and we can consider it for our next ECHO.

reference_conclusion: The patient had biopsy-confirmed recurrent metastatic disease involving the left inguinal lymph node and concurrent deep vein thrombosis. Management consisted of anticoagulation with Clexane 60 mg once daily, gynecology review with fine needle aspiration of the lymph node to confirm recurrence, and palliative chemotherapy with carboplatin plus taxane for six cycles, which was completed in September 2024. Ongoing symptom-directed palliative care included morphine for severe pain and crushed metronidazole for management of the foul-smelling ulcerated lesion.
reference_conclusion_quote: the left inguinal lymph node, it showed that this was metastatic. This was from the CT scan report and the Doppler confirmed the deep vein thrombosis. So she was commenced on Clexane 60 milligrams once a day. [...] there was a recommendation for her to be reviewed in the gynecology clinic for fine needle aspiration of the lymph node. So this was done and it was confirmed from results that there was recurrence. [...] And the recommendation was for her to have palliative chemotherapy of carboplatin and taxane for six cycles, which she completed in September of 2024. [...] She was put back on morphine because her pain was unbearable. And then also there was a recommendation that the ulcer is treated with a crushed metronidazole. because it was foul-getting and foul-smelling.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive hoarseness for 6 months; voice was described as pressed and high-pitched.

[ diagnosis ]: Left glottic laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, staged as T1a.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy demonstrated laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging results were documented for this patient.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were documented.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Referred by a local otolaryngologist for evaluation. No other medical problems were documented. No smoking history was documented. Prior surgical history included cesarean sections only.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so let's see. This is a 55-year-old female with hoarseness that has, 55-year-old female with hoarseness that has progressed for the past six months. She has a pressed and a high-pitched voice, and she was referred from one of the local otolaryngologists for evaluation. No other medical problems, no past history of smoking, only surgical history and the past history of C-sections. So I'm going to bring you two different strobes, and this is the same female, two different lesions, so that we get our heads going. So this is the left. And this turned out to be a laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma biopsy in DOR. And then we have this other patient who has a left vocal bone vision that is referred to as a laryngeal carcinoma for evaluation and treatment. So first of all, what is the staging of these two lesions, Diana and Andrew? Patient one and patient two?
I'll take patient one, it's pretty easy. It's a T1A.
Okay, and Dr. McWhorter?

Yeah. The other, you know, this is part of the limits of our staging system because these are very different tumors, but this is also a T1A. I don't think it's crossing anterior commissure. We couldn't quite see it, but it doesn't, I don't think so, but it's a large volume tumor in the anterior third, which is a different animal in terms of functional outcome, potentially compared to what you had with the other one, but they're both T1As.

You're going to end up my presentation before I go through it. But yes, yes. So for the fellows out there, there's a small T1 lesion versus an angry T1 lesion. Those are managed differently. And the discussions that have to be had with those patients about endoscopic surgery are completely different. And who would send the first lesion to a radiation oncologist? And I'm going to let Miriam answer that.

You know, I think the first one, yeah, the first one, I think it's just perfect for, for surgery. And for me, I like to do it cold steel actually without a laser. And it looks like it's going to come right off. I mean, it's perfect for that.
That is correct.
The second one, a little bit trickier, of course, but for the first one, absolutely.
Would you have the second patient have a discussion with the radiation oncologist before surgery?
Yes.
Do you guys agree with that, Diana and Andrew and Kendra? Would you see this patient? Yeah.

Well, I guess something to bring up is that when this lesion is that small, like patient number one, Laureano, I'd be curious to ask some of our discussants, how do you approach the tissue confirmation prior to excision? Or do you excise with the presumption that it's squamous or carcinoma because your biopsy would essentially you know, remove the lesion.

So, that is a great, great question. So, so I disagree a little bit with Dr. McWhorter's statement that he would take, you know, these lesions to the OR before surgery. I actually don't necessarily take everyone to the OR before surgery. I agree that you can't get a grasp of a lesion for surgery completely in the office, but first of all, you know, I get a biopsy in the office in all of these patients, even if it's a small leukoplakia, and I prepare the patient for surgical excision in the OR, okay? If it's a small lesion that I think it's confined to the epithelium, I, you know, I go through a thorough discussion of, you know, epithelial resection and ATP laser treatment. So I biopsy all of my lesions in the office before surgery. If it's going to be an extensive resection, like the patient number two, you know, then we have a different kind of discussion. I send them to see the radiation oncologist and then I have a second visit after we have, you know, the result of the biopsy to discuss what the patient would want to approach in terms of treatment, you know, and see what the voice result will be and whatnot. So I biopsy all of these patients. Let me see if I have, let me see this right here for a second. So when I biopsy them, I topicalize them with 4% lidocaine, and I perform, you know, a thorough endoscopy, which includes sort of an upper tracheoscopy. It's a bulk deletion with a saccular cyst. This is obviously another patient. you know, but I try to look at the superglottis and the subglottis from the posterior larynx to the front, so I get a good idea of what the extension of the lesion will be before going to the OR. And that's sort of the way that I see things in my practice. So following up on Diana's data on in-office biopsy, so This is from Seth Bailey and he did a small study on in-office biopsy of upper airway lesions and basically they biopsied 92 tumors transnasally and 24 transoral. Biopsies were performed on 116 patients, and 97 out of the 116 patients had a diagnosis of malignancy, you know, doing in-office endoscopies with biopsy. So, I fairly, you know, when you're doing, when I do surgery on these T1 carcinomas, I try to, if it's not a bulky tumor, I try to biopsy it off in the office. Jeffrey, and this is not a question, I try to avoid going to the OR without a preemptive tissue diagnosis, unless it's something really small, just to prepare for the patient for what the diagnosis will be at the end. You know, sometimes you can get a full breadth of the lesion and you get high grade dysplasia on them or moderate dysplasia, but that'll give you an idea of what you might have, you know, at the end. And at least you can tell the patient, look, this looks like premalignant tissue. And we'll probably go forward with the surgery to remove the lesion and it might end up being, you know, a squamous cell carcinoma. Okay. I don't know if you guys would like to comment on that, Andrew.

Oh, I think it's very doable. You know, I think it's, you can definitely, it's a high value technique. It depends upon, you know, in terms of, I think a lot of that's your referral base in terms of how they're coming to you in terms of whether they didn't diopsy ahead of time or not, and whether you need to make that. And then I think it needs to, for me, Anytime I choose to do a procedure like that, it's whether or not, do I think this is going to change my treatment decision? You know, is this going to be a decision point in terms of, am I going left or I going right here? And I don't think there's anything, I think it's a, you know, a perfectly fine way of doing it just based pretty much on how my practice is that I'm doing it. I think those tumors that you showed, I think that the, uh, the difference in the Diana's original tumor is there is a lot to be gained in that lesion when you are with that bulky, you know, large tumor that was T1 then being a T2 from in terms of, like Dr. Liu said, in terms of looking with a 70 degree telescope, what is that roof of ventricle? What's the apex like? How deep does that go? If you're doing that resection, you know, are you going to be an ELS type 5 complete chordectomy? Or is that more, you know, it's not quite as endophytic as it appears. And those are hard to judge. You can be confused in the office in that anterior component. I think, you know, I think it's perfectly fine. It's a great technique to be able to help make that treatment decision for the in the office if you don't have a diagnosis ahead of time. For sure, the small lesion, I would just cut it off. You know what I mean? Because if it's just if it's a leukoplastic lesion, if it's severe dysplasia, or it's CIS, or it's early T1, I'm going to give them the same treatment.
Yeah, they're still going to have a great outcome.
Yeah. So I just, I would just excise it.

Laureano, your office-based biopsy strategy, is that a physician preference on your end because you find it expeditious, or are there any systemic or financial considerations in your practice environment that make this the best way to take care of things?

That's a great question. So yeah, my practice is hybrid academic and hybrid private. One, I have three main considerations. One is OR time. I don't have enough OR time to, you know, I do a fair amount of laryngeal, endoscopic laryngeal cancer like some of you guys. So I don't have enough OR time in between, you know, big head and neck surgery and, you know, thyroidectomies and all this and that to take these patients to the OR for a biopsy. That's one reason. The other reason is I trained in laryngology and head and neck cancer just as Diana. You know, it's just ease of doing it in the office. I see the patient, you know, on a Tuesday or Wednesday, and I see him next week over, biopsy him. I already have a tissue diagnosis, and he's already scheduled for surgery in the OR by the time I biopsy the lesion, if it's something that I think we're going to go forward with surgery. So, yes. There are considerations. I don't look at it in terms of, I mean, biopsy in the OR, monetary wise in Puerto Rico, you get billed better for it than doing it in the office. So it's just convenience in the way that I do it in my practice. It's just easier for the patient to get him soon to the OR for surgery, basically. So patient one versus patient two, would you get a CT scan? I'm going to ask Diana, I'm going to ask Miriam, I'm going to ask Andrew. Would you get a CT scan on patient one?
Absolutely not. Patient two, definitely, because it looks like it's creeping forwards up to the anterior commissure and you really want to see what's happening up there.
What else would you, on an angry T1 lesion like this, what else would you be looking for in a CT scan?
Yeah, cartilaginous involvement, erosion of the inner cortex, and possibly less likely, though, the outer cortices.

I also look at the paraglottic fat, you know, and that's and I discuss it with I have, you know, my my I have a group of head and neck radiologists here who look at my scan. So I ask them specifically to look at the extension to the paraglottic fat. just because I can sort of tell the patient, you know, what the extent of the resection will be. And this obviously would impact their voice outcome significantly. You know, if you have to take a whole bunch of the muscle out and go lateral to, you know, ligament and cartilage, it's the different, the voice outcome will completely be different than, you know, not having to do that. So, so, um, what are, what would be the treatment options for these patients? You know, if it's a, and we already discussed this, if it's a large, bulky, T1A carcinoma, extending a lateral into, you know, close to the cartilage or deep into the muscle, I always discuss voice outcomes in them. I've had a few of those patients who, you know, I sent them over to the radiation oncologist and they have opted for radiotherapy, just because, you know, I have been clear that they probably going to have a breathy voice, you know, and that's probably an irreversible thing after surgery. So we have a thorough discussion on voice outcomes. If it's a small lesion confined to the epithelium, then I'd probably go ahead with surgery. And again, I agree with not sending them to the radiation oncologist. I don't know if you guys agree with that or have anything to add.

Can I make a comment here? Yeah. Yeah, I was going to say, I kind of feel that all these early stage glottic cancers should see the radiation oncologist and have a discussion as an option. I agree the very first one is incredibly superficial, very favorable for surgery. But my experience has been more recently that I think patients just need to hear both options. And especially from a I don't know, around here, just like the medical legal standpoint, I think it's actually, I've looked into this a little bit. It's like, I think you actually kind of have to just kind of at least, you know, discuss that as an option and often recommend that they actually see them for the actual discussion about it. So.

Kendra, what do you think? I think that this is something that varies very substantially depending on where you're at. If you have a radiation oncologist that's on your team, that's part of multidisciplinary care and who specializes in head and neck cancer, I don't think it's wrong. I can't speak to medical legal, but I do think that a radiation oncologist that radiated that first lesion has not done the right thing. They have made an error. That is not a lesion that should ever be radiated. And if you're never gonna radiate a lesion, that is, I would refuse radiation to that patient without some other consideration. I'm not sure that a discussion is necessary from an informed standpoint. The other comment I will make is, Though I trained in a very big place filled with many, many excellent people, I then went out into the world. And in the world, radiation oncologists, just like surgeons, differ substantially. And so you could end up in a situation where the information that the patient receives from such a consultation is bad. And as I said at the beginning, just as my disclaimer, In general, patients who can have good functional outcomes with something less than a total laryngectomy, in my view, should always have surgeries. Radiation is a pathway when you're talking about organ loss and when the risk for regional recurrences is high. I think in some settings, fine, but there are considerations that If someone sent me that first lesion, I'd be confused.
happy to have it. It's not, you know, in the world outside of big academic institutions, if you send this patient to a radiation oncologist, they're probably going to get radiated.
Yeah, they might. And that's really what I'm saying is.

Exactly. And that's what I'm and I'm going to ask and I'm going to answer somewhere. I agree with you in the in the sense that you have to have this discussion. But our my reality, the reality of my practice is that if I send a small T1 lesion and this has happened before, for a discussion with the radiation oncologist, they're gonna be like, okay, you need radiation for this, right? It's not an open discussion. There's no back and forth communication. They just get radiated. So I try to avoid being in that position, especially with small epithelial lesions, or lesions confined to the epithelium.
I used to be so offended when people said that in open forums, and then I went into the world.

No, I, no, I understand. I mean, I get referrals from community setting and radox and community that I know personally. reference_conclusion: For the small superficial T1a glottic lesion confined to the epithelium, management is endoscopic surgical excision, with epithelial resection and laser treatment as appropriate; radiation oncology consultation is not indicated for this lesion. For the larger bulky T1a glottic lesion, office biopsy should be obtained before definitive treatment, CT imaging should be performed to assess anterior commissure extension, cartilage involvement, and paraglottic fat, and the patient should be referred for radiation oncology consultation prior to treatment selection. Treatment choice for the bulky lesion should be individualized after discussion of expected voice outcomes, with either endoscopic resection or radiotherapy considered based on extent of resection and functional implications.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 78-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Shortness of breath.

[ diagnosis ]: Right pleural mesothelioma.

[ histopathology results ]: Mesothelioma was diagnosed on pathology from right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) pleural biopsy. Histologic subtype was not specified.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial chest imaging demonstrated a right pleural effusion. CT chest showed right-sided pleural fluid with mild pleural thickening and relative volume loss/collapse of the right hemithorax. PET/CT demonstrated limited hypermetabolic activity along the right lateral and posterior pleural/chest wall region. Imaging was described as showing low overall disease burden. No imaging evidence of disease spread outside one hemithorax was reported.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right VATS with drainage of pleural fluid and pleural biopsy, establishing the diagnosis of mesothelioma. Cardiopulmonary functional testing was acceptable for surgery. Invasive staging included thoracic lymph node assessment and diagnostic laparoscopy with abdominal biopsies; no extra-thoracic/intra-abdominal spread was identified.

[ current disease status ]: No specific residual disease measurements or interval imaging results were provided.

[ other clinical data ]: ECOG performance status was 0-1 for trial eligibility. Disease was considered surgically resectable and confined to the right pleural space based on staging evaluation.
