reference_discussion.text: I'm Adam Bograd, I'm one of the thoracic surgeons from out in Seattle, a little bit farther than Penn. These slides were created by Taylor Ripley, who unfortunately got stuck, so I'm going to do my best to go through them, and everyone feel free to chime in. So the tumor boards typically start with just general case presentation. You give some patient demographics and presentation, so that's how the flow of this will go. So this is a 78-year-old man with some shortness of breath. He went into the emergency room. They got some chest imaging, and they noted some fluid in the pleural space. That's fluid outside of the lung but inside of the chest. They got some additional imaging with a CT scan and a PET scan. So I know where I am. There is a large variety of places people get their medical care. There's big tertiary medical centers. There's small community centers. So the workup for a new effusion can vary pretty significantly. So I guess that's always a good first question is what is a typical workup for new effusions?

I think we see a new fusion. Of course, we do like to get the imaging to figure out if it is one site or two site. Second thing, we examine the patients and what the clinical symptoms and what the chronicity is, and if there are any additional constitutional symptoms with it. fever, weight loss, or any other. And of course, the most critical thing is to get a sample from the effusion and look at the biochemistry and looking at if there is any signs of cancer cells inside of that fluid. And these are the first steps. And usually what has been done is when we drain this fluid, we spin and we try to collect sediment and we look under the microscope, do some specific stainings to figure out if there is a cancer cell and if there is a cancer cell, what might be the origin of that cancer. And this is generally the first step. Of course, it can be by itself not adequate. I think we will be discussing further. But for example, in mesothelioma, only one-fourth of the fluid samples can get malignant cells, the cancer cells. So, by itself, it might not be diagnostic, but when we look at it, how urgent, how critical, the chronicity, additional symptoms that may come up with, and after that, analysis of the fluid is the first step.

Just to add to that, I mean, talking to the patient about kind of underlying risk factors and exposures. If you see a person with a pleural effusion who, you know, has symptoms or concerns for exposure for tuberculosis, or you think they have heart failure, or if they were a pipe fitter in the Navy, you may put out a different algorithmic kind of thought process. But as my colleague said, you will sample the fluid, you take a look. There are different criteria to analyze it. A negative sample does not mean that the space itself is pristine. So further evaluations may be needed. And I'm sure that's probably what we'll be talking about moving forward.
How many times do you sample an effusion before you're sure?
Our institutional standard is if we have high clinical suspicion after even one or two negative taps, we would go for a surgical intervention to adequately sample the pleural space.
Great. Thank you guys. All right. Walk us through the imaging.

So this is a CT scan of the previous patient we just mentioned. The images is as if they're laying down and you're kind of looking up from their feet. So the top of the image is the front of their chest, the back. Towards the bottom is their back of their chest. Towards screen right is actually the patient left. Towards screen left is the patient right. So, you can see on the patient's right side, screen left, there's some fluid, there's a little bit of pleural thickening, and then one of the more subtle things that you can actually see is you see some asymmetry in the, Into your posterior diameter of the chest. It's almost like the one side is collapsed down a little bit On the right side is a PET CT scan. That is a CT scan that's fused with some metabolic imaging where you get essentially sugar injected into you and it's tagged to a fluorine atom and then when that Sugar gets used as fuel. Most cells use sugar as fuel. It sends off a light particle or a positron. And that functional imaging gets fused on top of a CT scan. So things that glow tend to take up more fuel than the cells around it. And one of the things that uses more fuel is cancer cells. And so indirectly, it implies that there's something abnormal if it glows brighter. So you see a little bit of hypermetabolic activity along the right lateral chest wall, posteriorly and laterally.
I'll ask you a question about this. So I know you're not a radiologist, but that was a very good job, but just a spot read. Is this a high burden of disease, just from this?
No, this is not a CT scan that I would look at and say there's a lot of disease burden there.
Any other comments about the imaging? OK, so what do you know from these images and what would you do next? Since this might come to you normally, I'm going to have you start that conversation.

So I think the findings are concerning for something going on in the pleural space, and in particular if somebody's had a pleural effusion before. So I would probably go directly to a pleural biopsy. We do them thoracoscopically. You can do them percutaneously, so from the outside with an interventional radiologist putting a needle in, but I think you get a ton of information from thoracoscopy or putting a camera in the chest. really see disease extent in terms of what's on the parietal pleura, which is the undersurface of the chest wall, what's on the visceral pleura, which is the pleural surface surrounding the lung. You can see within the fissures how much disease there is, which is the fighting spaces between the lobes in the lung. You can see how much is on the diaphragm. So it really gives you a good idea of disease burden and you can take really good samples And I know sometimes when you're doing FNAs from the outside, you can sometimes have a little bit of confusion as to the histologic subtypes, which is really important actually for figuring out treatment strategies afterwards. I would vote for a pleural biopsy, but I'm a surgeon. That's like asking the pizza guy what's for dinner. He's going to tell you pizza. If I could just ask one more leading question, would you during the initial diagnostic procedure for a pleural effusion NOS go right to pleurodesis? And I think that's important because we will see that in the community, which can limit my surgical colleagues' abilities.
Can you explain what pleurodesis is?

I'll let the gentleman who does it, if he'd like. So a pleuridesis is a procedure where you want to try to get the lung to stick up against the chest wall. And the purpose of that is to obliterate the space that sits between the lung and the chest wall. That is a potential space. That potential space can fill up with fluid. Fluid building up can be really symptomatic. It can give people shortness of breath, chest pain. And so what he was mentioning is, while you're there, you're in the chest, why not just do it? In theory, it sounds like a great idea to just do it. However, if your initial biopsies are non-diagnostic, you've kind of hosed yourself in going back. It makes it really difficult. So I personally do not. I wait for a diagnosis. And then, you know, the other thing that you can assess at the time of surgery is, does the lung actually come up? Right? Because if you want to try to pleuridize somebody, the most common thing we use is talc. I'm not sure what you guys use elsewhere. Yeah, but we use talc. If you can't get apposition between the lung and the chest wall, then the talc's not going to work, right? Because you can't get things to stick up. And so you start thinking about other things like pleurex catheters and things like that. So I personally don't initially until I have a definitive diagnosis. And I agree with that. The other reason to bring it up is if there was going to be consideration for a section once the diagnosis was made. So I personally think pleuridesis makes the subsequent surgery easier. We can talk about it, but I think it actually makes it easier. I was going to say, my surgeons say the opposite. I guess it's apples and oranges.

So I think probably the summary there is that pleurodesis can be really good for fluid management, and actually we do do it quite a bit. And it's not a contraindication to surgery. But I think we're saying we should be thoughtful about when to do it, essentially. All right.

All right, so it looks like Taylor did a right vats. I'm gonna say vats for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, because that's really a tongue twister. Drain the fluid, and you biopsy the pleura. So you take this device, and you just sort of nibble a little bit at the pleura. This is important. You actually need to make sure that your biopsies are deep enough, because you have to document invasion. If you just do these little superficial surface bites, you can sometimes get a non-diagnostic biopsy. So that's important. I was always taught to biopsy down to things that either you either see fat, muscle, or it bleeds. And usually that gives you an answer. So a mesothelioma diagnosis was obtained from pathology. Second part of this is important too, and it gets to functional testing to make sure people are fit enough to undergo surgery. So it sounds like the cardiopulmonary testing was fine. And then the last line is important because you need to stage people appropriately. I am pretty conservative about surgical resection. I think it really needs to, in 2025 going into 2026, it really needs to be the right person you're operating on. And so I am a very big proponent of very, very aggressive preoperative staging. And so it sounds like they check some of the lymph nodes in the chest and did some biopsies in the abdomen with laparoscopy to make sure that there was no disease spread.
OK, so you gave us a lot of information. The workup sounds very similar to what you would have done. Is there anything else you would do? So I.

So I typically stage people pretty aggressively, right? So there's staging by imaging. So you saw some of it, right? So a PET scan. I very aggressively do lymph node staging. So I trained doing bronchoscopy biopsies for lymph nodes. It's one of the few instances where I do media stenoscopies. is you want to make sure you're actually biopsying a lymph node and not a pleural tumor. So there's a way you can put a camera just beneath the breastbone, go down, and you can biopsy some lymph nodes that typically live along and between the airway where the airway splits. And so that's one. You want to make sure you're not operating on, you're not getting yourself to an instance where you're doing a big surgery on somebody who may not benefit from the surgery. And then one of the more common places where mesothelioma can be outside of the chest is intra-abdominally. And so you want to check to make sure there's no intra-abdominal spread in particular on the surface of the under surface of the abdominal wall, the omentum, which is some of the fat that lives in your belly. And then I in particular look for trans-diaphragmatic invasion, so I look at both diaphragms. Typically, if the tumor has invaded through the diaphragm, there's probably going to be a pretty high chance that they'll be spread in the belly or intraperitoneal dissemination, so you really want to get a good look at the diaphragms. I guess we're going to talk about it because there's some slides in terms of surgery. I tend to stay away from extra pleural pneumonectomies. However, I work everybody up as if they're going to get one because if you're in the operating room and you have to transition your surgical plan, you don't want to be wondering is this something they're going to be able to tolerate. So, yeah, so one of the surgeries involves removing the entire lung. One of them involves not removing the entire lung. So if you need to transition from going from a lung sparing surgery to a remove the whole lung surgery, you don't want to be wondering in the back of your mind, okay, is this person going to actually tolerate this? I didn't get, you know, X or Y or Z tests, which are impossible to get afterwards, right? So I tend to get everybody stress tests, tend to get VQ scans on everybody, which looks at the perfusion to the right and the left side of the lungs. And I also tend to get echoes on everybody to make sure that I have pulmonary hypertension. One piece of additional information that wasn't on the other slide was the type of mesothelioma. So I will steal a page out of Hedy Kindler's book. I don't think she's here yet. She'll be here tomorrow. Mesothelioma can come in two different flavors. It can be vanilla or chocolate or a swirl of the two. So vanilla being epithelioid, the most common, about 70% of plural disease will be epithelioid. The chocolate in that case would be a sarcomatoid or a mixture of the two, biphasic. For the most part, surgery is most appropriate in patients with epithelioid disease. There can be equipoison and epithelioid predominant biphasic. But I think that's a big decision point for us would be the type of meso to make a decision if surgery makes sense.

Yeah, I agree for sure. The other thing that you were alluding to, but I just want to be more explicit about is that we do really want to make sure the disease is isolated to where we think it's isolated. So, you know, we saw on the PET scan that it was just those few little spots that were lining up along the lining of the lung. And one of the spaces that's really hard to see on imaging is the abdomen. So actually prior to any surgery our patients will get a surgical laparoscopy to look in the abdomen and make sure that it hasn't spread because it is very hard to see it on imaging. So that's one extra check just to make sure we are dealing with what we think we're dealing with. Any additional comments on this part?

So Taylor had a trial open at the time. I tried to get this open at our hospital, but I couldn't. I failed miserably. I think you guys have it or know about it. Time in if I mess this up. So this is a study that Taylor had open at the time. It's neoadjuvant. ICI is immune checkpoint inhibitor. Those are drugs that work in a certain pathway that help the immune system in mesothelioma. So it's abbreviated NEMO. So if I say NEMO, that's what it is. So this is for mesothelioma patients, stage one to three, good functional status, which is that ECOG zero to one, any histology, right? So that touches on what you said, sarcomatoid, biphasic, and epithelioid patients. The patients were broken down into two separate cohorts or two different groups. One cohort A got durvalumab and tremulimumab, I think I pronounced that right. So these are, Gervalumab is a PD-L1 inhibitor that blocks a certain pathway. PD stands for programmed death, so it stops the T cells from dying when they interact with tumor cells. And Tremolimumab, I think, is a CTLA-4 inhibitor. Yeah, so that's a chemo-sparing regimen, I would say. Cohort B involves chemotherapy and those two different immunotherapies. Then they get surgery, if you filter ahead. It can be one of the two. It can either be a pneumonectomy, an extra pleural pneumonectomy, which is removal of the lung, or an extended pleurectomy decortication, which tends to be what Taylor prefers, and then since we trained at the same place, it's also what I prefer. That is a, I think the best way I can explain what a pleurectomy decortication is, there's a slide next, is if you think about your lung like an orange, and the pulp is your lung, skin is the tumor, and you just sort of peel it off. So there's certain inclusion criteria. You gotta make sure that you're putting the right patients on trial. You can't just put everybody on. These are people that are potentially resectable. I think this is where a tumor board is helpful to discuss patients, right? You gotta figure out who is resectable and who is potentially resectable and who's not. They have to have a path diagnosis, so it has to be confirmed. The imaging can't show any disease spread outside of one side of the chest, which is what she was just mentioning. You can't have any obvious chest wall invasion or invasion into the mediastinum. The mediastinum is just the center of the chest. You need to have a surgical evaluation by surgeons who actually know a thing or two about mesothelioma. I think some people have a very nihilistic view of mesothelioma, and if you ask a surgeon, some of them just say, no way, which I definitely do not think is the right thing. On the flip side of the coin, you can't find a surgeon who just operates on everything. That's also bad. All histologies were included in this one. So these were all three. This is the chocolate, the vanilla, and the swirl, all of them. And they could have either no nodal disease detected or nodal disease that's isolated to either the same side as the tumor in the hilum, which is out towards the lung, or the mediastinum. The nodal staging system for meso is a little bit different than lung cancer, so. So this is a picture of an extended pleurectomy decortication. So the slide on the left is getting the parietal pleura off from the chest wall. So this is really the first step in the surgery in determining whether or not somebody's resectable or not. So there are instances where you think somebody's resectable and you get into the operating room and they're not. And it is a very simple test. If you get between the chest wall and that tumor rind, if your finger slides, it's resectable. If it doesn't slide, it's not resectable. Because that implies that it's T4 and there's some evidence of chest wall invasion if the tumor doesn't come down off the chest wall. And then the right side is the peeling the orange skin off of an orange. So the underlying reddish pink structure is the lung and the, I guess, salmon pink is with the hand peeling back, that's the tumor rind that's coming off. So it's two components. It's taking tumor off the bottom of the chest wall as well as peeling tumor off of the lung. And then typically for an extended pleurectomy decortication, it involves removal and resection and reconstruction of part of the diaphragm and often part of the pericardium.

Surgeons have sometimes described it to me as actually peeling the white pith off of an orange instead of the, it's harder than the peel. And yeah, and has anyone ever gotten all of the white pith off of an orange? No, it's very hard. So I think that's not a, it's not a bad analogy for the surgery either. OK, so this patient has checked all of the boxes that we've asked for in terms of being a surgical candidate. And they received three cycles of the chemotherapy and immunotherapy. So they must have been in the combo arm. They had surgery with removal of the disease. And then they continued on immunotherapy after. And I guess this patient is thankfully doing very well. So that's great. Dr. Ruffin.

We don't have NEMO open at our institution. We also lost the fight to get it funded to be open. This data was actually published, like the little sister of this now randomized trial was published in CCR. So just kudos to Taylor's group. Really interesting trial with a lot of interesting work came out of this. One thing that's not mentioned here, because I don't think it's necessarily spoken to on the trial, but there's a radiation oncologist staring at me. When we talk about surgery, we talk about usually a multi-modality or a three-pronged approach. We've addressed two of those, something that goes in the body, something that comes out of the body with a surgeon, and then there's usually something else. That something else is somewhat institutionally specific. Some people will do intrathoracic chemotherapy. Our institution and Penn, I believe, are much more inclined to do imprint or IMRT, which is radiating where the peel used to be. The reason being you can't peel all the white pith off. I can't promise my medicine can kill all the white pith, but at least we can say that if there's any white pith left, the best we can do is to try to radiate it away. So it's important to understand that these kind of group discussions aren't just surgeons and med-oncs. It's not just surgeons, med-oncs, and rad-oncs. It's supportive care, pulmonologists. It's a large group that kind of comes up with this multi-pronged approach for a patient like this.

There are a few things I also want to review about this patient's case and in general. So one of the reason we review our patients in multidisciplinary group is, again, we would like to get a synergistic or at least additive effect from the contribution of these different elements. That is because generally, if we do even a very aggressive surgery, We cannot cure most of our patients because we cannot get rid of it all. And the intent is how we can increase the cytoreduction, how we can try to get rid of most of resistant tumor clones by surgery, by radiation, so systemic therapies can be more effective. And this decision was a little bit based on earlier stages of data related with surgery. And what has been historically studied is for patients who had surgery followed with aggressive consultative therapies, such as systemic treatment or radiation, did better than historical controls. But of course there was a bias because we were selecting the fittest patients for surgery. And two years ago, there was a study that has been published that make all of us hesitate to surgery as much. But there was some flaws, or at least we believe it was not in the right, perfect setting. But that study, for patients who were treatment naive, diagnosed with early mesothelioma, underwent surgery or they did get systemic treatment on patients who got surgery after that got additional therapies if needed. But there was not a significant advantage if actually there was a increased early mortality in the surgical arm. But when we look at the patient selection, the selection criterias were not very typical. So some of the cancers, some of the biologies are more aggressive, and we generally do not offer surgeries most of the time. That is biphasic and sarcomatoid. And there were a number of patients who had that histology. The second thing, we know lymph node involvement shows what is the extent of the disease, or at least a surrogate of it. The tumor is trying to get out of the chest. and there were a number of patients who had lymph node positivity. The other thing is surgeries were done in surgical centers, but those centers did not have enough expertise, at least some of them, which probably explain why the outcomes were inferior than most of the centers that we expect to see in terms of outcomes, 30, 90 day outcomes from the surgery. So those are the reasons, at least few reasons, While the current highest level of evidence does not support surgery, we still believe surgery can play a role in the treatment of mesothelioma, but we need to select patients. And that is one of the reasons we discuss our cases in tumor board. And the other thing, it is going to be important because we cannot cure our patients in general. We will talk about different strategies, how we can try to convert this disease more of a chronic disease. And one of the key thing is how we can decrease the disease burden. so that we can alter or slow down the progress of the disease. It is why we'll be talking about these different strategies, and this is gonna be also important discussion for the medical part, what we can do in terms of combination, and if we are gonna do maintenance or not, because you need to consider the risk and the toll to the patient, but also what might be the benefit in terms of these treatment decisions. The other thing I would like to highlight is neoadjuvant treatment. So this is a systemic treatment that is given before surgery. We have a lot of experience in different cancers, in breast cancer and lung cancer, and that is the success that we are trying to replicate in some of these studies. Giving systemic treatments before surgery provides a couple of additional benefits. Number one, patient tolerance is better because after a surgery with recovery, sometimes patients may not be able to get these therapies the way that we plan to deliver. Second thing, if we give these drugs up front, when we do surgeries, we can see in real life, what the treatment response may look like. So that is an important aspect of it. And the third thing is, of course, if we have a good global systemic control of the disease before a surgery, it is likely that we may have a better outcome with cytoreductive approaches. So that is one of the reasons we've been trying to bring these neoadjuvant studies not only we can hopefully improve the outcome of surgery, which has been, again, at least in high level of evidence, not as good as we would like to see, but also if we can identify patient-specific therapies that works well, because when we remove the cancer under the microscope, we can see how many cancer cells died, what is the viability of the leftover tissue? And the third thing is because we won't be able to get rid of all the cancer, we will be leaving some micrometastatic disease. If we have a good systemic control, can we have better outcomes?

One of the things I just wanted to touch on, he mentioned, you know, what is the goal of the surgery, right? Because I think the most common question that I get after really any surgery is, did you get it all? Hey doc, did you get it all? I'm like, for these, I'm like, kinda. So the goal of surgery is what's called a macroscopic complete resection. But what is that? Did you remove all tumor that you can see with your eyeballs? And is the only thing left behind microscopic, which is an R1 resection. So that's really the goal of surgery. So that's sort of a tough conversation afterwards. Did you get it all conversation? You think you did. But you probably didn't. There's probably microscopic disease that's left behind. Which is why when I read papers about mesothelioma, if they cite R0 resections, I immediately trash the paper. And then something that you touched on about the Mars 2 trial. I have a tough time really altering my thought pattern and practice based on that trial considering the large percentage of patients in that study who got operated on who I would never ever operate on. And most mesosurgeons would not operate on. I agree with that. What I would say is the MARS II is the trial he was alluding to. It's a European-based trial. And I always try to be politically correct. It was appropriate in the time and geographic environment it was done, but we have a different practice pattern here. We have different surgical centers and mesothelioma centers of excellence here. We could sit here and talk about it until I'm blue in the face why we also still think for the properly selected individual surgery makes sense. But I think that's the most important thing. This is not the type of a procedure or decision that is going to be totalitarian recommended to a patient based on the kind of conflicting literature. So you talk to a team to discuss do they think you're healthy enough to go through this procedure and have good quality afterwards. And do they think realistically they can get enough of this out to make it worth your while. But at the same time, if the person sitting in front of me says, listen, I don't want a week-long hospital stay for that surgery, it's not something I personally want at this juncture, it's not definitively wrong to hold off and forego the surgery. So it's definitely a shared discussion. But in our center and centers like it, the people on the stage, those types of centers, we offer it to people that we deem operable, well enough to tolerate the surgery, and resectable. After our surgeons do their full evaluations, they think they can get enough out, we would offer it. For instance, the predecessor of the NEMO trial, patients lived well over two and a half years, give or take, as compared to MARS-2, which was 18 months. And the trial that I'm publishing now is 36 months. So again, it's about patient selection. And to say whether we're better at surgery or we're just better at picking patients, it's really hard to say. But I don't think MARS-2 is the end of surgery, it's just the more thoughtful utilization of surgery.

So I'm going to open it up for questions. This is our, our, um, case about surgery. So we'll move on. The case after this will be about systemic therapies. So let's focus the questions on the surgical cases. So, um, I saw you in the back. Oh, you. Yeah.

In other approaches to cancer, people have talked about concomitant tumor resistance. And there's poor, from what I can tell, evidence for that for mesothelioma, but not very much. What do you think? Do you think that's a possibility?
Are you asking about like an acquired resistance mechanism to therapy?

No, it's the idea that many of these cells secrete, a large tumor will secrete a tumor-suppressing hormone for other cells, right? I know it's been shown for certain kinds of lung cancer, for example.

Yes, I mean, the tumor itself, by definition, can secrete different what we can think of as hormones or chemokines. that may affect the way in which the body can respond to certain drugs. Surgery itself, the actual manipulation of the pleura and the lung, can also affect what we call tumor microenvironments. So it makes it very difficult to study. So if you get a biopsy sample for us to figure out what is the tumor secreting, the needle itself or the scalpel itself may alter what it's secreting. So it's a very nuanced discussion. But I would say extrapolating from the experience in lung, having lymph nodes and native tumor inside and exposure to immunotherapy during that course seems to be more beneficial than not because you still have the proper immune milieu. Now again, that is much more conjecture than anything else. And in a rare tumor like this, we're likely going to be consigned to conjecture from other tumors. I think I understood that you said that if the lymph nodes were already infected that you're not a candidate for surgery.
Is that in all cases? Also, what happens if you also have nodes inside your lung?

Yeah, so it depends how extensive the nodal involvement is and which lymph nodes are or are not involved. So if you have, you know, microscopic involvement of one lymph node that is out towards, you know, not a non-mediastinal lymph node, a high-lymph node, something that's more out towards the lung, we probably still would proceed forward with surgery for that. Conversely, if somebody has a lymph node on the opposite side of the chest from where their tumor is located, right? So if you're on the right side of the airway but your mesothelioma is on the left side of your chest, that's not somebody we'd operate on. Or if somebody has multiple stations that are involved, that's somebody that we probably would not operate on. Or if there was a lymph node involved in the abdomen, we probably wouldn't operate on them. So it's nuanced in terms of who you would and wouldn't offer surgery to. I don't think there's a one-size-fits-all plan for mesothelioma, which I think it's important to present all of them at tumor boards. So every new mesodiagnosis that I get, I present at tumor board, because it's important. There's a lot of nuances. And so I wouldn't say all lymph node involvement is exclusionary for surgery, but you have to be very thoughtful about it. And you have to make sure the lymph node disease burden is low. It also is a good reason, if there's a lymph node involved, at least where we are and I assume many other institutions, if surgery was going to be considered, that's a person we would almost de facto recommend some sort of medical therapy first because we want to prove we can control this disease that's already starting to move a little bit before we put somebody through a large surgery.
You mentioned you don't do surgery on biphasic or sarcomic tumors. Why is that, or what if it's discovered that after surgery it is now biphasic, not epithelioid?

So as a clarifying point, we don't routinely do it on patients that have any chocolate. If it's a swirl, vanilla mostly, though. It's like an epithelioid predominant. So 90% epithelioid, 10% sarcomatoid. In a healthy, fit person who understands the risk and benefit of the procedure in that setting, we may still well offer it. For what you're describing, this is a conversation I have with every patient before surgery. I think right now you have vanilla based on where the needle went. But when my surgeon takes out the entire thing, you may be surprised and upstage or change the diagnosis. So for us, we've had patients that happens to, of course. We can get some hints off of PET scans sometimes, but a lot of the time we will give the patient the benefit of the doubt. For what it's worth, PET scans, if you have a spot that's super bright and everything else is low-level bright, those super bright spots may be a different flavor. But if the biphasic component was found after surgery, in my practice, I'd be curious to hear what Melina would say, that may influence my post-surgical plan towards an immunotherapy approach. Because we know in the advanced non-surgical setting, immunotherapy is more beneficial than chemo in the initial setting. So if I have a person that I gave, let's say, standard chemo to, we didn't extend the pleurectomy to cortication, and we found a hint of a biphasic, that's reason for me to think about pivoting towards immunotherapy in the after-surgical setting.

I think the other thing I want to add is that it comes from a historical adage that patients with biphasic or sarcomatoid mesothelioma did not do as well. And so surgery ended up just delaying their systemic therapy, and they sometimes didn't make it to systemic therapy. And so it just didn't serve them well. Now with immunotherapy, with dual immunotherapy, the playing field has leveled quite a bit. And so some of these trials actually are designed with the question of, now can we do surgery for biphasics and sarcomatoids since we have dual immunotherapy? And I know this one was, and there's another one at Mayo Clinic that was asking that very specific question. So I think it's changing a bit.

And I think that's a key point. Standard of care right now, we don't normally do it if we know a priori, but this is the exact setting for the trials. Because if we prove that immunotherapy has changed the landscape, nothing would make me happier than to offer patients with those specific diagnosis this procedure. I agree, from a standard of care standpoint, it's not routine to offer surgery if you know upfront that somebody has either sarcomatoid or sarcomatoid predominant biphasic. But all of us who operate have our, I call them the oops biphasic patients, where you thought they were epithelioid going in, and then on final path, there's sarcomatoid components. So I think on a trial basis, it's fine, because it's an important question to ask, because the older data, Those studies weren't powered to look specifically at sarcomatoid patients, so I think it's important. I think you can do it on a trial basis. I wouldn't routinely be doing it. I don't think that's a great idea, but I think that needs more information.

I actually have two. One would be easy. What if the family or the patient herself tries to convince you to do it even if you don't see them as? They say, I don't care if I die. I don't want to live this way. Would you try? That's one question. The others, this is primarily what I've heard is more for Laurel. What about the people with peritoneal or other types?
Yeah, the peritoneal part we'll defer to tomorrow's tumor board, because I think that's actually very interesting.
I'll be back on stage for that tomorrow, but I can talk to you after this if you want.

But the first question you asked about surgery is interesting. And I'm curious about everybody on this panel's view. My general feeling is that because surgery is not a cure, And we have a lot of other systemic therapies. If I don't feel that someone is a good surgical candidate, then I'm not the surgeon, so I'm not the one actually doing the scalpel, but I certainly wouldn't be recommending it, and I don't think our surgeon would proceed.

And I would agree with that. I mean these are not easy surgeries. I mean our surgeons after they're in there for a 10 hour surgeries our patients could be admitted for several days for pain control and management. These are not necessarily easy procedures that we would go into just because an individual personally wants it if we don't think it's going to benefit them. That would be my thought. Yeah, I agree. It's usually a conversation between care team trying to figure out if surgery is the right thing to do. They're very, very difficult surgeries. They're difficult on patients. They're very difficult on the care teams afterwards. So to do them for the sake of doing them, I personally think is a terrible idea. But there are, you know, sometimes patients make you reconsider your viewpoint on things, right? And sometimes the no isn't no ever, it's just a no right now, right? You know, somebody gets, you know, I have a patient, my first year of practice, very large treatment, very large burden of disease. They got treated with dual agent immunotherapy. They had a really good response. A year later, there's just like one or two spots towards their back that were just causing a lot of pain. And they already had a bunch of radiation for another reason, so they couldn't get any more radiation. And so we ended up operating, right? So there's reasons to do it on the line, and a no is not a no always. And sometimes that no can turn into a yes. But typically when you have a lot of people agreeing up front that surgery is a bad idea, it's usually a bad idea.

reference_conclusion: Thoracoscopic pleural biopsy was performed, establishing a pathologic diagnosis of mesothelioma. Given adequate cardiopulmonary reserve and comprehensive staging demonstrating no extra-thoracic spread, the patient proceeded with multimodality therapy on a neoadjuvant protocol consisting of three cycles of chemotherapy plus immunotherapy, followed by surgical resection with removal of disease and continuation of immunotherapy postoperatively. The case was considered appropriate for surgery based on fulfillment of surgical candidacy criteria and disease confined to the hemithorax.

And then the last line is important because you need to stage people appropriately. [...] it sounds like they check some of the lymph nodes in the chest and did some biopsies in the abdomen with laparoscopy to make sure that there was no disease spread. [...] This patient has checked all of the boxes that we've asked for in terms of being a surgical candidate. And they received three cycles of the chemotherapy and immunotherapy. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: B symptoms with bulky cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), diagnosed by peripheral blood flow cytometry.

[ histopathology results ]: Bone marrow examination showed approximately 70% marrow involvement by CLL.

[ imaging findings ]: Bulky lymphadenopathy was present in the neck and axillae bilaterally.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: FISH demonstrated del(13q). IGHV was unmutated.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 11 g/dL; platelet count 110,000/µL; white blood cell count 94,000/µL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Ibrutinib was started at 420 mg daily in the frontline setting. The patient responded well and tolerated treatment for approximately 1 year. Atrial fibrillation subsequently developed while on ibrutinib.

[ current disease status ]: Disease had responded to BTK inhibitor therapy prior to treatment interruption for toxicity. No progression on ibrutinib was documented in the available clinical information.

[ other clinical data ]: Treatment indications at presentation included B symptoms and bulky lymphadenopathy. Mild anemia and thrombocytopenia were present at baseline.

reference_discussion.text: All right, thanks, everybody. We'll get going. There's a lot to talk about with CLL. We will start with a case just like the follicular lymphoma discussion. So we've got Penny, a 58-year-old female. She presents with B symptoms. And she has bulky nodes in both the neck and axilla. So you've got two indications for treatment right there, the B symptoms and the bulky nodes, particularly if they're If they're painful, don't have a slide on this just for the sake of time, but we're still not treating asymptomatic CLL patients. We're waiting for indications for treatment just like with follicular lymphoma. So she gets worked up, and while anemic, not really significantly so. Hemoglobin is 11, has still a decent amount of platelets with 110,000. White count is 94,000, so moderately high. Flow confirms CLL. And she gets a marrow. It's not always necessary to get a marrow in CLL these days. You can make the diagnosis on flow as she got here. But there's still some utility in certain circumstances. Marrow shows that her disease has taken up about 70% of the marrow space. She gets prognostic workup done correctly with fish that shows 13Q deletion. And she is IGHV unmutated. So this is a younger patient. But she is IGHV unmutated. Traditionally, probably would have gotten FCR. In 2019, we now have additional options in the frontline setting beyond just chemo immunotherapy, which is good for a patient like Penny, who historically we know IGHV unmutated patients have not been doing so well in terms of long-term progression-free survival with our traditional chemo immunotherapy options. So for the sake of discussion in terms of relating this patient to a cooperative group alliance trial that we're gonna discuss later, we'll say Penny gets a Brutinib at 420 milligrams daily. It would be very appropriate and perhaps given the young age maybe in my clinic I would actually even lean towards the option of venetoclaxonobinutuzumab in this patient though. So Penny starts on a Brutonib. Responds well, tolerates the drug for a year. Long-term follow-up on a Brutonib patient is now out to seven years for the early phase clinical studies, and over 70% of patients are still free of progression, so that's pretty remarkable. But unfortunately, sometimes patients have toxicity on a Brutinib. Again, it's given orally, daily, continuously. So toxicities do occur. Overall, well-tolerated drug, as I'll show you later. But atrial fibrillation is a toxicity that certainly gets a lot of notoriety in terms of a Brutinib treatment. So say this patient gets atrial fibrillation. We now luckily have an alternative BTK inhibitor option in a calibrutinib, which, while we're still awaiting on head-to-head data that I'll show you later, There is some hope that this agent does not have the same cardiac comorbidities that a Brutinib does. So for a patient that's responding to BTK inhibition that has to come off treatment due to toxicity, we now have an off-label option with a Calibrutinib. Although it's not currently FDA approved for the treatment of CLL, it is approved for mantle cell lymphoma. But it does get a lot of off-label use in CLL. It has breakthrough designation by the FDA recently for the treatment of CLL. And as I'll show you later, it's on the NCCN guidelines. Would not think about a calibrutinib in a patient though that progressed, say Penny progresses on a brutinib after responding for quite some time. The majority of patients that do progress on a brutinib, 80 plus percent are gonna have mutations at the C481S binding site where a brutinib and a calibrutinib both hit. So you would not try a calibrutinib in a patient that has has progressed on a brutinib and you think about an alternative option like venetoclax that we'll discuss. So we'll change the scenario a little bit. We'll make Penny a little older, a little more comorbid. 72-year-old with COPD now. Same prognostic workup. You do want to send the fish an IGHV mutational analysis, also TP53 mutational analysis on all your patients prior to treatment. So she is unmutated at the IgHV gene, still in this circumstance. And again, both the Brutinib and Venetoclax are category one options that I'll show you later in the frontline setting. And both would be appropriate. So I know Ian covered some of the remarkable improvements we've had in the therapy across the lymphoma spectrum and specifically to CLL these small molecule inhibitors have all become available since 2014 and how different the CLL treatment landscape is for patients now in 2019 than where we were at in 2014. We're going to focus on the BTK and BCL2 inhibitors today. Ian did a great job of talking about the PI3 kinase inhibitors already. So we'll start with BTK because they were around first, or specifically Abrutinib in terms of approval for treatment of CLL all the way back in what seems like a long time ago, but actually not that long ago, just in 2014. So this slide reads better from from right to left. The original resonate study was what led to a brute nibs approval in 2014 in the relapse setting. It was a big breakthrough for CLL patients relapse CLL patients were maybe getting a year or two of benefit with treatment with chemo immunotherapy. And we now know that a brute nibs benefit in the relapse setting. is, you know, between four and five years median. So, rutinib quickly became the treatment of choice in the relapse setting based on the Resonate study. We did have some extended approval for the high risk 17p patients in the frontline setting all the way back in 2014. But that was based on how the 17p patients were actually doing in the relapse setting on the Resonate study. 17p patients even with our strongest chemo immunotherapy of FCR maybe get a year or so of PFS. So the FDA saw that the 17p deleted patients were doing significantly better even in the relapse setting. So they extended the approval in the frontline setting. But in 2016, we had extended approval of Abrutinib based on the Resonate 2 study. They compared Abrutinib to Chlorambucil in older comorbid patients. So now, starting in 2016, all CLL patients, be it frontline or relapse, could get Abrutinib. A lot of oncologists did not like the comparator arm of chlorambucil in the Resonate 2 study. Thankfully, now in 20, towards the end of 2018 and in 2019, we've had the publication of two cooperative group studies that has compared Abrutinib to our most common chemo immunotherapy treatments that we were using in the frontline setting. So, we don't have to complain about the Chlorambacil comparator anymore. So, more notable of these two cooperative group studies, but we'll cover them both, this was a plenary presentation at ASH last year, the Alliance Study, released in the New England Journal after the presentation at ASH. And it looked at patients over the age of 65. So these are the patients that you wouldn't be thinking about giving FCR to because of their older age. We know FCR has more morbidity in patients over the age of 65. So the control arm was Bindamustine and Rituximab. And the two investigational arms was a Brutinib single agent and a Brutinib with Rituximab given in a similar way as Rituximab on the Bindamustine arm. So a three arm study deletion 17 P patients were included but they were a small fraction. Here are the PFS curves. So there was a statistically significant benefit in progression free survival when compared to been a Mustang and retoximab in both the abrutinib arms versus been a Mustang retoximab. You can see here though that there is no difference between the abrutinib and rituximab arm when compared to the single agent abrutinib arm. And this is now the third study that we've had that has looked at abrutinib with rituximab versus abrutinib alone and shown no difference. significant difference between the two. So I think one of the big positive elements of treatment with the Brutinib is its simplicity and its ease of starting treatment with, you know, at my institution, I'm just sending an electronic script to my specialty pharmacy. And the drug shows up on the patient's doorstep two or three days later. They don't have to worry about the infusion center, et cetera. So I'm not jumping at adding a monoclonal to a Brutinib, be it rituximab or obinutuzumab, unless I ultimately see compelling evidence saying it improves outcomes. Notably, there is no difference in overall survival in this study, but that can be hard to show in chronic cancers. Here is the ECOG study very recently published in the New England Journal. This was a late breaking presentation at Ash and it compared the FCR to a Bruton with Rituximab and it was looking mainly in younger patients but it did take patients up to the age of 70 and deletion 17 P were excluded. So at three years, there was a statistically significant progression-free survival benefit. And while that was maybe surprising to some, what was actually more notable is at that same point in follow-up, there was a statistically significant benefit in overall survival. And when they looked at the causes of death, it's not surprising to anybody that's treated with FCR before, but some early deaths due to infection. So clearly benefits the unmutated group in terms of progression free survival notably no statistical significant benefit in the IGHV mutated patient. So there are still some that are holding on to FCR's use in the young IGHV mutated patient. Notably, you'd want one without high-risk findings on fish as well. That represents about a total of 12% of the CLL population, so you're not talking about a large group of patients. The biggest argument for that was the ability to give a time-defined treatment as opposed to indefinite therapy. I would argue now that we have an option of time-defined therapy with venetoclax that the one big plus with FCR has now been kind of negated. But FCR, it's still certainly an option to discuss with patients. In terms of toxicities, this is a long-term follow-up by Susan O'Brien looking at high-grade toxicities. And you can see hypertension here. That appears to be the only cumulative toxicity that a Brutinib has over time. So there hasn't been any other with long term follow up emerging toxicities that have popped up. We mentioned the atrial fibrillation. Overall when you look at the trials between 5 and 10 percent the low grade toxicities that get noted by patients are usually diarrhea bruising. Those usually do not lead to discontinuation. Rash is another notable one. So I'd mentioned a calibrutinib. This is a, you know, when you look at this kinome here, felt to be a more specific BTK inhibitor, has less off-target BTK effects, and so the hypothesis is then it will ultimately prove to have less toxicities. A really exciting initial phase 1B slash 2 study presented at ASH about three years ago now and published in the New England Journal. Nice flat PFS curve in a relapsed refractory population. But ultimately still not approved by the FDA for treatment in CLL. have it available now for a while because of its approval in mantle cell lymphoma and a lot of its use is actually off label and CLL mainly in patients that have as I mentioned earlier had to come off of a brute nib because of a toxicity issue. And studies have shown notably a prospective study by Farouk one The 70 plus percent of patients that have had to come off of a Brutinib because of a toxicity can be switched to a Calibrutinib and continue on treatment without having that toxicity that they had on a Brutinib recur. It has made it onto the NCCN guidelines in the relapse setting based on some recently presented ASCEND data at EHA that looked at a calibrutinib versus a kind of dealer's choice of idilisib and rituximab or benamustine and rituximab in the relapse setting. And you can see the difference in the PFS curves here at 12 months. What the studies that we're waiting on that are pending are listed here. I would note the top two are looking at PFS differences. I don't think there will be a big surprise with the Elevate CLL trial showing PFS benefit when compared to Obinutuzumab. It'll be interesting to look at if Obinutuzumab seems to be additive to Acalabrutinib though. What I'm interested in seeing and is supposed to maybe be reported early next year is this bottom study that's a non-inferiority study between a Brutinib and a Calibrutinib. And we should finally get some head-to-head data in terms of what are the differences between these two and particularly looking at the toxicity. Because they hit the same, you know, point on the BTK at the C481S binding site, I'm not confident that a calibrutinib will ultimately show superiority in terms of PFS, but I won't be surprised if there are differences between the two in terms of toxicity. So what are the toxicities of a caliber to begin. You look at the grade three to four column overall a well tolerated drug but like a brute nib you know discontinuations are less than 10 percent when you look at the study in terms of discontinuing due to adverse events some notable toxicities that appear to be unique. You know the diarrhea is still there enlisted up at the top but headache can happen that seems to be unique to a caliber nib. It's restricted to earlier in treatment. It's usually low grade. Often a patient won't mention it unless you ask them, and usually don't even need Tylenol, but Tylenol seems to be effective enough if they do need it. I've not had it lead to a discontinuation in a patient. And then edema is another one that can, while also low grade, be something that's maybe a bit different between a calibrutinib and a brutinib. And we'll conclude here by discussing venetoclax. So while we've been talking about kinase inhibitors mostly with PI3 kinase inhibitors, BTK inhibitor, venetoclax is not a kinase inhibitor, but it does fall in this small molecule inhibitor category, these newer oral targeted treatments that we that have been such a great breakthrough for our patients. So the BCL2 protein has been found to be overexpressed in CLL, but also, as opposed to BTK, which is more unique to B-cell malignancies, BCL2 is not restricted to CLL. You might be aware of the drugs approval and the treatment of AML. And there's even breast cancer trials going on. So it will likely be something that shows up on the solid malignancy side. So when BCL2 is overexpressed, it binds up pro-apoptotic proteins released by the cell in response to DNA damage. So then, therefore, the cell's more resistant to apoptosis. So you throw in venetoclax, and rather abruptly, those preapoptotic proteins are released and lead to mitochondrial membrane permeabilization. Caspases get released into the cell, and the cell apoptosis through breaking up its outer cell membrane. So it's abrupt activity is in contrast to BTK inhibition which can take a median of four months before you see you know kind of the what you would mark as an official response in terms of 50 percent disease burden reduction. and leads to the tumor lysis syndrome issues that I'll discuss later in the deck. So here we're not going to discuss the initial trial that led to the drug's approval. which was single agent use back in 2016 for high-risk CLL patients defined as having a 17p deletion on fish. What was really exciting was in 2018, the Murano study led to the approval in the relapse setting where venetoclax is given with rituximab. And it was compared to Benamustine and Rituximab in a head-to-head study. And the really exciting part about this approval was that Venetoclax was given over a two-year period after six months of Rituximab and stopped. So this is the first example of one of these small molecule inhibitors with a defined treatment timeline, because we were all happy that we had these new treatments and that they worked well for so long, but we were concerned about the cost over time. So you can see, and this is with now extended follow-up that we got last ASH, so now three years of follow-up, a big difference in PFS curves. And at the three-year follow-up that's now been published as well, there was an overall survival improvement that was seen. So we all want to know how these patients are doing once you stop. Didn't have a whole lot of data at the initial publication. It was only two years of follow-up. With last year's ASH, we got an additional year. We're about to get another year's worth of data at this year's ASH. So, the short of it is, the patients that obtain minimal residual disease negativity are doing quite well and not relapsing after they stop. And even the patients, and that's in this black line at the top here, that get near MRD negative, so 10 to the minus two or worse, seem to be doing quite well. And for those of you that aren't necessarily familiar with MRD testing, not part of standard clinical practice guidelines yet in CLL, probably still a send out at most institutions. It can be done with flow cytometry or PCR, and it's where we're looking at one cancer cell in 10,000. The rate of MRD negativity in the relapse setting with venetoclax was around 57%, which is comparable to what FCR was doing in the frontline setting. So you have this chemo-free option that in the relapse setting was getting a depth of response equal to that of our strongest chemo immunotherapy combination, and it was really exciting. But more recently, We now have this combination of Obinutuzumab with Venetoclax and Venetoclax given over a year and just approved in May of this year for frontline treatment of CLL. So for everyone that was really concerned about the implications of all these patients on indefinite Abrutinib we now have a time defined treatment option recently published in the New England Journal and leading to to approval, this was a study that, because of its comparative of obinutuzumab and chloramacil, was looking at older patients that you wouldn't give chemoimmunotherapy to, but because of the impressive PFS curve, the FDA approved it for all frontline CLL patients. And here is the MRD negativity rates that was exciting. 76% in the peripheral blood, so better than we had been able to do with chemoimmunotherapy. When you looked in the marrow, while numerically less, the, you know, they found really with venetoclax-based treatments that the peripheral blood MRD testing correlates to about 92% degree with the bone marrow. So you can, you know, in clinical practice save an invasive procedure and just test the peripheral blood and be pretty confident in it. In terms of toxicities of venetoclax, The TLS on the right is what most think about. But since the five week dose ramp up and appropriate risk stratification has been in place, there's actually been no cases of clinically significant tumor lysis syndrome on any prospective venetoclax trials. So it's quite safe if you follow the package insert instructions in terms of the ramp up. What you actually will deal with is neutropenia. In the Murano study specifically, 3 quarters of patients ended up having to hold treatment at some point. And the large majority of those patients were having to hold because of neutropenia. But diarrhea can be something you deal with. Joint pain is another one. And because of the neutropenia issues, you want to watch out for infection. Just like with a Brutinib, with a Calibrutinib, you can use growth factor and not interrupt treatment. And I often do that. It's a bit different from IV chemotherapy in that way. So here's the NCCN updates, and it's basically the BTK versus BCL2 options in both the frontline and the relapse setting as being the category one indications. Everything else has been moved to category two or less. And as I mentioned earlier in the talk, we don't really have data to support one option over the other in terms of BTK versus BCL2 inhibition. So in conclusion it's it's it's really a great time for our CLL patients in terms of treatment options. BCL 2 is is is an option that we're excited about in terms of time defined treatment but. when it may take a long time, but it's possible that perhaps in terms of long term outcomes, a disease modulating agent targeting BTK given indefinitely ends up being ultimately the best approach. We just don't know at this point. and there's advantages and disadvantages to both. We'll have some exciting data on looking at these two agents given together at ASH this year, a trial that both Ian and myself participated in.

reference_conclusion: Treatment is indicated for symptomatic, bulky CLL. Frontline therapy with ibrutinib 420 mg daily was selected as an appropriate option; venetoclax plus obinutuzumab was also identified as an appropriate category 1 frontline alternative, including as a time-defined regimen. If intolerance to ibrutinib occurs, particularly atrial fibrillation, acalabrutinib may be used off label for patients responding to BTK inhibition who discontinue ibrutinib because of toxicity; however, acalabrutinib should not be used after progression on ibrutinib, in which case venetoclax is the preferred alternative.
reference_conclusion_quote: So we've got Penny, a 58-year-old female. She presents with B symptoms. And she has bulky nodes in both the neck and axilla. So you've got two indications for treatment right there, the B symptoms and the bulky nodes [...] we'll say Penny gets a Brutinib at 420 milligrams daily. It would be very appropriate and perhaps given the young age maybe in my clinic I would actually even lean towards the option of venetoclaxonobinutuzumab in this patient though. So Penny starts on a Brutonib. [...] So say this patient gets atrial fibrillation. We now luckily have an alternative BTK inhibitor option in a calibrutinib [...] So for a patient that's responding to BTK inhibition that has to come off treatment due to toxicity, we now have an off-label option with a Calibrutinib. [...] So you would not try a calibrutinib in a patient that has has progressed on a brutinib and you think about an alternative option like venetoclax that we'll discuss. [...] And again, both the Brutinib and Venetoclax are category one options that I'll show you later in the frontline setting. And both would be appropriate.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 73-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Hyperparathyroidism identified during pre-transplant evaluation for renal transplantation in the setting of worsening renal function.

[ diagnosis ]: 
- Severe hyperparathyroidism with multigland parathyroid hyperplasia.
- Papillary thyroid carcinoma with multifocal thyroid involvement and nodal metastases, including central neck and deep mediastinal nodal disease.
- Chronic renal failure secondary to lithium toxicity in a solitary kidney; status post renal transplant in March 1994, with recurrent graft dysfunction/incipient renal failure by 2019.
- Severe osteoporosis.
- Bipolar affective disorder.

[ histopathology results ]: 
- Parathyroid pathology showed four hyperplastic glands.
- Two intrathyroidal parathyroid glands were identified, for a total of six parathyroid glands.
- Thyroid pathology showed 10 foci of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Two central neck lymph nodes were positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- A deep mediastinal node removed by mediastinoscopy was positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Histologic description of the thyroid carcinoma included papillary and follicular architectural features with calcifications/sclerotic change.
- Lymph node metastases showed papillary and follicular features with psammomatous calcification.

[ imaging findings ]: 
- Preoperative MIBI scan demonstrated at least four foci consistent with hyperparathyroidism.
- Cross-sectional neck/chest imaging demonstrated four visible parathyroid glands and an additional fifth mass inferior to the innominate artery.
- The mediastinal mass beneath the innominate artery was subsequently confirmed as metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- In April 2020, ultrasound demonstrated a right level IV cervical lymph node measuring approximately 1 cm.
- CT imaging confirmed the right level IV cervical lymph node.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: 
- Parathyroid hormone: 93 (reference range in local jurisdiction stated as 1.6-6.9).
- Serum calcium: 1.6, described as elevated.
- Alkaline phosphatase: 435.
- Postoperatively, thyroglobulin was undetectable.
- Severe renal impairment was present by 2019, with rising creatinine and incipient renal failure.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- Underwent dialysis for two years prior to renal transplantation.
- Underwent renal transplant in March 1994 for renal failure secondary to lithium toxicity.
- During pre-transplant endocrine surgery, underwent four-gland parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation of partial parathyroid tissue into the right intraclavicular pectoralis major muscle.
- Intraoperatively, a blue-black right central compartment node was identified; frozen section confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection.
- Underwent mediastinoscopic excision of the deep mediastinal node; pathology confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Postoperative course was complicated by severe hungry bone syndrome/homeostatic disturbance and psychotic decompensation requiring psychiatric ICU admission for three months.
- Did not receive radioactive iodine initially.
- In April 2020, fine-needle aspiration of the right level IV lymph node confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Underwent ethanol/alcohol ablation of the right level IV nodal metastasis in two sessions; this failed.
- Subsequently underwent neck dissection; multiple involved lymph nodes were found that had not been identified on imaging.
- Two months after the neck dissection, had another psychiatric breakdown requiring prolonged hospitalization.

[ current disease status ]: 
- Following initial thyroid surgery, postoperative thyroglobulin was undetectable.
- Subsequently developed biopsy-proven recurrent/persistent nodal metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma in the right lateral neck (level IV) in April 2020.
- After failed alcohol ablation, neck dissection demonstrated additional metastatic lymph node involvement not detected on imaging.
- At the latest documented point, radioactive iodine therapy had not yet been administered and was under consideration.
- Renal impairment persisted, and renal transplantation remained under consideration.

[ other clinical data ]: 
- Bipolar affective disorder had been present since age 14, with multiple prior psychiatric admissions.
- Family support was described as excellent.
- A second sister had been willing to serve as a kidney donor.
- The patient had a cochlear implant.
- She was taking 18 medications, including immunosuppressive and psychotropic agents.
- She was unwilling to undergo dialysis.
- Radioactive iodine administration was considered complex because of renal impairment requiring dialysis considerations and psychiatric stability concerns.
