reference_discussion.text: So that was in our awareness, by the way, and still is. Okay, so we have a 73-year-old woman with a bipolar affective disorder. Since age 14, she's had multiple admissions to mental health facilities, but otherwise functions well and has excellent family support. March 1994, had a renal transplant due to renal failure, secondary to lithium toxicity in an only kidney with no monitoring. No lawsuit. She was on dialysis for two years and did well until 2019 when her creatinine started rising and had incipient renal failure. The need for dialysis, of course, or a renal transplant. Her second sister was willing to be a donor and a patient was unwilling to have dialysis, so she had a transplant, incidental cochlear implant, She is on 18 medications a day which are immunosuppressive and psychotropic. Her PPH is 93. Here's the normal and our jurisdiction is 1.6 to 9.3. Sorry, it's 1.6 to 6.9, sorry about that. Her serum calcium is 1.6, rather high. Her ALK-FOS is 435. She has severe osteoporosis. We worked her up before her transplant, and you can see at least four foci on her MIBI scan of hyperparathyroidism. Just want to ask the panelists, perhaps Janice, more and more I'm getting asked to deal with hyperparathyroidism in pre-transplant patients. Is that what's happening out West?

Yes, so the feeling is now, and there's some data to support it, that if you can get their calcium homeostasis normalized before their transplant, that there's better graft function. So if you can correct that, get their calciums in the normal range, and then they go on to transplant, that is ideal. And I think we're seeing more of it because of living related donors and a little bit more, not all hit and miss looking for cadaveric. There is some scheduling of some of the transplants. And I think that's where it really came out that it helps with the graft function. And that's my interpretation of the literature, but I know it's an area of controversy.

Yes, we're asked more and more to deal with this now because of all the issues that you've alluded to. And here's a cross-sectional image of that particular patient. You can actually see four of her parathyroids, but I draw your attention to a mass, a fifth mass, just under her anominate artery. Let's keep that in the back of our minds for a few minutes. So what do we do here? Janice, maybe I'll come back to you. What's your standard operation for pre transplant when the parathyroids are dysfunctional?

Yeah, so I would ideally like to do a subtotal parathyroidectomy leaving a portion in place in the neck if the parathyroids would allow me. Unfortunately, when you can see them and they're that big on CT, I may have to then go with a total with auto transplant. But she's got likely some degree of hungry bone where she does get transplanted soon. I don't want her to be hypoparathyroid and then go into the transplant. So I try to do a subtotal if possible.

Yeah, so that's what we did. We did a four gland removal. and an auto-implant of a partial gland to the right intraclavicular pectoralis major muscle. But here's the big but intraoperatively. So her thyroid appeared thyroididic. And there was a blue-blackish node in the central compartment on the right. So I suspected she may have papillary thyroid cancer, which we confirmed in the node on frozen section. So Eyal, what would you suggest we do now?
It depends what you saw on the ultrasound before surgery.
It was a thyroiditic appearing gland.

Yeah, so many times when you have Hashimoto's thyroiditis, you can miss on the ultrasound the papillary thyroid carcinoma because the gland itself is hypoechoic and you have a hypoechoic nodule. and sometimes you can miss it. So we would do what you did, frozen section, to see if indeed it was cancerous. I guess our surgeons would probably do a hemidectomy and just reevaluate after that.
Her whole gland was involved.
Oh, so you saw it during surgery?
Yes. We looked at the gland, We sent a note for frozen section. She had metastatic disease. What would you recommend now?

So total thyroidectomy, you go bilaterally anyway because of the parathyroid, central neck dissection. If you see that the whole thyroid is involved, then bilateral central neck dissection. This case, you don't have to worry too much about the parathyroid because you're treating them. So really taking care of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and we would do what you did during surgery.
Okay, but remember, I showed you this. What do you think of that, Monica?
It looks like a lymph node in the mediastinum, and with a lymph node in the central neck, it's probably disease from her papillary thyroid cancer.

Yeah, so this took us by surprise. You know, I personally thought this might have been a supernumerary parathyroid gland, but what we did was a mediastinoscopic removal, and in fact, it showed metastatic papillary thyroid cancer, no other lesions. So ultimately, her pathology showed four hyperplastic glands, two intrathyroidal parathartes, for a total of six glands, 10 foci of papillary, two central neck nodes, and this other deep mediastinal node was positive.
So, Zuber, what does this show? I think you're on mute, Zuber. Zuber? There we go, we got you.

All right, so it looks like a paliparoid adenoma. It's very cellular. It is a little bit onchocytic in the middle on the right-hand side, so it has pink cells, but it has a beautiful border, so it looks like a classic hypercellular paliparoid gland. I do not see a rim, which you can see in adenomas, but to me, it looks like a classic case of a hypercellular paliparoid, like an adenoma. And here is the PTC, which has a follicular pattern because you see the colloid on the left-hand side among the follicles. So it is not a classic papillary and there is a sclerosis. I don't know whether that's taken from the middle of the tumor or on the edge. So it does appear infiltrative. It doesn't appear the encapsulated looking, you know, classic, I mean, follicular variant that you see, but it does look like, And here, what you have is, so I don't know whether that's the lymph node or that's a thyroid gland. Right hand is the lymph node metastasis. So now, which is very common in papillaries, that it can be a classic papillaries and the mets can look like follicular variant, or it can be a follicular variant with the mets looking like a classic PTC. So on the met, you can see it has papillary formations, and that dark stuff on the top is the somomatous calcification of body and the left hand side in this papillary also which is infiltrative both papillary and follicular with calcifications. This is a lymph node and you can see this is forming follicles now. So this looks like a follicular variant plus it has some cystic spaces with papillary formations. It is confined to the nodes. At this power I do not see any extra normal extension. That's an intrathyroidal parathyroid, which is, you know, very gorgeous. I mean, but it is very cellular. And we do see them, you know, in the total thyroidectomies when we get for goiter and this stuff, but definitely this is a hyperplastic looking parathyroid in the gland.

Thank you, Zubair. So her postoperative course was extremely stormy. She, goes over the deep end if you just look at her. She had severe bone hunger. Her whole homeostasis was disturbed. She had a psychotic breakdown. She was in the psychiatric ICU for three months. Post-operatively, her TG was undetectable. And now we started COVID. COVID is rampant. She doesn't want REI. She doesn't want to go anywhere near a hospital because of her immunological status. In April 2020, she had a lymph node in level four on the right side, and an FNA showed capillary thyroid cancer. Here's my ultrasound. You can see this one centimeter lymph node. Here it is on a CT scan. I'll just point it with the cursor. So what do we do now, Eyal? We have a solitary, what appears to be a solitary lymph node.

So this lady was treated with surgery and she didn't have radioactive iodine. So we want to do something because if we just leave this lymph node untreated, follow up, it's probably going to grow. Maybe she has more metastasis. The optimal treatment, if her medical condition allows it, is neck dissection, cleaning the neck, the lateral neck, and the central neck was already operated on, and then radioiodine, if her condition allows it. Now when we see only one lesion, only one metastatic lymph node, we can think of local therapies. So either ethanol injection or thermal ablation, it's not gonna cure probably the patient because if we see one, she probably has more. It depends what she can tolerate and what her general condition is.

So are there... Well, you've mentioned alternatives. Just as an aside, she was deathly scared of another open operation because of her mix-up, not mix-up, but her problems with her psychotropic medication and her psychiatric ICU admission. So yes, what we suggested to her was alcohol ablation, which I did in two sessions, and sadly this failed. So in the interest of time, ALU suggested she have a neck dissection. We finally persuaded her to have it. And in fact, she did have several lymph nodes involved that were not picked up on the imaging. And of course, she had another breakdown two months post-surgery, necessitating another prolonged hospitalization. So the question is now, what do we do? Do we give her RAI? When do we do a transplant? If ever. So Mike, why don't you hone in on this? Because you've probably seen more of this than anybody.

Yeah, I mean, this is a common thing because anybody gets a transplant that had thyroid cancer, the transplant guys want you to say there's no cancer, right? I mean, let's be honest with you, we've all seen patients that have had organ transplants with persistent thyroid cancer and generally, we don't see the cancer explode. I mean, it doesn't, you know, whether they're talking about immunotherapies that everybody always worries about or chemotherapies for other stuff or, you know, I've had heart transplants and kidney transplants for years after that with low-level thymoglobin. So the immunosuppression after transplant, while we don't have great data, doesn't really bother me all that much. I don't think it's a great factor for their doing poorly. So I try to find a time where I can declare them no evidence of disease. that there's no structural disease. Once I get that, I send them to transplant before somebody else does another ultrasound or measures another thyroglobin or does something. So it's a silly game to play, but I would be looking for the best opportunity I could get to declare her no evidence of disease, which to my mind would be a clean ultrasound or a CT scan of the neck. a thyroid globulin that's as low as I can get it. If it's undetectable, that makes it even easier. I don't demand a time. There's no logic to me for six months, nine months, a year, two years, five years. There's no data on that at all. So I try to do what's the minimum I can do. And in follow-up, I try to do the minimum detection that I can do so that we don't end up keep finding these little teeny tiny things. So I would say, yeah, if she would accept radioactive iodine, I would do it. If she would not accept radioactive iodine and her thyroid globulin was undetectable and your cross-sectional imaging is fine, I'd say you have no evidence of disease right now and you can go on to transplant.

Yeah, so she's now negotiating with the radiation oncologist about RAI. And I tried to get deep into the literature, and as you say, All the current literature suggests is there's an increased frequency of thyroid cancer in renal transplant patients, if they haven't already had it. And if she does have it, there's a good chance she'll crop up others, as A.L. suggested. And there is no optimal wait time. Are there any other comments on this complicated problem?
Yeah.

I just want to say. Oh, sorry. Two issues, she's already got renal impairment. So we would need to dialyze off the radioactive iodine. And sometimes when you start with dialysis, then you can't get them off dialysis. And so she has to accept that she'll be on dialysis until she gets transplanted. And the other issue is she has to be in a stable mental state to receive radioactive iodine for a number of factors, apart from informed consent. that she will abide by radiation safety measures. And we admit patients in our country until the level is down to 15 millicuries. So there's an occupational health and safety issue for staff and a patient safety issue. So I think she's a very difficult patient to give radioactive iodine to.
And you would do it with thyrogen rather than thyroid hormone withdrawal, right Martha?
Yeah, yeah. but she'll have to be dialyzed. Any other comments?

I just want to say one sentence. My hospital is a huge transplant center and we hardly see thyroid cancer in these patients. So we're starting a study now to show that, but we really don't believe it's increasing the risk of thyroid cancer.

Last issue, Jeremy, before you go to your last case, there's a really good question that says, what's the effect of renal impairment on thyroglobulin level? We haven't ever published this, but in our experience, it's interesting to see what A.L. says. When we see renal failure, we do see thyroglobulin numbers trail up. And I can't find their disease. You know, renal failure, it may be 3, 4, or 5, as opposed to 0.5. So when folks get in that sort of severe renal failure, I do think we see a little higher thyroglobulin. A.L., anecdotally, have you seen
Any what?
The thyroglobulin levels be a little higher in people in renal failure than in the same clinical state without that? Not so much, hard to tell.
It's hard to tell, yeah.

reference_conclusion: Following identification of metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma during parathyroid surgery, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck dissection and mediastinoscopic excision of the mediastinal metastatic node. For subsequent nodal recurrence in the right lateral neck, ethanol ablation was attempted in two sessions but was unsuccessful, after which neck dissection was performed and revealed additional involved lymph nodes not detected on imaging. Radioactive iodine may be administered if clinically feasible, recognizing the need for dialysis support and psychiatric stability; if radioactive iodine is not undertaken, transplant candidacy may proceed once there is no structural evidence of disease on imaging and thyroglobulin is as low as possible, ideally undetectable.
reference_conclusion_quote: So total thyroidectomy, you go bilaterally anyway because of the parathyroid, central neck dissection. If you see that the whole thyroid is involved, then bilateral central neck dissection. [...] what we did was a mediastinoscopic removal, and in fact, it showed metastatic papillary thyroid cancer [...] what we suggested to her was alcohol ablation, which I did in two sessions, and sadly this failed. So in the interest of time, ALU suggested she have a neck dissection. We finally persuaded her to have it. And in fact, she did have several lymph nodes involved that were not picked up on the imaging. [...] So I would say, yeah, if she would accept radioactive iodine, I would do it. If she would not accept radioactive iodine and her thyroid globulin was undetectable and your cross-sectional imaging is fine, I'd say you have no evidence of disease right now and you can go on to transplant. [...] Yeah, yeah. but she'll have to be dialyzed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 24-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Symptomatic hydrocephalus.

[ diagnosis ]: Large third ventricular mass causing obstructive hydrocephalus. The lesion extended from the anterior to posterior third ventricle. Tissue diagnosis had not yet been established.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology results were available.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain demonstrated a multicystic, heterogeneous lesion extending front-to-back within the third ventricle. T1-weighted non-contrast imaging showed the lesion in association with enlarged temporal horns consistent with hydrocephalus. Coronal post-contrast imaging showed superior extension of the lesion. The lesion showed minimal enhancement. T2-weighted imaging was described as isointense. Sagittal imaging showed the optic chiasm displaced anterior to the lesion. CT venography was obtained and showed no venous limitation to the contemplated surgical corridor. CT showed no calcification.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic results were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain with tumor rupture while on vacation.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal bilobar hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) without cirrhosis, presenting with ruptured hepatic tumor.

[ histopathology results ]: Liver lesions were biopsy proven HCC.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT demonstrated multifocal bilobar hepatic disease with approximately 5-6 visible lesions. Angiography demonstrated diffuse multifocal hepatic tumors, with greater tumor burden than appreciated on CT and a near-miliary pattern of numerous small lesions. Post-embolization imaging demonstrated extensive necrosis, particularly involving the dominant right hepatic tumors. Left hepatic tumors remained viable and were not targeted initially because they were not ruptured. MRI obtained approximately 2 months later demonstrated three small residual hepatic tumors.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial hepatic embolization was performed for hemorrhage control after tumor rupture. This resulted in extensive necrosis of the dominant right-sided hepatic tumors; untreated left-sided lesions remained viable. Systemic immunotherapy with STRIDE was subsequently initiated.

[ current disease status ]: No peritoneal disease had been identified by 2 months after rupture.

[ other clinical data ]: No cirrhosis was present. No risk factors for chronic liver disease were reported. Liver function was described as good unless otherwise specified, and the patient was described as very physically fit. Chronic pulmonary disease was not reported for this patient.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, we worked this patient up for a section. Unfortunately, the pulmonary, they had chronic pulmonary disease, so they were not a candidate. We ended up doing radioembolization and they had a good response. I want to show a similar but slightly different situation. This patient, 64-year-old female, she was on vacation. She was also found to have abdominal pain and rupture. However, instead of having a solitary tumor, you can see she has multifocal bilobar disease. doesn't have cirrhosis, but these are biopsy proven HCC. Maybe there's five or six that we can see on this picture here. She was taken for immersion angiography just like before. We did the angiograms and at least to my eye, and I'd love to get your thoughts too, Sid, it looks like there's more tumors on the angiogram here than we saw on the CT scan. It looks like almost on the left screen, almost a milliary pattern where you can see a bunch of small little tumors throughout. I don't know if you have a similar

Yeah, I mean, I agree. This patient's got diffuse multifocal tumors. They've ruptured their prognosis. Short-term prognosis, you can still be reasonable, but their long-term prognosis, no matter what you do, is poor. And so just like you did here, we would do an embolization. I think it ends up being dealer's choice in terms of how you embolize this, whether it's particles or gel foam, et cetera. The embolizations tend to be quite effective in stopping bleeding. Then the question becomes, what do you do next? And that's not so easy.

On the post-scan, you can see extensive necrosis, particularly of the dominant tumors on the right side of the liver. The left side tumors are still viable. They weren't targeted because they weren't ruptured. However, now we have three small tumors that we can see on this MRI. What do we think? More local regional therapy, systemic therapy? Patients stable?
Are their patients stable?
Outpatient now? This is two months later.

Two months later. So I'm assuming they haven't at least yet declared peritoneal disease. So, you know, we would still consider local regional therapy at this point, but then everything has to come on the table. Like, are they a transplant candidate eventually, right? Clearly not now, but if they're downstate, do they have peritoneal disease where they would need systemic therapy and so on. We would probably do some kind of embolization, whether it be a TACE or a radio embolization. It's hard to say. We would have to do a mapping angiogram and determine that. I would lean away towards ablation because this patient has multifocal. It's not just the three tumors that are highlighted. There's definitely more than three, so doing an ablation on the three that you can actually see is not really in the patient's best interest.

I would advocate for systemic therapy for a person like this. I mean, unlike the last case, the cat's at least starting to come out of the bag here. We have multifocal disease. Obviously, she's also at risk for peritoneal seeding. And I think similar to our prior discussion, I think you lose little by starting with immunotherapy here, seeing where things head. Of course, considering additional local regional therapy to some of those lesions that may or may not be responding is always on the table if it needs to be. And then again, similarly, would not offer Bevis as a map with a recent rupture, but could potentially be a good candidate for stride.

I would say it's probably worth mentioning that downstaging and getting to transplant, the burden of proof that the cancer was completely controlled to pursue transplant is pretty high in a case like this. It wouldn't qualify for the standard exceptions, but you'd have to really watch this person for a very long time.
And I'm assuming you'd have to give some test of time, like one to two years. Yeah.
And I don't think there's a hard answer about what that time is exactly, but it'd have to be a real long time to make sure.

I agree with that. I mean, the dogma used to be rupture equals no transplant. I think we've been a little bit more thoughtful about that and not lumped everyone into one basket. you still have a high burden of proof to get past it. I just wonder, if you go back to the last image there, I feel like we're on the matrix where you see these screens coming, the numbers, and you guys are reading it like, oh yeah, that's a milliary pattern in ICR. All I see is I was like, oh, is that the kidney?
It's the same when our transplant surgeons send me pics of the surgical resection. I'm like, I don't know what's head and tails here. So it's the same way.
Got it. Okay.
And we have to have some magic too. We can't have you doing all of this.
Appreciate that.

So, we decided to go with Stride for the exact reasons. She ended up having a recurrence, particularly in segment 5 where it was about 3 cm. We did radioembolization, as you can see the cone beam CT there, and it had a complete response. And so she's doing well. This is about a year now after radioembolization. She's continued on immunotherapy. She's having no side effects or issues with the immunotherapy. Do we consider immunotherapy indefinitely? Do we have a stop date? When do we consider transplant, if ever?

I'll start. We don't know the answer for these patients. The other thing I will just add is that I know you gave us the caveat that everyone has, you know, good liver function unless told otherwise. This person has zero risk factors for chronic liver disease and is more physically fit than anyone at this table. So what is the best answer for someone like that that's extremely healthy, now has NED? And for me, when we don't know the answers to these questions and you have a patient that's capable of shared decision-making, it's being very honest with them that, look, if you're nervous and want to continue immunotherapy for the short to medium to long term, we'll do it. if you're tired of this and want a break after a year or two to see how things declare herself, let's do that. But I'm curious too as to Heather's opinion here on would a transplant benefit her at this point?

You know, assuming that with everything that's been done to her liver, her liver is, you know, still in good shape, then it really, that's an oncologic question, right? She doesn't need it for you know, liver function, it would be more a matter of would that give her a better durable response to the cancer than, you know, any other approach including continuing her immunotherapy on an indefinite basis.

Yeah, these cases on the margin are really interesting and we just don't know the answer, right? So, I think this is an area that's really It's going to be interesting to see how this progresses, how this develops over time, because you're right. I mean, the immunotherapy can go on indefinitely as far as we know. Is that fair?
It could. We also could stop and she could never recur. Right.

Yeah. So how do you decide when to stop? Because that to me, I would be like so nervous that she's going to blossom and pop up. And then the other question is, if they do stop and you see disease come back, how responsive are they to restarting that same immunotherapy? Or do you have to switch?

We can re-challenge and get a response. Obviously, these are small numbers of people. It's not like we have these enormous case series, but we know either from other tumor types in melanoma, for example, where our kind of history with immunotherapy is a bit longer, that patients that stop immunotherapy that are re-challenged can respond. I would not feel comfortable stopping any earlier than one year after her tear. Two years would probably be better, but it really is a bit of a judgment call based upon how everyone's feeling at the time.

I guess my one plug for pushing for transplant in this case, I'm trying to think of patients where I've seen 10, 15 or more tumors and you got an NED and it didn't ever recur again. That doesn't happen. I mean, that happens like in fairy tales, right? So this patient is going to recur. Whether they're on immunotherapy or not, you had that many tumors, the chance of them not recurring are way less than 10%. So my push would be for a transplant where now your post-OLT recurrence becomes sub-10%, assuming you have, you know, not fulminant HCC at the time of transplant.

I think I agree with you in some sense. I do worry in that scenario though, you're now subjecting a person to a treatment that, yes, we historically think of it as providing long-term durable disease control, but we're now immunosuppressing her. Is that the trigger that causes her to recur? And then I know that she's very immunotherapy responsive now. Immunotherapy becomes off the table post transplant. And if she does recur, we run into a whole lot of trouble. So I think those are the, all the variables to think about, but you're right. There's no right answer.
And it's even, but even you mentioned in the, the five-year survival for now the immunotherapies is what? 20%. Right. So that means 80% are dead.
But we know that people that are responders have, um, are driving that curve, that tail of the curve.

But it's still not... What's the five-year survival after a transplant? And again, this is a dividend of 80%, right? So when I think about those numbers, and again, we're not talking about 80% of these patients, right? This might be a very different patient population.
You say that's 80% of all comers. Of all comers, yeah. I don't know for her. Absolutely.

Yeah. But we're talking 20% at five years for immunotherapy. 80% at five years for transplant. And again, it's not a fair comparison, but it is one, two very different ends of the spectrum in terms of overall survival. So that's why in this specific case, I think there's no right answer here, but to me, this patient's going to recur. There's just a matter of time. That was great. Hot one.

reference_conclusion: For multifocal bilobar hepatocellular carcinoma following rupture and initial embolization, systemic immunotherapy with the STRIDE regimen was selected, with bevacizumab avoided because of the recent rupture. Subsequent focal recurrence in segment 5 was treated with radioembolization, achieving a complete response, and immunotherapy has been continued given ongoing tolerance and disease control. Transplant candidacy remains uncertain and would require prolonged observation and sustained oncologic control before reconsideration.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman; gravida 1. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred with cervical squamous carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous carcinoma, clinically staged as stage IIB. Extension studies were negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Post-radical hysterectomy pathology showed squamous carcinoma in situ. Residual tumor size was 3 mm. Parametria were free of tumor. Internal iliac nodes were reported as negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Extension studies were negative for metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered with paclitaxel, cisplatin, and fluorouracil for 3 cycles. After 3 cycles, tumor size was reported as 1 cm, and pelvic examination was negative for parametrial involvement. One additional chemotherapy cycle was scheduled, followed by radical hysterectomy. Surgical pathology after hysterectomy demonstrated squamous carcinoma in situ with 3 mm residual disease, negative parametria, and negative internal iliac nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after radical hysterectomy with minimal residual in situ squamous carcinoma (3 mm), negative parametria, and negative nodal assessment as reported.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

The literature, though, unfortunately, if you look at the old historical data, two of the cases from the meta-analysis had all the patients receiving radiation therapy. So it's unclear. I personally would observe this patient because I'm not sure she really truly had to be disease or whether she just really had a 3CM tumor, which actually would be a perfect candidate for new adjuvant chemotherapy followed by hysterectomy. The EORTC has a trial that just finished, and hopefully those studies will come up in, what, in a year or two? They finished accruing about two years ago. So my thought is I would just observe her. That's just my thought. Because it's only a clinical staging. You don't really know if she really had 2B disease.
Well, you know, Anuja, I mean, I think, but if you assume that the stage is correct, if you were sure she had 2B disease, would that influence your decision on whether or not to radiate?
Well, she has to.
She had a primary drug.
Well, then she's saying it's a clinical stage.
So she's unclear. What if you were sure it was a 2B?

If I was sure it was a TB, I would then probably add, but there's no data that shows one way or the other, right? The data that we have is from the post-operative specimens, and you add the radiation depending on what is residual after the neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Well, you know, that's different from breast, and I know when you give neoadjuvant therapy for breast, Paul, you want to comment on that.

Yeah, I want to begin a discussion that I'm extrapolating from breast to cardio and see if it applies. We have discovered in our research that most South American countries, the biggest difference in causing mortality is a clinical upstaging of stage 3 and 4 versus 1 and 2 in the United States. So the single biggest, we think, the single biggest reason for the mortality being so much higher is a great upstaging. Now in that path of diagnosis to treatment, one problem we've identified in breast is a very lengthy delay between pathological diagnosis and the institution of surgery. Because of the weight on the surgical unit and busyness, they're not often able to schedule, like we do. So, in breast, a trial has been done where adjuvant chemotherapy has been given amicably versus adjuvantly by the NSABP, and no difference in outcome and survival has been shown. So, that has resulted in breast cancer. If a patient has a pathological diagnosis of breast cancer and you know that the patient's going to require adjuvant chemotherapy, so you can clinically stage or radiologically stage two, three, or four, for instance, then people will sometimes give adjuvant to start the cycles of chemotherapy, adjuvant, neoadjuvant, and just interrupt it at the right time for surgery and then complete it off. So if it's four or five or six, Is that something that could be done or should be done or would be done for cervix cancer? That's staging with periaortic nose or stage 3 or 2B?

Well, I mean, that's been the practice, I think, outside of the U.S., sort of getting people treated urgently because they tend to have more locally advanced disease. I think the dilemma now, and Anuja and I are sort of grappling with it, What do you do with the pathological response in someone who first presented with advanced disease? So breast, for example, the role of radiation therapy depends on what patient's presented with, not the pathologic response. So someone who had a T4 breast lesion who had an incredible response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy will still get comprehensive breast radiation. you know, even if there was a pathologic CR. So I think that's sort of what has been the experience in the breast world. In cervix, it's a little bit more difficult. Like, Anuja, I think I agree with you. Sort of, it's not technically new angiotherapy the way we think about it a la breast. You give some therapy up front, then you give some therapy at the back end. So if you weren't going to radiate this patient, I probably would commit her to three more cycles of chemo just to complete it.

Yeah, there's really no data, so you could do either or. If you really truly believe it's a 2B, I think I'd be more comfortable in giving radiation. I'm really concerned with the 3CM tumor that had such an amazing response, whether she really had true 2B disease. But I agree. If you truly believe it's a 2B, she needs some sort of therapy, whether it's radiation or chemo.

Yeah, and I think most of us would agree it would be radiation rather than chemo. But it doesn't negate, I guess the pathological response shouldn't negate the adjuvant treatment paradigm at this point. I mean, the neoadjuvant data is just not that clear.

So maybe I should also add that in July, I have two new fellows joining me from Brazil, one from Belo Horizonte and one from Rio de Janeiro, and at the request of my colleagues at Mass General, we want to start a global database, as we've done in breast cancer, we want to start a global database looking at the outcome of patients with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, because stage 3 and 4 cervix cancer is so rare now, thank God, in the United States, Our doctors are losing the opportunity and experience to treat those patients, which you sometimes see, but not often, if I'm not wrong, and also to do clinical trials as well. So advanced cervix cancer is not a U.S. disease as a rule, but it is very common in South America. We see patients presented on these tumor boards and in the literature with stage 3 and 4 disease. So neoadjuvant chemotherapy is of great interest to our expert doctors, in the United States, but they don't get it. So they have no experience, and they can't do clinical trials of new regimens or new strategies. So it is up to our global colleagues in South America to help us study and to involve, to let U.S. doctors participate in clinical trials occasionally, but to leave the charge on advanced cervix cancer until we get it under control better. So that's one thing I wanted to tell you about coming in June and July, we're going to start building in collaboration with our gynecologist, we're going to start building an important database.

Great. Paul, can we, can you just see how many people, so you've got a good audience of South American and Central Americans who do a lot of neoadjuvant, can they raise their hand, how many would give for adjuvant therapy? It may be interesting to see what our audience would say. Can you ask that question? Will you ask it?
So if our doctors could respond to Dr. Jing Ren, please, for this question. Go ahead, Anuja, ask the question, please.
How many people would give adjuvant radiation therapy for this patient? from our audience.

Can you just raise your hand in South America if you would give adjuvant radiation? Just put your hand right up in the air so we can see you. Or type into the chat box for viewers please. Would you give this patient post-operative radiation therapy? Who would give radiation therapy? I don't see any hands or any comments.
Eduardo from Brazil says yes, he would.
So Eduardo from Brazil says he would, from Inca in Brazil. Eduardo Paulino is one of the doctors joining us.
Argentina would. OK. We decided to make the radiotherapy.
OK. Thank you.
Thank you.

So it's not 100%, but it's not nobody. That's the answer, yeah. And there's a lot of people answering by typing in their answers to say that they would give it. So there is a diversity of opinion around this topic, as we have discussed. So that was a very great question, Myra. Thank you for that case. Perhaps we can move on to our second case from Dr. Zaina Meranti from Lima in Peru. Dr. Meranti, can you go ahead and present your case, please? We'll just show the slides. Okay, here's the case, here's Dr. Morente from INED, and here's the case. Can you start presenting, please?

reference_conclusion: Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy and radical hysterectomy with pathology showing squamous carcinoma in situ measuring 3 mm, negative parametria, and negative lymph nodes, the multidisciplinary discussion acknowledged uncertainty regarding the original clinical stage and the limited evidence base for management after neoadjuvant therapy. Despite differing opinions regarding observation versus adjuvant treatment, the agreed next step was to proceed with postoperative radiotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Dysphonia for 6 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Right glottic squamous cell carcinoma, staged as cT2N0.

[ histopathology results ]: Direct laryngoscopy with biopsy demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma on frozen section, with invasion identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Office laryngeal examination demonstrated a right vocal fold lesion, primarily confined to the right true vocal fold, with extension to the right false vocal cord. No subglottic extension was identified. Stroboscopic examination showed slight limitation of vocal cord mobility without complete fixation. Direct laryngoscopy demonstrated tumor extending the full length of the right vocal cord and up to the right false vocal cord, without subglottic extension. PET-CT showed uptake in the right vocal cord and no lymphadenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent direct laryngoscopy with biopsy confirming squamous cell carcinoma. Endoscopic resection was not feasible because of poor laryngeal exposure. He subsequently underwent vertical partial laryngectomy. No neck dissection was performed.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He was an ex-smoker with a reported 20-pack-year history and used alcohol. He was otherwise described as generally healthy.

reference_discussion.text: Good evening, everyone. It's my great pleasure to be here and talk to you about open partial laryngectomy. As some of you may know, I'm dual fellowship trained in laryngology and head and neck surgery, so larynx cancer certainly falls in my sweet spot of practice. So we'll kick off with the case, and I'll throw out some questions to our discussants. So we have a 77-year-old male here who presents with dysphonia for six months. He's otherwise pretty healthy and well, apart from hypertension and a history of GERD. He's an ex-smoker with a reported 20-pack year history, and he's a drinker. Laureano, I've heard so much about you. It's a pleasure to finally meet you in this setting, given that you're also at Sinai previously. Can you show me or tell me what you see here in this in this picture?
Well, you have a right vocal fold lesion confined to a right vocal fold, maybe extending a little bit of the paralytic space. Is this a video or just a picture?
Just a picture.

It's a picture. OK. It seems confined to the right side mainly. And I don't see that it's extending, at least from the picture, subglottically or superglottically. So it's an airway obstruction, obviously.

Yeah, I agree with all those statements. I think there's a little bit of false focal cord extension up here and a little bit of fullness. Certainly in the stroboscopic examination, which I didn't include for ease of time, there was some slight limitation of mobility, but not complete limitation of mobility. So, Andrew, when you see a lesion like this, do you think about biopsying in the office or do you take them straight to the OR?

So I'll tell you that for a case like this, if I'm seeing it, they've been sent for consideration of conservation laryngeal surgery. And so I think the indications for office biopsy are someone who you know you're going to radiate. Because I think if you're considering operating, I do not think that that patient should be evaluated just with an office endoscopy. Because you gain too much by going to the operating room to palpate this. You're going to appreciate the extent of the tumor. What is the mobility of that cricorhytenoid joint? What is that extension into the ventricle? And those pieces of information you cannot gain with the same, you know, certainty that you would gain by taking that patient in the operating. So the only time I've seen in the office is say this guy was 89 with multiple medical problems with this large T1, maybe T2 lesion. And we're trying to get an answer because we're going to get this guy into radiation. Otherwise, this guy definitely deserves a trip to the operating room, in my opinion, for a full endoscopic evaluation.

I am I completely agree with that and do exactly the same thing for our for our fellows and residents joining us this evening, this is a double channeled scope I highly implore you to learn at a biopsy. you know, learn how to do in-office biopsies for the reason of facilitating patients faster through to radiation therapy, but completely agree with you. You can't, you can't minimize the information that you get from taking a patient to the operating room and planning for further surgery. So I did take a look into this in the, in the data and, and, you know, the office biopsies, even though the biopsy forceps are small, they do give you a result quite a lot of a large percentage of the time, 64% in this particular study, which comes out of my old alma mater at Boston Medical Center. And certainly there's definitely a cost advantage to doing it in the office as well. So it's definitely something to add to your armamentarium if you haven't already been trained in how to do it. So just quickly, a bit of a competition matrix here. You know, obviously, local anesthesia in the office, general anesthesia in the OR, you know, less cost in the office, there's more sampling error in the office and the time to result is less. So if you really want to get someone quickly to radiation therapy, it's a very good tool to have as part of your armamentarium. So I proceeded to a direct laryngoscopy. And, you know, as Andrew knows, sometimes I'm a little bit colorful in my descriptions, as you saw in my prior presentation at Academy. And here, basically all I'm saying is that dental guard was placed and And, you know, couldn't really get a good examination of the patient with the Lindholm. Then I tried the Dido, I tried additional manoeuvres, I tried the Louis suspension, and then essentially I got a monocular view through the Hollinger. And I was able to see that extended the full length of the vocal cord and up to the right false vocal cord. There was no subglottic extension. I was able to take a biopsy and the frozen came back as squamous cell carcinoma, and I was surprised that they were able to tell me that there was invasion, because you don't always get that on your frozen section. So I'm going to throw this one back to Andrew. What are predictors of exposure? Do you look at the patient and have things run through your mind when you're in a situation like this in terms of how difficult it's going to be, how easy it's going to be?

Yeah. So, you know, there are different people who have published different things, whether it's the tease of exposure or, you know, Georgia Peretti and Cesar Piazza have put forth their laryngoscope in terms of what they're thinking about, you know, in terms of things to do. Big questions, you know, in terms of my mindset are interstitial distance in terms of is there any trismus and, looking for, do they have tori on the mandible? How high is the larynx? Any other preexisting issues that may make that difficult. As you were able to do, you had to work through the algorithm of scopes that you were going to get into using this with a monocular Hollinger to get your view, because you couldn't get it with a Lindholm or the Dito. But I think you can have all those tools available and see. And obviously, that's going to change how you think about approaching this tumor, potentially, based on what that exposure is.

So, Diana, Diana, could you comment and do you use any other adjuncts during your direct on gossipy do use telescopes to like angle telescopes and such because that's a great picture that you got there, but that may have been from the office and I was curious what you use in addition to the learning scope access.

Yeah, routinely we use a zero degree in a 70 degree scope, but once again. you know, it was very clear to me that that was something that I wasn't going to be able to remove endoscopically. And I always tell a patient when I'm taking them to the OR, I give them the option. I give them the option that I'm either just going to biopsy this, confirm the biopsy. But most patients want biopsy and treatment at the same time. So I tell them mostly that if I can access it endoscopically, I will try and remove this. I always have the CO2 laser set up and stand at the standby. But clearly, that wasn't you know, going to work in my favor that day. But I worked through the range of the scopes. I, you know, put the patient into neck flexion. I even tried to suspend to see if that gave me anything. I just really wasn't getting much. So I knew at that stage that this patient was either going to go to open partial laryngeal surgery or radiation therapy. But I really love this laryngoscore. I think it's a nice way of trying to determine laryngeal exposure. It's just particularly a nice score for the residents and the fellows, too. in this in this paper and for the residents and fellows Cesare Piazza and his team out of Italy published a lot of study, a lot of studies on larynx cancer so he's really one of you know one of the world authorities on these things. But the Laryngoscore is anything less than six, you're going to get a good laryngeal exposure 94% of the time. Anything greater than six is difficult laryngeal exposure 40% of the time, and anything greater than nine, then you're looking at an almost 70% chance of difficulty laryngeal exposure. And the things that they thought were most important were upper jaw dental status, macroglossia, micronathia, degree of neck flexion and extension, and BMI. You know in this gentleman, I was trying to understand at that time, I think if I was to go through this he probably was just above a six. But it is it is what it is and it sort of delineates him down through the algorithm is to exactly what you're going to do with him so. In terms of workup, you know, obviously, I definitely get a CT. I absolutely get a PET CT if they're going on to radiation. That's definitely my algorithm in terms of imaging. Once I've treated the patient and then I'm monitoring them, then I'll absolutely get a PET CT down the line, too. I don't know if everyone's in agreement with that. Would anyone like to add anything there in terms of imaging?

Actually, I'll ask Kendra as a radiation oncologist. This looks to be like a T2N0. I'm assuming that Diana would know cervical lymphadenopathy on imaging. Would you need a PET to proceed with the radiation? This one has a little superglottic extension. Is that right, Diana?
Yeah, false cord. So it's still within the glottis.

So Kendra, I'd be interested for pure glottic lesions. Do you feel like you need a PET versus one that you come across in the superglottis where you might want to think about radiating a neck? How do you approach these?

So I think in general, getting a PET-CT is standard if you're going to be moving forward with radiotherapy. I'm not clear what the value is in the very early stage larynx in terms of, you know, the predicted likelihood of finding nodal disease for a T1 and zero is very, very low. But what I have found is that in these exposure exclusive malignancies, The likelihood of identifying an additional primary or a tertiary primary in a patient who is gonna be coming to radiotherapy is relevant and serves an important purpose, an important percentage of the time. I don't often use post-treatment PET-CT in the early stage glottics because really your eyes are the best tool that you have. I don't know if that addressed your question.
Yeah, no, definitely. Definitely.
If a patient presented with a CT neck and chest, would you still get the PET, or would you just go ahead and proceed with stem and radiation, if it was referred for radiation specifically?
I often do get the PET, and it's because of the competing risks.
OK. Diana, please continue.

So this gentleman, I mean, I'll get into this discussion, but there was a lot of to and froing about whether he should get radiation or open surgery. So he did get a PET and that obviously showed the the uptake of the right vocal cord, there was no lymphadenopathy seen. So staging here, he's, as you said, a T2, you know, end stage is zero based on the PET image on the PET. And so we're left with our management options here, which really come from the NCECN guidelines and what we probably all agree on. He's either going to go to RT or the option is with this because he can't be exposed endoscopically to go to open partial laryngeal surgery. So generally what I do at my institution is I don't really think I can have that discussion about radiation very well. So I always send them on for a discussion to our radiation therapists and obviously discussion in a tumor board setting as well. So Kendra, what are some of the things that you discuss with your patients regarding the benefits, risks of surgery, the radiation therapy for a T2N0? Yeah. So,

This is a really easy report for me. I mean, this setting is a really easy set of discussions, because I think in general, anyone who can safely go to an appropriate margin negative surgery and have appropriate laryngeal function thereafter should be surgically addressed. That's my position. For those who either due to function issues are going to end up going to TL, or are not able to get something less than a total laryngectomy and have elected for non-operative management in that context, the focus is really on defining the extent of supra and subglottic extension to ensure that it's an appropriate candidate for so-called limited field radiotherapy, which is focused just on the larynx itself. This is a completely different and much less difficult course than most of the definitive chemo-rad and definitive-rad treatments we give in the aerodigestive track. And the focus really needs to be on odynophagia and dermatitis. I put these patients on high-dose gabapentin. They use mometasone cream twice daily, which has been shown to reduce the absolute maximum acute toxicity in the skin. And we talk about sort of six to 10 week window at the end of radiotherapy and in the aftermath of radiotherapy where the voice hoarseness worsens, the throat pain intensifies, and the skin becomes highly irritated. We talk about the treatments themselves not having sensation lasting 10 minutes, and that I actually do daily image guidance with the early stage larynx patients and They're set up as in a long mask, which is immediately against the skin. We workshop whether we think it is likely to cause a significant problem so that we can be proactive about it.
Miriam, how would this patient get discussed at Anderson and what do you think the recommendation would be in your disease team?

At Anderson, a patient like this would be seen by all the modalities. I actually think that this patient would probably also end up seeing the medical oncologist as well. It is a stage two, but there's some impairment in vocal cord mobility if I understood correctly. We would all have the opportunity to see the patient to talk about what the treatment would be and the patient would also be seen by our speech therapist. They would almost certainly undergo a stroboscopy to get a full idea of the function. as well as a careful laryngoscopy and an interoperative examination. In terms of discussion, I mean, I think this would be one of those cases where, you know, a lot of this would depend on the interest and the expertise of the surgeon. I mean, this is, this case clearly can't be done with a laser. You don't have the exposure for it. I'm not sure that it's, you know, certainly not ideal from that standpoint. So it would be open partial laryngectomy versus radiation or chemoradiation. Then the results of that could be potentially quite good. I mean, one of the factors that would concern me as a surgeon seeing this patient is it looked like there was a lot of posterior extension. And so if you're chasing a margin on the posterior commissure, that would make me pretty nervous. The other thing is that this is definitely somebody that should be considered for kind of a hemi laryngectomy as opposed to something like a super cricoid, which I am personally more comfortable doing. But I don't think a super cricoid is the right thing for this patient. And then finally, with partial laryngectomy, you're going to be looking at the reconstruction is really going to be what drives the vocal outcomes on someone like this. And so you really need to go to someone who is very good at that reconstruction. And so for me, I would probably send it to a colleague who does a lot of vertical partials, which are very rare at this point, I think.
Thanks, Donna. We've got three minutes. Do you want to tell us what you did?

So yeah, I'll just breeze through it. This was just a paper regarding outcomes. And it did say that outcomes were better with open partial laryngeal and CO2 in terms of laryngeal preservation. So I go through the indications here for open partial laryngeal surgeries. There's limited indications now, but it can be helpful, obviously, in poor endoscopic access and a limited recurrence post-RT. You know, I'm doing an NCDV analysis of some other larynx stuff at the moment. It's still being done in the United States. This is from 2010 to 2019. I think open local excision is probably a variant of open partial laryngeal surgery. For this gentleman, vertical partial laryngectomy was what he had, but the other options for open partial laryngeal surgery, not in this case, horizontal supraglottic laryngectomy. In terms of vertical partial laryngectomy, the indications are really for a lesion of a, you know, a mobile cord and this cord was still mobile, they can't have that much in the way of subglottic extension it has pretty good local control rates. You have to be very cautious if there's extension. you know, beyond the glottis, it sort of becomes a no-no when that happens. And if there's truly impaired, you know, almost verging on a paralysis of cord mobility, you should really be cautious in that because that does signify cartilage invasion. There's, you know, several variants of this and the reconstruction is definitely with strap muscle rotation and imbrication. I won't go through the surgical steps. I think that you can all refer to that in this PowerPoint. But essentially, we got negative margins on this all around the complete cancer. It was a 2.2 centimetre. It didn't go into any of the, you know, the angiolymphatic invasion, rather, and peri-annual invasion was not identified. And then in terms of what it looks like now, I mean, I would be sort of somewhat critical of myself here that it could look a little better here on this side. You know, but it doesn't look too bad. He's cancer free currently.
I know we're running out of time. Did you do a neck dissection?

No, not for this, not for this. So I would I would also say that this is an excellent schematic from the European Laryngological Society on open partial horizontal laryngectomies that I would encourage everyone to look at. And finally, I do have some another reference here, which does give step by step anatomic dissections on open partial laryngectomies. And I'll leave it at that.

Thank you so much, Diana. Well, If you want to unshare slides and move on to Laureano. I just have a question for Kendra while I bring up the slides. Kendra, would you have irradiated the neck if you had done this patient as a single modality, or would you have just done the primary as parallel opposing fields?

Yeah. If it's not broke, don't fix it. Fairly old school. If you're going to irradiate just the glottis, it should be parallel opposed fields. You should do daily image guidance, and you should measure the dose at the anterior commissure. Thanks, everyone.

reference_conclusion: For cT2N0 glottic squamous cell carcinoma with false cord extension and inadequate endoscopic exposure, management options were radiation therapy or open partial laryngeal surgery. The patient underwent PET imaging, which demonstrated uptake confined to the right vocal cord without lymphadenopathy, and proceeded with vertical partial laryngectomy without neck dissection. Final pathology showed negative margins with no angiolymphatic or perineural invasion, and the patient is currently without evidence of disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 24-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, pathologic stage I (TNM stated as stage 1). Risk stratification was described as intermediate to high risk due to vascular invasion.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial fine-needle aspiration in May 2016 from another center was reported as Bethesda category II.  
- Repeat fine-needle aspiration in 2019 was reported as follicular neoplasm, Bethesda category IV.  
- Surgical pathology after total thyroidectomy showed papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular variant, measuring 1.5 cm (also reported as 1.3 cm), with four foci of vascular invasion and no extrathyroidal extension.  
- No histologic description of lymph node involvement was available.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in May 2016 showed a hypoechoic heterogeneous solid nodule with irregular borders measuring 10 × 11 × 13 mm in the left lobe.  
- In 2019, the thyroid nodule had enlarged to 17 × 18 × 16 mm; it was described as very posterior in the left lobe.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Stimulated thyroglobulin at the time of radioactive iodine treatment preparation after thyroid hormone withdrawal was 174 ng/mL.  
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were negative at that time.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Total thyroidectomy was performed in 2019 after repeat cytology showed Bethesda IV follicular neoplasm. Lobectomy had initially been indicated.

[ current disease status ]: Status post total thyroidectomy for follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with four foci of vascular invasion, prepared for radioactive iodine after thyroid hormone withdrawal with a stimulated thyroglobulin of 174 ng/mL.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus with renal involvement (2013), ischemic stroke (August 2015), and deep vein thrombosis (March 2016).

[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old female; postmenopausal. No comorbid conditions were reported. No family history of breast cancer or ovarian cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast carcinoma with metastatic disease to the lungs.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative carcinoma of the left breast, staged as T4b N2 M1, with multiple pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Triple-negative breast carcinoma. Ki-67 was 12%.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline disease included multiple lung secondaries. After completion of six cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin, PET-CT showed an almost near-complete response in both the breast primary and the lung nodules.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline BRCA variant of uncertain significance (VUS) was identified on germline testing. Variant allele fraction was reported as 44%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received six cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin. Carboplatin was added in the context of the germline BRCA VUS. Following six cycles, PET-CT demonstrated an almost near-complete response in the primary breast lesion and pulmonary metastases.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with radiologic near-complete response after six cycles of systemic chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain in January 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Melanoma, initially diagnosed in 2012 after excision of a lesion on the foot/dorsum of foot. Metastatic recurrence was identified in January 2025 with abdominal nodal masses, inguinal nodal disease, and lytic bone metastases. Subsequent pathology from recurrent disease was reported as metastatic melanoma; an inguinal node biopsy was also obtained. One account described recurrent disease as amelanotic melanoma; subtype classification was otherwise not documented.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2012: Melanoma diagnosed following excision of a skin lesion on the foot; detailed original pathology was not available.  
- Recurrent disease: Inguinal node biopsy confirmed melanoma and was used for tissue next-generation sequencing.  
- Specimen from decompressive laminectomy was reported as metastatic melanoma.  
- Amelanotic melanoma was referenced in relation to recurrence in one pathology description; no definitive melanoma subtype was otherwise documented.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- January 2025 evaluation demonstrated abdominal nodal masses, inguinal nodes, and lytic bone lesions.  
- PET-CT after 4 cycles of nivolumab plus ipilimumab showed disease progression, including progression at the D4-D5 spine site.  
- Repeat PET after an approximately 2-month interval again showed disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue NGS from inguinal node biopsy showed:  
- NF2 mutation, variant allele frequency/WAF 50%  
- TET2 copy number gain  
- FGFR3 copy number gain  
- BRAF copy number gain  
- CCND3 copy number loss  
- CDKN2A/2B copy number loss

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2012: Excision of primary melanoma lesion. Details of any additional treatment were not available.  
- January 2025: Decompressive laminectomy performed in the setting of metastatic recurrence.  
- Systemic chemotherapy with dacarbazine plus cisplatin for 3 cycles; no symptomatic improvement was reported.  
- Switched to nivolumab plus ipilimumab; after 4 cycles, PET-CT showed disease progression.  
- Repeat decompressive laminectomy was performed for progression involving the D4-D5 spine region.  
- Palliative radiotherapy was delivered to the spine lesion and an additional pelvic bone lesion.  
- Temozolomide was subsequently started and was the current systemic treatment at the time of reporting.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic melanoma involving non-regional nodal disease and bone, with progression documented on PET imaging after dacarbazine/cisplatin and after nivolumab/ipilimumab. The patient was receiving temozolomide at the time of reporting.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Hepatitis C positive.  
- Anti-HBc total positive.  
- Under treatment for viral hepatitis-related comorbidity.  
- No significant family history was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Pelvic pain and numbness in the left leg.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma, primary site not identified.

[ other clinical data ]: None provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Vaginal lesion initially; later presented with bleeding per vaginum associated with locoregional recurrence and liver metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Vaginal mucosal melanoma, initially diagnosed in March 2024, with subsequent locoregional recurrence and multiple liver metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Wide excision of the vaginal lesion was performed. Histopathology reported vaginal melanoma. Biopsy was obtained from a liver lesion after development of metastatic disease; no further histopathologic details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Multiple liver metastases were documented at recurrence. Locoregional recurrence was also present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing showed high homologous recombination deficiency (HRD-high). TP53 mutation was identified. ATRX loss-of-function mutation was identified with allele fraction 35%. RAF1 copy number gain was present with copy number 9. NF1 copy number loss was present with copy number 0, consistent with biallelic loss. No DNA repair gene positivity was reported otherwise. No c-KIT alteration was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Wide excision of the primary vaginal lesion was performed in March 2024. Adjuvant radiotherapy had been advised after surgery, but this was not received. After recurrence with bleeding per vaginum, palliative radiotherapy was started for bleeding control. No systemic anticancer therapy had been given prior to referral.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic vaginal mucosal melanoma with active locoregional disease and multiple liver metastases. Bleeding per vaginum had required palliative radiotherapy. First-line systemic treatment had not yet been initiated.

[ other clinical data ]: Financial constraints affecting treatment access were documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old male. Good baseline general health. No comorbidities were reported. Performance status was described as fit.

[ chief complaint ]: Symptomatic rectal lesion with constipation, rectal bleeding, false diarrhea, tenesmus, obstructive defecation, and pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated invasive rectal adenocarcinoma with synchronous liver-only metastatic disease. Locally advanced low rectal cancer with involvement of the right puborectalis muscle and suspected mesorectal nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Rectal biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Digital rectal examination identified a fixed rectal tumor approximately 3 cm from the anal verge, involving three quarters of the circumference.  
- Rigid rectoscopy confirmed a fixed rectal tumor.  
- Colonoscopy was completed and showed no colonic polyps and no synchronous colorectal tumors.  
- CT demonstrated nine liver metastases involving both hepatic lobes, predominantly the right lobe.  
- Pelvic MRI showed a bulky low rectal tumor below the levators, located approximately 1 cm from the anal verge, involving all three bowel wall layers, with extension close to the pelvic wall and involvement of the right puborectalis muscle. Several lymph nodes were suspicious for neoplastic involvement, including a node at the mesorectal fascia. No extramesorectal nodes were detected. No EMVI/MVI was detected on the reported MRI assessment.  
- Restaging MRI after treatment showed marked shrinkage of the primary rectal tumor with radiologic features of tumor regression.  
- Restaging liver imaging showed response of hepatic metastases, with residual lesions still visible prior to surgery.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: RAS wild type. BRAF wild type.

[ laboratory results ]: CEA was mildly elevated at 12.9.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Short-course pelvic radiotherapy was administered at 25 Gy in 5 fractions for symptom control.  
- Systemic chemotherapy was started 2 weeks later in the setting of a randomized phase II trial: FOLFOX plus bevacizumab with or without an experimental agent.  
- Oxaliplatin was discontinued after 8 cycles per trial protocol; treatment then continued with 4 additional cycles of fluorouracil/leucovorin plus bevacizumab.  
- Clinical response after systemic therapy was marked, with complete resolution of rectal symptoms.  
- On reassessment after 8 weeks of chemotherapy, digital rectal examination was normal and rigid rectoscopy showed no mucosal damage.  
- Right hepatic artery embolization was performed prior to liver surgery.  
- Right hepatectomy was performed 6 weeks after the last bevacizumab dose.  
- The primary rectal tumor was not resected; abdominoperineal resection had been the surgical option considered for the rectal primary, but surveillance was pursued instead.

[ current disease status ]: The rectal primary had shown complete clinical response on examination/endoscopy after chemoradiation and chemotherapy, and was under surveillance.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable apart from the rectal findings. Planned surveillance consisted of rectal examination, proctoscopy, and pelvic MRI every 4 months, and CT imaging every 3 months.

reference_discussion.text: So thank you very much. I'm going to challenge you with this case that challenged us some weeks ago. It is a 62-year-old male. So, physical examination was unremarkable, except in the digital rectal exam, where a fixed tumor was located at three centimeters from the anal verge, involving three quarters of the circumference. So in the rigid rectoscopy, a fixed tumor was confirmed. The biopsy showed a poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma in the rectum. And colonoscopy, because the tumor was not completely obstructed, could be completed without showing any polyps or any synchronous tumors in the colon. This is the axial view of the tumor showing involvement of all three layer of the bowel and reaching almost the pelvic wall. So, the report was in that sense, so it's a bulky rectal tumor below the levators, located at one centimeter from the anal verge, and several nodes with suspected neoplastic involvement, and also pro-rectal muscle involvement. No MV was detected, and no extra mesorectal nodes were detected. So, in summary, this is a symptomatic locally advanced rectal cancer with synchronous metastatic disease, liver only, and all RAS and BRAF was well-typed. This patient was fit without comorbidities, and we were willing not to miss any opportunities with this patient. So, what would be your treatment plan? Because this is a situation that it happens frequently in the clinic where we may have synchronous, locally advanced rectal tumors with limited metastatic disease. I mean limited, not in number, but limited to a single organ. In this case, it's the liver. So, what would be your approach? Who of you would be in favor of chemo radiation followed by chemotherapy? No? Chemotherapy plus anti-EGFR. Let's see what happened. Okay, some of you. Thank you. Who would go for five times five followed by chemotherapy? Okay, Rolf and Karin are going, and also some of you. Direct TMA upfront plus chemotherapy. almost no one, and liver resection first plus chemo-radiation thereafter. Our decision was to go five times five, followed by chemotherapy. The point of this was that our patient was very severely symptomatic, having pain, having bleeding, so we decided to go for radiation. And this, in general, if you go for five times five, you may get a very quick control of those symptoms. So we went to a multidisciplinary team discussion, and then we went for this. Radiation was given, five times, five gray, for symptomatic purposes. And then chemotherapy was started two weeks later. the patient was considered eligible for a randomized phase two trial with Folfox plus Bev plus minus an experimental agent. And then what we did is that we went back to reassess tumor size and eight weeks after starting chemotherapy. So, the patient got much better, clinically much better, no symptoms at all. And in the MRI, there are very clear signs of this tumor shrinkage. And also, our radiologist, who is a very experienced MRI pelvic person, told us that there was some kind of important features indicating tumor regression in the primary tumor. The digital rectal examination was normal and even there was no mucosal damage in the rigid rectoscopy we performed. So we went then to the liver, and of course there was also a nice response, but some nodes were still present. So this is really a challenging case, having good response in both sides. And no further therapy and reintroduced treatment upon progression. That's the other possibility. I don't know if some members of the panels like to have any comments on this point.

Yeah, I think the idea of giving chemotherapy upfront is something that we share. In the United States, the 5 times 5 is not very popular, but I see the appealing in this case, giving the radiation, the so-called radiation, to not delay the systemic chemotherapy. I don't know if I would have used VEV at the beginning, because that condition, the time of the surgery, a little bit, and have this patient not responded well and require surgery, would have compromised that. But I would have agreed with starting the chemotherapy. Now, if the response is very good, at the end of the day, the fate of this patient is going to be determined by the liver meds. So that's going to probably drive the whole surgical approach. Some patients are going to need to have removal of the primary tumor if there is no response for, you know, just symptomatic control. But I think this is a case that I will discuss very closely with my liver colleagues. and probably time it well in relation to the maximal response before the patient, you know, achieve, develop some liver toxicity from the chemotherapy. But if they feel that they can be, the liver can be cured or at least attentive to complete resection, I think I will go probably with liver surgery. In our institution, depending on the performance of the patient, sometimes we do synchronous resection, not infrequently. APR is not something that we do that often with liver surgery, particularly if the liver surgery is extensive. So I would be inclined to just do liver surgery if there are residual lesions after achieving maximum clinical response.
So, go ahead.

Yeah, well, I think that five times five followed by chemotherapy is a very flexible way of doing things. We would then, usually then, if the liver is resectable, we would go and resect the liver and probably talk to the patient and say, you know, there's still quite a big risk that you'll develop other metastatic disease, so why don't we defer, if we think that you've got a complete clinical response, we could defer that decision for six or 12 months. and then sit down and talk that through in about 6 to 12 months. But many patients will relapse again and it will be irrelevant really.

So then we went for liver surgery. Then liver surgery was planned after eight courses of Folfax-Bev and plus four courses of fluoroethylleukovirin and devacizumab because we stopped oxaliplatin after eight courses according to this trial. So, a right hepatectomy after right hepatic artery embolization was performed six weeks after the last dose of Bevacizumab. And then we decided to do only follow-up for the primary rectal tumor after discussing with the patient. But the only, I mean, the recommended surgical approach would be APR, and this was not... I mean, very well accepted by the patient. So the patient was operated in the liver. He stayed in the hospital only for seven days. And our case shows a successful multimodality treatment of a patient with a difficult disease. When my surgeons challenge me, this approach is curative or palliative, I answer, I don't know, but we have to try to do the best in any moment, and this was our approach. Thank you.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old female. ECOG performance status was 1. No comorbid illness was documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly increasing neck swelling of 1 month duration.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy performed at an outside center was reported as anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified TP53 mutation, HRAS mutation, TERT promoter alteration, and KMT2D alteration. BRAF was wild type. [ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 1 cycle of paclitaxel plus carboplatin chemotherapy on a 3-weekly schedule. There was no significant response after the first cycle; disease was described as static.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent anaplastic thyroid carcinoma after 1 cycle of systemic chemotherapy, with no objective response documented to date.

[ other clinical data ]: None documented.
