case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Left preauricular/left parotid mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the left temple with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma involving the left parotid, favored to represent intraparotid metastasis. Initial stage was documented as cTxN2bM0.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Mohs resection of the left temple approximately 3 months before presentation showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Biopsy of the left preauricular/left parotid mass showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Left parotidectomy specimen showed squamous cell carcinoma of the left parotid, favoring intraparotid metastasis.  
- Perineural invasion was present.  
- Left neck dissection specimen: 0/36 lymph nodes positive.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT neck demonstrated multifocal left parotid-region disease without neck adenopathy.  
- PET/CT obtained 5 weeks after surgery and before adjuvant radiation showed a hypermetabolic lesion in the operative region.  
- CT neck at recurrence demonstrated a lesion over the left temple and a lesion in the region corresponding to the prior PET-avid focus near the left zygoma/TMJ region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Mohs excision of left temple cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma was performed approximately 3 months before presentation.  
- Left parotidectomy with sacrifice of the upper division of the facial nerve and left neck dissection levels IB-IV was performed.  
- Adjuvant radiation therapy was completed at an outside facility.  
- Disease progressed during/after adjuvant radiation, with recurrent lesions over the left zygoma/TMJ region and left temple.  
- Neoadjuvant cemiplimab was administered for 4 cycles.  
- Definitive salvage surgery was subsequently performed.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Former smoker with approximately 15-year smoking history.  
- Initial physical examination showed a left temple scar from prior Mohs excision and a firm left parotid mass without fixation or dermal involvement.  
- No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy was present initially.  
- No facial nerve weakness was present initially.  
- After initial surgery, the upper division of the facial nerve had been sacrificed; the lower division was weak and had not fully recovered, though remained functional at the time recurrent disease was identified.  
- At recurrence, examination showed a 3 cm firm fixed lesion overlying the left zygoma/TMJ region tethered to skin and a 1 cm subcutaneous nodularity overlying the left temple at the prior Mohs site.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old woman; no comorbidities.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive painless swelling involving the right lower alveolar/submandibular region.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), limited-stage disease; stage IA, revised IPI score 0.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy showed high-grade lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell type. Immunohistochemistry classified the tumor as germinal center B-cell phenotype (GCB/GCP) by Hans algorithm.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline PET scan showed localized bulky locoregional disease centered in the right alveolar/submandibular region, measuring approximately 6 × 5 cm. No bone involvement was identified. No other sites of disease were reported on staging PET.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No FISH or other molecular cytogenetic abnormality was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Complete blood count and biochemical parameters were normal. LDH was at the upper limit of normal. Bone marrow examination was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 3 cycles of chemotherapy. Consolidative radiotherapy was subsequently delivered because of proximity to bone and possible soft tissue component.

[ other clinical data ]: Oral cavity examination was normal except for mild fullness of the gingivobuccal sulcus/fossa. No other clinically evident swelling or lymphadenopathy was identified. Systemic evaluation was otherwise normal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 94-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging painful right parotid mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Regional metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma involving the right parotid gland and cervical lymph nodes, in the setting of a prior right temple cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma treated with Mohs surgery.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior right temple cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma had been removed by Mohs surgery. No additional histopathology details were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a large right parotid mass with multiple right-sided nodal metastases. The right temple Mohs site appeared well healed. Disease was initially considered resectable. Follow-up imaging in September, after two doses of immunotherapy, demonstrated interval progression with blossoming/enlarging disease. Subsequent disease extent was considered not resectable with clear margins.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior right temple lesion had been treated with Mohs surgery. The patient had received neoadjuvant immunotherapy and completed two doses. Treatment was complicated by severe arthritis, which improved with steroids. She declined further immunotherapy after the second dose and did not receive a third cycle. Disease progressed on treatment. Hypofractionated palliative radiotherapy (“quad shot”) was subsequently administered.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive locoregional disease involving the right parotid region and regional nodes, associated with significant pain. Disease was no longer considered surgically resectable with meaningful margins after progression on immunotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: Facial nerve function was intact at presentation. Past medical history included recurrent deep vein thromboses treated with warfarin (Coumadin). The interval between Mohs surgery and development of the enlarging parotid-region mass was approximately 1-2 months.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 39-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Dysphagia and forgetfulness for 3 weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Known acute myeloid leukemia. Intracranial lesion in the left frontal region was diagnosed on biopsy as myeloid sarcoma, consistent with CNS relapse of prior acute myeloid leukemia.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the brain lesion showed myeloid origin with involvement by myeloid sarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain with contrast dated 05 May 2004 showed a focal abnormal mass lesion in the left frontal region with extensive surrounding vasogenic edema. The lesion caused significant mass effect with effacement/replacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, subfalcine herniation, and midline shift. The lesion crossed the midline through the genu and proximal body of the corpus callosum. It demonstrated significant post-contrast enhancement with a few central non-enhancing/T2 hyperintense areas interpreted as probable internal necrosis. One to two adjacent smaller enhancing foci/satellite nodules were seen lateral to the dominant lesion. The lesion was described as relatively hypo- to isointense on T2-weighted imaging. Diffusion restriction was described, consistent with dense cellular packing. No susceptibility was identified on the available review.

[ laboratory results ]: At emergency presentation, hemoglobin was 15.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count was 9.6, neutrophils were 72.5%, and lymphocytes were within normal limits. At initial AML diagnosis in 2021, blast count was 90 and total leukocyte count was 30.3.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a prior diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia in 2021 and had previously received chemotherapy. At the time of current emergency presentation, peripheral blood counts were within normal range. A biopsy of the intracranial lesion was performed; no surgical resection was performed.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic intracranial left frontal myeloid sarcoma with extensive edema, mass effect, ventricular effacement, subfalcine herniation, and midline crossing through the corpus callosum, representing relapse of acute myeloid leukemia in the CNS.

[ other clinical data ]: Karnofsky Performance Status was documented as 90. The patient had been residing outside Karachi prior to presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old man at initial presentation; otherwise healthy. He was approximately 30 years old at the time of later tertiary referral.

[ chief complaint ]: Left parotid mass with parapharyngeal space involvement at initial presentation. He later developed recurrent post-auricular/parotid bed disease and subsequently distant metastatic disease involving the sternum/manubrium.

[ diagnosis ]: Low-grade acinic cell carcinoma of the left parotid gland with parapharyngeal extension. The disease was multiply locally recurrent despite surgery and repeated radiotherapy. He later developed distant osseous metastasis to the manubrium/sternum. Recurrent disease at tertiary evaluation was associated with mandibular osteoradionecrosis and condylar fracture.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial fine-needle aspiration of the parotid mass showed low-grade acinic cell carcinoma.  
- Following total parotidectomy and parapharyngeal mass removal in March 2019, margins were reportedly negative.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of a post-auricular recurrence approximately 1 year later again confirmed low-grade acinic cell carcinoma.  
- Persistent disease after radiotherapy was biopsied and again showed acinic cell carcinoma.  
- Wide local excision of skin-involving recurrent disease confirmed persistent low-grade acinic cell carcinoma; margins were reportedly negative.  
- Outside pathology was re-reviewed at the tertiary center and remained consistent with low-grade acinic cell carcinoma. Re-review of a CT-guided biopsy from recurrence also confirmed acinic cell carcinoma.  
- Pathology from salvage surgery at the tertiary center showed another focus of acinic cell carcinoma with vascular involvement. Margins were negative.  
- Elective neck dissection specimen from levels I-IV showed no positive lymph nodes.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial tumor involved the parotid gland and parapharyngeal space.  
- PET imaging at tertiary presentation showed FDG-avid recurrent disease in the parapharyngeal/peripheral operative bed region adjacent to surgical clips.  
- PET imaging also showed avidity in the glottis; direct laryngoscopy and serial follow-up did not identify malignancy at that site.  
- Imaging demonstrated fracture of the mandibular condyle with the condylar fragment displaced in the glenoid fossa, in the previously treated field, consistent clinically with osteoradionecrosis.  
- Approximately 1 year after salvage surgery, imaging showed another soft tissue recurrence in the parapharyngeal space and a lytic lesion in the manubrium/sternum.  
- No distant metastases were identified at the time of tertiary referral. No cervical nodal disease was identified on imaging at that time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing performed on tissue from the initial resection showed androgen receptor expression 0%, HER2 negative, and a RET rearrangement/fusion with an unknown fusion partner.  
- Testing did not support secretory carcinoma/NTRK-driven disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- March 2019: Total parotidectomy with parapharyngeal mass removal for clinically node-negative low-grade acinic cell carcinoma; margins were reportedly negative.  
- Approximately 1 year later: Recurrent post-auricular disease confirmed by FNA; treated with radiotherapy to the left parotid bed to 70 Gy. Persistent disease remained after treatment.  
- Persistent biopsy-proven acinic cell carcinoma was then treated with proton radiotherapy to the parotid bed to 70 Gy.  
- After the second radiation course, persistent disease involved the overlying skin; this was treated with wide local excision with reportedly negative margins, followed by an additional 60 Gy of adjuvant proton radiotherapy completed in January 2023.  
- Post-treatment PET after these therapies showed persistent disease.  
- After transfer of care, he underwent salvage surgery including revision parotidectomy, repeat parapharyngeal dissection, mandibular resection/reconstruction using scapular tip free flap, and elective neck dissection. Operative findings included bone appearance consistent with osteoradionecrosis, no gross bone tumor involvement, and multifocal diffuse parapharyngeal involvement with severe radiation fibrosis and concern for tumor deposits.  
- Postoperatively, jaw function, pain, and mouth opening improved.  
- Approximately 1 year later, he developed recurrent parapharyngeal soft tissue disease and a lytic manubrial/sternal metastasis.  

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Clinically node-negative neck at initial presentation.  
- No positive cervical lymph nodes were identified despite later elective neck dissection of levels I-IV.  
- Reconstruction planning initially considered fibula free flap, but this was not used because of two-vessel runoff and congenitally absent posterior tibial artery in the leg. Scapular tip free flap reconstruction was performed instead.  
- Available records did not include additional initial pathologic details such as lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, or full operative reports from the outside hospital.

Thank you for having us. Let me figure out how to advance. We have nothing to disclose. So briefly, here's our objectives. We'll go through a case, and then we'll use that as a jumping-off point for some interesting discussions and literature review regarding topics including the clinically node-negative neck management in major salivary gland cancer, adjuvant radiation for low-grade salivary carcinomas, surgical and other management of recurrent disease, and then risks and management of distant disease. So this story starts off with a 28 year old gentleman who presented with a parotid mass, which involved the peripheral space. This was at an outside hospital, so unfortunately I don't have any pictures to show you. But this was a young, otherwise healthy gentleman who had an FNA and found a low-grade acinic cell carcinoma. He had no nodes clinically, so he appropriately underwent a total parotidectomy, parapharyngeal mass removal in March of 2019 and had reportedly some negative margins at that time. So this leads into the first discussion point, which is management of the node negative neck in low-grade salivary carcinomas. So there is some data to think about when guiding this decision-making. Vora et al reviewed the National Cancer Database and looked into the rates of occult nodal metastases. Their cohort included 6,977 patients. Among these, only eight 0.2% of low-grade tumor patients had acotinodal metastases versus 30.9% of the high-grade tumor patients. Specifically looking at low-grade acinic cell carcinomas, there was a very low rate of 4.7% of those patients had acotinodal metastases. Elective neck dissection was not associated with an overall survival benefit among these with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.10. In parotid malignancies, the nodal metastases were found to be most dependent on histology and tumor grade, with high-grade tumors in certain histologies, such as salivary ductal carcinoma and adenocarcinoma, having higher rates of occult nodal metastases.

I agree with you, though. I do this pretty much the same thing. It really depends on the histology pre-op. And I have a unique practice at Stanford where I get an MRI on all parotid tumors. Only eight out of their cohort were patients who had acinic cell carcinoma that developed distant mets. The median time from diagnosis to developing those mets was about 17 months. That's a very small number to try and figure out risk factors specifically for that histology type, but amongst their larger cohort, the independent risk factors for distant mets were tumor grade, higher T-stage, and positive nodal disease at the time of diagnosis. This was where I was going to make that mention of keeping in mind to test for that NTRK gene fusion to make sure you're not misclassifying and dealing with a different histology than you think you are, because that does lead to the misclassification of secretory carcinomas as acinic cell carcinomas. So the next thing to think about is the targeted therapy that he was started on. So he received sulprocatinib. This is a highly selective RET inhibitor involved in ATP competition. The efficacy and safety of sulprocatinib was established during the Libereto-001 trial, which was published in the New England Journal in 2020 and led to the rapid approval by the FDA of sulprocatinib for non-small cell lung cancer and solid tumors that harbor a RET fusion mutation. As a reminder, the RET proto-oncogene encodes a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase that is involved in normal embryologic development. Fusions between the sequences that encode the kinase domain at the terminal region of RET and various upstream gene partners lead to abnormal expression of chimeric kinase fusion proteins. Selprocatinib is a highly selective small molecule inhibitor of RET kinase with specific potency against diverse RET alterations, including fusions, activating point mutations, and against predicted acquired resistant mutations. But it does spare non-RET kinases and other non-kinase targets, as opposed to some of the other small molecules out there that can target RET, so it's kind of unique in that it targets only the mutated form of RET. So the LIBERETO-01 trial explored the efficacy and safety mostly among non-small cell lung cancer patients, but it did include some other solid tumors. They found in 68% of the lung cancer patients who received cell procatenib were progression-free during the interval of the trial with a median progression-free survival of 18.4 months. They did include other solid tumors, as I mentioned, including four salivary gland tumors, which led to the FDA approval of the use of this medication for any solid tumor that harbors a RET fusion. mutation in 2020. They also included 65 thyroid patients, which they published separately and led to approval for the use of RET-mutated thyroid cancers. There have been follow-up trials since that time, including LIBORETO-531, which considered RET fusion-mutated medullary thyroid cancer specifically and led to FDA approval of it in the setting of medullary thyroid cancer last year for adults and beads.

OK, thanks, Colleen. I think we're about 30 minutes in, so I'm going to move us along. But a really challenging case, one where you wish that they could have been referred earlier in that disease course, of course. And it's really tragic to see the complications that they suffered from it. And I think one of the last discussion points is just it's a very challenging decision about how to frame that operation to that patient, right? They have possibly resectable, possibly curable disease, but in reality, With that much radiation with multiple prior recurrences, you know, it may be best to consider that more of a palliative operation. And so they need to understand the risks associated with it. And it's a controversial operation to do. In a young person like that, I think it sounds like you did the right thing, but it's not an easy discussion to have with the patient in terms of framing what their expectations are. So thanks again for sharing that. And we'll move on to Annie.
Thanks for having us.

reference_conclusion: Given multiply recurrent parotid acinic cell carcinoma after prior surgery and multiple courses of radiation, further irradiation was not recommended. The consensus favored comprehensive genomic profiling and definitive salvage surgery because of persistent locoregional disease with mandibular osteoradionecrosis/fracture in a young, otherwise healthy patient. The patient subsequently underwent revision parotidectomy with parapharyngeal resection, mandibular resection and scapular tip free flap reconstruction, along with elective neck dissection. After later development of a parapharyngeal recurrence and sternal metastasis, RET fusion testing supported referral to medical oncology for selpercatinib, and palliative radiation was delivered to the sternal metastasis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 35-year-old premenopausal woman with a family history of breast cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic relapse of triple-negative breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative breast cancer, initially early stage after pregnancy, with subsequent metastatic recurrence. Metastatic disease included lung nodules and a brain lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: Primary breast cancer was triple negative. Biopsy of metastatic lung nodules confirmed triple-negative disease. Residual disease was present after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

[ imaging findings ]: Metastatic relapse occurred 18 months after the last chemotherapy cycle and consisted of three lung nodules. A brain lesion was subsequently identified and treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. During treatment with talazoparib plus a bromodomain inhibitor on study, radiographic response was documented prior to later disease progression at 10 months.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor genomic profiling on a lung biopsy obtained after progression identified a somatic BRCA1 mutation. Prior germline BRCA1/BRCA2 testing was negative. Repeat testing for the same BRCA1 variant was performed and remained classified as non-germline in the available data. PD-L1 had not been tested at the time metastatic disease was diagnosed.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: For early-stage disease, she received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with anthracycline/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel, then had residual disease. Metastatic relapse occurred 18 months after completion of chemotherapy. In the metastatic setting, she underwent surgery at another institution. She was enrolled on the phase III KEYNOTE-355 study and achieved a partial response. A brain lesion was treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. Subsequent systemic therapies included capecitabine and eribulin. She then received talazoparib in combination with a bromodomain inhibitor on a clinical study and remained on treatment for 10 months before disease progression.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with progression after 10 months on talazoparib plus bromodomain inhibitor. Prior metastatic sites included lung and brain.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was described as young and premenopausal. The breast cancer developed after pregnancy.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. OK, so it's going to be our final case. So in the interest of time, we're going to discuss it and discuss the objectives of this case. So it's a patient with metastatic triple negative breast cancer with a somatic BRCA1 mutation. So a young premenopausal woman, 35 years old, with a family history of breast cancer. After pregnancy, she had a triple negative breast cancer that was early stage. She got a new adjuvant. Chemotherapy, which was standard at the time of the case, you see those dents followed by paclitaxel. She had residual disease, and she had metastatic relapse 18 months after the last chemotherapy cycle, which was three long nodules. The biopsy was triple negative. PD-L1 at the time was not tested. And those are the treatments she had in the metastatic settings. She was in another institution where they performed surgery. She was enrolled in Keynote 355, the phase 3 study that got Pembrolizumab approved. She got a partial response. She had a brain lesion that was treated with SRS. She had capcitabine. She had aribuline. And then she stayed in 10 months on a study with a combination of telazoparib and the bromodomain inhibitor. So telazoparib is a PARP inhibitor. And the study was recruiting patients without germline BRCA1, BRCA2 mutations. And you can see here the response he had before disease progression 10 months later. And actually the rationale for this combination was that the bromodermin inhibitor would downregulate BRCA1 and RAD51, rendering the patients, the tumors sensitive to PARP inhibition. And actually there was nice, I think the response rate in the study was 30%, but then with the advent of sasitizumab, the development of this combination stopped. Now, we analyzed a long biopsy later after progression, and there we found what was described as a BRCA1 somatic mutation, because the patient had germline testing, which was negative, and then we tested again for the same variant. So I don't know, Dara, if you want to comment the somatic BRCA mutations. So, yeah.

So, one of the things I think to consider here is given the strong family history and this VAF, the repeat testing I think is very reasonable to, you know, query again whether or not this might be a germline alteration. Another consideration, and I really think this is where you need to bring in genetic counselors, is whether this could be a germline mosaic condition. And it gets really challenging because with a matrilineal history, it's a little harder to invoke a mosaic condition, but it's not unheard of. And so I think the question for somebody who is young with a strong family history in the setting of a negative routine germline assessment, I think querying somatic mosaicism or germline mosaicism is an important consideration.

Okay, so I think another impact here is an ethical issue also. So when we, at least where I work, we patients sign in from consent form before doing genomic profiling because we can have incidental findings that could be germline. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 14-year-old boy; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache for 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-mutant.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy specimen was obtained. Pathology review confirmed diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-mutant.

[ imaging findings ]: Brain MRI dated 06 January 2024 demonstrated an infiltrative lesion centered in the posteromedial thalamus, extending into the adjacent temporal lobe cortex, with dilatation/entrapment of the left temporal horn. The lesion was T1 hypointense and showed heterogeneous nodular/patchy post-contrast enhancement with central necrotic areas. FLAIR imaging demonstrated tumor extent; the lesion appeared relatively circumscribed with some infiltrative margins. The lesion was described as more medial thalamic than caudate; bilateral caudate heads were symmetric without abnormal T2 signal. A small additional right perisylvian/cortical-based nodule was identified on volumetric imaging from 06 January 2024; it was very low signal on T1, non-enhancing, and did not project into the CSF on review of volumetric sequences. This additional lesion was reported as nonspecific and follow-up imaging was requested. Prior MRI from 13 December 2023 had also been available for comparison; the thalamic lesion increased over an interval of approximately 20 days, whereas the small right perisylvian/cortical-based lesion did not show interval growth.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: H3 K27 mutation was identified. The tumor was classified as H3 K27-mutant diffuse midline glioma.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Biopsy only had been performed. No resection data were documented.

[ current disease status ]: Intracranial thalamic/temporal lesion remained present on latest described imaging, with interval growth of the primary thalamic lesion between 13 December 2023 and 06 January 2024. Additional small right perisylvian/cortical-based non-enhancing lesion remained nonspecific without documented interval growth.

[ other clinical data ]: MRI sequences available for review were limited in part to T2 axial sections at the level of the thalamus. Follow-up MRI with volumetric post-contrast T1 imaging was discussed as useful for further assessment of the additional small lesion.

[ other clinical data ]: COVID vaccination had been administered in the right arm 10 days before the PSMA PET scan.

So we are going to be seeing imaging changes quite soon when patients start having that fourth vaccine dose. I remember last year when the COVID vaccines first came out, there were concerns with women having mammograms because of auxiliary lymphadenopathy. And I certainly saw changes in my patients with FDG PETs and even DOTATATE PET scans as well. But I haven't actually seen any changes on a PSMA PET scan that's been attributed to just reactive changes.

And I think- Can I just pause you, Louise, because we want to take a vote while you're talking. Voting is going to take 20, 30 seconds. We want to vote on this question, if everyone can open their app. And the question is, do you think these nodes are benign due to COVID and you don't need to do anything? Would you report them as equivocal? I don't know. Maybe you should biopsy them. Or are they definitely just malignant because they're a PSMA avid and after all, it's prostate-specific membrane antigen? So interested in people's thoughts and sorry to interrupt you Louise, you can continue.

No, that's all right. So I think we heard very nicely this morning about PSMA expression and it is quite specific to prostate cancer. There is uptake in other cancers as we heard and in some normal tissues like salivary glands, but it really isn't expressed in normal lymph nodes. So my opinion would be that it's malignant. Particularly looking at that SEV, which was quite high at 17, you could see that lymph node was quite hot on the PET scan.

You're in the minority. Only 7.4% of people agree with you. Less than 1 in 10, Louise. But the PhD students, they're always the smartest in the room. Always. Declan, what do you think? Does prostate cancer spread to auxiliary nodes?

Well, I voted with Louise on that one, I must say. And one of the things that I think PSMA PET CT has taught us is the quite extraordinary distribution of prostate cancer in the body, even in patients you think have localized disease or local regional. And we usually think that the lymph nodes are in certain templates, but guess what? They're not. They're in the mesorectin, they're in the presacral region. So I think PET-CT has shown us the extraordinary ability that prostate cancer has to metastasize to odd places. And because the specificity is so high, when these things light up like that, not like a celiac ganglion, this is, you know, In a guy with metastatic cancer, I'm usually very, very convinced. We published a big systematic review like this, about this in European Urology, and that was one of our big findings is the specificity is very high. When they light up like that, you know, you got to presume it's prostate cancer in that type of location in a guy with metastatic disease.
Michael, was that 7% from the panellists voting for that number there?

Oh, no, that's the audience. And I was told there were 300 people online, virtually, in addition to what we see in the audience. So we've got a lot of people voting. So that's statistically significant, the p-value for that was 0.01. I'm told. But of course, you know, this lymph node, this is the follow-up PET. You can see that it progressed and it's had an SUV of max of 54 a few weeks later. So these were clearly malignant. And do you want to talk us through this paper seating? Someone's off. There's a study on COVID for everything.

Everything. You name the tracer and it's got a COVID slant to it because that's how you get published these days, you know. Internal medicine, anything with COVID will get published. So this paper quite nicely showed, and that was in PSMA 1007 that you all heard about before and saw that there was actually quite a bit of I can't see that. It was metastasis, I think, in that far right graph. Yes.

Yeah, that's right. So on the y-axis is the SVMAX, so it's a lot higher, whereas the other three boxes are for the nodal react... Anyway, essentially there was a group of patients with COVID vaccines. Some of them had none, so you had controls. And there was a slighter increase in those who had a vaccine, but only around 2 to 3 SVMAX. So it can be mildly increased, but nothing in the order of 17. Once you get above 4 or 5 SVMAX, it's already getting a lot more suspicious than that low-grade uptake.

And I think once you get an SUV, I mean, there's no rule, but it increases with higher intensity. Once you've got an SUV max over 10, it's extremely likely to be prostate cancer and nothing else in that two to three range. That's when you need to think, could it be reactive?
That's right. And we might move on to the next case, because I think that's where the SUVs get a little bit more interesting.

The right axillary nodal uptake was interpreted as malignant metastatic prostate cancer rather than vaccine-related reactive adenopathy, supported by very high SUVmax and interval progression on follow-up PET.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodule identified on pre-employment examination.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the thyroid with nodal metastases in the central neck.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was diagnostic of medullary thyroid carcinoma. Total thyroidectomy specimen showed medullary thyroid carcinoma measuring 2.4 cm, with reported intrathyroidal micro-multifocality and lymphovascular invasion. Central neck lymph nodes were positive for metastatic disease in 6 of 13 nodes examined. Left lateral neck dissection was negative for metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial physical examination showed a small mobile thyroid nodule without clinical adenopathy. Serial postoperative neck ultrasounds showed an approximately 1 cm thyroid bed nodule interpreted as most likely residual thyroid tissue; fine-needle aspiration of this lesion showed benign thyroid tissue. No abnormal cervical lymph nodes were identified on earlier surveillance ultrasounds. After subsequent calcitonin rise, CT chest, liver MRI, and repeat neck ultrasound did not identify disease. Nuclear medicine bone scan showed multiple nonspecific findings, with a potentially suspicious right iliac site. DOTATATE PET demonstrated a superior/left neck focus without other abnormal uptake or evidence of distant metastatic disease. Targeted ultrasound at referral identified abnormal low-neck/central neck lymph nodes, including a lesion measuring approximately 2 cm, and FNA was positive for metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET testing was negative. No family history of relevant tumors was reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment consisted of total thyroidectomy with left lateral lymph node dissection. Postoperative calcitonin measured 12 a few months after surgery. The patient then underwent surveillance with serial calcitonin measurements and neck ultrasound. Calcitonin remained relatively stable between approximately 10 and 40 for a period of time. Subsequently, calcitonin gradually increased to 177, with an estimated doubling time of approximately 3 years.

[ current disease status ]: No distant metastatic disease had been identified on CT chest, liver MRI, DOTATATE PET, or available bone scan evaluation.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism on long-term anticoagulation and diabetes mellitus.

reference_discussion.text: All right, so a 60-year-old man was found to have a thyroid nodule on a pre-employment examination. He had a history of DVTPE, was on long-term anticoagulation, a history of diabetes. Neither of those meant to be secret kernels, just of interest to flush out the patient. He was diagnosed with medullary thyroid carcinoma on FNA. He didn't have any family members with relevant tumors. And on physical exam, he had a somewhat small mobile nodule without any clinical evidence of adenopathy. He underwent a total thyroidectomy and a left lateral lymph node dissection as part of his initial treatment. That confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma is 2.4 centimeter and to what we were saying before, reportedly with micro multifocality within the gland, there was lymphovascular invasion and positive lymph nodes in the central neck, six out of 13 with negative lateral neck disease. He did undergo germline red testing that was negative, and he had initial postoperative calcitonin of 12 a few months after surgery.

Okay, Mara, so now we've got a medullary that's a little more straightforward, typical size, a few lymph nodes involved, and here we are after surgery now. He's not cured because we've still got a calcitonin. What do you tell the patient, your expectation, what's going to happen here? Sort of think out loud a little bit there, Mara.

Yeah, so I mean with his staging, I don't have a pre operative calcitonin here but and then with this post operative calcitonin and the lymph node involvement, you know, in general, this still can be quite an indolent disease, and, but he does have a risk of recurrence most likely local recurrence in the lymph nodes. Typically, we're going to follow with surveillance here generally every 6-12 months, following by neck ultrasound primarily and the calcitonin and CEA. We would consider additional anatomic imaging depending on what happens with his tumor markers as we go along.

Dr. Langer, the role of ultrasound sort of in the post-op neck, my reports can say anything from atypical to secretly suspicious, or I get an email that says I'm a little worried about this. Do you guys have any kind of standard language to describe these lymph nodes and how much I'm supposed to worry when you take pictures of all these?

Yeah, that is a challenge. And basically, we will give you the size of lymph nodes in three dimensions. We will report pertinent positive and negative findings. So the findings that would be considered positive would be around the shape, not so much for medullary, but in papillary, any cystic change, any echogenic foci in a lymph node, which is less challenging than in a nodule because they're not supposed to be there any which way. And we'll do a vascular analysis, which I think is very important. In the setting of papillary cancer, we're looking for abnormal peripheral vascularity. In the central compartment of the neck, we are looking for sort of any sort of vascularity because that's far less common in the central compartment of the neck. And then for the oppression, we try to have three results, no abnormality seen. a finding suspicious for metastatic disease, or indeterminate, cannot exclude a low burden of metastatic disease, which I really think is very fair to our endocrinology colleagues to allow them to just carry on with further surveillance.

It sounds good. Liz, when we're dealing with small volume disease, do any of those functional imaging, so you talked about the FTG PET scan being largely big tumors and aggressive tumors. Any role for nuclear imaging in this small volume stuff?

No, not really. I mean, we generally reserve, you know, FDOPEP for calcitonin levels, you know, 150 and above. Similar argument to our follicular derived thyroid neoplasms. I'm not sure the benefit of identifying very small lymph nodes in the neck and how aggressive you have to be. I think possibly just, you know, if everything's stable, you don't need to rush in to confirm it. a small, like a three millimeter, slightly suspicious lymph node contains metastatic disease, but we kept under surveillance. But I wouldn't be rushing into doing any functional imaging at this sort of calcitonin level.

Dana, just sort of your management philosophy. I mean, we're zero surprised that there's still a little calcitonin because they had lymph nodes to begin with. Is your approach to find every teeny, tiny lymph node medullary and operate on it as soon as you can or watch for a little bit? How do you think about that, Dana?

No, I agree with this level of post-operative calcitonin. He had this surgery. We don't have the calcitonin pre-op, but he did have total therapeutic central neck and a lateral neck. So no, I think we just want to follow that up. And then nodes, the problem is going back. It's risk-benefit. Maybe has a central node, you know, somewhere kind of in the periphery of what was dissected out. And so, we are not that aggressive. If we find something that's suspicious that's five millimeters or six millimeters, we're going to wait until we do have proof that it's actually growing before sticking a needle into it to get the diagnosis. and even before discussing going in. So, no, we're trying not to be too aggressive in terms of morbidity because, as was said already, these can stay indolent and the prognosis can remain excellent in terms of survival. So, we don't want to bring in too much surgical morbidity here.

Right. So what's the goal of the surgery? Maura, some of these patients just want a biopsy and they want a surgery. They want it out of their body. That's not a judgment thing. That's just the way some people think. If you end up doing a surgery, what do you tell the patients in terms of expectations? It's going to cure them and they're done, which is what they want, or we're going to keep an eye on it. So how do you frame that, Maura?

Yeah, you know, I really try and dissuade patients from having additional surgery with particularly a low-level calcitonin. And I really talk to them about the risk that, particularly if these are micrometastases, that they're not actually going to be resected. And so there's a high risk actually that they could potentially have more surgery and most often will not have a surgical cure. And that's where I think there really needs to be a lot of shared decision-making and reassuring patients that this is very common for us to see this low-level calcitonin and even potentially to see small micrometastases remaining in the neck that we can follow for an extended period of time.

Yeah, and I've seen a good number of these folks get a surgery, they find some medullary on the surgery, and then we do the ultrasound six months later, and Jill reads it as stable. Because what we took out wasn't the five millimeter place in the scar tissue, it was something besides it. And then some that went to surgery and didn't find medullary cancer. So you know, when you're dealing with that small stuff. Alright, Jeff, so what happened with this one? So your initial one was a calcitonin 12? Where'd you go?

So, you know, underwent ongoing monitoring over time. That calcitonin was relatively stable, you know, between about 10 and 40. And he was undergoing neck ultrasounds to monitor over time. And that showed around a one centimeter thyroid bed nodule that looked most likely like thyroid tissue. A needle was stuck in it at some point that was benign thyroid tissue. and otherwise there were no abnormal lymph node findings in the cervical neck.

Phil, can you, we often get this sort of ultrasound report that says could be benign tissue, could be residual thyroid cancer, could be scar tissue. Is there a way for you to kind of tell or you're just describing the local area for us?

Yeah, it can be tricky. So in these medullary patients who have not had ablation, I think it's much more at play that there could be a little bit of tissue left. In patients that have had total thyroidectomy and ablation, really, I think a lot of radiologists are seeing the normal fibro fatty connective tissue that lives in the neck and misinterpreting that as thyroid remnant. I'll look at the OP report. Occasionally, you do have a patient who has a very extensive tumor and the surgeon will note that they could not get a complete resection. and they've left tissue behind. Usually those patients are referred to radiation oncology and are on oral medications and so forth. So I think radiologists are just very confused about sort of the fibrofatty connective tissue, which is bright, not exactly the same, but somewhat similar to thyroid tissue, whereas most residual disease or recurrent disease in the bed is hypoechoic and vascular.
Very good. All right, Trevor, take me through toward the end of this one now.

So the patient had a change in the velocity of things thereafter with a gradual increase in calcitonin up to a level of 177. And trying to evaluate that in terms of a doubling time comes out around three years for doubling in that sense. So at that point, started to undergo additional imaging. I had CT of the chest, MRI of the liver, and another ultrasound of the neck, none of which revealed anything to us, and then had a nuclear medicine bone scan as the next step in the evaluation.
Okay, I cannot possibly read this. Liz, quick, quick peek at that. This is a protecnotate bone scan, I assume? Yes.

An HDP bone scan. I'm struggling to read it too, Mike. It's OK. There's a lot of degenerative change in the spine, and we've only got the planar images here. The problem of bone scans is that they're not specific, very sensitive, increased osteoblastic activity, but not at all specific. The changes we can see in the spine and the periarticular activity, particularly at the knees and the ankles and the feet and the cramicovicular joints would all be in keeping with degenerative change. I note that there was some minor asymmetry at the right ischium and perhaps at the left anterior iliac crest, but you probably want to do specs with this to really see whether there's any focal abnormality. We wouldn't, we don't often do bone scans in this setting, probably because we're lucky at our institution where we have access to a range of pet traces. But if there were any, you know, if there were any questions raised after this and the calcitonin was continuing to rise, we would offer F-dopa PET imaging. Okay.
And you guys read this as normal, non-specific, Trevor?

It was many nonspecific findings. They actually looked at that right iliac site and said that was potentially suspicious. Yeah, I mean, just kind of a note on the practicalities of medicine, you know, insurance, this is what they wanted before getting another.

But pre test pre test probability of distant mets with a slow, a three year doubling time a castle and 177 is pretty low right. Those are usually in the thousands by the time we find something not always, but okay so let's keep going.

Now we had this finding that remarked about a potential metastatic site. Obviously, now the patient's in a different state of mind, so did get a functional imaging study with DOTATATE PET scan. This is another snowstorm to me, but tried to highlight where to pick something up. So other than this superior neck finding going down through the bones, there was nothing else that was abnormal at all.
OK, so no distant mets and probably something in the left neck there, right? Yes.
Yeah, about now.
Yeah, now. Good job, Liz. You have to hit the buzzer. Yeah, okay. So obviously then, so onto an ultrasound to go find this, okay?

Yeah, yeah. So, you know, I think the patient was brought in, you know, to our center, you know, had ultrasound done, you know, with potential to biopsy, identified more abnormal looking lymph nodes in the low neck and underwent FNA that was positive.

So Dana, assume for me this is kind of left paratracheal. We'll make it central neck, which is where they often are, just left paratracheal somewhere. So now it's been biopsied. And you mentioned when you were talking before, don't biopsy unless you plan on doing surgery. That gets the train running and kind of hard to stop. So what do you tell this patient about sort of surgery, your expectations? Can you watch one that's biopsied? You get these referrals. So how do you think here?

Yeah, that's a great question. I think it's really going to depend on the size of this lymph node. Like we've said earlier, very small lymph nodes are really hard to find. So if we really, really want to go back into that neck that's already been operated on, we can make use some colloidal charcoal tattooing there, ultrasound-guided tattooing before going in when we've really discussed the need to go back in. I think it's really a risk-benefit. The patient needs to understand that if we remove this, that the calcitonin levels aren't necessarily going to even go down much. or it might go down a little bit, but it's not going to be something that's…it's very unlikely to cure him, and then it's in the central neck, so we have the current nerve that's there, and really, there is a high risk for a postoperative for current a nerve paralysis, temporary for sure, permanent also. The patient really has to be aware of the risk-benefit of going back. I would probably get a contrast and have CT also before going back in just to see where that is in terms of the esophagus trachea and the tracheoesophageal groove.

Right. And Jill, can you speak to that a little bit? Because our team tends to do the same thing. We tend not to operate just on an ultrasound in this recurrent setting. What additional information does CT with contrast or MRI bring to us?

Yeah, I think the anatomic localization. So with ultrasound, some lesions can be hiding, particularly in the TE groove. We know that from all of our parathyroid patients, that that's a real hiding space. Ultrasound also, again, as before, would not do as good a job for tracheal or esophageal invasion. Sometimes lesions that sort of are wrapping themselves around the carotid sheath space can be very challenging for tumors like this. So I think that when surgery is planned, really the CT map is very much more valuable to the surgeon.

Yeah, we often get faced with either a little recurrent disease in the neck or whether it's medullary or papillary. And we sort of talk about five things that we think about. What makes us move from watching the surgery? We talk about size. We talk about location, right? Because sometimes small things and bad locations need to be treated. Size, location, rate of change, not the tumor marker, but the nodule itself, right? How quickly is it changing? Is it causing symptoms or likely to cause symptoms? And the last one is patient preference. It sort of gathers those together there. All right, so Trevor, so this one, he ended up, she ended up having surgery?

Yeah, he ended up going back having a lymph node dissection. Yes, it was in the central neck area. The size on ultrasound was around two centimeters or so. And the went back a little bit into the neck and found sort of what they called multiple nodules or replacement of lymph nodes with disease. He came back quite recently after this with postoperative calcitonin, now maybe back to the baseline, but not negative. And did very well, didn't have any even temporary complications, fortunately. And, and, you know, this was where he had sort of been for many years was very motivated and is happy that he's back to this place, which is good for all of us. But, you know, kind of seeing where the scalcitonin will go now.

This is what Maura was talking about. Hey, Dana, for the non-surgeons in the audience, when you go back to take out a lymph node like that, I mean, we have the picture, you just go find it and pluck one out. What really happens when you're in there? And you guys always seem to take out more than I knew about. So, you know, we won't tell anybody. Can you tell us what really happens in the operating room when you're hunting down one of these little places?

In the central neck, it really depends on what has been done initially. And often we don't really have the operating report or it's not very detailed of what had been done before. But yeah, generally speaking, we go back, if the central neck hadn't been completely dissected out, we go and try to redo a whole central neck dissection. It's really hard, though, because it's fibrotic. I can't even really see these nodules. If it's two centimeters, I might be able to palpate it. I might be able to see it, but often they're sort of in this fibrotic tissue, so that really what we're doing is we're going in and we're taking out whatever isn't vascular, nervous, esophagus, and trachea, and maybe if we see a parathyroid, we might want to try it, but that's really, really tough to find parathyroids in re-op surgery. So really, we're limited because of just not being able to dissect into this fibrotic tissue, if you will. It's like I tell my residents, it's like dissecting in your table. It's hard like wood. So I guess, I hope that answers your question.
Yeah, it does, exactly. Yeah, it's a different picture than we had.
It's not easy.

Frank, there was one question from the audience that was the same as what I had. Because when Trevor presented this case, the patient had a DVT. Some tumors do make folks hypercoagulable. In the small papillaries, the small medullaries, I don't think I see DVTs. But anecdotally, in the bad medullaries, I think I do. From your, I mean, you see a lot of these distant meds, not only in the medullary, but in the poorly differentiated. Do we need to worry about hypercoagulability, Frank?

You know, in this, I'm not sure that I thought the same thing. And I was wondering about that. Sure, I guess you could say cancer is an inflammatory state, which would put you at higher risk for DVT. In this particular case, I agree with everything that's been discussed, that it's taking on a more kindling approach. And this gentleman can probably live for years being managed with local treatment, et cetera. So, you know, the question comes up really, is this a person that should be on lifelong anticoagulation is kind of what you're asking because they have cancer. And the answer is, we don't know. The hematologist will tell you we don't know, because the patient does have cancer. And we do know that there's some underlying degree of cancer living at this level of 17 or whatnot in the neck. To be on the safe side, did the DVT predate the tumor? Perhaps that it probably does now that we have DOACs and people are not having to undergo injections with Levinox and things like that. It probably does warrant continued treatment versus someone who should be treated for six months and stop therapy.
But in the absence of the history of a DVT, we don't routinely put our dysthematous folks on that, right?
We'd be looking- Absolutely not. No, no, no. Even people with aggressive tumors, no. We would wait until something occurred. Yeah.

reference_conclusion: Post-thyroidectomy medullary thyroid carcinoma with low-level persistent calcitonin should be managed with active surveillance, including serial neck ultrasound and calcitonin/CEA assessment at 6–12 month intervals, with additional anatomic imaging guided by tumor marker kinetics. Functional imaging is not indicated at low calcitonin levels, and reoperation for small-volume suspected nodal disease should be deferred unless there is documented structural progression or clinically significant disease because repeat surgery is unlikely to be curative and carries substantial morbidity. After subsequent calcitonin rise and localization of biopsy-proven recurrent central neck nodal disease of approximately 2 cm, contrast-enhanced CT should be obtained for operative mapping if reoperation is planned. The patient ultimately underwent repeat central neck lymph node dissection, with postoperative calcitonin returning near baseline but remaining detectable.

And so there's a high risk actually that they could potentially have more surgery and most often will not have a surgical cure. [...] Yeah, he ended up going back having a lymph node dissection. Yes, it was in the central neck area. The size on ultrasound was around two centimeters or so. [ patient demographics ]: Age and sex were not documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic malignancy with uncertain cell of origin in a patient with prior cervical adenocarcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Prior diagnosis in 2021: adenocarcinoma of the cervix.  
- Current metastatic disease involving the lung.  
- Current metastatic lesion had been regarded histopathologically as a poorly differentiated or undifferentiated malignant neoplasm with uncertain primary site.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial cervical biopsy from 2021 showed a well-differentiated gland-forming tumor, reported as cervical adenocarcinoma.  
- Lung metastatic lesion showed morphology different from the original cervical adenocarcinoma.  
- The metastatic lesion had not been classified as small cell carcinoma because of pancytokeratin negativity.  
- INSM1 was negative.  
- The metastatic lesion was described as very poorly differentiated or undifferentiated on histopathology.  
- p16 showed block-type positivity.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Lung metastasis was present.  
- No additional imaging details were documented.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive genomic profiling had been performed and was reported as negative.  
- KRAS G12D mutation was identified.  
- Variant allele frequency for KRAS G12D was reported at greater than 40%.

[ laboratory results ]: Not documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient had been treatment-naive in the metastatic setting at the time of review.  
- Multiple investigations had already been performed.  
- Prior cervical tissue biopsy had been obtained in 2021 at an outside hospital.

[ current disease status ]:  
- The patient had metastatic disease involving the lung.  
- The relationship between the current metastatic lesion and the prior cervical adenocarcinoma remained unresolved on available pathology and molecular data.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Cytokeratin/pancytokeratin was negative in the metastatic lesion.  
- Neuroendocrine differentiation was not supported by the available immunohistochemistry, including negative INSM1.  
- Retrieval of the 2021 cervical biopsy block from the outside hospital was being pursued for review and possible additional testing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Loss of appetite, jaundice, abdominal pain, and pancreatitis at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of pancreatobiliary origin with uncertain primary site; imaging suggested possible gallbladder or bile duct primary. Liver metastases were present at diagnosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from a liver lesion showed adenocarcinoma of pancreaticobiliary origin.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging showed multiple liver space-occupying lesions. PET/imaging demonstrated a bulky pancreas with diffuse uptake in the setting of pancreatitis, small peripancreatic collections, and multiple hypermetabolic liver lesions. The gallbladder was distended with diffuse wall thickening. Multiple lymph nodes were present in the porta hepatis, peripancreatic, periportal, portocaval, and aortocaval regions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling showed low tumor mutational burden, microsatellite stable status, and HRD positivity with a GIS score of 49. TP53 in-frame deletion was detected with variant allele frequency 14.8%. CCNE1 copy number gain was detected.

[ laboratory results ]: CA 19-9 was 1.4. AFP was 33. CEA was 12.1.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine and oxaliplatin was started. Four cycles had been completed over approximately 2 months. No post-chemotherapy imaging had yet been performed. Tumor markers had not yet been repeated.

[ current disease status ]: Clinically stable after four cycles of chemotherapy, with no reported clinical worsening. Formal radiologic response assessment after chemotherapy had not yet been performed.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history included a sister’s daughter diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Three- to four-month history of dysphagia, globus sensation, and palpable low right neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with regional nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid lesion demonstrated medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound identified a thyroid lesion and suspicious lateral neck adenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT neck demonstrated a multilobulated right-predominant thyroid mass with a right lateral neck lymph node. The mass abutted the tracheal wall and caused compression without tracheal invasion. Flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated right vocal cord paresis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET mutation was positive.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven medullary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with suspicious right lateral neck adenopathy, tracheal compression without invasion, and right vocal cord paresis.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included lung disease and hypertension. There was no prior head and neck surgery. Social tobacco use was reported. No known family history of thyroid cancer was available; the patient was adopted. Examination demonstrated mild breathy dysphonia, right lower neck/thyroid asymmetry, and a palpable focal lower neck lymph node without other palpable lateral neck nodes.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female sex.

[ chief complaint ]: Appendiceal cancer with local-regional peritoneal disease and nodal metastasis.

[ diagnosis ]: Appendiceal carcinoma with local-regional peritoneal studding/implants, nodal metastases, and positive peritoneal washings.

[ histopathology results ]: Positive peritoneal washings for malignant cells. Non-mucinous neoplasm was described.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT imaging demonstrated local-regional peritoneal implants/studding and nodal disease. Interval imaging showed marked radiographic response after treatment, with a mass reported to have largely disappeared between September and December. PET/CT was considered insufficient to exclude residual intraluminal disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Pathogenic POLE alteration identified, involving the active domain. Tumor was described as mismatch repair proficient/microsatellite stable. Blood tumor mutational burden was reported as 70. Germline testing was negative for a germline alteration.

[ laboratory results ]: A quantifiable methylation marker assay was followed on a clinical study: value was approximately 15,000 before treatment and declined to 0 within 3 weeks after one dose of therapy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Combination immunotherapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab was initiated. No significant treatment-related side effects were reported. Radiographic response was dramatic, with substantial regression of tumor burden on interval scans. Methylation marker response was rapid, declining to zero within 3 weeks.

[ current disease status ]: At most recent assessment, there was no evidence of disease reported clinically/radiographically, and the DNA methylation marker remained down to zero. Ongoing concern remained regarding possible residual intraluminal disease.

[ other clinical data ]: This case was described as the first appendiceal cancer with a POLE mutation identified in the referenced CARES database.

reference_conclusion: For stage IB squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, the agreed management is radical hysterectomy. The preferred minimally invasive approach discussed was robotic radical hysterectomy with pelvic node dissection, while acknowledging recently presented interim data suggesting inferior survival with minimally invasive compared with abdominal radical hysterectomy. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 94-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic lung cancer at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with widespread metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Lung adenocarcinoma. SMARCA4-deficient tumor was reported.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT demonstrated widespread metastatic disease, including a large pulmonary mass extending toward the mediastinum, a left lower lobe pulmonary nodule, contralateral right upper lobe/apical tumor nodules, thoracic nodal disease, and liver metastases. Follow-up imaging after approximately 2 months of capmatinib showed marked disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: MET exon 14 splice-site alteration consistent with MET exon 14 skipping was identified. MDM2 amplification was identified. SMARCA4 loss was identified.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially received 1 cycle of chemoimmunotherapy and reportedly tolerated it well. After molecular results became available, treatment was changed to capmatinib. After approximately 2 months of capmatinib, there was profound radiographic progression. Capmatinib was also associated with gastrointestinal toxicity and fatigue.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic stage IV lung adenocarcinoma after approximately 2 months of capmatinib, with persistent widespread thoracic and hepatic metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: No laboratory values were provided.

Yeah, so we basically just do an overview of MET for people. So this is mesenchymal epithelial transition factor. MET's located here. It's located on chromosome 7q2131. It is a receptor tyrosine kinase like everything else, EGFR, HER2, FGFR, blah, blah, blah. It has really one known ligand, and that's hepatocyte growth factor, so HGF. But there are two shorter splicing isoforms, which I think people don't really know that much about. So NK1 and NK2. NK1 is a partial agonist, and NK2 is an antagonist. These are the only really known MET ligands. So really, you'll see a lot of people targeting HGF. We're going to show that also later on today. HGF binds the semidomain. So here's the semidomain of the protein, which causes homodimerization, just like other receptor-containing kinases that leads to activation of MET. This ultimately leads to activation of STAT3, which you can see here. You can see RAS, so activates RAS, which is here, activates PI3 kinase, and then what's not shown here is phospholipase C at gamma. Again, a lot of people forget phospholipase C. I'm not sure why. This is a very important mechanism and a very important pathway that we need to kind of focus on. So, as we continue, we know that there's a number of different MET aberrations. To Ram's point, there's a lot of different MET aberrations, and people don't really know if they're actual or not. You can see gene amplifications, point mutations, gene fusions, exon-14 skipping mutations. So there's a lot. Certainly, exon-14 skipping mutations we're focused on today is absolutely a driver mutation. It's absolutely actionable. Ram, any thoughts here?

Yes. You know the met mutation I think you'll be talking about this, you know, the way this functions as a driver is not. what we normally think about drivers. Like when we look at EGFR mutants where you have this kinase that is locked into the activated position, or an ALK fusion where you have the kinase domain bound to a driver to another gene, which, again, constitutively activates this kinase. This is a slightly different mechanism. And the key feature of that is that the exon 14 is lost. So the mutation, it's very important, does not necessarily have to be in the exons, which is what we normally see in EGFR mutant. This can be both in the introns and the exons. Essentially, as the protein is being coded on the DNA, and this exon has to be coded, and after 13 and 15, in between, the 14th exon will have to come and sit. And anything at that splice site or somewhere in the beginning or the end of the exon, if there is an aberration that just prevents that part of the exon being coded and gets dropped, and you miss it. So it's a slightly different mutation. There's a variety of mutations that can make it happen. So it's impossible, not like L858R and exon 19 deletion, the most common that you see. You can have a variety. You can have splice site mutations. You can have point mutations. at the beginning or end of the exon. And the bottom line is, does it skip the exon 14? That's the bottom line. And that the testing companies need to make clear that the exon 14 has been skipped. And that if they make it clear, then all of us can be very, you know, be sure that yes, we are dealing with an exon 14 skipping mutation that's actionable here.

Awesome. So trials we'd like to see, you know, I've been thinking a lot about this, and here's the deal. You know, there's just not going to be enough patients here to do a significant randomized phase three study, particularly when you start talking about combination trials, where you say, okay, let's look at patients with MedExon14 skipping, and let's take a look at what other mutations they have, and let's see if we can do combination therapies for those patients. There's no way to do significant trials where you randomize patients to say, the MET inhibitor plus minus the drug that targets the other mutation you're seeing versus the MET inhibitor alone. There's just not enough of that. So you have to start getting creative with some of these trials. There's a lot of Agile trials ongoing, like the Agile trial in the glioblastoma space. We have to get better at this where we say, okay, let's do a match trial where we take the MET inhibitor and have that be the backbone for exon 14 skip mutations and let's just say okay if you've got another kind of code commutation, we can use a drug there at the same time on trial, but that the hurdle that you have to jump to get approved doesn't have to be as high. You know I think one very nice thing that happened last couple months was that tumor agnostic approval of the BRAF-MEK inhibitor combination, the RAF-NIB and TREMETINib. That was really important. And I think a lot of people have died, in my personal opinion, a lot of people have died with ELK mutations outside of lung cancer that could have benefited from an ELK inhibitor. I mean, I think a lot of people have died waiting on those trials to finally take place. And I think we have to do better at figuring out how to do these combination trials when there's an N of 1 or an N of 2. And so my instinct would be to do a match-like trial with a backbone and come around that. But that's obviously very complicated. But I think the combination met inhibitor trials would be nice to try and circumvent that resistance issue. So maybe a type 1B with a type 2, those are ongoing. But I think more of those would be nice. Ram, any thoughts here?

I completely agree with you. I think, you know, the fact that the raffinib and covetinib, you know, has this pan-tumor indication is, you know, tells us that this is not just tied to lung cancer. This is going to be across tumor types. And you hit the nail on the need of the other is these large, you know, pan-tumor studies that needs to be done. so that we understand the biology of these tumors better, and we also make sure the need, the unmet needs in different tumor types are addressed. So I don't have much else to add.

reference_conclusion: For metastatic non-small cell lung cancer harboring a MET exon 14 skipping alteration, the panel favored frontline treatment with a MET inhibitor, given the higher response rates, longer progression-free survival in treatment-naive patients, and generally better tolerability than chemoimmunotherapy. Following progression on capmatinib, repeat molecular profiling at progression was recommended, preferably with tissue if feasible or ctDNA if re-biopsy is not possible, to define resistance mechanisms and guide subsequent therapy or clinical trial selection. If an on-target resistance mutation such as D1228 or Y1230 is identified after a type 1B MET inhibitor, consideration may be given to a type 2 MET inhibitor.
reference_conclusion_quote: So I think I would go case by cases. But more and more, I think I'm leaning towards using the metinobiter in the front line for patients. Because I think the depth of response and survival benefit in terms of progression-free survival seems to be better when we use it in pre-prenative patients. And it's also better tolerated. Plus, generally with targeted therapy, what we have seen is patients who are we put the best therapy up front seems to do better. So that's what I would do. [...] Yes. [...] Absolutely. I think we should. there are different reasons to resequence. One we already talked about is resistance mechanisms, you know, what drives the resistance mechanism here. [...] In terms of clinical trials, again, resequencing is important to find out what trials to go with. Yes, the problem of re-biopsying is difficult, but nothing wrong in trying that. I think as clinicians, we need to be ready to do it. We need to educate our patients that they are also for it. And ctDNA helps quite a bit in many situations where we are not able to re-biopsy. So a blood-based biopsy can help. So my answer is always absolutely yes here. [...] Consider type 2 metin inhibitors if the mutation from a type 1B inhibitor is at D1228 or Y1230 if that's the resistance mechanism. Really consider a type 2 metin inhibitor.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Pediatric female patient; presented at age 6 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with extensive cervical and mediastinal nodal involvement, diffuse miliary pulmonary metastases, and osseous metastases. Disease was stage IV at post-therapy radioiodine imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration/biopsy of the thyroid lesion was positive for malignancy, Bethesda category VI. Surgical pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma with psammoma bodies and solid/paraganglioma-like areas. Lymph node metastases were present with definite extranodal extension. Extensive angioinvasion was present. Following total thyroidectomy with central and bilateral modified radical neck dissection plus sternotomy, 354 lymph nodes were removed, of which 321 were positive for metastatic disease. Extrathyroidal extension was present.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound showed an enlarged thyroid gland with markedly heterogeneous parenchyma and multiple echogenic foci throughout the thyroid, consistent with intrathyroidal lymphatic spread. Metastatic cervical lymph nodes with echogenic foci were present.  
- Chest CT demonstrated diffuse miliary pulmonary metastases.  
- PET imaging showed FDG-avid nodal disease in the neck extending contiguously into the mediastinum. No clear skeletal metastatic disease was identified on the initial PET study.  
- Abdominal CT showed hepatic congestion, considered attributable to congenital heart disease.  
- Post-therapy whole-body radioiodine scan demonstrated diffuse pulmonary uptake consistent with miliary lung metastases and multiple skeletal metastases involving the femora, pelvis, and skull. MRI was performed to exclude intracranial metastases. An additional focus of uptake in the upper abdomen was described as suspicious for either hepatic or osseous metastasis.  
- Serial chest CT over the subsequent follow-up period showed progression of pulmonary metastases in both number and size; lesions were typically 2–3 mm, up to 4 mm maximum.  
- Subsequent diagnostic whole-body scan did not demonstrate the previously seen bone activity.  
- Follow-up PET imaging continued to show neck activity.  
- After 5 months of RET inhibitor therapy, imaging showed marked reduction in visible pulmonary metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Somatic oncogene testing identified a RET-PTC1 fusion.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Initial etiologic workup for lymphadenopathy was negative.  
- TSH was normal at presentation.  
- Six weeks postoperatively, non-stimulated thyroglobulin remained significantly elevated.  
- At the time of radioactive iodine treatment, stimulated thyroglobulin increased markedly following thyroid hormone withdrawal and 2 weeks of low-iodine diet.  
- Approximately 6 months after radioactive iodine, non-stimulated thyroglobulin decreased from approximately 500 to 45.  
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were mildly positive and later increased over time.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient was initially followed with serial clinical examinations by the primary care provider.  
- Preoperative laryngeal evaluation showed normal vocal cord mobility.  
- The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, bilateral modified radical neck dissection, and sternotomy for mediastinal disease. Recurrent laryngeal nerves remained intact postoperatively.  
- Radioactive iodine therapy was administered at a dose of 150 mCi after thyroid hormone withdrawal and low-iodine diet. Post-therapy imaging demonstrated persistent widespread iodine-avid metastatic disease in lungs and bone.  
- During surveillance after radioactive iodine, thyroglobulin declined but pulmonary metastases progressed radiographically.  
- Systemic therapy with a RET inhibitor was initiated. After 5 months, pulmonary metastases showed marked radiographic reduction. Treatment was tolerated well, with no concerning adverse effects reported; growth and linear progression remained on track.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with prior evidence of pulmonary, nodal, mediastinal, and osseous disease. Following RET inhibitor therapy, pulmonary metastatic burden decreased markedly on imaging. Neck PET activity persisted. The patient remained clinically well and tolerated systemic therapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history was significant for complex congenital heart disease, including Ebstein anomaly, multiple large ventricular septal defects, prior pulmonary artery banding, Glenn procedure, and Fontan procedure, with multiple prior sternotomies.  
- Family history was negative for thyroid cancer predisposition.  
- The patient developed permanent hypoparathyroidism after surgery.

And this gets overlooked and misdiagnosed as a benign type of diffuse thyroid disease, most commonly chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, which it can coexist with, not uncommonly. The other important thing that you had mentioned is examination of the lymph nodes. Almost always these patients will have evidence of metastatic lymph nodes with these echogenic foci in the nodes.
