And so in discussion with the family, this patient, again, for time-wise, was started on a RET inhibitor. And you can see, as Stephen described, these medications work wonderfully. Our goal is not to keep patients on it long-term, but this is even after five months of therapy, you can see just the marked reduction in visible pulmonary metastasis. has tolerated the medicine quite nicely, is growing and tracking as far as linear growth and progression and side effects, adverse reactions, nothing currently that's concerning. I'm not the treating physician, I'm the partner. We have an oncologist that's helping. Ted Leach, who's our developmental therapeutics expert at CHOP is helping me. So this is a patient that is, you know, doing quite well. And the question now, I think in the last and final slide with two minutes left is, you know, what to do. So as Steven mentioned, this is not a long-term plan for the patient. We didn't go into it thinking that way. And thinking six, at least a year of treatment, and then repeating as was previously suggested, the diagnostic scan scene. what's there and if there actually is activity, which we've seen in another patient on larotrectinib after six months, after a year of treatment, that their CT scan was actually really nice anatomic response and the activity on the diagnostic scan a year after larotrectinib was remarkable as far as having an avid uptake.

Steven, let me give you one minute. In adults, when we start these kinase inhibitors, they're on them forever, unless they re-differentiate, right? So how are you guys, you keep saying we're going to use them for a little while. In a minute or so, give me the logic of that and how you guys are thinking about that right now.

Yeah, so we now know that, I mean, we've always had evidence, but we know that the median disease-specific survival in advanced papillary carcinoma diagnosed in childhood is excellent in over 50 years. So the long-term outcomes are really good. And then just anecdotally, Patients that at least I've treated as teenagers with systemic therapies have been able to come off without rebounds like we worry about in adults. And I think partly it's just the molecular makeup. We don't see TURK promoter mutations. We don't see other, you know, acquired mutations that occur in these tumors that make it more aggressive. So yeah, so in children, I think it's, you know, I kind of say it's like a metronomic approach. Like, you know, do you consider treating for a year or two to maximal response, reset the clock and then take them off. And then maybe you have, you know, many years of just doing nothing, but we need to prove that. And I think through right now, it's just case individual cases that we could, we could document that, but at least I can share some people off of larotrectinib that I've treated have not had rapid progression after coming off. So, So I think that is the logic behind it.

And it comes up even in the adult arena. Sometimes we've talked about maybe doing discontinuation studies, right? Maybe they don't really need to be on these for the long time. All right, we're right up against the thing. We got 30 seconds. Mark, you want to finish this out? I'll say thank you to the panel. Terrific discussion. Mark, take it over there.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 27-year-old male. Karnofsky Performance Status Score (KPSS) 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent episodes of facial and body weakness, with 4-5 episodes since January 2024.

[ diagnosis ]: Clival chordoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Postoperative histopathology was consistent with chordoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI demonstrated a midline extra-axial clival mass centered at the skull base/prepontine region, with heterogeneous T2 signal and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement. The lesion involved the clivus, with the posterior clival surface not separately visualized. It caused significant compression of the pons/brainstem and midbrain, with pressure effect on the basilar artery, and minimal superior displacement of the pituitary/sellar structures and optic chiasm. The pituitary gland, infundibulum, and optic chiasm were separately identifiable, and the pituitary fossa was preserved without expansion. Paranasal sinuses were clear. Postoperative MRI showed a CSF-containing cavity and smooth pachymeningeal enhancement attributed to postoperative change, without definite solid enhancing residual lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgical resection of the clival lesion via a transcranial lateral skull base approach. Postoperative imaging did not demonstrate definite significant residual enhancing tumor.

[ current disease status ]: Status post resection of clival chordoma. Postoperative MRI showed no definite solid enhancing residual lesion; only postoperative pachymeningeal enhancement was seen.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone pain; referred for assessment of suitability for lutetium therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with osseous metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET demonstrated heterogeneous tracer uptake overall, with relatively low-intensity uptake in the majority of sites, less than parotid uptake in most locations. Reported PSMA PET quantitative metrics were SUVmax 13.8 and SUVmean 4.8. FDG PET demonstrated multifocal avid lesions in the pelvis with spatial discordance relative to PSMA PET; the extent of FDG-avid disease was greater than that seen on PSMA PET in some sites. Some bone lesions showed greater FDG uptake than PSMA uptake.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 430. PSA doubling time 0.6 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior systemic therapy included docetaxel, enzalutamide, and cabazitaxel. Prior radiotherapy had been delivered to the spine. Bone pain had been controlled on multiple opioids. Castration resistance had developed within 12 months. Disease had progressed through docetaxel, enzalutamide, and cabazitaxel in less than 2 years.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after multiple prior lines of therapy. Performance status was ECOG 1–2 at referral.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient lived several hours from the treating center and had a difficult social situation with social isolation.

reference_discussion.text: Case number five, 67-year-old, so a young patient, post-carbazetaxel, who's also had docetaxel enzalutamide radiotherapy to the spine. Bone pain is controlled on multiple opioids. He's got ECOG 1 to 2, PSA 430, doubling time of 0.6 months, referred for suitability for lutetium therapy. And we've done a PSMA and also an FDG, as we always do.

All right, so we'll just start these MIP images going again and have a little bit of a look. So the impression that we're getting straight away here is that the overall PSMA activity is quite heterogeneous. In fact, I can tell you that the SUV max here is 13.8 and the SUV mean is 4.8. And then when we come down on the FDG PET towards the pelvis, we can see these multifocal avidities that when you go through carefully, you can see that there is some spatial discordance where the extent of FDG activity is probably a little bit more than what we see on the PSMA PET.

Can we just window that image out a little bit? Because that's windowed quite heavily. So I think this is actually the ... that's the DOTATATE. This is the PSMA windowing, so you can see that the uptake is kind of less than parotted in the majority of locations. So I think you probably had it over windowed to start with and you can give a false impression that it's intense uptake, but it's actually quite low intensity uptake. And then if you look closely you do see sites like this rib. Oh no, that's not a rib. There are some bone sites that have more FDG uptake like here than the PSMA PET scan.
I was about to say, it doesn't look like SV-mean of 4.7 on the previous one, so I think windowing, that's a really good point. You'd really have to standardize these.
Just trying to catch up.
Yeah, I know, I was confused. Testing the limits of your skill. I was like, this has got to be the wrong patient.
I mean, obviously, this candidate's not ideal, right? But they're post-gabazitaxel. I'm assuming they don't have a DNA damage repair. They're not suitable for Olaparib or another option.

Yeah, I think this is a complex decision. Again, it depends upon cost, availability, social factors, comorbidities, everything else. It's not an imaging or SUV criteria. I think this patient had a difficult social situation and lived quite a few hours drive from the city and was, we had a cancellation actually a day later, so we had an opportunity to treat this patient quickly and the person seeing, the doctor seeing the patient thought this is great, let's book him in and it was discussed at the MDT but it was already booked in for the next day. And I was actually a bit reluctant to treat this patient because the low SUV mean really worried me. The quick decision-making, the long drive, I think the patient had some social isolation. I was a bit concerned.
Yeah, it's not optimal.

Not optimal. We did treat the patient and despite the suboptimal imaging phenotype, but we had a dose available and I actually remember getting it. He was treated on a Thursday and then at Friday at 5 p.m. I got a phone call from a patient's relative who was very upset because the patient had come down to Melbourne through transport and we do this as an outpatient treatment but accommodation was arranged for this patient nearby to Peter Mac and post-therapy, the patient was very unwell, couldn't get out of bed and the relative was like, what do you mean? You didn't admit this patient. There's no nurse looking after him. You've just treated him and there's no nurse. Like, what were you thinking? This is unconscionable. there should be a nurse with him 24-7. If we had known that he wouldn't be looked after afterwards, we wouldn't have sent him down to Melbourne for treatment. So it was quite an angry call on a Friday afternoon. And after the first dose, his PSA continued to rise and he was admitted for local palliative care and pain management support. And he had some delirium worsening, symptomatic anemia, malnutrition, and I think he passed away very soon after that. Less than eight weeks.
Did the patient want treatment?
Sorry?
Did the patient want treatment?
The patient wanted treatment, yes.

I think, though, this is one of those cases that highlights the power of the in-person review. So when we saw him for his post-therapy review, one, we could see how cachectic he was. And I think you have that sense when you look at that sort of patient that their time is shortening, and they might not only have weeks anyway. And there's also the subtle body language cues that you pick up on. began to get the sense that perhaps he hadn't accepted treatment for himself but for others in his life and I think that's the sort of nuance that you get in an in-person review that you don't necessarily see via telehealth and certainly not via telephone if we can't hook up with telehealth which is a consideration because Often we book many of these patients in for telehealth but when it comes to the appointment time they might not be able to get their technology to work and then we have to make a decision whether we try to consult them via the phone to get things moving or if we try to rebook, which can cause delays.

Look, I think we have to be careful not to oversell the treatment and just inform the patient honestly. So if this patient had super high SUVs, I'd be very keen to treat him. But with an SUV that barely reaches 15, wouldn't be suitable for the therapy trial, I'm hesitant to treat him. I still may give him the option, but I'll be honest and tell him, look, it's not likely to help you and it does have side effects. You may be worse after this treatment. You may have fatigue, you may have nausea and it may not benefit you and you may be symptomatically worse and if the patient's still keen for treatment despite informed consent, it's quite reasonable, but too many people are just overselling it as a treatment without side effects. There's no downside in having treatments. Come try it, but there is a downside. I think this patient had a miserable last few weeks of life as a consequence.

Sometimes it's very difficult for people to accept that there are no treatments, and we can't say that this patient definitely won't have any response. Do you think it's a bad thing to give someone that option of treating them?

Yeah, it's a complex discussion because some patients can't accept, or their families can't accept when they're reaching the end. I think part of the discussion I'd have with the patient here is if you look at the dates, we don't know what the month of some of these treatments was, but he had castration resistance within 12 months. That's a very poor prognostic sign, very poor prognostic sign, and he's cycled through docetaxel, enzalutamide and cabazetaxel in less than 2 years. I would actually say that even if it had higher or more favourable PET phenotype, that his duration response would have still been low. He might have responded and improved quality of life and had symptoms, but I don't think this patient would have done, would have had long survival typically, even if, even with better pet, you know, different pet phenotypes. So, you know, that's part of the discussion you have with these patients is, look, you know, your cancer's gone from, cancer's just, you know, been rapidly progressing despite all these treatments over less than two years, and it's time to, you know, I mean, I think, you know, whether or not you blue tissue him, he's not gonna do well, and I think that's part of the discussion you have to have at this stage. Case number six.

reference_conclusion: The panel concluded that this patient was a suboptimal candidate for lutetium therapy given the low-intensity, heterogeneous PSMA uptake with FDG/PSMA discordance and the very poor overall prognosis. If treatment were to be considered, it should only be offered with explicit informed consent that benefit is unlikely, toxicity may worsen symptoms, and the patient may be clinically worse after therapy. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Older adult male. Former tobacco smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Solitary kidney with bulky upper tract urothelial tumor in the upper calyx.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma of the left upper tract in a solitary kidney. Personal history also included colorectal cancer diagnosed at age 54 and metastatic prostate cancer treated with hormonal therapy with good PSA response.

[ histopathology results ]: Endoscopic biopsy of the upper tract lesion showed high-grade urothelial carcinoma. Upper tract washings were positive for high-grade disease.

[ imaging findings ]: CT chest was negative. There was no evidence of metastatic disease on staging imaging. Imaging demonstrated a bulky tumor in the upper calyx. Follow-up CT after pembrolizumab showed marked interval tumor reduction, described as a partial response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor showed deficient mismatch repair with loss of expression of a DNA repair gene and was described as MSI-high. BRCA mutation testing was negative. The patient was referred to a high-risk gastrointestinal clinic. First-degree relatives qualified for genetic counseling and testing.

[ laboratory results ]: Estimated glomerular filtration rate was reduced at 43 mL/min/1.73 m² in the setting of a solitary kidney. During pembrolizumab treatment, renal function remained stable to slightly improved. PSA had responded well to hormonal therapy for metastatic prostate cancer.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Left upper tract cancer had previously undergone deferred ureterectomy more than 5 years earlier; no neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy had been given.  
- For the current bulky upper calyceal lesion, subtotal endoscopic laser ablation was initially performed.  
- The patient was not considered eligible for cisplatin-based chemotherapy because of reduced renal function in a solitary kidney.  
- Pembrolizumab was administered for 3 cycles. Treatment was tolerated but caused significant bothersome symptoms affecting quality of life. Radiographic and ureteroscopic reassessment after 3 cycles showed a good partial response with substantial tumor size reduction.  
- The patient declined further immunotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: After 3 cycles of pembrolizumab, the upper tract tumor had shown a partial response on CT and ureteroscopy. No metastatic disease had been identified on available imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus and sleep apnea. Family history was notable for breast cancer in the mother and two maternal relatives. Clinical family history did not meet Amsterdam-type criteria for Lynch syndrome. Cardiac disease was also referenced in the comorbidity profile.

Yeah, I think, you know, I'm not going to say that I wouldn't do it, but it would be something in my back pocket that I would have as a desperation move, and I'm not sure I would use it in this case. Because also, I think, you can see the laser probe there to give you a sense for how big that residual tumor is. I mean, it's very, you know, with your tholium or with my diode laser, that's going to be lasered away within two minutes, right? And even underneath that necrotic tissue, you can scrape that away. And if you're worried that there's something at the base, then just treat all of that. Clearly, for high grade, you're going to worry a little bit. But the patient had such a good response that you would think that anything that potentially may have been invasive was treated also. And so you rely on these two modalities to get the tumor from the inside on the outside, if you will. So patient did pretty good, but refused any more immunotherapy, was miserable from it. And then six months later, we thought we saw a recurrence in the upper tract, so I performed a ureteroscopy. It was negative, great, except we gave him a stricture. Six weeks later, presented with renal failure. My colleague who was on call placed an emergent stent and then basically about a month later I went up to make sure that I didn't miss disease or something and it was just a regular old endoscopy caused stricture and where you would expect it to be in the distal ureter. So we basically left the stent I think for two, three months and then took it out and just very carefully monitored to make sure it didn't recur. Would you have done anything differently, Adam?
No, no, I think exactly the same way.

Okay, very good. Any questions about that case? And actually, go ahead, if you're asked, but I am gonna slowly start moving on. If you have other, if you have, if there's other questions, this is also about inheritable syndrome, but we'll talk a little bit more about treatment. Sure.
What if the germline testing showed VUS? Would you offer him Pembro? Let's say insurance will approve it, he has Medicare, straight Medicare, no insurance issues.

If he was truly MSI high, we have no problem. But I don't think you're going to see that on a variant. I don't think it would show up as a variant of the DNA mismatch repair. It's either missing or it's there. I've never run into that problem, but when people have other indications for a specific mutation, if it is a variant, we cannot get it paid for. They will fight.

I think the differentiator here is that there was no expression. So it's not a VUS because pathologically it is not being expressed. But your point is if you don't have the IHC and you're just doing mutation profiling and that's the only data you have. then that might be a harder call. And that's why maybe doing immediate or only mutation profiling may not be very helpful. And that has been highlighted to me by my pathologist, because I asked him, why don't we just do that? And the point that was made to me is because not every mutation that we find is necessarily translated to an actionable mutation. And that's why the tissue testing can be very helpful that way.

Is this a good time? So there's one question here. It says, and I think this was referring to the prior case, but it says, what would you do for high-grade CIS confirmed by cytology and fish? I lasered the strawberry patches and I'm now doing surveillance. Ruptured calyx, low volume, flat. Sounds like two to three doses of gelmido. So I'll comment that gelmido is really for low-grade disease. and that there, for imperative indications, such as a solitary kidney or bilateral disease, we do have, it has been, we have used it for high grade, and there is some evidence in the response rate, it will confirm that, was 40%, but that's very short-term follow-up. And so, I know you are a fan of BCG, other, yeah.

Yeah, I think if it's, see, I am very reluctant to give gelmito for high-grade disease. In the clinical trial, a lot of recurrence. We unmasked high-grade disease that was not treated by it. So I'm very reluctant to do that. For CIS, I absolutely would not use it. I totally agree. And if it is a case where I think it's really just, quote unquote, pure CIS, and there's no visible papillary or solid tumors, we have given BCG. And with that, it's retrospective, single institution data, so take that for what it is. But we see a roughly 60 to 65% response rate similar to the bladder. And so it seems to be, it's high risk disease, but it seems to favorably respond to at least the induction BCG. And in my case, I actually, as much as I can, I do it like the bladder, where I will give them at least two cycles of maintenance afterward. It's a huge hassle for the patient, but if they wanna save their kidney, that's what we do.
I agree.

The patient declined further immunotherapy because of treatment-related symptoms; subsequent suspected recurrence was evaluated by ureteroscopy, which was negative, and a procedure-related distal ureteral stricture was managed with emergent stenting followed by temporary stent maintenance and close surveillance after removal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male. Non-smoker. No significant past medical history apart from prior laryngeal cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Worsening dysphonia.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma following prior treatment for glottic squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior outside diagnosis had been squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx, staged T2N0. On subsequent operative evaluation for recurrence, targeted biopsies were obtained from the left-sided lesion, right-sided extension, and petiole region. These showed squamous carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma in situ.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Prior outside description of the original laryngeal tumor: involved the anterior left true vocal cord, superior medial surfaces, extended across to the right side from the left, and extended to the subglottis at the anterior commissure; vocal fold mobility had been normal.  
- Office stroboscopic examination at recurrence showed a largely left-sided lesion with reduced mucosal wave through the left vocal cord.  
- CT neck appeared largely clean on axial images, with mild thickening seen on coronal imaging.  
- Operative endoscopic examination demonstrated tumor extending to the ventricle, reaching the petiole/base of the epiglottis, and crossing to the contralateral side.  
- Swallowing was clinically normal, with no aspiration reported.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Previously treated at an outside community hospital in New York for T2N0 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Prior treatment consisted of radiation therapy to 63 Gy with cetuximab.  
- At recurrence, operative biopsy confirmed persistent/recurrent squamous neoplasia.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent/recurrent laryngeal squamous neoplasia involving the left glottis with extension to the ventricle, petiole/base of epiglottis, and contralateral side on operative assessment. The patient had moderate dysphonia and preserved swallowing on a normal diet without aspiration.

[ other clinical data ]: Voice was described as moderately dysphonic overall. Previous scar was present on operative examination. Vocal fold mobility had been normal in the original tumor assessment.

reference_discussion.text: Hi, everybody. Once again, thanks for inviting me. It's always an honour to be here. And I'm going to also be presenting on a recurrent case, which actually touches on a lot of the themes we've already spoken on tonight. So I think repetition is probably good. And it's a patient that I'm operating on in a couple of weeks, but have certainly run through all the steps leading up to that point. And we can talk about all those. So 64 year old male he presents to my office hours with worsening dysphonia he doesn't really have any significant past medical history apart from his prior laryngeal cancer which I'll get to shortly, because that in itself is very interesting he's a non smoker so. Previously at an outside community hospital in the New York area, he had a prior squamous cell carcinoma, which was a T2N0. And it was large-ish from this report from the notes that he brought me. So it involved the anterior left true vocal cord. This was taken cut and paste directly from the notes that were sent in. involved the superior medial surfaces. It extended across to the right side from the left, and it also extended to the subglottis at the anterior commissure. But he had vocal fold mobility, normal vocal fold mobility. Interestingly, this was treated with radiation therapy, but also chemotherapy. And as we all know, that's not really standard of care for a T2 lesion. And I couldn't really get any further insight into this and why he received it. And certainly, he also got cituximab, which, as we know now, is certainly not the chemotherapeutic of choice in an otherwise healthy patient. Does anyone else want to comment on this, you know, treatment modality at all?
So, Diana, just as a question, so this was cisplatin cytotoxic therapy plus cituximab and then 63 gray?
Cituximab and 63 gray. at an outside hospital.
So it's interesting choice.

Agreed, agreed. So just for the trainees, not standard of care for a T2 lesion at all. So this is his voice. I tend to do a voice recording, you know, of all my patients pre and post-operatively and during their recovery. I'll just play this.
Would anyone like to comment on his voice at all before I play the stroboscopy of his examination? Dr. Young,
I apologize, Dr. Kirk, it was a little garbly for me, I think, because my Wi-Fi, I told you, was a little iffy. No problem. I apologize.

Oh, no, no, no problem at all. So I think he has like a moderate overall grubas, and I always rate them on the grubas scale or moderate overall dysphonia. This is a view of his stroboscopic examination.
They got me.
Does anyone want to comment on his stroboscopic examination at all?

It's a really nice exam. It's very clear to see exactly where the lesion is located. That subglottis looks much better than I expected it to look. It looks to be largely left-sided, that anterior commissure aspect looks a little erythematous, so I worry about it, but I don't know, I'm kind of excited about this.

I hear you. So, you know, I would agree with all that. He also has, just for the trainees, he definitely has reduced mucosal wave through this left vocal cord. There's no question about that. That may be a reflection of either the previous radiation therapy, or it may be a reflection of the tumor itself. We won't really know that until we go in and and assess it with the micro laryngoscopy. Also, because he was a recurrent, you know, patient and because of this possible anterior commissure that you alluded to, Dr. Young there, I also got a CT scan. Now, it looks pretty clean on the axial, but this there is a little bit of thickening on the coronal if you just have a look at it closely here but that that may be with the retrospective scope of having already taken him to the operating room that I look back on that and go oh yeah I see some thickening there so just a demonstration that always you know look at these things look back at the scans once you've also taken the patient to the to the to the OR

So, unfortunately, make one comment on your video that you had just one thing, ignoring that we have the seat, you just showed the CT scan. It looked like it was almost going into the ventricle, and that's one thing for the trainees is. Look at that carefully when you're in doing an endoscopy or something because that may be may end up behaving like a supraglottic cancer. So you're right there, it looked like it was maybe going into the ventricle right there. So just a point for the trainees. That's a nice picture you have there, by the way.

Absolutely. So yeah, I agree with that. And I also think that on this view here, I stopped it early. You could almost see some increased erythema on this side too, and extending up to the PDL. So, I don't know, this seems to happen a lot to me. I lost him to follow up. I actually sent him off for a pet and I tend to routinely send these recurrent And even primary Laringi is now off for a pet T2 and up, T1 not necessarily. And he obviously fails to show up for his OR even though I've booked him. And I feel like, you know, this is a problem, you know, for all of us. And I would be curious to know how, how everyone manages it. Obviously we tried to call him multiple number of times. We tried to call his family a multiple number of times, but how do you all manage this very problematic situation. I'd love to hear your thoughts because I think it's something that we can do better. I'm just not too sure how.

So I just want to make a comment on this number one. I think this is separate just for education because I do a lot of expert review as well. This terminology loss to follow up, I think we should be very careful. And I think Diana, you've heard me say this many times even when you were doing a fellowship with us. It's a very double-edged sword because this puts the onus on the physician team and your team. This sounds like someone who is non-compliant. I think we have to make this distinction between non-compliance and if your service failed to follow up with the patient and bring him in. So that's one point, because this does not look good on a medical record. I'm just going to be honest about it. We are all learning here. I'd be open to anyone else's suggestions, Uma or Bharath or Dr. Young, anyone. So I have a big problem with just this notation. When someone doesn't show up, I mean, our biggest issue we have in our unit is the patient die. So that's where the phone calls start going out. And we have had patients over my career which have found dead at home because they just died from cancer. So making sure there's a secondary phone number to get in touch with these people is important. And obviously, I think it brings you to a very important point that all you are young surgeons or mid-career surgeons that we need to have coordinators in our practice to help. You and I cannot do this alone. You need people to help get these patients in and out. and I cannot understress that and how much we have to discuss with the hospitals if you're an academic center to pay for those coordinators. So that's all I want to stop at and anyone else to make a comment I'd really love to.
It's going to be very difficult to get a dead patient to show up.

I put in that terminology, Dr. Jalici, just to fire you up, because I knew that would get you going when I saw you on the panel. But you'll also have to tell the authors of this article to change their terminology too. This comes out of Kansas, obviously. And it shows you out of 353 patients that they lost 15%, which is a significant amount. And they sent out a survey to those that that didn't follow up and interestingly enough they responded even though they didn't want to go to their clinic appointments or show up for their therapy but I think that these are all the issues, difficulty scheduling and certainly our phone room can be an issue sometimes, you know, transportation. We, you know, we do have, um, uh, transportation in, in, in New York, but may not be, you know, maybe a problem elsewhere in the country, but we still have difficulty getting them in, you know, some people just have to work. They need to make money and, you know, their medical problems become a secondary consideration, which is sad. 17% felt better, their symptoms got better. And then interestingly, 39% said that they were following up closer to home, which I think is important to get communication from the patients about. And sorry, this is a typo here, 13% only, I should say, were aware of the five-year surveillance, which means the rest weren't. I think that there's a lot more, there was very few papers on this particular topic, by the way, and there's a lot more that we can do to help these patients. And a lot of it may come down to communication, which I think I do well, but obviously not for this gentleman. So eventually we got him, sorry. Oh, no, I was just going to say, thank you for bringing this up, right?

Like this is so important because you're right, we all deal with this. And I think that Exactly what was said like patient care coordinators are so key for this because, I mean, I'll be honest, we don't always know what it is like, is it because they have to work, is it because they don't have anyone to watch their kid. Is it because they can't pay for gas money or their car broke down? We don't know these things, but I don't know about you. I don't have time to ask these questions in my clinic, right? And a care coordinator or a social worker or a patient navigator or someone else that can do that may actually help us identify and address these. It may not be that the patient doesn't care about they have cancer or they don't care to follow up with you or they weren't listening to what you had to say, which are things maybe we assume. like, or we didn't do a good enough job of explaining, maybe there's other logistical things that prevent them from adhering to the treatment plan, which we may or may not be able to help with, if only we knew what they were.

But on that note, you know, maybe one of the things that we have to be careful of is being paternalistic, you know, there's really good data from Australia, from the NHS, that shows that patients will actually will accept a decrement in survival, for quality of life, quality of life, meaning not having to travel four hours in Kansas, or I'm making a long distance to have care, you know, fighting the traffic of New York to come and see Dr. Kirk in, you know, in the city, right? So that's, you're never going to get you know, a 0% non-compliance rate to Dr. Yalisi's terminology, right? There are some people that will accept this. They will prefer to have a better quality of life and stay close to the home. Having said that, you know, we want to, of course, optimize their survival. And we focus on that a lot as surgeons, as American surgeons. But sometimes the holistic view means that these guys are going to be better off paying their mortgage and keeping a roof over their head than you know, than living. I hate to sound so cynical about it, but these are the things that I think, to Sherouk's point, social workers and patient navigators and case managers have a better training and time and aptitude to deal with versus, you know, the head and neck surgeon who is trying to, you know, cure the cancer.

Yeah, all great points and definitely something that I wanted to touch on. So I got into the OR eventually, and this is what it looked like. This was with a lintolm actually, so very nice view. I don't have my 70 degree picture in here, but essentially, as you can see, the tumour does extend right out to the ventricle and I don't show it all here, but it does come up to the petiole of the epiglottis and does cross to about here. So I did targeted biopsies of all those areas and he does have previous scar, which I think was the reason why he had decreased mucosal wave in that initial examination. So I did targeted biopsies of this. and they all of the left, the right and the PDO and they all came back as you know squamous carcinoma or at least squamous cell carcinoma inside you. So a couple of considerations to run through, a lot of which we've touched on, and in the interest of time, that's probably a good thing. But obviously, you know, you're going to discuss this case in a multidisciplinary setting. And, you know, with all that information and with the views I've provided, and keeping in mind, he's had previous radiation therapy, how would you all approach this? What would be your surgical plan? I'm going to go into a couple of treatment considerations on the next slide, and that'll round out the presentation.
But Dr. Kirk, just to clarify, when you say biopsy of the superclotus, where did you biopsy the superclotus?
Right at the PDL, right at the base.
Great. So not up the epiglottis, for example, or into the... That was pretty clean looking. Got it.
Yeah.
I'll let my...
what would everyone, um, you know, we had a very robust conversation about this, a tumor board, um, you know, fairly recently, what, what would, um, everyone offer this, this patient.
Diana, did you, uh, I'm sorry, Mr. Do you talk about it? Uh, the swallowing.

Yeah, I put that on my next with counseling actually. Yeah. So swallowing normally, um, not aspirating, um, You know, this one, I didn't do it because he's got a normal diet, but I think it's also important to maybe add a fees into your assessment of these patients too. It's very easy to do in the office, especially if you have access to, you know, generally I'll do a fees and I'll have the SLPs there at the same time. And if the fees is really abnormal, then I'll do a modified barium swallow. And it's something that you can really easily add into your office hours as well. So no significant past medical history, normal swallow, moderate dysphonia, previously radiation and chemotherapy. I mean, you could go either way, right?

So- From your perspective, I think this guy is a wonderful candidate for either an endoscopic or open partial lateral surgery. Given that anterior release, I would do a petiolar release as my first step, drop the true vocal folds or the commissure into the field. you've got a great view, then you can clear the disease. I'm a little worried about the lack of a wave and the fact that there could be some paraglottic space extension, because then you're starting to get into a sort of a type 3, type 4 situation where you're getting all the way out to the cartilage. But the bigger issue with this guy is, I think, his compliance. Yeah, he doesn't show up to his pad if he doesn't show up to his first or, you know, this, these endoscopic resections these fancy superglottis super cricoids vertical frontal lateral hemilangiectomies, we can we can we can pontificate very elegantly but the reality is if this guy doesn't show up for his follow ups. he's gonna die from his disease, right? And if you think that this is a sort of a flight risk, essentially, I hate to say it, but a total longectomy is, you know, been around for 150 years and it works.

Yeah, exactly. And these are all the things that were discussed at tumor board too. And I think ultimately what we settled on is that, you know, it's probably important to be able to pivot between the two, right? Be able to do your endoscopic techniques, but also be able to do your partial laryngectomy techniques. If if as a trainee you don't get a ton of exposure to partial laryngectomy techniques in your fellowship, go and do them in the cadaveric lab and get up to speed on how you do those. So my plan for him, given the decent exposure, is absolutely to start endoscopically and then just pivot really quickly to open if I'm not getting a good clearance around it. And I did entertain the idea initially of a total laryngectomy, but I just couldn't convince myself to do it based on that anterior disease. So that's why I'm going to definitely keep it in reserve. So just very quickly, these are all the things that you just need to keep in mind here. And this is mostly for the trainees. And we've obviously touched on all of these issues throughout tonight's session. Definitely, he may need voice therapy afterwards. He may even need a trach, especially if we end up doing an open partial. He definitely needs swallow therapy, probably post his surgery. Didn't need it pre, I certainly did a phase. He may even need a G tube. This is a guy that's had radiation therapy and chemotherapy before. This may be the thing that tips him over the edge. So these are the things that you want to discuss. Is there a higher risk of chondroradionecrosis with a endoscopic approach? There's no evidence for that at all. I've looked in the literature. There's nothing there. You know, with an open partial, you know, you bring in a muscle flap, some fresh tissue, and even with a total laryngectomy, you would bring in some fresh tissue as well. And obviously you have to counsel him, look, we could try these limited things, but you may end up having a laryngectomy down the track. So I'm going to be operating on him a couple of weeks. So at the next time that we, that we meet, I, I can, you know, present my outcomes. We'll see how it goes. But thank you, everybody.

What I think is interesting here is this risk of chondronecrosis because most of the endoscopic data, of course, comes from Europe, and the vast majority of those patients are primary cases. So in the context of a post-radiation patient who is going to have aspiration, who's going to have saliva and microblading saliva running down that open cartilage. I have a fear of this. While I understand that there is no clear data to say that it is high, there's also not clear data to say that it is not a problem.
Exactly.

I think we just have to be cognizant of that and recognize that and be able to diagnose it. And as you said, pivot as necessary. In that ideal world, we'd be able to book a person for the OR and do all of them, this, possible that, possible that. But the difference between a two-hour, two-and-a-half-hour laser case and a four-hour total lingectomy, it's a little hard to schedule around that. But in the ideal world, that would be great. So please let us know how it works out.

Yeah, definitely. And the reason why I put the chondroradionecrosis is that, you know, larynges are highly sensitive after radiation therapy. I saw once in my laryngology fellowship a CRN that was precipitated by an injection augmentation. So definitely, you know, that was a discussion in our tumor board as well. But no one has the answers to this. I think, as you rightly say, just be able to recognize the problem if it at all arises. And certainly I've counseled him about it. So that's it. Thank you everyone. Really appreciate all your input there.

reference_conclusion: For this recurrent previously irradiated laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, the agreed management is to proceed with surgery beginning via an endoscopic approach, with readiness to convert promptly to an open partial laryngectomy if adequate oncologic clearance cannot be achieved. Total laryngectomy was considered but reserved rather than selected upfront. Preoperative and postoperative counseling should address the potential need for tracheostomy, swallow therapy, possible gastrostomy tube placement, and the possibility of subsequent total laryngectomy.

And I did entertain the idea initially of a total laryngectomy, but I just couldn't convince myself to do it based on that anterior disease. So that's why I'm going to definitely keep it in reserve. [...] He may even need a trach, especially if we end up doing an open partial. He definitely needs swallow therapy, probably post his surgery. [...] He may even need a G tube. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid with central and lateral cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the thyroid nodule was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Final pathology demonstrated large nodal metastatic deposits measuring 5 cm. Papillary thyroid carcinoma showed hobnail cell features.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated gross nodal disease in the lateral neck compartment and gross central compartment lymphadenopathy. The interface between nodal disease and the esophagus was identified on imaging; assessment of esophageal involvement was indeterminate on imaging.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Diagnostic biopsy confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]: Regional nodal metastatic disease was present in the central and lateral neck compartments. Pathologic features placed the patient in a high-risk category.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with thyroid nodal disease and pulmonary metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the thyroid with metastatic disease to the lungs.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2008: Fine-needle aspiration of thyroid nodules showed fibrotic tissue without definitive malignancy.  
- Prior to 2014 CABG workup: Biopsy of lung nodules showed no evidence of malignancy.  
- 2014: Lung nodule biopsy demonstrated metastatic thyroid carcinoma.  
- 2019: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the left thyroid nodule was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- During pre-CABG evaluation approximately five years after 2008, multiple pulmonary nodules were identified, measuring up to 1 cm.  
- Thyroid ultrasound in March 2019 demonstrated highly suspicious bilateral thyroid nodules measuring 2.7 cm on the right and 2.6 cm on the left.  
- Repeat thyroid/neck ultrasound in August 2019 showed interval progression over 5 months, with concern for enlargement of the right thyroid nodule to approximately 2.75 cm and concern for progression of the left thyroid nodule.  
- CT neck with contrast showed less marked progression by CT criteria than on ultrasound, but persistent concern for growth of the left thyroid nodule.  
- Imaging review described the left thyroid lobe lesion as becoming more centrally necrotic over 5 months.  
- The right thyroid lobe lesion was described as having chunky calcification.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Tumor molecular testing was positive for BRAF V600E.  
- TERT promoter mutation was also identified.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- 2019 TSH was within normal range.  
- Thyroglobulin was 23.  
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were positive at 52.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2014: Total thyroidectomy was offered after diagnosis of metastatic thyroid carcinoma, but surgery was declined.  
- 2019: Surgical evaluation by approximately three surgeons concluded he was not a surgical candidate because of poor cardiovascular status.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent thyroid primary disease with interval progression in the neck on serial imaging in 2019.  
- Metastatic pulmonary disease was present.  
- Disease was considered unresectable/inoperable in 2019 because of medical comorbidity.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Underwent CABG in 2014.  
- Poor cardiovascular status limited surgical candidacy in 2019.  
- Required supplemental oxygen by 2019.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 34-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Neck lumps for approximately 3 months. Associated longer-standing systemic/gastrointestinal symptoms over approximately 18 months, including loose stools, bloating, and weight loss. Prior history of intermittent irritable bowel syndrome symptoms. No relevant drug history. No family history of note.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology from the thyroid lesion and cervical lymph nodes was consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma. Postoperative histopathology demonstrated multifocal medullary thyroid carcinoma. The largest lesion was in the right thyroid lobe and measured 50 mm. Additional contralateral subcentimeter foci were present. Metastatic lymph node involvement was identified in the right neck and central compartment, including levels II, III, IV, VI, and superior VII.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial ultrasound identified a thyroid mass and suspicious lymph nodes. Subsequent MRI neck and CT thorax demonstrated a right-sided thyroid nodule with multiple pathological lymph nodes in the right neck from levels II to IV and in level VI. No pathological disease was identified in the contralateral neck on preoperative imaging. At approximately 6 months postoperatively, imaging demonstrated low-volume but pathological lymph nodes again in the right neck; the contralateral neck remained clear. Contrast-enhanced CT with triple-phase liver imaging showed no other sites of disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET testing was negative. Somatic RET mutation was identified, specifically RET M918.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative serum calcitonin was approximately 13,000. At 5 weeks following surgery, calcitonin had fallen to approximately 600 and continued to decline thereafter before a subsequent slight rise. No other laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with right neck dissection. Surgery was based on radiologic evidence of right-sided disease without contralateral neck involvement. Postoperatively, serum calcitonin declined substantially but remained detectable. At approximately 6 months after surgery, recurrent/persistent low-volume nodal disease was identified in the right neck. Fine-needle aspiration confirmed viable medullary thyroid carcinoma in right level II and level IV lymph nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent/recurrent low-volume structural disease was present in the right neck at approximately 6 months after surgery, involving right level II and IV lymph nodes confirmed by fine-needle aspiration. No contralateral cervical disease was identified. No distant metastatic disease was identified on body imaging, including triple-phase liver CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Given the patient’s age and diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma, biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma was discussed as relevant perioperative evaluation; no test result was provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old woman. ECOG performance status was 3 at initial oncology assessment. Body surface area was 1.43 m². Comorbidities included coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial presentation in 2022 followed post-COVID lower respiratory tract infection admission. Geriatric assessment identified anemia, weight loss, recurrent falls, and inguinal lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-depleted subtype, stage IIIB.

[ histopathology results ]: Excision biopsy of an inguinal lymph node showed lymphoma consistent on immunohistochemistry with classical Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-depleted type.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline whole-body PET-CT showed extensive lymphadenopathy with both supradiaphragmatic and infradiaphragmatic involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Anemia was present at baseline; hemoglobin was 9.4 g/dL.  
- Albumin was 3.4 g/dL.  
- Creatinine was normal at baseline.  
- LDH was mildly elevated.  
- Left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Comprehensive geriatric assessment was performed before treatment. Findings included: Charlson Comorbidity Index 7; CIRS-G 19; dependence in mobility and transfers; dependence in activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living; timed up-and-go test 20 seconds with difficulty; high fall risk; MMSE 24; Geriatric Depression Scale 11; significant weight loss over 6 months; malnourishment; frailty by Fried criteria; Clinical Frailty Scale 6 (moderately frail). Identified geriatric syndromes included falls, frailty, depression, probable pseudodementia, insomnia, malnourishment, and polypharmacy.

[ current disease status ]: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-depleted subtype, stage IIIB, with extensive supradiaphragmatic and infradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy on baseline PET-CT. ECOG performance status was 3, and comprehensive geriatric assessment performed before treatment identified frailty, malnourishment, depression, recurrent falls, dependence in mobility and activities of daily living, and polypharmacy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- CARG score was 14, corresponding to high predicted chemotherapy toxicity risk.  
- Cardiac disease was described as stable at baseline.  
- Social assessment showed that she lived with her son and family and had good caregiver support and insurance/resources.  
- Vaccination history was incomplete.

So, in this patient, in fact, prior to the diagnosis itself, we had the opportunity to evaluate the patient because like Dr. Varun told us, the patient had actually was admitted with an LRTI post-COVID issues in pulmonary medicine where we were evaluating her for recurrent falls. So we thought that we generally do a CGA whenever we are called for a consultation. And in that process, we found out that she has a type 2 diabetes mellitus, which was fairly controlled. She had hypertension. She was taking medications. We always do a Brown Bag examination. And we found that she had five medicines for her diabetes and hypertension, plus multiple supplements. Because those days, following COVID, everybody was, the tendency was to take more supplements. We found that she had not taken vaccinations. At that point, COVID vaccine also was not available. We found that her comorbidity indexes, the Charleston comorbidity index was 7, and SIRS-C was 19. We went into deeper geriatric assessments where the functional assessments we found that she was actually dependent in her mobility and transverse. she was actually requiring, because of her recurrent falls, she required to hold on to somebody to walk. She required support for activities of daily living and IADLs as well because she was always dependent on a caretaker. The tuck test which we did showed that she had taken 20 seconds to complete with much difficulty when she was asked to walk alone. And we definitely considered she has a high fall risk. And moving on, our cognitive assessment actually showed that her MMSE was 24. Her geriatric depression scale was 11, indicative of clinical depression. And psychological depression was also assessed and found that she could be probably fitting into depression. However, what we found that she had an excellent social domain. stays with her son and family with adequate support. The family participation was very evident right from the beginning and when we started working her up and she was supported by good insurance and good resources otherwise. Nutritionally, like the initial presentation itself was weight loss. So we found that she had a significant weight loss in the past six months. Nutritional assessment also showed that she had malnourishment. And her frailty assessment, we use a frail criteria. And she was fitting into a category of frail. And with the CFS score, she had six, which was putting her as a moderately frail lady to begin with. So at the end of our CGA, we found that she has issues in multiple domains. And the issues which were identified included false frailty, depression, probably pseudodementia at that point, insomnia and malnourishment. So these were the syndromes identified in this lady who was otherwise probably when we were taking discussions on RMDT on whether we should treat or not, these were the issues which we had in our hand. So again, my questions to my fellow geriatricians in this board, I would like to begin with Dr. Rakesh Mishra. On These geriatric syndromes, mainly especially on this malnourishment, the depression and the polypharmacy, prior to the oncological treatment, how would you like to optimize and how do you want to generally take up the decisions on these issues, Dr. Rakesh?

Am I audible? Yes. Hi, thank you so much for this opportunity. Now, a very wonderful presentation and good approach. This is how we usually go about addressing an older person who has come to us prior to initiation of chemotherapy. Now I'd like to take a moment to say that G8 screening tool that we were talking about, it's actually a screening tool which actually identifies the patients who warrant a more comprehensive geriatric assessment. So in case they score higher on the G8 screening tool, here the radiation therapy people refer these patients to us. We're actually currently having a study with them, which is using the ES13 as well as G8 screening tools along with comprehensive geriatric assessment. Now, like Dr. Gino said, that polypharmacy was an issue here. This patient was on five different medications for her sugars. Definitely, when we do a comprehensive geriatric assessment, it also includes a detailed history and a thorough examination and a brown bag check. and if we find that the patient is on more than five medications, it qualifies as polypharmacy. Now, definitely, if possible, we would like to give her higher doses of, reach the maximal doses of one oral anti-hyperglycemic agent before introducing another. Then again, the causes of malnutrition in this patient, we have to see whether it is because of her depression itself, whether it is loss of appetite because of her malignancy, whether it is because of something like an edentulous state, which many of our older people have, or poor dentition. whether it is because of a lack of social support or whether it is because of a combination of all these. So this is something which is usually picked up quite well if you do a thorough comprehensive geriatric assessment. There are certain markers for malnutrition which we can use. For instance, this patient had an albumin of 3.4 and this patient also had a hemoglobin which was a little low, 9.4. Now, so we have to find out the cause for her anemia. Is it only because of malnutrition? Does she have any GI loss? Is it because of any vitamin deficiencies? So we would like to check her B12. We would like to check her iron stores. As regards depression, identifying depression in such a patient becomes a little difficult. So because she has scored so high on the geriatric depression scale, definitely she is having depression, whether it only warrants psychotherapy or whether it also warrants pharmacological therapy, something which needs to be seen. Having said that, initiating antidepressants if your psychotherapy is not working would be helpful in helping her regain her appetite as well. The problem is all the antidepressants that we start, they usually take some time to act. So before initiating the chemotherapy, it might make sense that if warranted, we start the appropriate antidepressants as well.

Thank you, Dr. Rakesh. So, Dr. Rakesh, you could continue on answering the questions. What you would think about the frailty factor in this patient? We found that the patient is very frail. So, what are the interventions you would think that is impactful in reversing the frailty or modifying the risk before or during the treatment?

So there are a few interventions, like if in a CGA we identify the patient has malnutrition, we do a mini nutritional assessment and we find that the patient has, or is at risk of malnutrition, definitely making the meals more palatable, making the meals, if it's an edentulous patient, making it more suitable for her. In case you need to increase the protein or the calories, work in tandem with dietary to help modify the meals, making them high calorie and high protein. look at the sugars and see whether you need to give a diabetic diet or not. This goes a long way. Nutrition goes a long way in addressing frailty. Apart from that, certain exercises, whatever the patient can tolerate, can be prescribed based on the patient's functional status.

Thank you. I think I'll, I mean, put this question to Dr. Divya Maul. So, Dr. Divya, I think everybody is worried about how to screen in busy clinics. So, I'm sure in all the discussions we had in the latest meeting which we had in Kochi also, we had a lot of debate how to screen this very fast. So, a CGA comes quite fast for a geriatrician, but then it comes with practice probably. So, any practical tips or how do you tell us, you know, how can we handle a CGA in a very busy clinic?

Thank you, Gino, for this opportunity. Basically, in many of this screening that we do in CGA involves basic questioning about how their routine day-to-day life is going about. So we can ask them regarding if it is the malnutrition, we can ask them regarding how many meals they have during the day. We can ask them what is there in their meal, meaning do they have rice alone. Sometimes when elderly leave alone, they have just rice and maybe one curry with them. So is it a balanced diet? We can explore through just that one question. What all do you have during the day? And also we can ask, have their appetite come down recently? that itself will give you an idea of whether the patient is eating well. Regarding depression, we can ask two questionnaires. There are simple questions regarding, have you been feeling low lately? Simple questions itself can screen most of the items that we do in a CGA, and which can actually hint us on what to dig in deeper.

Yeah, I think that's what the consensus which we reached last time when we had the discussion on geriatric oncology in Cochin under EGOS, that we all have kind of modified our CGAs. We have tailor-made CGAs to fit into our busy clinics. And we had shared a couple of our models last time, the Amrita model and the medical dress model, as well as the CMC Vellore model. So what we all have done is we have tailor-made into asking very significant questions and identifying things as we go on, so that the CG actually can be done in a much shorter time, but touching on most of the factors. So I think we'll move on with the case. So we had, I mean, as our team had decided to give the clearance for the patient and oncological treatment was undertaken and initiated by Dr. Varun and team. Also, our side, we thought we definitely need to treat the depression apart from the psychotherapy part. We initiated Mirtazapine, we chose Mirtazapine because we thought it will also boost their appetite. We taught her sleep hygiene measures, nutritional rehabilitation and diet supplements were started. Her occupational therapy, physiotherapy team both started working on her because of mobility issues, recurrent falls. We provided her walking aids, made her walk independently. We gave her vaccines in between. Influenza, pneumonia, and herpes zoster were considered from our side. And the government had issued COVID also subsequently to her. We ensured adequate diabetes and hypertension control. We were done with minimal medicines and insulin. And we took care of her polypharmacy. We reduced her overall medicines to just five medicines. And that's how we supported the journey in the oncology part with Dr. Varun.

So as Chinnam mentioned, actually, we have decided to proceed with the treatment of hot skin lymphoma in this elderly lady. As everybody knows, the hot skin and the myeloma, these all are the favorite topics for all madams. So we don't want to leave that disease, so we actually decided to treat it. So the issues to address here is that here we have an elderly lady who is frail, and we identified a lot of geriatric syndromes. So what about the use of anthracyclines in frail patients? So how would you approach this case, Dr. Chandrakant?

Yes, Chandrakant? Right, right, right. So well, again, it's tricky to assess for anthracycline. In fact, for any chemotherapy fitness, again, we should go back to the same CGA functional status, cognition and the frailty score. If all things are fine, then the cumulative dose of anthrax in Hodgkin's is not much. So you would have a cardiac assessment. In fact, we can do a GLS and a 3D echo and we can have a baseline cardiac biomarkers in the hand. So if by the CGA this patient is fit for anthracycline then we can actually use anthracycline and we have used dexrazoxane in some of our patients. So if you can use dexrazoxane it has yeah as a prophylactic measure you can use it in these patients and maybe you can prolong the infusion time of anthra. So maybe these are some ways to be a little cautious. Of course, we need to have a proper IV line in this patient because a PICC is important because they're frail and extravasation is common. So I think the CGA plus specifically assessing the cardiac status, the liver function, renal function, I think these are more important. We find the cumulative dose is not much. I think that's the way to go. We can use some protective agents like dexrazoxin.

Yeah. Yeah, all are valid points, Chandrakant. And so questions are actually, is there any cutoff for the use of BLEO in elderly? Because we all are actually scared to use BLEO in elderly because of the risk of pulmonary fibrosis, which is irreversible. So is there any cutoff? What about your practice in elderly patients?

Yeah, actually, bleomycin is an important drug in the treatment of Hodgkin's disease. But the issues are that what we are worried is about the lung toxicity. And this lung toxicity increases as the age advances. Because if the patient is above 70, risk of bleomycin toxicity is more than 25%. Like that, if the renal function is low, that is increased creatinine, or previous UOPD, or some lung disease, then smoking history. All these increases the risk of bleomycin toxicity. So if such risk factors are there, better to avoid. Otherwise, you can use it. But again, it depends on the number of cycles used. So if you use four cycles of ABBD versus two cycles, or two cycles of ABD and two cycles of ABBD, the risk of toxicity is almost same, ABVD versus two cycles of ABVD. So in a very fit patient, maybe you can use about 60. Maybe you can maximum maybe two cycles, not more than that, because as the dose increases, the risk of toxicity also increases. Yes, sir.
And now we have actually the better molecules.
There are other agents like you.

Yeah, yeah. So Krishnakumar, so what about your take on the use of brentoximab or immune checkpoint inhibitors? Actually, at that time, when I treated this patient, the NEVA was not approved as first line. Only brentoximab was approved. So how you approach this case if you omit BLEO?

There have been few patients for whom AVD backbone we are given, assuming that the echo with the GLS scoring is normal. There have been some rare patients where we haven't gone up to the extent to see the LV function properly to make sure that there is no even subtle cardiac dysfunction because as Pavitran sir mentioned, just like bleomycin has the cumulative dose, even if it has not reached a particular level, patients tend to have So baseline biomarkers in some patients who have real high risk. And when we do the, actually very recently, I can't tell you about our experience. We've just started incorporating slowly into the geriatric oncology assessment, which is the CGA, as well as we are doing for patients with very high risk, we do baseline biomarkers. Now I know that this is not the standard of care. We tried adopting it from the ESA recommendation, the first guidelines, which came on Asian, I mean, on the geriatric oncology guidelines for managing various toxicities, cardio-oncology. So they say that actually it's a two-year recommendation. We can do baseline troponin. So some of the patients who are very high risk, we even follow up with serial troponin. There's a sudden rise, then we stop. So we have done it for one patient, but now that is for the anthra. Then coming to avoiding BLEO, definitely yes. I would be scared even with one or two dose of BLEO. very apprehensive. I don't use bleomycin. I have AVD as my backbone. Even a choice, it would be Nivo first in today's context, followed by BV. Hopefully, post-COVID, there is no lung ILD issues or other problems, then Nivo would be my choice to go. Otherwise, we can go for a BV-AVD. BV with AVD. So treatment completed with the AVD into 6, and the end of treatment PET showed a complete response. And the end of treatment, the ECOG PS became 1. At the onset, it was 3. And at the end of treatment, it was actually, it became one. And also we evaluated the end of treatment CGA also as a dynamic measure. So you can see actually the patient actually improved all aspects of CGA, the functional variables, the cognitive, the memory, nutrition, And actually almost all the bariatric syndromes were not concerning her at that point when patient achieved remission. So it is about the treatment of that patient. So she was kept on follow-up after that. Then she relapsed exactly after two years, that is in November, 2024. So she presented with a fever, anemia, and cough. And again, she developed anemia. So the PET scan showed mainly disease in the mediastinum and abdomen lymph nodes. You can see the PET images, mainly in the lymph node-limited disease. So actually, surprisingly, at that point, actually, her performance status was preserved. She was still ECOG PS1, and also CGA-wise also, she's actually fit for further chemotherapy. So at the time of relapse, actually I have treated, I have used the branduximab for this patient. I have treated with the branduximab plus bendamastine for three cycles. And she achieved almost complete response after three cycles. So I omitted the bendamastine. Then I completed the six cycles with the branduximab alone. And the end of treatment, better after six cycles, showed a complete response. So now the patient is on BV maintenance. So, so the points to consider here. So it's an open question to all panelists. So my fellow, the oncologist and geriatricians and everyone actually can contribute. So what is the role of dynamic CGA in our practice, even though it is not the standard practice. So, so I think you can actually can put forward your views one by one.

Dynamic CG is important because the CG can vary because like in this patient initially it was she was in a very poor condition but after chemotherapy she improved to the normal stage. So assessment in between during the treatment as well as initially during treatment as well as end of the treatment is important.

All right, ma'am. Actually, the dynamic CGA become the standoff care. Actually, who should treat it? Is it the oncologist or the geriatrician, or it should be a combined approach?

Yeah, you have a follow-up, like you have a patient who has been under geriatrician, they will know. But if, say, the geriatrician sees for the first time, and like say many of the questions we ask about like how was she six months in the last six months so that that will tell us her status so somebody says no in the last one or two months only she's not eating she's losing weight And then this malignancy was diagnosed. We know that one month or two months back, she was fit. So we can go back and ask the same PGA question. There is a 10-minute comprehensive geriatric assessment, which is there as a WHO toolkit for primary health centers. That is good enough for us. We use it in our day-to-day practice, because that can be done in 10 minutes. And even a nurse, even my department attendant was doing it for us. And look at the components. Her cognition is assessed just by three-word recall. If she can recall at least two of the three words that you have told after some time, that means a cognitician is okay. Then comes depression. The question is, are you sad or depressed and how long? So everybody will be sad after a diagnosis of malignancy for sure. That we will not assess as depression. because depression means it has it should be there with the patient for some time. Then the third question that we ask is about incontinence and the fourth one that we ask is history of fall. So again, the patient has been following after patient developed malignancy. That means it is all due to malignancy. So we have to of course improve the nutritional condition, exercise, high protein diet, if she has sleep issues that has to be addressed. So all that we do for a geriatric patient, we have to continue to be doing while the oncologist assess the patient for fitness for chemotherapy in their own way. That is based on the toxicities of the drug. So, I was thinking that for cardiac assessment, even nitroproBNP is a very good biomarker because if they have subclinical heart failure already, such a patient may go into overt heart failure after your anthracycline. So, not only troponin, you can also do a nitroproBNP because many of the patients do have a subclinical heart failure already. in which case just giving anthracycline can push them off balance because all these frail patients they won't have exercised much they would just maybe walk to the washroom and come back but if a challenge if they put on a challenge they may develop overt heart failure so nitroproBNP is a very good biomarker that can be used because that if that is elevated already we know that there is a possibility of patient going into overt heart failure so that is also a good biomarker that we can use if it's very high you know this is not the patient for you but if it is just normal or just outside the reference range it's okay we can still take the patient and give the patient of course those I know for a frail patient you will adjust the dosage as well and then give the treatment. So if somebody has been really fit, like what we do in geriatrics is somebody who has been exercising regularly, okay, for maybe many years, 10 years, we assess their age as 10 years less. Whereas somebody who has been not exercising at all, mobility is restricted for a long time, such a patient is really frail and even if they are 60, probably we would put them as 70, like that. So all that matters. The fitness that they had before they developed cancer is what matters a lot. In addition to doing CGA at the point and then serially as we go through the chemotherapy and suppose the patient is becoming frail and frail with chemotherapy, we know, like we have to stop, watch, see what has happened. but if the patient is improving and improving, and what you did was absolutely right. You gave steroids first, with which many of these frailty markers will improve. There will be significant improvement with the steroid that you give, then the patient becomes fit, patient will eat better, nutritionally better, mobilize better, and then you have given chemo. I feel that's the right approach, I would say.

Yeah. Thank you for the Bible book. Yeah. Yeah. The next question, actually, it is actually this person is more or less like a. Now, which comes first, the chicken or the egg? That is, yeah, in this patient, the patient's CGA improved after treatment. So do you see this as evidence that treating cancer reverses frailty or the interventions by the treatment enhance cancer outcome? So Chandragana, what's your take about that? Or Dr. Ragesh also can answer that.
What was the question, Varun?

Yeah, in this patient, the patient's CGA improved. Actually, it was a dramatic improvement after treatment. So do you see this as an evidence that treating cancer, it reverses frailty or the geriatric intervention enhanced cancer outcome?

Yeah, so CGA is important to plan the initial treatment. And in this situation, what is the response to treatment? There's also a CGA can guide us. So if the CGA is worsening, then probably your initial selection of chemotherapeutic regimen is not good, or the disease is bad, then you need to probably change the plan. If there is an improvement in the CGA score, then probably you can add a better chemotherapy regimen. That's a good sign. Yeah. Supposing, let's say, I didn't give chemotherapy, I just give prednisone for this patient and the patient's CGA has improved over a period of time, then I would go ahead and add an anthracycline based chemo. So CGA is dynamic. The problem with static CGA is it's only a single time assessment, but this keeps changing. So if there is an improvement in CGA score, that means the treatment is working, the disease is becoming better, we can actually escalate on to the treatment.

Yeah, nice. So, let's move on to the next slide. So, the key takeaways from this case is the CGA is both diagnostic and prognostic, frailty and all other syndromes, that is geriatric syndromes, were as significant as malignancy in an elderly patient. So holistic intervention improved resilience because remission was accompanied by actually the reversal of frailty, malnutrition, and depression in our patient. So at the end of the initial, at the end of the treatment, then relapse, the patient was more fitter, more independent, and psychologically stronger. So it actually demonstrate the long-term benefit of integrated geriatric interventions. So, after this case, I think we can move on to the second case. It's a totally different case when compared to the first one. So, Dr. Chino, you can summarize.

reference_conclusion: Comprehensive geriatric assessment identified frailty, malnutrition, depression, recurrent falls, mobility impairment, and polypharmacy; multidisciplinary optimization was undertaken with mirtazapine, sleep hygiene measures, nutritional rehabilitation with supplements, occupational therapy and physiotherapy, provision of walking aids, vaccination, optimization of diabetes and hypertension control, and medication rationalization.
