case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old male. Current smoker, approximately 1 pack per day for at least 30 years. Past medical history included hypertension.

[ chief complaint ]: Left throat pain, left otalgia, and left neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: HPV-mediated squamous cell carcinoma of the left tonsil with ipsilateral cervical nodal metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial fine-needle aspiration of the left neck mass was non-diagnostic. Repeat clinic biopsy was positive for squamous cell carcinoma. Initial p16 testing on the biopsy specimen was negative, and HPV in situ hybridization was equivocal. Following transoral robotic surgery tonsillectomy and ipsilateral neck dissection, pathology showed a 1.5 cm HPV-mediated tumor in the left tonsil with negative margins and no adverse features. One metastatic lymph node was identified with a 3.6 cm tumor deposit. No extranodal extension was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinical examination identified a 3 cm left level II neck mass and an enlarged, firm left tonsil with asymmetry but no obvious mucosal lesion on nasal endoscopy. Initial CT demonstrated a left tonsillar mass with glossotonsillar sulcus extension and a 2 x 3 cm necrotic left level II lymph node. Updated CT/PET imaging showed a similar left tonsillar lesion, described as slightly extending into the glossotonsillar sulcus, and a slightly enlarged left level II node compared with prior imaging. No additional suspicious lymphadenopathy or other areas of concern were identified. PET showed minimal FDG avidity in the cystic nodal lesion; assessment of the tongue was limited by motion artifact from tongue movement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NavDx was positive preoperatively. Postoperative NavDx had been drawn but result was not yet available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent transoral robotic surgery left tonsillectomy and ipsilateral neck dissection. Surgical pathology demonstrated complete resection of a 1.5 cm left tonsillar primary with negative margins. One metastatic cervical lymph node was resected; no extranodal extension was present. No adjuvant therapy had been administered.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after resection of left tonsillar primary and ipsilateral nodal disease. Under close surveillance. No documented residual disease after surgery. Postoperative circulating tumor DNA testing was pending.

[ other clinical data ]: The left tonsillar lesion was clinically firm on palpation and appeared contained within the tonsil. The tongue base was soft and not fixed on examination. The metastatic neck node was described as mobile and cystic on clinical assessment.

reference_discussion.text: OK. So just get straight into the history. This is a 56 year old male. He is a current smoker, one pack per day for at least 30 years. And he presented with left throat pain, otalgia, and a left neck mass. Otherwise he's relatively healthy, just some hypertension. And when he was seen in clinic, he had a three centimeter left level two neck mass. And on nasal endoscopy, he had an enlarged left tonsil, but there was no obvious lesion, just some asymmetry in the tonsils. He was initially worked up by one of our colleagues in the community and saw he had this sort of left tonsil mass on CT with they called GTS extension, and it's two by three centimeter necrotic left level two mass. He had an initial FNA, which was non-diagnostic, which again is pretty common for these cystic nodes, and then was referred to us. So I biopsied him in clinic, and it was positive for squamous cell. His initial, it was still pretty cystic, so his initial P16 was negative on those cells, and they said the HPV in situ was equivocal. but then he had a positive NavDX. So we sort of, you know, from there, presumed this was an HPV-mediated disease and discussed with him treatment based on that.
So just to pause there really quick, Molly, could you see the tumor in the tonsil?
It was mostly just like a enlarged left tonsil. You could feel it, it was pretty firm, but it seemed completely contained within the tonsil.

Perfect. I think that's helpful to have a, just a quick 12 second discussion with the fellows that, you know, I don't, I'm not a big fan of taking the tonsil out for a diagnostic biopsy in these situations. reference_conclusion: Following transoral robotic left tonsillectomy and ipsilateral neck dissection demonstrating a 1.5 cm HPV-mediated tonsillar primary with negative margins, no adverse features, and a single 3.6 cm nodal metastasis without extranodal extension, the multidisciplinary recommendation was close observation rather than adjuvant radiotherapy. Postoperative surveillance includes close monitoring with postoperative NavDx/ctDNA assessment; if the postoperative NavDx returns positive, reconsideration of adjuvant radiation was discussed. Radiation oncology consultation was obtained to establish care should adjuvant treatment become necessary.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient (“Ellen”), aged 60 years at initial diagnosis; aged 63 years at first relapse assessment. ECOG performance status was 0–1.

[ chief complaint ]: Disease progression after approximately 3 years of lenalidomide maintenance therapy, with mild renal insufficiency at relapse.

[ diagnosis ]: Multiple myeloma, Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) stage I at diagnosis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial therapy consisted of VRD/BRD induction followed by autologous stem cell transplantation. This was followed by lenalidomide maintenance therapy. Disease progression occurred after approximately 3 years of maintenance therapy.

[ current disease status ]: First relapse/progressive multiple myeloma after prior induction therapy, autologous transplantation, and lenalidomide maintenance. Mild renal insufficiency was present at relapse. Performance status remained good (ECOG 0–1).

[ other clinical data ]: No histopathology, imaging, molecular/genomic findings, or laboratory values beyond staging, performance status, and mild renal insufficiency were provided.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks, Nina. So Sorry, we'll start off with a case. And Ellen was diagnosed at 60 years of age with revised ISS stage one disease. ECOG performance status, good, zero to one. She was treated with BRD and then autologous transplant, and then subsequently received lenalidomide as maintenance-based therapy. And then progression was noted after three years. And we could take that two ways. We could take that on lenalidomide maintenance or off lenalidomide maintenance. And that's obviously going to make a difference. And she has mild renal insufficiency. I'll just start off with a few comments about doing relapse-based therapy. And the first, when you're thinking about the selection of regimen for these patients, I think you have to think about patient-related factors, disease-related factors, and then treatment-related factors. And Dr. Rajkumar gave us a nice acronym of TRAP, the timing of the relapse, the response to prior therapy and what they're sensitive to or refractory to, the aggressiveness of the relapse, and then maybe what their performance status and comorbidities are. And I do want to say that in some patients, you can take a wait and watch approach. In patients that have just biochemical progression, sometimes if they don't have anemia, they don't have any new bone lesions, it's maybe light chain escape and they only have a very low level of light change, nothing in the urine, you might be able to watch the pace of their disease for a small bit of time. But patients that have any clinical symptoms, you know, new bone lesion, hypercalcemia, anemia, renal insufficiency. And this person does have renal insufficiency, I think. So this person has to actually get therapy. Or if they have a history of high risk disease, you want to start their therapy right away. So I will give you some of my A few pearls for me for treating relapsed refractory myeloma. The first is, when they're progressing on a maintenance drug or maintenance therapy, that, in my mind, equals resistance. If they're on 10 of lenalidomide, then they are resistant to lenalidomide. I would consider them refractory to lenalidomide. When we consider our treatment, and here on this slide shows the various studies that have been done in the early relapse setting, we have three big classes of drugs, right? We have proteasome inhibitors, we have immunomodulatory drugs, and then we have monoclonal antibodies. For the monoclonal antibodies, we have CD38 antibodies, we have daratumab and e-cetuximab, and then we have elotuzumab, an antibody that targets LAMF7. I will say another, and so those three big classes are going to be the ones that we switch around for our relapse based therapy. We choose a couple, put them together for our first relapse, and then we switch it around for second relapse, third relapse, etc. I will say a couple of things, and that is if somebody's refractory to say carfilzomib, then probably going back to bortezomib or exazomib is probably not therapeutic. If somebody's refractory to pomalidomide, then going back to lenalidomide is probably not therapeutic. We always think about going back to something people had in the past, and we'll talk a little bit more about when you can go back to a CD38 if you're exposed to a CD38 in the future. But in these studies that we have in front of us, we have the CASTOR and the POLIX trial that were done more than five years ago. But they really established a CD38 antibody, in my mind, as a really good choice for early relapse. In fact, the CASTOR trial, which lends sensitive patients, randomized patients, to daratumab lenalidomide dexamethasone versus lenalidomide dexamethasone and showed the longest PFS that we've ever seen in a relapse trial, 45 months. So it still is a really excellent choice of therapy in patients that are len sensitive. In the Pollack's trial was daratumab plus bortezomib and dexamethasone. Didn't have as long of a progression-free survival, but certainly would be an okay choice in somebody that has len refractory disease. And as first As out-of-the-gate patients have first relapse, it's actually a good regimen to choose with a PFS that's right around 20, 21 months. On the bottom right, we have the eloquent trials, which elotuzumab Lendex, I think is a hard one to choose because we have so many active partners, and I think elotuzumab may not be the most active partner with linoleumide dexamethasone, but trials looking at elotuzumab with Palmdex actually were pretty, pretty positive with a PFS in that group of patients with elopalmdex of 10, 10 and a half months versus Palmdex which is half, half of that PFS. So then the more recent trials have really been the Daratumab and the Isituximab trials. And I want to talk more further about the CANDOR and the APOLLO trials using Daratumab with a PI or an IMID, and then the Icaria and Ikema trials using Isituximab with pomalidomide and carfilzomib, a PI. So here's, here's the candor trial looking at the PFS of a triplet versus a doublet and I'll say that kind of every triplet versus doublet trial that we've done right has shown a benefit for the triplet over the doublet. In essence, the standard of therapy and somebody that has relapsed right now is to go with a triplet we haven't really done so many quadruplets although I'm sure that's going to come up in the next, you know, three to five years but right now it's we're looking at triplet combinations. Daratumab, carfilzomib, and dexamethasone in the maroon curve, and then carfilzomib and dexamethasone in the yellow curve. And you can see a marked difference. The medium PFS, in fact, one of the highest that we've seen in relapse refractory trial, 28.6 months, whereas the control group had a PFS of about 15 months with a really low hazard ratio of 0.59. Now if we look at across subgroups who actually benefited from DERA-KD versus KD, pretty much every subgroup benefited. Those with low stage or high stage, low age or higher age, and all the cytogenetic risk groups all actually benefited from getting the triplet versus doublet. I think no surprise. from that. And let's look at the Apollo study. So the Apollo study looked at sub-q deratumab plus pomalidomide and dexamethasone versus POMDEX, again, a relapse refractory myeloma. These patients all had prior lenalidomide exposure, but they could have just one prior line of therapy. In this one, Again, you can see that the median PFS was 12.4 months versus 6.9 months so marked advantage for the triplet with their two members is the doublet of just palm decks. And I think that led to us using those Daratumab-based triplets, Daracarfilzomabdex or Darapalmdex for a lot of patients in early relapse. Now on came the Ikeria or the Isatuximab trials. This is the Ikeria study looking at Isatuximab and Palmdex and relapse refractory myeloma. These patients had two prior lines of therapy. And if you look at the Isapalmdex PFS, 11.5 months versus six and a half months. So very similar to the Apollo trial. And you can see here that the time to next therapy, if you went on ESA POMDEX, obviously, if you have a longer PFS, you also have a longer time to the next therapy. So a marked difference with ESA POMDEX versus POMDEX. And these are data that were actually recently presented at ASCO from Paul Richardson. The other interesting thing I will point out is, What they looked at if patients receive ESA Palm Dex and then went on to receive a Daratumumab regimen as the next regimen, you can see that the PFS with a Daratumumab-based regimen is much lower than if you choose a non-Daratumumab regimen, so 2.2 months versus 4.5 months. I think the take home from this is it's really hard to go from a CD38 containing regimen directly to another CD38 antibody containing regimen. I do think you can go back to CD38 at some point in time, but you have to have some duration in between, maybe three or six months in between. And the belief is that maybe that actually allows for increased expression of CD38 back on the cell surface, or maybe for some of the mechanisms of resistance to fade away so that they can actually respond to CD38 in the future line of therapy. And then one of my favorite studies, and that's the IKEMA study, looking at isatuximab, carfilzomib, and dexamethasone versus carfilzomib and dexamethasone. And here is data that was originally presented by Philippe Moreau at the American hematology, sorry, the European hematology meetings. And basically, the PFS with 20 months of follow up was not reached with EISA-KD. It's believed to be at least 28 months, maybe a little bit better, similar to the CANDOR data, versus 19 months in the carfilzomib and dexamethasone, so a marked advantage. If we look at, similar to CANDOR, if we looked at the patients who are benefiting, we see that the high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities and FISH abnormalities benefit. There was only a small number of patients who had deletion 17P, so the error bar is cross one. But the 414 and the 1416 also have benefit, as well as patients who have isolated gain 1q21 or have no gain of Q21 and standard risk cytogenetics. Now, the other thing that we have looked at in the ITEMA study, we looked at patients who had renal insufficiency going on to therapy. And there is actually a benefit to ISA-KD versus KD in terms of improvement in renal function. And you can see on on this curve. This is a capital Meyer estimate. Over time, you can see that that he said KD is in blue above with patients that have a low ejection fraction, as well as those that have. a higher, sorry not ejection fraction, GFR versus those that have a normal GFR. You see there's a benefit in really both of those. And the worst patients are the patients who get KD who have the lowest GFR. We also looked at depth of response from a chemo. You can see, I'll focus your attention over to the right, looking at MRD analysis. We looked at, by intent to treat, 30 percent of the patients with ISA-KD achieved MRD negativity versus only 13 percent of the patients are receiving KD, so a marked difference. Now, the MRD was only done on patients who achieved MRD negativity. If you look just at the patients who had a VGPR or better, it was actually the MRD negative rate was 41 percent, so really a pretty amazing MRD negative rate. I think the monoclonal antibodies, this is a common theme in early redox trials, that the monoclonal antibodies using CD38 antibodies have the best chance of getting deep MRD negative responses, even in early relapse. And that's why I think using a CD38 antibody-based therapy is really important at early therapy. So summary points. Generally, antibody platforms, they have been extremely well-tolerated. Adding an antibody to KD, PD, whatever backbone you see, it doesn't really add all that much in terms of toxicity. They are associated with hypogammaglobulin anemia and potentially a small increased risk of infections, including pneumonias. Many of those are viral infections. We do consider, especially for patients who have severe hypogammaglobulin anemia, some say less than 400, some say less than 300, of using prophylactic IVIG. And then obviously you need to treat infections aggressively. Now it's been nice that with subcutaneous dairy tube map, especially through the COVID pandemic, we get people in quick and out quick. And it essentially really eliminated severe infusion-associated reactions by using subcutaneous therapy. I will say that there is a clinical trial ongoing using isatuximab as subcutaneous administration and we're looking forward to seeing more of those data in the future. Now I will say in terms of cytopenias, which is common in the relapsed refractory setting, that They're more common when you combine a CD38 antibody with pomalidomide versus a CD38 antibody and a PI. And so if somebody has baseline cytopenias, I might choose a PI over pomalidomide. So some take-home thoughts from me. Antibody therapy and early relapse has really shown some deep and durable responses that patients are able to achieve in some scenarios MRD negativity. And it's especially important in my mind in antibody naive patients. Triplets are certainly the best therapies for patients for early relapse. I try to use a triplet over a doublet for almost everybody. And I think you can come up with a triplet that In transplant, the patients who had prior transplant are not that they'd be able to tolerate. In LEN refractory patients, if they're refractory to an IMID, I usually gravitate to a CD38 antibody together with a PI, and especially carfilzomib because the data from IKEMA and CANDOR is so positive. Then like I said, subsequent CD38 antibody treatment is difficult if you do it one directly following the other. So back to the, back to the case, Ellen was diagnosed at age 60, revised ISS stage one disease, ECOG performance data zero to one, treated with VRD then to transplant and subsequently received lenalidomide as maintenance. And then progression. After three years on land maintenance, and had mild renal insufficiency. So she's now 63 there's a ton of options. I certainly would recommend a CD 38 base triplet. And that could feature dare to map or use a text map. And the backbone could be POM with dexamethasone or carfilzomib with dexamethasone. I think the Akema data with showing improvements in renal insufficiency and good responses in those patients might push me in this case to go with e-cetuximab plus carfilzomib and dexamethasone or a CD38 plus carfilzomib and dexamethasone. There are other platforms. I'll hand it back to you, Nina.

Great, fantastic discussion. And there's, it's funny because there's so many choices in newly diagnosed, and now it's like, there's so many choices in the one to three prior lines. So just to kind of get an idea, I want to hit on some points that you talked about. The dosing of carfilzomib, when you combine it with daratumumab or isatuximab, can you talk a little bit about that and how easy is it to get in those doses? It seems a little bit more than what we'd be used to. And what about weekly dosing?

Nina, that is really an excellent question, and a question that I feel to our referring doctors all the time and that is, you know, with the candor and I chemo study the carfilzomib dosing was 56 milligrams per meter squared on day 1289 1516, which a lot of us don't use anymore. I'll say the phase one study that we did here at UCSF as part of the MMRC was in combination with carfilzomab at 27 milligrams per meter squared at day 1, 8, 9, 15, 16. And we saw that together with e-cituximab, we saw really good responses at that dose. There are also, Dr. Chari published a study using daratumab with carfilzomab at 70 milligrams per meter squared weekly. And that's actually approved on the label for daratumab in combination with carfilzomab at 70 milligrams per meter squared. And I certainly have gravitated towards the towards the weekly dosing of carfilzomib together with a CD38 antibody. As you know, we have a study here doing the same thing with isatuximab together with 70 milligrams per meter squared of carfilzomib weekly, day 1, 8, and 15.

Yeah. I want to kind of go around and see, start again, you know, with this case, this is sort of our garden variety patient who has a progression. And we, and you talked a little bit about what leads you to, to, to cause to change treatment, you know, not just the numbers, but maybe something else going on as well. Shaji, if this was your patient, you know, pretty good performance status transplant, three years of maintenance therapy, a little bit of renal insufficiency, what would you choose as your second line therapy?

I think one of the important questions, and I think Tom alluded to this as well, is for somebody who has learned refractory at the time of the first relapse, do you change the class of drug and use a K-combination, a PI-based combination, or a second-generation IMID-based combination? I think there's agreement in terms of the monoclonal antibody being there. The big question is, what do you combine it with? In my own practice, I tend to use more of the PI. So I think the data or isatexamab in combination with cafelsimab, again, cafelsimab weekly and dex is my favorite go-to combination, unless the patient says, you know, sub-Q data is going to become once a month. They would rather be on a pill. Then, of course, the data or isatexamab pomdex might be a reasonable option as well.
Yeah. What about you, Nupur? What would you do for this patient?

So I honestly think this patient has a choice, Nina, and you know I've been listening to both Tom and Shaji agree, but there is a lot of data in REV refractory patients where we've used pomalidomide. So pomalidomide with a CD38 monoclonal antibody whichever one you want to choose. would be perfectly reasonable, specifically in renal failure, because pomelos does not require a whole lot of dose adjustment when you're giving it in renal disease. One thing to be careful about when you're combining pomalidomide with a CD30 monoclonal antibody, and I think Tom alluded to that already, is you might need a little bit of dose adjustment of pomalidomide given the cytopenias. Using a proteasome inhibitor, whether you use it with bortezomib or carfilzomib is perfectly reasonable. I think with renal insufficiency, if there are issues around fluid retention, et cetera, I'd be a little careful with the use of carfilzomib, that's all.
And are you using weekly carfilzomib for this combination as well?

Yeah, routinely, weekly. I can't remember the last time I've used twice a week carfilzomib. You know, I don't go all the way up to 70 mg per meter square. I don't know if you need that. So 56 is what we typically do. There are times when we also in the relapse setting are, you know, there's data at this year's meetings looking at quadruplets. So the 56 migs per meter square seems reasonable. I've rarely had to go all the way up to 70 migs per meter square.

Great. And just, Tom mentioned it a little bit. Anybody here, maybe I'll just ask Shaji, subcutaneous daratumumab, really, have you just moved completely to sub-q daratumumab? Anytime you do IV before sub-q, any issues?

No, we have been uniformly using sub-Q data for all the new patients who have started on it. Majority of the patients who have been on IV have opted to convert to sub-Q, and that has become the default. If someone has significant local infusion reaction or local skin reaction, that's probably the only place where we would switch over to an IV formulation.

Great. And Tom, last question for you. Nubra mentioned it, and you also talked about it, the cytopenias that you do see with daratumumab and potentially to pomalidomide, and maybe less so if you use a proteasome inhibitor. Can you comment on the cytopenias that you guys saw in Ikema, and possibly similar to Kandor, if they were a real issue for you?

Yeah, so specifically in Aikima, the grade three neutropenia was really low. It was less than 20% actually. And it's actually more, like Nupur said, it's more significant when you use it together with pomalidomide. And I do think people have to watch that closely. A, you can dose reduce the pomalidomide, but you also can use growth factor. So the other possibility is to give them, and I've done, a couple of days daily dosing of growth factor, but also it's quite convenient to give them a pegylated GCSF and to get them through the cycle, which is pretty effective at eliminating some of the neutropenia. Thrombocytopenia isn't as severe, and so you can use platelet growth factors too if need be.

Yeah. I'd say for this patient, I probably, it would depend on the other sort of vital sign of the patient, you know, convenience, could the patient come or not. And so if they couldn't come that often, I would give Darapalm Dex. And I agree with you, Tom, that using growth factor, which I actually traditionally do sometimes on day two or day nine with NuLasta, and it totally solves the problem. You can get them through the cycle. Or if the patient was willing to come and, or maybe, had some issues which would push me towards PI, I would give daratumab, carfilzomib, or isatuximab, carfilzomib. So any of those is a great option. This has been a really good discussion about the early relapses, and I think a lot of food for thought, and it can't go wrong, basically. So now we're going to move on to the next section, which is the challenge of pre-treated disease, choosing a path from novel mechanisms to BCMA. So we'll look at a slightly different case. This is Michael, who's a 62-year-old man with revised ISS stage 2 myeloma. initially treated with BRD induction, transplant, and lead maintenance, achieved a CR. Ultimately, three years later, did have progression and got daratumumab, pomalidomide, dexamethasone, and did achieve a VGPR, was doing fine for about a year, but then was diagnosed with a new L2 plasma cytoma and a rising M protein, then got carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone. But unfortunately, that only held him for seven months, at which point he then had progressive disease. So I want to talk about some of the newer agents that we're seeing in the space for multiple myeloma. And what's exciting about a lot of these is some are new ideas on an old agent, or some are just completely new ideas. And I think that's great because if we know anything about the myeloma cell, it's smart. So we want to target it in different ways. So first drug we want to talk about is melflufen, which has a new combination partner. It could be a new combination partner in relapse for fracturing multiple myeloma. And it's interesting because this is one of those new twists on an old idea where it's a first-in-class peptide drug conjugate. And it's interesting to think about this. It's actually kind of a targeted therapy because it's targeting the aminopeptidase, which is actually more frequently found in these myeloma cells. So the drug is actually conjugated as it is initially given, and then it's very lipophilic, gets into these myeloma cells where there happen to be more aminopeptidases. and therefore it's targeting the myeloma cells. Now with the aminopeptidase in the myeloma cell, the drug can be cleaved and very active, and it allows this very active melphalan, essentially alkylating agent, to be effective in the myeloma cell. So we know that melphalan or alkylating agents in general are very active in multiple myeloma cells. So this is sort of a targeted way of delivering it, taking advantage of the myeloma cells own metabolism and cellular characteristics. So that's kind of an interesting take and again, a new twist on an old drug. The phase two horizon trial, which was very important in getting this drug approved, Melflufen, excuse me, plus dexamethasone was very active in heavily pretreated relapsed refractory multiple myeloma. And again, this was what ultimately led to FDA approval. And then the ANCHER study assessed melflupin plus dexamethasone with daratumumab or bortezomib in relapsed refractory multiple myeloma, and this did include patients' refractory to IMIDs and PIs. And it's just important to know that, like all drugs, we start out with single-agent activity and then try to start using them in combinations, again, because the myeloma cell is very smart and you want to sort of punch it from different directions to get rid of it. So you can see here the melpufonidexamethasone has a clinically meaningful efficacy in heavily pretreated relapsed refractory multiple myeloma patients, and this includes triple class refractory and extramedullary disease patients. And you can see here, this is the data from the Verizon trial, 157 patients that were treated, and the overall response rate here was 29%, which pretty held up in the triple class refractory a 26% overall response rate in those patients that were triple class refractory, the median duration of response for these patients was 5.5 months with the PFS around there 4.2 months, and an overall survival of 11.6 months, I will point out that this drug is. kind of easy from a user perspective. It's a day one of a 28-day cycle with weekly dexamethasone, and as of now, has to be given centrally, but there are studies ongoing to evaluate if it will be able to be given peripherally. And I think it's important to know that this kind of schedule actually is something that we're used to, and it's kind of user-friendly, and the main thing to watch out for with this drug is cytopenias, and we'll talk about that in the discussion. Now, the ANCHR study we talked about as melflupin as a combination partner in relapse refractory multiple myeloma, and this looked at the efficacy and the safety of this. Again, patients got melflupin in combination with dexamethasone and daratumumab or dexamethasone and bortezomib, but you can see here that the combination was well tolerated. And again, cytopenias were the most pertinent AE that was seen And you can see in ASCO, the overall response rate for the melphalofen dexamethasone daratumumab was 57% with the 30 milligram dose. And that's been identified as the optimal dose for combination, excuse me, with bortezomib. So with this in mind, we can think of how there may be new drugs that we're going to be able to use a single agent and thinking about our patient in this case, and that we also might be able to use in combination. And we look forward to seeing how we may be able to combine these new mechanisms of action with drugs that already exist. Another drug that has a completely new mechanism of action is selonexor, and this is an XPO1 inhibitor. So, XPO1 is a nuclear exportant, and selonexor inhibits this and ultimately allows for retention or nuclear retention and activation of tumor suppressor proteins. And this allows for the tumor suppressor proteins to do their activity and to suppress the tumor growth of, in particular, multiple myeloma cells. So, this is a very interesting and novel way of approaching multiple myeloma cells, such that they're particularly targeted to not grow and take advantage of its internal mechanisms to prevent that. So, Cellinexor was originally studied sort of as a single agent, well, with dexamethasone, and this data was originally presented several years ago and then published in the New England Journal in 2019. This is the STORM data showing its effect on patients with relapsed refractory multiple myeloma, and you can see here in the waterfall plot that the overall response rate was 26% and then getting to an MR or better clinical benefit response rate of about 40% in these patients. And this was a way for us to see how this drug could be used. This was used in a twice weekly setting and did have some significant adverse effects including nausea and decrease in appetite, but then was studied in other ways, not just with dexamethasone, but in a subsequent sort of basket way in the stomp data and ultimately in the Boston study. The Boston study, as you can see here, is selonexor with bortezomib and dexamethasone versus bortezomib and dexamethasone. And I want to point out some interesting things about the Boston study. Again, as we've seen sort of with the other drugs as well, we see single agent activity initially, so patients can get this drug but then if you combine it, you can actually get better activity which is true of most multiple myeloma agents. Interestingly, in the Boston study, the Selenexor bortezomib dexamethasone arm was with weekly bortezomib. So the Selenexor was weekly, the bortezomib was weekly, and the dexamethasone was twice weekly. But the control arm of bortezomib and dexamethasone was twice weekly bortezomib and dexamethasone as it has been traditionally used. But even with more bortezomib and dexamethasone, excuse me, more bortezomib in the control arm, you can see here that there was a significant improvement in PFS for the selenex or bortezomib dexamethasone arm versus the bortezomib dexamethasone arm, as you can see in the orange versus black curves here. As many of you know, there are different AEs associated with this combination, and you can see that the cytopenias definitely were more present in the triplet arm versus the doublet arm, particularly thrombocytopenia. This is something that we have also noticed using this drug and oftentimes can be ameliorated with judicious use of growth factor, which is actually more permitted now than it used to be. And I would say that once you get the patient sort of set up on a system of growth factor, even for platelets, it's actually not so bad and you can get them through the cycles and then they can have a benefit from this combination of therapies. Very interesting sub-analysis that has happened for the Boston has been different updates that have happened over the past year at ASH and ASCO. So the first one is for patients who've been prior exposed to PIs. And I think this is important because they did an analysis to see which patients, and it was about a 70 or so percent of patients that had been exposed to prior PIs. And they looked at them to see how they did in this particular randomization. And it turns out that the patients who had prior PI versus who didn't, still benefited from Selenexor bortezomib dexamethasone versus the doublet. And I think this is important because these are our patients, right? We have a lot of patients that are getting BRD up front, then transplant, and then maintenance, and then progress, and they're not actually bortezomib refractory. So, this shows us that we could potentially use bortezomib again with a novel agent. So, I thought this analysis that Ash was actually very pertinent to our patient population And you can also see that there was other analyses in older patient populations. And in that case, XPD, as it's now called with Selenix or Fortesnit Dex, was associated with a significant survival benefit of both improved PFS and improved overall, excuse me, overall response rate without worsening peripheral neuropathy. Now, I will point out that the peripheral neuropathy actually was worse in the control arm because of the dosing of bortezomib-likely, because of the dosing of bortezomib being the 1, 4, 8, and 11, the twice-weekly bortezomib dosing versus the weekly bortezomib dosing that was seen in the triplet arm. So that was an interesting way of looking at the data, an interesting outcome that actually, as far as peripheral neuropathy goes, the triplet was better than the doublet. Another very interesting drug that has come onto the scene is bilantam and mapadotan. This is the first BCMA targeting drug that was FDA approved. This is an antibody drug conjugate, which has with it an antibody against BCMA conjugated to MMAF, which is a toxin. So this allows for a correctly deployed toxin to the myeloma cell. And this was studied in both the DREAM1 and the DREAM2 program. This is very interesting because, again, novel mechanism of action and novel target. So, this is the first ADC and the first PCMA drug that was approved for multiple myeloma patients. And again, this was based on the DREAM-2 data, where single-agent valentamine methadotin was studied in heavily pretreated multiple myeloma patient populations, median of six prior lines of therapy, And you can see here, the overall response rate was 31%. This is the curves that you can see here. And interestingly, they looked at the duration of response. And for those who did respond, there was a duration of response median of about 11 months. So again, another drug that we can use now as a single agent, and we have to consider that we may be able to use it in combination. which leads us to DREAM-6, and there are a variety of DREAM programs looking at different combinations of drugs with belantamab, mapidotin. And in DREAM-6, it was studied belantamab, mapidotin plus bortezomib and dexamethasone. Again, this is a multi-arm study, but they reported on the VD arm with belantamab, mapidotin. And you can see that the 2.5 milligrams per kilogram every three weeks schedule was active and safe, and this is in patients with at least three prior lines of therapy, which included bortezomib and daratumumab you can see here overall response rate of 78%. So this is a good. sort of launching pad to think about what we can do with our novel drugs, how we can maybe use them in the relapse refractory multiple myeloma setting where patients have already gotten so many drugs of the ones that we've talked about already in this session. So going back to this case, we can talk again about Michael, who's a 62-year-old man with revised ISS stage two myeloma. Again, he got VRD induction transplant, lenalidomide maintenance, had a CR three years, then had PD, got DPD, had a VGPR, and then a year later had another progression, so now third-line treatment with KCD, carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone, and then progresses again. So the patient's had three lines of therapy, and I want to talk about what the options are for Michael. Could he use something like XVD or XPD, which is selenix or pomalidomide dexamethasone, another army studied in stomp, another novel mechanism of action, for example, philanthromab, methadone, eventually when you would consider cellular therapy. So, I want to kick it back to my colleagues and talk about this. I think this is where we get into uncharted territory, right? There's no right answer here. Tom, what do you think about a patient like this, considering that these new drugs that we've talked about, what might you use in this situation and why?

reference_conclusion: At first relapse after progression on lenalidomide maintenance, treatment should be initiated rather than observation given the presence of renal insufficiency. The consensus favored a CD38 antibody–based triplet regimen, with preference for a proteasome inhibitor backbone in lenalidomide-refractory disease. Isatuximab plus carfilzomib and dexamethasone was identified as the preferred option in view of the IKEMA data, including activity in patients with renal insufficiency; daratumumab- or isatuximab-based pomalidomide/dexamethasone or carfilzomib/dexamethasone combinations were also considered appropriate alternatives based on patient convenience and tolerance.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female; pregnant with second child at time of thyroid cancer diagnosis. She was 10 weeks pregnant at initial specialty evaluation.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable goitre and bilateral palpable thyroid nodules.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of both thyroid nodules was malignant (Bethesda category VI).

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in September 2019 showed bilateral thyroid nodules with thyromegaly.  
- Right thyroid nodule measured 1.7 cm, solid with hypoechoic areas and smooth margins; categorized as TI-RADS 4.  
- Left thyroid nodule measured 3.7 cm, heterogeneous, slightly hypoechoic, with lobulated margins and possible microcalcifications; categorized as TI-RADS 5.  
- Repeat thyroid and neck ultrasound at 10 weeks’ gestation showed grossly stable thyroid nodules and no suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genomic classifier testing performed externally showed BRAF V600E mutation positivity in both nodules.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma (Bethesda category VI, BRAF V600E positive) in a woman 10 weeks pregnant at initial specialty evaluation, where repeat thyroid and neck ultrasound showed grossly stable thyroid nodules and no suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No symptoms of hoarseness, dysphagia, or shortness of breath were reported at presentation.  
- No history of radiation exposure was reported.  
- Family history was notable for a maternal aunt with papillary thyroid cancer.

She's also a fantastic thyroid person, so she'll be a panelist with me as well. She just found that out. So let's start with case number one. Show the slides for case number one, and Valentina, tell us what you got. Next slide, please.

So today, the first case that we'll discuss is thyroid cancer management during pregnancy. So, next slide. So, 26-year-old female who was found to have palpable goitre on physical exam. At that time, ultrasound of the thyroid was done, and in September 2019, it showed bilateral thyroid nodules and some thyromegidine. Next slide. So, here are the nodules, and she has bilateral thyroid nodules, two, one on the right, one on the left side. On the right side, thyroid nodule was measuring 1.7 centimetres. It was solid with hypoechoic areas. Margins were rather smooth and it was characterised as thyrus 4. On the right side, the thyroid nodule was measuring 3.7 centimetres, and it was heterogeneous, slightly hypoechoic with labellated margins, with possible some micro-classifications which we cannot really see well on that representative slide, but it was characterised as thyroid 5. Next slide. She had biopsy of both nodules, right 1.4 and left 3.7 centimeters, and both come back as Bethesda Category 6 malignant. A former genomic sequencing classifier determined that she has BRAF B600 imitation. We're not sure why that was sent, it was done outside, but now we know that both of them were BRAF positive. On the day when she was found that she has papillary thyroid cancer, she was found she's pregnant with her second child. So she came to appointment with her mother, with her husband, with her one-year-old son, and of course, everybody was very worried about that new diagnosis. Just of note that her thyroid nodules were symptomatic and she did not experience any symptoms of hoarseness or dysphagia or shortness of breath. She actually, she felt them, but they were not really
Next slide.

There was no history of radiation exposure. Her maternal aunt was diagnosed with papillary thyroid cancer, but did really well. So, at the time she went, when I saw her, she was already 10 weeks pregnant. And at that time, we obtained ultrasound of the thyroid and neck. ultrasound of the neck did not reveal any suspicious lymphadenopathy. Thyroid nodules at that time remained grossly stable. We also did fibro-optic laryngoscopy, and we found out that her vocal cords were mobile, and she did not have a vocal cord paralysis. So she was there for discussion, what to do with her now biopsy-proven bilateral pathogenic thyroid cancer that was BRAF positive. And of course, she read about it all, and she was quite concerned about the new diagnosis. Next slide. That's called an ultrasound of the thyroid at 10 weeks, and it basically showed grossly stable thyroid nodules, and so there was no really, like, worrisome lymph nodes to show on the imaging.

Okay, perfect, Valentina. Dr. Pettore, I'm going to come to you. Um, you know, we watch a lot of these small thyroid cancers during pregnancy, but this is a 3.7 centimeter nodule. So when you see, I mean, she's obviously devastated. You get pregnant and cancer at the same time. You know, talk to me, how do you sort of set the stage for her? What do you present to her when you meet her the first time?

Well, probably I will try to calm her down and calm the family down, trying to say that we are not in a rush in this case. And of course, that there are some cases that escape from what we usually see. But we have clearly seen that thyroid cancer during pregnancy probably does not have a worse outcome than thyroid cancer during outside this time of the life. So probably I will try to talk with the patient, with the family, and try to calm them down and decide together which pathway we should go. together with the decision, putting clearly that we do not need to rush in this case. We wouldn't indicate surgery probably from our side to a patient with this situation.
Dr. Tarascova, how did you factor in this BRAF positivity? I mean, everybody always worries about BRAF. Did that change, Valentina, how you were thinking about it in terms of watching or not?

From my standpoint, I definitely took into consideration in terms of like, I was certain that it would be papillary thyroid cancer. We know that 63% of papillary thyroid cancer are positive. And from my standpoint, it's basically saying that it's classical papillary thyroid cancer and does not necessarily upgrade the risk. Yes, we'll know that it will present with some probably lymph node involvement. We know that there will be lymphatic involvement, but in the absence of other mutations, I think that this represents classical papillary thyroid cancer.
Dr. Hartle, what do you say when she comes to see you, Dana? These are pretty good-sized papillary cancer nodules. I'm sure she can probably feel them.

reference_conclusion: During pregnancy, the patient was managed with active surveillance rather than immediate surgery, with serial thyroid and neck ultrasonography demonstrating overall stability and no new lymphadenopathy. Following delivery, total thyroidectomy was performed without lymph node dissection because no nodal disease was identified. Postoperatively, thyroid hormone replacement was adjusted to achieve TSH goals, and radioactive iodine was not recommended. Ongoing surveillance with thyroglobulin monitoring and follow-up neck ultrasonography was planned, with reassessment in six months.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 18-year-old female; senior in high school; previously healthy and active.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodule identified on routine physical examination/wellness check by pediatrician.

[ diagnosis ]: Cribriform morular thyroid carcinoma, initially identified on fine-needle aspiration as papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was positive for papillary carcinoma. Surgical pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm cribriform morular thyroid carcinoma. Histologic description included absence of colloid, cribriform architecture, morular formations, and papillary structures. The tumor was intrathyroidal. No lymph node involvement was identified. No other high-risk pathologic features were reported.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated several small thyroid nodules measuring approximately 10-15 mm, generally classified as TI-RADS 3 and 4. A suspicious hypoechoic solid isthmus nodule was described. No abnormal cervical lymph nodes were identified on ultrasound.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Prior parental whole-genome sequencing reportedly showed no abnormal FAP-associated mutation in either parent.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed and was positive for papillary carcinoma. Surgical resection of the thyroid lesion was performed. Postoperative thyroglobulin was reported as very low/less than 1.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after thyroid surgery for a 1.4 cm intrathyroidal cribriform morular thyroid carcinoma, without documented nodal disease and without reported high-risk features.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history of thyroid disease or thyroid cancer. No childhood radiation exposure. No symptoms concerning for thyroid malignancy were reported. No family history of colorectal cancer was reported. The presentation included multiple thyroid nodules.

I know we've got two other great cases ahead and time moves quickly. It's a pleasure to present to you a case that I thought taught me a lot and had me reflect on a few things, share it with all of you. This is an 18-year-old female who's referred for a thyroid nodule. She's completely healthy, active. She's a senior in high school and it was just a routine physical exam, a wellness check where her pediatrician actually noticed the nodule, and she has no family history of thyroid problems, let alone thyroid cancer, and also the usual questions, no childhood radiation or symptoms of concern. She was completely healthy and not worried about this at all. To keep us moving, obviously, I think most people when you would have a nodule suspected would pursue an ultrasound. And I'm just going to cut to the chase on that. This is the report of the ultrasound, which, as you see, shows several small nodules, roughly 10 to 15 millimeters, and generally classified tirads three and four, and notably no abnormal lymph nodes. And the first teaching point for me a little bit was the questions I posed at the bottom of the slide, which Increasingly, I've been a bit more tuned to this question of how to think about age as a risk factor for thyroid cancer, but I'll throw that out to Eyal maybe a little bit, which is, is there really a meaningful difference in overall risk when you think of a nodule in a younger person than an older person, however you want to define those terms? And then also, do we think about cancer risk at all differently, whether it's one or whether it's multiple? So maybe Eyal, I'll toss it to you for a second.

Yeah, so I think the answer is yes and yes. With age people, healthy people, have more and more nodules and the risk per nodule decreases. So most patients after the age, most people after the age of 60 or 70 have nodules. A younger patient like this one, 18 years old, the risk of malignancy in an autule is as high as 30%, as opposed to in older patients where it's down to 5%. So yes, so this is suspicious already by just existing, even before we see the ultrasound features. And Multiple macroscopic nodules are also uncommon because many times we have multifocal disease. We have one dominant nodule and several small ones. So when we see a younger patient with several macroscopic lesions, we need to think whether it's part of a syndrome. Does she have a genetic tendency for malignancy?

No, well said, and I agree, and I'll go very briefly, but I'm always drawn to these data. Nora Kwong was one of our fellows now a decade ago or so, and clearly, at least in our data set here in Boston, there's a clear age related. decline in risk as you age forward, but the younger individual, I do worry about a little bit more, just average entering a nodule workup, that they have a higher risk. And as you quoted, A.L., Ari Wassner's data on the pediatric population clearly shows that line continuing. So, I also just throw out that, you know, we should think about, I think, pediatric or younger adult nodules in cancer is also driven likely by different processes, and there's a wealth of data thinking about the different mutations. These are earlier data. It's not as in-depth as we likely would genetically screen now, but for the sake of time, I'll move on. And the data is showing, just as we've all said, the risk of cancer per nodule is much higher in children. That said, it is important for radiologists to sort of harmonize their reporting in a standard that is uniform that makes sense. So on one hand, I would say, yes, this is a suspicious nodule. Absolutely. And that's what we did. And it did return positive for papillary carcinoma. And obviously the next step here would be, I think, surgical resection. Margie.

I can.

So a morula is just kind of squamoid, but not really characterizing a kind of round knot. of squamoid cells. And so, those, those are the two features that I just described the big empty wide spaces, that's cribriform, and then the squamoid balls, that's the morula. Now that's not those are not the only findings but those are the two findings for the name. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma with symptomatic relapse manifested by an L2 plasmacytoma and rising paraprotein.

[ diagnosis ]: Multiple myeloma, Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) stage II at initial diagnosis. Subsequently developed triple-class refractory relapsed/refractory disease after exposure to immunomodulatory therapy, proteasome inhibitors, and anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody therapy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial therapy consisted of bortezomib/lenalidomide/dexamethasone followed by autologous stem cell transplant and lenalidomide maintenance. Complete response was achieved, followed by disease progression after 3 years. Second-line therapy with daratumumab/pomalidomide/dexamethasone produced remission for approximately 1 year. At subsequent symptomatic relapse with L2 plasmacytoma and rising paraprotein, treatment with carfilzomib/cyclophosphamide/dexamethasone was given, with response duration of approximately 7 months before progressive disease. Subsequent selinexor/bortezomib/dexamethasone resulted in stable disease for a few months, followed by rapid progression.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma after 4 prior lines of therapy, with shortening duration of response at each relapse. Overall health status was described as good. Residual treatment-related toxicity consisted of grade 1 peripheral neuropathy involving the toes.

[ other clinical data ]: Prior exposure included bortezomib, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, carfilzomib, daratumumab, cyclophosphamide, selinexor, and dexamethasone. Autologous stem cell transplant had been performed.

reference_discussion.text: So thank you, Nina. This is, you know, you've gone through a whirlwind tour of myeloma from newly diagnosed all the way to new novel treatments. We'll start out as we did previously with a case. So 62 year old, a gentleman with the RISS stage two was treated with BRD followed by stem cell transplant, rev maintenance, achieved a CR but progressed after three years, got DPD or darapalm dex. developed, had a nice remission for about a year, was symptomatic with an L2 plasma cytoma and a rising paraprotein, got KCD at that time, had, and as you can see with every relapse, you know, the duration of response is decreasing with time, got seven months with this, had progressive disease, ended up getting Selinexor with Bortezomib dexamethasone, had stable disease for a few months and progressed very quickly. Overall, he's in good health, has only side effect from all the treatment he's had is grade one neuropathy of his toes. So obviously, you know, I'm setting the stage for BCMA targeted therapies, you've talked about one such BCMA targeted approach, but just to take a step back here, BCMA is an exciting target which where we've seen a lot of new data now. BCMA stands for B-cell maturation antigen as you all are familiar with, and we know that BCMA is expressed on all myeloma cells, all plasma cells in fact, and excitingly we have several different ways of approaching or targeting BCMA. Nina, you've already mentioned bilantamab mafidotin, which is the antibody drug conjugate, which has been tested and is now FDA approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma. It uses the MFA toxin warhead. And the biggest toxicity that is seen with bilantamab mafidotin is the ocular toxicity, which sort of limits the use of bilantamab mafidotin in the treatment of myeloma. There are other approaches to the use of targeting BCMA. These include bispecific T cell engagers, which we're going to touch on a little bit, but most of this we're going to focus on is cellular therapy or CAR T cells. And this is specifically important because of all the data you've just heard about right now. And this was what you mentioned earlier, Nina, is real-world data. This is the mammoth study. And this is essentially the patient population that we are dealing with in our practices today. These are patients, 275 patients, who were refractory to an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody. And if you look at patients who were either triple or quadruple refractory, you see that the median progression-free survival of these patients is anywhere between three to nine months. The overall survival of these patients is also quite dismal, suggesting that this is a patient population which has an unmet medical need, and using a BCMA-directed targeted approach in this patient population may actually be quite useful. So obviously we've looked at CAR T cell therapy and just to give some background on what CAR T cells entail. CAR stands for chimeric antigen receptors and what CAR T cell technology involves is taking your T cells, inserting a car, in this case what we are using right now in myeloma, second generation cars, including these cars in your lymphocytes, which are then recognizing BCMA. All of these cars have CD3 Zeta which activates your T-cells and most of the cars that we're using in multiple myeloma has the co-stimulatory domain of 4-1BB which allows the expansion of the CAR T-cells so that they can go ahead and then target the BCMA that we've all been talking about. As I mentioned earlier, CAR T-cells are not off the shelf, they require a little bit of manufacturing, so we go through a process of T-cell collection or leukophoresis, which a patient has to undergo. Once these T-cells are collected, they have then to be transfected with the CAR insertion. That usually takes anywhere between two and three weeks, but by the time it comes back to the patient for reinfusion, it's about three or four weeks. And during that time, most of these patients, because we've treated these patients sort of end stage of their disease, have required some form of treatment before they go on to receiving these CAR T-cells. We've had the most recent CAR T cell approval now for myeloma very excitingly in March of this year. This was with IdaCell, which was approved. This was based on some of the data that we have presented and published now. Dr. Munshi presented this data at ASCO last year. This has now been published. in the New England Journal of Medicine earlier this year and has been approved, and as Nina has pointed out, has been approved after four lines of treatment in this patient population. This was the CARMA 2 CARMA trial, which was the phase 2 trial, which got the IDA cell its approval. These are relapsed refractory multiple myeloma patients who've had more than three prior regimens, and they were exposed to both IMIDs, most of them exposed to both lenalidomide as well as pomalidomide, as well as both PIs, that is bortezomib as well as carfilzomib, as well as the majority of patients had seen the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies as well. As mentioned already, you have to go through the leukophoresis process, and prior to giving back these CAR T-cells, most of these patients get lymphodepleting chemotherapy with fludarabine and cytoxan. 128 patients were treated on this CARMA Phase II trial, which got IDACEL its approval. Again, I just want to highlight the baseline demographics of these patients. These were heavily pretreated patients. We did not really look for BCMA on any of these patients because it is assumed that all plasma cells would express BCMA. Most of these patients were extremely heavily pretreated and the majority of these patients, actually close to 90% of these patients required bridging therapy, underscoring how refractory these patients were so that we could not leave them without any treatment for the three or four weeks that the manufacturing of these CAR T cells was ongoing. If you look at the overall response rate of this and if you look at the target dose, which is the recommended dose of 450 million cells, it was more than 80%, with about 39% of these patients actually achieving a complete response or a stringent complete response in this patient population. Again, really important to remember that the median time to first response is very quick with these immunotherapies, one month in the majority of patients. If you look at the progression-free survival of all patients combined, it was close to one year. Again, looking at target dose of 450 million cells was close to about a year. And if you look at progression-free survival by best response, I mentioned that 39% of these patients achieved a complete response or a stringent complete response, and their median progression-free survival was close to 20 months in this patient population. So really quite remarkable from what you've seen with some of the earlier data that we've seen with the novel drug targets as well. The updated overall survival of this was presented at this year's ASCO meeting. And again, if you look at all comers, it's again about one year or close to two years of an overall survival in this karma patient population. Obviously we're concerned about toxicity with these cellular therapy approaches and the two on target toxicities that we're familiar with include cytokine release syndrome, or CRS, as well as neurotoxicity, The good news here with CRS and neurotoxicity, I'll start off with CRS first. The majority of CRS with either cell was grade 1 and 2 with very little, if any, grade 3 CRS. This was well managed with just the use of either tocilizumab, which is an IL-6 receptor, antibody, or steroids. Neurotoxicity fortunately for us graded by icons was hardly seen in this patient population, we did see some grade one and two neurotoxicity with very little, if any, grade three and four neurotoxicity in this patient population. car T cells in myeloma the toxicity was quite manageable, most of it grade one and two, and I think as we've gotten familiar with the use of these technologies. We've also gotten a lot better with management of these toxicities. Similar to the IDA cell or the Karma trial, the CARTITUDE trial has now been presented and updated data has been presented at this year's ASCO meeting. What has been seen with the CARTITUDE trial is again, the CAR construct here has a bi-epitopic binding to BCMA and with that we are seeing very high response rates in this CAR-TU trial in excess of 95% with very high VGPR rates as well as MRD negative disease. This translates it into a progression-free survival, and the updated results which were presented by Dr. Osmani at this year's ASCO showed an overall PFS at two years of about 22 months, which is quite remarkable with this siltacel drug product. Again, if you compare now Siltacel and Idacel, and again, not a good idea to compare across trials, but just wanted to show you high response rates with all CAR T cell products, whether you use Idacel or Siltacel, you're seeing response rates in excess of 80%. And this is translating into complete response rates of more than 40% in the majority of patients, translating now into PFSs of 12 to 24 months, depending on whichever drug product you're using. Again, one wants to focus on toxicities, obviously with this slight differences between Idacel and Siltacel. Idacel had CRS, in the majority of patients, but most of that CRS occurred early, started at day one. If you look at Siltacel, most of the CRS occurs one week into treatment. With Siltacel, again, very manageable. Majority of CRS with Siltacel as well is grade one and two, very little in terms of grade three and four, and easy to manage with both tocilizumab as well as steroids. We are seeing some other toxicities as well, such as neurotoxicity, which has been seen with both siltacel and idacel. Most of the ICANN's neurotoxicity, which is the early neurotoxicity, is easy to manage, most times with steroids. Occasionally, we've had to use anakinra, but very few patients, if any, have needed that. With cell-to-cell, we have seen a subset of patients with a delayed neurotoxicity, and I think longer follow-up will be able to be more informative in this. This is in a small minority of patients. There's recovery in more than half of these patients, but there have been some toxicities which have gone out three months into the use of cell-to-cell as well. Excitingly we have a whole lot of new anti-BCMA CAR T cell strategies and I've just highlighted all of these which have been presented at different meetings. I will mention one which is the Allogene CAR T cell. This is an off-the-shelf CAR T cell approach so that you do not have to wait for those four to five weeks of actual manufacturing of the shelf CAR T-cells. Again, when you get to the recommended phase two dose of this allogenic CAR T-cell product, we are seeing MRD negative disease in this patient population. And again, no increase in CRS or neurotoxicity. Again, excitingly, we have not seen any graft versus host disease in this patient population. and we're looking forward to seeing longer follow-up to see sustained responses with this as well. So targeting BCMA, I think, is a new standard. It's not a future anymore. We already have drug products in this space. We have the antibody drug conjugate, which Nina has presented. I've shown you data with CAR T-cells. We have the CAR T-cell, IDA cell approved, and we hope to see CILTA cell approved soon. We have a whole lot of bispecific T-cell engagers, which are being studied in this space, which are now in either phase one or phase two trials as we speak, and we're seeing very high response rates with bispecific T cell engagers as well. They were being used intravenously initially, but most of us are now using them succutaneously. We do see the same toxicity that we see with CAR T cells, specifically CRS and neurotoxicity with bispecific T cell engagers as well. So the question often asked, obviously, is who should I refer to for CAR T-cells? I think in the context of myeloma, we should be considering CAR T-cells for all patients with multiple myeloma. And I think it's really important to remember that the toxicity of CAR T-cells is very different from what you imagine with autologous stem cell transplant. So early referral to a center for cellular therapy is critical because it does include us trying to coordinate getting CAR T-cells for these patients. They're not readily available. There is a little bit of logistics involved. So think about CAR T-cells in patients, refer to your centers, and think about clinical trials in this space as well. So I think the current understanding in this space is that immune system is very important across the spectrum of multiple myeloma. We've already demonstrated that BCMA is a validated target in the context of relapsed refractory myeloma. You've seen that antibody drug conjugates are approved now. We've got really exciting data with bispecific T cell engagers, and we have the first CAR T cell drug product approved also in the context of myeloma. And in the future, I do think we're going to try and define how best to combine or sequence some of these approaches. And in the future, we would like to look at next generation approaches to even improve upon some of the efficacy and duration of response that we are seeing with CAR T cells or some of these immune strategies. So coming back to our patient again, our 62-year-old gentleman, Michael, who was initially treated with RVD stem cell transplant, achieved a response, got DPD. Is this patient now somebody you would consider CAR T-cells and how would you sort of approach this patient? I'll open it up to everybody on this panel and send it back to you, Nina, to discuss this case.

Great. Thank you so much for going through all of this data, which is so exciting, so much to know about it, and not just how it works, but what's the efficacy, what are the differences between the modalities we're seeing. This case, I think, is probably what's going to happen to a lot of our patients, I think, because it's a very standard way to approach a patient. We're talking about four lines of therapy here, as you can see listed here. So, I would venture to say that this person is a good candidate for CAR T cell therapy, good health, grade one neuropathy. This is pretty good for our patient population. This patient is probably about 67 years old, which is definitely on track for where a lot of the patients were in CAR T. So, Tom, what do you think are the next practical steps when you have a patient like this? And we get referrals like this all the time from the community.

Yeah, so this, this patient has triple class refractory disease and so this patient certainly is a candidate for the immunotherapies which we're also excited about. For us, the first step is to try to see do we have a trial that's open that this person can could step into either trial using a by specific detail engager or a car. CAR T cell therapy. And then the second thing, if not, then the best therapy for him is what Newport just presented and that is Ida cell is to give them a clinical standard of care CAR T cell therapeutic. And so the first, you know, thing to do is to actually try to get them a slot for an apheresis slot so they can collect the lymphocytes and then send them off. And then you have to do bridging chemotherapy, etc. And so for me, I'm looking for many avenues of therapy. And that's either other treatments to hold them over right to CAR T cell therapy or clinical trial.

Great. Shaji, Nupur brought up a really good point, which is that CAR T cell, and I agree with her, not really as toxic as a Mel 200 transplant. What do you think about that? Do you think our CAR Ts are something that we could give our patients that might not be completely fit for a transplant, but would be okay here?

Yeah, I completely agree. I think the the threshold for how fit the patient needs to be to going into that transplant or the CAR-T is quite different, I think. Even though many of the trials have, you know, had used a very high threshold for the eligibility, it seems like, you know, most of the patients, it's a very short-lasting phase where we have to kind of tie them through the CRS, And the cytopenias, again, you know, it's lymphodepression chemo isn't as intense as what we give them with the high-dose melphalan. The cytopenia duration, certainly at least the significant neutropenia that we get with the transplant certainly isn't here. Certainly some of the, you know, the ability to withstand the infections is important. And, you know, anybody with a reasonable cardiopulmonary status should be able to safely get through those CRS-related symptoms.

reference_conclusion: The patient has triple-class refractory multiple myeloma and is an appropriate candidate for BCMA-directed immunotherapy, with preference for enrollment in an available clinical trial using either a bispecific T-cell engager or CAR T-cell therapy. If no suitable trial is available, standard-of-care idecabtagene vicleucel should be pursued. Next steps are to secure an apheresis slot for lymphocyte collection and proceed with bridging chemotherapy as needed while awaiting CAR T-cell manufacture.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old male from Aldai. Married with six children. Small-scale farmer. NHIF contributor. Admitted from the male surgical ward on 09 June.

[ chief complaint ]: Tongue lesion for 10 months and left facial swelling for 1 week.

[ diagnosis ]: Well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue with locally advanced head and neck disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the tongue lesion showed features consistent with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: CT head and neck demonstrated a heterogeneous tongue mass measuring approximately 4.4 x 4.7 x 4.1 cm. The mass was continuous with the left retromolar space and left parapharyngeal space and filled the left fossa of Rosenmüller. There were diffuse ill-defined left posterior neck masses with loss of normal fascial planes extending from the left retromandibular region to level VII. Both submandibular glands showed heterogeneous enhancing lesions, with possible gland infiltration. Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy was present at levels I-V, with some nodes showing central necrosis. Radiologic impression described a diffuse mass involving the tongue, left buccal/masticator region, and left posterior neck space, with bilateral cervical adenopathy. Paranasal sinuses were clear. No intracranial lesion was identified on the reported study.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Urea was 1.58. Creatinine was 51. CBC: white blood cell count 5.74, hemoglobin 13.8, platelets 410. UECs were reported as normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Tongue lesion biopsy had been performed prior to admission. Left facial swelling began after the biopsy. The patient had been treated with antibiotics during admission for suspected infection. Dental assessment had initially considered Ludwig’s angina; CT imaging did not support Ludwig’s angina. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound had been requested, but results were not yet available.

[ current disease status ]: The tongue lesion had been slowly increasing in size over 10 months and was painful. It was associated with difficulty feeding, excessive saliva and mucus secretion, and inability to protrude the tongue. Mouth opening was limited by pain. The lesion appeared exophytic and erythematous on limited examination. Left facial swelling was painful and affected vision in the left eye. The patient reported difficulty breathing, snoring at night, hotness of body, mild fevers, and weight loss related to poor oral intake. He was able to take soup but not solid food. ECOG performance status was documented as 1. General condition was fair. Cervical, submandibular, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy were present. Vital signs were normal.

[ other clinical data ]: No history of trauma was reported. No family history of malignancy was reported. Smoking history was denied in one part of the record; elsewhere, a remote history of smoking and alcohol use more than 20 years earlier was documented. Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. No significant past medical or surgical history was documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Sudden-onset dysphonia and hoarseness after 3 months of progressive odynophagia, with more recent mild dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma with locally advanced invasive disease involving the trachea and esophagus. Right vocal cord paralysis was present.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy showed follicular neoplasm. Subsequent core biopsy of the primary lesion demonstrated poorly differentiated follicular thyroid cancer. Pathology reported no evidence of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma in the sampled core biopsy, although unsampled anaplastic component elsewhere could not be excluded on that specimen.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinical examination identified a large right neck mass with tracheal deviation to the contralateral side. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a large thyroid mass with posterior invasion extending toward the prevertebral fascia, tracheal involvement at multiple levels, and probable esophageal invasion. Imaging suggested at least 4 cm length of tracheal wall invasion. PET imaging showed the tumor to be highly FDG-avid. PET staging reportedly showed no distant metastatic disease prior to operative consideration.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Laryngoscopy demonstrated right vocal cord paralysis. Bronchoscopy showed through-and-through tracheal invasion with tumor visible within the tracheal lumen; intraluminal tumor measured at least 3 cm. Esophagoscopy demonstrated frank invasion of the esophageal mucosal wall. The patient declined aggressive surgical resection because of anticipated loss of voice and possible loss of swallowing.

[ current disease status ]: Locally advanced invasive poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma involving the trachea and esophagus, with right vocal cord paralysis. No distant metastatic disease had been identified on staging PET.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient reported several days of mild hemoptysis before bronchoscopy. He had a history of heavy smoking. Examination described a hyperinflated chest and a short, bulky neck. No stridor was present clinically.
