reference_discussion.text: And certainly you're singing to the choir because that has always been my perspective as well. But I do find that the art of compromise is an important art to practice, which is why occasionally I will treat some of these folks nowadays with radioactive iodine that I would not have in the past, recognizing that we can do it with negligible risk. I think we need a trial. So we have enough time, I think, to deal with case four, if we're prompt about it. It's a 68-year-old man, sudden onset of dysphonia and hoarseness following three months of progressive discomfort on swallowing, and then more recently, a little dysphagia. He has a large right neck mass palpated in the neck with tracheal deviation to the contralateral side, and laryngoscopy reveals a right vocal cord paralysis. There's no stride or clinically. Imaging, in this case, I presume everyone would want some kind of cross-sectional imaging, CT with contrast. Anybody who wants a PET scan at this early stage? What are we getting out of our imaging? Dr. Orloff, what's the purpose of that CT versus the PET?
Well, your primary goal is to control the local disease, so the imaging is more focused on the surgical decision making and executing adequate surgery. So a PET scan is perhaps premature.
But you know this is a cancer, right? I mean, this is not going to be benign. Good luck getting it approved. You don't have a diagnosis.

Well, that's true. So CT with contrast, I would say that it really varies by institution, but MRI with contrast is also reasonable. I think there's probably a majority of people who favor CT. I personally had a lot of preference for MRI by my neuroradiologist and by just the goal of minimizing radiation exposure, but I think either type of study is appropriate. And it needs to be performed to include the mediastinum as well as the neck. So when you order a CT scan of the neck, you will often have the tumor cut off at the level of the clavicles. I think it's really important to emphasize CT from the skull base to and including the mediastinum. CT scans, I've been taught by my radiology colleagues, when a CT scan of the neck is done with the patient's arms down at their side, whereas a CT scan of the chest is done with their arms up over their head, so it does change the relationship of the anatomy. So, it just helps to know your regional protocol for imaging and to request that the scan go down below the clavicles. But as you're showing here, I mean, you are looking for where this tumor is invading. You already know that there's some invasive component because of the vocal fold paralysis. looking up and down from there to include the relationship with the trachea, the esophagus, the larynx, the retropharynx, and the mediastinum, as well as the great vessels.

So I've picked just one cross-sectional image of this tumor mass, which I think is evident there. You can see this big mass kind of invading posteriorly, heading at least towards the prevertebral fascia. It appears to be involving the trachea at multiple levels, and although we're not seeing a good view of the esophagus there, the read was that we probably had esophageal invasion of this tumor as well. So there was a PET scan done as part of staging for more distant metastases before this patient could be sent to the OR, and I'll explain the background to that in a moment. But you can see that this is very highly PET avid, as you might expect for presumably a poorly differentiated version of thyroid cancer. I would just make one comment about that, and that is that not all large and invasive cancers are necessarily poorly differentiated. And I think it's important to make a distinction between an aggressive cancer, which I believe this one actually is, poorly differentiated, deeply invasive, non-iodine avid, not a very effective thyroglobulin producer, probably. versus cancer that's just been sitting there for a long time and has had a long incubation period to become more locally advanced. I think there's a difference between those two things. But in this case, the time course, the invasion, the loss of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the size of the tumor, and its invasive characteristics all suggest it's probably poorly differentiated thyroid cancer. A biopsy is performed, which reveals follicular neoplasm. Anybody still want to do Molecular markers on that you PMC. Would you do molecular markers on this follicular neoplasm?

It's a reflexive test for any indeterminate nodules So we would have this automatically and how helpful is that going to be at the cost of how many thousand dollars? You know, it's been analyzed as a cost-effective test since we use it with a high positive predictive value to avoid the lobectomy and second surgery But aren't you gonna have to take this guy to the OR? Yeah, well, this case is not, I mean, the cytology is inaccurate. It's not a follicular neoplasm. So if the cytology hit the appropriate malignant area of the tumor, you know, we would not do a molecular test. So this is one of the quirks where the reflexive test probably does it. On the other hand, it would likely be BRAF positive, and so we would have our diagnosis that we know. I think in this case, you want to make sure that you get excised tissue and not rely on cytologic tissue, honestly, because you want to know what the differentiation status is of this very likely, you know, malignancy.

Well, it's a topic for another day, but I think this business of reflexing tests is one that should be open to some additional discussion. I know it's very popular in the commercial field right now to simply take cytology that's indeterminate and reflex it. But I think, as this case demonstrates, we already know this is a cancer. I'm not convinced that a reflex test makes a lot of sense, whether it was the Afirma assay, the UPMC assay, a surgeon's version of this, you know, whatever it is, I think it's evident that the molecular markers, unless you think BRAF is useful, the molecular markers probably aren't all that helpful. But what would be the surgical approach? How are we going to manage this big, nasty, invasive cancer in this man who's lost a vocal cord already? Dr. Shah. Did everybody hear that? He said, carefully.

I think you need to sort out what is the level of understanding of the patient and the patient's willingness to have the type of surgery he may need. And that will allow you to decide whether you want to do a two-stage operation or one stage. And when I say two-stage, meaning endoscopic assessment to define what you will have to do and have the patient mentally prepared for that. Or if the patient is ready, doctor, do whatever is necessary. Cure me of my cancer. That makes your job easier, and you can do everything at one time. After imaging, this patient needs careful endoscopy of the trachea and the esophagus. You would probably find tracheal invasion through the mucosa on the right-hand side, where you saw the regular tracheal wall. At esophagoscopy, what you want to see more carefully, you may not see intraluminal tumor. but you want to see whether the mucosa easily glides over the involved muscular wall or not. And that would help you decide whether you need to do through and through esophagectomy or will a section of only muscular wall be adequate, leaving the mucosa and therefore the lumen intact. So endoscopic assessment is crucial before you put the incision.

So it turns out that prior to going through that procedure, the patient acknowledged a little haemoptysis over a couple of days. And at the time of bronchoscopy, there was indeed through and through tracheal invasion with disease visible in the lumen of the trachea.

So at that point, you need to be careful as to what is the length of invasion of the trachea that you may have to reset. you can easily dissect and do primary repair or primary anastomosis up to six or even seven rings of trachea, but it depends upon the physiognomy of the patient, long neck, short neck, et cetera. But those are technical issues. In most instances, the vertical involvement of the tracheal wall is within reach of the surgeon to be able to accomplish primary anastomosis.

So this was a man who had been a heavy smoker for much of his life. He had a hyperinflated chest, a rather short and bulky neck. He had imaging that suggested at least a four centimeter length of invasion into the tracheal wall. And intraluminally, there was at least three centimeters of tumor visible. In addition, when the esophagoscopy was performed, there was also frank invasion of the esophageal wall.
Mucosal wall of the esophagus.
Mucosal wall, correct.

So in this setting, now you are committing yourself to a much bigger operation, which may mean letting go tracheal resection and esophagectomy. And in that setting, I want to have the histology confirmed. I won't do that on follicular invasion or follicular lesion. So I would be inclined to do, after endoscopies, either an open biopsy frozen section, or if I have staged my endoscopies, then I want a core biopsy to give me a more clear histologic diagnosis.
So a core biopsy was performed of the primary lesion and it turned out to be a poorly differentiated follicular thyroid cancer.

So when you get that diagnosis, now you need to go to the pathology lab, because that to me is not enough. I want the pathologist to tell me, are you seeing this tumor leaning towards an aplastic carcinoma? or this is poorly differentiated carcinoma leaning towards differentiated carcinoma with focal areas of anaplasia. Because that will make the difference. If truly this is a poorly differentiated carcinoma with anaplastic features, the probability of surgical cure, mind you, my word, cure, becomes less and less. Surgical control of neck disease is possible. But surgical cure for anaplastic carcinoma is unlikely.

So the pathologist is adamant that they do not see any signs of anaplastic thyroid cancer. This is poorly differentiated cancer, and that's all they see in this core biopsy. But they could not exclude the possibility of having anaplastic cancer elsewhere that has not been sampled at this point. So other surgical views on this. Is this a surgically approachable disease?
I'd be looking for reasons not to do surgery on this patient.
Don't you have lots of them?

Very unlikely to cure this individual if there's true invasion of the laryngotracheal structure. So I would want to get a CT scan higher. I didn't quite see that cricoid in the larynx. But 68 years old, the patient, if fit, could certainly tolerate a major procedure. It's clearly the best curative chance, but you're going to have to reconstruct both the laryngotracheal complex with pull-up type procedures, microvascular procedures. It's a major problem that you'd want to make sure the distant disease, I gather the PET has been already cleared, but I think from the local regional standpoint, surgery would be not advised.

So just in the last few minutes, is there a role for a neoadjuvant approach to the management of these deeply invasive and rather nasty, poorly differentiated cancers? Could we give a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, for example, and shrink this cancer down, make it more easily operable?

I think the points that have already been raised is very critical because we need to know whether truly this is anaplastic thyroid cancer or poorly differentiated variant of well-differentiated thyroid cancer. And the reason for saying that is even when we are talking of neoadjuvant approach, that presupposes we are thinking of going back to surgery at one point or the other. If this is truly anaplastic, then the use of cytotoxic chemotherapy as a new adjuvant approach has been shown to be equivalent to doing adjuvant chemotherapy after debulking surgery. So if we think this is anaplastic, and the surgeons have already decided this is not something we want to jump into, at that point, it would be reasonable to use a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen as an either neoadjuvant approach along with radiation. I know some surgeons don't want the radiation in the mix. Or if it is a poorly differentiated follicular neoplasm, then one can then consider the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors. But I think in that regard, the ability to actually shrink the tumor is relatively less. And therefore, you will not be looking at that as a neoadjuvant intervention with the plan of going to surgery.

So just to wrap this case up, the patient actually made the decision for us. He was not interested in accepting the aggressive surgical approach with loss of voice and the chance of loss of swallowing that that might ensue. And he elected for a chemo radiation program with cisplatin-based chemotherapy and external beam radiation, which I think completed about a week ago. So I can update this conference next year and let you know how he's doing. I'd like to thank the panelists for an interesting and fascinating discussion. I'd like to thank the audience for attention.

reference_conclusion: Following staging and endoscopic evaluation demonstrating transmural tracheal invasion and frank esophageal mucosal invasion, core biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma without definitive anaplastic features on sampled tissue. Extensive surgery was considered unlikely to provide cure and was declined by the patient because of the anticipated morbidity, including loss of voice and possible loss of swallowing. The agreed next step was nonoperative treatment with a cisplatin-based chemoradiation regimen consisting of external beam radiation and concurrent cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical progression after definitive treatment for localized prostate cancer, with subsequent urinary complications including clot retention, bladder neck contracture, gross hematuria, dysuria, and pain with orgasm.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, unfavorable intermediate-risk at initial diagnosis (PSA 10.5 ng/mL, Gleason score 4+3=7 / Grade Group 3). Subsequent biochemical recurrence/progression after proton radiotherapy and short-course androgen deprivation therapy, with imaging findings suspicious for nodal metastatic disease involving pelvic and retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial prostate biopsy: Gleason score 7; later characterized as Gleason 4+3=7 / Grade Group 3. Cancer involved 6 of 12 cores, predominantly on the left.  
- Bladder/trigonal biopsies performed during evaluation of clot retention and bladder neck contracture showed necrosis and inflammation; pathologic changes were considered likely due to radiation cystitis/radiation effect.  
- Repeat prostate biopsy on 8 March (year not explicitly stated, subsequent to imaging for recurrence) showed radiation changes and no malignancy identified.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial conventional imaging at diagnosis: negative.  
- Prostate MRI after PSA rise: prostate volume 42 g; decreased signal in seminal vesicles reported.  
- Bone scan: no definitive evidence of osseous metastatic disease.  
- Fluciclovine PET: radiotracer activity in the prostate gland; subcentimeter bilateral retroperitoneal and left pelvic lymph nodes demonstrated avidity suspicious for metastatic disease; bilateral inguinal nodes were also described.  
- PSMA PET (obtained subsequently): multiple foci of increased uptake within the prostate gland; increased uptake in a left external iliac node; multiple retroperitoneal nodes with increased PSMA uptake, interpreted as suspicious for metastatic disease.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA at diagnosis: 10.5 ng/mL.  
- Post-treatment PSA nadir: 0.9 ng/mL.  
- PSA in May 2022: 1.23 ng/mL.  
- Subsequent PSA: 8.32 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- In 2020, received definitive proton radiotherapy plus 6 months of androgen deprivation therapy for localized prostate cancer.  
- Testosterone replacement therapy was administered for approximately 2.5 months after treatment because of hot flashes and sexual side effects; this was subsequently discontinued.  
- Developed urinary complications after radiotherapy, including clot retention and bladder neck contracture requiring opening/incision, with trigonal biopsies showing radiation-related changes.  
- Had recurrent urinary retention.  
- In November 2022, received hyperbaric oxygen therapy and ciprofloxacin for radiation cystitis symptoms; gross hematuria and burning improved somewhat.

[ current disease status ]: Biochemical progression after prior definitive local therapy, with persistent PSA rise and PET-avid pelvic and retroperitoneal lymph nodes suspicious for metastatic nodal recurrence. No definitive osseous metastatic disease had been identified on bone scan. Persistent post-radiation lower urinary tract/bladder toxicity had been documented.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had been sexually active at the time testosterone replacement was initiated.  
- Pain with orgasm was reported during the post-treatment course.

reference_discussion.text: Hi everyone, my name is E. David Crawford from the University of California in San Diego and welcome to our PET Tumor Board. PET imaging, especially PSMA PET, in my opinion, is one of the most significant advances in prostate cancer management in the last decade. It has created a lot of opportunities and also challenges. I have observed that in many tumor or second opinion boards, Almost half of the cases now are focused around PET scanning, particularly PSMA PET. We recently published our latest Radar 6 and 7 guidelines, which goes through in detail a lot of the indications for PET, the pitfalls and the ups and downs. We have a lot to learn, and we hope that these monthly tumor boards will broaden your knowledge in this area. I would like to thank Blue Earth Diagnostics who recently developed and launched a PSMA pet product called RH-PSMA or PASLUMA for this educational grant. We have gathered for this tumor board panel, three international experts in this field. They have not seen these cases beforehand, and so they are as blinded as you are to what's gonna happen in these cases. First panel member is Dr. Phil Koo. Phil is at MD Anderson Banner in Phoenix, Arizona. He is a nuclear medicine physician. Also, Dr. Daniel Petrulak, a medical oncologist from Yale, well-known in the field of prostate cancer is joining us. And a radiation oncologist, Dr. Paul Nguyen from Harvard Brigham in Boston, Massachusetts. So gentlemen, let's go ahead and get started. This case is a 60-year-old wire. who had a PSA of 10.5 and he had a biopsy and had a Gleason 7 and half of the core 6 to 12 primarily on the left. Conventional imaging was negative and he chose, we have a proton center here, in 2020, to receive proton therapy and six months of ADT. Let me ask Phil to begin with, what's sort of the cutoff where conventional imaging is still indicated? With this guy, I mean, according to our radar guidelines we did, he would have qualified for conventional imaging because his PSA was above 10, but he didn't have a nodule and he did have a Gleason He didn't have a, uh, uh, well, he had a, he didn't have an eight, nine or 10, but he had a seven. Nope.

You know, in our, in our radar article, the first one, we talked about having two out of three criteria, a PSA greater than 10 T three B disease, um, or greater than equal to seven. I think, you know, when we first wrote radar one, we didn't have access to PSMA pet. Now that we have PSMA pet, uh, what we're seeing and what all the, approvals are for are for unfavorable intermediate or worse disease. So we're seeing more and more use of PSMA PET up front without getting conventional imaging first.
Okay. So let's just talk about some stuff here. Grade group. Paul, radiation oncology catching on to the grade group one through five. Are we still on the the Gleason 3-4 and 3-3 in that era?

I mean, I admit I still use both of them. I still liked seeing 4 plus 3 like this, but I can translate it to grade group 3. With his 4 plus 3 and PSA above 10, he's in the unfavorable intermediate group.
Dan?
Yeah, I mean, I think that we use both our institutions, so it just gives me a little bit more feel for what's going on.
All right, so let me just start. What about MTI? Phil, one of the indications is the high-risk local disease, whatever that means. Does this guy meet it?
Yeah, unfavorable intermediate, it is a recommendation to get PSMA PET. And again, you don't necessarily need to get conventional imaging first. In fact, you shouldn't.
So we did. I mean, 2020 was sort of a transition era. We're beginning to get that. But today, without question, you would say, get PSMAPAT?
Yes.
OK. And what about you, Paul? Would you radiate this guy without getting that? I mean, we have some problems with insurance coverage, too.

It's a tough call for me, certainly for high risk. We're trying to get the PSMA pets. Availability is an issue sometimes. Sometimes we have to wait six weeks for them. So this is a patient where I'm kind of plus minus. I wouldn't, I would be willing to radiate him without a PSMA pet, but I would prefer to have one if I could.
Okay. And then I guess the other thing is this guy is six months of ADT. Dan, is that? Good for you or?

Yeah, I think also that's why I would like to see if it's my path. I'm going to see a Colton Mill disease. I'm going to probably add to both length as well as the intensity of the ADT. It probably would add a next generation to it. Although there's no data for it, but you would assume that this is potentially micrometastatic and that we'd want more therapy in this situation.
What does ADT mean to you? I mean, does that double therapy? Is it something for flare? What does it mean to you?

So, I mean, ADT, in my mind, is just simply single therapy. You know, double therapy would be ADT plus a next generation, and triple, of course, would be adding chemotherapy to that. So I think we need a little bit more of a standardized term because, you know, ADT is a bit of a vestige, but, again, I think we have to be clear with our definitions.

So we, you know, we have we have doublet there, you know, we had the first and second generation anti antigens now we're in the third and they still call them the second but. And we use the word ADT and we have antigen biosynthesis inhibitors and other things. And that stands for androgen deprivation therapy and people are talking about some other terminology. I think, and just writing a paper on this is that we ought to keep the word ADT and just this make it androgen. directed therapy, so we're doing something to do something to androgens, and I think that could be widely accepted without getting rid of our ADT term, but other people want to use ADT plus this and that. I don't know, what do you think?

I mean, I think it's I think, again, if it's used consistently, it's not a problem. But as we saw with the terms hormone resistant, castration resistant, then you and I came up with the term endocrine resistant years ago. We just have to be careful about our definitions that we're talking the same language.

Well, you and I wrote a paper about not doing that. And you know what? We were right now. Everybody's going back to what we said 10 years ago. about that when that came out. Okay, let's get let's get going on this case. So his nadir PSA is point nine. Paul, not good. Good.
Well, not good if he got six months of ADT. I mean, I would expect these patients to be well below point one undetectable after radiation and six months of ADT.

So he he had double trouble. He was having a lot of hot flashes and was sexually active, but he got his doctor to start him on testosterone replacement therapy for two and a half months. And he subsequently stopped that he had pain with orgasm and other things like that. But after that, the following year, his PSA was now in May. of 22, 1.23. He was in the clinic with clot retention. He had a water neck contracture, which was opened and he had abnormal suspicious areas in his trigon, which were biopsy and determined to be radiation cystitis. He had another episode of retention. Here's his pathologic diagnosis from his biopsies. He had necrosis and he had inflammation. Down here, they say pathologic changes are likely due to radiation. Radiation oncologist, Paul, what do we do about this guy here?

Yeah, this is a tough situation. You know, we, we try our best to minimize the dose of the bladder and we try all this daily imaging, but these kinds of things can happen. And it looks like this patient's had a particularly strong late reaction to the radiation. So, you know, at this point we're, we're trying to do supportive care. If he's, if he's bleeding, we send them to our urology colleagues and see if there's anything that can be, fulgurated or any way to create hemostasis. And then otherwise, we're trying to let them heal. And so that could be observation, that could be all the way up to sending them for hyperbaric oxygen.

OK, well, you're right on. So this guy also went to Duke and worked there also. And then in November of 22, he got hyperbaric oxygen, plus Cipro. And he had gross hematuria GH with burning for a while, got a little bit better. And now we see him with a PSA of 8.32. Bill, imaging, what do we do?

You know, it's interesting, earlier on when he went up to 1.23, probably wouldn't have imaging. But now that it's rising and it's rising pretty rapidly, I'm getting a little concerned and would definitely want to be aggressive. This seems faster than I would have expected. So I think a PSMA PET here should be considered.
Okay. Anybody disagree?
Nope.

All right. So what happened was He ended up getting imaging. And the first thing he got was MR of the prostate, 42 grams. That's kind of large for a guy that's got ADT and radiation, but he had, you can read it here, decreased signal on seminal vesicles. I guess, how hard is MR to read after radiation, Phil?
I mean, I don't read prostate MRs, but from what I know and speaking to colleagues, I think it is challenging and it's oftentimes difficult to separate inflammation from a tumor.

Okay, well, I had a bone scan and no definitive evidence of alseus metastatic disease. And that was it. And this was a guy that we got a lot of pushback from insurance companies about getting a scan and availability of some of the new PSMA scans. we were able to get a fluciclovine oxygen scan on him. And I need to go back here. And you can see he had activity in his prostate gland. And so it had some nodes. What do you think of subcentimeter bilateral retroperitoneum on left pelvic nodes, Phil?

You know, the fact that they're subcentimeter to me, irrelevant. If they were fluciclovian avid in the setting of elevated PSA, I would be very concerned those were sites of metastatic disease. It's interesting, you know, they commented in the impression about these bilateral inguinal nodes. We know that prostate cancer rarely goes bilateral inguinal, but the comment here, so I wouldn't worry about them. But it's really those retroperitoneal nodes that concern me. And I'd also like to point out that MRI, I read the impression there, you know, it's challenging because the MRI is just looking at the pelvis. And you could see that these nodes that were outside of the pelvis potentially in the retroperitoneum would not be called. And even if it was in the field of view, they may have not called it because they were sub-centimeter. Because on MRI and CT, we often use CT as the cutoff or we use size as a cutoff, not physiology.

Okay. So, um, I like, I like the biopsy prostate so I did that on March the eighth of this year, and didn't find anything but radiation changes and are. tumor board said radiate the lesion, whatever that was, some of them and start ADT. Dan, would you at this point start ADT or not?
Yeah. I mean, based upon these small lesions, small lymph nodes, I would start the, I would definitely start ADT.
Okay. And, So you would treat him like metastatic disease, right?
Yeah, I mean, I think, again, I'm pretty convinced from the data and I agree completely with what Phil said before about the avidity of these particular areas.
So what does ADHC mean to you in this guy? Are we talking about his LHR antagonist or antagonist?
That's a great question. I would give him an LHRH plus the next generation.
Okay. So like apalutamide, enzalutamide, darolutamide, something like that. You wouldn't give chemo in this guy, right? No.
No.
Okay. Paul, what would you do? Is there anything you'd radiate here?

Yeah. I mean, it sounds to me like he still has potentially quote unquote curable disease in the extent that he's got the nodes in the pelvic region and the retroperitoneal is a little bit higher than I like to go, but, um, he's a young man, I think you said he was 60 initially, so I would try to radiate a nodal region, like basically try to patch on a retroperitoneal pelvic nodal field, try not to overlap with the prior proton field, and try to stay off of his bladder, because obviously his bladder is very sensitive right now.
Yeah. Bill, is there any reason to get a PSMA scan on him or anything at this point? At this point,
I don't think so. I don't think it would necessarily change what we're doing, and to your point earlier about actionable findings, I don't know if it would necessarily change anything right now.

Okay. Well, I tried to get one, a PSMA scan in May or June, and was unable to get it. kept being persistent and we got one. It was an interesting one, a conversation. I remember being on the phone for 20 minutes, talking to various people about trying to get approval and then getting passed to the next one and next one, and then I got disconnected. I don't know if anybody else has experienced that harassment, but it happened. So I was able to get a scan on him, and this is what it showed, Phil. It showed that he has multiple foci of increased uptake within the gland. Biopsy proven cancer that I missed, something when we did it, I didn't do 12 core biopsies. Again, uptake in left external iliac, suspicious multiple retroperitoneal modes, increased PSMA uptake. So they think it's probably, it is probably metastatic disease. Do you feel comfortable calling it that or?

You know, I would like to see the images here. It's interesting, you know, the first impression talks about the prostate gland, but that was biopsied and it was shown to be, you know, inflammation. And I think this is a good example how just cause it has uptake with PSMA doesn't make it prostate cancer and inflammation can have increased activity. You know, the second impression that makes sense. I think they point out something that we should all be aware of that ganglia can have uptake with PSMA. I imagine if we looked at the CT images closely, hopefully we could identify lymph nodes actually rather than ganglia that are concentrating the radio tracer. So based on this, and we also have the AXIMR results, I think we should, we'd feel pretty comfortable that those lymph nodes are metastatic.

So our group thought that this is, that, you know, this probably, I mean, with this PSA level being what it is and that ADT and third generation antiandrogen should be started. And that's, that's the direction we're going. Does anybody disagree with that, Dan?
Absolutely not. Great. Exactly what I would do.

Well, I want to thank you all for looking at this case. As you know, we see a lot of different cases now and a whole change in the environment with molecular target and imaging. And I think we have to really be on our toes to sort of know what to deal with these people. So again, thank you all. And we'll see you for next month for our next case. Thank you.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old postmenopausal woman. No family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented initially with a large left breast mass measuring greater than 7 cm.

[ diagnosis ]: Invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, initially localized at presentation. Subsequent metastatic recurrence occurred 16 years after the primary diagnosis, involving ovary, bone, and later liver.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the primary breast lesion showed invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 1, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, Ki-67 less than 10%. Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, mastectomy specimen showed residual tumor measuring 7 cm with 1 positive lymph node. Liver biopsy was performed at metastatic progression for genomic profiling.

[ imaging findings ]: At initial diagnosis, chest radiograph, liver ultrasound, and bone scan were negative for metastatic disease. At metastatic relapse, ovarian and bone metastases were identified. After 20 months of first-line metastatic therapy, there was reactivation/progression of bone lesions and development of a liver metastasis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: FoundationOne assay on liver biopsy demonstrated a PIK3CA mutation in the helical domain, a KRAS mutation involving codon 12, and tumor mutational burden of 33 mutations/Mb.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with anthracycline- and taxane-based treatment for primary breast cancer, with no response. Underwent mastectomy, which showed persistent 7 cm residual tumor and 1 positive lymph node. Received adjuvant radiotherapy. Received tamoxifen for 10 years; subsequent aromatase inhibitor therapy was not tolerated. After metastatic relapse, received letrozole plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor as first-line metastatic therapy, with progression after 20 months. Subsequently received fulvestrant plus alpelisib; treatment was poorly tolerated and disease progressed after 5 months. Immunotherapy was later administered in the context of high tumor mutational burden.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative lobular breast cancer with prior ovarian, bone, and liver involvement. Disease had progressed on letrozole plus CDK4/6 inhibitor and fulvestrant plus alpelisib.

[ other clinical data ]: Lobular histology. High tumor mutational burden was documented at 33 mutations/Mb.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. So we're going to move to case number two, which is a case of a patient with lobular metastatic breast cancer and a high tumor mutational burden. So this is a 50-year-old postmenopausal woman with no family history of breast or ovarian cancer that came in for a large left breast mass, more than 7 centimeters. The biopsy showed invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 1 hormone receptor positive. Her 2 negative was a key 67, less than 10%. Chest x-ray, liver ultrasound, and wound scan were negative for metastasis. So this patient was treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, anthracycline and taxanes. And obviously, there was no response to this neoadjuvant therapy. At mastectomy, there was a tumor that was still 7 centimeters and one positive lymph node. She then had radiotherapy. and then 10 years of tamoxifen and switched to an aromatase inhibitor was not tolerated. So I'd like to ask George a question about the lobular histology. So how interesting is that and is it easy to diagnose lobular breast cancer?

Loblar carcinoma is the most frequent histological special type of breast cancer. It's characterized by the sole characteristic discohesiveness of the cancer cells. The classical variant presents as infiltrating the breast stroma as single cell or single cell files, but there are variants of loblar carcinoma as well, going from the pleomorphic, the solid, trabecular, the alveolar. It's an interesting tumor in terms of reproducibility of the diagnosis. There are several studies now showing that the pure cases of lobular can be diagnosed with, let's say, a good agreement across pathologists, but there is a number of cases where the agreement is far from ideal. And then the utilization of additional immunochemical assays like CDH1, in immunochemistry can help firm up the diagnosis as well, always in conjunction with the histology. There are also now approaches based on artificial intelligence to classify lobular carcinoma with a great deal of accuracy. There was a work by Frasier Pareja from Memorial Sloan Kettering showing that you can attain very high levels of accuracy in the diagnosis of a lobular on the basis of computer vision.
So Janet, would you use a MAMA print or ONCO type in this case? So I'm just anticipating a question from online.

Lobular breast cancer tends to be less responsive to chemotherapy, as was seen in this case where this patient didn't have any response from neoadjuvant chemotherapy. I think it's still within the guidelines to use Oncotype for a patient along these lines. Although, if it was known to be T3N1, maybe not. But I think the bang for your buck that you're going to get with chemotherapy is pretty low for lobular. Definitely more endocrine therapy.

So the patient had a relapse 16 years after the primary tumor diagnosis. And I put a graph below just to show you a hormone receptor positive or negative disease. Late relapses are not infrequent. And she had ovarian and bone metastasis. And she was treated with a combination of letrozole and the CDK46 inhibitor. And this progression occurred after 20 months. So she got 20 months of her first line therapy with the reactivation of bone lesions and the development of a liver metastasis. Now, just this slide to show you that lobular cancer can have different genomic alterations when compared to ductal, so I don't know if you want to comment that, George, also, regarding the differences in ductal and lobular and the number of mutations and the types of mutations you can get.

It's indeed interesting. The most striking difference, which is, let's say, An underpinning cause of the sole characteristic discohesiveness of lobular carcinoma cells is the presence of CDH1 echaduring mutations. And these are usually loss of function mutations and with loss of the wild type allele as well. We see additional alterations that are more frequent in lobular carcinoma, but thinking about the luminal genes, there's an enrichment for them. It's not exclusively in lobular here in this context. Different studies have highlighted different genes that have a slightly higher prevalence or significantly higher prevalence in lobular. In some of the target genes as well that we think like Herbichew mutations are reported to be more frequent in lobulars as well. An important observation, however, is that the repertoire of mutational signatures in lobular carcinomas appears to be different from the garden variety of, let's say, luminal tumors of other histologic types.

Thank you. So you mentioned HER2 mutations. So this is a question for you, Phil. Do you treat in the metastatic setting differently, lobular carcinoma versus ductal? Because in this slide, this was an interesting data coming from a study using fluvescent and ratinib. All patients had the ERBB2 activity mutations, ductal and lobular. But you would see that in lobular breast cancer, the response rate seemed a bit higher.

Yeah, I mean, I think definitely, as you alluded to, ERBB2 mutations occur at a higher frequency in lobular cancer. It's about 5% of patients. So these are different from HER2 or ERBB2 amplifications. So these are sort of hotspot mutations often that activate the tyrosine kinase domain of the HER2 receptor. So there is single arm data to support that. I think it's also included in the NCCN guidelines. You know, the availability of that, I think, is a different question. That may differ of using For instance, a HER2 TKI like neratinib in combination with fulvestrin, plus or minus trastuzumab. So I think it certainly does speak to, as you highlighted, that there are opportunities for precision medicine in patients with lobular cancer, and I think it's important to know some information about whether or not there are any genomic targets that can guide therapy.

So let's go to the genomic data. So this patient had a liver biopsy. And then those were the results. So she had the foundation one assay. There was a PCCA mutation in the helical domain and then a tumor mutational burden of 33. So maybe Dara, can you comment the results?

Sure, so we see here a PIK3CA mutation, much like we saw in the last case. I do think it's important to note that there's also a KRAS mutation here, which, when you think about targeted therapy opportunities, a built-in bypass mechanism that allows for sustained cellular signaling that would not be impacted by many inhibitors of the PI3 pathway is really, really important. The tumor mutational burden, I think, is also very interesting here. It's certainly uncommon for breast cancer to have this high of a tumor mutational burden. And tumor mutational burden as an assay itself also has some challenges, although what I will say is that at 33 mutations per megabase, I would expect that any lab that reports tumor mutation burden would would call this a high tumor mutation burden.

My first question, looking at this high TMB, the frequency of C2Ts and C2Gs in this case, and to think about apobac metagenesis as the underlying cause, rather than other causes of an increased tumor mutation burden.

Yeah. So, PIX4C mutations are quite prevalent in hormone receptor-positive or to negative disease. Janet, would there be more frequent in lobular than in ductal, or would you believe that the prevalence is the same for PIX4C mutations?

Again, here, it depends on the subtype of Let's say the luminal subtype, as you can see here in this figure from the TCJ study, if you look at the frequency of PIK3C mutation in luminal A and luminal B, it's different already. So given that this interrelationship between lobular and ductal and the molecular subtypes, you can see a higher frequency of PIK3C mutation. And if you think about the APOBAC metagenesis, APOBAC metagenesis is associated with a higher frequency of some PIK3CA hotspot mutations. You expect a higher frequency in lobulars.
Thank you. So this patient got fulvescent alopecia. Would that have been your first choice of therapy after a CDK46? So she had 20 months on first line endocrine therapy.

Certainly at the time, it would have been my first choice. I would have definitely done a second line endocrine-based therapy with something to target the PIK3CA. I think now we have other options other than Alpalocib, you know, capivacertib that was approved in the United States. So, today I may have a slightly different choice, but at the time, yes, I would have done Alpalocib.
Okay. And then Tom, I put this way because this is something we discussed with Dara prior to the session. So, would you like to comment on the different variants?

Yeah. So, on the right here, you see a plot of PIK3CA mutations, and the portions of it that are the protein structure are the PIK3CA variants that are approved related to alpelicib. And I think what's important about this is that there's a number of known activating mutations that are on the bottom half of this chart. And those were not included in the approval. And so different drugs have different spectra of mutations that are considered cognate for different drugs. So alpelicib specifically, The trial that, the registrational trial included a smaller number of mutations, and for the newer drugs that are looking more at pathway alterations, the number of mutations has been more inclusive. So, you know, do I have biologic reason to think that one of these mutations on the bottom would be less responsive to alpelicib? No, I don't have biological reason to think that, but we don't have empiric proof from the level of the registrational studies.
Thanks. And Phil, would that impact your choice between capivaciratib and alpelizib, the type of variant?

Yeah. I mean, I think as was alluded to by the other speakers, it's obviously important to look at what the variants are and whether or not they're included in the drug label. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old female; Karnofsky Performance Status 80. Known case of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), diagnosed in 2016.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, vertigo, gait disturbance, and neck pain; right-sided hearing loss. Symptoms had relapsed in November 2023 and persisted without symptomatic improvement after CyberKnife treatment. She also had a prior history in 2016 of headache and left-sided hearing loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Neurofibromatosis type 2 with multiple intracranial and spinal extra-axial enhancing lesions consistent with meningiomatosis, bilateral vestibulocochlear schwannomas, and spinal ependymomas.

[ histopathology results ]: Resection of the right parietal lesion in 2016 showed low-grade meningioma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial MRI in 2016 showed a right parieto-occipital lesion with mass effect and a left cerebellopontine angle lesion.  
- Whole-spine MRI in 2016 revealed multiple lesions in the cervical and dorsal spine.  
- MRI brain and whole spine performed in 2023 showed multiple enhancing lesions involving the brain and whole spine, including cervical, dorsal, and lumbar regions.  
- Brain MRI demonstrated multiple supratentorial and infratentorial extra-axial lesions with CSF cleft, broad dural attachment, buckling of gray-white matter, and intense homogeneous post-contrast enhancement, consistent with multiple meningiomas/meningiomatosis.  
- A left cerebellopontine angle lesion showed widening of the internal auditory canal with intracanalicular extension and enhancement, consistent with vestibular schwannoma.  
- Additional enhancement was present in the right vestibulocochlear nerve complex, consistent with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.  
- An enhancing lesion was present at the cervicomedullary junction and posterior to C2.  
- Cervical and dorsal spine post-contrast sagittal imaging showed multiple enhancing lesions along the cord surface, suggestive of meningiomas.  
- Central intramedullary spinal lesions in the cervical region were described as ependymomas.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2016: Surgical resection of right parietal lesion; histopathology showed low-grade meningioma.  
- No further treatment was given after initial evaluation in 2016.  
- November 2023: CyberKnife delivered in 5 sessions for recurrent symptoms.  
- No symptomatic improvement was reported after CyberKnife.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent symptomatic multifocal intracranial and spinal disease with headache, vertigo, gait disturbance, neck pain, and right-sided hearing loss after CyberKnife treatment.

[ other clinical data ]: Symptoms had been present since March 2024 at current presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss for approximately 2 months prior to diagnosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced gastric carcinoma, diagnosed in April 2018.

[ histopathology results ]: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated thickened gastric wall. Gastric biopsy showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, signet ring type.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal ultrasound showed circumferential gastric wall thickening. Liver segment 4A showed a focal area of fatty infiltration, with no evidence of hepatic parenchymal metastasis. CT chest/upper abdomen showed irregular circumferential gastric wall thickening involving the body/antrum. Post-chemotherapy CT showed persistent gastric wall thickening involving the cardia and body, in keeping with gastric carcinoma. No abdominal lymphadenopathy was identified. Endoscopy performed subsequently did not show a gross visible lesion.

[ laboratory results ]: Routine laboratory tests were reported within normal limits overall. Creatinine was elevated on the most recent chemotherapy assessment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was started on 20 April 2018 with docetaxel, cisplatin, and capecitabine. Three cycles were completed. Clinical response was reported, with marked symptomatic improvement; vomiting subsided and oral intake improved.

[ current disease status ]: After 3 cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the patient remained clinically stable with ECOG performance status 1. Presenting gastrointestinal symptoms had improved. Disease remained radiologically evident as gastric wall thickening without identified abdominal lymphadenopathy or hepatic parenchymal metastasis.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history, past surgical history, family history, social history, and review of systems were otherwise unremarkable. General examination was stable. Local examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits.

The immediate next step is diagnostic laparoscopy to assess for gross lymphadenopathy and minimize the morbidity of a laparotomy; if gross lymphadenopathy is identified, the procedure will be aborted, and if not, total gastrectomy will proceed. The tumor board concurred that surgical resection offers the best potential for prolonged survival in this setting and endorsed the surgical oncology plan.
reference_conclusion_quote: So I think at this point, I'm preparing him for a total gastrectomy [...] My next step will be to do a diagnostic microscopy to minimize the morbidity of an incision and make sure there are no gross lymphadenopathy when I go in to look with a camera. If there is, I will stop there. And if there is no gross lymphadenopathy, then we will proceed with a total gastrectomy. [...] So I like the idea that the surgeons are going in to first of all look and see. [...] but from my standpoint I think the plan by the oncology team is pretty good

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Diarrhea, flushing, abdominal cramps, and weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic well-differentiated small bowel neuroendocrine tumor (functional/carcinoid syndrome), grade 2, with hepatic metastases and ileocolic nodal involvement at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopy and liver biopsy demonstrated well-differentiated small bowel neuroendocrine tumor with Ki-67 10%. Subsequent surgical pathology after laparoscopic right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and liver wedge resection showed well-differentiated small bowel neuroendocrine tumor, grade 2, with 3/27 positive lymph nodes and Ki-67 6%. Later hepatic debulking/resection specimens demonstrated intrapatient Ki-67 heterogeneity: segment 2 lesion Ki-67 20%, segment 4/5 lesion Ki-67 12.5%, and other sampled lesions Ki-67 1%.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT abdomen/pelvis showed numerous hepatic lesions, a 2 cm ileocolic lymph node, and a primary tumor in the distal small bowel that was nearly obstructive in the small bowel lumen. Initial DOTATATE PET showed numerous liver lesions, the primary small bowel tumor, and ileocolic lymph nodes. MRI with Eovist showed innumerable bilobar hepatic lesions. After bland embolization, interval imaging reportedly showed no major changes for approximately 6-8 months, but repeat DOTATATE PET later demonstrated worsening hepatic disease and new retrocrural lymph nodes despite MRI being read as grossly stable. After peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, repeat DOTATATE PET/CT approximately 1 year later showed stable disease with retrocrural lymph nodes less conspicuous. Two years after PRRT, imaging showed predominantly hepatic progression, especially a rapidly enlarging segment 2 lesion measuring approximately 3.5 cm, with additional progression in segment 4.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Initial molecular profiling (OncoPlus) identified a BCOR mutation and equivocal NOTCH1 loss. Repeat molecular profiling from later hepatic tumor samples again showed BCOR mutation and additionally demonstrated SMAD4 loss and RB1 loss.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum serotonin at diagnosis was 1330. Postoperatively after bowel surgery, serotonin remained approximately unchanged. After bland embolization, serotonin decreased to 364. During PRRT, serotonin ranged from 274 down to 46 over an 8-month treatment period. Two years after PRRT, serotonin again rose to >1000. After later hepatic debulking/resection, serotonin decreased to 4.4. Echocardiogram was negative. No symptoms of carcinoid heart disease were reported, including no shortness of breath or edema.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Long-acting somatostatin analog therapy was initiated first-line; lanreotide 120 mg every 28 days was documented. This produced mild improvement in diarrhea and flushing, but abdominal cramping persisted. Because of persistent crampy abdominal pain, weight loss, and a nearly obstructive primary lesion, she underwent laparoscopic right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and liver wedge resection; postoperative recovery was uncomplicated and cramping resolved. Persistent flushing and diarrhea continued after surgery. She subsequently underwent bland hepatic embolization, after which symptoms improved and serotonin declined substantially. Approximately 6-8 months later, symptoms worsened again with biochemical progression. Telotristat was administered for at least 8 weeks to 3 months without major symptomatic improvement. PRRT was then given; symptoms improved markedly and serotonin declined during the 8-month treatment period. Approximately 1 year after PRRT, disease was stable on DOTATATE PET/CT. Two years after PRRT, symptoms and serotonin worsened again with predominantly hepatic progression. She then underwent further hepatic debulking/resection with removal of multiple tumor deposits ranging from 4 to 8 cm; postoperative symptoms improved and serotonin fell markedly.

[ current disease status ]: Following the most recent hepatic debulking/resection, symptoms improved and serotonin decreased to 4.4. The postoperative interval described was approximately 3 months, with no documented immediate recurrence during that period.

[ other clinical data ]: Diarrhea remained present after bowel surgery and cholecystectomy without clear postoperative worsening; persistent serotonin elevation supported ongoing serotonin-mediated symptoms. She was described as highly functional, working full time, and caring for three children.
