reference_discussion.text: Okay, welcome everybody to our 2024 Virtual Education Conference from the Neuroendocrine Tumor Research Foundation. We're really excited to have you here today for our Virtual Tumor Board. We have a great team We have Dr. Hilary Zasarias from the University of Utah, Dr. Aman Shohan from the University of Miami, Dr. Mark Lewis from Intermountain in Salt Lake City as well, and then Dr. Ahmed and Dr. Liao as well as myself from the University of Chicago. Again, thank you for being here today. So let's dive right into it. This first case is a 50-year-old female that presents with diarrhea, flushing, and abdominal cramps. She goes to the emergency room. She also reports some weight loss. Her CT abdomen pelvis shows numerous hepatic lesions, as well as a 2-centimeter ileocolic lymph node. and she gets worked up for this. She gets a colonoscopy and a liver biopsy that eventually show a well-differentiated small bowel neuroendocrine tumor with a Ki67 of 10%. A serotonin level is quite high at 1330. That's much higher than normal. As we all know usually serotonin levels are below 200 or 250 depending on the laboratory. And so as a workup she gets a CT scan. This is the one from the emergency room. that, as you can see, shows numerous lesions in the liver here, but then the blue arrow points towards the primary tumor within the small bowel here, the distal part of the small bowel. She gets a DOTATATE PET scan, which shows numerous lesions within the liver, as well as the primary tumor and the ileocolic lymph nodes that were seen on the CT scan in the emergency room. and then she also gets an MRI with Eovist which shows like the radiologists would call it innumerable bilobaryopathic lesions. Certainly you can count them but they're quite a bit here. So she is being started on long-acting octeotitis first line as we all know both for symptom improvement as well as for tumor improvement and she reports some mild improvements in her diarrhea and flushing. So before we move on to the next part of what we did, I would ask perhaps Dr. Soares whether there is anything else that she would want to do at this sort of early stage. And you will see this is a multi-year story, so obviously this is the very beginning after the diagnosis. A lot of things are going to happen, but is there something in particular at this point? You have a patient that has some mild improvement in her diarrhea and flushing, still reports some cramping. You've seen the images. Is there something else that you would recommend that we do at this time, or would you just continue to follow her?

Thank you so much. Unfortunately, this is a presentation that we see not so infrequently as the first presentation. I think, obviously, there is the concern that all this is related to carcinoid syndrome. So in addition to the serotonin, I'll probably get to complement that 5-HIA. potentially a raw BNP and an echo, depending on the results to rule out carcinoid heart disease as part of the screening. That's in terms of thinking about some of the issues with her carcinoid syndrome. Then, because of her tumor intact in the small bowel and the history of cramping, there certainly, I think, deserves a conversation about resection of the primary tumor, because that can improve her symptoms. whether or not, you know, consideration for liver debulking can be considered. I think it really depends on the institution that the patient is being seen. Some institutions are more aggressive than others. There's data that suggests that debulking up to 70% if it's achievable can also improve survival, at least in retrospective analysis. So all these are considerations for this patient. Consider a section of the priming, whether or not there's a role for liver, the bulking, and again, that's a larger conversation. And we shouldn't forget about screening for carcinoid heart disease. These are initial thoughts. I'm sure there's more for my colleagues.

Dr. Saur, anything you want to add to this? Yeah, with such high serotonin, I think I always worry about getting a baseline screening for carcinoid. So Dr. Saur has covered those bases. The other thing that we can potentially add on here is maybe Zermelo. This patient is still having carcinoid syndrome diarrhea, which is technically refractory to SSA alone at this point in time. It's not fully resolved. So that's the classic FDA approved indication for Zermelo or teletrostat ethyl. Now, this drug, it targets the production of serotonin in the neuroendocrine tumor cell, unlike SSA, which blocks the secretion of serotonin. So it really complements, and if diarrhea is still a quality of life limiting issue for this particular patient, we can certainly add Zermelo and that I've shown to improve carcinoid syndrome diarrhea. But beyond that, for medical management for metastatic disease, I think the case needs to be reviewed in a multidisciplinary setting to really chart what's the next best treatment. I think Dr. Soares brings out a good point about debulking for functional nets that could be hugely beneficial. But in this particular case, Some might say there's too much disease, unless there's a concern for bowel obstruction. Maybe surgical developing can be, we can trend the tumor biology, tumor growth rate. This is a grade two tumor. And those KIs, 6, 7, 10% can be very tricky. That's really the borderline where they can be either aggressive or very indolent. So understanding the biology of the cancer, is a fast-growing grade 2 or slow-growing grade 2. It's very important. There are other therapies like liver directed therapies that can be used. Those are relatively less invasive as compared to a debulking surgery for immediate relief or some sort of cytoreduction if it's needed for functional neuroendocrine tumor management. So again, we have multiple tools and I think we have to factor in patients risk for individual procedures, their choices and their goals, and also factor in the multidisciplinary tumor board recommendations and what expertise are available. For example, you guys at the University of Chicago, you're very well known for NET surgeries. Not every center might have very expert NET debunking surgeons. So we've got to factor those things in.

Thank you very much. So to both yours and Dr. Soraya's point, we obviously got an echo that was all negative. She also had no symptoms. I would also add that occasionally, you know, patients certainly with carcinogenic heart disease don't have any symptoms, so no shortness of breath. no swelling or relax and still i don't know what your thoughts is but generally we tend to once the serotonin level are above 1000 even if there are no symptoms we tend to definitely check for that especially if we plan on doing something a little bit more on the invasive side. This case was presented in the Neuroendocrine Tumor Board, and believe it or not, you know, we judged this, at least from a liver perspective, to be too high a tumor burden for debulking. Like Dr. Suarez said, there's different thresholds. We generally try to aim for greater than 90% because those are the better results that we've seen, especially in very symptomatic patients like she is. But, you know, we just thought there was too much. However, one of the things that I think you both mentioned as well is to really pay attention to the patients right so in this particular case her crampy abdominal pain didn't really resolve and if you remember from the ct i showed you that lesion was almost completely obstructive in the small bowel lumen and so we did decide to take her to the operating room or to remove the primary tumor we thought that this was necessary to relieve her symptoms that she had not so much the flushing and the diarrhea but rather the crampy abdominal pain and the weight loss that she had. And so we did a laparoscopic ritemic colectomy, we took her gallbladder out, which we often do in patients with metastatic disease that actually are projected to be on long-acting octeotide for a while. And then we did a liver waste resection just to be sure that we're dealing with the same Ki-67 or tumor grade Like you said, Dr. Shahan, which is really important to understand sometimes for tumor biology in the primary tumor as we see in the liver. And so it turned out that the operation went very well. She recovered quickly. This was a small bowel neuroendocrine tumor, well differentiated, grade 2, 3 out of 27 positive lymph nodes, and a calc 67. of 6% actually. Now we, for some reason, run Oncoplus, which is a molecular testing platform on all our neuroendocrine tumors, including the small bowel neuroendocrine tumors, which generally is not that helpful for small bowel neuroendocrine tumors. But these were the results. She was found to have two pathogenetic findings. One, a mutation in B-Core, which is really, I think, a loss of function mostly, and then an echo vocal notch one loss. Anything any of the medical oncologists wants to add here that makes you nervous, unnervous? You know, I know B-Core can be found in small bowel neuroendocrine tumors, but I don't think it has any particular prognostic value. Anything you want to add before I move on?
Yeah, I don't know we know enough about prognostic or predictive value of these two.

I would agree. I think notch one, we are increasingly learning notch pathway signaling in general, broadly with neuroendocrine cancers, definitely well established with higher grade, poorly different neuroendocrine carcinomas. But again, this is one of those biomarkers, we don't understand what they mean, and they're not very commonly found either. So I think it's too difficult to make sense of these things at this stage of time.

I might just add, maybe the one time I do find genomics fairly helpful in these settings is, as we all know, there are occasionally times, at least before patients go to the operating room, where you might actually not be able to distinguish readily a pancreatic from a mid-gut primary. I certainly see that from time to time and there I find loss of heterozygosity in chromosome 18 to be a hallmark of the midgut origins. That's sometimes helpful. But yeah, I agree. I wouldn't see anything actionable here.

Okay, so she's continued to have symptoms despite being on long-acting Octreotide, on this case Lyme Rheotide, 120 milligrams every 28 days. So what now? Anybody wants to chime in and think about You know, anything else we could do for this patient that still is symptomatic? Obviously, her cramps go away. That's not an issue anymore, but she still has the flushing and the diarrhea.

I think like Dr. Chauhan said, you know, telotristat or Zermelo is an option, but controlling the symptom also goes hand-in-hand with controlling the disease. So, you know, if the tumor is not debulkable by surgery, then perhaps we could consider diverteric therapy, otherwise a different type of systemic therapy.

Great. So, Dr. Ahmed, can you talk to us a little bit about liver-directed therapy in your endocrine tumors, specifically in those cases where liver debulking is not a good option, either because the patient couldn't get through it or because the tumor volume is too high?

Quick, quick, quick comment before we go. So it might not be fully serving this particular case, but after the debulking or primary tumor resection, you know, for the audience, it's important to know the diarrhea and neuroendocrine tumor can be multifactorial. And especially after the surgery, shortcut diarrhea can be particularly playing a role now in addition to carcinoid syndrome diarrhea. So it'd be interesting to see how the serotonin levels or 5-HIA levels trended pre and post-operatively. so that we can really fine-tune. If it is purely a carcinoma syndrome, diarrhea issue, then again, I think we will hear more about what we did to develop further disease. But if there are additional components, some patients might get gallbladder removed, might have some bilacid diarrhea component, vector overgrowth, shortcut syndrome. So it's really important to understand what could be contributing to worsening GI issues.

Yeah, it's a very good point, especially as we remove the right colon, you know, the terminal ilium and the gallbladder, you could have bowel reabsorption issues, which hopefully most surgeons will know about. And so if the diarrhea gets worse, I mean, you would definitely expect that there's a component there. In her case, her diarrhea pretty much remained the same, and the serotonin level, I'll show you in a little bit, was also about the same. So we assumed that this was serotonin-induced diarrhea still at this point. Back to our IR colleagues.

Yeah, sounds good. This is honestly, you know, where I think there's a nice role for what Dr. Chauhan talked about in terms of local regional therapy. So from an interventional radiology perspective, we have a role when patients have disease, especially localized to one organ, particularly the liver. And we tend to sort of work well when you have a lot of tumor in the liver or very little, like one or two lesions. And so in this case, as Dr. Koiken mentioned, there is a lot, a lot of tumor in the liver, so much that, you know, sort of going out in there surgically and removing all of it doesn't seem possible or would potentially be more risky than, than beneficial. So, um, the way that we treat tumor when there's a lot of tumor in the liver is through what are known as intra-arterial therapies. And intra-arterial therapies is where we take a catheter through the groin. And we thread it through the artery, very small catheter, about one or two millimeters in size. Using x-ray guidance, we can take it into the liver and then we can inject a material through that catheter. And depending on what we inject is what the procedure is known as. For patients with neuroendocrine tumors, we most often do what's known as bland embolization, where we inject basically inert beads, almost like grains of sand, essentially, to plug up the arteries and starve the tumor of its blood supply. As you can see here from the PowerPoint, because there's tumor in both the right and left lobes of the liver, we can treat the whole liver, but we typically have to split that up into two procedures because treating half the liver at one time is a lot to recover from. And then so patients usually need about a month or so to recover from that, and then we can treat the other side.

Great, thank you. And, you know, obviously I didn't give you a real time frame here, but this happened relatively shortly. So the first few slides here I showed you happened within three to four months. So, you know, I think one of the issues which we haven't touched based on directly, but it's also, it's not always about biology and tumor progression, but also I think about quality of life. This patient was a highly functional patient. that worked full time, was a mother to three children, you know, and had to go on with her life. So she really was bothered by the diarrhea, which was really keeping her from doing a lot of the things she would normally do. So she sort of, you know, needed to move on. And that's why we don't necessarily have to be that aggressive with most patients. But quality of life, I think, is a really important part, especially with carcinoid syndrome. And so I think that it's important to consider that. Her symptoms did finally improve after a blood embolus. Serotonin level went down by almost a thousand points to 364. So that's a pretty good success. And I think it also speaks for, you know, the knowledge and the savoir faire of our interventional radiology colleagues. But, you know, about six to eight months later, she came back to clinic. And again, you know, we're scanning her in the meantime, no major changes, but she reports worsening symptoms again and her serotonin shoots back up. But the MRI read at the time, you know, says that things look grossly stable. Is there anything you would want to do at this time point? Maybe Dr. Soraris, you could comment if there's anything else that you think this patient would need?

Again, it's all about the conversation with the patient and goals of care, because, you know, there's other strategies. If you believe, really, that it is just a progression of the functional status, then you can discuss, in addition to the later stat, you can discuss strategies to increase the frequency of the somatostein analog or the dose if you are in octreotide, and if you are in laryotide, you can do every two weeks. But this is a patient that actually if we think about an error to study that was recently presented and published with Ki67 of 10% and quality of life being something very affected and the high tumor burden of disease, it's not unreasonable to consider here are three treatments, again, depending on the conversations with the patient is at least worth the conversation here. And, you know, six months later, you can argue that, would you want to try more liver embolizations? I personally prefer to see at least a good year of benefit before trying again, but it's certainly conversations that can take place.

Yeah, very good. So I think, like you suggested previously, studying her on teloresat was thought to be the next step because, you know, again, she was very active, she was working, she didn't want anything really more at that time. And this was sort of an easy thing for us to just do. But unfortunately, she didn't have any major improvements in her symptoms.
And may I just ask, did she stay on the Ritostat for a good three months?

Yeah, she did. So we'll make sure that she always tries eight weeks at the minimum. I think it's an important point you bring up because symptoms may not improve within two weeks. We know that, right? So we generally tell our patients to stay on it for at least two months before they stop. So we got to repeat DOTATATE PET because, you know, I think it's important to remember that MRIs sometimes will show obviously what happens in the liver, especially when you have a lot of liver disease, confluent liver disease, like she has. It's sometimes challenging to really assess true progression. I don't know if you've found similar things, but she got a repeat DOTATATE PET and the DOTATATE PET showed worsening of her liver disease as well as some new retrocural lymph nodes. So, sort of a very mild and small extra hepatic disease. Dr. Lewis, at this point, symptoms getting worse, clearly had some progression, some although very small amount of extra hepatic disease. Anything you would recommend that this patient be started on at this time?

Yeah, I think I'll combine my colleagues' comments, which I thought were extremely insightful. You know, the word aggressive has always struck me as very subjective. So sometimes patients will ask me, even the very first visit, Doctor, is this aggressive? I like the way that Dr. Shahan put it that you know, honestly, disease biology will declare itself in time. And the KS67 of 10% is really an interesting sort of liminal number that yes, is grade two, but as he was saying, can kind of go either way. And so I would again reiterate what Dr. Suarez was saying that as of this year, as of ASCOGI, and the publication of the NNR2 data, which of course places PRT with somatostatin analogs right up front, I would strongly consider PRT given this dodotate PET, which really by the lock and key hypothesis shows that there is still disease that's targetable, not just with analog, but with therapeutic radionuclide.

So this is exactly what we did. We started on PRT. She had improvements in her symptoms and her serotonin level ranged from 274 to 46 over the treatment period of eight months. So she definitely improved dramatically and probably felt the best that she had. in many years. A repeat DOTATATE PET CT a year later, so it's stable disease. You even see maybe some of this extra hepatic disease. These retrocrural lymph nodes are not as obvious anymore under DOTATATE PET. But two years post PRT, her symptoms worsened again and her serotonin went back up again above a thousand. So what now, Dr. Liao, any recommendations?

Yeah, I think, you know, we would be worried about disease progression. And then the question is, does it mean the liver or outside the liver? Because our treatment options may be different. So if it's within the liver, we may still be able to consider something liver directed, such as embolization or debulking, which is not a candidate. But if it's more systemic progression, then we will choose another systemic therapy. So I think the MRI here shows mainly liver progression, right?

That's right, yeah. So this is a really interesting case because what ended up happening, and you have the two dotatates next to each other here within a year period, is that she mostly had progression of a single lesion in segment two that sort of rapidly appeared out of nowhere. And she had some progression in segment four, but not dramatic really, it was the segment a two lesion here that you could see very clearly on the dotated that really significantly changed came out of nowhere so as from an ir perspective anything you can offer for lesion this measured about three and a half centimeters.

Yeah, definitely. So this is now we're talking about sort of the other spectrum where we often are asked to evaluate patients is when you have maybe one lesion in this situation that's growing out of control, whereas the rest of the disease is stable. So when we're trying to target just one lesion, we can start thinking about some of our percutaneous treatments, which are treatments through the skin. directly into the tumor, and that's specifically ablation is one good option. Ablation is where you take a needle through the skin directly into the tumor. You can either burn it or freeze it or even electrocute it. Ideally, we like to do it for lesions that are three centimeters or smaller because those tend to be treated best. And again, depending on the location, we can also do very focal embolization as well. So I don't recall what we did here, but this does look like it's in a favorable location for ablation.

Right. So, yeah, in this particular case, you know, I have to smile because Dr. Shahan, before we started the tumor board said, well, the case you're going to present, the answer is easy. Everybody goes through surgery. Well, you know, this was presented at tumor board and we went back and forth and we thought that certainly we could destroy this, but we weren't sure. whether percutaneous approach would really significantly help her symptoms. And so we also wanted a good chunk of tumor because we wanted to run some more additional tests, especially to see whether this is a tumor that is slowly de-differentiating. We sort of bit the bullet and I gotta tell you this is not generally cases that I as a surgeon like to debunk because, like I said, we generally aim to go over 90% debunking, which clearly, look at the DOTA 3 patent, in this case is not possible. But we did take it to the operating room. and we removed quite a bit of tumor. So you can see here multiple deposits ranging from four to eight centimeters essentially. So you know looking at putting all of these tumors together was basically bigger than an orange in terms of what we were able to remove. The fascinating part was this. So we asked our pathologist to specifically look at different blocks and, you know, the segment 2s turned out to be with a cat 6-7 of 20%. The segment 5, which was the other one, 4-5 that was growing, was 12.5% and the other ones were 1%. So, this, I think, is a really interesting finding. I'm curious to see what the team is going to say about this. But before I give you the floor, I will add that, again, we run an Oncoplus, and again, it showed a B-core mutation, but also now we had a SMAT4 loss and, perhaps more importantly, an RB1 loss. So, when you see this report here, and I know we don't always get to see reports like this after PRT, after liver-directed therapy, to have so many multiple samples, but what runs through your mind? Let's start with Dr. Soraris.

Yeah, it certainly is concerning that, you know, things are picking up more. We tend to see this in more aggressive tumors, so that goes along with the imaging that we're seeing in the growth of some of the lesions.
Dr. Shahan, how often do you see this heterogeneity of Ki-67s within tumors?

Actually, quite frequently, especially in the era of heightened PRRT use and also in PNets where people have gotten alkylator-based chemotherapy for a longer time. I'm seeing a lot of grade migration and aggressive or up-regulation of the grades. So this is not uncommon and rarely I'm also noticing complete transformation from well-differentiated to poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma as well. This particular case, it looks like kind of genetic fingerprinting, it's acquiring like loss of RB1, which is more like pathogenomic of neuroendocrine carcinoma rather than neuroendocrine tumor. These tumors are definitely evolving and getting more aggressive as we can see here. So I'm glad that you did do the biopsy or at least surgical debunking so you can understand that. So if I see rapid growth in otherwise indolent disease, I'm worried about great migration and kind of worsening of the tumor biology and I almost always do a biopsy. And I also like to do both DOTATATE and FTG PET in these cases, because what happens in these heterogeneous diseases, you have to really target the more aggressive biology first. So you have to understand which lesions are more hypermetabolic and which are more SSTR, positive, negative, to really get a very comprehensive understanding of whether you're going to in future need chemotherapy, or you will be okay with some sort of targeted therapies.

Yeah, and postoperatively, your serotonin dropped to 4.4, the symptoms improved, so that's obviously positive for us, but to what we have discussed right now, I think that certainly this is not going to be a case that's just going to, you know, sit quiet for a while. It has for the last three months or so, but we expect that something again within the next six months is going to change. I guess that occasionally you could be lucky and just have wedged out just the one clone, you know, that was the problematic one. But similar to what you said, we do think that generally this has changed overall in terms of probably multiple foci throughout this liver that now have more aggressive features. Dr. Liao, if this patient recurs relatively rapidly, and assuming there are no FTG positive lesion, but still high uptake on dodatate, would you consider retreatment with PRT? Or would you, because of the Ki-67, likely go to a chemotherapy-based approach next?

I'll consider retreating with PRT given that it seems like she had a good progression-free interval with the first course of PRT and we're seeing more and more data, you know, from the NETR2 for the activity of PRT for the higher grade disease. Now had the biopsy shown something different, you know, with the RP loss, had it shown neuroendocrine, poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma with a very high KX67, like 70%, I would probably move on to chemotherapy instead.
Dr. Lewis, do you think the clonal change here, so the changes of the neuroendocrine tumor cells, perhaps getting a little bit more aggressive with a high Ki67, is due to PRT?

Oh gosh, that's an excellent question. I would infer that not. I liked what Dr. Chauhan said, that in the era of more and more alkylator use, and of course we see sort of CAPTEM used more and more, especially in our PNAT patients, You know, temozolomide certainly has the sort of hyper-mutational profile. We sometimes do that on purpose, actually, to try to raise, say, candidacy for immunotherapy. Just based on our understanding of the rates of your therapy-related MDS with PRT alone, meaning without alkylators, I think it's less likely that temozolomide did this. I do like the points you're driving home here, though, that when the disease is not acting in a manner that is congruent with your understanding of the proliferative rate, I think we are obligated to obtain more tissue. And I think it's really important to get across this point of heterogeneity. Dr. Suarez and I are involved in a very active support group here in Salt Lake. And just as most breast cancer patients would know their ER, PR, HER2 status, the leader of the support group here almost inculcates in our members and our patients that they need to know their Ki-67. I think the problem is the overly simplistic assumption that the Ki-67 is static or is homogenous. And as Dr. Shohan said, we sometimes see what I would say is sort of a solid tumor version of a Richter's transformation where you go from a relatively low-grade biology to something much more threatening. And again, this is happening, as you've shown very elegantly, in the same patient at the same time. So I always focus my efforts on what I think is the most aggressive, and sometimes that means the most unexpected. Like you said, that segment two lesion just kind of popped up, and you showed that very nicely. And, you know, short of a very extensive surgery like you, I think very expertly performed, I think I would have sampled the segment two lesion and then based a lot of my treatment decisions around that.

reference_conclusion: Baseline evaluation for carcinoid syndrome should include 5-HIAA assessment and screening for carcinoid heart disease with BNP and echocardiography. Given persistent crampy abdominal pain and a near-obstructing small-bowel primary, resection of the primary tumor was undertaken; hepatic debulking was not pursued initially because the liver tumor burden was considered too extensive. For persistent carcinoid syndrome symptoms despite somatostatin analogue therapy, telotristat was considered, and liver-directed bland embolization was used for symptomatic hepatic disease when surgical debulking was not feasible. After subsequent symptomatic and radiographic progression on DOTATATE PET, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy was initiated, with consideration of PRRT retreatment at future recurrence if disease remains DOTATATE-avid and without FDG-positive transformation; chemotherapy would be favored if biopsy demonstrates poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma with very high Ki-67.
reference_conclusion_quote: I'll probably get to complement that 5-HIA. potentially a raw BNP and an echo, depending on the results to rule out carcinoid heart disease as part of the screening. [...] we did decide to take her to the operating room or to remove the primary tumor we thought that this was necessary to relieve her symptoms [...] This case was presented in the Neuroendocrine Tumor Board, and believe it or not, you know, we judged this, at least from a liver perspective, to be too high a tumor burden for debulking. [...] The other thing that we can potentially add on here is maybe Zermelo. [...] For patients with neuroendocrine tumors, we most often do what's known as bland embolization [...] Her symptoms did finally improve after a blood embolus. [...] I would strongly consider PRT given this dodotate PET [...] So this is exactly what we did. We started on PRT. [...] I'll consider retreating with PRT given that it seems like she had a good progression-free interval with the first course of PRT [...] had it shown neuroendocrine, poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma with a very high KX67, like 70%, I would probably move on to chemotherapy instead.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old left-handed woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive right superior visual field deficit. Jerking of the right arm was also reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Left temporal/insular glioma, molecularly classified as IDH-mutant lower-grade astrocytoma, molecular grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Tumor pathology was consistent with an IDH-mutant lower-grade glioma. Immunohistochemistry and molecular testing were performed, including assessment of IDH1 R132H, ATRX, and p53. DNA methylation classification identified the tumor as an IDH-mutant lower-grade neoplasm. Copy number profile was described as significantly less genomically complex than that of an IDH-wildtype high-grade glioma and as a calm copy number profile. No concerning molecular biomarkers suggesting a more aggressive variant were identified. MGMT promoter was unmethylated.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI demonstrated a large left temporal insular lesion with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and expansion/mass-like growth of the left temporal lobe. The lesion was heterogeneous internally, with dark foci interpreted as vascular structures. The lesion was described as non-enhancing. No additional sites of disease were described. Postoperative MRI demonstrated resection of the majority of the tumor, with residual T2 hyperintensity along the posterior aspect and possibly along the medial/central aspect, consistent with residual abnormal tissue in the postoperative bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-mutant tumor. Molecular testing included DNA/RNA next-generation sequencing and whole-genome DNA methylation profiling. DNA methylation classifier categorized the tumor as IDH-mutant lower grade. Copy number profile was calm/less genomically complex. MGMT promoter was unmethylated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Surgical resection was performed. Postoperative imaging showed that the majority of the tumor had been resected, with residual T2-hyperintense abnormality remaining posteriorly and medially.

[ current disease status ]: Status post subtotal resection of a left temporal/insular IDH-mutant molecular grade 2 glioma, with residual postoperative T2-hyperintense abnormality.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypothyroidism. The patient had been previously healthy and active. She was recently engaged and worked as an attorney. She was in the adolescent and young adult age range. Potential need for laboratory monitoring of liver enzymes was referenced in the context of systemic therapy considerations, but no baseline laboratory values were provided.

reference_discussion.text: I think that's an outstanding point. So over the course of my career, I took care of over 5,000 patients. And I felt the most important thing was at each decision juncture, we made the decision that irrespective of the result, when we look back, we had no regrets of the decision that we made. And that's a really, really difficult but such an important point. And I think the benefit of a tumor board and experts like we have here on our panel is they will tell you what the various options mean so that each person can make the right decision for themselves. There is no one right decision. If we knew how a treatment would work, we wouldn't actually need to see people. We could dial it in. If we knew it didn't work, we wouldn't do it. If we knew it worked, we would just do it. And so I think those are really important. And I hope you get a sense from this first discussion how important conversation is, discussion, and consensus. So with that, we'll segue to case two, which is a little, I think it's going to be a little briefer. It has to be. We have 20 minutes and 33 seconds left. But you guys have all heard the way this works, so we can actually go through the various components a little quicker. So it's a 32-year-old left-handed woman presented with progressive right superior visual field deficit, and as you will see, a large left temporal insular lesion, previously healthy, active, only has hypothyroidism, notice some jerking. of her right arm, recently engaged with a wedding plan, an attorney, busy law firm, emigrated to the country from college, parents, so we're thinking support, they live in China. So Javier, a little more briefly, but there you go. Absolutely. So what I'm showing or what we're looking at here is another axial image. So from the top down, this is a T2 flare sequence. I know on the last case we looked at T1 post contrast. I just want to make clear that when we're looking at the imaging, we're looking at all of the sequences for every patient. We're just pulling out the ones that we think are relevant for the discussion here. So here we have T2 flare. We see some bright signal and some expansion or mass-like growth of the left temporal lobe. T2 signal hyperintensity is that bright signal that you're seeing. It's also fairly nonspecific and it can represent tumor or swelling, edema is what we call it, or swelling. It can also represent scarring in the post-treatment setting. This patient has not yet been treated, so we're not necessarily concerned about scarring or gliosis. But the challenge we face is determining or defining what is the edge of the tumor? Where does the tumor stop and just edema or swelling kind of begin? One additional thing I'll point out here looking at this, in addition to that swelling, is kind of the internal aspect. There's some dark areas. It's got what we would call some heterogeneity to it. So I'm looking at this and I'm thinking this looks to me like it's an IDH mutant tumor by imaging characteristics. I can tell you I don't have the contrast enhancement up here, but let's say it's not enhancing, so I'm thinking it's probably a lower grade tumor. But that's kind of where I would stop. And as I mentioned in the other case, one of the critically important roles of a neuroradiologist here is to also identify additional sites of disease because that's gonna be critical for management. So that's fantastic. So this is actually where our neurosurgical colleagues shine. And this is, you're gonna hear why it's so important that the person who does the operation is a skilled brain tumor neurosurgeon. So Dr. Lim.

Yeah. Could you go back to that picture? Of course. So I think at this point, again, the principles of getting as much as you can out is critical for this type of diagnosis. For low-grade gliomas, the data seems even clearer. The more you get out, the better the patients can do. What we have right now where the field sits is if you can get at least 75% of it out, patients can live a pretty long time. Now that's a nuanced conversation because 25% of a bigger tumor like this is still a lot of tumor, whereas 25% of a small tumor is a very small residual, and that's kind of where experience and comes in. In this situation, again, the principles are to try to get as much of it as you can out. And there's actually a new principle in this we call GTR plus, gross total resection plus. We actually get a margin of almost normal brain out. And when you do that, some of the patients can do really, really well. I mean, decades if you can achieve that. For this person, it's a dominant hemisphere lesion, we think, which means speech is probably in or near it. And in this situation, I'll have the patient go through what's called a functional MRI. You'll get an MRI, you'll be asked to talk, move your fingers, and we'll be able to map out where your speech is, where your tracks are, where the wires are for movement, and I can see where that is in relationship to the tumor. The tumors can either infiltrate into it and in essence envelop it or they can be pushing all those structures away and that's a critical decision point for me as I plan for surgery. For these what's different is I will keep my patients awake as we remove these tumors because I again, want to achieve as much or get out as much of the tumor as possible. And if you look, there are little black dots in that tumor. Those are blood vessels, and we don't want to cause injury to that. And it's critical, again, to be using what I call neuro-navigation. We have special instruments that can remove these types of tumors and preserve vessels. And again, having the intraoperative mapping done, which is to keep patients awake, that requires, again, a big multidisciplinary team. I have neurologists in the room, special anesthesiologists in the room to help me do this. But again, the goal is to, even if I could get what's called a GTR+, patients can do really, really well from that.
So what are the implications of this patient's left-handedness?

So with someone being left-handed, still a good majority of patients have speech on the left side. Depending on the literature you read, for right-handed people, about 90% of people have speech on the left, and for left-handed people, still about 80% can have speech on the left. That functional MRI, I think, is critical. Fantastic.

So this is the post-surgery scan. Yeah, I'll just mention a couple of things here really quickly. So you can see that a majority of the tumor was resected. There still is some residual T2 hyperintensity along the posterior or back aspect, as well as maybe along the medial or aspect along the middle or closer to the central aspect of the brain. And now, I mentioned earlier also that this T2 hyperintensity, it's not specific. It can represent edema or tumor. Now that there's been surgery, we add that additional element of post-surgical change. scarring with radiation, same sort of thing, scarring. And so now you're sitting there scratching your head, what of these three things could it be? And this is where it's important to look back at the prior imaging, understand what was resected, understand the surgical plan so you can truly say, okay, this here looks like it's, you know, it was there before, so it's probably tumor. We also have some newer technologies that we're applying, some newer molecular imaging technologies where we're trying to understand what's happening in terms of the metabolites present within those tissues. IDH mutant tumors are known to make certain metabolites that are specific to that IDH mutation. So you may have heard of MR spectroscopy, which can be used to help us make that differentiation. There are also some PET imaging agents and some other advanced imaging or MR imaging agents that are being looked at to give us greater specificity, help us understand that. And a lot of this is being driven by some of the newer treatments that you're about to hear from this group. Great. Thank you so much. Dr. Sniderl, you are on with pathology.

Yes, so a lot of same things that I've showed you are shown here as before, but I want to emphasize that it is molecular pathology to really completely redefine how we think about gliomas. We have mentioned the word IDH, not sure how many of them, how many of you are familiar with that. It's one of the critical genes that helped us to basically separate adult gliomas into two major categories. For simplicity, IDH mutants, the good ones, if you will, and IDH wild types, which was our first case, the not-so-good ones or the bad ones. And what we did here is something very similar. Some of these mutations we can test with immunohistochemistry directly in a slide, like IDH1R132H, but it's only one of the mutations that's tested this way, ATRX and P53, and then a variety of molecular tests that help us determine how busy genomically this tumor is. You can see copy number profile in this tumor. It's significantly less busy than the previous one, and MGMT is against methylated. I want to emphasize molecular testing is not equally available to every patient at every institution. At NYU, we employ the strategy, every molecular test for every brain tumor patient, DNA, RNA, next-generation sequencing, and whole genome DNA methylation to really get a complete genomic picture of every patient. And this way we can really confirm not only it's an IDH mutant tumor, which there was a good suspicion based on the radiology, but we can also use some advanced molecular techniques such as DNA methylation classification. As you can see at the middle left, it classifies an IDH mutant lower grade. And that is very good news for these patients because we know now molecularly that these patients are truly lower grade by molecular techniques, not only based on the microscope.

That's fantastic. So I want to really emphasize a point. So for IDH mutated tumors The staining which you see on the second panel from the left will only Be positive in 90% of IDH mutated tumors. Okay, we call those canonical So you can impress people at you know parties If you have one of them, you have a canonical IDH. If you have one of the other 10%, you have a non-canonical. You cannot diagnose an IDH mutation in a non-canonical mutation with staining. That requires DNA sequencing. So if a patient has a tumor and the pathologist says the IDH stain was negative, this is not IDH mutated, There should be a buzzer that goes off. What did the DNA sequencing show? I think it's a really, really important point. Doing a stain takes a day. Doing the sequencing has to be sent to a laboratory, et cetera. But it is essential. Would you agree, Dr. Sniderol?

Absolutely. I think it's imperative that every glioma, no matter what radiology or basic pathology says, should be sequenced. Absolutely everyone. It doesn't matter. We have shown over and over that molecular testing is significantly better than pathology estimate of a diagnosis. Fantastic.
So very important message. So in the interest of time, I'm going to pass it on to the treatment team for a quick discussion.

Thank you. So the majority of brain tumor patients in the country come to community hospitals. I am in a community hospital. And so I want to emphasize, again, for the people in the back, for people virtually, your tumor should go for genetic testing. And these are the cases, the lower grade tumors, where we really see a huge variety based on where you were diagnosed. So if you're in a small town in rural Montana, you may not even have heard of genetic sequencing. You may have had a different kind of surgery. You may immediately have gotten radiation. So there's a lot of variety in treatment. So this is where an opinion, a second opinion, even if it's just virtual, even if it's just tumor board, really will allow you to be on the best treatment that everyone else in the country is getting. So equity and disparity is high in brain tumor care. and especially when it comes to grade two, grade three gliomas, because there is a lot of variety in it, and the research is changing so rapidly, as we'll talk about, and so we really wanna make sure you're getting the most up-to-date information, and the most up-to-date guidelines are being followed. And so here, this is where a lot of our conversations in the tumor board are about, should this patient get radiation? And that'll be a controversy and a discussion, and again, going back to who this patient is, what's important to them, and I think if we go to the next slide, we'll talk a little bit about that. We also discuss clinical trials here, this is very important. Now I discussed a young woman who, we presented a young woman who is about to get married, she has to think about fertility, family planning. And for women, it's not very simple in terms of banking, so that takes time, that takes a referral to a reproductive endocrinologist. And so we want to make sure that we discuss clinical trials, we want to discuss fertility family planning, and then we want to discuss if or not, if this patient should get radiation right now, or can we wait on radiation. And some of this discussion comes from very new data from the INDIGO trial. So this was a trial done with a drug called woricidinib, which is specifically targeted to IDH mutant tumors. And so this is our new brave world of targeted therapy, and we're really trying to treat every patient personalized with their mutations. So warasitinib in patients who had low-grade, grade 2 tumors, if they did not get radiation, but a year after, if they were randomized to warasitinib, they had significant control of their tumor, and they also had seizure control for patients with low-grade glomazolfil have seizures. So based on that, we consider warasitinib for these patients. Again, each patient is individual. It depends a lot on what grade and mutations they have, but we have that conversation in Tumor Board.
Excellent, so Dr. Shi, you're asked, radiation or no radiation? To be or not to be?

At some point, radiation is usually part of the story for these patients. The opportunity with the voracitinib is that we have data that shows that it can control these tumor for quite some time. If you only had one option at this fork and said it's either a drug like voracitinib or radiation, Radiation has a longer durability, but radiation has risks of side effects, and going through radiation itself can be arduous and tough. And so we don't know all the right answers there, so what we're doing is taking the data that we have and thinking together as a team, again, as the multidisciplinary team to figure out and incorporating with the patient and family what is right for each individual. We don't really know. We don't have the crystal ball, but we take, we make this decision individualized with each person. If there's concerns that, you know, the surgery wasn't that 75, 80% of Dr. Lim mentioned. There's concerns from the molecular features of the tumor that it could be a more aggressive variant. Then we're more likely to go with radiation, because that's been a little bit more tried and true. And radiation also always comes with chemotherapy. So there's a lot of effects. One decision impacts the rest of the decision pathway. But if a person had great surgery, they're young, they're doing a lot of other things in their life, radiation actually seems really disruptive. And you're worried about always, what if there are neurocognitive effects with radiation? Sometimes, it may make, right now, for a lot of patients, it's made sense to go the route of for acidinib if they have the mutation and they seem to, they're likely to be responsive to this tumor, to this treatment.

So again, emphasizing 90% it's easy to make the IDH diagnosis by a stain. 10% needs that extra testing, but it's so pivotal and critical in the decision making, not only for treatment, but also for guiding the patient with prognosis. So another emphasis. And so dr. Snooter all just to get back so very important. Dr. Sharma said for grade 2 IDH mutant tumors So what do you do you look at a you look at an entire tumor? This was a large tumor mass and you see it's 95% grade 2 and you see one island that looks grade 3 and

Yeah, no, this is a huge point because people often think that making a diagnosis is easy. You look at a slide and that's what it is, right? It's quite the opposite. Grade fours are easy, and I think I would say the clinical decision there is a little bit easier because we know it's a bad disease. Grade twos are usually easy. It's all benign looking or low-grade looking. But then there's that grade 3. And it's important to keep that word sitting there. It's only approved, I believe, for grade 2. And many of the pathologists just don't want to be wrong. They don't want to be wrong in a way, you know what? I'm not so sure. Maybe I'll call it grade 3. That's kind of like in between, right? I cannot be wrong. It's halfway between good and bad. So if it's good, I'm not wrong. If it behaves bad, I'm not wrong either. People hate to be wrong, right? And it's just human nature. You hedge your bets. And I've been on a passionate quest to eradicate grade 3. I think it's a scourge of our decision making. And we have shown that we can get rid of grade 3 IDH astrocytoma by using molecular tools and really determine this young lady. She has molecular grade 2 tumor. Calm copy number profile, no scary biomarkers. It is molecular grade 2. So even if I see a small focus that gives me a pause histologically, I will not call this grade 3. I will not push my clinical colleagues in the direction of aggressive treatment because this is molecular grade 2. And we've seen it over and over that even if these patients come back after no therapy, In 90% of the time, they don't have any additional molecular changes. So it would be imprudent to push our clinical colleagues into more aggressive treatment. So I think this is where molecular diagnostics really shines, helps to give you a definitive answer molecularly, rather than an opinion based on human feelings.
But conversely, it could look great, too, and molecular look more aggressive, and you would reflect that in your pathology.

Yeah, you are absolutely right. We've shown that about 25% to 28% in the big academic centers, 25% to 28% of these diagnoses are wrong. Not because people are bad diagnosticians, but because you cannot make these assumptions based on histology. That's why molecular testing is so critical. That's a lot of patients that are either over-diagnosed or under-diagnosed. So Dr. Lim, did you?

Oh, I was just going to go back on one point, but the other point of confusion sometimes is, as we mentioned in surgery, I do intraoperative MRIs for my cases, and statistically, 60% of the times when you do an intraop MRI, we actually find there's still a little bit left, and we can get gross total resections. or GTR plus, but another question that's also there is right now the voracitaminib is approved for even if you get it all out, but that's another one where the tumor board may have another interesting conversation, because even if we get it all out, some will wait and some will treat. Excellent.
So, Ivalu, you actually get the last word in the big picture, the psychosocial considerations.

OK, yes, it's trying to wrap it up. But so these are things we want to consider for this patient if they chose, you know, divorce it in a brow. Can they go back to work? This patient is busy. It's an attorney works in a law firm. Like, what would that look like? Because we want to talk about side effects as well with fatigues, nausea, vomiting and also elevated liver enzymes. So we want to make sure this patient's being followed up. with labs, and just the stress of it all, right? This patient is recently engaged. You're planning a wedding. I remember how stressful it was planning my wedding. So now you're dealing with that in a brain tumor treatment. So that's a lot. And then Dr. Shama mentioned about family planning for this patient. you know, egg preservation typically is not covered by insurance. It's a lot of out-of-pocket costs. We want to make sure, you know, we can present resources of financial assistance for this patient if available and just provide that mental health and social support for the patient and the fiancee as well. You know, they're newly, they're only 32, they have so much, you know, to go for and like They also qualify for the AYA group, so that's called the Adolescents and Young Adults, ages from 15 to 39. So they are this unique gap, this unique age gap that, you know, we don't, they have different needs, and they're starting out their career, you know, starting a family. We want to make sure that they have other resources available for them. And there's other organizations dedicated for the AYA group, such as the Stupid Cancer and the Deer Jack Foundation.

I want to make a plug here for my talk later. But I will be talking, sometimes people think lower grade glioma, there's no reason for palliative care to get involved. And so we'll be talking about how palliative care can be a resource for all patients, including and especially patients who are dealing with all these issues that Jenny so greatly summarized.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Asymptomatic right ventral tongue mass identified by dentist on 20 October 2023.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the right ventral oral tongue/floor of mouth. Initial clinical stage was cT1N0M0, stage I. Final pathologic stage after identification of nodal metastasis was pT1N2aM0, stage IVA.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside incisional biopsy demonstrated adenoid cystic carcinoma with cribriform and tubular growth patterns invading skeletal muscle. Definitive resection pathology showed a 1.9 cm adenoid cystic carcinoma with cribriform and tubular patterns and no solid component. Margins were negative. No lymphovascular invasion was identified. Multifocal intratumoral perineural invasion was present; the largest involved nerve measured 0.4 mm in diameter. In the right level IB nodal specimen, 1 lymph node was positive for metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma with a 7 mm focus and microscopic extranodal extension measuring less than 1 mm. Completion bilateral neck dissection pathology showed no additional positive lymph nodes.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan in December 2023 showed ill-defined hypermetabolic activity in the anterior tongue with SUV 5.8. Bilateral level II cervical nodes were present and interpreted as nonspecific, with SUV 3.3 on the right and 2.7 on the left. MRI demonstrated the tongue lesion and bilateral cervical nodes that were considered nonspecific, including a 1.5 cm right level II node and a 1.3 cm left level II node. Surveillance imaging remained negative through September 2024.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right partial glossectomy with partial floor-of-mouth resection, with 1.5 cm margins taken. Reconstruction was performed with a left radial forearm free flap. Tracheostomy was performed. A right level IB neck dissection was performed for vessel exploration; the submandibular gland was preserved. Intraoperative frozen-section margins were negative. The resection defect involved the anterior one-third of the right oral tongue, extended across the midline, and involved the floor of mouth. Following final pathology showing a positive right level IB node with microscopic extranodal extension, the patient underwent completion bilateral neck dissections. Operative findings included a moderately firm level IA node; all cranial nerves and vessels were intact at the end of the procedure. Final pathology from the completion neck dissections was negative for additional nodal metastasis. Adjuvant intensity-modulated radiotherapy was delivered to the oral cavity and bilateral neck to a total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions, completed in April 2024.

[ current disease status ]: No evidence of disease on clinical follow-up and surveillance imaging at last follow-up. Last documented surveillance imaging in September 2024 was negative.

[ other clinical data ]: Review of systems was notable only for weight loss since April 2023 following gastric sleeve surgery. Past medical history was otherwise non-contributory. Initial physical examination showed a submucosal right ventral tongue mass measuring approximately 1.5 cm, abutting the midline. The tongue was mobile, the floor of mouth was soft, and there were no palpable neck masses or adenopathy. There was no preoperative tongue anesthesia or impairment of tongue movement.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Distal ureteral tumor with nodal metastatic disease in the upper retroperitoneum; recent history of high-risk bladder disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma of the distal ureter, clinical stage cT2N1. Nodal disease involved an upper retroperitoneal lymph node; no pelvic lymphadenopathy was identified on staging.

[ histopathology results ]: Interventional radiology biopsy was obtained from the nodal lesion located between the great vessels. Following systemic therapy and surgery, pathology demonstrated complete response with ypT0N0.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial disease included a distal ureteral lesion and upper retroperitoneal nodal metastasis without pelvic lymph node involvement. Post-chemotherapy imaging demonstrated complete radiographic response, with interval opening of the previously involved ureteral segment.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Estimated glomerular filtration rate was reported in the 70 mL/min range.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received neoadjuvant dose-dense MVAC chemotherapy for 6 cycles. A tolerability issue with MVAC was reported. Post-treatment imaging showed complete response. Repeat ureteroscopy was performed before surgery and showed no new disease higher in the collecting system. The patient subsequently underwent distal ureterectomy with right pelvic lymph node dissection, retroperitoneal lymph node dissection including the previously involved area, and ureteral reimplantation with psoas hitch. Surgical pathology confirmed pathologic complete response (ypT0N0). Renal preservation was achieved. Maintenance BCG was continued because of the history of high-risk bladder disease.

[ current disease status ]: No residual carcinoma was identified on post-treatment surgical pathology (ypT0N0). Imaging after chemotherapy showed complete response.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient desired renal preservation. Preoperative evaluation for kidney-sparing surgery included repeat ureteroscopy to exclude additional proximal upper tract disease. Bladder evaluation was considered relevant because of the recent history of high-risk bladder disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid mass with compressive symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated oncocytic thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe with extensive vascular invasion; metastatic disease to lung identified on FDG PET and confirmed by resection of a small lung lesion showing poorly differentiated oncocytic thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion showed an oncocytic neoplasm. Left thyroid lobectomy specimen demonstrated an oncocytic carcinoma with fibrosis and extensive blood vessel invasion, with at least 3-4 foci/sides of vascular invasion described. Necrosis was present and was considered tumor necrosis for classification purposes. Three mitotic figures were identified. The tumor was described as encapsulated. There was no evidence of extrathyroidal extension on surgical assessment. The resected small lung lesion was positive for poorly differentiated oncocytic thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a large left thyroid lobe mass with retrosternal extension into the anterior mediastinum. No concerning cervical adenopathy was identified. Ultrasound demonstrated a large heterogeneous mixed-echogenicity lobulated left thyroid mass. FDG PET identified a small lung lesion; no additional sites of disease were reported on PET.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing identified a TERT mutation without BRAF mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent left thyroid lobectomy for the thyroid mass. Surgery was completed smoothly, the mass was removed intact, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve was preserved. No gross vascular invasion or extrathyroidal extension was identified intraoperatively. A small lung lesion detected on FDG PET was subsequently resected and pathology confirmed metastatic poorly differentiated oncocytic thyroid carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]: Status post left thyroid lobectomy and resection of a solitary PET-avid lung metastasis. Post-resection FDG PET reportedly showed no other sites of disease. The patient had postoperative pain at last clinic review. Follow-up regarding headaches was not yet available.

[ other clinical data ]: Laryngeal examination was normal preoperatively. No adenopathy was identified on imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old female from Molo; married; occupation recorded as farmer; NHIF contributor.

[ chief complaint ]: Painful anterior chest wall/sternal mass present for approximately 1 year and increasing in size.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma, initially diagnosed in September 2013. Recurrent disease was documented in 2015 and again in April 2017, with left axillary nodal involvement and lung and liver metastases. Current symptomatic anterior chest wall/sternal mass was present by February 2018.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- September 2013 lumpectomy: invasive ductal carcinoma with positive margins.  
- 2014 mastectomy specimen: ER negative, PR negative; HER2 negative was also recorded subsequently, consistent with triple-negative disease.  
- 2015 recurrent mass/lumpectomy specimen: grade 3 carcinoma with positive margins and lymphovascular invasion.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Post-mastectomy CT scan: lung fields were normal; no evidence of metastasis; no pleural effusion; cystic anterior sternal mass measuring approximately 4 × 6 cm; bony calvarium appeared normal; other visualized organs were reported as normal.  
- Follow-up CT in April 2017 after recurrence: left axillary lymph node involvement with lung and liver metastases.  
- CT in 2017 also described a mass measuring 1.3 × 1.2 cm with liver lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: ER negative, PR negative, HER2 negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- September 2013: lumpectomy performed for primary breast cancer.  
- 2014: mastectomy performed; referred for radiotherapy but was lost to follow-up.  
- 2015: returned with recurrent mass.  
- November 2015 to February 2016: adjuvant chemotherapy administered, comprising 4 cycles of AC followed by 4 cycles of taxane-based chemotherapy; completed February 2016.  
- 2016: resection of recurrent mass performed.  
- June 2016: radiotherapy delivered, 30 sessions at Texas Cancer Center.  
- April 2017: evaluation demonstrated recurrent metastatic disease involving left axillary nodes, lungs, and liver.  
- May 2017 to 31 October 2017: palliative capecitabine (Xeloda/Zaloda), 8 cycles completed.  
- February 2018: developed enlarging painful anterior chest wall mass over the sternum.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with prior documented lung and liver metastases and current painful fixed sternal/anterior chest wall mass. On examination, performance status was 1. General condition was fair. She was not pale, not jaundiced, and had no sinus formation. Right breast was normal with no axillary lymphadenopathy. Left chest wall showed a healed, dry mastectomy scar without obvious local breast-site mass. There was a hard, tender, elevated, fixed mass over the sternum measuring approximately 4 cm. No axillary lymphadenopathy was detected on current local examination.

[ other clinical data ]: Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. Previous admissions were recorded. No biopsy of the sternal mass had been performed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old woman; previously healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodule detected on examination by gynecologist.

[ diagnosis ]: Right thyroid nodule with indeterminate cytology; final surgical pathology demonstrated Hurthle cell adenoma and incidental papillary thyroid microcarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration cytology: follicular lesion of undetermined significance (Bethesda III), with multiple oncocytes/Hurthle cell type; specimen described as cellular and composed almost exclusively of Hurthle cells in clusters, without significant colloid or lymphocytes.  
- Surgical pathology after hemithyroidectomy: 3.5 cm Hurthle cell adenoma, completely excised.  
- Additional findings: adjacent hyperplastic nodule; incidental 6 mm papillary microcarcinoma.  
- Pathology review of the adenoma showed individual cell apoptosis without necrosis, mitoses, or significant solid areas.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated an approximately 4 cm right thyroid nodule.  
- Nodule characteristics included solid composition, well-defined margins, hyper/isoechoic echogenicity, and wider-than-tall shape.  
- No punctate echogenic foci/microcalcifications were identified.  
- ACR TI-RADS score: TR3.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- ThyroSeq testing was positive, with an estimated 60% risk of malignancy.  
- No point mutation or gene fusion was identified.  
- Multiple chromosomal copy number alterations were detected, reported as associated with follicular-pattern carcinoma, including Hurthle cell carcinoma.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed and yielded Bethesda III cytology.  
- Molecular testing with ThyroSeq was performed.  
- Hemithyroidectomy was performed.  
- Postoperative pathology showed benign Hurthle cell adenoma with incidental 6 mm papillary microcarcinoma; adenoma was completely excised.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post hemithyroidectomy with complete excision of a 3.5 cm Hurthle cell adenoma.  
- Incidental 6 mm papillary thyroid microcarcinoma was identified on surgical pathology.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Physical examination before workup showed a mobile, non-tender thyroid nodule measuring approximately 2-3 cm by palpation; remainder of examination was normal.  
- No history of radiation exposure.  
- No family history of endocrine disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old male. Smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Lung squamous cell carcinoma with extensive bone metastases involving the spine; poor performance status related to bony metastatic disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with extensive osseous metastases in the spine. Performance status was ECOG/PS 3.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy did not show fully differentiated carcinoma. Subsequent biopsy reported squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Extensive bone metastases were present in the spine.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified a KRAS G12C mutation. EGFR testing showed an exon 20 point mutation classified as a variant of uncertain significance. EGFR variant allele frequency was reported as 44%. No STK11, KEAP1, or SMARCA4 co-mutations were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: PD-L1 testing by Dako 22C3 showed expression less than 1%. PD-L1 testing by Ventana SP263 showed approximately 1% expression (low expression).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Radiation therapy was started after the initial biopsy, before final histologic classification. No systemic anticancer treatment outcome was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic squamous cell lung carcinoma with persistent extensive spinal bone metastases and poor performance status (PS 3).

[ other clinical data ]: Poor performance status was attributed to extensive bone metastases.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Slowly enlarging right parotid mass, initially noticed approximately 3 months before presentation, with pain developing 3 weeks before consultation and isolated right upper eyelid drooping for 1 week.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade squamous cell carcinoma involving the right parotid region, favored to represent metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma to an intraparotid lymph node rather than a primary salivary/parotid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the right parotid lesion demonstrated malignant cells consistent with a high-grade carcinoma with squamous differentiation. Immunohistochemical studies showed S100 negative, SOX10 negative, CK7 negative, and p53 overexpression.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT neck demonstrated a 3.0 x 3.0 x 3.0 cm heterogeneously enhancing solid lesion in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland.  
- CT chest at initial staging was negative.  
- MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed, mildly lobulated 3.3 cm enhancing lesion in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland with mild fat stranding and no positive cervical lymph nodes.  
- Post-immunotherapy baseline MRI after hospital discharge demonstrated marked interval decrease in size and degree of enhancement of the superficial right parotid mass, consistent with treatment effect, with no evidence of tumor progression or cervical adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic sequencing results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Following the second cycle of cemiplimab, he was febrile and was found to have acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, and transaminitis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Prior history included cutaneous malignancies treated with local procedures.  
- He received neoadjuvant cemiplimab off trial: cycle 1 on 22 June 2025 and cycle 2 on 16 July 2025.  
- After the second cycle, he developed severe immune-related toxicity felt to represent capillary leak syndrome, with fever, acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, transaminitis, acute respiratory decompensation, intubation, and ICU admission.  
- He was treated with high-dose dexamethasone and supportive/conservative measures, improved, was transferred from ICU to the medical ward in August, and was subsequently discharged home.  
- Due to toxicity, further planned cemiplimab was not administered.  
- In September 2025, he underwent right superficial parotidectomy with limited level II/III neck dissection and facial nerve preservation. No operative complications were reported.  
- Postoperatively, he developed a small sialocele that failed repeat aspirations; a small drain was placed under local anesthetic in clinic, and this resolved.

[ current disease status ]: After two cycles of neoadjuvant cemiplimab, imaging showed marked interval response without progression or cervical adenopathy. He remained under close surveillance and was awaiting postoperative imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included cerebrovascular accident approximately 2.5 years earlier; he remained on aspirin.  
- On examination at presentation, there was right frontal branch facial nerve weakness and a mobile 3 cm right parotid mass free of overlying skin.  
- No overt cutaneous malignancy was identified on examination.  
- Intraoperatively, there was no frank facial nerve invasion; scar/treatment effect was present around the nerve.

For this gentleman in particular, given the previous history of cutaneous malignancies and the fact that he was traveling down to Florida and wasn't using sunscreen. We ultimately did favor a cutaneous primary after tumor board discussion. They did do some stains, which again did point to a cutaneous primary. Most specifically, his S100, SOX10, and CK7 were all negative, which made it less likely that it was a primary salivary carcinoma. And he did have some P53 overexpression as well. He then met with our medical oncology team and radiation oncology team and was presented at our tumor boards. Again, it felt that his path was consistent with a cutaneous primary that was metastatic to an intraparotid lymph node. As such, the recommendation was that we would start with two to four cycles of neoadjuvant semiplimab followed by surgery. And with this, we would do a repeat CT neck and chest after the first two cycles. He ultimately was admitted to the medicine unit, but unfortunately experienced acute respiratory decompensation requiring intubation and an ICU stay. He was ultimately treated with conservative measures, most notably high dose dexamethasone and was discharged from the ICU back to the medicine floor in August, continued to do well and was then discharged home. And for a quick word, the capillary leak syndrome is often associated with this myeloma. It's a rare but life-threatening immune-related adverse event where they get endothelial dysfunction as seen here with the resulting sequelae. So then he came in to see us after discharge and a new baseline MRI was obtained, which ultimately demonstrated marked interval decrease in the size and degree of enhancement of the superficial prodded mass consistent with treatment effect. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent right-sided neck mass in 2023.

[ diagnosis ]: Cutaneous melanoma of the vertex scalp, initially diagnosed in 2012. Initial stage was pT4b N2c M0, stage IIIC melanoma. Disease course included regional nodal micrometastatic involvement and in-transit metastasis in 2012, followed by recurrent regional melanoma in the right posterolateral neck in 2023 without distant metastatic disease identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial 2012 wide local excision specimen showed nodular melanoma of the vertex scalp, Breslow thickness 5 mm, ulcerated. Lymphovascular invasion was not identified. Perineural invasion was not commented on. Margins were clear. Bilateral sentinel node biopsies showed one micrometastasis in a right level II neck sentinel node. Completion right posterolateral neck dissection levels II-V yielded 27 lymph nodes negative for tumor; however, a small perinodal soft tissue deposit was present in scar tissue near the prior sentinel node biopsy site, not within a lymph node. Five months later in 2012, a small anterior scalp nodule at the prior excision site was excised and was consistent with in-transit metastasis. In 2023, biopsy of the right neck mass showed recurrent melanoma.

[ imaging findings ]: In 2023, MRI demonstrated an extensive right posterior level V neck mass infiltrating into the floor of the neck, not encasing the great vessels and not involving the brachial plexus, although extending toward that region. PET imaging showed FDG-avid disease confined to the posterolateral neck mass with no distant disease. Previously followed lung nodules were stable and non-FDG-avid. MRI brain was negative for intracranial disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF testing in 2012 showed no targetable BRAF mutation. Molecular testing on the 2023 recurrent melanoma again showed no targetable mutations, including no BRAF mutation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In 2012, the patient underwent wide local excision of vertex scalp melanoma with bilateral sentinel lymph node biopsies. Completion right posterolateral neck dissection levels II-V was subsequently performed. Adjuvant radiation was offered and declined. Systemic therapy was discussed at that time, but the patient was observed. Five months later in 2012, an in-transit scalp metastasis was excised. The patient then received 4 cycles on a clinical trial consisting of ipilimumab plus an IDO inhibitor. Treatment was discontinued because of immune-mediated colitis and panhypopituitarism. The patient was then observed and followed for more than 10 years. In 2023, for recurrent regional neck melanoma, the patient received 3 cycles of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab followed by surgery. Revision neck dissection resected two level V nodules. The patient then proceeded to adjuvant pembrolizumab, planned for 15 additional doses.

[ current disease status ]: No distant metastatic disease had been identified on PET imaging, and MRI brain remained negative. The patient was receiving adjuvant pembrolizumab.

[ other clinical data ]: Prior immune-related adverse events from ipilimumab plus IDO inhibitor included colitis and panhypopituitarism. Cranial nerve XI was preserved at the time of revision neck dissection.
