case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of suspected intraprostatic recurrence following prior focal ablation for localized prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma after prior focal therapy. Initial disease had been a focal left transition zone anterior lesion, Grade Group 2. On subsequent biopsy approximately 4 years after ablation, recurrent Gleason score 4+3 adenocarcinoma was identified in the prior target lesion and in the left posterior base.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial biopsy: focal left transition zone anterior lesion, Grade Group 2; all other sampled areas were negative.  
- Post-treatment biopsy at approximately 1 year of a small focal enhancing area: negative.  
- Repeat biopsy approximately 4 years after ablation: recurrent Gleason score 4+3 adenocarcinoma in the focal enhancing target lesion, with 90% pattern 4. Additional Gleason score 4+3 adenocarcinoma was present in the left posterior base.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pre-treatment prostate MRI demonstrated a focal left transition zone anterior lesion. A dense nodule with relatively less enhancement but marked hyperintensity on high b-value diffusion imaging (B2000) was also present and was included within the planned ablation zone.  
- MRI at 48 hours after focal ablation showed a homogeneous ablation zone with complete lack of enhancement, encompassing the treated lesion and the adjacent dense nodule.  
- MRI at approximately 1 year showed no significant enhancement and normal B2000 appearance; a small focal area of enhancement was biopsied and was negative.  
- MRI at approximately 4 years showed recurrent focal enhancement in the treated region.  
- A left posterior base lesion with Gleason 4+3 on biopsy had not been clearly visualized on MRI; T2 appearance remained normal, with only minimal nonspecific enhancement described.  
- Conventional staging imaging was negative.  
- PSMA PET/CT was not obtained.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Pre-treatment PSA: 13.8 ng/mL.  
- PSA at 1 month after ablation: 1.2 ng/mL.  
- Subsequent PSA values remained low and stable over follow-up; values reported included 1.9 ng/mL and 1.28 ng/mL.  
- At approximately 4 years after treatment, PSA remained low despite biopsy-proven recurrence.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Enrolled in a clinical trial using focal ablation with intravenously infused nanoshell-based therapy.  
- Treated lesion was the left transition zone anterior prostate lesion; the adjacent dense nodule was included within the ablation margin.  
- Early post-treatment imaging demonstrated complete nonenhancement of the ablation zone.  
- PSA declined from 13.8 ng/mL to 1.2 ng/mL at 1 month and remained low for several years.  
- Surveillance MRI and biopsy at approximately 1 year showed no confirmed residual malignancy.  
- At approximately 4 years after focal ablation, biopsy confirmed recurrent Gleason 4+3 disease in the prior target region and separate Gleason 4+3 disease in the left posterior base.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven intraprostatic recurrent prostate cancer approximately 4 years after focal ablation, with multifocal left-sided disease involving the prior treated anterior target and the left posterior base. Conventional staging was negative for metastatic disease. PSA remained low.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Baseline erectile function was preserved.  
- No lower urinary tract symptoms were reported at initial presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old man; smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough for 3 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Left lower lobe lung squamous cell carcinoma, clinical stage T2N0M0.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- CT-guided biopsy from the left lower lobe lesion showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Endobronchial ultrasound-guided nodal sampling from N2/N3 stations was negative for malignancy.  
- Lymph node biopsy showed granulomatous pathology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Chest radiograph showed left lower zone haziness.  
- PET-CT showed a fibrocavitary lesion in the left lower lobe with SUV 23.6, extending to the costal pleura.  
- PET-CT also showed tracer uptake in bilateral hilar and a few mediastinal lymph nodes.  
- CT imaging demonstrated a peripheral cavitary lesion in the left lower lobe with eccentric cavitation and associated emphysematous changes.  
- Brain MRI was performed; no abnormal findings were specified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- GeneXpert from an EBUS-sampled lymph node was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, reported as medium signal intensity.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- EBUS and CT-guided biopsy were performed during diagnostic workup.  
- Antitubercular therapy was started after EBUS GeneXpert positivity.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Clinical stage T2N0M0 left lower lobe squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Endobronchial ultrasound-guided nodal sampling from N2/N3 stations was negative for malignancy.  
- Granulomatous lymph node pathology in the setting of MTB GeneXpert positivity, with antitubercular therapy started.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Preoperative fitness assessment included cardiac evaluation, pulmonary function testing, DLCO, and stair-climbing assessment; the patient was considered fit for surgery.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old female. Past medical history was unremarkable. There was no family history of thyroid cancer, no history of benign thyroid disease, and no history of radiation exposure.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable left-sided neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Thyroid carcinoma of papillary type, described histologically as solid subtype papillary thyroid carcinoma. Initial thyroid FNA cytology was Bethesda IV (follicular lesion/follicular neoplasm). The patient subsequently underwent thyroid lobectomy followed by completion thyroidectomy.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma with nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma. The tumor showed prominent solid areas/nests of tumor cells with mitotic activity, consistent with solid subtype papillary thyroid carcinoma. Follicles with colloid were also present in parts of the tumor. Capsular invasion was identified. Necrosis was considered present on histologic review. A focus concerning for possible vascular invasion/angioinvasion was identified and investigated further on pathology review.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thyroid ultrasound images were not available for review. Ultrasound at the time of FNA demonstrated a solid lesion replacing essentially the entirety of the thyroid lobe/gland visualized, isoechoic relative to thyroid parenchyma, with tiny cystic areas, smooth margins, echogenic foci, wider-than-tall configuration on the captured image, and size of approximately 5 cm. There was no evidence of contralateral thyroid disease preoperatively.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing performed on the FNA specimen identified a PAX8-PPARG rearrangement/mutation. No additional molecular alterations were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was normal at presentation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent thyroid FNA, which yielded Bethesda IV cytology. She subsequently underwent thyroid lobectomy at an outside institution. After postoperative pathology review and molecular results, completion thyroidectomy was performed. She then received radioactive iodine, 50 mCi.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

reference_discussion.text: She also refused the clinical trial, and hence was started on ertifitinib Belversa 8 mg daily. She was advised to restrict any phosphate intake. She monitored for changes in vision, and after about 14 to 21 days, as long as her phosphate levels were under 5.5 mg per deciliter, she could increase her dose to 9 mg once daily. On follow-up, her hemoptysis has since resolved, her appetite is back, she's putting on some weight, and a repeat CT test three months later doesn't show a complete slam dunk, but pretty good as compared to what it was before, as you guys can appreciate. So let's talk about the FGFR receptor a little bit, which binds the members of the fibroblast growth factor family of proteins, which is one of the largest families of growth factor ligands, consisting of 22 different members. The FGFR receptor comprises of an extracellular ligand, a single transmembrane helix, and an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain, which fires down multiple pathways eventually to promote survival, growth, differentiation, and migration. There's at least five different subtypes of the FGFR receptor, including FGFR1 through 4, as well as FGFRL-1. What's important to point out here is that FGFR1 amplifications are seen in squamous cell, non-small cell lung cancers. But unfortunately, targeting these mutations have only promoted about 5 to 10 percent response rate. FGFR3 mutations have been found, like in our cancer patient with bladder cancer in 50 to 60 percent of non-small cell. and 10 to 15 percent of muscle-invasive. And obviously, with Dr. Kuznir being here, we want to make sure that we mention the FGFR2 receptor, which is frequently found in cholangiocarcinomas. And obviously, there's an approved medication for that as well, pemigatinib. And the drug reps didn't tell me to say that. Subtypes of muscle-invasive blood or cancers. So, mutations and fusions of such FGFR2 and 3s are common in patients that have urethelial cancers. and particularly the luminal subtype, which is about 20%. 40% of upper urothelial tracts also have this mutation. It's important because the luminal subtype has been associated with a much poorer response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, and it has a lower PD-L1 expression. Hence, FGFR inhibitors here are very interesting as this is probably the way to go, as you've both seen in our patient and you'll see in the following subtypes. Last year, there was a molecular NGS analysis of all the bladder tumors that were done in Europe. It was published in a European journal, because obviously they weren't publishing anything else. And what you're able to appreciate here is that there's six distinct subtypes for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, with luminal papillary and the basal squamous being the predominant subtypes, being about 55%. What's important to note here is that they each have distinct oncogenic mechanisms and mutations, with the luminal papillary having an FGFR3 mutation, the luminal unstable having an ERB2 or HER2, and the basal squamous having an EGFR. Unfortunately, targeting these subsequent mutations have not led to response rates. What else is important to point out here is that this is not only prognostic based on overall survival being four years for laminal papillaries and neuroendocrines around one year. But it's also predictive, because we know in the basal squamous subtypes, there is a very enriched CD4 count and CD8 count in the cellular matrix. Hence, these are more likely to respond to immunotherapy, whereas our FGFR mutator luminal subtypes are less likely to respond to immunotherapy. So let's talk about Belversa a little bit, or Dafitinib, which is a pan-FGFR kinase inhibitor, which inhibits multiple targets, including FGFR1-4, RET, CSF1R, PTGFR-alpha-beta, FLP4, KIT, and VEGFR2. The FDA granted approval for rhodofitinib for patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinomas with FGFR2 and 3 genetic alterations that have progressed during the following platinum-containing chemotherapy including within 12 months of neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemo. It's a mouthful, but bottom line, it's based on this BCL2001 trial, which was an open-label, non-randomized phase two. It included 99 patients, of which 43% had received at least two prior lines of therapy. To dive a little bit deeper into the trial, The response rates here were 40%, and out of which 60% of these patients had had prior immunotherapy. Out of those 60 patients, only five had responses to immunotherapy. The median duration of response here was 5.6 months. The median PFS was about 5.5 months, and the median OS was 14 months. Toxicities include grade 3s, which are hyponatremia at 11%, stomatitis at 10%, asthenia at 7. The most common adverse events are hyperphosphatemia, which is a known class effect of FGFR inhibitors. It's also important to note that there's multiple ocular toxicities that can happen. Those ocular toxicities happen within the first 50 days, so it's important that these patients see ophthalmology and get evaluations almost weekly for the first four weeks. They also get stomatitis at 58%, diarrhea at 51%, and dry mouth at 46%. So super easy to take. Very well tolerated drug. Yeah. You know, what else do we have? And what do we have? So, well, before 2016, medical oncologists were arguing between giving dose-dense NVAC or cisgen and which one was more toxic and which one had better overall survivals. They're both pretty crappy regimens. But in the past five years, we've had an explosion of immunotherapies. We've had multiple targets. And before 2016, our median overall survival was 13 months. The most recent immunotherapy based on the Javelin now has 22 months, which was in September 2020, which was followed by Infortinab with a median overall survival of 13 months at second line, and last but not least, the most recent approval of Sastatuzumab in third line with a 30% response rate. We're doing OK. I think we're doing OK. So where's the future? And like Dr. Kuznir said, it's not going to be a one size fits all type of store. I think in the near future, we're going to have personalized medicine with next gene sequencing. We're going to detect the right appropriate biomarkers for the right patients at the right time. And we're going to individualize treatments that are algorithmic based for our patients in front of us. And that's all I got. Thank you, guys.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male. No comorbidities were reported. Performance status was described as fit.

[ chief complaint ]: Pain in the upper thigh region.

[ diagnosis ]: Primary lung carcinoma with metastatic lytic bone lesion involving the upper thigh/femoral region. Clinical-pathologic classification favored lung adenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: EBUS-guided biopsy from the lung primary showed poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was inconclusive overall. TTF-1 was positive. Synaptophysin was positive. Small-cell carcinoma markers were reported positive, but morphology was not consistent with small-cell carcinoma or neuroendocrine morphology. Ki-67 was not performed.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a lytic lesion corresponding to the painful upper thigh region and identified a primary lesion in the lung.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genomic panel/NGS identified:
- EGFR exon 19 deletion, tier I pathogenic
- EGFR exon 20 mutation: L792F missense mutation, variant allele frequency 23%
- MET amplification, tier I pathogenic
- HER2 mutation, variant allele frequency 5.8%
- TP53 frameshift loss-of-function mutation

MET amplification copy number was not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine and carboplatin was initiated before availability of NGS results, due to absence of definite evidence of adenocarcinoma at treatment start. No response assessment or treatment outcome data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic lung carcinoma with bone involvement at the time of referral. Disease remained under active systemic treatment evaluation after identification of concurrent EGFR exon 19 deletion, EGFR exon 20 L792F mutation, and MET amplification.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional laboratory results were available.

So it's like saying, you know, it's a poor prognostic indicator. That's it. But you know, you cannot say that Osimodinib will not work here.

Not Lessernib, sir. Lessernib is not available. My question is Amivantinib with chemo.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic prostate cancer identified on staging imaging.

[ diagnosis ]: High-risk metastatic prostate cancer; hormone-sensitive status was referenced as relevant to treatment sequencing, but no confirmed castration-resistant disease was documented.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET/CT demonstrated a highly PSMA-avid primary prostate lesion with SUVmax approximately 40. PSMA PET/CT also demonstrated widespread small-volume osseous metastases, with more than 20 bone metastatic sites identified. CT showed little to no interval change for the vast majority of lesions. Conventional bone scan demonstrated only 3 sites of mild uptake, consistent with low-volume metastatic disease by conventional imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was 26.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent both PSMA PET/CT and conventional imaging within a trial setting. No systemic therapy, radiotherapy, surgery, or other prior cancer-directed treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: De novo metastatic prostate cancer with discordant staging between PSMA PET/CT and conventional imaging: extensive osseous metastatic burden on PSMA PET/CT and low-volume metastatic burden on bone scan.

[ other clinical data ]: Conventional imaging was available in addition to PSMA PET/CT. The case illustrated marked discordance between PSMA PET/CT and bone scan assessment of metastatic volume.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so this one, I just have the screen cap. Great. But Michael raised a good question just now, like, you know, should we be doing PSMA PET for all these patients now as we do mainly here in Australia? So if you saw our, so if you only had the PSMA PET without the conventional imaging, how does that change your management? You know, both of you and also Louise, would you?

I think from a systemic therapy perspective the volume of disease nowadays doesn't make too much of a difference in terms of the options available and how you decide which agent you would prescribe. It's more from a trial point of view, as Shanker mentioned, working at Peter Mac which is a very academic centre with lots of trials, Patients are still eligible based on having measurable disease based on resist on the CT or measurable bone lesions on the bone scan. Would you send them for lutetium PSMA treatment?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Self-detected palpable breast mass on breast self-examination.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage I triple-negative breast cancer of the breast.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy demonstrated invasive breast carcinoma, grade 3. Estrogen receptor was negative. Tumor was triple negative. Ki-67 was elevated, consistent with rapidly proliferating tumor cells.

[ imaging findings ]: Mammography was abnormal at the site of the palpable lesion. Breast ultrasound demonstrated a small breast mass with an adjacent nearby lesion. Breast MRI demonstrated the enhancing primary tumor with biopsy clip visible centrally and showed no evidence of additional disease elsewhere in the breast; the lesion was near the central breast but not involving the nipple. On clinical examination, the palpable mass was located at the edge of the areola without skin or nipple retraction. No palpable lymphadenopathy was present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline BRCA1 mutation was identified on genetic testing.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed stage I triple-negative breast cancer in a BRCA1 carrier, with no additional disease in the breast on MRI and no palpable lymphadenopathy. She was a candidate for nipple-sparing mastectomy.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included anxiety and depression. Family history included paternal grandmother with breast cancer and grandfather with prostate cancer. Fertility preservation was a relevant consideration given age.

reference_discussion.text: We can go one more ahead. We'll catch up to our next case. So in summary, this lady was treated with oncoplastic surgery, sentinel node biopsy. She got whole breast radiotherapy. She had an oncotype test and then was treated with endocrine therapy with a high expectation of cure. And then we can move along to the next case. We'll come back to survivorship at the end. So the second case is a young woman. She's 38 years old who presented with a mass that she identified on her own breast self-exam. And she had abnormal imaging and a biopsy. And her only medical history is anxiety and depression. Next slide. Her family history includes a paternal grandmother with breast cancer, grandfather with prostate cancer and she had a palpable mass at the edge of the areola, the pigmented area of the breast, but it wasn't pulling on the skin or the nipple and she had no lymph nodes. Next slide. The mammogram is done with, you can see the triangle on the skin there that seems to overlie, you can almost see a little triangle underneath there in the breast tissue. Next slide. And on ultrasound, there was a small mass and then another one right nearby. Next slide. She had a biopsy that showed that this was a breast cancer, but this was a different biology breast cancer. This was a higher grade. It was grade three. And it was estrogen receptor negative. In fact, it was what we call triple negative breast cancer. There were no receptors that were found on the cell surface that regulating the cell growth. And the KI67 shows that this is a cancer where the cells are dividing very rapidly. Next slide. A breast MRI was done to make sure that there was no sign of disease elsewhere. And you can see, I see your question. I'll jump in in a minute. You can see the tumor there that lights up. It's kind of whitish, and you can see the dark area in the middle, which is the biopsy clip. The other slide shows that this tumor is not close to the nipple, though. Even though it's near the center of the breast, the MRI is very helpful in very finely mapping the tumor extent, which can help us in surgical planning down the road. And I saw the question in the chat box about grade three versus stage three. which is a great question. And you notice that we talk about the stage quite a bit in both of these cases. The stage of the cancer is determined by the tumor size, the involvement of local lymph nodes, any sign of metastatic disease, and then we take into account the receptors on the cell surface. The grade is how the cells look under the microscope and how big are the nuclei, the middle of the cells, and how rapidly are the cells dividing? Do we see things like mitoses and how are the cells organized next to each other? So the stage takes into account all of these factors and the grade is just how it looks under the microscope. Thanks for that question. Next slide. So this patient is still early stage cancer, like the other one was also stage one. This is stage one, but it's a different tumor biology. And so she then was brought to tumor board for discussion and the discussion leaned towards chemotherapy as first course of treatment. Next slide. Back to Pam. When we meet this type of a patient, what are some of the issues involved in navigation?

So younger ladies have a little bit other issues going on as a little bit different than our first case. She may have issues with finances and working just like the other lady did. But given her age, we would talk to her about fertility preservation if she's thinking about having more children in the future. And if she is, we would refer her to our endocrine a reproductive endocrinology clinic. We would also talk to her about if she has children, how do you tell your kids you have cancer? And depending on the age of the child, we have different resources to help her to do that. But we also noticed that this lady has a history of anxiety and depression. So while we're always assessing for that, we would really be keeping a close eye on her, making sure that her depression or her anxiety aren't a barrier to her care. And if her depression was getting worse, we would make sure we would put the appropriate referrals in, whether it be to social work or psychiatry. We would also refer her to the psychologist. We also have different support groups for younger ladies. We have triple negative support groups. And we also know that our percentage of our triple negative ladies do tend to be African-American. And there are support groups that are specific to African-American ladies. So again, we would follow this woman very closely. We would meet with her with Dr. Fenn, most likely in a multidisciplinary clinic. And just make sure she gets to the right doctors at the right time and meet any of her needs that may come up. With both ladies, we would also be talking to them about sexuality and intimacy and how does breast cancer and the treatment of it affect them. So next slide, please. Thank you.

All right, so I want to take us into considerations for this case and whether or not she has a high chance to have a hereditary cancer risk. And so first let's start with the fact that she has a triple negative breast cancer, which is definitely a more rare type of breast cancer and can be more highly associated with genes that cause a hereditary breast cancer risk. And she's 38. So that alone are two factors independent of any other factors in her family history that would qualify her for an evaluation and genetic testing. But she also has a family history of breast cancer in her grandmother on her paternal side, as well as prostate cancer in her grandfather. Next. And with triple negative cancers in particular, as much as 20% of these women, regardless of family history, will have a hereditary cause for that triple negative type breast cancer. So that is one reason which just within the last month or two, the NCCN guidelines have changed and now recommend that all women with triple negative type breast cancer regardless of when they were diagnosed and regardless of what their family history might look like, should be referred and considered genetic testing. So that is certainly something that has changed based on our recognition of how, what high percentage of these women have a genetic cause. Next. And so she would meet criteria and we would definitely recommend that she come and see us and consider genetic testing. Next. And so in this particular case, my suspicion for a hereditary risk is really high. And so this patient undergoes genetic testing before she has surgery, let's say, and she's found to have a BRCA1 mutation, which is just a fancy way of saying she has a genetic risk. And BRCA1 is the gene in which that defect was identified. And so for this woman who has this new diagnosis of a triple negative breast cancer, these genetic test results now tell us that she has an additional risk to get a new primary cancer. So separate then from this new triple negative breast cancer. And that lifetime risk for her is 20 to 40% that she'd get a second breast cancer. Given how young she is, she's probably on the higher end of that risk range. So maybe even closer to the 40% risk. And so her options based on this risk might include increased screening of remaining breast tissue, depending on what surgical option is decided, or she might meet with Dr. Lynch and the plastic surgeon to decide that the best approach is to undergo a bilateral mastectomy where removing both breasts, including the cancer that's there, removing the rest of the healthy breast tissue to reduce as much as possible that risk for the second primary breast cancer. BRCA1 is also associated with ovarian cancer and that risk ranges between a 40 to 60 percent chance. The hard part is that there's no effective screening to identify ovarian cancer at an early stage, meaning we caught it where we can easily treat it and have long-term survival for that woman. In the absence of effective ovarian cancer screening, We strongly encourage and recommend that women with a BRCA1 mutation elect to have their ovaries and both of their fallopian tubes surgically removed between the ages of 35 to 40 or whenever they're done with their family planning. And so certainly the breast cancer diagnosis is first and foremost in our priority in her care right now at this time. But this is information for future planning for us to think about after we get her through this stage, that ovarian cancer risk is the next thing that we should be focusing our attention on. And then with BRCA1, you can see a less than 5% risk for individuals to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in their lifetime, although it's still rather low in all. Most individuals with a BRCA1 mutation will not go on to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. And so pancreatic cancer screening has its limitations. It has its risks. We're still trying to prove benefit. And so we really reserve pancreatic cancer screening in individuals who have a BRCA1 mutation, but whom also have a family history of pancreatic cancer in a close relative. So in this case, since she did not have a family history of pancreatic cancer, we would not strongly encourage consideration of pancreatic cancer screening in her case. And next slide for the next.

So this is someone who in medical oncology, I would meet, you know, before surgery and with an eye on time, I'll go through, you know, how we treat systemically triple negative breast cancer and our thoughts about, you know, timing of chemotherapy. So as we had mentioned, you know, triple negative breast cancer is a subtype of breast cancer that can have a particularly aggressive biology. and have a propensity to spread elsewhere in the body quickly. So this is something, a diagnosis where unfortunately because it's not expressing the estrogen receptors or another protein called HER2, we don't have traditionally targeted therapy such as endocrine therapy that I mentioned in the last case to treat these patients with. And so what we think of as traditional quote unquote cytotoxic chemotherapy So traditional IV chemotherapy is really the mainstay of systemic treatment for triple negative breast cancer and the vast majority of patients with triple negative breast cancer will need chemotherapy as part of their treatment. When we know that someone is going to need chemotherapy, we think about whether they would benefit from chemotherapy before surgery, which is called neoadjuvant therapy, versus going to surgery first and doing chemotherapy afterwards. But for patients with triple negative breast cancer, there are particular advantages of giving chemotherapy upfront prior to surgery. So these advantages include for certain patients, especially those who have more advanced tumors, we can shrink the tumor with chemotherapy and may allow for less extensive surgery and improved surgical and cosmetic outcomes. But from my perspective in medical oncology, and more relevant to this case in this woman who has a relatively small tumor, is that giving chemotherapy before surgery allows us to assess the response to chemotherapy at the time of surgery. We know a proportion of patients will have what we call a pathologic complete response or no active viable cancer cells in the pathology tissue at the time of surgery. Those patients generally have a good prognosis. For patients who have residual disease or active tumor still left over after preoperative chemotherapy, we know those patients may benefit from additional therapy after surgery. But we wouldn't be able to identify those patients unless we gave the chemotherapy up front and assess the response. So when we think about who should receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy for triple negative breast cancer, certainly this is the standard of care for more advanced early stage breast cancer, such as stage two and three. But when we know patients are going to need chemotherapy, we will certainly consider it preoperatively for patients who have slightly smaller tumors, including this patient who has a tumor between one and two centimeters. Certainly, she's young, she has aggressive biology, she's a candidate for chemotherapy. I would advocate for her to receive chemotherapy before surgery so we can assess response. And in my next slide, I'll explain potential options for her after chemotherapy if she doesn't have the optimal response at the time of surgery. So when we think of post-operative therapies for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, You know, I wanted to mention, you know, two options just to make aware of, you know, options that would be available to her if she did have a suboptimal response at the time of surgery. This includes briefly oral chemotherapy called Zolota, which we know improves disease-free and overall survival in triple negative patients with residual disease. But for her situation in particular where she has a germline BRCA1 mutation that she inherited, from her family members. There is a drug called Olaparib, or brand name Lymparza, that's in the class called a PARP inhibitor, which prevents, in general terms, prevents cancer cells from repairing DNA damage leading to cell death. And the patients with BRCA mutations are particularly susceptible, their tumors are susceptible to this drug. And so we have a recent study that came out just over the summer called the Olympia trial that notes that adjuvant olaparib can improve disease-free survival in patients with high-risk early breast cancer and BRCA1 mutation. And so if she had residual disease at the time of surgery, she could potentially benefit from this drug. And that's a pretty new development. And that's all I'll say to preserve time.

It's very exciting, those changes. I mean, thinking about it in the course of my career, how treatment of women with triple negative breast cancer has improved is really, really thrilling. So this patient, because she has a BRCA mutation elected to have a bilateral mastectomy, I just wanted to comment briefly on nipple sparing mastectomy, which she is a candidate for. This is a technique for both treating breast cancer and for doing prophylactic surgeries. And it allows us to preserve the entire skin of the breast, including the nipple. This picture, which is from a research publication, I think really gives a wonderful picture because patients often don't understand how we do the operation through a very small incision underneath the breast, where we're able to remove all of the breast tissue and maintain all of the skin and provide exposure. So the plastic surgeon, my partner, Dr. Mastriani, who have done a few of these cases with can then place an implant or can even use the patient's own tissue to create a reconstruction. These really require, the breast can't be too large. So we have to choose the right patient for the right operation. And it's also better for patients that are not smokers. Next slide. And the outcomes are safe. And so there is both a registry and a large review of multiple studies with multiple patients that show that these are both safe from a surgical perspective and from a cancer perspective and that we can still achieve a cure using these new operations. Next slide. Dr. Mastriani.

I forgot I was on mute. So in general, when we remove the whole gland, what you're left with is a skin skeleton or a shell, basically. So we have two different options currently available to fill up that skin envelope. One is with using an implant, and that's something that we make synthetically. It is made of silicone. All of them have silicone shells. Some of them can be filled with silicone gel itself, or they can also be filled with saline, but all of the shells have silicone on the outside. And it's something that we've studied for the past 50 years and we know that it's safe. The other option is that we can fill in your skin envelope with your own tissue. And this is not an implant. You don't have to take any rejection medications for this. It's your body. It's going to feel the most natural. Next slide, please. The two different kinds of implants that we can do, you'll notice on that former slide, there was a one stage and a two stage. The two stages where I have to put in a tissue expander, which is the device you see on the left, that is an inflatable expander. It allows me to add more volume or take it away as we need to based on how your wounds heal. When we do remove most of the breast, you're removing about 80 to 90% of the blood flow to that skin. So I wanna make sure that you heal well. So this, I guess, adjustable implant allows me to tailor make your reconstruction for you. It also gives you an opportunity to try on the size and you can walk around with that size in your body and decide if that's what you really like. Oftentimes, and more and more often, we're able to go directly to the implant, which is what you see on the right. And as you'll notice, it's not a round sphere like a water balloon. We've also come a long way as far as implant technology to make it more breast shaped and to help it move more fluidly with you and to feel more natural under the skin. Next slide. And then finally, I just wanted to talk briefly about using your own skin. This is probably your own tissue to reconstruct. This is probably the most popular option and it's been around for more than a decade, but we're now becoming more facile and it's becoming more mainstream. More people are training to do this kind of procedure. It is a bit more involved. We can't just move up skin and fat from anywhere. It actually has to come with a blood supply to it. We need to nourish that area. So one common place that we take this extra tissue from is the lower abdomen. Oftentimes women have a little bit of extra fat down there. Perhaps they've had pregnancies and they have a little extra skin down there that is hard to exercise away. So those kinds of patients are ideal candidates for this. Even if you've had a cesarean section, you're still a candidate for this. So we are able to trace all of the blood vessels down into your groin and reconnect them up in your chest using a microscope and we use sutures as fine as hair. So this is an intensive operation. It does require special training, but a place like Yale, we can offer services like this. We can offer a whole range of reconstruction options. And then the beauty of this kind of reconstruction is you don't need any long-term follow-up. With implants, I tell my patients it's a lot like getting an oil change. You're going to come in every 10 to 15 years to get the implant switched out. And while that's an outpatient surgery, it's still another surgery. Whereas if you undergo this option, you're done with reconstruction for the rest of your life. You don't need to come in for oil changes or anything like that.

So our patient had that operation. She had an implant-based reconstruction. Next slide. And she had a complete pathologic response. So she had a tumor there. She received her chemotherapy. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent bleeding per rectum.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).  
- Rectal adenocarcinoma, clinical stage III, cT3N1M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Rectal lesion was diagnosed as adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Rectal cancer was staged clinically as cT3N1M0.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Clinical whole-exome sequencing performed on blood with germline testing intent identified an APC exon 16 missense variant classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS).  
- Cytogenetic study for CLL showed no dividing cells obtained in culture; no specific cytogenetic finding was reported.  
- MYD88 had been verified.  
- No somatic tumor testing results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Following diagnosis of CLL, treatment with acalabrutinib was started.  
- Approximately 1 month later, rectal carcinoma was diagnosed.  
- Long-course neoadjuvant radiotherapy with capecitabine was administered for rectal cancer.  
- Neoadjuvant long-course radiotherapy had been completed.

[ current disease status ]:  
- CLL and rectal adenocarcinoma were both present.  
- Rectal cancer status after completion of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy had not been otherwise documented.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No significant family history of cancer, including colorectal cancer.  
- Colonoscopy had been completed up to the cecum/terminal ileum; only rectal growth was identified.  
- No polyposis was reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman. Member of the Air Force.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable right thyroid nodule measuring approximately 3 cm.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Right thyroid Hurthle cell neoplasm on fine-needle aspiration, with Afirma gene expression classifier result reported as suspicious.  
- Status post thyroid lobectomy.  
- Final surgical pathology demonstrated a benign 3.5 cm Hurthle cell neoplasm without capsular or vascular invasion.  
- Incidental 1.3 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma in the same lobe.  
- Pathologic stage described as T1b, presumed N0, Mx.  
- One sampled lymph node was negative for malignancy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration cytology: suspicious for Hurthle cell neoplasm.  
- Intraoperative frozen section: follicular lesion with Hurthle cell features.  
- Final pathology of dominant nodule: benign 3.5 cm well-encapsulated Hurthle cell neoplasm; no capsular invasion; no vascular invasion.  
- Separate nodule: 1.3 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Surgical margins were microscopically positive for the papillary carcinoma.  
- Multifocal disease within the involved lobe was described, including foci measuring 1.3 cm, 2 mm, and 3 mm.  
- One lymph node removed with the lobectomy specimen was negative for carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, well-circumscribed complex thyroid nodule with cystic and solid components, without evident microcalcifications.  
- Neck ultrasound was negative for abnormal cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- An additional ipsilateral thyroid nodule measuring just over 1 cm was identified in the same lobe and was characterized as nonspecific/indeterminate.  
- The second nodule was later reported pathologically as 1.3 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Afirma gene expression classifier on the indeterminate thyroid nodule: suspicious.  
- Subsequent testing of the papillary thyroid carcinoma demonstrated BRAF V600E mutation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed and was suspicious for Hurthle cell neoplasm.  
- Thyroid lobectomy was performed.  
- Lobectomy pathology showed benign Hurthle cell neoplasm as the dominant lesion and incidental follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma in a separate nodule.  
- No metastatic carcinoma was identified in the single sampled lymph node.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post lobectomy with incidental multifocal follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma identified in the resected lobe.  
- Microscopic positive surgical margins were present.  
- No radiographic cervical nodal disease was identified preoperatively.  
- No nodal metastasis was identified in the single sampled lymph node.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Preoperative TSH was normal.  
- A low-TSH/hyperfunctioning nodule scenario did not apply in this case.

When I went in to operate on this woman for a hurtful cell lesion, I didn't want to have to go back into that compartment at a later date, so I would have sampled lymph nodes if I could find any, and that would have given me information on both the hurtful cell and the possible existence of metastatic papillary carcinoma at the time. So I would have liked to know what the actual pathologic nodal status of the original thyroid lobectomy side was.
So there was one node that came out with that lobe and it was node negative for cancer.

And that sort of points out the shortcomings of our staging system that with one single node you have a pathologic stage N0 which may not be reflective of the rest of the nodes in the area. But if, as the surgeon in that original case, you had at least inspected that ipsilateral side and confirmed that there were no other prominent lymph nodes, then I think that that's at least more supportive of this being a case of papillary carcinoma that's not metastatic to the highest risk area, which is the ipsilateral central net.

So we're going to talk a little bit more about central neck node management in the next case. So we'll skip on there. Anybody here on the panel willing to say this patient does not need the completion? She had a 1.3 centimeters. She's T1. She's a young patient. She's going to live forever. Why on earth are we going to go ahead and take out that other lobe? Dr. Shah, I know I can call on you to be a minimalist.

You know, there is a saying in medicine which is called primum non nocere, do no harm to the patient. This patient is cured, and you can't cure her more than 100%. Whether you do total thyroidectomy, you do total thyroidectomy and give radioactive iodine, you do elective central compartment dissection or elective lateral neck dissection, it's not going to improve the longevity of this patient. So doing more, you have to convince me that completion thyroidectomy, completion thyroidectomy in radioactive iodine, or elective node dissection has any statistical data supporting your recommendation. If you do not have statistics to support your contention, then I think we are talking about personal biases which should not apply into a forum like this.
But Dr. Shah, when did you ever see any statistics in thyroid cancer that were meaningful?

There's plenty of statistics. And there are very few meaningful statistics. And you will never find a prospective randomized trial because the biology of the disease is such that all of us will be long gone before you report a 20 or a 30 year survivorship and recurrence-free survivorship in a 32-year-old woman.
So would you treat her with thyroid hormone suppressive therapy with that?

That is a very provocative question. Does this woman need to be suppressed? Mind you, she's 32, and she's going to live at least another 60 years of her life. She will get older, and she will get osteoporotic. And do you want to precipitate her osteoporosis by keeping her TSH down to zero? And there are some enthusiasts to keep the TSH to zero. So I think I would get a baseline TSH perhaps two months out. I'm in no rush to put the patient on suppression the week after thyroidectomy. I'm not aware of any data which says that if you don't suppress within one week of thyroidectomy, the patient will die. No such thing exists. And if you do immediate post-op TSH, it's going to be elevated. You just took out a part of the thyroid gland. It takes that information some time to get to the brain to affect on TSH. So two months out, I'll do TSH. If the TSH is elevated or on the high range of normal, I may think about suppression. If it is one or around, I will not put her on thyroid suppression.
So are you going to treat her just to normalize her TSH or will you suppress her if you treat her with thyroid hormone?

Well, I think that is a question which is debatable. Again, there is no data to show that suppression of TSH to 1, 0.9, 0.05, or 0.04 has any statistical validity that higher suppression means better patient care or better survivorship.

All right, so we're going to take a vote from the panel first. Who on the panel then is going to be comfortable with a lobectomy alone? OK. And let's just take a brief poll from the audience. Is there anybody in the audience who feels strongly that this patient really should have the total thyroidectomy, the completion thyroidectomy? So we've got a few people who really do feel, maybe a dozen or 20 people who really feel that thyroidectomy is necessary. How about a show of hands who would say a lobectomy is sufficient? The majority of the audience would say lobectomy. I can tell you that amongst an endocrinology audience, this case would raise probably 95% of people's hands saying, let's get rid of that other half. Because otherwise, how do I monitor this patient into the future? So let's take this minimalist audience and ask the question, would it matter to you if those surgical margins were microscopically positive?
This is one of those that she would then be a T3. And that would put her in a category where she's a candidate for RAI.

If I can interrupt a second, it wouldn't necessarily make her T3. Only surgical margins are positive. You're assuming that the entire thyroid has been removed. So you could have a T1 that has positive surgical margins.

It would be hard to envision that, but usually those two go together. But that would raise my concern for whether this patient needs adjuvant RAI, at which point the completion thyroidectomy would be part of that package.
Okay, and the rest of the panel, any still want to stick with the lobectomy alone? Dr. Shah, justifying.

OK, so I think the most important part of this patient's care is educating the patient about the biology of her cancer. Needless to say, this patient will go and seek many consultations. She will get confused with a diversity of opinions. And then she'll come back to you that Dr. Ferris says thyroidectomy and radioiodine. Dr. Orloff says thyroidectomy and elective Guys, don't take it personally. Elective node dissection and what have you. So I think your first or second post-operative visit is going to be the longest one. Because you are now telling the patient that this cancer is symbiotic with you. Presence of microscopic cancer doesn't mean anything. I can prove microscopic cancer even in your lateral neck node. If I do elective neck dissection of the whole neck, there's a 50% probability that you will have myocardial metastasis. And all of this means very little. And it takes time for the patient to understand the biology of this disease. But once they do, they're in sync with you. This patient will be coming to see you once a year for the rest of her and your life, and your discussion at that time will be mostly social, how her family is doing.
So you're going to leave this residual cancer in the neck. Are the other panelists happy with that approach?

First of all, at the time of surgery, you should have put your cross clamp away from the nodule so that you don't get this scenario. But assuming that this was done elsewhere, then you need to go back to pathology. and help pull out the specimen, how microscopically positive it is. If there is gross transaction through tumor, and the cut margin shows the tumor throughout up and down, then I will take her back to the operating room. If I see a focal microscopic area of papillary carcinoma, that's fine. I'm not worried about it.
Focal microscopic. Rest of the panel happy to leave it behind, or do people want to be a bit more aggressive?

I think if you go by the HCA guideline, This patient will fall, going back to what Dr. Farris was alluding to, assuming that this is true extra thyroid extension, but not just positive surgical margin. You're now talking of someone in intermediate to high-risk category. But if you're only saying that this is microscopically positive, we don't know how he got there, and it may not be that you actually left tumor behind, then you have a lot of discussion to hold with the patient. And that would actually be a patient where you are thinking may be following the guideline of low normal TSH suppression. And Dr. Shah would not.
But isn't it the case that your endocrinologist with whom you work closely is going to freak out if you don't do something more?

That's exactly what I'm saying, that the endocrinologist in this instance would not be comfortable saying, we're not going to do anything. You're fine. And I think the multidisciplinary approach will actually help the patient to reach the most appropriate decision going forward.

Well, not only were her surgical margins microscopically positive, but she also has a BRAF V600E mutation, which we didn't know about ahead of time, but it was tested on the sample subsequently. Dr. Ferris, you're still leaving that cancer behind?

I'm just, my heart sunk. Because we could have packaged up this patient's entire surgical therapy with her upfront total thyroidectomy with the Nikki Forov panel We would have not had any frozen section. We would have saved the health care system.
But remember that we didn't biopsy the cancer. We biopsied the benign nodule. So we would have been no further ahead. Oh, you're right about that.

Fair enough. Well, I do think there's a question as to whether on the histopathology there's any value for doing molecular testing. I think there's a real stretch besides curiosity and research. But doing it after the fact, given Particularly, I think, is the point of this bullet point is to raise the question about the prognostic value of this common mutation, which is, I'd say, relatively controversial at present, particularly in the absence of other histopathologic features, which we already know have prognostic variables.
So how about in Kobe, Japan? Would we be following the same path, or would we have a different strategy in Japan?

So in this case, T1N0, M0, so I recommend Lobectomy. So this is surgical margin positive, mean external thyroid extension. But microscopically positive. So the prognosis is not changed. So I observe alone.

You would observe alone and not complete the thyroidectomy or treat with radioactive iodine. So you would fit very much into Dr. Shah's approach. All right. What happens if it's multifocal? Dr. Orloff.
Lisa, he's trying to corner you into completion.

It's getting tougher here. I would agree with the other panelists about the BRAF mutation itself. We did a study. I'm currently located at Stanford University, but while I was at UCSF, we did a review of our BRAF positive histology and agree with Bob's comment that It was present in the majority of our papillary carcinomas in the range of 80 plus percent of the cases and really did not have a direct correlation with more aggressive behavior. The additional foci does raise the question of if there are these microscopic foci that you saw, are there additional microscopic foci that you didn't see? And I have tended to rely on the three rule of three microscopic foci as a... Well, she has three because there's a 1.3 centimeter, a two, and a three millimeter.
Exactly.

So she would qualify as having three foci in this lobe, and therefore, and I'm sorry I can't recall the study that cited numbers of foci of microscopic disease, but the rule of thumb that I followed is three or more foci of disease is more predictive of diffuse disease in the other lobe.

So we looked at this at Mayo. I say we, it's really Ian Hay who looked at this at Mayo and demonstrated that multifocality predicts more than anything else the involvement of central compartment lymph nodes. And of course, central compartment lymph nodes then predict a higher risk for future recurrence of the disease, but didn't really impact on the long-term survival of these patients, which remains, of course, for normal life expectancy. But I think each of these adverse impacts, including the finding of lymphovascular invasion on pathology, arguably raises the risk of this patient, and I think pushes us more and more towards a completion. But I think this case, more than anything, illustrates why it's fascinating to be in a department of head and neck and endocrine oncology, as I am, because the challenge with thyroid cancer is not that the disease is so aggressive and nasty as it is with most of the head and neck squames. but rather that it is so benign and innocuous, and you have to make these terribly tough decisions about how aggressive to make the treatment. And so we're balancing the risk and the benefit of surgery against the risk of the disease. So I find thyroid fascinating, as I say. So let's talk about a second case, then. A 46-year-old woman. It's an incidentally discovered three centimeter nodule, so very similar to the last case, just a little older. No radiation history, no family history for thyroid cancer, no abnormalities of thyroid function. There's the nodule on the ultrasound.

reference_conclusion: Initial evaluation should include a dedicated thyroid ultrasound performed by an experienced thyroid ultrasonographer, comprehensive history and physical examination with palpation of the entire neck, serum TSH testing, and pre-decision laryngoscopy. Given the 3 cm thyroid nodule with normal TSH, ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is indicated. After cytology suspicious for Hürthle cell neoplasm and a suspicious Afirma result, the agreed next surgical step is thyroid lobectomy rather than total thyroidectomy. Following incidental identification of a 1.3 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma after lobectomy, the consensus favored observation with lobectomy alone, with completion thyroidectomy not routinely recommended.
reference_conclusion_quote: I would always want to have an ultrasound, and even one with one from the outside would repeat one by an experienced thyroid ultrasonographer [...] Ordering blood tests, part of the physical exam should always include a pre-decision making laryngoscopy, as well as palpation of the entire neck. [...] So I try biopsy and fine needle biopsy and US guide. [...] I'd say most practices would lead to a lobectomy. [...] we're still back at the same lobectomy that the cytologic diagnosis would have indicated. [...] We have consensus. Surgical consensus. [...] Who on the panel then is going to be comfortable with a lobectomy alone? OK. [...] The majority of the audience would say lobectomy. [...] So in this case, T1N0, M0, so I recommend Lobectomy. So this is surgical margin positive, mean external thyroid extension. But microscopically positive. So the prognosis is not changed. So I observe alone.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old male; retired bank manager; lived with family; remained independently mobile and performed routine activities. Past medical history included coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting in 2014, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

[ chief complaint ]: In 2018, presented with 1 year of weight loss and abdominal discomfort.

[ diagnosis ]: Follicular lymphoma, grade 3A, initially diagnosed in 2018 with supra- and infradiaphragmatic nodal disease and splenic involvement. In 2023, histologic transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma/large B-cell lymphoma arising from follicular lymphoma was documented. In 2025, second relapse with recurrent diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal center subtype, was documented.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2018 external iliac lymph node biopsy: follicular lymphoma grade 3A.  
- 2023 left axillary lymph node biopsy: large B-cell lymphoma arising from follicular lymphoma; Ki-67 approximately 70%.  
- 2025 repeat lymph node biopsy at relapse: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal center subtype.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2018 PET-CT: supra- and infradiaphragmatic lymph node enlargement with moderately enlarged spleen.  
- Interim PET-CT after 4 cycles of bendamustine-rituximab: near-complete metabolic response at all disease sites.  
- End-of-treatment PET-CT after 6 cycles: complete metabolic response with no residual disease identified.  
- 2023 routine PET-CT: multiple confluent enlarged cervical level I/II/III and axillary lymph nodes, with supraclavicular and medial external iliac nodal involvement.  
- August 2025 PET-CT: recurrent lymphomatous disease involving axillary, infrapectoral, and infraclavicular regions, with additional periportal and portocaval lymph nodes; splenomegaly with diffuse uptake.  
- Reassessment PET-CT after 3 cycles of R-polatuzumab-GemOx: complete reduction in size and metabolic activity at all sites, consistent with near-complete metabolic response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- FISH at initial diagnosis: negative for BCL2, BCL6, and MYC rearrangements.  
- Gain of 3q27 detected.  
- Chromosomal analysis was normal.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- At transformation/relapse in 2023, LDH was elevated at approximately 800.  
- Hypercalcemia was referenced as a clinical pointer for relapse/transformation, but no patient-specific calcium value was provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2018 first-line therapy: bendamustine plus rituximab for 4 cycles, followed by interim PET-CT showing near-complete metabolic response; consolidated with 2 additional cycles for a total of 6 cycles, achieving complete metabolic response.  
- Maintenance rituximab was started after first-line therapy; 2 cycles were administered. Further maintenance was deferred in March 2020.  
- Disease-free interval was approximately 3 years.  
- 2023 treatment for transformed disease: initially 2 cycles of R-COP followed by R-mini-CHOP; after response, 2 additional cycles of R-mini-CHOP were given. Complete metabolic response (CR2) was achieved.  
- Autologous transplant was discussed after CR2 but was not pursued.  
- 2025 third-line therapy for second relapse: R-polatuzumab-GemOx was initiated as bridging-type therapy; 3 cycles were administered with near-complete metabolic response. Treatment was ongoing on cycle 5 at last update, with plan to complete 4-6 cycles and omit polatuzumab if neuropathy developed.  
- No significant treatment-related toxicity was reported with R-polatuzumab-GemOx: no neuropathy, no neutropenia, and no treatment-related admissions other than admission for chemotherapy administration/insurance purposes.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent diffuse large B-cell lymphoma had shown near-complete metabolic response after 3 cycles of R-polatuzumab-GemOx in 2025. The patient remained on treatment and was receiving the fifth cycle at last documentation.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- At time of transformed disease treatment in 2023, performance status was documented as ECOG 1.  
- Cardiac reassessment before anthracycline-based therapy showed normal cardiac function including echocardiography; physical activity was described as unlimited.  
- Geriatric assessment in 2025: G8 score >14; nutritional assessment normal; MOCA normal; Charlson Comorbidity Index 7; CARG score 4 with intermediate risk.  
- Polypharmacy and comorbidity burden were documented.  
- The patient declined autologous stem cell transplant.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. So we will quickly start with our first case. So today we have got two cases from Jerry Care Hospitals, Chennai. The first case is a 77-year-old gentleman who has gone through a lot in the last six years. And Dr. Vinod, our colleague and consultant medical oncologist will be presenting the case and we'll put some of the interesting questions to the panelists. Over to you, Dr. Vinod. Thank you, sir. Good evening all. First of all, I would like to thank Professor Purvish sir for this opportunity and my colleague and mentor Dr. Rajiv sir for giving me this opportunity. So, today we will be seeing a case of follicular lymphoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma which has progressed through three lines of treatment, an elderly gentleman. So he's a 71 year male who was a retired bank manager living with his family and busy with his own business post retirement. He has an extended health insurance coverage. He's a known case of CID, underwent a coronary bypass in 2014. Again, it was a regular medical checkup in which he was found to have a CID for which he'd underwent a bypass but was not symptomatic. And later, after three years, he developed diabetes and then hypertension. but patient is mobile and he is on his own doing his routine activities. So in 2018 he was evaluated for loss of weight for one year and abdominal discomfort. So on evaluation PET-CT was done. It found to have a supra-infra-diaphragmatic lymph node enlargement with moderately enlarged spleen. So we ordered a biopsy from the external iliac lymph node which came out to be follicular lymphoma grade 3A. and fish testing was done which was negative for BCL-2, BCL-6 and MYC, but he had this gain of 3q27 and chromosomal analysis was normal. In view of advanced stage and GELF positive, he was symptomatic and FIPI high risk patient was planned for chemotherapy. He received four cycles of BR regimen, Vendamastine and Rituximab, post which the interim patch showed near complete metabolic response in all disease sites. and he was consolidated with two more cycles and achieved a complete metabolic response and was started on maintenance rituximab. So post two cycles of rituximab in March 2020, there was a COVID situation. So due to COVID situation as well as the guideline recommendation at that time, further cycles were deferred after having a discussion with the patient and the family. Here we can see the PET CT at the end of treatment, there was no disease anywhere. So after a three-year of DFS, patient was again on follow-up for the past two years from 2022. So in 2023, on routine, PET-CT showed a multiple confluent enlarged level 1, 2, 3 axillary lymph node, as well as supraclavicular and medial external lymph node. So we did a biopsy from the left axillary lymph node, which came out to be large B-cell lymphoma arising from follicular lymphoma. And the K67 was 70%. suggestive of Richter's transformation. So Dr. Varun sir, can you please share with us your experience on Richter's transformation and follicular lymphoma incidences and how do you prove it?

Hi Rajiv sir and Dr. Vinny and all the members of the RICARD team. Yeah, it's an interesting case. Again, we know in low-grade follicle lymphomas, the incidence of which is transformation we see in our practice. So, usually when the patient transforms to a high-grade lymphoma, usually patient presents with B symptoms or usually some other symptoms. But actually in this patient, it was quite surprising that patient didn't had any symptoms. Isn't it? Is the patient had any symptoms?
He did not have any B symptoms but he had this large infraclavicular node which was clinically palpable but no major B symptoms.
What was the LDH?
Is there any jump? LDH was reasonably high. I think it was around 800.

But it fits with the histology. It can happen. And even actually the incidence is around actually in the tune of 10% even in the retuximab era. And maybe you should treat those patients as high-grade lymphomas. And I believe the age of this patient at that time was around 75, right?

Correct. Correct. So he was 71 at presentation. Now he's around 74, 75. That's the question that we have for you. So we have now DL-BCL who is already exposed to rituximab and a few doses of maintenance rituximab, what would be your choice if you in the second life?
Yeah, how is the performance status there at that time?
Excellent, SPS1 and we will give the geriatric parameters when we do the next line of treatment.

But still 75 years good performance status and also we had a reasonable DFS of around three years. So what I would do in my practice is I will try with the chop, R-chop. So what I will do is that I will start with the R-mini-chop in the first cycle. And if the patient tolerates, then I will try to escalate it to at least a modified R-chop.

So here he had a coronary artery disease and he had undergone a CABG in 2014 but now the cardiac functions including an echo was normal and he had unlimited physical activity. So will that be a concern for you to start on CHOP? being taken care of.
If the cardiac LV systolic function is actually fair enough then I will try the adreamycin based chemotherapy.

Sure, sure. So I think that's what we did. So we gave him initially two cycles of R-COP and then R-mini-CHOP and again he went into a complete metabolic response and we gave two more cycles of R-mini-CHOP and he was in complete metabolic response. And now, here comes the dilemma. Now, we have achieved a CR2, a reasonably well-preserved lentiment, but now it is an aggressive DL-BCL with CR2. What would be your discussion point at this point?

Again, actually patient achieved CR after six cycles of ARCHOV, again in a 75 year old man. Actually, discussing about an autologous transplant, I would be a bit skeptical. So, we have two options. I can actually, we can again consult it because it's a richer transformation, high grade. Yes. So we can consolidate with the CAR T cell therapy. It's an option.
And this was in 2023.

Yes, sir. Yes, sir. If that option is not there, then I will continue with the rituximab maintenance. OK. Because we have the, actually, even though in the lab setting, we do not have much data, but extrapolating the PRIMA trial, I think I would prefer to continue with the rituximab maintenance.

I think we were discussing exactly what your thoughts were. We actually discussed the option of autologous transplant with him. Our transplant team also, though a bit apprehensive, was OK for a discussion, but the patient was very clear that he doesn't want any treatment which can be life-threatening. So we actually kept him under follow-up. So the patient was on follow-up for the next two years. after which again he was asymptomatic doing his own activities. But routine PET-CT showed in August 2025 a lymphomatous recurrence, again in the same site, the axillary intrafectolar, infraclavicular, and this time even in the periportal and portocaval lymph nodes were positive, with splenoma galli having a diffuse uptake. Biopsy from the lymph node again came out to be DLBCL, germicenter subtype. So here you can see there is an extensive disease which has come back. patient was asymptomatic. As sir has rightly pointed out, other than these symptoms, any rise in LDH, hypercalcemia as well as lymph nodal enlargement are pointers for relapse or stress transformation for that matter. So, here we had again extensive disease. So this time he was around 77 years old at this juncture so we wanted to do a pediatric assessment. The G8 was more than 14 points but still considering his age we also wanted to do the other parameters to know his nutritional status and any depression and mental status. complete point in both nutritional assessment as well as in MOCA, but his Charleston coma bit index was high. There were seven points because he had three coma bits, was on multiple treatment. Here, sir, we would like to know your experience on CARG scoring. Suppose patient has a reduced dose, he has four points, what would you do? And if we give a standard dose with an intermediate risk, how would you proceed, sir?

Yeah, it is mainly we do CARG after doing the geriatric assessment because actually we had to know actually how will be the outcome if we use the standard of chemotherapy or modified dose. Usually if you're planning for a combination chemotherapy, then if the risk is more than 50% in an elderly person, What we usually do in our practice is to try to modify the dose. I think in the case of lymphoma labs, we have no other choice rather than a combination of chemotherapy. Actually, we cannot treat with a single agent chemotherapy here. So, actually our options are actually really limited. So, we have to treat with the combination therapy. So, but again, if we apply the standard dose, it will be much toxic for this patient. So, I prefer to modify the dose.

Thank you, sir. So, we have few questions for our GTI patient. Dr. Magesh, sir, can you explain us about How do you stratify this chronological versus functional age and polypharmacy in this patient? Yes, we moved away from the concept of number as an age and now we more look at the function and most of us in oncogeriatrics now we are used to this and we use the various scales comprehensive geriatric assessment and activities of daily living to come to a conclusion about the patient's functional age or functional status And particularly with this patient, even though the comorbidities are more and the number of drugs are more, and there was no red flags highlighted in the CGA, G8, the risk of still know when they're on diabetic and on good diabetic control, I would prophylactically ask them to kind of reduce the number of medications for diabetes or hypertension if it's under good control. Because those who have had good control, when they start chemotherapy, especially with minimal side effects, they tend to have hyperglycemia and more of a decline in their function. And we want to prevent an hospital admission. So for trying to counsel the family, especially to kind of lifelong they've been educated to have good glycemic and good hypertension control, but to kind of reassure them for a temporary period, it doesn't matter if the sugars go high. So to try and look at the medications and try to scale back temporarily, somebody like him who has a good glycemic control. So the functional status in him was very good. I think there is a point we wanted to make, sir, where, for example, in many of our oncology forums, we feel this patient is performance status one and G8 screening actually has shown very excellent score. Most of us would go ahead and give treatment at that point of stage, but when we go into the CGA, we could find out, you know, that some of these parameters like comorbid and polypharmacy, even the CARG had intermediate risk for him. So that actually brings us to the point on irrespective of the performance status and irrespective of the initial scale, screening scale showing good scores, a comprehensive geriatric assessment and a complete geriatricians review will still help us in polypharmacy management and comorbidities which can have impact on our oncological outcomes also. I totally agree with you. I think definitely because many things, especially nutrition and cognition are two big things in elderly population. And no, we definitely need to have a baseline. And so sometimes it's not possible in oncological settings. So the geriatrician being a part or some arrangements to get the nutrition and the cognition screened in fit and well patients on G8 is very essential because they can tend to fluctuate once chemotherapy started. I think that's the message.
And can I add one thing?
Yes, please.

Yeah, actually, one more important thing, as Dr. Magesh mentioned here, is the cognitive dysfunction. Because he is a 77-year-old man, he already received two lanes of chemotherapy. And I think patient is clear about his actual decision and all, right sir? Yes, sir. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old male. Otherwise healthy. No personal or family history of neurofibromatosis.

[ chief complaint ]: One to two months of numbness involving the right fourth and fifth digits.

[ diagnosis ]: Right lower neck/upper thoracic mass with neural foraminal widening at approximately T1 level. Preoperative differential included nerve sheath tumor. CT-guided core biopsy was reported as a fibrous lesion/fibrous tumor consistent with fibromatosis. Intraoperative frozen section from the superior aspect of the mass was consistent with neurofibroma. Final permanent pathology was not available.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided core biopsy demonstrated a fibrous lesion, reported as a fibrous tumor/fibromatosis. Intraoperative incisional biopsy with frozen section was more consistent with neurofibroma. Lymphoma was excluded intraoperatively. Final pathology was pending.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial cervical spine MRI demonstrated an incompletely evaluated right lower neck mass extending into the upper chest. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a non-enhancing mass in the right lower neck/upper thoracic region, extending posterior to the trachea with deviation of the esophagus to the contralateral side. The vertebral artery was markedly displaced anteriorly and closely approximated the carotid artery. The mass extended inferiorly into the upper thoracic space and partially dumbbelled around the subclavian artery. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated widening of the neural foramina, described at the T1 level. PET scan showed a low-avidity lesion with no other sites of disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent CT-guided core biopsy prior to surgery. He subsequently underwent operative resection via low collar incision and upper clamshell thoracotomy between the fourth and fifth ribs, with cervical and thoracic exposure. Intraoperatively, the vertebral artery was dissected free from tumor but was approximately 270 degrees encased and was ultimately ligated and sacrificed due to vessel damage from retraction/dissection. The subclavian artery sustained two to three puncture injuries requiring oversewing. The mass was not resectable en bloc because of dense adherence to surrounding structures; piecemeal resection/debulking was performed from the thoracic component into the neck, down to the neural foramina. A posterior rind of tumor was left along the spine. Operative duration was approximately 8 hours.

[ current disease status ]: Status post subtotal resection/debulking of right cervicothoracic mass with residual posterior tumor rind at the spine/neural foraminal region. Postoperatively, the phrenic nerve was nonfunctional. The vagus nerve remained intact. Swallowing was intact. The patient was otherwise neurologically intact.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination before surgery showed mild right eye ptosis, intact motor strength, and subjective diminished sensation in the right fourth and fifth digits. Intraoperatively, the mass was located between the vagus nerve and phrenic nerve, with prolonged retraction of both during dissection. The retrotracheal component was delivered after medial-lateral dissection adjacent to the trachea.
