reference_discussion.text: No worries, no worries. It's all good. So this is just a couple slides from a case I was asked to be involved in on Monday that I thought I'd show you guys briefly. So this was... Am I sharing my screen? So this was a 62-year-old male who I was asked to be involved in a surgical case from thoracic surgery. 62, otherwise healthy guy. I presented to his PCP with a couple of months history or one month history of numbness in his right fourth and fifth digit. The physical exam was notable for a little bit of right eye ptosis. His motor exam was, his strength was intact, but he did have subjective diminished sensation over the fourth and fifth digits. He underwent a C-spine MRI per his PCP that demonstrated what they call an incompletely evaluated right lower neck mass extending into the upper chest. And radiologists recommended definitive imaging with a MRI, contrast enhanced MRI, and a CT with contrast as well. So can you guys see these images?
Yeah. Okay, great. Are you playing radiologist today too?
What's that?
Are you playing radiologist today too?

I'm playing radiologist as well. So here's, I'll scroll you through the contrast enhanced CT scan on the left side of the screen. So you're seeing this kind of non-enhancing mass here that's pushing behind the trachea and deviating the esophagus to the contralateral side.
Oh boy.

The arrow here is pointing to the vertebral artery. So that's really displaced pretty far anterior. The vertebral is really kissing with the carotid and then extends down into the upper thoracic space pushing along inferiorly. So the big mass MRI scan, this is contrast enhanced MRI scan. And you can see that there's some widening of the neural foramina here. And then so really widening what the radiologist called is at the T1 level. So the next step was a CT guided biopsy and the CT guided biopsy was consistent with, um, I can pull that report up with, they called it a fibrous lesion, uh, consistent with, they called it a fibrous tumor or fibromatosis.
Hmm. Any history of NF1 or NF2 in this patient, 60 years?
No, no history of NF, no personal history, no family history of NF.
Oh, oh boy.
So the neurosurgery saw the patient, I saw the patient, and thoracic surgery saw the patient. I was asked to manage the neck for potential surgical resection.
Was that an FNA or a core?
That was a core biopsy.

I guess in the interest of time, if the fellows want to, Arno, you proceed. And then after hours, we will just have to open the floor for others who would like to stay on and comment. I definitely want to hear more from other attending how they would approach these. These are rare cases, and I'm definitely going to learn. So you go ahead first, and then we'll all discuss it and see if others have any comments.

Yeah, so this is not something I'd ever encountered before. And so I was eager to hear what people's thoughts were in terms of approaching it. It seemed like a nerve sheath tumor of some kind, obviously with the widening of the foramen there, neurofibroma or schwannoma. The core didn't definitively show that, but we proceeded under the assumption that it was because the imaging findings were so specific. Basically, I did a low collar incision. And then we did an upper clamshell thoracognosy between the fourth and fifth rib. We divided the SCM and the straps off of the clavicular head. And then they used this like medieval, looked like a medieval torture device with this big hook that basically just ratchet up the chest on that side. And the vertebral was a big concern of mine there. I don't know, I'm interested to hear people have experienced sacrificing the vertebral or whether they prepare for that or sacrificing that. We had a vascular surgeon who said that it looked like the non-dominant vertebral and that if we had to ligate it, we should. We were able to trace it out of the tumor successfully. It was about 270 degrees encased. You can see kind of on these images that it really had to be kind of...
the brachiocephalic vein or artery that's up there, were they okay?

So the subclavian artery here was basically this thing was kind of dumbbelling a little bit around the subclavian. Just as kind of a a pre-op question or two. Sometimes these solitary fibrous tumors on the spectrum of sarcoma or malignant nerve sheath tumors, and I'm just wondering whether, you know, an incisional biopsy and or metastatic workup or some sort of imaging of the chest, just things like that, I would kind of think about, especially with something growing into the neural frame and I like that and the complete resection being somewhat challenging. Yeah, no, absolutely. I think it's a great point. So he did have a PET scan, which showed basically a low avidity lesion, no other sites of disease. And on opening, basically on getting onto the surface of the tumor, I did an incisional biopsy and took it down to frozen section. And at that point, they felt much more confident that it was a neurofibroma and not a fibrosis.

In terms of differential diagnosis, no. But preoperatively, we routinely perform brachial plexus MRI here to try to identify the nerves and provide some sort of surgical guidance.
Okay, great. Thank you. So Arna, tell us, how did you approach the rest of the case?

So I, you know, from a cervical standpoint, I dissected free the vertebral artery down to its insertion on the subclavian. We found the vagus and the carotid are basically lateralized, you know, medialized all those structures. And actually this retro tracheal component actually delivered very, very nicely once we were able to get the finger medial to the lateral to the trachea. Then the vascular surgeon dissected free this subclavian vessel. And a neurofibroma, I haven't done many of them, but my experience generally is that they're like fibrous tumors. The subclavian artery sustained, I think, two or three puncture wounds during the dissection that required oversewing. And the vertebral actually, in time, started to fatigue just with the level of retraction. And actually, by the end of the case, it looked so damaged that we ligated and sacrificed the vertebral.

In my NL1, I had the same experience that these are very sticky and they kind of, you're absolutely right, you don't have that nice plane around them and they are really hard to kind of dissect the vessel out of them. As you said, exactly, once you do that even, the vessel gets really beat up. And I'm really interested to hear, so what happened? How did you finish the case and what was the end product?

So then laterally we found the brachial plexus and the phrenic. And this thing's basically squeezed between the vagus and the phrenic. And so both are being retracted medially and laterally. So there's a lot of kind of prolonged stretch on those nerves during the course of the procedure. Ultimately, it's not something that we could take out on block because it's so stuck to everything. And so we basically did a piecemeal resection starting from the thoracic component, dissecting it out, and then just followed it up basically into the neck and then just dissected it and then just basically debulked it down to the neural foramina. So it was just tedious, slow. It took, you know, eight hours to get the entire thing out finally. And we left, I'd say, a rind of neurofibroma tumor posteriorly on the spine. But otherwise, it went well. I mean, his phrenic is out, just from trying it. But otherwise, he's neuro-intact.
Is his vagus intact? And how's his head?
Vagus is intact.
Yeah. Swallowing?
Swallowing fine. Just uncomfortable.
Wow. Well, that's, as Pete used to tell me, that's success. All right, we're open for comments. I'm really interested to hear other comments. Mike, Jeff, Dr. Ridge, Don, Chad, Jennifer.

I don't have a whole lot to add. I mean, I think the important thing that was pointed out by Arnold is really trying to make every effort to identify the pathology, even if you couldn't get it preoperatively, at least intraoperatively. And you want to make sure, most importantly, it's not a lymphoma, which it's not. It's a fibrous tumor. But even intraoperatively, if you're dealing with a malignancy, you may feel either more inclined to be aggressive or even less inclined to be aggressive because you know at best you're gonna get an R2 resection and an R2 resection that leaves cancer behind may not be worth all the engendered morbidity when you might need some other non-surgical modality for treatment. So I applaud the strategy of trying to get as much preoperative identification of the tumor and then subsequent intraoperative identification of the tumor.
Yeah, very good point. And I think that that move that you made, Arno, to actually get a proven infection in the beginning of the case was very important. And I applaud that. Others, comments?

I was going to kind of echo that. And some of these, depending on the pathology, there's some TKIs, which actually show pretty good efficacy in desmoid tumors and aggressive fibromatosis. So confirming the pathology is paramount.
Very, yeah, absolutely. Very true. Charlie, what do you do? Call Edward Cohen right away?
I'd call Dr. Bewley. Say, Arno, get on a plane, fly down. No, that all sounds spot on.
With vertebral, I mean vertebral artery we don't often think of in in salvaged neck, but if you're low enough in the neck, the vertebral artery sometimes can be pretty close to... Yeah, very true.
There was one thought I had was whether in consultation with the vascular surgeon might be worth preoperative stenting.
Uh-huh.
Which just helps, doesn't guarantee you safety by any stretch, but it may help your confidence.
If that's big enough for a stent, that seems to be pretty small, but you might be right.
It's not the most impressive vessel, yeah, when you have it stretched out.
Yeah.
If they can put dents in your coronaries.
Yeah, that's true. For some reason, neurosurgeons are very uncomfortable with taking the vertebral, and they always try to save it. I think it's a little bit unpredictable. how the patient reacts.

In the literature in terms of pre-op balloon occlusion, even I found some studies supporting, and the literature seemed to be all over the place. And so I was, yeah, very interested to hear if anybody had any practical experience with guidance. Because I felt, I didn't feel like I had prepared myself well enough for that aspect of it, you know, when I was staring at this thing.
Yeah. These are tough cases. Anybody of the other attendings on call would like to make any comments?

So this was Monday. The frozen, the piece I took in the superior aspect of the mass was consistent with neurofibroma, but I don't have final pathways.

Unknown prior to the numbness.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male sex.

[ chief complaint ]: Post-transplant recurrent hepatocellular carcinoma with adrenal metastasis.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma, status post liver transplantation, with subsequent metastatic recurrence involving the adrenal gland.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent liver transplantation. Following post-transplant recurrence, he was treated with lenvatinib. He subsequently underwent cryoablation of the adrenal metastatic lesion.

reference_discussion.text: I've said it three times now, so hopefully it's getting across. No immunotherapy post-transplant. And there are case series showing fatalities in this circumstance, both in HCC and in other tumor types. And unlike patients that are post-kidney transplant, for example, where we have dialysis as a backup, if someone rejects their liver on immunotherapy post-transplant, we're in a really bad place. So, that does leave us towards additional mechanism of action. So, as you mentioned here, this patient was challenged with lenvatinib. We don't have great data in the post-transplant space on which systemic therapy to use, so we're kind of just putting our best thinking caps on from, again, a mechanism of action perspective and what do we use in advanced disease. I would say most people agree that lenvatinib is the most active TKI in advanced HCC, which is why that was chosen.

And he did well for two and a half years, though eventually did develop intolerance from a side effect profile, for which we then did a cryoablation. And now you can see on a post-cryoablation, he has no evidence of disease, as far as we can tell, about a year out off of all systemic therapy. I just wanted to have a quick conversation about how we can treat these patients post-transplant.
I have one patient who had an adrenal met who did well with SBRT as well, yeah.

I mean, I think you have to be careful and we probably would have done the same thing. If they get an immediate recurrence, jumping into a local regional approach before systemic approach is probably unwarranted, right? Because, okay, I see this one adrenal met, yeah, we can technically treat it. And then three months later, they have five lung mets or three other adrenal mets, right? So they need some kind of systemic approach assuming they can tolerate it. And I would argue not just a systemic reproach, but then some demonstration of stability before you consider doing, let's say a percutaneous ablation in this case. Okay. Because I don't want to just jump into it and find out on the next scan that you were just treating one 10th of the patient's cancer cells in the body.
You haven't even helped that.
You haven't helped at all.
What does stability mean?
Six months? Yeah, it's five months. It's like a good long time.
Five to six months.

I mean, at the very least, three months, because if you just assume that we often restage patients every three months, which again, there's no reasoning to do it every three months, but we do that. So at the very least, I want a three-month scan showing some relative stability where this patient didn't blossom out with five lung and bone meds, where doing a single adrenal cryo was really not worth it for him.
247 days. That's the magic number, Zach. You're looking for it.
I'm happy to provide it. We'll have to publish it. Yeah, I'll give you credit. And with that, thank you guys for Surviving Tumor Board. Thank you. Thanks, Zach.

reference_conclusion: Post-transplant immunotherapy is contraindicated because of the risk of fatal graft rejection; therefore, subsequent management should use an alternative mechanism of action, with lenvatinib favored as the systemic therapy given its activity in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. For isolated recurrence after transplant, local therapy such as percutaneous ablation should not be undertaken immediately; systemic therapy should be administered first if tolerated, with radiographic demonstration of disease stability for at least 3 months, and preferably 5–6 months, before considering local regional treatment.

[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer with rapid progression in the liver after PI3K inhibitor plus fulvestrant.

[ diagnosis ]: Hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast carcinoma with liver metastasis. Primary breast cancer had been diagnosed in June 2012 as grade II, ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative, stage T2N1 disease. Metastatic recurrence presented as a solitary liver lesion. Subsequent metastatic biopsy remained consistent with ER-positive, HER2-negative breast carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- June 2012 radical mastectomy with axillary dissection: grade II invasive breast carcinoma, ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative; pathologic stage T2N1.  
- Liver lesion biopsy at recurrence: ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative metastatic breast carcinoma.  
- Biopsy at progression in March 2023: ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative disease, consistent with prior metastatic phenotype.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a solitary liver lesion suspicious for recurrence.  
- Additional imaging at that time showed no disease outside the liver.  
- Imaging during metastatic course demonstrated a solitary liver metastasis.  
- After approximately 3 months of alpelisib plus fulvestrant, imaging showed progression of liver disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Liquid biopsy identified a PIK3CA mutation, p.E542K.  
- Liquid biopsy also detected DNMT3A and ATM alterations, considered most consistent with clonal hematopoiesis.  
- Tissue NGS from liver biopsy confirmed the PIK3CA mutation.  
- Tissue NGS identified PTEN deletion.  
- Tissue NGS identified an ESR1 p.F404 mutation.  
- Tissue NGS identified an ESR1 fusion.  
- Tumor profiling also showed CDK6 amplification.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- June 2012: Radical mastectomy and axillary dissection for primary breast cancer.  
- Adjuvant endocrine therapy: ovarian suppression and tamoxifen.  
- First-line treatment for metastatic disease: palbociclib plus letrozole, with good progression-free survival.  
- March 2023: Disease progression documented.  
- Subsequent treatment: alpelisib plus fulvestrant for PIK3CA-mutant metastatic disease.  
- Outcome on alpelisib plus fulvestrant: rapid progression after approximately 3 months, with progression in the liver.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with progressive liver-dominant disease following alpelisib plus fulvestrant.

[ other clinical data ]: Disease distribution was described as solitary oligometastatic liver involvement at recurrence.

reference_discussion.text: So fantastic. So I think this particular case highlighted the fact that we can question the diagnosis by genomic data and also change of the diagnosis for this particular patient, open multiple treatment options for the patients that would not be available if the patient was a GI origin neuroendocrine tumor. And we'll see how the patient responds to any of those, but I think This opened a lot of treatment options for the patient. So let's just go to case number four. This is a 56-year-old woman with ER-positive, HER2-negative, PIK3CA mutant metastatic breast cancer with rapid progression on PI3K-inhibited plus-fluvestrin. History goes back to June of 2012, when she had a radical mastectomy axillary dissection, showed a grade II ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative disease. The tumor was T2N1. She received OS and tamoxifen. Then she had an abdominal ultrasound that showed a solitary liver lesion suspected for recurrence. Additional imaging didn't show any signs of disease outside. The patient had a solitary oligometastatic disease, had a biopsy of the lesion that showed ER positive, PR negative, HER2 negative disease. She received first-line palbocyclic plus letrozole with good progression-free survival. And in March 23, she had a progression. She had a biopsy of that, showed an ER-positive, ER-negative, HER2-negative disease consistent with what she had before. I'm showing the liver metastases here. I don't think that we need the radiologist. There's a solitary liver metastasis here. The patient had a liquid biopsy, and the liquid biopsy at the time showed a PIK3CA mutation that was 542K, and the patient received alpelicity. There were also multiple other alterations, including DNMT3A and ATM, that most likely were coming from clonal metabolism. So, Dr. Coriano.

You know, according to the data that we have from Solar One and by leave, this was a patient with a liquid biopsy positive for PI3 kinase. She had a longer exposure to AI plus palbo. So the idea was to propose a full-face strand plus some palisade, finally. So this is what we did.

So the patient received alpha-leucine and fluversin. She had a very rapid progression, three months on alpha-leucine fluversin. You see that there's a progression of the disease in the liver. And the question was, why this patient didn't have a good response? One issue that was raised was that maybe, Dr. Koriyama and colleagues, they thought that maybe cell-free DNA didn't capture the whole landscape of the mutations in this case, and they performed additional testing. Dr. Koriyama, what do we see here?

So we performed an analysis NGS on the tissue biopsy and we discovered that, okay, the PI3 kinase mutation was confirmed, but there was a P10 deletion. That is the primary mechanism of resistance to alpelicin. So, the message for us was the liquid biopsy alone maybe is not reliable to predict the activity of a targeted agent like Alpelicib. We need an expanded panel to better understand if there are molecular markers of resistance. And here, it's very clear that P10 deletion was the reason why Alpelicib and fulvestrant was not so effective in this patient. So, Dr. Turner, it seems like this patient had multiple... And then we have an ESM1 mutation also. And the question is whether to use or not the Lassa strand since there was a longer exposure to PAL-BOEI, and this is the question for Joyce.

Well, I'd like to hear from Nick with regard to this particular F404B, because you'd be tempted certainly to think about L-acestrin for the patient, because there's data that it actually is efficacious in patients with visceral disease compared to standard endocrine therapy physician's choice. So just because she's progressed through alpella so quickly, I wouldn't necessarily not treat her with L-acestrin. But I don't know if there's any information, Nick, about whether L-acestrin inhibits this particular mutation.

L-acestrin is active against ESL1F404 mutations. These aren't mutations that activate the estrogen receptor, but they can cause resistance to fulvestrin. because the phenylalanine of F404 is involved in fulvestrin binding to the estrogen receptor. It forms what's called a pi-stacking bond. So if you mutate it, you make fulvestrin less effective, but the oral SIRDS are potentially still active. But there's strong reasons to think oral SIRDS are not going to be effective in her cancer, because as you've pointed out at the bottom here, she's got an ESL1 fusion. And these are a very important, but relatively rare way of activating the estrogen receptor and hormone receptor positive breast cancer. The point being is it makes them completely resistant to all endocrine therapy, because you don't have the ligand binding domain, you have the DNA binding domain fused to another protein. And so the estrogen receptor is still activating all of the genes that the estrogen receptor activates, but it doesn't have the ligand binding domain in the fusion. So all of our current endocrine therapies, of course, bind to the ligand binding domain. And so these tumors, we assume, although there's relatively little evidence, we assume they won't respond to endocrine therapy.

So the question is, are all of these fusions activating? And a lot of them are actually not. But as mentioned, the ones that usually lose the LBD domain, but they keep the DNA binding domain, depends on the partner, so on and so forth, that can result in resistance. And the problem here is that they are resistant to all sorts of endocrine therapy that we have, including SIRTs, including the current PROTACs that we have, and how we can target them. I'm just going to provide some of the, one of the solutions is just going for translation of ER. This is a trial done by the Herosin-EI-4A inhibitor preventing the translation of the ER, and it showed that in this trial, the trial is ongoing. We see how the trial goes, but there is good preclinical data that such an approach can help in this type of setting. P10 loss, a major mechanism of resistance to alpelicin. Dr. Coriano, can you run us through the data?

You know, this was the original paper of Dejan Duric and your paper also demonstrating with multiple biopsies on clones resistant that this was the major driver of resistance to alpelicin. So for sure, with a molecular profile like this, you should not give a PI3K in ACE inhibitor.

Fantastic. So the tumor also had CDK-6 amplification tumor, had multiple different mechanisms of resistance to endocrine therapy. This is a work that was done by Cheng Li and Dr. Chandralapati from MSK, showing that the CDK-6 overexpression and amplifications result in resistance. It's actually a very interesting mechanism for resistance. It's through the trimer of P18, ink protein, cyclin D, and CDK6. And the P18, this blocks the site that the CDK4-6 actually binds, and that by itself, it's a results in a weak suppression of ATP and prevents the binding of CDK4-6 inhibitor that results in a complete activation of the molecule and results in resistance. So we will skip this part for the sake of time. And we'll probably spend a few minutes talking about some of the challenges in the liquid biopsy, which is a highlight of this case. Dr. Coriano, what do you think about this?

You know, of course, you have technical challenges in detecting fusions on ctDNA-based NGS panels, of course, and sometimes also the copy number alteration may require higher level of detection. That's why in our cases there was absolutely this discordance, because the quality of the sample was not optimal.

So there are also some interesting and technical issues with the liquid biopsies that we should be aware of. Often for copy number alterations, unless there is a good amount of ctDNA in the blood, the limits of detection for liquid biopsies are not as good as tissue biopsy and tissue sequencing. There are also some of the alterations such as fusion, so on and so forth, are not captured with these type of liquid biopsy analyses because Sometimes that exonic region is not even included or intronic region not included in the panel to be captured. So we should be aware and often as it was done in this case when there is a discordance or there is a reason that to order more tests, order liquid biopsy and tumor tissue sequencing to understand the cases better. So, the MTB recommendation was for the patient to have the ablation of the liver. Dr. Gupta, what do you think about oligometastatic disease and radiation therapy or local therapy?

You know, it's easier in retrospect to say that there may have been a role for, you know, focal therapy for that oligometastatic or oligoprogressive liver lesion, but I think we don't have prospective evidence to know that this is beneficial in all cases. There's actually a randomized trial that was conducted out of MSK, actually, that was looking at SBRT for oligoprogressive, you know, one to three metastatic lesions. And while there was a benefit and outcome in the lung cancer patients in that study, the breast cancer patients as a whole did not benefit. So there is, and I believe that's in press at Lancet. There's a need for better selection, and I think what happened here was appropriate, but given that there's local progression, I think considering palliative focal therapy, whether radiation or thermal ablation or other approaches could be considered.

Fantastic. We have another case, but we are running out of time. So with that, I would like to conclude this session. Thank you so much for participating, and thank you to the panelists for a fantastic discussion.

reference_conclusion: Tumor tissue next-generation sequencing demonstrated PTEN deletion and an ESR1 fusion, indicating resistance to alpelisib and broad resistance to endocrine therapy. Further PI3K inhibitor therapy should not be administered. Given the isolated liver progression, local treatment with liver ablation was recommended, with consideration of palliative focal therapy to the liver lesion.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 29-year-old man; rancher from Montana.

[ chief complaint ]: Several months of nasal obstruction and epistaxis, with approximately 1.5-2 months of subjective diplopia.

[ diagnosis ]: Sinonasal moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with left orbital/periorbital involvement on imaging; no regional or distant metastatic disease on staging workup.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy demonstrated moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. No papilloma was identified on pathology.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial examination demonstrated left-sided proptosis with intact extraocular movements. CT imaging showed a left sinonasal mass with orbital involvement and hyperostosis in the ethmoid region. T1 post-gadolinium MRI demonstrated left-sided orbital involvement, fairly anteriorly. PET-CT showed no regional or distant disease. Post-induction MRI obtained approximately 3-4 weeks after completion of chemotherapy showed a marked reduction in tumor volume, with improved orbital appearance but persistent/questionable periorbital involvement; residual frontal sinus disease and a suspicious piece of dura over the orbit were identified preoperatively.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 3 cycles of platinum-based induction chemotherapy. Restaging MRI after induction demonstrated substantial interval tumor reduction. He subsequently underwent combined craniofacial surgical resection. The periorbita was involved intraoperatively and was completely resected. He then received adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: On initial clinical examination, left-sided proptosis was present; extraocular movements were intact.

reference_discussion.text: Matt, great case. Thanks for presenting that. It seems that young people may be the theme of the day, unbeknownst to us. If you could sort of comment on, when you look at imaging, CT, MRI, PET scan, et cetera, how do you like to evaluate the orbit as far as invasiveness of tumor, at least as well as you can predict on preoperative imaging?

Yeah, sure. So absolutely, so there's no definitive way to know certainly or for sure on imaging. However, there are some characteristics that may lead you to think in one direction or the other. So at least initially when I'm looking at it, I'm looking mostly for at least initially for the borders. What is that border that's pushing into the orbit look like? Is it smooth? Is it well circumscribed, rounded? To me, that suggests a little bit more of kind pushing or compression kind of process so less likely to be invasive. If you lose that nice smooth border, especially if you lose kind of fat planes there, harder to distinguish the muscles from the fat nearby, those are all going to be signs that are going to be a little bit more suggestive of possibly invasion. However, even in those cases where it does look more pushing and it does look like it may not be involving the intracranial contents or potentially going through the periorbita, it does ultimately depend on the tumor histopathology. Some of those more aggressive tumors like a squame may still have some infiltration that you can see once you get in there that may not have actually been picked up on imaging.

And Dr. Hong, if I could ask you to maybe comment on imaging and how you look at it, as well as perhaps if you were seeing this patient in your office, what kind of exam do you do if you can to delineate, you know, is tumor actually involving musculature or intracranial content, or is it merely pushing?

Exactly. So, like what Dr. Rabinowitz was saying, like often, you know, on imaging, it's just impossible to tell when you have the effacement of the normal fat plane between the rectus muscle and the tumor edge. And so on exam, what I specifically am looking for is whether there is limitation of eye movement, so ductions, whether, you know, because if the medial rectus, for example, were involved, you know, that would normally cause some mechanical restriction of eye movement. So the eye would be limited in abduction, and sometimes it can cause pain too. So looking for pain with eye movement and limitations of ductions causing double vision would be specifically what I would be looking for.
Dr. Bleier, any other comments on imaging or what you look for with these challenging cases?

Yeah, a couple of things. The first is, I think it's interesting on the left, the hyperostosis and the ethmoid. So that kind of makes me think is this a squam that arose within a pre-existing papilloma, invertebrate papilloma. And in that context, it's not just the plane of the tumor, but also the location within the orbit where the tumor is extending. So if this was basically pushing the lamina, it's just strictly lateral and you're looking at the border, that's one thing. In this case, what concerns me is that the tumor is actually pushing in the orbit and then taking an anterior turn. You can see that it actually extends past the meridian of the globe, and that's why you're having that significant, not only proptosis, but sort of lateral positioning of the globe. So in this situation, it's that sort of track of the tumor as it tracks anteriorly in the orbit, likely away from its origin, that makes me more concerned for the potential for actual invasion as opposed to a pushing border here.

Yeah, I agree. This is a bit more anterior than you typically expect from a tumor like this. I agree with you. So I'm going to just throw once more back to Dr. Hong. In a case like this, forget about this particular patient or approach to this particular tumor. But when there is anterior orbital involvement, what makes you sort of more highly consider an orbitotomy versus attacking something endonasally in your hands?

I think with the anterior, very anterior involvement, so i.e. at the level of like the nasal lacrimal sac and duct and anterior to that, that's gonna be tough to get at endonasally. And I would approach that with a anterior approach. And this would involve, doing like a like a modified lynch type of incision rather than like a transcurricular which would be going more posteriorly.

So sort of nasal oculomotor duct in anterior you tend to prefer an orbitotomy approach? Correct. Very good. Dr. Raza, if you could comment, you know, this is a young gentleman. He's 29 years old. He's actually a rancher from Montana. Does age affect how you think about definitive management for a patient, whether this gentleman was 29 or whether he was, you know, 70, for instance?

You know, quite honestly, I don't think age would affect it. I mean, if we're putting a patient through surgery for definitive treatment, I think it'd be the same overall treatment strategy, whether they're 29 or 70. Yeah.
Any other comments from the group on that?

I mean, just to jump in for a quick, just a squeam and a 29 year old, if there was no papilloma previously, that's bad, at least in other sites of the head and neck. There's not as much data in that in sinonasal specifically, but people in their twenties who get head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, just generally speaking, tend to have a worse prognosis. I think we're gonna get into the management of this, but I, but it's very different if it came out of a papilloma. Yeah. This one, you know, given the hyperesthesia, I was kind of suspicious, although in a young person, a little bit more unusual than an older person. This one just was straight up squam though, no papilloma in the path. So in this gentleman, I'm just going to sort of jump to the punch. We can move to the case a little bit. You know, with with over involvement, a young guy, we've been favoring induction therapy more and more in an attempt for older preservation. Sean, you obviously and the industry group is a big proponent of that as well. Talk to us a little bit about your experience with induction for swings and what your typical protocol is, if you don't mind.

And I think, you know, the response rates that, you know, uh, you have had reported in his paper, we're on the order of like two thirds of patients, uh, with squint undergoing induction chemo. And, you know, we typically start out the CIS platen based therapy and, you know, give about three cycles and then re-image after three cycles of therapy to assess the response. And that's really what guides sort of further, uh, you know, treatment.

Yeah. Yeah, so essentially our approach is very similar to that as well. So he got three cycles. He got a platinum-based as well. And then we re-image. So one of the questions is, when you re-image a patient, how long do you wait after their third cycle, if you will? What imaging do you like? And how do you assess response? Is it a 50% reduction? Is it any reduction? Is it no progression? How do you look at that and say, this is a good response or not so good?

So, you know, it would typically probably get an MRI scan a week or two after the last cycle of chemo and, you know, greater than 50% response would be, you know, a good response, anything less, try to see if we can push it a little bit further. Yeah, yeah.

Dr. McDonough, if I could get some input from you, you know, with our snooks, with this patient is not, if they have a good response to induction therapy, we tend to move on to definitive chemo radiotherapy. Yeah, I think sort of echoing those sentiments, I think a good take-home point is that, you know, a lot of our treatment is driven by the histopathology. Well, I, I work with Dr McDonald, so we, we definitely at least give the patient and attempted a surgical extra patient. Sure, so I think that it really depends on the doses to the cornea, retina, optic nerves, optic chiasm. So visual acuity can be impaired if the doses to the optic chiasm or nerves were more than 50 to 54. That risk is pretty low. But at a dose of 60, you may have been pushing that. And then the retina is sensitive to radio, a little more sensitive radiation so doses on the order of 45 which I would imagine they could have received even with proton therapy could lead to damage to the retina in the medial portion so not, you know, complete vision loss but field loss. And then if the cornea, we try to keep to 30 gray if we can. It's a little bit, there's a little less data on that, but corneal abrasion is possible as well. And then with adjuvant proton radiation, hopefully lacrimal glands were spared and dry eye would not be an issue.

Last question, Dr. Raza, just comment, you know, we were, we had a discussion in operating room today about a different patient and, you know, dealing with potentially a radiated orbit that has no longer function, it's painful, etc. What's your experience with those patients? Do you end up doing an exoneration down the road for a lot of these? Do they sort of limp by and get along? Do they regret, quote unquote, keeping the orbit? What's your experience with that?

Yeah, I definitely have had a few patients. I know some of my partners have had patients over the years where an organ sparing strategy was done and then the radiated orbit just becomes painful. And we ended up doing an orbital exent later on down the road, purely for palliative reasons. You know, of course, there's a selection bias to that patient population, right, in terms of they may have regretted keeping the orbit. But it's always a consideration when you're trying an organ sparing strategy, an orbit sparing strategy, that we definitely counsel patients on the potential risk of a, you know, radiated orbit down the road that could be painful and require further intervention.

Yeah, good. So I think, you know, take home points from this case are histopathologies are different and are treated differently. So squaim is much different than a chondrosarcoma. Organ preservation strategies can be very effective. Induction chemo is a game changer for both, you know, snooks and squaims in some cases, although there may be downsides to adjuvant therapy occasionally and additional surgery on the road is probably warranted in some cases, especially if it's a painful, non-functional orbit. All right, we'll move on to case number three. It's our last case for the evening. And Dr. Geltsiler, this one is yours.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus favored induction platinum-based chemotherapy for three cycles followed by interval MRI reassessment to evaluate response. Given the favorable radiographic response and the feasibility of complete resection, the recommended definitive management was surgical exploration and resection with the goal of negative margins, including resection of involved periorbita as indicated while preserving the orbit if the orbital contents were not invaded. Adjuvant radiotherapy with chemotherapy was planned following surgery.
reference_conclusion_quote: we've been favoring induction therapy more and more in an attempt for older preservation [...] we typically start out the CIS platen based therapy and, you know, give about three cycles and then re-image after three cycles of therapy to assess the response. And that's really what guides sort of further, uh, you know, treatment. [...] For a 29-year-old, I'd definitely favor definitive surgical resection if it's feasible to get a GTR. [...] And then adjuvant radiation for closer positive margins. [...] I think at a minimum you need to explore You need to determine what the margins are. And even if you have to focally resect some periorbita or even some extraconal fat, I think that's reasonable in a patient of this age in anticipation of post-adjuvant therapy. [...] So of course, if you're going to go for surgery, our goal is negative margins. [...] He did get adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female; age 32 years at initial presentation in 2004.

[ chief complaint ]: Surveillance imaging in 2021 demonstrated new bilateral pulmonary nodules.

[ diagnosis ]: Cribriform-type adenoid cystic carcinoma originating in the right maxillary sinus, initially diagnosed in 2004; recurrent metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma to the lungs confirmed in 2021.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Primary tumor: cribriform-type adenoid cystic carcinoma of the right maxillary sinus.  
- CT-guided biopsy of the left upper lobe lung nodule in 2021 confirmed recurrent metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- Left upper lobe lung resection specimen showed a 2.0 cm adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the inked pleural surface, with resection margins negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Surveillance CT chest in 2021 showed approximately 3-4 new bilateral pulmonary nodules.  
- Largest pulmonary lesion measured 2.1 cm in the left upper lobe.  
- PET-CT demonstrated a metabolically avid cavitary left upper lobe lung nodule measuring approximately 2.0 cm, corresponding to the CT abnormality.  
- Additional small pulmonary nodules were present, including a small right lung lesion and another lesion near the liver.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2004: Surgery followed by radiation for primary right maxillary sinus adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- 2021: CT-guided biopsy of left upper lobe pulmonary nodule confirmed metastatic recurrence.  
- Left upper lobe lung resection was performed for the dominant pulmonary lesion.  
- Postoperative course was complicated by significant postoperative pain.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Residual small pulmonary metastases remained after resection of the dominant left upper lobe lesion.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Long interval between initial diagnosis in 2004 and detection of pulmonary metastatic disease in 2021.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. It's really a privilege to be here this morning. Thank you for the invitation. And I will bring up my slides. So, in a, in a normal tumor board, we would have a number of cases to discuss and typically the discussion starts with 1 of the members of the team presenting a case. And so I will present the 1st case, and then we'll have some discussion as we would in a real tumor board. And so this case begins back in 2004, at which point in time, the patient who came to us for care was 32 years old. And this woman developed a cribriform type adenoid cystic carcinoma that originated in the right maxillary sinus. Now, the focus of this patient's original treatment is not the topic of this tumor board, but she originally was treated with surgery followed by radiation. So a pretty typical initial treatment course. And then was seen regularly in follow up until more recently when in 2021, she had a surveillance cat scan of the chest. So a CT or cat scan of the chest, which demonstrated new bilateral lung nodules. So, lung nodules on both sides of the lungs, approximately 3 to 4 as determined by our radiologist. The largest was 2.1 centimeters within the left upper lobe of the lung. And on the right, you can see the patient went on to have a PET-CT. And this is the PET-CT. PET-CT shows activity, or what we call avidity, within normal tissues, such as the heart, that are metabolically active, such as the heart muscle, but also within tumors. And so this here in the lung, and this is the left lung, is a 2 centimeter cavitary left upper lobe lung nodule corresponding to the abnormality that was seen on the CT imaging. And this is kind of a view from the front. So, looking at the patient scan kind of head on. And this patient went on to have a CT guided. So using the CAT scan as guidance to do a biopsy of this left upper lung nodule. And when the pathologist looked at this biopsy tissue, it confirmed that the lung nodule that was seen was recurrent metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma. So, you know, normally during a tumor board at multiple points, when we're thinking about decisions, we would stop and have a discussion about management or what we think of scans and treatment course. And so maybe at this point, I'll stop and we'll, we'll have a little bit of a discussion. Um, you know, the 1st, the 1st question that comes up and management is, you know. What should we do for surveillance? Um, and that means after a patient is treated, uh, you know, in this case, it was surgery and radiation, uh, back in 2004, you know, how is the, what is the best way to follow these patients? Um, and subsequently, when, um, this patient developed a nodule. what defines a suspicious nodule? So maybe I'll ask Paul to comment first on what his practice is, and then I'll comment also.

Boy, it's a fantastic question. Once again, thank you for hosting. Surveillance is difficult. Typically, most cancers, breast cancer, colon cancer, we think 5 years and your risk of recurrence is very low. What we've seen for adenoids, it's extremely variable, shown by this case in 2004, the original case, and now 2021 and finally recurring. ACCRF actually has been funding some research, both at our institution and others, to look at how often we should be screening people for how long. And I think that will be very useful. Overall, this is for some time, because recurrences can happen 20, 30, even 40 years later. In general, our practice at University of Michigan has been yearly CT scans. And if there's something suspicious, follow up with a little bit closer interval scans every six months. Hopefully with research between different endocytic sites, we can have a more precision type surveillance strategy. In terms of when and how to biopsy, that's a multidisciplinary discussion. between ourselves, the thoracic surgeons, the radiation oncologists, and the radiologists. Normally we look for it to be growing over time. And once again, that's very, it changes from case to case. It's very hard to define. Often we wait for it to get at least to about a centimeter. And then if there's only one lesion, we actually may do a surgery to remove it. Once again, we defer to our thoracic surgeons. If there's several spots in both lungs, then we might just do a CT guided biopsy as shown here. The reason of the difference is if there's a single spot, we do remove it with a surgery, we're done with it. There's no other spots to deal with. However, if there's multiple spots, then we can just biopsy it with a needle. Then it brings up the question of how do we address it appropriately? I think that's what Dr. Schoenfeld is about to discuss. But I'm curious, what about at Brigham? What's your practice?

Yeah, it's pretty pretty similar. I mean, I think we, we admittedly wish we had more kind of data. So it's very helpful to continue to do research to really see what the best way is to to follow patients. But I completely agree. I mean, we, we treat this differently than. Uh, other types of head and neck cancers, you know, other types of cancers that we see, and that we typically don't think there is an interval, um, after which we stop doing surveillance. So, you know, and other types of cancers, you might stop after 3 years or 5 years. Um, in patients with, we typically would do maybe some more frequent scans the 1st, few years after initial treatment, um, and then, you know, enter what we call kind of longer term follow up where we typically would still kind of do imaging about once a year in most cases. But that's also a discussion with patients because we admit we don't have the data to really guide us about the frequency of scans or what types of scans we want to do. So usually we will do a CAT scan of the chest and we'd recommend a CAT scan of the chest once a year. Sorry, just a quick follow up.
Should should every scan also include the abdomen to view the liver and how do you recommend that?

So, we typically don't, um, you know, I think that's a good question and that gets back to the fact that we, you know, we can't no scan is perfect and no scan is going to catch, you know, kind of everything and scans also have what we call false positives. And, you know, if you scan. people that have no cancer, with a history of cancer, without a history of cancer, you will get abnormalities that turn out to be just scar tissue or evidence of a prior infection or things completely unrelated. So we always are balancing kind of the risks and benefits of doing scans. And that is how frequently we do scans, but also what types of scans to do. And for ACC, we usually just focus on the lungs or the site in the head and neck. That was originally treated because we think at least according to the data that we have for most patients, those are going to be the areas of most risk. But what do you think?

I think that it's a couple of very important points. For 1, our technology is getting better over time. And 1 thing that we run to an issue with is technology gets better that sometimes presents new diagnostic challenges because now they see things smaller and smaller and smaller. And after you've had. a viral infection, or even after you've done a beautiful fall day, you actually develop pulmonary nodules, which are very, very common. And now we can see very, you know, sub-centimeter, three, four millimeter spots, and that's completely benign. However, of course, in cancer, we always get concerned. And so that's why it's so important. I think in the coming slides, we're going to discuss how do we follow this over time? I think the other question I hear very frequently is, well, why CT? Why not PET scan? You know, it's beautiful colors. Why can't we do that? CT and what I tell all my patients is actually much more high definition. You can see spots in much better anatomic resolution. I always give the analogy of a 1990s TV and watching football being in Ann Arbor here. versus a high-definition TV of today where you can see sweat rolling down people's faces. You can see very, very small spots on CAT scans and follow it over time. And so in general, our practice has actually been to favor CTs when at all possible. There's some contradications there. If I had a question about liver metastases, it's a great topic, but in general, if you look at the statistics, when people develop metastases outside of the lungs, for example, liver, the bones, the right leg, most of those people have lung metastases. And so we would have caught it if we're just scanning the chest and avoiding unnecessary radiation.

Yeah. And I will just add that if we do see something in the chest, like what was seen in this case, then we will go on to do more imaging. So then we would do either a PET scan or a CAT scan for high resolution. And we typically would do the entire body or kind of restage patients at that point. Um, and so I think here, we've talked about, you know, surveillance, we talked about suspicious nodules again, you know, there's, we would always discuss with our radiologists and tumor board and with our surgeons about radio, you know, how best to biopsy it. And often we would do, you know, as we did in this case, a CT or CAT scan guided biopsy. So maybe I'll go on in the interest of time. Um. And and so, you know, in this case, you know, getting to the management options, we had a biopsy that that showed, um, you know, recurrent. And so at this point, we think about various management options. And then, in terms of the general options that we always consider, is one, not every cancer, not every ACC that spreads to the lung, especially with very small metastases, needs treatment. And we'll talk more about that. So one option that we always think about is just watch it and watch it closely. The other option we think about is systemic therapy. So that would be, you know, Paul's area of expertise and expertise and he'll talk more about it in a minute. But and then finally would be local treatment. Would be, you know, should we treat just the lesions that we see and within local treatment is a kind of some nested questions. How many so in this patient, there were a few lesions that we're seeing that we think we're suspicious. Do we treat all of the lesions or do we treat some of them? And what type of local treatment should we should we pursue? So, should we do surgery? Should we do what we call ablation and the several different types of ablation such as cryo ablation using cold thermal energy to kind of ablate the tumor radio frequency ablation or my specialty, which is to do therapeutic radiation. And often we think about a very focused type of radiation called stereotactic body radiotherapy, otherwise known as, as for short, as an acronym. So, you know, I think there's a lot of considerations. How would you, how would this discussion typically go at University of Michigan, Paul?

Yeah. So it's a great multidisciplinary case here. And I always really depend on the expertise in my head and neck radiation oncologist. I think this is very important to engage people that specialize in this type of cancer. In this case, we would follow up the patient with probably scans at approximately six months to judge the pace of disease and understand really how this is growing. Because it looks like the original case was 04, Now we're seeing lesions in 2021. The largest was 2.1 centimeters. And to really assess, is that disease velocity increasing rapidly? Or does it sound like they're symptomatic? And based on that change in disease, if they're stable, if they're growing, then we would consider radiation to all of them, given the limited number, versus active surveillance.

Great. And so, you know, I think You know, 1 of the things I wanted to highlight just in terms of those different options is, um, is that there is a lot of uncertainty and I think, you know, when we talk about the case, this, this type of case, all of those issues that that Paul brought up, you know, do we monitored how stable have the lesions been? You know, we really, I think, as a field. Um, you know, don't know the right answer in many cases. Um, and so it's a very individualized discussion about. You know, what we think where the, where the nodules are located, how easy are they to treat? You know, what's the risk? Um, what are the side effects that are associated with each of the treatment? What's the best treatment? Um, but more broadly. Um, is conceptually a question that I think we all struggle with in the field, which is, you know, how aggressive, you know, what should our general philosophy be? Um, and, you know, in that context, I wanted to mention that a trial that we have started at the Brigham and Women's Hospital Dana Farber, which is the solar trial. And as I'll talk about in a minute, we found that the early treatment of oligo metastases may improve outcomes in patients we had treated over the last few decades. And so what does that mean? You know, I think in historically, we've kind of. Divided cancer patients into 2 kind of groups. Um, so people that have what we call localized cancer and patients that have metastatic cancer that spread to other parts of the body. But that we're learning over time that probably in many cases, as we learn more about the biology, as we get as our anatomy is our ways of following patients get more sophisticated that there's kind of this intermediate group and oligo means that these patients may just have a few kind of areas. Um, and so, you know, there's a thought that maybe treating these few areas aggressive locally might be beneficial. But we don't know that and what we always like to do is, you know, not just look back at our outcomes over historically. but also just actually test the question by doing a randomized trial of early radiation of metastases versus observation. And so this follows on a number of other trials that have been done in the United States and other countries. for patients with this type of condition, oligometastases, and they've really had mixed results. You might have strong feelings one way or the other, and we certainly see patients and doctors that feel strongly, like, of course, if you see a few cancer spots, why wouldn't you treat them? And then another school of thought is, well, what are you really doing to benefit the patient if there's still a risk that the cancer comes back somewhere else? And so I think it really depends on the situation and you can see that by results of other trials. So there was a trial called the saber comment trial, and that was multiple different types of cancers, including some salivary cancers. And they're treating these oligo metastases actually. Seem to improve survival. Similarly, in patients with prostate cancer, there's been a couple of trials. All these trials have, you know, they try to get good acronyms for the trials. So, STAMP and ORIEL were the names of 2 of these other trials. And there was a benefit in prostate cancer for localized treatment. But in contrast, just to show that it can be different from 1 cancer to another, just recently, we've had results from 2, 2 trials that were done on what we call a cooperative group. So, within the United States, and that was the energy is the name of the cooperative group. And so there was a lung cancer trial that was negative. It showed that treating these oligo metastases with radiation or localized treatment didn't benefit patients overall. And similarly, for patients with breast cancer, there was a recent report of a trial that was negative.

I don't know about you, but I always find it difficult to interpret these because there's a little bit of patient selection that goes into these. And it's always judging. Each cancer is completely different, especially an adenoid cystic. And sometimes the patients may be driving benefit, as you've kind of implied, or those that are growing slowly over time are very stable versus those are you know, tripling oversize, developing new lesions within a matter of a couple of months, and it's parsing out which group of patients, which disease biology may be driving a benefit oligomet. And so, as you're putting it here, I think that it's, your prospective study will be so important to address that, about who can we really address in that early setting, and how do we really prescreen them with, you know, scans a couple of months apart to figure out what that best therapy is.

Yeah, yeah, that's a great point. It's really comes, and that's the discussions, right, we have in Tumor Board all the time. It's like, what are the patient factors that really kind of drive us to think one way or the other? Here's the data that I mentioned. This is what we call retrospective data, so it's not a trial. We just looked back at the patients that we treated over many years, and this was research that was supported by the ACCRF, where we looked back and saw how many of our ACC patients had oligometastatic versus polymetastatic disease, and so might be eligible for kind of this type of approach. And we saw that, especially with our way of monitoring patients, we did see patients with just a few lung metastases or other metastases. And that when we looked back, it was some suggestion that maybe patients did better with earlier treatment. Now, I will say that there's a lot of caveats because, again, what Paul just said goes into this data that we do our best. This wasn't randomized. We selected the patients for local treatment based on maybe some favorable factors, and that might have contributed to this. But at least it makes us think that it's a question that's worth testing. And so this is the trial. This is the SOLAR trial. This is what we call a trial schema. where we have, I won't go through all the details of the trial, but basically we take patients that come to us and we say, we don't know what the best option is. So, we are going to follow you closely and either monitor things closely or be more aggressive and treat with radiation, SBRT. or other types of local therapy. And then really look to see over time, is there a benefit in how quickly the cancer progresses in your quality of life, in the toxicities, and how well do our treatments work? And so that's the goal of this ongoing trial. So to go back to this first case, so this patient had a, we discussed all the issues and we decided because they had that one larger lesion to go ahead with surgery. And so the patient had a left upper lobe lung resection, which showed a 2 centimeter lesion of adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the inked plural surface, but not at the resection margins. And I will just say that, you know, it is a, it is a good question. So everybody, of course, feels reassured that the cancer comes out, but there are downsides, obviously, to any procedure. And so one of the side effects of surgery is that this patient had significant post-operative pain. And then we're still left with the question of what to do about the other lung metastasis. And so getting back to Paul's points that he was making before, Um, you know, here are the other lesions that we saw, you know, 1 was small and was close to the liver. Another 1 was very small. You can see here in the right lung. You can see that it's just a little bit of a dot here. That's not present on the other side. And so actually, for this case, when we then gave advice to this patient after discussing it in our tumor board, just like Paul was commenting, we thought given the long interval between the initial presentation and metastases, the low overall tumor burden, And the trickier location to treat, because it was closer to the liver, we decided to observe. And just to highlight, as Paul mentioned, there are data that suggests that certain factors, such as the long interval from initial diagnosis, predict more slow growth. And this patient has fortunately gone on to have stability of these other small lesions for approximately 2 years, which brings us to the current time. So, I think that was the end of the 1st case. Do you have any final comments, Paul? on this case?
No, not at all. This is a great case to cover some very important points and some important trials.

Dr. Schoenfeld, can I just ask one question that we saw in the chat that relates to this last point about the interval between initial presentation of metastases? Is there generally a breakpoint at which you say, oh, this is a case where it's clearly less aggressive versus perhaps more aggressive?

Uh, that's a great question. You know, I don't I don't think we, we know what that that cut off is. Um, I think again, it depends on a number of factors. The way. We typically think about it is, is, is like we were saying, you know, for for other types of cancers, you know, we use that kind of 3 year, roughly 3 year time point, or even like a shorter time span where. you know, these cancers would grow and if they've grown within the 1st, certainly within the 1st year, but within the 1st, you know, couple years, um, it, it, it, we do think about treating more broadly, but, but clearly when there's been, you know, decades or more than 5 years, then we think that we hope that even if there's cancer growing somewhere else, it's more indolent, slow growing. Okay. So, I'll go ahead and then the 2nd case brings up some of the same issues a little bit different. This was a 61 year old man who was diagnosed with a 6.8 centimeter ACC of the right maxilla in 2021, underwent surgery, and then developed 4 lung nodules in late 2023. So, for lung lesions, 1.3 centimeter sub plural nodule in the left lower lobe biopsy confirmed adenoid cystic carcinoma and then 3 additional what we call sub centimeter nodules 2 in the left lower lobe and then 1 in the right upper lobe. And so here are the scans that we would review in our, in our tumor board, and you can see this 1.2 centimeter left lower lobe, what we call power vertebral. So it's next to the vertebral body lesion. You can see this other nodule here in the left lower lobe looking kind of face on. You can see this nodule here in the left lobe of the lung. And here you can see, you know, this peripheral, so kind of this smaller lung lesion kind of here and here, as I had mentioned. And then a very small lesion that's very, you know, it's hard to even see, but this tinier lesion right here, left lower lobe. And then the right upper lobe, again, you can see a small lesion here in the right upper lobe. So we would go through these in our tumor board with our radiologists and discuss. And so here we decided on a little bit of a different approach. Again, it was a shorter interval. These areas are more tricky to remove for surgery. There's fewer nodules. And we were a little bit worried that this nodule here close to the vertebral body might eventually start to cause pain because it's close to the chest wall. And so we actually discussed the protocol with this patient. This patient enrolled in our solar protocol, and we did radiation to the 2 largest lesions that we saw in the left lower lobe. And here's a typical, what we call a radiation isodose curve or heat map, and it just shows where the radiation goes. you know, the colors are what radiation dose, and you can see how targeted we try to be with our radiation, giving the highest dose, you know, right around the tumor and a much lower dose to the normal lung tissue and to the heart and to other tissues in the body. And, you know, again, we did this on protocol, but we also discussed, you know, in our tumor board, you know, whether or not we should treat this patient, and if so, what approach. And so maybe, you know, would this patient have been considered for radiation at Michigan, Paul?

reference_conclusion: Following multidisciplinary review of biopsy-confirmed pulmonary metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma, the dominant left upper lobe lesion was managed with left upper lobe lung resection. Given the prolonged interval from initial diagnosis to metastatic presentation, low overall pulmonary tumor burden, and the technically challenging location of the remaining small lesions near the liver, the residual lung metastases were managed with observation and close surveillance. The remaining lesions have remained stable for approximately 2 years.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 73-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Left upper tract urothelial carcinoma involving the mid and distal ureter; high-grade disease without radiographic evidence of metastatic disease at staging.

[ histopathology results ]: Ureteroscopic biopsy from the left ureter was consistent with high-grade urothelial carcinoma. There was suspicion for lamina propria invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a left ureteral filling defect spanning a substantial portion of the mid and distal ureter. Staging evaluation showed no clear radiographic metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Baseline glomerular filtration rate was 58.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent cystoscopic evaluation, cross-sectional imaging, and ureteroscopic evaluation. Ureteroscopy demonstrated extensive circumferential tumor involving the distal and mid left ureter. He was enrolled on ECOG-ACRIN 8192 and was randomized to chemotherapy alone in the neoadjuvant arm; he completed 4 cycles. He subsequently underwent left robotic radical nephroureterectomy with retroperitoneal and pelvic lymph node dissection.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included atrial fibrillation. Performance status was described as reasonable. He had two functional kidneys prior to surgery.
