reference_discussion.text: Can't say it better. Wonderful discussion. Thank you, Dr. Schmidt. Let's move on to our second case. I know we have a lot of excellent points to cover today. For our second case, we have a 73-year-old gentleman, history of atrial fibrillation, who had gross hematuria, for which he underwent both cystoscopic evaluation and cross-sectional imaging. As you can tell from these areas highlighted from these single cuts, On the left side, he was found to have a filling defect that spanned a decent portion of his both mid and distal ureter. Overall, he had a reasonable performance status. His GFR was 58. He underwent a ureteroscopic evaluation that revealed extensive tumor, again, spanning throughout the distal and mid-ureter circumferentially. A biopsy was acquired. The interpretation of the biopsy was that it was consistent with high-grade urothelial carcinoma. There was some suspicion for lamina propria invasion. Before I jump into the options, maybe another question for Dr. Schmidt. Maybe, you know, we see this when it comes to kind of understanding the depth of invasion on these pathology reports. In this case, there's some suspicion for lamina propria invasion. I'd be curious to know how you would interpret this. Do you consider this to be a T1 tumor just based on this pathology report? Is this something that you feel confident in?

Yeah, this is the bane of all of our existence, right? So these ureteroscopic biopsies are notoriously challenging. I think our ability to get to the depth of the tumor is very limited by the equipment that we use. So for me, if it's a high-grade tumor, I almost never believe the path that I get, and I almost always think it's worse. than they say it is. So if they say it's suspicious for lamina propria invasion, in my mind it's for sure at least lamina propria invasion with the concern that this might actually be T2 in reality. I've toyed around with the different biopsy techniques and different So, I used to use the bigopsies exclusively, which I hate, but I think they give you a better sample. I've transitioned somewhat now to using an alligator forcep, and I do the biopsy a little bit differently. So, I was taught to do it kind of a slow pull technique, right? So, you grab it and you pull, pull, pull, pull, pull until you get it off. And now I've started doing a forward push technique. So you grab it and you kind of try to shear it off by pushing it with the ureteroscope forward. I find that you get that lining a little bit better to get that depth. But to answer your question more directly, that suspicious for lamina propria invasion makes me worried. It's at least T1, likely T2.

Dr. Hoffman, since this patient had undergone a staging evaluation that revealed no evidence, no clear evidence of radiographic metastases, with this information, is there a role for a medical oncologist to be involved in this patient's care? Maybe can you comment on whether there's any role for, for example, perioperative or for systemic therapy at all?

Yeah, absolutely. I think a few things with this case. So first, it really highlights who are the patients that are walking into our clinic. And they are that kind of average 73-year-old patient with a host of medical comorbidities that maybe potentially can complicate the administration, perioperative therapy. you know, atrial fibrillation on eloquence with bleeding and then thinking about, you know, giving a chemotherapy that can cause thrombocytopenia, it can be a little bit nerve-wracking. But, you know, in general, with hydration and oftentimes some early clinical benefit that we can see, that's often not too much of an issue. I think from a medical oncologist standpoint, seeing a patient like this in clinic, especially if this is not a common consult, I think one of the points that was brought up earlier about staging, I think we As med-ons, we're pretty comfortable seeing patients with the same disease, you know, a few inches south, muscle invasive bladder cancer, and knowing that there's level one evidence to give platinum-based chemotherapy in the pre-op setting, but maybe potentially not as familiar with the fact that it's really, really challenging. to get adequate biopsies. And in fact, going back, as you mentioned, again and again, to get more biopsies to feel more comfortable with this diagnosis can, in fact, hurt the patient or maybe even cause a radial structure and radial insufficiency down the line. So, you know, in our practice, this is actually completely like what the information we would need in order to treat this patient or at least to discuss a perioperative therapy. There's a few trials now. Two trials, one, the ECOG81-41 trial, as well as Jonathan Coleman's preoperative study, both using cisplatin-based chemotherapy and showing what we had seen in some previous historic studies. that platinum-based chemotherapy can be safe in appropriately selected patients and get them to a point where there's a percentage, somewhere between 14% and 19% of patients that can be significantly downstaged to a CR at the time of surgery, at the time of nephro-ureterectomy. And it does seem to be those patients that, just like those with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, tend to ultimately do do better. Looking at this case with this patient with a GFR of 58 with looks like two functional kidneys, you know, I would be concerned that this patient has kind of one shot on goal to get platinum-based chemotherapy safely. And I think that would be in the pre-op setting before that kidney came out. Sometimes, it's not the case. Sometimes, you know, we're talking about a kidney that's been in trophic, you know, potentially because of obstruction for years. But I think in this case, I would, as long as the other medical comorbidities that we think about when we are counseling patients about platinum, so do they have peripheral neuropathy? Is their cardiac function okay? Can they handle the volume of IV fluids that we give with the chemotherapy? Do they have peripheral neuropathy, hearing issues, those kinds of things. But as long as the patient is a good candidate, I think It would be reasonable to consider a new HIV chemo. We actually do have a large-scale randomized phase 3 trial going on in the part group setting right now. It's ECOG 8192. And that trial randomizes patients like this to MVAC chemotherapy for four preoperative cycles versus MVAC plus your value map. that study might be open at a cancer center near you. And in fact, this pathology would meet eligibility criteria. So really, in the upper tract setting, we're really not expecting to get muscle invasive samples. So any high-grade sample with a visible lesion on a biopsy specimen or on a radiographic scans would fit those eligibility criteria. If this patient came to us and had these scans but went straight to surgery and had a high-risk tumor, so in upper tract cancer, we're talking about a pathologic T2 or higher, or with lentopositive disease, if they were still a platinum candidate, of course, the PALT trial showed that platinum-based chemotherapy was beneficial in the post-operative setting. improved disease-free survival. There's a follow-up that was recently published about a year or so ago in the JCO with longer follow-up. So, adjuvant chemotherapy for the high-risk patients post-op, absolutely an important tool in the toolkit. I think the challenge with our population of patients in the upper tract sytomy is how much platinum can they get and whether or not they're eligible for cisplatin. In the PALP trial, patients could get carboplatin if they were not cisplatin candidates, mostly based on renal function. And a lot of people actually had to transition from cisplatin to carboplatin in the postoperative setting. in that study. So that's another option if the patient had worrisome pathology. And then finally, we also have two positive immunotherapy studies in the adjuvant setting. So those studies were both designed for patients who had high-risk urothelial cancer. And in about 20% in the patients in both the adjuvant nivolumab and adjuvant pembrolizumab trials had upper tract tumors. So either patients who had preoperative platinum-based chemotherapy or for patients who were not eligible for platinum pre- or post-op, they were randomized to a year of adjuvant checkpoint inhibitor versus either placebo or observation alone. And both of those studies were positive. And so adjuvant immunotherapy is a tool that we have in our toolkit. It seems interesting in both studies. In a subgroup analysis, it seemed that even though the intent to treat population, which included all patients in those trials, with lower tract disease and upper tract disease, but those studies both met their primary endpoint in terms of disease-free survival. It seemed like those with upper tract disease potentially were not getting the same benefit. We don't have discrete data on why that is. We also know that at least from the Novolumab trial, Patients who also didn't have a lymph node dissection and also didn't have neoadjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy and also had impaired creatinine clearance may not have gotten the same degree of benefit. Whether or not those patients happen to also be more represented by those with upper tract disease, it's hard to say. We don't have that information. In the perioperative setting, there's certainly room for discussion with your local medical oncologist and treatment options that we have for these patients.

Can I hijack this for just one second? So you brought up something that I struggle with in this setting exactly. So the ambassador trial, nivolumab adjuvant, really did not, in the subgroup analysis, demonstrate a benefit. So when you have this clinical scenario, right, that patient that goes straight to surgery, we know from POUT that there was a benefit from CARBO. And we don't have convincing evidence that there was benefit from immunotherapy. Obviously, immunotherapy patients look at more favorably. CARBO is generally well-tolerated. But in that cis and eligible patient now, what do you lean towards? Do you still go for CARBO per pout, or are you leaning towards a nivolumab or a pembrolizumab?

Yeah, I think that's where the conversation can get a little bit tricky. So one thing to remember is if you go to the eligibility criteria for those adjuvant trials, patients had to have either not been a candidate for adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy, and that includes carboplatin, or refuse it. So how that conversation comes about is a different story. So I always think about, well, if the patient was coming to me on that trial, what would that conversation look like? And I try and mirror that in clinic. At least in the adjuvant volume map data, those that had PD-L1 positive tumors maybe got a little bit more of a benefit. So if the patient is really on the fence, you're really not quite sure if they're even a good candidate for colonoscopy. Sometimes, I let that make the decision for me. But otherwise, I'm not checking PD-L1 status in order to make that decision. But it's tough. And again, none of these studies are powered to look for patients with upper tract disease. And tragically, none of the future adjuvant trials are including patients with upper tract disease. So we've got a lot of great adjuvant data that will be coming out in the next couple of years. But unfortunately, we're not going to have as much in the upper tract setting.

Thank you so much, Dr. Hoffman-Sensitz, for really taking a deep dive and summarizing the recent and emerging data pertaining to perioperative therapies in this space. As we've heard, it's a very nuanced space, even compared to like muscle invasive bladder cancer, where maybe the role for the timing of systemic therapy in a perioperative space is a little bit more clear cut. Here, there are certainly nuances related both to baseline comorbidities in generally what's a more elderly population affected by this disease, in addition to what the implications may entail with removal of a renal unit surgically. And so then it becomes really a weighted discussion about neoadjuvant versus adjuvant space, and then also transitioning from cisplatin-based approaches, which we know have nephrotoxic implications to utility of alternative strategies such as immunotherapy. I will also mention, since Dr. Huffins didn't mention it, that she is the global PI on the ECOG ACRIN 8192 trial and was also for the ACRIN 8141 trial. I think we're certainly very excited to continue to see the data emerge with one of our leaders here on the call itself. Dr. Schmidt, just out of curiosity, in your institutional experience, is there a greater inclination to the use of neoadjuvant systemic therapies? Are you finding that there's a little bit more of a mixed bag, or is there more of a preference towards the adjuvant setting?

I think that's a rapidly evolving space. When I was a trainee, we had to really push to get neoadjuvant chemo and almost never were able to get our medical oncologist to give it in the space of before power trial data. Now, I think it's more of a conversation and it's a conversation with the medical oncologist and the patient. I lean towards neoadjuvant chemo as much as I can encourage a patient to do it. think that that's the right setting to get the therapy to the patient. I worry about that 30% of patients who will become ineligible for adjuvant therapy based on that loss of a renal unit. So my personal preference is always to encourage neoadjuvant therapy, to send every patient in this setting to a medical oncologist to discuss exactly what that looks like and really emphasize to the patient that I think this is the time to get that therapy in. But institutionally, and obviously every patient will make a decision based on what makes sense to them in that moment, especially when you take care of patients from far away. Sometimes they come in and say, I just want my surgery. I'll deal with it later if I need to. So it's always a patient-specific decision, but my personal preference is for neoadjuvant.

And I think another plug, too, for some recently put together guidelines that were published in the Journal of Urology, again, led by many of our urology colleagues looking at guidelines for diagnosis and management of upper tract urethelial cancer that did include recommendations for perioperative chemotherapy for high-risk patients with urethra, high-grade upper tract disease.
Yes, and that has actually helped us. We ended up discussing those in tumor board and saying, look, we've all been asking you guys to do this. Here it is in our guidelines. So absolutely.

Yeah, it definitely was a long time coming to finally have an actual guideline within the AUA for UTUC. And I think that's a great way to also recognize the nuances of UTUC as its own entity. So just switching gears here, we talked about the role for perioperative therapies. Dr. Schmidt, this one is more for you. Can you comment a little bit on how you would approach this patient surgically?

Yeah, so that looks like a pretty lengthy tumor, distal midurator, so I wouldn't try a segmental nephrons bearing option in this case. I think this is a radical nephro-U. I think the guidelines actually spell out exactly how you should perform this surgery, so I'm a guidelines-driven surgeon in this case. I think you have to take the kidney, you have to do a node dissection, you have to do a real bladder cuff. And the node dissection, in this case, would be basically a unilateral bladder node dissection, as well as everything that kind of tracks along that ureter. Probably would get all the nodes that are periaortic in this side. I probably wouldn't go interaorta caval for a more distal midureteral tumor.

Excellent. And if let's say this were more of a just isolated to the distal ureter, would you consider something like a renal scan to make a determination between a radical nephro-uretectomy versus a distal uretectomy? Is there a role for that?

I think there is a role. I think about that sometimes, especially when you're making the decision for neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy as well. I think that there certainly could be a role. If it's a smaller tumor, yes, I would consider trying to do a segmental case, certainly with concern for needing to put the patient on dialysis. But we know these tumors can be really aggressive, and you don't want to underdeliver for these patients.
Absolutely.

I didn't mention because I apologize, but I want to be totally complete. I do use intravascular chemotherapy in these cases. I know everyone's institution has a different protocol. I try to do it simple. I do it in the OR at the time of the surgery. I put it in immediately at the start of the case. And I start my surgery usually with the bladder cuff. I kind of dissect around it, but I try to get that chemo in for an hour and then drain it out, get the bladder cuff, sew up the bladder, do the rest of the case.

And it's great that you brought that up, especially that we know that there is an elevated risk of distal seeding antegrade into the bladder, especially with the manipulation surgically with these tumors. We have a similar, I certainly have a similar approach with installation. intravestigally at the beginning of the case, but there is certainly data that supports the utility of intravestigal chemotherapy, at least in some regards in the perioperative setting as well. And you make excellent points in terms of a proper surgical technique and lymph node templates. So, to sort of reveal what happened, this patient actually was enrolled on the ECOG-ACRIN 8192 trial. He was actually randomized to the chemotherapy arm alone and completed all four cycles, followed by a left robotic radical nephro-uderectomy. At the time, because of the span of the tumor, that sort of included both the pelvic as well as the retroperitoneal parts of the ureter. The decision was made to do both a retroperitoneal as well as a pelvic lymph node dissection. His final pathology was favorable, a YPT1N0 high-grade UTUC, all 25 lymph nodes negative, margins negative. And he's now 12 months out from his surgery and remains NED. I think the one unfortunate thing is that he did have some worsening of his baseline renal function, as you can see from his GFR. And so perhaps the call of giving him treatment in the neoadjuvant setting was the right one, perhaps.
Yeah. And I think, honestly, that's a great outcome for a patient. You know, he has enough renal unit to maintain his life off dialysis. Hopefully he stays that way. He's cancer-free.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board favored neoadjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy in the preoperative setting, provided the patient remained an appropriate candidate for cisplatin-based treatment after assessment of comorbidities and treatment tolerance. Definitive local therapy should consist of radical nephroureterectomy with formal bladder cuff excision and regional lymph node dissection rather than a segmental nephron-sparing approach, given the extensive mid- and distal-ureteral high-grade tumor. Intravesical chemotherapy at the time of surgery was also incorporated into the operative approach.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old female; postmenopausal since age 45 years; performance status PS 1.

[ chief complaint ]: Fatigue, body pain, and right breast central quadrant ulcerative lesion measuring 4 × 6 cm with bleeding.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic right breast invasive carcinoma with axillary, subpectoral, pulmonary, skeletal, hepatic, and bone marrow involvement. Hormone receptor profile showed ER weak positive (30%), PR negative, HER2 0; Ki-67 was high.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy from the breast showed invasive carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated ER weak positive 30%, PR negative, HER2 0, and high Ki-67. Bone marrow biopsy later showed metastatic carcinoma breast.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline PET-CT: spiculated soft tissue lesion in the upper inner quadrant of the right breast involving the overlying skin with retraction; multiple enlarged right axillary and right subpectoral lymph nodes; multiple bilateral lung metastases; multiple ill-defined sclerotic lesions in the axial and appendicular skeleton; no other lesions reported. Overall impression was locally advanced right breast malignancy with axillary, subpectoral nodal, pulmonary, and skeletal metastases.  
- PET-CT in July 2025: disease progression with a newly developed hypodense lesion in segment VI of the liver; breast lesion, bone lesions, and lymphadenopathy were otherwise stable.  
- Most recent PET-CT: partial favorable response in all lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive hereditary cancer panel: no pathogenic variant detected.  
- NGS: HRD positive; no other actionable finding reported apart from HRD positivity. TP53 mutation was reported. Gene amplifications reported included MYC, MCL1, and SGK1. RAD51C variant of uncertain significance was reported. HRD score was reported as 80.  
- MSI: stable.  
- Tumor mutational burden: low.  
- PD-L1: CPS score 1.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- During progression after initial systemic therapy, liver function tests were deranged; thrombocytopenia was approximately 75,000/µL.  
- During weekly paclitaxel, platelet counts ranged from approximately 65,000 to 80,000/µL.  
- Latest available laboratory values: total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, SGOT/AST 130 U/L, SGPT/ALT 156 U/L, hemoglobin 9 g/dL, total leukocyte count 8,000/µL, platelet count 75,000/µL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Systemic therapy was started in April 2025 with ribociclib plus letrozole and zoledronic acid every 3 months.  
- PET-CT in July 2025 showed disease progression with new liver lesion while breast, bone, and nodal disease remained stable.  
- In the setting of progression with deranged liver function tests and thrombocytopenia, repeat biopsy from liver or marrow was initially not performed.  
- Weekly paclitaxel was started thereafter. Treatment was administered with delays because of thrombocytopenia.  
- Palliative radiotherapy to the breast lesion was delivered for bleeding control: 20 Gy in 5 fractions.  
- Weekly cisplatin was subsequently added to weekly paclitaxel. The patient received a total of 9 cycles of paclitaxel and 8 weeks of cisplatin with paclitaxel.  
- Most recent PET-CT showed partial favorable response.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma with documented partial radiologic response to paclitaxel plus cisplatin. Bone marrow involvement was confirmed on biopsy. Persistent thrombocytopenia and abnormal liver function tests remained present.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history was significant for carcinoma stomach in the mother at age 85 years.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 18-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Self-palpated right neck mass/lymph node.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral thyroid microcarcinomas and cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Total thyroidectomy specimen demonstrated papillary thyroid microcarcinoma in the right thyroid lobe and papillary thyroid microcarcinoma in the left thyroid lobe. Neck dissection pathology demonstrated four metastatic lymph nodes in the right lateral neck; the largest metastatic node measured 15 mm. There was also one micrometastatic lymph node in each central neck compartment.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial neck ultrasound demonstrated a 15 mm right level III lymph node with cystic areas. Thyroid ultrasound showed thyroid micronodules that were not highly suspicious, with reported microcalcifications and cystic features. Post-radioiodine whole-body scan showed remnant uptake and a focal area of uptake in the left lateral neck. Subsequent neck ultrasound was negative, with no structural correlate identified for the left lateral neck uptake.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Fine-needle aspiration with thyroglobulin measurement in needle washout fluid confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma. Stimulated thyroglobulin after radioactive iodine was 5.3, with negative thyroglobulin antibodies.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, bilateral central neck dissection, and selective therapeutic right lateral neck dissection of levels III and IV. He subsequently received adjuvant radioactive iodine, 100 mCi (approximately 4 GBq), with recombinant human TSH preparation. Post-therapy whole-body scanning demonstrated focal uptake in the left lateral neck not seen on ultrasound.

[ current disease status ]: Post-thyroidectomy and post-radioiodine status with no macroscopic structural disease identified on neck ultrasound. Biochemical and scintigraphic findings showed stimulated thyroglobulin of 5.3 and focal left lateral neck radioiodine uptake without ultrasound correlate.

[ other clinical data ]: Risk stratification was described as intermediate risk.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 17-year-old married female; described as a housewife from poor socioeconomic background.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent vaginal bleeding after evacuation of molar pregnancy; later re-presented on 10 October 2020 with per-vaginal bleeding after approximately 1 year without follow-up.

[ diagnosis ]: Hydatidiform mole. Histopathology dated 08 November 2019 showed high-grade disease consistent with hydatidiform mole. The case was initially recorded as stage I with score 6 before evacuation. After subsequent relapse/progression, pulmonary metastatic disease was described, consistent with stage III gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology report from 08 November 2019 documented hydatidiform mole with high-grade features.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pelvic ultrasonography showed two separate cystic adnexal structures measuring approximately 7.3 × 7.4 cm and 10 × 5.8 cm, interpreted as bilateral theca lutein cysts.  
- Uterus measured approximately 10 × 4 × 6 cm.  
- There was discussion of incomplete evacuation requiring repeat evacuation 48 hours after the first procedure because of bleeding.  
- MRI was advised after readmission on 10 October 2020; detailed MRI findings were not available in the record provided.  
- Pulmonary metastases/multiple lung shadows were subsequently described, indicating lung involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum beta-hCG before evacuation: 127,000 IU/L.  
- Serum beta-hCG after evacuation: >147,000 IU/L.  
- After 1st cycle methotrexate-based chemotherapy: 14,000 IU/L.  
- After 2nd cycle: 5,000 IU/L.  
- After 3rd cycle: 4,000 IU/L.  
- After 4th cycle: 2,000 IU/L.  
- Moderate anemia was documented on examination.  
- CBC, liver function tests, and renal function tests were checked before chemotherapy administration, but specific values were not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial uterine evacuation was performed for molar pregnancy.  
- Ongoing bleeding after the first evacuation led to referral for higher-level care.  
- Repeat evacuation was performed 48 hours later for incomplete evacuation with bleeding.  
- Single-agent chemotherapy with methotrexate plus folinic/folic acid rescue was started on 13 November 2019 and continued through 14 January 2020 for 4 cycles. Regimen described as methotrexate 1 mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 with folic acid on alternate days in an 8-day course.  
- Beta-hCG declined from >147,000 IU/L post-evacuation to 2,000 IU/L after 4 cycles.  
- The patient did not continue scheduled follow-up after completion of these 4 cycles.  
- She was readmitted on 10 October 2020 with recurrent vaginal bleeding after approximately 1 year.  
- Subsequent disease was described as having lung metastases and prior exposure/failure of single-agent chemotherapy.

reference_conclusion: After molar evacuation, management should consist of confirming complete uterine evacuation with ultrasound and performing serial weekly beta-hCG surveillance rather than initiating chemotherapy immediately on the basis of a single elevated post-evacuation value. Chemotherapy should be started only if beta-hCG demonstrates plateauing or a rising trend consistent with gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. If residual intrauterine tissue is identified after one week, repeat curettage should be performed to complete evacuation. Once beta-hCG normalizes after chemotherapy, at least one additional consolidation course should be administered, followed by continued beta-hCG follow-up.
reference_conclusion_quote: So the take-home message from here is that even after it is 140,000 or 50,000, even after evacuation, immediately just after that, we should not start the chemotherapy. We must follow up the patient and we must have to do ultrasound to see whether there is residual disease and weekly vitiligo. If it is plateauing or if it is rising, then we may start chemotherapy. But after evacuation, she should report after one week. Do a scan to see that the uterus is empty. Do a beta CG after one week so that you are going to get that levels coming up or plateauing or coming down. And in spite of that, at the end of one week, do a second ultrasound study, and if there is anything remaining, do a second QR-TAC to make it complete. [ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old female; never-smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Pleuritic chest pain.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT and PET demonstrated a hypermetabolic mass in the superior segment of the left lower lobe, adjacent to the pleura without clear pleural invasion on imaging. Endobronchial ultrasound staging had indicated resectable disease preoperatively. Brain MRI was negative for intracranial metastases. At surgery, pleural implants and diaphragmatic implants were identified. After prolonged disease control on osimertinib, disease remained stable in the left chest without complete response for over 2.5 years. Subsequent PET showed no hypermetabolic lesions, but within a few months the patient developed clinical progression in the left chest with a new pleural effusion. By November, new osseous metastases were identified at T8 and in the left pelvis; by January these had become symptomatic, with an additional new painful lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling on tissue identified an EGFR exon 19 deletion. This was further characterized on plasma testing as a rare EGFR exon 19 deletion-insertion with proline insertion. PD-L1 expression was 5%. A 2023 liquid biopsy detected the persistent EGFR exon 19 deletion-insertion. Repeat liquid biopsy after progression detected EGFR exon 19 deletion-insertion at 1.5% variant allele fraction, TP53 mutation, KRAS amplification, and BRAF V600E at 0.2% variant allele fraction. Methylation tumor fraction was 0.8%. MSI-high was not detected. Tumor mutational burden was just over 20.

[ laboratory results ]: PD-L1 5%. MSI-high not detected on liquid biopsy. Tumor mutational burden just over 20. Methylation tumor fraction 0.8%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent lobectomy in 2021 after initial assessment as resectable; metastatic pleural and diaphragmatic disease was identified intraoperatively. She subsequently started osimertinib and had prolonged disease control, with stable residual disease in the left chest for more than 2.5 years without complete response. After progression with malignant pleural effusion, she began carboplatin plus pemetrexed while continuing osimertinib. She had a response to this regimen and remained clinically improving by June.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma after prior osimertinib and subsequent carboplatin/pemetrexed plus continued osimertinib. Current progression included malignant pleural effusion and symptomatic bone metastases involving T8, the left pelvis, and an additional new painful osseous lesion. Repeat liquid biopsy demonstrated persistent EGFR alteration with emergent TP53 mutation, KRAS amplification, and BRAF V600E.

[ other clinical data ]: Past surgical history included gastric sleeve and cholecystectomy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Slowly rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) following prior treatment for prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma previously classified as Gleason score 3+3=6, Grade Group 1, managed with active surveillance and low-dose brachytherapy in 2008. Biochemical rise in PSA to 5 with PSMA PET findings consistent with intraprostatic recurrence/persistence. Additional PSMA-avid focus was identified in the left inferior pubic ramus, interpreted as a likely bone metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior prostate cancer histology showed Gleason score 3+3=6, Grade Group 1.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET demonstrated moderate to high uptake within the prostate, with SUVmax approximately 13, in the setting of visible brachytherapy seeds, consistent with in-gland recurrence/persistence. No nodal metastases were identified. A mild PSMA-avid focus was present in the left inferior pubic ramus with SUVmax approximately 4.5. No definite corresponding lesion was visible on CT, although there may have been very subtle sclerosis at that site.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA had risen slowly to 5.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had been managed with active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer. Low-dose brachytherapy was performed in 2008. Subsequent course was notable for slowly rising PSA.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent/recurrent PSMA-avid disease was present within the prostate after prior brachytherapy. No nodal metastatic disease was seen on PSMA PET. A solitary PSMA-avid lesion in the left inferior pubic ramus was present and was regarded as likely metastatic disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic right lung malignancy with diffuse skeletal metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the right lung with diffuse bone metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumor tissue biopsy from the lung showed adenocarcinoma. Tissue was inadequate for next-generation sequencing.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT after 6 cycles of chemotherapy showed partial response, with reduction in size of disease and previously lytic bone lesions becoming sclerotic. Follow-up scan also showed partial response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy demonstrated an EGFR compound mutation comprising exon 19 deletion and T790M mutation. Reported variant allele frequency was approximately 14% for the exon 19 deletion and 53.5% for T790M. The exon 19 deletion was described as atypical, starting at codon 747 rather than the more typical codon 746.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 6 cycles of pemetrexed plus carboplatin-based chemotherapy. No prior EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy had been given. Chemotherapy resulted in partial radiologic response, including reduction in tumor burden and sclerosis of bone lesions.

[ current disease status ]: Partial response following pemetrexed-carboplatin chemotherapy. EGFR TKI-naive. Solid repeat biopsy had not been performed because the patient declined repeat tissue biopsy; liquid biopsy had been performed instead.

[ other clinical data ]: Molecular testing was not performed upfront on tumor tissue because of inadequate sample for NGS. The patient declined repeat solid biopsy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected FDG-avid thyroid lesion identified during routine surveillance PET/CT performed for prior colon adenocarcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe. Initial clinical stage was cT1b cN0 cM0, stage I. Final pathologic stage was pT2 pN1b, stage IVA. Incidental papillary thyroid carcinoma was also identified on final pathology.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion was consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma. Surgical pathology demonstrated a 2.1 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma. There was no lymphovascular invasion and no perineural invasion. Four lymph nodes were involved in total, including one paratracheal node and three lateral neck nodes. Nodal disease was described as microscopic, with no extranodal extension. Incidental papillary thyroid carcinoma was present.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance PET/CT demonstrated a single FDG-avid thyroid lesion. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a single well-defined 1.4 cm hypoechoic nodule in the left thyroid lobe, with no visible central or lateral neck lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no cervical lymphadenopathy, no distant metastatic disease, and no adrenal tumors.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET status was assessed but was not available at the time of referral.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was normal. Serum calcium was normal. Urine metanephrines and catecholamines were normal. Calcitonin was elevated to just over 200. CEA was elevated at 5.6.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Colon adenocarcinoma had been treated surgically in 2010 followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. It recurred in 2019 and was treated with chemoradiation approximately 1 year before thyroid cancer evaluation; there had been no evidence of disease since that treatment. For medullary thyroid carcinoma, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection (level VI) and ipsilateral lateral neck dissection (levels II-V). Postoperative PTH stabilized, and he was discharged on postoperative day 1.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after resection of medullary thyroid carcinoma with microscopic nodal metastases in the central and ipsilateral lateral neck. No distant metastatic disease had been identified on preoperative imaging. Baseline postoperative biomarkers were planned for approximately 3 months after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included vasculopathy with below-knee amputation approximately 1 year earlier, prior deep venous thrombosis, and IVC filter placement; he was not on anticoagulation. There was no family history of thyroid malignancy, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, and no personal or family history of hypercalcemia or other endocrine tumors. Physical examination of the neck had been unremarkable, with no palpable thyroid mass or cervical adenopathy. Bilateral vocal fold motion was intact.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of elevated serum calcitonin and a small right thyroid nodule identified in October 2020 during assessment while traveling.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe; primary hyperparathyroidism due to left upper parathyroid adenoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial ultrasound in Romania showed a 9 mm right thyroid nodule. Repeat neck ultrasound in Canada showed a 6 mm right thyroid lobe nodule with no other neck masses. Neck examination was normal, and vocal cord mobility was normal. MIBI scan was negative. Systemic imaging identified a right renal/suprarenal lesion on cross-sectional imaging; blood pressure was normal and urine metanephrines were negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline/serum RET testing was negative for RET gene variants. Somatic testing on the tumor specimen identified a RET mutation/variant, reported as codon 634.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum calcitonin measured 180 pg/mL and 150 pg/mL in Romania; repeat calcitonin in Canada remained markedly elevated. CEA was normal. Routine laboratory studies were normal. TSH was normal. Serum calcium was 1.23 (reported as normal). Vitamin D was very low. PTH was elevated at 11.3. Urine metanephrines were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was performed and was insufficient for diagnosis. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck dissection and excision of a left upper parathyroid adenoma.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had no comorbidities, no family history of thyroid cancer, and was taking no medications. Blood pressure was normal.

So here is, we do our own ultrasounds. So this is what it looked like on the ultrasound. Her blood pressure was normal, and as I said, metanephrines were normal. Here is a cross-sectional image of what we think is a lesion. And of course, I consulted my good friend, Dr. Tuttle. OK. That's what Mike actually recommended. The thing that perturbed me most of all was the size of her calcitonin measurements. It was 150 and I was concerned about other foci of disease. What does the panel think of that small primary, very large calcitonin level? Eyal, what do you think of that?

So there were several studies looking at the calcitonin level and the spread, lymph node spread of the disease. So with increasing calcitonin, you have first in the thyroid, then in the central neck, then in the lateral neck. Some centers, especially in Europe, guide surgery according to calcitonin levels. We don't. So we rely on good imaging. Just to mention that these studies were done 10, 20 years ago, and today we have better imaging, better ultrasounds, so we do rely more heavily on good quality imaging in our center, rather than looking just at the calcitonin level.
Would you agree that this particular patient should have a central neck dissection only, no other? no other dissections of any other compartments.

Yeah, so this is what we would also do. The minimal surgery that we do and according to the guidelines are total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection. If you have good imaging of the lateral neck, it looks clean, we wouldn't touch it.
Okay, you're not bothered by the size of the calcitonin?
So in real life, we see patients with this type of calcitonin and then after surgery have undetectable levels. So I know the studies, but in real life, we see quite a bit of these patients.

Well, you know, when I first started doing this a hundred years ago, I paid a lot of attention to the studies by Quayle and Moley and others. And basically they were recommending you know, widespread bilateral, lateral, and central neck dissection regardless of tumor size because of their finding of high incidence of neck metastases. And I was scratching my head after I did a whole bunch of patients and found very little in the way of lateral and central neck dissection. So then onto the scene came, and this is what their quoted rate was of the incidence of neck disease in various medullary syndromes. So then we looked at the studies of Machen and looked at the incidence of positive nodes in the central compartment. We looked at the French study group, French medullary study group, and found that they based a lot of their surgery on calcitonin levels. Machen's even did a study and showed incremental increases in the rate of neck disease in all compartments based on CEA levels. And Machen's also looked at the contralateral rate. Here's a slide I lifted from Hemingdrala, who generously let me use it. And you can see with basal levels of calcitonin, incrementally the incidence of neck disease increases, and he's recommending more extensive neck disease as the higher the calcitonin and the tumor size goes. So here we had a very small tumor, but calcitonin's in the range of 150. Should we have done a bilateral lateral neck dissection, Janice? Did we blow it here or did we do the right thing if we did a central neck only?

No, I think that you can go back to the lateral neck afterwards. So if you do a good total thyroidectomy and a central lymph node dissection and then see what response you get because As stated earlier, I've always been surprised sometimes the calcitonin is 500, you do that and it goes down to undetectable. If it's still elevated, then you can go back. If you don't reach that plane, it's safe to go back and stage it. So I've gone to more of a staging based on good lymph node mapping.

Good point, good point. What I do personally is look at the lymph node mapping and look at the size of the tumor, and look at the calcitonin, and base my surgical strategy on a blending of all three of those, which I think has stood me in good stead in my latter years. So anyway, yes, we decided to do surgery. She had a total thyroidectomy, a bilateral central neck, and of course, we found a parathyroid in the left upper field. Pathology showed a 0.6 sonometer right lobe medullary. No nodes were positive. And we found a 1.5 sonometer parathyroid adenoma in the upper left. So, I mean, it looks like a classic case of medullary carcinoma. it has these, it's forming nests of tumor cells. It does have a little pleomorphism and it's growing by infiltration. So it's kind of, you know, taking over a little bit of a follicular stuff. You can see the colloid in that follicle, which is kind of embedded in that tumor. What I do not notice, which I am becoming more and more sensitive to, so there's no necrosis, there's no mitoses. in this because, um, you know, the study that came from Memorial showed that you can now should actually be grading these medullary parotid carcinomas based on pathology. So I don't see any, so it does look like a, another medullary parotid carcinoma. Naturally we have to do immunostains to confirm it. But in this case, you know, the calcitonin is very high. Um, so there's calcitonin and as you can see, it's beautifully, on the left side, highlighting the tumor cells. And you can see in the background thyroid follicular cells are negative. So that tells you that is basically embedded thyroid tissue rather than part of the tumor, because there is a small subset of medullary carcinomas, which have dual differentiation between follicular and C cells. And on the right side, you have a CEA. Personally, I like CEA much better because it does stain beautifully, strongly these tumor cells.
Is there any C-cell hyperplasia on this?

So the C-cell hyperplasia for me, I mean, these are, should be like in the surrounding thyroid, right? So you're not going to see that in the tumor. So, and here it is beautiful adenoma of the parathyroid, which is on the right side. And It looks like a cellular parathyroid. There's nothing funny about it. And on the left side of my screen is a papillary microcarcinoma, which was listed and which is going to be incidental in this case.

How reliable is when I see on a PATH report There's no C-cell hyperplasia. There is C-cell hyperplasia, provided you have to read it before you get to see the red oncogene testing. How should we read those path reports?

So, I mean, you know, I will say that, and you know, there are people who will say that they can see C-cell hyperplasia on HNE, which is the cheapest test. I don't think that it's so reliable. So for me, the C-cell hyperplasia, when it is looking, you have that really bunch of cells that's forming almost like a nodular growth pattern. Definitely you can see it. But to me at that point, if it's infiltrating, it's already a microcarcinoma. If I have to say, if I am forced to say it on HNE, I need a calcitonin immunostain on the uninvolved thyroid. to look at it. You have to be careful because if the patient's thyroid has chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, or the patient is young, you are going to see some hyperplastic C-cells in the upper and the mid portion of the thyroid lateral, because that's where the C-cells are concentrated. So you really have to do these stains to see that multifocal hyperplasia. You know, the jury is still out, but I usually say that it has to be like 50 or more cells. I'm kind of surrounded by basement membrane, not infiltrating to say that this is definitely a focus of C-cell hyperplasia. But personally to me, CE and calcitonin immunostain, which really confirms it.

So can I just ask Jeremy what the other parathyroids look like? Because I know she's ret negative, but you're now got medullary thyroid cancer and you found, you know, primary hyperparathyroidism. So, Did you see the other three glands? Were they completely normal?
Yes, they were. So let's segue into that part of it. Do you think this patient has MEN?

Well, clinically she does. Before we had genetic testing, we would say she does. She has hyperparathyroidism and medullary thyroid cancer, and then we would rely on our pathologist to tell us, you know, is it bilateral? Is there C-cell hyperplasia? And if there wasn't, then we'd go, oh, two sporadic diseases in one patient with a micropapillary.

Yeah. Yeah. So your calcitonin came down quite nicely. Your CEA was always normal. Here's something interesting. Maybe, Mike, you could comment on this. Her genetic report did show a RET mutation, which is an RET variant. This is on the specimen. What do you think of that in the face of a systemic RET negativity?

So two comments. One, when somebody tells you they have a negative RET gene, you actually have to see the report. I saw one last year, and the RET gene they had tested was something called R-H-E-T. It's a pediatric thing, and the endocrinologist thought he ordered a RET gene, and it was the wrong RET gene, and she had M-E-N-2-A. So looking at the source documentation, making sure it really is J. And then over the last several years, we've learned that there are mutations within the tumor that are not germline. And so finding a 634 or in some of the really aggressive medullaries, the 918, what would have been an MEN2B mutation, it's not in the rest of the body. It's just in that cancer cell. Those are really important to know now because we have RET-targeted therapies. So we used to say if you have a sporadic medullary, it's not RET, we can't use any of those RET inhibitors. And now we know, particularly some of the aggressive medullaries, They don't have MEN2A, their body is fine. But in that tumor, there's a RET mutation, often 918, many times 634. So it doesn't do anything for her right now. But if we got in the setting of distant metastasis, it would bring RET inhibitors into play with her, even though she was a sporadic medullary. So important to note, we call this somatic testing, somatic inside the tumor. versus germline. So interesting, and you file that away. This lady's never going to need it. But if you were dealing with a more aggressive one, it would. Along those same lines, Monica, there was a question from Dr. Al-Qahtani that wanted to know, what's the role of DOPA PET, either in pre-op imaging for distant metastasis or post-op? From a nuclear standpoint, where would you come into play with those, Monica?

I think if you can get ectopa imaging, it's more if the calcitonin remains elevated after you've done your surgery, then you can screen with ectopa imaging to find out where the disease is. But we don't, I mean, we only have one center in Australia that does it, that's in another state. I know Dr. Varshavski in Alberta has got it. But I don't know in New York if you can even get it. But it is the best tracer for imaging medullary thyroid cancer.

Yeah, another question from the audience. It's very limited in New York as well. Zuber, there's a question from Dr. Abadri that says, what's the percentage of medullary cancer where we see a high serum calcitonin and yet negative calcitonin immunohistochemistry? So can you have a medullary that I have sky high calcitonin and when I send it to you, no calcitonin immunostain?

To be honest, I've seen it other way around, where the medullary is calcitonin positive and the serum calcitonin is pretty low. So I personally have not come across these. So I will repeat. That's why I rely more on the CEA, because I have seen it the other way around.
That'd be my guess too. I'd repeat that immunostain and make sure.
All right, Jeremy? Would anybody send this patient for genetic counseling?
Monica?
Well, I don't know the answer to that because systemically it's not positive. I don't know what the answer to that is.
Okay, any other panellists?
So I just have a very quick question from Mike. Mike, in the setting of MEN, that 634 is a high-risk mutation, right?

It depends on where the range is. So in the ME and 2A, the 634 would be one of the higher risk. But to my mind, it's the 918, the ME and 2Bs that are really high risk. I'm probably using that risk stratification inappropriately. But 634 in the germline would be one of the most common ones and would be one of those that we take the thyroid out when they were five prophylactically. At least in terms of genetic counseling in New York, Jeremy, we've got all kinds of rules. about genetic testing and consent in that. So we were, I used to 20 years ago, just order the Rett gene myself and not worry about it. But the last 10 or 15 years, we actually don't order the Rett testing ourselves. We always go through genetic counselors. So every medullary that we see, whether we think they're sporadic or whatever, we would go through a genetic counselor to invoke all of that sort of language. So with us, that's how we have to do it.

The thing that I've struggled with over the last many years has been the privacy issue. And if you read some of the literature, the legal literature on this, there are three cases that are quoted. The most famous one is this Tarasoff versus Regents of University of California. Briefly, Tarasoff was a woman whose boyfriend She broke up with her boyfriend and he threatened homicide. And it was a whole comedy of errors. And at the end of the day, he was incarcerated for a while and they thought he was normal. They let him go and he ended up killing this young woman, tragically. So the privacy issue is in play to a point But when, and if you look at my last sentence here, protective privilege ends when the public peril begins. And this is a well-known maxim now in legal circles. So when you wish to test for any disease, test family members, and if there's any danger in the family members because of presence of disease or psychological imbalance. It's incumbent on society, I guess, to protect the public. And there are three cases cited here. One involved medullary thyroid cancer where the surgeon was negligent for failure to warn. And then there was one about familial polyposis. So I don't have that struggle anymore about privacy issues. If somebody, threatens to kill or has a disease that could kill other members, they go to genetic counseling and they do what they need to do as far as agent of harm goes. Any other comments on that?

I mean, I think you're exactly right. Doing this through the clinical genetics and the ethics folks, they know how to do it. The two cases at the bottom were actually failure to warn the patient that they had a hereditary syndrome. It wasn't necessarily their kids. So there's one level that we would all say, For a patient with medullary, we're obviously gonna tell that patient that there's the risk of having hereditary, right? So that solves most of this. Where it gets a little more complicated is if the person decides not to tell the rest of their family. I've had this a couple times, and honestly, after six months or a year of working through it, we usually work through those issues. But just be aware that that's a good time to get genetic counselors involved and medical ethics and stuff involved. So by and large, we're in pretty good shape there. So, we want the patient to be, yeah.
Test serum RET was negative, so I just don't know how you can test the RET.

Well, yeah, you're done with it. So once we have the RET negative, then there's, you know, you've done your part, which is you've told the patient that they could have something hereditary, and now if it's negative, even if they were positive, we encourage the patients to tell their own family members, not to get too deep, but there's also a right not to know your genetic testing. So when we deal with it on the IRB, you have the right to know and you have the right not to know. So you can't be so paternalistic to say, I'm gonna tell your kid without knowing whether they have the option of knowing or not knowing. And the clinical genetics folks know how to do that. So it's really best left in their hands to help you work through it. Janice, you were gonna say something here?

Yeah, I just, you know, we have somebody that also has hyperparathyroidism and a super renal mass. And so for us, I mean, our genetic testing in medullary, just like you, Mike, would have gone through genetics. Yes, they would have been told you don't have anything, but we would be keeping their file because who knows when there's another genetic abnormality. And I think that suprarenal mass just needs a little bit more investigation.

I agree, because if that turned out to be an adrenal thing, then we would sequence the entire Rett gene, right? Because the Rett testing she's had done has been very focused on the most common mutations, which works like 98% of the time. We don't generally do that for a single parathyroid adenoma, because you're allowed to have an adenoma and sporadic medullary. But if you threw an adrenal thing in there, then we would probably sequence the entire Rett gene to see if we found something more unusual in there. All right, Jeremy, we're running on. What do you got?

reference_conclusion: The panel agreed that the patient should undergo total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection, with no lateral neck dissection in the absence of suspicious findings on high-quality lateral neck imaging. Management should be guided by careful lymph node mapping rather than calcitonin level alone, with postoperative reassessment of calcitonin response and consideration of staged lateral neck surgery only if biochemical disease persists. The suprarenal mass warrants further investigation, and referral through genetic counseling was supported for RET evaluation and follow-up of potential hereditary implications.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Compressive thyroid symptoms in late 2023, including dysphagia predominantly for solids, fatigue, constipation, depression, and cognitive symptoms described as “brain fog.”

[ diagnosis ]: Graves disease diagnosed in 2003. Right thyroid lobe neoplasm resected in April 2023, reported as thyroid tumor of uncertain malignant potential. Post-thyroidectomy left thyroid bed hypoechoic lesion identified on surveillance ultrasound in 2024.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroidectomy specimen from April 2023 showed a 1.7 × 1.1 × 1.2 cm well-circumscribed nodule in the mid portion of the right lobe. No other focal lesions were identified. Surgical margins were negative. Two lymph nodes were negative for malignancy. Background thyroid tissue showed hyperplasia consistent with Graves disease. Pathology was reviewed at the treating institution and by Mayo Clinic, with final interpretation reported as tumor of uncertain malignant potential.

Fine-needle aspiration of the left thyroid bed lesion in 2024 yielded scant cellularity with few follicular cells and a background of mixed lymphocytes and histiocytes, interpreted as consistent with lymphoid tissue. TTF-1 was non-contributory. LCA highlighted lymphocytes. Molecular testing submission was insufficient for analysis.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI cervical spine in 2022 reportedly demonstrated a left thyroid lobe abnormality; outside records were unavailable. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated an approximately 1.5 cm solid isoechoic-to-hypoechoic right lobe nodule. The gland was described as heterogeneous. Follow-up ultrasound in 2024 showed an empty right thyroid bed, a small remnant in the left thyroid bed, and a suspicious hypoechoic lesion in the left thyroid bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No contributory molecular/genomic result was available. Specimen submitted for molecular analysis from the thyroid bed lesion was insufficient.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- 2022: Laboratory findings were consistent with active Graves disease, with suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, positive thyroid antibodies, and elevated TSI/TSHR antibodies.  
- Late 2023 preoperatively: Developed hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low free T4.  
- Immediate postoperative period: TSH 0.1.  
- August 2023: TSH 7.3; thyroglobulin undetectable; thyroglobulin antibodies positive.  
- November 2023: TSH 4.9; thyroglobulin antibodies remained positive.  
- September 2024: TSH 1.2; free T4 1.6; thyroglobulin 2; thyroglobulin antibodies positive.  
- At time of thyroid bed lesion evaluation: TSH 6.6; free T4 1.1; thyroglobulin negative; anti-thyroglobulin result unavailable at that draw, although prior positivity was documented.  
- FNA washout studies from thyroid bed lesion: calcitonin negative; thyroglobulin negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Methimazole therapy had been administered for Graves disease since 2003 with long-term control of hyperthyroidism. Thyroidectomy was performed in April 2023 for compressive symptoms and goiter. Postoperatively, levothyroxine replacement was required and titrated according to TSH. Compressive and hypothyroid symptoms reportedly resolved after surgery.

[ current disease status ]: As of 2024, there were no palpable neck masses. Surveillance ultrasound demonstrated a small left thyroid bed remnant and a suspicious hypoechoic lesion in the left thyroid bed. FNA of this lesion was non-diagnostic for malignancy and favored lymphoid tissue. No confirmed recurrent or metastatic malignancy had been demonstrated.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included Graves disease. Family history included a cousin with thyroid cancer and a mother with thyroid disease of unspecified etiology. The patient was an active smoker at presentation.

She was current a smoker when she was presented to the clinic. Just a brief story about her. In 2003, she was having hyperthyroid symptoms. She was treated with methimazole for many years and she was controlled. But in 2022, she had an MRI of cervical spine that showed left thyroid loop in another hospital and the outside records were not available. Yeah. Yeah, the ultrasound showed like around 1.5 centimeter solid isotohypoechoic right lobe nodule.

And it's a fairly well circumscribed nodule. It's abutting the capsule of the thyroid. No really obvious extra thyroid extension. No, it does not bother me that much. But if patient is persisting to get an ultrasound, I do it, to be honest, just for relief of the patient. But yeah, it does not.
Yeah, we try to reassure him. Okay, so keep going, Ibrahim, and let's see what we see.

Sure. So yeah, as part of her course, she developed hypothyroidism in late 2023, TSH was elevated, free T4 was low, and also she started to have some symptoms, like compressive symptoms, dysphagia, mainly for solids, fatigue, constipation, depression, and also brain fog. So just for the compression symptoms and for the goiter, patient had a thyroidectomy in 2023, like in April. and the pathology came back as a tumor of uncertain malignant potential. The pathology was read in our institution and also we sent a specimen to May Clinic for a second opinion and review. And then within like this is like I just copied the report it said like within the mid portion of the right loop there was like 1.7 by 1.1 by 1.2 centimeter of well circumscribed nodule And also no focal lesions were identified. And the surgical margins were negative. There was like two lymph nodes negative for malignancy. And the other cells were like hyperplasia consistent with Graves' disease. And also have a copy of the formal pathology here.
All right, Margie. The first time I heard about this tumor of uncertain malignant potential is in the early Chernobyl days, right? Right, right, right. Tell me what the heck this thing is.

Well, you know, this is a term that, you know, we've heard this said at this forum many a time. It's a term that pathologists should try to avoid if at all possible, because it sounds more ominous than it usually is. You know, if you say unknown potential, just, you know, in the void, it sounds like, well, it could be okay, it could be a disaster, right? We don't know, right? Where in reality, it might be benign or it might be a tumor of low-grade malignant, you know, a low-risk tumor. So, you know, I really can't say anything more than that because there's nothing to look at, right? It's not big. It's 1.7. That decreases my suspicion. The bigger something is, the more likely it is to be malignant. Of course, you could see something that's highly malignant, that's 1.7. But then, you know, it wouldn't be of uncertain malignant potential. We'd have a handle on it. We would see invasion, whatever, you know. So I like to avoid that term.
Dr. Duong, practically when you get this, how do you treat this? Is this benign? Is it cancer? How do you sort of think about this from the endocrine perspective?
You know, for me, I will treat this as a benign because it doesn't show any malignant thing. So I will treat this as benign.

And Catherine, you're the one that gets to talk to the patient first because they see you a week after surgery to look at the scar and you've got the path report. What do you tell the patient with this report, Catherine?

I think the main thing is to reassure them that when the word uncertain appears on a pathology report, it actually makes the patient pretty concerned usually. the first thing is to kind of reassure them that, you know, that we're not uncertain about the diagnosis here and that this is, you know, consistent with benign, it's not invading anywhere, there's no evidence of lymph nodes, and to go through all of the positive factors of that histology report rather than focusing on that one word of uncertain, I think. And then malignant as well, when you get uncertain malignant patients sort of panic, so I agree with And Dr. Brown, you know this is not a great term to have on a pathology report because it usually breeds panic by the time they come in to see you. So reassurance and explanation of what it is and why it's called that as opposed to a malignant tumor.

So Margie, is it fair for me to think about this as somewhere between a follicular adenoma and worst case scenario, like a minimally invasive low risk follicular thyroid cancer that's likely cured with lobectomy or am I on a different path?

Bingo. I think that it's probably something that, you know, maybe has invasion, maybe a capsular invasion, maybe not. Maybe has vascular, maybe not. But, you know, I don't want to say these are highly subjective. That's not true. But they're not, sometimes capsular invasion is not easy, right? So it's probably around that realm.

Yeah, I think so. I mean, we don't see this very often, as Margie said. I mean, this was really brought to us by some really, really expert pathologists that sometimes you just can't tell. But we see this a handful of times. This is not a common diagnosis that we get handed. I do measure one thyroid globulin a few weeks after surgery, the same I would do for a minimally invasive follicular thyroid cancer, and then I follow it. I tell the patient, I think it's benign. If I'm wrong, it's a really low risk thyroid cancer that you're probably cured with lobectomy. So that's how we set kind of the follow-up. All right. So where did we go from there? Go ahead, Dr. Ibrahim.

Thank you. So yeah, post-op labs, we have like the immediately post-op like TSH was 0.1 and then it increased 7.3 by August. Thyroglobulin was undetected but also they have like the antibodies was positive also limiting the TG interpretation as well. Post-op course she required levothyroxine and was titrated according to the TSH. Last one was or like November 2023 her TSH was 4.9, TG antibodies again positive with symptoms completely improved. She does not have any palpable neck masses. Fast forward in September of 2024, TSH is 1.2, 3T4 1.6, TG is 2, again, TG is positive. In the follow-up session, she had an ultrasound again, right thyroid bed was empty, but the left thyroid bed was showing small remnant, and there was a suspicious hypoechoic lesion. I will show you now this. This is the hypoechoic lesion on the left thyroid bed, and also we did an FNA during that time.

All right, Catherine, before we get down this rabbit trail, can you make the case for me that we should have never, ever done a follow-up neck ultrasound on this patient? We're only going to get false positives here, right? case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 17-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with bulky thyroid primary causing severe tracheal compression; regional nodal metastasis in the right lateral neck; distant metastatic disease was suspected based on markedly elevated calcitonin and indeterminate pulmonary nodules. Germline RET M918T mutation was present, consistent with MEN2B.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroid biopsy performed at the time of tracheostomy showed medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT neck/chest demonstrated a thyroid mass with significant tracheal compression.  
- A pathologic right lateral neck lymph node was present at level II.  
- The common carotid artery was abutted/partially encased by tumor on imaging.  
- The innominate artery was completely encased by tumor.  
- DOTATATE PET demonstrated the known right level II nodal disease, multiple small pulmonary nodules interpreted as indeterminate, and no other evidence of disease elsewhere in the body at baseline.  
- Airway evaluation including bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy showed no transmural tracheal invasion and no transmural esophageal invasion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Germline RET M918T pathogenic mutation was identified.  
- Somatic RET mutation was also identified in the tumor.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Calcitonin was >11,000 at initial workup.  
- BMI was 13 at presentation.  
- Other initial laboratory testing was reported as otherwise unremarkable/within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- During EGD/colonoscopy, the patient developed ventilation difficulty followed by significant respiratory distress in recovery.  
- Urgent airway management was performed by pediatric otolaryngology with intubation using a size 5 endotracheal tube.  
- Urgent tracheostomy and thyroid biopsy were performed.  
- The patient was initially tracheostomy-dependent and unable to tolerate capping.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Medullary thyroid carcinoma in the setting of MEN2B, with a bulky thyroid primary causing severe tracheal compression, complete encasement of the innominate artery, right level II nodal metastasis, and indeterminate pulmonary nodules.  
- Calcitonin was >11,000.  
- He remained tracheostomy-dependent and unable to tolerate capping.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Left vocal cord paralysis was present at initial specialist evaluation; right vocal cord function was intact at that time.  
- Mucosal neuromas were present.  
- Phenotypic features characteristic of MEN2B were present.  
- Past medical history and social history were otherwise unremarkable.
