reference_discussion.text: All right. Do you guys see that there? We do. All right, cool. Yeah, thanks all for the invitation of presenting this medullary thyroid cancer case that I've been taking care of this young man for the last year or so. So he's 17. His past history and social history is pretty much unremarkable, only due to the fact that he never saw it. great medical care, but he presented with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss that had been persistent, presented to our pediatric hospital for EGD and colonoscopy. During that procedure, he had a challenge with ventilation during the procedure. And then immediately in the recovery, he developed significant respiratory distress, and our pediatric otolaryngologists were called urgently. They were able to intubate him with a size five endotracheal tube. At that point, they scoped through the tube and this is what they saw. So obviously significant compression of the trachea. The patient was stable enough with the size five endotracheal tube in. They elected to get an urgent CT neck and chest on their way to the operating room for more definitive surgical area. But this is what the initial CT scan showed us. And I can just walk briefly through this, but clearly a pathologic lymph node in the right lateral neck. There's a level two node there. You can see this thyroid mass here with significant compression of the trachea. And you can see the common carotid, at least in this view, probably just shy of 180 in case. And then further down, you'll see that the anominate is completely encased in this tumor. So their plan was, proceeded the operating room for a trach and biopsy of the thyroid at the same time. So that is what they did. and pathology showed medullary thyroid cancer. So this is when I was called. Um, so I think we can just pause there and talk a little bit about what we would all do at this point.
Yeah.
As much information as needed for the history.
Yeah. Why don't, um, why don't we go through some of the basic workup for medullary thyroid cancer? What, uh, what do you guys usually do for like the initial package?

Yeah. Um, so, you know, the full lab workup, so TSH, uh, you know, calcium, PTH, calcium. I check a calcitonin and the CEA, and I just do the serum metanephrines to start. I don't typically get the urine metanephrines. That's just what our endocrinologists have recommended to me. Um, in terms of imaging, you know, I am, I'm definitely a huge fan of the ultrasound. So I do my own ultrasounds in clinic, um, so thyroid, neck ultrasound, um, For the medullary patients, they do need some type of cross-sectional imaging. I think that the exact modality used is a little up for debate. Our radiologists do prefer using the DOTATATE PET, so we get the DOTATATE PET. FDG PET, I think, is fine as well. We do the genetics on the tumors, so testing for RET on the specimen, and then all these patients should be evaluated, in my opinion, by genetics for whole blood testing. So that's what we do here at the University of Minnesota.

Thank you. Yeah. I think just to summarize some of that for the fellows, medullary thyroid cancer can be, um, part of inherited syndromes. Um, so they need to be referred to genetics typically. Um, and then while you're waiting for all that, doing the testing for some of those syndromes, like MEN syndromes, having, uh, calcium, PTH, screening plasma, metanephrines, just to make sure they don't have any kind of field chromocytoma. Dr. Tarasova, anything you want to add to that for an initial diagnosis of medullary thyroid cancer?

No, I think that this definitely completes the workup. That's what we will do if, let's say, if it is not patented, it's not available. We do sit-in neck, chest, abdomen. Very important to assess the liver because that's the most common site of this metastatic spread for medullary thyroid cancer, and it's typically MRI of the liver or three-phase CT of the liver, and then evaluation of the bones. So, if you do just CT of the neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis as a baseline, that's not complete the staging. You need to evaluate the bone, whether it's going to be bone scan or peridototate scan of FTG path, like either of these modalities.

And in terms of the genetic testing, also to be very clear for the trainees, we're talking about both germline and somatic testing. So germline looking for MEN2 syndromes and looking at the tumor itself to see what mutations it has, potentially something actionable. And they get a ton of imaging and a ton of blood work. So Dr. Jethwa, what's going on next?

Sure. So here is his labs, you know, Notably, you can see the calcitonin over 11,000. The rest of his testing, fortunately pretty normal for him. Like I said, we did the DOTATAPE PET. He had that right level two node that I previously showed, no other evidence of regional disease, multiple small pulmonary nodules that were read as indeterminate, nothing else in the rest of the body. And then his genetic testing.

So. That makes sense because it's so rare for a 17-year-old to present with such advanced MTC. Most of the sporadics happen in older patients or if it is, you know, there are some germline mutations where patients will present later in life, usually with the less aggressive ones, but the 918 is one of the more aggressive types that you can have both as a somatic and both as a germline mutation. So the fact that he's 17 and has so much disease, this kind of makes sense.
Yeah, I agree.

But the fact that there's a Rett mutation at the same time is good because only about 60, 70% of the somatic mutations have Rett mutations and the others are mostly RAS and others. So with a Rett mutation, it offers some therapeutic possibilities at least.

And the risk of pheochromocytoma with germline pathogenic RETM918T is about 50%. So that has to be evaluated really clearly. And if you really need to assess it urgently, you can just look at the adrenals on the CAT scan and see evidence of adrenal nodules that will increase the pre-test probability. Plasma meds are frequently false positive. So if in doubt, need to confirm with 24-hour urinary cuts and meds and look for medications would interfere with the measurement of this test.

Very helpful. And I think just to hammer home this particular mutation, Do you guys know when we would need to do a prophylactic thyroidectomy if this was already a known mutation in the family history? Dr. Wong, do you do much, I don't know if you guys do.

I don't do a lot of the pediatric, but I'm a firm believer that we should be doing this over the pediatric surgeons. Cause you know, we do like almost a thousand a year here and the pediatric surgeons do like five, you know, so I keep saying that we should be doing these, but this is one of the highest, highest risk category where by guidelines, you think about it like, you know, like what is it below age five or something, or it's like, it's like, even first year of life. But honestly, the, to operate on someone, that's below one is really harrowing. I mean, that's not something that I do regularly, but the people that do this, the parathyroids are like impossible to find, you know? The nerves are like nothing. So it's really hard. It's really hard to do that.

But it just goes to show for the trainees, if you know that this patient has this inherited mutation, this is somebody that gets a prophylactic thyroidectomy early in life. All right, next slide, if you want to keep going.

So, you know, when he, you know, he was so malnourished, his BMI was 13. At this point when I met him, he was trach dependent, could not tolerate capping. As I showed you that the bulk of that disease was on the right side, but he had a left cord paralysis when I met him. The right side was actually functioning normally. And that's, you know, those typical mucosal neuromas you see in MEN2B. And he did have all the characteristic bases, that somehow just was not detected in his childhood pediatric evaluations. So then, yeah, just going through some of the different treatment considerations, discuss new adjuvant considerations. What is the extent of surgery? Do we go ahead and do elective lateral necks? Obviously a disease on the right neck, but a lot of controversial topics in this case.

Yeah, for sure. So I think that's the point of this case is that there are a lot of nuances. It's complicated. I think we can all agree though, that with a nominate encasement like that, this is not a surgical case up front. Unreceptible. So what do we do for unreceptible medullary thyroid cancers? Dr. Tarasova, what kind of options do we have?

So in this specific case, the presence of rat somatic and germline obviously like mutations opens opportunities for selective rat inhibitors and they change the landscape of management for patients with medullary thyroid cancer. they are very well-tolerated. Basically, initially, it was silprocaltenib and pralseltenib, but like the silprocaltenib is the only one that is approved for the treatment of medullary thyroid cancer, red mutant medullary thyroid cancer. So that could be used as a neoadjuvant agent with great tolerability, great response. And so I think that that's something that could be considered.
I think, Dr. Wong, you probably have more experience than I do with neoadjuvant, but if it's clearly unresectable up front, it's a little harder to call it neoadjuvant, right?

Right. That's right. So the whole idea of neoadjuvant is that you're planning to do surgery and you're using the sulforacaptive as a modality to get some regression to make the surgery less morbid. If it's clearly unreceptable from the start, like if the anomaly is completely encased or if the trach is, you know, extensively invaded and, and, you know, you would have to do some kind of laryngopharyngectomy and the anomaly resection, then it's, it's really all semantics. Then you can put them on a Rett inhibitor just as therapy and see how things go without a plan for surgery. But it's all, it's all semantics really. But it sounds like this is pretty bad. I mean, the trachea looked pretty bad to me, Dr. Jethmo. And then the inominate, I couldn't even see. I assume it goes much more inferiorly into the superior mediastinum.

Yeah, it did not go too far into the mediastinum. But as you guys saw there, the inominate was totally encased. In very close review of his imaging, there was no signs of transmural tracheal invasion. I, of course, bronched him and did esophagoscopy as part of the workup. There was no transmural invasion. And if time permits, you'll see some imaging coming up of the trachea.
I think we are running short on time. Um, I want to be respectful of everybody's time. Do you want to just summarize for us what happened with them?

Sure. Yeah. So you got, he had suffragette and maybe he was on it for four months, had a pretty remarkable response. Um, you can see the shrinkage of the tumor in, in these images here. Um, the anominate was able to get freed there. And so I actually did take him to surgery. I did have a cardiovascular surgery who was willing to resect the anominate if needed. I felt I needed to be aggressive with the 17-year-old, even though with a calcitonin of over 11,000, he obviously has distant disease. It was extremely challenging surgery, the right vagus. Remember, left cord paralyzed, right nerve working. The right vagus was encased in tumor. So I was able to preserve that, maintain a functioning right nerve, did the right neck dissection, total thyroid and central neck, but it was extremely challenging. But he's actually done well. He's recovered both nerve function now. I was able to get him decannulated. He is eating everything by mouth, so I got his G-tube out. And his DOTATATE PET showed no evidence of disease. His calcitonin is ranging around 500, so still diseased.
you know, excellent, excellent work. Outstanding.
Outstanding.
Great job.

Yeah. Just so you know, Mark Saffario presented at the ATA about three or four months ago, the neoadjuvant sulfur captinib study with four institutions. And he showed like an over 50% major response rate. And I think in his study, almost everyone made it to surgery and they had like an over 90% R0, R1 resection rate. So this definitely has legs and we do, we do it too here. This is definitely a target you want to go after. So congratulations. That's a fantastic surgery, Dr. Jethwa. Fantastic.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 9-year-old female child.

[ chief complaint ]: Pulmonary lesion identified on surveillance imaging 3 years after liver transplantation.

[ diagnosis ]: Calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumor of the liver with biopsy-proven pulmonary metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]: Primary tumor demonstrated nested epithelial and mesenchymal components, consistent with calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumor. Immunohistochemistry showed strong beta-catenin expression and WT1 expression. Lung lesion biopsy confirmed metastatic calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance scans performed 3 years after liver transplantation demonstrated a lung lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive molecular profiling (Tempus xT and Tempus xF) identified CTNNB1 mutation and TERT promoter mutation. Tumor mutation burden was low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent liver transplantation in 2021 for calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumor. Subsequent surveillance identified pulmonary metastatic disease, indicating post-transplant recurrence/progression. The patient also received systemic chemotherapy, with subsequent persistent metastatic disease. Compassionate-use tegavivint was initiated thereafter.

[ current disease status ]: After 6 months of tegavivint, the patient remained symptom-free, had no significant adverse effects, and had stable disease without significant radiographic improvement.

[ other clinical data ]: The pulmonary metastasis occurred after prior liver transplantation for the primary hepatic tumor.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Renal mass initially suspected to represent renal cell carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma, pathologic stage T4N1, high grade.

[ histopathology results ]: Pathology from laparoscopic nephrectomy demonstrated high-grade urothelial carcinoma, stage T4N1. No ureteral tumors were identified in the specimen. The ureteral margin was negative. A residual ureteral stump remained following nephrectomy. One high lymph node was positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Pre-surgical imaging demonstrated a very central renal tumor, initially suspected to be renal cell carcinoma with possible invasion into the renal sinus. No clinically enlarged lymph nodes were identified subsequently.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent laparoscopic nephrectomy at an outside institution. Following pathologic diagnosis of T4N1 high-grade urothelial carcinoma, the patient received adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient then underwent surveillance, including endoscopic monitoring, with no residual tumor identified in the ureteral stump or bladder at initial post-nephrectomy evaluation. The patient subsequently underwent salvage ureterectomy with bladder cuff. No lymph node dissection was performed at the time of salvage ureterectomy.

[ current disease status ]: No residual tumor was identified in the ureteral stump or bladder on endoscopic evaluation after nephrectomy. No clinically enlarged lymph nodes were present at the time of later management.

[ other clinical data ]: Estimated recurrence-free survival at 2 years, based on CRAB nomogram assessment, was 23.8%, consistent with very high-risk disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old man; never-smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough and breathlessness for 4 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma of the right lung, with bony metastases and soft tissue deposits.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the lung.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline imaging demonstrated a right lung mass with bony metastases and soft tissue deposits. After 3 cycles of pembrolizumab, PET scan showed slight reduction in the lung mass and slight reduction in lymph nodes, with interval development of new bony lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: PD-L1 expression was 70% by 22C3 assay. EGFR negative. ALK negative. ROS1 negative. Subsequent next-generation sequencing was negative for actionable alterations.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Single-agent pembrolizumab was started as first-line systemic therapy. One cycle had been administered before next-generation sequencing results became available. After 3 cycles, PET imaging showed slight reduction in the primary lung mass and lymph nodes but new bony lesions. Pembrolizumab was continued for 3 additional cycles.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic NSCLC remained present on pembrolizumab, with mixed radiologic response: partial reduction in primary lung mass initially, new osseous lesions after 3 cycles. The patient was reported to have some pain but remained reasonably well.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbid illness was documented. Genetic panel turnaround time was reported as approximately 15 days.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 89-year-old female at initial presentation in 2020.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid carcinoma, subsequently with rising serum thyroglobulin after thyroidectomy and later progressive pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Oncocytic thyroid carcinoma (encapsulated angioinvasive), initially localized to the left thyroid lobe; later progressive metastatic disease involving the lungs, with additional FDG-avid lesions in the thyroidectomy bed, left retropharyngeal lymph node, and C6-C7 region on follow-up PET imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial surgical pathology from 2020 showed a 7 cm left encapsulated angioinvasive oncocytic thyroid carcinoma. Capsular invasion was present. Extensive vascular/angioinvasion was present in more than 4 foci. No extrathyroidal extension was identified. The tumor was completely resected. Two resected lymph nodes were negative for oncocytic thyroid carcinoma. Pathology was subsequently reviewed at the treating institution and the diagnosis of oncocytic thyroid carcinoma was confirmed.

[ imaging findings ]: Post-radioactive iodine imaging after the first treatment in 2020 reportedly showed no evidence of radioactive iodine-avid distant metastatic disease. After a second radioactive iodine treatment in August 2025, post-therapy imaging showed scattered diffuse and focal pulmonary activity associated with extensive reticulonodular opacities. PET imaging obtained after referral showed disease predominantly consistent with pulmonary metastases; suspected osseous lesions were subsequently considered degenerative rather than metastatic. Repeat PET imaging over a 4-month interval demonstrated progression, with bilateral FDG-avid lung nodules increased in number, size, and uptake; an FDG-avid lesion in the right thyroidectomy bed increased from 1.6 cm to 1.9 cm; a left retropharyngeal lymph node lesion was present; and a new FDG-avid lesion at C6-C7 was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing demonstrated two TP53 mutations, two DAXX mutations, an ARID1A mutation, and a CDK4 gene alteration. TSH receptor mutation testing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Approximately 10 weeks after thyroidectomy in 2020, with minimally suppressed TSH, thyroglobulin was 12 and thyroglobulin antibodies were negative/undetectable. Thyroglobulin subsequently rose steadily over 4 years to 70 with suppressed TSH; thyroglobulin doubling time was approximately 5 years. Thyroglobulin antibodies remained negative throughout follow-up. After the second radioactive iodine treatment, thyroglobulin continued to rise; by February 2026 it increased from 127 to 170 despite TSH suppression.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Total thyroidectomy was performed in 2020 with complete resection. Radioactive iodine ablation was administered in 2020 at a dose of 100 mCi following Thyrogen preparation; post-therapy imaging reportedly showed no iodine-avid distant metastatic disease. A second radioactive iodine treatment was administered in August 2025 at a dose of 150 mCi, also following Thyrogen preparation. Following the second treatment, the patient developed hypoxemia and required continuous supplemental oxygen day and night; at review in October 2025 she was short of breath on exertion while receiving 2 L continuous oxygen. This was considered consistent with treatment-related pneumonitis and/or subsequent fibrosis causing chronic respiratory failure.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic thyroid carcinoma, predominantly involving the lungs, with radiographic progression on serial PET imaging and rising thyroglobulin despite TSH suppression. The patient had chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring continuous oxygen after the second radioactive iodine treatment.

[ other clinical data ]: The first and second radioactive iodine treatments were performed at different institutions. Original outside imaging from the first radioactive iodine treatment was not available for review. Initial community management was by endocrinology, followed later by oncology referral.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old woman; otherwise healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Acute onset right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever.

[ diagnosis ]: Acute appendicitis with incidental well-differentiated appendiceal carcinoid tumor (appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor) identified on appendectomy specimen.

[ histopathology results ]: Appendectomy pathology demonstrated acute appendicitis and a well-differentiated appendiceal carcinoid tumor. The tumor showed morphology described as tubular/gland-like in areas, with linear arraying in some sections. The lesion stained with synaptophysin.

[ imaging findings ]: CT abdomen/pelvis showed stranding/inflammation around the appendix, consistent with acute appendicitis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Fever was documented on presentation. No additional laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent appendectomy for acute appendicitis. The appendiceal carcinoid tumor was identified on surgical pathology.

[ current disease status ]: No post-operative disease status data were available.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination in the emergency setting showed fever and marked right lower quadrant tenderness.

reference_discussion.text: And so, a multiplicity of different options, those two most recently approved ones are certainly on the list. But we always like to discuss clinical trials, which we won't do right now, but which would be part of our tumor board discussion. The only reason we won't right now is because Pam will conclude this afternoon with some clinical trial discussions. So, moving away from the pancreas to the appendiceal carcinoid tumors. A 30-year-old woman develops acute onset right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fevers, and she's otherwise healthy. Sounds like appendicitis. You go to the emergency room, the physical examination, she has a fever. She's very tender. You touch here and she jumps. She has a CT scan which shows some stranding inflammation around the appendix consistent with acute appendicitis. I'm amazed at the radiologists now that can see the appendix. In the old days, we couldn't see the pancreas or the appendix with our scans. Now we can actually see something that's that big and pencil thin. and even see some inflammation around it and make a radiographic diagnosis. However, she ultimately needs an appendectomy, and surprisingly, the pathology reveals not just appendicitis, but a well-differentiated appendiceal carcinoid tumor. And I'd say that this is a fairly typical way of finding these, and I'll let Terry talk about what she sees through the microscope.

Yeah, we see this not all that infrequently. And the good news about it is the vast majorities are really quite small and they're almost all well differentiated and they're very, very slow growing and they don't spread. The vast majority don't really spread beyond the appendix unless they're starting to get really quite large or more mitotically active. The interesting thing is I remember when I talked about the immunostains that we use to confirm neuroendocrine tumors, some of these appendiceal carcinoid tumors don't stain with neuroendocrine markers or do so very weakly. And they can show, these tumors can also show a little bit different morphology. Here what you're seeing is more tubular shape. They almost look like they're making little glands. rather than this nice little ribbony nest that I showed you for the pancreatic. Here's another example of this carcinoid. That looks a little bit more typical for the appendiceal carcinoid. But here you start seeing it's almost lining up, a linear array. And what happens sometimes with these is Because these often occur in younger patients, because that's generally who's getting acute appendicitis, and you often see an association with acute appendicitis, is a pathologist might look at it and think, oh, this looks like metastatic carcinoma, because it looks like it's making glands, and it looks a little bit like breast cancer. So, it's really important for pathologists to be really, really aware that this is a pattern that you can see with these appendiceal carcinoids, because metastatic breast cancer is obviously a completely different sort of prognosis, and not a good prognosis at all, as opposed to an appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor. And I think that that's all I have to show on it. So, once again, this one, though, fortunately, stained with synaptophycin, and so you could say, oh, you know, don't worry about that. That's, and this is a neuroendocrine tumor. But every once in a while we'll get cases in on our consultation service where they're worried because they think it's a neuroendocrine tumor and they've done their chromogranin stain and their synaptophysin stain and they're negative. And they're worried that maybe it's some very well differentiated carcinoma that spread to the appendix. And it never has been in my experience. It's almost always going to be one of these incidental neuroendocrine tumors. So this is actually sort of a good news tumor if you're going to get one.

reference_conclusion: Following appendectomy for presumed acute appendicitis, pathology demonstrated a well-differentiated appendiceal carcinoid tumor. The tumor board characterized this as a typically incidental, indolent appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor with very low risk of spread unless large or more mitotically active, supporting appendectomy/pathologic diagnosis as the key management step in this presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of right neck mass with dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma centered in the post-cricoid region, clinically staged as cT4a cN2b cM0 at initial presentation. Disease later progressed with biopsy-confirmed pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration/biopsy and endoscopic evaluation demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma. Residual tumor was identified on post-treatment endoscopy in the post-cricoid area, with extension into the lateral wall of the piriform sinus.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT neck demonstrated a hypopharyngeal tumor with cortical destruction and extension into the strap muscles.  
- Right level III cervical lymphadenopathy was present, with two metastatic cervical nodes identified.  
- PET imaging showed intense uptake in the primary tumor and neck disease; uptake extended into the strap muscles.  
- PET imaging also showed chest uptake, prompting CT chest. Initial chest imaging demonstrated mediastinal nodes; thoracic evaluation did not identify definite metastatic disease at that time, and the patient was considered M0.  
- Three months after completion of chemoradiation, PET imaging showed significant interval improvement but persistent disease.  
- Subsequent CT chest demonstrated multiple lower lobe pulmonary nodules.  
- Interventional radiology biopsy of lung nodules was positive for metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No patient-specific molecular or genomic test result was documented.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial office examination showed a 3 x 3 cm right neck mass that was poorly mobile/fixed, right vocal cord immobility on fiberoptic examination, and mucus pooling at the hypopharyngeal inlet.  
- Baseline swallow evaluation demonstrated aspiration.  
- The patient declined primary surgery.  
- He underwent primary chemoradiation.  
- Post-treatment course was complicated by PEG-tube dependence.  
- Shortly after the 3-month post-treatment PET scan, he presented emergently with respiratory distress and underwent emergency tracheostomy.  
- Endoscopy at that time demonstrated residual post-cricoid tumor with extension into the lateral wall of the piriform sinus; the upper esophageal sphincter was scarred over and could not be traversed with the scope.  
- The PEG tube had been dislodged and was replaced.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent locoregional disease after primary chemoradiation, with residual post-cricoid/piriform sinus tumor, nonfunctional swallowing requiring PEG dependence, tracheostomy dependence after respiratory distress, and biopsy-confirmed pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No weight loss was reported at presentation.  
- Past medical history included alcoholic hepatitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism.  
- He had extensive alcohol use history and smoking history, and continued smoking and drinking during treatment.  
- Functional status was limited by COPD; he was able to walk approximately one block before becoming short of breath.

reference_conclusion: The panel agreed that this T4aN2bM0 post-cricoid/hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma represented a clear indication for primary surgical management, with preoperative direct laryngoscopy/endoscopic assessment to define inferior tumor extent and reconstructive requirements, and planning for likely circumferential repair. After failure of chemoradiation with persistent disease and suspicious pulmonary nodules, restaging with diagnostic workup of the lung nodules was recommended before considering salvage surgery. Following biopsy confirmation of pulmonary metastases, curative-intent laryngopharyngeal surgery was no longer appropriate; the remaining management options discussed were palliative systemic therapy, including immunotherapy, and goals-of-care discussion with DNR/DNI and hospice planning.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent upper abdominal pain for 6 months, associated with loss of appetite, weight loss of approximately 10-15 kg over 4-5 months, and low backache.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma of unknown primary at presentation, based on metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma identified on left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy. Subsequent imaging demonstrated a pancreatic mass with metastatic disease involving liver, retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and left supraclavicular lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the left supraclavicular lymph node showed metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry showed strong positivity for MUC1, patchy nuclear positivity for NKX3.1, and occasional cells positive for PAX8. Tumor cells were negative for CK7, CK20, glypican, CD10, p40, and Hepar-1. The outside pathology interpretation reported the findings as most compatible with prostatic primary adenocarcinoma, with clinicoradiologic correlation advised. A repeat biopsy had been performed and additional immunohistochemical workup, including neuroendocrine markers, had been sent; results were not available.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial outside CECT showed a well-defined heterogeneous abdominal lesion measuring approximately 7-8 cm near the liver, involving hepatic segments V, VII, and VIII, without venous washout. Multiple enlarged lesser omental and retroperitoneal lymph nodes were present, along with an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node measuring approximately 2.8 cm. Prostate and bladder were reported as normal. Whole-body PET imaging, including FAPI PET and PSMA PET, showed a FAPI-expressing soft tissue mass involving the proximal body/head region of the pancreas, with additional uptake in liver lesions, retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and left supraclavicular lymph node. Prostate was reported as normal, with only mild prostatomegaly and no abnormal prostate uptake on PET.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue NGS showed TERT positivity, CREBBP positivity, and TP53 mutation. Tumor mutational burden was low. Microsatellite status was stable. Genomic instability metric was low.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor markers were within normal limits, including CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, and PSA. ECOG performance status was 1. BAC was documented as 1.7.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had been started on gemcitabine plus carboplatin on a day 1/day 8 schedule for carcinoma of unknown primary. After 2 cycles, he had symptomatic improvement.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma with pancreatic mass and metastatic involvement of liver, retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and left supraclavicular lymph node. The patient had symptomatic response after 2 cycles of gemcitabine/carboplatin.

[ other clinical data ]: Past history included diabetes mellitus. He had a history of tobacco chewing for more than 30 years, alcohol intake for approximately 10 years at 7-8 drinks per week, and no smoking history. On examination, ECOG performance status was 1. A hard left supraclavicular lymph node measuring approximately 2.5-3 cm was palpable. Abdominal examination showed epigastric fullness. Upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal.

<image> Comprehensive NGS report showing likely oncogenic TERT, TP53, and CREBBP alterations, low tumor mutational burden, microsatellite stability, and a low genomic-instability score.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Left vertex scalp lesion. The patient reported a palpable scalp lump present since November of the prior year and denied other symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Mixed desmoplastic melanoma of the vertex scalp. Initial outside biopsy had been reported as desmoplastic melanoma, Breslow thickness 1.0 mm, Clark level IV, 7 mitoses/mm², no ulceration, staged pT1b. Repeat institutional biopsies from three separate scalp foci demonstrated melanoma with spindle cell proliferation, mixed desmoplastic type, depth of invasion 1.4 mm, no ulceration, no dermal mitotic figures. Clinical stage was documented as pT2a pN1c cM0, stage III, based on concern for satellite/in-transit dermal foci.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside shave biopsy of the scalp lesion showed desmoplastic melanoma, Breslow thickness 1.0 mm, Clark level IV, 7 mitotic figures/mm², no ulceration. The outside report did not specify pure versus mixed desmoplasia. Repeat punch biopsies were obtained from three distinct areas of the scalp lesion. These showed melanoma with atypical spindle cell proliferation, mixed desmoplastic type, with measured depth of invasion 1.4 mm, no ulceration, and no dermal mitotic figures. All three biopsy specimens showed dermal tumor extension without an epidermal component. Histologic review described deep dermal spread consistent with desmoplastic melanoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Physical examination demonstrated a raised horseshoe-shaped vertex scalp lesion measuring approximately 3 cm in diameter, with three clinically distinct foci. No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy or parotid masses were present. CT brain and neck showed no intracranial invasion and no calvarial invasion. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Castle genetic testing had been reported as low risk.

[ laboratory results ]: LDH was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: An outside shave biopsy had been performed initially. Repeat diagnostic sampling was performed with three punch biopsies of the three visible scalp foci, confirming mixed desmoplastic melanoma. Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab was initiated. Pembrolizumab monotherapy was selected in the setting of a history of diarrhea. Response assessment had remained pending.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven mixed desmoplastic melanoma of the vertex scalp remained present, with multifocal dermal involvement across three sampled scalp sites and no radiographic evidence of distant metastatic disease. There was no evidence of intracranial or calvarial invasion on CT imaging. The patient was undergoing neoadjuvant pembrolizumab at the time of review.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included anxiety with claustrophobia, bilateral glaucoma, irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea, colon perforation with colon resection in 2015, mixed hyperlipidemia, and osteoporosis. Brain MRI was not obtained because of claustrophobia.

[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old male. Former smoker. Childhood tonsillectomy. No significant comorbidities were documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Left neck mass, persistent sore throat despite multiple courses of antibiotics, and mild dysphagia developing over the preceding week.

[ diagnosis ]: HPV-associated, p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the left base of tongue/oropharynx with metastatic left cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical pathology demonstrated a 3.4 cm base of tongue squamous cell carcinoma, HPV-positive and p16-positive. Lymphovascular invasion was absent. Perineural invasion was absent. Surgical margins were negative. Left neck dissection showed metastatic carcinoma in 2 of 20 lymph nodes; the largest metastatic deposit measured 3.2 cm. No extranodal/extracapsular extension was identified. Right neck dissection showed 0 of 24 lymph nodes involved.

[ imaging findings ]: Office laryngoscopy demonstrated a left base of tongue mass involving the base of tongue without involvement of the lingual surface of the epiglottis. There was minimal extension into the glossotonsillar sulcus/tonsillar fossa, and the lesion extended toward the midline. CT imaging showed a left-sided base of tongue mass extending toward midline with some deep extension into the base of tongue musculature, without clear extension into the intrinsic tongue musculature. A left cervical lymph node was present. PET scan showed locoregional disease in the left neck without distant metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor was HPV-positive and p16-positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior to oncologic evaluation, the patient had received multiple antibiotic courses from the primary care physician for persistent sore throat without resolution. He subsequently underwent surgical resection of the base of tongue primary with bilateral neck dissection and ligation of left-sided arteries. Postoperatively, he was admitted for 2 days and discharged on a soft diet. At 2-week follow-up, he was functioning well with minimal swallowing deficit, no appreciated aspiration symptoms, improved pain, and well-healing incisions. He participated in a clinical trial postoperatively.

[ current disease status ]: Status post resection of primary tumor and bilateral neck dissection with negative margins, pathologically node-positive disease in the left neck only, and no distant metastases identified on PET imaging. Early postoperative recovery was favorable.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination showed a firm but mobile left neck mass. A lesion at the left base of tongue was palpable. Tonsils were surgically absent. Intraoperative management included bilateral neck dissection and ligation of arteries on the left side.

reference_conclusion: Following transoral surgical resection and bilateral neck dissection, adjuvant postoperative radiation therapy is recommended based on intermediate-risk pathologic features, specifically two involved lymph nodes without extranodal extension and negative margins. Radiation should be directed to the primary site and the left neck, with omission of the right neck given the pathologically node-negative contralateral dissection. Off protocol, treatment would follow ECOG-based postoperative dosing, with an anticipated dose of 50 Gy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic carcinoma of the lung with disease progression on prior EGFR-targeted therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV lung carcinoma, initially diagnosed in July 2023 as metastatic lung cancer with EGFR-mutated disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Histologic subtype was not documented.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan performed in July 2025 showed progressive disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- NGS panel at initial diagnosis in 2023 showed EGFR exon 19 deletion.  
- Liquid biopsy performed in October 2025 showed acquired EGFR T790M mutation and TP53 mutation.  
- Additional report details indicated EGFR exon 19 deletion remained detectable and dominant, with variant allele fraction 27.6%.  
- EGFR T790M was detected with variant allele fraction 12.9%.  
- Two additional low-level variants were reported at 0.12% and 0.25%; one TP53 alteration was described as TP53 R175 mutation.  
- An EGFR exon 20 variant was also referenced in the report material, but the exact alteration was inconsistently documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Afatinib was started in 2023 following identification of EGFR exon 19 deletion.  
- Afatinib was continued from 2023 to 2025.  
- Best documented response on afatinib was partial response.  
- Disease progression was subsequently documented on PET scan in July 2025.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic EGFR-mutated lung cancer after prior afatinib, with acquired EGFR T790M resistance mutation and TP53 co-mutation.

[ other clinical data ]: No laboratory values were provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally identified thyroid nodule. The patient was asymptomatic, without dysphonia, dysphagia, or dyspnea.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Left thyroid papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), classic type.  
- Left thyroid follicular carcinoma, minimally invasive.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the left superior thyroid nodule: malignant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the left mid-thyroid nodule: benign, consistent with benign follicular nodule.  
- Left hemithyroidectomy pathology:  
  - Lesion 1: 1.6 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma, classic type, with lymphovascular invasion; posterior margin focally positive.  
  - Lesion 2: minimally invasive follicular carcinoma; no lymphovascular invasion; no perineural invasion; margins negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated:  
  - Right thyroid nodule not meeting criteria for biopsy.  
  - Two left thyroid nodules meeting criteria for biopsy.  
  - Left superior nodule measured 1.8 cm and was TI-RADS 5/highly suspicious. Sonographic features included mostly solid/almost completely solid composition, hypoechogenicity, taller-than-wide shape, microcalcifications, and punctate echogenic foci.  
  - Second left thyroid nodule measured 1.8 cm and was TI-RADS 4.  
  - Isthmus was normal.  
  - No notable cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- Laryngoscopy demonstrated normal bilateral vocal fold mobility.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- TSH: 1.552 (normal).  
- Free T4: 0.8 (normal).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Left hemithyroidectomy was performed.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post left hemithyroidectomy, with pathology showing a 1.6 cm classic papillary thyroid carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion and a focally positive posterior margin, together with a minimally invasive follicular carcinoma with negative margins.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Physical examination was unremarkable.  
- Thyroid nodule was not palpable.  
- No history of radiation exposure.  
- No family history of thyroid cancer.

And I thought it's really good that they're separating now PTC from follicular because they're different and they're also invasive encapsulated variant PTC. But take a look at this one that comes out. It's just really clear because when you look at the current ATA guidelines published in Thyroid, it's so hard to figure all this out. And the case that we just saw, it follows here where it says low-intermediate rates. It says here is margins negative or positive at the posterior margin R1. That's what we just presented, which is why it was pertinent for you to bring that up. It was a very smart idea to bring that up. And the completion is completely, it is completely reasonable. Just because that's not what we do, I would do here, it doesn't mean that it's wrong. But the guidelines are still guidelines. The guidelines are not rules. And so just because it's written on a guideline doesn't mean that we should feel compelled to follow everything to the letter. But thank you.

Thank you for sharing that. Yes. I think there's one question here and Dr. Wang, I'm going to put it to you because you had mentioned it. If you're doing a TG on patients who've had a lobectomy only. How do you know when to do any more work or intervention?

So this is controversial. Some people don't believe in this because there's natural fluctuation of TG with intact low, but we all know this, it goes up and down with the TSH. And so what we're looking for is something catastrophic. We're looking for like a real jump that's out of the ordinary, not like one or two points higher, but something that's a trend that's going up where that'll prompt like distant imaging. This might be reasonable if you have like some kind of follicular lesion or, you know, a follicular variant of PTC or follicular one where you're worried about the small chance of distant meds or RAS-mutated cancer. So, for that reason, we do check it even though it's not likely to be sensitive for any small local recurrence. It's more for that rare catastrophic event where you have something brewing distantly.
Awesome. All right. Great discussion. Excellent case. Important points. We got to keep going. So next up we have Dr. Thornton and a case from Dr. Dylan Johns Hopkins.

reference_conclusion: Following left hemithyroidectomy demonstrating a 1.6 cm classic papillary thyroid carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion and a focally positive posterior margin, as well as a minimally invasive follicular carcinoma without vascular invasion or other high-risk features, the consensus favored surveillance rather than completion thyroidectomy. Management should consist of serial neck ultrasound, thyroglobulin monitoring, and clinical follow-up, with prognosis considered very favorable provided the resection was clinically clean. Completion thyroidectomy was considered reasonable only if operative findings suggested gross residual disease or if additional concern arose from the surgical assessment.
reference_conclusion_quote: We would monitor here. this patient would get, you know, serial ultrasound images. And we would, we would follow, even though there's an attack low, we would still do TG and we would see the patient back. And this patient's prognosis remains, remains very, very favorable as long as the surgeon felt like the resection was clean. [...] But overall, if it's good quality surgery, no need for completion based on the path. [...] No high risk features here, which is great. [...] So only the patient with extensive vascular invasion, or let's say high-grade features, or gross external extension, they are the ones who require completion pterodectomy in follicular carcinomas. But just vascular invasion, no need for completion.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old female. No relevant comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: In 2012, she presented with progressive abdominal enlargement, bloating, abdominal pain, approximately 1 year of vaginal bleeding, weight loss, ascites, pleural effusion, and enlarged uterus with vaginal involvement on gynecologic examination. Performance status was reported as ECOG 2.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic endometrial adenocarcinoma, initially misclassified on biopsy as cervical carcinoma. At presentation in 2012, metastatic disease was documented with supraclavicular nodal involvement and thoracic/abdominopelvic metastatic disease. Final surgical pathology after hysterectomy demonstrated endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium, grade 3, with myometrial invasion and bilateral ovarian infiltration.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial biopsy in 2012: solid carcinoma with clear cell components; initially interpreted as cervical primary.  
- Left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy at presentation: positive for metastatic carcinoma.  
- Post-chemotherapy surgical specimen following total hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy: endometrioid adenocarcinoma, grade 3, arising in the endometrium, with myometrial involvement and infiltration of both ovaries.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT chest in 2012: left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, and para-aortic/mediastinal lymphadenopathy.  
- Initial CT abdomen/pelvis in 2012: large uterine-associated mass, multiple retroperitoneal and pelvic lymph nodes, ascites, and peritoneal invasion involving the uterus, rectum, and pelvis.  
- Post-chemotherapy imaging after 3 cycles and after 6 cycles of carboplatin/paclitaxel: marked response with only a small residual uterine mass.  
- Laparoscopy after chemotherapy: no carcinomatosis identified.  
- Imaging in 2015: pelvic mass, supraclavicular lymph node recurrence, iliac lymph node involvement, and a 5 cm pelvic mass.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- CA-125 at initial presentation: 485.  
- CA-125 after 6 cycles of first-line carboplatin/paclitaxel: 14.  
- CA-125 at recurrence in 2015: 265.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line systemic chemotherapy in 2012: carboplatin plus paclitaxel for 6 cycles.  
- Outcome of first-line chemotherapy: major clinical and radiologic response; post-treatment imaging showed only a small residual uterine mass, and CA-125 decreased from 485 to 14.  
- Surgical treatment after response to chemotherapy: laparoscopy followed by total hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy. No lymph node sampling was performed at surgery.  
- Postoperative management: observation without further treatment.  
- At recurrence in 2015: rechallenge with carboplatin plus paclitaxel for 2 cycles.  
- Outcome of rechallenge chemotherapy: clinical and radiologic progression.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent progressive metastatic disease as of 2015, with pelvic mass, iliac nodal disease, and supraclavicular nodal recurrence after 2 cycles of platinum-taxane rechallenge.

[ other clinical data ]: Colonoscopy at initial presentation was normal.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, this is a 56-year-old female with no relevant comorbidities. She was a very healthy woman But as many of our patients come in very late, she came in in 2012 with an increased abdominal size, bloating, abdominal pain. She had been for a year with vaginal bleeding. She had weight loss and a kneecog that went up to two. In the physical examination, she had ascites, pleural effusion, we didn't assess, and her gynecology exam viewed an enlarged uterus with vaginal involvement. Their images at that time, the CT of the chest, showed left supraclavicular lymph nodes, the pleural fusion, the periortic and mediastinal lymph nodes, and the abdominal and pelvis CT showed a large mass associated with her uterus, multiple lymph nodes in the retroperitoneum and the pelvic areas, a situs, and invasion of the peritoneum surrounded the uterus, the rectum, and all the pelvic area. Her colonoscopy was normal and her CA125 was 485. The biopsy that was performed showed a solid carcinoma with clear cell components and everybody diagnosed at that moment and thought that it was of the cervix. So we decided to go on with chemo and we started chemotherapy, Cargoplatin and Paclitaxel and we went in on doing six cycles of this and the images and the imaging post the three cycles and after the sixth cycle, only showed a small mass in the uterus. She had a great, great effective response to the chemotherapy. And her CA, 125, went down to 14. So, the surgeons decided they wanted to see what was going on. And finally, after performing a laparoscopy, they saw that there was no carcinomatosis. So, they went on and performing a total hysterectomy with bilateral anexectomy. and the biopsy showed that this was not a cervix carcinoma, but it was an adenocarcinoma of the endometrium. It was an endometroid adenocarcinoma, grade three, with myometrial involvement and infiltration of both ovaries. So, she went on with no more... treatment, she was just on observation, and on 2015, her images showed that there was a pelvic mass and, again, a supraclavicular lymph node. The CD scan showed iliac lymph node involvement and a 5-centimeter pelvic mass. And her CA, 125, went up again to 265. So we challenged the chemotherapy again, the same scheme, and she went on with two cycles of that, but she had now clinical and radiological progression. So the questions are, what other treatments can we offer this patient if there's a second and a third line chemotherapy for this endometrial carcinoma, and if there's a role for the radiotherapy?

And dare I say, a role for palliative therapy as well. This is a different topic that I'll cover in another tumor board. But there's been a large increase in palliative services over the past years in South America. There's also been the introduction of signed patient directives for end-of-life care legislatively in many countries, led by Mexico, I think, first in the continent, but there's a very low utilization of palliative services and signing of patient directives by patients. So this is something that's radically different from the United States. This is the kind of patient who will probably show up in an emergency room and slow down the pace of clinic resources and beds and things for her care, which could be avoided, perhaps, by involving palliative care earlier. But I'm interested in general comments from Dr. Dazon, first of all.
Yeah, I guess the biggest question I have is what was the rationale to proceed with hysterectomy in this patient?

Well, the surgeons wanted to see how much involvement was there. that there was no carcinomatosis, so they just decided to go on and do the surgery, the total hysterectomy, because they saw very little disease that was left over after the chemo.
But there was no biopsies ever done of the supraclavicular nodes that she presented with in 2012 to prove stage 4?
Yes, absolutely. But she had a complete response as images were, she had a complete response everywhere. So you did biopsy the nodes in the supercloth? At the beginning, yes.
Oh, and it was proven to be?
And it was positive.
Ah, okay.
Yes. Okay.

I agree completely with the treatment that she has received so far. I think, to me, if she had a beautiful response to chemotherapy after six cycles, I have no problem taking her back to the OR and do a hysterectomy. For what purpose? What is your intent of the surgery? I don't think there's any paradigm that shows any benefit here. To me, I would offer her surgery, no doubt if she has a nice response, and I'm extrapolating Fair amount from ovarian cancer.
You're extrapolating hugely from ovarian cancer. I would not be able to even justify that on the board.

When I worked in Toronto, there were patients operated on with diagnosis of stage 4 cancer. for 20, 30 years, for many decades, and it was finally abandoned. We used to refer to this as heroic surgery. It has no hope of curative intent.

I would say that. I mean, she got—I mean, stage 4 individual cancer has a horrible prognosis, right? I mean, this patient had two extra years of life without cancer. And you think it's because of the surgery? I mean, I don't know if it's chemotherapy or surgery, the combination of both. There's no way to know. But are stage 4 individual cancer patients ever cured with chemotherapy? No. I don't think so. I think all of them have poor prognosis. They're not cured with surgery either? No, no. I'm not saying that she's going to cure.

I'm just saying that you have to allow me to assert. So this woman was having a supraclavicular nodal involvement from carcinoma, had a phenomenal response to chemotherapy. The role for surgery of removing the uterus is what? Curative? Palliative? Control? None of the above. There was no reason to do surgery.
I think, can I talk now? I think it's for curative intent. Oh, really?
Stage four was supraclav nodes.
That's what you're hoping for. I will still offer her surgery despite Don's disagreement.

That's my personal opinion. I just think that this is a critical question in solid tumor malignancies. And we have to come down to what's out there. You're not listening to the biology. The surgeons do this all the time. All today in breast cancer. And there has never been shown an advantage of surgery other than for local reasons. If a patient has a flungating breast tumor, a bleeding And for pelvic bleeding or severe pelvic pain, fine. But no way can you ever convince me there is not a shred of literature to suggest that you can cure a patient with stage four disease surgically. No.

So you have to have an intent. Well, not only that. You did a THBSO in this patient. I'm going to have to go over it. I'll be in a couple of weeks. Well, no, no. But my point is you had a THBSO in this patient who also had nodes throughout the entire abdominal cavity.
Well, she had a response, right?
I know, but you wouldn't even bother to sample the nodes? Yeah, absolutely. Did you sample the nodes?
No, they did not sample the nodes.

Then I don't understand the intent of surgery. I think that's what we're—but here's the point. In the United States, this would be the discussion of this case even in our tumor board. People saying you should absolutely do surgery, some of us saying There is no, I don't understand the intent of the surgery, and you're talking about a palliative procedure, the woman has stage four cancer. It's a continental difference. It's a complete, yeah. It's a disciplinary difference. Yeah, oh yeah, yeah.
And I think medical oncologists, Anuja, you say what you say. And we've always got a radiation oncologist to like broker the decision.
I have to say, at MD Anderson, we would have done the surgery as well. It is based on the ovarian data. Dr. Pompa But cervix is so different. Oh my gosh.
You didn't even know it at the time. It was cervix. That's why they did the surgery, not uterine.
I know, but I have to say, at MD Anderson, that would have been—even though there is no data, and I totally agree, but it is based on the ovarian data where the debulking is important.

Actually, you can extrapolate from ovary to endometrial, because I do think endometrial—stage 4 endometrial with carcinomatosis, we do see some of those women cured with an aggressive surgical approach and chemotherapy. You can cure stage—but this wasn't endometrial. You did the surgery for stage 4. cervical cancer.
And that's what they thought. We thought it was cervical.
If they thought it was cervical cancer, I would never have done the surgery. That's the truth. I think Dawn has a point there. That's true.
I agree.

If my thought was a cervical cancer, I would never have done a surgery. If I thought that there was a concern whether there was endometrial, I would definitely have offered a surgery. But you're absolutely right. If it's cervical, then there's no room for surgery. Right? And that's a good point.

Yeah, so all of us are starting to say, you know, endometrial, we do apply an ovarian cancer algorithm with advanced endometrial. I am more comfortable with someone who has uterine cancer and carcinomatosis going to surgery than getting chemotherapy alone. This is not endometrial cancer. At least you didn't think it was endometrial cancer when you started. and you guys did surgery for stage 4 cervix cancer. That's a totally different thing.
Yes, absolutely.
Brittany, you haven't said anything. Do you want to make a comment?

Sorry, I joined late today. But I agree. I think, you know, I'm a medical oncologist, too. And I think probably my opinion would align with Don's in regards to the fact that I think this patient with stage 4 cervical cancer probably shouldn't have had a surgery. You know, it'd be one thing if there was an indication where she was having severe abdominal pain or they were trying to control bleeding and they couldn't do radiation, but that wasn't the situation it sounds like. It sounds like she wasn't very symptomatic and she was doing well after chemotherapy that I think, you know, I think here, we probably would not have done surgery.
Does chemotherapy prolong survival? For cervical cancer? Either, endometrial or cervical?

Well, we do. We do. Yes. Yes, it does. I think for metastatic disease, compared to historical controls, chemotherapy does have a role in prolonged survival. That's in the first line setting, like most solid tumors. So first line, you have a bigger benefit than second, third, and fourth line therapies. But we tend to continue to give treatments with the hope that we're extending survival. The problem with endometrial and for the large extent of cervical cancer, after you progress on one line of therapy, median survival across the board for any drug you give is less than a year. Yeah. And that's based on phase two trials, really. And, you know, the attempts at getting a US approval for a second line agent, say, after platinum taxane and endometrial cancer, I can think of two randomized trials, both of which were negative for a new agent. One was Nixabethalone versus Agent.

Just to go back to non-sexy chemotherapy individuals, I'm intrigued by the literature showing that ambulatory patterns of care for patients end-stage cancer improves survival a little bit. So I think for a resource-constrained environment, an aggressive move towards palliative services and ambulatory palliative services is a mandatory part of stage 4 solitary malignancy and should be focused on a lot, I think. Because it would free resources to treat earlier stage disease better.

I think this is a case that this is a patient that you know that you're not going to be able to cure. And chemotherapy, the response rates in chemotherapy in someone with recurrence in the middle of cancer after going through a second line of carbotaxel, I mean, there is very limited data. I mean, I would offer her a single agent that has low toxicity. I would think about Doxil. I think the response rates with Doxil in this setting is 8% to 10%. So that's an agent that it has low toxicity. It's easy to administer. And other than that, you know, I don't see any other, you know, you can use single-pane taxol, but she already kind of progressed to carbon taxol. Yeah.

Yeah, so an anthracycline, like Ali mentioned, would be our probably a second, is what we would offer her now. If I needed the response, I'd use Adriamycin rather than Doxil, but if she was doing okay and not, didn't have a lot of symptoms, I think doxil does make a lot of sense, and it's better tolerated than adriamycin. It can keep things stable, not as high of a response rate perhaps, but again, this is not a curative situation. And if she did maybe six months of adriamycin or doxil and then had progression, I would probably try taxol again. If she got it weekly, then try the every-three-week dose.

And I think the other question about radiation, I'll let Anish respond to that, but my sense widespread metastasis, there is little role for radiation. Especially with humans, she has multiple sites of metastasis.
I'm sorry, I didn't get that.
So with multiple cytometastases, if she has a lymph node, positive pelvic mass, I don't think radiation has a role, but I'll let Anuja respond to that.
I think it's only palliative. I totally 100% agree. If she needs palliative radiation, I would do it, but otherwise, I agree. She does not have a role for radiation right now. Definitive.

So Anuja, here in Boston, it's becoming more frequent that our preferred second line choice is Taxolabastin. And we're using that quite frequently on our patients here. And it's producing disease control that we don't have any phase 2 data saying how how durable the response is. But what are you guys using second line over there? You know?
I know it's Bev, but I don't know if it's with Taxol if it is with something else. But I can find out, Don, and I can email you.

OK. I know we're using Bev. I did a calculation on the back of an envelope. But for something like a 2.4-month or 2.5-month prolongation of survival, it costs about $100,000, for which you can do about 100,000 pepsimums. Yes. So I think for a resource, constrained environment, the use of invested in surface cancer is really not fully justified.
Right, right. And I totally agree with that. It's hard to justify it here in the U.S. even. But, you know, where it's accessed, that tends to be our go-to in the second line.
Well, Dr. Salmon, you've managed to do what I hope with tuberculosis. You've created a fist fight in Boston and I'm sure across the world. This was a great case, so thank you very much.

On subsequent progression after approximately six months of anthracycline-based therapy, paclitaxel rechallenge may be considered. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient. Presentation occurred in November 2025.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache; progressive loss of vision in the right eye over approximately 3 months; right squint; subsequent blurring/progressive visual loss in the left eye for approximately 1 week at initial presentation, with preserved ability to read.

[ diagnosis ]: Destructive clival-centered skull base mass. Two endonasal biopsies identified a fibrous lesion without evidence of malignancy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- First transnasal/endonasal biopsy performed in December 2025.  
- Specimens included soft tissue and osseous tissue.  
- Histopathology showed a fibrous lesion/fibrous tissue without features of malignancy.  
- Second endonasal biopsy showed the same result, with no malignant component identified.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain demonstrated a large skull base lesion centered in the midline clivus.  
- Lesion was described as T2 hyperintense and lobulated.  
- Partial encasement of both internal carotid arteries was present.  
- Inferior/anterior extension into the paranasal sinuses was present.  
- Mass effect on the brainstem, including pons and midbrain, was present.  
- Margins were described as well defined/well corticated.  
- Peripheral enhancement was present on post-contrast imaging, without central enhancement.  
- CT demonstrated a focal lytic expansile clival lesion with well-defined margins.  
- Cortical surface/cortex was described as largely intact on CT.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Two endonasal/transnasal biopsies were performed.  
- Both biopsies were nondiagnostic for malignancy and showed a fibrous lesion.  
- Despite biopsy, visual symptoms progressed, including complete right eye vision loss and progressive visual decline in the left eye.

[ current disease status ]:  
- At presentation, the patient was awake, alert, and oriented.  
- Right eye: absolute/complete vision loss.  
- Left eye: progressive blurring/visual loss, but still able to read.  
- Right abducens palsy was present.  
- No other focal neurological deficits were identified; trigeminal and facial nerve function were intact.  
- Disease remained symptomatic with progressive visual compromise after two biopsies.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Right squint was present.

reference_discussion.text: November 2025 with a history of headache and progressive loss of vision in right eye followed by squint of the right eye as well. All this for just three months. He presented to us with a completely awake alert oriented state, absolute vision loss in right eye and now he has been having this blurring of vision for past week in the remaining left eye as well but he's still able to read. Right side is completely In terms of vision, it is lost. However, it has right abducens palsy as well. No other deficits are present. Trigeminal, facial, everything else is okay. The MRI brain at that time showed a large aggressive skull-based tumor, confirmed with CT that it's a destructive clival-centered skull-based mass. So we recommended a trans-nasal biopsy first to look at the pathology. The first biopsy was done in December, when it was about two months of symptom onset. and that came out to be a fibrocious lesion without any features of malignancy. So we advised them to repeat another biopsy. But the results of that biopsy are exactly the same. And now the patient has been having progressive vision loss in the only functioning eye. And we have nothing in the two consecutive biopsies. The question to the board is for further plans. I'll move on to the scans now. Scans, may I tell you, we have a...
Okay, that's Dr. Shumaila... Yeah, yeah, doctor. So Nasser, we have Dr. Shumaila, we can ask her.
If you want any other sequence, any other view, let me know. I'll put it right away.
OK.

So we have a slide of T2 weighted axial images and we can appreciate that there is a T2 hyper intense lobulated lesion centered in the midline in the region of clivus and it is partially encasing bilateral ICA. It is showing extension interiorly in the paranasal sinuses. If you go to the next slide on sagittal images, So I can appreciate that there is an abnormal signal intensity area, but it is well corticated. It is causing mass effect on the brainstem, pons, midbrain, but still it has well-defined margins. It is showing peripheral enhancement. And same is appreciated on the next set of images, which are coronal. I would like to move on to the CT images. And on CT scan axial bone window images, I can appreciate that there is a focal lytic expensile lesion. More or less the lesion has well-defined margins. So I was just thinking of, since I knew the histopathology, I was just thinking that can it be some kind of fibrous dysplasia, benign bony lesion? which is expensile, causing compression on neural foramina and rest of the structures, but it is centered in the midline on Clivus. So that was the thought which was coming to my mind after looking at the CT images and after, because I knew the histopathology. It is partly centered on the Clivus. It is going interiorly as well, but it's all over its cortical surface is intact more or less. Especially when you look at these sagittal set of images, I can appreciate that the cortex is intact everywhere. So it is probably some benign bony lesion and as the histopathology already reveals that it is a fibrous lesion, I was thinking in lines of fibrous dysplasia.
Can I ask if there is any soft tissue ossification at all?

When I look at the images, the post-contrast even weighted images, there is peripheral wall enhancement, but probably that can come in fibrous dysplasia as well because because it is it is like the the characteristics of lesions are more evident since it's a bony lesion so they are better depicted on CT images instead of MR because on MR the calcifications they are not that you know the picture is not that clear in case in case for example if I see a fibrous dysplasia in a limb so I need an x-ray or a CT to confirm my bony details So probably it is some kind of fibrous dysplasia. It does not look like a chordoma. When we look at the surgical T1 post-contrast images, there is no central enhancement. The enhancement is only along the periphery. And that is probably the fibrous and the osseous because the fibrous scars, they also enhance. So the fibrous component is going to show enhancement.
So my question was whether there's any possibility it could be a base of scoliosis or sarcoma if there is soft defrostification.

Actually, the osteosarcomas, they have bony spicules, a lot of bony spicules, because they have a lot of osteoid material. They are osteosarcomas. So the osteoid material should be too much on CT as well. But it does not look like an osteosarcoma. There is not too much osteoid material. Any other question?
No, I don't think we can.
So, Nasser, do we have an astropathology report with us?
Yes, Nasser, that's what I'm sharing right now. Can you see it on the screen now?
Was the second biopsy also endonasal?

Yes, both the biopsies were endonasal. I'm sharing the first biopsy report as well which has a little more details because there were two specimens sent on this one. One was soft tissue and one was osseous. So I'm going to share that as well.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 48-year-old right-handed man; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Transient numbness and weakness in the left lower limb in 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent right parietal astrocytoma with malignant transformation. Initial diagnosis in 2015 was CNS WHO grade 2 astrocytoma. Following resection in November 2025, pathology showed astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4, IDH-mutant.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- First resection (2015): CNS astrocytoma, grade 2.  
- Second resection (November 2025): Astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4, IDH-mutant; Ki-67 greater than 60%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial preoperative MRI: T2-hyperintense lesion in the right parasagittal region, involving both frontal and parietal lobes; hyperintense on T1-weighted imaging; no significant post-contrast enhancement. Imaging appearance was of a neoplastic lesion without high-grade radiologic features.  
- Follow-up MRI (2022): Additional area anterior to the original lesion, more evident on FLAIR; surgical bed showed peripheral gliosis as FLAIR hyperintensity.  
- Preoperative MRI (October 2025): Interval progression compared with 2022. Previously subtle anterior focus had become more conspicuous. There was finger-like vasogenic edema, widening of the resection cavity on T2-weighted imaging, T1 hypo- to isointense signal, and significant thick nodular solid post-contrast enhancement along the medial parasagittal region with inner wall nodularity. The prior surgical bed and adjacent lesion appeared coalescent into a solid-cystic lesion. Vasogenic edema had progressed with extension into the frontal lobe.  
- Postoperative MRI after second surgery (November 2025): Postsurgical hemorrhagic change within the surgical bed and residual patchy contrast enhancement, including enhancement near the falx; residual vasogenic edema remained. Most of the lesion had been resected.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-mutant astrocytoma on 2025 histopathology.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2015: Surgical resection of right parietal astrocytoma.  
- 2016: Radiation therapy, 30 fractions.  
- Clinical course after initial treatment: remained clinically well for several years; last available interval MRI before recurrence was in 2022; no additional treatment was given between prior radiation and presentation in 2025.  
- November 2025: NNG-guided right parietal awake craniotomy with resection of recurrent lesion. Postoperative imaging showed residual patchy enhancing disease.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative state after second resection in November 2025 with residual enhancing tumor in the surgical bed and persistent vasogenic edema.

[ other clinical data ]: This was the first presentation to the current treating institution in October 2025.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old postmenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic recurrence of left breast carcinoma with lung, liver, nodal, skeletal, and central nervous system involvement after prior curative-intent treatment.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast carcinoma, initially staged clinically as cT3N1M0. Metastatic recurrent disease was identified in March 2025, involving bilateral lungs, liver, mediastinal/sternal nodal disease, skeleton, and brain/pituitary-sellar region.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial breast malignancy was reported as invasive ductal carcinoma. Following left modified radical mastectomy, pathological stage was ypT1bN1a. No biopsy of metastatic lesions was performed at recurrence.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- During surveillance after completion of adjuvant therapy, PET-CT had been performed at 3-month intervals.  
- After a disease-free interval of approximately 1 year and 3 months, metastatic recurrence was detected in March 2025.  
- PET-CT/imaging at recurrence showed multiple bilateral lung nodules, including a right lower lobe lung lesion measuring 5 × 4 cm; metastatic lesions in both lobes of the liver; mediastinal/sternal lymph node involvement; skeletal lesions; a nodular suprasellar lesion; and bulky pituitary gland.  
- MRI brain demonstrated an enhancing sellar mass involving the hypothalamus and contacting the optic chiasm; radiologic impression favored metastasis rather than pituitary adenoma.  
- Repeat MRI after 1 cycle of ado-trastuzumab emtansine showed a new lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere, in addition to the sellar lesion.  
- Stereotactic radiosurgery was delivered to the sellar and right cerebellar lesions in 5 fractions to 25 Gy.  
- After 6 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, response PET-CT showed complete metabolic response of all lesions, including brain lesions.  
- After 10 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, MRI performed following seizure episodes showed multiple new small nodular lesions in the cerebellum, brainstem, cerebral hemispheres, and thalamus.  
- At the time of reporting, repeat PET-CT and MRI for response assessment after 12 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan had been planned but not yet performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No next-generation sequencing had been performed. No liquid biopsy results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy: 4 cycles of TCHP (docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab, pertuzumab), with clinical partial response.

- Subsequent systemic therapy: trastuzumab deruxtecan was started at 300 mg; 6 cycles were administered, followed by complete metabolic response on PET-CT.
