- Supportive treatment after seizures included antiepileptic therapy and blood glucose control.

[ current disease status ]: After 6 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, there had been complete metabolic response of systemic and intracranial lesions on PET-CT. After 10 cycles, MRI demonstrated new multifocal intracranial lesions in the cerebellum, brainstem, cerebral hemispheres, and thalamus, with no contemporaneous extracranial response assessment available. The patient had completed 12 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, and repeat PET-CT and MRI were pending.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Two seizure episodes occurred the day after cycle 10 of trastuzumab deruxtecan.  
- Apart from seizures, no other neurologic symptoms were reported at that time.  
- Reduction of trastuzumab deruxtecan dose from 300 mg to 200 mg was due to financial constraints.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male. Past medical history included hypertension and atrial flutter. Lifelong never smoker. Did not drink alcohol. Employed by the US government. Regular medication was metoprolol.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent right-sided epistaxis, facial pain, and new-onset right facial numbness for approximately 4 months prior to initial evaluation in January 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Malignant sinonasal mucosal melanoma centered in the right maxillary sinus, initially staged as cT4a versus cT4b N0 M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Endoscopic operative biopsy of the sinonasal mass demonstrated malignant melanoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a destructive mass centered in the right maxillary sinus with opacification of the right ethmoid sinus, demineralization/erosion of the right lamina papyracea, extension into the orbit, and bony destruction involving the posterior maxillary wall and orbital floor. The fovea appeared intact on initial CT.

Post-biopsy MRI demonstrated a large mass centered within the maxillary sinus. The lesion abutted the dura at the olfactory recess without obvious brain involvement, dural invasion, or intracranial invasion. There was concern for orbital involvement, with tumor extending through the orbital floor and lamina.

PET/CT demonstrated no metastatic disease. Chest imaging demonstrated no evidence of distant metastasis. No cervical nodal disease was identified on staging.

Follow-up MRI in May 2019 after 4 cycles of ipilimumab/nivolumab demonstrated persistent tumor with progression, including extension into the cribriform region and through the ethmoid roof, with increased mass effect on the eye.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mutational status was not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent initial endoscopic biopsy by a community otolaryngologist.

He subsequently received 4 cycles of combination immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab beginning in January 2019. Follow-up imaging after 3-4 months demonstrated radiographic progression of disease.

He then underwent combined open and endoscopic-assisted resection of the anterior skull base with infratemporal fossa resection and orbital exenteration. Reconstruction was performed with a chimeric anterolateral thigh free flap, including vastus muscle for skull base closure and fat/fascia for orbital reconstruction.

He subsequently completed adjuvant radiation therapy to a total dose of 70 Gy. He later underwent removal of the monitoring skin paddle.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial examination documented a fixed dilated right pupil, reported as a lifelong abnormality following childhood facial trauma from a baseball bat. Vision in the right eye was intact at presentation. Extraocular movements were intact. No obvious mass was seen on anterior rhinoscopy. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present. No cerebrospinal fluid leak was present at initial evaluation.

[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Ovarian carcinoma, initially diagnosed in July 2023; subsequent biochemical and radiologic relapse identified in March 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade serous carcinoma of bilateral ovaries, FIGO stage IIIA after interval cytoreduction; ypT3aN0.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy with immunohistochemistry was suggestive of serous adenocarcinoma. Postoperative histopathological examination after interval cytoreduction and HIPEC showed high-grade serous carcinoma involving both ovaries. Omentum showed tumor deposit.

[ imaging findings ]: After four cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin, follow-up imaging showed complete response. In March 2025, imaging demonstrated liver metastases. After six cycles of gemcitabine-cisplatin completed in July 2025, follow-up PET showed complete response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Initial germline BRCA testing showed a BRCA2 variant of uncertain significance. Hereditary cancer deletion/duplication analysis by digital MLPA detected no pathogenic or likely pathogenic deletions or duplications. HRD testing was negative. Tumor/somatic BRCA testing again showed a BRCA2 variant of uncertain significance.

[ laboratory results ]: In March 2025, CA-125 was elevated/increasing.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received four cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin after initial diagnosis, with complete response on follow-up imaging. Subsequently underwent interval cytoreduction with HIPEC. Received two additional cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin postoperatively. Was on regular follow-up from February 2024. Following relapse with rising CA-125 and liver metastases in March 2025, received six cycles of gemcitabine-cisplatin through July 2025. Follow-up PET after gemcitabine-cisplatin showed complete response.

[ current disease status ]: Complete metabolic/radiologic response on follow-up PET after completion of six cycles of gemcitabine-cisplatin in July 2025.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history was positive for breast cancer in a maternal aunt diagnosed at age 60 years.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old man; retired iron worker. Tobacco exposure exceeded 50 pack-years. Occupational history included prior employment at a nuclear reactor. Past medical history was not otherwise detailed.

[ chief complaint ]: Dysphagia for approximately 1 year.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the supraglottic larynx/epiglottis, clinically staged as cT1N0M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial direct laryngoscopy with biopsy performed externally showed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the epiglottis. Following transoral resection, final pathology showed pT1 disease with negative margins and no adverse pathologic features. Additional specimens taken from the base of the epiglottis on the right and left were negative on frozen section and permanent section, showing only minor salivary gland tissue. Bilateral neck dissection yielded 37 negative lymph nodes.

[ imaging findings ]: External CT neck was reported as normal, with no lymphadenopathy and no reported laryngeal lesion. Review of the CT demonstrated a lesion involving the mid-epiglottis, extending toward the tip. CT chest showed emphysema and scarring. PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic activity in the right epiglottis, with no hypermetabolic activity near the hyoid. Preepiglottic fat was preserved. PET-CT also showed a lung opacity. No cervical nodal disease was identified on imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: External otolaryngology evaluation included flexible endoscopic examination identifying an epiglottic lesion, followed by operative laryngoscopy and biopsy confirming moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. The patient declined radiation therapy. He subsequently underwent transoral robotic supraglottic resection with bilateral neck dissection. Hospital stay was 4 days postoperatively.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative pathology showed pT1 disease with negative margins, no adverse features, and 37 negative cervical lymph nodes. The patient was managed with close observation after surgery. Endoscopic appearance at approximately 2 weeks postoperatively showed expected healing/granulation tissue.

[ other clinical data ]: Office and operative examination showed an ulcerative/exophytic lesion confined to the right lateral mid-epiglottis/aryepiglottic fold region with minimal lingual epiglottic involvement. The lesion did not involve the epiglottic tip, infrahyoid epiglottis by appearance, false cords, or true vocal cords. Vocal cords were mobile and appeared normal. Baseline voice was raspy. The patient was edentulous. Pulmonary comorbidity included emphysema, and lung status was considered poor. Speech-language pathology evaluation had not been completed preoperatively.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Right lower eyelid melanoma inferior to the lateral canthus; lesion had been present for 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Cutaneous melanoma of the right lower eyelid. Initial biopsy indicated at least pT4b disease with Breslow thickness at least 4.7 mm. Final pathologic stage was pT4bN0, corresponding to stage IIC.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside shave biopsy demonstrated melanoma with thickness at least 4.7 mm, at least T4b. Following wide local excision, final pathology showed no residual invasive melanoma. Four sentinel lymph nodes were identified and all were negative for metastasis.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative PET scan was negative, with no evidence of FDG-avid residual or metastatic melanoma.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent wide local excision of the right lower eyelid lesion with 2 cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Reconstruction was staged. Temporary tarsorrhaphy was performed at the time of excision. Definitive reconstruction was performed several weeks later with an oculoplastic surgeon, including a Mustardé flap, full-thickness skin graft to the upper lid, use of upper lid tissue as a flap for lower lid reconstruction, and canthopexy. She subsequently underwent one additional revision surgery with the oculoplastic surgeon.

[ current disease status ]: Post-excision pathology demonstrated no residual invasive melanoma and sentinel lymph nodes were negative. No metastatic disease was identified on PET imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No prior history of other cutaneous malignancies. History of significant sun exposure.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Left anterolateral chest wall lesion at initial presentation; later developed recurrent disease with dyspnea in the setting of lung and pleural metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Skin adnexal adenocarcinoma of the left chest wall, reported as syringocystadenocarcinoma/syringocystidinocarcinoma, with subsequent axillary nodal recurrence and later metastatic recurrence involving lungs and pleura.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- September 2023: Local excision of left chest wall lesion showed adenocarcinoma.  
- December 2023: Axillary lymph node dissection specimen showed syringocystidinocarcinoma.  
- Nodal status: 19 axillary lymph nodes were dissected; 1/19 was positive with extranodal extension.  
- Immunohistochemistry: CK7 positive, CK20 negative, CK19 positive, TTF1 negative, HER2 negative, GCDFP-15 negative, mammaglobin negative, GATA3 weak positive in <5% of cells. Breast markers were considered negative overall. ER and PR were not performed.  
- Clinicopathologic impression favored skin-origin adnexal adenocarcinoma; gastrointestinal primary was considered and investigated.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline MRI (September 2023): Left-sided anterolateral chest wall lesion in the skin/subcutaneous plane, measuring 3.5 × 3.1 cm, with cystic degeneration.  
- Baseline PET-CT: No disease elsewhere.  
- After recurrence following adjuvant radiotherapy: Lung and pleural metastases were identified.  
- September 2025 PET-CT: Progressive disease with lung deposits, pleural deposits, and pleural effusion.  
- December 2025 PET-CT after 3 cycles of paclitaxel/carboplatin: Progressive disease.  
- Post second-line gemcitabine/cisplatin (after 4 cycles): Final PET-CT showed progressive disease.  
- At latest description: No local chest wall recurrence; disease was lung-limited with multiple lung nodules, pleural-based nodules, and left-sided massive pleural effusion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive NGS on archival tissue showed PIK3CA mutation with variant allele frequency 76.5%.  
- PD-L1 immune cell score: 2%.  
- Tumor mutational burden could not be determined from the tested specimen.  
- Copy number variation assessment could not be determined from the tested specimen.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Pleural fluid cytology from initial tapping was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- September 2023: Wide local excision/local excision of left chest wall lesion.  
- December 2023: Axillary lymph node dissection for nodal recurrence; 1/19 nodes positive with extranodal extension.  
- January 2024: Adjuvant radiotherapy to chest wall and axilla.  
- Subsequently remained on follow-up until metastatic recurrence approximately 1 year after completion of adjuvant radiation.  
- Palliative chemotherapy was advised at metastatic recurrence, but treatment was initially defaulted; patient underwent unspecified native therapy for approximately 8 months.  
- First-line palliative chemotherapy: Paclitaxel plus carboplatin for 3 cycles; outcome was primary progression.  
- Second-line palliative chemotherapy: Initially single-agent gemcitabine, then gemcitabine plus cisplatin; 4 cycles completed; outcome was progressive disease.

[ current disease status ]:  
Metastatic progressive disease after two lines of palliative chemotherapy, with multiple pulmonary nodules, pleural-based metastases, and left-sided pleural effusion. No local recurrence at the primary chest wall site was described.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Upper/lower gastrointestinal endoscopic evaluation was negative.  
- Repeat biopsy was not performed because the patient was unwilling due to pain and pleural disease burden.  
- NGS was performed on archival tissue block from the original specimen.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 86-year-old man; widower; father of two children; occupation: farmer.

[ chief complaint ]: Bleeding per rectum and constipation for 3 weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, staged as cT4N1M0 / stage T4N1 with no distant metastases identified on PET. Lesion was located 5 cm from the anal verge. Mesorectal fascia involvement was present.

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopic biopsy showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Colonoscopy demonstrated a circumferential rectal lesion 5 cm from the anal verge. MRI pelvis showed locally advanced rectal disease with nodal involvement, staged T4N1, with mesorectal fascia involvement. Whole-body PET showed no distant metastatic disease and demonstrated local nodal involvement only.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial blood investigations were reported as within normal limits. Hemoglobin and albumin were available; despite rectal bleeding, anemia was not present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior oncologic treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated locally advanced non-metastatic rectal cancer with local nodal involvement; performance status was reported as PS 1.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included systemic hypertension and obstructive airway disease. Regular medications included one antihypertensive tablet and one inhaler. No family history of malignancy or genetic disorders was reported. Baseline general and systemic examinations were unremarkable; vital signs were normal. Digital rectal examination identified a rectal mass. Comprehensive geriatric assessment showed independence in all activities of daily living, active involvement in farming, independent mobility, robust handgrip strength, normal 3-word recall, no documented cognitive impairment, negative PHQ-2 screening for depression, good family support, and no significant frailty identified. Additional findings included bilateral cataracts with minor visual impairment, nocturia/lower urinary tract symptoms, unintentional weight loss, mild loss of appetite, and constipation. He had received 2 doses of COVID vaccination.

reference_conclusion: The patient was considered fit for multimodality treatment following comprehensive geriatric assessment. For this locally advanced rectal cancer, the agreed approach was long-course chemoradiotherapy as the initial modality, followed by reassessment; if a good or clinical complete response is achieved, a nonoperative watch-and-wait strategy may be considered, whereas if feasible and acceptable, chemoradiation followed by surgery remains the preferred option. If systemic therapy is administered, treatment should favor single-agent fluoropyrimidine-based therapy such as capecitabine rather than oxaliplatin-containing combination chemotherapy because of age-related toxicity concerns.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 6-year-old female child.

[ chief complaint ]: Symptomatic local recurrence presenting with headache in August 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Right parieto-temporal brain tumor diagnosed on 20 March 2025. Initial diagnosis after first surgery was ependymoma. Following re-excision on 11 October 2025, the lesion from the right temporal lobe was diagnosed as desmoplastic infantile astrocytoma. Stage at diagnosis was documented as stage II. Performance status at diagnosis was 2.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial postoperative histopathology after gross total excision on 28 March 2025 was reported as ependymoma.  
- Histopathology from re-excision specimen dated 11 October 2025, site: right temporal lobe, was reported as desmoplastic infantile astrocytoma.  
- Immunohistochemistry: GFAP positive; CD34 positive; synaptophysin negative; OLIG2 retained; H3G34R/H3G34V negative; ATRX retained; H3K27me3 retained; BRAF V600E positive; ALK positive; ROS negative; pan-TRK negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Disease progression/recurrence was identified in August 2025 in the same side/right temporal region. Recurrence was associated with edema and no midline shift. Residual disease remained after the second surgery.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BRAF V600E mutation was confirmed.  
- RT-PCR confirmed BRAF V600E mutation.  
- NGS showed no fusions identified.  
- The NGS assay used was a 12-gene fusion panel and did not identify ALK fusion.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 28 March 2025: Gross total excision of the right parieto-temporal tumor.  
- Postoperative response after initial surgery was documented as partial response.  
- No adjuvant radiation was given initially.  
- The patient defaulted further treatment after the initial surgery.  
- August 2025: Disease progression/recurrence occurred approximately 5 months after initial surgery.  
- 11 October 2025: Re-excision/near-total excision of recurrent right temporal lesion was performed.  
- Adjuvant radiation was subsequently initiated/given for residual disease after the second surgery.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent right temporal/parieto-temporal tumor status post re-excision with residual disease present; receiving adjuvant radiation with curative intent.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbidities were documented. No family history was documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable left breast lump for 3 months, associated with nipple retraction.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced left breast invasive ductal carcinoma, stage IIIB, with axillary lymph node involvement; estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, HER2 negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. Hormone receptor positive (ER positive, PR positive). HER2 negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Axillary lymph node involvement was present. No other imaging details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HER2 negative. No additional molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- HbA1c: 8.2%  
- Estimated GFR: 45 mL/min  
- Serum albumin: 3.2 g/dL  
- Hemoglobin: 11.2 g/dL  
- Creatinine clearance: not less than 34 mL/min

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- No prior cancer-directed treatment was documented.  
- Hypertension had been treated with amlodipine and losartan.  
- Ischemic heart disease status post angioplasty had been treated with dual antiplatelet therapy, beta blocker, and statin.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated locally advanced hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative left breast cancer requiring neoadjuvant treatment consideration; not described as upfront operable.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Comorbidities: hypertension for 20 years; type 2 diabetes mellitus for 15 years with suboptimal glycemic control; chronic kidney disease stage 3a; ischemic heart disease status post angioplasty; osteoarthritis with mobility restriction; mild cognitive impairment.  
- Functional/geriatric assessment: Timed Up and Go test 18 seconds, indicating high fall risk; activities of daily living were dependent; instrumental activities of daily living were dependent; reduced social engagement; mild depression was recorded; borderline nutritional status on MNA; BMI 21; Charlson Comorbidity Index 7; taking 8 medications; potential drug-drug interactions were present; social support was good, with financial limitations.  
- Falls history: no falls in the preceding 6 months, but high fall risk was documented.  
- Mobility: limited in walking one block; used a walking stick.  
- Chemotherapy toxicity assessment: CARG assessment categorized the patient as high risk for grade 3 or higher chemotherapy-related toxicity.

reference_conclusion: For this patient with locally advanced, strongly hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer and substantial medical comorbidity, optimization of comorbid conditions should be undertaken before cancer-directed intervention, with particular attention to cardiac risk assessment, glycemic control, renal function, and supportive geriatric measures. Neoadjuvant endocrine therapy is favored and may be initiated while assessing fitness for surgery. Surgical management should be considered only if cardiology and anesthesia clearance are obtained; chemotherapy is less favored given the comorbidity burden and high anticipated toxicity risk. Ongoing geriatric follow-up, supportive care, and shared decision-making with the caregiver should be incorporated.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 36-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Right thyroid nodule with bulky cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, infiltrative follicular subtype, involving the right thyroid with metastatic cervical lymph node disease. Residual/recurrent cervical nodal disease and suspected contralateral thyroid involvement were subsequently identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the right thyroid nodule at an outside hospital showed atypia of undetermined significance and was suspicious for ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. Surgical pathology from the outside operation showed papillary thyroid carcinoma, infiltrative follicular subtype. Skeletal muscle was present in the specimen without microscopic skeletal muscle invasion. A right cricothyroid mass specimen contained positive papillary thyroid carcinoma, submitted in the context of margin assessment. Multiple lymph nodes were positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma in both the central and lateral neck. Histology demonstrated an infiltrative follicular-pattern papillary carcinoma with papillary-type nuclear features and colloid-containing follicles. Subsequent biopsy of abnormal bilateral level II lymph nodes showed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial presentation included a right thyroid nodule and bulky lymphadenopathy. Postoperative neck ultrasound demonstrated a remaining left thyroid lobe containing multiple tiny foci without a discrete nodule, concerning for infiltrative intrathyroidal disease. Ultrasound also showed two abnormal level VI lymph nodes with hyperechoic foci, irregular margins, and enlargement, suspicious for metastatic disease. Bilateral lateral cervical lymphadenopathy was present, including abnormal level II nodes with cystic change and echogenic foci. Neck CT demonstrated medialization of the right vocal cord, consistent with right recurrent laryngeal nerve sacrifice, bilateral abnormal enhancing lymph nodes at the level of the carotid bifurcation, and a small enhancing abnormal lymph node in the lower neck at level VI/VII. Radioiodine whole-body scan/SPECT showed avid uptake throughout the left thyroid lobe and uptake in lymph nodes adjacent to the clavicles.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Cytology/molecular assessment of the right thyroid nodule was suspicious for ETV6::NTRK3 fusion.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum thyroglobulin was 39. Thyroglobulin in lymph node aspirates was markedly elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: At an outside institution, the patient underwent right thyroidectomy, excision of a right cricothyroid mass, right central neck dissection, and right modified radical neck dissection. Left thyroidectomy was not performed. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve was sacrificed intraoperatively because of tumor encasement. After referral, abnormal bilateral level II lymph nodes were biopsied and confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. The patient subsequently underwent left modified radical neck dissection and revision/selective right lymph node dissection. Left thyroidectomy was not performed at that operation because of concern regarding the only remaining recurrent laryngeal nerve. A diagnostic radioiodine scan was then obtained and demonstrated avid uptake in the residual left thyroid lobe and nodal uptake near the clavicles.

[ current disease status ]: Residual left thyroid lobe remained in situ with imaging findings concerning for infiltrative thyroid carcinoma. Persistent metastatic cervical nodal disease had been documented by ultrasound, CT, biopsy, and radioiodine imaging. The patient had right vocal cord paralysis following sacrifice of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve.

[ other clinical data ]: Operative findings from the outside surgery documented tumor encasement of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve. The residual left thyroid lobe was described on palpation as very firm. The patient had expressed strong concern about any intervention that might risk loss of the remaining recurrent laryngeal nerve and possible tracheostomy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 48-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: In June, he presented with a 1-month history of right neck mass, right-sided otalgia, and dysphagia to pills.

[ diagnosis ]: p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsil with ipsilateral cervical nodal metastasis and ipsilateral retropharyngeal lymph node involvement; clinical stage T2N1.

[ histopathology results ]: Direct laryngoscopy biopsy of the right tonsil demonstrated p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a right tonsillar mass and a cystic right level II lymph node. PET scan demonstrated FDG-avid disease in the right tonsil and right neck mass. Updated CT demonstrated an ipsilateral retropharyngeal lymph node.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NavDx ctDNA was 32 at initial multidisciplinary evaluation. Postoperatively, ctDNA was negative on postoperative day 1.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: He was referred from primary care to ENT after initial CT imaging. ENT performed direct laryngoscopy with biopsy confirming p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma. He subsequently underwent tonsillectomy, transoral robotic excision of the retropharyngeal lymph node, and right neck dissection. Postoperative pathology reportedly demonstrated only one additional involved node in level II. No extranodal extension was described intraoperatively for the retropharyngeal node.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative ctDNA was negative on day 1 after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: Former smokeless tobacco user; had quit approximately 10 years earlier. Current alcohol use was approximately 10 drinks per week. No trismus was described.

Yeah.

Yeah.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old woman. Heavy smoking history. No reported occupational or environmental exposure history.

[ chief complaint ]: Right-sided epistaxis, epiphora, nasal obstruction, and right facial fullness. Symptoms had reportedly been present for approximately 2 years before presentation. No vision changes were reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the right nasal cavity/anterior nasal passage, with cribriform and tubular histologic patterns. Initial postoperative stage was documented as T3N0Mx. Recurrent disease later involved an anterior site and a posterior pterygopalatine fossa (PPF) region site.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial outside biopsy of the right nasal cavity mass was interpreted as pleomorphic adenoma. Outside slides were reviewed and were considered consistent with pleomorphic adenoma on the limited fragmented tissue available. Final pathology after initial resection demonstrated adenoid cystic carcinoma, cribriform and tubular types. No perineural invasion was identified on the resection specimen. Surgical margins were positive. Biopsy of recurrent disease later confirmed adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI skull base protocol at presentation demonstrated a 3.6 cm mass in the right anterior nasal passageway. Imaging showed marked enhancement. The lesion was not particularly T2 bright. There was difficulty distinguishing involvement of the middle versus inferior turbinate. No orbital invasion or anterior skull base involvement was identified on the initial MRI. Possible involvement of the canalicular system was questioned. A small cystic component was also described. After loss to follow-up, repeat MRI and PET demonstrated two concerning sites of recurrent disease: an anterior recurrence and a posterior recurrence in the PPF region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially underwent endoscopic and combined open resection, including resection of the middle and inferior turbinates, ethmoidectomy, dacryocystorhinostomy, and planned lateral rhinotomy to address the lateral nasal wall. Intraoperatively, bony expansion was present; there was no concern for skin involvement. Resection was performed piecemeal. Final pathology showed adenoid cystic carcinoma with positive margins. Postoperative radiation therapy was declined. The patient was followed for approximately 4 months for serial debridements and was then lost to follow-up for 18 months. After documented recurrence, she underwent revision medial maxillectomy, open ethmoidectomy, and endoscopic pterygopalatine resection, with reconstruction involving oculoplastic and facial plastic reconstructive procedures including a paramedian flap. She subsequently received adjuvant radiation therapy and completed treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent adenoid cystic carcinoma had been documented after an 18-month interval without follow-up, with anterior and posterior/PPF sites of disease. Following revision resection, adjuvant radiation therapy was completed. No later post-treatment surveillance findings were provided.

[ other clinical data ]: On initial examination, the right nasal bridge and upper midface appeared fuller and more expanded than the left side. Initial endoscopy demonstrated a right nasal cavity mass with fibrinous material/cautery artifact. Orbit was considered not directly involved at the time recurrent disease was evaluated.

reference_discussion.text: Okay. So this case, and I'll try to keep it brief, just being respectful of everyone's time, is kind of a little bit of a different flavor for a salivary gland malignancy. So we have a 67-year-old lady who came in actually to see one of our rhinology anterior skull base partners who had this prior history of some right-sided epistaxis. epiphora, and then some nasal obstruction as well as some right facial fullness. She had been seen by an outside general ENT in the community who did a nasal endoscopy and actually had done a biopsy of a right nasal cavity mass. The patient didn't have really any other associated symptoms other than listed above, no vision changes. She thinks that it had been ongoing for actually a couple of years prior to her presentation, heavy smoking history, but no other kind of environmental work-related exposures. So on her presentation, you can see the right side of her nasal bridge and kind of upper mid-faces, full and expanded as compared to the left side. This was just a clip of her initial nasal endoscopy, again, by a rhinologist. So you can see some kind of fibrinous stuff and probably some cautery artifact and whatnot, who knows from the prior biopsy, but that's septum to the right of the screen and then inferior turbinate to the left. So she underwent an MRI skull base protocol. And this identified a 3.6 centimeter mass was in the right anterior nasal passageway and just kind of benign versus malignant considerations. She also likely had a little cyst present. And it was really difficult to determine kind of or differentiate middle turbinate and inferior turbinate, but felt pretty confident they didn't see any orbital invasion or skull base, anterior skull base involvement. And this is just a still shot. I also don't have videos, I'm sorry, but just a still of a couple of different samples of her initial MRI. just capturing the anterior extent there on the upper right, and some of the orbital extent on the upper left. Great case.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 60-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Lung malignancy diagnosed in September 2025.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IIIB lung squamous cell carcinoma with mediastinal nodal involvement. ECOG performance status was 1. Comorbidities included type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. The patient was a non-smoker.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology was reported as squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT performed after 4 cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed partial response. No post-radiotherapy imaging had been performed at the time of reporting.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NGS on tumor tissue identified EGFR exon 19 deletion. TP53 co-mutation was also reported. Testing was performed on an FFPE sample using a hotspot panel. PD-L1 expression was reported with DPS score 15%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial treatment plan had been neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by reassessment and surgery. The patient received neoadjuvant paclitaxel plus carboplatin for 4 cycles. Post-chemotherapy PET-CT demonstrated partial response. Surgery was planned after response assessment, but the patient declined surgery. The patient subsequently received consolidation radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy were completed by March 2026.

[ current disease status ]: Partial radiologic response had been documented after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Following completion of radiotherapy, no repeat imaging had yet been performed. Clinically, the patient was reported to be symptomatically better.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old male; retired accountant in the civil service. Reported weekend alcohol intake of approximately six beers. Did not smoke.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive painless neck swelling of 3 months’ duration, associated with dyspnea worse when supine and dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Thymoma, clinically staged as stage III on the basis of locally invasive mediastinal mass involving major neck vessels. No distant metastases were identified at initial staging.

[ histopathology results ]: Tissue sampling included fine-needle aspiration followed by biopsy of the mass. Histology was reported as suggestive of thymoma. Detailed thymoma subtype/grade was not available.

[ imaging findings ]: CT chest demonstrated a mediastinal mass extending into the lower anterior neck/chest region and surrounding the major vessels in the neck. No mediastinal adenopathy was identified on the reported scan. The tumor was described as locally invasive, extending through the capsule into surrounding fat and involving adjacent vessels. On physical examination at presentation, there was a soft, tender anterior neck swelling over the lower anterior neck measuring approximately 15 cm in width and extending retroclavicularly into the chest.

[ laboratory results ]: Complete blood count, renal function tests, and liver function tests were within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The mass was initially considered unresectable because of involvement of neck vessels. The patient received cisplatin, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide chemotherapy and completed 6 cycles. Following treatment, the anterior neck swelling significantly reduced in size, with no palpable mass on current examination. Presenting symptoms of dyspnea when supine and dysphagia resolved.

[ current disease status ]: Completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy approximately 3 weeks previously. Clinically improved, with no palpable anterior neck mass and resolution of presenting compressive symptoms. Post-treatment CT reassessment had not yet been documented.

[ other clinical data ]: At presentation, there were no reported fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or other body swellings. There were no reported symptoms suggestive of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. No prior history of dysphagia, reflux disease, or other major illness was reported. On examination, general condition was fair. There was no pallor, cyanosis, or dehydration. Cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological examinations were normal. Respiratory examination demonstrated expiratory wheeze. No autoimmune manifestations, pure red cell aplasia, or other hematologic abnormalities were documented.

Because if you told me I have a 35-year-old with breast cancer, you've told me nothing. There's a lot of features that I would really like to know from that best answer. So the entire report is actually very essential. And then obviously staging from the beginning, which we already have. And for the purpose of these meetings, because people do not really know how to stage thymoma very well, you need to actually say what specific features on the CT scan put this patient to stage three. So you can actually pull out the staging of thymoma, stage one, two, three, or the three, just the three. and then, you know, black out or, you know, hide the areas that this patient had that made them stay today. That would be very educative.
Okay.
Any other questions? On this patient?
Yes, Dr. Achite? Yes. Hello. Hello. This is Dr. Ezura. Just a question for the general group. How was this histology obtained?
So, from what I can recall, we had an FNA.
Oh, it was an FNA?

They did an FNA first and then a biopsy of the mouse. On FNA you may not really be able to differentiate. I mean it's very abnormal for somebody to put it on FNA. It will just show some abnormal tissues with no characterization. So they must have done a core. But we really need to know. That's part of the reason why the pathology report is very important because it tells you what samples are taken, how many samples are taken from the specimen. and whether they use the, because you can actually make the diagnosis from just the cervical lymph node. You don't necessarily have to get, you know, have some guided biopsy or CT guided biopsy from the anterior mediastinum. If they already have some lymphadenopathy, the easiest lymph node to get to can give you the diagnosis.
Okay, thanks.

Any other questions? We'll be moving to number two. But for this one, there are several things that are unresolved. So Dr. Mwaniki will present to us this data, or at least send to the hematology group, to the hemo group, the pathology report, just a copy of it. The staging itself, the patient comes today, so we'll do other staging to see post-treatment, and then we can actually definitively say what is the best plan.

reference_conclusion: Post-treatment restaging with contrast-enhanced CT is indicated to compare with the baseline study, confirm the extent of response, and identify any residual or additional lesions. Subsequent management should be determined by the restaging findings in a multidisciplinary setting: residual disease would favor radiotherapy to remaining sites, followed by repeat imaging 4–6 weeks after completion of radiation; surgical resection should be considered only if subsequent imaging demonstrates operability without evidence of other disease. The pathology report should also be reviewed in full to confirm the diagnosis and subtype of thymoma, as this has prognostic and management implications.
reference_conclusion_quote: So then today, the best one of the things to do is actually to repeat CT scan and compare it with the previous CT scan to be sure that the lesion has actually completely resolved. If not, we see where we have any other lesions that can be seen. Now, from that CT scan, it's what you decide what to do next. Usually, the treatment of thymic carcinomas and thymomas is, you know, we involve all the disciplines. So you have chemotherapy, which you've already given. with what seems to be appreciable response at least from clinical and then they would probably benefit from radiation if you see any mass that is remaining because sick cycle is usually the maximum with you. You radiate the sites that are remaining and then after that once the patient finishes radiation you go for four to six weeks and then they'll require another scanning to see whether there is any other lesions that can be seen at that time. If there is now that is the time the patient is available to surgery. Otherwise, doing surgery without knowing where else the disease would be, it actually would not be good for this patient. [...] And then the other thing is that we need to follow up with the pathology because just reporting thymoma is actually not sufficient. You have to break them. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old male; occupation: lawyer.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarged right tonsil identified on evaluation; patient had otherwise been asymptomatic.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma involving both thyroid lobes, with aggressive histologic variants (columnar cell and tall cell variant with hobnail features), extrathyroidal extension into strap muscles, intraoperative tracheal invasion, cervical nodal metastases, pulmonary metastasis, and liver lesion described as consistent with metastasis. Concurrent primary hyperparathyroidism due to left upper parathyroid adenoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid showed bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma. Thyroidectomy pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma, columnar and tall cell variant with hobnail features, with 4 mitoses per high-power field and necrosis. Both thyroid lobes were involved. Primary tumor size was 7.2 cm. Tumor was positive for extrathyroidal extension into strap muscles. One central neck lymph node was positive. Two lymph nodes were positive among 22 lateral neck nodes. Left upper parathyroidectomy specimen showed parathyroid adenoma with residual rim of normal cellular parathyroid tissue. Tonsil pathology was normal.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT performed for enlarged right tonsil showed diffusely enlarged thyroid in addition to the tonsillar abnormality. Thyroid imaging demonstrated diffuse bilateral thyroid tumor with marked airway compression. Sagittal and coronal imaging demonstrated an enlarged left-sided parathyroid gland. Imaging showed a lesion consistent with a metastatic left level II cervical lymph node. During staging workup, a lung lesion was identified; CT-guided needle biopsy confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. A cystic liver lesion was described as consistent with metastasis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No patient-specific molecular or genomic test result was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum calcium was elevated at 1.42. Parathyroid hormone was elevated at 25. Following left upper parathyroidectomy, calcium normalized and parathyroid hormone fell to appropriate levels.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, left lateral neck dissection, left upper parathyroidectomy, resection of strap muscles for tumor invasion, and bilateral inferiorly based sternomastoid flaps for strap muscle reconstruction. Postoperatively, calcium normalized and parathyroid hormone decreased appropriately.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after thyroidectomy and neck surgery for locally advanced papillary thyroid carcinoma. Distant metastatic disease had been documented in the lung by biopsy. A liver lesion had been identified and described as consistent with metastasis. Clinical T4 disease was present based on intraoperative tracheal invasion. Gross residual disease was considered present after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: No compressive symptoms were reported despite imaging evidence of airway compression. No malignancy risk factors were reported. No comorbidities were reported.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, Jeremy, you're doing good. One more? One more. I think I'm going to rush through this because the only issue is at the end. So I'm going to go through the case and then we'll get some commentary. This is a 62 year old lawyer who was found to have an enlarged left tonsil. And a CT done to work this up showed a diffusely enlarged thyroid reported as well as the abnormal tonsil. Otherwise asymptomatic, no risk factors for malignancy, no compressive symptoms, no comorbidity. His serum calcium was elevated, 1.42. PTH was very high, 25. Spinal aspirate showed bilateral papillary thyroid cancer, and here is his thyroid cancer. It's very diffuse. It's crushing his airway. Here it is on the other side, and here it is on a sagittal view. The arrow is pointing to an enlarged parathyroid gland on the left side, and shown in the coronal view over here. This was a, sorry, I might have said left tonsil. It was his right tonsil that was enlarged. And here we have a lesion consistent with a metastatic node in level two on the left side. During his workup, it was found that he had a lesion in his lung and a needle biopsy, CT guided, showed this to be metastatic papillary thyroid cancer. And of course, he had a, a hypoechoic lesion, not hypoechoic, sorry, a cystic lesion consistent with a MET in the liver. So we went ahead and did a total thyroidectomy, central neck, left lateral neck, left upper parathyroidectomy with normalization of his calcium and PTH, resection of his strap muscles because of invasion, bilateral inferiorly based sternomastoid flaps to reconstitute his straps, PTH fell to appropriate levels. His pathology showed columnar and tall cell variant with podnail features, four mitosis per high-powered field. Both lobes were involved, 7.2 centimeter size of his thyroid cancer. It was positive for extra thyroid extension into the straps. He had one central node positive. He had two nodes positive of 22 nodes on the right side. a left upper parathyroid. Clinically, this is a T4 tumor based on tracheal invasion detected intraoperatively. So Zuber, would you give us a commentary on the pathology?

So, you know, this is a combination of aggressive variants of aggressive subtypes of papillary thyroid carcinoma. This is beautifully illustrated here is the columnar cell variant. It's called columnar cell because it mimics the adenomatous epithelium that you see in colon, in colonic adenomas. So it has that gorgeous columnar look. And also it looks like an endometrium. So definitely this is, this is an aggressive variant of papillary carcinoma. And on the right hand side is the, what is called the hobnail variant because it has nuclei kind of pushed to the edge of the cell. And also it has this very tiny micro papillary appearance. You know, micropapillary tumors throughout the body tend to be aggressive tumors because they can be very decisive, and they can really get into the lymphatics and vascular areas. And as known, these tumors are really have a high rate of BDAP mutations, especially VX600E, and they can also have TERT-promoted mutations, which is also refracted in histology, as you said, mitoses and necrosis. So Even if you look at the ATA risk, these will be more in the intermediate risk. And now some of these tumors, we do classify them as high-grade thyroid carcinomas because they almost act like poorly differentiated carcinomas prognostically, but they have really aggressive pathologic features. And here you can see there's, um, you know, microscopic extra thyroid extension. Um, it is going into the soft tissues as well as the muscle on the left-hand side. You can see the skeletal muscle, and this is actually sitting at the ink and this is the columnar variant. So it has all those aggressive pathologic features. Um, and there is the necrosis. So the necrosis is actually no-no in, um, in papillary thyroid carcinoma. So that is the aggressive features. And I really respect that. As you can see on the left-hand side, there is that pink area, which is the necrosis. And on the right-hand side, you can see mitosis. So whenever you see mitosis in a papillary carcinoma, you have to be very careful. And that's why I like to do sometimes Ki67 on them to really look at a proliferative index.

Before before you leave this slide, there's a very good. There's a question about this is reminiscent of tall cell versus tall fill features. A question about hobnail features versus true hobnail. And is there any association with FAP? I don't know if they're thinking about moreular variant or something different.

I don't know. I don't know. So you're correct. That is no. There is no association of the tall cell with the. with the FAP, but definitely for the tall cell, you have to have 30% or more of a tumor to call it outright tall cell. But if you see tall cell, you should mention it because sometimes the aggressiveness of the tumor in the lymph nodes and the distant metastasis, maybe the tall cell component. So we always mention it. And here is the parathyroid adenoma again. And this one on the left hand side, that's beautiful. The rim of which at the bottom left, you can see a gorgeous normal cellular parathyroid, which is forming the brim of that central portion of the hypercellular parathyroid.
Interestingly, his tonsil pathology was normal after all, and this was what set us off on the pathway. So that brings us to this part, which I wanted to discuss. Who wants to take this part on?

Let's start with Monica. Monica, the imaging, what can help? I mean, we're about to enter this distant metastasis. Zuber showed us the poorly differentiated thing. What do you have to offer that would help us?

Okay, well, I think this patient needs radioactive iodine, but prior to, at the time of TSH stimulation, I would also do an FDG PET because this is an aggressive tumour, so the FDG PET may demonstrate further sites of disease. But I think you need to get rid of any residual thyroid tissue and then you'll see if any of the iodine goes to these lesions, which may be demonstrable on the CT or the FDG PET. If it doesn't go to those sites, then you have to consider re-differentiation therapy, potentially.

Eyal, can you tell us sort of how you're thinking now, so the next surgery's been done, it's poorly differentiated, you know, all the gross diseases out there, you got distant mets. How do you begin thinking about sequence, what you're gonna do, what you're gonna manage? So think out loud a little bit there for us, Eyal.

So today, we do things very differently than we did three, four, five years ago. So we have to be really structured. First, we need to have a map of all the involved lesions. we have some local treatments. For example, for this metastasis in the neck, we can have stereotactic radiation instead of systemic therapy, if it's the major foci of the disease, what we call SBRT. And before we move forward and think about systemic therapy, we have to have next generation sequencing. We have to know what's the driver mutation of this disease, because today 10 to 20% of patients can have really good personalized treatments, RET mutations, in this instance, RET-PTC or N-TRAC mutations. So really, instead of all comers getting lenvatinib today, we start with genetic testing. We see how many foci we have. We see if we can treat locally. And if it's a progressive disease, then we see if we have targeted treatments. And if not, we'll use the all comers drug that we use, which is lenvatinib.

Janice, let me ask you, A.L. is dealing with the distant mets. Jeremy just mentioned in passing that there was tracheal invasion, which is not uncommon in these hobnails and that sort of stuff. Where do you, when you walk out of the operating room, say, boy, that's somebody that needs external beam radiation afterwards versus, boy, I'm a happy surgeon, everything is good? Not a lot of great data, but how do you do that, Janice? So let the rest of the team know when you're thinking about external beam radiation.

You know, I think that's the beauty of a multidisciplinary tumor boards and having the surgeons really give you the gestalt at the tumor board that is not conveyed in an operative report. Taking it off the trachea and seeing that the trachea is nice and smooth versus cutting into it and having carved it into the cartilage itself, two very different things, both of them will have quote, positive margins, but I'm obviously worried about the one that I know there is actually disease that I've left behind. So I can't stress enough how important having a surgeon at your multidisciplinary tumor board is to get their real impression. And I'm never happy until they're home.

That sounds good. Jeremy, how do you think about that in terms of, when do you call me and say, hey, we need to think about external beam radiation versus And has that changed over the years and how you've used it?

Well, when I think that I've left gross disease, and I think I have in this particular individual, I like to get an opinion from our radiation oncologists who are excellent. And usually they'll treat these guys and gals with both RAI and external beam radiation. Yes.
RAI before the external beam, because if you do the external beam first, the radioactive iodine doesn't go there.
So you give the RAI first, and then you follow with external beam. Yes. Are there any other comments about this? I mean, why treat him at all? He's asymptomatic.

He's asymptomatic now. He's not going to be for long. I worry about recurrent disease in the neck and, you know, depending on what you found in there. If we've only got one place in the lung, I've been known to just resect these big places like this, just be done with it, and still get radioactive iodine. I will use an FDG PET scan to help me understand because, you know, how much other PET positive disease is still in the neck or the chest. So the molecular testing, the PET scanning, and then I think as A.L. talked about, is there a localized therapy we can offer? If that's the only place in the lung, then I probably wouldn't put him on a systemic therapy yet if I could treat that one place in the lung with a surgery or a radiation or something. But if you find other places, so, you know, we're kind of guessing what this would look like in six months. to help us know what we would do now.
Mike, what's your drug of choice? Or what's your oncologist drug of choice?

We do it exactly what Eyal did. We base it off of the molecular testing. So we use a big commercial gene panel. And then whether it's BRAF or RED or NTRK or TRK. So it's all very, very done that way. If it's agnostic, then most of us use Linvima or Linvatinib because it's sort of a good across the board. All right, guys, we are at 8.59. I cannot believe you guys pulled this off. Jeremy, thank you for the wonderful cases. To the panelists, great discussion. Zubair, fantastic. You don't even need a microscope anymore. We just send you slides, and you can charge for that. That's awesome. Thank you very much for a wonderful presentation. Thanks to the audience, and we'll finish it there, stopping right at the hour. Thanks to all, and you can send your voting in specifically to Dr. Erkin's house. If you don't have that, email me and I'll provide you his email and address. Send him the votes in. So who's the, what'd you say, the most attractive one, Jeremy, is that what you said? Ansimous. Ansimous, that's pretty good, yeah. Well, I'm voting for Dr. Paseka and signing off. We're done. Thanks guys, good job.

Comprehensive next-generation sequencing should be performed to identify actionable driver alterations and guide systemic therapy selection; localized treatment such as stereotactic radiation may be considered for limited metastatic foci, with lenvatinib reserved for progressive disease without an actionable target. Given concern for residual gross tracheal disease, external beam radiation should be considered after radioactive iodine.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Floor-of-mouth swelling in August 2016.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left floor of mouth with synchronous metastatic pulmonary disease at initial staging; later metastatic involvement included pleural-based thoracic lesions and a renal lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy of the floor-of-mouth lesion demonstrated adenoid cystic carcinoma. Surgical resection of the primary floor-of-mouth tumor was performed; the resection specimen showed high-risk pathologic features. Because the pulmonary nodules were too small for CT-guided biopsy at presentation, one lung lesion was surgically excised, and pathology confirmed metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial staging CT in August 2016 showed approximately 7 bilateral pulmonary nodules, all subcentimeter, involving all 5 lobes.  
- Serial CT surveillance was performed every 6 months.  
- By 2018, the pulmonary nodules had shown slow interval enlargement, increasing by approximately 2-3 mm on each 6-month scan; only one lesion was greater than 1 cm at that time.  
- In 2018, imaging also showed a renal mass of uncertain etiology and pleural thickening.  
- By 2019, there were greater than 10 pulmonary lesions, with multiple lesions measuring 1.5-2 cm.  
- In January 2020, the pulmonary lesions had continued to enlarge; the largest lung lesion measured 3.5 cm. The renal lesion measured 4 cm. Imaging demonstrated pleural-based nodularity/lesions along the outer lung/chest wall region, including lesions enlarging over time and appearing to abut/push toward the rib. Additional fissural and pulmonary nodules were also present.  
- Approximately 6 months after local radiation treatments, follow-up imaging showed further progression, including increase of one lesion from 2.2 cm to 3.6 cm (>20% growth over 6 months), with additional enlarging and new lesions seen by 2021.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Repeat biopsy in 2019 for molecular testing identified a MYB-NFIB fusion, described as common in adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Primary surgery was performed to remove the left floor-of-mouth primary tumor.  
- Adjuvant radiation therapy was delivered to the floor of mouth after surgery.  
- The metastatic pulmonary disease was initially managed with surveillance only, with CT imaging every 6 months, for approximately 4 years from diagnosis because of indolent growth and lack of significant symptoms.  
- In 2020, radiation therapy was delivered to pleural-based thoracic lesions because of concern for current or impending symptoms; this improved the patient's intermittent side discomfort/twinge.  
- Radiation therapy was subsequently delivered to the renal lesion because of concern for future renal complications.  
- Radiation therapy was also later delivered to a lung lesion.  
- Despite local therapies, imaging approximately 6 months later demonstrated continued disease progression, with enlarging and new lesions.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma after a prolonged indolent course, with multiple enlarging pulmonary metastases, pleural-based thoracic disease, and a renal lesion. Disease progression was documented despite local radiation treatments, including >20% growth over 6 months and development of new lesions.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- At multiple time points through progression, the patient remained highly functional and largely asymptomatic.  
- In January 2020, he remained active enough to run 10 km and reported only an occasional side twinge/pulling sensation.
