reference_discussion.text: Either that or observation, I personally will talk about an upcoming case. I would at least push for radiation or advocate for radiation for that subplural lesion, the 1.2 centimeter. That is a high likelihood of becoming symptomatic either in the very near future or possibly even now, just based on that location. So even off trial, I'd consider radiation for that lesion.
Dr. Schoenfeld, I feel I need to stand up for the surgeons. What do you think the surgical perspective would be on this?

Again, as not a surgeon, I'll do my best. The surgeons always, I think, as Paul was saying in the beginning, there's some situations where we do, I think, really do try to favor surgery and that's kind of uniform in our tumor boards. And that's when it's a single nodule, especially if we don't have a diagnosis and it's an easier spot to remove. because then we answer multiple questions at once. We get a diagnosis, we remove potentially all the disease we can see, and hopefully patients do well, not just from a tumor perspective, but also from a quality of life perspective, in terms of a quick recovery. Um, we think less about surgery, the more nodules there are generally because again, you know, every time we're doing surgery, that's time on 1 nodule. We're not addressing the other nodule. We also shy away from surgery when we think that the recovery is going to be more challenging. Sometimes these nodules right at the chest wall can be a little bit of an issue because they're right by kind of the lining of the lung. and that can be a little bit riskier in some situations. But again, we would discuss, that's one of the important roles of the tumor board, because we would have a surgeon and a radiologist and usually multiple surgeons there to discuss kind of the pros and cons for each individual situation.
So there's some questions here about, are you always biopsying these lesions? Did you biopsy both before you would treat? Talk a little bit about that.

I think that's a great question. And in general, the 1st time lung lesions or bone lesions, anything appear after the initial diagnosis, you have the initial surgery. After that, there's a new spot that shows up in the lung. It's worth biopsying that to confirm it is in fact, to even consider molecular testing at that point. That being said, when there's subsequent spots that show up, we don't biopsy every single one. And in general, there may even be a lag time from when the spot shows up in the lung to when we find the stick and needle in it. And that's because we wait until it's a safer size. When spots are very, very small, there's a possibility we don't get a sample of it and we just get normal lung and have complications. And so it's a complex decision-making process that the multidisciplinary tumor board always talks about.

We don't just talk about treatment. We often talk about imaging and other management questions too in the tumor board. That's a great point. And so, after treatment for this patient, there were what we call post-treatment changes. Sometimes right after radiation, it can be challenging to kind of see exactly what's happening because of the changes caused by radiation. But we usually follow these changes over time. and the other lung tumors remain stable. And I will just add that we've done a previous study where we looked at SBRT kind of prospectively, either with or without immune therapy, and we really did show that radiation is a good local treatment where we give the radiation. It's just a matter of trying to select the patients who would benefit the most from this type of approach. So, I think that wraps up my 2 cases and so I will stop sharing and turn it over to Paul.
John, a quick question. A couple of people are asking versus proton. Can you can you comment at all?

Yeah, it's a complicated question that I don't know that I'll have time to do complete justice to. There's multiple different types of radiation that we give that might have some advantages versus another. Photons is the most common type of radiation that we give. And then there's another type, protons. Sometimes we think about protons, especially in the head and neck area. for a variety of reasons. Usually when we're treating metastases in the lung or in some other organs of the body, some centers will think about protons in specialized situations, but usually we do photons because we do a stereotactic body radiotherapy. And because of some of the uncertainty within the air, for physic reasons, we often would not use protons for this type of situation.
And I would also recommend anybody interested in the SBRT proton conversation, check out our 3rd webinar, because there was a good discussion among docs within that webinar as well. Okay.

So, this case that I'm presenting is 1 that goes over a pattern of years, and we're going to have a repeated discussion about treatment decisions, because I think it gets at many of these points we've been talking about. So this is a 47-year-old gentleman who had a newly diagnosed metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the lung. So to go back, just to keep this in perspective, it's August, 2016, and this person had flora mouth swelling. The dentist, very full, body age with an infection. Fortunately, this was biopsied and found to be adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left bottom of the mouth. At that point, just for reasons of staging, CAT scan was done, showed very many, I think it was about 7 pulmonary nodules. The largest was under a centimeter on both sides of the chest, all 5 lobes of the lungs. So it wasn't something we could just remove with surgery. in order to get an accurate biopsy, because they're so small, we couldn't do a CT guided biopsy. We had to do a surgery to remove one of the spots. And in fact, that was shown to be adenoid cystic carcinoma. So the question was how to treat this person with adenoids that was found to have metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma upfront. So, we chose to do a primary surgery to remove the cancer at the bottom of the mouth. And also, this person had, when they removed it, had high risk features. We looked at it under the microscope. And so the question was, do we do radiation to the mouth afterwards as well? So, what would you guys have done at Brigham, out of curiosity?

Yeah, first and foremost, I think we want to treat patients who are having symptoms to see if we could help. And so in this type of case, there are multiple kind of small lung nodules. Hopefully those are not growing too quickly. And then there's kind of a symptomatic area in the floor of the mouth. And so then it's always a question, you know, we're really talking about, in addition to trying to control the disease, what would what would provide the most palliative symptomatic benefit? And that's always a discussion with medical oncology usually or surgery about, you know, what are the options in terms of drug treatments? What are the options in terms of surgery? We do often consider radiation for these type of situations to try to stabilize or shrink the swelling in the floor of the mouth. The issue with radiation in the mouth can be that we're trying to relieve symptoms, but it's a tough area to give radiation to because it also causes significant symptoms. And so it's always a discussion to think about whether or not we should do radiation. So, I think in this type of situation, sometimes doing surgery 1st would be reasonable to kind of remove the mass because it's on the larger side. And then in patients that have gone through a surgery, who have these high-risk features in the setting of kind of small lung disease, we would think about them in some way similar to an initial presentation of a patient, and then actually talk to the patient about giving radiation after surgery to try to make sure what we call consolidate that local treatment and reduce the risk the tumor came back.

In fact, that's the same thing we did. We have adjunct radiation, as you said, to ensure it doesn't come back to the bottom of the mouth. and followed this person with a CAT scans every 6 months. And over time, I have pictures here and even as a medical oncologist, I think I can do this and please don't get angry at me. I'm not a radiation oncologist, but we saw a slow increase in these pulmonary nodules. Going up top here, we can see the small lesion right there, that white spot, perhaps that's the most prominent, and that was in 2018. And every scan, every six months, it increased by about two to three millimeters. Each time, asthmatic, and only one was greater than one centimeter. And six months later, as you can see in 2018, we were accused of having a renal mass, but it was hard to say, couldn't really say if it was cancer or not. And he also was noted at pleural thickening. So that's where the lung joins up with the outer portion. Once again, continue to follow his lung spots. We had this discussion repeatedly. This patient was very well-informed and very involved with the research area. And finally, in 2019, we decided to biopsy it again, just for molecular testing. At that point, we were looking mainly to see if there's anything we could do treatments with. And we found this MIB-NFIB fusion, which is very common in ACC. We'll talk about in just a second with some emerging therapeutics that are very promising. And so at this point, slowly increasing in size over time, What would you guys do? I think he had greater than 10 lesions by 2019, multiple lesions over 1.5 to 2 centimeters. Would you consider treating this as oligo and going for the lesions greater than 1 centimeter or continued after surveillance given less than 20% growth?

Yeah, this is a tough one. I mean, I think that typically Historically, 5 lesions have been our cutoff for what we think of as oligometastases. And even there, I think, once you start getting more than 3, there's some question. Now, there's also a question, maybe 5 to 10 counts as oligometastases as our radiation techniques improve. But I would say generally when there's more than 5, you know, we, we, we don't treat locally unless there's, we're worried about symptoms or growth in that area. And then we would have a discussion, I think about, you know, given that growth, you know, whether it's time to initiate systemic treatment.

Perfect. I'm glad we're all on the same page. We didn't commit malpractice. Sure enough, in January 2020, continued to increase in size, asymptomatic. Finally, as we saw, I think we kind of alluded to before, adenoid cystic over time increases in the speed it's growing. I think about this and discuss it with my patients. It's like a stone rolling down the side of a mountain. At first it's going slowly, but at some point it starts to speed up quicker and quicker and quicker. And what we saw was that these lesions were getting larger, but he was still asymptomatic. The largest spot in the lung was now 3.5 centimeters. The kidney spot was up to four centimeters. So it was getting rather sizable. He was still running a 10K faster than I could, which is saying a lot. This person had an occasional twinge in his side, but it was running six mile, and the twinge could be just sitting around. And here we can see his scans, once again, 2018 versus 2020. To make this confusing, the 2018 scans are at the top and 2020 are at the bottom. And we can see this is the pleural base nodularity, very similar to the previous case he presented. You can see a little bump here, and a couple of years later, this large lesion kind of pushing into the rib here. And similarly, we can see maybe nothing here, maybe a little bit of thickness. And once again, a bump at the rib here on the outside of the lung. Same thing, this little white speck. And now there's a larger white lesion, significantly increased in size over those two years. And then along this fissure of the lung here, a little bit of thickness. And now you can see definitely more nodularity bumps there. You can also see a small lesion that was present. You can't really see it now, but several other metastatic cancer spots just in that field of vision alone. So at that point, especially given these spots on the outside of the lung, per our conversation earlier, we already got to it. These were starting to be concerning for either symptoms now or symptoms in the near future. And so talking to radiation oncology, we pursued radiation to those pleural base lesions. And that actually did help this patient's twinge, still kept to the six minute mile, unfortunately. And shortly thereafter, we were getting concerned about the kidney spot, that that could actually cause some kidney problems in the future. And so we performed radiation to the kidney spot and eventually to a lesion in the lungs too. But despite all of that, about six months later, we performed scans and we could see that it was once again, picking up in size. Compared to six months prior, it went from 2.2 centimeters to 3.1. 3.6, so greater than 20% growth in six months, despite our local therapies. Still active, but occasional pulling sensation.

Can I ask a quick question before you move on? Yeah. John, they've irradiated at several sites. Could you go back if a new lesion showed up in a similar location? Can you re-irradiate that site, or does that change how you might do a treatment?

That's a great question. We often try to avoid giving radiation to the same site. There's some side effects of radiation that can be cumulative, depending on the total dose that's given. but it varies. I mean, it depends on the timing when the radiation was given, the dose of radiation, the situation. So I would say that's a really individualized discussion, but in general, a prior course of radiation to that same area, we can give radiation to other areas, but prior radiation to one area does make the discussion about future radiation to that same area more complicated.

So once again, pictures here to kind of put it in perspective this time. This is out of order to like we do in tumor boards. So actually 2020 is over here, 2021 is over here to keep us out of just paying attention. We can see that the lesions are increasing in size even within the matter of year, almost double. Once again, here's another lesion slowly increasing in size. And also we saw new lesions popping up. So what's the point of the story? We went from 2016 with the initial diagnosis of metastatic adenoid cystic. He eventually got radiation almost four years later. And finally, because it's increased growth, new lesions, that's when we finally started systemic therapy. So here's a person asymptomatic and we're able to just watch for four years with nothing at all and no impairment in the patient's quality of life. So I think this points to the fact of the multidisciplinary discussion and when to finally Choose those tricks out of our belt and it's also a complex discussion with our patients and, you know, in the end of the day, it's you all are very, you know, the ultimate decision makers here. But I think this is points the complexity around to some of these things. And I think it gets the question to about when is a medical oncologist do we do we reach for a systemic therapy? I think that goes into here. Yep. And so it's hard given the variable history of adenoid cystic cancer, how these grow in every single cancer is different. What we're realizing more and more is that we wait until it's picked up that disease trajectory when it's growing faster and faster, at least increasing in size by 20%. within six to 12 months, as well as being at least two centimeters in multiple spots. We can't just radiate those two spots that John's talked about. It's something that's many, many spots, and it's growing quicker. That's when we start talking about a systemic therapy. And our go-to, if available, is a clinical trial, because we really think clinical trials offer us a way to move the field forward and offer us something better than what we currently have. Um, right now targeted therapies, um, they're called, um, all these, what's called a VEGF inhibitor are typically our go to based on some clinical trials. It gets kind of complicated here, but I have some of the information shown here showing that we were making a ground, but still have some, some room to grow. Um, what we see with a lot of these drugs. Here are 2 typical agents, exitinib and lindatinib, is that tumors very rarely shrink. In fact, no growth is a very good thing. We're just looking to stabilize the cancer. However, what we're hoping to do is just stabilize that growth for some period. On average, with our oral pills, with some of our agents, it stabilizes it for about six months to about a year. And then we just look for the next tool on our belt. Immunotherapy has been tested, including by the Harvard group. And unfortunately, it hasn't been as effective as other head and neck cancers, but we're looking at different combinations there. But so far, it hasn't really made the change that we would hope for. Currently, some areas that are clinical trials are evolving. There's directed clinical trials for this MIB fusion I mentioned before. Adenoid cystic, when we started doing molecular testing, we thought it'd be like lung cancer or melanoma, where there's a very specific mutation. We could use a pill and it would reverse the cancer and get rid of it right away. Unfortunately, it hasn't been that easy. But there's now a fusion about 80% of patients, which there's several companies coming up with a drug that might be able to at least stabilize the growth in those patients. And those studies are ongoing. And so hopefully within the next couple of years, we can get a sense of how those targeted therapies will work. There's also some next generation kind of chemotherapy type drugs that are IV called antibody drug conjugates. The idea of kind of depositing chemo just inside the adenoid cystic cancer cells. And I think those are very promising in the next couple of years. But once again, these are all clinical trials. And for the first time ever, we have several clinical trials in this area. So it's an exciting time to be moving the field forward. So I think that's it for that case. We have one more, but I think in the interest of time, we could stop there if you want, Jeff. It's up to you.

reference_conclusion: The primary floor-of-mouth adenoid cystic carcinoma was managed with surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiation to consolidate local control, with surveillance imaging performed at 6-month intervals. Given the multiplicity of pulmonary metastases, local therapy was deferred initially in favor of observation. As pleural-based and renal lesions enlarged and became concerning for current or impending symptoms, radiation was delivered to those sites and subsequently to a lung lesion. With further progression characterized by new lesions and accelerated growth despite local therapy, systemic therapy was initiated; clinical trial enrollment was identified as the preferred approach when available.
reference_conclusion_quote: So, we chose to do a primary surgery to remove the cancer at the bottom of the mouth. [...] In fact, that's the same thing we did. We have adjunct radiation, as you said, to ensure it doesn't come back to the bottom of the mouth. and followed this person with a CAT scans every 6 months. [...] we don't treat locally unless there's, we're worried about symptoms or growth in that area. And then we would have a discussion, I think about, you know, given that growth, you know, whether it's time to initiate systemic treatment. [...] And so talking to radiation oncology, we pursued radiation to those pleural base lesions. [...] And shortly thereafter, we were getting concerned about the kidney spot, that that could actually cause some kidney problems in the future. And so we performed radiation to the kidney spot and eventually to a lesion in the lungs too. [...] And finally, because it's increased growth, new lesions, that's when we finally started systemic therapy. [...] And our go-to, if available, is a clinical trial

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with multifocal total-body bony pain, constipation, fatigue, and weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), pre-cabazitaxel, with extensive osseous metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET/CT demonstrated multiple bone metastases with high PSMA uptake and no obvious discordance on FDG PET. PSMA PET molecular tumor volume was greater than 1 liter. PSMA PET SUVmax was 31.5 and SUVmean was 6.5. FDG PET demonstrated metabolic tumor volume of 170 mL, SUVmax 7.5 at a sacral lesion, and overall SUVmean 3.7.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was 64 micrograms/L at referral, with PSA doubling time 0.9 months. Hemoglobin was 117 g/L. Platelet count was 121 × 10^9/L. eGFR was greater than 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2. PSA peaked at 65 prior to the first cycle of lutetium-PSMA therapy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Prior systemic and local treatments included androgen deprivation therapy, docetaxel, enzalutamide, and radiotherapy to the thoracic spine for pain control. The patient was subsequently treated on the LuCAB trial with lutetium-PSMA therapy.

[ current disease status ]: ECOG performance status was 1–2 at referral. The patient had symptomatic high-volume bone-predominant metastatic disease prior to lutetium-PSMA therapy.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had been a construction worker. Opioid analgesia had been required for cancer-related pain. Constipation was present.

reference_discussion.text: Excellent, so case number one. So this is a 69-year-old with MCRPC, pre-cabazitaxel, has had, already had ADT, docetaxel, endalidomide, and radiotherapy for pain control to the thoracic spine. He's got multifocal, so total body bony pain. He's got a problem with constipation, fatigue, weight loss, ECO 1 to 2, doesn't sound very comfortable. PSA is currently 64 micrograms per liter, with a doubling time of, a very rapid doubling time, .9 months, and he's been referred for consideration of next treatment, including potential of lutetium PSMA.
Louise, can I ask you, how do you do your, something really simple, how do you calculate your PSA doubling times?
You're asking Louise Emmett or Louise Costas?
You're trying to duck the question.
Exactly what I'm trying to do when I think about the answer.

I've got to tell you, most referrals don't tell me the PSA doubling time, they just tell me what the current PSA is. They sometimes don't even tell me what the previous PSA is and that's part of Liz's job screening our referrals is, Liz, how do you calculate the doubling time?
There's a website that does it for you.
I was about to say that there's a website. There's a phone app as well, which is very handy.

Yeah, there's an app from South America that I use for PSA doubling time and PSA density called PSAPP. I can't remember which of our South American colleagues developed it. You did, Luke. No, you didn't. But it was definitely a South American urology trainee, I think. So we use that all the time, PSAPP.
I think we use the MSKCC website. It's very convenient and quick.

I think practically in clinic, the main thing we have to remember to do is reverse the day and month when we're putting our figures in so that we don't get the wrong date in. Because we format them correctly in the day, the month. Hopefully that's the most controversial thing I say for the session.
So these are the imaging, so we've got PSMA and FDG, just looking at that. And I might ask James. Yeah, we can do it together if you'd like, James.

Sounds good. First time I see these. Good. Very high uptake, PSMA PET scan to the left, you know, multiple bone metastases, a little lower uptake in the lumbar spine, probably an SCV mean around 8, I'll guess.
You're guessing 8?
I'll guess 8. Would you like to know for sure?
Just keep rotating.
I don't know, maybe 7.5. No discordance on the FDG.
Can I ask a basic question? You've put the image like this, but why didn't you do it like that? How do you choose how to window it?
Yeah, it looks much nicer.
Yeah, like some people, I think that looks better.

That's wrong. No. Look, I think that when we window it for the SUV-15, it gives it a really nice balance. So on the MIP for a visual assessment, we can easily pick out where our sites are and give some context to the intensity of the uptake. Practically, when we are reviewing these images in clinic, we might move it up or down a little bit to maybe pick up some subtle lesions we might not pick up if we were windowed for 15. But I think keeping a consistent SUV windowing and getting used to that is useful for repetition and seeing high volume cases because you start to get a sense quite quickly for what you're looking at within a few seconds of seeing the image.
Yeah, so I think there is no standardisation here globally, but we like 0 to 15, so you'll see on the scale, so that means anything which is black is 15 or over.

Yeah, perfect. So again, in our MDM, we like to put the PSMA and FDG PET up together. We often have a couple of screens, so we won't necessarily have the fusion image of the transaxial through at the same time, but it just allows us to explain the case in the context of both images side by side. And so as we can see with this case that we have a nice high PSMA uptake with no obvious discordance on the FDG PET.
And do you have the SEV mean?
Sorry, what was the?
Do you have the SEV mean?

Yeah, I do. So I can tell you for this PSMA PET CT that the, I will mention the volume for the PSMA PET, although that's not something that we're going to do for every case, but there's over a liter of molecular volume there. For the SEV max, we're 31.5, and for the mean, we're 6.5. When we look at the FDG PET, the volume there is 170 mils. The max is 7.5 at the sacral lesion, with an overall mean on the FDG of 3.7. But I guess, Michael, I've given the full gamut of stats for that case.

But... And I can tell you in my international travels, when I present some slides like this, I'm usually told, Michael, can you not talk about SUV means and volumes? Because we can't do them. So they're not of value to us.
Is there a visual way to quantify it? Louise?

There's actually two visual ways. One of them got accepted for publication this morning. So there's the visual PSG score where you can actually use the parotid and the liver and you can dictate whether more than 80% are above liver and parotid and that's usually reasonably accurate. And we also have something called the HIT score, the heterogeneity intensity score. Because one of the things that's quite interesting when you look at PSMA PET is sometimes it's really high variation. They might be suitable but there can be a whole lot of variation between the intensity between the lesions. not just because of size. And in fact, that's a bit of an adverse prognostic reporter for response as well, and it's one of the reasons why people with quite high SEVmax can also have quite low SEVmean. So, you know, there's a number of ways you can do it.
So I think these quantitative measures are very useful, and you should try to find some software so that you can do it in your center.
I agree.
All right, do you want to get on to
Oh, there's a vote.

Yeah. So now that you've had the opportunity to have a look at those images and you're part of the MDT with us, what would you like to do with this patient? Would you like to watch and wait? Would you like to start lupus? Anyone, any takers for chemotherapy or maybe some radiotherapy?

And while you're thinking about that, you're all gonna be asking this question. I can let you know that the bloods look pretty good. The hemoglobin was 117, platelets a little bit low, 121, and kidney function, EGFR greater than 90.
Kerry, what about radium-223? Is that not an option for this patient?
Sorry, what was the?
Radium-223, bone-only progressive MC or PC? Have we all forgotten about Radium-22? In many countries it's still available.

Nice if it was funded in Australia. Yeah, and I guess I'm still in mindset of being the therapy fellow last year and having high volume, working things through quickly and knowing that radium's not an option to us at the moment outside a clinical trial, so probably having to dismiss it at this stage.
But very few people here are from Australia. They're up there from everywhere else. They probably have Radium-22.
They probably do, but in Australia it's $8,000 a month. for radium, so yeah.
But cost aside, would you put radium as a treatment option for this patient? If you had access to lutetium and radium and they were both available and reimbursed, would you consider radium?

Personally, I actually think Letitia and PSMA and this kind of patient's an excellent treatment option. If this patient didn't have a target, did not have a target, then I think radium's a good option.

You don't need a target as long as you've got bright disease on the bone skin. I guess one question, and anyone on the panel can have a look at this. I'm looking towards our medical oncologist as well. So we were talking about the SUV mean being 6.5 in this case. Do you think that affects our decision making tree for how we look at this patient?

Yeah, definitely. So we're lucky, as Michael said, at Peter Mac we get very lovely detailed pet reports with all of those parameters. And I guess in this case, my concern is the patient's symptomatic and they've got a rapid PSA doubling time, so we really want to make sure they get the most effective treatment next. get their disease under control. And we, I guess, mainly look at the SEV max but the SEV mean is helpful for, I guess, giving some kind of indication as to how successful treatment with lupus may be. So with an SEV mean less than 10, I'd be a bit worried they may not have a great response. Also, I think their FDG metabolic tumor volume is quite high, almost. I think it was 170, so they do have quite a large burden of disease. So I For this patient, I think based on their imaging, I would be happy to treat them with loopy SMA, but at Peter Mac we do have combination trials as well. So this would be someone we'd sort of be considering one of the combination trials for to try and give them the most aggressive treatment possible and enhance their response.

Yeah, sorry, Louise, I'll let you. I was gonna say, so we had the voting, and that was showing 88% of people would vote for recommending for lutetia and pierce-may, 11% for gabasitaxel, and 2% for watch and wait.

I think Louise raised a really interesting point and if we go back to the main presentation, actually we were very fortunate to put this patient on the LUCAB trial and if we click one more over, we'll see a summary of their post-therapy SPECT CTs from their first five cycles and we can see that this patient's having a really nice response. In addition to our post-therapy imaging, I can tell you that the PSA peaked at 65 prior to the first cycle, and it's down now to 1.9, so a greater than 99% response rate there.
It's a question I've got. Peaked, so the PSA actually went up a little bit before it went down. That's something you see commonly?
I think, sorry, Louise is looking at a lovely little PSA graph in front of her, but I think the peak was just prior to the first cycle, and if I've not annotated that well, I apologize.
But it's a good question, and it's a common question we get asked is, is there a PSA flare that occurs after lutetium PSMA? That's a question for you, Louise.

I know, certainly with the LUCAV trial, we do put patients with more aggressive disease on that trial, so often the PSA does actually go up, sometimes for the first three weeks or even the first cycle before it comes down again.

So I'm not sure that we see a flare after lutetium PSMA therapy. I don't think that actually happens. A flare meaning release. I think sometimes the PSA trajectory is just so fast. If you've got a doubling time of 0.5 months, it's going up so fast that it takes some time to plateau before it goes down.
It's almost like it's doing that. Correct.
What about pain flare, Michael? I've seen that a couple of times. Pain flare after lutetium. So I think there is a clinical flare. That's a real problem. Yeah, yeah.

And that was certainly a consideration in this case. This patient construction worker was on opioid analgesia, having a lot of trouble with pain, and I believe had a little bit more pain after the first cycle or two, but subsequently feeling much improved now and getting back to some social hobbies that he was involved in prior to becoming unwell.
I think when the patients do have a flare of pain, they call Liz up, actually. What do you do, Liz, when they do that?

Usually I speak to my medical oncologist. But usually it also helps us with planning for the second cycle. So if they have a pain flare with cycle one, usually we can discuss whether we give some dex as a pre-med for the second cycle just to try and combat it.

And if we're talking about high volume patients in that first injection, they get a pain flare in a significant percentage of patients with high volume disease, and I pre-warn them of that if they've got high volume. The other flare they get is severe fatigue. So those high volume patients are particularly at risk of quite severe fatigue in that first six weeks, and they really need bathing through. I don't know if you noticed that.

Yeah, the fatigue can, I guess in my experience usually, especially if they're really high volume and they have a really big PSA drop, and especially in that first kind of three weeks, the fatigue can be quite profound before they start to feel better. And then they get a bit worried about having the second cycle because they don't want to feel as bad as they did the first, but I think it's just the initial kind of response that we see.
I'm sure it must be something to do with release of, you know, tumor necrosis factors and interleukins if you've got a massive cell turnover happening there.

We do need to get through seven or eight cases, but there are two questions in Slido, anonymous questions. Given the lack of OS benefit, would that impact your sequencing decision? So I think what someone's getting at is why not give carbazitaxel rather than lutetium in this patient? Arun, do you have a comment on sequencing? What would you suggest for this patient?

Yeah, I mean, look, I think that this patient was appropriate to treat with Lutetium. I think, you know, yesterday we were talking about this. I think the key is to try and get as many of these treatments into patients as possible. I think that going with Lutetium is good in this patient, but perhaps potentially, if you were just giving Lutetium alone, giving the SUV means a little lower, I would definitely, counsel them about the fact that cabazitaxel is next and we shouldn't leave that on the table if at all possible. Look, in the end, cabazitaxel has a survival benefit, but that was against mitoxantrone, it's old data. We don't use mitoxantrone anymore. You can argue about the design of the control arms from the vision trial versus therapy, but I think they're both active and life-prolonging agents, and if we can get both in, it's more important than the sequence, to be honest.

But I think there's two things that ultimately matter and it's not survival is one of them and the other one is quality of life. And in the therapy trial, we showed unequivocally that it was a very strong, favorable outcome for patient experience. And so symptoms with improvement with lutetium compared to carbazitaxel. So that's why we recommend lutetium prior to carbazitaxel. Case two, 71-year-old whose post-carbazitaxel has also had abiraterone, radiotherapy to the prostate, docetaxel, ADT and most recently olaparib. So really has had the whole kitchen sink and now has a right nephrostomy due to extrinsic compression. with a EGFR of 70, which is okay. A widespread pain on opioids, fatigue, weight loss, 15 kilograms, ECOG. PSA 60 with a doubling time of 1.5 months and referred for consideration of Lutetium PSMA versus best supportive care with no other treatment options available. I think we've done a, would you even do a scan? Is this patient too sick or should we do a scan? We've done a scan, so maybe we can look at the PSMA and FDG.

Given the low SUV mean and high disease burden, enrollment in a combination trial was favored where available to maximize treatment efficacy. Cabazitaxel should remain the subsequent systemic option and should not be omitted if feasible.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old man. Former occupation: engineer. Smoking history: 20 years, approximately 2 packs/day. No family history of malignancy was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent refractory cough and chest pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV right lung adenocarcinoma with nodal and hepatic metastatic disease at presentation. Subsequent progression included osseous metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy of the right lung lesion showed grade 3 adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 positive, CK7 positive. PD-L1 expression: 20%. Biopsy of a hepatic lesion was also performed after progression.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT chest showed a right lung mass with multiple lymph nodes.  
- PET scan demonstrated a significant right lung lesion with areas of consolidation and SUV 11.2.  
- PET imaging also showed a solitary hepatic lesion at baseline.  
- After 3 months of osimertinib, imaging showed marked response in the primary thoracic lesion, described as a very good partial response of greater than 80%, with concurrent development of multiple hepatic focal lesions.  
- After 2 cycles of pemetrexed/carboplatin, imaging showed disease flare with massive liver involvement.  
- Later disease assessment also demonstrated bone metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- EGFR L858R mutation was detected by next-generation sequencing.  
- Repeat biopsy from the hepatic lesion after progression did not identify any additional mutation; EGFR L858R was again detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line osimertinib monotherapy was administered. Chemotherapy had initially been proposed, but the patient declined it.  
- After 3 months of osimertinib, the primary lung lesion showed a durable marked partial response (>80%), but hepatic disease progressed with development of multiple liver lesions.  
- Chemotherapy was then added with pemetrexed and carboplatin.  
- After 2 cycles of pemetrexed/carboplatin, the patient had radiologic disease flare with massive hepatic progression and subsequent clinical deterioration.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic disease with massive hepatic involvement and bone metastases. The patient became clinically decompensated after progression on osimertinib followed by pemetrexed/carboplatin.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Echocardiogram was unremarkable.  
- Performance status was described as good at the time of initial systemic treatment selection.

reference_conclusion: For EGFR L858R-mutated metastatic lung adenocarcinoma progressing rapidly on first-line osimertinib, repeat molecular reassessment is indicated, preferably with liquid biopsy and, when feasible, biopsy of a newly appearing or progressing lesion to define resistance mechanisms and tumor heterogeneity. In the absence of an actionable co-mutation, the preferred subsequent systemic therapy is amivantamab plus chemotherapy rather than continuation of osimertinib with added chemotherapy. Immunotherapy is not recommended routinely in EGFR-mutated disease and should be considered only on a case-by-case basis when other treatment options are unavailable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidental thyroid nodule identified on carotid ultrasound; patient was asymptomatic.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, primary tumor 1.3 cm, staged postoperatively as pT1bN1a. Disease was confined to the thyroid on preoperative imaging, with one small central compartment lymph node metastasis identified on surgical pathology.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the 1.3 cm thyroid nodule was reported as atypia of undetermined significance / Bethesda III. Thyroidectomy pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma with follicular architecture and papillary structures with nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. Pathology reported no angioinvasion and no lymphatic invasion. One small lymph node metastasis was present.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a 1.3 cm hypoechoic lobulated nodule in the lower pole with interspersed punctate microcalcifications and a taller-than-wide configuration on transverse view. No extrathyroidal extension was seen. A rim of normal thyroid tissue was present anteriorly and posteriorly. The contralateral thyroid lobe was normal without nodules. No abnormal cervical lymphadenopathy was identified. No distant metastatic disease was identified on preoperative radiologic assessment.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing on the FNA specimen was positive for RET fusion, TP53 mutation, and TERT mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative thyroid function: euthyroid; TSH 3.8; not receiving levothyroxine. Postoperative thyroglobulin was <0.1 with negative thyroglobulin antibodies.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy. Radioactive iodine was not administered. She tolerated treatment well.

[ other clinical data ]: Medical comorbidities were present and described as reasonably controlled. No vocal cord paresis symptoms were reported preoperatively.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 24-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Symptomatic hydrocephalus.

[ diagnosis ]: Third ventricular mass causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Differential diagnosis discussed in the record included primary intraventricular craniopharyngioma, glial neoplasm/astrocytoma, optic pathway glioma, hypothalamic glioma, and germinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: No tissue diagnosis had been obtained.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain demonstrated obstructive hydrocephalus with enlarged temporal horns. There was a multicystic, heterogeneous lesion extending from the anterior to posterior third ventricle. On T1-weighted imaging without contrast, the lesion was visible within the third ventricle. Coronal post-contrast imaging showed superior extension of the lesion. The lesion showed minimal enhancement. T2-weighted imaging reportedly showed the lesion to be isointense. Sagittal imaging demonstrated the optic chiasm displaced anterior to the lesion. CT venography was reported as favorable, without venous limitations for a transcallosal route. CT showed no calcification.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Pituitary function was intact.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: An external ventricular drain was placed after transfer from another hospital for management of hydrocephalus. The drain was reported to decompress both lateral ventricles.

[ current disease status ]: The patient remained with an untreated third ventricular mass and CSF diversion via external ventricular drain. No definitive tumor-directed treatment had yet been performed.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion was described as involving the suprasellar/third ventricular region. The septum pellucidum may already have been fenestrated or deficient, inferred from bilateral ventricular drainage and chronic ventricular enlargement.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for management of newly diagnosed high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer following outside transurethral resection of bladder tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with concomitant carcinoma in situ (CIS); high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside TURBT demonstrated multifocal T1 disease and CIS. Tumor volume was not clearly documented in the operative note. Presence or absence of muscularis propria in the specimen was not provided.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed high-risk NMIBC after initial outside TURBT, with extent of residual disease not yet fully characterized in the available record.

reference_discussion.text: So non-muscle invasive bladder cancer is getting more complex every day. We have more and more agents. It's a good problem to have, but it's complicated to manage. So I wanted to pick your brain on some cases and see how you think through these situations. So let's say we have a pretty standard patient, 74-year-old male, average age for bladder cancer. Referring urologist does a TRBT. He finds multifocal T1 and CIS. Not really clear what the volume of disease is based on his op note. Patient comes to see you in the office. Can you walk us through what your first steps are?

Yeah so I think first things first when you hear high volume T1 plus CIS all of the bells go off that this is a patient who very much needs to have a thorough staging and evaluation so you really have characterized that disease and you make sure this is one of those moments where making the right decision at this point is critical because it will change that patient's clinical trajectory. So I think at this point the first thing is we do a path 3 review and I think I talk to patients to say at this point we need to look back in your bladder and make sure that all of the disease that can be resected has been resected and fully understand everything, especially if there's not muscle in the specimen. But I actually re-resect all high-grade T1 irrespective of muscularis propria in the first specimen. I just think it's rude. I call it a quality check. I tell the patients before I take them to the OR if I find high-grade T1 Even when I'm doing your first resection, four to six weeks later we're going back and that's to make sure that we didn't miss anything because of that historic data that 25% of people are upstaged. But I think also I want to be thinking about the prostatic urethra and I want to make sure that the upper tracts are staged. I do get a chest CT even though the likelihood of pulmonary metastases is low. It's more because I want to have a baseline so that I have something to compare to in the future if and when we get further CTs down the line. So I think at this point it's kind of start from scratch, do all the work, make sure you fully understand that tumor.

Yeah, I think most of us will have a low threshold to do a repeat evaluation. Let's say the patient did not have T1 disease. Do you do an office systole sometimes or are you still taking that patient to the operating room?
I think it depends on, I don't know what you think, Mark, but I think the volume of high-grade TA, I think high-grade TA, if it's a larger tumor, I will still often re-resect those.
And are you doing those with blue light?
If there's carcinoma in situ in that first biopsy, absolutely, I do.

Any other thoughts, Mark? No, I think Sarah and I see it pretty much the same. I don't routinely re-resect TA. So I'll read the op note if the outside urologist, and they're somebody I know and trust especially, they've done a complete TUR, it's a smaller tumor, then I might not re-resect that because there is some data in the BCG immunoablation setting where BCG can ablate residual disease. So if we think there's some residual high-grade TA, that's probably not a big deal, just give them induction BCG. I'm not sure you have to totally clear it. But high grade T1, obviously we're worried about the potential for muscle invasive disease. And so that obviously changes the trajectory for the patient. So I think resection is very important, like Sarah said, for all high grade T1s.

Yeah. Let's go through some different potential scenarios once you're in the operating room. And to be honest, I don't know the best answer for this. Let's say bladder looks really good. You see the prior scar from the site where presumed T1 disease was. Are you doing a biopsy of that area? Are you doing a full loop resection? Are you re-resecting the entire scar? Walk us through that.

So I honestly will usually re-resect the whole scar, especially if there wasn't muscle. If it looks like sometimes you have those sort of little dystrophic calcifications and you sort of have one area where it looks like that was truly where the stalk was and I'll cold cup that just to make sure I don't get cautery artifact because I do think a lot of times you resect the scar and you just get that sort of denuded epithelium and you don't get anything definitive. But I otherwise just like taking the loop and doing the sort of staccato method and basically I tell my residents it's like Mohs surgery and just shave it down until we see some muscle fibers. Personally that's my preference. And then I will often take like a satellite biopsy sort of right next to it because I think sometimes you get that sort of halo of CIS and I kind of want to make sure that I fully understand that.

Yeah, I think it's tough because we want to sample muscle, we want to make sure we're not missing occult muscle invasive disease, but a lot of the time these scars come back benign and we'll see a rim of CIS, but I think it still seems to help these patients. Let's say we find a lot of CIS in the bladder, you know, with or without blue light, do you think it's important to resect all of the disease or just sample some and let the intravascular therapy handle the rest?

I generally try to resect all of it. I'm not sure how important it is for CIS, but I think it's an assumption when you see something light up on blue light that it's CIS. It could be invasive disease. So in general, I try to resect everything that we see. Now there are those patients that have very high volume disease and they're heading towards a cystectomy anyway. I may not in those situations. I may just get a representative sample and the patient's really not going to go for intravascular therapy anyway because they have symptoms or they can't tolerate it or they've been through a lot already and now it's time for a cystectomy. So in those cases, I may not, but generally I try to.

Philosophically to me, it kind of makes sense to try to get rid of as much cancer as we can so that the intravascular therapy works, but there's definitely no answer. I don't think a trial has actually assessed that rigorously. Now, I have seen this, sometimes it can be a little frustrating. Let's say we didn't do an office cysto, you go to the operating room, you see a rim of tumor around the ureteral orifice. You're not totally sure if there's more going inside. What do you do then?

I think that's a really challenging situation because the way that you manage the UO has implications for that patient's bladder and upper tract health. My practice has been to resect on cut and not cauterize and basically just take the UO. I was having a conversation with somebody this morning actually about this about do you stent or not stent and my practice has been to try to avoid stenting but then if it looks like it's really narrow I will sometimes put a stent up just to try to avoid that stenotic UO situation because that can be a really tough problem later on if that scars down and you end up threatening the function of the upper tract and the drainage and then you're in there trying to sort of resect to find the UO. That can be really hard. But in general, I know the level of the evidence for sort of the risk of upper tract seeding with a stent after an immediate resection. It's low, it's retrospective data, but I still try to avoid seeding the upper tract if I can.
I cringe a little bit at putting a ureter scope in there, but that would be a definitive way to rule out the extent of upper tract involvement.

If there is tumor coming out of the ureter, I generally will scope them just to understand what's going on. But it's tricky. And so the upper tract guidelines do say that though if we have concomitant upper tract and lower tract disease, generally what I do is I will take care of everything. I like to take care of the lower tract first and then I will rinse the bladder a couple of times just on continuous flows. I mean you hope that there isn't anything floating around. and then I'll do my upper tract work. In general, that's how I've approached it. But I know that some people say, no, you should do the upper tract first and then clear the lower tracts and you avoid the bleeding. So I think there's really not a perfect answer. You sort of have to do what you're most comfortable with.

Definitely case by case. The stent issue is a tough one because I've had stenotic ureters with stenting or without stenting. I don't think there's one right answer. I've asked some of my recon colleagues and there's no consensus on that.

And I think that the intravascular therapy probably causes also a fair amount of irritation and I worry sometimes that that actually exacerbates if a ureter is going to become stenotic that can sometimes make it worse. I've seen that. So it's tricky.

Now let's say you left a stent and you're planning on giving intravascular therapy. Are you going to leave that stent in through the induction course to try to get a little bit of treatment up there or not an important consideration?

I wanted to hear what you think about this, but my personal reading of the literature is that that doesn't really work terribly well. I think that in training we did that, but based on some of the animal studies that have looked at sort of transfer of like dyed intravascular therapy, we just don't get the kind of treatment in the upper tract that we would like to think we get with reflux from the bladder. So, especially if, I mean, if there's upper tract disease, I'm going to treat that upper tract disease according to what it needs. If the upper tract is not involved, then that stent is in there just usually for five days and I'll leave it on a tether so that they can take it out at home and avoid another procedure in the office.

My thought process is sometimes there's some low-volume papillary disease or CIS that kind of retrograde ascends up the ureter and maybe that stent will let some treatment affect that, but it's definitely a soft call. All right, Mark, so this patient comes to the office, you've done the full restaging, let's say maybe just find a little bit of CIS. Are you using any biomarkers to help guide the next steps, or are you just going based on the PATH report?

Going just based upon the PATH report. Saw the data at the AUA for the Vesta, I think the Valor Labs, data for GEMDOSI versus BCG. In the biomarker-selected population, GEMDOSI did better than BCG, which, you know, I think we were joking about this yesterday, that might be the first time GEMDOSI took down BCG. in any setting, you know? I am trying to get that process up and running, that workflow up and running at Mayo and Arizona, but I'm not routinely using any biomarkers at this stage, primarily because I'm not convinced that at this stage there's like enough diversity in therapeutics to really make a difference. I mean, we're going to be putting most of these patients on BCG if we haven't, if we don't, Tymdosy. So, no, not typically.
Well, good segue there. What treatment options are there? Do you think that's true, that we only have BCG, or are there other treatments you're talking about?

For a high-grade T1 with CIS? Yes, newly diagnosed. Newly diagnosed. I mean, so, I mean, we just, the BRIDGE trial just finished accrual, so we were very enthusiastic about trying to put people on that trial, I think, especially for a lot of reasons. One, I think that question needs to be answered, whether or not gemdose should be used in the frontline setting. But also in the setting of the BCG shortage, it was a way of getting more people treatment. You know, kudos to Max Cates and everyone who did that and ran that study. But in general, if it's a high-grade T1 with carcinoma in situ, I'm having the conversation about afferent cystectomy versus BCG. And at this point, I don't think we have anything else that I would consider in the frontline setting.
Do you think about clinical trials or, you know, the new CREST data is interesting as well?

Yeah. I mean, well, and we'll see, you know, once that's ready for primetime, I think that's going to be a conversation we will be having. But at least at this point for BCG Naive, we don't personally have any trials open at our shop in that space. Obviously, I am one of those people who believes very strongly that if there's a trial available, we should be talking to patients about it. But until we have our next round, right now, it's BCG or bust.
Yep. All right. Well, let's say, you know, you don't have BCG, complete shortage. What's your next step in that situation?

Like Sarah said, usually a trial. So we were enrolling on Keynote 676 and Patapsco. We weren't enrolling on Crest, but you know, for this, somebody who has a high grade T1, and concomitant CIS on re-resection, obviously very high-risk phenotype. This is somebody that I would consider an iotherapy combination with BCG clinical trial concept as a hedge against metastatic disease. You know, there's a not non-zero chance of metastatic disease in a patient like this, and so if they were young and healthy and otherwise willing to take on the systemic risks of iotherapy, I would offer that. I'm not necessarily saying I would recommend it, but But that's certainly an option. Otherwise, yeah, BCG would be the go-to for somebody with residual CIS. If we're out of BCG, then we're, you know, then we're kind of stuck. Because, you know, Max had some really nice phase 2 data for T1 patients, predominantly T1 patients in the BCG naive setting. I think a 25 patient cohort that he published last year, the year before, and the CR rate was impressive, like 90 plus percent at a year or something. So, Jim Dosey was insured based upon that phase 2 trial. But, you know, that's problematic for some people, you know, given dosetaxel and there's challenges there too. So, I'd have that conversation with the patient and say, it's going to be a long day in the clinic and it's two chemotherapies and it's not easy sometimes. And so, you know, it would be a dialogue, but that would probably be where I would ultimately land if they weren't a candidate for cystectomy, if they declined a clinical trial and there's no BCG available.
I guess in your mind, is the data for GEMDOSI compelling enough that you think that's a reasonable choice rather than, you know, referring to another center that has BCG?

Great question. I think Max's GEMDOSI data is compelling in that phase two trial they published, and obviously we're awaiting the results of Bridge. But yeah, I mean, because that was, I mean, there was a lot of T1 patients in that trial. And so, and this patient has residual CIS, you know, that's probably shouldering the original lesion. It's not like the rest of the bladder looked okay. This patient's fairly young, 74, hasn't tried any other intravascular therapy, so. Yeah, I am leaning for this patient, I'm leaning a little bit more toward intravascular therapy. And yeah, if I knew if there was somebody in town that I knew had BCG, which is not the case for me, then I would then I would definitely make a referral for consideration of BCG. But I don't, I wouldn't hesitate to do gym dosi in this setting.

Yeah, I find the GEMDOSI data to be relatively compelling, and we have some good retrospective outcomes, and the prospective data is really lining up with that. So I personally have zero qualms giving GEMDOSI in that situation. But of course, if you have BCG, that's a level one recommendation that those patients can get. So let's say, you know, BCG shortage happens, patient gets gemdosy, maintenance for six months, they recur. Now we have BCG, patient gets induction maintenance of BCG, another small recurrence with CIS now, bladder function starting to get a little bit worse, some more nocturia, some more frequency. How do you think through the next options for this patient?

So it's CIS only recurrence within six months of induction BCG in a patient who's already had induction and maintenance gem dosing. And at this point, you know, I think this is where you start to have a very thoughtful conversation with that patient not only about the now but about the future. And this is where having a really good relationship with your patients I think helps. And the one thing is this patient would be sitting down and it would not be the first time I would be bringing up cystectomy. So I bring up cystectomy early and often, not because I want people to have a cystectomy right away, but because when it comes time to talk about it when they really need it, I don't want that to be the first time they're hearing about having their bladder removed. Because I think that it takes a long time for people to get to the point, especially someone who has non-muscle invasive disease, where bladder preservation, they come in the very first time and they say, my goal is to die with my bladder in my body. I say, okay, I can meet you there. But I want you to hear the conversation about cystectomy so that if we ever have to talk about it and we don't have any other options, you already kind of know what this spiel is. just because mostly that conversation is such a dated heavy conversation that I think it's a lot for people to not just walk away from completely overwhelmed. So in this situation obviously you know immunotherapy unless you can get to we can talk about with just a little bit of CIS I would have a conversation about cystectomy. I don't think this patient needs a cystectomy but unless the bladder function and their quality of life is driving them towards that where they're not sleeping, it's affecting their cognitive function, they're, you know, unable to do the things that they enjoy, it's disrupting their independence at home. So at that point, you know, I think bladder removal is a quality of life option. And the SISTO data could be used to support that conversation obviously that was recently presented at the AUA. I think that's very compelling that taking out the bladder in someone with BCG, unresponsive, high-risk disease, is associated with improvements in physical function and quality of life.
I think it's smart to bring up cystectomy early, and it's part of the education about the disease process. But let's say this patient's very motivated to keep their bladder at this point.

Well, the nice thing is we have options, right? So I think in our practice, we would be talking about notopharyngeal I think that now I will say that in someone who has a really irritated bladder, you're going to have to work to make sure that that natto stays where it's supposed to stay for an hour. And so you want to work on maximally controlling their bladder symptoms and the sort of spasticity of that bladder in order to get as much bang for your buck as you can get.

So just to interrupt there, is that a consideration that you're making for these specific patients? If they have a lot of tolerability issues, are you going to steer a little bit away from that? Or do you think you can overcome that?

No, I think you can overcome it. And I actually draw on Mark's data that was just published with the rectal benzodiazepines. I think that I've found to be very, very helpful. We also have BNO suppositories which are compounded locally that we can utilize. And then we'll just make sure that they're obviously on maximum antispasticity medications, whether it's an anticholinergic or a beta-3 agonist. And also thinking about hydration and just trying to optimize their lower tract. Definitely think about a clinical trial. In the setting of a BCG shortage, we are not using a lot of Vanctiva, to be totally honest with you, just because I think that we are limited, especially in our region, with how much BCG we have. So it's just not as much of an option. And I think the cost considerations come into play a little bit from a pragmatism standpoint. I do think though that one of the benefits of thanato is that it's a once quarterly drug. So you're not getting, you know, six weeks of sort of increasing bladder intolerability. You sort of, it's one and done, see back in three months. And I think that especially the real world data that's recently been published shows improved durability compared to even the initial study that led to its regulatory approval.
Yeah, those are great points. And do you have the same type of thinking about bladder symptoms and how you're thinking about these treatment options?

Yeah, I agree with what Sarah said. I think laying the groundwork for cystectomy is important for this patient. For this particular patient, I would probably do one more course of BCG. patient that's BCG exposed. If I could give a full induction course, I would land there. If I was really short, then another course of maintenance. But let's say he was BCG unresponsive. He got an induction and a maintenance. Yeah. And then in that case, then yeah, I would probably not give more BCG. Although there's some interesting data from Ashish Kamat.
Ashish's data.

Even in well-selected patients that are BCG unresponsive, you can get some nice responses. And that's why I say probably not. You know, I think for this particular patient, I generally, if they were exposed, I would generally start thinking about a trial, like Sarah said. You know, there's a bunch of trial concepts. CORE, CORE 8, The Legend's got a cohort coming. ADVANCE 2, I think, just might have a cohort coming too. So there's options out there still. For BCG expose and of course the gain trial Eugene's trial, which we're gonna open and support. I'm excited about that, too So if there wasn't a trial, can you tell the audience a little bit about that? Yeah, so gain is a gem BCG concept It's the phase 2 data for that concept who looked really good like like the gem to host seed data phase 2 data looked You know like 90 plus percent see how incredible I think 93 percent.
So I

So yeah, so I mean if I have gain open and the patient's interested and they're exposed, BCG exposed, then I would not hesitate to land there or just get more BCG if I had it and they were not, let's say they were not interested in the clinical trial. But if they were BCG unresponsive, then like Sarah, I'd talk to the patient. About all the options and that affair gene being one we do use no the pendicon as well And I use both of those probably about half the time when the patient's not getting gem dosi or a clinical trial So I really think it's great for patients right now to have kind of a choice. Yeah a lot of choice

Yeah, I'm not going to try to say NAI like you did nicely, but with the BCG shortage, I totally agree. It's tough to kind of rationalize using an agent that's also using BCG, but now they're making a push to give recombinant BCG. I don't know how much data there is that's very strong to support that. Is that something that you guys are using in your practice?
Not at this point, we're not. Are you?

Yeah, we're opening the EAP. Yeah, we haven't started using it yet, but we're going to open it and I'm going to use it because I think it's an opportunity for me to go back to 6 plus 3. And I agree there's questions about comparative efficacy, but right now in my practice I'm doing 5 of 6 doses for BCG and 2 of 3 for maintenance routinely. You know, I just I will also talk to them about that and that the data is pretty good and it's pretty easy to give. And for us at Mayo, it's not hard to give. I mean, GEMDOSI is difficult, I think, for some of our independent practice colleagues, but it's not hard for, I don't think, the three of us to give. Yeah, it's interesting. I think we preferentially start with GEMDOSY for a couple of reasons. One, I think it's something that our office from a workflow standpoint is just very comfortable and accustomed to giving and we can get patients through it well. I think that the two-year sort of durability is something that has pushed me and I do recognize the differences in the quality of the data. This is the tricky thing. We can't compare across trials because the populations that got into each of those studies were so very different in terms of their prior treatment burden and just, I mean, just even we know that there are differences in who gets into trials and who doesn't. I think that the real world data that's coming out, sort of the phase four EAP data, the sort of the real world NATO data is interesting because looking at how these drugs are actually used in the real world and what responses we are seeing in clinical practice off trial, I think is interesting and to the fact that it was better the durability especially it was better with nano after in the real-world data than it was in the phase 3 or in the registrational studies. Interesting. But I also, and maybe this is just the Canadian in me, the cost piece comes into play. I have a really hard time with how expensive those drugs are. And I have patients who are selling their homes to pay for their medical care. So that does come into it. And I also think about keeping those drugs. I think if we can salvage somebody with Gemdose and have a good durable response and we keep all those other drugs in our back pocket for when we need them later. So I go into it with no preconceived notions about what patients are going to tolerate. And sometimes a patient says, look, I'm coming from Alaska. I can come down four times a year. I can't come down for six weeks and then once a month. And that's not something I can make happen. So we have to think about the practice settings that we're all working into. But it's interesting, I do think at this point in the absence of comparative data, it's the logistics that end up oftentimes driving patients towards one decision versus another. So I'm a heavy believer in enrollment to clinical trials if I have them available. We are also opening the Credo EAP and there's going to be a TAR 200 sort of further registry that will open up if and when we get the registration on that. But I think that right now, I guess what I'm seeing is that most patients are definitely starting with gemdosy and then we're gonna sort of ratchet up as we go.

Yeah, I think really great points. I personally find the GEMDOSI data to be pretty compelling. There's multiple large retrospective multi-institutional series that are consistently showing one-year complete response in the 60 to 70 percent range. There was recently a study in Europe also where they reproduced this as well, so I find that interesting. I totally agree with your point that it's not prospective data, and it's tough to do these cross trial comparisons. But when I walk patients through these numbers, a lot of them end up electing for GEMDOSY. But very good point about the logistics. Sometimes that's going to end up shifting the decision considerably too.

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended comprehensive restaging for newly diagnosed high-grade T1 bladder cancer with concomitant CIS, including pathology review, repeat transurethral resection of all high-grade T1 disease, assessment of the prostatic urethra and upper tracts, and baseline chest CT imaging. Following restaging, management should consist of a discussion of upfront radical cystectomy versus intravesical BCG as frontline therapy. If BCG is unavailable, enrollment in a clinical trial is preferred; if trial participation is not feasible and cystectomy is declined or not appropriate, intravesical gemcitabine/docetaxel is a reasonable alternative.
reference_conclusion_quote: the first thing is we do a path 3 review [...] we need to look back in your bladder and make sure that all of the disease that can be resected has been resected and fully understand everything, especially if there's not muscle in the specimen. But I actually re-resect all high-grade T1 irrespective of muscularis propria in the first specimen. [...] But I think also I want to be thinking about the prostatic urethra and I want to make sure that the upper tracts are staged. I do get a chest CT even though the likelihood of pulmonary metastases is low. It's more because I want to have a baseline [...] But in general, if it's a high-grade T1 with carcinoma in situ, I'm having the conversation about afferent cystectomy versus BCG. And at this point, I don't think we have anything else that I would consider in the frontline setting. [...] Like Sarah said, usually a trial. [...] that would probably be where I would ultimately land if they weren't a candidate for cystectomy, if they declined a clinical trial and there's no BCG available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 92-year-old postmenopausal woman; weight 68 kg; parity 7. Menopause had occurred approximately 40 years previously. Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%, and presence of a cardiac pacemaker.

[ chief complaint ]: Per-vaginal bleeding for 3 weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Endometrial adenocarcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Dilatation and curettage specimen showed endometrial adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Pelvic ultrasound showed diffuse endometrial thickening. MRI was not performed because of the cardiac pacemaker. PET-CT had been arranged/planned. CT imaging was under consideration subject to renal function.

[ laboratory results ]: COVID-19 test was positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Dilatation and curettage had been performed, leading to histopathological diagnosis of endometrial adenocarcinoma.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed carcinoma endometrium following evaluation for postmenopausal bleeding. Further staging work-up was pending at the time of documentation. No final surgical specimen was available.

[ other clinical data ]: Cardiac pacemaker in situ. Reduced ejection fraction was 40%. Renal function/creatinine had been identified as a relevant consideration for contrast-enhanced CT imaging, but no creatinine value was available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old man. Comorbid hypertension. Reformed smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough for 2 years. Loss of appetite for 6 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma of the left lung. Final recorded clinical stage was T4N3M0.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy from the left lung showed non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma type.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT chest showed an area of consolidation in the left lung involving the apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe, left perihilar region, and superior basal segment of the left lower lobe. The consolidation extended toward the hilum and encased the left descending pulmonary artery. A left pretracheal lymph node measured 16 x 10 mm. An enlarged subcarinal lymph node measured 2.0 x 1.4 cm.

PET-CT performed after tissue diagnosis showed a mildly FDG-avid ill-defined area of consolidation in the left upper lobe with SUV 3.4. There was an FDG-avid right paratracheal lymph node with SUV 5.3. A tiny nodule in the apical segment of the right upper lobe was non-FDG-avid. An additional subcentimeter left lung nodule was non-FDG-avid. No distant metastases were identified on the reported PET-CT.

Follow-up PET-CT after completion of chemoradiotherapy showed persistent lesion in the left lower lobe with adjoining left upper lobe involvement and significant perilesional lymphangitis. FDG-avid right paratracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes were present and had increased in size; the right paratracheal node had increased from 1.1 cm previously to 1.9 cm. The study was interpreted as showing residual disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing had not been performed. The patient declined molecular analysis. EGFR, ALK, and PD-L1 results were not available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available. Echocardiography was normal. Performance status was 1.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent CT-guided biopsy for diagnosis. He subsequently received concurrent chemoradiotherapy, completed on 25 August 2023. Post-treatment PET-CT demonstrated residual/progressive intrathoracic disease.

[ current disease status ]: Residual/progressive disease after completion of concurrent chemoradiotherapy, with persistent left lung lesion and enlarging FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy. No documented distant metastatic disease was reported on the available imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: MRI brain was normal. EBUS-guided nodal sampling was not performed because EBUS was not available locally and the patient was unwilling to travel outside the city for the procedure.

Recommended baseline evaluation included MRI brain with contrast and molecular profiling for EGFR, ALK, and PD-L1. Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy was advised as primary treatment, with subsequent consolidation immunotherapy or other adjuvant systemic therapy guided by molecular results and affordability. Following post-chemoradiotherapy progression, the disease was to be managed as stage IV, with molecular testing on prior or repeat biopsy material to guide biomarker-directed therapy; if biomarkers were negative, systemic chemotherapy plus immunotherapy was recommended.
