[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Flushing, diarrhea, and lower extremity swelling.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV well-differentiated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor with hepatic metastases and mesenteric nodal disease, consistent with functional metastatic neuroendocrine tumor/carcinoid syndrome. Subsequent metastatic recurrence/progression included cervical soft tissue metastasis and extensive osseous metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Liver biopsy demonstrated well-differentiated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor. Resection of a cervical mass approximately 2.5 years later demonstrated metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 2, with Ki-67 5%.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT demonstrated a few small right hepatic lesions and a dominant large lesion in the left lateral segment of the liver. CT also demonstrated clustered lymph nodes around mesenteric vessels supplying the small bowel. The primary tumor was not visualized on the initial CT. Echocardiography demonstrated tricuspid regurgitation with severe valvular damage. DOTATATE PET showed four small foci of uptake at T5-T6. After 3 months of octreotide, repeat imaging showed stable disease. Postoperative surveillance showed no recurrent liver disease on MRI. Approximately 2.5 years later, DOTATATE PET/CT demonstrated a few small liver lesions with predominantly skeletal metastatic disease. After 2 years on resumed octreotide, surveillance DOTATATE PET/CT demonstrated progression from a moderate burden of bone metastases to extensive osseous metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Serotonin was 1,500 at presentation. Chromogranin was 3,554 at presentation. Serotonin normalized after hepatic and primary tumor resection. After later metastatic recurrence, serotonin increased mildly after resumption of somatostatin analogue therapy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Cardiology evaluation was obtained for carcinoid heart disease, and tricuspid valve replacement was performed successfully; the patient recovered well postoperatively. Octreotide therapy was initiated. After 3 months of octreotide, imaging demonstrated stable disease. The patient subsequently underwent resection of the dominant left lateral hepatic lesion/debulking, resection of the small bowel primary tumor, and cholecystectomy. Postoperatively, recovery was good, serotonin normalized, and carcinoid symptoms resolved. Somatostatin analogue therapy was then discontinued, and the patient was followed with serotonin monitoring and MRI surveillance. Approximately 2.5 years later, a cervical mass was resected locally and pathology confirmed metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. Somatostatin analogue therapy was then resumed. After 2 years of resumed octreotide, surveillance imaging demonstrated progression of osseous metastatic disease.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with predominantly bone metastases and a few small residual liver lesions on DOTATATE PET/CT after 2 years of resumed octreotide. Prior liver disease had remained controlled postoperatively for an interval, with no recurrent liver disease seen on surveillance MRI during that period. Carcinoid symptoms had resolved after surgery; later serotonin elevation was mild.

[ other clinical data ]: Clinical features were consistent with carcinoid syndrome and carcinoid heart disease. Lower extremity swelling was associated with severe tricuspid valve involvement requiring valve replacement.

Like Dr. Liao suggested before, we want to be wary about these patients that have high serotonin level to make sure that they don't have any problems with their heart valves before we intervene further. Dr. Liao, what would you do for this patient at this point?

Good. So I assume we all agreed that we would start him on Octeotide as well. We did get our cardiology colleagues involved and they actually recommended a valve replacement because the valve was so damaged and the patient was severely symptomatic that this was the only way that they thought would be reasonable to manage him. And so that was done successfully. The patient did well afterwards. What now? Now we got the patient on a triotide, the heart valve's fixed. You saw the tumor burden, which is mostly in the left lobe of the liver, and there's a primary tumor there in the small valve. Dr. Chan, is this something you would send to your surgeons, or is this something that you would watch for a little bit, or what would you do?

I would, in a case like this, definitely have one of my surgical oncology colleagues weigh in. especially with that large mass involving the left lobe, that may be something that can be resected. And then you've really essentially debulked a lot of the liver disease, and at the same time also get an opinion about potentially also removing the primary tumor. It's not symptomatic now, so it may not be quite as critical as in the first case, but still I think something to potentially consider.

Fantastic. So he was on three months of Octreotide. We did some repeat imaging, no surprises. Everything stayed stable. And by the way, we did get a DOTATATE patch just to make Dr. Lon Heath happy. She got four small, or he had four small foci of uptake in T5 and T6. But really, like you said, Dr. Chen, the bulk of the disease was in that left lateral segment. And so because of the symptoms, he was presented to me and I thought that exactly like you that I thought it was very reasonable to go ahead. And, you know, since I'm in the abdomen, I may as well just take the primary tumor out at the same time. So, and the gallbladder as well. So that's what we did. And the patient actually had a really good recovery. His serotonin level normalized actually after surgery, proving that most of, at least the functioning tumor mass was in that left lateral segment. And he became asymptomatic. Now, do we continue SSA after this? Dr. Liao, any idea?

I would say it depends on how much of the disease the surgeon was able to reset. In this case, I was very confident, 99%. Then it may be, you know, if she's asymptomatic, her serotonin is dropping, then it may be time to take a break from the SSA.
Courtney, any recommendations on your end on this?

We do know SSA is fairly benign from a side effects standpoint, so I feel pretty ambivalent about whether or not to continue. I think it would be fine to continue, but I understand the rationale behind stopping. Definitely don't think PRT is a good thing at this point.
Dr. Chan, do you continue octreotide after surgical debauchery at your institution?

Yeah, I think in a case like this, I think there are, you know, the two options that have been discussed, continue or stop, are both quite reasonable, where you've debulked most of the disease. I will say that I do have a low threshold for continuing SSA in patients who we know have functional tumors, and especially in this patient who had carcinoid heart disease. I think the long-term hormone control can be beneficial, so I think my inclination would be, even though you've removed much of the disease, to probably continue.

Okay, so in this case, actually, we had a discussion with the patient. He wanted to rather not have the shot in the butt unless he had to on a monthly basis. So we continued with just closed serotonin and MRI levels. So there was no recurrent disease in the liver, as you can see here. And lo and behold, the resection showed a metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, this time grade 2 with a KI 67 of 5%. We obtained a DOTATATE PET CT, and this is what it showed. So what now, Andy?
You can consider resuming that. If he was on SSA and this developed, then maybe consider PRT.

So we started him back on his SSA, serotonin level grew or clamped mildly. Jen, is this something that you see often that the functioning part of the disease is the one that's in the abdomen or the liver and that patients with bone metastasis don't necessarily have a high serotonin level and don't have that many symptoms like this patient?

I think a lot of the symptoms with carcinoid syndrome are probably driven by hormone that's secreted by liver disease. So I think it's not entirely surprising, especially where it's now bone predominant, not so much in the liver.

Two years after Octreotide, he gets a surveillance toiletate PET CT and this is what it shows now. So we're going from, you know, a fair amount of liver disease to really a lot of, excuse me, a fair amount of bone disease to a lot of bone disease. Courtney, what now?

I think now would be a great time for PRRT. Like the previous patient, this patient has very strong uptake in their tumors. Sometimes people ask me, you know, in patients with really an extensive amount of tumor in the bones, like we see in this patient in the after picture, sometimes other physicians will raise concerns, you know, are you worried treating this patient with PRRT? that they'll have more toxicity to their bone marrow than patients with less disease. But really, we've not really seen that. I think the disease must have to be really extensive and really just replacing all the marrow to see that. We do know there's some marrow toxicity to begin with, with PRRT. But somebody with this much disease, even though it looks like quite a lot, As long as their blood cell counts were good at baseline and were strong enough for us to be safe to do PRRT, I'd expect them to be able to handle it just like anybody else.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Posterior scalp lesion first noticed approximately 4 months before presentation; palpable right supraclavicular lymph node.

[ diagnosis ]: Cutaneous melanoma of the posterior scalp with regional nodal metastases. Clinical stage was T2b N2b M0, stage IIIB. Disease involved the posterior scalp primary and right cervical/supraclavicular nodal basin. No distant metastatic disease was identified on staging or restaging imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial outside biopsy of the posterior scalp lesion showed unclassified invasive melanoma, Clark level at least IV, Breslow thickness at least 1.4 mm, with ulceration. Fine-needle aspiration of the right supraclavicular node was positive for metastatic melanoma.

Definitive surgical pathology from wide local excision showed melanoma with Breslow thickness 13.4 mm, Clark level V, ulceration present, and microscopic satellitosis. Neck dissection pathology showed 4 lymph nodes positive for metastatic melanoma with focal therapy effect. Tumor bed composition was reported as 70% viable tumor, 10% necrosis, 10% pigmented macrophages, and 10% fibrosis.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial PET scan showed an FDG-avid posterior scalp lesion and 2 FDG-avid right neck lymph nodes. MRI brain was obtained; no intracranial metastatic disease was documented. Initial staging showed no distant metastases. Restaging PET after neoadjuvant systemic therapy showed progression of locoregional disease with increased size of previously identified nodal disease and enlargement of the primary scalp lesion; no distant metastases were identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600K mutation was present.

[ laboratory results ]: After the first neoadjuvant treatment cycle, liver enzymes were mildly elevated but remained within treatment parameters. At follow-up after the second cycle, liver enzymes were significantly elevated, consistent with transaminitis during immunotherapy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neoadjuvant immunotherapy with nivolumab plus relatlimab, administered as 2 treatments 4 weeks apart. During treatment, transaminitis developed. Clinical and PET restaging demonstrated progression of the primary lesion and regional nodal disease despite therapy.

He subsequently underwent wide local excision of the posterior scalp melanoma with 2 cm margins to a depth including the muscular fascia, reconstruction with a full-thickness skin graft, and formal posterolateral neck dissection including levels II-V.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status following resection of posterior scalp melanoma and regional neck dissection. Pathology demonstrated residual thick ulcerated primary melanoma with microscopic satellitosis and persistent nodal metastatic disease in 4 lymph nodes, with predominantly viable tumor after neoadjuvant immunotherapy. No distant metastatic disease had been identified on restaging imaging. The patient was approximately 3 weeks postoperative at the time documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Relevant past medical history included prior corneal transplant and splenectomy. Ophthalmology evaluation had been completed before immunotherapy, and no prohibitive ocular contraindication to treatment was identified.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 37-year-old woman at initial presentation; age 40–41 years at later metastatic progression.

[ chief complaint ]: Skin change in the left breast with a 3 cm left breast mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast triple-negative invasive carcinoma, clinical stage cT2N1M0, stage IIB at initial diagnosis. Subsequent metastatic recurrence involving lung, bone, and metastatic lymph nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the left breast showed invasive carcinoma, grade 3. Estrogen receptor negative, progesterone receptor negative, HER2 negative; HER2 FISH negative. Ki-67 was 35% in the primary tumor. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery, residual invasive carcinoma measuring 15 mm was present in the left breast; 14 axillary lymph nodes were negative. At metastatic relapse, biopsy of a lymph node confirmed malignancy morphologically compatible with breast primary; Ki-67 was 80%.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline clinical and imaging assessment demonstrated a 3 cm tumor in the outer part of the left breast with clinically palpable mobile lymph nodes measuring 2 cm. Post-neoadjuvant clinical and imaging assessment showed a very good response. At first metastatic relapse, PET-CT demonstrated multiple lung metastases, bone metastases, and metastatic lymphadenopathy. Post-treatment PET-CT after first-line metastatic therapy showed a good partial response. Subsequent PET-CT after second-line metastatic therapy later demonstrated progression. Fourth progression was described as extensive disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline BRCA testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic BRCA1 mutation in exon 20. Tissue NGS (FoundationOne) performed on lymph node tissue during metastatic disease identified PTEN, PIK3R1, NOTCH2, and TP53 alterations. Tumor mutational burden was 8 mutations/Mb. PD-L1 testing on metastatic lymph node biopsy by SP142 assay was positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy consisted of epirubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by 12 weekly cycles of paclitaxel and carboplatin, with very good clinical and imaging response. Surgery was then performed; pathology showed residual invasive carcinoma 15 mm in the breast with 14 negative lymph nodes. Adjuvant radiotherapy was administered. Adjuvant capecitabine was given for 8 cycles. The patient remained disease-free for approximately 2 years after initial treatment.

At first metastatic progression, treatment with atezolizumab plus nab-paclitaxel produced a good partial and durable response lasting approximately 13 months.

At second progression, treatment with carboplatin plus gemcitabine for 6 cycles produced a partial response with good symptomatic relief; response duration was approximately 6 months.

At third progression, olaparib was started in the setting of germline BRCA1 mutation and patient preference to avoid further intravenous therapy; this produced a good partial response lasting approximately 9 months.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic triple-negative breast cancer after prior treatment with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery, adjuvant radiotherapy, adjuvant capecitabine, atezolizumab plus nab-paclitaxel, carboplatin plus gemcitabine, and olaparib. Disease had progressed to a fourth progression with extensive metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history was significant for mother and aunt with ovarian cancer, both treated and alive. At initial presentation, axillary lymph nodes were clinically palpable, mobile, and measured approximately 2 cm. Symptomatic disease was present at second metastatic progression.

There is a target. and reach a clinical trial or therapeutic target for which you have an approved therapy, that's great. Obviously, we know the benefit and we know the studies that go to that. Thank you, professor. We are reasonably aware of the clinical subgroups of the triple negative and we can talk about. But it's getting deeper and deeper. But again, there is no really good therapeutic target associated with this specific mutation. There's been a proof of that indication to show that you really need to pay attention to an MRA derived subtype of triple negative. There is no consideration for this type of subtypes in our molecular tumor board because we don't have the data to support that and we don't have the information that suggests a specific subtype, except for the androgen receptor. Of course, if you have an androgen receptor, our pathology, by the way, they test for androgen receptor. some of the triple negative patients, they have a tissue biopsy. So there is a pathology assessment with standard immunohistochemistry that in our case include androgen receptors, and there is an NGS. reference_conclusion: For early-stage germline BRCA1-mutated triple-negative breast cancer, adjuvant olaparib for up to 1 year would now be considered standard practice, including in patients previously exposed to platinum-based chemotherapy. In the metastatic setting, broad-panel NGS testing is recommended after first-line failure to identify actionable alterations and clinical trial options. At later progression, sacituzumab govitecan was identified as the preferred subsequent systemic therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult patient; sex and age were not documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Upper tract urothelial tumors with multiple papillary lesions.

[ diagnosis ]: Low-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma involving the renal pelvis/calyceal system. Subsequent non-muscle-invasive bladder tumor recurrence was identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Upper tract lesions were described as low grade. Histopathologic details for the subsequent bladder tumors were not provided.

[ imaging findings ]: Retrograde pyelography was used during treatment administration. Calculated renal pelvis/calyceal volume was approximately 10 mL. CT urography performed 3 months after treatment was negative for upper tract disease and demonstrated two new bladder tumors.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Ureteroscopic laser ablation of multiple papillary upper tract tumors was performed. Adjuvant mitomycin hydrogel was administered with adjuvant intent for 3 weekly doses. Follow-up ureteroscopy at 6 weeks after completion of hydrogel treatment was negative for residual upper tract disease. At 3 months, CT urography was negative for upper tract recurrence but showed two new bladder tumors. Transurethral resection of bladder tumor was then performed. Concurrent upper tract endoscopic reassessment at that time showed no evidence of disease. Intravesical chemotherapy was subsequently administered for the bladder tumors.

[ current disease status ]: No visible upper tract disease was present on repeat ureteroscopy 6 weeks after mitomycin hydrogel treatment and on subsequent upper tract reassessment performed at the time of bladder tumor resection. Two new bladder tumors developed by 3 months after upper tract treatment.

[ other clinical data ]: Mitomycin hydrogel treatment was delivered based on a measured collecting-system volume of approximately 10 mL. Treatment was given in the adjuvant setting for 3 weekly doses.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma with segmental portal vein tumor invasion.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), 3 cm lesion in hepatic segments 2-3, with adjacent segmental portal vein tumor invasion; described as BCLC stage C.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated a 3 cm HCC in segments 2-3 with small adjacent portal vein invasion. On repeat imaging after 1-2 cycles of systemic therapy, the primary tumor showed partial response, with a new small adjacent lesion identified near the tumor. Subsequent angiography performed for radioembolization demonstrated an additional 2-3 small tumors in the same segment 3 region, located slightly downstream from the original tumor. Post-radioembolization imaging demonstrated non-progressive disease with treatment-related parenchymal changes and residual small focal abnormality at the site of a prior nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor markers were rising prior to local-regional therapy. No specific values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had portal hypertension and a TIPS in situ. Surgical resection was not pursued. Systemic therapy with STRIDE was initiated. After 1-2 cycles, partial response was observed in the primary tumor, but a new small adjacent lesion was detected on repeat imaging. The patient subsequently underwent TARE (transarterial radioembolization). At the time of angiography for TARE, additional small segment 3 lesions were identified. Following TARE, imaging showed non-progressive disease. Immunotherapy was continued.

[ current disease status ]: Non-progressive intrahepatic disease following TARE, with ongoing immunotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: Significant portal hypertension was present. A TIPS had been placed. No extrahepatic disease was reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/progressive ovarian carcinoma after multiple prior systemic therapies; intolerance to ongoing chemotherapy and unwillingness to continue further chemotherapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma ovary, diagnosed in 2019. Disease was described as platinum-resistant after progression on gemcitabine/carboplatin.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- HRR gene panel testing performed approximately 4 months earlier was negative.  
- HRD testing was negative.  
- Re-biopsy was performed during cycle 2 of liposomal doxorubicin plus platinum and sent for comprehensive genomic profiling.  
- KRAS mutation was identified.  
- KRAS variant allele frequency was reported as 5%.  
- Microsatellite instability status was low.  
- Tumor mutational burden was 11 mutations/Mb.  
- No other significant mutations were identified on comprehensive genomic profiling.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line paclitaxel plus carboplatin.  
- Subsequent gemcitabine plus carboplatin; disease progressed after 4 cycles.  
- Weekly nab-paclitaxel.  
- Metronomic oral cyclophosphamide/etoposide regimen (recorded as oral “BP16”).  
- Nab-paclitaxel plus bevacizumab had been administered approximately 1 year earlier.  
- Disease progression was documented in July 2025.  
- Liposomal doxorubicin plus platinum was started after progression in July 2025.  
- At the time of reporting, the patient was on cycle 2 of liposomal doxorubicin plus platinum.  
- After 2 cycles, chemotherapy was not tolerated.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive ovarian carcinoma after multiple prior lines of therapy. On second cycle of liposomal doxorubicin plus platinum at the time of re-biopsy and genomic profiling. The patient had not tolerated chemotherapy after 2 cycles and was unwilling to continue further chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: Multiple comorbidities were present. The interval since prior platinum exposure was approximately 1 year.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male with prior liver transplantation performed multiple years earlier. He had remained on substantial chronic immunosuppression.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly growing lesion of the left face. Additional lesions were present on the left lower eyelid and left forehead.

[ diagnosis ]: High-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the left nasal sidewall/face; synchronous basal cell carcinoma of the left lower eyelid; carcinoma in situ of the left forehead.

[ histopathology results ]: Office biopsies of three facial lesions showed:
- Left nasal sidewall: moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
- Left lower eyelid ulcer: basal cell carcinoma.
- Left forehead: carcinoma in situ.

Definitive pathology from resection of the nasal lesion showed:
- Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma measuring 3.6 cm.
- Deep invasion present.
- No perineural invasion.
- No lymphovascular invasion.
- Close deep margin on permanent section measuring 1.5 mm, corresponding to resection at the nasal bone.
- Pathologic stage recorded as pT2N0Mx.

The additional excised lesions were reported as adequately treated without adverse pathologic findings.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinical examination demonstrated an exophytic approximately 3 x 3 cm facial lesion with ulceration, not fixed to bone. No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy was identified.

CT neck showed the facial lesion without obvious cervical lymphadenopathy.

PET scan demonstrated uptake in the three known facial lesions and was negative for cervical or other occult metastatic disease.

Sentinel lymph node lymphoscintigraphy identified a bright draining node in the left neck.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: History of multiple prior skin cancers treated surgically. Three current facial lesions were biopsied in clinic. The patient subsequently underwent resection of the left cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma with sentinel lymph node procedure, excision of the additional facial lesions, and reconstruction. Immunosuppression was later reduced. Adjuvant radiation therapy was discussed but not administered; the patient elected observation.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had chronic immunosuppression in the setting of prior liver transplantation and recurrent cutaneous malignancies. On initial examination, no cervical lymph nodes were palpable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging neck mass over approximately 4–6 weeks with dysphagia and compressive symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid mass was reported as malignant and interpreted as consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma on immunostaining, with calcitonin positive and TTF, PAX, and A103 negative.  
- Definitive surgical pathology after operation in August 2018 showed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.  
- Tumor size was 8.9 cm.  
- Extensive necrosis was present.  
- Ki-67 proliferation index was 80%.  
- Extrathyroidal extension was present.  
- Surgical margins were positive.  
- Six lymph nodes were examined and were negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT neck in 2018 showed a large relatively hypodense mass replacing the right thyroid lobe.  
- The mass circumferentially involved the right common carotid artery.  
- There was significant mass effect on the trachea with tracheal narrowing, without tracheal invasion identified on the reviewed images.  
- The mass extended into the tracheoesophageal groove.  
- Retrosternal extension was present.  
- Cervical lymph nodes were described on imaging.  
- PET/CT performed 8 days after surgery showed increased FDG avidity in the resection bed and superior mediastinum, with FDG-avid level II lymph nodes.  
- PET/CT performed 65 days after surgery again showed increased avidity in the right thyroid bed and superior mediastinum.  
- PET/CT in October 2021 showed no suspicious lesions.  
- Subsequent CT showed stable postsurgical changes with no recurrent mass in the surgical bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BRAF testing was negative.  
- FoundationOne testing identified NRAS as a potential target for off-label trametinib therapy.  
- PD-L1 status was not provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum calcitonin was negative.  
- CEA was not elevated.  
- TSH was 3.4 initially.  
- Free T4 was 0.99 initially.  
- TPO antibody was 1.5.  
- Postoperatively, TSH remained within normal range.  
- Postoperative free T4 was 1.4.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent right thyroid lobectomy and right central neck dissection in August 2018. The operation was described as technically difficult because of involvement of multiple adjacent structures.  
- Received aggressive adjuvant chemoradiation consisting of 33 fractions of radiation therapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin.  
- Subsequently received trametinib 2 mg daily as consolidation treatment; dose was reduced to 1.5 mg daily because of severe rash/eruption requiring antibiotic treatment.  
- Remained on trametinib from 2019 until June 2021.  
- Trametinib was discontinued in June 2021.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Off trametinib since June 2021.  
- No evidence of recurrence since discontinuation.  
- Imaging through October 2021 showed no evidence of recurrent disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Physical examination at presentation was notable for marked non-tender thyromegaly.  
- Family history included lung cancer in both maternal grandparents and prostate cancer in the father.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old woman from Northern Ontario.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive left eye proptosis and diplopia on lateral gaze.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the sinonasal region involving the left ethmoid/nasal cavity with orbital invasion and skull base involvement.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial biopsy of the nasal mass showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- p16 status was not available on the initial biopsy.  
- Post-resection pathology showed persistent squamous cell carcinoma in the orbit, ethmoids, and dura.  
- Dural margins were clear.  
- Primary site margins were clear.  
- Three perifacial nodes were excised; one node contained a 1 mm focus of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Endoscopy showed an obvious anteriorly visible nasal mass.  
- Coronal MRI demonstrated left orbital proptosis with tumor invading the intraconal fat, extending through the lamina papyracea, into the frontal recess, and up to the cribriform plate.  
- MRI showed mild dural enhancement without obvious dural nodularity.  
- Tumor extended along the medial rectus posteriorly toward the sphenoid sinus.  
- Neck imaging showed no clearly reported cervical nodal disease by radiology.  
- A small left level IB/perifacial node adjacent to the submandibular gland was visible on MRI.  
- Preoperative PET-CT showed no uptake in the neck.  
- Post-treatment/post-surgical imaging showed the primary site to be clear with the orbit obliterated surgically.  
- A new contralateral PET-positive cervical node was identified on post-surgical imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 status was not reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Because of operative delays during the COVID-19 pandemic, the patient received preoperative radiation therapy rather than immediate surgery.  
- Preoperative radiation therapy was delivered to 50 Gy in 25 fractions.  
- She subsequently underwent planned combined open anterior craniofacial resection with left orbital exenteration and skull base/dural resection.  
- Reconstruction included free tissue transfer to reconstruct the orbit and line the skull base, with use of a pericranial flap.  
- No formal neck dissection was performed at the time of primary surgery because the neck had been clinically N0 and PET-negative.  
- During flap vessel preparation, three perifacial nodes were removed; one contained a 1 mm metastatic focus.  
- Following identification of a new contralateral PET-positive node after surgery, bilateral neck dissections and ipsilateral parotid surgery were performed; final pathology from that procedure was not yet available.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Primary sinonasal/orbital/skull base disease had been surgically resected with clear primary and dural margins.  
- Occult regional nodal metastasis had been identified in a left perifacial node.  
- Subsequent imaging demonstrated a contralateral PET-positive cervical node after primary treatment.  
- Final pathology from the bilateral neck surgery and ipsilateral parotid procedure was pending.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On clinical examination, she had marked left proptosis and disconjugate lateral gaze.  
- She was otherwise described as healthy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Young woman of childbearing age planning pregnancy.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodules identified on pre-pregnancy ultrasound evaluation.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal differentiated thyroid carcinoma following surgery, consisting of:
- Right follicular thyroid carcinoma, minimally invasive type
- Left papillary thyroid carcinoma, classical type
- Additional incidental papillary thyroid microcarcinoma
- Central neck lymph node metastases (3 involved lymph nodes, all small-volume)
Overall stage was documented as stage I low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed:
- One thyroid nodule: Bethesda III (atypia of undetermined significance)
- Contralateral thyroid nodule: Bethesda V/VI consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma

Intraoperative frozen section pathology showed:
- Left lobe: papillary thyroid carcinoma
- Right lobe: follicular neoplasm

Final postoperative pathology showed:
- Right thyroid: minimally invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma
- Additional incidental papillary thyroid carcinoma in the right thyroid
- Left thyroid: papillary thyroid carcinoma, classical type, measuring 7 mm
- Central neck lymph nodes: 3 metastatic lymph nodes, all small-volume metastases

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated two suspicious nodules:
- Left-sided nodule classified as TI-RADS 5
- Right-sided nodule classified as TI-RADS 4

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: 
- Right-sided nodule/follicular carcinoma: RAS-positive; final diagnosis specified NRAS-positive
- Left-sided papillary thyroid carcinoma: BRAF-positive

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- Past history included treatment with methimazole, subsequently discontinued.
- Thyroid function tests were normal after discontinuation of methimazole.
- In August, the patient underwent near-total thyroidectomy consisting of total left lobectomy and near-total right lobectomy with central neck dissection.
- Intraoperative assessment showed no gross extrathyroidal extension.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after near-total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection for stage I low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer. The patient was receiving levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily.

[ other clinical data ]: 
- Past history of Graves disease.
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone target was documented as 0.5-2.0 in the setting of planned pregnancy.
- Planned surveillance included thyroid function testing every 3-6 months and neck ultrasound at 6 months postoperatively.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid nodule initially palpated by primary care provider.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid nodule was Bethesda category VI (malignant), positive for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound demonstrated a 4-5 cm left thyroid nodule that was nearly entirely solid and hypoechoic, with sharp margins, macrolobulations, and scattered echogenic foci; no gross macrocalcifications were described. The right thyroid lobe appeared normal in background parenchymal echogenicity. No cervical adenopathy was identified on physical examination. DOTATATE PET demonstrated an avid thyroid lesion measuring 6.0 x 4.0 x 3.5 cm with SUVmax 29. No additional lesions or metastatic sites were identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET testing was not performed preoperatively.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was 0.73. Preoperative calcitonin was 14,973 (upper limit of normal 5.1). Preoperative CEA was 242 (normal <3). Plasma metanephrine assessment was performed preoperatively. Calcium evaluation for MEN-associated workup was also performed preoperatively.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection and limited additional nodal dissection including levels III and IV.

[ current disease status ]: No metastatic disease had been identified on preoperative DOTATATE PET.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had no prior thyroid history. She reported fatigue, thinning hair, and brain fog. She denied dysphagia, positional dyspnea, hoarseness, flushing, and diarrhea. She was otherwise healthy and took no regular medications. Family history was negative for thyroid cancer and other malignancies. Physical examination showed a mobile left thyroid nodule estimated at approximately 4-5 cm, with no palpable cervical adenopathy.

But when someone has a palpable nodule, certainly we want to evaluate with a neck ultrasound and understand what this looks like. The fact that she has no compressive symptoms despite the size is very reassuring because that gives us a sense that this has been growing fairly slowly over time. And so sometimes with a nodule this size, it may actually be visible when the patient walks in the room. Yes, sorry about that. I know, not necessarily. I think I, as years go by, I'm more and more conservative about this. And if it were, we're going to, of course, go to FNA on this. I would discuss, you know, pros and cons of surgery with the patient. Gotcha. So in the absence of some sign or symptom of structural invasion, we're probably going with ultrasound to begin with. Okay, Trevor, even though you're from California, I assume we did a normal evaluation here and stuck a needle into this or did an ultrasound. What'd you do next?

So when we look at the border of a nodule, we could define it, first of all, as distinct or indistinct. If it's distinct, then we can look to see if there are jagged, speculated, irregular margins. Gotcha. Yeah. Got it. So we wouldn't, we probably wouldn't do somatic testing up front on every medullary, but if it was one of those presentations where we were thinking about neoadjuvant or something like that, we'd want to know the target. reference_conclusion: The agreed next steps were preoperative biochemical and genetic evaluation for medullary thyroid carcinoma, including plasma calcitonin, CEA, and RET proto-oncogene testing, with syndromic assessment for MEN by calcium testing and urine metanephrines. Given the markedly elevated calcitonin level, metastatic evaluation was indicated before surgery, using cross-sectional imaging and/or functional imaging, with consideration of liver MRI. Definitive management consisted of total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection, with the extent of nodal dissection guided by calcitonin level and imaging findings.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 6-year-old female child.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal distension and abdominal lump for 1.5 months, associated with loss of appetite, weight loss, nausea, and constipation.

[ diagnosis ]: Abdominal neuroblastoma, staged as L2 disease after evaluation. Primary mass was located in the left upper quadrant/upper abdomen.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided FNAC from the abdominal mass showed features of a small round cell tumor, with neuroblastoma considered. Immunohistochemistry was positive for neuron-specific enolase, and the diagnosis of neuroblastoma was made. No core biopsy histology, Shimada classification, or favorable/unfavorable histology was available.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound abdomen showed a tumor encasing major vessels including the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery, without documented vascular invasion.  
- Left kidney was visualized separately from the mass.  
- Inferior vena cava was compressed but remained patent, with no thrombus.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a large left upper quadrant abdominal mass with calcifications.  
- Descending aorta was displaced by the mass.  
- Left kidney was separate from the mass, and the mass did not appear to arise from the kidney.  
- Mild left hydronephrosis and minimal ascites were present on initial CT.  
- CT chest showed no evidence of metastatic disease.  
- After 6 cycles of chemotherapy, repeat CT abdomen/pelvis showed good interval response; clinically the mass was no longer palpable, but persistent encasement of the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery branches, and bilateral renal pedicles remained.  
- After 1 additional cycle of chemotherapy, repeat CT showed persistent encasement of the superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis, bilateral renal arteries, and portal vein by more than 180 degrees.  
- Inferior vena cava remained compressed but patent on venous phase imaging.  
- No skeletal lesions were identified on bone scan.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: N-MYC amplification testing was not performed. No MLPA or segmented chromosomal aberration analysis was available. MIBG scan was not performed due to unavailability.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Child was not anemic.  
- Renal function tests were normal.  
- Electrolytes were normal.  
- 24-hour urinary VMA was negative.  
- 24-hour urinary HVA was negative.  
- LDH was elevated; value reported at approximately 1600.  
- Other tumor markers were within normal range.  
- Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were negative for malignancy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy planned as 6 cycles of a 4-drug regimen: cyclophosphamide, etoposide, cisplatin, and adriamycin.  
- Following 6 cycles, general condition improved and the abdominal mass was no longer palpable clinically; however, residual tumor with persistent major vascular encasement remained on CT.  
- One additional cycle of neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered.  
- After the additional cycle, imaging continued to show persistent encasement of major abdominal vessels.

[ current disease status ]: Residual abdominal neuroblastoma persisted after 7 cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, with ongoing encasement of the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery, bilateral renal arteries/pedicles, portal vein, and compression of the inferior vena cava without thrombosis. No documented distant metastatic disease was identified on CT chest, bone marrow evaluation, or bone scan. Clinically, the child had improved after chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On general examination at presentation, the child appeared cachectic.  
- Abdominal examination showed a 22 × 18 cm large non-tender nodular mass involving the entire upper abdomen with well-defined margins; it was not possible to insinuate between the costal margin and the mass.  
- Per-rectal examination was normal.  
- External genitalia examination was normal.  
- Rapid progression of abdominal distension with onset of respiratory distress had been documented prior to initiation of treatment.  
- The child was not hypertensive at presentation.

reference_conclusion: Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the consensus was to proceed with operative debulking rather than further observation or metabolic imaging. Surgical management should aim for at least 50% tumor resection, with piecemeal excision as feasible and acceptance of residual disease along major vessels if required to preserve critical structures; nephrectomy should be avoided unless necessitated by a life-saving intraoperative circumstance. Resected tissue should be submitted for histology and MYCN amplification or other feasible molecular studies to clarify tumor biology and guide subsequent management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old man; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache and confusion for 10 days.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal high-grade glioma, with histopathologic features favoring astrocytoma, WHO grade 4.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical tissue diagnosis from the left parietal lesion showed high-grade glioma with features favoring astrocytoma, WHO grade 4.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain demonstrated two contrast-enhancing intra-axial lesions in the left cerebral hemisphere: one left frontal and one left parietotemporal/parietal lesion. Both lesions were heterogeneously T2 hyperintense with significant surrounding vasogenic edema and mass effect, including effacement/replacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle. Subfalcine herniation was present, with possible descending transtentorial herniation. There were T1 hyperintense foci consistent with hemorrhagic component, particularly in the parietotemporal lesion. Post-contrast imaging showed thick/nodular enhancement with internal non-enhancing necrotic areas. Edema possibly extended across the corpus callosum, with corpus callosal involvement/crossing of the midline described. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast showed no extracranial lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old White male.

[ chief complaint ]: Odynophagia for more than 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Posterior pharyngeal wall hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Resection specimen showed a 2.3 cm moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. There was no perineural invasion and no lymphovascular invasion. Initial inferior/distal margin was close at 1.5 mm (also described as 1 mm). Additional inferior margin re-excision was negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT neck demonstrated a subtle submucosal lesion of the posterior pharyngeal wall. A plane with the prevertebral fascia/spine was present. No obvious cervical lymphadenopathy was identified. Endoscopic examination demonstrated an exophytic lesion arising from the posterior pharyngeal wall, extending to the level of the arytenoids and subtly into the pharyngoesophageal junction; lateral pharyngeal walls were not involved. PET imaging showed uptake at the primary site only, with no evidence of nodal disease or distant metastatic spread at that time; stomach was reported as unremarkable.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Prior gastric cancer had been treated 2 years earlier with partial gastrectomy and adjuvant chemoradiation.  
- The patient had an indwelling gastrostomy tube and received some nutrition via tube feeding.  
- For the hypopharyngeal primary, examination under anesthesia with direct laryngoscopy was performed.  
- Transoral robotic resection of the posterior pharyngeal wall lesion was performed using CO2 laser.  
- Postoperatively, dysphagia occurred and subsequently resolved over time.  
- Additional inferior margin re-excision was performed and was negative.  
- No further adjuvant treatment was undertaken.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- At presentation, oral intake was tolerated.  
- No stridor or respiratory distress was present.  
- Past medical history was otherwise not significant.  
- Tobacco history: 1.5 packs per day.  
- Alcohol history: prior drinker.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old premenopausal woman. No significant past medical history was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for breast medical oncology consultation following left breast lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node evaluation.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer, status post breast-conserving surgery, with 1 of 2 sentinel lymph nodes positive. Systemic staging showed no evidence of distant metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Left breast lumpectomy specimen showed a 2.1 cm grade 2 tumor. Estrogen receptor expression was 100% positive. Progesterone receptor expression was 90% positive. HER2 immunohistochemistry was 1+ and HER2 FISH was negative. Sentinel lymph node evaluation showed 1 of 2 nodes positive for a 4 mm tumor deposit with extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Systemic staging was negative for distant metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Oncotype DX Recurrence Score was 20.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent left breast lumpectomy with sentinel lymph node evaluation. Surgical pathology demonstrated a 2.1 cm grade 2 ER-positive/PR-positive/HER2-negative tumor with 1 of 2 sentinel nodes positive and extranodal extension. No distant metastatic disease was identified on systemic staging.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative early-stage node-positive breast cancer without evidence of distant metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Premenopausal status was documented. Ki-67 was not reported. Histologic subtype was not reported. Germline genetic testing results were not reported. Laboratory values were not reported.

reference_discussion.text: Yes, of course. Good day, everyone. Thank you to all who have joined. So the case that we will be discussing as a multidisciplinary team is of a 41-year-old female with no significant past medical history presenting for breast medical consultation after a left breast lumpectomy and sentinel node evaluation. Her breast pathology report shows a 2.1 centimeter grade two tumor that is 100% estrogen receptor positive, 90% progesterone receptor positive. Her HER2 immunohistochemistry is one plus, but FISH negative. One of the two sentinel lymph nodes that were evaluated was positive for a 4 millimeter tumor deposit with extra nodal extension. Systemic staging is negative and an Oncotype DX is ordered. and returns with a score of 20. So in summary, you have a younger premenopausal woman with a node positive strongly hormone receptor positive breast cancer with one positive node and an oncotype DX recurrence score of 20. So the section that I will be speaking of will be systemic therapy considerations and node positive hormone receptor positive breast cancer. And to guide our decision making, we're fortunate enough to have results of the responder data, which was a clinical trial that prospectively evaluated the use of the recurrence score in lymph node positive breast cancer in patients who had one to three positive lymph nodes. with a recurrence score of 25 or less, just like the individual in our case. And this was a multi-site study under SWOG 11007. The schema for responder, as you can hopefully see, the eligibility criteria included hormone receptor positivity with one to three lymph nodes positive without evidence of distant metastases. That patients be eligible to receive chemotherapy. And that the axilla was evaluated by either sentinel lymph node or axillary node dissection. And patients who had a score above 25 actually were off study where chemotherapy followed by endocrine therapy was recommended as part of standard of care. Those who enrolled in the study with scores of 0 to 25 were randomized to chemotherapy followed by endocrine therapy versus endocrine therapy alone. Stratification factors included recurrence score, 0 to 13 versus 14 to 25, menopausal status, and the type of axillary surgery that they had. I should note that the prior data supporting this design was based on a retrospective analysis of the phase 3 SWOG8814 study for postmenopausal women with node positive, which had shown previously that those with recurrence scores under 25 do not appear to benefit from chemotherapy. The results of the study are shown, and as previously shown in the retrospective analysis, there was no added benefit with the addition of chemotherapy in postmenopausal women with recurrent score of 0 to 25. However, in premenopausal women, regardless of the recurrence score, there was a significant benefit to invasive disease free survival and distant relapse free survival with the absolute chemotherapy benefit being close to 5%. So the takeaway points from the responder data is that the data have currently matured to a median follow-up of 6.1 years. And we can clearly see that there is no chemotherapy benefit in node positive women with 1 to 3 positive nodes who are postmenopausal with recurrent scores of 0 to 25. However, the current data do show a benefit of chemotherapy in premenopausal women regardless of the recurrence score. And so in this particular case, we have a node positive premenopausal woman in her 40s with a recurrence score of 20. So in this particular case, chemotherapy would be advisable. I will add that there is ongoing debate in our field about how much of the benefit from chemotherapy is actually coming from chemotherapy itself or is it from the ovarian suppression effect of chemotherapy. And this is not an answer that the responder is able to fully answer. However, I will say that exploratory analysis in premenopausal women and responder showed that there was improved disease-free survival in both arms in women who stopped having periods. So as a next step, future studies are being planned that will further help us decide whether ovarian suppression alone can replace chemotherapy benefit in premenopausal women. However, at this time, the data are supportive of systemic chemotherapy in this particular case. Thank you, and I'll stop talking here.
Thank you very much, Dr. Lozberg. Can Dr. Lambertini follow up?

Yeah, sure. Thanks, Gil. Hi, dear colleagues. It's a pleasure to join this fantastic faculty and this great initiative from the Oncolab Network. So we are discussing here a case of a premenopausal woman that will be potentially candidates to receive adjuvant chemotherapy. So I'm going to discuss the oncofertility issues that are being faced by this patient by starting with the updated ESMO guidelines published a year ago on this topic with two important statements from this guideline. First important statement that all patients of reproductive age should receive complete oncofertility counseling as early as possible in the treatment planning process irrespective of type and stage of disease. There are here a few key words. First, all women should be informed about this side effect irrespective of type and stage of disease and as early as possible after treatment. The second important point that there is no an absolute threshold of exposure to anti-cancer therapies to determine risk of gonotoxicity. So in theory, all women receiving a systemic therapy should be considered a potential risk of gonotoxicity. We should not over or underestimate this risk, but potentially all women may face this side effect. So what is the first important step of the Oncofertility Council is actually discussing the risk of gonadal toxicity with the treatment we propose to our patient. The risk of gonadal toxicity, if we look at the breast cancer regimens, is mostly dependent on two main key factors. The first one is the age of the patient at the time of treatment. So the older the age, the closer to the natural age of menopause, the higher the risk of developing this toxicity. The second is the use of chemotherapy and the type of chemotherapy to be used, with alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide being associated with the highest risk. So in this specific case, we have a patient above the age of 40 years that will be candidates probably to adjuvant chemotherapy. If we go for a full course chemotherapy, anthracycline, cyclophosphamide, and toxin-based chemotherapy, we can estimate the risk of godotoxicity to be quite high. Of course, this will be different if we decide to go, for example, for a anthracycline cyclophosphamide-free regimen with a toxin alone-based treatment. Second important step of the Oncofertility Council is first to inform the patient about the risk of the side effect, and then second, to propose to the patient the different available strategies that we have to counteract the side effect. We have two important questions to ask to our patient. The first is the interest in fertility preservation, meaning the interest in a potential future pregnancy. In patient that will desire a potential future pregnancy, we should offer fertility preservation strategies that are cryopreservation options. The first and standard option is oocyte or embryo cryopreservation, should be considered as the first and standard option to be proposed to all patients that have at least two weeks available before initiating chemotherapy, so that they have no urgent need to start chemotherapy. We have to mention, however, that the success of this strategy is strongly dependent by the age of the patient at the time of the procedure. The guidelines recommend usually to propose this strategy in patient up to the age of 40 years, with this gray zone between 38 and 42 years, that should be this case on a case-by-case basis, including in our patient. And the decision should be made according to different factors, including the ovarian reserve of this patient, that usually is related to the age of the patient, but sometimes can have some variation, especially in this zone between 38 and 42 years. The second important question that we should ask our patient is the risk of premature ovarian insufficiency, which is a more general concept that does not only include infertility, but also all the side effects of early menopause. So we may have patients that are not interested to have a future pregnancy, so not interested in fertility preservation, but may be interested in reducing the risk of early menopause. They don't want to enter menopause earlier than one. So, what we could propose to this patient is the use of ovarian suppression during chemotherapy as a way to reduce the risk of premature ovarian insufficiency. Of course, this patient has a hormone receptor-positive disease, so she would be candidates to ovarian function suppression as part of adjuvant endocrine therapy up to probably five years. However, by the age of 46 years, there is no reason why this patient should enter permanent menopause. So I would still propose ovarian function suppression during chemotherapy as a way to reduce this risk of future early menopause. As a final point I wanted to make regarding a misconception that many of us as medical oncologists have had for a long time regarding the safety of having a pregnancy following treatment completion and the safety of access in fertility preservation strategies. What we can say now, we have large meta-analysis including several studies highlighting the fact that having a pregnancy following treatment completion proper treatment, proper period of follow-up should be considered safe for our patient. So a patient should not be discouraged to try to have a pregnancy following appropriate treatment and period of follow-up. And the same applies to fertility preservation strategies received before initiating chemotherapy. We have still one unmet issue in this field, and we will probably hear a lot about this at the upcoming San Antonio Breast Cancer Symposium, hopefully when we hope to have the results of the positive trial that is investigating the safety of stopping endocrine therapy for a window of two years in patients like the case we are discussing. that receive at least one and a half year of adjuvant endocrine therapy. The study is looking at the safety of stopping treatment to have a pregnancy before moving back to endocrine therapy and completing the five to 10 years of adjuvant endocrine therapy. And with that, I will leave again the floor to Gil Morgan.
Thank you very much, Dr. Lambertini. Now following up, Dr. Igor Miattini.

Hi everybody, thank you very much for this really kind invitation. So here we are going to discuss the approach in terms of radiation therapy for this patient. I remind you that is a premenopausal patient with no significant past medical history, presents for breast medical oncology consultation after a left breast lumpectomy, so is a conservative surgery, and sentinel node evaluation. With a final path, they show two centimeter grade two tumor with estrogen receptor positive, progesterone regester positive, R2 negative, with two sentinel nodes, positive, and extra nodal extension. So basically, this is a really debated point, starting from the 3.11 trial, as you know, randomized around less than 1,000 patients, and it's been published in 2011 and updated in 2017. Demonstrating that among patients with limited sentinel node metastatic breast cancer, patients enrolled T1, T2 with 1 to 2 sentinel nodes containing metastasis basically show that after breast conservation and systemic therapy, because patients receive 90% of cases of systemic therapy with chemotherapy, The use of sentinel node alone compared to axillary lymph node dissection did not result in inferior survival. However, this has been really a highly debated study due to the limitations, some bias, the mix of micro and macro metastasis in the setting of the trial, and these patients should be considered for lymphadenectomy. But you have to consider also data that was added by the AMAROS trial with more than 4,000 patients that have been evaluated for randomization. to axillary lymphoid dissection or axillary radiation therapy in case of a sentinel node biopsy. As you know, these trials show an equivalence at five years and the updated in terms of DFS and overall survival. Basically, both treatments show excellent results and comparable axillary control with toxicity in favor of the radiation therapy arm. However, Amaro's trial could be not considered a practice-changing trial due to the low rate of basically of axillary recurrence that does not allow to draw any definitive conclusions. And we have to take in account the very low-risk patients that could be reasonably not undergo any intervention in the axilla and their potential suboptimal dose delivery in the adjuvant setting in case of presence of residual axillary This is being a technical challenge in case of irradiation. Of course, axillary irradiation therapy is a valid option also in this case. In case of no indication to axillary lymph node section, it represents one more option in the end of the oncologist. The main problem is based on the role of biology in all the trials that evaluated both the role of treatment, auxiliary dissection, or radiation therapy. So ZOO11 and the MAROS trial, but also the role of regional node irradiation, you know that we have got two main phase 3 trials, the MAE20 and the ERTC22922. And there, there's also the non-randomized Danish breast cancer group internally mammary node. All the studies basically lack data in terms of biology, estrogen receptor status, progesterone receptor status, basically calling for further research in terms of trials based on biology. However, in case of positive sentinel node without axillary dissection, so also in this case, for patients with higher risk factors, both diseases more advanced than the one that were typically eroded in the ZOO11, Targeting the undissected node in addition to level 1 and 2 is a reasonable option that should be always discussed in a multidisciplinary approach, of course using the modern radiation therapy technique and the volume-based radiation therapy. Basically, the risk that should always be considered when there are higher risks than the inclusion criteria of the ZU11 and the EBCG2301, for example, study, where you may avoid axillary lymphoid dissection or nodal radiation therapy, are based on the presence of lymphovascular invasion, estrogen receptor status, the benefit of modern systemic therapy. This is the framework where we are going to analyze the cases, also because you have to take into account that the main regional non-deradiation trial did not meet the DFS and overall survival endpoint. If you exclude the Danish trial, that is not randomized, it's randomized on a basis of left or right-sided irradiation, including the internal mammary node that did not meet the endpoint of DFS and met the endpoint of overall survival. Basically, in conclusion, I, of course, will consider this premenopausal patients for further action on the axilla, also because it's present an extra nodal component. However, I would like to conclude that if you observe the 10-year overall survival rates in terms of sentinel node alone, axillary lymph node section groups, both in the ZOO11 trial, were really comparable in the nodal irradiation group of the MA20, that's basically our 86, between 86 and 83 percent of rate, suggesting that the main of the ZOO11 eligibility criteria identify the population that basically may not benefit from comprehensive nodal irradiation. Although nodal irradiation may of course be added in the management of some patients with not positive tumors based on the evaluation of their overall risk profile, we can't consider the routine use of nodal irradiation for all patients with one or two sentinel node metastases managed with only sentinel node biopsies. A final comment on the role of endocrine therapy. This is a case of a G2 tumor of premenopausal candidate to receive endocrine therapy could be one reason more to avoid any further axillary treatment for this patient that will receive, of course, radiation therapy to the whole breast and tumor bed boost. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Dr. Martini. Now following up, Dr. Hamilton.

Great, thank you so much. I have enjoyed the conversation so far. So my role is really to talk about whether we may be thinking about adjuvant abimiciclib for this patient, you know, based on the Monarch-E trial that recently came out. And as you all recall, Monarch-E was a trial that randomized node-positive high-risk early breast cancer patients to either receive endocrine therapy alone or endocrine therapy in combination with abimacyclob for two years of that time at 150 milligrams twice daily. It was a bit complicated how we defined high risk in this trial, but high risk was defined as at least four positive nodes, or if one to three positive nodes, they had to have another high risk factor, either grade three tumor histology, tumor size of at least five centimeters, or a key 67 of at least 20%. Now, what I'm thinking about for this patient is that she does not meet the fact that she has four positive nodes. She has one positive node. And in fact, her tumor size really isn't that large. She also is grade two, not grade three. But the piece of information that we don't know is what her key 67 is. And there are two small pieces of her case in the sea of otherwise things that seem pretty reassuring to me. her young age at 41, and then also that she had extranodal extension on that lymph node, that I think would be worth ordering the Key 67 to see whether this patient may be higher risk than we think. In the Monarch E data, the disease-free survival, essentially at three years, had improved from 83.4% up to 88.8. So right now, still pretty immature follow-up, but about a 5% difference if we look at three years. And so this really was increasing if we looked kind of at two years to what we see now. Additionally, in the key 67 high subset, we saw a benefit from 80.8% up to 86.8. So that really widened. And so that's why we think that looking at key 67 may be particularly helpful for these patients. But as with anything else, just like the excellent conversation about chemotherapy, we really have to think about what is her actual benefit and is that benefit worth it. any medication, certainly Abemacyclob, they're not without side effects. And so the key adverse events within Monarch E was diarrhea was the most common, a little over 80% of patients having at least some grade diarrhea. Luckily, with supportive care, grade 3 was rare at about 7.7%. But any patient that's had diarrhea can tell you that even grade 2 diarrhea can be significant and can impact quality of life. Additionally, we also saw about 40% fatigue on trial, very rare, less than 3% to be grade three, as well as neutropenia, although it's not as common with the bemacyclob as it is with the other CDK4-6 inhibitors, certainly can occur. And if we look at adverse events leading to dose reductions or holds on trial, diarrhea accounted for about 18% of that, neutropenia for about 10 to 15%, and fatigue for only about 4%. We have gotten better at managing the side effects of abemocycline. We certainly make our patients have loperamide on hand. So if they do have diarrhea, they can quickly treat this at home before it becomes more of an issue. But I think that this is an important point for this patient. You know, there are multiple things that make us think that maybe she's a little bit on the lower end of the spectrum. I would, however, order the key 67 to help us quantify her risk. And if she does have a key 67 of over 20%, I think this is a patient that is young that I would have the conversation with. Thank you so much.
Thank you very much, Dr. Hamilton. Ms. Mapes?

Hi, Gil. Thank you so much, and sorry about the technical difficulties. I am honored to be asked to join this tumor board. I really appreciate you including the patient voice. So I have many, many questions about this case. One of my first questions, of course, is do we have the full picture? And there was a study that came out of the Cleveland Clinic on lobular breast cancer and decision-making, and they favored an MRI for accurate tumor staging. and to be able to tell if you have more than a few lumps in one breast or if you have tumors in both breasts. The other question that I have is, has she had genetic testing done? Because as Dr. Hamilton just said, 41 at diagnosis is just so very, very young. So it makes me suspicious that there might be something else going on. I'm also, with regard to the question on chemo versus no chemo, as the admin for a very large Facebook group for lobular breast cancer patients, I see women struggle with this decision all the time. And it is a really tough individual decision. Chemo means huge change in circumstances and the quality of life at a really key point in her life. So there's tons to decide. As discussed earlier, does she want to have fertility preservation? 41, she could still want kids. If she doesn't have them, she could have many, many kids. And that means a lot of pressure if she does go through with this chemotherapy, because you need to understand where she is in life. Does she have a family? Does she work full time? Does she have a partner? Is she single and dating? You know, what, what is she going to need? Where is she in life? What is she going to need? Because if she's working full time, and she has a bunch of kids, and she has no partner, this is a different conversation and very different circumstances for her than somebody who has, you know, doesn't work for a living. has a partner, has lots of resources and lots of support. It's just a huge issue in the U.S. just because of our dysfunctional system that we have here. So another huge question, can she even afford these proposed treatments? Will she be forced to stop short? Can she get financial navigation? Can she get patient navigation? Does she have the ability to get to the clinic through the treatment and all of that? So as I said, many questions. Another huge one is, does she fully understand her risk? I see women. debating this question a lot. And if she doesn't do chemo, will she regret? Will she have regrets? Will she kick herself down the line and say, I didn't do everything I could to help myself? And then when we get to talking about the additional medication that was proposed, the Ademocyclib, otherwise known as Fresenio. The questions that I would have for that is, is it overkill? Is this going to be too much? Or is it just enough? The side effect profile is, of this medication is super, super daunting. As Dr. Hamilton mentioned, the diarrhea, nausea, the white blood cells, red blood cells, platelets, liver issues, blood clots. Is she that high risk that you want to subject her to those side effects? The other question is that, does she need the full dose of that drug, or can it be tailored? There's a new initiative, or maybe not so new, but the Patient-Centered Dosing Initiative. It encourages conversations between oncologists and patients to discuss dosing. And this is particularly important in metastatic breast cancer, because metastatic breast cancer patients are on treatment for the rest of their life. And in this case, this woman is a, you know, she's early stage, but it It's still a really interesting discussion, this idea of patient-centered dosing. There's a website where you can learn more about it, therightdose.org, and there have been publications in the Journal of Clinical Oncology and the AACR Journal. and presentations done at ASCO and AACR last year and this year. Patient advocate Ann Loser has done She's spoken about it and led a study that surveyed metastatic breast cancer patients who found that 86% of these patients had at least one significant treatment side effect, and 83% of the side effects improved with dosage reduction. Excellent. Thank you all very much. Now we're rounding up about the hour, so I would just like to start wrapping it up by asking the faculty if they could just give me a 10 to 30 second wrap-up of the take-homes of this case in their views.

From my part, we are discussing the case of a premenopausal woman, so that is potentially candidates to chemotherapy. reference_conclusion: Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy is recommended for this premenopausal patient with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, node-positive breast cancer and an Oncotype DX recurrence score of 20. Oncofertility counseling should be provided before treatment initiation, including discussion of gonadotoxicity risk, fertility preservation options if desired, and ovarian function suppression during chemotherapy to reduce the risk of premature ovarian insufficiency. Adjuvant radiation therapy to the whole breast with tumor bed boost is planned, with further axillary management to be considered given extranodal extension. Ki-67 testing should be obtained to further assess eligibility for adjuvant abemaciclib, and germline genetic testing is indicated based on age at diagnosis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistently detectable and rising PSA following radical prostatectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma previously treated with robotic radical prostatectomy in 2020. Post-prostatectomy biochemical persistence/recurrence was present, with PSA never becoming undetectable. Subsequent evaluation identified a large bladder neck/prostate bed mass on multiparametric MRI; biopsies of this tissue showed benign prostatic hyperplasia and inflammation without carcinoma. PSMA PET demonstrated focal uptake in the prostate bed, a right iliac bone lesion, and low-level rib uptake. Axumin PET demonstrated focal uptake in the prostate bed mass without corresponding uptake in the right ilium or ribs.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial prostate biopsy before prostatectomy showed bilateral Gleason grade group 2 and 3 disease in 4 of 12 cores. Biopsy of the right iliac lesion was negative for malignancy. Biopsy of residual prostate/bladder neck tissue showed benign prostatic hyperplasia and inflammation, with no prostate cancer identified. Seminal vesicle tissue was also present in the biopsy specimen and was negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PSMA PET dated 2023-02-06 showed:
  - low-level uptake in a right rib lesion (described as right second or third rib), SUVmax 1.9;
  - a more intense focal lesion in the right iliac bone;
  - subtle focal uptake in the left aspect of the prostate bed/prostate region, concerning for local recurrence.  
- Multiparametric MRI demonstrated a 12 cm mass at the bladder neck/prostate bed.  
- Axumin PET showed no uptake in the right ilium and no uptake in the ribs, with focal/homogeneous uptake in the prostate/prostate bed mass.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Preoperative PSA: 6.2 ng/mL.  
- Post-radical prostatectomy PSA in 2021: 0.8 ng/mL.  
- PSA in November 2022: 1.54 ng/mL.  
- Repeat PSA: 1.52 ng/mL.  
- PSA nadir after prostatectomy never became undetectable and did not fall below 0.1 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Robotic radical prostatectomy was performed in 2020.  
- No prior radiation therapy was given.  
- Diagnostic workup after biochemical persistence/recurrence included PSMA PET, multiparametric MRI, Axumin PET, right iliac bone biopsy, digital rectal examination, and biopsy of residual prostate/bladder neck tissue.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent biochemical disease after prostatectomy, with PSA 1.52 ng/mL at most recent reported measurement. Imaging and biopsy findings did not confirm metastatic disease. Residual tissue/mass at the bladder neck/prostate bed was present on MRI and PET imaging, but biopsy showed benign tissue and inflammation without carcinoma.

[ other clinical data ]: Digital rectal examination identified palpable tissue that did not feel like a hard mass and was described as resembling normal prostate tissue. The original prostatectomy pathology report was not available. Concern was raised for residual benign prostate tissue remaining after prostatectomy.

reference_discussion.text: Hi everyone, my name is E. David Crawford from the University of California in San Diego and welcome to our PET Tumor Board. PET imaging, especially PSMA PET, in my opinion, is one of the most significant advances in prostate cancer management in the last decade. It has created a lot of opportunities and also challenges. I have observed that in many tumor or second opinion boards, Almost half of the cases now are focused around PET scanning, particularly PSMA PET. We recently published our latest Radar 6 and 7 guidelines, which goes through in detail a lot of the indications for PET, the pitfalls and the ups and downs. We have a lot to learn, and we hope that these monthly tumor boards will broaden your knowledge in this area. I would like to thank Blue Earth Diagnostics who recently developed and launched a PSMA pet product called RH-PSMA or PASLUMA for this educational grant. We have gathered for this tumor board panel, three international experts in this field. They have not seen these cases beforehand, and so they are as blinded as you are to what's gonna happen in these cases. First panel member is Dr. Phil Koo. reference_conclusion: PSMA PET imaging was obtained for biochemical persistence after prostatectomy. Following clarification with multiparametric MRI, negative iliac biopsy, Axumin imaging demonstrating no uptake in the ilium or ribs, and biopsy of the prostate bed mass showing benign prostatic hyperplasia and inflammation without carcinoma, the consensus shifted away from immediate radiation or systemic therapy. The agreed next step was observation with finasteride and PSA monitoring, with repeat imaging using PSMA PET if the PSA rises and consideration of repeat biopsy if clinically indicated.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old female; housewife. Height 146 cm; weight 45 kg; BMI 21 kg/m². Lived alone with no immediate caregiver support; children lived out of state. Known type 2 diabetes mellitus for 8 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Dysphagia for 4 months with weight loss of more than 7 kg over 3 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma base of tongue, clinical stage cT2N1.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from base of tongue lesion showed squamous cell carcinoma. p16 negative.

[ imaging findings ]: CT head, neck, and thorax showed a left base of tongue lesion measuring 3 × 2 cm and a single left-sided lymph node measuring 2 × 1 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL. Transferrin saturation 25%. Serum ferritin 132 ng/mL. Serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. DTPA-GFR 54 mL/min. Serum albumin 2.7 g/dL. HbA1c 8.9%. Other routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Echocardiography showed LVEF 63%. Pure tone audiometry was normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Long-standing diabetes had been treated with glimepiride 1 mg and metformin 500 mg twice daily. During pretreatment optimization, a Ryle’s tube was placed after counseling because of baseline dysphagia and >10% weight loss. The patient was accommodated in hospital-supported lodging during treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed non-metastatic base of tongue squamous cell carcinoma, p16 negative, with baseline malnutrition, hypoalbuminemia, anemia, borderline renal function, and poorly controlled diabetes.

[ other clinical data ]:  
Geriatric assessment: Clinical Frailty Scale 2; G8 score 11. Mini Nutritional Assessment 15. Instrumental Activities of Daily Living 5/8. Timed Up and Go 21 seconds. No history of spontaneous falls. Geriatric Depression Scale 2. MMSE 28. Fatigue score 2/10. Polypharmacy absent; only metformin and glimepiride were being taken. No near or far vision difficulty. No hearing impairment. CARC/CARG toxicity scoring documented positive factors including planned full-dose polychemotherapy and inability to walk one block; score 6, corresponding to a 44% risk of grade 3 adverse effects for full-dose polychemotherapy. Socioeconomic support included partial financial support from children and enrollment in Ayushman coverage.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board recommended definitive concurrent chemoradiation with radical intent for cT2N1 p16-negative base-of-tongue squamous cell carcinoma, using weekly cisplatin rather than 3-weekly dosing, with delivery of full-dose radiation by IMRT and close weekly supportive review. Pre-treatment optimization should include early enteral nutritional support with Ryle’s tube placement, correction of anemia, swallowing assessment, and intensive social-support planning including accessible accommodation during treatment. Diabetes management should be modified by discontinuing glimepiride, continuing metformin, and initiating a DPP-4 inhibitor with a target HbA1c below 8.5; adult vaccination and assessment for diabetic end-organ damage should also be completed.
